# Book Thirty-Four.

[[notes: This text is from Marsilio Ficino's 15th-century Latin translation of Plato’s *Laws* (*Leges*), specifically Book III. The speakers are an Athenian Stranger, Clinias the Cretan, and Megillus the Spartan.]]

Dignity is to be placed sixth, by which the ignorant are indeed ordered to follow, while the prudent are ordered to lead and dominate. I would affirm, O wisest Pindar (the Greek lyric poet), that this authority is not contrary to nature, but according to the nature of the law and undertaken willingly, not by violence. [[term: CLIN.]] Well said. [[term: ATHEN.]] Let us bring forth a seventh type of sovereignty based on the lot, asserting that it falls to one by the grace of God and a certain good fortune: and let us consider it most just that he whom the lot has chosen should command, while he whom it has rejected should obey. [[term: CLIN.]] You speak the truth. [[term: ATHENIAN.]] We shall say, therefore, in a certain place to one of those who undertake the duty of establishing laws: "Do you see, O legislator, how many ranks of dignity regarding those who command must be weighed, and how they are opposed to each other? Indeed, we have now found a certain fountain of seditions, which you must guard against." First, consider diligently with us what happened, and how it was that those kings at Argos and Messene, by acting badly in these matters, destroyed both themselves and the power of the Greeks, which was then wonderful. [[margin: How one should understand that the Half is more than the whole.]] Did they not fail because they were ignorant of that most correctly spoken saying by Hesiod (the ancient Greek poet), "The half is sometimes more than the whole"? Namely, when it is harmful to grasp the whole, but the half is a moderate amount, then surely he judged the moderate to be more than the immoderate, as the better is better than the worse. [[term: CLIN.]] Most correctly. [[term: ATHENIEN.]] Shall we believe this was ruinous to the kings before it was to the common people? [[term: CLIN.]] It is probable that this is especially a disease of kings, who live haughtily because of their luxuries. [[term: ATHEN.]] It is clear, then, that those kings first possessed this: they wished to be able to do more than the laws allowed, and they did not remain in harmony with what they had praised in words and by oath. But their disagreement—which, though it is the greatest ignorance, appears to be wisdom—overturned all those things through error and bitter rudeness. [[term: CLIN.]] So it seems. [[term: ATH.]] So be it. What, then, ought a legislator who fears this disease to have guarded against? By the gods, is the recognition of this now neither a matter for praise of wisdom, nor difficult to say? But if someone had foreseen it then, he certainly would have appeared wiser to us. [[term: MEG.]] What is it that you say? [[term: ATHEN.]] It is possible now, Megillus, to observe what was done by your ancestors long ago, and from that to understand the matter itself, and thus more easily to say what could have been done then. [[term: MEG.]] Speak more plainly. [[term: ATHEN.]] It shall certainly be made most clear. [[term: MEG.]] In what way? [[term: ATHEN.]] If someone grants a greater power to lesser things while neglecting moderation (*mediocritas*)—sails to ships, food to bodies, or authority to souls—everything will be overturned. For things raised beyond measure become insolent; some fall into diseases, others into the injustice that is the daughter of excessive insolence. What, then, do we say? Is it not this? That there is absolutely no human nature, O my dearest friends, which, if it were both youthful and subject to no one, could bear the greatest power in such a way that its mind would not be filled with the greatest disease of folly, and thus incur the envy of even its closest friends; when this happens, it immediately loses its soul and obscures all its power. To guard against this by the observation of moderation itself is the work of excellent legislators. What was done then is easy to see now; and it seems to be this. [[term: MEG.]] What exactly? [[term: ATHEN.]] Some God, as I believe, had a care for you, who, foreseeing the future, established for you a twin generation of kings from a single one, and so contracted it more toward moderation. Furthermore, a certain human nature joined with divine powers, perceiving your treading upon the swelling authority, joined the moderate power of those who deal in the judicial forum with the power of the haughty nobility, making the opinion of the twenty-eight elders equal to the power of the kings in the greatest matters. [[notes: The 28 elders refer to the Spartan *Gerousia* (Council of Elders)]]. To these, a third savior appeared [[notes: referring to the reformer Lycurgus or the establishment of the Ephors]], who, considering the still luxuriant and roaring authority, applied a bridle to it by the censorship of the Ephors (Spartan overseers), whose power was chosen by lot. By this reasoning, your kingdom, composed of what was fitting and established moderately, was itself preserved and was the cause of safety for others. Since, under Temenus and Cresphontes and the others who founded laws for them—whoever they were—not even the faction of Aristodemus itself would have been saved. For they were not sufficiently skilled in the making of laws. If they had been, they would never have thought that a youthful soul, having accepted an authority from which a tyranny could arise, would be restrained by an oath. But now God has shown what kind of authority ought to have been, and must be, chiefly established. That this is understood by us after it has happened, as I said before, is no wonder. For it is not difficult to see if you are warned by an example. But if someone had foreseen it then, and could have moderated the authorities and perfected one out of three, he would have saved all their magnificent thoughts, and neither the Persian fleet nor any other would have ever sailed into Greece, despising us as if we were worth nothing. [[term: CLIN.]] You speak the truth. [[term: ATHEN.]] They resisted them shamefully, then, O Clinias. I say shamefully, not because those who then conquered by land and sea did not conduct themselves with decent bravery in fighting; but I call it shameful because only one of those three cities fought for Greece, while two were so corrupted that one even prohibited Lacedaemon (Sparta) from helping by bringing a significant war against it, and the other, Argos, although it was first in Greece in those times of distribution, when summoned to repel the Barbarian, would not listen to those praying, nor did it defend them. I could relate many things that were done in Greece at that time that could be accused as shameful. Nor do those who say they defended Greece speak truly. For unless the common counsel and power of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians had repelled the imminent servitude, almost everything would now be confused: Greeks with Greeks, Greeks with Barbarians, and Barbarians with Greeks. Just as those Greek cities which are now subject to the tyrants of the Persians are confused without any order, and even badly scattered. These are the things, O Clinias and Megillus, which we may oppose both to the ancient statesmen and legislators and to the younger ones, so that by searching out their causes, we may find what else should have been done besides these things: such as what we have now explained, namely that one ought not to establish great or [[margin: That the city ought to be free, wise, and a friend to itself.]] unmixed authorities, always keeping in mind that a city must always be free, wise, and a friend to itself. This is what he who is to make laws must look toward. Do not wonder if we have already proposed several other things to which the legislator must look, which may not appear to be the same as these. But one must consider that when we say one must look to temperance, or wisdom, or friendship, our intention is not different but the same; and if we use many other words of this kind, do not be disturbed. [[term: CLIN.]] We shall try to do so, repeating your words in order. But now explain what you were going to say, when you said the legislator ought to look to friendship, liberty, and wisdom. [[margin: Two mothers of civil governments.]] [[term: ATHEN.]] Only listen.

[[page number: 527]]
# On the Laws; Or, the Third Dialogue on the Legislator.

There are, as it were, two mothers of civil governments, from which if someone says the others derive their origin, he will certainly speak correctly. One of these it is proper to call monarchy (the rule of one), the other democracy (the rule of the people). The race of the Persians holds the height of the former, and it should not be thought that any other holds the height of the latter [democracy] more than the Athenians. All other forms are composed, as I said, of these in various ways. It is necessary for a city to participate in both of these if it is to have liberty, friendship, and wisdom. Indeed, the discourse wishes to command us this when it says that a city devoid of these can never be well governed. [[term: CL.]] How so? [[term: ATH.]] Since, therefore, one city embraced Monarchy (the rule of one) and the other liberty more than was fitting, neither maintained the moderation (*mediocritas*) between servitude and liberty. But your cities, I mean the Lacedaemonian and Cretan, did so more. But the Athenians and Persians did so once in almost this way, but now they do so less. But shall we also state the causes, [[margin: Much concerning the government of Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius.]] or not? [[term: CLIN.]] By all means, if we desire to complete what has been proposed. [[term: ATHEN.]] Let us hear, then. During the time of Cyrus, the Persians had more of a balance between servitude and liberty; first, they were free themselves, and then they subjected many others. For since the leaders themselves imparted liberty to their subjects and reduced matters more toward equality, the soldiers were more friendly to their leaders and showed themselves ready in dangers. And if there was anyone among them who was wiser and strong in counsel, since the king was not envious but gave the faculty of speaking freely to all and honored those who shared in counsel, he brought the faculty of wisdom into the common midst. Everything then was made easy for them by liberty, friendship, and the communion of mind. [[term: CLIN.]] These things seem to have happened as they are told. [[term: ATHEN.]] Why, then, in the time of Cambyses did that kingdom almost fall, and was restored again in the time of Darius? Do you wish that we speak as if using divination? [[term: CLIN.]] Why should we not? For this contributes to the goal toward which we tend. [[term: ATHEN.]] Thus, then, I prophesy concerning Cyrus: in other matters he was both a good leader and a friend to civil life, but he never attained correct discipline, nor did he ever apply his mind to the administration of the household. [[term: CLIN.]] Why so? [[term: ATHEN.]] Occupied in military service throughout his whole life from his youth, he handed over his sons to women to be educated; these women educated them as boys who were immediately happy and blessed, lacking nothing, in such a way that they prohibited anyone from opposing them in any matter as they were "blessed," forcing everyone to praise whatever they said or did. Thus they educated them to be such men. [[term: CLIN.]] You seem to have described a fine education indeed. [[term: ATHEN.]] A feminine one, certainly, which the royal women introduced, being puffed up by new riches and left alone by the men who were occupied with war and dangers. [[term: CLIN.]] That is consistent. [[term: ATHEN.]] Their father, indeed, had many flocks of sheep and men, and many herds; but he did not know that his sons, to whom he was going to leave these things, were not being taught his own Persian art, since the Persians were shepherds born in a rough region, and the Persian art itself was hard, sufficient to make robust shepherds who could both keep guard and watch, and serve as soldiers if the situation required. But he permitted the women and eunuchs to nourish his sons in the manner of the Medes (the Median people); their education was corrupted by that which is commonly thought to be happiness. Hence they turned out to be such as it was fitting for those to become who had been nourished in the highest license. When, therefore, upon the death of Cyrus, they gained control of affairs, being full of luxuries, impunity, and license, first one, not bearing equality, killed the other; then he himself, raging with ignorance and drunkenness, lost the sovereignty. For the Medes and a certain eunuch, then mentioned, despised him as if he were insane. [[term: CLIN.]] So it is said, and so it seems to have happened. [[term: ATHEN.]] And yet it is also said that through Darius and those seven men, the sovereignty returned to the Persians. [[term: CLIN.]] Clearly. [[term: ATHEN.]] Let us inspect this, then, following the reason. Darius was not the son of a king, nor was he brought up in luxuries. When he came to the sovereignty, as the seventh who had received it, he divided it into seven parts, of which today some small dreams still remain; and he judged that they should live under laws contributing to a certain common equality. And he sanctioned this, and he included in the law that distribution which Cyrus had promised to the Persians, offering friendship and community to all Persians, and attracting the Persian people with money and gifts. Thus, loved by his soldiers, he subjugated no fewer regions than Cyrus had left. After Darius came Xerxes, who was educated in the luxuries of a king. But I rightly call upon you now, O Darius, who were not warned by the evil example of Cyrus, but educated Xerxes in the same habits in which Cyrus had nourished Cambyses. He himself, therefore, being educated in the same way, suffered similar things. Since that time, almost no king of the Persians has been "Great" except in name. Nor do I think this was a result of fortune, but of a bad life, which is the kind that the very wealthy and the majority of tyrants live. For never can a boy, a man, or an old man emerge as excellent in virtue from such a life. These things, we judge, must be considered by the legislator and observed by us at present. And it is also right for you, O Lacedaemonians, to grant that you do not commit any excellent magistracy to poverty, nor to riches, nor to a kingdom, nor to private persons, which from the beginning the voice of some god has not commanded to be committed. For it is not proper in a city to confer excellent honors on anyone because he excels in riches, or because he is swift, or beautiful, or robust, if he lacks virtue. But neither if he has some other virtue, but lacks temperance (*temperantia*). [[term: MEGIL.]] In what way do you say that, stranger? [[term: ATHEN.]] Is not fortitude one certain part of virtue? [[term: MEG.]] It is. [[term: ATHEN.]] You yourself, then, having heard this, judge. Would you wish to have a neighbor or a servant who is very brave, but not at all temperate, but rather insolent and one who pours himself into every vice? [[term: MEG.]] May the gods grant better. [[term: ATHEN.]] Or one skilled in many arts and wise in them, but unjust? [[term: MEG.]] By no means. [[term: ATHEN.]] But justice can have no origin without temperance. [[term: MEGIL.]] How could it be otherwise? [[term: ATHENIEN.]] But neither can that man whom we just called wise, because he has his pleasures and pains in harmony with and obedient to right reason. [[term: MEGIL.]] Certainly not. [[term: ATHENIEN.]] Let us consider this further, so that we may see how honors are correctly or incorrectly distributed among citizens. [[term: MEG.]] What is that? [[term: ATHEN.]] If temperance were destitute of every other kind of virtue in someone's soul, is it rightly to be honored, or the opposite? [[term: MEGIL.]] I do not have an answer. [[term: ATHENIEN.]] You have answered modestly and sufficiently. For if you had conceded either of those, you would have answered, I think, discordantly. [[term: MEGIL.]] Then it is well done. [[term: ATHEN.]] So be it. Indeed, the addition of honor—and

[[summary: This dialogue from Plato's Laws explores the necessity of moderation (the "middle way") in government, contrasting the balanced Persian state under Cyrus and Darius with its decline under spoiled heirs like Cambyses and Xerxes. It emphasizes that a stable state requires a mix of monarchy and democracy to ensure liberty, wisdom, and friendship.]]

# Book Three
<note>original: "Liber Tertius". Note: The previous page header "Book Thirty-Four" likely refers to a volume or section in this specific 15th-century binding, while the text itself is Plato’s *Laws*, Book III.</note>

**ATHENIAN:** Do we then think that this destruction was present in the kings at that time, but not in the others?

**CLINIAS:** It seems likely it was especially in the kings, who were living in luxury and pride.

**ATHENIAN:** Is it not clear, then, that the kings were the first to desire to have more than the established laws allowed? They did not harmonize with one another in what they had agreed upon and sworn to. This discord, which they falsely called "wisdom" but was actually the greatest ignorance <note>Plato often argues that the greatest ignorance is not lack of knowledge, but the soul's lack of harmony between what it likes and what it knows to be right.</note>, destroyed all those affairs through its harsh dissonance.

**CLINIAS:** It seems likely.

**ATHENIAN:** Very well. What then should the legislator have done at that time to prevent this disaster? By the gods, it is easy to know now, after the event has occurred, but it would have been a more skillful man who could have foreseen it then and corrected it.

**CLINIAS:** To what are you referring?

**ATHENIAN:** One can see what happened among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> by looking at your own history, Clinias, and use it as a model. 

**CLINIAS:** In what way?

**ATHENIAN:** A certain god, taking care of you and foreseeing what would happen, gave you a twin line of kings from one source <note>original: "duplicem regiam progeniem ex una". Referring to the unique Spartan system of having two kings at once to check each other's power.</note>, thus reducing the power to more moderate proportions. Afterward, a human nature combined with a certain divine power <note>This refers to the legendary lawgiver Lycurgus.</note> noticed that your government was still feverish and puffed up. He mixed the cautious power of the twenty-eight elders with the pride of the royal birth, giving them an equal vote in the most important matters. 

<margin>The third savior.</margin>

Then, a "third savior" <note>The Ephors. In Greek thought, the "third cup" or "third act" was often dedicated to Zeus the Savior.</note>, seeing the government still swelling and turbulent, imposed the power of the Ephors <term>Ephors</term><note>A group of five senior Spartan magistrates elected annually to balance the power of the kings and the elders.</note> as a sort of bridle. In this way, the royal power among you, being mixed from the right elements and possessing a measure <note>original: "modum". A central concept in Plato's philosophy: the "golden mean" or limit that prevents excess.</note>, saved itself and became the cause of safety for the rest.

**CLINIAS:** You speak very well.

**ATHENIAN:** Indeed, for if any man grants a power that exceeds the measure to someone whose nature cannot bear it—sails to a small boat, food to a small body, or supreme authority to a small soul—everything is overturned. The bodies become diseased, and the souls, through insolence, give birth to injustice. 

<summary>The Athenian Stranger explains that the Spartan government survived while others failed because its power was "mixed" and tempered by the dual monarchy, the council of elders, and the Ephors, preventing the corruption of absolute rule.</summary>
<keywords>Sparta, Lacedaemon, Lycurgus, Ephors, kingship, moderation, political stability, mixed constitution</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page serves as a preface or "Letter to the Reader" from the publisher Antoine Vincent, introducing a new Latin edition of Plato's works, likely building upon the famous translations of Marsilio Ficino but claiming significant improvements.</meta>

->ANTOINE VINCENT GREETS THE READERS.<-
[fleuron]

**D**UABUS <note>The large ornate initial "D" begins the Latin word "Duabus," meaning "For two [reasons]."</note> for two reasons we wish to give an account of the logic behind this new edition of ours. First, so that we may not be thought to follow the treachery of certain printers, who profess corrections and comparisons with both Greek and ancient manuscripts in the tables of contents of their books with letters nearly a <term>cubit high</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length (about 18 inches); the author is mocking printers who use "massive lettering" to make false claims about their book's accuracy.</note>: while in the meantime they substitute monstrous errors for us in place of the most chaste and polished books. Secondly, so that the industry of a most learned man—who, at our great and constant pleading, gave us his own Plato, corrected against a Greek exemplar, to be used—might not, through our fault, lack the praise and gratitude owed to them by all grateful men. 

Therefore, so that we may leave it testified among all scholars that a comparison to the Greek text was employed, we say that in Plato’s dialogue titled *Crito*, this remarkable passage was neither translated by <term>Marsilio</term> <note>Referring to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the priest and scholar whose Latin translations of Plato were the standard for centuries.</note>, nor restored by anyone until now, but has been replaced by us for the first time in this edition:

,, *But it was always said, I think, in this way by those who thought they were saying something significant, just as I myself was saying just now: namely, that the opinions of men are in part to be highly valued and followed, but in part not at all. By the Gods, O Crito, does this not seem to you to be rightly said? For you, as the condition of men goes, are far from the danger of dying tomorrow, and your present calamity does not lead you into error.* <note>original: "Dicebatur autem, vt opinor..." This passage from the Crito (46d-47a) discusses whose opinions a wise person should value.</note>

All these things, I say, were still missing in the *Crito* dialogue on page 326 of our previous edition.

Furthermore, a most charming passage in the *Charmides* was required, which we are the first of all to display for scholars to read, translated from the Greek. The passage is on page 191.

,, *Then I, my friend, was already stuck; and that confidence which I had a little while before—that I would very easily dispute with him—deserted me. But after Critias said that I was the one who knew the remedy, he looked at me with eyes as if at something marvelous; and as if about to ask a question, he approached us. And everyone who was in the <term>palæstra</term> <note>A wrestling school or gymnasium in ancient Greece.</note> immediately flocked to us and surrounded us in a circle. Then indeed, O noble one, when I saw what lay hidden beneath his cloak, I was all on fire, and I was no longer master of myself. And I judged Critias to be most wise in matters of love, who, speaking of a beautiful boy but using the likeness of another thing, warned me again and again to watch out, lest like a fawn coming into the sight of a lion I should have a piece of my flesh torn away. Indeed, I seemed to myself to have certainly been captured by that bait. Then, however, he himself asked whether I knew the cure for a head...* <note>original: "Tum ego, ô amice..." This is a famous moment in the Charmides (155c-e) where Socrates is overwhelmed by the physical beauty of the young Charmides.</note>

Thus far, therefore, two great and foul <term>lacunae</term> <note>Missing sections or gaps in a manuscript.</note> have most basely deformed the Latin translation of Plato, and they most basely and foully escaped those "diligent collators" who, before this time, were boasting their corrections to us. Where are the ingenious men who have previously basely abused the name of <term>Simon Grynaeus</term> <note>A 16th-century German scholar and reformer who edited major editions of Greek texts.</note>, a most famous man, for their own gain? Those who boasted in the titles of their books of the comparison and correction of Marsilio's interpretation applied by him—by the reading of which titles even a <term>legal summons</term> <note>original: "vadimonium." A legal term for a guarantee to appear in court; here it implies the titles were so fraudulent they deserved legal action.</note> could have been served? With how much honor, I ask, do they treat that distinguished man, when they wish it to seem that he either concealed such great gaps out of malice or passed over them out of laziness? And yet there are almost innumerable faults of this same kind. In the *Cratylus*, page 228.

* 2 <margin>Signature mark for the printer's gathering.</margin>

<summary>In this preface, the publisher Antoine Vincent justifies his new Latin edition of Plato by exposing significant omissions in previous editions (including Ficino's) and criticizing rival printers who make false claims of accuracy. He provides two specific examples of "restored" passages from the Crito and the Charmides to prove the superior scholarly value of his work.</summary>

For in the Codex <note>an ancient manuscript book</note> which we obtained, we saw margins filled with innumerable corrections of this kind, and we gladly shared them with friends, most of whom looked upon such a "Hydra of errors" <note>original: "lernam vitiorum"; a reference to the many-headed Lernean Hydra</note> with great wonder. Nor was there anyone who did not judge the industry and diligence of the most learned man—by whom these almost Herculean labors were exhausted—to be worthy of the greatest praise and gratitude. For it was by his benefit that Plato’s translation, which was once so defiled by many foul stains that it deterred students from reading him, now invites and entices them with its own beauty and charm.

Furthermore, to explain the third kind of emendation: even several passages which had been translated so unskillfully and so childishly that they seemed intolerable by any reckoning, this same learned man did not hesitate to render into Latin—although this was done in very few places, lest anyone complain that their own judgment was not left to them. In the *Letters*, we stumbled upon this remarkable passage. No one even moderately learned is ignorant that the <term>Latomiae</term> <note>stone quarries</note> were a prison in Syracuse, so named from the cut stones. Plato, therefore, in the third letter to Dionysius, the Tyrant of Sicily, writes thus:

,, <note>original Greek: "ὑπέσχετο δ᾽έ μοι καὶ Φιλιστίωῃ. εἰ σὺ ἀφῆς λυτὸν, ἥξειν προθύμως ἀδύναζε. τὸν ἐκ τω̅ λαθωμιω̅ εὖ ἐποίησας ἀφείς."</note> Which passage, expressed word for word, means this:
,, "Philistion promised me that if you release him, he will come quickly to Athens. You did
,, well in releasing him from the stone-quarries."

This is the easiest interpretation of that passage. But in other editions, it was read in this way:
,, "But to have released that Lithotonian was praiseworthy." <note>The translator here mocks a previous error where "Latomiae" was garbled into a non-existent word</note>

Who, finally, could have been so dull as to allow such a foul error to remain any longer in these most beautiful books? But there was also another much more laudable diligence of this same most learned man, who did not wish to be named for the present, lest he be thought to want to appear clever in another's work, or to grow from the mistakes of others. It is well established that countless passages of Plato were brilliantly and almost divinely expressed by Cicero—the sole master of Latin writing and translating—everywhere in his own books. When he had begun to write all these passages in the margin, partly moved by the narrowness of the margins, and partly to serve the interests of the lovers of Cicero (of whom he understood there to be a great number at this time), he placed them into the text itself, having carefully noted and indicated the book of Cicero from which he had copied them in the margin. In this matter, truly, we believe there will be no one to complain that an injury has been done to anyone—unless perhaps someone seeks an interpreter better and more learned than Cicero, or thinks the translation of any of our people is to be preferred to the Julian <note>Ciceronian</note> one. In the translation of the *Timaeus*, however, since on account of the longer discourse he had written nothing in the very narrow margins, but had only designated the translation of passages with this mark [manicule pointing right], we have relegated that part of Cicero’s book which exists to the end of this volume, from where whatever is useful to anyone may easily be taken. Furthermore, to this diligence, this was also added, especially to be commemorated and worthy of great praise: since infinite passages from Homer and Hesiod were brought forward by Plato, having searched for them with great labor in so many books and finally found them, he indicated in the margin, as if with fingers pointed toward the sources, from which book each was taken. Finally, by another kind of diligence also, this edition of ours has been greatly illustrated: for since neither the last letter of Plato, nor six Dialogues of the same (which are nevertheless noted as spurious) had been translated by Marsilio [Ficino], or ever received into this volume, he first made that letter Latin; then he took care to replace the six Dialogues elegantly translated by Sebastian Conrad, a most learned man, in their proper place, so that nothing should be missed hereafter.

Since these things are so, in my opinion, no excuse will be left to our people hereafter to prevent them from studiously leafing through the books of Plato and keeping them perpetually in their hands. To us, indeed, the will to assist in their studies, and perhaps also the ability, was not lacking; nor hereafter, if the Greatest and Best God preserves this spirit in us, will it ever be lacking, however much good and useful books may cost us. For we wish both to foster the goodwill of learned men with our resources, and to serve the interests of the Republic of Letters as much as is in our power. And we detest the greed of certain printers, who by their own meanness commonly deter talented men from the labor and diligence of correcting books. Many marvel—and truly they do not marvel without reason—at the incredible diligence of Pliny in amassing such a great history. But what kind of spur do we think there was for Pliny

### Thirty-Fourth Book.
[[page number: 536]]

Toward what mark should we aim our sight? And what are the proper arrows to strike it, and what is their specific flight? To speak most correctly: first, after the honors due to the celestial gods and the gods who preside over the city, if one pays the second and principal tributes to the terrestrial gods, he will most rightly hit the mark of piety itself. Following the honors of these gods mentioned above, and in alternating response to what was said, a man of sound mind will sacrifice to the *daemones* (spirits), and to the heroes after the *daemones*. Next follow the established shrines of the ancestral gods, consecrated according to the law. Finally comes the cult of living parents, to whom it is right to pay the first and greatest debts—the oldest of all obligations. For every person ought to believe that everything they possess belongs to those who fathered and raised them, so that they should provide for them with all their strength: first with external goods, then with those of the body, and finally with those pertaining to the *animus* (soul or mind). By doing this, one repays the loans given long ago; in exchange for the cares and old pains of the parents, the children return fresh care in their parents' old age, when they need it most. 

Furthermore, throughout one's whole life, it is most fitting to venerate parents in speech. For a very heavy penalty hangs over light and "winged" words. Indeed, **Nemesis**, the [[margin: Nemesis.]] messenger of judgment, is placed over all such things as an overseer. Therefore, one must yield to parents when they are angry and venting their spirit, whether they do so in words or deeds, recognizing that a father has a great right to be angry with his son if he thinks he has been wronged by him. When parents have died, the most fitting monuments are those built with the greatest moderation. One should not exceed the customary size, nor make them smaller than those our ancestors built for their own parents. It is also fitting to maintain the annual care for the deceased, which brings them honor, and to always honor parents with a memory renewed daily, spending moderately according to one's fortune. If we observe these things and lead our lives accordingly, each of us will receive worthy rewards from the gods and all those superior to our nature, living our lives with great good hope. 

As for what each person should do regarding children, grandchildren, kinsmen, friends, citizens, and guests—always worshiping the gods and acting rightly in the company of all these—the treatment of the laws themselves will demonstrate how to illuminate one's life according to the law. This is done partly by persuading, and partly by compelling harder characters through force and punishment. In this way, with the gods favoring us, the laws will make our city happy and blessed. 

But there are other things the legislator (who shares my concerns) ought to explain, which yet do not seem convenient to state in the form of a law itself. I believe an example of these should be presented first, both for the law-giver and those to be instructed by the law. Then the positioning of the laws should begin, discussing all remaining matters as best as possible. It is not easy to capture in a single formula how such things should best be handled. But let us take a certain measure of them, so we can assert something clearly. 

**Clin.** Speak then, what is this measure? 

**Athen.** I would wish for them to be as persuaded and obedient to the duties of virtue as possible, and the legislator will attempt to do this everywhere. 

**Cli.** Why not? 

**Athen.** What has been said seems to contribute something to this: if the listener’s soul is not entirely raw, it may become gentler and more benevolent in hearing the precepts. Having been made more benevolent, the listener learns more easily. Even if this is not fully achieved, if it is done in some small way, we should consider it sufficient. For there is no great abundance of people who strive to become the best as quickly as possible. Many proclaim **Hesiodus** (Hesiod, the ancient Greek poet) [[margin: In *Works and Days*]] to be wise when he says the road to vice is flat and traveled without sweat, since it is very short. But before virtue, he says, the immortal gods placed sweat. And the path that leads to it is long, steep, and rough at first; but after one has been carried to the highest peaks, the path that was difficult becomes an easy track. 

**Cl.** He seems to speak well. 

**Athen.** Indeed he does. But I want to set before you the point toward which this discourse was progressing. 

**Cli.** Set it forth. 

**Athen.** Let us turn our speech to the legislator thus: "Tell us, O Legislator, if you knew what we ought to do and say, would you not tell us?" 

**Cli.** Necessarily. 

**Athen.** Did we not hear him saying a little while ago that the legislator ought not to permit poets to fashion whatever pleases them? For they do not understand which words, spoken against the laws, might harm the city, etc. 

**Cli.** You speak the truth. 

**Athen.** If we say these things to him regarding the poets, will they be spoken with moderation? 

**Cli.** Which things? 

**Athen.** An old story, O Legislator, is commonly told by us and confirmed by everyone else: when a poet sits upon the tripod of the Muse, he is not of sound mind, but flows like a fountain, pouring out whatever rushes in. And since his art is a kind of imitation, and expresses the contrary emotions of men, it often forces the poet to say things contrary to himself, not knowing whether these or those are true. But a legislator is not permitted to say two different things about one matter in a law; he must always announce one thing about one thing. You will notice this from what you were just saying. Since some tombs are excessive, others deficient, and others hold the middle, you simply praised the moderate ones and ordered them alone to be made. But if I had a very rich wife who ordered me to bury her magnificently, I would praise the excessive tomb in a poem; whereas a poor and greedy man would praise the deficient one. But he who possesses moderate wealth and is himself moderate will praise the middle. You, however, should not speak as you did just now—merely saying "the moderate"—but you must explain what the moderate is and how much it consists of. Otherwise, do not think such a speech is a law." 

**Clin.** You speak the truth. 

**Athen.** Should he who applies himself to founding laws say nothing of the sort in the preamble of the laws, but immediately set forth what must be done and what not? And having imposed the penalty, turn to another law, bringing no reason to exhort or persuade? 

Let us bring into the middle two modes of healing, by which different doctors are accustomed to cure differently. Just as children beg a doctor to cure them in the easiest possible way, so we beg the legislator. To make this clearer: do we not say there are some doctors, and some assistants to doctors, whom we also call doctors? 

**Clin.** Entirely so. 

**Athen.** Whether they are free men or slaves, who possess the art by the command of masters, through observation, use, and experience, but not according to nature—unlike the free doctors, who learned it themselves and instruct their own sons? Do you posit these two types of doctors? 

**Athen.** [[notes: The speaker here remains the Athenian; this is a rhetorical continuation.]] What forbids it? Do you then understand that when slaves and free men in the city are sick, the slaves are mostly cured by slaves? These assistants hang around the doctors' workshops and go about everything; they neither give nor receive any rational account (*ratio*) for each of the slaves' diseases. Instead, they command proudly and stubbornly like tyrants, as if they knew exactly what they were doing, based on what seems to work in practice. And so, they fly from slave 

[[page number: 537]]
### On the Laws, or, The Fourth Dialogue on Legislation.

from slave to slave, practicing medicine. In this, they provide ease for the master in curing the sick. But the free doctor, for the most part, cures and considers the diseases of free men. He searches out the nature of the disease from its beginning; he consults with the patient and his friends, learning something from them and, as far as possible, teaching the patient. He does not command anything until he has persuaded him. And so, by always using persuasion, he attempts to lead the sick back to health with mildness. 

Which is the better doctor or trainer? The one who heals and trains in this way, or the one who uses the other mode? That is, the one who accomplishes one thing in a double way, or the one who uses the single, harsher, and inferior mode? 

**Cli.** The one who does it in the double way, Guest, is far superior. 

**Athen.** Do you wish then for us to consider how this "double" and "simple" method occurs in the making of laws? 

**Cli.** I certainly do. 

**Athen.** Tell me, by the gods, which is the first law the founder of a law will write? Will he not, according to nature, first adorn with laws the very beginning of generation in the city? 

**Cli.** Clearly. 

**Athen.** But the beginning of generation for all cities is the union and communion of marriage. 

**Cli.** Certainly. 

**Athen.** Therefore, if the marriage laws are placed first, they will seem well-suited to the correct constitution of the whole city. 

**Cli.** It is entirely so. 

**Athen.** Let us state the simple law first, which might perhaps be like this: "Every man shall marry between his thirtieth and thirty-fifth year. If he does not, he shall be punished with a fine and dishonor: the fine shall be such-and-such an amount, and the dishonor of such-and-such a kind." Let this be the simple law of marriage. 

The double law, however, would be like this: "Every man ought to marry when he is thirty years old, reflecting that by a certain nature, the human race somehow attains immortality. [[margin: Man becomes eternal through generation.]] Everyone is by nature most desirous of this; for there is no one who does not desire to have a perpetual name among posterity. Thus, the race of humans lasts forever in this way: by leaving children’s children, it achieves immortality through generation, remaining one and the same always. It is a wicked thing for a man to voluntarily deprive himself of immortality. But he deprives himself of this from his very soul who neglects children and a wife. Whoever obeys this law shall go unpunished. But he who does not obey, and reaches thirty-five years of age without a wife, let him not think his solitary life will bring him profit or pleasure; he shall be fined a certain sum every year, and shall not share in those honors which the younger men in the city daily show to the elders." 

Comparing these two laws, one can judge whether they should be written with the double length, interposing persuasion along with threats, or use threats alone and make the laws simple in length. 

**Meg.** [[notes: Megillus, the Spartan participant.]] It is the Laconian (Spartan) habit, Guest, to always choose the shorter way. But if someone made me the judge of these, to choose which law I would want in the city, I would choose the longer one. And in all other laws, if these two options were proposed, I would do the same according to this very model. Nevertheless, these laws must also be approved by Clinias; for it is his city for which these laws are being founded. 

**Clin.** You speak rightly, Megillus. 

**Athen.** It is quite foolish to worry too much about the length or brevity of writing. For I believe we should choose not the shortest or longest, but the best. In the laws proposed just now, it is not only that the double version contributes more to virtue than the other; but the analogy of the two kinds of doctors was most rightly applied. No legislator seems to have ever considered this. For although they can use two methods for bringing laws—persuasion and force—they use only one, as far as they are able, when dealing with the crowd that lacks discipline. They do not join threats with persuasion; they employ pure force alone. 

But I, blessed man, see a third thing that ought to be done in laws, which we see done nowhere. 

**Cli.** What is that? 

**Athen.** That which has been done by us, with a certain God breathing upon us, through the things we have discussed. For we began to dispute about laws in the morning, and now it is noon, and we are resting most comfortably in this pleasant place, disputing only about laws. And [[margin: Concerning preambles.]] now we seem to be making the beginning of the laws we are to treat. Everything before this was the *exordia* (preambles) of the laws. 

Why do I say this? Because I wanted to say that for all speeches and other things where there is vocal imitation, there are prefaces—and, as it were, certain preludes—which provide a skillful and useful approach to the matter to be discussed. Indeed, for those songs called the "laws" of the cithara-players, and for the rest of the Muses, wonderfully invented *prooemia* (preambles) are placed first. But for the true laws, which we call civil laws, no one has ever pronounced or published a preamble, as if none existed by nature. 

However, our delay and our discussion seem to signify that there is such a thing. The laws which were just now called "double" are not simply double, but consist of two parts: the law itself, and the preamble of the law. That part which we compared to the tyrannical command of the slave-doctors is the "mere law." But what was placed before this, spoken in a persuasive manner, truly belongs to persuasion, but has the force of a preamble. For that whole speech was introduced for the sake of persuasion, so that the citizens might hear the legislator’s command (which is the law) more benevolently and thus accept it more easily. Therefore, in my opinion, this whole part should be rightly called not the "reasoning of the law," but the *prooemium* (preamble). 

After this, what else do I desire to add? This: that the legislator ought always to place a preamble before every law, making them differ from each other just as those two parts we related differed. 

**Cli.** I, for one, would never desire anyone but a man skilled in these things to bring laws. 

**Athen.** You seem to me, Clinias, to have spoken well: that a certain preamble should precede all laws, and that in the beginning of every legal composition, a preamble suited to each law should be placed before the discourse. For what is said afterward is of no small importance, nor is it of small consequence whether such things are commemorated clearly or obscurely. However, if we were to order that preambles for both great and small laws be fashioned similarly, we would not be ordering rightly. For this is not to be done in every song or every speech. Even if a preamble *could* be found for all, it does not follow that it *must* be used for all. That decision must be left to the rhetorician, the singer, and the legislator. 

**Clin.** You speak the truth, Guest. But let us not linger further; rather, let us return to the proposed discourse, and begin, if it pleases you, from those things you said above without using a preamble. So, as those at play say, "let us return the second turnings better from the start," treating it now as a certain preamble and not just any speech as we did recently. Let us begin, then, and profess to make an opening. And concerning the honor of the gods and ancestors...

THE PREFACE OF
MARSILIO FICINO
THE FLORENTINE, TO THE BOOKS
OF PLATO, ADDRESSED TO LORENZO
DE' MEDICI, A MAN
OF GREAT MAGNANIMITY.
*
<note>Large decorative initial D</note> Divine providence, powerfully reaching all things and sweetly disposing them, magnanimous Lorenzo, has decreed that holy religion should be armed not only with Prophets, Sibyls, and sacred doctors, but also uniquely adorned by a certain path of elegant philosophy. Thus piety itself, the source of all good things, might finally walk as securely among all professors of wisdom and eloquence as it rests safely among those of its own household. For it was necessary that religion (which is the only way to happiness) be common not only to the simple, but also to the more skilled. With religion as our guide, we may all more easily and safely reach that blessedness for which we were born, and toward which we labor with common zeal. Therefore, almighty God, at the appointed times, sent down the divine soul of Plato from on high, who, by his life, talent, and miraculous eloquence, would illuminate sacred religion among all nations. But since until this present age the Platonic sun had not yet risen openly for the Latin world, Cosimo <note>de' Medici</note>, the glory of Italy and a man of distinguished piety, striving to propagate the Platonic light (so beneficial to religion) from the Greeks to the Latins, destined me—who was raised largely within his own household—for such a great work. Although I have been a worshiper of the Platonic name from a tender age, I undertook so heavy a task not by my own, but by the prosperous auspices of your grandfather Cosimo, hoping that divine help would not be lacking for so necessary and pious a duty. Led primarily by this hope, I entered the Academy, and from there I rendered Plato's dialogues into Latin before Cosimo yielded to nature <note>died</note>. After his death, I gave nine dialogues to be read by your father Piero, a most excellent man. But after Piero departed from this life, fortune, often envious of noble works, against my will drew me away from the duty of translation. But you, a worshiper of religion and a patron of philosophy, called me back to the beginning with all favor and help. For this reason, I have returned to the appointed task under happy auspices once again, and I have not only translated, but also partly touched upon the Platonic mind with arguments, and partly explained it with brief commentaries as far as I was able. And so, the whole work now completed by divine help, I most gladly dedicate it to you. To you also belong, by hereditary right, those things which were inscribed to your elders—you who are truly the heir of your grandfather's and father's virtue in cultivating the fatherland. Among the dialogues you will read the funeral oration of Plato dedicated to your pious brother Giuliano. Furthermore, when you come to the book *On Kingship*, you will see Federico, Duke of Urbino, honored by me on that day when he honorably visited your home. Not only are the thirty-seven books which are marked by your title alone yours, but all of them in the end are yours, since they were all completed for your sake, and I am yours. Indeed, I do not profess that I have entirely captured the Platonic style in these books, nor again do I trust that it could ever be captured by anyone, however much more learned they may be. I speak of a style not so much like human eloquence as like a divine oracle, often thundering from on high, often flowing with nectarean sweetness, but always embracing celestial secrets. Indeed, just as the world is fortified by three principal gifts—utility, order, and ornament—and by these it testifies to us of the divine architect: so the Platonic style, containing the universe, abounds in three gifts especially: the philosophical utility of its sentiments, the oratorical order of its arrangement and expression, and the ornament of poetic flowers; and everywhere it uses divine witnesses and offers the most certain testimony concerning God, the architect of the world. Farewell then, magnanimous Lorenzo; let all those stand far off who demand from Plato only the most minute methods for the instruction of childhood. Let others instruct the more unrefined; let the learned at last approach the Platonic doors, to bring back from there not so much childish rudiments as divine mysteries. I said "at last," Lorenzo, because our Plato, before he pours out divine oracles—lest sacred things become common to the profane—leads the minds of his listeners by a triple path gradually to the summit: through purification, resolution, and conversion. For this reason, many things are read in Plato pertaining to the purging of the mind from disturbances. Many more again to the releasing <note>resolutione</note> of minds from the senses; and most of all to the converting of them, both into themselves and into God, the author of all, toward whom, when they are rightly turned as toward the sun, they may be happily illuminated by the desired rays of truth. Meanwhile, our Plato, while he treats the duty necessary for the human race in often hidden ways, sometimes seems to joke and play. But the Platonic games and jokes are much more serious than the solemnities of the Stoics. For he does not disdain to wander through certain humbler things, provided that by gradually capturing the humbler listeners, he may more easily lead them to the heights. He frequently mixes, by some very serious plan, the useful with the sweet, so that by the charming graces of a modest discourse, he may entice minds naturally more prone to pleasure through the bait of pleasure itself toward healthy food. He often devises myths in the poetic manner: for indeed, the very style of Plato seems not so much philosophical as truly poetic. For he sometimes rages and wanders like a prophet <note>vates</note>, and meanwhile he maintains an order not human, but prophetic and divine; and he acts not so much the part of a teacher as that of a certain priest and prophet: partly indeed raging <note>in divine frenzy</note>, but partly expiating others and snatching them up similarly into a divine frenzy. He seems to use myths among these things for this reason especially: so that among the various flowers of the Academy everyone may indeed be delighted, but that only the purified may pluck the fruit, eat more sweetly, digest more easily, and be more perfectly nourished. Moreover, he does all things through dialogues, so that the living discourse may place the speaking persons before one's eyes, persuade more effectively, and move more vehemently.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino dedicates his translation of Plato to Lorenzo de' Medici, explaining the history of the project through three generations of the Medici family and describing Plato's style as a divine, multi-layered tool for spiritual purification.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Lorenzo de' Medici, Cosimo de' Medici, Piero de' Medici, divine providence, Academy, Platonic style, purification</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
Added to this is the fact that he honors his friends (as is fitting) opportunely in his dialogues, more easily commending many to posterity. Furthermore, different opinions on the same matter are more conveniently reviewed in a dialogue. I pass over how a dialogue delights with a certain wonderful variety and holds the attention of those listening and reading. But why do we digress further through certain minute and humbler things? Wisdom <note>Sophia</note>, magnanimous Lorenzo, who was born from the head of Jove alone and was with him from the beginning arranging all things—imitating her father, she also bore a daughter from her head alone, named Philosophy, whose delight it would be to be with the sons of men. Therefore, while she was once wandering on earth through various nations, the more excellent minds everywhere admired her. Among their number, our Plato not only admired her, but was the first and only one to cultivate her to the highest degree. For he was the first to bind her temples with a miter, as if with the priesthood of sacred things; furthermore, he clothed her in a robe <note>peplum</note> which would befit the August daughter of Minerva; he also anointed her head, hands, and feet with sweetly-smelling ointments. Finally, he scattered various flowers and decorated the very ground wherever the philosophical deity might walk. Such was, and still is, the habit and ornament of this goddess as she walks within the boundaries of the Academy. But as often as she wanders outside the Academic gardens, not only does she always lose her ointments and flowers, but also (oh, the wickedness!) she often falls among thieves; and having lost the insignia of her priesthood and gravity, she wanders everywhere naked and as if profane, and appears so deformed that she no longer pleases Apollo or Mercury, her familiars; nor, moreover, is she approved by either her grandfather Jove or her mother Minerva. But immediately, by her mother's counsel, withdrawing herself within the walls and gardens of the Academy, she resumes her ancient glory, and there, as if in her own country, she rests most gladly. Therefore, it is a joy to exhort all those—along with you, Platonic Lorenzo—who are desirous both of learning and of living well, to the Platonic Academy. For here young men, either amidst joking, will attain the precepts of character, or amidst playing, they will attain the industry of debating very pleasantly and easily. Here men will also thoroughly learn the discipline of both household and public affairs. Here old men, in exchange for mortal life, will hope for eternal life. In the gardens of the Academy, poets will hear Apollo singing under the laurels. In the vestibule of the Academy, orators will watch Mercury declaiming. In the portico and the hall, lawyers and governors of cities will listen to Jove himself, enacting laws, dictating rights, and governing empires. Finally, in the inner sanctum itself, philosophers will recognize their Saturn, the contemplator of celestial secrets. Everywhere, indeed, priests and overseers of sacred things will find weapons with which to protect piety strenuously against the impious. To this place, therefore—to this place, I pray—let all of you approach who cultivate the liberal disciplines, here to obtain them and the liberty of life alike. To this place, finally, let all those run together whom a perpetual ardor for attaining truth and achieving blessedness inflames: here, by the inspiration of God, having attained truth according to your wish, and happiness. But meanwhile, you must be warned not to pass judgment rashly on Platonic things—or rather, divine things—but to judge by a long and fair examination; nor should you exercise envious censure against those who watch and labor for you, far from all envy. Rather, favor the pious author gladly; favor also the translator, who is consulting the common utility of all to the best of his strength, not only by the translation of words but by the explanation of sentiments. Do not, I pray, cruelly pursue and oppress this ancient and healthy doctrine—alas, already oppressed for too long, but recently coming forth into the light by divine providence—lest perhaps what Almighty God wishes to be alive everywhere, a mortal man should wish lost in vain. For "the right hand of the Lord has done valiantly, the right hand of the Lord has now exalted it; it shall not die, but live, and shall declare the works of the Lord." <note>Psalm 118:15-17</note>

But whither, O best Lorenzo, has our immense love for Plato—knowing no measure—carried us? Have we declaimed in the cause of Plato, the prince of oratorical eloquence? For he will have declaimed enough and more than enough for his own cause, especially among those who, free from disturbances, show themselves to be fair listeners. You, however, I will not exhort at all at present, as you are inclined by will in a wonderful way to all these things, prompt in talent, and learned in study. But I shall only wish that you may both read happily and live most happily, mindful of your Marsilio. While I name Marsilio Ficino, understand that Filippo Valori, our fellow Academic, is equally named. For if Valori and Marsilio are the same in defending Plato and in loving you, they are undoubtedly also the same between themselves. His singular virtue proves Valori to you, Lorenzo; his Platonic honor praises him; his incredible love for you commends him greatly.

THE LIFE OF PLATO.
AND FIRST, HIS GENEALOGY
AND BIRTH.
*
<note>Large decorative initial P</note> Plato the Athenian was the son of Ariston and Perictione. For Solon descended from Neleus and Neptune. Solon's brother, Dropides, fathered the elder Critias, from whom Calaescrus was born; he had two sons, namely the younger Critias (who was one of the thirty governors of Athens) and Glaucon, the father of Charmides and Perictione. Perictione, married to Ariston, gave birth to Plato, Adeimantus, and Glaucon; also a daughter, Potone, who, married to Eurymedon, gave birth to Speusippus. Again, Ariston, Plato's father, descended from Codrus the son of Melanthus, who likewise traces his origin back to Neptune, just as Solon does. They say it was famous in Athens that Ariston attempted to lie with Perictione, as she was of a most beautiful form. But his attempts were in vain, and he saw Apollo in a dream, and was commanded by him to keep her pure from conjugal union until she should give birth. Both Laertius and Polycrates write this. He was born in Athens or in Aegina, in the seven hundred and fifty-sixth year from the capture of Troy <note>ca. 427-423 BC</note>; in the three hundred and third year from the founding of the city <note>Rome</note>; and in the four hundred and twenty-third year before the coming of Christ. The birth-chart <note>genesis</note> of Plato, such as I heard when a youth, I indicated in the book *On Love*; but now I will bring forward such as Julius Firmicus the Astronomer describes. I consider his opinion in this matter to be truer. It is as follows: with Mars, Mercury, and Venus in the ascending Aquarius. In the second house, the Sun in Pisces. In the fifth, the Moon in Gemini. In the seventh, Jupiter in Leo. In the ninth, Saturn in Libra. Julius Firmicus asserts that this birth-chart signifies a man who prevails with wonderful eloquence and approaches all the secrets of divinity with a celestial talent.

THE EDUCATION, CHARACTER, LEARNING,
AND SOBRIETY OF PLATO.
IT IS SAID that while he was in his cradle, bees placed honey on the infant's lips—a presage of his future eloquence. They say Socrates saw in a dream a swan chick fledging in his lap, which, as soon as its feathers grew, flew up into the heights with outspread wings and uttered the sweetest songs. On the next day, when Plato was commended to him by his father, he saw him and said that he was that swan. He flourished in his youth with a poetic style. He composed elegies and two tragedies, which he himself gave to the fire as soon as he first applied his mind to philosophy. He was imbued with his first letters by Dionysius his teacher; then he heard Socrates when he was in his twentieth year of age. After Socrates' death, he attached himself to Cratylus, a disciple of Heraclitus, and to Hermogenes, to protect the philosophy of Parmenides. When he was twenty-eight years old, he went to Megara to Euclid with other Socratics. Then having set out for Cyrene, he heard Theodorus the mathematician, and from there he went to Italy to the Pythagoreans Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum and Eurytus. From these, he withdrew to Egypt to the prophets and priests. He had decided to go on to the Indians and the Magi, but because of the wars in Asia, he abandoned the plan. Having finally returned to Athens, he lived his life in the Academy—which unhealthy spot in Attica he is said to have chosen (as both Saint Basil and Jerome confirm) so that an excessively good condition of the body, like a vine with too much luxury, might be pruned back. For he was of a most beautiful and robust physical build. From this, on account of his broad shoulders, wide forehead, and the excellent habit of his whole body and the richness of his speech, he was named "Plato" <note>from the Greek 'platys', meaning broad</note>; whereas he had previously been named Aristocles. There was nothing deformed in him, unless perhaps a somewhat thin voice and I know not what lump under his neck deformed him slightly. Because of his living in the Academy, he suffered a quartan fever for eighteen months; but by his sobriety and diligence, he recovered stronger forces after the fever than before.

MILITARY SERVICE AND THE THREE
VOYAGES OF PLATO.
HE SERVED as a soldier three times. First at Tanagra, second at Corinth, third at Delos, where he also obtained a victory. He sailed to Sicily three times. First, so that he might see the island and the wonders of Etna and its craters. He was then in the fortieth year of his age, at which time Dionysius, son of Hermocrates, urged him to speak with him. There, when Plato discoursed on tyranny, saying that nothing was excellent which was only useful to oneself unless it also excelled in virtue, they say the offended and angry tyrant said: "Your words are those of idle old men." But he replied: "And yours smack of tyranny." At this, the indignant tyrant first wished to kill him. But then, entreated by Dion and Aristomenes, he did not do so; but he handed him over to Pollis the Lacedaemonian, who had come to him as an ambassador at that time, to be sold. Pollis took him to Aegina and sold him. At which time Charmander also accused him as one guilty of death. Indeed, according to a law commonly held among them, it was a capital crime if any Athenian should go to that island. But when it was alleged by someone that the philosopher had come there for the sake of learning, and that the law spoke of men, not of philosophers who are above men, they dismissed him acquitted; and they decreed not that he should be killed, but sold. By chance Anniceris of Cyrene was present, who redeemed him for twenty minae and sent him back to Athens to his friends. There is a story that Pollis was defeated by Chabrias and afterwards drowned in Helice, a spirit announcing to him that he suffered such things for the sake of the philosopher. Nevertheless, Dionysius did not rest. But when he learned what had happened to him, he wrote to Plato, praying him not to hurl insults at him. To whom Plato wrote back that he did not have so much leisure from philosophy that he would remember Dionysius. To certain detractors who objected that Plato was abandoned by Dionysius, he replied: "On the contrary, Dionysius was abandoned by Plato." A second time he set out to the younger Dionysius, summoned by him and Dion for the sake of philosophizing; led also by the hope that he would bring it about by his counsels that a republic or a kingdom might be made there out of a tyranny; and that he would see what he had long and vehemently desired, namely a certain most philosophical government, in which either philosophers should govern or governors should philosophize. For he thought that cities could not otherwise avoid misery. He desired all this to be done for Dionysius not by force or fraud, but by persuasion through philosophical reasons. But about the fourth month after Plato's arrival, Dionysius, driven by false slanders, expelled Dion as if he were plotting against the tyranny. But he embraced Plato willingly. Yet Plato returned to his fatherland. A third time he went to reconcile Dion to Dionysius, being entreated again and again by both, and also asked by Archytas. Then Dionysius even sent a trireme adorned with fillets to meet him, and Archedemus the Pythagorean orator, and many nobles; and he himself received him as he arrived in a chariot with four white horses. Plato demanded the promised restoration of Dion, and furthermore a city and men who would live according to the republic established by him. Although Dionysius promised this, he declined to fulfill it. When Plato openly rebuked Dionysius because he had broken his word—both concerning the restoring of Dion and concerning the keeping of Theodotus regarding Heraclides—he then had Dionysius as an enemy. Wherefore he was in the greatest danger of being killed by the soldiers. But Archytas of Tarentum sent Lamiscus as an orator to Dionysius with a ship, asking that he dismiss Plato. He dismissed him and provided provisions; Plato returned to his fatherland. Shortly after, Dionysius, expelled from his tyranny by Dion and his men, paid the penalty for the crime committed against the philosopher. Plato was received with wonderful honor in his fatherland. When summoned there to the Republic, he refused to enter because the common people had accustomed themselves to bad morals.

TO WHOM PLATO GAVE
LAWS.
IT IS SAID that the Arcadians and the Thebans, having founded a city of honorable size, asked him to establish that republic. But when he understood they were unwilling to follow equality, he did not set out. To the Syracusans, however, after the tyrant was expelled, he gave laws; and for the Cretans, when the city of Magnesia was recently founded or restored, he wrote twelve laws arranged into books. He sent from his familiars Aristonymus to the Arcadians to establish laws, Phormio to the Elians, and Menedemus to the Pyrrhaeans.

THE CONTINENCE, GRAVITY, AND
COURTESY OF PLATO.
HE LIVED celibate and very sober, and as Aurelius Augustine asserts, chaste. Wherefore also in old age he is said to have performed the sacred rites of nature, so that he might absolve himself among the common people from the charge of sterility. As a youth he was so modest and so composed that he was never found to laugh except moderately. Indeed, no one saw him angry. Wherefore a boy educated at Plato's house, when he returned to his parents and saw his father shouting, said: "I never saw this at Plato's." Only once was he secretly a little angry at a boy who had gravely transgressed. But he said to Xenocrates: "You beat this boy, for I cannot, because I am angry." He ate every day either only once or twice, most sparingly. He slept alone. He greatly criticized the opposite way of life. Toward loving youths, he seemed a little more prone, just as his teacher Socrates did; but both were as continent in reason as they were inclined in sense. How divinely these men loved, and in what way the things they spoke about love should be explained, we have sufficiently treated in the book *On Love*. He desired...

And although he was of a melancholic temperament and possessed the most profound genius—as Aristotle writes—he nevertheless employed many jests. He very often advised the more severe Xenocrates and Dion to "make sacrifices to the Graces" <note>In Greek mythology, the Graces represented charm and beauty; Plato was telling his friends to be more pleasant and approachable</note>, so that they might become more agreeable and gracious. Thus, a sense of courtesy was mingled with Plato's gravity.

## THE PRINCIPAL DISCIPLES OF PLATO
His disciples were: Speusippus of Athens, Xenocrates of Chalcedon, Aristotle of Stagira, Philippus of Opus, Hestiaeus of Perinthus, Dion of Syracuse, Amycles of Heraclea, Erastus and Coriscus of Scepsis, Timolaus of Cyzicus, Hebion of Lampsacus, Python and Heraclides of Aenus, Hippothales and Callippus of Athens, Demetrius of Amphipolis, Heraclides of Pontus, and many others. Among these were two women, Lasthenia of Mantinea and Axiothea of Phlius, who wore men's clothing. It is said that Theophrastus was also his pupil, as were the orator Hyperides, Chamaeleon, Lycurgus, and even Demosthenes, who was a devoted student, along with Mnestistratus. Inscribed upon the vestibule of the Academy was: *Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here.* <note>original: "Nemo huc geometriæ expers ingrediatur"</note> This was intended to be understood not only regarding the measurement of lines, but also regarding the proper measurement of one's emotions.

## THE BOOKS WHICH PLATO WROTE, COLLECTED BY POSTERITY INTO NINE TETRALOGIES <note>A "tetralogy" is a group of four works.</note>

**Euthyphro:** or, on holiness

**The Letters (twelve)**

All these books of Plato we have translated ourselves from the Greek language into Latin. <note>This identifies the author as Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century scholar who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin.</note> There are three types of Platonic dialogues: he either refutes the sophists, exhorts youth, or teaches adults. What Plato himself discusses in his letters, or in the books of the *Laws* and the *Epinomis*, he wishes to be held as most certain. However, what he disputes through the mouths of Socrates, Timaeus, Parmenides, or Zeno in the other books, he considers to be likely truths.

## THE ELOQUENCE, WISDOM, AND AUTHORITY OF PLATO
Plato's style, as Aristotle says, flows midway between prose and poetry; such is its sweetness and abundance that Cicero said Plato was the weightiest author of both understanding and speaking. He added that if Jupiter had wished to speak in a human tongue, he would have spoken in no other than that of Plato. Indeed, such was the learning in him that while before him all the illustrious Greeks had traveled to foreign nations for the sake of wisdom, after Plato's time other nations flocked to Athens. Even Aristotle, endowed with such a miraculous genius and most eager for new doctrines, having come to Plato almost as a young man, listened to him for twenty continuous years. Furthermore, before he came to Plato, he was already advanced in letters; thereafter, he had Plato as his only teacher. I pass over what is written by Cicero: "I would rather err with Plato than think rightly with the others" <note>original: "Malo cum Platone errare, quàm cü cæteris recte sentire"</note>. Additionally, along with Panaetius, he calls him the "Homer of philosophers." I pass over that saying of Quintilian: "Who would doubt that Plato is the foremost, whether in the sharpness of his debating or in a certain divine and Homeric eloquence of speaking?" For his speech rises far above ordinary speech—which the Greeks call "pedestrian"—so that he seems to me to be inspired not by human genius, but by some Delphic oracle.

Through a certain divine wisdom and integrity, he seems to have acquired for himself a wonderful authority even in his own homeland, which very rarely happens. When Plato returned from Sicily and arrived at that most magnificent celebration of the Olympics—a gathering of nearly the whole world—he was received with such joyful greetings by everyone that he seemed like a God sent down from heaven to mortals. You could see the games deserted, the spectacles of the athletes left behind, and the boxers left alone. And what is more marvelous: those who had come to the Olympics from such long stretches of land and sea for the sake of feeding their eyes and minds and for other reasons, forgetting all pleasure, went to Plato. They gazed at Plato; they rested in Plato as if in the most pleasant of inns. Once, when someone was reciting a tragedy and no one was present except Plato, and some objected that it was unbecoming for him to be there when no one else was present, he replied: "And this one man is worth more than the whole Athenian people."

## THE CHARITY, MAGNANIMITY, AND HOLINESS OF PLATO
His letters declare how great and constant his spirit was, especially in the cause of his friends. He boldly rebuked the Tyrant <note>Referring to Dionysius of Syracuse</note> even in the presence of witnesses because he governed unjustly or because he deceived his friends; he was so far from flattering him. I pass over those smaller details, such as when Dionysius had ordered at a banquet that everyone should dance clothed in purple; Aristippus danced immediately, but Plato refused, saying it did not befit a philosopher to wear women's clothing. Consider also his contempt for the tyrant and his defense of Dion. Furthermore, when the wicked accuser Crobylus had named a day for the trial of the most brave general Chabrias and had sought a capital judgment, and while Chabrias was ascending to the citadel deserted by the rest of the citizens for fear of danger, Plato alone was always present to offer him aid. When the slanderer Crobylus, to deter him from his patronage, said threateningly: "You come to offer defense to others, not knowing that the poison of Socrates awaits you as well," Plato himself replied: "Long ago, Crobylus, when I fought for the dignity of my country, I was not slow in enduring dangers; now, for my duty and the safety of a friend, though you may threaten iron and poisons and fire, I refuse no danger."

When Socrates was most unjustly shut in prison, Plato collected money to ransom the innocent man. And while the trial was being held, ascending the platform, he began to speak thus: "Since I am younger, O men of Athens, than all these who have ascended the tribunal..." But the tyrannical judges, fearing lest he move the citizens by his authority and eloquence, suddenly interrupted and shouted: "Get down!" Plato went home. For as much as those men labored under a disease of the evil mind, he then labored under a disease of the body. However, the persecutors of Socrates paid the penalty shortly thereafter. When one of his fellow students, driven by envy that Xenocrates was so pleasing and acceptable to Plato, tried to stir up enmities against him and reported many insults from Xenocrates against Plato, Plato, rejecting the accusation in mid-speech, fell silent. The detractor insisted, affirming the crime with a severe expression. Finally, having called all the gods and goddesses to witness, Plato, to free himself from the man's persistence, said: "So be it. But Xenocrates is so powerful in faith and gravity that unless he had judged it to be profitable, he would never have said those things." That Xenocrates, his beloved disciple, imitated the gravity and magnanimity of Plato is evidenced by the life of Xenocrates in Diogenes <note>Diogenes Laërtius, author of "Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers"</note>, which is indeed an exemplar of fortitude and holiness. Plutarch is witness that Dion also imitated him. Furthermore, Philiscus, in describing the life of the orator Lycurgus, says: "He was a great man <unclear>...</unclear>"
