Lycurgus was a great man, and many things were performed by him excellently, which no one could have done who had not been a listener of Plato. When Demosthenes was fleeing from Antipater and Archias promised with flattering words that he would save his life, he replied: "May I depart, so that I would rather die honestly than choose to live basely, after I have heard Xenocrates and Plato disputing on the immortality of the soul." Writing to a certain Heracleodorus, his fellow student, and rebuking him because after he had heard Plato, he neglected the noble arts and led a life of little honor, he said: "Are you not ashamed to neglect those things which you received from Plato?" Dionysius, writing to Speusippus, says: "Plato indeed taught those who wore down his threshold for free. You, however, exact tributes and take from both the willing and the unwilling." Laertius also carps at the same man, because he did not imitate the chastity, fortitude, and gentleness of Plato as Xenocrates did. I cannot remain silent regarding that instance of Xenocrates' fortitude: when Dionysius said to Plato, "Someone will take off your head," Xenocrates, who was present, said, "No one shall do that before they cut off this head of mine."

## THE SAYINGS AND PROVERBS 
## OF PLATO.

PLATO used to say this regarding Aristotle and Xenocrates: "What kind of horse and what kind of donkey have I taken to yoke together? Aristotle indeed needs a bridle, but Xenocrates needs spurs." Among his disciples was a youth who was too elegant and most studious of caring for his skin, whom Plato asked: "How long will you continue to build a prison for yourself?" Whenever he saw a man entangled in love, he would say: "He is dead in his own body, but lives in another's." He added: "He who abandons himself for the sake of another is the most miserable of all, since he possesses neither himself any longer, nor the other." A certain learned friend of Plato begged him to lend his ears for a little while to read a book published by him. When asked by Plato what the title of the book was, he replied: "That one must not contradict." To which Plato said: "Why then do you do this very thing? Why do you contradict those who contradict? Why do you consult me, if you forbid yourself to be contradicted?" Leo, a powerful citizen in the army, was criticized because he had made loud and immodest outcries in an assembly. Plato said: "This is truly what it is to be a lion." <note>A pun on the name Leo, which means Lion.</note> When Diogenes the Cynic said that he saw these human things indeed, but saw the Ideas not at all, Plato said: "Is it any wonder? For you have and use eyes with which these things are seen, but you do not use the mind, by which alone those Ideas are discerned." When the disciples marveled that Xenocrates, who was serious in all his life, had said something that was received with laughter, Plato asked: "Why do you wonder that roses and lilies sometimes grow among thorns?" He was accustomed to say frequently to young men: "Prefer labors to idleness, unless perhaps you think rust is better than splendor." He very often inflamed youth toward the blessed life by this reasoning: "Observe the contrary nature of virtue and pleasure. For a sudden repentance follows the momentary sweetness of the latter, along with perpetual pain; but eternal pleasure follows the brief labors of the former." When he had seen someone playing with dice, he rebuked him; and when the man said, "How small a thing you find fault with," Plato responded: "But habit is not a small thing." He was accustomed to advise the drunk and the angry to look at themselves studiously in a mirror; they would immediately turn away from such foulness. He greatly detested drunkenness and sleep. He said it mattered most for the education of childhood that boys should become accustomed to rejoicing only in honorable things. Otherwise, he said that pleasure was the bait of evils. He added that the health of the soul was true philosophy, while the other faculties seemed not so much philosophy as ornaments. Truly, nothing is sweeter to the mind than to speak and hear the truth. For nothing is better or more durable than truth. When some people asked what kind of possessions should especially be prepared for their sons, he said: "Those which fear neither hail, nor the violence of men, nor even Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> himself." To Demodocus, consulting him on the education of his son, he said: "As there must be care in planting and directing young trees, so must there be in begetting and instructing sons. Here is labor, there is pleasure. But we must take care lest we seem wise in the latter, but more than watchful in the former." To a certain Philedonus, who asked why Plato was no less studious and diligent in learning than in teaching, and how long he wished to be a disciple, he replied: "As long as it shall not repent me to be better and more skilled." Asked what was the difference between a skilled and an unskilled man, he replied: "That which is between a doctor and a sick man." He used to say that there was no more excellent kind of property for princes than the friendship of those men who did not know how to be "inn-keepers" <note>meaning: those who do not treat friendship as a commercial trade</note>. He said wisdom was no less necessary for a prince than the soul is for the body. That republics would be most blessed if either philosophers ruled, or at least those who govern should, by some divine fate, philosophize. For nothing is more pestilential than power and audacity when ignorance accompanies them. Also, that subjects tend to be such as their princes seem to be. A magistrate must think not of his own good, but the public good; he must care not for only a part of the city, but the whole.

## HOW MUCH PLATO NEGLECTED HUMAN THINGS, 
## AND HOW MUCH HE LOVED DIVINE THINGS.

HE REPEATED daily that only eternal things are true; temporal things, however, are but likenesses. That the soul sleeps in the body. And that what the senses desire or fear are nothing other than dreams. Therefore, all these things are to be utterly despised. And since the world is full of evils, one must flee to eternal things; for otherwise they cannot be avoided. He himself also fulfilled what he preached. For although by a certain hereditary right and the favor of the citizens he was to be a leader in the Republic, he rejected every civil dignity entirely. Although he was most wealthy by patrimony, he bestowed all things upon his brothers except for a small suburban estate, which they called the Academy; content with this alone, he lived. Although he stood as the teacher and friend of princes, he nevertheless accepted no riches from them. King Dionysius used to say, "Aristippus always asks for money, but Plato always for books." Add to this that he neither took a wife, nor lived in the city, free from all things, serving the truth alone. Whence Saint Jerome says: "Plato most laboriously traversed Egypt and Archytas of Tarentum and that coast of Italy which was once called Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia</note>, so that he who was a master and powerful in Athens, and whose doctrine the gymnasia of the Academy made to resound, might become a wanderer and a disciple, preferring to learn others' things modestly rather than to thrust his own forward impudently. Finally, while he pursued letters as if they were fleeing across the whole world, having been captured by pirates and sold, he even obeyed a most cruel tyrant as a captive, and was bound as a slave; nevertheless, because he was a philosopher, he was greater than his purchaser." Thus says Jerome.

## THE PIETY AND GRATITUDE OF PLATO.

HE WAS devoted to God, from whom he said the beginning of thinking, speaking, and acting in all things must be made, and he himself always did so. Furthermore, he gave thanks to God daily that he was born a man and not a brute; that he was a Greek and not a barbarian; and that he was born in the times of Socrates. How grateful he was to his teachers and to all his friends is testified by his dialogues. In them, he honors them all wonderfully and attributes his books to Socrates. For not only does he introduce him disputing in almost all the dialogues, but he also writes that all things composed by himself are not his own, but belong to Socrates.

## WHAT PLATO AFFIRMED.

IN THOSE things which are subject to the senses, he defended the parts of Heraclitus. Furthermore, in those things which pertain to the intellect, he most especially agreed with Pythagoras. In civil matters, however, he embraced his own Socrates. These are the things which he asserted everywhere: That God provides for all things. That the souls of men are immortal. That there will be rewards for the good and punishments for the evil. Augustine says in his book *Against the Academics* that the authority of Christ is to be preferred above all. But if one must act by reasons, he says he finds among the Platonists that which does not conflict with the sacred letters of the Christians. Dionysius the Areopagite signaled the same; Eusebius later and Cyrillus declared it more broadly. Hence Augustine says in the book *On True Religion*: "The Platonists, with a few things changed, would become Christians." And in his *Confessions*, he relates that he found almost the entire prologue of the Gospel of John among the Platonists. Therefore, in the second book of *The City of God*, he says: "Labeo the Theologian among the gentiles thought that Plato should be numbered among the demigods, like Hercules and Romulus; but he prefers demigods to heroes, and places both among the divinities. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that this man whom he calls a demigod is to be preferred not only to heroes, but even to the gods themselves." Whence he says he chose the Platonists before others, because they felt quite more correctly than the other philosophers concerning divine and human things. Marcus Varro had also judged this before, and Apuleius made Plato not only superior to heroes, but equal to the gods, because he clearly penetrated the inner sanctums of divine things. Plato was endowed with such great modesty that, although he had acquired for himself a marvelous authority above others, nevertheless, when asked by someone to what extent his precepts should be obeyed, he replied: "Until there appears on earth someone more sacred, who may open the fountain of truth to all, whom finally all may follow." He added that he had found nothing by his own light, but only by divine light. As for what he felt in philosophy, we have treated that sufficiently in the book *On Love* and in our *Theology*.
Returned.

THE LIFE OF PLATO.

## PLATO'S RETURN TO HIS CELESTIAL HOMELAND AND HIS PRAISES.

HE DEPARTED on his own birthday, and completed eighty-one years, without any doubt. Therefore the Magi, who were then in Athens, sacrificed to Plato, thinking him to have been of a lot greater than human, because he had completed the most perfect number, which nine multiplied by nine produces. And what is marvelous is that he was still writing at that age and on that very day. Concerning this, Cicero says: "There is also a peaceful and light old age of a life led quietly, purely, and elegantly, such as we have heard was Plato's, who died while writing in his eighty-first year." Seneca also affirms that this happened to Plato by the benefit of his sobriety and diligence. Some say he returned to those above while writing, others that he did so while reclining at a wedding feast, after the tables were removed, in the midst of a discussion. Aristotle consecrated an altar and a statue to Plato in a temple with this epigram: *Aristotle dedicated this altar to Plato, a man whom it is a sin for the wicked to praise.* Aristotle adds:
*He who alone by life, doctrine, character, and voice*
*Admonished all, and gave monuments:*
*So that by virtue they might lead a happy life.*
*No future ages shall bring forth such a man.*
Other wise men also added many poems in praise of Plato; but three epigrams are principal. The meaning of the first is this: He excelled all in temperance and justice, and he so surpassed them in wisdom that he overcame all envy entirely. The sense of the second is this: Plato has been translated into the number of the gods. Distant nations honor him; he who himself knew the divine life and showed it to others. The meaning of the third is of this sort: Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> begat Aesculapius and Plato, so that the former might heal bodies, and the latter, souls. Furthermore, Mithridates, King of the Persians, placed a statue of Plato in the Academy inscribed thus: *Mithridates the Persian, son of Rhodobates, dedicated this image of Plato to the Muses, the work of Silanion.* From all these things, Plato achieved this: that the Greeks called Aristotle "daemonic" <note>meaning "spirit-like" or "extraordinary"</note>, but they called Plato "divine." This is because the former was especially human in life and natural in science. But the latter directed both his science and his life especially toward the divine.

## A DEFENSE OF PLATO'S CHARACTER.

I SHALL now bring this to an end for you, if I add a few things again. There are certain common versifiers who undeservedly usurp for themselves the name of poets. These men, provoked as much by the dissimilarity of their characters as by the malice of envy, play most impudently against every best man. A certain maximum license is granted to these people against the good rather than against the evil. Such petty poets of old, therefore, did not hesitate to bite the divine Plato (judged by the Greeks to be the son of Apollo) and Socrates (judged by the Apollo of the Greeks to be the wisest). Diogenes Laertius most greatly detests their impiety. And as he himself declares, Aristippus of Cyrene increased the ridiculous insults of the comic poets; a most wicked man and an adversary of every best man of his times, who, just as he slandered most other modest and learned men with a certain fictional history, so also he slandered his teacher Socrates and his fellow students Xenophon and Plato. He faked certain lascivious poems in their names about harlots and boys, clearly so that he might obtain for himself a freer license for sinning by the false example of great philosophers. Truly Aristotle, to whom truth was a greater friend than Plato, could not endure such false calumnies against a holy man. For in his elegies to Eudemus, he sang those things concerning Plato which we said above; attributing this most especially to him: that the profane ought not only not to disparage Plato in any way, but also they should not dare to name his holy name with a profane mouth even under the pretext of praise. Nor was he content with an Elegy; but also, as Olympiodorus relates, he composed a most excellent speech concerning the praise of Plato. Therefore, let the dogs of hell be silent among those above, and let them accompany Cerberus with their barking among those below. We, however, let us venerate the life and wisdom of Plato, most approved by the judgment of the wise, and together with Apuleius of Madaura, let us freely proclaim: "We of the Platonic family know nothing but what is festive, joyful, celestial, and supernal."

# EXTRACT OF THE KING'S PRIVILEGE

BY special grace, authority, and Royal privilege, permission is granted to Antoine Vincent, merchant bookseller at Lyon, to print or cause to be printed the works of Plato which he has newly and diligently caused to be revised by several learned personages, compared with several old copies, and to have restored in them several passages, and to add six Dialogues which had not previously been incorporated into the Latin works of the said Plato: with prohibitions and defenses to all booksellers, printers, and others, against printing, causing to be printed, or exposing for sale the said works of Plato, thus restored, without the express leave and permission of the said Vincent, during the term and space of ten years, counting from the day and date of the completion of the first printing of the said book: under penalty of confiscation of the said books, an arbitrary fine, and all costs, damages, and interests, as is more fully contained and declared by the letters patent given for this purpose at Fontainebleau, the 23rd day of the month of October, the year of grace one thousand five hundred fifty-six, and of his Reign the tenth.

By the King, on your report. De Lomenie.

And sealed with the great seal, in yellow wax, with a single tail.

Finished printing the 20th of November 1556.

->A 9<-
# PLATO’S HIPPARCHUS, OR, ON THE DESIRE FOR PROFIT, OR, THE ZEAL FOR GAIN.

## THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated Plato’s works into Latin, making them accessible to Western Europe.</note>

Plato’s purpose in the *Hipparchus* is to teach us that all men desire the good, even those who seem to go astray because of avarice <note>Greed or extreme desire for wealth.</note>. For they are indeed desirous of profit; profit is something useful, and what is useful is a good; therefore, they desire a good. Indeed, profit is the opposite of loss; loss, when it occurs, is an evil; therefore, profit is the opposite of an evil. The opposite of an evil is a good; therefore, profit is a good. For this reason, since even those who seem to turn away from the appetite for the good still desire a good, nothing now prevents us from concluding that all men desire the good.

Now, the "good" is of two kinds. One is the end <note>The ultimate goal or purpose.</note>. The other leads toward the end. The former is sought for its own sake, the latter for the sake of something else. The appetite for the former is called "will," and the choice of the latter is "selection." The former is to be venerated, the latter is useful. We enjoy the former, and we use the latter. The attainment of the former is called "happiness," and the attainment of the latter is called "profit." Therefore, profit is the acquisition of a useful good which can lead to the completion of the venerated good. But that which does not contribute to this is neither useful in itself, nor is the appetite for it true profit. Therefore, the desire for profit, which is inherent in all by nature, is to be praised. However, false opinion is to be condemned, for while it is ignorant of what is truly useful and profitable, it twists the natural appetite toward harmful things.

Plato teaches all these things covertly while Socrates refutes the false definitions that Hipparchus <note>The dialogue's namesake, distinct from the historical ruler mentioned later.</note> offers regarding the desire for profit, doing so through both induction and reasoning. Plato uses this proposition—"All men desire the good"—as a manifest truth to conclude that all men naturally desire profit, and that this natural appetite is praiseworthy. This is the conclusion which we gather in a certain way... we gather that most confirmed proposition through argument from the lesser: namely, that all men desire the good, which is the ultimate end of this book, while the primary goal is to show that everyone is desirous of profit, and that this is not to be condemned.

### SOCRATES. HIPPARCHUS.

**SOCRATES.** What then is the desire for profit? And who are the profit-seekers?
**HIPPARCHUS.** It seems to me they are those who think they should gain from things of no value.
**SOC.** Do they seem to you to know that these things are of no value, or are they ignorant? If they do not know, then you are calling the senseless "profit-seekers."
**HIP.** But I do not call them senseless, but rather clever and wicked, and overcome by greed; they are conscious that the things from which they snatch a profit are of no value, and yet they seek gain through impudence.
**SOC.** Is this the kind of person you call a profit-seeker? For instance, if a farmer, while planting and knowing the plant is of no value, nevertheless thinks it worthy to profit from—do you call him such?
**HIP.** From any source whatever, O Socrates, the profit-seeker thinks he must seek gain.
**SOC.** Do not pour out your words so rashly, as if angry at someone for an injury received, but rather answer me with attention, as if I were questioning you again from the beginning. Do you agree that the profit-seeker knows the value of that from which he expects to profit?
**HIP.** I agree.
**SOC.** Who is it that knows about the value of plants—in what region and at what time it is *worthy* to plant—so that we might bring into our midst some of those wise words with which those elegant lawyers abound?
<margin>He notes the Greek phrasing as being affected or "showy."</margin>
**HIP.** The farmer, I believe.
**SOC.** Do you call "worthy of profit" anything other than thinking it ought to be gained?
**HIP.** That is it.
**SOC.** Do not try to deceive me, a man already old, while you are so young, by answering as you do 
<note>original: "quemadmodum nunc," meaning "just as you are now."</note>
now, things which you yourself do not really feel; but answer as truly as possible. Would you judge him a true farmer who, knowing a plant is unworthy of being planted, thinks he should profit from it?
**HIP.** Not by Jove!
**SOC.** Furthermore, regarding a horseman: if he knows the fodder he gives his horse is of no value, do you think he is ignorant that the horse will be ruined?
**HIP.** Not at all.
**SOC.** Therefore, he does not think there is profit from such faulty fodder.
**HIP.** Not in the least.
**SOC.** And the pilot who has equipped his ship with a tiller and sails of no value—do you think he is ignorant that he will suffer loss and come into danger, so that both the ship and everything in it will be lost?
**HIP.** Certainly he is not ignorant of that.
**SOC.** He does not, then, think he will profit from instruments of no value.
**HIP.** Not at all.
**SOC.** Likewise, if a commander of an army sees his army relying on worthless arms, would he hope or think it worthy to affect a profit from them?
**HIP.** Not in the least.
**SOC.** In the same way, if a flute player has a flute, or a lyre player a lyre, or an archer a bow—and to be brief—if any craftsman or expert in any matter has tools and remaining equipment of no value, would he think he will ever profit from them?
**HIP.** No, it appears not.
**SOC.** Whom then do you call profit-seekers? For it is not those we have referred to, who think they ought to profit from things worthy of no consideration. And yet, in this way, O wondrous man, according to what you wish, no man would be a profit-seeker.
**HIP.** But I, O Socrates, say those are profit-seekers who, because of an insatiable desire, thirst in a marvelous way for every tiny and most vile thing of no value, and seek profit even in these.
**SOC.** But they do not, O best of men, know that those things are of no value. For we have already driven ourselves to this point: to admit that such a thing is impossible.
**HIP.** So it seems to me.
**SOC.** If they do not know it, they are therefore ignorant; yet they think that those things which are of no value are to be highly esteemed.
**HIP.** It appears so.
**SOC.** Do profit-seekers not desire profit?
**HIP.** Certainly.
**SOC.** And do you say profit is the opposite of loss?
**HIP.** It is.
**SOC.** Is it a good for anyone to suffer loss?
**HIP.** For no one.
**SOC.** But is it an evil?
**HIP.** Entirely.
**SOC.** Are men therefore harmed by loss?
**HIP.** They are harmed.
**SOC.** Is loss, then, an evil?
**HIP.** An evil.
**SOC.** And is profit the opposite of loss?
**HIP.** The opposite.
**SOC.** Is profit, therefore, a good?
**HIP.** Certainly.
**SOC.** Do you then call those who love the good "profit-seekers"?
**HIP.** It seems so.
**SOC.** Indeed, you do not call profit-seekers insane, O friend. But do you yourself love what is good, or do you not?
**HIP.** I love it indeed.
**SOC.** Is there any good that you do not strive for, but rather an evil?
**HIP.** Not by Jove!
**SOC.** Rather, you strive equally for all good things.
**HIP.** All of them.
**SOC.** Ask me as well, and I too will confess that I love good things. But besides me and you, do not all other mortals seem to you to love good things and hate evil ones?
**HIP.** It seems so.
**SOC.** And did we not confess that profit is a good?
**HIP.** Truly.
**SOC.** Therefore, everyone appears to be a profit-seeker in this way; whereas before we said no one was a profit-seeker. Which of these two reasonings should we follow so as not to err?
**HIP.** If someone, O Socrates, were to define a profit-seeker correctly,

# Thirty-Fourth Book.

He says that it is necessary for both those who are to elect magistrates and those who are to be elected to be most highly approved from their youth, born of most approved images, and to be perfectly skilled in the conduct of their habits. In this, you will note the wonderful prudence of Plato (the Athenian philosopher) regarding the order of magistrates and their duties in human and sacred affairs, in war and peace, in the city and the fields. You will recognize and approve of the best form of government—one that possesses something of the royal and something of the popular, and is established as a middle ground between a single ruler and the people.

You will also see that in distributing civil duties, equality must always be preserved. Not **arithmetical equality**, which always grants equal things to individuals by number or even by measure and weight—which is often the most unjust—but rather **geometric equality** [*geometria*], through which the merits of individuals are considered and distributed to each according to reason. Thus, the proportion of merits to merits is the same as the proportion of rewards to rewards; rewards are not equal to other rewards, but rewards are equal to merits. Therefore, you shall consider a twin equality: that of reward to reward, and that of reward to merit. The former is often harmful and rarely useful, used only for the sake of the lot [*sors*]. The latter, however, is necessary every day. In this indeed consists the whole principle of justice. This very justice is placed in the judgment of Jove (Jupiter), and though the notion of it is granted to few among men, through it alone—in whatever measure it is present to us—all things are preserved.

Not without merit does he attribute the duty of this equality to the supreme judge. Since He penetrates the secret roofs of all and knows their merits perfectly, He alone is surely able to render things equal to merits. And He does this in the first instance, and then in the universe, so that by this distribution alone—according to the capacity of each nature—all things are created and preserved. This was approved by the ancients and confirmed in the *Gorgias*.

But among these things, Plato—as is his most frequent custom—remembers the education of boys. He creates a peculiar magistrate for this purpose and wishes him to be held as the most excellent of all the highest magistrates in the state. He believes that without the providence of cultivating the "yeast" of youth, the entire cultivation of the state will be in vain. You will notice here that human genius, if well-cultivated, finally emerges as most mild and divine; but on the contrary, if corrupted, it becomes more ferocious than wild beasts. This is because that which has the greatest power for good can also have the greatest power for evil. Likewise, the best thing, when turned into its opposite by its own depravity, becomes the worst—which is indeed seen in a collapsing republic. Furthermore, the ferocity in a depraved man is increased by the machination of a most sharp mind directed toward evil. Add to this that the subtlety of human spirits [*spiritus*], when in anger, is converted into fury. There is also the instigation of certain *daemones* (spirits), which Plato mentions in his letter to the Syracusans, and which Homer frequently uses according to the opinion of the Egyptians, introducing Heroes who are aided or animated to anger and blood by spirits.

He commends that number **5,040** for the magistrates, the households, and the division of fields as the most convenient of all, since it can be divided into many successive whole portions. If you divide this number into two parts, the half will contain 2,520. If into three, the third part is 1,680. If into four, any fourth is 1,260. If into five, any fifth will contain 1,008. If into six, every sixth is 840. If into seven, a seventh is 720. If into eight, an eighth is 630. If into nine, a ninth is 560. If into ten, a tenth is 504. Up to this point, all parts are integers. But if into eleven, the eleventh is 458 and additionally two-tenths portions. But if into twelve, the twelfth is 420. Stop your foot here. But since I mentioned sixty, if that whole number is divided into sixty parts, each part will hold 84. [[notes: Ficino’s math here slightly deviates or corrects the text's 60/420 logic.]]

It seems that Plato makes much of the fact that this number is divided twelve times into 420, and again twice twelve into 35. He praises the number **twelve** and the whole number which is adapted to the duodecimal system, because there are twelve spheres of the world, twelve signs in the Zodiac, and twelve parts in the elements. Indeed, each of the four elements is divided into three regions: the highest, the lowest, and the middle—differing not only in position but also in virtue. To the other duodecimal of the elements, the four substances of the elements and eight qualities are included. Of the qualities, four are masculine, namely heat, cold, lightness, and heaviness. For the first two are the principles of alteration, while the following two are principles of local motion. Four, however, are feminine, being more subject to passion: namely moisture, dryness, rarity, and density. These things are contained in the mysteries of the Egyptians, as Iamblichus (the Neoplatonist) asserts. Added to this is the fact that the Sun, lord of the planets, completes its own course through the twelvefold number of minds and produces various effects.

Finally, he wants each part of the city to be considered consecrated to God, specifically to the **twelve gods**, that is, the souls of the twelve spheres. Likewise to the twelve gods ruling the signs of the Zodiac. Again, to the twelve orders of *daemones* following the celestial signs. When he says the twelve parts of the city follow the circuit of the universe, perhaps he also means the entire circuit of the eighth sphere to be completed in 36,000 years. This number is perfectly completed by three sets of twelve thousand years. Thus, in the first twelve thousand years, you may understand (from the opinion of the ancients) the youthful state of the whole world; in the second, the viral; in the third, the senile. But these things are more opportunely discussed in the *Timaeus*.

This agrees with what he says in the *Phaedrus*: that the army of gods and spirits is arranged into twelve orders under Jove the leader. He concludes here that the parts of the city are established partly through the twelvefold number of districts and temples, and partly through divine worship solemnly renewed twice in each of the twelve months. Thus, they are prepared for the gifts of God so that they may be governed by the gods themselves. He specifically wants public solemnities to be renewed twice so that both the twelve tribes and the remains of the city and fields are satisfied by the number twelve. When he orders sacred rites to be made for the gods and the sons of gods, he wants the gods to be understood as the souls of the spheres, and the sons as the purer spirits. He orders all these things to be done for the sake of the one Prince of all.

Nor should it be passed over in silence: the duodecimals we mentioned pertaining to the universe are represented, as it were, by the duodecimal proper to each human. This seems to consist of the four humors of the body, and the same number of perturbations and virtues. After the sacred rites of the gods, he descends to the sacred rites of marriage. There you will consider the wedding laws and rituals: the exhortation to marriage, and the duties of husband and wife both toward each other and toward children both to be born and to be educated. You will note above all that it is not fitting to give effort to procreating children while in a state of drunkenness or other mental perturbation. Because of this kind of fault, children are born every day sick in soul as much as in body.

He also mandates a mystery when he says: *The Principle and the Divinity [*numen*] implanted in men preserves all things, provided it is affected with fitting honor by individuals using its gift.* What then is this principle, what divinity? The Principle is the **Idea** of human formation. The Divinity is the **familiar spirit** [*daemon*], also the prince of generation often signified under the name Lucina (goddess of childbirth). This is to be understood not just as a number being present, but as one who diligently fosters and cherishes: especially favoring and preserving if it is gratefully worshipped by those who use its gift.

After the mutual duties of husband and wife, he consequently descends to the mutual duties of masters and servants. After these things, by a certain art, he returns to the walls, temples, and palaces, which he says should have been treated before marriage. There you will note especially that the courts of judgment and the palaces of the magistrates are placed closest to the temples, so that human judges may always remember they are judged by God, and the guardians of cities may remember they cannot guard unless God guards. Likewise, nothing in the city, even the smallest thing, should be without a certain order. For things lacking order confound other ordered things. Women's affairs especially need order and continuous care. Otherwise, if women's affairs are neglected, more than double the detriment comes to the state than if men's affairs were neglected.

Among these things, where the antiquity of the world is repeated—that the very beginning of generation did not precede by an inestimable magnitude of time—you will understand that he observes Moses regarding the inestimable number of days and hours. He concludes the book with the sentiment that we should not be precipitated by the threefold impulse—namely toward food, drink, and sex—but should restrain them with a threefold bridle: namely fear, law, and true reason, and furthermore by the moderate use of honorable games from childhood. Thus, through honorable solace, we may be recalled from shameful things and provoked gradually toward serious studies.

***

ATHENIAN: After all we have said so far, it seems magistrates must now be established in the city.
CLINIAS: Certainly so.
ATHENIAN: There are indeed two species in the adornment of a republic. First, the constitution of magistrates—how many there should be and how they are established. The other is about the laws to be attributed to the magistrate—which ones, how many, and of what kind are suited to each.

[[page number: 547]]

# On the Laws, or the Sixth Dialogue on Legislation.

But for a little while before we elect the magistrates, let us declare some things pertaining to their election.
CLINIAS: What things?
ATHENIAN: These. Listen now. No one doubts that since legislation is a great matter, if someone establishes unfit magistrates for a city well-prepared by laws, even if the laws are well-placed, it will not only be useless and provoke laughter, but will also produce the greatest damage and calamities for the states.
CLINIAS: Plainly.
ATHENIAN: This must be considered, friend, just as it happens in this city and republic of yours. For you see that those who are to correctly receive a magistracy must have been sufficiently approved from youth—both themselves and their kin—up to the election itself. Then, those who are to cast votes must be educated in legitimate habits, so they can easily recognize who should be admitted or rejected, and conduct themselves toward both according to dignity. But those who have recently come together, since they neither know each other sufficiently nor are yet educated, how will they ever be able to correctly elect magistrates?
CLINIAS: Almost by no means.
ATHENIAN: But the contest (as they say) does not easily accept excuses. This must be done by me now, and by you: since you have willingly undertaken the duty of instituting the city for the Cretans and are the tenth in this work, as you say; and I have promised to bring help to you in the present conversation. Therefore, I will not allow this discourse of ours to be headless and mutilated. For if it were to wander, it would appear deformed to everyone.
CLINIAS: You have spoken best, guest.
ATHENIAN: Indeed, let us do so according to our strength.
CLINIAS: Let us do exactly as we say.
ATHENIAN: We shall do so if God wills, and we shall overcome old age in this part.
CLINIAS: It is to be believed that God wills it.
ATHENIAN: Truly to be believed. Therefore, following Him, let us say this.
CLINIAS: What?
ATHENIAN: How boldly and dangerously the city is being established by us at this time.
CLINIAS: Why so?
ATHENIAN: Because we easily and intrepidly give laws to unrefined men and order them to receive them; while it is clear to almost everyone, even those not very wise, O Clinias, that no one will easily receive new laws. But if we waited until boys instituted by the laws, having lived with them a long time, could cast votes with the whole city, and that were done correctly according to their strength, surely both then and in the future, a city so instructed would remain far from error.
CLINIAS: So reason advises.
ATHENIAN: Let us proceed then, if we can find a certain convenient mode for these things. It is necessary for the Gnosians (the people of Knossos), O Clinias, above the other Cretans, not just to taste the beginning of this republic you now found, but to provide with all zeal that the first magistrates are established as safely and best as possible. In establishing the others, the task is shorter; but to create the **Guardians of the Laws** (*Nomophylakes*) before others is necessary with the highest diligence.
CLINIAS: By what way and reason shall we do this?
ATHENIAN: I say this, O Cretans. It is necessary for the Gnosians, since they are the first of many cities, to act in common with those who have gathered into this same colony. They should elect thirty-seven men from among themselves and from the others. Nineteen indeed from the number of those who will inhabit the colony, and the Gnosians themselves shall provide the rest from their own number. Let the Gnosians give these to your city, including yourself, Clinias, as a citizen of this colony and one of the eighteen, either by persuading or by moderately compelling these men.
CLINIAS: But guest, do not you and Megillus here participate in this Republic with us?
ATHENIAN: The Athenian (me) and the Lacedaemonian (Megillus) have granted much to you, Clinias, but we both live far away. For you, all things are conveniently situated; and for the other inhabitants similarly, according to what has just been said about you, and what can most conveniently be done for you and them at this time. But as time progresses and the Republic remains, the designation of such magistrates shall be done thus: Whoever, whether cavalry or infantry, can bear arms and has participated in wars when their age allowed, shall enter the voting process. Let the assemblies be held in the temple which the city considers most excellent.

# On the Laws...

...There remains the leader who shall have care of the whole discipline for both females and males. We wish this one leader to be according to the laws: not born fewer than fifty years, who has legitimate children of both sexes especially, but if fewer, at least of one sex. Both the one who elects and the one elected must think that **this magistracy is the most excellent of all the highest magistrates in the city.** In all living things, the first sprouts, if they begin aptly toward the virtue of their nature, have the greatest power to impose the end due to them. This happens in plants, in beasts (both wild and tame), and in humans. We say that man is a tame animal. Furthermore, when he has attained a right discipline along with a happy nature, he is accustomed to emerge as the most divine and mildest animal. But if he is not sufficiently or well educated, he is rendered the most ferocious animal of all that are born on earth.

Wherefore, the lawgiver must not postpone the education of youth, which is a most necessary thing, but must give effort first—if he is to care for this matter diligently—that of all citizens, the best man is elected for this duty and placed over the education of boys. Therefore, all magistrates except the Senate and the Quaestors (treasurers), having gone to the temple of Apollo, shall cast a secret vote with the Guardians of the Laws, each selecting whom they think will best preside over the discipline of boys. He who prevails in the voting, having been approved by the magistrates who selected him, shall preside for five years. And in the sixth year, another leader shall be similarly established.

... [[Ficino translates the judicial sections, the role of the Aediles, the Rural Police (Agronomoi), and the regulation of marriage feasts and drunkenness.]] ...

[[page number: 554]]

...One must not drink to drunkenness anywhere, except in the solemnities of that god who granted wine (Dionysus), nor is it safe. Especially, those joined in marriage, the groom and bride, must then be masters of their minds, when they enter upon no small change of life. For the generation should always come from those who are most moderate. For it is uncertain which night or day God will complete it. Therefore, so that a solid, stable, and quiet conception may occur, it is not fitting for bodies diffused with drunkenness to give effort to children. For he who is filled with wine, stirred by the rage of both soul and body, is pulled and pulls wherever. Therefore, a drunkard, like one captured in mind, is useless for sowing. It is likely that he will procreate fetuses that are unequal, unstable, and crooked, both in their limbs and their character.

Wherefore, throughout the whole of life, and especially while one is vacant for generation, each shall abstain and beware, lest he do things which by their nature induce diseases, or which decline toward insolence and injury. For these things are necessarily translated into the souls and bodies of those being born and are impressed there, and worse children are born from them. But especially on that day and night, one must abstain from such things. **For the Principle and the Divinity [*numen*] implanted in men, if it is affected with fitting honor by individuals using its gift, preserves all things.**

The Lovers, or, On Philosophy. 3
...You call both "good profit" and "bad profit" by the name "profit." What do you see as the same in both good and bad profit, because of which you call each "profit"? If you have nothing to answer, then listen to me while I speak. Do you call "profit" every possession which someone has acquired, either spending nothing at all or very little, when he receives more?
**HIP.** I think I would call that profit.
**SOC.** Do you mean it in this way: if someone, spending nothing, has feasted abundantly, and from the feast has acquired a disease?
**HIP.** No, by Jove.
**SOC.** But if he attained good health from the feast, would he have attained a profit or a loss?
**HIP.** A profit.
**SOC.** Therefore, it is not "profit" to acquire just anything.
**HIP.** Certainly not.
**SOC.** Is it not the case, then, that he does not "profit" who attains whatever he wants, whether it be good or bad?
**HIP.** It appears so.
**SOC.** Nor does he incur a "loss" who incurs just anything, whether good or bad?
**HIP.** So it seems to me.
**SOC.** Do you see, then, that you have revolved back to the same point? For profit appears to be a good, and loss an evil.
**HIP.** I do not know what to say.
**SOC.** And rightly so. But answer me this as well: if someone, spending less, receives more, would you say this man profits?
**HIP.** I say so, provided he does not "profit" from an evil, but rather, while laying out less gold or silver, he receives more.
**SOC.** Indeed, I will ask this further: if someone, laying out half a pound of gold, receives back double the amount of silver, is it a profit or a loss?
**HIP.** A loss certainly, O Socrates; for instead of twelve-fold, he receives only double.
**SOC.** Nevertheless, he received *more*. Is not double more than half?
**HIP.** Silver is not of the same dignity and price as gold.
**SOC.** Therefore, it is necessary to add this to "profit": namely, the estimation and the price. Now, although the silver is more in quantity than the gold, you say it is not to be estimated as equally precious; whereas the gold, though it is less, is precious and worthy.
**HIP.** Very much so, for that is how things are.
**SOC.** Therefore, the estimation and dignity themselves contain the "profit," whether the thing be small or large. But that which is unworthy of estimation lacks profit?
**HIP.** Certainly.
**SOC.** Do you call "precious and worthy" anything other than "worthy of acquisition"?
**HIP.** Worthy of acquisition.
**SOC.** But is that which is worthy of being sought useful or useless?
**HIP.** Useful.
**SOC.** Is not the useful a good?
**HIP.** It is.
**SOC.** O bravest of men, has it not now been concluded by us a third and fourth time that profit is a good?
**HIP.** It seems so.
**SOC.** Do you remember where this conversation began?
**HIP.** I believe so.
**SOC.** But if you yourself do not remember, I will bring it back to your memory. It began from the fact that you denied it was the way of good men to accept just any profit, but rather only good profits, and never bad ones.
**HIP.** From there, indeed.
**SOC.** And did not reason compel us to admit that all profits are good, whether they be large or small?
**HIP.** It compelled me indeed, O Socrates, more than it persuaded me.
**SOC.** But perhaps it will persuade you later. For now, whether you have been persuaded or are affected in whatever other way, do you agree with us that all profits, both large and small, are good?
**HIP.** I agree.
**SOC.** And you confess that all good men want good things, do you not?
**HIP.** I confess it.
**SOC.** But you said that bad men desire all profits, both small and large.
**HIP.** I said so.
**SOC.** Therefore, according to your speech, would not all men—the good and the bad alike—be profit-seekers?
**HIP.** It seems so.
**SOC.** No one, therefore, will rightly condemn profit-seekers, since he himself is also a profit-seeker.

# PLATO’S DIALOGUE ON PHILOSOPHY, OR, THE LOVERS.

## THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.

The sum of this dialogue is to define what philosophy is and what kind of duty belongs to the philosopher. It is the philosopher's duty to know divine things and to govern human ones; in the former, contemplative philosophy is understood, and in the latter, active philosophy. Thus, the philosopher first contemplates through wisdom the divine—that is, the absolute nature of the good itself. Then, directing human operations toward that good as toward an end, he governs human affairs. 

This governance requires two things. First, that he know what human nature is, and by what means it is led to the good and removed from the evil; this the philosopher does through prudence. Second, that he so establish both the affections and the acts of men, so tempering and restraining them, that they easily tend toward the good which wisdom itself had found, and toward which prudence then directed them. This is indeed accomplished through the moral virtues, all of which Plato embraces under the single name of justice. And from these two, the governance of human affairs consists. 

It belongs to the same person to know how to rightly govern one man, a family, and a republic. Wherefore he who is moral would also be a master, a citizen, and a suitable king. From these things, it is concluded that in the very duty of the one who philosophizes, all these are contained: wisdom, prudence, justice, and moral, domestic, civil, and royal discipline. Through wisdom, he knows divine things; through prudence and justice, he governs human things while administering his own business, family business, and the republic. 

Such is the duty of the philosopher himself, which Plato explains more broadly in the books on the *Republic* and signifies more briefly here. And first, he refutes two opinions of others regarding the philosopher’s duty. The first seems to have been Solon's, or someone similar, saying it is to learn as many things as possible; the second is that of Hippias the Sophist, wanting philosophy to be the skill in all arts. These having finally been refuted, he briefly hints at the opinion we have stated before. Socrates is thus imagined to have disputed these things in the school of Dionysius—who taught the elements of grammar to Plato—against two disciples of Dionysius; then he recounts from the beginning what he had treated in the schools to a circle of his friends.

### SOCRATES.
Having entered the school of Dionysius the Grammarian, I saw certain youths who seemed of a noble character, born of famous parents, and with them also their companions. There were also present two young men contending with each other, but what the contention was about, I had not quite noticed. Nevertheless, they seemed to be debating about Anaxagoras or Oenopides <note>Two famous early Greek astronomers and mathematicians.</note>, describing circles and depicting certain inclinations of the sphere, leaning on their elbows and very intent. 

But I, touching with my elbow the friend of one of them next to whom I was sitting, asked what the young men were so contending about, and whether it was something great and beautiful in which they placed such great study. Then he said, "What 'great and beautiful'? For they are trifles about sublime things and they are babbling about philosophy." I, marveling at this response, said, "O youth, does it seem shameful to you to philosophize? Or why do you answer so bitterly?" 

But the other—for a certain rival of that one was sitting nearby—when he had heard both me questioning and that one answering, said, "It does not help you, Socrates, to ask this one whether he thinks philosophy is shameful or not. Do you not see that he has spent his entire age in a certain puffed-up state, and in satiety and sleepiness, so that you might believe he would answer you anything else than that philosophy is shameful?" 

This one was from among the "lovers" <note>Referring to the title of the dialogue; here, he is a 'lover' of the arts and intellect.</note> educated in music; the other, whom he was criticizing, was in gymnastics. It seemed to me that I ought to let go of the one I had first questioned, because he seemed to wish to be considered exercised in action rather than in disputing. 
a ii

--- Page 23 ---
4 Book Two.
...rather than being practiced in debating. I decided, however, to question the one who wanted to seem wiser, so that I might carry away some benefit if possible. I said to him, therefore, that I had raised a common question: if you think you will answer this better, I now ask you that same thing—whether it seems that to philosophize is a beautiful thing, or otherwise? 

While we were saying these things, the young men heard us, and having let go of the contention that was between them, they prepared themselves in silence to hear what we were discussing. But what happened to the lovers, I do not know. I certainly was struck with awe. For I am always awestruck by new and beautiful things. It seemed to me, therefore, that the other was competing no less; and indeed he answered me, and quite ambitiously: "If ever, O Socrates, I should consider philosophizing to be shameful, I would not think myself a man, nor anyone else so affected." 

Insinuating this against his rival, he said these things in such a voice that his friends could overhear. At this I said, "So it seems beautiful to you to philosophize?" "Very much so," he said. "What then," I said, "does it seem possible to you that anyone can know whether something is shameful or beautiful, unless he first knows what the thing itself is?" "No." "Do you know, then," I said, "that there is something called philosophizing?" "Certainly I do." "What is it?" "What else than according to Solon? For Solon said somewhere: 'Old age comes to one constantly learning many things.' And it seems to me indeed that he who is to be a philosopher ought always to learn something in this way, whether he be young or old, so that in life he learns as many things as possible." 

And at first he seemed to me to have said something. Then, reflecting with myself, I asked whether philosophy seemed to him the same as "learning many things." And he said, "Entirely." I said, "Do you think philosophy is only something beautiful, or also something good?" "Good as well," he said. "Do you make that proper to philosophy alone, or do you also attribute it to others in the same way: as, for example, the study of gymnastics—is it not only beautiful, but also good?" 

Then he, playing both sides, brought forward two points. "Against this one," he said, "I say that it is neither; but against you, O Socrates, I confess it is both beautiful and good at once." "Therefore, in the gymnasiums, do you think much labor is the 'study of gymnastics'?" "Very much so," he said, "just as in philosophizing, I think 'learning many things' is philosophy." 

And I said, "Do you believe those studious of gymnastics desire anything else than that their bodies be in good condition?" "That is it," he said. "Do many labors produce a good condition of the body?" "How," he said, "could a robust body be made from few labors?" 

At this point, it seemed to me that I should provoke that gymnastic fellow, who might bring me help because of his skill in gymnastics. I therefore asked him, "What, O best of men, are you silent while he is speaking? Does it also seem to you that men acquire strength from many labors rather than from moderate ones?" "Indeed, O Socrates, I seem to see that which is usually said: namely, that the body is in good condition from moderate things." "Whence," I said, "do you see it? Do they not rather render a man sleepless and nauseated, and with a soft neck and exhausted by cares?" And when he had nodded to these things, the young men, delighted, laughed. 

But that other one blushed. Then I said, "What about you then? Do you concede that neither small nor great labors produce a good condition of the body, but moderate ones? Or do you resist us two who are in the same opinion?" "I would gladly resist this one," he said, "and I would be strong against him to defend what I proposed, even if I had a less valid cause. For he is of no value. But it is not fitting to contend more insolently with you; I confess, therefore, that not many, but moderate exercises provide a good habit of body to men." 

"What about food?" I said, "much or moderate?" "Food too," he said. Furthermore, I compelled him to concede that all other things that concern the body are most beneficial when moderate, but that few or excessive things are of no use. And he confessed that moderate things help. 

"But what about those things that look to the soul?" I said, "when moderate things are applied, do they help more, or immoderate ones?" "Moderate." "Are not teachings among those things which are applied to and benefit the soul?" He agreed. "Therefore, do not teachings which are moderate, rather than those which are many, bring utility?" He conceded. "Whom then is it rightly fitting to ask what kind of labors and foods are suitable for bodies?" 

"In this, I think we three agree," I said, "that the doctor or the physical trainer <note>original: "pædotribam," a teacher of gymnastics.</note> must be questioned." "But who about the sowing of seeds, how much is suitable?" "The farmer, it is agreed." "But indeed, regarding the sowing and planting of teachings in the soul, whom should we rightly ask what kind and how many are sufficient?" 

Here, when we were full of ambiguity, I said jokingly, "Since we are ambiguous in this, do you want us to ask these young men here? Or perhaps we are ashamed, as Homer introduces the suitors, when they were unwilling that anyone else besides themselves should bend the bow?" 

But since they seemed to take it heavily, I began to investigate by another way, saying, "On what shall we conjecture those things to be which a philosopher ought to learn, since he should follow neither 'all' nor 'many'?" 

Answering, that wiser one said, "Those are the most beautiful and most fitting teachings for the soul, from which someone may attain the greatest glory in philosophy; and the greatest glory is obtained if one is skilled in all arts; or if not all, at least most of them, and especially those that are worthy of estimation, learning those above others which become free men, or which are accomplished by the reason of intelligence and not by the ministry of hands." 

Then I said, "Do you speak of it in the way it happens in workshops? Where you might buy a workman for five or at most six minae <note>An ancient unit of currency.</note>, but an architect not even for ten thousand drachmae; for through all Greece they are found very rarely; do you mean something like that?" He, having assented, confessed that he was saying that very thing. 

I then asked him whether it was possible for the same person to perceive even just two arts in this way, let alone very many and great ones. And he said, "Do not think me to be saying, O Socrates, that it is necessary for one philosophizing to pursue individual arts to the highest degree, like those craftsmen; but, as becomes a free and educated man, that he be able to perceive what is brought forward by each craftsman, and that more than the others who are then present; furthermore, to conjecture all things in his mind, so that he himself always appears the most elegant and wisest of all in each of those things which is brought forward by anyone." 

And I (for I still doubted where he was tending) said, "Do I understand what kind of man you say the philosopher is? For you seem to me to be saying he is such as the pentathletes <note>original: "pentathli," athletes who competed in five different events.</note> are in a contest, compared to runners or javelin throwers. For those are inferior to runners or peltasts <note>Light infantry/skirmishers, often used here as a metaphor for specialists.</note> in their specific contests, and hold the second place, but are the first and victors over the rest of the athletes. Perhaps you say the study of philosophy confers something like this on philosophers: that they are surpassed in intelligence by those who are supreme in any art, holding the second place in that art, but they precede the rest, so that the philosopher exists as a man of a certain second-rate lot in individual faculties." 

"You seem to show such a man in one who philosophizes. You rightly accept what is said of the philosopher, O Socrates, who compared him to a pentathlete. For he is undoubtedly such as to wish to serve no business entirely, nor to labor in any one thing until the highest point, lest because of the exact diligence of one thing he be surpassed in all others as craftsmen are surpassed; but he touches all things moderately and temperately."

--- Page 24 ---
The Lovers, or, On Philosophy. 5
...After this response, desiring to know more clearly what he was saying, I said, "Do you judge good men to be useful or useless?" "Useful," he said, O Socrates. "Is it not the case, if the good are useful, that the bad will be useless?" He agreed. "What about philosophers—do you think they are useful or useless men?" At this, he asserted that philosophers are useful above all. 

"Come then, let us distinguish if you indeed speak the truth, how those men of the second rank are useful to us. For it is manifest that the philosopher is inferior to each specific craftsman." He nodded. "Come," I said, "if either you or someone most dear to you from among your friends were sick, would you bring that secondary philosopher into your house for the care of your health, or the doctor?" "Both." "Do not say 'both' to me; but which one preferably?" "No one," he said, "would doubt: the doctor, both more and sooner." 

"What then in a ship tossed by waves—would you commit yourself and your things to the pilot or to the philosopher?" "To the pilot," he said. "And in all other things, as long as a craftsman is present, will there be no place for the philosopher?" "It appears so," he said. "The philosopher, therefore, is now useless, provided that craftsmen are not lacking." 

But we confessed that the good are useful and the bad are useless. He was forced to confess this. "What then shall I ask after this? Or is it perhaps more uncivil to search further?" "Ask whatever you like," he said. "I ask nothing else but that the things already said be conceded again; they stand in this way: We confessed that philosophy is good, and that philosophers exist, and that they themselves are good, and that the good are useful, while the bad, on the contrary, are useless. Then we conceded that while craftsmen are present, philosophers are useless, and that craftsmen are always present. Have these things not been conceded?" "They have." 

"We confess therefore, as it seems according to your speech—if indeed to philosophize is to be knowledgeable in arts in the way you said—that philosophers are bad and useless, as long as there are arts among men. But it is not so, O friend. Neither is to philosophize to be studiously occupied around arts, nor to lie upon many businesses, nor to learn many things thoroughly, but something else; since I think this is even absurd, and those who apply themselves to arts are more rightly called 'mechanics.'" 

"But we will understand more clearly in this way whether I speak the truth or not, if you answer this: Who know how to break horses correctly? Is it those who make them better, or others?" "Those who make them better." "What about dogs? Do not those who know how to make them better also know how to restrain them correctly?" "Entirely." "Therefore, does the same art both make them better and restrain them correctly?" "The same." "What then? Does the same art which both makes them better and restrains them correctly also discern the good and the bad, or another?" "The same," he said. 

"Do you want us, then," I said, "to establish the same thing about men: that the art which makes men best is the same which both correctly restrains them and discerns who are good and who are bad?" "Certainly," he said. "Is it not the case that whatever knows one, knows also many; and what knows many, knows also one?" "So it is." "And furthermore, in horses and all other things in the same way?" "The same," he said. 

"What is the science which rightly punishes the intemperate and the transgressors of laws in the city? Is it not the judiciary?" "Entirely." "Do you call 'justice' any other than that?" "None," he said. "Is it not the case that by the science with which they rightly chastise and punish, they also discern the good and the bad?" "The same." "Whoever indeed knows one, will also know many?" "He will know." "But he who is ignorant of many, will he also be ignorant of one?" He agreed. 

"If therefore, being a horse, one were ignorant of good and bad horses, would he be ignorant of himself?" He conceded. "And if, being an ox, one did not know who were good or bad oxen, must he also be ignorant of what kind of thing he himself is?" "It is so," he said. "In the same way also if he were a dog?" He confessed. 

"But now, since someone is a man, if he is ignorant of good and bad men, will he not also be ignorant of himself—whether he be good or bad?" He nodded. "Is to be ignorant of oneself to be wise or to be foolish?" "To be foolish." "To know oneself, therefore, is to be wise?" "It is," he said. 

"This, then, as it seems, is also what the inscription at Delphi commands: namely, to cultivate Prudence and Justice." "It appears so." "By this same art we also know how to restrain correctly." He nodded. "Therefore, that by which we know how to restrain correctly is surely justice. But that by which we are able to distinguish both ourselves and others is prudence." "It seems so." "Therefore, justice and prudence are the same." "It appears so." 

"Because cities also are then best governed when the unjust pay the penalty." "You tell the truth." "And this is the civil science <note>The science of politics or governing the state.</note>." "It is," he said. "But what when one man rightly establishes a city—what name will befit him? Is it not that of tyrant and king?" He nodded. "Does he not govern by the tyrannical or royal art?" "Indeed." "Therefore, these faculties are the same as the ones above." "They seem so." 

"What about when one man rightly disposes a house—what name most fits him? Is it not 'manager' <note>original: "œconomus," head of a household.</note> and 'master'?" "It fits." "Does this one also rule his family well by justice, or by another faculty?" "By justice." "The same thing, then, it appears, is the king, the tyrant, the statesman, the manager, the master, the prudent man, and the just man; and there is also one art: the royal, the tyrannical, the civil, the masterly, the managerial, justice, and prudence." "It seems so." 

"What then? For a philosopher man, whenever a doctor has said anything about the sick, is it shameful not to be able to follow his words or to contribute anything here, like any of the other craftsmen? And when either a judge or someone else from among those we referred to a little while ago speaks, is it not absurd not to follow their words nor be able to contribute anything in those matters?" 

"Why would it not be absurd, O Socrates, in such great matters to have nothing to contribute?" "Therefore," I said, "do we say that in these things also the philosopher ought to be like a pentathlete—holding the second place and being useless as long as one of those specialists is present? Or rather, should he first not provide his own house to be administered by anyone else, nor hold the second place in this, but correct all things from himself, judging rightly, if indeed he desires to administer his family correctly?" He assented to me. 

And I added: "Then if either some friend should commit the reason of his life to him, or the city should commit something to be discerned or judged—would it not be shameful, O friend, for him to hold the second or third place in these things, and not rather to exist as the leader?" "So it seems to me," he said. 

"Be it far from us, then, O best of men, that to philosophize should be to learn very many things and to handle arts." When he had said these things, that wise one, affected by a blush from the things said before, was silent. But the unlearned one affirmed it was so, and all the rest praised the words spoken.
