# Third Book

## THEAGES, OR
## ON WISDOM.

### MARSILIO FICINO’S
### ARGUMENT.

In this dialogue, Wisdom is categorized, and the final branch of this division is examined to reveal how men acquire it. In the first division, Wisdom is said to be of two kinds: one is absolute, the other conditional. Absolute wisdom is that which is simply called "wisdom" without any further qualification. Conditional wisdom is not called wisdom simply, but is called "a certain kind of wisdom." The former is defined as: The knowledge of those things about which certain science can be held. Now, science is held concerning things that are always the same and exist in the same way; these are the highest principles of things and the eternal reasons of all things. These are called divine, which is why absolute wisdom is the science of divine things.

Conditional wisdom, however, is common to all arts and faculties. For the peak of any art is called a "certain wisdom," such as the wisdom of piloting, the wisdom of charioteering, or military wisdom. Out of all those things called wisdom with an addition, the chief is that which uses the others as servants, which is the nature of civil <note>original: "civilis," meaning relating to the state or citizens</note> wisdom. This faculty, which aims for the common good of the city and its people, is so defined. It is called both civil and royal discipline. Its subject is the city; its end is the common good; its servants are all the arts. It has two duties: to establish laws and to execute those established. It performs the former through legislative prudence and the latter through legal and judicial justice.

Truly, in many of his discussions, Plato doubts how a man might obtain civil wisdom. In the present *Theages*, he asks whether statesmen, or sophists, or perhaps only contemplative philosophers teach it. That it is learned from statesmen, or sophists, or those devoted solely to contemplation, he denies in the *Meno* and here to some extent; for the first group never even taught their own sons, the second have no account of the good, and the third are least experienced in human affairs. It remains, therefore, that this is perceived either by philosophers who are excellently skilled in both contemplation and action, or perhaps it happens by divine gift. The former are found nowhere. 

Thus, in the *Meno* and in the *Theages*, he asserts that it happens by divine favor that God's providence pours into the souls of temperate citizens an understanding of the good itself and the laws leading to it. He calls this notion "civil wisdom" here, but in the *Meno* he calls it a "certain prophecy" <note>original: "vaticinium," a divinely inspired foretelling or insight</note>, comparing statesmen to those in a frenzy. He also often says that the human race will never cease from evils unless either true philosophers rule, or those who govern the republic philosophize by a certain divine lot. 

In this book, when Socrates had divided wisdom into its parts and said, under a shadow of irony, that Theages could not obtain this civil wisdom from statesmen, nor from himself (as a philosopher devoted to contemplation), he added that the power of the *daemon* <note>The "daimonion," or divine sign, that Socrates famously claimed guided his actions</note> must be tested, and finally the will of God must be sought through prayers, as if these things are learned from there, and God's providence often reveals oracles of what must be done to men through intermediary spirits. Those ministers who, by God’s command, illuminate the minds of good and lawful citizens for the sake of good government, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian (c. 5th century) whom Ficino often synchronized with Plato</note> calls "Principalities." It might be necessary to discuss Socrates' *daemon* here, but the brevity of the argument forbids it. Moreover, Maximus of Tyre, Hermias, and Apuleius have discussed this abundantly. Plato introduces three persons here: Demodocus, an Athenian citizen, along with his son Theages who desires wisdom, and Socrates. The dialogue begins with Demodocus’s petition.

->**DEMODOCUS. SOCRATES,**<-
->**THEAGES.**<-

**DEMODOCUS.** I had need, O Socrates, to communicate certain things privately with you, if indeed there is leisure, or even if there is business, provided it is not altogether great; for I would wish you to be at leisure for my sake. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, I am at leisure anyway, but especially for your sake. If you wish to say anything, you may. **DEMOD.** Do you wish us to step aside from here into the nearby portico of Zeus the Liberator? **SOCR.** As you please. **DEMOD.** Let us go then, O Socrates. All plants seem to behave in the same way, both those that grow from the earth, and all animals, and finally men themselves. For as in plants, it is easiest for us who cultivate the earth to prepare everything before we plant, and even the planting itself; but after that which was planted lives, then its cultivation is varied and difficult; so it seems to be in men. From my own affairs, I conjecture the rest. For this planting, or generation if it should be called that, of my son was the easiest of all; but his education has been difficult and always full of fear, causing the greatest dread for his sake. And many other things could be said about this; but specifically, a desire that is now in him troubles me greatly. It is not an ignoble desire, but it is such that it might deceive. For he desires, O Socrates, as he says himself, to become wise. And as it seems to me, certain of his peers from the district coming into the city have filled him with certain speeches and incited him vehemently; he began to emulate them, and for a long time now he has been troublesome to me, wanting me to take care of him and pay money to some sophist who might make him wise. To me, the money is a minor care; but I think that because of this pursuit, he will run into no small danger. Hitherto I have resisted him by consoling him; but when I can no longer do so, I thought it would be worthwhile to comply with him, lest without me, living frequently with others, he should be corrupted. Now, I am setting out for this purpose, to commend him to one of those who are considered sophists. You, therefore, have met us most opportunely, whom I especially desired as a counselor in this matter. Therefore, if you have anything you can advise me in what you have heard, it is permitted and expedient.

**SOCRATES.** Moreover, O Demodocus, it is commonly said that "counsel is a sacred thing"; and if ever any other was, this is especially so, about which you ask. For there is nothing more divine about which one can consult than the education of oneself and one's own. First, then, let us agree on what we think this thing is that we are consulting about, lest oftentimes I think it is one thing and you another, and then we disagree at length, both appearing ridiculous—I who give, and you who ask for counsel, when we have not yet agreed. **DEMOD.** You seem to me to speak rightly, O Socrates. Therefore, I judge it should be done. **SOCR.** Rightly, I say, yet not altogether rightly; for I change that slightly: I doubt whether perhaps this youth desires something other than what we thought; if it is something else, we would also be acting quite absurdly consulting about something else. It seems most right to me, then, taking a start from here, that we ask him what he most intends. **DEMOD.** It seems best as you say. **SOCR.** Tell me then, what is the boy's beautiful name? By what name shall we call him? **DEMOD.** Theages, O Socrates. **SOCR.** You have given your son a beautiful and divine name, O Demodocus. But tell me, Theages, do you desire to be wise? And do you think it is worthy that this father of yours should find a man who, by his company, may make you wise? **THEAGES.** I do desire it. **SOCR.** Do you call wise men those having knowledge, whatever those things are that they know, or not? **THEAGES.** Those who know, indeed. **SOCR.** What then, did your father not have you taught what the sons of noble men are taught here? Namely, letters, playing the lyre, wrestling, and other contests? **THEAGES.** He did. **SOCR.** Do you think...

--- Page 26 ---
# Theages, Or, On Wisdom. 7

...you further need some knowledge, for which it is proper for your father to take care for your sake? **THEAGES.** I do. **SOCRATES.** What then is it? Tell us, so that we may gratify you. **THEAGES.** He also knows, O Socrates, since I have told him very often, but he says these things with you now on purpose, as if he did not know what I desire; for in this way, he fights with me in many other things, and does not want to hand me over to anyone. **SOCRATES.** But what has been said by you against him so far lacks witnesses; now, however, bring a witness, and recount it again in my presence. What is this wisdom that you seek? Come, if you desired that by which men govern ships, and I asked you, "O Theages, lacking what wisdom do you get angry with your father because he does not hand you over to those by whom you can be made wise?" what would you answer it to be? Would it not be the art of piloting? **THEAGES.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But if you desired to become learned in that by which chariots are driven, and were angry with your father, and I should ask what it was, would you not answer the art of charioteering? **THEAGES.** Surely. **SOCRATES.** But this which you now seek, does it have a name or not? **THEAGES.** I think it has. **SOCRATES.** Is it that we know the thing but you are ignorant of the name? Or do you also know the name? **THEAGES.** I know the name too. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, what is it? **THEAGES.** What other name would you say fits this, O Socrates, than "wisdom"? **SOCRATES.** Is not charioteering also wisdom? Or does it seem to be ignorance to you? **THEAGES.** By no means. **SOCRATES.** Is it not wisdom? **THEAGES.** It is wisdom. **SOCRATES.** Which we use for what? Is it not that by which we know how to manage yokes of horses? **THEAGES.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** And the art of piloting, is it not also itself wisdom? **THEAGES.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** Is it not that by which we govern ships? **THEAGES.** That indeed. **SOCRATES.** But that which you now desire, what kind of wisdom is it? Or having obtained it, what do we know how to govern? **THEAGES.** It seems to me to be that by which we know how to command men. **SOCRATES.** Those who are sick? **THEAGES.** Least of all. **SOCRATES.** For that is medicine itself, is it not? **THEAGES.** It is. **SOCRATES.** But that by which we know how to lead those singing in choirs? **THEAGES.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** For that is music. **THEAGES.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** But is it that by which we lead those in contests? **THEAGES.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** For that is gymnastics. **THEAGES.** It is. **SOCRATES.** But for those doing what? Try to express it just as I did those above. **THEAGES.** It clearly seems to me to be that for those who are in the city. **SOCRATES.** Are there not also sick people in the city? **THEAGES.** There are indeed, but I do not speak of those only, but of everyone who dwells in the city. **SOCRATES.** I understand what art you mean. For you seem to mean not that by which we know how to lead reapers, or vintagers, or planters, or sowers, or threshers; for that by which we command those is agriculture. **THEAGES.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Nor again that for those cutting, or boring, or polishing, or making something with a lathe; for this belongs to craftsmen. **THEAGES.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** But perhaps you call that wisdom by which we command all these, both farmers and craftsmen, and all private citizens, and women and men. **THEAGES.** That is the very one, O Socrates, I have been wanting to say for a long time. **SOCRATES.** Can you say whether Aegisthus, who killed Agamemnon at Argos, commanded all these you mentioned—craftsmen, private men, and all the women—or some others? **THEAGES.** Not others, but all these. **SOCRATES.** What about Peleus the son of Aeacus in Phthia, did he not rule the same? **THEAGES.** The same. **SOCRATES.** Have you not heard that Periander son of Cypselus ruled among the Corinthians? **THEAGES.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Did he not rule the same people in his city? **THEAGES.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And what about Archelaus son of Perdiccas recently ruling in Macedonia, do you think he ruled the same? **THEAGES.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** And Hippias son of Pisistratus ruling in this city, whom do you think he was over? Was it not the same? **THEAGES.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** But Bacis, and the Sibyl, and our own Amphilytus—by what name would they seem to you to be called? **THEAGES.** By no other name than prophets. **SOCRATES.** You say rightly; in the same way, try to find by what name you would call Hippias and Periander on account of the same kind of rule. **THEAGES.** What would I call them but tyrants? **SOCRATES.** Therefore, whoever desires to rule all his citizens in that manner, desires a tyranny and strives to be a tyrant? **THEAGES.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Is this what you desire? **THEAGES.** It seems so from what I have said. **SOCRATES.** You rogue, do you desire to rule over us in the manner of a tyrant? And you have been angry with your father all this time because he does not send you to some teacher of tyranny? And are you not ashamed, Demodocus, you who have known for a long time what he desired, and because you could have made him a master of that wisdom he seeks, do you envy him and refuse to send him? But now you see. Since he has accused you to your face, let us consult together, I and you—is there anywhere we might send him, so that by someone's company he may become a wise tyrant? **DEMOD.** By Jove, O Socrates, let us consult; for it seems to me there is need of counsel, and the greatest. **SOCR.** Wait, good man, let us ask him first. **DEMOD.** Ask him. **SOCR.** What if we used Euripides for something, O Theages? For he says: "Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise." If someone were to ask Euripides, "O Euripides, in what matter do you say tyrants are wise by the company of the wise?" just as if he had said "Farmers are wise by the company of the wise" and we asked in what matter, what do you think he would say? Anything other than in farming? **THEAGES.** Nothing else. **SOCR.** In the same way, if he had said "Cooks are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked in what matter, what else would he answer than in cooking? **THEAGES.** That very thing. **SOCR.** What if he had said "Athletes are wise by the company of the wise," and we asked in what of the wise, would he not answer in competing? **THEAGES.** Indeed. **SOCR.** And since he said "Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise," if we asked him "In what matter, O Euripides?" what do you think he would answer? **THEAGES.** By Jove, I do not know. **SOCR.** Do you want me to tell you? **THEAGES.** As you please. **SOCR.** These are the things that Anacreon says Callicrete herself knew. Have you heard the song? **THEAGES.** I have. **SOCR.** What then, do you desire the company of such a man as holds that art which Callicrete, born of Cyane, held, and who knew the tyrannical things which the poet says Callicrete knew, so that you might exercise tyranny over us and the city? **THEAGES.** You have been biting and mocking me for a long time, Socrates. **SOCR.** Why so? Do you not say you desire this wisdom by which you may command everyone? And doing this, would you be anything other than a tyrant? **THEAGES.** I would indeed desire, like an arbiter, to possess tyranny over all men or as many as possible—as I am persuaded you and all others would, or even to be a God. Nevertheless, I was not saying that I sought this. **SOCR.** What then is it that you desire? Is it not to lead the citizens? **THEAGES.** Not by force indeed, nor as tyrants do; but over those who are willing, just as other well-mannered and good men in the city. **SOCR.** Do you mean...

# 8 Third Book.

...kind Themistocles was, and Pericles, and Cimon, and whoever else flourished in the administration of the republic? **THEAGES.** By Jove, those are the ones I mean. **SOCRATES.** But what if you were eager to be a noble horseman, and wise in that art, to what others would you go than to horsemen? **THEAGES.** To no others. **SOCRATES.** Surely to those very ones who excel in the equestrian art, and who use many horses, both our own and many from elsewhere. **THEAGES.** Of course. **SOCRATES.** And in the same way, if you desired to obtain the art of wise javelin-throwing, you would set out to those who throw javelins best, and who use many targets, both foreign and their own. **THEAGES.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** Come then, since you wish to be instructed in civil matters, so that you may become wise in them, do you think you should go to any others than to these statesmen, who are exceedingly strong in civil discipline, and deal with both their own country and other cities, and are occupied for that reason among both Greeks and barbarians? Or do you think that by conversing with some others, you will turn out wise in those things in which they themselves are, and not in these very men? **THEAGES.** I have heard certain speeches, Socrates, which they say are yours, that the children of statesmen are no better than those of cobblers. And in my opinion, you speak the truth. I would be foolish, therefore, if I could be among their number, if I persuaded myself that any of them would hand over their wisdom to me, when they did not even help their own sons; and I would think they could be of use either to me or to any mortal in this matter. 

**SOCRATES.** What then would you do, best of men, if you had a son and he brought such business to you, showing he desired to turn out to be the best painter, and was angry with you because you would not spend any money on him for that sake, yet he thought little of the actual masters of painting and did not want to learn anything from them? Or flute-players, wanting to become a flute-player, or even lyre-players? Would you have anything to do with him, or where would you finally send him, since he was unwilling to learn from those masters? **THEAGES.** I certainly would not have any place. **SOCRATES.** Do you not then, doing these same things, wonder at and get angry with your father when he doubts what to do with you and where to send you? We were going to commend you to whichever of the most outstanding Athenians in administering the republic you wished, who would have spent time with you without a price; and at once you would have spared expenses and gained more of a name from such company than from all the others. **THEAGES.** What then, Socrates, are you not among the good men? If you will take me on, I have enough, and I seek no other. **SOCRATES.** Why do you say this? **DEMODOCUS.** He does not speak badly, O Socrates, nor could anything be more pleasant or useful to me, as I judge, than if your company should please him, and if you would be willing to spend time with him; and indeed I am hindered by shame from saying how vehemently I desire it. Therefore, I would wish both of you to be asked: you, to be willing to take him on, and you, my son, not to seek anyone other than Socrates; and I pray you free me from the greatest cares and those full of dread, since now I fear vehemently lest he seek the company of someone else by whom he might then be ruined. **THEAGES.** Fear no further for me, my father, if you can persuade him to take me on. **DEMODOCUS.** You speak rightly, and to you, O Socrates, all speech will hereafter be turned. I, indeed, to speak as briefly as possible, most willingly hand over myself and all my dearest things, whatever you might need, if you will take on this Theages and do him good according to your ability. 

**SOCRATES.** Indeed, O Demodocus, I do not wonder at this zeal of yours, if indeed you think he can be helped most by me. For I do not see where there is need of greater diligence, if anyone has a mind, than that he should make his son the best. But from where did it seem so to you—namely, that I could make your son a better citizen than you yourself could? And from where did he persuade himself that he could be helped more by me than by you in this matter? For I wonder at that greatly: for you are first of all older than I, then you have held many and great magistracies among the Athenians, and no one is more honored by the people of Agnagryusia and other citizens. In me, however, neither of you sees any of these things. But if this Theages despises the company of statesmen and seeks others who profess to instruct youth, here is Prodicus of Ceos, and Gorgias of Leontini, and Polus of Agrigentum, and many others, who are so wise that when they visit cities, they entice the noblest and richest youths to themselves. Although these youths could have used the friendship of any of the best men for free, having left their company, they turn to those men, offering a price, and a huge one at that, and feeling the greatest gratitude besides. You and your son should have chosen one of these; it was not fitting to choose me for that. For I know and speak none of those blessed and beautiful disciplines (and to speak in a few words, I would wish nonetheless that they were known to me). But I always know nothing, except a certain small discipline of love <note>original: "amandi disciplinam," referring to Socrates' "erotics" or art of seeking what is beautiful and good</note>, in which I generally seem to be superior both to past and present men. 

**THEAGES.** Do you see, father, that this Socrates does not quite accept my acquaintance? For as far as I am concerned, I was ready, provided he himself wished it; but he says all these things in jest against us. For I know some of my peers, and some somewhat older, who before they spent time with him were of no value; but after they used his company, they shortly turned out to be the highest of all, though they were the lowest before. **SOCRATES.** Do you know what kind of thing this is, O son of Demodocus? **THEAGES.** By Jove, I know: for if you will, I shall become such as they were. **SOCRATES.** Not so, O best of men, but this has deceived you as to what it is; therefore, I shall tell you. There is present with me by a certain divine lot a certain *daemon* <note>The "daimonion" or divine sign</note> that has followed me from early childhood. This is a certain voice which, when it occurs, always signifies a dissuasion from that thing which I am about to do, but it never provokes me to act. If any of my friends ever communicates something with me, and the voice comes, it dissuades him from it and does not allow him to do it. Of which thing I will give you witnesses. You know Charmides, a good man, the son of Glaucon; he was once about to practice in the stadium at Nemea and communicated it with me. And as soon as he began to say that he was going to practice, the voice was present; I prohibited him, declaring that as he was speaking the voice of the *daemon* had occurred, that he should not practice. But he said, "Perhaps it signifies to you that I will not turn out the victor; but even if I do not obtain victory, yet practicing at this time, I shall make some progress." And having spoken thus, he went away to the contest. It is worthwhile, therefore, to hear from him what happened to him from that contest. Now, if you wish, ask also Clitomachus the brother of Timarchus what Timarchus said to him when he was already about to die; for he and a certain runner named Euathlus, who received him as he fled, will relate to you what he said then. **THEAGES.** What was it? **SOCRATES.** "O Clitomachus," he said, "I am indeed coming to die as soon as possible, because I was unwilling to obey Socrates." Why Timarchus said this, I will explain. For...

->a iiij<-

--- Page 28 ---
# Theages, Or, On Wisdom. 9

...when they had risen from the banquet, Timarchus and Philemon the son of Philemonides killed Nicias the son of Heroscamadarus, for they alone were conscious of the ambush. Here Timarchus said, "What do you say, O Socrates? You all indeed drink, but I must go elsewhere; I will return a little later if there is an opportunity." Then the voice was present to me. And so I said, "Do not rise, for the usual sign has been made to me by the *daemon*." He stayed. Then, having delayed a little while, he was burning again with the desire of going, saying, "I am going now, Socrates." And because I heard the voice again, I restrained him once more, until he, wanting to hide from me, rose a third time, saying nothing to me, but watching for when I had turned my mind elsewhere; and so having set out, he perpetrated those things which were the cause of death for him. He said these same things to his brother, just as I do now to you, that he was coming to die because he had been unwilling to believe me. You will hear besides from many who were in Sicily what it predicted about the slaughter of the army. And past things indeed can be heard from those who knew them. But we can even now test the sign of the *daemon* if it says anything. For the famous son of Calis has gone out on an expedition. The sign was present to me; he sets out now with Thrasyllus to fight against Ephesus and Ionia. But I think that he will either be killed or will run into something of this sort, and I fear vehemently for the rest of the business. 

I tell you all these things because all power for establishing acquaintances with those who are with me is in the hands of the *daemon*. For it opposes many, and it is not permitted to bring help to those who converse with me against the *daemon's* will; therefore it is impossible for me to live with them. But it does not prohibit sticking with many, yet they are helped not at all by our company. Those however whom the power of the *daemon* favors in that very acquaintance, they are those whom you noticed, for they make progress shortly. But some of them have this benefit firm and durable, while most are wonderfully powerful as long as they are with me, but when they have departed, they again differ in nothing from the rest. This once happened to Aristides the son of Lysimachus, he who was the son of Aristides. For staying with me, he made much progress in a short time; afterwards he went on military service. Returning then, he found Thucydides the son of Melesias acting with me; this Thucydides had objected to me the day before during a dispute about I don't know what matter. When Aristides had greeted me and spoken some things besides, he said, "O Socrates, I hear Thucydides boasting and even contending with you in some things, as if he were something." "He is," I said, "as you say." Then he said, "Does he not remember, before he adhered to you, what kind of slave he was?" "It does not seem so, by the gods," I said. "But I," he said, "am ridiculous." "In what especially?" I said. "Because before I went away from here, I dared to dispute with anyone, and I seemed inferior to no one in arguing, so that I boldly approached gatherings of outstanding men. Now, on the contrary, I flee whoever I understand to be learned, I am led to such shame by my ignorance." "Did that power leave you suddenly," I said, "or gradually?" "Gradually," he said. "But when it came upon you, did it happen to you by learning something from me, or otherwise?" "I will tell you, O Socrates, a thing indeed incredible by the gods, yet true. I never learned anything from you, as you yourself know, but I made progress whenever I was with you, even if I were only in the same house, though not in the same part of the house, yet more whenever I was in the same part. And I seemed to myself much more so when, being in the same part, I looked at you saying something, than when I was turned elsewhere. But I made far more progress when, sitting near you, I touched you. Now, however, all that habit has flowed away." 

Such, therefore, O Theages, is our company. For if it is pleasing to God, you will make very much progress and in a short time; but if otherwise, not at all. See, therefore, whether it is safer for you to be instructed by one of those who have the utility with which they benefit others in their own power, rather than to pursue it by some fortune from me. **THEAGES.** It seems to me I should do so, Socrates, that we may understand our situation regarding the *daemon*. If it grants it to us, all will be well; if not, we will then consult what should be done, whether we should adhere to someone else, or whether we should try to appease this divine thing which is implanted in you by prayers and sacrifices and any other way finally that the prophets command. **DEMODOCUS.** Do not resist this youth in these things, O Socrates, for Theages speaks well. **SOCRATES.** But if it seems you ought to act so, let us act so.

## MENO, OR, ON
## VIRTUE.
### MARSILIO FICINO’S
### ARGUMENT.

There are four kinds of argument which Plato uses: example, induction, reasoning <note>syllogism</note>, and enthymeme; and how they are made is sufficiently declared in the compendium of Alcinous, which we also translated. There we also find three species of Platonic dialogues, and which arguments he usually uses in each species of dialogue. For a dialogue either only inquires and refutes what is false, or only explains and teaches truths, or deals with both. The first is called inquisitive and confused, the second expository, and the last mixed. Now the *Meno*, although it is mixed, nonetheless for the greater part contends and refutes, and touches on all arguments. So that unless someone collects the meanings from Plato’s other dialogues, which pertain more to exposition than to debate, and adds them to this *Meno*, he could hardly elicit the sum of this discussion. 

The task is to inquire what virtue is and how it is present in us. Socrates performs this while he refutes four definitions of virtue by Meno, Aristippus, Gorgias, and Prodicus, and retracts his own definition introduced after those with twin objections. Indeed, truth shines out from the refutation of falsehood. Now, the virtue of a man is an affection, or a habit of the soul, by which its natural power performs its work as well as possible; this definition is handed down in the books on the Republic. The work of any power is then performed best when it is directed to its end. That which contributes to the end is called useful. Deservedly, therefore, in this discussion, it is handed down that the common duty of virtue is this: that it makes both actions and those things which we use in acting useful. That definition therefore harmonizes with this dialogue and is common to all virtues. 

Of virtues indeed there are many species, according to the diversity of the soul's powers and acts, in which nonetheless that one common account of virtue which was mentioned is always seen. The first power of the soul is the mind, whose act is the perpetual contemplation of truth. The second is reason, whose act is the investigation of truth. The third is imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, whose act is the collection of those things which the senses offer to its messengers, and discourse through them. And these are the powers of the soul which are called cognitive. There remain three others, which they call appetitive: Will, the power of anger, and the power of desire. The act of the Will is to seek what the mind and reason offer. The act of the irascible is to attack what reason and imagination propose. The act of the concupiscible is to grasp what imagination and the senses object. Above these six, two are placed beneath: the vigor of moving and of nourishing; but these have either nothing or very little to do with virtue. 

The affection of the mind which perfects contemplation is wisdom; that which perfects the search of reason is science and prudence. Science indeed is the investigation of those things which nature makes; prudence is consultation in those things which we do. That which perfects the discourse of imagination is right opinion, which some call sagacity. Justice and liberality perfect the will. Fortitude and its followers perfect the irascible. Continence and temperance together perfect the concupiscible. In all these, it is common that any of them, being such an affection perfecting the act of natural power, makes it both decorous and useful for following the ultimate end. But various virtues are held in different ways. Wisdom indeed is by nature: for it is the eternal...

# 10 Fourth Book.

...eternal embrace of all reasons in the mind, and a perpetual intuition of truth. Science is acquired through the doctrine of philosophy which provides remembrance, while the reason, which once cast away its wings, recovers them again by remembering as it turns toward the mind. Prudence comes through doctrine together with long use of things. Right opinion comes through examples, authority, induction, and lot. For which reason prudence oftentimes usurps the name of the whole moral virtue in Plato. There is also a certain virtue pertaining to right opinion, by which lawful princes and citizens, honest in acting yet lacking contemplation, care for the public good, which they also call civil virtue. And Plato argues both in the *Theages* and in the present *Meno* that this faculty is given to statesmen in no other way than by divine lot. 

With this summary, one may collect the mind of Plato in the *Meno*, and with this kind of distinction premised, one will refuse contradiction and avoid objections. Now, I did not choose to treat that discussion about remembrance with geometric figures in the argument, because it was inserted not as the principal matter, but as an accessory. For an argument requires the sum and head of the matter. Indeed, to discuss individual points is the duty not of an argument, but rather of a commentary.

**MENO.** Can you show me, Socrates, whether virtue can be taught or not, or whether it is acquired rather by practice? Or does it perhaps come to men neither by doctrine nor by use, but is it in men by nature itself, or in some other way? **SOCRATES.** Hitherto, O Meno, the Thessalian men have been held illustrious among the Greeks, both for their equestrian faculty and for their riches. Now, however, as it seems to me, for the name of wisdom; and no less your friends the fellow citizens of Aristippus of Larissa. And Gorgias <note>A famous Sophist known for rhetoric</note> was the author of this matter for you, who having set out into your city, gained friends for himself because of his wisdom, both of the Thessalians and especially of the first of the Aleuadae, from whom your friend Aristippus draws his origin. For which reason Gorgias so accustomed you that you answer those questioning you intrepidly and with a high mind, as becomes those who know; since he also allowed any of the Greeks to ask whatever anyone wished, and he did not fail to answer anyone. To us, however, O friend Meno, the contrary has happened: for our wisdom has somehow already dried up, and seems to have diverted from these places to you. 

So if you ask any of our men in this way, there will be no one who does not laugh and say: "O stranger, perhaps I seem to you to be some blessed man, and to know whether virtue is obtained by men through doctrine or some other reason. I, however, am so far from this knowledge that I plainly do not even understand what virtue itself is." And I myself also, O Meno, am so affected: for I live in the same poverty of mind as my fellow citizens, and I often accuse myself, as one who is utterly ignorant of what virtue is. Now when I do not know what it is, how can I know what sort of thing it is? Or does it seem possible to you that he who in no way knows who Meno is, could know whether he is good, rich, noble, or the contrary? **MENO.** To me, not at all. But do you truly, O Socrates, not know what virtue is? Shall we report these things about you back home? **SOCRATES.** I ask you not only to say that, Meno, but also that I have never met anyone, as it seems to me, who knew it. **MENO.** Did you never then meet Gorgias when he was staying here? **SOCRATES.** Indeed. **MENO.** Did he seem to you to be ignorant of these things? **SOCRATES.** I do not remember well enough, O Meno, and therefore I cannot relate at present what seemed to me then. But perhaps both he knew, and you hold what he taught: bring back to me the memory of those things he said. Or if that does not please you, you yourself declare it. For perhaps you agree with him. **MENO.** I do indeed agree. **SOCRATES.** Let us leave him then, since he is absent: but you yourself, O Meno, tell me by the gods I pray, what you think virtue is: tell me, I say, and do not envy me, so that I may be refuted by a certain fortunate lie: since you and Gorgias seem to know it, but I would say I have never met anyone who knew it. 

**MENO.** But, O Socrates, it is in no way difficult to say that: and first indeed if you like, what is the virtue of a man. This is clearly to be sufficient for the administration of civil affairs, and in handling them to help friends, to harm enemies, and also to take care diligently lest he himself suffer any such thing sometime. But if you further require to know what is the virtue of a woman, that will not be hard either. For it is the virtue of a woman to govern the home rightly, while she cares for domestic things and obeys her husband. There is also another virtue of a boy and a female and a male, and of a man already heavy with age: and also of a free man, if you wish, another, and another again if you wish, of a slave. And there are very many other virtues. For which reason there is no lack of what we may say about virtue. For indeed in every action and age, virtue is present to individual men for every work. Just as many things besides about vice, O Socrates, as I think, could be said. 

**SOCRATES.** I seem to myself not a little fortunate, O Meno: since seeking one virtue, I have found a certain swarm of virtues dwelling with you. Nevertheless, O Meno, if to me asking by the same similarity of a swarm, "What is the substance of a bee?" you had answered that their substances are multiple, and I should ask you again, "Do you say they are many and various and differing among themselves in that by which they are bees, or in some other way such as beauty, or magnitude, or some other way?" what, I say, would you most likely answer to one questioning thus? **MENO.** That in that they are bees, they differ not at all from one another. **SOCRATES.** And if I ask after these things, "What then is it, O Meno, in which they differ not at all from each other, but all are the same?" do you have what you may answer? **MENO.** I certainly do. **SOCRATES.** By the same reason then, although virtues are many and various, they nonetheless all have one certain species the same, by which they exist as virtues, upon which he who is about to answer anyone asking what virtue is ought to look. Do you hold what I say? **MENO.** I seem to understand, yet not yet as I would wish; I do not plainly grasp what you seek. 

**SOCRATES.** But does it seem to you thus only about virtue, O Meno, that one indeed is of a man, another of a woman, and another of the rest, or also about health and magnitude and strength in the same way, so that one indeed is the health of a man, another of a woman? Or rather is the species of health the same everywhere, if indeed it is health, whether it be present to a man, or a woman, or any other? **MENO.** Health seems to me to be the same both of a man and a woman together. **SOCRATES.** Is it not then that if a female should be strong, she will be strong by the same species of strength? For when I say the same, it differs nothing in that it is strength, that strength may be strength, whether it be in a man or a woman; does it seem to you to differ at all? **MENO.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Therefore also virtue, that it may be virtue, does it matter at all whether it adorns a youth, or an old man, or a man, or a woman? **MENO.** To me indeed, O Socrates, this seems in no way to be similar to the others. **SOCRATES.** Did you not then say virtue was to govern the Republic rightly, and for a woman the home? **MENO.** I did indeed. **SOCRATES.** Can anyone dispose of a city, or a home, or anything else rightly, unless...

SOCRATES. Therefore both, the man as well as the woman, have need of the same things if they are to be good: namely, moderation and justice. MENO. It appears so. SOCRATES. For example, regarding roundness, I would say it is *a* shape, not simply "shape" itself. I would speak this way for the reason that there are also other shapes besides roundness. MENO. You speak rightly. And I myself say that not only is justice a virtue, but there are also other virtues. SOCRATES. Then explain what these others are, I pray. Just as if you had asked me about other shapes, I would have answered; so you, show me what the other virtues are. MENO. Courage, then, seems to me to be a virtue, as do moderation, wisdom, magnificence <note>greatness of spirit or generous scale</note>, and many others. SOCRATES. We have fallen into the same trap again! We have found many virtues while looking for one, though in a different way; but the one virtue that is diffused through all of them, we are unable to find. MENO. I am not yet able, Socrates, to grasp that one virtue in all things as I can in other cases. SOCRATES. Not without reason; but if I am able, I will try to lead us there. Do you see how it happens in all things? If someone asked you what I just mentioned—what is "shape"—and you answered "roundness," and he asked you what I would ask: "Is roundness shape, or *a* shape?" would you not say it is a certain shape? MENO. Certainly. SOCRATES. Is that not because there are also other shapes? MENO. Yes. SOCRATES. And if he asked what those others were, would you answer immediately? MENO. I would. SOCRATES. Furthermore, if he asked in the same way what "color" is, and you said "whiteness," and he then asked whether whiteness is color or *a* color, would you say it is a certain color because other colors are also found? MENO. Most certainly. SOCRATES. And if he ordered you to name the other colors, you would tell of many others that are no less colors than whiteness is? MENO. I would. SOCRATES. What if he proceeded in the conversation as I do now, and said that we are always falling into "the many," which he would by no means permit? Since you call these many things by one name, and say they are all "shape," even though they are contrary to one another: what is this thing which contains the round no less than the straight, which you call "shape"? When you say this, do you mean the round is no more round than it is straight, or the straight no more straight than it is round? MENO. Certainly not, Socrates. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, you assert that the round is no more a "shape" than the straight is, and the straight no more than the round. MENO. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Try then to declare what that thing is to which the name "shape" applies. If, when someone questioned you about shape or color, you answered that you did not understand what he wanted, he would be greatly surprised, I think, and would say: "Do you not understand that I am seeking the same thing in all of these?" Would you have nothing to say, Meno, if someone asked what is the same in the round and the straight, and the others you call shapes—the same thing in all of them? Explain it, I beg you, so that in this way you may prepare yourself for the discussion of virtue. MENO. By no means, Socrates; you explain it yourself. SOCRATES. Do you wish me to gratify you? MENO. Entirely. SOCRATES. And will you in turn be willing to solve the question of virtue afterwards? MENO. I will. SOCRATES. Then it must be done, for it is proper. MENO. Most certainly. SOCRATES. Come then, let us try to express what shape is, and see whether you admit this. Let "shape" be for us that which alone of all things always follows color. Is this enough for you, or do you perhaps require something else? For I would be satisfied if you would show me virtue itself in such a way hereafter. MENO. But that is an absurd thing, Socrates. SOCRATES. Why so? MENO. Because shape, according to your definition, is that which always follows color. But if someone said they did not know what color was—doubting it in the same way they doubted shape—what would you answer him? SOCRATES. The truth. For if the questioner were one of those wise, contentious, and litigious men <note>likely referring to the Eristics, who argued for victory rather than truth</note>, I would tell him that I have spoken; and if I spoke wrongly, it is now your turn to answer and refute my words. But if, as we are, they were friends and wished only to discuss, it is surely proper to answer more mildly and in a more **dialectical manner** <note>the method of seeking truth through reasoned dialogue</note>. It is perhaps more dialectical not only to bring forth the truth, but to prove it by those arguments which the questioner himself admits he knows. I will try to use this method in speaking with you now. Tell me then, do you call an "end" a certain limit or extremity? For I offer all these as the same, though perhaps Prodicus <note>a Sophist famous for distinguishing between synonyms</note> might use them as different things. But do you say that something is "limited" or "finished"? I understand nothing different by these words. MENO. I do indeed say so, and I think I understand what you mean. SOCRATES. And do you call something a "plane" and another a "solid," such as those treated in Geometry? MENO. I do. SOCRATES. Now then, you can perceive from these what I call "shape." Indeed, in every shape I assert this: shape is that in which a solid terminates. To say it briefly, I call shape the limit of a solid. MENO. And what do you call color, Socrates? SOCRATES. You are not being fair, Meno. You impose the burden of answering on an old man, yet you yourself do not wish to define what Gorgias said virtue was, even though you remember it. MENO. ...they will live together, and they will not beget children beyond their means, guarding against poverty and war. To this Glaucon, responding, said: "It seems, Socrates, that you have prepared a feast without any *obsonium* (savory side-dishes)."

"You speak the truth," I said. "For I had forgotten this: that they will indeed have *obsonium*—namely salt, olives, cheese, and onions. Moreover, they will cook vegetables like the pottages of the fields. And we will set delicacies before them: figs, chickpeas, and beans; they will roast myrtle berries and beech-nuts in the coals, drinking in moderation. And so, living quietly and healthily as is fitting, when they are worn out by old age, they will leave a similar life to their descendants."

"If you were establishing a city of pigs, O Socrates," Glaucon replied, "what other fodder would you have prepared for them?"

"What then should be done, Glaucon?" I asked.

"What most people are accustomed to," he said. "Unless we wish to live miserably, they should recline on couches, eat feasts from a table, and have the *obsonia* (side-dishes) that people use in these times."

"So be it, Glaucon," I replied. "I understand: it seems we are not only considering how a city is made, but how a luxurious city is made. Perhaps, therefore, this will not be a bad thing. For by looking at such a city, we might perhaps discover where justice and injustice are born in states. To me, the city we described truly seems to be a 'healthy' one. But if you wish, let us also consider the 'swollen' city [[notes: Latin *turgidam*, often translated in this context as 'inflamed']]. For nothing prevents it."

"Certainly, as it seems, the basic things will by no means be enough for some, and this modest way of life will not please them. Instead, couches will be added, and tables, and other furnishings, and vessels, and savory dishes, and perfumes, and incense, harlots, spices, seasonings, and delights—and every kind of each of these. Nor must we only provide those necessary things we mentioned above—houses, clothes, and shoes—but we must also introduce painting and the arts of variety, gold and ivory, and everything else of that kind. Is it not so?"

"Entirely," he said.

"Must we not therefore establish a larger city? For that healthy one is no longer sufficient, but it must be filled with a great mass and multitude of those who are no longer in cities for the sake of necessity. Such are all kinds of hunters and mimes (performers), and imitators—some dealing with shapes and colors, others with music. These include poets and their servants: rhapsodes [[notes: professional performers of epic poetry]], reciters of poems, actors, singers, dancers, contractors, and craftsmen of various equipment and instruments—both for general use and those pertaining to the *mundum muliebrem* (women’s finery).

Furthermore, we will need many more servants. Does it not seem necessary to you to have *paedagogi* (tutors), nurses, educators, hairdressers, barbers, and those who prepare savory dishes and work in the kitchen? Moreover, we will need swineherds. For these were not with us in the former city, as there was no need. But in this one, we will also need many other foods from the flesh of animals, if anyone eats them. Is it not so?"

"Why not?" 

"And will we not also need doctors much more, living in this way, than we did before?"

"Very much so."

"And yet the region, which then nourished those people comfortably enough, will become small instead of spacious. Or what do we say?"

"It is as you say."

"Shall we not then seize something from our neighbors' region, so that we have enough land for grazing and plowing? And will our neighbors not do likewise to ours, if they also give themselves over to the infinite accumulation of wealth, exceeding the bounds of necessity?"

"It will be quite necessary, O Socrates."

"Will we go to war then? Or what shall we do?"

"We will go to war."

"And we are not yet saying whether war brings anything bad or good; only this: that we have discovered the origin of wars—from which, when they happen, great calamities invade cities both publicly and privately."

"That is exactly what happens."

"Therefore, there is need of a still larger city to prepare a very great army, which, because of the things we have said, may go out to meet invading enemies. Are those whom we have already mentioned not sufficient for fighting?"

"No," Glaucon replied. "If indeed you and all of us rightly conceded the previous points when, in establishing the city, we agreed that it is impossible for one man to practice many arts well."

"You speak the truth," I said. "But tell me: is not the contest of war a specialized skill (*artificiosa facultas*)?"

"It is, and very much so."

"Should we then care more about shoemaking than about the art of warfare?"

"Not at all."

"But did we not forbid a shoemaker from attempting at the same time the work of a farmer, or a weaver, or an architect? We ordered him to be occupied only in his own art, so that his work might be performed as well as possible for us. We assigned to each of the others a single task according to each one's nature, so that each..."

# Meno, Or, on Virtue. 13

...previously in my answer to you about shape, we rejected that answer which is made through those things which still need further proof and are not yet established. MENO. And we rejected it rightly. SOCRATES. Therefore, most excellent man, when the question is "what is virtue in its entirety and as a whole," you should not answer by showing parts to the questioners, nor answer anything else in the same way, but the same interrogation will be needed again: what is this virtue of which you say these things are subjects? Does it seem to you that I am saying anything? MENO. You seem to me to speak correctly. SOCRATES. Answer then again from the beginning: what do both you and that friend of yours <note>Gorgias</note> assert virtue to be? MENO. I had heard indeed, Socrates, before I spoke with you, that your habit is nothing other than to doubt, and to cast the stumbling blocks of doubt into others. And now indeed, as it seems to me, you disturb me with spells, and poisons, and incantations, so that I am full of ambiguity. And you seem to me entirely—if it is proper to bite you a little in jest—to be most similar in form and in all other things to that very broad sea fish which is called the Torpedo <note>an electric ray fish</note>. For it makes anyone who approaches it and touches it go numb. You too now seem to have done something of the kind to make me numb. For in truth, I am numb in both my mind and my *mouth <margin>*body in the Greek</margin>, and I hesitate, nor do I find what to answer you, although I have already argued ten thousand times about virtue, and many things, and against many people, as I thought, most excellently. But at present, I am in no way able to bring forth what virtue itself is. Therefore, I think you have counseled yourself cautiously by never traveling abroad. For if, as a stranger in a foreign city, you did these things—acting like a sorcerer and a wizard—you would perhaps be punished. SOCRATES. You are clever, Meno, and you have almost deceived me just now. MENO. For what reason, Socrates? SOCRATES. For I see now for what cause you depict me with this image. MENO. What do you think the cause was? SOCRATES. So that I might also depict you in return. For when men endowed with a handsome appearance are portrayed, they are accustomed to be delighted, because that is beneficial; for the images of the handsome are also handsome. But I will not portray your person at all. Indeed, if that numb fish is itself numb while making others numb, then I am like it; otherwise, not at all. For I do not make others waver while being clear myself, but being more in doubt than anyone else, I make others doubt as well. For at present, I certainly do not know what virtue is; you, however, perhaps knew before you met me, but now you have become like one who is ignorant. Nevertheless, I have determined to discuss this one thing with you, and to investigate what virtue might be. MENO. But by what path will you investigate that which you are entirely ignorant of, Socrates? For what sort of thing will you propose to inquire into, when you do not know it? Or even if you stumble upon it, by what sign will you recognize that it is the thing you were ignorant of? SOCRATES. I understand what you want, Meno. But do you notice what a contentious <note>original: "religiosam," perhaps meaning "scrupulous" or "difficult" in this context of argumentation</note> argument you have brought into our midst? Namely, that a man can inquire into neither what he knows nor what he is ignorant of. For if he knows it, there is no need of inquiry. But neither will he investigate what he does not know, for he does not know what to seek. MENO. Do you not think this reasoning is rightly introduced, Socrates? SOCRATES. By no means. MENO. Can you say why it does not please you? SOCRATES. I can. For I have heard it from men and women skilled in divine matters. MENO. What is their discourse? SOCRATES. True, as it seems to me, and excellent. MENO. Who is it, I say? And who are the witnesses? SOCRATES. Those who assert this are holy men, and also holy women, who have taken care to be able to give an account of the things they profess. Furthermore, Pindar and the other poets who are divine hand down such things; listen, I pray, to whether they seem true to you. For they say that the soul of man is immortal, and that it sometimes departs—which they call "dying"—and then returns again, but never perishes. For which reason they warn to lead life as holily as possible. For whoever has paid the penalty for ancient misery to Proserpine <note>Goddess of the Underworld</note>, she gives back their soul to the upper sun again in the ninth year, from whom glorious kings, mighty in strength and wisdom, arise. For the rest of time, they are called holy heroes among men. Since, therefore, the soul is immortal, and has returned many times into this life, and has seen many things both in this and in the other life, and has perceived all things, there is nothing left that it has not learned. Thus, it is no wonder if it is able to remember those things concerning virtue and other things, since it knew them of old. For since all nature is akin and consistent with itself, and the soul has learned all things, nothing prevents a man, by remembering one certain thing—which they call "learning"—from recovering all the rest, if he is so constant as not to grow weary in seeking. For seeking and learning is all recollection. Therefore, one ought by no means to believe that contentious argument, for it would make us lazy in a way. That also wonderfully pleases softer men. But our reasoning makes us skillful investigators of things; and I, trusting in it as true, desire to search out with you what virtue is. MENO. Yes, Socrates. But do you assert this absolutely, that we do not learn? And that what we call learning is recollection? Can you teach me that this is so? SOCRATES. I said in the previous parts also, Meno, that you are clever; and now you ask whether I can teach you, when I have just asserted that there is no "learning" but only "recollection," so that I might immediately seem to contradict myself. MENO. By Jove, Socrates, I did not intend that, but I spoke that way out of habit. But if by any means you can show it to me, show it, I pray. SOCRATES. It is by no means easy, but for your sake I will try. But call here to me any one you wish from the many who follow you, so that we may test this demonstration in him. MENO. Gladly. Hey you, come here. SOCRATES. Is he Greek? And does he speak Greek? MENO. He is Greek, born and raised in my house. SOCRATES. Attend then to whether I seem to remind him or to teach him. MENO. I will certainly attend. SOCRATES. Tell me, boy, do you know that such a space as this is a square? BOY. I do. SOCRATES. ->[DIAGRAM OF SQUARE]<- Has a square all these four lines equal? BOY. It has. # Meno, Or, on Virtue. 15

...any other opinion than his own? MENO. Never, but always from his own. SOCRATES. And yet he did not know, as we confessed a little while ago. MENO. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Therefore these opinions were in him. MENO. They were. SOCRATES. Therefore true opinions about things he is ignorant of are in him while he is ignorant. MENO. It appears so. SOCRATES. Now these opinions have been stirred up in him like a dream; and if someone questions him about such things often and in many ways, you will know for certain that he will eventually know these things as perfectly as anyone else. MENO. So it seems. SOCRATES. Therefore, will he not know without anyone teaching him, but rather by someone questioning him, recalling the knowledge into himself from within himself? MENO. It is so. SOCRATES. But to recover knowledge within oneself—is that not called "remembering"? MENO. Entirely. SOCRATES. But the knowledge he now has, he either received at some time or always had. MENO. TRUE. SOCRATES. If he always had it, he was always knowing; but if he received it at some time, it was not in this life. For no one taught him geometry, though he will do these same things in all other matters which belong either to geometry or to other disciplines. Is there someone who taught him all those things? It is likely that you know him, especially since he was born and raised in your house. MENO. But I am certain that no one ever taught him. SOCRATES. Yet he has these opinions? MENO. That appears necessary, Socrates. SOCRATES. But if he did not acquire them in this present life, and yet he knows them, it is clear that he had them and learned them at some other time. MENO. It appears so. SOCRATES. And was that not the time when he was not yet a human being? MENO. That very time. SOCRATES. Therefore, if there is always a time when he is not a human being, yet true opinions are in him which are awakened by questioning and become knowledge, then surely his soul will know these things for all time. For through all time, he either is or is not a human being. MENO. So it seems. SOCRATES. Therefore, if the truth of all things is always in the soul, is it not immortal? For which reason one ought to be bold and have great confidence to seek out and remember what you do not know at present—that is, what you do not remember. MENO. You seem to me to speak well, Socrates, I know not how. SOCRATES. To me too, O Meno. I do not contend very much for the rest; but that those who think we must seek what we do not know are better, more courageous, and less lazy in searching than those who think that what they do not know cannot even be sought—that I will contend for both in words and, if I can, in deeds. MENO. You seem to say this rightly as well, Socrates. SOCRATES. Since we have confessed that it is permitted to search for the unknown, do you wish then that we investigate together what virtue is? MENO. Most certainly. Yet it would be more pleasing to me to consider and hear first what I asked at the beginning of the discussion: how one must apply oneself to virtue—whether it is perceived through doctrine <note>being taught</note>, or whether it is in us by nature, or by some other way that it is provided to men. SOCRATES. But if I commanded you, Meno, as I command myself, we would not have searched whether virtue is taught or not before we had tracked down what it is. But since you do not even try to rule yourself, so that you may live as a free man, and yet you wish to rule me, and indeed you do rule me, I will yield to you. For what else is there to do? It seems, therefore, that we must consider what sort of thing it is, though we do not yet know what it is. Nevertheless, turn aside a little from your purpose, and permit us to consider "by hypothesis" <note>original: "ex suppositione," a method of making a preliminary assumption to see what follows</note> whether virtue is possessed through doctrine or some other way. By concession, then, I speak as...

...geometricians often discuss after someone has questioned them: for example, concerning a space, whether it is possible for this triangular space to be expanded within this circle. Where, if someone should say that he does not yet know whether it is of such a kind, I think such a concession would be useful. By permission <note>or "granting the hypothesis"</note>, therefore, I have decided to argue about what happens regarding the expansion of that into the circle, whether it can be done or not. So let us also seek concerning virtue, since we know neither what it is nor of what quality it is; by this permission, let us ask whether it can be taught in this way. If virtue is something that belongs to the soul, can it be taught, or not? First, if it is something other than knowledge, can it be taught or not? Next, I think we should investigate whether virtue is knowledge or something else. MENO. It seems to me that the same must be sought. SOCRATES. Do we say virtue is anything other than a good? And does this position remain stable for us—namely, that virtue is a good? MENO. Very much so. SOCRATES. If indeed there is some good separate from knowledge, then perhaps virtue will not be knowledge? But if there is no good that is not comprehended by knowledge, then in suspecting that knowledge is virtue, we will surely suspect rightly? MENO. These things are true. SOCRATES. Furthermore, are we good by virtue? MENO. We are. SOCRATES. And if good, then useful? For all good things are useful. MENO. It is so. SOCRATES. Therefore virtue is something useful. MENO. From what we have confessed, it follows necessarily. SOCRATES. Let us consider again in individual cases what sorts of things benefit us: are health, strength, beauty, and riches, and other such things said to be beneficial? MENO. Yes. SOCRATES. We confess that these same things sometimes harm us. Or do you feel otherwise? MENO. I certainly feel that way. SOCRATES. See then, with what guide these things harm or benefit: is it not when right use is present that they help, but otherwise they harm? MENO. Entirely. SOCRATES. Furthermore, let us consider what concerns the soul. Do you call something moderation, and justice, and courage, and docility <note>readiness to be taught</note>, and memory, and magnificence, and all other such things? MENO. I do. SOCRATES. Observe, I pray, whichever of these seems to be not knowledge at all, but something else besides knowledge: do they not sometimes help and sometimes hurt? For example, courage without prudence <note>practical wisdom</note>? Is courage anything other than a kind of boldness? And when anyone is bold with reason, he is helped; but without reason, he is harmed? MENO. It is so. SOCRATES. Are moderation and docility the same way—when perceived and established with reason they are an advantage, but otherwise a detriment? MENO. Most certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, to say it briefly, all the impulses of the soul and all its inclinations, with prudence leading, tend toward happiness; but with imprudence, toward the contrary. MENO. So it seems. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Meno regarding the nature of virtue and whether it can be taught. It transitions from a logical proof that virtue is a form of wisdom to a practical search for teachers of virtue, introducing the character Anytus.</meta>

# 16 Book Four.

if it resides in the soul and is necessarily useful, this must be wisdom; <note>original: "prudentiam"</note> for all things concerning the soul are, in and of themselves, neither advantageous nor disadvantageous; but when wisdom or folly is added, they immediately become either useful or harmful. By this reasoning, since virtue is the most beneficial thing of all, it is clear that it must be a kind of wisdom. **MENO.** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, regarding the other things we were just mentioning—wealth and the like—which are sometimes useful and sometimes harmful: just as wisdom, presiding over the other powers and duties of the soul, makes them useful, while folly makes them the opposite, is it not also true that the soul, by using and leading these external things rightly, makes them good, but by using them wrongly makes them bad? **MENO.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** The wise soul leads rightly, while the foolish soul leads astray. **MENO.** These things are true. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must assert generally that all other human affairs depend upon the soul, and the things of the soul itself depend upon wisdom, if they are to be good. By this reasoning, wisdom itself is the "useful" element, and we have already said that virtue is useful. **MENO.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, virtue is wisdom, either in its entirety or some part of it. **MENO.** All these things seem to me to be well said. **SOCRATES.** If this is how things stand, then men are surely not good by nature? **MENO.** It does not seem so to me. **SOCRATES.** Moreover, if they were made good by nature, we would surely have people who could recognize which of our sons were naturally good. We would take those children they identified and guard them in a <term>citadel</term> <note>Socrates uses the image of an "acropolis" or fortress to suggest that naturally virtuous people would be more valuable than gold.</note> even more carefully than gold, so that no one could corrupt them, so that when they grew up, they would be useful citizens to the State. **MENO.** That seems likely, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But since they are not good by nature, could it be through instruction? **MENO.** That appears necessary. And according to our reasoning, it follows that if virtue is knowledge, it must be something learned through teaching. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps, by Hercules! <note>A common Greek oath of surprise or emphasis.</note> And yet, I fear we may have been too hasty in agreeing to that. **MENO.** It certainly seemed to be rightly said just a moment ago. **SOCRATES.** But it ought to seem right not only in the past, but also in the present and the future, if there is to be any truth in it. **MENO.** What is it, then, that you see which displeases you, and makes you doubt that virtue is knowledge? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you, Meno. I do not take back the claim that virtue can be taught if it is indeed knowledge—that was well said. But see if I am not right to doubt that it *is* knowledge. Tell me this: if anything can be taught—and I speak not only of virtue, but of any subject—must there not necessarily be teachers and students of it? **MENO.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** But on the other hand, if there are neither teachers nor students of a subject, would we not be right to guess that it cannot be taught? **MENO.** That is true; but do you really think there are no teachers of virtue? **SOCRATES.** I have often searched with great effort to find if there were any masters of this, but I have never found them, even though I have searched for it with many others, specifically those who seemed most experienced in this faculty. And look, Meno, at just the right moment, this man has sat down with us, <note>Referring to Anytus, who has just joined the scene.</note> and we should make him a partner in our discussion. We are right to bring him in as a companion. For first, he is the son of a wealthy and wise father, Anthemion, who did not become rich by chance or by some gift—like the Theban Ismenias who recently came into the wealth of Polycrates—but increased his fortune through his own wisdom and vigilance. Furthermore, he is not a proud citizen, nor puffed up or difficult, but has proven to be a modest, upright, and easy-going man. Finally, he educated and instructed this son well, as the whole Athenian people can testify, for they chose him for the highest offices of the state. It is right to investigate with such men whether there are any teachers of virtue, and who they might be. Come then, Anytus, join me and your guest Meno in searching for who the teachers of this matter might be. Consider it in this way: if we wanted Meno here to become an excellent doctor, to which teachers would we lead him? Would it not be to the doctors? **ANYTUS.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** And if we desired him to become an excellent <term>cobbler</term>, <note>original: "cerdonem"; a manual laborer or shoemaker.</note> would we not go to the cobblers? **ANYTUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And in other matters likewise? **ANYTUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then again about the doctors: when we said he should be sent to the doctors if we wanted him to be a doctor, did we not mean that he should be placed with those who profess that art and who openly take a fee from students for it, showing themselves to be willing to teach those who want to learn? Should we not have this in mind if we are to place him wisely? **ANYTUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And the same judgment applies to flute-playing and all other things. For it would be great folly, if we wanted someone to become a flute-player, to refuse to send him to those who promise this faculty and take a fee for it, but instead to burden those who neither profess to be masters nor have any students in the art we want the person to learn. Does that not seem very absurd to you? **ANYTUS.** By Jove! <note>original: "Per Iouem"; a common Latin translation for the Greek oath "By Zeus."</note> Not only absurd, but a kind of stupidity. **SOCRATES.** You speak well. Now then, you can deliberate together with me about this guest of yours, Meno. For he, Anytus, told me long ago that he desires this wisdom and virtue by which states and homes are rightly governed, children are educated as well as possible, and citizens and guests are welcomed and sent away skillfully, as befits a good man. Meditate, therefore, to whom it is most fitting to send him for the sake of acquiring this virtue. Or is it clear from what we just said: that he must be committed to those who promise to teach such things, and who always offer themselves openly to any of the Greeks who wish to learn, taking a prescribed price for this instruction? **ANYTUS.** But who do you mean, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** I believe you know yourself that these are the ones who are publicly called <term>Sophists</term>. <note>The Sophists were professional teachers in Ancient Greece who traveled from city to city, charging fees to teach various subjects, including rhetoric and "virtue."</note> **ANYTUS.** Oh, Hercules! Good words, I pray you, Socrates! <note>Anytus is expressing shock and offense at the mention of the Sophists.</note> May it never happen that any of my relatives, household, friends, citizens, or guests fall into such madness as to be ruined by associating with them; for the company of those men is a certain plague to those who follow them. **SOCRATES.** Why do you say this, Anytus? Are they the only ones out of all types of men who, while professing to benefit people, are so much worse than the rest that they not only do not help (as others do with what is entrusted to them) but, on the contrary, corrupt them—and then demand a fee for it? I truly do not see how I can believe you. For I know one man, Protagoras, who amassed more money from this wisdom than that famous Phidias, whose works are so conspicuous and beautiful, or any ten other sculptors. Surely it would be absurd if those who mend old shoes or repair clothes could not hide for thirty days if they returned the clothes or shoes in worse condition; they would soon die of hunger if they did such things. Yet Protagoras, for more than forty years, corrupted his associates and returned them in worse condition than he received them, without anyone in all of Greece noticing! For I believe he died nearly seventy years old, having spent forty years in this art. And throughout all that time, even to this day, he remains famous...

He introduces Anytus to the conversation, suggesting the Sophists as potential teachers, which provokes a hostile and disgusted reaction from Anytus.</summary>
