# Meno, Or, on Virtue. 17

... remained famous. And not only Protagoras, but many others as well, some before him and some still living today. Shall we say, according to your opinion, that they knowingly and prudently deceive and strive to harm the young? Or do they also deceive themselves, and shall we say they are insane because there are some who say they are the wisest of mortals? ANYTUS. They are far from being called insane, Socrates; but much more so are the young men who give them money. And even worse than these are those who commit those under their care to such men. Most insane of all are the cities that receive them and do not expel them, whether a stranger or a citizen attempts such a thing. SOCRATES. Has any of the Sophists ever wronged you, Anytus? Or why are you so angry with them? ANYTUS. I have never had any dealing with any of them, nor would I permit any of my people to use them. SOCRATES. <unclear>Therefore</unclear> you have never experienced their ways. ANYTUS. And I hope I never shall. SOCRATES. By what reason, then, O divine man, can you distinguish whether a thing be good or bad when you have made no trial of it? ANYTUS. I know clearly what sort they are, whether I have tried them or not. SOCRATES. Perhaps you are a prophet, Anytus; for it would be a wonder if you knew this by any other means from what you have just said. But we are not seeking those with whom Meno might go and turn out wicked; for let those be the Sophists if you wish. But help your father's friend: show him to whom, among those who inhabit this great city, he should cling to acquire the virtue we described. ANYTUS. Why do you not indicate it yourself? SOCRATES. But I have already produced those whom I thought were masters of these things; but according to your opinion, I have accomplished nothing at all. ANYTUS. Perhaps you speak the truth. SOCRATES. Therefore, you also now fulfill your part of this duty. Show to which of the Athenians he should go. Name anyone you wish. ANYTUS. Why is there a need to hear the name of one man? Whomever of the good and famous Athenians he happens upon, he will turn out better for that man's company—if only he follows him—than from the company of Sophists. SOCRATES. But did those excellent and good men become such by themselves, with no one instructing them, and can they teach others, even though they themselves learned from no one? ANYTUS. I believe they learned from the older excellent and good men. Do you not think there have been many distinguished and very good men in this city? SOCRATES. It seems to me, Anytus, that there are men here skilled in civil administration, and that there were no fewer in the past. But were they suitable teachers of their own virtue? For this is what is now being discussed: not whether there are or were good men here, but whether virtue can be taught. And because of this, whether good men—either those of old or those now living—knew how to hand down to another the virtue with which they were endowed, or whether perhaps virtue can neither be handed down to another nor received. That, I say, is what Meno and I have been inquiring into for a long time. Consider the matter thus from your own speech: Do you confess that Themistocles was a good man? ANYTUS. Most of all. SOCRATES. And that Themistocles was a good teacher of his own virtue, if anyone was ever a master of virtue? ANYTUS. I believe so, provided he had wished to be. SOCRATES. Do you think he did not wish others to become good too? Especially his own son? Or do you think he envied his son and deliberately failed to communicate the virtue he had acquired? Have you not heard that Themistocles made his son Cleophantus strenuous in equestrian skill, so that he could stand upright on horses, and throw a javelin while standing on a horse, and do many other amazing things in which his parent diligently instructed him, and made him wise in those particular things that belong to the best teachers? Have you not received these things from your elders? ANYTUS. I have received them. SOCRATES. No one, therefore, could blame the son's nature as being bad. ANYTUS. No one, I think. SOCRATES. But what of this? Have you heard from any senior or junior that Cleophantus, the son of Themistocles, turned out good and wise in the things his father was? ANYTUS. Never. SOCRATES. Do we believe that Themistocles wished to imbue his son with foreign arts, but took no care to make him better than his neighbors in his father's own virtue, if indeed virtue could be taught by any means? ANYTUS. Perhaps, by Jove, not at all. SOCRATES. Such a master of virtue, then, was this man whom you assert to be the best among the ancients. Let us now consider another, Aristides, son of Lysimachus. Do you not also think he was good? ANYTUS. And most certainly. SOCRATES. Did he not also want his son Lysimachus to turn out the best educated of all Athenians in everything taught by masters? Yet did he make him better than anyone else? For you have spoken with him, and you know very well what he is like. Furthermore, if you wish, consider Pericles, a man of great wisdom: he educated two sons, as you well know, Paralus and Xanthippus. ANYTUS. I know them indeed. SOCRATES. These, as you know, he instructed better than other Athenians in equestrian art, and music, and also athletics. And finally, he did not want them to be inferior to others in anything perceived by art; but did he desire that they should turn out good? I think he did desire it, but that it could not be taught. Lest you think only a few most ignoble Athenians could not achieve this, look at Thucydides: he educated two sons, Melesias and Stephanus, whom he taught other things diligently, and wrestling in particular, so that they easily surpassed the rest of the Athenians in it, commending one to Xanthias and the other to Eudorus; and these were thought to excel all others in wrestling in those times. Do you not remember? ANYTUS. I have heard so. SOCRATES. Surely that man, when he wanted his sons to be skilled in things learned at great expense, would not have been unwilling to teach the only virtue which he could hand down without money, if only it could have been taught? Was Thucydides perhaps an ignoble man, and did he not have many friends among both citizens and allies? On the contrary, he was born of a great family and was of the highest authority both among his fellow citizens and all other Greeks. Therefore, if goodness could have been acquired through doctrine, he would have found at least some citizen or stranger who would have made his sons good, if he himself lacked the leisure for that teaching due to the business of the republic. But see, friend Anytus, lest perhaps virtue cannot be taught. ANYTUS. Socrates, you seem to me to disparage men more freely than is becoming. Therefore, I advise you, if you are willing to obey, to take care: for perhaps in another city it is easy to affect citizens either with injury or benefit, but in this one it is very difficult and dangerous. And I do not think this escapes you. SOCRATES. O Meno, Anytus here seems to me to be angry, and I do not wonder at it. First, because he thinks I am disparaging these men, and secondly, because he considers himself one of them. But if he ever learns what it is to detract from men, he will no longer be angry; for the present, however, he is ignorant. But tell me yourself, are there not famous and good men among us? MENO. There certainly are. SOCRATES. Are these men willing to offer themselves as teachers to the youth? And do they profess it? Or do they confess that virtue can be taught? MENO. No, by Jove, Socrates; but now you will hear from them that it can...

<summary>Socrates argues that even the greatest Athenian statesmen, such as Themistocles and Pericles, were unable to teach virtue to their sons, suggesting it is not a teachable skill. Anytus takes offense at this criticism and warns Socrates of the legal dangers of his speech.</summary>

# Book Four. 18

...be taught, and now that it cannot. SOCRATES. Shall we say those are masters of this matter, among whom there is no agreement? MENO. By no means, it seems to me, Socrates. SOCRATES. What then, do you consider the Sophists to be masters of virtue, since they alone proclaim it? MENO. I greatly admire and love Gorgias for this, that you never hear him promising this. Indeed, he laughs at others whenever he hears them promising it; he thinks, however, that one should only promise to make men eloquent. SOCRATES. Therefore, the Sophists do not seem to you to be teachers of this matter. MENO. I do not know what to say, Socrates, for the same thing happens to me as to many: now I think it possible, now I deny it. SOCRATES. It does not happen only to you and the other citizens that you sometimes believe virtue is taught and sometimes deny it, but even to the poet Theognis, for he says exactly the same things. MENO. In which poems? SOCRATES. In the elegies, in this manner: "Drink and eat near these, sit with them, and obey those whose power is great. For from the good you will learn good things. But if you cling to the bad, you will undoubtedly lose the mind you have." <margin>The precepts of Theognis are worthy of knowing.</margin> Do you see how in these he speaks as if virtue could be learned? MENO. It appears so. SOCRATES. But elsewhere, changing a little, he says: "If a healthy mind could be handed over to a man, those who accomplished it would surely receive a great and high reward, nor would a bad son ever come from a good father, being imbued with wise warnings; but by teaching, you will never make a good man out of a bad one." Do you see him establishing the opposite to himself regarding the same things? MENO. It seems so. SOCRATES. Can you then indicate to me any matter at all whose professed doctors are not doctors of anything else, nor do they hold that matter, but confess themselves to be base and of no account in that which they profess to teach; or if they confess themselves to be excellent, they affirm now that the matter can be perceived, and now deny it? Would you rightly call those who are so uncertain in any matter doctors of that thing? MENO. Not at all. SOCRATES. Therefore, if neither the Sophists nor the good and famous men are doctors of this matter, much less will others be. MENO. Certainly. SOCRATES. If there are no teachers, then there are no students either. MENO. It seems as you say. SOCRATES. Have we not confessed that that for which there are neither masters nor students cannot be taught? MENO. We have confessed it. SOCRATES. And are teachers of virtue found nowhere? MENO. Nowhere. SOCRATES. If no teachers, then no students either. MENO. So it appears. SOCRATES. Virtue, therefore, cannot be taught. MENO. So it seems, if indeed we have judged rightly. For which reason I greatly wonder, Socrates, that many good men are found among people, and I am uncertain what the reason is by which they become good. SOCRATES. It seems, Meno, that you and I are both bad; <margin>Prodicus was a teacher of Socrates.</margin> it seems Gorgias has not sufficiently instructed you, nor Prodicus me. Therefore, most of all, we must recall our own minds and seek someone who might make us better in this one way. But I say these things looking back at our previous inquiry. Was it not ridiculous that we overlooked that it is not only by the guidance of knowledge that right business proceeds for men? Unless that is conceded, that there is something else besides knowledge, perhaps there would be no reason why men become good. MENO. How do you say that, Socrates? SOCRATES. Thus: that it is necessary for good men to be useful, we have correctly confessed, since things are never otherwise, is it not so? MENO. Yes. SOCRATES. And that they will be useful if they preside over things to be done rightly, also correctly agrees between us. MENO. Correctly. SOCRATES. But that no one can preside rightly unless he is prudent, it is clear that this was not quite rightly asserted by both of us. MENO. Why do you say "rightly"? SOCRATES. I will tell you. He who knows the way to Larissa, or anywhere else, and goes there himself or leads others, will he not lead rightly and well? MENO. Entirely. SOCRATES. But what if someone has a right opinion as to which way leads to Larissa, yet has never gone there nor known it, would he not also lead rightly? MENO. Greatly so. SOCRATES. And as long as he has a right opinion about the same things of which the other has knowledge, he will be no worse a leader, though thinking true things but not knowing them, than he who knows those things thoroughly? MENO. No worse, certainly. SOCRATES. True opinion, therefore, is no less effective for right action than prudence. <margin>Right opinion and knowledge.</margin> And that is what we overlooked in the consideration of virtue before, when we asserted that prudence alone was the leader of right action, for this other was true opinion. MENO. It seems so. SOCRATES. Does right opinion then benefit no less than knowledge? MENO. It benefits less in this way, Socrates: that whoever has knowledge always succeeds; but he who has right opinion sometimes succeeds, and sometimes is deceived. MENO. What are you saying? He who walks with right opinion, as long as he opines rightly, is he not always achieving his wish? MENO. It appears necessary. For which reason I wonder, since it is so, why knowledge is held to be so much more excellent than right opinion, and I doubt why they are two different things. SOCRATES. Do you know the reason why you wonder? Or do you want me to tell you? MENO. Tell me, by all means. SOCRATES. Because you have never considered the statues of Daedalus <note>Daedalus was a mythical inventor said to make statues so lifelike they moved.</note>; perhaps they do not exist among you. MENO. To what purpose is this? SOCRATES. Because these, unless they are tied down, depart and run away; but tied down, they remain. MENO. What then? SOCRATES. What is loose of his works is of no great value, like a runaway slave, for it does not remain; but tied down, it is worthy of admiration, for they are very beautiful works. For what sake do I say this? For the sake of true opinions: for these, as long as they remain stable, are beautiful works and accomplish all good things. Yet they do not wish to stay for long, but flee from the soul of a man at once, wherefore they are not of much price, until someone ties them down by reasoning derived from causes. <margin>Right opinion is recollection.</margin> And this, friend Meno, is "recollection," as was agreed between us above. But after they are tied down, first they become knowledge, then they become lasting, and for that reason knowledge is more excellent than right opinion, and differs from it by a certain bond. MENO. By Jove, Socrates, a fitting comparison. SOCRATES. Furthermore, I myself speak not as one knowing, but as one guessing. But that true opinion is something other than knowledge, I do not seem to myself to be guessing altogether. If I were to confess that I knew anything else—which are few indeed—I would number this one among the things I know. MENO. You speak rightly, Socrates. SOCRATES. And what of this? Is it not also right that true opinion, leading any work, achieves it no worse than knowledge? MENO. This also is true. SOCRATES. Therefore, true opinion is no worse than knowledge, nor is it less useful for actions, nor is the man having true opinion less useful than the one endowed with knowledge. MENO. It is so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, it was agreed that the good man is useful. MENO. It was agreed. SOCRATES. If, therefore, men were good and useful to cities not through knowledge alone, if such could be found, but also through right opinion; and neither of these is in men by nature, neither knowledge nor true opinion, nor are these things innate; does it seem that any of these ...

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between "True Opinion" and "Knowledge," using the metaphor of Daedalus's statues to show that knowledge is more valuable because it is "tied down" by an understanding of causes (recollection). He concludes that virtue might come from right opinion rather than teachable knowledge.</summary>

# Meno, Or, on Virtue. 19

...exist by nature? MENO. Not at all to me. SOCRATES. Since they are not there by nature, then good men will not be good by nature either? MENO. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Since it is not by nature, were we considering whether it is by teaching? MENO. Yes. SOCRATES. And did it seem comparable to teaching if virtue is prudence? MENO. It did. SOCRATES. And if it were comparable through teaching, would it not also seem to be prudence? MENO. Entirely. SOCRATES. And if there were teachers, it could be taught; if not, not at all? MENO. So it is. SOCRATES. And we denied by common consent that there are teachers of it. MENO. We denied it. SOCRATES. We concluded, therefore, that it is neither taught, nor is it prudence? MENO. We concluded so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, we conceded that it is a good thing. MENO. We conceded it. SOCRATES. And that what leads rightly is good and useful. MENO. Most certainly. <margin>Two things lead rightly: true opinion and knowledge.</margin> SOCRATES. Finally, these two alone lead rightly: true opinion and knowledge, by which a man endowed with them can truly be a leader to others. For those things that happen by fortune are by no means by human command; but those things in which a man is a leader to what is right are these two: true opinion and knowledge. MENO. The same seems to me. SOCRATES. Therefore, since virtue cannot be perceived by teaching, it is by no means knowledge. MENO. It does not appear so. SOCRATES. Since there are two good and useful things, one of them is rejected, namely knowledge, nor does it hold the leadership in civil action. MENO. Not as it seems to me. SOCRATES. Therefore, it is not by some wisdom, nor as wise men, that those civil men administer the republic, like Themistocles and those whom Anytus mentioned a little while ago. Whence they cannot make others such as they are, since they are endowed with no such knowledge. MENO. It seems to be as you say, Socrates. SOCRATES. If not by knowledge, it remains that civil men govern states by using right opinion, and they are in no other relation to prudence than are prophets and those seized by divine frenzy. For these announce many true things, yet they understand nothing of what they speak. MENO. So it seems to be. SOCRATES. Is it not fitting then, Meno, to call such men divine, who, not using their minds, yet do many and great things, and dispose of them both in acting and speaking? MENO. Entirely. SOCRATES. For which reason we shall rightly call divine those whom we just spoke of: the prophets, the seers, and all poetic men; and we shall consider civil men no less divine than the rest, as being inspired by a divine power and possessed by God, since they direct the republic, saying many and greatest things, which they by no means understand. MENO. Most certainly. SOCRATES. Women also, Meno, call good men divine. And the Spartans, whenever they wish to commend some good man, say, "This is a divine man." MENO. And they seem to speak rightly indeed, Socrates, although Anytus here perhaps is angry at you for saying such things. SOCRATES. It is of no concern to me; <margin>From whence virtue comes.</margin> for we shall discuss this again with him, Meno. But if we have investigated rightly in all this dispute, virtue will come to us neither by teaching nor by nature, but will flow by a divine lot <note>The Latin is *divina sorte*, meaning by divine fate or gift.</note> without the mind into him who has obtained it; unless perhaps there exists someone among the civil men who is such that he can also make another man a civil leader. If such a one existed, he would be among the living as Homer says Tiresias is among the dead, saying: <margin>Odyssey, Book 10.</margin> "Among those who are in the underworld, he alone is wise, the rest flit about as shadows." Similarly, this citizen would be to others as a reality to shadows. For it would be a true thing, if you look at virtue. MENO. You seem to me to speak excellently, Socrates. SOCRATES. From this reasoning, Meno, it appears that divine virtue is present to whomever...

-> THE ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO <-
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the Italian scholar who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin, making them accessible to the Renaissance world.</note>
This most candid book of our Plato, which is titled the First Alcibiades, more beautiful than Alcibiades himself and dearer than all gold, teaches what man is and what his duty is. Now, man is a rational soul, partaking of the mind, using a body. From this definition, his duty is drawn, distributed in three ways. For as he is a rational soul, he reflects upon himself in a certain circle of reasoning by noticing himself. As he partakes of the mind, he flows back into the divine mind like a stream into its source. As using a body, he applies himself to governing human affairs. The perfect and absolute duty of man, therefore, is first that he should notice his own nature, then from that, as from an image and effect, he should turn to the divine mind, its exemplar and cause. By which the mind of man, being illustrated, understands the good itself, the useful itself, the beautiful itself, and the just itself, and perfectly comprehends his own good, useful, beautiful, and just. Whence he knows what is the good and what is the useful of other men with whom he lives, or whom he commands; and when he has known the absolute good, his own good, and the good of others, he must now approach the care of himself and of every other person according to the norm of the known good. By the study of philosophy, there is need for work in morals, mathematics, and theology, so that he may return to himself and to the mind, his cause. For moral and mathematical discipline restores the soul submerged in the body to itself; theology carries it above itself and lifts it outside itself into God. The knowledge of the divine mind and the ideas is called wisdom. The knowledge of oneself, and the discovery of the good and useful for oneself and one's own, flowing from the intuition of the divine mind, is called prudence. Prudence, indeed, as it understands the good, refers human actions, both public and private, to the best end. As it understands the useful, it directs them through convenient and proper ways by which they may reach that end. As it understands the beautiful, it institutes what order and what measure should be kept in this progress as if on a journey. As it understands the just, it prescribes the distinction of individual works, the observance of the imposed order, the punishment for the transgressor, and the reward for the one observing the law of this journey. From philosophy, therefore, to wisdom, and from wisdom to prudence, is the access made: prudence, truly the mistress of life, gives the discipline of one's own domestic affairs and of the republic. Man governs through prudence, but the house and the city are preserved through public friendship and justice. I call public friendship that consensus by which all freely meet under the same law and prince, and look to the same end. I name public justice that legitimate distinction by which individual men, though under the same prince and toward the same end (that is, the public good), yet proceed by different paths and keep the various distributions of duties assigned by nature and laws according to the nature and dignity of each, and perform their own duty without usurping another's. In this dialogue are two theological terms: "the self-same" and "the thing itself." Concerning man, the former signifies the soul as the same, and the latter the soul in the body. But of these more fully in the commentaries, which I have now begun to write on these ten dialogues of Plato.

The cause of this matter was not any human... <margin>The occasion of the dialogue, in which he finds, and having found seeks, and seeking he thinks he is ignorant.</margin> <margin>Alcibiades was a very beautiful youth, noble, wealthy, having a talent and hope for great deeds, and that man is not in these parts.</margin>

# Book Five. 20

...human thing: but it was a certain opposing power of a daemon, the power of which you will hear in what follows. But now, since it no longer opposes me, I have come here thus. I hope, moreover, that it will not be against us in the future. For almost all this time, I was considering how you conducted yourself toward your friends. Who, although they were many and proud, not one of them was there who did not go away surpassed by you in pride. But for what reason you despised them, I will explain. For you say that you need other men in no thing, since those things that are in you are so excellent that you lack nothing of anyone's goods, whether of body or soul. You think yourself to excel most of all in a tall and handsome habit of body. And indeed it is clear to anyone that you are not at all lying. Furthermore, you proclaim yourself to be born of the most strenuous race in this greatest of Greek cities: from your father's side, indeed, that your friends and kinsmen are as many and as excellent men as possible, who can supply you with all things when there is need. Those on your mother's side are neither inferior nor fewer. But you think Pericles the son of Xanthippus brings you a much greater authority for conducting affairs, whom indeed your father left as a guardian to you and your brother, and who can do whatever he wants not only in this city, but in all Greece, and even among many and great nations of the barbarians. I would also add the very great riches of your people, unless I knew you gloried in them least of all: for the sake of all these things, elate with pride, you have subdued all your friends. And they, as being inferior, gave way to you. Nor did these things escape you. For which reason I know well that you wonder with what mind I have persevered in my benevolence toward you, or what hope I have conceived of you, that while others were fleeing, I alone of all have remained. ALCIBIADES. But you do not know, Socrates, that you have just now anticipated me a little. For it had come into my mind that I should attack you first and ask these same things of you. What do you want? With what hope, at last, are you troublesome to me, you who are always present most accurately wherever I am? For in truth, I wonder what your counsel is, and I would gladly hear it. SOCRATES. You shall hear it then from me as is fitting as soon as possible, since, as you say, you desire to know and hear what I am thinking. For I shall relate it as if to one expecting and ready to listen. ALCIBIADES. Most certainly: only speak. SOCRATES. See then; for it ought not to seem a wonder if, just as I have barely begun, so I should barely finish. ALCIBIADES. Come, only speak, for I will listen. SOCRATES. I must speak indeed. <margin>He catches his benevolence from the matter itself and attention.</margin> It is difficult, truly, to enter into an acquaintance with one who yields to none of his friends. Yet I must dare, and my opinion must be expressed. Indeed, Alcibiades, if I had known you to be content with those things which we recounted above, and to pass your life in them, I would long ago (so I persuade myself) have laid down my benevolence toward you. But now I will indicate to you certain other thoughts of yours about yourself, so that you may understand from the time I once applied my mind to you, how I have never ceased. You seem to me surely, if some god should say to you: "O Alcibiades, do you wish to live possessing only those things which you now have? Or to die at once unless it be permitted to achieve certain more excellent things?" you seem likely to choose death instead. But now I will open with what hope you lead your life: for you think that if you soon ascend into the assembly of the Athenian people—which indeed you think will be in a few days—you will demonstrate to the Athenians that you are worthy of greater honor than either Pericles is, or anyone else has been of those who flourished in previous ages. And if you show this, you will achieve the greatest authority among your citizens. And if you can do most in this city, you would also be the most famous of all the Greeks and even of whatever barbarians inhabit the same region as the Greeks: and if that same God should grant the empire of Europe, you would not yet, it seems to me, choose to lead your life with these alone, unless you could propagate your name and power, so to speak, through all kinds of men. And I think you consider no one worthy of memory except Cyrus and Xerxes. That you are nourished by a hope of this kind, I know not by a guess indeed, but for certain. You will say perhaps, as being conscious that I have spoken true things: "What are these things, Socrates, to that reason which you wanted to assign, for which you have not yet deserted me?" I will tell you, O son of Clinias and Dinomache: you cannot at all lead these thoughts of yours to the desired end without me: to such an extent I trust myself to be able in you and your affairs. Wherefore I think God himself did not permit me to discuss with you before: and I waited until he should permit. For just as you hope to be able to show to your city that you are worthy of every honor in it, and having demonstrated these things, that nothing remains so great that you cannot at once accomplish it: so also I trust to have most power with you, as soon as I shall have shown to all that I am more worthy: neither a guardian, nor a kinsman, nor anyone else except me alone, God favoring, will hand over to you that power which you desire. Therefore, as long as you were younger, and had not yet come into such great hope, in my opinion, God prohibited me from disputing with you, lest I should contend in vain. But now he has impelled me. Now therefore you shall hear. ALCIBIADES. You seem much more wonderful to me now, Socrates, after you have begun to speak with me, than while you were following me in silence: although even then you seemed most of all such a one by your look. Whether I was turning these things in my mind or not, you have known so well, as it seems, that even if I should deny it, I would yet gain nothing further by persuasion: let it be so. But if I intend these things most of all, in what way shall I follow them through you, and those things will not be perfected without you? Can you say? SOCRATES. Do you ask whether I am about to begin a long speech, such as you are accustomed to hear? That is not my manner. Indeed, I can demonstrate to you, as I believe, that these things are so, provided you are willing to obey me in this one thing only for a little while. ALCIBIADES. Unless it is a hard obedience, I am willing. SOCRATES. Does it seem difficult to you to answer questions? ALCIBIADES. Not at all. SOCRATES. Answer then. ALCIBIADES. Ask. SOCRATES. Shall I ask you as if you were deliberating about those things which I said you were thinking? ALCIBIADES. Let it be so, if you please, so that I may at last see what you bring. SOCRATES. Come then; for you intend, as I said above, shortly to go to the Athenian people to advise them on some matter. If, therefore, as you were about to go to the assembly, I should meet you and say, "O Alcibiades, since the Athenians have determined to deliberate, and you have stood up to deliberate on the same: is it about those things which you know better than they?" <margin>From the person of the speaker.</margin> What would you answer to this? ALCIBIADES. I would answer, surely, about those things which I know better than they. SOCRATES. Those things which you know, then—about those are you also a good counselor? ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. <margin>We know in two ways.</margin> Do you not know only these things, which you have either learned from others or found out yourself? ALCIBIADES. What other things are there? SOCRATES. Is there anything which you have learned or found out already when you were unwilling to find or say it? ALCIBIADES. There is not. SOCRATES. Have you ever wished to inquire or say what you thought you knew? ALCIBIADES. Never. SOCRATES. What you now know, there was once a time when you thought you were ignorant...

-> Alcibiades I; or, On the Nature of Man. 21 <-

Did you consider this? ALCIBIADES. It must be so. SOCRATES. And yet, I almost certainly know what things you have learned; but if anything has escaped me, do say so. You learned, as I recall, your letters, how to play the lyre, and wrestling; for you did not wish to play the flute. These are the things in which you have knowledge—unless perhaps you learned something else while I was unaware. I think, however, that you did not leave the house by night or by day without my knowledge. ALCIBIADES. I have listened to no teachers except those of these three subjects.

SOCRATES. Then, whenever the Athenians consult about letters—that is, how they ought to be written—will you step forward to advise them? ALCIBIADES. Not by Jove! <note>original: "per Iouem." An oath to Zeus/Jupiter, common in Greek dialogue.</note> SOCRATES. But what when they consult about playing the lyre? ALCIBIADES. Not at all. SOCRATES. Nor are they accustomed to debate about wrestling in the public assembly? ALCIBIADES. Not in the least.

SOCRATES. When, then, and concerning what matter will we consult? Surely not when they deliberate about buildings? ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. SOCRATES. For a builder will advise better than you. ALCIBIADES. [Agrees]. SOCRATES. Nor when they debate about prophecy. ALCIBIADES. Not at all. SOCRATES. For a diviner knows these things better than you. ALCIBIADES. Better. SOCRATES. Whether he be small or great, handsome or deformed, noble or ignoble. ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. For I think it belongs to the one who knows, not the one who is rich, to give counsel on any matter. ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. And therefore, whether the one who advises be rich or poor, it would make no difference to the Athenians when they deliberate on how the citizens may be healthy, but they would seek only that a physician be their counselor. ALCIBIADES. And rightly so.

SOCRATES. When, therefore, and in what deliberation will you be a suitable counselor? ALCIBIADES. When they deliberate on their own affairs. SOCRATES. Do you mean when they ask about naval matters, what kind of ships they ought to build? ALCIBIADES. No, Socrates. SOCRATES. For, I suppose, you do not know how to build ships. Is this the reason, or is it something else? ALCIBIADES. Nothing else. SOCRATES. But truly, about which of their affairs were you speaking? ALCIBIADES. When they speak of war, O Socrates, or peace, or some other business of the state.

SOCRATES. Do you mean when they discuss with whom peace should be made, and against whom war should be waged, and in what manner? ALCIBIADES. Exactly. SOCRATES. And must they not do this with those for whom it is worthwhile? ALCIBIADES. With those very ones. SOCRATES. And only then when it is better? ALCIBIADES. Entirely so. SOCRATES. And for as long as it is preferable? ALCIBIADES. Certainly.

SOCRATES. If, therefore, the Athenians were asking against whom they should wrestle, or whether they should use only their fingertips or their whole body, and how they should compete, would you advise better than the master of the gymnasium? ALCIBIADES. The master of the gymnasium would advise better. SOCRATES. Could you say, looking toward what standard, that man advises with whom one must wrestle in the gymnasium, or not, and when, and in what way? I say it this way: must they not compete with those for whom it is worthwhile? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. And as much as is better? ALCIBIADES. And as much as is better. SOCRATES. And then when it is better? ALCIBIADES. Precisely.

SOCRATES. Furthermore, must not a singer play the lyre and dance to the song? ALCIBIADES. He must. SOCRATES. Is it not then when it is better? ALCIBIADES. Then, certainly. SOCRATES. And as much as it is better? ALCIBIADES. I confess it.

SOCRATES. What, then, since you have used the word "better" in both cases—in the singing of the lyre and in wrestling—what do you call that which is "better" in the correct sound of a song? For my part, in wrestling, I call it "gymnastic." But you, what do you call it? <margin>That which is better in every pursuit is that which is correct in all respects.</margin> ALCIBIADES. I do not understand. SOCRATES. But try to imitate me. Indeed, I would call that thing "better" which is correct in all respects. Now, it is correct when it is according to the art, is it not? ALCIBIADES. That is it. SOCRATES. Is not the art gymnastic? ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. So, that which is better in wrestling, I have called gymnastic. ALCIBIADES. You have so called it. SOCRATES. And is it not correct? ALCIBIADES. So it seems to me.

SOCRATES. Come then, you too; for it becomes you also to discourse correctly. Say first, what is the art to which belongs the right way of singing, playing, and dancing? How is this art collectively named? Can you not yet express it? ALCIBIADES. Not yet. SOCRATES. But strive thus: who are the goddesses of this art? ALCIBIADES. Do you mean the Muses, Socrates? SOCRATES. I do indeed; see now what name the art takes from them. ALCIBIADES. You seem to be speaking of Music. SOCRATES. I am indeed. What, then, is that which is correct according to this art? Just as in that other art I called that which was done correctly according to the art "gymnastic," what do you call that which is "better" in this one, and how is it done? ALCIBIADES. It seems to me it is called "musical."

SOCRATES. You speak well. Come now, what do you call that which is better in war and better in peace? Just as you showed above what was better in each case: in one that which is more musical, in the other that which is more gymnastic. Try to pronounce what is "better" in these things in a similar way. ALCIBIADES. I have nothing to say.

SOCRATES. But truly, it would be shameful if, while someone was bringing you food and saying this is better than that, and when and how much, and then someone asked, "What do you call this 'better' thing, O Alcibiades?" and you had no answer—namely, that it is "healthier"—even though you do not profess to be a physician. Yet in a matter where you boast of being an expert, and rise to give counsel as one who is learned, you fail to answer when questioned. Is this not, I say, a disgrace to you? ALCIBIADES. Most shameful.

SOCRATES. Consider, then, and try to show us what this "better" tends toward in making peace with those whom it is necessary, and also in war against those it is necessary? ALCIBIADES. Though I seek it, I cannot find it. SOCRATES. Have you not noticed, when we go to war, what it is we accuse each other of as we set out, and what name we give to the reason for which the war is undertaken? ALCIBIADES. I have noticed indeed that we are provoked to arms when we are either deceived, or coerced, or despoiled of something.

SOCRATES. Come, tell me, how does suffering those things in this way or that way differ? ALCIBIADES. When you say "in this way or that way," do you mean the same as if you said "justly or unjustly"? SOCRATES. That very thing. ALCIBIADES. Entirely so; and this makes all the difference. SOCRATES. Against whom will you exhort the Athenians to go to war? Against those who act unjustly or those who act justly? ALCIBIADES. What you ask is hard; for even if someone thought war should be waged against those who practice justice, he would not admit it to you. SOCRATES. For it is not lawful, as it seems. ALCIBIADES. Not at all, nor does it even appear honorable. SOCRATES. Here, then, you will make your speeches about what is just. ALCIBIADES. It is necessary. SOCRATES. Is there, then, any other "better" in waging war or not, and with whom one must or must not, and when one must or must not, than that which is "more just"? ALCIBIADES. This seems to be the "better."

SOCRATES. One thing, then, O friend Alcibiades, escapes you: you are ignorant of this. Or, if you went to a teacher without my knowledge, from whom you learned to judge what is more just and what is more unjust, come and show him to me, so that you may make me his student and guest. ALCIBIADES. You are mocking me, Socrates. SOCRATES. Not by the god who is a friend to both of us, whom I would least of all deceive by an oath; but if you have one, say who it is. ALCIBIADES. What if I do not have one? Do you not think I could distinguish just and unjust things in another way? SOCRATES. Indeed, if you have found it out for yourself. ALCIBIADES. Do you not think I have found it out? <margin>He who finds it out distinguishes it; that which is found is that which is sought; he seeks who thinks he is ignorant.</margin> SOCRATES. Most certainly, provided you have sought it.

# ## Thirty-Fourth Book.

[[notes: This section corresponds to the translation and commentary on Plato’s *Laws*, Book VIII, by Marsilio Ficino (the 15th-century Florentine philosopher who revived Platonism).]]

...is [fitting], nor do we speak it as a baneful omen, fleeing the new state. We have already said much concerning dancing and all gymnastic motion. For we call all military exercises "gymnasia," such as archery, javelin-throwing, light-shield combat (*peltastucen*), and all armed skirmishes, formations of battle lines, the leading of armies, the positioning of camps, and whatever pertains to the discipline of cavalry. 

There ought to be public masters for all these things, hired by the city, who may teach boys and girls, men and women, so that everyone in the city knows these things. 

[[margin: Why women ought to handle camps and arms.]] 

Indeed, girls should become accustomed to dancing and fighting with arms; women, however, should move camps, draw up ranks, and take up or lay down arms—if for no other reason, then at least so that if necessity forces everyone to go out on a military campaign, they themselves can meanwhile defend the city if any adversity happens. Or, if a great multitude of enemies, whether Greeks or barbarians, invades the fields, it might be necessary for women also to take up arms for the city, for none of these things is impossible to occur. It must certainly be attributed to a great vice of the republic to educate women so lazily that they do not even dare to fight for their little ones against fierce beasts like birds do, but would rather die and undergo all dangers than immediately flee to the altars and temples, giving the impression that the human race is the most cowardly of all animals. 

**CLINIAS:** By Jove, Stranger, this is both a disgrace and a detriment to the city. 

**ATHENIAN:** Therefore, let us sanction this law: that women do not neglect military matters, but that all citizens, both women and men, give their attention to it. 

**CLINIAS:** Let us sanction it. 

**ATHENIAN:** Regarding wrestling, we have partly spoken. But what is arguably the most important, we have not said, nor is it easy to say, unless someone adds physical gestures to the declaration of words. We shall judge this then, when words joined to things will signify something more clearly about the rest: that wrestling is the most related of all motions to battle, and one ought to give attention to it not for its own sake, but for the sake of battle. 

**CLINIAS:** That is indeed proper.

**ATHENIAN:** But let this be said for now regarding the faculty of wrestling. We divide the other motions of the whole body—most of which can rightly be called by the name of dancing—into two species. For one motion, with more decent gestures of the body, imitates something honorable and worthy; another, on the contrary, with more indecent gestures, leads down to imitating something base. 

And of each, there are again two species. For the honorable and more worthy motion is of one kind when we are involved in war and violent labors with an excellent body and brave spirit. Another is while the spirit is moderately joyful in favorable circumstances. If someone calls this the "peaceful" motion, he will seem to call it according to nature. But one will rightly call that other motion, different from the peaceful one, the *Pyrrhichen* (Pyrrhic dance), which imitates the bending of bodies by which weapons and blows are avoided—by dodging, retreating, leaping upward, and crouching to the ground. Likewise, the contrary gestures which contribute to the motions of the body suitable for preparing agility—whether in shooting bows, throwing spears, or in the attacks of all blows—strive to imitate the likenesses of battle, and at the same time the rectitude, strength, and vigor of good bodies and souls. Whenever it is an imitation that generally confers to the firmness of the limbs of the body, it is approved as right; but what is contrary to these is not. 

But let us also consider the dance suitable for peace in each instance, whether someone conducts himself correctly or not, according to the nature of honorable dancing, with decency in the choruses under the best law of learned men. First, however, the "ambiguous" dance, which falls into controversy, must be distinguished from the non-ambiguous. What then is this, and how is each to be distinguished? 

We consider as ambiguous that which belongs to the Bacchants and those following Bacchus—whom they call Nymphs, Pans, Sileni, and Satyrs—which, as they say, imitates drunken people performing lustrations and sacred rites. This whole genus of dancing is neither suitable for war nor for peace, nor can it easily be determined what it intends for itself. It seems most right to me, therefore, to distinguish it so that we place it separately from the dance of peace, denying that this is "civil" (pertaining to the citizen's life); and therefore, let it be left aside by the dances of war and peace. Let us now return to the dance belonging to us, which is without controversy. 

That genus of the *Musa* (Muse/Art) which we use in peace and in the opinion of prosperity, honoring the gods and sons of gods, is distinguished into two parts. For one is used when we have escaped dangers and labors and have obtained good things; it contains greater pleasures. The other is usually performed when prior goods are preserved and increased, in which pleasure is more relaxed. In such matters, everyone is moved more rapidly from greater pleasure and more calmly from lesser pleasure. Also, anyone more modest and more practiced in fortitude moves more peacefully. On the contrary, the cowardly person, least practiced in temperance, performs greater and more vehement changes of motion. Generally, whether by song or otherwise someone speaks, they cannot do it with a quiet body. 

Wherefore, the imitation of words expressed by the figures of the body gave birth to the whole art of dancing, in which some move harmoniously and others inharmoniously. And since antiquity is to be praised for many other names well and naturally placed, it is also to be approved in this: that it correctly named all the dances of moderate men rejoicing temperately in favorable things as "concinnities" (harmonies) according to music and reason. It established two species of honorable dancing: the *Pyrrhichẽ* for war, and the *commode concinnitatem* (fitting harmony) for peace. 

The legislator ought to explain these in certain figures; the guardian, however, should seek them out and join them with other music in youth, and having distributed them in solemn sacrifices, dedicate each to each. Once ordered, they should be established so that none of them thereafter is done otherwise, neither in dance nor in song, but the same city persevering in the same pleasures, and its citizens always remaining similar according to their powers, may live well and blessedly. 

But now we have spoken of the choruses of honorable and beautiful bodies and noble souls. It is necessary to consider and know the motions of deformed bodies and thoughts, which pertain to laughter and comedy, in words, song, dancing, and all such imitations. For it is impossible for anyone who is to be prudent to know serious things without ridiculous things, and generally opposites without their opposites. However, it is impossible to do both if we are to be participants in virtue. But these ridiculous things must be known for this sake: lest through ignorance something ridiculous be done or said when it is least appropriate. 

Therefore, let slaves and foreigners hired for a price imitate such things, but let no study be applied to them. Nor let a citizen, whether man or woman, be so "free" that they are seen learning those things, but let a new imitation always appear in them; and thus the plays looking toward laughter, which are called by the name of comedy, are disposed by reason and law. 

But as for the poets of Tragedy, who narrate, as they say, serious things: if they ask us thus: 

[[margin: Tragedians.]] 

"Is it permitted, O friends, for us to come into your region and city, and to bring our poems to you? Or has it seemed otherwise to you concerning the tragic matter?" 

What shall we rightly answer to these divine men? 

[[page number: 567]]

# ## On the Laws, or Dialogue VIII on Legislation.

For so it seems to me: We ourselves, O best men, are poets of a tragedy that is as beautiful and excellent as possible. For our entire republic is an imitation of the most beautiful and best life; which thing we certainly judge to be the truest tragedy. You are poets; we ourselves are also poets of the same poem, and as if rivals, we contend for the most beautiful work of tragedy, which only the true law, as we hope, can perfect. 

But do not believe that we will easily permit you to set up stages in the forum and lead out loud actors who shout louder than we do, and thus harangue our children, our wives, and the whole crowd of the city about the same things, not saying the same as we do, but often the opposite. For we and the whole city would be entirely insane if, before the magistrates had seen what you composed and judged what should be said to the people, you were admitted. 

Now therefore, O best men, sons of the soft Muses, we shall compare those songs of yours with ours before the leaders; and if what is said seems to be the same or better than ours, we shall give you a chorus. But if otherwise, O friends, we can never give it. Let these things be so constituted concerning every chorus and its doctrine, laws, and customs—and for slaves separately from the duties of masters, if it also seems so to you. 

**CLINIAS:** It certainly seems so. 

**ATHENIAN:** But for free men, three doctrines still remain. One is the computation of numbers. The second is the measure of length, width, and depth. The third is the knowledge of the circuit of the stars. Not many will learn all these things exactly, but the few whom we shall signify as having progressed to the end. For so it is fitting. 

[[margin: It is shameful to be ignorant of what is necessary.]] 

But for the multitude, it is most right to say it is shameful to be ignorant of what is necessary. However, to seek out all things exquisitely is neither easy nor entirely possible. What is necessary from these cannot be rejected. Indeed, he seems to have looked to this very thing who first spoke thus of God in a proverb: 

[[margin: God will never fight against necessity.]] 

"Neither will God ever fight against necessity," which I indeed think is to be understood regarding divine necessities. For if this were said about human necessities, to which many looking say such a thing, the speech will be by far the most foolish of all. 

**CLINIAS:** What then, Stranger, are the necessities not of human, but of divine doctrines? 

**ATHENIAN:** I think those are they which he who does not learn or experience in any way can never be a god to men, nor a demon, nor a hero, so that he could studiously have care for men. He will also be far from becoming a divine man if he can know neither one, nor two, nor three, nor even numbers and odd numbers at all; if he knows not how to count, nor to number days and nights, nor has he grasped the circumvolutions of the sun and moon and the other stars. If anyone denies these as necessary to a man about to perceive any of the most beautiful doctrines, he will think most foolishly. 

But what kind each of these is, and how many, and when they are to be learned, and what with another, and what alone without others, and what is the universal mixture of these, must be learned rightly before all else. Then, with these doctrines as leaders, one must step toward others. For nature and necessity itself have so obtained, by which we say none of the gods either fights now or will ever fight. 

**CLINIAS:** Correct, Stranger; what you say seems to be said according to nature. 

**ATHENIAN:** So the matter stands, O Clinias. But it is difficult to make laws about these things proposed in this order. Therefore, if it seems best, having delayed to another time, we shall sanction these more diligently by laws. 

**CLINIAS:** You seem, Stranger, to fear our inexperience in these matters. And not without cause. Nevertheless, strive to explain, fearing nothing on this account. 

**ATHENIAN:** I indeed fear what is said, but I dread much more those who have tasted these doctrines, but tasted them badly. For inexperience in all things is not a very heavy or hard thing, nor the highest evil; but much more pernicious is the badly acquired experience and knowledge of many things. 

**CLINIAS:** You speak the truth. 

**ATHENIAN:** It is necessary, therefore, that free men learn those things, as the doctrine has been so devised for the boyish genius that it may be perceived with play and pleasure. Let there be a distribution of apples and garlands, more or fewer, in numbers fitting for the same. Also, the assembly of boxers and wrestlers, and the order of other companionship and consequence, as is usually done, is arranged. 

Mixing in golden, bronze, and silver bowls and other similar things while playing—or handing over the whole sets to one another—they adapt the necessary numbers, as I said, to games. Thus they provide utility to the learners for leading armies, the orders of camps, for household management (*oeconomiam*), and for all other things, and they render them more vigilant. Then, since the shameful and ridiculous ignorance of nature regarding the measure of length, width, and depth holds all men, they lead them far away from this. 

**CLINIAS:** What and what kind of ignorance do you mean? 

**ATHENIAN:** O friend Clinias, when I once heard of it, I finally wondered at this ignorance of ours late in the day; it seemed to me to be the consideration not of men, but of swine and cattle. And therefore, I blushed vehemently not only for my own sake, but also for the sake of all Greeks. 

**CLINIAS:** Speak more plainly, Stranger; what is this? 

**ATHENIAN:** I shall say it indeed. Or rather, I will open it by questioning. Answer, I pray. Do you know length? 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN:** What of width? 

**CLINIAS:** Certainly. 

**ATHENIAN:** And that these are two, and depth is the third? 

**CLINIAS:** That also. 

**ATHENIAN:** Do all these seem to you to be able to be measured against one another? 

**CLINIAS:** Surely. 

**ATHENIAN:** I mean that length can be measured against length, width against width, and depth similarly by nature. 

**CLINIAS:** Vehemently indeed. 

**ATHENIAN:** But if some can do so neither vehemently nor weakly—but some can indeed, and others not at all—and you think all can, how are you affected toward this? 

**CLINIAS:** Badly. 

**ATHENIAN:** Again, length and width and depth, or width and length against each other? Do not all Greeks think they can be measured in some way? 

**CLINIAS:** Entirely. 

**ATHENIAN:** But if they can by no means, and all Greeks, as I was saying, think they can, is it not right that we, moved by a blush for everyone's sake, say to them: "This indeed is one of those things, O best of Greeks, which we said it was shameful to be ignorant of, but to know is necessary, and not at all especially noble"? 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN:** Besides, there are certain other things related to these, in which we mostly err similarly. 

**CLINIAS:** Which ones? 

**ATHENIAN:** What has been done by nature, so that some things can indeed be measured against each other, but others cannot; to know these is surely necessary, or else he who is ignorant is entirely useless. In these, therefore, one must linger for the sake of the mind. For this "old man's game" will be much more pleasant than dice and counters, and more worthy of a free man. 

**CLINIAS:** Perhaps. For these dice and these doctrines seem to differ much from each other. 

**ATHENIAN:** I think these things, O Clinias, should be learned by the younger ones. For they are neither harmful nor difficult, and perceived through play, they will profit the city and never hinder it. But it must be observed if anyone says otherwise. 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

[[page number: 568]]

**ATHENIAN:** if these things seem to be so, we shall certainly approve them. If otherwise, we shall reject them. 

**CLINIAS:** Certainly so. Should not these be sanctioned by us now as necessary doctrines, Stranger, lest our treatment of the laws be empty? 

**ATHENIAN:** Let them be sanctioned indeed, but on the condition that they can be loosened from the rest of the discipline of their order, if by chance they are approved in no way either by us who set them or by you for whom they were set. 

**CLINIAS:** This constitution is just. 

**ATHENIAN:** But let us now notice whether the doctrine of the stars pleases us. 

**CLINIAS:** Speak now. 

**ATHENIAN:** Something strange happens in these, which can least be tolerated. 

**CLINIAS:** What is that? 

**ATHENIAN:** We say that the greatest god and the whole world (the *cosmos*) are not to be inquired into, nor are the causes of things to be searched out with much study; nor do we deem it pious. Yet the contrary seems to be able to be done rightly. 

**CLINIAS:** In what way do you say this? 

**ATHENIAN:** Truly, this doctrine seems foreign to elders; but since I think it good, true, useful to the city, and friendly to God himself, I cannot be silent. 

**CLINIAS:** You speak consistently. But shall we find such a doctrine concerning the stars? 

**ATHENIAN:** We lie now, O good men, about the great gods—I mean the sun and moon, to speak briefly—all we Greeks. 

**CLINIAS:** By what reason do we lie? 

**ATHENIAN:** We think the sun and moon never make the same journey, and we say certain other stars with these "wander," which we call *planetas* (planets). 

**CLINIAS:** By Jove, Stranger, what you say is true. For often I myself have seen with my eyes Lucifer and Hesperus [[notes: Venus as morning and evening star]] and certain others never making the same course, but wandering entirely; we have all known that the sun and moon always wander. 

**ATHENIAN:** These are the things, O Megillus and Clinias, which I think are to be learned by our younger citizens concerning the celestial gods to such an extent that they speak nothing profane against them, but always honor them with praises, sacrificing and vowing piously. 

**CLINIAS:** This is indeed right; provided that first, what you say is possible to learn thoroughly; second, even if we speak less correctly about these things now, after we have learned, we shall speak correctly. If, I say, it is so, I also concede that such a doctrine is to be learned to that extent. Therefore, strive to explain diligently how these things stand; we indeed shall listen and learn. 

**ATHENIAN:** It is not easy to perceive what I say, nor again entirely difficult; nor does it require a long time to be discussed. A sign of which is that I myself heard it neither recently nor long ago, and now in a short time I can signify it to you. Yet if these things were deeply difficult, I could not declare them, nor could you perceive them at this age. 

**CLINIAS:** You speak the truth, but what is this doctrine which you say is wonderful, and necessary for the younger ones, and unknown to us? Strive to show that most clearly. 

**ATHENIAN:** I shall indeed strive. This opinion about the sun and moon and the other stars is not true, O best men, that they ever wander; but the matter stands to the contrary. For each of them accomplishes the same way—not many—by circling; although it seems to be carried through many. But what is fastest in them, we judge not correctly as slowest, and the contrary to be the contrary. Since these things are so, we would be in another state. For if in the Olympic games, we watched those contending in a race, and we proclaimed the fastest to run slowest, and the slowest fastest, and sang praises for the loser as the winner, our praises would not please the runners, I think. But now when we sin similarly regarding the gods, are we not ridiculous, and do we not wander similarly from the right? 

**CLINIAS:** Ridiculous indeed. 

**ATHENIAN:** And in no way acceptable to the gods, when we sing false things about them. 

**CLINIAS:** If these things stand so, you speak the truth. 

**ATHENIAN:** And yet if I show they stand so, all these things must be learned to that extent. If not at all, they must be dismissed; and let it be conceded to us thus concerning these things. 

**CLINIAS:** Thoroughly. 

**ATHENIAN:** But let the institutions already concerning the discipline of doctrines have an end. Concerning hunting, it must be judged similarly as about all things of this kind. 

For the office of the lawgiver seems to be not only this, that he writes laws, but also that he uses that middle ground which is between admonition and law, which we have also used more often, especially when we spoke of the education of infants. For in this matter we said there are many things which cannot be so said that laws be placed about them, and that to attempt it is the part of an insane person. 

But with laws so written and the republic constituted, the perfect praise of a citizen outstanding in virtue is not that by which he is said to be a good citizen who has served the laws as best as possible and obeyed them as much as possible; but that is more perfect: that he is such a one who has entirely obeyed the writings of the lawgiver—proposing, praising, and blaming laws—throughout his whole life. This is the chief praise of a citizen. 

Indeed, it is necessary that the founder of the law not only writes laws, but also adds a certain declaration to them, by which he signifies what things seem to him honorable or base. It is also necessary that the highest citizen observes these no less than what has been commanded by laws imposed on the many. 

But to this matter, of which we treat, we lead a sort of comparison. For it opens more what we wish. 

[[margin: Concerning hunting.]] 

For hunting is a broader thing, compressed by one name. One is of aquatic creatures, another of winged creatures, another of pedestrians; and not only of wild beasts, but truly also of men—and of these, not only warlike but also that which is through friendship; and one indeed has praise, another blame. The plunder of thieves and of camps are also hunts. Wherefore, he who is to establish laws about hunting can neither pass those by, nor impose threatening laws on each in a certain order and with a fine. 

What then is to be done about these? It is necessary that the lawgiver praises what is to be praised in hunting and blames the contrary, for the exercise of youth. Youth, when they have heard, ought to obey so that, recalled by neither labor nor pleasure, they do otherwise than the lawgiver has advised. Indeed, let them honor more what has been said with praise and proposed by exhortation than what has been firmed by a threatening and vengeful law. 

With these things so proposed, a congruent praise and blame of hunting can be written hereafter: so that what makes the souls of the youth better may be praised; what contrary, blamed. Let us say then hereafter to them thus, with prayers interposed: 

"I wish that you, O dearest ones, never be taken by the desire for marine hunting and the hook; nor generally of aquatic animals during the day or also night through lazy hunting by nets to be taken; nor let the love of piracy, through the seas, make you unjust and atrocious hunters of men. Let the desire for theft and robbery in the city or region not even come into your mind, nor the pleasant hunting of birds, which is more servile than free. 

Therefore, only the hunting of pedestrians remains for you. But even that of sleepers which is done by certain intervals interposed, and is called nocturnal, and is of lazy men, is not held worthy of praise; nor also that which is done in the remission of labor, and by nets and snares does not tame the atrocity of wild beasts by the strength of a constant soul. 

Only that hunting of quadrupeds, therefore, remains best for all: which is done with horses, dogs, and the strength of the body. For whoever have a divine strength of this kind, they ought to conquer all quadrupeds in a race, with wounds and weapons, hunting with their own hand." 

[[page number: 569]]

But let the praise and blame of hunting be so distinguished. And this law: Let no one prohibit these sacred hunters wherever they wish to hunt. Let no one anywhere permit a nocturnal hunter trusting in his nets and dogs to hunt. A fowler may be permitted to wander through uncultivated fields and mountains. Let him be driven away from cultivated places and uncultivated sacred places by anyone. A fisherman shall hunt neither in harbors nor in sacred rivers, marshes, or ponds; in others let it be permitted, provided he does not use a mixture of juices [[notes: i.e., poison]]. But let the institutions regarding discipline now have an end. 

**CLINIAS:** You speak excellently. 

### THE EIGHTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, OR ON LEGISLATION.
*
**ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.**

What we just asserted regarding the chief and singular worship of the one God from many testimonies of Plato: we can besides confirm through the *Phaedrus*, *Gorgias*, *Protagoras*, *Statesman*, *Critias*, and the fourth book of the *Laws* without controversy. For in these, he subjects the universal synagogue of gods, if I may say so, to a single king, as one commanding individuals: and justly distributing duties to some and others: and dispensing human affairs through them in order: not as if he were absent from here, but so that he appears in the fourth of the laws, rather so willing...

[[summary: This section of Plato's *Laws*, translated by Marsilio Ficino, discusses the necessity of physical and military education for all citizens (including women), the classification of music and dance into honorable and base categories, the vital importance of mathematics and astronomy for a well-ordered soul, and the ethical regulation of hunting and sexual conduct within the state.]]

...and you answer, which of us will be the one who speaks? ALCIBIADES. I. SOCRATES. Come, say in a word, whenever there is questioning and answering, which one is the speaker? The one asking or the one answering? ALCIBIADES. The one answering, it seems to me, Socrates. SOCRATES. In the previous parts, I have always questioned. ALCIBIADES. Always. SOCRATES. And you have answered? ALCIBIADES. I have answered. SOCRATES. Then for what has been said so far, which of us spoke? ALCIBIADES. From what has been conceded, I seem to have spoken.

SOCRATES. Was it not said that Alcibiades, the handsome son of Clinias, ignorant of just and unjust things, thought he knew them, and was about to address the Athenian assembly to advise them on things he did not know? Are these things true? ALCIBIADES. They are. SOCRATES. That saying of Euripides now applies to us, Alcibiades: "You seem to have heard these things from yourself, not from me." <note>original: "Abs te quippe istauideris audisse non à me." A reference to Euripides' *Hippolytus*.</note> Neither did I say these things, but you did; you accuse me in vain. ALCIBIADES. And indeed you speak well. SOCRATES. For you have decided, O best of men, to attempt something mad: to teach those things which you neither know nor care to learn.

ALCIBIADES. I think, Socrates, that the Athenians and other Greeks rarely ask which things are more just or which are more unjust. For they think such things are obvious. Therefore, omitting these, they inquire into what is advantageous <note>original: "conducant." Refers to utility or political expediency.</note> for those acting. For I do not think the just and the useful are the same, since injustice has benefited many who act unjustly; others, on the contrary, acting justly, were helped not at all by justice itself.

SOCRATES. What then? Even if they are very different—some things being just and others being useful—do you again think you know what is useful to men, and for what reason? ALCIBIADES. And what forbids it, Socrates? Unless you ask again from whom I learned it or how I found it myself. SOCRATES. See what you are doing—that you do not speak correctly—for while it could be shown by the same reasoning as before, you nevertheless think you should hear something new and new demonstrations should be brought forth. It is as if the former ones were like the worn-out equipment and garments used on a stage, which you will no longer put on unless someone brings something else pure and unspotted. But I, setting aside the preludes of your speech, will nonetheless ask: from where did you learn that these things are useful, and who was your teacher? And all the other things I asked before, I will seek in a single question. Yet you will be turned back, I think, to the same point, and you will not be able to show whether you know what is useful through instruction or discovery.

But since you are so delicate that you seem unwilling to taste the same discourse again, I will let this pass—whether you know or not what is useful or useless to the Athenians. However, why do you not demonstrate whether the just and the useful are the same or different—either by questioning me, as I did you, or, if you prefer, using a continuous speech? ALCIBIADES. I do not know, Socrates, if I am strong enough to dispute against you or not. SOCRATES. But, my good man, imagine that I am the assembly or the people in the present moment; will you not have to persuade each one there? ALCIBIADES. I will have to. SOCRATES. Is it not the property of the same man to be able to demonstrate what he knows both to one person separately and to many together? Just as a grammarian educates one person in letters as well as many? ALCIBIADES. It is. SOCRATES. And in the same way, can one show numbers to one and to many? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. And this man is the arithmetician. ALCIBIADES. He is. SOCRATES. And so you, too, can persuade one person of the same things you can persuade many. ALCIBIADES. It is consistent. SOCRATES. And these are clearly the things you know. ALCIBIADES. Exactly.

SOCRATES. This only differs between the rhetorician who speaks before the people and the one who speaks in this kind of meeting: the former persuades all at once, the latter persuades individuals separately. ALCIBIADES. So it seems. SOCRATES. Come then, since it appears to be the property of the same man to show things to many and to one, practice now before me and strive to show me that what is just is sometimes not profitable. ALCIBIADES. You are being insulting, Socrates. SOCRATES. Now, through this "insult," I am going to demonstrate to you the opposite of what you do not want. ALCIBIADES. Speak. SOCRATES. Just answer the one questioning. ALCIBIADES. No, you say it yourself. SOCRATES. Do you not wish to be persuaded as much as possible? ALCIBIADES. Entirely. SOCRATES. If you say that these things are so, will you not be most persuaded? ALCIBIADES. It seems so to me. SOCRATES. Answer then; for unless you hear from yourself that all just things are useful, do not believe anyone else saying it. ALCIBIADES. I will not; but I must answer now, for I think there is no danger.

SOCRATES. You are truly a prophet; speak then. Do you assert that some just things are beneficial and some are not at all? ALCIBIADES. I assert it. SOCRATES. What about this? Are some of them beautiful/noble, and others the opposite? ALCIBIADES. How do you ask this? SOCRATES. Whether anyone ever seemed to you to do things that were shameful but nonetheless just? ALCIBIADES. Never to me. SOCRATES. All just things, then, are also beautiful? ALCIBIADES. Yes.

SOCRATES. Again, are all beautiful things good, or are they partly good and partly bad? ALCIBIADES. I think indeed, Socrates, that some beautiful things are bad. SOCRATES. And some shameful things are good? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. Do you mean something like this: as if some men, while wanting to help a friend or kinsman in battle, were wounded and died; while those who did not bring help when they should have, departed safe? ALCIBIADES. Exactly. SOCRATES. Do you not call such help "beautiful," where one tries to save those they ought to? And that is courage. ALCIBIADES. Exactly. SOCRATES. But you call it "bad" because of the deaths and wounds, do you not? ALCIBIADES. I do. SOCRATES. Is not courage one thing, and death another? ALCIBIADES. Another. SOCRATES. It is not, therefore, according to the same thing that helping friends is both beautiful and bad. ALCIBIADES. It seems not.

SOCRATES. See then whether, by the same reason it is beautiful, it is also good—just as in these things. For perhaps you concede that bringing help is beautiful; but is courage itself good or bad? Consider it thus: which would you choose to have, good things or bad? ALCIBIADES. Good things. SOCRATES. Would you not most of all desire the greatest goods? ALCIBIADES. Most of all. SOCRATES. And you would least of all wish to be deprived of them? ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. What do you say of courage? For how much would you trade it? ALCIBIADES. I would not even wish to live if I were a coward. SOCRATES. Does cowardice seem to you the extreme evil? ALCIBIADES. It does to me. SOCRATES. As much as dying, as it appears. ALCIBIADES. As much. SOCRATES. Life and courage are the opposites of death and cowardice? ALCIBIADES. They are. SOCRATES. And you would most desire the former to be present, and the latter least of all? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. Is it not because you think those are the best and these the worst? ALCIBIADES. Entirely. SOCRATES. Therefore, bringing help to friends in battle, you were calling "beautiful" according to the action of the good—that is, courage. ALCIBIADES. I seem to indeed. SOCRATES. But according to the action of the evil—that is, death—you called it "bad." ALCIBIADES. So it seems to me.

SOCRATES. Is it not appropriate to name each action thus: if you call it bad insofar as it brings evil, should you not call it good insofar as it brings good? ALCIBIADES. It seems so. <margin>Insofar as something is good, it is beautiful; insofar as it is bad, it is shameful.</margin> SOCRATES. Is it not also beautiful insofar as it is good, and shameful insofar as it is bad? ALCIBIADES. Most certainly. SOCRATES. When therefore you say that bringing help to friends in war is beautiful but bad...

...it is as if you were saying that it is good but also bad. ALCIBIADES. You seem to me to speak the truth, Socrates. SOCRATES. Nothing beautiful, then, is bad insofar as it is beautiful, nor is anything shameful good insofar as it is shameful. ALCIBIADES. It seems not. SOCRATES. Furthermore, consider it in this way: whoever acts beautifully, does he not act well? ALCIBIADES. Yes. SOCRATES. And those acting well, are they not happy? ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. And are they not happy because of the possession of good things? <margin>Happy because of the possession of good things.</margin> ALCIBIADES. Most certainly. SOCRATES. And they acquire these because they act beautifully and well? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, acting well is good. ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. Is not a beautiful action a good action? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. The same thing, therefore, appears to us again to be both beautiful and good. ALCIBIADES. It appears so. SOCRATES. Whatever we find to be beautiful, we shall also find to exist as good by this reasoning. ALCIBIADES. It must be. SOCRATES. Do good things benefit us or not? ALCIBIADES. They benefit. SOCRATES. Do you remember what we confessed above concerning just things? ALCIBIADES. I think we said it is necessary for those acting justly to do beautiful things. SOCRATES.
