ALCIBIADES. It seems so. SOCRATES. Did you not say these things yourself, while I only questioned? ALCIBIADES. It appears so.

SOCRATES. If someone, then, should rise up to advise the Athenians or the Peparethians, boasting that he can distinguish just and unjust things, and saying he knows that just things are sometimes bad, would you not mock him, since you yourself assert that the same things are both just and useful? ALCIBIADES. By the gods, Socrates, I do not know what to say, but I seem to find myself in an absurd state. For now some things seem one way to me when you question me, and now they seem another. SOCRATES. Are you ignorant, O friend, of what this condition is? ALCIBIADES. I am ignorant. SOCRATES. If someone asked you whether you have two eyes or three, or two hands or four, or something else of this sort, do you think you would answer now this way, now that, or always the same? ALCIBIADES. I am beginning to fear for myself, but I think I would answer the same. SOCRATES. Is the cause of this not that you know? ALCIBIADES. I suppose so. SOCRATES. Concerning those things, then, where you unwillingly give contrary answers, it is clear that you are ignorant of them. <margin>Ignorance is not the cause of this, but of varying and non-identical responses.</margin> ALCIBIADES. It is consistent. SOCRATES. Do you not confess that you erred in answering about just and unjust, beautiful and shameful, good and bad, useful and useless? Then is it not manifest that you erred because you were ignorant? ALCIBIADES. It seems so.

SOCRATES. Is it not so that if someone is ignorant, his mind must necessarily wander concerning that matter? ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. Do you know how to ascend to heaven? ALCIBIADES. Not at all, by Jove. SOCRATES. Does your opinion wander about this? ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Do you know the cause of this, or would you rather I say it? ALCIBIADES. Say it. SOCRATES. It is because while you do not know, you do not *think* you know. ALCIBIADES. My friend, how can you say that again? SOCRATES. Think with me also about the things you do not know, and you recognize that you do not know them; do you stumble in those? Just as regarding the preparation of sauces, you know surely that you do not know it? ALCIBIADES. Thoroughly. SOCRATES. Do you form an opinion about how it is proper to prepare them and thus err? Or do you rather yield to the one who knows? ALCIBIADES. In that way. SOCRATES. What if you were sailing; would you form an opinion whether the rudder should be turned inward or outward, and being ignorant, would you err? Or would you rather yield to the pilot and remain quiet? ALCIBIADES. To the pilot. SOCRATES. You do not err, therefore, in the things you do not know, if you know that you do not know them. ALCIBIADES. It seems not. SOCRATES. Do you perceive that errors in actions are due to this ignorance: that one who does not know thinks he knows? ALCIBIADES. In what way do you say that? SOCRATES. We then begin to act when we think we know what we are doing. ALCIBIADES. So it is.

SOCRATES. On the contrary, those who are conscious of their own ignorance commit themselves to others. ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. Wherefore, among those who are ignorant, these alone live their lives without fault, because they entrust themselves to the care of others. ALCIBIADES. Exactly. SOCRATES. Who then are those who sin? For surely not those who know. ALCIBIADES. Not at all. SOCRATES. Since neither those who know, nor those among the ignorant who are conscious of their own ignorance, are the ones who err, what others remain but those who, while they do not know, think they know? ALCIBIADES. Only those. SOCRATES. This ignorance, therefore, is the cause of evils, and is a blameworthy lack of knowledge. ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. And when it concerns the greatest things, then it is the worst and most shameful. ALCIBIADES. Most of all. SOCRATES. Do you have anything greater than the just, the good, and the useful? ALCIBIADES. Not at all. SOCRATES. Do you not assert that you have erred concerning these? ALCIBIADES. I do. SOCRATES. But if you err, is it not clear from what was said above that you are not only ignorant in the greatest matters, but even though you are ignorant, you think you know? ALCIBIADES. I seem to.

SOCRATES. Oh, Alcibiades, with what disease are you afflicted! I shudder even to name it. Nevertheless, since we are alone, it must be said: You are involved, my good man, in the most shameful ignorance, which you yourself sufficiently declare by your own speech—you who betake yourself to civil affairs before you are skilled in governing. Nor has this disease held you alone, but also all those who administer this Republic, except for a very few, and perhaps except for your guardian, Pericles. ALCIBIADES. It is said, Socrates, that Pericles did not become wise by some chance, but that he associated familiarly with many wise men, Pythoclides first among them, and Anaxagoras; and even now, at such a great age, he uses Damon for the sake of wisdom.

SOCRATES. Have you ever seen a wise man who, in that matter in which he himself is wise, could not make another person wise? Just as the one who educated you in letters was himself wise, and likewise made you wise; and in the same way, he could have made anyone else. ALCIBIADES. Exactly. SOCRATES. And you also, having been taught by him, could instruct another. ALCIBIADES. I could. SOCRATES. Similarly the lyre-player and the master of the gymnasium. ALCIBIADES. Thoroughly. SOCRATES. This, therefore, is the best proof: that there are some who, since they themselves know, can show it to those they have taught. <margin>The best proof of knowing.</margin> ALCIBIADES. So it seems to me. SOCRATES. Can you name anyone who has been made wise by Pericles? Starting with his sons, were they not foolish? ALCIBIADES. What if Pericles' sons are dull? SOCRATES. But what about your brother Clinias? ALCIBIADES. Why do you mention Clinias, a man who is mad? SOCRATES. Since Clinias was mad and the sons of Pericles were born dull, what cause shall we ascribe to the fact that he neglects you, being such as you are? ALCIBIADES. I myself, I think, am to blame, as I have not applied my mind to him.

SOCRATES. But among the Athenians and other guests, tell me whom, whether slave or free, he has made wiser by his company, as I can show you that through Zeno's familiarity, Pythodorus son of Isolochus and Callias son of Calliades were made worthy and wise men, each of whom paid Zeno a hundred minas. <note>original: "centum minas." A mina was a significant weight of silver, roughly 100 drachmae.</note> ALCIBIADES. By Jove, I have no one to name. SOCRATES. So be it. What then do you think of yourself? Do you mature as you are now, or will you rather try something? ALCIBIADES. There is need for common counsel, Socrates. Indeed, I understand your words and I agree with them. For those who administer the Republic, except for a very few, seem to me also to be unlearned. SOCRATES. What then? ALCIBIADES. If they were skilled, it would be necessary for him who is going to compete with them, after he has learned the same art and exercised himself...

...and exercised himself: only then go to them as if to athletes. But now, since even these unskilled men have approached the republic, why do I need exercise? Why the study of discipline? For I know that by the gifts of nature I will far surpass these men. SOCRATES. Oh, what have you said, my good man? Something unworthy of your nature and your other gifts. ALCIBIADES. Why this, Socrates? SOCRATES. For it pains me both for your sake and because of our mutual goodwill. ALCIBIADES. What is it? SOCRATES. That you should think your contest will be against the men who are here. ALCIBIADES. Against whom else, then? SOCRATES. Is it becoming for a man who values himself so highly to ask that? ALCIBIADES. What do you mean? Is my contest not against these men?

SOCRATES. If you were determined to steer a trireme <note>original: "triremem." An ancient galley with three banks of oars, the primary warship of the era.</note> about to go into battle, would you think it enough to surpass your fellow sailors in steering? Or, understanding that this must be so, would you rather look toward strenuous adversaries—not, as you do now, toward your own defenders, whom you should excel so much that you do not think of fighting against them, but rather consider them as servants to be used against the enemy, if indeed you truly wish to perform some noble deed worthy of yourself and your republic? ALCIBIADES. Indeed, I do think so. SOCRATES. Is it fitting, then, to think it enough if you are the most excellent of your own soldiers, rather than looking toward the leaders of the enemy, to see how you may excel them instead—being always intent upon them and fortifying yourself against them?

ALCIBIADES. Whom do you mean, Socrates? SOCRATES. Do you not know that our city is waging war everywhere with the Spartans and the great King of the Persians? ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Is it not right, when you intend to be the leader of this city, to think that you will undergo a contest against the Kings of the Spartans and the Persians? ALCIBIADES. You seem to speak the truth. SOCRATES. No, my good man; but you ought to be intent upon Midias, the breeder of quails, and others of that sort, who (as the common women say) have not yet shaved from their minds the hair they grew as slaves because of their lack of skill, yet they approach the handling of the republic while still smelling of barbarism. They come forth in such a state to flatter the city, not to rule it. In looking at these men, I say, does it become you to be secure in yourself, and not learn whatever pertains to education—since you are about to enter such a great contest—nor to exercise yourself in what is necessary, nor to prepare what must be prepared, so that having been thus trained, you may finally take up civil administration?

ALCIBIADES. O Socrates, you seem to me to speak the truth. Yet I think the leaders of the Spartans and the King of the Persians do not differ at all from others. SOCRATES. But, O best of men, observe, I pray, what kind of opinion this of yours is. ALCIBIADES. In what matter? SOCRATES. Do you think you would care for yourself more diligently if you feared them as being most powerful, or if you did not fear them at all? ALCIBIADES. If I considered them powerful. SOCRATES. Do you think the care you have for yourself could harm you in any way? ALCIBIADES. In no way; on the contrary, it would profit me greatly. SOCRATES. This one thing, then, is the primary great evil your opinion holds. ALCIBIADES. You speak truly. SOCRATES. The second is that it is false, as can be shown to you as probable. ALCIBIADES. How? SOCRATES. Is it not consistent that better natures are found in a noble race than in an ignoble one? <margin>Proverb.</margin> <margin>It is consistent that better talents are in a noble race than in an ignoble one.</margin> ALCIBIADES. It is manifest that they are in the noble. SOCRATES. Are not the well-born, if they are also well educated, thus brought to virtue? ALCIBIADES. It must be so. SOCRATES. Let us then compare our things to theirs: first, indeed, whether the kings of the Spartans and Persians seem to be sprung from an ignobler race than we. Or are we ignorant that those trace their descent from Hercules, and these from Achæmenes? And the origin of both Hercules and Achæmenes is referred to Perseus, the son of Jove.

ALCIBIADES. And our line, Socrates, goes to Eurysaces, and from Eurysaces to Jove. SOCRATES. And mine too, noble Alcibiades, goes to Daedalus, and Daedalus to Vulcan, the son of Jove. But the ancestors of those kings, starting from them, are kings of kings all the way to Jove. Those indeed are kings of the Argives and Sparta. These, on the other hand, are kings of Persia always, and often of Asia as well, as they are now. But we and our ancestors are private citizens. If you had to show Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes, the progenitors and the homeland of Eurysaces—Salamis—or even the homeland of the earlier Aeacus—Aegina—with what laughter do you think you would be received? But see that we are not inferior to them both in the dignity of race and in education besides. Have you heard how great the dignity of the Spartan kings is? Whose wives are publicly watched by the Ephors, <note>original: "ab Ephoris." The Ephors were high-ranking magistrates in Sparta who oversaw the kings.</note> so that as far as possible, the king may not be born secretly from any other than the race of the Heraclidae. But the King of the Persians so excels that no one suspects the king is born from anyone but himself; wherefore the king's wife is guarded by nothing other than fear.

Once the firstborn is born, who succeeds to the kingdom, all who are under the kingdom celebrate that day; and thus in the future, every year all Asia honors the king's birthday with sacrifices and feasts. But when one of us is born, not even the neighbors notice, as the Comedian says, Alcibiades. Thereafter the boy is nurtured, not by a nurse of little honor, but by eunuchs, who seem the best of those around the king, to whom the care of the boy is demanded, especially that they make the child as handsome as possible, arranging and directing his limbs. And in doing these things, they are held in great honor.

When the boys have completed their seventh year, they go to masters of the equestrian art, and then they go to the hunt. <margin>Education of the Persian kings.</margin> But in the fourteenth year, they are taken up by those whom they call the royal pedagogues. They are surely four chosen from all the Persians of that age as the best: one most wise, one most just, one most temperate, and one most brave. The first of these teaches the magic of Zoroaster, son of Oromasius: that is the worship of the gods; <margin>The magic of Zoroaster is the worship of the gods.</margin> and he also teaches the royal institutes. The second admonishes him to be truthful in all his life. The third teaches him not to be overcome by any desire, so that he may be accustomed to live freely, and truly be a king, ruling over all things within himself before all others, and serving none. The fourth, finally, makes him undaunted and intrepid, so that he may never become a slave by fearing anything.

But for you, Alcibiades, Pericles appointed as a pedagogue Zopyrus the Thracian, the most useless of all his slaves because of his old age. I would tell you the rest of the education and discipline of your adversaries, were it not too long. But these things are clear enough to show what follows. As for your birth, education, and discipline, or that of other Athenians, no one among your kinsmen cares, so to speak, unless perhaps your lovers care for it. Now, if you wish to consider the riches, the delights, the luxurious ornament of garments, the scents of ointments, the crowd of following servants, and the rest of the Persian softness, you will be ashamed of yourself when you realize how much you are left behind by them. On the contrary, if you consider the temperance of the Spartans, their modesty, their ease... <margin>Praise of the Spartans.</margin>

<summary>In this portion of the dialogue, Socrates systematically dismantles Alcibiades' confidence by showing he lacks knowledge of justice—the true foundation of politics—and then humbles his pride by comparing his lackluster upbringing to the rigorous education of the Persian and Spartan kings.</summary>

26 Book Five.

...gentleness, magnanimity, moderation, composure, fortitude, constancy, endurance, the desire for victory, and the love of glory, you will judge yourself a mere child in all these matters. If you place any value at all on wealth, and think you are someone of importance here in that regard, let us not pass over this in silence. Once you realize where you stand and look upon the riches of the Spartans, you will surely recognize that we are surpassed by them by a great distance. For regarding whatever they possess—whether of their own land or that of the Messenians—no one would doubt that they excel us in the extent and fertility of their estates, and in the multitude of their servants (both others and especially the Helots <note>original: "Elotorum." The Helots were a subjugated population in Sparta who worked the land.</note>), and furthermore in their horses and the abundance of other livestock which the land of Messene produces. But for the moment, I omit all these things. 

Of gold and silver, however, there is such a great abundance among the Spartans as not even the whole of the rest of Greece possesses. For many generations now, wealth has been flowing there from all of Greece, and often even from the Barbarian <note>In ancient Greek context, "Barbarian" refers to anyone who did not speak Greek, particularly the Persians.</note> lands, yet it never flows out. Truly, just as the fox in Aesop’s fable said to the lion regarding the footprints of the beasts, so too the footprints of money entering Sparta are clearly worn into the dust, but the tracks of it leaving are nowhere to be seen. From this, one may conjecture that the Spartans are the wealthiest of all the Greeks in gold and silver. Furthermore, their king is the most monied of all. For the greatest part of this wealth reaches him. Moreover, a very large tribute is paid to the king. Indeed, the affairs of the Spartans are grand compared to the rest of the Greeks, but compared to the Persians and the kings of the Persians, they are narrow. 

Indeed, a certain grave man reported to us—one of those who had traveled to the King of the Persians—that he once journeyed for almost an entire day through a broad and fertile province which the inhabitants called the "Queen's Girdle" <note>original: "zonam." A belt or sash.</note>; there was also another named the "Veil" <note>original: "Calyptram."</note>, and thus many other beautiful and fertile regions were dedicated solely to the queen's adornment, with the names of individual places being imposed based on individual ornaments. 

<margin>Provinces named after the queen's ornaments.</margin>

Therefore, if someone were to say to Amastris (the wife of Xerxes and mother of the King) that the son of Dinomache <note>Socrates refers to Alcibiades by his mother's name to highlight his lineage.</note> intends to fight with her son—though Dinomache’s finery might be worth fifty minae <note>original: "minarū." An ancient Greek unit of currency; fifty minae was a substantial but not royal sum.</note> at most, and her son’s land at Erchia perhaps less than three hundred plethra <note>original: "plethra." A unit of land measurement, roughly 100 feet.</note>—she would marvel at what Alcibiades relies upon to dare to fight with Artaxerxes. I believe she would think this man is attempting this relying on nothing other than diligence and wisdom, as these are the only things worthy of esteem among the Greeks. 

But if she should understand that this Alcibiades is entering such a great contest when he is not yet twenty years old, and furthermore entirely unlearned, and not obedient to his friend who advises him to first learn, take care, and exercise himself before attacking such a great king—and she heard him say he is satisfied with the way things are now—I believe she would be moved by wonder and ask what it is this youth trusts in. If we were to respond that you trust in your beauty, your stature, your noble birth, your riches, and your spirit, she would think us insane, oh Alcibiades, knowing that all these things are far superior among her own people. In the same way, Lampido, the daughter of Leotychides, wife of Archidamus, and mother of Agis (all of whom were kings), would marvel—knowing what things surround her—that you, so poorly prepared, do not hesitate to stir up war against her son. Does it not seem shameful if the women of our enemies judge more correctly than we ourselves do about how we ought to be equipped against them? 

Therefore, my blessed friend, obey both me and the inscription that is at Delphi: <term>Know Thyself</term> <note>original: "nosce teipsum." The famous Delphic maxim "Gnothi Seauton."</note>. For these are our adversaries, not those whom you supposed; they are men whom it is permitted to surpass by no other means than industry and art. If you are inferior in these, you will also lack the glory among the Greeks and Barbarians which you seem to desire so ardently that no one has ever craved anything more fiercely.

ALCIBIADES. What care then do you think should be applied, Socrates? Can you show me? For you seem to me to have spoken the truth beyond what can be said. 

SOCRATES. I can indeed. But there is need of a common counsel as to by what reasoning we may become as excellent as possible. For I say that not only you, but even I myself, stand in need of discipline. For there is only one thing in which I differ from you. 

ALCIBIADES. What is that? 

SOCRATES. My guardian is better and wiser than your guardian, Pericles. 

ALCIBIADES. Who is this, Socrates? 

SOCRATES. God <note>original: "Deus." Likely referring to Socrates's *daimonion* or divine sign.</note>, oh Alcibiades, who forbade me to converse with you before this day; trusting in Him, I assert that through no other than me will you attain greatness. 

ALCIBIADES. You are joking, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. Perhaps, yet I speak the truth, that we both stand in need of care—indeed, all men do, but we especially. 

ALCIBIADES. In that I am in need, you are not at all mistaken. 

SOCRATES. Nor even that I am myself. 

ALCIBIADES. What then is to be done? 

SOCRATES. We must neither hesitate nor indulge in weakness, my friend. 

ALCIBIADES. It is not fitting, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. Certainly not, but we must consider this in common. Tell me, do we wish to be the best? 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly. 

SOCRATES. In what faculty? 

ALCIBIADES. In that, clearly, of good men. 

SOCRATES. Good in what thing? 

ALCIBIADES. In conducting affairs. 

SOCRATES. In which affairs? In horsemanship? 

ALCIBIADES. No. 

SOCRATES. For we would go to horsemen for that. 

ALCIBIADES. Indeed. 

SOCRATES. Did you mean in the steering of a ship? 

ALCIBIADES. By no means. 

SOCRATES. For we would go to sailors for that. 

ALCIBIADES. We would. 

SOCRATES. In what business then, and in the duty of which men? 

ALCIBIADES. In those things which the famous and good men of the Athenians do. 

SOCRATES. Do you call the famous and good "prudent" or "imprudent"? 

ALCIBIADES. Prudent. 

<margin>In whatever one is prudent, in the same he is good.</margin>

SOCRATES. Is each man good in that which he is prudent? 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly. 

SOCRATES. And the imprudent man is bad? 

ALCIBIADES. Bad. 

SOCRATES. Is the shoemaker prudent in the work of shoes? 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely. 

SOCRATES. Therefore he is good at this? 

ALCIBIADES. Good. 

SOCRATES. But regarding the making of clothes, is this cobbler not imprudent? 

ALCIBIADES. Yes. 

SOCRATES. Therefore he is bad at this? 

ALCIBIADES. Yes. 

SOCRATES. And so, according to this reasoning, the same man will be both good and bad. 

ALCIBIADES. So it seems. 

SOCRATES. Do you say that good men are also bad men? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. Whom then do you call good? 

ALCIBIADES. Those who are able to preside in the city. 

SOCRATES. But not over horses? 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. 

SOCRATES. But over men? 

ALCIBIADES. Yes. 

SOCRATES. Over sick men? 

ALCIBIADES. No. 

SOCRATES. Or perhaps over those sailing? 

ALCIBIADES. I do not mean those. 

SOCRATES. Over those harvesting? 

ALCIBIADES. Nor these. 

SOCRATES. Over those doing something, or nothing? 

ALCIBIADES. Those doing something. 

SOCRATES. Doing what exactly? Declare that to me. 

ALCIBIADES. Those conducting commerce, I say, and those using mutual services just as we live our lives in cities. 

SOCRATES. Do you say they command men who make use of men? 

ALCIBIADES. I do. 

SOCRATES. Like pilots who use rowers? 

ALCIBIADES. No. 

SOCRATES. For that is the virtue of the pilot’s faculty. 

ALCIBIADES. It is. 

SOCRATES. Perhaps you were saying to command the flute-player, who presides over those singing and uses choral dancers. 

ALCIBIADES. Not these either. 

SOCRATES. For this belongs to the faculty of the choir-master. 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely. 

SOCRATES. Finally, what do you call being able to command men...

<summary>Socrates humbles Alcibiades by comparing his meager wealth to the vast riches of the Spartan and Persian kings, then begins a philosophical investigation into what "goodness" and "prudence" mean in leadership.</summary>

Alcibiades I; or, On the Nature of Man. 27

...who make use of men? 

ALCIBIADES. Presiding over men communicating with one another in the administration and commerce of the Republic. 

SOCRATES. What art is this? Just as if I were to ask you again, what faculty makes it so that we know how to preside over those communicating by sailing? 

ALCIBIADES. The art of navigation. 

SOCRATES. And among those communicating in song, as was said a little before, what science teaches how to preside? 

ALCIBIADES. That which you recently mentioned, choral discipline. 

SOCRATES. But in those communicating in the Republic, what do you call the science? 

ALCIBIADES. Good counsel, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. Does it seem to you that the pilot's art lacks counsel? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. It too is good counsel. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so to me. 

SOCRATES. For the safety of those sailing. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak rightly. 

SOCRATES. But what you call good counsel, toward what does it look? 

ALCIBIADES. Toward the better institution and safety of the city. 

SOCRATES. What thing is better arranged and preserved by its presence, or ruined by its absence? Just as if you were to ask me by whose presence or absence bodies are well off: I would surely answer by the presence of health and the removal of disease. Do you think the same? 

ALCIBIADES. The same. 

SOCRATES. And if you ask the same regarding the eyes, I will answer by the same reasoning: when blindness is driven out and sight is present. And that ears are cured when deafness is put to flight and hearing is present. 

ALCIBIADES. Correct. 

SOCRATES. By the removal of what, and by the application of what, does a city become better and better instituted? 

ALCIBIADES. It seems to me, Socrates, when there is friendship among the citizens, and hatreds and seditions are absent. 

SOCRATES. Do you call friendship agreement <note>original: "consenśionem."</note> or disagreement? 

ALCIBIADES. Agreement. 

SOCRATES. Through what art do cities agree regarding numbers? 

ALCIBIADES. Through arithmetic. 

SOCRATES. And private individuals, do they not agree because of the same? 

ALCIBIADES. Indeed. 

SOCRATES. And each man with himself? 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly. 

SOCRATES. Through what art does each man agree with himself about whether a span or a cubit is greater? Is it not through the skill of measuring? 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. Is this not so both privately and publicly? 

ALCIBIADES. Indeed. 

SOCRATES. And about weights in the same way. 

ALCIBIADES. I agree. 

SOCRATES. What then is this agreement you were speaking of? Concerning what? What art provides it? For that agreement is of such a kind that it exists in the Republic and in each private person toward himself and toward others. 

ALCIBIADES. It is consistent. 

SOCRATES. What then is it? Do not be reluctant to answer, but speak promptly. 

ALCIBIADES. I truly think it is the friendship and agreement by which a father and mother love their son, and a brother his brother, and a wife her husband. 

SOCRATES. Do you think, oh Alcibiades, that a husband agrees with his wife regarding wool-working—an unskilled man with a skilled woman? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. Nor is it even necessary; for this is a woman's discipline. 

ALCIBIADES. Indeed. 

SOCRATES. But will a woman agree with her husband about military work, when she has not learned it at all? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. For you would say that this is, in turn, a man's work. 

ALCIBIADES. Truly. 

SOCRATES. There are, therefore, certain disciplines of women and certain ones of men, according to this opinion of yours. 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. Therefore, in these things there is no agreement between women and men. 

ALCIBIADES. None. 

SOCRATES. Nor therefore friendship; since friendship is a kind of agreement. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems not. 

SOCRATES. And therefore, insofar as women exercise their own duties, they are not loved by their husbands. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears not. 

SOCRATES. Nor men by women, while they handle manly things. 

ALCIBIADES. No. 

SOCRATES. Therefore cities are not then best instituted when individuals apply themselves to their own works. 

ALCIBIADES. However, Socrates, I think they are. 

SOCRATES. How do you say this when friendship is removed, by the presence of which we agreed cities are well constituted, and otherwise the opposite? 

ALCIBIADES. But it seems to me that friendship consists among men for this very reason: that each person performs his own duty. 

SOCRATES. Yet you were saying something else a little before: now, however, in what way do you say again that friendship is made by the application of agreement? Can agreement exist regarding these things in which some are skilled and others unskilled? 

ALCIBIADES. It cannot be. 

SOCRATES. Do they do just or unjust things when individuals perform what pertains to themselves? 

ALCIBIADES. Just things, surely. 

SOCRATES. Therefore, when citizens act justly, there is no friendship in the city. 

ALCIBIADES. This likewise seems necessary, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. What then do you call friendship or agreement, concerning which we ought to be wise and counselors in order to be good men? For I cannot perceive what it is, or in what things it exists: since from your speech it seems at times to be in the same things, and sometimes to be absent from them. 

ALCIBIADES. By the Gods, Socrates, I do not even understand what I am saying myself: and I seem to have been deceiving myself for a long time, as I am in a most shameful state. 

SOCRATES. You ought to be confident. For if you had only noticed this when you were fifty years old, it would surely be arduous to care for yourself; but now you are at that age in which it is fitting to notice it. 

ALCIBIADES. What then ought one who notices this do? 

SOCRATES. Answer those things which I shall ask you, Alcibiades. If you do this, and God wills it—if any faith at all is to be placed in my divinations—both you and I will be better off. 

ALCIBIADES. It shall be so, as far as it concerns me answering. 

SOCRATES. Come, what is it to take care of oneself? Lest we often deceive ourselves, not taking care of ourselves while we think we are taking care of ourselves well. And when does a man do this? Is it not whenever he takes care of his own things, that he also takes care of himself? 

ALCIBIADES. So it seems to me. 

SOCRATES. Does someone then take care of his feet when he takes care of those things which belong to the feet? 

ALCIBIADES. I do not understand. 

SOCRATES. Do you say there is something belonging to the hand itself, just as a ring is? Do you think the ring belongs to any other member than the finger? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. And the shoe to the foot in the same way? 

ALCIBIADES. Yes. 

SOCRATES. When we take care of shoes, do we also take care of the feet? 

ALCIBIADES. I don't quite understand, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. What then, Alcibiades, do you call the correct care of something? 

ALCIBIADES. I do. 

SOCRATES. Do you not say something is correctly cared for when it becomes better? 

ALCIBIADES. I do. 

SOCRATES. What art makes shoes better? 

ALCIBIADES. Shoemaking. 

SOCRATES. Therefore by shoemaking we have care of shoes? 

ALCIBIADES. By this very thing. 

SOCRATES. And do we also care for feet by shoemaking? Or rather by that which makes the feet better? 

ALCIBIADES. By that one. 

SOCRATES. And are the feet better by that which also makes the rest of the body better? 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. Is this not gymnastics? 

ALCIBIADES. Most certainly. 

SOCRATES. Therefore by gymnastics we care for feet, but by shoemaking for those things which belong to the feet. 

ALCIBIADES. Exactly. 

SOCRATES. And by gymnastics also the hands, but by ring-making those things which belong to the hands. 

ALCIBIADES. So it is. 

SOCRATES. And by gymnastics the body, but by weaving and other faculties those things which belong to the body. 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely. 

SOCRATES. Therefore we care for each thing with one art, and for the things that belong to it with another. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. Therefore when a man cares for his own things, he does not then also care for himself. 

ALCIBIADES. In no way. 

SOCRATES. For it is not the same art, as it seems, which cares for us and which cares for our things. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears not. 

SOCRATES. Come then, by what art can we care for ourselves? 

ALCIBIADES. I have nothing to say. 

SOCRATES. But this much at least is agreed between us: that we do not care for ourselves by that art with which we make some of our things better, but by that with which we correct ourselves toward a better state. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. Could we ever know what art makes a shoe better, unless we knew the shoe itself?

28 Book Five.

...unless we knew the shoe itself? 

ALCIBIADES. It would be impossible. 

SOCRATES. Nor even what makes a ring better, if we are ignorant of the ring. 

ALCIBIADES. True. 

SOCRATES. Shall we ever know by what art we might become better, as long as we are ignorant of our ourselves? 

ALCIBIADES. Never. 

SOCRATES. Is it an easy thing to know oneself, and was he ridiculous who inscribed it on the temple of Apollo, or is it rather an arduous thing, not for just any man? 

ALCIBIADES. To me, Socrates, it has sometimes seemed easy and for anyone, but at other times the most difficult thing of all. 

SOCRATES. But whether it be easy, Alcibiades, or difficult, it is certainly this way for us: that understanding this, we may also understand by what reasoning we are to be cared for; but being ignorant of it, we will not. 

ALCIBIADES. It is as you say. 

SOCRATES. Come, how shall we find that thing itself? For thus perhaps we might find what we ourselves are. But while ignorant of this, never. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak rightly. 

SOCRATES. Attend then, by God: with whom else but me are you disputing? 

ALCIBIADES. With you. 

SOCRATES. And I, am I not with you? 

ALCIBIADES. And you with me. 

SOCRATES. It is Socrates, therefore, who disputes. 

ALCIBIADES. It is. 

SOCRATES. And Alcibiades who listens. 

ALCIBIADES. So it is. 

SOCRATES. Does Socrates not dispute with reason? 

ALCIBIADES. Why not. 

SOCRATES. And to dispute and to use reason, do you call these the same in a way? 

ALCIBIADES. The same. 

SOCRATES. But the one who uses and that which we use, are they not different? 

ALCIBIADES. How do you mean? 

SOCRATES. Just as a cobbler cuts with a circular and a semi-circular tool, and other instruments. 

ALCIBIADES. It is as you say. 

SOCRATES. Is the one who divides not something other than that by which something is divided? 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. Likewise, is the harper one thing, and that with which he strikes the harp another? 

ALCIBIADES. Another. 

<margin>The one who uses and that which he uses are always different.</margin>

SOCRATES. This is what I was asking just before: whether the one who uses and that which he uses always seem to be different. 

ALCIBIADES. They seem so. 

SOCRATES. Do we say the cobbler cuts with instruments only, or also with his hands? 

ALCIBIADES. With his hands too. 

SOCRATES. And so he uses them. 

ALCIBIADES. He uses them. 

SOCRATES. Does he not also use his eyes when cutting leather? 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely. 

SOCRATES. But we conceded that the one who uses is something different from those things he uses. 

ALCIBIADES. We conceded it. 

SOCRATES. Therefore the cobbler and the harper are something other than the eyes and hands they use. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. Does a man not use his whole body? 

ALCIBIADES. Completely. 

<margin>Man is something other than his body.</margin>

SOCRATES. Certainly the one who uses is different from that which he uses. 

ALCIBIADES. So it is. 

SOCRATES. Therefore, man is something other than his body. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. What then is man? 

ALCIBIADES. I do not know. 

SOCRATES. You know he is that which uses the body. 

ALCIBIADES. I know. 

SOCRATES. Does anything else use it but the soul? 

ALCIBIADES. Nothing else. 

SOCRATES. Does it not use it by commanding it? 

ALCIBIADES. By commanding. 

SOCRATES. Moreover, I think no one would estimate this otherwise. 

ALCIBIADES. What? 

SOCRATES. That man must be one of three things. 

ALCIBIADES. Which things? 

SOCRATES. Either the soul, clearly, or the body, or the whole composed of both. 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. Nevertheless, we confessed that man is that which commands the body. 

ALCIBIADES. We confessed it. 

SOCRATES. What then is man? Does the body command itself? 

ALCIBIADES. In no way. 

SOCRATES. For we said it is subjected. 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly. 

SOCRATES. Therefore this is not what we seek. 

ALCIBIADES. Not as it seems. 

SOCRATES. But perhaps both together rule the body, and that is man. 

ALCIBIADES. Perhaps. 

SOCRATES. No, least of all: for if one of them does not rule, there is no way that both rule together. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak rightly. 

<margin>Man is nothing other than the soul.</margin>

SOCRATES. Since then neither the body nor both together is man, it remains, I believe, that either man is nothing at all, or if he is something, he is nothing other than the soul. 

ALCIBIADES. Exactly. 

SOCRATES. Must it be shown even more clearly to you that the soul is man? 

ALCIBIADES. No, by Jove: for this seems to me sufficient. 

SOCRATES. And even if these things have not been discussed in full, they suffice for the present as a moderate introduction. For then finally we shall comprehend it perfectly when we find that which we have now passed over because it required a more extensive investigation. 

ALCIBIADES. What was that? 

SOCRATES. It was said a little before that we must first consider "the self itself," but now instead of "the self itself," we have considered what each thing itself is. And that perhaps will suffice. For we could say nothing in ourselves is greater than the soul. 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. 

SOCRATES. Is it not to be thought thus: that I and you conspire with one another, soul to soul, using speech? 

ALCIBIADES. Most especially indeed. 

SOCRATES. This therefore was what we were saying a little before: that Socrates disputes with Alcibiades, using speech not directed at your person, as it appears, but directing words to the Alcibiades who is the soul. 

ALCIBIADES. It surely seems so to me. 

SOCRATES. He who commands "Know thyself," therefore, bids us to know the soul. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. Whoever therefore knows the body, knows his own things, but not himself. 

ALCIBIADES. So it is. 

SOCRATES. And therefore no physician insofar as he is a physician, nor gymnast insofar as he is a gymnast, knows himself. 

ALCIBIADES. Not as it seems. 

SOCRATES. Much less do farmers and other craftsmen know themselves: for they do not know themselves, nor their own things, but certain things even more remote from their arts: for they are intent upon those things by which the body is cared for. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. Therefore if prudence is to know oneself, none of these is prudent according to his own art. 

ALCIBIADES. Not as it seems. 

SOCRATES. Because of this, these mechanical arts seem not to be the disciplines of good men. 

ALCIBIADES. Exactly. 

SOCRATES. Again, does not whoever has care for the body care for his own things, not for himself? 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. But truly, he whose care is for money cares neither for himself nor for his own things, but for things far from his own. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. Therefore he does not study his own affairs who accumulates money. 

ALCIBIADES. Correct. 

SOCRATES. Whoever also loved the body of Alcibiades at any time, did not love Alcibiades himself, but those things which were Alcibiades’s. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. But he who loves you, loves the soul. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems to follow necessarily from your reasoning. 

SOCRATES. Does the lover of your body not depart and desert you as soon as your beauty fades? 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. But truly, he who loves your soul never deserts you, as long as you arrive at a better state. 

ALCIBIADES. It is consistent. 

SOCRATES. For this reason, I am the one who least deserts you; rather, I persevere in friendship, while others depart as your body ages. 

ALCIBIADES. How well you do, my Socrates; I pray you do not desert me in the future. 

SOCRATES. Then strive to become as beautiful as possible. 

ALCIBIADES. I shall try. 

SOCRATES. This is how your case stands: there was never, nor is there, I think, any lover of Alcibiades, son of Clinias, except one—and he a lovable one—Socrates, son of Sophroniscus and Phaenarete. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. Did I not say I had somewhat anticipated you when I came to greet you? For you had determined that you would meet me first and ask why I alone have not left you. 

ALCIBIADES. It was so. 

SOCRATES. This was undoubtedly the cause: because I alone was the lover of *you*, while the others were lovers of *yours*. Your things are indeed sliding away with time, but you yourself are now first coming into bloom. And hereafter, unless you are corrupted by the Athenian people and become more base, I shall never desert you. For I fear this vehemently, that becoming a lover of the people, you may be corrupted by us. For this has happened to many and indeed noble men among the Athenians. For the people of the magnanimous Erechtheus <note>A legendary king of Athens; Socrates uses this to refer to the Athenian populace.</note> are well-masked; but it is necessary to behold them naked. Therefore apply this caution of which I speak. 

ALCIBIADES. What caution? 

SOCRATES. Strip them first, my blessed friend, and learn whatever is to be known before you handle civic affairs or approach the Republic, bringing with you an antidote <note>original: "alexipharmacum." A protective medicine or charm against poison.</note>, lest you suffer any adversity.

Alcibiades I; or, On the Nature of Man. 29

...Erechtheus: but it is necessary to behold him naked. Therefore apply this caution of which I speak. 

ALCIBIADES. What caution? 

SOCRATES. Strip him first, oh blessed one, and learn whatever things are to be known before you handle civic matters or approach the Republic, carrying with you an antidote <note>original: "alexipharmacum."</note>, lest you suffer anything adverse. 

ALCIBIADES. You seem to me to speak well, Socrates, but try now to explain to us by what reasoning we may care for ourselves. 

SOCRATES. Have we not already defined this in the previous parts? For we defined what we are by common consent. We feared that if we were deceived in this, we might perhaps fail ourselves, having care for something else and not for ourselves. 

ALCIBIADES. It is as you say. 

SOCRATES. Next, it was conceded that care must be had for the soul, and that one must always look toward it. 

ALCIBIADES. It is manifest. 

SOCRATES. And that care for bodies and money should be left to others. 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. In what way then might we clearly know those things, since having understood this, we also understand our very selves? Perhaps, by the Gods, we have not yet understood that Delphic inscription which gives correct warning, of which we made mention above? 

<margin>Explanation of the Delphic inscription, Know Thyself.</margin>

ALCIBIADES. What kind? What are you thinking, Socrates, when you speak thus? 

SOCRATES. I will tell you what I suspect this inscription advises us. Indeed, it seems its example is not to be found everywhere, but in sight alone. 

ALCIBIADES. How do you say that? 

SOCRATES. Consider you also, as if it had advised our eye just as it advised a man, "See thyself," how would we think it had admonished us? Would it not be that the eye should look into that in whose gaze it was about to see itself? 

ALCIBIADES. It is established. 

SOCRATES. Let us consider therefore in what we might most look, so that we might see that thing and ourselves at the same time. 

ALCIBIADES. Without doubt, Socrates, in mirrors and other things of that kind. 

SOCRATES. You speak rightly: but in the eye with which we see, is there not something of this kind? 

ALCIBIADES. Very much so. 

SOCRATES. Have you noticed that the face of a man looking into an eye shines back in the sight of the one opposite as if in a mirror, which we call the pupil <note>original: "pupillam."</note>, being an image of the one looking in? 

ALCIBIADES. I have noticed. 

SOCRATES. The eye therefore only then perceives itself when it looks into an eye, and moreover into that which is the best part of the eye, and that by which the eye itself sees. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. But if it looks into any other member of a man, or into anything else at all except that to which this is similar, it will in no way perceive itself. 

ALCIBIADES. True. 

SOCRATES. Therefore the eye, when it is about to see itself, must look into an eye, and into that place of the eye in which the virtue of the eye exists. That is the sight and the sharpness of the pupil. 

ALCIBIADES. So it is. 

SOCRATES. In the same way, my friend Alcibiades, if the soul wishes to know itself, let it look into a soul, and especially into that place of the soul in which the virtue of the soul exists—wisdom—and into another thing to which this is similar. 

ALCIBIADES. So it seems to me, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. Can we find anything in the soul more divine than that around which intelligence and wisdom are occupied? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. That part of the soul is similar to the divine; and someone looking into it and perceiving all that is divine—God and wisdom—will thus also come to know himself. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. And to know oneself, we concede, is prudence. 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely. 

SOCRATES. But if we did not know ourselves, nor were prudent, could we know our own things, whether evil or good? 

ALCIBIADES. How could it be done, Socrates? 

SOCRATES. It seems impossible to you, perhaps, that anyone who does not know Alcibiades could nevertheless know that the things belonging to Alcibiades are indeed his? 

ALCIBIADES. Impossible, by Jove. 

SOCRATES. Nor can we know that our things are ours, unless we first know ourselves? 

ALCIBIADES. In no way. 

SOCRATES. If we are ignorant of our ourselves, we do not understand those things which belong to our things either? 

ALCIBIADES. No, as it seems. 

SOCRATES. Therefore we did not entirely agree correctly when we asserted above that there were some who, though ignorant of themselves, nevertheless distinguished their own things. Rather, not even those things which belong to their things. For to distinguish all these seems to be the duty of one and the same art: to know oneself, one's own things, and the things belonging to one's own things. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. But he who is ignorant of his own things is likewise ignorant of the things of others. 

ALCIBIADES. Why so? 

SOCRATES. If he is ignorant of the things of others, will he not also be ignorant of the things which belong to the republic? 

ALCIBIADES. It must be so. 

SOCRATES. Never, therefore, could such a man be a statesman. 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. 

SOCRATES. Nor even an economist <note>original: "œconomicus." One who manages a household.</note>. 

ALCIBIADES. Nor that. 

SOCRATES. Nor does he understand what he does? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. And being ignorant, will he not err? 

ALCIBIADES. Greatly. 

SOCRATES. Does he who errs not act badly, both privately and publicly? 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. And acting badly, is he not miserable? 

ALCIBIADES. Most especially. 

SOCRATES. And also those with whom he does these things? 

ALCIBIADES. These as well. 

<margin>No one is happy unless wise.</margin>

SOCRATES. No one therefore can be happy unless he be wise and good. 

ALCIBIADES. No one. 

<margin>The evil are miserable.</margin>

SOCRATES. It follows that evil men are miserable. 

ALCIBIADES. Very much so. 

SOCRATES. Therefore it is not he who is rich, but he who is prudent, who avoids misery. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. Wherefore, Alcibiades, a city has no need of walls, nor ships, nor triremes, nor naval docks, nor multitude, nor magnitude without virtue, if it is to achieve happiness. 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. If you are going to govern the city correctly and nobly, the citizens must be imbued with virtue. 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. Can anyone give to others what he does not have himself? 

ALCIBIADES. How could he? 

SOCRATES. Therefore, he who is about to command not only himself and his own, but also the republic and those things that pertain to it, must first be adorned with virtue himself? 

ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. Therefore, neither absolute power nor the license to do whatever one pleases must be acquired for yourself or the republic, but rather justice and prudence. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. For acting justly and prudently, both you and your republic will do a work pleasing to God. 

ALCIBIADES. It is fitting. 

SOCRATES. And thus, just as we said above, you will act while looking into the divine splendor. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. Moreover, looking there, you will clearly discern yourselves and your own goods. 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly. 

SOCRATES. Will you not then act correctly and well? 

ALCIBIADES. We shall. 

SOCRATES. Indeed, I am ready to guarantee that if you live thus, you will be happy. 

ALCIBIADES. A reliable guarantor, certainly. 

SOCRATES. On the contrary, if you live unjustly, looking into darkness devoid of divinity, you will do works similar to darkness, as is necessary, being entirely ignorant of yourselves. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. For if someone, my friend Alcibiades, has the power of doing whatever he pleases, but his mind is captured <note>i.e., he lacks reason or is insane.</note>, what do you think will happen to him, whether he be a private citizen or the republic? Just as if a sick man had free license to have no regard for the doctor's reasoning, but to exercise a kind of tyranny so that no one could deter him, what do you think would happen to him? Is it not likely that his body would be destroyed? 

ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. What if on a ship someone has all license to do whatever seems best, but lacks the mind and the skill of steering—do you see what would happen to him and his companions? 

ALCIBIADES. I think indeed he would destroy both himself and his companions together. 

SOCRATES. Does it not then happen to every republic and every command and domination where virtue is absent, that it acts badly? 

ALCIBIADES. It must be so. 

SOCRATES. Therefore, most excellent Alcibiades, not tyranny must be prepared for ourselves or the republic, but virtue, if indeed we wish to be happy. 

ALCIBIADES. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. But before virtue is present, it is better...

<summary>Socrates uses the analogy of an eye seeing itself in a pupil to explain that the soul knows itself by looking into the divine and wise part of another soul, concluding that virtue is the only path to private and public happiness.</summary>

30 Book Six.

...for a man, not only for a boy, to be ruled by a better person than to rule. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. Is not that which is better also more beautiful? 

ALCIBIADES. So it is. 

SOCRATES. And what is more beautiful is more fitting? 

ALCIBIADES. Why not? 

SOCRATES. It is fitting therefore for the evil person to serve: for it is better. 

ALCIBIADES. It is fitting. 

SOCRATES. Therefore depravity is servile. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. But virtue is noble <note>original: "liberalis." Befitting a free person.</note>. 

ALCIBIADES. So it is. 

SOCRATES. Must not servitude be fled, my friend? 

ALCIBIADES. Most especially indeed. 

SOCRATES. Do you notice how you are now? Whether freely, or the opposite? 

ALCIBIADES. Most especially indeed, as it seems to me, I feel this. 

SOCRATES. Do you know in what way you might flee that which now occupies you? For I would not wish to name that [servitude] in a famous man. 

ALCIBIADES. I know indeed. 

SOCRATES. How then? 

ALCIBIADES. If you yourself should wish it, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. You do not speak correctly, Alcibiades. 

ALCIBIADES. But how must it be said? 

SOCRATES. If God wills it. 

ALCIBIADES. I say it indeed, and I add this further: there is a danger that we may exchange roles, I assuming yours and you assuming mine. For it cannot be but that I shall follow you hereafter, and you shall be led by me. 

SOCRATES. Oh noble youth, my love for you then differs not at all from a stork's; for after it has cherished its winged love in the nest, as it were, it is nourished by it in turn. 

ALCIBIADES. Truly so it is, and I will begin from this moment to meditate upon justice. 

SOCRATES. Oh how I wish you would persevere! But I fear, distrusting your nature and understanding the force of this city, lest it overcome both me and you at once.

-> ALCIBIADES II; <-
-> OR, ON PRAYER. <-

-> MARSILIO FICINO'S <-
-> ARGUMENT. <-

SINCE the second book of Alcibiades is indeed most holy and inscribed "On Prayer," we must collect in summary what prayer is, what is to be sought in prayer, and when, and how. The definition of prayer, taken partly from Orpheus and partly from Plato, is this: Prayer is the ardent affection of a chaste mind, dedicated to God, and desiring what seems good. To this, Zoroaster and Orpheus added fumigations and characters whenever prayers were directed to secondary deities. Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> and Plato, when they venerated the majesty of the supreme deity, took away all external ceremonies, leaving only the pure fragrance of the mind. But concerning all these things, we shall speak more diligently in our commentaries. 

Plato wishes that "the good" be sought in prayer; and this is evident from the fact that he is able to prove this petition by the testimony of the Spartans, and thinks it safe and prudent for both the wise and the unwise, and that such a prayer can be made by anyone and always. But a specific petition for one's own [supposed] good is only then secure when one has attained prudence; otherwise, it is dangerous. Here he discusses much concerning prudence, which I pray you, Cosmo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino's patron.</note>, man of all men most prudent, read diligently, so that you may recognize entirely how much he values prudence. 

A universal prayer, therefore, by which only the good is sought, can always be made. But a specific one, by which something certain that seems [good] is desired, must then be done when one knows what ought to be asked. One will know this when he has understood what is good and what is evil. He will understand this when he has learned it from the Mind. He will learn it when he has turned himself toward it. He will turn himself when he has purged the soul and expelled the darkness. He will purge it when he has given himself over to legitimate philosophy. He will give himself when he has recognized his own ignorance. 

<term>Know Thyself</term>, therefore, was inscribed on the temple of Apollo, lest anyone should approach to pray to God rashly. In what order one must pray in a specific prayer, Hermes taught in his prayers, Orpheus in his hymns, and Pythagoras in his Golden Verses, whose rites we shall explain elsewhere. Plato then, imitating these theologians, introduces Socrates praying thus in the book *On Beauty* <note>Referring to the *Phaedrus*.</note>: "O friend Pan and other deities, grant, I pray, that I may become beautiful within; and whatever things lie outside me, let them be friendly to those within. Let me think only the wise man rich. But grant me as much of this gold as no one can carry or lead but a temperate man." 

What does Socrates seek? The Good. What good? Wisdom, that is, the knowledge of divine truth, which God alone can give, and which only a beautiful soul—that is, a temperate, pure, and bright one—is able to receive. What does he ask first? That He make him worthy of wisdom. For it is surely the part of a rash man to seek some gift of which he is unworthy. Who is worthy of divine wisdom? He who is prepared to bear its light. Who is prepared? He who through continence first, then through temperance, and finally through sanctity—that is, the civic, purgatorial, and purged virtue of the soul—has so expiated his soul that it has turned out beautiful, that is, entirely pure and shining. And then he will have desired the exemplary virtue, namely divine wisdom alone, as the treasure of all riches. 

Therefore Socrates prays that God, the father of all, and his ministers, may breathe upon him as a friend, so that purged by their kind and proper favor, he may emerge. But he passes lightly over corporeal and external things, choosing to have them be such that they do not impede the tranquil purity of the soul. Then, with this beauty already obtained, he hopes that he may estimate wisdom alone—that is, the knowledge of God—to be all wealth and sufficiency, and that he may thirst for it alone. Finally, as if prepared by the aforementioned things, he asks for this glowing gold of divine wisdom. Nor does he ask it out of pride, nor yet with slackness. For intemperate men obtain the smallest knowledge of truth; God embraces the highest and infinite within himself; but the temperate man attains a great and ample portion. He therefore asked for as much of this gold as only a temperate man is able to bear. This indeed I think is the "gold refined in fire" which John commanded to be bought in the Apocalypse.

-> SOCRATES. ALCIBIADES. <-

<margin>Occasion of the dialogue.</margin>

SOCRATES. Are you going to pray to God, oh Alcibiades? 

ALCIBIADES. Most especially indeed, Socrates. 

SOCRATES. You seem to show a certain sadness, and to fix your eyes on the ground, as if thinking something over with yourself. 

ALCIBIADES. And what should I think, Socrates? 

SOCRATES. Great things, as it seems to me: for tell me by Jove, I pray, do you not think the gods sometimes grant part and sometimes deny part of those things which we pray for, whether privately or publicly, and that they nod to some, but not at all to others? 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely so. 

SOCRATES. Does it not therefore seem to you that there is need of great foresight, lest someone deceive himself while seeking great evils, believing he seeks good things—and the habit and reason of the Gods be such that they grant what one asks? Just as they say Oedipus prayed to God regarding his father's kingdom, that his sons should decide it by the sword. Although it was permitted to him to ask for the averting of present evils, he imprecated other things besides. Whence those things came to that event, and from them many other grave things, which there is no need to relate individually. 

ALCIBIADES. But you have brought a raging man as an example; for what man of sound mind do you think would dare to seek such things? 

SOCRATES. Is to be insane not the contrary of being prudent? 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely. 

SOCRATES. Come then, let us consider who these people are. For it is now agreed that some are imprudent, others prudent, and some insane. 

ALCIBIADES. It is agreed. 

SOCRATES. Furthermore, some are in good health. 

ALCIBIADES. They are. 

SOCRATES. Others are sick. 

ALCIBIADES. Entirely. 

<margin>Plato denies that there is a middle ground between the healthy and the sick.</margin>

SOCRATES. Therefore they are not the same. 

ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. 

SOCRATES. Are there some who suffer neither of these? Such as to be sick, or not to be sick. 

ALCIBIADES. It seems so. 

SOCRATES. And do you judge the same regarding prudence and imprudence? 

ALCIBIADES. How do you say? 

<margin>Between the prudent...</margin>

SOCRATES. Do you think a man must be either prudent, or imprudent, or a third thing besides, as a kind of middle ground, by which he is neither prudent nor imprudent? 

ALCIBIADES. Not at all. 

SOCRATES. It is necessary therefore to suffer one of these. 

ALCIBIADES. It appears so. 

SOCRATES. Do you remember having conceded that insanity is the contrary of prudence? 

ALCIBIADES. Indeed. 

SOCRATES. And that there is no middle ground or third thing which makes a man neither prudent nor imprudent? 

ALCIBIADES. I agreed indeed. 

SOCRATES. But...

### Book Thirty-Four.

[[margin: The system of provisions (*annona*).]]
...shall be transported. Similarly, those things which are suitable for these purposes: plants, bronze tools, ropes, and animals which contribute to war. The masters of the cavalry and the leaders of the army shall have care of these things, so that the city is not deprived of the capacity for importing and exporting at the same time when the need arises. Concerning these matters, the guardians of the laws shall enact sufficient and becoming laws. 

Indeed, in no matter shall there be any retail trade (*cauponatio*) for the sake of amassing money, either in the city or in the entire region. The distribution of the *annona* (grain supply/provisions) which is gathered from the fields shall be rightly established according to the law of the Cretans. For those things produced by the region must be distributed by everyone into twelve parts, and consumed in a similar fashion. Every twelfth part—such as of wheat, barley, and other crops and fruits, and also of all animals for sale—shall be distributed by a threefold and competent proportion: one part shall be given to the free citizens, the second to the slaves, and the third to the craftsmen and to foreigners in general. This includes those who have come from elsewhere to inhabit the city for some time and are in need of necessities, or those who have come for the sake of some public or private utility of a citizen. Therefore, this third part of all necessities shall always be for sale, and only out of necessity. Of the other two parts, nothing shall be sold by necessity. 

How then will these be rightly distributed? It is clear, first of all, that it can be done rightly if the distribution is made partly equally and partly unequally. 

**CLINIAS (the Cretan):** **THE ATHENIAN:** In what way? 

**ATHENIAN:** It is necessary that the earth produce and nourish each of these things, whether better or worse. 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN:** Since there are three parts, as far as this is concerned, no one—neither master, nor slave, nor foreigner—should have more, but every distribution should be equal and similar. However, each citizen, when he has received his two parts, may distribute to his slaves and the free-born as many and of such quality as he wishes, by his own judgment. That which is in excess of these must be distributed by measure and number, so that a count is taken of all the animals for which food is provided by the land, and only then should the partition be made. 

Dwellings must thereafter be arranged separately. Such an order is most fitting: there should be one of twelve villages in the middle of each of the twelve parts. In each one, places for things for sale, temples of the gods, and of the *daemones* (spirits) following the gods must be constructed—whether of the indigenous Magnetians or of others whose statues have been consecrated from the most ancient memory. Honors must be rendered to these ancient men. Also, there should be temples of Vesta, Jupiter, and Minerva, and of the others presiding over each of the twelve parts in the highest places, and the houses of the guards should be most fortified on all sides. 

Then, the rest of the region shall be distributed into thirteen parts for the craftsmen. One part shall live in the city, divided through the twelve parts of the city; the others shall occupy the outer places everywhere, and in each village, the craftsmen suitable for the convenience of agriculture shall be compelled to live. The magistrates who preside over the fields shall have care of all these, and they shall foresee how many and which craftsmen each area needs, and where they should live so as not to be an impediment to the farmers, but rather to bring them great utility. The *aediles* (city officers) shall similarly have care of the urban craftsmen. 

Matters for sale shall be under the care of the city prefects, who should first attend to sacred matters. Then, they should vehemently provide that no one commits an injury in selling or buying; they should restrain all those who are immoderate and insolent. They should consider whether the citizens sell individual things to foreigners appropriately and as cautioned by the law. 

Let the law be this: On the first day of the month, the curators shall display to the foreigners the portion of those things which must be sold—namely, the citizens and their servants shall sell the twelfth part of the wheat, and the foreigners shall buy wheat and similar things for the duration of the whole month at the first market. On the tenth day, the sale and purchase of liquids sufficient for the month shall be established. On the twenty-third day, the sale of animals which men need shall take place, as well as of furniture, such as leather, clothes, and similar items. It is necessary for foreigners to buy all things from the owners, so that no retail trade (*cauponatio*) in wheat, barley, flour, or other nutrients occurs. It shall not be permitted for citizens or their slaves to engage in retail trade at all. 

However, in the foreigners' market, it shall be permitted for foreign craftsmen and their slaves to exchange and sell wine and food, and similarly cooked meats—which business is called retail trade (*cauponatio*) by many. A foreigner may buy the entire supply of firewood daily from those who take care of it in the fields, and resell it to other foreigners as and when he wishes. The sale of all other things and furniture which we use shall take place in the common market in designated places, where the guardians of the laws and the prefects, together with the *aediles*, have designated the spot and imposed prices on the items for sale. Here, coins shall be exchanged for things, and things for coins. Each person shall exchange for himself, committing it to no one else. If he does commit it, whether he receives it or not, he must let it rest. For there is no legal judgment for such exchanges. If anything sold or bought is worth more or less than the law has ordered, according to the measures and prices of goods established, that excess should be recorded by the guardians of the laws, and the contrary deleted. 

The same should be done regarding the registration of goods possessed by inhabitants and foreigners. It should be permitted for anyone to migrate to the city under certain conditions, provided they practice some craft, and they shall not remain for more than twenty years from the day of registration. During this time, they shall not be compelled to pay any tax for inhabitancy except for the example of frugality, nor shall they owe anything to the treasury for buying or selling. When twenty years have passed, they shall take their property and leave. But if someone has conferred a great benefit upon the city within twenty years and wishes to stay longer, or even for life, let what they seek be granted, provided they have persuaded the council and the assembly. For the children of inhabitants, if they are also craftsmen, the time of residency shall begin after the fifteenth year of age, so that they may stay for twenty years thereafter; then let them depart as they wish, or if they wish to stay, let them stay after similarly persuading the council. He who departs, having deleted the description which was registered with the magistrates, shall go his way.

# THE NINTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, 
# OR, ON THE ENACTMENT OF LAWS.

***
### MARSILIO FICINO’S
### ARGUMENT (Introduction).
***

The ninth dialogue, after the general discipline of morals and the tradition of many laws, now approaches judgments (legal proceedings). And this is quite opportune. For those who are educated in morals and instructed in the laws are now able to judge; and those who have not obeyed the preceding education and instruction are now to be judged. This "healer of souls" of ours [Plato] has prudently strived until now to preserve an integral health of the soul through warnings; but now he strives to repair what has been lost by every means. 

But such is Platonic charity: merciful, grieving, and compelled as if he were being dragged to cut or burn [like a surgeon]. He does this with such benign caution that he consoles the gravely ill with the sweetest words. He exhorts them as if with magical incantations to make them healthy before he applies the medical hand, which he then moves in such a way that the languishing patient hardly feels it, and conceives far more hope than pain—and from that pain, he reports not ruin, but salvation. 

A man of remarkable clemency, he punishes no one without consolation; he destroys no one by punishment; he preserves everyone according to his power. Even those he punishes with death, he professes to liberate from the diseases of the soul. By the minimal evil of death, he withstands the immense and daily-increasing evil of the soul. He asserts that it is better to depart from here than to live in an incurable disease of either soul or body. Yet he deprives no one of this life unless he has recognized them to be incurable. Nor does he want any punishment inflicted by a law that is good to tend toward evil. Indeed, he says punishment itself is good for many reasons: because it is just, and justice is good; because it either purges a present evil or prevents a future one; because in punishing one, he benefits many by the example, and purges the city of evils. 

To say the sum of it: he wonderfully mixes justice with clemency everywhere. He neither tortures the hard with rigidity nor leaves anything unpunished by softness. Just as in the earlier parts he prescribed divine duties before human ones, so in the present he prudently takes notice of sacrilege before other crimes. He shows how grave the crime of *laesa maiestas* (treason) against divine majesty is. With God standing by, he signifies that nothing of the sort was ever perpetrated by men as long as a certain divine grace flourished in them. But after that grace was lost because of other sins, men, now as if estranged from God, began to sin against God himself through sacrilege. Thus, sacrilege itself is not only a sin but also the punishment for sin—a punishment, I say, not purging someone, but killing them. For such punishment is inferred not by law, but by the transgression of law.

As for his saying that the ancient legislators were "sons of gods" and gave laws to heroes who were also born from gods: this must be explained through what is treated in the *Critias* and *Politicus* and often elsewhere. The "sons of gods" here are understood to be the gods under the Moon, some adapted to governing some tracts of the earth, others to others. These we may call "angels" after the Platonic fashion. Through these, under the name of Mercury in the *Protagoras*, he teaches that the human race received laws. Through these in the *Critias*, he says the first men born from the earth received rights; and he calls those men "heroes" sprung from gods—that is, generated from the earth by the work of the gods. But those laws, he says in the *Critias*, were not written for the ears but were infused into human minds from divine minds by a certain inspiration. Men lived happily under them as long as they obeyed. He adds that by the transgression of such laws, men lost divine grace; and having lost it, they also lost happiness. Falling into misery, they broke into sacrileges, and through sacrilege they finally became the worst and most unhappy. One can recognize here the mystery of the terrestrial paradise and the ejection from it. 

Consider, when he searches for the causes of sacrilege, that three causes are assigned for grave crimes. First: common human fragility confirmed by habit. Second: the persuasion or suggestion of a *daemon* (spirit/devil). Third, finally: a ruinous fault inflicted from ancient and unpurged sins, stimulating one to the gravest crimes. This seems very similar to the "original fault" (original sin) about which many theologians dispute. 

Therefore, when the divine Plato, addressing the sacrilegious person, says: "No human evil impelled you to sacrilege, nor divine evil," understand "human evil" as human fragility prone to lower things, and "divine evil" as diabolical fraud, as he says. He denies these two not because they are not involved in the cause of sacrilege, but because they are not the sole causes. For there is a third, proper cause of sacrilege, which he subjoins: "But a certain deadly attendant, born from ancient and unexpiated sins." By this, evidently, the mind is no longer human but feral; surely through sacrilege, it sins against God, having no further regard for God, since it has already lost human reason, which is the image of divine reason. 

Soon, Plato meets the first instigation to sacrilege with three remedies, as if it were a nascent disease—just as this disease arises from three causes. First, so that the monstrous impulse may be repressed, he sends one to sacred expiations, which in the Christian manner we can call by the names of penance, confession, almsgiving, and fasting. Second, to resist diabolical snares, he sends one to orations and supplications, through which protection may be obtained from the higher and liberating spirits against the lower ones. Finally, so that he may contain human weakness, he mandates that, avoiding the familiarity of evil men, one should adopt the custom of the good. 

Furthermore, since he had ordered the fatherland to be worshiped after God in the Pythagorean manner, he rightly proceeds from the sacrileges perpetrated against persons or things consecrated to God to punishing crimes and faults committed specifically against the fatherland. These he judges to be not only close to sacrilege but numbers them among them and punishes them similarly. He judges these to be three: To sin against the fatherland and to be considered an enemy of the fatherland is: [1] he who, having set aside the laws, reduces the government to human will and lust; [2] the citizen who was able but did not succor the fatherland in danger; and [3] he who, either from avarice or another cause, turns out to be a traitor of the fatherland for his son's sake.

Among these, he repeats the duty of the legislator. He wants it to be this: that the legislator writes laws not as a master for a slave, but as a father for sons—not less persuading than threatening, not less teaching than commanding, not less enticing than terrifying. The work of the legislator should not be so much the prescription of mandates as the discipline of morals. For his end is, by whatever reason it happens, to make citizens good and happy; to punish the wicked is a necessity for him rather than a desire. 

And because the Platonic laws embrace all these things among human laws, they are the most perfect of all human laws and are to be numbered almost among the divine rather than the human. It is not for nothing that the first beginning of this disputation was made from God; then it was added by Plato that all these things seemed to him to be divinely inspired. Finally, from this very disputation, one arrives at the blessed temple of the highest Jupiter—that is, the heaven—by a straight path. 

But since not only in sacrileges and parricides, but also in other crimes, according to the different degrees of fault, other degrees of punishment are to be described by the legislator and assessed by the judge, he brings forward a most convenient distinction for discerning such degrees. Every habit is either of virtue or of vice. If it is of virtue, it is entirely voluntary, because it was acquired by free counsel, ready choice, and the mind's own actions. But if the habit is of vice, it is judged entirely involuntary. For it is a disease of the mind, just as the intemperance of humors is a disease of the body. No one would call a disease voluntary, although you could in some way call voluntary those things which, contrary to expectation, bring on the disease. Furthermore, such a habit grows from obstructed counsel, distracted choice, and passions rather than actions. From these is fashioned that most famous Platonic saying: "Habits of vice are involuntary, and no one is evil by choice," just as no one is sick, deformed, or poor by choice. 

After this distinction of habits follows the distinction of actions. These tend properly toward the production of either a habit of virtue or of vice. If toward virtue, they are voluntary in the way that the habit itself is voluntary. If toward vice, they are called partly voluntary because they are done with the mind somehow consenting and could have not been done before they were; but partly involuntary, both because they secretly lead to detriment, deformity, and disease (which no one would want) and because they arise from a certain ignorance of the end and of itself. Insofar as they are done through ignorance, they are judged to be done outside the will of reason. 

Distinguish again in this way: Human actions, as far as the matter of laws and judgments is concerned, are reduced to five heads. Either they sprout from the affections of concupiscence (desire), or they break out from the irascible impulse of nature; or they come from a certain simple ignorance, through which one is ignorant of the things themselves, though he knows he is ignorant; or they arise from double ignorance, through which one both does not know the things themselves and is simultaneously ignorant of his own ignorance, thinking himself to know; or finally, they proceed from a certain rational opinion—an opinion, I say, about the just and unjust, believed by reason and the laws. 

After such a distinction, he also distinguishes the rules of judgment, through which one notices those who sin by desire differently from those who sin by anger; and in these, it is discerned whether they offended deliberately or undeliberately. Furthermore, whether it was done by force and openly, or rather secretly and by fraud. Then, whether the error was through ignorance—either simple or double. 

Where he deals with the judgments of homicides, he brings in the ancient mystery of the slain taking vengeance on their killers.
