Note that in Plato's opinion, perturbations pertaining to the senses are able to remain in the soul separated from this body. Since, according to his opinion, there remains a certain primary nature of sensing—the substantial origin of the other senses—through which the soul both explains its powers of sensing in this body and, departing from it, somehow folds them back into itself, or, to speak more Platonically, exercises them in the *aereo corpore* (aerial body). Wrapped in this, it enters this [terrestrial] body and exits from it. 

Concerning these, the Platonists distinguish thus: the soul inhabits this grosser body for a short time; the aerial body for many ages; and the celestial body for all time. Why this? Do not wonder if the perturbations of the deceased soul survive, if the senses and memories of these things survive. The ancient theologians thought it probable that the souls of men suddenly killed, being unexpiated, are driven by perturbations; indeed, that they harass their enemies, this being effected not only by human indignation but also by divine nemesis and a presiding *daemon*. 

Our Platonist Virgil occurs as a witness that sense and vengeful perturbation survive in the soul according to the opinion of the ancients, and that it uses an aerial body. For what does he mean by, "And now my great *imago* (image) will go under the earth"? In a very Platonic way, he calls the primary nature of sensing the "image" of the rational soul.

[[page number: 578]]

### Book Thirty-Four.

But why "great"? Because it is both the source of the other senses and the common sense, and it uses a large body after this body—namely, the aerial one. This is somehow constricted while insinuated into this [terrestrial] body; once stripped of it, it is explained into a wide space, as the nature of the aerial element requires. Furthermore, "I shall be present as a shadow in all places; you, wicked one, shall pay the penalty." He distinguishes between the *imago* (image) and the *umbra* (shadow). He wants the "image" to be the sense of the soul in the aerial body, while the aerial body itself is the "shadow" of the soul. But he calls the terrestrial body a "blind prison." 

As for what he says in the judgments on homicide, especially parricide, about the regression of the human soul back into human bodies (where it often pays penalties exactly equal to the faults conceived in the previous life), this is the ancient opinion of the Magi and the Egyptian priests. For they judged no purgatory of human faults to be more convenient than that souls should at some time suffer in human bodies the very things they did. 

Plotinus the Egyptian uses this reasoning in his books *On Providence* to solve the doubts daily rising against divine providence and justice. For he says that what is not repaid by divine providence in the present life is repaid in another, and indeed a human life, in an entirely equal manner. Moreover, it is repaid in brutes, in which often the soul that was once a man's becomes the soul of a brute. But in this last opinion, he seems to have stood alone. For to other Platonists, it seemed [unlikely] that the soul proper to a man should ever become the soul proper to a brute. However, they were content that it transmigrate into other humans. Although Plato does not hold this as certain, he holds it as very probable. 

As for the soul migrating into beasts, he often recounts this, but he does so with such a lack of his usual gravity—narrating it almost ridiculously—that he clearly demonstrates the thing itself is to be denied, and an allegory sought. Namely, that passing into a brute is taken in two ways. First, in the affection, imagination, and habit fitting for a brute. Second, in the habitation and company among wild beasts for the sake of punishment. For the ancients thought that a brutish custom and affection was merely a punishment; but the regression into a man, where a fatherland and family are undertaken, is not only a punishment but a purgatory. 

After this, falling opportunely into a mention of the necessity of law, he asserts that law is necessary for the human race. For without laws, it would differ in nothing from the most atrocious wild beasts. He asserts the cause of this is that no man's genius is so constituted by nature that he sufficiently knows all things which must be known for the public good; or if perhaps he does know, that he is always able and willing to do the best of what he knows. 

But if by some divine grace a mind should arise among men which entirely knew the public good and always generously intended it, there would be no need for laws for him or for his fatherland at that time. For a true and free mind is more excellent than any law and should rule over all by right itself. But since that is granted to no one’s genius, he concludes that we must necessarily live under laws. 

He also says that the study of one's own private good utterly dissipates the city, while the study of the public good connects it. Likewise, a ruinous pestilence dominates in a city when judgment is conducted by magistrates either mutually or clamorously. And when he says the *daemon* of families often withstands many evils, call that *daemon* a "protector," or with Plato's permission, an "angel." And let our mind be called our *daemon* and genius—not only, as some think, our intellect, but a divinity (*numen*). 

He soon prescribes that elders be worshiped with paternal reverence, such that even if beaten by them, you ought not to be angry but bear it patiently. But the "natal gods" he commemorates here are not the ascending signs or the planetary lords of the houses in the astronomical fashion; rather, we should understand them as the Idea of the human race as a principle, and the *daemon* who is the guardian of our life. 

Finally, he warns that the indignation of those above and the punishment of those below must be feared. He warns that death is not the ultimate punishment, but that beyond it are the punishments of the infernal regions, and these are narrated most truly.

***

### JUDGMENTS, however, if they are rendered hereafter as fitting to all the superior actions, the natural order of enacting laws will be preserved. 

But regarding the judgments of agriculture and similar matters, we have spoken; concerning the greatest judgments and judges specifically, we have not yet spoken. Therefore, we shall speak of these next. 

**CLINIAS:** Excellent. 

**ATHENIAN:** It may seem shameful in a way to grant laws about such matters as we are about to treat to that city which we say will rightly possess virtue. For who would not think it absurd if someone, in an established city, thought a most wicked man would be born, as in others—so much so that it is necessary to prevent him with the threats of laws lest he become such, or lest such things be committed, and that those committed be punished by established laws? As if the most flagitious men could be found in this republic as well? 

But since we do not act like the ancient legislators who, being sons of gods, gave laws to heroes (who were also said to be born from gods), but as men establishing these for men, it is right to fear lest some citizen be born to us so untamed and inexorable by nature that [[margin: *]] like legumes hardened by a lightning strike, he cannot be softened even by the fire of the strongest laws. Therefore, if someone should dare to commit sacrilege, we will enact a law about this, however burdensome and unpleasant it may be for us. 

Indeed, a rightly educated citizen we neither want nor greatly fear will labor under so grave a disease. But their slaves perhaps, and foreigners, and the slaves of foreigners, will attempt many such things. For their sake especially, and because the entire nature of men is weak, I will write laws both about sacrilege and about other things which can hardly, or in no way, be cured. But first, preambles according to the order established in the previous parts must be placed before all these as briefly as possible. 

To him, therefore, who—drawn by day and excited by night by a nefarious desire—seeks out temples to steal, someone might say these things for the sake of instruction and warning: 

"O wonderful man, no human evil, nor divine, turns you to sacrilege; but a certain deadly gadfly (*asilus*), born from ancient and unexpiated flagrant crimes in men, is driving you about—which you ought to flee with all your strength. How you shall flee, listen: When such a thought arises in your mind, flee to expiations, I beseech you. Flee as a suppliant to the sacrifices of the liberating gods. Flee to the company of good men, where you may partly hear and partly say yourself that the just and honorable things must be worshiped by everyone. Above all, flee the company of the wicked. If you do these things, and the disease ceases, it will be well with you. Otherwise, thinking it better to die, cease to live." 

When we have sung these exordia (preambles) to those into whose minds an impious and pestilential thought toward the city has fallen, whichever of them obeys, we will dismiss them in silence. For those men not persuaded by the preamble, we will then enact the law, thundering more loudly: 

"Whoever is caught in sacrilege, if he is a slave or a foreigner, let the calamity of his deed be branded in letters on his face and hands; having been beaten as seems fit to the judges, let him be driven naked outside the borders. For perhaps, made more self-controlled by this punishment, he will finally turn out better. For no punishment made by law tends toward evil. But it is almost always accustomed to effect one of two things: for he who has paid the penalty usually becomes either better or certainly less bad. 

But if some citizen is caught attempting to perpetrate such a thing against the gods, or parents, or the fatherland, and having set his mind to the greatest injury: let the judge consider that this man, because he was well-taught and educated from a boy and yet did not abstain from the greatest crime, cannot be cured. For him, the penalty of death is the minimum of evils. Having been disgraced so that he may help others by example, let him be destroyed outside the borders. To his children, however, and to his entire kin, if they have shunned their father's morals—because, being born from evil, they have bravely followed virtue—let honor and praise be shown. 

None of their money shall be confiscated into the treasury in a republic in which the [[shares of land]] must always remain the same and equal.

[[margin: * The Greek codex has "σκληρόν" (skleron). See the Chiliades (of Erasmus).]]

[[page number: 579]]

### De Legib. Vel, de Legumlat. Dial. IX.

...in which it is necessary that the shares of land (*sortes*) always remain the same and equal. But when someone has committed those things which must be paid for by a fine, whatever he possesses above his share shall be expended; the share itself shall remain intact. The guardians of the laws shall always report the exact truth of this matter to the judges from the recorded census, lest anyone ever be deprived of his share on account of poverty. 

But if someone should seem worthy of a greater penalty and is not freed by the bail and liberality of friends, let him be punished with manifest and long-lasting chains and other shames. Let no sin be unpunished, nor let any fugitive go away unpunished. But let him pay the penalty either by death, or chains, or lashes, or by sitting or standing ignobly in sacred places, or being led to the extremities of the region, or being fined in money by that ratio which we described. 

The judges of capital crimes shall be the guardians of the laws, and the best ones elected from their number who served as magistrates in the immediately preceding year. In what way the accusations, citations, and similar things should be done, later legislators shall determine. But the manner of voting and giving sentence is our duty to prescribe by law. 

Manifestly, therefore, let these be enacted. But before this, the judges shall sit as close as possible in the presence of the accuser and the defender, preserving their dignity. There, let all citizens who abound in leisure be present and diligently hear such judgments. In these, when the first speech has been made by the accuser, the defender shall say the second. Then, the senior among the judges shall examine what has been said with all diligence; after him, all the others shall consider whatever they think ought to be inquired into, whether said or unsaid by the adversaries. He who thinks nothing worthy of his discussion should leave the examination to another. 

At last, the written conclusions reached then shall be deposited in the shrine of Vesta, with the seals of all the judges attached. The next day, congregating in the same place, they shall examine and judge in the same way, and having applied the seals to all that was said, they shall deposit them. When they have done this similarly a third time, with seals and witnesses sufficiently assumed, each bringing a sacred vote, let them affirm by an oath by Vesta that they will judge truly and justly to the best of their power; and so they shall put an end to this judgment.

After sins committed against the gods, let us speak of those committed to the ruin of the republic. He who reduces the government to a man's whim and subjects the laws to him, and thus subjects the city to factions and fills it with seditions by force used against the laws—this man must be judged the greatest enemy of the whole city. 

The second enemy is he who, although not a participant in this crime, nevertheless, while functioning in the highest offices in that republic, does not notice these conspiracies; or if he does notice them, does not succor the fatherland out of a certain timidity. Therefore, every man who strives to be a citizen of any value should report these things to the judges and drag him into judgment who, having plotted against the fatherland, tries to turn it to an iniquitous government by force. The judges of this crime shall be the same as for sacrilege, and the entire judgment shall be carried out similarly; and the votes which win by majority shall condemn him to death. 

To speak briefly, let the sons not pay for the sins of the father, unless the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have been consecutively guilty of capital crimes. These the city should send back to their ancient fatherland with their goods, the share of land (*sors*) always excepted. And from the sons of citizens of whom there are more than one, not fewer than ten years old, let them choose by lot those whom the fathers or paternal and maternal grandfathers have named. Let their names be sent to Delphi, and he who is approved by the oracle of Apollo, to him let the share and the destitute house be restored by a luckier fortune. 

**CLINIAS:** That is right. 

**ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, there is a third common law concerning judges and the manner of judgment against those accused of treason. And concerning the staying of sons and grandsons or their departure from the fatherland, let there be one law against three similarly: the traitor, the sacrilegious, and the violent overthrower of civil laws. 

Concerning theft: whether someone has stolen something great or small, let there be one law and a similar penalty for all. For anyone condemned for theft, if his goods beyond his share of land are sufficient, let him pay double; otherwise, let him be bound in chains until he either persuades him to whom he owes it or pays it back. If it was a public theft, let him only then be freed from prison when he has persuaded the city or paid double. 

**CLINIAS:** In what way, Guest, do we say it makes no difference whether the theft is great or small, or taken from a sacred place or not, or however else it happens? Since theft can be committed in many ways, the legislator ought to infer the variety and dissimilarity of the crime and not punish with similar penalties those things which are not similar. 

**ATHENIAN:** Oportunely, O Clinias, you have pulled me back from my running impetus and brought to my memory what I had once thought: that up to this day, laws have in no way been rightly constituted, as it occurs to us to say while considering the present matters. 

**CLINIAS:** How so? 

**ATHENIAN:** We have used a fitting image when we compared all those who have received laws until now to those slaves who are cared for by other slaves. Surely it is not right to be ignorant of this: if some doctor of those who heal by a certain use without reason should hear a free doctor and a student of philosophy talking to a free patient—while he investigates the beginnings of the disease with reasons and discourses more diligently on the nature of bodies—he will immediately laugh. He will say against him what is always ready for most doctors in this matter: "You are not healing the sick man, O fool; but as if he needed doctrine and not health, you are teaching him." 

**CLINIAS:** Will he not seem to speak rightly? 

**ATHENIAN:** Will he not rightly object the same to us? That whoever discourses on laws as we are doing now is not establishing laws, but educating citizens? 

**CLINIAS:** Perhaps. 

**ATHENIAN:** But it happens luckily for us at present. 

**CLINIAS:** What? 

**ATHENIAN:** That nothing urges us to enact laws; but we ourselves, having undertaken this consideration spontaneously, strive to perceive regarding every discipline of the republic what is best and necessary, and how it may be accomplished. Since it is permitted to us, if we wish, to consider what is best or what is most necessary in laws, let us choose which seems best to us to treat at present. 

**CLINIAS:** This is a ridiculous option, Guest. It clearly makes us like those who are so compelled by huge necessity to enact laws at present that it does not seem permitted to wait until tomorrow. But to us, by the help of God—just as to those who construct something from stones or any other material—it is permitted to collect them easily, from which future conveniences for the work will be chosen without any haste. As if we were builders by no means hurrying, let us now pour some foundations and take other things from here for building, so that in enacting laws, some things are placed now as if for the first time, and others are added to those already placed. 

**ATHENIAN:** In this way, more according to nature, O Clinias, our view of the laws will become a shorthand. But let us consider this by the gods regarding legislators. 

**CLINIAS:** What?

[[page number: 580]]

### Book Thirty-Four.

**ATHENIAN:** The writings and discourses of many are extant in cities, but there are also the writings and discourses of the legislator. 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN:** Shall we then apply our minds to the works of poets and other writers composed concerning the manner of living, but to the legislators' works not at all? Or to these most of all? 

**CLINIAS:** To these entirely. 

**ATHENIAN:** Therefore, it is necessary for the legislator alone among those writing to consult concerning the honorable, the good, and the just, and to teach what sort of things these are, and how they are to be done by those who are to be happy. 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN:** For it is shameful, when Homer, Tyrtaeus, and other poets have written well concerning the life and studies of men—it is shameful, I say, for Lycurgus and Solon, and other legislators, to do it less. Rightly, therefore, the laws themselves ought to show forth this excellence above all other writings; the writings of others should be approved if they are in agreement with the laws, but if dissonant, they should be mocked. Thus, let laws be written for cities so that the maker of the laws acts entirely in the persona of a father and mother. Let the writings have the virtue of charity and prudence rather than the command of a master and tyrant only threatening and describing, while assigning no reason at all. Let us consider, therefore, if we must proceed in this way, whether we can or not. But let us be girded now; and proceeding by this way according to our powers, even if it is necessary to suffer anything, let us endure it. May it be successful—and it will be, surely, if God wills. 

**CLINIAS:** You have spoken rightly; therefore let us do so. 

**ATHENIAN:** We must consider first, then, as we began, diligently concerning sacrilege, theft, and all other injuries; nor should we take it hard if, in that very description of laws, we have already placed some and are debating others. For we are not yet legislators, but are being made so, and perhaps will be soon. But if it seems we must consider these things I proposed as I said, let us consider them. 

**CLINIAS:** By all means. 

**ATHENIAN:** Concerning all honorable and just things, let us strive to see wherein we (who desire to excel others, even if we cannot) agree with ourselves, and wherein we differ, and likewise how others differ from themselves. 

**CLINIAS:** What differences do you mean? 

**ATHENIAN:** I will try to explain. Concerning justice entirely and just men and things and actions, we all somehow agree: namely, that all these things are honorable and beautiful. So much so that if someone asserts that just men, even if deformed in body, are most beautiful according to the habit of justice itself, no one would reprove his judgment. 

**CLINIAS:** Almost no one who speaks thus will seem to speak wrongly. 

**ATHENIAN:** Rightly, therefore, all things which are done justly are honorable and beautiful. But the *passiones* (passions/sufferings) of all are almost similar to their actions. 

**CLINIAS:** What is this? 

**ATHENIAN:** Every action which is just, insofar as it is justice, is a participant in the honorable. 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN:** Wherefore, if a just *passio* (suffering/penalty) were said to be a participant in equity, the honorable, and justice, the speech will not be dissonant for us. 

**CLINIAS:** You speak the truth. 

**ATHENIAN:** But if we affirm a certain suffering to be just but deny it to be honorable, the just and the honorable will be dissonant with each other. For just things will be said to be most shameful. 

**CLINIAS:** How did you say that? 

**ATHENIAN:** Nothing difficult to know. For the laws which were placed for us a little before will seem to prescribe things entirely contrary in these words. 

**CLINIAS:** In what way? 

**ATHENIAN:** We judged that the sacrilegious man would justly die, and likewise the enemy of well-placed laws. And when we were about to write many laws of this kind, we pulled back, considering these sufferings to be infinite both in number and magnitude: the most just of all sufferings, but also the most shameful of all. Will not the honorable and the just now seem sometimes as the same, and sometimes as contrary? 

**CLINIAS:** So it seems. 

**ATHENIAN:** Many, therefore, call the honorable and the just dissonant in this way, as if they were discrepant. 

**CLINIAS:** So it clearly appears. 

**ATHENIAN:** But again, let us see, O Clinias, how we agree on these. 

**CLINIAS:** What agreement do you mean? 

**ATHENIAN:** I think it was stated by me clearly in the previous parts. 

**CLINIAS:** In what way? 

**ATHENIAN:** If it was not said above, at least consider me to be saying it now. 

**CLINIAS:** What? 

**ATHENIAN:** That all evil men are entirely not evil by choice (*non sponte*). If this is so, it is necessary that this also follows. 

**CLINIAS:** What? 

**ATHENIAN:** That to be unjust is an evil, and an evil is not such by choice. To be done not by choice can by no means ever be voluntary. He, therefore, who thinks justice is involuntary will think that a man acting unjustly acts unjustly not by choice. I must also agree with myself, since I confess that all men do injury not by choice—although someone might object to us for the sake of ambition or contention: that the unjust are indeed not unjust by choice, but many of them do injury by choice. Surely my opinion is not this, but the former. How then shall I agree with my own words if you ask me thus, O Clinias and Megillus: "If these things are so, Guest, what do you advise us concerning the city of the Magnetians? Should we give them laws or not?" I would advise giving laws. Then you would say: "Will you then distinguish for them injuries done by choice and those not by choice? And will you write greater fines for the former and lesser for the latter? Or equal for all, since no injuries are done entirely by choice?" 

**CLINIAS:** You are right, Guest. But for what shall we use these things which were just said? 

**ATHENIAN:** You have asked well. We shall use them first for this. 

**CLINIAS:** For what? 

**ATHENIAN:** Let us repeat by memory that we stated in the previous parts that there is much and great turbulence and dissension among us concerning the just. Resuming this, let us ask ourselves: is it becoming, when we have in no way declared the difference of these, to bring into the middle this opinion of ours as if it were divinely spoken (which in any city are placed by all ancient legislators as two species of injuries—namely, those done by choice and those not by choice—and are thus variedly punished), and to not confirm in any way how it stands rightly? It is by no means becoming. But it is necessary before we place the laws to signify how these two are and what difference they have; so that when we impose punishment on both, everyone may understand and be able to judge somehow whether it was imposed conveniently or otherwise. 

**CLINIAS:** You seem to us to speak rightly, Guest. For it is necessary for us to do one of two things: either not to say that no injuries are done by choice, or before we proceed to other things, to explain how it is rightly said. 

**ATHENIAN:** I will by no means suffer either of these—namely, that I should deny what I think to be so. Nor would that be my duty, nor pious. How these two differ (if they do not differ in being done by choice or not by choice), and in what else they differ, let us somehow try to open. 

**CLINIAS:** In no other way, Guest, can we understand these.

[[page number: 581]]

### De Legib. Vel, de Legumlat. Dial. IX.

**ATHENIAN:** So let it be. Come then, do not many damages and inconveniences happen among citizens in exchange and custom, in which the voluntary and the involuntary seem to abound? 

**CLINIAS:** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN:** No one would not think inconveniences and harms to be injuries, and they would think there is a twofold injury in them: one not by choice, the other by choice. For all damages done not by choice are not less in number or magnitude than those done by choice. But consider, I pray, whether I bring forward something true next, or nothing at all. For, O Clinias and Megillus, if someone harms someone else unwillingly, shall I say he injures him unwillingly? Or because of that, shall I place that as an injury done not by choice in the laws? Rather, I would call that damage no injury, whether it be greater or smaller. Often we even say that he who conferred a utility incorrectly is doing an injury, if this utility does not surpass the harm. For almost, O friends, it is not right that he should be called just or unjust simply because he confers something or takes something away. 

Therefore, it is not that, but whether he benefits or harms someone in honest ways and a just manner, or the contrary, that the legislator must consider. He must look to these two things: to the injury and the damage. So that he may bring back each thing to an unharmed and whole state according to his powers, restore what is lost, raise up what fell, and repair the killed or wounded. He should always strive so that discords raised by damages may be reduced to friendship through the laws. 

**CLINIAS:** These things are spoken well. 

**ATHENIAN:** Unjust damages and gains, therefore, if perhaps some lucre follows from an injury, must be cured as if they were diseases of the soul, if they are curable. Let the cure of injustice be led thither. 

**CLINIAS:** To where? 

**ATHENIAN:** So that whoever has committed injuries, whether great or small, may be corrected by the law through teaching, and be compelled entirely, either so that he may never again dare to commit such a thing by choice, or at least much more rarely, having been deterred by the imposition of the penalty. Indeed, we say it is the duty of the best laws to so instruct the minds of men that they hate injustice; and that they either love the nature of the just or at least do not hate it—whether the legislator achieves this by works or words, by pleasure or pain, by honor or infamy, or by fining in money or by gifts, or in any other way. 

Those whom the legislator has perceived to be incurable, he will affect with the ultimate punishment, not being ignorant that it will be better for those who are incurable to die than to live; and if they are deprived of life, they benefit others in a twofold way. For by their example, others are deterred from sin, and the city itself is purged of wicked men. For this reason, the conditor of the law will punish incurable men with death, and by no other means. 

**CLINIAS:** These things seem to have been said by you with great moderation. But we would gladly hear you speak more clearly again on the difference between injury and damage, and how they are done by choice. 

**ATHENIAN:** I will try both to do and to say as you command. It is certainly established that, in speaking between you about the soul, you often say and hear that one affection or part is present in it by nature, which we call irascibility (*iracundia*), contentious and difficult, which, being unconsidered, overthrows many things. 

**CLINIAS:** Without a doubt. 

**ATHENIAN:** But we say pleasure is not the same as anger (*ira*), but dominating from a contrary power; which compels by persuasion together with a certain violent deception, so that whatever it wants, you do it. 

**CLINIAS:** Most especially. 

**ATHENIAN:** Whoever places ignorance as the third cause of offending will not err. But he who distinguishes this twofold will be a better legislator: he will place one as simple, the other as double. Simple ignorance he will judge to be the cause of light sins; but he will call it double when someone is not only held by ignorance but, inflated by the opinion of wisdom, thinks he knows those things which he is entirely ignorant of. If this has attained strength and robustness, he will judge it to be the cause of huge and most shameful crimes; if it is pressed by weakness, he will think the sins proceeding from it—both of boys and of elders—are indeed sins, and will prescribe laws for them as for sins, but the mildest of all and full of much mercy and indulgence. 

**CLINIAS:** That is equitable. 

**ATHENIAN:** Concerning pleasure and anger, almost all of us agree that some men conquer them and others are conquered. And so it is entirely. 

**CLINIAS:** Entirely so. 

**ATHENIAN:** But that some overcome ignorance and are overcome by others, we have never heard. 

**CLINIAS:** You tell the truth. 

**ATHENIAN:** We say each of these drags a man to itself, often pulled to contrary things at the same time. 

**CLINIAS:** Indeed, most often. 

**ATHENIAN:** Now I will explain to you clearly and without any ambiguity what I call just and what unjust. For the tyranny of anger and fear, of pleasure and pain, of envy and desire in the soul—whether it harms or not—I call "injustice" entirely. But the opinion of the best, by which reason a city or some private persons think, if it dominates the soul and adorns every man (even if something turned out less rightly for him), I call "justice." Whatever is done from there, I call "just," and I hold those who willingly obey this kind of principality to live best. Such damage is thought by many to be an injury committed not by choice. But we do not contend about words. 

Truly, since three species of sins have been spoken of, these must first be repeated more diligently in memory. One species we judge to be of pain, which we call anger (*ira*) and fear. 

**CLINIAS:** Entirely. 

**ATHENIAN:** The second is of pleasure and desires. The third species is the appetite and longing of hope and of true opinion concerning the best. These being again divided twofold, five species are fashioned; for which five species of laws differing among themselves must be placed in two genera. 

**CLINIAS:** What are these genera? 

**ATHENIAN:** One which is committed by force and openly; the other which is committed secretly and with deception in the shadows. But sometimes it is done by both. If that is treated by right, it will be coerced by the harshest laws. 

**CLINIAS:** It is equitable. 

**ATHENIAN:** But let us return there now, from whence we digressed here; and let us apply ourselves to terminating the laws. We had proposed to speak of the sacrilegious, of traitors, and of those who corrupt the laws by changing the republic. Someone will perhaps commit one of these on account of insanity, either pressed by disease, or by old age, or being in the state of a boy, so that he differs in nothing from those. And if it shall be declared to the elected judges that he did such a thing, and by the defense referring it he shall be judged to have committed it so affected, let him restore the damage he brought simply; let the other things be remitted to him, unless—a man having been killed—the world is not yet clean of the slaughter. For thus, having set out elsewhere, let him be a pilgrim for a year. And if he returns before the time established by law has passed, or is even caught within the borders, let him be detained in the public prison for two years by the guardians of the laws; thereafter let him be free from chains. 

But as we began, let us write the absolute laws concerning each species of slaughter. And first, let us speak of those done by force and not by choice. If anyone—not by choice, whether in a contest or in public gymnasia, whether by choice immediately or from wounds followed thereafter by death—has killed a friend, or similarly in war, or in a warlike exercise instituted by the magistrates (whether with naked bodies or armed in imitation of true war), let him be clean according to the law brought from Delphic Apollo. Let all doctors who have killed not by choice while healing be clean. 

But if someone by his own hand, not by choice—whether with a naked body, or with an instrument, a weapon, or food or drink, by the addition of fire or cold or the surge of waves, or the privation of breath (whether he does this with his own body or through other things)—has killed someone, let him be thought an interfector (killer) by his own hand; and let him be punished as I shall say. 

If he has killed someone else's slave, thinking him his own: let him restore the damage to the master or pay double the price. How much the price was shall be determined by the judges. But let him use more and greater purgations than he who killed someone while competing. Suitable interpreters of these are those whom the oracle of the god has approved. But if he killed his own slave, having been purged according to the law, let him be absolved. 

But if someone has killed a free man not by choice, let him use the same purgations as he who slew a slave. And let him not despise the ancient mystery. For it is said that a free man killed by force is angry at his killer immediately in the time after death; and being full of terror and turbulence because of the violent death, especially if he sees the killer living in his usual way among his people, the memory supplying strength for this, he terrifies and disturbs the killer himself and his actions with all his might. Wherefore it is necessary that the homicide, for the sake of the killed man, lead a life as an exile for a whole year from his fatherland and from that entire region. But if he who died was a foreigner, the homicide shall also be driven from the fatherland of the foreigner for the duration of a year. 

If he willingly obeys this law, the next of kin to the slain, who will attend to whether he obeyed, shall grant him pardon, and will even be reconciled to him in peace and entirely equitable. But if he does not obey, but while he is unclean dares to seek the temples of the gods and to sacrifice, or does not travel for the whole established time, the next of kin shall report this to the judges and accuse him of the slaughter and take double penalties from him. But if that kin neglects it—as if the crime were revolved upon himself, the slain man himself converting the suffering upon him—let him be accused by anyone who wishes and be compelled to be without his fatherland for five years. 

If a foreigner kills a foreigner in the city not by choice, let it be reported to the judges by anyone who wishes under the same law, and let it be judged similarly. But if an inhabitant did it, let him be an exile for one year. 

But if a foreigner kills an entirely foreign man, or an inhabitant, or a citizen, beyond the purgation, let him be an exile for his entire life from the entire region in which such laws dominate. And if he returns against the laws, let him be punished with death by the guardians of the laws; and let his goods, if he possesses any, be handed over to the next of kin of the slain. 

But if someone has been brought to that region not by choice: driven by the force of a storm and the waves of the sea, let him wait for the opportunity of sailing while touching the sea with his feet; but if he was brought through the land by some people by force, he is to be released by the magistrate to whom the matter was first reported, and pushed back into exile untouched. 

If someone by his own hand has killed a free man, stirred by anger (*ira*), first the anger must be distinguished twofold. For he does it by anger who kills suddenly without the will to kill, by blows or in any way, so that repentance immediately follows after the impetus; and he who, provoked by an insult or injury, and therefore following in the desire of vengeance, killed later by choice and does not repent having done it. It pleases us to place a twofold slaughter, both done by anger. These they might rightly place in the middle between voluntary and involuntary actions. For neither is truly voluntary or involuntary, but one is the image of the other. For he who keeps his anger and later avenges himself with snares not suddenly is very similar to a voluntary homicide; and he who does not keep it but is carried by the first impetus of anger and killed without premeditation is judged similar to an involuntary homicide. Yet he is not entirely involuntary but is said to have the similitude of the involuntary. Wherefore slaughters committed through anger are difficult to determine: whether they are to be placed as voluntary or the contrary. 

The best and truest opinion is to call both "images" and to distinguish them separately, so that one is said to be committed deliberately and the other undeliberately. It is becoming to impose greater punishments on those who killed through anger deliberately. On those, on the contrary, who did it suddenly and undeliberately, lighter ones. For that which is similar to a heavier evil should be punished more harshly; that which is similar to a lighter one, more mildly. So certainly we must act in our laws. 

**CLINIAS:** Entirely so. 

**ATHENIAN:** But repeating again concerning anger, let us say this: If someone by his own hand has killed a free man stirred by anger undeliberately, let him suffer the other evils which are owed to the homicide who killed not through anger; but for two years he shall be an exile to coerce his anger. But he who killed any free man through anger but from snares: let him be compelled to do other things similarly as before. But let him be an exile not for two years only like the former, but for three years, so that his longer anger is punished longer. 

Let this be the universal disposition for these. Surely it is difficult to place laws concerning these specifically and exactly. For sometimes a slaughter which is established as more truculent by law seems lighter; sometimes on the contrary, that which is lighter seems more truculent, according to how atrociously or mildly it was done. For the most part, however, these things happen as we just said. But the guardians of the laws will recognize all these things. 

When the time for restoring the exiles arrives, let them send twelve judges to the borders of the region, who, having diligently considered all the actions of the exiles during that time, shall become the judges of their shame and reception. Let them acquiesce to the judgment of these magistrates. But if after restoration either of these, moved by anger similarly, has sinned, let him be an exile perpetually; and if he returns again, let him be punished no differently than a returning foreigner. 

If someone has thus killed his own slave, let him be purged; if another's, let him restore double to the master. 

If any homicide does not obey the laws but, not yet purged, has contaminated the market, gymnasia, and other sacred places by his entry, let anyone who wishes call into judgment both him and the kinsman of the slain who neglects these things, and compel them to pay double both in money and other things: which, when paid, he himself shall receive according to the law. 

If a slave, stirred by anger, kills his master, let the kinsmen of the killed man kill him however they wish, and let them be clean of the crime, provided they did not preserve him alive. But if his own slave killed not his master but another free man through anger, let him be handed over by his master to the kinsmen of the killed man; who, however they wish, shall entirely kill him. 

If a father or mother (for it happens, though rarely) through anger kills a son or daughter by blows or in any way, let them be purged just as other homicides and be an exile for three years. And after the restoration itself, let the husband be separated from the wife, and the wife from the husband. Nor shall they further give effort to procreating children together; nor shall either of them live together with him whose son or brother he killed, nor communicate with him in sacred rites. And he who by the impiety of his mind does not obey these laws, let him be accused by anyone who wishes as guilty of impiety. 

If a husband kills his wife, or a wife her husband through anger, let them be purged similarly and be an exile for three full years; and when they return, let them not communicate in sacred rites with their children, nor use the same table. If a parent or son does not keep this, let him be accused by anyone who wishes as guilty of impiety. 

If a brother kills a brother or sister, and a sister a sister or brother, through anger, let them be purged and exiled no differently than parents who killed their children; nor after return let them communicate in sacred rites and the table with those whom they deprived of brothers or sisters or sons. He who transgresses this law shall be rightly condemned as impious. 

But truly, when someone has been so conquered by anger that in an insane fury of irascibility he kills a parent—if the parent, before they died, voluntarily liberated their killer from the slaughter, let him be clean, purged like those who committed slaughter voluntarily, the other things being done similarly. But if they did not liberate him, let him who killed be guilty under many laws. For he will be subject to the ultimate punishments of slaughter, impiety, and sacrilege, because he took away the soul of a parent by sacrilege. Wherefore, if it were possible for someone to die more than once, it would be most just for the parricide to be killed more than once. For him to whom it is not granted by any law to kill the parents from whom he was brought into the light, even for his own defense if he sees he is about to be killed by them—but rather commands to suffer all things than to do anything of the sort—how otherwise will it be right to punish him? Therefore, the death penalty for parricide stirred by anger is sanctioned by law. 

If, with sedition having arisen or in any way, a brother kills a brother making an impetus upon him, for his own defense, let him be pure as if he had slain an enemy. Furthermore, if a citizen kills a citizen or a foreigner a foreigner, or a citizen a foreigner or vice versa, in defending himself, let him be similarly clean. In the same way, if a slave kills a slave. But if a slave kills a free man defending himself, he shall be subject to the same laws as a parricide. 

But what we said about liberation from the slaughter of a parent, let the same be understood as said about the liberation of all others. If someone therefore has voluntarily dismissed any of the others, let him who killed be purged as if the slaughter was committed not by choice, and be an exile for one year. 

But now, slaughters that are violent, involuntary, and committed through anger have been moderately explained. Let us next speak of those which are committed by choice in these matters according to every injustice from snares, on account of the tyranny of pleasure, desire, and envy. 

**CLINIAS:** You say rightly. 

**ATHENIAN:** First, therefore, let us declare to the best of our power how many causes of voluntary slaughter there are. The greatest cause of this is desire dominating a soul agitated by lusts: which consists most of all in that heat which vehemently inflames the minds of many. This surely is that power which, on account of nature and ignorance of riches, begets an insatiable greed. Ignorance is the cause because riches are not rightly praised. For both Greeks and barbarians, although riches hold the third place of goods, put them in the first; and by this opinion, they destroy both themselves and their posterity. Surely we would live best and most beautifully if the true opinion concerning riches were preached everywhere: which is that riches are for the sake of the body, and the body for the sake of the soul. Therefore, since those goods are for whose sake riches are to be possessed, they will hold the third degree after the virtue of the soul and the body. This reason, therefore, like a mistress, will teach us that it is not becoming for a man who is to be happy to seek riches in any way whatsoever, but with justice and temperance. For thus no slaughters to be punished by slaughters would be committed in cities. 

Now truly, as we said in the beginning of this disputation, this one thing is the greatest: that it makes the maximum punishments for voluntary slaughter. The second is the habit of an ambitious mind, from which envies are born—first indeed to the man himself, then even to the best men of the city. Fear occupies the third place: which begets many slaughters when those things are done by someone or are being done at present of which they would want no one to be conscious. Therefore, those who seem likely to reveal such things, if it cannot be otherwise, he removes from the middle by death. 

To all these, the preambles which we said apply; and furthermore the discourse which many of those who study sacred solemnities both hear and believe: that homicides are punished among the infernal regions; and returning here again, they neccesarily pay the debts and penalties according to nature. Surely what they did to others, they are compelled to suffer by others with a similar lot in this life. He, therefore, who shall have been persuaded, having been warned by such a preamble and having feared such punishments, there is no need to place any law for him; but for a man affected to the contrary, let this law be written: 

"Whoever deliberately kills his fellow citizen by his own hand through injury: first, let him be far from the temples, from the market, from the ports, and from every common assembly, lest he contaminate these by his presence—whether anyone has forbidden him to be present or no one has. For the law itself forbids it, and so forbids it that it seems to always forbid it and to be about to forbid it for the whole city. 

Then, he who does not prosecute him as is becoming, nor restrains him from these things, from the kinship of the slain up to second cousins: first, let the crime and the hatred of the gods turn upon him, as the imprecation and curse of the law commonly dictates; then, let him be guilty to anyone wishing to avenge the slain. But he who wishes to prosecute, when he has done all things which either concerning the observation of paying for the crime or concerning any other things to be done the god has instituted, and has foretold what must be foretold, let him proceed and compel the homicide to pay the penalty according to the law." 

That these things must be done can be easily persuaded by the legislator by prayers and the sacrifices of the gods who have a care lest slaughters happen in cities. But who those gods are, and how these judgments may be most carried out according to the mind of god, let the guardians of the laws declare with the interpreters, the soothsayers (*aruspices*), and the god, and thus let them dispose the judgments and penalties. 

The judges of these matters shall be those to whom the authority of punishing sacrilege was given. He who shall have been condemned, let him pay the penalty by death; and since he has sinned not only impiously but also imprudently, he ought not to be buried in the region of the slain. But if he flees and does not sustain the judgment, let him be an exile perpetually. And if he is ever caught within the borders, let whoever of the kinsmen of the slain or of the citizens first meets him kill him with impunity; or let him hand him over bound to the magistrates to be killed by the judges of this matter. 

But if anyone comes forward to defend him, let him give bail for him whom he protects, and let him provide three sureties whom the judges themselves shall think sufficient, who promise that he will present himself to the judgment. If anyone is unwilling or unable to do this, let him be bound by the magistrates and reserved for the judgment. 

Truly, if someone kills a man not by his own hand but by will, counsel, and snares, and though he is the cause of the slaughter and impure in his mind, he lives in the city: let him be punished similarly when condemned; except that he will not provide sureties, and though condemned, he will not lack his own burial. Let the other things be done for him as we said of the former. These same things are established for foreigners against foreigners, and for citizens and foreigners mutually, and for slaves against slaves, concerning slaughter done by one's own hand and concerning that which was committed by counsel and snares—except that we judge those to provide bail just as those who killed by their own hand. 

If a slave kills a free man by his own choice by his hand or by counsel, and was condemned, let him be dragged by the public punisher and avenger to the monument of the slain, or where he can see it; and having been beaten as he who convicted him in judgment orders, if thus beaten he still lives, let him be beaten even unto death. 

If someone killed a slave doing no injury, fearing lest some shameful thing done by him be revealed, or led by another cause of this kind: there are some things about which it is grave and troublesome to place laws, and impossible not to place them. Of this kind are the voluntary and unjust slaughters of kinsmen, whether brought by one's own hand or by counsel and snares, which are committed most in cities poorly governed; but they also sometimes happen where no one would expect. To avoid these crimes, let the superior speech be repeated. For perhaps, having heard these, someone will voluntarily abstain from a most wicked slaughter. For the fable or discourse—or whatever other name the speech should be called—was manifestly said by the ancient priests: that Justice is the watcher of all things and the avenger, to avenge kindred blood by the law which we just spoke of. 

Surely she has established this: that whoever has perpetrated anything of this kind must necessarily suffer the same. So that if someone has delivered his father to death, he himself later at certain times will be violently killed by his sons. But if he slew his mother, he himself later, having been made a participant in the female nature, will necessarily finally be killed by his own sons. For when common blood is contaminated, there is no other purgation, nor can the stain be otherwise wiped away, unless a similar slaughtered soul has expiated a similar slaughter and has settled the anger of the entire kinship. 

From these crimes, therefore, it is becoming to restrain men by the fear of punishments of this kind which are inferred by the gods. If any have truly fallen into such a miserable calamity that they dare to deprive a father or mother, brother, or son of life by choice and deliberately, the mortal legislator will thus sanction concerning such a crime: that both by the promulgation made they restrain them from public and sacred places, as was said above, and similarly require sureties. And he who shall have been condemned for such a slaughter, let him be killed both by the ministers of the judges and by the magistrates; and let him be dragged outside the city to an established crossroads naked, where each of the magistrates for the whole city shall throw a stone at the head of the dead man, and thus they shall purify the whole city. Finally, having been carried beyond the borders of the region, let them cast him out unburied according to the laws. 

But what is to be judged of him who has destroyed his nearest and dearest by slaughter? He who, I say, has deprived himself of life and the lot of the fates by a wicked force: not compelled by the judgment of the city, nor by a sad and inevitable accident of fortune, nor compelled by some extreme shame, but by the sloth and weakness of a fearful mind has unjustly inflicted death upon himself? What purgations and what burial befit him by law, God himself knows. Yet the next of kin should seek these from the interpreters and the laws of these matters, and let them do as it shall have been established by them. Let burial, therefore, be solitary for these, where no one else is buried; then let them be buried in those places which are the last, deserted, and unnamed of the twelve parts of the region: so obscure that the graves are noted neither by a statue nor an inscribed name. 

If a beast of burden or another animal kills a man, unless it did so in a public contest, let the next of kin of the killed man report it to the judges. And let those curators of the fields to whom the kinsman himself has mandated it judge, and kill the condemned beast beyond the borders of the region. 

If some inanimate thing (except for a lightning bolt or another weapon sent divinely) has deprived a man of life by falling upon him or by striking him, let the next of kin to the slain appoint the nearest person in the vicinity as a judge for this matter; and let him perform these and other things as befit the dead man himself, for the expiation of himself and the entire kinship. What shall have been condemned, as was said of the animals, let it be exterminated. 

If someone is found deprived of a pious life and the homicide is unknown and is not found by those searching diligently: let there be proclamations as in other cases; and let it be proclaimed publicly in the market by a crier that he who killed this or that person, because he is guilty of slaughter, must not enter sacred places and must leave the entire region. For if he is caught, he will be killed and cast out unburied beyond the borders of the region. Let this one law, therefore, be principal for us concerning slaughter. And enough of these. 

Now let us say in which cases he who kills is rightly clean. He who kills one who has entered his house at night by right, let him be clean. And he who kills a plunderer in his own defense, similarly. And he who has subjected a free woman or a boy to a venereal act by force, let him be deprived of life with impunity not only by him on whom the force was brought, but also by the father, brothers, or sons. And a husband, if he kills one bringing force upon his wife, let him be clean by law. And if anyone also, bringing help to a father not at all performing a slaughter through crime, or to a mother, or to sons, brothers, or a spouse, has killed someone, let him be clean. 

Hitherto we have written laws concerning the education and discipline of the living soul—which, if it is endowed with it, should live; but if not, should not live. Furthermore, concerning slaughters and violences, how they are to be punished, and also concerning the nutrition and discipline of bodies, enough was said in the previous parts. 

Next, what actions are violent, voluntary, and involuntary, and how many there are, and by what punishments they are conveniently to be repressed, let it be determined to the best of our power. For these are rightly treated after those. For wounds and the truncations of members through wounds, even a vile legislator will place after slaughter. These are distinguished like slaughters. For some are not by choice, some by anger, some by fear, some by choice and deliberately. 

Of all these, let this be the exordium (preamble): It is necessary to place laws for men, that they may live according to the laws. For if they lived without these, they would differ in nothing from the most atrocious wild beasts. The cause of this is that no man's genius is so constituted by nature that he sufficiently knows what things confer to the public good of human life; and if he knew, that he would always be able and willing to do the best of what he knows. 

For first, it is difficult to know what is not proper to the civil and true art but is necessary to be cared for as public. Surely the public connects and joins cities, while the private dissipates them; it benefits both publicly and privately to dispose the common better than the private. Then, although someone might perhaps know by art that these things are so, nevertheless, if he holds the command of a city with such license that he is subject to no relation of reasons, he will never be able to remain in that opinion for his whole life: namely, that he increases the public good in the city as the principal good, and puts the private after the public. 

But a mortal nature will always impel him to his own utility and private convenience; which, without reason, flees pain as much as it pursues pleasure, and will prefer both of these to the more just and better things; and buried in darkness, it will finally fill itself and the city entirely with all evils. Indeed, if some man by the favor of divine lot were endowed with that nature that he knew the public good and always generously intended it, he would need no laws to rule him. Since no law, no order, is held better or more excellent than knowledge; nor is it right for the mind to be subjected to someone and to serve, but rather if it is thus truly free...

[[page number: 585]]

### De Legib. Vel, de Legumlat. Dial. IX.

...and truly free, it should dominate all things. But now, nowhere is this found—only a minimal part of it appears. Wherefore, what is in the second place must be chosen: order and law, by which many things are indeed perceived, but all things cannot be seen. 

But with these things proposed for their sake, let us now establish what he who wounded another or otherwise harmed him ought to suffer or pay. For it is easy for anyone to rightly comprehend individual cases of this kind: whether namely someone has wounded or not, whom, in what part, and in what way. For these individual things are almost innumerable and differ greatly among themselves. But to commit all these to a judgment, or none of them, is impossible. 

Surely it is necessary to commit this one thing in all: whether each of these things was done or not. Also, to commit nothing concerning the fine of the injuring party, but to determine all great and small things by law, is nearly impossible. 

**CLINIAS:** How then must it be spoken after this? 

**ATHENIAN:** Surely thus: that the legislator ought to grant some things to the judgment, and some things he ought not, but determine them himself. 

**CLINIAS:** But which are to be left to the arbitrament and prudence of the judges, and which are to be determined by the conditor of the laws himself? 

**ATHENIAN:** These we will explain next in the best way. Surely a more grave and common pestilence is born in the whole city where judgments are slothful and silent, the opinions of the judges remain hidden from each other, and they give their sentence secretly. To that, it is harder when it is not conducted in silence, but as if in theatres, all things resound with clamor, and the rhetoricians now praise, now vituperate, and thus judge in turn. To such judgments, if someone were urged by a certain necessity to give laws, we would hold him to be unfortunate. But he who is compelled to give them, let him commit only the minimal fines to those judges, but let him declare most and all greatest things in enacting the laws. 

Where truly judgments are rightly constituted to the best of our power and the judges are well-educated and approved by all diligence, very many things can be rightly committed to the judges concerning the punishment and condition of the condemned. Let no one therefore accuse us if we do not now ordain most and many other things for these by laws, which even less-educated judges could perceive and accommodate a worthy fine and penalty for individual delicts. Since we hope that those for whom we describe the laws will be no inept judges of these matters, we judge that many things are to be committed to them. 

Truly, what we often said and did in the previous parts, thinking that with the description and form of punishments spoken, examples ought to be given to the judges which they should never transgress—that was both rightly done then, and we wish to observe it now, returning again to the enacting of laws. 

Concerning wounds, therefore, let us thus sanction: "If someone has willed and thought to kill a friend among those whom the law forbids, but wounded him and was not able to kill him: we would compel this man, with all mercy removed, to pay the penalty for slaughter no differently than if he had deprived him of life—unless we worshiped his fortune, not entirely perverse, and his *daemon* (spirit/luck); who, having prosecuted both the wounded and the wounding with mercy, withstood the unhappiness of both, and caused it that a lethal wound was not inflicted on the former, nor an execrable calamity of fortune on the latter. To this *daemon*, therefore, we will have gratitude, by no means opposing his benefit; we will take away the penalty of death from him who wounded and will decree that he be an exile in a neighboring city for his whole life, lacking the fruit of none of all his things—the damage, however, being first restored, if he harmed the wounded man in anything, as shall have been established by the judgment of this matter. 

The judges shall be those who would have been for slaughter if the wounded man had died. If a son wounds a parent, or a slave his master deliberately similarly, and was thus condemned to have done it, let him pay for the crime with death. Furthermore, if a brother wounds a brother or sister, or a sister a sister or brother, with the counsel of killing, let him pay for the crime with death. And a wife, if she wounds her husband with the counsel of killing, or a husband his wife similarly, let them be an exile perpetually. 

For these, if they have sons or daughters still children, let tutors administer the family property of the exile, who protect them as orphans. But if they are adults, let them permit them to have the things themselves, but they are not compelled to nourish the exile. 

If anyone truly lacking children has fallen into such calamities, let his kinsmen up to second cousins from both the male and female part assemble, and having held a council together with the guardians of the laws and the priests, let them appoint heirs to this house of the exile from the forty-five thousand houses of the city. In which they ought to think this: that no house of the five thousand forty-five is more of the inhabitant himself and his kind than of the city, both privately and publicly. 

It is becoming that the city possess its houses as most holy and happy according to its powers. Therefore, when some house is contaminated by misfortune and some impiety, because he who possessed it died without children, or was condemned for voluntary slaughter or some crime against the gods or citizens whose penalty is death or everlasting exile: first, let the house itself be expiated according to the law; then, let the kinsmen, as we said, assembling with the guardians of the laws, search for some family in the city most excellent in virtue and fortunate, in which there are more youths. One of these let them adopt as a son for the father of that failing house and his superiors, having prayed to the god that this man may be a propagator of offspring, a successor of the house and of deeds and a cultivator of all the rest under happier auspices than the previous householder; and finally let them appoint him the heir according to the law. But let him who sinned lie without a name, without children, without any share, since he is pressed by calamities of this kind." 

But there is not in all things a boundary joined to a boundary. For where some common border is, there let this medium between the boundaries of things be agreed upon for both. And indeed, between those sins which are done by choice and those which are not by choice, we have said that what is done through anger is such a thing. 

Of a wound made by anger, he who shall condemn: if the event itself shall show that the wound was curable, let him restore double the damage; but if incurable, fourfold. But if it is indeed curable, but brings a huge shame to the wounded man, he shall pay fourfold. 

Truly, if someone not only harmed the wounded man but also harmed the fatherland, because he deprived it of a soldier against enemies, let him be punished similarly; and furthermore, let him restore the damage to the city, and beyond that military service which he himself owes, let him also serve for the wounded man; and whatever was to be done by him in war, let he himself do it. If he does not do it, let him be guilty according to the law to anyone wishing to accuse him as a neglector of military service; and let him restore double, triple, or fourfold the damage as shall have seemed fit to the judges. 

If a full brother has similarly wounded a brother, let the tribesmen and kinsmen up to second cousins from the men and women assembling—both males and females—judge, and hand him over to the parents, that they themselves may punish him according to nature. But if the punishment is ambiguous, let the relatives on the side of the man determine it. If they themselves cannot, let them finally report the cause to the guardians of the laws. If children or grandsons have brought such a thing upon parents, let only those judge who have passed their sixtieth year; for whom not adopted but true...

rightly say that this republic is full of the greatest tumult and iniquity? 
ALCIBIADES. Rightly, by Jupiter. 
SOCRATES. Did it not seem necessary to us, first indeed either to think we know, or truly to know, this which we are about to do or speak readily? 
ALCIBIADES. It seemed so. 
SOCRATES. If someone adds the science of the best to what he knows or thinks he knows, does it not follow that he acts usefully both for himself and for the republic? 
ALCIBIADES. Why not? 
SOCRATES. But on the contrary, neither for the republic nor for himself? 
ALCIBIADES. So it is. 
SOCRATES. But how does it seem to you now, or otherwise? 
ALCIBIADES. Not otherwise.

ALCIBIADES. We clearly said so. 
SOCRATES. It is therefore beneficial for many neither to know anything, nor to think they know: since they will be more ready to perform those things which they either know or think they know. But in acting, they will harm themselves more frequently than they will help. 
ALCIBIADES. You speak the truest things. 
SOCRATES. When, therefore, I was saying that all the remaining sciences, if the science of the best is absent, harm more often than they benefit those having them, did I seem to you then to speak correctly? 
ALCIBIADES. If not then, at least now, Socrates. 
SOCRATES. It is therefore necessary for a city and a soul that is to live correctly to embrace this science beyond doubt: just as one who is sick needs a doctor, and one who wishes to sail without danger needs a pilot. For the more the mind attempts without this science concerning riches, or strength of body, or any such thing, the more it is necessary that great sins are committed from them. But he who is adorned with many and various arts and sciences, yet is devoid of this science, being led by each of the others, will he not deservedly be tossed by a great tempest? Indeed, since he wanders in the deep without a pilot, he is about to perish in a short time. 
<margin>Homer in Margites.</margin>
To this man certainly seems to apply that song of the poet, in which, blaming a certain person, he says: "He knew many things, but he knew them all badly." 
<note>The Margites was a comic poem attributed to Homer in antiquity, now mostly lost.</note>
ALCIBIADES. But to what does that saying of the poet pertain? It seems to me certainly to not fit our purpose at all. 
SOCRATES. On the contrary, it fits perfectly, but both this and nearly all other poets speak through riddles. 
<margin>Poetry is full of riddles.</margin>
For the whole of nature is itself poetry full of riddles, nor does anyone at all discern it. To this nature of poetry is added the fact that if it is ever in an envious man, unwilling to reveal his thoughts to other men, it is a wonder how difficult it is to know what the poet intended. Nor should you think that Homer, that most divine and wise poet, was ignorant that to "know badly" is impossible; for it is he who says that Margites knew many things, but knew them all badly. But he hides the meaning in a riddle, I think, putting "badly" for "evil," and "he knows" for "knowing": from which a certain composition outside the measure of the song is made. But what he means is this: "He knew many things indeed, but it was evil for him to know these things," and he himself was evil, if any faith is to be given to the aforementioned words. 
ALCIBIADES. It certainly seems so to me, Socrates. For what words would I ever believe, if I do not believe these? 
SOCRATES. And it certainly seems right to you. But come, by Jupiter, do you see how great and of what kind is the ambiguity in this? You yourself seem to be turned about in this: for tossed up and down, you truly stand nowhere, but what you once affirmed, you now condemn. If perhaps the God whom you are approaching to pray to, placing himself before your eyes before you make your vow, should ask you thus: whether it is enough for you to have any of those things mentioned in the beginning, or if he granted you license to ask for what you please, what would you think would be opportune for you? Either to accept what God offered, or to ask? 
ALCIBIADES. By the gods, Socrates, I do not have what to answer. But it seems to me a kind of insanity to pray to God rashly, and it must be diligently considered lest one should deceive oneself, seeking evils while thinking he prays for good things, and a little later, as you were saying, transfer himself to contrary vows. 
SOCRATES. Is not the poet more prudent than us, of whom we made mention at the beginning of the discussion, who prayed that even evils should be absent from those praying? 
ALCIBIADES. It seems so to me. 
SOCRATES. The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> also, Alcibiades, whether imitating this poet or observing from themselves, maintain the same vow, both privately and publicly, praying to the gods to grant them beautiful things along with good things, nor would anyone hear them pray for more. Nor yet up to these times are they less happy than other men. If however anything ever succeeded less prosperously for them, their prayer is not the cause, since it is in the gods, I think, to grant what we pray for, or the opposite. I wish moreover to relate another thing to you, which I once received from certain elders. For they were saying it always happened to our city that as often as the Athenians waged war with the Lacedaemonians, our people were unfortunate both on land and at sea, nor did they ever return as victors. Wherefore the indignant Athenians, since they did not have any art by which they might avoid so great a calamity, decided to consult Ammon <note>The Oracle of Zeus Ammon in Libya.</note> as to why the gods granted victory to the Lacedaemonians rather than to the Athenians, since they themselves nevertheless offered sacrifices both more numerous and more decent than the rest of the Greeks, thus adorning the temples with statues and gifts such as no others did, and celebrated processions as expensive and as beautiful as could be, and in every expense which looks toward divine matters, they were more magnificent than all the Greeks—while for the Lacedaemonians there was no care for these things, being so sparing regarding divine worship that they slaughtered mutilated animals everywhere, and were in all other ceremonies far more sparing than the Athenians, even though they were not surpassed by us in the magnitude of their wealth. After the messenger had said these things, asking by what means they could be liberated from the present calamity, the prophet did not answer much to these things: for the God did not permit it; but having approached the legate of the Athenians, he spoke in this manner: "These things says Ammon: the acclamation of the Lacedaemonians is more pleasing to him than all the sacrifices of the rest of the Greeks." And he answered no more to them. Truly, it seems to me that the God meant no other acclamation than their prayers; for indeed those differ very much from the rest. For the rest of the Greeks, partly sacrificing oxen with gilded horns, partly adorning temples with excellent gifts, seek from the gods whatever occurs to them, whether good or evil. But the gods, when they hear them praying, do not accept their most wealthy processions and sacrifices. For which reason it seems to me it must be diligently considered what ought to be said or what ought not to be said. You will also find other similar things in Homer. For he says that the Trojans, when they were laboring on a suburban <margin>Iliad, Book 21.</margin> building, dedicated to the immortal gods precious sacrifices of a hundred oxen: and the sweet smell from the shore was carried by the winds up to heaven: but the blessed gods did not feast upon it at all, because Ilion and Priam and Priam's people were hateful to them. Therefore, nothing...

nothing profited the Trojans, since they had the gods against them, to offer sacrifices and gifts to them rashly. For the nature of god is not such as to be led by gifts, like a wicked moneylender. But we are too delirious if we ever think we are more acceptable to God than the Lacedaemonians on account of gifts. For it would be a grave matter if God looked rather at our gifts and sacrifices than at the soul, whether it be just and holy. 
<margin>Justice and prudence honored among gods and men.</margin>
To which soul I think God attends much more than to processions of great expense and sacrifices, which nothing prevents him who has sinned much against God and men, whether he be a private citizen or a republic, from performing every year. But God, being incorruptible by gifts, spurns all these things, as he himself and his prophet have foretold. Whence it is clear that both with God and with men of sound mind, justice and prudence are especially honored. 
<margin>Who are prudent and just.</margin>
But the prudent and just are those who know what things are fitting to do and say toward God and men. I desire, however, to hear from you what you yourself feel in these matters. 
ALCIBIADES. To me indeed, Socrates, it seems no differently than it does to you and to God; for it would not be right for me to dissent from God. 
SOCRATES. Do you remember that you said you were in the greatest doubt and danger, lest you should deceive yourself, since you sometimes wished for evils instead of goods? 
ALCIBIADES. I remember. 
SOCRATES. Do you see that it is not safe enough for you to proceed to pray, lest perhaps God, hearing you praying, rejects those sacrifices of yours, and you bring back something else by chance? It seems to me, therefore, to be worthwhile to keep quiet: for I do not think you wish to use the prayer of the Lacedaemonians on account of magnanimity—
<margin>Magnanimity is a most honorable name for foolishness.</margin>
for that is the most honorable name of all by which foolishness is signified. Wherefore it is necessary to wait until it is learned how one ought to behave toward God and toward men. 
ALCIBIADES. When will that be, Socrates, and who will be the teacher? For I would most gladly recognize this man, whoever he shall be. 
SOCRATES. This is the one who has a care for you. But it seems to me, just as Homer says Minerva took away the mist from the eyes of Diomedes so that he might discern God from man, so also it is necessary first to take away from your soul the gloom which is now poured over it; then to move closer those things through which you may distinguish what is good or what is evil: for now you seem to be unable. 
ALCIBIADES. Let him take away the mist if he wishes, or whatever else. For I am prepared to omit nothing at all which he shall prescribe, whoever he may finally be, provided that I myself shall turn out better. 
SOCRATES. But he provides for you in a wonderful way. 
ALCIBIADES. Therefore I think it will be best to defer this sacrifice to that time. 
SOCRATES. And indeed correctly: for it is safer than to subject oneself to so great a danger. 
ALCIBIADES. So it is, Socrates. Meanwhile, however, since you seem to me to have counseled me well, I will place this crown upon you. But we will offer to the gods both crowns and all other things that are fitting then at last, when I shall know that that day has arrived. And it will arrive as soon as possible, if the gods are willing. 
SOCRATES. I accept this also, and whatever else has been given by you to me, I see gladly when I have received it from you. Just as Creon in Euripides, seeing Tiresias crowned and hearing that he had received the crown as first-fruits from the soldiers on account of his art, said: "I was considering it an omen, these triumphal crowns, for we are turned about in a tempest, as you yourself know." So also I consider this crowning by you to be an omen. For I seem to myself to be tossed by no less a tempest than Creon, and I strive to depart as victor over all your friends.
