-> MINOS, OR, <-
-> ON LAW. <-

-> MARSILIO FICINO'S <-
-> ARGUMENT. <-

MINOS asks about law, that we might comprehend in a few words what law is commonly, how many are its species, and whence it comes. 
<margin>What law is.</margin>
If anyone diligently attends to the words of Plato in this book *On Law*, and in the books *On Laws*, as well as in *The Republic*, he will describe law by a universal definition thus: Law is the true rationale of governing, which directs those governed through convenient means to the best end, establishing punishment for the transgressor and reward for the obedient. From which it happens that the institutions of princes, when they are not true nor proceed correctly to the best, are not laws at all, but rather are decrees, edicts, or institutes than laws. For from "law" comes "legitimate," from "legitimate" comes "just," and from "just" an "honest, right, and true work" is frequently named; therefore it is necessary for law to be true and good. It follows also that law is eternal and entirely immutable, and the same among all nations concerning the same things, if it is true in this way: for that which is changed by times and places and opinions is called not law, but an institution. 
<margin>Four species of law.</margin>
Moreover, the species of law, as is gathered from the *Timaeus*, *Phaedrus*, and *Gorgias*, are four. First divine, which Plato calls providence. Second celestial, which he calls fate. Third moving, which he calls nature. Fourth human, which he calls natural prudence. The first is in the divine mind, which Orpheus and Plato wish to be the law of Saturn. The second is in the superior part of the soul of the world, which they call the law of Jove. The third is in the moving and inferior power of it, which they call the law of the first Venus. The last is in the mind of man, which they call the law of the second Venus. The first flows from the highest good, which is above the mind. The second from the mind and the highest good. The third from the highest good, mind, and the universal soul. The fourth likewise from the highest good, mind, and soul. But all are reflected back to the good itself. The first is in ideas, around the highest good, above reasons. The second is in reasons, around ideas, above seeds. The third is in seeds, around reasons, above forms. The fourth is in notions, around reasons, over acts and arts, which they call the royal law, the imitator of the supernal king. Whence law proceeds is elicited from those things which have been said. For from the very principle of things all flow, but in various ways, as has been said. Wherefore all illustrious founders of laws have referred the invention of laws to God, but through different names and means. Zoroaster, giving laws to the Bactrians and Persians, referred them to Horomasis <note>Ahura Mazda.</note>. Trismegistus to the Egyptians, to Mercury <note>Thoth.</note>. Moses most rightly to the Jews, to God the father of all nature. Minos to the Cretans, to Jove. Charondas to the Carthaginians, to Saturn. Lycurgus to the Lacedaemonians, to Apollo. Draco and Solon to the Athenians, to Minerva. Pompilius to the Romans, to Egeria. Muhammad to the Arabs, to Gabriel. Zamolxis to the Scythians, to Vesta. Our Plato to the Magnesians and Sicilians, to Jove and Apollo. Arcadius, however, denied laws to both the Thebans and the Cyrenaeans when they requested them.

SOCRATES. COMPANION <note>original: "Minos." Ficino identifies the anonymous interlocutor with Minos, though modern scholars call him "Companion."</note>.

SOCRATES. What is law among us? 
<margin>Socrates is asked simply, not correctly to doubt what is a part.</margin>
MINOS. About which law do you ask? 
SOCRATES. Is there anything by which law differs from law according to what law is? Attend clearly to what I ask. For I ask thus, as if I said: what is gold? And if you asked in the same way about which gold I was asking, I would think you were not questioning correctly. For gold does not differ from gold insofar as it is gold, nor does stone differ from stone insofar as it is stone; in the same way law does not differ from law, but all are the same thing. For each one of them is similarly law, not one more and another less. I ask therefore about this very universal thing, what law is, generically; if you have it ready now, explain. 
<margin>A definition is gathered from translation.</margin>
MINOS. And what else would law be, Socrates, than what is received and approved by law? 
SOCRATES. Does speech seem to you to be those things which are spoken, or sight those things which are seen, or hearing those things which are heard? Or is speech one thing and the things pronounced another, sight one thing and the things seen another, and hearing similarly another and the things heard another—and likewise law one thing and that which is received by law another? Does it seem so to you, or otherwise? 
MINOS. So indeed. 
SOCRATES. Therefore law is not that which is received by law. 
MINOS. It does not seem so. 
SOCRATES. What then...

--- Page 54 ---
Minos, Or, On Law. 35

...what law might be, let us consider in this way. If anyone should ask about those things we just mentioned, saying: "Since you assert that things seen are perceived by sight, what is sight by which they are perceived?" we would answer that it is the kind of sense that reveals colors through the eyes; and to one asking about hearing, the sense that drinks in the voice through the ears. In the same way if he asks: "Since things are established by legitimate law, what is the law by which they are received when they are accepted? Is it some sense, or a declaration, as those things which are learned are comprehended by the science that declares them, or as an invention by the invention that shows them?" Just as healthy and harmful things are shown by medicine; but those things which the gods think, as the prophets say, are known by the faculty of divining. 
<margin>What a prophecy/vaticination is.</margin>
For prophecy is the discovery of such things; is it not? 
MINOS. Entirely so. 
SOCRATES. Which of these do we especially presume law to be? Those institutes and decrees? 
MINOS. So it seems to me. For what else would anyone say law is? From which it appears that the whole of what you were asking is that law is the institute of the city. 
SOCRATES. Do you call the opinion of the city law? 
MINOS. Indeed. 
SOCRATES. And perhaps you speak correctly; but perhaps in this way we shall understand better. Do you call some people wise? 
<margin>Another false definition of law, and refutation.</margin>
MINOS. I do. 
SOCRATES. Are not the wise wise by wisdom? 
MINOS. So it is. 
SOCRATES. And the just just by justice? 
MINOS. Entirely. 
SOCRATES. Therefore also the legitimate are legitimate by law? 
MINOS. Surely. 
SOCRATES. But the lawless are lawless by lawlessness? 
MINOS. Certainly. 
SOCRATES. And are the legitimate just? 
MINOS. So they are. 
SOCRATES. And the lawless unjust? 
MINOS. Unjust. 
SOCRATES. Is not law and justice something most beautiful? 
MINOS. It is so. 
SOCRATES. And lawlessness and injustice most foul? 
MINOS. Most foul. 
SOCRATES. And the former indeed preserves cities and all other things, but the latter perverts and corrupts them? 
MINOS. So it is. 
SOCRATES. Therefore it is necessary to think of law as something beautiful, and to seek it as a good. 
MINOS. Why not? 
SOCRATES. Did we not say that the institute of the city is law? 
MINOS. We said it. 
SOCRATES. Are not some decrees good, and some even bad? 
MINOS. They are certainly. 
SOCRATES. But law was not bad. 
MINOS. Certainly not. 
SOCRATES. Therefore it is not to be asserted so simply that law is the institute of the city. 
MINOS. By no means does it seem so to me. 
SOCRATES. For it is not fitting that an unjust constitution be law. 
MINOS. No. 
<margin>Law is a certain opinion.</margin>
SOCRATES. Nevertheless, law also seems to me to be a certain opinion; and since it is by no means a wicked opinion, is it not clear that if it is indeed an opinion, it is a worthy opinion? 
MINOS. It is established. 
SOCRATES. And a worthy opinion, is it not a true opinion? 
MINOS. It is. 
SOCRATES. But a true opinion is the discovery of truth. 
MINOS. Certainly. 
SOCRATES. Law, therefore, wishes to be the discovery of truth. 
MINOS. But how, Socrates, if law is the discovery of truth, do we not always use the same laws concerning the same things, since the truth of things has been found? 
SOCRATES. Nevertheless, law wishes to be the discovery of truth. But if men do not use the same laws, as it seems, those who expect law cannot always find the truth. But come, let us see if it may appear more clearly to us from here, whether we live always by the same laws, or at other times by others? 
MINOS. But that is not difficult to know, Socrates: that neither do the same people always live by the same laws, nor do different people always live by different ones. For our laws do not permit sacrificing human victims, but it is a nefarious thing; 
<margin>Among the Carthaginians it is legitimate to sacrifice sons.</margin>
among the Carthaginians, however, it is held to be just and holy, so much so that some of them sacrifice their sons to Saturn, which perhaps you yourself have heard. Nor do only barbarian men follow different laws than we do, but also those who inhabit Lycia: those successors of Athamas, what kind of sacrifices do they offer, though they are Greeks? 
<margin>Ancient ceremonies around the deceased.</margin>
You have also heard what kind of laws we once observed concerning burials, slaughtering victims before the cadaver was carried out, and summoning professional mourners. And those even more ancient than these even buried the deceased at home, none of which we observe at all in these times. We could relate innumerable other examples of this kind. For the field of demonstration is very wide, that neither do we always live with the same laws as ourselves, nor do men live by them in turn. 
SOCRATES. It is no wonder, O best of men, if you speak correctly but it escaped me. But as long as you yourself relate in a long speech what seems right to you, and I again do the same, we shall never, I think, agree. But if a common discussion is proposed, perhaps we shall agree; therefore if you wish, you yourself question me, and consider it together with me; but if you prefer to answer, answer. 
MINOS. I wish indeed, Socrates, to answer to whatever you please. 
SOCRATES. Come then, do you think just things are unjust, and unjust things just? Or rather just things just, and unjust things only unjust? 
MINOS. Indeed, things that are just are just; and likewise unjust whatever things are unjust. 
SOCRATES. And is it not as it is here, so also everywhere among nations? 
MINOS. So it is. 
SOCRATES. And among the Persians, is it not? 
MINOS. Also among the Persians. 
SOCRATES. And is it not always? 
MINOS. Also always. 
SOCRATES. Are those things which pull more weighed heavier here, and those which pull less lighter; or the opposite of this? 
MINOS. No, rather the more pulling are heavier, and the less pulling are lighter. 
SOCRATES. And in Lycia and Carthage the same? 
MINOS. The same. 
SOCRATES. Beautiful things, as it seems, are everywhere thought beautiful; and foul things the opposite, foul; but not beautiful things foul, or foul things beautiful. 
MINOS. So it is. 
SOCRATES. Generatelly through all things, are not those things which are true thought to be so? And those which are not true, not true, both among us and among all men? 
MINOS. It seems so. 
SOCRATES. Therefore whoever wanders from the true, also wanders from the legitimate. 
MINOS. According to your reasoning, Socrates, the same legitimate things always seem to be both among us and among others. But when I notice us without end daily changing laws up and down, I cannot have faith in you. 
SOCRATES. Perhaps you do not perceive that these transposed things remain the same. But look at this with me: have you ever found a book about the curing of diseases? 
MINOS. Indeed. 
SOCRATES. Do you know of what art that book is? 
MINOS. I know it is of medicine. 
SOCRATES. Do you call those who know these things doctors? 
MINOS. I do. 
SOCRATES. Do those who know establish the same things about the same, or different things about different? 
MINOS. The same. 
SOCRATES. Do only Greeks agree with Greeks, or also Barbarians, both with themselves and with Greeks, about those things which they know? 
MINOS. It is entirely necessary for Greeks and Barbarians to think the same about those things which they know. 
SOCRATES. You have answered well; but is it not also always? 
MINOS. And always. 
SOCRATES. Do not doctors write down about health those things which they think to be? 
MINOS. Yes. 
<margin>All prescriptions are laws.</margin>
SOCRATES. Therefore the writings of doctors are the laws of doctors? 
MINOS. They are. 
SOCRATES. And geometric writings are the laws of geometers? 
MINOS. Certainly. 
SOCRATES. Whose are the writings and constitutions concerning the cultivation of gardens? 
MINOS. Of the horticulturists. 
SOCRATES. These laws therefore are horticultural laws? 
MINOS. So they are. 
SOCRATES. Of those who know how to preside over gardens? 
MINOS. Why not? 
SOCRATES. And the horticulturists know? 
MINOS. Surely. 
SOCRATES. But whose are the writings and institutes concerning the seasonings of foods? 
MINOS. Of the cooks. 
SOCRATES. These laws therefore are of the cooks. 
MINOS. They are. 
SOCRATES. Namely of those who know how to preside over the preparing of foods? 
MINOS. Beyond doubt. The cooks know these things, as they say.

**MIN.** They know this. **SOCR.** Come then, tell me: whose writings and institutions concern the government of a city? Is it not those who are skilled in administering the state? **MIN.** It appears so. **SOCR.** Do any others besides statesmen and kings know these things? **MIN.** Only they. **SOCR.** These then are "civil writings," which men call the decrees of kings and good men. **MIN.** You speak the truth. **SOCR.** Those who know do not establish different things at different times regarding the same matters. **MIN.** Certainly not. **SOCR.** Therefore, laws are not one thing at one time and another at another. **MIN.** Not at all. **SOCR.** If we see some people disagreeing or changing things, shall we say they know, or are they ignorant? **MIN.** They are ignorant. **SOCR.** Is it not true that what is right in each case must be called "lawful"? Just as what is done according to the reasoning of a doctor, or a cook, or a gardener, is the law in those matters? **MIN.** Without a doubt. **SOCR.** On the other hand, that which is not right can no longer be called lawful. **MIN.** No longer. **SOCR.** It becomes, therefore, unlawful. **MIN.** It must be so. **SOCR.** <margin>What a royal law is.</margin> For this reason, in the constitutions concerning the just and unjust, and universally concerning the order and governing of the city, whatever is right for those handling them constitutes a "royal law." What is not right, however, is by no means a royal law; because where knowledge is lacking, it only seems to be law, whereas in fact it is unlawful. <margin>Law is the discovery of truth.</margin> **MIN.** That is so. **SOCR.** We have rightly agreed, then, that law is the discovery of truth. **MIN.** It appears so. **SOCR.** Furthermore, let us consider this as well: who is skilled in scattering seeds into the earth? **MIN.** The farmer. **SOCR.** He distributes the appropriate seeds to each type of soil. **MIN.** Certainly. **SOCR.** The farmer, therefore, is a good lawgiver in these matters, and his laws and distributions for them are correct. **MIN.** True. **SOCR.** Who is a good lawgiver regarding the striking of strings in harmony, who imparts them according to merit, and whose laws are correct? **MIN.** The flute-player and the lyre-player do these things. **SOCR.** He who is most "lawful" in these matters is therefore the best flute-player. **MIN.** Yes. **SOCR.** Who can best adapt nourishment to bodies? Is it not he who knows how to apply what is suitable to each? **MIN.** That very person. **SOCR.** His partitions and instructions are the best; and whoever is most "lawful" regarding these things is the best lawgiver. **MIN.** Exactly. **SOCR.** Who is he? **MIN.** The physical trainer. **SOCR.** He knows best how to shepherd the flock of the human body. **MIN.** Certainly. **SOCR.** And what is the name of him who knows how to shepherd a flock of sheep? **MIN.** A shepherd. **SOCR.** Therefore, the shepherd's laws are best for sheep. **MIN.** The best. **SOCR.** And the cowherd's for cows. **MIN.** Also. **SOCR.** <margin>The king's laws are best for human souls.</margin> But whose laws are best for the souls of men? Are they not the king's? **MIN.** The king's. **SOCR.** You speak well. But can you say which of the men of old was the best lawgiver regarding the blowing of flutes? Perhaps you do not remember; do you want me to remind you? **MIN.** Very much so. **SOCR.** <margin>Marsyas first imposed laws on flutes.</margin> It was Marsyas <note>In mythology, a satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest.</note>, and the one he loved most, Olympus the Phrygian. **MIN.** You speak the truth. **SOCR.** Indeed, the flute harmonies of these men are most divine, and they alone stir the listeners; they specifically reveal the gods who are of help to us, and they alone have endured to this day as being divine. **MIN.** These things are true. **SOCR.** <margin>Who the first lawgivers among the Greeks were.</margin> But which of the ancient kings is said to have been the best lawgiver, whose institutions still remain as if they were divine? **MIN.** I do not remember at all. **SOCR.** Do you not know which of the Greek nations use the most ancient laws? **MIN.** Perhaps you mean the Lacedæmonians <note>The Spartans.</note> and Lycurgus, the lawgiver of the Lacedæmonians. **SOCR.** But these institutions have perhaps not yet reached three hundred years, or only a little more. Do you know where the most excellent of those laws came from? **MIN.** They say from Crete. **SOCR.** Therefore, those people live by the most ancient laws of all the Greeks. **MIN.** True. **SOCR.** <margin>Concerning Rhadamanthus and Minos.</margin> Do you know who were the most excellent kings among them? Minos, of course, and Rhadamanthus, the sons of Jupiter <note>Original Latin: Iouis (Jove/Zeus).</note> and Europa, to whom these laws belong. **MIN.** They say, O Socrates, that Rhadamanthus was a just man, but that Minos was savage, harsh, and unjust. **SOCR.** My dear friend, you are repeating an Attic <note>Athenian.</note> and tragic fable. **MIN.** Is this not what is circulated about Minos? **SOCR.** However, Homer and Hesiod do not testify to such things; and they are far more reliable witnesses than all the tragic poets, by whose testimony you speak. **MIN.** And what do they say about Minos? **SOCR.** I will tell you, lest you, like many others, speak impiously. For nothing is more impious than this. <margin>Caution must be taken in praising and accusing.</margin> First, one must be careful never to sin against God in word or deed, and secondly, never against divine men. Indeed, one ought to be diligently careful whenever you are about to praise or blame a man, lest you fall into error. For this reason, we must take primary care to distinguish between good and bad men. For God is greatly indignant whenever someone disparages one who is like Him, or praises one who is unlike Him. <margin>A good man is like God.</margin> Now, a good man is like God. Do not think that stones and wood, birds and serpents are sacred, while men are not. <margin>A good man is a most sacred thing.</margin> On the contrary, a good man is the most sacred of all things, while a bad man is the most profane. And now I will relate how Homer and Hesiod extolled Minos himself, so that you, a man born of man, do not speak wrongly against a hero who was the son of Jupiter. <margin>Crete of ninety cities.</margin> For Homer, when he made mention of Crete, saying it was very populous and had ninety cities, said: "Among them is Knossos, a great city, where Minos reigned for nine years, conversing with great Jupiter." This is such great praise of Minos by Homer, explained in few words, that he never extolled any of the heroes with equal praise. <margin>Jupiter the teacher.</margin> For he reveals here, as he often does elsewhere, that Jupiter is a "sophist" <note>In this context, a wise teacher or master of an art.</note> and that his art is most noble. For he says that Minos conversed with Jupiter for nine years, and used to go to him for the sake of instruction, as if Jupiter were a sophist. That Homer granted to no other hero such a great gift—to have been educated by Jupiter—must be considered a marvelous praise. Furthermore, in the *Odyssey*, where the funeral rites are described, he depicted Minos judging the souls of the dead, holding a golden scepter. But he never depicts Rhadamanthus judging or conversing with Jupiter, either here or elsewhere. Therefore, I assert that Minos was honored by Homer above all others. For it is not a great praise merely to be the son of Jupiter, unless one was also educated by Him. Indeed, that poem signifies this: "Minos reigned for nine years, accustomed to converse with great Jupiter." That is, Minos met with Jupiter in discourse for nine years. For *entychia* <note>original Greek: ἐντυχίᾳ; meaning meeting or social intercourse.</note> signifies discourses, and *entychias* <note>original Greek: ἐντυχίας</note> is one who meets for discourse. Thus, Minos went to the cave of Jupiter for nine years to be instructed. From there he learned, and from there he taught others what he had received from Jupiter in those nine years. Yet there are some who interpret *sympoten* <note>original: συμπότην; drinking companion.</note> otherwise, as a fellow-drinker or a companion at a banquet, and a conversation of Jupiter. But we can conclude that those people do not interpret correctly, chiefly because no Greeks or Barbarians abstain from *symposia* <note>original: sympoßijs</note>—that is, drinking parties and such games—except for the Cretans and the Lacedæmonians, who learned from the Cretans...

<summary>In this dialogue, Socrates argues that true law is the "discovery of truth" and defends the legendary King Minos of Crete against his reputation as a tyrant. He cites Homer to argue that Minos was a divinely inspired lawgiver who was personally tutored by Zeus for nine years.</summary>

...learned. In Crete, moreover, among the other laws of Minos himself, this one stands out: "Do not drink together to the point of drunkenness." It is clear that he commanded his citizens to observe what he considered honest. Nor would Minos, like an wicked man, have done one thing himself and commanded others to do another. But that custom was, as I said, a conference of words for the sake of instruction; and for that reason, he established laws of this kind for his citizens, by the observation of which Crete has been happy through all time, as has Lacedaemon, since it began to use those laws as if they were divine. But Rhadamanthus was indeed a good man, <margin>Rhadamanthus stood out as a judge, having been instructed by Minos; yet he did not learn all royal discipline, but only to serve the king in judgments; whence he was called a good judge.</margin> for he had been instructed by Minos; yet he did not learn the whole royal discipline, but learned only to serve the king in judgments; hence he was called a good judge. Minos used him clearly as a guardian of the laws throughout the city, but for the rest of Crete he used Talus as a guardian. For Talus visited all the villages three times a year to observe their laws, carrying around the laws engraved on bronze tablets; hence he was called "the bronze one." Hesiod, moreover, brought similar things to bear regarding Minos himself. For when he mentioned that name, he said: "Who excelled mortal kings, and ruled over many nations, holding the scepter of Jupiter with which he governed the cities." Here also he calls the scepter of Jupiter nothing other than the teaching of Jupiter, by which he moderated all of Crete. MINOS. For what reason, then, Socrates, has this rumor spread among men that Minos himself was a rude and harsh man? SOCRATES. For the same reason that you, my good man, and everyone else who cares for a good reputation, if you are wise, must diligently take care not to have any poet as an enemy. For poets have the greatest power in both directions, both for praising and for blaming. In this matter, Minos certainly failed when he declared war on this city <note>Athens</note>, which is filled not only with many other wise men, but especially with poets of every kind, and particularly tragic ones. For tragedy here is very ancient, and it did not begin, as most people think, with Thespis or Phrynichus; but if you wish to investigate, you will find tragedy to be a much older invention of this city. This part of poetry greatly delights the people and attracts listeners, and we have used it to strike at Minos in revenge; but for this reason, he also forced us to pay those tributes. In this, therefore, Minos failed: when he provoked us, from which it happened, as you yourself ask, that he became infamous. Since he was a good and lawful man, as we said above, and an excellent shepherd of the people, his laws are the proof, which persevere unchanged, as having been found through the true government of the city. MINOS. You seem, Socrates, to have found a likely reason. SOCRATES. Does it not seem to you, then, if I speak the truth, that the Cretans, the citizens of Minos and Rhadamanthus, use the most ancient laws? MINOS. It certainly seems so. SOCRATES. These, therefore, were the most excellent of all ancient lawgivers and shepherds of men, just as Homer calls a good leader of an army the "shepherd of the people." MINOS. Entirely. SOCRATES. Come then, by Jupiter the friend, if some good legislator and shepherd of men should ask you, regarding the health of the body, what he applies to the body to maintain good health? We would answer correctly and briefly: nourishment and exercise, sometimes increasing, then relaxing, and thus composing the body. MINOS. Correct. SOCRATES. If afterward the same good legislator and shepherd of men should ask us, what does he apply and impart to the soul that makes it better? What shall we answer him above all, so that we might be less ashamed of ourselves and our age? MINOS. I do not know what to say. SOCRATES. But it is a great shame for both our souls if they are ignorant of what things are good or evil for themselves, while they seem to know what pertains to the body and to other things.

### THE EUTHYPHRO OF PLATO, OR, ON HOLINESS.

#### THE ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO
*

*Euthyphro* is entirely engaged in refutation. Thus it happened that some Platonists called this book "litigious," just like the *Euthydemus* and the *Hippias*. But in truth, while Socrates refutes Euthyphro's false opinions about holiness, he points out the tracks of truth to those hunting for it. In this book, and also in the *Gorgias*, Plato calls that part of justice "holiness" which gives God His due. He gives to God His due who returns to God those things which he received from God without an intermediary. The body, indeed, as Plato discusses in the book *On Nature*, we received from the four elements; the natural complexion of the species from the celestial spheres; the parts of the soul which are drawn by affections from the demons and the souls of the stars and spheres. But reason and mind, the image of our Parent, we received from the Architect of the whole world Himself, without any ministry of the heavenly inhabitants or demons. These things, therefore, belong to God; these must be returned to God; and this retribution is called holiness. <margin>Piety.</margin> <margin>Holiness.</margin> <margin>Religion.</margin> Piety precedes it, and religion follows it. For piety is the recognition of God our Parent. Holiness is the returning to God of what is God's, once He is recognized. Religion is the indissoluble binding back to God Himself of that which has been returned to Him, through constant meditation and just works. So that wise man rightly said, <margin>An indissoluble triple cord.</margin> "a triple cord is difficult to break"—a cord, I say, woven from piety, holiness, and religion. Piety excites holiness; holiness confirms and sancitifies piety. Holiness also moves religion. Religion binds holiness. For a pious person needs this by instinct, inspiration, or admonition: that we should think with undoubting faith that the one God is our Parent, which they wish to be piety. When someone has conceived these things, he soon fixes every intention of mind and reason on knowing and loving God. And Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> also defines this frequent gaze in knowing and loving divinity as holiness. From this burning intention of the mind and ardor, it happens that we meditate on and practice all the works, institutes, and commands of God, and constantly "re-read" <note>Ficino here links 'religio' to 'relegere' (to re-read/gather again).</note> whatever pertains to His veneration. Therefore, by binding ourselves back to God, we are religious. With this definition and distinction premised, what is said about holiness in the *Euthyphro* or elsewhere by Plato becomes clear. And when it is said that what is loved by God is holy, it is true; but because it is holy, it is loved by God, not because it is loved is it holy. And because it is loved, it is something "loved"; yet it is not because it is a "loved thing" that it is being loved; since being "holy" and being "loved" are not the same thing at all. For the nature of holiness does not consist in the mere fact of being loved, but rather in that retribution and devotion. Furthermore, when it is said, "Holiness is the service that cares for God," it is also true. But for what work of God is it the servant? For the conversion of the soul. For the work of God is to create, convert, purge, illuminate, and perfect. As soon as God begins to convert the mind to Himself by inspiring it through the instinct of piety, that very assent by which the mind itself restores itself to the converting God is called holiness, which is indeed the servant of God for completing the conversion. Lastly, it is added: "Holiness is the science of vowing and sacrificing to God." This pertains especially to religion, which, as we said, accompanies holiness. By vowing one asks, by sacrificing one gives. What does he ask of God? Himself. What does he give to God? Himself. He asks for the Idea, if any exists in the divine mind, which Mercury asked from Pymander. But he gives his own nature as a participant in the Idea.

**EUTHYPHRO, SOCRATES.**

WHAT news has happened, Socrates, that leaving the exercises of the Lyceum, you are now lingering here around the King’s Porch? For surely you do not have some case before the King, as I do. SOCRATES. The Athenians do not call this a "case," Euthyphro, but an indictment. EUTHYPHRO. What are you saying? Has someone accused you? For I wouldn't think that you...

--- Page 57 ---
38 Book Eight.

...had accused another. SOCRATES. Certainly not. EUTHYPHRO. But has another accused you? SOCRATES. Indeed. EUTHYPHRO. Who is he? SOCRATES. I do not quite know this man myself, Euthyphro. For he seems to be a young man and unknown; but they call him, I believe, Meletus, from the Pitthean district—if you know a Pitthean Meletus with long, flowing hair, an eagle-like and hooked nose, and a thin beard. EUTHYPHRO. I do not recall him, Socrates; but of what has he accused you? SOCRATES. Of what? Truly of a thing which does not seem to me to be lazy or from a lowly or neglected mind. For a young man to have known such a great matter is no small thing. For he says he understands how the youth are corrupted, and who they are that corrupt them; and he seems to be a kind of wise man, who, having observed my ignorance—as if I were perverting his peers—fled to the city to accuse me as if to a mother, so that he alone seems to me to correctly oversee civil affairs. For in the first place, care for the youth must be undertaken, so that they may become as good as possible; just as it is fitting for a good farmer to care for the tender plants first, and afterward to look after the others. And so Meletus perhaps first purges us, who, as he says, are corrupting the buds of the youth, and afterward, by applying care to the elders as well, he will be the cause of many and great benefits to the city, as is consistent for him to do who has made such a beginning. EUTHYPHRO. I would hope so, Socrates, but I fear the opposite may happen. For he seems to me to want to harm this city from the very hearth <margin>See Erasmus: "From the very hearth."</margin>, <note>A Greek proverb meaning to start at the most essential or sacred point.</note> he who attempts to treat you with injustice. And tell me, what does he say you are doing to infect the youth? SOCRATES. Things absurd to hear, and wonderful. For he says I am a maker of gods, and as if I were introducing new gods and denying the old ones; he has called me into court, as he says, for these reasons. EUTHYPHRO. I understand now, Socrates, because you claim that a divine sign <note>The 'daimonion' or inner voice of Socrates.</note> is present with you everywhere. Hence he has written this indictment against you as if you were innovating in divine things, and he comes into court to slander you, since he knows that such things can easily be subjected to the slander of the crowd. They also laugh at me as if I were insane when I discuss divine things in the assembly and predict the future, although I have never predicted anything but the truth. They envy us and all others of this kind; but we must not care about them, but continue in the same way. SOCRATES. O friend Euthyphro, perhaps to be laughed at is of no consequence. For it seems to me that the Athenians do not much care if they think someone excels in doctrine and learning, provided he does not teach his own things to others. But they are indignant with him whom they perceive to be imbueing others with his own expertise, whether they are moved by some envy, as you assert, or for some other reason. EUTHYPHRO. I certainly do not much desire to experience how they are disposed toward me. SOCRATES. For perhaps you seem to exhibit yourself rarely to others, and to be unwilling to propagate your wisdom. But I fear that because of my humanity, which I have toward all mortals, I may seem to the Athenians to offer myself too everywhere and too lavishly to every man, not only without a fee, but even being accustomed to offer myself and my things voluntarily, if anyone should only wish to listen. If they were going to laugh at me, as I was just saying, just as you say you are laughed at, it would certainly not be troublesome to be dragged into court by those joking and laughing. But if they contend in earnest, where the matter may end is uncertain except to you prophets. EUTHYPHRO. Perhaps it will be no trouble, Socrates; indeed, you will fight your case according to the strength of your mind, and I, as I think, will fight mine. SOCRATES. Do you also have a case? Are you the defendant, or the accuser? EUTHYPHRO. I am the accuser. SOCRATES. Whom? EUTHYPHRO. One whom, in pursuing, I seem to be insane. SOCRATES. What? Are you perhaps pursuing someone who can fly? EUTHYPHRO. He is very far from flying, as he is already advanced in age. SOCRATES. Who is he? EUTHYPHRO. My father. SOCRATES. Your own, my good man? EUTHYPHRO. My very own, I say. SOCRATES. What crime? What is the case? EUTHYPHRO. Of homicide, Socrates. SOCRATES. By Hercules! Surely, Euthyphro, it is generally unknown how this may be done rightly. For I do not think it is the work of just anyone to do these things correctly, but of someone far advanced in wisdom. EUTHYPHRO. Far indeed, by Jupiter. SOCRATES. Was it one of your household who was killed by your father? Surely it must be? For you would not accuse your father of homicide for the sake of some stranger. EUTHYPHRO. It is ridiculous, Socrates, if you think it makes any difference whether the person killed was a household member or a stranger, and that this alone should not be observed: whether he who killed, killed justly or not. If justly, he should be let go; but if unjustly, he should be prosecuted, especially if the killer is a member of the household and a companion. For we would be equally polluted if, being conscious of the crime, we were to acquiesce and did not expiate him and ourselves through a trial. Although the one who died was a client and servant of mine, who, when we were working in agriculture in Naxos, served us for a wage. Moved by insult and anger against one of our household servants, he immediately slit his throat. Whereupon my father threw him into a pit with his hands and feet bound; and he sent a man here to ask the interpreter of the law what should be done. Meanwhile, he neglected the bound man as a murderer, as if it mattered nothing at all if he should happen to die—which is what happened. For before the messenger could return from the interpreter, he died of hunger, cold, and his bonds. For this reason, my father and the rest of my relatives are indignant that, on account of a murderer's death, I should bring a charge of death against my father, who, as they say, did not kill him; or even if he had killed him, that one should not care about the death of a murderer. For they say it is impious for a son to sue his father, judging poorly, Socrates, how the divine power stands regarding what is holy or profane. SOCRATES. By Jupiter, Euthyphro, do you presume that you so sincerely know divine, holy, and profane things as they are, that once these things have been done as you say, you do not fear that in accusing your father of a death charge, you might be undertaking something profane? EUTHYPHRO. My study would be of no use to me, Socrates, nor would Euthyphro excel so many mortals in any way, unless I clearly distinguished such things. SOCRATES. O admirable Euthyphro, nothing is better than for me to become your disciple, and in the contention I have with Meletus, I shall first object this: that previously I had indeed made much of the knowledge of divine things; but now, after he has said that I am making up new gods by my own vain opinion and error, I have become your disciple. "If therefore, O Meletus," I shall say, "you think Euthyphro feels rightly in these matters, then think the same of me, and do not condemn me. If not, summon that teacher to court before me, for corrupting old men—namely, me and his father—me by teaching, and him by correcting and punishing." And if he does not obey me, nor drop the case, nor accuse you instead of me, you will say those same things in court which I objected. EUTHYPHRO. Yes, by Jupiter, Socrates! For if he attempts to accuse me, I shall find, I think, where he is weak and infirm, and he will be discussed in court much sooner than I. SOCRATES. But I, my sweet friend, considering these things, wish to be your disciple; since...

--- Page 58 ---
Euthyphro, Or, On Holiness. 39

...I know that while perhaps someone else and this Meletus do not even seem to have noticed you, he has perceived me so acutely and easily that he has accused me here of impiety. Now, therefore, by Jupiter, tell me what you just claimed to know clearly: what you would have holiness and unholiness to be, both in murder and in all other things. Is not the holy itself the same as itself in every action, and on the other hand, is not everything profane the opposite of the holy, yet similar to itself, having one single idea according to which it is profane, whatever is to be profane? EUTHYPHRO. Entirely so, Socrates. SOCRATES. Tell me then, what do you call holy, and what profane? <margin>First definition of the holy.</margin> EUTHYPHRO. I call holy exactly what I am doing now: to prosecute in court anyone who acts unjustly, whether in murder, or sacrilege, or anything else of this kind, whether it be father, or mother, or anyone else who has sinned. But not to prosecute is profane. Indeed, look, Socrates, I pray, at what a strong proof of the law I will bring you—that it is so, as I have told others as well—that it is fitting then and only then to act rightly when we spare no one who sins, whoever he may be. For these men believe that Jupiter himself is the best and most just of all the gods, yet they confess that he bound his own father because he had unjustly devoured his children. They also claim that he castrated his father for such things. But they are angry with me because I prosecute my father who is guilty of injustice. And so these men think the opposite about the gods and about me. SOCRATES. But this is the reason, Euthyphro, why I am being accused, and I do not have enough of an answer. For whenever someone says such things about the gods, I take it hard; for which reason, it seems, they say I am sinning. Now, however, if these things seem so to you who are an expert in these matters, we must also necessarily agree. For what else could we say, since we proclaim that we understand nothing of these things? But by Jupiter the friend, tell me, do you really think these things happened so? EUTHYPHRO. And even more wonderful things besides, Socrates, which are hidden from many. SOCRATES. Do you then think that war is waged among the gods against each other, and grave enmities and battles and many other things, such as are recounted by the poets and skilled writers? Whence also our other sacred things are full of such variety, and in the great Panathenaea the robe full of these varieties is carried into the citadel. Shall we confess these things to be true, Euthyphro? EUTHYPHRO. Not these alone, Socrates, but as I said a little while ago, I can explain many other things about divine matters to you, if you wish; when you hear them, I know for sure you will be stunned. SOCRATES. I would not wonder at all; but you shall tell me those things later at greater leisure; for now, <margin>Refutation.</margin> strive to explain more clearly what I just asked. For you did not sufficiently teach me at first when I asked what holiness was; but you said that it was holy to do what you are doing now, while you accuse your father of a charge of death. EUTHYPHRO. And I said things that were true, Socrates. SOCRATES. Perhaps. But do you call many other things holy, Euthyphro? EUTHYPHRO. Yes, others too. SOCRATES. Remember, therefore, that I was not urging you to teach me one or two out of many holy things, but that very form <note>original: "speciem"</note> by which all holy things are holy. For you said that by one idea all holy things are holy, and by one again those that are profane are profane. Do you not remember? EUTHYPHRO. I do. SOCRATES. Demonstrate to me then what that idea itself is, so that looking upon it and using it as a kind of pattern, I may say that whatever you or anyone else does of that kind is holy; but whatever is unlike it, I may deny. EUTHYPHRO. If you wish it so, Socrates, I will say it. SOCRATES. I do wish it. EUTHYPHRO. <margin>Second definition of the holy rendered.</margin> What is indeed loved by the gods is holy; but what is not loved, is profane. SOCRATES. Most beautifully, Euthyphro, and just as I wanted you to answer, so you have now answered. However, whether you have answered the truth, I do not yet know, but you will clearly show us that these things are true. EUTHYPHRO. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Come then, let us consider that of which we speak. An act loved by God is holy, and a man loved by God is holy; but an act hated by God is profane, and a man hated by God is called profane. But the holy and the profane are not the same, but entirely opposite. Is it not so? EUTHYPHRO. It is so. SOCRATES. Does this seem to have been well said? EUTHYPHRO. I think so, for it was said. SOCRATES. Was it not also said that the gods disagree with each other and fight, and that there are enmities among them? Was this also said? EUTHYPHRO. It was said, certainly. SOCRATES. <margin>Dissent about a matter causes anger and enmities.</margin> But enmities and angers, my good man, are produced by dissent about certain things. Let us consider it this way: if you and I disagreed about a number, discussing which was more, would a dissent of this kind make us enemies and stir up anger? Or would we, fleeing to the method of calculation, soon cease from this dissent? EUTHYPHRO. Entirely. SOCRATES. And if we disagreed about the greater and the lesser, would we not, recurring to measurement, immediately solve the controversy? EUTHYPHRO. These things are true. SOCRATES. And if we should turn to weighing and balancing, we would dissolve a controversy about the heavier and the lighter? EUTHYPHRO. Why not? SOCRATES. What are those things, then, about which when we disagree and cannot easily judge, we are made enemies and become angry? Perhaps you do not have it at hand. But I will tell you, and you consider whether they are these: the just and the unjust, the beautiful <margin>Just and unjust, beautiful and ugly, good and evil are the things that those who cannot judge become angry about.</margin> and the ugly, and the good and the evil. Are not these the things about which when we disagree and cannot reach a sufficient judgment, we become enemies whenever we do, both you and I, and finally all men? EUTHYPHRO. This is certainly the dissent, Socrates, and it turns upon these things. SOCRATES. And the gods, Euthyphro, if they disagree about anything, they will certainly disagree about these. EUTHYPHRO. It must be so entirely. SOCRATES. Therefore, noble Euthyphro, among the gods, some think some things are just according to your speech, and beautiful and ugly, and good and evil. For they would never fight with each other unless they disagreed about these. Would they? EUTHYPHRO. You speak rightly. SOCRATES. Do they not love those things which they individually think are beautiful and good and just? And those that are opposite, they entirely hate? EUTHYPHRO. Entirely. SOCRATES. But the same things, as you say, some judge to be just and others unjust, about which they contend and fight with each other. Is it so? EUTHYPHRO. So it is. SOCRATES. Therefore, as it seems, the same things are loved by the gods and held in hatred, and these same things are both dear to the gods and also hated by them. EUTHYPHRO. It seems so. SOCRATES. By this reasoning, Euthyphro, the same things will be holy and profane at the same time. EUTHYPHRO. It appears so. SOCRATES. You did not, therefore, admirable man, answer what I had asked. For I did not want that which happens to be both holy and profane at once; but what is dear to God appears to be also hated by God. For which reason, Euthyphro, what you are now doing in punishing your father, it would be nothing surprising if in doing this, you were doing something that would be approved by Jupiter, but hated by Saturn and Uranus; and pleasing to Vulcan, but troublesome to Juno, and similarly if any other of the gods differs from another about him. EUTHYPHRO. But I think, Socrates, that in this none of the gods disagree with another: that he who has unjustly killed anyone ought not to pay the penalty. SOCRATES. Have you ever heard any man...

--- Page 59 ---
40 Book Eight.

...Euthyphro, doubting this at some time: that it is not fitting for a man who kills unjustly, or does anything else unjustly, to pay the penalty? EUTHYPHRO. They never cease disputing about these things, both elsewhere and in the courts. For those who have sinned try to say and do everything to avoid punishment. SOCRATES. But do they confess to acting unjustly? And at the same time do they say they ought not to pay the penalty? EUTHYPHRO. In no way. SOCRATES. They do not then say and do everything; for I think they in no way dare to say or argue that punishment should not be taken for unjust things; but rather they say they have not acted unjustly, is it not so? EUTHYPHRO. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. They do not then argue about this, whether the unjust person ought to be punished; but rather they dispute about this among themselves: who acted unjustly, and by doing what, and when. EUTHYPHRO. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Do not these same things happen to the gods, if they disagree about just and unjust things, as your speech testifies? And they indeed claim some act unjustly, and others deny it, since, O wonderful man, no one of men or gods dares to say this: namely, that the unjust man ought by no means to pay the penalty. EUTHYPHRO. So it is. For you speak the truth in summary, Socrates. SOCRATES. They dispute, I think, about each of the things that have been done, Euthyphro, whoever they are that argue, whether men or gods; if indeed the gods argue when they disagree about some action, some saying it was just, and others saying it was unjust. Is it not that way? EUTHYPHRO. Entirely. SOCRATES. Come then, friend Euthyphro, teach me also so that I may become wiser: by what proof do you especially assert that all the gods think that man was unjustly killed, who, being a servant for a wage, became a murderer and was bound by the master of the slain man, and died in his bonds before he who had bound him could learn from the interpreter of the law what should be done? And that because of this, it is right for a son to bring his father into danger of his life? Come, I pray, try to demonstrate something clearly to me about these things, that all the gods think this action is especially right; if you show it sufficiently, I shall never cease to proclaim the praises of your wisdom. EUTHYPHRO. But perhaps this is no small work, Socrates; though I could indeed show it to you quite clearly. SOCRATES. I understand now: that I seem to you to be slower in perceiving than the judges, since you are going to show them clearly that these things are unjust, and that the gods hate all such things. EUTHYPHRO. Very clearly indeed, Socrates, provided they listen to me speaking. SOCRATES. But they will listen, if you seem to speak well to them. But while you were speaking, I thought of this, and I observe myself: that even if Euthyphro should teach me most of all that all the gods consider this death unjust, how will I have learned more from Euthyphro what the holy is, and what the profane is? This work would indeed be hated by God; yet it appeared just a little while ago that holy and unholy are not defined by this, for what was dear to God appeared also hated by God. Therefore I will let you go on this point, Euthyphro: and if you wish, let all the gods think it unjust and hate it. But let us now correct this in our speech, so that what all the gods hate is profane, and what all the gods love is holy. But what some love and others hate is neither, or both at once. Do you want the holy and profane to be distinguished by us in this way now? <margin>Third definition.</margin> EUTHYPHRO. What prevents it, Socrates? SOCRATES. Nothing on my part, Euthyphro; but you, for your part, consider whether by positing this you will easily teach me what you promised. EUTHYPHRO. I would certainly confess that the holy is what all the gods love, and the profane, on the contrary, is what all they hate. SOCRATES. Should this be discussed again, whether it is said correctly or not? Or should it rather be omitted, and thus we ought to indulge both ourselves and others, so that whatever is said, we admit it? Or should what is said be examined? EUTHYPHRO. It should be discussed, although I think this has been well said now. SOCRATES. Perhaps, my good man, we will understand this better; for consider it this way: Is the holy loved by the gods because it is holy? Or is it holy because it is loved by the gods? EUTHYPHRO. I do not understand what you are saying, Socrates. SOCRATES. I will try to explain it more clearly. We say something is "carried" and "carrying," "led" and "leading," "seen" and "seeing," and all such things: do you understand that these are different, and in what way they are different? EUTHYPHRO. I seem to understand. SOCRATES. Is there not also something "loved," and another thing besides this that is "loving"? EUTHYPHRO. Why not? SOCRATES. Tell me, I pray: is a thing "carried" because it is being carried, or for some other reason? EUTHYPHRO. By no means; it is for this very reason. SOCRATES. And "led" similarly because it is being led, and "seen" because it is being seen? EUTHYPHRO. Exactly. SOCRATES. It is not, then, because it is a "seen thing" that it is being seen, but on the contrary, because it is being seen, it is a "seen thing"; nor because it is a "led thing" is it being led, but because it is being led, it is a "led thing"; nor because it is a "carried thing" is it being carried, but because it is being carried, it is a "carried thing." Is it not clear, Euthyphro, what I want to infer? I want this: if something "becomes" or "suffers" something, it is not because it is a "finished thing" that it becomes, but because it "becomes," it is therefore "finished"; nor because it is a "sufferer" does it suffer, but because it "suffers," it is a "sufferer." Do you admit these things? EUTHYPHRO. I certainly admit them. SOCRATES. Is not a "loved thing" either something that has become so, or something that suffers something from someone? EUTHYPHRO. Entirely. SOCRATES. This, therefore, is in the same state as the previous things: it is not because it is a "loved thing" that it is being loved by those who love it, but because it is being loved, it is a "loved thing." EUTHYPHRO. Necessarily. SOCRATES. What then do we say about the holy, Euthyphro? Is it not that which is loved by all the gods, as your speech testifies? EUTHYPHRO. Yes. SOCRATES. Is it because of this, because it is holy, or because of something else? EUTHYPHRO. Because of this itself. SOCRATES. Therefore, since it is holy, it is loved; it is not holy because it is loved. EUTHYPHRO. It seems so. SOCRATES. However, because it is loved by the gods, it is a "loved thing" and dear to the gods. EUTHYPHRO. What prevents it? SOCRATES. Then being "dear to God" is not the same as being "holy," Euthyphro, nor is being "holy" the same as being "dear to God," as you say, but this is one thing and that is another. EUTHYPHRO. For what reason, Socrates? SOCRATES. Because we confess the holy is loved for this reason, because it is holy; but it is not holy because it is loved. Is it not so? EUTHYPHRO. Certainly. SOCRATES. But the thing loved by God, by the very fact that it is loved by God, is a "loved thing," not because it is a "loved thing" by God is it being loved. EUTHYPHRO. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. If, friend Euthyphro, "loved by God" and "holy" were the same, then either because it is holy, that which is holy would be loved, and so because it is loved by God, that which is loved by God would be loved by God. Or because it was loved by God that which is loved by God, it would be loved by God, and so that which is holy, from the fact that it was loved, would be holy. But now you see that they are in opposite states, since they are different from each other. For the one, namely the "loved thing" of God, is such as to be loved because it is being loved. But the other, namely the "holy," is being loved and is a "loved thing" because it is such as to be loved. You seem, Euthyphro, when you were asked what the holy is, to have been unwilling to show its essence, but to have assigned a certain passion <note>An accidental quality or experience.</note> which this holy thing has undergone—namely, to be loved by all the gods. But what it is, you have not yet explained. If therefore it pleases you, do not hide it from me, but define again from the beginning what the holy is itself, whether it is loved by God or experiences anything else; for we shall not disagree about this. But tell me now what is holy, or what is profane...

<summary>This portion of the dialogue refutes the definition of holiness as "what the gods love" by pointing out that the gods often disagree, and further argues that holiness must be an inherent quality of an action rather than a result of being loved by divine beings.</summary>

profane. E U T H. But O Socrates, I do not find a way to express to you what I am thinking. For whatever we have proposed always wanders away from us and refuses to remain where we establish it. S O C R. Our ancestor Daedalus, <note>In Greek mythology, Daedalus was a master craftsman famous for creating statues so lifelike they would walk away if not tied down. Socrates traditionally claimed descent from him because his father was a stone-cutter.</note> O Euthyphro, seems to be the creator of the works you have spoken of. If I had said and proposed those things myself, perhaps you would have mocked me (as if casting a joke) because the inventions of my speech flee away according to that kinship of his, and they do not wish to remain where someone has placed them. But now, since these suppositions are yours, there is need for another sort of wit: for they do not wish to stay put for you, as it also seems to you. E U T H. On the contrary, O Socrates, it seems to me that the things spoken by you can be marked with almost that same wit and jest: for I am <margin>The Works of Daedalus.</margin> least of all the cause of why they wander about, but you seem to me to be Daedalus himself: for as far as it depends on me, those things would have remained as they were. S O C R. I seem, then, O friend, to be more excellent in this art than he was, in that he made only his own works unstable, while I, it appears, do so for those of others besides my own. And this is for me the most beautiful part of the art, that I am wise against my will. For I would prefer that my arguments remain and stand immobile, rather than to attain the wisdom of Daedalus along with the riches of Tantalus. <note>Tantalus was a king famous for his immense wealth, though he is better known for his eternal punishment in the underworld.</note> But enough of this. Since you seem to me to be shrinking from the labor like a pampered person, I shall strive to explain it together with you, so that you may instruct me concerning the holy itself; do not fail in the middle of the speech. For see whether it does not seem necessary to you that everything holy is just. E U T H. It does indeed. S O C. Is everything just also holy? Or is everything holy just? Is everything just not indeed holy, but partly holy and partly something else? E U T. I do not follow those words of yours. S O C R. *Why should I fear to write, when I write of highest Jove?* <note>original: "Scribere cur metuā, quū scribo de Ioue summo?"</note>
*For fear always draws shame along as its companion.* <note>original: "Namq; metus secum fociū trahit vsq; pudorē."</note>

I disagree with this Poet: do you want me to tell you how I disagree? E U T H. Certainly. S O C. It does not <margin>That point is criticized: where there is fear, there is shame.</margin> seem to me that wherever there is fear, there is also shame. For many seem to me to fear poverty and diseases and other things of this sort—fearing them, certainly, yet not being affected by any shame in those things which they fear: does it not seem the same to you? E U T H. It does. S O C. But wherever there is shame, there is also fear. For is there anyone who is affected by shame and blushes, who does not dread the reputation of wickedness? E U T H. He certainly dreads it. S O C. Therefore it is not rightly said, "where there is fear, there is shame," but "where there is shame, there is also fear": yet it is not (vice versa) that wherever there is fear, there is also shame. For fear, I believe, is broader than shame, since shame is a part of fear, just as "odd" is a part of "number." Therefore it is not that wherever there is number, there is the odd; but where there is the odd, there is also number: do you not now follow? E U T H. Entirely. S O C. This, then, is what I was asking earlier: whether where there is justice, there is also holiness: or where there is holiness, there is justice: where, however, there is justice, there is not always holiness: for holiness is a part of justice. Shall we say this, or otherwise? E U T H. Thus indeed, for it seems to be spoken rightly. S O C. See then what follows: if holiness is a part of justice, it is necessary for us, as it appears, to find what kind of part of justice holiness is. If you were therefore to ask me something from before, for example, what kind of part of number the "even" is, and what number it is: I would surely answer, that it is not one of all unequal sides, but of two equal ones. <note>A classical way of defining an even number as divisible into two equal whole parts.</note> Does it not seem so to you? E U T. To me, certainly. S O C. Endeavor therefore that you also teach me in this way, what kind of part of justice holiness is, so that I may immediately object to Meletus, <note>Meletus was the primary prosecutor of Socrates at his trial.</note> lest he accuse us further of injustice and impiety: since we will have learned sufficiently from you what things are pious, what are holy, and what are the opposite. E U T. I think, O Socrates, that the holy and the pious is that part of <margin>The definition of the holy begins to appear.</margin> justice which is concerned with the care of the gods: while that part which pertains to the care of men is the remaining part of justice. E U T H. I assert it. S O C. And dogs by the skill of hunters, and oxen by the ox-herd's, and all other things similarly. Or do you think care tends toward the damage of that which is cared for? E U T. Not by Jove! <note>A common oath to Jupiter/Zeus.</note> S O C. But toward utility? E U T. Why not? S O C. Since holiness is the care of the gods, does it profit the gods?
