### Dialogue V. on the Republic, or, on Justice.

[[page number: 405]]

...Barbarians will rise up, and they will restrain themselves from one another. But what then? Is it honorable to strip the dead of anything besides their weapons after a victory, or not? Does this not provide an opportunity for cowards to avoid facing the enemy, as if they were performing some magnificent deed while they wallow among corpses? Indeed, many armies have perished through a lust for plundering. Most certainly. Does it not seem a sign of an illiberal and greedy mind—something womanish and petty—to despoil a corpse and to regard the body of the dead as an enemy when the adversary himself has flown away, leaving behind the instrument with which he fought? Do we not think those who do this differ little from dogs who snap at the stones thrown at them while ignoring the person who threw them? I think they differ not at all. Therefore, we must abstain from such plundering, for it hinders victory. We must abstain entirely. Nor shall we carry weapons into a temple to dedicate them to God, especially the weapons of Greeks, if we care at all for goodwill with other Greeks. Indeed, we should greatly fear that it might be an impious crime to bring such things from our own people into a sacred place, unless God says otherwise. Quite right. 

And will your soldiers ravage the fields and burn the houses of the Greeks with whom they fight? I would gladly hear what you think of this. To me, it seems no such thing should be done, but only that the annual harvest should be taken. Shall I tell you the reason? Please do. It seems to me that just as there are these two names, **War** and **Sedition** (civil discord), so there are two things underlying these two differences. I mean these two: one is internal and related, the other is foreign and external. The enmity among ourselves we call *seditionem* (discord); that which is with foreigners, we call *bellum* (war). What you say is not off the mark. 

Consider whether this also hits the mark: I say that all Greeks are neighbors and kin to one another, but distinct and foreign from the barbarians. You speak excellently. Therefore, whenever Greeks fight against barbarians, or barbarians against Greeks, we shall say they are waging war and are enemies by nature; we shall call these enmities "war." But when Greeks rise against Greeks, we shall say they are friends by nature, but that Greece is laboring under a disease and is shaken by discord; we shall call these enmities "sedition." I agree. 

If, in a city divided by discord, the men of both factions were to ravage the fields and burn the houses of their adversaries, do you see how destructive that discord would be, as neither side truly loves their fatherland? Surely, if they loved it, they would never dare to devastate their nurse and mother. Rather, they would think it enough if the victors took the harvest of the others, realizing they would not fight forever but would eventually be reconciled. Truly, this is the sentiment of civilized men. 

Is not this city you are founding a Greek one? It should be. Therefore, the citizens in it will be fair and mild. Most certainly. Thus, they will be friends of the Greeks. They will surely consider all Greece as joined to them and will hold sacred the shrines that are common to all. Entirely so. Therefore, they will regard a contention arising with other Greeks as something conducted with their own people, and they will call it "sedition," not "war." They will act exactly so. Thus, they will argue as people who must one day be reconciled. Certainly. They will handle the matter with a benevolent and temperate mind, not looking toward slavery or death, as they are not enemies in the least. Exactly in this way. 

Therefore, being Greeks, they will not destroy Greece, nor burn houses, nor believe that everyone in every city—men, women, and children—is their enemy. They will recognize only the few who were the authors of the discord as their enemies. For this reason, they will not devastate the land of those who are mostly friends, nor will they subvert their homes; they will fight only until those who gave cause for the discord are compelled by the innocent to pay the penalty. I agree that one should fight against Greeks in this way, but against barbarians, one should be minded as Greeks are currently minded toward each other. 

Let us then establish this law for the guardians: neither to ravage fields nor to consume dwellings with fire. Let us establish it, he said, and let us assert that these things, along with the previous ones, are well-ordered. 

But it seems to me, Socrates, that if one allows you to go on speaking, you will never remember the point you set aside in order to bring all this up: namely, whether it is possible for this Republic to exist, and in what way it can be done. For if it were to exist, I have no doubt that every good thing would come to the city... 

[[notes: This section concludes Book V's discussion on the ethics of war among Greeks, which Socrates argues should be seen as civil discord rather than total war.]]

...Now we are pushed into the third and greatest wave, the most difficult. When you have seen and heard it, you will surely grant me pardon, knowing that I was not wrong to fear entering a discourse so far removed from common opinion. The more you pile up such arguments, he said, the less we will let you go until you show how this Republic can become possible. Therefore, speak now, and do not delay. 

First, I said, we must remember that we arrived here while inquiring into the nature of Justice and Injustice. We must, but why? Because if we see what justice is, shall we then judge that the just man must differ not at all from justice itself, but be exactly as justice is? Or shall we be satisfied if he approaches it as closely as possible and participates in it more than any other? We shall be quite satisfied with that. 

For the sake of an example, then, we sought what justice is, and what a perfectly just man would be if he existed; and similarly for injustice and the most unjust man. We did this so that, by looking at how they appeared to us regarding happiness and misery, we would be forced to admit about ourselves that whoever among us shows himself most like them will have a lot similar to theirs. We did not search these things out to prove they *could* happen. This is true. 

Do you think a painter is any less good because, after producing a perfect model of human beauty and omitting no detail of its appearance, he cannot demonstrate that such a person can actually be found? Not at all. And have we not likewise fashioned a model of a most excellent city in our speech? Entirely so. Do you think we speak any less correctly if we cannot show that such a city can exist as we have depicted it? By no means. 

[[page number: 406]]

### Book Thirty-One.

...Is it possible for anything to be done exactly as it is said? Or is it in the nature of things that action touches truth less than speech does, even if it does not seem so to some? Will you admit this or not? I admit it. Therefore, do not force me to demonstrate that these things we have run through in words must be realized exactly in every detail. But if we are able to find how a political institution might most closely approach these ideals, you must admit we have discovered how your requirements can be fulfilled. Would you not be satisfied if you achieved this? I would be. I too. 

Let us then attempt to declare hereafter what it is in cities that is currently done badly, preventing them from being so governed, and whether by the change of one small thing a city might be brought to this form—what that thing is, and whether it is best done by the change of one person, or two, or at least as few as possible. 

...I return to that which we compared to a massive wave. It shall be said, though I suspect it may be overwhelmed by the overflowing laughter of the persistent. Consider what I am about to say. Speak. **Unless either philosophers rule in cities, or those who are now called kings and potentates genuinely and adequately philosophize, and these two—political power and philosophy—coalesce into the same person... there will be no rest from evils for cities, nor, I think, for the human race.** 

[[notes: This is the famous "Philosopher King" passage, cf. Republic 473c-d.]]

...From this speech of yours, Socrates, imagine that very many people—and not insignificant little men—will cast off their clothes, pick up whatever weapons are at hand, and rush at you to do something drastic. Unless you meet them with speech and defend yourself, you will truly suffer the penalty of being shredded by their insults. 

...If we wish to escape those you mention, it seems necessary to declare to them first whom we mean when we say that philosophers must rule. Once these are revealed, someone may be able to offer help, showing that it befits these people by their very nature both to touch upon the study of philosophy and to lead the state, while it befits others not to touch it, but to follow those who lead. 

...Do you need to be reminded, or do you remember well enough, that when we say someone loves something, if it is said truly, it must appear that he does not love one part and not another, but is devoted to the whole? I need a reminder, for I do not quite grasp it. 

...Shall we say the philosopher is a seeker of wisdom—not of one part while rejecting another, but of *all* wisdom? You speak the truth. Therefore, the one who hates a branch of learning—especially while young and not yet possessing the reason to discern what is useful and what is not—we shall not call a lover of learning or a lover of wisdom. Just as we do not call one who is disgusted by feasts hungry, nor a lover of food, but a despiser of it. And rightly so. But the person who is inclined to taste every branch of learning, who is prompt to learn and hangs on it insatiably, we shall rightly name a philosopher. Shall we not? 

Glaucon agreed. But, he said, many absurd people will be found to be such. For those who are greedy for spectacles seem to be lovers of learning, and it is absurd to call "curious" people who hate to approach reason or discussion but run around to every chorus in the *Bacchanalia* (festivals of Bacchus) as if their ears were hired for pay. Shall we call all these, and others who desire such perceptions or pursue the lowest arts, philosophers? By no means, I said, but they are *like* philosophers. 

Whom then do you call true philosophers? Those who are lovers of seeing the Truth. 

...Since "beautiful" is the opposite of "ugly," these are two. Why not? And since they are two, each is one. That too. And the same logic applies to the just and the unjust, the good and the bad, and all the *species* (Forms). For each of these is itself one; but because they appear everywhere in communion with actions and bodies and each other, each appears to be many. 

...Those who are greedy for hearing and seeing are delighted by beautiful voices, colors, and shapes, but their thought cannot touch the nature of the Beautiful itself. That is so. But those who are able to ascend to the Beautiful itself and see it in its own nature—are they not rare? Very rare. 

One who thinks these beautiful things are real, but does not believe in Beauty itself, nor can follow if someone leads him to the perception of it—does he seem to you to be truly wise, or to be playing in a dream? Consider this: is dreaming not exactly this—when someone, whether asleep or awake, thinks that which is like something is not merely like it, but is the very thing it resembles? I would say such a person is dreaming. 

What about the person who is the opposite? Who understands what the Beautiful itself is, and can discern both it and the things that participate in it, and does not think the participants are the Beautiful, nor the Beautiful the participants? Does he live awake or dreaming? Certainly awake. Therefore, we shall rightly call his thought "knowledge" (*cognitionem*), because he knows; but the other's we shall call "opinion" (*opinionem*), because he opines. 

[[notes: Ficino uses *cognitio* for *episteme* (knowledge) and *opinio* for *doxa* (opinion).]]

[[page number: 407]]

### Dialogue V. on the Republic, or, on Justice.

...If the person whom we say "opines but does not know" gets angry at us and denies we speak the truth, how shall we soothe him and gently persuade him that he is not in his right mind? We must indeed. 

Observe what we shall say to him... "If you know something, we do not begrudge it; it will be a pleasure to us for you to know something, so tell us: Does the one who knows know something or nothing?" Answer for him. Something, certainly. Something that *is* or that *is not*? Something that *is*. For how could that which is not be known? 

...That which is entirely "being" (*ens*) is entirely knowable; that which is in no way "being" is in no way knowable. Quite sufficient. Now, if something is such that it both is and is not, will it not lie in the middle between that which is purely and that which is not at all? In the middle. 

Knowledge (*cognitio*) is directed toward that which *is*. Ignorance (*ignoratio*) necessarily concerns that which *is not*. Concerning the middle between these, we must seek a middle state between science and ignorance, if such a thing is found. Exactly. 

Do we say that "opinion" is something? Why not? Is it the same power as science, or a different one? A different one. Therefore, opinion is directed toward one thing, and science toward another. 

...I call "powers" (*potentias*) a certain genus of things by which we can do whatever we do... I do not see the color or shape of a power itself, as I do with many other things... but in a power I look only at what it is directed toward and what it accomplishes. 

...Do you say science is a power? Yes, the most powerful of all. And opinion? A power certainly, for by nothing other than opinion can we opine. But a little while ago you admitted science and opinion are not the same. How could anyone with a mind say that what can be mistaken is the same as what cannot? Excellent. 

...Science knows "being" (*ens*) as it is. Opinion opines. 

...It is impossible for that which is perceived by science and that which is conceived by opinion to be the same. Therefore, if "being" is perceived by knowledge, that which is conceived by opinion must be something other than being. 

...What is conceived by opinion is not "nothing," for it is impossible to opine nothing. But neither is it "being." It must be a middle. Does opinion seem to you darker than knowledge but clearer than ignorance? Exactly. It lies between both. 

...Now it remains to find that which participates in both—in being and not-being—and which cannot be purely called either... so that we may rightly call it the "opinable." 

...Now I shall ask the man who denies the Beautiful itself and the Idea of Beauty as something always the same, yet believes there are many beautiful things... "Is there anything among these many beautiful things, my good man, which might not also appear ugly? Or among the just things that might not appear unjust?" No, they must appear so. 

What about "double"? Do things seem any less "half" than "double"? No. Great and small, light and heavy—will they be called these things any more than their opposites? No, each will always participate in both. 

...These many things are like the riddles told at banquets... They are ambiguous; one cannot firmly understand them as being, or as not being, or as both, or as neither. 

[[page number: 408]]

...We have found, it seems, that the many things which the masses think are beautiful or otherwise are rolling around in the middle between being and non-being. Those who look at these many beautiful things but do not see the Beautiful itself... we shall say they *opine* everything but *know* nothing of what they opine. 

But those who contemplate the things themselves that are always the same—do they not *know* rather than *opine*? Necessarily. Shall we not say they love and admire the things that are the object of knowledge? 

...Shall we call them *philodoxos* (lovers of opinion) rather than *philosophos* (lovers of wisdom)? They will be angry if we say so. But it is a sin to be angry at the truth. Those who admire and love the "being" of each thing itself, we shall call philosophers. 

---

# SIXTH DIALOGUE ON THE JUST.
# MARSILIO FICINO’S ARGUMENT.

Since all laws, even the best, are dead without highly approved magistrates, and the best magistrates are themselves divine laws even without written statutes, our Plato—as we have explained elsewhere—labors with all diligence in his excellent Republic not on the founding of laws, but on the forming of magistrates. He contends for this not only from a tender age but even from the very womb, so that from chosen seeds and continuous cultivation the best fruit may be reached. 

Because he calls these men "guardians" (*custodes*), and the most proper task of guardians is to look forward and look around, he therefore chooses the **philosophical genius**—the most perspicacious of all without controversy—to guard the human flock. For only to the eye of this man is the model of the Good itself and of Justice open, after whose image the city must be painted well, justly, and happily. 

Furthermore, it belongs to the guardian to be truthful, liberal, temperate, brave, just, magnanimous, and mild. He will prove these same qualities are proper to the philosopher... 

[[notes: Ficino’s *Argumentum* (Introduction) summarizes Book VI, emphasizing that the philosopher is the only one fit to rule because he perceives the "Idea of the Good."]]

[[page number: 409]]

...Ficino explains that the Idea of the Good is not this or that species, but the fecundity of the most eminent Divinity. Its image in the visible world is the sun. But before this sun we see, Plato conceives of another in the invisible world—the first image of God the Father, and his true Son. Thus he spoke of the "children of the Good." 

[[notes: Ficino here bridges Platonic thought with Christian Theology, identifying the "Sun" of the Republic with the "Son of God" (the Logos/Word).]]

...Iamblichus (the Neoplatonist) testifies that this is the mystery of Hermes. Just as the Good is above pleasures, and morals, and wisdom, so Plato signifies it here briefly... it is also above "being" (*ens*), for you desire to exist so that it may be well with you. 

---

### Dialogue VI. on the Republic, or, on Justice.

"Who the philosophers are," I said, "and who are those foreign to philosophy, Glaucon, has finally been established after a long discourse." 

...Since philosophers are those who can reach that which is always the same, while those who cannot—who wander through many changing things—are not philosophers, which of these should be the leaders of the city? 

...Does it seem to you that they differ at all from the blind—those who lack the knowledge of that which truly is in each thing, and have no clear model in their minds? Like painters looking at the truest model, they cannot refer to it and contemplate it accurately to establish laws here about the beautiful, the just, and the good. 

...Let us first agree on the nature of philosophers: they always love that learning which makes known to them that nature which always exists and is not changed by generation or corruption. 

...Next, notice this: must it not be in the nature of those who will be such as we described to be free from all falsehood? They must never lie voluntarily but must hate all falsehood and love the truth. 

...For one who is truly a lover of learning, it is necessary from childhood to seek all truth above all else. When desires pull a person toward one certain thing, his desires for other things become weaker, like water diverted into other channels. 

Whoever, then, burns with desire for the sciences and such things seeks the pure pleasure of the soul itself and despises the pleasures of the body—unless he is a fake and not a true philosopher. 

Such a person will be temperate and not a lover of money... He will have a magnificence of thought and the contemplation of all time and all substance; human life cannot seem a great thing to him. Therefore, he will not think death is a thing to be feared. 

...A modest man, not given to profit, not illiberal, not proud, not timid—will he be difficult or unjust in his dealings? Not at all. 

[[page number: 410]]

...Will he be quick to perceive or slow? Do you think anyone would ever love that which he does with great difficulty and little progress? Never. What if he forgets everything he learns? He will be empty of knowledge. 

...Therefore, we should not think a forgetful soul belongs to the genius of legitimate philosophers, but rather a very mindful one. 

...Can you in any way damn this study, which no one can sufficiently carry out unless he is by nature perspicacious, mindful, magnificent, gracious, a friend and kinsman of truth, justice, courage, and temperance? Even **Momus** (the god of mockery) could not find fault with it. 

...To this, **Adeimantus** replied: "No one, Socrates, could contradict you. But here is how those who hear what you say are affected: they think that because of their lack of skill in questioning and answering, they are led astray a little bit by reason at each step. When these small errors are collected at the end, a massive error results... like those who are not skilled at playing a board game are eventually blocked by those who are. 

...They would say that in reality, those who pursue philosophy—not just tasting it in youth for the sake of education and then leaving it, but staying in it longer—mostly turn out to be quite absurd, if not entirely wicked. Even the most excellent among them are rendered useless to the state by the very study you praise." 

"Do you think those who say these things are lying?" I asked. 

"I don't know," he said, "but I would gladly hear what you think." 

"You shall hear that I think they speak the truth." 

"Then how is it right to say that there will be no rest from evils for cities until philosophers rule, whom we admit are useless to the republic?" 

"Your question needs an answer through an **image** (a metaphor)." 

[[notes: Socrates now introduces the famous "Ship of State" allegory.]]

...Imagine a pilot of a ship who exceeds the other sailors in size and strength, but is somewhat deaf, has failing eyesight, and is ignorant of navigation. Imagine the sailors fighting among themselves over the steering, each thinking he is worthy of the helm, though he has never learned the art... They surround the pilot, begging and striving for him to hand over the tiller. 

If they do not persuade him, but others do, they kill the others or throw them overboard. Then, having drugged the noble pilot with mandragora or wine, they seize the ship, indulge in the stores, and drink and feast... They praise and call "navigator" and "pilot" anyone who is clever at helping them seize the command. The man who is not useful for this, they despise as useless. 

They do not even consider that a true pilot must pay attention to the year, the seasons, the sky, the stars, and the winds if he is to be truly a ruler of a ship. 

In such a ship, do you not think the true pilot would be called a "star-gazer," a "useless babbler," and "good-for-nothing" by those who sail in such a way? 

[[page number: 411]]

...I do not think I need to explain how this image applies to cities and their attitude toward true philosophers. 

...The most vehement calumny against philosophy arises because of the morals of those who profess to be philosophers... and I have conceded this to you, have I not? Yes. 

...Why are most of them wicked? Let us declare that the fault is not in philosophy. 

...The man who is a lover of knowledge is naturally inclined to strive for that which truly is. He does not linger among those many particulars where opinion wanders, but moves forward until he touches the nature of each thing with that power of the soul which is fit to grasp it. 

When he has adhered to and mixed with that which truly is, and from that has generated intelligence and truth, he will truly live and be nourished. Only then will his labor cease. 

...Where Truth is the leader, we will not say a chorus of evils follows, but rather a healthy and just character, followed by temperance. 

...We are now searching for why the nature of the philosopher is corrupted in so many. 

...We must observe that even the qualities we praised in the philosopher—courage, temperance, etc.—each one of them can ruin the soul and pull it away from philosophy. 

This sounds absurd. 

Furthermore, everything that is called a "good" by the masses corrupts the soul: beauty, riches, physical strength, a powerful family in the city... You have a formula for what I mean. 

...We know that every seed and plant, if it does not receive the nutrition, climate, or location it requires, the more vigorous it is, the more it fails. For "evil" is more contrary to "good" than to the "not-good." 

...Therefore, it is consistent that the most excellent nature, if fed on alien food, becomes worse than a lazy nature. Do you think unspeakable crimes and extreme wickedness proceed from a lazy mind rather than a noble one corrupted by education? A weak nature is never the cause of anything great, either good or evil. 

[[page number: 412]]

...If the nature of the philosopher finds the right discipline, it must reach every virtue. But if it is sown and nourished perversely, it falls into all the opposites, unless some god helps it. 

Do you think, as many do, that it is only "sophists" (paid teachers of rhetoric) who corrupt the youth? Or should we believe that the very people who say this—the public—are the greatest sophists of all? 

When do they do this? When they sit in crowds in the assemblies, the courts, the theaters, or the camps, and with a huge noise they blame some things and praise others, both in excess... while the walls and the places they are in echo the tumult. In such a crowd, what do you think is the "heart" of a young man? What private education can resist such a flood? He will say the same things are honorable or shameful as they do. 

...And yet we haven't mentioned the greatest necessity. Which? The one these sophists and teachers apply with *deeds* when they fail to persuade with words. Do you not see that they punish the one who does not obey with infamy, fines, and even death? 

...Truly, whoever escapes and remains upright in such a constitution of public affairs, know for certain that he escaped by **divine aid**. 

...Every one of these paid teachers, whom they call sophists, teaches nothing other than the opinions of the masses which they hold when they are gathered together; and they call this "wisdom." 

It is as if someone had nourished a **vast, brute, powerful animal** and observed its angers and desires: how to approach it, how to touch it, when it is most fierce or mild, and from what causes. He learns the noises it makes and which words soothe or provoke it. After long habit, he calls this "skill" and "wisdom" and sets up a school. 

But in reality, he is ignorant of which of these opinions and desires is truly honorable or shameful, good or evil, just or unjust. He names everything according to the opinion of that great beast: "good" is what delights it, "evil" is what offends it. 

Does such a teacher not seem absurd to you? To me, yes. 

...And is he any different from the one who thinks "wisdom" is knowing the anger and pleasures of a gathered crowd, whether in painting, music, or politics? 

...Can the masses ever admit that "Beauty itself" exists, rather than just many beautiful things? Not at all. Therefore, the masses cannot be philosophers. And they must necessarily blame those who philosophize. 

[[page number: 413]]

...When a young man has a magnificent soul, and is born in a great city, wealthy and noble, and is handsome and tall—will he not be filled with immense hope? He will think himself sufficient to manage the affairs of both Greeks and Barbarians. He will be puffed up with empty pride. 

If someone approaches such a person and says he has no mind, but needs one—and that a mind cannot be acquired unless one slaves for it—do you think he will listen? Far from it. 

...Thus the nature of the philosopher is corrupted. From these come the men who commit the most heinous crimes, both private and public. A petty nature never does anything great. 

...Philosophy, left desolate by those who should love her, is invaded by men unworthy of her, who bring upon her the infamy you mentioned. 

Other little men, seeing this seat vacant—though it is still full of noble titles and dignity—flee from their trades to philosophy, like people who flee from a prison to a temple. For philosophy, even in this state, still holds a higher dignity than the other arts. 

These men are naturally imperfect, their bodies warped by their trades and their souls crushed and broken by "mechanical" (menial) labors. Does he seem any different to you than a little bald blacksmith who has come into some money, just got out of chains, washed himself in a bath, put on a new suit like a bridegroom, and is about to marry his master’s daughter because the master is poor and has no one else to give her to? 

What kind of children will they produce? Bastards and base ones. 

...A very few remain, Adeimantus, who worthily consort with philosophy. These are those who, born with a good character and well-bred, were perhaps held in exile and so found the leisure for philosophy... or someone like our friend **Theages**, who was held back from politics by the poor health of his body. 

...As for my own "divine sign" (*daemonis nostri signum*), it is not worth mentioning now, for it has happened to almost no one else. 

[[notes: Socrates refers to his *daimonion*, the inner voice that warned him away from certain actions.]]

Those who have tasted how sweet and blessed a possession philosophy is... see the madness of the many. They see that no one acts rightly in public affairs... and like a man who has fallen among wild beasts, he will not join in their injustice, but he cannot resist all the beasts alone. He would perish before he could help his city or friends. 

Observing all this, the philosopher keeps quiet and minds his own business. Like someone in a storm when the wind whips up the dust and the rain, he stands aside under the shelter of a wall. Seeing others filled with lawlessness, he is content if he can live his life pure from injustice and unholy deeds, and depart with good hope, cheerful and at peace. 

"He will have accomplished no small thing," said Adeimantus. 

"But not the greatest thing either," I said, "unless he finds a Republic that fits him. In such a state, he will grow more and will preserve both private and public affairs." 

[[page number: 414]]

### Dialogue VI. on the Republic, or, on Justice.

...Which of the current republics is suitable for philosophy? "None at all," I said. "And that is my complaint: I see no current institution worthy of the philosophical nature." 

...Unless a philosopher finds the best Republic, he will never show that he is something divine. 

"You will probably ask me which one that is." 

"No, I was going to ask if it is this one we have been founding, or another?" 

"In most respects, it is this one." 

...How should a city take up philosophy so as not to be destroyed? For all great things are precarious, and as the proverb says, "Beautiful things are difficult." 

...Currently, those who study philosophy are mere adolescents. They take up the most difficult part—dialectic—while they are still managing their family affairs, and then they leave it. 

In old age, with few exceptions, they are extinguished more completely than the **Sun of Heraclitus**, for they are never lit again. 

[[notes: Heraclitus said the sun is new every day; Socrates suggests these people never renew their light.]]

We must do the opposite. Boys and youths should handle a youthful discipline and philosophy, and take care of their bodies as they grow, to prepare them as servants for philosophy. As they mature, they should increase the soul’s exercises. And when their strength fails in old age, they should be released from civil and military labors to live as they wish—those, at least, who are to live happily and receive a lot after death that fits their life. 

...You speak with great promptness, Socrates. But I think many will oppose you even more promptly. **Thrasymachus** (the angry sophist from Book I) especially. 

"Do not try to make an enemy of Thrasymachus and me," I said. "We have just become friends, and we weren't enemies before." 

...We have said that no city, no republic, and no man will be perfect until these few philosophers—who are called not wicked but useless—are forced by some necessity to take care of the city, or until a true love of true philosophy is breathed by some divine inspiration into those who currently rule. 

...If, in the infinite time of the past, or now in some barbarian region far from our sight, or in the future, such men are compelled to rule, we affirm that this Republic has existed, exists, and will exist. 

...Do not be so hard on the masses, my friend. They will have a different opinion if you show them, with friendly advice rather than contention, who the philosophers really are... 

Do you think a mild man gets angry at someone who is not angry? Or that a person without envy envies one who is not envious? 

...The reason the multitude is hostile to philosophy is because of those people who, being unfit for philosophy, have invaded it and spend their time insulting people and enjoying conflict. 

But the man whose mind is truly directed toward "being" has no leisure to look down at the petty affairs of men or to fight with them. He contemplates things that always keep the same order... He imitates these and makes himself as much like them as possible. 

The philosopher, by consorting with the divine and the orderly, becomes as divine and orderly as is possible for a human. 

If he is compelled to transfer what he sees there into the morals of men, both privately and publicly, do you think he will be a poor craftsman of temperance and justice? Not at all. 

When these philosophers take the city and the morals of men like a canvas, they will first wipe it clean, which is not easy. This is how they differ from others: they will not touch a person or a city, nor make laws, until they have either received it clean or made it clean themselves. 

Then they will sketch the form of the republic... Looking frequently in both directions: toward that which is naturally Just, Honorable, and Temperate, and toward the human world. They will arrange the human according to the model of the divine. 

They will erase some parts and paint others, until they have joined human morals as much as possible to the love of God. 

"This would be a most beautiful painting," he said. 

...The sons of kings and potentates may be born philosophers. And if even one is saved from corruption and finds an obedient city, he is sufficient to accomplish all these things that now seem incredible. 

Therefore, it is possible. It is difficult, but not impossible. 

...Now that we have finally reached the end of this, we must proceed to the rest: by what disciplines and studies they will be instructed...

***

[[summary: This text covers the transition from Book V to Book VI of Plato's Republic as translated and interpreted by Marsilio Ficino. It establishes the ethical distinctions between civil discord and foreign war, defines the philosopher as a lover of eternal Truth rather than mere opinion, and introduces the famous "Philosopher King" doctrine and the "Ship of State" allegory to explain why true philosophers are currently maligned by society.]]

[[keywords: Plato, Republic, Marsilio Ficino, Philosopher King, Knowledge vs Opinion, Ship of State, Idea of the Good, Justice, Greek Unity, Sophists]]

--- Page 62 ---
Parmenides, Or, On the One Principle of all things, and on Ideas. 43

In all these things Parmenides generally intends most of all to assert this: that the One is the principle of all things; and with it positioned, all things are positioned; but with it removed, they are destroyed. Thus in the first five suppositions he hands down five grades of things with the One positioned in the order of things. In the four following, indeed, he inquires how many absurdities, how many errors, and what great evils follow if the One itself is removed. The first of the five above discourses on the One and the supreme God, how he procreates and disposes the orders of the following gods. The second is about the individual orders of the gods, in what way they proceed from God himself. The third is about divine souls. The fourth is about those things which happen around matter, how they are produced by celestial causes. The fifth is about primary matter, how by its own nature it is void of species, and depends on the first One. Furthermore, it should be noted that in this dialogue, when the "One" is mentioned, in the Pythagorean manner any substance entirely absolved from matter can be signified, such as God, mind, or soul. But when "another" and "other things" are said, one may understand both matter and those things which occur in matter. These things therefore having been premised and preserved, let us come to the dialogue itself.

***

### CEPHALUS, ADIMANTUS, ANTIPHON, GLAUCON, PYTHO, SOCRATES, PARMENIDES.

WHEN we had set out from our home in Clazomenae to Athens, we met Adimantus and Glaucon near the forum. And taking my hand, Adimantus said, "Hail, O Cephalus, and if you need anything that is within our power, speak." And I said, "I have come for this, because I will need your help." "Explain," he said, "what it is you need." Then I said, "What was your half-brother's name? For I do not remember. For he was a boy when I first came here from Clazomenae, and a long interval of time has passed. I think his father's name, however, was Pyrilampes." "Exactly," he said, "and his own name is Antiphon. But why do you ask especially?" "These citizens of mine," I said, "are ardent lovers of wisdom; they heard that this Antiphon lived for a long time in close familiarity with Pythodorus, the associate of Zeno, and they think he retains in memory the arguments which Socrates, Zeno, and Parmenides once treated among themselves, since he heard them more frequently from Pythodorus." "You speak the truth," he said. "Therefore we desire to hear them." "It is not difficult," he said, "for while he was a young youth, he meditated on them diligently. But now, around his grandfather, who has the same name, he is mostly occupied with equestrian matters. However, if there is need, let us go to him; for he just left here for home. He lives near Melita." When these things had been said, we went and found Antiphon at home, handing a certain bit to a smith to be fitted. But after he left him, and the brothers reported the cause of our arrival, he recognized me because I had come there before, and he saluted me with an embrace. When we prayed him to relate that disputation, at first indeed he refused; for it would be a work of no small labor. Then, however, he set it forth.

Antiphon said, then, that Pythodorus narrated that Zeno and Parmenides once came to the celebration of the Great Panathenaea, and Parmenides was already old and gray-haired, decorous in appearance, being almost sixty-five years of age; but Zeno was born nearly forty years, tall moreover, and of a graceful habit of body: and he was said to be in Parmenides' favor. They lodged with Pythodorus outside the walls, in the Ceramicus, and Socrates came there, and many others with Socrates, desiring to hear the writings of Zeno: for they were then first brought by them.

Socrates was at that time quite young, and Zeno himself read to them. For Parmenides happened to be out of the house. Pythodorus said that little remained to be read when he himself entered the house together with Parmenides and Aristotle, who was one of the Thirty Men. <note>Aristotle here is not the famous philosopher, but a member of the "Thirty Tyrants" of Athens.</note> Therefore he heard the few things that remained to be read: yet he had perceived all things before from Zeno.

SOCRATES then, when he had heard them, ordered the first hypothesis of the first speech to be read again: and it having been read, he brought this in: "How do you say that, O Zeno, if those things which are are many, they must be both similar and dissimilar? For that is impossible. For neither can dissimilar things be similar, nor similar things dissimilar. Is it not thus you say?" "So indeed," Zeno replied. "If it is impossible for dissimilar things to be similar, or similar things dissimilar, is it also impossible for many things to be? For if there were many, something impossible would happen to them. Is this what your speeches want? and they intend nothing else than to assert through all things that there are not many, and do you think each of your arguments is a proof of this, and do you judge yourself to have brought as many proofs as the arguments you brought that there are not many? Do you say so? Or do I not perceive correctly?" "On the contrary," Zeno replied, "you have understood best what these writings mean." "I understand, O Parmenides," said Socrates, "that this Zeno wishes to consult with me not only in friendship, but also in those things which he composed. For he wrote in a way the same thing that you did: but by a certain permutation he tries to deceive us, as if he were saying something else than you. For you in your poems want this whole which is to be one, and you exhibit most beautiful arguments for this. But he denies that there are many, providing many and valid proofs himself. While therefore one says 'one,' and the other 'not many,' and each speaks in a way that they do not seem to bring in the same thing, though they say almost the same things, those things seem to us to be said above us." "It is so, O Socrates," Zeno said. "Yet you do not entirely grasp the matter, although like Laconian hounds you follow well and track what is said. For first this deceives you: that the writings are put forth for the reason that if, as you think, others cannot follow, something great has been achieved by us. But what you think was sought happens of its own accord. For these are in truth written in support of Parmenides, against those who strive to pluck at him, saying: if indeed there is one, many ridiculous things will happen to this opinion, and even things deeply repugnant to itself. This writing therefore opposes those who want there to be many, and throws back more in turn, so that it may be clear that much more absurd things follow from their opinion, namely that there are many, than from the opinion of Parmenides that there is one, if anyone examines it diligently. Because of this contention, then, in my youth I composed the book, which someone stealing published before I could consult whether it should be brought to light or not. This then escapes you, O Socrates, that you think it was written not from youthful contention, but from elderly ambition. However, as I said, you have not conjectured ineptly." "I accept it," said Socrates, "and I think it is as you say."

### CERTAIN THINGS ABOUT THE IDEAS.

...things which we certainly call many? and whatever things participate in likeness, become similar to that extent, insofar as they participate? and those in unlikeness, dissimilar, and those in both, both? but if all things participate in both contraries being present, in that they participate in both, they are similar and dissimilar among themselves, what is the wonder? For if someone said that similar things themselves were dissimilar, or dissimilar things themselves similar, he would say a kind of monster, as I think. But if someone asserted that those things participating in both suffered both, it would seem to me, O Zeno, nothing to be wondered at. Nor would I wonder if someone said all things were one from the fact that they participate in the one, and these same things again many, because they also participate in multitude. But if he showed that that which is the one itself is many, and the many themselves one, then I shall wonder exceedingly. And concerning all other things in the same way. For if he should say the genera themselves and species receive those contraries in themselves, it will certainly be worthy of wonder. For if anyone demonstrates that I am one and many, it is no wonder. If indeed, wishing to assert me to be many, he should say my right parts are some, my left others, some front, some back, and finally superior and inferior similarly: for I am a participant in multitude, as I think: but wishing to show me as one, he should say that out of us who are seven, I am one man, a participant in the one, similarly it is no wonder. For which reason both are affirmed truly. If therefore anyone should attempt such things, to demonstrate the same things as one and many, namely stones and wood and other things of this sort, we shall confess that he has shown one and many, yet not the one as many, nor many as one, nor has he said anything wonderful, but what we would all confess. But if someone first distinguished the species themselves according to themselves separately, as I said a little while ago, such as likeness, unlikeness, multitude, the one, rest, motion, and other things of this sort, then asserted that in themselves those things could be mixed and separated, I would be amazed indeed, O Zeno. And if I think those things you wrote have been treated as becomes a brave man, I would yet wonder much more and rejoice if someone could explain more clearly this same question which is deeply implicit in the species themselves, just as it is set forth in things which are seen, so also in those things which are comprehended by reason." While Socrates said these things, Pythodorus said he thought Parmenides and Zeno were each indignant against Socrates, but they listened with a certain greatest attention, and frequently looking at one another they smiled, as if admiring Socrates. Whence when Socrates had made an end of speaking, Parmenides said: "O Socrates, how worthy of admiration you are because of that impetus of disputing!"

"BUT tell me, I pray. Did you thus, as you say, yourself distinguish the species separately, and separately also those things participating in the species, and does it seem to you that there is something that is the species themselves separately—likeness, of which we also are participants, and something separately the one, something separately the many, and all things whatever you just heard from Zeno?" "So it seems to me," Socrates replied. "Do you mean such things," asked Parmenides, "as a certain species of justice itself by itself, and of the beautiful, and of the good, and finally of all such things?" "Entirely." "Is there then a species of man separate from us, and from others of the same kind, and also a species of fire and water?" "Oftentimes," said Socrates, "I have been turned in this ambiguity, whether it should be said about these just as about the former, or otherwise." "Have you also doubted about these, O Socrates, which someone perhaps might think ridiculous, such as hair or mud, and stain, and other most ignoble and vilest things? Do you doubt whether a separate species of each of these should be positioned, existing as something else from those which we handle, or not?" "In no way," said Socrates: "but what we see, these things also are: but to think there is a certain species of them would perhaps be too ridiculous. Yet sometimes this thought has disturbed me, lest there perhaps be something the same in all: but when I have stood there a little while, from there I have again departed, fearing lest falling into trifles to be explained by no words I might perish. Whence having returned to those things which we said before have species, I am now occupied with them." "You are still young, O Socrates, and philosophy has not yet embraced you. But it will embrace you, as my opinion holds, when you neglect none of those things; but now because of your age you look to the opinions of men."

"TELL me this then. Does it seem to you, as you were saying, that certain species exist, and those things which participate in them receive their names from them? Such as those participating in likeness are called similar, in greatness great, in beauty and justice beautiful and just?" "And most especially," said Socrates. "Does not whatever is a participant in a species participate in either the whole species or a part? Or is there another way of participating besides these?" "And what other?" Socrates said. "Does it seem to you that the whole species is in each of the many things, existing as one? Or otherwise?" "What prohibits it from being one?" "One and the same thing then in many things placed separately, the whole will be one at the same time, and thus it will exist separately from itself." "In no way," said Socrates. "But just as one day is present everywhere at once, yet it is not separated from itself, so nothing prohibits any one and the same species from being present to many at the same time, yet not being separated from itself." "Beautifully, O Socrates, you show one and the same at once in many, as if covering many men with a sail, you should say one thing is whole in many. Do you not say such a thing?" "Perhaps." "Will then the whole sail be present to each, or a part of it to one and another to another?" "A part." "The species therefore will be divisible," he said, "O Socrates, and those things which participate in them will take a part, nor anymore the whole in each, but a part of each will be one." "So it appears." "What then, will you say one species is truly both divided and one?" "In no way." "Consider then, if you divide greatness itself, and each of many great things will be great by a part of greatness smaller than greatness itself is, will it not seem far from reason?" "Entirely." "What then, each one participating a little in a part of the equal itself, will it have that by which, since it is smaller than the equal itself, that which it has is equal to something?" "Impossible." "But also some of us will have a part of the small itself, by which the small itself is greater, since that part of it exists, and thus the small itself will be greater. But that from which the part is taken away will be smaller, and in no way greater than it was before." "That," he said, "cannot happen." "In what way then, O Socrates," he said, "will others participate in species, when they can participate neither according to the whole, nor according to the parts?" "By Jove, this seems to me not an easy thing to determine." "But what do you say to this?" "What is it?" "Therefore another species of greatness besides greatness itself and those participating in greatness will shine out again, and in all those again another, by which all are great, nor will each species any longer be one, but rather infinite in number." "But perhaps," Socrates said, "each of these species is a certain notion, and cannot be anywhere else than in minds. For thus each will be one, and those things you said will not happen." "What then?" he said. "Is each notion one? but a notion of nothing?" "But that is impossible." "But of something?" "Of something, surely." "Of an existing thing, or a non-existing thing?" "Of an existing thing." "Is it not of one certain thing, which that notion understands as one idea in all things?" "Entirely." "Furthermore, will it not be a species, this which is understood to be one, always the same in all things?" "This also seems necessary." "What then?" said Parmenides, "is it not necessary, since others participate in species, that each consist of notions, and each understand? or although they are notions, yet understand nothing?" "But neither does that have reason," he said, "but most especially these things seem to me to be so: that these species stand as patterns in nature, but other things become similar to them, and are likenesses, nor do those things participate in species otherwise than that they become similar to them." "If then, as you say, something is similar to a species, is it possible for the species itself not to be similar to that which has been made similar to it, insofar as it has been made similar to it? Or can it be thought that the similar is not similar to the similar?" "Certainly not." "And must not the similar necessarily participate in the same species as that to which it is similar?" "It is necessary." "But that by which the similar things participating become similar, will not that be the species itself?" "Absolutely." "It is not possible then for anything to be similar to the species, nor the species to another. For besides the species itself, another species would always emerge: and if that were similar to any, another again. Nor will that progress ever cease, but a new species will always occur, if the species is similar to the participant." "You speak very true things." "Therefore not through similarity do others participate in species, but some other way of participating must be sought besides." "It appears so." "Do you see, O Socrates, how much ambiguity follows if anyone distinguishes the species, which are species, as they are according to themselves?" "And most especially," he said. "Know moreover that you do not yet, so to speak, comprehend how great the difficulty is if you position each species of things segregated from others." "How so?" he said. "There are indeed many other things: but this is the greatest: because if anyone should contend that they ought not to be known, since they are such as we say species ought to be, surely no one could refute him who says those things, unless he be a man of much experience and ingenious, who would contend for that, and be prepared moreover to follow the one demonstrating, and bringing in many things by a long circuit; but he who contends they are unknown cannot be persuaded." "Why, O Parmenides?" said Socrates. "Since, O Socrates, I think both you and anyone else whoever positions a certain essence itself existing according to itself, would not grant it to be in us." "For in what way," said Socrates, "would it be according to itself?" "You speak rightly. Are not then however many of the ideas look to each other, what they are, they have essence toward themselves, and not toward those things which <margin>The beautiful itself and the good itself are unknown to us.</margin> are around us, whether they be likenesses, or however anyone may name them, by which we participating are named as individual things? But those which are around us, equivocal to them, are similarly toward themselves and not toward the species, and of themselves and not of those which are again named similarly." "How do you say?" said Socrates. "As if someone of us were a master or a servant of someone, he is not a servant of the master itself which is a master, nor is he a master who is called master of the servant itself which is a servant: but both of these are as a man. But domination itself exists as what it is of servitude itself, and servitude itself again in the same way is servitude of domination itself: neither those things which are in us are toward them, nor those which are there are referred toward us: but, as I said, they are of themselves and toward themselves, and those which are here similarly look toward themselves. Do you understand what I say?" "I understand entirely." "Is not also science itself what it is, science of that truth which is itself?" "Absolutely indeed." "Again, whichever of the sciences is what it is, is it not the science of some one of existing things?" "Surely." "But our science, will it not be science of the truth which is around us? And again, each one of our sciences, science of each of those things which are around us?" "It is necessary." "However, do you assent that we neither have the species themselves, nor can they be around us?" "Not surely." "Are not individual genera known by the species of science?" "Certainly." "Which species we do not have." "Certainly not." "No species then is known by us, since we are in no way participants in science itself." "It does not appear so." "Unknown to us then is the beautiful itself, and the good itself, and finally all things which we suppose as ideas." "It seems so." "Consider also this, even more grave." "What is it?" "Do you confess, if there is a certain genus of science itself, it would be much more excellent than this our science, and beauty itself and the rest in the same way?" "Indeed." "Is it not that if anything else is a participant in science itself, you will say no one but God has the supreme science?" "It is necessary." "Will God, when he has embraced science itself, be able to discern these things of ours?" "Why not?" "Because," said Parmenides, "we have confessed, O Socrates, that neither those species have the power they have toward ours, nor ours toward the celestial ones, but both are referred toward themselves." "We confessed it clearly." "Therefore if with God there is the supreme domination itself, and the supreme science itself, never will either domination itself dominate us, or science itself know us, or any other of our things: but we also similarly will in no way rule the gods by our rule, nor perceive anything divine by our science. And they likewise by the same reason will neither be our masters, nor will they notice human things since they are gods." "But will not this speech seem very wonderful," he said, "if someone deprives God of knowledge?" "These things indeed, O Socrates," said Parmenides, "and many others besides these, necessarily happen to species, if indeed these are the ideas of things, and someone separates each one of them from others, since it is of itself. Whence whoever hears these things wavers and doubts, lest perhaps the ideas are nothing at all: or if they are, that it be necessary for them to be unknown to human nature, so that he who says these things, although he seems to have said something, soon that appears wonderful and incredible, as was clear a little while ago. And that it is the work of a man of very ingenious mind to be able to perceive what is the genus itself of each thing by itself, and the essence itself according to itself..."

COME THEN, if there is "One," the One itself will certainly not be "many." "How could it be?" "Therefore it is necessary that there be neither any part of it, nor that it be a whole." "Why?" "A part is certainly a part of a whole." "What then? Is not a whole that which lacks no part?" "Certainly." "In both cases, then, the One itself would be made of parts, being both a whole and having parts." "It must be so." "In both cases, again, the One itself would be many rather than one." "It must, however, exist not as many, but as the One itself." "It must indeed." "Therefore it will neither be a whole, nor will it have parts, if the One is to be the One itself." "Certainly not." "If it has no part, it will have neither a beginning, nor an end, nor a middle. For these would be parts of it." "Rightly so." "Furthermore, the beginning and the end are the limits of anything." "Why not?" "Therefore the One itself is infinite, since it lacks a beginning and an end." "Infinite." "Therefore it is also without figure <note>original: *figura*, meaning shape or form</note>: for it participates in neither the round nor the straight." "Why?" "The round is that whose extremes and middle are equally distant from the center." "Exactly so." "But the straight is that whose middle is in a line with both extremes." "So it is." "Would not the One have parts and be many if it participated in a straight or circular figure?" "Entirely so." "Therefore, it is neither straight nor round, since it has no parts." "Right." "Furthermore, since it is such, it is nowhere. For it can be neither in another, nor in itself." "Why?" does the One appear? What prevents it? This indeed. Because if it spends the same age either with itself or with some other, it will participate in equality and similarity of time. Yet it has been shown that no equality or similarity can be present in the One itself. It has been shown indeed. Did we not also say this, that it exists without possessing inequality or dissimilarity? Most certainly. In what way then can that which is of this sort be older or younger than anything, or equal in age to any? In no way. Therefore, the One itself will not be younger, not older, not equal in age either to itself or to another? It does not appear so. Likewise, in no way does the One itself become or exist in time. For it is necessary that whatever is in time always becomes older than itself. Necessary. And that which is older is always older than something younger. Why not? Therefore, that which becomes older than itself also simultaneously becomes younger than itself, if indeed it must be older than something. How do you mean? In this way: it is necessary that nothing becomes "different" than another when it is already "different," but for that which already exists, it is; for the past, it was; for the future, it will be. But for that which is becoming, it has not passed, nor will it be, nor is it "different"; but it is becoming, and cannot be otherwise. It is necessary. But "older" is something opposite to "younger," and to no other thing at all. It is. That which therefore becomes older than itself must necessarily also become younger than itself at the same time. It seems so. Furthermore, it does not become for a longer time than itself, nor a shorter, but always becomes and is and was and will be for an equal time with itself. These are also necessary. It seems necessary therefore that any of those things which are in time, and participate in this sort of thing, spend the same age with themselves, and become older and younger than themselves at the same time. It appears so. But to the One itself, none of these affections happens at all. None. Therefore, it is a participant of no time, nor is it in any time. Not indeed, as reason dictates. What then? Does the "was," "has been," or "was becoming" not seem to signify a participation in time that is past? <margin>The words "Is," "Was," etc. signify time.</margin> Indeed. And will not "will be," "will become," or "will have been made" designate the future for us? The future. And "is" and "becomes" are marks of the present time. Entirely so. If therefore the One itself participates in no time at all, it never "was," nor "became," nor "is," nor "will become," nor "will have been made," nor "will be." These things are most true. Can anything participate in essence <note>original: "essentia." This refers to "being" or "existence."</note> otherwise than according to one of these? <margin>In the word "Is," there is both time and essence.</margin> Not otherwise. In no way, therefore, is the One itself. It appears not at all. It is not therefore even so as to be "one." For it would then already be a being and a participant in essence; indeed, as it seems, the One itself is neither "one" nor is it at all, if this reasoning is to be believed. It appears so. But for that which is not, is there either anything for it or of it? And how? Therefore, there is no name for it, no discourse, no certain knowledge, no sense, no opinion. It does not seem so. Wherefore it is neither named, nor spoken of, nor thought of by opinion, nor known, nor is it perceived by any of those things which are. It certainly does not seem so. Is it possible for these things to be so concerning the One itself? Not, as it seems to me.

<margin>The second supposition concerning the One, if it is.</margin>
DO YOU wish then for us to return to the beginning of the position itself, considering if perhaps something might appear to us to be otherwise upon our return? I wish it indeed. If the One is, have we not confessed what the things that happen around it must be like? Certainly; meditate again from the beginning: if the One is, is it possible for it to be, yet in no way participate in essence? Impossible. But the essence of the One will not be the same as the One itself. Otherwise, if it were the same, it would not be its essence, nor would the One itself have participated in it, but whenever it was uttered that "the One is," it would signify something similar to if we said "one." Now, however, our position is not of this sort—namely, if "one," what will happen—but "if the One *is*," is it not so? Exactly so. Is it not said thus as if "is" signifies one thing and "the One" another? Necessary. Therefore, when we say briefly "the One is," does that speech signify anything other than to communicate one essence? <note>meaning "one existence."</note> Entirely. Again, let us say it this way: if the One is, what follows? Come, observe that. Is it not necessary by this supposition to predicate of the One itself as if it has parts? In what way? In this way. If "to be" is said of the one-being, and "one" is said of the being-one, and essence and "one" are not the same, yet belong to the same "one" which we supposed, is it not necessary that the whole "one-being" is itself, and its parts <margin>Whether "one" and "being" exist?</margin> exist as both "one" and "being"? Necessary. Do we call each of these parts merely a "part"? Or must we predicate a part as a part of a whole? Of a whole. It is a whole, therefore, which is one, and it has a part. Completely. What then? Do these parts of the one-being—namely, "one" and "being"—so desert each other that "one" is missing from "being," and "being" from "one"? Certainly not. Therefore, each part embraces both "one" and "being" together; so that any part is constituted of at least two small particles; and according to the same reasoning, whatever particle occurs, both are always enclosed in it. For "one" always embraces "being," and "being" always embraces "one" in mutual bonds. Whence, since two emerge everywhere in any particle, it is necessary that "one" never exists alone. Entirely. By this reasoning, will not the "one-being" be an infinite multitude? It seems so. Come, I pray, and proceed this way. Which way? Did we say the One participates in essence in <margin>That the One becomes many in relation to essence.</margin>sofar as it is? We did. And for this cause, did the "one-being" appear to be many? So it is. What then if we think of the One itself, which we said participates in essence, solely by the intellect according to itself, apart from that in which we said it participates: will it appear as one alone? Or even this as many? One alone, I think. Let us consider now another thing. It is necessary that its essence is one thing, and itself another. If indeed not essence is the One itself, but as one, it participates in essence. It is necessary. But if essence is one thing and the One another, the One itself is not other than essence by virtue of being "one"; nor is essence other than the One insofaras it is essence; but by that which is "the other" in itself and "different" in itself, they are other than each other. Exactly. For which reason, "the other" itself is the same as neither the One nor essence. True. What then? If we choose from these either essence and "the other," or essence and "one," or "one" and "the other," will we not in any assumption elicit some things which can rightly be called "both"? How? In this way, I say. Is it permitted to say "essence"? It is. And again to say "one"? That too. Has not each of those been spoken? Spoken. But when I say "essence and one," do I not say both? You do. And if "essence and the other," or "the other and one," do I not in each of these say "both"? Exactly. But can those things which are rightly called "both" be "both" yet not be "two"? In no way. But can those things which are "two" be thought of in such a way that each of them is not "one"? Not at all. Since therefore these are two together, each one exists as "one." It seems so. If any one of them is, and both ones are joined in a certain mutual

union, do not three result in total? Most certainly. And are not three odd, but two even? Why not? And if there are two, is it not necessary that these also be present: "twice" for the two, and for the three, "thrice"? Since in two there is "twice one," and in three "thrice one." Necessary. Finally, since there are two and there is "twice," is it not necessary that there be "twice two"? And since there are three and there is "thrice," is it not necessary again that there be "thrice three"? Why not? What then: if there are three and "twice," and two and "thrice," is it not necessary that there be "twice three"? It is entirely necessary. There will therefore be even-even, and odd-odd, as well as even-odd, and odd-even. Certainly. If these things are so, do you think any number is left out which does not necessarily exist there? None. Therefore, if the One is, it is necessary that number also exists. Without a doubt. Likewise, if number exists, many things surely are, and an infinite multitude of beings; or does not infinite number also become a participant in essence by its multitude? Most certainly. But if the whole of number is a participant in essence, each particle of number will also participate in essence. Exactly. Essence is therefore distributed through all things that are many, and it is absent from none of those things which are, whether it be the smallest or the largest. And it is absurd to doubt that. For how can essence be absent from any of those things which are? In no way. It is therefore divided as much as possible into the smallest and largest, and into all things that are in any way whatever, and most especially distributed of all; and the parts of essence are infinite. Thus it stands. The parts of it are therefore very many. Very many indeed. What then? Is there any of these which is indeed a part of essence, yet the part itself is not "one" thing? But how could that happen? But after it is, as I think, it is necessary that it always be "one" thing as long as it is, for it is impossible to be nothing. Without a doubt. Not only therefore is "one" present in the whole of essence, but also in its individual parts, deserting no part, whether it be larger or smaller, or however it may be. So it is. Since it is "one," is it everywhere a whole at the same time? Consider that carefully. I consider it, and I see that this is impossible. Divided therefore, if not a whole. For it will not be present in all parts of essence at once unless it is divided. So it is. Furthermore, that which is partible is necessarily as many as the parts are. Necessarily. For this reason, we were not correctly saying a little while ago that essence is distributed into "very many" parts; since it is not divided into more parts than the One itself, but equal parts. For neither is being missing from the One, nor the One from being, but these two are always thoroughly equalized in all things. It appears entirely so. The One itself, therefore, distributed by essence, is an infinite multitude. It is clear. Not only therefore is the "one-being" many, but also the One itself, distributed by essence, must be many. It must indeed. Furthermore, from the fact that all parts are parts of a whole, the One will be limited according to the whole. Are not all particles encompassed by the whole? They are encompassed. But that which <margin>That the One is many: both whole and parts, etc.</margin> encompasses is a limit. It is. Therefore, the "one-being" is somehow "one" and "many," "whole" and "parts," as well as "finite" and "infinite in multitude." <margin>Every whole has a beginning, a middle, and an end.</margin> It appears so. Since it is limited, does it not also have extremes? It is necessary. Furthermore, if it is a whole, will it have a beginning, a middle, and an end? Can any whole be found without these three? And if any of them is distant from that which is "one," will it still be a whole? Not at all. Wherefore the One has a beginning, a middle, and an end. It has. But the middle 

is equally distant from the extremes on all sides, for otherwise it would not be the middle. Certainly not. Furthermore, since the One is such, it is a participant in some shape, whether straight or round, or some other composed of both. A participant without a doubt. Moreover, if it is of this sort, it will be in itself and in another. In what way? Any part is in the whole, and none is entirely outside the whole. Granted. Are not the individual parts enclosed under the whole? Yes. But the One exists as all its parts, and neither more nor less than all of them. So it is. Is not the whole also "one"? Why not? If all parts are enclosed by the whole, <margin>How the One is understood to be contained by the One and itself.</margin> and the One is all things and the whole itself, and the individuals are contained under the whole, then the One will surely be contained by the One, and thus the One itself will be in itself. It seems so. Nevertheless, the whole is not in the parts, neither in all nor in any. For if it were in all, it must also be in one; and if it were not in some one, it could not be in all. If, however, this "one" consists of all, and the whole is in it, yet it is not in "one," in what way will the One be in all any longer? In no way. But no more is it in certain parts. For if the whole were in some, the larger would be in the smaller. But that is impossible. Impossible. Since therefore the whole is neither in several, nor in one, nor even in all parts, is it not necessary that it either be in some other thing or exist nowhere? Necessary. If it were nowhere, would it not be absolutely nothing? And yet since it is <margin>That which is nowhere is absolutely nothing.</margin> a whole, and is not in itself, does it remain that it consists in another? Completely. Therefore, insofar as the One is a whole, it is in another; but insofar as all things are its parts, and it is all the parts, it is in itself. And therefore it is necessary for the One to be both in itself and in another. Without a doubt. And since such is the nature of the One, does it not necessarily follow that it stands still and is also moved? Why so? It stands still, surely, if it consists in itself. For being <margin>How anything stands still and moves.</margin> inherent in the One, and not departing from it, it is in the same thing—in itself. It is indeed. But that which is always in the same thing must always stand still. It must. But that which is always in another, on the contrary, must never be in the same; if never in the same, then never standing still; but that which does not stand still must be moved. So it is. It is necessary therefore that the One, since it is always in itself and in another, always both stands still and is moved. It seems so. Furthermore, it must be the "same" as itself, and "other" than itself, and similarly "the same" and "other" in relation to other things, if indeed what was said above applies to it. By what reasoning? In this way: everything relates to anything else such that it is either the "same" as it, or "different"; if neither "the same" nor "other," it will surely be a part of that to which it so relates, or as a whole to a part. It is clear. Is the One itself a part of itself? In no way. It will therefore not be a whole in relation to itself, as if it were a part of itself. For that is not possible. Or perhaps the One is "other" than the One? Not in the least. Therefore, it is not "other" than itself. Certainly not. If it is neither "other," nor "whole," nor "part" in relation to itself, what else remains but that it be "the same" as itself? That very thing. What then? That which is "elsewhere" than itself, existing in the same thing—in itself—is it not forced to become "other" than itself, if indeed it exists "elsewhere" than itself? It seems so to me. The One was plainly shown to be of this sort, namely, being in itself and in another. It was shown indeed. From this therefore it is established that the One is "other" than itself. It seems so. If something is "other" than something, is it not "other" than an "other"? Necessary. Whatever things are not "one," are they not "other" than the One, and the One "other" than those things which are not "one"? Why not? Therefore, the One will appear "other" than all other things. "Other." Look furthermore,
