whether "the other" itself and "the same" itself are mutually contrary. Why not? Will "the same" ever wish to consist in "the other," or "the other" in "the same"? Never. Therefore, if "the other" is never in "the same," there is nothing among those things which are in which "the other" itself is for any time. For if it were in anything for any time, during that time "the other" itself would be in the "same." Would it not? Certainly. But since it never consists in the "same," "the other" itself will certainly never be in any of those things which are. You speak the truth. For that reason, "the other" will be neither in those things which are not "one," nor in the "one." Not indeed. It follows that the One cannot be "other" than those things which are not "one," nor those which are not "one" be "other" than the One, by means of "the other" itself. It follows plainly. But unless they participate in "the other" itself, they cannot be "other" than each other according to themselves. For by what way? But if they are "other" neither by themselves nor by "the other" itself, they can in no way be "other" than each other. In no way. Furthermore, those things which are not "one" participate not at all in the "one," for otherwise they would not be "not one," but in some way "one." True. For this reason, those things which are not "one" are not even number. Otherwise they would not be entirely devoid of the "one" if they had any number. Certainly not. Or are those things which are not "one" parts of the "one"? Or would those things which are not "one" thus participate in the "one"? They would participate. If therefore this is entirely "one," and those are "not one," neither will "one" be a part of those things which are not "one," nor a whole to them, as if they were parts; nor again will those which are not "one" be particles of the "one," nor even wholes, as if the "one" existed as a part. Not indeed. But we have asserted that those things which are neither wholes, nor parts, nor mutually "other," must be "the same" as each other. We have asserted it. Do we therefore confess that the One, when it relates thus to those things which are not "one," is "the same" as them? We confess it. Therefore the One, as it seems, is a certain "other" than others and than itself, and again "the same" as itself and them. So reason persuades. Is it also similar and dissimilar to itself and others? Perhaps. Since it was shown to be "other" than others, others will also be "other" than it. What prevents it? Is it not "other" than others in the same way as others are than it, neither more nor less? Why not? If neither more nor less, it remains that it is similarly. Similarly. Furthermore, if it happens to the One that it is "other" than others in the same way as others are than it, from this it follows that the same condition applies to both the One and the others. How do you say that? Thus: Does not every name have its own signified meaning? It has. Do you not pronounce the same name either many times or once? Indeed. When you utter it once, do you call that thing to which the name belongs; and when many times, not that thing? Or rather, whether you pronounce the same name once, or again and again, is it not necessary that you always mean the same thing? Always the same. Is not "the other" itself also a name imposed to signify something proper? It is. Therefore, as often as you utter this name, whether once or many times, you do not refer to another thing, nor do you name anything other than that whose name this is. Necessary. Therefore, when we say that the One is "other" than others, and those "other" than the One, pronouncing this word "other" twice, we never bring it in to signify anything else than the nature of which it is the proper name. Entirely so. If therefore the One is "other" than them, and others "other" than the One, undergoing that same "otherness" which is in the others, according to that, and not according to something else, the One is "other" than others; but whatever undergoes "the same" is similar, is it not? Indeed. But according to what the One has, such that it is "other" than others, according to this same thing anything is similar to anything; for anything is "other" than anything. It seems so. And is "similar" contrary to "dissimilar"? It is indeed. And "the other" itself to "the same" itself? That too. Nevertheless, this was also shown, that the One itself becomes both "the same" as others and "other." It was shown plainly. But it is a contrary affection to be "the same" as others and to be "other" than others? Exactly. Yet insofar as it is "other," it appeared similar. And this too. Therefore, insofar as it is "the same," it will be dissimilar according to the affection contrary to that affection which had made it similar. But did not "the other" itself make it similar? Exactly. Therefore "the same" itself will render it dissimilar; otherwise it will be in no way the contrary of "the other" itself. It appears so. From these things it is concluded that the One is both similar and dissimilar to others: insofar as it is "other," similar; but insofar as it is "the same," dissimilar. It has such a reasoning, as it seems. And it certainly has this one. Which? That insofar as it has undergone "the same," it has not undergone what is "alien"; if it has not undergone what is "alien," it is not dissimilar; if not dissimilar, it remains that it is similar; but if it has received "another" and what is "alien"; if "alien," it also becomes dissimilar. You speak truly. Therefore the One, both because it is "the same" as the others and because it is "other," will be both similar and dissimilar to the others according to both these and according to each of them. Most certainly. And will it not appear in the same way to itself, if indeed it appeared "other" than itself and "the same" as itself, according to both and each, both similar and dissimilar? It is necessary. Consider furthermore, I pray, in what way the One relates to touching, or not touching, itself and others. I consider it indeed. It was established that the One is in itself as a whole. Correct. And is not the One also in others? And in others. Therefore, insofar as it is in others, it touches others; insofar as it is in itself, it is prevented from touching others, but it touches itself, since it is in itself. It appears so. By this reasoning, the One touches both itself and others. It touches. What about this? Must not whatever is going to touch something lie near that which it is going to touch, and occupy that seat which follows the seat of that which it first touched? This is necessary. Therefore, if the One must touch itself, it must exist continuously after itself, occupying the seat next to the place in which it is. It must entirely. Would it not do this if the One were two, and existed in two places at once; but as long as it is one, it does this not at all? It is as you say. The same necessity therefore makes it so that the One is neither two nor touches itself. The same. But no more will it touch others. For what reason? Because we said that what is going to touch something must be placed separately, next to that which is to be touched, with no third intermediate between them. True. Wherefore at least two must be present as often as there is to be a touch. It must. But if besides the two terms a third intermediate something intervenes, three will indeed follow in order, but the touches will be double. Exactly. And thus, as one is always added to the number, one touch is also added. From which it happens that the touches themselves are exceeded by the multitude of numbers by one; for as much as the first two exceeded the touches themselves, so that they were more in number than the touches, by so much thereafter the whole number exceeds the whole of the touches. For in the future, one is added to the number at the same time, and one touch is set against the touches themselves. Correct. As many as the things that are, therefore, are in number, there are always just as many touches, with only one excepted. You speak the truth. ...are from the One, nor is it the One, nor does it even participate in the One, as long as they are "others." This we have said. From these points, it is concluded that there is no "one number" among the others, especially since the One is in no way present in them. Truly, how could it be so? Wherefore the others are neither one, nor two, nor designated by any other number. Certainly not. Therefore, the One itself is only one, but they are not two. Not so, it appears. And if they are not two, there will also be no touch. None. Therefore, neither does the One touch the others, nor do they touch the One, by an internal touch. Not at all. For all these reasons, the One touches itself and the others equally, and yet does not touch them. So it seems. Is it furthermore equal and unequal, both to itself and also to the rest? But in what way does this happen? If the One were greater or smaller than the others, or the others again greater or smaller than it, would not the One (from the fact that it is the One) and the others (from the fact that they are others than the One) be either greater or smaller than each other based on their own essences? But if, beyond these reasons, both were to possess equality besides, they would exist as equals to one another; but if these possessed magnitude and those smallness, or the One itself magnitude and the others smallness, then whichever species magnitude were present in would exist as greater; and whichever smallness were in, as smaller. Necessarily. Are there not two such species, magnitude and smallness? For if they did not exist, they would never exist as contraries to one another, nor be present in things themselves. It is as you say. Therefore, if smallness comes to the One, it either resides in the whole One or in some part. Necessarily. If it resides in the whole, it will either go through the entire One with equal extension or encompass it with external limits. Clearly. From which it follows that smallness infused into the One will undoubtedly be equal to the One; but if it encompasses it, it will be greater. Why not? Is smallness able to be equal to anything, or larger? And to exercise the effects of magnitude and equality in another, unless it could do so in itself? It certainly cannot. From which it is concluded that smallness cannot be in the whole One. It remains, perhaps, that it is in a part. It remains. Yet not in the whole part. For it would effect the same thing against the part as it had against the whole: namely, it will always be either equal to or greater than that very part in which it resides. Necessarily follows. Therefore, smallness will never dwell in any thing, since it dwells in neither the part nor the whole. From which it follows that nothing will be small except smallness itself. It seems so. But neither will magnitude be present. For anything else besides magnitude itself would be greater, namely that in which magnitude resides. Nevertheless, nothing is small, which indeed must be surpassed by the great, if anything were great. For in what way will you find anything small, since smallness resides in nothing? You speak the truth. Moreover, magnitude itself will be greater than nothing other than smallness, nor will smallness itself be smaller than anything other than magnitude itself. Nothing. For which reason the others besides the One will be neither greater nor smaller than the One, since they are devoid of magnitude and smallness. Nor will these two have any power against the One itself by which they might either exceed or be exceeded, but they will effect this between themselves. Nor will the One itself be greater or smaller than these two or any others, as it is devoid of both magnitude and smallness. So indeed it appears. And therefore, since the One is neither greater nor smaller than the rest, it will neither surpass the others nor be surpassed by the others. Without a doubt. Does it not necessarily follow that what neither surpasses nor is surpassed must be in an equal state? And if in an equal state, that it is equal? Indeed. But in this way, the One itself relates to itself,

being devoid of both magnitude and smallness so that it neither exceeds itself nor is exceeded by itself, but being in an equal state, it is always equal to itself. And most certainly. Therefore the One is equal to itself and to the others. It seems so. Nevertheless, since the One is in itself, it circles itself from the outside, and thus encompassing itself, it stands out as larger than itself; and since it is also contained, it is narrower. By which it happens that the One is both greater and smaller than itself. It happens indeed. Is this also not necessary, that nothing is found besides the One and the others? Necessary. Likewise, whatever is, must it not always be somewhere? It must. Furthermore, that which is in something, is it not always the smaller in the greater? For otherwise one thing would not be in another. It is as you say. Since truly there is nothing besides the One and the others, and it is necessary that these things be in something, is it necessary that they be in the One, and the One in the others, or exist nowhere at all? It is established. Because the One is in the others, therefore the others are greater than the One, insofar as they contain the One; but the One is smaller than the others because it is contained. Because truly the others are in the One, the One for the same reason is greater than the others, and those are smaller. It seems so. The One therefore is equal, greater, and smaller than itself and the others. It appears so. But if it is greater, smaller, and equal, it will be of equal measures and of more or fewer measures relative to itself and to the others; and if of measure, also of parts. What prevents it? Having the same measures and more and fewer, it will also be more and less in number both to itself and to the rest, and also equal to itself and the others for the same reasons. In what way? Those things it is greater than, it has more measures than they; and as many measures, so many parts; and those it is smaller than, in the same way; and those it is equal to, similarly. So it is. Is it not, when it is greater and smaller than itself and equal, that it participates in equal measures and more and fewer relative to itself, and since in measures, also in parts? Why not? And having parts equal to itself, it will also be equal to itself in multitude; but more parts makes it more, fewer parts makes it less in number than itself? It seems so. Will not the One relate similarly to the others? Because it appears greater than them, it must be more in number than they; because truly it is smaller in magnitude, also smaller in number; because finally it is equal in magnitude, it must also be equal in number. Necessarily so. By this reasoning again, the One will be equal, more, and less according to number relative to itself and the rest. It will be indeed. Does the One not also participate in time, and is it, and does it become younger and older than itself and others simultaneously? And again, on the contrary, neither younger nor older than itself or others while it participates in time? But how can that be? To be certainly belongs to it, if indeed it is <margin>What the word "to be" means.</margin> the One. It belongs. But what else is "to be" itself than participation in essence with the present time, just as "was" is the communication of its essence with the past, and "will be" with the future? That very thing. Therefore, if it participates in "being," it must also be a participant in time. Certainly. Is it not in flowing time? Surely. Therefore it always becomes older than itself, if indeed it runs through time. Necessary. Do we remember that "older" always becomes older than that which is becoming "younger"? We remember. Therefore, since the One becomes older than itself, does it not also become older than itself while it is becoming younger? It is necessary. It becomes, therefore, in this manner younger and older than itself. It does. But is it not "older" when it reaches the present time, which is the middle between "was" and "will be"? # Book Thirty-Four.
[[notes: This section corresponds to the conclusion of Plato’s *Laws*, Book X.]]

**Atheniensis (The Athenian):** But it must in no way be permitted to say that the gods are corrupted by the gifts of wicked men; if such a thing is said, it must be refuted with all our might. **Clinia (Clinias):** Well said; let us proceed accordingly. **Atheniensis:** Come then, by the gods themselves, in what way do they become appeasable, if they are appeased at all? And who and of what sort are they, if they can be pacified? For it is necessary that those who are to perpetually govern the whole *caelum* (heaven) be leaders. **Clinia:** Certainly. **Atheniensis:** But to what kind of leaders are they similar? Or which leaders are similar to them, so that it is possible for us to compare the lesser to the greater? Are they like the charioteers of competing teams? Or the pilots of ships? Perhaps they can be compared to the generals of armies, or to physicians who ward off and repel the "wars" of diseases from human bodies. Or perhaps to farmers who fear and guard against storms hostile to rising crops, or even to the shepherds of flocks and herds. 

For since we have agreed among ourselves that the heaven is full of many good things and many evils—and indeed more of the former—this is a kind of immortal war, and it requires a marvelous guardianship. But the gods and *daemones* (spirits) help us. Indeed, we are the possession of the gods and spirits. Truly, injustice and intemperance along with imprudence corrupt us. But justice and temperance along with prudence, which dwells in the animated powers of the gods, bring us safety. 

A small portion of these qualities may be seen clearly dwelling within us. For certain unjust souls dwelling on earth, fierce like wild beasts, rise up against the souls of the guardians—be they dogs, shepherds, or even the most eminent lords. Through the charms of words and the plea of certain chants, they persuade others (as the rumor of the wicked goes) that it is permitted to seize many things for themselves by acting badly among men, without paying any penalty. This crime, in which one gapes for the usurpation of many things, we call "disease" in the bodies of animals, "pestilence" in the seasons of the year, and, with a changed name, "injustice" in cities and republics. 

**Clinia:** Exactly. **Atheniensis:** Therefore, it is necessary for him who believes the gods grant pardon to unjust men (if someone grants them a portion of the plunder) to say that the gods are like dogs to whom wolves grant a small piece of the kill, and those dogs, pacified by these gifts, allow the flocks to be torn apart. Is this not the speech of those who proclaim that the gods are appeasable? **Clinia:** It is indeed. **Atheniensis:** But to which of the aforementioned guardians could someone compare the gods without being the most ridiculous of all men? To pilots, who, overcome by the libation of wine and the smoke of burning meat, overturn both ship and sailors? **Clinia:** Not at all. **Atheniensis:** Nor even to charioteers, who, while competing, are corrupted by bribes and concede the victory to the chariots of their adversaries. **Clinia:** Certainly not. Such a comparison toward the gods is foul. **Atheniensis:** And yet, they are not similar to commanders, nor physicians, nor farmers, nor shepherds, nor even to dogs who are smoothly seduced by the cunning of wolves. **Clinia:** Heaven forbid [[notes: literally "good words, I pray"]]. For such things are not to be heard. 

**Atheniensis:** Are not all the gods the greatest of all guardians, and over the greatest things? **Clinia:** Absolutely. **Atheniensis:** Shall we say that the guardians of the best things, who excel exceedingly in the virtue of guardianship, are worse than dogs or mediocre men, who would never betray justice for impious gifts received from unjust men? **Clinia:** By no means is this speech of impious men to be endured, and he who suffers from this opinion shall rightly be judged the worst and most profane of all the impious. **Atheniensis:** Therefore, those three things which we proposed—namely, that the gods exist, that they have care for all things, and that they cannot be turned from justice by any prayers—we seem to have shown sufficiently. 

**Clinia:** Certainly, and we assent to these arguments. **Atheniensis:** We have spoken somewhat more vehemently because of the controversies of wicked men. But for this reason, my friend Clinias, we have used a contentious oration, lest the base, thinking they have won in the speaking, believe they have been given license to do whatever they want, and think whatever they please against the gods. For this reason, I say, we wished to use a new and more vehement style of speaking. If we have brought anything toward persuasion so that they might now wish to hate their own habits and embrace the opposite, our prelude to the laws concerning impiety has been well spoken. **Clinia:** We hope it will be so; if not, at least the style of the speech will not be a disgrace to the legislator. 

**Atheniensis:** After the prelude, the speech that interprets the laws follows correctly: it should proclaim to all the impious that they should turn from their ways to piety. Against those who do not obey, let this law of impiety be placed: If anyone acts or speaks impiously in any way, let whoever happens to be present defend the gods and inform the magistrates. Let the first who hear it bring the matter to the judgment of these things according to the laws. If any magistrate hears and does not report it, let him be guilty of impiety himself, and let anyone who wishes prosecute him under the provision of the laws. And if anyone is condemned, let the judges punish him for each impious act committed with specific punishments. 

Indeed, let all be restrained by prisons. There are three prisons in the city. [[margin: Prisons.]] One is common to the majority in the forum where goods are sold, where many are guarded so they do not escape. The second is where the assembly of those who gather at night takes place, called by the name of "Correction" [[notes: the *Sophronisterion*]]. The third is in the middle of the region, where the place is most deserted and wild, known by the name of "Punishment." 

There are also three causes of impiety, as we narrated above. And since two kinds of behavior proceed from each of these causes, there will be six types of sins against the gods which are worthy of being judged, and they do not require equal or similar punishment. For some, although they do not believe gods exist, nevertheless, because of a certain just disposition of nature, they hate the wicked; moved by a certain hatred against injustice, they abstain from injuries, flee the iniquitous, and love just men. 

Others, however, are led to this opinion—that all things are destitute of the presence of the gods—and are more prone to pleasures and pains; they also excel in sharp wit and memory. To both types, it is common that they deny the gods exist. But they differ in this: the former harms other men less, the latter more. The former speaks freely against the gods, sacrifices, and oaths, and by mocking others with his anger, unless he is punished, he will perhaps make many similar to himself. But the latter holds the same opinion yet is thought by the common people to be endowed with a sharper talent; he is full of guile and snares. From these come many sorcerers, prompt toward every kind of poisoning and witchcraft. From these also come, at times, tyrants, leaders of armies, demagogues, those who perform private rites [[notes: literally "who are initiated into private solemnities"]], and those who deceive men with the tricks of sophists. 

Indeed, there are many species of these; but two are worthy of legislation: the one filled with dissimulation produces crimes worthy not just of one or two deaths, but many. The other requires both chastisement and chains. Similarly, the opinion by which the gods are thought negligent produces two types; and that by which they are thought easily appeasable by vows and gifts produces another two. Since the impious are thus distinguished, those who are not of wicked 

[[page number: 597]]
# On the Laws. Or, Dialogue on Legislation X.
### ELEVENTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, 
### OR, ON THE LAYING DOWN 
### OF LAWS.
-> MARSILIO FICINO'S <-
-> ARGUMENT (INTRODUCTION). <-

Our **Plato**, just as he is the wisest of all philosophers and the most eloquent of orators, is also the most prudent of all Jurisconsults (Legal Experts). Lest he be forced in contracts—as others usually are—to complete a work by a vast interpretation of laws (and that in vain), he rightly studied to make the citizens good through disciplines, laws, judgments, and religion before descending to contracts and the business of the courts. He hoped that just men, even without laws, would spontaneously provide faith and truth in every transaction. 

And indeed, very opportunely after the laws concerning judgments pertaining to persons, he brings into the midst the laws of judgments regarding things, by which both foreigners and citizens may learn to deposit justly and preserve what is deposited and agreed upon: not to move what belongs to another, and to return to each his own; how to deal with free men, freedmen, and slaves; how to sell, buy, return, lead, serve in the military, protect orphans, make a will, preserve testaments, administer inheritances, arrange marriages, perform divorce, and govern the family. 

But above all, they should religiously revere their parents, adulterate nothing, hate sorcery, and avoid anger and infamy; they should flee quarrels, insults, and slanders, restore damages, and preserve truth in testimonies and oaths. And this is roughly the subject matter of this eleventh book. 

We, however, as is our custom, think certain more obscure points should be briefly explained. In the beginning, he indicates that the goddess of youth is twofold in the rites: namely, a heifer and a young cow. And that one is indeed the light under the name of the Moon, while this one is faith under the name of Diana. Also, that whatever has been found by some chance belonging to another on the road must be dedicated to the god; so that you may recognize that prosperous fortune is to be referred to the providence of god. 

Contemplate the Platonic goodness, namely truth in buying and selling: not only to not adulterate the thing, lie, or commit perjury, but even to avoid swearing oaths; nay, rather even to avoid praising the thing for sale and changing the price on the same day. Here he proclaims: *Let no one say a lie with the gods invoked, or deceive, or dare anything by word or deed in an adulterated way, unless he wishes to be an object of hatred to God.* First, he is an object of hatred who, by swearing falsely, thinks little of the gods; then, he who lies before his elders. 

And look again and again at how free and integrity-filled Plato wishes the characters of the citizens to be, from whom he expels all license for peddling far away. He adds also that both opulence and poverty are a disease of character. For from the former comes inflation (arrogance), and from the latter, men become weaker and more abject. 

Where he says that **Pallas** (Athena), **Vulcanus** (Hephaestus), and **Mars** preside over the arts, gather from many of Plato’s mysteries handed down in various places: a certain trinity of divinities, which we Platonically call "demiurgic" (*opificia*), always stands by **Iuppiter** (Zeus), the supreme architect of the world. In this trinity, Pallas is first, Vulcan is second, and Mars is third. But just as the whole trinity is referred to Jupiter himself from whom it comes, so Vulcan and Mars are generally referred to Pallas. I pass over for now that he seems to have dreamed of power in Mars, wisdom in Pallas, and a fiery spirit in Vulcan. 

Certainly, three things are required for the very art of Jupiter by which he perfects the universe. First, the reason (*ratio*) itself through which he is going to make individual things. Second, the effective execution (*expeditio*) of those things which he had conceived by reason. Third, the safety and defense of those things which have been executed in effect. He names the idea of the first "Pallas," of the second "Vulcan," and of the third "Mars." And because both—namely, conservation or defense as well as the execution or expression of things—require reason and wisdom, therefore Pallas presides over both Vulcan and Mars. Whatever is either fabricated by Vulcan or defended by Mars after it has been fabricated and preserved in its form, is carried out under the leadership of Pallas. 

Of these three reigning in divine art, we also see three traces in nature: through Pallas, the order by which individual things are disposed; through Vulcan, the effective progress and prompt birth, as it were, toward which all things hasten; finally, through Mars, the most fortified structure applied by generators to those generated, and the various bulwarks defending their own nature from contraries. 

Similarly, three things must be in every human art, but especially in the civil art: that individual things be wisely thought out before they are done, that they be executed maturely and strenuously, and that the form which was thought out and expressed be preserved and strongly defended. And so that we may know that human art in completing all these things depends no less than nature on God himself, he says those three gods preside over human arts. But lest we think we have only the arts from the gods, he adds that the gods, the givers of life, must be revered...

[[margin: Let no one make or have [shrines] in a private house.]]
...morals, but have become such through a certain madness, the judge should cast them into the prison of correction to remain for no less than five years. During this time, let no citizen speak with them, except those who participate in the nocturnal assembly; let these, by admonishing them, speak for the salvation of the soul. When the time of chains is finished, let him who has become more modest dwell among the modest; but if he is convicted again of the crime of impiety, let him be punished with death. 

But there are some who, in addition to the opinion that the gods either do not exist, or are negligent or appeasable, also become monstrous and despise men; they allure many living people to themselves and attract them; they also say they draw and console the dead, and they profess to soothe the gods themselves with chants, sacrifices, and vows. By this charm, they attempt for the sake of money to ruin ignorant people, and likewise whole houses and cities. 

Let whoever of these is condemned be bound in the prisons in the interior, and let no free man ever approach him; but let slaves bring the food determined by the guardians of the laws. Finally, when he has finished his life, let them cast him out unburied beyond the borders of the region. If any free man buries him, let him be accused of the crime of impiety by whoever wishes. But if he leaves behind children sufficient for the city, let the tutors of orphans have care for these no less than others, from the day he was condemned. 

But let this common law be placed concerning all these, which will make many sin less in word and deed against the gods and be recalled from madness: because it will not be permitted to fashion gods for oneself or the sacred rites of the gods against the laws. If, however, such a law is imposed simply on all: Let no one have shrines in a private house. When anyone is moved in his soul to sacrifice, let him go to the public places to sacrifice, and let him offer the victims to the priests, both men and women, who perform the care of these things most purely. With whom he himself may pray, and whoever wishes to pray together with him. 

These things are so for this reason: because it is not easy to institute shrines and gods. Indeed, it belongs to a great talent to do this thing correctly. But it is the custom especially for women, and the weaker, and those placed in danger and in need wherever someone is in want, and conversely when an abundance of any thing flows in, to always consecrate what seems to be present and to vow victims, and to promise statues to gods and spirits and the sons of the gods. Moved by phantasms while awake, and similarly remembering out of fear having seen many things in dreams, they attempt to bring remedies to each thing and fill all houses and streets with altars and shrines. 

For the sake of all these, this law must be placed—and moreover for the sake of the impious—lest they, usurping these things in their operations, set up shrines and altars in their own houses and think to pacify the gods secretly with vows and sacrifices; and thus they increase their injustice unto infinity, whence they provoke the indignation of the gods both toward themselves and toward those who permit these things to them (even if the latter are better), by which means the whole city is held, in a certain way, by the crime of impiety. 

The god will by no means be angry with the legislator. For let the law be: That no one possess shrines of the gods in private houses. If, however, anyone is caught having possessed one and sacrificed elsewhere than in public, let whoever perceived it report it to the guardians of the laws. But they, if no great crime has been done by the woman or man, should order the private sacred objects to be brought to the public temples; and if they are not brought immediately, let them fine them until they are brought. 

But if anyone has committed not a childish but a nefarious impiety, whether he has offended in his own house privately or in public in sacrificing to the cult of the gods, let him be condemned to death as one who sacrifices impurely. But whether it is "childish" or not, let the guardians of the laws judge, and let them declare the impious thus dragged into judgment to be guilty of impiety.

[[summary: This text discusses the legal and theological foundations for punishing impiety and organizing a just society. It concludes Plato's arguments against the bribe-ability of gods and details the three-tiered prison system, while Ficino's introduction to the next section explains the divine trinity of Pallas, Vulcan, and Mars as the archetypes of civil order.]]

...than before, relative to those things for which it was the older? Younger, without a doubt. If that is younger, will not those things, if you compare them with the One, be older than before? Entirely. That which was previously becoming younger, becomes older relative to that which was previously being made and was older; it is however never older, but it is always becoming older than it; that one moreover grows young, while this one on the contrary grows old. That which is again older is similarly made younger than the younger. For since these tend in the contrary direction, they become contraries to each other. The younger indeed becomes older than the older, and the older on the contrary becomes younger than the younger. But they cannot have been "made" so. For if they had been made, they would no longer be becoming, but would already be. Now, however, they are made both younger and older than each other. The One indeed becomes younger than the rest, from the fact that it appeared to be older and was made first; but the others become older than the One, from the fact that they were made later. And according to the same reasoning, the others also relate similarly to the One, since they appeared to have been made older and earlier than it. The same seems so to me as well. Is it not by the same reason that neither of them becomes either younger or older than the other, according to the fact that they differ from each other by an equal number, neither the One becoming older or younger than the others, nor the others than the One? But by the reason that it is necessary that the earlier always differ from the later and the later from the earlier by another part, from this it is necessary that they become older and younger than each other, both the others than the One and the One than the others? And most certainly. For all these reasons, the One from itself and from the others is and becomes both older and younger, and again it neither is nor ever becomes younger or older than itself or the rest. Entirely. But since the One is a participant in time, and can become older and younger, is it not furthermore necessary that it be a participant in the past, the present, and the future, since it participates in time? It necessarily follows. Therefore the One was, and is, and will be; and it was becoming, and is becoming, and will become. Why not? There would also be something for it and of it, both was, and is, and will be. Most certainly. And therefore there would be knowledge of it, and opinion, and sense, since even we at present are treating all these things concerning it. You say rightly. Likewise, a name and discourse belong to it, and it is named and spoken of. And as many things of this kind as are found concerning other things, also exist concerning the One. Entirely so indeed is the matter.

<margin>Third supposition, that is, if the One is considered under being.</margin>

BUT truly, let us discuss for a third time, whether the One is as we said above: is it not therefore necessary, since it is One and Many, and again, neither One nor Many, and a participant in time, that because it is One, it participates in essence at some time; but because it is not, it does not participate at some time? This is necessary. Is it possible, when it participates, that it then not participate at all? Or when it does not participate, to participate? Impossible. Therefore it participates at one time, and is devoid of it at another; for only in this way can it happen that it is both a participant and devoid of the same thing. Correct. Is there not that time when it receives being, and when it loses being? Or how can it be that it sometimes has the same thing, and at other times does not, unless at one time it takes it, and at another loses it? Not otherwise. To receive essence, do you not call "to become"? I do. But to be deprived of essence, is that not "to be destroyed"? Most certainly. The One therefore, as it seems, assuming and laying aside essence, becomes and perishes. Necessary. And since it is One and Many, whether when it becomes or when it perishes, is it not that when it becomes One it ceases to be Many, and when it becomes Many, it ceases to be One? Greatly. And since it becomes One and Many, must it not be dispersed and gathered together? It must. Furthermore, as often as it is made dissimilar and similar, must it not be assimilated and, so to speak, "dis-assimilated"? <note term="assimilated">Becoming like or unlike something else; in Platonic terms, taking on or losing a form.</note> Indeed. And when it becomes greater and smaller and equal, must it not grow, decrease, and be equalized? So it is. But as often as it passes from motion into rest, or from rest into motion, this must not be in one [single] time. By what reason? Because, naturally, it stood before, and moves afterward; and since it moved before, it then stops. For without transformation, it cannot undergo these things. It cannot. But there is no time in which anything can so hold itself that it simultaneously neither stands still nor moves. None. Nevertheless, it does not pass through without transformation. It would not be consistent. When then does it pass? For it passes neither while it stands, nor while it moves, nor while it is in time. Certainly not. Is there not this wonderful thing, in which it is when it passes? What is it? <margin>The moment and the instant are found.</margin> The "indivisible moment," I say. <margin>The moment is the middle of motion and rest.</margin> For this moment signifies a certain thing from which there is a transition into either state. For it does not yet pass from a state of rest while it stands, nor from a state of motion while it moves. But this momentary nature, wonderful as it is, is placed in the middle between motion and rest, and is in no time at all; and into this and from this, that which was moved passes into rest, and that which rested, into motion. It appears so. Therefore the One, if indeed it stands and moves, undoubtedly passes into both. For only in this way does it do both. But passing, it passes in an indivisible moment. And when it migrates, it is in no time, nor does it stand then, nor move. Not at all. Does it not relate in the same way to other mutations? When it migrates from being itself into destruction, or from non-being into becoming itself, it then becomes the medium of certain motions and states, and it neither "is" then, nor "is not," nor does it "become," nor perish? It seems so. By the same reasoning, migrating from the One into the many, and from the many into the One, it is neither one nor many, nor is it gathered together nor dispersed; and migrating from similar into dissimilar, and again from dissimilar into similar, it is neither similar nor dissimilar, nor assimilated, nor so to speak, dis-assimilated; and passing from small into great, and into the equal itself, and passing through contraries, it is not small, not great, not growing, not decreasing, not equalized. It does not seem so. All these things, therefore, the One undergoes if it exists. Why not?

<margin>Fourth supposition.</margin>

SHALL we not consider furthermore what the "others" undergo, if the One exists? It should be considered. Let us say then, if the One is, what must the others from the One undergo? Let us say. Is it not because they are "others" than the One, they are not the One? Otherwise they would not be "others" than the One. Correct. Yet they are not entirely deprived of the One, but in some way they participate in the One. By what reason? Because the others from the One, from the fact that they consist of parts, are "others" than the One; for unless they had parts, they would be entirely one. Right. But parts, we have asserted, are parts of that which is a whole. We have clearly asserted it. But the whole itself must be one [thing] made from many, of which they are parts, which are called parts; for any of the parts is not a part of many, but exists as a part of the whole. But how is that? If anything were a part of many, in which it were present, it would also be in some way a part of itself (which is impossible) and of each of the others, if indeed it is a part of all. <margin>A part is not of many, but of a whole.</margin> For not existing as a part of one, it will be a part of all others except one; and thus it will not be a part of each one. Not existing as a part of each, it will be a part of none of the many. And, if it is a part of none, it will be impossible for it to be anything of all those things of which it is neither a part nor anything else. It appears so indeed. Therefore, whatever part is made is not a part of many, nor of all, but of one certain "idea," and of one certain thing that we call a "whole," made from all things as one and perfect. Of this, I say...

--- Page 73 ---
->54 Book Nine.<-

...I say it is a part, whatever part it may be. Entirely indeed. If therefore the others have parts, they participate in the whole and the One. Most certainly. Whence it is necessary that the one perfect whole containing parts is those very "others" from the One. Necessary. Moreover, the same reasoning applies to each part. For it must be a participant in this one [thing]. For if each of them is a part, this very word "each" signifies "one" in some way; for it signifies something distinct from the rest, and existing according to itself, if indeed they are "each." Right. But it will be a participant in the One, if it were something other than the One; otherwise it would by no means participate, but it would be the One itself. But truly, nothing can be "one thing" besides the One itself. Nothing. But it is necessary to participate in the One, both the whole together and the part. For the One itself will be a whole, of which the parts are individual parts; but each of the parts is a part of the whole, whatever part of the whole it may be. So it is. Is it not therefore, since they are "others" than the One, all things that participate, participate in the One? Why not? But the others than the One are in some way "many." For if they were others besides the One, yet neither one nor more than one, they would be absolutely nothing. Nothing indeed. But after they are more than one, which are participants in one part and one whole, is it not necessary that the things participating in the One be infinite in multitude? In what way? This clearly: they are something other than the One, nor do they participate in the One at the moment when they first participate in the One. Certainly. Are they not multitudes, in which the One is not present? Multitudes certainly. But if we wished by intelligence itself to extract some smallest thing from them, would it not be necessary that the thing extracted, being devoid of the One, be a multitude and not one? Necessary. Does it not seem to you, always considering the other nature of the species itself according to itself in this way, that however much of it you inspect, it will always occur as an infinite multitude? And most certainly indeed. Nevertheless, after any one part has been made, the parts now have a limit relative to each other and to the whole; and the whole has a limit relative to the parts. Very much so indeed. Therefore it happens to the others than the One, from the One itself and from themselves already communicating in the One, that another thing comes to be in them: which indeed provided a limit to each other, though their nature according to itself is infinity. It is manifest. In this manner, therefore, the others than the One are both wholes and also according to their particles, and they are both infinite and participate in a certain limit. Entirely. Are they not therefore similar and dissimilar to each other and to themselves? For what reason? Insofar as they are infinite according to their own nature, they all in some way suffer the same thing from this relative to each other. They suffer. Likewise, insofar as they all participate in a limit, from this also they all suffer the same thing. Why not? Yet insofar as it happens to them to be finite and infinite at the same time, which are contrary passions, they are as dissimilar as possible. Surely. Therefore according to either reason they will be similar to themselves and to each other, but according to both reasons on both sides, they will be as contrary and dissimilar as possible. It is established. Thus therefore the others will be the same as themselves and each other, both similar and dissimilar. They will be. And again, both the same and other, moved and standing, and receiving the rest of the contrary reasons, we shall easily find the rest of the things that happen to those which are "others" than the One, since these things are now established for us. You say rightly.

<margin>Fifth supposition.</margin>

WHAT then? shall we not pass over these things as if they were clear, and look again, if indeed the One exists, whether the rest which are not the One do not relate in that way, or only in that way? Entirely. First, therefore, let us see, if the One is, what must happen to the others. Let us see. Will not the One be separate from the others, and the others separate from the One? Why? Because there is nothing besides these, which is either other than the One, or other than all the others; for all things have been encompassed when "the One and the others" were said. All. Wherefore nothing remains besides these, in which both the One and the others might be considered as if in the same seat. Nothing at all. Therefore, never do the One and the others concur into the same "one." Never. Therefore they are separate? Separate. Furthermore, it was said that the One in reality has no parts. How could it have them? Therefore neither the whole One will be in the others, nor its particles, since it is separate from the others and is constituted of no particles. So it is. Therefore in no way will the others participate in the One, since they take neither the whole of it nor a part of it. In no way, as it seems. And therefore the others are in no way one, nor have they any "one" in themselves. Not at all. Whence the others are not "many" either. For if they were many, each of them, as a part of the whole, would be one. But now they are not one, not many, not a whole, not parts, since they participate in nothing of the One. Correct. For which reason they are neither two, nor three, nor is "one" in them, since they are entirely bereaved of the One. So it is. Therefore the others are neither similar nor dissimilar to the One, nor is similarity or dissimilarity in them. For if they were similar and dissimilar, from the fact that they would have similarity and dissimilarity in themselves, the others than the One would already comprehend two contrary species in themselves. It appears so. And it cannot be that things which participate in nothing, participate in two things. Certainly not. Therefore they are neither similar, nor even dissimilar—any two things other than the One; for if they were similar or dissimilar, they would participate in one other certain species; and if both, in two certain contrary species, but these were shown to be impossible. You speak the truth. Therefore they will be neither the same, nor other, nor moved, nor quiet, nor rising, nor perishing, nor greater, nor smaller, nor equal, nor finally will anything else of this kind happen. For if they received anything such, they would participate in each thing and in two and in three, and in even and odd, which we saw to be impossible, since they are destitute of the One in all things. These things are most true. For these reasons, therefore, if the One is, the One is all things and it is nothing, both toward itself and toward the others in the same way. The matter stands entirely so.

<margin>Sixth supposition. A negative from an infinite subject is contrary to a negative from a finite subject.</margin>

BUT truly, if the One is not, what follows must we not consider hereafter? It should be considered. What is this supposition, "if the One is not"? Does it differ in any way from this, "if not-one is not"? It differs indeed. Does it only differ? Or is this also entirely contrary—"if not-one is not" to that, "if the One is not"? Entirely contrary. But what? if someone should say, "if magnitude is not," or "smallness is not," or anything else of this kind, does he not indicate in each case that he says something else is "not being"? Entirely. Does he not therefore now declare that he calls something else "not being" besides the others, when he says "if the One is not"? Do we understand what he says? We understand. First, therefore, he expresses something that can be known; then, something other than the others, when he says "the One," whether adding "to be" to it or "not to be." Nevertheless, it is known what is said not to be, and that it is a certain thing different from the others, is it not? Necessary. In this manner, therefore, it must be said from the beginning, if the One is not, what it must be. First, therefore, this must happen to it, as it seems: that there be a certain knowledge of it, or we would understand nothing...

--- Page 74 ---
->Parmenides, Or, on the One as the Universal Principle & on Ideas. 55<-

...we would understand nothing of what we say, when we utter "if the One is not." You speak the truth. Is it not that the others are "other" than it, or else that "it" is not called other than the rest? Most certainly. Therefore diversity also is present in it besides knowledge; for one does not speak of the diversity of the others when one calls the One "other" than the others, but of its own diversity. It appears so. Furthermore, this "not being" itself is said to be a participant in "this thing," and "of some," and "of this," and "to this," and "of these," and all things of this kind. For the One would not be spoken of, nor the others from the One, nor anything be to it, nor anything of it, nor would it be called anything, unless it were a participant in a certain thing, or certain things of this kind. Right. To be "the One," however, is impossible unless it exists; but to participate in many things, nothing prevents it. But it is also necessary. If indeed that very One alone, and nothing else, is "not," but if neither the One itself nor "that" will be "not," but a discourse is held concerning something else, then nothing ought to be pronounced; but if that One alone and no other is presupposed "not to be," it must be said to be a participant both in that very thing and in many others. And most certainly indeed. For which reason there is dissimilarity in it toward the others; for since the others are "other" than the One, they must be foreign. They must. But are not foreign things "alien"? Why not? And are not alien things "dissimilar"? Dissimilar clearly. But if they are dissimilar to the One, they will be dissimilar to a dissimilar thing. Clearly. Therefore dissimilarity will also be present in the One, according to which the others are dissimilar to it. It seems so. And if dissimilarity to the others belongs to it, will not similarity to itself be appropriate? In what way? If dissimilarity were in the One toward the One, a discourse would certainly not be held about such a thing as "the One," nor would the supposition be about the One, but about some other thing. Entirely. But that is not fitting. Certainly not. For this reason similarity to itself must be present in the One. It must. Likewise it is not equal to the others. For if it were equal, it would now certainly also be similar to them according to equality. Both of these are impossible, since the One in no way "is." Impossible. But since it is not equal to the rest, is it not also necessary that the others are by no means equal to it? Necessary. But those things which are not equal, are unequal. Unequal. But are unequals unequal to some unequal thing? Certainly. Whence the One also appears to be a participant in inequality, according to which the rest are unequal to it. A participant indeed. Moreover, magnitude and smallness pertain to inequality. They pertain. And magnitude therefore and smallness are appropriate to such a One. It seems so. Magnitude again and smallness are always distant from each other. They are distant. And therefore a certain medium always intervenes. Surely. Do you find any other medium between these besides equality? None other. To whatever, therefore, magnitude and smallness happen, equality also happens, obtaining the medium of these. It is established. Equality, magnitude, and smallness seem to happen to the One while it is not. Furthermore, it must also participate in essence in some way. But how? It must hold itself in that way which we have said, for unless it held itself so, we would by no means speak the truth when we confess the One "not to be." But if we speak the truth, it is manifest that we are uttering things that "are." <margin>If a thing is made, and a speech from it is true, if the speech from the made thing is made true, the thing also is true.</margin> Is it not so? So it is. But when we have said that we speak true things, it is necessary that we profess that we assert things that "are." Necessary. The One is therefore, as it seems, "not being." For if it does not become "not being," but relaxes something of its "being" so as that it "is not," it will immediately be "being." Entirely indeed. Therefore it is necessary that "not being" has "being not being" as a bond of its "not being," if it ought "not to be"; just as on the contrary, "being" has the bond of its "not being not being," so that it may be allowed to be perfectly again. For thus "being" itself will most greatly be, and "not being" itself will most greatly not be, if "being" itself indeed participates in the essence of "being being," but not in the essence of "being not being," if it ought to be at all; but "not being" itself does not participate in the essence of "not being not being," but in the essence of "not being being," if indeed it ought to appear entirely "not being." These things are most true. Is it not therefore, since "being" is a participant in "not being," and "not being" is a participant in "being," the One also when it "is not," must necessarily participate in "being" itself for this purpose, that it truly "is not"? Necessary. Essence therefore seems to be present in the One if it "is not." It seems so. And yet not essence again, if indeed it is not at all. Why not? Can anything, which is said to be affected in a certain way, "be" so, not "to be" so, when it has not yet been transmuted from such a habit? It cannot. Therefore whatever holds itself so and not so, undergoes a certain change. It undergoes. But shall we say change is "motion," or something else? Motion. But did the One not appear as both "being" and "not being"? It appeared. Therefore as both holding itself so and not so. It seems so. Therefore the One "not being" seems to be moved, if indeed it receives a change from "being" itself into "not being." It is clear. Truly if it is nowhere in the nature of things, since it "is not," it certainly cannot migrate from elsewhere to here. In what way could it? Therefore it is not moved by the fact that it passes. Not at all. Nor yet can it turn in the same place. For it never touches "the same" itself; for "the same" itself is "being," but it is impossible for "not being" to be in any of those things that "are." Impossible certainly. Therefore the One, since it is not, could never turn in that in which it by no means is. Never. Nor even is the One altered from itself, neither "being" nor "not being"; for a discourse would no longer be held concerning the One if it had been altered from itself, but concerning some other thing besides the One. Correct. If it is neither altered, nor revolves in the same place, nor proceeds, in what way will it be moved? In no way. But that which cannot be moved, must necessarily act in rest, and what rests must stand still. Necessary. Therefore the One, if it is not, stands and is moved. It seems so. Furthermore, if it is moved, it is necessary undoubtedly that it be altered; for insofar as anything is moved, to that extent it holds itself not in the same way as before, but in another. Clearly. Therefore the One, while it is moved, is also altered. Certainly. Nevertheless, by no means moved, it is by no means altered. In no way at all. For which reason the One which is not, insofar indeed as it is moved, is undoubtedly altered; but insofar as it is not moved, it is by no means altered. Not at all. And therefore the One, if it is not, is altered; and also by no means altered. It is established. But must not that which is altered become "other" than it was before, and put off its pristine habit? But that which is not altered, does it neither become, nor even perish? It necessarily follows. Whence the One which is not, because it is altered, is made and perishes; but because it is not altered, it neither becomes nor perishes. And thus it both becomes and perishes at the same time, and again neither becomes nor perishes. So it is.

<margin>Seventh supposition.</margin>

LET us return again now to the beginning, clearly to inspect whether these things thereafter appear to be as they have been so far, or otherwise. This is worth the effort. Have we not already discussed what happens concerning the One if it by no means is? We have discussed it. But as often as we utter "not being," does it signify anything else to us than the absence of essence from that which we pronounce not to be? Nothing else. Whether when we say something "is not," do we in some way understand that it "is not" and in some way "is"? Or rather does this very phrase, "is not," as often as it is pronounced, signify simply that it is in no way at all? And when it is not... <margin>Not being.</margin>

<summary>This section of the Parmenides explores the logical paradoxes of "the One," examining how it can simultaneously possess contrary attributes like magnitude and smallness, being and non-being, and how it relates to time and the "others." It introduces the concept of the "instant" as the indivisible transition between rest and motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical deductions regarding the "One" (the concept of absolute unity) from Plato's Parmenides. The previous section likely explored the consequences of the One's non-existence for the One itself; here, the text concludes that analysis and moves into how "other things" are affected if unity does not exist.</meta>

56 Book Nine.

->That which is simply non-being cannot be, nor can it touch upon essence.<-

<note>original: "Non ens simpliciter esse non potest, neque essentiam attingere." This section explores the radical consequences of a thing having no "being" at all.</note>

If it is <term>becoming</term> <note>original: "fit"; the process of coming into existence</note>, is it in no part capable of essence? It signifies that absolutely. Therefore, neither can non-being itself "be," nor can it in any other way touch upon essence. Not at all. And is "becoming" and "perishing" anything other than the former receiving essence and the latter losing it? Nothing else. Therefore, that to which no part of essence can belong can never either receive it or lose it. Never. Thus, for the One, since it in no way *is*, it is not fitting for it to obtain, or cast away, or in any other way take hold of essence. That is proper. Therefore, the One itself does not perish when it does not "become," nor does it "become," insofar as it is in no way capable of essence. It does not seem so. Nor, again, is it altered in any way. For it would already be both becoming and perishing if it could suffer this. True. If it is not altered at all, is it not also necessary that it is in no way moved? Necessary. Yet we shall not assert that what in no way *is* can stand still anywhere; for that which stands still must always be in some same place. Why not? Thus, we shall clearly admit that non-being itself never either stands still or moves. Never. Furthermore, nothing from those things which *are* is present to it. For then it would already participate in essence, insofar as it would be a participant in something existing. That is manifest. Therefore, neither magnitude, nor smallness, nor equality happens to it. Certainly not. But neither similarity nor diversity will be present to it, either toward other things or toward itself. It in no way seems so. Now, can other things be present to it in any way, when nothing at all can be for it? It is not possible. For which reason, other things are not similar, nor dissimilar, nor the same, nor different. Truly not. But can that which is "of it," or "to it," or "something," or "this," or "of this," or "of another," or "to another," or "once," or "hereafter," or "now," or "knowledge," or "opinion," or "sense," or "speech," or "a name," or anything else from those things which *are*, exist around that which is not at all? Not at all. By these reasons, therefore, if the One is not, it does not have itself in any way whatsoever or anywhere. It truly does not seem to have itself in any way or anywhere.

<margin>Eighth Hypothesis</margin>

Must it be discussed again, if the One is not, what must happen to the things *other* than the One? It must be discussed. First, therefore, these "others" must be something; for unless they are "others," there would be no discussion at all about these others. That is so. And if the speech is about others, the others are surely "different." Or do you not call "other" and "different" the same thing? I do. Do we not say that the "different" is different from another different thing, and the "other" is other than another thing? Certainly. Therefore, if there are to be "others" at all, there will be something from which they will be "others." Necessary. What then will that most likely be? They will not be "others" from the One, since that does not exist. Certainly not. They are, therefore, "others" of each other; for that alone remains, otherwise they would be "others" of nothing. Rightly so. Therefore, they are "others" of each other according to <term>multitudes</term> <note>original: "multitudines"; groups or masses lacking internal unity</note>. For they cannot be so according to a "one," since the One does not exist. But any mass of them, as it seems, exists as an infinite multitude. And even if someone takes what appears to be the smallest part, just as in a dream, suddenly instead of what had seemed to be "one," a multitude occurs; and instead of what had appeared to be smallest, it already appears as very great if you compare it to the pieces into which it is dissected. Most rightly. I say that such masses will be "others" to each other besides the One, if the others exist while the One does not. Most certainly. And will there not be many masses, of which each will seem to be "one" at first glance, yet none will be "one," since the One itself is not? Certainly. Likewise, some number of them will seem to exist, if indeed each seems to be "one" even though they are many. Quite so. Furthermore, even and odd will falsely seem to exist within them, if the One is entirely absent? Falsely.

Moreover, that which at first will seem small in them, as was said, immediately shows itself to us as very great and very many in relation to the individual small parts, which are also many. What forbids it? Furthermore, each mass will seem to be equal to many small masses. For it would not clearly seem to have passed from the greater into the lesser unless it first seemed to have arrived in the middle; but this will be a certain <term>phantasm</term> <note>original: "phantasma"; an illusion or mere appearance rather than a reality</note> of equality. It is likely. Does it not, having a limit toward another mass, have in itself neither beginning, nor middle, nor end? For what reason? Because whenever anyone contemplates one of these things with the intellect, another beginning always occurs before the beginning; and after the end, another end always follows; and in the middle, there are always other things more internal than the middle, and always smaller, because a "single thing" cannot be grasped in these, since the One is not. You speak most truly. Finally, I think it is necessary that whatever is grasped without the "One" is torn apart and dispersed. Without a doubt. Does not such a thing appear as "one" to someone looking from a distance and dimly? Necessary. But to one looking closely and sharply with the intellect, does not each thing appear as an infinite multitude, since it is forsaken by the One which does not exist? This is necessary above all else. In this way, therefore, it is necessary that each of the others appear as infinite, and as having a limit, and as "one," and as many, if the others exist besides the One, which is not. It must be so. And will they not also seem similar and dissimilar? But how? For when they appear as "one" to someone looking from a distance like a shaded sketch, they will all seem to communicate in something of the same, and to be similar. Entirely. But to one approaching closer, they appear as many and different, and by that very phantasm of diversity, they happen to be different from themselves and dissimilar. So it is necessary that the masses themselves appear both similar and dissimilar, both to themselves and to each other. Most certainly indeed. And will they not also seem to be the same and different from each other, and in contact with themselves, and separate from themselves, and agitated by every motion, and standing still everywhere, and rising and falling, and neither, and all things of this sort, which indeed would be easy for us to run through, if many things exist while the One does not? You tell the truest things.

<margin>Ninth Hypothesis</margin>

Returning now again to the beginning, let us declare what will happen to the things other than the One, if the One is not. Let us declare. In the first place, therefore, the others will not be the "One." How could they? Nor yet will they be "many." For in those things which are many, the "one" is also present. For if none of them is one, they are all nothing, for which reason they are not even many. You speak truly. Since, therefore, the One is not in the others, they are neither many nor one. Clearly not. Nor even do they appear as one or many. Why? Because the others have no commerce at all with those things which are not, nor does anything from those things which are not at all pertain to any of the others; for no part is present to those things which are not. True. Therefore, there is neither an opinion of that which is not at all, nor is a phantasm present in the others, nor in any way is that which is not conceived by the others through opinion. Certainly not. For which reason, if the One is not, none of the others is conceived by opinion to be either one or many. For without the One, it is utterly impossible to form an opinion of "many." Impossible indeed. Therefore, if the One is not, the others neither *are*, nor are they even thought by opinion to be one or many. It does not seem so. Whence they are neither similar, nor even dissimilar. No. Nor are they the same, or different, nor in contact, nor separate, nor any of the remaining things we narrated in the previous sections as those things which seemed to regard the others; neither are there others, nor do they seem to be others, if the One is not. True.

<note>The text ends mid-sentence ("Vera..."), likely continuing as "Vera loqueris" (You speak truly) on the following page.</note>

->Philebus, Or, on the Highest Good. 57<-

True. Shall we not say, to speak summarily, that if the One is not, nothing is? And most certainly indeed. Thus let this be said by us, and that besides, which as it seems, whether the One is or is not, both itself and also the others, toward themselves and toward each other, all things entirely are and are not, and appear, and do not appear. These things are most true.

->THE PHILEBUS<-
->OF PLATO, OR, ON THE<-
->HIGHEST GOOD.<-

->MARSILIO FICINO'S<-
->ARGUMENT.<-
*

<margin>The highest good.</margin>
The purpose of this book is to discuss the highest good of the soul, which is indeed called the highest good with a certain condition, while the principle of all things itself is called the highest good absolutely. Concerning this, therefore, which is the good with a condition, it is discussed in this book: concerning that which is absolute, it is disputed in the *Parmenides*. This, however, flows from the absolute, just as a certain light depends on the very source of the entire light. For which reason it was said by Plato in the *Phaedo* and the *Theaetetus* that the highest good of the soul is likeness to God. Nothing, truly, becomes similar to the sun except by a certain infusion of its own light. Whence also the good of the soul will be the complete attainment of the divine light. That 
<margin>Ambrosia. Nectar.</margin>
light descends first into the mind, and then into the will. In the mind is truth, in the will joy; in the mind is ambrosia, in the will nectar; they are so named by Plato here and in the *Phaedrus*. <margin>The highest good in the mixture of wisdom and pleasure.</margin> Therefore he placed the highest good of man in the mixture of wisdom and pleasure. But before this, he denied that beatitude could consist in the ratio of either wisdom or pleasure alone, because the triple condition of the highest good is found in neither. 
<margin>Three conditions of the highest good.</margin>
That is, that it be exceedingly perfect, and sufficient, and desirable. Perfect, because nothing is lacking to itself. Sufficient, because nothing is lacking to him who receives it. Desirable, because in it and from it is whatever can be desired. Whence because it is perfect, it is sufficient: because it is sufficient, it is desirable. Indeed, because it is enough for itself, it suffices for another: because it suffices for another, it is desired by another. These things are demonstrated to belong neither to wisdom alone, nor to pleasure alone, but to a certain mixture of both. Where many things are said concerning the genus, origin, and nature of pleasure and wisdom, concerning the infinite and the limit, concerning the composite and the principle of composition. <margin>The highest and absolute good in nature is the measure of all things.</margin> And finally it is concluded that the highest and absolute good in nature is the measure of all things; that is, the principle of the whole of nature. The highest good of the mind and soul, however, is the possession of that first good, which belongs to the mixture of wisdom and pleasure through truth, commensuration, and beauty. 
<margin>Grades of goods.</margin>
Wherefore in the first grade of goods is placed the measure of all things; in the second, truth, commensuration, and beauty; in the third, mind and wisdom; in the fourth, science, art, and opinion; in the fifth, temperate pleasure. And the blessed man is said to be he who has both attained the wisdom of divine things and the experience of human things consisting in a certain science and art and opinion; he exults entirely in the joy of contemplation, and commits himself to the pleasure of the senses only so far as wisdom, science, and joy receive no impediment therefrom. The introduction to the dialogue is as follows: When Socrates and Philebus had conferred much back and forth concerning the highest good, and Philebus was now weary of debating, he congratulated Protarchus who had recently arrived, and signaled that he should take up his province in the debate. Protarchus, being a youth, suddenly assented. Turning to him, Socrates says, "Consider what guardianship you are undertaking, and do not hasten rashly to the dispute. Rather, hear the opinion of both first, and take up the defense of that which appears more probable to you as you examine it with right reason." But now let us come to the dialogue.

->SOCRATES, PROTARCHUS,<-
->PHILEBUS.<-

SEE, O Protarchus, what speech you are now to receive from Philebus, and against which of us you will rather fight, if it should please you little. Do you wish that we reduce both opinions to a summary? PROT. I certainly wish it. SOCRA. Philebus indeed says that for all living things the good is 

joy, pleasure, delight, and all other things of this kind. Our discussion against him, however, is that not those things, but to be wise, to understand, to remember, and those things related to these—right opinion and the discourse of true reason—are better and more excellent than pleasure for all things that are capable of them, and that the attainment of these is the most useful of all, both for those present and those to come. Was this not the opinion of both, Philebus? PHIL. Most certainly indeed, O Socrates. SOCRAT. Do you take up, O Protarchus, the dispute that is now offered to you? PROT. It is necessary for me to take it up, since that beautiful Philebus is weary. SOCRAT. We must indeed define with all zeal what is involved in these matters. PROT. We certainly must. SOCRA. Come then, let us assert this in addition to these things. PROT. What is that? SOC. That each of us tries to demonstrate a certain habit and affection of the soul which can provide a blessed life to all men. Is it not so? PROT. Certainly. SOCRA. And you indeed propose the habit and affection of rejoicing, while we propose that of being wise. PROT. So it is. SOC. If, however, some habit appears more excellent than both of these, and the same is more akin to pleasure, and excels in a stable quality of life, will we not both be surpassed, but pleasure will surpass wisdom? PROT. Indeed. SOC. If, however, it is nearer to wisdom, then wisdom will surely conquer pleasure, and pleasure on the contrary will succumb. Do you concede these things, or how? PROT. They seem to me to be conceded. SOC. But what does Philebus think? What do you say? PHIL. To me indeed pleasure seems to excel, and always will seem so. But you see for yourself, O Protarchus. PROT. Since you have now conceded to us the duty of the dispute, Philebus, you will no longer have the power of assenting to Socrates or dissenting. PHIL. You say the truth. I indeed refuse, and now call the goddess to witness. PROT. And we also will be witnesses that you said those things which you say. But let us hereafter, O Socrates, whether Philebus is willing or in whatever way you wish, try to settle the matter. SOCRAT. Let us try, beginning from the goddess herself, whom he says is called Venus here, but her truest name is Pleasure. PROT. Most rightly. SOCRAT. I always have a reverence toward the power of the gods, not a human one, but one exceeding every greatest fear. And now indeed I call her Venus, just as it is pleasing to him: but I know that Pleasure is a varied thing. But making a beginning from it, as I said, we ought to investigate what nature it has. We hear one thing indeed: yet it has forms quite varied, and in a way dissimilar to each other. For see, we say an intemperate man is delighted; but also a temperate man by temperance; an unwise man is delighted 
<margin>Many modes of delighting.</margin>
by unwise opinions, and full of vain hope; but also a wise man by wisdom. Which pleasures if anyone should say are inimically similar, he would rightly seem unwise. PROTAR. These indeed, O Socrates, come from contrary things, yet they are not themselves contrary. For how would pleasure not be most similar of all things to pleasure, since it is the same as itself? SOCRAT. Indeed, O blessed one, neither does color differ from color in that each is a color, yet we all know that black, besides being different from white, is also most contrary to it. Furthermore, figure is the same in genus as figure as a whole: but the parts of that genus either differ immensely among themselves, or are even contrary, and many other things of this
