kind we shall find. For which reason, do not trust this reason, which makes all most contrary things one. For I fear lest perhaps we find some pleasures contrary to each other. PROT. Perhaps, but how will this harm our reason? SOCRA. This will certainly harm it, that you call these things, though they are dissimilar, by another name (so to speak): for you say all sweet things are good: but no reason prohibits sweet things from being sweet. Since, however, many of them are evil, and many also—as we indeed say—are good, yet you call them all good, being forced to confess they are also dissimilar to each other, if anyone should compel you. What, therefore, is found in all pleasures, both evil and good, as a certain same thing in common, for the sake of which you call them all good? PROT. What do you say, O Socrates? Do you think anyone, when he has posited that pleasure is the good, will then concede to you and tolerate you saying that some are good and some are evil? SOCR. Nevertheless, you will confess that many are dissimilar, and most even contrary to each other. PROT. Not indeed insofar as they are pleasures. SOCRA. We fall back into the same thing again, O Protarchus, and we shall say that pleasure differs nothing from pleasure, but all are similar: and the examples brought into the middle a little before will move nothing. And like those who are inept and unrefined in disputes, we shall contend. PROT. Why do you say those things? SOCR. Because if I, imitating you, should not fear to say that the most dissimilar of all things is most similar to the most dissimilar, I could say the same things as you. And so we shall appear more unrefined than is proper. And our speech will have fallen away, and be already finished: let us therefore begin it again: for perhaps having progressed deeper we shall concede to the same opinion. PROT. Tell me how? SOCR. Imagine me in turn being interrogated by you, Protarchus. PROT. What indeed? SOCRA. Wisdom, science, mind, and whatever I—having been asked from the beginning what the good itself is—called good, will they not suffer the same thing as your speech? PROTAR. By what reason? SOC. For all sciences will seem many, and some of them dissimilar to each other, and if some should even be contrary, should I be worthy of the present dispute if, fearing this very thing, I said no science is dissimilar to science? Thus at last our speech would vanish like a fable, and we would be held by a certain unrefinedness. But it is by no way decent to happen so, but rather the ratio of safety must be held. To me therefore, both in your speech and in mine, this equally pleases: namely, that there are many and dissimilar pleasures, and furthermore many and different sciences. Let us therefore bear the difference of my good and yours, O Protarchus, by no means hiding it, but rather bringing it into the light, if any examiners should inquire whether it is right to call pleasure, or wisdom, or a third thing besides these, the good. For now we ought by no means to contend for this, that what I pose or what you pose should win, but let us favor that which is most true. PROT. So it must be. SOCR. Let us also stabilize this much more by mutual confession. PROT. What indeed? SOC. That which is troublesome to all men, both to the willing and sometimes even to the unwilling. PROT. Speak more clearly. SOCRA. I say the speech which will soon fall in, wonderful by nature. That many are one, and one is many, is wonderful to say. In which it is easy to defend either part, and likewise to move it. PROTAR. Is this not for those when someone—for example—asserts that I, Protarchus, am one born by nature, and then again says I am many? Again, those who pose me as even contrary to myself, 

heavy, light, great, small, do they pose the same and one man, and many things of this kind? SOCRA. You indeed, O Protarchus, bring in things concerning the one and the many which have ceased to seem wonderful, and which—to speak so—all agree are by no means to be tried, since they are certain childish things, and easy to know, and most likely to obstruct speeches if anyone admits them: nor are they to be judged wonderful if someone, dividing the members and parts of something by reason and having confessed all those to be that one thing, soon refutes and derides it, as if forced to confess monsters, namely that the one is many and infinite, and the many are one. PROT. But what other things do you say, O Socrates, which have not yet been conceded or made public concerning the same speech? SOCRA. When someone, O boy, poses the "one" itself as nothing from those things which are born and die, as we said a little before, then it is conceded that such a "one" ought by no means to be refuted. But when one tries to affirm "one man," "one ox," "one beauty," and "one good," now surely in these and such unities, there is anxious study and even ambiguous division. PROT. In what way? SOCRAT. First indeed, whether it must be admitted that certain unities of this kind truly exist: then, how each of them is to be thought to be always one and the same, receiving neither generation nor destruction, and most firm in its unity: finally, whether in things generated and infinite each is to be placed, either dispersed and having now become many from one, or the whole itself apart from itself, which seems the most impossible of all, that one and the same should be at once in one and many. Those things, therefore, O Protarchus, are not the cause of all difficulty and defect, but these things concerning the one and the many, when poorly conceded; but when well examined, they are the cause of facility. PROT. We ought, O Socrates, to discuss this first at present. SOCR. So I indeed would judge. PROT. Therefore, think that all these men concede these things to you. Perhaps, however, it is better now not to move Philebus, like an evil (as it is said) which lies well. <margin>Do not move an evil well-slept.</margin> SOCR. So be it. But from where shall we most likely begin, since there is a great and varied fight in these doubts? From here? PROT. From where indeed? SOCR. The one and the many having become the same by reasons, wander through every speech everywhere both formerly and now, because as it will never not be, so now for the first time it has not begun, but there is—as it seems to me indeed—in this kind of disputes, Protarchus, a certain immortal and never-aging reason implanted in us. As soon as any youth has tasted it, he congratulates himself, as if having found some treasure of wisdom, and exults full of pleasure, and is moved, and willingly tries every dispute, then indeed reflecting into the other part and mixing into one, then truly unfolding again and distributing into many: where surely he first and chiefly throws himself into doubt and difficulty, then his neighbor, whether he be younger or older or equal, sparing neither father nor mother, nor any of the listeners, not even sparing other living things, let alone men, since he spares none of the barbarians, provided he finds an interpreter from somewhere. Nevertheless (for we understand what you say), if there is any way, if there is any machine <note>original: *machinamentum*, referring to a logical device or method.</note> by which this perturbation can be kindly rejected from the dispute, and some more

I do not contend that the mind should obtain the first place in life. Regarding the **second place**, however, we must see what we shall do. For perhaps one of us might assert that the mind is the cause of our common life, and the other might assert pleasure, and thus the "Good" itself will be neither of those: but perhaps someone will judge one of these two to be the cause. Therefore, I should strive all the more against Philebus, because in this mixed life, whatever it is that makes life itself desirable and good, the mind is more closely related and more similar to it than pleasure is. And from this reasoning, the mind will truly hold the second place, but it will be further from the third, perhaps, if any faith is now to be placed by us in my reasoning.

PROTARCHUS. And yet, O Socrates, pleasure now seems prostrate, as if struck down by your arguments: for even while fighting for victory, it lies low. Regarding the mind, however, it seems it must be said that it would not wisely claim victory for itself. For it would suffer the same fate. But if pleasure is perhaps deprived of the second place, it will be altogether despised by its lovers; for it will no longer appear equally beautiful.

SOCRATES. What then? Is it not better to let it go, and not to cause it pain by an exquisite examination and refutation?

PROTARCHUS. You say nothing, O Socrates. <note>A Greek-style idiom meaning "You are talking nonsense" or "You are evading the point."</note>

SOCRATES. Is it because I proposed something impossible—that "pleasure should be affected by pain"?

PROTARCHUS. What kind of beginning do you mean?

SOCRATES. Let us distinguish all things that are now in the universe into two parts. Or rather, if you wish, into three.

PROTARCHUS. In what way?

SOCRATES. Let us take some of the things that were just said by us.

PROTARCHUS. Which ones?

SOCRATES. We were saying that God has shown, among the things that are, one to be **infinite** <note>original: *infinitum*, referring to the 'Unlimited' or things without inherent boundaries</note> and the other to be a **limit** <note>original: *terminum*, referring to 'Limit' or definite measure</note>.

SOCRATES. It is clear that a **fourth genus** <note>A "genus" is a category or class of things.</note> is still needed.

PROTARCHUS. Which one?

SOCRATES. Consider the **cause** of the mutual mixing of these things. And place that as a fourth besides those three.

PROTARCHUS. Will you not perhaps need a fifth in addition, some discerning factor?

SOCRATES. Perhaps; but not at present, as I think. But if there should be a need, you will forgive me for pursuing a fifth life.

PROTARCHUS. What stops us?

SOCRATES. In the beginning, therefore, dividing three of these four, and seeing each of the two split and torn into many parts, let us soon join each back together into one, and let us strive to perceive to what extent each of these is either one or many.

<margin>That the infinite is like many.</margin>

SOCRATES. I speak of the two that were proposed: the **finite** and the **infinite**. I will strive to show that the infinite is, in a way, many; but let the finite be deferred for later.

PROTARCHUS. Let it be deferred.

SOCRATES. Attend then: for what I bid you consider is difficult and highly controversial. Nevertheless, take note. First, consider concerning the **hotter and colder**, whether you find any limit in them;

<margin>The "more" and "less" reject an end and a "how much."</margin>

or rather, while the **"more" and "less"** are present in these kinds, they reject an end; for if an end were applied, they themselves would also be finished.

PROTARCHUS. You speak most truly.

SOCRATES. But indeed, we admit that "more" and "less" are always in the hotter and colder themselves.

PROTARCHUS. Very much so.

SOCRATES. Therefore, this reasoning always shows us that an end is absent from them: and since they are without end, let them be altogether infinite.

PROTARCHUS. Absolutely, O Socrates.

SOCRATES. Well done, friend Protarchus! You have understood, and you have noted now that this very thing which was just vehemently pronounced by you, and also that which is said mildly, have the same force as the "more" and the "less." For wherever they are present, they do not allow each thing to be a specific amount, but always inserting a "more vehement" into the "milder," and conversely a "milder" into the "more vehement" in all actions, they produce "more and less"; but they always destroy "how much" <note>Meaning they destroy fixed quantity or measurement.</note>. For as was just said, if they did not destroy "how much," but allowed it and measure to be born in the place of the "more" and "less," "vehement" and "mild," these would depart from their own region in which they were. For the hotter and colder would no longer exist if they received a fixed quantity. For the "hotter" would flee away and not stand still, and the "colder" likewise: but a "quantity" stands still and ceases to progress. Therefore, by this reasoning, it is clear that the hotter and colder are now infinite.

PROTARCHUS. So it appears, O Socrates: nevertheless, as you said, these things can hardly be perceived. But perhaps, repeated again in succession, they will declare the questioner and the responder to be in mutual agreement.

SOCRATES. You speak well, and so we must act according to our strength. But look first, whether we should place this mark of an

<margin>A sign of infinite nature.</margin>

infinite nature, lest by running through every single thing we stretch our speech out too long.

PROTARCHUS. What mark do you mean?

SOCRATES. Whatever things admit of "more and less," "vehemently and mildly," "too much," and such things, all are to be reduced into the **one genus of the infinite**,

<margin>Things in the genus of the infinite.</margin>

just as we said above, asserting that all things which are divided and dispersed ought to be collected into one, and marked according to one power, as if one single nature. Do you remember?

PROTARCHUS. I remember.

SOCRATES. But those things which do not accept such things, but accept all their opposites—first the **equal** itself and **equality**, and after the equal, the **double**, and every single proportion that number has to number, or measure to measure—if we referred

<margin>Things in the genus of the finite.</margin>

all these into the **genus of the finite**, would we be doing rightly? What do you say to this?

PROTARCHUS. Excellently, O Socrates.

SOCRATES. Come then. But the **third**, mixed from both of these, what idea shall we say it has?

PROTARCHUS. You will tell me that, I think.

SOCRATES. Rather, a God will, if only some God would graciously hear my prayers.

PROTARCHUS. Pray then, and contemplate.

SOCRATES. I am contemplating indeed. And it seems to me that some one of the gods has now breathed upon us in a friendly way.

PROTARCHUS. How do you say that? And what conjecture do you use?

SOCRATES. I will say it plainly, but you stand by with attentive ears.

PROTARCHUS. Just say it.

SOCRATES. Were we just now speaking of something "hotter" and "colder"?

PROTARCHUS. Certainly.

SOCRATES. Add furthermore the "drier" and "moister," the "more" and "less," the "faster" and "slower," the "greater" and "smaller": and finally, as many as we reduced above to the one nature that receives "more and less."

PROTARCHUS. Do you mean the nature of the infinite?

SOCRATES. Yes. But after this, mix into it that offspring of the **limit**.

PROTARCHUS. Which one?

SOCRATES. That which, although it was fitting to collect into one just as we had collected the nature of the infinite, we have not yet collected: but perhaps now you will do the same: for when these both are driven together, that **third** will immediately be revealed.

PROTARCHUS. What do you mean, and in what way?

SOCRATES. The offspring of the **equal** and the **double**, which does not allow whatever different things there are to be contrary and hostile, but by rendering them commensurate and harmonious,

it produces **number**.

He uses this framework to argue that "Mind" is superior to "Pleasure" because it brings order and measure.</summary>
