# Book Thirty-Four.

## THE TWELFTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS,
### OR, ON THE ENACTMENT OF LAWS.

->MARSILIO FICINO<-
->INTRODUCTION.<-

**P**lato, divine in all his dialogues on laws, was so delighted by the number twelve—imitating the divine work of the universe—that he intended this twelfth dialogue to be the common mystery of laws, just as the twelfth circle of the world is the common firmament of the stars. And just as one who penetrates that twelfth circle immediately finds, or rather attains, the soul in its perfection and happiness, so Plato, as he moves toward the end of this twelfth book, demonstrates in the *Epinomis* (the "After-law") not just laws, but the blessed perfection of the soul acquired through laws. 

In the previous books, he dealt with laws pertaining partly to public duties and partly to private business, some urban and some foreign, whether in peace or war. In the twelfth, however, all things are gathered together in a way that pertains to everything—not just individual laws, but certain singular ones from every category. To the laws is added that which is greatest: the *ratio* (reason or principle) that both preserves and corrects the laws. To the magistrates is added that which is greatest: the principle of *repetundae* (the recovery of property and the rendering of accounts). This is placed over the public duties of magistrates just as the examination of conscience is placed over the private actions of souls. Upon this examination, the entire health of souls depends privately, and the entire health of the city depends publicly. This is the summary argument of the twelfth book. 

At the very beginning, and in what follows—as often in the preceding parts—he mentions the vengeance of the gods. He calls some gods the sons of other gods, and men the sons of gods. It is important to remember that in Plato, there are two ways gods are sons of gods, and two ways men are sons of gods. First, as the *Timaeus* teaches, all the rulers of the world-spheres—whether the souls of the spheres themselves, or the *daemones* (spirits) within the spheres, or the angelic intellects beyond the spheres—are sons of the omnipotent God, created as benefits by His will. Second, in each of these three classes, the lower are called sons of the higher because they continuously receive rays and forms from the higher, are shaped by them, and seem to obey them as fathers. 

Similarly, men are said to be born from the higher powers, either because they were brought into the light from the bowels of the earth at the beginning of things by the nourishment of the higher powers, or because some are so intensely inspired daily by higher powers that they are "reborn" from their usual human state into a divine state of life. In this rank, Plato often places pious philosophers and philosophical princes. 

When he places Jupiter and Mercury over ambassadors and messengers at the start of the book, it must be understood first that Jupiter signifies God the Architect of the world, and Mercury signifies the entire number of angels. Secondly, Jupiter signifies the planet indicating emperors and laws, while Mercury signifies the planet of interpretation and swift execution. I call the planets "signifiers" because, as the *Timaeus* and Plotinus (the Neoplatonist) testify, the planets and celestial things signify and announce to everyone what the higher powers are about to do, or what we ourselves will sometimes do, or more often, suffer. 

He soon detests the poets who, by transferring human crimes to the higher powers, have both sinned impiously against divinity and gravely harmed men by the bad example of the gods. Furthermore, he believes thefts and other crimes should be judged more by the intention and the habit of the sinner—whether curable or incurable—than by the mere impulse. 

Among the military laws, he prescribes what he considers the best for all of life: that no one should know what it is to live for himself alone or do anything apart from others. Instead, each should direct every action toward the nod of a wise superior and toward common use. He teaches judges not to deliver a sentence contrary to right, whether voluntarily or under compulsion. For Judgment itself, according to the opinion of the ancients (especially Orpheus and Hesiod), is a modest virgin; Lie is hateful above all to Modesty and Judgment. He considers the goddess presiding over judgment to be Divine Providence, who must be venerated by human judges. 

After this, where he condemns those who shamefully threw away their weapons and those war leaders who receive them back to serve again: he mentions the number of ten *minae* (a Greek currency unit) in our translation, though the laws elsewhere mention a thousand. A little later, he asserts that the "knot" of the Republic is the judgment of the rendering of accounts (*repetundae*), so that no judge in the Republic is without his own judge. Otherwise, through unregulated license in judging, justice would perish first, and then the city, having lost justice, would die like a body without a soul. 

By the "Temple of the Sun and Apollo," he understands a shrine dedicated not only to the planetary soul of the sun, but much more to the light of the Highest Good, of which the sun is the image. You will hear that sins are committed out of an "envious absence of religion." But the worst of all the impious are those who trust they can appease God with prayers and sacrifices so that they may extort great sums of money with impunity. 

After this, he gives very cautious laws about receiving foreigners and the travel of citizens, so that the city's customs are not confused by foreign habits, yet the Republic does not lack the expertise of others. You will note here that a certain divine power exists in a few people, through which they discern the capacity of geniuses. This shows that a certain divinity is not only "acquired" by us, so to speak, but is innate. 

He commands that it should not be considered a small thing whether you seem honest or wicked. The reputation for virtue must be sought—but sought only through virtue itself. He mentions that divine men sometimes exist even among the common people and in poorly governed cities. 

Next, he treats many matters: legal actions, accusations, defenses, appeals, sureties, proscriptions, and such. He mixes in various things to be dedicated to the deities, a symbolic tradition in the Pythagorean rite. He says the Earth and Vesta are the sacred habitation of all gods. By adding "Vesta," he signifies that under the name of this Earth, something deeper should be understood: this elemental earth, the lunar earth, and finally the star-bearing earth. Likewise, the three souls of these three earths, and their three angels. 

Remember that among the ancients, whatever in the universe is effective for forming and moving is metaphorically called "Fire." Whatever is most easily formed is called "Air." That which is purgative is "Water." That which is solid, stable, and consistent is named "Earth." Such a nature, due to its dense or consistent quality, is called "Earth" by the Platonists both here, on the moon, and in the firmament. Why should it be a wonder, then, that Earth is the sacred habitation of all gods, if the universe is contained within the three boundaries of these three Earths? 

Since he says the gods are consecrated by the soul, he forbids them to be consecrated again, warning that you cannot trust yourself to offer God anything that was not already God's own. He forbids statues to be made of gold or silver, lest we trust we can purge great crimes with their high price. He forbids ivory, since it has been abandoned by the sensible soul, lest we work in sacred matters without "sense"—that is, without vigilance and attention. He rejects bronze and iron, blaming them as instruments of war. For if the soul is at odds within itself or with others, we perform sacrifices in vain. Finally, he considers wood and stone for the images of gods. In stone, he commends the stability of the mind in sacred rites. In wood, he sees the "food of fire"—that is, the ardor of the soul that is easily ignited in divine matters. He commands images to be carved from a single piece of stone or wood, commending simplicity and integrity above all. 

Nor should it be passed over in silence that in the previous parts, ambassadors were sent to four oracles, so that we might know that God, the author of all, provides for all parts of the world equally (designated by the four corners: East, West, North, and South). In whatever rite God is worshipped, provided He is worshipped with a pure mind and grace, it is in some way acceptable. But these matters are discussed more diligently elsewhere. 

Among these things, he forbids those who serve the father in any matter from receiving gifts. He deals with taxes. He says no one can learn anything better than that which makes him better. He says the Law is a wondrous and divine thing, taking its name from "Mind" (*nous* in Greek, *nomos* for law) [[notes: Ficino is making a linguistic connection frequent in Plato between *nous* (mind) and *nomos* (law)]]—from the Divine Mind as its father, and the human mind as its mother. He wants judgment to follow the law. These two are the greatest of human goods. 

But here it comes to mind what he said at the end of the eleventh book: that our goods are often stained by their own calamities. He says elsewhere that the "calamity of law" is the wickedness of the magistrate himself. He called the "calamity of judgment" a certain legalistic trickery which, having no regard for right but only for greed and ambition, accepts any case for defense without distinction. This he detests above all others as the plague of the Republic. 

After this, when he sets laws for funerals, he wants the man himself to be considered primarily the substance of the rational soul. The body of the man is an "image," and as he calls it elsewhere, a "shadow." What is "man" in us and what is "animal" is known from the *Timaeus*, the *Alcibiades*, and Plotinus—matters we discuss more broadly in our *Theology*. There he concludes that "man" is the substance of the rational soul, which, beyond reason, also has a certain internal, impassible, and common sense. The "animal" is a composite of the shaped body and a certain "trace of life" impressed by the soul. In this impressed trace is that other "sense"—secondary to the first—which is distributed through the various organs and is capable of suffering. 

[[page number: 607]]

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation. Dialogue XII.

This seems to harmonize greatly with some of the sayings of the Apostle Paul. When he says the soul goes away to "other gods" to give an account of its deeds, he calls the angelic minds outside bodies "other gods," who are distinct from the souls of the spheres. For our souls, while joined to these bodies, are placed under the kingdom of the higher souls; when separated, they are transferred to the judgment of the separated beings. 

Thus far he has established laws; but he says laws are established in vain unless one thinks about their health, stability, and preservation. Therefore, for their stability, he will devise a certain wondrous council of magistrates. But before creating this, he touches on the power of the Fates, as he understands that human prudence is not enough for the health of human affairs if the fatal power is utterly opposed. In this, he certainly seems to approve of those who, in building cities, enacting laws, creating magistrates, and even "planting" men, carefully guard against the adverse positions of the stars. 

Regarding Fate, many things are said elsewhere, which are brought in here as briefly as they are opportunely. Fate is a certain immovable disposition of movable things within the Soul of the World. The instrument of Fate is the celestial nature. But the matter upon which it acts through that instrument is the mass of the elements. He accepts three names: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos, pertaining both to the instrument and the matter. For we can call Lachesis the firmament, in whose stars the strong powers of all lower things are contained. Clotho is the assembly of planets, unfolding the lots of things while the firmament provides the material. Finally, Atropos is Saturn especially, who by his stability inevitably confirms the lots unfolded into effect. 

In matter, too, we count three Fates, because the fatal power infused into the elements through the celestial instrument acts on matter and form and the composite. Likewise on essence, power, and action. Likewise on the beginning, middle, and end. Since it acts not only on bodies, but also on souls insofar as they are affected by or use bodies, Plato says here that the Fates can preserve the prosperity of both bodies and souls, and of the laws. 

And since the Mind, by its nature (relying on the providence of the Divine Mind), sometimes overcomes Fate or uses Fate successfully, he added that for the safety of life, both public and private, sense must be joined with mind, so that sense obeys and serves mind. Similarly, this union composed of mind, sight, and hearing creates a certain assembly of magistrates in the Republic who look out for the stability of laws. This assembly first looks to the goal of the Republic, then to what power best leads to that goal. It studies how everything in the city, whether private or public, may lead toward the One. It directs all things toward virtue, and the other virtues toward Prudence. Finally, it leads Prudence to Wisdom, which he often signifies under the name of "Mind." By the standard of this Wisdom, all virtues are to be approved, insofar as they lead to Wisdom, which is itself approved because it partakes in the one Divine Good. 

He asserts that the most exquisite consideration of things is that which sees not only the "many" insofar as they are many, but also the "one common nature" within all. Likewise, from what "one principle" they have this nature. Again, toward what "one goal" they can be led through it. Without this kind of contemplation, no one can perfectly govern life, either privately or publicly. Since this speculation belongs to the philosopher—especially the divine one—he rightly judges that the highest matters should be referred to the divine philosophers gathered in that most elect assembly. "Divine," I say, meaning those who inspect and cultivate divine things. Therefore, those who are dull in inspecting divine things, or lazy in worshipping them, or inept in teaching them, he keeps far away from the highest offices of the Republic. 

Soon he proves that for a firm faith in the highest divinity, two things are primarily necessary. First, that we know the class of rational souls is divine and older than bodies, by which the spheres of the world are moved and all things within the spheres are generated. Second, that we consider the class of Minds (namely, the angelic ones) to be more excellent than the class of souls. And that souls move the spheres in an orderly way because they participate in Mind. For if anyone knows these two things, he will easily understand that just as Mind is the form and order of the soul, so the Divine Good is the life and light of both Mind and soul. 

These three—the Divine Good, Mind, and Soul—Plato undoubtedly demonstrates or hints at as the principles of all things in almost all his writings. He wrapped this in obscure words in his *Letter to Dionysius*. Regarding our soul being older than the body, he does not mean it is older in time, but rather older in dignity and prior because it has its origin from a principle superior to bodies. Therefore, he placed motion "from itself" in the soul, but "from the soul" in the body. And because mutability exists in the body from a mutable soul, the body is changed not only in action but even in substance.

[[page number: 608]]

# Book Thirty-Four.

...of daughters who are under the charge of men. All dances should be celebrated so that war may be waged well, and all dexterity, ease, and promptness should be prepared for this same cause. For the same reason, we must accustom ourselves to abstain from excessive food and drink, to endure cold and heat and the hardness of the bed, and especially not to corrupt the strength of the head and feet with foreign coverings, nor to ruin the nature of the caps and shoes given at birth. For these extremities, when they preserve their nature, provide the greatest strength to the whole body; the opposite produces the opposite. One part serves the whole body most, while the other leads the whole, since it naturally possesses all the principal senses. Let the youth hear these praises of the military life.

As for these laws: Let whoever is conscripted or assigned to any part serve. If anyone, out of cowardice and without the general's permission, refuses to serve, let him be accused of deserting military service when he returns to the leaders of the war. Let all who have served judge—the infantry separately, the cavalry separately, and others likewise. Indeed, infantry should be brought before infantry, cavalry before cavalry, and others before leaders of the same rank. Whoever is condemned shall be prohibited from entering any later contest or accusing another of neglected service. Furthermore, let the judges decide what he must give or suffer. 

Once the judgment for desertion is over, let the leaders hold assemblies of the infantry, cavalry, and others, so that military rewards may be given to those who conducted themselves strenuously. Let whoever wishes judge the victory among his own rank, provided he does not use conjectures or witnesses from past battles, but considers only the fight that was recently waged. Let those who are seen to have fought excellently be given a crown woven from the leaves of an ever-green tree. Let those who receive this hang it in the temples of the warlike gods, however they please, with an inscription of their title, so that the testimony of virtue may be lasting. Let those declared in second and third place do likewise. 

If anyone has set out for war and leaves the army before the leaders have dismissed them, let him be accused of deserting his rank before the same judges as the one accused of neglected service, and let him be punished similarly if condemned. Whoever is about to judge must take care with all his strength not to inflict a punishment or fine falsely and undeservedly, whether voluntarily or involuntarily; for Judgment is truly said to be a modest virgin. To Modesty and Judgment, a lie is naturally hateful. Therefore, in all things, and especially in the throwing away of weapons in war, we must take care not to offend the goddess presiding over judgment. Let no one, out of ignorance, judge necessary abandonments of weapons as shameful and punish someone undeserving of penalty. 

It is indeed difficult to distinguish these things. However, the law must try to distinguish each part. Let us therefore use a story for this. If Patroclus had been carried back to the tents half-dead without weapons (as happens to many), and the weapons that Peleus had given to the gods—which the poet says were given as a dowry to Thetis—had been snatched by Hector, would the son of Menoetius [[notes: Patroclus]] have been blamed by detractors as one who threw away his weapons? Furthermore, if some are cast down from a height, or in the sea, or in a clash of storms and waters, and are forced to lose their weapons, should they be blamed? Effort must be made to separate the greater and heavier evil from its opposite. 

In the very act of blaming, the use of the words themselves shows a difference. For a "thrower-away" is not rightly said of everyone, but a "loser of weapons" is said of everyone; and he who lost them by force should not be judged like one who threw them away voluntarily. They are entirely different. So let us do this: if someone is surrounded by enemies while armed and does not defend himself against them, but voluntarily drops or throws away his weapons, preferring to obtain a shameful life through speed rather than an honorable and happy death through fortitude—let there be a judgment for such a "throwing away," but none for the former. For the cowardly and wicked must always be punished so they become better and stronger. But the unfortunate, not at all; it achieves nothing. 

But what punishment is fitting for one condemned for throwing away weapons and degenerating from manly fortitude? Especially since it is impossible for such a person to be changed into his opposite, as they say the Thessalian Caeneus was changed from a woman into the nature of a man by divine power. For it would be most fitting for a thrower-away of weapons to be punished by being transformed from a man into a woman. But since that cannot happen, let us devise something close to it: since he is so desirous of living, let him thereafter face no danger, but live the rest of his life—and a very long one at that—wickedly and with disgrace. 

Let this be the law: Let no general or any prefect ever use a man condemned for shamefully throwing away his weapons as a soldier, nor receive him into the battle line. If a leader does otherwise, the judge of the rendering of accounts shall take note of it. If the leader is of the highest property class, let him be fined ten *minae*; if the second, five; if the third, three; if the fourth, one. The one condemned for throwing away weapons shall not only be barred from manly dangers due to his cowardly nature but, if he is of the highest class, shall similarly be fined ten *minae*; five for the second; three for the third; one for the fourth. 

What shall we say of the recovery of property (*repetundae*) [[notes: This refers to the accounting of a magistrate's conduct and finances at the end of their term]], which magistrates—whether created by lot for a year or chosen by a council for many years—must render? Who will be a sufficient judge of these accounts if some magistrate, weighed down by the importance of affairs, has said or done something unworthy of his office? This is difficult to find. For since the chosen magistrates excel others in virtue, how shall we find someone more excellent than them? 

And yet, some divine men must be sought as exactors and judges of these accounts. For the matter stands thus: many occasions for the dissolution of a Republic seem to exist, just as for a ship or an animal. Although their nature is one and diffused everywhere, we call them tensions, supports, extensions of nerves, and many other names. But this occasion for either the safety or the destruction of the Republic is not small. For if the judges who demand the account of the conducted magistracy excel the magistrates in virtue, and if it is done so that no one can rightly complain, then the whole region and city will flourish happily. But if the judgment of accounts proceeds otherwise, then that judgment—by which all civil things are bound into one—is dissolved. All magistrates are torn away from each other; and having become "many" instead of "one," they make a multiple city out of a single one. From this, everything is quickly overturned by full sedition. Therefore, the exactors of accounts must wonderfully excel everyone in every kind of virtue.

[[page number: 609]]

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation. Dialogue XII.

Let us devise their generation in this way. Each year, after the summer solstice, the entire city shall gather at a place commonly dedicated to the Sun and Apollo to elect three men, whom each person judges to be better than himself (himself alone excepted), and who is not less than fifty years old. Then, of the elected, let them put forward the half who were preferred by the most voters. If they are equal, let them go forward; if unequal, excepting the one who received fewer votes, let them similarly take the half of the remaining ones, judged by the number of votes. If many have an equal number of votes and increase the half-number, let the younger be placed after. Once the others are taken, let votes be cast again until three unequal ones obtain the position. If votes are equal for all these or for two, let the matter be committed to good fortune; let them be discerned by lot. 

Let them crown the one who surpasses in votes, and the ones declared in second and third place, with a crown woven from the leaves of an ever-green tree. Once the prizes are given, let them declare by a herald how the city of the Magnesians, having again obtained safety under God's leadership, consecrates its three best citizens as common first-fruits to the Sun and Apollo according to the ancient law, insofar as they are to follow the judgment. 

In the first year, let them appoint twelve examiners of the recovery of accounts. Let them do this until for each, the seventy-fifth year is completed; thereafter, let three always be added each year. Let these magistrates, distributed into twelve parts, observe all things diligently, judging with every free examination. Let them live, during the time the accounts are rendered to them, in the place where they were elected, dedicated to the Sun and Apollo. And whether each one alone or all together in common, after diligent inquiry, let them write down publicly concerning each magistrate what he ought to suffer or give according to the sentence of the judges of accounts. 

And if any magistrate complains that he was not rightly condemned by their judgment, let him bring the judges of the accounts to an elected court. If he escapes, let him accuse them if he wishes; but if he is condemned there as well, and had previously been condemned to death by the judges of accounts, let him die as necessity requires. If he is condemned to a fine by them which can be paid double, let him pay double. 

But now we must hear what their sentences for accounts are and how they are to be delivered. For those who have been placed over everyone by the consensus of the whole city, let the first seats always be provided in all solemnities for as long as they live. And whenever it is necessary for some judges and prefecters to be sent from the city to the common spectacles and sacrifices of the Greeks, let them be sent from these. Let these alone in the city be crowned with a laurel crown; let these be the priests of the Sun and Apollo. Also, let the High Priest each year be that one from among them who was judged to have excelled the other priests in the previous year. Let the eras be distinguished by their names for as long as the city is inhabited. 

When they die, let their funerals and tombs be more excellent than those of other citizens. Let all their garments be white. Let mourning and wailing be absent. Also, let two choirs—one of fifteen girls, the other of as many boys—standing around the bier on each side, praise the priest in turn with songs and chant his happiness throughout the whole day. In the morning, let the younger men who labor in the gymnasia, whom the relatives of the deceased have chosen, carry the bier to the monument. Let the first of the unmarried men, armed as if for battle, lead the way: cavalry with horses, infantry with light arms, and others likewise. Let the boys sing the ancestral song before the bier, and the girls after them, and let the women past childbearing follow. 

Finally, although the high priests of either gender are barred from other monuments, if the Pythian [[notes: Apollo's oracle at Delphi]] also confirms it, there is nothing preventing them from coming to this tomb, as if it were something pure. Let his monument be a certain longer vault under the earth made of the hardest and most beautiful stones, where there are stone beds on both sides; here let them bury that blessed man, and plant trees in a circle, except for one part, so that this tomb can be enlarged. Then, each year, let them honor these men with musical, gymnastic, and equestrian contests. 

Let these rewards be returned to those whose judgments on the reported accounts were not condemned. But if any of them, trusting in the judgment by which he was preferred, reveals the fragile condition of human nature—that is, falling into error after he was considered excellent—let it be established by law that he may be accused by anyone who wishes. Let the judgment regarding him be conducted thus: first, the guardians of the laws shall be present; then the colleagues of the accused himself; and finally the judges of the elected court. Let the accuser write down that the accused is unworthy of both the office and the rewards of the office. If he is condemned, let him be deprived of the office, the tomb, and the other rewards belonging to that office. But if the accuser does not obtain a fifth part of the votes, let him pay: if he is of the first class, twelve *minae*; if the second, eight; if the third, six; if the fourth, two. 

I see that Rhadamanthus [[notes: a mythical wise king, son of Zeus, and judge of the dead]] was worthy of great admiration in judging. For he perceived that in those times, all men confessed with one mouth that there were gods. And not without reason, since many in those times were born of gods, in whose number he himself was counted. Therefore, he seems to have thought that judgments should be committed to gods, not to men. For this reason, he performed judgments simply and swiftly. For by requiring an oath from the litigants in each case, he used to judge both quickly and safely. 

Now, however, some deny there are gods, others think they do not care for human affairs, and the most numerous and worst believe that the gods are so reconciled to them by many sacrifices and flatteries that they may extort great money with impunity. Therefore, that Rhadamanthine way of judging does not fit these men at all. For since the opinions of men about the gods have changed, the laws also must be changed. Therefore, a wise legislator will prohibit the oath of litigants in the discussion of judgments, so that both the intention of the accuser and the plea of the defender may be written in the judgments without an oath. For if the license of swearing is given to anyone in the city, where more cases are brought before the judges daily, almost all will be perjurers, especially those joined by present banquets, other customs, and private necessity. 

Therefore, let it be established by law that the judge who is about to judge shall swear, as well as those who will appoint the magistrates of the Republic by vote. Also, let the judge of the choir, and the presidents and givers of all music, gymnastic, and equestrian duties in the contest, swear; and in short, in whatever cases, according to human opinion, there is no gain from perjury. But in those where someone would pursue utility from perjury, let them be judged without an oath. And let the judges in no way permit the litigants either to swear for the sake of persuasion, or to call down curses on themselves or their kin, or to supplicate shamefully, or to use feminine commiseration.

[[page number: 610]]

# Book Thirty-Four.

...but let them teach mildly what they think is just, and let them listen to the one teaching. If he wanders from these things, let him be brought back to the matter by the magistrate. When foreigners litigate among themselves, let them be allowed to swear if they wish, just as now. For since they are not to grow old in the city, there is no fear that they will corrupt others. In the same way, let the execution of judgment be done among free men, if a free man does not obey the city in those matters which are not punished by lashes, bonds, or death. And if someone does not come to celebrate a dance or a procession, or some other common matter of this kind, for the service of sacrifice and sacred peace or war, or has not contributed a tax: in all these, let the loss be restored as soon as possible, or a pledge which the city and law have committed be brought, and the pledge being sold at the exacted time, let the money be brought into the treasury. 

If there is need of a greater fine, let the individual magistrates call the stubborn men into judgment and compel them to obey the laws by imposing the debt fine. But for a city that does not give effort to collecting money and has money only from agriculture—since it has time for neither commerce nor travel, nor receives foreigners from elsewhere—it is necessary to deliberate what must be done. Therefore, the legislator, first by persuading, should consult for its strength thus. 

The mixing of different nations usually confuses various customs, and the association of foreigners with foreigners introduces many innovations. This harms a city well and rightly instituted by laws most of all. In poorly instituted cities, it matters nothing if both old and young travel abroad at will and receive foreigners from elsewhere. On the contrary, never to receive any newcomers, nor for them to set out elsewhere, is both impossible and would seem cruel and arrogant to other men, who would mark the city with a shameful term, calling it an enemy of foreigners and difficult and inhuman. 

One ought never to make light of whether you seem honest or wicked to others. For many, though they lack virtue, judge who is honest and who is wicked. For even in wicked men, a certain divine power of conjecture is innate, through which many, even the worst, rightly distinguish better people from worse, both by opinion and words. Therefore, it is usefully commanded to cities that they do not weigh a good reputation among the many as a small thing. It is surely the greatest and most right thing that, since you are honest, you should seek glory; otherwise not at all, if you are to be a perfect man. Therefore, the Cretan city also ought to strive to obtain the best reputation for virtue among other men. The greatest hope is that, living by reason, it will deservedly see the Sun and the other gods, along with other well-governed cities and regions. 

Thus, regarding travel to other places and regions, and the reception of foreigners, let it be decreed: First, let it be allowed in no way for anyone who is less than forty years old to travel. Let it be allowed to no private person. But publicly, let it be allowed to heralds, ambassadors, and scouts. Indeed, travel outside the region to wage war should not be considered civil travel. To Pythian Apollo, to Olympic Jupiter, and also to Nemea and the Isthmus, some should be sent through whom our city may commonly bring sacrifices and games to these gods. Let as many as possible be sent, the most beautiful and best, who in the sacred and peaceful unions may obtain honor and glory for their city corresponding to its military glory. 

When they return, let them teach the younger that the civil institutions of others are far inferior to their own. Let no law prohibit other spectators who, abounding in leisure, desire to consider the affairs of other men, according to the institution of the guardians of the laws. For a city ignorant of good or bad men and lacking foreign experience can never be sufficiently human and perfect, nor can it preserve laws by habits and custom alone, unless it also becomes wiser by the knowledge of laws. 

Even in the common people and the multitude, there exist certain divine men, though few, yet worthy with whom you should have association. These arise no more in well-governed cities than in others. Therefore, whoever in a rightly governed city is incorrupt, setting out from his fatherland, will follow their tracks by land and sea, so that finally returning, he may approve some of the laws of the fatherland and correct others if they fail in some matter. Indeed, without this inspection and investigation, a city will never remain at its best, nor will it be poorly investigated. 

[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] How will both of these happen? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Certainly in this way. First, let such a spectator be more than fifty years old; then, proven both in other things and especially in war, if he is to leave an example of the guardians of the laws in other cities. Let him wander no more beyond his sixtieth year. But within the tenth year, when he wishes to return home, let him enter the assembly of those who examine the laws. 

Let this assembly consist of younger and older men, and let it meet daily in the morning until the sun rises: first regarding the priests who have been affected with duties as being more excellent than others; then ten of the older guardians of the laws; and finally the censor of universal discipline, both he who holds this office and those who have already completed it. And let none of these be alone, but with some younger man whom he has chosen, born between thirty and forty years of age. Let these always discuss the laws and the Republic, and compare with one another if they have heard anything excellent about them. Let them also speak of the disciplines leading to that end, which those who know will more easily understand the intention of the laws, and those who do not will understand with more difficulty. 

What the elders approve from these, let the younger learn with great study. If any younger man brought in is seen to be unworthy, let the whole assembly reproach the one who brought him. Let the whole city honor and preserve the youths who have conducted themselves rightly in these things. But if they make themselves worse than others, let them be affected with greater disgrace than others. Let the one who inspected the laws and customs of others proceed immediately to this assembly; if he found anything among others regarding the enactment of laws or discipline or education, let him set it forth. If he himself found anything, let him declare it to the entire assembly. If he is seen to have returned not worse, let him be praised because he freely did what he could. If he returned much better, let him both while alive be affected with great honors and let the whole assembly decorate him when dead. 

But if he is seen to have returned corrupted, while he pretends to be wise, let him not dare to mix with any younger or older man. If he obeys the magistrates, let him live as a private citizen. But if, against the will of the magistrates, he is condemned in judgment for disputing about discipline and civil laws, let him die. And if, when he ought to have been led into judgment by right, he was led by no magistrate, let this matter be a disgrace to the magistrates when offices are decreed afterward. 

He who is about to set out elsewhere ought to be of this kind and travel thus. But foreigners also are to be kindly received.

[[page number: 611]]

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation. Dialogue XII.

There are four types of foreigners of whom mention must be made. The first are those who are always "summer birds," and like birds fly across the sea mostly for the sake of acquiring money, coming to other cities in the summer time. Let the magistrates in charge of such places receive these in the forum, ports, and public houses outside the city in the suburbs, observing lest any of them do anything new. Let judgments also be rightly rendered to them there, so that familiarity is had with them no more than necessity compels. 

The second type is of those who come as spectators and to hear the muses of the city there. Let all these have inns next to the temples, which are most convenient for receiving guests. Let the priests and sacristans have care of them, so they can stay pleasantly for a sufficient time and see and hear those things for which they came, and finally depart without harm both to themselves and others. If any of them brings injury to anyone or is affected by injury, let the priests take cognizance of it up to fifty drachmas. Let greater crimes be referred to the curators of commercial affairs. 

The third type of foreigners is to be received publicly, when someone comes from elsewhere sent for a public cause. Let the Generals, masters of the horse, and military tribunes alone receive him. And he with whom he stays, along with the leaders of the council, shall have care of him. 

The fourth type is very rare. However, someone may arrive from elsewhere, responding to our spectators on the other side. He shall be received thus: first, if he has completed fifty years; then, if he came with that mind that he may either consider what is held as excellent among others or teach his own. Let him surely go to the doors of the wealthy and wise as one not unwelcome, since he himself is of this kind; and as a guest of discipline, let him rightly seek the prefect's house, not doubting that it will be hospitable to him because of the connection of virtue. And when he has learned from others and taught what he thought should be learned and taught, let him depart as a friend from friends, affected with fitting honor and gifts. 

By these laws let us receive foreigners and send out our own, fearing Hospitable Jupiter. For foreigners are not to be driven away by exclusion from food and sacrifices, as happens near the Nile; nor are they to be barred from our borders by a harsh edict. 

Let any surety (fideiussor) give surety openly and clearly, and let him confess the whole business in writing before three and no fewer witnesses, if the surety is made for less than a thousand drachmas. If it is beyond a thousand, let five witnesses at least be used. Let the surety be he who previously sold the item, of whom it is doubted whether he can sell by right; and he who is seen to be less sufficient for his promises; similarly, let both the one who pre-sold and the one who sells be subject to judgment as one liable. 

If anyone wishes to seek anything in the house of another as his own, let him first affirm by oath that he hopes to find there what he seeks; then let him enter naked or wearing only an inner tunic and girded, and let the house and the furniture, both sealed and unsealed, be offered to him. If anyone does not permit him to search by force, the one who prohibits shall be charged with the price of the lost item being fixed, and he who drove him away shall be accused, and if he is condemned, let him restore double. If the master of the house is absent, let only the unsealed things be offered by those present; but the sealed things let him also bind, and let him leave a guard for five days. In which time if the patron does not come, taking the aediles (city officers) with him, let him unseal the bound things, and when he has searched before the eyes of the household and aediles, let him seal it again. 

In ambiguous matters, a space of time must be determined for prescription. Regarding houses and fields, there will be no dispute by this reason. But if any other thing is held by anyone, and he has used that thing openly in the city, forum, or sacred rites for an entire year, and it is certain he did not hide it; nor did anyone meanwhile, however much seeking it, demand it: let it thereafter be allowed to no one to reclaim that thing as his own. But if he uses it manifestly not in the city but in the fields, and the master of the thing is not found within five years, let him use it at home; and for up to three years, he who lost it can apprehend it. In the fields, however, if he holds it secretly, up to ten years. If outside the region, let him always apprehend it whenever he finds it. 

When someone by force prohibits him who litigates or the witnesses from coming into judgment, if he is his own servant, whether his own or another's, let the act be of no importance. But if a free man, let both the sentence be void, and let the one who drove him away be bound for a year; and if anyone wishes to accuse him of robbery, let it be lawful. If anyone by force prohibits another who is about to compete with him in music or gymnastics or any other faculty from entering the contest, let whoever wishes signify this to the declarers of rewards, who shall procure that any free man can compete. If he cannot do that, let the rewards of victory be given to the prohibited person; if the prohibitor wins, let the name of the victor also be inscribed in whatever temples he wishes. But let it not be allowed to the prohibitor to inscribe his name or offer the insignia of victory. And whether he wins in the contest or is defeated, let him be guilty of the crime of the damage inflicted. 

If anyone knowingly receives a thing stolen by theft, let him be in the same guilt as he who stole it. He who receives an exile or anyone fleeing of this kind, let him die. For whoever the city has decreed as its friend or enemy, each person ought similarly to consider him. If anyone by his own counsel and without common authority enters peace or moves war, let him be condemned to the ultimate punishment. If some part of the city attempted that, let the authors of this matter be dragged into judgment by the military generals and, if condemned, be punished by death. 

Let those who serve the fatherland in any matter in no way receive gifts; nor by any occasion or reason should we persuade ourselves that in good things gifts should be received, but in others not at all. For it is not easy to know, nor when you have known, to contain yourself. Therefore, it is safer to obey the laws, which say that no gifts are to be received for the service of the fatherland. If anyone is condemned for having obeyed less, let him die. 

Let public taxes be arranged thus: first, for the sake of many things, let there be an assessment of all the property of every citizen. Then let the tribesmen bring the written annual fruits from the fields to the magistrates, so that since there are two taxes, the Republic can use either one as it sees fit each year: namely, either a part of the universal assessment or a part of the annual fruits. Whence those things which are given for food should always be excepted. 

Let moderate gifts to the gods be offered by moderate men. The Earth, therefore, as the forum of the home of men, is sacred to all the gods. Therefore, let no one consecrate the same again. Gold and silver in cities, both privately and in shrines, is an enviable thing. Then ivory, extracted from a lifeless body, is a gift hardly pure enough for God. Now bronze and iron, instruments of war, are not for the shrine. But wood, whatever one wishes, dedicated from one piece of wood; likewise of stone, in common shrines. Woven work should be no more laborious than a woman's monthly work. The color white is especially decorous for God, both in other things and especially in woven work. Let dyed things be absent, except from military insignia. The most divine gifts are birds and forms completed by one painter in one day. And let other gifts of this example be, in their craftsmanship,

[[page number: 612]]

# Book Thirty-Four.

...fitting for the gods. But things dyed with other colors should be exhibited only for military insignia. The most divine offerings are birds and pictures which a single painter has painted in one day. Let all other donations be similar to these. 

Afterwards, the parts of the city which and how many they ought to be have been distinguished, and laws concerning contracts and the greatest commerce have been placed as far as possible: it remains that we speak now of judgments. First, therefore, let the arbitrator-judges whom the litigants have chosen have a place. These can be more conveniently called "conciliators" than "judges." Then the neighbors and tribesmen distributed according to the twelfth part. Before whom, if they were not reconciled by the first, let them litigate with greater loss. Where if the debtor is condemned again, let him pay a fifth part of the debt. Whoever appeals even from this judgment and wishes to contest a third time, let him seek the elected judges. And if he is again condemned by them, let him bring both the debt itself and a half part of the debt in addition. And if the accuser, repulsed from the first judgment, did not rest but wished to contest again in a second judgment, if he wins let him receive a fifth part, but if defeated let him lose as much. When they seek third judges, not yet being reconciled through the first and second, let the defeated debtor deposit as much and a half part of the debt in addition for the victor, as we said. The previously defeated accuser, a half. 

But concerning the creating and declaring of judges, the administration of all these, the times in which individual things are to be done, the casting of votes, the delay and dilation of judgment, the term, the citation, the rejection, and all other things which are necessary for judgments, we have touched upon in the previous parts: however, what is beautiful, as the proverb has it, can be said rightly both twice and three times. Small things and those easy to find, if an older legislator passed them over, let the younger fill in. 

But regarding private judgments, enough has now been said. Public and common ones which the magistrates use, performing what pertains to them, are found rightly established by wise men in many cities. Whence it is necessary for the guardians of the laws to receive what is fitting for this new Republic, so that they may both diligently correct and approve individual things examined by risk, until they think they have them sufficiently; and finally, let them use these as immovable for their whole life, without an end placed on the discussion. 

Regarding silence, praise, and blame, and about the just, good, and honorable which differ in other cities, it has been said and will be said in the end. A judge who is to be equitable ought to look back to all these, and give effort that he learns these constitutions of the laws before all things and holds them firmly in his mind. For toward making a man who has learned good, the writings of the laws confer more than other doctrines if they hold themselves rightly. Nor does the wondrous and divine law possess a name closest to "Mind" by chance ([[abbrev: νοῦς → nous]] indeed signifies mind, but [[abbrev: νόμος → nomos]] laws). For since many speeches about the praise and blame of some are circulated partly in songs and partly in prose, both written and held daily in circles either by contending or by false assenting, the writings of the legislator are for us the clear examination of all these. The honest judge will always hold these with him like a remedy and medicine against the poisons of other speeches; by which he will emend himself and the city, confirm and extol the good, and recall the wicked from ignorance, incontinence, fear, and in summary, from universal injustice as far as possible if they are curable. For if they cannot be cured, those who affect them with death seem to be called judges and princes of judges by all, not undeservedly, quite often. 

But after the annual judgments are finished, let them use these laws. First, let the magistrate who already exercises the office of judge hand over all the money of the condemned debtor to the petitioner, leaving only the things necessary for use. And let that be done immediately after the votes are cast, the herald announcing it and the judges hearing. Then if a second month is present from the delivered sentence, nor has the defeated paid the victor voluntarily and justly: let the judges who delivered the sentence hand over all the money of the debtor to the victor. But if the present things are less than sufficient, nor does less than one drachma fail, let it not thereafter be allowed to the debtor to drag any other into judgment before he restores the whole debt to the creditor. But he can be dragged by others. If anyone condemned in judgment has harmed the judges themselves or taken anything of theirs against their will, let those same judges refer it to the guardians of the laws. By whom if he is condemned of this crime, as if he had overturned the whole city and the laws, let him die. 

Those who, born and educated under these laws, have similarly begotten and educated children, having lived with others so that their commerce was moderate, have given penalties for injuries inflicted and exacted them for injuries received, just as they live justly by these laws until old age, so they depart from life according to nature. For the dead, both men and women, let the parental rites and those which pertain to the gods, whether infernal or celestial, be done according to the responses of the interpreters. 

Let no tomb be made in a fertile place and a field fit for cultivation. But let that place receive the bodies of the dead which is useless for other things and, being convenient for that only, least harms the living. For the fertility of Mother Earth is to be impeded neither by the living nor by the dead. Therefore, let no one, either living or dead, deprive any living person of food. Let a mound be no higher than that heap which five men can construct in five days. Also, let stones be built upon it no larger than can contain the praises of the dead person's life delivered in only four heroic verses. Let the lying-in-state be held within for no shorter or longer time than the truly dead can be known and recognized. And as human affairs go, a three-day lying-in-state until the tomb seems moderate. 

One must believe both the legislator and others about the soul, when he says it differs entirely from the body, and that there is nothing besides it which in this life makes each of us this very thing which we are. The body, however, follows the man like a certain imaginary thing. It is convenient also that bodies be called the "images" of the dead. And in truth, each of us—the soul itself—is immortal, and it goes away to other gods to give an account of its deeds, as the ancestral law contains. In which certainly good men are to trust and wicked men are to fear; since after death they lack all help. While living, however, all relatives ought to have brought help, so that they may live most justly and holily, lest the greatest punishments for crimes await them after death. 

Since these things are so, we ought by no means to waste the family estate, as if we thought this mass of flesh which is buried is that "self" of ours, when that son or brother or whoever else is missed by us, whom we think is being buried, has departed from here elsewhere, his fates being completed. It will indeed be well done if we use moderate expense as if for the altar of the spirits (manes) for one lacking a soul. But how much is moderate will be rightly established by the legislator. Let the law therefore be this: that he who is of the highest class should spend on the funeral and burial no more than five *minae*;

[[page number: 613]]

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation. Dialogue XII.

...he who is of the second, three; of the third, two; of the fourth, one: and thus the expense of each will be moderate. 

Furthermore, the guardians of the laws, along with many other things, ought to take care of this especially: that boys and men, and to speak summarily, people of whatever sex or age, being continually observed by them, live well. And at the end of each person's life, let one of them, whom the relatives of the dead man have chosen, observe the whole funeral and provide that all things are done well and moderately, not otherwise; and let that be an honor to him, and the opposite a disgrace. Let the expositions and processions and all other things be done according to the laws written about these. 

Regarding civil matters, let these be granted to the legislator. To decorate the dead with tears or not, it is shameful for the legislator to compel; but to wail and to cry out outside the house should be prohibited. Also, it is not allowed to carry out the corpse manifestly through the more frequent ways of the city, and to howl in public, or to afflict oneself outside the city before daybreak. Let these things remain thus instituted concerning them. He who obeys, let him be exempt from loss. But he who does not obey one guardian of the laws, let him be punished by all as it will commonly be seen. The rest which pertain either to the monuments of the dead or to those who on account of parricide and sacrilege are unworthy of burial, we have comprised in the previous laws. 

Therefore, the positioning of laws almost has its end. But the end of all is not in that they were made or possessed or inhabited, but rather in that, just as they were made rightly, so they are firmly established. For in such conservation, it is to be thought that as much as was necessary was done; otherwise, not at all. 

[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] You speak rightly, guest, but to what purpose is this? Tell it more clearly. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Many things, O Clinias, were excellently said by the ancients: and not least the names of the Fates. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Which ones? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] That Lachesis is the first, Clotho the second, and Atropos the third, who brings safety to the aforementioned. These are compared to things twisted by fire, possessing an inconvertible power. These things indeed in the city and Republic ought to bring not only a stable health to bodies, but also the cult of laws to souls, or rather the safety of laws. But it seems to me that to the business of laws this still lacks: that it be discerned in what way an inconvertible power can be in them according to nature. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] It is not a small thing that you say, if it is possible to find in what way that may be done rightly in each thing. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] It is indeed possible, as it seems to me at present. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Let us not therefore depart hence, I beseech you, before we attribute that to our laws. For it is ridiculous to have taken up labor in any matter in vain, and not to have founded something stable. 
[[abbrev: MEG. → Megillus]] You advise rightly: you will find me such as well. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Well said. What therefore is this safety? And by what reason will it be present to our Republic and laws? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Did we not say such an assembly is to be established in the city, in which ten of the older guardians of the laws always meet? To these let all those be added who have been honored with duties and prizes. Furthermore, those also who have traveled through many cities, so that they might find something conferring to the conservation of ancestral laws. But let these not be received into such an assembly unless they are proven to have returned from that travel incorrupt and whole, and to be worthy of the assembly. And let each of these associate with himself one younger man, born no fewer than thirty years, who by nature and education seems worthy to the one inviting him, and finally to the whole assembly. If any unworthy person is admitted, let the sentence be of no importance. This assembly, we said, ought to meet before light, when one is at leisure from other private as well as public business. Did we not say something like this in the previous parts? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Certainly. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] About this assembly I will say this again. I say indeed, if anyone casts this like an anchor of the whole city, containing in itself whatever things are required for this, it will preserve all things that we wish. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] In what way? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] We will say opportunely now, and we will apply ourselves with all our strength. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] You said it well, and do as you think. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] It is indeed necessary, O Clinias, to devise a fitting savior for individual works in each matter. What sort of place the soul and the head seem to have in animals. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] By what reason do you say that again? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Namely, their virtue provides safety to every animal. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] In what way, I say? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] For into the soul, indeed, mind is infused for other things; into the head also, sight and hearing are inserted for other things. And thus summarily, joined to the most beautiful senses of the mind and reduced into one, the safety of individuals is effected. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] So it seems. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Certainly. For also mind joined to the senses is accustomed to bring safety to ships in storm and tranquility. Do you not see that the pilot and sailors, joining sense together with the governing mind, protect themselves and the ship? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Why not? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] There is no need of many examples. But let us consider in an army and medicine: looking toward what goal and exit do generals and physicians most rightly follow safety? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Rightly. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Do they not look to the flight of the enemies and their own victory? And those to the health of the body? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Without doubt. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] If the physician is ignorant of the health of the body, or the general of victory, and the rest which we were saying, will they seem to have mind or know anything in these? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] In no way. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] What further in the city? If anyone seems to be ignorant of the end toward which a civil man ought to look back, can he first be called a prince by right? Then can he preserve that whose end he utterly ignores? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Not at all. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] It is necessary therefore now also, as it seems, if the construction of this new city is to have a good exit, that there be something in it which knows, first, what indeed is the civil end: then how we may follow it: and finally what law first, then which of men rightly consults toward that, or not rightly. Indeed, the city which will lack these will not be a wonder, since it is captured by mind and sense, if by chance and fortune it does individual things. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] You speak the truth. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Can we say in what part of our city especially, or by what study, some such protection for safety is sufficiently established? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Although I do not dare to assert it clearly, guest, I conjecture however that this speech of yours contends toward that nocturnal assembly which you just mentioned. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] You conjectured rightly, O Clinias. And it is necessary that it, as present reason signifies, be endowed with all virtue. But its first and principal virtue is that it not wander through many and various things: but always look back to one, toward which all things like arrows are always to be directed by it. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Thus indeed. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Now therefore we understand that it is not a wonder if the laws of cities wander far. For in any city, one positioning of laws looks to one thing, and another to another. And for some, the end of the just is that some—whether those better indeed or worse—rule in the republic. For others, that they grow rich, whether they serve or not. The study of others is turned to liberty. Others establish laws for two things: that they themselves be free, and that they subdue other cities. But those who think themselves most wise, to all such things at once. But one principal thing toward which they should direct the rest,

[[page number: 614]]

# Book Thirty-Four.

...they do not have. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] We therefore, guest, have rightly thought in our laws to look back toward one thing, and we allowed that to be called virtue. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] So it is. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] And we placed virtue as four certain things. [[notes: The four cardinal virtues: Courage, Temperance, Justice, and Prudence.]]
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Certainly. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] But mind the leader of all these, toward which also all other things, and those three of theirs, it would be necessary to look back. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] You follow most beautifully, O Clinias. And follow similarly in the rest. We were saying that the mind of the pilot, physician, and general looks back toward a certain thing. But we proceeded here to the mind of a civil man redarguing, and now like a man, let us ask this civil mind. O wonderful man, where are you tending? What is that one thing which the physician can clearly assign in his art, and you, who say you excel other prudent ones, will not be able to in your faculty? Can you, O Clinias and Megillus, respond for him what this thing itself is, as I have often done for you on behalf of others? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Not at all, guest. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Do you not think it is to be sought, what that is, and in what things? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Speak clearly. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Since we have placed four species of virtue, it is evident that each of them is one, if four together complete it. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Why not? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] We also name all these one. For we say fortitude is virtue, prudence virtue, and the other two similarly, as if in truth they were not many, but that one thing alone, which is virtue. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Entirely indeed. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Insofar as these two differ among themselves and received two names, and the other two similarly, it is not difficult to say. But insofar as we placed one in both, and called it virtue, and similarly in the remaining two, it is not so easy. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] How do you say that? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] What I say is not hard to explain. Come then, let us divide the duty of asking and responding among us. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] In what way? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] You ask me what indeed we called one, naming it virtue, and then said there were two again, one fortitude, but the other prudence. I assert the cause to you, that one was occupied about fears. Whence beasts also are partakers of fortitude, and the souls of infants. For the soul is made brave in a way by nature and without reason; but without reason, a soul prudent and composed of mind neither was ever, nor is, nor will be. Therefore, this is something other than that. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] You speak the truth. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] How therefore these two and their difference are by reason, you received from me. But how indeed they are one and the same, you in turn should teach me, so that you think you will say in what way since they are four, they are again one, and I afterwards to you again how they are four, to be declared. Next, however, let us consider whether he who is to understand some things sufficiently, which have both a name and a reason, ought to know the name only, but not the reason. Or rather if it is of some price, it is shameful to ignore both the names and the reasons of things excelling in magnitude and beauty. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] So it seems. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] But for the founder and guardian of laws, and for him who thinks himself to excel others in virtue, and received rewards for these things, is there anything greater than fortitude, temperance, justice, and prudence? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] How could it be anything else? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Regarding these therefore, the interpreters, teachers, founders of laws, and guardians of others, ought they not to teach others who desire to know, or are in need of punishment and rebuke, what powers virtue has, what powers vice has, and excel others in declaring these? Or will some poet or master of youth recently entered into the city be judged more excellent than he who professes that he excels in all virtue? and then will it seem a wonder if that city where the guardians do not hold the name and reason of virtue, like a city deserted by its guardian, suffers the same things which also many other cities suffer today? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Nothing indeed is a wonder. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Let us therefore apply ourselves to this. How therefore shall we render the guardians more exquisite than others in virtue, both in deed and word? Or by what reason will our city become similar to the head and senses of the prudent on account of such a guardianship? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] In what way, O wonderful man, shall we make this similarity? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] It is evident because the city will be a certain capacity of the head, but the younger guardians, sagacious and skillful, will be placed in the supreme summit. Whence they will look around the whole city, and by guarding what they perceive, they will commend it to memory, and announce all things to the elders, who, very similar to the mind on account of the cognition of many things, will consult for the city using the ministry of the youths. And thus both together will commonly preserve the whole city. Do we think they are to be prepared thus or otherwise? Or do we think all are to be had as equal? nor do we wish some to be educated and learned by a more exquisite reason, and those to be preferred to the rest? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] But that indeed, O wonderful man, is impossible. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Let us therefore come to the exquisite discipline, how superior it may be. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Thus indeed. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] But that which we just touched upon is perhaps this very thing which we seek. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Entirely. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] But we were saying that the principal worker and guardian in individual things ought not only to be able to discern many things, but also to tend toward one, and know it, and when he has known it, direct all things toward that whither he looks. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Rightly. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Is there therefore another more exquisite consideration of things than that you can look to one Idea from many dissimilar and different things? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Perhaps. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Do not say "Perhaps," but in truth, O blessed man, no one will ever have a surer way and reason than this. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Persuaded by your reasons, guest, I concede; wherefore let us proceed thus. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] The guardians of the divine Republic are to be compelled by us, therefore, to inspect exactly, first what is the same in all four, which since it is in fortitude, temperance, justice, and prudence, we rightly wish to call by the one name of virtue. This, O friends, if you wish, let us now especially hold: nor let us dismiss it before it is sufficiently evident what that is, to which—whether as if to one, or as if to a whole, or to both, or in whatever way it holds itself—one must look back. Or do we think if this escapes us, it is sufficiently evident to us what pertains to virtue, about which we can explain neither if many, nor if four, nor if one. Either therefore if you believe our counsel, we will strive to find the mode in which that will be present to us in the city, or if it will be seen, we will dismiss it. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] By no means, by the hospitable god, O guest, is this to be dismissed. For you seem to say that most rightly. But by what way will someone find this? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Not yet let us say how it is to be done: but first let us agree among ourselves, whether it is necessary or not. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] It is necessary certainly, if it is possible. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] What further of the honorable and good? whether only that they are many, our guardians will know? or also how they are one will they know? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] It seems necessary that they also understand how they are one. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] What then? Ought they only to understand, but not be able to declare by speech what they understand? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] By what way would that be?
