# On the Laws, or, On Legislation. Dialogue XII.

...for it would be a state of stupidity. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Is the same reason also for all things worthy of study, that it is necessary for those who are to be true guardians to understand the truth of the laws best, and to set it forth sufficiently by speech, and to follow it in works, judging according to nature what is done rightly and what is not? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Why not? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Is not one of the best things that about which we seriously disputed above? Where we demonstrated that there are gods, and that they have the greatest powers: and that this is to be known by a man as far as possible: so that we forgive many if they only follow the sentence of the laws: but we commit the guardianship to no one who has not by much labor and firm faith followed whatever things pertain to the gods: so that we choose no one ever as a guardian of the laws or prefer him to others in virtue, unless he is divine, and has given effort to divine studies. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] It is equal therefore, as you say, if someone is slow and inept in divine matters, that he be driven far from the most beautiful things. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Do we know therefore that there are two things which make those things which were set forth above about the gods to be believed? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Which ones? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] One indeed is that mentioned above about the soul, that it is the oldest and most divine of all things, whose motion, having obtained generation, produced substance always flowing. The other is about order: by which the stars and other things are carried which the intellect leading, adorned all things. For no one who has diligently considered and perceived these things was ever so impious that he was not affected in the opposite way than many suspect. For most people think that those who treat these things, given to astronomy and other arts necessary for these, are alienated from religion. Indeed, since they have inspected as far as possible the necessity by which things are done, they think those do not believe all things are born by divine will for the sake of good. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] How therefore does that hold itself? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] It holds itself entirely the opposite now, and when these things were thought to be without a soul. Although also then whoever searched those things with other diligences, touched the truth wonderfully: namely that they would never use so exquisite a reason if they lacked a soul, things expert of mind; some dared to affirm that the celestial mind adorned all things. But those same ones, not knowing the nature of the soul to be older than bodies, overturned all things again, so to speak, or rather themselves, since they thought it younger. For those things which are before the eyes, they believed these were also in heaven. Therefore, believing the celestial things were filled with earth, stones, and other inanimate bodies, they gave the causes of the whole world to these. By these things therefore it happened that the philosophers who treat these things were commonly thought impious, and were compared by poets to dogs barking in vain, and other things full of folly were said against them. Now however, as we said, the matter holds itself entirely the opposite. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] In what way? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Never will any mortal be able to worship God firmly, who has not first received these two things. First, that of all things which are partakers of generation, the oldest is the soul, and also immortal: and since it is such, it dominates all. Then what we said more often, he should not be ignorant that there is true mind in the stars, and the disciplines which precede these do not escape him. Also not ignorant of many things convenient to these, let him use them for composing habits and preserving laws: and let him be able to render the reason of those things which have a reason. But he who will not have possessed these in addition to public virtues, he will almost never be a sufficient prince of the whole city: but a minister of others. It is to be considered indeed now, O Clinias and Megillus, whether we ought to place this as a summit and guardian to the predicted laws, that for the sake of safety the nocturnal assembly of princes be present, endowed with the discipline which we predicted. What therefore shall we do? 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] What prohibits, most excellent man, that we place it, as much as we can? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Certainly we all ought to contend for that. I indeed will gladly assist you. Perhaps also on account of the skill in these things and frequent meditation, I will find many other helpers. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] By this way, O guest, let us most especially proceed, where God himself seems to lead. But let us now devise the mode in which this may be done rightly. 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] Laws about these, O Clinias and Megillus, cannot be written before the whole city has been adorned. For then they will seem to be established with due authority. But these will be proven no otherwise rightly than many doctrines and by a long examination of disputation. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] What does this again mean for itself? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] First therefore let the assembly of those men who are suitable for guardianship by age, doctrine, habits, and custom, be established. Then what things are to be learned, those are neither easy to find, nor the disciple of the invention easy to become. The times furthermore in which it is necessary to perceive individual things will be written in vain. For those who learn cannot know when anything may be learned opportunely: before the science of the thing itself is in their soul. Therefore those things which cannot be said openly in these are not rightly attempted: I say they cannot be said, indeed: since if they are said, they explain nothing more clearly. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] Since these things hold themselves thus, guest, what do you think we should do? 
[[abbrev: ATH. → Athenian]] What is said by the proverb, O friends: it seemed to us equal that we confer the matter into the common and public, and be willing to undergo the risk about the whole Republic: and do nothing not to do, that we may throw three sixes, or three dice. [[notes: A metaphor for taking a decisive gamble or high-stakes action.]] I indeed will undergo that risk with you, by saying and setting forth what will seem to me about this discipline and education which we just touched upon: the risk however is not small, nor similar to others. Which I command to be your care now, O Clinias. For you will flourish with the highest glory in the Magnesian city, or that to which God will make the same name, if you establish it rightly. Certainly you will never escape but that you appear the strongest of all posterity. If therefore this divine assembly will be established for us, O friends, the city is to be handed over to it. Nor will the remaining legislators oppose these as if less sufficient. Indeed what we touched upon a little before in words as if dreaming, when we brought through a certain image the communion of the head and the mind, that we will almost perform waking, if these men exquisitely taught have met us, and have inhabited in the citadel of the region as guardians of the city established, such as we never in past life have known to have been for carrying out guardianship. 
[[abbrev: MEG. → Megillus]] From all things which we said, O friend Clinias, it is evident, either such a constitution of the city is to be passed over, or this guest is not to be dismissed, but by prayers and all modes he is to be accepted as a companion for arranging the city. 
[[abbrev: CLE. → Clinias]] You speak rightly, O Megillus. I indeed will so entirely effect it, but you also bring help. 
[[abbrev: MEG. → Megillus]] I indeed will bring it.

[[summary: This text is Marsilio Ficino’s introduction and summary translation of Book 12 of Plato's Laws. It emphasizes the "Nocturnal Council" as the ultimate anchor of the state, requiring its members to possess both civil virtue and a deep metaphysical understanding of the Soul and the Divine Mind to ensure the laws remain stable and directed toward the Highest Good.]]

->Philebus, or, Concerning the Supreme Good. 63<-

should be so hard and vehement as to contend that these things are not so, but are carried along without order?

PROTARCHUS. Why would I not wish it?

SOCRATES. Come then, contemplate the discussion that follows for us concerning this matter.

PROTARCHUS. Just speak.

SOCRATES. We see that in the composition of the bodies of living things, **fire, water, air, and earth** are present, but like those who are "tossing about," as they say.

<margin>The utility of the elements in us.</margin>

PROTARCHUS. And very much so: for in these speeches we truly "toss about" because of ambiguity.

SOCRATES. Therefore, regarding each of those things which are around us, accept this.

PROTARCHUS. What?

SOCRATES. That each of these in us is small and base, and in no way pure and whole, nor carrying a power worthy of its nature: and observing this in one, judge the same concerning all the rest. For instance, **fire** exists in us, and it also exists in the universe.

PROTARCHUS. It does.

SOCRATES. Is not this fire of ours small, weak, and base, but that which is in the universe is marvelous in quantity and beauty, and in every power that belongs to fire?

PROTARCHUS. You speak too truly.

SOCRATES. But is it otherwise—is the fire of the whole world led from our fire, or on the contrary, is mine and yours and that of all other living things led from it?

PROTARCHUS. These things are not worthy of a response.

SOCRATES. Correct. You would say the same about the earth of animals and of the world, I think, and similarly you respond concerning all other things which we sought a little while ago?

PROTARCHUS. Who, in responding otherwise, would be esteemed of sound mind?

SOCRATES. No one, perhaps. But now to the rest. Looking at all these things just mentioned, composed into one, we call it a **body**.

PROTARCHUS. Why not?

SOCRATES. Take the same also concerning this which we call the **world** [cosmos]. For by the same reasoning, it is a body, composed of the same things.

PROTARCHUS. You speak most rightly.

SOCRATES. Is our body nourished entirely from this [cosmic] body, or on the contrary, is it [the world] nourished from ours, and does it receive and have whatever we mentioned just before?

PROTARCHUS. This other thing also, O Socrates, is not worthy of a response.

SOCRATES. But the other? Is it worthy, or not?

PROTARCHUS. Say, which?

SOCRATES. Shall we confess that our body has a **soul**?

PROTARCHUS. It is clear.

SOCRATES. From where, O friend Protarchus, did it receive it, unless the body of the universe—which contains the same things as ours and even more excellent things—has a soul?

PROTARCHUS. It is clear. From nowhere else.

SOCRATES. For it must not be thought, O Protarchus, that those four things—the limit, the infinite, the mixture, and the **genus of cause** existing as the fourth among them all—which provides the soul and body to the things in us, while it imprints a shadow, and prepares remedies for a failing body, and establishes and restores different things in different places, is called all the wisdom of every kind; and yet, while these same things are in the whole heaven and its larger parts, which are purer and more excellent, the nature of the most noble and precious things is not to be found in them?

PROTARCHUS. That would truly have no reason.

SOCRATES. Therefore, following that reason further, we would better say, as we have often said, that the **infinite** exists throughout this universe, and a sufficient **limit** and a **cause**—by no means ignoble—is always present, adorning and disposing the hours, months, and years, and is deservedly called **mind and wisdom**.

PROTARCHUS. Deservedly.

SOCRATES. But wisdom and mind are never without a soul.

PROTARCHUS. Never indeed.

SOCRATES. Therefore, you will confess that in the nature of **Jupiter** [Zeus] himself, there is a **royal soul** and a **royal mind** because of the power of the cause, and in other things likewise other beautiful things, as it pleases each of them to be called.

PROTARCHUS. Most certainly.

SOCRATES. Do not think, O Protarchus, that the preceding speech was introduced at random: for it aids the opinion of those who long ago showed that mind presides in every way.

PROTARCHUS. Truly.

SOCRATES. And it provides an answer to my petition: that **mind is a certain offspring of that cause** which is called the cause of all things, and which is one thing from these four that have been related. You have, then, our exposition.

PROTARCHUS. I have it, and sufficiently indeed. Although when you responded before, I did not understand.

SOCRATES. A certain relaxation of study, O Protarchus, is often a **jest**.

<margin>A jest is often a relaxation of study.</margin>

PROTARCHUS. You speak excellently.

SOCRATES. Now therefore, O friend, it has been shown well enough in what genus [mind] is, and what power it has.

PROTARCHUS. Entirely.

SOCRATES. Furthermore, the genus of **pleasure** was made clear long ago.

PROTARCHUS. Certainly.

SOCRATES. Let us now remember this about both: that the **mind was recognized as related to the cause**, and of almost the same genus with it; but **pleasure is infinite**, and of that genus which contains in itself, by its very nature, neither beginning, nor middle, nor end, nor will it ever contain them.

PROTARCHUS. Why should we not remember?

SOCRATES. It is necessary therefore to observe hereafter in which of these two each consists, and because of what passion it happens whenever it happens. And as we first investigated the genus of pleasure itself, so we will now inquire first into these things concerning it. Nevertheless, we cannot sufficiently examine pleasure apart from **pain**.

PROTARCHUS. If we must walk this way, let us indeed walk this way.

SOCRATES. Does the same thing seem to you as to me concerning their generation?

PROTARCHUS. What is that?

SOCRATES. **Pain and pleasure** seem to be according to nature in the same common genus.

PROTARCHUS. This common genus, friend Socrates, brings back to our memory what you wish to be understood from those things which were distinguished above.

SOCRATES. I will do so to the best of my ability, O wonderful man.

PROTARCHUS. You say well.

SOCRATES. Let us understand the **common**, therefore, as that which we numbered as the **third** of the four.

PROTARCHUS. Do you mean what you placed after the infinite and the finite, in which you placed health and harmony, as I think?

SOCRATES. You say correctly, but now apply your mind most especially.

PROTARCHUS. Speak then.

SOCRATES. I say that when **harmony is dissolved** in living things, at that time a dissolution of nature and a generation of **pains** occur.

PROTARCHUS. It is consistent.

SOCRATES. Conversely, when **harmony is recomposed**, and immediately restored into its own nature, it must be said that **pleasure** occurs, if indeed the greatest things are to be concluded in a few words.

PROTARCHUS. I think indeed you speak rightly, O Socrates; nevertheless, we must strive to express the same things more clearly.

SOCRATES. Are not common and well-known things easy to know?

PROTARCHUS. Which are those?

SOCRATES. **Hunger** indeed is a dissolution and a distress.

PROTARCHUS. It is.

SOCRATES. But **eating** is a replenishment and a pleasure.

PROTARCHUS. So it is.

SOCRATES. **Thirst** again is a corruption, a dissolution, and a pain. But the power of moisture, refilling what was dried up, is pleasure. Furthermore, a separation and dissolution beyond nature, caused by a certain heat, is distress. But a restoration and cooling according to nature is pleasure.

PROTARCHUS. Exactly.

SOCRATES. Also the **congealing** of moisture against the nature of the animal, caused by cold, is pain. Conversely, when the moisture is liquefied and returns into its own nature, that return is pleasure. And consider summarily whether this speech seems tolerable to you: Whenever the animated species, generated from the infinite and the limit according to nature (as we said in the previous sections), is **corrupted**, such corruption is **pain**. But when these flow back into their own essence, we call this return **pleasure**.

PROTARCHUS. Let it be so. For this seems very likely to me.

SOCRATES. Let us therefore place this as one species of pleasure and pain in both these passions.

<summary>Socrates compares the individual body to the cosmic body, arguing that just as we have a soul, the universe must have a "royal soul" and mind (Jupiter). He defines pain as the dissolution of natural harmony (like hunger) and pleasure as its restoration (like eating).</summary>

PROTARCHUS. Let it be placed.

SOCRATES. Place next the **expectation** of these passions in the soul. I mean the expectation which precedes the pleasurable, being hopeful, rejoicing, and secure; but that which precedes the painful, being fearful and mournful.

PROTARCHUS. This is therefore another species of pleasure and pain, separate from the body, proceeding from the expectation of the soul alone.

SOCRATES. You have understood correctly. In these, as my opinion goes—both existing as pure and not mixed—it will be seen concerning pleasure and pain; we will clearly discern whether the whole genus of pleasure is to be loved, or whether this is rather to be attributed to some other of the previously mentioned things: but to pleasure and pain, just as to hot and cold and other such things, it belongs that they are sometimes to be loved, and at other times not to be loved; as things which are in no way "goods," but which, sometimes receiving a certain quality, follow the nature of the good.

PROTARCHUS. You speak rightly; one who examines such things must proceed so.

SOCRATES. First, therefore, let us look at this: if it is true what was said, that when those [harmonies] are destroyed, pain follows, and when they are safe, pleasure follows: when they are neither perishing nor being preserved, what disposition should we then attribute most especially to each animal? Answer me with an intent mind, whether it seems necessary to you that any animal at that time should in no way be either delighted or distressed.

PROTARCHUS. Necessary indeed.

SOCRATES. There is therefore this **third state** besides the affect of the mourning and the rejoicing person.

PROTARCHUS. There is indeed.

SOCRATES. Come then, try to remember this: for it is of no small importance for judging pleasure to remember it, yet if you wish, let us touch upon something brief about it.

PROTARCHUS. Speak then, what is it?

SOCRATES. Nothing prevents the one who chooses the **life of contemplation** from living so.

PROTARCHUS. Do you mean apart from joy and distress?

SOCRATES. For it was said in the comparison of each life that the man dedicated to contemplation does not in any part either rejoice or be distressed.

PROTARCHUS. So it was entirely said.

SOCRATES. Is it not fitting for him so? And perhaps it would be no wonder if this life is the most divine of all the rest.

<margin>The contemplative life is the most divine. The gods neither rejoice nor are saddened.</margin>

PROTARCHUS. Is it absurd that the gods rejoice or, on the contrary, are saddened?

SOCRATES. Altogether absurd. For both are indecent. Let us investigate this next, if it contributes anything to this discussion: and let us accommodate it to the mind for the second prize of victory, even if we cannot for the first.

PROTARCHUS. You speak rightly.

SOCRATES. But indeed, the other species of pleasures, which we assigned as proper to the soul, consists entirely of **memory**.

PROTARCHUS. In what way?

SOCRATES. First, it seems we must understand what **memory** is; and even perhaps what **sensation** is, if we wish these things to be more clearly elucidated.

PROTARCHUS. In what way do you mean?

SOCRATES. Suppose that from all the passions of the body, some are extinguished in the body before they flow through into the soul, leaving it void of passion: others are diffused through both and bring about a certain confusion, as much proper as common to both equally.

PROTARCHUS. Let them be supposed.

SOCRATES. If we say that the passions which are not propagated through both remain **hidden** [unperceived], and those flowing through both become **known to the soul**, shall we say rightly?

PROTARCHUS. Certainly.

SOCRATES. Therefore, in no way think that this "being hidden" is the generation of **forgetfulness**. For forgetfulness is the exit of memory. But in those things that were just said, it [memory] was not yet present. It is absurd that a loss should be made of that which neither is nor was.

PROTARCHUS. Absurd.

SOCRATES. Only change the names, then.

PROTARCHUS. How?

SOCRATES. Instead of saying that the soul is "hidden" when it exists without the passion of the bodily tumult, call it **insensibility** or **void of sensation**, which you now seem to call forgetfulness.

PROTARCHUS. I grasp it.

SOCRATES. But if you call the movement made in the common passion of the body and the soul **sensation**, you will not name it out of place.

PROTARCHUS. You speak the truth.

SOCRATES. Do we not perceive now what we wish to call sensation?

PROTARCHUS. We perceive it.

SOCRATES. Furthermore, one will rightly call the preservation of sensation **memory**, in my opinion.

<margin>Memory.</margin>

PROTARCHUS. Too rightly.

SOCRATES. And we admit that **reminiscence** differs from memory, or not?

PROTARCHUS. Perhaps.

SOCRATES. Is it not especially in this?

PROTARCHUS. In what?

SOCRATES. Whenever the soul resumes in itself, without the body, those same things which it once suffered together with the body, then we assert that it **remembers**, do we not?

PROTARCHUS. Very much so.

SOCRATES. Furthermore, when having suffered the loss of a memory, it then recalls it again in itself, either by sensation or by the teaching of a discipline, it is thought to **reminisce**. And all these we call memories and reminiscences.

PROTARCHUS. You speak well.

SOCRATES. But the reason for which all these things have been said is this.

PROTARCHUS. What?

SOCRATES. That we may grasp the pleasure of the soul without the body as greatly and clearly as possible, and along with it **desire**; for through these two both of those things seem to be declared.

<margin>Passion belongs to the body, but not desire.</margin>

PROTARCHUS. Let us proceed now to the rest, Socrates.

SOCRATES. It is fitting to consider many things, as it seems, investigating the origin and every form of pleasure. And now indeed we must first see what it is, and where **desire** is born.

PROTARCHUS. Let us see now, I beseech you. For we will lose nothing.

SOCRATES. Rather, O Protarchus, when we have found what we were just seeking, we will lose something concerning these matters—namely, **doubt**.

PROTARCHUS. How beautifully you turned that back! But let us now expedite what follows.

SOCRATES. Did we not say that **hunger and thirst** and many such things are certain desires?

PROTARCHUS. Very much so.

SOCRATES. Looking back at what same thing do we call such diverse things by one name?

PROTARCHUS. By Jupiter, it is not easy to say, O Socrates. Yet it must be said.

SOCRATES. Let us begin again from the same things.

PROTARCHUS. Which?

SOCRATES. Do we say someone **thirsts**?

<margin>To thirst is not of the body, but to be dried out.</margin>

PROTARCHUS. We do.

SOCRATES. And this is to be empty?

PROTARCHUS. Why not?

SOCRATES. And thirst is a desire?

PROTARCHUS. It is.

SOCRATES. Of a drink?

PROTARCHUS. Of a drink.

SOCRATES. Is it not of the replenishment of the drink?

PROTARCHUS. Of this, certainly.

SOCRATES. He who is empty, therefore, and exhausted, desires the opposites of those things which he suffers. For when he is empty, he desires to be filled.

PROTARCHUS. It is manifest.

SOCRATES. What then? Can he who is first empty attain its replenishment either by sensation or by some memory of what he has suffered neither in the present nor ever in a past time?

PROTARCHUS. In no way.

SOCRATES. But we confess that he who desires, desires something.

PROTARCHUS. Why not?

SOCRATES. He does not, therefore, desire what he suffers. For he thirsts, and thirst is an emptiness, but he affects replenishment.

PROTARCHUS. So it is.

SOCRATES. Something, therefore, of that which he desires will attain to the fulfillment.

PROTARCHUS. Necessarily.

SOCRATES. The body certainly cannot; for it is exhausted.

PROTARCHUS. Certainly.

SOCRATES. It remains that the soul follows the fulfillment through **memory**.

PROTARCHUS. It is evident.

SOCRATES. For by what else would it follow?

PROTARCHUS. Almost nothing.

SOCRATES. Do we note what is produced for us from these reasons?

PROTARCHUS. What?

SOCRATES. This reasoning does not dictate that desire belongs to the body.

PROTARCHUS. In what way?

SOCRATES. Because in every animal, desire shows an effort contrary to the passions of the living thing.

PROTARCHUS. Deeply so.

SOCRATES. But the impulse drawing toward the contrary of what it suffers, through the

memory, indicates a memory contrary to the passions.

<summary>Socrates distinguishes between the body’s "insensibility" and the soul’s "sensation." He argues that desire (like thirst) must belong to the soul rather than the body, because the body only feels its current state (emptiness), whereas the soul "remembers" and seeks the opposite state (replenishment).</summary>
<keywords>Expectation, Third State, Contemplative Life, Gods, Memory, Reminiscence, Sensation, Desire, Soul and Body</keywords>

indicates a memory contrary to the passions.

PROTARCHUS. Entirely.

SOCRATES. Therefore, the reasoning showing that memory leads every impulse and desire of the soul toward the things desired, attributes the principality of every living thing to the soul.

PROTARCHUS. Too rightly.

SOCRATES. This reasoning, therefore, in no way admits that our body thirsts or hungers, or suffers anything of that kind.

PROTARCHUS. You speak the truth.

SOCRATES. Furthermore, we will consider this about these things: that this reasoning seems to wish to demonstrate a certain species of life in them.

PROTARCHUS. In what things? And of what life do you speak?

SOCRATES. I mean in **replenishing and emptying**, and in all things that pertain to the health or destruction of animals. And if anyone of us, being constituted in either one, is affected by pain, then he rejoices according to the changes.

PROTARCHUS. It is so.

SOCRATES. What, whenever he remains in the middle of these?

PROTARCHUS. How in the middle?

SOCRATES. While he is indeed saddened by the affliction, but in the meantime remembers past pleasures: the sadness indeed ceases, yet he is not yet filled: what is to be said then? Is he not in the middle of passions?

PROTARCHUS. It must be said.

SOCRATES. Whether as one grieving altogether, or on the contrary, as one rejoicing?

PROTARCHUS. Not rejoicing, by Jupiter, but rather affected by a **double sadness**: according to the body in passion, and according to the soul in the ardor of expectation.

SOCRATES. In what way, Protarchus, were you saying the pain was double? Does not someone who is empty sometimes hope for a certain replenishment, and at other times, on the contrary, despair of it?

PROTARCHUS. Very much so.

SOCRATES. Does he not, while he hopes to attain it, seem to rejoice by that very recollection? And at the same time, being empty, he is tortured at that time?

PROTARCHUS. Necessarily.

SOCRATES. Then, therefore, both man and the rest of animals rejoice and mourn at the same time.

PROTARCHUS. It appears so.

SOCRATES. But when someone who is empty altogether despairs of fulfillment, does not a **double passion** then arise concerning pains, which you yourself, having seen it a little before, thought was simply double?

PROTARCHUS. These things are true.

SOCRATES. Let us use this consideration of such passions for this purpose.

PROTARCHUS. For what purpose do you say?

SOCRATES. Whether we ought to call these pleasures and distresses **true or false**, or some true and others false?

PROTARCHUS. In what way, O Socrates, can pleasures or distresses be false?

SOCRATES. How also, O Protarchus, can fears be true or false? Or expectations true, or least true? Or opinions true or false?

PROTARCHUS. Opinions indeed I would confess: but these others, least of all.

SOCRATES. What do you say? We seem to be beginning a not-brief discussion.

PROTARCHUS. You tell the truth.

SOCRATES. But if it is consistent with the preceding things, O son of that man, it must be considered.

PROTARCHUS. That perhaps.

SOCRATES. Everything superfluous, therefore, and whatever is said beyond what is fitting, must be omitted.

PROTARCHUS. Rightly.

SOCRATES. Speak then. Indeed, a continual wonder always holds me concerning the questions which we have now introduced.

PROTARCHUS. In what way, do you mean?

SOCRATES. Are there not some **false pleasures** from the number of pleasures, and others true?

PROTARCHUS. Why not?

SOCRATES. Therefore, in truth or in falsehood, will anyone be said to rejoice when he does not rejoice, or to be saddened when he is not saddened—whether he be a madman or an insane person?

PROTARCHUS. We all suspect that all these things hold themselves so, O Socrates.

SOCRATES. But rightly? Or perhaps it must be considered whether these things are said rightly or not?

PROTARCHUS. It must be considered indeed, in my opinion.

SOCRATES. Let us therefore distinguish more evidently what was just said about pleasure and opinion. Is there anything among men, **to opine**?

PROTARCHUS. There is.

SOCRATES. And **to rejoice**?

PROTARCHUS. And to rejoice.

SOCRATES. Because even that which we opine is something?

PROTARCHUS. Why not?

SOCRATES. And this by which we rejoice?

PROTARCHUS. And this.

SOCRATES. He who opines, whether he opines rightly or not rightly, nevertheless does not lose the fact that he is truly opining.

PROTARCHUS. For how could he?

SOCRATES. Also he who rejoices, whether he rejoices rightly or not, nevertheless does not lose the fact that he is truly rejoicing.

PROTARCHUS. Nay, and these things hold themselves so.

SOCRATES. In what way, therefore, does **opinion become true and false**, but pleasure only true, even though both have similarly accepted to opine truly and to rejoice?

PROTARCHUS. This must be considered.

SOCRATES. Is it from the fact that truth and falsehood are added to opinion? And not only because of these has it become an opinion, but what kind of opinion is each? Is this what you say must be considered?

PROTARCHUS. Yes.

SOCRATES. Furthermore, it must be investigated whether pleasure and pain remain only those things that they are, and never become a certain kind of thing.

PROTARCHUS. It is evident.

SOCRATES. But it is by no means difficult to see that they do become a certain kind. Long ago we admitted that pleasures and distresses become large and small, vehement and mild.

PROTARCHUS. We admitted it.

SOCRATES. But if **wickedness** is added to any of these, we will confess that just as a wicked opinion is made, so also a **wicked pleasure** is made.

PROTARCHUS. What prevents it?

SOCRATES. What if **rectitude** [correctness] or the contrary to rectitude is moved toward any of these, shall we not similarly call the opinion "right" which has undergone rectitude, and similarly pleasure?

PROTARCHUS. It necessarily follows.

SOCRATES. Even if that which is comprehended by opinion is fallacious, shall we not call the opinion **false** rather than right?

PROTARCHUS. Indeed.

SOCRATES. Likewise, if we discern that pleasure or pain errs about that in which we rejoice or are distressed, shall we call it a right or good pleasure, or honor it with some noble name?

PROTARCHUS. But that cannot happen, if indeed pleasure itself should fail.

SOCRATES. Nevertheless, often pleasure arises for us not from a true but from a **false opinion**.

PROTARCHUS. Without a doubt. However, O Socrates, we call such an opinion false, but no one would ever name the pleasure itself false.

SOCRATES. You defend the reason of pleasure too promptly at present, O Protarchus.

PROTARCHUS. Not at all, but I speak what I hear.

SOCRATES. Does pleasure proceeding from a right opinion and science differ nothing for us, O friend, from that which follows a false opinion and ignorance?

PROTARCHUS. It is consistent that they differ by no small interval.

SOCRATES. But let us come to scrutinizing this very distance.

PROTARCHUS. Lead on, then, where it pleases you.

SOCRATES. Behold, I lead you this way.

PROTARCHUS. Which way?

SOCRATES. Opinion, we say, is partly true and partly false.

PROTARCHUS. Let it be so.

SOCRATES. Often (as we were saying) pleasure and pain follow these—I mean, true and false opinion.

PROTARCHUS. They follow.

SOCRATES. Does not opinion arise in us from **sensation and memory**, and the very power to opine?

PROTARCHUS. Especially.

SOCRATES. Must it not be thought that we hold ourselves thus concerning these things?

PROTARCHUS. How?

SOCRATES. As you might admit that a man sometimes clearly discerning from afar some confused things, desires to discern more clearly the things he sees?

PROTARCHUS. I admit it indeed.

SOCRATES. He will therefore question himself in a way.

PROTARCHUS. In what way do you mean?

SOCRATES. "What is that which appears from afar next to a rock under a tree?" Does he not seem to you to say these things to himself, while he looks at such things as have sometimes appeared to him?

PROTARCHUS. Why not?

SOCRATES. Then, as if responding to himself, he says, "It is a man," speaking to himself as if having now affected the thing.

PROTARCHUS. Certainly.

SOCRATES. Again, perhaps having progressed, [he says] it is a certain **statue**...

<summary>Socrates argues that while the act of feeling pleasure is always "real," the pleasure itself can be "false" if it is based on a false opinion. He uses the analogy of a man misidentifying an object in the distance to show how our internal "writer" or "painter" can create false mental images that lead to false joys.</summary>
<keywords>Double Sadness, True and False Pleasures, False Opinion, Madman, Insanity, Sensation, Socratic Analogy, Statue vs. Man</keywords>

SOCRATES: If someone were present here, pouring out into speech the same things he was turning over in his mind, he would say to those present what we previously called an "opinion." PROTARCHUS: That is manifest. SOCRATES: But if he is alone, he proceeds by considering this same thing with himself, and sometimes keeping it within himself for a long time. PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: What then? Do you feel the same way here as I do? <margin>The soul is like a book and a blank slate.</margin> PROTARCHUS: What is that? SOCRATES: It seems to me then that a man's soul is very similar to a certain book. <note>original: "Anima libro & tabulæ rasæ similis" — This is a classic philosophical metaphor where the mind begins as a blank slate or "tabula rasa" upon which experience writes.</note> PROTARCHUS: In what way? SOCRATES: Memory, coinciding with the senses, and those things which concern these experiences, seem to me to somehow write certain words in the soul. And when they write true things, we call the resulting experience a true opinion, and true speeches in us proceed from this very act. But when this scribe of ours writes false things, the opposite of the truth occurs. PROTARCHUS: It seems entirely so to me, and I gladly accept what has been said. SOCRATES: Accept also, they say, the craftsman of those things which then occur in our souls. PROTARCHUS: Whom? SOCRATES: The Painter, who following the scribe, paints images of the things said in the soul. PROTARCHUS: How and when should we say he does this? SOCRATES: When someone, drawing out the things said and perceived by opinion from sight or another sense, somehow contemplates in himself the images of the things said and perceived by opinion. Does this not happen in us? PROTARCHUS: Very much so. SOCRATES: Are not the images of true opinions and speeches true, but the images of false ones false? PROTARCHUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: If we have said these things correctly, let us consider this further. PROTARCHUS: What is it? SOCRATES: Is it necessary that this happens to us concerning the present and the past, but not at all concerning the future? PROTARCHUS: By the same logic, it concerns all times. <margin>Pleasure and sadness, which belong to the soul, precede the pleasures and pains of the body.</margin> SOCRATES: Was it not said earlier that the pleasures and pains proper to the soul itself precede the pleasures and pains of the body? And because of this, it happens that we "pre-rejoice" and "pre-grieve" over things to come? PROTARCHUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Do the letters and pictures which we just now imagined being imprinted on us look to the present and the past, and not at all to the future? PROTARCHUS: To all of them. SOCRATES: Do you agree then that all these things are certain hopes for the future, and that we are nourished throughout our whole lives by perpetual hope? PROTARCHUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: Come, answer this in addition to those things. PROTARCHUS: What do you ask? SOCRATES: The just, pious, and good man—is he not a friend of God? PROTARCHUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Is the unjust and wicked man not the opposite? PROTARCHUS: The opposite. SOCRATES: Yet, as we were saying, everyone is led by many hopes. PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: There are speeches in each of us which we have named "hopes." PROTARCHUS: They are present. SOCRATES: And also painted fantasies. For anyone may imagine themselves possessing a vast pile of gold and, abounding in various delights, being drenched in every sweetness. PROTARCHUS: Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES: Must we not say that these internal writings often turn out true for good men because they are friends of God, but often the opposite for the wicked? PROTARCHUS: We must certainly say so. SOCRATES: And for wicked men, pleasures are nonetheless often present that are fabricated and, ultimately, false. PROTARCHUS: Why should they not be? SOCRATES: Therefore, the depraved for the most part exult in false pleasures, while good men are nourished by true ones. <margin>It is concluded that there are true and false pleasures and pains.</margin> PROTARCHUS: You say what is necessary. SOCRATES: According to this reasoning, there are therefore certain false pleasures in the souls of men, which nonetheless imitate true ones, though ridiculously; and pains in the same way. PROTARCHUS: There are indeed. SOCRATES: Was it not possible for someone holding such an opinion to hold an opinion about things that never were, are not, and never will be? PROTARCHUS: It was possible. SOCRATES: And these were the things that then made for a false opinion, and for "opining falsely." Was it not so? PROTARCHUS: It was. SOCRATES: Must we not grant a similar condition to pleasures and pains in return? PROTARCHUS: In what way? SOCRATES: That it is possible for someone to truly rejoice, even if exulting in a random or reckless way, and yet the things for which he rejoices neither are, nor were; and often he even rejoices in things that will never happen. PROTARCHUS: These things too, O Socrates, are necessary. SOCRATES: And the same reasoning applies to fears and desires and all such things: that all of them are often false. PROTARCHUS: Truly the same. SOCRATES: Do we call opinions good or bad for any other reason than that they are true or false? PROTARCHUS: For that very reason. SOCRATES: And do we not think pleasures are bad for any other reason than because they are false? PROTARCHUS: Entirely the opposite, Socrates! For one should by no means assert that pleasures and pains are bad solely because they are false, since they frequently crash into the greatest and most manifold wickednesses besides. SOCRATES: Those bad pleasures which are such because of wickedness, we will refer to a little later, if you like. But as for false ones, we must say that they are many and occur in us in another way; for this perhaps helps us to judge. PROTARCHUS: Why not? As long as they exist. SOCRATES: And yet, O Protarchus, in my opinion, they do exist. And as long as this dogma remains with us, it is impossible for it to be safe from refutation. PROTARCHUS: Well said. SOCRATES: Let us approach this dispute again in the manner of athletes. PROTARCHUS: Let us approach it. SOCRATES: In the things said above, if we remember, we said that as long as the desires (as they are called) were in us separately, the body was occupied with experiences without the soul's experience. PROTARCHUS: We remember, and these things were undoubtedly said. SOCRATES: Did the soul not desire a state contrary to that of the body? And was the body not the receptacle of the pain and pleasure that comes from experience? PROTARCHUS: It was. SOCRATES: Gather what follows from this. PROTARCHUS: Speak. SOCRATES: Whenever these concur, pleasures and pains also meet, along with the senses of those things which are contrary—as has now become clear. PROTARCHUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: And has this not been agreed upon between us and set down above as confessed? PROTARCHUS: What is it? SOCRATES: That both pleasure and pain admit of "more" or "less," and are referred to the <term>infinite kind</term>? <note>original: "genus infiniti" — In Platonic philosophy, this refers to things that have no inherent limit or boundary, like heat, cold, or in this case, pleasure.</note> PROTARCHUS: It is certainly agreed. SOCRATES: There is, therefore, a certain way of judging these things correctly. PROTARCHUS: Where, and how? SOCRATES: In this judgment, is our purpose not to distinguish everywhere which of these is greater, which is smaller, and which is more intense—namely, pleasure compared to pain, and pain to pain, and again pleasure to pleasure? PROTARCHUS: These things are so, and that is the purpose of our judgment. SOCRATES: What then? In sight, looking at sizes from a distance or up close destroys the truth and forces one to form false opinions. Does the same thing not happen in pains and pleasures? PROTARCHUS: Much more so, Socrates. SOCRATES: Indeed, that is the opposite of what was told a little while ago. PROTARCHUS: What do you mean? SOCRATES: For then, these opinions, having become false and true, filled up the pains and pleasures along with their own experience. PROTARCHUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: But now, because these appear to change everywhere depending on whether they are seen from a distance or up close, and are compared to one another—pleasures to pains, the greater...

He argues that just as we can have false opinions, we can experience "false" pleasures and pains based on incorrect expectations of the future.</summary>

...they seem more vehement, and pains, conversely, more so when compared to pleasures. PROTARCHUS. It is necessary that such things happen for those reasons. SOCRATES. But if you were to cut away as much as each appears larger or smaller than it really is, would you not say that which appears to be both, yet is not, is neither appearing correctly, nor would you ever dare to assert that the portions of such pleasure or distress are right or true? PROTARCHUS. That is so. SOCRATES. After this, then, let us see if we encounter by this reasoning pleasures and distresses that are false in a much greater way than those which either appear or exist in living things. PROTARCHUS. What kind do you mean, and how? SOCRATES. It has been said many times that when the nature of anything is corrupted by gatherings or separations, by fillings or emptyings, by increases or decreases, then pains, distress, tortures, and other things called by such names arise. PROTARCHUS. This has been said often. SOCRATES. But when they are restored to their own nature, we established that such **restoration** is pleasure in us. PROTARCHUS. Well said. SOCRATES. But what when none of these things happen concerning our body? PROTARCHUS. But when does that occur, O Socrates? SOCRATES. That question of yours, Protarchus, is nothing to the point. PROTARCHUS. Why so? SOCRATES. Because nothing prevents me from asking you again what I asked before. PROTARCHUS. What was that? SOCRATES. If I say that no such thing happens, O Protarchus, what must necessarily result for us from this? PROTARCHUS. Do you mean when the body is not moved in either direction? SOCRATES. Exactly. PROTARCHUS. It is clear, O Socrates, that neither pleasure nor pain is perceived at that time. SOCRATES. You have answered all too correctly. But I think you feel that it is necessary that one of these things must always happen to us, as the **wise men** <note>original: "sapientes," likely referring to the followers of Heraclitus who believed in universal flux</note> hand down; for they say all things are always flowing up or down. PROTARCHUS. They do indeed say so, and they do not seem to speak badly. SOCRATES. How could they speak badly, since they were not bad men? But I wish to avoid the discourse that hangs over us, and I intend to flee this way—and you flee with me. PROTARCHUS. Tell me, which way? SOCRATES. Let us concede to them that these things are so. But you answer me: whether whatever an animal ever suffers, it also feels in the suffering—neither does it escape us while we grow, nor while anything else of this kind happens to us? Or is it entirely the opposite? For almost all such things escape us. PROTARCHUS. Entirely the opposite. SOCRATES. Therefore, what we just said was not correctly stated: that changes made up or down bring pleasures and pains. PROTARCHUS. What then? SOCRATES. It is possible to speak more correctly and safely in this way. PROTARCHUS. How? SOCRATES. That **great changes** bring pleasures and pains, but moderate and small ones do not at all. PROTARCHUS. It is said more correctly in that way than the other, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Indeed, if these things are so, the life mentioned earlier will soon return. PROTARCHUS. Which one? SOCRATES. The one we set down as being without sorrow and without joy. <margin>A triple life.</margin> PROTARCHUS. You speak most truly. SOCRATES. From these, let us establish three lives: the pleasant, the sad, and the neutral. Or do you feel otherwise? PROTARCHUS. Not otherwise than that there are three lives. SOCRATES. Therefore, not feeling pain will not be the same as rejoicing. PROTARCHUS. By no means. SOCRATES. Whenever you hear that it is the sweetest of all things to spend one's whole life without sorrow, what do you think the person saying that means? PROTARCHUS. He seems to me to mean that not feeling pain is itself "sweet." SOCRATES. Set down three things, as you like, and so that we may use more beautiful names, call one gold, the other silver, and the remaining one neither. PROTARCHUS. They are set down. SOCRATES. Can that which is neither of these become either of them—either silver or gold? PROTARCHUS. It cannot. SOCRATES. Therefore, if the **middle life** is ever said or thought to be pleasant or sad, it is by no means correctly thought or said. PROTARCHUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. And yet, O friend, we perceive some people speaking and opining this way. PROTARCHUS. Very much so. SOCRATES. Do they then think they are rejoicing when they are not grieving? PROTARCHUS. They say so, at least. SOCRATES. Do they not then think they are rejoicing? For they would not say it otherwise. PROTARCHUS. Perhaps. SOCRATES. They opine falsely about joy, if indeed its nature is different from the nature of the other <note>meaning the state of not feeling pain</note>. PROTARCHUS. It is indeed different. SOCRATES. What then shall we inquire among ourselves? Whether these are three, or only two, and whether pain is an evil to men, but the avoidance of pain—by that very name a good—should be called "sweet." PROTARCHUS. How that might be, O Socrates, let us ask ourselves, for I do not understand. SOCRATES. Because, Protarchus, you do not truly understand the adversaries of this Philebus. PROTARCHUS. Of whom do you speak? SOCRATES. Those who are said to be especially skilled in the nature of things, who deny that pleasures exist. <margin>Pleasures as escapes from pain.</margin> PROTARCHUS. What then? SOCRATES. They call all those things "escapes from pains" which the followers of Philebus call "pleasures." PROTARCHUS. Do you advise us to believe these men, O Socrates? SOCRATES. By no means, but let us use them like certain **prophets**—not by art, but by a certain grumpiness of a not-unrefined nature, who abhor pleasure too much and think nothing in it is healthy, so much so that they call those very allurements of hers a certain "evil entangling" rather than pleasure. Use these men for this purpose, considering also their other grumpinesses. After this, accept also what pleasures I consider true, so that considering the force of it from the speeches of both sides, we may finally apply ourselves to judgment. PROTARCHUS. You speak rightly. SOCRATES. Let us then follow these men like defenders, in the footprint of their grumpiness and harshness. I think they will say something of this sort, having repeated it from a somewhat distant beginning: if we wish to know the nature of any species, such as the nature of "hardness," would we know it best by looking at the hardest things, or the least hard? You must answer these grumpy men, Protarchus, just as you answer me. PROTARCHUS. I must indeed, and I answer them that we must look to the highest magnitudes. <margin>What should be looked at when a species must be distinguished.</margin> SOCRATES. If we wish to know what nature the genus of pleasure has, we must look not at small pleasures far removed from the highest, but at those which are called the supreme and most vehement. <margin>Whether pleasures are greater in the healthy or the sick.</margin> PROTARCHUS. Anyone would concede that to you now. SOCRATES. Are not the pleasures that are most at hand and the greatest, as we have often said, those which exist concerning the body? PROTARCHUS. Why wouldn't they be? SOCRATES. Are they found to be more vehement in those who are sick, or those who are in good health? Let us beware, I pray, lest we offend by answering recklessly. PROTARCHUS. In what way? SOCRATES. For perhaps we would confess they are in those in good health. PROTARCHUS. That is likely. SOCRATES. Do not those pleasures greatly exceed where the greatest desires are present? PROTARCHUS. That is true. SOCRATES. Do not men affected by fevers and such diseases both thirst vehemently and grow cold, and whatever they are accustomed to suffer in the body, do they not suffer it much more than others? From which it happens that they have greater need, and in filling the need, they are more vehemently delighted. Or shall we deny this is true? PROTARCHUS. It appears entirely so, as has been said. SOCRATES. What then, shall we seem to feel correctly...

...asserting, if anyone wishes to see the greatest pleasures, he should look not to health, but to disease? And see that you do not think I am asking this with the thought that those who are sick are soothed by more delights than those in good health, but rather think I am asking where the greatest magnitude and vehemence of pleasure is mostly found. For we said before that we must scrutinize its nature and what they say who have asserted that it does not exist at all. PROTARCHUS. I almost catch what you are saying. SOCRATES. Perhaps also, O Protarchus, you will demonstrate it no less. Just answer. In **lewdness and wantonness**, do you not see not more, but more vehement and greater in force pleasures than in a temperate life? Tell me, I pray, paying attention. PROTARCHUS. I perceive what you want, and I see the excess is very great. For the temperate are always restrained by the proverb "nothing in excess," and they obey it. But the heat of pleasure, occupying intemperate and wanton men even unto madness, compels them to exult with immoderate clamors. SOCRATES. You speak rightly. And if this is true, it is clear that vehement pleasures and vehement tortures consist in a certain depravity of both the soul and the body, rather than in virtue. PROTARCHUS. It is certainly clear. SOCRATES. Is it not fitting to elicit some from the many and investigate by what reasoning they should be called the greatest? PROTARCHUS. It is necessary. SOCRATES. Observe therefore the pleasures of such diseases, and what their nature is. PROTARCHUS. Which ones? SOCRATES. The pleasures of the deformed <note>perhaps meaning unseemly or base states</note>, which those whom we called difficult and grumpy utterly abhor. PROTARCHUS. What kind, I ask? SOCRATES. As in the remedy for **scabies** <note>a skin disease causing intense itching</note> which is done by scratching, and other things of this kind, needing no other medicine. For this evil—by the immortal gods!—shall we call it pleasure, or rather pain? PROTARCHUS. It seems to be a certain evil, O Socrates, mixed in this way. SOCRATES. Indeed, I would not have produced this example for Philebus's sake; but unless these pleasures, O Protarchus, and those that follow them, are inspected, we can almost never judge what is now sought. PROTARCHUS. Therefore, we must proceed to their relatives. SOCRATES. Do you mean, he says, those which communicate by **mixture**? <margin>Mixtures of pleasure and pain in the body.</margin> PROTARCHUS. These very ones. SOCRATES. There are therefore mixtures of the body itself in bodies, and of the soul in the soul. And we will find the pains of the soul and the body mixed with pleasures, and that commixture of both sometimes called pleasure, and sometimes pain. PROTARCHUS. In what way? SOCRATES. As, for example, when someone in restoration simultaneously suffers the contrary corruption: one who is cold often grows warm, and one who is warm sometimes grows cold, seeking, I think, to attain the one and cast off the other; and what is called "sweet mixed with bitter," and with the difficulty of rejection, a distress remains which makes it a harsh encounter. PROTARCHUS. What you say is very true. SOCRATES. Are not some of these mixtures composed of equal parts from both pleasure and pain, and some from one or the other exceeding? PROTARCHUS. Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES. Say then, among their number, those which contain more pain than delight are those that follow scabies and ticklings, when that which is within boils and grows, and one does not reach it by scratching or agitation, but only spreads what is around the skin. Then indeed, bringing those parts to the fire, and turning this way and that in lack of a plan, they often produce inestimable pleasures. Sometimes, on the contrary, with internal pleasures mixed with external distresses, they show in which direction the inclination goes, because they spread the mixtures by violence, or confound the dispersed, and at the same time apply pains to pleasures. PROTARCHUS. You tell the truth. SOCRATES. Again, when a more ample pleasure is mixed according to all these, then a portion of pain mixed in **tickles** it and produces a certain light indignation. And again, the more abundant part of pleasure infused provokes, and sometimes compels one to leap out, and produces colors of every kind, figures of every sort, every kind of breath with every incitement, and exclamations with madness. PROTARCHUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. It compels him besides, O friend, to cry out about himself, sometimes to himself or to another, that bathed in these pleasures he almost dies. And the more someone is intemperate and imprudent, the more he follows pleasures of this kind. And he calls these besides the supreme delights, and he counts as most blessed the man who spends his whole life especially in these delicacies. PROTARCHUS. You have gathered all the things that come into the estimation of the many, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Concerning the pleasures, O Protarchus, which are mixed from without or within in the common passions of the body, we have spoken. <margin>Mixtures of pleasure and pain of the soul in the soul.</margin> But concerning those which are mixed in the soul, certain contraries are cast together toward the body—namely, pleasure with pain, and pain with pleasure, meeting in one mixture. And we ran through these in the previous sections, that when it is emptied, it desires replenishment, and hoping it rejoices, but being empty it is anguished. We did not confirm those things then by testimonies, but now we say that when the soul is at variance with the body in all these things—of which the multitude is not sufficiently grasped—one mixture of pain and pleasure emerges. PROTARCHUS. You seem to speak all too correctly. SOCRATES. One further meeting of pain and pleasure remains. <margin>Pleasures of the soul in the soul.</margin> PROTARCHUS. Which one? SOCRATES. That which we said the soul often receives within itself. PROTARCHUS. By what reasoning do we assert this? SOCRATES. Anger, fear, desire, lamentation, love, emulation, envy, and the rest of this kind—do you not set all these down as certain pains of the soul itself? PROTARCHUS. I do. SOCRATES. Can we not find such pains full of certain marvelous pleasures? Or perhaps we ought to recall to our memory that: "Which made even the most prudent man rage with glowing heat and anger," and "Much sweeter than flowing honey," and pleasures mixed with distress in lamentations and desires? <note>References to Homer's Iliad describing the sweetness of anger and the mixed nature of grief.</note> PROTARCHUS. By no means <note>meaning he does not disagree</note>, for these things happen so, and not otherwise. SOCRATES. Furthermore, do you remember those who attend **tragic spectacles**, that while they are delighted, they often mourn? PROTARCHUS. I remember. SOCRATES. And in comedies, have you perceived the affect of our mind declining toward delight and sorrow at the same time? PROTARCHUS. I have not sufficiently noticed. SOCRATES. For it is not easy, O Protarchus, to grasp such an affect everywhere. PROTARCHUS. Certainly not, as it seems to me. SOCRATES. Let us therefore accept it all the more as it is more obscure, so that one may more easily perceive the meeting of pleasure and distress in the rest. <margin>Envy was a new name.</margin> PROTARCHUS. Tell me. SOCRATES. The name of **Envy** <note>original: "Inuidia"</note> introduced a little while ago—do you think it signifies a certain pain, or not? PROTARCHUS. I do. SOCRATES. Yet the envious man is caught rejoicing at the misfortunes of his neighbors. PROTARCHUS. Vehemently so. SOCRATES. Indeed, ignorance is an evil, and as we now speak, a certain stupidity. <margin>Ignorance...</margin> PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. From these, see what nature that "ridiculous" thing has. PROTARCHUS. Just tell me. SOCRATES. It is surely, in summary, a certain depravity of some habit named by its nickname, but it is a genus of universal wickedness which...

Philebus, or, Concerning the Supreme Good. 69

...is a certain kind, having exactly the opposite of what the **Delphic precepts** teach. PROTARCHUS. Do you mean this precept, O Socrates: "**Know thyself**"? SOCRATES. I do. Would the opposite to this be if it were perhaps commanded: "In no way know thyself"? PROTARCHUS. It would. SOCRATES. O Protarchus, try now to distribute this in a threefold way. PROTARCHUS. You tell me, for I cannot. SOCRATES. You say then that I must divide this now? PROTARCHUS. And I even pray you to, which is more. SOCRATES. Even more who think themselves greater and more beautiful, and whatever pertains to the body, beyond what they really are. PROTARCHUS. Even more indeed. SOCRATES. And as far as the virtues of the mind go, is not the common crowd, claiming wisdom entirely for itself, full of contentions and a false opinion of that very wisdom? PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. If anyone therefore calls that affliction entirely an evil, he will surely name it correctly. PROTARCHUS. Very much so. SOCRATES. This therefore again, O Protarchus, must be divided in two, if we wish to know the marvelous mixture of pleasure and distress by recognizing the **ridiculous** envy. PROTARCHUS. How must it be divided in two? SOCRATES. Thus. Whoever foolishly presumes this false opinion of themselves—it must necessarily happen to them as to all other mortals, that some of them have strength and power in what they profess, and others by no means. PROTARCHUS. It is necessary. SOCRATES. By this reasoning, therefore, distinguish: those among them who are weak and mocked, and cannot avenge injuries, are deservedly called **ridiculous**. But those who can are justly called terrible, strong, and hostile. <margin>The ignorance of the powerful is a most foul thing.</margin> For the ignorance of powerful and strong men is a hostile and most foul thing; for this and whatever is similar to it is harmful to all neighbors. But if ignorance be weak, it takes on the nature of the ridiculous. PROTARCHUS. You speak rightly. Yet the meeting of pleasure and pain has not yet become clear to us in these. SOCRATES. First, accept the force of **malice** <note>original: "liuor," meaning envy or ill-will</note>. <margin>The force of malice.</margin> PROTARCHUS. Speak. SOCRATES. Is it not a certain sadness and an unjust joy? PROTARCHUS. This is necessary. SOCRATES. To rejoice at the evils of enemies is neither unjust nor envious. PROTARCHUS. No. SOCRATES. But to rejoice rather than be saddened at the evils of friends—is that not unjust? PROTARCHUS. It is. SOCRATES. We said ignorance was an evil to everyone. PROTARCHUS. And correctly so. SOCRATES. Therefore, the arrogance of friends regarding wisdom and beauty, and whatever we said a little while ago happens in the three species—ridiculous indeed when weak, but hateful when strong—do we not confess that this habit of friends, when someone has it harmlessly toward others, is ridiculous? PROTARCHUS. We certainly confess it. SOCRATES. And that this, since it is ignorance, is an evil? PROTARCHUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Do we rejoice or are we saddened while we mock these things? PROTARCHUS. We clearly rejoice. SOCRATES. But did we not say before that pleasure in the evils of friends proceeds from malice? PROTARCHUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, our reasoning concludes that we, smiling at the ridiculous things in our friends' affairs, mix pleasure with pain, while we add joy to envy. For it was established long ago that malice is a certain sadness of the soul, and mockery a joy, and it became clear that these meet at the same time. PROTARCHUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Reason therefore dictates this to us: that not only in lamentations and in tragedies, nor in fables alone, but in the **tragedy and comedy of the whole of life**, pains are mixed with pleasures, and in six hundred <note>meaning "countless"</note> other things. For I think if I say a few more things, you will let me go; for I promise I will speak to you about all these tomorrow. For I do not entirely agree with those who say all pleasures are cessations of pains. <margin>What are true pleasures.</margin> However, as I said, using them as witnesses, by showing that most appear to be pleasures when they are not, and others appear great and many but are mixed with sadness and with the cessations of great pains, both concerning the defect of the body and the soul. Those which consist in beautiful colors and figures, and most smells, and sounds, and besides those which concern things in which there is a defect indeed, but one which is neither felt nor hurts. SOCRATES. I say besides that clear and sweet voices, and any one that sounds entirely pure, harmonizing a melody, compared to nothing else, but are beautiful by their nature, and bring an innate...

And those which receive the "more intensely," "more gently," "great," "small," "rarely," or "frequently," it is fitting to refer to the genus of the **infinite**, which runs through the soul and body according to the more and the less. What do you want, while you ask those things, O Socrates? SOCRATES. Nothing, O Protarchus, that I would wish to omit in the very debate over pleasure and knowledge. Rightly, without doubt. SOCRATES. Shall we need more such examples for judging pleasure? Or will it suffice to know from here that any pleasure, small rather than great, few rather than many—provided it is removed from pain—is sweeter and truer, and finally more beautiful? PROTARCHUS. Very much so indeed, and this example is suitable. SOCRATES. But what about this? That we have heard that **pleasure is always a generation** <note>original: "generatio," meaning a process of becoming or coming-to-be</note>, but an **essence** <note>original: "essentia," meaning stable being</note> never exists. For certain elegant men try to hand this down to us, and we must be grateful to them. <margin>Pleasure is a generation, but essence never exists.</margin> PROTARCHUS. What then? SOCRATES. Do you wish, friend Protarchus, that I run through it by questioning? PROTARCHUS. Speak, and just ask. SOCRATES. There are therefore two certain things: one indeed according to itself, the other always desiring another. PROTARCHUS. By what reasoning? And what do you say these are? SOCRATES. The one is by its own nature most venerable, but the other is deficient. PROTARCHUS. Express it more clearly. SOCRATES. We have often seen boys who are both beautiful and good, and men who are their lovers. PROTARCHUS. We have seen them. SOCRATES. From these two existing things, seek two other similar things throughout everything we say: that a third exists for the sake of the second. PROTARCHUS. Bring forth more clearly still what you feel, Socrates, I pray. SOCRATES. Nothing is different here, O Protarchus, but we are joking. But we say that of the things which are, something is always for the sake of another, but there is something for whose sake that which is made for the sake of another is always produced. PROTARCHUS. I have barely perceived it after frequent repetition. SOCRATES. Perhaps, my boy, as the dispute proceeds, we will grasp it more clearly. PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Let us take up these other two again. PROTARCHUS. Which ones? SOCRATES. One indeed the **generation** of all things, the other **essence**. PROTARCHUS. I accept these two from you: essence and generation. SOCRATES. Rightly: but which of these do we say is for the sake of the other? Generation for the sake of essence? Or essence for the cause of generation? PROTARCHUS. This which is called "Essence"—do we say it is the cause of generation? Is this what you are now asking? SOCRATES. It seems so. PROTARCHUS. But by the gods, what are you asking me? SOCRATES. I am asking something of this sort, Protarchus: whether the building of ships is for the sake of the voyage? Or on the contrary, the voyage for the sake of ship-building? And concerning all such things, I say the same, Protarchus. PROTARCHUS. Why do you not, Socrates, answer yourself? SOCRATES. Nothing prevents it. However, you speak at the same time. PROTARCHUS. Indeed. SOCRATES. For the sake of generation, I say, medicines and all tools and all material are applied to all things; but each generation is for the sake of each individual essence, and finally the whole for the sake of the whole essence. PROTARCHUS. Very clearly indeed. SOCRATES. Is not pleasure also, if indeed it is a generation, necessarily made for the sake of some essence? PROTARCHUS. Why wouldn't it be? SOCRATES. That which is of such a kind that it is made for the sake of something else, which is always for the sake of another, is perhaps placed in the lot of the "good"; but that which is for the sake of another must be reduced to another lot, O best of men. <margin>That for whose sake it is made is the good.</margin> PROTARCHUS. That is entirely necessary. SOCRATES. Wherefore, if pleasure is a generation, we will deservedly refer it to a lot other than that of the good. <margin>That pleasure is not the good.</margin> PROTARCHUS. Deservedly indeed. SOCRATES. As I said at the beginning of this dispute, must we not be grateful to the one who says pleasure is a generation, but no essence exists? For it is clear that those who proclaim pleasure to be the good are mocked by this. PROTARCHUS. Greatly. SOCRATES. Furthermore, this same thing will mock those who are too zealously devoted to generation. PROTARCHUS. In what way, and what kind do you mean? SOCRATES. Those who, while they quench hunger and thirst, or something else of those things which generation cures and settles, rejoice in generation, as if it were the good itself; and they say they would not care for life at all unless they were thirsty and hungry, and were affected by other things that follow these. PROTARCHUS. They certainly seem so. SOCRATES. But the contrary of that which is "to become" is "to be destroyed," as we all confess. PROTARCHUS. Necessarily. SOCRATES. Whoever seeks these things chooses corruption and generation; but not that third life, which we proposed as being void of both joy and sadness, but partaking in intelligence as purely as possible. PROTARCHUS. It will be far from reason, O Socrates, for whoever shall assert that pleasure is the good to us. SOCRATES. Far indeed, since even these things beyond...

# Book Thirty-Five.

# PLATO’S EPINOMIS, OR, THE PHILOSOPHER.
### MARSILIO FICINO’S INTRODUCTION.

**N**o Platonist should doubt, great-souled Lorenzo [[notes: Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron]], that this *Epinomis* (which is also titled *The Philosopher*) is a treasure—a foundation stone—of the divine Plato. But to bring this work fully into the light, much labor is required. Although your Marsilio promises these introductions, he is not permitted to make them too lengthy. This is especially true since the messengers of the writers and printers are constantly urging the work forward; they snatch the arguments almost provocatively from my hands, scarcely allowing me to pursue the highest peaks of these matters in each volume. 

The purpose of the preceding *Laws* was to compose the souls of citizens as much as possible so that, having achieved a ready tranquility, they might examine the reasons and causes of divine works. In these works, as if in mirrors, they might contemplate and love God the author. Indeed, *sapientia* (wisdom) consists in contemplation, while *religio* (religion) consists in worship; in both together lies the whole of human happiness and the end of the laws. The preceding *Laws* promised this kind of end, but the *Epinomis* actually provides it, God granting. Therefore, having prophesied this perfect habit of mind in the opening, he then seeks it from God through a certain suppliant prayer. 

Some have judged that happiness can be possessed in this life; others in the next; and others, indeed, nowhere. Surely, whoever thinks it can be acquired in this life by human power is clearly deceived, as the testimony of our whole life cries out against it. But those who say "nowhere" are as if empty-headed, for they would have it that even the instinct of the whole of nature is in vain. Our Plato quite wisely hopes for happiness in the next life, to be obtained both through the virtues of the present life and by the gift of God. Yet he does not despair that a very few may taste the sweetness of happiness even in this life. In the *Phaedrus* and the *Republic*, he maintains that such people are those who live outside the body rather than in it—in short, they live for God rather than for themselves. The result is that, by God’s inspiration, even amid the Lethean floods [[notes: the waters of forgetfulness/the material world]] of human existence, they seem to sip something of the ethereal nectar. 

It is not without reason that he inscribed this *Epinomis* as *The Philosopher*. For, as is clear in the sixth and seventh books of the *Republic* and in the present book, the duty of the philosopher is to investigate the reasons for all things so that they may find the very Divine Reason by which they were made; once found, they may worship it, and once worshiped, enjoy it. In this book, while he strives to lead us toward happiness—which religious wisdom undoubtedly establishes—he depicts the specific character of the legitimate philosopher and educates and forms him through the appropriate levels of the disciplines. And everywhere he seems to demand from the philosopher no less—indeed, much more—virtue and piety than knowledge. Whatever knowledge he requires, he requires it so that the philosopher may venerate God himself, the true master of knowledge and the author of the things known, above all else. 

First, he proves that the power for divine happiness is naturally implanted in us by the fact that we all prophesy and seek it in all our actions, and the soul is filled by nothing else. Second, enumerating the individual faculties in order, he shows that this happiness is not prepared by the natural, necessary, playful, or auxiliary arts. Third, he demonstrates that wisdom and piety, the foundations of blessedness, are acquired by both moral and speculative virtues. When he enumerates the speculative doctrines, he first not only praises but admires arithmetic. In his earlier books, he says this art most of all whets the character, confirms the memory, and makes the soul most fit and ready for all speculation and action. He adds here that number was handed down to men by God himself as a necessary instrument for the discourse of reason. If it were removed, the soul would appear mindless, and the sciences and arts would utterly vanish. 

Furthermore, he praises geometry, which looks at measurements; stereometry, which balances weights; astronomy, which observes the heavens; and music, which imitates the harmony of the heavens. He also commends physics, where he treats the types of bodies, compositions, animals, and the principle of motion and generation. However, he leaves the most minute details of natural things to the physicians, as being least relevant to one who is turning himself toward divine things. Finally, he places Dialectic—that is, Metaphysics, the pinnacle of this theology—before all others as a queen; specifically as the rightful step for finding and adoring God. He proves that the duties of this "Queen" regarding the other faculties are threefold. First, that she surveys the multitude of all these arts. Second, that she perceives what single communion and connection exists among them all. Third, that she clearly observes by what logic this multitude and its union contribute to the One itself and the Divine Good.

# Book Thirty-Five.

# CLINIAS, THE ATHENIAN GUEST, MEGILLUS.

[[margin: Which arts do not grant wisdom.]]
**C**LINIAS: Now, as we had commonly agreed, all three of us have finally arrived here rightly, O Guest [[notes: The "Athenian Guest" or Stranger is the lead speaker, usually identified with Plato himself]]—I, you, and Megillus here—to inquire about *prudentia* (prudence). We seek the logic by which we might attain that state where the human intellect, as far as nature allows, is best disposed toward prudence. We have already treated the other matters pertaining to the making of laws. But that which is greatest both to discover and to say—namely, by what knowledge a man becomes wise—we have neither discovered nor stated. Yet I think it must by no means be skipped over, lest we leave imperfect that for which we have traveled this far to open up.

ATHENIAN: You speak skillfully, friend Clinias. But I think you are about to hear a discourse that is at once wonderful and yet, in another way, not wonderful. For many, tossed by the waves of this life, proclaim that the human race cannot be happy and blessed. Pay attention, therefore, and consider whether I myself seem to speak rightly on this matter. I judge it impossible for men to attain happiness and blessedness in this life, except for a very few. There is, however, good hope that after death one may fully obtain those things, for the desire of which he lived and finished his life as well as he could. 

I am not bringing forward something unheard of or new, but something that all we Barbarians and Greeks recognize in a certain way. For no one is ignorant of how great the difficulty is in the first generation of animals: first in conception and the womb, then in birth and labor, and afterwards in nutrition and education. We are not ignorant that these things happen through a thousand labors. Moreover, the time is short—not only in respect to the long duration of evils, but in whatever way one considers it—which lets us breathe a little around the middle of human life. But quickly, gloomy old age arrives and ensures that no one would wish to return to life again when he considers past troubles, unless he is carried away by a childish opinion. All these things being so, the proof for me is the very thing we are now seeking. For we ask by what means we can become wise, as if some such power were implanted in each of us. Indeed, this reality does not escape us: when one has proceeded toward any of those faculties commonly called by the name of art, prudence, or science—as if none of those in such human affairs were worthy to be called by the name of "wisdom"—the soul nevertheless settles down and prophesies that there is some such power...

...these things remain the same in the same way. And looking toward truth itself, we think those are more true. 

PROT. Quite right. 

SOC. If we first mix the truest portions of both together, will this mixture be sufficient to provide us with the most desirable life? Or will we need something else besides, and not such things? 

PROT. It seems to me we should do so. 

SOC. Let there be, then, a certain wise man who knows what justice itself is, and who possesses the reason that accompanies intelligence, and let him similarly understand all other things that exist. 

PROT. Let it be so. 

SOC. Will this man be endowed with sufficient knowledge if he holds the logic of the divine circle and sphere themselves, but is entirely ignorant of this human sphere and these circles, even while he uses <term>canons</term> <note>original: "canonib." — a Greek-derived word for a carpenter's rule or standard of measurement</note>—that is, rules and circles—in architecture and similar works?
