SOC. What do you say? Must we bring in and mix together the impure and unstable art of the false rule and circle into the common pool? 

PROT. This is necessary, if any of us is ever to find the way home. 

SOC. And what about music, which we said a little earlier was full of conjecture and imitation, and lacks purity? 

PROT. That too is necessary, if our life is to be a life at all. 

SOC. Do you wish then, like a gatekeeper pushed and forced by a crowd, that I should now throw open the doors and let all the sciences flow together and be mingled, the pure with the inferior? 

<margin>No one is harmed by the other sciences if he holds the primary ones.</margin> 

PROT. I do not know, O Socrates, if anyone is harmed by the other sciences who holds the primary ones. 

SOC. I now permit them all to flow together into a sort of valley of <term>Homeric mixing</term> <note>An allusion to the Iliad, where rivers join together in a valley; Socrates uses it to describe the confluence of different types of knowledge.</note>, and a very poetic one at that. 

PROT. Let them flow. 

SOC. Now it seems we must go back to the fountain of pleasures. For when we thought of mixing them, did not certain "true" pleasures arise for us? But for the love of all knowledge, we permitted all sciences to run together before the pleasures. 

PROT. You speak the truth. 

SOC. It is time, therefore, that we also consult about the pleasures, whether all of them should be admitted together, or only the primary and true ones. 

PROT. It makes a great difference for safety to admit the primary and true ones. 

SOC. Let their commerce be admitted then. But what next? If there are some that are necessary, must these also be accepted into the mixture just as the others were? 

PROT. What prevents it? But which ones are necessary? 

SOC. If, just as it was established that knowing all the arts is harmless and useful in life, it should now be established regarding pleasures—namely, that enjoying all of them is harmless and useful—then perhaps they should all be mixed together. What do you say to this? 

PROT. How shall we speak of these, and how shall we act? 

SOC. Not from us, Protarchus, but from the pleasures and sciences themselves should this be asked. 

PROT. How so? 

SOC. "O friends (whether it is right to call you pleasures or by some other name), do you choose to associate with all wisdom, or to be apart from wisdom?" I think they would necessarily respond as follows. 

PROT. What? 

SOC. That, as was said above, it is neither possible nor useful for any genus to be pure, separate, and solitary. Indeed, we think that the best of all kinds, if one is compared to another, would be that genus by which all other things, and even our individual powers, are perfectly known. 

PROT. And we shall rightly confess that they have answered correctly. 

SOC. It remains for us to ask Mind and Wisdom, as we say they need pleasures in a certain way in the mixture, what kind of pleasures they specifically require. 

PROT. Rightly so. 

SOC. Our question hereafter will be this: "Besides those true pleasures, do you need the commerce of the most vehement and greatest pleasures?" Perhaps they will answer thus: "And how, O Socrates? For these offer us innumerable impediments. They disturb the souls we inhabit with fury, they do not permit us to grow, and for the most part, they entirely ruin our offspring by bringing about forgetfulness through negligence. But the other pleasures—the true and pure ones you described—consider those almost like members of our household. And besides those, admit also the pleasures taken with health, temperance, and the other virtues." 

<margin>Which pleasures are proper to wisdom, and which are foreign.</margin> 

"For these pleasures, which follow virtue as if she were a goddess, we gladly admit. But as for those that associate with madness and other wickedness, it is absurd to mix them with Mind, if anyone wishes to discern that most beautiful and harmonious mixture and temperament, to learn what is good by its own nature in man and in the universe, and to divine what the Idea of the Good itself is." Shall we not say that Mind has answered wisely and as if in control of itself, both about itself and about memory and right opinion? 

PROT. Entirely so. 

SOC. And yet this is also necessary, and could never be otherwise. 

PROT. What is that? 

SOC. That to which we do not mix Truth would never become true, nor would it have been made so. 

PROT. For in what way could it? 

SOC. In no way. But if anything further is missing from this mixture, you and Philebus must say so. For to me, this discourse seems to have been completed like an incorporeal world beautifully ruling over an animated body. 

PROT. Know, O Socrates, that the same seems true to me. 

SOC. If we say that we have just now entered the vestibule of the house of the Good itself, perhaps we shall be professing rightly in some way? 

PROT. It certainly seems so to me. 

SOC. What then seems to be the cause of why this mixture is most precious and why this constitution is most pleasing to all? For if we know that, we shall soon weigh whether it is more closely related and more akin to Pleasure or to Mind in the universe. 

PROT. Shrewdly put. For that will contribute greatly to our dispute. 

SOC. And yet it is by no means difficult to find the cause for which any mixture is to be valued either most or least. 

PROT. How do you mean? 

SOC. No man is ignorant of this. 

PROT. What is it, then? 

SOC. That whatever mixture lacks measure or a commensurate nature, necessarily destroys all the things that are mixed, and first of all, it destroys itself. For this is not a temperament, but some intemperate heap; such a thing is usually a calamity to those who possess it. 

PROT. You speak the truth. 

SOC. Now the power of the Good, transferring itself into the nature of the Beautiful, has escaped our notice. 

<margin>Beauty.</margin> 

For measure and commensurability everywhere become beauty and virtue. 

PROT. Entirely. 

SOC. Furthermore, we said that Truth was mixed with them in that temperament. 

PROT. Absolutely. 

SOC. Therefore, if we cannot capture the Good itself in one single idea, let us at least grasp it with three: Beauty, Commensurability, and Truth. Let us say that this trio, as if they were one, is the cause of what is in the mixture, and because of this—that is, because it is good—the mixture becomes what it is. 

PROT. Most rightly. 

SOC. Now, Protarchus, I think anyone could easily judge concerning wisdom and pleasure, which of them happens to be more akin to this "best" and more excellent both among men and among the Gods. 

PROT. It is clear, yet by the reason that...

...and it will be better to run through that too in speech. SOC. Therefore, according to each of these three, let us judge concerning pleasure and wisdom. For we must see to which of the three we may assert each is more closely related. PROT. Do you speak of beauty, truth, and measure? SOC. Certainly. First, therefore, take truth, Protarchus; and when you have taken it, look now to the three: mind, truth, and pleasure. And after you have considered it long and maturely, answer yourself whether pleasure or mind is closer to truth. PROT. What need is there of long meditation? There is a great difference, as I think. For pleasure is the most reckless of all things. For it is said of Venusian <note>sexual</note> pleasures, which are estimated to be the greatest of all, that the gods entirely forgive those who forswear themselves, as if pleasures were some kind of children, 

<margin>Mind either is truth itself, or is most like it.</margin> 

capable of no intelligence. But mind is either the same as truth, or certainly of all things the most similar and the truest. SOC. Does it then remain to consider that measure and moderation, whether pleasure or wisdom is more capable of it? PROT. That too which you now bring in is very easy to investigate. I think that nothing can be found more immoderate than pleasure and its exultation; on the contrary, nothing is more moderate than mind and science. SOC. Excellently. But nonetheless, answer the third as well. Does the mind partake more of beauty, or does pleasure itself? Or which is more beautiful: the mind than pleasure, or the contrary? PROT. Mind and wisdom indeed, O Socrates, no one ever, whether truly or falsely, saw as deformed or thought in any way to have been, to be, or to be in the future. SOC. Right. PROT. But if we observe someone enjoying pleasures, especially the greatest ones, because they are either ridiculous or obscene, we ourselves blush and hide them, committing such things to the darkness of night, as if they were unworthy of the sight of daily light. SOC. Therefore, O Protarchus, declare to everyone, both through messengers and with your present voice, that the possession of pleasure 

<margin>Distinction of goods.</margin> 

is neither the first nor the second good. But the first is concerning measure, and the moderated, and the opportune, and whatever such things must be thought to have obtained a certain eternal nature. PROT. It appears so from what has just been said. SOC. The second, then, is concerning the commensurate and the beautiful, perfect and sufficient, and as many as are of this kind. PROT. So it seems. SOC. The third, as I myself divine, if you place mind and wisdom there, you will not depart far from the truth. PROT. Perhaps. SOC. The fourth are those which we placed as proper to the soul itself: sciences and arts and right opinions. These, therefore, follow immediately after those three, because they are more related to the good than pleasure is. PROT. Perhaps. SOC. In the fifth place, put those pleasures which we defined as devoid of pain, which we called the pure sciences of the soul itself, following the senses. PROT. Perhaps. SOC. "But in the sixth generation," says Orpheus, "finish the ornament of the song." Our discourse also seems to be finished in the sixth judgment. Hence nothing else remains for us hereafter, except that we add a head, as it were, to what has been said. PROT. It is indeed proper. SOC. Now for the third time, having called upon the Savior God, let us briefly run through the same discourse. PROT. Of what sort do you mean? SOC. Philebus indeed said that every pleasure entirely is the good itself for us. PROT. For the third time, O Socrates, as it seems; you were saying a little while ago that the discourse must be repeated. SOC. This very thing. But let us hear what follows. Indeed, considering and bearing heavily what I just said regarding the discourse of Philebus and of countless others, I contended that the mind is far better and more preferable for the life of men than pleasure. PROT. These things were said. SOC. Suspecting, however, that there were many other things, I introduced this: that if anything appeared more excellent than both of these, I would perhaps fight for the mind itself against pleasure for the second place, and pleasure would be stripped even of second honors. PROT. You said these things too. SOC. Furthermore, when I had said that the good itself is the most sufficient of all things, it nonetheless was established that neither of these is sufficient. PROT. You tell the truth. SOC. And when in that discourse neither mind nor pleasure seemed to have a sufficient and perfect power for themselves, it appeared that neither was the good itself. PROT. Very rightly. SOC. Moreover, when it was established that a certain third thing was better than both, the mind certainly shone forth at a long interval as closer to the more powerful and surpassing idea than pleasure. PROT. Why not? SOC. Therefore, would not the power of pleasure obtain the fifth rank from that opinion which the present judgment has brought forth? PROT. See to it. SOC. Yet all oxen and horses and all wild beasts would give the first place to pleasure; most people, trusting in them just as augurs trust in birds, think pleasures are the most powerful of all things for living well; and they assert that the loves of wild beasts are richer witnesses than so many responses of philosophers. PROTARCH. We all confess, O Socrates, that you have told the truest things. SOC. Will you not then dismiss me now? PROTAR. A little something still remains, O Socrates; for you shall not depart first; and I will bring back to your memory those things that remain.

PLATONIS HIPPIAS MAIOR, VEL, DE PVLCHRO.
->PLATO’S GREATER HIPPIAS, OR, ON THE BEAUTIFUL.<-

->MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT.<-

The beautiful is discussed in the *Phaedrus*, *Symposium*, and *Hippias*. In the *Hippias*, because Socrates acts against Hippias the sophist <note>a professional teacher of rhetoric</note>, who, although he was ignorant, thought he knew—which ignorance renders the soul unteachable—he does not sufficiently teach what the beautiful is, but shows what it is not, and refutes false opinions. He calls him a "sophist" who strives to seem wise rather than to be so, for the sake of money and honor. That Hippias is such a person is declared in the prologue and at the end of the prologue. Having taken the occasion from a certain speech of Hippias which discussed beautiful duties, Socrates asks what is beautiful in itself, by which all other things become beautiful. 

<margin>Occasion of the dialogue with a challenge and boast of the sophist.</margin> 

For it is necessary to refer particulars to the universal that is in particulars, and the universal in particulars to that universal which is above individual things. For individual beautiful men are rendered beautiful through a certain form common to each; but the common form is imprinted on the many from the divine species as if by a seal’s character: since every multitude is reduced to the one which is in the multitude, and the one in the multitude to the one which is above the multitude. Wherefore, since there are many beautiful things, it is necessary that each one be beautiful through a beauty common to all and implanted in all: and that the beauty which is in all, just as it is in another, not in itself, so it depends on another, not on itself. Each of the individual beautiful things Plato calls "this beautiful thing"; the form in all, he calls "beauty"; the species and idea above all, he calls "the beautiful itself." Opinion and the senses reach the first. Reason thinks the second. The mind intuits the third. 

<margin>Ancient wise men abstained from civil actions.</margin> 

Hippias, being questioned, defines it thrice according to sense and opinion. These being refuted, Socrates also defines it thrice: twice according to reason, and finally according to the mind. For the sophist walks by sense and opinion; the philosopher rather by reason and mind. In the first place, Hippias answers that a beautiful young woman is the beautiful itself. That this is false is clear from the fact that not all things which are beautiful become beautiful through a young woman. And a young woman, if she is compared with beasts, appears beautiful; if with the gods, she appears deformed. Wherefore she seems no more beautiful...

--- Page 94 ---
Hippias Major, Or, on the Beautiful. 75

...than she seems ugly. Then Hippias answers with another thing similarly from individual beautiful things, not a common one: namely, that Gold is the beautiful itself, by which all things become beautiful. Which Socrates rejects on this ground: because gold, to whatever things it is suitable, makes those things beautiful; but other things it deforms. Therefore, it does not make things beautiful simply, but it is "fitting." For this reason, it does not adorn a thing more by its own reason than by the reason of another. Nor is gold the only thing by which all things are adorned, but also silver and ivory, and other things of this kind. In the third place, he brings in another thing, which is also particular rather than common: "It is beautiful," he says, "to be in good health of body, to be rich and honored, to die an old man, to be buried by one's sons, and to have buried one's parents." This is clearly false, because not all things besides man are rendered beautiful by this. Furthermore, this is perhaps beautiful among men; but among the gods and the sons of gods it is ugly, where parents do not die. Having refuted these things which Hippias brought forward concerning individual corporeal things through sense and opinion, Socrates, now tending toward higher things, brings in not what sense offers to opinion, but what reason offers to opinion. For first he says the "fitting" <term>decorum - the seemly or appropriate</term> is the beautiful. This is indeed more incorporeal and common to many. Yet he refutes it by this division: the fitting either makes a thing seem beautiful only, or it excels both in seeming and in being. If the first, the fitting is a certain deception concerning the beautiful, rather than the beautiful itself. For true beauty makes things be beautiful: just as true magnitude makes things large, even if they are not seen. If you say the second, you will have spoken falsely. For if the beautiful itself, as often as it grants being beautiful, also granted appearing so equally, then whatever things are beautiful would appear so to all just as they are. That this is false, the contentions and controversies concerning beautiful things show us. Secondly, he brings in another thing which reason offers to opinion. Furthermore, he calls the "Useful" the beautiful. Utility is something incorporeal and common to many. Nor is it a wonder that thought is deceived concerning the fitting and the useful. For the former has the order of part to part, and of parts to the whole; but the latter has the order of some whole to another whole, and order truly seems to represent beauty. For this reason, anyone easily accepts the fitting or the useful for the beautiful. That the fitting is not the beautiful has been established; that the useful is not, he shows thus: the useful is that which has power for doing something. Therefore, power and utility are the same. Whatever we do, we do by some power, but for the most part we do evil things; therefore, power and utility for the most part bring in evil, but the beautiful is never the cause of evil. Therefore, not simply whatever utility there is, is the beautiful. "But at least that which contributes to the good," someone will answer; against whom he argues thus: "That which tends toward the good is conducive. The conducive makes the good: that which makes something is other than that which is made; for this reason, the conducive is one thing, the good is another. The conducive and the beautiful are the same. Therefore, the beautiful and the good are different." Consequently, neither is the beautiful the good, nor the good the beautiful—which is entirely absurd. Finally, the errors of sense, opinion, and thought having been conquered, the mind dictates to reason that the beautiful is a certain "grace" which moves and allures the soul through the mind, sight, and hearing. Which surely is elicited partly from the end of this dialogue, and partly from Plato's *Phaedrus* and *Symposium*. In what way this grace is present, and by what name it is to be called, Socrates inquires; yet he does not declare to the ambitious sophist what he revealed to Phaedrus and Agathon, who, since they were ignorant, yet acknowledging their ignorance, were teachable. Truly, beauty is grace, not by reason of the sense, because it would not suit the mind, and would belong to the other senses equally as to hearing and sight. Not by reason of the mind, because it would escape the eyes and ears. Nor also by reason of pleasure, because this is found not only in hearing and sight, but in all senses. Not by reason of hearing alone: for it would not suit the mind and sight. Not by reason of sight: for it would be lacking to hearing and the mind. Not by reason of hearing and sight together, because beauty would be in sight and hearing joined together as one: but in each of them acting separately from the other, there would be no beauty. But we want that grace to be perceived commonly by the three powers of the soul, and to be present commonly in their three objects. For this reason, he adds that the pleasures of the mind, sight, and hearing are beautiful from the fact that they are the most harmless and best of all pleasures. If the best is the same as the conducive, it makes the good; therefore, it is for the sake of the good. Cause and effect are different. Therefore, the conducive is one thing, the good is another. From which it follows that the beautiful is one thing, the good another. Therefore, neither is the beautiful the good, nor the good the beautiful. But if you explain the best as being "harmless, easy, spiritual, luminous, and vital," so to speak, you will be made a master of the truth. For beauty is nothing else than the splendor of the highest good, shining in those things which are perceived by the eyes, ears, and mind, and through those things turning the sight, hearing, and mind toward the good itself. From which it happens that beauty is a certain circle of divine light, flowing from the good, residing in the good, and eternally reflected through the good and to the good. This mystery, which Socrates asserted he had learned from the sibyl Diotima, he revealed not to the sophists, but to his disciples. What is the good itself? It is the one principle of all things, pure act, an act vivifying all subsequent things. What is the beautiful itself? A vivifying act flowing from the first fountain of goods, decorating first the divine Mind with the infinite order of ideas, then filling the subsequent divinities and minds with a series of reasons, thirdly adorning souls with numerous discourses, fourthly natures with seeds, and fifthly matter with forms. Truly, the sun procreates visible bodies and seeing eyes. To the eyes, so that they may see, it infuses a lucid spirit. Bodies, so that they may be seen, it paints with colors. Yet neither the ray proper to the eyes nor the colors proper to the bodies are sufficient for completing vision, unless the light itself—one above the many, from which many and proper lights have been distributed to the eyes and bodies—comes, illustrates, excites, and strengthens. In the same way, the first act itself, that is, God, has granted species and act to individual things by producing them. Which act indeed, when it has been received in a suffering subject, is weak and powerless for the execution of work. But the perpetual and invisible light of the divine sun always stands by all things as one; it cherishes, vivifies, excites, completes, and strengthens. Of which Orpheus divinely said: "Cherishing all things and himself bearing himself above all." Insofar as it is the act of all things and strengthens them, it is called the Good. Insofar as it vivifies, soothes, softens, and excites, it is called the Beautiful. Insofar as it allures those three powers of the cognizing soul in the objects that are to be known, it is beauty. Insofar as in the cognizing power it applies it to the known, it is truth. Insofar as it is good, it procreates, rules, and completes. Insofar as it is beautiful, it illuminates and infuses grace. But it is necessary for all things to be prepared for receiving the grace of the divine splendor. Bodies indeed by proportion, which consists in order, mode, and species. Voices by harmony, which is composed of numbers and intervals. Duties of morals by rectitude toward a good end. Disciplines by order toward a true object. The soul by purity through aversion from lower things and conversion to higher things. The mind, through an eternal intuition into the good itself. Through all these things, the ray of divine beauty penetrates by steps. Around the body, it shines in numerous inequality, subject to place and change. Around voices, in harmony outside a fixed place, but dispersed by motion. Around duties and disciplines and the soul, it consists in motion indeed but in a vital reason. Around the mind, above motion, sparkling in an eternal series of ideas. Around the good itself, it is pure act, bringing life and grace to all. These things, I pray, Peter de' Medici <note>Piero the Unfortunate, son of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note>, most distinguished of all men, that you read with your usual diligence. For you will both entirely recognize the wondrous beauty of your own mind, and you will notice how very closely you approach the beautiful itself, which is discussed here.

SOCRATES.
HIPPIAS.

<margin>Occasion of the dialogue with a provocation and boast against the sophist.</margin>

SOC. Wise and beautiful Hippias, after how long an interval have you come to Athens? HIP. I have no leisure, O Socrates. For as often as the citizens of Elis have something to be treated with some city, they commit the embassies to me above others, judging me a fit judge and messenger of those things which are said among the individual cities. For which reason I have often gone as an ambassador to other cities, and even more often to Lacedæmon <note>Sparta</note> concerning the greatest matters. For which reason I frequent these places less, as you were asking. SOC. This certainly, O Hippias, is proper to a wise and perfect man. You indeed, in private, having received much money from young men, are able to confer more upon them than what you have received; and in public you are able to benefit your country, as befits him who should not be despised by the common people, but should be held in the highest price. But what, O Hippias, is the cause that those ancients who obtained the great name of wise men—Pittacus and Bias, and those who 

<margin>Ancient wise men abstained from civil actions.</margin> 

flourished in the study of wisdom in the time of Thales the Milesian, or thereafter down to Anaxagoras—either all or most of them abstained from civil affairs? HIP. What else do you think, O Socrates, than weakness of...

...talent, since they could not prudently manage both private and public affairs? SOC. Or do you think that just as the other arts have received increment in time, so that the artisans of our time far excel those of earlier times, so also your faculty—the study

<margin>Gorgias.</margin> 

Since Gorgias here, the Leontine sophist, came here as an ambassador of his country, as one who was the most excellent of all the Leontines for managing those public duties: he was judged both to speak most excellently to the people, and by disputing privately and conversing with young men, he made a great profit, and began from this city. But each of those whom I just mentioned has accumulated more silver by his wisdom than any other artisan 

<margin>Protagoras before Gorgias and Prodicus.</margin> 

from any art whatever. And the same Protagoras, before those fellows Gorgias and Prodicus, gained very much silver, at which you would wonder. I omit other things. <margin>Anaxagoras dissipated a large patrimony so that he might philosophize.</margin> 

must the ignorance of those who were before the times of Anaxagoras seem? Since he, contrary to what happens to you, when he had received a large patrimony, is said to have neglected and dissipated it, he philosophized so stupidly: and they pass down certain other such things about the other wise men of those times. Wherefore you seem to have brought this best conjecture, that our wise men excel their predecessors, and many agree in this, that a wise man ought especially to be wise for himself. No, by Jove, O Socrates. SOC. What do you say? Was it the least? HIP. On the contrary, nothing at all ever. SOC. What you say is a marvel and a wonder, O Hippias; and tell me: can your wisdom make those who converse with you and learn from you better toward virtue, or not? HIP. Most greatly indeed. SOC. Were you able to make the sons of the Inycian citizens better? But the sons of the Spartans not at all? HIP. Far be it. SOC. Or perhaps the Sicilians strive to become better, while the Lacedæmonians neglect it? HIP. On the contrary, the Lacedæmonians also affect the same thing. SOC. Did they lack your company through a lack of money? HIP. By no means, for they are rich enough. SOC. Could you not persuade the young men in Lacedæmon that by adhering to you they would profit more toward virtue than if they lived with their own people? Or could you not induce the parents to commit their sons to you rather than to their own diligence, if only they had a care for their sons? For they were not so envious of their sons that they would not wish them to turn out the best. HIP. Indeed, I do not think they were envious. SOC. Is not Lacedæmon instituted with good laws? HIP. With good ones indeed. SOC. In cities instituted with good laws, virtue is honored most of all. HIP. Most indeed. SOC. But you know best of all men how to hand this over to others. HIP. Entirely, O Socrates. SOC. He who can teach the equestrian faculty excellently, would he not be honored more in Thessaly than in the rest of Greece, and make the most profit, and similarly elsewhere wherever this art is in price? HIP. That is indeed agreeable. SOC. He therefore who is able to institute young men with the most noble precepts of virtue, why is he not honored most greatly in Lacedæmon, and there accumulate innumerable sums of money, and similarly in whatever city of the Greeks virtue is most greatly valued? But perhaps in Sicily rather and Inyca; do you think we ought to believe those things, Hippias? If you command it, it must be believed. HIP. It is not the paternal custom for the Lacedæmonians, O Socrates, to change the laws, or to educate their sons contrary to the usual ways. SOC. What do you say? It is not paternal for the Lacedæmonians to act rightly, but to wander from the path? HIP. I would not assert that. SOC. But they would act rightly if they educated their young men better, not if worse? HIP. Rightly, but their law does not admit foreign disciplines. Otherwise, if anyone else had ever gained anything there for the sake of teaching, know that I would have gained the most. They rejoice, therefore, when they hear me, and they praise me: but as I was saying, their foreign law forbids it. SOC. Do you call law, O Hippias, the destruction of a city, or its safety? HIP. In my opinion, law is established for the sake of utility, but sometimes it hinders, if it be badly established. SOC. Do not the makers of laws establish the law as a certain greatest good for the city, and when the law is taken away, we cannot live legitimately in the city? HIP. You speak the truth. SOC. As often, therefore, as those who strive to bring laws wander from the good, they depart from the legitimate and the law. What do you say to this? HIP. By exact reason, it is so, O Socrates. Yet men are not accustomed to name it so. SOC. Do they do so, O Hippias, knowing or ignorant? HIP. The common people. SOC. Are those who know the truth the common people? HIP. By no means. SOC. But truly those who know, they judge that what is more useful is more legitimate than what is useless, indeed for all men. Do you not confess it? HIP. I confess indeed that it is so in truth. SOC. Is it not so, as those who know think? HIP. Entirely. SOC. But it is better, as you say, for the Lacedæmonians to be imbued with your discipline, even if it is foreign...

...rather than their paternal one. HIP. And I speak the truth. SOC. Furthermore, whatever things are more useful are more legitimate. Is this what you say, O Hippias? HIP. I said it indeed. SOC. Therefore, according to your reasoning, it is more according to the law that the sons of the Lacedæmonians be taught by Hippias than by their parents, since you would benefit them more than they would in truth. HIP. I would benefit them without a doubt, Socrates. SOC. The Lacedæmonians act against the law, therefore, when they do not hand over their sons to you to be educated for a reward of gold. HIP. I agree indeed; for you seem to speak for me: wherefore it is not proper to oppose you. SOC. We find the Spartans, O friend, to be devoid of good laws, and indeed in the greatest matters, although they seem to use the best laws. Is it when you tell those things which you yourself know excellently, the stars and the celestial progresses? HIP. In no way do they endure these. SOC. Does the speech of geometry delight them? HIP. Least of all: for very many of them, so to speak, do not even know how to count. SOC. It is far off, therefore, that they would gladly hear calculations. HIP. Far off, by Jove. SOC. Is it those things which you understand most acutely of all men, the distinctions of letters and syllables, the natures of rhythms and harmonies? HIP. What harmonies and letters, O good man? SOC. But what then are those things which they rejoice in hearing, and praise you for? Tell me at least, since I cannot find out. HIP. The lineage of heroes and men, and habitations—how cities were once built—and in summary, they listen attentively to all the history of antiquity. Wherefore for their sake I was forced to learn and meditate on all things of this kind. SOC. How well it has gone for you, O Hippias, that the Lacedæmonians take it ill if someone begins by reciting our leaders starting from Solon. Otherwise, in learning their names, you would have had to be fatigued. HIP. Why fatigued, Socrates? Hearing fifty names once, I can repeat them from memory. SOC. Do you say so truly? But I had not noticed that you were so powerful in memory. Wherefore I now understand that you are deservedly enjoyed by the Lacedæmonians as one skilled in many things, and that they use you just as children use old women, for the pleasantness of storytelling. HIP. By Jove, O Socrates, recently in that same place, discoursing on beautiful studies in which it befits a young man to be occupied, I was an object of admiration. For there exists a certain brilliant oration composed by me about them, which is powerful in the special elegance of its words; the form and beginning of the oration is of this sort: "Troy having been captured, Neoptolemus asked Nestor what things were most beautiful, by occupying himself in which a young man might turn out an illustrious man." To whom Nestor, answering, recites many and beautiful precepts. For Eudices, the son of Apemantus, asked me. Wherefore see that you also are present, and bring others with you, whoever know how to judge words of that kind. SOC. Recently, O best of men, when in a certain sermon I was praising some things as beautiful and vituperating others as ugly, someone brought this doubt into the middle, interrogating me very insultingly thus: "From where do you, Socrates, know beautiful or ugly things? Are you able to define what the beautiful is?" But I, on account of my worthlessness, hesitated, nor did I have what I might respond appropriately, and departing from the gathering of men, I was angry with myself, and vehemently accused my own rudeness: and I threatened that when I first should have any of you who profess wisdom in my way, I would endeavor to hear and learn it, and having diligently premeditated it, return to him who had asked, so that I might fight again about the same thing. Wherefore now you, as I was saying, have come most opportunely. Teach me, I beseech you, what the beautiful itself is: endeavor, I say, most diligently to open the whole matter by answering, lest I be laughed at again, having been refuted. I shall therefore easily learn, nor shall anyone further refute me. HIP. None certainly. For my study would be worthless and rude. SOC. By Juno, you speak well, Hippias, if we catch that man. SOC. Are not all beautiful things beautiful by the beautiful itself? HIP. By the beautiful certainly. SOC. Is it therefore the beautiful itself? HIP. It is without a doubt, but to what purpose? SOC. Excellently, by the dog <note>a favorite oath of Socrates</note>, O Hippias, and you have answered very decorously. ...that he would dare to rebuke you further, as if what you say were not beautiful? Or if by chance he did dare, would he not be laughed at by everyone? SOCRATES. That he will indeed dare, O wonderful man, I know for certain; but whether his daring will turn out to be ridiculous, the event itself will show. However, I desire to tell you what objections he will bring. HIPPIAS. Tell them now. SOCRATES. "How charming you are, Socrates," he will say. "Is a beautiful mare not beautiful? The God himself praised one in an oracle." <note>This likely refers to an oracle concerning the best things in Greece, where the mares of Thessaly were praised.</note> What shall we say to this, Hippias? Shall we not confess that a beautiful mare is a beautiful thing? For how could we deny that what is beautiful is beautiful? HIPPIAS. You speak the truth, Socrates; the God indeed sang rightly, for the most beautiful mares are bred among us. SOCRATES. After this he will add, "Is a beautiful lyre not beautiful?" HIPPIAS. Yes. SOCRATES. He will ask again (for I am certain of this, making a conjecture from his character), "O best of men, is a beautiful pot not beautiful?" SOCRATES, who is so unrefined as to mix such cheap names into a serious matter? SOCRATES. Such is that man, O Hippias: for he is not polished or urbane, but sordid, caring for nothing else besides the truth. Nevertheless, he must be answered, and I shall speak first. If a pot has been fashioned by a good potter, smooth and round and sufficiently fired, like certain pots with two handles and very beautiful, which hold six pitchers: if he should ask about such a pot, we must answer that it is beautiful. For how shall we assert that what is beautiful is not beautiful? HIPPIAS. In no way, Socrates. SOCRATES. "Will not the pot also," he will ask, "be a beautiful thing?" Answer. HIPPIAS. I think it is so; a vessel is also beautiful when it is fashioned with art, but all this, if compared with a mare and a maiden, and all other such beautiful things, is unworthy of the name. SOCRATES. Behold, Hippias, now I understand what must be thrown back at that man who questions. "O man, you are ignorant of how wise that saying of Heraclitus is: 'The most beautiful of monkeys is deformed when compared with another genus of animals.' <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine of universal change and the unity of opposites.</note> Likewise, the most beautiful of pots is ugly if compared with the genus of maidens, as the wise Hippias has judged." Is it not so, Hippias? HIPPIAS. You have answered rightly indeed, Socrates. SOCRATES. Listen, for I know he will next bring this up: "What if someone compares the genus of maidens, Socrates, with the genus of gods? Will not the same thing happen as when the pot was compared with the maiden? Will not the most shapely of maidens appear deformed? Does not Heraclitus, whom you just brought in as a witness, teach this same thing—that the wisest man appears as a monkey to God in regard to wisdom, beauty, and all other things?" Shall we confess, Hippias, that the most shapely maiden is deformed when compared with the genus of gods? HIPPIAS. Who would contradict this, Socrates? SOCRATES. If we admit these things, he will laugh immediately and address me again in this manner: "Do you remember, Socrates, what you were asked?" And I will say, "I remember indeed that I was asked what the 'Beautiful' itself is." Then he will say: "When asked what is beautiful, you answer with something that happens to be no more beautiful than it is ugly, as you yourself confess. Shall I say it appears so?" Tell me, my friend, what you advise me to answer. HIPPIAS. This very thing. SOCRATES. He will also concede that compared to the gods, the human race is not beautiful. "But if," he will say, "I had asked you from the beginning what is both beautiful and ugly, and you had answered me the same things you have now, would you have answered rightly? Furthermore, does the 'Beautiful' itself, by which all things are decorated and appear beautiful whenever that form is present—does it seem to you to be a maiden, or a mare, or a lyre?" HIPPIAS. If he asks that, Socrates, it will be very easily answered what the 'Beautiful' itself is, by which all other things are decorated, or by whose presence they appear beautiful. The man is clearly most foolish and introduces nothing of noble substance. For if you answer him that the 'Beautiful' itself which he seeks is nothing other than **gold**, he will surely be at a loss and will not attempt to refute you. For it is agreed among all men that to whatever this is present, even if it seemed ugly before, it appears beautiful when adorned with gold. SOCRATES. You do not know, Hippias, how troublesome that man is, and how difficult it is for him to assent to those who speak. HIPPIAS. What then? He must necessarily concede what is rightly said. For if he rejects this, he will be a laughingstock to all. SOCRATES. And yet he will not only refuse this answer, but he will bite at me sharply. "O inflated man," he will say, "do you think Phidias was a crude craftsman?" <note>Phidias was the most famous sculptor of classical Greece, known for the statue of Athena Parthenos.</note> And I, as I think, will say I do not think so in any way. HIPPIAS. And rightly so. SOCRATES. Rightly, without a doubt. But after I have conceded that Phidias was a skilled craftsman, he will add this: "Do you think Phidias was ignorant of that which you call the Beautiful?" And I will say, "Why should he be?" Then he will say, "Since he did not make the eyes of Athena out of gold, nor the rest of the face, nor the feet, nor the hands—even though if they had been gold, they would have been most beautiful—but he made them of ivory. In this he surely erred through ignorance, since he did not know that gold is that whose presence makes all things beautiful to which it adheres." What shall we answer him when he says these things, O Hippias? HIPPIAS. Nothing difficult. For we shall confess that he did rightly. For ivory is also beautiful. SOCRATES. But he will ask, "Why did he not also make the pupils of the eyes ivory, but of stone, finding as far as possible a likeness of stone to ivory? Shall we answer, Hippias, that a beautiful stone is beautiful?" HIPPIAS. Yes, certainly, when it is appropriate. SOCRATES. But when it is not appropriate, must it be confessed as ugly, or not? HIPPIAS. It must be confessed, surely, when it is not at all appropriate. SOCRATES. To this he will add, "O wise man, do not ivory and gold, when they are appropriate, make all things beautiful? But on the contrary, when they are inappropriate?" Shall we deny it, or confess that he speaks rightly? HIPPIAS. We shall plainly confess that whatever is appropriate to a thing makes it beautiful. SOCRATES. Here he will bring this up: "Which is more appropriate for the beautiful pot of which we spoke above: when someone has moved it to the fire, to add a golden stirring-stick <term>tudecula: a stirring ladle or spatula</term> for the good legumes, or one made of fig-wood?" HIPPIAS. By Hercules! What kind of man are you describing? Do you not wish to utter his name? SOCRATES. You would not recognize the man even if you heard his name. HIPPIAS. Nevertheless, I recognize even now that he is unlearned. SOCRATES. He is far too inquisitive, Hippias. But what shall we say? Which of the two stirring-sticks rather fits the legumes and the pot? The one of fig-wood? For it provides a sweeter smell to the beans, and it will not spill the legumes by striking and breaking the pot, nor will it extinguish the fire with water, nor deprive the guests of a precious meal. On the contrary, the golden stirring-stick will do all these things. Therefore, it seems to me that the fig-wood is more appropriate than the golden one, unless you say something else. HIPPIAS. It is indeed more appropriate, although I... it is not fitting to be filled with such men when you are adorned with such a beautiful cloak and shoes, and excel in wisdom among all Greeks. But nothing prevents me from dealing with him. Therefore, instruct me beforehand, and deign to answer for my sake. For he will proceed thus: "If the fig-wood is more appropriate than the golden one, is it not more beautiful?" HIPPIAS. Since you have confessed, Socrates, that what is appropriate is more beautiful than what is inappropriate. SOCRATES. Must we confess, Hippias, that the fig-wood is more beautiful than the golden one? HIPPIAS.

<summary>Socrates challenges Hippias's claim that beauty is a specific material like gold by using the example of a common pot and the masterful artistry of Phidias. They conclude that beauty depends on what is "appropriate" or fitting for a specific use rather than intrinsic material value.</summary>

HIPPIAS. Do you want me to tell you, Socrates, how, by defining the Beautiful, you can distance him with long speeches? SOCRATES. Why wouldn't I? Provided you first tell me which of those two stirring-sticks should be answered as more appropriate and more beautiful. HIPPIAS. Well, if you wish, answer that the one made of fig-wood is more beautiful. SOCRATES... Now tell me what you were starting just a little while ago. For by this answer, in which I say that the Beautiful itself is gold, gold will appear no more beautiful, I think, than fig-wood. Now, what do you assert the Beautiful itself to be? HIPPIAS. I will tell you indeed: for you seem to me to require such a definition of the beautiful that can never appear ugly to anyone. SOCRATES. Entirely so, O Hippias; now you understand rightly. Only listen, and see if anyone could object against this, and say that I can praise nothing. Speak quickly, by the Gods. HIPPIAS. I say indeed that it is always, for anyone, and everywhere most beautiful to be healthy, wealthy, and honored among the Greeks until old age: and just as he decorated his deceased parents with an excellent funeral, so to be buried nobly and magnificently by his own children. SOCRATES. Oh, oh, Hippias! How wonderfully and excellently, and as befits you, you have spoken. By Juno, I love you greatly, because you seem to help me with the greatest goodwill according to your strength. Yet we have not yet caught that man; rather, believe me, he will now laugh at us more unrestrainedly. HIPPIAS. A wicked laugh, Socrates. For when he is unable to bring forth anything against these things, yet laughs, he will be laughing at himself, and he himself will be a laughingstock to all present. SOCRATES. Perhaps that is how it is; perhaps also from this response, as I divine, he will not only dare to mock me. HIPPIAS. But what then? SOCRATES. If by chance he has a stick, and I, fleeing, do not escape him, he will try to reach me thoroughly. HIPPIAS. What are you saying? Is he your master? If he does this, will he not be called to account and suffer punishment? Is your city unjust, and does it permit him to strike citizens? SOCRATES. Not at all. HIPPIAS. Will he not then be punished if he strikes you unjustly? SOCRATES. Not unjustly indeed, O Hippias, if I were to answer such things, but justly, it seems to me. HIPPIAS. To me also, since you think this. SOCRATES. Do you want me to tell you for what reason I think myself worthy of stripes for answering such things? Or will you strike me without knowing the cause? Or will you admit reason? HIPPIAS. It would be a grave thing, Socrates, if I did not admit it; but by what reason do you say that? SOCRATES. I will speak in the same way as a little before, imitating him, so that I do not bring forth before you the words he uses with me, which are too harsh and absurd. For he will undoubtedly address me thus: "Come now, Socrates, do you think he is struck unjustly who, having pronounced a Dithyramb <note>A wild, choral hymn of ancient Greece, often dedicated to Dionysus.</note> so inharmoniously, has strayed so far from the proposed question?" And I will ask, "In what way?" Then he will say: "Because you cannot remember that the question was about the Beautiful itself, which makes everything in which it is present beautiful—stone, wood, man, God, every action and every branch of learning—this very thing, O man, I seek: what is the Beautiful? But you have no more heard me than if a stone were sitting before me, or a millstone, having neither ears nor brain." If I, terrified, should answer thus to these things, will you take it heavily, Hippias? HIPPIAS. In what way? SOCRATES. Like this, I say. "However, Hippias said this was beautiful, although I asked him, as you now ask me, what is beautiful for all and exists always." What do you say? Will you take it hard if I say this? HIPPIAS. I know for certain, Socrates, that what I said is beautiful for everyone, and so it will appear. SOCRATES. "And will it be so?" he will say. "For is the beautiful always beautiful?" HIPPIAS. Entirely. SOCRATES. "And was it also so?" he will ask. HIPPIAS. And it was. SOCRATES. To this he will say, "And did the guest from Elis <note>Hippias was from the city of Elis.</note> say it was beautiful for Achilles to be buried after his parents, and for his grandfather Aeacus, and for others whoever were born of the gods, and finally for the gods themselves?" HIPPIAS. To the bad place with him! What kind of man is this? For such questions are profane, Socrates. SOCRATES. What indeed? When another asks SOCRATES. "Perhaps then you are the one," he will say, "who says to anyone and always it is beautiful to be honored by children with a funeral, and to perform funeral rites for parents. Was not Hercules one of all these, and others whom we mentioned before?" HIPPIAS. But I was not speaking of the gods. SOCRATES. Nor of heroes even, as it seems. HIPPIAS. Not certainly those who were sons of gods. SOCRATES. But those who were not of the gods? HIPPIAS. These very ones. SOCRATES. Therefore, according to your speech, among the number of heroes, for Tantalus and Dardanus and Zethus it is grave, profane, and ugly; but for Pelops and others similarly born, it is beautiful. HIPPIAS. So it seems to me. SOCRATES. To this he will say: "It seems to you then—which you did not say in the previous points—that to bury parents and be buried by children sometimes and for some happens to be ugly, or rather impossible; yet this is beautiful for all. Therefore, this is similar to those previous things, namely the maiden and the pot: and even more ridiculously, it is beautiful for some, and for others not at all." Wherefore he will rebuke me thus: "Can you not even today, Socrates, express what the Beautiful itself is, about which we ask?" And he will rightly scold me so, while I answer him such things. Such is our dispute, O Hippias. But sometimes, as if pitying my lack of skill and my ignorance, he himself meets me and asks whether such a thing seems to me to be the Beautiful itself, or about whatever else is disputed and mentioned. HIPPIAS. How do you say that, Socrates? SOCRATES. I will tell you. "O blessed Socrates," he says, "stop answering such things. For they are inept and easily refuted. But consider whether the Beautiful itself appears to be such a thing as we touched on above, when we were saying gold was beautiful for those to whom it is appropriate, but on the contrary for those to whom it is not; and all other things to which the 'appropriate' itself and its nature belongs become beautiful. See then whether this 'Appropriate' itself is the Beautiful; I, however, have been accustomed to concede these things everywhere. For I do not find anything to object. Does it seem to you that the Decorous <note>original: "decorum," referring to that which is fitting or appropriate.</note> is the Beautiful itself?" HIPPIAS. Entirely so, Socrates. SOCRATES. Let us take care lest we be deceived in something. HIPPIAS. We must certainly take care. SOCRATES. See therefore: do we call the 'Appropriate' that which, by its arrival, makes each thing in which it is present *appear* beautiful, or that which *makes it be* beautiful, or neither of these? HIPPIAS. To me indeed it makes it so, just as if someone deformed, adorned with decorous cloak and shoes, should appear more beautiful. SOCRATES. Is it not so that if the 'Appropriate' makes those things in which it is present appear more beautiful than they are, the 'Appropriate' would be a kind of deception concerning the beautiful? And this would not be what we are seeking, Hippias? For we were seeking that by which all beautiful things are beautiful; just as all great things are great by excess. For all these things are great: and even if they do not appear so, if they exceed, they must necessarily be great. So also we sought the Beautiful, by which all things are beautiful, whether they appear so or not—what would it be? It is not the 'Appropriate': for it makes things appear more beautiful than they are, as you yourself were saying; it does not allow them to appear as they are. But that which makes them *be* beautiful, as I was saying just now, whether they appear so or not, what is...

The fourth definition is false.
Refutation of the fourth definition.
The fifth definition of the beautiful.
Refutation.

<summary>Hippias proposes that a life of health, wealth, and honorable burial is the definition of beauty, but Socrates refutes this by showing it cannot apply to gods or heroes. They then pivot to exploring whether "The Appropriate" or "The Decorous" is the true essence of beauty.</summary>

80 Book Eleven.

...to be said: this indeed is sought, if only the Beautiful is sought. HIPPIAS. But the 'Appropriate', Socrates, makes things both *be* and *appear* beautiful when it is present. SOCRATES. Therefore it is impossible that things which are truly beautiful do not appear beautiful, while that which makes them appear is present. HIPPIAS. Impossible. SOCRATES. Shall we confess this, O Hippias? That all truly beautiful institutions and pursuits are also thought to be beautiful by men? Or on the contrary, are they unknown, so much so that concerning these things men fight most bitterly both privately and publicly? HIPPIAS. I think they are rather unknown, Socrates. SOCRATES. Yet they would not be unknown if, as they are beautiful, they also appeared beautiful: and they would appear so if the 'Appropriate' were the Beautiful, and forced things not only to be, but also to seem beautiful. Wherefore, if it is the 'Appropriate' that makes things *be* beautiful, it is indeed what we seek as the Beautiful, yet it is not that which forces them to *seem* so; but if the 'Appropriate' only makes them *seem* so, it is in no way the Beautiful itself which we seek. For that compels them to *be*. But the same thing cannot make things both appear and be at the same time, neither beautiful nor anything else. Let us choose now whether we think the 'Appropriate' is that which makes things appear beautiful, or that which makes them be so. HIPPIAS. I think it is what makes them appear, Socrates. SOCRATES. Oh my, how far the knowledge of the Beautiful itself has fled from us, Hippias, after the 'Appropriate' appeared to be something else besides the Beautiful itself. HIPPIAS. By Jove, Socrates, it seems to me very absurd. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, my friend, let us not yet give up: for I have not cast away all hope of finding what the Beautiful is. HIPPIAS. We must certainly hope, Socrates, for it is not difficult to find: I am conscious within myself that if I were to withdraw for a little while and consider it by myself, I could explain it to you more accurately than accuracy itself. SOCRATES. Alas, do not say that with a loud voice, O Hippias, lest it be indignant and escape us for a long time. Do you not see how much it has fatigued us so far? But I say nothing. For when you are alone, you will find it easily and safely. But come, by the gods, find it while I am present: and if you wish, as before, let us seek it together from now on. If we find it, it will be well. If not, I indeed will be content with my lot; but you, after you have gone, will find it easily. However, if we find it now, I will no longer be troublesome to you, asking what you have thought out with yourself. In the present, consider whether this seems to you to be the Beautiful. Attend diligently, I pray, lest I be delirious. Let this indeed be the Beautiful: **that which is useful**. I make a conjecture of this matter chiefly from this: because eyes are beautiful not when they are unable to see, but those which are fit and useful for seeing. HIPPIAS. Certainly. SOCRATES. And we call the whole body beautiful in the same way, one for running, another for wrestling. Likewise all animals, such as a beautiful horse, or a cock, or a quail; and all vessels and vehicles, both terrestrial and maritime, ships and triremes; also all instruments pertaining both to music and to other arts; likewise, if you wish, pursuits and laws—we call each of these beautiful in almost the same way, looking, of course, to the condition in which each was born, or manufactured, or placed as useful, and in what way useful, and for what useful, and when useful, calling it beautiful: but what is useless according to these things, we call ugly. Does the same not seem so to you as well, Hippias? HIPPIAS. To me indeed. SOCRATES. We speak well then now, that above all other things, that which is **useful** is the Beautiful itself. HIPPIAS. Very well indeed, Socrates. SOCRATES. Is it not that what can effect something is useful for that which can be effected; and what cannot is useless? HIPPIAS. Entirely. SOCRATES. Therefore power is beautiful, and impotence is ugly. HIPPIAS. Most especially, for all other things testify to this for us, and civic matters particularly. Since to be powerful in one's own city and republic is the most beautiful of all things, but to be impotent is most ugly. SOCRATES. You speak excellently. But is it not for this very reason that wisdom is the most beautiful of all things, and ignorance on the contrary the most ugly? HIPPIAS. And what do you think, Socrates? SOCRATES. Rest a little, my sweet friend. For I suspect and fear concerning what we are saying. HIPPIAS. What do you fear, Socrates? Are these things not cleverly said? SOCRATES. I would wish it so, but consider this with me: does anyone ever effect what he neither knows how to do nor can do? HIPPIAS. In no way. For how could he do what he cannot? SOCRATES. Those who err and do evil things, and effect them through imprudence—if they had not been able to do these things, would they have done them? HIPPIAS. Least of all. SOCRATES. But indeed those who can, can by power: for they do not do it by impotence. HIPPIAS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. And can all men do what they do? HIPPIAS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. But all men do many more evil things than good ones, starting from their early age and throughout their whole life, nor do they leave them of their own accord. HIPPIAS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. What further? This power and these useful things which lead to the execution of evils—shall we call them beautiful, or is it far from that? HIPPIAS. Far from it, it seems to me, Socrates. SOCRATES. Therefore the powerful and the useful, as it seems, is not the Beautiful itself for us. HIPPIAS. Unless it is able to do good things, and contributes to them. SOCRATES. That idea is therefore rejected: that the powerful and useful is simply the beautiful. But was it this, O Hippias, to which our mind was looking—namely, that the powerful and useful for producing **good** is the beautiful? HIPPIAS. It seems so to me. SOCRATES. This is the **beneficial**, is it not? HIPPIAS. Greatly. SOCRATES. Thus indeed beautiful bodies, beautiful institutions of laws, and wisdom, and other things which we related a little before, are all beautiful because they are beneficial. HIPPIAS. It is agreed. SOCRATES. Therefore the beneficial itself seems to us to be the beautiful. HIPPIAS. Most of all. SOCRATES. And yet the beneficial is that which produces good. HIPPIAS. That very thing. SOCRATES. But the producer is nothing other than the **cause**, is it not? HIPPIAS. It is so. SOCRATES. Therefore the cause of good is the beautiful. HIPPIAS. It is indeed. SOCRATES. But the cause is one thing, and that of which it is the cause is another. For the cause cannot be the cause of the cause itself. This can be conjectured most from here: was it not established that the cause is efficient? HIPPIAS. Plainly. SOCRATES. But by the efficient, the effect is made, not the efficient. HIPPIAS. It is true. SOCRATES. The efficient is one thing, the effect another. HIPPIAS. Another, certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore the cause is not the cause of itself, but of that which is produced by it. HIPPIAS. It is so. SOCRATES. Therefore, if the beautiful is the cause of good, the good is made by the beautiful. And for this reason, as it seems, we desire prudence and all other beautiful things, because the work which is born from these, which is the good, is to be desired. Whence, through those things we have found, the beautiful seems to have the character of a certain father toward the good. HIPPIAS. Entirely so, for you speak excellently. SOCRATES. Is this also excellent: that neither the father is the son, nor the son in turn the father? HIPPIAS. This too. SOCRATES. Indeed, neither is the cause the effect, nor the effect the cause. HIPPIAS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. By Jove, O best of men, neither is the beautiful the good, nor is the good the beautiful. Does it seem possible to you from these things which have been said? HIPPIAS. Not to me, by Jove. SOCRATES. Does this please us, and do we want to assert it, that neither the beautiful is good...

<margin>
Utility is proposed, that the genus of the beautiful may be sought.
Whether the beneficial is the genus of the beautiful.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates and Hippias investigate the "Useful" as a definition for beauty, refining it to the "Beneficial" (useful for good). However, they encounter a logical paradox: if the beautiful is the cause of the good, they must be distinct things, meaning the beautiful itself is not good—a conclusion they find unacceptable.</summary>

Hippias Major, Or, on the Beautiful. 81

...good, nor the good beautiful. HIPPIAS. Not by Jove, it does not please me. SOCRATES. By Jove, it pleases me no less, O Hippias, from these things that have been said. HIPPIAS. So indeed it seems. SOCRATES. No longer, therefore, does that speech seem excellent, as it did above, by which the beautiful was asserted to be that which is beneficial and useful and powerful for producing some good. Rather, if it is possible, it is to be judged more absurd than those previous ones, in which we called the maiden, and the individual things we related above, the beautiful itself. HIPPIAS. It appears so. SOCRATES. Indeed, Hippias, I do not know where to turn, for I hesitate and am in doubt. But do you perhaps have something? HIPPIAS. At present, not at all; but as I said at another time, if I consider it with myself, I know for certain I shall find something. SOCRATES. But I seem to myself, because of a burning greed for learning, in no way able to tolerate your delay. But look, now something else comes to my mind. Attend, I pray. Is it **that which delights us**? (I do not speak of any pleasure, but of that which is through sight and hearing). Should such a thing be called beautiful? For how can we fight against it, when beautiful men and all ornaments, beautiful paintings and figurines delight us when we look at them? Beautiful songs also and voices, and all music, speeches and conversations similarly affect us? Wherefore, if we were to answer that bold and stubborn man that the beautiful is what delights through sight and hearing, would we not restrain his boldness? What do you think? HIPPIAS. Now, Socrates, it seems to me that what the beautiful itself is has been cleverly said. SOCRATES. What then of beautiful pursuits and laws? Shall we say they are beautiful because they are pleasant through sight and hearing, or are they contained in some other form? HIPPIAS. These things are perhaps so, Socrates, even if they escape the man. SOCRATES. By the dog, Hippias, not that man whom I would fear most of all whenever I was delirious or professed to say something when I said nothing. HIPPIAS. Whom do you mean? SOCRATES. Socrates the son of Sophroniscus, <note>Socrates refers to himself as if he were another person, a typical Socratic irony to represent his internal critical faculty.</note> who would no more allow me to judge these things easily without discussion than to think I knew what I do not know. HIPPIAS. And yet to me also, after you have spoken, that which pertains to laws seems to be something else. SOCRATES. Rest a little, Hippias. For we seem to have fallen into the same ambiguity concerning the beautiful as a little before, while we thought we had something certain. HIPPIAS. In what way do you say that, Socrates? SOCRATES. I will tell you indeed what seems to me, if I am saying anything. For these things which pertain to pursuits and laws are perhaps not outside the sense of seeing and hearing. Furthermore, let us bear this speech which asserts that what is pleasant to these senses is beautiful, and let us not bring laws into the middle. But if someone should ask us—either he whom I mention or anyone else—in this manner: "What, Hippias and Socrates? Do you judge only that pleasure which is perceived by two senses to be beautiful? But those which drench the other senses with sweetness—food, drink, the act of love, and all other things of this kind—do you not call them beautiful? Or perhaps you do not place any pleasure in these sweet things, nor in the senses except in hearing and seeing?" What, I say, Hippias, shall we answer? HIPPIAS. We shall assent, Socrates, that great pleasures are present in the other senses. SOCRATES. But he will say, "For what cause, since these are no less pleasures than those others, do you deprive them of the name of beautiful?" Because, we will answer, there is no one who would not laugh at us if we said eating is not sweet but beautiful; likewise that a sweet odor is not sweet but beautiful. Also concerning the movements of love, everyone would equally not contend that it is a most sweet thing, but when anyone performs it, he ought to perform it so that he removes it from the sight of men as if it were a most ugly thing. When we have said these things, Hippias, he will perhaps answer: "I have understood for a long time that shame hinders you from calling pleasures of this kind beautiful, because they do not seem so to men. But I was not seeking what commonly seems beautiful, but what the beautiful itself is." For we shall say, I think, what we have posited as being beautiful, namely that part of the pleasant which soothes through the eyes and ears. But can you, Hippias, use this same argument, or shall we say something else? HIPPIAS. We shall say nothing else besides this, Socrates. SOCRATES. "You speak excellently," he will bring in. "If therefore only what comes through sight and hearing is beautiful, then what delights through another sense is not at all beautiful." Shall we confess? HIPPIAS. We shall confess. SOCRATES. But he will ask again: "Is that which is pleasant through sight also pleasant through sight and hearing? And that which is pleasant through hearing, also pleasant through hearing and sight?" To these things we would say, in no way is that which is through one through both; for you seem to seek this. But we said that either of the two pleasures is beautiful in itself, and also if both are together. Must it not be answered thus? HIPPIAS. Exactly so. SOCRATES. "Is it then," he will say, "that a pleasure differs from a pleasure in that very thing by which it is a pleasure? I am not asking whether one pleasure is greater or less, or more or less a pleasure, but whether one from among many pleasures differs from another by this very thing, that this is a pleasure and that is not." We shall say it does not seem so to us. HIPPIAS. It does not seem so, plainly. SOCRATES. So he will bring this up: "Is it not for some other thing than because they are pleasures that you have chosen these pleasures especially from the number of all others, looking at something in both of them, because they evidently have a certain nature differing from others, to which you were indeed looking when you asserted they were beautiful? For the pleasure of sight is not beautiful for this reason, because it is through sight. For if this were the cause of that beauty, in no way would that which is through hearing be beautiful, since it is in no way effected through sight." Shall we confess that he speaks the truth? HIPPIAS. We shall certainly confess it. SOCRATES. "Nor again is the pleasure of hearing beautiful because it happens through hearing? Otherwise that which is perceived through sight would not be beautiful, since it is not the same as that which is effected through hearing." Shall we confess, Hippias, that the man who speaks thus tells the truth? HIPPIAS. The truth indeed. SOCRATES. "But nevertheless both," he will say, "are beautiful, as you say." Do we say so? HIPPIAS. We certainly say so. SOCRATES. Therefore they have something common and the same, which makes them beautiful, or which is present commonly to both, and properly to each. Otherwise both would not be beautiful, and each one as well. Come, answer me as if to him. HIPPIAS. I answer that it seems to me as you say. SOCRATES. For if these pleasures both received something which neither of them experienced individually, they would never exist as beautiful through a passion of this kind. HIPPIAS. It is so, Socrates. For how can it be that what neither of them suffers, both should endure? SOCRATES. Does it not seem so to you? HIPPIAS. I would be entirely unskillful in such matters and such speech. SOCRATES. They are pleasant indeed, Hippias. But perhaps there is a danger lest it seems to me that I perceive something which is in such a way as it seems impossible to you to be. But I see nothing. HIPPIAS. No...

<margin>
Delight as the genus of the beautiful.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates proposes that beauty is "pleasure through sight and hearing." They debate why other sensory pleasures (like taste or sex) are excluded and begin to analyze whether beauty is a property that must belong to individual pleasures or can exist only when they are combined as a pair.</summary>

This translation renders the Neo-Latin text of Marsilio Ficino’s 15th-century translation of Plato’s *Hippias Major* (the end of the dialogue) and the beginning of the *Lysis*. The text focuses on the metaphysical and logical distinctions between attributes of a pair versus attributes of individuals, leading to the famous conclusion that "beautiful things are difficult."

# Book Eleven.

**SOCRATES**
There is no danger, O Socrates—rather, you perceive it most clearly. For indeed, many things of this kind turn over in my mind, to which I do not grant belief, since they are not approved by you, who have accumulated more money through the pursuit of wisdom than any other mortals of our time. But I, O friend, as one who has never gained anything, think that perhaps you are playing with me out of [deliberate] [Note: *industriaque*] effort; you deceive me, so many things seem to me [to be thus].

**HIPPIAS**
No one will understand better than you, Socrates, whether I am playing or not, if you begin to bring forth those things which occur to you: for you will seem to say nothing, since [Note: *quoniam*] you will never [Note: *nunquam*] find [Note: *quam*] a thing which neither I suffer nor you, yet we both suffer together.

**SOCRATES**
How do you mean, Hippias? Perhaps you are saying something that I do not quite understand. But listen to me, I will explain more clearly what I feel. It seems to me that it might happen that I am not [a certain way], nor am I, nor you likewise; yet it is possible for us both to suffer this [condition]. Likewise, there are other things which we both suffer, yet neither of us exists as that thing.

**HIPPIAS**
You seem to be asserting monsters again, O Socrates, and certainly more so than you answered a little while ago.

**SOCRATES**
Just pay attention. If we were both just, would not each of us be so? Or if each were unjust, would not both be? Or if both were healthy, would not each be? And if each of us suffers from something, or is wounded, or struck, or has suffered anything else, do we not both suffer the same thing? Furthermore, if we were both golden, or silver, or ivory, and even, if you wish, well-born, or wise, or honored, or old, or young, or anything else human—would it not be entirely necessary for each of us to be that thing?

**SOCRATES** [Note: Likely a misprint in the source for **HIPPIAS** based on the context of the dialogue].
Entirely so.

**SOCRATES**
But you yourself, O Hippias, do not consider things as wholes, nor do those with whom you are accustomed to dispute; you applaud immediately because you have grasped [the concept of] the beautiful, and you tear apart each thing by debating it: and for that reason, great bodies [of truth] escape you, which have obtained a continuous essence from nature. And now the truth flees you concerning these things to such an extent that you think there is some affection or essence which concerns both together, but in no way concerns each one: and conversely, that which is indeed [Note: *quidem*] present in each, is by no means present in both. Thus absurd, rash, inept, and foolish you are.

**SOCRATES**
Such are our affairs, Hippias—not as one might wish, as the trite

[Margin: **Proverb.**]

proverb goes, but as they are able to be. But you always help us by advising. For before you advised us on these matters, how stupidly we were affected—I will reveal it to you even more clearly: I shall relate what we think about these things. Shall I speak?

**HIPPIAS**
Relate it to one who knows, Socrates; for I know the condition of all those who are engaged in disputation. Nevertheless, if you desire, tell it.

**SOCRATES**
I do indeed desire it. For indeed, best of men, we were so ignorant before you said these things to us, that we thought of me and you that each of us is one, yet we are not both that which each of us is—for we are not one, but two. So foolish were we! But now we have learned from you that if we are both two, it is necessary for each of us to be two likewise; and if each is one, both are equally one. For it is impossible, according to the universal and continuous reason of essence, Hippias, for it to be otherwise. But what both were, the same is also each: and conversely, what each is, both are equally. Now, therefore, persuaded by you, I sit here; but first, O Hippias, remind me of this: whether I and you are one, or you are two and I am two?

**HIPPIAS**
What are you saying, Socrates?

**SOCRATES**
These very things I say. For I fear to speak openly before you: for you are angry with me and you disturb me when you seem to yourself to be saying something [important]. At the same time, tell me, is not each of us one, and it happens that each is one?

**HIPPIAS**
Entirely so, Socrates.

**SOCRATES**
But if one, then also odd; or do you not think "one" is odd?

**HIPPIAS**
I do indeed.

**SOCRATES**
Are we both, since we are two, therefore odd?

**HIPPIAS**
By no means, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES**
But both are even, are they not?

**HIPPIAS**
Even.

**SOCRATES**
Then because both are even, is each of us also even?

**HIPPIAS**
Not at all.

**SOCRATES**
Therefore, it does not follow entirely, as you just said, that whatever is true of both is true of each, and whatever is true of each is true of both.

**HIPPIAS**
Not in things of this sort, but in those things which I recounted above.

**SOCRATES**
That is enough for me, Hippias. For those suffice, since some things seem to be one way, and others another. Indeed, I said—if you remember from where this discourse arose—that pleasures through sight and through hearing are not beautiful because of that which each of them has [individually], but the pair [does not have], or because the pair has it, but each does not; rather, [they are beautiful] because both have it and each has it. And for that reason, both and each are beautiful, and you conceded this. And for this reason, through that very essence which follows both, I judged both to be beautiful, if indeed they are beautiful; but through that which deserts the one [individually], I did not. And now I still think the same. But tell me as if from the beginning: if pleasures which occur through sight and hearing are beautiful, both and each, does that which makes them beautiful not follow both and each?

**HIPPIAS**
Entirely.

**SOCRATES**
Is it because each and both are pleasures that they are beautiful? Or by this reasoning, would other pleasures be no less beautiful? For it is established that those are no less pleasures.

**HIPPIAS**
Not at all.

**SOCRATES**
But because they occur through sight and hearing, for that reason they are said to be beautiful.

**SOCRATES** [Note: Likely **HIPPIAS**]
So it is said.

**SOCRATES**

**HIPPIAS**
Exactly so.

**SOCRATES**

**HIPPIAS**
It is.

**SOCRATES**
Therefore, each is not beautiful by that which does not follow each; for that which belongs to "both" does not follow "each." Wherefore it is permitted to call those two "beautiful" according to the hypothesis, but each of them by no means. Or do we say otherwise? Is this not necessary?

**HIPPIAS**
It seems so.

**SOCRATES**
Must it be said that both are indeed beautiful, but each is not?

**HIPPIAS**
What prevents it?

**SOCRATES**
This, my friend, seems to stand in my way: that certain things were judged to be present in others in such a way that if they are present in both, they are present in each; and conversely, if in each, then in both. Are these all the things you recounted?

**HIPPIAS**
They certainly were.

**SOCRATES**
But the things I related are not: in the number of which was that which is called "both" and that which is called "each." Is it not so?

**HIPPIAS**
It is.

**SOCRATES**
Which does it seem to you, O Hippias? In which category is the beautiful? From those you set forth? As in, if I am robust and you are, we are both robust. Likewise, if I am just and you are, we are both; and conversely, if both, then each. Or does nothing prevent it from happening as it occurs in even and odd numbers? Where both are sometimes even, yet each is odd, and sometimes both are even [and each is even]. Furthermore, each is sometimes such that they cannot be expressed [irrational], yet both can be expressed, and sometimes they cannot. And many other things of this kind which I said occurred to me—in which of these do you place the beautiful? Does it appear to you as it does to me? For it seems to me too absurd that we both should be beautiful, yet each is not. Or conversely, each is beautiful, but not both, or anything else of that sort. Do you choose as I do? Or rather in that [other] way?

**HIPPIAS**
Thus indeed [I choose as you do].
