# Hippias Major, or, On Beauty.

**SOCRATES**
You do well, Hippias, so that we may free ourselves from a longer inquiry. For if the beautiful is from these things, then that which delights through sight and hearing will no longer be the beautiful. For it makes "both" beautiful, but "each" not at all. But this is impossible, as is agreed between us.

**HIPPIAS**
It is certainly agreed.

**SOCRATES**
It is therefore impossible that the pleasant through sight and hearing is the beautiful; for if that were the beautiful, something impossible would follow.

**HIPPIAS**
These things are true.

**SOCRATES**
At this point, that contentious fellow will say: "Explain again from the beginning, since this has failed you: what do you say this 'beautiful' is, which is in both pleasures, on account of which you called them beautiful, honoring them above the rest?" It seems necessary to me, O Hippias, that we answer that they are harmless beyond other pleasures, and the best, both the pair and each. Or do you have anything else

[Margin: **Another false definition of beauty.**]

by which they differ from the others?

**HIPPIAS**

Socrates, do you think all these things are but certain scrapings and clippings of speeches, as I said before, broken down into the smallest bits? But a certain marvelous fortune detains me: for I am always wandering and in need. Whenever I show my poverty to you wise men, I am rebuked again by you with words. For you object continually, as you have also objected now, that I deal in stupid, meager, and worthless things. Finally, when persuaded by you, I bring forth the same things as you—that it is by far the best to be able to deliver an elegantly and ornately composed speech in court or any other assembly—then some of our people, and especially that man who always refutes me, scolds me gravely. That man is very close to me in kin, and lives together with me. Therefore, as soon as I enter the house and he hears me saying such things, he asks why I am not ashamed to dispute about beautiful institutions of life, when I have been so clearly refuted concerning the beautiful, such that I am ignorant of what the beautiful itself is. For he says: "By what reason will you understand which speech is beautifully composed and which is not, or any other action to be beautiful or base, while you remain ignorant of what the beautiful itself is? And when you are so affected, do you not think it is better for you to die than to live?" Thus it happens to me, as I was saying, that I am badly treated with words both by you and by him, and I hear ill [of myself]. But perhaps it is worthwhile to tolerate all these things; for it is not absurd, provided I have gained something. For I have profited so much from the company of both of you, Hippias, that I seem to myself now to understand that proverb: "Beautiful things are difficult."

**SOCRATES.** You do well, Hippias, to free us from a longer inquiry. For if the beautiful is among these things, then that which delights through sight and hearing would no longer be the beautiful. For it makes both beautiful, but each one not at all <note>Socrates is pointing out a logical paradox: if the "beautiful" is defined by two things together, it implies that neither thing is beautiful on its own, which seems impossible</note>. ## PLATO'S LYSIS, OR, ON FRIENDSHIP.
### ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.

WHERE Socrates disputes with the <term>sophists</term> <note>professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized for prioritizing persuasion over truth</note> and their followers, he refutes false opinions and signifies the truth rather than teaching it. For sharp minds, once false things are refuted, hunt down the truth from a small track. This is clear in the *Euthydemus*, *Protagoras*, *Meno*, *Hippias*, *Euthyphro*, and *Lysis*. But where he holds discourse with his own disciples and students, he shows and teaches, as is understood from many dialogues. In the *Lysis*, therefore, since friendship is disputed among the disciples of the sophists, Socrates strives to confute false ideas rather than show the truth. But what Plato's opinion on friendship and love is, we can gather not just from this book, but from the books on *Laws* and many others. He wishes friendship to be an honest communion of perpetual will. Its end is one life. Its principle is kinship. Its medium is love. By calling it "honest," he excludes the company of wicked men and the gatherings of the lustful. By "perpetual," he warns that the light-hearted goodwill of youths, even if honest, is not yet to be called friendship. By "will," he signifies that a mere similarity of opinion or art is not sufficient to perfect friendship. By "communion," he indicates a reciprocity of goodwill. The end of this is that from two souls, one might be made by will; from one will, one life; and finally from one life, the enjoyment of one and the same divine idea. The principle by which the desire for this communion is excited is kinship. Kinship signifies a harmony in the Idea, the star, the genius, and a certain affection of soul and body. For those who hang from the One, strive to return into the One, through the One, and toward the One. Love exists as the medium and a kind of path to friendship. Since love is a desire for the beautiful, and friendship is both led by and named from love, it is necessary that those who are to be friends be beautiful. Beautiful, I say, in that their souls are beautiful. For man is his soul; the body of man is his instrument; and whoever loves a beautiful body loves not the man, but the things which belong to the man. Therefore, whenever that kinship is present and the beauty of souls concurs, perfect friendship is born. If the form of the body is added to this beauty of souls, they begin to love more quickly and attain the habit of friendship in a short time. This happened in the mutual goodwill of Plato and Dion. But if the form of the body is joined with deformity of soul, a desire for shameful intercourse arises, not for honest communion. Whence not friendship, but rather petulance first, and then discord proceeds. Wherefore, if kinship is lacking, they are never friends. If kinship is present but all beauty is lacking, they are sometimes well-wishers rather than friends. But if to kinship the beauty of the body is joined without that of the soul, the heat of obscene intercourse arises instead of the desire for friendship. When one is beautiful in soul and the other ugly, that kinship produces a zeal for admonition and rebuke. But if the soul of one is beautiful and the other is neither beautiful nor ugly, the will of teaching and learning from one another arises from the kinship. Finally, from that rebuke and this teaching, friendship is born. This is indeed shown by the love of Socrates for Phaedrus and Alcibiades. But truly, kinship having found beauty on both sides quickly procreates an indissoluble friendship. This was established in the goodwill of Plato and Aster. And as is gathered from many things, this is our Plato's opinion on friendship. In this dialogue, first he rebukes those who abuse love and serve shameful lust under the appearance of friendship. Then he admonishes those who, from the form of the body alone, think themselves worthy to be loved. Thirdly, he refutes those who thought less truly about friendship. Lastly, he indicates a certain track for sagacious souls to hunt for friendship. The individual parts are clear to those reading them in their places. For while Socrates derides Hippothales and Ctesippus with irony and jokes, he signifies that they were captured by shameful love. And while he instructs the youths in morals in their presence, he admonishes lovers in what way they should love and how they should live together. And when he had instructed the lovers, he proceeds to the second part of the dialogue to instruct those who are loved, where by a long series of induction he teaches that it is proper to fish for friends not by the shadowy form of this little body, but by the true beauty of the soul—namely, wisdom and prudence. In the third place, he refutes, first, the opinion of Solon, who said that those who are loved are friends—yet those who love are often hated. He adds also that it is not only lovers who are friends, because those who love are often held in hatred. Where he concludes that reciprocal goodwill should be called friendship. Then he reprehends Empedocles, who wished that any simple likeness should suffice for friendship. The similarity of many arts declares this to be false, for they more often produce envy and hatred than...

--- Page 103 ---
84 Book Twelve.

...than they produce friendship. Next comes the opinion of Hesiod and Heraclitus: that dissimilar things are friends. This is established as false from the fact that hatred and love, since they are dissimilar, are not friends, nor are a just man and an unjust man, and so on for others. If something ever seems to desire its dissimilar—as the dry desires moisture, and the cold heat—it must be said that it does not love its contrary, but seeks the restoration of itself from its contrary. For that which uses excessive heat beyond its nature is reduced to its natural temperance through cold. Therefore it loves not the cold, but temperance through the cold. The same is to be judged of other contraries. Having refuted these, Socrates introduces a certain opinion as if he were prophesying. He divides the affections of the soul in three ways: the good soul, the bad, and the neutral. The bad can never be a friend to the good because of their diversity. The bad is harmed by the bad because of injustice. Therefore, these are not friends to each other. It is also impossible for the neutral to love the bad; for since the bad is harmful, it is always held in hatred by its very nature. It remains that friendship must be between the good and the bad, or the neutral and the good. And that indeed consists in joy, this in desire. From these, two species of friendship have arisen. But certain objections arise which seem to disturb this, which Socrates brings out openly, while he hints at the solutions secretly. First, because the good is like the good; and as we saw, it was said against Empedocles that likes are not friends. Here it must be understood that it was not said that likes can in no way become friends, but rather it was denied that simply any similarity suffices to procreate friendship. Likewise, when it is objected secondly: the good man is sufficient to himself, therefore he does not desire another; hence he does not love, wherefore he is not a friend of the good. It must be explained that this absurdity does not follow from Plato's mind, but from the sayings of Empedocles and Heraclitus, in which they do not distinguish the desire of love from friendship; therefore, where there is friendship, there must be perpetual craving. Plato, however, wishes friendship to be a certain habit contracted from long-lasting love. Thus it happens that love is friendship being born. Friendship, however, is long-standing love, in which much more of pleasure remains than of desire. From which it follows that he who had once craved, now takes delight. Thus the habit of friendship does not necessarily require the heat of desire for one who is present, but rather delight. Therefore, if the good man desires the good man less, he does not rejoice in him any less; and this is very powerful for preserving the reason for friendship. And this is one species of friendship—namely, between good and good, established in joy rather than in desire. There is also another, which includes more desire than pleasure, arising between the neutral and the good. In what way this happens, and for whose sake, and because of what, is clear enough in the text. He describes it first as opinion offers it, then gradually amends it. For when he had said that the neutral loves the good friend for the sake of the bad enemy, for the sake of the friendship of the good, he immediately corrects it by objecting to what was said. Here he first teaches that all friendships directed toward men are imperfect, and are images of the friendship that looks toward the first good itself and the author of all things, which is loved first and is the cause for all these things to be loved. And whoever loves anything has that first thing as the end of his love. For from the first good, goodness is in all things; from the first beauty, grace is present in individuals; goodness draws us, beauty allures us. Therefore, it is not these lower things that move us, but that first thing in these things draws and allures us. Therefore, we love that thing in these things and at the same time out of these things, not the things themselves. In this, our Plato's piety toward God and his supreme religion shine forth wonderfully. He shows, moreover, that we are not always friends for the sake of another. For we do not desire the first good for the sake of another good. Likewise, you would not desire the good because of the bad. For even if all evil were removed from the nature of things, the good would remain pleasing by its own nature, and the appetite in that which is less good would be drawn toward attaining the greater good. For it is not the bad that excites the appetite for the highest good, but the lack of the less good itself turns it toward its own replenishment in the highest good: which is indeed not bad, because the bad never leads to the good, nor contrary to contrary, but it should rather be called the beginning of the good. Having brought these points for amendment, he introduces a certain principle for investigating perfect friendship. He says that kinship and harmony of nature produce friendship, about which we have said enough at the beginning. Lastly, he bites at those youths and adolescents because they are ignorant of what is worthily to be loved; what true friendship is; in what way it may be honestly and stably forged; and before they learn these things, they strive to enter into friendship rashly, procaciously, and petulantly. But lest he make them hostile to himself, he signified these things secretly, and rebuked himself along with them. This is enough for the argument. Let us come to the *Lysis*.

**SOCRATES. HIPPOTHALES. CTESIPPVS. MENEXENVS. LYSIS.**

**The Occasion of the Dialogue.**

I WAS GOING from the Academy straight to the Lyceum by the suburban way next to the walls, and when I had come to the gate where the fountain of Panops is, I came upon Hippothales the son of Hieronymus, and Ctesippus the Paeanian, and many other youths with them. And when Hippothales saw me coming, he said: "O Socrates, whither and from whence?" And I said: "I am going from the Academy straight to the Lyceum." Then he said: "Come here, why do you not come straight to us? For it is proper." To this I indeed said: "It is proper; but where, and with whom among you do you want me to be?" He then said, pointing to a certain gymnasium <term>gymnasium</term> <note>a place for both physical exercise and philosophical discussion</note> across from the walls surrounded by a wall and with an open door: "Here," he said, "we and many others, and indeed honest ones, exercise ourselves." "In what thing especially is this exercise of yours?" "In the <term>palæstra</term> <note>a wrestling school or area for physical training</note> which has recently been constructed, and for the most part in speeches, which we would gladly share with you." "You do well. But who is the teacher there?" <margin>Miccus, Socrates' companion</margin> "Your companion and praiser, Miccus." "By Jove, he is not a bad one, but a sufficiently great <term>sophist</term>." "Do you wish to follow me inside, so that you may see those who are there?" "I would first gladly hear why I should enter, and who is the beautiful one there." "One seems so to one of us, O Socrates, and another to another." "But to you, who, O Hippothales? Tell me, I beseech you." But he, being asked, blushed. Then I said: "O Hippothales, son of Hieronymus, there is no need for you to open whether you love someone or not. For I know that you not only love, but that you have progressed so far in love. For in other things I am dull and useless: but this one gift has been given to me by God, that at first sight I recognize both lovers and the beloved." When he heard this, he blushed much more. But Ctesippus said: "How polite you are, Hippothales, who refuse to tell the name of your beloved to Socrates. For if he stays here for a little while, he will be killed by hearing it constantly from you. For he has long since filled our ears, O Socrates, and made them deaf with the name of Lysis. And when he drinks a little, it is easy that even if we were awakened from sleep, we would seem to hear the name of Lysis. And it would not be so troublesome, even if it were troublesome, to hear him speaking of him in prose, if he did not try to exhaust us with his poems and commentaries, and what is most troublesome, he sings of his loves in a wonderful voice, which we are forced to endure: but now, being asked by you, he blushes." "This Lysis," I said, "seems to be a youth: I guess this, for hearing his name, I did not recognize it." "You," he said, "rarely hear his name pronounced, but he is still called a youth by his father's name, since he is a very noble man: for I am persuaded of this, it cannot be that you are ignorant of the boy's form: for he is endowed with such excellence that he could be known by all by that alone." "Whose son is he?" I asked; "tell me, I pray." "He is the eldest son of Democrates of Aexone." Then I said: "May it be so, O Hippothales, that you have found a noble and constant love. But come, show me also those things which you show to these, that I may see whether you know what it is proper to say concerning the beloved, either to himself or to others." "Do you think any of these things he says, O Socrates, are worth weighing?" "Would you deny that you love him whom he named here?" "By no means," he said: "but I say I compose or write nothing about my loves." To this Ctesippus said: "He is not of sound mind, but he raves and is insane." Then I said: "O Hippothales, I do not care much to hear either the poems or even the song, if you have composed any to the youth: but I desire to understand what your mind is toward boys in matters of love." Then he said: "Ctesippus here will tell you; for he knows and remembers it, if indeed, as he says, every day...

--- Page 104 ---
## Lysis, Or, on Friendship. 85

...every day he is beaten over the head by hearing it from me." "Very much so, by the gods," said Ctesippus. "For it is truly ridiculous that although he loves this boy above all others, he can bring forth nothing from his own wit that even a child would say. For that which the whole city proclaims about Democrates and Lysis, this boy's grandfather, and about all their ancestors—wealth, a multitude of horses, victories at the Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean games with chariots and horses—he also goes around repeating these things, and even older things than these. And recently he recounted to us at a certain banquet that Hercules was received as a guest, because their great-grandfather had received Hercules in hospitality on account of kinship, since he also was born from Jove and the daughter of a certain prince of the people—things which even old women sing. And many other such things, O Socrates. These are the things which he forces us to hear by narrating and singing them." When I heard these things, I said: "O ridiculous Hippothales, before you have conquered, you compose and sing an encomium <note>a speech of high praise</note> to yourself." "I do not prepare or sing these to myself, O Socrates," he said. "You do not think so," I said. "Why do you say that?" he asked. "Most of all, these odes redound to you alone. For if you should catch such a friend, such praises will be an ornament to you, as to a certain conqueror, since you have found such a friend. But if he escapes you, the greater the praises you have attributed to him, the more you will be judged ridiculous for being deprived of such great goods. <margin>A precept in acquiring friends.</margin> Whoever, therefore, is wise in acquiring friends does not praise any of them before he has attained their familiarity; for he fears the future: for most people, when they perceive themselves being praised and extolled, swell with pride and insolence; does it not seem the same to you?" "To me, indeed." "Is it not true that the prouder they are, the more difficult they are to catch?" "It is likely." "What kind of hunter would he seem to be to you, if someone drove the wild beasts away in such a way that they became both safer and harder to catch in the future?" "An unskilled one, obviously." "And is it not the mark of an unskilled man not to soothe but rather to provoke people with speeches and songs?" "It seems so." "See therefore, O Hippothales, lest you make yourself liable to all these things on account of your study of poems. I truly think you will consider no one a good poet who has harmed himself by his poem." "None, by Jove, for what an absurdity would that be?" "For this very reason, O Socrates, I communicate my mind to you: and if you have anything else, advise me by what means one might, either by speaking or by acting, reconcile to himself those whom he loves." "It is not easy to say," I replied. "But if you would join me in a conversation with him, perhaps I could show you what things ought to be said to him, instead of these things which they say you speak and sing." "Nothing shall be an impediment. For if you enter with Ctesippus and sit there and dispute, of his own accord, I believe, he will be present. For he is exceedingly eager to listen. And there also, celebrating the <term>Hermaea</term> <note>original: "Mercurialia"; a festival in honor of the god Hermes/Mercury</note>, both the youths and the boys gather together. Therefore he will come to you, and if he does not, he is an intimate of Ctesippus on account of Menexenus, his cousin, of whom he is a most dear companion. Therefore let him summon the boy, if he does not come by himself." "It must be done thus," I said, and having taken Ctesippus, I followed him into the palæstra, and others followed behind us. Having entered, we found the youths sacrificing, and the sacred rites almost finished; and they were dressed up, playing with pebbles and dice, some in the very vestibule outside, some in a corner of the gymnasium, playing odd-or-even, picking out pebbles from certain baskets. Others stood around watching these, among whom was Lysis, who stood among the youths and boys crowned and excelling all in appearance—to be judged not only beautiful, but also honest and good. We sat down in turn out of sight where there was a quiet place. <margin>A benevolent conversation to allure someone to speak.</margin> Turning around, Lysis frequently cast his eyes toward us, as if he desired to come closer, but he was afraid to come alone. Meanwhile Menexenus, while playing, entered from the vestibule, and seeing me and Ctesippus, came to sit with us. When Lysis saw him, he followed and sat down next to him. Others also arrived. Hippothales, however, after he saw that many had gathered, desiring to be hidden, withdrew to a place where he thought he could not be seen by Lysis, lest perhaps he should be troublesome to him; and thus standing, he listened. But I, looking at Menexenus, said: "O son of Demophon, which of you is the elder?" "We are in doubt," he replied. "And do you also doubt which is of more noble birth?" I asked. "Entirely," he said. "And also which is more beautiful?" They both smiled. "Which of you is richer, I shall by no means ask. For you are friends, are you not?" "Very much so," they replied. "And it is said that the things of friends are common; wherefore in this you differ in nothing, if indeed you say that truly about friendship." They agreed. But when I wanted to inquire which was more just and wise, someone interrupted us, who summoned Menexenus, saying he was called by the gymnasium master. He seemed to me to be a priest of the sacred rites. He went away, therefore, and I questioned Lysis. "Tell me then, O Lysis, do your father and mother love you vehemently?" "Greatly." "Do they not desire you to be most happy?" "Why not?" "Does he seem happy to you who is a slave, and to whom it is permitted to do nothing of those things which he desires?" "No, by Jove," he said. "Therefore if your father and mother love you and want you to become happy, they will take care with all effort and diligence that you live happily." "What forbids it?" "They will therefore permit you to do whatever you please, and they will not oppose your desires." "By Jove, O Socrates, they stand in my way in many things." "How do you say that? While they desire you to be happy, do they prevent you from doing what you want? Answer me this. If you desired to be carried in some chariot of your father's, taking the reins when he competes, would he not permit it?" "Nothing less." "Whom then would he permit?" "There is a certain charioteer hired by my father for a wage." "What do you say? Your parents allow a mercenary rather than you the free administration of the horses? and they will spend money besides for the sake of this work. But what then? To drive a yoke of mules and to strike them with thongs—will they grant that to you?" "Why would they grant it to me?" "Is no one allowed to beat them?" "Very much so—the muleteer, of course." "A slave or a free man?" "A slave." "So they value a slave, as it seems, more than you, their son, and they permit their property to him rather than to you: and they permit him to do whatever he likes, but they prohibit you. Furthermore, answer me this. Do they permit you to rule yourself, or not?" "Not in any way." "Who rules you?" "The pedagogue." "Is he a slave?" "Our slave." "It is a grave thing for a free person to be subjected to a slave. But by doing what does this pedagogue command you?" "While he leads me to the teachers." "And these teachers also command you." "Entirely." "Therefore your father has voluntarily set many masters and princes over you. But when you return home to your mother, does she let you do whatever you like so that you may be happy, either concerning the wool-work or the loom when she weaves? Does she let you handle the sword and shears, the shuttle and the comb, and other instruments of wool-work?" Then he, laughing, said: "By Jove, Socrates, she would not only forbid it, but would also strike me if I dared to touch them." "By God, have you done some injury to your father or mother?" "None at all." "For what cause, then, do they not want you to be happy and to dispose of individual things by your own judgment, and every day they educate you thus, so that you always serve someone, and to embrace it briefly, you do nothing according to your own will? By which it happens that such great riches seem to be of no use to you, since anyone else more than you...

86 Book Twelve.

...manages them: and what is greater, not even a body so noble, since another feeds and cares for this: but you have no power, O Lysis, nor are you made master of any wish." "It is not yet permitted because of my age, O Socrates." "See lest that be less of an impediment to you, O son of Democrates. For these things, as I believe, both father and mother grant to you, and they do not wait for a more advanced age, whenever they want something to be read or written for them. "In these things it is permitted to you, both in writing and in reading, to preserve any order of letters: and when you take up the lyre, your parents do not prohibit you, I think, from tightening or loosening any of the strings, and playing, and striking it with the plectrum." "Certainly not." "What is the cause, O Lysis, that they permit those things, but prohibit the former ones?" "Because I know those things, but on the contrary, I am ignorant of those." "Behold, most excellent Lysis, your father does not wait for age to exhibit license to you, but as soon as he perceives that you have been made more prudent than himself, he will immediately commit both all his things and you yourself freely to you." "I hope so, indeed." "What further of your neighbors? Will they not conduct themselves toward you by the same reason as your parents? Do you think a neighbor will commit the governance of his house to you, if he understands that you are more skilled in domestic affairs, or that he will manage it through himself?" "I think he would commit it to me." <margin>How much dignity prudence brings to faith.</margin> "Do you doubt that the Athenians also would commend the republic to you, when they perceive that you are vehemently wise?" "I do not doubt it." "What of the Great King <note>Referring to the King of Persia</note>? Whether would he permit his eldest son, to whom the kingdom of Asia will belong, to throw into the boiling meat whatever he wants, rather than us, if we, having gone to him, made it plain to him that we are more skilled in preparing seasoned dishes than his son?" "Us, clearly." "And he would permit him nothing at all, but us, even if we wanted to take a great deal of salt and throw it in, he would certainly permit." "Why not?" "And if his son were sick in his eyes, would he permit him to touch his own eyes, or would he prohibit him, since he did not consider him a physician?" "He would surely prohibit him." "But us, if only he thought we were physicians, he would not hinder at all, even if we wanted to open the eyelids and cure them by sprinkling ash over them?" "You speak true." "Furthermore, he would commit all other things to us rather than either to himself or his son, in which things he thought we were wiser." "It is necessary, O Socrates." "So the matter stands, friend Lysis; individual things in which we are prudent, all will concede to us, both Greeks and Barbarians, both men and women, and in those we shall act by our own judgment, nor will anyone voluntarily oppose us, so that we may both be free and the leaders of others. And when they confer these things on us, they will be ours. <margin>In those things which we know, we glory and are proud.</margin> But those things which we are ignorant of, no one will permit us to act as we please, but all will resist us to their power, not only strangers but even parents, and what is closer to us, we ourselves also will not serve ourselves, but others: and since these things are of no advantage to us, they will be alien to us. Do you agree?" "I agree, indeed." "Shall we be friends to any of the people, and will anyone love us in those things in which we are useless?" "Never." "Therefore neither does your father, nor anyone else, love any other person insofar as he is useless." "Not, as it seems." "If therefore you escape into wisdom, all will be friends to you and intimates. For you will be useful and good. If not, neither anyone else to you, nor parents, nor neighbors will be friends. Can someone be proud and glory in those things in which no one is yet wise?" "How can he?" "If you lack a teacher, you are not yet wise?" "Not yet, certainly." "Therefore you are not proudly wise, if you know nothing." "No, by Jove, as it seems to me." When I had heard these things, I turned my eyes toward Hippothales, and I was just about to offend him; for it came into my mind to say: "O Hippothales, it is in this way one must dispute with youths, rebuking them and casting them down, not flattering them as you do, and corrupting them." But when I saw him greatly troubled by the things said before, I remembered that he wanted to be hidden from Lysis just now. I therefore restrained myself and held my tongue. Meanwhile Menexenus returned and sat down next to Lysis, from where he had risen. Then Lysis, very sweetly and friendly, whispered in my ears, hidden from Menexenus: "O Socrates, those things you say to me, I beseech you, explain the same to Menexenus also." "You, Lysis," I said, "recount them to him. For you have listened to us attentively." "Attentively indeed," he replied. "Therefore apply yourself so that you may diligently remember, that you may clearly report individual things to him. But if anything should perhaps escape you, you will ask of me again when you first meet me." "I will apply myself, and know this for certain, O Socrates," he replied. "But at least tell him something new, so that I may hear, until it is time to return home." And I said: "It must be done, especially since you command it; but consider by what means you will help me if this Menexenus here strives to refute me. Or are you ignorant that he is contentious?" "Entirely; and therefore I very much desire to hear you disputing with him." "So that I may be held as ridiculous?" "Far from it, but rather so that you may chastise and coerce him." "It is not easy; for he is vehement and eloquent, a disciple of Ctesippus. Furthermore, Ctesippus himself is present; do you not see?" "Care for nothing, O Socrates; come, I beseech you, discourse." "It seems I must discourse. But let these things be between us talking apart from the others." "Why," said Ctesippus, "do you two handle these things alone among yourselves? Why not impart these things of yours to the others also?" I responded that they should be imparted. "Furthermore, this one here perceives nothing of those things which we discuss, and he thinks Menexenus understands: wherefore he commands me to inquire from him." "Why do you not ask?" "I will ask. Tell me, I pray, O Menexenus, what I shall ask of you; there has been innate in me from my early age a certain desire for one possession, just as in others. For behold, one desires horses, another dogs, another gold, another honors; I indeed value these things little, nor do they move me much. But I burn with the desire to acquire good friends. Therefore I would rather have a good friend than the most precious quail or cock, and by Jove rather than a horse and dog; furthermore, as I think, by the Dog, rather than to obtain the gold of Darius, or to capture Darius himself, I would choose a best friend. You see how greedy I am for friendship. When therefore I observe you and Lysis, I am truly amazed, and I judge you happy, because you have reconciled at such a tender age, and he has embraced you with mutual love: but that gift is so far from me, that I do not even know in what way... I ask, when someone loves another, which of the two is made the friend of the other? The lover of the beloved, or the beloved of the lover? Or does it make no difference?" "It seems to me to make no difference," he said. "What do you say?" I asked; "do both become friends in turn if only one loves the other?" "So it seems to me." "What further? Can there not be found a certain lover to whom the friend by no means responds in friendship in return?" "There can." "And does it not often happen that a friend is held in hatred? Which sometimes happens to lovers toward the beloved. For lovers sometimes love most ardently, but are least...

## Lysis, Or, on Friendship. 87

...least loved in return, and indeed are sometimes even held in hatred. Do I not seem to you to speak the truth?" "Most truly." "In these cases, does not this one love, while that one is loved?" "Certainly." "Which of the two then is the friend of the other? Is the lover the friend of the beloved, whether he be loved in return or held in hatred? Or is the beloved the friend of the lover? Or is neither the friend of the other then, when both do not love in turn?" "So the matter seems to be." "We judge differently now than we did above. For then it seemed that if only one loved, both were friends: <margin>Unless both love, neither is a friend.</margin> now on the contrary, unless both love each other, we must say neither is a friend." "It appears so." "Nothing therefore is a friend to him who loves that by which he is not loved in return." "It does not seem so." "Therefore they are not friends of horses whom the horses do not love in return, nor friends of quails, nor of dogs, nor of wine, nor of exercise, nor friends of wisdom, unless wisdom loves them in return: for they love these individual things, but these are not friends to them. Wherefore that poet lies who says:
*Happy is he for whom boys are sweet, for whom there is a wealth of horses,*
*And for whom there is a pack of dogs and for whom a guest is a stranger.*"
"By no means does it seem so to me." "Does he seem to you to speak the truth?" "The truth." "The beloved, therefore, is a friend to the lover, as it appears, O Menexenus, whether he loves or hates: just as younger boys sometimes do not yet love, and sometimes hate, when they are beaten by their parents; then indeed while they vehemently hate them, they are the dearest of all to their parents." "I think so indeed." "Therefore not the lover but the beloved will be the friend according to this reasoning." "It seems so." "And that which is hated is an enemy, not he who hates." "It appears so." "So many are loved by enemies, and are held in hatred by friends, and are friends to enemies, and on the contrary enemies to friends, if the beloved rather than the lover is the friend. But what would this absurdity be, O sweet friend? Indeed it is impossible for the enemy to be a friend to the friend, or the friend to the enemy." "You seem to speak true, O Socrates." "And if this can in no way happen, it remains that the lover is the friend of the beloved." "It appears so." "Similarly, that which hates is the enemy of that which is hated." "It is necessary." "The same things must now be conceded by us as in the previous points, that frequently something is a friend of a non-friend, and frequently also of an enemy, whenever one loves one who does not love or who loathes him. Sometimes an enemy will be an enemy of a non-enemy, or even of a friend, whenever one hates one who does not loathe him, or loathes a lover." "So it seems." "What then shall we say, if neither the lovers will be friends, nor the beloved, nor the lovers and beloved together? Shall we say some others besides these are friends to one another?" "By Jove, O Socrates, I do not find what to answer." "See, O Menexenus, lest perhaps we have sought less than rightly in the previous points." Then Lysis said: "It seems so to me, O Socrates," and having spoken thus he blushed. For it seemed to me that what was being said had escaped him against his will, because he was observing more attentively. But it was clear that, although he was listening otherwise, it was not so. I, therefore, wishing Menexenus to rest, and being excessively delighted by that boy's philosophy, spoke thus to Lysis. "O Lysis, you seem to me to speak the truth, because if we had considered rightly, we would not have wandered so now. Wherefore let us not proceed further by this way. For this consideration seems to me like a certain difficult and rough way. But the journey which we have now entered must be finished with the helps of the poets. For these are to us as parents and leaders of wisdom. <margin>Friends are made by the guidance of God. Homer, Odyssey Book 17.</margin> They say indeed not badly, while they admonish who are friends; furthermore, they wish friends to be made by the guidance of a conciliating God. For they say thus: *God always leads like to like, and makes them known.* Have you not sometimes come upon these verses?" "I have." "Perhaps also in the writings of the wisest men, in which they affirm these same things, that like is necessarily always a friend to like. <margin>Like is a friend to like.</margin> And this is the opinion of those who have treated of nature and the universe." "You speak true." "Do they speak well?" "Perhaps." "And this is perhaps true in part, perhaps even in whole: but we do not yet understand. For it seems to us that the wicked man, the closer he adheres to a wicked man and the more frequently he deals with him, the more he becomes an enemy. For he does injury: but it cannot be that he who does and he who receives injury are friends, can it?" "Not at all." "By this reasoning, half of that opinion will be false, if indeed the wicked are alike." "Certainly." "But they seem to me to say that the good are like one another and are friends: but the wicked, as is often said of them, are never like either themselves or one another, but are entirely unstable and inconsistent. But he who disagrees with himself will in no way agree with another, nor can he be a friend to anyone. Do you not think the same?" "Truly." "Therefore, as my opinion goes, they signify this, O friend, who say that like is a friend to like: that only the good is a friend to the only good, but the bad is never truly made a friend to either the good or the bad. Do you agree?" "I assent." <margin>A certain definition of friends.</margin> "We have now those who are friends. For reason dictates that those who are good exist as friends." "It is established." "I think the same. But there is something that disturbs me. And see, I pray, what I suspect. <margin>Refutation.</margin> In what way is like a friend to like insofar as he is like, and such a one useful to such a one? Indeed let us consider it thus. What advantage or detriment can any like thing bring to any like thing, which it could not bring to itself? Or what can it suffer from that thing, which it could not suffer from itself in like manner? These things, then, since they are such that they help each other in nothing, in what way are they sought by each other?" "In no way." "That which does not seek, how is it a friend?" "In no way." "Or perhaps like is not a friend to like insofar as he is like? But the good exists as a friend to the good, insofar as he is good, not insofar as he is like?" "Perhaps." "What truly, is not the good man, insofar as he is good, so far sufficient to himself?" "So." "He who is sufficient to himself, in that which he is sufficient to himself, lacks nothing at all." "What prevents it?" "He who lacks nothing, seeks nothing." "Nothing indeed." "If he does not seek, he does not love." "No." "He who does not love is not a friend." "It does not seem so." "How then will the good be friends to the good, when they neither desire each other while absent, as each is sufficient to himself separately, nor when present does either need anything of the other's work? In what way can such men value each other?" "In none." "They will never be friends who do not value each other much." "Never." "Consider now, O Lysis, where we have slipped, and whether we have been altogether deceived." "In what way?" "I heard long ago from someone (indeed I remember still) that like is adverse to like, and the good are most inimical to the good. <margin>The opinion of Hesiod, that not likes but dissimilars seem to be friends.</margin> He also used the testimony of Hesiod, saying that a potter envies a potter, and a singer also a singer, and a beggar a beggar. And in others similarly he thought it necessary that likes should abound among themselves with envy, emulation, and contention, but dissimilars with friendship. Furthermore, he said that the poor man is made a friend to the rich by necessity, and the weak to the strong for the sake of help, and similarly the sick man to the physician, and every ignorant man desires and loves the skilled man. He added besides certain greater things, that it is so far from a friend being like to like, that on the contrary, the contrary is most of all, most of all a friend to the contrary. For each thing desires not its like, but its contrary: as the dry desires the moist, the cold the hot, the bitter the sweet, the sharp the obtuse, the empty replenishment, the full emptiness, and others similarly. For the contrary provides nourishment to the contrary: but like enjoys like not at all."

Indeed, O companion, he who taught such things seemed to be a most eloquent and elegant man. For he spoke well. But how does it seem to us? Rightly, said Menexenus, as it appears at first glance. Do we say then that the opposite is most friendly to the opposite? Certainly. Let it be so, O Menexenus. But I ask, is this not strange and foreign? Immediately those wise men who excel in the eloquence of refutation <note>Socrates refers to the "Eristics," philosophers who specialized in logical arguments and verbal disputes.</note> will rise up against us and ask whether hatred and friendship are not most opposite. What shall we answer them? Shall we not be forced to answer that they speak the truth? Forced. Will they say the enemy is a friend to the friend? Or the friend a friend to the enemy? Neither. What about the just to the unjust, or the temperate to the intemperate? Or the good to the bad? It does not seem so to me. And yet if something is a friend to another according to the law of contrariety <note>The idea that "opposites attract."</note>, these must be friends. They must indeed. Why then is neither like a friend to like, nor opposite to opposite? It does not seem so. Come, let us also notice this, lest we be even more deceived: that truly none of these things we have mentioned is a friend, but that which is **neither good nor evil** sometimes becomes a friend to the good. What do you say? I myself do not know, by Jupiter! <note>original: "per Iouem." A standard oath in Platonic dialogue.</note> For I waver because of the ambiguity of the speech.

<margin>Proverb: The beautiful is a friend. Properties of the beautiful.</margin>
And it seems, as the old proverb has it, that the beautiful itself is a friend. For it appears to be something soft, smooth, and sleek, and therefore it easily slips into us, creeps in and penetrates like something slippery and smooth. For I say the good itself is beautiful. Don't you? I do too. I divine this for you: that what is neither good nor evil is a friend to the good and the beautiful. 

<margin>Three kinds: good, evil, neutral. Another definition of friends.</margin>
Hear why I prophesy this. It seems to me there are three kinds. One good, another evil; the last, which is neither good nor evil. And to you? To me also. Neither good to good, nor evil to evil, nor good to evil is a friend, as our previous reasoning showed. It remains that if anything is a friend to another, it is that which is neither good nor evil; it must be a friend either to the good, or to something like itself. For nothing is a friend to evil. Certainly. And yet, not like to like, as we showed a little while ago. Indeed. Therefore, that which is neither good nor evil will not be a friend to that which is the same as itself. It does not seem so. Only that which is neither good nor evil can become a friend to the good alone. It seems to follow necessarily.

Is this now rightly set forth by us, O boys? If we consider a healthy body, it does not need the medical art, nor any help at all, for it is self-sufficient. Thus no healthy person is a friend to a doctor because of health itself. No one. But the sick person is, I think, because of the disease. Why not? Disease is indeed an evil, while the skill of medicine is something good and useful. So it is. The body, in that it is a body, is neither good nor evil. True. But the body is compelled because of disease to seek and love medicine. It appears so. It follows, then, that what is neither good nor evil becomes a friend of the good because of the presence of evil. It seems so. It is certain, however, that this happens before that thing becomes evil itself due to the presence of the evil. For it has not yet become evil in the place of the good which it desires and of which it is a friend; for we have shown it is impossible for evil to be a friend to the good. Impossible, without a doubt.

Observe, I pray, what I am saying. I assert that some things become like that which is present to them, and some do not; just as if someone wanted to dye something with a certain color, the "infection" of the color would be present in some way to the thing colored. It would. Is the thing then also of such a kind as the color itself usually is? I do not quite understand. Perhaps you will understand it this way: if someone should dye your hair, which is blond, with white lead, would it become white? Or rather would it only *seem* so? It would seem so. Nevertheless, whiteness would be present to it. It would. Yet they will be no more white for all that; and despite the presence of brightness, they will be neither bright nor black. You speak the truth. But when, O friend, they grow white with old age, then they become such as that which has arrived: white by the presence of the white color. Why not? This is what I was asking: whether everything to which something is present immediately becomes such as that thing; or rather, if it is present in a certain way it becomes so, but otherwise not at all. Rather in this way. By the same reasoning, that which is neither good nor evil, when evil is present, is not yet evil; but it becomes so when it has already turned into such a thing. Entirely. When it is not yet evil, though evil is present, this presence compels it to desire the good; but the presence which makes it evil rejects both the desire for the good and friendship, for it is no longer neutral, but evil. But an evil friend to the good, or a good friend to the evil, cannot be. Certainly not.

For this reason, those who are already wise no longer <term>philosophize</term> <note>Socrates uses "philosophize" in its literal Greek sense: "to love or seek wisdom." If one is already wise, one does not need to seek it.</note>, whether they be gods or men; nor do those who are so corrupted by ignorance that they have become wicked, for no one who is evil and utterly ignorant should philosophize. There remain, therefore, those who possess this evil—namely, ignorance—but are not yet utterly unlearned or ignorant; rather, they acknowledge their own ignorance, because of which awareness they philosophize (that is, they love wisdom), being not yet good or evil. For the evil by no means philosophize, nor do the good. For neither opposite to opposite, nor like to like, appeared to us above. Do you remember? We certainly remember.

Altogether, O Lysis and Menexenus, we have found what a friend is and what is not. For we concluded this regarding the soul as well as the body: that which is neither good nor evil, because of the presence of evil itself, becomes a friend of the good. They conceded all these things. And I rejoiced greatly, like a hunter who has successfully caught what I was tracking in my thoughts. Then, I know not how, a certain strange and absurd suspicion arose in me, as if those things we had just conceded were less than true. And immediately disturbed, I said: "Alas, O Lysis and Menexenus, we seem to have found only a dream." "Why is that?" replied Menexenus. "I fear lest we have fallen into false talk about the friend, as if into proud and vain men." "By what reasoning?" "This way, clearly. Is a friend a friend to someone, or not?" "Necessarily." "Is it for the sake of nothing and because of nothing, or for the sake of someone and because of something?" "Certainly for the sake of someone and because of something." "Is that thing a 'friend' <note>Here used in the sense of a 'dear' or 'cherished' thing.</note> for the sake of which the friend is a friend to someone? Or perhaps it is neither friend nor enemy?" "I do not quite understand." "It is likely, but in this way both you and I, as I think, will understand better. Did we say the sick man is a friend to the doctor?" "We did." "Is he not a friend to the doctor because of disease and for the sake of health?" "Yes." "Is disease an evil?" "Why not?" "Is health a good, an evil, or neutral?" "A good." "We said before that the body, since it is neither good nor evil, is a friend to medicine because of disease—and thus because of an evil—but medicine is a good. And medicine obtains friendship for the sake of health, and health is a good." "Exactly." "Is health a friend, or not a friend?" "A friend." "Is disease an enemy?" 

<margin>That which is neutral, because of the evil within it, becomes a friend to the good, for the sake of the good.</margin>
"Utterly. Therefore, that which is neither good nor evil, because of an evil and an enemy, is a friend of the good, for the sake of the good and a friend." "It is clear." "Therefore, for the sake of a friend, the friend is because of..."

<summary>Socrates explores the idea that friendship arises when a neutral entity (like the body or the soul) seeks the "Good" (like health or wisdom) because of the presence of an "Evil" (like disease or ignorance). He concludes that true philosophers are those who recognize their own ignorance and thus "befriend" wisdom to remedy it.</summary>

...of an enemy. I suppose so. Come boys, since we have reached this point in our discussion, let us, I pray, attend diligently, lest by chance we be deceived. At the start, I will pass over the fact that a friend has become a friend of a friend, which is like of like—a thing we established as impossible in the earlier parts. But let us nevertheless consider this, lest our present opinion deceive us. We said medicine is a friend for the sake of health. We affirmed it. Is health therefore a friend? Very much so. If it is a friend, it is a friend for the sake of something. It is. For the sake of a friend, if what was granted above holds. And a friend. Will that again be a friend for the sake of a friend? Certainly. It is necessary that in this progression we arrive at a certain first principle, which is no longer referred back to another friend, but to that which is the primary friend, for whose sake all other things said to be such are friends. It is necessary. This is what I was saying just now must be considered: lest all the other things which we previously said were friends for the sake of that one deceive us like certain phantoms of it, while that first thing is the true friend.
Let us therefore consider it in this way. Whatever someone values highly—as, for instance, a father his son—he prefers before all other things. And such a man, because he values his son highly, also values some other things highly for his sake. For example, if he perceives that his son has drunk hemlock, he will value wine very highly, if indeed he hopes this will cure the poison. Most certainly. Will he not also value the jar in which the wine is? Very much. Does he then esteem the earthen cup, or three measures of wine, more than his son? Or is it rather the opposite? So that all this zeal does not look to those things which are prepared for the sake of another, but tends toward that for whose sake the other things are sought. Nor is it true what we often say, that we value silver and gold highly. For every intention and estimation belongs to that alone for which these things are prepared. Shall we say it so? Most certainly. The same reasoning applies to a friend. For whatever things we said were friendly to us for the sake of some friend, we named with an improper term? But it appears that the true friend is that toward which all these things called friendships tend. So it seems. Wherefore the true friend
<margin>A friend is a friend for the sake of nothing else.</margin>
is a friend for the sake of no other friend. True. This, therefore, has been rejected: that a friend is a friend for the sake of some other friend. But is not the good a friend? So I think. Is the good loved because of evil? Is that how the matter stands? If of the three things we mentioned—good, evil, neutral—two are taken, but evil departs and touches nothing, neither the body nor the soul nor any of the things we said were of themselves neither good nor evil, would the good then be entirely useless to us? For if nothing further harmed us, we would have no need of any favor from the good. And thus it would now be manifest that we sought and loved the good because of evil; as if the good were the remedy for evil, and evil the disease; and when there is no disease, we have no need of a remedy. Is the good itself so instituted by nature that it is loved by us—who are in the middle between good and evil—because of evil? While of its own nature it contributes nothing? So it seems.
That friend, therefore, in which all the other things called friendly for the sake of another friend ended, is far different from those things. For those were called friendly for the sake of a friend; but the thing itself which is truly a friend appeared to us, on the contrary, to be a friend because of an enemy. But if the enemy were absent, it would no longer be a friend to us. Not as the present reasoning persuades me. If evil were extirpated, by Jove, would no hunger or thirst remain, or anything of this kind? Or perhaps some hunger would be left, so that men and other animals might exist, yet it would not be harmful? And thirst and other desires would remain, yet not be evil, evil having been utterly extirpated? Or is it perhaps a ridiculous question, what would happen then? Or not? For who knows? But yet we know this, which happens now: that it happens that he who hungers is harmed, and it happens that he is helped. Certainly. Does it not also happen that he who thirsts, and whoever desires other things of this kind, sometimes desires usefully, sometimes harmfully, and sometimes in neither way? Very much so. If evils are destroyed, things which are not evil will not perish along with them? By no means. There will be, therefore, desires that are neither good nor evil, even if evils have been destroyed. Likely. Is it possible that he who desires something, and burns for it, does not love that very thing? Not as it seems to me. For this reason also, even if evils are destroyed, as it seems, some friendly things will remain. Yes. But if evil were the cause of one being a friend to another, with evil removed, nothing would be a friend. For with the cause removed, that which existed because of it cannot remain. You speak rightly. Did we not agree above among ourselves that a friend loves something, and because of something? And that because of evil, that which is neither evil nor good loves the good itself? We agreed. But at present, as it seems, another cause for loving in return appears. It seems so.
Does desire, as we were just saying, cause friendship? And is that which desires a friend of what is desired at the time when it desires? But what we said above
<margin>Whether desire is the cause of friendship.</margin>
about being a friend—is it some nonsense, like a long poem composed? Perhaps. Indeed, what it craves, it craves because it lacks it. That very thing. Therefore, that which is in need is a friend to that which it needs. So I think. Anything lacks that of which it is deprived. What forbids it? Therefore, of that which is proper and kindred, as it seems, love, friendship, and desire exist, O Menexenus and Lysis. We grant it. Wherefore, if you are friends to each other, you are in a certain way kindred by nature. Most certainly. And whoever else desires another, O boys, or loves, desires and esteems and loves for this reason: because the person is kindred to him either according to the soul, or the soul's habit, or character, or appearance; otherwise he would never love. Menexenus agreed plainly. But Lysis was silent. But I said: it is necessary that we love what is by nature our own. It seems so. Therefore it is necessary that a legitimate and not at all feigning lover be loved in return by those he loves. To this Lysis and Menexenus at last barely nodded. But Hippothales, leaping with joy, changed in face and color. However, wishing to discuss the discourse more diligently, I added this: if "one's own" and "like" are different, we have already stated, O Lysis and Menexenus, what a friend is; but if "like" and "one's own" are the same, it is not easy to reject the earlier discourse: that the like is useless to the like according to its likeness; and the useless is in no way a friend. Do you wish then, after we have become as if drunk by debating, that we confess "one's own" is one thing, and "like" another? We certainly wish it. Shall we set the good as "one's own" to each person, and the evil as "alien"? Or evil as "own" to evil, good to good, and neutral to neutral? Each of these things seemed to be own to each...

--- Page 109 ---
90 Book Thirteen.

...seemed to us. Again, O boys, we have fallen into those discourses about friendship which we refuted at the beginning. For the unjust will be no less a friend to the unjust, and the evil to the evil, than the good to the good. So it seems. What if we were to say that the good and "one's own" are the same; then is not only the good a friend to the good? Entirely. But we considered that also to have been refuted by us long ago. Do you remember? Most perfectly. What discourse then shall we use hereafter? To nothing, it seems. It is worthwhile, therefore, like wise men in judgments, to resume by enumerating. For if neither lovers, nor the beloved, nor the like, nor the unlike, nor the good, nor those who are "own," nor any of the others we have numbered—the multitude of which I do not remember—if, I say, none of these is a friend, I have nothing further to offer.
When I had said these things, I noticed one of the older men moving, but immediately certain tutors <note>Original: "paedagogi," attendants who supervised boys' behavior and education.</note>, like certain demons, both of Lysis and Menexenus, along with their brothers, ordered them to return home. For Hesperus <note>The evening star.</note> had come. At first, therefore, we and the others standing around pushed the tutors back. But when they paid no attention to us, and, muttering in a certain barbarous way, took it ill, and nevertheless called the boys, we, overcome by their persistence, dissolved the gathering. For it seemed to us, because they had yielded to the festival, they had nothing further to bring into our midst. Afterward, as they were leaving, I turned to Menexenus and Lysis and briefly added: "At present we seem to have turned out ridiculous and silly—both I, an old man, and you boys. For those leaving will carp at us, because we think we are friends to each other—for I count myself among you—though we have not yet been able to find what a friend is."

THE THEAETETUS OF PLATO, OR, ON KNOWLEDGE.

EPITOME OF MARSILIO FICINO ON THE THEAETETUS, OR, ON KNOWLEDGE.

This dialogue on knowledge, Peter de' Medici <note>Piero de' Medici, son of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note>, rises higher and raises questions worthy of the wondrous sharpness of your talent, the heads and solutions of which you will notice summarily in this compendium. Wherein you will find disputed what knowledge is not, what it is, and whence, and how. Socrates indeed asks what knowledge is. Theaetetus, however, answers that knowledge is geometry, arithmetic, and other disciplines and individual arts of this kind. Socrates rejects this answer as less than
<margin>Definition by enumeration is flawed.</margin>
suitable to the question. Because when he was asked what knowledge is, he enumerates not *what* it is, but *how many* knowledges there are, and explains *of what* things they are knowledges. For he who says arithmetic does not state knowledge itself, but the knowledge of counting; and he who says geometry says the knowledge of measuring. Then, the answer is ridiculous when it is given through things unknown. For no one can know what this knowledge of numbers or figures is, unless he knows what knowledge is. Furthermore, the answer is superfluous. For when he could have embraced the rational nature of knowledge itself in a few words, he enters upon an infinite journey by enumerating individual types.
After this, he brings forward the definition of Protagoras, who says that knowledge is perception <note>Original: "sensum."</note>. For Protagoras judges man to be the measure of all things:
<margin>Whether knowledge is perception.</margin>
of things that are, that they are; and of things that are not, that they are not; and that whatever things are to each person, such they seem to each. For such as things are, such are they perceived. Such as they are perceived, such they appear to the *phantasia*—that is, the interior sense. By which he wishes to effect that perception is knowledge. In this, certainly, Thales of Miletus, Homer, Epicharmus, Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Protagoras agreed. For when Thales says water is the principle of all things, and Homer that Ocean is the father of all and Tethys the mother, they all show that things are in a state of flux. The rest whom we mentioned, imitating these, said that nothing ever *is*, but each thing is always *becoming*. Whence nothing in itself is absolutely such rather than such, but through motion, mixture, and the relation of one to another, it becomes and appears such to one, and such to another.
They think it is established that all things are in motion because all things are made by motion. Moreover, they conjecture that all things come from motion because by that through which anything exists, it is also preserved. But both those things pertaining to the soul and those pertaining to the body are preserved by motion and exercise, and perish by leisure and torpor. From motion, therefore, are all things. Furthermore, as long as the spheres of the heavens are moved, the four elements are mixed. Insofar as these are mixed, internal things are generated; which, after they have been generated, are preserved by exercise. Motion, therefore, effects all these things. They add that generation comes from heat, and heat from the motion of the sun or the collision of bodies.
But that nothing is one certain thing according to itself, they show by this example: whiteness, and every color, is neither the sight of the eyes nor the motion of bodies, but from sight and motion a certain medium result arises—that is, such an affection around the eyes. And from the diverse disposition of the one looking and the various way of intuiting, various colors appear and become, sometimes one, sometimes another. Furthermore, the various motion of rays striking bodies and hitting the eyes offers diverse and omniform images. Indeed, often around the same thing a diverse color appears and is to diverse men and animals; and often to the same person, and around the same thing, although not at the same time but at another, because of the mutation of nature itself.
They judge, therefore, that whatever is, is motion. Of motion there are two species: one in acting, the other in suffering <note>In the sense of "receiving an action."</note>. By the mixture of these motions, as they say, all things are completed. The outcomes are twin in species, but infinite in number: namely, the sensible thing and perception, which is always with the sensible thing and meets it. For as often as some power of perceiving and something consonant to it cling together, from their concurrence two things arise: around that which is the object, the species to be perceived—color, taste, smell, and other things of this kind; around the power of the soul, perception. When these are disjoined, those things do not happen. From which it follows that of the things offered to the five senses, nothing is such by its own nature, but meeting with perception, it becomes now one thing, now another. For nothing is acting or suffering according to itself, but in the alternate meeting each is both. Wherefore nothing is one thing by itself, but is always becoming toward another and for someone, nor ever *is*, but is always becoming and flowing.
Socrates refutes these things by this:
<margin>Socrates' refutation of the aforementioned.</margin>
that the drunk, and those suffering from frenzy, and the insane, and the sleeping when they dream, as well as those who have their senses corrupted in some other way, affirm that they perceive and think true things, even though we say all their visions are false. From which it follows that not all things which appear are true. Into the same doubt fall those things which we are said to perceive while awake and sober. For we give equal time to sleep and wakefulness in turn. Therefore it is doubtful whether these or those are rather dreams and false. But those who wish to think all appearances are true
<margin>Protagoras' response to Socrates.</margin>
would certainly answer thus: that various affections of those acting or suffering produce different things; and the objects which are perceived act according to the affection of the perception of the sufferer. This is one thing in the waking and another in the sleeping, one in the sick and another in the healthy. Wherefore different judgments arise, yet all are true, because all things are such to each as they are judged. For it is necessary to remember what was said above: that nothing by its nature is absolutely one thing, but whatever something is, it is toward another, and for another, and of another. Indeed, whatever becomes something, *becomes* it, but *is* nothing. These things, therefore, are consonant with each other: according to Homer and Heraclitus, all things flow; according to Protagoras, man is the measure of all things; according to Theaetetus, knowledge is perception. Against these Socrates argues thus: If perception is knowledge,
<margin>Another refutation by Socrates.</margin>
beasts, which excel man in senses, will excel in knowledge. Likewise, if whatever things appear are true, the thoughts of any man are equally right, nor is any man wiser than another, nor God wiser than man. To this is added that the faculty of teaching, debating, and refuting would be vain, since it would be unnecessary for those who judge truly about individual things to learn, nor should they inquire...

<summary>These pages conclude the Lysis, exploring the "First Friend" as the ultimate object of desire, and begin the Theaetetus with Ficino's summary of why knowledge cannot simply be defined as perception or a list of arts.</summary>
