# Theaetetus, Or, on Knowledge. 91

What each person possesses must be accepted, and nothing should be refuted, since any thought whatsoever would be true. Furthermore, if sensing and knowing are the same—just as seeing and hearing are—then when uneducated children first look at letters, they see them, and therefore would "know" them; or if they are said not to know them, they must also be said not to see them. And when we first hear foreigners pronouncing their own language, not yet being skilled in that tongue, just as we hear them, we would also claim to "know" <margin>Protagoras’s second response.</margin> what they utter. But if someone denies they understand, they must similarly deny they hear. Protagoras would respond to this last point by saying that what we see or hear, we know; but what we are ignorant of, we do not even truly sense. For instance, in letters, children see the shape, the placement of parts, and the color, and in seeing these, they know them. Hearing foreign voices, they know the high and low tones as they hear them; but since they do not sense the meanings of the letters and voices, they remain entirely <margin>Against Protagoras.</margin> ignorant. Against him, it is inferred thus: From this, O Protagoras, it follows that when people know meanings, they know by something other than sense. Knowledge, therefore, is something other than sensation.

Likewise, if to see is to know, then not to see will be not to know. However, what someone has seen and learned and remembers, he knows. Yet often he no longer sees it; therefore, he would not know it. Thus, the same person would both know and not know at the same time. Furthermore, if you see something with one eye while the other is closed, you see and do not see it at once. Therefore, a litigious person might say: "If seeing is knowing, and not seeing is not knowing, you both know and do not know the same thing at once." Add to this that when you look at something from a distance and confusedly, you see it indeed, yet you do not know it, since you doubt. Therefore, <margin>Response of Protagoras.</margin> knowledge is not sensation. 

Protagoras might perhaps respond by first distinguishing between memory and knowledge. For when someone first experiences something through sensing, he begins to hold it in memory; then, even when not experiencing it, he remembers; and when he senses and experiences the same thing again, he recollects it. In the first case, he knows by action; in the second, by habit <note>original: "habitu," meaning a settled state or disposition</note>; in the third, by both action and habit together. Therefore, he sometimes both knows and does not know. Yet these are not contraries, for he does not ignore it in the same way that he knows it. Therefore, when he does not see, he nevertheless remembers; he knows by habit, but is ignorant in action. These are not contraries.

And when Socrates says that one person is wiser than another, Protagoras responds that some should not be called wise and others foolish because some think true things and others false things. For everyone thinks those things which they experience; they experience those things by which they are moved; they are moved by those things that act; and those things that act are true while they exist. From this, he concludes that everyone thinks true things, yet not everyone thinks good and proper things. He asserts that the wise are those who, being well-disposed, receive whatever is offered as good, and think things are good for themselves, and as they think, so they are. The foolish are those who, being ill-disposed, judge things to be bad, and things are bad for them as they judge. 

Against the claim that everyone thinks true things, Socrates argues thus: It happens in all of life and in individual skills that we think ourselves to judge truly in some things, and others to judge truly in others. For everyone professes some skill and yields to another in an unfamiliar art. Either this estimation is true, or it is false. From both, it follows that not all men think truly. For if that estimation is true, it will be true that some judge truly in many things in which we ourselves think falsely. Therefore, not everyone thinks true things. If the estimation is false, then at least in this we are often deceived, and thus not every opinion is true. 

Moreover, it often happens that what one person thinks as true is abhorred by the opinion of all others. To that person, those things will seem true, but to others, false. They will therefore be false, yet more so than true, as there are more people by whom they are thought false than those by whom they are thought true. Therefore, he is not the measure of things, but others are. Thus, not everyone is the measure of all things. Likewise, Protagoras’s sentiment that every opinion is true is a paradox and contrary to everyone’s common sense. From this, almost the entire human race deems his opinion false. But if every opinion is true, then this universal judgment is also true; therefore, as it is thought false, so also is Protagoras’s own position (which says every opinion is true) false. To think those who disagree with his words are thinking falsely—from this also follows the same conclusion: namely, that not every opinion is true. 

Furthermore, he who is ignorant cannot be the measure of that which he ignores. He who doubts is ignorant; all men doubt, therefore they are ignorant of many things. Thus, not all men are the measure of all things. And when he says that things are such as they appear to each individual, he errs. Whatever things appear healthy or harmful to the body to those ignorant of the medical art are not always so. Often, opinion deceives them. And what citizens, in deliberating the administration of the republic, decree as useful or harmful are not always such for the republic. For many things hinder which they hoped would be profitable, and things which they thought would be harmful actually help. But if the healthy and the useful do not consist only in the opinion and custom of men but have some substance by their own nature, then much more so do the honorable and the good, since they are the principle and the end of useful things. Therefore, neither in those things which pertain to the care of the body, nor in those which look to the governance of the soul and the republic, are things such as they appear to each. 

Indeed, if whatever appeared were so, then as often as someone predicted the future, he would surely prophesy truly. Which is indeed false: for rarely do future things happen as they are thought. And if someone judges about future things, not just anyone does it, but the expert in those things that look to his art. For a physician foresees a future fever better than a musician, and a musician foresees a future consonance better than a physician.

Finally, having refuted these points, Socrates, taking occasion from the freedom or servitude of speaking, disputes the freedom of those practicing philosophy and the servitude of civil and rhetorical men—what the life of each is like. The end of the philosopher is to ascend from human evils to celestial goods. He speaks of the rewards of those who seek heavenly things and the punishments of those who pant for earthly things. 

After this digression is finished, he returns to the proposed question. Its foundation was the sentiment of Heraclitus: that all things are moved <note>original: "omnia moueantur," the doctrine of universal flux</note>. Parmenides, Melissus, and Zeno of Elea felt the contrary. For they posited that "All is One and immobile." <margin>Plato approves of Heraclitus and Protagoras.</margin> Plato explains and approves of their dogma in the book *Concerning the One Principle of All Things*, which we have translated. On the other hand, he begins to argue against Heraclitus and Protagoras by the division of motion. 

There are two kinds of motion. One is motion according to place; the other is according to the nature of the thing. The former is called <term>translation</term> <note>local motion</note>, the latter <term>alteration</term>. There are two species of translation: passage and circulation. For translation happens either from place to place or <margin>Distinction of motions.</margin> in a circuit around one and the same place. Motion in the nature of the moved thing itself is effected either according to substance, or around quantity or quality. If it is moved according to substance toward "being" itself, it is <term>generation</term>; if toward "non-being," it is <term>corruption</term>. According to quantity toward the greater, it is called <term>increase</term>; toward the lesser, <term>decrease</term>. Motion which goes from quality to quality is named <term>affection</term> <note>modification</note>. It then receives various names from various qualities. For that which moves toward heat is heating; toward cold, cooling; toward color, coloring; and similarly for the rest.

Having set forth this distinction, Socrates asks: if all things are moved, are individuals moved by those two kinds of motion, or are many moved by one kind and others by two? If many are moved by only one, it follows that they are no more moved than they are standing still. For if they are moved in a certain way, they also rest in a certain way. But the opinion of those men does not want this, but that all things are moved entirely without any state of rest. Thus it happens that they are agitated by all motions. Therefore, while things are carried from place to place, they meanwhile pass continually from affection to affection—as from heat into cold, whiteness into blackness, or the contrary. It is asked whether they remain for any length of time under one of these forms or not. If they remain, it follows that not every state of rest has been expelled. If they do not remain, while something is pronounced "hot" or "white," it ceases to be hot or white. Indeed, before the accepted pronunciation can end, the form itself ends. Hence, nothing is ever truly pronounced or perceived; nor should that thing be predicated as "hot" more than "not hot," or "white" more than "not white," since it persists in nothing, and it both is and is not equally while it is being spoken of. For this reason, the forms of things are unknown to us.

The same must be said of sensation. For neither sight in vision, nor hearing in auditory perception, remains for a moment. Wherefore it happens that we see or hear no more than we do not see and do not hear, even while we profess that we are seeing and hearing. From this it follows that if the senses are removed, the truth of the senses is also removed; and once that is removed, it can in no way be said that there is a knowledge of the senses. He adds another reason, for the understanding of which it must be noted that Plato attributes no cognition to the body, just as he attributes no life to it. What lives, that senses; the soul lives, and the soul senses. In the body, however, neither life nor sensation is found, but the works of life and sensation are declared. Therefore, what others call the five senses, he wishes to be called the five organs of sense; he thinks nothing senses *with* these instruments, but *through* them, as if they were passages by which individual things are sensed by one power of the soul, which he calls the "common sense," into which the various passions flow from every side from the individual organs of the body, like lines to the center of a circle from the circumference. Colors flow through the eyes, sounds through the ears, odors through the nostrils, tastes through the tongue, and finally heat, cold, moist, dry, heavy, light, soft, hard, smooth, rough, rare, dense, sharp, and similarly obtuse through the whole body. That this soul senses not with many, but with one power, is clear: because by sensing color, we say it is not a voice; and by sensing a taste, we pronounce that it is not an odor. He who does not know both cannot distinguish one from the other. No organ provides the same things as another organ; and if the same, not in the same way. Therefore, the distinction of those things which are sensed is not in the organs, but in one perceiving power of the soul which perceives each and distinguishes each from the others simultaneously. Since the soul alone can do all these things—which even the Peripatetics do not deny—what need is there for many senses? This sense which they call "common" is present in all animals as soon as they are born. Besides this, there is also another power, which...

# Theaetetus, Or, on Knowledge. 93

We distinguish the false [by the true]. Therefore, it seems knowledge must be defined before false opinion can be declared, if we desire to comprehend it perfectly. Hence, Theaetetus asserts that knowledge is true opinion. Socrates refutes this from the fact that the oratorical faculty persuades, it does not teach: he who persuades induces an opinion, and a true opinion when he reports the truth, yet not knowledge. For concerning those things which are always in motion and are sometimes one way and sometimes another, there is never certain knowledge. Such are human affairs, which orators deal with, especially since they often lead listeners to believe those things which they themselves doubt and at which they were never present. 

After this, Theaetetus adds the definition of Leucippus and Theodorus of Cyrene: "Knowledge is true opinion with an account <note>original: "cum ratione," meaning with a rational explanation or logos</note>." And therefore, things that have an account can be known; things that lack an account, not at all. And Prodicus of Chios, imitating Leucippus, asserted that the elements of things, because they are simple and therefore without an account, are unknown; but compounds, because they can have an account, are known. They understand an account to be a definition and a certain speech declaring the substance and property of a thing. Because this includes several things—subject and predicate, sometimes also the copula (that is, the verb), and nouns—it signifies a certain compound. But the element is simple, and therefore devoid of an account, and is left unknown. 

Socrates refutes both things that have been said—first indeed this latter point, by which it is said that "Elements, because simple, are unknown; things made from them, because compound, are known." Then the former point: "Knowledge is true opinion with an account." And for the sake of example, he takes letters for the elements and the syllable for the compound. But what he delivers concerning these, he wants to be understood concerning all things. 

The first reason against them is this: because just as compounds depend on elements, so the cognition of compounds is perfected by the cognition of elements. For things that are from a cause cannot be known without the cause. Therefore, it is impossible to know compounds if the elements are ignored. Likewise, take a certain compound, for example "So," the first syllable of the name Socrates. Is this syllable both elements? Or some one form born from the meeting elements? If it is both, then whoever knows this syllable "So" knows both elements. And being asked what "So" is, he will answer "S" and "O." And if he is ignorant of "S" and "O," he will never know "So." For he who does not know each, does not know both. It is therefore impossible to know compounds when the elements are ignored. 

But someone will perhaps say that the syllable, and each form, is not the elements, but some one thing existing besides them. Socrates asks him: "Does this form and syllable have parts or not?" If it has, it is a certain whole and "all." But the "whole" and the "all" are nothing other than all the parts, which is clear in numbers. For the whole number is nothing other than all the units it contains; and thus this form will consist of parts, and the parts, by the very fact that they exist, will belong to the whole. Just as, therefore, the form is known, so also are the elements known. For if he knows the form, he knows the whole and the all. If the whole and the all, he knows that none of its parts are missing. Therefore, he knows that individual parts have existence; thus he knows each one. If he were ignorant whether all were present or not, he could not know the whole. It is therefore impossible to know the form when the elements are ignored. 

But if someone says that the form itself, being one, has no parts because the elements of which it consists are not its parts, it follows that it is simple and impartible. Wherefore, just as the element was said to be unknown because it is simple, so also the form itself will be said to be unknown because it is simple. And therefore, it can in no way happen that the forms made from elements are known when the elements themselves are ignored. This is also clearly evident from the fact that in individual arts, the foundation of understanding each art is to comprehend the elements of the very things with which the art deals. Otherwise, all labor is in vain. 

This having finally been refuted, Socrates now begins to refute the principal part of the proposition, where it was said: "Knowledge is true opinion with an account." For three things can be signified by the name of "account": either speech, or a discourse through the elements of the thing, or a definition. 
1. If the first, every opinion will be knowledge. For whether we opine true or false things, we are able to utter what we feel in speech; therefore, even he who opines false things will opine with an account. 
2. If the second, as often as someone discourses through the elements, he will be said to know. But that is false for this reason: because in discoursing, he can transpose elements, pervert the order, refer the element of one thing to another, and fit it to another of the elements. He who confuses these things is not to be said to know. 
3. If he understands the third, that is, definition, and calls knowledge "true opinion with a definition," he argues against him thus: Definition is the interpretation of the difference; therefore, whoever defines assigns the proper difference besides the common things of the thing. But he who opines Socrates and Theaetetus truly, does he perceive the differences of Socrates and Theaetetus in his opining or not? If he does not perceive them, nor opine truly, for I would never truly distinguish one from the other unless I discerned the differences of both. Therefore, by the very fact that he opines truly, he understands the differences. Wherefore, there is no need, besides true opinion, to add an account—that is, the notion of the difference. 

But someone will perhaps say that in the opinion itself, a certain sense and imagination of the difference is included, rather than a certain understanding of the natural difference; therefore, "understanding of the difference" should be added to the definition of knowledge. Socrates argues against this thus: A definition is surely absurd by which the same is described by the same. When we say knowledge is true opinion with an account (that is, with an understanding of the difference), we define knowledge through knowledge. For the understanding of the difference is the *knowledge* of the difference; hence knowledge will be true opinion with the *knowledge* of the difference—which is ridiculous to say. 

From all these things, the false definitions of the sophists have now been refuted: 
- First, which said knowledge is the individual faculties that are learned. 
- Second, that knowledge is sensation. <margin>Seven definitions of knowledge returned by the sophists.</margin> 
- Third, that knowledge is true opinion. 
- Fourth, that knowledge is true opinion with the utterance of speech. 
- Fifth, true opinion with discourse through elements. 
- Sixth, true opinion with the imagination of the difference. 
- Seventh, true opinion with the knowledge of the difference. 

These having finally been refuted, we must see what Plato teaches, who indeed in the sixth book of the *Republic*, imitating the Pythagoreans Brontinus and Archytas, posits two kinds of things: the intelligible and the sensible. The former is stable and incorporeal; the latter mobile and corporeal. He calls the way to knowing the former "reason," the way to knowing the latter "sense." The common notion of the former is "intellect"; of the latter, "opinion." But he divides both kinds into two. He wants there to be a first and second intelligible: in the first are ideas (that is, the forms and notions of the divine mind) and other minds and souls; in the second are numbers and figures. For although numbers and figures are incorporeal, yet because they admit of some division, they are not to be deemed of equal dignity with impartible substances. He calls the cognition of the former by the proper name "intellect," and of the latter "intellectual cogitation." 

He also divides the sensible by a similar division into first and second. In the first, he places all bodies and corporeal things. In the second, shadows and images of bodies, whether appearing in water or in mirrors. And he thinks these relate to bodies as mathematics relates to divine things. He names the perception of bodies properly "belief" <note>original: "credulitatem," translating the Greek *pistis*</note>; and of shadows, "imagination." Then, concerning shadows of bodies, or bodies, or mathematics, he denies there is knowledge, but places it in the intellect of divine things alone. 

This he also signified in this dialogue at the beginning, when he proposed that knowledge and wisdom are the same. For he everywhere testifies that wisdom is the contemplation of divine things. But how the intellect itself (that is, knowledge) differs from opinion, he shows in the book *On Nature* <note>the *Timaeus*</note> with these words: "If intellect and true opinion are two things, it is necessary that ideas be comprehended through themselves by intellect rather than by sense. But if, as it seems to some, true opinion differs not at all from intellect, then all things we sense as corporeal must be held as certain. But I think two things must be said, because both differ by a great difference: for indeed, instruction instills one in us, but the assumption of persuasion the other. One is always with true reason; the other is without any reason. One of them is not transferable by any reason, the other is wavering and uncertain. What? That every man is a participant in right opinion? But intellect is proper to God, and to a very few chosen men?" 

He testifies almost the same things in the *Meno* and *Philebus*. What then is knowledge? The certain rational comprehension of divine things. This is in the intellect, first and always. In reason second, and not always. For reason, once it has understood and is intermediate to opinion, as often as it is extended toward inferior things, is filled with the errors of opinion and ceases to think divine things. But when it is turned back to the mind, its leader, it drinks in the cognition of divine things. This, Plato names by the proper name "wisdom" in the mind, and "reminiscence" in reason. 

And therefore, he disputed in this dialogue about the obstetric <note>midwifery</note> faculty through which we remember, so that we might understand not only what knowledge is, but also how it is acquired. Nay, he even explained from whence it is and through whom, when he said Socrates performs the obstetric duty by the command of God. 

->Knowledge is, therefore, the certain rational comprehension of divine things, residing in the mind, flowing into reason, inserted into the mind by God, led back into reason by a dialectical teacher with God’s inspiration, directing reason into the mind, and joining the mind with divinity.<-

EUCLID, TERPSION, SOCRATES, THEODORUS, THEAETETUS.

**[Initial M]** Just now, O Terpsion, or have you long since come from the country? 
TERPSION. Long enough ago, and I sought you in the forum, and wondered that I could not find you. 
EUCLID. I was not in the city. 
TERPSION. But where? 
EUCLID. When I had gone down to the harbor, I encountered Theaetetus, who was being carried from the camp at Corinth to Athens. 
TERPSION. Living or dead? 
EUCLID. Half-living, for he is afflicted by certain wounds, and what is worse, he was also wasted by a long illness in the camp. 
TERPSION. Not dysentery? 
EUCLID. That very thing. 
TERPSION. O, what a man you describe placed in peril. 
EUCLID. Truly a most noble and excellent man, O Terpsion: for just a little while ago I heard some who were extolling him with wonderful praises concerning military matters. 
TERPSION. Nor should that seem a wonder; indeed, it would be far more wonderful if it were otherwise. But why did he not turn aside to Megara? 
EUCLID. He was hurrying home. I both advised and beseeched him, but he would not. Indeed, having accompanied him as I was leaving, I remembered Socrates, and wondered how divinely he prophesied both often elsewhere, and especially about this man. For a few days before he departed from life, having met Theaetetus while he was still a young youth, he discussed with him, and both approved of and wondered at his nature. Then, he narrated to me, having set out for Athens, the individual accounts of that disputation most worthy of hearing, and moreover added that he would be an altogether outstanding man if he reached maturity. And he seems to have predicted all too truly. 

TERPSION. Certainly, but what were the speeches? Can you report them? 
EUCLID. Not by word, by Jupiter, but by letters. For having returned home, I immediately sketched them out in commentaries: then, at my leisure, by remembering, I wrote them out more broadly; and as often as I set out for Athens, if anything had slipped my mind, I would ask Socrates and amend it upon returning here. Whereby it happened that almost that entire disputation was written down. 
TERPSION. You speak the truth. For I heard these things from you long ago, and desiring to know them, I often came here to ask you. What then hinders us now from running through them? For truly I have need of rest, for coming from the field, I am exhausted. 
EUCLID. I also accompanied Theaetetus as far as Erineus, wherefore I would rest most gladly. Let us go then. For while we are resting, a boy shall read to us. 
TERPSION. Excellent. 

EUCLID. Here, O Terpsion, is the book, not composed as if Socrates were reporting to me, as he in truth did, but as if he were present and disputing with those with whom he told me he disputed. <margin>Why speaking persons are introduced in dialogues. Cicero imitated this place in his book *On Old Age*.</margin> He said these were the geometer Theodorus and Theaetetus. Lest, therefore, it should be troublesome in the writing if I were to interpose "I said" and "he said," "he agreed," and "he denied" too often, having avoided these, I have introduced Socrates himself disputing together with them. 
TERPSION. Cleverly done, Euclid. 
EUCLID. Hey you [boy], take the book and read. 

SOCRATES. If the Cyrenians, O Theodorus, were my chief care, I would especially inquire from you about what pertains to them—whether any youths there were ardently applying themselves to the study of geometry or some other philosophy. But now I love our own more than those, and I rather desire to understand which of our youths seem likely to turn out as upright men. These things I always explore for myself as much as I can, and I often inquire of others to whom I see the youths flocking. For no few follow you, and rightly so. For both for the sake of other things, and especially for geometry, you seem worthy of the gathering. If therefore you have found anyone worthy of mention, I would gladly hear. 

THEODORUS. And yet, O Socrates, it is fitting for both me to report and you to listen to what kind of youth I have found from among your citizens. If he were handsome, I would fear to praise him, lest I might seem to someone to be captured by love for him. <margin>A face similar to Socrates is reported.</margin> Now, however—do not be angry with me—he is not beautiful. He is similar to you, with a flat nose and protruding eyes, although he exceeds the limit in these less than you do. I speak freely with you. Know that in the first place, I have found no youth yet, although I have been acquainted with many, endowed with such a wonderful happiness of nature. <margin>Difficult to find a man both talented and gentle and manly.</margin> It is exceedingly difficult to find a man both docile and at the same time gentle beyond others, and yet manly with everyone. Indeed, I do not think such a one ever existed, nor do I see those who are so constituted by nature. Otherwise, those who are sharp and sagacious like this, and have good memories and are docile, are for the most part prone to outbursts of anger and are headlong; for they rush out and are carried away just like ships without anchors, and they turn out to be furious rather than brave. Those who are grave, however, when they apply themselves to studies, are often sluggish, torpid, and forgetful. But this one moves toward studies and questions so smoothly, freely, sweetly, and expeditiously, with the greatest gentleness, that it seems like the silent flow of oil, softer and sweeter, and it is a wonder that such a great genius performs these things so maturely. 

SOCRATES. You bring excellent news; but whose son of our citizens is he? 
THEODORUS. I heard his name indeed, but it has slipped my memory. But he is the middle one of those who are approaching; just a little while ago they were anointing themselves outside the stadium, but now they are anointed. He and some of his companions seem to be coming here. See whether you recognize him or not. 

SOCRATES. I recognize him indeed. He is the son of Euphronius of Sunium, a man, O friend, undoubtedly such as you described the son to be, highly approved before all, who left an ample patrimony. But I have not heard the name of the boy. 
THEODORUS. Theaetetus, O Socrates, is the name, but his guardians seem to have dissipated his patrimony. Nevertheless, he is wonderfully strong in liberality. 
SOCRATES. You describe a generous man. Command him to come here and sit with us. 
THEODORUS. So be it. O Theaetetus, come here to Socrates. 

SOCRATES. Come, I beseech you, Theaetetus, so that I may contemplate myself, to see what kind of face I present. For Theodorus says my face is similar to yours. But if he asserted that the lyres of both of us were similarly tuned, would we immediately believe that? Or would we first inquire whether he was a musician? 
THEAETETUS. We would inquire. 
SOCRATES. And if we found him to be such, we would believe it; but if he were devoid of music, not at all? 
THEAETETUS. It is so. 
SOCRATES. Now then, if the similarity of our faces is of concern to us, we must see whether he who says so is a painter or not. 
THEAETETUS. So it seems. 
SOCRATES. Is Theodorus a painter? 
THEAETETUS. Not that I know of. 
SOCRATES. Is he a geometer then? 
THEAETETUS. Most certainly, O Socrates. 
SOCRATES. And an astronomer, a dialectician, a musician, and skilled in the rest of the disciplines? 
THEAETETUS. To me indeed he seems so. 
SOCRATES. While therefore he declares us to be similar in some part of the body, <margin>Faith is not to be given to one who ignores what he praises or blames.</margin> praising or blaming in a certain way, not much faith should be given to him. 
THEAETETUS. Not as it appears. 
SOCRATES. But if he were to praise someone for the virtue and wisdom of the mind, would it not be fitting for the one hearing this to consider the person praised, and for the praised one to show himself? 
THEAETETUS. Altogether, O Socrates. 
SOCRATES. See, therefore, O friend Theaetetus, it is in your interest to show, and in mine to consider. Know that although Theodorus has praised many foreigners and citizens to me, he has extolled no one with greater praises than you. 
THEAETETUS. It is well, O Socrates...

# Theaetetus, Or, on Knowledge. 95

...O Socrates, but see that he did not say it in jest. 
SOCRATES. This is not the manner of Theodorus; but do not refuse what has been conceded, objecting that he acts in jest, lest you be forced to testify. It is not easy to refute his testimony, but persist boldly in the concessions. 
THEAETETUS. It must be done, if it seems so to you. 
SOCRATES. Come tell me, do you learn some geometric things from Theodorus? 
THEAETETUS. Indeed. 
SOCRATES. And those things which pertain to astronomy and harmony, do you learn them? 
THEAETETUS. I strive indeed. 
SOCRATES. I also, O boy, strive from him and from others whom I think understand something of these things; and although I hold myself moderately in other matters, I doubt a certain small thing which must be investigated with you and with these men. Therefore, I pray you answer me. Is not learning to become wiser in that which each person learns? 
THEAETETUS. That very thing. 
SOCRATES. But are the wise wise by wisdom? <margin>Whether wisdom and knowledge are the same.</margin>
THEAETETUS. Certainly. 
SOCRATES. Does this differ in anything from knowledge? 
THEAETETUS. What specifically? 
SOCRATES. Wisdom, to be sure. In those things in which they are knowing, are they also wise? 
THEAETETUS. What prevents it? 
SOCRATES. Are wisdom and knowledge therefore the same? 
THEAETETUS. The same. 

SOCRATES. This is what I doubt, nor am I able to conclude with myself what knowledge is. Do we have anything to say to these things? What do you assert it to be? Which of us shall show it first? But whoever errs and always hallucinates <note>original: "hallucinetur," to be deceived or wander in mind</note> shall be the "ass" and sit, just as boys playing with a ball say. But he who wins and errs in nothing shall be King for us, and shall command whatever he wishes to be answered. Why are you silent? Do I, out of a desire for discourse, fall into rusticity? Wishing to lead you into a disputation, so that friends and familiars may become so to each other. 
THEAETETUS. In no way, O Socrates, would this be rustic. But you should command one of these boys to answer you. For this manner of disputing is unaccustomed to me, and my age now prevents me from becoming accustomed to it; but these things better suit them, and they will profit far more. For indeed youth profits in all things; and as you have begun, do not let Theaetetus go, but question him. 

SOCRATES. Do you hear this, O Theaetetus, what Theodorus says? Whom you, as I think, will gladly obey. For it is not right that in such matters a youth should obey a wise man less. Ingenuously therefore answer, what do you think knowledge is? <margin>First definition of knowledge.</margin>
THEAETETUS. I must obey, O Socrates, since you both command it; for if I err in anything, you will correct me. 
SOCRATES. We shall do so undoubtedly, if in any way we are able. 
THEAETETUS. It seems to me that the knowledges <note>plural: "scientiae"</note> are those which someone can learn from Theodorus—geometry and the rest which you enumerated above; furthermore, the arts of cobblers and other craftsmen; all and each are nothing other than knowledges. 
SOCRATES. Generously and magnificently, O friend, being asked for one thing, you have given many and varied things for a simple one. 
THEAETETUS. In what way do you say that, O Socrates? 
SOCRATES. Perhaps I say nothing, yet I will indicate what I think. As often as you say the "cobbling art," do you say anything other than the knowledge of making shoes? 
THEAETETUS. Nothing else. 
SOCRATES. What further, when you say the "tectonic" (that is, the building) art? Is it anything other than the knowledge of wooden works? 
THEAETETUS. Nothing certainly. 
SOCRATES. In both, therefore, you declare that of which each is the knowledge? 
THEAETETUS. Truly. 
SOCRATES. But our question was not this—of what things are there knowledges, and how many are they? For we were not seeking for the sake of counting, but to know what knowledge itself is. Do I say nothing? 
THEAETETUS. Nay, rightly. 

SOCRATES. Observe also this: if someone should ask us about one of these cheap and common things, such as clay, "What is it?" and we should answer him, "the clay of those who make pots, the clay of those who make dolls, the clay of those who mold bricks," would we not seem ridiculous? 
THEAETETUS. Perhaps. 
SOCRATES. First indeed because we would think that he who asks can understand from our answer if we say "clay," and only add "either of the doll-makers or of whatever other craftsmen." Or do you think anyone understands the name of any thing when he does not know what the thing itself is? <margin>To the one who ignores the simple, its own [nature] is ignored.</margin>
THEAETETUS. In no way. 
SOCRATES. Therefore, he does not understand the knowledge of shoes who does not know knowledge. 
THEAETETUS. Not certainly. 
SOCRATES. He also does not understand the cobbling art, whoever is ignorant of knowledge, nor any other art. 
THEAETETUS. It is so. 
SOCRATES. Therefore, the response is ridiculous if someone, being asked what knowledge is, answers the name of some art. For he answers that it is the knowledge *of something*, when this was not asked. 
THEAETETUS. It seems so. 
SOCRATES. Furthermore, when it is permitted to answer simply and briefly, he wanders around through an immense circuit. Just as in the question about clay, something light and simple can be returned: that earth mixed with moisture is clay. But whose clay it is should be omitted. 

THEAETETUS. Easily now, O Socrates, it seems so. For you seem to seek what recently came into my mind and that of this Socrates <note>referring to "Young Socrates," a silent character in the dialogue</note> who is similar to you in name, while we were disputing. 
SOCRATES. What was that, O Theaetetus? 
THEAETETUS. Theodorus here was writing about the powers <note>original: "potestatib," referring to square roots of non-square numbers</note> of the three-foot and five-foot magnitude, showing that in length they are not commensurable with the one-foot magnitude. Running through in the same way and eliciting individuals up to the magnitude of seventeen feet, he finally stopped there. Something of this kind came into our minds: since the "powers" emerged infinite in number, we must try to comprehend them into one, by which we may express them all. 
SOCRATES. Was some such thing found then? 
THEAETETUS. To me indeed it seems so; you consider it also. 
SOCRATES. Speak. 
THEAETETUS. We divided all number into two. One which can be made "equal times equal" <note>a square number</note>, which we compared to the square figure, calling it quadrangular and equilateral. 
SOCRATES. Excellent. 
THEAETETUS. And that which is in the middle between these—such as are three and five, and every number which cannot be made "equal times equal," but is taken either "greater fewer times" or "lesser more times" <note>factors that are not equal</note>, and always contains a greater and a lesser side—we compared to the "oblong" <note>original: "altera parte longiori," literally 'longer in the other part'</note> figure, and called it an oblong number. <margin>The sides of this square are the means between three and five, and are incommensurable to them in length, but commensurable in power: for the [square] of them is equal to the square, as is clear.</margin>
SOCRATES. Outstandingly done; what then after that? 
THEAETETUS. All lines which square an equilateral and plane number, we defined as "length"; but those which square an oblong number, we called "powers," as being in no way commensurable to those in length, but commensurable to the planes which they are able to form; and something of this kind also concerning solids. 
SOCRATES. Best of all, O boys. Wherefore Theodorus will in no way be found guilty of false testimony. 

THEAETETUS. Truly, O Socrates, what you ask about knowledge, I am not able to answer in the same way as about length and power, although you seem to me to be inquiring for something of this kind. Whereby it happens that Theodorus appears false in turn. 
SOCRATES. What then? If he had praised you for speed in running, adding that he had seen none of the boys more prompt in the course: then, in running, you were beaten by an adult and some very swift person, would you think he had praised you any less truly? 
THEAETETUS. In no way. 
SOCRATES. But knowledge—as I was saying a little while ago—is it something "light" to find, or rather something "grave" and supreme? 
THEAETETUS. By Jupiter, I think it is something supreme. 
SOCRATES. Have confidence in your powers, and do not weigh the testimony of Theodorus lightly. Strive with all study, both concerning other things and also concerning knowledge itself, to attain the reason of what it is. 
THEAETETUS. For the sake of striving, O Socrates, we shall do these things. 
SOCRATES. Come now, be of good heart, for you just now explained excellently. Try to imitate the response...

that division regarding powers; just as you grouped many of them into one species, so too you should embrace many sciences [branches of knowledge] within one reasoning. THEAETETUS. Know, O Socrates, that I have often attempted this when I heard these questions of yours being circulated. But I can neither persuade myself that I am fit for this, or that I have sufficient ability, nor have I heard anyone else disputing as you command; yet I have not given up on the inquiry. SOCRATES. Are you in pain, O friend Theaetetus, because you are not empty, but pregnant? THEAETETUS. I do not know, O Socrates, but I am telling you what has happened to me. SOCRATES. O ridiculous man, have you not heard that I am the son of a very noble and stern midwife, Phaenarete? THEAETETUS. I have heard it indeed. SOCRATES. And have you heard that I practice the same art? THEAETETUS. Not at all. SOCRATES. Know that it is so, but do not betray me to others. For it has remained hidden from everyone until now that I am endowed with this art, and they, being ignorant, do not proclaim this about me, but rather that I am most absurd and lead men into ambiguity—have you heard this? THEAETETUS. Exactly that. SOCRATES. Do you want me to assign the cause of this to you? THEAETETUS. Why wouldn't I? SOCRATES. Consider what midwives are like, and you will easily perceive what I mean. For you know that none of them helps others in labor as long as she herself conceives and bears children, but only when they are already unfit for bearing. THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. They say the cause of this is <term>Diana</term> <note>Original: "Dianam," the Roman name for the Greek goddess Artemis, patron of childbirth</note>, who, though she is sterile, took up the protection of births; she forbade sterile women from becoming midwives, because human nature is too weak to master arts of things it has never experienced. However, to those who can no longer conceive due to age, she gave this duty, honoring their likeness to herself. THEAETETUS. That is indeed likely. SOCRATES. Is it not also probable and necessary that those who are pregnant and those who are not are noticed more sharply by midwives than by others? THEAETETUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, by medicines and incantations, midwives are able to arouse or soften the pains of labor, and to help those laboring with difficulty to bring forth the fetus, and if it seems it will be untimely, to blunt and push it back. THEAETETUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. And have you heard this about them: that they are most fit as matchmakers in arranging marriages? For they know best which man should be joined to which woman for the procreation of noble offspring. THEAETETUS. I did not know that well enough. SOCRATES. Indeed, you should know they glory in this no less than in the cutting of the umbilical cord itself. For do you think it belongs to another art, or to the same one, to care for and gather the fruits of the earth, and again to distinguish which seed or plant should be cast into which soil? THEAETETUS. To the same art. SOCRATES. In the case of women, then, O friend, do you think this is a matter of one faculty and that of another? THEAETETUS. It is not likely. SOCRATES. Certainly not; but because of the unjust and absurd joining of male and female, which is called <term>pandering</term> <note>Socrates distinguishes between legitimate matchmaking and the illegal or shameful act of procuring</note>, chaste midwives avoid the office of reconciling marriage, fearing lest they be branded as panders for their zeal in matchmaking, even if they join legitimate couples. THEAETETUS. That is clear. SOCRATES. Therefore, the duty of midwives is a lesser work compared to mine. For it does not happen to women that they sometimes give birth to mere images and sometimes to various real things. But it is not easy to discern this, and if it were possible, it would be the greatest and most magnificent task of midwives to discern the true from the false. But what do you think? THEAETETUS. Exactly the same. SOCRATES. My art possesses everything that pertains to the diligence of those midwives. But it excels in this: that it assists men, not women, in labor, and it watches over the births of souls, not bodies.

<margin>Midwives.</margin>
<margin>Diana wished for sterile midwives to be made.</margin>
<margin>Why midwives do not wish to be matchmakers.</margin>
<margin>The midwifery art of Socrates.</margin>

But the greatest thing in my art is this: the ability to examine diligently whether the thought of the young man brings forth an image and a falsehood, or something native and true. Furthermore, the same thing happens to me as to the midwives: I am sterile and void of wisdom. And what many have objected to me—that I question individuals but answer no one, because I have nothing wise that I can answer—they object quite truly. Indeed, this is the cause: God compels me to assist those in labor but has forbidden me to generate. Therefore, I am not myself wise in any matter at all, nor does there exist any discovery of my mind born from me. But those who associate with me appear at first to be ignorant, but then, through my company, those whom God favors make wonderful progress, as it seems both to themselves and to others. This much is certain: they never learn anything from me, but rather they themselves, possessing many excellent things within themselves, find them. God and I are the cause of this midwifery duty, which can be most clearly conjectured from this: for many, being ignorant of this in the past and thinking themselves the cause, despised me, perhaps persuaded by others. Thus they departed from me sooner than they should have. These, departing, miscarried the rest because of their wicked company; and moreover, the things I had already rescued from the bowels of their souls through my midwifery aid, they lost entirely by nourishing them badly, since they preferred falsehoods and images far above the truth. Finally, they appeared ignorant both to themselves and to others. One of their number was Aristides, the son of Lysimachus, and many others. But when they return to me, needing my company again and desiring it wonderfully, my <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "daemonium." Socrates's inner guiding spirit or divine sign.</note> forbids me from trusting some of them immediately, but permits it for others, who then make great progress again. For my associates suffer this in common with those in labor: they are tormented and filled with difficulty day and night, much more than those women. My art is able to both arouse and soothe this pain. And so it is with them. But sometimes, O Theaetetus, when some do not seem to me to be fertile, and noticing that they do not need my help, I gladly join them in marriage to others, and—to speak with God's help—I acutely foresee which unions will be most profitable for them. Many of these I have handed over to Prodicus, and many to other wise and divine men. I have recounted all these things at length, O best of men, for this reason: I suspected you were pregnant with a certain concept and in labor, as you yourself think. Commit yourself, therefore, to me as to the son of a midwife, and as one long skilled in the midwifery faculty; and when I inquire, strive to answer with all your strength. And if, in discussing what you have said, I should refute it as an image appearing rather than the truth and cast it away, I pray you do not be angry, just as women in their first labor are prone to be. Many already, O wonderful youth, have been so affected toward me that they wished to attack me with their teeth if I took away some nonsense from them, not thinking that I do this out of benevolence—for it was hidden from them that no God is malevolent toward men, nor do I do any such thing out of ill will. It seems to me clearly forbidden by divine law to admit the false or to refute the truth. Therefore, from the beginning again, Theaetetus, try to explain what knowledge is, as far as you are able; but do not say that you cannot. For if God wills it and helps you, you will be able. THEAETETUS. Since you so command, O Socrates, it would be shameful if one did not bring forth his own opinion. It seems to me that he who knows something perceives what he knows; and as it now appears, knowledge is nothing other than perception. SOCRATES. How nobly you have answered, O boy; for thus it is necessary for one to speak who

--- Page 116 ---
->Theaetetus, or, Concerning Science [Knowledge]. 97<-

wishes to define anything. But let us consider together whether this fetus is solid or empty. You say that perception is knowledge. THEAETETUS. I do. SOCRATES. You seem to have brought forth a definition of knowledge that is not to be cast aside, but which Protagoras introduced in another way. For he says that man is the measure of all things: of those that are, that they are; and of those that are not, that they are not. Have you ever read this? THEAETETUS. I have indeed read it often. SOCRATES. Does he not say it thus: as each thing appears to me, such it is to me; and as it appears to you, such it is to you—and we are both men? THEAETETUS. He certainly says that. SOCRATES. Yet it is probable that a wise man does not talk nonsense. Let us follow him, therefore. Does it not often happen that when the same wind is blowing, one of us feels cold and the other not at all? And one slightly, the other severely? THEAETETUS. Without doubt. SOCRATES. Shall we say then that the wind itself is cold in itself, or not cold? Or shall we believe Protagoras, that it is cold to the one who feels cold, and not to the one who does not? THEAETETUS. So it seems. SOCRATES. Does it not thus appear to both? THEAETETUS. Yes. SOCRATES. But "to appear" is "to perceive"? THEAETETUS. It is. SOCRATES. Therefore, <term>phantasia</term> <note>The faculty of appearance or imagination</note> and perception are the same in heat and other things of this kind. For as each person perceives things, such they appear to him to be. THEAETETUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. Perception, therefore, is always of an existing thing, and it is never false, since it is knowledge. THEAETETUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. By the powers of the Graces, was not Protagoras an exceptionally wise man? And did he not signal this obscurely to us common folk, while explaining the truth to his disciples in secret? THEAETETUS. In what way do you say this, O Socrates? SOCRATES. I will tell you, and it is not to be despised: that nothing is one certain thing in itself, nor can one rightly name it as "this" or "of such a kind" from itself. For if you call it large, it again appears small; and if heavy, it appears light. The same reasoning applies to all other things, as if nothing were one, or anything, or any quality. But from motion, movement, and mutual mixture, all things arise which we say "are," though we name them incorrectly. For nothing ever *is*, but always *becomes*. And in this, all the wise in order, except Parmenides, have agreed: Protagoras, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and the greatest of the poets in both types of poetry: Epicharmus in comedy, and Homer in tragedy. For when Homer spoke of the Ocean as the generation of the gods and Tethys as their mother, he proclaimed that all things are born from flux and motion. Does he not seem to put it that way? THEAETETUS. To me, indeed. SOCRATES. Who then would dare to fight against such an army, and its leader Homer, without being considered ridiculous? THEAETETUS. It is difficult, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Difficult without doubt, Theaetetus, especially since these things can serve as an argument for this discourse: that motion makes things seem to be or to become, while rest makes them not be and perish. For fire and heat, which beget and govern other things, are themselves produced from movement and friction; and this is motion—is this not the origin of fire? THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Furthermore, the race of animals is born from these same things. THEAETETUS. Why not? SOCRATES. What about the condition of bodies? Is it not corrupted by idleness and sluggishness, but preserved for the most part by exercise and motion? THEAETETUS. Yes. SOCRATES. The condition of the soul also, through discipline and meditation, which are motions, attains doctrines, is preserved, and is perfected; but through idleness—that is, negligence and laziness—it learns nothing at all, and if it has learned anything, it forgets it. THEAETETUS. Most definitely. SOCRATES. Therefore, motion is good both in the soul and in the body, but rest is the contrary. THEAETETUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. Moreover, regarding those things called calm and tranquility, I assert this: that states of rest cause rot and destruction, while other things preserve. And so I will finally bring the messenger from Colophon, adding the <term>Golden Chain</term> itself. By which Homer means nothing other than the sun: because as long as the sun's circuit continues, all things of gods and men exist and are preserved. But if this were to stand still as if locked, immediately all things would be dissolved, and that saying would happen: "everything turned upside down." THEAETETUS. To me also, O Socrates, it seems to be as you say. SOCRATES. Think then this way, O best of men, regarding the eyes: first, that the color we call white is not itself anything else outside your eyes, nor in your eyes, nor should you attribute a certain place to it. For then it would be in an order and would remain, and would no longer be in the process of becoming. THEAETETUS. But how? SOCRATES. Let us follow the previous discourse, positing nothing as one certain thing in itself; and thus black and white and every other color appears to us as generated from the meeting of the eyes and the proper motion. And each thing that we call by the name of color will be neither the thing striking the eyes nor the thing struck, but a certain middle effect peculiar to each. Or would you assert that as each color appears to you, it appears the same to dogs and every other animal? THEAETETUS. By Jupiter, no. SOCRATES. What about to another man and to you? Does each thing seem to appear similarly? Or rather, does it not even seem the same to yourself, because you are never similar to yourself? THEAETETUS. I think the latter rather than the former. SOCRATES. If, therefore, that by which we measure, or that which we touch, were large, or white, or hot, it would never, in meeting something else, become something else itself, provided nothing changed. But if the thing measured which we touch were white or hot, even if nothing else happened to it, it would be changed without suffering anything itself. For in the present case, my friend, we are forced to say some strange and easily ridiculed things, as Protagoras himself and anyone else of the same opinion would confess. THEAETETUS. In what way? And what kind of things do you mean? SOCRATES. Take a brief example, and you will understand what I want. If you have six dice and you add four, we say they are more than four and exceed them by half, which is called a <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio</note> proportion. But if you have twelve, they are fewer and by half. It cannot be said otherwise. Or do you? THEAETETUS. Certainly in no way. SOCRATES. What then? If Protagoras, or anyone else, asked you: "O Theaetetus, can anything become larger or more in any other way than by being increased?" what would you answer? THEAETETUS. If I bring forth what seems to me, O Socrates, I would assert that it cannot. But if I respond with the previous position in mind, I will say it is possible, lest I contradict myself. SOCRATES. Well and divinely said, by Juno, O friend. Therefore, it seems, if you answer that it is so, that saying of Euripides will happen: "The tongue will remain unrefuted, but the mind will be refuted." THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. If, therefore, you and I were eloquent and wise, after we had searched all the corners of the mind, soon, as if from an abundance, each trying his own strength and meeting in this arena in the manner of sophists, we would clash in our speeches. But now, being unlearned folk, we wish first to contemplate these things in themselves, to see what kind of things we are thinking, and whether they agree among ourselves or not. THEAETETUS. I would like that very much. SOCRATES. No less than I. But since we are so disposed, let us calmly, since we are at leisure, look again, not succeeding one another, but truly examining ourselves, what these appearances and phantasms within us are. Having considered these first, we will say, I believe, that nothing ever becomes greater or smaller

in either mass or number, as long as it remains equal to itself, is it not so? THEAETETUS. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Secondly, that to which nothing is added and from which nothing is subtracted, this neither ever grows nor decreases, but always stands equal. THEAETETUS. Very much so. SOCRATES. Thirdly, we will say that what was not before and is afterwards cannot exist unless it happens and is made. THEAETETUS. So it certainly seems. SOCRATES. These three concessions fight against each other in our mind when we speak of those things, or when we admit that I, an old man, while remaining so great, neither increased nor diminished in any part, am now greater than you, a youth, in the same year, and later will be smaller, though my mass was not taken away, but yours alone increased. For I am later what I was not before, yet without having become anything, for to have become without becoming is impossible. Yet losing nothing of mass, I never became smaller. And infinite other things of this kind happen in many cases, if we admit these. Come, speak, O Theaetetus. For you seem to me not unskilled in these matters. THEAETETUS. By the gods, O Socrates, I greatly wonder what those things are, and sometimes, looking at them most intently, I am overwhelmed by darkness. SOCRATES. Theodorus, O friend, seems to have conjectured not badly about your nature. For this happens most of all to philosophers: to wonder. For there is no other beginning of philosophy than this. And he who said that <term>Iris</term> <note>The goddess of the rainbow and messenger of the gods</note> was the daughter of Thaumas (that is, of Wonder) did not explain her origin absurdly. But do you perceive for what reason such things are from which we asserted Protagoras spoke, or not? THEAETETUS. I do not seem to yet. SOCRATES. Will you then be grateful to me if I reveal the due truth of the intelligence of the man, or rather of most celebrated men? THEAETETUS. Why wouldn't I be? And a huge gratitude indeed. SOCRATES. Contemplate now, and at the same time be diligently careful lest any profane person hear these things. The profane are those who think nothing else exists except what they can hold in their fist. But actions, generations, and whatever is invisible, they do not hold to be in the number of things that are. THEAETETUS. You describe two very stubborn and impudent men, O Socrates. SOCRATES. These are indeed, O boy, quite alienated from the Muses. Nor are there lacking certain more elegant others whose mysteries I am about to tell you. The beginning will follow from which those things we just said flow: namely, that this universe is motion, and nothing exists besides motion. Of motion, however, there are two species: and both are infinite in multitude, but one has the power of acting, the other of suffering. From their meeting and mutual collision, effects occur, infinite in number but twin in species: namely, the sensible thing and the perception, which always coincides and meets with the sensible. These are the names of the perceptions: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and the touch of cold and heat. These are followed by pleasures, pains, desires, and fears, and other innumerable unnamed affects, as well as many that are named. But the sensible genus is kindred to each perception. To all-natured visions, all-natured colors; likewise to ears, voices; and to the other senses, other kindred sensible things are similarly present. What then, O Theaetetus, does this discourse have to do with the previous ones? Do you notice? THEAETETUS. Not much, O Socrates. SOCRATES. See then if it is brought to a conclusion in this way. For it means this to you: that all these things, as we said, are in motion, and in their motions there is speed or slowness. As far as slowness is present, it holds its motion in the same place and toward things nearby, and thus generates. But the things thus begotten are swifter. For they are carried, and their motion is in that carrying. When therefore the eye, or something that has approached, generates whiteness and the kindred perception, which would never have been born while either of them had approached something else, then indeed in the meantime, while sight is carried from the eyes and whiteness from that which then gives forth color from itself, the eyes are filled with sight and see, and become not sight, but a seeing eye. But that which then gives forth color from itself is filled with whiteness, and becomes not whiteness, but a white thing, whether wood or stone, or whatever else may happen to be colored with color of this kind. And in the same way, judgment must be made about other things, like the hot and the hard, and all the rest. None of these is anything in itself, which we also discussed in the previous parts, but all things become all kinds of things in their mutual meeting, because of motion. Since one cannot firmly think, as they say, that either the acting or the suffering thing is any one thing by itself. For the acting thing is nothing before it meets with the suffering thing, nor the suffering before the acting. For that which meets with something and has the power of acting, when it falls upon another, only then first appears as suffering. From all these things it follows, as we also said from the beginning, that nothing is one thing according to itself, but always becomes to something, and "to be" itself must be excluded from everywhere. Although we have often been forced by a certain habit and ignorance to use that very word "to be." Nevertheless, as the speech of the wise dictates, one should in no way predicate anything either to someone, or of me, or "this," or "that," or any other name that signifies existence; but it is necessary to pronounce according to nature that they are moved, that they become, that they are corrupted, that they are changed. For if anyone asserts that anything stands firm in speech, he will be easily refuted. It is necessary to speak thus both individually and about all things collected into one: in which collection they place man, and stone, and every animal and species. Does this, O Theaetetus, seem pleasant to you? And will you taste it as if it pleased you? THEAETETUS. I do not know, O Socrates, and I am even ambiguous about you, whether you report these things as consonant with your own mind, or rather to test me. SOCRATES. You do not remember, friend, that I know nothing of these things, and I claim none such as my own? For I am sterile of them. But I stir and exercise you according to the midwife's rite, and for this sake I enchant you, and I offer the sayings of each of the wise to be tasted until I bring your own opinion into the light. When at last it has been brought out, then first I will examine whether it be empty and sterile, or fertile and solid. Boldly and constantly then, well and manfully, bring forth your opinion in these things which I shall now ask you. THEAETETUS. Ask then. SOCRATES. Say whether it pleases you that nothing *is*, but the good and the beautiful always *become*, and all those things we enumerated a little while ago. THEAETETUS. While I hear you arguing, they seem wonderfully probable and to be admitted. SOCRATES. Let us not pass over then what remains. For it remains that I speak of dreams and diseases, among other things, especially insanity, and of that which is perversely seen, or heard, or otherwise perceived in any way. For you know that in all these things the discourse we reported above is refuted without any controversy, since the senses are entirely deceived in them. And so far is it from being the case that all things which appear to anyone are true, that on the contrary, none of the things that appear exist. THEAETETUS. You tell the truth, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Where then, O boy, will he flee who affirmed that perception is knowledge, and that whatever things appear to anyone, such they are to him as they seemed? THEAETETUS. I am ashamed to speak further, Socrates. For I have nothing to bring into the middle. For what I had posited, you have utterly overturned by terrifying me.

overturned. Truly I could never deny that those who are mad and dreaming think things that are far too false, since some of them think they are gods, others believe they fly like birds. SOCRATES. That which I think you have often heard, whenever it is asked by what conjecture it can best be shown whether we are all dreaming now and dreaming each of the things we think, or whether we are awake and truly differ from one another. THEAETETUS. Indeed it is doubtful, O Socrates, because one might discern it by conjecture. So much does each follow upon each as if reciprocal. For the things we are now discussing, nothing prevents us from seeming to speak while dreaming. And when in a dream we think we are recounting dreams, these things are wonderfully similar to those. SOCRATES. You see now how easily it comes into controversy; since it can even be doubted whether the things seen are dreams or true things. Moreover, since the time given to sleep and to waking is equal, in both our soul contends to assert the present opinions as true. Wherefore for an equal time we will say these are true, and for an equal time those, and we will maintain ourselves in both. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. The same reasoning applies to diseases and fits of madness, except that the time is unequal. THEAETETUS. Quite rightly. SOCRATES. Is truth determined by the length or brevity of time? THEAETETUS. But that would be very ridiculous. SOCRATES. Can you show by any other argument which of these opinions are true? THEAETETUS. Not as it seems to me. SOCRATES. Listen then to me, for what those who want the appearances always to be true to the one to whom they appear might answer. For thus, I think, they would ask you: "O Theaetetus, can that which is entirely other ever have the same power as another thing? And let us understand not 'the same in part and other in part,' but entirely other." THEAETETUS. It is impossible then for this to have anything the same as that, either in power or in any way, when it is entirely other. SOCRATES. Does it not necessarily follow that it is also dissimilar? THEAETETUS. It seems so to me. SOCRATES. If therefore something becomes similar or dissimilar to anything, either to itself or to another, we will confess that as far as it becomes similar, it is the same; as far as dissimilar, it is made other. THEAETETUS. It follows necessarily. SOCRATES. Did we not concede above that there are many and innumerable acting things, and similarly suffering things? THEAETETUS. We conceded it. SOCRATES. And that what is other from another, when mixed with one and then another, will generate not the same things but other things. THEAETETUS. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Let us say then of me and you and others according to the same reasoning—namely, Socrates being well, and Socrates being sick—shall we say this is similar to that, or dissimilar? THEAETETUS. Do you mean this whole "sick Socrates" to that whole "well Socrates"? SOCRATES. You have taken it quite rightly; that is exactly what I was saying. THEAETETUS. Clearly dissimilar and other. SOCRATES. Then, in that it is dissimilar, is it also other? THEAETETUS. Necessarily. SOCRATES. And will you assert the same for the sleeping and the waking man, and all those things we recounted above? THEAETETUS. I will indeed. SOCRATES. Will each of those things which by nature can effect anything, when it receives the healthy Socrates, use me as one person, and when weak, as another? THEAETETUS. Why not? SOCRATES. And we will generate other things in both cases—I suffering, and that effecting? THEAETETUS. Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES. Whenever I drink wine being healthy, it seems sweet and pleasant to me. THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Further, from these things which were conceded—the acting and the suffering—they produced sweetness and perception, and both were moved: and the perception, existing from the suffering part, made the tongue perceive; but the sweetness, moved from the wine around it, made the wine both *be* and *appear* sweet to the healthy tongue. THEAETETUS. Thus the previous things were entirely conceded. SOCRATES. But when it receives me being sick, first of all it does not in truth find the same person, for it comes to a dissimilar one. THEAETETUS. It is so. SOCRATES. Then the wine-drinking and Socrates being thus affected generate other things: around the tongue, a perception of bitter sleepiness; around the wine, a bitterness—not making me perception itself, but rather a perceiver. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. And I shall never become anything else thus perceiving. For the perception of another thing is other, and it makes the perceiver different and other; nor will that which makes me such, if it ever meets another, generate the same thing and exist as such. For generating one thing from another, it will become different and other. THEAETETUS. These things are true. SOCRATES. Nor shall I become such to myself, nor will that become such to itself. THEAETETUS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. But it is necessary that I become *something's* perceiver whenever I become a perceiver. For it is impossible for a perceiver to perceive nothing. And it is also necessary for that to become *something's* whenever it is rendered sweet or bitter or anything of this kind. For sweet cannot be sweet to no one. THEAETETUS. It is entirely so. SOCRATES. It remains then, I believe, that whether we "are," we are not to each other; or whether we "become," we become to each other; since necessity itself connects our essence. But it connects it to none of the others, nor to ourselves; it follows then that we are bound to each other. Wherefore if anyone says something "is" or "becomes," it must be understood thus: it is or becomes for someone, or of someone, or toward something; but that anything *is* or *becomes* in itself, he should neither profess it himself, nor allow another to assert it, just as the previous reasoning admonishes. THEAETETUS. It is exactly so, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Since, then, that which effects me is for me and not another, do I not also perceive it, and not another? THEAETETUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Therefore my perception is true to me: for it always exists for my essence, and I, according to Protagoras, am the judge of those things that are, as they are to me, and of those things that are not, as they are not. THEAETETUS. So it seems. SOCRATES. What now hinders me from being knowing [wise], just as I am perceiving? Especially since I am neither deceived nor do I wander in thought regarding those things which either are or become? THEAETETUS. Nothing at all. SOCRATES. Excellently then did you say that knowledge is nothing else than perception. Indeed, these things coincide: according to Homer and Heraclitus and all that kind, all things flow along like a river; according to Protagoras, the wisest man, man is the measure of all things; and finally, according to Theaetetus, the previous concessions being granted, knowledge is perception. Shall we say, O Theaetetus, that this opinion is like your offspring, recently generated by you, and now brought into the light by me through a certain midwifery work? What do you say? THEAETETUS. It must be so, O Socrates. SOCRATES. This offspring, it seems, whatever it may be, we have at last barely generated; but after the birth, as is the custom, on the fifth day after its birth, let us celebrate the solemnities by running through the circle of disputes, to see if it might deceive us, if perhaps it is not worthy of being raised but is empty and false: or do you think your newborn must be nourished at all costs and in no way cast away? Or perhaps if you see your firstborn rejected, will you not take it badly that it is removed? THEAETETUS. Theaetetus, O Socrates, will bear it with a calm mind. For he is not peevish. But say, by the gods, is it not so if the matter stands thus? SOCRATES. You are very eager for dispute and a good man, O Theodorus, who thinks I am a certain chest of speeches, from which I will soon bring forth a monster showing that these things are not so: no,

When nevertheless each person is the measure of his own wisdom. Or how shall we not say that in these things Protagoras is not talking nonsense? To pass over my own zeal for the midwifery faculty, how much laughter shall we provide? Indeed, I think, and the whole duty of arguing. For that attempt to discuss and refute each other's phantasms and opinions, when all are right for each person, will be nothing else than great and long nonsense, if that truth of Protagoras, which he so names, is true—and yet he is not joking, but spoke as if from the inner sanctuary of his book. Not by Jupiter; and I greatly wonder at what you ask: for while we were explaining above the reason why what seems to each is true to each, it seemed to be said quite skillfully; but now a contrary opinion immediately comes to mind. SOCRATES. You are still young, O friend boy, and therefore you are easily persuaded by a public assembly. For to these things Protagoras, and any other follower of his, will say: "O noble boys and men, apply your mind to the assembly with confidence, and bring the gods into the middle, about whom I think one should neither speak nor write as to whether they exist or not; and say these things which many hearing would admit (which would be grave, unless any man were far superior in wisdom to any brute beast); but bring no demonstration or necessity, but use only a likely reasoning." If Theodorus or any other geometer wished to use such reasoning in geometrical disputes, he would be valued at nothing at all. Consider then, both you and Theodorus, whether you wish to receive speeches about such great matters confirmed only by probable reasoning. THEAETETUS. Shall we confess that whatever we perceive by seeing or hearing, we also simultaneously know? For example, the voice of barbarians <note>meaning foreigners who do not speak Greek</note> before we have learned it—shall we say we do not hear them when they speak? Or that we hear and know at the same time? And being entirely ignorant of letters when we look at their context, shall we deny that we see them? Or shall we assert that we also know them, if only we have seen them? THEAETETUS. That very thing which we discern and hear in these, O Socrates, we shall affirm that we know: that we see and similarly know their shape and color, and likewise that we hear and know their high and low voice. But what grammarians and interpreters hand down about these, we say we neither perceive by seeing and hearing, nor even know. SOCRATES. But look at another thing that is added to these, and consider how it can be repelled and avoided. THEAETETUS. What is that? SOCRATES. This surely: if someone asks whether it is possible that what someone once knew, and still holds in memory and preserves fixed, he nevertheless does not know that very thing. I am drawing into a long speech, wishing to ask whether someone who retains in memory what he learned does not know it. THEAETETUS. How could this happen, O Socrates? What you say would be a monster. He who sees something—does he not know the same thing that he sees, as the present speech proposes? THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Do you call "memory" something? THEAETETUS. I do indeed. SOCRATES. I too, by Jupiter, suspect it, though I do not yet quite understand. Tell me, I pray, in what way? SOCRATES. <summary>In these pages, Socrates explains his "midwifery" of the soul, through which he helps others bring forth their own ideas, and begins a rigorous examination of Theaetetus's proposal that "knowledge is perception." He links this definition to Protagoras’s relativism and Heraclitus’s theory of universal flux, while raising initial challenges regarding dreams, memory, and the equality of all perceptions.</summary>

# Theaetetus, or, Concerning Knowledge. 101

Indeed, we predicted that if this were to happen, it would be a kind of monster. THEAETETUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. It seems impossible for something to occur if one assumes that **knowledge and sense-perception** are the same. THEAETETUS. So it appears. SOCRATES. Therefore, we must admit they are two different things. THEAETETUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. For which reason, we must search again from the beginning for what knowledge actually is. But what are we doing, O Theaetetus? THEAETETUS. About what are you asking? SOCRATES. We seem to me like **lazy roosters** <note>original: "ignaui galli". Socrates uses this metaphor to describe someone who claims victory or starts "crowing" before the argument is actually won.</note>, leaping away from the discussion to start crowing before we have conquered. THEAETETUS. How so? SOCRATES. We seem to have reached an agreement based on the contradictory use of names, and by dealing with such things, we have scrutinized words and remained stuck in them. While we profess to be philosophers rather than professional babblers <note>original: "rabulas". A "rabula" was a loud, unlearned lawyer or a petty wrangler.</note>, we are meanwhile doing nothing different than those fierce men do in secret. THEAETETUS. I do not yet understand what you mean. SOCRATES. I will try to explain what I feel about these things. We asked whether someone who says and remembers something could be ignorant of it. By showing that someone who has seen a thing remembers it even with his eyes closed, yet does not see it, we demonstrated that he is both ignorant and remembering at the same time—which is quite impossible. And thus, the fable of Protagoras has vanished, and along with it yours, which sang that sense-perception and knowledge were the same thing. THEAETETUS. That is established. SOCRATES.
