Not at all, I think, my friend, if the father of that other fable <note>Socrates refers to Protagoras as the "father" of the idea that "man is the measure of all things."</note> were still alive; he would defend it most vehemently. But now, we pursue it as an orphan and strip it bare, and the guardians Protagoras left behind—one of whom is Theodorus here—refuse to help. Therefore, for the sake of justice, we ourselves shall attempt to support it. THEAETETUS. Not I, Socrates; rather, Callias, son of Hipponicus, is the guardian of Protagoras's affairs. We, indeed, have suddenly turned from "naked" <note>This refers to "naked" dialectic or pure philosophical talk as opposed to the "clothed" or technical proofs of geometry.</note> speeches to geometry. We will be grateful to you, however, if you bring him aid. SOCRATES. You speak skillfully, O Theodorus. Pay attention, then, to the way I shall help. If someone does not notice the power of words, by which we are usually accustomed to affirm or deny anything, he will be forced to admit things even more absurd than what came before. Shall I tell you how, or shall I tell Theaetetus? THEODORUS. To both of us together. But let the younger one answer. For if he slips, he will do less harm. SOCRATES. I state a very difficult question: is it possible that someone who knows something is also ignorant of what he does not know? THEODORUS. What shall we answer, Theaetetus? THEAETETUS. I think it is impossible. SOCRATES. Not at all, if you assume that "seeing" is "knowing." For what would you answer to an inexplicable question—trapped in a "well," as they say—if someone truly intrepid asked you, while covering one of your eyes with his hand, whether you see your cloak with the covered eye? THEODORUS. I would say not with that one, but with the other. SOCRATES. Do you not then see and not see the same thing at the same time? THEAETETUS. Yes, in a way. SOCRATES. He will say: I do not ask "how" or "in what way," but whether what you know, you also do not know. In the present case, you seem to see what you do not see. And it was previously admitted that seeing is knowing, and not seeing is not knowing. Consider what is concluded against you from these points. THEAETETUS. The exact opposite of what I proposed. SOCRATES. Perhaps many more such things would have happened to you, O wonderful boy, if someone had asked you whether it is possible to know both sharply and dully, or to know up close but not at all from a distance, or to know the same thing intensely and weakly, and many other things besides. A "shield-bearing" man <note>original: "vir clypeatus". Socrates uses military imagery to describe a professional debater or Sophist who fights with words for pay.</note>, hired for pay to speak, would have lain in wait for you when you claimed knowledge and sense-perception were the same. He would have thrown you into questions about hearing, smelling, and the other senses, and he would have refuted you diligently and eagerly. Having caught you, he would not let you go until you, having admired his exquisite wisdom, were bound by him—where, captured and tied, you would redeem yourself for as much money as he might set. You might ask, then: what reasoning will Protagoras assign to defend his opinions? Must we try something else? THEAETETUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. He will proceed with all these things we are saying to help him, and on the contrary, I think, he will look down on us deeply, saying: "That good man Socrates, when a boy he questioned was terrified by whether one can know and be ignorant of what he remembers at the same time, and when that terrified boy denied it because he could not see the matter clearly, Socrates showed me to be ridiculous in the dispute. But the matter, O most lazy Socrates, stands like this: Whenever you consider something by questioning one of my followers, if the questioned person answers the same things I would have answered and is refuted, then consider me refuted as well. But if he answers differently, then only he who answered is refuted." <margin>Proverb.</margin> <margin>For Protagoras.</margin>

<summary>Socrates begins to challenge Theaetetus's definition of knowledge as sense-perception, arguing that such a definition leads to logical contradictions, specifically regarding memory.</summary>
<keywords>Theaetetus, Socrates, Protagoras, knowledge, sense-perception, memory, dialectic</keywords>

--- Page 121 ---
This text is a Latin translation of Plato’s *Theaetetus*, specifically the section spanning from approximately 167a to 197c. Based on the "Liber Decimustertius" heading and the marginalia, this is the version translated by the Renaissance humanist **Marsilio Ficino**.

The dialogue features **Socrates**, **Theodorus**, and **Theaetetus** discussing the nature of knowledge, the doctrines of Protagoras and Heraclitus, and the possibility of false opinion.

***

### Book Thirteen [Theaetetus]

**[Page 102]**
...Moreover, friend Socrates, I by no means call them frogs [*ranas*]; rather, as far as bodies are concerned, I call them doctors; as far as plants are concerned, husbandmen. For I assert that these men, whenever such a thing is sick, instill good, healthy, and true sensations into their plants in place of depraved ones. Likewise, wise and good rhetoricians make good things seem just to cities instead of bad ones; for whatever things seem just and honorable to any city, these are so for that city as long as it thinks them so. But the wise man causes good things both to be judged and to be in place of these individual bad things. By the same reasoning, the sophist, being capable of so instructing those who are taught, is wise and is held worthy of a large reward by his listeners. And thus some are wiser than others, yet no one thinks false things; and you, whether you wish it or not, must admit this very thing, since you are the measure of things. For the discourse is preserved in these points. If you can oppose this again from the beginning in any way, oppose it by meeting it with an oration. Or if you wish to do so by questioning, perform it by questioning. For this is not to be avoided, but especially pursued by all those of sound mind. Yet do it in such a way that you are not unjust in your questioning. It is indeed absurd for that man, who professes especially to meditate on virtue, to be always unjust in his discourses. To act unjustly in these matters occurs when one does not distinguish between contending in exercise and discussing in dialogue. In the former contest, one may jest and deceive as much as possible; but in the latter—namely, in disputation—one acts seriously and corrects the disputant, pointing out to him only those errors by which he was led astray both by himself and from past disputations. If you do so, those who associate with you will blame themselves, not you, for their own confusion and deficiency; they will follow and love you at once, and conversely, they will hate themselves and flee from themselves toward philosophy, so that, having become different in a certain way, they may lay aside their former habit. But if you do the opposite, as many others do, the opposite will happen to you as well, and you will render your associates enemies of this study when they grow up, instead of philosophers. 

If, therefore, you follow me, as was said above, you will consider with a calm and mild spirit, not hostilely or contentiously, how we say all things are moved, and how that which seems to each person is so both privately and publicly. From these you shall inquire whether knowledge and sensation are the same or different—and you shall not discuss it, as you just began, from the common usage of words and names, which many people drag about in whatever way they please, injecting various difficulties of doubt. These things, O Theodorus, I have attempted in defense of your friend to the best of my power, small things from small resources. For if he himself were alive, he would fight more strongly and magnificently for himself. 

**THEODORUS:** You are joking, Socrates, for you have fought bravely for him. 
**SOCRATES:** You speak rightly, my friend. But tell me: have you noticed that Protagoras just now rebuked us because, in disputing with a boy, we fought against his writings using the fear of a child? And since he rejected this kind of urbanity but praised a middle course in all things, he ordered us to deal seriously with his words? 
**THEAETETUS:** Why should I not have noticed, Socrates? 
**SOCRATES:** What then? Do you bid us obey him? 
**THEAETETUS:** Most certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Do you see that all these here, except you, are boys? Therefore, if we believe him, it behooves me and you together, by questioning and responding in turn, to examine his discourse seriously, lest he accuse us again of troubling his discourse by playing with boys. 
**THEAETETUS:** What prevents Theaetetus from following your scrutiny better than many barbarian men? 
**SOCRATES:** Not better than you, however, O Theodorus. Therefore, do not think it right for me to bring every aid to your deceased friend, while you bring none. But come, best of men, follow me for a little while, until we find this at least: whether it is fitting for you to be the measure in geometric figures, or whether all are as skilled as you in astronomy and other faculties in which you are deservedly seen to excel. 

**THEODORUS:** It is difficult, Socrates, for one who sits by you not to answer when you ask. I was indeed raving a little while ago when I said you would allow me not to gird myself for the fight and that I would not be compelled after the manner of the Lacedaemonians. Now you seem rather to incline toward Sciron. For the Lacedaemonians say "depart or stay"; but you seem to imitate Antaeus. For you do not let go of the one who meets you until you have compelled him to contend with you stripped. 
**SOCRATES:** You have found an appropriate comparison for my malady, Theodorus. Yet I am more robust than they. For innumerable Herculean and Thesean men, strong in speaking, have met with me and been exhausted; yet I do not desist at all, so vehement a love of this exercise has invaded me. Therefore, do not grudge me, that you may be exercised with me and help yourself as well as me. 

**THEODORUS:** I resist no further; lead where you please. This fate-like necessity which you have established must be endured by conviction. Yet I cannot offer myself to you beyond what you have proposed. 
**SOCRATES:** That will be enough. But observe this carefully for me: let us not secretly slip into a childish way of speaking, and for that reason, someone might carp at us again. 
**THEAETETUS:** I shall certainly try with all my power. 
**SOCRATES:** Let us therefore first resume what we touched upon above, and let us see whether we rightly or wrongly disapproved of his discourse, in which he says that each one is sufficient unto himself for being wise. Furthermore, Protagoras granted us that most people differ from one another in that which is better or worse, and that these are the wise. Did he not? 
**THEODORUS:** He granted it. 
**SOCRATES:** For if he himself were present and had confessed these things, and we had not granted them in his favor, there would be no need to confirm the same things by repeating them. But now, since it might perhaps seem that we are not sufficiently suitable advocates of his dogmas, it is better to grant clearly how the matter stands. For it is of no small importance whether it is so or otherwise. 
**THEODORUS:** You speak the truth. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, let us receive the consensus as briefly as possible, not from others, but from his own discourse. 
**THEODORUS:** How? 
**SOCRATES:** Thus: he said that what seems to each person is so to the one to whom it seems. 
**THEODORUS:** He certainly said so. 
**SOCRATES:** Do we not also, Protagoras, speak of the opinions of a man—nay, of all men—and do we not assert that absolutely no one thinks partly that he knows, and that he is wiser than others, and partly that others are wiser than himself? For in the greatest dangers, as often as they are tossed in camps, or diseases, or the sea, do they not hold as gods those who excel in each matter, and think they are their searchers, excelling the others in nothing else but knowledge? And in all human affairs, do they not seek teachers and leaders for themselves and other living creatures and works, who are commonly estimated to be sufficient both for teaching and for commanding? In all these things, what else shall we say, except that men think there is wisdom and ignorance among themselves? 
**THEODORUS:** Nothing else. 
**SOCRATES:** Do they not consider wisdom to be true thought, and ignorance to be false opinion? 
**THEODORUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** To what end, Protagoras, shall we turn the discourse? Shall we say that men always have true opinions? Or sometimes true, and sometimes false? For from both sides it follows that they do not always have true opinions, but both true and false. Attend, Theodorus, whether Protagoras or you perhaps...

**[Page 103]**
...himself would wish to contend that there is no one who thinks that another is either unskilled or holds such opinions. 
**THEODORUS:** This is incredible, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** And yet that discourse which proclaims man the measure of all things falls into this necessity. 
**THEODORUS:** In what way? 
**SOCRATES:** When you determine something within yourself, and then declare your opinion to me, let it be true for you according to his discourse; but can we not become judges of your sentence, or do we judge that you always have true opinions? Rather, do not innumerable men fight with you daily, thinking contrary to what you think, and believing that you judge and think wrongly? 
**THEODORUS:** By Jove, Socrates, as Homer says, there are very many men who cause me trouble. 
**SOCRATES:** What then? Do you want us to say that you then have true opinions for yourself, but false for very many others? 
**THEODORUS:** From what has been said, it seems to follow necessarily. 
**SOCRATES:** What about Protagoras himself? Is it not necessary? For if neither he himself thought man to be the measure, nor did those many (as they do not think), then this truth which he wrote would be true for no one. But if he himself judged so, but the multitude does not agree, know first that by as much as those to whom it does not seem so are more numerous than those to whom it does, by so much more it *is not* than it *is*. 
**THEODORUS:** It is necessary, if indeed according to individual opinions, it both will be and will not be. 
**SOCRATES:** Then it holds itself most beautifully. For he, concerning his own opinion, grants that the sentiment of those who disagree—by which they believe him to lie—is in a certain way true, while he confesses that everyone thinks true things. 
**THEODORUS:** Without doubt. 
**SOCRATES:** Does he not admit that his own is false, if he confesses that the judgment of those who want him to think false things is true? 
**THEODORUS:** Necessary. 
**SOCRATES:** But others by no means concede that you are lying. 
**THEODORUS:** Certainly not. 
**SOCRATES:** But he, from what he wrote, confesses that even this opinion is true. 
**THEODORUS:** It is clear. 
**SOCRATES:** From all things, therefore, that Protagoras published, it will be doubted—nay, it will be especially conceded by him. For if he concedes that the one who contradicts him thinks true things, then surely Protagoras himself will confess that neither a dog nor any man is the measure, if he has not learned it. Is it not so? 
**THEODORUS:** So it is, certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Since it is therefore doubted by all, the truth of Protagoras will be true to no one, neither to others nor even to himself. 

**THEODORUS:** We are attacking my friend too much, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** But truly, friend, it is obscure whether we are also passing over the right. For it is likely that, since he was older, he was also wiser than us. If he were suddenly to pop up here as far as his shoulders and invade us, he would refute me for raving in many things (as is probable) and you for agreeing, and then he would vanish. Nevertheless, we must use ourselves as we are, and always confess those things which seem to be. And now indeed we judge that anyone would concede this very thing: that one person stands out as wiser or more ignorant than another. 
**THEODORUS:** It seems so to me. 
**SOCRATES:** Shall we say that he insisted most on this discourse, which we also conceded while supporting Protagoras: that many things which seem so are so to each person—hot, dry, sweet, and others of this kind? But if he confesses that in certain things one differs from another—concerning things healthy and harmful—he will surely assert that not just any woman, or girl, or beast is sufficient to cure itself through the knowledge of healthy things; but in this, if anywhere else, they differ most. 
**THEODORUS:** The same seems so to me as well. 
**SOCRATES:** Moreover, in civil matters also—honorable and base, just and unjust, holy and impious—whatever things each city, thinking them so, establishes as lawful for itself, will he say these are truly so for each? And in these things, is no private person wiser than another private person, and no city wiser than another city? But truly, in that which a republic establishes as useful or useless to itself, here, if anywhere else, he will confess that one counselor differs from another, and one republic from another in finding the truth. Nor will he ever dare to admit this: that whatever a city institutes while thinking them useful to itself, these will always be conducive to it. But I say to you, in those matters of just and unjust, holy and profane, they cautiously place a defense: that none of these things have any substance by their own nature, but what commonly seems so is true at the time it seems so, and for as long as it seems so. And whoever does not entirely relate the sentiment of Protagoras, they philosophize in some such way. 

But us, Theodorus, a greater discussion continually emerges from a smaller one. 
**THEODORUS:** We are not at leisure then, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** So it seems. And often elsewhere, blessed man, I have noticed this, and now especially: that it is not without reason that those who spend a long time in philosophy, when they betake themselves to the forum [the law courts], appear as ridiculous rhetoricians. 
**THEODORUS:** Why do you say this? 
**SOCRATES:** Those who have been tossed about in the courts and the forum from an early age seem, when compared to those who are accustomed to philosophy and such studies, like a servant educated among free men. 
**THEODORUS:** In what way? 
**SOCRATES:** Because for these [philosophers], as you were saying, leisure is always present, and they converse in tranquil leisure; just as we are now renewing our discourse for the third time. So too with them, if something else beyond the proposed question falls in which happens to please them more (as is happening to us now), they do not care whether they speak at length or briefly, provided they master the truth. But those others [the lawyers] are agitated by the narrowness of time in speaking. For the flowing water [the water clock] urges them on, nor is it permitted to speak of what they desire: but necessity brings the adversary, bringing the formula of the brief, outside of which nothing must be said, which they call the oath for avoiding calumny. Their discourses are always about a fellow-servant against a master who sits in judgment and holds the sentence in his hand. Their contests are never for nothing, but always for a specific matter, and often even concerning death and life. Therefore, for all these reasons, they are intent and sharp, knowing how to flatter the master with words and comply with him in deeds—men who are small-souled and not endowed with right minds. For servitude from childhood has taken away their magnitude of soul, rectitude, and liberty, forcing them to perform crooked and perverse deeds while casting great dangers and terrors upon their still soft minds; all of which, since they cannot endure with justice and truth, they immediately turn into lies and mutual injuries; they are bent and broken on every side, so that, having nothing more of sound mind, they grow from youths into men who are eloquent and wise, as they think. And such are these, Theodorus; but shall we describe the men of our choir? Or shall we rather dismiss them and return to the proposed discourse, lest, as we were just saying, we abuse the liberty and digression of discourse too much? 

**THEODORUS:** By no means, Socrates, but let us describe them. For you said well that in the choir of philosophers we are not servants to our discourses, but our discourses are servants to us, and each of them waits to be perfected by us when it seems good to us. For neither a judge nor a spectator, like a censor or master over the poets, presides over us. 

**[Page 104]**
**SOCRATES:** Let us speak then, since it seems good to you, about those who are the leaders. For what shall we say of those who abuse the study of philosophy? They, from an early age, first do not know the way to the forum, nor do they know where the court, or the council, or any other assembly of the city is; they neither see nor hear the laws and decrees, whether promulgated or written. They do not even dream of the factions of societies for creating magistrates, or meetings, or dinners, or wanton banquets. Whether something has gone well or ill in the city for a long time, or what evil or base mark someone has from their ancestors, whether female or male, is more hidden from them than the sand of the sea, as the saying goes. And they do not even know that they do not know all these things. For they do not abstain from them for the sake of common glory, but in truth only their body dwells and stays in the city; but their mind, thinking all these things of little or no value, flies everywhere, as Pindar says, measuring both what is under the earth and what is above, and transcending the heaven by art, scrutinizing the whole nature of all things that belong to the universe, but in no way applying itself to those things which are near. 

**THEODORUS:** How so, Socrates? 
**SOCRATES:** Just as they say a certain Thracian maidservant, witty and graceful, mocked **Thales** while he was looking up at the heaven intent on the stars and fell into a pit, because he contended to see into the things in the sky, but did not see what was next to him and at his feet. The same can be objected against all who spend time in philosophy. For it is hidden from the philosopher not only what his neighbor does, but almost whether he is a man or a beast. But what a man himself is, and what is most fitting for his nature to do or suffer, he inquires into and laboriously scrutinizes. Do you understand, Theodorus, or not? 
**THEODORUS:** I understand indeed, and I approve of what you say. 
**SOCRATES:** Indeed, my friend, as we said in the previous points, if such a man is ever forced to discuss, either privately with someone or publicly in court or elsewhere, those things which are at his feet and in sight, he moves laughter—not only for Thracian maids but also for other people—since he falls into pits and many ambiguities because of his ignorance of these things. Here an absurd ineptitude brands him with the mark of sloth. For when someone is perhaps to be vituperated, he has nothing to bring as a reproach, being ignorant of vices, since he never noticed the individual evils of individuals; therefore he is laughed at as one who does not know. In praising and extolling men also, since he does not simulate or dissimulate anything but laughs openly, he seems to be raving. For when he hears a tyrant or king being praised, he thinks some swineherd, or shepherd of sheep, or cowherd is being extolled because he milks abundantly. Yet he considers that it differs in this: that kings and tyrants tend and milk a more hostile and insidious animal. And it is necessary that they be no less rustic and rude because of leisure than shepherds, so enclosed within walls in the city as a shepherd in a fold on a mountain. When he hears ten thousand acres of land or more being proclaimed as if some great thing were possessed by the one who has it, he thinks he hears some small things, since he is accustomed to look at the whole circle of the earth. Moreover, as often as someone relates the nobility of their race—that he can enumerate seven wealthy ancestors—he considers such praises to be of a dull mind that thinks nothing great because of ignorance, as if it cannot look back at the nature of the whole world and see that innumerable grandfathers and great-grandfathers have preceded each of us, in whose number innumerable rich and poor, kings and slaves, Barbarians and Greeks have preceded. Furthermore, when someone counts twenty-five ancestors and refers their origin to Hercules, son of Amphitryon, the matter seems unworthy of mention to him. For he laughs that the twenty-fifth person from Hercules is such as fortune made him, even if he were the fiftieth from Hercules, as if they cannot calculate and drive away the vanity of an insane mind. In all these things, the philosopher is commonly held as ridiculous, partly because he appears a proud contemner, partly because he is ignorant and wavers in things that are manifest. 

**THEODORUS:** You have narrated the matter exactly as it happens, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** But when he draws someone upward, my friend, and the person is prepared to depart from here, having sent away the lawsuits in which it is asked in what I have harmed you or you me, and ascends to the speculation of justice and injustice itself—what each of them is, and how they differ from all other things among themselves—or also that controversy being dismissed in which it is asked whether a king is happy who possesses much gold, and ascends to the contemplation of the kingdom itself and of human happiness and misery—what kind each is to each, and in what way it befits human nature to attain the one and flee the other: when, I say, it is necessary to give an account of all these things, that small-souled and sharp lawyer then in turn pays the penalty to the philosopher. For he suffers vertigo from the high watchtower with clouding eyes, since he is unaccustomed to look upward. He grieves, stumbles, and speaks barbarously. Wherefore he moves laughter not for the Thracians, nor for any rude person (for they do not perceive it), but rather for all those who have been educated freely and far from a servile life. This, Theodorus, is the condition of each. The one is of that man who was educated in liberty and leisure, whom you call a philosopher. Though he truly ought not to be vituperated, he appears foolish and inept whenever he approaches servile ministries, since he could neither tie up bundles of bedding, nor prepare the seasonings of delicacies, nor fashion flattering blandishments of words. The other is the condition of that man who can supply these things expeditiously and quickly, but does not know how to use the decent clothing of a free man properly. He is entirely ignorant of how to sing the true life of gods and happy men with a fitting harmony of discourse. 

**THEODORUS:** If you could persuade other men of what you say, Socrates, as much as you persuade me, greater peace and fewer evils would be born among men. 
**SOCRATES:** But it is impossible, Theodorus, for evils to be entirely extirpated. For it is always necessary that there be something opposite to the good. Nor can those things have a place among the gods. But they necessarily circulate around mortal nature and the lower region. Wherefore we must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible; but the flight is to become as like to God as possible according to our power. Wisdom, justice, and holiness together make one like God. But, best of men, it can hardly be persuaded that virtue is to be followed and vice fled, not for the sake of that which the vulgar think—namely, that you may not seem bad and that you may appear good; for these seem to me to be the trifles of old women. But let us say what is true. God is nowhere and in no way unjust, but most just, having embraced the whole power of justice, and nothing is more like Him than a most just man. Around this, true industry and fortitude of a man, as well as inertia and weakness, are turned. Indeed, the knowledge of these is true virtue and wisdom; ignorance, on the contrary, is manifest unskillfulness and wickedness. Other things which seem to be faculties and wisdoms are troublesome in civil magistrates, and illiberal in other arts. 

**[Page 105]**
...Therefore, for him who has performed something unjustly, and either says or does profane things, it is much safest if he can do nothing by craftiness nor use bad arts. For men of this kind exult in reproach, and they wish to be seen as not at all abject and empty mannikins, nor as the "inert weight of the earth," but as such men who can live safely in a republic. Therefore, the truth must be expressed that they are all the more such as they do not think, because they do not think it; they are entirely ignorant of the penalty of injustice, of which it least becomes one to be ignorant. For it is not, as they perhaps think, stripes and slaughters, which those who have done nothing unjust often suffer, and which the unjust themselves often avoid, but rather that which cannot be avoided. 
**THEODORUS:** Which do you mean? 
**SOCRATES:** Since in the order of things, my friend, there are two patterns—the divine indeed most blessed, but that which is void of God most miserable—they, occupied with extreme folly and dementia, do not see that the matter stands so, and they are secretly rendered like the latter on account of their iniquitous actions, and dissimilar to the former. Of which crime they certainly pay the penalty while they lead a life fitting for that which they have been made like. Indeed, if we say that these, unless they cease from their wickedness, will not be received after death into that place void of evils, and here they will carry the likeness of their own life always living as evil men among evil men: those sharp and malicious men will respond that they are hearing certain ravings. 
**THEODORUS:** And most especially, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** I know indeed, my friend. One thing at least happens to them: that if they are ever forced privately to give and receive reasons for those things which they vituperate, and if they are willing to endure the delay of manfully disputing and not flee cowardly, then at last—which is absurd, O blessed one—they will disapprove of even their own words, and their rhetoric entirely vanishes, so that they seem to differ in nothing from boys. But let us now put an end to these things, since they are beside the purpose. Otherwise, very much matter flowing together from every side will overwhelm the discourse instituted from the beginning. Let us return therefore to the prior things, if it seems good to you also. 

**THEODORUS:** To me indeed, Socrates, those things are no less pleasant to hear. For at my age I easily follow this. Nevertheless, if it pleases you, let us return to where we digressed. 
**SOCRATES:** We certainly arrived in disputing at the point where we said that those who placed all essence in agitation, and said that whatever seems to each is so to the same, would assert this most vehemently in other things, but not least in just things: that whatever appearances a city establishes as just for itself, these are just for it so long as they remain established. But truly no one will be so brave as to dare to contend the same in good and useful things: namely, that whatever appearances a city institutes as useful to itself, these are conducive to it for as long as they have been so established—unless perhaps someone should say "the name"; but this would rather be a mockery [*scomma*] of what we want, would it not? 
**THEODORUS:** Undoubtedly. 
**SOCRATES:** Let him not say the name; but let him look at the thing named. And what the city has called such, it looks to in founding laws, and it founds individual laws as much as it thinks and can, to be as useful as possible to itself. Does it intend anything else in passing laws? 
**THEODORUS:** Nothing else. 
**SOCRATES:** Is it always successful in its wish? Or does opinion often deceive it? 
**THEODORUS:** I think it often deceives. 
**SOCRATES:** Moreover, by this reasoning, anyone will more readily confess these same things if he inquires concerning every species in which the useful consists. It is also in a certain way concerning future time. For whenever we found laws, we found them as if they will be profitable for the future, which we might more rightly call the "future." 
**THEODORUS:** Most especially. 
**SOCRATES:** Come then, let us ask either Protagoras or anyone else who is his follower. You assert, Protagoras, that man is the measure of all things—of white, heavy, light, and each of such things. For since he contains the judicial power within himself, and judges them to be such as he suffers, he judges true things for himself, and things that are. Is it not so? 
**THEODORUS:** Quite so. 
**SOCRATES:** Shall we say also of future things, Protagoras, that he has in himself judicial power? And such things as he thinks will be for you, such happen to you thinking so. When someone unskilled in medicine thinks he is about to fall into a fever and will thus be made hot, but the doctor disagrees, thinking the opposite: which of them do we think will have the true opinion of the future? Surely both? And for the doctor he will be neither hot nor feverish, but for himself both? 
**THEODORUS:** That would be ridiculous. 
**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, concerning wine, whether it will be sweet or harsh, the opinion of the husbandman, not the harper, prevails. 
**THEODORUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** Nor concerning a consonant or dissonant future does a gymnast judge better than a musician what will then seem consonant to the gymnast himself. 
**THEODORUS:** In no way. 
**SOCRATES:** But when a prepared table is offered for a banquet, and something is to be predicted concerning the future sweetness of those dishes, is not the opinion of the cook more powerful than that of any other unskilled in cookery? We do not fight about what either is or was sweet to each, but rather about that which in the future ought to be and seem so to each: is each person a suitable judge for himself, or would you, Protagoras, foresee more rightly than any of the unskilled what will seem probable to individuals in a judicial discourse? 
**THEODORUS:** In this very thing especially, Socrates, Protagoras professed to excel all. 
**SOCRATES:** O miserable man. No one, by Jove, would have followed him with offered money unless he had persuaded his associates that he alone could presage what would be probable and seem so in the future better than any seer or anyone else. 
**THEODORUS:** You speak most true things. 
**SOCRATES:** Do not the passings of laws and utility also look toward the future? And would not anyone without controversy confess that the constitution of a republic more often misses what is useful? 
**THEODORUS:** Very much so. 
**SOCRATES:** Let it now have been sufficiently said against your teacher that he is forced to confess that one person stands out as wiser than another, and such a man is the measure. But it forces me, since I am void of knowledge, not to become a measure, just as his discourse recently urged—that I would be such whether I wished it or not. 
**THEODORUS:** I think, Socrates, his discourse is especially refuted by this, and also somewhat by this: that it makes the opinions of others valid; but these openly reprove his discourses, thinking them false. 
**SOCRATES:** In many things besides, Theodorus, this can be detected: that not every opinion of all men is true. But concerning the present passion to each, from which the senses and opinions according to senses are born, it is more difficult to detect that the opinions of the sense are not true. But perhaps I say nothing. For if they have attained them, they cannot be refuted; and those who would assert that they are certain and are knowledges might perhaps not be wandering. And therefore Theaetetus here said not without reason that sense and knowledge are the same. Wherefore we must approach closer, as your teacher Protagoras...

**[Page 106]**
...prescribed, and examine this agitated essence by striking it, to see whether it gives an integral or a shattered sound. Indeed, no small fight, and not among few, has arisen about it. 
**THEODORUS:** It is far from being a cheap contention, which has been propagated everywhere through Ionia; for the students of Heraclitus support this discourse most vehemently. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, friend Theodorus, these things must be inspected from the principles, as they oppose them. 
**THEODORUS:** Entirely. For, Socrates, concerning the Heracliteans, or as you say, the Homerics, and even those more ancient among the Ephesians, especially those who wish to seem more skilled, it is no more permitted to speak with them than with those driven by a gadfly. For their writings are clearly carried along by impulse. But delay and waiting in discourse, and questions, and quiet between responding and questioning are less present to them than nothing. Nay, even less than nothing: so little rest is there in the minds of those men. But if you ask any of them something about a matter, they shoot little obscure words as if taking them from a hidden quiver. And if you seek the reason for this, they strike with another one, but with the name changed; you will never accomplish anything with any of them, nor they among themselves. And they take care of this one thing most observedly: that they permit nothing stable either in discourse or in their own minds, thinking (as it seems to me) that stability itself is something, and they pursue it with all their powers and vehemently expel it from everywhere. 
**SOCRATES:** Perhaps, Theodorus, you saw these men in battle, but in peace not at all. For they are not friends to you. But they say certain such things to their disciples, as I think, in leisure, whom they wish to render like themselves. 
**THEODORUS:** What disciples, O blessed one? For among those men, no one becomes a disciple of another, but they are born spontaneously from wherever; it happens that each of them is seized by fury. And each thinks the other knows nothing. From these therefore you will never receive a reason, as I was just saying, neither from the willing nor the unwilling. But we must consider it as a received proposition. 

**SOCRATES:** You speak skillfully. For we received another certain sentiment from the ancients concealing it from the common herd of men by poetry: that the origin of all other things is Oceanus and Tethys, and that all things are in flux and nothing stands firm. But from the more recent and wiser ones demonstrating the matter so clearly that even cobblers could perceive their wisdom by hearing it, and would cease foolishly to think that some things stand firm and others, on the contrary, are moved—from those, I say, we have received that all things are moved, whom those authors venerate. But I had almost forgotten, Theodorus, that others have shown things contrary to these: namely, that "immobile" is the congruent name for this existing whole, and whatever other things Melissus and Parmenides, opposing all these, assert: that all things are one, and that one itself consists in itself, having no place at all in which it might be moved. What is to be said of all these, my friend? For progressing gradually, we have secretly escaped between the two. But if we depart as weaklings without defending either side, we shall pay the penalty like those who play at the line in the wrestling schools, when, being caught by both sides, they are dragged in contrary directions. Therefore, it seems that we must first deal with those whom we first approached—namely, the "flowing" ones. And if they seem to say anything probable, we shall drag ourselves along with them, trying to escape the others. But if those who place the whole as stable produce truer things, we shall flee to them from those who even move the immobile. But if neither seem to bring anything plausible to us, we shall emerge as ridiculous, thinking that we, vile mannikins, know something great, when nothing but...

**[Page 107]**
...as seeing or hearing? Is it ever to remain in vision or hearing? 
**THEODORUS:** Least of all, if indeed all things are moved. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, one must not say that he sees anything rather than that he does not see, nor use any other sense rather than not use it, since all things are entirely transmuted. 
**THEODORUS:** Certainly not. 
**SOCRATES:** Nevertheless, sense itself is knowledge, as I and Theaetetus said. 
**THEODORUS:** So it was said. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we were not responding what knowledge is, when asked, any more than what non-knowledge is. 
**THEODORUS:** So you certainly seem to be. 
**SOCRATES:** We should therefore opportunely amend that response if we were contending to demonstrate that all things are moved, so that the response would seem right; but this appeared, as it seems: that if all things are moved, any response about whatever anyone responds is equally right—whether it be responded that it holds itself so or does not hold itself so. But if we must rather say "it becomes," let us not stop our discourse with those people. 
**THEODORUS:** You speak rightly. 
**SOCRATES:** Except in this, Theodorus, that I was saying "so" and "not so." But it is necessary neither to say "so" in this way. For it would no longer be moved "so," nor again "not so." For this is not motion, but another name must be imposed by those who discuss such things; since now they have no words for their supposition, unless perhaps they seem to have this phrase, namely "not in whatever way," which indeed especially fits them, being prolated infinitely. 
**THEODORUS:** That phrase is very convenient there. 
**SOCRATES:** Now, Theodorus, we have dispatched what pertains to your friend; nor yet have we conceded to him that any man is the measure of all things, unless he be a wise man. Furthermore, we shall by no means concede that knowledge is sense according to that reasoning which proclaims that all things are moved—unless perhaps Theaetetus here says so in some other way. 

**THEAETETUS:** You have spoken excellently, Socrates. For these being finished, it is fitting for me also to be dispatched from these, as was agreed between us. After the disputation against Protagoras has received its end, do not desist, I pray, Theodorus, before you and Socrates run through those besides who wished all things to stand, just as you proposed a little while ago. 
**THEODORUS:** Since you are a youth, Theaetetus, you teach your elders to do injury, while you exhort them to transgress the agreements. But gird yourself, so that you may render an account of the remaining things to Socrates, if he wishes. 
**THEAETETUS:** Most willingly, however, I wish to hear those things of which I speak. 
**THEODORUS:** You provoke knights into the field when you summon Socrates to dispute. Question him, therefore, and you shall hear. 

**SOCRATES:** I seem indeed, Theodorus, not at all likely to obey Theaetetus in what he orders. 
**THEODORUS:** What prevents you from obeying? 
**SOCRATES:** Although I fear lest we seem burdensome harassing Melissus and others who say the universe is one and consistent, yet I fear even more—not to use Homeric words—it seems I must fear the sharp and venerable [Parmenides]. I spoke once with that old man when I was still very much a youth, and he seemed to me to possess a profound and generous wisdom entirely. I fear, therefore, lest we by no means understand his words and voices; and what he sub-understands in words may much more be hidden from us; and what is greatest, for the sake of which the disputation began between us—inquiring what knowledge is—may be left undiscussed because of the disputations rushing in rashly if anyone obeys them; especially since that most ample question which we just introduced, if it were treated beside the purpose and as if by digressing, would suffer too much; and if it were perfected more broadly and exactly, it would impede the investigation of knowledge itself. But neither...

**[Page 108]**
...and these are the very things I ask. 
**THEAETETUS:** By Jove, Socrates, I do not know what I should say, except that it seemed to me from the beginning that no such proper organ is accommodated to these as to those [the senses], but rather the soul itself through itself judges the communion in all things. 
**SOCRATES:** You are beautiful, Theaetetus, and not, as Theodorus was saying, deformed. For he who speaks beautifully is beautiful and good. To these is added that you have conferred a huge benefit on me. For you have liberated me from a long and grave disputation, after it seems to you that the soul animates certain things through itself, and apprehends others through the powers of the body. For this was my sentiment, which I was also desiring to persuade you of. 
**THEAETETUS:** To me it is certainly persuaded. 
**SOCRATES:** In the number of which do you place essence? For this especially follows all things. 
**THEAETETUS:** Of those which the soul itself by itself affects and attains. 
**SOCRATES:** Surely also like and unlike, and same and other? 
**THEAETETUS:** These also. 
**SOCRATES:** What of beautiful and base, and good and evil? 
**THEAETETUS:** Of these also it seems to me that the soul especially considers the essence of all in turn, reputing and comparing in itself the past and present toward the future. 
**SOCRATES:** Attend also to this: it will feel the hardness of a hard thing through touch, and the softness of a soft thing by a similar reasoning. 
**THEAETETUS:** So it is. 
**SOCRATES:** But the essence, and what they are, and their mutual contrariety, and the essence of the contrariety itself, the soul itself revolving through itself and comparing them in turn, strives to discern. 
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** Does not a certain natural faculty belong to men and beasts as soon as they are born, by which they feel the passions flowing through the body into the soul? But the reasoning and comparison of those toward essence and utility comes only at last after long courses of time, by frequent study and discipline, to those to whom it competes? 
**THEAETETUS:** So it is exactly. 
**SOCRATES:** Can we perceive truth by that by which we do not perceive essence? 
**THEAETETUS:** Least of all. 
**SOCRATES:** But he who lacks the truth of something, will he have any knowledge of it? 
**THEAETETUS:** How could that happen? 
**SOCRATES:** In passions, therefore, knowledge by no means exists, but in the reasoning which is turned around them, it seems to be. For we can touch essence and truth by this, but by those [passions] in no way. 
**THEAETETUS:** It is certain. 
**SOCRATES:** Do you call that and this the same, when they differ with such a great difference among themselves? 
**THEAETETUS:** It would hardly be fitting. 
**SOCRATES:** What name do you attribute to that? Namely, to that which is seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, being warmed, and being chilled? 
**THEAETETUS:** To sense. 
**SOCRATES:** Do you therefore call this whole "sense"? 
**THEAETETUS:** Necessarily. 
**SOCRATES:** We denied that the perception of truth fits this, since it does not perceive essence. 
**THEAETETUS:** So it is. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, it will not be possessed of knowledge. 
**THEAETETUS:** No. 
**SOCRATES:** From these it follows, Theaetetus, that knowledge and sense will never be the same. 
**THEAETETUS:** Never entirely. 
**SOCRATES:** In these it has clearly appeared that sense is one thing, and knowledge another. But we did not begin to discuss for the sake of finding what knowledge is not, but rather what it is. We have progressed so far in disputing as to judge that knowledge is in no way to be sought in sense, but in that name rather which the soul then sorts, when it itself according to itself is turned and acts around those things which are. 
**THEAETETUS:** But this, Socrates, as I myself think, is called "to think" [*opinari*]. 
**SOCRATES:** You think rightly, friend. And now from the beginning attend again, all previous things having been deleted from your mind, whether you perceive anything greater, after you have been carried this far. Explain again what knowledge might be. 
**THEAETETUS:** It is impossible to say that any opinion, Socrates, is knowledge, since there is also a certain false opinion. But true opinion appears to be knowledge. 

**[Page 109]**
...let that be my answer for now: if it seems otherwise in disputing thereafter, we shall try to bring something else. 
**SOCRATES:** Well done, Theaetetus. It is fitting to dispute with such a prompt mind, and not to hesitate as you began. For if we do so, one of two things will happen: either we shall find what we affect, or we shall certainly think we know less of what we are ignorant; nor will that be a mediocre gain. And now what do you say? Since there are two species of opinion, one true and the other false, do you define true opinion as knowledge? 
**THEAETETUS:** I define it so. For this seems to me in the present. 
**SOCRATES:** Must we then treat of opinion from the beginning? 
**THEAETETUS:** Why do you say no? 
**SOCRATES:** It disturbs me now and often elsewhere, so that I am turned in very much ambiguity as to myself and as to others, not being able to explain what this affection in us is, and in what way it comes. 
**THEAETETUS:** What is this? 
**SOCRATES:** Namely, that someone thinks false things. About which I also now doubt, whether we should omit it or consider it otherwise than above. 
**THEAETETUS:** Why not, Socrates, if you think it fits in any way? For you and Theodorus were speaking excellently in the previous points about leisure, that nothing urges in such things. 
**SOCRATES:** You have reminded me opportunely; for perhaps it will not be beside the purpose to run through the trace again: for it is better to determine a little well, than much not sufficiently. 
**THEAETETUS:** It is better indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** How then, and what do we say? We say that false opinion is frequent, and that some one of us thinks such things, as if these things so hold themselves by nature. 
**THEAETETUS:** We say so without doubt. 
**SOCRATES:** Does this not compete for us both concerning all things and concerning individual things? Namely, to know or to be ignorant? For I pass over for the present learning and forgetting, as media of those things, since they confer nothing to our purpose. 
**THEAETETUS:** Nothing at all, Socrates, remains except to know or to be ignorant around each thing. 
**SOCRATES:** Is it not therefore necessary for the one who thinks to think those things about which he knows something, or does not know? 
**THEAETETUS:** Necessary. 
**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, for one who knows to be ignorant of the same, or for one who is ignorant to know, is impossible. 
**[Marsilio Ficino's marginal table notes]:**
* *What he knows, to think they are what he knows.*
* *What he does not know, to think they are what he does not know.*
* *What he knows, to think they are what he does not know.*
* *What he does not know, to think they are what he knows.*

**THEAETETUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** Does the one who thinks false things about what he knows think they are not those things, but some other things which he also knows: and knowing both, is he again ignorant of both? 
**THEAETETUS:** That cannot happen, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** Or perhaps what he does not know, he thinks are certain other things which he does not know? And can one who has recognized neither Theaetetus nor Socrates ever think that Socrates is Theaetetus, or conversely that Theaetetus is Socrates? 
**THEAETETUS:** Never. 
**SOCRATES:** Nor yet does he think that those things which someone knows are those which he does not know: nor again those which he does not know, are those which he knows. 
**THEAETETUS:** For it would be a monster. 
**SOCRATES:** In what way then will someone think false things? Beyond these indeed it is not permitted to think, since indeed we either know or are ignorant of all things: but in these no one seems to be able to think false things in any way. 
**THEAETETUS:** You speak true things. 
**SOCRATES:** Or perhaps, what we seek is not to be considered according to knowing and not knowing, but according to being and not being? 
**THEAETETUS:** How do you say this? 
**SOCRATES:** Lest it be simple. Since he who thinks things which are nowhere, in whatever thing he thinks, he cannot but think false things, in whatever way he may finally think. 
**THEAETETUS:** That too is decent, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** How then, and what shall we respond, Theaetetus, if someone asks us (for it is possible for anyone what I say): "Who of men would think that which is not? Whether about some of those things which are, or about it itself according to itself?" To these surely we shall respond: "Namely, whenever someone in thinking does not think true things." Or what shall we say? 
**THEAETETUS:** So certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Does such a thing also happen elsewhere? 
**THEAETETUS:** What is that? 
**SOCRATES:** That someone sees something indeed, but sees nothing? 
**THEODORUS:** And in what way? 
**SOCRATES:** But truly if he sees some one thing, he sees some one of existing things. Or do you think "one" is in those things which are not? 
**THEAETETUS:** Least of all. 
**SOCRATES:** He therefore who sees some one thing, sees some existing thing. 
**THEAETETUS:** It appears so. 
**SOCRATES:** And he who hears something, hears some one thing, and hears an existing thing. 
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Likewise he who touches something, touches some one thing, and an existing thing likewise, if indeed it is one. 
**THEAETETUS:** That too. 
**SOCRATES:** But he who thinks, does he not think some one thing? 
**THEAETETUS:** It is necessary. 
**SOCRATES:** And he who thinks some one thing, does he not think some existing thing? 
**THEAETETUS:** I assent. 
**SOCRATES:** He therefore who thinks what does not exist, thinks nothing. 
**THEAETETUS:** It does not seem so. 
**SOCRATES:** But he who does not seem, thinks nothing, he does not think at all. 
**THEAETETUS:** It is certain. 
**SOCRATES:** It is therefore impossible to think what is not, whether about some of those things which are, or about it itself according to itself. 
**THEODORUS:** It seems impossible. 
**SOCRATES:** It is therefore one thing to think false things, and another to think those things which are not. 
**THEAETETUS:** It appears different. 
**SOCRATES:** Neither therefore in this way, nor as we considered a little ago, does false opinion exist in us. 
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly not. 
**SOCRATES:** But perhaps we call it this in this way? 
**THEAETETUS:** Which? 
**SOCRATES:** We say a certain other-opinion is false opinion, whenever someone says that some of those things which are, is some other thing of those which are also, the thought of the mind having changed. For thus he will always think some existing thing, but one thing for another: and since he wanders from what he thought, he will rightly be said to think false things. 
**THEAETETUS:** You seem to me now to have spoken most rightly. For as often as someone thinks a base thing instead of a beautiful one, or on the contrary a beautiful one instead of a base one, so often he may be judged to think false things not without reason. 
**SOCRATES:** You openly contemn me, Theaetetus, and do you not fear? 
**THEAETETUS:** To what end is this? 
**SOCRATES:** For I do not think I seem to you to have apprehended what is truly false, being asked whether "fast" could be "slow," or "light" "heavy," or some other contrary thing not according to its own nature, but according to the nature of the contrary to become contrary to yourself. Lest you therefore dare that in vain or rashly, I let it go, and it pleases you, as you say, that to think false things is to think other things. 
**THEAETETUS:** To me indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** It is therefore permitted, as you yourself think, to place one thing as another in thought, and not as that thing. 
**THEODORUS:** It is permitted indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** When therefore the thought does that, is it not necessary for it to think either both, or one? 
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely necessary. 
**SOCRATES:** Or together, or separately? 
**THEAETETUS:** That too. 
**SOCRATES:** Do you call "to think" the same as I do? 
**THEAETETUS:** What do you call it? 
**SOCRATES:** The discourse which the soul itself revolves within itself concerning those things which it considers. I declare the matter to you, and that as one not at all skilled. For this seems to me: namely, that the thought of the soul does nothing else than discuss with itself, questioning and responding, affirming and denying. But after it has defined, and asserting the same thing whether more slowly or more quickly, and does not wander, we place this very thing as opinion. Wherefore I call "to think" to speak, and opinion a discourse, not to another, nor by voice, but in silence and to oneself. But what do you feel? 
**THEODORUS:** The same. 

**[Page 110]**
**SOCRATES:** When therefore someone thinks one thing for another, then as it seems he says to himself that one thing is another. 
**THEODORUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** Record, I pray, if you ever said to yourself that a beautiful thing is entirely base, or an uninvited thing is just: nay, that I may speak in sum, did you ever try to persuade yourself that one thing is especially another, or on the contrary: nor in dreams did you ever dare to say to yourself that equal things are entirely unequal, or some other thing of this kind. 
**THEODORUS:** Never certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Do you think anyone else, whether prudent or insane, would dare to persuade himself by speaking with himself that an ox is necessarily a horse, or two are one? 
**THEAETETUS:** Least of all, by Jove. 
**SOCRATES:** If to speak with oneself is to think, no one while he learns both, thinks and attains them in his mind, would ever prolate and think that one thing is another. Let go, if it pleases, of this word "other," for this is what I want: no one thinks that a base thing is beautiful, or anything else of the same kind. 
**THEAETETUS:** I let it go indeed, Socrates, and what you say pleases me very much. 
**SOCRATES:** Wherefore it cannot happen that he who thinks both thinks that one is another. 
**THEAETETUS:** It is clear. 
**SOCRATES:** But neither he who thinks only one, and not the other, will ever think that one is the other. 
**THEAETETUS:** You tell true things: for he would also be forced to attain what he does not think. 
**SOCRATES:** Neither therefore he who both, nor he who only one, can think other things. Wherefore what defines false opinion as thinking other things, achieves nothing. Whence neither in this way, nor according to the previous points, is it certain that false opinion exists in us. 
**THEAETETUS:** It does not seem so. 
**SOCRATES:** Nevertheless, Theaetetus, if this has not appeared to be, we shall be forced to confess many and absurd things. 
**THEAETETUS:** Which ones? 
**SOCRATES:** I shall not tell you until I have contended to consider entirely: for I would be ashamed of us in those things which we doubt, if we were forced to confess what I say: but if we find it, and emerge free, then at last we shall speak of others to whom such things happen, as ones entirely alien from such a ridiculous error. But if we fail entirely, having been made humble, like those tossing and suffering nausea, we shall permit ourselves to the oration, that it may either trample us or drive us where it will. Therefore, if I find any exit for this question, listen now. 
**THEAETETUS:** Just speak. 
**SOCRATES:** I do not confess that we agreed rightly when we conceded that someone who knows something cannot think those things which he does not know, and thus lie. Nay, it can happen in a certain way. 
**THEAETETUS:** Do you say what I also then suspected, when we said it was such a thing, that sometimes I, knowing Socrates, and seeing from afar some old man unknown to me, thought he was Socrates known to me? For it happens in what you say. 
**SOCRATES:** Were we not already driven away from that, because it caused us, while knowing what we know, to not know it? 
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely. 
**SOCRATES:** Let us therefore not do so any longer, but let us place it in this way. And perhaps someone will assent to us, perhaps also it will be brought against us. But let us attend to that in which it is necessary to examine that discourse which inverts all things. See therefore: can he who was formerly ignorant of something, afterwards learn it? 
**THEAETETUS:** He can certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** Does he not learn one thing after another? 
**THEAETETUS:** What prevents it? 
**SOCRATES:** Place for the sake of example a certain wax effigy in our minds, in this one larger, in that one smaller, in this of purer wax, in another of filthier or harder, in some softer, in some also tempered. 
**THEAETETUS:** I place it. 
**SOCRATES:** Let us therefore say this is a gift of the mother of the Muses, Memory, and in this whatever of those things we either see, or hear, or think ourselves, we desire to remember, insinuating it into the senses and intelligences, we mark it like signing with rings, and whatever has been signed, we remember and know as long as the figure remains: but when it is abolished, or cannot be inscribed, we forget and do not know. 
**THEAETETUS:** So it is. 

**[Page 111]**
**SOCRATES:** He therefore who knows those things, but considers something of those which he sees or hears, see in what way he might think false things. 
**THEAETETUS:** In what way? 
**SOCRATES:** Thinking what he knows to be what he knows, now indeed what he knows, and now what he does not know. These surely we did not rightly concede above, contending they were impossible. 
**[Marsilio Ficino's marginal table notes]:**
* *In notice without sense:*
    * *Knowing. what he knows.*
    * *Knowing. what he does not know.*
    * *Not knowing. what he does not know.*
    * *Not knowing. what he knows.*
* *In sense alone:*
    * *Feeling, what he feels.*
    * *Feeling, what he does not feel.*
    * *Not feeling, what he does not feel.*
    * *Not feeling, what he feels.*
* *In both joined:*
    * *Knowing and feeling, what he knows and feels.*
    * *Knowing and feeling, what he knows and does not feel.*
    * *Knowing and feeling, what he feels and does not know.*
    * *Not knowing and not feeling, what he does not know and does not feel.*
    * *Not knowing and not feeling, what he does not know and feels.*
    * *Not knowing and not feeling, what he knows and does not feel.*

**SOCRATES:** How do you say? Let us speak of those from the beginning by distinguishing: that this thing which someone knows, and preserves its monument in his soul, but does not feel it, he cannot think it is some other of those things which he also knows, and preserves its image, but does not feel; and on the contrary, to think what he knows is what he does not know, of which he preserves no image; and what he does not know, that besides what he does not know; and what he does not know, that which he knows; or what he feels, some other of those things which he feels; or what he feels, something which he does not feel at all; or what he does not feel, some of those things which he does not feel; or what he does not feel, anything from those which he feels. And much less can he think what he knows and feels, and preserves its image according to sense, is some other thing which he also knows, and feels, and preserves in the same way; or what he knows, and feels, and retains, rightly what he knows, to think; or what he knows and feels, and similarly retains, that to be what he feels; or what neither knows nor feels, that to be what he neither knows nor feels; or what neither knows nor feels, that which he least knows; or what neither knows nor feels, that which he least feels. All these things are such that no one in them can think false things by any reasoning. It remains therefore that in some such things, if only such a thing happens anywhere. 
**THEAETETUS:** In which then? 
**SOCRATES:** Let us see, I pray, if I understand more from them. For in the present I hardly follow, in which things someone knows, he thinks they are certain other things which he both knows and feels, or which he does not know but feels, or which he knows and feels, those which he both knows and feels. Wherefore now I fail far more than above. 
**SOCRATES:** Come, listen again thus. I indeed recognizing Theodorus, and holding his likeness in memory, and Theaetetus similarly, sometimes I see them, sometimes I do not see them. And I touch them sometimes, at other times not at all, and in the same way I hear, and apprehend with other senses: yet I perceive you with no sense, but I know and remember you within me nonetheless. 
**THEODORUS:** Entirely. 
**SOCRATES:** This therefore first of those which I am about to set forth, notice: that someone can not feel what he knows, and he can also feel it. 
**THEAETETUS:** So it is. 
**SOCRATES:** Can he not also often not feel what he does not know, and often only feel it? 
**THEAETETUS:** This too is true. 
**SOCRATES:** See if you now follow it more in the present. Socrates, while he recognizes Theodorus and Theaetetus, but sees neither, nor perceives them with another sense, never thinks with himself that Theaetetus is Theodorus. What to these? 
**THEAETETUS:** They are true. 
**SOCRATES:** This was indeed the first of those things I was saying. 
**THEAETETUS:** It was. 
**SOCRATES:** The second was this: that while I recognize one of you, but am ignorant of the other, and feel neither, I never think that he whom I recognize is the one whom I am ignorant of. 
**THEAETETUS:** Correctly. 
**SOCRATES:** The third indeed is that: while I recognize neither, and feel neither, I never think that he whom I am ignorant of is some other whom I am again ignorant of. And so on, imagine all the above-said repeated similarly: in which I shall never think false things of you and Theodorus, neither knowing nor being ignorant of both, nor indeed knowing one but being ignorant of the other. And the same reasoning for the senses, if only you perceive it. 
**THEAETETUS:** I perceive it indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** It remains therefore that we think false things in this: when knowing you and Theodorus, and preserving in other effigies of both, the figures from a long time, as the signets of your rings, not clearly seeing both, I try to accommodate the proper sign of each to its trace by its vision so that recognition may happen: but I wander, and like those who err by changing shoes, I change, and transfer the vision of each to the alien likeness, and I suffer certain things similar to those which result in mirrors with a transverse aspect, when the sight changes right for left. And thus I am deceived, and an other-opinion is born, and that is what is called to think false things. 
**THEAETETUS:** Entirely, Socrates, the passion of opinion is such as you have wonderfully figured it. 
**SOCRATES:** Moreover, when knowing both, I feel one besides, but not the other, but I do not have the knowledge of the other according to sense: which I said thus above, and you did not understand me. 
**THEAETETUS:** Certainly not. 
**SOCRATES:** Yet I was saying this: that he who recognizes one and feels him, and has the knowledge according to his sense, will never think that he is some other, whom he also recognizes and feels, or of whom he has the knowledge according to sense. Was this it? 
**THEAETETUS:** Yes. 
**SOCRATES:** What was just said was in some way omitted, when we were asserting in the previous points that false opinion happens whenever someone, knowing and seeing both, or perceiving them by some other sense, and holding the signets of both, does not have each according to his own proper sense, but like an unskilled archer wanders far from the sign, which indeed was called a lie. 
**THEAETETUS:** Not unjustly. 
**SOCRATES:** And when sense is present to one of the signets, but not to the other, but he ascribes to the present one what is of the absent sense, this thought is entirely deceived: and that I may say in sum, concerning those things which someone never either knew or felt, he cannot lie or be false, and have a false opinion, if only we now speak something of the truth. But in those in which we know and feel, in those very things true or false opinion is turned: which when it collects its proper likenesses from sight and a direct effort and figures them, is true. But when transverse and oblique, false. 
**THEAETETUS:** Have these not been spoken excellently, Socrates? 
**SOCRATES:** When you have heard these, you will assert the same more vehemently. Moreover, to think true things is beautiful, to lie is base. 
**THEAETETUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** These surely they say happen most from here. When someone has that wax effigy in his soul deep and much, and smooth and properly kneaded, those things which flow through the senses into this are inscribed, which Homer called the heart of the soul, sub-understanding the similarity of wax, as pure and deep-seated signets. And at first indeed men so instituted are docile and sharp, then also mindful, finally they do not change the likenesses of the senses, whence they certainly think true things. For since those things are clear and ample in the region, they quickly distribute and divide individual things into their own effigy, which indeed are called existing and true, and such men are said to be wise. Does not the same seem to you? 

**THEAETETUS:** In a wonderful way. 
**SOCRATES:** When therefore someone's heart is dense, which the most wise poet praised, or when muddy, not from purified wax, or too soft, or hard, it does not hold itself altogether rightly. For too soft wax makes them quick to perceive, but the same forgetful. Hard wax, on the contrary, makes them mindful for a long time, but inept and slow to perceive: and those who have a dense and rough, stony, or earthy or foul heart, contain obscure likenesses: those who have a hard heart also contain obscure ones, for depth is not present. Moreover, those who have a softer one, for from confusion they easily vanish: if besides these, they are also crowded together on account of the narrowness of the seat itself, if indeed the little soul be small, the likenesses in them will become even more obscure. All men therefore of this kind, such as we have described, are rendered prone to false opinion. For he who sees something, or hears, or thinks, because they cannot soon render individual things to individual things, they are slow, and they prevaricate; for they see very many things perversely, and hear them, and are often deceived by thinking one thing for another: and these are called false, lying, and ignorant. 

**THEAETETUS:** You speak most rightly of all, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** It must be confessed therefore that false opinions exist in men. 
**THEAETETUS:** Most definitely. 
**SOCRATES:** And true ones besides. 
**THEAETETUS:** And true ones. 
**SOCRATES:** Now surely it must be thought sufficiently established that two opinions exist. 
**THEAETETUS:** Greatly. 
**SOCRATES:** Truly a troublesome and very much annoying man, Theaetetus, a talkative man seems to be. 
**THEAETETUS:** To what end do you say this? 
**SOCRATES:** Bearing my rudeness, and to speak truly, my talkativeness, with difficulty. For what other name should someone impose on him who on account of the slowness of his genius turns discourses up and down, since he cannot be persuaded, and like a dull man cannot expedite any disputation at all, and cannot escape doubts? 
**THEAETETUS:** But why do you bear it with difficulty? 
**SOCRATES:** Not only do I suffer it with difficulty, but I also doubted what I should respond if someone asked thus: "Socrates, have you now found that false opinion consists not among senses among themselves, nor among thoughts, but in the congress of sense and thought?" But I shall confess, as I think, boastfully, as if we have found some excellent thing. 
**THEAETETUS:** It seems to me, Socrates, that it is by no means base what has now been shown. 
**SOCRATES:** "Surely therefore," that person will say, "we shall never think that a man whom we only think of, but see in no way, is a horse, whom in the present we neither see nor touch, but only think of, and feel nothing else around him?" I indeed, as I think, shall confess that I assert these things. 
**THEAETETUS:** And deservedly. 
**SOCRATES:** "Then," he says, "he who only thinks of eleven, according to this reasoning, will never think they are twelve, which he also only thinks of. What do you respond to these?" 
**THEAETETUS:** I shall respond: that perhaps someone seeing or touching eleven, would think they were twelve: yet those things which he has in thought, he would never judge similarly. 
**SOCRATES:** "What further," he says, "do you think someone will think with himself five and seven—not men, I say, but five and seven—nor anything else of this kind, but those very five and seven which we say are monuments there in effigy, and that no one can think false things in those?" These things, I say, if someone should consider with himself, inquiring how many they are, will not some of them judge they are eleven, some twelve? Or will all say and think they are twelve? 
**THEODORUS:** Not by Jove, but most will say eleven: and if someone asks about a larger number, he is more deceived. For I think you speak about every number. 
**SOCRATES:** You think rightly. Notice therefore whether this also happens, that is, that someone thinks twelve itself, which is in effigy, is eleven. 
**THEAETETUS:** It seems so. 
**SOCRATES:** Does this not revolve back to the previous points? For he who suffers what he knows, thinks it is some other thing which he similarly knows, which we rejected above as impossible. And from this very thing we force anyone to confess that false opinion does not exist, lest one and the same man be forced to know and not know the same things at the same time. 
**THEAETETUS:** You speak the truth. 
**SOCRATES:** From these it is now established that false opinion is to be defined otherwise than as the permutation of thought to sense. For if it were so, we would never be deceived in thoughts themselves. But now either there is no false opinion: or if there is any, it can happen that what someone knows, he is at the same time ignorant of. Which do you rather choose? 
**THEAETETUS:** You have proposed an ambiguous choice, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** Reason seems to forbid admitting both. Nevertheless, all things must be dared. What if we dare to lay aside shame? 
**THEAETETUS:** In what way? 
**SOCRATES:** To dare to pronounce what knowing itself is. 
**THEAETETUS:** Why is this impudent? 
**SOCRATES:** You seem not to have noticed sufficiently that our whole discourse from the beginning has been an investigation of knowledge, as if we are ignorant of what it itself is. 
**THEAETETUS:** I hold it. 
**SOCRATES:** Is it not of an impudent mind, as ones ignorant of knowledge, to strike at what knowing is? But, Theaetetus, we have been wandering far from the purity of disputing for a long time. For a thousand times we have said these things: "we recognize," "we do not recognize," "we know," "we do not know," as if we understand something in turn, of which we meanwhile are ignorant of the knowledge. Therefore even now also, if it pleases, let us use those vocables, namely "to be ignorant" and "to understand," as it is fitting to use them, if indeed we are void of knowledge. 
**THEAETETUS:** But in what way, these having been taken away, Socrates, would you be able to dispute? 
**SOCRATES:** In no way, while I remain such as I am: yet I could in some way, if I were contentious. And now if any such person were present, he would profess to abstain from these vocables, and would vehemently deter us from those things which I tell. But after we are simple and idle, do you want me to dare to prolate what knowing itself is like? For it seems worth the effort to me. 
**THEAETETUS:** Dare, by Jove. For we shall give pardon to you using these. 
**SOCRATES:** Have you heard what they say knowing is at this time? 
**THEAETETUS:** Perhaps, yet I do not remember in the present. 
**SOCRATES:** They say this is to have knowledge. 
**THEAETETUS:** So it is. 
**SOCRATES:** But let us, changing it a little, say it is to **possess** knowledge. You will perhaps ask how this differs from that. Perhaps in nothing. But after you have heard what seems to me, examine it with me. 
**THEAETETUS:** If only I can. 
**SOCRATES:** To possess does not seem the same as to have: as if someone having bought a garment, preserving it, and being able to use it as he judges, does not wear it, we would by no means confess that he has it, but that he possesses it. 
**THEAETETUS:** And rightly indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** See moreover whether it can happen that someone who similarly possesses knowledge does not have it: just as if someone having hunted forest birds, whether pigeons or any others, nourishes them in an aviary constructed at home, he will in a certain way be said always to have them, because he possesses them. 
**THEAETETUS:** Surely. 
**SOCRATES:** In what way...
