# 104 Book Thirteen.

"...since it seems good to you, let us speak of those who are the leaders. For why speak of those who abuse the study of philosophy? The former, from their youth, first do not even know the way to the marketplace, nor do they know where the court, or the council-chamber, or any other public gathering of the city is. They neither see nor hear the laws and decrees, whether promulgated or written. The factions of political clubs seeking to create magistrates, the meetings, the banquets, and the decadent feasts—they do not even dream of them. Whether the city has fared well or ill for a long time, or what evil or stain of disgrace has come to someone from his ancestors (whether men or women), is more hidden from them than 'the sands of the sea,' as the saying goes. And he does not even know that he does not know all these things. For he does not abstain from them for the sake of common glory, but because in reality, only his body dwells and lives in the city; but his mind, considering all these things small or rather of no value, flies everywhere, as Pindarus says, measuring both what is under the earth and what is above, transcending the heavens by its art, and searching out the entire nature of all things that pertain to the universe—but in no way applying itself to those things which are near at hand." THEODORUS. "In what way do you say this, Socrates?" SOCRATES. "Just as it is said that a certain clever and charming Thracian servant girl <note>This refers to the famous anecdote of the astronomer Thales of Miletus. While he was looking up at the stars, he fell into a well, and a servant girl laughed at him for wanting to know what was in the heavens while being blind to what was at his feet.</note> mocked Thales while he was looking at the sky, intent on the stars, and fell into a pit. She argued that he was striving to see what was in the heavens, but did not see what was right before him at his feet. The same can be charged against all who spend their lives in philosophy. For it is hidden from the philosopher not only what his neighbor does, but almost whether he is a man or a beast. But as to what a human being is, and what it most befits his nature to do or suffer, he seeks out and laboriously scrutinizes. Do you understand, Theodorus, or not?" THEODORUS. "I understand indeed, and I approve of what you say." SOCRATES. "Indeed, my friend, as we said before, if ever such a man is forced to speak, either privately with someone or publicly in court or elsewhere, about the things at his feet and in his sight, he causes laughter not only to the Thracians but also to other nations, since he falls into pits and many ambiguities because of his inexperience in these matters. There, an absurd clumsiness stamps him with the mark of laziness. For when someone must be disparaged, he has nothing to bring as a reproach, since he is ignorant of vices, having never noticed the particular evils of individuals; therefore, he is laughed at as if he were ignorant. In praising and extolling men, since he simulates or dissimulates nothing but laughs openly, he seems to be raving. For when he hears a tyrant or a king being praised, he thinks he is hearing about some swineherd, or shepherd, or cowherd being extolled because he milks abundantly. However, he considers that kings and tyrants care for and 'milk' a more difficult and treacherous animal. Such rulers must be no less rustic and unrefined than shepherds because of their lack of leisure, being surrounded by walls in the city just as a shepherd is in a fold on a mountain. When he hears that someone possesses a 'vast estate' as if it were something great, he thinks he is hearing about something tiny, since he is accustomed to looking at the entire orb of the earth. Moreover, whenever someone recounts the nobility of his lineage—because he can count seven wealthy ancestors—he thinks such praises belong to a dull mind that thinks of nothing great because of ignorance, as if it cannot look toward the nature of the whole world and see that countless ancestors and great-grandparents preceded every one of us, among whom were countless rich and poor, kings and slaves, barbarians and Greeks. Furthermore, when someone counts a lineage of twenty-five ancestors and traces his origin back to Hercules, the son of Amphitryon, it seems a thing unworthy of mention to him. For that man is the twenty-fifth in line from Hercules, but fortune made him so; even if he were the fiftieth from Hercules, the philosopher laughs, as if at those who cannot calculate and drive away the vanity of an insane mind. In all these things, the philosopher is commonly held to be a ridiculous man, partly because he appears proud and a scorner, and partly because he is ignorant and wavering about things that are plain to see." THEODORUS. "You have narrated the matter exactly as it happens, Socrates." SOCRATES. "But when he draws someone, O friend, toward the things above, and having moved away from lawsuits (in which the question is how I have harmed you or you me) he ascends to the speculation of justice and injustice themselves—what both are, and how they differ from all other things and from each other—or when he sets aside the controversy about whether a king is happy because he possesses much gold and turns to the contemplation of kingship itself and of human happiness and misery (what kind they are for each person and in what way it befits human nature to attain the one and flee the other): when, I say, that small-souled and sharp-witted lawyer is required to give a reason for all these things, then he in turn pays the penalty to the philosopher. For he suffers from vertigo looking down from that high watchtower with blurred eyes, as he is unaccustomed to looking from above. He grieves, he stumbles, and he speaks like a barbarian. Therefore, he causes laughter not to Thracians, nor to any unrefined person—for they do not perceive it—but rather to all those who have been educated freely and far from a servile life. This, O Theodorus, is the condition of each. One is that of the man raised in freedom and leisure, whom you call a philosopher. Although he truly ought not to be blamed, he appears foolish and clumsy whenever he attempts servile tasks—since he would not know how to tie up a bundle of bedding, nor how to prepare the seasonings of a meal, nor how to fashion flattering words of adulation. The other is the condition of the man who can perform these things quickly and skillfully, but does not know how to wear the dress of a free man becomingly. Moreover, he is completely ignorant of how to sing the true life of gods and blessed men with a harmonious speech." THEODORUS. "If you could persuade other men of what you say, Socrates, just as you persuade me, there would be more peace and fewer evils among men." SOCRATES. "But it is impossible, Theodorus, for evils to be completely uprooted. For there must always be something opposite to the good. Nor can they have a place among the gods. But they necessarily circulate around mortal nature and the lower region. Therefore, we must strive to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. The flight consists in becoming as like God as possible according to our strength. We are made like God through prudence, justice, and holiness. But, O best of men, it is not easy to persuade people that virtue is to be followed and vice fled from, not for the reason the common people believe—namely, so that you do not seem bad and so that you appear good. For these seem to me to be the trifles of old women. But let us say what is true: God is never and in no way unjust, but most just, embracing the whole power of justice, and nothing is more like Him than a most just man. About this, the true industry and strength of a man, as well as his laziness and weakness, are concerned. The knowledge of these things is true virtue and wisdom; ignorance, on the contrary, is manifest lack of skill..." <margin>Proverb.</margin> <margin>The fall of Thales.</margin> <margin>The philosopher is unskilled in forensic disputes.</margin> <margin>It is impossible for evils to be completely uprooted. Evils are in the lower things.</margin>

<summary>Socrates describes the philosopher as someone whose mind dwells on universal truths rather than local gossip or politics, often appearing ridiculous in practical life. He concludes that one must strive for "homoiosis theoi"—becoming like God through justice and wisdom—to escape earthly evil.</summary>

# Theaetetus, or, Concerning Knowledge. 105

"...and manifest wickedness. But other things that seem to be powers and wisdoms are troublesome in civil magistrates and illiberal in the other arts. Therefore, for him who has committed some injustice or said or done something profane, it is safest if he has no cunning and does not use evil arts. For such men exult in their disgrace, and they do not seem to be abject and empty little men, nor 'the inert weight of the earth,' as the said; but they seem to be such men as can live safely in a republic. Therefore, the truth must be expressed: they are all the more what they do not think they are, the less they think it. For they are ignorant of the penalty of injustice, which it is least fitting to be ignorant of. For it is not, as they perhaps think, beatings and killings—which those who have done nothing unjust often suffer, and the unjust often avoid—but rather that penalty which cannot be escaped." THEODORUS. "Which one do you mean?" SOCRATES. "Since in the order of things, my friend, there are two patterns <note>original: "exemplaria duo". Socrates describes two models of life: the divine/happy and the godless/miserable.</note>—the divine one, most blessed, and the one devoid of God, most miserable—they do not see that this is the case. Occupied by extreme folly and madness, they secretly become like the latter through their unjust actions, and unlike the former. They certainly pay the penalty for this fault while they lead a life fitting for that which they have become like. Indeed, if we say that unless they cease from their wickedness, that holy place free of evils will not receive them, but they will always live here in a likeness of their own life—evils dwelling with the evil—then these clever and malicious men will answer that they are hearing mere ravings." THEODORUS. "They certainly will, Socrates." SOCRATES. "I know it well, my friend. But one thing at least happens to them: if ever it becomes necessary to give an account in private and to bring forth reasons for the things they disparage, and if they are willing to endure a delay for manly disputation and not flee lazily, then finally—O blessed man, it is absurd—they will disapprove of their own words, and their rhetoric will utterly vanish, so that they seem no different from children. But let us now put an end to these things, as they are beyond our proposal. Otherwise, the abundance of material flowing in from every side will overwhelm the speech we began. Let us return to the earlier points, if it seems good to you." THEODORUS. "To me, Socrates, those things were no less pleasant to hear. For at my age, I can easily follow this. Nevertheless, if you please, let us return to where we digressed." SOCRATES. "We had come to the point in our dispute where we said that those who placed all essence in motion <note>referring to Heraclitus and his followers</note> and held that what seems to each person exists for him, would assert this most vehemently in other things, especially in justice. They say that whatever a city establishes as appearing just to itself, these things are just for it so long as the statutes remain. But no one would be so bold as to dare to contend the same regarding 'good' and 'useful' things—namely, that whatever things a city establishes as appearing useful to itself are beneficial to it for as long as they are decreed, unless perhaps he were just speaking of the 'name' <note>i.e., just calling it "useful" without it actually being so</note>. But that would be a joke <note>original: "scomma". A taunt or mockery.</note> regarding what we want, would it not?" THEODORUS. "Undoubtedly." SOCRATES. "Let him not speak of the name, but look at the thing named. A city, in making laws, looks to what it calls useful, and it establishes each law as being as useful to itself as it can and thinks. Does it intend anything else in passing laws?" THEODORUS. "Nothing else." SOCRATES. "Does it always achieve its wish? Or does opinion often fail it?" THEODORUS. "I think it often fails." SOCRATES. "Furthermore, anyone will confess these same things more readily if one asks about every species in which the 'useful' consists. It also concerns, in a way, the future time. For whenever we make laws, we make them as being about to be useful in the future, which we would more correctly call the 'future.'" THEODORUS. "Most certainly." SOCRATES. "Come then, let us ask Protagoras, or any other of his followers. You assert, O Protagoras, that man is the measure of all things: of white things, heavy things, light things, and every such thing. For since he contains the power of judging them in himself, and judges them to be such as he experiences them, he judges things that are true for himself and that exist. Is it not so?" THEODORUS. "Plainly so." SOCRATES. "Shall we say, O Protagoras, that he also has the power of judging future things in himself? And such as he thinks they will be for him, so they happen to the one who thinks so. For example, when someone unskilled in medicine thinks he is going to catch a fever and that he will become hot, but a doctor disagrees, thinking the opposite: whose opinion do we think will be true for the future? Or both? For the doctor, he will be neither hot nor feverish, but for himself, he will be both?" THEODORUS. "That would indeed be ridiculous." SOCRATES. "Furthermore, regarding whether wine will be sweet or tart, the opinion of the farmer prevails, not that of the lyre-player." THEODORUS. "Of course." SOCRATES. "Nor does a gymnast judge better than a musician about what will be consonant or dissonant—even though it will later seem consonant to the gymnast himself." THEODORUS. "Not at all." SOCRATES. "And when a table is prepared and a feast is to be offered, and something must be predicted about their future sweetness, is not the cook's opinion more powerful than that of any person unskilled in catering? We do not fight about what 'is' or 'was' sweet to each person, but rather about what 'ought to be' and 'seem' sweet to each in the future. Is each person a sufficient judge for himself, or would you, Protagoras, better foresee what will seem 'probable' to each person in a court case than any unskilled person could?" THEODORUS. "In this very thing, Socrates, Protagoras professed to excel all people." SOCRATES. "O wretched man! No one, by Jupiter, would have followed him and offered him money if he had not persuaded his associates that he could foresee what would be probable and seem so in the future better than a prophet or anyone else." THEODORUS. "You speak most truly." SOCRATES. "Do not the making of laws and their utilities also look to the future? And would not everyone admit without controversy that a constitution of a republic often misses what is useful?" THEODORUS. "Very much so." SOCRATES. "Let it be said sufficiently against your teacher that he is forced to confess that one person is wiser than another, and that such a person is a 'measure.' But as for me, since I am unskilled in science, the argument does not force me to become a measure—as his speech recently urged—stating that whether I like it or not, I was such a thing." THEODORUS. "From that, Socrates, his speech seems most convicted, and also from this: that it makes the opinions of others valid; but these opinions openly reject his words, thinking them false." SOCRATES. "In many other ways, Theodorus, it can be grasped that not every opinion of every person is true. But concerning the present experience of each, from which sense-perception and opinions according to sense arise, it is more difficult to grasp that they are not true. But perhaps I say nothing. For if they have been attained, they cannot be refuted; and those who assert that they are certain and are 'knowledges' perhaps would not be wandering from the mark. And for that reason, Theaetetus here said, not without cause, that sense-perception and knowledge are the same. Therefore, we must approach more closely, just as the Protagorean speech teaches..."

<summary>Socrates argues that while perception might seem true in the present moment, it fails as a "measure" for the future, where experts (like doctors or cooks) are clearly better judges than laypeople. This refutes the idea that every man is an equal measure of what is useful or true.</summary>

-># Theaetetus, or, On Knowledge. 105<-

...and manifest wickedness. Other qualities, which seem like capacities or wisdom, are troublesome in civil magistrates and unrefined in other arts. Therefore, for the man who has committed some injustice, or says or does profane things, it is much safer if he has no cleverness <note>original: "vafricie," referring to a sneaky, dishonest kind of skill</note> and does not use evil arts. For men of this sort exult in their own disgrace, believing that they appear to be not at all cast down, nor "useless burdens upon the earth," as the saying goes, but rather the kind of men who can live safely in a republic. Therefore, the truth must be expressed: they are all the more the sort of men they think they are not, precisely because they do not think they are so. Indeed, they are ignorant of the penalty for injustice—an ignorance that is least becoming. For the penalty is not what they perhaps imagine—beatings and executions, which those who have done no injustice often suffer, and which the unjust often avoid—but rather a penalty that cannot be escaped. 

THEO. Which penalty do you mean? 

SOC. Since in the order of things, my friend, there are **two patterns** <note>These "exemplaria" or patterns are central to Platonic ethics: the "likeness to God" vs. the "likeness to the world."</note>—one divine and most blessed, the other devoid of God and most wretched—those who do not see that this is the case, being occupied by stupidity and extreme madness, secretly become like the latter through their wicked actions, and unlike the former. They pay the penalty for this fault by leading a life consistent with the one they have become like. Indeed, if we say that, unless they cease from their wickedness, that place free of evils will not receive them after they have finished their lives, and that here on earth they will always bear a resemblance to their own lives, dwelling as evil men among the evil—these cunning and malicious men will reply that they are hearing mere ravings. 

THEO. And most especially so, Socrates. 

SOC. I know it well, my friend. Yet one thing at least happens to them: if ever it becomes necessary for them to give and receive reasons in private regarding the things they disparage, and they are willing to endure a long, manly dispute rather than fleeing like cowards—then at last, my blessed friend, a strange thing happens: they end up disapproving of their own words, and their rhetoric utterly vanishes, so that they seem no different from children. 

But let us put an end to these matters, as they are outside our main purpose. Otherwise, the many subjects flowing in from every side will overwhelm the discourse we began at the start. Let us return to our previous points, if you agree. 

THEO. To me, Socrates, those things are no less pleasant to hear. For at my age, I can easily follow them. Nevertheless, if you please, let us return to where we left off. 

SOC. We had reached the point in the dispute where we were saying that those who place all essence in motion <note>Referring to the Heraclitean doctrine that everything is always changing.</note>, and hold that whatever seems to each person actually exists for that person, would assert this most vehemently in other matters, and not least in matters of justice. They claim that whatever a city establishes as appearing "just" to itself, these things are indeed just for that city for as long as the statutes remain. But no one would be so bold as to contend the same regarding **good and useful** things—namely, that whatever a city establishes as appearing "useful" to itself, these things are beneficial to it only for as long as they are decreed. Unless, perhaps, someone is merely speaking of the *name* "useful"; but that would be a mockery <note>original: "scōmma," a Greek-derived term for a taunt or jest</note> of what we are trying to discuss. Is it not so? 

THEO. Without a doubt. 

SOC. Let him not speak of the name, but look at the thing named. When a city names something "useful," it looks to this in making its laws; it establishes individual laws as being as useful to itself as it possibly can. Does it intend anything else in making laws? 

THEO. Nothing else. 

SOC. And does it always achieve its wish? Or does its opinion often fail it? 

THEO. I think it often fails. 

SOC. Furthermore, everyone will more readily admit these same things if one inquires about the whole class in which the "useful" consists. This also concerns, in a way, the **future time**. For whenever we make laws, we make them as things that will be beneficial in the future—which we might more rightly call the "future." 

THEO. Most certainly. 

SOCR. Come then, let us ask Protagoras, or anyone else who follows him: You assert, Protagoras, that "man is the measure of all things"—of white things, heavy things, light things, and every such thing. For since he contains the power of judging them within himself, and judges them as he experiences them, he judges things that are true for him and which exist. Is it not so? 

THEOD. Quite so. 

SOC. Shall we say then, Protagoras, that he also has the power of judgment within himself regarding **future things**? And that whatever he thinks will happen to him, these things actually happen to the one who expects them? For instance, when someone unskilled in medicine thinks he is going to catch a fever and become hot, but a doctor thinks the opposite—whose opinion do we believe will be true in the future? Or both? Will it be that for the doctor, the man will be neither hot nor feverish, but for the man himself, he will be both? 

THEO. That would be ridiculous. 

SOCR. Moreover, regarding whether wine will be sweet or tart, the opinion of the farmer prevails over that of the lyre-player. 

THEO. Why wouldn't it? 

SOC. Nor can a gymnastics teacher judge better than a musician whether a sound will be harmonious or discordant in the future—even if it later seems harmonious to the gymnastics teacher himself. 

THEO. In no way. 

SOCRA. And when a feast is to be prepared and served, and someone must predict the future sweetness of the dishes, is not the cook’s opinion more valid than that of anyone unskilled in the culinary arts? We are not fighting over what is or was pleasant to each person, but rather about what *ought* to be and seem so to each person in the future. Is each person a fit judge for himself, or would you, Protagoras, better foresee what will be persuasive to individuals in a legal judgment than any unskilled person could? 

THEODO. In this very thing, Socrates, Protagoras claimed to excel everyone. 

SOC. Oh, you poor man! No one would have followed him and offered him money by the god Jove if he had not persuaded his associates that he could foresee what would be persuasive and appear to be the case in the future better than any prophet or anyone else. 

THEO. You speak most truly. 

SOC. And do not the making of laws and their utility also look to the future? And would not anyone admit without controversy that the constitution of a republic often misses what is actually useful? 

THEO. Very much so. 

SOCR. Let this be a sufficient argument against your teacher: he is forced to admit that one person is wiser than another, and that such a person is a "measure." As for me, though I am unskilled in knowledge, he does not force me to become a "measure," as that recent argument of his urged—namely, that whether I liked it or not, I was such a measure. 

THEOD. Socrates, his argument seems most refuted by that point, and also by the fact that he makes the opinions of others valid; yet these very opinions openly reject his own words, considering them false. 

SOCRAT. In many other ways, Theodorus, it is possible to catch this error and show that not every opinion of every person is true. But regarding the present sensation <note>original: "passio," a physical or mental impression</note> from which senses and the opinions based on senses are born, it is more difficult to prove that these are not true. But perhaps I say nothing. For if they are grasped, they cannot be refuted; and those who assert that these are certain and are "knowledge" might not be wandering from the truth. And therefore, our friend Theaetetus here said not without reason that sensation and knowledge are the same. We must therefore draw closer, as the Protagorean argument instructed...

<summary>Socrates argues that while people may be judges of their own current sensations, they are not equal judges of future utility, where the expert's opinion (like a doctor's or a cook's) is superior to the layman's. This refutes Protagoras's claim that every man's opinion is equally true.</summary>
<keywords>Protagoras, Socrates, Theodorus, Relativism, Man is the Measure, Knowledge, Future Utility, Expertise, Likeness to God, Divine Pattern</keywords>

# Thirteen Book.

<margin>The habit of the followers of Heraclitus in disputation.</margin>

He has commanded that this agitated <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentia"; referring to the nature of reality as being in constant flux.</note> be examined by striking it, to see if it gives off a whole or a cracked sound. Indeed, no small battle has arisen concerning it, and not among a few people. 

**THEODORUS.** It is certainly far from being a trivial contention, for it has been spread everywhere through Ionia. Indeed, the students of Heraclitus support this discourse with the greatest zeal. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, my friend Theodorus, these things must be inspected from their principles, as those men propose them. 

**THEODORUS.** Entirely. For indeed, Socrates, regarding these Heracliteans—or, as you say, Homericists <note>Socrates often links Heraclitus's idea of flux to Homer's line about Oceanus being the father of all things.</note>—and even those more ancient ones among the Ephesians, it is no more possible to speak with those who wish to seem more skilled than with people driven by a <term>gadfly</term> <note>original: "œstro"; meaning a stinging impulse or frenzy.</note>. For their writings are clearly carried along by an impulse. But delay and expectation in discourse and questions, and the quietness between responding and questioning, are less present in them than nothing at all. Or rather, even less than nothing; so little rest is there in the minds of those men. But if you ask any of them about any matter, they shoot off little obscure words as if from a dark quiver. And if you seek the reason for this, they strike with another, but with the name changed. You will never achieve anything with any of them, nor they with each other. They take the utmost care for this one thing: that they permit nothing to be stable, either in discourse or in their own minds, thinking (as it seems to me) that the stable itself is an enemy, and they pursue it with all their strength and drive it out from everywhere.

**SOCRATES.** Perhaps, Theodorus, you have seen these men in battle, but in peace never. For they are not your friends. But I suppose they say such things to their disciples in leisure, whom they wish to make like themselves.

**THEODORUS.** What disciples, blessed man? For among such people, one is not the disciple of another, but they spring up spontaneously, wherever any of them happens to be seized by frenzy. And one thinks the other knows nothing. From them, therefore, as I was just saying, you will never receive a rational account, whether they are willing or unwilling. But we must consider it as if we had received a formal <term>proposition</term>.

**SOCRATES.** You speak skillfully. Indeed, we have received a certain other opinion from the ancients who hid it from the common people with poetry: that the origin of all other things is <note>original: "Oceanus atq; Tethys"</note> **Oceanus and Tethys**, and that all things are in flux and nothing stands still. From the more recent and wiser men, however, demonstrating the matter so clearly that even cobblers could perceive their wisdom by hearing it—and might cease to foolishly think that some things stand still while others move—from these, I say, we have received the doctrine that all things move, whom those authors revere. 

But I had almost forgotten, Theodorus, that others have shown the opposite of these: namely, that the name for the <term>universe</term> is "The One" existing immobile; and other such things which Melissus and Parmenides assert in opposition to all these, saying that all things are one, and this "one" itself consists in itself, having no place at all in which it might move. 

What shall we say of all these, my friend? For gradually progressing, we have secretly escaped into the middle of both sides. If we go away without defending either, like cowards, we shall pay the penalty like those who play at the line in the wrestling grounds <note>A reference to a game where players are pulled across a central line.</note>, whenever they are seized by both sides and dragged in opposite directions. It seems, therefore, that we must first deal with those whom we first approached: those who say all is in flux. And if they seem to say anything probable, we will pull ourselves along with them, trying to escape the others. But if those who posit a stable universe bring forth truer things, we will flee to them from the ones who move even the immobile. But if neither side appears to bring forward anything plausible, we shall turn out ridiculous, thinking that we, trivial little men, know something great when we have done nothing but disparage those ancient and wise men. Look then, Theodorus, whether it is better or not to undergo such a great danger.

**THEODORUS.** It is by no means to be allowed, Socrates, that we should fail to discuss what truth or falsehood the senses of both sides hold.

**SOCRATES.** It must be discussed now, since you desire it so much. It seems to me that the beginning of this disputation should be taken from **motion**, namely, by what motion they say all things move. What I say is this: whether they introduce one species of motion, or, as it seems to me, two species. I do not wish this to seem so to me alone, but to you also, so that we may both suffer together whatever is necessary. Say, then: Do you call it "moving" when something changes place for place, or turns in the same spot?

**THEODORUS.** Indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, let this be one species. But when something remains in the same place but grows old, or becomes black from white, or hard from soft, or is changed by any other <term>alteration</term>, shall we not rightly call this another species of motion?

**THEODORUS.** Rightly.

**SOCRATES.** From these it is necessary that twin species of motion exist: namely, **alteration** and **local motion**.

**THEODORUS.** Correct.

**SOCRATES.** This distinction having been made, let us now go to those who wish all things to move, and let us question them in this manner: Do you admit that anything moves in both ways, both altered and carried along? Or some in both ways, and some in only one?

**THEODORUS.** Indeed, I do not know what I should assert, but I think they would say in both ways.

**SOCRATES.** Otherwise, my friend, things would seem to them both to be agitated and to be consistent with themselves at the same time, and it would be no more permitted to assert that all things move than that all things stand still.

**THEODORUS.** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES.** Since it is necessary that they move, and the absence of motion cannot belong to them, then all things are always moved by every motion.

**THEODORUS.** It follows necessarily.

**SOCRATES.** Consider this from their words: the generation of heat, or whiteness, or anything else. Did we not say they think each of these is carried along at the same time as the sensation between the <term>agent</term> and the <term>patient</term>? <note>In this theory, perception is the result of an interaction between an active force (agent) and a passive receiver (patient).</note> And that the patient becomes "sensible" but not "sensation," while the agent becomes an "efficient" something, but not yet a "quality"? 

Perhaps "quality" <note>original: "qualitas"</note> seems like a strange name to you, and you do not perceive it spoken of in a general sense; hear it then in its parts. For the agent is neither heat nor whiteness, but rather "the hot" and "the white," and the rest in the same way. You remember we said above that <margin>Nothing is one thing by itself.</margin> nothing is one thing according to itself, nor is there simply an agent or a patient, but from both meeting in turn, sensations and sensibles emanate, partly becoming certain qualities, and partly becoming the act of sensing?

**THEODORUS.** I remember; why would they not say so?

**SOCRATES.** Let us leave the rest aside, whether they say it thus or otherwise. But let us diligently search out this one thing for the sake of which we are disputing. All things move and flow, as you say. Is it not so?

**THEODORUS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Are they not both carried along and altered by those two motions we distinguished?

**THEODORUS.** Why not, if it is necessary that they be perfectly moved?

**SOCRATES.** If, therefore, it were only carried along, but not altered, we could say what kind of things flow as they are carried; or how shall we say?

**THEODORUS.** In this way.

**SOCRATES.** But since not even this remains—as for instance "white"—so that the white which flows remains flowing as white, but it is changed so that there is a flux of this very whiteness, and a transition into another color, so that it can in no way be caught remaining the same, can we ever pronounce any color such that we name it correctly?

**THEODORUS.** But how, Socrates, can that be done, either in this or in any other thing, if indeed while we are pronouncing it, it continually slips away, being something that always flows?

**SOCRATES.** What then shall be said of any sense, such as seeing or hearing?

<summary>Socrates and Theodorus discuss the radical "flux" theory of the Heracliteans, concluding that if everything is constantly changing in both position and quality, language itself fails because nothing remains stable enough to be named.</summary>
<keywords>Heraclitus, flux, motion, alteration, local motion, Parmenides, Oceanus, perception, language, Ephesian philosophers</keywords>

# Theaetetus, or, Concerning Knowledge. 107

Does it ever remain stable in vision or hearing?

**THEODORUS.** Least of all, if indeed all things are moved.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, one should not say one is "seeing" any more than "not seeing," nor use any other sense more than not using it, since all things are entirely transmuted.

**THEODORUS.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** Furthermore, sensation itself is knowledge, as I and Theaetetus said.

**THEODORUS.** It was said.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, when asked what knowledge is, we were responding "not knowledge" no less than "knowledge."

**THEODORUS.** So you certainly seem to be.

**SOCRATES.** We would have corrected that response opportunely if we were striving to demonstrate that all things move, so that the response would seem correct. But this, it seems, has appeared: that if all things move, every response, about whatever one may respond, is equally correct—whether one responds that it is "thus" or "not thus." Or if you prefer to say "becomes" rather than "is," so that we do not stop them in their speech.

**THEODORUS.** You speak correctly.

**SOCRATES.** Except in this, Theodorus: I said "thus" and "not thus," but one ought not even say "this." For it would no longer be moved "thus," nor again "not thus." For this is not motion, but another name must be imposed by those who hold such doctrines; since now they have no words for their supposition, unless perhaps this expression: "not in any way whatsoever," which would most suit them if uttered infinitely.

**THEODORUS.** That expression is very fitting there.

**SOCRATES.** Now, Theodorus, we have dispatched with what pertains to your friend Protagoras: we have not yet granted him that every man is the measure of all things, unless he happens to be wise. Furthermore, we will not at all concede that knowledge is sensation according to that reasoning which proclaims that all things move, unless perhaps Theaetetus here says it in some other way.

**THEAETETUS.** You have spoken best, Socrates. For these things being finished, it is right that I also be dispatched from these duties, as was agreed between us. But since the disputation against Protagoras has reached its end, do not stop, I pray, Theodorus, before you and Socrates run through those others who wanted all things to stand still, just as you proposed a little while ago.

**THEODORUS.** Being a young man, Theaetetus, you teach your elders to do injury, while you exhort us to transgress our pacts. But gird yourself so that you may give an account of the remaining things to Socrates, if he wishes.

**THEAETETUS.** I would most willingly hear those things of which I speak.

**THEODORUS.** You are "challenging cavalry to the plain" <note>A Greek proverb meaning to challenge someone to a contest in which they are superior.</note> when you invite Socrates to dispute. Question him, therefore, and you shall hear.

**SOCRATES.** Indeed, Theodorus, I seem unlikely to obey Theaetetus in these things he commands.

**THEODORUS.** What prevents you from obeying?

**SOCRATES.** Although I fear Melissus and the others who say the universe is one and consistent, lest perhaps we seem burdensome in harassing them, I fear even more the unique Parmenides. Parmenides, to use Homeric words, seems to me "venerable and awesome." <note>original: "verendus... acerq;" citing Homer's Iliad.</note> I spoke once with that man when he was quite old and I was still very young, and he seemed to me to possess a profound and altogether noble wisdom. I dread, therefore, that we might not at all understand his words and voices; and what he implies beneath his words might hide from us much more. And what is greatest is that the reason for which this disputation began among us—inquiring what knowledge is—might be left unexamined because of arguments rushing in at random, if one obeys them. Especially since that most ample question we just introduced, if it were treated outside of our purpose and as if by digressing, would suffer too much indignity; and if it were completed more broadly and exactly, it would impede the investigation of knowledge itself. Neither is fitting; rather, it is better to lead Theaetetus's offspring concerning knowledge into the light by the <term>obstetric faculty</term> <note>Socrates' famous "midwifery" of the soul.</note> and examine it diligently.

**THEAETETUS.** If it seems so, it must be done so.

**SOCRATES.** Consider this further, Theaetetus, about the things said above. You responded that knowledge is sensation, did you not?

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** If someone asked by what a man sees white and black things, and by what he hears high and low sounds, you would respond, I suppose, "with eyes" and "with ears."

**THEAETETUS.** Indeed.

**SOCRATES.** To use common names and words and not to inquire exactly and curiously is often the mark of a noble mind, while the contrary is illiberal. Yet sometimes it is necessary, as we are compelled in the present to examine in what part your response might be less than correct. Attend to which response is more correct: that which says "that by which <note>original: "quo"</note> we see are the eyes" or "that *through* which <note>original: "per quod"</note> we see." Likewise, "by which we hear are the ears" or "*through* which we hear."

**THEAETETUS.** It seems to me better to respond "through which" we sense each thing, rather than "by which" we sense, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** It would be absurd, my boy, if many senses sat within us <margin>Allusion to the Trojan Horse.</margin> as if in wooden horses, and all these did not tend toward one thing—whether an <term>idea</term> or a <term>soul</term>, or whatever it is right to call it—by which we sense the things subject to the senses through these organs.

**THEAETETUS.** This seems to me better than that other way.

**SOCRATES.** For this reason I search these things out with you diligently, so that we may see whether by some one and the same thing that is in us, we perceive white and black things through the eyes, and other things through other organs; and whether, when questioned, you can refer each of these to the body. It is perhaps better for you to respond to each yourself than for me to be exhausted by acting in your place. Tell me then: the things through which you sense the hot and the dry, the light and the sweet, do you not place each in the organs of the body? Or in something else?

**THEAETETUS.** In nothing else.

**SOCRATES.** Will you not admit that what you sense through one power, you cannot sense through another? Such as what you perceive through hearing, you cannot see through sight; and conversely, what you perceive through sight, you cannot hear?

**THEAETETUS.** Why would I not admit it?

**SOCRATES.** If therefore you think something about both, you do not sense it through the one organ, nor through the other about both.

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** Concerning a voice and a color at the same time, you first think this: that both exist.

**THEAETETUS.** I think so.

**SOCRATES.** Likewise, that each is different from the other, and the same as itself.

**THEAETETUS.** It is so.

**SOCRATES.** And that both are two, and each is one.

**THEAETETUS.** That also.

**SOCRATES.** Can you furthermore judge whether they are similar to each other or dissimilar?

**THEAETETUS.** Perhaps.

**SOCRATES.** Through what, primarily, do you think all these things about them? For neither through hearing nor through sight can anything common to them both be received. From this, moreover, we can conjecture: if it were possible to judge about both whether they are false or not, you could undoubtedly declare by what you judged; and it is certain that this is neither sight nor hearing, but something else.

**THEAETETUS.** Why should the power of the tongue not effect it?

**SOCRATES.** You speak skillfully. But what is that power through which it shows you what is common to each, and what is over each, by which you name "to be" and "not to be"—those things we were just asking about? What kind of organs will you assign to all these, through which that which senses in us senses each part?

**THEAETETUS.** You mean <term>essence</term> (being) and non-being, and likeness and dissimilarity, and also the same and the different, and the one and other numbers regarding each. For it is clear what you ask: by what corporeal instrument the soul itself perceives even and odd, and those things that follow.

<margin>In this place Plato seems to agree with Parmenides.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** Excellently, Theaetetus, you follow...

<summary>Socrates argues that the senses are merely conduits ("through which") for a unified soul or mind to perceive. He demonstrates that common concepts like "existence," "number," and "likeness" are not perceived by any physical organ but by the soul itself.</summary>
<keywords>Parmenides, sensation vs. perception, the unified soul, Trojan Horse, common notions, essence, being, midwifery, Socrates</keywords>

# Thirteen Book. 108

...and these are the very things I am asking.

**THEAETETUS.** By Jove, Socrates, I do not know what to say, except what seemed to me from the beginning: that no such proper organ is accommodated to these things as to those others, but rather the soul itself, through itself, judges the commonality in all things.

**SOCRATES.** You are beautiful, Theaetetus, and not, as Theodorus said, deformed. For he who speaks beautifully is both beautiful and good. To this is added that you have conferred a great benefit upon me. For you have liberated me from a long and heavy disputation, since it seems to you that the soul notices some things through itself, and apprehends others through the powers of the body. For this was my opinion, which I wished to persuade you of as well.

**THEAETETUS.** I am certainly persuaded.

**SOCRATES.** In which category do you place <term>essence</term> (being)? For this especially follows upon all things.

**THEAETETUS.** Among those things which the soul itself, through itself, aims at and attains.

<margin>A certain soul through itself apprehends the body.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** And what of the similar and the dissimilar, and the same and the different?

**THEAETETUS.** These also.

**SOCRATES.** What about the beautiful and the ugly, the good and the evil?

**THEAETETUS.** Of these also it seems to me most of all that the soul considers their essence in relation to one another, reflecting upon and comparing within itself the past and the present toward the future.

**SOCRATES.** Notice this too: it will sense the hardness of a hard thing through touch, and the softness of a soft thing in a similar way.

**THEAETETUS.** Yes.

**SOCRATES.** But their essence, and what they are, and their mutual contrariety, and the essence of that very contrariety—the soul itself, revolving these things through itself and comparing them with each other, strives to discern.

<margin>The senses do not perceive essence.</margin>

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Do not both men and beasts, as soon as they are born, possess a certain natural faculty by which they sense the passions flowing through the body into the soul? But reasoning and comparison of these things toward their essence and utility—does this not arrive, if it arrives at all, only with difficulty after long periods of time, through much study and discipline?

**THEAETETUS.** Exactly so.

**SOCRATES.** Can we perceive truth in that in which we do not perceive essence?

**THEAETETUS.** Not at all.

**SOCRATES.** But if someone lacks the truth of a thing, does he have any knowledge of it?

**THEAETETUS.** And how could that be possible?

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, knowledge does not at all lie in the passions (sensations), but it seems to lie in the reasoning that is occupied with them. For we can reach essence and truth through the latter, but in no way through the former.

**THEAETETUS.** It is certain.

**SOCRATES.** Do you call that and this the same, when they differ by such a great difference?

**THEAETETUS.** It would not be right.

**SOCRATES.** What name do you attribute to that—namely, the act of seeing, hearing, smelling, <note>missing in the Greek</note> tasting, being warmed and being cooled? Is it not "to sense"?

**THEAETETUS.** That very thing. For what else?

**SOCRATES.** Therefore you call this whole thing "sensation"?

**THEAETETUS.** Necessarily.

**SOCRATES.** To this we have denied the perception of truth, since it does not perceive essence.

**THEAETETUS.** It is so.

**SOCRATES.** Neither, therefore, will it possess knowledge.

**THEAETETUS.** No.

**SOCRATES.** From these things it follows, Theaetetus, that knowledge and sensation will never be the same.

**THEAETETUS.** Never at all.

**SOCRATES.** In these things it has clearly appeared that sensation is one thing, and knowledge another. But we did not begin to discourse for this reason, to find what knowledge is *not*, but rather what it *is*. We have proceeded so far in disputing, however, that we have judged that knowledge is by no means to be sought in sensation, but rather in that name which the mind then strongly holds, when it is occupied and acting according to itself regarding those things which are.

<margin>When there is opinion.</margin>

**THEAETETUS.** But this, Socrates, as I think, is called "to opine" (forming an opinion).

**SOCRATES.** You think correctly, friend. And now look again from the beginning, all previous things having been deleted from your mind, whether you see more clearly, now that you have been carried this far. Explain again what knowledge might be.

<margin>Second definition of knowledge.</margin>

**THEAETETUS.** It is impossible, Socrates, to say that any opinion whatsoever is knowledge, since there is also a certain false opinion. But it appears that **true opinion** is knowledge. Let that be my answer for now: but if it appears otherwise in disputing thereafter, we will try to bring forward something else.

**SOCRATES.** Well done, Theaetetus. It is fitting to dispute with such a prompt mind, and not to waver as you had begun. For if we do this, one of two things will happen: either we will find what we seek, or at least we will think we know less of what we are ignorant of; and that will be no small gain. And now what do you say? Since there are two species of opinion, one true and the other false, do you define true opinion as knowledge?

**THEAETETUS.** I define it so. For this seems right to me at present.

**SOCRATES.** Should we then treat opinion from the beginning?

**THEAETETUS.** What do you mean?

**SOCRATES.** It troubles me now, and often at other times, so that I am in much ambiguity regarding myself and others, being unable to explain what this affection in us is, or in what way it arrives.

**THEAETETUS.** Which one?

**SOCRATES.** Namely, that someone opines falsely. Regarding which I now also doubt, whether we should omit it or consider it otherwise than above.

**THEAETETUS.** Why not, Socrates, if you think it is somehow fitting? For you and Theodorus spoke excellently in the previous pages about leisure, that nothing urges us in such matters.

<margin>It is better to determine a little well than much insufficiently.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** You have reminded me opportunely; for perhaps it will not be beside the point to run through the track again: for it is better to determine a little well, than much insufficiently.

**THEAETETUS.** It is better indeed.

**SOCRATES.** How then, and what do we say? Do we say that opinion is mostly false, and that one of us opines falsely and another truly, as if these things were so by nature?

**THEAETETUS.** We say so without doubt.

<margin>Knowing and ignoring, regarding all things and individual things.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** Does this not apply to us both regarding all things and regarding individual things—namely, to know or to be ignorant? For I pass over "learning" and "forgetting," as they are the middle ground between these, since they confer nothing to our purpose at present.

**THEAETETUS.** Nothing else remains, Socrates, besides knowing or being ignorant regarding each thing.

**SOCRATES.** Is it not therefore necessary that one who opines, opines those things about which he knows something, or does not know?

**THEAETETUS.** Necessary.

<margin>These notes from Marsilio Ficino: To know what one knows. To know what one does not know. Not to know what one does not know. Not to know what one knows. In sensation alone. To sense what one senses. To sense what one does not sense. Not to sense what one does not sense. Not to sense what one senses. In both joined. To know and sense what one knows and senses. To know and sense what one knows and does not sense. To know and sense what one senses and does not know. Not to know and not to sense what one does not know and does not sense. Not to know and not to sense what one does not know and senses. Not to know and not to sense what one does not sense and knows. There are also other combinations which, because they can easily be made from these, are omitted.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** Furthermore, is it not impossible for someone who knows to be ignorant of the same thing, or for one who is ignorant to know?

**THEAETETUS.** How could it not be?

**SOCRATES.** Does he who opines falsely about what he knows, think those things are not what they are, but some other things which he also knows: and knowing both, is he again ignorant of both?

**THEAETETUS.** But this cannot happen, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Or perhaps those things he does not know, he thinks are certain other things which he does not know? And if he has recognized neither Theaetetus nor Socrates, can he ever think that Socrates is Theaetetus, or conversely that Theaetetus is Socrates?

**THEAETETUS.** Never.

**SOCRATES.** Nor indeed does one think those things he knows are those he does not know; nor again those he does not know are those he knows.

**THEAETETUS.** For it would be a monster.

**SOCRATES.** In what way then will anyone opine falsely? Indeed, it is not permitted to opine besides these, since we either know all things or are ignorant of them: and in these it seems that in no way can anyone opine falsely.

**THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth.

<margin>Second mode of disputing. Whether anyone opines what is not.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** Or perhaps we should not consider what we seek in this way, proceeding according to knowing and not knowing, but according to being and non-being?

**THEAETETUS.** How do you say that?

**SOCRATES.** Whether it is simply because he who opines those things which are nowhere, in whatever thing it may be, cannot but opine falsely, in whatever way he may think.

**THEAETETUS.** That is also fitting, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** How then, and what shall we respond, Theaetetus, if someone asks us (for what I say is possible for anyone): "Which of men can opine that which is not? Whether about any of those things that are, or...

<note>Translator's Note: The following text in the OCR contains a significant repetition of the line "potéstne qui antè aliqd ignorauit, postea discere?" (Can he who was previously ignorant of something later learn it?). This appears to be a printer's error or OCR glitch and is omitted for readability, as the dialogue resumes normally on the next page.</note>

...itself according to itself?" To these things we will respond: namely, whenever someone opining does not opine the truth. Or what shall we say?

**THEAETETUS.** So certainly.

<summary>Theaetetus proposes that true opinion is knowledge. Socrates begins a logical dissection of how "false opinion" could even exist, exploring the paradoxes of knowing and not knowing, and being versus non-being.</summary>

# Theaetetus, or, Concerning Knowledge. 109

...itself according to itself? To these things we will respond: namely, whenever someone opining does not opine the truth. Or what shall we say?

**THEAETETUS.** So certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Does such a thing happen elsewhere?

**THEAETETUS.** What do you mean?

**SOCRATES.** That someone sees something, yet sees nothing?

**THEAETETUS.** And in what way?

**SOCRATES.** But truly, if he sees some one thing, he sees one of the things that exist. Or do you yourself think that "one" can be among those things that are not?

**THEAETETUS.** Not at all.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who sees some one thing, sees something that exists.

**THEAETETUS.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** And he who hears something, hears some one thing, and hears what exists.

**THEAETETUS.** Indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Likewise, he who touches something, touches some one thing, and what exists besides, if indeed it is one.

**THEAETETUS.** That too.

**SOCRATES.** But he who opines, does he not opine some one thing?

**THEAETETUS.** It is necessary.

**SOCRATES.** And he who opines some one thing, does he not opine something that exists?

**THEAETETUS.** I agree.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who opines what does not exist, opines nothing.

**THEAETETUS.** It does not seem so.

**SOCRATES.** But he who, as it seems, opines nothing, does not opine at all.

**THEAETETUS.** It is certain.

**SOCRATES.** It is therefore impossible to opine that which is not, whether about any of those things that are, or about it itself according to itself.

**THEODORUS.** It seems impossible.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, to opine falsely is something other than to opine those things which are not.

**THEAETETUS.** It appears to be something else.

**SOCRATES.** Neither in this way, nor as we considered a little while ago, does false opinion exist in us.

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** But perhaps we call it this in this manner?

**THEAETETUS.** In what manner?

**SOCRATES.** We say that a certain "alien" opinion is a false opinion, when someone says that one of the things that are is another of the things that are, having changed them in the thought of the mind. For thus he always opines something that exists, but he opines one thing in place of another; and since he has wandered away from what he thought, he is rightly said to opine falsely.

**THEAETETUS.** Now you seem to me to have spoken most correctly. For as often as someone opines the ugly in place of the beautiful, or conversely the beautiful in place of the ugly, so often it is judged not without reason that he opines falsely.

**SOCRATES.** You openly despise me, Theaetetus, and do not fear?

**THEAETETUS.** Why so?

**SOCRATES.** For I do not think it seems to you that I have apprehended what is truly false, when I am asked whether the swift can become the slow, or the light the heavy, or any other contrary become its own contrary—not according to its own nature, but according to the nature of the contrary. Therefore, lest you venture that in vain or rashly, I dismiss it; and it pleases me, as you say, that to opine falsely is to opine "alien" things.

**THEAETETUS.** To me indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Is it therefore permitted, as you think, to place one thing as another, and not as itself, in thought?

**THEODORUS.** It is certainly permitted.

**SOCRATES.** When the thought does that, therefore, is it not necessary for it to think either both, or one of the two?

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely necessary.

**SOCRATES.** Either simultaneously, or separately?

**THEAETETUS.** That too.

**SOCRATES.** But to think itself—do you call it the same as I do?

**THEAETETUS.** What do you call it?

**SOCRATES.** The discourse which the soul itself revolves within itself concerning those things which it considers. I declare the matter to you as one not very skilled. For this is what it seems to me: that in thinking, the soul does nothing else than discourse with itself, questioning and responding, affirming and denying. But after it defines, and asserts something—noticing it either more slowly or more swiftly—and does not wander, this we call opinion. Wherefore I call "to opine" to speak, and opinion a discourse, not to another, nor with a voice, but in silence and to oneself. But what do you feel?

**THEODORUS.** The same.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, when someone opines one thing to be another, then as it seems, he says to himself that the one is the other.

**THEODORUS.** Why not?

**SOCRATES.** Recall, I pray, if you have ever said to yourself that the beautiful is altogether ugly, or the unjust is just; or, to speak in sum, whether you have ever tried to persuade yourself that most of all one thing is another—or on the contrary: have you ever dared even in dreams to say to yourself that even things are altogether odd, or anything else of this kind?

**THEODORUS.** Never, certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Do you think anyone else, whether prudent or insane, would dare to try to persuade themselves by speaking to themselves that a cow is necessarily a horse, or that two are one?

**THEAETETUS.** Not at all, by Jove.

**SOCRATES.** If to opine is to speak with oneself, no one while saying both things and attaining them in the mind would ever pronounce or opine that one is the other. Let us dismiss, if it pleases, this word "other"; but this is what I want: that no one opines that the ugly is beautiful, or anything else of the same kind.

**THEAETETUS.** I dismiss it indeed, Socrates, and what you say pleases me very much.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore it cannot happen that he who has both in his mind opines that one is the other.

**THEAETETUS.** It is clear.

**SOCRATES.** But neither will he who opines only the one, and not the other at all, ever opine that one is the other.

**THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth: for he would be compelled to also touch upon that which he does not opine.

**SOCRATES.** Neither he who opines both, therefore, nor he who opines one, can opine "alien" things. Wherefore he who defines false opinion as opining "alien" things achieves nothing. Hence it is certain that neither in this way, nor according to the previous ways, does false opinion exist in us.

**THEAETETUS.** So it seems.

**SOCRATES.** Yet, Theaetetus, if this does not appear to be so, we will be compelled to confess many and absurd things.

**THEAETETUS.** Which ones?

**SOCRATES.** I will not tell you until I strive to consider it entirely: for I would be ashamed of us in those things we doubt, if we were compelled to confess what I say. But if we find it and escape free, then at last we will speak of others to whom such things happen, as we ourselves are entirely foreign to such ridiculous error. But if we fail altogether, being made humble, like those tossed by waves and suffering seasickness, we will permit ourselves to the discourse, so that it may either trample us or drive us where it will. Therefore, if I find any exit to this question, hear it now.

**THEAETETUS.** Speak then.

**SOCRATES.** I will not confess that we consented rightly when we conceded that what someone knows, he cannot opine to be what he does not know, and thus be mistaken. Rather, it can happen in a certain way.

**THEAETETUS.** Do you mean what I also suspected then, when we said it was such a thing—that sometimes I, knowing Socrates, but seeing another unknown to me from a distance, might think that the one I know is Socrates? For it happens in what you say.

**SOCRATES.** Have we not already been driven away from that, because it made it so that what we know, we would not know while knowing it?

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, let us not put it that way any longer, but in this way. And perhaps someone will agree with us, or perhaps someone will oppose us. But let us attend to that in which it is necessary to examine that discourse which inverts all things. Look then, can he who was previously ignorant of something later learn it?

**THEAETETUS.** He can, certainly.

<summary>Socrates explores the idea of "alien opinion"—mistaking one known thing for another—and defines thinking as a silent dialogue of the soul with itself. He concludes that error must be possible even if their current logical models haven't yet explained it.</summary>
<keywords>alien opinion, dialogue of the soul, false opinion, Socrates, Theaetetus, logic, paradox, being and non-being</keywords>

# Thirteen Book. 110

Therefore, he who knows those things, but considers anything of those which he sees or hears—look whether he opines falsely in this way.

**THEAETETUS.** In what way?

**SOCRATES.** Thinking that what he knows is, at one time, what he knows, but at another time, what he does not know. These things we certainly did not rightly concede above, confessing them to be impossible.

**THEODORUS.** But now, how do you say?

<margin>These notes from Marsilio Ficino: 
In knowledge without sensation: 
To know what one knows. 
To know what one does not know. 
Not to know what one does not know. 
Not to know what one knows. 

In sensation alone: 
To sense what one senses. 
To sense what one does not sense. 
Not to sense what one does not sense. 
Not to sense what one senses. 

In both joined: 
To know and sense what one knows and senses. 
To know and sense what one knows and does not sense. 
To know and sense what one senses and does not know. 
Not to know and not to sense what one does not know and does not sense. 
Not to know and not to sense what one does not know and senses. 
Not to know and not to sense what one does not sense and knows. 

There are also other combinations which, because they can easily be made from these, are omitted.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** Let us speak of them by distinguishing from the beginning in this manner: that what someone knows, and of which he preserves a monument in his mind, but does not sense, he cannot think is something else of the things he also knows and of which he preserves an image, but does not sense. 

Conversely, he cannot think what he knows is what he does not know, or of which he preserves no image; nor what he does not know to be what he does not know; nor what he does not know to be what he knows; or what he senses to be something else of the things he senses; or what he senses to be something he does not at all sense; or what he does not sense to be some of those things he does not sense; or what he does not sense to be anything of those which he senses. 

And much less can he think that what he knows and senses, and of which he preserves an image according to sense, is something else which he also knows and senses and preserves in the same way; or what he knows and senses and retains correctly, to think it is what he knows; or what he knows and senses and similarly retains, that it is what he senses; or what he neither knows nor senses, that it is what he neither knows nor senses; or what he neither knows nor senses, that it is what he least knows; or what he neither knows nor senses, that it is what he least senses. 

All these are such that no one can opine falsely in them by any reasoning. It remains, therefore, that it must happen in certain things of this kind, if such a thing happens anywhere.

**THEAETETUS.** In what things? Let us see, I pray, if I may understand better from them. For at present I do not follow how, in those things someone knows, he could think they are certain others which he both knows and senses, or which he does not know but senses, or which he knows and senses to be those which he both knows and senses. Wherefore I am now much more at a loss than before.

**SOCRATES.** Come, hear it again in this way. Indeed, I, recognizing Theodorus and holding his likeness in memory, and similarly Theaetetus—sometimes I see them, sometimes I do not see them. And sometimes I touch them, other times not at all, and in the same way I hear them and apprehend them with other senses; yet often I perceive you with no sense, but nevertheless I know and remember you within myself.

**THEODORUS.** Entirely.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, first notice this from what I am about to explain: that someone can not sense what he knows, or he can also sense it.

**THEAETETUS.** It is so.

**SOCRATES.** And what he does not know, does he not often neither sense, nor often only sense?

**THEAETETUS.** This is also true.

**SOCRATES.** See whether you now follow this better. Socrates, while he recognizes Theodorus and Theaetetus but sees neither, nor perceives them with any other sense, never opines within himself that Theaetetus is Theodorus. What do you say to this?

**THEAETETUS.** They are true things.

**SOCRATES.** This was surely the first of the things I was saying.

**THEAETETUS.** It was.

**SOCRATES.** The second was this: that while I recognize one of you, but am ignorant of the other, and sense neither, I never think that the one I recognize is the one I am ignorant of.

**THEAETETUS.** Correct.

**SOCRATES.** The third is this: while I know neither and sense neither, I never think that the one I am ignorant of is some other whom I am again ignorant of. And so on, consider all the things mentioned above repeated similarly: in which I will never opine falsely about you and Theaetetus, neither knowing nor being ignorant of both, nor knowing one and being ignorant of the other. And the same reasoning applies to the senses, if only you perceive it.

**THEAETETUS.** I perceive it indeed.

**SOCRATES.** It remains, therefore, that we opine falsely in this: when knowing you and Theodorus, and preserving in that remainder the figures of each as imprints for a long time—like the signs of your rings—but not seeing both sharply, I attempt to attribute the proper sign of each to my own vision by accommodating it to its trace so that recognition may occur; but I wander, and like those who err by switching their shoes, I switch them, and transfer the vision of each to an alien likeness. I suffer something similar to what results in mirrors when the reflection is transverse, when the sight of the right is switched to the left. And thus I am deceived, and an "alien" opinion is born, and that is what is called opining falsely.

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely, Socrates; the passion of opinion is such as you have wonderfully pictured.

**SOCRATES.** Furthermore, when knowing both, I sense one besides, but the other not at all, yet I have the cognition of the other not according to sense; that is what I said above, and you did not understand me.

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** Yet I was saying this: that he who recognizes the other and senses it, and has the cognition of it according to sense, will never think it is some other whom he also recognizes and senses, and of which he has cognition according to sense. Was that it?

**THEAETETUS.** Yes.

**SOCRATES.** We somehow passed over what is now said, when we were asserting above that false opinion happens whenever someone, knowing and seeing both, or perceiving by some other sense and holding the signs of both, does not have each according to its own proper sense, but like an unskilled archer wanders far from the mark, which indeed has been called a lie.

**THEAETETUS.** And not without justice.

**SOCRATES.** And when the sense is present for one of the signs, but not for the other, he attributes the sense of the absent one to the one present, <margin>In what things false opinion is not, and in which it seems to be.</margin> this thought is altogether deceived. To say it in sum: regarding those things which one never either knew or sensed, he cannot be deceived or lie, or have a false opinion, if what we are saying now is true. But in those things which we know and sense, in those very things true or false opinion revolves: that which collects and figures the proper images from sight and direct effort is true. But when it is transverse and oblique, it is false.

**THEAETETUS.** Have these things not been spoken excellently, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** When you have heard this, you will assert the same more vehemently. Furthermore, to opine truly is beautiful; to lie is base.

**THEAETETUS.** Why not?

**SOCRATES.** They say these things especially happen from this: When the <margin>The heart of the soul.</margin> waxen image in someone's soul is deep and abundant, and smooth and properly worked, those things which flow through the senses are inscribed in this, which Homer called the **heart of the soul** <note>original: "animae cor"; Socrates plays on the Greek words 'kear' (heart) and 'keros' (wax).</note>, implying this similarity of wax, as they are pure signs...

<summary>Socrates introduces the "Wax Tablet" metaphor of the soul, explaining that false opinion (error) occurs not from purely knowing or purely sensing, but from a mismatch between present sensations and past memory-imprints.</summary>
<keywords>wax tablet metaphor, memory imprints, false opinion, Socrates, Theaetetus, Marsilio Ficino, cognition, sensation, error</keywords>
