242 Twenty-Fourth Book.

...therefore it drives away poverty; Medicine, in truth, drives away diseases; and finally, the judicial art removes intemperance and injustice. POLUS. So it appears. SOCRATES. Which, then, of these is the most beautiful? POLUS. Of which do you speak? SOCRATES. The art of business, medicine, or justice? POLUS. Justice excels far among these, Socrates. SOCRATES. Therefore it either brings the most pleasure, or utility, or both, since it is the most beautiful. POLUS. That is so. SOCRATES. Is it then delightful to be cured by a doctor? And do the sick take pleasure in the hands of the doctor while they are being cured? POLUS. It does not seem so. SOCRATES. Yet it is beneficial, is it not? POLUS. It is advantageous. SOCRATES. Because, clearly, they are freed from a great evil, and therefore it is useful to endure pain so that you may emerge healthy. POLUS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. Would he then be the happiest man, as far as the body is concerned, who recovered through medical treatment, or rather he who was not sick from the beginning? POLUS. Certainly he who was not sick. SOCRATES. For it seems that happiness does not consist in being freed from evils, but in being unharmed from the very start. POLUS. It is so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, if two were badly affected in either body or soul, which of these would be more miserable: the one who is cured and freed from the evil, or the one who is not? POLUS. The one who is not cured, in my opinion at least. SOCRATES. Was not being punished in a court of law a liberation from a certain maximum evil, that is, from depravity? POLUS. It certainly was. SOCRATES. Indeed, since just punishment moderates and makes men more just, serving as a kind of medicine for wickedness. POLUS. It is so. SOCRATES. He is therefore happiest who has no vice of the soul, since that appeared to be the greatest evil. POLUS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. And next is he who is freed from such an evil. POLUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. This, in truth, is the one who, having been corrected and terrified, has paid the penalty. POLUS. That very one. SOCRATES. He lives most wretchedly, then, who is unjust and is not released from his injustice. POLUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. Is this not the man who, having committed the greatest wrongs and used the greatest violence, ensures that he is neither corrected, nor punished, nor pays the penalty—just as you say Archelaus <note>A Macedonian king cited as a tyrant who escaped earthly punishment</note> did, along with other tyrants, orators, and powerful men? POLUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. For such men, my best friend, behave almost as if someone seized by a most serious disease were to take care that he should not face the doctor's penalties for the vices within his body, nor be cured—fearing surgery and cautery like a child, as if they were painful things. Does it not seem so to you as well? POLUS. It does to me. SOCRATES. Clearly they are ignorant of how great a thing health and the virtue of the body are. It seems, by what we have just conceded, O Polus, that those who flee judgment do something similar: they look only at the pain of it, but are blind to its utility. They are ignorant of how much more miserable it is to live with a soul that is not healthy, but broken, unjust, and impious, than to carry around a sick body. And so they take care not to undergo judgment, lest they be released from the greatest evil. For that reason, they amass wealth, acquire friends, and study eloquence. But if we have confessed the truth to one another, do you perceive what finally follows from this discussion? Or do you wish for us to collect the points in order? POLUS. Unless it seems otherwise to you. SOCRATES. Did we not agree that injustice and wrongdoing is the greatest evil? POLUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. Moreover, that the solution to this evil is to pay the penalty? POLUS. It appeared so. SOCRATES. And to flee those penalties is the persistence of the evil? POLUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, among evils, committing an injury holds the second place in magnitude. But to ensure that the punishment for injuries is not undergone is, by the nature of all things, the greatest and first of evils. POLUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. This, then, my friend, is what we were debating. You, indeed, asserted that Archelaus was happy, because although he committed the greatest wrongs, he paid no penalties. I, however, felt the opposite: that whether it be Archelaus or any other mortal who does not bear the punishment for his wrongs, he is especially miserable. And always, he who inflicts an injury is more miserable than he who suffers it; and finally, he who does not pay the penalty is more miserable than he who does. Were these not the things I was saying? POLUS. These very things. SOCRATES. Has it not been demonstrated that these things were truly said? POLUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. Come then, Polus, if it is established that these things are true, what use is there for rhetoric? Surely it follows from what went before that we must observe ourselves most diligently, first, lest we inflict injury on anyone, as we would have enough evil from that very act; is it not so? POLUS. Certainly so. SOCRATES. But secondly, if an injury is inflicted by us, or by anyone else dear to us, we should offer ourselves of our own accord to be punished by the judge as if hurrying to a doctor: lest the long-standing disease of injustice so infect the soul as to make it incurable. In what other way shall we speak, O Polus, if those prior concessions between us remain? Do these things not necessarily harmonize, and can they be otherwise? POLUS. What more can we say then? SOCRATES. <margin>Socrates wishes here that we accuse the wrongs of our friends and reveal them to the judge.</margin> To defend or excuse our injustice, therefore, or that of our parents, or friends, or children, or of our country when it does wrong, rhetoric brings us no utility. Unless one judges that rhetoric should be used for the opposite purpose—that is, for accusation: first against ourselves, then against our household, family, and others, if any of those dear to us have committed wrongs. We should not hide their crimes but bring them forward, so that they may pay the penalty and emerge healthy. Moreover, one should use it to compel oneself and others not to be sluggish or terrified, but with a brave soul and as if with closed eyes, to surrender oneself to the judge as if to a surgeon to be cut and burned, following the good and the honorable itself, with pain disregarded. Thus, if they have committed acts worthy of stripes, they should offer themselves to be beaten; if worthy of bonds, to be bound; if a fine, to pay; if exile, to be expelled; if death, to be killed. In this matter, let each man be the accuser of himself and his own, and let him use the oratorical faculty for this: so that by revealing their injustices, they may be released from the greatest evil of injustice. Is it so, Polus, or do we say otherwise? POLUS. These things seem absurd to me, Socrates. Yet, perhaps they harmonize with your previous points. SOCRATES. Is it not necessary either that those earlier points be rejected, or that these consequences be granted? POLUS. That is how it stands. SOCRATES. On the contrary, if one must do harm to someone, whether an enemy or anyone else, one must only take care that he himself does not suffer injury from his adversary. But if an enemy has done injury to others, one must provide with all zeal, both in words and deeds, that he does not pay the penalty, nor is dragged to a judge. But if he is snatched there, perhaps one should strive so that the enemy escapes and no punishment is taken from him. Nay, if he has stolen much gold, let him not restore it, but possessing it, let him spend it unjustly and impiously on himself and his own. If he has committed acts worthy of death, let him never die, if possible, but let the wicked man be immortal. At the very least, let him live for a long time. For these and such things, Polus, rhetoric seems useful to me. But to him who is not going to inflict injury, it seems to be of no great benefit—if indeed there is any advantage or utility in it at all. For in those things said above, nothing of the sort appeared. CHAEREPHON. Tell me, Chaerephon, is Socrates speaking seriously, or is he joking? CHAEREPHON. It seems to me, Callicles, that he is speaking seriously in a marvelous way. However, it would not be inconvenient to ask him himself. CALLICLES. By the gods, I desire to know, Socrates, whether we ought to think you are speaking seriously or joking. For if these things are serious and true...

<summary>Socrates argues that injustice is a disease of the soul and that punishment acts as its medicine; therefore, the most miserable person is the one who commits evil and escapes punishment. He paradoxically suggests rhetoric is only useful for accusing oneself or one's friends to ensure they are healed through justice.</summary>

### Book Thirteen.

In a certain way, however, it is not to possess, but to be a certain power; and when he has shut them in a dovecote, he is able to take them as often as he wishes, and to have any one he wants at his will, and again to let it go: and it is permitted for him to do this as often as it pleases him. THEETETUS: So it is. SOCRATES: Again, just as before we devised in the mind some sort of waxen figment, so let us now fabricate in any soul a certain aviary [bird-cage] of every kind of birds: some of which wander about separately from others in distinct flocks, others in small number, and some solitary, flying about everywhere wherever they happen to go. THEETETUS: Let it be so; what then after that? SOCRATES: Let us say that this cage is empty in children, but in place of birds let us understand "knowledges" [scientias]: and whoever, having obtained a knowledge, has confined it in this circuit, we say that he has found and learned the thing itself of which it is the knowledge, and this is what it is to "know." THEETETUS: Be it so. SOCRATES: Then again, let him consider what names all these things are to be expressed by—whenever he wishes to hunt for any knowledge he wants and to have it captured, and again to let it go—are they not the same as those before, when they were possessed merely as acquired? From this, perhaps, you will understand me more clearly. Do you call Arithmetic an art? THEETETUS: I do. SOCRATES: Suppose this is the hunting of knowledges of every even and odd. THEETETUS: I so suppose. SOCRATES: By this art, the arithmetician himself has the knowledges of numbers subjected to him as if they were certain slaves, and he hands them over to others. THEETETUS: Precisely. SOCRATES: And him who hands them over, we say "teaches"; but him who receives them, "learns": and him who has them from what he possesses in the cage itself, "knows." THEETETUS: Very much so. SOCRATES: Observe diligently what follows. Does not he who is a perfect arithmetician know all numbers? For indeed, the knowledges of all numbers are within his mind. THEETETUS: Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES: Does he not sometimes count either internal things with himself, or certain external things which consist of number? THEETETUS: Why not? SOCRATES: But we shall posit that to count is nothing other than to consider how great each number is. THEETETUS: Certainly nothing else. SOCRATES: Therefore, he who we have confessed knows every number seems to consider what he knows as if he were ignorant. Have you heard ambiguities of this sort? THEETETUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: When we compared them to the possession and hunting of doves, we said the hunting was twofold: one before acquisition for the sake of possessing; the other after he has acquired and possessed it, for the sake of taking in hand those things which he has long possessed. And so, concerning those things of whose knowledges he is already endowed by learning, or which he knew before, he can learn them again, resuming and detaining each knowledge: that is, by thought, which he possessed indeed before, but did not have in his hand. THEETETUS: You tell the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, a little while ago I was asking how names are to be used when we speak of them; as for example when an arithmetician is about to count, or a grammarian to read. For then, as one who knows, he seeks again within himself what he knows, attempting to learn. THEETETUS: But this is absurd, Socrates. SOCRATES: Or perhaps should it be said that he counts or reads things he does not know, when we have already granted him the understanding of all letters or numbers? THEETETUS: This also is absurd. SOCRATES: Do you wish then that we say we do not care in what way anyone uses the names of knowing and learning? But after we have determined that possessing knowledge is one thing, and having what one possesses is another, we say it is impossible for what one possesses not to be possessed. Wherefore it never happens that someone does not know the very thing he knows. Yet a false opinion can be received concerning that very thing. For it can happen that we take the knowledge of one thing instead of the knowledge of another, when some one of us, hunting for one of the internal knowledges,

instead of that one, is deceived and apprehends another flying before him. Just as when he thinks eleven is twelve, taking the knowledge of eleven in place of the knowledge of twelve, since both remain within, taking as it were a wood-pigeon for a dove. THEETETUS: That is indeed likely. SOCRATES: But when he apprehends that which he seeks, then he must be said to be free of falsehood and to judge those things which are. And in this way true and false opinion exist, and nothing of those things which troubled us above will be an impediment to us. Perhaps you will agree with me, or what will you do? THEETETUS: I agree. SOCRATES: Now we have escaped that dilemma, by which some were forced to not know what they know. For it does not happen that what we possess we do not possess; neither if we are deceived, nor if we judge truly. Nevertheless, another more serious thing seems to me to arise. THEETETUS: What is this? SOCRATES: If the exchange of knowledges becomes false opinion. THEETETUS: How so? SOCRATES: First, indeed. Is it not very absurd that he who has knowledge of a certain thing should be ignorant of that very thing, not indeed by ignorance, but by knowledge of the same? Then, that he should think this thing is some other, and on the contrary that that is this? How beyond reason is it that, with knowledge present, the soul knows nothing and is ignorant of everything? Indeed, according to this reasoning, nothing prevents present ignorance from making one know anything, and blindness from making one see, if knowledge makes anyone ignorant. THEETETUS: Perhaps, O Socrates, we did not introduce the birds rightly when we placed only knowledges in the soul; it was necessary also to introduce "un-knowledges" [inscientias] flying about in the soul together with knowledges, and the hunting man sometimes receiving a knowledge, often an un-knowledge concerning the same thing; and when he runs into knowledge, he thinks truly: when into ignorance, falsely. SOCRATES: It is difficult not to praise you, Theaetetus; yet consider again what you have said. For let it be as you say. He who falls into ignorance will think falsely, as you say; will he not? THEETETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Yet he will not think that he thinks falsely. THEETETUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: But rather truly, and he will be affected as one who knows toward those things in which he errs. THEETETUS: Why not? SOCRATES: And therefore he will think that he has obtained knowledge by his hunting, not un-knowledge. THEETETUS: It is clear. SOCRATES: Now by a certain long circuit we have fallen back into the first doubt. For that contentious rebuker will say, smiling: "Whether, O good men, someone knowing both knowledge and un-knowledge, which he knows, deems one to be another which he also knows? Or knowing neither, which he does not know, he deems it to be another which he also does not know? Or knowing one indeed, but the other not at all, does he deem the one he knows to be the one he does not know; or on the contrary, the one he does not know to be the one he knows? Or again will you tell me that there are knowledges of knowledges and of un-knowledges, which he who possesses, enclosed in some other ridiculous cages or waxen figments, knows insofar as he possesses them, even if he does not have them at hand?" And so you will be forced to revolve in an infinite loop around the same point, profiting nothing. What shall we answer to these things, O Theaetetus? THEETETUS: By Jove, O Socrates, I do not know what should be answered. SOCRATES: Does not reason rightly both chide and admonish us, O boy, that it was not right to investigate false opinion before knowledge, and to leave knowledge un-discussed? For it is impossible to know those things before knowledge has been sufficiently defined. THEETETUS: It is necessary, O Socrates, to assert what you say in the present instance. SOCRATES: What then? Shall we discuss knowledge again from the beginning? For we are not yet weary of speaking. THEETETUS: Certainly not, if indeed you yourself do not refuse. SOCRATES: Come then, in what way will you define it, so that we may least disagree with ourselves? THEETETUS: Just as we contended above.

---

### [Page 113]
### Theaetetus, Or, Concerning Science [Knowledge].

THEETETUS: ...as we contended above; for I have nothing else. SOCRATES: How above? THEETETUS: I wanted true opinion to be knowledge. For to judge truly is far from error: and those things which proceed from true opinion are all decorous and good. SOCRATES: He who, O Theaetetus, goes before those following in crossing a river, when they ask how deep the water is, says "It will show itself." And if we, having entered, search, perhaps the very impediment which is sought will demonstrate itself; if we remain, nothing will be open to us. THEETETUS: You speak well. Let us go now to seek. SOCRATES: Is this not a matter of a brief investigation? For the whole art is an argument to us that this is by no means knowledge. THEETETUS: By what reasoning? What is this faculty? SOCRATES: Of those who are wise above others, whom they call orators and lawyers [causidicos]. These, indeed, by their art persuade, they do not teach. For they induce the auditors to think what they themselves desire. Or do you think some are so vehement in teaching that when no witnesses were present at robberies and other injuries, they nevertheless teach the truth of the crimes committed by a little water [i.e., the water-clock in court]? THEETETUS: I think they by no means teach, but persuade. SOCRATES: But to persuade, do you not assert the same as to induce an opinion? THEETETUS: Exactly the same. SOCRATES: Is it not true that when judges are justly persuaded in those things which only he who saw knows, and otherwise by no means, then judging those very things from hearing, and having obtained true opinion without knowledge, they judge rightly those things in which they were persuaded, if only they judge well? THEETETUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: Yet if true opinion, judgment, and knowledge were the same thing, O friend, that highest judge would never judge rightly without knowledge. But now each seems to be a certain different thing. THEETETUS: What I once heard from someone concerning knowledge, O Socrates, I had forgotten, but now I remember. He said, however, that true opinion with an account [ratione] is knowledge, but without an account it is devoid of knowledge: and things which lack an account cannot be known: but those which have an account can be known. SOCRATES: How excellently you speak. But these very things which can be known, and those which cannot, say how you distinguished them, so that we may see whether you and I have received them similarly. THEETETUS: Whether I am about to find it I do not know, but perhaps if someone else explained it I would follow. SOCRATES: Hear therefore a dream for a dream. I too seem to have heard from certain people that the first elements themselves, as it were, from which men and other things are composed, do not admit of an account. For each of them can be named according to itself, but to call it anything else is by no means possible, neither that it is, nor that it is not. For already essence or non-essence would happen to be applied to it. One ought to add nothing, if one would speak of that thing itself alone. Indeed, they wish that neither "itself," nor "that," nor "each," nor "alone," nor "this," nor other such things be applied. For they say these things run around and are applied to all things, and are certain other things besides that to which they are added. But it would be necessary, if it were possible for it to be spoken of and it admitted its own account, that it be spoken of apart from all others. But now you express that no [element] can be brought forth by speech. For nothing else is present to it but a name, and it has only a name. But those things composed from them, just as they are coupled together, so also their names being coupled together become a discourse [*oratio*].
[Margin: The substance of discourse.]
For the coupling of names is the substance of discourse. Wherefore elements are without discourse and account, and are unknown, yet to be perceived by the senses: but syllables can both be known and learned, and apprehended by true opinion. Therefore, when someone obtains a true opinion about something without an account,

they say his soul indeed perceives the truth about it, but by no means knows it. For he who is unable to receive and return an account is ignorant. But when he follows the account, he is able to know all these things and to obtain perfect knowledge. Did you hear it thus in your dream, or otherwise? THEETETUS: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Does it please you? And in this way do you assert that true opinion together with an account is knowledge? THEETETUS: Most certainly. SOCRATES: Thus, Theaetetus, have we today apprehended that which very many wise men of old, investigating before they found it, grew old? THEETETUS: To me indeed, O Socrates, what has just been said seems to be well said. SOCRATES: And deservedly, for what knowledge could ever exist without discourse and right opinion? Yet one thing of those said displeases me. THEETETUS: What is that? SOCRATES: That which seemed to be said more magnificently: that elements are unknown, but the genus of syllables is known. THEETETUS: Is it not right? SOCRATES: We must certainly observe. For we have the examples themselves as pledges of the discourse, which he used who said all these things. THEETETUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: The elements of letters and syllables. Or do you think he who says what we are narrating was looking elsewhere than at these? THEETETUS: Certainly not to other things, but to these only. SOCRATES: Therefore let us examine them by reviewing them. Or rather thus ourselves: do we not say letters are these things? Answer to this first: do not syllables have an account and definition, but elements by no means? THEETETUS: Perhaps. SOCRATES: To me also it entirely seems so. If someone therefore should ask concerning the first syllable of "Socrates," O Theaetetus, say what it is? What will you answer most especially? THEETETUS: That it is S and O. SOCRATES: You have therefore this account of the syllable. THEETETUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: Come, say moreover the account of the S itself. THEETETUS: But in what way could anyone report the elements of an element? For indeed the S itself, O Socrates, is only a certain sound of the mute letters, as if the tongue were hissing: but of the B itself, there is neither voice, nor sound, nor of very many elements. Wherefore they are said quite rightly to be without an account. Of which those seven most well-known have a voice, but an account by no means. SOCRATES: This therefore, O friend, we have rightly asserted concerning knowledge. THEETETUS: So we seem. SOCRATES: But what when we said the element is unknown, but the syllable is known? Have we correctly established it? THEETETUS: It is probable. SOCRATES: But do we say a syllable is both elements? Or even if more than two are in it, are they all? Or rather a single Idea generated from those composed? THEETETUS: We seem to say all of them. SOCRATES: Behold therefore regarding the two, S and O; if both are the first syllable of my name, whoever knows it, knows both. THEETETUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Therefore he knows S and O. THEETETUS: Plainly. SOCRATES: What further? If he were ignorant of both, would he know both while knowing neither? THEETETUS: This would be both absurd and beyond reason. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, if it is necessary to know both, since indeed he knows both, it follows that it is necessary that he who is ever to know the syllable must first know the elements; and thus [the theory] fails completely. SOCRATES: For neither do we guard it well. It was necessary perhaps to posit the syllable not as the elements, but as a certain single form constituted from them, which has one idea of itself, and differs from the elements. THEETETUS: Exactly so, and perhaps in this way rather than that it holds itself. SOCRATES: Therefore it must be considered diligently, nor does it befit us to betray so great and so noble a discourse so lazily. THEETETUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Let it be then, as we were just saying, that the syllable is one idea from each of the fitting elements, both in letters...

---

### [Page 114]
### Book Thirteen.

...as in all other things. THEETETUS: Exactly. SOCRATES: Ought it not to be that it has no parts? THEETETUS: Why so? SOCRATES: Because of whatever there are parts, it is necessary that the "all" [*omne*] be all the parts. Or do you call the "whole" [*totum*] a certain single form made from parts, differing from all the parts? THEETETUS: Indeed.
[Margin: Whether "all" and "whole" are the same.]
SOCRATES: But do you call "all" [*omne*] and "whole" [*totum*] the same, or each different? THEETETUS: Although I have nothing certain, yet because you bid me to answer promptly, making a trial I say they differ. SOCRATES: Promptness, O Theaetetus, is right. But whether the answer is right must be considered. THEETETUS: Indeed.
[Margin: Whether "everything" and "all" are the same.]
SOCRATES: Does it not follow from this discourse that the "whole" and the "all" differ? THEETETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: What further: do "everything" [*omnia*] and "all" [*omne*] differ in anything? Just as when we say one, two, three, four, five, six, or twice three, or thrice two, or four and two, or three and two and one, do we say the same or something else in all these? THEETETUS: Entirely the same. SOCRATES: Anything other than six? THEETETUS: Nothing else. SOCRATES: Do we not find "all six" in each way of speaking? THEETETUS: Yes. SOCRATES: But again, do we not say some one thing when we say "all"? THEETETUS: It is necessary. SOCRATES: Anything other than six? THEETETUS: Nothing else. SOCRATES: Therefore in these things which consist of number, we say that the "all" and "everything" are the same. THEETETUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: Let us speak of them in this way: the number of an acre and the acre are the same, are they not? THEETETUS: Yes. SOCRATES: And the number of a furlong and the furlong similarly. THEETETUS: This too. SOCRATES: Also the number of the army itself and the army itself, and other such things in the same way? For every number being the "all" is each one of those. THEETETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: But is the number of individual things anything other than the parts? THEETETUS: By no means. SOCRATES: Whatever things therefore have parts, consist of parts. THEETETUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: But all the parts have been granted to be the "whole," if indeed every number is the "all." THEETETUS: So it is. SOCRATES: Therefore the "whole" does not consist of parts; for it would be the "all," since it would be all the parts. THEETETUS: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: Is a part what it is of something other than a whole? THEETETUS: Of the whole "all," surely. SOCRATES: Strenuously you fight, Theaetetus; is not the "all" itself that from which it is all because nothing is missing? THEETETUS: Necessary. SOCRATES: And is not the "whole" by the same reasoning a whole because nothing is absent? But that from which nothing is missing, and yet is not a whole, nor is the "all" itself six itself. THEETETUS: It seems to me now that "whole" and "all" do not differ at all. SOCRATES: Did we not say that of which there are parts, the whole and the all are all the parts? THEETETUS: Plainly. SOCRATES: Again, what we tried a little before: if the syllable is not the elements, is it not necessary that it not have the elements as its parts? Or if it is the same with them, that it be able to be known equally as they are? THEETETUS: So certainly. SOCRATES: Lest this should happen, we posited it as something other than them. THEETETUS: Other. SOCRATES: What if the elements are indeed parts of the syllable, yet not the elements of that thing? THEETETUS: I would never call parts those which are not elements. Indeed, omitting elements to seek others is a root. SOCRATES: Entirely therefore according to this reasoning, O Theaetetus, the syllable seems to be a certain single indivisible form [*idea*]. THEETETUS: It seems so indeed. SOCRATES: Do you remember, friend, that we admitted in the previous things that there was no account of the first things from which others are composed, because each itself according to itself existed simply, nor could "to be" be said of it fittingly, nor "this," nor "so," as if these were extraneous and alien; and we said this very cause prevented it from being described and known? THEETETUS: I remember. SOCRATES: Is there any other cause besides this which makes it uniform and indivisible? For I see no other. THEETETUS: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: Does not the syllable also run into the same thing with it, since it is a species, and has no parts, but is a single idea? THEETETUS: Most especially. SOCRATES: If therefore the syllable is many elements, and a certain whole, and its parts, those things similarly—the syllable and elements—can be known and described: since it has been established that all parts are the same as the whole. THEETETUS: Principally. SOCRATES: But if it is some one thing, and simple, equally the syllable as the element is devoid of the cognition of a definition. For the same cause will effect such things. THEETETUS: I cannot assert otherwise. SOCRATES: Therefore let us not admit his discourse who said that the syllable indeed can be spoken of and known, but the elements by no means. THEETETUS: Certainly not, if we believe this reasoning. SOCRATES: What if someone said the contrary? Would you not rather grant those things from those matters in which you yourself became conscious in the first rudiments of letters? THEETETUS: What are those? SOCRATES: That you studied to do nothing else than to discern elements with eyes and ears, and to note each according to itself, lest their position either when spoken or when written should trouble you. THEETETUS: You tell the truth. SOCRATES: But to have learned the art of a cithara player, what else is it than to distinguish each tone of each string? For anyone would call these the elements of music. THEETETUS: Nothing else. SOCRATES: When therefore we are skilled in elements and syllables, and wish from these to make a conjecture toward other things, we shall surely assert that the genus of elements contains a clearer and more principal intelligence than the syllable, for the absolute perceiving of individual disciplines. And if anyone says the syllable is known, but the element unknown by nature, we shall think he is playing, whether willingly or unwillingly. THEETETUS: And most especially indeed. SOCRATES: But those are also demonstrations of the same thing, as it seems to me: yet lest we forget the proposal on account of these, what indeed is to be judged of this which is said: that an account, if it meets with true opinion, is perfect knowledge. THEETETUS: We must inquire entirely. SOCRATES: Come then, what does *logos* [reason/word/account] signify for us here? For it seems to me to signify one thing out of three. THEETETUS: Out of which? SOCRATES: First, I think it is to express one's thought by voice through words and names, showing one's own opinion in the voice just as in a mirror or water. Does not such a thing seem to you to be discourse? THEETETUS: To me indeed. SOCRATES: We say he who does this speaks. Could not anyone do this? Namely, to show more quickly or more slowly what seems to you concerning individual things? Unless perhaps he is mute or deaf by nature. And so whoever thinks anything rightly, seems to think it "with an account" [*met' elogon*]. And never will right opinion be without knowledge. THEETETUS: These things are true. SOCRATES: Therefore let us not easily condemn him who affirmed that knowledge is what we have now said, as if he said nothing. For perhaps he did not mean that, but being asked what each thing is, he could answer the inquirer through elements. THEETETUS: What is that you say, O Socrates? SOCRATES: Just as Hesiod says of a chariot: "A chariot is a hundred pieces of wood," which indeed I could hardly say, nor you either, as I think. But it will be enough for us if, to the one asking what is a chariot, we can answer: wheels, axle, boards, semicircles, yoke. THEETETUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: But he perhaps would think us—as if asked about your name and answering by syllable—worthy of laughter, indeed thinking rightly and saying what we say, but thinking that we are grammarians, and have and speak grammatically the account of the name of Theaetetus: but that this is not to speak according to knowledge until one determines each thing through elements along with true opinion, as has been said above. THEETETUS: It has been said without doubt. SOCRATES: Thus for both of us we have a right opinion concerning the chariot. But he who is able to run through those hundred things, receiving the essence of the chariot itself, has also apprehended the account together with true opinion: in place of an opiner, he has emerged as one skillful and possessed of knowledge concerning the essence of the chariot, determining the whole through elements. THEETETUS: Does it not seem well to you, O Socrates? SOCRATES: If it seems so to you, O friend, and you approve this discourse through elements concerning each thing as being an account, but that he who goes through syllables or anything greater is devoid of account, I want you to tell me, so that we may consider more diligently. THEETETUS: I approve, and most especially indeed. SOCRATES: Is it thus, that you think anyone is knowing of anything, when the same thing seems to him now to be of one and the same, now of another? Or when he thinks now this, now that of one and the same thing? THEETETUS: Not by Jove. SOCRATES: Has it escaped your memory that in learning letters this happened often to you and others? THEETETUS: Do you mean they were accustomed to think now this, now that letter of the same syllable? Or to refer the same letter sometimes to its own syllable, sometimes to a foreign one? SOCRATES: These things I say. THEETETUS: By Jove, I have not forgotten, nor do I think those who are so affected know. SOCRATES: What indeed? If someone at that time writing "Theaetetus" thinks TH and E should be written, and writes them: and again wanting to write "Theodorus" thinks TH and E should be written and writes them, shall we say he knows the first syllable of your name? THEETETUS: A little while ago it was agreed between us that he who is thus instructed does not yet know. SOCRATES: What prevents someone from suffering this same thing regarding the second, third, and fourth syllable? THEETETUS: Nothing at all. SOCRATES: Will he then, having the course through the element, write "Theaetetus" with right opinion, when he writes it in its order? THEETETUS: Without doubt. SOCRATES: Is he not still ignorant, but thinking rightly, as we said? THEETETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: And having an account with right opinion: for having the discourse through the element, he wrote, which account we agreed was *logos*. THEETETUS: True. SOCRATES: There is therefore, O friend, a certain right opinion with an account, which it does not yet befit us to call knowledge. THEETETUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: We have obtained a certain dream, as it seems, while we consider we have the truest account of science. THEETETUS: Or we ought not yet to find fault, for perhaps someone would not so define *logos*: but would choose the remaining from the three species, of which we said he would choose one, who affirmed that knowledge was right opinion with an account. SOCRATES: You have admonished me opportunely. For still one species remains: the first indeed was as it were an idol of thought in the voice, the second a process into the whole through elements. THEETETUS: But what do you say the third is? SOCRATES: What very many would confess: namely, to be able to bring forward a certain mark, as it were, by which the thing under discussion differs from all others. THEETETUS: Of what, or of whom, can you assign such a definition? SOCRATES: Use the example of the sun, if you wish; you will approve, I think, that it excels all things in light which revolve around the earth in heaven. THEETETUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: Receive the reason why this was said. It is what we were just reporting. If you take the difference of each thing by which it is distinguished from others, you have received the definition as they hand it down: but as long as you touch upon something common, you will have the definition of those whose community it is. THEETETUS: I understand, and I think such a thing is rightly called an account. SOCRATES: But he who with right opinion receives the difference by which each is separated from any other, will then know that very thing which he previously opined. THEETETUS: It is consistent. SOCRATES: Now at last, O Theaetetus, when I first came closer to this certain sketch, as it were, I notice that I understand nothing at all in these matters. But as far as I could see from a distance, it seemed to me that something was said. THEETETUS: How so? SOCRATES: I will say if I can. Having indeed a right opinion concerning you, if I furthermore receive your definition, I know you; otherwise I merely opine. THEETETUS: So it is.
[Margin: Difference between knowing and opining.]
SOCRATES: But the definition was the interpretation of your difference. THEETETUS: It was certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore when I only opined, did I perceive in thought none of those things by which you are distinguished from others? THEETETUS: Nothing, as it seems. SOCRATES: Therefore I was attending to certain common things, of which you have nothing more than anyone else. THEETETUS: It necessarily follows. SOCRATES: Come, say by Jove, in what way did I then opine you rather than any other? Suppose me thinking thus: "Theaetetus is he who is both a man, and has a nose, and a mouth, and eyes, and similarly the rest of the members." Will that thought effect that I notice Theaetetus rather than Theodorus, or (as is commonly said) the last of the Mysians? THEETETUS: Who indeed? SOCRATES: But if I should think not only of one having a nose and eyes, but also a snub nose and prominent eyes, I will not opine you any more than myself, and others whoever are such. THEETETUS: Equally indeed. SOCRATES: But truly I shall not opine Theaetetus, as I think, until this snub-nosed figure—distinguished from all other snub figures I have seen by some monument [mark] of its own impressed upon me—distinguishes you and other similar things; which indeed will remind me tomorrow even if I run into you, and make me opine rightly of you. THEETETUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore right opinion concerning each thing is turned toward the proper difference. THEETETUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: What then will it be, if together with right opinion we also aid the definition? For it is a ridiculous precept if it bids us to opine how anything differs from others. THEETETUS: How? SOCRATES: Regarding those things of which we rightly opine insofar as they differ from others, it bids us to assume a right opinion concerning those same things insofar as they differ from others. And so your discourse will be similar to the revolution of either a whip or a pestle, or anything whatever; but to this precept it says absolutely nothing. For it might more rightly be called the precept of a blind man. Since to bid us to receive what we have, for the purpose of learning those things which we opine, seems to be the command of a blind man. THEETETUS: Come, say what were you just seeking? SOCRATES: If while it commanded us to receive an account, O boy, it commanded us to *know*, but not to opine the difference, the account would be a very sweet thing indeed, and the most beautiful of all that pertain to knowledge. For to know is to receive knowledge. THEETETUS: It is indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore being asked what knowledge is, it answers that it is right opinion with the knowledge of the difference. For the assumption of an account according to him would be this. THEETETUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: It is entirely fatuous, while we are seeking knowledge, to say it is right opinion with knowledge, whether of the difference or of anything else. Therefore neither sense, O Theaetetus, nor true opinion, nor an account assumed together with true opinion is knowledge. THEETETUS: Not, as it seems.

---

### [Page 116]
### Book Thirteen.

SOCRATES: Does any other fetus remain in us concerning knowledge, O friend? Or have we already given birth to all? THEETETUS: By Jove, I have brought forth more things than I had in me, you drawing them out. SOCRATES: Does not this obstetric art of ours show that all these things were born vain and unworthy of being reared? THEETETUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: If therefore you should strive to become full and fecund with others hereafter, and should become pregnant, you will be full of better things on account of the present discussion. But if perhaps you remain empty and sterile, you will certainly be less troublesome to your familiars, and more moderate and milder, by no means thinking you know what you do not know. My art can do only this much, and nothing else besides: nor do I know those things which many others, whoever they are, great and admirable men, both are and have been. But I and my mother have been allotted this obstetric faculty; she indeed concerning women, but I concerning noble and honest youths. But now I must go to the King's porch: for Meletus has summoned me to judgment. Tomorrow at early morning, O Theodorus, we shall return here.

---

### ION OF PLATO, OR, CONCERNING POETIC FURY.
### THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.

Our Plato, best Laurentius, defines fury in the *Phaedrus* as an alienation of the mind. He hands down two kinds of alienation. One from human diseases. The other proceeding from God. That one he calls insanity, this one divine fury. In insanity, a man is cast down below the human species, and from a man is rendered in a certain way a brute. By divine fury, he is raised above human nature and passes into God. Divine fury is a rational illumination of the soul, through which God draws back the soul, which had fallen from the heavens to the underworld, from the underworld to the heavens. The fall of the soul from the very One principle of all things to bodies is effected through four steps: through Mind [*mens*], Reason [*ratio*], Opinion [*opinio*], and Nature [*natura*]. For since in the whole order of things there exist six steps, the highest of which the One itself holds; the lowest the body; but the middle are the four which we have mentioned, it is necessary that whatever falls from the first to the last should fall through the four middle steps. The One itself is the end and measure of all things, devoid of infinity and multitude. Mind is indeed a multitude, but stable and eternal. Reason is a mobile multitude, but finite. Opinion is an infinite mobile multitude, but united in substance and points; Nature similarly, except that it is diffused through the points of the body. But the body is an infinite multitude subject to motion, and a substance divided into points and moments. Our soul regards all these; through these it descends, and through these it also ascends. For as it is produced by the One itself which is the principle of all things: it has obtained a certain unity which unites all its essence, powers, and actions: from which, and toward which, the other things which are in the soul hold themselves, just as lines from the center and to the center of a circle. Indeed, it unites not only the parts of the soul to each other and to the whole soul, but the whole soul to the One itself, the cause of all things. But as it depends on the divine Mind, it contemplates the ideas of all things through the Mind by a stable act. As it regards itself, it thinks the universal reasons of things, and runs from principles to conclusions by reason. As it regards the body, it conceives by opinion the particular forms of mobile things, and runs through them. As it touches matter, it uses nature as an instrument, by which it unites matter, moves, and forms it: whence generations, increases, and their contraries proceed. You see therefore that from the One which is above eternity, it falls into eternal multitude; from eternity into time; from time into place and matter. Wherefore, just as it descends through four steps, so it must ascend through four. Divine fury is that which turns toward the supernal things, as it consisted in its definition. Therefore four species of divine fury exist: first indeed, poetic fury; second, the ministerial [mystery]; third, prophecy; fourth, the amatory affection. Moreover, poetry is from the Muses, mystery from Dionysus, prophecy from Apollo, love from Venus. For the soul cannot return to the One unless it itself is made one. But it has been made many; it has fallen into the body, distributed into various operations, and looking toward individual things. From which its superior parts almost fall asleep, and its inferior parts dominate the others; those are affected by the body, these by perturbation; but the whole soul is filled with discord and lack of harmony. Therefore there is need of poetic fury first of all, which through musical tones may arouse what is torpid, and through harmonic sweetness may soothe what is troubled: finally, through the consonance of diverse things, it may drive out dissonant discord, and temper the various parts of the soul. Nor is this enough. For multitude still remains in the soul. Therefore there follows mystery, which by sacred expiations and all worship of the gods directs the intention of all parts into the mind, by which God is worshiped. Whence, when the individual parts of the soul have been reduced to one mind, the soul has now become a certain whole one out of many. But thirdly there is still need of fury, which may reduce the mind to the very unity which is the head of the soul. Apollo effects this through prophecy. For when the soul rises above the mind into unity, it presages future things. Finally, when the soul has been made one—one, I say, which is in the very essence of the soul—it remains that it immediately be turned into the One which is above essence. Celestial Venus herself completes this through love, that is, the desire for divine beauty, and the ardor for the good. Thus the first fury tempers the unharmonious and dissonant. The second makes one whole out of the tempered parts. The third makes one whole above the parts. The fourth leads into the One which is above essence. The first distinguishes the good horse, that is reason and opinion, from the bad horse, that is from confused fantasy and nature. The second subjects the bad horse to the good, and the good to the charioteer, that is the mind. The third directs the charioteer into his own head, that is into the unity, the apex of the mind. The last turns the head of the charioteer into the head of all things. Where the charioteer is blessed, and standing at the manger, that is divine beauty, he offers ambrosia to the horses, and over that, nectar to be drunk: that is, the vision of beauty, and joy from the vision. These are the four works of the furies, which Plato discusses generally in the *Phaedrus*, but properly concerning the last fury, that is love, in the *Symposium*; concerning the first, that is poetic fury, in the present dialogue which is inscribed *Ion*: which he so defines in the *Phaedrus*: "Poetic fury is a certain occupation from the Muses, which having obtained a gentle and insuperable soul, arouses it and agitates it through songs and other poetry, for the instruction of the race of men." "Occupation" signifies the rapture of the soul and its conversion into the divinities of the Muses. He says "gentle" meaning as it were agile and formable by the Muses: for unless it is prepared, it is not occupied. "Insuperable," because after it has been snatched up, it overcomes all things, and can be polluted or overcome by no inferior things. It arouses from the sleep of the body to the vigilance of the mind, from the darkness of ignorance to light, from death to life, from Lethean oblivion to the remembrance of divine things. It agitates, stimulates, and inflames to those things which it contemplates and presages, to be expressed in songs. After the definition he adds: he who approaches the poetic gates without the fury of the Muses is himself empty and his poetry likewise, as if poetry were so great that without the supreme favor of God it cannot be compared. He hands down the same in the *Ion*, and teaches whence this fury is, and through how many steps it descends. Plato says in the fourth book of the *Laws* that God, fortune, and art govern all human things. Whence it is that poetry is either a gift of God, or a lot of fortune, or a work of art. Which of these is most especially true, Socrates investigates with the rhapsode Ion.
[Margin: What a rhapsode is.]
A rhapsode in this book signifies a reciter, interpreter, and singer of songs. Ion interpreted the songs of Homer, and sang to the lyre before the people, and was so affected that he would explain no other poet besides Homer, even if they related the same things with the same facility as Homer. But he would explain all things of Homer quickly. Whence he argued thus: either Ion brings forth by chance what Homer writes, or by art, or by divine inspiration. Not by chance, because he would interpret not all things, but some few, and without continuation and order. Not by art, because whoever has an entire art judges whatever is subjected to the same art. But the poems of Hesiod and other poets are subjected to the same poetic study as those of Homer, especially those which treat of the same things, which nevertheless Ion does not perceive, although he explains Homer perfectly. Therefore he does not judge by art. It remains that it is by divine inspiration. From which it is clear that Ion, the interpreter of the poet, and many others who are similarly affected, interpret another's poetry by divine instinct. But if human genius does not suffice for perceiving poetry already handed down, much less will it suffice for invention. Therefore neither Homer, nor any other truly a poet, has attained poetry without celestial inspiration. Which Socrates here shows to others in another way. First thus: poets hand down all arts and sciences, but it is impossible to have learned all by human study, since to perceive one in part is most difficult. Therefore they do not bring them forth by human art, but by a certain divine infusion. An argument of this matter is that most prophets, after the impetus of fury has subsided, do not immediately understand what they have written, although they have treated rightly of individual arts in their fury, which individual craftsmen of those arts judge by reading. Furthermore, we often see a rude and inept man suddenly emerge as a good poet, and sing something magnificent and divine.

---

### [Page 117]
### Ion, Or, concerning poetic fury.

...and to sing something divine. But to attain great things in a moment is not of human genius, but to be inspired by God. Because in this clear matter God shows that this intelligence is infused by his own nod. And to demonstrate that it is so, he often seizes certain inept men rather than urban ones, insane rather than prudent, lest if he used acute and prudent men for these things, they might be thought to be done by human subtlety and industry. Since therefore poetry is not from fortune, nor from art, it is granted by God and by the Muses. When he says God, he signifies Apollo: when he says the Muses, the souls of the world's spheres. Jupiter indeed is the mind of God; from him Apollo: the mind of the soul of the world, and of the soul of the whole world. And the eight souls of the celestial spheres, which nine souls are called the nine Muses, because while they move the heavens harmonically, they produce musical melody: which, distributed into nine sounds—namely the eight tones of the spheres and one concord of all—produces the nine Sirens singing to God. Wherefore from Jove, Apollo: and the Muses from Apollo, that is, from the mind of the soul of the world, the chorus of Muses is led, by which that mind, just as it is illuminated by Jove, so also it illuminates the souls of the world and of the spheres. But the steps by which that fury descends are these. Jove seizes Apollo. Apollo illuminates the Muses. The Muses arouse and agitate the gentle and insuperable souls of the poets. The inspired poets inspire their interpreters. The interpreters move the auditors. But other souls are seized by other Muses, because also other souls have been attributed to other spheres and stars, as is handed down in the *Timaeus*. The Muse Calliope is the voice resulting from all the voices of the spheres. Urania, of the starry heaven, so called for its dignity. Polymnia of Saturn, on account of the memory of ancient things which Saturn exhibits, and its dry and cold complexion. Terpsichore, Jupiter, for he is health-bearing to the chorus of men. Clio of Mars, on account of the desire for glory. Melpomene of the sun, which is the tempering of the whole world. Erato of Venus, on account of love. Euterpe of Mercury, on account of honest delight in serious things. Thalia of the moon, on account of the greenness exhibited to things by its humor. Apollo likewise is of the sun's mind, and his lyre is the sun's body: nine of which, its four motions—annual, monthly, diurnal, oblique: four voices—*acates, hypotes, dorious, gemini*: there are four triplicities of signs, from which the four qualities of the seasons are produced. Calliope inspired Orpheus, Urania Musaeus, Clio Homer. Polymnia Pindarus. Erato Sappho, Melpomene Thamyris, Terpsichore Hesiod, Thalia Maro [Virgil], Euterpe Naso [Ovid]. The same Phoebus who now agitates you, best Laurentius, seized Linus; Phoebus, I say, who in your age gave prophecy to Cosimo; to your parent Piero, the bow and medicines; to you finally, the lyre and songs.

---

### SOCRATES, ION.

**ION** I bid you be well. Whence have you now come to us? Do you come from your country Ephesus? ION: By no means, O Socrates, but from Epidaurus from the festival of Asclepius. SOCRATES: Did the Epidaurians also institute a contest for rhapsodes, that is, of those who recite the songs of poets? ION: Not only in these, but also in another kind of music. SOCRATES: What then, did you not compete there for us? How was it, did you compete? ION: We brought back the first prizes of the contests, O Socrates. SOCRATES: You say well. Come, let us pursue victory in the celebration of Pallas. ION: These things will happen if God wills. SOCRATES: Indeed, O Ion, I have always valued your art very much, because it befits your art that you adorn your body, and always appear as beautiful as possible, and also because it is necessary to be assiduously engaged with very many and good poets, especially with Homer, the best and most divine of all poets, and to learn not only his songs, but also his meanings. For never would anyone emerge as a rhapsode unless he understood those things said by the poet. For the rhapsode ought to interpret the poet's mind to the auditors: which cannot rightly be done if one is ignorant of the poet's sentiment. These things are all worthy of our emulation. ION: You say true things, O Socrates: and I indeed have labored very much in this. I profess that I will explain most clearly concerning Homer beyond all others, so that neither Metrodorus of Lampsacus, nor Stesimbrotus the Thasian, nor Glaucon, nor any of the ancients could ever explain so many and such clear sentiments of Homer as I. SOCRATES: Rightly, O Ion: for it is established that no envy will prevent you from opening these things to me. ION: And it is indeed worthy of hearing, O Socrates, how vehemently I have adorned Homer. Whence it is just that those things which pertain to the poet, but now for this one... [Ion mentions being crowned with a golden crown]. SOCRATES: I shall surely obtain leisure for hearing you sometime: but for now answer me this one thing: whether you are skilled only concerning Homer, or also concerning Hesiod and Archilochus. ION: By no means, but concerning Homer only, for that seems enough to me. SOCRATES: Are there any things about which Homer and Hesiod report the same? ION: I think there are many indeed. SOCRATES: Would you explain better those things which Homer says, or those which Hesiod says? ION: Equally of both, O Socrates, in those things in which they report the same. SOCRATES: What however in those things about which they do not say the same? As for example, Homer and Hesiod speak of prophecy. ION: Most especially indeed. SOCRATES: And in what these poets agree or disagree when they speak of prophecy, would you explain better than some skilled prophet? ION: A prophet better. SOCRATES: But if you were a prophet, could you explain not only those things in which they agree, but also those in which they differ? ION: It is clear. SOCRATES: What further? Are you vehement and eloquent only concerning Homer? But concerning Hesiod and other poets very little? Does Homer treat of other things than those which other poets also treat?
[Margin: What things are explained in all the poetry of Homer.]
Did he not narrate many things which pertain to war, and to the mutual customs of good and bad men, private persons and craftsmen? And concerning the gods, how they deal with each other and with men, and concerning celestial affections? Also concerning those things which are in the underworld, and did he not sing the generations of gods and heroes? Does not all Homer's poetry turn around these things? ION: You speak true things, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Do not other poets sing the same things? ION: The same certainly, but others not as Homer does. SOCRATES: Or perhaps worse? ION: Much worse. SOCRATES: Better therefore Homer? ION: Better certainly. SOCRATES: O Ion, charming head, when many speak about number, and one of them speaks rightly, cannot someone know him who speaks well in that matter? ION: He can. SOCRATES: Is it he himself who knows him who speaks ill, or another? ION: He himself, the same. SOCRATES: Is not this he who is endowed with the arithmetical art? ION: Indeed. SOCRATES: When many speak concerning foods, what kinds are healthful, and someone speaks rightly on that matter, will some other person notice him who speaks well that he speaks rightly, and another him who speaks ill that he speaks ill? Or one and the same? ION: The same without doubt. SOCRATES: Who is this? What is his name? ION: A physician. SOCRATES: Do we not say summarily that when several speak concerning the same matter, one and the same will distinguish both him who speaks ill and him who speaks well: and unless he knows him who errs in the same matter, he will never recognize him who thinks rightly? ION: Indeed. SOCRATES: Is not he himself the same skilled in both? ION: Exactly. SOCRATES: Do you assert that Homer and other poets, in whose number are Hesiod and Archilochus, report the same things? Yet not in the same way, but Homer better, but others worse? ION: I speak true things.

---

### [Page 118]
### Book Fourteen.

SOCRATES: If you know him who speaks well, you understand those who speak ill, that they err. ION: It is agreed. SOCRATES: If therefore we say, O best man, that Ion is similarly skilled and vehement concerning Homer and other poets, we shall by no means err: since he himself confesses that the same judge is suitable regarding all those who are engaged in the same matter, and that almost all poets fashion the same things. ION: Why therefore, O Socrates, when someone speaks of another poet, except of Homer, can I say nothing at all worthy of being understood, but I immediately fall asleep and become torpid: but as soon as someone makes mention of Homer, I immediately wake up and apply my mind, and whatever is intended follows? SOCRATES: It is by no means difficult, O friend, to conjecture the cause of this. For it is established that you can speak skillfully of Homer neither by art nor by knowledge. For if by art, you would be able to speak similarly of all other poets, for poetry is a whole. Is it not? ION: It is certainly. SOCRATES: Does not anyone, after he has prepared some other entire art, judge equally of all things which are under that art? Indeed there is the same reason for considering all arts. Do you want me to tell you for what reason I say this? ION: I desire it by Jove, O Socrates. For as often as I have heard you wise men, I am immediately affected by a certain marvelous joy. SOCRATES: I wish you were telling the truth, O Ion. But you rhapsodes and actors are wise men, and those whose poems you sing. But I speak nothing besides the truth, as becomes an unlearned man. For behold how light that is of which I was just asking, and easy to know: so that anyone could perceive what I was narrating, that there is the same consideration throughout the rest, if someone has prepared for himself an entire art. For example, is not the art of painting a certain whole? ION: It is. SOCRATES: Have there not been and are many painters, partly good, partly bad? ION: Certainly. SOCRATES: Have you seen anyone who could sufficiently show both those things which Polygnotus son of Aglaophon painted rightly and those not rightly: but regarding other painters, he could not: and if someone showed the work of other painters, he would fall asleep, nor would the faculty be available to him for saying anything and conjecturing: but when he must judge of Polygnotus, or of any one painter, he would wake up, and apply his mind, and have the faculty of speaking? ION: Not by Jove. SOCRATES: What in statuary? Have you seen anyone who could explain those things which Daedalus of Metion, or Epeius son of Panopeus, or Theodorus the Samian, or any other sculptor fashioned well, but in the works of other sculptors he would be torpid and mute? ION: By Jove, I never found one such person. SOCRATES: But surely neither in the blowing of flutes as I think, nor in the striking of the lyre: nor in that singing to the lyre, nor in rhapsody have you beheld a man who, in the works of Olympus, or Thamyris, or Orpheus, or Phemius the rhapsode of Ithaca, would fail, and could not perceive and compare what they modulate well and what otherwise. ION: I have nothing to contradict you in this, but nevertheless I am conscious to myself that I report the most beautiful things concerning Homer beyond all other men, nor do I lack abundance of speaking: and all others praise me in this matter, but in the rest by no means. See what this may be. SOCRATES: I see, O Ion, and I will begin to open to you what it seems to me to be. That you speak well of Homer, art does not provide for you, as I was just saying, but it is a divine power which moves you, just as in the stone which Euripides named the Magnet, and some call the Heraclean stone. This stone

not only draws iron rings, but even infuses power into the rings themselves, by which they can effect this same thing, and just like the stone, draw other rings. Whence a long concatenation of iron and rings often hangs from each other, and for all these, the power is drawn from that stone. So the Muse herself inspires poets with divine instinct; the inspired poets seize others with fury. Wherefore from all these a series itself is woven. And so all epic poets...
[Margin: It seems he does this to show that Homer himself did not write from art, but a certain divine force of genius.]
...good epic poets say all these clear poems not by art, but captured by divine inspiration; and good lyric poets similarly: as the Corybantes dance with a mind not sane, so the excellent lyric poets fashion these songs with a mind not sane: but when they rise into harmony and rhythm, and snatched up they become bacchic, just as bacchic women, with a mind not sane, draw honey and milk from rivers, but with a sane mind they cannot draw them; and that the soul of lyric poets effects, which they themselves narrate. For the poets tell us that drawing from fountains where honey flows, and plucking from the gardens and hills of the Muses, they bring songs to us, just as bees bring honey from flowers, and they say they fly like bees. In which they speak truly: for the poet is a light, volatile, and sacred thing, nor can he sing before he is full of the god, and placed outside himself, and alienated from his mind. For as long as one is well in his mind, no one can either fashion songs nor give oracles. Not by some art therefore do they sing these clear things which you report concerning Homer, but by divine lot each can effect that rightly to which the Muse has incited him. This one sings Dithyrambs, that one praises of someone else, this one Hypochemata and choral dances, another epic songs, another likewise iambics. For the rest of these, each is rude and inept. For not by art, but by divine power do they say these things. For if they knew how to speak rightly of one of these by art, they would be able to do the same of all others. But for this cause God, stealing their mind, uses them as ministers and messengers of oracles and divine prophets, so that we who hear may perceive that it is not they who report such worthy things, when they are by no means masters of their mind, but that God speaks these things, and through them shouts these things to us. To this matter Tynnichus the Chalcidian can be a most evident argument, who before had composed no poem worthy of memory: but he says he found by the inspiration of the Muses the hymn to Apollo which everyone sings, almost the most beautiful of all songs. In this most especially God shows that it seems we ought not to doubt that these clear poems are divine and the works of gods rather than human and the works of men.
[Margin: Poets are the interpreters of the gods.]
But poets are nothing other than interpreters of the gods, while they are seized by fury, by whatever divinity anyone may be seized. Which God indeed wishing to show, deliberately sang the most beautiful melody through the most inept poet. Do I not seem to you to report true things? ION: To me certainly by Jove. And you soothe and affect my soul with these discourses, Socrates. And by a certain divine lot from the gods, distinguished poets seem to interpret these things for us. SOCRATES: Do you rhapsodes not interpret the writings of poets? ION: You tell the truth. SOCRATES: Are you not interpreters of interpreters? ION: We are. SOCRATES: Notice what I wish, and answer me this, O Ion: nor hide from me that about which I shall ask you. When you report songs aptly, and render the spectators struck with stupor, whether when you sing Ulysses jumping onto the threshold and showing himself openly to the suitors and pouring out arrows before his feet, or Achilles making an attack on Hector, or when...
[Margin: Odyssey, Iliad.]
...when you...

### [Page 119]
### Ion, Or, concerning poetic fury.

...when you bring forth something miserable and querulous concerning Andromache, or Hecuba, or Priam, are you then in control of your mind? Or is the mind alienated from itself, and the inspired soul thinks itself to be present among the deeds which you relate, whether they were done in Ithaca, or at Troy, or wherever else the songs may snatch you? ION: You have brought a clear conjecture to me, nor shall I review it hidden from you. For as often as I say anything miserable, my eyes are filled with tears...

--- Page 132 ---
Theaetetus, Or, On Knowledge.
113

...nothing else do I have. SOCRATES. How "above"? THEAETETUS. I wished to say that true opinion is knowledge. For to opine truly is far from error, and all things that proceed from true opinion are decorous and good. SOCRATES. O Theaetetus, he who precedes others in crossing a river, when they ask how deep the water is, says, "the water itself will show." So if we enter and search, perhaps the very obstacle we seek will demonstrate itself; if we stay still, nothing will be revealed. THEAETETUS. You speak well. Let us go and seek. SOCRATES. Is this not a matter for a brief investigation? For the whole of art is proof to us that knowledge is not this. THEAETETUS. By what reasoning? And what is this faculty? SOCRATES. That of those who are wise above others, whom they call orators and lawyers. For these people persuade by their art, they do not teach. They induce the listeners to opine what they themselves desire. Or do you think some are so powerful in teaching that when no witnesses were present at robberies and other injuries, they could teach the truth of the committed crimes in the short time the water-clock allows? <note>In Athenian courts, a water-clock or 'clepsydra' timed the speeches.</note> THEAETETUS. I do not think they teach them at all, but persuade them. SOCRATES. And to persuade, do you not assert it is the same as to induce an opinion? THEAETETUS. Exactly. SOCRATES. When judges are justly persuaded of things which only he who saw them knows, and otherwise not at all, then judging those things from hearsay and having obtained a true opinion without knowledge, do they not judge rightly if they judge well? THEAETETUS. Entirely. SOCRATES. Yet if true opinion and knowledge were the same thing, O friend, that excellent judge would never opine rightly without knowledge. Now, however, each seems to be something different. THEAETETUS. What I once heard from someone about knowledge, O Socrates, I had forgotten, but now I remember. He said that true opinion with an account <note>original: "cum ratione" / logos</note> is knowledge, and without an account it is outside of knowledge; and those things that lack an account cannot be known, but those which have an account can be known. SOCRATES. How excellently you speak. But those very things that can be known and those that cannot—tell me how he distinguished them, so that we may see if you and I have received it similarly. THEAETETUS. Whether I shall find it I do not know, but perhaps if someone else explained it I could follow. SOCRATES. Hear then a dream for a dream. I also seem to have heard from certain people that the first elements themselves, from which men and other things are composed, do not admit of an account. For each of them can be named by itself, but it is not possible to call it anything else, neither that it "is" nor that it "is not." For already existence or non-existence would be added to it. One ought to add nothing if one speaks of that thing alone. For they wish that neither "itself," nor "that," nor "each," nor "alone," nor "this," nor other such things be applied. For these things run around and are applied to all, being something else besides that to which they are added. But it would be necessary, if it were somehow possible for the thing itself to be spoken and to admit its own account, for it to be spoken apart from all others. Now, however, you cannot express any of the elements in a discourse. For the element itself has nothing but a name, and only has a name. But those things composed of them—just as the elements themselves are joined, so the names of them joined together become a discourse <note>original: "orationem" / logos</note>. Indeed, the joining of names is the substance of discourse. Wherefore the elements are without discourse and account, and are unknown, yet perceivable by the senses; but syllables can be both known and learned, and grasped by true opinion. When therefore anyone obtains a true opinion about something without an account, they say his soul perceives the truth about it, but does not know it. For he who cannot give and receive an account is ignorant. But when he attains the account, he is able to know all these things and obtain perfect knowledge. Did you hear it this way in your dream, or otherwise? THEAETETUS. Exactly thus. SOCRATES. Does that please you? And do you thus assert that true opinion together with an account is knowledge? THEAETETUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. Have we then, Theaetetus, today grasped that which many wise men of old sought and grew old before they found it? THEAETETUS. To me, O Socrates, what has just been said seems to be well said. SOCRATES. And rightly so; for what knowledge could ever exist without discourse and right opinion? Yet one of the things said displeases me. THEAETETUS. What is that? SOCRATES. That which seemed to be said most magnificently: that the elements are unknown, but the class of syllables is known. THEAETETUS. Is that not right? SOCRATES. We must certainly observe. For we have as guarantees of the argument the very examples which he used to say all these things. THEAETETUS. Which ones? SOCRATES. The elements of letters and syllables—or do you think he who says what we are recounting was looking at anything else? THEAETETUS. Not at anything else, certainly, but at those very things. SOCRATES. Let us then review and examine them. Or rather, let us examine ourselves: did we not learn our letters this way? Respond to this first: do not syllables have an account and definition, but elements do not? THEAETETUS. Perhaps. SOCRATES. It seems so to me entirely. If someone should ask about the first syllable of "Socrates," O Theaetetus, tell me: what is it? What will you most especially respond? THEAETETUS. That it is S and O. SOCRATES. You have, then, this account of the syllable. THEAETETUS. Indeed. SOCRATES. Come, tell me further the account of the S itself. THEAETETUS. But how could anyone refer to the elements of an element? For the S itself, O Socrates, is only a certain sound of the mute letters, like the tongue hissing; but for B, there is neither voice nor sound, nor for most of the elements. Wherefore they are very rightly said to be without an account. Of these, only those seven best known have a voice, but no account. This, then, my friend, we have rightly asserted concerning knowledge. THEAETETUS. We seem to have. SOCRATES. But when we said the element is unknown and the syllable known, did we establish it correctly? THEAETETUS. It is probable. SOCRATES. But do we say the syllable is both elements? Or even if more than two are in it, are it all of them? Or rather a single idea generated from those very composites? THEAETETUS. We seem to mean all of them. SOCRATES. Look then at these two, S and O; if both are the first syllable of my name, whoever knows the syllable knows both. THEAETETUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Therefore he knows S and O. THEAETETUS. Plainly. SOCRATES. What further, if he is ignorant of both, and knowing neither, will he know them both together? THEAETETUS. That would be both absurd and beyond reason. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, if it is necessary to know both since someone knows them both together, it follows that it is necessary for him to have foreknowledge of the elements who is eventually to know the syllable, and thus it happens too suddenly. SOCRATES. For we do not guard the argument well. Perhaps we ought to posit the syllable not as the elements, but as a certain single form constituted from them, which has a single idea of its own, and differs from the elements. THEAETETUS. Exactly so, and perhaps it is this way rather than that. SOCRATES. For which reason it must be considered diligently; it is not becoming to betray so great and noble a discourse so lazily. THEAETETUS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Let the syllable be, as we were just saying, a single idea from each of the fitting elements, both in letters...
