...as in all other things made. THEAETETUS. Exactly. SOCRATES. Is it not necessary that there be no parts of it? THEAETETUS. Why? SOCRATES. Because of whatever things there are parts, the whole must necessarily be all the parts. Or do you call the whole a certain single form made from parts, different from all the parts? THEAETETUS. Indeed. SOCRATES. But do you call "everything" and "the whole" the same, or is each different? THEAETETUS. Although I have nothing certain, yet because you bid me respond promptly, making the attempt I say they differ. SOCRATES. Promptness, O Theaetetus, is right. But whether the response is right must be considered. THEAETETUS. Indeed. SOCRATES. Does not the whole and everything differ according to this discourse? THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. What further, "all things" and "everything"—do they differ in any way? As when we say: one, two, three, four, five, six; or twice three; or thrice two; or four and two; or three and two and one—in all these, do we say the same thing or something else? THEAETETUS. Entirely the same. SOCRATES. Anything other than six? THEAETETUS. Nothing else. SOCRATES. Do we not in every way of speaking find all six? THEAETETUS. So it is. SOCRATES. But again, do we not say some one thing when we say "all"? THEAETETUS. It is necessary. SOCRATES. Is it anything other than six? THEAETETUS. Nothing else. SOCRATES. Therefore, in things that consist of number, we say "everything" and "all" are the same. THEAETETUS. So it appears. SOCRATES. So indeed let us speak of them: the number of an acre and the acre are the same, are they not? THEAETETUS. The same. SOCRATES. And the number of a furlong and the furlong similarly? THEAETETUS. This also. SOCRATES. Also the number of the army and the army itself, and other such things in the same way? For the entire number existing is everything of each of them. THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. But is the number of each thing anything else than its parts? THEAETETUS. In no way. SOCRATES. Whatever things therefore have parts, consist of parts. THEAETETUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. But all the parts have been conceded to be the whole, if indeed every number is "everything." THEAETETUS. It is so. SOCRATES. The whole, therefore, does not consist of parts; for it would be "everything," since it would be all the parts. THEAETETUS. It does not seem so. SOCRATES. Is a part what it is of anything other than a whole? THEAETETUS. Of "everything" itself, surely. SOCRATES. You fight strenuously, Theaetetus; is not "everything" itself "everything" from the fact that nothing is missing? THEAETETUS. Necessary. SOCRATES. Is not a "whole" also a "whole" by the same reasoning, because nothing is absent? But that from which nothing is missing is neither the whole nor "everything" itself of itself. THEAETETUS. It seems to me now that "whole" and "everything" do not differ at all. SOCRATES. Did we not say that of whatever there are parts, the whole and "everything" are all the parts? THEAETETUS. Plainly. SOCRATES. Again, what we attempted a little before: if the syllable is not the elements, is it not necessary that it does not have its elements as parts? Or if it is the same with them, must it not be known just as they are? THEAETETUS. So it is. SOCRATES. Lest this should happen, we posited it as something other than them. THEAETETUS. Other. SOCRATES. What if the elements are not parts of the syllable, can you ever refer to any other things which are parts of the syllable, yet are not its elements? THEAETETUS. Never would I call things parts that are not elements. It would be ridiculous to omit the elements and seek other things. SOCRATES. Entirely, then, according to this reasoning, O Theaetetus, the syllable seems to be a certain single indivisible idea. THEAETETUS. It seems so indeed. SOCRATES. Do you remember, friend, that we admitted in the previous points that there was no account of the first things from which others are composed, because each thing itself existed simply according to itself, and neither "to be" could be congruently said of it, nor "this," nor "so," as if these were external and foreign—and we said this very cause stood in the way of its being described and known? THEAETETUS. I remember. SOCRATES. Is there any other cause besides this which makes a thing uniform and indivisible? For I see no other. THEAETETUS. None appears. SOCRATES. Does not the syllable also run into the same fate as that, since it is a form and has no parts, but is a single idea? THEAETETUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. If, therefore, the syllable is many elements and a certain whole, and these are its parts, then the syllable and elements can be known and described similarly: since it has been established that all the parts are the same as the whole. THEAETETUS. Especially. SOCRATES. But if it is one thing and simple, the syllable is just as devoid of definition and knowledge as the element. For the same cause will make them such. THEAETETUS. I cannot assert otherwise. SOCRATES. Let us then not admit the discourse of him who said the syllable can be spoken of and known, but the elements not at all. THEAETETUS. Certainly not, if we believe this reasoning. SOCRATES. What if someone said the opposite, would you not rather concede those things from the knowledge you have of your own very first rudiments of letters? THEAETETUS. What are those? SOCRATES. That you studied to learn nothing else than to discern the elements with eyes and ears, and to note each one according to itself, lest their position should disturb you when they were either spoken or written. THEAETETUS. You tell the truth. SOCRATES. But to have learned the art of the lyre-player—what else is it than to distinguish each tone of each string? For anyone would call these the elements of music. THEAETETUS. Nothing else. SOCRATES. Since then we have become skilled in elements and syllables, and we wish to make a conjecture from these to other things, we shall surely bring it about that the class of elements contains a clearer and more principal intelligence than the syllable, for the absolute perception of individual disciplines. And if anyone should say the syllable is known but the element is by nature unknown, we shall think he is playing, whether he likes it or not. THEAETETUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. But let there be other demonstrations of the same thing, as it seems to me; yet let us not forget the proposal because of these: namely, what should be judged of this which is said—that an account, if it joins with true opinion, is perfect knowledge. THEAETETUS. We must investigate it entirely. SOCRATES. Come tell me, what does <term>logos</term> <note>original: "λόγος" — word, reason, or account</note> signify to us here? For it seems to me to signify one of three things. THEAETETUS. Which ones? SOCRATES. I think the first is to express one's thought by voice through words and names, showing one's own opinion in the voice as if in a mirror or in water. Does not discourse <note>original: "oratio"</note> seem to you to be such a thing? THEAETETUS. To me indeed. SOCRATES. We say that he who does this "speaks." Can not everyone do this sooner or later: namely, show what he thinks about individual things? Unless perhaps he is mute or deaf by nature. And so, whoever opines anything rightly will have it "with an account," and it will be knowledge. THEAETETUS. These things are true. SOCRATES. Let us then not easily condemn him who affirmed that knowledge is what we have just said, as if he says nothing. For perhaps he did not mean that, but being asked what each thing is, he could respond to the questioner through elements. THEAETETUS. What sort of thing do you mean, O Socrates? SOCRATES. Just as Hesiod says of a chariot: "A chariot of a hundred timbers," which I indeed could not name, nor you either, as I think. But it will be enough for us if, to the one asking "what is a chariot?", we can respond: wheels, axle, body, rails, yoke. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. But he perhaps would think us ridiculous—as if being asked about your name, we responded by the syllable—rightly indeed opining...

Theaetetus, Or, On Knowledge.

...opining and saying what we say, but thinking that we are grammarians, and that we have and speak the account of the name "Theaetetus" grammatically. But this is not to speak according to knowledge, before one determines each thing through elements along with true opinion, as was said above. THEAETETUS. It was said, without a doubt. SOCRATES. So indeed, we have a right opinion about a chariot. But he who can run through those hundred parts, grasping the essence of the chariot itself, has also grasped the account along with true opinion: instead of a mere opiner, he has emerged as one skilled in knowledge concerning the essence of the chariot, determining the whole through its elements. THEAETETUS. Does it not seem good to you, O Socrates? SOCRATES. If it seems so to you, my friend, and you approve this discourse through elements concerning each thing as being an "account," and that he who does it through syllables or anything larger is devoid of an account, I want you to tell me, so that we may consider it more diligently. THEAETETUS. I approve, and most certainly. SOCRATES. But is it so, that you think anyone is a knower of anything when the one and same thing seems to him now to belong to one and the same thing, and now to another? Or when he opines that one and the same thing is now this, now that? THEAETETUS. Not by Jove! SOCRATES. Has it escaped your memory that in learning letters this happened often to you and others? THEAETETUS. Do you mean we used to opine now this letter and now that for the same syllable? Or refer the same letter sometimes to its own syllable and sometimes to another? SOCRATES. These things, I say. THEAETETUS. By Jove, I have not forgotten, nor do I think those who are thus affected "know." SOCRATES. What then? If someone at that time, writing "Theaetetus," thinks he should write "Th" and "e," and does write it; and again, wishing to write "Theodorus," thinks he should write "Th" and "e," and does write it—shall we say he knows the first syllable of your name? THEAETETUS. A little while ago we agreed that he who is thus situated does not yet know. SOCRATES. What prevents this same person from suffering the same thing regarding the second, third, and fourth syllables? THEAETETUS. Nothing at all. SOCRATES. Will he not then, having the discourse through the element, write "Theaetetus" with right opinion when he writes it in its order? THEAETETUS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. But still as one ignorant, but opining rightly, as we said? THEAETETUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. And having the account along with right opinion? For having the discourse through the element, he wrote it—which we agreed was an "account." THEAETETUS. True. SOCRATES. There is therefore, O friend, a certain right opinion with an account which it is not yet fitting to call knowledge. THEAETETUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. We have obtained a certain dream, it seems, while we consider how to have the truest account of knowledge. THEAETETUS. Or perhaps we ought not to find fault yet; for perhaps someone would not define <term>logos</term> <note>original: "λόγος"</note> that way, but would choose the remaining of the three species, from which we said he would choose one who pursued the idea that knowledge is right opinion with an account. SOCRATES. You have admonished me opportunely. For there still remains one species: the first was as it were the image of thought in the voice; the second was the process toward the whole through the elements. THEAETETUS. And what do you call the third? SOCRATES. That which most people would agree on: namely, being able to bring forward a certain mark by which the thing in question differs from all others. THEAETETUS. Of what thing, or of what kind of definition can you assign such a thing to me? SOCRATES. As, for example, regarding the sun: if you wish, you will approve, I think, that it surpasses in light all the things that revolve in the heavens around the earth. THEAETETUS. Entirely. SOCRATES. Take the reason why this was said. It is what we were just referring to. If you take the difference of each thing by which it is distinguished from others, you will have received the definition, as some hand down; but as long as you touch on something common, you will have the definition of those things whose community it is. THEAETETUS. I understand, and I think such a thing is rightly called an account. SOCRATES. But he who, with right opinion, takes the difference by which each thing is separated from any other, he will then know that very thing which he previously opined. THEAETETUS. It is agreed. SOCRATES. Now at last, O Theaetetus, since I have come closer to this, as it were, a certain sketch, I notice that I understand nothing at all in these things. For as long as I was looking from far off, something seemed to be said to me. THEAETETUS. Why so? SOCRATES. I will tell you if I can. Having indeed a right opinion of you, if I furthermore take your definition, I know you; otherwise I only opine. THEAETETUS. It was so, certainly. SOCRATES. When therefore I was only opining, I perceived in thought none of those things by which you are distinguished from others. THEAETETUS. Nothing, as it seems. SOCRATES. I was therefore attending to certain common things, of which you have nothing more than anyone else. THEAETETUS. It follows necessarily. SOCRATES. Come tell me, by Jove, how then did I opine you rather than anyone else? Suppose it were so in my thinking: "Theaetetus is he who is both a man, and has a nose, and a mouth, and eyes, and similarly the other members." Does that thought make me perceive Theaetetus rather than Theodorus, or (as they say) the "last of the Mysians"? <note>A Greek proverb for someone of no account or the lowest rank</note> THEAETETUS. How so? SOCRATES. But if I do not only think of someone having a nose and eyes, but also a snub nose and protruding eyes, I shall no more opine you than myself, and others whoever are such. THEAETETUS. Quite so. SOCRATES. But indeed, I shall not opine Theaetetus, as I think, before this snub figure is distinguished for me from all other snub figures I have seen by some mark proper to it, and similarly other things of which you consist. Which indeed will remind me tomorrow, even if I run into you, and make me opine rightly about you. THEAETETUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Therefore, right opinion concerning each thing is concerned with the proper difference. THEAETETUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. What then will it be if we assume the definition along with the right opinion? For it is a ridiculous precept if it bids us opine how something differs from others. THEAETETUS. How? SOCRATES. To those things about which we already opine rightly insofar as they differ from others, it bids us assume a right opinion insofar as they differ from others. And so your discourse will be like a <term>scytica</term> <note>meaning unclear, perhaps a reference to a 'scytale' or staff, or a 'pistillus' (pestle), implying something turning in circles</note> or a pestle, or any circular motion; to this precept it says absolutely nothing. For it might more rightly be called the precept of a blind man. Since to bid us take what we already have, in order to learn those things we opine, seems to be the command of a blind man. THEAETETUS. Come tell me, what were you just asking? SOCRATES. If, while he commanded us to receive an account, O boy, he commanded us to know, and not to opine the difference, the account would indeed be a sweet thing, and the most beautiful of all things pertaining to knowledge. For "to know" is to receive knowledge. THEAETETUS. It is indeed. SOCRATES. Asked therefore what knowledge is, he responds that it is right opinion with the knowledge of the difference. For according to him, the assumption of an account would be this. THEAETETUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. It is entirely fatuous, when we are seeking knowledge, to say it is right opinion with knowledge, whether it be knowledge of the difference or of anything else. Therefore, neither sense, O Theaetetus, nor true opinion, nor an account assumed with true opinion is knowledge. THEAETETUS. Not, as it seems. SOCRATES.

Book Thirteen.

**SOCRATES:** Is there any other offspring within us concerning knowledge, my friend? Or have we now brought forth everything? **THEAETETUS:** By Jove, I have uttered more than I had in me, thanks to your delivery. **SOCRATES:** And does not our art of midwifery show that all these have been born vain and unworthy of upbringing? **THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** If, therefore, you should strive hereafter to become full and fertile with others, and you become pregnant, you will be full of better things because of this present examination. But if you remain empty and sterile, you will certainly be less troublesome to your companions, more moderate and gentle, by no means thinking you know what you do not know. My art can do this much, and nothing more; nor do I know the things that many others—great and wonderful men, both now and in the past—know. But I and my mother were allotted this midwife's faculty: she for women, and I for noble and honest young men. But now I must go to the King's Porch <note>The Stoa Basileios in Athens, where the Archon Basileus heard religious and legal indictments</note>; for Meletus has summoned me to court. Tomorrow at dawn, O Theodorus, we shall return here.

->**PLATO'S ION, OR, ON POETIC FRENZY.**<-

->**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI, A MAGNANIMOUS MAN.**<-

Our Plato, excellent Lorenzo, defines frenzy in the *Phaedrus* as an alienation of the mind. He teaches that there are two types of alienation: one arising from human illnesses, the other proceeding from God. He calls the former madness, and the latter **divine frenzy**. In madness, a person is cast down below the human species and is turned, in a way, from a human into a brute. By divine frenzy, one is raised above human nature and passes into God. Divine frenzy is the illumination of the rational soul, through which God draws the soul, which had fallen from the upper realms to the lower, back from the lower to the upper. The soul’s fall from the "One" itself <note>In Neoplatonism, 'The One' is the ultimate source of all existence</note>—the principle of all things—to bodies occurs through four stages: through mind <term>mens: the highest intuitive intellect</term>, reason, opinion, and nature. For since there are six levels in the whole order of things—the highest of which is held by the One, the lowest by the body, and the middle four being those we mentioned—it is necessary that whatever falls from the first to the last must drop through the four intermediaries. The "One" is the boundary and measure of all things, free of infinity and multitude. The **mind** is a multitude, yet stable and eternal. **Reason** is a moving multitude, yet finite. **Opinion** is an infinite moving multitude, yet united in substance and points. **Nature** is similar, but divided. Our soul looks upon all these; through these it descends, and through these it also ascends. For as it is produced by the One itself (which is the principle of all), it has been allotted a certain unity which unites all its essence, powers, and actions. From this unity, and toward it, the other things in the soul relate, just as lines of a circle relate from and toward the center. It unites not only the parts of the soul to each other and to the whole soul, but the whole soul to the One itself, the cause of all things. As it depends on the divine mind, it contemplates the ideas of all things through the mind with stable action. As it looks at itself, it thinks of the universal reasons of things and runs through them by reason from principles to conclusions. As it looks at the body, it conceives particular forms of moving things through opinion and runs through them. As it touches matter, it uses nature as an instrument by which it unites, moves, and shapes matter; from this, generations, growth, and their opposites proceed. You see, then, that the soul falls from the One (which is above eternity) into eternal multitude, from eternity into time, and from time into place and matter. Therefore, as it descends through four steps, it must ascend through four.

Divine frenzy is that which turns the soul back toward the heavens, as established in its definition. There are four species of divine frenzy: first, the poetic frenzy; second, the mystery frenzy; third, prophecy; and fourth, the affection of love. Poetry comes from the Muses, mystery from Dionysus, prophecy from Apollo, and love from Venus. Indeed, the soul cannot return to the "One" unless it itself becomes one. But through its effects, the soul has become many; it has fallen into the body, distracted by various operations, and looking toward individual things. Because of this, its higher parts almost fall asleep, and its lower parts dominate the others; the former are affected by torpor, the latter by perturbation. The whole soul is filled with discord and lack of harmony. Therefore, there is a need first for **poetic frenzy**, which rouses what is sluggish through musical tones, soothes what is disturbed through harmonic sweetness, and finally drives away discordant strife through the consonance of diverse things, tempering the various parts of the soul. But this is not enough. Multitude still stands in the soul. Therefore, **mystery** <note>sacred rites and initiations</note> approaches, which through expiations and sacrifices and the whole worship of the gods, directs the intention of all parts toward the mind, by which God is worshipped. When the individual parts of the soul are reduced to one mind, the soul has already become a certain whole "one" made of many. Yet there is still need for a third frenzy, which leads the mind back to the very unity that is the head of the soul. Apollo effects this through **prophecy**. For when the soul rises above the mind into unity, it foretells the future. Finally, when the soul has been made "one"—a unity, I say, which exists in the very essence of the soul—it remains for it to be turned immediately into the "One" which is *above* essence. The celestial Venus herself fulfills this through **love**, that is, the desire for divine beauty and the ardor for the Good.

The first frenzy thus tempers what is unharmonious and dissonant. The second makes the tempered parts into one whole. The third makes the whole "one" rise above its parts. The fourth leads into the "One" which is above essence and the whole. The first distinguishes the "good horse" (that is, reason and opinion) from the "bad horse" (that is, confused phantasy and nature). The second subjects the bad horse to the good, and the good to the charioteer (the mind). The third directs the charioteer to his own head (the peak of the mind's unity). The last turns the head of the charioteer toward the Head of all things. There, the charioteer is blessed, and standing his horses at the manger (divine beauty), he offers them ambrosia and nectar to drink—that is, the vision of beauty and the joy derived from that vision. These are the works of the four frenzies, about which Plato disputes generally in the *Phaedrus*, but specifically about the last frenzy (love) in the *Symposium*, and about the first (poetic frenzy) in the present dialogue titled *Ion*. He defines it in the *Phaedrus* thus: "Poetic frenzy is a certain possession by the Muses, which, having allotted a tender and insurmountable soul, awakens and excites it through songs and other poetry, for the instruction of the human race." "Possession" signifies the soul's rapture and its turning toward the divine power of the Muses. He calls the soul "tender" meaning agile and shapeable by the Muses; for unless it is prepared, it is not possessed. He calls it "insurmountable" because after it is seized, it overcomes all things, and can be neither polluted nor conquered by any inferior thing. It rouses the body from sleep to the vigilance of the mind, calls it back from the shadows of ignorance to light, from death to life, and from Lethean forgetfulness to the remembrance of divine things; it excites, goads, and inflames the soul to express in verse those things it contemplates and foretells. After this definition, he adds that he who approaches the gates of poetry without the frenzy of the Muses is himself empty and his poetry is naught—as if poetry were so great a thing that it cannot be obtained without the highest favor of God.

He teaches these same things in the *Ion*, showing where this frenzy comes from and through how many steps it descends. Plato says in the fourth book of *Laws* that God, fortune, and art govern all human affairs. Thus, poetry is either a gift of God, a lot of fortune, or a work of art. Socrates searches with Ion the rhapsode <margin>Rhapsode</margin> <note>A performer who recited epic poetry</note> to see which of these is most true. In this book, a "rhapsode" signifies a reciter, interpreter, and singer of poems. Ion interpreted the poems of Homer and sang them to the lyre before the people; he was so affected that he could explain no other poet except Homer, even if they spoke of the same things with the same ease. He explained everything in Homer quickly. From this, Socrates argued: either Ion brings forth what Homer wrote by chance, by art, or by divine inspiration. Not by chance, because it is not random but ordered. Not by art; for in art, whoever possesses the complete art can judge whatever is subject to that same art. The poems of Hesiod and others are subject to the same poetic study as Homer's, especially those dealing with the same subjects, yet Ion does not grasp them, though he explains Homer perfectly. Therefore, he does not judge by art. It remains that he acts by divine inspiration. From this it is clear that Ion, the interpreter of the poet, and many others who are similarly affected, interpret another's poetry by divine instinct. If human genius is not sufficient to perceive poetry already delivered, it will be much less sufficient for its invention. Therefore, neither Homer nor any other who was truly a poet achieved poetry without heavenly inspiration. Socrates shows this in other ways here. First: poets deliver all arts and sciences, but it is impossible for a human to have learned them all through study, when it is difficult to perceive even one in part. Therefore, they bring them forth not by human art, but by a certain divine infusion. The proof of this is that most prophets, after the impulse of frenzy has receded, do not immediately understand what they have written, even though they treated individual arts correctly while in the frenzy—things which the craftsmen of those arts can judge by reading. Furthermore, we often see a crude and inept man suddenly emerge as a good poet and produce something magnificent and divine...

<summary>This page contains the conclusion of Plato's Theaetetus and the beginning of Marsilio Ficino's influential introduction to the Ion, where he details the Neoplatonic theory of the four divine frenzies (Poetry, Mystery, Prophecy, and Love) as a path for the soul's ascent back to the One.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Theaetetus, Marsilio Ficino, Lorenzo de' Medici, Ion, Divine Frenzy, Neoplatonism, The One, Poetic Inspiration, Rhapsode, Muses, Apollo, Dionysus, Venus, Chariot Allegory</keywords>

--- Page 136 ---
->Ion, Or, On Poetic Frenzy.<- 117

...and sing something divine. To achieve great things in a moment is not characteristic of human genius, but of one inspired by divinity. In this matter, see how God shows that this intelligence is infused by His will. To demonstrate that this is so, He often seizes inept men rather than the clever, and the mad rather than the prudent, lest if He used sharp and prudent men for this, it might be thought these things happened through human subtlety and industry. Since, therefore, it is not from fortune nor from art, it is granted to poets by God and the Muses. When he says "God," he means Apollo; when "Muses," he means the souls of the spheres of the world. Jupiter is indeed the mind of God; from him comes Apollo, the mind of the soul of the world, and the soul of the whole world; and the souls of the eight celestial spheres. These nine souls are called the nine Muses because, while they move the heavens harmonically, they produce musical melody; which, distributed into nine sounds—namely, the tones of the eight spheres and the one concord of them all—produces the nine Sirens singing to God. Therefore, from Jupiter comes Apollo; and the Muses come from Apollo—that is, the chorus of the Muses is led by the mind of the soul of the world. For just as that mind is illuminated by Jupiter, so it illuminates the souls of the world and the spheres. The steps by which that frenzy descends are these: Jupiter seizes Apollo. Apollo illuminates the Muses. The Muses awaken and drive the gentle and insuperable souls of the prophets <note>original: "vatum"</note>. The inspired prophets inspire their interpreters. The interpreters move the listeners. Other souls are seized by other Muses, because other souls are attributed to other spheres and stars, as is taught in the *Timaeus*. The Muse Calliope is the voice resulting from all the voices of the spheres. Urania is the Muse of the starry sky, so named for its dignity. Polymnia is of Saturn, because of the memory of ancient things which Saturn provides, and a dry, cold complexion. Terpsichore is Jupiter, for he is health-bringing to the chorus of men. Clio is Mars, because of the desire for glory. Melpomene is the Sun, because it is the tempering of the whole world. Erato is Venus, because of love. Euterpe is Mercury, because of honest delight in serious matters. Thalia is the Moon, because of the greenness <note>vitality/growth</note> she provides to things here. Likewise, Apollo is the flower of the soul, his lyre is the body of the sun; its four strings are his four movements: annual, monthly, daily, and oblique; the four voices are *neates*, *hypates*, *doriones*, and *gemini*; the four triplicities of the lunar signs, from which the four qualities of the seasons are produced. Calliope inspired Orpheus, Urania inspired Musaeus, Clio inspired Homer, Polymnia inspired Pindar. Erato inspired Sappho, Melpomene inspired Thamyras, Terpsichore inspired Hesiod, Thalia inspired Maro <note>Virgil</note>, Euterpe inspired Naso <note>Ovid</note>. Phœbus seized Linus, and the same Phœbus now drives you, noble Lorenzo—Phœbus, I say, who gave prophecy to your grandfather Cosimo, but gave the bow and medicines to your father Piero, and finally gave the lyre and songs to you.

->SOCRATES, ION.<-

**SOCRATES.** I bid Ion welcome. From where have you come to us now? Do you come from your home in Ephesus? **ION.** By no means, O Socrates, but from Epidaurus, from the festivals of Asclepius. **SOCRATES.** Did the Epidaurians establish a contest for the rhapsodes—that is, those who recite the poems of poets—in honor of the God? **ION.** Not in these alone, but also in every other kind of music. **SOCRATES.** What then? Did you not compete there for us? How was it; did you compete? **ION.** We carried away the first prizes of the contests, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Well said. Come, let us also obtain victory in the celebration of Pallas. **ION.** These things shall be, if God wills. **SOCRATES.** Truly, O Ion, I have always valued your art highly, because it is fitting for your art that you adorn your body and always appear as beautiful as possible, and that you must be constantly occupied with many good poets, and especially with Homer, the best and most divine of all poets; and not only to learn his songs by heart, but also his meanings. For no one could ever become a rhapsode unless he understood the things said by the poet. For the rhapsode must interpret the mind of the poet to the listeners; which certainly cannot be done rightly if one is ignorant of the poet's meaning. All these things are worthy of our emulation. **ION.** You speak the truth, O Socrates; and I have indeed labored most on this. I profess that I can explain Homer more brilliantly than any other, so that neither Metrodorus of Lampsacus, nor Stesimbrotus of Thasos, nor Glaucon, nor any of the ancients could ever explain so many and such brilliant meanings of Homer as I. **SOCRATES.** Rightly so, O Ion. It is clear that no envy will prevent you from opening these to me. **ION.** And it is truly worth hearing, O Socrates, how magnificently I have adorned Homer. For which reason I think it is just that I be crowned with a golden crown by those who are students of Homer. **SOCRATES.** I shall certainly find leisure to hear you at some point; but now answer me this one thing: can you do this only regarding Homer, or also regarding Hesiod and Archilochus? **ION.** By no means; only regarding Homer. For that seems sufficient to me. **SOCRATES.** Are there some things about which Homer and Hesiod say the same? **ION.** I think there are many. **SOCRATES.** Would you explain better the things that Homer says, or what Hesiod says? **ION.** Equally concerning both, O Socrates, in those matters where they say the same. **SOCRATES.** But what about those things where they do not say the same? For example, Homer and Hesiod both speak about prophecy. **ION.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And in what these poets agree or disagree when they speak of prophecy, would you explain better than some skilled prophet? **ION.** A prophet would explain it better. **SOCRATES.** But if you were a prophet, could you not explain not only those things where they agree, but also where they disagree? **ION.** It is obvious. **SOCRATES.** What further? Are you only powerful and eloquent regarding Homer? And regarding Hesiod and other poets not at all? Does Homer deal with other subjects than those which other poets also treat? Has he not narrated many things pertaining to war, and the customs of the good and the bad toward each other, both private citizens and craftsmen? And about the gods, how they deal with each other and with men, and about celestial affections? Likewise about those things that are in the underworld, and the genealogies of gods and heroes? Does not all the poetry of Homer revolve around these? **ION.** You speak the truth, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Do not other poets sing the same things? **ION.** The same, certainly, but not the others as Homer does. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps worse? **ION.** Much worse. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, Homer better? **ION.** Better, certainly. **SOCRATES.** O Ion, you charming head, when many speak about numbers, and one of them speaks correctly, can anyone not recognize the one who speaks well in that matter? **ION.** One can. **SOCRATES.** Is it that same person who recognizes the one speaking poorly, or another? **ION.** The same one. **SOCRATES.** Is this not the one who is gifted in the art of arithmetic? **ION.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** When many speak about foods, which are healthy, and someone speaks correctly about that matter, will one person notice the one speaking well because he is correct, and another notice the one speaking poorly because he is wrong? Or the one and the same? **ION.** The same, without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Who is this? What is his name? **ION.** A doctor. **SOCRATES.** Do we not say generally, when many speak about the same thing, that one and the same person will distinguish both the one who speaks poorly and the one who speaks well? And unless he knows the one who errs in that same matter, he will never recognize the one who thinks correctly? **ION.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Is not the same person skilled in both? **ION.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** You assert that Homer and other poets, among whom are Hesiod and Archilochus, say the same things? Yet not in the same way, but Homer better, and the others worse? **ION.** And I speak the truth.

**SOCRATES.**

**SOCRATES.** If you recognize the one who speaks well, you understand those who speak poorly, that they err. **ION.** That is agreed. **SOCRATES.** If therefore we say, O best of men, that Ion is similarly skilled and powerful regarding Homer and other poets, we shall by no means err: since he himself admits that the same judge is suitable regarding all those who are occupied in the same matter, and that almost all poets imagine the same things. **ION.** Why is it then, O Socrates, that when someone discusses another poet, I neither pay attention, nor can I say anything worthy of consideration, but I utterly yawn and am numb; but as soon as someone makes mention of Homer, I am immediately awakened and pay attention, and whatever I set out to say follows? **SOCRATES.** It is by no means difficult, O friend, to guess the cause of this. For it is clear that you are able to speak skillfully about Homer neither by art nor by knowledge. For if it were by art, you would be able to speak similarly about all other poets, for poetry is a whole. Is it not? **ION.** It is, certainly. **SOCRATES.** Is it not true that after someone has acquired any other complete art, he judges equally all things that fall under that art? Indeed, the same reasoning must be considered concerning all arts. Do you want me to tell you how I mean this? **ION.** I desire it, by Jove, O Socrates. For as often as I have heard you wise men, I am immediately affected by a certain wonderful joy. **SOCRATES.** I wish, O Ion, that you were telling the truth. But you rhapsodes and actors are the wise ones, and those whose poems you sing. I, however, speak nothing but the truth, as becomes a common man <note>original: "idiotam"</note>. For look at how light and easy to know is the thing I was just testing: so that anyone could perceive what I was narrating—that the consideration is the same for the rest, if someone has acquired a complete art for himself. Consider the cause: is not the art of painting a certain whole? **ION.** It is. **SOCRATES.** Have there not been and are there not many painters, some good and some bad? **ION.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Have you ever seen anyone who could sufficiently show those things which Polygnotus the son of Aglaophon painted correctly and not correctly, but could not do so for other painters; and if someone showed the work of other painters, he would fall asleep, and have no faculty for saying or guessing anything; but when a judgment must be made about Polygnotus, or about any single painter, he would wake up, pay attention, and have the faculty of speaking? **ION.** No, by Jove. **SOCRATES.** What about in the crafting of statues? Have you seen anyone who can explain what Daedalus son of Metion, or Epius son of Panopeus, or Theodorus of Samos, or any other maker of statues has well engineered, but in the works of other sculptors he is numb and silent? **ION.** By Jove, I have never found one such person. **SOCRATES.** And yet, neither in the playing of flutes, I think, nor in the plucking of the cithara; nor in that singing to the cithara, nor in rhapsodizing have you seen a man who can express the works of Olympus, or of Thamyras, or of Orpheus, or of Phemius the rhapsode of Ithaca, but in the works of Ion of Ephesus he fails, and can neither perceive nor compare what is played well and what is played otherwise. **ION.** I have nothing to say against you in this, but nevertheless I am conscious in myself that I report the most beautiful things about Homer more than all other men, and that a bounty of speech does not fail me; and that all others praise me in this matter, but in other poets they do not at all. See why this seems so to you. **SOCRATES.** I see, O Ion, and I will begin to open to you what it seems to me to be. Your ability to speak well about Homer is not an art, as I was just saying, but it is a divine power that moves you, like that in the stone which Euripides named the Magnet, and which some call the Heraclean stone. This stone not only attracts iron rings, but even infuses power into the rings themselves, so that they can do this same thing and, just like the stone, attract other rings. Thus a long chain of iron and rings often hangs from one another, and for all of them the power is drawn from that stone. So the Muse herself inspires poets by divine instinct; those inspired poets catch others in their frenzy. Therefore, from all these, the series itself is woven together. Thus all good epic poets utter all those brilliant poems not by art, but by being possessed by a divine inspiration—and good lyric poets similarly: just as the Corybantes dance when they are not in their right mind, so the excellent lyric poets imagine these songs when they are not in their right mind. But when they rise into harmony and rhythm, they are seized and become like Bacchants—as the Bacchant women, when they are not in their right mind, draw honey and milk from the rivers, but cannot draw them when in their right mind—and the soul of the lyric poets does that which they themselves narrate. For the poets tell us that, drawing from the springs where honey gushes forth, and plucking from the gardens and hills of the Muses, they bring songs to us, just as bees bring honey from flowers; and they say they fly like bees. In this matter they speak the truth: for a poet is a light, winged, and sacred thing, and he cannot sing before he is full of God, and placed outside himself, and alienated from his mind. For as long as someone is healthy in mind, no one can either imagine songs or give oracles. Therefore, they do not sing these brilliant things which you report about Homer by any art, but by a certain divine lot each can correctly achieve that to which the Muse has incited him. This one sings Dithyrambs, that one praises of someone, this one *Hyporchemata* <note>dance-songs</note> and choruses, another epic poems, another again iambic verses. But in the rest, each of them is rude and inept. For they say these things not by art, but by divine power. For if they knew how to speak correctly about any one of these by art, they would be able to do the same for all others. For this reason, God, snatching away their mind, uses them as His ministers and as messengers of oracles and as divine prophets, so that we who hear may perceive that it is not they who report such worthy things when they are not in possession of their minds, but that it is God who speaks these things and shouts them to us through them. Tynnichus of Chalcis can be an evident proof of this matter, who before had composed no poem worthy of memory; but he says he discovered the hymn to Apollo which everyone sings—almost the most beautiful of all songs—by the inspiration of the Muses. In this especially, God seems to have shown us that we must not doubt that these brilliant poems are works of the divine and the gods rather than human works and those of men. Poets, moreover, are nothing else than interpreters of the gods, while they are seized by frenzy, by whichever deity one may be seized. Desiring to show this, God intentionally sang the most beautiful melody through the most inept poet. Do I not seem to you to speak the truth? **ION.** To me certainly, by Jove. And with these speeches, Socrates, you soothe and affect my soul. And by a certain divine lot from the gods, distinguished poets seem to interpret these things to us. **SOCRATES.** Do you rhapsodes not interpret the writings of the poets? **ION.** You say the truth. **SOCRATES.** Are you not therefore interpreters of interpreters? **ION.** We are. **SOCRATES.** Pay attention to what I want, and answer me this, O Ion: do not hide from me what I shall ask you: when you report songs aptly, and render the spectators struck with wonder—whether when you sing of Ulysses leaping onto the threshold, revealing himself openly to the suitors and pouring out the arrows before his feet, or Achilles making an onset against Hector, or...

...or when you bring forth something miserable and complaining about Andromache, or Hecuba, or Priam, are you then in possession of your mind? Or are you alienated from your mind? And does your soul, inspired by the deeds you report, think it is present at them, whether they happened in Ithaca, or at Troy, or wherever the songs may snatch you? **ION.** It is perceived clearly by me; my heart leaps. **SOCRATES.** I shall recount this to you, nor will I hide it. For as often as I say anything miserable, my eyes are filled with tears. When I say something terrible or powerful, my hair stands up because of terror, and my heart leaps. **SOCRATES.** Shall we then say that man is in possession of his mind who, adorned with a beautiful robe and golden crowns in sacrifices and celebrations, weeps, though he has lost none of these things? Or he who trembles too much when he is situated among twenty thousand friendly people, with no one either stripping him or doing him injury? **ION.** No, by Jove, O Socrates, if we are willing to confess the truth. **SOCRATES.** Do you not affect the multitude of spectators with these same things? **ION.** Truly, very much so: for I always look down from the platform itself at those weeping, and looking grim, and struck with wonder at the things which are narrated. And I must pay great attention to them. For if I strike tears from them, I myself, receiving money, will laugh. But if I move them to laughter, I myself, losing money, will weep. **SOCRATES.** Do you see that the spectator is the last of the rings—of those, I say, whom I mentioned as receiving power from one another under the magnet stone? You, the reciter and actor, are the middle; and the poet himself is the first; but God, through all those, draws the soul of men wherever He wishes, while He suspends and transmits the power from one to another. From this, just as from that stone, a long series hangs, by which those who dance in the chorus, and the masters and sub-masters, are linked step by step on the side; the rings are suspended from the Muse of this chain, and of the poets, one is suspended from one Muse, and another again from another Muse. We call it "being possessed," which is indeed very close to it. For from these first rings, which are the poets, others again are seized by others, and become divine: some are possessed by Orpheus, others by Musaeus; and not a few are occupied and held by Homer, of whom you, O Ion, are one who has been seized by frenzy from Homer. And if someone should sing the writings of another poet, you fall asleep, and the faculty of speaking fails you; but if someone sings a melody of this poet, you are immediately awakened, your soul leaps, and the faculty of speaking is sufficient. For you do not recount those things which you say about Homer by art or knowledge, but by a certain divine lot and occupation of the mind. And just as the Corybantes are keenly sensitive only to that melody which belongs to that god by whom they are seized, and they abound in words and figures fitting to that harmony, but despise others: so you too, O Ion, if anyone mentions Homer, are eloquent in speaking, but in others your abundance fails you. Therefore, the cause of that which we were seeking—why you are copious regarding Homer, but fail regarding others—is this: that you are a heavy praiser of Homer not by art, but by a divine lot. **ION.** You speak rightly, O Socrates; yet I would be surprised if you discussed so keenly as to persuade me entirely that I celebrate Homer with praises when I am crazed and frantic <note>original: "lymphatus at que fures"</note>; for I do not think I seem frantic to you if you were to hear me speaking about Homer. **SOCRATES.** And yet I wish to hear, but not before you answer me from those things of which Homer speaks, which he speaks best. **ION.** About everything. **SOCRATES.** Do you not know, O Ion, that he does not speak about everything? **ION.** Yes, about everything, I say. **SOCRATES.** However, you do not handle well those things which you are ignorant of, but which Homer writes. **ION.** What are those things which Homer narrates, but I do not know? **SOCRATES.** Does he not frequently explain many things about arts? As about the discipline of chariot-driving. If I remember, I will recite his verses to you. **ION.** But I will report them; for I remember. **SOCRATES.** Tell me what Nestor commands his son Antilochus, when he warns him to turn the horses cautiously in the horse race established for the sake of Patroclus. **ION.**
"Lean yourself in the well-polished chariot a little to the left of the horses, and urge the right-hand horse with a shout and blows, and give him the reins with your hands. But let the left-hand horse draw near the post, so that the hub of the well-wrought wheel seems to touch the edge, but avoid touching the stone." <note>This is a Latin poetic rendering of Iliad 23.335-340</note>
**SOCRATES.** These are enough, O Ion. Whether Homer speaks correctly or otherwise in these verses, would a doctor or a charioteer perceive better? **ION.** A charioteer, without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Is this judgment made by art, or by something else? **ION.** By nothing else but art. **SOCRATES.** Is not the faculty of judging a certain work granted by God to each art? For we will not perceive by the medical art those things which we know by the art of steering. **ION.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Nor will we notice by architecture those things which we see by medicine. **ION.** No indeed. **SOCRATES.** Is it not similarly in all arts: that those things which we comprehend by one certain art, we will by no means comprehend by another? But answer me this first. Do you assert that one art is different from another? **ION.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Do you distinguish arts by the same conjecture as I? For when the knowledge of these things is of one kind, and that of other things is another, I call this one art and that another art. Do you? **ION.** I do. **SOCRATES.** For if the knowledge were about the same things, why would we call this one thing and that another? Since the same would be known by both. Just as it is perceived by me that these are five fingers, and you notice this same thing just as I do. Whence if I were to ask you whether we know these same things by the same art of arithmetic or by another, you would certainly answer by the same. **ION.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Tell me what I had asked a little before: whether it seems to you that it should be said according to all arts, that it is necessary that the same things be known by the same art, but not the same things by another art, but certain other things, since the art itself is different. **ION.** So it seems to me, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** If someone has not attained a certain art, he will by no means be able to discern the words or deeds of this art well. **ION.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Those verses which you reported, whether they are sung well or poorly by Homer, would you or a charioteer perceive better? **ION.** A charioteer. **SOCRATES.** For you are a reciter, not a charioteer. **ION.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** The faculty of a reciter is different from that of a charioteer. **ION.** Obviously. **SOCRATES.** But if it is another art, it is also a knowledge of other things. **ION.** Of other things, certainly. **SOCRATES.** What then when Homer brings forward that Hecamede, the mistress of Nestor, offers a healing potion to the wounded Machaon, into which she pours Pramnian wine, and moreover grates goat cheese with a certain bronze instrument, and also mixes flour with the cheese, and adds an onion as a relish to these? Whether these are said correctly or otherwise by Homer, is it a judgment of the medical art or the reciter's art? **ION.** Of medicine. **SOCRATES.** What when Homer says,
"She plunged into the sea like a leaden weight, which, fastened to the horn of an ox, goes down to the bottom, bringing death to the ravenous fish." <note>Iliad 24.80-82</note>
What these things mean, and whether they are said correctly or otherwise, will not the art of fishermen notice better than that of reciters? **ION.** It is clear that the art of fishermen judges that. **SOCRATES.** If you were to ask me thus: "Since, O Socrates, you have found in the poems of Homer what belongs to each of those arts that were mentioned, come now, find for me what things it is fitting to be judged by a prophet and prophecy, whether they are said correctly or otherwise by Homer"—see how easily and truly I would answer you. ...frequently in the *Odyssey* he writes, especially those things which the prophet Theoclymenus, son of Melampus, says against the suitors:
"O miserable men, what evil is this that you suffer? Your heads and faces and knees are wrapped in night. A cry of wailing blazes forth, your cheeks are wet with tears. Frequently also in the *Iliad*, as in the storming of the walls, he touches upon those things which pertain to a prophet. There he says thus:
"For an omen had come to them as they were eager to cross, a high-flying eagle, skirting the host on the left, bearing in its talons a monstrous blood-red snake, still alive and struggling; nor had it yet forgotten the joy of battle. For it bit the eagle that held it on the breast beside the neck, writhing backward. The eagle, stung by the pain, cast it from him to the ground, and it fell in the midst of the throng; and he himself, with a cry, flew away on the blasts of the wind." <note>Iliad 12.200-207</note>

Are you so forgetful? And yet it does not become a reciter to be a forgetful man. **ION.** What do I forget? **SOCRATES.** Do you not hold in memory that you said the art of reciting was different from that of the charioteer? **ION.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Did you not confess that since it is different, it has a different knowledge? **ION.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, according to your mind, the art of reciting will not perceive everything, nor will the reciter himself. **ION.** Nay, everything except for such things. **SOCRATES.** When you say "except for such things," you mean almost those which belong to other arts. But what things will he know, since he does not know everything? **ION.** He will know what it is decent for a man to say, what a woman, a slave, a free man, a subject, a prince—he will know all these things. **SOCRATES.** What it is decent for a prince to say on a ship tossed by a storm at sea, will the reciter know better than the navigator? **ION.** No, but the navigator will perceive this better. **SOCRATES.** But those things which are decent for a prince to say in sickness, will the reciter understand better than the doctor? **ION.** Nor these. **SOCRATES.** But those things which are fitting for a slave, you say? **ION.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** For example, what it is decent for a slave who is a cowherd to say when he is talking about raging and wild cattle—will the reciter himself know, and not the cowherd? **ION.** By no means. **SOCRATES.** What about those things which are decent for a woman to report to a weaver about wool-working? **ION.** No. **SOCRATES.** Those things which it is decent for a man who is a general of an army to say when he is exhorting the soldiers, will he know? **ION.** Such things, certainly, are what the reciter recognizes. **SOCRATES.** Is the art of reciting the same as that of the general? **ION.** I, at least, would understand what it is decent for a general to say, if it were necessary. **SOCRATES.** For perhaps you are also a general, Ion. For if you were powerful in both the equestrian and the cithara-playing disciplines at once, you would recognize those who ride well and those who ride poorly. And if I were to ask you, O Ion, by which art—equestrian or the art of the cithara-player—you recognize those who ride well, what would you answer me? **ION.** By the equestrian art. **SOCRATES.** And if you recognized those who pluck the cithara well, would you confess that you recognized them not by the equestrian art, but by the discipline of the cithara-player? **ION.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** But since you understand those things which pertain to a general, do you know them by the general's art or the reciter's art? **ION.** It seems to me to make no difference. **SOCRATES.** How do you say it makes no difference? Do you posit the general's art and the reciter's art as one, or two? **ION.** It seems one to me. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, whoever is a good reciter will also be a good general? **ION.** Most especially, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** And he who is the best general of an army, is he also a good reciter? **ION.** I do not think so. **SOCRATES.** However, you admit that whoever is a good reciter is a good general. **ION.** Strongly so. **SOCRATES.** Are you not the best reciter of the Greeks? **ION.** Clearly, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Are you not the best general of the Greeks? **ION.** Certainly, O Socrates. For I learned these things in the writings of Homer. **SOCRATES.** Why then, by the gods, since you are the best leader of an army of all Greeks, and the best reciter, do you sing songs everywhere but never serve as a soldier? Does it seem to you that a reciter adorned with a golden crown is of more use to the Greeks than a general by no means? **ION.** Our city, O Socrates <note>Ephesus</note>, is under yours and is governed with you, and therefore does not need a general. But your republic and that of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> would never choose me as a leader of an army. For you think you are suitable leaders. **SOCRATES.** O best Ion, do you not know Apollodorus of Cyzicus? **ION.** Which Apollodorus? **SOCRATES.** The one whom the Athenians often chose as general, even though he was a guest, and Phanosthenes of Andros, and Heraclides of Clazomenae. To these men, though they were foreigners, because they were held to be outstanding men, this city mandates commands and other powers. Will it not then decree an Ephesian general, and affect him with honor, if he is seen to excel in virtue? What then, are not you Ephesians Athenians by ancient origin, and Ephesus inferior to no city? But you, O Ion, if indeed you speak the truth and are able to praise Homer by knowledge and art, you do me an injury: you who, having professed to know many and beautiful things about Homer, and having promised to show them to me, now deceive me, and are very far from showing them. Indeed, you do not even wish to open what those things are in which you are skilled, nor with what faculty you are instructed, despite my long pleading. Instead, like a varied Proteus, you change in various ways, turning yourself up and down and into everything, so that finally escaping me, you have turned into a General, lest you show me how much faculty you are gifted with in promulgating the wisdom of Homer. For if this is in you by art, as I just said, and you deceive me after promising to explain, you are certainly unjust. But if you lack art, and by a certain divine lot are seized by Homer, though you understand nothing, you say many and beautiful things about this poet—as I was judging about you—you do no injury. Choose which you prefer: to be thought an unjust man by us, or a divine one. **ION.** It differs greatly, O Socrates, and it is much more beautiful to be judged divine. **SOCRATES.** This, therefore, which is more beautiful, is granted to you by us, O Ion: that you are a divine rather than an artful praiser of Homer.

->PREFACE OF PROCLUS TO PLATO'S SOPHIST, translated by Marsilio Ficino.<-

Plato calls the "Sophist" not only a certain man, but also Love, Pluto, Jupiter; and he calls the sophistic art most brilliant. From which we understand that this dialogue regards a more noble subject than it appears. For the invention, according to the great Iamblichus, is to treat of the sublunary craftsman. For he is a maker of idols, a purifier of souls, always separating them from contrary reasons, a transmutator, and a mercenary hunter of wealthy youths. While he receives souls full of reasons coming from above, he receives a reward from them, the very fabric of animals, which is made according to the reason of mortals. Here to that which is not...

# Sophist, Or, on Being. 121

<margin>Love as a mage and nature as a mage.</margin>
The Sophist leans toward that which is not <note>original: "non ens"</note>, because he produces things that exist in matter. And he loves what is truly false, which is to say, matter. At the same time, he looks toward that which is truly real. He is also "many-headed" <note>original: "multiceps"</note>, since he claims many essences and lives for himself, through which he arranges the variety of generation itself. Likewise, he is a "mage" <term>Magus (Mage): Here used to mean a sorcerer or someone who uses charms to enchant others, rather than a wise man.</term> of generation, as he soothes and allures souls with natural reasons, to such an extent that by the spell and nature of the mage he is moved by generation. Indeed, both love and nature are called "mages" by some because of the reciprocal attractions and allurements that proceed according to nature. Now, therefore, he wishes to declare the Sophist in every way. For even the philosopher is a kind of sophist, insofar as he imitates the celestial creator and the creator of generation. And the power of distinction imitates the progress of things from the One, and the creator of generation imitates the celestial creator; therefore, he is a sophist. And even man himself is called a sophist because he imitates great things. For this reason, he called the sophist "manifold." The Stranger from Elea represents the father of creators, the super-celestial and absolute. The listeners, however, represent the intelligences of the creator. The former represents Jove (Jupiter), the latter represents the angelic nature, acting as an interpreter and geometer. and since the work of the creators begins from the imperfect and ends in the perfect, that Stranger deals first with Theodorus, and then, through a conversion, with Socrates himself.

## PLATO’S SOPHIST, OR, ON THAT WHICH IS, OR, ON BEING.
*
### THE ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.

AFTER the *Theaetetus*, which dealt with knowledge, the *Sophist* must be read, which deals with Being itself, which is the object of knowledge. While Being is discussed here—which is the concern of the philosopher—non-being <note>original: "non ente"</note> is also treated, toward which the sophist declines. <margin>Among the Pythagoreans and Plato, only God is "sophos" (wise). Who is a philosopher?</margin> Among the Pythagoreans and Plato, only God is "sophos," that is, wise. The true philosopher is an imitator of God. The Sophist is an ambitious and deceptive emulator of the philosopher. Plato brings forward six definitions of the Sophist. But since a definition cannot be had without division—through which those things which do not belong to the thing being defined are separated from it, and its genus is divided by differences, from which finally the species is composed and defined alongside the genus—therefore, Plato, intending to define the Sophist, first devises the most exact partitions. He warns that no one can discern the hidden nature of any thing unless he has thoroughly separated it from foreign qualities. Accordingly, he brings forth descriptions of Being and non-being according to his ability; Being, just as in the *Parmenides*, he subjects to the One. He counts five genera of Being: Essence, the Same, the Other, Rest, and Motion. He teaches that true essence belongs to incorporeal things, while imaginary essence belongs to corporeal ones. Furthermore, he greatly detests those who deny the incorporeal, as well as those who think either that all things only move, or only stay still. Likewise, he disputes concerning knowledge and concerning true or false opinion and speech, and concerning the verb and the noun, insofar as it seems to pertain to the dispute over Being itself. Finally, after he has disputed concerning the sophist and the philosopher together, he concludes the book with a certain divinely inspired sentence: namely, that natural things are the works of God. <margin>Natural things are the works of God.</margin> For he had proved that all works of nature proceed from a certain divine wisdom infused into the world. Shadowy and deceptive things, however, he says are the tricks of demons. In the same place, he says that the sophist is hidden from us as if wrapped in the darkness of non-being—that is, falsehood—and that the philosopher is likewise hidden, though for a different reason: namely, because he is surrounded on all sides by the splendor of Being itself, which is divine truth, utterly surpassing the gaze of ordinary minds.

->THEODORUS, SOCRATES, THE STRANGER FROM ELEA (WHO IS PERHAPS MELISSUS), THEAETETUS.<-

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue.</margin>
**THEODORUS.** We have come, O Socrates, just as we agreed among ourselves, and we bring this Stranger here with us. He is an Eleatic by nation, but a very different and unlike man from Parmenides and Zeno, his contemporaries; yet he is an excellent philosopher. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps, O Theodorus, while you believe you are bringing a guest-man with you, you are bringing some god. For Homer says that while other gods visit, the god of hospitality especially dwells among men who partake in just shame, <margin>Odyssey 17. God is among the prudent men.</margin> to inspect the insults and injuries of men. Perhaps one of the higher powers has followed you here to observe and correct us who wander from the methods of disputation—a god of refutation, as it were. **THEODORUS.** This is not the custom, O Socrates, of this Stranger. He is more modest than those who are devoted to contentions. And he seems to me to be not a god, though he is a man, but certainly divine. Indeed, I call all philosophers divine. **SOCRATES.** And rightly so, my friend. But the genus of philosophers is not much easier to discern, so to speak, than that of the gods. For all those who philosophize not fictitiously, but truly, appear in many forms because of the ignorance of others, as they go about cities and look down from above upon the life of those below. And these men are estimated by some as nothing, while by others they are honored most highly. Sometimes they appear as statesmen, at other times as sophists, and sometimes, in the opinion of some, they are considered altogether insane. Therefore, I desire to inquire of this Stranger, if it should be pleasing to him, what his associates in Elea feel about these things, and what they say they are, and how they name them. **THEODORUS.** What things? **SOCRATES.** The Sophist, I mean, the Statesman, and the Philosopher. **THEODORUS.** What specifically, and what sort of doubt regarding these things would you like to ask? **SOCRATES.** This: whether they wish all these to be one thing, or two. Or just as there are three names, whether they distinguished three genera, assigning individual names to individual genera. **THEODORUS.** But will you not be burdened, or how shall we say, O Stranger? <note>to the Stranger</note> He will not be burdened, O Theodorus, for I think he will explain these things to us, nor is it difficult to say that they thought there were three. But to distinguish them individually and define what each one is, is neither a small task nor an easy one. **THEODORUS.** You have happened upon the same question, O Socrates, that we were asking him before we came here; and he then replied to us the same things he now replies to you: that he has indeed heard and remembers. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, in that which we first asked, you ought to gratify us, O Stranger. But first declare this to us: whether you are accustomed to explain what you wish to teach by yourself in a continuous speech, or rather by questioning, as Parmenides used to do? I heard him once when I was a youth disputing in that way when he was a very old man, and bringing forth most beautiful arguments. <margin>Parmenides used to dispute by questioning.</margin> **STRANGER.** If someone responds in a friendly and calm manner, it is easier to discourse with another by questioning; if not, it is easier for each to dispute by himself. **SOCRATES.** You may therefore choose whomever you wish from these. For all will obey most willingly. I indeed advise you to choose some youth, either this Theaetetus, or another who seems more fit to you. **STRANGER.** It would shame me, O Socrates, since I am speaking with you for the first time, not to return word for word in turn, but to begin a prolix sermon, whether I dispute alone by myself, or with another responding for the sake of demonstration. For no one should trust that what was just asked can be easily explained. For it requires a long disputation. On the other hand, if I do not comply with you and these others, especially when you have asked so modestly, it seems to me it would be something rustic and foreign to the gentleness of a guest. Especially since I am to have this Theaetetus as a companion in the disputation, based on what I said and what you just ordered. **THEODORUS.** Certainly, O Stranger, as Socrates says, you will gratify everyone. **STRANGER.** Nothing further needs to be said against this, Theaetetus. It is with you that I must deal next; if perhaps the length of the speech becomes tedious to you, and you are burdened by the labor, I pray you, do not accuse me, but these your associates who are the cause. **THEAETETUS.** I do not think it will be bothersome; for if...
