<margin>Life, soul, and mind cannot be absent from that which truly is.</margin> Regarding that which is altogether and truly, must we really be persuaded that it is completely devoid of wisdom—that it neither lives, nor thinks, nor possesses a venerable and holy mind, but instead stands completely still and motionless? THEAETETUS. That would be an altogether absurd thing to grant, Stranger. STRANGER. Shall we say then that it has a mind, but not life? THEAETETUS. How could that be? STRANGER. Or shall we say both are in it, but that they are not contained within a soul? THEAETETUS. But in what other way could it contain them? STRANGER. Then must we say it possesses mind, life, and soul? And yet, though it is fully animate, does it stand motionless? THEAETETUS. All these things seem to me to be devoid of reason. STRANGER. We must therefore admit that what is moved and motion itself are present as things that exist. THEAETETUS. What stands in the way? STRANGER. From this, O Theaetetus, it follows that mind is present in nothing among the things that are motionless, anywhere or in any way. THEAETETUS. That follows clearly. <margin>Second definition of being.</margin> STRANGER. Nevertheless, if we agree that all things are in flux and agitated, by this discourse we shall remove "the same" itself from the class of existing things. THEAETETUS. In what way? STRANGER. Does it seem to you that what is said to be "according to the same things, in the same way, and regarding the same" could ever exist without stability? THEAETETUS. Not at all. STRANGER. Do you ever perceive mind, either past or present, existing without these? THEAETETUS. Minimally. STRANGER. One must fight with every effort of reason against anyone who, by removing knowledge, prudence, and mind, asserts anything else. THEAETETUS. And quite vehemently too. <margin>Third definition of being.</margin> STRANGER. It is necessary for the one who philosophizes and honors these things above all others, for this reason, neither to admit the speech of those who, introducing one or many forms of things, claim the whole stands alone, nor to listen to those who affirm only that <term>being</term> <note>original: "ens"</note> is moved. Rather, following the opinion of children, he should grasp all things together—as many as stand still or are moved—and call them both together "being" and "the all." THEAETETUS. You speak the truth. STRANGER. Does it not seem that we have now appropriately grasped "being" in our discourse? THEAETETUS. Entirely. STRANGER. My goodness, O Theaetetus, in what great ambiguity are we now tossed! For we seem to ourselves to know nothing now except the difficulty of the inquiry. THEAETETUS. To what end is this? STRANGER. Do you see, blessed one, that while we are deeply ignorant of it, we nevertheless think we are saying something about it? THEAETETUS. I think so too, but where we have deceived ourselves, I do not clearly understand. STRANGER. Observe more diligently, I pray you, whether if we grant these things, someone might rightly question us just as we ourselves previously questioned those who wanted the "all" to be hot and cold. THEAETETUS. In what way? Remind me, if you please. STRANGER. It pleases me indeed, and I shall try to do so; he would ask you now in the same way as he asked them, so that we might make some progress. THEAETETUS. Excellent. STRANGER. Do you not call motion and rest the most contrary to each other? THEAETETUS. Why not? STRANGER. Indeed, you say they "are" similarly, and both equally, and each of them. THEAETETUS. I certainly do. STRANGER. When you grant that each and both "are," do you then proclaim that they are moved? THEAETETUS. In no way. STRANGER. Or do you perhaps mean that they "stand," when you say both and each "are"? THEAETETUS. Neither this. STRANGER. Therefore, you are thinking of "being" itself as a third something, as if motion and rest were contained under it; you encompass both, and looking at their communion in essence, you name them both as "being" in this way. THEAETETUS. We truly seem to be prophesying a third something, "being" itself, when we say that motion and rest "are." STRANGER. For this reason, "being" itself is not these two—motion and rest—but something else besides them. THEAETETUS. So it appears. STRANGER. Thus, "being" by its own nature neither stands still entirely, nor is it moved. THEAETETUS. That is almost what must be said. STRANGER. Where then must the thought be turned so that the soul may have something certain and manifest concerning "being"? THEAETETUS. I do not know. STRANGER. I do not think it is easy anywhere. For if something is not moved, why does it not at least stand still? Or if it does not stand still, why is it not moved? But "being" appeared to us to be outside both of these; can that be possible? THEAETETUS. Least of all things. STRANGER. We must certainly remember this at present. THEAETETUS. What is that? STRANGER. That when we were asked about the name of <term>non-being</term> <note>original: "non ens"</note>, we were unable to declare to what it belonged. Do you remember? THEAETETUS. Why shouldn't I remember? STRANGER. Are we now in any less doubt regarding "being"? THEAETETUS. To me at least, Stranger, if it can be said, we seem to be even more at a loss now. STRANGER. Let this ambiguity be placed here; yet after both "being" and "non-being" have appeared equally obscure to us, there remains hope that henceforth, if one appears more clearly or obscurely, the other will appear similarly; and if one is entirely unknown, the other will be so as well. Therefore, let us pursue our discourse as much as we can together concerning both equally. THEAETETUS. Wisely said. STRANGER. Let us say plainly in what way we call this same thing by many names. THEAETETUS. Bring an example of this. STRANGER. Calling a man "one," we name him with many surnames, as we attribute to him colors, shapes, magnitudes, virtues, and vices—in all of which, and many others, we say he is not only a "man," but also "good" and many other things; and we act similarly in other cases. For taking any one thing, we then call it many things by many names. THEAETETUS. You speak truly. STRANGER. From this, I think, we have given occasion for opposition to young men and to old men of slow wit. For anyone can immediately object that it is impossible for many to be one, and one to be many. For this reason they exult while they do not allow a man to be called "good," but say "the good is good" and "the man is man." You have often encountered, I think, Theaetetus, men who study such quibbles, often even elders, who admire these things due to a poverty of wisdom, and boast as if they have discovered something magnificent. THEAETETUS. Quite so. STRANGER. So that our discourse may encompass all who have ever spoken anything about essence, let what we next submit by questioning be understood as being said against these people, as well as against those others we mentioned above. THEAETETUS. What are those things? STRANGER. Whether we shall join essence with neither motion nor rest, nor anything else with anything else, but rather treat things as if they cannot communicate with each other, separating them entirely in our speeches? Or shall we force all things into one, as if each could be mixed? Or will it be permitted in part, and in part not at all? Which of these, Theaetetus, do we think they will choose? THEAETETUS. I do not know what to answer for them. Why not investigate what follows from each by answering individually? STRANGER. You advise correctly. Let us assume then, if you wish, that they say nothing can communicate with anything in any way. Would not motion and rest, therefore, participate in essence in no way? THEAETETUS. Certainly in no way. STRANGER. Will either of them "be" something, since neither would be a participant in essence? THEAETETUS. It would not. STRANGER. Immediately, by this agreement, all things are overturned, as it seems—both the dogmas of those who want all things to be moved, and those who want them to stand as one; and even those who always think that the things that are exist in the same way and according to the same things, according to their forms. For all of them add "to be" to their claims, some saying things truly move, others saying they truly stand. THEAETETUS. It is exactly so. STRANGER. ### Book Fifteen [of Ficinus’s Plato Edition]

**[[page number: 132]]**

…all things, they sometimes divide into one, whether they divide from the one into infinite or into finite elements, and compose from these: similarly, whether they posit that this happens sometimes, or always: in all these things, I say, they say nothing of the truth, since there is no mixing of things.

**THE.** Correct.
**HOS.** Furthermore, we ourselves would transact speech most absurdly if we permitted nothing to be called by the name of another through the communion of an affection.
**THE.** How so?
**HOS.** They are forced to use “being” itself regarding each individual thing in some way, and “itself,” and “the other,” and “according to itself,” and innumerable other terms: since they cannot abstain from interfering with these in their speeches, they need no refutations from others, but, as it is said, they have an enemy and adversary at home, murmuring within, always walking about like that absurd **Eurycles** [the ventriloquist]. 
*[[margin: Eurycles, a proverb.]]*
**THE.** What you say is true and a fitting likeness.
**HOS.** But what if we say all things have the power of mutual communion? This, surely, they themselves can refute.
**THE.** By what reasoning?
**HOS.** Because Motion itself would rest entirely, and Rest would be agitated, if they were mixed with one another. By a certain supreme necessity, it is impossible for Motion to stand or for Rest to move.
**THE.** Why not?
**HOS.** Therefore, only a third [option] remains.
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** For one of these is necessary: either all things mix, or none do, or some do and others not at all.
**THE.** Necessary indeed.
**HOS.** The first two certainly cannot be found [to be true].
**THE.** Certainly not.
**HOS.** It follows that whoever wishes to answer rightly must posit the remaining of the three.
**THE.** Most certainly.
**HOS.** Since some things wish to combine and others not at all, it happens nearly the same with things as it does with letters. For some letters are coupled with each other, others not at all.
**THE.** It is clear.
**HOS.** Indeed, the series of vowel letters is extended through all the others like a kind of bond, without which no letters can be bound to each other.
**THE.** Very much so.
**HOS.** Does everyone understand which letters agree with which? Or is there need of art to do this correctly?
**THE.** Of art.
**HOS.** Which?
**THE.** Grammar.
**HOS.** Is it not the same regarding the sounds of low and high pitches? For he who distinguishes consonant or dissonant voices by art is a musician; he who is ignorant is unskilled in music.
**THE.** It is so.
**HOS.** And in other arts and the defects of arts, we shall find other things of this kind.
**THE.** That is manifest indeed.
**HOS.** But when we have said that the kinds (*genera*) of things have mutual communion in the same way, must not he who is to show which kinds agree or disagree with which conduct his discourse by a certain science? And indeed, must he not know through all things if they agree so that they can be mixed, and in divisions again, if through all things there is another cause for the division?
**THE.** There is altogether a need for science, and perhaps the greatest of all.
**HOS.** What then shall we call this, **Theaetetus**? Have we not, by Jove, unknowingly stumbled into the science of free men? And while we were seeking the Sophist, we seem to have first found the Philosopher.
**THE.** How so?
**HOS.** To divide by kinds, and to think neither the same species to be another, nor another again to be the same—shall we not say this is the duty of Dialectic?
**THE.** We shall indeed.
**HOS.** Whoever can do this perceives acutely one idea stretched throughout many things, each one being placed separately; and many ideas which are diverse among themselves, contained externally under one; and again one idea coupled in one through many whole things; and many distinct things apart on every side. This, however, is to know: to discern through the kind (*genus*) how individuals can communicate in turn, and how they cannot.
**THE.** Entirely.
**HOS.** But indeed, you will give the work of Dialectic to no other, I think, than to him who purely and legitimately philosophizes.
**THE.** How could it be given to another?
**HOS.** We shall find the Philosopher indeed in such a place both now and hereafter, if we seek him, though even here he is not easily perceived. But the Sophist and the Philosopher flee the sight of the eyes by different reasons.
*[[margin: How the philosopher and the sophist hide.]]*
**THE.** By what?
**HOS.** I place the Sophist as fleeing into the darkness of non-being, and by long custom he is covered by that darkness; therefore, he is discerned with the greatest difficulty.
**THE.** It is so.
**HOS.** But the Philosopher, always clinging by reasoning to the idea of Being itself, is not easily perceived because of the brilliance of that region. For the eyes of common souls cannot sustain the rays of divinity.
*[[margin: The eyes of common souls cannot sustain the rays of divinity.]]*
**THE.** It is likely that these things are no less so than those.
**HOS.** We shall treat of this more clearly elsewhere, if it shall be permitted by will. But the Sophist is not to be dismissed until he is sufficiently known by us.
**THE.** Excellent.
**HOS.** Since, therefore, it is agreed among us that some kinds meet in turn, and others totally disagree, and some indeed with a few, others with many, and some also cohere with all things through all, let us follow the reasoning of this discourse, considering it in this manner. Not regarding all species, I say, lest we be confounded by the multitude, but choosing some of those which are called "greatest," first [seeing] what kind each is, then what power of mutual communion they have—such as Being and Non-being—so that if we cannot grasp them with a perfectly clear notion, at least we may not lack a reasoned discussion about them, as far as the condition of this investigation allows. For if we say that Non-being *is*, truly Non-being, as if imagining it, we may perhaps escape [the difficulty].
**THE.** It is fitting.
**HOS.** The greatest kinds of all, which we were just mentioning, are Being itself, and Rest, and Motion.
**THE.** Very much so.
**HOS.** It was said that these two [Rest and Motion] cannot be mixed together.
**THE.** Certainly.
**HOS.** But Being mixes with both: for both are, in some way.
**THE.** Nothing prevents it.
**HOS.** It follows that these are three.
**THE.** It follows.
**HOS.** Is not any one of these "other" than the remaining two, and "the same" as itself?
**HOS.** What? Have we now called "The Same" and "The Other" two kinds other than the three above, yet always necessarily annexed to them, such that we must think of five kinds? Or have we announced this "Same" and "Other" as something of those [three], though it escaped our notice?
**THE.** Perhaps.
**HOS.** But indeed, Motion and Rest are neither "The Other" nor "The Same."
**THE.** For what reason?
**HOS.** Because whatever we commonly call Motion or Rest cannot be either of those.
**THE.** Why?
**HOS.** Because Motion would rest, and Rest likewise would move. For regarding both, whichever of those two were effected would force the other to pass into the nature of its contrary, as a participant in the contrary.
**THE.** Entirely.
**HOS.** Yet both participate in "The Same" and "The Other."
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** Let us not say, then, that Motion is "The Same" or "The Other," or Rest similarly.
**THE.** Certainly not.
**HOS.** But should we think of "Being" and "The Same" as if they were one thing?
**THE.** Perhaps.
**HOS.** But if "Being" and "The Same" differ in no way from each other, whenever we say that Motion and Rest both *are*, we would be calling them both "the same" just as we call them "beings," but this is impossible.
**THE.** But this is impossible.
**HOS.** Therefore, "The Same" and "Being" cannot be one.
*[[margin: That being and the same are not one.]]*
**THE.** So it must almost be said.
**HOS.** Let us then place "The Same" itself as a fourth species besides the three above.
**THE.** Let us so place it.
**HOS.** Should we not place...

**[[page number: 133]]**

...“The Other” itself in the fifth place? Or should we think that this and “Being” denote one thing by two names?
**THE.** Perhaps.
**HOS.** I think, however, you will grant that of the things which are, some are themselves according to themselves, and others are referred to other things.
**THE.** Why not?
**HOS.** But “The Other” is always to another, is it not?
**THE.** Always.
**HOS.** This would not be so unless “The Other” and “Being” differed greatly from each other. But if “The Other” participated in both species, like “Being,” it would surely be something of those things which are “others,” and yet not “other” in relation to another; but now, whatever is truly “other,” it follows by necessity that according to what it is, it is “other” [to something else].
**THE.** It is as you say.
**HOS.** Therefore, it is fitting to place the nature of “The Other” itself as a fifth among the species to which we have joined it.
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** It must also be said that this runs through all of them. For each one of the others is “other,” not through its own nature, but because it is a participant in the idea of “The Other.”
**THE.** In truth.
**HOS.** Thus let us speak of the five, repeating them individually.
**THE.** What?
**HOS.** First, that Motion is entirely something other than Rest. Is it to be asserted so, or otherwise?
**THE.** Entirely so.
**HOS.** Therefore, it is not Rest.
**THE.** By no means.
**HOS.** But it *is*, because it is a participant in Being.
**THE.** It is.
**HOS.** Again, Motion is other than “The Same” itself.
**THE.** Precisely.
**HOS.** Therefore, it is not “The Same” itself.
**THE.** Certainly not.
**HOS.** Yet it is "the same" in some way because of participation. For all things participate in that same thing.
**THE.** Exceedingly so.
**HOS.** It must be granted, therefore, without controversy, that Motion is equally "the same" and "not the same." For when we say it is not "the same," we do not pronounce it in a similar sense to saying it *is* "the same": rather, it is "the same" because it participates in the self-same, and it is "the same" as itself. But it is "not the same" because it also receives "the other," by which it is separated from "the same," and is not that, but something else. Wherefore it is rightly called "not the same."
**THE.** Rightly, indeed.
**HOS.** Furthermore, if in some way Motion itself admitted Rest, it would by no means be absurd to call Motion "stable."
**THE.** Rightly, if indeed we have granted that among the kinds some wish to communicate with each other, and some not at all.
**HOS.** But indeed, before the demonstration of this, we arrived by refuting present matters—namely, that this is how things are in nature.
**THE.** Why not?
**HOS.** Let us say again that Motion is "other" than "The Other" itself, just as it was something other than "The Same" and "Rest."
**THE.** It is necessary.
**HOS.** Therefore, Motion is also "other" in some way and "not other."
**THE.** True.
**HOS.** What then next? Shall we say that "The Other" itself is other than the [first] three, yet not different from the fourth, since we confessed there are those five, of which we proposed one to be considered?
**THE.** But how?
**HOS.** For we cannot grant a lesser number of them than was established above. Therefore, fearing nothing, let us fight to show that Motion is something other than Being.
**THE.** Let us become accustomed to this immediately.
**HOS.** Wherefore Motion truly exists as "non-being," and also as "being," since it is a participant in Being.
*[[margin: In which things Non-being is.]]*
**THE.** That is manifest indeed.
**HOS.** It follows, therefore, that Non-being is in Motion and in all other kinds. For in each, the nature of "The Other" itself, while it makes each thing "other" than Being itself, makes each "non-being"; and thus we shall predicate all things similarly as "non-beings," and because they participate in Being, we shall again say they "are," and call them "beings."
**THE.** Perhaps.
**HOS.** Therefore, regarding any species, Being is manifold, but Non-being is infinite in multitude.
**THE.** It seems so.
**HOS.** Must not Being itself also be called "other" than each of the others?
**THE.** It is necessary.
**HOS.** Therefore, Being "is not" as many things as there are other things: for while it is not those, it is itself one; but it is not the others, which are infinite in number.
**THE.** It must almost be said so.
**HOS.** We ought not be troubled by these things, since the nature of the kinds has mutual communion. If anyone does not accept these things, having posited the earlier points, he must grant these as well.
**THE.** So you say.
**HOS.** Let us see this also.
**THE.** What?
**HOS.** Whenever we say "non-being," as we seem to, we by no means say the contrary of "being," but only something "other."
**THE.** How?
**HOS.** As when we say something is "not large," we do not signify "small" by that word any more than we signify "equal."
**THE.** It is so.
**HOS.** Therefore, we shall not admit that a contrary is signified when a negation is spoken; we shall only assert that "not" and "no" signify something from the number of others, when they precede names, or rather as often as they precede the things themselves about which the names following the negations are pronounced.
*[[margin: When a negation does not signify a contrary.]]*
**THE.** It is so entirely.
**HOS.** Furthermore, if it seems right to you, let us meditate on this.
**THE.** What is that?
*[[margin: Meditation on the Other itself.]]*
**HOS.** The nature of "The Other" itself seems to be cut up in the same way as science.
**THE.** In what way?
**HOS.** That too is one, but a part of it residing in something, and separately determined, has obtained its own name: wherefore many arts and sciences are said to be.
**THE.** Entirely.
**HOS.** Do not the parts of the nature of "The Other" itself, which is one, suffer the same as the parts of science?
**THE.** Perhaps. But let us say by what reasoning.
**HOS.** Is there some part of "The Other" itself opposed to "The Beautiful"?
**THE.** There is.
**HOS.** Shall we say this lacks any name, or rather that it is named?
**THE.** It is named. For that which we pronounce "not beautiful" everywhere is "other" from nothing else than from the nature of "The Beautiful."
**HOS.** Come then, answer this.
**THE.** To what shall I answer?
**HOS.** When something is determined in a certain part of beings, and again is opposed to some of the beings, does it not happen that it is called "not beautiful"?
**THE.** So it is.
**HOS.** Truly it follows that "the not-beautiful" is something, since indeed that to which it is opposed exists.
**THE.** Very correctly.
**HOS.** Must "the beautiful" be placed more in the number of beings, and "the not-beautiful" less, because of this discourse?
**THE.** In no way more.
**HOS.** Therefore, "the not-large" must be said to exist just as much as "the large."
**THE.** Similarly.
**HOS.** Furthermore, we shall place "the not-just" and "the just" according to these things: so that the one is in no way more than the other.
**THE.** Without doubt.
*[[margin: It is proved that Non-being exists.]]*
**HOS.** And the reasoning will be the same for the rest, after the nature of "The Other" itself appeared to be from the kind of beings. Since that exists, it is necessary that its parts also exist no less.
**THE.** Why not?
**HOS.** The opposition itself which is between a part of the nature of "The Other" itself and a part of Being is an essence no less—if it is right to say so—than Being itself: nor does it signify the contrary of that, but only something "other."
**THE.** Clearly.
**HOS.** What then shall we call it?
**THE.** It is certainly established that this is "non-being," which was sought by us for the sake of the Sophist.
**HOS.** And does it have essence no less than anything of the rest, as you were saying? And must we now boldly say that non-being firmly has its own nature, just as "large" was large, and "beautiful" was beautiful, and also "not large" and "not beautiful"?
*[[margin: That Non-being firmly has its own nature.]]*
**HOS.** And in the same way, Non-being, according to the same, was and is one species of "non-being" numbered among many other beings. Do we disagree any further about this, **Theaetetus**?
**THE.** Not at all.
**HOS.** Do you...

**[[page number: 134]]**

...notice how far we have diverted from the mind of **Parmenides**?
**THE.** Why so?
**HOS.** We have transgressed his limits, while we have considered and shown further than he established.
*[[margin: The poems of Parmenides.]]*
**THE.** In what way?
**HOS.** Because, he says, "never and in no way are non-beings. But you, seeking, restrain your mind from this progress."* 
*[[margin: *In the Greek, Theaetetus answers; Hospes replied, which, because it did not please me, I omitted, following Ficinus.]]*
These are his words. But we have not only shown that non-beings exist, but we have demonstrated what the species of non-being is. For when we asserted that beings are divided and dispersed among each other, then we said that the part opposed to that which each thing is, is truly non-being itself.
**THE.** We seem to me, O Stranger, to have said entirely true things.
**HOS.** Let no one say, then, that after we showed non-being as the contrary of being, we dare to say that it exists. For we have long since said farewell to him who asks whether that which is contrary to something truly exists or not, and whether it subsists by some reason or lacks reason.
*[[margin: He who does not believe the position ought to refute it; he who cannot refute it ought to believe.]]*
But what we have now said "non-being" is, he who believes less must either refute, or if he cannot refute it, he must believe it so far as he cannot contradict it: namely, that the kinds are mixed with each other, and Being and "The Other," by penetrating through each other and through all other things, mutually catch each other, while "The Other" participates in Being. It *is*, indeed, on account of such participation, yet it is not that very thing in which it participates, but something else. But since it is something else than Being itself, it necessarily follows that it is said to be non-being. Being also, from the fact that it is a participant in "The Other," must be said to be something other than the other kinds. And since it is something other than all the rest, it exists neither as any one of those, nor as all of them together, but only as that which it is; wherefore Being, without doubt, in very many things is not very many things. And other things also similarly, both the universal and the individuals, in many ways *are*, and in many ways *are not*.
**THE.** You tell the truth.
**HOS.** If anyone does not grant faith to these contrary conversions, he ought to think of bringing in better things than these. Or if someone, having found something seemingly arduous, rejoices in drawing the discourse now here, now there, let him know he has devised things not worthy of much study, as these discourses testify. For this is neither something extraordinary nor difficult to find, but that which is arduous and noble.
**THE.** What is that?
**HOS.** What was also said above: that, having omitted these as light things, one might be able to refute in each thing those which are clearly the same: whether what is other is the same, or what is the same is other, and each by the same reasoning, convicting it to be so. For to show that what is the same is other, or what is other is the same in some way, or that what is large is small, and what is similar is also dissimilar, and to connect contraries in this way, is not a true refutation, but one scarcely touching the matter lightly, rude and newly born.
**THE.** Entirely so.
**HOS.** For to separate everything from everything, O best youth, is both unharmonious and the mark of a man entirely unskilled in music and philosophy.
**THE.** For what reason?
**HOS.** All speech is utterly destroyed if each thing is segregated from all. For it is because of the mutual coupling of species that speech exists.
**THE.** It is so.
**HOS.** Observe, I pray, how opportunely we have now fought against those, forcing them to permit one thing to be mixed with another.
**THE.** To what end especially?
**HOS.** To the end that speech might be one of the kinds; for if we were deprived of this, we would for the most part lack philosophy. It is necessary, moreover, to define in the present by common consent what speech is; for if it were entirely removed from the midst, we could speak of nothing. It would be removed, however, if it were granted that there is no mixture of things.
**THE.** That is right indeed. But for what cause speech must now be defined, I do not understand.
**HOS.** But perhaps you will perceive it in this way.
**THE.** How?
**HOS.** Non-being was established as being one of the remaining kinds, diffused through all things that are.
**THE.** It was established.
**HOS.** We must consider, then, next, whether it is mixed with opinion and speech.
**THE.** Why?
**HOS.** Because if it is mixed with these in no way, it is necessary that all things are true. But if it is mixed, false opinion and false speech arise. For to say and to opine "non-beings"—this itself is the "false," happening to speech and thought.
*[[margin: From non-being comes falsehood, from falsehood deception etc.]]*
**THE.** It is so.
**HOS.** But when there is falsehood, deception follows.
**THE.** Immediately.
**HOS.** Deception having arisen, it is necessary that all things be filled with images and likenesses and phantasy.
**THE.** Nothing contradicts it.
**HOS.** But we said the Sophist had fled into this place, while he said that the false in no way exists, because no one thinks or pronounces non-being, since non-being is in no part a participant in essence.
**THE.** So it was said.
**HOS.** But now this has appeared to us as a participant in Being: wherefore he will no longer fight in this part. But perhaps he will say that some of the species participate in non-being, and some do not; and that speech and opinion are among the number of those which do not participate; and therefore he will contend that that phantastic faculty, the mistress of images in which we placed him, is nowhere, since opinion and speech in no way participate with non-being; or at least he will say it is nothing, since no such communion is found. Wherefore, what speech is, and opinion, and phantasy, must first be investigated, so that these having been declared, we may see their communion with non-being: which being inspected, we may show that something is false: and having shown this, we may bind the Sophist in it, if indeed he is guilty, or else absolve him and seek him thereafter in some other kind.
**THE.** It seems entirely true, O Stranger, what we predicted from the beginning about the Sophist: namely, that this kind is entirely difficult to catch. For he seems hedged in by many obstacles, such that no one can reach him unless he first removes the obstacle that he has placed. And now indeed we have scarcely escaped that objection by which he inferred that non-being in no way exists. Immediately, another obstacle is clear. Whence it is necessary to show that both speech and opinion can be false, and perhaps after this another, and another after that, and no end will be found.
**HOS.** He ought to follow with a brave heart, **Theaetetus**, whoever can go forward or at any time in what he has begun. For how should he who hesitates in these dare to do anything in others? For he who either effects nothing in those or is repelled backward will never, as the proverb says, capture the city. But now, since what you were saying has been transacted by us, and the great rampart taken, the remaining things hereafter are smaller and lighter.
*[[margin: Proverb.]]*
**THE.** You speak excellently.
**HOS.** Let us therefore first take up speech or opinion, as has been said, so that we may more clearly show whether non-being touches these, or whether both are entirely [real], and neither is false.
**THE.** Most excellent.
**HOS.** Come, just as we spoke regarding species and letters, let us likewise think again regarding names. For it seems that what is now sought is so.
**THE.** What especially do you wish to be understood about names?
**HOS.** Whether all agree with each other, or none, or some sound together...

**[[page number: 135]]**

...and others are dissonant.
**THE.** It is clear that some agree, some not at all.
**HOS.** Perhaps you mean such a thing: that those which being said in sequence express something, agree with each other; but those which, being continued, signify nothing, do not agree.
**THE.** How were you saying that?
**HOS.** What I thought you understood and confessed. For there are two kinds of declarations which are made by the voice concerning essence.
**THE.** In what way?
**HOS.** One kind of names, another of verbs.
**THE.** Tell both.
**HOS.** The declaration which signifies actions, we call a verb.
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** But the sign of the voice imposed on the agents themselves, a name.
**THE.** Exactly.
**HOS.** Speech is never made from names alone uttered in order, nor again from verbs pronounced without names.
**THE.** I have not learned this.
**HOS.** It is certainly established that you, intending your mind elsewhere, were assenting a little before. For this is the very thing I wished to say: that if those things are pronounced only so continued, they do not make speech.
**THE.** How?
**HOS.** As "goes," "runs," "sleeps," and whatever other verbs signify actions: if someone joins them all together, he no more makes speech.
**THE.** It is so.
**HOS.** And again when it is said, "lion," "stag," "horse," and the other names which signify the agents themselves, no speech is yet fashioned by this continuation. For those things which are brought forth do not show an action, or the impediment of an action, or essence, whether of an existing thing or a non-existing thing, until verbs are mixed with names. Then indeed they first agree, and immediately speech is made, and the first complex of these is the first speech, even if it be very short.
**THE.** How do you investigate this?
**HOS.** When someone says, "man learns," do you say this speech is the first and shortest?
**THE.** I do.
**HOS.** Then surely it declares something about those things which are, or were, or have been now, or will be. Nor does he only name, but also defines something, coupling verbs with names. And therefore we say he not only names, but talks, and we have given the name of "speech" (*oratio*) to such a context of names.
**THE.** Rightly.
**HOS.** Indeed, just as some things sound together, as we said above, and some are dissonant, so also signs of voices: some in no way agree, but some, agreeing, fashion speech.
**THE.** Exactly.
**HOS.** Take also this brief point.
**THE.** What is that?
**HOS.** It is necessary that speech, whenever it exists, be speech *of something*: for it is impossible for speech to be of nothing.
**THE.** So it seems.
**HOS.** And must it not also be of some quality?
**THE.** It must indeed.
**HOS.** Let us observe, I pray, diligently.
**THE.** It is fitting.
**HOS.** I shall offer speech to you, you will join a thing with an action through a name and a verb: but you say of whom the speech is.
**THE.** I shall do so as I can.
**HOS.** "Theaetetus sits," is that a long speech?
**THE.** No, but moderate.
**HOS.** It is yours now to say of whom and whose the speech is.
**THE.** Of me, obviously, and it is mine.
**HOS.** This also?
**THE.** Which?
**HOS.** "This Theaetetus with whom I now dispute, flies."
**THE.** No one would say otherwise of this also, except that it is of me and is mine.
**HOS.** We said any speech must be of some quality.
**THE.** We said so.
**HOS.** Of what quality then shall we say each of these is?
**THE.** One true, the other false.
**HOS.** True speech predicates those things which are, as they are, concerning you.
**THE.** Certainly.
**HOS.** But false speech predicates other things than those which are.
**THE.** Exactly.
**HOS.** It asserts, therefore, those which are not, as if they are.
**THE.** Nearly so.
**HOS.** And it says other things concerning you than those which truly are. For we said before that there are many beings about each thing, and many non-beings.
**THE.** Entirely.
**HOS.** First indeed, it is necessary that that speech which I brought forth concerning you in the second place, according to the definition of speech, is one of the shortest.
**THE.** So it was agreed between us.
**HOS.** Then express whether it is of someone.
**THE.** Of someone.
**HOS.** If it is not yours, it is much less of another.
**THE.** It is clear.
**HOS.** If it is of no one, it is not speech at all. For it was shown to be impossible that what is speech is the speech of no one.
**THE.** Cleverly.
**HOS.** Therefore, as often as other things are predicated of you in this way as if they were the same, and those which are not as if they are, such a composition of verbs and names is undoubtedly false speech.
**THE.** You speak very true things.
**HOS.** But what shall we say of thought, opinion, and phantasy? Does it not now stand that all these kinds, both true and false, are fashioned in our souls?
**THE.** By what reasoning?
**HOS.** You will understand easily if you first receive what each of these is, and how they differ among themselves.
**THE.** Show me now.
**HOS.** Are not thought and speech the same? Except that thought is called that interior conversation without the sound of the voice, by which our soul speaks to itself.
**THE.** Entirely.
**HOS.** But the flow of utterance from it through the mouth is named speech (*oratio*).
**THE.** True.
**HOS.** Furthermore, we notice this in speech.
**THE.** What?
**HOS.** Affirmation, I say, and negation.
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** When therefore this happens in the soul by thought in silence, can it be called by any name other than opinion?
**THE.** By no means.
**HOS.** But what when such a passion occurs not by thought itself but through sense again? Can it be called otherwise than phantasy?
**THE.** Not otherwise.
**HOS.** Since speech appeared partly true and partly false, and thought is the interior conversation of the soul itself, and opinion the conclusion of thought, in which the mixture of opinion and sense is found, it seems to be necessary that thoughts and opinions are partly true and partly false: since they are kindred to speech.
**THE.** Nothing contradicts it.
**HOS.** Do you notice that we have found more easily than we thought that speech and thought are sometimes false? We were fearing indeed lest we were undertaking a vain and inexplicable work in seeking these.
**THE.** I notice.
**HOS.** Therefore, let us not lose heart in the remaining things: but after these have been made open, let us recall to memory those earlier divisions according to species.
**THE.** Which ones?
**HOS.** We divided the imaginary art into two, namely the assimilative and the phantastic.
**THE.** So we did.
**HOS.** But in which art we should place the Sophist, we were uncertain.
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** After this ambiguity, suddenly a deeper darkness emerged, when that discourse was brought in, doubtful to all: that neither an image, nor a likeness, nor a phantom exists at all anywhere, because the false in no way, anywhere, ever exists.
**THE.** You tell true things.
**HOS.** But now, after speech appeared, and false opinion appeared, it is possible that there are some likenesses of true things, and that the art of deceiving flows from this disposition.
**THE.** Possible certainly.
**HOS.** Furthermore, was it not granted by us in the earlier parts that the Sophist is occupied in these?
**THE.** It was.
**HOS.** Let us strive again, dividing the proposed kind in two, always to progress to the right part of the division, and to look around for what things communicate with the Sophist in any way, so that all communions having been cut away, we may behold his proper seat and image, and show it as closely as possible to those who by nature approach the progress of this kind of discipline.
**THE.** Excellent.
**HOS.** Did we not at the beginning introduce the art of effecting as one part and that of acquiring as another?
**THE.** Certainly.
**HOS.** Having later divided the art of acquiring, we imagined the Sophist under it in hunting, contest, trade, and species of this kind.
**THE.** So it was done.
**HOS.** But now, after the art of imitating has also embraced the Sophist, it stands first that this art of effecting must be divided in two. For imitation is a certain effecting, namely of likenesses and not of true things, as we said above. Is it not?
**THE.** Without doubt.
**HOS.** Therefore, let there first be two parts of the effective faculty.
**THE.** Which ones?
**HOS.** Divine and human.
**THE.** I do not yet understand.
**HOS.** If we only remember what was said at the beginning, we call the effective faculty a certain power which is the cause that things which were not before should exist afterwards.
**THE.** We remember.
**HOS.** All mortal animals, and plants, whatever grow from seeds or roots on the earth, and whatever inanimate things consist in the earth, whether they can be liquefied or not—do we say they were made, not having been before, by any other craftsman than God? Or shall we follow the doctrine and speeches of many?
**THE.** Of whom?
**HOS.** Of those who say these are born by nature itself from some fortuitous cause, without a mind acting; or rather with reason and divine science which arose from God himself.
**THE.** I, perhaps because of my age, sometimes opine this, sometimes that. But at present, looking to you and thinking that you judge all these to be born through God, I myself judge the same.
**HOS.** Very rightly, **Theaetetus**. And if we thought you would opine otherwise in the future, we would now effect by reason together with a certain necessary persuasion that you should believe us. But since I know you are of such a character that even without our demonstration you will of your own accord proceed to those things to which you say you are now drawn, I will let it go. For such a dispute would be superfluous. I shall posit, indeed, that those things which are said to be born by nature are made by divine art; but those which are composed from these by men are human: and in this way there are two kinds of the effective faculty, namely human and divine.
**THE.** Pre-eminently.
**HOS.** Since there are two arts, divide each in two.
**THE.** How?
**HOS.** Just as the universal effective art was divided through its breadth, so let it now be divided through its length, and so four parts of it are effected: two human as far as us, two again divine as far as the gods.
**THE.** Exactly.
**HOS.** From these again, divided differently now, one part of each partition is effective, but the remaining are named imaginary. Whence the faculty of effecting is again divided in two.
**THE.** Say again how both are.
**HOS.** We ourselves and the other animals, and those things from which these are born, fire and water and their kin—do we not know all these are procreated by God as individual things effected and wrought?
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** After these, likenesses of them follow, produced by a certain divine industry.
**THE.** What kind?
**HOS.** Phantoms indeed which occur to those sleeping, and those which are seen in the day without art by you, such as a shadow when darkness is mixed with fire: and a double thing, when own and extraneous light concur in one around clear and smooth things, providing a contrary sense of accustomed vision, and effects a species.
**THE.** There are then those two works of divine effecting: the individual things, and the likenesses following the things.
**HOS.** But human art, does it not fabricate a house through architecture, and through painting the image of the house, like a certain human dream made for those awake?
**THE.** No one doubts it.
**HOS.** In other things also similarly, by partitioning through two, we shall find twin works of our effective action. Making the thing itself by the principal faculty, but the image by that emulating one.
**THE.** Now I understand better, and I place two species of the effective faculty: first I part it into divine and human according to the second division; but according to the other into the effective of things themselves and of images.
**HOS.** Let us remember, I pray, that we said there must be two kinds of the imaginary faculty: the assimilative and the phantastic, if indeed something truly false, and one false something of those which are, is to exist.
**THE.** So it was said.
**HOS.** Does it not stand? And therefore shall we not now count two species without controversy?
**THE.** Indeed.
**HOS.** Therefore, cut the phantastic again into two.
**THE.** How?
**HOS.** One made through instruments, the other of him who exhibits himself as the instrument effecting the phantom.
**THE.** How do you say that?
**HOS.** Whenever someone, usurping your figure, makes his body or voice seem similar to yours, that imitation is called phantastic.
**THE.** Certainly.
**HOS.** Calling this the "imitative," let us so distribute it, and let us pass over all the rest as if already desiring rest, and let us grant to another to collect it into one and attribute a convenient name to it.
**THE.** Let it be distributed as you wish, and let this be dismissed.
**HOS.** This moreover, **Theaetetus**, must be thought double. For what cause, observe.
**THE.** Tell me.
**HOS.** Of those who imitate, some do this knowing what they imitate, but others ignorant. Shall we place any greater discrepancy and division than that of ignorance and knowledge?
**THE.** None.
**HOS.** Was not that which we were saying the imitation of those who know? For he who knows you imitates your figure.
**THE.** He himself.
**HOS.** But what must be said about the figure of justice and of universal virtue? Do not many, while they are ignorant, but opine that they know this, striving to imitate what seems so to them, both in words and works, so that it may appear to be in them?
**THE.** And very many indeed.
**HOS.** Does hope fail them so that, just as they are not just, so they do not even seem to be? Or on the contrary?
**THE.** On the contrary.
**HOS.** Shall we say this imitator is diverse from that earlier one, the ignorant from the knowing?
**THE.** We shall say so plainly.
**HOS.** Whence then shall the proper name of each be deduced? Or is it perhaps difficult because an old cause of the division of kinds into species was unknown to our predecessors, such that no one contended to part them, and therefore we must be in want of names? And if it can seem somewhat bold to say, yet for the sake of declaration and discretion, let us call that imitation which is the companion of opinion "opinable imitation"; but that which is of science, a certain "historical and knowing imitation."
**THE.** So be it.
**HOS.** Of these names, only one is to be used. For we placed the Sophist, though in the kind of imitators, yet not in the kind of those who know.
**THE.** It is so.
**HOS.** Let us therefore examine this "opinionated" imitator as if he were iron, whether he is solid and simple, or on the contrary twin and double, having something within.
**THE.** Let us examine.
**HOS.** Certainly he is very manifold. For one Sophist is fatuous and inept, who...

**[[page number: 137]]**

...thinks he knows. But the form of the other, on account of the varied revolution in speeches, certainly has much suspicion and fear lest he be ignorant of those things which he simulates he knows before others.
**THE.** It is entirely from both kinds, as you have related.
**HOS.** Shall we not then place one as a simple and the other as an ironic imitator?
**THE.** It is likely.
**HOS.** Again, do we say there is one kind of this or two?
**THE.** You see to it.
**HOS.** I am thinking, and two offer themselves to me as I think. One indeed using irony in public by a prolix speech before the people; the other privately by certain small captious arguments forcing him who disputes with him to contradict himself in his speeches.
**THE.** You speak very correctly.
**HOS.** How shall we name that earlier one? Civil, or popular?
**THE.** Popular.
**HOS.** But the other: *Sophon* (that is, wise) or *Sophisticum* (Sophistic)?
**THE.** To call him wise is not permitted, since we have placed him as ignorant. But since he imitates the wise, he shall obtain a certain name similar to that.
*[[margin: Whence the Sophist is named.]]*
And at last I understand: it is fitting that this very man be called properly and truly the Sophist.
**HOS.** Shall we not now bind together his name as above, encompassing all things again from the end to the beginning?
**THE.** Entirely.
*[[margin: The final definition of the Sophist.]]*
**HOS.** He at last will truly define the Sophist who shall assert that his generation and stock is this: the Sophist, I say, is he who in speeches forces the disputant to contradict himself, who is part of the ironic, coming from the opinionated imitator, also of the phantastic kind, flowing from the imaginary faculty, a determined progeny not of divine but of human effecting, and from the number of those who by words, as if by certain juggleries, deceive the listeners in a marvelous way.
**THE.** So it must entirely be said.

***

### MARSILIUS FICINUS’S APOLOGUE FOR THE BOOK OF PLATO
#### On Kingship, to Federico, the always unconquered Duke of Urbino.

Jupiter, the best and greatest, since he desired at some time to look upon such a kingdom on earth as he always beholds in heaven with himself, has already long ago sent down to earth through that divine idea of kingship a certain royal and divine soul. And having called together the dwellers in heaven, he commanded that all should vote for this future king, whom the gods indeed already named *Piderēgum* [protector of the faith] from royal faith and *Orbinantem Ducem* [ruling duke] from the empire of the world, but whom men, with changed letters, were to call **Federico, Duke of Urbino**. All the deities assented to Jupiter except Juno. For Juno alone, the ambitious queen of the thicker air, has hitherto envied the heavenly kingdom on earth. But Pallas and Mercury, with the others favoring and Truth being witness, have long since most willingly conferred the crown and royal scepter upon this same man, on whom Jupiter also did. Since the Academy everywhere worships and follows Pallas and Mercury, it also most happily grants the kingdom and monarchy of the whole world—such as the divine Plato describes—to Federico, Duke of Urbino, most deserving both from the judgment of Jupiter and from the testimony of Truth.

***

### PLATO’S CIVIL [STATESMAN], OR, ON KINGSHIP.
#### MARSILIUS FICINUS’S ARGUMENT.

Since God and nature produce man by acting, they certainly produce him that he may act, I say, for the sake of divine things... [Ficinus proceeds to explain the teleological purpose of human society and the necessity of a single ruler (Monarch) to guide the diverse human race toward a single end of contemplation and virtuous action, comparing the king to a shepherd, a pilot, and a physician.]

...shall we place "another" itself in the fifth place? Or must we think that this and "being" are two names signifying one thing? THEAETETUS. Perhaps. STRANGER. I think, however, you will grant that of the things that are, some are "according to themselves," while others are referred to other things. THEAETETUS. Why not? STRANGER. But "another" is always referred to another. Is it not so? THEAETETUS. Always. STRANGER. This would not be so unless "another" and "being" differed greatly from each other. If "another" participated in both forms like "being," it would certainly be something among those things which are other, but not necessarily other relative to something else; but now, whatever is truly "another," it follows of necessity that it is "another" according to that which it is. THEAETETUS. It is as you say. STRANGER. It is fitting then to place the fifth nature of "another" itself among the forms to which we joined the others. THEAETETUS. Certainly. STRANGER. We must also say that this nature runs through all of them. For each one is "other" than the others, not by its own nature, but because it becomes a participant in the idea of the "other." THEAETETUS. Truly. STRANGER. Thus let us speak of the five, repeating them individually. THEAETETUS. What? STRANGER. First, that motion is entirely another something than rest. Is it to be asserted thus, or otherwise? THEAETETUS. Exactly thus. STRANGER. Therefore it is not rest. THEAETETUS. In no way. STRANGER. But it "is," because it is a participant in being. THEAETETUS. It is. STRANGER. Again, motion is another than "the same" itself. THEAETETUS. Nearly so. STRANGER. Therefore it is not "the same" itself. THEAETETUS. Certainly not. STRANGER. Nevertheless, it is "the same" in a certain way because of participation. For all things participate in that same thing. THEAETETUS. Most definitely. STRANGER. It must be granted, then, without controversy that motion is equally "the same" and "not the same." For when we say "the same" itself is "not the same," we are not speaking in a similar way: it is "the same" because it is a participant in that same thing in relation to itself. But it is "not the same" because it also receives "the other," by which it is separated from that same thing; it is not that, but something else. For which reason it is rightly called "not the same." THEAETETUS. Rightly indeed. STRANGER. Furthermore, if in some way motion itself admitted "rest," it would be in no way absurd to call motion "stable." THEAETETUS. Correct, if indeed we have granted that some among the classes want to communicate with each other and some do not at all. STRANGER. But we arrived at the demonstration of this before refuting the present things—namely, that nature is clearly disposed in this way. THEAETETUS. Why not? STRANGER. Let us say again that motion is another than "the other" itself, just as it was something else than "the same" and "rest." THEAETETUS. It is necessary. STRANGER. It is, therefore, in a certain way "the other" and "not the other" by this reasoning. THEAETETUS. True. STRANGER. What follows? Shall we say "the other" itself is different from the three, but not different from the fourth, since we confessed those five to be the ones among which we proposed to consider one? THEAETETUS. But how? STRANGER. For we cannot grant a smaller number of them than was established above. Therefore, fearing nothing, let us fight to say that motion is something other than "being." <margin>Where non-being resides.</margin> THEAETETUS. Let us assert it immediately. STRANGER. Wherefore motion truly exists as "non-being," and also as "being," since it is a participant in being. THEAETETUS. That is certainly manifest. STRANGER. It follows, therefore, that "non-being" is in motion and in all the other classes. For in each, the nature of "the other" itself—while it makes each thing "other" than being itself—makes each thing "non-being." And thus we shall proclaim all things to be similarly "non-beings" for this reason, and because they participate in being, we shall say they "are" again, and call them "beings." THEAETETUS. Perhaps. STRANGER. Therefore, concerning any form whatever, "being" is manifold, while "non-being" is infinite in multitude. THEAETETUS. So it seems. STRANGER. And must not "being" itself be called "other" than each of the others? THEAETETUS. It is necessary. STRANGER. Therefore, being is "not" as many things as there are other things in number; for since it is not those things, it is itself one thing, but it is not the other things, which are infinite in number. THEAETETUS. It must almost be said so. STRANGER. We certainly should not be troubled by these things, since the nature of the classes has mutual communion. If anyone does not accept these things, he must know that once the previous points are posited, he must further grant these. THEAETETUS. You speak rightly. STRANGER. Let us see this as well. THEAETETUS. What is it? STRANGER. Whenever we say "non-being," as it seems, we do not at all say the "contrary" of being, but only something "other." THEAETETUS. How so? STRANGER. Just as when we say something is "not large," we do not signify "small" by that word any more than "equal." THEAETETUS. It is so. STRANGER. Therefore, we will not admit that a "contrary" is signified when a <margin>When negation does not signify a contrary. "Not."</margin> negation is spoken. We shall only assert this much: that "not" and "neither" signify something from the number of other things when they precede names—rather, as often as they precede the things themselves, concerning which the names following the negations are pronounced. THEAETETUS. It is exactly so. STRANGER. Let us furthermore meditate on this, if it seems good to you. THEAETETUS. What is that? STRANGER. <margin>Meditation on the "other" itself.</margin> The nature of "the other" itself seems to be divided into parts, in the same way as "science" <note>original: "scientia," here meaning knowledge or a field of study</note>. THEAETETUS. In what way? STRANGER. That also is one, but a part of it residing in something and being individually determined has received its own surname; for which reason many arts and sciences are said to exist. THEAETETUS. Entirely. STRANGER. Do not the parts of the nature of "the other" itself, which is one, undergo the same thing as the parts of science? THEAETETUS. Perhaps. But tell us by what reason. STRANGER. Is there some part of "the other" itself opposed to "the beautiful"? THEAETETUS. There is. STRANGER. Shall we say this lacks all surname? Or rather that it is named? THEAETETUS. That it is named. For that which we pronounce "not beautiful" everywhere is "other" than nothing else than the nature of the beautiful. STRANGER. Come then, answer this. THEAETETUS. To what shall I answer? STRANGER. When something is determined in a certain part of things that are, and again is opposed to something of the things that are, does it not happen that it is called "not beautiful"? THEAETETUS. Yes. STRANGER. It truly follows that "not beautiful" is something, since indeed that which it is opposed to exists. THEAETETUS. Quite rightly. STRANGER. From this discourse, should the "beautiful" be placed more among the number of existing things, and the "not beautiful" less? THEAETETUS. Not at all more. STRANGER. Similarly, then, "not large" must be said to exist as much as "large." THEAETETUS. Similarly. STRANGER. Furthermore, we shall posit "not just" according to these things alongside "just," so that one is no more than the other. THEAETETUS. Without a doubt. STRANGER. <margin>It is proved that non-being exists.</margin> And there will be the same reason for the rest, since the nature of "the other" itself has appeared to be from the class of existing things. And that existing, it is necessary that its parts exist no less. THEAETETUS. What does it prove? STRANGER. The opposition itself which exists between the part of the nature of "the other" itself and the part of "being" is no less an essence than "being" itself, if it is permitted to say so; nor does it signify its contrary, but only something "other." THEAETETUS. Clearly. STRANGER. What then shall we call it? THEAETETUS. It is certain that this is that very "non-being" which was sought by us for the sake of the sophist. STRANGER. And does it have essence no less than anything else, as you were saying? And must we now say boldly that "non-being" firmly possesses its own nature, <margin>That non-being firmly has its own nature.</margin> just as "large" was large, and "beautiful" was beautiful, and also "not large" and "not beautiful"? And in the same way, "non-being" according to the same was and is "non-being," one species numbered among many other beings. Do we distrust this anymore, Theaetetus? THEAETETUS. Not at all. STRANGER. Do you...

...do you notice how far we have diverted from the mind of Parmenides? THEAETETUS. Why so? STRANGER. We have transgressed his limits, while we have considered and shown further than he established. THEAETETUS. In what way? STRANGER. <margin>The verses of Parmenides.</margin> Because, he says, "Never, and in no way, are non-beings. But you, seeking, restrain your mind from this path."* So says he. But we have not only shown that non-beings exist, but we have demonstrated what the form of non-being is. For when we showed that the nature of "the other" itself exists, divided and dispersed throughout all existing things in turn, then we asserted that the part of it opposed to what is the "being" of each thing is itself truly "non-being." <margin>*In the Greek, Theaetetus speaks and the Stranger responds; because it was not pleasing, I have omitted it, following Ficino.</margin> THEAETETUS. We truly seem to have spoken the truth, O Stranger. STRANGER. Let no one say, then, that after we have shown non-being to be the "other" of being, we dare to say it "is." For we have long since said goodbye to anyone who asks whether what is contrary to something truly exists or not, and whether it subsists by some reason or lacks reason. But what we have now said "non-being" is, <margin>He who does not believe the position must refute it; he who cannot refute it must believe.</margin> one must either refute, if he believes it less, or if he is unable to refute it, he must believe it until he can contradict it: namely, that the classes are mixed with each other, and "being" and "the other" penetrate through each other and through all other things, capturing each other mutually, while "the other" participates in being. For because of such participation, it "is," but yet it is not that very thing in which it participates, but something else. But since it is something else than "being" itself, it follows necessarily that it is said "not to be." Being also, because it is a participant in "the other" itself, must be called something other than the other classes. And since it is something other than all the rest, it exists as not any one of them, nor all of them, but only itself which it is; wherefore being without doubt "is not" many things in many instances. And other things likewise, both universal and singular, in many ways "are," and in many ways "are not." THEAETETUS. You speak the truth. STRANGER. If anyone does not grant faith to these contrary conversions, he should consider whether he can bring forward something better than these. Or if someone, as if he had found something difficult, rejoices in pulling discourses now here, now there, let him know that he has not thought out things worthy of much study, as these discourses testify. For this is neither something extraordinary, nor difficult to find, but that which is difficult and illustrious. THEAETETUS. What is that? STRANGER. What was also said above: that leaving these things aside as light matters, you can refute in each thing those things which are plainly the same—whether what is "other" is "the same," or what is "the same" is "other," and both by the same reasoning, convincing them to "be." For to show that what is "the same" is "other," or what is "other" is also "the same" in any way, and what is "large" is "small," and what is "similar" is "dissimilar," and to connect contraries in this way, is not a true refutation, but one scarcely touching the matter lightly, rude and recently born. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. STRANGER. For to separate everything from everything, O excellent youth, is both unharmonious and the mark of a man entirely devoid of music and philosophy. THEAETETUS. Why? STRANGER. All speech is entirely destroyed if each thing is segregated from all others. For speech consists because of the mutual coupling of forms. THEAETETUS. It is so. STRANGER. Observe, I pray, how opportunely we have now forced those fighters to permit one thing to be mixed with another. THEAETETUS. To what end especially? STRANGER. To this end: that speech may be one of the classes of things; for if we were deprived of this, we would for the most part lack philosophy. It is necessary, moreover, to define by common consent what speech is at present. For if it were entirely removed from our midst, we could speak of nothing. And it would be removed if it were granted that there is no mixing of things. THEAETETUS. That is indeed correct. But for what cause speech must now be defined, I do not understand. STRANGER. But perhaps you will perceive it in this way. THEAETETUS. How? STRANGER. "Non-being" was established as one of the remaining classes that exists, diffused through all things that are. THEAETETUS. It was established. STRANGER. We must consider next, therefore, whether it is mingled with opinion and speech. THEAETETUS. Why? STRANGER. Because if it were mingled with these in no way, all things must be true. But if it were mixed, false opinion and false speech arise. For to speak and to think <margin>From non-being comes falsity, from falsity deception, etc.</margin> "non-beings"—this itself is falsity, happening in speech and thought. THEAETETUS. It is so. STRANGER. But where there is falsity, deception follows. THEAETETUS. Immediately. STRANGER. When deception arises, it is necessary that all things be filled with images, and likenesses, and phantasia. THEAETETUS. Nothing stands against it. STRANGER. But we were saying the sophist fled into this place when he said that "false" exists in no way, because no one thinks or pronounces "non-being," since "non-being" is in no part a participant in essence. THEAETETUS. So it was said. STRANGER. But now this has appeared to us as a participant in being; wherefore he will no longer fight in this part at least. But perhaps he will say that some of the forms participate in "non-being," and some do not; and that speech and opinion are among those which do not participate. And therefore he will contend that that <margin>The phantastic power, mistress of images.</margin> "phantastic" power, the mistress of images, in which we placed him, exists nowhere, after opinion and speech in no way participate with "non-being"; and he will say nothing is false, since no such communion is found. For which reason, what speech is, and opinion, and phantasia, must first be investigated, so that once these are declared, we may perceive their communion with "non-being"; and having inspected this, we may show that something is false; and when we have shown this, we may bind the sophist in it, if indeed he is guilty, or else set him free and seek him in some other class. THEAETETUS. It seems entirely true, Stranger, what we said from the beginning about the sophist—namely, that this class is altogether difficult to catch. For he seems surrounded by many barriers, and no one can reach him unless he first removes the obstacle he has thrown up. And now indeed we have scarcely at last escaped that objection by which he inferred that "non-being" in no way exists. Immediately another objection follows. Whence it is necessary to show that both speech and opinion can be false, and perhaps after this another, and another after that, and no end will be found. STRANGER. He who can proceed, or at some time succeed in what he began, must pursue it with a brave heart, Theaetetus. For how could he who hesitates in these things ever dare in others? For he who either effects nothing or is repelled backward by them will never, as the <margin>Proverb.</margin> proverb says, "capture the city." But now, since what you were saying has been transacted by us, and the great rampart captured, the remaining things are hereafter smaller and lighter. THEAETETUS. You speak excellently. STRANGER. Let us then first take up speech, as was said, or opinion, to show more clearly whether "non-being" touches these, or whether both are entirely true and neither is false. THEAETETUS. Best of all. What especially do you want to be understood regarding names? STRANGER. Whether they all harmonize with each other, or none, or some sound together...

...sound together, and others discord. THEAETETUS. It is clear that some harmonize, and some do not at all. STRANGER. How? And what were you saying? STRANGER. What I thought you understood and confessed. For there are two classes of declarations of those things which are made by the voice regarding essence. THEAETETUS. In what way? <margin>Verb.</margin> <margin>Noun.</margin> STRANGER. One is the class of "nouns," the other of "verbs." THEAETETUS. Tell us each. STRANGER. The declaration by which actions are signified, we call a "verb." THEAETETUS. Indeed. STRANGER. But the sign of the voice imposed upon those who act themselves, we call a "noun." THEAETETUS. Precisely. STRANGER. From names alone uttered in order, speech is never effected, nor again from verbs pronounced without nouns. THEAETETUS. I have not learned these things. STRANGER. It is certain indeed that you were just now assenting while intending your mind elsewhere. For this is the very thing I wanted to say: that if these are only continued in such a way, they do not make speech. THEAETETUS. How so? STRANGER. Like "goes," "runs," "sleeps," and other verbs whatever signify actions: if anyone joins them all together, he no more makes speech. THEAETETUS. It is so. STRANGER. And again when it is said, "lion," "stag," "horse," and other nouns which signify the agents themselves, as yet no speech is fashioned by this continuation. For the things brought forth do not show action, or the impediment of action, or the essence of a thing existing or not existing, until verbs are mixed with nouns. But then first they harmonize, and immediately speech is made, and the first complexity of these is the first speech, even if it be <margin>The first and shortest speech: man learns.</margin> very short. THEAETETUS. Why do you say so? STRANGER. When someone says, "Man learns," do you say this is the first and shortest speech? THEAETETUS. I do. STRANGER. Then indeed he declares something about those things which "are" or "become," or "have been" already, or "will be." He does not only name, but he also defines something, coupling verbs with nouns. Therefore we say he not only "names" but "speaks," and to such a context of names we have given the name "speech." THEAETETUS. Correct. STRANGER. Indeed, just as some things harmonize with each other, as we said above, and some discord, so also the signs of voices: some in no way agree, but some by their congruence fashion speech. THEAETETUS. Entirely. STRANGER. Take this brief point too. THEAETETUS. What is that? STRANGER. It is necessary that speech, as often as it is made, be the speech "of something"; for it is impossible for it to be the speech "of nothing." THEAETETUS. So it seems. STRANGER. And must it not also be of a certain quality? THEAETETUS. It must indeed. STRANGER. Let us observe diligently, I pray. THEAETETUS. It is fitting. STRANGER. I shall assert a speech to you, joining a thing with an action through a noun and a verb; you tell us "whose" speech it is. THEAETETUS. I shall do so as I can. STRANGER. "Theaetetus sits"—now is that a long speech? THEAETETUS. No, but moderate. STRANGER. It is your part now to say of whom and whose speech it is. THEAETETUS. Of me, obviously, and it is mine. STRANGER. What of this one too? THEAETETUS. Which? STRANGER. "Theaetetus, this one with whom I am now disputing, flies." THEAETETUS. No one would say otherwise of this also, except that it is about me and mine. STRANGER. We said any speech whatever must be of a certain quality. THEAETETUS. We did. STRANGER. But what quality shall we say each of these is? THEAETETUS. One truly, the other false. STRANGER. True speech predicates those things which "are," as they "are," concerning you. THEAETETUS. Certainly. STRANGER. But false speech predicates other things than those which "are." THEAETETUS. Indeed. STRANGER. Therefore it asserts things which "are not," as if they "are." THEAETETUS. Almost so. STRANGER. And it says other things about you than those which truly "are." For we said many beings exist concerning each individual, and many non-beings too. THEAETETUS. Entirely. STRANGER. First indeed, it is necessary that that speech which I brought forth concerning you in the second place, according to the definition of speech, be one of the shortest. THEAETETUS. So it was agreed between us. STRANGER. Next, express whether it is "of someone." THEAETETUS. Of someone. STRANGER. If it is not yours, it is much less another's. THEAETETUS. It is clear. STRANGER. If it is of no one, it is not speech at all. For it has been shown that it cannot happen that what is speech is the speech of no one. THEAETETUS. Wisely said. STRANGER. Therefore, as often as "others" are predicated of you as if they were the "same," and things that "are not" as if they "are," a composition of this kind from verbs and nouns undoubtedly becomes "false speech." THEAETETUS. You speak very truly. STRANGER. But what shall we say of thought, opinion, and phantasia? Is it not now manifest that all these classes, both true and false, are produced in our minds? THEAETETUS. By what reason? STRANGER. You will understand easily if you first receive what each of these is, and how they differ from each other. THEAETETUS. <margin>What thought is; speech is the same.</margin> Show us now. STRANGER. Are not thought and speech the same? Except that "thought" is called that silent interior conversation by which our soul speaks to itself. THEAETETUS. Exactly. <margin>Speech.</margin> STRANGER. But the flow from it through the mouth in utterance is named "speech." THEAETETUS. True. STRANGER. Furthermore, we observe this in speech. THEAETETUS. What? STRANGER. "Affirmation," I mean, and "negation." THEAETETUS. Indeed. STRANGER. <margin>Opinion.</margin> When this happens in the soul through thought in silence, can it be called by any name other than "opinion"? THEAETETUS. In no way. STRANGER. But what when such a passion occurs not through itself, but through sensation—can it be called anything else than "phantasia"? THEAETETUS. Not otherwise. <margin>Phantasia.</margin> STRANGER. Since speech has appeared to be partly true and partly false—and thought is the interior conversation of the soul itself, and opinion is the conclusion of thought, and in phantasia a mixing of sensation and opinion is found—it seems necessary that thoughts and opinions are partly true and partly false, since they are cognate to speech. THEAETETUS. Nothing stands against it. STRANGER. Do you notice that we have found more easily than we thought that speech and thought are sometimes false? We feared indeed lest we were undertaking a vain and inexplicable work in seeking these things. THEAETETUS. I notice it. STRANGER. Let us not lose heart in the remaining matters, then; but after these have been revealed, let us recall to memory those former divisions according to forms. THEAETETUS. Which ones? STRANGER. We divided the "image-making" art into two: namely, the "assimilative" and the "phantastic." THEAETETUS. So we did. STRANGER. But in which art we should place the sophist, we were in doubt. THEAETETUS. Truly. STRANGER. After this ambiguity, a deeper darkness suddenly emerged, when that discourse brought doubt to all—claiming that neither an image, nor a likeness, nor a phantom exists anywhere at all, because "false" exists nowhere, ever, in any way. THEAETETUS. You speak truly. STRANGER. But now, after speech has appeared, and false opinion has appeared, it is possible for there to be certain "images" of true things as rivals, and from this disposition the art of deceiving may flow. THEAETETUS. Certainly possible. STRANGER. Furthermore, was it not granted by us in the former parts that the sophist is engaged in these things? THEAETETUS. It was. STRANGER. Let us strive again to divide the proposed class in two, always proceeding to the right side of the part divided, and look around at whatever communicates in any way with the Sophist, so that all commonalities being pruned away, we may behold both his proper seat and his effigy, and show them to those who are following the progress of this discipline...

<summary>In this pivotal section of the Sophist, the Stranger and Theaetetus establish that "non-being" exists not as a contrary to being, but as "the other" or difference. They then demonstrate that falsity is possible in speech, opinion, and appearance (phantasia) by showing how "being" and "the other" can be combined in language.</summary>

nature, we should show it as closely as possible. THEAETETUS. Well said. STRANGER. Didn’t we, from the beginning, introduce the <term>art of production</term> <note>original: "artem efficiendi," often translated as the "productive art."</note> as one part, and the art of acquisition as the other? THEAETETUS. Certainly. STRANGER. Having then divided the art of acquisition, did we not imagine the Sophist within it, in the categories of hunting, combat, commerce, and species of that kind? THEAETETUS. That is exactly what happened. STRANGER. But now, since the art of imitation has also embraced the Sophist, it is clear that first, this art of production must be divided into two parts.
