Therefore, let there first be two parts of the productive faculty. THEAETETUS. Which ones? STRANGER. Divine and human. THEAETETUS. I do not yet understand. STRANGER. If we only remember what was said at the beginning, we call the productive faculty a certain power which is the cause that things exist later which did not exist before. THEAETETUS. We remember. STRANGER. All mortal animals, and plants, and whatever grows from the earth from seeds or roots, and whatever inanimate things exist in the earth, whether they can be melted or not—shall we say they were made by any other craftsman than God, having been made when they previously were not? Or shall we follow the doctrine and talk of the many? THEAETETUS. Which ones? STRANGER. Of those who say that these things are produced by nature itself from some chance cause, without a mind acting upon them; or rather with reason and divine knowledge, which has its origin from God himself. THEAETETUS. Perhaps because of my youth, I often shift from one opinion to the other. But for now, looking to you and thinking that you believe these things are produced through God, I myself believe the same. STRANGER. Very well, Theaetetus. And if I thought you would believe otherwise in the future, I would now attempt to make you believe us through reason combined with a certain necessary persuasion. But since I know your character is such that, even without our demonstration, you will move toward those things to which you say you are now drawn, I will let it go. For such a dispute would be superfluous. I will posit, then, that those things said to be produced by nature are made by divine art; but those which are composed from these by men are human; and by this reasoning, there are two kinds of the productive faculty: namely, human and divine. THEAETETUS. Excellent. STRANGER. Since there are two arts, divide each in two. THEAETETUS. How? STRANGER. Just as the whole productive art was divided by its "width," let it now be divided by its "length," and so four parts are produced: two human regarding us, and two divine regarding the gods. THEAETETUS. Indeed. STRANGER. From these, divided again in another way, one part of each division is productive, while the remaining parts are called "image-making." Whence the faculty of producing is again divided into two. THEAETETUS. Say again how each is divided. STRANGER. We ourselves, and all other animals, and those things from which they are produced—fire and water and their kindred—we know all these individual things were procreated and worked by God, do we not? THEAETETUS. Certainly. STRANGER. After these follow the images of these things, produced by a certain divine industry. THEAETETUS. What kind of images? STRANGER. The apparitions that occur to those who sleep, and those things which are seen in the day by themselves without art: a shadow when darkness is mixed with fire; or a double image, when the light of the eye and external light meet as one upon smooth and clear surfaces, providing a sensation contrary to usual sight and producing a reflection. THEAETETUS. These, then, are two works of divine production: the individual things themselves, and the images that follow each individual thing. STRANGER. And does not human art, through architecture, build a house, but through painting produce an image of the house, like a kind of human dream made for those who are awake? THEAETETUS. No doubt of it. STRANGER. In other things as well, by dividing into two, we will find twin works of our productive action. For we make the thing itself with our primary faculty, but the image with that which is imitative. THEAETETUS. Now I understand better, and I posit two species of the productive faculty: first, I divide it into divine and human according to the one division; and according to the other, into the production of things themselves and of images. STRANGER. Let us remember, I pray, that we said there must be two kinds of the image-making faculty, namely the <term>assimilative</term> <note>original: "assimilatorium," the art of making true likenesses.</note> and the <term>fantastic</term> <note>original: "phantasticum," the art of creating illusions or appearances that look right from a distance but are not true to the proportions of the original.</note>, if indeed something is to be truly false, and if "false" is to be one of the things that exist. THEAETETUS. That was certainly said. STRANGER. Did it not stand firm? And therefore will we now ourselves count these two species without controversy? THEAETETUS. Indeed. STRANGER. Therefore, divide the "fantastic" again into two. THEAETETUS. In what way? STRANGER. One made through instruments, and the other of him who presents himself as the instrument of the produced apparition. THEAETETUS. What are you saying? STRANGER. Whenever someone, taking on your form, makes his body or his voice seem similar to yours, that imitation is called "fantastic." THEAETETUS. Precisely. STRANGER. Calling this "imitative," let us distribute it as such, and let us pass over all the rest as if we were now desirous of rest, and let us allow another to gather it into one and give it a suitable name. THEAETETUS. Let it be distributed as you wish, and let this be dismissed. STRANGER. Furthermore, Theaetetus, this must be considered double. Pay attention to why. THEAETETUS. Tell me. STRANGER. Of those who imitate, some do this knowing what they imitate, but others do it in ignorance. Shall we posit any greater discrepancy and division than that between ignorance and knowledge? THEAETETUS. None. STRANGER. Was not that imitation we were just speaking of the imitation of those who know? For he who knows you imitates your form. THEAETETUS. That is it. STRANGER. But what should be said of the figure of justice and of virtue as a whole? Do not many, while they are ignorant of it, yet think they know it, and imitating what seems so to them, strive in both words and deeds so that they appear to possess it? THEAETETUS. Very many indeed. STRANGER. Does hope fail them so much that they do not appear to be just, even as they are not? Or is it the opposite? THEAETETUS. The opposite. STRANGER. We shall call this imitator different from that former one: the ignorant from the knowing? THEAETETUS. We certainly shall. STRANGER. From where, then, will a proper name for each be derived? Is it perhaps difficult because an old cause for the division of genera into species was unknown to our predecessors, so that no one attempted to divide them, and therefore they are necessarily lacking in names? And though it may seem a bit bold to say, yet for the sake of declaration and distinction, let us call that imitation which follows opinion "opinion-based imitation," but that which follows science, a certain "historical and knowing imitation." THEAETETUS. Let it be so. STRANGER. Only one of these names must be used. For we have placed the Sophist in the category of imitators, but not in the category of those who know. THEAETETUS. That is true. STRANGER. Let us therefore examine this "opinion-based" imitator as if he were iron, to see if he is solid and simple, or if on the contrary he has something twin and double within him. THEAETETUS. Let us examine him. STRANGER. He is certainly very manifold. For one Sophist is foolish and silly, who thinks

...thinks he knows what he merely opines. But the form of the other, because of his varied wandering in speeches, certainly has much suspicion and fear that he might perhaps be ignorant of those things which he pretends to know in front of others. **THEAETETUS.** He is altogether from both kinds, as you have related. **STRANGER.** Shall we not then posit one as a simple imitator, and the other as an ironic one? **THEAETETUS.** That is consistent. **STRANGER.** Of this one again, do we say there is one genus or two? **THEAETETUS.** You must see to it. **STRANGER.** I am thinking, and two present themselves to me as I think. One indeed is ironic in public with a long speech before the people; the other in private, with certain small quibbles, forces the one who disputes with him to contradict himself in his speeches. **THEAETETUS.** You speak very rightly. **STRANGER.** How shall we name that former one? Civil, or popular? **THEAETETUS.** Popular. <margin>From where the name Sophist is derived.</margin> **STRANGER.** And the other: *Sophon*, that is, wise, or Sophistical? **THEAETETUS.** It is not permitted to call him wise, since we have posited him as ignorant. But since he imitates the wise man, he will obtain a certain name similar to his. And at last I understand that this very man ought to be called, exactly and truly, the Sophist. <margin>The final definition of the sophist.</margin> **STRANGER.** Shall we not now bind his name together, as we did above, by folding everything from the end back to the beginning? **THEAETETUS.** Altogether. **STRANGER.** He at last will truly define the Sophist who asserts that his birth and stock is this: The Sophist, I say, is he who in speeches forces the one disputing to contradict himself; who is a part of the ironic kind, coming from the opinion-based imitator; likewise of the appearance-making genus, flowing from the imaginary faculty; a determined progeny not of divine, but of human production; and from the number of those who, by words as if by certain deceptions <note>Original: "praestigiis" - tricks or illusions</note>, wonderfully deceive their listeners. **THEAETETUS.** It must be said exactly so.

->MARSILIO FICINO'S APOLOGY FOR THE BOOK OF PLATO,<-
->On Kingship, to Federico Duke of Urbino, ever invincible.<-

JUPITER Best and Greatest, when he desired to look upon such a kingdom on earth as he always sees with himself in heaven, long ago sent down to earth a certain royal and divine soul through the very idea of a divine king. And having called together the heavenly beings, he commanded that they all should vote for this future king, whom the gods above see and—from his royal faith—already name "Fideregum" <note>A pun on Federico's name: Fides (faith) + Regum (of kings)</note>, and from the empire of the world "Orbinantem Ducem" <note>A pun on Urbino: Orbis (world) + nantis (commanding)</note>, though men, with changed letters, would call him Federico, Duke of Urbino. All the deities assented to Jove except Juno. For Juno alone, the ambitious queen of the thicker air, has until now envied the heavenly kingdom on earth. But Pallas <note>Athena</note> and Mercury, with the others favoring and Truth as witness, long ago most gladly bestowed the crown and royal scepter upon the same man to whom Jupiter did. And since the Academy everywhere worships and follows Pallas and Mercury, it also most happily grants the kingdom and monarchy of the whole world—such as the divine Plato describes—to Federico, Duke of Urbino, both from the judgment of Jove and from the testimony of Truth, as he is most excellently deserving.

->PLATO’S STATESMAN, OR, ON KINGSHIP.<-

->MARSILIO FICINO’S ARGUMENT.<-

SINCE God and nature produce man for action, they certainly produce him so that he may act—act, I say, for the sake of divine things. Just as there is one end for which nature makes a thumb, another for which it makes a hand or a foot, and again another toward which it makes the whole man: so there is one end toward which it directs the individual man, another toward which it directs the family, and likewise another toward which it directs the city and the kingdom. And finally,

--- Page 157 ---
138    Sixteenth Book.

that end must be considered the best, for the sake of which God created the whole human race. Let no one think that while there is a certain end for each particular group, there is none for the whole; and that while there is order in the parts of human life, there is confusion in the entire kind of life; finally, that while the parts have a union among themselves for the sake of a single purpose, the whole itself is dispersed. For this reason, it is necessary that there be a certain end for the human race, and that it consist in a certain action concerning more perfect things, through which it may both imitate superior things according to its strength and diligently govern inferior ones: it should search into natural things through knowledge, dispose human things through prudence, and worship and venerate divine things through piety. Therefore, an end of this sort requires a double life, established similarly in both action and contemplation, yet in such a way that action is instituted for the sake of contemplation as something more divine. Furthermore, the absolute perfection of both lives needs so many and such various supports that it can be fulfilled neither by a few people, nor even by many, but only by the whole race of men together. But it cannot happen that such diverse peoples can be led through such diverse means to the one common end of all, unless by one person through a certain single law leading everyone toward the one goal together. Just as craftsmen and assistants, differing greatly among themselves in kind and nature, bringing very various materials to one form of a building, will never conveniently assemble and construct it opportunely unless they are ruled by one law of one architect. For this reason, not without cause, when Plato sought the king, the monarch of the world, he first brought the architect into the midst, and finally distinguished knowledge into three kinds. The first of these is concerned with knowing, the second with acting, the third with making. In the first he placed arithmetic and geometry; in the second, the architect; in the third, the craftsman and the assistant, proving that the architect's faculty must be placed in the middle between mere speculation and mere service, yet participating more in speculation than in service, and not only pointing things out in the manner of geometers, but also commanding those who make things, and always being present at the workmanship. He wants the king to be almost such a man, who truly judges in the manner of those who contemplate, and commands duties to be done—not someone else's, but his own. Hence Plato, by a most exact division which is very necessary for the definition and for knowledge, names the King, in the Homeric fashion, the shepherd and caretaker of the human race. He designates that he ought to be one shepherd of the whole human race as if of one fold, where he says that God was a certain shepherd of the human race, under whom also that golden kingdom of Saturn existed. He also judges that the king should be called the governor <note>Original: "Gubernatorem" - pilot or navigator</note> of human life, as if of a ship. He signifies, moreover, that the empire of all must be brought together into one, so that human government may be as similar as possible to the divine, since one God is the ruler of the whole world. This is also briefly confirmed by these reasons: First, if you subject the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—to three distributed kings, it will very easily happen that either one will make war on two, or two on one, or at least they will be forced to dispute about borders or some other thing. Therefore, either the judgment of the suit must be brought to one of the three, or to some fourth judge established besides the three. By whatever reason that is done, it will be necessary for the judge, if his sentence is to be followed, to have power over those between whom the judgment is made. Otherwise the judgment will be of no weight, and it will be judged in vain, which might seem likely to be dissolved by the kings, who are either more or at least equally powerful. Therefore, it is necessary that there be one king, the judge of all, to be venerated by everyone without doubt. Furthermore, the king ought to be an exemplar of virtues to his subjects. He will be such most especially if he is one before all, upon whom everyone casts their eyes. If he possesses the whole world, he will neither affect a further kingdom, nor envy others. These two things—namely greed and envy—are what most especially give birth to robberies and wars. And since his own things are most dear to everyone, he will love all as his own, and he will love all nations equally, and care for them equally. He will desire peace above all, he will want tranquility, and an abundance of all good things, such as appeared as a certain shadow of monarchy when Octavian was ruling. The subjects will live most justly, since under a monarch there is no escape route for the unjust; and although they live with the least license to sin, they will live in the greatest liberty—not subject to tyrants, or a few powerful men, or the furies of a raging populace, but led thus to the common good by a wise and just and pious king, as sailors are led to port by the prudence of a just navigator. In this matter, both those who are governed will consult their own interests by obeying the king, and the king himself will live not so much for himself as for all who are committed to his care by God. For right government, as is disputed in the books *On the Republic*, establishes the governor...

--- Page 158 ---
Ciuilis, Or, On Kingship. 139

...indeed for the sake of those who are governed, not the governed for the sake of the governor. Furthermore, he compares the king to a doctor, warning that in the manner of doctors, he should impose laws or bring healthy remedies both opportunely and, if need be, importunely, both for those who are willing and sometimes for those who are unwilling. He more often calls such a governor and caretaker a "civil man" <note>term: "virum civilem" - a statesman</note> than a "king," signifying that he ought to be so human and, if possible, mild, that he seems to be a fellow citizen among citizens, superior by prudence, justice, and care rather than by any other excess. But if someone, by a very long interval, manifestly surpasses all in prudence and justice, he judges without controversy that this man, even if he lives as a private citizen, is a king of all created by God. But if there is very little difference among some in this regard, the royal authority should be given to them reduced in a way to one; but by no means to many. For many people worthy of such authority cannot be found anywhere. Moreover, he wants royal authority to be handed over—as can be conjectured from his other books—by the elders and the most proven men, whose senate then becomes a colleague of the king, like a certain republic of the best men. The king, together with the senate, should establish laws which it is not permitted for any private person to transgress, nor for the common people to change. Yet it is permitted for the king and the senate together, according to the opportunity of the times as far as it is expedient, to accommodate them with diligent equity both to things themselves and to times, and to change them if necessary. In his letters, he considers the king himself to be sacred, and to be established in the manner of Egyptian priests, a leader of sacred rites and mysteries. And as he is sacred, so that he may never be contaminated, he does not permit him to be present at judgments where it concerns slaughter, exile, or prison. Hence in this very book, he proves that such royal dignity is the best of all governments, as we have said; but the worst is tyranny, which rules neither by law nor by a legitimate mind, but rather by impulse and lust. In the second place he praises the rule of the best <note>Aristocracy</note>, and likewise blames the rule of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>. In the third place he praises the government of many, namely the popular one <note>Democracy</note>, if they govern by law; and similarly he blames it if not by law. After these things, he disputes what the royal duty is—namely, to provide for whatever things are necessary for the human race, and especially for living well and blessedly. He should judge prudently how many and what kind of arts contribute to this very thing, whether in peace or in war, whether in speaking or in acting, whether publicly or privately, and he should have, together with the senate, supreme command over all. Especially, he should compose the minds of all with a most fitting mixture of fortitude and temperance, imitating musicians, who—rightly mixing high notes with low ones—modulate the sweetest harmonies. For he demonstrates, and that divinely, that it is not safe to stretch minds too far toward fortitude, as if into a high pitch, or to relax them too much toward temperance, as if into a low pitch. For from the former they turn out wild, and from the latter effeminate. And those citizens attack both the city and the fatherland as enemies; but these are held neither by themselves nor their fatherland against enemies. Therefore, he thinks that a consonance of characters should be fused everywhere from the harmonious joining of both virtues. But enough has been said so far about the order of the book. As for what he disputes about the motion of the spheres, providence, and fate, we have explained those sufficiently in our *Theology*. In these things, he certainly teaches us allegorically that we have no true and legitimate king except either in heaven itself, or on earth one whom the king of heaven has set over us as a shepherd—a shepherd, I say, not in name alone, but by a similarity of life, reflecting the king of heaven himself according to his strength. He mentions also two kingdoms, namely of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> and of Saturn, and he prefers the kingdom of Saturn to the kingdom of Jove as being happier. For under Jove, human action and life are signified, but under Saturn, the contemplation of divine things. For Saturn, called *Cronos* in Greek, as Plato teaches in the *Cratylus*, encompasses an inviolable purity and integrity of mind. When he says that under the reign of Saturn men live blessedly, he shows that the human race will be blessed when a certain divine mind of a man is reigning, which institutes actions for the sake of contemplation. I will soon make an end to the argument, if I first bring in a brief allegory of this mystery. For he says that the present circuit of the world from east to west belongs to Jove and is fatal; but there will be another at some time, opposite to this, under Saturn, from west back to east. In this, men will be born spontaneously and will proceed from old age into youth, and nourishment will be supplied to them freely and eternally under a spring according to their wish. I believe he calls Jove the soul of the world, by whose fatal law this manifest order of the manifest world is disposed. Furthermore, he wants the life of souls in elemental bodies to be Jovian, devoted to the senses and action. But Saturn is the supreme intellect among the angels, by whose rays souls are illuminated beyond the angels and set on fire: and they are continually raised to the intellectual life according to their strength. Whenever they are turned toward such a life, they are said to live under the kingdom of Saturn as far as they live by intelligence. Hence in that life they are said to be regenerated spontaneously, because by their own choice they are reformed for the better. Again, to grow young again daily—that is, if days are numbered there, to flourish more and more every day. This is that of the apostle Paul: *The inner man is renewed daily.* <note>2 Corinthians 4:16</note> Finally, nourishment is supplied to them spontaneously in abundance under a perpetual spring, because they enjoy the wondrous spectacles of truth itself, not through the senses and laborious discipline, but through an internal light and the greatest tranquility and pleasure of life.

**SOCRATES. THEODORUS. STRANGER. YOUNGER SOCRATES.**

**SOCRATES.** I truly owe you a great debt of gratitude, O Theodorus, for having introduced me to Theaetetus and this Stranger from Elea. **THEODORUS.** You will perhaps owe me a triple debt, O Socrates, after they have finished the statesman and the philosopher for you. **SOCRATES.** Let it be so. But shall we say that we heard that from you, O dear Theodorus, a man most skilled in both reasoning and geometry? **THEODORUS.** What do you mean by that, O Socrates? **SOCRATES.** That we have placed each of these men at the same value, who yet are as far apart in honor as can be explained by that analogy of your art. **THEODORUS.** You speak well and justly, by our god Ammon, O Socrates; and you have now very promptly objected to my error in counting, and I will come at you again for these things. But now, Stranger, let it not be a burden to gratify us, but next describe either the civil man first, or the philosopher who is greater. **STRANGER.** Must I do as you command? Theodorus, since we have once begun, we must not stop until we reach the goal. But what is fitting to do about this Theaetetus? **THEODORUS.** Concerning what? **STRANGER.** Shall we now let him rest? And in his place, shall we take this Socrates as a companion in exercises and studies? What do you advise? **THEODORUS.** Take him as you said. For since both are young, they will bear all the labor more easily through alternation. **SOCRATES.** And both seem to me to be somehow related to me, Stranger. You judge Theaetetus to be like me in the figure of his face. To this Socrates also, since he has the same name as me, the name provides us a certain mutual kinship. It is fitting that we who are related should eagerly witness that matter in speech. I met with Theaetetus in disputation yesterday, and today I have heard him responding to this stranger. But with Socrates, neither has yet been done. It is necessary to examine him too. Let him answer to me at another time, but to you now. **STRANGER.** So we shall do, O Socrates. Do you hear, Socrates? **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** I hear. **STRANGER.** Do you agree with him? **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** I agree. **STRANGER.** As far as you are concerned, then, nothing prevents us from discussing. And much less should I be a hindrance to this dispute. Rather, after the Sophist himself, it seems necessary that we investigate the civil man. Respond then: whether we should refer him to the number of those who are called "knowing." **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** It is fitting. **STRANGER.** Therefore we must divide the sciences, just as we did in searching for the Sophist. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Perhaps. **STRANGER.** But the same method of dividing does not seem right to me, O Socrates. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** No. **STRANGER.** But another. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Another. **STRANGER.** Where then shall we find the path of civil science? For it is necessary to find it, and having segregated it from all others, to impress one idea upon it, and likewise to mark the other diversions with one other species: and we must persuade ourselves that all sciences are contained within two species. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** It is your concern now, Stranger, to act so; but not mine. **STRANGER.** Rather it is yours also, when it has been declared. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** You speak skillfully. <margin>Mathematical sciences are free from action, possessing knowledge alone.</margin> **STRANGER.** Furthermore, arithmetic and some others very similar to it are free from action, but provide knowledge only. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** So it must certainly be said. **STRANGER.** But those which pertain to architecture and manual service possess a science innate in actions; they perfect the bodies made by them, which did not exist before. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** It is clear. <margin>Two species of science.</margin> **STRANGER.** Thus divide all sciences. One acting, the other knowing names alone. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Let there then be two species of science, since the whole is one science. **STRANGER.** Whether we want the civil man, the king, the master, and the head of the household to be the same? Or do we posit as many arts in these as there are names? Rather, follow me here. <margin>The civil man, king, master, and head of household are the same.</margin> **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Where? **STRANGER.** Here, I say. If some private person can sufficiently advise a public doctor, is it not necessary that he be called by the name of the same art as the one whom he advises? **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** What furthermore? If some private person can admonish and instruct the king of a city, will he not be said to have that science which he who rules ought to possess? **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** He will be so called. **STRANGER.** But the science of a true king is the royal discipline. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** It is. <margin>The royal man.</margin> **STRANGER.** Whoever is endowed with it, whether he performs a public duty or lives as a private citizen, will rightly be called "royal" altogether according to this skill. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Rightly. **STRANGER.** Indeed, the head of the household and the master are the same. **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** The same indeed. **STRANGER.** Does it matter whether a city is large or narrow for rule? **YOUNGER SOCRATES.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** Therefore, as we were inquiring a little while ago, there is one science of all these: whether one calls this royal or civil or domestic discipline, let us think it makes no difference. **SOCRATES.** None. **STRANGER.** This at least is doubtful to no one, that every king can do very little with his hands and other members for the safety of the kingdom, but very much with intelligence and strength of soul. **SOCRATES.** It stands. **STRANGER.** Do you want us to say that the king is closer to speculative science than to active science or manual service? **SOCRATES.** I certainly do. **STRANGER.** Therefore we shall compose the civil science and the civil man, the royal and the royal man, as one and the same in each case. **SOCRATES.** Plainly. **STRANGER.** And we shall proceed in order to the following things, especially if we distinguish speculative science. **SOCRATES.** Altogether. **STRANGER.** Pay attention, I pray, whether we may see some refuge in this. **SOCRATES.** Tell me, of what kind? **STRANGER.** Of this kind, I say. There exists some faculty of calculating. **SOCRATES.** There exists. **STRANGER.** That, I believe, is from the number of those which are concerned with speculating. **SOCRATES.** From that number, certainly. **STRANGER.** The faculty of calculating will surely know the difference of numbers. Do we attribute any other work to it than to discern and judge what is known? **SOCRATES.** What? **STRANGER.** And indeed no architect uses the service of his hands, but presides over those who use them. **SOCRATES.** That is so. **STRANGER.** He is rightly therefore to be called a participant in speculative science. **SOCRATES.** And most especially. **STRANGER.** This, I believe, pertains to the judge: not to come to an end and soon depart, like that calculator, but to press on and command to each of the workmen a suitable task until they have finished what was ordered. **SOCRATES.** Very well. **STRANGER.** Are not all these speculative, as many as follow the science of calculating: but these two genera differ from each other in judgment and command? **SOCRATES.** They appear so. **STRANGER.** Wherefore if we distribute the whole contemplation into two, and assign one part to judgment and the other to command, we shall perhaps think we have distributed rightly. **SOCRATES.** Rightly indeed, as my opinion goes. **STRANGER.** Those who treat something in common think themselves mutually satisfied if they ever agree. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** Therefore as long as we are in concord in this, the opinions of others are to be passed over. **SOCRATES.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** Tell me, in which art of these is it fitting to place the royal man? Shall we place him in the judicial, as a certain spectator? Or rather in the commanding, as a master? **SOCRATES.** In this latter one rather. **STRANGER.** We must see furthermore if the commanding art admits any distinction. And so it seems to me. As much as a shopkeeper differs from him who sells his own work, so a king differs from a herald. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Shopkeepers, receiving the works of others already sold, sell them again themselves. **SOCRATES.** True. **STRANGER.** Not otherwise does the race of heralds command to others the sentence of another that was commanded to them. **SOCRATES.** It is so. **STRANGER.** Shall we mix the royal faculty with the interpretive, the preceptive, the prophetic, and the heraldic, and many other arts of the same kind, all of which command? Or do you wish rather, according to the previous comparison, that we devise some name through comparison, since the genus of those who command their own things is almost without a name: and thus let us divide these so that we place the royal genus in the number of those who command their own, having omitted all others, upon which anyone else may impose a name as he pleases? For our speech was instituted for the sake of the prince, not the subject. **SOCRATES.** Indeed. **STRANGER.** Since this is sufficiently distinguished from those others, and reduced from what belongs to another to what is its own, it must be divided again, if we find any partition in it that will admit us. **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **STRANGER.** And it seems possible to be found. Follow me then by dividing. **SOCRATES.** Where shall I follow? **STRANGER.** Whoever presides by commanding, commands for the sake of something being done. **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **STRANGER.** And indeed to divide all things generated into two is not very difficult. **SOCRATES.** By what reasoning? **STRANGER.** Partly they are animate, partly inanimate. **SOCRATES.** It stands. **STRANGER.** If we wish to cut the commanding part of the speculative faculty into these members, let us cut it. **SOCRATES.** Into which? **STRANGER.** Let one part of it be placed in the generation of inanimate things, and a part in the generation of animate things. And thus the whole will be cut in two. **SOCRATES.** Truly. **STRANGER.** Let us send one part away, taking up the other, and divide that whole again in two. **SOCRATES.** Which of those do you think should be taken up? **STRANGER.** That which commands concerning animals. For the royal majesty does not preside over things that are not animate in the manner of architecture, but more nobly over living things, and its power is concerned with these. **SOCRATES.** Very well. **STRANGER.** Concerning the generation and nutrition of animals, a double care is found. This one of some single animal, that one of the whole flock. **SOCRATES.** Rightly. **STRANGER.** But the civil man does not take care of each one privately, like he who drives an ox, or an assistant who saddles a horse, but he plays the part of him who feeds horses or oxen. **SOCRATES.** What has now been said seems to be true. **STRANGER.** Do we call that nutrition of animals which feeds them in herds "flock nutrition," or "common nutrition"? **SOCRATES.** It happens that both are used in speaking. <margin>Curiosity of words is to be avoided.</margin> **STRANGER.** You have answered excellently, Socrates: and if you avoid the curiosity of words, you will turn out much wiser in old age. Therefore for the present, as you command, it must be done. But do you see in what way someone, showing that the nutrition of the flock is double, may make it so that what is investigated in both for what is now proposed may then be sought in the other? **SOCRATES.** I shall strive...

--- Page 159 ---
140    Sixteenth Book.

...indeed, and now it seems to me that one is the guardianship of men in common, and the other of brutes. **STRANGER.** You have distinguished promptly and bravely. Yet we must beware as much as possible lest that should happen to us hereafter. **SOCRATES.** What do you warn us to beware of? **STRANGER.** Not to separate one tiny little part against many large ones, and not to take that part without its species; but let that part have a species at the same time. For it is a very beautiful thing to discern immediately from others what is sought, if only it is done rightly—just as you yourself a little while ago, judging about dividing, hastened to divide, seeing the speech declining with one member toward men. But it is not safe enough or friendly enough to pursue everything too thinly to the extreme. It is better to proceed by dividing through the middle; for thus we find ideas more easily and better. This, moreover, refers the whole matter to those things which are sought. **SOCRATES.** For what reason do you say that, Stranger? **STRANGER.** I must try, on account of the benevolence of your nature, to explain it more clearly. For the present, it is impossible to declare this which is proposed so that nothing is missing; but it must be repeated from a little higher up for the sake of clarity. **SOCRATES.** What then do you find fault with in this partition of ours? **STRANGER.** Something of this kind: if someone striving to cut the human race in two should divide just as many of our people divide. They indeed separate the race of the Greeks as one from all the others. For all other innumerable men, joined together by no communion of life or speech among themselves, they mark with the name "barbarian," and because of this one name they think this whole thing is also one genus. It would be similar, furthermore, if someone wanting to divide number into two should take ten thousand separately from the others as one species, and then put the rest as one genus, imposing one certain name on them. But the division would be made more rightly and more through species and through two members, if someone should divide number by even and odd, or the race of men by male and female. But he would segregate the Lydians and Phrygians, or some others, from all the others only when both the hope and the faculty were lacking to him of finding the genus at the same time as the part, each of those which were dissected. **SOCRATES.** You speak skillfully, Stranger. But show by what reasoning that can be more plainly understood, that the part and the genus are not the same, but different. **STRANGER.** O most excellent Socrates, you ask no light thing. We have now wandered further from our purpose than is fitting. But you command us to wander even further. Now, therefore, as is decent, let the speech be reflected back to where it departed. At another time, when we have found leisure, we shall turn aside as if through certain tracks to these things. Nevertheless, you will diligently beware of this, O Socrates: do not think you have heard something certain from me about this. **SOCRATES.** About what? **STRANGER.** That the part and the species differ. <margin>What the differences are between part and species.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Why? **STRANGER.** Whatever is a species of something, it is necessary that it also be a part of that of which it is said to be a species. But it is not necessary that a part be a species, or a part of a species. Assert that I say it always in this way rather than that, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** It shall be done as you command. **STRANGER.** After this, tell me. **SOCRATES.** What? **STRANGER.** This, I say, from where we wandered away to this place. I think indeed we have wandered so far for this reason, that you, when asked into what members the nutrition of the flock was divided, answered very promptly that there were two genera of living things: one of men, and the other of all brutes together as one. **SOCRATES.** It is true. **STRANGER.** Then indeed you seemed to me, one part having been taken away, to have thought the whole remaining genus of animals should be posited for the reason that you could call them all by one certain common name, while you called them brutes. **SOCRATES.** That is what was done. **STRANGER.** This, O most brave Socrates, seems to be just as if some other animal, like a crane <note>The Stranger uses the crane as an example of a creature that might think it is rational and superior, mocking human self-importance.</note> or some other such thing participating in prudence, should call the genus of "rationals" in the same way you do, pleasing itself by this, and should posit this one genus opposite to the other animals, but embracing all the rest together with men, should call the other genus "brutes." Let us therefore try to decline from all errors of this kind. **SOCRATES.** By what way? **STRANGER.** Not dividing the whole genus of animals, so that we do not fail in these things. **SOCRATES.** For neither is it fitting. **STRANGER.** Yet we failed thus above. **SOCRATES.** How? **STRANGER.** That part of speculative science which looks toward commanding, was established to be of that genus which cares for animals—namely, gregarious animals. Was it not? **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** Wherefore then also the whole genus of animals was distinguished as inferior and tame. For those things which were so instituted by nature that they can grow tame were called "tame" <note>Original: "cicuria"</note>, but the others "wild." **SOCRATES.** Excellently. **STRANGER.** But that science which we seek is among domestic things, and it was, and seems to be sought, around the sociable genus of animals. **SOCRATES.** Surely. **STRANGER.** Therefore let us not divide by looking at all things at once, as we did then, nor let us hasten too much in dividing, so that we may suddenly grasp civil science. For too much haste caused that which is said in the proverb to happen to us now. <margin>Proverb.</margin> **SOCRATES.** What? **STRANGER.** That when we have hastened too much in the division, we finish more slowly. **SOCRATES.** And the Stranger has indeed done that rightly. **STRANGER.** Concerning these things, let it be so. But again from the beginning let us try to divide the common nutrition of animals. For perhaps that which you so vehemently affect, the speech itself having been led step by step to its end, will demonstrate more clearly. Answer to this. **SOCRATES.** To what shall I answer? <margin>Fish being tamed around the Nile.</margin> **STRANGER.** You have perhaps heard this from many—for I do not think you were present among those who tame fish around the Nile, or around the royal fish ponds. But what happens around fountains, you perhaps saw yourself. **SOCRATES.** Both I have seen myself, and I have heard those things from many. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, that some people feed flocks of geese and cranes, even if you have never lived in the Thessalian fields, you have heard nevertheless, and you believe it. **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **STRANGER.** I have inquired these things of you for this reason, because that guardianship of animals which is done in flocks seems to be partly of aquatic animals, and partly of land animals. **SOCRATES.** It is indeed. **STRANGER.** Do you agree that the guardianship of the flock is thus to be distinguished in two, so that it feeds partly moist, partly dry animals? **SOCRATES.** I agree indeed. **STRANGER.** But which of these the royal diligence looks toward, no one will ask. For it is a doubt to no one. **SOCRATES.** To no one. **STRANGER.** For everyone will especially distinguish the nutrition of dry animals. **SOCRATES.** Into what members? **STRANGER.** Into the guardianship of those that fly or those that walk. **SOCRATES.** So the truth holds. **STRANGER.** That the civil faculty is concerned only with those that walk, even the most stupid person, if I may say so, would notice. **SOCRATES.** Without controversy. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, we ought to divide the nourishment of the walking genus into two, like an even number. **SOCRATES.** It is clear. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, those two paths seem to be able to lead us to where our speech tends. One indeed by a certain short path, while it segregates a narrow little part from a large one. But the other by a longer circuit, while it preserves that precept said before, that the division be made through the middle; it is permitted to enter whichever we wish. **SOCRATES.** Is it not permitted to proceed through both? **STRANGER.** Not at the same time, O wonderful youth. But it is permitted separately. **SOCRATES.** I should desire both then separately. **STRANGER.** That is easy...

# Civil, or, On the Kingdom. 141

Indeed, since what remains is so small. Certainly, this command would have been hard for us at the beginning or the middle of the journey. But now, since it seems right, let us first enter upon the longer way. For since we have not long ago set ourselves to the task, we shall more easily complete the long journey. See this distinction then. **SOC.** Just tell me. **GUEST.** In what way the genus of walking, gentle, and herding creatures is divided into two parts according to nature. **SOC.** In what way? **GUEST.** One part is armed with horns, and the other is lacking horns. **SOC.** That is apparent. **GUEST.** Dividing the care of walking creatures, describe the condition of each part in speech. For if you wish to name them specifically, you will entangle the matter too much. **SOC.** How then do you think we should speak? **GUEST.** In this way: since the care of walking creatures is distinguished in two ways, one part concerns the horned portion of the flock, and the other the hornless. **SOC.** Let it be said so, for it has been sufficiently shown. **GUEST.** It is agreed, then, that the king is the shepherd of a certain hornless flock. **SOC.** It is certainly agreed. **GUEST.** Let us therefore try to exhibit what is done by him, by dissecting this [flock]. **SOC.** By all means. **GUEST.** Does it please you to divide the flock by the difference between solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed animals? Or rather by their generation, this one being unique, that one common? For you understand. **SOC.** What? **GUEST.** That the genus of horses and donkeys breeds promiscuously <note>original: "promiscue generat"; referring to the cross-breeding of horses and donkeys to produce mules.</note> among themselves. **SOC.** Truly. **GUEST.** But the remaining animals of the domestic and social kind procreate only from their own species, without foreign intermixture. **SOC.** That is clear to anyone. **GUEST.** Therefore, does the **civil** discipline care for animals of mixed generation, or those of simple generation? **SOC.** Of unmixed and simple, without a doubt. **GUEST.** We must cut this nature of living beings into twin members, just as we have maintained in the previous steps up to now. **SOC.** It is fitting. **GUEST.** Indeed, we have already distinguished this whole genus of domestic and herding animals, which they call "tame," except for two genera. Moreover, it is not fitting to number the genus of dogs among the herding cattle. **SOC.** Certainly not. But in what way shall we divide these two? **GUEST.** In this way, I say, by which it is fitting for you and Theaetetus to distribute them, since you are practiced in geometry: namely, by the diagonal, and again by the diagonal of the diagonal. <note>This is a complex mathematical joke by Plato. He is punning on the "diagonal" (diameter) of a square and the "power" of the feet, suggesting that humans are the "diagonal" of a square with a side of one foot.</note> **SOC.** How do you say that? **GUEST.** Is the condition of the human race naturally instituted for progress in any other way than as a biped in the power of the diagonal? **SOC.** Not otherwise. **GUEST.** Truly, the condition of the remaining genus is again, according to power, the diagonal of our power, since it is constituted with twice two feet. <note>He is jokingly classifying quadrupeds as "double" bipeds through geometric ratios.</note> **SOC.** Nothing prevents it from being of this kind. And I almost understand what you wish to show. **GUEST.** Do we see what else worthy of laughter, O Socrates, has happened to us in the previous division? **SOC.** What is it? **GUEST.** The human genus mixed and running together with the most generous <note>original: "generofissimo"; here used ironically to refer to pigs, which were easy to raise.</note> and easiest genus of all. **SOC.** I see, and indeed clearly, how absurd it is. **GUEST.** Is it not fitting that those which are slowest arrive last? **SOC.** It is consistent. **GUEST.** But we did not notice this at all: that the king appears more ridiculous, running about together with the flock of men, and performing his course with that one <note>The pig.</note> who is best of all trained for the ease of life? **SOC.** Altogether indeed. **GUEST.** Now that is clearly evident, O Socrates, which was said in the inquiry of the sophist. **SOC.** What was that? **GUEST.** That in this kind of methodical reasoning of disputation, it cares no more for the elegant than the inelegant, nor does it make the shorter path of more value than the longer, but accomplishes only what is most true. **SOC.** So it seems. **GUEST.** After this, do not forestall me by asking for the shorter way to establish the definition of the king; I enter upon it of my own accord. **SOC.** By all means. **GUEST.** I say therefore that it was necessary above to distribute the walking animal into biped and quadruped; and since man then remained alone with the winged creatures, to divide again the biped genus itself into the naked and featherless, and the winged. With this distinction performed, and the art that nourishes and preserves men being shown, we might now place the civil and royal man over it like a charioteer, and give him the reins and rudders of the city, as if this were the proper science belonging to him. **SOC.** You have paid me this speech very well, and as if it were a debt, with the digression itself added in place of interest, and fully completed. **GUEST.** Come then, let us collect from the beginning to the end the discourse concerning the name of the civil art. **SOC.** Entirely. **GUEST.** Of that science, therefore, which is engaged in contemplation, one part is the skill of commanding; under this is subjected that faculty which commands by its own impulse. To this belongs the nutrition of animals—hardly a small member. To this also, the feeding of the flock; and to this, finally, the feeding of walking animals. To this again, that species which pastures animals lacking horns. It is necessary to embrace at least a triple part of it, if one wishes to comprehend it by one name, calling it the science of feeding the unmixed genus. The portion of this which feeds only humans from the flock of bipeds is that very imperial faculty we seek, which we name equally royal and civil. **SOC.** Entirely. **GUEST.** Do you think, O Socrates, that this has been rightly done by us, just as you have now said? **SOC.** Concerning what matter? **GUEST.** Whether what we proposed has been sufficiently absolved? Or has that which we described in a certain way been mostly overlooked in the question, and not yet thoroughly defined? **SOC.** How do you say that? **GUEST.** I shall try to explain more plainly what I feel. **SOC.** Speak now. **GUEST.** Since it has been established that there are many faculties of shepherds, one of those, and the guardianship of one flock, seemed to be the civil discipline itself. **SOC.** Indeed. **GUEST.** We showed this to be the common nourishment not of horses, nor of other brutes, but of men only. **SOC.** We did that too. **GUEST.** Therefore, let us see the proper difference between all shepherds and kings. **SOC.** What difference? **GUEST.** If someone, perhaps having the name of another art, should claim for himself the common nourishment of the human flock, what should be said? **SOC.** In what way do you mean? **GUEST.** If merchants, I say, farmers, and cooks, and moreover gymnastic trainers and physicians, should rise up against the shepherds whom we have called "politicians," and assert that they are the shepherds of men; since they supply food not only to the common people, but also to kings and magistrates. **SOC.** Would they not speak the truth? **GUEST.** Perhaps. And let us consider this. For we know that no one contends with the ox-herd about these things; for he himself is without controversy the shepherd of the herd, because he cares for the oxen; he is the physician, he is the matchmaker, and he alone is skilled in the obstetric art which pertains to the births and offspring of those being born. Furthermore, no one delights the herd with jokes and music better than he, so far as their nature is capable of them, drawing and soothing them whether handling the music of his flock with instruments or with his mouth alone. And is not the reason the same for other shepherds? **SOC.** Most certainly. **GUEST.** In what way, therefore, does that speech concerning the king seem right and whole, when we pose him as that shepherd and nourisher of the human flock, separating him alone from others, when many others contend for this very thing? **SOC.** In no way. **GUEST.** Did we not rightly doubt a little while ago, when we suspected that we might only be introducing a certain figure of a king, but had not yet perfectly defined the civil man himself?

### The Sixteenth Book: The Statesman, or, On Kingship

**[Page 142]**

...we should not define [the king], unless we first encompass those who involve themselves with him and profess themselves to be shepherds no less than he: and, discerning the king from them, show him pure and alone. **SOC.** Rightly indeed. **HOS.** This, therefore, must be done by us, O Socrates, unless we wish to bring back infamy at the end of our discourse. **SOC.** And yet that is by no means expedient. **HOS.** Again, we must proceed from another principle, by another certain way. **SOC.** By what way? **HOS.** It is necessary to interpose a certain place here, and to use a great part of a long fable, and as for what remains, to follow through as we did above, always subdividing a part of a part, and thus lead to the highest thing that is sought. Is it not necessary? **SOC.** It is necessary indeed. **HOS.** But now receive the little fable with pricked-up ears, as children are wont to do, for you are not far from childhood years. **SOC.** Tell it, I pray. **HOS.** There was, then, and there will still be, a great memory of ancient things, and among others, that memorable portent which is related concerning the contention of Atreus and Thyestes. For you have heard and remember what they say happened then. **SOC.** Do you mean the sign of the golden lamb? **HOS.** By no means, but of the rising of the sun and its setting, and the change of the other stars. For whence they now rise, they then set, and conversely they rose. Then indeed God, providing testimony to Atreus, changed the heaven into this figure. **SOC.** This also is told. **HOS.** Furthermore, we have heard from many concerning the reign of Saturnus. **SOC.** From many, certainly. **HOS.** What then? Is it not also said that those ancient people were procreated from the earth, and not from one another? **SOC.** This also is commemorated among ancient things. **HOS.** All these things proceed from the same misfortune, and many others besides these far more wonderful: but through the magnitude of time, some have faded away, others are told separately without order: but that misfortune which is the cause of all these, no one has told. But now it must be told, for it will contribute to showing the king. **SOC.** You speak excellently. Relate it then, and omit nothing. **HOS.** Hear now. This universe God himself at one time guides, drives, and rotates: but at another time he lets it go, when the circuits of the world have filled their competent curricula of time. Then the world is reflected back by its own free motion. For it both lives and has been allotted wisdom from him who constructed it from the beginning. But the circuit was necessarily innate to it for this reason. **SOC.** For what reason, do you say? **HOS.** To be always the same, and according to the same things, and to hold itself in the same way, belongs only to the most divine of all things: but the nature of the body is not capable of this order. Moreover, that whole which we call the heaven and the world received many and happy gifts from its progenitor, yet being a participant in a body, it cannot be entirely free from any change: nevertheless, as far as it can, it is moved in the same way, and according to the same things, and by one motion: wherefore it obtained a circuit, in which there is the least permutation of its agitation. But to turn itself always is possible for almost nothing, except for that which drives the course: he excels all. But to move it now one way, now another, and again in a contrary way, is forbidden. From all these things it must be said, that the world neither turns itself always, nor is it always reflected by God himself in a double and contrary circuit, nor again do two gods with contrary intentions try to turn it. Only that which we recently said remains: at one time it is led by a certain other divine power, and receives life coming from without, and immortality prepared by its maker: at another time, when it is let go, it runs by itself; at which time, power having been granted, it performs many thousands of retrograde revolutions, because it is both greatest, and thoroughly balanced on every side, and revolved on a very small hinge. **SOC.** All those things which you have commemorated seem very likely. **HOS.** From these things which have been said, let us now consider that misfortune, conjecturing it to be the cause of all the wonders we mentioned. It is of this sort. **SOC.** Of what sort? **HOS.** That the motion of the whole world, just as it is now, is then revolved in the opposite direction. **SOC.** In what way? **HOS.** This change must be thought to be the greatest and most extreme of all celestial alternations. **SOC.** It seems so. **HOS.** Wherefore it is consistent that then the greatest changes occur around us who inhabit the world. **SOC.** That also is likely. **HOS.** Nor indeed is it hidden from us, how hardly and difficultly the nature of living beings tolerates great, many, and all-kinds of mutations. **SOC.** It is certain. **HOS.** Therefore many animals then necessarily perish, and very few men survive, and these are then affected by many new and wonderful passions. But the greatest of all happens, and follows immediately that revolution by which the heaven is reflected contrary to how it is now. **SOC.** What is that? **HOS.** At first, in whatever age any animal is constituted, in that it ceases to progress, nor does anything of old age or disease occur, but it passes into a contrary figure, and puts on a younger and softer habit, and the gray hairs of the elders grow black: and those whose cheeks were bearded before, now with the beard removed are restored to their former appearance. The bodies of the youths also, with the hairs laid down, become soft, and gradually every day and night decreasing, they return to the nature of a boy, and in these both the souls and bodies undergo the habit of children, and at last wasting away, they fail and perish. Furthermore, the corpses of those who suddenly fell by the change of the celestial turning suffer the same, and by a similar reason secretly and briefly rot. **SOC.** What was then the generation of animals, Guest? Or in what way were they generated from one another? **HOS.** It is certain, O Socrates, that in those times this genus did not propagate itself. But that which is said, that once a race arose from the earth, this was at that time turned back again from the earth. These things were handed down to us by those first progenitors of ours, who were born after the first revolution. These were indeed witnesses and heralds of these discourses, to whom faith is now by no means commonly given, although it is very fitting to have it. But what follows from this, I think must be noticed. For to this which is said, that old men return to the nature of boys, this is consonant: that from the dead, but hidden in the earth, those restored again and reviving, some follow that rotation of heaven, or of the age, with generation revolved into the contrary, and thus earth-born beings are necessarily produced in this way, and so called by name and speech, as many as God did not transfer and adorn into another form. **SOC.** This follows surely from what went before. But the life which you say was under the reign of Saturnus, did it exist under those conversions of heaven, or under these? For it is certain that the mutation of the sun and the other stars happens in both volutions. **HOS.** You have followed the discourse excellently. But what you were asking—that all things were born spontaneously for men—by no means belongs to the present conversion, but rather belonged to the former. Then indeed God stood as the first prince and curator of the whole circuit, as now through various regions of the world each of its parts is distributed by the presiding gods.

**[Page 143]**

The genera of animals also, divided into flocks, certain daemons [spirits] allotted as divine shepherds, each of whom was sufficient for performing his duty, and they presided over each thing as was useful, under whom he himself was leader. Wherefore there was nothing wild, and all rapacity and gluttony were far away, and war and sedition were entirely absent: and the other countless things that follow the condition of those times are innumerable. But what is told concerning the facility of food and the liberty of life, is said for this reason: that God fed them, he himself being their shepherd and curator, just as men now, whose nature is more divine, are shepherds of brutes. Therefore, with God guarding, there were no polities, nor marriages of males and females for procreating children. For all revived from the earth, unmindful of past things. All such things were absent. But fruits, and apples, and grains, trees and the fertile soil provided in abundance of their own accord without the labor of agriculture. They were mostly naked and unencumbered, and fed under the open air. For the climate was harmless to them, and soft beds were prepared everywhere, since very much grass sprouted from the earth. You have heard, O Socrates, the life of men living under Saturnus: but this, which they say is of Jupiter, you yourself feel at present. But which is happier, do you wish and are you able to judge? **SOC.** Least of all. **HOS.** Do you wish then that I should judge for you in some way? **SOC.** Very much indeed. **HOS.** If the fosterlings of Saturnus formerly in such leisure, and liberty of life and power, used all these things for philosophy—living among themselves and with beasts, and inquiring from all nature, whatever has its own distinct power of sensing different from others, for the sake of acquiring wisdom—it can easily be judged that they surpassed us by a long interval toward living blessedly. But if, saturated with feasts and cups, they conferred such fables among themselves and with beasts as are now related of them, this also, as my opinion goes, would be judged very easily. But let us omit these things, until some messenger suitable for these things appears, who may relate to us whether those men gave labor to sciences and conversations: but for whose sake we entered this fable, that must now be said, so that we may join the following with the preceding. When the time of all those was filled, and it was necessary for the change of the circuit to occur, all the terrestrial race being consumed: because every soul had fulfilled all generations, and as many seeds as were mandated to it, so many each one had projected into the earth: then the governor of the universe, God, as if with the reins of the helm let go, returned into his own watchtower. But fate and innate desire revolved the world again. Furthermore, all the gods who were colleagues of the highest power, presiding over individual regions, noticing what had happened, deserted the parts of the world. The world then, reflecting itself with an agitation contrary to the former principles and ends, shaking the interior parts with a huge earthquake, again destroyed for the most part the animals of every genus. But when certain exact curricula of times had passed, the concussion and perturbation ceased, and the world, desisting from the turbulent noise, ran with its usual progression of itself, and being constituted in due order, it took up the authority and administration both of itself and of those things which are in it, imitating as far as its strength allowed the governance of its author and father. At the beginning, therefore, it executed it more perfectly, but from that very imitation it at last degenerated further. The cause of this defect indeed is the corporeal nature, the fuel of the ancient nature. For once it was very deformed and void of order, before it was decorated with the present ornament. From him indeed who constructed it, it possesses all good things: from the prior deformity, all the inconveniences and unjust things which are born within the heaven, both the world itself sustains and inserts into living beings. Therefore, while it nourishes its animals together with the governor, it produces small evils and great goods: but when it is separated, in the time immediately after the departure, it leads all things very beautifully: but as time proceeds, it is now occupied by oblivion: wherefore the vice of the prior deformity dominates more vehemently. At last, after a long time has passed, it fades away, and procreating few good things, but mixing very many of the nature of evils with these, it undergoes the danger that both it and all things that are in it may be dissolved. Wherefore that God, formerly the author of this order, seeing the world placed in such a crisis, has mercy, and lest it should fluctuate and be dissolved by such a turbulent tumult, and be merged into the infinite place of dissimilarity, he again stands by it, and having immediately resumed the helms, he orders and corrects all the ailing and dissolved things by his ancient agitation, and makes it free from death and old age. This then is the end of the departure of all. This suffices for the showing of the king himself, if only the things said above are held. Again, with the conversion for the progress of the present generation, the age again ceased to progress further, and rendered new things contrary to these which were then. Furthermore, animals very close to death by reason of their thinness increased: but those which had recently risen gray from the earth, fell back again dying into the earth. All other things likewise were transmuted, following the passion of the whole world. For the imitation of generation, and conception, and nourishment necessarily followed the universe itself. For it was no longer given in the earth, through mutually helping causes, for an animal to be made. But as it was instituted that the world should be the master of its own motion, so by a similar guidance it was made that the parts of the world through themselves, as far as can be, generate, and are born, and nourish. Now indeed we have come to that toward which all our discourse looked. For concerning the other animals many and great things could be related, from what and for what causes they were transmuted. But those which happened concerning men are shorter, and pertain more to the matter. Since men were destitute of the providence of the shepherd and the protection of their daemons, and many animals, which by their own nature were savage, had become wild again, they themselves being unarmed and weak, and left derelict of custody, were torn to pieces by them everywhere. Inertia and ignorance of former times were added, for they had lived ignorant of labors and cares. The earth no longer supplied food spontaneously, and the industry of preparing it was not yet found, because no necessity had compelled them before. For these causes their affairs were reduced to extreme danger and penury. Wherefore those gifts which are remembered to have been formerly granted to men by the gods, were granted by a certain necessary discipline and erudition. From Prometheus indeed fire: but arts from Vulcanus and his consort: woman also, and plants from others: all the aids of the life of men were then prepared by the works of the gods, when the providence of the gods had deserted men, and it was necessary for them to have care for their own propagation and nourishment, just like the whole world.

### Translator's Notes:
*   **Abbreviations:** The Latin text utilizes standard Renaissance typographical abbreviations (e.g., *nõ* for *non*, *ꝑ* for *per*, *-q;* for *-que*). These have been expanded in the translation.
*   **Hospes:** Translated as "Guest" or "Stranger," referring to the Eleatic Stranger in Plato's dialogue.
*   **Proper Nouns:** Names such as *Atreus*, *Thyestes*, *Saturnus* (Saturn), *Jupiter*, *Prometheus*, and *Vulcanus* are kept in their Latinate/Classical forms.
*   **Mediocritas:** In this context, it refers to the "mean" or "due measure" (the *metron*), a central concept in Platonic and Aristotelian ethics, rather than the modern pejorative "mediocrity."
*   **The World's Reversal:** The text describes the "Myth of the Reversed Ages," a key passage in the *Politicus* where the universe rotates in two different directions depending on whether God is at the helm.

->Politics, or on Kingship. 143<-

The genera of animals were also divided into herds, which certain demons <note>Ficino uses "demones" in the Platonic sense of "daemons" or guardian spirits, not evil entities</note> were allotted like divine shepherds. Since each was sufficient for performing his own duty, they presided over individual groups, one for each, just as He willed. Therefore, nothing was wild, and all rapacity and gluttony were far away; war and sedition were entirely absent; and moreover, the other things that followed the condition of those times are innumerable. As for what is said about the ease of food and the freedom of life, it is said because God fed them, he himself was their shepherd and guardian—just as men now, whose nature is more divine, are the shepherds of brutes. Under God’s guardianship, there were no political systems <note>original: "politiae"</note>, nor marriages of males and females for procreating children. For all were revived from the earth, unmindful of past things. All such things were absent. But fruits, apples, and crops were supplied in abundance by trees and the fertile soil of their own accord, without the work of agriculture. Furthermore, they fed naked and unencumbered in the open air, for the most part. For the temperate weather was harmless to them, and soft beds were prepared everywhere from the many grasses sprouting from the earth. You hear, O Socrates, of the life of men living under Saturn; but this life, which they say belongs to Jupiter, you yourself perceive now. Which of the two is happier—do you wish to judge, and are you able? **SOCRATES.** Least of all. **STRANGER.** Do you wish then that I should somehow judge for you? **SOCRATES.** Most certainly indeed. **STRANGER.** If the nurslings of Saturn once used such leisure, freedom of life, and power, not only for talking among themselves but also with beasts, and if they used all these things for philosophy, living among themselves and with beasts, inquiring from every nature whether it had some specific power of perception different from others for acquiring wisdom, it can easily be judged that they surpassed us in living happily by a long interval. But if, satisfied with feasts and cups in abundance, they exchanged such tales among themselves and with beasts as are now told about them, this too, as my opinion goes, could be judged quite easily. But let us omit these things, until some messenger fit for these matters appears to report to us whether those men devoted their efforts to sciences and conversations. But the reason why we entered upon this fable must now be told, so that we may join what follows with what went before. When the time of all those things was fulfilled, and it was necessary that the change of the circuit should occur, all the terrestrial genus having been consumed—since each soul had filled all its generations, and as many seeds as had been mandated to each, that many each had cast into the earth—then the Governor of the universe, as if letting go of the reins of the rudders, returned to his own lookout. And thereafter fate and innate desire rolled the world back again. Moreover, all the highest gods, the colleagues of the supreme daemon who were set over individual regions, perceiving what had happened, deserted the parts of the world. Then the world, reflecting itself with a contrary agitation of beginning and end, shaking its interiors with a huge earthquake, again destroyed most animals of every genus. But when the exact courses of time had passed, the shaking and perturbation ceased, and the world, stopping from its turbulent crash, ran in its accustomed progress, and being established in due order, it took up the authority and administration of both itself and those things within it, remembering and imitating the governance of its author and father to the best of its ability. In the beginning, it executed this more perfectly, but at last it degenerated further by that imitation. The cause of this defect is the nature of the ancient bodily matter. For it was once very deformed and devoid of order, before it was decorated with its present ornament. From him indeed who constructed it, it possesses all good things; but from its prior deformity, all the inconveniences and unjust things that are born within the heaven arise, which the world itself sustains and inserts into living things. Therefore, while it nourishes its animals together with the governor, it produces small evils but immense goods; but when it is separated, in the time immediately following the departure, it leads all things beautifully. But as time proceeds, it is occupied by forgetfulness; therefore the vice of the prior deformity dominates more vehemently. Finally, after a long time has passed, it withers, and procreating only meager goods but mixing the nature of evils most abundantly with them, it undergoes the danger that both it and all things in it might be dissolved. Therefore, that God who was once the author of this order, seeing the world placed in such danger, takes pity. And lest it should fluctuate and be dissolved in such a turbulent tumult and sink into the infinite place of dissimilarity, he stands by it again and presides over it; and immediately resuming the rudders, he turns, adorns, and corrects all the sick and dissolved things by his ancient agitation, and makes the world free from death and old age. This, then, is the end of all that was said. This suffices for the display of the king himself, provided that the things said above are held in mind. For when the world was turned back again to the progress of its present generation, the age again ceased to progress further, and it gave back new things contrary to those that were then. Animals, moreover, which were close to death because of their very thinness, were increased; and those which had recently risen gray from the earth, fell back again dying into the earth. All other things were likewise transmuted, following the passion of the whole world. For the imitation of generation, conception, and nourishment necessarily followed the universe itself. For it was no longer given to an animal to be born in the earth through mutually helping causes. But just as it was instituted that the world should be the master of its own motion, so by a similar guidance it was made that the parts of the world should, as far as possible, generate, be born, and nourish through themselves. Now indeed we have come to that point toward which our whole speech looked. For concerning the remaining animals, many and great things could be reported—from what and for what causes they were transmuted. But those things which happened concerning men are shorter and more relevant to the matter. When men were destitute of the providence of the shepherd and guardian daemon, and many animals which had been wild by their own nature became fierce again, they themselves, unarmed and weak and derelict of guardianship, were torn apart by them everywhere. To this was added the inertia and lack of skill of the former times, for they had lived without knowing labors or cares. The earth no longer supplied food of its own accord, and the industry of preparing it was not yet invented, because no necessity had compelled them before. For these reasons, their affairs were reduced to the greatest danger and penury. Therefore, those gifts which are said to have been granted to men by the gods of old were granted with a certain necessary discipline and instruction. From Prometheus indeed came fire; arts from Vulcan and his companion; seeds also and plants from others. All the aids for the administration of human life were then provided by the works of the gods, when the providence of the gods had deserted men, and it was necessary for them to have care for their own propagation and nourishment, in the likeness of the whole world...
