->Sixteenth Book. 144<-

...in the likeness of the whole world, which they imitate through all time and follow, being born and living in various ways. But let the fable now have an end. It will indeed help us to discern how much we erred above in the definition of the royal and civil man. **SOCRATES.** In what matter, and how much do you say we erred? **STRANGER.** Partly less, partly more generously and more than we erred then. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Because while the king and the statesman were being sought from the present circuit and generation, we brought in a shepherd from the contrary conversion; and instead of a mortal shepherd of the human herd, we commemorated a God, and so we transgressed too far. But as for showing him to be the prince of the whole state, we did not declare in what way he was prince; we spoke the truth, yet we did not describe it perfectly and clearly. Therefore, we seem to have failed less in this than in that. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. **STRANGER.** We must therefore think that we have only then sufficiently explained the statesman when we have distinguished the mode of governing the state with sufficiency. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **STRANGER.** For this reason we began the fable: not only that it might be shown who they are who claim for themselves that communal nourishment of the human herd against the king, but that we might more clearly behold him whom alone it is fitting to call thus, who, like a shepherd of oxen and sheep, carries the care of pasturing the human genus. **SOCRATES.** Right. **STRANGER.** I believe indeed, O Socrates, that the figure of that divine shepherd is too great to fit a king. But these civil men are more similar to their subjects, whether we look at nature, education, or disciplines. **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. **STRANGER.** And it must not be examined whether they were more or less, or whether they were born thus or otherwise. **SOCRATES.** Why not indeed? **STRANGER.** Thus let us resume again. The art that prescribes by its own command, and provides for animals not privately but publicly, we immediately called the nourishment of the herd above. Do you remember? **SOCRATES.** I remember. **STRANGER.** But in this there was an error. For we have neither grasped the statesman yet, nor named him, but his name still escapes us. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** To pasture individual herds is appropriate to all other shepherds. But we did not give a fitting name to the statesman, when it was proper to apply something common to all. **SOCRATES.** You tell the truth, if it were allowed. **STRANGER.** Indeed, it was allowed to attribute "care" <note>original: "curationem"</note> in common, without the distinction of "nourishment" or another business; and to bring in some other common appellation, calling it either the leading of the herd, or care, or diligence, and so embrace the statesman together with others, after reason had dictated that it should be so. **SOCRATES.** Very good. But in what way was it to be distinguished afterward? **STRANGER.** Just as we divided the nourishment of the herd according to the species of walking and winged creatures, and of unmixed and hornless ones, so it was allowed to divide the leading of the herd according to those same things; and thus both the reign of Saturn and the present one would have been embraced in the speech. **SOCRATES.** It seems so. But what then? **STRANGER.** If the name had been so imposed on that faculty that we had called it "herd-leading" instead of what we called "herd-nourishing," it is certain that no one would have contended against us, as if there were no care at all. Just as this also might be argued not absurdly: that there is no art in us worthy of the name "nourishing"; and if there were, that name would fit many others sooner and more than the royal art. **SOCRATES.** Right. **STRANGER.** No other art contends about this, as being the care of the whole human community, which is greater and milder than the royal one. **SOCRATES.** You speak correctly. **STRANGER.** After this, Socrates, do we notice how seriously we failed near the end? **SOCRATES.** Where do you say the failure is? **STRANGER.** In this, I say: that even if we thought some art was the nourisher of the biped herd, we should not have immediately called it that royal and civil art as if it were absolute. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** First indeed, it was necessary, as I was saying, to accommodate the name to "care" rather than "nourishment"; afterward to divide the care. For it undergoes no small divisions besides. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **STRANGER.** Into the divine shepherd and the human curator. **SOCRATES.** Skilfully done. **STRANGER.** It is likewise necessary to part human care into two. **SOCRATES.** What parts? **STRANGER.** Into that which commands the unwilling, and that which commands the willing. **SOCRATES.** What then? **STRANGER.** Erring in this, we more ineptly than was fitting brought the king and the tyrant into the same thing, though they themselves are most dissimilar, and their mode of governing is far different. **SOCRATES.** You report the truth. **STRANGER.** Now, therefore, correcting it again, as I was saying, let us part human care in two ways: into the violent and the voluntary. **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **STRANGER.** Let us name the violent "tyrannical," but the voluntary leadership of a herd of willing bipeds the "civil art"; and let us call him who is endowed with this faculty truly the civil man and the king. **SOCRATES.** It seems, Guest, that the demonstrations of the statesman are now at last fully absolute for us. **STRANGER.** It would be well with us, O Socrates. But it must seem so not to you alone, but to me along with you. And now the king does not yet seem to me to have a perfect form. But just as sculptors sometimes, hurrying not quite seasonably, when they use more and larger emblems than are necessary, finish the work later; so we too—so that we might quickly and magnificently show the errors of the previous explanation concerning the king, thinking that great examples should be placed—exaggerated a huge mass of a fable, and were forced to use a larger part of it than was necessary. Therefore we brought in a more prolix demonstration, and did not entirely impose an end on the fable. And our speech really seems, like a living animal, to have its outer circumference absolute, but is not yet decorated with a clear mixture of pigments and colors. It is fitting to describe each animal with words and speech more than with a painting or manual craftsmanship, and to display it to those who can follow with reason; to the others let them be displayed with the brush and paint. **SOCRATES.** Enough of this. Show us for what reason you say it has not yet been sufficiently spoken. **STRANGER.** It is arduous, O blessed one, to show great things clearly without examples. For it seems each of us knows all things as if through a dream, but in reality, again, knows nothing. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Quite absurdly, we have begun in great and arduous things what should have been begun in the smallest and easiest by order. **SOCRATES.** To what purpose is this? **STRANGER.** An example, O happy one, requires an example in turn. **SOCRATES.** For what reason? Speak, fearing nothing for my sake. **STRANGER.** It must be said since you yourself are ready to hear. Do we know what boys do when they first learn letters? **SOCRATES.** What is that? **STRANGER.** That they sufficiently perceive each of the letters in the shortest and easiest syllables, and can speak the truth about them. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** These same boys, being ambiguous in others, are deceived in opinion and speech. **SOCRATES.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** Is it not therefore most easily and best that they be led to unknown things? **SOCRATES.** In what way?

->Politics, or on Kingship. 145<-

...how can they be led most easily and best to unknown things? **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** One must first lead them back to those things in which they correctly held these same opinions, and offer to them what they do not yet know, and by comparing them in turn, show that the same similarity and nature is in the internal complexes, until all the unknown things are shown to be compared with those conceived by true opinion. When demonstrated, they finally become examples of those things, so that from all the elements of any syllable, they may now name what is different from others as different; and what is the same, as always the same with itself according to the same things. **SOCRATES.** Exactly so. **STRANGER.** Have we not sufficiently grasped this? That namely, the generation of an example occurs when that which is the same is in one of two separate things, conceived with right opinion and accommodated to both, and produces one common opinion of both? **SOCRATES.** It seems so. **STRANGER.** What wonder if our soul, suffering the same nature concerning the elements of all things, is now established in truth itself concerning each thing in some matters, but again fluctuates about all things in others? And when in certain couplings it opines correctly in a way, but when transferred into the great and difficult syllables of things, it is again ignorant of these same things. **SOCRATES.** Nothing indeed should seem wonderful. **STRANGER.** For by what reasoning, O friend, could anyone starting from a false opinion, and arriving at some even smallest part of truth, acquire wisdom? **SOCRATES.** Almost none. **STRANGER.** If these things are thus by nature, we would by no means wander from the act if we first try to look into the nature of the whole example in some other small separate example; then, having approached that greatest example of the king, translating that very thing from smaller things, we should try again through an example to discern the care of civil things by art, and follow it by dream with the truth. **SOCRATES.** Quite right. **STRANGER.** The previous speech must be repeated again, where it was inserted that after very many people contend with the royal genus for the government of the state and usurp it for themselves, it is necessary to separate all of them from him and leave him alone. And for this, we said a certain example is needed. **SOCRATES.** Greatly so. **STRANGER.** What small example, indeed, containing the same civil faculty, could someone bring forward that would sufficiently find what is being investigated? Do you wish, by Jupiter, O Socrates, unless we have something else at hand, that we choose the art of weaving? Not the whole of it indeed, for I think the working of wool will suffice. For perhaps this chosen part will indicate what we desire. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** Why did we not, as we were dividing each thing into parts of parts before, do the same now concerning the art of weaving, and by passing through all things as briefly as possible, choose what leads to the proposal? **SOCRATES.** How do you mean? **STRANGER.** I shall give the narration itself in place of an answer. **SOCRATES.** You speak excellently. **STRANGER.** Of the things we do and possess, some are for the sake of doing something, others so that we may not suffer anything inconvenient, like defenses. Of defenses, some are remedies, both divine and human; others are obstacles. Of obstacles, some are military armor, others are fortifications. Of fortifications, some are coverings, others are protections against heat and cold. Of protections, some are roofs and awnings, others are coverings. Of coverings, some are under-layers, others are garments. Of those that are garments, some are simple, others indeed double and composite. Of the composite, some are perforated, others are joined without perforation. Of these indeed, some are made of sinews from those things born from the earth, some are felt <note>original: "pilea"</note>. Of felt, some are glued together with water and earth, others are connected to one another. To these defenses and supports which are made from these things bound together, we have given the name "clothes." But the art that is most engaged around clothes, let us call it "clothing-making" from the effect of the clothes themselves, just as we named the discipline that cares for the city "civil" from the city itself. And let us say that the faculty of weaving, insofar as it weaves clothes in the greatest part, differs in no other thing except the name from that which we called clothing-making, just as above we said the royal art differs from the civil. **SOCRATES.** Very rightly. **STRANGER.** After this, let us think that perhaps someone might think the weaving art has been sufficiently described; but he might not be able to notice that although it was not yet distinguished from those things which cooperate more closely, it was separated from many other things related to it. **SOCRATES.** Which related things? **STRANGER.** You seem not to have attended to what was said above. Therefore, as it seems, we must return from the end to the beginning. For if you understand the kinship, we have indeed distinguished this from it, when we separated the composition of blankets from cloaks and supports. **SOCRATES.** I understand. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, we have already separated every craft that uses flax, cords, and twigs, and summarily those things born from the earth, which we a little while ago called "sinewy." Nay, we also separated the composition of hats, and that which works by perforating and sewing, which for the most part belongs to the leather-working faculty. **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. **STRANGER.** We have besides separated the making of simple coverings, which uses skins. Likewise the mechanisms of coverings and stays as many as are made in building; and in other arts whatsoever for the retention and repulsion of waters, and whatsoever works around folds and violent actions by which something is restrained, and they place hedges and a stone wall in opposition, and cast up certain heaps, and those which cover something. Likewise the fixings of doors and lattices, which pertain to the craft of nails. Furthermore, we segregated armor, which is a portion of that ample faculty which places defenses and obstacles. Moreover, we separated the culinary arts, which profess to provide remedies for human life, from the beginning. But we left a certain art, which seemed to be the one we are looking for: the effective art, namely, of supports against the cold made of wool, and named weaving. **SOCRATES.** So it seems. **STRANGER.** But we have not yet, O boy, perfectly expedited the matter with these words. For he who first handles the craft of clothes seems to act contrary to the weaver. **SOCRATES.** For what reason? **STRANGER.** For the weaver somehow folds and connects. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** But the other dissolves those things which are inserted and implied together. **SOCRATES.** What is that? **STRANGER.** The work of him who cards and discerns. For should we call the carding and discerning work the same as the weaving art? And shall we call the carder and discerner the same as the weaver? **SOCRATES.** By no means. **STRANGER.** If someone indeed approaches the diligence with that appellation. **SOCRATES.** Clearly. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, do we say the work of fullers and tailors contributes nothing to the making of garments? Or do we call all these things "weaving"? **SOCRATES.** Neither should be said, it seems. **STRANGER.** Nevertheless, all these will contend with the art of the weaver concerning the care of clothes; and they will indeed give most of this work to him, but will also claim much of the same work for themselves. **SOCRATES.** So it is entirely. **STRANGER.** Besides these, it is necessary to think moreover of the arts of the instruments which the weaver uses...

146 ->Book Sixteen<-

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the "Statesman" (Politicus) by Plato, where the characters use the craft of weaving as a metaphor to define the role of a King or Statesman. The "Stranger" (Hospes) leads the discussion with Young Socrates.</meta>

...they are the efficient causes, claiming a part for themselves in the production of the fabric. **SOCRATES:** Quite right. **STRANGER:** Will the definition of the weaver's craft, which we chose as our specific part, be sufficiently distinguished if we call it the greatest and most beautiful of all the crafts that deal with woolen clothing? Or would that be a true statement, yet neither perfect nor clear, until we have separated it from all the others? **SOCRATES:** Certainly so. **STRANGER:** Should we not proceed then, so that our discourse may follow a consistent order? **SOCRATES:** Nothing prevents it. **STRANGER:** First, then, let us consider two types of arts regarding everything that is produced. **SOCRATES:** Which ones? **STRANGER:** One is the contributory cause <note>original: "causam adiuvantem"</note>, and the other is the cause itself. **SOCRATES:** In what way? **STRANGER:** Those which do not manufacture the thing itself, but provide the tools for the manufacturers—without which the intended work could never be completed—these we call "contributory causes." Those which actually produce the thing itself, we call "principal causes." **SOCRATES:** That is reasonable. **STRANGER:** Following this, let us call all the arts that produce the distaff, the spindle, the shuttle, the comb, and other instruments for the labor of clothing, "contributory causes"; but those that actually care for and produce the garments, "causes." **SOCRATES:** Correct. **STRANGER:** From these "causes," let us take the part that washes and repairs, and others of this kind which provide care; since there is much diligence in beautification, it is fitting to collect them under one name and call it the fuller's art. **SOCRATES:** Very well. **STRANGER:** But that part which cards, separates, and spins, and everything concerning the production of garments, is encompassed by one art, which is commonly called wool-working. **SOCRATES:** Why not? **STRANGER:** Furthermore, there are two divisions of wool-working, and both are simultaneously parts of two arts. **SOCRATES:** In what way? **STRANGER:** That faculty which cards, and that which uses a certain comb, and generally everything that separates what is joined; all of this, to embrace it in a single word, is called a part of wool-working. Its two greatest parts are the <term>analytical art<gloss>discretoria</gloss></term> and the <term>synthetic art<gloss>concretoria</gloss></term>. **SOCRATES:** It is entirely so. **STRANGER:** Within the analytical part are the carding and the other faculties we just mentioned. For that which divides the wool and the <term>warp<gloss>stamen</gloss></term>, whether with a comb or by hand, has received all the names we just uttered in different ways. **SOCRATES:** Exactly. **STRANGER:** Conversely, let us take the part of the synthetic art that is also contained within wool-working; let us pass over whatever analytical parts were there, dividing all wool-working into two parts: the synthetic and the analytical. **SOCRATES:** Let us divide them. **STRANGER:** Therefore, Socrates, it is right to divide the synthetic part of wool-working if we wish to sufficiently grasp the art of weaving we have proposed. **SOCRATES:** We certainly must. **STRANGER:** Without a doubt. And so, let us say one part consists in twisting and turning, and the other in intertwining. **SOCRATES:** Do I understand this? You seem to place the work of the warp in the twisting. **STRANGER:** Not just this, but the <term>woof<gloss>subtegmen</gloss></term> as well. Shall we find any production of this without twisting? **SOCRATES:** By no means. **STRANGER:** Describe each of these; for perhaps such a description will be timely. **SOCRATES:** How so? **STRANGER:** Behold, when the carder’s work is drawn out in length and width, we call it a "deduction." **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** When this, having been made into a weight, is twisted by the spindle and becomes a solid thread, they call it the "warp"; the art itself which directs and draws this out is called "warp-making." **SOCRATES:** Correct. **STRANGER:** However, those threads which receive a soft twist, and by the intertwining of the warp achieve a softness moderate enough for the pull of the turn, these they call the "woof"; the art itself, however, is the "woof-spinning" art. **SOCRATES:** Very well. **STRANGER:** And yet that part of the weaver's art which I proposed is now clear to anyone. For when that part of the synthetic faculty in wool-working—through the straight drawing out of the woof and the warp—achieves their intertwining and weaving together, the entire interwoven thing is called a woolen garment, and the art of this kind we call "weaving." **SOCRATES:** Quite rightly. **STRANGER:** But why did we not immediately answer that the art of weaving is that which intertwines the woof and the warp, instead of wandering in circles through long delays? **SOCRATES:** To me, Guest, nothing of what has been said seems to have been said in vain. **STRANGER:** It is no wonder. But perhaps, my friend, it will seem so if you frequently fall into this "disease" in the future. For why is it a wonder? Listen to a principle that should always be brought forward concerning all such matters. **SOCRATES:** Just tell me. **STRANGER:** First, let us look at the nature of excess and defect, so that we may praise moderated things according to reason, and criticize in each case whatever does not observe the proper measure of speech, whether we speak more prolixly <note>at greater length</note> than is fitting in such disputes, or more briefly. **SOCRATES:** We certainly must. **STRANGER:** Rightly so, we must take account of these things. **SOCRATES:** Of what things? **STRANGER:** Of prolixity and brevity, I say, and of all excess and defect. For the faculty of measurement pertains to all these things. **SOCRATES:** Truly. **STRANGER:** Let us therefore distinguish it in two ways. For it serves our purpose. **SOCRATES:** Tell me how it is to be distinguished. **STRANGER:** Thus: One part is according to the mutual relationship of greatness and smallness; the other according to the necessary essence of production. **SOCRATES:** What are you saying? **STRANGER:** Does it not seem to you to be according to nature that what is larger should be called larger than nothing else but the smaller? And the smaller, smaller only than the larger? **SOCRATES:** To me, yes. <margin>Greater is spoken of in a twofold way.</margin> **STRANGER:** What then? That which exceeds the <term>Mean<gloss>mediocritatem</gloss></term>, and that which is exceeded by it—whether in speaking or in acting—shall we not say that this is where good men differ from bad? <margin>How good men differ from evil ones.</margin> **SOCRATES:** It appears so. **STRANGER:** Therefore, it is fitting to establish two kinds of essences and judgments of the great and the small: and not, as we were saying just before, that they should only be referred to one another, but rather, as has now been said, partly to one another and partly compared to the Mean <note>The "Mean" refers to the concept of the "Right Measure" or "Golden Mean"—the idea that virtue and excellence lie between two extremes.</note>. Do we wish to understand the reason for this? **SOCRATES:** Why would we not? **STRANGER:** If someone refers the nature of the larger only to the smaller, will it not be referred to the Mean? What do you say? **SOCRATES:** That is the point. **STRANGER:** Do we not separate the arts themselves and all their works by this reasoning? And shall we remove from our midst the "civil" art which we seek, and the weaver's art? For all these avoid what is greater or smaller than the Mean—not as if it does not exist, but as something difficult to manage in actions—and by thus preserving the Mean, they produce all things good and beautiful. **SOCRATES:** Without a doubt. **STRANGER:** Will not the investigation of the royal science be in doubt <note>if we do not accept this measurement</note>? **SOCRATES:** Greatly. **STRANGER:** Just as in the discussion about the Sophist, where we proved that "non-being" exists after the argument failed us, should we now also prove that the "more" and the "less" are measurable not only against each other, but also toward the production of the Mean? For no one can be skilled in the civil discipline, nor any other human faculty, unless he admits this. **SOCRATES:** Must this then be done with the greatest effort now? **STRANGER:** This is a greater work, Socrates, than that other one, even though that one was very long; remember...

<summary>This page explores the definition of weaving as a metaphor for statesmanship, distinguishing between the tools used (contributory causes) and the act of creation (principal causes). It introduces a crucial philosophical argument that "measurement" must be judged not just relatively (big vs. small), but against an absolute "Mean" or proper standard of excellence.</summary>

...remember. Truly, something of this kind must be supposed concerning them. **SOCRATES.** What kind? **STRANGER.** That there is a need for what has now been said, if indeed we wish to teach what the absolute and pure nature is. However, for what pertains to the present matters, it will be excellently and sufficiently demonstrated, and this discourse seems to me to suggest strongly that it must be considered that all arts similarly measure the "more" and the "less" at the same time, not only in relation to each other, but also to the generation of the mean itself. For when this exists, those exist; and when those exist, this exists; if either of these is removed, both are taken away. **SOCRATES.** This is indeed correct. But what next? **STRANGER.** It is proper to distinguish the art of measurement into two parts, as we said above: to place in one part all those arts that measure number, length, width, depth, and speed against their opposites; and in the other part those arts that look to the moderate and the balanced, the fitting, the opportune, and the due, and in short to all those which, having avoided the extremes, have taken refuge in the middle. **SOCRATES.** Both portions are indeed large, and one differs far from the other. **STRANGER.** What those elegant men often say, O Socrates, who think they speak something great and wise when they proclaim that the faculty of measurement is concerned with all things that are made, has now been stated. For whatever is made by craft appeared to be in some way a participant in measure. But because some are not accustomed to consider by going through divisions by specific kinds, they immediately bring these things, though they differ so far from one another, into one, judging them to be similar. But they also do the opposite of this: things that are different, they do not distinguish by parts. Whereas one ought, when he first perceives a commonality among many things, not to stop until he has inspected all the differences within it which are enclosed in species; and again, as often as he feels many dissimilarities in a multitude, he cannot stop from this annoyance of sight until he clothes all the things that are related within one kinship and property, concluding them as the essence of one genus. Concerning these things, therefore, and concerning excesses and defects, let these sayings suffice; only this must be preserved, that two kinds of measurement have been found here, and we must keep in mind what they are. **SOCRATES.** We will keep them. **STRANGER.** After this discourse, let us take up another, concerning the things that were just being sought, and concerning every treatment of such discourses. **SOCRATES.** What is that? **STRANGER.** If someone were to ask us about the exercise of boys learning letters, when they are asked what letters a certain name consists of, do we think they are then being asked for the sake of declaring that one name only, or rather so that they may become more learned in all grammar? What shall we answer? **SOCRATES.** So that they may be more learned in all grammar. **STRANGER.** What then? Is the investigation of the statesman proposed to us more for his own sake, or so that we may become sharper in every disputation? **SOCRATES.** That too is clear: for the sake of all things. **STRANGER.** Surely no one in his right mind would contend to hunt for the definition of the weaver's faculty for its own sake alone. But it escapes many, I think, that there are some sensible images of certain things that are easy to know, which it is not at all difficult to declare as often as any of them wishes to demonstrate quickly to someone inquiring about a reason for something—not with the things themselves, but without reason. But of the greatest and most precious things, there is no image that has been clearly fashioned for human sense and grasp, which, when shown, could satisfy the mind of the inquirer by accommodating it to some sense. Therefore, we must think how we may be able to give and receive a reason for anything. For incorporeal things, since they are the greatest and most beautiful, are declared by reason alone, and by nothing else clearly. Furthermore, for the sake of these things, all that we have said has been spoken. Moreover, the consideration of any matter is easier in smaller things than in larger ones. **SOCRATES.** You speak excellently. **STRANGER.** Finally, let us remember for what sake all these things have been said. **SOCRATES.** For what? **STRANGER.** Especially for the sake of that annoyance which we felt concerning the long-winded speech about the art of weaving, and also about the revolution of the whole world; and we thought the Sophist’s discourse about the essence of non-being was indeed longer than the disputation warranted. And in all these things we deterred ourselves, fearing lest we were perhaps lingering too long in superfluous matters. Therefore, so that something of this kind does not happen to us again in the future, think that all these things were said for the sake of these. **SOCRATES.** It shall be so; just say what remains. **STRANGER.** I say, therefore, that it is necessary for both me and you to always be mindful of what we have said, whenever either brevity or length of speech is blamed, so that we do not compare the lengths themselves with each other, but refer them to the part of the faculty of measurement which we said above must be referred to the norm of the fitting. **SOCRATES.** Wisely said. **STRANGER.** But not all things seem to be referred to this alone. For we shall not need length that suits no one for the sake of pleasure, except in passing. Nor is what is sought, so that we may find it most easily and quickly, the first thing we should strive for, but the second; but most of all, we should honor that first progress by which we are able to distinguish according to species, and not to bear a long disputation with annoyance, but rather to affect it, if in any way it contributes to discovery; and similarly the brief one. It also befits him who blames longer speeches and does not admit the circuits of such disputations, not to condemn length so lightly and rashly, but first to show that a shorter disputation makes us both readier to discuss and more sagacious to discover; but other rebukes or praises tending elsewhere, he should neither care for nor listen to at all. And enough of these things, if it also seems so to you; let us return again to the civil faculty, bringing together the example of the weaver which we set forth above. **SOCRATES.** You have spoken excellently, and let us do as you command. **STRANGER.** Has not the king now been distinguished from many duties of shepherds, indeed from all guardians of herds? There remain the urban faculties of assisting causes and causes alike, which we must first separate from one another. **SOCRATES.** Rightly. **STRANGER.** To divide these in two is difficult. The cause of this difficulty will be clear in the following discourse. **SOCRATES.** It must be done exactly so. **STRANGER.** Therefore, let us tear them apart limb by limb like a sacrificial victim, since we are not able to cut them into two. For it is always necessary to distribute into the nearest number. **SOCRATES.** In what way would we do that now? **STRANGER.** Just as in the earlier parts we placed all who prepared the instruments of weaving as assisting causes. **SOCRATES.** Indeed. **STRANGER.** The same thing must also be done in the present, and much more so. For whatever things fabricate some great or small instrument in the city must be placed as assisting causes, for without these the city cannot exist, nor can political science consist. Yet we shall place none of these as the work of the kingly art. **SOCRATES.** None at all. **STRANGER.** Yet we are approaching something difficult, distinguishing this genus from others. For he who says that an instrument is of some one of those things which are in...

...the instrument is, seems to say something likely: yet another of those things which are possessed in the city must be mentioned. **SOCRATES.** What is that? **STRANGER.** That which does not have this power. For causes are not so glued together to generation as an instrument, but to the safety of that which has been completed. **SOCRATES.** What kind is that? **STRANGER.** That which is an effect of various kinds of dry and wet, heated by fire and cold, which we call by one name "vessel," although the species is very numerous. But this is not the work of that science which we are seeking. **SOCRATES.** Certainly not. **STRANGER.** The third species of possessions appears multiform: terrestrial and aquatic, much-wandering and not straying, precious and cheap, signified by one name: because this whole is always made into a seat for someone, for the sake of sitting. **SOCRATES.** What is this? **STRANGER.** We call it a "vehicle," not at all much the work of civil skill, but rather of architecture and pottery. **SOCRATES.** I understand indeed. **STRANGER.** Must not a fourth be mentioned besides these, in which many of those things we related above are contained? All clothing, many weapons, walls, and enclosures of earth and stone, and many other things. Since all these are made for the sake of protecting and obstructing, they can rightly be called "defenses" and "obstacles" in common, and are much more the works of architects and weavers than of the statesman. **SOCRATES.** It is entirely so. **STRANGER.** Shall we place in the fifth position the arts of decorating, painting, and singing? And whatever things use these, and the imitations made by them for the sake of pleasure alone, which are deservedly embraced by one name. **SOCRATES.** What? **STRANGER.** This whole is denominated as something "playful." <note>original: "iocofum," meaning leisure activities or the arts.</note> **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **STRANGER.** This one name will suit all these, for none of them is ever made for the sake of study, but of play. **SOCRATES.** I almost understand this too. **STRANGER.** That faculty which prepares bodies for all these, from which and in which the works of the arts we just narrated are finished—shall we not place it as a sixth species, varied and depending on many arts? **SOCRATES.** Which do you mean? **STRANGER.** That which prepares gold and silver and other metals from the bowels of the earth. Likewise, that which cuts timber, which shears, which constructs something from these, which folds and weaves, or which cuts and polishes the barks of trees or the skins of animals, and whatever arts are concerned with such things. Again, those by which cork, bark, paper, <note>original: "liber, codex"</note> and bonds are prepared, so that composite species may be made from non-composite genera: we call this whole the "first-born possession" for men, and simple, which is in no way the work of the kingly art. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **STRANGER.** The seventh place is held by the possession of nourishment, and whatever things, mixed with the body, can nourish and care for the parts of the body with their own parts: all of which should be called "aliment," unless we find something more beautiful. But this whole is more rightly attributed to agriculture, hunting, gymnastics, medicine, and cooking than to the statesman. **SOCRATES.** Rightly indeed. **STRANGER.** Almost all things that are possessed, besides the species of domestic animals, are counted, I believe, in these seven. Think of it thus: It was proper to bring in first that species we call "first-born," then the instrument, the vessel, the vehicle, the defense, the pastime, and the nourishment. We pass over, however, if anything not great has been hidden, which can be accommodated to any of these, such as the form of coins, and of seals, and of every mark. For these do not have a genus very closely related to those, but partly in ornament and partly in instruments—perhaps more violently—yet they fit when treated in some way. But the possession of domestic animals, except for slaves, seems to have been encompassed first by the distinct nurturing of the herd. **SOCRATES.** And most especially. **STRANGER.** There remains the genus of all slaves and ministers, where I foresee that they will openly cry out against it—those who contend for this part with the king, just as they did with the weaver who combs and spins, and those who do other things of which we spoke. But all the others, called assisting causes, together with the works now mentioned, have been separated and distinguished from the kingly and civil action. **SOCRATES.** It has appeared so. **STRANGER.** Let us consider the rest who approach most closely, so that we may know them more certainly. **SOCRATES.** It is entirely necessary. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, as far as we can see from here, we shall find that the greatest ministers have an exercise and passion contrary to what we suspected. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **STRANGER.** Purchased slaves and men forced into servitude in a similar way. Whom we can without controversy call "slaves," standing farthest from kingly dignity. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** What shall we say of free men, whoever of their own will perform the ministries we mentioned above—those who transport the works of agriculture and other arts, and exchange them in mutual commerce, whether from market to market in the same city, or transferring them from city to city by land and sea, exchanging coins for other things, or something similar for similar—whom we have named money-changers, merchants, ship-owners, and innkeepers? Will they claim civil skill for themselves? **SOCRATES.** Perhaps the art of merchants. **STRANGER.** Yet those whom we see as mercenaries exposed everywhere to serve all men will not be found to usurp kingly dignity. **SOCRATES.** It is as you say. **STRANGER.** But what of those who provide such things to us everywhere? **SOCRATES.** Whom do you mean, and ministers of what things? **STRANGER.** I mean the genus of heralds, and those who wisely assist concerning public letters, and some other skillful elaborate-workers of things pertaining to the ministry of princes. What should be said of these, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** What you yourself were saying: that they are ministers, not princes of cities. **STRANGER.** It is not in vain, therefore, I think, what I said earlier: that most people would not be found contending vehemently about civil care in this way, although it might seem very absurd to someone to seek them in the number of ministers. **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **STRANGER.** Let us approach, moreover, more closely to those who have not yet been examined: these are they who have a small part of some ministerial science concerning divination. For they are considered interpreters of divine things to men. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, the genus of priests, as is held by law, understands in what way gifts should be skillfully offered to the gods with slaughtered victims. Likewise, by what reasoning one should vow, or what good should be asked from the gods. Both of these are parts of the ministerial art. **SOCRATES.** So it seems. **STRANGER.** Now, therefore, we seem to touch upon a certain footprint of what we are inquiring into. For that reasoning of priests and diviners abounds in magnanimity, intelligence, and clarity, because of the magnificence of the things they treat. Therefore, among the Egyptians, it is not permitted for a king to rule without the priesthood; indeed, if someone from another genus should usurp the kingdom by force, he is compelled after the assumption of the kingdom to be initiated into the sacred rites, so that he may finally be king and priest. Furthermore, in many cities of the Greeks, especially among you, you will find that the principal sacred rites are instituted by the highest magistrates...

...by the highest magistrates. For among you also it is said that to the chosen king are granted the greatest ancestral and solemn rites, the most pure of all others. **SOCRATES.** And most especially. **STRANGER.** We must, therefore, consider these chosen kings and priests, and their ministers, as well as another certain frequent crowd which came to light a little before, after the higher ones were set aside. **SOCRATES.** Whom do you mean? **STRANGER.** I mean certain wonderful ones. **SOCRATES.** Why? **STRANGER.** For already a multiform genus of these appears to me as I think on it. For many of the men are like lions, and centaurs, and others of this kind; very many also like satyrs, and weaklings, and multiform beasts; they change their forms and power in turn. Indeed, only now do I seem to have noticed men of this kind, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Tell me, I pray. For you seem to see something wonderful now. **STRANGER.** Indeed. For ignorance causes something to always seem wonderful to us. And the same has just happened to me. For suddenly it happened that I was in doubt when I looked at the chorus of civil affairs. **SOCRATES.** Which one? **STRANGER.** The greatest juggler of all sophists, <note>In this context, a "sophist" is not just a teacher but a deceptive pretender to wisdom.</note> and the most skilled in this art above the rest, whom it is proper to discern from men truly kingly and civil, however arduous that may be, if only we wish to clearly know what we are seeking. **SOCRATES.** This must in no way be omitted. **STRANGER.** Certainly not, as I think. And tell me: **SOCRATES.** What? **STRANGER.** Is not monarchy, that is, the rule of one, one certain kind of civil governance? **SOCRATES.** It is. **STRANGER.** After this, we can place the power of a few. **SOCRATES.** Surely. **STRANGER.** And third, the government of the multitude, which they call popular. **SOCRATES.** Exactly. **STRANGER.** Do not these three in some way become five, when they give birth to two other names besides? **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **STRANGER.** Those who consider that rule can be over both the unwilling and the willing, and also by law and by will, and that those who preside can be either poor or raised to power by riches—they divide rule into two species, for the one as well as for the few. And the rule of one they thus call, as if containing two species, by two names: Tyranny and Kingship. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** And the governance which is in the hands of a few, into the power of the few (Oligarchy), and the power of the best (Aristocracy). **SOCRATES.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** But no one would ever be accustomed to change the name of popular governance (Democracy), whether the people preside over certain rich men willingly or by force, whether they rule by law or by will. **SOCRATES.** You tell the truth. **STRANGER.** Do we think that any of these civil governances is right, being determined by these limits and distinctions: namely, by one, by few, by many, by poverty, by riches, by violence, by will, by laws, and by choice? **SOCRATES.** What prevents it? **STRANGER.** Consider more diligently, and follow me this way. **SOCRATES.** Which way? **STRANGER.** Shall we stand in that which was said in the beginning or not? **SOCRATES.** In what? **STRANGER.** We said that kingly dignity is one certain kind of science. **SOCRATES.** We said so. **STRANGER.** Nor did we place it in just any kind of science. Out of many other faculties, we selected that which judges and commands at the same time. **SOCRATES.** Indeed. **STRANGER.** Then, dividing that which commands into part over inanimate things and part over animate things, and dividing in the same order, we progressed this far, so that we might preserve the name of science; but what science it is most of all, we have not yet been able to declare. **SOCRATES.** You speak correctly. **STRANGER.** Do we not see, therefore, that the description of them ought to be made neither according to violence and will, nor according to few and many, nor through poverty and wealth, but through a certain science, if we follow what was said before? **SOCRATES.** It must be so. **STRANGER.** Necessarily, therefore, we must now consider this: in which of these does the science of the commanding faculty most exist, which is almost the greatest of all and the most difficult to obtain. For it is proper to look into it, so that we may see which ones are to be separated from the wise king, who claim civil skill for themselves and persuade many of it, when they are very far from it. **SOCRATES.** It must be done exactly so, as the earlier reasoning advised. **STRANGER.** Does the multitude in the city seem to you to be a possessor of this science? **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** Can it happen in a city of a thousand men that a hundred, or fifty men, should sufficiently attain it? **SOCRATES.** This would be the easiest of all arts. For we know that in a number of a thousand men, just as many men who excel the other Greeks in the game of dice could in no way be found, let alone kings. Yet that man, whoever is instructed in kingly skill, must be called a king, whether he rules or lives as a private citizen, according to that earlier reasoning. **STRANGER.** You have advised beautifully. I think, however, according to this discourse, that right government, if it is ever right, must be sought around one, or two, or a few. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** But it is proper to consider those men as civil and kingly who rule by a certain art, whether over the willing or the unwilling, whether according to writings or without writings and institutions and laws, whether they themselves rule as poor or rich, it matters nothing. For we call doctors no less so, whether they heal the unwilling or the willing by cutting, or burning, or bringing other pain, or whether they heal by writings or by practice, being poor themselves or rich—provided that they use a certain art for the care of bodies, either by purging, or thinning, or filling and increasing. For we call them equally doctors, as long as those who care for the body look toward its good, and restore it from a worse habit to a better and preserve it. In this way only, I think, shall we say that the definition of medicine, or of any other leadership, is right, and in no other. **SOCRATES.** It must be thought exactly so. **STRANGER.** It is necessary, therefore, to consider that republic most, and alone, right, in which those who perform the magistracies truly know how to govern, and do not merely seem to; whether they rule by laws or without laws, whether over the willing or the unwilling, or even if they are poor or rich. For nothing of these refers at all to the right reason of governing. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **STRANGER.** Nor does it matter, moreover, whether they purge the city by capital punishments and certain exiles for the sake of the common good, or send out colonies like swarms of bees and diminish the people, or summon men from elsewhere to be future citizens and enlarge the city. For as long as, relying on science and justice, they make the city better from worse according to their power and preserve it, so far do we wish the republic to be called right, and in that alone the definition of right government consists. But all the others must be thought to be called so neither legitimately nor truly. But those which imitate this one, we willingly praise, as if rightly tending toward better things; others, on the contrary, we blame as prone toward worse things by imitation of the bad. **SOCRATES.** The other things, O Stranger, seem to have been well said: but that which you say, that government without laws can be right, cannot easily be admitted. **STRANGER.** You have anticipated me a little by asking, O Socrates. For I was about to ask whether you admit all these things, or if anything of what has been said is troublesome to you. But now it is clear that we wish to discuss those who rightly preside without laws. **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **STRANGER.** It is clear, in a way...

...that legislation pertains to the king. But that it is best not for the laws to prevail, but for a man who is prudent and kingly. **SOCRATES.** Do you understand the reason for this? **STRANGER.** Declare it. **STRANGER.** Because the law cannot, by sincerely embracing what is best and most just for all, always command so as to be worthwhile. For the dissimilarity of men and actions, and the unstable condition of human affairs, makes it so that no art can constitute anything simple and universally valid for all, and for all time. Do we concede these things? **SOCRATES.** Clearly. **STRANGER.** But we see the law striving for this very thing, like a certain stubborn and commanding man who permits nothing to be done except what he himself has established, nor even to be asked, if something new besides his order seems rather better to someone. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. For just as you were saying, the law constrains men. **STRANGER.** But it cannot be that a certain and simple order of one kind should prevail in these things which are always varied, and never of one kind. **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **STRANGER.** Therefore, the cause must be found why it is necessary to bring in laws, even though the law itself is not the best and most right thing. **SOCRATES.** Who doubts it? **STRANGER.** Are there not, both among us and among any other mortals, certain common exercises of all together, whether you wish to contend in a race or in any other kind? **SOCRATES.** Very many. **STRANGER.** Come now, let us recall to memory the precepts of those who, by a certain art, preside over gymnastics. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **STRANGER.** They indeed think it is not possible for what fits each one individually and separately to be prescribed. Therefore, they think that what is more common, and what they believe will be most conducive to the most people, should be instituted. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **STRANGER.** For this reason, while they today bind all with equal labors and drive them with parts of exercises, it happens that they either incite them too much or weaken them, and render the bodies unfit for the race, the wrestling-school, and other contests. **SOCRATES.** So it happens. **STRANGER.** Let us also think of the founder of laws presiding over his herds, and giving laws about just works and mutual commerce, that he cannot—while he consults for all in one—provide accurately for the convenience or right of individuals. **SOCRATES.** It is reasonable. **STRANGER.** Moreover, I think, what is most conducive to the most people, he will institute in common, and will bring in such laws both in writings and not in writings, but in ancestral customs. **SOCRATES.** Rightly. **STRANGER.** Very rightly. For in what way could anyone look around at individuals through his whole life, and diligently sit by each, and consult for each one's convenience? For if anyone endowed with kingly discipline could do this, he would hardly ever prescribe for himself those impediments which are called laws. **SOCRATES.** It appears exactly so from these things that have been said. **STRANGER.** Indeed more so, O best one, from these things which will be said. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **STRANGER.** These, I say: if a certain doctor or trainer, with a long journey imminent, thinks he will be far away from those he cares for for a long time, and thinks that either those who are exercising or those who are sick will not remember his precepts, will he not think to write down for them certain monuments of things to be done, or not? **SOCRATES.** He will certainly think so. **STRANGER.** What if, contrary to expectation, he returns sooner than he had thought; will he fear to prescribe other things for them besides those he had once written, if any better things can be applied to the sick because of winds or something else accustomed to happen unexpectedly by the will of God? Will he persevere, I say, in his first purpose, nor allow anyone to transgress the first institutions, nor himself command other things, nor allow other things besides the usual to be observed by the sick man, as if those were both proper to the art of medicine and most healthy; but those things which are done otherwise are outside the art and harmful? Or rather, would not whatever of that kind happens concerning true science and art provoke much laughter for all those authors? **SOCRATES.** And most especially. **STRANGER.** For him who brought and introduced just and unjust things, honest and shameful, good and evil, whether by written laws or unwritten customs, to the herds of men—whoever in the city lives according to the norm of written laws—will it not be permitted to do certain other things besides those which are written, neither if he himself who previously wrote them returns, nor if anyone else similar to him comes? Or rather, would not such a doubt appear no less truly ridiculous than that higher one? **SOCRATES.** Nothing prevents it. **STRANGER.** Do you know, therefore, what is commonly said about this matter? **SOCRATES.** At present, I do not remember. **STRANGER.** Yet they say beautiful things. For they say if anyone finds some laws better than the previous ones and persuades the citizens of them, he ought to bring the laws; if he does not persuade them, he ought not. **SOCRATES.** Is that right? **STRANGER.** Perhaps. But if someone should introduce what is more right not by persuasion but by force, what will be the most fitting name for that violence? Answer—or rather, not yet to those things, but to the higher ones first. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **STRANGER.** If someone truly endowed with the medical art does not persuade but forces him whom he cures—a boy, or a man, or a woman—to do what is better besides the writings, what will be the name for that violence? Would it not be anything else rather than a transgression of the art, which is the bringing in of disease? And must it not be said that anything else rather happened to the forced man than a transgression of art and disease? **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. **STRANGER.** But what was the offense against the civil art? Was it not what is called shameful, what is evil, and what is unjust? **SOCRATES.** Exactly that. **STRANGER.** Come, when some are forced to do what is more just, better, and more honest besides the ancestral laws and customs, will not anyone be the most ridiculous of all who blames that force, and says that they have suffered shameful, evil, and unjust things from the caretakers who forced them? **SOCRATES.** You speak entirely the truth. **STRANGER.** Whether he is rich who forces, are the compulsions just; but if poor, unjust? Or rather, whether he persuaded or did not persuade, whether he be poor or rich, and according to writings or besides writings, provided he introduces useful things, must it be said that this is the true definition of right civil government? By which reasoning a wise and good man will always govern thus looking to the safety of the subjects, as a pilot looks to the safety of the sailors and the ship. For just as he preserves the sailors not by writings but by art as a certain law, so also that truly civil man; and among those who can so rule, there is a right administration of civil affairs, applying the power of art as something more powerful than laws. And in summary, whatever prudent princes do, they never fail, as long as they preserve this one most important thing: that by mind and art they introduce what is most just to the citizens, and are able to protect them, and make them better from worse as far as possible. **SOCRATES.** One cannot disagree with these things that have just been said. **STRANGER.** Nor with those besides. **SOCRATES.** Which were you saying? **STRANGER.** That no multitude can ever excel in that discipline by which a city is ruled according to the mind. But that one right administration of the city must be sought either in one man or in very few indeed. But the others must be placed as certain imitations, as was said a little above, imitating this one now in a better part, now in a worse. **SOCRATES.** How were you saying that? For...

<meta>This page transitions from a discussion on the imitation of a true ruler to a critique of rigid legalism. It features a dialogue between the "Stranger" (Hospes) and "Socrates" regarding the "second-best" method of government: strict adherence to written laws when a perfect, wise ruler is absent.</meta>

-># Civil Affairs, or, Concerning Kingship. 151<-

<note>original: "Ciuilis, Vel, de Regno"</note> Regarding what you said a little while ago about imitation, I understood it well enough then.
**STRANGER.** One would not do poorly if, having introduced this speech, they paused before showing the error that has been committed regarding this matter. **SOCRATES.** What error do you mean?
**STRANGER.** It is now necessary to seek out something of this sort; although it is neither customary nor easy to understand, let us nevertheless strive to grasp it. Since this alone is the "correct" civil government which we have mentioned, is it not necessary that the other forms, using its institutions, be preserved while they do what we just now praised, even if that is not the most perfect way? **SOCRATES.** What do you mean by that? **STRANGER.** That no one should dare to commit anything contrary to the laws, and whoever dares to do so should be punished by death and afflicted with all the ultimate punishments. <margin>Whether laws should be established,</margin> Yet this is the most righteous and honorable path in the *second* degree; for that which was just spoken of must be placed in the *first* degree. Let us declare, then, in what manner that which we just called the "second-best" comes to be. Shall we? **SOCRATES.** Most certainly. **STRANGER.** Let us return again to the analogies to which it is always necessary to compare royal princes. **SOCRATES.** Which analogies do you mean? **STRANGER.** I mean the noble navigator of a ship, and the doctor who—as the saying goes—is equal to many others. Let us now consider an image of this matter by imagining something. **SOCRATES.** What sort of thing? **STRANGER.** Imagine something like this: suppose we all persuaded ourselves that we were suffering grave injuries from them. For instance, suppose they save those of us whom they wish to save, but on the other hand, they destroy those they wish to destroy by cutting or burning them, <note>A reference to ancient medical practices of surgery and cautery.</note> and from this practice of theirs, they take a tribute as a reward. Suppose that while they force the sick person to spend much, they themselves provide nothing for the sick person, but they and their families use the remaining resources. Finally, having accepted money either from the relatives or the enemies of the sick person, they cause him to die. Navigators, too, are said to perpetrate many other things of this kind; for example, those who often by agreement leave men alone in remote retreats, or who, when they have damaged something on the sea, cast them into the depths, and injure them in many other ways. Let us, therefore, persuade ourselves—having been provoked by these causes—to deliberate on how we might strip authority from those arts, so that they may no longer freely dominate either slaves or free men. And for this purpose, having formed an assembly, we should run together and call either the whole people or only the wealthy, where the advice of even unlearned men and other craftsmen regarding the ship and diseases might be heard: in what manner doctors ought to use their medicines and instruments with the sick; likewise concerning ships and their instruments for navigating, avoiding the dangers of storms and waves, and escaping the ambushes of pirates; and even if a battle must be fought at sea with long ships against similar foes, by what reasoning it is proper to use them. I say, let us imagine that whatever seems best regarding these things to the crowd of unlearned men—or to the doctors and navigators—be inscribed on certain public tablets and columns, and that certain unwritten ancestral customs and rites be established, according to which standard we must navigate and heal. **SOCRATES.** You have imagined something utterly absurd. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, imagine that every year the leaders of the people are appointed, chosen by lot either from the wealthy or from the whole populace, who should govern the ships and heal the sick according to those written institutions. **SOCRATES.** These things seem even harsher than the previous ones. **STRANGER.** Let us see, moreover, what follows from this. When the term of each annual magistrate has expired, it will be necessary—either by a judgment of the chosen wealthy or by the people at large appointed by lot—to bring those men who have performed their magistracies to stand trial and demand an accounting from them. Thus, any person who wishes may bring a lawsuit against them, claiming that they navigated the ships or cured the sick otherwise than the laws command and ancestral custom teaches. And those who are found to have done otherwise shall be afflicted by the judges with a sentence, either of punishment or some other penalty. **SOCRATES.** Would not anyone who voluntarily undertakes a magistracy among men of this sort deserve to suffer any punishment or loss? **STRANGER.** Moreover, it will be necessary to carry a law: if anyone, contrary to the written constitutions, introduces some new method of navigation, or searches for that true method of preserving health handed down by the laws by transferring it to the winds, heat, and cold, and <margin>By this law, all arts could be overturned both for the present and the future.</margin> "philosophizes" about these things from his own genius and teaches it: first, indeed, such a person must be named neither a navigator nor a doctor, but some meddlesome and delirious <term>sophist</term>. <note>In this context, a "sophist" is used pejoratively to mean a deceptive or overly clever person who subverts traditional wisdom.</note> Next, he can be dragged into court by anyone, as one who corrupts the youth and persuades them that navigation and medicine should be handled according to each person's own judgment rather than the institutions of the laws, in the same way ships and diseases are treated. And if he is found persuading any young or old person of anything contrary to the laws and writings, he shall be afflicted with the ultimate punishments. For nothing ought to be wiser than the laws. For no one is allowed to be ignorant of the nature of medicine and health, or the best method of governing and navigating, if they are willing to learn the writings and ancestral customs. If these things should happen regarding the sciences we have described, and many others, so that actions are taken according to prescriptions rather than according to the art, what shall we say, O Socrates? For example, if the same were established regarding military matters, every kind of hunting, painting, and universal imitation, architecture, and the making of all instruments and furniture, agriculture and all care of planting, the keeping of horses and all herds, oracles and the various services of attendants, the game of dice, pure arithmetic, or that which concerns the plane, the solid, or speed and slowness. **SOCRATES.** It is certain that if things were so, all arts would be utterly subverted, nor would they ever again be reborn because of this very law which forbids the investigation of new things. Whence life, which is now difficult, would then become altogether intolerable. **STRANGER.** What about this? If we forced each thing to be done according to prescribed laws, and we placed over those laws a certain man—either designated by the consent of the people or created by lot—who, <margin>If any unskilled person is placed in charge of the laws, what evils follow.</margin> having despised the laws for the sake of gain or his own lust, though unskilled in affairs, should attempt to do things other than those which have been instituted, would this not be an evil worse than the first? **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **STRANGER.** For indeed, whoever, being unskilled, dares to commit anything contrary to those laws—which were established from long experience by those who gracefully persuaded the people to accept them—commits a crime far worse than the previous error, and much more than the written laws, he confuses and perverts the duties of life. **SOCRATES.** Greatly so. **STRANGER.** For which reason, once the laws are established, there is now (as the saying goes) a "second voyage," and no one should ever be permitted to do anything contrary to them, whether individuals or the people attempt it. **SOCRATES.** Wisely said. **STRANGER.** <margin>That laws are imitations of the truth.</margin> Will not these laws be certain imitations of the truth, which were established to the best of their ability by those who understand? **SOCRATES.** Nothing prevents it. **STRANGER.** And yet, if we remember, we said above that a truly political and skilled man would often do many things based on his art contrary to the institutions he had written previously, whenever some better things occurred to him than those that were absent—

Using the metaphors of medicine and navigation, it illustrates how rigid legalism might stifle progress but is still preferable to the rule of an unskilled or corrupt individual who ignores established wisdom.</summary>

### [Page 152]
**Book Sixteen.**

*[Margin: How a king should govern.]*
...left behind among those present, he might think he has found. SOCRATES: We said [this] without doubt. STRANGER: Is it not true that if individuals, or the people themselves to whom laws have been prescribed, attempt something else as if it were better, beyond what has been handed down by those laws, they are doing to the best of their strength exactly what that true statesman does? SOCRATES: Most certainly. STRANGER: Therefore, if the unskillful were to do this, they would strive to imitate the truth itself, yet they would imitate it perversely. But if the skillful strive for the same, this will no longer be an imitation, but that very thing which is most true. SOCRATES: Entirely so. STRANGER: Indeed, it was agreed between us earlier that no art belongs to the many. SOCRATES: It was certainly agreed. STRANGER: Therefore, if the royal art is a certain faculty, the crowd of the wealthy and the whole people will never attain this civil science. SOCRATES: Never. STRANGER: It is necessary, therefore, that republics of this kind (since they are to imitate to the best of their power that true governance of a single man ruling by art) never do anything contrary to the written laws and ancestral customs. SOCRATES: You have spoken excellently. STRANGER: When the wealthy imitate that same [true state], we call that republic the governance of the best (*optimatum*); but when they hold the laws as nothing, it is the power of the few (*paucorum potentia*). SOCRATES: Perhaps. STRANGER: Furthermore, whenever one man rules according to the laws, imitating that knowing man, we call him a King, not distinguishing by name the one who alone rules by science from the one who alone rules according to opinion following the laws. SOCRATES: So it seems. STRANGER: Therefore, if one man endowed with that true science rules, does he not have the same name, that is "Royal," and is called by no other title? For out of the five names of civil governments we recounted, this was the only one. SOCRATES: It seems so. STRANGER: What then, whenever someone rules neither by law nor by custom, and at the same time pretends to know, asserting that things ought to be done more rightly in this way beyond the laws—yet there is in him a certain lust and ignorance which leads to such an imitation—is not such a man to be called a Tyrant? SOCRATES: Most certainly. STRANGER: By this reasoning, there exists the King, as we said, and the Tyrant, the power of the few, the governance of the best, as well as popular administration; for men grew weary of the rule of one man, despairing that such a man could ever be found worthy of such great power, who would both be able and willing to rule with virtue and science, and holily and justly grant each man his right. They feared, moreover, lest one man having gained license might harm, oppress, or kill anyone according to his lust. Since if such a man as we have described should occur to us, his administration would surely be loved, which alone of all is most right and leads to living well and blessedly. SOCRATES: Truly. STRANGER: But now, since such a king is not born in cities, as one among the swarms of bees immediately excels the rest in both body and soul from the beginning, it is necessary, it seems, to form an assembly of consultants to write down institutions and follow the tracks of that truest republic. SOCRATES: So it appears. STRANGER: And do we wonder, O Socrates, that in governments such evils occur and will occur as we see, because the foundation is laid not on science, but rests only on certain written institutions and customs in the conduct of affairs? If any other governance or city were to use this, it is certain it would utterly overturn all things. Or perhaps that ought to seem more wonderful, how robust a thing a city is by nature: for though some cities have been so affected for a long time, they nevertheless remain and do not collapse; yet many, like ships, have perished submerged, are perishing, and will perish, because of the wickedness of the governors and sailors who are held in a certain extreme ignorance regarding the greatest matters. For although they are entirely ignorant of civil affairs, they seem to themselves to be most wise in them. SOCRATES: You speak the truth. STRANGER: Since, therefore, all republics that are not right are difficult for living together, we must see which is the lightest and which is the most burdensome of all. Although this seems to pertain less to our current task, we will perhaps find that we do all things for the sake of this. SOCRATES: Thus it must be done. STRANGER: Of the three, they say one and the same is both the easiest and the most difficult. SOCRATES: How do you say that? STRANGER: Not otherwise than before, there are surely three civil governances: of one, of the few, and of the many, speaking first in a confused way. SOCRATES: It will be as above. STRANGER: But by dividing each into two, let us make six, and set apart the right one itself as a seventh from the others. SOCRATES: In what way? STRANGER: We divide the principality of one into Kingdom and Tyranny. The domination which belongs to the few we divide into one form which is praised, namely the governance of the best (*optimatum*); the other which is blamed, the power of the few (*paucorum potentia*). But the administration of the many we can call simple, naming it popular governance; yet now let us say even this is twofold. SOCRATES: By what reasoning shall we divide it? STRANGER: By no other than the others, even if the name is the same. But this is common to this as to the others: whether they keep the laws or transgress them. SOCRATES: Certainly. STRANGER: Then surely, for those seeking the right governance, this partition was of no use, as we showed above. But after we set that one apart and considered the others necessary, in these the custody or transgression of the laws divides each in two. SOCRATES: From the discourse just spoken, it seems so. STRANGER: Therefore, the domination of one joined with good constitutions, which we call laws, is the best of all those six; that which is void of laws is harsh and the most burdensome of all for the subjects. SOCRATES: It appears so. STRANGER: But the governance in which the few rule, we ought to consider middle, just as what is "few" holds the middle between "one" and "many." But the administration of the many is weak in all things, as being compared to the others, it can produce nothing magnificent, whether good or evil, because the magistracies are reduced to trifles and divided among many. Wherefore, of all lawful Republics, this is the worst; of the unjust, it is the best of all. And if all are intemperate, it is better to live in a popular one; if all are temperate, one should live in that one least of all. But in the first [Kingdom] it is most powerful and best to lead one's life, the seventh being excepted. For it is fitting to set that one apart from all other governances, no differently than a God from men. SOCRATES: These things seem to happen and occur thus; we must act as you say. STRANGER: Therefore, is it not right to set aside all administrators of these Republics, except for that one who belongs to that wise man, as being men who are not truly civil, but seditious, and presiding over great masks—indeed, the masks themselves, the greatest mimics, the greatest tricksters, and the sophists of sophists? SOCRATES: This title seems to rightly apply to those who are called civil. STRANGER: Now at last we have barely separated from the civil art that dance of Centaurs and Satyrs which we said we saw above, and we think it must be separated from the civil. SOCRATES: It seems so. STRANGER: A certain harder thing remains for these, which is all the more difficult to discern from the King because it is more closely joined to his nature, just as...
