### [Page 153]
**Civil, or On Kingship.**

*[Margin: That the judiciary is the king's peculiar duty.]*
...it seems to have happened to those digging for gold. SOCRATES: In what way? STRANGER: The craftsmen first separate the earth and stones and many other things from it; but after these there remain certain things more akin to gold and more precious, to be separated from the gold by fire alone—bronze, silver, and sometimes even adamant—which are barely explored by the test of fire, and allow us to see pure gold. SOCRATES: So it is said of them. STRANGER: By the same reasoning, we too seem to have separated from civil science things that are vehemently alien and distant, but have left those things which are closest and honorable. In this number is the command of the army, the judicial praetorship, and the oratorical dignity communicating with royal authority, while it persuades what is just and with that [authority] governs public affairs. If someone easily separates these, he will show us that civil [man] whom we seek, naked and alone. SOCRATES: There is no doubt this must be attempted with all zeal. STRANGER: Indeed, for the sake of experience it will be revealed, but we must try to reveal it through music. Tell me then. SOCRATES: What do you wish me to say? STRANGER: Is there for us any discipline of music and generally of the arts performed by the ministry of hands? SOCRATES: There is. STRANGER: What then, shall we say there is some science here which teaches which of the arts is to be learned and which is not? SOCRATES: We shall plainly say so. STRANGER: Shall we not confess this is different from the others? SOCRATES: And this too. STRANGER: Then shall we say none of them rules the other, or do those rule this one, or does this one preside over all as a leader? SOCRATES: That one which judges which arts are to be learned and which not. STRANGER: Do you assert then that it rules both the teacher and the learner? SOCRATES: Entirely. STRANGER: And does the art which judges whether one should persuade or not rule the one which can persuade? SOCRATES: Why not? STRANGER: To which science shall we chiefly attribute that persuasion which is made to the crowd through conversation and exhortation rather than doctrine? SOCRATES: It is clear it must be attributed to the oratorical [art]. STRANGER: Whose duty do we say it is to judge whether to use force or persuasion, and in what matters, and against whom it is fitting to use it? SOCRATES: His who rules the skill of persuading and speaking. STRANGER: But I think there is no such faculty except that of the civil man. SOCRATES: Excellent. STRANGER: Thus, then, the oratorical faculty seems immediately distinct from the civil, as a certain other species subject to the civil. SOCRATES: Certainly. STRANGER: What further should be thought of this faculty? SOCRATES: Which one? STRANGER: By which we fight against those on whom we have declared war. Shall we say this is skillful or void of art? SOCRATES: Who would say it is without art, seeing all those things which belong to the imperial and military discipline? STRANGER: But that faculty which can prudently deliberate by consulting with whom war is to be waged or peace made—shall we think it different from that one [the military], or the same? SOCRATES: Different, if indeed we stand by our previous points. STRANGER: If we follow the previous reasoning, shall we not say that this one which consults about war rules that one which wages war? SOCRATES: Exactly so. STRANGER: What faculty, besides that royal discipline of civil affairs, shall we say truly presides over the most powerful art of the whole military? SOCRATES: Absolutely no other. STRANGER: Therefore, we shall by no means posit that the science of those who lead armies is the civil faculty itself, since it obeys and serves another. SOCRATES: It is indeed not fitting. STRANGER: Come now, let us consider the duty of judges who judge individual matters justly. SOCRATES: Let us consider it. STRANGER: Does it ever extend further than to consider what is just and what is not regarding all kinds of contracts, and looking toward the norm of the laws which the king himself established, to judge individual things, with his own virtue always applied, through which neither by gifts, nor threats, nor mercy, nor hatred, nor love, having transgressed the laws, he dissolves mutual accusations? SOCRATES: Certainly the duty of a judge is nothing other than what has now been said by you. STRANGER: It is clear, therefore, that the power of judges is not that royal majesty, but the guardian of the laws and the minister of the king. SOCRATES: It appears so. STRANGER: Whoever considers all the arts we have mentioned must think that none of them is the civil discipline we seek: since the duty of royal majesty is not to act itself, but to rule those capable of acting, and to recognize the command and power of those things which are greatest in the city, then what is decorous, what is opportune, and what is contrary; while the other faculties carry out orders and transact mandates. SOCRATES: Optimally. STRANGER: Wherefore those arts we just recounted, since they are masters neither of themselves nor of each other, but each is incumbent upon certain proper works, have deservedly obtained proper names for their proper duties. SOCRATES: It appears so. STRANGER: But that art which presides over all these, and has care of the laws and of all things in the city, and weaves all things together, we rightly call "Civil Science," comprehending its faculty by a common name. SOCRATES: Entirely. STRANGER: Is it fitting now to run through this according to the example of the weaving faculty, after we have revealed all the kinds that are in the city? SOCRATES: Most certainly. STRANGER: It must next be declared, it seems, what the royal composition is, and by what reasoning it folds together and produces what kind of texture for us. SOCRATES: So it is. STRANGER: The matter is indeed difficult to demonstrate; but since it seemed necessary, it must be declared to the best of our power. SOCRATES: It must be declared entirely. STRANGER: For that a part of virtue differs from a species of virtue can easily be proven even against contentious men by the opinion of many. SOCRATES: I do not quite understand. STRANGER: Perhaps you will understand this way. I think you consider Fortitude to be some part of virtue. SOCRATES: Completely. STRANGER: And Temperance to be different from fortitude, yet to be a part of the same thing of which fortitude is a part. SOCRATES: Yes. STRANGER: Something wonderful must be dared to be stated about these. SOCRATES: What is it? STRANGER: That these two, in many things, are in a way very much opposed to each other. SOCRATES: By what reasoning do you say this? STRANGER: This is unheard of, if indeed all parts of virtue are said to be bound by mutual friendship. SOCRATES: Certainly. STRANGER: Let us therefore consider diligently whether this is so simple, or whether it has a very great difference in things that are in a way kindred. SOCRATES: Indeed. But tell me where it should be considered. STRANGER: In all things which we call beautiful, and we refer them to two species contrary to each other. SOCRATES: Speak more plainly. STRANGER: Velocity of bodies, or of souls, or of voices—whether of these themselves or even of any images which express them by imitating in music or painting—have you ever praised any of these yourself, or heard another praise them? SOCRATES: Why ask? STRANGER: Do you remember how those things are praised in each of them? SOCRATES: Not at all. STRANGER: I wish I could explain these things in words as they seem to me. SOCRATES: What prohibits it? STRANGER: This seems easy to you, as I see. Wherefore let us consider it in contrary genera. This happens whenever we admire the velocity, vehemence, and sharpness of many things, whether in thought, or body, or voice, we are accustomed to use one name of "Fortitude" in praising them. SOCRATES: In what way?

### [Page 154]
**Book Sixteen.**

STRANGER: We say "sharp and strong," "swift and strong," "vehement and strong": and we are accustomed to praise these natures by the common name of fortitude. SOCRATES: Assuredly. STRANGER: Do we not also often praise a thing in many actions when it is done gradually and lightly? SOCRATES: Very much. STRANGER: Do we not, on the contrary, use different praises here than there? SOCRATES: How? STRANGER: We often call these things "quiet," and "temperate," and we love these in thought, and in actions the slow and soft, in voices the light and grave, and every rhythmic and numerous motion, and every muse using an opportune slowness: and to all these we apply the name of "Moderation" (*moderatio*), not "Fortitude." SOCRATES: You speak truly. STRANGER: But whenever these do not observe opportuneness, we conversely blame them with changed names. SOCRATES: How? STRANGER: When they become sharper and swifter, and harsher or harder than opportuneness requires, we call them "insulting," "petulant," "furious"; but when they become graver and slower, and softer, we call them "timid," "inept," and "slothful." And almost always we find these and the natures of temperance and fortitude to be contrary, like hostile forms, and stirring up sedition among themselves; nor do those who are occupied with these ever mix in actions, nor do those in whose souls these reside agree among themselves, but rather they disagree, if only we investigate diligently. SOCRATES: Where do you say? STRANGER: In all those things I mentioned, and it is likely in many others: for since both, according to the affinity of their nature, praise some things as their own and reprove others as alien and strange, it happens in many things that they are vehemently opposed to each other. SOCRATES: They seem so. STRANGER: This altercation of such species is a kind of game to some, but in the greatest matters it becomes the most serious disease for all cities. SOCRATES: In what kind of matters? STRANGER: In every constitution of living, as is likely. For those who excel the rest in modesty study the tranquility of life, always doing their own things privately, loving peace and concord both toward foreigners and toward fellow citizens. And by the excess of this love it happens that, while they are privately intent on their own works, they themselves are rendered un-warlike and weakened, and they soften and effeminate the younger by their example. Hence they are exposed to any invaders, and in a short time they and their children and the whole fatherland succumb, having gradually lost their liberty. SOCRATES: You have described a very hard and grave disease. STRANGER: But those who, inclining more toward fortitude, affect a warlike life too much, often incite and exhort their country to war, whereby they render many and powerful nations hostile to their city. Wherefore they either utterly overturn their cities or imprudently bring them into the slavery of enemies. SOCRATES: So it also happens. STRANGER: Therefore, who would deny that in these both are very much opposed to each other? SOCRATES: No one, surely. STRANGER: Have we not now found what we were seeking from the beginning? Namely, that some not small parts of virtue are by nature fighting with themselves, and make those who possess them disagree greatly among themselves? SOCRATES: It appears so. STRANGER: Let us see this likewise. SOCRATES: What? STRANGER: Whether there is any science among those whose action consists in composing, which would voluntarily construct any work of its own, even the vilest, out of bad and good things together? Or rather does every science always avoid the wicked to the best of its power, and catch the fit and useful: and from these, part similar and part dissimilar, collected into one, forge one certain power and idea? SOCRATES: The latter rather. STRANGER: Therefore, the true skill in civil affairs according to nature will never voluntarily constitute any city from bad and good men: but it will explore each one by discipline and some trial, and having made an examination, it will afterwards commit that same duty to those who can teach others and obey themselves: over whom it will diligently preside and command, just as the weaving art presides over the carders and other preparers of wool-making, prescribing such things to each as it thinks will lead to its texture. SOCRATES: Entirely so. STRANGER: By the same reasoning, royal majesty seems to me presiding over all others who imbue and educate according to the institutes of the laws; it permits them to exercise and teach only that which, pertaining to its reasoning, induces decorous manners: but those who cannot attain the power of fortitude or temperance or other virtues, but are drawn by the depravity of nature to impiety, petulance, and injustice, it ejects from the assembly of citizens, and damns them with exile, death, and extreme reproach. SOCRATES: So it is handed down in a way. STRANGER: But the ignorant and small-souled little men it subjugates to servile ministry. SOCRATES: Very skillfully. STRANGER: But the others, whose wits can be raised to a noble habit through discipline, and allow the art to be tempered among them, it saves and protects. Of these, those which verge more toward fortitude, it judges to be in place of the warp on account of their solid manners: but those toward modesty, like soft and tender material, have the image of the woof of a saffron color. Finally, those which tend toward a contrary and diverse nature, it strives to conquer and weave together in this way. SOCRATES: How? STRANGER: First, according to the reason of kinship, it binds the eternal part of the soul with a divine bond; then after the divine, it binds that which is of animal nature with human bonds. SOCRATES: How is that? STRANGER: Whenever there is in souls a true and stable opinion about the beautiful, just, and good, or their contraries, I assert that it becomes divine in a demonic genus, that is, in a knowing and happy one. SOCRATES: It is indeed fitting. STRANGER: Do you not think it belongs to the civil man and the good lawgiver, that only the royal muse can insert this into those who are participants of right discipline as is fitting, whom we just mentioned? SOCRATES: That also is likely. STRANGER: But he who cannot do this, O Socrates, ought not to be called by the names we were just seeking. SOCRATES: Certainly not. STRANGER: Does not a brave soul, if it participates in this kind of truth, become mild, and thus most greatly desires to live and act justly among others? But if it is entirely void of it, does it not fall into a beastly nature? SOCRATES: Without doubt. STRANGER: And yet a soul modest by nature, imbued with those opinions, is rendered truly temperate and moderated so as to be useful to the republic. But being empty, it most rightly bears the foul infamy of stupidity and sloth. SOCRATES: Greatly so. STRANGER: Must it not be said that such a complication and bond is never stable between the wicked themselves, nor between the good and the wicked? And that no science would intentionally use this to bind such men? SOCRATES: Entirely. STRANGER: But for those to whom nature gave noble manners, and whom custom educated according to the norm of nature, to them alone is that bond given through the laws: and in these is that civil art like a remedy, and by this reasoning that very conciliation of the parts of virtue, naturally contrary and fighting, becomes something divine. SOCRATES: These things are true. STRANGER: Where this divine bond stands, it is easy both to find and to perfect human bonds once found. SOCRATES: By what reasoning? and which...

*[Margin: What evils arise from intemperance.]*
*[Margin: Every science rejects evils, seeks the useful.]*
*[Margin: Duties of royal majesty.]*

### [Page 155]
**Commentary.**

*[Margin: Condition of a strong nature.]*
...especially? STRANGER: The affinities of children and those necessities which are in betrothals and marriages: for many are not rightly coupled for procreating children in these things. SOCRATES: For what reason? STRANGER: How eagerly they pursue riches and power in these things—what pertains to reviewing this more diligently in speech? SOCRATES: Nothing. STRANGER: But it is better to speak of those who care for lineage, if they happen to act beyond measure. SOCRATES: It is fair. STRANGER: For they act by no right reason, following present pleasure, and from the fact that they are delighted only by their likes, and not at all by dissimilars, they stir up a great deal of difficulty. SOCRATES: In what way? STRANGER: Modest men seek manners similar to their own, and as far as they can, they both marry from such and give their daughters to such. In the same way, the brave kind takes its likes to itself, when it ought to happen entirely the opposite for both kinds. SOCRATES: How? and for what cause? STRANGER: Because this is the condition of a strong nature, that if it remains void of temperance through many successions, in the beginning it becomes more robust, but finally it fails, turning into madness. SOCRATES: It agrees. STRANGER: Conversely, a soul abounding in shame, but everywhere lacking the audacity of fortitude, if it passes through many generations similarly, becomes more sluggish than is fitting, and finally is merged in a certain extreme lethargy. SOCRATES: It is clear that happens also. STRANGER: We can easily bind both kinds of men with these ligaments, as we said, if, as we said, both have the same opinion about the good and beautiful. This one and integral work belongs to the royal texture, that it never permits moderated manners to be separate from the brave ones, but weaving both wits together through the consensus of the same opinion, through honors and reproaches, and through alternate marriages, it produces from these a smooth and best-cohering web, and always commits civil magistracies and duties to these in common. SOCRATES: In what way? STRANGER: Where the governance of one will suffice, it will set over it a man endowed with both manners. Where there is need of more, it will mix some parts of each kind. For the manners of temperate princes are very cautious and just and salutary: they need sharp promptness and a certain vehemence suitable for acting. SOCRATES: So it seems of these also. STRANGER: But fortitude yields to those in caution and justice: but in acting it excels greatly. Nor can all things be done well in a city privately and publicly, unless both of these are present. SOCRATES: Certainly not. STRANGER: Therefore let us say the end of civil action, woven by right publication, then exists, when conciliating the wits of the brave and temperate by concord and friendship, it makes their life common: which context is indeed the most noble of all and best, protecting and embracing all others in the city, both slaves and free men, and comprehending them in this texture and series: and thus it rules and presides over the city, so that it omits nothing of those things which, as far as possible, make a city blessed. SOCRATES: Truly, guest, you have excellently defined the royal and civil man for us.

### [The Protagoras of Plato, or, The Sophists.]
**Marsilio Ficino's Argument.**

There exists among the Greeks a very true saying about Plato: that Phoebus seems to have fathered two sons especially, Aesculapius and Plato. Aesculapius indeed to heal bodies, but Plato to heal souls. All the Socratics also testify that Socrates was sent by god for the sake of purging souls. The disease of the soul seems to consist in false opinions and bad manners. Such great evil is not so easily brought upon noble souls by others as by sophists. Truly philosophers are those who studiously seek the truth solely for the love of truth itself. Sophists, however, affect opinion, similarly for the love of opinion. For these, like merchants and innkeepers of disciplines, gather various opinions from everywhere without selection, pertaining both to thinking and speaking however one pleases, which they then sell like venal goods to wealthy youths, for the sake of riches and empty glory... [Ficino continues with a long introduction to the Protagoras, discussing Prometheus, Epimetheus, and the nature of virtue as a divine gift.]

---

### [Page 157]
**Protagoras, or, the Sophists.**

...himself. Finally, when Protagoras began to evade due to ignorance of responding, and therefore Socrates pretended he would depart, the Sophist was called back to discourse by the auditors. In which altercation the superstitious curiosity of the Sophist Prodicus about words is demonstrated; then the ostentation of the Sophist Hippias in more timid preaching. Finally, Protagoras, recalled to disputing, digresses too importunately and ineptly into songs and poetry... [Summary of the dialogue's action continues].

**FRIEND, SOCRATES, HIPPOCRATES, PROTAGORAS, ALCIBIADES, CALLIAS, CRITIAS, PRODICUS, HIPPIAS.**

*[Margin: The narration ought to have been a continuous one without the personas.]*

**FRIEND:** From where, O Socrates, do you come? Do you perhaps return from that hunt which the beauty of Alcibiades is accustomed to provoke in you? For lately as I contemplated him, he seemed a beautiful man—already a man, I say, who could be counted among ourselves, as for instance his cheeks are already covered with much down. SOCRATES: Be it so, what then? Do you not approve of Homer, who says the age of the first down is most pleasing? Indeed Alcibiades now enjoys that age. FRIEND: But at present do you return from him? and how is the youth now disposed toward you? SOCRATES: Well indeed, especially today he seemed so to me, for he often came to my aid today in speaking, and I come now from him. And I will tell you something wonderful: I was not looking at him when he was present, and looking elsewhere I barely noticed him. FRIEND: What then was so great as to divert you from him? For no more handsome man from our citizens could be present. SOCRATES: On the contrary, there was one present much more beautiful. FRIEND: What do you say? A citizen or a foreigner? SOCRATES: A foreigner. FRIEND: From where? SOCRATES: From Abdera. FRIEND: Was that foreigner seen by you to be endowed with such remarkable form that he seemed more handsome to you than the son of Clinias? SOCRATES: What prohibits, O blessed one, that which is wiser from being also more beautiful? FRIEND: Do you perhaps come from the conversation of some wise man? SOCRATES: Of the wisest indeed of all men of our age, if only Protagoras seems to you the wisest of all. FRIEND: Ah, what do you say? Has Protagoras come here? SOCRATES: Two days ago. FRIEND: And have you just been with him? SOCRATES: Just now, and I spoke many things, and also heard many. FRIEND: Will you not relate those to us? unless something prohibits it. You may sit here. This boy will give way to you. SOCRATES: I will indeed relate them, and I shall be grateful if you listen. FRIEND: And we to you, if you speak. SOCRATES: Therefore there will be a double grace. Listen then. Last night before the rising of light, Hippocrates the son of Apollodorus, brother of Phason, struck my door vehemently with his staff: and when someone had opened the door, suddenly entering in haste and shouting with a great voice, "Are you sleeping, O Socrates, or are you awake?" And I, by his voice, said, "This is Hippocrates." "Hippocrates, is there anything new?" "Nothing," he said, "except I come announcing a pleasant thing." "Excellent," I said. "But what is it? what cause drove you here?" "Protagoras has come, and is staying near me." Then I: "He came long ago; did you only now hear?" "Yesterday evening indeed," he said; and grabbing a stool in the darkness, he sat at my feet and added: "late yesterday evening returning from Oenoe, for my boy Satyrus had fled: and when I wanted to signify to you that I was pursuing him, I forgot because of something else intervening. But when I had come, and we had dined and wanted to give ourselves to sleep, then my brother first announces that Protagoras has come. I immediately tried to hurry to you, but the untimely night detained me. But having awakened from sleep and being relieved of labor, I have just now come here to you." And I, observing the magnanimity and amazement of the man: "What is this to you?" I asked. "Does Protagoras do you some injury?" Then he smiling: "Certainly," he said, "because he alone is wise, but does not make me wise." SOCRATES: Nay, he will certainly also make you wise, if you persuade him by offering a fee. HIPPOCRATES: O Jupiter and the other gods, I would spare neither my own nor my friends' things, provided I consider I would attain it: and therefore I come to you now, so that you may intercede for me with him. For I am younger, and I have never seen nor heard Protagoras, for I was then a boy when he first came here. All men indeed praise this man, O Socrates, and they say he is most wise in speaking. But why do we not hurry to him, so that we may meet him at home? He is staying, as I heard, with Callias the son of Hipponicus. Let us go now. SOCRATES: Not yet, O good man, I said, must we go there. For it is still very early morning. But let us go to the court, where we will walk until the dawn shines, afterwards we will go to Protagoras himself: for Protagoras spends most of his time at home. Therefore be confident, for we shall find him at home. Having said these things, we rose and went to the court: and I, wanting to make a trial of his confidence, looked at him diligently, and thus interrogated him: "Tell me then, O Hippocrates, you want to go now to Protagoras, to give him a fee for yourself? to what kind of man are you going? and you yourself, what kind of man are you to turn out from him? Just as if you wanted to go to Hippocrates, that namesake of yours from Cos, born from the stock of Aesculapius, to pay a fee for yourself, and someone asked, 'Tell me, O Hippocrates, will you give a fee to Hippocrates? to what kind of man, and for what reason?' what would you respond?" HIPPOCRATES: As to a physician. SOCRATES: What will you yourself become, that is, for whose sake? HIPPOCRATES: To turn out as a physician. SOCRATES: But if you went to Polycletus the Argive or Phidias the Athenian with a fee offered for yourself, and someone asked to what kind of men and for what reason you intended to give money to Polycletus and Phidias, what would you say to this? HIPPOCRATES: As to sculptors. SOCRATES: And you yourself, what kind of man will you become? HIPPOCRATES: A sculptor, obviously. SOCRATES: Attend, I pray: I and you now set out to Protagoras, and we are prepared to give your money as a favor to you, if only our money suffices and if it is permitted to obtain it; if not, we will also spend the money of friends. If anyone therefore asks us as we hurry to this: "Tell me please, O Socrates and Hippocrates, to what kind of man and for what reason do you think to give money to Protagoras?" what should we answer him? What title especially have we heard for Protagoras? They name Phidias a sculptor. Homer a poet. But Protagoras what? HIPPOCRATES: A Sophist, O Socrates, they call this man. SOCRATES: Therefore we proceed to him as to a sophist to be hired for a fee? HIPPOCRATES: Exactly. SOCRATES: If someone asks you with what mind and what kind of man you yourself are going to Protagoras to become, what would you say to him? Here Hippocrates blushed, for now the dawn had shone a little, by which his face could be seen; he responded then: "To conclude from the above, surely as a sophist myself to be." SOCRATES: By the gods, are you not ashamed to present yourself as a Sophist among the Greeks? HIPPOCRATES: Vehemently, O Socrates, if I must bring forth what I feel. SOCRATES: But see, O Hippocrates, lest perhaps your study of this Protagorean art leads elsewhere than that you should become a sophist. Just as you attended the school of the grammarian, the citharode, and the gymnast, not for the sake of exercising the art itself, but rather with a certain greed for learning, as becomes a private and free man. HIPPOCRATES: Such entirely seems to be the reason for my study with Protagoras. SOCRATES: Do you know what you are about to do now, or does it escape you? HIPPOCRATES: Concerning what? SOCRATES: You are about to commit the care of your soul to a man who is, as you say, a sophist. But if you know what a sophist is, I shall marvel greatly. And if you are ignorant, you do not know what kind of thing this is, whether good or bad, upon which you study to bestow your effort. HIPPOCRATES: I think indeed I know. SOCRATES: Tell me then, what do you think a sophist is? HIPPOCRATES: I think he is, as the name signifies, one who understands things pertaining to wisdom. SOCRATES: One may say the same also of painters and craftsmen, that they are those who understand things pertaining to wisdom. But if someone asked about painters, to what things' wisdom, we would respond to the wisdom of producing images, and similarly of the others. And if we were interrogated in the same way about the sophist, what kind of wisdom would we answer his is? the teacher of what art? HIPPOCRATES: The teacher, O Socrates, of eloquence and the faculty of speaking. SOCRATES: Perhaps we would speak truly thus, but not sufficiently. For that response requires another interrogation: in what matters does the sophist make men skilled in learning? For the citharist makes them fit for the same things in which they are also learned, namely in striking the cithara, does he not? HIPPOCRATES: Certainly. SOCRATES: But indeed, what faculty of speaking does the sophist provide? in what things? It is clear that in those which he understands. HIPPOCRATES: That is likely. SOCRATES: What then is that which the Sophist himself understands and teaches others? HIPPOCRATES: By Hercules, I am ignorant. SOCRATES: Do you not see to how great a danger you subject your soul? if you were to subject your body to the same danger, by which it could be turned either for better or for worse, would you not first commit it to someone about to make such a trial only after you had diligently considered whether it ought to be committed or not: and would you not have consulted friends and relatives for a long time about this very thing? But when you value your soul more than your body, and from its either disease or integrity it happens that all your things are either badly or well disposed, you did not consult your father, nor your brother, nor any of us who are your friends and familiars, whether your soul should be committed to this guest or not. But when you heard of his arrival yesterday evening, you hurry to him in the early morning, with no counsel taken about this, whether you ought to believe yourself to him or not. Nay, you are prepared to spend both your own and your friends' money, as if you already knew it was entirely necessary to adhere to Protagoras, whom you have never seen, as you say, nor spoken with. You call him a Sophist, and you clearly do not know what a sophist is, to whom you are about to give yourself. HIPPOCRATES: You seem to speak the truth, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Is not a sophist, O Hippocrates, a certain merchant and innkeeper of the provisions by which the soul is nourished? HIPPOCRATES: He indeed seems so to me; but by what is the soul nourished? SOCRATES: By disciplines; but we must be careful, O friend, lest while the sophist praises what he sells, he deceives us, as those do who sell food for the body, both merchants and innkeepers. They indeed praise all their things, nor is it understood whether what they sell is healthy or noxious for the body, and they are ignorant of this, as are those who buy, unless perhaps one of them happens to be a physician or a gymnastic trainer. No differently those who carry various disciplines for sale through the cities and peddle them to those who wish to buy, praise all things they sell. And perhaps some of them are often ignorant of what is useful to the soul and what is useless from these things they sell: similarly also those who buy from them: unless some one of them is a physician of the soul. If therefore you understand yourself what from these is profitable and what is harmful, you can safely buy disciplines both from Protagoras and from any other. Otherwise, take care, O blessed youth, lest you lead your most dear things into the greatest danger of loss. For the danger is far more grave in buying disciplines than in buying foods. For he who buys eatables and drinkables from an innkeeper or a merchant can, before he consumes them, carry them home in some other vessels, and there deposited, diligently examine them, and having called some expert in these things, deliberate what should be eaten or drunk, what not, how much, and when; wherefore the danger in buying is not grave. But disciplines cannot be transferred into another vessel, but it is necessary that he who buys them takes them into his soul, and having left the price, he has them, carrying them within himself, either already polluted or advanced toward better things. Let us therefore discuss these with those older than both of us; for we are younger than such a great matter of judgment requires. In the present, however, let us proceed where we began, and hear this man; having heard him, we will communicate with others. For Protagoras is not alone there, but also Hippias of Elis, and Prodicus, I think, of Chios, and many other men, and very wise ones. These things pleased us, and we went on. And having entered the vestibule, we treated a certain discourse which we had by chance fallen into while going. Lest it be left imperfect, we progressed so far as to talk in the vestibule until we agreed... [The narrative continues into the house of Callias].

*[Margin: Far more grave danger in buying disciplines than foods.]*

--- Page 172 ---
->The Statesman, Or Concerning Kingship. 153<-

...to have happened to us as to those digging for gold.
**SOCRATES.** How so?
**STRANGER.** Earth and stones and many other things the craftsmen first separate from it. But after these there remain certain things more closely related to gold, more precious and mixed with it, which are to be separated from gold by fire alone—copper, silver, and sometimes even diamond—which are barely explored at last by a test made at the fire, and permit us to see pure and unadulterated gold.
**SOCRATES.** So it is said of them.
**STRANGER.** By the same reasoning, we too seem to have separated from civil science things that are vehemently alien and very distant; but we have left behind things that are near and to be honored. In their number is the command of the army, the judicial office, and the oratorical dignity communicating with royal authority, while it persuades what is just and governs public affairs with it. If someone were to easily separate these, he would show us that civil man whom we seek, now naked and alone.
**SOCRATES.** There is no doubt that this must be attempted with all zeal.
**STRANGER.** For the sake of experience, the thing itself will be revealed, but we should attempt to reveal it through music. And tell me.
**SOCRATES.** What do you wish me to say?
**STRANGER.** Is there any discipline for us of music and of all the arts which are performed by the service of hands?
**SOCRATES.** There is.
**STRANGER.** What then, shall we say that here also there is some science which teaches which of the arts is to be learned and which is not?
**SOCRATES.** We shall plainly say there is.
**STRANGER.** Shall we not confess that this is performed by others?
**SOCRATES.** This also.
**STRANGER.** Then shall we say that none of them rule over each other, or that one rules another, or that this one presides over all of them as a leader?
**SOCRATES.** That one which judges which of the individual arts are to be learned and which are not.

<margin>The majesty of the oratorical faculty.</margin>

**STRANGER.** Do you assert, therefore, that it commands both the teacher and the learner?
**SOCRATES.** Entirely.
**STRANGER.** And does that which judges whether persuasion should be used, or not, command that which can persuade?
**SOCRATES.** Why not?

<margin>How oratory is distinguished from the civil art.</margin>

**STRANGER.** To which science shall we especially attribute that persuasion which is made to the crowd through a certain conversation and exhortation rather than through teaching?
**SOCRATES.** It is clear it must be attributed to the oratorical art.
**STRANGER.** To which art's duty do we say it belongs to judge whether force or persuasion is to be used, and in what things and against whom it is proper to use them?
**SOCRATES.** To that which rules over the skill of persuading and speaking.
**STRANGER.** But that, as I think, is no other faculty than that of the civil man.
**SOCRATES.** Excellently said.
**STRANGER.** Thus, therefore, the oratorical faculty seems immediately distinguished from the civil faculty, as a certain other species subject to that civil one.
**SOCRATES.** Certainly.

<margin>The science of military affairs is subject to the civil art.</margin>

**STRANGER.** What furthermore must be thought of this faculty?
**SOCRATES.** Which one?
**STRANGER.** That by which we fight against those on whom we have declared war. Shall we say this is based on art, or is it expert-less?
**SOCRATES.** Who would say that all those things which belong to the imperial and military discipline lack art?
**STRANGER.** But that faculty which by consulting can prudently deliberate with whom war must be waged or peace entered into—shall we think it different from that one, or the same?
**SOCRATES.** Different, if indeed we stand by the previous points.
**STRANGER.** If we follow the reasoning of the previous points, shall we not say that this which consults about war rules over that which carries out war?
**SOCRATES.** That very thing.
**STRANGER.** What faculty, indeed, truly besides that royal discipline of civil affairs, shall we say presides over the most powerful art of all military matters?
**SOCRATES.** Absolutely no other.
**STRANGER.** Therefore, the science of those who lead armies, because it obeys and serves another, we shall by no means place as the civil faculty itself.
**SOCRATES.** It is indeed not fitting.
**STRANGER.** Come now, let us consider the office of judges who justly judge individual things.
**SOCRATES.** Let us consider it.

<margin>That the judiciary is the handmaid of the king.</margin>

**STRANGER.** Does it extend further than that it should consider what is just and what is not concerning all kinds of contracts, and looking to the standard of the laws which the king himself has established, judge concerning individual matters—always using its own virtue, through which it dissolves mutual accusations, transgressing the laws neither by gifts, nor by threats, nor by mercy, nor by hatred, nor by love?
**SOCRATES.** Truly, the office of a judge is nothing other than what has now been said by you.
**STRANGER.** It is established, therefore, that the power of judges is not that royal majesty, but a guardian of the laws and a minister of the king.
**SOCRATES.** It appears so.

<margin>What is civil science.</margin>

**STRANGER.** Whoever considers all the arts we have mentioned must think that none of them is the civil discipline we seek. For it is the office of royal majesty not that it should act itself, but that it should command those who are able to act, and that it should know the empire and power of those things which are greatest in the city, as well as what is decorous, what is opportune, and what is the contrary; but that the other faculties should take up the orders and carry out the mandates.
**SOCRATES.** Excellently.
**STRANGER.** Wherefore those arts which we just recounted, since they are mistresses neither of themselves nor of each other, but each one is intent upon certain proper works, they have deservedly obtained proper names for their proper duties.
**SOCRATES.** It appears so.
**STRANGER.** But that which presides over all these, and has the care of the laws and of all things that are in the city, and weaves all things together, we rightly call civil science, comprehending its faculty by a common appellation.
**SOCRATES.** Entirely.

<margin>What the king's texture is like.</margin>

**STRANGER.** Is it fitting at present to run through this according to the example of the weaver's faculty, after we have revealed all the kinds that are in the city?
**SOCRATES.** Very much so.
**STRANGER.** Next, it seems, it must be declared what the royal fitting-together is, and by what reasoning it complicates and weaves, and what kind of texture it produces for us.
**SOCRATES.** So it is.
**STRANGER.** A matter indeed difficult to demonstrate; but since it has seemed necessary, it seems it must be declared to the best of our ability.
**SOCRATES.** It must be declared entirely.
**STRANGER.** For that a part of virtue differs from a species of virtue can easily be proved by the opinion of many, even against contentious men.
**SOCRATES.** I do not understand.
**STRANGER.** Perhaps you will understand thus. I think you consider fortitude to be some part of virtue.
**SOCRATES.** Fully.
**STRANGER.** And that temperance is different from fortitude, but nevertheless is a part of the same thing of which fortitude is a part.
**SOCRATES.** Yes.
**STRANGER.** Something wonderful must be dared to be stated about these.
**SOCRATES.** What then?
**STRANGER.** That these two, in some way, in many things are very much opposed to each other.
**SOCRATES.** By what reasoning do you say that?
**STRANGER.** This is unheard of, if indeed all the parts of virtue are said to be bound together by mutual friendship.
**SOCRATES.** Indeed.
**STRANGER.** Let us therefore consider diligently whether this is so simple, or whether it has a very great difference of these things in some way in related things.
**SOCRATES.** Certainly. But you should say where it is to be considered.
**STRANGER.** In all things whatever we call beautiful, and we refer them to two species contrary to each other.
**SOCRATES.** Speak more clearly.
**STRANGER.** Speed, whether of bodies, or of minds, or of voices—whether of these themselves, or even of whatever images music or painting expresses by imitating: have you ever praised any of these yourself, or heard another praise them?
**SOCRATES.** What then?
**STRANGER.** Do you remember how those things are praised in each of them?
**SOCRATES.** Not at all.
**STRANGER.** I wish I could explain these in words just as they seem to me.
**SOCRATES.** What forbids it?
**STRANGER.** This seems easy to you, as I see. Therefore let us consider it in contrary kinds. These things happen whenever we admire the speed, vehemence, and sharpness of many things, whether in thought, or body, or even in voice; we are accustomed to use one certain appellation of fortitude in praising.
**SOCRATES.** In what way?

**STRANGER.**

--- Page 173 ---
154                                               Book Sixteen.

**STRANGER.** We say "sharp and brave," "swift and brave," "vehement and brave"; and we are accustomed to praise these natures with the common name of fortitude.
**SOCRATES.** Certainly.
**STRANGER.** For do we not often praise something in many actions when it is done gradually and gently?
**SOCRATES.** Greatly.
**STRANGER.** On the contrary, do we not say this here using praise rather than there?
**SOCRATES.** How?
**STRANGER.** We often call these things quiet and temperate, and we love these things regarding thought; regarding actions, we call them slow and soft; regarding voices, smooth and deep, and every rhythmic and numerous motion, and every muse using an opportune slowness: and to all these we apply the name of moderation, not fortitude.
**SOCRATES.** You speak the truth.
**STRANGER.** But whenever those things do not keep to opportunity, on the contrary, we blame them with changed names.
**SOCRATES.** How?
**STRANGER.** When they become sharper and swifter, and harsher or harder than opportunity requires, we call them insolent, petulant, and furious; but when they become deeper and slower, and softer, we call them timid and inept, and sluggish. And we shall find that almost both these and the nature of temperance and fortitude are contrary, like hostile forms and stirring up sedition among themselves; nor are they ever mixed in actions which are concerned with these, nor moreover do those in whose minds these things are present agree among themselves, but rather disagree, if only we investigate diligently.
**SOCRATES.** Where do you mean?

<margin>What evils arise from a lack of moderation.</margin>

**STRANGER.** I say in all those things which we have reported, and it is consistent that it is so in very many others. For since both, according to the affinity of their nature, partly praise things as their own and proper, and partly reprove things as alien and strange, it happens that in many things they are vehemently opposed to themselves.
**SOCRATES.** They seem so.
**STRANGER.** This altercation of such species is a certain game to some; but in the greatest matters, it becomes the most grave disease of all for cities.
**SOCRATES.** In what kind of matters do you mean?
**STRANGER.** In every constitution of living, as is consistent. For those who excel others in modesty are eager for the tranquility of life, always doing their own things privately, greedy for peace and concord both toward foreigners and toward fellow citizens. And by the excess of this love it happens that, while they are intent upon their own private works, they themselves are secretly rendered unwarlike and enervated, and they soften and effeminate the younger ones by their own example. Whence they are exposed to any invaders whatever, and in a short time they themselves, their children, and the whole country, having gradually lost their liberty, succumb.
**SOCRATES.** You have recounted a very hard and grave disease.
**STRANGER.** But those who, declining more toward fortitude, excessively affect a warlike life, these often incite and exhort their country to war, whence they render very many and powerful nations hostile to their city. Wherefore they either utterly overturn their cities or imprudently bring them into the slavery of enemies.
**SOCRATES.** So also it happens.

<margin>Every science rejects evils and captures useful things.</margin>

**STRANGER.** Therefore, who would deny that in these things these are very much opposed to each other?
**SOCRATES.** No one indeed.
**STRANGER.** Have we not now found what we were seeking from the beginning? Namely, that certain not small parts of virtue are by nature both at war with themselves and make those who have them disagree much among themselves?
**SOCRATES.** It appears so.
**STRANGER.** Let us likewise see this.
**SOCRATES.** What then?
**STRANGER.** Is there any science among those whose action consists in composing, which would voluntarily construct any work of its own, even the most worthless, from evils and goods mixed together? Or rather, does every science always avoid depraved things to the best of its ability, and capture fit and useful things: and from these, having collected into one all things—partly similar, partly dissimilar—blow together one certain power and idea?
**SOCRATES.** That rather.

<margin>Certain offices of royal majesty.</margin>

**STRANGER.** Never, therefore, will the true skill of civil affairs according to nature voluntarily constitute any city from bad and good men. But it will explore each one by discipline and some trial, and the examination having been made, it will afterwards commit that same office to those who can both teach others and obey themselves. Over these it will so diligently preside and command, as the art of weaving presides over the combers and other preparers of wool-working, prescribing such things to each as it thinks will lead to its texture.
**SOCRATES.** Exactly so.
**STRANGER.** By the same reasoning, royal majesty seems to me to preside over those imbuing and educating all others according to the institutes of the laws, permitting them to exercise and teach only that which, pertaining to its own reasoning, induces decorous manners. But those who cannot attain the power of fortitude, or temperance, or of the other virtues, but by the depravity of nature are drawn to impiety, petulance, and injustice, it ejects from the assembly of citizens, and damns with exile, death, and extreme reproach.
**SOCRATES.** So it is handed down in a way.
**STRANGER.** But it subjects the ignorant and small-souled little men to servile ministry.
**SOCRATES.** Very wisely.
**STRANGER.** But the rest, whose geniuses can be raised to a noble habit through discipline, and permit themselves to be tempered together by art, it saves and protects. From these, indeed, which verge more toward fortitude, it judges them to be as the warp <note>original: "staminis vice" — the vertical threads in a loom.</note> because of their solid manners; but those which verge toward modesty, similar to soft and tender material, to have the image of the woof <note>original: "subtegminis" — the horizontal threads in a loom.</note> of a saffron color. Finally, those things which tend in a contrary and different direction of nature, it strives to overcome each other and to weave together in this way.
**SOCRATES.** In what way?
**STRANGER.** First, indeed, according to the reasoning of affinity, it binds the everlasting part of the soul with a divine bond; but after the divine, it binds that which is of an animal nature with human ones.
**SOCRATES.** How is that?
**STRANGER.** Whenever in minds there is a true and stable opinion about the beautiful, the just, the good, and the contrary things of these, I say that it becomes divine in that demonic genus, that is, knowing and happy.
**SOCRATES.** It is indeed fitting.
**STRANGER.** Should we not think that a civil man and a good bringer-of-laws, alone by the royal muse, can infer this into those who are participants of right discipline as is fitting, as far as we have just mentioned?
**SOCRATES.** That also is consistent.
**STRANGER.** But he who cannot do that, O Socrates, ought not to be called by the names which we were just seeking.
**SOCRATES.** Certainly not.
**STRANGER.** Is it not that a brave soul, if it be a participant of such truth, becomes mild, and thus most greatly desires to live and act justly among others? But if it should be altogether expert-less, it slides down to a beastly nature?
**SOCRATES.** Without a doubt.
**STRANGER.** And yet a soul modest by nature, imbued with those opinions, truly becomes temperate and moderated, so that it is useful to the republic. But being void, it rightly reports a shameful infamy of stolidity and sluggishness.
**SOCRATES.** Greatly.
**STRANGER.** Must it not be said that such a complication and bond is never stable, both among the bad themselves and among the good toward the bad? Nor does any science use this for the sake of binding such men by industry?
**SOCRATES.** Entirely.
**STRANGER.** But to those whom nature has gifted with noble manners, and whom custom has educated to the standard of nature, that bond alone is put in through the laws. And in these, the civil art is like a remedy, and by this reasoning that very conciliation of the parts of virtue, contrary by nature and fighting, becomes a certain divine thing.
**SOCRATES.** These things are true.
**STRANGER.** Where this divine bond is established, it is easy both to find and to perfect the human bonds once found.
**SOCRATES.** By what reasoning? And which...

--- Page 174 ---
->Commentary. 155<-

...especially?
**STRANGER.** Those affinities and necessities of children, and those which are in marriages and weddings. For very many people do not correctly couple for the sake of procreating children.
**SOCRATES.** Wherefore?
**STRANGER.** For what purpose is it to recount more diligently in a speech how greedily they pursue riches and power in these things?
**SOCRATES.** None.
**STRANGER.** But it is better to speak of those for whom the race is a care, if perhaps they should do something beyond measure.
**SOCRATES.** It is fair.
**STRANGER.** But they do it by no right reasoning, following present pleasure; and from the fact that they are delighted only by similar things, and by dissimilar things not at all, they excite very much difficulty.
**SOCRATES.** In what way?
**STRANGER.** For indeed, modest men seek manners similar to themselves, and as much as they can, they both marry from such and give their own to such. In the same way, perhaps, that brave genus takes to itself those similar to itself, when on the contrary it ought to be done altogether by both kinds.
**SOCRATES.** How? And for what cause?

<margin>The condition of a brave nature.</margin>

**STRANGER.** Because this is the condition of a brave nature: that if it remains void of temperance through many successions, at first it becomes more robust, but finally, having turned into fury, it fails.
**SOCRATES.** It is consistent.
**STRANGER.** Again, a soul abounding in shame, but everywhere lacking the audacity of fortitude, if it passes through many generations similarly, becomes more sluggish than is proper, and finally is submerged in a certain extreme torpor.
**SOCRATES.** It is established that that also so happens.
**STRANGER.** As we said, we can easily bind both kinds of men with these ligaments if, as we said, both should have the same opinion concerning good and beautiful things. But this is the one and whole work of royal weaving: that it never permits moderated manners to be separate from brave ones, but weaving together both geniuses through the consent of the same opinion, through honors and reproaches, and through alternate marriages, it produces from these a smooth and most excellently cohering web, and to these it should always commit the civil magistracies and duties in common.
**SOCRATES.** In what way?
**STRANGER.** Where the government of one man will suffice, it will place a man endowed with both manners over it. Where there will be need for more, it will mix together some parts of both kinds. For the manners of temperate princes are very cautious and just and salutary; they lack a certain sharp promptness and vehemence suitable for acting.
**SOCRATES.** So it seems concerning these also.
**STRANGER.** But fortitude yields to those in caution and justice; but in acting, it excels very much. Nor can all things be done well in a city privately and publicly unless both these are present.
**SOCRATES.** Certainly not.
**STRANGER.** Let us say then that the end of civil action, woven with a right publication, then stands forth, when conciliation of the geniuses of the brave and the temperate through concord and friendship makes their life common. This texture is surely the most noble of all and the best, protecting and embracing all others besides in the city—both slaves and free men—it comprehends them in this texture and series. And thus it rules and presides over the city, so that it omits nothing of those things which, as far as can be done, make a city blessed.
**SOCRATES.** Truly, O Stranger, you have excellently defined the royal and civil man for us.

# PLATO'S PROTAGORAS, OR, THE SOPHISTS.

## MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT.

There exists among the Greeks a very true saying about Plato: namely, that Phoebus <note>Phoebus: Apollo, the god of light, music, and healing.</note> begat two principal sons, Aesculapius and Plato. Aesculapius, indeed, who might heal bodies; but Plato, who might heal minds. All the Socratics also testify that Socrates was sent by God for the sake of purging minds. But the disease of the mind seems to consist in false opinions and bad manners. So great an evil is not usually brought upon noble minds so easily by others as by the Sophists. Truly, philosophers are those who studiously seek the truth for the sake of the love of the truth itself; but the Sophists affect opinion, similarly for the love of opinion. For these, as if they were merchants and tavern-keepers of disciplines, collect various opinions from everywhere without selection—pertaining both to thinking and to speaking in whatever way it has pleased—which they then sell as if for sale to wealthy adolescents, for the sake of riches and vain glory. Therefore, they never have any concern whether they themselves learn or teach others true or good things, or the contrary; but they both confound and everywhere pour out very many errors daily, having held no reasoning at all of a right elation, provided only they accumulate riches and obtain vulgar glory. Wherefore it is necessary that adolescents and men, who make much of the Sophists because of the opinion of wisdom and the paint of eloquence, daily drink in from them the poisons of false opinions and of the worst manners. Since indeed bad manners both follow false opinions and are easily transfused from greedy and ambitious teachers (who are nevertheless very highly regarded) into disciples. Plato, therefore, having pitied the minds of those so prone and so gravely endangered, very frequently in the person of Socrates detests as much as he can the wicked and poisonous Sophists, so that namely men desirous of learning may cautiously avoid the deceptive songs of the Sirens and the harmful cups of Circe <note>Ficino uses classical myths to warn against the seductive but dangerous teachings of the Sophists.</note>. Nor yet does he thunder against them with manifest invectives, lest either he himself seem led by any perturbation and hatred against them, or they and their followers should retort the poisonous weapons of a most impudent tongue against him. Therefore, partly by irony, partly by laughter, often by jest and play, and more often by a certain honest redargution, he attempts to take away from the Sophists their unmerited authority. That indeed he performs most sharply in the *Sophist*. The same most elegantly in the *Gorgias*. Very facetiously and urbanely in the *Hippias*. Wisely and acutely in the *Euthydemus*. Artfully also in the *Protagoras*, and frequently similarly. Everywhere indeed he introduces the Sophists professing all things, boastful and glorious, moreover rash and greedy. In the beginning of the dispute, indeed, they are fit enough; but gradually they become more inept; and last of all, the most inept, who understand nothing about any matter—especially a graver one—either what it is, or how great, or of what kind. And although they profess all things, he convinces them that they know nothing at all. Thus far let it suffice to have prefaced all Plato's dialogues in which mention of the Sophists is made. Let us proceed now to the *Protagoras*. Socrates learned the amatory art from Diotima the prophetess, through which he knew how to hunt sagaciously through the beauty of bodies, as if through certain tracks, both the beauty of the mind and of the angelic mind, and of God; and he taught that same art everywhere. Plato treated of this art of his, both often elsewhere and especially in the *Symposium* and *Phaedrus*. He signified the same in the beginning of this book. Therefore he added that he loves a man no less than an adolescent. And a little after, that he loves the seniors also more ardently, provided they appear wiser. After these things, while Socrates most artfully warns the adolescent Hippocrates—most greedy for disciplines—not to commit himself rashly to anyone's discipline, he warns not only him but also us that we should have a care of the mind far more than of the body. And let us take care diligently lest we imbue it with harmful disciplines. For indeed, poison is more harmful to the mind than to our body. Soon, as if a painter, he places before our eyes the pride and vanity of the Sophists. He demonstrates also how much a credulous youth admires their pomp and is captured by their allurements. Then he descends to those things which are of the greatest weight for life, and in which the Sophists most greatly glory, seeking indeed concerning all virtue, but especially concerning the principal one—that is, the civil one—through which both the private affair of each one, and the domestic and public affair, is disposed by right reasoning toward the highest good: which Plato seeks in almost all his dialogues as if it were more necessary than the rest; and meanwhile he shows that this is by no means to be sought from the Sophists, but in a certain way from philosophers: who, since they understand the truth and cultivate the good, can doubtless lead to it by a straight path with God as their guide. But let us return now to the Sophist, who, that he cannot hand down such a virtue either by example or teach it by dispute, is plainly perceived from this: that he himself is void of virtue, and does not observe the right order of disputing. For when this Protagoras is questioned by Socrates whether virtue can be taught or not, as one who is ignorant of the true art of differing, he immediately undertakes that he will show that virtue can be taught, before he opens what it is itself or into how many parts it is divided. But Socrates, for the sake of trying the Sophist, argues that it cannot be taught, in almost these words. When it is consulted publicly concerning any work of that art which can be taught by certain teachers, no one is admitted to...

<meta>This page continues a discussion on whether civic virtue can be taught, moving into an allegorical interpretation of the myths of Prometheus and Epimetheus as presented in Plato’s Protagoras and Philebus dialogues.</meta>

# 156 Book Seventeen.

...to the council, except for those who have learned such an art from the teachers themselves and have practiced it. However, when it is deliberated concerning public affairs which pertain to civic virtue, almost everyone is admitted similarly. No one is asked whether, or from whom, or when they received their civic skill, as if everyone understands that it cannot be learned in specific schools. Furthermore, if it were passed from one person to another, the most famous men in this field would often leave this precious thing to their heirs by a kind of hereditary right. To this, Protagoras proves through long, winding stories that virtue can be taught. In these, he recounts certain <term>mysteries</term> <note>In this context, "mysteries" refers to secret or sacred teachings of the ancient Greeks.</note> of the ancients that should be noted. For it is fitting, even though he is a <term>Sophist</term> <note>A paid teacher of philosophy and rhetoric in ancient Greece, often criticized by Plato for prioritizing persuasion over truth.</note>, that he has read some good things; and since he speaks at length in Plato’s writings, he brings forward some useful points.

The <note>original: "theologi veteres"</note> ancient theologians relate that animals once lay hidden under the earth—that is, that the seeds of things existed beforehand in the <term>prime matter</term> <note>The basic, formless substance from which the universe was created.</note> of the world. Furthermore, they say that Jupiter—that is, God the creator of the world—composed animals out of the elements through the "following gods," which is to say, through the stars. They say the gods, using the ministry of <term>demons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, "demons" (daemones) are not evil spirits, but intermediary beings or guardian spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>, armed the animals with instruments and supports necessary for life. This was done in such a way that Prometheus, who signifies the order of the sublime demons, loved humans; while Epimetheus, who represents the army of the inferior demons, supported the brute animals. This was not done without reason: for the higher demons favor the incorporeal and rational nature, while the lower ones favor the corporeal and irrational. Just as much as Epimetheus, belonging to the lower nature, favored the brutes in matters pertaining to the body, so Prometheus and the superior providence seem to have consulted for humans in matters pertaining to the soul. 

For when he granted the faculty of art, he displayed a craftsman who was more skilled than all those things nature had given to the beasts. He received this art itself along with fire from the workshop of Minerva and Vulcan. Minerva contains the genius in art, Vulcan contains the efficacy, and fire is the instrument. These twin deities, Minerva and Vulcan, are first conceived in the very ideas of the arts; then in the virtues of Mercury and Mars; and finally in the demons who govern the arts. And so, from all these, Prometheus—the governor of the rational soul—transferred the industry of art into man. 

Since this was a divine gift, man immediately worshipped God because of his kinship with the superior realm, even before he spoke or practiced any arts. Indeed, because of its wonderful power, a person directs a divine gift toward divine things rather than extending it through human ones. The story that Prometheus was affected by pain because of this gift signifies that our very "demonic" caretaker—in whom emotions can exist—is moved by a kind of mercy toward us. He considers that we, because of the gift of reason either given or rather awakened by him, lead a life on earth that is as much more miserable than that of a beast as it is more anxious and inexplicable. 

Pythagoras, noticing this, placed Epimetheus above Prometheus in this specific regard. This seems in some way similar to the saying: <note>original: "Pœnitet me fecisse hominem"</note> "It repents me that I have made man." <note>A reference to Genesis 6:6.</note> Therefore, remember that man is created here, as in the writings of Moses, on the outside and last. Likewise, in a Mosaic fashion, the world had a beginning. But more on these things elsewhere. 

Through this same Prometheus, it is said in the *Philebus* that the art of discourse was given to us by the gods along with fire. For when one discourses, dividing universals into particulars, he represents the procession of things from higher sources. When he, in turn, resolves particulars back into universals, he signifies the return of things to the higher sources. Where he defines and where he demonstrates, he shows the existence of things—here in themselves, there depending on others. Therefore, the faculty of discourse is a divine gift, as it reflects the divine order of the universe. It is said to be given with fire because fire similarly divides, resolves, defines, and demonstrates. Likewise, the rational faculty, like fire, illuminates the intellect, inflames the will, and raises both to sublime heights. 

As for the tradition that Prometheus could not grant the civic virtue entirely necessary for human safety because such virtue stays with Jupiter, where Prometheus is not permitted to ascend—it is to be understood in this way: the duty of civic virtue is to command not only human affairs, but also the arts, to ordain each one with the other, and finally to direct them all toward the common form of all. This same office belongs to Jupiter himself in the universe, just as the office of civic science appears in the human race. For this reason, it is not without justice that it belongs to Jupiter himself to grant this to us from on high. For universal virtue pertains to the universal providence of Jupiter. The providence of the demons is particular and narrow, and therefore it cannot ascend to the citadel of Jupiter; for a narrower and humbler providence cannot equal the most ample and eminent one. 

Jupiter, therefore, through Mercury—that is, through the angel who interprets the divine will—inscribes in our minds the laws of civic science, which are the decrees of his will looking toward the safety of human society and the human race. I say he inscribes them both from the beginning (which the *Timaeus* clearly teaches) and daily through the angels who interpret the divine will to us. From this, an internal judge presides over us: the unquenchable light of reason, the right examination of true and false and of good and evil, and the unavoidable sting of conscience. Through this law infused into everyone, God directs all people toward the common good, just as he raises all flames toward the heavens by their lightness. From this innate law, the written law then takes its origin. Plato revealed this at the very beginning of the book of *Laws*, saying that laws had their beginning not from man, but from God himself. 

But to return to the present dialogue: he adds that Jupiter, through Mercury, established a law by which all are commanded to be participants in civility, since this alone is the bond of the city. He says that he sent down from heaven to all people the city which consists of justice and <term>shame</term> <note>The Latin 'pudor' implies a sense of moral decency, respect, and the capacity to feel healthy shame at wrongdoing.</note>. This was done with the agreement that whoever was hereafter found entirely devoid of this virtue should be punished with the ultimate penalty as a plague to the city. What he first called shame, he then named temperance. For innate shame is the foundation of temperance. Temperance moderates each citizen's own emotions and composes their gestures. Justice, however, directs each person's actions toward others. Remember that "civility" in a private person is satisfied with almost these two things, but in a public person, according to Plato’s mind, prudence must be added to them. And that would be almost enough in peace; but in war, add fortitude, and thus the description of civility will be complete. 

After this, Protagoras confirms from the common opinion of men that everyone ought to be participants in this virtue, because if someone were to openly admit their own injustice, they would be considered insane by the public. It is as if everyone thinks common justice is so necessary to the city that even if one does not have it, they ought at least to pretend to have it. 

Since he has shown so far that civic virtue is the most necessary of all for everyone, and that a certain inclination, or fuel and seed of it, was infused into us by God from the beginning, he next proceeds to demonstrate that civic virtue—and indeed others (for it encompasses them all)—cannot obtain a perfect and firm habit by nature or chance, but that its habit is acquired only by doctrine and custom. For this, he first brings a reason showing that men are not accustomed to ever approve or disapprove of anyone for things that happen by nature or chance; but they always praise or blame actions of virtue or vice. 

Then he arranges the education of childhood and adolescence under domestic tutors, grammarians, musicians, gymnasts, and laws in a certain long order, showing that the whole institution of life strives with all its might toward this goal: that vices be avoided and virtues possessed. It is as if neither vices nor virtues arise by fortune or fate, but by choice and exercise. 

Meanwhile, he touches upon the opinion of the ancients regarding the punishment of vices, which is worthy of consideration: namely, that no one should be punished *because* they have sinned, but rather so that they themselves may not sin further, or others by their example. He then responds to those objections Socrates had raised. 

We, however, out of everything that has been disputed so far, will hold that golden opinion of the ancients deep in our minds. First, that God himself provides for and consults for our life and safety in every way and from every side. Second, that civic virtue is a divine gift, lest anyone should happen to trust that they will govern the republic rightly and happily without divine grace. For Plato, confirming this in the *Laws* and elsewhere, says: just as many beasts cannot be led rightly by one of their own unless under a human shepherd, so many men cannot be led happily by one king unless that one is also ruled by God. Therefore, he proves in the *Theages* and *Meno* that the faculty of ruling is held from nowhere else but God. As for what the sophist Protagoras wants, he can see to that himself. 

Finally, let us remember how necessary is that inviolable justice sent from heaven, if those voices of the ancients continually ring in our ears: "Mortals were once miserable before civility was sent from heaven; they could not live apart without being torn apart everywhere by wild beasts, nor could they gather together without tearing each other apart." Therefore, justice alone finally provided the safety for us which all the arts together could not provide. 

After these things, Socrates—lest the Sophist be admired by the listeners because of some good things he had recounted from others—makes him an object of ridicule to those present through a certain ironic, polite, and skillful method of refutation. For after Protagoras had spoken so magnificently about virtue, Socrates asks whether there is only one virtue or not. Furthermore, if there are many, whether they are parts of one or not. Again, if they are parts, are they similar to each other and to the whole, or dissimilar on both sides? To these questions, Protagoras does not know how to respond correctly, nor how to define or divide the virtues, nor to distinguish in what way they are similar and in what way dissimilar—and what is most shameful in disputing, he cannot avoid being easily led to the point where he often [contradicts] himself.

<summary>This page explores the myth of Prometheus and Epimetheus to explain the origins of human skill and civic virtue, arguing that while technical arts come from lower divine orders, true justice and social harmony are unique gifts directly from Jupiter (God). It concludes by transitioning to Socrates's logical critique of the Sophist Protagoras's inconsistent definitions of virtue.</summary>

Protagoras, or, the Sophists. 157

himself. At last, when Protagoras began to evade the questions because of his ignorance in responding, Socrates pretended he was going to leave, and the Sophist was called back to the discussion by the listeners. In this altercation, first the superstitious curiosity concerning words of Prodicus the Sophist is demonstrated; then the somewhat timid ostentation of Hippias the Sophist in speaking is shown. Finally, Protagoras, called back to the dispute, digresses quite inappropriately and ineptly into songs and poetry, questioning Socrates about a certain opinion of the poet Simonides. Socrates soon convicts him of not understanding this himself, as Socrates explains Simonides’ mind, as if he had said that it is indeed difficult for a man to *become* good, but impossible to *remain* so. Here you will hear that the wisdom of the ancients was content with as few words as possible, and that to be able to embrace many things in a few words is the work of an absolutely learned man. Likewise, that no one commits bad and disgraceful things willingly, but through ignorance. Finally, where the discussion is carried out in a dialectical manner <note>A method of philosophical argument involving question and answer.</note>, poetic matters are to be rejected. After these acts, the Sophist evades again and is barely called back by those present. Then Socrates returns to the prior dispute concerning virtue: whether there are many parts of one virtue, and in what relation they stand to each other. Protagoras, however, slips again, affirming elsewhere that the virtues are very similar to each other, which he had not admitted in previous parts; likewise, he separates fortitude very far from the others, agreeing that men can be brave without prudence and the other virtues. In this matter, he is then forced to contradict himself and to confess that not only fortitude, but no virtues at all can exist without prudence. Then indeed, many things are treated concerning good and evil. For prudence is the science of choosing the good and avoiding the evil. It is debated, however, whether good and evil are exactly the same as pleasure and pain. That is neither entirely affirmed nor clearly denied. For concerning this in the *Gorgias*, *Philebus*, and elsewhere, it is proved overall that prudence itself—in which the knowledge of the end of life and the choice of the ways conducive to this end consist—is the prince and leader of the moral virtues. This is asserted to such an extent that the virtues seem to be like sciences (that is, types of prudence), while vices seem to be types of ignorance (that is, imprudence). It is then added that all sins proceed from ignorance, and that no one will ever choose evils unless deceived by the image of good; nor will they flee from goods unless terrified by some image of evil. But if someone should say that a man discerning goods and evils nonetheless turns away from the former and toward the latter because he is overcome by pleasure or some other emotion of the senses, Socrates will deny it. He asserts that the very thing said to be "overcome by emotion" is nothing other than ignorance, and that knowledge of all things within and around us is most powerful and can never be overcome by anything. Finally, he concludes that science contributes most—indeed, everything—to virtue and happiness, while ignorance contributes similarly to their opposites. And again he rebukes Protagoras, because he both contradicted himself and used a backwards order. For before he defined what virtue is, he attempted to divide it and disputed whether it could be taught. Socrates even simulates that he himself has been led into a contradiction, only because he followed the wandering Sophist; and he warns that we should imitate the providence of Prometheus rather than the haste of Epimetheus in all our life to the best of our power.
