**FRIEND, SOCRATES, HIPPOCRATES, PROTAGORAS, ALCIBIADES, CALLIAS, CRITIAS, PRODICUS, HIPPIAS.**

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue.</margin>

**FRIEND.** From where, O Socrates, are you appearing? Is it perhaps that you are returning from that hunt to which the beauty of Alcibiades <note>A prominent and beautiful Athenian statesman and general, known for his close relationship with Socrates.</note> is accustomed to provoke you? For to me, as I was watching lately, he seemed a beautiful man—a man now, I say, who could certainly be counted among us, seeing as a thick down already creeps over his cheeks.
**SOCRATES.** So be it, what of it? Do you not approve of Homer, who says the most pleasing age is that of the first down? That is the age Alcibiades is now leading.
**FRIEND.** But are you coming from him now? And how is the young man disposed toward you now?
**SOCRATES.** Well indeed; he seemed especially so to me today, for he often came to my aid in speaking today, and I am coming from him now. And I will tell you something wonderful: I was hardly looking at him while he was present, and turning my mind elsewhere, I scarcely noticed him.
**FRIEND.** What was so great that it turned you away from him? For no one of our citizens more shapely could have been present.
**SOCRATES.** On the contrary, someone much more beautiful was present.
**FRIEND.** What are you saying? A citizen or a stranger?
**SOCRATES.** A stranger.
**FRIEND.** From where?
**SOCRATES.** From Abdera.
**FRIEND.** Did that stranger seem to you endowed with such a remarkable form that he seemed more beautiful to you than the son of Clinias <note>Alcibiades.</note>?
**SOCRATES.** What prevents it, O blessed one, from that which is wiser being also more beautiful?
**FRIEND.** Are you perhaps coming from a conversation with some wise man?
**SOCRATES.** From the wisest indeed of all the men of our age, if indeed Protagoras seems to you to be the wisest of all others.
**FRIEND.** Look what you are saying! Has Protagoras arrived here?
**SOCRATES.** The day before yesterday.
**FRIEND.** And have you been with him just now?
**SOCRATES.** Just now, and I spoke many things, and also heard many things.
**FRIEND.** Why do you not recount those to us? Unless something prevents it, you may sit here. This boy will give up his seat for you.
**SOCRATES.** I will indeed recount them, and I will have gratitude besides if you listen.
**FRIEND.** And we to you, if you speak.
**SOCRATES.** The gratitude will therefore be double. Listen then. Last night, before the rising of light, Hippocrates the son of Apollodorus, brother of Phason, pounded on my door violently with his staff. And when someone had opened the door, he suddenly entered in haste and crying with a loud voice: "Are you sleeping, O Socrates, or are you awake?" But I, recognizing his voice, said: "This is Hippocrates. O Hippocrates, is there any news?" "Nothing," he said, "except I come to bring a welcome message." "Excellent," I said. "But what is it? What cause has brought you here?" "Protagoras has come," he said, "and is staying near me." Then I said: "He arrived some time ago; have you only just heard?" "Yesterday evening indeed," he said. And grasping a footstool in the darkness, he sat down at my feet and added: "Yesterday evening, very late, having returned from Oenoe—for my boy Satyrus had fled—and when I wanted to signal to you that I was pursuing him, I forgot because something else intervened. But when I had come and we had dined and wanted to give ourselves to sleep, then for the first time my brother announced that Protagoras had come. Immediately I tried to hasten to you, but the unseasonable night held me back. But having woken from sleep and been relieved of labor, I arrived here to you soon." But I, noticing the man's high-mindedness and amazement, said: "What is this to you? Does Protagoras do you any injury?" Then he, smiling, said: "Certainly, because he alone is wise, but does not make me wise."
**SOCRATES.** Nay, surely he will also make you wise, if you persuade him with an offered fee.
**HIPPOCRATES.** O Jupiter and the other gods! I would spare neither my own things nor those of my friends, if only I were confident that I would attain that. And for that reason I come to you now, so that you may intercede with him for me. For I am both younger, and I have never seen or heard Protagoras, for I was a boy when he first arrived here. All men indeed praise this man, O Socrates, and say he is most wise in speaking. But why do we not hasten to him, so that we may meet him at home? He is staying, as I heard, at the house of Callias son of Hippocinus. Let us go now.
**SOCRATES.** Not yet, O good man, I say, must we go there. For it is still very early morning. But let us go to the courtyard, where we will walk until dawn breaks; afterward we will go to Protagoras himself. For indeed Protagoras is at home most of the time. Therefore be confident, for we will find him at home. With these words, we rose and went into the courtyard. And wanting myself to make a trial of his confidence, I looked at him diligently and questioned him thus: "Come, tell me, O Hippocrates, you wish to go to Protagoras now, intending to give him a fee for yourself? To what kind of man are you going? And what kind of man are you yourself going to turn out to be from him? Just as if you wished to go to Hippocrates...

...the namesake, that Hippocrates of Cos born of the stock of Aesculapius <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, to pay him a fee for yourself, and someone asked: "Tell me, O Hippocrates, you will give a fee to Hippocrates? To what kind of man, and for what reason?" What would you answer?
**HIPPOCRATES.** As to a physician.
**SOCRATES.** And what would you yourself become, that is, for what purpose?
**HIPPOCRATES.** I would turn out to be a physician.
**SOCRATES.** But if you were to go to either Polyclitus of Argos or Phidias of Athens <note>Famous Greek sculptors.</note> with a fee offered to them for yourself, and someone inquired: "To what kind of men and for what reason are we proceeding to hire them? What do you offer? What do you say to these things?"
**HIPPOCRATES.** As to sculptors.
**SOCRATES.** And what kind of man would you become?
**HIPPOCRATES.** A sculptor, obviously.
**SOCRATES.** Attend, I pray: you and I are now proceeding to Protagoras, and we are prepared to give money on your behalf, if only our money will suffice and if it is permitted to obtain it; if not, we will expend the money of our friends besides. If someone, therefore, asks us as we are hastening so much to these things: "Tell me, I pray, O Socrates and Hippocrates, to what kind of man and for what reason do you intend to give money to Protagoras?" What would we answer him? What name of Protagoras have we most especially heard? They call Phidias a sculptor. They call Homer a poet. But Protagoras—what do they call him?
**HIPPOCRATES.** A Sophist, O Socrates; they call this man a Sophist.
**SOCRATES.** Therefore we are proceeding to hire him as a Sophist?
**HIPPOCRATES.** Exactly.
**SOCRATES.** If anyone should ask you with what mind and what kind of person you yourself are going to Protagoras to become, what would you say to him? Here Hippocrates blushed, for now the dawn had shone a little, so that his face could be seen; he answered then: "As the above things conclude, surely as if I were going to become a Sophist myself."
**SOCRATES.** But are you not ashamed, by the gods, to present yourself as a Sophist among the Greeks?
**HIPPOCRATES.** Greatly, O Socrates, if I must bring forth what I feel.
**SOCRATES.** But look, O Hippocrates, lest perhaps this study of yours in the Protagorean art tends elsewhere than toward your becoming a Sophist. Just as you frequented the school of the grammarian, the cithara-player, and the gymnast, not for the sake of practicing the art itself, but rather with a certain greed for learning, as befits a private and free man.
**HIPPOCRATES.** Such entirely seems to be the reason for my study with Protagoras.
**SOCRATES.** Do you know what you are about to do now? Or does it escape you?
**HIPPOCRATES.** Concerning what matter?
**SOCRATES.** You are about to commit the care of your soul to a man who is, as you say, a Sophist. But if you know what a Sophist is, I shall wonder greatly. But if you are ignorant, you do not know what kind of thing that is—whether good or bad—to which you strive to devote your effort.
**HIPPOCRATES.** I think I certainly know.
**SOCRATES.** Tell me then, what do you think a Sophist is?
**HIPPOCRATES.** I think he is, as the name signifies, one who understands matters pertaining to wisdom.
**SOCRATES.** One can also say the same about painters and craftsmen: that they are those who understand matters pertaining to wisdom. But if someone asked about painters, "To the wisdom of which things?" we would surely answer, "To the wisdom of making images," and similarly about the others. And if we were asked in the same way about a Sophist, what kind of wisdom would we answer his is? Of what art is he a teacher?
**HIPPOCRATES.** A teacher, O Socrates, of eloquence and the faculty of speaking.
**SOCRATES.** Truly, perhaps we would say that, yet not sufficiently. For that answer requires another question: about what things does a Sophist make men skilled in speaking? A cithara-player makes them fit for speaking about the same things in which he also educates them—namely, in striking the cithara, does he not?
**HIPPOCRATES.** Certainly.
**SOCRATES.** But what faculty of speaking does a Sophist provide? About what things? It is clear that it is about those things which he understands.
**HIPPOCRATES.** That is indeed likely.
**SOCRATES.** What then is that which the Sophist himself understands and teaches others?
**HIPPOCRATES.** By Hercules, I do not know.
**SOCRATES.** Do you not see to what danger you subject your soul? If you were going to subject your body to the same danger, whereby it could turn for the better or for the worse, would you not first commit it to someone about to make so much trial of the danger only after you had diligently considered whether it should be committed or not? Would you not have consulted friends and relatives for a long time about this very thing? But since you value your soul more than your body, and from its either sickness or health all your affairs happen to be either ill or well, have you consulted either father, or brother, or any of us who are your friends and intimates, whether your soul should be committed to this stranger or not? But since you heard of his arrival yesterday evening, you hasten to him very early in the morning, with no counsel taken about this, whether you ought to trust yourself to him or not. Indeed, you are prepared to expend all your own money and that of your friends, as if you already knew it was entirely necessary to adhere to Protagoras, whom you have neither seen, as you say, nor spoken to. You call him a Sophist, and you clearly do not know what a Sophist is, to whom you are about to give yourself.
**HIPPOCRATES.** You seem to speak the truth, O Socrates.
**SOCRATES.** Is not a Sophist, O Hippocrates, a kind of merchant and a huckster of certain provisions by which the soul is nourished?
**HIPPOCRATES.** He certainly seems so to me; but by what things is the soul nourished?
**SOCRATES.** By teachings. But we must be careful, O friend, lest while the Sophist praises what he sells, he deceives us, as do those who sell feasts for the body, merchants and hucksters. They indeed praise all their own things, nor do they understand whether those things they sell are healthy or harmful to the body, and those who buy are also ignorant of it, unless perhaps one of them is a physician or a gymnast. In no other way do those who carry various teachings for sale through cities and hawk them to those who desire to buy, praise all things they sell. And perhaps some of them are often ignorant of what is useful for the soul and what is useless from these things they sell; similarly those who buy from them, unless one of them is a physician of the soul. If therefore you yourself understand what from these things is beneficial and what is harmful, you can safely buy teachings both from Protagoras and from anyone else. Otherwise take care, O blessed youth, lest you lead what is most dear to you into the greatest danger of loss. 

<margin>The danger in teachings is far more serious than in buying foods.</margin>

For the danger in teachings is far more serious than in buying foods. For he who buys eatables and drinkables from a huckster or merchant can, before he consumes them, carry them home in certain other vessels, and there, having deposited them, examine them diligently, and having called in someone skilled in these things, deliberate what should be eaten or drunk, and what not, how much, and when; wherefore the danger in buying is not heavy. But teachings cannot be transferred into another vessel, but it is necessary that he who buys them takes them into his soul, and having left the price, he has them, carrying them within himself, either already polluted or moved toward better things. Let us therefore discuss these things with those older than both of us, for we are younger than the judgment of so great a matter requires. For the present, however, let us proceed where we began, and let us hear this man; having heard him, we will communicate with others. For not only Protagoras is present there, but also Hippias of Elis, and Prodicus, as I think, of Chios, and very many other men, and quite wise. These things pleased us, and we proceeded. And having entered the vestibule, we treated a certain discourse which we had by chance fallen into while walking. Lest it be left imperfect, we progressed so far talking in the vestibule until we agreed...

...in our dispute. I think a certain eunuch janitor heard us, but because of the frequency of Sophists coming there, he was angry at those arriving. We knocked; he opened. When he saw us, he said: "There are some people; he has no leisure." And at the same time, leaning with both hands, he closed the door. We knocked again, but he, with the doors closed, said: "Did you not hear that he has no leisure?" "O good man," I said, "we have not come to Callias, nor are we Sophists; but be confident, we have need of Protagoras, we desire to see him." With this announced, he at last barely opened the doors. Having entered, we found Protagoras walking in the vestibule of the portico. Many followed him: on this side indeed Callias son of Hipponicus, and his half-brother Paralus son of Pericles, and Charmides son of Glaucon; on the other side indeed the other son of Pericles, Xanthippus, and Philippides son of Philomelus, and Antimirus of Mende, who was considered the most distinguished among all Protagoras’ listeners, and was learning that faculty with the intention that he himself would one day profess the same as a Sophist. Behind them, moreover, others followed listening to Protagoras, most of whom seemed to be strangers, whom he gathers from each city through which he wanders, charming them with his voice like a certain Orpheus, and alluring them. They, indeed, enchanted by his voice, follow everywhere. Some of our own people were also present in that chorus. When I contemplated this chorus, its order delighted me wonderfully. For with diligent caution, each one observed lest they should precede Protagoras by a step. But when he turned his foot back, the follower-listeners quite aptly and divided into a circle on both sides, yielded so that they were always behind him. After him I saw—to speak in the words of Homer—Hippias of Elis sitting on a throne in the opposite vestibule of the portico. Around him, some sat on benches: Eryximachus son of Acumenus, and Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian, Andro son of Androtion, and some others, partly citizens, partly also strangers: who seemed to be questioning Hippias about sublime things of nature and the movements of the stars; he, however, sitting on his throne, unraveled the doubts for each. I saw besides Tantalus <note>A mythological reference; here likely referring to Prodicus, who is described as being tucked away.</note>. Furthermore, Prodicus of Chios was present, who had withdrawn into a certain small room, which Hipponicus had previously used as a storehouse; but so that the whole crowd of flocking guests might be received, Callias had given that corner also for the guests to inhabit, having cleared out the provisions. Prodicus, therefore, wrapped in shaggy blankets—and indeed many, as it seemed—was still reclining there. On the seats nearest to him sat Pausanias of Cerameis, and near him a certain youth endowed with an excellent genius, as it seemed to me, and a noble disposition, Agathon by name as I heard; nor ought it to seem strange if he were from the loves of Pausanias. Both Adeimantuses were also there, both the son of Cepis and the son of Leucolophus, and very many others. What they were debating among themselves I could not sufficiently perceive from outside, although I vehemently desired to hear Prodicus. For he seems to me to be a most wise and divine man, but a certain sound from the gravity of his own voice, continuously rolling under the vault, confused individual words. Immediately after our entry, Alcibiades entered—as you say, beautiful, and I believe it—and Critias son of Callaeschrus. But when we had entered and discussed some things together, and had contemplated those spectacles, we approached Protagoras. "Then, O Protagoras," I said, "for a certain cause I and Hippocrates have come here to you."
**PROTAGORAS.** Do you wish to speak with me privately from the others? Or in the presence of everyone?
**SOCRATES.** It is all the same to us, but when you have heard for what cause we have come, you yourself will see.
**PROTAGORAS.** What is that, then, for the sake of which you have arrived here?
**SOCRATES.** Hippocrates, this fellow-citizen of ours, son of Apollodorus, is sprung from a noble and happy race. He himself contends with his equals concerning virtue, stirred by emulation, and he desires to turn out an illustrious man in the republic, and he hopes he will be master of this matter by your company. See whether it befits us to consult about this alone with you, or in the presence of others.

<margin>Defense of the Sophistic art.</margin>

**PROTAGORAS.** You counsel me rightly, O Socrates, for a stranger needs prudent caution, who, traveling through great cities, persuades famous youths everywhere that they should adhere to you alone, having left the company of all others, both their own and foreigners, both old and young, as if they were going to turn out superior to all others by his company; for many envies, ill-wills, and snares rise up against him. 

<margin>Apparent reasons.</margin>

But I say that the Sophistic art is ancient, but the ancient men skilled in it, fearing this envy and offense, disguised it under the appearance of other arts: partly indeed under the appearance of poems, as Homer did, and Hesiod, and Simonides; partly indeed under the name of sacred things and oracles, as Orpheus and Musaeus and also their followers. I have heard besides that some called that art "gymnastics," which Iccus of Tarentum seems to have done, and he who still survives, a Sophist inferior to none, Herodicus of Selymbria, who draws his genus by ancient origin from the Megarians. Pythodes furthermore, a most learned Sophist of Chios, and very many others, concealed the Sophistic faculty under the veil of the musical art. All these, as has been said, both to avoid envy vehemently disguised the name, and concealed the Sophistic art under the pretext of other arts. But I disagree with all these in this, nor do I think those trickeries are conducive. For I do not think they become masters of their wish. For the prominent men in the city understand all such dissimulations. The common people, however, in a way do not notice, but praise those things which they themselves proclaim. But that study of escaping, when it does not attain what it attempts, indicates an inert person fleeing, and makes men who notice more hostile. For they think that besides other things, this man is a crafty deceiver; I, therefore, have entered upon a certain contrary way. I confess that I am a Sophist, and teach others, and I think that by this ingenuous confession, envy is more safely avoided than by that dissimulation. I have looked out for myself by other reasons besides, so that I have suffered nothing of evil, God helping, on account of the profession of Sophistry, although I have practiced this faculty for many years. I am indeed great in age, and I could be the father in age of any of you. Wherefore it will be most pleasing to me if you wish to speak about these things with me, while all who are within are listening. Here I, having suspected that he wanted to show off and boast before Prodicus and Hippias, because we had set out to hear him inflamed by greed for his wisdom, said: "Why do we not call Prodicus and Hippias, and those who accompany them, here, so that they also may hear us?"
**PROTAGORAS.** Let us call them.
**CALLIAS.** "Do you wish then," Callias said, "that we prepare seats here, so that you may dispute sitting?" We all consented. Joyful, all of us—as we were about to hear wise men—each one took hold of benches and quickly prepared them next to Hippias. For there were very many benches there. There Callias and Alcibiades come, bringing Prodicus and those who were with him...

...bringing them with them. After we had all sat down, Protagoras said: "Repeat, O Socrates, in the presence of these people, what you were entreating of me a little while ago for this youth." "Let us therefore," I said, "use the same beginning as above. Hippocrates here vehemently desires to adhere to you; but he would gladly hear what he is going to carry away from this company of yours." This was our speech.
**PROTAGORAS.** O youth, you will never approach me without going away more learned, and each day you will profit more and more.
**SOCRATES.** This is no wonder, O Protagoras; for so it is fitting: since even you, being so great in age and so wise, if you should learn things you do not know from someone, would go away superior. But indeed we do not seek only that. But just as if this Hippocrates, having changed his mind, desired to spend time with this youth—recently here indeed, Zeuxippus son of Heraclentus—and having approached him in the same way as now you, should hear from him the same things as from you, namely that he would profit beautifully with him daily: if he should ask Zeuxippus in what thing most especially he was going to profit, he would surely answer: in the art of painting. And if he should meet Orthagoras the Theban, and hear from him the same things he heard from you, and should inquire of him in what thing he would become superior daily by spending time with him in the sound of the pipes, Orthagoras would answer. In the same way, you also answer this youth and me asking on his behalf. For you say that Hippocrates, if indeed he adheres to Protagoras, will be more learned daily: in what thing, finally? Declare it.
**PROTAGORAS.** You question cleverly indeed, O Socrates; and I rejoice to answer those who question properly. Hippocrates indeed, if he spends time with me, will not fall into that error into which he would undoubtedly have fallen if he had spent time with other Sophists. 

<margin>What the Sophist promises to teach.</margin>

For others harm youths. For they drag back the unwilling to those arts which they had even fled: teaching arithmetic, astronomy, geometry, and music. (And looking at Hippias at the same time, he added:) But whoever comes to me will learn only that for the sake of which he came: such a discipline is prudent deliberation in domestic and public affairs, whereby one both governs his home rightly and transacts the business of the city best, both by speaking and by acting.
**SOCRATES.** I understand what you want, Protagoras; for you seem to me to say "civil art," and to promise how they may turn out as good men and citizens.
**PROTAGORAS.** This is the very thing, O Socrates, which you proclaim everywhere.
**SOCRATES.** O what a most noble craft you have found, if only you have found it! Surely nothing else should be brought forth to you than what I feel. I had indeed thought, O Protagoras, that this could not be taught. Yet I cannot fail to trust you when you assert it. 

<margin>It is shown by trial that virtue can be taught.</margin>

But for what cause I should think it can neither be taught nor passed on by men in turn, it is fair, I think, that I should say. Indeed, as the rest of the Greeks testify, I call the Athenians wise men. I see therefore, when the city, having gathered an assembly, wants to deliberate something about building, that the counsel of builders is sought concerning the buildings; and when concerning the manufacture of ships, the ship-builders are summoned. They also do the same in all other things which they think can be taught and learned. But if anyone else proceeds to consult about the work of that art, whom they think to be unskilled in that art—though he be most distinguished in other things, most wealthy and most noble—they nevertheless admit him no more, but hiss him and hoot him off, until either he himself, deterred by the tumult, ceases from speaking, or the archers, at the command of the magistrates, either drag him out immediately or carry him away. This, therefore, they are accustomed to observe in all things pertaining to the perception of the arts. But when it is to be consulted concerning the public administration of the city, the architect consults equally with the blacksmith, equally also the cobbler, the merchant, the sailor, the rich, the poor, the ignoble, the noble; nor does any of these hiss anyone off, as happened in the above things, as if one who has nowhere learned it, and perceives it with no teacher, should dare to consult. It is further established that they do not think it can be taught. Not only is this seen publicly, but also privately. For those who excel in civil wisdom are unable to pour this virtue into another. Indeed Pericles, the father of these youths, diligently educated them in those things which are learned under a master; but in those things in which he himself is wise, neither does he educate them himself, nor does he commit them to any other to be educated, but they wander about everywhere as if grazing without a shepherd, if perhaps by some chance they might fall into this virtue. The same Pericles, when he was the tutor of Clinias, the younger brother of this Alcibiades, and feared for him from Alcibiades lest perhaps he should be polluted by his company, separated them and educated Clinias at the house of Ariphron; but before six months had passed from then, he returned him to him, as he did not know what he should do. I could commemorate many others besides, who although they were excellent men in the republic, yet never taught any of their relatives or strangers. Indeed, O Protagoras, while I notice these things, I distrust that virtue can be taught. On the contrary, while I hear you asserting these things, I am forced to change my opinion, and I think what you say should by no means be despised, considering that you are both skilled in many things, and have both learned most things and found them out through yourself. Therefore, if you can show us more clearly that virtue is acquired by some teaching, show it I pray, and do not be envious.
**PROTAGORAS.** I will not be envious, O Socrates. But shall I, as an elder to younger men, recount a story <note>original: "fabulam"; often translated as "myth."</note>? Or shall I proceed by disputing? Then indeed most of those sitting by allowed him to speak in whichever way he preferred. 

<margin>This story strives to demonstrate that virtue is taught.</margin>

**PROTAGORAS.** I think a story will be more pleasing to you. Once upon a time, the gods alone existed, but no races of mortals; but when the fatal time of generation came, the gods themselves fashioned them in the bowels of the earth out of fire and earth, with the intervention of those things which are mixed with fire and earth. But when they wanted to bring them forth into the light, they commanded Prometheus and Epimetheus to distribute to each its powers and ornament, as was fitting. Epimetheus, therefore, asked Prometheus that he might grant to him the office of that distribution, and that Prometheus should present himself as the spectator of the distribution. Prometheus consented. He distributed: to some therefore he gave strength without speed, to some weaker ones he granted velocity; he armed some, but for the unarmed he devised some other contrivance for safety. For those whom he had enclosed in a small body, he commanded to be raised partly through the air with wings, partly to creep through the earth. But those whom he had increased into a large mass, he fortified by that very mass for their safety. And similarly in the other things, equaling them, he partitioned each, so that no genus should be entirely obscured. After he so instructed them, lest they perish by mutual destruction, he began to devise escapes by what reasoning they might most easily lead their life under the open sky. Therefore he clothed them either with very thick hair and bristles or with very hard skins, by which they might easily tolerate both the intemperance of winter and of summer, and he prepared for them natural bedding from the same things, and lairs; and to their feet he added soles, claws, bristles, and likewise skins as hard as possible. Then he supplied some with one food, others with another: to some herbs from the earth, to some the fruits of trees, roots, to others...

# Protagoras, Or, the Sophists. 161

others. Nor were those lacking to whom he gave food through mutual slaughter. But he made the predatory animals somewhat sterile, while he made those subject to their ferocity prolific, so that in this way their kind might be preserved. Now, since Epimetheus <note>The name Epimetheus means "afterthought"; he is the brother of Prometheus ("forethought").</note> was not entirely wise, he ignorantly poured out all the strengths upon the beasts (and did not notice that nothing would remain for him from such a great distribution with which to then gift our race). Therefore, he was in doubt as to where he should turn. While he was doubting, Prometheus stood by as a spectator of that partition, and saw that the other animals were each supported by their own gifts and filled with good things, but man was naked, unarmed, without shoes, and without bedding. Now the fatal day itself was imminent, which forced man to go out from the earth into the light. And since Prometheus, consulting another way for human safety, could not find one, he stole the skilled wisdom of Vulcan <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, god of fire and smithing.</note> and Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, goddess of wisdom and war.</note> together with fire. For it was not possible for anyone to obtain or even use it without fire. He thus brought it to the human race, and so we attained the wisdom that provides for life. 

Yet men still lacked political wisdom. For that was with Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods.</note>, whose citadel Prometheus was not yet allowed to ascend; the terrifying guards standing around the citadel of Jupiter deterred Prometheus. However, having secretly entered the common workshop of Vulcan and Minerva in which the arts were cultivated, he stole the fiery art of Vulcan and the other of Minerva, and handed them to man, by which the faculty of living was obtained. But Prometheus, as it is said, paid the penalty for the theft because of Epimetheus <note>Because Epimetheus’s poor planning forced the theft.</note>. Since, truly, man was made a sharer of a divine lot, he alone because of this kinship thought at first that there were gods, and dedicated altars and statues to them. Then he distinguished voice and words articulately by art, constructed houses, made clothes and shoes, worked on blankets, and gathered food from the earth. 

Thus men, constituted from the beginning, wandered scattered and lived apart, for they had not yet built cities. Therefore, since they were weaker, they were slaughtered everywhere by wild beasts. For the faculty of the arts was sufficient for obtaining food, but not at all for fighting against fierce beasts. For they were devoid of political skill, of which military matters are a certain part. Therefore, so that they might fortify themselves against that plague, they were gathered together in built cities. But once gathered, they injured one another, inasmuch as they lacked political art; therefore, being dispersed again, they were torn apart by beasts. But Jupiter, consulting for human safety, sent Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes, the messenger god.</note> to bring shame and justice to the assemblies of men, so that these two things might adorn cities and bind them together, and reconcile citizens through mutual goodwill. 

Therefore, Mercury asked under what condition he should hand over shame and justice to men. "Shall I distribute these," he said, "as the arts were distributed?" For they were distributed in such a way that one man skilled in the art of medicine suffices for many unlearned ones, and others similarly. "Shall I give shame and justice to men in this way? Or shall I implant them in all?" "In all," Jupiter replied: "let all indeed be sharers of these: for no cities would stand if only a few, as with the other arts, were sharers of these. Furthermore, establish a law in my name, that whoever is entirely devoid of either justice or shame should be put to death as a plague of the city." For this reason, O Socrates, both all others and the Athenians, whenever a speech is to be held about

<margin>These [symbol] are from the Greek.</margin>

architecture or some other craftsmanship, they call on a few for advice and exclude the rest as unlearned, as you say and I approve. But as often as a council is entered upon regarding civil administration, which consists of the virtues of temperance and justice, they rightly admit everyone, since it is necessary that everyone be a sharer of this virtue, or no cities would exist. This, O Socrates, is the cause of that which was doubted. But lest you suspect you are being deceived, take this conjecture in addition: namely, that all mortals think every mortal is a sharer of this civil virtue, specifically of temperance and justice. For in the other faculties, as you say, if someone boasts—suppose he says he is an excellent flute player, when he is actually unlearned in it—those hearing him either laugh or are indignant. His relatives advise him as if he were insane and rebuke him. But on the contrary, in justice and other civil virtues, it happens that even if some know someone to be unjust, yet if he admits this before those who do not know, they think him insane; they do not think iniquity should be revealed, but rather that justice should always be displayed, whether he possesses it or not. They think he who does not pretend to be just is raving, as if it were necessary for everyone to either be a sharer of civil virtue or be exterminated from the assembly and life of men. From these things I think it is sufficiently shown that they deservedly admit anyone as a consultant on civil matters, because they judge anyone to be possessed of this virtue. 

But next I will try to show you that they do not think virtue is inborn, nor that it happens by chance, but that it is acquired by teaching and study. No one is angry with anyone on account of those evils which they think have happened by nature or chance. Nor does anyone rebuke, or teach, or punish those who are weighed down by these evils, so that they may not be such: but rather we pity everyone, such as the deformed, the small, or the sickly. For who is so mad as to try to do any of those things? They understand clearly, I think, that all these evils and their opposites come to men by nature and fortune. On the contrary, when they judge that certain evils are produced in someone either by study or habit and teaching, then they are indignant, they rebuke, and they punish. In the number of these are iniquity and impiety, and in summary whatever is repugnant to civil virtue. Which things, for that reason, everyone everywhere condemns and corrects, because both wickedness and that civil virtue proceed from industry and discipline. 

For if you wish to consider, Socrates, what power punishing the unjust has, you will understand from that as well that men think virtue is acquired by study. For no one punishes for the sake of the past, and afflicts the unjust with penalties for this reason—because they have committed an injury—unless someone strikes like a brute without reason. But he who undertakes to punish with reason does not punish because of a past crime; for he cannot achieve that what has been done be undone: but he looks to the future, lest again either the perpetrator himself or anyone else, led by his example, should commit a fault. Whoever, moreover, with this purpose and such a judgment punishes errors, thinks that virtue can be acquired by teaching. For he strikes for the sake of deterring. With this mind and opinion, all who punish sinners approach punishing both publicly and privately. Now, everyone else condemns and punishes those whom they judge to be sinners, and especially your citizens, the Athenians. Wherefore, from this reasoning, it is clear that the Athenians are also in the number of those who think virtue can be taught. From these things, I think it has been shown openly, O Socrates, that it is not without justice that your citizens

# Protagoras, Or, the Sophists. 163

those arts which their fathers and others of the same art practice, or which the sons imitate, it would not be easy, O Socrates, to find a teacher for them; but for innumerable others, it would be very easy. So it must be said of virtue, and other such things. But we must think it enough if someone leads us to virtue a little more conveniently than other youths. Of these, I profess myself to be one, to know the reason by which men become good and honorable more subtly than other men, and so to perfect the thing itself, as is worthy of the reward which I demand, or even a greater reward, as the students themselves judge. This, however, is the condition of my charging: after someone has learned from me, if he wishes, he pays back as much money as I demand. If not, having entered a temple, he estimates by an oath how much my teachings seem to him to be worth, and pays that much. 

Therefore, O Socrates, let it be proved to you by this fable and reason that virtue can be taught and learned. Which the Athenians themselves also testify. We have shown likewise that it should not seem a wonder if the sons of good fathers are bad, or the sons of bad fathers are good, since indeed the sons of Polycletus, the equals of Paralus and Xanthippus here, if compared with their father, are surpassed by a very long interval; and similarly the sons of other craftsmen. Nor are these youths yet to be rejected, for they indeed offer some hope, since they are young. 

When Protagoras had shown these and similar things, he made an end of speaking. But I, for a long time after, being as it were still charmed by the previous speech, continued to look at him, inflamed with the desire for the words that might follow. But after I noticed he had entirely ceased, I finally recovered myself with difficulty, and turning to Hippocrates: "O son of Apollodorus," I said, "how great the thanks I owe you for bringing me here today. For I value it very much to have heard these things from Protagoras. For before I thought it was hardly a human care by which those who are good are made good; but now I am persuaded it is. But a certain small doubt remains that troubles me, which Protagoras will clearly remove easily after he has taught all these many things. For if someone should deal with one of the public orators about these same matters, perhaps he will hear such speeches as those of Pericles are wont to be, and of the rest of the eloquent men. But if he insists on questioning and urges someone about anything, like books, they have nothing either to answer or to ask themselves. But if someone asks about anything mentioned briefly and in passing by them, they resound loudly and shout for a long time like struck brass, unless you immediately catch their words. And thus the rhetoricians, asked a brief thing, produce a prolix speech. 

But Protagoras here can speak copiously and ornately, as the previous speech testifies, and he can also, when asked, answer summarily and briefly: and questioning himself, stand firm and receive an answer, which indeed can be said of few. At present, therefore, O Protagoras, I desire a little something, which if you declare, I will think myself satisfied in all things. You say virtue is attainable by the study of teaching, and I believe you most of all, if I believe anyone. But what I wondered at while you were speaking, I beseech you to open.

<margin>He finds certain sayings of Protagoras, so as to convict him.</margin>

For you were saying that Jupiter had clothed men with justice and shame. Then as the speech proceeded, you often named justice, temperance, and holiness, just as if all those things were contained under one certain virtue, and virtue itself existed as one thing. I would like this to be clearly explained to me, whether virtue is one certain thing, of which justice, temperance, and holiness are parts; or whether all these names I have now reported are of one and the same thing—this, I say, is what I further require." 

**PROTAGORAS.** But the answer to those things is easy, O Socrates: that all the things you ask are parts of virtue itself, which summarily is one. 

**SOCRATES.** Is it just as the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears are parts of one face? Or like parts of gold, which differ not at all from the whole, except in a certain magnitude and smallness? 

**PROTAGORAS.** They seem to me to be so, O Socrates; the parts of virtue to the whole, as all the parts of the face to the whole. 

**SOCRATES.** Do some men receive one part of virtue and some another? Or is it necessary that he who has one, has all? 

**PROTAGORAS.** In no way, since many are indeed brave, but unjust: and others are indeed just, but not at all wise. 

**SOCRATES.** Are wisdom and courage parts of virtue? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Entirely indeed, and wisdom is the most excellent part of all. 

**SOCRATES.** Is this one thing, and that another? 

**PROTAGORAS.** It is. 

**SOCRATES.** Does each also have its own power? Just as from the parts of the face the eye is not like the ears, nor is their power the same, nor is any other part like another, either in power or in anything else. Do the parts of virtue stand so, that neither is like the others, nor the same, nor the power the same? Or does it happen to be so? Indeed, the example of the nature of virtues we introduced agrees. 

**PROTAGORAS.** So it certainly is, O Socrates. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, one part of virtue is not such as knowledge is, nor such as justice, or courage, or temperance, or holiness. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Certainly not. 

**SOCRATES.** Come, let us consider together. What sort of thing is any of these: first indeed thus: Is justice a certain thing, or nothing? To me indeed it seems to be a certain thing. But to you? 

**PROTAGORAS.** To me also. 

**SOCRATES.** What then? If someone should ask of me and you, O Protagoras and Socrates: 'Tell me, please, is that thing which you were just now calling justice, by the very fact that it is justice, also just, or unjust?' I indeed would say it is just; but do you feel with me? Or not? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Plainly with you. 

**SOCRATES.** I, therefore, would answer the questioner that justice is such as the just is; but you? 

**PROTAGORAS.** I also. 

**SOCRATES.** If he asked again, 'Should we say there is also some holiness?' we would certainly agree, as I think. 

**PROTAGORAS.** We would agree. 

**SOCRATES.** 'And do you not say this is some thing?' If he asks, shall we not also assent to this? 

**PROTAGORAS.** To this also. 

**SOCRATES.** 'Do you think the nature of that thing is such that it is holy, or such that it is profane?' I would be annoyed at this question, and turning to him I would say, 'Better words, please!' Nothing else would ever be holy, unless holiness itself were holy. What about you? Would you not answer similarly? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Similarly. 

**SOCRATES.** If he added to these: 'Have I correctly received what you said above?' For you seemed a little while ago to assert that the parts of virtue relate to each other such that one part is not like another. I would interject to this, that he received some things correctly; but that he thought I had agreed in that, not correctly. For this Protagoras answered those things; but I asked. Therefore, if he should say, 'O Protagoras, Socrates speaks truly; you are the one who says one part of virtue is not such as another: this is your speech.' What will you answer him? 

**PROTAGORAS.** It is necessary, O Socrates, to confess it. 

**SOCRATES.** These things having been granted, what shall we answer him most especially if he objects further thus: 'Therefore holiness is not such that it is a just thing: nor justice such that it is

I indeed in my opinion would say justice is holy, and holiness is just. For I think you will permit me to answer that very thing for you: namely, that either justice is the same as holiness, or they are most similar to each other; that justice is most of all such as holiness is, and such as holiness is, such is justice. See whether you prohibit me from answering thus, or whether you agree. 

**PROTAGORAS.** That does not seem to me so simple, O Socrates, that it can be granted that holiness is just, or justice is holy. Yet a certain difference in being appears, but what does that finally matter? If you wish, let holiness be just for us, and justice holy. 

**SOCRATES.** But not for me. Nor do I have need that this—'if you wish' and 'if it pleases you'—be refuted. But I want it to be said for 'me and you.' I say 'me and you' because I think the speech is then finally discussed correctly if that 'if' is removed from it. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Truly justice has something similar to holiness. For anything has something similar to anything else, except those things which are entirely contrary to each other, like white and black, soft and hard. And yet even those things which we said above had different powers from each other, and that one was not such as another, like the parts of the face themselves, have something similar between them, and in a way one is such as another. And by this reasoning you may refute these things if it pleases you, because all things are mutually similar: yet not everything that has something similar is to be called 'similar,' nor even everything that has something dissimilar called 'mutually dissimilar' if they have some tiny similar thing. 

**SOCRATES.** I wonder indeed, O Protagoras, if justice and holiness are so mutually related that they have only a little something similar between them. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Not entirely thus, yet not quite so either as you yourself seem to think. 

**SOCRATES.** Since these things are a trouble to you, let us dismiss them; but let us consider another certain thing from what you were saying. Do you call something 'folly'? And do you say wisdom is its contrary? 

**PROTAGORAS.** I do. 

**SOCRATES.** When men live rightly and frugally, acting thus, do you think they act temperately, or when they act otherwise? 

**PROTAGORAS.** They seem to me to act temperately when they act frugally and rightly. 

**SOCRATES.** Do they not act temperately by temperance? 

**PROTAGORAS.** It is necessary. 

**SOCRATES.** Do not all who act not rightly act foolishly? And those who act thus, do they not act temperately? 

**PROTAGORAS.** So it seems. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, acting foolishly is the contrary of what is called acting temperately. 

**PROTAGORAS.** It is indeed. 

**SOCRATES.** Are not those things which are done foolishly done by folly? And those done temperately by temperance? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** Is not whatever is done by strength done strongly? And by weakness whatever is done, weakly? 

**PROTAGORAS.** It appears so. 

**SOCRATES.** And whatever is done by speed, speedily; but whatever by slowness, slowly? 

**PROTAGORAS.** This too. 

**SOCRATES.** And what is done in the same way entirely, is effected by the same thing; but what is done in a contrary way, is effected by a contrary. 

**PROTAGORAS.** I assent. 

**SOCRATES.** Tell me, please, is there something beautiful? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Certainly there is. 

**SOCRATES.** Is there any other contrary to this except the base? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Nothing else. 

**SOCRATES.** Is there also something good? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Also good. 

**SOCRATES.** And is there any other contrary except the evil? 

**PROTAGORAS.** No other. 

**SOCRATES.** Is there something 'acute' <note>High-pitched</note> in the voice? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Surely. 

**SOCRATES.** Is there any other contrary to it except 'grave' <note>Low-pitched</note>? 

**PROTAGORAS.** That very thing. 

**SOCRATES.** Is there not to each one of the contraries not many, but one contrary? 

**PROTAGORAS.** One only. 

**SOCRATES.** Let us resume now what has been granted by us so far. We granted plainly that for one thing there is only one contrary; but more than one, not at all. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Indeed. 

**SOCRATES.** Likewise that what is done in a contrary way is effected by contraries. 

**PROTAGORAS.** This also. 

**SOCRATES.** We admitted besides that what is done foolishly and what is done temperately are done in a contrary way. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Yes. 

**SOCRATES.** Again, that what is acted temperately proceeds from temperance; what foolishly, from folly. 

**PROTAGORAS.** It agrees. 

**SOCRATES.** If it is done in a contrary way, is it not done by a contrary? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** But this indeed is done by temperance, and that by folly. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** In a contrary way? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Contrary. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore not by contraries? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Also by contraries. 

**SOCRATES.** Folly, therefore, is the contrary of temperance? 

**PROTAGORAS.** It appears so. 

**SOCRATES.** Do we remember that we granted above that folly is contrary to wisdom? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** And that for one thing there is only one contrary? 

**PROTAGORAS.** This too. 

**SOCRATES.** Which of these speeches, then, shall we reject, Protagoras? That one by which it is said there is only one contrary for one thing? Or that which wanted wisdom to differ from temperance, since each was a part of virtue? And also besides that these two are different, that they themselves are as dissimilar as their powers, just as those parts in the face? Which of these shall we refute? Both are indeed not spoken quite fitly, for they do not harmonize or agree between themselves. For by what reasoning would they sound together if indeed it is necessary that for one thing there be only one contrary, and not at all for more; but of folly, while there is one, wisdom and temperance appear as contraries? Is it thus or otherwise, O Protagoras? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Let it be so, finally; what then? 

**SOCRATES.** By this reasoning, will not wisdom and temperance be one thing? And above it was established that justice and holiness were in a way the same? Come, Protagoras, do not be annoyed, but let us proceed to the rest. Does an unjust man seem to you, in acting unjustly, to be temperately wise? 

**PROTAGORAS.** I indeed, O Socrates, would not dare to confess this, but very many men assert it. 

**SOCRATES.** Shall I direct my words to them, or to you? 

**PROTAGORAS.** If it pleases you, explain this speech of the common people first. 

**SOCRATES.** It matters nothing to me, provided you yourself answer whether these things seem so to you or not. For I am discussing the speech itself in the first place. But that which happens both with me asking and you answering, happens by chance. 

Here Protagoras was first showing the difficulty of the speech by making excuses, but afterwards he granted he would answer. 

"Come," I said, "answer me from the beginning. Do some people seem to you, in acting unjustly, to be temperately wise?" 

**PROTAGORAS.** Let it be so. 

**SOCRATES.** But do you call 'being temperately wise' 'being well wise'? 

**PROTAGORAS.** I do. 

**SOCRATES.** And is 'being well wise' to consult well in that in which others commit injury? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Let it be so. 

**SOCRATES.** Is it if they do well because they act injuriously, or if they do badly? 

**PROTAGORAS.** If well. 

**SOCRATES.** Do you say some things are good? 

**PROTAGORAS.** I do. 

**SOCRATES.** Are those things good which are useful to men? 

**PROTAGORAS.** Nay, by Jupiter, I call some things good even if they are not useful to men. 

**SOCRATES.** Since Protagoras seemed to me to be getting angry and descending to the answer unwillingly, I asked all with caution and step by step. "Do you say, Protagoras, things which are useful to no man? Or which are in no way useful? And do you call such things good?" 

**PROTAGORAS.** Not at all. But I know many things useless to men—foods, and drinks, and medicines, and very many other things—but others useful. Some indeed which are the same for men bring great benefit to horses. And some only to oxen, some to dogs; some indeed to none of these, but rather to trees.

# Protagoras, Or, the Sophists. 163

And of those which are for trees, some are such that they often benefit the roots but harm the buds. Just as manure is useful to roots, it is very harmful to young branches and shoots. Oil also is most beneficial to all trees and herbs; but to the hairs of all animals, human except, it is most harmful. For it benefits the hairs of men and the whole body. And thus good exists as a certain varied and multiform thing. Whence also oil is best for the external parts of our body, but worst for the internal. For which reason all physicians forbid the use of oil to the sick, nor permit them to use it except as sparingly as possible to reject the offense of certain foul-smelling foods. 

When Protagoras had said these things, those present, acclaiming with frequent applause, approved his words. But I said, "O Protagoras, I am indeed too forgetful, and if anyone protracts a speech into a long one about which words are being made, I immediately forget. Surely if I were hard of hearing and you entered into a speech with me, you would think you had to shout louder to me than to the rest; so at present since you are addressing a forgetful man, act with me with more concise answers, if only you want me to follow you." 

**PROTAGORAS.** How much brevity do you demand? Do you command me to act with you in fewer words than is necessary? 

**SOCRATES.** Not at all. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Or perhaps as many words as are needed? 

**SOCRATES.** Just so many. 

**PROTAGORAS.** Shall I impose the measure on the speech at my own discretion? Or will you rather establish the due limit? 

**SOCRATES.** I have indeed heard that you can speak copiously as often as it is pleasing, so that speech never fails you, and also that you can touch upon the same matters in fewer words than any mortal; and that you can teach that very power to others, as I hear. If therefore you are going to dispute with me, use that brief and concise way of speaking, I beseech you. 

**PROTAGORAS.** O Socrates, I have fought in speaking with many men in the past. But if I had done what you advise, if, I say, I had made words according to the norm prescribed to me by the listener, I would be no better than anyone, nor would the name of Protagoras resound through all Greece. 

But when I recognized that the previous way of answering had not at all pleased Protagoras, and that he would by no means answer so willingly thereafter, I judged it not at all expedient for me to be present at those disputes, and therefore I said, "O Protagoras, I do not demand that we dispute together contrary to what is convenient for you, but if you wish to discourse so that I can follow, I will indeed stand by: for you indeed, as it is said of you and you yourself profess, are equally able both to touch on things summarily and to explain most amply: for you are wise. I, however, am inept at a prolix speech; and would that I were master of it, but it was in your interest to indulge us a little, since you are equally prepared for both, so that the dispute might be carried through. But since you do not wish, and business so urges me that I cannot stay here with you for long, although I would have heard those things gladly, I go now where the matter itself calls me." 

Having said these things, I rose immediately to depart. But as I was rising, Callias, taking me with his right hand and this cloak with his left, said, "We shall not let you go, Socrates: for if you leave now, it will hardly be possible to talk thus hereafter. Stay, I beseech you; no one's speech will delight me as much as that of yours with Protagoras. Therefore gratify both me and all these." 

But I had already risen to leave, and I said to Callias, "O son of Hipponicus, I have always admired your philosophy; now I praise and love it besides. Wherefore I would vehemently desire to gratify you, if you asked possible things. But what you now ask is just as if I were to follow the orators, like Crison of Himera <note>A famous Olympic runner.</note>, the young runner, with equal steps, or any of those who are accustomed to run a very long distance, or perform a day's course; for I would object much more that I myself desire, than you, to be able to equal these runners in the race, but I cannot. But if you want to see me and this man, as if another Crison, running together equally, ask him to accompany me with equal steps. For I indeed cannot run quickly, but he can run slowly. Therefore if you desire to hear me and Protagoras disputing, entreat him that, as he did from the beginning, so now he should answer in a few words and to the proposed question. Otherwise what will be the mode of disputing? I thought surely it was one thing to talk by mutual discourse, another to give a public oration." 

"But see, O Socrates," said Callias, "Protagoras seems to ask fair things, while he thinks it is permitted to him to discourse at his discretion, and to you likewise at yours." 

Here Alcibiades said, "You do not speak correctly, O Callias. For Socrates here confesses himself to be incapable of speaking copiously, and in this he yields to Protagoras. But if he should yield to anyone in disputing, and in receiving and giving reasons, I shall wonder greatly. If therefore Protagoras confesses himself to be inferior to Socrates in disputing, Socrates has enough now; but if he claims this for himself too, let him dispute, now by questioning, now by answering: nor in individual answers let him produce a speech at length, intercepting the discourse so that another may not speak, but he is so wordy that a great part of the listeners forgets what the proposed question was. I indeed warrant for Socrates that he will by no means commit to oblivion the things that are said, even though he jokes with us, saying he is forgetful. To me surely Socrates seems to demand quite fair things. For it becomes each one to express his own opinion." 

After Alcibiades, as I think, Critias said, "O Prodicus and Hippias, Callias indeed seems to favor Protagoras vehemently. Alcibiades, however, is too contentious and stubborn, whichever way he turns. But it does not become us to favor one more than the other, either Socrates or Protagoras, but to ask both in common that, after they have begun, they do not cease in the middle of the dispute." 

When he had said these things, Prodicus said, "You speak well, O Critias: for it becomes those who are present at these disputes to be common listeners of both, but not at all equal. For this is not one and the same thing; for it becomes one to hear both in common, but not to attribute equally to both. To the wiser indeed more, but to the more unlearned less. I indeed, O Protagoras and Socrates, think you ought to concede something to each other, and concerning those things which shall be said, to doubt indeed together, but by no means to contend. For friends doubt with friends because of benevolence, but adversaries and enemies contend. And thus our dispute would proceed best. You indeed would be כך, I would not say praised. The listeners indeed approve by the judgment of the mind without deception; they praise with words, mostly falsely, extolling something contrary to their opinion. We likewise as listeners would thus be most affected with joy, not pleasure. He is affected with joy who is delighted by learning and contemplating with intelligence itself; those are steeped in pleasure who, while eating or enjoying some other amusement, are delighted by the sense of the body itself."

Then Prodicus, along with most of those present, agreed. After that, the wise Hippias rose and spoke: "I believe, O men present, that you are all kinsmen, relatives, and fellow-citizens to one another by nature, if not by law. For by nature, like is akin to like. Law, however, the tyrant of men, forces many things upon us contrary to nature. It would therefore be a disgrace if we, who understand the nature of things and are the wisest of all the Greeks, having come together in this city—the very center of Greece—and assembled in this grandest and most magnificent of houses, should show nothing worthy of such great dignity, but instead should quarrel and disagree with one another like common, lowly men. Indeed, I urge and beseech you, Socrates and Protagoras, to be willing to submit to us as if to arbiters, who shall lead you to a middle ground. Neither should you, Socrates, demand that exact form of dialogue and that overly brief 'brevity of speech' if it is troublesome to Protagoras; rather, I pray you, loosen the reins for a little while, so that the speeches may be more magnificent and splendid. And to you, Protagoras, I ask that you do not immediately glide out into the deep sea of discourse with all ropes tight and sails full, until the land is nowhere in sight; instead, both of you should strive to preserve a middle course as much as possible. Therefore, do as I wish: obey and choose an overseer, a master of the contest, and a judge who shall set a limit to the words of each." This pleased those present, and everyone praised the idea. Callias even urged me to do this, and asked me to choose an arbiter. But I said, "It is not fitting to appoint a judge over this discussion. For if the judge is less skilled than we are, it would be unjust for someone inferior to preside over those who are better. If he is our equal, things will still not be handled correctly, for an equal to us will act as we do, and thus be superfluous. To choose someone truly more outstanding than ourselves is, I believe, impossible in reality—certainly, another man wiser than Protagoras cannot be chosen. If you choose someone who is no more learned but pretend he is, it will be a disgrace to Protagoras to have a judge appointed over him as if he were ignorant and of no account. For my part, it makes no difference. But so that we may proceed with the discussion as you wish, here is how I think we should act: If Protagoras does not wish to answer, let him at least ask the questions, and I will answer; I will try to show him in what manner, in my judgment, one ought to answer another. And when I have answered whatever questions he asks, let him in turn promise to perform the same duty for me. If he should seem a bit reluctant to answer, then I and all of you together shall entreat the man—just as you are now entreating me—not to break up the gathering. There is no need to propose a single judge; for you shall all judge together as one." Everyone agreed that this was the way to act. Protagoras, however, seemed to descend to this unwillingly. At last he was compelled to concede that he would ask questions, and after he had asked enough, he would answer briefly. Thus, he began to question me in this manner: "I believe, Socrates, that the chief part of education consists in being well-versed in poems. This means being able to understand the words of poets—knowing which are right and which are not—and being able to distinguish them and give an account when questioned. So now, let the questioning be about the very subject we have both been investigating: virtue. The only difference is that the discussion is now transferred to poetry. For Simonides says to Scopas, son of Creon of Thessaly, that it is 'difficult to become a truly good man, four-square <note>The original term implies being "perfect" or "perfectly balanced" in hands, feet, and mind.</note> in hands, feet, and mind.' Do you remember the poem, or do you want me to recite the whole thing?" SOCRATES: "There is no need. For I remember it, and I have given these poems diligent care." PROTAGORAS: "Well said. Does Simonides seem to you to have spoken well and correctly, or not?" SOCRATES: "Quite excellently." PROTAGORAS: "Does a poet seem to speak correctly if he contradicts himself?" SOCRATES: "Not at all." PROTAGORAS: "Then attend more diligently." SOCRATES: "My good man, I am attending well enough." PROTAGORAS: "In the same poem, he later says that the opinion of the wise Pittacus seems 'discordant' to him, where Pittacus says, 'It is difficult to remain good.' Do you see that the same Simonides said both this and the former thing?" SOCRATES: "Indeed." PROTAGORAS: "Do these two statements not seem consistent to you?" "They do," I said, or so it seemed to me. And at the same time, fearing he might add something further, I asked if they did not seem so to him as well. He replied, "Do you ask if I think he is consistent with himself, when he said both? First, he proposed that to become a good man is truly difficult, but a little later, as if forgetting himself, he rebukes Pittacus for saying the same thing—namely, that it is difficult for a man to remain good—rejecting his words even though he had said the same? Truly, when he accuses Pittacus of the same opinion as his own, he condemns himself. Therefore, either his first statement or his second is incorrect." When this was said, many of the listeners shouted and praised Protagoras. I, however, felt at first like I had been struck by a powerful boxer; my eyes grew dizzy and I stumbled. For both his voice and the shouting of the others had completely overwhelmed me. Then, to tell you the honest truth, in order to gain time to investigate the poet's meaning, I turned to Prodicus and said, "Simonides was your fellow-citizen, O Prodicus. Therefore, it is in your interest to bring him aid. I seem to be calling upon you just as, in Homer, the Scamander, when beset by Achilles, called upon Simoeis <note>original: "Iliad. φ." A reference to Book 21 (Phi) of the Iliad where the river god Scamander calls for help against Achilles.</note>: 'O sweet brother, let us both together restrain the force of this man.' In the same way, I summon you now, lest Protagoras conquer our Simonides. Indeed, to rescue Simonides, I have need of that subtle skill of yours, by which you distinguish between 'to will' and 'to desire,' and many other excellent things you were saying a moment ago. And now, tell me if you see it as I do; for I do not think Simonides contradicts himself in his speech. But you, Prodicus, state your opinion first: does 'to become' and 'to be' seem the same to you, or different?" "Different, by Jove!" said Prodicus. "Did not Simonides first," I said, "set forth his own opinion, that it is difficult for a man to *become* truly good?" "You speak the truth," said Prodicus. "But he disapproves of Pittacus—not as Protagoras thinks, for saying the same thing, but for saying something different. For Pittacus did not say it is difficult for a man to *become* good, as Simonides did, but to *remain* so. Now, to be and to become are not the same, O Protagoras, as this man Prodicus believes. And if being is not the same as becoming, Simonides is by no means contradicting himself. Perhaps Prodicus and many others could quote that line of Hesiod <note>original: "In opere cui titulus Erga η̉ η̉μέραι." Reference to Hesiod's 'Works and Days'.</note>, saying that to become good is indeed difficult, for the gods have placed sweat before virtue. But when one has reached the highest peak, it is easy, though it was difficult to attain." Prodicus, having heard this, praised me. But Protagoras said, "That correction, Socrates, contains more fault than the thing you are correcting." "Then I have fared poorly, Protagoras," I said, "and I am a ridiculous doctor: while I strive to cure the disease, I increase it." PROTAGORAS: "But that is how it is." SOCRATES: "In what way?" PROTAGORAS: "Because that poet would have been far too ignorant if he thought virtue was of so little value..."

SOCRATES: "By Jove, Protagoras, this Prodicus of ours has intervened in our discourse at just the right moment. For it seems, Protagoras, that the divine wisdom of Prodicus is an ancient thing, either long ago drawing its origin from Simonides, or perhaps even older. You, however, though you are skilled in many other matters, seem to be unacquainted with this. I, on the other hand, am experienced in it, since I was a disciple of this man Prodicus. Yet at present, you do not seem to notice that perhaps Simonides did not use the word 'difficult' in the way you are using it now. Prodicus frequently warns me that 'difficult' should be understood as something 'bad' and 'grievous.' For whenever I, praising either someone else or yourself, say: 'Protagoras is a wise and <term>vehement</term> <note>original: "δεινός" (deinos), meaning powerful, wondrous, or dangerously clever.</note> man,' he immediately rebukes me and asks if I am not ashamed to call what is good 'grievous'—since what is 'grievous' is 'bad.' For no one calls wealth 'grievous,' or peace 'grievous,' or health 'grievous'; rather, they speak of a 'grievous' disease, a 'grievous' war, or 'grievous' poverty, as if 'grievous' means a burdensome evil. Perhaps therefore both the people of Chios and Simonides himself, when they say 'difficult,' imply 'bad,' or something else that you do not understand. Therefore, let us ask Prodicus. For it is most fitting to consult him about the writings of Simonides. What, Prodicus, did Simonides intend to be understood by the word 'difficult'?" PRODICUS: "An evil, certainly." SOCRATES: "For this reason, I believe, Prodicus, he rebuked Pittacus for saying 'It is difficult to remain good,' as if he had said it is 'bad' to remain good." PRODICUS: "And what else do you think Simonides intended, Socrates, than to rebuke Pittacus for not knowing how to distinguish names correctly, seeing as he was from Lesbos and educated among barbarians?" SOCRATES: "Do you hear, Protagoras, what Prodicus says? What do you say to this?" PROTAGORAS: "It is far from being so, Prodicus. I certainly know that Simonides, by the word 'difficult,' intended what others usually do: not 'bad,' but that which is not easy, and which is attained with much labor." SOCRATES: "I also believe Simonides intended this, Protagoras, and that Prodicus understands this as well, but he is playing with you and testing whether you are able to defend your own argument. For that Simonides did not mean 'bad' by 'difficult' is proven by what follows; for he adds that 'only God is worthy to enjoy this gift.' Surely, if he meant it was 'bad' to be good, he would not add shortly after that only God possesses this, or attribute such a gift to God alone. Prodicus would surely call Simonides a dissolute man, and not at all a Chian. However, I will tell you what I think Simonides finally felt in these poems, if you wish to make a trial of me and see how I stand regarding poetry. Or, if you prefer, I will listen to you." Protagoras, having heard this, said, "As you like, Socrates." But Prodicus and Hippias and all the others urged me to proceed. "I will try," I said, "to explain to you what I think of these poems. Philosophy is most ancient and most abundant among the Greeks in Crete and Lacedaemon <note>The ancient name for Sparta.</note>, and more sophists are found there than anywhere else. But they disguise it and pretend to be ignorant, so that they might not be discovered surpassing the rest of the Greeks in wisdom—exactly as Protagoras was saying about the sophists earlier. Instead, they want to seem to excel others in military matters and courage, fearing that if their true nature were revealed, everyone else would pursue the same study. Therefore, they hide and deceive those who imitate the customs of the Lacedaemonians in other cities. For there are those who, because they have their ears cropped and wrap themselves in thongs, because they enjoy exercises and wear short garments, want to appear like Spartans—as if the Lacedaemonians surpassed the other Greeks in such things. But the Lacedaemonians, whenever they wish to speak more freely with their sophists, find it hard to tolerate foreigners; they gather in secret, excluding all strangers, and practice philosophy with the sophists. Furthermore, both they and the Cretans forbid the young men of their nation to visit other cities, lest they perhaps unlearn elsewhere what is taught among them. In these states, one finds not only men of excellent learning, but also women. That I speak the truth, and that the Lacedaemonians are best educated for philosophy and discourse, can be seen most clearly from this: if anyone talks with even the lowliest of the Lacedaemonians, he will find him appearing crude in his words at first. Then, whenever the opportunity of the matter demands, like a powerful javelin-thrower, he hurls a word, brief and twisted, but of some great weight, so that the one talking to him seems no different from a child. That the virtue of the Lacedaemonians consists more in the study of wisdom than in exercise is understood by some men of our age, and many in the past noticed the same, seeing that to be able to utter such words is the mark of a perfectly learned man. Among their number was Thales of Miletus, and Pittacus of Mitylene, Bias of Priene, our Solon, Cleobulus of Lindus, Myson of Chenae, and the seventh of these was said to be Chilo the Lacedaemonian. <margin>The Wise Men of Greece.</margin> <margin>Lacedaemonian Wisdom.</margin> All these were rivals and students of Lacedaemonian wisdom. We have found it to be of such a kind: brief words, worthy for each person to remember. These men, having met together by common consent, dedicated these first-fruits of wisdom at the temple of Apollo at Delphi, which are inscribed on the temple and celebrated by all: *Know thyself* and *Nothing in excess*. I mention these things for this reason: to show that the style of ancient philosophy was exactly this—a certain 'Laconism,' if I may call it that, or brevity of speech. Now, this particular saying of Pittacus was circulated and celebrated by the wise: 'It is difficult to remain good.' Simonides, therefore, since he desired the glory of wisdom, knew that if he could refute and conquer this proverb as if it were a famous athlete, he himself would be held as illustrious by all. For this reason he composed those poems, in order to disrupt, as I believe, the words of the one whose glory he envied. But let us all discuss these things together and see if I speak the truth. First, those earlier lines would indicate an insane man if, wishing to say that 'to become a good man is difficult,' he then threw in the particle 'indeed' <note>referring to the Greek particle 'men'.</note>. For it seems to have been inserted for no reason, unless we say Simonides is speaking against the words of Pittacus. When Pittacus said, 'It is difficult to remain good,' Simonides objects: 'It is not so, O Pittacus; rather, it is difficult *indeed* to *become* a good man, truly'—not 'truly good.' For he does not say 'truly' because some are truly good and others are good but not truly. That would seem discordant and unworthy of Simonides. But we shall say that in the wording, 'truly' is a hyperbaton <note>A figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed.</note> in the poem, which he placed after the words of Pittacus: as if we suppose Pittacus himself were saying, 'O men, it is difficult to remain good,' and Simonides replied, 'O Pittacus, you do not speak the truth at all. For it is not to *be*, but to *become* a good man, in hands and feet and mind...'"
