"...perfectly squared to the mind <note>original: "mente adamusim quadratum," a metaphor for moral perfection, like a stone cut perfectly on all sides.</note>, is truly difficult," so this little word "truly" seems to have been inserted with good reason: and "truly" itself is placed at the end for a purpose. And indeed, everything that follows bears witness to this, as it is said in this manner. There are, moreover, many things in these verses which we could show piece by piece, seeing how beautifully they were written. For they are composed skillfully and accurately, but the discourse would be too long. Therefore, let us explain the form and intention of this poet in summary. He intends, in all these verses, to refute the saying of Pittacus. For he says a little later, almost in this way, that "to be made a good man is truly difficult," but there is a certain time when it is possible. However, once one is made good, to persevere in that state and "to be good," as you, Pittacus, contend, is impossible and not a human feat; only God enjoys this gift. For a man to remain good in such a way that he does not slip again is impossible, for he is one whom unexpected fate might snatch away. What kind of person does an unexpected accident most of all sink in the steering of a ship? Not an unskillful man, for he is always down; and just as no one knocks down a man already lying on the ground, but someone might knock down a man who is standing and force him to lie down—never the one already down—so too does an unexpected accident sometimes circumvent the clever and sagacious man. Truly, it does not affect the one who never cares for anything. And a great sudden force of a storm overcomes the pilot, and the inclemency of the year overcomes the farmer, and similar things happen to the doctor, so that they then seem to have been improvident. For a good person can become bad, as another poet testifies, saying: "A good man is now bad, now good." But for a bad man to be made bad is impossible, for he must always be so. Therefore, whenever an unexpected accident strikes a provident, wise, and good man, he is made bad. But you say, O Pittacus, that it is "difficult to remain good." The matter, however, stands thus: it is possible to become good, though difficult; but to endure as good is utterly impossible. For anyone who acts well is good; on the contrary, he who acts badly is bad. What is the "good thing" regarding letters? Or what action makes a man good in them? It is clear that it is the learning of them. Likewise, what good action makes a good doctor? Clearly, the skill of curing diseases. He who cures well is a good doctor; on the contrary, he who cures badly is bad. Who, therefore, is sometimes made a bad doctor? Certainly he in whom this first exists: that he is a doctor, and then that he is a good doctor. For this man can sometimes be made a bad doctor. But we who are ignorant of the medical art would never be made either doctors or craftsmen by acting badly, or anything of that sort. Whoever does not become a doctor by performing his duty badly is not even a bad doctor. Thus, a good man can sometimes become bad, either because of time, or labor, or disease, or some other accident. For this is the only truly "bad action": to be deprived of knowledge. A bad man, however, would never become bad <note>original: "malus vir nunquam malus fieret," implying he is already in that state and cannot "become" what he already is.</note>, for the reason that to become bad, he must have been good before. And so these verses tend toward this: that he affirms it is impossible for a good man always to persevere; but that it is possible for the same man to become good and then again bad; and for the most part, those whom the gods love are the best. All these things were said against Pittacus, which what follows declares more clearly. "For this reason," he says, "I, never searching in vain for what cannot be, shall hope for a good man who will live perpetually without reproach among those of us who eat the fruits of the earth." Then he continues to you with what I have discovered...

<margin>And other things that follow. So vehemently does he attack Pittacus’ saying throughout the whole poem. That I never praise and love him who does nothing shameful willingly. But even the gods do not fight against necessity.</margin>

...and other things that follow. So vehemently does he attack the saying of Pittacus throughout the whole poem. "But I never praise and love him who, of his own will, commits nothing shameful. Even the gods do not fight against necessity." But this is said to the same point. For Simonides was not so ignorant of things that he would say he praises the one who commits no evil willingly, as if there were some who commit evil voluntarily. I believe indeed that no wise man thinks that any man errs of his own accord, or commits evil and shameful things willingly. For they know that those who commit evil and shameful things sin against their will. And yet Simonides by no means says he praises the one who does not commit crimes willingly; rather, he wanted that phrase "willingly" to be understood regarding himself. For he thought that a noble and good man would often force himself to become the friend and praiser of someone, and would love and praise them—as when people often happen to have cross and unjust parents, or a fatherland, or something similar. If they are wicked men, they are accustomed to attack the errors of parents and country willingly and of their own accord, and to spread them everywhere so that no one can criticize them for neglecting their parents and country. Therefore, they blame their parents and country and harass them with hatred and enmity beyond necessity. But those who are good men rather hide the disgraces of their country and force themselves to praise them; and if in some matter they are affected by injury and could justly be indignant with their parents and country, they console themselves, reconcile themselves, and drive themselves to the love and praise of their elders even against their will. I believe often Simonides himself, not from his own heart's opinion but unwillingly, came to praise and exalt some tyrant or other such person. This, then, he says to Pittacus: "I indeed, O Pittacus, do not rebuke you because I enjoy detracting from nature; for whoever is not bad or too lazy satisfies it. A healthy man, knowing justice, will help the city. Yet I will not detract; for I do not enjoy detraction. For the race of fools is infinite, so that if one were to continue to blame them, he would necessarily be exhausted. Furthermore, all things are honorable in which shameful things are not mixed." He does not say this as if he were saying all things are white in which no black is mixed—for that would be ridiculous—but as if to say he will tolerate mediocre things and not blame them. "I do not seek," he says, "an irreproachable man among as many of us as pluck the fruit of the wide earth. Then I announce to you what I have discovered: that for this cause I shall praise no one. But it is enough for me whoever holds the middle ground and does nothing shameful. Thus I love all, thus I praise them." Here he used the language of the Mityleneans <note>Simonides is addressing Pittacus, who was from Mitylene.</note> as if against Pittacus, saying: "I praise all thus, I love all thus willingly." Here one must distinguish the word "willingly" from the following, "whoever commits nothing shameful." For there are some whom I do not praise and love willingly. "But if you, my dear Pittacus, had said even moderately consistent and true things, I would never have rebuked you. Now, however, since you bring forth things that are both very false and about the greatest matters, which appear true to many, I am forced to rebuke you." This, O Prodicus and Protagoras, seems to me to have been the opinion of Simonides himself in those verses. Then Hippias said: "Well, Socrates, you seem to have explained these verses. I also have an account suited to them, which I will show to you if you wish." "On the contrary," said Alcibiades, "but later: first it is proper to complete what was agreed between Socrates and Protagoras. And if Protagoras wants to question further, Socrates must answer."

Protagoras, Or, the Sophists.                              169

"But if Protagoras wants to answer, Socrates should question." "And yet," I said, "I grant to Protagoras whichever of these will be more pleasing to him. But if it is agreeable, let us set aside the verses, and let us gladly finish with you, Protagoras, those things which I first asked you. For it seems to me that a dispute about poetic matters is very similar to the banquets of ignorant and common people. Who, since they are unable to converse among themselves with their own voice and their own words because of their ignorance, bring in flute-girls for a fee, and conduct the banquet with a foreign voice—that is, the blowing of flutes. But where good, excellent, and educated guests gather, you see there neither flute-girls, nor dancing-girls, nor any singing-girls, but they celebrate the banquet with their own voice, having removed those trifles and jests, and they discourse modestly with alternate questions and answers, even if they drink wine in abundance. In the same way, if such men gather for disputes of this kind—as most of us claim to be—there is no need for the foreign voice and words of poets, whom it is not possible to question about what they write; and those who bring their testimonies into the midst say the poet thinks one thing, while others say another, yet they cannot prove the matter about which they differ, nor resolve it. Therefore, wise men dismiss such conversations and talk among themselves, and in turn, they make a trial of their own talent with each other. Such disputants, I believe, you and I should now imitate; and having set aside the poets, let us discuss the matter itself with our own reasons, and make a trial of our talent as much as of the truth. If then you wish to question, I am prepared to answer; if you wish otherwise, offer yourself to me and help to complete those things which we left unfinished." When I had brought in these and other such things, Protagoras did not clearly declare what he would most prefer to do. Here Alcibiades, turned toward Callias, said: "O Callias, does it seem to you that Protagoras is acting rightly now, when he refuses to declare whether he wishes to answer or not? It does not seem so to me. But let him either dispute now, or say he does not wish to dispute, so that we may know this about him. Then Socrates can discourse with anyone else, or anyone else who wishes can do so with another." Here Protagoras, as it seemed to me, moved by shame because of Alcibiades' speech and the prayers of Callias and others present, finally descended to the discussion and ordered Socrates himself to question, promising to answer. "O Protagoras," I said, "do not think that I discourse with you for any other reason than because I want to discuss the things I doubt here and there. For I think it was said not without reason by Homer: 'If two go together, one understands more than the other.' For we are all more ready for any work, word, or investigating a sense. But if someone thinks of something alone, he soon goes around everywhere seeking someone to communicate with and by whom he may be confirmed until he finds it. For which reason, I now dispute more gladly with you than with anyone else, thinking that you will best of all judge concerning all other things that pertain to the judgment of an honest man, and especially concerning those things which I myself was seeking—namely, virtue. For whom could I hope would do it better than you? You who not only think yourself honest, as some others are honest themselves but cannot make others so; but you are not only endowed with virtue, you also promise to adorn other men with the same. And you trust your talent so much that while all others conceal their art, you alone profess it, and you openly proclaim yourself throughout all Greece, calling yourself a 'sophist' as if by a public announcement, declaring yourself a master of doctrine and virtue, and you are the first to demand a fee for that craft. What then prevents you, above all others, from being employed and questioned for the discussion of these matters, and why should not all things be communicated with you? Nothing at all prevents it. And yet I myself now desire partly to be reminded by you of those things which I first asked, and partly to have them discussed by common judgment. The question was, I believe, this: whether wisdom, temperance, courage, justice, and holiness are five names of the same thing, or whether some proper essence underlies each of these names, and each thing has its own power, so that one is not like the other. You said then that these are by no means names of one thing, but that individual names are applied to individual things. Furthermore, that all these are parts of virtue, not indeed like the parts of gold which are similar to each other and the whole, but like the parts of the face, which are mutually dissimilar to each other and the whole, distinct by their own power. And say if these things are now still so, as you confirmed above. If you feel otherwise now, distinguish all things clearly. I will certainly not hold it against you if you say something else now. For I do not wonder if you said those things then for the sake of testing Socrates." PROTAGORAS: "I say all these are parts of virtue, of which four are fairly similar to each other. Courage, however, differs far from the others. That I speak truly, you will know in this manner. You will find some men who are most unjust, most profane, most intemperate, and most ignorant, who nevertheless excel others in courage." SOCRATES: "Attend, please; what you say must be considered. Do you call the courageous 'daring,' or some others?" PROTAGORAS: "Indeed, even those headlong toward those things from which most people are deterred." SOCRATES: "Come then, do you assert virtue is something honest and beautiful, and do you teach it as something beautiful?" PROTAGORAS: "Most beautiful indeed, unless perhaps I am insane." SOCRATES: "Is some part of it shameful and some part beautiful? Or is it all beautiful?" PROTAGORAS: "The whole is as beautiful as can be." SOCRATES: "Do you know those who daringly plunge themselves into wells?" PROTAGORAS: "Indeed I do. Divers <note>original: "urinatores," meaning breath-holding divers or pearl divers.</note>." SOCRATES: "Is it because of what they know, or for some other reason?" PROTAGORAS: "Because of what they know." SOCRATES: "Which men dare to fight most bravely from horses? The horsemen, or those unlearned in equestrian industry?" PROTAGORAS: "The horsemen." SOCRATES: "Which fight daringly with small shields? The targeteers <note>original: "peltatine," likely a typo for peltastae (peltasts), light infantry.</note> or others?" PROTAGORAS: "Those indeed; and in all other things, if you ask this, those who know are more daring than those who do not know; and the same men, after they have learned, dare anything more vehemently than when they were ignorant." SOCRATES: "Have you ever seen any who are ignorant of all these things, but are nevertheless daring toward all of them?" PROTAGORAS: "I have indeed, and very daring." SOCRATES: "Are those daring ones courageous?" PROTAGORAS: "Courage would be something shameful, since those daring ones are furious <note>In the sense of being mad or raving.</note>." SOCRATES: "But do you not say the courageous are themselves daring?" PROTAGORAS: "I said so indeed, and I do say so." SOCRATES: "Do not those who are thus daring appear to be by no means courageous, but mad? And above, again, those wisest appeared to us to be most daring, and because most daring, therefore also most courageous; and so according to this reason, would not wisdom itself be courage?" PROTAGORAS: "You do not sufficiently remember, O Socrates, what I said above and answered to you. Indeed, asked by you whether courageous men are daring or not, I agreed. But whether daring men were courageous, you did not ask. If you had asked then, I would have answered: certainly not all. But that courageous men are not daring, you have never shown me to have granted, for indeed I would not have correctly granted it. Furthermore, you show that knowing men are more daring than the ignorant, both than themselves and others, and therefore you think wisdom and courage are the same. By which line of reasoning, you might think strength and wisdom are the same. For if you had asked me in the same way, whether strong men are powerful, and after they have learned are more powerful than themselves when they were ignorant, and more than the unlearned, and I had admitted this after they learned... by my concession it would have been permitted to you to infer in the same way that wisdom is strength. But I nowhere at present confess that powerful men are strong. I say, however, that strong men are powerful. And I do not think strength and power are the same. For power can come from knowledge, from madness, and from anger; but strength comes from nature alone and the due nutrition of bodies. Similarly, in those others, courage and audacity should by no means be considered the same. Wherefore it happens that the courageous are indeed daring, but truly not all daring men are courageous. For audacity is given to men by art, by anger, and by madness, just as we said of power; but courage proceeds from nature and the due education of the souls."

<summary>Socrates moves the discussion away from poetry to direct dialectic. Protagoras argues that courage is distinct from other virtues because one can be brave while lacking other qualities, leading to a debate on the difference between mere daring (audacity) and true courage.</summary>

"...you would never have shown, nor indeed would I have correctly granted it. Therefore, you show that knowing men are more daring than the ignorant, and more than themselves and others, and for that reason you think wisdom and courage are the same. By which reasoning, you might think strength and wisdom are the same. For if you had asked me in this way: whether strong men are powerful, and if after they have learned they are more powerful than themselves while they were ignorant, and more so than the unskillful; and if I had then admitted this... by my concession it would have been permitted to you to conclude in the same way that wisdom is strength. But I nowhere at present confess that powerful men are strong. I say, however, that strong men are powerful. And I do not think strength and power are the same. For power can come from knowledge, from madness, and from anger; but strength comes from nature alone and the due nutrition of bodies. Similarly, in those others, courage and audacity should by no means be considered the same. Wherefore it happens that the courageous are indeed daring, but truly not all daring men are courageous. For audacity is given to men by art, by anger, and by madness, just as we said of power; but courage proceeds from nature and the due education of souls." SOCRATES: "Do you say, O Protagoras, that some men live well, and others badly?" PROTAGORAS: "I say so indeed." SOCRATES: "Does a man seem to you to live well if he lives with annoyance and pain?" PROTAGORAS: "Not at all." SOCRATES: "But if he has lived pleasantly until the end of his life, should he be said to have lived well?" PROTAGORAS: "Certainly." SOCRATES: "Therefore, to live pleasantly is good, and to live with annoyance is bad." PROTAGORAS: "If only one is delighted by honorable things." SOCRATES: "Do you yourself, Protagoras, like many others, call some pleasant things 'bad,' and some sad things 'good'?" PROTAGORAS: "I do." SOCRATES: "Insofar as they are pleasant, are they not good? And is it not so if something else comes from them? And again, sad things in the same way?" PROTAGORAS: "I do not know, Socrates, whether I should answer as simply as you ask, that all pleasant things are good and all sad things are bad. But it seems safer to me, not only for the present question but also for the whole reason of my life, to answer that there are some pleasant things that are not good, and some sad things that are not bad; and again, there are others that are neutral, which are neither good nor bad." SOCRATES: "Do you call pleasant things those which either participate in pleasure or produce pleasure?" PROTAGORAS: "Exactly." SOCRATES: "I ask this, then: whether from the fact that they are pleasant, they are not good. Whether, namely, pleasure itself is not a good." PROTAGORAS: "As you yourself say everywhere, O Socrates, let us consider this; and if that consideration seems to lead to the matter, and the pleasant and the good appear to be the same, let us grant it; if not, then let us proceed to discuss it." SOCRATES: "Do you wish to be the leader of the dispute? Or do you bid me to go first?" PROTAGORAS: "It is fair that you be the leader. For you began." SOCRATES: "In this way perhaps what we seek will be revealed: just as if someone, to consider a man's health or another bodily habit or work, having looked at his face and the extremities of his hands, should say, 'come now, strip your chest and back for me, so that I may inspect more clearly.' So I now require the same for this dispute. For since I have learned your opinion toward the good and pleasure from your words, it is useful for me to say something of this sort. Come, Protagoras, and open your mind in this also: what do you feel about knowledge? Does it please you the same as it does others, or differently? For concerning knowledge, very many judge thus: that it is not something robust, nor does it lead, nor even dominate. Nor do they suspect it to be like a leader or a prince. But when knowledge is often not lacking to a man, they think not knowledge itself but something else—such as anger, or pleasure, or pain, or love, or fear—dominates. And they think of knowledge as if it were a certain slave dragged around by all others from every side. Do you also feel the same? Or rather, do you think knowledge is something excellent and a prince in man, so that if one discerns good and evil, he can never be induced by anything else to do anything other than what knowledge has commanded; but that prudence alone is sufficiently suitable to be at hand for a man?" PROTAGORAS: "What you say seems so to me, O Socrates. For if it is shameful for any man to deny that wisdom and knowledge are the most powerful of all human things, it is certainly most shameful for me." SOCRATES: "You speak very excellently and truly. But do you know that many do not believe you and me? They say, moreover, that most people, conscious of the good, when it is possible to do good, do not wish to do good, but other things. And whomever I have asked what the cause of this thing is, they answer that they are overcome by pleasure, or pain, or some other of those things we recalled above, and they do these things." PROTAGORAS: "There are also many other things, O Socrates, in which men err." SOCRATES: "Come then, try with me to persuade men and teach them what this evil is, by which they say they are overcome by pleasures, and for this reason they do not do the goods they know. For perhaps if we say, 'O men, you are mistaken,' they will ask: 'If it is not, O Protagoras and Socrates, this "evil of pleasure" to which one succumbs, what else is it? Explain in your words.'" PROTAGORAS: "Why should we attend to the opinion of the many, who speak however it happens?" SOCRATES: "I believe this will be profitable for us to find how courage relates to the other parts of virtue. Therefore, if you think we should stand by the former agreement—namely, that I lead the way where I think what we seek can best be found—follow me. If not, and you prefer to dismiss this, I will dismiss it." PROTAGORAS: "You speak rightly: proceed then, as you began." SOCRATES: "I, if they asked us again: 'What is this that you say we call being conquered by pleasures?' I would answer them thus: Listen then, I and Protagoras will try to declare it to you. For do you say, O men, that anything else happens here than what often occurs: that men, enticed and conquered by the pleasure of food, drink, and sex, adopt those things for themselves, even if they know they are bad? They would agree. But we would ask them thus: 'But why do you say those things are bad? Is it because they offer this present pleasure and soothe with sweetness? Or because in the future they bring diseases, poverty, and many other things of this kind? Or even if they bring nothing of the sort in the future, are they bad only because they delight, so that a man learns to rejoice?' Do we think, O Protagoras, they would answer otherwise than that they are bad not because of present pleasure, but because of diseases and other things that follow?" PROTAGORAS: "I think the crowd would answer thus." SOCRATES: "While they bring diseases, do they not bring pains? While they bring want, pain? They would agree, as I believe." PROTAGORAS: "Indeed." SOCRATES: "Therefore, O men, for no other reason, as I and Protagoras think, do these things appear bad to you than that they end in pains and deprive you of other pleasures. They would confess." PROTAGORAS: "Without a doubt."

<summary>Socrates and Protagoras discuss the nature of pleasure and knowledge. They begin to analyze the common claim that people are "overcome by pleasure," with Socrates arguing that knowledge should be the sovereign ruler of human action.</summary>

Protagoras, Or, the Sophists.                              171

"Without a doubt." SOCRATES: "If on the contrary we asked again: 'O men, you admit that sad things are good, do you not speak of certain things of this kind? Such as bodily exercises, the labors of military service, the treatments of doctors, which are done either by cutting, or by burning, or by drugs, or by hunger—you call these good because these are indeed good, but troublesome?' They would agree." PROTAGORAS: "And this also." SOCRATES: "Do you call these things good because they finish with present pains and tortures? Or rather because from these things, health follows in the future, and a good habit of the body, the safety of the country, power, and riches? They would say it is for that reason, as I think." PROTAGORAS: "I also judge so." SOCRATES: "Is there any other reason these are good than that they end in pleasures and drive away troubles? Can you assign another end, looking to which you call these good, other than pleasures and pains? They would answer, as I believe: 'We cannot.'" PROTAGORAS: "I think so indeed." SOCRATES: "Do you not follow pleasure as a good, and flee pain as an evil? They would grant it." PROTAGORAS: "Certainly." SOCRATES: "Therefore you think that is an evil—namely, pain—and pleasure a good, since you then surely call delight itself bad when it deprives one of greater pleasures than it affects, or when it brings more vehement pains than the pleasures it offers. Since if you called delight itself bad for some other reason—looking, for instance, toward some other end—you could show it to us. But you will by no means be able." PROTAGORAS: "It does not seem to me that they could." SOCRATES: "Similarly also, you call pain itself good only when it puts to flight greater pains than it brings, or induces pleasures more vehement than the troubles. Since if you judged pain to be good looking toward another end, you could show it everywhere, but you will not be able." PROTAGORAS: "You tell the truth, O Socrates." SOCRATES: "If you in turn ask me, O men: 'Why do you speak so much about this everywhere?' forgive me, I will answer immediately. First, for it is not easy to demonstrate what this is that you say: to be 'overcome by pleasure.' Second, because all demonstrations are in this. And now even if there is something pressing which you wish to explain, you may, if you have any other way to say what is good other than pleasure, and what is bad other than pain. Or is it enough for you to lead a life pleasantly without sadness? If it is enough, and you cannot say there is another good or evil that does not tend toward these, hear what follows. I say indeed, these things being so, that your speech is ridiculous, in which you say that a man does bad things, knowing they are bad, yet nevertheless does them although he could not do them, because he is drawn and conquered by pleasures. Likewise when you say a man conscious of the good does not wish to act well, being bound by present pleasure. These things, I say, will be shown to be ridiculous, unless we wish to use many names: the pleasant, the sad, the good, and the bad. Since it is agreed that these are two in general, let us call them by only two names: first indeed, good and bad; later, pleasant and sad. These things being positioned, let us say thus: 'There is a man who knows that bad things are bad, and he does them nevertheless.' If someone asks why, we answer: 'Because he was conquered.' 'By what?' he will ask. It will not be permitted to us to say further 'conquered by pleasure.' For it has taken another name in place of pleasure: 'the good.' Let us answer him then, and say: 'Because he was conquered.' 'By what?' he will ask. 'By heaven, by the good,' we shall answer. If then he who questions us happens to be an insulting man, he will surely laugh and say it is an absurd statement. 'For if someone does bad things, knowing they are bad, when he ought not to do them, because he was conquered by goods... are these goods worthy to conquer bad things, or unworthy?' We shall say they are unworthy, for he whom we say was overcome by pleasures would not have erred. To this he will say: 'For what reason are those goods unworthy to conquer evils, or evils to conquer goods? Is it for any other reason than because these are greater, and those smaller? Or these more, and those fewer?' We certainly will have no other cause. He will add: 'It is clear, therefore, that to be overcome is to take up greater evils in place of smaller goods.' Let these things be so. Let us change the names, and let us accept in the same matter 'pleasant' and 'sad.' In this way: we said before a man does bad things; let us now say 'sad things,' although he knows they are sad, because he is conquered by pleasures—by such ones, namely, that are unworthy of victory. And what other unworthiness is in pleasure compared to pain than the excess and defect between them? That is, when they become greater or smaller than each other, or more and fewer, or more vehement and more remiss. If someone should say: 'But it differs much, O Socrates, between present pleasure and future pleasure and trouble,' I would say indeed: 'Is it by any other thing than pleasure and trouble? For it cannot be by anything else.' But it is just as if a man skilled in weighing, having collected pleasant things on this side and sad things on that side—both those which are near and those which are far—should search with a balance and say which are more. For if you weigh pleasant things against pleasant things, the greater and more are always to be chosen; but if you compare sad things to sad things, the fewer and smaller; if pleasant with sad, and the sad are overcome by the pleasant—whether near by remote, or remote by near—that reckoning is to be chosen in which these are present; but if the pleasant are overcome by the sad, not at all. Or does the matter stand otherwise, O men? I know indeed they can assert nothing else." PROTAGORAS: "I also judge the same." SOCRATES: "Since truly it is so, I will ask them in this way. Do the same masses appear to your eyes larger close at hand, and smaller far off? They will affirm it, I think. And thick things and many things similarly? And equal voices larger near, but smaller far away? They will agree. If in this our acting well and happiness consisted—that is, in building and receiving great masses, but rejecting small ones—what would be our most powerful safety of life? Would it be the art of measurement? Or rather optics, showing how great a thing appears? Rather, this would deceive us, and confusing us with error would often force us to judge the same things differently at different times, and to change our counsel too often in the choices of great and small things. But the faculty of measurement would abrogate and refute this appearance, and opening the truth it would give rest to the soul relying on truth, and thus would save life. Would men agree to this, or not: that we are saved by the measuring art?" PROTAGORAS: "By this very one." SOCRATES: "What further? If our safety of life consisted in the choice itself of even and odd, when it would be necessary to choose correctly what is more and when what is less—either itself compared to itself, or perhaps one to another, whether near or far—what would most of all save our life? Would it not be knowledge? And indeed of measuring, since that art is of excess and defect. But when the ratio of even and odd is to be had, it is no other than the science of numbering. Would men grant us these things, or not?" PROTAGORAS: "Without controversy." SOCRATES: "Come, O men. Since indeed the safety of life is certain to consist in the right choice of pleasure and pain—that is, in the selection of more and fewer, greater and smaller, nearer and more remote—is not the faculty of measurement first a considerer of excess, defect, and mutual equality?" PROTAGORAS: "Necessarily." SOCRATES: "Since truly it is the faculty of measurement..."

<summary>Socrates develops the "hedonistic calculus," arguing that what people call "being overcome by pleasure" is actually a failure of measurement—an intellectual error in which people choose a small immediate pleasure over a future greater good, simply because it is closer in time.</summary>
<keywords>hedonistic calculus, art of measurement, optics, appearance vs. truth, safety of life, weighing pleasures, ignorance</keywords>

### [Page 172]
# Book Seventeen [Protagoras]

...it is necessary that there be an art and a science. PROTAGORAS: They will admit it.
SOCRATES: What this science may specifically be, we shall consider elsewhere. For now, it suffices that it is a science, which pertains to that demonstration which I and Protagoras were going to give in response to your question. This, if you remember, was the question: We indeed agreed that nothing is more powerful than knowledge; rather, that wherever it is present, it always rules over pleasure and all other things. But you objected that pleasure and pain rule over choice. Since we in no way granted this to you, you immediately asked: "If this, O Protagoras and Socrates, is not 'to be overcome by pleasures,' but something else, declare what it is." Here, if we had immediately replied that it is "ignorance," you would have laughed at us. But now, if you laugh at us, you will also laugh at yourselves. For you yourselves confessed a little while ago that those who fail in their choice regarding pleasure and pain err through a defect of knowledge—these being goods and evils. And you did not say merely through a defect of knowledge, but you added: through a defect of the science of measurement. An action that errs and which science does not govern, as is not hidden from you, proceeds from ignorance. Wherefore, what is commonly said—to be overcome by pleasures—is the extreme of ignorance. Of which disease [OCR: *iut morbi*] Protagoras here, and Prodicus, and Hippias, profess themselves to be doctors. But you, because you think this is something other than ignorance, give neither yourselves nor your sons to these sophists, the teachers of these matters, to be cared for, as if virtue cannot be taught; but by using your money unprofitably, and not applying it to these instructors, you fail both privately and publicly. This is clearly what we would have responded to the common people.

But now I ask you also, O Prodicus and Hippias, together with Protagoras—for let this discourse be common with you—whether I seem to speak the truth to you, or false things? It seemed to all that it was said very truly. "Do you grant then," I said, "that what is pleasant is good, and what is sad is evil?" Indeed, I reject that distinction of names which Prodicus here is accustomed to introduce, and I require his judgment. For whether you call it 'pleasurable,' or 'delightful,' or 'joyous,' or however else you might name it, most excellent Prodicus, answer me now what I wish. Prodicus, smiling, assented, and the others likewise agreed.

Then I said: "What of this, O men? Are not all actions which pertain to living pleasantly and without trouble honorable and useful? And is an honorable work not good and useful?" They assented. "If therefore the pleasant is good," I said, "no one, either knowing or thinking other things to be better than those he does, and being able to do them, then does these [lesser] things when he could do the better. For what is said to be 'overcome by affections' is nothing other than ignorance; and to 'rule over affections' is nothing other than wisdom." This pleased everyone. "What then of ignorance? Do you not say it is something such as when one is deceived by a false opinion concerning things of great value?" This too they granted. "No one indeed willingly descends toward evils, or toward those things which he deems to be evil. Nor does it seem to be in the nature of man to wish to decline toward what he judges evil in place of goods. And when he is forced to choose one of two evils, no one chooses the worse when it is permitted to choose that which is the lesser evil." All these things seemed to be held as settled by us.

"What," I said, "do you call fear and terror? Is it not what I say to you, Prodicus? A certain expectation of evil—whether you call it fear or terror—is what I say." It seemed to Protagoras and Hippias that fear and terror were this; but to Prodicus, fear was indeed this, but terror was not. "That matters nothing," I said, "O Prodicus, but this: whether the things said above are true. Who among mortals would wish to proceed toward those things which he fears, while it is permitted to go toward those he does not fear? Or is it impossible, according to those things we have already granted? For it was established that what someone fears, he thinks to be evil; and that no one willingly descends to those things, or takes up those things which he believes to be evil." These things also pleased everyone.

"These things being established, O Prodicus," I said, "and Hippias, let that which Protagoras first answered now be brought down [examined]. Or rather, not what he said at the very first. For he said that of the five parts of virtue, none was similar to the other, but each had its own private power. I do not press this now, but what followed. For he said in the following: that four parts of virtue are close enough to each other, but one of them, namely courage, differs far from the rest. Which he said could be conjectured from the fact that many men are found to be most brave, who are yet most profane, most unjust, most intemperate, and most ignorant; from which he wished it to be evident that courage differs most from all other parts of virtue. At which response I was immediately greatly astonished, and even more so after I treated these things with you. Therefore I inquired of him whether he called the brave 'bold' [audacious]. He indeed added 'precipitate' [headlong] besides. Do you remember, Protagoras, that you answered these things?"

PROTAGORAS: I remember.
SOCRATES: Tell us, I pray, for what reason do you call precipitate men brave? Is it toward those things which the timid approach?
PROTAGORAS: No.
SOCRATES: Therefore toward other things?
PROTAGORAS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: Do the timid approach things to be dared? And the brave things to be feared?
PROTAGORAS: So it is said, O Socrates.
SOCRATES: You tell the truth. But I do not ask this; rather, for what reason do you call the precipitate brave? Is it toward evils, knowing them to be evil and ruinous, or rather toward those which are not such?
PROTAGORAS: It was shown by you in the previous arguments that this is impossible.
SOCRATES: And in this too you speak truly. Wherefore, if this has been correctly demonstrated, no one approaches those things which he indicates to be evil and ruinous, since it was established that what is called 'being overcome by affections' is ignorance.
PROTAGORAS: Clearly.
SOCRATES: But indeed, everyone approaches those things which they dare, both the timid and the brave. And by this reasoning, both the timid and the brave approach the same things.
PROTAGORAS: On the contrary, O Socrates, those things toward which the brave and the timid strive are altogether opposite. For these are willing to go to war, but those are unwilling.
SOCRATES: Is going [to war] honorable or base?
PROTAGORAS: Honorable.
SOCRATES: If it is honorable, did we not also agree above that it is good? For it is agreed that all honorable and beautiful actions are also good.
PROTAGORAS: You speak the truth, and it always seems so to me.
SOCRATES: Correct. But whom do you say are unwilling to go into battle, when that journey is beautiful and good?
PROTAGORAS: The timid.
SOCRATES: If it is beautiful and good, is it not also pleasant?
PROTAGORAS: It has been granted.
SOCRATES: Do the timid, knowing this, refuse to proceed toward that which is more beautiful, better, and more pleasant?
PROTAGORAS: But if we admit this, we shall overturn what was agreed upon earlier.
SOCRATES: What further? Does the brave man not tend toward that which is more beautiful, better, and more pleasant?
PROTAGORAS: It is necessary to confess it.
SOCRATES: Altogether, therefore, brave men do not fear basely, if ever they fear, nor do they dare basely.
PROTAGORAS: It is so.
SOCRATES: If not basely, then honorably and beautifully.
PROTAGORAS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: If honorably, then also well.
PROTAGORAS: Truly.
SOCRATES: And do not the timid...

***

### [Page 173]
# Protagoras, Or, the Sophists.

...and the fierce and the furious, on the contrary, dare basely and fear basely?
PROTAGORAS: That is so.
SOCRATES: But for what other cause do they dare basely and badly, if not because of lack of skill and ignorance?
PROTAGORAS: Because of this very thing.
SOCRATES: This thing by which they are timid, do you call it timidity or courage?
PROTAGORAS: Timidity.
SOCRATES: But have the timid not appeared to be so because of ignorance of things to be feared?
PROTAGORAS: Surely.
SOCRATES: Because of this ignorance, therefore, they are timid?
PROTAGORAS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: You asserted that that which makes them timid is timidity.
PROTAGORAS: I asserted it.
SOCRATES: Is not, therefore, the ignorance of what is to be feared and what is not to be feared, timidity?
PROTAGORAS: It will be.
SOCRATES: But indeed, courage is the opposite of timidity.
PROTAGORAS: Without a doubt.
SOCRATES: Is not the wisdom concerning what is to be feared and what is not to be feared the opposite of the ignorance of those same things?
PROTAGORAS: Entirely.
SOCRATES: And the ignorance of these things is timidity.
PROTAGORAS: Very much so.
SOCRATES: Therefore, the wisdom of what is to be feared and what is not to be feared is courage, being the opposite of the ignorance of the same.

Protagoras no longer assented further, but was silent. Then I said: "Why are you silent, Protagoras? Why do you neither assent nor deny?" He said: "Finish the matter yourself." "I shall conclude immediately," I said, "if I may ask only this one thing: whether it still seems to you now, as before, that there are some who are most unskilled, yet who are nevertheless most brave."

"You seem to strive obstinately, O Socrates," he said, "that I myself should answer; therefore I will comply with you. I say it seems impossible, from those things which were granted above."

"For no other cause," I said, "do I inquire of you concerning all these things, than that I desire to know of what sort they are which pertain to virtue, or what virtue itself is. I know indeed that with this declared, that thing will immediately be known about which you and I have consumed so many words: while I denied that virtue could be taught, and you asserted it could. And yet I think the outcome of our dispute, if it could take voice like a human [being], would laugh at us, and would rebuke us in this way: 'How foolish you are, O Socrates and Protagoras. You, Socrates, said from the beginning that virtue could not be taught, yet now you strive to contradict yourself, while you wish to show that all these—namely justice, temperance, and courage—are knowledge. By which reasoning it most clearly follows that virtue can be taught. For if virtue were something other than knowledge, which Protagoras first asserted, it clearly could not be taught. But now if it appears to be knowledge, as you, O Socrates, endeavor to infer, it would be a wonder if virtue could not be acquired through doctrine. Protagoras, however, at first wished virtue to be taught: now on the contrary he seems to labor so that virtue may appear to be anything else rather than knowledge; by which means it would be taught least of all.'

Indeed, O Protagoras, seeing all these things heavily disturbed upside-down, I apply myself vehemently so that they may come into the light. I would wish, these things having been run through between us, that we might show what virtue is, and likewise consider whether it can be taught or not; lest that Epimetheus deceive us again in the dispute, just as he neglected us in the distribution, as you related. For Prometheus in the fable pleases me more than Epimetheus; using whose example and being 'promethume'—that is, provident—of my whole life, I treat all these things. And if you wish, I would most gladly deliberate with you concerning these matters as I said from the beginning."

Then Protagoras said: "I praise this zeal of yours, O Socrates, and the course of your discourse. For since other vices, unless opinion deceives me, are absent from me, envy certainly is absent most of all. And concerning you indeed, I have already said often among many that I marvel at you most of all those I have met, certainly of those of your age. I add furthermore that it will be no wonder to me if you turn out famous in the study of wisdom. And concerning these things we shall discourse at another time whenever you wish. Now it is time that I betake myself to other things."

"So it must be done," I said, "if it seems so to you, since already for some time, as I said, it was time for me to depart; nevertheless, I persisted to comply with the honorable youth Callias." These things having been said and heard, we departed.

### [Page 175]
# Euthydemus, Or, the Disputatious.

# CRITO, SOCRATES, EUTHYDEMUS, DIONYSODORUS, CLINIAS, CTESIPPUS.

**C**RITO: Who was that, O Socrates, with whom you were disputing yesterday in the Lyceum? A large crowd was surrounding you. Wherefore, although I wished to approach closer to hear the matter, I could not perceive anything clearly. But when, standing on tiptoe, I looked in, he seemed to me to be a certain stranger with whom you were debating. Who was he?

SOCRATES: Which one are you asking about, Crito? For there was not only one, but two were present.

CRITO: The third one, sitting at your right, is the one I mean. But in the middle was that youth, the son of Axiochus, who seemed to me to have progressed quite a bit. He is nearly the same age as our Critobulus. But while that one has a leaner habit of body, this one seems to present the appearance of one more grown in years, of a truly honorable and excellent character.

SOCRATES: Euthydemus is the one you seek, O Crito. The one who sat at my left was Dionysodorus his brother, who also himself was disputing.

CRITO: I know neither of them, O Socrates.

SOCRATES: They are new, it seems, sophists.

CRITO: What is their native land? What is their wisdom?

SOCRATES: They are from Chios, I believe, by birth; but they migrated to Thurii. Fleeing from there, they have been living in these parts for many years now. Concerning their wisdom which you ask about, O Crito, they are plainly most wise. And until now, I did not know that they were perfect athletes. For they are equipped for every kind of contesting, not in the manner of the Acarnanian athlete brothers. For those are strong only in body, but these are first of all most strong in speech, and in that kind of fight by which everything is overcome. For they are most skilled in arms, and can make others skilled in arms if anyone gives them a fee. Then they can handle and expedite judicial fighting, and instruct anyone, both in writing and in pleading cases. And until now they were skilled in these things only, but now they have imposed a limit on perfect athletics. For whatever kind of contesting was lacking, they have recently attained it so that no one can resist them; they are so strong in speaking, and prompt to repel any statement, whether true or false. Wherefore, O Crito, I am thinking of handing myself over to these men; for they promise that they will make anyone else a master of the same things in a short time.

[Margin: *That a greater age ought not to frighten one away from discipline.*]

CRITO: Does not your older age deter you, O Socrates?

SOCRATES: Not at all, Crito. For there is something that consoles me and does not let me distrust. For these men too, now old, so to speak, have given themselves with contention to this faculty which I now affect. For in the previous year, or certainly the third from now, they were not yet skilled. But I fear this one thing only, lest I be a disgrace to these strangers, just as to Connus the son of Metrobius, the lyre-player, who even now teaches me the strings. The boys, my fellow-disciples, therefore laugh at me every day, and call Connus himself "the teacher of old men." Lest someone object the same to these strangers, and they, deterred by that, reject me, I have exhorted some others, O Crito, great in age, to set out there with me for the sake of learning; and here likewise I shall try to persuade some. Why don't you also go along? Rather, let us even bring your sons as an enticement to them. For when they hope for the gathering of your sons, they, led by these enticements, will more willingly receive us to be educated.

CRITO: Nothing prevents it, Socrates, if it seems so to you. But first tell me what their wisdom is, so that I may know what we are about to perceive.

SOCRATES: You wait in vain for me to say I cannot, as if I had not listened enough; rather, I both listened diligently and I remember, and I shall try to relate everything to you from the beginning. By a certain divine chance, I was sitting alone in the place where the athletes undress, where you saw me, and I was already thinking of departing from there, when suddenly that usual sign of the daemon obstructed me as I was rising. I stopped, therefore, and a little later Euthydemus and Dionysodorus entered, and with them many others, who seemed to me to be their disciples. Having entered, they were walking about in the covered track. They had scarcely completed the space a second and third time when that Clinias arrived, who you say has progressed greatly—and you speak truly. Many friends and others followed him, then a certain youth Ctesippus of Paeania, of good character indeed and handsome, but more wanton because of his very youth. Clinias, having caught sight of me sitting alone from the entrance, came toward me and sat down at my right, just as you said. Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, having seen him, first stood still and spoke to each other, turning their eyes on us from here and there. For I was observing them most diligently. Then, approaching closer, they sat down: Euthydemus indeed next to the youth himself, but Dionysodorus next to me at my left, and the others as there was a place for each. Therefore I congratulated them, as not having seen them for a long time.

After this, turning to Clinias: "These men, Clinias," I said, "Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, are wise not in small matters, but in the greatest. They know all things that pertain to military matters, whatever it becomes a strenuous commander to know, the instructions of the line and ranks, and of the army. Then also they can teach how someone may vindicate himself from injury in a court." But they looked down upon me speaking so, and looking at each other, both laughed. And Euthydemus indeed said: "We no longer treat these things seriously, O Socrates, but in passing." But I, marveling, said: "Your studies must be magnificent, if your diversions are so great. Tell me, I pray, what is this most excellent work of yours?"

EUTHYDEMUS: Virtue, O Socrates, we persuade ourselves can be taught by us most easily and best of all.

SOCRATES: By Jupiter, what a precious thing you promise! By what stroke of luck did that gain reach you? For until now I thought of you, as I said, as men excelling in military matters, and I preached that of you. For I remember when you first came here, you professed this only; but if now you have truly attained this science, be propitious—indeed I salute you just as gods, beseeching that you forgive what I said before. But see, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, whether you speak the truth. For it is no wonder...

# Protagoras, or, The Sophist. 173

...and do the timid, the fierce, and the frenzied, on the contrary, dare things shamefully, and fear things shamefully? PROTAGORAS: That is so. SOCRATES: But is there any other reason they dare things shamefully and badly, except through ignorance and lack of skill? PROTAGORAS: For that very reason. SOCRATES: Now this, which makes them timid—do you call it cowardice or courage? PROTAGORAS: Cowardice. SOCRATES: And did the timid not appear to be so because of their lack of skill regarding things to be feared? PROTAGORAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: It is because of this lack of skill, then, that they are timid—if cowardice is indeed what it could be. PROTAGORAS: I have agreed to that. SOCRATES: Therefore, will not cowardice be the lack of skill regarding what is to be feared and what is not to be feared? PROTAGORAS: It will be. SOCRATES: Yet courage is the opposite of cowardice. PROTAGORAS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: And is not wisdom regarding what is to be feared and what is not to be feared the opposite of the lack of skill regarding those same things? PROTAGORAS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And the lack of skill regarding these things is cowardice. PROTAGORAS: Most certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, wisdom regarding what is to be feared and what is not to be feared is courage, <note>Socrates concludes his "intellectualist" argument: if you truly know what is dangerous and what isn't, you will act rightly. Thus, courage is a type of knowledge.</note> existing as the opposite of the lack of skill regarding those same things.

Protagoras nodded no further, but remained silent. Then I said: Why are you silent, Protagoras? Why do you neither nod in agreement nor refuse? He said: Finish the matter yourself. I said: I shall conclude immediately, if I may ask just this one thing: whether you still think now, as you did before, that there are some who are extremely ignorant and yet extremely courageous. You seem, O Socrates, he said, to contend stubbornly that I should be the one to answer; therefore, I will grant you your way. I say that it appears impossible, based on those things that were conceded above.

I am not, I said, inquiring about all these things for any other reason than that I desire to know what sort of things pertain to virtue, and what virtue itself is. Indeed, I know that once this is explained, that other point will immediately become known—the one about which you and I have already spent so many words: I denying that virtue could be taught, while you asserted it could be. And yet, I think the outcome of our dispute, if it could use a human voice, would laugh at us and rebuke us in this way: "How foolish you are, O Socrates and Protagoras! You, Socrates, were saying from the beginning that virtue could not be taught, yet now you strive to contradict yourself by wanting to show that all these things—namely justice, temperance, and courage—are knowledge. By this reasoning, it is most clear that virtue *can* be taught. For if virtue were something other than knowledge, as Protagoras first asserted, it clearly could not be taught. But now, if it appears to be knowledge, as you, Socrates, are trying to infer, it would be a wonder if virtue could not be acquired through instruction. Protagoras, on the other hand, at first wanted virtue to be taught; now, conversely, he seems to strive so that virtue appears to be anything else rather than knowledge—in which case it would be taught least of all."

Indeed, Protagoras, seeing that all these things are so heavily disturbed and turned upside down, I am leaning in with great effort so that they might come into the light. I would wish that, after these matters have been run through between us, we might show what virtue is, and likewise consider whether it can be taught or not—lest that Epimetheus <note>In Greek mythology, Epimetheus means "afterthought." He forgot to give humans natural defenses (claws, fur) during creation.</note> deceive us again in our dispute, just as he neglected us in the distribution of gifts, as you narrated. For Prometheus <note>Prometheus means "forethought." He stole fire to save humanity after his brother's mistake.</note> in the fable pleases me more than Epimetheus; using his example and being *promethumenus* <note original: "promethumenus, id est, prospiciens">forethinking—that is, looking forward</note> in my whole life, I handle all these matters. And if you are willing, as I said from the beginning, I would most gladly deliberate with you about these things.

Then Protagoras said: I praise this zeal of yours, Socrates, and the course of your discourse. For while other vices, unless my opinion deceives me, are absent from me, envy is certainly absent most of all. And indeed, I have already said of you to many people often that of all those I have met, I admire you most—certainly among those of your own age. I add, moreover, that it would be no wonder to me if you should become famous for your pursuit of wisdom. But we shall discuss these things at some other time whenever you wish. Now it is already the hour for me to attend to other matters. So be it, I said, if it seems right to you, since for a long time now, as I said, it was time for me to depart; nevertheless, to indulge the noble youth Callias, I stayed. After these things were said and heard, we departed.

->**PLATO’S EUTHYDEMUS, OR, THE CONTENTIOUS.**<-

->**MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT.**<-

Plato, a man of remarkable charity, strives in the *Euthydemus* (as he often does elsewhere) to turn minds born for serious things away from the empty trifles of the sophists. He shows that even when the gravest matters are discussed, they play games and everywhere delude the hopes of their audience. These men he describes elsewhere in other ways, but here he describes them as curious and vain contestants in the altercation of words, ready to refute any statement, whether it be true or false.

**First**, he shows how greedy the character of the sophists is, since Euthydemus and his brother Dionysodorus—both sophists—are ready to teach for a fee the military art in which they boast, which no one has ever sold before. **Secondly**, how ambitious they are. For they profess judicial skill together with military skill, and both together with the sophistic art—things which are vastly different from one another. **Thirdly**, how vain they are: for they often turn from things to words, and from the pursuit of truth to lies. **Fourthly**, how contemptible: for in a short time—within two years at most—any caviller can attain this faculty. **Fifthly**, how dangerous: for who should wonder that simple youths are easily ensnared by the painted cleverness of the sophists, and are imbued with false opinions and ruinous habits? Especially since Socrates himself, the wisest of old men, is portrayed as being caught by the same bait and hastening with wonder to the sophists' schools.

Add to this that the Socratic *daemon* <note>The "daimonion" was Socrates' internal divine sign or "voice" that warned him against certain actions.</note> which seems unable to be deceived by anyone, is portrayed as being deceived by the sophistic tricks of these rascals. Meanwhile, Socrates, even in his old age, frequenting the schools of boys, music lessons, and the rudiments of words, warns us: first, that we should not despise even the smallest thing for the perfection of disciplines; second, that we should not (as often happens) be kept from the study of disciplines by a rustic blush of shame; third, that we should think, in the manner of Solon <note>Solon of Athens famously said, "I grow old ever learning many things."</note>, that we must learn for as long as we must live.

Furthermore, the fact that the sophists never notice the Socratic irony directed against them—rather, nothing so magnificent is brought forward in their praise that they do not very easily believe and openly accept it—declares two things to us especially: first, that nothing more empty than these rascals can be found; and second, that while they study more intensely to deceive others, they are surely most easily deceived by their own fallacy. Moreover, the fact that jugglers of this sort never provide the virtue they promise, nor do they ever exhort anyone toward it, but everywhere flee to their accustomed verbal quibbles—setting these above other studies as if they were serious matters—signifies three things to us: **First**, those who are not themselves adorned with virtue can never teach it by reason or example. **Second**, men too curious about words never attain or bring about good things. **Third**, those who most easily promise the most things are the ones who least of all keep their promises.

To these is added the fact that Socrates lures the sophists into teaching virtue by mentioning a crowd of wealthy disciples, as they are exceedingly ambitious and greedy. But there, under the persona of Crito, we are warned not to rashly commit our minds to just anyone's care. But the fact that Socrates, while the sophists promise virtue, meanwhile implores them as if they were gods, clearly declares that virtue must be sought from God himself, and that men endowed with virtue are to be held as divine. Likewise, the fact that he considers them happier than kings because of their pursuit of virtue clearly signifies that a man endowed with virtue is, first of all, king of himself, and then of a kingdom. Socrates further teaches, in the care of Clinias, how great...

--- Page 193 ---
174 . Book Eighteen.

...with what charity and how much diligence we ought to apply ourselves to the care of youth. But soon, under the promises of the most insolent sophists, "the mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse is born" <note>A quote from Horace, meaning a great deal of fuss resulting in a tiny outcome.</note>. But one must also note there the hyperbolic irony of Socrates used to mock vain men. Then there is the incomparable vanity of these scoundrels, offering words instead of things—and the most inept words at that—everywhere falling back into childish nonsense even when they have promised an exhortation to wisdom. Then Socrates says the entire school of the sophists is a game of words, and that the nature of things is entirely hidden from them, and that their artificial webs can be dissolved by the mere exposition of words and the distinction of meanings. 

He then implores the sophists with a most witty irony to come to serious matters after their games; and he proposes a certain formula, by the example of which he will demand from them an exhortation to philosophy. In this formula, he first describes happiness by a common notion: "living well." Then he proves that this "living well" consists either in the attainment of things according to one's wish, or in the right use of those same things. And from both sides, he concludes through inductions. He concludes that wisdom alone, since it both attains things according to the wish and uses them rightly, alone makes men blessed. 

There, such an order is seen in the inductions: if through the individual parts of the way wisdom both attains the wish and uses it rightly, then wisdom brings the same common end of life and the highest good in the successful attainment and right use of life as a whole. In the course of arguing, a brilliant sentiment shines forth which is the foundation of the Stoic sect: namely, that external and bodily things are "indifferent" <note>In Stoic philosophy, things like wealth or health are neither good nor bad in themselves; only virtue is good.</note> and common, rather than to be called either good or bad. Properly speaking, wisdom is good, while foolishness is bad. Since through the former all things turn out good for us, and through the latter all things turn out bad. Therefore, only wisdom can make men blessed. 

That the power to achieve happiness consists entirely in knowledge is declared by the three names for happiness established by the ancient Greek authors: namely, *Eudaimonia*, *Eutychia*, and *Eupragia*. The first signifies the knowledge of the good, the second the attainment, and the third the use; all of which knowledge perfects for us. Plato says here and elsewhere that this knowledge of the good is in a way all virtue. Wisdom is the absolute and divine knowledge of the good. Prudence <note>original: "prudentia"</note> is the knowledge of goods and evils properly pertaining to man. Justice is also the knowledge of goods and evils to be distributed according to merit. Courage is the knowledge concerning goods and evils to be dared or feared. Finally, temperance is the knowledge concerning goods and evils to be similarly adopted or fled. 

One must remember above all things here that Plato hints, both here and often elsewhere, that wisdom is not so much acquired by human study as it is usually infused by divine power into purified minds. Therefore, when the soul joined to this body is rendered inept for things entirely separate from the body, it grows dim like an owl in the excessive splendor of divine things. For this reason, the Socratic exhortation to wisdom pertains not so much to speculation as to morals. By these morals, the soul is finally purified and attains wisdom from God, as well as knowledge and prudence. Through these things, while Socrates feigns to demand from the sophists an exhortation to philosophy (which is the study of wisdom), he meanwhile, with a most apt dissimulation, wonderfully exhorts them to philosophize. 

Nevertheless, the sophists do not yet accept the exhortation for themselves or for others, but roll back into their usual nonsense. Here it appears how stubborn an intellect always is, whether in vices or in trifles, when it is either wrongly born or poorly educated. Among these things, observe most diligently the divine sentiment of Plato, by which we are commanded, for the sake of attaining virtue and wisdom, to endure not only inconveniences, losses, labors, and servitude: but even if we hope that from our very dissolution we shall finally emerge better, we should permit ourselves to be flayed, liquefied, and entirely dissolved by him who has promised this very thing. Here it appears how much the good of the soul exceeds bodily things, and how much those ancient and most brave Christian martyrs are to be praised. This is similar to that saying: "He who loves his soul in this world shall lose it; but he who loses it here shall receive it back in eternal life." 

Furthermore, Socrates, by refuting the sophists' little traps, demonstrates that sophisms can most easily be turned back against the sophists, especially because he forces them both to contradict themselves and to confess the most absurd things. Having done this, by feigning a formula similar to the previous one, he declares that the listeners receive no good from the sophists, and that the sophists themselves, like the most ruined men, cannot be brought back to good fruit. Because he often repeats three names during the dispute—wisdom, science, and prudence—it must be noted that when he speaks more precisely, he defines wisdom as the knowledge of divine things, science as knowledge of natural things, and prudence as knowledge of human things. Where he speaks less precisely, he usually uses the name of "science" <note>original: "scientia"; here meaning systematic knowledge.</note> to signify all three. But where he speaks more freely, he uses each one equally for all. 

Moreover, he introduces two kinds of arts: those that produce works, and those that use the things made. And since the art that uses the work of another art both prescribes the end of its manufacture and provides the model for completing the work, we not unjustly place the "using" art above the "making" art in dignity. Notice here that Plato makes so little of the making art, and so much of the using art, that he most clearly wants it understood that if someone could convert all materials into gold at will, or even provide immortality itself among men, neither that great mass of gold nor immortality would profit him unless he knew how to use it. Notice again that the common abuse of the oratorical art is criticized here as being entirely similar to the sophistical art—like a kind of wicked enchantment, struggling everywhere to infect souls with disturbances like a poison. For a similar reason, he elsewhere detests the common abuse of poets. 

But because in numbering the arts here he names "dialectics"—lest I should say "dialectice" in the manner of some, for "dialectics" <note>original: "dialectica"</note> sounds more Latin to me—one must remember that logic in Plato signifies the art that arranges the rules of names, speeches, and arguments; but dialectics signifies the wise investigation of the philosopher, using these rules to investigate the reasons for things, especially divine things, from which the highest reasons of the following things are also received; therefore, dialectics for the most part in Plato signifies theology for us. He names in the same place the "royal and civil art," namely the prudence of happily governing the human race. Whether this be in a private or public person, or in one or many, it is equally called by him "civil" as it is "royal." To this art, truly as if to a queen, he subjects all faculties that are occupied in acting and making, to which she gives laws and uses them as instruments and handmaidens. 

Similarly, he subjects to theology all the sciences that are occupied in speculation, to which these sciences relate just as the private arts relate to the royal art. Wherefore Socrates, while in the formula following the previous formula he seeks the faculty most conducive to happiness, rightly dismisses others and flees to the royal and theological art—especially since happiness consists in the best use of things, and these arts strive to bring the most correct use of both speculating and acting and making to all people in all things. He taught the same in the *Philebus*, the same in the last book of the *Laws*, the same in the books on the *Republic*, where for the happiness of the human race he instructs the future governor first in theology, and then in civil discipline, asserting that the divine Idea of the Good itself is hardly perceived except by the legitimate theologian; and unless it has been perceived, nothing can be acted rightly or disposed happily, either privately or publicly. 

Although this is so, Socrates nevertheless does not think these mysteries should be revealed here among adolescents and sophists. For soon the Socratic figure only exhorts the adolescents, only refutes the sophists, and finally teaches legitimate men. Here, therefore, under irony and dissimulation, he touches on such mysteries and feigns to hesitate, as if suffering from vertigo among the dizzy sophists. Perhaps he feigns to doubt whether theology and civil discipline provide happiness because he often confirms that the absolute perfection of neither theology nor civil discipline can be had by a human way, but rather by divine inspiration. Therefore, not unjustly distrusting human powers, he refers happiness to divine bounty, to which he undoubtedly also referred the wisdom of theology and the prudence of the civil art. 

Finally, all these things are to be accepted by us in such a way that human duties prepare minds for happiness, especially those most correctly governed under theological and civil discipline; but the most merciful goodness of God himself may finally grant the highest good of man through these things as if through intermediaries to those who have turned toward Him. I had determined to place an end here, sufficient for an argument or even a commentary; but a necessary question still detains me: to what purpose does the frequent irony of Socrates serve? This irony always hides Socrates' own good qualities, but often feigns the good qualities of those superior to him; and as much as it always detracts from Socrates, it just as often attributes to the proud. He achieves this with frequent jokes and wit, and often beyond belief, so that by depressing himself he makes the listeners more modest; while by extolling the proud beyond the measure of belief, he makes their pride a thing to be mocked by all. Truly, those who are praised beyond measure by Socrates, if they are not entirely lost, amend themselves, being confused by the blush of shame; but if they are already entirely lost, they themselves do not change, but those present avoid such ridiculous vanity of pride most cautiously by the example of his correction. 

Socratic irony is a very skillful, urbane, witty, and charming thing. It supports the truth more safely and avoids hatred, while it both aptly dissimulates its profession and clearly detracts from itself before it can be caught even secretly detracting from another; and what is greatest in correcting vices, it avoids the mark of being a slanderer. Through this, certainly near the end of this dialogue, he gathers the criticism of sophistical caviling into three heads. First, that

--- Page 194 ---
# Euthydemus, or, The Litigious One. 175

all the most esteemed people despise such trifles. Second, that sophisms confound themselves. Third, that even boys can achieve this flower of nonsense in a mere two days. Soon he descends from the sophist to the rhetorician. For both falsely profess civil virtue, as is written in the *Gorgias*: the sophist feigns the speculation of the philosopher, while the rhetorician feigns the moral discipline of the philosopher, far from the truth. He shows that rhetoricians and orators, while they profess to be both philosophers and statesmen at the same time, are entirely useless for both. 

Finally, he concludes the dialogue with a twin and most excellent sentiment. One is that we must care more that our sons be good than that they simply exist; and that you should leave them behind as good men, rather than leaving goods to them. The other is that one must philosophize entirely: since philosophy itself is a divine thing, and such a precious possession is not to be abandoned either because of its false professors or because of lying slanderers.
