### CRITO, SOCRATES, EUTHYDEMUS, DIONYSODORUS, CLINIAS, CTESIPPUS.

**CRITO:** Who was that, Socrates, with whom you were disputing yesterday in the Lyceum? A large crowd was standing around you. Therefore, although I approached closely, being desirous of hearing, I could perceive nothing clearly. But when I stood on my toes to look, he seemed to me to be some stranger with whom you were debating. Who was he?
**SOCRATES:** About which one are you asking, Crito? For there was not just one, but two were present.
**CRITO:** The third one, sitting at your right hand—he is the one I mean. Between you was that young boy, the son of Axiochus, who seemed to me to have made quite enough progress. He is about the same age as our Critobulus. But while Critobulus has a leaner habit of body, this boy seems to have the appearance of a more mature age, with a truly honorable and excellent nature.
**SOCRATES:** Euthydemus is the one you seek, O Crito. The one who sat on my left was Dionysodorus, his brother, who also took part in the debate.
**CRITO:** I know neither of them, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** They are, it seems, new sophists.
**CRITO:** What is their homeland? What is their wisdom?
**SOCRATES:** Chios is their homeland, I think; but they migrated to Thurii. Fleeing from there, they have lived in these parts for many years now. As for their wisdom about which you ask, Crito, they are plainly most wise. And until now, I did not even know they were perfect athletes. For they are trained in every kind of combat—not like the Acarnanian athlete brothers. For those only have strength in their bodies, but these are primarily strong in their speech, and in that kind of fighting by which all things are overcome. They are most skilled in arms, and can make others skilled in arms if someone pays them a fee. Furthermore, they can handle and prepare for judicial combat, and can instruct anyone both in writing and in pleading cases. And until now, they were skilled only in these things, but now they have perfectly put the finishing touch on their athletic faculty. For the kind of combat that was missing they have recently attained, so that no one can resist them; they are so strong in speaking, and ready to refute any statement, whether true or false. Therefore, Crito, I am thinking of handing myself over to these men. For they promise to make anyone else a master of the same things in a short time.
**CRITO:** Does your older age not deter you, Socrates?
<margin>That older age ought not to deter one from learning.</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Not at all, Crito. For there is something that consoles me and does not let me despair. For even these men, being already old, so to speak, have recently devoted themselves to this faculty which I now affect—namely, the litigious one. For in the previous year, or certainly three years ago, they were not yet skilled. One thing only I fear: that I may be a disgrace to these strangers, just as I am to Connus the son of Metrobius, the harpist, who even now teaches me the lyre. The boys who are my fellow-disciples laugh at me every day and call Connus "the teacher of old men." Lest someone should object the same to these strangers, and they, being deterred by that matter, reject me, I have exhorted some others, Crito—men of great age—to go there with me for the sake of learning; and here I will try to persuade some likewise. Why don't you come along too? Indeed, let us even bring your sons as bait for them. For when they hope for the attendance of your sons as well, being led by these baits, they will more willingly accept us for instruction.
**CRITO:** Nothing prevents it, Socrates, if it seems right to you. But first, tell me what their wisdom is, so that I may know what we are to perceive.
**SOCRATES:** You wait in vain for me to say I cannot, as if I had not listened enough; on the contrary, I both listened diligently and remember, and I will try to relate everything to you from the beginning. By some divine luck, I was sitting alone in the place where the athletes undress, where you saw me, and I was just thinking of leaving when the usual sign of the *daemon* <note>original: "dæmonis signũ"; Socrates' inner warning voice.</note> suddenly blocked me as I rose. So I stayed, and a little later Euthydemus and Dionysodorus entered, and with them many others who seemed to me to be their disciples. Having entered, they began to walk in the covered track. They had hardly completed their second or third lap when that Clinias arrived—who you say has progressed greatly, and you speak truly. He was followed by many friends and others besides, including a certain young man, Ctesippus the Paeanian, who is good and beautiful in nature, but rather wanton in his youth. 

Clinias, seeing me sitting alone from the entrance, came toward me and sat on my right, as you also said. Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, having noticed him, first stood and talked to each other, turning their eyes on us from here and there. For I was observing them most diligently. Then, approaching closer, they sat down: Euthydemus next to the youth himself, and Dionysodorus next to me on the left, the others as each found a place. I congratulated them, as people I had not seen for a long time. 

After this, turning to Clinias, I said, "These men, Clinias—Euthydemus and Dionysodorus—are wise not in small matters, but in the greatest. They know everything pertaining to military matters that it befits a future strenuous general to know: the arrangement of the line, the ranks, and the instructions of the army. Moreover, they can teach how someone might defend himself from injury in court." 

They, however, despised my speaking so, and looking at each other, both laughed. Euthydemus said, "We no longer treat these things seriously, Socrates, but only in passing." I, being amazed, said, "Your studies must be truly excellent if your diversions are so great. Tell me, I pray, what is this extraordinary work of yours?" 
**EUTHYDEMUS:** Virtue, O Socrates, we are persuaded can be taught by us most easily and best of all. 
**SOCRATES:** By Jupiter, what a precious thing you promise! By what luck did this gain come to you? Indeed, I had thought of you until now, as I said, as men outstanding in military matters, and I proclaimed that of you. For I remember when you first came here, you professed only this. But if you have now truly attained this knowledge, be propitious—indeed, I salute you just like gods, imploring you to forgive what I said before. But see, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, whether you speak the truth. For it should not seem a wonder if someone, estimating the magnitude of this thing you promise, finds it difficult to believe. 
**EUTHYDEMUS:** Know that it is so, O Socrates, entirely.

176 . Book Eighteen.

**SOCRATES:** ...it should not seem a wonder. I count you more blessed for the possession of this thing than that great king for his kingdom. But tell me, I pray, whether you intend to exhibit this wisdom of yours, or whether you have decided otherwise. 
**EUTHYDEMUS:** We have come for this very purpose, Socrates—to demonstrate it, and to teach it if anyone wishes to learn. 
**SOCRATES:** But as for whether everyone who lacks it wishes to learn, I myself bind my faith to you as a guarantor. I first, then also Clinias here, and furthermore Ctesippus himself, and the others you see here—pointing to Clinias' friends who were then standing around us. 

Ctesippus happened to be sitting at a distance from Clinias. When Euthydemus, during the dispute, leaned forward, he blocked Ctesippus' view of Clinias, as Clinias was sitting in the middle between us. Ctesippus rose and stood directly across from us, so that he could both see his friend and hear the disputants. Soon the others followed him—both Clinias' friends and the companions of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus—and immediately stood by us. Pointing to all these, I promised Euthydemus they would be his disciples. Ctesippus vehemently agreed, as did the others; they all encouraged him together to show the power of his wisdom. 

Then I said, "O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, you must gratify these people in all these ways, and demonstrate it even for my sake. To show everything would be a long task; but tell me this: can you make a man a good man only if he is already persuaded that he ought to learn from you? Or can you also do so for one who is not yet persuaded, and who does not think virtue can be taught at all, or that you are teachers of that matter? Is it the work of the same art to persuade a man so affected that virtue can be taught, and that you are the ones who can do it best? Is it so, I ask?" 
"It is the work of the same art, O Socrates," said Dionysodorus. 
"So you, above all other men," I said, "can exhort men to philosophy and the care of virtue as best as possible?" 
"So we think, Socrates," he said. 
"Show the rest later," I said, "but for now, I pray, persuade this young boy that he should apply himself with all his strength to the study of philosophy and virtue, and humor me and all these people. Furthermore, this young boy is of such care to me and all these that we desire most greatly that he turn out to be the best of men. He is the son of Axiochus, born from the elder Alcibiades <note>original: "Alcibiade maiore," though historically Clinias was the cousin of the famous Alcibiades.</note>; he is the cousin of the younger Alcibiades <margin>The elder and younger Alcibiades.</margin> who is now living. His name is Clinias. He is young. We fear for him as a youth, lest someone should perhaps get ahead of us and deflect his mind elsewhere and stain it. Therefore, you have come most opportunely. Unless it makes a difference, test the boy, and discourse with him while we are present." 

When I had said these things, Euthydemus said strongly and confidently, "It makes no difference, Socrates, provided the youth is willing to answer us." 
"He is not unaccustomed to it," I said. "For these people frequently meet and dispute among themselves, and ask many things. Therefore, it is likely he can answer." 

What followed, Crito—I wish I could recount it with the dignity it deserves! For it must not be thought a small thing to be able to narrate that inestimable wisdom. Wherefore I see that I must first, in the manner of poets, invoke the Muses and Memory. Euthydemus, I believe, began in this way: 
"Which men are they, O Clinias, who learn something? The wise, or the ignorant?" 

The boy, because of the weight of that question, blushed and looked at me in hesitation. I, noticing his disturbance, said, "Be of good courage, Clinias, and answer bravely whatever seems right to you. For I think you will attain the greatest advantage from this." As I was saying this, Dionysodorus whispered in my ear and said with a laugh, "I predict to you, Socrates, that whatever the boy answers, he will be refuted." 

Meanwhile, Clinias had answered—whence I was not permitted to warn the boy. He had answered that it is the wise who learn. To him, Euthydemus said: "Do you call some people teachers, or not?" He agreed. "Are teachers not the teachers of those who learn? Just as the harpist and the grammarian were the teachers of you and the other boys, and you were the disciples." He consented. "When you were learning, did you not yet know these same things you were learning?" "Not yet." "Were you wise when you were ignorant of these things?" "By no means." "If not wise, then ignorant." "Entirely." "So while you were learning what you were ignorant of, you were learning as ignorant ones." The youth nodded. "From this it follows that the ignorant learn, O Clinias, and not the wise, as you yourself thought." 

When he had said this, just as a chorus at the signal of their master, the followers of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus shouted and laughed with the greatest applause. And before the boy could catch his breath, Dionysodorus, taking up the discourse most brilliantly, said: "What then, O Clinias? When the grammarian has pronounced some things, which of the boys learn them? The wise, or the ignorant?" 
"The wise," said Clinias. 
"Therefore, the wise learn, and not the ignorant. Wherefore you did not answer correctly to Euthydemus a moment ago." 

At this, their friends shouted louder and laughed, wondering at the wisdom of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus. We, however, were silent as if stunned. When Euthydemus saw that we were rendered stunned, so that we might be drawn into even greater admiration of him, he did not yet let the boy go, but questioned him further, and in the manner of those who are vehemently trained in a chorus, he moved a double question on the same matter, saying: "Do those who learn, then, learn what they know, or what they do not know?" 

Then Dionysodorus again whispered in my ear, saying, "This too, Socrates, is such a thing as that which was brought forward above." 
"By Jupiter," I said, "even the previous one seemed brilliant to us." 
"We always propose inevitable questions in this way," he said. 
"Therefore," I said, "you seem to have no small authority among your disciples." 

Meanwhile, Clinias answered Euthydemus that those who learn, learn what they are ignorant of. Immediately he questioned him as before: "Do you yourself know your letters?" "I know them." "Do you not know them all?" "Yes, all." "When someone recites, does he not recite letters?" He conceded. "Therefore he recites what you know, since you yourself know all letters." He admitted this too. "Do you not learn what he recounts?" He agreed. "Do you learn while ignorant of letters?" "Not at all." "Rather, I learn while knowing them." "Do you not therefore learn what you know, since you know all letters?" He nodded. "You did not answer correctly, then." 

Hardly had Euthydemus said these things when Dionysodorus, taking up the speech like a ball, thus attacked the adolescent: "Euthydemus is deceiving you, O Clinias. Tell me: is not 'learning' the taking in of the knowledge of that which one learns?" Clinias admitted it. "But 'to know'—is it anything else than already having that knowledge itself?" He conceded. "Is 'not to know,' therefore, not yet having the knowledge?" He granted this too. "Which ones take something? Those who have it, or those who do not have it?" "Those who do not have it." "Did you not confess that ignorant men are among the number of those who do not have it?" He nodded. "Those who learn, therefore, are among the number of those who take, not of those who have." He proved it. "Therefore, those who do not know, O Clinias, learn—not those who know."

# Euthydemus, or, The Litigious One. 177

...those who do not know, O Clinias, learn, not those who know. After this, truly for the third time as if seeking a wrestling match, Euthydemus was attacking the adolescent. But I, pitying him as he was falling, began to console him in this way to refresh him a little, lest perhaps he should become too terrified. 

"Do not wonder, O Clinias, if these discourses are unfamiliar to you. For perhaps you do not know what these strangers intend. Indeed, they do the very thing that the Corybantes <note>Priests of the goddess Cybele known for wild, ecstatic dances and clashing cymbals.</note> are accustomed to do in the mysteries, when they place the one they are about to initiate on a throne, applaud, and lead dances around him. I think you understand, if you have been initiated. Similarly, these men are playing now, and leading dances and jumping around you, as if they are purifying you now so that they may soon initiate you into the sacred rites. Therefore, for the present, think that some first sacred ceremonies of the sophistical rites are being celebrated. 

For in the beginning, as Prodicus commands, it is fitting to hold to the proper meanings of names; which these strangers are also showing you. For you did not know how people use the word 'to learn' when they speak of these things. For they call it 'learning' both when someone attains something he did not hold before, and also when, having attained the knowledge of it, he considers that same thing with that same knowledge—whether it is when it exists or when it is spoken. You should call the latter 'to understand' rather than 'to learn,' although not rarely it is called 'to learn.' But that escaped you, as these men showed: namely, that the same name is attributed by men to contrary things—to knowing and to not knowing. 

And similar to this is that other thing they proposed in the second question, asking which people learn—those who know or those who do not know. All these things are a kind of play <note>original: "ludi," meaning a game or diversion.</note> in the disciplines, and I say these men are playing with you. I call it a game for this reason: because even if someone knew many or even all things of this kind, he would understand the nature of things no better, yet he could play with men by that diversity of names—tripping them up and laying them prostrate like someone using a pipe, in the manner of those who secretly pull stools away from those who wish to sit, and laugh more loudly when they see the one who fell lying on his back. Therefore, take these things for games. 

Next, however, these men will treat serious matters with you, and I will demand from them what they promised: namely, in what way someone might be impelled toward wisdom. But now it seems to me they thought they should joke with you first. Therefore, let this be enough of your playing, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus. And perhaps it is enough. Show now what follows. It remains for you to lead this adolescent toward the study of virtue and wisdom. And I will say in the beginning what seems right to me, and what I most of all desire to hear. But if I do so unskillfully and ridiculously, I pray, do not laugh. It is the desire for hearing your wisdom that makes me not hesitate to bring forth my ineptitudes before you. You and your disciples will therefore contain your laughter. 

You, son of Axiochus, answer me: do we all desire to 'act well,' that is, to 'live well'? Or perhaps this question, as I feared, is among the number of those that are ridiculous? For it is the part of a madman, I think, to ask such things. For who is there among all men who does not desire to live well?" 
"No one," said Clinias. 
"Come then," I said, "since we wish to live well, in what way is it possible to attain it? Would it be if we have many good things? Or is someone so inept as to deny this? For it is agreed to be so." 
"It is agreed," he said. 
"But which things from every kind of thing are good?" I said. "Is that perhaps not hard to find, nor to be doubted by an elegant man? For who is there who would deny that it is good to be rich? Is it not so?" 
"Most certainly," he said. 
"And is it not also good to be healthy," I said, "and beautiful, and endowed with the other gifts of the body?" 
"Certainly," he said. 
"Furthermore, are noble birth, power, and honors in each man's city not good things?" 
"Those too," he said. 
"What good things remain besides?" I said. "If we say that temperance, justice, and courage are good, shall we be speaking correctly? For someone might perhaps doubt it. But what do you say?" 
"They must certainly be called good," he said. 
"And wisdom," I said, "in what class shall we place it? Among the good things, or otherwise?" 
"In the class of good things," he said. 
"See," I said, "lest we overlook any of the good things worthy of any reason." 
"It seems to me," he said, "that we have overlooked none." 

Here, thinking for a little while, I said: "We seem, O Clinias, to have postponed the greatest of all good things." 
"What is this?" he said. 
"Happiness <note>original: "Felicitatem"</note>," I said, "which even the most ignorant of men call the highest good." 
"You speak the truth," he said. 
And I, with a changed sentiment, said: "We almost moved our guests to laughter, O Clinias." 
"Why so?" he said. 
"Because when we had already placed 'happiness' before," I said, "we were talking about that same matter again." 
"How so?" he said. 
"It is ridiculous to place again what was placed before, and to recount the same things twice." 
"For what reason do you say that?" 
"Wisdom itself is happiness," I said, "which indeed even any boy might understand." 
<margin>A certain definition of happiness and *eutychia* <note>Good luck or success.</note>.</margin>
<margin>Wisdom makes us happy.</margin>
When he had wondered at this because of his boyish rudeness, and I noticed his wonder, I questioned him in this way: "Do you not know, O Clinias, that skilled flute-players attain the best of all things regarding the use of flutes?" He agreed. "And learned grammarians regarding letters, both in writing and reading?" "Entirely," he said. "What then about the dangers that happen at sea? Do wise pilots also attain the desired port of navigation before others?" "It is so." "And likewise a wise leader of war, regarding military matters—does he conduct them more safely, and will you serve more safely with him than with an ignorant one?" "Without a doubt," he said. "And will a wise doctor lead you to the desired health of the body," I said, "better than an unwise one, and will you commit yourself to him more willingly?" "Certainly," he said. "Is it because you think it will turn out more happily for you with a wise man than with a fool?" He consented. 

"Wisdom, therefore, in all human matters," I said, "makes us happy. For wisdom never errs, nor is it deceived, but it performs the work correctly and attains it—otherwise it would not even be wisdom." 

We agreed finally, I know not how, that in short we should say that when wisdom is present, there is no need of anything else for happiness. But having conceded these things, I asked again what we thought of those things that had been conceded above. "For we confessed," I said, "that if we have many good things, we live well and blessedly." He admitted it. "Now, do we live blessedly," I said, "because of the presence of good things if they profit nothing, or if they profit?" 
"If they profit," he said. 
"But do they confer anything if we only have them but do not use them? Just as if we had many banquets and drinks, but did not eat them—would they help?" 
"Nothing," he said. 
"Furthermore, if for craftsmen all the things for completing a work were set out and prepared, but they did not use them, would they act well because of the abundance of equipment and tools? As if for a blacksmith all the tools were prepared, and likewise the material, but he forged nothing—would he be helped by the possession?" 
"In no way," he said. 
"What then? If someone attained riches and all the good things we mentioned, but never used them, would he be blessed by the mere possession of good things?" 
"Not at all, Socrates," he said. 
"It is necessary, therefore, for him who is to be blessed," I said, "not only to have good..."

...to possess such goods, but to use them. For possession alone is of no help. "Correct," he said. "Does the possession and use of goods, O Clinias," I said, "suffice for living happily?" "It seems so to me," he replied. "Do you say this provided one uses them correctly, or even if one does not use them correctly?" "If correctly," he said. "Excellent," I replied. "For I think it is more significant when someone uses a thing wrongly than when he does not touch it at all. For the former is an evil, while the latter is neither good nor evil. Should it not be said so?" He agreed. "In the working and use of wood," I asked, "does anything besides the craft of carpentry produce the ability to use each thing correctly?" "Nothing else," he said. "Furthermore, regarding the making of vessels, does knowledge provide the correct use?" He nodded. "And regarding the use of the goods we mentioned above—wealth, health, and beauty—was not knowledge itself the leader, teaching how to use these correctly and directing the work?" "Entirely," he said. "Therefore, it seems that in every possession and action, knowledge provides men not only with success, but also with good work." He assented. "I pray, is any of all these possessions useful without prudence and wisdom? Or which of these two brings back greater utility: the one who is deprived of mind though he abounds in things and does many things, or the one who does few things and possesses few things, but is of sound mind? Think of it this way. Does not the one who does fewer things err more rarely? Erring less, does he not do less poorly? Doing less poorly, is he not less miserable?" "Entirely," he said. "By what means, then," I said, "does someone do fewer things? If he is poor, or if he is rich?" "If poor," he said. "If he is weak, or if he is robust?" "If weak," he said. "If he is honored, or if he is cast down?" "If cast down," he said. "If he is brave and temperate, or if he is cowardly?" "If cowardly." "And does not the lazy man accomplish less than the one ready for action?" He admitted it. "And the slow man less than the swift? The one dull of sight and hearing less than the one sharp in both?" All these things were agreed upon between us. There, truly, I concluded in this manner. "It seems the dispute was not about all those things we previously said were good, as to how they might be good by their own nature, but as it seems, the matter stands thus: if ignorance presides over them, they are worse than their opposites, because they can provide more abundant tools of wickedness to an evil leader. But if prudence and wisdom preside over them, then finally they are better. In themselves, however, by their very nature, none of them are worthy of being esteemed as either good or evil." "It seems to be," he said, "as you say." "What else follows from this," I asked, "than that none of the other things are either good or evil? But of these two, wisdom is indeed a good, and folly indeed an evil?" He approved. "Now, therefore, let us consider what remains. Since we all desire to be happy, and we are made happy, as it appeared, by the fact that we use things and use them correctly—and knowledge provides the correctness of use and the prosperity of the result—everyone ought to strive with all zeal, setting aside all other things, to become as wise as possible. Is it not so?" "Certainly," he said. "Moreover, everyone ought to think that from parents, from tutors, from friends, and others, especially those who love them—whether they are strangers or citizens—this should be sought rather than immense riches; and all should be entreated to impart wisdom. Nor is it shameful, nor unworthy, Clinias, to serve anyone for the sake of wisdom, and to deserve well of everyone with honorable compliance. Do you feel the same?" "The very same," he said. "For you seem to speak rightly." "Provided," I said, "wisdom can be taught, and does not perhaps come to men by chance. For this must be investigated further; nor is it yet established between us." Then he said: "To me indeed, O Socrates, it seems it can be taught." Delighted by this response, I said, "O best of men, you have done me a very great favor, freeing me from a long inquiry as to whether wisdom can be taught or not. Now, truly, since it seems to you that learning can be acquired, and this alone of all things renders a man blessed and fortunate, what else would you say than that one must practice philosophy? Will you not do this?" "Most certainly," he said, "O Socrates, as much as it is possible to do so." When I had heard these things gladly, I said, "O Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, you have here an example of the exhortation I want, though perhaps poorly gathered by me in unpolished and long-winded words. Whichever of you wishes, let him show us the same thing, weaving it together skillfully; or if this does not please you, at least pursue for the youth's sake what is missing from my speech: namely, whether it is necessary for him who wishes to be a good and happy man to acquire every branch of knowledge, or rather one specific kind; and then what this knowledge is. For, as I said at the beginning, we vehemently desire this young man to turn out wise and good." When I had said these things, O Crito, I was now intent on what followed, observing what kind of opening they would make in their speech, and by what reasoning especially they would exhort Clinias to the study of wisdom and virtue. Here, Dionysodorus, who is older, began first; and we were all turned with our eyes toward him, about to hear some marvelous speech immediately—which is what happened. For he began a strange discourse, O Crito, worthy of being heard by you, to see how beautifully, forsooth, he provokes one to virtue. "Tell me," he said, "O Socrates, and you others, whoever you are who wish this young man to become wise, whether you are joking, or if you are doing this in earnest and truly desire it." At this, realizing that they had thought I was playing when I asked them to dispute with the youth, and that for this reason they too had handled nothing serious so far, I said, "We desire it most greatly." Then Dionysodorus said, "Watch out, O Socrates, lest you later deny what you now assert." "I know," I said, "that I will by no means deny it." "What then do you say?" he asked. "Do you want him to become wise?" "We want it," I said. "Why not?" "Is Clinias wise now, or not?" he asked. "Not yet," I said. "For he is not at all boastful." "But you," he said, "want him to become wise, and by no means to be ignorant?" We admitted it. "Therefore, you desire him to become what he is not," he said, "and to be no longer what he now is." When I had heard this, I was troubled; and he, noticing I was troubled, said, "Since you want what he now is to be no longer, you want, it seems, this man to perish. What fine friends and lovers they are, who strive with all care to destroy the ones they love!" Hearing this, Ctesippus <note>A friend of Socrates known for his fiery temperament.</note> took it ill for the sake of his beloved boy; and being indignant, he said, "Stranger from Thurii, if it were not a boorish thing to say, I would say to your face that you fasten a wicked and unworthy lie upon me and them—that I, forsooth, desire him to perish." At this, Euthydemus, turning to Ctesippus, said, "Does it seem to you possible, perhaps, for a lie to occur? He who lies," he asked, "does he speak the thing itself about which the speech is, or does he not speak it?" "He speaks it," he said. "If he speaks the thing itself, he speaks nothing else besides that which he speaks." "How," Ctesippus said, "could it happen otherwise?" "Is not the thing he speaks one certain thing," he asked, "distinct from others?" "Entirely," said Ctesippus. "Does not he who speaks it, utter that which is?" "So it is." "But truly, whoever speaks what is, and the things that are, speaks the truth. Wherefore Dionysodorus, if he speaks the things that are, proclaims the truth, and lies in no way against you." "So it is," said Ctesippus...

--- Page 198 ---
Euthydemus, or, The Litigious One. 179

Ctesippus. "But he who says these things, O Euthydemus, does not say the things that are." To him Euthydemus said: "Are non-existent things not nothing?" "They are not," he said. "Are the things that are not, existent anywhere?" "Nowhere." "Can it happen that someone does anything regarding those things which are not, so that someone makes those things to exist which are nowhere?" "By no means does it seem so to me," said Ctesippus. "When the orators harangue the people, do they do nothing?" "They do something." "If they act, they therefore also make or produce. It follows, then, that to speak is itself to act and to make." He agreed. "No one, therefore, speaks of non-existent things, for he would then be making something; but you," he said, "have confessed it is impossible for anyone to make non-existent things. Wherefore, according to your own speech, no one speaks falsely. On the contrary, if Dionysodorus speaks, he speaks things that are true and existent." "It is so, Euthydemus," Ctesippus said. "For he says things that exist, but he does not say them as they are." "Why do you say that, Ctesippus?" Dionysodorus asked. "Are there those who speak of things themselves as they are?" "There are certainly," he replied, "men who are good, noble, and truthful." "What further?" he said. "Do not good things stand well, and bad things, on the contrary, stand badly?" He approved. "And you confess that good and noble men speak of things themselves just as they are?" "I confess it," he said. "Therefore good men, O Ctesippus, speak badly of bad things, if indeed they speak of them as they are." "Most certainly indeed," he said, "and they speak badly of bad men. You must take care, if you believe me, not to be of their number, lest good men speak badly of you. For you know that the good speak badly of the bad." At this Euthydemus said: "Do they also speak greatly of great things, and hotly of hot things?" "Exceedingly so," said Ctesippus. "And they speak coldly of cold things, and say they discuss things 'coldly' <note>To speak 'coldly' was a Greek idiom for being boring or making poor jokes.</note>." At this Dionysodorus said, "You are being abusive, Ctesippus, you are being abusive!" "Not by Jove, Dionysodorus," he said. "For I love you; rather, I even warn you as a friend and strive to persuade you never to speak so boorishly in my presence as to say I desire those whom I hold most dear to be destroyed." But I, as I perceived they were fired up, joked with Ctesippus: "It is fitting, Ctesippus," I said, "as it seems to me, to accept from these strangers what they give, if only they wish to impart anything, and not to bicker about names. For if they know how to 'destroy' men in such a way as to make honest and prudent men out of bad and imprudent ones—whether they themselves are the inventors of this destruction, or have learned it from another—so that by exterminating the bad man, they can restore a good one. It is clear, however, that they know this: for they said just now that an art had been recently acquired by them, by which they make good men out of bad ones. If they know this," I said, "let us surely permit them to thus 'destroy' the youth, provided they make him wise; nay, let us even hand ourselves over to be cared for by them in this way. But if you young men are afraid, let them try their art on me, as if on some Carian <note>The Carians were often used as cheap mercenaries or experimental subjects in antiquity; "to risk it on a Carian" was a proverb for trying something dangerous on a person of little consequence.</note>. Indeed, since I am an old man, I am ready to undergo the danger and I surrender myself to this Dionysodorus, as if to Medea the Colchian <note>A sorceress from Greek myth who rejuvenated the elderly by cutting them up and boiling them in a cauldron.</note>, so that he may dissolve me, and if he wishes, boil me, or perform any other experiment upon me, provided he makes me a good man." Ctesippus also said, "I likewise, O Socrates, commit myself to the will of the strangers: and if they wish to skin me even more than they are skinning me now, provided my skin is turned not into a wine-skin like Marsyas <note>A satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest and was flayed alive after losing; his skin was said to have been made into a wine-flask.</note>, but into virtue. And Dionysodorus here thinks I am angry with him; but I am not angry at all, but I oppose what he said against me incorrectly. But you, Dionysodorus, should not think it an insult that I reclaim the truth. For it is one thing to contradict, and another to be abusive." Here Dionysodorus said: "I ask you, do you speak of contradicting in such a way that you think contradicting is actually anything at all?" "Most certainly indeed," said Ctesippus. "Do you not think so, Dionysodorus?" "But you will never show," said Dionysodorus, "where you have heard one person contradicting another." "You speak the truth," he said. "But now let us hear if I can show you Ctesippus contradicting you, Dionysodorus." "Do you then promise this to us?" he asked. "Entirely," he said. "Are there," he asked, "speeches and reasons concerning each thing?" "There are," he said. "Is it as each thing is, or as it is not?" "As it is," he said. "If you remember, Ctesippus," he said, "we showed a little while ago that no one speaks what is not. For it is established that no one can speak what does not exist." "What then?" said Ctesippus. "Does that prevent you and me from contradicting each other?" Then he said, "Would we be contradicting if we both thought of the same reason for the same thing? Or would we not rather be saying the same thing?" He agreed. "But if neither of us," he asked, "should say what the thing is, do we contradict? Or do we rather not grasp the thing at all?" He admitted that too. "Surely," he said, "when I say what the thing is, but you say something else, is it only then that we contradict? Or rather, when I say what the thing is, and you say what is entirely not the thing? And will it be that the one not speaking contradicts the one speaking?" At this, Ctesippus was silenced. But I, marveling at what was said, said: "By what reasoning, Dionysodorus, do you say that? Indeed, though I have heard this kind of discourse many times from many people, I am always accustomed to marvel at it. For the followers of Protagoras, and those more ancient than they, used it frequently. But to me it has always seemed wonderful, and such a thing as subverts both others and itself. But I think I shall now hear the truth of it from you especially: for does it mean that to speak falsely is impossible, and that he who speaks must either speak the truth or not speak at all?" He asserted it. "Is it indeed impossible to speak falsely," I asked, "but possible to think falsely?" "Not even to think it," he said. "Therefore there is no such thing," I said, "as a false opinion." "None at all." "Nor are men infected by ignorance," I said, "for what would ignorance be, if it were possible to be deceived about things?" "Entirely," he said. "But that does not exist," I said. "Certainly not," he replied. "Do you introduce these things for the sake of conversation, O Dionysodorus," I said, "to bring in something marvelous? Or in reality, does no man seem to you to be ignorant?" "You, then," he said, "refute it." "Can anything be refuted," I asked, "if, as you say, no one can lie?" "It cannot," Euthydemus said; "nor did Dionysodorus command that you refute him. For by what means could anyone command what is not?" "I indeed, Euthydemus," I said, "hardly learn these clever and noble things perfectly, but I touch upon them in passing. It will therefore be burdensome, perhaps, what I shall ask, but forgive me, I pray. See, I beg you: if no one can lie, nor think falsely, nor be ignorant, no one can even err in what he does. For he would not err from what he does. Is this what you say?" "Plainly so," he said. "This is," I said, "that grave question. For if we never err, neither in acting, nor in speaking, nor even in thinking, what then have you come here to teach? Did you not proclaim above that you, beyond all others, could best hand over virtue to anyone who wished?" "Are you so much of a Cronus <note>A reference to the ancient god Cronus, used here as a slang term for someone who is old-fashioned, "out of touch," or "in their dotage."</note>, O Socrates," Dionysodorus said, "that you remember now what we said at the beginning? And if I said something last year, you will also remember it now; but you have nothing to answer to what has been said in the present." "Because they are difficult," I said, "and not without reason. For they are produced by wise men. Indeed, even to that which you said last, it is most difficult to respond. For when you say I do not have anything to answer...

180 The Eighteenth Book.

...O Dionysodorus, what especially do you wish to imply? Is it, forsooth, that I have no way to convict that speech? For tell me what else that word means—that 'I do not have' anything with which to respond to those speeches by my own means. Do you mean anything else," he asked, "than that it is difficult to respond?" "Certainly, but answer first." "Before you answer," I said, "Dionysodorus?" "What, do you not answer?" he said. "Is it fair?" I asked. "Fair," he said. "By what reasoning?" I asked. "Is it perhaps because you come to us endowed with the faculty of speaking, and you know when one ought to respond and when one ought not, and therefore," he said, "is there not any word possessing a soul?" "None, for my part," I said. "Why then were you asking just now what the word meant?" "For no other reason," I said, "except on account of my own dullness, which compelled me to err. But perhaps I did not err, but spoke correctly when I attributed thought to words. But do you say that I erred, or not? For if I did not err, neither will you now refute me, wise though you may be, nor do you have anything to oppose. But if I did err, even so you do not speak correctly when you say that no one can err. And indeed I do not bring these things up against what you were saying last year, but it seems to me, O Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, that this discourse revolves to the same point: and even now, as was also accustomed to happen formerly, while it casts down, it falls itself. As for how that might not happen even to you, it seems your art has not yet provided for it, though it is admirable regarding the sharper diligence of speeches." At this Ctesippus said, "You say marvelous things, O men of Thurii, or of Chios, or whatever other name you please to claim: for whom to be delirious is all the same." But I, fearing lest it come to insults, again mitigated Ctesippus thus: "I say the same things to you now, Ctesippus," I said, "that I was also saying to Clinias. For you do not know how marvelous is the wisdom of these strangers. But they do not wish to show it to us with deliberate effort just yet, but in the manner of that Egyptian sophist Proteus <note>A sea-god who could change his shape to avoid being caught and questioned.</note>, they deceive us with certain tricks. Let us therefore imitate Menelaus, and not let go before they reveal what they have in mind. For they will exhibit something most beautiful, I think, if they truly bring it forth. Wherefore let us exhort and entreat them with suppliant prayers to exhibit it. But it seems necessary to set forth again what form of study I require of them. I will try to continue the discourse from where we left off above, if by some means I may provoke them, so that having pitied me, who am so heavily occupied, they may then handle the matter seriously. But you, Clinias, tell me where we broke off the speech. For, as I think, we were stuck here, where we were confessing that one must practice philosophy. Was it not so?" "Certainly," he said. "Philosophy is indeed the acquisition of knowledge?" I asked. "Certainly," he said. "Which knowledge, then, is it most fitting to acquire?" I asked. "Is it not, to speak briefly, that which is profitable to us?" "That very one," he said. "Would that knowledge profit us most if we knew in which lands much gold might be dug up?" "Surely," he said. "And yet we recently refuted that, because even if without labor, and without the earth being dug, all things were golden for us, and even if we could make the stones themselves golden, nevertheless this knowledge would be cheap and of no price. For if we do not know how to use gold, it is useful for nothing. Do you not remember?" "I remember," he said, "and most especially indeed."

"Nor is any knowledge of any thing—whether money-changing, or medicine, or whatever other kind—useful," I said, "if it only teaches how to make, but does not teach how to use. Is it not so?" "Exactly so," he said. "To such an extent," I said, "that if any knowledge should make us immortal, but does not teach how to use immortality, it would be entirely useless, if any faith is to be placed in what was said before." "All these things seemed so to us." "There is need, therefore, my noble boy," I said, "of this knowledge, in which the work, the production, and the use come together." "It appears so," he said. "There is therefore a very great difference between the makers of lyres and those who have attained the knowledge of playing the lyre. For the art which makes is one thing, and the art which uses these things is another. For the art that builds a lyre and the one that strikes the lyre differ far from each other. Do they not?" "It is so," he said. "Nor, again," I said, "is there need of a maker of flutes. Since that art differs from the one that uses them." "True," he said. "Could it be perhaps," I said, "that the faculty of composing speeches is to be sought, so that you might become happy?" "I do not think so," he said. "What reason moves you?" I asked. "I know indeed," he said, "certain authors of speeches who know how to use these speeches they have composed just as lyre-makers use lyres, who have constructed lyres for the use of others, which they themselves do not know how to play. It is established similarly that concerning speeches, the art that composes them is one thing, and the art that uses the composed ones is another." "You seem to have shown by a most evident argument," I said, "that the art of those who compose speeches by no means suffices for happiness. Although I hope that in this kind of knowledge we shall find that which we have long been seeking. For these authors of speeches, Clinias, as often as I have addressed them, seem wise above other mortals, and their very art seems profoundly divine and lofty. Nor is it a wonder. For it is a certain part of that incantatory art <note>The art of spells and charms.</note>, not much inferior to it. Furthermore, the faculty of incanting is the mitigation of vipers, spiders, scorpions, and other wild beasts, and of diseases. But oratory is a certain delight and charming of judges, assembly-goers, and other crowds. Or do you feel otherwise?" "Not otherwise," he said, "but exactly as you say." "To what, then, shall we turn?" I asked, "and to what art?" "I am uncertain," he said. "But I think I have found it," I said. "Which one?" "The art of generalship <note>Latin: *Imperatoria*.</note> seems especially to be the one that makes a young man happy." "It does not seem so to me," he said. "Why?" I asked. "Because it seems to be a certain hunting art of men," he said. "What do you mean?" I asked. "Because no hunter," he said, "extends the work of hunting further than tracking and capturing; after they have seized what they were hunting, they cannot use it. But both those who hunt with dogs and those who fish show their prey to the cooks. Similarly, geometers, astronomers, and calculators are certain hunters. For they do not make the figures and descriptions themselves, but since they exist, they discover them. Since, therefore, they do not know how to use them themselves, but only hunt them, whoever among them is not senseless gives their discoveries to the dialecticians <note>Philosophers who use logic and reasoning to examine the truth.</note>, so that they may use them." "Well done, most beautiful and wise Clinias," I said, "is it so?" "Exactly so," he said. "And by the same reasoning, leaders of an army, after they have occupied either a city or an army, hand over the prey and spoils to the civil authorities. For they themselves do not know how to use those things they have seized, just as bird-catchers, after they have caught quails, hand them over to the bird-keepers. If, therefore, you lack that art which knows how to use what has been sought either by making or by hunting, and which makes its possessors happy, one must seek another than the military one." "What do you say, O Socrates? Did that youth say such things?" c r i t o. "Do you not think so, Crito?" c r i t o. "Not by Jove. "At least I remember this: that neither Euthydemus brought these things forward, nor Dionysodorus. But, O blessed Crito, I suspect some more excellent man present said these things. For I do not doubt that I heard them." c r i t o. "By Jove, O Socrates, some more excellent person seems to have brought those things forth. But after these, what art at last did you scrutinize? Did you find the one you were seeking, or not?" s o c r a t e s. "Whence, O blessed one, would we have found it? Something ridiculous happened. For in the manner of children who chase larks or crested larks, we were pursuing each branch of knowledge with a certain vehement affection, and always, as soon as we thought we were about to catch each one, it failed us and suddenly slipped away. Why should I enumerate many to you? We approached the 'Kingly Art' <note>The art of ruling or statesmanship.</note>, contemplating whether or not it was the one that makes people happy. But as if having fallen into a Labyrinth, while we were now hoping to be near the end, we were turned back and returned again to the beginning, affected in the same way as we were at the start of the dispute." c r i t o. "Since the military art and all other faculties seemed to submit the command of their works to the civil art, as if it were the only one that knows, we thought nothing would be an impediment to us from this being the one we were seeking: the cause of correctly administering the republic, and according to that iambic verse of Aeschylus, sitting alone at the stern of the city, and holding the rudders of the whole, ruling all things, and rendering all things useful." c r i t o. "Did it not seem correct to you, Socrates?" s o c r a t e s. "You shall judge yourself, Crito, if you hear what happened next. For again we were seeking in this manner: 'Come, does that kingly art presiding over all produce some work, or not?' 'Entirely some work,' we all agreed. For would not you too, Crito, concede this?" c r i t o. "Without doubt." s o c r a t e s. "What then would you say its work is? Just as if I were to ask you, while Medicine rules over all things of which it is mistress, what work does it exhibit? Would you not immediately answer 'health'?" c r i t o. "Certainly." s o c r a t e s. "Similarly your Agriculture, while it rules over all things of which it is mistress, what work does it perform? Will you not say 'to provide nourishment from the earth'?" c r i t o. "Indeed." s o c r a t e s. "The kingly faculty, therefore, since it rules over all things of which it is mistress, what work does it complete? Perhaps it is not at hand." c r i t o. "Not by Hercules, O Socrates." s o c r a t e s. "Nor was it for us, O Crito; but at least you know this: if this is the one we desire, it must be useful." c r i t o. "Exceedingly so." s o c r a t e s. "Is it not therefore necessary that it bring some good to us?" c r i t o. "It is entirely so." s o c r a t e s. "But Clinias and I agreed that the good is nothing else than a certain knowledge." c r i t o. "So you were saying, certainly." s o c r a t e s. "And although each one would especially confess that the works of civil governance are many other things—to make citizens rich, free, and harmonious—all these appeared to be neither good nor evil. But it must, as was established, make them wise and grant them knowledge, if indeed it is to be that which profits and makes them happy." c r i t o. "You tell the truth. For so it was established between you then, as you yourself have recounted." s o c r a t e s. "Does the kingly discipline make men wise and good?" c r i t o. "What prevents it, Socrates?" s o c r a t e s. "Does it make them all good, and in all things? And does it provide all knowledge? Shoemaking, carpentry, and all the rest?" c r i t o. "I certainly do not think so, O Socrates." s o c r a t e s. "But what knowledge? And in what shall we be helped? Indeed, it must not be the maker of those works which are neither good nor evil. But it is fitting that it provide no other knowledge than itself. Let us say, therefore, what this is, and by what we are helped. Do you wish us to say, O Crito, that it is that by which we can make others good?" c r i t o. "I certainly wish it." s o c r a t e s. "To what will the good lead? Or in what will they be useful? "Did Euthydemus then wish to show it to you?" s o c r a t e s. "Why not? Quite magnificently, O friend, he began to address me in this manner: 'Shall I teach you, O Socrates, this knowledge which you have long been seeking,' he asked, 'or shall I show that you already have it?' 'O blessed man,' I said, 'are you really able to do this?' 'Very much so,' he said. 'Show me then,' I said, 'that I have it. For that will be easier for me than to learn it anew at this age.' 'Come say,' he said, 'do you know anything?' 'I know many things indeed,' I said, 'but small things.' 'It suffices,' he said. 'Do you think it possible for any of those things which are, to not be that very thing which it is?' 'In no way,' I said. 'Do you not assert that you know something?' he asked. 'Certainly.' 'Are you not then knowing, if indeed you know?' 'I am indeed, but of that very thing which I know.' 'It matters not,' he said. 'If you do not know something,' he said, 'are you not unknowing?' 'Of that very thing, O friend,' I said, 'which I do not know.' 'Nonetheless you are unknowing,' he said, 'you who a little while ago proclaimed yourself to be knowing. And so it happens that you are the very one who both is, and again is not, at the same time and according to the same things.' 'Let it be, Euthydemus,' I said. Because, forsooth, it is impossible for the same thing both to be and not to be. Whence if I know one certain thing, I know all things. For I cannot be knowing and unknowing at the same time. But if I know all things, I also have that knowledge. Is this not how you speak? And is this that wisdom?' 'You refute yourself, Socrates,' he said. 'But what about you, Euthydemus?' I asked. This is a scholarly translation of the provided Latin text, which contains Marsilio Ficino’s translation of Plato’s *Euthydemus*, *Hippias Minor*, and the introductory material for the *Charmides*.

### **Note on Abbreviations and Readings**
The text employs standard Renaissance Latin abbreviations:
- **-q;** or **-q[ue]**: translated as "-que" (and).
- **m** or **n** represented by a tilde/macron over a vowel (e.g., *inquā* = *inquam*, *nūc* = *nunc*).
- **v** and **u** are interchangeable depending on position; **ſ** is the "long s."
- **-rū** = **-rum** (genitive plural).
- **p** with a stroke = **per**, **pre**, or **pro** depending on the mark.
- **oia** = **omnia**.

### **Translation**

[[page number: 182]]
# Book Eighteen.

... "Dionysodorus," I said, "now at last you seem to me to be speaking seriously, and I have finally prevailed upon you to act in earnest. Do you truly know all things? Even the craft of the smith and the tanner?" "Altogether everything," he said. "Do you even know the number of the stars and the sand?" "Certainly," he said, "and even how to make shoes." "And," I said, "the number of the stars and the sand?" "Those too," he said. "Do you think we would grant these things?" I asked. Here Ctesippus, responding, said: "O Dionysodorus, bring forth some such proof for us, by which we may infer that you speak the truth." "What sort?" he asked. "Do you know," he said, "how many teeth Euthydemus has? And does Euthydemus know how many you have?" "Is it not enough for you," he replied, "to have heard that we know all things?" "By no means," he said, "but show us only this one thing: that you speak the truth. For if you say how many teeth each has, and afterward we, by counting, find you to have spoken the truth, we shall believe you in other matters as well." But they, thinking that Ctesippus was mocking them, refused to answer anything else except that they knew all things, when questioned about individual points by Ctesippus; for Ctesippus questioned them openly about each thing, even the smallest or most base, whether they knew it. They, however, with a bold spirit, responded equally in turn that they understood all things, like boars that rush against the blow. Wherefore I also, O Crito, was finally forced to ask Euthydemus whether Dionysodorus also knew how to dance. And he agreed. "But," I said, "can he leap over swords with his head inclined to the ground, and be rolled upon a wheel, at such a great age? Is he so advanced in wisdom?" "There is nothing," he said, "that he does not know." Then I said: "Do you know all things only now? Or always?" "Always," they replied. "Did you know all things from a tender age, immediately upon being born?" "Everything," they both replied together. To us, indeed, the thing seemed incredible. Then Euthydemus asked, "Do you not believe it, O Socrates?" "Except for this," I said, "that it is likely that you are wise." "And if you will answer me," he said, "I will show that you also possess these marvelous things." "It would be most pleasing if you convince me of this: for if I were wise and did not know it until now, and you show that I know everything and have always known it, what a profit I might find in life! Ask now," I said. "Ask, as if I were about to answer," I said. "Are you a knower of something," he said, "O Socrates, or of nothing?" "Of something," I said. "Do you know by that same thing by which you are a knower, or by something else?" "By that which I am a knower. For I think you mean the soul. Do you mean this?" "Are you not ashamed," he said, "O Socrates, to ask in turn when you are being questioned?" "But what shall I do?" I asked. "I will do whatever you command, since I am ignorant of what you seek. You command that I answer something, not that I ask." "Do you think in any way," he said, "about that which I ask?" "Certainly," I said. "Then answer that which you think. What if," I said, "you ask with one mind and I answer with another? If I conceive of something different from you, will it be enough for you if I answer nothing to the point?" "It will be enough for me," he said, "though not for you, I think." Then I said, "By Jove, I will not answer before I hear more." "You do not answer," he said, "always to those things which you conceive in your mind; because you are trifling, Socrates, and you are more unrefined than you ought to be." I recognized then that he was now angry with me, because I distinguished the words with which he was striving to ensnare me. Moreover, it came into my mind that Connus, who himself is often indignant with me whenever I do not yield to him, then scorns me as if I were unrefined. Since I thought to hand myself over to their teaching, I decided it was necessary to obey, lest any of them reject me as inept or unteachable. Therefore I said, "If it seems so to you, Euthydemus, let it be done. For you understand the method of disputation much better than I, since you possess this art, while I am unrefined. Therefore ask again from the beginning." "Answer again," he said, "whether you know by something by which you know, or by nothing?" "By the soul," I said. At this he said, "He answers more than what was asked. I do not ask by what you know, but whether you know by something, or not." I said, "I have answered more than was fitting because of my inexperience. But forgive me, I pray. I will now answer simply, that I always know by something whatever I know." "Is it always by this same thing," he said, "or sometimes by this, sometimes by another?" "Always," I said, "whenever I know, I know by this." At this he said, "Will you not cease answering beside the point?" "Lest perhaps," I said, "the word 'always' should deceive us, I answered thus." "Do not say 'us'," he said, "but 'you.' But answer: do you always know this?" "Always," I said, "after the 'Whenever' is removed." "Do you not always know this? And always knowing, do you know some things by this by which you know, and some by another, or everything by this itself?" "By this," I said, "all things whatsoever I know." "Here again you overstep, Socrates." "Let it be excepted," I said, "whatever I know." "I demand no exception," he said, "rather answer: could you know all things unless you knew all things?" "That would be a monster," I said. "Add now," he said, "whatever you please. For you confess to knowing all things." "So I seem," I said, "after this 'I know everything, however, I know' is of no consequence." "Did you not confess to knowing always by this by which one knows, whether whenever you know, or however it pleases you? For you confessed to knowing always, and all things at once. It is settled, therefore, that you knew as a boy, and when you were conceived, and when you were born, and indeed even before you were born, and before the rising of heaven and earth, you knew all things, if indeed you always know. And by Jove, you will always know, and all things, if I wish it." "But you will wish it," I said, "O most honored Euthydemus, if indeed you speak the truth. But I do not have much confidence that you can do it, unless this brother of yours, Dionysodorus, wishes it with you; for so perhaps you will be able. Speak further. How I should not grant you the rest, I know not, since you are endowed with such miraculous and new wisdom, so that I may know all things, since you assert it. By what reason should I say I know such things, Euthydemus? For instance, that good men are unjust. Tell me, do I know that, or not?" "You certainly know it," he said. "What?" I asked. "That good men are not unjust." "I knew this long ago," I said. "But I do not ask that, but where did I learn that good men are unjust?" "Nowhere," said Dionysodorus. "Therefore," I said, "I do not know this." Then Euthydemus, turning to Dionysodorus, said, "You are destroying the argument, and it will appear that this man, if he does not know, is both knowing and not knowing at the same time." Dionysodorus indeed blushed, but I said, "But what do you say, Euthydemus? Does it not seem to you that your brother speaks the truth, since he knows all things?" "I am the brother of Euthydemus," Dionysodorus said. "Set those things aside," I said, "O good man, until Euthydemus teaches me that I know good men to be unjust, and do not envy me this lesson." "You flee, O Socrates," said Dionysodorus, "and do not wish to answer." "Not without cause," I said, "do I flee: for since I am weaker than either of you, why should I not flee two? I am indeed much weaker than Hercules, who was not able to fight at the same time against the Sophistic Hydra, which because of its wisdom, for every head of speech cut off, many grew back, and even against a certain Sophistic Crab arriving from the sea, and recently, as I think, brought by ship; by which when Hercules was being distressed on the left...

[[margin: Hercules against the sophistic hydra and the sophistic crab.]]

[[page number: 183]]
# Euthydemus, Or, The Contentious.

...and was being sharply bitten by its words, he implored the help of his nephew Iolaus, who greatly assisted him. But if my Iolaus, Patrocles, should come, he would do far differently." "Answer then," said Dionysodorus, "since you yourself proclaim these things, whether Iolaus was more the son of Hercules' brother than yours." "I think it would be worthwhile to answer you, Dionysodorus. For you would not cease questioning and disturb the order out of some envy, lest Euthydemus teach me that wise thing." "Answer then," he said. "I answer," I said, "that Iolaus was the son of Hercules' brother: but mine, it seems, in no way. For Patrocles his father was not my brother, but someone close in name, Iphicles, was the brother of Hercules." "Was Patrocles, then, yours?" "Certainly," I said, "but from the same mother, not the same father." "He is therefore a brother to you," he said, "and not a brother." "Not from the same father," I said, "O best of men. For his father was Chaeredemus, but mine was Sophronicus." "Was Sophronicus and Chaeredemus a father?" "Entirely; he was mine, the other was his." "Was Chaeredemus someone other than a father?" "Other than my father, certainly." "Was he a father, since he was other than a father? Are you the same thing as a stone?" "I feared," I said, "lest I should seem to be the same by your assertion. But I do not seem so to myself." "Are you not therefore something other than a stone?" "Other, certainly." "If you are other than a stone, you are not a stone. And if other than gold, you are not gold." "So it is," I said. "By the same reasoning, since Chaeredemus is other than a father, will he not be a father?" "It seems," I said, "that he is not a father." To this Euthydemus added: "Chaeredemus is not a father: and again, since Sophronicus is other than a father, he is not a father. Wherefore you are without a father, O Socrates." Taking up the speech, Ctesippus interjected: "But since the same has happened to your father, is he not someone else who is my father?" "Far from it," said Euthydemus. "Is he the same?" "The same indeed." "I would not agree. But Euthydemus, is he my father only, or also the father of all other men?" "Of the others as well." "Do you think the same man, being a father, is not a father?" "I thought so indeed," said Ctesippus. "Is gold, being gold, not gold? And a man, being a man, not a man?" Then Ctesippus: "You are not, as they say, Euthydemus, connecting flax to flax. You say a heavy thing, if your father is the father of all." "He is, however," he said. "Of men only," asked Ctesippus, "or also of horses and all other animals?" "Of all entirely." "Is your mother also the mother of all?" "Also the mother." "Therefore your mother is the mother of sea urchins." "And yours," he said. "And you, in turn, are the brother of gobies, puppies, and piglets." "And you," he said. "Furthermore, your father is a dog." "And yours as well." Here Dionysodorus said, "If you are willing to answer me, Ctesippus, I will make you concede these things. Tell me, do you have a dog?" "And a very bad dog at that," Ctesippus said. "Does he have puppies?" "He has many such." "Is not the dog their father?" "I certainly saw him mating with the mother dog." "Is the dog not yours?" "He is." "Therefore, being a father, is he not yours? Wherefore your father is a dog, and you are the brother of puppies." But lest Ctesippus object first, Dionysodorus suddenly added: "Answer a little more. Do you beat this dog?" Laughing, Ctesippus said, "I beat him, but I cannot beat you." "Do you not therefore beat your father?" "It would be far more just," he replied, "if I beat your father, who, having acquired a certain discipline, begot such wise sons." "But tell me, Euthydemus, has your father and the father of puppies obtained many good things from your wisdom?" "Neither he nor you, Ctesippus, are in need of many good things." "Nor you either, Euthydemus, nor any other of men," he said. "For tell me, Ctesippus, whether you think it good for a sick man to drink medicine when he needs it, or not? Or is it good for a man about to fight to go forth armed, or unarmed?" "I think so indeed," he said, "certainly I expect something extraordinary from you." "You will see for yourself best," he said. "But answer: after you have confessed that it is good to drink medicine when the matter requires it, should one drink as much of this good as possible? And will it be best if someone grinds it and pours into a cup as much hellebore as a wagon can carry?" "Certainly so," Ctesippus said, "if the one who is to drink it is as large as the Delphic statue." "Similarly in war," he said, "if it is good to be clothed in arms, should one have many arms, and should a pack of javelins and shields be carried about? Since it is a good thing." "Most certainly," Ctesippus said. "But you do not think, Euthydemus, that only one javelin should be carried?" "I do," he said. "Would you thus arm Geryon and Briareus? I thought you were more robust, and this companion of yours similarly, as armigerous men." Euthydemus was silent. But Dionysodorus, against what Ctesippus had first answered, said: "Does it seem good to you to have gold?" "Very much indeed," answered Ctesippus. "And to have money always and everywhere?" "Most of all," he said. "Do you not confess that gold is good?" "We have already confessed." "Should one always have it, and everywhere, and in himself as much as possible?" "Most blessed would be he who had three talents of gold in his belly, one talent under the bone of his head, and a stater—that is, a certain coin and weight of gold—in each eye." "They say," Ctesippus said, "O Euthydemus, among the Scythians those are the most happy and best men who contain much gold in the bones of their heads, just as you a little before called a dog a father. And what is more marvelous, they drink from their gilded heads and look into these, raising their own crown and forehead with their hands." At this Euthydemus: "Do the Scythians and other men see, Ctesippus, what they can see, or what they cannot see?" "What they can, clearly." "Do you not also?" "And I similarly." "Do you see our garments?" "I see them." "Can these then be seen?" "Wonderfully," Ctesippus said. "What further," he said. "Nothing. But do you not think they see?" "Are you such a pleasant man? You seem to me, Euthydemus, to have fallen asleep outside of sleep, and I think you can say nothing while speaking." "And you seem to do this. Is it not impossible," said Dionysodorus, "for one who is silent to speak?" "Impossible," Ctesippus said. "And for one who speaks to be silent?" "Much less possible." "When you speak of a stone, are you not speaking of a silent thing? And similarly when you speak of wood and iron?" "I will not grant you that iron things are silent," Ctesippus said, "for if one strikes them, they are said to sound and resound. Wherefore, in your wisdom, you have not sufficiently noticed how you say nothing. But as for what remains, show that it is possible for one who speaks to be silent." Certainly Ctesippus then seemed to me to contend vehemently on behalf of his friend. "When you are silent," said Euthydemus, "are you not silent about all things?" "Indeed." "Are you not silent about any thing that speaks? Since those things which speak are computed in the number of all things." "What then?" asked Ctesippus, "do not all things keep silent?" "No," said Euthydemus. "Or do all things speak, O best of men?" "Yes, certainly, those that speak." "I was not asking that," he said, "but whether all things are silent or speak." Then, snatching away the speech...

[[margin: A proverb.]]

[[page number: 184]]
# Book Eighteen.

...Dionysodorus said, "Neither and both. For I know certainly that you will be ignorant of what to object to this response." Immediately Ctesippus, as is his custom, breaking out into laughter, shouted: "O Euthydemus, your brother is already defeated." Clinias also, being very delighted, smiled. Wherefore Ctesippus, exulting, grew more than tenfold in joy. But it seemed to me that Ctesippus, like a veteran, had extorted these very things from them by cunning. For such wisdom is not found among other men of our time. After this I said, "Why do you laugh, Clinias, at things so serious and so beautiful?" But Dionysodorus, turning to me, said, "Have you ever seen a beautiful thing, Socrates?" "Many indeed, Dionysodorus." "Are they other than the beautiful itself? Or the same?" I was momentarily hesitant, and I thought I had suffered this not without cause, since I could not keep silent any longer. I answered, however, that they are other than the beautiful itself, yet a certain beauty is present in each. "If an ox is present to you," he said, "will you be an ox? And because I am now present to you, are you Dionysodorus?" "Good words, I pray," I said. But he: "In what way is one present to the other, since one is one, and the other is another?" "Do you," I said, "doubt this?" For I was already striving to imitate their wisdom, being kindled with desire for it. "Why should I not doubt it," he said, "I and all others, concerning that which in no way exists?" "What do you say, Dionysodorus? Is not the beautiful beautiful, and the base, base?" "If it seems so to me," he said. "Does it not seem so?" "Entirely," he said. "And is not the same the same," I asked, "and the other similarly other? Not merely that the other is the same?" "But I did not think even a boy would suspect this, that what is other is anything but other. But, O Dionysodorus, you have omitted this by choice. You seem to me like craftsmen who ought to complete individual tasks, to conduct and hand over the method of disputing decorously. Do you know," he said, "what is fitting for individual craftsmen to complete? First, do you know whom it befits to hammer bronze?" "The bronze-smith," I said. "And to mold clay?" "The potter." "Who again is to slaughter and skin, and roast or boil meat cut into pieces?" "The cook." "Does not whoever does what is fitting, do rightly?" "Most of all," I said. "But it is fitting, as you say, for the cook to cut and skin. Do you agree to this, or not?" "I agree," I said, "but forgive me, I pray." "It is settled then," he said, "if someone, slaughtering and cutting up a cook, boils or roasts him, he does what is fitting. Furthermore, if someone hammers a bronze-smith as bronze, and molds a potter, he will work similarly fittingly." "O Neptune," I said, "now you have placed the finishing stroke on this wisdom of yours. Will this ever be present to me here and become my own?" "Would you recognize it," he said, "O Socrates, once it has become your own?" "If you wish it," I said, "I indeed would." "What further," he said, "do you think to know your own?" "Certainly," I said, "unless perhaps you say otherwise. For it is necessary to begin with you, and end with this Euthydemus." "Do you not think those things are yours," he said, "of which you are the master? and which you may use at your discretion, like oxen and sheep? Do you think those things are yours which you can sell and give away, and vow to any of the gods? But those which you cannot, are not yours?" I, thinking that some noble question would arise from this, and being entirely inflamed with greed for hearing, said, "Entirely so. Such things are indeed mine." "Do you call those 'animals'," he said, "which have a soul?" "Those very things," I said. "Do you admit therefore that only those of the animals are yours concerning which you can do all these things which I just mentioned?" "I confess it," I said. Here he, quite ironically, restrained himself as if about to contemplate something great, then said, "Tell me, O Socrates. Do you have a paternal Jove?" But I, suspecting the speech would return to where it led, and turning away through a certain ambiguous bypass, escaped the net in which I was already as if entangled, and answered: "He is not mine, O Dionysodorus." "You are a wretched man," he said, "and not an Athenian, who has neither paternal gods, nor sacrifices, nor anything else noble and magnificent." "Set those things aside, Dionysodorus," I said, "lest you omen poorly, and do not teach so sharply. For I have both altars and domestic and paternal sacrifices, and whatever else of that kind is present to Athenians." "Is paternal Jove present to the other Athenians?" "There is no such kinship among the Ionians," I said, "nor among those who flowed from this city, nor among us, but Apollo is paternal because of the begetting of Ion. Jove however is not called paternal by us, yet he is called the protector of the city and guardian of the tribes, and Minerva is the guardian of the tribes." "It is enough," said Dionysodorus. "For you have, it seems, Apollo, Jove, and Minerva." "Entirely." "Will these gods not be yours, namely as progenitors and masters? Are they not yours? Did you not confess them to be yours?" "I confessed," I said, "what then?" "Are these gods not animals?" he asked. "You confessed, furthermore, that whatever has a soul is an animal; do these gods not have a soul?" "They certainly have one," I said. "Are they therefore animals?" "They are, surely." "But you said those among the animals were yours, of which you have the power to sell, give away, and dedicate to gods as you please." I cannot refute Euthydemus, since I have conceded these things. Immediately he interjected thus: "After you confess that Jove is yours, and other gods are yours, is it not permitted to you to sell them and give them away, and to treat them as you wish, like the other animals that are yours?" I therefore, Crito, as if struck by the speech, was silent. Ctesippus however, trying to assist me, said, "Wonderful, by Hercules, a noble speech." To whom Dionysodorus: "Is Hercules wonderful, or is 'wonderful' Hercules?" Then Ctesippus said, "By Neptune, harsh and hard speeches. I desist now. Both are invincible." Here, my friend Crito, no one present could contain himself further from extolling their speech with the highest praise: and those guests, Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, exulting with laughter, applause, and joy, were almost dissolved. For in the previous parts, while individual points were brought forth, only their followers applauded. But here, almost the very columns of the Lyceum seemed to shout, applaud, and exult. I indeed was so affected that I asserted I had never seen any men of equal wisdom. And being entirely enslaved to their wisdom, I began to praise and celebrate them exceedingly. "O men," I said, "blessed by the wonderful gifts of nature: who have completed so great a thing so easily and in so short a time. Many other things are indeed noble in your speeches, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, in which this is especially magnificent: that you have no care for the common people, or even for illustrious men, or those held in any price, but only for those like yourselves. I know certainly that there are few who love this kind of speech, and those indeed are like you: but others are so ignorant and scornful of them that they would blush more vehemently if they convicted others by them than if they themselves were convicted by others. Moreover, your speeches have this popular and mild quality: that when you say...

[[page number: 185]]
# Euthydemus, Or, The Contentious.

...that nothing is good or bad, nor white, nor anything else of such kind, nor anything at all different from others: truly, as you boast, you have completely stopped the mouths of men. Because you have stopped not only the mouths of others, but your own as well, it is a gracious thing: and you avoid the hatred and offense of the audience. But this is the greatest thing: that these have been so artfully habituated and instituted by you that you can hand them over to anyone in a short time. I recognized this indeed, and I pay attention to Ctesippus, and consider how suddenly he began to imitate you. To be able to teach the mystery of this matter as quickly as possible is noble, yet it does not seem it would be worthwhile for you to discourse before many men: rather, if you believe me, you will entirely beware not to speak in a crowd of many: lest perhaps, perceiving these things quickly, they give no thanks. Therefore, communicate these things only among yourselves in turn, nor let any other hear them unless he pays money. If you are wise, you will also advise your disciples never to speak of these things with anyone except themselves and you. For that which is rare, Euthydemus, is to be honored. Water indeed is bought at a very cheap price, although it is a thing most precious by nature, as Pindarus says. But come," I said, "receive this Clinias and me."
