When we had discussed these and some other brief matters, O Crito, we departed. Consider therefore whether you will come with me to these men. For they promise to teach all who are prepared to give money, nor do they make exception for any natural talent or age. What is most useful for you to hear, they say that no study of accumulating money prevents anyone from easily perceiving their wisdom.
CRIT. Indeed, O Socrates, I am desirous of hearing, and I would learn most willingly. Yet I seem to be one of those who are not like Euthydemus, but rather those whom you mentioned a little before, who would rather be refuted by others with such little traps than refute others. Truly it would be ridiculous if I proceeded to advise you. Yet nothing prevents me from relating to you now what I heard from those who, when the assembly was dismissed, departed from you. As I was walking, I met one of those who are considered to excel most in judicial cases: "O Crito," he said, "did you hear nothing from those wise men?" "Nothing, by Jove," I said. "For the frequent crowd and tumult prevented me from hearing." "Yet," he said, "it was a thing worthy of hearing." "Why?" I asked. "So that you might have heard those men disputing, who in this kind of speech excel the rest." To him I asked, "What did it seem to you?" "What else," he said, "than what is always heard from such men, while they trifle and argue with one another with an unworthy zeal about matters of no consequence?" He used this speech specifically. Then I said, "Nevertheless, philosophy is a gracious thing." "How gracious," he said, "O blessed one, when it is of no price? But if you had been present a little before, you would have blushed, I think, for the sake of your friend: who was so inept that he desired to hand himself over to men who have no care for what they say, but snatch at every point and object to words, although they, as I was saying, excel other such men of our age. Truly, O Crito, both this study is most vile, and those who are engaged in it are ridiculous." To me indeed, O Socrates, he seemed wrongly to disapprove of the thing itself, whoever he or another might be who disapproves. But that someone should strive to dispute with such men in a gathering of many, he seemed to me to rebuke deservedly.
SOC. O Crito, these men are worthy of admiration. But I do not yet know what I am about to say. From which group was he who met you and disparaged philosophy? Was he some orator from those who are strong in judicial contest? Or from those who compose and write such speeches with which orators contend in court?
CRIT. By no means an orator, nor do I think he ever pleaded in court, but they say he understands judicial matters best and composes elegant speeches.
SOC. I understand now. Indeed, I was just about to say the same. These are the ones, O Crito, whom Prodicus placed between the philosopher and the statesman. They think they are the wisest of all, and furthermore appear so to many: but only philosophers are an impediment to them, preventing them from being equally approved by all. They think, therefore, that if they spread this common opinion against philosophers—that they are of no price—they will carry off the highest glory of wisdom among all without controversy. For they think they are truly the wisest, but are hindered in private speeches when the followers of Euthydemus oppose them. That they are wise, however, they wish to seem consistent from this: that they have enough of philosophy, enough also of civil skill, and are participants of both as much as is necessary, and placed outside the turbulent tumults of civil business, they enjoy the fruits of wisdom pleasantly.
CRIT. Do these men seem to you to say anything, Socrates?
SOC. By no means.
CRIT. Nevertheless, the speech of these men has something plausible.
SOC. It has, as you say, O Crito, plausibility rather than truth. Nor can they easily be persuaded that both men and all other things whatsoever which are midway between two certain things and participate in both are so held that those which are from evil and good become better than the one and worse than the other; but those which are from two goods not leading to the same end are worse than both for completing that work for which both those things from which the composition is made are intended. But those which are constituted from two evils not tending to the same end, these alone are better than both of those in which they participate. If therefore philosophy is good, and civil action is good, but each contributing to one thing and another, and these men participate in both of these, they are placed in the middle. For they are worse than both. But if one of these is good and the other evil, they are better than the latter and worse than the former. But if both are evil, then finally they would speak the truth, but otherwise in no way. Nor do I think they would confess that both are evil, nor one good and the other evil. But truly, being participants of both, they are more inept than either for that to which philosophy and civil action belong, and although they hold the third place, they do not hesitate to usurp the first. Their desire should be forgiven, and we should not be indignant, yet they are to be considered such as they are. For we ought to love everyone who, being a participant of prudence, says something and acts manfully.
CRIT. Indeed, O Socrates, as I often speak with you, I am in doubt in what way to educate my sons. The younger in age is still more tender than discipline requires: but Critobolus is already an adult, and needs someone by whose work he may profit. Whenever I speak with you, I am so affected that I think it is madness to be occupied with other things for the sake of sons, such as concerning marriage, that they may be born from a most noble mother, then that a large patrimony may be left to them, but to neglect their education...

[[page number: 186]]
# Book Nineteen.

...Yet when I look at those who profess to educate men, I am deterred, and it seems to me, considering each one of them, that he is far from what he proclaims and is alien to it. And to confess the truth to you, I do not know how to exhort and provoke my son to philosophy.
SOC. O friend Crito, are you ignorant that in any study there are many vile and worthless men? But the upright are few, and those are to be held in the highest price? Does it not seem to you that gymnastics, commerce, rhetoric, and military affairs are something beautiful?
CRIT. To me certainly.
SOC. Do you not see in each of these arts many who are inept and ridiculous for each work?
CRIT. It is so, and you speak too truly.
SOC. Therefore, for this reason will you flee all studies and dissuade your son from them?
CRIT. It is not fitting, O Socrates.
SOC. Beware then, O Crito, lest you do what is unfitting. Lay aside this care, whether men studious of philosophy are good or bad: but examine the thing itself diligently: if upon inquiry the thing seems base, deter not only your sons but all men. But if it appears to you such as it appears to me, follow it manfully and exercise it, and exhort your sons to the same study.

[[margin: In any study the vile are many, the upright few.]]

# HIPPIAS MINOR,
## OR, ON LYING.
### MARSILIO FICINO'S
### ARGUMENT.

THE WONDERFUL goodness of our Socrates and Plato, since it most diligently provides in many ways everywhere lest credulous youth be captured by the crafty snares of sophists and, being captured, be lost, not without cause agitates Hippias of Elis, the most unlearned and most deceitful of sophists, in two dialogues: namely, the Greater and the Lesser. In the Greater, he demonstrates that Hippias, a professor of most beautiful things, is entirely ignorant of what beauty itself is. In the Lesser, he shows that the same man, boasting that he discerns the liar from the truthful man better than others, errs entirely in the definition of both: so that it may be clear that Hippias, just as he is the most arrogant of all, so also is he the most ignorant and appears most inept. He depicts him now, as is the custom of sophists, as boastful, rash, and greedy: and since he promises all things, in all things giving words but performing nothing; and though he boasts himself the greatest, he falters even in the smallest things. But to return to the definition of the liar and the truthful man, the liar ought to have been described as he who most wishes and however he can knows how to lie. The truthful man, on the contrary, as he who most wishes and however he can and knows how, speaks the truth. But Hippias, the most inert master of all arts and the most confused director of the truthful and the liar, departed in the opposite order, saying that a liar is he who most can and knows how to lie whenever he wishes: and the truthful man, he who whenever he wishes can and knows how to speak the truth. Whence he is first forced to confess that liars are powerful, knowing, prudent, and wise. Then also good at those things for which they are powerful and wise. Thirdly, by leading through individual arts, he is compelled in any matter or art to confess that the same man is truthful and a liar, which he had denied from the beginning. Since in any matter he who knows best, the same is most able and knows at his discretion to speak truly as well as to lie. Fourthly, he is led to concede that the truthful man is in no way better than the liar, since when the truthful man is sufficient and good for speaking the truth, so also the liar appears sufficient and good for lying. After these things Socrates leads the sophist into an ambiguity, which of the two offends more gravely: he who lies willingly, or he who lies unwillingly. The sophist does not know how to solve this, nor does Socrates wish to solve it for the sophist. But it is to be solved thus: those err less in those things which pertain to the intellect who lie spontaneously; but in those things which pertain to morals, they err more. Then truly he who willingly tells a lie has the argument against himself. Then it is doubted whether they err more, those who do so by deliberate effort, or those who sin by unskillfulness or ignorance. It is proved by long circuitous inductions that in those things which pertain to nature and art and their instruments, it is a graver vice committed by impotence or ignorance than that perpetrated by malice. Since the good of nature consists in power itself, and the good of art in this itself and furthermore in knowledge. Evil therefore consists in the opposites. From these things, however, outside the proposal, Socrates transfers Hippias to morals, concluding the same in the genus of morals as in the genus of nature and art. Which indeed, although Socrates understands it ought not to be done, he nevertheless strives to declare that the sophist in no way notices it. Truly in those things which pertain to the will and morals, one offends more gravely by malice, that is, by a certain will of sinning, than if one offends either by impotence or by ignorance. Finally, Socrates says that justice is either power or knowledge or both. He knew how to add, but did not wish to, the third: namely, the will. For justice consists especially in the will. That he wished to declare lay hidden from the sophist. But let us now conclude the argument for the preceding precepts. One must teach without envy. One must learn without shame. Thanks must always be given to the teacher. Another's youth is not to be usurped by you.

# EUDICUS, SOCRATES,
## HIPPIAS.

"BUT WHY are you silent, Socrates, when Hippias here has shown so many things? Why do you not either approve of some of his sayings or refute them if something seems to you not rightly said? Especially since we, who claim for ourselves no mediocre study of philosophy, have departed as inferiors?"
SOC. "Eudicus, there are some things among those which Hippias was saying about Homer concerning which I desire to inquire. I have heard indeed from your father Apemantus that the *Iliad* in Homer is a more noble poem than the *Odyssey* in proportion as Achilles is more excellent than Ulysses. For he said one poem was composed for Achilles, the other for Ulysses. Concerning this, therefore, I am eager to inquire of Hippias, if it only pleases him, which of those men he asserts to be more excellent, since many and varied other things about Homer and the other poets have been shown to us."
EUD. "No envy at all will prevent Hippias from answering when questioned. Will you not answer, Hippias, if Socrates asks something?"
HIP. "I would not be acting rightly, Eudicus, if I now fled Socrates' questioning, I who am accustomed always to go from Elis, my country, to the Olympic feasts where the Greeks flow together from everywhere for common celebration, and to offer myself there at the temple to anyone, declaring whatever anyone desires to be demonstrated and answering individual questions."
SOC. "O what a happy lot has fallen to you, Hippias, if you arrive at every Olympiad so confident in the wisdom of your mind: I would truly wonder if any athlete, about to compete in bodily exercise there, approached as confident in the strengths of his body as you are in the subtlety of your mind."
HIP. "I am deservedly affected here, Socrates: for from that time I began to exercise in the Olympics, I have found no one yet superior to me in any matter."
SOC. "What you say is noble indeed, Hippias, and this glory of yours from the city of the Eleans and your parents will be a certain monument of wisdom. But what do you judge concerning Achilles and Ulysses? Which of these do you think is more excellent, and in what way? Furthermore, while many of us were inside and you were discoursing, some words escaped me: yet it irked me to inquire, both because the crowd was very large inside and also lest I be an impediment to your speech. But now, since we are fewer and Eudicus here bids me ask, show us more clearly what you were saying about these men, and in what way you judged them."
HIP. "I am willing, Socrates, to relate more openly than I did then what I think of these and of others. I assert that Homer fashioned Achilles as the best man of all who came to Troy, Nestor as the wisest, and Ulysses as the most wily and many-formed."
SOC. "Wonderful, O Hippias. Will..."

[[page number: 187]]
# Hippias Minor, Or, on lying.

"...you gratify me in this? That is, lest you laugh at me if I am slower in perceiving and ask too often? Deign to answer me, I pray, freely and easily."
HIP. "It would be base indeed, O Socrates, since I teach others the same and demand money for it, if I did not indulge your questioning and did not answer with a glad mind."
SOC. "You speak very well. Indeed, you were saying Achilles was fashioned as the best man, Nestor as the wisest; I seemed to understand what you were saying. But when you called Ulysses wily and many-formed, to confess the truth, I did not understand what you meant. Tell me, perhaps I will perceive it better from this: was Achilles also induced by Homer as many-formed and wily, or not?"
HIP. "In no way, O Socrates, but entirely simple. Since in the supplications themselves, when he induces them disputing, he makes Achilles speak thus against Ulysses:
[[margin: Iliad.]]
'O much noble fabricator of guile, Ulysses,
It befits me to refute your words intrepidly,
As I think it ought to be done, lest you yourself
With deceitful words stun me sitting here and there.
Since he is more hated by us than the gate of black Dis,
Who hides one thing in his heart and speaks another openly.
But I will say now, as I believe it will be.'
In these verses he declares the character of both: Achilles to be truthful and simple, Ulysses wily and lying. Achilles inserts these things plainly against Ulysses."
SOC. "I seem now to understand what you say, O Hippias. For you call the wily man a liar, it appears."
HIP. "Most of all, O Socrates. For Homer fashions such a Ulysses often in both the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*."
SOC. "Therefore Homer thought that one man was truthful and another a liar, and that both were not the same."
HIP. "What prevents it, Socrates?"
SOC. "Do you yourself think the same, Hippias?"
HIP. "Most of all. For I would err too much if I thought otherwise."
SOC. "Let us then set Homer aside, since it is not permitted to inquire of him what his opinion was in composing these verses. But since you take up the cause, and those things seem so to you which you assert Homer said, answer for Homer and yourself at the same time."
HIP. "Let it be so. Ask in few words what you please."
SOC. "Do you call those liars who are unable to do something, like the weak or the weary, or those who can do something?"
HIP. "The powerful, and most of all, both in many other things and also in deceiving men."
SOC. "They are powerful then according to your speech, and wily, are they not?"
HIP. "Certainly."
SOC. "But are they wily and crafty out of some stupidity and imprudence? Or rather by cunning and prudence?"
HIP. "By cunning most of all, and prudence."
SOC. "They are prudent then, as it seems."
HIP. "Greatly, by Jove."
SOC. "Being prudent, are they ignorant of what they do, or do they know?"
HIP. "On the contrary, they know most of all. For because of this they seduce others."
SOC. "Since they are knowing of these things which they know, are they foolish, or rather wise?"
HIP. "Wise, clearly, in these very things for deceiving."
SOC. "Stop, I pray, let us repeat the words, so that we may see what you say. You say liars are powerful and prudent, likewise knowing and wise concerning those things about which they are liars?"
HIP. "I do."
SOC. "But that others are truthful, others on the contrary liars, and these are far contrary between themselves?"
HIP. "I say that too."
SOC. "From this it follows, then, that liars are from the number of the powerful and wise."
HIP. "Most of all."
SOC. "But when you say liars themselves are powerful and wise at the same things, do you say they are powerful to lie if they wish, or powerless at those things which they lie about?"
HIP. "Powerful, indeed."
SOC. "To say it summarily, then, liars are those who are powerful and wise at lying."
HIP. "Clearly."
SOC. "Therefore a man who cannot lie, nor knows anything, will not be a liar."
HIP. "So it is."
SOC. "But he is powerful who can... just as you can write my name whenever you wish, so I ask now. Do you not call a man so affected powerful?"
HIP. "Truly."
SOC. "Tell me, O Hippias, are you not skilled in counting and computing?"
HIP. "Most of all."
SOC. "If someone asks you how much thrice seven hundred makes, will you not, provided you wish, answer concerning these as quickly and as greatly as possible?"
HIP. "Entirely."
SOC. "Is it not because you are most powerful and wisest concerning these things?"
HIP. "Certainly."
SOC. "Are you only the wisest and most powerful? Or also the best concerning the same things, about which you excel in wisdom and power, that is, in computing numbers?"
HIP. "And the best furthermore, Socrates."
SOC. "Therefore you could speak the truth about these things most of all above others, could you not?"
HIP. "I think so indeed."
SOC. "And false things concerning the same? Come now, Hippias, answer generously and magnificently as before. If someone asks how many thrice seven hundred are, will you lie more about these, and always pronounce false things according to the same, wishing to lie and never bring forth the truth? Or can he who is ignorant of numbers lie more than you, even if you wish to lie? Or on the contrary, while the ignorant man often wishes to bring forth false things, will he perhaps by chance bring forth true things besides his intention, because he is ignorant of the matter itself? But you, since you are wise, will you always lie when you wish to lie?"
HIP. "It is as you say."
SOC. "Therefore, is the liar a liar concerning other things, but not concerning numbers, nor will he lie about a number?"
HIP. "Indeed, also about numbers."
SOC. "Let us assume this then, Hippias: that someone is a liar concerning computation and number."
HIP. "Certainly."
SOC. "Who will this be? It is necessary that he be able to lie, as you were saying, if he is to be a liar. For it was said by you, if you remember, that he who cannot lie is not a liar."
HIP. "I remember indeed, and it was so said."
SOC. "Did it not consist a little before that you were most powerful at lying in computing numbers?"
HIP. "That was also said."
SOC. "Are you not also most powerful at bringing forth true things about those same numbers?"
HIP. "Greatly."
SOC. "Therefore the same man can most of all speak the truth in computing and lie: and he is the one who is good at numbers, namely the computer."
HIP. "So entirely."
SOC. "Who then, Hippias, would be a liar in computing, unless he who is good at it? For this one is powerful, this one also truthful."
HIP. "It appears so."
SOC. "You see the same man is truthful and a liar in these things, and the truthful man is in no way better than the liar himself. For they are the same, nor are they very contrary, as you recently thought."
HIP. "It does not certainly appear so now in these things."
SOC. "Do you wish us to consider it in other things too?"
HIP. "As you please."
SOC. "Are you not also skilled in geometry?"
HIP. "I am."
SOC. "Does not the same happen in geometry? The same man can pronounce false things most of all about figures, who also speaks the truth. And he is the geometer."
HIP. "Truly."
SOC. "Is anyone else good at these besides him?"
HIP. "No other."
SOC. "Does not the good and wise geometer..."

[[page number: 188]]
# Book Nineteen.

"...can he do both? And if any other is a liar in figures, he is most of all the one who is good in them: for this one is powerful, but the bad man is powerless at lying. Nor can he ever be a liar who is powerless at lying, as has been conceded."
HIP. "These things are so."
SOC. "Let us inspect a third, the astronomer, which art you are accustomed, Hippias, to profess even more than the superior ones, is it not so?"
HIP. "So certainly."
SOC. "Do not the same things happen in Astronomy?"
HIP. "It is consistent, O Socrates."
SOC. "Wherefore also in astronomy, if any other is a liar, it will be most of all he who is a good astronomer. For he can lie most of all. For he who is powerless is ignorant."
HIP. "So it appears."
SOC. "Therefore the same man will be truthful and a liar in astronomy."
HIP. "It seems so."
SOC. "Come, Hippias, think thus generally through all the sciences, whether it is so, or otherwise. For before all others you are adorned with very many arts. Just as I heard you once boasting, that you abounded in much and desirable wisdom beyond the rest, and walking in the forum among the tables of the money-changers while disputing: when you said you had once gone to Olympia, and all the ornaments of your body which you had, you had made with your own hands. First, the ring you had (for you began from there), was your own work, as if you were skilled in engraving. Furthermore, a certain seal was your work, and a strigil, and a vessel for ointment was similarly your work, and shoes sewn by your hands, and a cloak and an inner garment woven by you. And what seemed most marvelous and an indication of singular wisdom, you said you showed a belt made by you similar to Persian and precious ones. Likewise some of your poems, epic verses, tragedies, dithyrambs, and many orations variedly composed in freer numbers: furthermore, that you held before all others those things which I was commemorating in the superior parts, and excelled in rhythms and harmonies and the right ratio of letters and in very many other things of this kind, if I remember correctly. But truly I had passed over your art of memory, in which you seem to me to be wonderfully polished. Perhaps indeed I have forgotten many other things. But as I said, looking both into your arts (which are too many) and into the arts of others, tell me if you have ever found from those things which were conceded between us, that a truthful man is different from a liar, and that the same man does not exist as both. In any wisdom or craft, or however you wish to call it, seek. But you will never find it, O friend: for it is nowhere. If it is anywhere, speak."
HIP. "I do not find it in the present, Socrates."
SOC. "Nor will you find it hereafter, I think. If I speak the truth, remember, Hippias, what follows from the superior things."
HIP. "I do not sufficiently heed what you say, Socrates."
SOC. "There is no need in the present for the art of memory: for it is clear that you do not think it necessary, but I will lead you back to memory. Do you remember saying Achilles was true and veracious, but Ulysses was a liar and wily?"
HIP. "Indeed."
SOC. "Now however you perceive that the same man appeared to be truthful and a liar. And therefore if Ulysses was a liar, he was also truthful. Likewise if Achilles was veracious, he was also a liar: nor were these two different from each other nor contrary, but they turned out to be similar."
HIP. "Always you, Socrates, weave such little traps, and occupying what is most troublesome in speech, you insist on this, and touch upon every smallest thing, nor do you contend against the whole matter itself about which the speech is. For if you wish, I will now show you with many arguments and sufficient reason that Homer fashioned Achilles as better than Ulysses and truthful: but Ulysses as crafty, and lying in many things, and worse than Achilles. But if it pleases you, answer in turn, and compare your oration with mine, by which I show the other to be better: and so those present will better understand which of us has spoken more rightly."
SOC. "I do not doubt that, nor do I contend, Hippias, that you seem wiser than I. But I am accustomed always, when someone disputes about some matter, to attend diligently, especially when he who speaks seems to me to be wise. Then indeed, being greedy for understanding what he says, I inquire, weigh, and estimate, so that I may perceive the sayings more clearly. But if I make little of the speaker himself, I neither require anything from him, nor do I attend to what he says. And by this very conjecture you will comprehend whom I estimate as wise. For you will see me listening most accurately to their words and inquiring of them, so that I may profit in life by learning something. And now indeed when I was noticing your words, by which you show Achilles by the testimony of those verses as speaking like a boastful man against Ulysses, it seemed a marvelous thing to me if you spoke the truth. Since Ulysses himself, being wily, cannot be convicted of any lie: but Achilles appears to be wily and varied according to your speech: for he lies. For when he had pronounced those verses which you just recited,
[[margin: Iliad.]]
'Since he is more hated by us than the gate of black Dis,
Who hides one thing in his heart and speaks another openly.'
A little after he adds, what will not be persuaded by Ulysses nor by Agamemnon, nor will he remain at Troy.
'But tomorrow I myself, having prepared sacrifices for Jove and the rest
Of the celestials, will lead down the ships collected on the curved shore
Into the sea, which you will see at the first light
Swimming through the Hellespontine sea suitable for fish.
In which you will behold, if only you wish to see, strong
And learned men leaning on the oars. For if
Neptune fills the sails with seconding winds,
The third fruit-bearing light will stand on the shores of Phthia.'
Likewise above, scolding Agamemnon, he says,
[[margin: Iliad.]]
'Behold, I will go home with black ships, because it is better,
Into my country Phthia: nor does my mind wish that here
I should fill you with valid riches and inglorious arms.'
Having said these things, then before the whole army, then to his friends, he nowhere appears either to gird himself for work or to draw the ships, as if about to return home, but rather to care very little that what he says should be true. Indeed, Hippias, I asked you from the beginning, since I doubted which of these is held as more excellent by the Poet, and I thought both were very good men, and it was difficult to know which of these excels more in lying, and truth, and other virtue. For both are very close in this."
HIP. "You do not discern rightly, O Socrates. For what Achilles lies, he seems to lie not from snares but unwillingly because of the fall of the army, being forced to remain and assist: but Ulysses lies spontaneously and by guile."
SOC. "You deceive me, dearest Hippias, and you yourself imitate Ulysses."
HIP. "By no means, Socrates. What do you say? And for what reason?"
SOC. "Because you say Achilles lies not from snares, who was so much a seducer and a snarer beyond his own boasting, as Homer fashions, that he was so much more wily than Ulysses that he hid his vanity from him while he dared to speak things contrary to himself before him, and he deceived Ulysses...

[[page number: 189]]
# Hippias Minor, Or, on lying.

...Wherefore Ulysses seems to infer nothing against him, as he who did not notice the lie."
HIP. "What are these things you say, O Socrates?"
SOC. "Do you not know that afterward he said to Ulysses that he would depart at first light: but to Ajax not so, but otherwise?"
HIP. "Where?"
SOC. "In these verses:
[[margin: Iliad.]]
'No care of war will hold me first,
Until I hear that Hector the son of Priam has come under arms
To the Myrmidons, seeking the ships and long tents,
And has pressed the Argives and hurled against the ships themselves.
For I think Hector, raging against my ships or camp,
Hardly touches them in the doubtful war of the halls.'
Do you think, Hippias, the son of Thetis, taught by the most wise Chiron, was so forgetful that when a little before he had attacked those vain boasters with a most vehement oration, he himself immediately said to Ulysses, as if forgetful of himself, that he would sail, but would remind Ajax: rather than having snared him, since he knew Ulysses was older, and he was far more powerful than his made-up machinations and guiles?"
HIP. "Achilles seems to me to have said those things not by guile, but persuaded otherwise by his very simplicity, to have spoken differently with Ajax than with Ulysses. But Ulysses, whether he speaks true or false things, always tends toward snares."
SOC. "Ulysses then, as it seems, is better than Achilles."
HIP. "By no means, O Socrates."
SOC. "Did it not appear above that those who speak a lie spontaneously are better than those who do so not spontaneously?"
HIP. "In what way, Socrates, can those who sin knowingly, willingly snare and harm, be better than those who do these things besides their intention? Since much is forgiven to him who infers injury through ignorance, speaks a lie, or commits some other evil: and the laws punish more severely those who willingly do evil things and lie than those who do so unwillingly."
SOC. "You see, Hippias, that I speak the truth when I say I am accurate at the interrogations of wise men: and since I fail greatly in other things, I have this much good. For what the nature of things is, I do not know. Which can be conjectured most from this, because as often as I speak with any of you who excel in the opinion of wisdom and have all the Greeks as witnesses of your doctrine, I appear to know nothing. For never does the same thing seem to me, so to speak, as to you. What is a more evident argument of ignorance than if someone dissents from wise men? Yet I have this little good, which helps me, because I prepare myself for learning without the blush of shame. I ask and inquire, and I have huge gratitude for the responder, nor have I ever been ungrateful to any, nor do I ever claim for myself the inventions of others before listeners, but I always extol the teacher with praises and attribute to him before all those things which are his. And indeed now I do not at all admit what you say, rather I dissent far, and I know certainly that this happens by my fault: who indeed confess myself to be such as I am, lest I extol myself. To me indeed, Hippias, it seems entirely contrary than it seems to you. I think indeed those who spontaneously harm men, do injury, lie, deceive, and sin, are better than those who do so not spontaneously. Sometimes however I judge the opposite and err about these things, as one who is ignorant of the matter itself. Behold now a certain disease of the mind has invaded me, and those who sin by purpose concerning something seem to me better than those who err besides their intention. I lead the superior speeches as the cause of this evil, by which it is that in the present I estimate those who do not sin spontaneously to be worse than those who do so spontaneously. Therefore you will forgive me, and let no envy detain you from curing my mind. You will confer a much greater benefit on me if you free my mind from ignorance than if you free my body from sickness. If you wish to effect this with many words, I predict to you that in this way you will least cure me. For I will not follow. But if you wish to answer as above, you will profit me greatly. I hope however this will not be harmful to you. Deservedly indeed I will now invoke you, son of Apemantus. For you yourself led me to dispute with Hippias. Wherefore if Hippias now refuses to answer, intercede for me yourself."
EUD. "I think there is no need for my prayers to Hippias, Socrates. For he did not propose to answer only by force: rather he promised to answer all things freely. Were these not the things you were saying, Hippias?"
HIP. "I was saying them indeed. But Socrates here, O Eudicus, always disturbs the speakers and seems to be like a certain prestidigitator."
SOC. "O best of men, Hippias, I do not do these things spontaneously. For I would be wise according to your speech and wily. But I act besides my intention, wherefore forgive me. For you say one should forgive him who does not sin spontaneously."
EUD. "Do not do otherwise, Hippias, but for our sake and because of those things said by you above, answer to those things which Socrates asks."
HIP. "I will answer indeed, since you ask. Seek then what you please."
SOC. "I vehemently desire, Hippias, to consider what was just said, which of the two are better: those who sin spontaneously and willingly, or those on the contrary. I hope it can be considered most rightly in this way. Answer now. Do you call some runner good?"
HIP. "Indeed."
SOC. "And bad?"
HIP. "Yes."
SOC. "Is not he good who runs well, and bad who runs poorly?"
HIP. "Certainly."
SOC. "Does not he who runs slowly, run poorly? But he who runs swiftly, runs well?"
HIP. "Without a doubt."
SOC. "In the running itself, therefore, speed is a good, but slowness an evil."
HIP. "What then?"
SOC. "Which runner then is better? He who runs slowly spontaneously, or he who does so otherwise?"
HIP. "He who does so voluntarily."
SOC. "Is not running doing something?"
HIP. "Doing indeed."
SOC. "But doing something is working."
HIP. "Truly."
SOC. "Therefore he who runs poorly works this evil and base thing in the race."
HIP. "Evil. Why not?"
SOC. "But he runs poorly who runs slowly."
HIP. "Truly."
SOC. "Therefore, does not the good runner work this evil and base thing by industry, and the bad runner besides his purpose?"
HIP. "It seems so."
SOC. "In the race, therefore, he is worse who acts poorly besides his will than he who does so willingly."
HIP. "In the race, clearly."
SOC. "What about in the wrestling ring? Which wrestler is better? He who falls by deliberate effort? Or he who falls unwillingly?"
HIP. "He who falls by deliberate effort."
SOC. "So it seems. But is it worse and more base to fall in the wrestling ring, or to throw down?"
HIP. "To fall."
SOC. "And in the wrestling ring, therefore, he who works evil and base things by study is a better wrestler than he who does so by weakness and inertia."
HIP. "It seems so."
SOC. "What about in all other use of the body? Is not he who is more robust and fitter of body able to do both at his discretion, both what belongs to a robust man and what belongs to a weak man, both beautiful and base things? Wherefore he who excels in the habit of the body, whenever he does poorly according to the body, he effects it willingly; but the weak man unwillingly."
HIP. "It seems also that the same happens concerning strength."
SOC. "What indeed of the elegance of the figure itself: is it not of the more beautiful and better body to join together base figures with expended effort, but the deformed on the contrary? What does it seem to you?"
HIP. "What it seems to you."
SOC. "Elegance of figure, therefore, when voluntary, pertains to the virtue of the body; but when contrary, to its vice."
HIP. "It appears so."
SOC. "Of the voice, what do you say? Which do you assert is better? That which is dissonant from the will of the mind, or from inertia?"
HIP. "From the will of the mind."
SOC. "The other, truly, is worse."
HIP. "Without a doubt."
SOC. "Do you wish to have good things or evil things?"
HIP. "Good."
SOC. "Which would you choose: to have feet which limp by deliberate effort, or which do so unwillingly?"
HIP. "Those clearly which limp by industry."
SOC. "Is not the limping of feet a vice and a deformity?"
HIP. "It is."
SOC. "And is not dullness of the eyes a vice?"
HIP. "A vice."
SOC. "Which eyes then will you rather choose? Those with which someone sees confusedly or inspects perversely spontaneously? Or on the contrary, those with which someone sees poorly unwillingly?"
HIP. "Those with which someone does so willingly."
SOC. "From these things which are yours, you think those better which act poorly spontaneously than those which do so unwillingly."
HIP. "Such things indeed."
SOC. "Does not one reason comprehend all the rest: ears, nostrils, mouth, and all senses, which teaches that senses sinning besides their purpose are never to be chosen, as being bad? But those which do so from institution are rather to be chosen as good?"
HIP. "It seems to me."
SOC. "Of which instruments is the use better? Those with which someone errs willingly, or those with which someone errs unwillingly? Such as a rudder: is that better by which someone steers poorly by industry, or that by which someone does so unwillingly?"
HIP. "That by which he does so by industry."
SOC. "Similarly a bow, a lyre, pipes, and all other things."
HIP. "You speak the truth."
SOC. "Which soul of a horse is better to possess? That by which one rides poorly spontaneously, or that by which one does so unwillingly?"
HIP. "That by which he does so spontaneously."
SOC. "It is therefore better."
HIP. "It is."
SOC. "To the better soul of a horse, therefore, one will do the evil works of this soul willingly, but contrary things on the contrary."
HIP. "Entirely."
SOC. "Is not the same reason of the soul of a dog and other animals?"
HIP. "The same."
SOC. "Which soul of an archer would you choose as better? That of him who misses the mark willingly, or that of him who misses unwillingly?"
HIP. "That of him who does so voluntarily."
SOC. "Is not this better for the art of archery?"
HIP. "Better."
SOC. "Wherefore the soul which misses while ignorant is worse than that which misses while knowing."
HIP. "In the faculty of archery, clearly."
SOC. "What indeed in the study of medicine? Is not that which by deliberate effort infers certain evil things to bodies, as far as pertains to the art of medicine, more skilled than that which sins through ignorance?"
HIP. "Clearly."
SOC. "Therefore this one is better in the art of medicine."
HIP. "Better."
SOC. "Which is better instructed for playing the cithara or blowing pipes, and other works of each art or science, and therefore better? That which, if ever it does something poorly besides the art, does so by industry: but the worse one does so besides its intention?"
HIP. "It appears so."
SOC. "Will we choose rather the souls of servants who knowingly sin concerning their ministry, than those who sin while ignorant, as being better for these works?"
HIP. "Truly."
SOC. "And our own soul, do we not desire to have it as best as possible?"
HIP. "Certainly."
SOC. "Will it not be better if it does evil things and sins spontaneously than if it does so unknowingly?"
HIP. "It would be grave, O Socrates, if those who do injury spontaneously were better than those who do so not spontaneously."
SOC. "From those things which were said above, however, it seems to follow."
HIP. "But to me in no way."
SOC. "I thought, Hippias, that it seemed the same to you as well. Answer therefore again. Is justice not either a certain power, or science, or both? Is it not necessary that justice be something of these?"
HIP. "Necessary."
SOC. "If justice is a certain power of the soul, will the more powerful soul be more just? For this one appeared better to us, O best of men."
HIP. "It appeared so."
SOC. "What if justice is science? Will not the wiser soul be more just? And the more foolish, on the contrary, more unjust?"
HIP. "It is so."
SOC. "What if it is both? Will not that which has both these—namely, science and power—be more just? And that which does not have science, more unjust? Is it not necessary that the matter be held so?"
HIP. "It appears so."
SOC. "But that which is more powerful and wiser appeared to be better, and more prepared for each—both beautiful and base things—concerning any action to be performed?"
HIP. "Certainly."
SOC. "Whenever therefore it does base things, it does so willingly because of art and power. These, however, either both or one, pertain to justice."
HIP. "It seems so."
SOC. "Truly to do injury is to do evil things: not to do injury is to do good things."
HIP. "It is so."
SOC. "Therefore, will not the more powerful and better soul, whenever it acts unjustly, act so spontaneously? But the base one on the contrary?"
HIP. "It appears so."
SOC. "Is not a good man he who has a good soul? And a bad man on the contrary he who has a bad one?"
HIP. "Without a doubt."
SOC. "Wherefore it belongs to a good man to do injury spontaneously, but to a bad man not spontaneously, if indeed a good man has a good soul."
HIP. "He has one indeed."
SOC. "If there is any man, therefore, who misses spontaneously and commits base and unjust things, he is no other, O Hippias, than a good man."
HIP. "I cannot concede those things to you, O Socrates."
SOC. "Nor can I to myself, Hippias, yet from the superior speech it is necessary that it seem so to us in the present. But truly, as I was saying above, I always wander up and down concerning these things, nor do I persist in the same opinion; nor is it a wonder that I and those like me, unrefined men, wander about to contraries, if even you wise men wander. But it is a grave evil to us if, having set out to you, we do not cease to err."

# CHARMIDES, OR,
## ON TEMPERANCE.
### MARSILIO FICINO'S
### ARGUMENT.

THE STUDY of Socrates in this dialogue is to exhort all indeed to temperance: but three groups especially, namely the young, the noble, and the beautiful. The young indeed for this reason, that medicine must be applied quickly to diseases. "Resist the beginnings; too late is medicine prepared when evils have grown strong through long delays." The noble also, both so that he may show that true nobility is to be placed in virtue, and because the noble are for the most part an example to the rest and are daily admitted to the republic, to the very grave detriment of the human race if they are bad. Finally, the beautiful: for these are most of all depraved by the company of the profligate, which is why they have more need of medicine. Furthermore, the beautiful ought to study so that, just as nature has handed down a brief beauty to the body, so they in turn may restore to God, the author of nature, a perpetual beauty of the soul. Nor indeed is it to be permitted that while our exterior parts please many with their beauty, the interior parts meanwhile displease with their deformity. Although all things in this dialogue have a wonderful allegory, especially amatory things, no differently than the Song of Solomon, I have nevertheless changed some things and passed over some. For those things which were in harmony with the most chaste ears of the Athenians might perhaps be least in harmony with more unrefined ears. And therefore a certain Aristarchus the Homeric, or rather the Platonic, might say that those things which are less in harmony do not belong to Plato but to Chronos. Three things indeed are to be noted in the beginning: first, those which transfer love from this form of the body to incorporeal beauty. First, that Socrates says he discerns nothing between this beautiful one and that beautiful one, but all beautiful ones please him equally: as if he would say, one's foot is not to be fixed in the form of one body, but one must ascend to the common beauty of the whole species itself. Which, since it is one in many, refers to one idea of beauty over many. Just as, therefore, we transcend by thinking from the individual to the species, and from the species to the idea, so also we are admonished to proceed from the love of this form to the love of the common form first, and then to the love of the ideal form. To these things Socrates added that the beauty of the body is not to be loved for itself, but to be estimated by us as an image of divine beauty. He bids finally to strip the soul, and having postponed the form of the body, to look more diligently at the natural decorum of the soul and to apply study to acquire it. And meanwhile he rebukes Chaerephon, who said something or other about the nudity of the body in the wrestling ring. Nor without cause does he begin the exhortation to temperance from the beauty of the body. For this is the temperance which is called of lines and colors. But from this he immediately passes to the health of the body, which is also a certain temperance and moderation: and in knowledge there is similarly a certain temperance, consisting in a certain harmony and congruence of the intellect to the things which are understood, so that not undeservedly Pythagoras called temperance the most healthy of all virtues, the preserver of human society both publicly and privately: especially since justice is also a certain temperance, that is, a convenient moderation in exchanging and distributing. Truly although temperance properly revolves around restraining vehement lusts and pleasures, yet by a certain similitude it is transferred both to amputating all desires and to moderating any act, so that even the office of fortitude consists in the moderation of audacity and fear, similarly of justice in the mode of rewards and punishments, also of liberality in the mode of expending, finally the health of the whole life, "nothing in excess." Hence that Pythagorean saying: "Measure is the best of all things." But remember those were denied to be temperate in the *Phaedo* who abstain from pleasures for the sake of bodily pleasure. For he bids that mortal actions be referred to purging the mind, for the sake of following wisdom and divine similitude. So great truly is the excellence of temperance that all elegant craftsmen observe it in their works, and by its virtue not only any body under the moon, but even the whole universe itself is preserved. Which is confirmed in the *Gorgias* by the testimony of the wise. To this is similar: "God disposes all things sweetly." Likewise he disposes all things in number, weight, and measure. But let us now return to the dialogue. Socrates, while he forbids curing the body before the soul is cured according to the opinion of the Magi, manifestly reproves those who, caring for the smallest things, neglect the greatest, as those who seek remedies for sick horses and dogs, but least of all consult doctors for the diseases of their own body and soul. They compose all the smallest household goods rightly, while they themselves are meanwhile uncomposed in both soul and body. To an intemperate soul, temperance is hateful. Daily they curiously handle other people's affairs but desert their own. All things truly besides the soul itself are alien to us. Therefore he called the medicine of the body a "folium" [leaf], a light, fragile thing, and entirely mutable, and to be utterly contemned. He signifies also that many inconveniences both of body and of fortune frequently happen to us because of intemperance, and on the contrary very many good things proceed through temperance. Likewise, to a perfectly composed soul, whatever happens is both prudently disposed and equally tolerated, so that nothing finally turns out as an evil. But to an uncomposed soul, nothing can be well composed either in the body or outside it. He expounds moreover in the *Cratylus* the Greek name for temperance, *Sophrosyne*, as a certain safety and preservation of prudence. For he thinks that the lights of all truths were innate in the mind, and therefore if it should look entirely into itself, it will behold all truths. But truly that it should not look, the cause is an immoderate affection toward the body and corporeal things: whence it is that temperance is needed in the beginning: which having expelled the darkness of perturbations, the mind, being made more serene, is abundantly surrounded by the light of the divine sun, whence it first recovers wisdom, and then acquires prudence. Since therefore wisdom and prudence accompany temperance, therefore Plato often elsewhere and in this dialogue under the very name of temperance wants wisdom also and prudence to be contained. Socrates advises Charmides to look into himself when about to make words about temperance. For this very turning into oneself is the office of this virtue: and he who, having turned entirely into himself, both understands human temperance through the innate idea of temperance in the mind, and also recognizes the moderation itself by which God tempered the parts of the soul among themselves from the beginning, will know by what reason the soul thus affected is to be tempered. To these things is added that in this precept he signifies that no one except the temperate ought or can speak of temperance for persuading. Furthermore it is handed down in the *Timaeus* that from a certain consonant modulation of the soul both to itself and to the body, all prosperous things happen to us. Furthermore the Pythagoreans, whom the Roman Censorinus follows in this, promise perpetual and true health and a long life to the body if the mind prudently moderates individual motions both of itself and of the body. Which indeed is found to have happened to many very holy and wise men, both Censorinus and we have. To the same cause or a similar one some refer the lives of the ancients. But something marvelous is added to these: that the Magi by their "charms" promise immortality to bodies. The Magic of Zoroaster, Plato says in the *Alcibiades*, is nothing other than divine worship. Here furthermore he added that by not only magical charms but also by philosophical reasons, both the soul is tempered and the body is preserved either always or at least for a long time far from death. Certainly that oration which is entirely about to persuade the audience of temperance and furthermore affect them, requires two things especially: a power infused by God, and reasons compared by philosophy. And an oration composed from these two Plato names a "magical incantation," by which Phoebus first, then the Pythagoreans, wonderfully expelled diseases from the soul and body. Nor truly ought it to be thought false that the body under a soul entirely tempered can be immortal, and under an intemperate one can fall into diseases and evils. For that contains the Mosaic mystery concerning the state and fall of the first parents. And Avicenna, following the Platonics and Hippocrates, proves that the mind from its very nature so much exceeds all matter that as soon as it is restored into itself, it can move the elements of the world by a certain marvelous virtue and have empire over bodies: whence it is that it can do so much more in its own body. Which indeed Adam could experience from the beginning, and some think Enoch and Elias, and some suspect the Evangelist still lives by a certain similar reason. But of all these things we dispute most widely in our *Theology*. Finally, to speak summarily, marvelous things are declared in this virtue of temperance, that it restores one who has fallen into baser things to himself happily. The marvelous power of the soul is also declared, from which all things both good and bad flow into the body, and by whose will the body can be preserved incorrupt. Which indeed is everywhere consonant with Mosaic mysteries. After these things follow what temperance is, which indeed neither Charmides nor Critias ever absolute. For the former brings into the middle not temperance properly, but those things which accompany it: the latter however pertains more to prudence: and that indeed always ineptly, namely so that it may be declared that it is not for anyone to discourse on such a noble virtue. Meanwhile note that the ancient priests were accustomed to keep the third of the libations of the sacrificial bowls for Jove the Savior especially, as declaring the principles, means, and ends of all things, as Plato relates in the *Laws*, to be disposed and preserved under the providence of Jove. But let us return to the ineptitudes of Critias, saying that it is a certain science which knows both itself and all sciences but is ignorant of the matters themselves of which they are sciences. Which indeed is therefore absurd, because the truth and reason of science consist in a certain contact and congruence of those things which are known. Furthermore science cannot be perfectly known unless it be discerned what science is: but that cannot be held unless it be held of what it is. Likewise Critias confesses that someone who in no way knows can meanwhile know that he does not know. But Socrates for that reason did not receive it, because those things which are in no way known cannot meanwhile be known in a certain way. For whoever notices that he is ignorant of something, by that very fact recognizes and knows that he lacks it. He indicates thus: therefore already a notion of that very thing which he lacks is described in himself, through which he judges both that he lacks it and of what he especially lacks. Whence it is that whoever knows he is ignorant of some matter, meanwhile does not entirely ignore the matter itself, rather he describes it with a certain general adumbration; I say general because science consists perfectly in the special distinction of things, which Plato seeks through all his disputations. But where he induces Socrates recognizing that he knows nothing, he judges that he had, even if not special, nevertheless general descriptions of things, otherwise he could not recognize his ignorance: and therefore while he knew nothing, he knew all things in a certain way. But because Critias had translated the speech about temperance to prudence, and that with a certain Platonic license, Socrates asserts prudence—that is, the science of good and evil—to obtain the highest authority for beatitude, both because it demonstrates both the end of the good and the means to that good, and because all things, both matters and arts, as far as they are ruled by it, are conducive to us for the good, but on the contrary in no way. Finally Socrates teaches that nothing is more difficult either to define or to acquire than temperance. The difficulty of the definition proceeds from this: that its force from the other virtues, of which it is a certain consonance, can be discerned. Add that it is understood and expressed by words more difficultly in proportion as it is possessed more difficultly within. Certainly since from the commerce of the body itself we are especially inclined to pleasure and intemperance, we acquire temperance most difficultly. Furthermore the first affections of the senses seem to lead some either to fortitude through anger and audacity, or to prudence through fear, or to patience through pain, or to justice and liberality through love. Temperance, however, is always opposed to all impulses. For since it can be placed only in a certain tranquility, it is hindered from every affection on all sides. Difficulty also increases because just as in the body an entirely consonant temper of humors and members is found, so in the soul an entire harmony of all its parts...

# Euthydemus, or, The Disputatious. 183

...he was distressed, and was being sharply bitten by words, he implored the help of his nephew Iolaus, who greatly assisted him. But if my Iolaus, Patrocles, should come, he would act far differently. <note>Socrates is comparing the logical "bites" of the sophists to the heads of the Hydra which Heracles fought with Iolaus's help. Patrocles was Socrates's half-brother.</note> "Respond then," said Dionysodorus, "since you yourself proclaim these things: was Iolaus more the son of Heracles' brother than he was yours?" "I think it would be worth the effort to answer you, Dionysodorus. For you would not cease from questioning and, out of a certain envy, causing a disturbance, lest Euthydemus the wise should teach me that." "Respond then," he said. "I respond," I said, "that Iolaus was the son of Heracles' brother; but mine, as it seems, he was not at all. For his father Patrocles was not my brother, but someone else close in name, Iphicles, was the brother of Heracles." "And Patrocles," he said, "is he yours?" "Certainly," I said, "but from the same mother, not the same father." "Therefore he is a brother to you," he said, "and he is not a brother." "Not from the same father, O best of men," I said. "For his father was Chaeredemus, but mine was Sophroniscus." "Was Sophroniscus and Chaeredemus a father?" he asked. "Entirely; the former was mine, the latter was his." "Was Chaeredemus anything other than a father?" "He was other than *my* father, certainly." "Was he a father, then, while being other than a father? Or are you the same thing as a stone?" <note>The sophist is using a word-play: because Chaeredemus is "other" than Socrates's father, they argue he is "not a father" at all, or that "fatherhood" cannot coexist with being "other."</note> "I feared," I said, "lest I might seem the same as a stone by your assertion. But it does not seem so to me." "Are you not, therefore, other than a stone?" "Other, certainly." "But if you are other than a stone, you are not a stone. And if you are other than gold, you are not gold." "That is so," I said. "By that same reasoning, since Chaeredemus is other than a father, will he not be a father?" "It seems," I said, "that he is not a father." To this Euthydemus added: "Chaeredemus is by no means a father; and again, since Sophroniscus is other than a father, he is not a father. Therefore, O Socrates, you are without a father." Taking up the conversation, Ctesippus broke in: "But as for your father, since the same condition applies to him, he is other than my father." "Far from it," said Euthydemus. "Is he the same?" "The same indeed." "I should not agree. But tell me, Euthydemus, is he only my father, or also the father of all other men?" "Of all others as well." "Do you think the same man, while being a father, can be not a father?" "I should have thought so," Ctesippus said. "And gold," he asked, "while being gold, can it be not gold? Or a man, while being a man, can he be not a man?" Then Ctesippus said, "You are not, as they say, Euthydemus, **connecting flax to flax**. <margin>Proverb.</margin> <note>original: "lino linum connectis". This is a proverb meaning to weave together things that are alike, or to spin a long, repetitive yarn.</note> You say a grave thing if your father is the father of all." "He is, however," he said. "Whether of men only," asked Ctesippus, "or also of horses and all other animals?" "Of all, absolutely." "And is your mother the mother of all?" "She is also the mother." "Therefore your mother is the mother of sea urchins." "And yours," he said. "And you, in turn, are the brother of gudgeons, puppies, and piglets." "And you," he said. "Furthermore, your father is a dog." "And yours as well." Here Dionysodorus said, "If you are willing to answer me, Ctesippus, I will make you concede these things. Tell me, do you have a dog?" "And a very bad dog at that," Ctesippus said. "Does he have puppies?" "He has many such puppies." "And is the dog not their father?" "I certainly saw him mating with the mother dog." "Is the dog not yours?" "He is." "Therefore, being a father, is he not yours? Wherefore your father is a dog, and you are the brother of puppies." But lest Ctesippus should object first, Dionysodorus suddenly added: "Answer a little more. Do you beat this dog?" Laughing, Ctesippus said, "I do beat him, but I cannot beat you." "Do you not, therefore, beat your own father?" "It would be far more just," he responded, "if I were to beat your father, who, having acquired such a 'discipline,' begat such wise sons." "But tell me, O Euthydemus, has your father and the father of the puppies obtained many good things from your wisdom?" "Neither he stands in need of many good things, O Ctesippus, nor do you." "Nor do you either, Euthydemus," he said, "nor any other of men. For tell me, Ctesippus, whether you think it is good for a sick man to drink a <term>pharmacum</term> <note>original: "pharmacum" (medicine/drug). In Greek medicine, this could refer to a healing potion or a poison.</note> when he needs it, or not? Or is it good for a man about to fight to go forth armed, or unarmed?" "I think so indeed," he said, "for I expect something extraordinary from you." "You shall see for yourself, O best one," he said. "But answer: after you have confessed it is good to drink medicine when the situation requires it, ought one to drink as much of this good as possible? And will it be best if someone grinds up and pours into the cup as much hellebore as a wagon could carry?" <note>Hellebore was a potent herbal remedy used for mental illness and purging; in large doses, it is lethal.</note> "Certainly so," Ctesippus said, "if the one who is to drink is as large as the statue at Delphi." "In the same way in war," he said, "if it is good to be clothed in arms, should one have the greatest number of arms, and should a pack of javelins and shields be carried about, since it is a good thing?" "Most certainly," Ctesippus said. "But you do not think, Euthydemus, that only one javelin should be carried?" "I think so," he said. "Would you then so arm Geryon and Briareus?" <note>Mythological giants; Geryon had three bodies and Briareus had a hundred arms.</note> Ctesippus said, "I thought you and this comrade of yours were more robust, seeing as you are men of arms." Euthydemus remained silent. But Dionysodorus, in response to what Ctesippus had first answered, broke in: "Does it seem good to you to possess gold?" "Very much so," Ctesippus responded. "And is it not good to have money always and everywhere?" "Most especially," he said. "Do you not confess that gold is good?" "We have already confessed it." "Should one then have it always, and everywhere, and as much as possible *inside* oneself?" "He would be most blessed who had three talents of gold in his belly, one talent under his skull-bone, and a <term>stater</term> <note>A gold coin or specific weight.</note>—that is, a certain coin and weight of gold—in each eye." Ctesippus said, "O Euthydemus, they say that among the Scythians those men are the most happy and best who contain much gold in their own skull-bones, just as you said a little while ago that a dog was a father. And what is more marvelous, they drink from their own gilded heads, and they look into these, lifting up their own crown and forehead with their hands." To this Euthydemus asked: "Do the Scythians and other men see what they are able to see, Ctesippus, or what they are not able to see?" "Clearly what they are able to see." "Do you not also?" "I as well." "Do you see our clothes?" "I see them." "Are these, therefore, able to see?" <note>The sophist is playing on the ambiguity of "able to be seen" vs "able to see."</note> "Wonderfully so," Ctesippus said. "What further?" he said. "Nothing. But do you not think they see? Are you so pleasant a man? You seem to me, Euthydemus, to have fallen asleep while awake, and I think you are able to say nothing while speaking." "And do you seem to do this?" "Is it not impossible," Dionysodorus said, "to speak while being silent?" "Impossible," Ctesippus said. "But is it possible for one who is speaking to be silent?" "Much less possible." "When, therefore, you speak of a stone, do you not speak of a silent thing? And when you speak of wood and iron likewise?" "I will not concede that iron things are silent to you," Ctesippus said, "for if someone strikes them, they are said to sound and ring out. Wherefore, because of your wisdom, you have not sufficiently noticed that you are saying nothing. But as for what remains, show that it is possible for one who is speaking to be silent." Certainly, it seemed to me then that Ctesippus was contending vehemently on behalf of his friend. "When you are silent," Euthydemus said, "are you not silent regarding all things?" "Indeed." "Are you not then silent regarding anything that is speaking? Since those things which speak are counted in the number of 'all things'." "What then?" Ctesippus asked, "Are all things not silent?" "No," said Euthydemus. "Then do all things speak, O best of men?" "Yes, certainly, those which speak." "I was not asking that," he said, "but whether all things are silent or speak." Then, smiling...

184 The Eighteenth Book.

...stealing the conversation, Dionysodorus said, "Neither and both. For I know certainly that you will be ignorant of what to object to this answer." Immediately Ctesippus, as he is wont, broke into laughter and shouted: "O Euthydemus, your brother has already been defeated!" Clinias also laughed, being quite delighted. Wherefore Ctesippus, exulting, grew more than tenfold in joy. But it seemed to me that Ctesippus, like a veteran, had extorted these very things from them by craft. For such wisdom does not exist among other men of our time. After these things I said, "Why do you laugh, O Clinias, at such serious and beautiful matters?" But Dionysodorus, turning to me, said, "Have you ever seen a beautiful thing, Socrates?" "Many indeed, Dionysodorus." "Are they anything other than beauty itself? Or are they the same?" I hesitated everywhere, and thought I suffered this not unjustly, since I could no longer remain silent. However, I replied that they were other than beauty itself, but that a certain beauty was present in each. "If an ox were present to you," he asked, "would you yourself be an ox? And because I am now present to you, are you Dionysodorus?" "Heaven forbid <note>original: "Bona verba quaeso," literally "Good words, I pray," used as a pious euphemism to ward off bad omens.</note>," I said. But he asked, "In what way is one thing present to another, since one is one, and the other is the other?" "Do you doubt this?" I asked. Truly I was now striving to imitate their wisdom, being inflamed with desire for it. "Why should I not doubt," he said, "both I and all others, concerning that which exists in no way?" "What are you saying, Dionysodorus? Is not the beautiful beautiful, or the ugly, ugly?" "If it seems so to me," he said. "Does it not seem so?" "Entirely," he said. "And is not the same thing the same," I said, "and the other similarly the other? But is that which is 'other' not the same?" "I did not think even a child would suspect this, but rather that what is other, is other. But, O Dionysodorus, you omitted this intentionally. You seem to me, like craftsmen who know how to finish individual tasks, to properly handle and deliver the method of disputation." "Do you know," he asked, "what it is fitting for individual craftsmen to finish? First, do you know whom it befits to hammer bronze?" "A blacksmith," I said. "And whom to mold clay?" "A potter." "And again, whom to slaughter and skin, and to roast or boil meat cut into pieces?" "A cook." "Does not whoever does the fitting things act rightly?" "Very much so," I said. "And it is fitting, as you say," he said, "for a cook to cut and skin. Did you concede these things, or not?" "I conceded them," I said, "but forgive me, I pray." "It stands therefore," he said, "that if someone, slaughtering and cutting a cook, should boil or roast him, he would be doing the fitting thing. Furthermore, if someone hammers a blacksmith with bronze, and molds a potter, he will be working similarly fitting things." "O Neptune!" I said, "now you have put the finishing touch <note>original: "colophonem," meaning the final stroke or peak of an achievement.</note> on this wisdom of yours. Will this ever be present to me so that it becomes my own?" "Would you recognize it, O Socrates, if it had already become your own?" "If you yourself wish it," I said, "I certainly would." "What further," he said, "do you think you know as your own?" "Indeed," I said, "unless perhaps you say otherwise. For it is necessary to begin from you, and to end with this Euthydemus." "Do you not think those things are yours," he said, "of which you are the master? And which you are allowed to use at your judgment, like oxen and sheep? Do you think those things are yours which you can sell and give away, and vow to any of the gods? And those which you cannot, are they not yours?" I, thinking that some noble question would arise from there, and being immediately inflamed with greed for hearing, said "Entirely so. Such things are indeed mine." "Do you not name as animals," he said, "those that have a soul?" "Those very ones," I said. "Do you confess then that of animals, only those are yours concerning which you can do all these things which I just mentioned?" "I confess it," I said. Here he restrained himself quite ironically, as if about to contemplate some great matter, then said: "Tell me, O Socrates: Do you have a fatherly Jupiter?" And I, suspecting the conversation would return to where it had arrived, and withdrawing through a certain ambiguous bypass, escaped the net in which I was already as if entangled, and replied, "He is not, O Dionysodorus." "You are a wretched man," he said, "and no Athenian, who has neither fatherly gods, nor sacred rites, nor any other noble and magnificent thing." "Leave those things, Dionysodorus," I said, "lest you speak ill omens, or teach too sharply. For I have both altars and domestic fatherly rites, and whatever other things of that kind are present for Athenians." "For the rest of the Athenians," he asked, "is there a fatherly Jupiter?" "There is not," I said, "among the Ionians such a kinship, nor among those who came from this city, nor among us, but Apollo is our fatherly god because of the birth of Ion. Jupiter is not called our fatherly god, but he is called the protector of the city and the caretaker of the tribe, and Athena is the caretaker of the tribe." "It is enough," said Dionysodorus. "For you have, as it seems, Apollo, Jupiter, and Athena." "Entirely." "Will these not be your gods? Forefathers, namely, and masters? Are they not yours? Have you not confessed they are yours?" "I have confessed it," I said. "What then?" "Are these gods not animals?" he asked. "You conceded further that whatever things have a soul are animals; do these gods not have a soul?" "They certainly have one," I said. "Are they therefore animals?" "They are certainly." "And of animals, you said those were yours of which you had the power, to sell, give away, and dedicate to the gods according to your judgment." "I cannot refuse, Euthydemus, that I conceded those things." Immediately he brought this in: "Since you confess Jupiter is yours, and the other gods are yours, is it not permitted for you to sell them and give them away, and to treat them at your whim just like the other animals that are yours?" I then, Crito, as if struck by his speech, became silent. But Ctesippus, trying to help me, said, "O Hercules! A magnificent speech!" To which Dionysodorus replied, "Is Hercules an 'oh' or is 'oh' Hercules?" Then Ctesippus said, "O Neptune, brave and hard speeches. I desist now. These men are invincible." Here certainly, friend Crito, no one present could contain their laughter, nor refrain from extolling their oration with the highest praises: and those guests Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, exulting with laughter, applause, and joy, were almost dissolved with delight. For in the previous parts, while individual points were being brought forward, only their followers would immediately applaud. But here, almost the very columns of the Lyceum <note>The gymnasium where the dialogue takes place.</note> seemed to shout, applaud, and exult. I indeed was so affected that I asserted I had never seen any men of equal wisdom. And being entirely enslaved to their wisdom, I began to praise and celebrate them exceedingly. "O men," I said, "blessed by the marvelous gifts of nature: you who have accomplished such a great thing so easily and in so short a time. Many other things indeed in your speeches, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, are noble, in which this is especially magnificent: that you have no care for the common people, or even for illustrious men, or those held in any esteem, but only for those like yourselves. Indeed I know for certain that there are few who love this kind of speech, and they indeed are like you; but others so ignore and despise them that they would be more vehemently ashamed if they convicted others with them than if they themselves were convicted by others. This, moreover, your speeches have that is popular and gentle: that when you say nothing...
