### Euthydemus, Or, The Litigious Man. 185

...is good or bad, neither white nor anything else of such things, nor anything at all different from others: truly, as you boast, you have completely blocked the mouths of men. Because not only the mouths of others, but yours in addition, it is a graceful thing: and you avoid the hatred and offense of the listeners. This is truly the greatest thing: that these have been so skillfully invented and established by you that you are able to hand them over to anyone in a short time. I have recognized this indeed, and I pay attention to Ctesippus, and I consider how suddenly he began to imitate you. It is noble to be able to teach the mystery of this thing as quickly as possible; nevertheless, it does not seem it would be worth the effort for you to discourse in the presence of many men: rather indeed, if you believe me, you will be entirely careful not to speak in a crowd of many: lest perhaps, perceiving these things as soon as possible, they should by no means be grateful. Therefore, communicate these things only among yourselves in turn, and let no one else hear them unless silver has been set out. If you are wise, you will advise your disciples the same: never to speak of these things with others except with themselves and with you. For what is rare, Euthydemus, that is to be honored. For water is bought at the cheapest price, though it is the most precious thing by nature, as Pindarus says. But come," I said, "accept this Clinias and me." When we had discussed these and certain other brief things, O Crito, we left. Deliberate therefore who might come with me to these men. For they promise they will teach all who are prepared to give silver, and they except no natural ability or age. What truly is most useful for you to hear: they say that the study of accumulating money does not prohibit anyone from being able to easily perceive their wisdom.

**CRITO:** Indeed, O Socrates, I am eager to hear, and I would most willingly learn. Yet I seem myself to be one of those who are not like Euthydemus, but rather of those whom you mentioned a little while ago, who prefer to be refuted by others by such little catches rather than to refute others. Truly it would be ridiculous if I proceeded to advise you. Yet nothing prohibits me from reporting to you now what I heard from one of those who, having left your gathering, departed from you. As I was walking, I happened upon one of those who are esteemed to excel most in judicial causes. "O Crito," he said, "have you heard nothing from these wise men?" "Nothing, by Jupiter," I said. "For a frequent crowd and tumult prohibited me, though I was desiring to hear." "The matter, however," he said, "is worthy of hearing." "Why?" I asked. "So that you might have heard those men disputing, who in this kind of speech excel the others." To him I said: "What did it seem to you?" "What else," he said, "than what is always heard from these men, while they trifle, and wrangle with each other with a certain unworthy zeal about matters of no moment?" Specifically, he used this speech. Then I said: "Nevertheless, philosophy is a graceful thing." "How graceful," he said, "O blessed man, when it is of no price? But if you had been present a little while ago, you would have been ashamed, as I think, for the sake of your friend: who was so inept that he desired to hand himself over to men who have no care for what they say, but catch at individual things, and object to words, when nevertheless they, as I was saying above, excel the other such men of our age. Truly, O Crito, both this study is most vile, and those who are engaged in it are ridiculous." To me indeed, O Socrates, that man did not seem rightly to disapprove of the thing itself, or whoever else might disapprove. But because someone should study to dispute with such men in a crowd of many, he seemed to me to have rightly blamed that.

**SOCRATES:** O Crito, these men are worthy of admiration. But I do not yet know what I am about to say. From which number was he who, meeting you, was disparaging philosophy? Was he some orator from those who are powerful in judicial contest? Or from those who produce and write such speeches with which the orator contends in court?

**CRITO:** By no means an orator, nor do I think he ever spoke in court, but they say he understands the judicial matter itself very well, and composes elegant speeches.

**SOCRATES:** I have it now. Truly I was about to say the same thing. For these are the ones, O Crito, whom Prodicus <note>A famous Greek philosopher and sophist, contemporary with Socrates.</note> established as borders between the philosopher and the statesman. These men think they are the wisest of all, and moreover seem such to very many: but that philosophers alone are an impediment to them, preventing them from being equally approved by all. They think, therefore, if they spread this common opinion against philosophers, that they are of no price, they will report the highest glory of wisdom among all without controversy. For they say they are truly the wisest, but are hindered in private conversations when the followers of Euthydemus oppose them. That they are wise, however, they want to seem agreeable from this: that they have enough of philosophy, enough also of civil skill, and they are participants in both as much as is necessary, and being placed outside the turbulent tumults of civil business, they enjoy the fruits of wisdom pleasantly.

**CRITO:** Do these men seem to you to say anything, O Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** Not at all.

**CRITO:** Nevertheless, the speech of these men has something plausible.

**SOCRATES:** It has, as you say, O Crito, plausibility rather than truth. Nor can they easily be persuaded that both men and all other things which are middle-grounds between two certain things, and participate in both, are so situated that those which are from the bad and the good, become better than the former but worse than the latter: but those which are from two good things not leading to the same, are worse than both for performing that work toward which each of those of which the composition consists looks. Those however which are constituted from two bad things, not tending to the same, these alone are better than both those in which they participate. If therefore philosophy is good, and civil action is good, but each contributing to one thing and another, and these men participating in both of these are established in the middle of both, they conclude nothing. For they are worse than both. But if one of these is good, but the other bad, they are better than the latter but worse than the former. But if both are bad, only then would they speak the truth, but otherwise by no means. Nor indeed do I think they will confess that both are bad, nor that one is good and the other bad. But truly these participants in both are more inept than both for that toward which philosophy and civil action pertain, and while they hold the third place, they do not hesitate to usurp the first. Their desire is indeed to be forgiven, not to be resented; nevertheless, they are to be considered such as they are. For we ought to love everyone who, participating in some part of prudence, says something and acts manfully.

**CRITO:** Indeed, O Socrates, as I often speak with you, I am in doubt in what way to educate my sons. The one younger in age is still more tender than discipline requires: but Critobulus is already an adult, and needs someone by whose work he may profit. Whenever I speak with you, I am so affected that I think it is madness to be occupied with other things for the sake of the sons, such as concerning marriage—namely, so that they may be born from the most noble mother—then so that an ample patrimony might be left to them, but to neglect their education...

...neglect. But when I look at those who profess to educate men, I am deterred, and to me considering them, each of them seems far removed from that thing which he proclaims. And to confess the truth to you, I do not know how to exhort and provoke my son to philosophy.

**CRITO:** To me certainly.

# THE LESSER HIPPIAS,
# OR, ON LYING.

### THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

The marvelous goodness of our Socrates and Plato, since it most diligently provides in many ways everywhere lest credulous youth be captured by the subtle traps of the sophists, and being captured be lost, not unjustly agitates Hippias of Elis—the most intolerable and deceitful of the sophists—in two dialogues: namely, the Greater and the Lesser. In the Greater indeed he demonstrates that Hippias, a professor of the most beautiful things, is entirely ignorant of what beauty itself is. In the Lesser, however, he shows that the same man, boasting that he discerns a liar from a truthful man better than others, errs entirely in the definition of both: so that it may be plain that Hippias, as he is the most arrogant of all, so he is also the most ignorant, and appears most inept. I pass over now that he depicts him, as is the custom of sophists, as boastful, rash, and greedy: and while he promises everything, in everything giving words but performing nothing in truth: and while he glories in the greatest things, stumbling even in the smallest. But to return to the definition of the liar and the truthful man: the liar was rightly to be described as he who most wants, and in whatever way he can and knows how, to lie. The truthful man, however, on the contrary, he who most wants, and in whatever way he can and knows how, to speak the truth. But Hippias, the most inert master of all arts, and the most confused distinguisher of the truthful and the liar, defines in the opposite order, and says the liar is he who can and knows how to lie most, whenever he wishes: the truthful man, however, who whenever he wishes can and knows how to speak the truth. Whence he is first compelled to confess that liars are powerful, knowing, prudent, and wise. Then also good at those things for which they are powerful and wise. Thirdly, by leading through individual arts, he is compelled in any art to confess that the same man is both truthful and a liar, which he had denied from the beginning. Since indeed in any art he who is best skilled, the same is most able and knows how to speak the truth and to lie equally at his judgment. Fourthly, he is induced to concede that the truthful man is in no way better than the liar, since as sufficient and good as the truthful man is for speaking the truth, so sufficient and good the liar appears for lying. After these things Socrates brings the sophist into ambiguity: which of the two offends more gravely, he who lies willingly, or he who lies unwillingly. The sophist does not know how to solve that, nor indeed does Socrates wish to solve it for the sophist. It is however to be solved thus: In those things which pertain to the understanding, those who lie voluntarily err less; but in those things which look to morals, they err more. But he who willingly speaks a lie, holds himself to the contrary. Then it is doubted which err more, those who do so with set purpose, or those who sin through infirmity or ignorance. And it is proved by long wanderings of induction in those things which pertain to nature and art, and their instruments, that the vice committed through impotence or ignorance is more grave than that perpetrated by malice. Since the good of nature consists in power itself, but the good of art in this itself, and moreover in knowledge. Evil therefore in the opposites. From these things, however, outside the proposal, Socrates transfers Hippias to morals, concluding the same in the genus of morals as in the genus of nature and art. Which indeed although Socrates understands ought not to be done, he nevertheless strives to declare that the sophist by no means notices it. Truly in those things which pertain to the will and morals, one offends more gravely by malice—that is, by a certain will to sin—than if one offends either through impotence or through ignorance. Finally Socrates says justice is either power or knowledge or both. He knew to add but did not wish the third, namely the will. For justice consists most in the will. He wished to declare that this truly escapes the sophist. But let us now conclude the argument with these previous precepts: One must teach without envy. One must learn without shame. Thanks must always be given to the teacher. The inventions of others must not be usurped for oneself.

### EUDICUS, SOCRATES, HIPPIAS.

But why indeed are you silent, Socrates, when Hippias here has shown so many things? Why do you not either approve something of what was said, or refute if anything seems to you to have been said less rightly? Especially since we ourselves have departed as inferiors, we who claim for ourselves no mediocre study of philosophy?

**SOCRATES:** There are, Eudicus, some of those things which Hippias was saying about Homer, concerning which I desire to inquire. I heard indeed from Apemantus your father, that the *Iliad* in Homer is a more noble poem than the *Odyssey*, by as much as Achilles is more excellent than Ulysses. For he was saying that one poem was composed for Achilles, the other for Ulysses. Concerning this, therefore, I am inclined to inquire from Hippias, if only it pleases him, which of those men he asserts to be more excellent, after many other and various things about Homer and other poets have been shown to us.

**EUDICUS:** No envy at all will prohibit Hippias from answering the one questioning. Will you answer or not, Hippias, if Socrates asks something?

**HIPPIAS:** I would hardly be acting rightly, Eudicus, if I now fled the interrogation of Socrates, I who have been accustomed always to go from Elis my homeland to the Olympic feasts—where the Greeks flow together from everywhere for the common celebration—and to offer myself there at the temple to anyone, declaring whatever anyone might desire to have demonstrated, and answering individual interrogations.

**SOCRATES:** O how happy it has happened for you, Hippias, if you arrive at the sacred gathering so confident in the wisdom of your mind at any Olympiad. I would certainly marvel if any athlete concerning the exercise of the body were to come there to compete as confident in the strengths of his body as you are in the subtlety of your mind.

**HIPPIAS:** I am deservedly thus affected, Socrates: for from that time when I began to exercise in the Olympics, I have found no one as yet superior to me in any matter.

**SOCRATES:** Noble by Hercules is what you say, Hippias, and this glory of yours will be a certain monument of wisdom both to the city of the Eleans and to your parents. But what indeed do you judge concerning Achilles and Ulysses? Which of these do you think more excellent, and in what matter? Furthermore, while many of us were inside, and you were discoursing, some words escaped me: yet I was loath to inquire, both because the crowd inside was very large, and also lest I should be an impediment to your oration. Now truly, after we are fewer, and Eudicus here bids me ask, show us more clearly what you were saying about these men, and in what way you were judging them.

**HIPPIAS:** I wish indeed, Socrates, to report more openly in the present what I feel about these and about others. I assert that Homer fashioned Achilles as the best man of all who came to Troy, Nestor as the wisest, and Ulysses as the most especially crafty and multifaceted.

**SOCRATES:** Oh, Hippias! Will...

### Hippias Minor, Or, On Lying. 187

...Hippias. Will you gratify me in this? That is, will you not laugh at me if I am slower to perceive, and ask too often? Deign, I beseech you, to answer me willingly and easily.

**HIPPIAS:** It would be shameful indeed, O Socrates, since I teach these same things to others and demand money for them, if I did not indulge you when you ask, nor answer with a glad mind.

**SOCRATES:** You speak very nobly. Indeed, when you were saying that Achilles was fashioned as the best man, and Nestor as the wisest, I seemed to myself to understand what you were saying. But when you called Ulysses crafty and multifaceted <note>original: "multiformem," a translation of the Greek *polytropon*.</note>, to confess the truth, I did not understand what you meant to signify. And tell me: for perhaps from here I may perceive more: was not Achilles also induced by Homer as multifaceted and crafty, or not?

**HIPPIAS:** By no means, O Socrates, but entirely simple. Since in the supplications themselves, when he induces them debating, he makes Achilles speak thus against Ulysses:

<margin>Iliad 9.</margin>
"O much noble fabricator of guile, Ulysses,
It befits me to intrepidly refute your words,
As I think it ought to be done, lest you yourself
Dull me with deceits, sitting here and there.
For he is more hateful to us than the gate of black Dis <note>The god of the underworld, equivalent to Hades.</note>,
Who hides one thing in his heart,
Then openly brings forth whatever else appears.
But I shall now say what I believe will be."
In these verses he declares the character of both: Achilles being truthful and simple, Ulysses crafty and lying. These things indeed Achilles brings against Ulysses in his presence.

**SOCRATES:** I seem now to understand what you say, O Hippias. For you call the crafty man a liar, as it appears.

**HIPPIAS:** Especially so, O Socrates. For Homer often fashions such a Ulysses both in the *Iliad* and in the *Odyssey*.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore Homer thought that one man was truthful, but another was a liar, and that both were not the same?

**HIPPIAS:** What prohibits it, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** Do you yourself also think the same, Hippias?

**HIPPIAS:** Most of all. For I would err too much if I myself felt otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** Let us therefore leave Homer, since it is not permitted to inquire from him what his opinion was in composing these verses. But since you take up the cause, and those things which you assert Homer to say seem so to you, answer for Homer and yourself together.

**HIPPIAS:** It shall be done. Ask in a few words what you please.

**SOCRATES:** Do you call those men liars who are unable to do something, like the weak or the exhausted, or those who are able to do something?

**HIPPIAS:** The powerful, and most especially so, both in many other things and also in deceiving men.

**SOCRATES:** They are therefore powerful according to your speech, and crafty, are they not?

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** But are they crafty and subtle through a certain stupidity and imprudence? Or rather through shrewdness and prudence?

**HIPPIAS:** Shrewdness most of all, and prudence.

**SOCRATES:** They are therefore prudent, as it seems.

**HIPPIAS:** Very much so, by Jupiter.

**SOCRATES:** Since they are prudent, do they ignore what they do, or do they know?

**HIPPIAS:** Rather, they know most especially. For because of this they seduce others.

**SOCRATES:** Since they are knowing of these things which they know, are they foolish, or rather wise?

**HIPPIAS:** Wise, namely, in these very things for deceiving.

**SOCRATES:** Stop, I beseech you; let us repeat what was said, so that we may inspect what you say. You say liars are powerful and prudent, likewise knowing and wise concerning those things about which they are liars?

**HIPPIAS:** I say so.

**SOCRATES:** And that some are truthful, but others on the contrary are liars, and these are far contrary among themselves?

**HIPPIAS:** I say those things as well.

**SOCRATES:** From this it follows, then, that liars are from the number of the powerful and wise.

**HIPPIAS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** When however you say liars are powerful and wise, do you say they are powerful for the same things—to lie if they wish—or powerless for those things which they lie about?

**HIPPIAS:** Powerful, indeed.

**SOCRATES:** So that we may speak summarily, liars are those who are powerful and wise for lying.

**HIPPIAS:** Clearly.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore he who wishes to lie but cannot, nor knows anything, will not be a liar.

**HIPPIAS:** So it is.

**SOCRATES:** But he is powerful who does what he wants, and when he wants. I do not mean one hindered by disease or some such thing, but truly just as you can write my name whenever you wish, so I ask now. Do you not call a man so affected 'powerful'?

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Tell me, O Hippias, are you not skilled in counting and computing?

**HIPPIAS:** Most of all.

**SOCRATES:** If someone therefore should ask you how much three times seven hundred <note>original: "ter septingenta"</note> completes as a number, would you not, if only you wished, answer about these as quickly and as much as anyone?

**HIPPIAS:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not because you are most powerful and wisest concerning those things?

**HIPPIAS:** Indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Are you only the wisest and most powerful? Or also the best concerning the same things, in which you excel in wisdom and power, that is, in computing numbers?

**HIPPIAS:** And the best in addition, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore you could speak the truth about these things especially above others, could you not?

**HIPPIAS:** I think so indeed.

**SOCRATES:** And also the false concerning the same? Come now, Hippias, answer generously and magnificently as before. If someone should ask how much three times seven hundred is, would you then lie more about these, and always pronounce false things according to the same, wishing to lie and never to bring forth true things? Or could he who is ignorant of numbers lie more than you, even if you wish to lie? Or on the contrary, while the ignorant man often wishes to bring forth false things, will he perhaps bring forth true things contrary to his intention, because he ignores the matter itself: but you, since you are wise, whenever you wish to lie, will you lie similarly?

**HIPPIAS:** It is as you say.

**SOCRATES:** Does the liar, therefore, lie about other things, but not about numbers, nor will he lie about a number?

**HIPPIAS:** Rather, also about numbers.

**SOCRATES:** Let us assume this then, Hippias: that there is some liar concerning computation and number.

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Who will this be? It is necessary that he be able to lie, as you yourself were saying, if he is to be a liar. Indeed it was said by you, if you remember, that he who cannot lie is not a liar.

**HIPPIAS:** I remember indeed, and it was so said.

**SOCRATES:** Did it not appear a little while ago that you were most powerful for lying in computing numbers?

**HIPPIAS:** That was also said.

**SOCRATES:** Are you not also most powerful for bringing forth true things about those same numbers?

**HIPPIAS:** Very much so.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore the same man is most able both to speak the truth and to lie in computing: but he is the one who is good in numbers, namely the computer <note>A person who computes.</note>.

**HIPPIAS:** So entirely.

**SOCRATES:** Who then else, Hippias, becomes a liar in computing, unless he who is good at the same? For he is powerful, and he is truthful.

**HIPPIAS:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** Do you see that the same man is truthful and a liar in these things, and that the truthful man is in no way better than the liar himself? For they are the same, and not far contrary, as you recently were thinking.

**HIPPIAS:** It certainly does not appear so now in these things.

**SOCRATES:** Do you wish that we consider in other things also?

**HIPPIAS:** As you please.

**SOCRATES:** Are you not also skilled in geometry?

**HIPPIAS:** I am.

**SOCRATES:** Does not the same happen in geometry? The same man can pronounce false things as much as possible about figures, who can also speak the true. That man is the geometer.

**HIPPIAS:** Indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Is any other good at these besides him?

**HIPPIAS:** No other.

**SOCRATES:** Is not the good and wise geometer both...

You profess this art even more than the previous ones, do you not, Hippias? **HIPPIAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Do not the same things hold true in astronomy? **HIPPIAS:** It is consistent, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, in astronomy as well, if anyone is a liar, it will be especially the good astronomer. For he is the one most capable of lying; for he who is incapable is merely ignorant. **HIPPIAS:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the same man in astronomy will be both truthful and a liar. 
**HIPPIAS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Come now, Hippias, consider this generally across all the sciences, whether it is so or otherwise. For you are adorned with more arts than all others. As I have heard you boasting at times, saying that you abound in much desirable wisdom beyond all others, while you were walking and disputing in the marketplace among the tables: when you said that you once went to Olympia, and that all the things you had as ornaments for your body you had made with your own hands. First, that the ring you had (for you began with this) was your own work, as if you were skilled in engraving; furthermore, a certain seal-ring was your work, and a strigil <note>A curved blade used by ancient Greeks to scrape sweat and oil from the body after exercise.</note>, and an oil-flask was similarly your work; shoes also fashioned by your own hands, and a cloak and an inner tunic woven by you. And what seemed truly marvelous and a sign of singular wisdom, you said you showed a belt that was your own work. You finished it to look like a precious thing. Also, certain poems of yours—epics, tragedies, dithyrambs <note>Wild, choral hymns usually dedicated to the god Dionysus.</note>, and many orations, and various pieces composed in freer meters; furthermore, that you held those subjects I mentioned before better than all others, and that you excelled in rhythms, harmonies, and the correct logic of letters <note>Grammar or orthography.</note>, and in many other things of this kind, if I remember correctly. But truly, I had overlooked your "art of memory," in which you seem to me to be wonderfully powerful. Perhaps I have forgotten many other things as well. But as I said, looking into your arts (which are quite numerous) and the arts of others, tell me, if you have ever found from these things we have agreed upon, that the truthful man is different from the liar, and that they are not the same. Search for this in whatever wisdom or cleverness, or whatever name you please to call it. But you will never find it, my friend; for it does not exist anywhere. If it does, say so. **HIPPIAS:** I cannot find it at present, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Nor will you find it hereafter, I think. But if I speak the truth, remember, Hippias, what follows from our previous points. **HIPPIAS:** I do not quite follow what you are saying, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** There is no need for your "art of memory" at the moment; it is clear that you do not think it necessary, but I will bring it back to your mind. You remember saying that Achilles was a truthful man, but Ulysses was a liar and multifaceted <note>original: "versutum."</note>. **HIPPIAS:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** But now you see that the same man has appeared to be both truthful and a liar. And therefore, if Ulysses was a liar, he was also truthful. Likewise, if Achilles was truthful, he was also a liar; these men were not different from one another nor opposites, but rather they were similar. **HIPPIAS:** You are always weaving such little traps <note>original: "captiunculas," referring to sophistical quibbles.</note>, Socrates; seizing upon what is most troublesome in the conversation, you insist upon it and touch upon every minor point, rather than contending against the whole matter of the discourse. For if you wish, I will now show you with many arguments and sufficient reason that Homer fashioned Achilles as better than Ulysses and truthful; but Ulysses as deceitful, lying in many things, and worse than Achilles. But if it pleases you, respond in turn, and compare your speech with mine, in which you show the other to be better; and thus those present will better understand which of us has spoken more correctly. **SOCRATES:** I do not doubt, nor do I contend, Hippias, that you appear wiser than I. But I have always been accustomed, when someone disputes about a matter, to attend diligently, especially when the speaker seems to me to be wise. Then, truly eager to understand what he says, I question, weigh, and estimate, so that I may perceive his words more clearly. But if I hold the speaker in low esteem, I neither ask him anything nor attend to what he says. And by this very conjecture you will understand whom I deem wise. For you will see me listening most accurately to their words and inquiring of them, so that I may profit in life by learning something. And now, as I was considering your words—by which you show Achilles against Ulysses with the testimony of those poems—it seemed a wonderful thing to me, if you spoke the truth. Since Ulysses himself, though versatile, cannot be proven guilty of any lie; but Achilles seems to be versatile and shifty according to your own speech: for he lies. For when he had pronounced those verses which you just recited,

"For he is more hateful to me than the gate of black Dis <note>original: "Is magis est quoniam quàm nigri ianua Ditis..." Achilles is speaking to Ulysses, expressing hatred for those who say one thing but think another.</note>,
Who hides one thing in his heart,
Then openly brings forth whatever else appears."

In which you will behold, if you desire to see, strong

For both are very close in this. **HIPPIAS:** You do not discern correctly, Socrates. For the things Achilles lies about, he seems to lie about not out of plot, but unwillingly because of the army's misfortune, being compelled to remain and help; Ulysses, however, lies voluntarily and with guile. **SOCRATES:** You deceive me, dearest Hippias, and you yourself imitate Ulysses. **HIPPIAS:** Not at all, Socrates, what are you saying? And for what reason? **SOCRATES:** Because you say Achilles does not lie out of a plot—he who was such a seducer and plotter beyond his own boasting, just as Homer fashions him, that he was so much more clever than Ulysses that he hid his own vanity from him, while he dared to speak contradictions to himself in his presence, and fooled Ulysses...

He then challenges Hippias's claim that Achilles is "simple and truthful" by pointing out that Achilles promises to leave Troy in the Iliad but never actually does, making him a liar by definition.</summary>

**HIPPIAS:** What are these things you say, O Socrates?

**HIPPIAS:** Where?

**SOCRATES:** In these verses:

Do you think, Hippias, that the son of Thetis <note>Achilles</note>, educated by the most wise Chiron, was so forgetful that—having just before attacked those vain boasters with a most vehement speech—he himself immediately told Ulysses (as if forgetting himself) that he would sail, but told Ajax he would stay? **HIPPIAS:** It does not seem to me that Achilles said those things by guile, but rather, by his very simplicity, he was persuaded differently at one time with Ajax and another with Ulysses. But Ulysses, whether he speaks true or false, always stretches his plots.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, as it seems, Ulysses is better than Achilles.

**HIPPIAS:** Not at all, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Did it not appear above that those who tell a lie willingly are better than those who do so unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS:** How can those who knowingly do injustice, who willingly plot and cause harm, be better than those who do these things unintentionally, Socrates? For much is forgiven to him who does injustice through ignorance, speaks a lie, or commits some other evil; and the laws act more severely against those who do evil and lie willingly than against those who do so unwillingly.

**SOCRATES:** You see, Hippias, that I speak the truth when I say I am accurate in the questioning of wise men; and while I fail greatly in other things, I have this one good quality: for I do not know the nature of things as they are. This can be most inferred from the fact that as often as I speak with any of you who excel in the reputation for wisdom—and have all the Greeks as witnesses of your learning—I appear to know nothing. For never, so to speak, does the same thing seem true to me as to you. And what is a more evident argument of ignorance than if one disagrees with wise men? 

Yet I have this wonderful good quality which saves me: I prepare myself to learn without the blush of shame. I ask and inquire, and I have great gratitude for the one who responds; I have never been ungrateful to anyone, nor have I ever claimed for myself the discoveries of others before an audience, but I always extol the teacher with praise and attribute to him what is his before all. 

And even now, I by no means admit what you say; rather, I disagree far more, and I know for certain that this happens by my own fault—since I confess myself to be such as I am, lest I extol myself. To me, Hippias, it seems entirely contrary to what you think. I believe that those who willingly hurt people, do injustice, lie, deceive, and fail are better than those who do so unwillingly. Sometimes, however, I judge the opposite and wander from this, being ignorant of the matter itself. Behold, now a certain sickness of the mind has invaded me, and those who sin by purpose in something seem better to me than those who err unintentionally. I consider the previous arguments the cause of this evil, by which it happens that I now think those who sin unwillingly are worse than those who do so willingly. 

Therefore, forgive me, and let no envy hold you back from curing my soul. You confer a much greater benefit upon me if you free my soul from ignorance than if you free my body from sickness. If you wish to achieve this with many words, I foretell that you will not cure me in this way, for I will not follow. But if you wish to respond as before, you will profit me greatly. I hope this will not be harmful to you. I will rightly invoke you now, son of Apemantus <note>Eudicus, who introduced Hippias to Socrates.</note>. For you yourself induced me to dispute with Hippias. Therefore, if Hippias now wishes to answer, you must intercede for me.

**EUDICUS:** I think there is no need for my prayers to Hippias, Socrates. For he did not propose to answer only by compulsion; rather, he promised he would answer everyone willingly. Were these not your words, Hippias?

**HIPPIAS:** I said them indeed. But this Socrates, O Eudicus, always disturbs those speaking, and seems to be like a sort of magician.

**SOCRATES:** O best of men, Hippias, I do not do these things willingly; I would indeed be wise and crafty according to your own speech. But I do it unintentionally; therefore, forgive me. For you say that one who sins unwillingly should be forgiven.

**EUDICUS:** Do not do otherwise, Hippias, but for our sake, and because of what was said by you before, answer what Socrates asks.

**HIPPIAS:** I will answer indeed, since you ask. Seek then whatever you please.

**SOCRATES:** I vehemently desire, Hippias, to consider what was just said: which are better, those who sin willingly and by choice, or those who do the opposite? I hope it can be most correctly considered in this way. Answer now: Do you call some runner good?

**HIPPIAS:** Indeed.

**SOCRATES:** And a bad one?

**HIPPIAS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** Is not the one who runs well good, and the one who runs poorly bad?

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Does not the one who runs slowly run poorly? And the one who runs quickly, run well?

**HIPPIAS:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, in running itself, speed is a good thing, and slowness an evil.

**HIPPIAS:** What then?

**SOCRATES:** Which runner is better? The one who runs slowly by choice, or the one who does so otherwise?

**HIPPIAS:** The one who does so by choice.

**SOCRATES:** Is not running a kind of doing?

**HIPPIAS:** It is a doing indeed.

**SOCRATES:** And is doing a kind of performing?

**HIPPIAS:** Truly.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, he who runs poorly performs something evil and shameful in his running.

**HIPPIAS:** Evil. Why not?

**SOCRATES:** But he runs poorly who runs slowly.

**HIPPIAS:** Indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, does the good runner perform this evil and shame by industry, while the bad runner does so against his purpose?

**HIPPIAS:** It seems so.

**SOCRATES:** In running, therefore, he is worse who does evil against his will than he who does so willingly.

**HIPPIAS:** In running, clearly.

**SOCRATES:** What about in the <term>palaestra</term> <note>A wrestling school or gymnasium.</note>? Which wrestler is better? The one who falls by deliberate effort? Or the one who falls against his will?

**HIPPIAS:** The one by deliberate effort.

**SOCRATES:** So it seems. But is it worse and more shameful in the palaestra to fall, or to throw someone?

**HIPPIAS:** To fall.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, in the palaestra, he who performs evil and shameful things by effort is a better wrestler than he who does so by weakness and inertia.

**HIPPIAS:** It seems so.

**SOCRATES:** What about in every other use of the body? Is not he who is more robust and fit in body able to do both things according to his judgment—the things of a strong man and the things of a weak man, both beautiful and shameful? For this reason, he who excels in the condition of his body, whenever he does something poorly regarding the body, does so willingly; but the weak man does so unwillingly.

**HIPPIAS:** The same seems to happen regarding strength.

**SOCRATES:** What should be said about the grace of the figure itself? Is it not the part of a more beautiful and better body to combine shameful figures by great effort, but for the deformed body to do the opposite? What do you think?

**SOCRATES:** Is not the limping of feet a vice and a deformity?

**HIPPIAS:** It is.

**HIPPIAS:** Those by choice.

**HIPPIAS:** Certain things of that kind, evidently.

**SOCRATES:** Does not one reason encompass all the rest—ears, nostrils, mouth, and all the senses—which teaches that senses which fail against their purpose are never to be chosen, as they are depraved; but those that do so by intent are rather to be chosen as good?

**HIPPIAS:** It seems so to me.

**SOCRATES:** And of which instruments is the use better? Those with which someone errs willingly, or those with which they do so unwillingly? As for a rudder, is that one better with which someone steers poorly by industry, or one with which they do so against their will?

**HIPPIAS:** The one by industry.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not the same for the bow, and the lyre, and the flutes, and all other things?

**HIPPIAS:** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES:** Which soul of a horse is better for possessing? That by which someone rides poorly by choice, or that by which they do so against their will?

**HIPPIAS:** That by which by choice.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is better.

**HIPPIAS:** It is.

**SOCRATES:** With the better soul of a horse, therefore, one will perform the evil works of this soul willingly, but the opposite in the contrary case.

**HIPPIAS:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** Is not the same reasoning true for the soul of a dog and other animals?

**HIPPIAS:** The same.

**SOCRATES:** And whose soul would you choose as better for an archer? The one who misses the mark by choice, or the one who does so against his will?

**HIPPIAS:** The one by choice.

**HIPPIAS:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** And we would rather choose the souls of servants who fail knowingly in their service than those who do so through ignorance, as being better for these tasks?

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly.

**HIPPIAS:** Indeed.

**HIPPIAS:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** And the soul which is more powerful and wiser appeared to be better and more prepared for both beautiful and shameful actions in any performance?

**HIPPIAS:** Certainly.

**HIPPIAS:** It seems so.

**HIPPIAS:** Thus it is.

**HIPPIAS:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** Is not a good man one who has a good soul? And a bad man, on the contrary, one who has a bad soul?

**HIPPIAS:** Without a doubt.

But it is a grave evil for us if, having come to you, we do not cease to err.

### CHARMIDES, OR, ON TEMPERANCE.

->THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.<-

THE AIM of Socrates in this dialogue is to exhort all people to temperance, but especially three groups: namely, the young, the noble, and the beautiful. The young, because a medicine of character must be applied quickly. "Oppose the beginnings; the medicine is prepared too late when the evils have gained strength through long delays." <note>Ficino quotes Ovid's *Remedia Amoris*.</note> The noble also, both to show that true nobility must be placed in virtue, and because the noble are most often an example to others and are daily admitted to the republic; if they are evil, it is to the gravest detriment of the human race. Finally, the beautiful: for these are most of all depraved by the company of the wicked, which makes them need the medicine more. Furthermore, the beautiful ought to strive so that, just as nature gave a brief beauty to the body, they in turn may restore to God, the author of nature, an everlasting beauty of the soul. Nor should it be permitted that our external parts please many with their beauty, while our internal parts meanwhile displease with their deformity. 

Although everything in this dialogue has a wonderful allegory, especially the amatory parts—no differently than the Songs of Solomon—nevertheless, I have changed some things and omitted others. For those things which harmonized with the most refined ears of the Athenians might perhaps not harmonize at all with ruder ears. Therefore, a certain Aristarchus <note>A famous grammarian and critic.</note> of Homeric, or rather Platonic sort, might say that those things which harmonize less are not of Plato, but of Chronos. Three things in the very beginning are especially to be noted, which transfer love from this form of the body to incorporeal beauty. First, that Socrates says he discerns nothing between this beautiful person and that one, but that all beautiful people please him equally; as if to say, one must not stop at the form of one body, but ascend to the common beauty of the entire species itself. Since this beauty is one in many, it reflects one Idea of beauty over many. Therefore, just as we transcend in thought from the individual to the species, and from the species to the Idea, so we are admonished to proceed from the love of this form to the love of the common form first, and then to the love of the ideal form...

--- Page 210 ---
Charmides, Or, on temperance 191

...admonished to proceed to love. To these Socrates added that the beauty of the body is not to be loved for itself, but is to be thought of by us as an image of divine beauty. Finally, he commands us to strip the soul naked and, having set aside the form of the body, to inspect the beauty of the soul, both that which is natural and that which is more diligently applied through study. And meanwhile, he corrects Chaerephon, who had said something about stripping the body as if in the wrestling school. Nor does he unjustly begin the exhortation to temperance from the beauty of the body. For this temperance is a certain arrangement of lines and colors. 

But from this he passes next to the health of the body, which is also a certain temperance—namely, of the humors and the limbs. Third, from this to the ornament of the soul itself, which in affection is temperance—the moderation of the motions themselves—and in cognition is similarly a certain temperance, consisting in a certain harmonious congruence of the intelligence with the things understood. Thus Pythagoras not undeservedly said that temperance is the most healthful virtue of all, the preserver of human society both publicly and privately: especially since justice is also a certain temperance, that is, a convenient moderation in exchanging and distributing. 

Truly, although temperance properly concerns the restraining of vehement lusts and pleasures, it is nevertheless transferred by a certain similarity to the cutting off of all desires and to the moderating of any act, so that even the duty of fortitude consists in the moderation of audacity and fear, similarly justice in the measure of rewards and punishments, and liberality in the measure of giving; finally, the safety of all life, so that there be "nothing in excess." Hence that Pythagorean saying, "Measure is best of all." But remember that in the *Phaedo* those are denied to be temperate who abstain from pleasures for the sake of bodily pleasure. For he commands that mortal actions be referred to the purging of the mind and for the sake of following wisdom and divine likeness. 

So great is the excellence of temperance that all elegant craftsmen observe it in their works, and by its virtue not only any body under the moon, but even the heaven itself and the whole universe are preserved. This is confirmed in the *Gorgias* by the testimony of wise men. To this it is similar: "God disposes all things sweetly." Likewise, in number, weight, and measure He disposes all things. 

But let us now return to the dialogue. Socrates, following the opinion of the Magi, forbids the body to be cured before the soul is cured; he clearly disapproves of those who, caring for the smallest things, neglect the greatest, just as those who seek remedies for sick horses and dogs but by no means consult physicians for the diseases of their own bodies and souls. They arrange all the smallest household items properly, while they themselves are meanwhile unarranged in soul and body. They tune the zither with an intemperate soul. Daily they curiously handle the affairs of others but desert their own. All things except the soul itself are foreign to us. Therefore, he called the medicine of the body a "leaf"—a light, fragile thing, entirely changeable, and to be thoroughly despised. 

He also signifies that many inconveniences both of body and fortune frequently happen to us because of intemperance, and on the contrary, many goods come through temperance. Likewise, in a perfectly composed soul, whatever happens is both prudently disposed and equally tolerated, so that nothing finally turns out as an evil. In an uncomposed soul, nothing can be well composed, either in the body or outside it. In the *Cratylus*, he explains the Greek name for temperance, <term>Sophrosyne</term> <note>Meaning soundness of mind or self-control.</note>, as a certain safety and preservation of prudence. For he thinks that the lights of all truths were innate to the soul, and therefore if it looks entirely into itself, it will see the truth in all things. But the cause that prevents it from looking in is the immoderate affection for the body and bodily things: for which reason temperance is needed first of all. Through temperance, the darkness of perturbations having been expelled, the mind is made more serene and is abundantly surrounded by the light of the divine sun, whence it first recovers wisdom and then attains prudence. 

Since, therefore, wisdom and prudence accompany temperance, Plato often elsewhere and in this dialogue wants wisdom and prudence to be contained under the very name of temperance. Socrates admonishes Charmides to look into himself when he is about to speak of temperance; for this turning into oneself is the duty of this virtue. And whoever is thoroughly turned into himself understands human temperance through that Idea of temperance innate to the mind; then, recognizing that very moderation by which God tempered the parts of the soul together from the beginning, he will know by what reason the affection of the soul is to be tempered. To these is added that in this precept he signifies that no one except a temperate person ought to or can speak of temperance to persuade others. 

Furthermore, it is handed down in the *Timaeus* that from a certain consonance of the soul both to itself and its modulation to the body, all prosperous things happen to us. Moreover, the Pythagoreans—whom the Roman Censorinus follows in this—promise perpetual health of both and a long life if the mind prudently moderates individual motions, both of itself and of the body. Censorinus and we ourselves have found that this has happened to many wise and holy men. Some refer the long lives of the ancients to this same or a similar cause. But something more wonderful is added to these: that the Magi promise immortality to bodies by their songs. Plato says in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of Zoroaster is nothing other than the worship of the divine; here he adds that not only by magic songs, but also by philosophical reasons, the soul is tempered and the body is preserved far from death, either always or at least for a long time. 

Truly, that speech which is to be entirely persuasive of temperance to listeners, and moreover to affect them, requires two things most of all: power infused from God and reasons prepared by philosophers. And Plato calls a speech composed of these two a "magic incantation." By this, Phoebus first, and then the Pythagoreans, wonderfully expelled diseases from the soul and body. Nor should it be thought false that a body under a soul that is entirely temperate can be made immortal, and under an intemperate one can fall into diseases and evils. For that Mosaic mystery concerning the state and fall of the first parent contains this. And Avicenna, following the Platonists and Hippocrates, proves that the soul by its very nature so exceeds all matter that as soon as it is restored into itself, it can move the elements of the world by a certain wonderful virtue and have command over any bodies; by which it happens that it can do much more in its own. This indeed Adam could experience from the beginning, and some think Enoch and Elias did, and some suspect the Evangelist <note>John the Evangelist, who was rumored in some traditions not to have died.</note> still lives in a similar way. But we dispute most broadly about all these things in our *Theology*. 

Finally, to speak in summary, a wonder of the virtue of temperance is declared in this: that it happily restores to itself the soul which had unhappily fallen into worse things. A wonderful power of the soul is also declared, from which all things both good and evil flow into the body, and by whose will the body can be preserved uncorrupted. These indeed harmonize almost everywhere with the Mosaic mysteries. 

After this, it is often asked what temperance is, which neither Charmides nor Critias ever settles. The former brings forth not temperance properly, but what accompanies it; the latter, however, brings forth what pertains more to prudence; and this always ineptly, namely so that it may be declared that it is not for just anyone to discourse on so noble a virtue. Meanwhile, note that the ancient priests were accustomed in sacred rites to consecrate the third bowl of libation to Jove the Savior especially, to declare that the beginnings, middles, and ends of all things—as Plato reports in the *Laws*—are disposed and preserved under the providence of Jove. 

But let us return to the ineptitudes of Critias, who says there is a science which knows both itself and all sciences, but does not know the things themselves of which they are sciences. This indeed is absurd because the truth and reason of science consist in a certain contact and congruence with the things which are known. Furthermore, a science cannot be perfectly known unless it is discerned of what it is a science; but that cannot be held unless the thing of which it is a science is held. Likewise, Critias confesses that someone can meanwhile know that he does not know things which he in no way knows. But Socrates does not receive this because things which are in no way known cannot meanwhile be known in any way. For whoever notices that he is ignorant of something, by that very fact recognizes that he lacks it. If he so judges, then he has already described a certain notion of it in himself, by which he judges both that he lacks it and what particularly he lacks. 

Thus it happens that whoever recognizes that he is ignorant of some thing does not entirely ignore the thing itself; rather, he describes it in a certain general outline—general, I say, because perfect science consists in the special distinction of things, which Plato seeks through all his disputations. But where Socrates induces one recognizing that he knows nothing, he judges him to have, if not special, at least general descriptions of things; otherwise he could not recognize his ignorance: therefore while he knew nothing, he in a certain way knew all things. Since indeed Critias had translated the speech about temperance to prudence—and that by a certain Platonic license—Socrates asserts prudence, that is, the knowledge of good and evil, to hold the highest authority for obtaining beatitude: both because it demonstrates the good end and the good means to it, and because all things and arts, insofar as they are ruled by it, are conducive to our good, but otherwise by no means. 

Finally, Socrates teaches that nothing is more difficult either to define or to acquire than temperance. The difficulty of definition proceeds from the fact that it can hardly be discerned from the other virtues, of which it is a certain consonance. Add that it is as much more difficult to understand and express in words as it is more difficult to possess internally. Truly, since from the very commerce of the body we are most of all prone to pleasure and intemperance, in which we are nourished from infancy, we attain temperance with the greatest difficulty. Furthermore, the first affections of the senses seem sometimes to contribute either to fortitude through anger and audacity, or to prudence through fear, or to patience through pain, or to justice and liberality through love. But every impulse is always opposed to temperance. Since it can be placed only in a certain highest tranquility, it is hindered from every side by any affection. The difficulty is also increased because, just as in the body it is most difficult to find an entirely consonant temper of humors and limbs, so in souls a harmonic temperance of all its parts...
