### [Page 192]
# Book Twenty.

...is the most difficult of all. For which reason Socrates, not without cause, says in the epilogue rather than in the beginning that to achieve a harmony most similar to celestial temperance, there is need of celestial and divine virtue, infused then into the reasonings and words of souls. But everywhere he warns that one must strive rather to be made temperate under the legitimate institutes of law, than to dispute about temperance under dialectical reasonings: since it is known only with a certain supreme difficulty, and once known without practice, it not only profits nothing, but even hinders a great deal; and what is more, unless it be possessed in reality, it cannot be perfectly known. For it is not permitted for the impure to touch the purest of all things.

## SOCRATES, CHAEREPHO, CRITIAS, CHARMIDES.

Yesterday, when I had returned in the evening from the army at **Potidaea**, I immediately repeated with great pleasure the usual exercises from which I had long been absent, and I entered the palaestra of **Taureas**, which is opposite the royal temple. There I found many, some unknown to me, others known, and those indeed the leading men. When they saw me entering unexpectedly from a distance, they immediately congratulated me, running up from various sides. **Chaerepho** especially, as if he were insane, immediately leaped forth from the middle and ran to me, and taking me by the hand, said, "O **Socrates**, by what means did you escape surviving the battle?" For a little before we left, a battle was joined at **Potidaea**, which these men here had recently heard of. But I, responding to them, said, "Just as you see." He said, "It was reported that the battle was most bitter, and that in it many men known to us fell." I said, "The things reported to you were true." "Were you present at the battle?" he asked. "I was present." "Sit here, and relate it to us, for we have not yet understood everything sufficiently." Having said this, he ordered me to sit near **Critias**, the son of **Callaeschrus**. Sitting therefore by **Critias**, I first congratulated him and the others, then I recounted what had happened in the military expedition, whatever each one asked (for one asked one thing, another another).

But when we had spoken abundantly of these matters, I in turn asked them what was the condition of philosophy in these times, and which of the youths were distinguished either for wisdom, or for natural talent, or for both. Then **Critias**, looking toward the doors and seeing certain youths entering and arguing with one another, and after them another crowd, said: "O **Socrates**, concerning the noble ones you were asking, you shall soon see and know. For those who are entering now are the precursors and lovers of a certain youth who is judged the noblest and most handsome of all at this time; and it seems he himself is just about to enter." "Who is he, and whose son?" I asked. He said, "Perhaps you also know him. But when you left from here, he had not yet reached puberty. Did you know **Charmides**, the son of our uncle **Glaucon**, my cousin?" "I knew him indeed, and even then he was not a boy to be despised. But now I think he is already a young man." "You will immediately understand," he said, "how great and of what sort he has turned out." While he was saying this, **Charmides** enters.

As for me, O friend, as far as it pertains to me, I consider nothing. Indeed, I am toward those distinguished by noble talent as a white level-line on a white stone. [[Margin: Proverb.]] For almost all men of that age seem beautiful to me. But especially then did he appear marvelous both for the stature of his body and his distinguished talent. All the others indeed seemed captured by his love, to such an extent were they stunned and disturbed by his entrance. Many lovers, moreover, followed after him. And as far as the men are concerned, it was no wonder; but I also noticed the boys, none of whom—even the smallest—looked at anyone else, but all contemplated him alone as if he were some divine image.

Here **Chaerepho**, turning to me, said, "How does the youth seem to you, O **Socrates**? Is he not of a handsome countenance?" "Wonderfully so," I said. "And yet," he said, "if he were willing to strip, you would call his countenance deformed compared to that beauty which lies hidden within." All the others agreed with these same words of **Chaerepho**. "By Hercules," I said, "you describe an insuperable man, if only some small thing in addition is present in him." "**Critias** said, "What is that?" I said, "If he were adorned by nature with the best habit of soul, which is fitting, O **Critias**, for one born from your stock." "Indeed, certainly in terms of genius, he is both most beautiful and best." "Why then," I said, "do we not strip the soul first, and contemplate the interior form instead? For since he is now so great, I think he will rejoice to discourse." "**Critias** said, "Certainly. For he is a student of wisdom and, as it seems to himself and others, quite poetic." I said, "O friend **Critias**, you draw this nobility from the lineage of **Solon** in a long series. But why do you not show me the youth now, summoning him hither? For it is not unbecoming, even if he were younger, to discourse with him, while you, his cousin and tutor, are present." "Rightly said," he replied. "He must be called now." And having said these things, turning to the one who followed behind, he said, "Call **Charmides**; but hey, tell him that I wish to commit him to a certain physician on account of the illness of which he complained recently." **Critias** said to me, "Recently, when **Charmides** rose in the morning, he complained of a headache. What prevents you, then, from pretending that you have some remedy against the heaviness of the head?" I said, "Nothing prevents it, provided he comes." "But he will come."

And so it was done: for he came, and provoked great laughter in everyone: for each of us sitting together, wishing to yield a place for **Charmides** to sit, intentionally pushed his neighbor. The result was that of those who sat on either end, we compelled one to stand up and the other we threw prostrate on the ground. He, however, approaching, sat down between **Critias** and me. Then I, O friend, was already stuck: and that confidence deserted me which I had a little before, that I would easily dispute with him. But after **Critias** said that I was the one to whom the medicine was known, he looked at me with eyes as if at some marvel, and as if about to ask a question, he approached us. And all those who were in the palaestra immediately flowed toward us and surrounded us in a circle. Then indeed, O noble one, when I saw what lay hidden under his cloak, I was entirely inflamed, nor was I any longer master of myself. And I judged **Critias** most wise in matters of love, who, speaking of a handsome boy but employing a metaphor of another thing, warned me to see again and again lest a fawn coming into the sight of a lion should lose a piece of its flesh: for I indeed seemed to have been captured by that bait. But when he himself asked whether I knew the cure for the head, I finally responded with difficulty that I knew it. "What is it?" he said. "A certain leaf," I replied. "But in addition, a certain incantation must be added, which if someone employs it and uses the leaf, health is restored. But without the incantation, the leaf confers nothing." To this he said, "I will indeed copy out this incantation as you dictate it." I said, "Whether you have persuaded me or even if you have not?" He, smiling, said, "If I shall have persuaded you, **Socrates**." "Aha," I said, "you clearly even know my name." "I know it indeed," he said, "unless I am mistaken. For frequent talk is had of you among my peers. I even remember when I was still a boy, you used to frequent this place with **Critias**." "You are right," I said. "For I will more boldly show you the mode of the incantation. But a little before I did not know by what means I should show its power to you. It is such, O **Charmides**, [[Margin: Certain precepts of medicine]] that it cannot cure the head alone: just as you have often heard from skilled physicians, who as often as anyone consults them afflicted with pain of the eyes, they say they cannot heal the eyes unless the head is first healed, nor...

### [Page 193]
# Charmides, Or, on Temperance.

...nor can the head be cured without the medicine of the whole body. For this reason, they use certain rules beneficial to the whole, and pass from the whole to the part to be restored; have you not heard them speak thus, and that it is so?" "Exactly," he said. "Do they seem to you to speak rightly," I said, "and do you approve of this discourse?" "Most of all," he said. Indeed, when I heard that these things were approved by him, I recovered my confidence, and my spirit was gradually excited again and I was refreshed. "Such," I said, "O **Charmides**, is the power of this incantation as well. Which I learned there in the army from a certain one of the **Thracian** physicians, followers of **Zamolxis**, who are said even to bring immortality. That **Thracian** physician added, moreover, that the Greek physicians also preach the things that were related above. But **Zamolxis**, our king and god, says: just as it is not right to cure the eyes without the head, nor the head without the rest of the body: so neither the body without the soul. And that is the cause why many diseases of bodies escape the Greek physicians, because they are ignorant of the whole itself, which ought to be cured first: for if it is badly affected, it is impossible for any part to be well. For all things, whether good or evil, flow from the soul into the body and the whole man, and from there similarly as from the head into the eyes they flow out. Therefore, he orders that [the soul] be cured first and most of all, if indeed the head and the entire body ought to be well. He teaches, O blessed one, that the medicines of the soul are certain incantations. That these are contained in noble reasonings, by which temperance is attributed to the soul: which being inserted and present, it is easy to provide health to the head and the whole body." He therefore, when he taught the medicine and the incantations, ordered that I should be moved by no prayers to apply the remedy against the headache to anyone, unless he had first committed his soul to be purged by those very incantations. Indeed, he said this was the error of our times, that many strive to be physicians without the study of temperance and health. Me, therefore, he forewarned in a wonderful way, and commanded that I should take care lest anyone, however rich or noble or beautiful, should persuade me to do otherwise. To him, I bound myself by an oath; wherefore it is necessary that I obey, and I will obey. If you wish, according to the precepts of the guest, to subject your soul first to all the incantations of that **Thracian**, I will apply it to the head. Otherwise, I will not be able, O friend **Charmides**, to profit you.

When **Critias** had heard these things, he said, "This heaviness of the head will be a gain to the youth, if he is compelled to become better in mind and soul because of it. But assure yourself that this **Charmides** excels all his peers not only in appearance, but even stands out above the others in that very thing of which you said you have the incantation. Did you not speak of temperance above?" "Of this very thing," I said. "Know then that of all the youths of his age, he seems the most temperate, and in all other things according to the increase of his age, he is inferior to none." "It is fitting, O **Charmides**," I said, "in these things which **Critias** has said, that you excel the others. For no one can easily report, I think, the union of two families among the **Athenians** from which it is more likely that a beautiful and noble offspring should be born than from the union of your ancestors. For the paternal line of this **Critias** [and] **Dropides** has been illustrated by **Anacreon**, **Solon**, and very many other poets, excelling in beauty, virtue, and other happiness. The maternal glory of the lineage is also the same. For no one appeared either more beautiful or greater than **Pyrilampes**, your uncle, to all who inhabit the continent: as often as he approached as an ambassador either to the Great King or to another inhabitant on the continent. And in sum, this entire house is inferior to no other whatsoever. Wherefore it is probable that you, created from such a stock, hold the first parts in all things. As much, therefore, as pertains to that beauty which is discerned by the eyes, O sweet son of **Glaucon**, you seem to me not to have degenerated at all from your superiors; if you are disposed by nature toward temperance and toward other things, as **Critias** here testifies, your mother bore you blessed, O dear **Charmides**. Therefore, this is how the matter stands. If temperance is in you, as **Critias** says, and you are sufficiently temperate, you need neither the incantations of **Zamolxis** nor of **Abaris** the **Hyperborean**, but now the medicine of the head must be applied to you. But if temperance is lacking to you, the incantation ought to precede the medicine. Respond, therefore, to me yourself, whether you agree with **Critias** and assert that you have enough temperance, or whether you recognize that something is lacking."

Then indeed the cheeks of **Charmides** himself, suffused with a blush, showed a more pleasing appearance. [[Margin: Modesty becomes a youth.]] For shame becomes that age. Then he responded quite nobly: "It is by no means easy to either admit or refuse the things that have been asked in the present. For if I deny that I am temperate, first indeed it will seem base that I should disparage myself; second, I would convict this **Critias** and many others, to whom I seem temperate, of an as-if false opinion. But if I affirm it, these boastings about myself will seem odious. Wherefore, I do not know where to turn." "You seem to speak rightly, **Charmides**," I said. "Therefore, I think we must investigate in common whether you possess what I seek, or not: lest either you be compelled to speak otherwise than you wish, or I hasten rashly to heal. If, therefore, it will be pleasing to you, I desire to investigate with you; if not, I think it should be dismissed." "On the contrary, certainly most pleasing of all," he said. "Wherefore, as you think best, so inquire." "In this way," I said, "the search seems likely to be more convenient. It is certain surely that if temperance is in you, you have something that you opine concerning it. For it is necessary that, if it is inherent in you, it should provide some sense of itself, from which some opinion about it might arise, by which you might conjecture what and of what sort temperance is, do you not think?" "I think so indeed." "Do you not think this: namely, that since you know how to speak Greek, you could certainly say what that seems to be to you?" "Perhaps," he said. "So that we may conjecture whether temperance is in you or not, come tell me, what in your opinion do you say temperance is?"

He was reluctant at first, and did not come willingly to respond; at last he responded thus: "That temperance consists of two things: doing each thing becomingly, and proceeding on the way quietly and calmly; speaking quietly, and doing all things quietly; and to embrace briefly what you seek, it seems to me to be a certain quietude and calmness." "Rightly said," I replied. "They say indeed that quiet and placid men are temperate; but let us see if you speak the truth. Tell me then, is temperance something beautiful?" "It is, entirely," he said. "In that skill of the grammarian, is it more beautiful to write the same letters quickly, or slowly?" "Quickly." "And as for reading, quickly or slowly?" "Quickly." "Furthermore, is it more beautiful to strike the cithara swiftly and to compete promptly," I said, "than quietly and slowly?" "It is," he said. "What indeed in the games of fists and arms—is not speed itself praised?" "Certainly." "To run and to jump, and the other acts of the body—if they are done hurriedly and promptly, do they not look toward the beautiful? If slowly, with difficulty, placidly and calmly, toward the base?" "It appears so," he said. "It is clear, therefore, as far as pertains to the body, that not what is slow and calm, but what is swiftest and fast is especially beautiful. Is it not so?" I said. "Altogether," he replied. "And was it agreed that temperance is something beautiful?" "It was agreed." "Therefore, concerning the body, quietude...

### [Page 194]
# Book Twenty.

...no, rather speed will pertain to temperance, if indeed temperance is something beautiful." "It seems so," he said. "And is not docility more beautiful than dullness?" "Certainly more beautiful." "And docility," I said, "is to learn quickly; dullness is to learn late and slowly." "Indeed," he said. "Is not to teach another as quickly as possible more beautiful than hesitatingly and slowly?" "Without a doubt." "Likewise, to recollect and to remember late and slowly, is it more beautiful than easily and promptly?" "Promptly," he said. "And is not shrewdness," I said, "rather a certain speed of the mind than slowness?" [[Margin: Shrewdness and a certain speed of the mind.]] "It is," he said. "And yet, to understand what the grammarians and cithara-players say in games and in all other things not as slowly as possible, but as swiftly as possible, is most beautiful." "And this too," he said. "Furthermore, in the very investigations and consultations of the mind, is not the one who gives counsel and thinks quietly and with difficulty to be praised, I think, but rather the one who does so briefly and most easily?" "These things are true," he said. "From these things it is gathered," I said, "O **Charmides**, both in those things which pertain to the body and those which pertain to the soul, that fast and prompt things seem more beautiful than slow and quiet ones." "So it appears," he said. "Therefore, quietude will not be temperance," I said, "nor a quiet life temperate, as is conjectured by this reasoning, since what is temperate must also be beautiful. For of two things, one is true: either never or very rarely in life have quiet actions appeared more beautiful to us than fast and vehement ones; but if, O friend, quiet actions were found to excel in beauty no fewer than fast and vehement ones, not even by this reasoning would it be established that to act quietly is temperance rather than acting vehemently and swiftly, neither in walking, nor in speech, nor in anything else: nor would a quiet life be more becoming and temperate than an unquiet one: since in the superior discourse it was supposed that temperance is something beautiful, but it was agreed that fast things are no less beautiful than quiet ones." "Rightly," he said, "you seem to me to have spoken, O **Socrates**."

"Again therefore, O **Charmides**," I said, "behold yourself more attentively, and think what sort of person the presence of temperance makes you, or what it is itself while it makes you such; observing all these things, answer well and manfully what it seems to you to be." He, immediately collecting himself and contemplating more diligently, said: "It seems to me that temperance induces a certain modest blush, and makes a man modest, and I think that temperance is shame (*pudor*)." "What are you saying?" I said. "Did you not a little before say that temperance is something beautiful?" "I did indeed," he said. "Are not good men themselves temperate?" I said. "They are," he replied. "Do you think that is good which does not make men good?" "By no means." "Therefore it is not only beautiful, but also good," I said. "So it seems to me," he replied. "Do you not believe," I said, "that **Homer** speaks rightly when he says that shame is not good for a needy man?" [[Margin: Odyssey 17]] "I believe it indeed," he said. "Shame, therefore, as it appears," I said, "is both not good and good." "It appears so," he said. "But temperance is only good, since it makes those in whom it is present good, but bad men by no means." "It seems to me to be as you speak," he said. "Therefore temperance will not be shame, since temperance is only good, but shame is no more good than evil." "This seems to me to be rightly said, O **Socrates**," he replied. "But attend, I pray, to what sort of thing I may bring forward again. For just now I remembered what was passed down to me by someone saying that temperance is that each one does his own business (*sua quisque agat*); consider whether he who says this seems to speak rightly to you."

"O wicked one, did you hear that from this **Critias**, or some other of the wise men?" "**Critias** said, "It seems indeed from another, for he never heard it from me." "What does it matter," he said, "O **Socrates**, from whom I heard it?" "Nothing, indeed," I replied, "for we must not consider who said it, but whether it is said truly or not." "Now you speak well," he said. "Rightly, by Jove," I said. "I will wonder, however, if we find how this stands, for it is very similar to a certain enigma." "Wherefore?" he asked. "Because I do not think that he meant it as the words sound," I replied, "namely, that temperance is that anyone does his own business. Do you think a grammarian does nothing when he writes or reads?" "I think he does something indeed," he said. "Does the grammarian seem to you to write and read his own name only? Or does he also instruct you boys? For you were writing the names of enemies no less than those of yourselves and your friends." "Certainly no less," he replied. "And when you were doing this," I said, "were you more meddlesome than is fitting, and were you departing from the law of temperance?" "Least of all," he said. "But you were not doing only your own things, if writing and reading is doing something." "It is indeed," he said. "Moreover, to heal, O friend, to build, to weave, and to fulfill the work of any art—is that doing something, or nothing?" "Something entirely," he replied. "Would that city seem to you well-instituted," I said, "in which the laws ordered that each one weave his own garment, wash it, and make his own shoes, and his own strigil and oil-flasks, or ointment-jars, and every piece of furniture? That he should never touch another's things, but perform and finish his own himself." "By no means," he said. "Nevertheless, if a city is temperately disposed, it is well-instituted," I said. "Why not?" he said. "Therefore temperance will not be to do such things, and to do one's own in this way?" "No, as it appears," he said. "Wherefore he was speaking in enigmas," I said, "as I said above, he who preached that temperance is to do one's own. For he is not to be thought so foolish that his meaning was the same as the sound of the words. Did some foolish person, O **Charmides**, pass this down to you?" "Least of all," he said, "of all men. Rather, one who is in my judgment most wise." "Altogether, therefore, he involved his meaning in obscure words," I said, "so that it might be difficult to know what it is to 'do one's own.'" "Perhaps," he said. "Can you open to us what it is to 'do one's own'?" I asked. "I indeed do not know," he said. "Perhaps even he who said these things did not sufficiently understand what he meant."

While he was speaking thus, **Charmides** smiled and looked at **Critias**. **Critias**, although before he had been instigated by a desire for glory to discourse against **Charmides** and others, had until now restrained himself; but he could no longer restrain himself at this. And it seemed to me that what I had suspected was true: namely, that **Charmides** had received that superior opinion about temperance from **Critias**. Therefore **Charmides**, not wishing to defend the response himself and desiring to throw this labor onto **Critias**, showed him as if refuted; which he [Critias] by no means tolerated, rather he seemed to have been no less indignant toward him than a poet toward an actor ineptly reciting his poems. And therefore, looking at him, he said, "Do you think thus, O **Charmides**, that if you by no means understand what was his meaning who asserted that temperance is to do one's own, that he himself did not understand it either?" "O best of men, **Critias**," I said, "it is no wonder that this youth does not understand. But it is fitting for you to know these things, both on account of your age and your study. If therefore you also affirm that temperance is what he said, and you take up this discourse, I will more willingly investigate with you whether it be true or not." "I affirm it indeed," he said, "and I take it up." "You do rightly," I replied. "But tell me, I pray: [p. 195] Whether you admit the things I was asking a little before? Namely, that all artisans 'do' something." "I do," he said.

### [Page 195]
# Charmides, Or, on Temperance.

"...Do they seem to you to 'do' their own only, or others' as well?" "Others' as well," he said. "Do they act temperately, then," I said, "who do not only their own things?" "What prevents it?" he asked. "As for me," I said, "nothing. But see lest something prevents it in him who, having supposed that temperance is to do one's own, then says nothing stands in the way of those who do others' things being temperate." "I indeed conceded," he said, "that those who do others' things are temperate; but did I concede it of those who 'make' (*faciunt*)?" "Tell me, **Critias**," I said, "do you not call 'to act' (*agere*) and 'to make' (*facere*) the same thing?" [[Margin: Those idle in work...]] "Certainly not," he said, "nor 'to work' (*operari*) and 'to make.' For I learned that from **Hesiod**, who says, 'No work is a disgrace.' Do you think that he, if he had named such works—working and acting—as you were relating above, would have said no work of anyone is a disgrace, whether to one cutting leather, or a tavern-keeper selling condiments and victuals, or sitting in a shop? It is not to be thought so, O **Socrates**. Rather, he, in my judgment, thought 'effecting' (*effectionem*) to be something other than 'action' (*actionem*) and 'operation' (*operationem*), and that 'effecting' is sometimes a reproach, when we do something besides what is noble; but that 'work' (*opus*) never turns out to be a disgrace to us. For those things which are done nobly and usefully, he called 'works,' and such 'operations' and 'actions' he called 'effectings.' One must think, moreover, that he thought only these were one's 'own'; but all harmful things were entirely 'alien.' Wherefore one ought to think that **Hesiod**, and every other man of sound mind, calls a man doing his own things in this way 'temperate.'"

"As soon as you began to speak, O **Critias**," I said, "I perceived that you call one's 'own' and 'proper' things good, and you denominate the 'effectings' of good things as 'actions.' For I have very often heard **Prodicus** distinguishing names in this manner. I indeed concede to you the use of names at your pleasure, provided you declare what you wish to signify by each name. Now, therefore, define again more clearly from the beginning, whether you say that the 'action' or 'effecting' of good things, or however else you wish to name it, is temperance." "This very thing," he said. "Therefore he does not act temperately," I said, "who does evil things, but rather he who does good things. Does it not seem so to you, O noble man?" he said. "Dismiss that for the present," I replied. "We are not yet considering what seems so to me, but what you are saying now." "Indeed," he said, "I would never say that he acts temperately who does not do good things, but evil. For I manifestly define the action of good things itself as temperance."

"Perhaps nothing prevents you from speaking truly," I said; "however, I wonder at this, if you think that men acting temperately are ignorant that they are acting temperately." "I by no means think so," he said. "Was it not said by you a little before," I said, "that nothing prevents artisans, even when they are doing others' things, from living temperately?" "It was indeed said," he replied, "but what then?" "Nothing else," I said. "But say whether some physician seems to you, while he makes someone healthy, to effect useful things both for himself and for the one he cures?" "He does, in my opinion," he said. "Does he not do becoming things," I asked, "whoever does these things?" "Certainly," he said. "But he who does becoming things," I said, "does he not also act temperately?" "And temperately," he replied. "Is it necessary for the physician to understand when he cures usefully and when not? And for every artisan [to know] when the work he effects will be profitable to him and when not?" "Perhaps not," he said. "Sometimes, therefore," I said, "when a physician has worked usefully or the contrary, he does not know himself how he has worked, even if he worked usefully; yet as you were confessing, he acted temperately, or did you not say so?" "I did indeed," he said. "Therefore," I said, "as it appears, sometimes having worked usefully, he acts indeed temperately and is temperate, but he himself is ignorant that he is acting temperately and is temperate?"

"This cannot happen, O **Socrates**," he said. "But if anything has been said in the preceding from which this follows necessarily, I will more willingly retract that than be forced to confess that I did not say something else correctly, rather than consent that he who is ignorant of himself is temperate. For I almost think this very thing is temperance: to know oneself; and I agree with him who inscribed this precept in the temple of **Apollo** himself. And yet this inscription seems like a certain salutation of the God to men who enter the temple, in place of that which bids one 'rejoice': as if it is not properly said 'rejoice,' nor does it befit men to command this to one another, but rather to 'live temperately.' Thus God addresses men entering the temple with a singular sentiment, and salutes us differently than men do, as he thought, in my judgment, who inscribed it. And he prescribes nothing else to the enterer than to live temperately. But he inserted this precept in obscure words as if he were a prophet. For 'Know thyself' is the same as 'Live temperately,' as the letters testify and I interpret. But perhaps someone will think it is something else: which I think happened to those who added the following: 'Nothing in excess' and 'Misery is the companion of a pledge.' For they thought 'Know thyself' was a piece of advice, not an admonition of God himself to those entering. Then, so that they might also hang up no less worthy advice, they added the rest. Therefore all these things, **Socrates**, have been said by me because I will concede all the superior points to you without controversy. For perhaps you said something more correctly about them, and perhaps I did; but nothing from what we have said is manifest. Hereafter, however, I wish to give you the reason for this, if you do not concede that temperance is to know oneself."

"You deal with me," I said, "O **Critias**, as if I affirmed that I knew the things I ask, and as if you would concede them to me if I wished; but this is not so. For I always seek with you concerning that which has been brought into the middle, for the reason that I am ignorant of it. I will see further whether I concede it or not. Wait a moment while I consider these things." "Consider," he said. "Behold, I am considering," I replied. [[Margin: Refutation of the fourth definition.]] "If temperance is to 'know something,' it is certain that it is some science and of something. Is it not?" "It is indeed," he said, "namely, of oneself." "Is not medicine the science of the healthy?" "Exactly," he said. "If therefore you were to ask, since medicine is the science of the healthy, what does it confer on us? Or what does it effect? I would certainly respond that it profits as much as possible, and health, moreover, is the beautiful work it performs for us. Do you accept this?" "I accept it," he said. "And if you were to ask again, since architecture is the science of building, what work it might build, I would certainly respond 'houses,' and in the same way I would give an answer for the other arts. Since you say temperance is the science of oneself, it is your business to respond if someone should inquire in this manner: 'O **Critias**, temperance, which is the science of oneself, what noble work does it effect for us, and one worthy of the name? Say, please.'"

"You do not ask correctly, **Socrates**," he said. "For this is not similar to the other sciences, nor are the others [similar to one another]: but you ask as if they were similar. For tell me, I pray. Of the science of computation or geometry, what sort of work is there such as a house is for architecture, and a garment the work of weaving, and very many other things of this kind which anyone could attribute to many arts? Can you show me any such work of these? You will not be able." "You speak the truth," I said, "however, I can show you this: of what each of these sciences is a science, which is something other than the science itself. Just as the skill of computing is the science of even and odd multitude, in what way they relate to themselves and to each other, is it not?" "Certainly," he said. "And is not even and odd something else," I said, "than the science of computation itself?" "It is," he replied. "Furthermore, the faculty of weighing is the balancing of heavier and lighter weight. But the heavy and light itself is something else than the art itself of weighing. Do you agree?" "I agree," he said. "Tell me then, of what especially is temperance the science, such that it is something other than temperance itself?" "This indeed," he said, "which you now ask, is that very thing by which temperance differs from all other sciences. But you demand some similarity of this to the others. But the matter stands otherwise. Namely, all the others are of some other science, not at all of themselves. This alone is the science of both other sciences and of itself."

"You are far from being ignorant of this if I think truly, what you were denying a little before: for you attempt to refute me, and you pass over that of which the discourse is. What are you doing?" I said. "Do you think if I refute you, I do it for the sake of anything else than that for which I examine myself, if I say anything, fearing lest while I think I know what I do not know, my ignorance deceives me? And now indeed I assert that I do this most of all, namely, to weigh and examine the discourse for my own sake first, perhaps also for the sake of my friends. Do you not think this is a common good for all men, that the condition of each thing should become known to all?" "Most of all, O **Socrates**." "Boldly then, O blessed one," I said, "responding to the questions as your opinion bears, do not care whether it be **Critias** or **Socrates** who is refuted, but attend to the discourse itself, to what end the refutation may turn out." "I will do so," he said, "for you seem to speak rightly."

"Come, repeat what you say concerning temperance," I said. "I say indeed," he replied, "that of all other sciences this alone is the science of both itself and of the remaining sciences." "Is it not also the science of ignorance," I asked, "since indeed it is of science?" "Altogether." "Therefore the temperate man alone," I said, "will know himself, and will be able to examine what he knows, what he is ignorant of: he will be able in addition to judge from other men what each knows and thinks he knows, if indeed he knows it, or what he is ignorant of and thinks he knows; but no other person will be able to do this. And this is to be temperate, and temperance: to know oneself, namely, to understand what things one knows and what one does not [[Margin: Proverb]] know. Are these the things you say?" "They are," he said. "Therefore," I said, "as the saying goes, let us consider for the third time as if from the beginning. First whether this can happen or not, that what each one knows and what he does not know, he can likewise both know and not know. Then if that can happen, what utility would there be for those who understand it." "One must inquire," he said.

"Observe, **Critias**," I said, "whether you have anything certain in these things: for I have nothing, and in whatever matter I doubt, if you wish, I will open it." "Indeed I wish it," he said. "These things will follow," I said, "if what you just now said stands: namely, that there is one certain science which is the science of no other than itself and other sciences: and likewise the science of ignorance." "Exactly," he said. "See," I said, "friend, how absurd this discourse of ours is. For if you were to consider this same thing in other cases, as I think, it will seem impossible to you." "In what way," he asked, "and where?" "Clearly here," I replied. "For think whether it seems to you that there is a certain vision which is not a vision of those things of which other visions are, but of itself and of other visions, and likewise of non-vision; and it sees no color since it is vision, but only inspects itself and other visions. Does any such vision seem to you to exist?" "None," he replied. "Can you trust that some power of hearing can be found," I said, "which hears no voice, but perceives itself and other hearings and non-hearings?" "That is not possible either," he said. "In sum, consider all the senses, whether some sense can be found that perceives itself and the other senses, yet feels none of those things which the other senses feel." "I think this also is impossible," he said. "Or perhaps is there some desire of the senses which affects no pleasure, but is a desire for itself and the remaining lusts?" "By no means," he said. "Nor will you say, I think," I said, "that there is a will which desires no good, but seeks itself and the other wills." "Least of all," he said. "Furthermore, will you say there is some such love that is a love of nothing beautiful, but rather is an ardor for itself and other loves?" "I indeed will not." "Have you ever thought of some fear that is afraid of itself and other fears, but dreads nothing terrible and dangerous?" "Never at all," he said. "Moreover, is there an opinion such that it is an opinion of other opinions and of itself, but opines none of those things which other opinions suspect?" "In no way." "Nevertheless, we said that there is some such science which is a science of no dogma, but is the science of itself and other sciences." "We did indeed say so," he replied. "Is it not a certain wonder, if it exists? For let us not yet contend that it is not, but let us consider whether it is." "You speak wisely," he said. "Tell me now, is this science the science of something? And does it have some power of this kind, such that it is of something?" "Exactly," he said. "Likewise, do we say it has the power of the greater, by which it is greater than something?" "Certainly it has," he said. "Will it not be greater than something smaller, if it is to be greater?" "It is necessary," he said. "If we find something greater which exists as greater than other greater things and itself, yet was not greater than any of those things by which the rest are greater, would it not entirely happen to this that just as it is greater than itself, so it is also smaller?" "It is entirely necessary, O **Socrates**." "Furthermore, if something be double," I said, "relative to other doubles and to itself, surely relative to itself it will be half of the double, and relative to other halves, double. For whatever is double is the double of no other than the half." "It is true," he said. "Moreover, that which is more than itself, is it not also less? And that which is heavier likewise lighter? Or that which is older also younger? and in all other things in the same way, whatever has the power of itself toward itself, will it not also have that essence toward which its power is? I speak of something like this. Do we say hearing is of nothing else than the hearing of a voice?" "Certainly," he said. "If it hears itself," I said, "will it not hear itself as having a voice? For it could not hear otherwise." "It follows necessarily," he said. "Vision also, O best man," I said, "if it sees itself, it will be necessary for it to have some color. For without color, vision can discern nothing." "It can do nothing," he said. "You see, **Critias**, that those things we have related partly seem entirely impossible to us, partly must be deeply doubted lest they do not have their power toward themselves, since that every magnitude and multitude and other things of this kind should have their power toward themselves is entirely impossible, is it not?" "It is altogether so," he said. "But that vision and hearing perceive themselves," I said, "that motion moves itself, and that heat heats itself, and other such things is not believed by some, although to others perhaps it seems to be believed. There is need of some great man, O friend, who may distinguish this sufficiently through all things, whether nothing at all can have its power toward itself except science, but only toward another; or whether some can and others cannot; and if there are some things which have their power toward themselves, whether among their number is this science which we call temperance. I indeed by no means trust that I am sufficient to discern these things. Wherefore I cannot even assert whether it can happen that there is a science of science. Even if that be given, I will not yet assent that temperance is of this sort, until I have investigated whether such a temperance being so profits us anything or profits nothing. For I divine that temperance is something useful and good. You therefore, son of **Callaeschrus**, since you place temperance as science in science and the science [of ignorance], show first that this which you said above is possible: afterward, besides its being possible, that it is also beneficial: and thus you will perhaps satisfy me concerning the definition of temperance itself."

But **Critias**, when he had heard these things and saw me doubting, in the manner of those who, seeing others yawning, yawn themselves, seemed to be compelled by my hesitating to similarly hesitate. But being fond of glory, he feared those present, nor did he wish to confess to me that he was not sufficient to discern those things I had offered, nor did he clearly bring forth anything, and he hid his hesitation. But I, so that our disputation might proceed, said: "If it seems so to you, **Critias**, we will grant now that there can be a science of science. But whether it can be or not, we will investigate elsewhere. Nevertheless, if that were possible to the highest degree, what is it more possible to know than what one knows and what one does not know: this surely we said was to know oneself and to be temperate. Is it not so?" "Most of all," he said, "and it follows in a certain way, **Socrates**. For if someone has that science which knows itself, he would be such as that which he has: just as when one has speed, he is fast: and when beauty, beautiful: and when knowledge, knowing. Wherefore when someone has the knowledge of himself, he then is made knowing himself." "I do not doubt that at all," I replied, "that if someone has something in himself knowing itself, he himself also knows himself. But what necessity compels a man thus affected to know what he knows and what he does not know?" "Namely this," he said, "because this and that are the same." "Perhaps it is so," I said, "but I always seem to be the same, nor again do I understand how it is the same thing to know what one knows and to know what one does not know." "How can you say that?" he asked. "Thus," I said, "science being itself science, can it discern further than that of these things one is science and the other is ignorance?" "No further, but to that extent," he replied. "Is it therefore the same thing," I asked, "to have science and ignorance of health, and likewise science and ignorance of the just?" "In no way," he said. "But truly this is medicine, and the other is civil skill... unless someone knows in addition the healthy and the just, but only science, since he has the science of this alone, what indeed he knows, or of what he has a certain science, he will recognize both concerning himself and concerning others. Is it not so? But by what reason will he understand that this science knows? For medicine knows the healthy and the wholesome, not temperance; music the harmonic, not temperance; architecture the building, not temperance; and similarly all things, is it not so?" "It appears so," he said.

"But temperance," I said, "if it is only the science of sciences, how will it understand what knows the healthy and wholesome, or what is a building?" "In no way," he replied. "Therefore it will not understand what it knows, being ignorant of this, but only that it knows. So it seems," he said. "Therefore to be temperate will not be this, nor temperance: to understand what one knows or what one does not know, but as it seems, only that one knows and that one does not know." "It appears so," he said. "Nor will this man be able to examine another professing some science, whether he knows what he promises or does not know. Rather only this, as it seems," I said, "will he recognize: that he has a certain science; but of what thing that science is, temperance will not show." "It does not seem so," he said. "Therefore he will not discern a simulated physician from a true one, nor any other knowing person from one who is ignorant. Let us consider it thus. If the temperate man, or anyone else, is to judge between a true and a false physician, will he not do it thus? Concerning the art of healing he will differ nothing from him. For the physician understands nothing else, as we were saying, than the healthy and the sick, the wholesome and the harmful, is it not so?" "Quite so," he replied. "Further, concerning science he knows nothing," I said, "for we will attribute this to temperance alone." "So it is," he said. "Therefore the physician knows nothing about medicine either," I said, "since medicine is a certain science." "You speak truly," he said. "The temperate man will recognize that he indeed has some science, but someone else will consider the skill of the physician, of what things it is. Which indeed then is clear, when it is known of what things it is the science. Is not every science determined, not only in that it is science, but which science it is, and what science it is known to be, these being known, of which it is the science?" "Quite so," he said. "The science of medicine," I said, "is distinguished from other sciences by this, that it is the skill of the wholesome and the unwholesome?" "Certainly," he said. "Is it not in these things," I asked, "that whoever comes to consider medicine ought to consider, namely in those things in which it is occupied? For it is not to be sought in extraneous things where it is not." "Certainly not," he said. "Therefore in wholesome things and their contraries he will consider the physician as a physician, whoever will correctly scrutinize him." "It seems so," he said. "Will he not notice in these things either said or done, what things are truly said and what are rightly done?" "It is necessary," he said. "Can anyone attain these things without the skill of medicine?" "None," he replied. "Nor another, as it seems, besides the physician; therefore not the temperate man either. For besides being temperate, he would also be a physician." "These things are true." "Altogether therefore temperance, if it is the science of science and ignorance, will not be able to discern a physician skilled in healing, and likewise one simulating skill in medicine or thinking himself to have it, nor any other of those who know anything, except a man of the same profession, just as other artisans [do]." "So it appears."

"What further utility, O **Critias**, is going to come to us from temperance when it is such? For if, what we supposed in the beginning, the temperate man knew what he knows and what he does not know—that indeed he knows this, and that he is ignorant of that—and could judge another thus affected, we would report an immense benefit endowed with temperance: since we would lead our lives without sin, both we ourselves who are participants in temperance, and all others who were ruled by our command. For we would not undertake to do those things which we are ignorant of, but having scrutinized knowing men we would surely yield to them: nor would we concede to others subject to our governance to do anything else than what they were going to do rightly having undertaken it, that is...

### [Page 199]
# Charmides Or, on Temperance. 299

"...is he the artisan of nothing? In no way does it seem so, O **Socrates**." "Do you see, **Critias**, that I did not fear without cause above, and blamed myself, because I perceived nothing great and useful concerning temperance. For never would that which is conceded by all to be the most beautiful have appeared useless to us if in some way I were useful for inquiring correctly. Now, however, we succumb on all sides, nor are we able to find to signify what especially the author of names himself instituted the name of temperance: although we have conceded many things entirely abhorrent to reason. Furthermore, we agreed that it is the science of science, with reason struggling against it and immediately repelling it. Moreover, by this very science we conceded that the works of the remaining sciences are known, with reason similarly resisting, so that the temperate man should be such that he knows what he knows, knows himself to know, and understands again that he is ignorant of what he does not know. This indeed we conceded too magnificently and freely, not noticing that it is impossible that what one in no way knows, he should in some way know. In this, however, we consented: namely, that someone being ignorant of something, knows that he does not know it: although there is nothing, as my opinion goes, which seems more absurd than this. Nevertheless, this investigation having found us inept rather than hard and persistent, it can find the truth no more: but it has mocked itself to such an extent that what we have for a long time fashioned by common consent and posed to be temperance, this finally has appeared as something useless, insolently and too contumeliously.

Indeed for your sake rather than mine, O **Charmides**, I am distressed, if you, endowed with such an excellent appearance and temperance of soul, are helped nothing by such virtue, and it profits you nothing in life. I also bear it more heavily on account of the incantation which I learned from that **Thracian**, if I have placed such great study in perceiving a thing of no value. Therefore I do not sufficiently believe that these things are so, but I think myself to be a lazy investigator, since I indeed judge temperance to be some great good: which if you have, you are blessed. But think whether you possess it, and do not need the incantation. For if you have it, I will indeed advise you to think me a madman and one impotent in investigating the truth, but you, by how much you are more temperate, by so much the more blessed."

And **Charmides** said, "I do not know, by Jove, O **Socrates**, whether I have it or not. For by what means should I understand that which you, as you say yourself, are not yet able to find what it is? Indeed I do not much believe you, **Socrates**. Rather I think myself to need the incantation, and as far as pertains to me, nothing prevents you from healing me with incantations every day, until you think I have enough." "**Critias** said, "Let it be so; and truly, O **Charmides**, if you do this, it will be an argument to me that you are temperate, because you subject yourself to the incantations of **Socrates**, and never depart from his side." "I will obey indeed and follow everywhere," he said. "For I would sin gravely unless I obeyed you, my tutor, and executed what you order." "I do indeed order it," said **Critias**. "I will do it diligently," he said, "and I will begin today." "What are these men deliberating?" I asked. "**Charmides** said, "Nothing more. For it is decreed." "Will you use force?" I asked; "and will you leave me no choice of consulting in turn?" "Think that I will entirely bring force," he said, "since he here commands it. Concerning this, you also consult what you are going to do." "There remains no place for consulting," I said, "for no one will be able to resist you affecting and compelling something." "Therefore you do not resist either," he said. "I indeed will not oppose you," I said.

# LACHES OF PLATO, OR, ON COURAGE.

### ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.

Plato frequently prefers the best magistrates to laws, because laws without them seem entirely useless: for no one will keep them. But the best magistrates are themselves the laws. But he says that magistrates cannot become the best unless the citizens are the best men: nor will men be such unless the adolescents and boys are also such. Wherefore in almost all the dialogues he exhorts parents first of all to educate their sons correctly, knowing that the human race cannot live either honestly or be governed happily without the best governors...

[Ficino's introduction continues, arguing for the necessity of training youth in virtue (courage/fortitude and temperance) to ensure a stable Republic.]

### [Page 200]
# Book Twenty-One.

[Ficino’s Argument continues...] He adds that it is not possible for anyone to exhort another to courage unless he knows how to express what courage itself is. Soon, having been asked what courage is, **Laches** responds more confidently that it is the virtue through which one, not deserting the rank, fights the enemy. Which indeed is refuted because someone can conquer the enemy in the **Scythian** manner no less by fleeing than by remaining, and be equally brave. And therefore **Homer** calls him brave who opportunely dares to be afraid. A little later, the victory of courage is drawn to any matter whatever, as if it becomes a brave man to overcome not only fears, but also pains, lusts, and pleasures. Hence this definition of all courage is sought in common. To these **Laches** responds that this is a certain endurance of the mind...

## LYSIMACHUS, MELESIAS, NICIAS, LACHES, THE SONS OF NICIAS AND LACHES, SOCRATES.

**Lysimachus**: You have seen a man fighting in noted arms, O **Nicias** and **Laches**; but for what cause I and **Melesias** here ordered you to watch this with us, we did not then declare. Now, however, we will open it: for we think we must speak freely with you. For there are some who mock these things: and if someone consults them, they do not express their opinion: but thinking that they hold the mind of the one consulting and the matter being consulted, they bring forth things other than what they feel. But since we judge you to be both sufficient for understanding and likely to explain simply what you know, we have taken you as partners for the deliberation of those things we shall relate. It is, however, of the sort which I have begun. These boys here are our sons, this one the son of this man, called **Thucydides** by his grandfather’s name: mine likewise another, serving the grandfather's name: for we name him **Aristides**. And it seems to us that the most diligent care of these must be undertaken, nor do we think we should do what many are accustomed to do, who allow their sons as soon as they have grown up to live according to their own lust; rather, now one must begin to have care for them as much as we are able. Since therefore we see that you have sons, we judged that you especially had thought by what reason they should be educated so that they might become the best; which if you have not much noticed, in the present we admonish you that you ought not to neglect it, and we exhort you that you deliberate with us concerning the education of the sons.

But for what cause these things seem so to us, O **Nicias** and **Laches**, it is right to hear, although the things that follow are a little more prolix. For I and **Melesias** here live together, and these youths dine with us and are present at our consultation. Whence, just as I signified in the beginning of the discourse, we speak freely and boldly with you. Indeed, each of us can relate many noble deeds of his own father done in peace and in war, by which they profited either their republic or their allies, but we can relate no deeds done by us. Wherefore we are both ashamed of these things, and we often blame our parents' negligence, that they permitted us after we grew up to live in a certain softness and luxury, meanwhile intent on the affairs of others. And showing these same things to these youths, we declare that if they neglect themselves and despise our precepts, they will be ignoble: but if they care for this, they will turn out worthy of their names. They indeed respond to us that they will obey. But as we consulted among ourselves by what discipline or custom they could especially become the best, someone explained that it is worthwhile that they should learn to fight in arms, and he praised this man whom you just now watched competing, and he ordered us to turn [to him]. It seemed best therefore that we should come to this spectacle, and summon you together, both to watch and also, if you wish, to deliberate with common counsel concerning the education of the youths...

### [Page 201]
# Laches, Or, on Courage.

...concerning this matter, whether it ought to be learned or not, as well as concerning other disciplines or studies of youth you have that are worthy of praise; then to predict what you are going to do regarding the counsel.

**Nicias**: I indeed approve your sentiment, O **Lysimachus** and **Melesias**, and I am prepared to investigate together with you, and I judge **Laches** here to be similarly affected.

**Laches**: You think rightly, O **Nicias**. Indeed, what **Lysimachus** was just now relating concerning his and **Melesias**'s father seems most aptly said against those, and us, and all whoever handle civil affairs: for, as **Lysimachus** complained, they neglect their sons as well as other domestic matters. In these things therefore, **Lysimachus**, you speak rightly. But that you summon us to consult about the institution of the youths, yet do not invite this **Socrates**, I wonder: first indeed a fellow-citizen, then one frequently occupied in that very thing which you require, either discipline or liberal study for the young.

**Lysimachus**: What do you say, **Laches**? Has **Socrates** here ever cared for such things?

**Laches**: Most certainly, **Lysimachus**.

**Nicias**: I also can be a witness of this matter no worse than **Laches**. For recently he led to me as a guest for the sake of instructing my son **Damon**, a disciple of **Agathocles**, a master of music, a man indeed polite above others, and skilled not only in music but also in other faculties, by which certainly he is worthy that youths of this sort be committed to his discipline and company.

**Lysimachus**: No longer, O **Socrates**, **Nicias**, and **Laches**, do I and my peers know the younger ones, since we mostly keep ourselves at home on account of our age. But if you can give any good advice to this fellow-citizen of yours, O son of **Sophroniscus**, give it. For it is fitting: for your father is our friend. For I and your father were often familiar and friends, and he departed from life before any grudge arose between us. To me also the name of **Socrates** somehow still rings in my ears, which these boys frequently use while arguing at home and celebrate most highly; I have not yet asked them whether they mean **Socrates** the son of **Sophroniscus**, or another. But O boys, tell me, is this that **Socrates** whom you are so frequently accustomed to mention?

**Boy**: That is him, father, without a doubt.

**Lysimachus**: It is well indeed, by Juno, O **Socrates**, that you extol and adorn your father, the best of men, and that our things will be yours, and yours ours.

**Laches**: Do not let this man go, **Lysimachus**. For I have noticed him elsewhere also, not only adorning his father, but even his fatherland; furthermore, in that flight at **Delium**, he retreated together with me, and I affirm this to you, that if the others had conducted themselves similarly, our city would stand, nor would it have suffered such a great ruin.

**Lysimachus**: This is the best praise, O **Socrates**, which is now attributed to you by men worthy of trust, who are themselves to be praised in the same things in which they praise you. Know therefore that I rejoice in your reputation, and consider me bound to you with the highest benevolence. It behooves you therefore first to approach us, and to think us domestic and familiar, as is fitting. Wherefore hereafter, after we have recognized each other, do not do otherwise, but embrace us and these younger ones with a certain domestic benevolence, so that mutual friendship between us may be preserved on both sides; these things you will do, and we hereafter will recall them again in memory. But regarding what we began to inquire, what do you say? Do you think it is beneficial for youths to learn this discipline, to fight in arms? [[Margin: Boys ought to learn the discipline of arms.]]

**Socrates**: I will indeed endeavor, O **Lysimachus**, if I can do anything to advise concerning these matters, and to do all that you ask: but it seems right to me that since I am both younger than these and more unskilled in these things, I should first hear what they themselves feel, and learn, and if I have anything besides their sentiments, then finally open it to you and them. And why do you not speak first, O **Nicias**?

**Nicias**: Nothing prevents it, **Socrates**. This skill seems to me to profit youths everywhere, nor should they linger in those things to which youths having found leisure are accustomed to give themselves, but it is better to acquire that faculty through which a robust habit of the body is acquired. For in no other exercise is this inferior or less laborious. Moreover, such exercise and equestrian skill especially becomes a free man. For in that contest of which we are athletes, and in those for which a contest is proposed to us, only those fight who exercise themselves in such instruments of war. This skill will also confer in the battle itself, as often as one must fight in the rank and order with very many others. But it will profit most of all then, when the ranks are dissolved, and it will be necessary in a singular contest either to pursue one resisting, or in flight to repel one attacking. Certainly he who is instructed in this faculty will never succumb to one, and perhaps not even to more, but will everywhere excel by this. Furthermore, this faculty brings a desire for a certain other noble discipline; for anyone when he has learned to fight with arms will affect the discipline concerning ordering ranks, which follows immediately: and having attained this, and being inflamed with a desire for glory concerning these things, he will take himself to the command of the army, and in sum, he will turn himself to all the noble studies and institutes concerning these things, worthy of knowledge and use, with that first one leading. We will also add something not to be despised, that this faculty would render each one in battle more daring and stronger in a wonderful way. Nor is that to be kept silent besides, although it might seem lighter, that you will make a man more fit and more capable there, where it is especially necessary to be seen as fit and prompt. There certainly on account of that very dexterity and capability he will appear more terrible to the enemies. It seems to me therefore, O **Lysimachus**, both worthwhile that youths should perceive these things: and I have explained for what cause I think so. Nevertheless, I will willingly hear if **Laches** wishes to bring anything besides these.

**Laches**: An absurd discourse would indeed be judged, O **Nicias**, if someone said any discipline were by no means to be acquired. [[Margin: The discipline of arms is depressed by reasons.]] For it seems better to know all things. Indeed, this faculty concerning arms, if it is a discipline as those who teach it say, and such besides as **Nicias** preaches, it must be learned. But if it is not a discipline, but those who promise this deceive us, or it is indeed a discipline but of no great price, why is it necessary to learn it? This I say because I think that if this were of any price, it would never have been hidden from the **Lacedaemonians**, to whom nothing else is a care in all of life than to prepare themselves so in all things that they excel all others in war. If by chance this escapes them, it would not have escaped the masters of this thing, because both the **Spartans** strive most highly for arms, and because he who is in price on account of the art would easily accumulate money among them and among others, just as the poet of tragedies among us is honored. For he who trusts in his tragedies does not wander outside of **Attica**, showing them through other cities, but immediately arrives here, and not without reason shows them to these men. But those who are occupied in the exercise of arms, I see they think **Lacedaemon** is as if some inaccessible temple, nor do they ever dare to ascend even with the top of their foot. Rather they wander around, and boast themselves rather among others, especially among those who themselves would confess themselves inferior to many others in military matters.

# Book Twenty-One.

"...confess. Furthermore, I was present with no few men of this kind, **Lysimachus**, when they were fighting, and I know what sort they are. Although anyone may conjecture the matter for himself. For as if by deliberate effort, no one of those who brooded over these games ever turned out illustrious in war, whereas in all other things those turn out distinguished and celebrated who frequently exercise themselves; only these [teachers of arms] are shown to be impotent of this wish. [[Margin: Stesilaus the gladiator.]] You watched [Stesilaus] boasting and promising wonderful things; elsewhere I once saw him more certainly demonstrating himself in truth to those who were not looking on of their own accord. For in the ship in which he was being carried, while attacking a certain transport ship, he was fighting with a hooked scythe, a very great one, and he himself very great. The other deeds of this man are not worthy of hearing, but this however must not be passed over in silence: what happened from such a marvelous machination of this man who added a scythe to his spear; for as he was fighting, the scythe became entangled in the rigging of the ship. **Stesilaus** pulled to disentangle it, but could not; the ship however was passing, meanwhile he accompanied the ship in its course holding the spear: but when the ship was now passing the other ship and he, holding the spear, was being pulled along, he finally came to the end of the weapon by hand. Laughter therefore and a din were raised in the transport ship on account of the figure of **Stesilaus**'s face, and on account of this besides, that someone having thrown a stone onto the deck near his feet compelled him to let go of the spear. Then indeed those who were carried in the trireme could no longer contain their laughter, as they watched that hooked scythe hanging from the ship. Perhaps these things are of some price, as **Nicias** asserts, but those at which I was present were such. Wherefore as I said from the beginning, if this is a discipline, it profits little; if it is not, but those who profess it simulate it, the matter does not seem worthy of study. For I think thus, that if some fearful person follows this faculty, having been made more daring on account of it, he will be more clearly [seen as a coward] than he was. But if some brave man follows it, it will be observed by everyone if he should err even a little, and he will undergo great calumnies; for the profession of this science is an invidious one, wherefore unless he excels others in virtue in a wonderful way, he who claims this science for himself will not be able to avoid being held ridiculous. Such seems to me, **Lysimachus**, the study of this discipline. It is necessary, however, as I was saying from the beginning, to pray this **Socrates** most highly that he himself consults with his own opinion concerning the proposed question."

**Lysimachus**: I do indeed ask, **Socrates**. For this consultation requires the opinion of a certain arbiter: for if these men had agreed with each other, there would be less need of such a consultation; now after **Laches**, as you see, and **Nicias** disagree, it is better to hear now whose opinion you would rather support.

**Socrates**: What truly, **Lysimachus**? Will you hold to this, if more of us praise it?

**Lysimachus**: What else should anyone do, O **Socrates**?

**Socrates**: Would you also do similarly, **Melesias**?

**Melesias**: Deservedly so, **Socrates**.

**Socrates**: Would you therefore attribute more faith to one, than to us four?

**Melesias**: Perhaps.

**Socrates**: For by science, not by multitude, must that be judged which is to be judged rightly.

**Melesias**: Without a doubt.

**Socrates**: Must it not first be considered if any among us is an artisan in that matter about which we are now deliberating? or not: and if any such is found, is he to be believed, the opinion of the rest being postponed? If none, must another be sought by us? Or do you think you are now imperiled by some small thing, you and **Lysimachus**, rather than concerning the most precious of all your possessions? [[Margin: As the sons are, so is the governing of the house.]] For the sons being instituted well or badly, the entire paternal house will be governed in the same way in which the sons are affected.

**Melesias**: You speak true things.

**Socrates**: Therefore one must watch this matter diligently.

**Melesias**: Greatly.

**Socrates**: In what way therefore should we have considered what I was just saying, if it had been proposed to find which of us is most skilled in competing? Would we not have scrutinized him who both learned and practiced? and to whom namely suitable teachers of this matter existed?

**Melesias**: So indeed I think.

**Socrates**: Must I not first also [find out] what that thing is, whose teachers I would seek?

**Melesias**: What is it you say?

**Socrates**: Thus perhaps you will perceive more clearly: it does not seem to have been agreed among us in the beginning what that is which we seek, which of us excels in it, and for the sake of this has had teachers, and who has not.

**Nicias**: Were we not seeking, **Socrates**, whether it behooves the youths to learn to fight with arms, or not?

**Socrates**: Quite so, **Nicias**, but when someone seeks concerning the medicine of the eyes whether it should be applied or not, then do you think the consultation is about the medicine or about the eyes?

**Nicias**: About the eyes.

**Socrates**: And when it is asked whether a bridle should be applied to a horse or not, and when, then is the consultation not about the bridle, but rather about the horse?

**Nicias**: True.

**Socrates**: But to embrace it in a few words, [[Margin: A beautiful rule in knowing things of which one treats.]] as often as someone seeks something for the sake of another thing, the consultation is about that very thing for whose sake the other thing is sought, not about that which is sought for the sake of another.

**Nicias**: Necessary.

**Socrates**: Therefore it behooves the consultant to consider whether he is skilled in caring for that thing for whose sake we are deliberating in the present.

**Nicias**: Altogether.

**Socrates**: Was it not said that we are inquiring about the discipline for the sake of the soul of the youths?

**Nicias**: It was said.

**Socrates**: Therefore, whether any of us is powerful in the art of those souls, and is able to cultivate them sufficiently and has had learned teachers, must be inquired into.

**Nicias**: Have you never seen, **Socrates**, some who without teachers turned out more skilled in a certain thing than those who had employed teachers?

**Socrates**: I have seen them indeed, **Laches**, whom you yourself however would not believe if they preached themselves the best artisans, unless they show some work of their art rightly perfected and elaborated, both one and many.

**Nicias**: What you say is true.

**Socrates**: It behooves us therefore, **Laches** and **Nicias**, after **Lysimachus** and **Melesias** have summoned us to consult about their sons, desiring to make their souls the best, if we confess that we have had teachers, to show those who were both themselves first the best, and have educated the souls of many adolescents, and afterward taught us. Or if any of us denies having had a teacher, he ought to show his works, and bring into the middle which of the **Athenians** or guests, either slave or free, has become good through their diligence without controversy. But if we can show neither, we ought to order them to go to other consultants, nor in depraving the sons of friends undergo that danger by which we may deserve the greatest accusation among the households of the youths. I indeed concerning myself first assert that no master of this matter has existed for me, although from a tender age I have always affected this thing. But truly I am not able to pay the fee to the Sophists, who alone have promised to make me good and honest. But I myself by my own genius am even now by no means able to find this art; which if **Nicias** here or **Laches** has found...
