# Charmides, or, On Temperance. 193

...nor can the head be cured without the medicine of the whole body. For this reason, they use certain rules that contribute to the whole, and they move from the whole to the part that is to be restored. Have you not heard them speak in this way, and that it is so? "Entirely," he said. "Does it seem to you that they speak correctly?" I asked, "and do you approve of this discourse?" "Most of all," he replied. Indeed, when I heard that he approved of these things, I regained my confidence, and my mind was gradually stirred again and I was refreshed. 

"Such," I said, "O Charmides, is the power of this incantation. I learned it there in the army from a certain Thracian physician, one of the followers of Zamolxis <note>Zamolxis was a legendary social and religious reformer among the Thracians, often regarded as a god or a king who taught the immortality of the soul.</note>, who are even said to bestow immortality. That Thracian physician added, moreover, that the Greek physicians also preach what was narrated above. But Zamolxis, our king and god, says: just as it is not right to treat the eyes without the head, nor the head without the rest of the body, so it is not right to treat the body without the soul. And this is the reason why many diseases of the body escape Greek physicians: because they are ignorant of the whole itself, which ought to be treated first; for if the whole is in a bad state, it is impossible for any part to be well. For all things, whether good or evil, flow from the soul into the body and the whole man, and from there they flow out just as they do from the head into the eyes. He orders, therefore, that the soul be treated first and most of all, if the head and the entire body are to be in good health. 

The soul, O blessed one, he teaches is healed by certain incantations. He says these consist of noble words and reasons <note>original: "praeclaris rationibus"</note>, by which temperance is granted to the soul: and once this is inserted and present, it is easy to provide health to the head and the whole body. Therefore, when he taught the medicine and the incantation, he commanded that I should apply the remedy for a headache to no one, moved by no prayers, unless they had first committed their soul to be purged by those very incantations. He said this was surely the error of our times, that most physicians strive to be doctors without a zeal for temperance and health. 

Therefore, he forewarned me in a wonderful way and commanded me to be careful lest any man, whether rich or noble or beautiful, should persuade me to do otherwise. I bound myself to him by an oath; for which reason it is necessary that I obey, and I will obey. So, if you wish, according to the stranger’s precepts, to subject your soul first to all the incantations of that Thracian, I will apply the remedy to your head. If not, I will not be able, O friend Charmides, to be of use to you." 

When Critias heard these things, he said, "This heaviness of the head will be a profit to the youth if he is compelled to become better in mind and soul because of his head. I assert to you, however, that this Charmides excels all his peers not only in appearance, but also in that very thing for which you said you have an incantation. Did you not say it was for temperance?" 

"I did," I replied. 

"Know then," he said, "that of all the youths of his age, this one seems the most temperate, and in all other things, according to the increase of his age, he is inferior to no one." 

"It is fitting, O Charmides," I said, "that in these things which Critias has said, you should excel others. For no one could easily report, I think, a union of two families among the Athenians from which a beautiful and noble offspring would more likely be born than from the union of your ancestors. For the paternal line of this Critias and Dropides has been made illustrious by Anacreon, Solon, and many other poets, excelling in beauty, virtue, and other happiness. The glory of the maternal line is the same. For no one ever seemed more beautiful or greater among all those who live on the continent than your uncle Pyrilampes <note>A prominent Athenian diplomat and friend of Pericles.</note>, whenever he went as an ambassador either to the Great King <note>The King of Persia.</note> or to another living on the continent. In short, this entire house is in no way inferior to any other. Therefore, it is probable that you, born of such a stock, should hold the first parts in all things. 

As far as that beauty which is seen by the eyes is concerned, O sweet son of Glaucon, you seem to me to have degenerated in nothing from your superiors; but if you are naturally inclined toward temperance and other virtues, as Critias here testifies, then your mother bore you a blessed man, O dear Charmides. So the matter stands: If temperance is in you, as Critias says, and you are sufficiently temperate, you need neither the incantations of Zamolxis nor of Abaris the Hyperborean <note>A legendary figure and priest of Apollo said to have traveled the world without eating.</note>, but the remedy for the head should already be applied to you. But if temperance is lacking in you, the incantation must precede the medicine. Respond to me yourself, therefore: do you agree with Critias and assert that you have enough temperance, or do you recognize that something is lacking?" 

Then the cheeks of Charmides were suffused with a blush, which gave him a more graceful appearance. For modesty becomes that age. <margin>Modesty becomes the young.</margin> Then he responded quite nobly: "It is by no means easy to either admit or deny the things that have been asked at present. For if I deny that I am temperate, it will first seem base that I should disparage myself; second, I would be accusing Critias here and many others to whom I seem temperate of holding a false opinion. But if I affirm it, this boast about myself will seem hateful. Therefore, I do not know which way to turn." 

"You seem to speak properly, Charmides," I said. "Therefore, I think we should investigate together whether you possess what I am asking for, or not: lest you be compelled to speak otherwise than you wish, or I should hasten to heal you rashly. If, therefore, it will be pleasing to you, I desire to investigate it together with you; if not, I think we should dismiss it." 

"On the contrary, it is certainly most pleasing of all," he said. "Therefore, as you yourself think best, search it out." 

"In this way," I said, "the inquiry seems likely to be more convenient. It is certain that if temperance is in you, you have some opinion about it. For it is necessary that, if it is inherent in you, it should provide some sense of itself, from which some opinion about it arises, by which you might conjecture what and of what kind temperance is; do you not think so?" 

"I do think so." 

"Do you not judge this: namely, that since you know how to speak Greek, you could certainly say what it seems to be to you?" 

"Perhaps," he said. 

"So that we may conjecture whether temperance is in you or not, come, tell me: what, according to your opinion, do you say temperance is?" 

At first he was reluctant and did not come forward willingly to respond; finally, he answered thus: "Temperance is two things: to act in each matter with decorum, and to walk along the way quietly and calmly, to speak quietly, and to do all things quietly; and to embrace what you ask in brief, it seems to me to be a certain quietness and calmness." 

"Rightly said," I replied. "They certainly say that quiet and placid men are temperate; but let us see if they speak the truth. Tell me then, is temperance something beautiful?" 

"It is, entirely," he said. 

"In the art of grammar, is it more beautiful to write the same letters quickly or slowly?" 

"Quickly." 

"And reading—is it better done quickly or slowly?" 

"Quickly." 

"Furthermore, is it more beautiful to strike the lyre rapidly and to compete promptly," I asked, "than to do so quietly and slowly?" 

"It is," he said. 

"What about in the games of boxing and wrestling? Is not speed itself praised?" 

"Certainly." 

"Running and jumping, and other acts of the body—if they are done hurriedly and promptly, do they not belong to the beautiful? If slowly, with difficulty, placidly and calmly, do they not belong to the base?" 

"It appears so," he replied. 

"It is clear, then, as far as the body is concerned, that not what is slow and calm, but what is swiftest and most rapid is the most beautiful. Is it not so?" I asked. 

"Entirely," he said. 

"And was it not agreed that temperance is something beautiful?" 

"It was agreed." 

"Therefore, regarding the body, quietness...

--- Page 213 ---
# Book Twenty. 194

...will not belong to temperance, but rather speed, provided that temperance is something beautiful." 

"It seems so," he said. 

"And is not teachability more beautiful than dullness?" 

"More beautiful, certainly." 

"But teachability," I said, "is to learn thoroughly and quickly, while dullness is to learn late and slowly." 

"Indeed," he said. 

"Is it not more beautiful to teach another as quickly as possible than hesitatingly and slowly?" 

"Without a doubt." 

"To recollect and remember: is it more beautiful to do so late and slowly, or easily and promptly?" 

"Promptly," he said. 

"And is not cleverness <margin>Cleverness is a certain speed of the soul.</margin> a certain speed of the mind," I asked, "rather than slowness?" 

"It is," he replied. 

"And even to understand what is said in the schools of the grammarian and the lyre-player, and in all other things, is it not most beautiful to do so as quickly as possible rather than as slowly as possible?" 

"This too," he said. 

"Furthermore, in the very investigations and consultations of the mind, it is not the one who gives counsel and thinks things through quietly and with difficulty who is to be praised, I think, but rather the one who does so briefly and most easily." 

"These things are true," he said. 

"From these things it is gathered, O Charmides," I said, "that both in those things which pertain to the body and in those which pertain to the soul, fast and prompt things seem more beautiful than slow and quiet ones." 

"So it appears," he said. 

"Therefore, temperance will not be a certain quietness," I said, "nor is the quiet life temperate, as is conjectured by this reasoning, since that which is temperate must also be beautiful. For of two things, one is true: either never, or only very rarely, have quiet actions appeared to us in life as more beautiful than fast and vehement ones; or, my friend, if quiet actions were found to excel fast and vehement ones in beauty no less frequently, even by this reasoning it would not be established that temperance is acting quietly rather than vehemently and quickly—neither in walking, nor in speech, nor in anything else. Nor would a quiet life be more decent and temperate than an unquiet one, since in the previous discourse it was posited that temperance is something beautiful, and it has been established that fast things are no less beautiful than quiet ones." 

"You seem to me to have spoken rightly, O Socrates," he said. 

"Again, therefore, O Charmides," I said, "look at yourself more attentively and think what kind of person the presence of temperance makes you, and what kind of thing it is itself while it produces such an effect; and observing all these things, answer well and manfully what it seems to be to you." 

He, immediately collecting himself and contemplating more diligently, said: "It seems to me that temperance induces a certain modest blush, and makes a man modest; and I judge that temperance is modesty <note>original: "pudorem", often translated as "shame" or "sense of shame/modesty" in a positive, social sense.</note>." 

"What do you say?" I asked. "Did you not say a little while ago that temperance was something beautiful?" 

"I did indeed," he said. 

"Are not good men themselves temperate?" 

"They are," he said. 

"Do you think that which does not make men good is good?" 

"By no means," he replied. 

"Not only is it beautiful, then, but it is also good," I said. 

"So it seems to me," he said. 

"Do you not believe," I asked, "that Homer speaks rightly when he says that modesty is not good for a needy man? <note>A reference to Odyssey, Book 17.</note>" 

"I do believe it," he said. 

"There is, then, as it appears," I said, "a modesty that is not good and a modesty that is good." 

"So it seems." 

"But temperance is only good, since it makes those to whom it is present good, and in no way makes them bad." 

"It seems to be as you say," he replied. 

"Therefore, temperance will not be modesty, since temperance is only good, while modesty is no more good than it is evil." 

"This seems to me to be rightly said, O Socrates," he replied. "But attend, I pray you, to what I bring forward again. For I have just remembered what was handed down to me by someone saying that temperance is for each person to do his own business <note>original: "ut sua quisque agat"</note>. Consider whether he who says this seems to speak rightly to you." 

"O you rogue! Have you heard this from Critias here, or from some other of the wise men?" 

"It certainly seems, Socrates," said Critias, "to have been from someone else, for he never heard it from me." 

"What does it matter," asked Charmides, "from whom I heard it?" 

"Nothing, certainly," I replied, "for we must not consider who said it, but whether it is said truly or not." 

"Now you speak properly," he said. 

"Rightly, by Jove," I said. "Yet I shall wonder if we find out how this stands, for it is very much like a certain riddle." 

"For what reason?" he asked. 

"Because I do not think he meant it as the words sound," I said, "namely, that temperance is for each person to do his own things. Do you think a grammarian does nothing when he writes or reads?" 

"I think he does something," he said. 

"Does it seem to you that the grammarian writes and reads only his own name? Or that you boys are also being taught? For you were writing the names of enemies no less than your own names and those of friends." 

"Certainly no less," he said. 

"And when you were doing this," I asked, "were you more meddlesome than is fitting, and were you departing from the law of temperance?" 

"Not at all," he said. 

"But truly, you were not doing only your own business, if writing and reading is to do something." 

"It is indeed," he said. 

"Furthermore, to heal, O friend, to build, to weave, and to fulfill the work of any art—is this to do something, or nothing?" 

"It is something, entirely," he said. 

"Would that city seem to you well-instituted," I asked, "in which the laws commanded that each man weave his own garment, and wash it, and make his own shoes, and his own strigil <note>A small, curved metal tool used in ancient Greece and Rome to scrape dirt and sweat from the body.</note> and oil-flasks, or ointment-jars, and every piece of furniture? That he should never touch the things of others, but perform and complete his own by himself." 

"By no means," he said. 

"Nonetheless, if a city is temperately disposed, it is well-instituted," I said. 

"Why not?" he asked. 

"Therefore, temperance will not be to do such things, or to do one's own business in this way?" 

"No, as it appears," he said. 

"Therefore, he was speaking in riddles," I said, "as I said before, he who preached that 'doing one's own' is temperance. For he must not be thought to have been so foolish that his meaning was the same as the sound of his words. Did some foolish person, O Charmides, hand this down to you?" 

"Not at all," he said, "on the contrary, one who is most wise in my judgment." 

"Then he entirely wrapped his meaning in obscure words, so that it is arduous to know what it is to 'do one's own'." 

"Perhaps," he said. 

"Can you open up to us what 'doing one's own' is?" I asked. 

"I do not know, indeed," he replied. 

"Perhaps even he who said this did not sufficiently understand what he meant." 

While I was speaking thus, Charmides smiled and looked at Critias. But Critias, although he had been instigated by a desire for glory to dispute against Charmides and others, had until now restrained himself; but he could no longer restrain himself at this. And it seemed to me to be true what I had suspected: namely, that Charmides had received that previous opinion about temperance from Critias. Therefore, Charmides, not wishing to defend the answer himself and desiring to throw the labor onto Critias, showed him as if he had been refuted. Critias did not tolerate this at all; on the contrary, he seems to have been no less indignant with him than a poet with an actor clumsily reciting his poems. 

And so, looking at him, he said: "Do you think, O Charmides, that if you by no means understand what the meaning was of him who asserted that temperance is 'doing one's own', that he himself did not understand it either?" 

"O best of men, Critias," I said, "it is no wonder that this youth does not understand. But it is fitting for you to know these things, both because of your age and because of your study. If, therefore, you yourself affirm that temperance is what he said, and you take up this discourse, I will more willingly investigate with you whether it is true or not." 

"I do affirm it," he said, "and I take it up." 

"You do rightly," I said. "But tell me, I pray: Whether...

# Charmides, or, On Temperance. 195

...you admit what I was asking a little while ago? Namely, that all craftsmen make something." 

"I do," he said. 

"Do they seem to you to make only their own things, or also those of others?" I asked. 

"Those of others as well," he said. 

"Do they act temperately, then, who do not make only their own things?" 

"What prevents it?" he asked. 

"As for me," I said, "nothing. But see lest something prevents him who, while he has posited that temperance is 'doing one's own', then nevertheless says that nothing stands in the way of those who do the things of others also being temperate." 

"I have indeed conceded," he said, "that those who do the things of others are temperate, but was it conceded regarding those who 'make'?" 

"Tell me, Critias," I asked, "do you not call 'doing' and 'making' the same thing?" 

"Certainly not," he replied, "nor is 'working' the same as 'making'. For I learned that from Hesiod, who said, 'No work is a disgrace' <note>From Hesiod’s *Works and Days*. Critias is making a semantic distinction common in Greek philosophy between *poiesis* (making/production) and *praxis* (action/doing).</note>. <margin>Work. <note>original Greek: "ἔργον" (ergon)</note></margin> Do you judge that he, if he had named such works, 'working' and 'doing', as those you narrated above—such as cutting leather, or a tavern-keeper selling condiments and victuals, or someone sitting in a shop—would have said that no work is a disgrace to anyone? We must not think so, O Socrates. On the contrary, in my judgment, he considered 'making' to be something different from 'action' and 'operation', and that 'making' is sometimes a reproach, when we make something beyond what is honorable; but 'work' never happens to be a disgrace to us. For those things which are done honorably and usefully, he called 'works', and such 'operations' and 'actions' are distinct from 'makings'. Furthermore, we must think that he considered only these to be one's own; but all harmful things to be utterly alien. For which reason we must believe that both Hesiod and every other man of sound mind calls a man 'temperate' who thus does his own business." 

"As soon as you began to speak, O Critias," I said, "I perceived that you call 'each one's own' things that are good, and the 'making' of good things you call 'actions'. For I have very often heard Prodicus <note>A Greek philosopher known for his interest in the precise meaning of words.</note> distinguishing names in this way. I certainly allow you to use names as you please, provided that you declare what you wish to signify by each name. Now, therefore, starting again from a clearer definition: do you say that temperance is the action or the making of good things, or whatever other name you wish to use?" 

"This very thing," he said. 

"Therefore, he who does evil things does not act temperately, but rather he who does good things," I said. 

"And does it not seem so to you, O good man?" he asked. 

"Leave that aside for the present," I said; "let us not yet consider what seems so to me, but what you are now saying." 

"Indeed," he replied, "I would never say that he acts temperately who does not do good things, but evil. For I clearly define temperance as the very action of good things." 

"Perhaps nothing prevents you from speaking the truth," I said; "yet I wonder at this, if you think that men acting temperately are ignorant that they are acting temperately." 

"I do not think so at all," he said. 

"Was it not said by you a little while ago," I asked, "that nothing prevents craftsmen, even when making the things of others, from living temperately?" 

"It was certainly said," he replied, "but what then?" 

"Nothing else," I said. "But tell me whether some physician seems to you, while he makes someone healthy, to be doing things useful both for himself and for the one he treats?" 

"He does, in my opinion," he said. 

"Does he not act as is fitting," I asked, "whoever does these things?" 

"Certainly," he said. 

"And he who acts as is fitting," I said, "does he not also act temperately?" 

"And temperately," he replied. 

"Is it not necessary for the physician to understand when he treats usefully and when not?" 

"Perhaps not," he said. 

"Sometimes, therefore," I said, "when the physician has worked usefully or otherwise, he does not know himself how he has worked, even if he has worked usefully, as you yourself admitted, and temperately—did you not say so?" 

"I did," he replied. 

"Is it not therefore, as it appears, that sometimes having worked usefully he acts indeed temperately, and is temperate, but he himself is ignorant that he acts temperately and is temperate?" 

"This cannot happen, Socrates," he said. "But if anything was said in the previous points from which this necessarily follows, I would more willingly retract it; rather than be compelled to admit that one who is ignorant of himself is temperate. For I almost think this very thing is temperance: to know oneself; and I agree with him who inscribed this precept in the temple of Apollo itself. And indeed, this inscription seems like a certain salutation from the God to the men who enter the temple, in place of the one which bids them to 'rejoice' <gloss>rejoice</gloss> <note>original Greek: "χαῖρε" (chaire), a standard greeting.</note>. As if it were not properly said, 'rejoice', and it were not fitting to command this to one another, but rather to live temperately. Thus the God addresses men entering the temple with a singular sentiment, and salutes us differently than men do, as he intended, in my judgment, who inscribed it. And he commands nothing else to the one entering than to live temperately. But he interjects this precept in obscure words, like a prophet. For 'Know thyself' is the same as 'Live temperately', as the letters testify and I interpret. 

But perhaps someone will think it is something else: which I think happened to those who added the following: 'Nothing in excess' and 'Pledge a surety, and ruin is at hand' <note>Three famous Delphic maxims: Know Thyself (Gnothi Seauton), Nothing in Excess (Meden Agan), and the warning against making legal/financial pledges (Engua para d'ate).</note>. For they thought that 'Know thyself' was a certain piece of advice, not an admonition from the God himself to those who enter. Then, so that they might also hang up advice no less significant, they added the rest besides. Therefore, all these things, Socrates, have been said by me because I will concede all the previous points to you without controversy. For perhaps you yourself said something more rightly about them, and perhaps I did too; yet nothing from what we have said is manifest. Next, however, I wish to give you a reason for this, if you will not concede that temperance is to know oneself." 

"You deal with me, Critias," I said, "as if I affirmed that I knew the things I ask; and you offer yourself to me, as if I will concede if I wish; but it is not so. For I am always searching with you for that which has been brought into the middle, precisely because I am ignorant of it. I will see, then, whether I concede it or not. Wait a moment while I consider these things." 

"Consider," he said. 

"Behold, I am considering," I said. <margin>Refutation of the fourth definition.</margin> "If temperance is to know something, it is certain that it is some science and is of something. Is it not?" 

"It is indeed," he replied, "namely, of itself." 

"Is not medicine also a science of the healthy?" 

"Entirely," he said. 

"If you were asked, therefore, since medicine is the science of the healthy, what it confers upon us, or what it produces, I would respond that it profits us greatly, and further that it perfects for us the beautiful work of health. Do you accept this?" 

"I accept it," he said. 

"And if you asked again, since architecture is the science of building, what work it might perform, I would respond 'houses', and I would give an answer for the other arts by the same reasoning. Since, therefore, you say temperance is the science of itself, it is your business to answer if someone should inquire in this way: 'O Critias, what beautiful work, worthy of the name, does temperance, which is the science of itself, produce for us?' Tell me, please." 

"You do not ask rightly, Socrates," he said. "For this is not like the other sciences, nor are the others like one another; but you ask as if they were similar. For tell me, I pray: of the science of calculation or geometry, what such work is there as a house is of architecture, or a garment of weaving, and many other things of this sort which anyone could attribute to many arts? Can you show me any such work of these?" 

"But you will not be able to."

# Book Twenty. 196

"You speak the truth," I said, "yet I can show you this: of what each of these sciences is a science, which is something other than the science itself. Just as the skill of calculation is the science of the even and the odd multitude, and in what way they relate to themselves and to each other, is it not?" 

"Certainly," he said. 

"Is not the even and the odd something other than the science of calculation itself?" I asked. 

"It is," he replied. 

"Furthermore, the faculty of weighing is the balancing of a heavier and a lighter weight. But the heavy itself and the light are something other than the art of weighing itself. Do you agree?" 

"I agree," he said. 

"Tell me, then: of what is temperance especially the science, which is something other than temperance itself?" 

"This is exactly it," he replied, "the very thing you are now asking, by which temperance differs from all other sciences. But you demand some similarity of this to the others. But the matter stands otherwise. For all the rest are of some other thing, not of themselves. This alone is the science of both the other sciences and of itself. You are far from being ignorant of these things: but I think you are doing what you denied a little while ago; for you are trying to refute me, and you pass over that of which we are speaking." 

"What are you doing?" I asked. "Do you think that if I refute you, I do it for any other reason than that for which I would examine myself—lest, while I think I know what I do not know, my ignorance should deceive me? And now indeed you seem to me to be doing this very thing: namely, examining the discourse for my own sake first, and perhaps also for the sake of my friends. Do you not think it is a common good for all men that the condition of each thing should become known to all?" 

"Most of all, Socrates." 

"Be bold, then, O blessed one," I said, "responding to the questions as your opinion carries you, and do not care whether it is Critias or Socrates who is refuted, but attend to the discourse itself, to see how it turns out when refuted." 

"I will do so," he said, "for you seem to speak properly." 

"Regarding temperance, come," I said, "repeat what you say." 

"I say indeed," he replied, "that of all other sciences, this alone is the science both of itself and of the remaining sciences." 

"Is it not also the science of ignorance <note>original: "inscientiae"</note>?" I asked. "If it is of science, entirely so." 

"Therefore only the temperate man," I said, "will know himself and will be able to examine what he knows and what he does not know; and moreover to judge from other men what each knows and thinks he knows (if indeed he knows it), or what he is ignorant of while he thinks he knows it. No one else will be able to do this. And this is to be temperate, and temperance, and to know oneself: namely, to understand what one knows and what one does not know. <margin>Proverb.</margin> Are these the things you say?" 

"They are," he replied. 

"Therefore, for the third time," I said, "as they say, 'to the Savior', let us consider it from the beginning. First, whether this can happen or not: that one can know both what he knows and what he does not know, and also know that he does not know. Second, if that can happen, what utility it would have for those who understand it." 

"It must be sought," he said. 

"Observe, Critias," I said, "whether you have anything certain in these things; for I have nothing, and in what matter I doubt, I will open up if you wish." 

"I certainly wish it," he replied. 

"This will follow, if what you just said stands: namely, that there is one certain science which is the science of no other thing than itself and other sciences; and the same is again the science of ignorance." 

"Entirely," he said. 

"See, friend," I said, "how absurd this discourse of ours is. For if you consider this same thing in certain others, as I think, it will seem impossible to you." 

"In what way?" he asked, "and where?" 

"Think clearly here," I said; "consider whether it seems to you that there is a certain sight which is not a sight of those things of which other visions are, but is a vision of itself and of other visions, and likewise a vision of non-vision; and being a vision, it sees no color, but only inspects itself and other visions. Does any such vision seem to be to you?" 

"None," he said. 

"And do you trust that some power of hearing can be found which hears no voice, but perceives itself and other hearings, and non-hearings?" 

"That is by no means possible," he said. 

"In short, strike through all the senses, and consider whether any can be found which perceives itself and the other senses, but yet feels none of those things which the other senses feel." 

"I judge this impossible," he replied. 

"Or perhaps that there is a certain desire <note>original: "cupiditatem"</note> which is a sense that affects no pleasure, but is a desire for itself and for the remaining lusts?" 

"Not at all," he said. 

"Nor a will <note>original: "voluntatem"</note>, I think," I said, "which desires no good, but seeks itself and other wills." 

"Least of all," he replied. 

"Will you even say there is such a love that is a love for no beauty, but is an ardor for itself and for other loves?" 

"Indeed not." 

"Have you ever thought of a fear which is terrified of itself and other fears, but dreads nothing terrible and dangerous?" 

"Never, entirely," he said. 

"Furthermore, an opinion such that it is an opinion of other opinions and of itself, but opines none of those things which other opinions suspect?" 

"In no way." 

"Nevertheless, we said that there is a certain science of this kind, which is the science of no dogma, but is the science of itself and other sciences." 

"We certainly said so," he replied. 

"Is it not a wonderful thing, if it exists? Let us not yet contend that it does not exist, but let us consider whether it does." 

"You speak skillfully," he said. 

"Tell me now: is this science a science of something? And does it have some power of this kind, by which it is of something?" 

"Entirely," he said. 

"For do we not also say that it has power by which it is greater than something?" 

"It surely has," he replied. 

"Is it not greater than some lesser thing, if it is to be greater?" 

"It is necessary," he said. 

"If we find something greater which exists as greater than other greater things and itself, but yet was not greater than any of those things than which the others are greater, would it not entirely happen that just as it is greater than itself, so it is also less?" 

"It is absolutely necessary, Socrates." 

"Furthermore, if something is double," I said, "to other doubles and to itself, surely it will be a half-double to itself, and a double to other halves. For whatever is double is nothing other than the double of a half." 

"True," he replied. 

"Moreover, that which is more than itself, is it not also less? And what is heavier, also lighter? And what is older, also younger? and in all other things in the same way: whatever has its own power toward itself, will it not also have that essence toward which its power is? I mean something like this. We say hearing is the hearing of nothing other than a voice?" 

"Certainly," he replied. 

"If it hears itself," I asked, "will it not hear itself as having a voice? For it could not hear otherwise." 

"It follows necessarily," he said. 

"Sight also, O best of men," I said, "if it sees itself, it will be necessary for it to have some color. For without color, sight can perceive nothing." 

"It can perceive nothing," he replied. 

"You see, Critias, that those things we have narrated seem partly impossible to us, and partly we must greatly distrust lest they have their power toward themselves. For that every magnitude and multitude and other things of this kind should have their power toward themselves is utterly impossible, is it not?" 

"So it is entirely," he said. 

"But that sight and hearing," I said, "should perceive themselves, that motion should move itself, and heat should heat itself, and so on...

# Charmides, or, On Temperance. 197

...and other such things, it is not believed by some, though perhaps it seems believable to others. There is need of some great man, O friend, who can sufficiently distinguish through all things whether nothing at all can have its power toward itself except science, but only toward something else; or whether some things can and others cannot; and if there are some which have power toward themselves, whether this science which we name temperance is among their number. Indeed, I do not trust myself to be sufficient for discerning these things. Wherefore, let it be the science of science. Even if this were granted, I would not yet agree that such a thing is temperance until I have investigated whether such an existing temperance profits us anything, or profits nothing. For I prophesy that temperance is something useful and good. 

You therefore, son of Callaeschrus, since you posit temperance as the science of science and of ignorance, show first that this is possible which I was saying above: afterward, that besides being possible, it is also beneficial; and thus you might perhaps satisfy me concerning the definition of temperance itself." 

Critias, when he had heard these things and saw me doubting, in the manner of those who, seeing others yawning, yawn themselves, he seemed indeed to be compelled by my hesitation to hesitate similarly himself. But being glorious <note>original: "gloriosus", meaning prideful or seeking renown.</note>, he stood in awe of those present, and did not wish to confess to me that he was not sufficient for discerning those things which I had offered, nor did he bring forth anything clearly, and he hid his hesitation. 

But I, so that our disputation might proceed, said: "If it seems good to you, Critias, we will grant now that there can be a science of science. Whether it is possible or not, we will investigate at another time. Nonetheless, even if it were possible as much as can be, what more is it possible to know of what someone knows and what he does not know? This, at any rate, we said was to know oneself and to be temperate. Is it not?" 

"Most of all," he said, "and it follows in a way, Socrates. For if someone has that science which knows itself, such a one would be as the thing he has: just as when one has speed, he is fast; and when beauty, beautiful; and when knowledge, knowing. For which reason, when someone has the knowledge of itself, he is then made knowing of himself." 

"I do not doubt that at all," I replied, "that if someone has something in himself that knows itself, he himself also knows himself. But what necessity compels a man thus affected to know what he knows and what he does not know?" 

"This, namely: because the one is the same as the other." 

"Perhaps it is so," I said, "but I always seem to be the same, and yet again I do not understand how it is the same to know what one knows and to know what one does not know." 

"Why do you say that?" he asked. 

"Thus," I said, "the science itself being of science, can it discern anything further than that of these things, this one indeed is science, and that one ignorance?" 

"Not further, but that far," he said. 

"Is it the same thing, therefore," I asked, "as the science and ignorance of the healthy, and likewise the science and ignorance of the just?" 

"In no way," he replied. 

"But truly, the one is medicine, and the other is political skill," I said, "while this is nothing other than science. How could it be otherwise?" 

"Unless someone should know healthy and just things in addition, but only science, as one having the science of this alone, he will recognize that he knows, or that he has a certain science, both concerning himself and concerning others. Is it not so?" 

"But what he knows by this science, by what reason will he understand it? For medicine knows the healthy and the wholesome, not temperance; music knows the harmonic, not temperance; architecture knows the building, not temperance; and similarly for all things, is it not so?" 

"It appears so," he said. 

"But temperance," I said, "if it is only the science of sciences, how will it understand what the physician knows as healthy and wholesome, or what the builder knows as a building?" 

"In no way," he replied. 

"Therefore he will not understand *what* he knows, being ignorant of this, but only *that* he knows." 

"It seems so," he said. 

"Therefore to be temperate will not be this, nor will temperance be to understand what he knows and what he does not know, but as it seems, only that he knows and that he does not know." 

"It appears so," he said. 

"Nor will he be able to examine another who professes some science, whether he knows what he promises, or does not know. On the contrary, he will recognize only this, as it seems," I said, "that he has a certain science: but of what matter the science is, temperance will not show." 

"It does not seem so," he replied. 

"Neither, therefore, will he discern a pretending physician from a true one, nor any other knowing person from one who is ignorant. But let us consider it thus: if a temperate man, or any other, is to judge between a true and a false physician, will he not do it thus? Concerning the art of healing, he will differ in nothing from him. For the physician understands nothing else, as we were saying, than the healthy and the sick, and the wholesome and the harmful, is it not so?" 

"Exactly so," he replied. 

"Furthermore, he knows nothing of science," I said, "for we attributed this to temperance alone." 

"So it is," he replied. 

"Neither, therefore, does the physician know anything of medicine," I said, "since medicine is a certain science." 

"You speak the truth," he said. 

"That he has some science, the temperate man will recognize; but some other will consider the skill of the physician, what it is and of what things it is. Which is then clear, when it is known of what things it is the science. Is not every science determined, not only by this that it is a science, but what science it is, and what kind of science it is—these being known by the things of which it is the science?" 

"Exactly so," he replied. 

"The science of medicine," I said, "is distinct from other sciences in that it is the skill of the healthy and the unhealthy?" 

"Indeed," he said. 

"Must not anyone who is about to consider medicine consider it in those things in which it is occupied? For it does not seem it should be sought in extraneous things, in which it is not." 

"Certainly not," he said. 

"Therefore, he will consider the physician in wholesome things and their contraries, insofar as he is a physician, whoever scrutinizes him rightly." 

"It seems so," he replied. 

"Will he not observe in these things, whether spoken or done, what things are truly said and what are rightly done?" 

"It is necessary," he said. 

"Can anyone attain these things without the skill of medicine?" 

"No one," he said. 

"Nor any other, as it seems, besides the physician; and therefore not the temperate man. For besides being temperate, he would also have to be a physician." 

"These things are true." 

"Entirely, therefore, temperance, if it is the science of science or of ignorance, will be able neither to discern a physician skilled in healing, nor likewise one pretending to have skill in medicine, or thinking himself to have it, nor anyone else of those who know something, except for a man who is a professor of the same art, just like other craftsmen." 

"So it appears." 

"What further utility, O Critias, will come to us from temperance when it is such? For if, as we supposed in the beginning, the temperate man knew what he knows and what he does not know—the former because he knows it, and the latter because he is ignorant of it—and could judge another thus affected, we would report a huge profit for those endowed with temperance: since we would lead our lives without sin, both ourselves, whoever are participants in temperance, and all others who were ruled by our command. For we would not undertake to do those things which we are ignorant of, but having scrutinized men who know, we would yield to them: nor would we concede to others subject to our governance to do anything else, except what they were about to do rightly..."

# Charmides, or, On Temperance. 299

...be a master of nothing? In no way does it seem so, O Socrates. Do you see, Critias, that I was not wrong to fear before, and to blame myself, because I can perceive nothing great or useful concerning temperance? For if I were at all useful in seeking the right path, this thing—which is conceded by all to be the most beautiful—would never have appeared useless to us. But now we are failing on every side, and we are unable to find what the author of names <note>Socrates refers to the "giver of names" or "legislator of language," a concept he explores more deeply in the *Cratylus*.</note> intended the name "temperance" <term>Temperance: The Greek word is *Sophrosyne*, which implies a healthy mind, self-control, and moderation.</term> to signify most, even though we have granted many points that are entirely at odds with reason. Furthermore, we agreed that there is a "science of science," even as reason resisted and immediately sought to refute it. We even granted that this very science could know the works of the other sciences, though reason similarly fought back: so that the temperate man would be such that he knows that he knows what he knows, and again understands that he does not know what he does not know. We certainly granted this too magnificently and too freely, not noticing that it is impossible for someone to know, in some way, what he in no way knows. Yet we agreed to this—namely, that someone ignorant of something could know that he does not know it—even though there is nothing, in my opinion, that seems more absurd than this. Nevertheless, having found us to be foolish rather than hard and stubborn, this investigation is still no more able to find the truth; instead, it has mocked itself to such an extent that what we have long ago constructed by common consent and posited to be "temperance" has finally appeared, quite insolently and insultingly, to be something useless. 

For your sake rather than mine, O Charmides, I take this poorly, if you—who are endowed with such an excellent appearance and such temperance of soul—are helped not at all by such great virtue, and if it profits you nothing in life. I also take it more heavily for the sake of the incantation <note>original: "incantationis". This refers to the "Thracian charm" Socrates mentioned at the start of the dialogue, which he claimed could cure Charmides' headache if accompanied by temperance.</note> which I learned from that Thracian, if I placed so much study in learning a thing of no value. I do not quite believe these things to be so; rather, I judge myself to be a lazy investigator, since I certainly consider temperance to be a great good—and if you possess it, you are blessed. Indeed, consider whether you possess it and have no need of the incantation. For if you have it, I would advise you to think of me as a rambling fool, incapable of investigating the truth, but think of yourself as being all the more blessed as you are more temperate. 

And Charmides said, "By Jupiter, O Socrates, I do not know whether I have it or not. For how could I understand that which you yourselves, as you say, are not yet able to find? Indeed, I do not believe you much, Socrates. Rather, I think I do need the incantation, and as far as I am concerned, nothing prevents you from healing me with your incantations every day, until you yourself think I have enough." 

"So be it," said Critias. "But, O Charmides, if you do this, it will be proof to me that you are temperate: if you submit yourself to the incantations of Socrates and never depart from his side." 

"Consider me as one who will follow and obey everywhere," he replied. "For I would sin gravely if I did not obey you, my guardian, and do what you command." 

"Indeed, I do command it," said Critias. 

"I shall do it diligently," he said, "and I shall begin today." 

"What are these two deliberating?" I asked. 

"Nothing more," said Charmides. "The decree is made." 

"Will you use force?" I asked. "And will you leave me no turn for deliberation?" 

"Consider that I will certainly bring force," he said, "since he has commanded it. In view of this, you too should deliberate what you will do." 

"No place for deliberation remains," I said, "for no one will be able to resist you when you are attempting and forcing an action." 

"Then do not resist," he said. 

"I certainly shall not oppose you," I said.

## THE LACHES OF PLATO, OR, ON FORTITUDE.
*
### THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.
*
Plato frequently places the best magistrates above the laws, because laws without them seem entirely useless; for no one will keep them, but the best magistrates are themselves the laws. But he says that magistrates cannot become the best unless the citizens are the best men; nor will the men be such unless the adolescents and boys are also such. Wherefore, in almost all his dialogues, he exhorts parents first of all to educate their sons rightly, knowing that the human race cannot live honorably or be governed happily without the best governors. Furthermore, there will never be good leaders in a republic unless they are men of the highest proven character, cultivated diligently from a tender age. 

However, since childhood is usually sufficiently ruled under the providence of those at home, while adolescence—having attained license—wanders everywhere without reins, our Plato rightly treats at length the correction and bridling of adolescents. He heavily laments that this age, which joins petulance and pride with softness and luxury, and is therefore placed in the greatest danger, is too little observed by those at home and unhappily neglected by laws and magistrates—especially since adolescents both corrupt each other and are infected by their elders everywhere. Therefore, in the *Laws* and the *Republic*, he places a specific magistrate over adolescence. Who, like a—so to speak—overseer <note>original: "episcopus", here used in the sense of a supervisor or guardian of morals.</note> should send out scouts daily, both by night and by day through the whole city, to observe the habits, words, and gestures of every single adolescent, and who would faithfully report their individual deeds and words to the magistrate as if to a shepherd and father. 

Nor was the necessary diligence regarding adolescents a concern for Plato alone, a matter in which even Aristotle himself could not but highly approve of Plato. But let us come to the dialogue. Lysimachus and Melesias are thinking about educating their sons, having complained about their own parents—who, while handling public cares too curiously, neglected their home and sons, even though the first care of the republic consists in caring for the youth. And although they are now old, nevertheless, so that they may deliberate more rightly on that matter, they likewise call together Nicias and Laches—also old men who have sons—to consult. And so that nothing may be overlooked, they invite Socrates to the council, not only as a companion but as a judge—Socrates, I say, who handled nothing else in all his life but the proper care of every age, and especially of adolescence. 

You, however, will meanwhile consider the wonderful praises of Socrates' life, and likewise that those are true praises which proceed from a man worthy of praise. But truly, since in some states the institution of laws leans more toward mildness than toward boldness, while in others it is the opposite, Plato, judging both to be dangerous, commands in the *Statesman* that mildness be mixed equally with boldness, and vice versa. If anyone joins the *Charmides* to the *Laches*, and joins the exhortation to temperance there with the exhortation to fortitude <term>Fortitude: From the Latin *fortitudo*, translating the Greek *Andreia* (courage).</term> here, he will rightly temper the minds of the young. I pass over how, in this present dialogue's exhortation to fortitude, both Nicias and Laches admire military fortitude more than is fitting; and Nicias, beyond the games of arms, extols them with praise beyond measure as if they were absolutely necessary preludes to military service. But Laches, not without cause, corrects him. 

After this, the opinion is transferred to Socrates. Here, notice that no harmony delights more than that which exists in a wise man from the very concord of his soul and speech. And on the contrary, no dissonance offends more than where the tongue and the mind are out of tune. Then, that a ruined man, even if he speaks beautifully, is not to be heard; nor is it permitted to speak of morals unless one is moral. Furthermore, Socrates was always accustomed, whatever the subject being disputed, to lead his companion in the dispute to the point where he would give an account of his whole life—as if you might know another's life in vain unless you know yourself. It is added that it is necessary, first of all, to submit oneself to someone examining us, to whom accounts of our past life are often rendered: which indeed strongly confirms the annual confession instituted by Christians. It is added also that one must learn as long as one must live. Socrates, however, the most cautious of all, says the judgment enjoined upon him should be transferred to the elders. But meanwhile, entreated by everyone, he approaches the matter itself, before all things approving diligence in educating sons and disapproving negligence. He adds that it cannot be that...

200 Twenty-first Book.

...someone can exhort another to courage unless he knows how to express what courage itself is. Soon, when Laches is asked what courage is, he responds rather confidently that it is the virtue through which one, not abandoning his rank, fights off the enemy. This is indeed refuted because someone can conquer the enemy by fleeing no less than by staying, in the manner of the Scythians, and be equally brave. And therefore Homer calls him brave who knows how to dare and to fear at the opportune time. 

A little later, the victory of courage is drawn toward any subject matter, as if it becomes a brave man to overcome not only fears but also pains, lusts, and pleasures. Hence, a common definition of courage for all these things is sought. To this, Laches responds that it is a certain endurance <term>tolerantia: the ability to bear or endure</term> of the mind. But since it is defined insufficiently, Socrates compels him to add that the endurance itself ought to be honorable and beneficial. It will not be of such a kind unless it is done prudently. And therefore he compels Laches to say that courage is properly "prudent endurance." Indeed, courage is something beautiful and good. Then it is asked what kind of endurance, and toward what it is prudent—that is, concerning what matter and what duty. 

Laches, however, slips when he is asked generally whether where there is greater boldness, there is greater courage, and he grants this: and again he admits that boldness is necessarily greater in him who, without skill in the thing itself yet knowing the danger, approaches the matter, than in him who proceeds instructed by skill. For the latter acts more cautiously and safely. Laches finally receives <note>Accepts the premise.</note> that where there is more boldness or less skill and prudence, there is greater courage. In which concession he both contradicts himself and admits a falsehood. For courage is indeed something beautiful and beneficial, but imprudent boldness is base and harmful. 

Among these things, note the well-worn sentiment of Socrates and Plato: "Each is good in those things in which he is wise; bad in those in which he is ignorant." Truly, just as all errors—both of the hand in grasping and the foot in walking—proceed from a defect of seeing itself, so Socrates judges that all the errors of men, both in choosing and in acting, proceed from a defect of intelligence. For where the leader himself is blind or blinking, everything falls into ruin. 

After Laches, Nicias defines courage as the science of things to be feared and not to be feared—namely, by what reason and to what extent they are to be feared or invaded. He certainly calls courage a certain constant habit with prudence concerning things to be feared and invaded. Boldness without prudence he calls rash ferocity. Socrates argues against Nicias thus: "Whatever things there is some science of, there is not one science of the past as they happened, another of the present as they are happening, another of the future as they can best happen; but it belongs to the same science to understand all these things." If, therefore, courage is the science of daring and fearing regarding good and evil—namely, as they are in the future—it is surely also the science of the same as they are in the present and past, and thus of all things simply. It is, therefore, universal virtue. But we were seeking courage from the beginning as some part of virtue. 

This objection was made not so much for the sake of refuting as for the sake of testing Nicias. But Nicias did not know how to defend his definition. Socrates, however, not wishing to act as a teacher among his elders because of modesty, simulates that he is similarly ignorant of the definition: and he exhorts them that they should seek out teachers of the virtues for themselves together with him, before they profess the faculty of educating the youth, showing that in every age moral discipline is greatly necessary, and that one must always learn without the blush of shame. 

The definitions, however, which he seeks either here concerning courage or in the *Charmides* concerning temperance, are not completed here or there, where the plan is only to exhort and admonish, but in the *Republic* and *Laws*. But to speak of courage and temperance together as siblings in summary: Plato in the *Phaedrus* and *Symposium* compares this life of ours to a certain journey, in the directing of which reason represents the charioteer; the affections, however, partly superior and partly inferior, represent twin horses, namely a white one and a black one. And so that we may more conveniently distinguish the question as far as it pertains to the purpose: He says that Divine Providence has determined to recall us from shameful things and to provoke us continuously toward honorable things. And therefore it has implanted in us shame and magnanimity, so that our charioteer, by shame as if by a certain rein, might restrain our affections—like horses—from shameful though sweet things; but with the spurs of magnanimity might stimulate us toward honorable though arduous things. 

Indeed, a certain evil demon allures us to base things with the enticements of pleasure; and deters us from honorable things by the bitterness of pain. For which reason, both temperance, using the reins of shame, brings it about that we always abstain from base things despite pleasure; and courage, relying on the spurs of magnanimity, takes care that we strive manfully toward honorable things, having despised the fear of difficulty and pain. And as much as it is more difficult to overcome pains than to abstain from pleasures, so much perhaps might it seem to someone that courage is to be preferred to temperance. Finally, temperance indeed brings it about that we are not cast down from being human into beasts, but courage brings it about beyond that, that we are even in a certain way transferred into a God who overcomes all things. On account of this virtue especially, all antiquity recorded Hercules in the number of the gods: Hercules, I say, while as victor of the earth he climbed the celestial steps, thus crying out: "Go now, brave ones, where the high path of a great example leads: why do you bared inert backs? The overcome earth gives the stars." <note>A quote from Seneca the Younger's tragedy *Hercules Furens*.</note>

-> LYSIMACHUS, MELESIAS, NICIAS, LACHES, THE SONS OF NICIAS AND LACHES, SOCRATES. <-

You have been watching a man fighting in armor, O Nicias and Laches; but for what cause I and Melesias here commanded you to watch this together with us, we did not then declare. Now, however, we will open it: for we judge that we must speak freely with you. For there are some who mock these things; and if anyone consults them, they do not express their opinion: but thinking they hold both the thing being consulted and the mind of the consultant, they bring forth things other than what they feel. But since we judge you both to be sufficient for understanding and to explain simply what you know, we have joined you as partners to the deliberation of those things which we will report. 

But that from which I have begun is of this kind. These are our sons; this one indeed is his son, called Thucydides by his grandfather's name; mine is the other, similarly keeping the grandfather's name: for we name him Aristides. And it seems to us that the most diligent care of these must be undertaken, nor do we think we should do what many are accustomed to do, who, as soon as their sons have grown up, allow them to live according to their own lust; rather, we must now begin to have care for them, as much as we are able to do so. Since, therefore, we see that you have sons, we judged that you, more than others, have thought by what reason they are to be educated so that they might become the best; and if you have not noticed much, we admonish you at present that you ought not to neglect it, and we exhort you to deliberate together with us concerning the education of the sons. 

But why these things seem so to us, O Nicias and Laches, it is fitting to hear, even though those things which follow are a little longer. For I and Melesias here live together, and these youths feast with us and are admitted to our banquet. Whence, as I signified in the beginning of my speech, we speak with you freely and boldly. Truly, each of us can tell these boys many noble deeds of his own father, performed both in peace and in war, by which they either served the republic or profited the allies; but of deeds performed by us, we can report none. Wherefore we are both ashamed of these things, and we often blame our parents' negligence, because after we grew up, they permitted us to live in a certain softness and luxury, being meanwhile intent on the affairs of others. And showing these same things to these adolescents, we proclaim that if they neglect themselves and despise our precepts, they will be ignoble; but if they take care, they will perhaps emerge worthy of their grandfathers' names. They, for their part, respond that they will obey us. 

But while we were consulting with one another by what discipline or habit they can best become the best, someone explained that it is worthwhile that they learn to fight in armor, and they praise this man whom you just watched competing, and he commanded us to turn our attention to it. Therefore, we thought it would be best that we both come to this spectacle and call you together, both to watch and also, if you wish, to deliberate by common counsel concerning the education of the youths. These are the things I desired to confer with you about. It is now your concern, both about this...

...this matter, whether it should be learned or not, and about other things if you have any discipline or study of an adolescent worthy of praise: then to predict what you are going to do regarding the counsel. 

NIC. Indeed, I approve of your sentiment, O Lysimachus and Melesias, and I am prepared to investigate together with you, and I judge Laches here to be similarly affected. 

LAC. You think rightly, O Nicias: for indeed what Lysimachus was reporting a little earlier about his and Melesias’ father seems most aptly said against those, and us, and all who handle civil affairs: for, as Lysimachus complained, they neglect their sons as much as other domestic matters. In these things, therefore, Lysimachus, you speak rightly; but that you summon us to consult about the institution of adolescents, but do not invite Socrates here, I wonder: first indeed a fellow citizen, then frequently occupied in that which involves either the discipline or the liberal study of youth, such as you require. 

LYS. What do you say, Laches? Has Socrates here ever cared for such things? 

LAC. And most greatly indeed, Lysimachus. 

NIC. I also can be a witness of this matter no worse than Laches. For recently he led a guest to me for the sake of educating my son—Damon, a disciple of Agathocles, a teacher of music, a man indeed refined above others, and skilled not in music alone, but also in other faculties, for which he would certainly be worthy that adolescents of this kind be committed to his discipline and company. 

LYS. No longer, O Socrates, Nicias, and Laches, do I and those of my age know the younger men, inasmuch as we stay at home most of the time because of age. But if you can advise this fellow citizen of yours any good, O son of Sophroniscus, advise it. For it is fitting: for you are a paternal friend to us. For I and your father were often familiar friends, and he departed from life before any enmity arose between us. To me also, the name of Socrates still rings in my ears in a certain way, which these boys frequently use while arguing with one another at home, and they celebrate it most greatly; I have not yet asked them whether they mean Socrates the son of Sophroniscus, or another. But, O boys, tell me, is this that Socrates whom you are so frequently accustomed to mention? 

BOYS. That is he, without a doubt, father. 

LYS. Well indeed, by Juno, O Socrates, that you extol and decorate your father, the best of men, and that our things will be your own, and yours will be ours. 

LAC. Do not dismiss this man, Lysimachus: for I have noticed him elsewhere as well, decorating not only his father but also his fatherland; furthermore, in the flight at Delium <note>The Battle of Delium (424 BCE), where the Athenians were defeated by the Boeotians. Socrates was noted for his calm bravery during the retreat.</note>, he retreated together with me, and I affirm this to you, that if the others had carried themselves similarly, our city would stand, nor would it have suffered such a great ruin. 

LYS. This is the best praise, O Socrates, which is now attributed to you by men worthy of faith, who are themselves to be praised in the same things in which they praise you. Know therefore that I rejoice in your reputation, and consider me bound to you with the highest benevolence. It behooves you, therefore, first to approach us, and to think of us as household and familiar friends, as is fitting. Wherefore hereafter, after we have recognized each other, do not do otherwise, but rather embrace both us and these younger ones with a certain domestic benevolence, so that mutual friendship might be kept between us on both sides; these things you will surely do, and we will again recall them to memory. 

But to that which we began to inquire: what do you say? Do you think it is conducive for adolescents to learn this discipline, to learn how to fight in armor? 

SOC. I will indeed try, O Lysimachus, if I can, to advise concerning these things and to do all that you ask: but it seems to me to be fair that, since I am both younger than these and less skilled in these things myself, I should first hear what they themselves think and learn; and if I have anything besides their sentiments, I will then at last open it to you and them. And why do you not speak first, O Nicias? 

NIC. Nothing prevents it, Socrates. It seems to me that this skill is useful for young men everywhere, and they should not linger in those things to which young men, having obtained leisure, are accustomed to give themselves, but it is better to acquire that faculty through which a robust habit of the body is acquired. For in no other exercise is this inferior or less laborious. Furthermore, such an exercise and equestrian skill especially befit a free man. For in that contest of which we are athletes, and in those things whose contest is proposed to us, only those fight who exercise themselves in such instruments of war. 

Furthermore, this skill will confer in the fight itself, as often as one must fight in the line and rank with very many others. But it will be most useful then, when the line is dissolved, and it will be necessary in a singular contest either to pursue an opponent or to repel an attacker in flight. Surely he who is instructed in this faculty will never succumb to one, and perhaps not even to many, but will rather excel everywhere by this. Furthermore, this faculty brings a desire for another certain noble discipline; for anyone, when he has learned to fight in armor, will turn himself to the discipline concerning the ordering of battle lines, which leads to the rank of commander, and summarily to all the noble studies and institutes which revolve around these things, worthy of knowledge and use, with that first one leading the way. We will also add something not to be despised: that this faculty would render everyone in battle wonderfully more daring and stronger. 

Nor is that to be kept silent besides, although it might seem lighter, that you will make a man more fitting and more capable there, where it is most fitting that he be seen as capable and prompt. There certainly, on account of his very dexterity and capability, he will appear more terrible to the enemies. It seems to me therefore, O Lysimachus, to be worthwhile that adolescents perceive these things: and I have explained why I think so. Nevertheless, I would gladly hear if Laches wishes to bring forward anything besides these. 

LAC. Indeed, O Nicias, it would be thought an absurd sermon if anyone said some discipline should not be acquired at all. For it seems better to know all things. 

<margin>Children ought to learn the discipline of arms.</margin> 

Truly, if this faculty concerning arms is a certain discipline, as those who teach it say, and such besides as Nicias proclaims, it must be learned. But if it is not a discipline, but those who promise this deceive us, or it is indeed a discipline but of little value, why is it necessary to learn this? My saying these things is from the fact that, as I think, if this were of any value, it would never have escaped the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, famous for their military focus.</note>, to whom nothing else is a care in all of life but to prepare themselves in all things so that they might excel all others in war. 

<margin>The discipline of arms is depressed by reasons.</margin> 

You might ask: if perhaps it escapes them, yet it would not have escaped the masters of this thing, because the Spartans study arms most greatly, and because he who is in price on account of an art would easily accumulate money both among them and among others, just as the poet of tragedies is honored among us. Indeed, he who trusts in his tragedies does not wander outside Attica, showing off through other cities, but immediately comes here and shows his works not without reason to these men. But those who are engaged in the exercise of arms, I see they think Lacedaemon is as if a certain inaccessible temple, and they never dare to ascend even with the top of their foot. Rather they wander around, and boast themselves rather among others, especially among those who would themselves confess that they are inferior to many others in military matters.

...confessed. Furthermore, O Lysimachus, I have been present with not a few men of this kind fighting, and I know what kind they are. Although it is permitted for anyone to conjecture the matter within himself. For as if by deliberate effort, no one of those who brooded over these games ever became illustrious in war, although in all other things those emerge clear and celebrated who exercise themselves frequently; yet these alone besides the rest are powerless of this wish, to such an extent do they seem unfortunate. 

For I beheld this Stesilaus, whom you contemplated showing himself off with me in such a crowd, and making too marvelous a profession, elsewhere once more certainly demonstrating himself to those looking on in truth not of his own will. For on the ship in which he was carried, when it was attacking a certain merchant vessel, he was fighting with a hooked scythe-spear, a very great man, and the weapon very great itself. The rest of this man's deeds are hardly worthy of hearing, yet this is not to be passed over in silence: what happened from such a marvelous machine of this man who added a scythe to the spear; for while he was fighting, the scythe entangled itself in the ship's rigging. 

Stesilaus was pulling so that he might disentangle it, and he was not able: the ship, however, was passing by; meanwhile, he accompanied the ship in its course holding the spear: but when the ship was now passing the other ship, and he was being drawn away holding the spear, he came to the very end of the weapon with his hand. Laughter therefore and a din were raised on the merchant ship because of the shape of Stesilaus's face, and because besides that, when a stone was thrown at the boards near his feet, someone forced him to let go of the spear. Then truly even those who were carried on the trireme were no longer able to contain their laughter, when they beheld that hooked scythe hanging from the ship. 

Perhaps these are of some value, as Nicias asserts, yet those at which I was present were such. Wherefore, as I said from the beginning, if this is a discipline, it profits little: if it is not, but those who profess it pretend, it does not seem a thing worthy of study. Thus indeed I judge: if someone timid should follow this faculty, having been made more daring because of this, he would be more clearly seen to be so than he was. But if some brave man should follow it, it would be observed by all if he should err even a little, and he would undergo great calumnies, for the profession of this science is invidious; wherefore unless he should excel the others in virtue in a marvelous way, he who claims this science for himself will not be able to avoid being held ridiculous. Such seems to me, Lysimachus, the study of this discipline. <margin>As the sons are, so is the governance of the house.</margin>

SOC. Would I not also first ask what that is, whose teachers I would seek?

SOC. Thus perhaps you will perceive more clearly: it does not seem to have been established among us in the beginning what that is which we seek, who among us excels most in it, and for the sake of this has had teachers, and who has not.

NIC. True. 

SOC. But that I may comprise it in a few words: as often as someone seeks something for the sake of something else, the consultation is about that very thing for whose sake the other is sought, not about that which is sought for the sake of the other. 

NIC. Necessarily. 

SOC. It behooves, therefore, the consultant to consider whether he is skilled in caring for that thing for whose sake we are deliberating at present. 

NIC. Altogether.

NIC. It was said.

...He found it or learned it, I shall certainly not wonder. But if you yourselves have found this, bring forth an example for the sake of the cause: if perhaps you have made any others, by your diligence, into good and famous men from depraved ones. For truly, if you are now beginning to teach for the first time, it must be considered lest the danger be made not "upon a Carian" (as they say), but upon your own sons and those of your friends, and that it clearly happen as is said in the proverb, "to practice pottery on a large jar." **LYS.** Socrates seems to me, O men, to speak rightly. If therefore it will be pleasing to you, O Nicias and Laches, to answer the questioners, you yourselves shall see to it: certainly it is pleasing to me and to this Melesias, if you are willing to run through everything Socrates asks with reason. For immediately from the beginning I said that you were brought in for consultation for this reason, because we thought these things were already considered by you, as is fitting; especially since you have sons as we do, now established in nearly that age in which one must think about education. If therefore nothing prohibits it, speak, I beseech you, and consider this together with Socrates, both giving and receiving a reason in turn. For he said this rightly also, that we are deliberating at present concerning a certain greatest matter of all our affairs. See therefore whether you think it must be done thus.

**NIC.** You certainly seem to me, Lysimachus, to know Socrates only in part, nor to have ever had intimacy with him, unless perhaps while he was a boy, following his father, he sometimes stayed with you either in a temple or some other public assembly.
