**LYS.** Why, O Nicias? 

**NIC.** You seem to be ignorant that whoever approaches Socrates in speech, as if in kinship, and clings to him in disputation, even if he began to dispute about something else, is finally forced, being led around by the words of Socrates, to give an account of his life—what the condition of his present life is, and what his past life was. And after he has fallen into these things, Socrates does not dismiss him before he has sufficiently examined all these points. But I have used this [habit] familiarly, and I know from his words that it is necessary that these things be perceived, and I am not ignorant that I must now undergo this. This habit of his delights me very much, O Lysimachus. Nor do I think it a hindrance that it be brought back to memory if we have done or are doing anything not rightly. Indeed, it is necessary that he who does not flee these things becomes more cautious for the future, thinking according to that saying of Solon: that one must learn as long as one lives, nor is it to be hoped that a [sound] mind will be given to us by old age. 
*[Margin: The precept of Solon]* 
To me, therefore, it is neither unusual nor unpleasant to be examined by Socrates in this way. And indeed, I knew long ago that the discourse for us would not be about the boys while Socrates was present, but about ourselves. Wherefore nothing prohibits me from discussing with Socrates in whatever way he himself wishes. But consider how Laches is affected toward these things.

**LAC.** Simply indeed, Nicias, I am affected toward discourses, or rather, if you wish, doubly. Furthermore, I might seem to someone to be a lover of words, and sometimes the opposite. For as often as I hear someone disputing about virtue or about a certain wisdom—someone truly a man and worthy of the words themselves—I am affected by a certain wonderful pleasure, contemplating the speaker as well as the words, how congruent and harmonious they are among themselves. And here truly the man seems to me to be a musician, having modulated a most sweet harmony, not on a lyre, nor on certain jocular instruments, but contemplating a life truly harmonizing by the concord of words and deeds, according to the Dorian melody, not the Ionian, or Phrygian, or Lydian, but certainly that which is the only Greek harmony. Such a man, therefore, delights me wonderfully with his words, and makes it appear that I am a lover of words: with such attention do I receive his sayings. But whoever acts to the contrary offends my ears, and the more elegantly he seems to speak, the more he makes it appear that I abhor discourses. Indeed, I have not yet experienced the words of Socrates, but certainly I have experienced his deeds before, and it has sometimes been found by me that he is worthy of distinguished discourses and every liberty of speaking. If therefore he has this also, I plainly agree with him, and most willingly shall I be examined by such a man, nor will it be troublesome to me to learn something from him. And even to Solon (let him permit this to be added now) I concede: namely, that being old I wish to learn many things, but only from good men. Let this therefore be granted to me, that he himself is a good teacher, lest perhaps while I learn as an unlearned man, I seem to be unteachable; nor is it a care to me whether the teacher is younger, or not yet famous in the opinion of men, or has any other such thing. To you therefore, Socrates, I declare that you may both teach and refute me in whatever way you wish, and say what I myself may know. For certainly I have been so affected toward you since that day on which you underwent danger with me, and made a trial of your virtue, providing such a specimen as anyone ought to exhibit who is justly to make a trial. Speak therefore what you please, not fearing our age.

**SOCR.** Therefore we shall not be able to accuse you as being less prepared for consultation and investigation. 

**LYS.** But this is certainly our business, O Socrates. For I count you as one of us. Think for me for the sake of the youths, what it is necessary for us to seek from them, and consult by discussing with these men: for many things have fallen from my memory on account of old age, from those things which I had determined to inquire into. Nor indeed shall I remember sufficiently those things which I hear, if any other discourses intervene. Wherefore, run through in turn what we have proposed; I truly shall listen, and when I have heard, together with this Melesias, I will perform whatever you determine. 

**SOCR.** O Nicias and Laches, Lysimachus and Melesias must be obeyed. Therefore, those things which we contended to investigate above—namely, who were our teachers of such a discipline, or whom others we ourselves...

### Page 204
**Book Twenty-One**

...we ourselves have made better—perhaps it would not hinder to examine among ourselves. But a certain consideration of this kind will fall back to the same point, indeed it will be just as from the beginning. For if it were found by us concerning any person whatsoever, that his presence makes better that to which he is present, then if we could apply this to him, we would also understand that very thing concerning which he took counsel: in what way one might acquire it for himself most easily and best. Perhaps you do not understand, but thus you will comprehend more easily. If we knew that sight, being present in the eyes, makes those eyes better in which it is present, and again we were able to apply it to the eyes, it is clear that we would also know what sight itself is, concerning which we would sometimes have to consult, by what reason one might most easily and conveniently acquire it. For if it were unknown to us what sight is, or what hearing is, we would never be suitable consultants of medicine regarding eyes or ears, investigating how someone might best recover sight or hearing.

**LAC.** You tell the truth, O Socrates. 

**SOCR.** Did these men not at present, O Laches, bring us into counsel, by what reason the virtue of the mind of their sons, being applied, might make them better? 

**LAC.** Indeed. 

**SOC.** Must it not therefore be established, namely, to understand what virtue itself is? For if we were entirely ignorant of what virtue is, in what way will we be able to consult for anyone, and show the best and easiest way to attain virtue? 

**LAC.** In no way, O Socrates. 

**SOC.** Do we confess, Laches, that we understand what virtue is? 

**LAC.** We certainly confess it. 

**SOC.** If we understand it, surely we are also able to express what it is. 

**LAC.** Nothing prohibits it. 

**SOC.** However, let us not immediately, O best of men, inquire into what universal virtue is. For that is a greater work. But let us first see concerning some part, whether it is sufficiently open to us; and in this way the investigation will be easier for us. 

**LAC.** In whatever way it pleases, let us act. 

**SOC.** Which part of virtue, therefore, shall we especially elicit? Is it namely that to which the discipline of arms itself seems to look? But it seems to many to look toward fortitude [courage], does it not? 

**LAC.** Very much so indeed. 

**SOC.** *[Margin: And here is the occasion of the dialogue]* First therefore, O Laches, let us attempt to open what fortitude is: then we shall investigate in what way it may be acquired by the youths, as far as it can be done by exercise and doctrine. *[Margin: A false definition of fortitude]* Wherefore, strive to explain to us what fortitude is. 

**LAC.** That is not difficult to say, O Socrates. Certainly know that he is brave who, keeping his rank, presses on in attacking the enemies and does not flee. 

**SOC.** You speak well, Laches. But perhaps because I asked you with more obscure words, it gave cause that you answered something other than what I myself, in asking, intended. 

**LAC.** By what reason do you say that, Socrates? 

**SOC.** I will explain if I can. A brave man is certainly he whom you yourself describe, whoever, not deserting his rank, fights against the enemies. *[Margin: Refutation]* 

**LAC.** This is the very one I mean. 

**SOC.** And I too. But what of him who fights not by remaining, but by fleeing? 

**LAC.** How, by fleeing? 

**SOC.** Just as the Scythians are said to fight no less by fleeing than by pursuing. Whence also Homer, praising the horses of Aeneas, says *[Margin: Iliad 8]* they pursue and flee very swiftly here and there: *[Margin: Iliad 17]* and he similarly praised Aeneas himself once for the knowledge of fearing, and said that he was skilled in fearing and fleeing. 

**LAC.** And rightly so, O Socrates: for he was speaking about chariots, but you speak about the horsemen of the Scythians; certainly their horsemen fight thus: but the Greeks are skilled in armor, just as I was saying. 

**SOCRA.** Except perhaps for the Lacedaemonians, O Laches. For the Lacedaemonians at Plataea, when they had fallen upon the wicker-shield bearers [Persians], did not sustain their first attack, nor did they persist, but rather fled. But after the ranks of the Persians were broken, they turned themselves in the manner of horsemen, and emerged victors in that battle. 

**LAC.** You tell the truth. 

**SOCR.** Deservedly, therefore, I was saying that from the fact that I had not questioned properly, it happened that you also did not answer rightly. *[Margin: An enumeration is made so that the question may be simply about fortitude]* For I was wanting to ask not only about those who are brave regarding light armor, but also about horsemen, and about all simply who are brave in any kind of war; and not only on land, but in maritime storms; indeed even about those whoever are brave against diseases or poverty or civil affairs. Nor only about those who are constant against pains or fears, but also about those who can fight bravely against pleasures and desires, whether by persisting or even by turning away. For there are also some brave men in these matters, O Laches. 

**LAC.** Very much so indeed, O Socrates. 

**SOC.** Are not all these brave? Nevertheless, some possess fortitude regarding pleasures, some regarding pains, some regarding desires, some regarding fears: and those who are timid, I think, are timid regarding the same things. 

**LAC.** It is entirely so. 

**SOCR.** I was asking what each of these is. Therefore, again according to your powers, express what fortitude itself is, which is found to be the same in all these things. Do you not yet understand what I say? 

**LAC.** Not sufficiently. 

**SOC.** I say it just as if I had asked: what is speed itself, which is present in us in running, in playing the cithara, in speaking, in learning, and in very many other things: which indeed, as is worthy to say, we possess in the movements either of the hands, or feet, or of the mouth and voice, or of the intelligence. Do you not speak similarly? 

**LAC.** Precisely. 

**SOC.** Therefore, if someone were to ask me, "O Socrates, what do you say that is which you name 'speed' in all these things?" *[Margin: Definition of speed]* I would certainly answer that it seems to me to be a power performing many things in a short time, whether regarding the voice, or the race, and all other things. 

**LAC.** Rightly. 

**SOC.** Try therefore you also, Laches, to define fortitude similarly: what is that power in pleasure, in pain, and in all those things which we were just saying it fits, that same fortitude named through each instance. 

**LAC.** It seems to me that fortitude is a certain endurance of the soul, if it must be said what fits fortitude through all things. *[Margin: A bad definition of fortitude. Refutation]* 

**SOC.** It must certainly be said, if we are to answer for ourselves to the things asked. But I think you do not consider every endurance to be fortitude. Which I conjecture from this: I nearly know this, Laches, that you think fortitude is something beautiful [noble]. 

**LAC.** Nay, certainly most beautiful. 

**SOC.** Is not that endurance which prudence accompanies both beautiful and good? 

**LAC.** Entirely. 

**SOCR.** But that which is with imprudence, is it not on the contrary damaging and harmful? 

**LAC.** Indeed. 

**SOC.** Will you call beautiful that which is such—damaging and harmful? 

**LAC.** That would be a sin, O Socrates. 

**SOC.** Therefore you will not call such endurance fortitude, since it is not at all beautiful, whereas fortitude itself is beautiful? 

**LAC.** You speak the truth. 

**SOC.** Therefore, according to your speech, prudent endurance is fortitude. 

**LAC.** So it seems. 

**SOCR.** Let us see therefore what endurance, and in what matter prudent, is fortitude; is it perhaps toward all things, both great and small? As if someone should endure while he prudently spends money, knowing that from this expense he will gain: will you call him brave? 

**LAC.** By no means. 

**SOCR.** Or truly if some physician, when his son, or anyone else burdened with a constriction of the lung, asks for drink and food, should endure and not be moved? 

**LAC.** Not even...

**Laches, or, On Fortitude**

...nor shall I call this endurance fortitude. 

**SOC.** But truly, a man in war who is enduring and prompt for battle, who prudently provides having looked around at each detail—both the reinforcements that will be present, and that he must fight against fewer and weaker ones, then would use a convenient place—will you, I say, call him who endures with such providence and preparation braver than him who stands and endures in some contrary army? 

**LAC.** Indeed this one in the contrary army, Socrates. 

**SOC.** Yet the endurance of this one is more imprudent than that of the other. 

**LAC.** You speak the truth. 

**SOC.** Therefore you will say that a man endowed with equestrian science, and enduring in an equestrian contest, is less brave than he who endures being ignorant of this science? 

**LAC.** To me indeed it seems so. 

**SOC.** And what of him besides who, knowing how to hurl with a sling or bend a bow, or should endure anything else, is he less brave? 

**LAC.** Entirely. 

**SOC.** Likewise, whoever, descending into a well without the art of swimming, dare to endure and persist in that work, or in any other work without art—will you say they are braver than those who are learned in those arts? 

**LAC.** What else would anyone say, Socrates? 

**SOC.** Nothing, if only one thinks so. 

**LAC.** I think it indeed. 

**SOC.** Yet these men undergo dangers and endure more imprudently than those who approach these things with art. 

**LAC.** They seem so. 

**SOC.** Did not imprudent audacity and endurance previously appear to us as base and harmful? 

**LAC.** Very much so. 

**SOC.** But it was conceded that fortitude is something beautiful. 

**LAC.** Clearly conceded. 

**SOC.** Now again we concede that that base and imprudent endurance is fortitude. 

**LAC.** So it appeared. 

**SOC.** Do we seem to you to speak rightly? 

**LAC.** To me indeed, by Jove, not at all, O Socrates. 

**SOC.** Therefore, according to the Dorian harmony—to use your words—you and I do not now harmonize: for our deeds do not sound together with our words. Someone might say that we are partakers of fortitude in deed, but in words not at all, I think, if he heard us disputing at present. 

**LAC.** You tell the truest things. 

**SOCR.** Does it seem to you to be beautiful that we should be so affected? 

**LAC.** By no means. 

**SOC.** Are you willing that we at least trust the discourse we have brought in, and follow it? 

**LAC.** What, and whom especially? 

**SOC.** The discourse, I say, which commands us to endure. If therefore it pleases you, let us also stand and endure in this very question, lest fortitude herself mock us, that we investigate her less bravely, if many times endurance itself and constancy is fortitude. 

**LAC.** I indeed, O Socrates, am already prepared for persevering, although these discourses are unusual to me: but a certain ardor instigates me to contend against the previous points, and truly I take it badly if I am so inept at bringing forth the things I feel. Truly I seem to myself to understand what fortitude is. I know not, however, in what way it escaped me a little while ago, so that I was unable to embrace in words what it is. 

**SOC.** Does it not become a good hunter, friend, to run about exploring, and to follow sagaciously, nor to cease lazily? 

**LAC.** It certainly becomes him. 

**SOC.** Are you willing then that we invite that Nicias to this hunt, if in some way he might be more sagacious than us? 

**LAC.** Why should I not wish it? 

**SOC.** Come, Nicias, help your friends nodding in the waves of discourses, and run to help those vacillating with whatever power you have. You see how much our things fail and are in doubt. You therefore explain what you think fortitude is, dissolve the ambiguity, and confirm your opinion with reason. 

**NIC.** You seem to me, O Socrates, to have long ago defined fortitude incorrectly. *[Margin: Frequent opinion of Socrates concerning every virtue and goodness]* Furthermore, you make no mention of that opinion which I have heard you bring forth sometimes correctly. 

**SOC.** Which opinion, Nicias? 

**NIC.** I have often heard from you that everyone is suitable in those things in which he is wise: but unsuitable in those in which he is unlearned. 

**SOC.** By Jove, you recall true things, O Nicias. 

**NIC.** Is it not therefore so, that if a brave man is good, he is also wise? 

**SOC.** Do you hear, Laches? 

**LAC.** I hear indeed, but what he says, I do not sufficiently understand. 

**SOC.** But I seem to myself to understand. For I think he calls fortitude a certain wisdom. 

**LAC.** What wisdom, Socrates? 

**SOC.** Do you not ask him this? 

**LAC.** Certainly. 

**SOC.** Come, Nicias, declare to him, what kind of wisdom is fortitude according to your speech; for it is not flute-playing. 

**NIC.** No. 

**SOC.** Nor even cithara-playing. 

**NIC.** Not at all indeed. 

**SOC.** But truly, what then, and the science of what thing? 

**LAC.** You ask him very rightly, O Socrates: and therefore let him explain what wisdom he says it is. 

**NIC.** The science of things to be feared, and things not to be feared, both in war and in all other things. 

**LAC.** How absurdly this man speaks, O Socrates. 

**SOC.** Why do you say so, Laches? 

**LAC.** Why? Because wisdom is different from fortitude. 

**SOC.** Nicias does not say so. 

**LAC.** By Hercules, he does not, and for that reason he raves. 

**SOC.** Nay, let us teach him, having omitted insults. 

**NIC.** But Laches desires, O Socrates, that I be refuted as saying nothing, after this very thing happened to him a little while ago. 

**LAC.** Without doubt, Nicias, and I shall try to show it: for you say nothing. Do not physicians know things to be feared in diseases? Or does it seem to you that the brave know those things? Or do you call physicians brave? 

**NIC.** Not at all. Nor do I think farmers, although they know in cultivating fields what things are to be feared. Moreover, other artisans know what they ought to dare and what to fear in their arts, who are no more brave for it. 

**SOC.** What does Laches seem to say to you, O Nicias? He certainly seems to say something. 

**NIC.** He certainly says something, but not the truth. 

**SOC.** Why? 

**NIC.** Because he thinks physicians want to know anything further concerning the sick besides what is sick and harmful, or what is healthy and salubrious. They truly only understand this. But whether to someone who is fearing, it is a bad thing to be healthy rather than to be sick, do you think, O Laches, that physicians understand this? Or do you not think it is better for some not to recover from a disease than to recover? For tell me, do you assert that for all it is better that they live, and that for many death is not more conductive? 

**LAC.** I indeed think this rather. 

**NIC.** Do you think those things are to be feared and bad for those for whom it is better to die, as they are for those for whom it is better to live? 

**LAC.** By no means. 

**NIC.** Do you attribute the judgment of these things to a physician? Or to some other artisan besides him who understands things to be feared and things not to be feared, whom I call brave? 

**SOC.** Do you observe, Laches, what he is saying? 

**LAC.** I observe indeed, that he calls seers [prophets] brave. For who else would know for whom it is better to die than to live? And yet, O Nicias, do you confess yourself to be a seer, or neither a seer nor brave? 

**NIC.** Do you think it is the office of a seer to discern how far one must yield and how far one must dare? 

**LAC.** I think so indeed: for whose is it besides? 

**NIC.** Clearly his whom I say, O best of men, much more so. Since it belongs to the seer only to foreknow the portents and signs of future things, whether death threatens anyone, or disease, or loss of things, or victory, or slaughter in war, or in any other contest. But what of these it is better for someone either to suffer or not to suffer, why will a seer judge rather than anyone else? 

**LAC.** I know not what this man wants, Socrates. For he declares neither a seer, nor a physician, nor any other to be the one he calls brave, unless perhaps he says he is some God. To me indeed Nicias seems to be unwilling to confess ingenuously that he says nothing, and...

*   **Doric harmony**: Laches (a soldier) prefers the Dorian mode because it was associated with military discipline and virility, as opposed to the softer Ionian or Phrygian modes.
*   **Marsilio Ficino**: The text transitions from Plato's dialogues to Ficino's *Argumentum* (his scholarly preface) for the *Cratylus*. Ficino was a key figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated the complete works of Plato into Latin.
*   **Tetragrammaton**: Mentioned in Ficino's introduction, referring to the four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH).

Nor would I call this endurance courage. SOCRATES: But in war, take a man who endures and is ready for battle, who prudently and with foresight considers each circumstance, knowing that help will arrive, and that he is fighting against fewer and weaker men, and that he holds a more advantageous position—would you say a man who endures with such foresight and preparation is braver than the man in the opposing army who stands firm and endures? SOCRATES: Likewise, those who, without the art of swimming, dare to descend into a well and endure and persist in that task, or in any other task without skill—will you say they are braver than those who are learned in those arts? LACHES: What else could one say, Socrates? SOCRATES: Nothing, if one thinks so. LACHES: Indeed, I do think so. SOCRATES: Yet these people undergo dangers and endure more imprudently than those who approach these things with skill. LACHES: So they seem. SOCRATES: Did we not previously conclude that imprudent audacity and endurance appeared to us base and harmful? LACHES: Most certainly. SOCRATES: And it was granted that courage is something noble. LACHES: It was clearly granted. SOCRATES: Now, on the other hand, we are granting that this base and imprudent endurance is courage. LACHES: So it has appeared. SOCRATES: Does it seem to you that we are speaking correctly? LACHES: To me, by Jupiter, not at all, Socrates. SOCRATES: Then we do not harmonize according to the Dorian mode <note>A Greek musical mode associated with being stern, manly, and steady</note>, to use your words, for our deeds do not harmonize with our words. In deed, someone might say we share in courage, but in words, I think, they would not, if they heard us disputing at present. LACHES: You speak the very truth. SOCRATES: Does it seem noble to you for us to be in this state? LACHES: Not at all. SOCRATES: Should we at least trust and yield to the argument we have introduced? LACHES: What argument, and to what end? SOCRATES: To the argument, I say, that commands us to "endure." If it pleases you, let us also stand firm and endure in this very inquiry, lest courage itself mock us for not investigating it courageously—if indeed endurance and steadfastness themselves are courage. LACHES: I am indeed ready to persevere, Socrates, although such arguments are unfamiliar to me. But a certain ardor goads me to contend against what has been said, and I am truly annoyed if I am so inept at expressing what I feel. For I seem to myself to understand what courage is; yet I know not how it escaped me just now, so that I was unable to encompass in words what it is. SOCRATES: Does it not become a good hunter, friend, to run about exploring, and sagaciously pursue, and not lazily give up? LACHES: It certainly becomes him. SOCRATES: Shall we then invite this Nicias to the hunt, to see if he might be more sagacious than we are? LACHES: Why should I not wish it? SOCRATES: Come then, Nicias, help your friends who are tossing in a tide of words; run to our aid as we falter, if you have any power. You see how much we fail and are in doubt. Explain, therefore, what you think courage is, resolve the ambiguity, and confirm your opinion with reason. <margin>A sentiment frequent in the mouth of Socrates concerning all virtue and goodness.</margin> NICIAS: It seems to me, Socrates, that you two have for some time failed to define courage correctly. Furthermore, you make no mention of that sentiment which I have often heard you introduce quite rightly. SOCRATES: Which sentiment, Nicias? NICIAS: I have often heard from you that every man is good in those things in which he is wise, and bad in those in which he is unlearned. SOCRATES: By Jupiter, you recall it truly, Nicias. NICIAS: Therefore, if the brave man is a good man, is he not also wise? SOCRATES: Do you hear, Laches? LACHES: I hear indeed, but I do not quite understand what he is saying. SOCRATES: But I seem to understand. For I think he is saying that courage is a certain kind of wisdom. LACHES: What wisdom, Socrates? SOCRATES: Are you not asking him this? LACHES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Come then, Nicias, declare to him what kind of wisdom courage is according to your speech; for it is surely not the wisdom of flute-playing. NICIAS: No. SOCRATES: Nor indeed of lyre-playing. NICIAS: Not at all. SOCRATES: But what then, and the knowledge of what thing? LACHES: You question him quite rightly, Socrates; therefore let him explain what wisdom he says it is. NICIAS: It is the knowledge of things to be feared and things not to be feared, both in war and in all other things. LACHES: How absurdly he speaks, Socrates. SOCRATES: Why do you say so, Laches? LACHES: Why? Because wisdom is different from courage. SOCRATES: Nicias does not say so. LACHES: By Hercules, he does, and therefore he is raving. SOCRATES: Let us rather teach him, omitting insults. NICIAS: Indeed, Laches desires, Socrates, to refute me as if I were saying nothing, since this very thing happened to him just now. LACHES: Without doubt, Nicias, and I shall try to show it; for you are saying nothing. Do not doctors know what is to be feared in diseases? Or does it seem to you that the brave know those things? Or do you call doctors brave? NICIAS: Not at all. LACHES: Nor farmers, I suppose, although they know what is to be feared in tilling the fields; and indeed other craftsmen know what they ought to dare and what to fear in their own arts, but they are no more brave for it. SOCRATES: What does Nicias seem to be saying to you, Laches? He certainly seems to be saying something. NICIAS: He is certainly saying something, but it is not true. SOCRATES: Why? NICIAS: Because he thinks doctors know anything more about the sick than what is harmful and what is healthy or curative. But they understand only this much. But whether it is a fearful thing and an evil for someone to be healthy rather than sick—do you think, Laches, that doctors understand this? Or do you not think it is better for some not to recover from sickness than to recover? Tell me, do you assert that it is better for everyone to live, and that death is not beneficial for many? LACHES: I think it is as you say. NICIAS: Do you think the same things are to be feared by those for whom it is better to die as by those for whom it is better to live? LACHES: Not at all. NICIAS: Do you attribute the judgment of these things to a doctor? Or to some other craftsman besides the one who understands what is to be feared and not to be feared, whom I call brave? SOCRATES: Do you notice, Laches, what he is saying? LACHES: I notice indeed, that he is calling seers <note>prophets or diviners</note> brave. For who else would know for whom it is better to die than to live? And yet, Nicias, do you admit that you are a seer, or neither a seer nor brave? NICIAS: Do you think it is the office of a seer to distinguish how far one should yield and how far one should dare? LACHES: I do indeed; for whose else would it be? NICIAS: It belongs clearly to the one I mean, my good man, much more so. For it belongs to a seer only to foreknow the omens and signs of future things, whether death threatens someone, or disease, or loss of property, or victory, or defeat in war, or in any other contest. But which of these things it is better for someone to suffer or not suffer—why will a seer judge this rather than anyone else? LACHES: I do not know what he means, Socrates. For he declares neither a seer, nor a doctor, nor any other person to be the one he calls brave, unless perhaps he says it is some God. It seems to me that Nicias is unwilling to frankly admit he is saying nothing, and is tossing...

Therefore let us inquire more clearly of him what he feels; and if he seems to bring anything of the truth, we will agree; if not, we will teach him. LACHES: You ask him if you wish, Socrates. For I have questioned enough. SOCRATES: Nothing prevents it. For the questioning will be common to both me and you. LACHES: Quite so. SOCRATES: Tell me, Nicias—or rather tell us, for this question is common to both me and Laches: do you say that courage is the science of things to be feared and not to be feared? NICIAS: Indeed. SOCRATES: And that to distinguish this is not the work of just any man, since neither the doctor nor the seer knows this, nor is he brave, unless he has attained this very science? See Plutarch in Theseus.</margin> not just any sow would know this, nor would she be brave. NICIAS: Certainly not, as it seems to me. SOCRATES: It is clear then, Nicias, that you do not believe even the Crommyonian sow <note>A legendary wild sow killed by Theseus</note> was brave. I do not say this for the sake of joking, but I believe he who speaks thus admits no bravery in any brute animal, nor concedes that any brute is so wise that it could know those things which very few men know because of their difficulty—things which a lion, or a leopard, or some wild boar might know. But he who defines courage as you do must say that the lion, the stag, the bull, and the ape are all equally constituted by nature toward courage. LACHES: By the gods, you speak rightly, Socrates. And answer us this truly, Nicias: do you say these beasts are wiser than us, whom we all admit to be brave? Or do you dare to deny they are brave, against the opinion of all? NICIAS: Indeed, Laches, I do not call brutes brave, nor anything else that, through ignorance of terrible things, fears nothing—the intrepid and the foolish. Or do you think I call all children brave, who through ignorance fear nothing? I think indeed that to be intrepid is not the same as being brave. For I think courage and foresight are found in very few; but ferocity and audacity lacking fear, and entirely without foresight, are found in many—in men, women, children, and beasts. Those things which you and many others call brave, I call ferocious; but I call brave those things which prudently discern what is worthy of audacity and what is worthy of fear. LACHES: Do you see, Socrates, how beautifully this man, as he himself thinks, adorns himself with words? But he strives to deprive of the honor of courage those whom everyone else agrees are brave. SOCRATES: Not at all, Laches, but be of good cheer. For I say that you and Lamachus are wise, if you are brave, and many other Athenians besides. LACHES: I will bring nothing against these things, even if I could, lest you say I am truly some foul-mouthed slanderer. SOCRATES: Do not say so, Laches; for you seem not to have noticed that he received this kind of wisdom from our friend Damon. And Damon is very studious of Prodicus. <note>Prodicus was a Sophist known for his precision in the meaning of words.</note> Prodicus is said to be marvelous among the other Sophists in explaining and distinguishing the force of names. LACHES: Truly, Socrates, it becomes a Sophist to exalt himself with these studies more than a man whom the city judges worthy to preside over it. SOCRATES: It becomes him, Laches, who manages the greatest affairs, to also have the greatest prudence. But I think we should now inquire what Nicias principally intended the name of courage to signify. LACHES: You yourself inquire into these things, Socrates. SOCRATES: I will do so, my good man; yet do not think you are excluded from the common dispute—you too pay attention and consider what is to be said with us. LACHES: Let it be so, if it seems it must be done. SOCRATES: It certainly does seem so. But you, Nicias, tell us again from the beginning. You know that at the start of the talk we were considering courage as a certain part of virtue? NICIAS: Indeed. SOCRATES: And did you not answer that it was a certain part, as was introduced above, as if there were also other parts, all of which are called by the name of virtue? NICIAS: Why not? SOCRATES: Do you name the same parts as I do? For I, besides courage, name temperance, justice, and such things. Do you also? NICIAS: I also. SOCRATES: Pay attention now. For we admit these things. Next, let us consider those things which are worthy of fear and terrible, and those which are worthy of audacity, lest perhaps you think they are one thing and we think they are another. We will set out to you what we think. But you, if you disagree, teach us. We think terrible things are those which strike fear; things to be dared are those which present no fear. But fear is instilled not by past evils, nor present ones, but by those which are expected. For we call fear the expectation of a future evil. Do you not feel the same, Laches? LACHES: Most certainly, Socrates. SOCRATES: You hear, Nicias, that we say terrible things and things to be feared are future evils; things to be dared are future goods, or at least not evils. Do you feel this way about them, or otherwise? NICIAS: In that way, certainly. SOCRATES: Do you call the science of these things courage? NICIAS: Precisely. SOCRATES: Let us see furthermore whether you also feel with us in this third point. NICIAS: What is that? SOCRATES: I will say it. It indeed seems to me and to this man that of whatever things there is some science, there is not one science of past things as they happened, another of present things as they happen, and another of future things as they might best happen; but it is the work of the same science to know all these. Just as regarding the healthy and curative, throughout all time, no science other than medicine alone foresees what happens, what has happened, and what will happen, and in what way it happens. And regarding those things which are born from the earth, agriculture behaves similarly. Indeed, in war you yourselves will be witnesses that military science foresightfully looks to all other things and future things; for it does not wish to be subject to a seer, but rather to rule over him, as one who foresees more acutely what happens in war and what will happen. And indeed the law so establishes, that the seer does not command the general of the army, but the general of the army presides over the seer. Shall we assert these things, Laches? LACHES: We shall. SOCRATES: Do you agree with us, Nicias, that it belongs to the same science to know the same things as they were in the past, as they are in the present, and as they will be in the future? NICIAS: Indeed; for so it seems to me, Socrates. SOCRATES: Is not courage, my good man, the science of things to be feared and their opposites, as you yourself proclaim? NICIAS: It is indeed. SOCRATES: But it was established that the things we fear are future evils, and the things we dare are future goods. NICIAS: Clearly. SOCRATES: But the same science is of the same things in the past, present, and future. NICIAS: These things are true. SOCRATES: Therefore, courage is not only the science of things to be feared and their opposites; for it understands not only future goods and evils, but also present and past ones, and simply all things, as other sciences do. NICIAS: So it seems. SOCRATES: Therefore, Nicias, you have answered us with only a third part of courage, although we asked what courage is as a whole. ...your speech, courage is not only the science of things to be feared and their opposites, but of all goods and evils, and simply of all things (as indeed follows from your words), in whatever state they may be. Do you judge it so now, or otherwise, Nicias? NICIAS: It seems so to me, Socrates. SOCRATES: Do you think, blessed man, that this person lacks any virtue, who knows all goods exactly as they have been, are, and will be, and evils likewise? And do you think that man is in need of temperance, and justice, or holiness—he to whom alone it belongs to prudently understand both divine and human goods and evils, to avoid the latter and embrace the former, and who knows how to live rightly with all men? NICIAS: You seem to speak the truth, Socrates. SOCRATES: Therefore, what was introduced by you, Nicias, is not a part of virtue, but all of virtue. NICIAS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, we said courage was some part of virtue. NICIAS: We clearly said so. SOCRATES: But what is now said does not appear so. NICIAS: No. SOCRATES: Therefore, Nicias, we have not found what courage itself is. NICIAS: We do not seem to have. You seem therefore truly to suffer something human, in that you look not at yourself, but at others. But I think these matters have been spoken of by me in a tolerable way. Furthermore, when I am solidly settled, I will even teach you about envy; for you seem to be in greatest need of that discipline. LACHES: You are indeed wise, Nicias. I also, if my sons were adults, would have done the same. NICIAS: Indeed, I also judge that if only Socrates wishes to undertake the care of the youths, no one else is to be sought. I think it is necessary, O men (for I want none of this to be leaked), that we all together seek, first indeed for ourselves the best teacher, for we are in need; and then for the youths, sparing neither money nor any other things. But to live as we now live, and to care for our sons so, I do not advise. And if anyone mocks us because at such a great age we decide to enter a teacher's school, that line of Homer's <margin>Odyssey, Book 17.</margin> should be thrown back: he says that shame is of no use to a needy man. Therefore, despising all the words of detractors, let us undertake the common care of ourselves and the youths. But hey you, do exactly this: come to my house tomorrow at first light, and do not fail, so that we may enter into council about these things. For today's assembly must now be dismissed. SOCRATES: I will do what you command, Lysimachus; and if God wills, I will come to you tomorrow.

THE CLITOPHON OF PLATO, OR, EXHORTATORY.

PERSONS OF THE FRAGMENTARY DIALOGUE: SOCRATES, CLITOPHON.

Someone recently reported to me that Clitophon the son of Aristonymus, <margin>The occasion of this dialogue. The rest is missing.</margin> speaking with Lysias, found fault with the company of Socrates, but greatly praised that of Thrasymachus. CLITOPHON: Whoever that was, Socrates, he did not correctly report what I spoke about you with Lysias. For in some things I praised you, and in some I did not. But since you are openly angry with me, although you pretend to care for nothing, I myself will most willingly report those things to you, especially since we are alone, lest you think you are so despised. For perhaps you have now heard incorrectly, which is why you have become more incensed with me than is proper. But if you yourself give me the power to speak freely, I will most willingly tell you the matter. SOCRATES: But it would be quite shameful if I did not tolerate you wanting to benefit me. For it is clear that once I have understood in what way I am bad and in what way I am good, I will decline the worse with all my strength and pursue the better. CLITOPHON: Hear then. Indeed, being with you, Socrates, I have often been vehemently amazed while hearing you speak, and you seemed to me to speak most excellently of all men, as often as, rebuking men like a God suddenly crying out from a <margin>Proverb.</margin> tragic machine <note>the "deus ex machina" used in Greek theater</note>, you exclaim: "Where are you rushing, men? You know not where you are being carried, nor do you do anything opportune, you who apply all your study to amassing money; but you neglect the sons to whom you will leave it, nor do you commend them to teachers of justice so they might know how to use it justly—who might teach justice, if it can be taught, and if it is to be acquired by exercise and habit, might diligently exercise them. Nor have you ever cared for yourselves. But when you see that you and your sons have sufficiently attained letters, music, and gymnastics, which you think is the perfect discipline of virtue, and yet nonetheless you are wicked regarding money, why do you not despise your current education? Why do you not seek some who might free you from this dissonance in music?" For on account of this fault and sluggishness more than on account of a foot moving out of tune with the lyre, both brother is carried against brother, and city against other cities immoderately, and they are carried into discordant sedition, and having joined battle they suffer and inflict the extreme. But you say that it is not through rudeness and ignorance, but voluntarily that those who are unjust are unjust. And again you do not hesitate to assert that injustice is a base thing and hateful to God. For what reason then does anyone voluntarily choose this so great an evil? You answer that a man overcome by pleasures undergoes it. Is not being overcome against one's will, since overcoming is by will? Therefore, reason entirely convinces us that to act unjustly is against one's will. A more diligent...

...care, then, than is usually applied, becomes both all men privately and cities publicly. As often as I hear you saying these things, Socrates, I am wonderfully delighted and I praise them, and I do the same when I listen to what follows. For you add that those whoever exercise the body but neglect the soul, are cultivating that which is by nature subject, but despising that which commands. Likewise, that to everyone should be left the use of that thing which he does not know how to use. For he who knows not how to use his eyes, ears, or whole body, it is better for him neither to see, nor hear, nor otherwise use the body, than to use it. Similarly also in the arts. For whoever knows not how to use his own lyre, it is clear as you yourself say, that he also knows not how to use another's lyre; and he who knows not how to use another's, knows not how to use his own. And the reason is the same for other instruments and possessions. And finally, your speech proceeds so excellently that you infer: he who knows not how to use his soul, it is better for him that his soul be at rest and that he not live, than that he live and be his own master in acting. And if some necessity forces him to live, it is better for him to lead his life as a slave than as a free man. This is like committing the rudders of thought to someone else, who has attained the pilot's discipline of human life—which you often, Socrates, call Political, and the same as judicial and justice. To these speeches and many other such noble ones, asserting that virtue can be taught and commanding one to take care of oneself first of all, I have almost never been opposed, nor do I think I shall be opposed in the future. For I judge them to be very useful and to have great power for exhortation, and to be conducive to waking men up as if from sleep. I have therefore applied my mind, as one who was about to hear the rest; I questioned not you first, Socrates, but your equals, or companions, or associates, or however else they ought to be called in relation to you. Of these, I say, I asked those who are held first among you before others, what speech would most especially follow after these things; and in your manner, having prefaced it in some such way, I set forth the question. "O best of men," I said, "in what way must we then receive the Socratic exhortations to virtue? As if this were the only thing that exists, but to go forward to the work and to perfect the matter not at all? But shall this be our duty through all our life: to provoke those who are not yet sufficiently incited, and thus always to exhort one another in turn? Or rather, is it fitting for both Socrates and ourselves, since we do not deny that this itself must be done, to inquire thus: what next? From where shall we begin the study of justice? If someone were to exhort us to care for the body, as if we were children who in no way noticed that the care of it is gymnastics and medicine, and were to rebuke us because we are always thinking of wheat and barley and vines, and of all things which we seek for the sake of the body, but we inquire into no art or industry by which a good habit of the body might be made, although there is some—perhaps we would ask him what arts he says there are regarding the cultivation of the body, and he would, I think, answer medicine and gymnastics. In the same way now, what art should we think is occupied with the virtue of the soul? Let whoever seems most skilled of these answer." He answers then to these things, "Know that this art which you have heard from Socrates is none other than justice." Then I said, "Do not only bring me the name, but explain it further thus. Medicine, moreover, is called a certain art; by this, two things are made: for both doctors are made from doctors, and health is restored. One of these is no longer an art; but the work of the art having been taught and perceived is what we call health. From architecture, similarly, two things are made, namely a building and architecture; the former indeed a work, the latter a doctrine. Let it be also for justice to make others just, as with the individual craftsmen above. But the other work which a just man can perform for us—what shall we say it is? Declare it." One indeed answered, I think, "the beneficial"; another, "the becoming"; another, "the conducive"; another, "the useful." But I, answering, objected that these same names are in the individual arts: and that there it is said and done rightly what are useful, conducive, and other things of this kind. But that which is proper to each art is that to which these things look. Just as in the craft of carpentry, what is said to be well, beautifully, and becomingly situated, tends toward this: that from wooden material, furniture might be aptly made, which are not at all the art, but the work of the art. Let it be said similarly of the work of justice itself. Here a certain one of your familiars, Socrates, answered, and indeed he seemed to speak very beautifully. "The work proper to justice," he said, "which belongs to no other faculty, is to produce friendship in cities." He, being asked again, asserted that friendship was a certain good, but never an evil. But when he was questioned about the benevolences of children and brutes, which we commonly call friendships, he denied they were friendships, since they more often harm than help; and he said those are falsely called friendships; but true friendship is undoubtedly concord. And when it was asked whether he called that concord an agreement of opinion or a concurrence of science, he indeed despised opinion, because concurrences of opinions among men are many and harmful; but he had granted that friendship was entirely a good and the work of justice. Therefore he said the same thing—that concord is science, not opinion. But when we had been carried this far in speaking, the ambiguous listeners immediately cried out against him, that the speech was revolving to the same point: since medicine also is a certain concord, as are the remaining arts, and they can declare what they are occupied with. But this of yours which you call justice, or concord, knows not where it tends, or what its work is—it is hidden. Finally, I asked these same things of you, Socrates. And you immediately said it was the work of justice to help friends and to harm enemies. But then it seemed to you that a just man never harms anyone, but helps everyone in all things. These things were attempted not once only, Socrates, or twice; but when I had followed you as a suppliant for a long time, I was finally exhausted, thinking that for inflaming men so that they might take up the study of virtue, you were more fit than others. But of two things, one must be true: either you are only powerful to that extent and no further—which indeed can happen in any art; as in the art of piloting, it can happen that he who knows not how to pilot has thought up some praises of that art by which he might provoke men to it, as if it were most worthy, and in the remaining arts in the same way. Perhaps someone will attribute the same to you: as if you know justice itself no more, although you praise it excellently. But I do not think so. For of two things, I say: either I think you do not know, or you are unwilling to communicate it with me. Therefore, I will betake myself to Thrasymachus, I suppose, and anywhere else I can, and I will hope to be freed from doubts. Nor indeed would I betake myself elsewhere, if you yourself were willing to sometime make an end to those exhortations. Furthermore, just as if you had already sufficiently incited me to the care of the body, which belongs to gymnastics, after such an exhortation you would open to me what kind of condition my body was in, and what kind of cure it needed; so do in the present: suppose Clitophon grants to you that it is ridiculous for anyone to place his study in other things, but to neglect the soul for the sake of which one labors in the rest, and whatever other things follow after these and have just been reported by me...

...think of me. I beseech you, Socrates, do not act otherwise; do not let it be necessary, as it is now and shall be hereafter, for Lycias and other men partly to praise you and partly to blame you. For to one who has not yet been provoked to virtue, I would assert that you contribute a great deal; but to one already persuaded, on the contrary, you are almost an obstacle to his reaching the goal of virtue and becoming happy.
