# THE CRATYLUS OF PLATO, OR, ON THE CORRECTNESS OF NAMES.
*

### MARSILIO FICINO’S ARGUMENT.
*

<term>Platonic Wisdom</term> <note>Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic tradition which seeks higher truths in all things.</note> always looks up to the lofty and never despises the lowly; for the knowledge of true names is not a lowly thing, but rather exalted, especially the knowledge of divine names. The wise Hebrews valued this so highly that they preferred it not only to all other sciences but even to the written Law, affirming that it was granted by God to the patriarchs and to Moses. I say it was granted to Moses not to be inscribed in letters, but in the minds of the holy—the minds, I mean, of the succeeding prophets, who thereafter propagated the wisdom of divine names into the minds of those who followed in a long series. By the power of these names, they say, their ancestors performed miraculous works. Furthermore, they inserted some of these names into their writings, but for the most part, they were either scattered or veiled; if anyone should know, collect, and pronounce them with the same purity of mind with which they were given, he would perform similar wonders. This is especially true of the primary name of God, which, since it is composed wonderfully of only four letters—and these being vowels <note>Ficino refers to the Tetragrammaton (YHWH), though he notes them here as vowels, likely following a tradition that associated the Hebrew letters with vowel-like breaths.</note>—can surely be pronounced correctly by no one unless divinely inspired. From this, they are forced to admit that Jesus, whom they call the Nazarene, was divine, since they confess that He performed miracles through the true understanding and perfect pronunciation of this four-letter name. Indeed, enough has been said by us on these matters in our book *On Religion*.

Origen also, when he had considered the marvelous power of divine names and prayers, said in his books *Against Celsus* that a wonderful power lies hidden in certain sacred names; therefore, these should not be translated from the Hebrew tongue into another, but preserved in their own characters. For perhaps just as life remains in a body composed in a certain way, but does not remain if it is composed otherwise or changed; so they think a certain vital power resides in divine names composed in a certain divine manner. And as <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric wisdom (Hermeticism).</note> taught from the beginning, and long after him Plotinus and Iamblichus, demons are in a way enclosed in certain statues composed in a certain order. By words tempered to a certain celestial likeness, certain divine gifts are distributed, and this by God’s providence, so that whenever the matter requires it, we might rightly invoke divine help. They say this was observed by Apollo himself and by Pythagoras, who are said to have wonderfully cured diseases of both mind and body with certain divine words alone. In this matter, we find that the entire wisdom of <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>The ancient Persian prophet, highly esteemed by Renaissance philosophers as a "pious philosopher."</note> consisted, which Plato calls divine in the *Alcibiades*, and in the *Charmides* the healer of diseases of mind and body. I omit that all nations and languages pronounce the principal name of God with only four letters. This is treated more extensively by us in the commentaries on the *Philebus*, where it is proved that all nations could not have agreed on this one thing unless divinely inspired. Hence the Egyptians call Him whom we call God, *Theut*; the Persians, *Syre*; the Magi, *Orsi* (from which comes *Oromasis*); the Hebrews express that ineffable name of four vowels as best they can through *Adonai*; the Greeks, *Theos*; the Arabs, *Alla*; Muhammad, *Abdi*; we received *Jesus* from the angel. But why did God wish to be invoked everywhere by four letters? Perhaps because He Himself disposes all things through four stages: composing them by essence, being, power, and action. Likewise, he arranges celestial things by four triplicities of signs—fiery, airy, watery, and earthy—and those under the heavens similarly by the four elements.

But no one will wonder that such great force lies hidden in true names, if only we consider the natural power of the thing itself: when we truly know, it reaches from the objects to the senses, from these to the imagination, and from this in a certain way even to the mind. Then, it is first conceived by the mind, then expressed through the voice like a birth. And in this very voice, constituted by its own articulations, the very power of the thing lies hidden under the form of its meaning like a life; a life, I say, first conceived from the mind itself through the "seeds of things," then brought forth through voices, and finally preserved through writings. If the names of other things in some way preserve the power of those things—so that through them, as images of things, the things themselves are recognized—much more do the divine names delivered by God Himself perpetually preserve their power. And not without reason. For a true name, as Plato pleases, is nothing other than a certain power of the thing itself, first conceived in the mind, then expressed by the voice, and finally signified by letters. It is necessary that the power of a divine thing be divine. Therefore, because divine power resides in them, Plato commands us to venerate the names of God both here and in the *Philebus*, and, as he indicates in the *Laws*, even more than shrines and divine statues. For a more express image of God is preserved in the craftsmanship of the mind, especially when divinely inspired, than in the works of hands. He judges the first and purest names of God to exist among the supernal and celestial minds, by whom God Himself is more expressly conceived. The second are in the purer <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. The third are in the souls of men, and these were brought forth through ancient men inspired by God as if they were the trumpets of God. Therefore, the names of God delivered to us through the ancients and the holy seem to be like images and rays of God Himself, penetrating through the higher powers and through the holier souls of men. Whoever admires the sun as is proper, rightly venerates also the light of the sun. So too one ought to worship God primarily, and at the same time the rays, powers, and images of God lurking in the meaning of sacred names. Let us hear Socrates crying out thus in the *Philebus*: "Reverence for the names of the gods is always in me; it is not a human fear, but it surpasses any greatest dread." Let us hear him again in the *Phaedrus* expiating himself, because in debating he perhaps offended against Love, the name of a god. Let us hear Plato in the eleventh book of the *Laws*, judging those who defile the names of the gods with lies and perjury to be utterly sacrilegious, and commanding that they may be killed by anyone with impunity; and strictly condemning as a traitor to the laws anyone who, being present, does not punish them.

Nor should it disturb us that he often names many gods. For in the *Parmenides* and the *Timaeus*, he proves there is one God through Himself, but when he names others as "gods"—angelic and celestial ministers of God—he understands them not so much as gods but as divine beings. After he finally compared all things to the One in the *Parmenides*, he did not think His names should be despised; since many gifts of God lie hidden in them, that divine theologian Dionysius the Areopagite not unjustly sought out all the mysteries of theology in the divine names. But why have we passed over in silence that splendor of truth, the Apostle Paul, saying that "the Word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword"? Likewise, that saying of the same: "God gave Him a name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth"?

But let us now return to the dialogue. Hermogenes, a disciple and follower of Parmenides, and Cratylus, a follower of Heraclitus, disagreeing about the correctness of names—while the former thinks names have power only by human will, and the latter by a certain natural reason—finally submit themselves to the judgment of Socrates. At the beginning, how beautifully the three teachers of Plato meet here! For he is said to have received morals from Socrates, physics from Cratylus, and metaphysics especially from Hermogenes, besides those things which he himself discovered. Cratylus is indeed a follower of Heraclitus and of the other ancients who philosophized many centuries before Heraclitus, and who thought nothing was stable anywhere, but that all things revolve in perpetual motion; hence they established names for things largely from motion itself. Hermogenes, however, a devotee of Parmenides and the Pythagoreans, on the contrary thought all things remain stable. Socrates and Plato settle this controversy between Hermogenes and Cratylus in such a way that Heraclitus’s opinion is to be approved in Physics, but Parmenides’s in Metaphysics; but if anyone should transfer the state of things to natural matters, or motion to divine matters, he is to be utterly disapproved.

But leaving these things aside, as far as names are concerned: Socrates seems to lean more toward Cratylus’s opinion, confirming it in this way: Some speeches are true, others false; and the parts of a true speech are true; the parts of a false speech are also false. But the parts of speech are names; thus it happens that some names are true, others false. A true speech is that which says things as they are; a false one, the opposite. Therefore, true names are those that bring forth things as they are, rather than as it pleases one's whim. Because Protagoras thinks

--- Page 228 ---
# Book Twenty-Three. 210

that things are such as they seem to each person, so that things have no essence of their own, but all human opinion is the measure; therefore Socrates inserts against Protagoras that some men are indeed the best, namely the most prudent, while others are the worst, namely the furthest from prudence. But if, as Protagoras thinks, those things are true for each which each one opines, there will certainly be no difference between the prudent and the imprudent. But Protagoras is most subtly refuted in the book *On Science* <note>Referring to Plato's *Theaetetus*.</note>; however, it was necessary to refute him briefly here too, so that Hermogenes’s opinion about names, which is somewhat similar, could be more easily rebuked. Indeed, Hermogenes does not at all turn away from Protagoras’s view on things; for while he confesses that names have their truth from human will, he secretly leans toward the Protagorean view on things. He also leans latently toward the opinion of Euthydemus, who says that all things are always present to all people in the same way; he is briefly rejected by the fact that some would not be good and others evil if both virtue and vice were equally present to all. You, meanwhile, note the very well-known opinion of our Plato: that the whole power of virtue is placed in prudence itself, and all vice in imprudence.

After the opinion of Protagoras and Euthydemus is refuted, it is concluded that things themselves exist not according to our opinion, but according to their own nature in the very order of things. If essences exist naturally, actions and passions are also natural. Therefore, if we study to divide or burn anything, we will do so not so much according to our will as according to the nature of the thing, so that we divide it in the manner and with the instrument by which it can more aptly be divided, and similarly burn it. But speaking and naming seem to be a certain action, and therefore must have their own nature, so that we name things not as it pleases us, but as the mode of the thing requires. For a name is a certain instrument by which we discern and divide the named thing from others. An instrument of this kind, as is clear in others, must be adapted to its own duty not by chance, nor according to whim, but by art, so that it is a form disposed through the very idea of the art, which leads as to a goal to the most apt discerning and dividing. An instrument of this sort—that is, a name accommodated both to discerning things and to teaching listeners—is not for anyone to manufacture, but for a certain craftsman, a founder of names, who is the rarest of all. He, however, manufactures names by the rule which the craftsman who is to use the names requires and instructs. Plato wants the <term>dialectician</term> <note>For Plato, the dialectician is the master of logical division and synthesis, the one who knows the true nature of things.</note> to be such a person. But he who manufactures them composes the name according to the very idea of the thing conceived in the mind, in which the true reason of the name consists, endowed with a certain meaning. And this very ideal reason and meaning is the true name, and it remains the same regarding the same thing in whatever material of letters it is made, among whatever nations, provided it teaches by discerning what the thing itself is. Conclude that names, if they are to be true and rightly placed, must be established by a wise founder of names, and indeed with the dialectician advising him, so that they are forged in such a form that they imitate and explain the properties of things according to their power.

After this, diligently inquiring from whom the correctness of names is to be learned—that is, the proper reason by which they were constituted—he mocks the sophists and leads us rather to the poets: not just any poets, but divine ones, who as it were received the true names of things from the gods, among whom names are true. Among these things, he shows that Homer's poetry is allegorical, even where he seems to narrate history; as appears in names allegorically fashioned. He mentions many names of heroes in Homer composed by a certain allegorical reason. Then he ascends to the names of the gods, whose reasons he received from more venerable theologians.

In the first position of names: <margin>What the masculine and feminine names of the gods signify in divine matters.</margin> **Heaven** <note>Caelus/Uranus</note> signifies the soul of the star-bearing sphere; **Saturn** <note>Cronus</note> the soul of the following sphere; **Jupiter** <note>Zeus</note> that of the third. In the second position: Heaven signifies God; Saturn the angelic mind; Jupiter the soul of the world and the celestial soul. In the third: Heaven signifies the fecundity of God Himself; Saturn His intelligence; Jupiter His beneficial will providing for all. In the fourth: Heaven in any divinity designates an outlook toward higher things; Saturn a respect toward itself; Jupiter a prospect providing for lower things. I would be forced to be more prolix if I wanted to interpret each god here theologically, and indeed we have treated this more extensively in the books *On Love* and *Theology*.

Since treating divine matters is not for one who always says he knows nothing, Socrates, where he acts more deeply concerning divine things, appropriately says that this wisdom recently shone upon him from whence he knows not, signifying that inspiration is needed for the true perception of divine things. This he confirms in the *Timaeus*, *Symposium*, and *Phaedrus*; he proves the same in the letters. That he says he received the contemplation of divine things from <term>Euthyphro</term> <note>A priest known for his legalistic and literalist views on piety, whom Socrates treats with irony.</note> is ironic, and he mocks him and similar ambitious professors of divine law. Thus it happens not unjustly that what he pretends to have heard from him, he asserts will be dismissed a little later, warning that one must not trust the doctrines of the ambitious, especially where they judge concerning divine things, about which even the most approved man can never speak as a man, but rather sometimes as the trumpet of God. To this is somewhat similar what Plutarch says, that a law existed among the Greeks by which it was commanded that the books of wicked men be removed from the midst, so that the memory of the authors might be deleted. He signifies besides that the ancients were accustomed to release a person who was seized by a daemon during sacred rites—so that he would no longer be fatigued by it—a little later with certain prayers and sacrifices. He teaches also that a long time should not be wasted on names.

Accordingly, he rebukes those who think only the world spheres and stars are divine; surely since from these, as things naturally closer to our sight and mobile, one must ascend to higher divinities, stable and unknown to our senses due to their greater excellence. He narrates besides that the names of the gods were found not by chance, but by the birth of human reason partly through divine inspiration. Heroic and human names, however, were often placed either from the surnames of ancestors or from a vow; therefore, the certain reason of names is to be sought in divine names rather than in others. After this, he descends to the daemons, and asserts by the opinion of Hesiod and the most approved ancient men that the souls of men ascend into airy daemons, who both excel in the wisdom of things and provide for the human race. You, however, notice here that every good man is wise, and in turn, a good man becomes wise because God fills the purged and earthly mind of a good man with the light of His wisdom. A wise man is also good for this reason: because he neither wanders from the goal, nor in these things which contribute to the goal, in choosing everywhere. Notice that heroes and demigods are thought to be the same, and to be born from mutual love between God and man. Hence that saying, "But they were born from God." In which matter the kinship between the human and divine race is shown.

Attend soon to the duty of man: not to feel, but to consider those things which he has felt. Then that the state of the soul in the body is not to be contained, but to contain the nature of the body. Nevertheless, the body is called by Orpheus the prison of the soul and a tomb, inasmuch as the soul is judged to be as if dead in the body. Remember also that Anaxagoras thought that one soul before others was the mind of the world machine, and that one mind presided. Hence that: "The Spirit nourishes within, and the Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass." <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, used by Ficino to illustrate Anaxagoras's philosophy.</note> Then consider the pious modesty of Plato saying: "Whoever is wise acknowledges that he is ignorant of the gods and the names of the gods among themselves." He adds that one must pray to God that He reveal to us His own proper name; it must also be thought that the names we attribute to God signify not the nature of God itself, but our affection toward God. Therefore, God must be beseeched that we do not displease Him in naming Him. The same in the *Philebus*, *Parmenides*, *Phaedrus*, and *Timaeus*.

He then interprets the names of the gods, narrating first the opinion of those who thought all things flow, which he will finally disapprove. But in these, truly remember that the goddess **Vesta** signifies the essence of separate forms and the stable foundation of divine things; therefore, the ancients were accustomed to sacrifice to Vesta before other gods. Likewise, names which signify stability in divine things are referred to their substance; but those which signify motion, to action: improperly indeed to intellectual action, but properly to animal action. Again, masculine names of gods signify in divine matters the efficient act, but feminine names signify the receiving power. Furthermore, that the heaven by its motion generates time, consuming and continually consuming, is a certain image referring to the god **Heaven** <note>Uranus</note> and **Rhea**, and **Saturn** devouring his sons. In these, however, Heaven is the divine essence itself, Rhea the life of the same, Saturn the mind of the same. The sons of Saturn are the ideas of things, generated within the divine intelligence, which just as they are produced from the mind, so also they are reduced back into the mind, which absorbs them in itself, so to speak. But the multitude of gods distributed around the different parts of the world is contained both in the ideas of those same parts, and in the angelic minds contemplating in many ways, and in the souls governing the world spheres and stars.

Notice above others that **Pluto** here signifies especially the divine providence pertaining to separate souls, which—you think—so ravishes and detains the souls of the good by perpetual allurements of its goods that they do not wish to return further to us. Which indeed does not agree with the infinite periods of souls in Plotinus and Proclus. He proves that souls are detained in Pluto’s power by a certain very tight and indissoluble bond because they are held by an amatory affection. Where that Platonic saying in the *Symposium*, *Laws*, and often elsewhere is confirmed: that the amatory and voluntary knot is more powerful than all others, and that not unjustly; namely, he who draws someone through appetite, both draws him more powerfully and retains him more firmly than he who tries to attract through other force, because he ravishes not only from without, but from within. Furthermore, what is so ravished not only does not struggle to be released, but even leans upon the binder, and involves itself more tightly in the same bond. I omit that another ravisher occurs as something superior and foreign. But the amatory ravisher insinuates himself into us both openly and secretly as something equal and domestic. Hence Boethius proves from the mind of Plotinus that God ravishes all things to Himself most powerfully and at the same time most sweetly,

--- Page 229 ---
# Cratylus, Or, On the Correctness of Names. 211

namely by the love of His own good, drawing them as if by bait. This also the Platonist Philo confirms: God from the beginning to the end touches all things powerfully and disposes them sweetly. We will show elsewhere that this whole idea was taken from the fourth book of the *Laws*. Concerning **Phoebus** <note>Apollo</note>, who in Orpheus signifies vital light, there are many and distinguished things in the Orphic hymn to Apollo: in the sixth book of the *Republic*, in the oration of the Platonist Julian, and in our own opuscule *On Light*. Here, however, the name Apollo is briefly explained. It signifies a triple sun: divine, angelic, and celestial. In the first, the light is superior to intellect. In the second, intellectual light is above sight. In the third, it is visible light. The second is called by the Platonists the son of the first. The third is called the image of both. But, to speak summarily, Apollo signifies first the divine and angelic simplicity of substance; second, the power through which God and the angel wash souls and purge them from lower affections; third, the benefit by which they release them from worse things and join them to better; fourth, the "archer" virtue, so to speak, by which they hurl their gifts from afar through all things, and afflict the unjust with their stings; fifth, the efficacy tempering all things and converting them with musical measures. In these, Apollo’s prophecy appears; the power is called simple, washing by purging, and releasing. In the same place, medicine also appears, as well as skill in archery and singing; where he powerfully extends his powers through all things, and sweetly tempers all things among themselves, and fortunately converts them to himself by tempering. Similar gifts and affections seem to be in the sun and toward the sun in the third and celestial sense.

Among these things, Socrates says he is joking in explaining the names of the gods, obviously knowing that he does not reach the divine substance with these names, but either narrates their affections or explains our affections toward them according to his power. He adds that the gods sometimes joke and play: we indeed joke about divine things, and the gods joke about ours; inasmuch as obviously our things, compared to theirs, are very small, and they govern these with no labor but with inestimable ease. I omit for the present that Platonic saying: "Man is a joke and a plaything of the gods." For we will explain that where the matter requires it. After this, for the third time, the exceptionally religious man says he reverences disputing about the matters of another. Namely, even at the very beginning of the disputation, it is to be feared lest we speak of God without God; and again in the middle of the disputation, lest we rashly measure the immeasurable; and again around the end, lest we prolong the speech about divinities further than their will inspires us.

Next, note that **Mercury** <note>Hermes</note> is occupied with speech, so that you understand the power of intelligence to belong rather to Saturn. Likewise, what he adds, that **Pan** is the biformed son of Mercury—namely because of twofold speech, true and false: note that where Pan speaks as a man, it signifies true speech; but where as a brute, false: so that being warned by this, you may fear to speak false things, lest by speaking false things you be a false man and a true brute. Accordingly, where he mocks many of the ancients who, while they themselves were suffering from vertigo, thought all things were turning, he warns lest we measure eternal things by a particularly temporal nature. Likewise, where he says that temperance is the safety and conservation of prudence, he shows that a soul drunk with the perturbations of the body cannot perceive the truth of things themselves, especially incorporeal ones.

Soon, where he interprets the name of the **Good**, he shows that three things pertain to the Good itself: namely, that it is to be admired, to be loved, and to be sweet. It is to be admired when it excites us, diverts us from others, and converts us to itself. To be loved when we approach it and cling to it. Sweet when we are filled by it. A little later, explaining the name of **Justice**, he teaches that divine judgment penetrates all things. Which Orpheus also sang. Then he signifies that justice is among the Anaxagoreans the divine mind, the ordainer of all things. Which Socrates indeed dares neither to affirm nor deny. He does not deny it, because justice pertains to God. He does not affirm it, because it would be said more appropriately that justice is the divine will distributing individual things according to the merits of either nature or will. Observe that the reason of the Good pertains to a certain nature diffusing itself through all things. But the reason of the **Beautiful** pertains to the wisdom and order flowing from it, and provoking to the rest. Finally, the power of **Love** looks to a certain influx penetrating from the eyes through the eyes.

After this, he asserts many things about names, which are sufficiently understood by the previous points. He touches upon a triple opinion on the origin of names: either that they were once received from the gods, or from barbarians, or that they have been so changed by the length of time from their first origin that the first positions of names are minimally discerned. Soon he mocks those who profess knowledge of subsequent things while they are ignorant of the antecedents. But you, in what follows, notice the golden sentiment: "The most serious of all deceptions is that by which a man deceives himself." For in that, the deceiver is never absent from the deceived.

Since Cratylus leans toward the sect of Euthydemus, which thinks no one says anything false—because whoever speaks, says what is, and therefore speaks the truth—Socrates refutes it in this way: We often say that some things are present to someone which are far away, and in turn that things are absent which are present, which is nothing other than to speak false things. And similarly, we can appropriately name, expressing through the name and the sounds of letters in some way the nature and action or passion of a thing; and on the contrary, name incongruously.

After this, where he makes mention of numbers and qualities, he says that in the order of numbers the species of a number is always changed by the addition or subtraction of a unit, which does not happen in quality. I think this happens for this reason: because the whole reason of number consists in unity and its replication. In quality, however, since besides unity and its replication there is a certain other nature, deservedly when one degree is added or subtracted, or even many, the species of quality is not changed. Similarly in an image, for it is an image insofar as it represents; but it can refer more or less. Almost the same happens to names. For some are images of the things themselves. Furthermore, since the end of a name is to refer to the thing itself, it is better to refer it by a certain likeness of the thing than by human convention. Again, since a name consists of letters, it cannot aptly express the thing unless it is composed of syllables and letters properly expressing it. And since it is a laborious thing to accommodate letters, syllables, and names to individual things entirely—indeed, it cannot even be done in numbers—therefore, nature's custom must be mixed, so that as far as can be done, the nature of things should have authority over names. But where it can be done either in no way or with great difficulty through the property of nature, let it be done through human custom and convention, whether alone or joined to nature.

Notice after this that the greatest diligence must be applied to principles, and much must be disputed in establishing them. Again, he goes to knowledge by a certain most fallacious way, whoever, as Cratylus advises, hunts for the properties of things through the properties of names; since the author of names did not institute such names as the things themselves are, but such as he thought, who is liable to be deceived. Add that different people can interpret the same names differently, and translate them with probability to signify opposites. Certainly, many names are so placed as if things flow, and many also as if they remain. It is therefore most fallacious to judge things through names. A little later, consider: the first who named things knew them before he named them. Also the ancient opinion by which it is asserted that a certain divine power instructed man from the beginning and taught the names of things. Which is consistent with those things said in the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman*. For it cannot be that the human race, either from the beginning of the world or after great illusions, was instructed otherwise than divinely.

But what Socrates says about dreaming concerning ideas declares both that Socrates was accustomed to be mocked on this very point both by the common people and by comic poets, and that the knowledge of ideas is had through the separation of the mind, similar to a prophetic dream. Soon he proves that ideas exist, because over imperfect forms there must be perfect ones. Likewise, that ideas are immutable, if indeed the specific reasons and definitions of things always remain in the same way. He adds: if all status is taken away from things, it follows that no thing truly is either "this something" or "such something," nor is it known, since in any moment it will deceive the judge and necessarily lie. He adds neither the knowledge of the marketplace, namely the specific idea of knowledge itself, which should always remain in the same way. He concludes that the science of things is to be sought not from names, but from ideas, whose innate notions in us are the first and true names of things. Finally, he warns young men not to easily pass judgment on serious matters; rather, they should learn for a long time and wait for a more mature age before they judge.

# HERMOGENES, CRATYLUS, SOCRATES.

**HERMOGENES:** Shall we then confer our speech with this Socrates? **CRATYLUS:** I certainly wish to, if it seems good to you. **HERMOGENES:** Cratylus here, O Socrates, says that in individual things there is naturally a right reason for a name, and that a name is not that which some call by convention, while they pronounce some little part of their voice, but that there is some right reason of names innate to all, both Greeks and Barbarians. I ask him, therefore, whether Cratylus is truly his name. He confesses it. But what name for Socrates, I say? He says Socrates. Is it not, I say, the name for all others by which we call each one? He says, however, that your name is not Hermogenes,

--- Page 230 ---
# Book Twenty-Three. 212

even if all men should call you so. And while I beseech him to open to me what he means when I inquire, he declares nothing at all, but mocking me, he pretends to be revolving something in his mind, as if he understands something about this matter which, if he wished to express it, would force me to confess that very thing and to say the same things he says. Therefore, I would gladly hear from you if you can guess Cratylus’s prophecy by any reason; however, I would more gladly hear your opinion about the correctness of names, if indeed it pleases you.

**SOCRATES:** O Hermogenes, son of Hipponicus, <margin>Proverb.</margin> it is said in an old proverb that "beautiful things are difficult to know." And yet that notice of names is no small matter. Indeed, if I had already heard that fifty-drachma demonstration from Prodicus—in whose tradition these things were also included, as he himself testifies—nothing would prevent you from immediately understanding the truth about the correctness of names. I have never heard that one, but only that of a single drachma. Therefore, what is true in these matters, I know not; but I am ready to investigate together with you and with Cratylus. But as for his saying that your name is not truly Hermogenes <note>The name "Hermogenes" implies being "born of Hermes," the god of gain and eloquence.</note>—which is said from "gain"—I think he bites you, as if you were greedy for money and unable to obtain your wish. But as I was saying just now, these things are difficult to know. We must search by bringing the reasons on both sides into the midst, whether it is as you yourself say, or rather as Cratylus says.

**HERMOGENES:** Indeed, O Socrates, although I have already disputed frequently with him and with many others, I cannot yet be persuaded that there is any other correctness of a name than convention and agreement itself. It seems to me that whatever name anyone imposes on anything, that is correct. And if he changes it again and imposes another, the name that succeeds it exists no less correctly than the first, just as we are accustomed to change the names of slaves; for no name is innate in anything by nature, but by the law and use of those who have become accustomed to call it so. If this is otherwise, I am ready to learn and hear not only from Cratylus but from anyone else.

**SOCRATES:** Perhaps you say something, Hermogenes. Let us consider then: whatever name anyone imposes on anything and calls it, do you assert that is its name? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And whether a private person calls it, or a city? **HERMOGENES:** I assert it. **SOCRATES:** What then if I myself call something—for instance, if what we now call a "man," I should name a "horse," and what we call a "horse," a "man"? Publicly it will be named a man, and privately a horse; and privately again a man, and publicly a horse. Is that how you speak? **HERMOGENES:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Say again, do you call something "speaking the truth" and something "speaking false"? **HERMOGENES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** <margin>Which speech will be true, which false.</margin> Will not one be true speech, and the other false speech? **HERMOGENES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** But is that speech true which says things as they are, and false which says them as they are not? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Is this, then, to speak in speech of those things which are and those which are not? **HERMOGENES:** That very thing. **SOCRATES:** Is a speech that is true wholly true, while its parts are not true? **HERMOGENES:** No, the parts are also true. **SOCRATES:** Are the large parts true, but the small particles false, or are they all true? **HERMOGENES:** All, I think. **SOCRATES:** <margin>The smallest part of speech is the name.</margin> Do you have any part of speech smaller than a name? **HERMOGENES:** By no means, for this is the smallest part. **SOCRATES:** And this name is a part of true speech. **HERMOGENES:** Undoubtedly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore a true part, as you yourself say. **HERMOGENES:** True. **SOCRATES:** And a false part. **HERMOGENES:** I say so. **SOCRATES:** It is permitted, then, to call a name true and a name false, if indeed one can so call a speech. **HERMOGENES:** What prevents it? **SOCRATES:** Whatever name anyone says belongs to anything, is that its name? **HERMOGENES:** That very thing. **SOCRATES:** Or even as many names as anyone attributes to it, will there be just as many? And also whenever he attributes them? **HERMOGENES:** Indeed Socrates, I have no other correctness of a name than this: namely, that it is permitted for me to call a thing by another name which I myself imposed, and for you by another which you imposed. Thus indeed I see in cities that some names are held as proper to the same things, both by Greeks to other Greeks, and by Greeks to Barbarians.

**SOCRATES:** Let us notice, Hermogenes, whether things themselves seem to you to be such that each thing has its own essence for each person, <margin>The opinion of Protagoras concerning the essence of things.</margin> as Protagoras delivered? saying that man is the measure of all things, so that as things seem to me, so they are to me; and as they seem to you, so they are to you. Or rather do you think there are some things which have a certain firmness of their essence? **HERMOGENES:** Sometimes, O Socrates, in my doubt I have been led to these things which Protagoras delivers. Yet I do not sufficiently persuade myself that it is so. **SOCRATES:** Were you also sometimes led to this: that it seemed to you that no man was altogether evil? **HERMOGENES:** Not by Jove; on the contrary, I have often been so affected that I thought some men were altogether evil, and indeed very many. **SOCRATES:** But have no good men appeared to you yet? **HERMOGENES:** Very few. **SOCRATES:** Some, then, have appeared? **HERMOGENES:** Some. **SOCRATES:** By what reason do you judge this? By this? That some indeed are altogether good, altogether prudent; but others altogether depraved, altogether imprudent? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** If Protagoras said true things, and this is the truth itself—that as things seem to each, so they are—is it possible that some men are prudent and others imprudent? **HERMOGENES:** By no means. **SOCRATES:** And yet this, as I think, seems altogether true to you: since there is a certain prudence and imprudence, Protagoras cannot speak altogether true things. For one will not truly be more prudent than another, if what seems to each will be true for each. **HERMOGENES:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** <margin>The opinion of Euthydemus: that all things are always similarly present to all.</margin> But neither do you agree with Euthydemus, I think, saying that all things are similarly and always for all people. For some would not be good and others evil if virtue and depravity were always and equally in all. **HERMOGENES:** You speak true things. **SOCRATES:** Therefore if all things are not in all always and similarly, nor is each thing proper to each, it is established that things themselves exist which have a certain firm essence in themselves; they are not distracted toward us or by us through imagination up and down, but according to themselves they remain in their own essence as they were instituted by nature. **HERMOGENES:** The same seems to me too, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Do things themselves thus consist by nature, but their actions not so, but otherwise? Or are actions themselves similarly certain species of things? **HERMOGENES:** They are altogether so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore actions themselves happen according to their own nature, not according to our opinion. Just as if we should decide to divide something: must each thing be divided as we wish and with what we wish? Or rather, if we divide each thing according to the nature by which it ought to divide and be divided, and also by that which according to nature the division ought to be made, will we divide correctly and gain something, and do that thing correctly? But if against nature, will we wander and gain nothing? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** And also if we should attempt to burn something, we must not burn according to every opinion, but according to the correct opinion; and this is by what reason each thing naturally ought to be burned and to burn, and with what it ought. **HERMOGENES:** These are true things.
**SOCRATES:**

[[page number: 213]]

# Cratylus, Or, On the Right Reason of Names

SOCRATES: Is not the same reasoning true for the rest? HERMOGENES: The same.
SOCRATES: And is not "speaking" also one of the operations? HERMOGENES: It is, clearly. SOCRATES: Whether then will he speak correctly who speaks as it seems he should speak? Or rather he who speaks as the nature of things itself requires one to speak and be spoken of? And if he speaks in the way nature demands, he will profit by speaking; but if otherwise, he will err and achieve nothing. HERMOGENES: I think it is even as you say. SOCRATES: [[Abbrev: Is not naming a certain part of speaking?]] and do those who name not speak in some manner? HERMOGENES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And naming is a certain action, since speaking is a certain action concerning things. HERMOGENES: Precisely. SOCRATES: Moreover, actions have appeared to us not to look toward ourselves, but to have a certain nature of their own. HERMOGENES: It is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, things must be named by that reason by which the nature of the things themselves demands them to name and be named, and by that which it demands, and not according to the arbitration of our own will, if we are to stand by those things which have been said. and thus we shall accomplish something and we shall name; but otherwise, in no way. HERMOGENES: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: That which is to be cut, must it be cut by something? HERMOGENES: By something. SOCRATES: And that which is to be woven, certainly by something it must be woven; and that which is to be pierced, by something it must be pierced. HERMOGENES: Clearly. SOCRATES: Likewise, that which is to be named, by something it must be named. HERMOGENES: So it must be. SOCRATES: What is that by which it is necessary to pierce something? HERMOGENES: A drill. SOCRATES: What by which to weave? HERMOGENES: The shuttle and the comb. SOCRATES: What by which to name? HERMOGENES: A name. SOCRATES: You speak well; therefore, the name is a certain instrument. [[Abbrev: HERMOGENES: It is.]] SOCRATES: If I were to ask what instrument the shuttle and the comb are, would you answer: that by which we weave? HERMOGENES: Nothing else. SOCRATES: But weaving, what do we do? Do we not discern the weft and the warp, which were confused, with the shuttle? HERMOGENES: That very thing. SOCRATES: Will you answer the same regarding the drill and the others? HERMOGENES: The same. SOCRATES: Can you similarly declare regarding the name, what do we do while we name something with the name itself, which is the instrument? HERMOGENES: I cannot. SOCRATES: Do we not teach one another something, and discern things as they are?

[[Margin: A name is an instrument for teaching and discerning the substances of things.]]

HERMOGENES: Indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, a name is an instrument for teaching and discerning the substances of things, just as the comb and the shuttle are for the web. HERMOGENES: So it must be said. SOCRATES: Furthermore, the shuttle is the instrument of the weavers. HERMOGENES: Why not? SOCRATES: Therefore, the weaver will use the shuttle and the comb correctly—correctly, I say, according to the reason of weaving; but will he who teaches use the name, and correctly—correctly, namely, according to the proper reason of teaching? HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Whose craftsman’s work does the weaver use well when he uses the shuttle and the comb? HERMOGENES: The carpenter’s. SOCRATES: Any carpenter, or rather one who possesses the art? HERMOGENES: He who possesses the art. SOCRATES: Likewise, whose work does the piercer use correctly when he uses the drill? HERMOGENES: The blacksmith’s. SOCRATES: Is every man a blacksmith, or rather he who possesses the art? HERMOGENES: He who possesses the art. SOCRATES: Come then, tell me whose work the teacher himself uses as often as he uses a name. HERMOGENES: I do not know. SOCRATES: Do you not even know this to assign: who delivers to us the names we use? HERMOGENES: I am ignorant of this as well. SOCRATES: Does it not seem to you that the law has established names for us? HERMOGENES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore, the teacher will use the work of the legislator when he uses the name itself. HERMOGENES: I suppose so. SOCRATES: Does any founder of the law seem to you equal [to the task], or he who is endowed with the art? HERMOGENES: He endowed with the art. SOCRATES: Wherefore, it is not for any man to impose a name, Hermogenes, as if for some author of names;

[[Margin: * Greek *onomathothetes* (institutor of names). Ficinus [Notes: OCR reads 'Ficanus']]

but here also, as it seems, [it is the work of] the institutor of names, who is found more rarely than any other craftsman among men. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Observe, I pray, to what the institutor of names looks when he imposes names upon things; rather, judge from the examples of the former [craftsmen], to what the carpenter looks when he fashions the shuttle and the comb. Does he not look to something of such a kind as is by nature fit for weaving? HERMOGENES: Precisely. SOCRATES: If in the work itself this shuttle is broken, will he fashion another again after the image of that broken one? Or will he rather look to the Form itself [the *speciẽ* / Idea], after whose exemplar he had made the shuttle that was broken? HERMOGENES: To the Form itself, as I think. SOCRATES: Shall we not rightly call that Form itself the "reason of the shuttle," and the "shuttle itself" in the highest degree? HERMOGENES: I suppose so. SOCRATES: If ever it is necessary to prepare a shuttle for making a thin garment or a thicker one, whether of linen or of wool or of any other kind, all the shuttles must have the Form of the shuttle itself; but whatever kind is naturally most accommodated to each, that kind must be applied to the work to be finished, as nature demands. HERMOGENES: It must be indeed. SOCRATES: The same is the reasoning regarding other instruments. For what fits each by nature, that instrument must be discovered, and it must be attributed to that thing, out of which the maker produces not just any sort he wishes, but such as nature herself requires. For one must know how to perfect in iron the drill accommodated to each thing. HERMOGENES: It is clear. SOCRATES: And furthermore, the shuttle competent for each thing in wood. HERMOGENES: These things are true. SOCRATES: Indeed, by the very reason of nature, one shuttle is competent for one web, and another for another, and in other things in the same way. HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: 

[[Margin: How he shall name and correctly name.]]

It is also necessary, O best of men, that the institutor of names express in voices and syllables the name naturally fit for individual things, and looking toward that which is the name itself, he should fashion and attribute individual names, if he is truly to be an author of names. [[Abbrev: But]] if every founder of names does not express the name in the same syllables, it must be observed that neither do all blacksmiths do it in the same iron, as often as they fashion the same instrument for the sake of the same thing. But insofar as they attribute the same Idea, although in one iron or another, so far the instrument is rightly held, whether they fashion it here or among the Barbarians. Is it not so? HERMOGENES: Very much so. SOCRATES: And will you not judge in the same way, so long as the institutor of names who is among us, and he who is among the Barbarians, gives the competent Form of the name to each thing, that in whatever syllables, the one is no worse than the other in imposing names? HERMOGENES: Indeed. SOCRATES: Who is to know whether the convenient Form of the shuttle has been impressed upon any wood? Is it the craftsman who makes it? Or the weaver who will use it? HERMOGENES: It is probable, O Socrates, that he who will use it knows better. SOCRATES: Who uses the work of the maker of the lyre? Is it not he who can instruct the one making it, and judge whether the work has been done correctly or otherwise? HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Who then? HERMOGENES: The lyre-player (*Citharista*). SOCRATES: And who the work of the builder of ships? HERMOGENES: The pilot (*Gubernator*). SOCRATES: Who likewise will best preside over the work of the founder of names, and judge it completed both among the Greeks and among the Barbarians? Is it not he who will use it? HERMOGENES: He certainly. SOCRATES: And is he not the one who knows how to ask questions? HERMOGENES: That one. SOCRATES: And also to answer? HERMOGENES: Indeed. SOCRATES: But do you call him who knows how to ask and answer anything other than a dialectician? HERMOGENES: A dialectician, surely. SOCRATES: It is the work of the carpenter to make a tiller with the pilot prescribing it, if it is to be a good tiller. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: And the author of names [must make] the name, with the dialectical man advising him, if names are to be correctly placed. 

[[Margin: The dialectician knows whether names are correctly imposed on things or not.]]

HERMOGENES: These things are true. SOCRATES: It appears then, Hermogenes, that the imposition of a name is no light matter, as you think, nor is it the work of unskillful men or just anyone. Indeed, Cratylus

[[page number: 214]]

# Book Twenty-Three

speaks the truth when he says names belong to things by nature, and that not just anyone is an author of names, but only he who looks to the name which fits each thing by nature, and afterwards interprets that Form in letters and syllables. HERMOGENES: I do not know, Socrates, by what reason I should resist what you have said; but perhaps it is not easy to be so suddenly persuaded. But I seem to myself more likely to agree with you in this manner, if you show me what you say is the naturally right reason of a name. SOCRATES: Indeed, O blessed Hermogenes, as yet I know none; for the speech which I said above has fallen from my memory: namely, that I am ignorant of this, but am searching together with you. Now, however, to me and you investigating together, this much at least beyond the former points has been found: that a name has by nature some rectitude, and not just anyone can accommodate a name to things. Is it not so? HERMOGENES: Very much so. SOCRATES: It remains to be considered, if you desire to know, what is the rectitude of the name itself—that is, its right reason. HERMOGENES: I do desire it indeed. SOCRATES: Observe therefore. HERMOGENES: By what path do you advise us to investigate? SOCRATES: The most right consideration, O friend, is to seek these things from those who know, by offering money and giving thanks besides; these are the sophists, through whom your brother Callias, having paid out much money, seems to have turned out wise. But since you have no right to your paternal property, it remains that you should as a suppliant pray your brother to teach you the rectitude of names, which he learned from Protagoras. HERMOGENES: How absurd this petition would be, Socrates, 

[[Margin: "Truth," the name of a writing, or ironic.]]

if while I in no way receive that "Truth" of Protagoras, I should value at an alien price those things which are said based on that "Truth." SOCRATES: But if these things do not please you, one must learn from Homerus and the other poets. HERMOGENES: What about names, and where does Homerus deliver this, O Socrates? SOCRATES: Everywhere in many places; but the greatest and most beautiful are those in which he distinguishes concerning the same names which men use, and those which the gods themselves bring in. Do you not think that in these he delivers something magnificent and wonderful regarding the right reason of names? For it is established that the gods use those names according to rectitude itself, which consist in nature. Do you not think so? HERMOGENES: I know for certain that if the gods call things anything, they name them quite correctly. But what are those? SOCRATES: 

[[Margin: Iliad 20.]] 

Are you ignorant of what he says concerning the Trojan river, which fought in singular combat with Vulcanus? "Which the gods call Xanthus, men call Scamandrus." HERMOGENES: I know it. SOCRATES: Do you not think it is a magnificent thing to know this: by what reason it is more correct to name that river Xanthus than Scamandrus? Likewise, if you wish, observe this: that he says the same bird is called Chalcis 

[[Margin: Iliad 14.]] 

by the gods, but Cymindis by men. Do you think this light knowledge, to know how much more correct it is to call the same bird Chalcis than Cymindis, or Batiea and Myrina, and many others, both in this poet and in others? But the discovery of these things requires a sharper wit than ours. Scamandrius, however, and Astyanax, can be comprehended by human wit, as it seems to me, and easily perceived (names which he says are of the son of Hector), what rectitude Homerus would have there be in these names. Do you know the verses in which these are contained, which I mean? HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Which of these names do you think Homerus thought more fitting for a boy: Astyanax or Scamandrius? HERMOGENES: I do not know. SOCRATES: Consider it thus: if someone were to ask you whether you think the wiser or the less wise impose names on things more correctly? HERMOGENES: I would answer: the wiser. SOCRATES: Do women in cities seem to you to be wiser than men? As far as the gender is concerned. HERMOGENES: Men. SOCRATES: 

[[Margin: Homerus says Scamandrius was named by Hector; Astyanax from *asty* (city).]]

Do you not know what Homerus says, that the son of Hector was called Astyanax by the Trojans, and Scamandrius by the women? since the men were accustomed to call him Astyanax. HERMOGENES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Did Homerus not think the Trojan men wiser than their women? HERMOGENES: I think so indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, he judged he was more correctly named Astyanax than Scamandrius. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Let us observe what cause he himself brings for this denomination. For he says: "He alone protected the city and the wide walls for them." Wherefore it is fitting, as it seems, to name the son of the Savior "Astyanax," that is, "king of the city"—of the city, I say, which his father saved, as Homerus says. HERMOGENES: It seems the same to me. SOCRATES: But why this is especially so, I myself do not yet sufficiently understand, O Hermogenes. Do you perceive it? HERMOGENES: No, by Jove. SOCRATES: And yet to Hector himself, O good man, Homerus himself imposed the name. HERMOGENES: For what reason? SOCRATES: Because it seems to me that the name "Hector" is very close to "Astyanax"; for they signify almost the same thing, and the Greeks think both these names are regal. For of whatever thing anyone is *anax*, that is, king, of the same he is also *hektor*, that is, possessor. For it is established that he rules over those things which he possesses and has. Or perhaps I seem to you to say nothing? and does the opinion deceive me, by which I trusted to reach the knowledge of Homerus concerning the rectitude of names, as if by certain tracks? HERMOGENES: In no way, as I think; for perhaps you are onto something. SOCRATES: It is fitting, as it seems to me, to similarly name the son of a lion a lion, and the son of a horse a horse. I certainly do not say [this] if something like a monster is born from a horse, something other than a horse; but what is born is of the same genus according to nature, I say. For if the son of a bull according to nature begets a horse, it is not a calf that is born, but a horse-foal that must be named. And if a horse against nature begets a calf, it must not be called a horse-foal, but a calf. Neither also if from a man any other progeny than a human one is produced, should that which is born be called a man. And the same is to be judged of trees and of all other things. Do you approve of these? HERMOGENES: I approve indeed. SOCRATES: Watch me, lest I defraud you. For by the same reason, if one is born of a king, he is to be named a king; but that the same is signified in different syllables, it matters not at all, nor does it matter if some letter be added or even subtracted, so long as the essence of the thing signified shines forth and dominates in the name itself. HERMOGENES: How do you say this? SOCRATES: I say nothing strange or new, but even as you see happening in the elements. For you know that we say the names of the elements, but not the elements themselves, except for four; for we say alpha, beta, epsilon, gamma, delta, mu, lambda, and so on. But to the others, both vowels and non-vowels, adding other letters, such as Beta, e, t, a, we constitute names, and so we utter them. But so long as we insert the power of the element itself shining forth, it is fitting to call that name the thing itself which signifies the element to us, as appears in "Beta," where with e, t, a added, nothing hindered the nature of that element from being shown in the whole name, which the author of names wished; to such an extent did he skillfully give names to letters. HERMOGENES: You seem to me to speak the truth. SOCRATES: Will not the same reasoning be for a king? There will be from a king a king, from a good man a good man, from a beautiful man a beautiful one, and in all others, similarly from any genus another such thing, unless a monster be made, and they are to be called by the same names.

### Notes on the Transcription:
*   **Ligatures/Abbreviations:**
    *   `q́;` is the common scribal abbreviation for the enclitic `-que` (and).
    *   `ã, õ, ũ` etc. indicate a following `n` or `m` (e.g., `operationum`, `quandam`).
    *   `ꝙ` stands for `quod`.
    *   `* Græc. legislat. Ficanus ὀνομαθοθετης`: The marginal note attributes the Greek term *onomatothetes* (lawgiver of names) to Ficino (likely "Ficanus" in the OCR).
*   **Greek terms:** Homeric names are discussed in their Latinized forms (*Scamandrius*, *Astyanax*), referencing the *Iliad* where gods and men use different names for the same objects.
*   **Proper Nouns:** All proper nouns (Socrates, Hermogenes, Homerus, etc.) have been retained as per instructions.

...speaks the truth when he says that names belong to things by nature, and that not just anyone is the author of names, but only he who looks toward the name which belongs by nature to each thing, and afterwards is able to implant that form into letters and syllables. I think I would be more likely to agree with you in this way if you showed me what you mean by the "natural correctness of a name." SOCRATES: Indeed, O blessed Hermogenes, I say I know none yet. For the speech I gave above has slipped my memory, namely that I am ignorant of this, but am searching for it along with you. Now, however, as we investigate together, only this much has been discovered beyond our previous points: that a name has a certain natural correctness, and that not just anyone can fit a name to things. HERMOGENES: How absurd this request would be, Socrates, if, since I in no way accept that "Truth" of Protagoras, I were to value at any price the things said based on that "truth." SOCRATES: But if these do not please you, we must learn from Homer and the other poets. HERMOGENES: Where and what does Homer, O Socrates, hand down concerning names? SOCRATES: In many places, but the greatest and most beautiful are those in which he distinguishes between the names that men use for the same things and those which the gods themselves bring forth. Do you not think that in these he hands down something magnificent and wonderful concerning the correct reason of names? For it is established that the gods use those names according to their actual correctness, which consist by nature. Do you not think so? HERMOGENES: I certainly know that if the gods call things anything, they name them quite correctly. But what are these names? SOCRATES:

<margin>The "Truth" is the name of the book, or it is ironic.</margin>

<margin>*Iliad* Book 20.</margin> Are you ignorant of what he says about the Trojan river, which fought in singular combat with Vulcan? That which the gods call <term>Xanthus</term> <note>original: "Xanthum"</note>, men call <term>Scamander</term> <note>original: "Scamandrū"</note>. HERMOGENES: I know it. SOCRATES: Do you not think it is a magnificent thing to know by what reason it is more correct to name that river Xanthus than Scamander? Likewise, if you wish, consider this: that he says the same bird is called 

<margin>*Iliad* Book 14.</margin> <term>Chalcis</term> <note>original: "Chalcidem"</note> by the gods, but <term>Cymindis</term> <note>original: "Cymindin"</note> by men. Do you think this is a light bit of knowledge, to know how much more correct it is to call the same bird Chalcis than Cymindis, or <term>Batiea</term> and <term>Myrine</term>, and many other such things in this poet and others? But the discovery of these matters requires a sharper wit than ours. However, the names <term>Scamandrius</term> and <term>Astyanax</term> can be grasped and easily perceived by human wit, as it seems to me—the names he says belong to the son of Hector—what correctness Homer wishes there to be in these names. Do you know those verses in which they appear? HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Which of these names do you think Homer thought more suitable for the boy: Astyanax or Scamandrius? HERMOGENES: I do not know. SOCRATES: Consider it thus: if someone asked you whether you think the wiser or the less wise impose names on things more correctly? HERMOGENES: I would certainly answer: the wiser. SOCRATES: Do the 

<margin>Homer says he was called Scamandrius by Hector; by others Astyanax.</margin>

women in the cities seem wiser to you, or the men? Insofar as the gender is concerned. HERMOGENES: The men. SOCRATES: Do you not know that Homer says the son of Hector was called Astyanax by the Trojans, but Scamandrius by the women? Since the men were accustomed to call him Astyanax. HERMOGENES: So it seems. SOCRATES: Did not Homer consider the Trojan men wiser than their women? HERMOGENES: I think so. SOCRATES: Therefore, he judged he was more correctly named Astyanax than Scamandrius. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Let us observe what cause he himself brings for this naming. "For he alone," he says, "guarded the city and the long walls for them." <note>A reference to *Iliad* 6.403.</note> Therefore it is fitting, as it seems, to name the son of the Savior <term>anakta</term> <note>original: "ἀκτίωντα" (likely a scribal error for ἄνακτα)</note>, that is, "king of the city"—of the city, I say, which his father saved, as Homer says. HERMOGENES: It seems the same to me as well. SOCRATES: But why this is so especially, I myself do not yet sufficiently understand, O Hermogenes. Do you perceive it? HERMOGENES: No, by Jove. SOCRATES: And yet Homer himself, O good man, imposed the name on Hector. HERMOGENES: For what reason? SOCRATES: Because it seems to me the name <term>Hector</term> is very close to <term>Astyanax</term>; for they signify almost the same thing, and the Greeks think both these names are kingly. For of whatever thing one is an <term>anax</term> <note>Greek: ἄναξ</note>, that is, "king," of the same thing he is also a <term>hektōr</term> <note>Greek: ἕκτωρ</note>, that is, a "possessor" or "holder." For it is established that he dominates, possesses, and holds it. Or perhaps I seem to be saying nothing to you? And am I deceived by the opinion by which I trusted I was reaching Homer's knowledge concerning the correctness of names, as if by certain footprints? HERMOGENES: Not at all, I think; for perhaps you are touching on something. SOCRATES: It is fitting, as it seems to me, to name the son of a lion likewise a lion, and the son of a horse a horse. I certainly do not mean if something like a monster is born from a horse, something other than a horse; but I mean that which is born according to the nature of its kind. For if, against nature, the son of an ox should beget a horse, it is not a calf that is born, but it must be called a horse-foal. And if a horse, contrary to nature, begets a calf, this must not be called a horse-foal, but a calf. Nor if from a human any offspring other than human is produced, should that which is born be called a human. The same is to be judged of trees and of all other things. Do you approve of these things? HERMOGENES: I certainly approve. SOCRATES: Watch me, lest I deceive you. By the same reasoning, if someone is born from a king, he must be named a king; but whether the same thing is signified in different syllables, it matters nothing, nor does it matter if some letter is added or even taken away, as long as the essence of the thing signified remains dominant, shining forth in the name itself. HERMOGENES: How do you say that? SOCRATES: I say nothing strange or new, but just as you see happen in the <term>elements</term> <note>Here referring to the letters of the alphabet.</note>. For you know that we speak the names of the elements, but by no means the elements themselves, with four exceptions: for we say <term>e</term> and <term>u psilon</term> <note>Epsilon and Upsilon ("simple" or "smooth" E and U).</note> and <term>o mikron</term> <note>Omicron ("little" O).</note> and <term>o mega</term> <note>Omega ("great" O).</note>. But for the rest, both vowels and non-vowels, we create names by adding other letters, as in <term>beta</term> <note>Greek: βῆτα</note> adding <term>e, t, a</term> <note>Greek: η, τ, α</note>, and thus we utter them. But as long as we insert the shining power of the element itself, it is fitting to call it by that name which signifies the element to us, as appears in "beta," where, although <term>e, t, a</term> are added, nothing prevents the nature of that element from being shown by the whole name, as the author of names intended; to such an extent did he skillfully give names to the letters. HERMOGENES: You seem to me to speak the truth. SOCRATES: Will not the same reasoning apply to a king? From a king will come a king, from a good man a good man, from a beautiful thing a beautiful thing, and in all others, similarly from any kind another such thing, unless a monster is created, and they must be called by the same names.

<summary>Socrates argues that names have a natural "rightness" rather than being arbitrary, citing Homeric distinctions between divine and human names and explaining the etymological link between Hector and his son Astyanax as "protectors" or "kings." He suggests that while letters or syllables may change, a name is correct as long as it preserves the essence of the thing it names, similar to how the name of a letter (like Beta) contains its primary sound.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Hermogenes, Cratylus, philosophy of language, etymology, Homer, Astyanax, Hector, Protagoras, linguistics, naturalism vs. conventionalism</keywords>

# Cratylus, Or, On the Correctness of Names. 215

...names. However, one may vary them by syllables so that, to an unrefined person, things that are the same seem different. Just as a doctor's medicines, often varied by colors and smells, seem different to us though they are the same; but to a doctor considering the power of the medicines, they are judged the same, and the additions do not confuse him. Similarly, perhaps, one who is learned in names considers their power and is not troubled in his judgment if a letter is added, changed, or removed, or if the same power of the name is found in different and many letters. As with the names we mentioned above, Astyanax and Hector: they have entirely different letters except for the 't' alone, yet they signify the same thing. Likewise, what is called <term>archepolis</term> <note>original: ἀρχέπολις — city-ruler</note>, what commonality of letters does it have with the two above? It signifies the same thing nonetheless. And there are many others that signify nothing but "king." Furthermore, there are many that signify "leader of an army," such as <term>Agis</term>, <term>Polemarchos</term>, and <term>Eupolemos</term>. Others declare a practitioner of medicine, like <term>Iatrocles</term> and <term>Akesimbrotos</term>. Many others can be found, differing in syllables and letters, but entirely harmonious in the power of their significance. Do you think so too, or otherwise? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly so. **SOCRATES:** To these things which occur according to nature, the same names should be attributed. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Whenever, however, men are born contrary to nature in some form of monster—such as an impious man being born from a good and pious man—the one born ought not to receive the name of the father, but the name of the kind to which he belongs. Just as we said before, if a horse produces the offspring of a bull, it should be called a bull, not a horse. **HERMOGENES:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the name of the kind, not the parent, should be attributed to an impious man born from a pious one. **HERMOGENES:** These things are true. **SOCRATES:** It is not fitting, then, to call such a son <term>Theophilus</term> <note>God-lover</note> or <term>Mnesitheus</term> <note>Mindful of God</note>, or any such thing, but to call him by names signifying the opposite, if indeed names are to be correctly established. **HERMOGENES:** It must be done exactly so, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Truly, the name **Orestes** seems correctly imposed, Hermogenes, whether some chance gave him the name or some poet, signifying by that name his beast-like nature, wild and mountain-dwelling. <note>Socrates links Orestes to 'oros' (mountain).</note> **HERMOGENES:** So it appears, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** It seems his father also has a name according to nature. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** **Agamemnon** certainly appears to be such a man who thinks you must labor and endure, and persevere through virtue in the things he has decreed. A proof of his endurance was his long stay at Troy with such a great army. Because this man was of wonderful perseverance, the name Agamemnon signifies it, as if from <term>agastos</term> <note>admirable</note> and <term>menōn</term> <note>remaining/enduring</note>. Perhaps **Atreus** was also correctly named. For the killing of Chrysippus and the cruelty he exercised against Thyestes show him to be harmful and destructive. From this, the name deviates slightly and secretly hints, so as not to declare the nature of this man to just anyone; but to those skilled in names, the significance of Atreus is clear enough. For he is called according to <term>ateires</term>, <term>atreston</term>, and <term>ateres</term>—as if he were indomitable, inexorable, harmful, and insolent. It seems the name **Pelops** was also not given without reason. For that name signifies that the man is worthy of this appellation because he sees what is near. **HERMOGENES:** Why does that fit him? **SOCRATES:** Because in the murder of Myrtilus, as it is told, he could foresee nothing, nor look from afar at how great a calamity was imminent for his whole race. He looked only at what was before his feet and at present things—that is, "looking near"—which he did when he contended with all his effort to enter into marriage with Hippodamia. Hence the name Pelops from <term>pēlas</term> <note>near</note> and <term>opsis</term> <note>vision</note>. Even to **Tantalus**, the name seems correctly and naturally imposed, if the stories circulating are true. **HERMOGENES:** Which ones? **SOCRATES:** That while still living, many grave misfortunes befell him, and finally his whole homeland was overturned. After death, a rock hangs over his head—a most hard fate indeed. These things entirely agree with the name, as if one wanted to name him <term>talantatou</term> <note>most miserable/unhappy</note>, but speaking a little more obscurely, put Tantalus for Talantatus. Such a name his adverse fortune seems to have provided through the rumors of the nations. Furthermore, for his father, whose name is **Jupiter** <note>Zeus</note>, the name is correctly bestowed, yet not easy to know. For the name of Jupiter is like a certain discourse; we divide it in two and use one part or the other. Some call him <term>Zēna</term>, some <term>Dia</term>. <note>Relating 'Dia' to the preposition 'through' (dia) and 'Zena' to 'living' (zēn).</note> These parts joined into one show the nature of the God himself, which is what a name should most be able to do. For there is no cause for living for us and all others more than the prince and king of all. Therefore, this God has received a fitting name, through whom life is always in all living things. But the one name is cut in two, as I was saying, into <term>Dia</term> and <term>Zēna</term>. When someone hears he is the son of **Saturn** <note>Cronus</note>, they might think him insolent and abusive. But it is probable that Jupiter is the offspring of some great intelligence. For when he is called <term>koros</term>, it does not signify "boy," but the purity of his mind and sincere integrity. He is, as is told, the son of **Uranus** <note>Heaven</note>. Indeed, looking to the things above is rightly called <term>horan ta anō</term>, as if "seeing the things above." Hence they affirm, Hermogenes—those who deal with sublime things—that a pure mind is present, and the name was justly imposed on Uranus. If I held the genealogy of the gods handed down by Hesiod in my mind, and remembered which progenitors he introduces, I would not cease to show you that names were correctly inscribed on them, until I had made a trial of this wisdom to see if it accomplishes anything, and whether it fails or not—this wisdom which has suddenly shone upon me from I know not where. **HERMOGENES:** Truly you seem to me, Socrates, like those who are seized by a divine spirit, to be pouring out oracles. **SOCRATES:** I think indeed, Hermogenes, that this wisdom has flowed into me from Euthyphro, son of Pantias. For I stood by him from early morning with constant attention and stretched out my ears. It seems, then, being inspired, he has not only filled my ears with blessed wisdom but has also occupied my soul. Thus I think we should act: today let us use it and investigate the rest that pertains to names. But tomorrow, if we agree, we will expiate it and renounce it, provided we find a man—either a priest or a Sophist—skilled in such expiations. **HERMOGENES:** I highly approve of this, Socrates, for I would most gladly hear what remains concerning names. **SOCRATES:** Let it be done then. Where do you judge we should best begin, now that we have prescribed a formula, so we may know if names themselves testify to us that they were not made by chance, but contain some correctness? The names of heroes and men might deceive us. For many of these are given according to the surnames of ancestors and often do not fit at all, as we said in the beginning. Many, however, are given as if by men wishing...

<margin>The Dialectician knows whether names are correctly imposed on things or not.</margin>

<summary>Socrates provides etymological explanations for the names of heroes like Orestes and Agamemnon and gods like Jupiter and Saturn, suggesting that names reflect the internal nature or history of the person, often influenced by a sudden "divine inspiration" he attributes to Euthyphro.</summary>
