# Book Twenty-three. 216

...men bestow names, such as **Eutychides** <note>son of good fortune</note>, **Sosias** <note>savior</note>, **Theophilus** <note>God-lover</note>, and many others. Therefore, I think such names should be passed over. For it is most fitting and consistent that we find those names which are correctly placed among things eternal and established by the order of nature. For in such things it is most fitting to have studied the founding of names. Perhaps some of them were established by some divine power rather than human. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak excellently, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Is it not right to begin with the gods themselves, and investigate the reason why they are called **gods** <note>original: θεοὶ (theoi)</note>? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, I conjecture this. It seems to me that the ancient Greeks thought the only gods were those whom many of the Barbarians still believe in today: the sun, moon, earth, stars, and sky. When they saw all these things in perpetual motion and running, from this nature of "running" <note>original: θέειν (theein) - to run</note>, it seems they named them "gods" <note>theoi</note>; then, noticing others, they called them all by the same name. Does what I say have some likelihood, or not? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly does. **SOCRATES:** What should be investigated next? **HERMOGENES:** It is clear we should ask about **demons**, **heroes**, and **men**. **SOCRATES:** About demons? And indeed it is so, Hermogenes. What then does the name of demons mean? Notice if I say anything. **HERMOGENES:** Just speak. **SOCRATES:** 

<margin>In the work *Works and Days*.</margin> Do you know who Hesiod says the demons are? **HERMOGENES:** No. **SOCRATES:** Nor even that he says a Golden Race of men existed in the beginning? **HERMOGENES:** This I do know. **SOCRATES:** For he says that from this race, after the fates of the present life, they become "holy demons, earthly, best, expellers of evils, and guardians of men." **HERMOGENES:** What then? **SOCRATES:** Certainly, I think he calls them the Golden Race not because they were made of gold, but because they were good and noble. I conjecture this because he says our race is of iron. **HERMOGENES:** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES:** Don't you think if someone among us now is good, he is estimated by Hesiod to be of the Golden Race? **HERMOGENES:** That is consistent. **SOCRATES:** But are the good anything other than the prudent? **HERMOGENES:** Prudent. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, as I think, he calls them demons especially because they were wise—<term>daēmones</term> <note>original: δαήμονες — knowing/wise</note>. And that name exists from our ancient language. Wherefore he and many other poets speak excellently, whoever say that after a good man has ended his life, he receives the greatest dignity and reward and becomes a demon, according to the surname of wisdom. Thus I too assert that every man who is good is a "demon," that is, wise; and that he is "demonic," that is, happy, while living and dead, and is correctly called a demon. **HERMOGENES:** I seem to agree with you most in this, Socrates. But what does **hero** signify? **SOCRATES:** That is not at all difficult to find, for the name of heroes differs only a little from its origin, indicating that their generation flowed from **love** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔρωτος (apo tou erōtos)</note>. **HERMOGENES:** By what reason do you say that? **SOCRATES:** Are you unaware that the heroes are demigods? **HERMOGENES:** What then? **SOCRATES:** All heroes were born either from the love of gods for human women, or the love of men for goddesses. Furthermore, if you consider this according to the ancient Attic tongue, you will understand more. For you will find it was changed slightly for the sake of the name from <term>eirein</term> <note>to speak</note>, from which the heroes were born: or either the name of heroes was drawn from here, or from the fact that they were wise men and rhetoricians, eloquent indeed, and most ready to question and discuss. For <term>eirein</term> means to speak. Wherefore, as we were just saying, in the Attic voice the heroes seem to be certain rhetoricians, and debaters, and lovers. Hence the race of rhetoricians and Sophists is an heroic offspring. But this indeed is not difficult to know; rather, that is more obscure: for what reason are men called **anthrōpoi**? Do you have something to offer? **HERMOGENES:** From where would I have it, good man? Even if I could find it in some way, I would not try, because I hope you will find it better and more easily than I. **SOCRATES:** You seem to trust in Euthyphro's inspiration. **HERMOGENES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** And you trust rightly. For I seem to myself now to have thought quite beautifully, and there is a danger, unless I am careful, that I might appear to have emerged wiser today than is fitting. Attend to what I say. First, it is fitting to notice about names that we often add letters, and often take them away, while we name things at our whim, and we frequently change the accents, as when we say **Dii philos** <note>Dear to Zeus</note>: so that this might be a name for us instead of a phrase, we removed one 'l' and 'i', and instead of an acute middle syllable, we pronounce a grave one. In some others, we insert letters, and we utter others more heavily. **HERMOGENES:** You speak truly. **SOCRATES:** This also happens in **anthrōpos** <note>Man</note>, as it seems to me. For the name was constituted from a phrase, with one 'a' cast out and the ending made heavier. **HERMOGENES:** How do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Thus that name of man signifies that, while other animals do not consider or notice or contemplate what they see, man both sees and contemplates at the same time, and notices what he sees. Hence, man alone of all living things was rightly called <term>anthrōpos</term>, as if <term>anathrōn ha opōpe</term>—contemplating what he has seen. What shall I seek after this? Perhaps what I would gladly perceive? **HERMOGENES:** By all means. **SOCRATES:** It seems to me the consideration of the **soul** and the **body** should immediately follow. For we call the combination of soul and body a "man." **HERMOGENES:** Without controversy. **SOCRATES:** Let us try to distinguish these as we did those above. Do you think we should first ask about the soul, so that it might be seen if **psychē** was correctly named? Then the body? **HERMOGENES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** To give what occurs to me first: I think those who so called the soul thought especially this—that whenever it is present in the body, it is the cause of its living, providing the power of breathing and cooling; and as soon as that which cools is absent, the body is dissolved and perishes. Hence they seem to have named it <term>psychēn</term>, as if <term>anapsychon</term>—cooling by breathing. But if you please, stay a moment. I seem to see something more probable among those who follow Euthyphro. For they would despise that, I think, and judge it to be something harsh. But see if this will please you. **HERMOGENES:** Just say it. **SOCRATES:** What else but the soul seems to you to contain the body, to carry it, and to make it live and walk? **HERMOGENES:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** Don't you believe Anaxagoras, that the nature of all things is at once adorned and contained by a certain mind and soul? **HERMOGENES:** I certainly believe it. **SOCRATES:** It is right, then, to name that power <term>physhechen</term>, which <term>physin</term> (nature) <term>ochei</term> and <term>echei</term>—that is, carries and contains. But it is more elegantly pronounced <term>psychē</term>. **HERMOGENES:** It is entirely so. **SOCRATES:** And that seems to me more artistic. **HERMOGENES:** It is indeed. **SOCRATES:** But it would appear ridiculous if it were named exactly as it was established. **HERMOGENES:** What follows after this? **SOCRATES:** Do you mean **sōma** (that is, the body)? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And yet it seems to me that in this name there is a slight deviation from the origin. For some say this body is the <term>sēma</term> (tomb) of the soul, as if it were buried in the present time; and also because the soul signifies <note>original: "significat" - links 'soma' to 'sema' (sign)</note> through the body whatever it can signify. Therefore it is justly called <term>sēma</term>. It seems to me besides...

<margin>Dear to Zeus.</margin>

<summary>Socrates explores the etymologies of "gods" (from running), "demons" (from wisdom), "heroes" (from love and speech), and "man" (the one who contemplates what he sees). He also discusses the soul (as the sustainer of nature) and the body (as a tomb or sign).</summary>

# Cratylus, Or, On the Correctness of Names. 217

...besides, that the followers of Orpheus established this name especially because the soul pays the penalties for its sins in this body, and is enclosed by this surrounding wall, as if in a certain prison, so that it might be <term>sōzetai</term> (saved/kept). They want it to be thus, as it is named, a <term>sōma</term> (enclosure) for saving the soul until it has paid all its debts, and they think no letter should be added. **HERMOGENES:** Enough has been said of these things, Socrates, I think. But could we consider the names of some gods, as was done with Jupiter, according to what correctness the names were imposed? **SOCRATES:** By Jove, Hermogenes, if we had any sense, we would consider the chief mode of correctness to be confessing that we know nothing about the gods—neither about them themselves, I say, nor about their names by which they call themselves. For it is clear that they call themselves by true names. But according to the second mode of correct naming, I think that just as the law has established in prayers to address the gods however it pleases them to be named, so we also should call them, as if knowing nothing else. For it seems to me to be rightly decreed. Therefore, if you wish, let us proceed to this investigation, first prefacing to the gods that we shall consider nothing about them—for we do not trust we are able—but rather about men: by what opinion concerning the gods they established the names. This is far from divine indignation. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to speak modestly, Socrates, and it should be done exactly so. **SOCRATES:** Must we not begin with **Vesta** <note>Hestia</note> according to the custom? **HERMOGENES:** That is certainly fitting. **SOCRATES:** For what reason shall we say she was named <term>Hestian</term>? **HERMOGENES:** That is not easily found. **SOCRATES:** Truly, my good Hermogenes, the first authors of names seem not to have been dullards, but sharp investigators of sublime things. **HERMOGENES:** Why? **SOCRATES:** Names appear to have been imposed by the invention of such men. And if one considers foreign names, he will nonetheless find what each one means. Just as what we call <term>esian</term> (essence), some call <term>osian</term>. First, according to one of these names, it seems not far from reason that the essence of things is called **Hestia**. And because we call that which is a partaker of essence <term>esian</term>, from this it could correctly be named **Hestia**. Our ancestors once called <term>esian</term> <term>osian</term>. Furthermore, if one observes the rites of sacrifices, he will judge that those who established these things thought so. For before all gods it is right to offer sacrifices to Vesta <note>Hestia</note> for those who surnamed the essence of all things Vesta. Those who also named her <term>osian</term> judged, almost according to Heraclitus, that all things are always flowing and nothing stands still. Therefore they derived the cause and origin of things from <term>ōthoun</term>, that which impels. Wherefore it is rightly named <term>osian</term>, the impelling cause. Let this much be said of these things, as if by those who understand nothing. After Vesta, it is fitting to consider **Rhea** and **Saturn** <note>Cronus</note>, although we spoke of Saturn's name earlier. But perhaps I am saying nothing. **HERMOGENES:** Why so, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** O good man, I have noticed a certain swarm of wisdom. **HERMOGENES:** What kind? **SOCRATES:** Ridiculous to say. Yet it has something probable. **HERMOGENES:** What probability? **SOCRATES:** I seem to see Heraclitus long ago wisely handing down things about Saturn and Rhea that Homer had also said. **HERMOGENES:** What do you mean? **SOCRATES:** For Heraclitus says that all things flow and nothing remains, comparing the progress of things themselves to the flux of a river; he says it is impossible to step into the same water twice. **HERMOGENES:** These things are true. **SOCRATES:** Does he seem to you to differ from Heraclitus, he who inserted Rhea and **Saturn** <note>Cronus</note> among the progenitors of the other gods? Do you think he randomly imposed the names of both as "flowing"? <note>Socrates links Rhea to 'rhoe' (flow) and Cronus to time or flux.</note> Indeed, Homer established Ocean as the origin of the gods, and Tethys as the mother. And I think Hesiod wanted the same. Besides, Orpheus says that Ocean was the first to begin a beautiful marriage, who mixed with Tethys his sister. See how greatly these things harmonize with each other, and all return to the opinion of Heraclitus. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to be onto something, Socrates. But the name of **Tethys** I do not quite understand. **SOCRATES:** This means almost the same thing; since it is a hidden name for a fountain. For <term>diattomenon</term> and <term>ethoumenon</term>, that is, "bubbling up" and "leaping through," bear the image of a fountain; and from both of these names the name **Tethys** is composed. **HERMOGENES:** This is most beautiful, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Why not? But what next? We have certainly spoken of Jupiter. **HERMOGENES:** So it is. **SOCRATES:** Let us speak of his brothers, **Neptune** <note>Poseidon</note> and **Pluto**, and the other name by which they call him. **HERMOGENES:** By all means. **SOCRATES:** It seems Neptune was called **Poseidōn** by the one who first named him because the nature of the sea detained him as he went and did not permit him to proceed further, but cast as it were chains on his feet. Therefore he called the prince of the sea <term>Poseidōna</term>, as if being <term>posidesmon</term>, that is, having a "chain of the feet." The 'e' was perhaps added for the sake of elegance. Perhaps it does not mean this, but 'm' was first put for 's', as if to say <term>pollaeidōs</term>, that is, a God knowing many things. Perhaps he was named from what is called <term>seiein</term>, that is, to shake—<term>seiōn</term>, meaning "shaking," to which 'p' and 'd' were added. We call **Pluto** as if from <term>ploutos</term>, that is, the giver of wealth, because wealth is dug out from the bowels of the earth. **Hades** however is interpreted as the multitude, as if <term>aeidēs</term>, meaning "sad" or "dark." And those who shudder at this name call him Pluto. **HERMOGENES:** And what do you think, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** It seems to me that men have erred in many ways concerning the power of this God, and have always shuddered at him when it is least fitting. Furthermore, everyone fears this: that no one returns from there after he is dead, and that the soul, stripped of the body, goes there. But all these things—both the kingdom and the name of this god—seem to me to tend toward the same thing. **HERMOGENES:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** I will say what I think; answer me. Which of these is a stronger chain for detaining any animal anywhere: necessity or desire? **HERMOGENES:** Desire, Socrates, is far superior. **SOCRATES:** Would not many flee from **Hades** daily if he did not bind those who descend there with the strongest chain? **HERMOGENES:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore he binds them by a certain desire, it seems, rather than by necessity, if indeed he binds them with the strongest chain. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Again, are there not many desires? **HERMOGENES:** Many. **SOCRATES:** Therefore he binds them with the most vehement desire of all, if indeed he is to connect them with an insoluble knot. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Is there any more vehement desire than that by which one is affected while hoping to become a better man through someone’s company? **HERMOGENES:** By Hercules, none, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** For this reason it must be said, Hermogenes, that no one wants to return from there to here, not even the Sirens themselves, but both they and all others are soothed and as it were bound by the most sweet orations of Pluto. And it is, as this reason testifies, that this god is undoubtedly a most eloquent Sophist, and confers immense benefits on those who dwell with him, who so abundantly overflows with riches that he supplies such great goods to us, whence he was named Pluto. Does it not seem to you the duty of a philosopher and a man...

<margin>*Cronos, that is, time.</margin>

<summary>Socrates analyzes the etymologies of the gods of the elements and the underworld—Vesta (essence), Rhea and Saturn (flux), Neptune (foot-fetter), and Pluto (wealth). He notably describes Hades not as a place of terror, but as a place where souls are bound by the "desire for virtue" and the "eloquent discourse" of the god.</summary>

# Book Twenty-three. 218

...and a man endowed with the highest prudence and counsel, that he does not want to cling to men having bodies, but only admits them when their soul is purged of all bodily evils and desires? Surely this god thought out this reason so he could best detain souls, if he bound them with the greed for virtue. But those who are infected with the stupor and insanity of the body, not even Pluto’s father Saturn himself can restrain with those chains of his and keep them with him. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to be saying something, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** It is far from the truth, Hermogenes, that the name **Hades** was said as if <term>aeidēs</term>, meaning "sad" or "dark"; rather, it is drawn much more from that which is <term>eidenai</term> (that is, to know) all beautiful things. From this, then, this god was named Hades by the establisher of names. **HERMOGENES:** So be it. What besides do we say of the name of **Ceres** <note>Demeter</note>, and **Juno** <note>Hera</note>, **Apollo** and **Minerva** <note>Athena</note>, and **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus</note> and **Mars** <note>Ares</note>, and the other gods? **SOCRATES:** Ceres indeed is called **Dēmētēr** from the very bounty of nourishment, as if <term>hē didousa mētēr</term>, that is, the "giving mother." **Juno** <note>Hera</note> however is <term>eratē</term>, that is, "lovable," because of the love with which Jupiter is affected toward her. Perhaps also he who established this name was looking at the sublime, <term>aera</term> (air); he changed the name and spoke obscurely, putting the beginning at the end. This will be clear to you if you pronounce the name frequently. Some fear to name **Proserpina** <note>Persephone</note> and **Apollo** because the correctness of the names is unknown to them. Indeed, changing it to <term>Pherephattē</term>, it appears grave to them. But this indicates the wisdom of the goddess herself. For wisdom is that which touches and can attain "flowing things." Wherefore she would be rightly named <term>Phersepapha</term> because of wisdom and <term>epaphēn</term> (contact) with that which is carried <term>pheromenou</term>, or something like that. Therefore the wise Hades himself clings to her, because she is such. But now they decline this name, valuing the sound of the pronunciation more than the truth, so they call her <term>Phersephattan</term>. The same also happened concerning the name of **Apollo**. For many shudder at that name as if it brought something terrible. Don't you know? **HERMOGENES:** I know indeed, and you speak truly. **SOCRATES:** But this, as I think, most fits the power of this god. **HERMOGENES:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** I will try to express my opinion. Surely no other single name could have been found more suitable for the four powers of this god, which would both comprise them all and in some way declare his music, prophecy, medicine, and skill in archery. **HERMOGENES:** Open it now. You say that name is something wonderful. **SOCRATES:** It is certainly harmoniously composed and consistent, as it pertains to the God of Music. First, purging and purifications, both according to medicine and according to prophecy, likewise those which are performed with the drugs of doctors and the incantations and expiations of prophets, washings and sprinklings—this one thing they intend: to make a man pure in both body and soul. **HERMOGENES:** Exactly so. **SOCRATES:** Is not the god who purges himself <term>apolouōn</term> and <term>apolyōn</term>, that is, "washing away from evils" and "releasing from evils," which Apollo himself signifies? **HERMOGENES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Insofar as he washes away and releases, as a doctor of such things, he is rightly called <term>apolouōn</term>. But according to divination and the true and <term>haploun</term> (simple), which is the same, we can rightly name him according to the manner of the Thessalians; for they all call this god <term>Haploun</term>. Insofar as he is always <term>aei ballōn ignōtēs esti</term>, that is, "always hitting the mark" when he stretches his bow, he has it always in his power; he can be called <term>aei ballōn</term>, that is, "perpetually aiming and directing." But according to music, one must think of him as one who is called <term>akolouthein</term> and <term>akolouthos</term>, that is, "follower," "companion," and "wife," in which the 'a' as in many other things signifies "together." Here too, 'a' and <term>keleuthos</term> signify the rotation which is performed together and at once in the heavens, which occurs through those things we call <term>polous</term> (poles); and in song <term>harmonia</term>, which we call <term>symphōnion</term> (symphony). Because in these things, as those skilled in music and astronomy hand down, all things are turned together in a certain harmony. But this god presides over harmony as <term>homopolōn</term>, that is, "turning all these together," both among gods and among men. Just as we called <term>homokeleuthon</term> and <term>homopolon</term> (going together and lying together) "following," by changing to 'a', so we named him **Apollo** who was <term>homopolōn</term>, with another 'l' inserted, because it would have been an equivocal and harsh name, which most people suspect in these times because they do not correctly notice the power of this name, and so they fear it as if it signified some destruction. But in truth this name embraces all the powers of this god, as we said above. For it signifies the "simple," the "perpetual archer," the "purifier," and the "converter." But the name of the **Muses** and **music** is drawn from <term>mōsthai</term>, that is, "to seek," and from "investigation" and the "study of wisdom." **Latona** <note>Leto</note> is named from "gentleness," because she is <term>ethelēmōn</term>, that is, "ready and exposed and willing" to provide what anyone asks. Perhaps, as foreigners call her—for many name her <term>Lēthō</term>—the name seems to have been given because she has not a rigid mind but a mild one, therefore <term>Lēthō</term>, as if <term>Leia tis</term>, meaning a "smooth and mild character." **Diana** <note>Artemis</note> is from the fact that she is <term>artemēs</term>, as it were "intact and modest," because of her choice of virginity. Perhaps also as if <term>aretēs istora</term>, that is, "conscious of virtue," the establisher of the name called her. Perhaps Artemis was also called as if <term>aroton misotokos</term>, that is, as if she "hates the union" of man and woman. For either because of one of these things, or because of all such things, the name was established. **HERMOGENES:** What about **Dionysus** and **Venus** <note>Aphrodite</note>? **SOCRATES:** You ask great things, son of Hipponicus. And yet the reason for the names imposed on these is twofold: serious and playful. Seek the serious from others, but nothing prevents me from recounting the playful. Surely the gods are also playful: **Dionysus** is "he who gives the wine" <note>original: ho didous ton oinon</note>, as if <term>Didoinysos</term>, surnamed by a certain joke. Wine however can rightly be called <term>oionous</term> because it makes most of those drinking it lose their minds and <term>oiesthai noun echein</term>, that is, "think they have a mind." Concerning **Venus**, it is not right to fight with Hesiod, but to grant that because of her generation from <term>aphro</term>, that is, from "foam," she is called **Aphrodite**. **HERMOGENES:** But **Minerva** <note>Athena</note>, O Socrates, since you are an Athenian, and **Vulcan** and **Mars**, you will not pass over in silence. **SOCRATES:** It is not at all fitting. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Why one of her names was imposed is not difficult to say. **HERMOGENES:** Which? **SOCRATES:** We call her **Pallas**. **HERMOGENES:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** This name should be thought to have been drawn from "dancing in arms"; furthermore, it will be to lift something from the earth or to carry something in the hands, which we call <term>pallein</term> and <term>pallesthai</term>, that is, to "vibrate," "shake," and "be shaken," and to "dance," and "endure dancing." **HERMOGENES:** Without controversy. **SOCRATES:** Therefore we call her Pallas for this reason. **HERMOGENES:** And rightly. But how do you interpret her other name? **SOCRATES:** You ask about **Athēnan**? **HERMOGENES:** That very one. **SOCRATES:** This is a graver matter, friend: the ancients seem to have thought of Athena as do those who in these times are learned in the interpretations of Homer. For most of these explain Homer’s Athena as if he had fashioned her as "mind" and "thought." And he who found the names felt something similar about her...

He concludes with playful takes on Dionysus and Aphrodite before beginning an analysis of the "mindful" nature of Athena.</summary>

### Cratylus, or, On the Correctness of Names 219

He seems to have perceived this, or even extolled her more highly, as he introduced the **Mind of God**, just as if he said *theonoē* <note>original: "ἡ θεονόη"; a play on "theou noēsis" or divine intelligence</note>, that is, using an "a" instead of an "e" by some foreign custom, and truly removing the "d" and "a." But perhaps not so, but rather *dia noēsis* <note>original: "ἡ διὰ νόησις"</note>, that is, as one who knows divine things, or he called her *ēthonoē* <note>original: "ἡ ἠθονόη"</note> above all others, that is, one who knows divine character. Nor would it be beside the point if we said he wanted to call her *thonoē* <note>original: "ἡ θονόην"</note>, as if she were **intelligence in her character**. He himself later, or perhaps his successors, changed it into something more beautiful, as it seemed, and named her **Athena**.

**HERMOGENES:** What do you say of **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus</note>, whom they name *Hephaistos*?

**SOCRATES:** Do you ask of that noble **knower of light** <note>original: "φάεος ἴστορα"</note>, that is, the guardian of illumination?

**HERMOGENES:** I seem to have asked of him.

**SOCRATES:** This is clear to anyone; he is *phaos* <note>light</note>, and claims to be "kindled." Whence he is called **Hephaestus**, that is, the **guardian of light**.

**HERMOGENES:** Perhaps, unless it seems otherwise to you in some way.

**SOCRATES:** Ask whether it seems otherwise regarding **Mars** <note>Ares</note>.

**HERMOGENES:** I am asking.

**SOCRATES:** If it pleases you, **Ares**, that is, **Mars**, is named according to *arrhēn* <note>original: "Ἄρρην"</note>, that is, **masculine**, and *andreion* <note>original: "ἀνδρεῖον"</note>, that is, **brave**. Furthermore, if you wish, because of a certain rough, hard, and unconquerable nature, and unchangeable, all of which is called *arrhēton* <note>unspoken or unutterable</note>, he was called **Ares**; this also fits a god who is thoroughly warlike.

**HERMOGENES:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** Let us leave the gods now, by the gods I beseech you! For I fear to discourse of them. But challenge me to whatever other things you wish, so that you may know what kind of horses those of Euthyphro are <note>Socrates jokingly refers to the "divine inspiration" he is receiving from the priest Euthyphro</note>.

**HERMOGENES:** I shall do as you ask, if I may ask about one more—for Cratylus denies that I am truly **Hermogenes** <note>The name Hermogenes means "born of Hermes"</note>. Let us investigate what the name **Hermes**, that is, **Mercury**, signifies, so that we may see if Cratylus speaks any truth here.

**SOCRATES:** **Hermes**, that is, **Mercury**, seems to pertain to **speech**, insofar as he is an *hermēneus* <note>original: "ἑρμηνεύς"</note>, that is, an **interpreter** and a messenger, a thief-like seducer in speaking, and a forceful orator. All of that revolves around speech. Indeed, as we said in the earlier parts, *eirein* <note>original: "εἴρειν"</note> is the use of speech. Often Homer says of him, *emēsato* <note>original: "ἐμήσατο"</note>, that is, "he contrived." From both, therefore, the name of this god is composed: both from that which is **to speak**, and from that which is **to contrive** and to think out things to be said, just as if the author of the name commanded us: "It is fitting, O men, that you call that god who *eirein emēsato* <note>contrived to speak</note>, **Hermes**." We, however, thinking to speak more elegantly, call him **Hermes**. Furthermore, **Pan** seems to have his name from *eirein*, that is, to speak, because he is a messenger.

**HERMOGENES:** By my faith, Cratylus seems to have rightly denied that I am Hermogenes. For I am dull when it comes to the invention of speech.

**SOCRATES:** It is also consistent, friend, that **Pan** is the two-formed son of **Mercury**.

**HERMOGENES:** By what reasoning?

**SOCRATES:** You know that **speech** <note>logos</note> signifies *pan*, that is, **all**, and it circles and revolves always, and it is double: namely **true** and **false**.

**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Is not that which is true in speech smooth and divine, dwelling above among the gods? On the other hand, is not the false below among the many of men, rough and tragic? For from here the fictions of myths and many falsehoods regarding the tragic life are found.

**HERMOGENES:** It is entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** Rightly, therefore, he who is *pan*, that is, announcing the whole, and *aei polōn* <note>original: "ἀεί πολῶν"</note>, that is, **always revolving**, would be called *pan aipolos*, the two-formed son of Mercury, smooth and delicate in his upper parts, but rough and goat-like in his lower parts. And **Pan** is speech itself, or the brother of speech, if indeed he is the son of Mercury. And what wonder is it for a brother to be like a brother? But now, O blessed one, as I asked a little while ago, let us break off the discourse about the gods.

**HERMOGENES:** We may leave such gods if you wish, O Socrates, but what prevents us from running through things of this kind? The **sun**, **moon**, **stars**, **earth**, **ether**, **air**, **fire**, **water**, **spring**, and the **year**?

**SOCRATES:** You ask for many and great things. Yet, if it will be pleasing to you, I shall comply.

**HERMOGENES:** It will be very pleasing indeed.

**SOCRATES:** What do you ask first? Or shall it be as you were just saying, first **Helios**, that is, the **sun**?

**HERMOGENES:** Indeed.

**SOCRATES:** It seems it would be clearer if one used the **Doric** name. For the Dorians call it *halion* <note>original: "ἅλιον"</note>, and so he calls it according to *halizein* <note>original: "ἁλίζειν"</note>, that is, from the fact that it **gathers** men into one when it rises. Likewise from the fact that it *aei eilein* <note>original: "ἀεί εἱλεῖν"</note>, that is, **always revolves** around the earth. Furthermore, because it varies by its circuit those things which are born from the earth. To vary <note>poikillein</note> and *aiolēn* <note>original: "αἰολήν"</note> are the same.

**HERMOGENES:** What should be said of **Selene**, that is, the **moon**?

**SOCRATES:** This name seems to press upon **Anaxagoras**.

**HERMOGENES:** Why?

**SOCRATES:** Because it brings to the fore something older, which he recently said: that the moon draws its light from the sun.

**HERMOGENES:** In what way?

**SOCRATES:** Is *selas* <note>original: "σέλας"</note> the same as light?

**HERMOGENES:** The same.

**SOCRATES:** This light is perpetually *neon* and *enon* <note>original: "νέον & ἔνον"</note>, that is, **new and old** around the moon, if indeed the followers of Anaxagoras speak the truth: for shining around it, it is continually renewed. But the "old" is the light of the past month.

**HERMOGENES:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Many call the moon *selaēno-neo-selēna* <note>a compound meaning light-new-moon</note>.

**HERMOGENES:** True.

**SOCRATES:** Because it always has new and old light, it ought rightly to be called *selaēno-neo-selēna*. But now, with the word shortened, it is called **Selene**.

**HERMOGENES:** This is a dithyrambic name, O Socrates. But **Meis**, that is, the **month**, and **Astra**, the **stars**—how do you interpret them?

**SOCRATES:** The month, *meis*, would rightly be named from *meiousthai* <note>original: "μειοῦσθαι"</note>, that is, from **diminishing**. And the stars, *astra*, have the name of *astrapas* <note>original: "ἀστραπάς"</note>, that is, of **flashing**. *Astrapē* <note>lightning</note>, however, because it *ta ōpa anaspā* <note>original: "τὰ ὦπα ἀνασπᾷ"</note>, that is, **draws the sight to itself**, ought to be called *anaspōpē*. Now it is named *astrapē* by a more elegant word.

**HERMOGENES:** From where do the names **Pyr** and **Hydōr**, that is, **fire** and **water**, draw their origin?

**SOCRATES:** I am indeed in doubt; it seems either the Muse of Euthyphro has deserted me, or this is something difficult. Observe, I pray, where I flee in all things about which I doubt.

**HERMOGENES:** To where?

**SOCRATES:** I shall tell you. Answer me: do you yourself know by what reasoning **fire** <note>pyr</note> is named?

**HERMOGENES:** Not by Hercules!

**SOCRATES:** See what I suspect about this. I truly believe the Greeks have many names from **Barbarians** <note>Meaning non-Greeks, specifically Phrygians here</note>, especially those who are under Barbarians.

**HERMOGENES:** To what end?

**SOCRATES:** If someone seeks the correct imposition of these names according to the Greek voice, and not according to that by which the name was invented, he will surely be in doubt.

**HERMOGENES:** That is indeed likely.

**SOCRATES:** Look then whether this name *pyr* <note>fire</note> is barbaric. For it is not easy to accommodate it to the Greek language, and it is established that the **Phrygians** name it thus, declining it only a little, as they do with *hydōr* <note>water</note> and *kynas* <note>dogs</note>, and many other things.

**HERMOGENES:** These things are true.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, one must not tear these apart, since no one can say anything about them. For that reason, I reject those names of fire and water in this way. **Air** <note>aer</note>, however, is so called as if it *airei* <note>original: "αἴρει"</note>, because it **lifts** those things which are around the earth. Or because it *aei thei* <note>original: "ἀεί θεῖ"</note>, that is, it **always flows**, or because a spirit is stirred by its flow. Poets indeed call blasts and winds *aētas* <note>original: "ἀήτας"</note>. Perhaps, therefore, air is said as if "spirit" <note>pneuma</note>, or "flowing spirit," or "flowing blast." Furthermore, I think **Ether** <note>aithēr</note> is to be explained thus: because it *aei thei peri ton aera rheōn* <note>original: "ἀεί θεῖ circa ἀέρα ῥέων"</note>, that is, it **always runs flowing around the air**, for which reason it can be called *aithēr*. **Gē** <note>original: "γῆ"</note>, however, that is, **earth**, expresses the sense more plainly if it is called *gaia*. For *gaia* can rightly be called *gegaasi* <note>original: "γεγάασι"</note>, that is, **mother** or **begetter**, as Homer says. For what is called *gegaasi*, he says, is **born within itself**.

**HERMOGENES:** So be it.

**SOCRATES:** What remains next?

**HERMOGENES:** **Spring** <note>ver</note> and the **year**, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** *Hōra* <note>original: "ὥρα"</note> indeed, that is, the times of spring, in the ancient and Attic voice...

## Book Twenty-three. 220
...spoken of if you wish to know what is fitting. For they are called **Horai** <note>The Seasons</note> because they **bound** <term>horizousi</term>, that is, they terminate winter and summer, the winds, and the fruits born from the earth. **Eniautos** and **etos**, meaning the **year**, seem to be the same thing. For that which brings forth in turn into the light whatever is born and made from the earth, and examines and discerns it within itself, is the year. And as we said above that the name of **Jupiter** <note>Zeus</note> was split in two, called **Zēna** by some and **Dia** by others, so also some call the year **eniautos** because it is in itself, and some **etos** because it scrutinizes and examines. The complete reasoning is that which "examines in itself." From this single phrase, two names were selected. For what is said together as **that which examines in itself** <note>original Greek: "to en hautō etazon"</note> is spoken distinctly as **eniautos** and **etos**, the year. **HERMOGENES:** But truly, O Socrates, you are now progressing far. **SOCRATES:** I seem indeed to be wandering quite far into philosophy. **HERMOGENES:** Quite so. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you will grant more. **HERMOGENES:** Truly, after this sort of thing, I would most gladly contemplate by what reason these noble names of the **virtues** were correctly imposed, such as **phronēsis**, that is, prudence; **synesis**, intelligence; **dikaiosynē**, justice; and all the rest of this kind. **SOCRATES:** You raise a type of name not to be despised, my friend. Nevertheless, since I have put on the **lion’s skin** <note>A reference to Hercules; Socrates means he has taken on a heroic or difficult task</note>, it is not becoming to be deterred; rather, I must consider those noble names of prudence, intelligence, thought, science, and the rest of this sort. **HERMOGENES:** Indeed, we must by no means stop before then. **SOCRATES:** By the dog, I think I am not guessing badly about what I was just considering: namely, that those most ancient authors of names (as has happened to many of our own wise men) fell into a **dizziness of the brain** due to their frequent revolving in the investigation of things. From this, I think, it happened that things themselves appeared to them to be carried along and to waver. They think the cause of this opinion is not an internal dizziness, but an external circuit of the things themselves. They think nature holds things such that nothing in them is firm and stable, but all things flow and are carried along, and are agitated in every way, always being born and flowing away. I see this indeed in these names which have now been cited. **HERMOGENES:** In what way, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Have you perhaps not noticed that the preceding names were imposed on things as if they were being carried along, flowing, and moved by a perpetual generation? **HERMOGENES:** I did not quite perceive it. **SOCRATES:** At the start, the very first one we cited pertains entirely to something of this kind. **HERMOGENES:** Which one is that? **SOCRATES:** **Phronēsis**, which is **prudence**, is the **perception of motion and flux** <note>original Greek: "phoras kai rhoou noēsis"</note>. It can also signify **the benefit of motion** <note>original Greek: "rhoou onēsis"</note>. Finally, it revolves around agitation itself. Furthermore, if you wish, **gnōmē**, meaning **thought**, signifies the **consideration of generation** <note>original Greek: "gonēs nōmēsin"</note>, for *nōmān* means to consider. And if it pleases you, **noēsis**, that is, **intellection**, is the **desire for the new** <note>original Greek: "neou esis"</note>. That things are "new" signifies they are always becoming. And this "desiring things to be" is what it means. For at the beginning, *noēsis* was not said, but instead of *nu*, two *epsilons* were to be pronounced, as *neoesis*, as if an appetite and approach for the **new** <term>neou</term>. **Sōphrosynē**, that is, **temperance**, is the health and preservation of that which we just called **phronēsis**, prudence. **Epistēmē**, that is, **science** or **knowledge**, has this notation: as if the soul, not to be despised, follows flowing things, and neither leaves them far behind nor goes before them. Therefore, with an *epsilon* inserted, it is right to call it **epistēmēn**. **Synesis**, intelligence, seems to be a certain **syllogism**, that is, a reasoning. But when it is said **to understand** <term>synienai</term>, the same is meant as if one said "to know." For *synienai* declares that the soul accompanies things and is at one with them. **Sophia**, that is, **wisdom**, is the touch of agitation. This is somewhat obscure and more foreign to us. But we must observe in the poets how often they wish to express someone arriving and rushing in, they say **esythē**, meaning "he broke out" or "he leaped forth." Indeed, a certain illustrious man among the Spartans had the name **Thouros**, meaning "swift." For thus the Spartans indicate the force of an impulse. Thus, as if all things are carried through, **sophia** demonstrates the **touch** <term>epaphēn</term> and perception of this very agitation, which is signified by that which is called **sousthai** <note>to rush</note>. **Agathon**, that is, the **good** of each nature, signifies **agaston**, meaning "admirable," "lovable," or "delightful." For since all things flow, there is partly speed and partly slowness. Therefore, not everything is swift, but there is something "admirable" of itself. This "admirable" thing is declared by the name of **good** itself. **Dikaiosynē**, that is, **justice**, we can easily guess imports the **intelligence of the just** <note>original Greek: "dikaiou synesis"</note>. But what the **just** <term>dikaion</term> itself means is difficult to know. It seems that up to this point, what has been said is conceded by many, but the rest remains in doubt. For whoever thinks the whole is mobile believes that it is most agitated, and that something permeates through everything by which each thing is made, which must be most thin and swift. For it could not run through all things unless it were so thin that nothing could resist its penetration, and so swift that it uses the rest as if they were standing still. Since, however, it governs all things, it was called **dia ion** <note>"going through"</note>, with an *alpha* inserted for the sake of a more polished pronunciation. So far, what we just said is agreed among many: that this is the "just." But I, O Hermogenes, being inflamed with the desire for learning, have scrutinized all these things, and perceived in the secret mysteries that this "just" is the **cause**. For that by which things are made is the cause; and someone handed down that it ought to be called by that name specifically. But when I gradually inquire from these people I've heard what the "just" itself is, since it is so, I seem to be demanding further than is fitting, and to be "overleaping the wall and the rampart," as they say <margin>Proverb.</margin>. For they say it is enough that I have always asked and heard their answer, and wishing to satisfy me, one brings forward one thing and another another, and they agree no further. One says this "just" is the **sun**. For the sun alone, by running through and heating, governs all things. But when I repeat this eagerly to someone as if it were a noble thing I had heard, he immediately laughs at me and asks if I think that after the sun sets, nothing remains for men? To me, asking what he thought, he said that **fire** itself is the "just." Nor is that easy to know. Wherefore another says, not fire itself, but rather the **heat** innate in fire. Another holds all these things as nothing: that the "just" is that **Mind** which **Anaxagoras** introduced. For he says that she, being mistress by her own nature and mixed with nothing, adorns all things, penetrating through all. Here, my friend, I have fallen into a greater ambiguity than before when I inquired nothing of justice. However, to return to that for the sake of which we dispute, such a name as we have said was attributed to it for these reasons. **HERMOGENES:** You seem, O Socrates, to have heard these things from someone, and not to have clumsily produced them from your own workshop. **SOCRATES:** What of the others? **HERMOGENES:** Not so. **SOCRATES:** Attend then, for perhaps in the rest I might deceive you, as if I had not heard what I bring forward. After justice, what remains? We have not yet completed **andreia**, that is, **fortitude** or **courage**. Indeed, **injustice** <note>in Latin: "iniustitia"</note> is obviously...

--- Page 239 ---
# Cratylus, or, On the Rightness of Names. 221
...the obstacle to that which runs through all things. **Andreia** <note>courage</note> is concerned with battle. Battle among things, if they indeed flow, is nothing other than the contrary flux itself. Therefore, if one subtracts the *alpha* from this name *andreia*, the name that remains, **dreia**, declares the work itself. It is clearly established that fortitude is not just any contrary **rhoē**, that is, flux, but the one opposite to that flux which is beyond the just. For otherwise fortitude would not be praiseworthy. Furthermore, **andreia**, meaning **male**, and **anēr**, **man**, draw their origin from something similar, namely from **anō rhoē**, meaning an "upward flux." **Gynē**, however, that is, **woman**, is as if **gonē**, meaning "fruitful" and "procreative." **Thēlu** is **female**. It is said from **thēlēs**, meaning the **nipple**. And it seems, Hermogenes, that she is called *thēlu* because she makes things **bloom** <term>tethēlenai</term>, that is, germinate and bud, like those things that are irrigated. **HERMOGENES:** So it appears, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** The terms **arrēn**, meaning to grow green, to mature, to bloom, represent the increase of the young, as if something swift and sudden, which he who forged the name hinted at from **anō**, meaning "to run," and **halmesthai**, meaning "to leap." Do you not notice me being carried as if out of the race-course, now that I have found smooth and passable ground? Many things also remain which seem to pertain to serious matters. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** One of which is that we see what **technē**, meaning **art**, imports. **HERMOGENES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** Does this not show **echein noun**, that is, the "habit of mind," if the *tau* is removed, and *upsilon* is inserted between the *chi* and *nu*, and between the *nu* and *eta*, resulting in **echonoē**? **HERMOGENES:** That is quite subtle, Socrates, and unrefined. **SOCRATES:** Do you not know, blessed man, that ancient names have been buried by those fond of tragic speech, who for the sake of elegance add and subtract letters, perverting them everywhere, partly by length of time and partly by a desire for decoration? As for example in **katoptron**, meaning a **mirror**, how absurd is the addition of the *rho*? Such things certainly, I think, are done by those who value an artificial shaping of the mouth more than the truth. Wherefore, since they added much to the names themselves, they finally brought it about that no one now notices the sense of the names. Just as when they utter **sphinga**, meaning the **Sphinx**, when they ought to pronounce **phinga**, and many other things. **HERMOGENES:** These things are indeed so, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, if it were granted to each to both subtract and add at his own discretion, there would surely be great license, and anyone would attribute any name to any thing. **HERMOGENES:** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES:** Plainly true. But it becomes you, as a wise guardian, to maintain a certain moderation and decorum. **HERMOGENES:** O, I wish I could. **SOCRATES:** And I too, O Hermogenes, wish it; but do not, fortunate man, seek too exact a discussion, lest you utterly exhaust my strength. For I shall ascend to the peak of the aforementioned things after we have considered, following "art," **mēchanēn**, that is, **machination** or clever contrivance. It seems to signify the same as to reach far and to ascend. It is composed therefore of these two: **mēkos**, meaning "length" or "much," and **anyein**, meaning "to ascend," "to penetrate," or "to reach." But as I was just saying, we must come to the sum of these sayings, and ask what these names signify: **aretē**, that is, **virtue**, and **kakia**, that is, **vice** or depravity. One indeed I do not yet find, but the other seems open. For it accords with all the previous ones: namely, as if all things go, **kakōs ion**, that is, "going badly," will be **kakia**. Wherefore, when the soul approaches things badly, it will commonly be called depraved. Specifically and most greatly, this faculty of proceeding is open in **deilia**, that is, **cowardice**, which we have not yet declared. For we passed it over. It was necessary to bring it in immediately after fortitude itself. We seem to have passed over many other things besides. **Deilia** signifies a hard **bond** of the soul. For **desmos** is a bond. And **lian** signifies something very strong and hard. Wherefore cowardice is a vehement and greatest bond of the soul; just as **aporia**, meaning "lack," "poverty," or "doubt," is a certain evil, and in summary whatever is an impediment to progress itself, and it seems to show "going badly," namely being impeded and detained in motion itself. When the soul undergoes this, it is said to be full of depravity. In the first place indeed, the impulse of a good soul ought to be an easy and agile progress, and then a free and unhindered one. Wherefore, without impediment and obstacle, that which is **always flowing** <note>original Greek: "aei rheon"</note> could rightly be nicknamed **aretē**. But perhaps someone also calls it **airetē**, because it is the **most choiceworthy choice** <note>original Greek: "hē hairesis hairetōtatēs"</note>. But it is named **aretē** with the word compressed. Perhaps you will say I am inventing; but I assert that if that name of depravity which I cited was correctly introduced, then this name of virtue is also correctly introduced. **HERMOGENES:** But **kakon**, meaning **evil**, through which you said many things in the preceding parts, what does it mean? **SOCRATES:** Something miraculous, by Jove, and difficult to see; as it seems to me, at least. Therefore, I shall bring forward that same "machination" from before for this too. **HERMOGENES:** Which one? **SOCRATES:** I will say that this too is something **barbarian**. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to speak rightly. **SOCRATES:** But let us now let these go if it pleases you, and let us consider these names **kalon** and **aischron**, that is, **beautiful** and **ugly**, how correctly they are fashioned. What **aischron** <note>ugly</note> hints at seems plain enough to me. Namely, it agrees with the previous ones. It seems he who established the names everywhere blamed the impediment to agitation. As for example, he gave the name **aeischoroun** to that which **always hinders the flux** <note>original Greek: "aei ischon to rhoun"</note>. Now, by compressing it, they call it **aischron**. **HERMOGENES:** What of **kalon**, that is, **beautiful**? **SOCRATES:** This is more difficult to know, although it is so deduced that the *alpha* was lengthened only for the sake of harmony and length. **HERMOGENES:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** This name seems to be a certain nickname for **thought**. **HERMOGENES:** Why do you say that? **SOCRATES:** What do you think is the cause of the naming of each thing? Is it not that it attributed names? **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Is not this cause thought, whether of gods, or of men, or of both? **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore **kaloun**, meaning "that which calls" things, and **kalon**, are the same as thought. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Whatever mind and thought do are to be praised; what they do not, are to be blamed. **HERMOGENES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** That which partakes in medicine effects the works of medicine; that which partakes in the smith’s art, the works of the smith. What do you think? **HERMOGENES:** The same. **SOCRATES:** Beautiful things, therefore, produce beautiful things. **HERMOGENES:** It is fitting. **SOCRATES:** And this is, as we said, thought. **HERMOGENES:** Most greatly. **SOCRATES:** The name **kalon**, therefore, will rightly be a nickname for **prudence**, doing such things as we, affirming them to be beautiful, love. **HERMOGENES:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** What besides of this kind remains to be investigated? **HERMOGENES:** Those things which look toward the good and the beautiful: namely **conferring**, **useful**, **profitable**, **emoluments**, and their contraries. **SOCRATES:** What **sympheron**, that is, **conferring**, is, you will find yourself if you consider it from the previous things. For it appears to be something kindred to that name which pertains to science. For it displays nothing other than **phoran**, meaning the **motion** of the soul together with things, which are called **sympheronta** and **symphora**, that is, "conferring," from the fact that they are **carried around together** <term>symperipherontai</term>. **HERMOGENES:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** **Kerdaleon**, however, that is...

## Book Twenty-three. 222
...**emolument** or **gain**, comes from **kerdos**, meaning **lucre**. **Kerdos** indeed, if one inserts *nu* instead of *delta* into this name, expresses what it wants. For it names the **good** in another way. For because it is **mixed** <term>kerannutai</term> with all things, diffused through everything, he devised that name signifying this very power of its, placing *nu* for *delta*, and pronounced it **kerdos**. **HERMOGENES:** But what of **lysiteloun**, meaning **useful**? **SOCRATES:** It seems, O Hermogenes, that this is not called **lysiteloun** as shopkeepers do, because it **avoids and diminishes expense** <term>analōma apolyei</term>; rather, because being most swift, it does not allow things to stand still, nor does it permit the motion **to stand** <term>stēnai</term>, that is, to receive an end of progress and to cease; but it always releases it from that and puts it to flight, if any limit should come upon it, and renders it unending and immortal. For this reason I think the good was called **lysiteloun**. For it seems to be called *lysiteloun* because it is **loosening the end** <note>original Greek: "lyon to telos"</note> of motion. **Ōphelimon**, meaning **conducive** or **helpful**, is a foreign name which Homer used many times. It is a nickname for increasing and making. **HERMOGENES:** What is to be said of their contraries? **SOCRATES:** Those which are said by the negation of these, it is by no means necessary to treat. **HERMOGENES:** Which are those? **SOCRATES:** **Asymphoron** <note>unprofitable</note>, **anōpheles** <note>useless</note>, **alysiteles** <note>unhelpful</note>, **akerdes** <note>gainless</note>. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** But **blaberon** and **zēmiōdes**, meaning **harmful** and **damaging**. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** **Blaberon** indeed is said to be **harming the flux** <note>original Greek: "blapton ton rhoun"</note>. To **harm** <term>blaptein</term> signifies **wishing to fasten** <note>original Greek: "boulomenon haptein"</note>, that is, what wants to impede and coerce. **Rhoun** means **flux**. He everywhere blames this; and that which wants to **fasten the flux** <note>original Greek: "haptein ton rhoun"</note> would rightly be called **blapteroun**. But for the sake of ornament, I think it was named **blaberon**. **HERMOGENES:** Various names occur to you, O Socrates. Indeed, you seem to me at present as if you were singing a prelude to the Palladian law when you pronounced this name *blapteroun*. **SOCRATES:** I am not the cause, Hermogenes, but those who established the name itself. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. But what is **zēmiōdes**? **SOCRATES:** I will tell you what **zēmiōdes** <note>damaging</note> ought to be, Hermogenes: and see how truly I speak whenever I say that by adding and subtracting letters, they vary the sense of names greatly, so much so that often by changing a tiny thing, it induces a contrary significance. This appears in this name **deon**, meaning **opportunely** or **as is binding**. This just came to my mind while thinking of what I am about to tell you. Indeed, that noble word is recent to us, and it forced **deon** and **zēmiōdes** to sound contrary to us, confusing the sense itself. But the ancient name explains what each wants. **HERMOGENES:** How do you say that? **SOCRATES:** I shall tell you. It does not escape our elders that they frequently used *iota* and *delta*, nor less frequently the women, who especially preserve the ancient speech. But now instead of *iota* they use either *epsilon* or *eta*; and for *delta*, they use *zeta*, as if these sound more magnificent. **HERMOGENES:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** As for example, the most ancient men called the day **himera**; later ones call it partly **hēmera**, and partly—indeed at this time—**hēmera**. **HERMOGENES:** These things are true. **SOCRATES:** You know therefore that by that ancient name only the mind of him who imposed the name is declared. For from the fact that light flashed out from the shadows for men **who yearn** <term>imeirousin</term> for it and rejoice, they nicknamed the day **hēmera**. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** But now you might by no means understand what that **hēmera** chanted by the tragedians means. Although some think it is called **hēmera** because it makes things **gentle** <term>hēmera</term>. **HERMOGENES:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** Nor does it escape you that the ancients called **zygon**, meaning a **yoke**, **duogon**. **HERMOGENES:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** Indeed **zygon** signifies nothing. But **lysiteloun**, **lysiteloun agathon**, meaning the **conduction of two** for the sake of binding together, shows it. And the same is to be judged of many others. **HERMOGENES:** It is evident. **SOCRATES:** By the same reasoning, **deon**, so pronounced, shows the contrary of all names that look toward the good. Furthermore, if there are species of the good, **deon** <note>here meaning "binding"</note> seems to be a **desmos**, that is, a bond and an impediment to progress, just like **blaberon**, meaning **harmful**, is something kindred. **HERMOGENES:** So it appears most greatly, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** But not so in the ancient name, which is more likely to have been correctly established than ours. Indeed, it will agree with the previous goods if you restore the ancient *delta* for *zeta*. For not **deon**, but **dion** signifies that good which the inventor of names always praises. And thus he does not disagree with himself; rather, they look toward the same thing: **deon**, **dion**, **ōphelimon**, **lysiteloun**, **kerdaleon**, **agathon**, **sympheron**, **euporon** <note>meaning "easy for progress"</note>. This whole set hints at something penetrating through all things and adorning everything by various names, and that everywhere praised; but what blocks and detains, it disapproves. Furthermore, in this name **zēmiōdes**, if you place *delta* for *zeta* after the manner of the ancients, it will appear to you that this name was imposed as **dēloun ton**, that is, **to one who binds and stays** that which proceeds. Hence it was nicknamed **zēmiōdes**. **HERMOGENES:** What of **hēdonē**, **lypē**, **epithymia**—namely **pleasure**, **pain**, **desire**—and the rest of this kind? **SOCRATES:** They do not seem very obscure to me, Hermogenes. **Hēdonē**, that is, **pleasure**, is the name of that action which tends toward **onēsin**, meaning **utility** and emolument. But the *hē* added makes it so that instead of *onēsis*, it utters **hēdonē**. **Lypē**, that is, **pain**, seems to be drawn from **dialyseōs**, meaning the **dissolution** of the body. For in such a passion the body is dissolved. **Ania**, that is, **sadness**, demonstrates that which impedes **ienai**, meaning **to go**. **Algēdōn**, that is, **torment**, seems a foreign name, said from **algēnos**. **Odynē**, that is, **pain** and affliction, is named from **endyseōs**, meaning the **entrance** of pain. **HERMOGENES:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** **Achthēdōn**, that is, **sorrow** and languor, signifies the weight and slowness of motion. For **achthos** is a burden, and **ion** is "going." **Chara**, that is, **joy** and gladness, is said from **diachyseōs**, meaning the **profusion** of **eunoias**, "goodwill," and **rhoēs**, the "motion" of the soul. **Terpsis**, that is, **delight**, is drawn from **terpnō**, meaning "pleasure." But **terpnon** is from **pnoē**, meaning the **inspiration** of delight into the soul. Therefore it would rightly be called **herpnoun**, meaning **inspiring**. But by the interval of time, it came to be **terpnon**. **Euphrosynē**, that is, **hilarity** and alacrity—there is no need to assign why it is said. For it is plain to anyone that this name is drawn from that which is called **eu**, meaning "well," and **sympheresthai**, meaning "to follow together," as if it were said that the soul "well attains things." Hence it ought to be called **eupherosynē**; yet we call it **euphrosynē**. But it is not difficult to assign what **epithymia**, that is, **desire**, means. Indeed, this name shows a force tending into the **thymon**, meaning the **soul**, and anger, and fury. **Thymos**, however, is from **thyseōs** and **zeseōs**, meaning the **flagrancy**, fervor, and impulse of the soul. Therefore **himeros**, that is, **sweet and bland persuasion**, is said because the **flux** <term>rhoou</term> vehemently allures the soul. For from the fact that it **flows incited** <note>original Greek: "hiemenos rhei"</note> and desiring things, it vehemently attracts the soul because of the impulse or incitement of the flux. From this whole force **himeros** was named. Furthermore, it is called **pothos**, that is, **longing**, which surely does not signify a present sweetness, as does *himeros*, but...

### Cratylus, or, On the Rightness of Names

...but he burns for the absent one. Whence *pothos* [longing] is so called, as if *apothos*, that is, the concupiscence for what is absent. The same [feeling] which in itself is mixed into that which is pleasing to the soul is called *himeros* [desire] when that which is desired is present, but is named *pothos* when it is absent. Moreover, *erōs*, that is love, [is so named] because it *eisrō*, that is, it flows in from without; nor is that *rhoē*, that is, that flux, innate to the one possessing it, but is infused through the eyes. For which reason, from *eisrō*, that is, to flow in, *erōs*—that is, "influxion"—was called love by our ancestors. For they used to use *o* [omicron] for *ō* [omega]. Now, however, it is called with *ē* [eta] instead of *o*, with *ō* interposed.

But what should be considered next as most important? *Doxa* [opinion], that is, opinion, and certain such things: from whence do they have their name? **SOCRATES:** It is said from *diōxis* [pursuit], or from *diōkein*, that is, from the persecution [pursuit] by which the soul proceeds and follows, investigating the condition of things; or it is named from *toxou bolē*, that is, the shot of a bow. It seems, however, rather to depend upon the latter. *Oiēsis* [estimation], that is, estimation, accords with this. For it shows *oisis* [bearing/carrying], that is, the ingress of the soul into each thing to be considered, *oion*, that is, of what kind it might be; just as *boulē* [counsel/will], that is, will, is said from *bolē*, that is, a shot; and *boulesthai*, that is, to wish, because of that very effort of reaching, signifies also *ephesis* [aiming/desire], that is, to desire; and *boulesthai*, that is, to deliberate. 

All these things following after opinion seem to be images of *bolē* itself, that is, of the shot and the effort: just as the contrary, *atychia* [misfortune/failure], that is, the privation of will, appears to be a certain failure of attaining, being powerless, as if they do not contend, nor does one obtain what he intends, wishes, desires, and investigates. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to be heaping these up quite frequently, O Socrates. Therefore, let there be an end now, God willing. Yet I still wish *anankaion* [necessary] and *hekousion* [voluntary], that is, the necessary and the voluntary, to be declared. For indeed these follow upon the previous ones. 

**SOCRATES:** *Hekousion*, indeed, is *eikon* [yielding], that is, yielding and not resisting. For by this name is declared *agon tō ionti*, that is, yielding to that which goes, or that which is performed out of will. *Anankaion*, however, that is, the necessary and resisting—since it is contrary to the will—will be concerned with error and ignorance. Moreover, it is derived from the process according to necessity, because in a rough way, thickets [Latin: *densa*]¹ prohibit the passage. Whence it was called *anankaion*, as if *an’ ankē ion*, that is, going through a valley. Truly, as long as our strength lasts, let us not abandon it. Therefore, ask, I pray, and do not cease. 

**HERMOGENES:** Behold, I ask about those things which are greatest and most beautiful: *alētheia* [truth], that is, truth, and *pseudos* [falsehood], that is, a lie, and *to on* [being], that is, being, and why that about which we are dealing here is called *onoma* [name], that is, a name. 

**SOCRATES:** What do you call *maiesthai*? **HERMOGENES:** I call it indeed "to seek." **SOCRATES:** This name [name] seems to be composed from that speech by which it is said *on*—that is, that being is—of which "name" is the investigation. Which you will certainly understand more clearly in that which we call *onomaston*, that is, "to be named." For here it is expressed what a name is: namely, an investigation of being. *Alētheia* [truth], however, just like the others, seems to be contracted and composed. For the divine motion of being is included in this name, *alētheia*, as if being *theia alē*, that is, a certain divine wandering. *Pseudos* [falsehood], however, is the contrary of motion. Again, here is used the obstacle to agitation, or that which compels one to stand still. For it is said from *katheudein*, that is, "I sleep." The *ps* [psi] added, however, hides the sense of the name. But *to* [the] and *deon* [binding/fitting], that is, being and essence, agree with *dion*, that is, with truth, if *i* [iota] be added. For it signifies *ion*, that is, "going." But *ouk on*, that is, non-being, some name *ouk ion*, that is, "not going." 

**HERMOGENES:** You seem to me, O Socrates, to have discussed these things quite bravely. But if someone should ask you what the correct interpretation is of those things which are called *dikaion* [just], that is, "going"; *deon* [fitting], that is, "flowing"; *blaberon* [harmful], that is, "binding and detaining," what shall we answer him especially? Do you have it? **SOCRATES:** I have it indeed now...

***
*(Page 224)*

...so indeed. **SOCRATES:** But after we wished to declare it by voice, tongue, and mouth, will not the demonstration then finally be made through these, if an imitation is made through them concerning anything? **HERMOGENES:** I think it is necessary. **SOCRATES:** A name, therefore, is, as it appears, an imitation of the voice, by which whoever imitates something, imitates and names it through the voice. **HERMOGENES:** The same seems so to me as well. 

**SOCRATES:** And yet, by Jove, I do not yet think it has been correctly stated, O friend. **HERMOGENES:** Why? **SOCRATES:** Because we would be compelled to admit that these imitators of sheep and cocks and other animals name the very things which they imitate. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Does this deter you? **HERMOGENES:** Not at all. But what sort of imitation, O Socrates, will a name be? 

**SOCRATES:** Not such an imitation as that which is made through music, although it is made by the voice, nor even of the same things of which music is an imitation; for we do not seem to name by musical imitation. But I say it thus: voice, figure, and color are present in many things. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** It seems to me that if someone should imitate these, the faculty of naming does not consist around those imitations. For these are partly music, and partly indeed painting, are they not? **HERMOGENES:** Clearly. 

**SOCRATES:** What of this? Do you not think there is an essence to each thing, just as to color and the others which we mentioned above? Or is there not in color and voice a certain essence, and in all other things whatsoever that are worthy of the appellation of "being"? **HERMOGENES:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** If someone were able to imitate the essence of each thing by letters and syllables, would he not declare what each thing is? **HERMOGENES:** Most greatly indeed. **SOCRATES:** Whom will you say this person is? The former ones you called partly a musician, partly a painter; but what will you call this one? **HERMOGENES:** This one seems to me, O Socrates, to be the "author of naming" whom we have long been seeking. 

**SOCRATES:** If this is true, we must now consider those names which you required: *rhoē*, that is, flux; *ion*, that is, to go; *schesis*, that is, detention—whether by their letters and syllables they truly imitate the essence, or not. **HERMOGENES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** Come, let us see whether these alone are the primary names, or whether there are others besides these. **HERMOGENES:** I think there are others indeed. **SOCRATES:** It is consistent. But what is the method of distinguishing from whence the imitator begins to imitate? Is it not since the imitation of essence is made by letters and syllables, that it is best first to distinguish the elements? Just as those who give labor to rhythms first distinguish the powers of the elements, then of the syllables, and finally they approach the rhythms themselves, and not before. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** And must we not also first distinguish the vocal letters [vowels], then the rest according to their species, the mutes and semi-vowels? For so learned men speak in these matters; and again the vowels themselves, yet not the semi-vowels, and the species of the vowels themselves differing from each other. And after we have well discerned all these things, we must again bring in the names, and consider if there are things to which all are referred, just like elements, from which it is possible to know both the things themselves, and if species are contained in them in the same way as in the elements. All these things having been diligently considered, one must know how to assign each thing according to its similarity, whether one thing to one thing in that manner, or many to be mixed with each other: just as painters, wishing to express a likeness, sometimes apply only the color purple, sometimes any other color, and sometimes mix many, as when they wish to fashion an image of a man as similar as possible, or some other such thing, insofar as each image requires certain colors. In no other way do we also [apply] the elements...

***
*(Page 229)*

### Critias, or, The Atlantic

...between us that [things] are to be learned and sought not from names, but rather from themselves. **CRATYLUS:** So it appears, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Let us also notice this besides, lest these many names tending toward the same thing deceive us, since those who imposed them thought that all things always run and flow, and they established them with that consideration. It seems to me indeed that they thought so: truly they, as if having fallen into a certain vertigo, are themselves wavering and tossed about, and they plunge us, dragging us into the same. 

Consider, O wonderful Cratylus, what I often dream: whether it must be said that there is something that is itself the Beautiful and the Good, and each of the existing things thus, or not. **CRATYLUS:** To me indeed, O Socrates, it seems to be so. **SOCRATES:** Let us therefore consider that thing itself: not if a certain face or something of such a kind is beautiful—since all these things flow—but do we say the Beautiful itself does not always remain such as it is? **CRATYLUS:** It is necessary. **SOCRATES:** Is it possible to name it rightly, if it always escapes, and first to say what it is, then of what kind it is? Or is it necessary, while we are speaking, that it immediately becomes something else and continually flows away, and is no longer such? **CRATYLUS:** Necessary. 

**SOCRATES:** In what way will that thing be anything, which never stays in the same state? For if it stays in the same state for a time, in that time while it so stays, it is clear that it is not changed at all; but if it always stays in the same state, and exists as the same, how does it pass away or move, since it does not desert its own idea? **CRATYLUS:** In no way. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, it would be known by no one. For while the power of knowing approached it, it would become something else and foreign; therefore what it is or of what kind could not be known. For no knowledge perceives a thing in such a way that it perceives it as having no state. **CRATYLUS:** It is as you say. 

**SOCRATES:** But neither is it to be affirmed that knowledge itself exists, O Cratylus, if all things fall away and nothing remains. For if knowledge does not fall away from being knowledge, it will remain always, and will always be knowledge; but if the species of knowledge itself departs, it will simultaneously fall into another species of knowledge, and it will not be knowledge. Because if it perpetually migrates, it will always not be knowledge. And by this reason, neither that which is to know, nor that which is to be known, will always exist. 

But if that which knows always is, and that which is known is, and the Beautiful is, and the Good is, and finally each of the existing things—the things we are now speaking of—they do not seem to me to be similar to flux or motion. Whether these things are so, or as the followers of Heraclitus and many others say, cannot easily be discerned. Nor is it the part of a man of very sound mind to trust himself and his soul to names, and to assert that the author of names is wise, and thus to feel ill concerning himself and all things, as to think that nothing exists whole and firm, but that all things flow and collapse like earthen vessels, and just as men sick with rheum of the head judge that the things themselves are similarly affected, so that all things are comprised by rheum and flux. 

Perhaps, O Cratylus, it is so, or perhaps it is otherwise; therefore the matter must be investigated with a brave soul and diligent study. For one must not easily assent. You are still young, and your age is sufficient. And if you find anything by searching, you ought to impart it to me also. **CRATYLUS:** I will give my effort, Socrates. And certainly know that even at present I am not sluggish; on the contrary, to me thinking and revolving many things in my mind, it seems much more as you yourself were saying, than as Heraclitus said. **SOCRATES:** Afterward, friend, after you have returned, teach me. Now, however, as you have decided, go into the field. And Hermogenes here will accompany you. **CRATYLUS:** It shall be as you advise, Socrates. But you also now think on these things.

***
*(Page 232)*

### Gorgias of Plato, or, On Rhetoric

**CALLICLES, SOCRATES, CHAEREPHO, GORGIAS, POLUS.**

*(Margin: The occasion of the dialogue. A proverb: We have come too late after the feast.)*

**CALLICLES:** So when one goes to war and battle, O Socrates, they say one ought to linger. **SOCRATES:** Have we come "after the feast," as is commonly said, and are we present too late? **CALLICLES:** Indeed, a most pleasant feast. For Gorgias has just now set forth many and excellent things for us. **SOCRATES:** This Chaerepho, O Callicles, was the cause of this tardiness, who compelled us to draw out a delay in the forum. **CHAEREPHO:** That shall be no inconvenience indeed, O Socrates; for I will apply a remedy, since Gorgias is a friend to me, who—whether now or at another time—will demonstrate the same things to us. **CALLICLES:** What, O Chaerepho? Does Socrates desire to hear Gorgias? **CHAEREPHO:** For that very reason indeed we were present. **CALLICLES:** Whenever, therefore, it shall please you to enter to me, it will be permitted; for Gorgias is staying with me, who will open and explain what you desire. **SOCRATES:** You speak well, Callicles. But would he be willing to discuss with us at present? For I desire to inquire from him what the force and power of his art is, and what he himself professes and teaches...

*   **Proper Nouns:** All names (Socrates, Hermogenes, Cratylus, Gorgias, etc.) have been retained.
*   **Abbreviations:** Common Renaissance Latin abbreviations (e.g., *ꝙ* for *quod*, *ꝑ* for *per*, *cõ* for *com/con*) have been expanded into full words.
*   **Greek Passages:** The Greek words provided in the OCR (often with Latin phonetic explanations) have been translated or transliterated according to the context of the etymological discussion.
