# Book Twenty-Three. 224

**SOCRATES:** Quite so. But after we have decided to express things through the voice, the tongue, and the mouth, will the manifestation not be completed only when an imitation of a thing is made through these means? **HERMOGENES:** I think that is necessary. **SOCRATES:** A name, then, as it appears, is an imitation of the voice; whoever imitates something by means of their voice, imitates and names it. **HERMOGENES:** It seems the same to me. **SOCRATES:** And yet, by Jove, my friend, I do not yet think this has been stated correctly. **HERMOGENES:** Why is that? **SOCRATES:** Because we would be forced to admit that those who imitate sheep, roosters, and other animals are "naming" the very things they imitate. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Do you think that is fitting? **HERMOGENES:** Not at all. But what kind of imitation, Socrates, will a name be? **SOCRATES:** Not the kind of imitation produced through music, even if it is done with the voice; nor is it an imitation of the same things that music imitates, for we do not seem to "name" things through musical imitation. Let me put it this way: voice, figure, and color belong to most things. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** It seems to me that even if someone imitates these things, the faculty of naming does not reside in those imitations. For those are partly the domain of music and partly the domain of painting. Is that not so? **HERMOGENES:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** What about this? Do you not think there is an essence <term>essentiam</term> <note>the fundamental nature or "what-it-is-ness" of a thing</note> for each thing, just as there is for color and the other things we mentioned? Does there not exist a certain essence in color and voice, and in all other things that are worthy of the name of "being"? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** If someone were able to imitate the essence of each thing using letters and syllables, would he not declare what each thing actually is? **HERMOGENES:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** What would you call such a person? You called the others "musician" or "painter"; what will you call this one? **HERMOGENES:** This person, Socrates, seems to be the one we have long been seeking: the author of naming. **SOCRATES:** If this is true, we must now consider those names you were demanding: **rhoēs** <note>original: ῥοῆς; meaning flux or flow</note>, that is, "flow"; **ienai** <note>original: ἰέναι; meaning to go</note>, that is, "to go"; and **staseōs** <note>original: στάσεως; meaning detention or rest</note>, that is, "stopping"—whether they truly imitate the essence with letters and syllables, or not. **HERMOGENES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** Come, let us see if these are the only primary names, or if there are others besides these. **HERMOGENES:** I believe there are others. **SOCRATES:** That is consistent. But what is the method of distinguishing where the imitator begins to imitate? Since the imitation of essence is done through letters and syllables, is it not better to first distinguish the elements? Just as those who work with rhythms first distinguish the powers of the elements, then of the syllables, and finally approach the rhythms themselves, and not before. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Must we not also first distinguish the vowels, then the rest according to their types—the mutes and the semivowels? For that is how learned men speak of them. And again, distinguish the vowels themselves, as well as the semivowels, and the different types of vowels from one another. And after we have distinguished all these well, we must then bring in the names and consider if there are things to which they all refer—just like elements, from which one can know the names themselves—and if types are contained within them in the same way as in elements. Having carefully considered all these things, one must know how to apply each one according to similarity, whether it is one thing for one, or many to be mixed together. Just as painters, wishing to express a likeness, sometimes use only purple color, sometimes any other color, and sometimes mix many, such as when they want to paint a man's image to be as similar as possible, or something else of this sort, as each image requires certain colors. In the same way, we shall accommodate the elements to things, one for one, wherever it seems most needed. We will produce "conjectures" <term>symballein</term> <note>original: συμβάλλειν; to throw together or compare</note>, which they call syllables. When we have joined these and constituted names and verbs from them, we will again construct something great, beautiful, and whole from those names and verbs. And just as the composite whole in painting is called an "animal," so we shall call this whole context "speech," whether produced by the skill of naming, or rhetoric, or any other art that accomplishes this. Indeed, it is not we who will do this; for I have exceeded the mode of speaking. For the ancients fashioned them this way, if it was so established. But we must, if we are to consider them skillfully, think it out by distinguishing all these things—whether the primary and subsequent names are placed as is fitting, or not. Otherwise, we must see how to connect them, friend Hermogenes, lest there be an error. **HERMOGENES:** Perhaps, by Jove, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Do you trust that you yourself can distinguish them so? For I distrust my own ability. **HERMOGENES:** Then I distrust mine much more. **SOCRATES:** Shall we give up then? Or shall we try as best we can? Even if we can know little of these things, let us approach it, just as we did a little earlier when speaking of the gods: acknowledging that we understand nothing of the truth, we only conjecture the opinions of men about them. So let us proceed now, telling ourselves the same thing—that if these things had to be distinguished perfectly, either by someone else or by us, they should have been distinguished in this way. But now, as they say, it will be proper for us to treat these things according to our strength. Do you accept this? Or what do you say? **HERMOGENES:** I think exactly so. **SOCRATES:** I think it will seem ridiculous, Hermogenes, that things are made manifest through an imitation made of letters and syllables. Yet it is necessary; for we have nothing better than this to look toward in order to judge the truth of the primary names. Unless, perhaps, just as the tragic poets flee to the "machines" <note>the "deus ex machina" crane used in Greek theater</note> of the gods whenever they are in doubt, we too should settle the matter quickly by saying that the gods established the first names, and therefore they were rightly instituted. Is this the best argument for us? Or the one that says we received them from certain barbarians? For barbarians are older than us; or perhaps because of their antiquity, they cannot be discerned, and so appear barbarian? These are evasions—and very clever ones—for those who do not wish to give an account of the correct imposition of the primary names. For whoever is ignorant of the correct rationale for primary names cannot know the subsequent ones. Furthermore, these later ones must be explained by the earlier ones, yet he is ignorant of those. Rather, it is necessary that before professing skill in the subsequent names, one should have grasped the antecedents much more perfectly and be able to show them. Otherwise, one must know that he will talk nonsense regarding the subsequent ones. Or do you think otherwise? **HERMOGENES:** Not otherwise, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** What I have felt regarding the primary names seems to me quite unusual and even ridiculous, and I will share it with you if you wish. If you find anything better, share it with me in turn. **HERMOGENES:** I will do so. But speak now with a brave heart. **SOCRATES:** In the beginning, the word **rhein** <note>to flow</note> itself seems to be the instrument of all motion. We have not said why motion is called **kinēsis**, but it is clear that it wants to be **kisis**, that is, "a going." For we used to use the letter *eta* rather than *epsilon*. The origin is from **kiein**, meaning "to go," which is a foreign word and signifies **ienai** <note>to go</note>. Therefore, if its ancient name were found translated into our voice, it would be rightly called **kiesis**. But now, from the foreign word **kiein**, and by the change of its *eta* and the insertion...

--- Page 243 ---
# Cratylus, or, On the Rightness of Names. 225

...of the letter, it is called **kinēsis** <note>motion</note>. It ought to have been called **kiein oisin** or **asin**. **Stasis** <note>standing/rest</note>, however, wants to be the negation of **ienai** <note>to go</note>, but for the sake of ornament, it is named **stasis**. Therefore, the element **rho** <note>the letter R</note> seemed to the author of names to be a suitable instrument for motion, as I just said, to express the likeness of movement; thus, he uses **rho** everywhere to express motion. In the very first place, in **rhein** and **rhoē**, meaning "flow," he imitates movement through the letter **rho**; then in **tromos**, meaning "tremor," and **trachys**, "rough." Likewise in words of this sort: **krouein** "to strike," **thrauein** "to wound," **erybein** "to drag," **ereiptein** "to break or weaken," **kermatizein** "to cut into pieces," and **rhymbō** "to vacillate, stir up, or whirl around." He fashions all these mostly through **rho** for the likeness of motion. I pass over the fact that the tongue does not linger at all when pronouncing this letter, but rather is moved most violently. Therefore, he seems to have used **rho** primarily for the expression of these things. He also used **iota** <note>the letter I</note> for thin things that penetrate most easily through everything. Therefore, he imitates **ienai** and **hiesthai**, meaning "to go" and "to proceed," through **iota**. Just as through **phi**, **psi**, **sigma**, and **zeta**, which are letters of more vehement breath, the author of names expresses such things as **psychron** "cold," **zeon** "fervent," **seiesthai** "to be shaken," and generally **seismon**, meaning "concussion or quaking." Whenever the founder of names wants to imitate something vehement and full of breath, he uses such letters for the most part. Furthermore, he seems to have judged the compression of **delta** <note>D</note> and **tau** <note>T</note>, and the retraction of the tongue as if it were sticking, to be very suitable for expressing the power of binding and standing still. And because in pronouncing **lambda** <note>L</note> the tongue especially slides forward, he named things from that likeness, such as **leia** "smooth," **olisthanein** "to slide," **kollōdes** "sticky or liquid," **liparon** "fatty," and others of this sort. Because the letter **gamma** <note>G</note> restrains the sliding tongue, by inserting it he formed **glischron** "slippery/gluey," **glyky** "sweet," and **gloiōdes** "viscous or muddy." Noticing also that the sound of **nu** <note>N</note> is held deep in the throat, he used it to name **to endon** and **ta entos**, meaning "that which is within" and "things that are internal," so that the letters would represent the reality. He assigned **alpha** <note>A</note> to **megalō**, meaning "great," and **eta** <note>long E</note> to **mēkei**, meaning "length," because they are large letters. In the name **strongylon**, meaning "round," needing the letter **omicron** <note>O</note>, he mixed in **epsilon** <note>short E</note> for the most part. By the same logic, the author of names seems to accommodate the rest to individual things according to letters and syllables, establishing a sign and a name, and from these, he then constitutes the remaining types through similarity. This, Hermogenes, seems to me to be the correct rationale for names, unless Cratylus here has something else to offer. **HERMOGENES:** Indeed, Socrates, Cratylus here has often caused me trouble, as I said from the beginning, by asserting that there is a certain correct rationale for names, but he does not explain what it is, so that I cannot discern whether he is being obscure on purpose or not. Therefore, Cratylus, say now in the presence of Socrates whether the things Socrates says about names please you, or if you can offer something more excellent. If you can, bring it into the open, so that you may either learn from Socrates or instruct us both. **CRATYLUS:** Does it seem easy to you, Hermogenes, to perceive and teach anything in such a short time, let alone so great a matter, which is considered one of the greatest of the great? **HERMOGENES:** Not to me, by Jove; rather, I think Hesiod spoke wisely when he said it is worthwhile <margin>In Book 1 of Works [and Days]</margin> to add a little to a little. Therefore, if you are able to accomplish anything, even if small, do not be reluctant, but help this Socrates, and me as well. **SOCRATES:** Truly, Cratylus, I would not assert any of the things I mentioned above as certain. Indeed, I have investigated this with Hermogenes just as it seemed best at the time. Therefore, if you have anything better, dare to express it, as I will be glad to accept what you say. For I would not wonder if you had something more excellent than these. Furthermore, you yourself seem to have considered such things and learned them from others. If you say something more excellent, count me as one among your disciples regarding the correct rationale for names. **CRATYLUS:** Certainly, Socrates, as you say, these things have been a care to me, and perhaps I might make you a disciple. Yet I fear the matter may be quite the opposite. It is fitting for me to say to you now what Achilles says to Ajax in the sacred poems <margin>Iliad</margin>. "Noble Ajax," he says, "son of Telamon, prince of the people, you have spoken everything according to my own mind." So you too, Socrates, seem to prophesy according to our mind, whether you were inspired by Euthyphro, or whether some Muse, long dwelling within you, has now suddenly stirred you. **SOCRATES:** O good Cratylus, I too have long admired my own wisdom, yet I do not trust it too much. Therefore, I think I must examine what I say. For to be deceived by oneself is most grave; it is a very dangerous thing when the deceiver is never absent but always accompanies the deceived person closely. One must therefore frequently look back at what was said before, and as that poet says, "look before and behind." So let us see what we have said. We said the correct rationale for a name is that which shows what kind of thing each thing is. Do we assert that this has been sufficiently stated? **CRATYLUS:** To me it clearly seems so, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Are names therefore spoken for the sake of teaching? **CRATYLUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And do we not say that this is an art, and that there are craftsmen of it? **CRATYLUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Who? **CRATYLUS:** Those whom you called from the beginning the founders of laws and names. **SOCRATES:** Does he think this art is present in men just like other arts, or otherwise? This is what I want to know: are some painters worse and some more excellent? **CRATYLUS:** There are. **SOCRATES:** Do the more excellent not make their works more beautiful—namely, the figures of animals—while the others do the opposite? And do not builders likewise make houses, some more beautiful, some uglier? **CRATYLUS:** So it is. **SOCRATES:** And do not the authors of laws themselves make their works some more beautiful, some uglier? **CRATYLUS:** I no longer admit that. **SOCRATES:** Do you not think, then, that some laws are better and others worse? **CRATYLUS:** No. **SOCRATES:** Nor do you think, apparently, that one name is imposed better and another worse. **CRATYLUS:** Not that either. **SOCRATES:** Therefore all names are rightly placed? **CRATYLUS:** At least those that are names. **SOCRATES:** What about the name of this Hermogenes that was mentioned a little while ago? Should we say that this was not imposed on him, unless the name "of the race of Hermes" <note>original: ἑρμοῦ γενεᾶς; Hermogenes' name literally means "born of Hermes"</note> belongs to him? Or was it imposed, but not rightly? **CRATYLUS:** I do not think it was imposed at all, Socrates, but that it seems to be his, while it is actually the name of someone else whose nature matches what is contained in the name. **SOCRATES:** Does he not lie, then, whoever says he is Hermogenes? For it is not to be doubted that he *calls* him Hermogenes, even though he is not. **CRATYLUS:** On what basis do you say that? **SOCRATES:** Does your argument consist in the idea that it is impossible to speak falsehoods? Many people, friend Cratylus, both now and in the past, have asserted this. **CRATYLUS:** How, Socrates, while someone says what he says, could he say that which is not? Is not speaking falsely saying things that "are not"? **SOCRATES:** This is a more excellent argument, friend, than my condition...

# Book Twenty-Three. 226

...and age demand. Nevertheless, tell me: does it seem to you that someone could not *speak* falsely, but could *talk* falsely? **CRATYLUS:** Not even talk. **SOCRATES:** And also neither speak, nor name, nor greet? Just as if someone met you and, taking your hand by the right of hospitality, said: "Greetings, Athenian guest, Hermogenes son of Smicrion." Would he be speaking those things, or said to be talking, or saying, or greeting, or naming—not you, indeed, but this Hermogenes, or no one at all? **CRATYLUS:** It seems to me, Socrates, that this man is shouting in vain. **SOCRATES:** But I ask, does he who shouts so shout truths or falsehoods? Or partly true, partly false? For even this would suffice. **CRATYLUS:** I would say he is making a sound, moving himself to no purpose, as if someone were striking bronze. **SOCRATES:** Consider, Cratylus, whether we agree in any way. Do you not say the name is one thing, and that which the name belongs to is another? **CRATYLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And do you admit that a name is a certain imitation of the thing itself? **CRATYLUS:** Most of all. **SOCRATES:** And that paintings are, in another way, imitations of certain things? **CRATYLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Come now, perhaps I do not quite understand what you are saying, but you might be speaking rightly. Can we attribute both these imitations—paintings and names—to the things of which they are imitations, or not? **CRATYLUS:** We can. **SOCRATES:** Notice this first: could someone attribute the image of a man to a man, and the image of a woman to a woman, and so on in other cases? **CRATYLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And what about the opposite: the image of a man to a woman, and that of a woman to a man? **CRATYLUS:** That too. **SOCRATES:** Are both such distributions "right"? Or rather only the one that attributes to each what is proper and similar? **CRATYLUS:** The latter, it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** Lest you and I, being friends, fight over words, notice what I say. I call such a distribution in both imitations—both names and paintings—"right." And in names, I call it not only right, but "true." But the other distribution, which attributes the dissimilar, I call "not right," and in names, I call it "false." **CRATYLUS:** But look, Socrates, lest perhaps this can only happen in paintings—that someone might distribute poorly—but in names it is not possible, and it is necessary to always assign them rightly. **SOCRATES:** What are you saying? How does this differ from that? Is it not possible that someone meeting a man might say, "This is your figure," and show him perhaps the figure of that man, or perhaps even that of a woman? To show, I say, to offer it to the senses of the eyes. **CRATYLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And again, meeting the same man, might he say, "This is your name"? For a name is a certain imitation, just like a figure. I say it this way: will it not be permitted for him to say, "This is your name," and then pour into his ear the imitation of a male, saying that he is a man; or perhaps the imitation of a certain human female, saying that he is a woman? Does it not seem to you that this can sometimes happen? **CRATYLUS:** I am willing to grant you this, Socrates; let it be so. **SOCRATES:** You do well, friend, if indeed it is so. For we need not fight much about that now. Furthermore, if there is a certain partition in these things, we call one "speaking truly" and the other "speaking falsely." If this happens, and we can incorrectly distribute names and give to each what is not proper, it will likewise be possible to err in verbs. And if we can heap up verbs and names in this way, it must be the same for sentences. For a sentence, I believe, is a composition of verbs and names. What say you to this, Cratylus? **CRATYLUS:** You seem to speak correctly. **SOCRATES:** Moreover, if we refer the primary names to the letters themselves by a certain imitation, it can happen in these just as in paintings, where it happens that we use all the appropriate figures and colors. And likewise, where we do not use all, but add some, subtract others, and show more or fewer. Can this not happen? **CRATYLUS:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** He who attributes all convenient things produces beautiful letters and images. But he who adds or takes away also makes letters and images, but bad ones. **CRATYLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** But he who imitates the essence of things through letters and syllables—by the same logic, if he attributes all competent things, does he not produce a beautiful image? And that exists as a name. But if he falls short in a few things or sometimes exceeds, an image will indeed be produced, but not a beautiful one. Therefore, some names will be well instituted, and others the opposite. **CRATYLUS:** Perhaps. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps, then, one will be a good craftsman of names, and another a bad one. **CRATYLUS:** Surely. **SOCRATES:** And was not the name for this person "the founder of names"? **CRATYLUS:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** There will be, therefore, in this art as in others, one good founder of names and another not good, provided our previous points hold. **CRATYLUS:** These things are true. But you see, Socrates, whenever we attribute these letters—alpha, beta, and any element—to names through the art of grammar, if we take anything away, or add, or even change, we are writing a name, but not correctly. Indeed, we are not writing it at all, but rather it immediately becomes something else as soon as it suffers any of these changes. **SOCRATES:** We must see, Cratylus, lest perhaps we are considering it incorrectly in this way. **CRATYLUS:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Perhaps whatever must consist of a certain number suffers what you say, like the number ten or any other number. For any number, if anything is added or taken away, immediately becomes another. But perhaps the rationale for the correctness of a quality or an image is not the same, but different. For an image does not need to have everything that the thing it is an image of has, if it is to be an image. Notice if I am saying something: will these be two things—namely, Cratylus and his image—if some god not only expressed your color and figure, as painters do, but also made all the internal parts similar to yours, with the same softness, warmth, motion, soul, and wisdom, and to put it briefly, fashioned all things exactly as they are in you? Would one of these be Cratylus and the other the image of Cratylus? Or would they rather be twin Cratyluses? **CRATYLUS:** Two Cratyluses, Socrates, I think. **SOCRATES:** Do you see, friend, that another kind of correctness for an image must be sought than what we said a little before? And that we should not force it so that if anything is added or taken away, it is no longer an image? Do you not perceive how much is missing from images, so that they do not have the same things as those of which they are images? **CRATYLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Something ridiculous would happen to things from names, Cratylus, if they were made exactly similar to them. For all things would become twins, and no one would be able to tell which was which. **CRATYLUS:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, noble man, admit frankly that one name is placed well and another poorly; and do not force names to contain every letter, so that they are entirely such as the thing they name. Rather, allow that sometimes an incongruous letter is brought in; and if a letter, then a name similarly in speech; and if a name in speech, then speech that is by no means fitting for things may be attributed, and the thing itself will nonetheless be named and spoken of, so long as the figure of the thing being spoken of is present, just as in the names of the elements that Hermogenes and I mentioned just now, if you remember.

--- Page 245 ---
# Cratylus, or, On the Rightness of Names. 227

**CRATYLUS:** I remember indeed. **SOCRATES:** Well said, by Hercules! Therefore, whenever this [figure] is present, although not all fitting parts are present, it will be said "well" when all are there, and "badly" when few are. Let us stop saying it is not "said," blessed one, lest like those who wander around Aegina at night and finish their journey too late, we too seem to have arrived at the truth of things much later than we should. Or at least, find some other correct rationale for a name, and do not confess that a name is a declaration of a thing made by letters and syllables. Furthermore, if you say both these things, you will not be able to be consistent with yourself. **CRATYLUS:** You seem to me to speak rightly, Socrates, and so I grant it. **SOCRATES:** Since we agree on these things, let us discuss what remains. If a name must be well placed, we said that appropriate letters must be in it. **CRATYLUS:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** And it is fitting that letters similar to things should be in it. **CRATYLUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, those that are rightly placed are placed כך. But if something is not rightly placed, for the most part it consists of appropriate and similar letters, if indeed it is an image; but it also has something inappropriate, because of which it is not right, nor is the name rightly instituted. Do we say it thus, or otherwise? **CRATYLUS:** I think, Socrates, there is nothing to contend: for it does not please me to say it is a name, but not rightly placed. **SOCRATES:** Does this not please you—that a name is a declaration of the thing itself? **CRATYLUS:** That pleases me. **SOCRATES:** But do you not think it was well said that names are partly constituted from primary ones, and partly are primary themselves? **CRATYLUS:** Well said. **SOCRATES:** Truly, if primary names must be declarations of certain things, do you have a more convenient way for that to happen than if they become such as the things they are meant to declare? Or does that mode rather please you which Hermogenes and many others teach—that names are certain conventions and declarations, and signs for those who so constituted them and already knew the things; and that the correct rationale of a name consists in convention, and it makes no difference whether one decides as it is now established, or the opposite? For example, that **o**, which is now called "small o" <note>omicron</note>, should be named "great o" <note>omega</note>, and the **ō**, which is now "great o," should be called "small o"? Which of these modes pleases you more? **CRATYLUS:** It is altogether better, Socrates, to refer by similarity to what one wants to show, than by any other way. **SOCRATES:** You speak wisely. If a name is similar to a thing, is it not necessary that the elements from which the primary names are composed be by their very nature similar to things? I put it this way: could someone ever have fashioned the painting we mentioned above, making it similar to any thing, unless the very colors of which the image consists were by nature similar to the thing the painter's study imitates? Is it not impossible? **CRATYLUS:** Plainly impossible. **SOCRATES:** By the same reasoning, names themselves would never become similar to anything unless those things of which names are composed had some similarity to those things of which the names are elements. **CRATYLUS:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** Now you be a participant in the argument in which Hermogenes was just now. Did we not try to say correctly that the letter **rho** fits motion, movement, and roughness? **CRATYLUS:** Correct to me, indeed. **SOCRATES:** And that **lambda** fits the smooth and soft, and the other things we recounted? **CRATYLUS:** Surely. **SOCRATES:** Do you know that the same thing—that is, roughness itself—is called **sklērotēs** by us, but **sklērotēr** by the Eretrians? **CRATYLUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Do both these, **rho** and **sigma**, seem to belong to the same family, and do they show the same thing—both to them through the termination of **rho**, and to us through **sigma**—or does one of them declare nothing to us? **CRATYLUS:** Clearly it demonstrates it to both. **SOCRATES:** Insofar as **rho** and **sigma** are similar, or insofar as they are dissimilar? **CRATYLUS:** Insofar as they are similar. **SOCRATES:** Are they entirely similar? **CRATYLUS:** Regarding movement, indeed, they signify equally. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, regarding the letter **lambda** inserted [in *sklērotēs*], why does it not signify the opposite of roughness? **CRATYLUS:** Perhaps it was not rightly inserted, Socrates, just like those things you were treating in the earlier part with Hermogenes, when you both took away and inserted letters where it was most appropriate. And you seemed to me to do rightly. And now, perhaps instead of **lambda**, **rho** should be applied. **SOCRATES:** You speak well. But what about this: as we speak now, do we not perceive anything from one another when someone pronounces **sklēron** <note>hard</note>? Do you not understand what I am saying now? **CRATYLUS:** I understand indeed, my friend, through custom <term>consuetudinem</term>. **SOCRATES:** When you say "custom," what else do you think you are saying besides "convention"? Do you call it custom for any other reason than that when I pronounce this, I think of that, and you perceive what I am thinking? Is this not what you say? **CRATYLUS:** This very thing. **SOCRATES:** If you know it while I am pronouncing it, a declaration is made to you through me. **CRATYLUS:** So it is. **SOCRATES:** Manifestly by means of something dissimilar to what I, thinking, bring forth; since the **lambda** itself is dissimilar to that which you call **sklērotēta**, that is, roughness. If this is so, then both dissimilar and similar letters represent things to you because of the acquisition of custom and convention. But if custom were not convention, it could not yet be rightly said that declaration is made by similarity; rather, one should say it is custom. Indeed, custom declares through both similarity and dissimilarity. With these things conceded, Cratylus (for I will take your silence as a concession), it is necessary that custom and convention contribute something to the expression of those things we feel and speak. For if you wish, excellent man, to descend to the consideration of numbers, how do you hope you will find names so proper that you can attribute a similar name to each individual number, if you do not permit your concession and convention to have some authority regarding the rationale of names? I too like the idea that names should be similar to things as much as possible. Yet I fear perhaps, as Hermogenes was saying, that the use of this similarity is in some way thin, and we are forced to use this "burdensome" thing—convention—for the correct rationale of names; since then perhaps it would be spoken best according to our strength, when we speak with either entirely or mostly similar (that is, fitting) elements, and most foully when the opposite. But tell me this besides: what power do names have for us, and what beauty do we assert is produced through them? **CRATYLUS:** Names seem to me to teach, Socrates, and it should be stated simply: that whoever knows the names also knows the things. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps, Cratylus, you are saying something like this: that when someone has learned what the name is like—and it is such as the thing is—he will also recognize the thing itself, since the thing is similar to the name. For the art is one and the same for all things similar to one another. You seem to have been led by this logic to say that whoever knows names will also know the things themselves. **CRATYLUS:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Come, let us see what this mode of teaching things is that you are now describing, and whether there is another besides it, though this one be held superior, or no other besides this one; which of these do you think? **CRATYLUS:** This certainly: that there is no other, but this one alone is best. **SOCRATES:** Do you think the things themselves are discovered in such a way that whoever discovers names also finds those things which...

--- Page 246 ---
228 Book Twenty-Three.

...the names belong to? Or should one rather seek and discover some other way, and learn this one? **CRATYLUS:** Most of all, according to those points, this very way is both to be sought and found. **SOCRATES:** Come, let us consider it this way, Cratylus: if someone, while investigating things, follows the names themselves and attends to what each one wants to be, do you see how great a danger of deception he undergoes? **CRATYLUS:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Because he who first established the names fashioned them, as we were saying, according to how he thought things were. Is it not so? **CRATYLUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** If he did not perceive correctly, and instituted them as he perceived, do you not think those who follow in his footsteps will be deceived? **CRATYLUS:** It is not so; rather, it is necessary that he who established the names was a knower. Otherwise, as I said long ago, they would not be names at all. This can be the most evident argument for you that the author of names did not wander from the truth: that if he had perceived poorly, all things would by no means harmonize with one another. Have you not noticed yourself, when you said that all things tend toward the same point? **SOCRATES:** That defense, good Cratylus, is worth nothing. For what is surprising if the founder of names, having been deceived at the first, pulled the subsequent things back to the first one by a certain force and compelled them to harmonize with it? Just as in geometric figures, sometimes when a certain first small point is unknown and false, the many subsequent parts then harmonize with each other. For every man <margin>About establishing a principle, one must delay much.</margin> ought to delay much and consider most diligently regarding the establishing of any principle of a thing, whether he decides correctly or not. Once that is sufficiently examined, the rest ought to follow the principle. I wonder, however, if names truly harmonize with themselves. Let us consider again what we related above. We said that names signify essence as if all things were running, being carried along, and flowing. Do you think they signify so? **CRATYLUS:** Certainly so; and rightly indeed. **SOCRATES:** Let us see, then, repeating some of them. First, this name **epistēmē** <note>knowledge</note> is ambiguous, and seems to signify more that the **gnōmē** <note>judgment/mind</note> **stops** <note>original: sistit</note> the soul in things, rather than being carried around together with things. And it seems to be more correct that we should call its principle, as we do now, **epistēmēn**, rather than **ōipēmēn** by the ejection of the **iota**; and we should rather add the **epsilon**. Then **bebaion**, meaning "firm," is so called because it is an imitation of **basis** and **stasis**, meaning "foundation" and "standing," rather than of motion. Furthermore, **ischousa** <note>holding/restraining</note> perhaps signifies that which **stops the flow** <note>original: sistit fluxū</note>; and **pistin** <note>faith/belief</note> itself signifies **histan** <note>to make stand</note>, meaning to make firm. Moreover, **mnēmēn** <note>memory</note> shows entirely that in the soul there is not motion and agitation, but **monē**, that is, "rest" and stable permanence. And if someone observes the names themselves, **hamartia** <note>error/sin</note> and **symphora** <note>contingency/misfortune</note> will seem to bring in the same as **oiēsis** <note>imagination/opinion</note> and **epistēmē** <note>knowledge</note>, and the other names that are imposed on excellent things. Likewise **amathia** <note>ignorance/stupidity</note> and **akolasia** <note>intemperance</note> seem very close to these. **Amathia** indeed seems to import the progress of one **going together with God** <note>original: simul cū deo euntis progressum</note>. **Akolasia** truly signifies a certain **following** <note>original: akolouthian</note> or gathering of the things themselves. And so, what we think are names for the foulest things will appear very similar to those names that concern the most beautiful things. I think many other things can be found, if someone applies himself to these, from which he will judge again that the author of names indicates not running and carried things, but stable ones. **CRATYLUS:** Nevertheless, Socrates, you see that he constituted many names according to the significance of agitation. **SOCRATES:** What shall we do, Cratylus? Shall we count the names themselves like votes or pebbles? And shall we judge the correct rationale of names by this norm—so that those are finally true which the majority of names support by their significance? **CRATYLUS:** That would not be fitting. **SOCRATES:** Certainly not, friend. But these things being now omitted, let us see whether you confess these things to us in this way, or not. Come, did we not a little while ago confess that those who imposed names in individual cities, both Greek and Barbarian, were **onomathetai**, that is, founders of names, and that the art which contains this faculty is the craft of name-founding? **CRATYLUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Now then, did the first name-founders impose the first names while knowing the things on which they were imposing them, or while being ignorant? **CRATYLUS:** Knowing them, as it seems to me at least, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** For they could not have done so while ignorant, friend Cratylus. **CRATYLUS:** Not in my opinion. **SOCRATES:** Let us return to where we digressed. You said just now, if you remember, that it is necessary for the one who established names to have foreknown those things to which he gave names: do you still persist in that opinion, or not? **CRATYLUS:** Still. **SOCRATES:** Do you say that even he who placed the first names knew them while he was placing them? **CRATYLUS:** He knew them. **SOCRATES:** From what names had he either learned or discovered the things, when the first names had not yet been instituted? Since it was said to be impossible to either find or learn things unless we have learned what the names are like, or found them ourselves? **CRATYLUS:** You seem to me, Socrates, to be saying something significant. **SOCRATES:** In what way, then, shall we say they placed the names while knowing? That the name-founders existed before the placing of any name, and that they knew the things beforehand, if indeed things cannot be learned otherwise than from names? **CRATYLUS:** I think, Socrates, that the most true argument is that which says a certain power more excellent than human gave the first names to things, by which it is necessary that they were rightly distributed. **SOCRATES:** Do you think the author of names—if indeed some Demon or God existed—placed things contrary to himself? Or does it seem to you that we have said nothing above? **CRATYLUS:** Perhaps one of those [sets of] names was not yet established. **SOCRATES:** Which ones were they then, excellent man? Those that verge toward stability? Or those toward motion? For, as we just said, it will not be judged by the multitude. **CRATYLUS:** So it is fitting, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Since, therefore, names dissent and contend with one another regarding the truth, and both these and those assert they are closer to the truth, by what norm shall we judge? Where shall we turn? For we shall not flee to other names, because there are none besides these. Rather, some other things besides names must be sought, which may show us without names which of these are true—things, that is, showing the truth of things. **CRATYLUS:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** If these things are true, Cratylus, it seems that things can be perceived without names. **CRATYLUS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Through what else do you especially hope to perceive the things themselves? Is it not through that which is consistent and fitting? Through their mutual communion—that is, if they are in some way related to one another—and especially through themselves. For that which is other than them signifies something other, not them. **CRATYLUS:** You seem to speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Tell me, I pray: have we not already often confessed that names which are rightly placed are similar to those things of which they are names, and are images of things? **CRATYLUS:** We have clearly confessed it. **SOCRATES:** If, then, it is permitted to learn things through names, and also through themselves, which will be the more excellent and clearer perception? Is it if one thinks from the image—and considers both whether the image itself is rightly expressed, and the truth of which it is an image? Or rather if one learns from the truth—both the truth itself and its image—to see if the image was fittingly instituted for it? **CRATYLUS:** If from the truth. **SOCRATES:** By what rationale things are to be grasped, whether through teaching or through discovery, seems to be a work of greater genius than yours or mine. But let it suffice now...

<summary>In this section of the Cratylus, Socrates and Cratylus debate whether names are naturally "correct" imitations of things or products of social convention. Socrates argues that while names are intended to be imitations of a thing's essence, they are often imperfect images, and that true knowledge must ultimately come from studying things in themselves rather than through the potentially flawed medium of language.</summary>

->Critias, or, The Atlantic. 229<- <note>original: "Critias, Vel, Atlanticus." Although the heading mentions the Critias, the text is actually the conclusion of the Cratylus. Such misprints or mislabeled headers were common in early printed editions of Plato.</note>

...we have agreed between us that things are to be learned and sought not from names, but rather from themselves. **CRATYLUS:** So it appears, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Let us also consider this further, lest these many names tending toward the same point deceive us—since those who established them thought that all things are always running and flowing, and established them with that consideration. Indeed, it seems to me they thought so; however, if their opinion was such, it must be held as false. Truly, they have fallen into a kind of dizziness, and they themselves waver and are tossed about, dragging us along and submerging us in the same state. Consider, wonderful Cratylus, a thing I often dream of: whether we should say there is something that is the "Beautiful itself" and the "Good itself," and each of the existing things likewise, or not? **CRATYLUS:** To me, Socrates, it certainly seems to be so. **SOCRATES:** Let us therefore consider that "itself"—not whether a certain face or something of that sort is beautiful, for all these things flow—but do we say the Beautiful itself remains always as it is? **CRATYLUS:** It must. **SOCRATES:** Is it possible to name it correctly if it always slips away? Can we first say what it is, and then of what quality it is? Or is it necessary that, while we are speaking, it immediately becomes something else and continuously flows away, and is no longer such as it was? **CRATYLUS:** It is necessary. **SOCRATES:** How then can that be something which never stays in the same state? For if it ever stays in the same state, in that time while it stays so, it is clear that it does not change at all. But if it always stays the same way and exists as the same thing, how does it pass away or move, since it does not abandon its own form? **CRATYLUS:** In no way. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, it would be known by no one. For while the power of knowing approached it, it would become something else and foreign. Therefore, what it is or of what quality could not be known. For no knowledge perceives a thing in such a way that it perceives it as having no state at all. **CRATYLUS:** It is as you say. **SOCRATES:** But neither should we affirm that knowledge itself exists, Cratylus, if all things fall away and nothing remains. For if knowledge does not fall away from being knowledge, it will remain always, and always be knowledge. But if the very form of knowledge departs, it will simultaneously fall into another form of knowledge, and there will be no knowledge. But if it perpetually migrates, there will always be no knowledge. And by this reasoning, neither that which is to know, nor that which is to be known, will ever exist. But if there is always that which knows, and that which is known, and the Beautiful exists, and the Good exists, and finally each of the existing things exists, then those things we are presently describing do not seem to me to be like a flow or a localized motion. Whether these things are so, or as the followers of Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus was a pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the doctrine that "everything flows" (panta rhei).</note> and many others say, cannot be easily discerned. Nor is it the part of a man of sound mind to entrust himself and his soul to names, and to assert that the author of names was wise, and thus to feel so poorly about himself and all things as to think that nothing is whole or firm, but that all things flow and collapse like pottery; and just as men sick with head-catarrhs <note>An old medical term for a "cold" or "running nose." Socrates uses the physical "flow" of a sick person's mucus as a metaphor for the philosophical theory of universal flux.</note>, he judges that things themselves are similarly affected, so that everything is encompassed by dripping and flux. Perhaps, Cratylus, it is so, or perhaps it is otherwise; therefore, the matter must be investigated with a brave spirit and diligent study. For one must not easily give assent. You are still young, and your age is sufficient for the task. And if you find anything in your searching, you ought to share it with me. **CRATYLUS:** I will do my best, Socrates. And know for certain that even now I am not idle; rather, to me as I think and revolve many things in my mind, things seem to be much more as you were saying than as Heraclitus says. **SOCRATES:** Then, my friend, teach me after you return. For now, as you have decided, go into the countryside. And Hermogenes here will accompany you. **CRATYLUS:** It shall be as you advise, Socrates. But you, too, think on these things now.

->**PLATO'S GORGIAS, OR, ON RHETORIC.**<-
\*
->**ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.**<-
\*

Since there are two most powerful things in the soul, knowledge and affection, the sophists distort knowledge toward falsehoods under the appearance of truth, while the popular poets often plunge affection into discordant disturbances under the bait of charming pleasure. Finally, popular orators both deceive knowledge with false conjectures and stir affection into various movements. Therefore, since by their work the minds of men are forced to be sick with both false opinions and ruinous affections, Plato—the physician of human souls—leads us entirely away from the sophists, and in a certain way away from the orators and poets as well. He indeed exterminates all sophists everywhere; but as for the poets, he does not remove them all, but only those who either invent shameful things about the gods or too sharply imitate and report disturbed minds. Nor does he remove them from everywhere, but from the city—that is, from the crowd of young and ignorant people who are quite prone to disturbances and do not penetrate the allegorical sense of the poets. For this reason, in his books *On the Republic*, he orders poets either to be expelled or forced to speak honorably of God, and not to accustom their listeners to disturbances, but to sing divine hymns and gravely recount the laws of the ancestors and the deeds of great men. But to return to the orators: Plato does not blame all of them either, but only those who apply themselves assiduously to persuading their listeners of whatever they please by any means they can, without selection—whether it be evil or good, whether the reasoning be false or true—using either pity, or provocation, or conjecture. Such had been the purpose of Lysias the Theban, and Tisias, and also Gorgias of Leontini. He prefers Pericles and Isocrates over others in the *Phaedrus* because they joined eloquence with philosophy. He adds that the legitimate orator ought to understand the reasons of things, the laws of character, the powers of words, and the natures of dispositions, and to compose words by a certain certain method accommodated to the dispositions of the listeners as far as possible, for the sake of persuading them of the common good; nor should he apply himself so much to making his speech pleasing to men as to making it acceptable to God. But he detests the man who, in the manner of Tisias and Gorgias, follows not truth itself and justice, but only a conjecture that is likely and probable to the crowd, as a man harmful to the state above others—as if eloquence without wisdom were a sharp sword in the hands of a madman. He attacks two men above others: Lysias in the *Phaedrus*, and here, Gorgias. For as their authority was greater, so they were more dangerous. Here they are brought in... [Ficino explains the structure of the dialogue]. Socrates first acts through his friend Chaerephon against Polus. Then he himself acts against Gorgias. Since these men were accustomed to boast wonderfully before the people in assigning reasons for other things, it is shown—so that all faith may be taken from them—that they do not know how to provide the reasons for their own profession. For when Polus was asked what Gorgias's art is, when he ought to have defined it only through necessary terms and explained what it is, he circumscribed it through superfluous ones and "what kind" it is, and that indeed in an overly affected style, which he is confirmed to have used in the *Phaedrus*, where the styles of orators are discussed. Then Gorgias himself, being asked what his art is, replied with a certain inept boasting that it is rhetoric. He is then asked to define what rhetoric is. We must remember that any thing, in what it is, partly agrees with other things and partly differs; and that by which it agrees is called the "genus," and that by which it differs, the "difference." Hence it happens that a definition, which encompasses what the thing is, ought to be assigned through such a genus and difference. Gorgias, therefore, as one who does not know how to define his art, puts forward its genus, and that indeed ineptly. The difference, which he ought to bring forward soon in the same response together with the genus, he is finally compelled to bring into the open after many...

--- Page 248 ---
->230 Book Twenty-Three.<-

...interrogations, with Socrates extorting it. At first, he answers that rhetoric is the art concerning speeches. And since there are other similar arts, he is asked concerning what kind of speeches, so that it may be discerned in what way it differs from other arts. He answers: concerning speeches that provide the power of speaking. Again, this is common to other arts. Whence he is again forced to add that rhetoric is occupied as much as possible with speeches and the power of speaking. But since that too is common with many, he is urged again to add "concerning speeches," namely, "about the greatest things." But when that too is common, he is compelled to bring forward something more distinct—that is, that through oratory we achieve the state of serving no one but ruling over others, and that the oratorical art is the effecter of persuasion at one's will. Meanwhile, Socrates warns that in disputing we should not intend our mind so much toward the person with whom we dispute, but toward the thing itself, the speech, and the soul. Then, since every art persuades about something, it is asked about what thing and of what kind is the orator's persuasion. Soon, persuasion is distinguished into two types: namely, that which produces knowledge, and that which produces belief. It is concluded that oratorical persuasion does not bring knowledge but belief; not properly about just anything, but about the just and the unjust; not everywhere, but mostly in a crowd, and about things which chiefly pertain to the republic. It is even added that an orator persuading about things properly pertaining to other arts can speak better than the artisans themselves—not indeed among those skilled in the arts themselves, but among the unskilled. Among these things, we are warned never to abuse power and art. Likewise, we are warned not to be disturbed in disputing where tranquility is necessary for perceiving the truth. Again, that a refutation ought to be received with an even and most willing mind, especially in correcting character. For nothing is worse than to feel falsely about character. After this, Gorgias concedes that it does not pertain to the orator to know in what way things themselves are, but to devise a certain machination for persuading such that he himself, though ignorant, may appear to understand more among the ignorant than those who actually know, and that his duty is to speak strenuously about anything in a crowd, not by teaching, but by persuading. He also concedes that the orator ought to know and be able to do what is "likely," even if he does not know what is "true." This, indeed, can in no way happen. For unless you know the thing itself, you will never recognize what is similar to it. Furthermore, it is asked whether, just as it does not pertain to oratory to know other things, so too it does not pertain to it to understand what is good, honorable, and just. Gorgias, although he said elsewhere that the orator relates similarly to these and those things, here contradicting himself, confesses that he ought at least to know these. Hence Socrates argues: if the orator knows just things, therefore he is just—testing, clearly, whether Gorgias holds the force of the consequence. He admits it immediately, since in the sciences and arts pertaining to the intellect it properly follows: he knows astrology or carpentry, therefore he is an astrologer or a carpenter. Does it not follow in those things which pertain to the will and character: he knows just things, therefore he is just? For work toward justice requires the will. Nevertheless, if someone has a certain divine knowledge about justice—which Plato wishes can sometimes happen when God breathes it in—it will follow correctly. For whoever knows most certainly how great a good justice is, and how great a reward remains for it; and on the contrary, how great an evil injustice is, and how great a punishment is due to it: he will undoubtedly flee injustice and embrace justice. By whatever reasoning the matter stood, Gorgias is forced to contradict himself. For since in the preceding parts he conceded that an orator can sometimes be unjust, here he denies it. After this, Socrates, out of the arrogance of Polus and under a certain irony, disapproves of younger men if they ever arrogantly rebuke their elders, and especially urges all to easily allow themselves to be emended by anyone. Furthermore, so that what follows may be clearly understood, it must be noted that oratory can be considered either in its genus or in its species: and in its genus indeed it is defined as a most prompt industry for persuading in civil matter, both by a certain faculty of proof and especially by the grace of eloquence. And therefore it is established in a certain way between the art of debating and poetry. Thus far, oratory is a good for the intellect, but for the will it is neither good nor evil. Of this, however, there are two species: the philosophical and the popular or flattering. The former is good, the latter is evil. The end of the former is to lead listeners to the common good through certain reasons of things, words, and character. This he praises most highly in the *Phaedrus*, composed of philosophy and the weightier kind of poetry. The end of the other, however, is to obtain whatever one wishes through conjectures likely to the crowd and provocations of the soul. This we place between sophistry and common poetry, mixed from both, which he detests in this dialogue. He divides the arts properly curative of man himself into two principal kinds. The first of these cures the soul, the second the body. In the soul, he says the "legal faculty" is the founder of laws and the moderator of character: it forms and stabilizes the soul itself in a certain habit agreeable to nature. The "judicial art," however, restores the soul if it has ever fallen from this. In the body, likewise, he places twin arts, similarly curative of the body: "gymnastics" indeed, the teacher of exercising this, confirming it in a good habit according to its strength; and "medicine," restoring lost health to the body. Therefore, as the legal is in the soul, such gymnastics appears to be in the body. Likewise, as the judicial is in the soul, such is medicine in the body. All these he calls "arts," because they lead to the good by a certain reason. He adds a certain nature or skill—flattering, servile, and deceptive—which falsely emulates these four. Through "sophistry" indeed it simulates the legal; through "oratory" (namely, the common kind) it fakes the judicial; through "cosmetics" <term>fucatoria: the art of using dyes or makeup to simulate health</term> it displays gymnastics; through "cookery" it represents the physician. This whole genus of flattering he denies is an art, because it strives for favor not by a certain reason toward the true good, but by enticements. But lest anyone think that Plato, the most eloquent of all, compares legitimate eloquence to cookery, let him read the *Phaedrus*, in which he approves of it, and most subtly hands down its end, duty, and precepts, asserting that it is similar to medicine. Since Polus, extolling oratorical power, says that orators have the greatest power because they can at their will condemn adversaries to prison and death, or despoil them of goods, or deprive them of the city: Socrates proves by two principal arguments that the unjust are not powerful. First indeed, since power is to be desired by each one as a good: it is established that the license to do whatever one pleases is not only not good but evil, and finally ruinous for unjust men as if they were captive in mind. Then, that the greatest power is to be able to effect that very thing which you want. It is clear, however, that all want the true good. But the bad never do or achieve the true good. Add that the evil mind, by the very fact that it is evil, is judged discordant in itself and insane, and is already overcome by those things which are asserted by the senses. Who, therefore, would say that a mind both languid and serving its own slaves in the manner of a slave is powerful? Meanwhile, all human things are distinguished into three: namely, the good, the evil, and the middle. The first of the goods is wisdom; the second, a desirable habit of the body; the third, the convenience of fortune. But these two are judged good only insofar as they exhibit a convenient ministry to the mind. The opposites of these are called evil; but the middle things are like indifferent things, which no more decline toward good than toward evil, like walking, sitting, and the like. It is added that no one wants either evil or middle things, or those things which he properly does; rather, he wants only those for the sake of which he is moved and acts. Therefore, those who do injuries do not want the injuries themselves, but the good for the sake of which they do them. But they do not achieve the good; therefore they do not achieve what they want. Therefore they are not powerful. Next, Socrates, having found an occasion from the common error of Polus, hands down holy precepts to us: he for whom it is permitted to sin gravely is almost miserable; he who sins gravely is already miserable; he who does not pay the penalty for his sin is more miserable. To suffer injuries is to be chosen rather than to inflict them. The license to do whatever one pleases is not power, unless it will finally be of advantage to us. It will be of advantage, however, only to those using it justly. The unjust, even if they obtain the empire of the whole world, are unhappy—indeed, most unhappy. For the more it is permitted to sin, and the less the penalty of sin is given, the more unhappy they are held to be. Happiness consists in wisdom and justice, unhappiness in their opposites. Since Polus places the judgment of truth—which ought to be referred to the quality of the judge rather than to the number of those judging—in the multitude of any witnesses whatever, Socrates answers that the best mode of proving is if you bring forward a single witness in the cause, namely the adversary convicted by reason; otherwise, a heaped-up multitude of witnesses from everywhere is of little moment for the truth. Furthermore, because Polus says that to do injury is indeed more shameful, but to suffer it is worse: Socrates argues against this, asserting that in human things and character, the good is the same as the beautiful or honorable; the evil the same as the shameful. Then, that very beauty is thought to exist either because of pleasure, or utility, or both; the shameful, on the contrary. Hence he argues: if to do injury is more shameful than to suffer it, it is not because it is more troublesome, but because it is more damaging; if so, therefore it is judged worse. Soon he adds that one ought to commit oneself to reason as to a physician for curing. He also affirms that the just punishment of sinners profits most the one who is punished. For if this is just, therefore it is beautiful and honorable; if so, therefore it is good; if good, it confers upon the soul, namely as medicine to the body. And much more so, for it frees it from the disease of the soul, which is the gravest of all diseases and evils. Among these things, notice the opinion of theologians: nothing is more necessary and useful for sinners than to confess sins, to be affected by penitence, to seek punishments from a judge, and to bear it with an even mind so that the soul may be purged before...

--- Page 249 ---
->Gorgias, Or, on Rhetoric. 231<-

...before its disease becomes incurable. After this, you will hear that it is very easy for us to signify our affection to him who labors with a similar affection. Also, that Socrates, captured by the love of philosophy, always obeys her. Furthermore, that it is to be chosen that all other things should be discordant with us, rather than that the soul should be discordant within itself. Accordingly, where Callicles corrects Socrates as if he were too studious of subtleties, understand that under the person of Socrates, the Sophists are being refuted by Plato. Callicles then touches upon the profane opinion of Thrasymachus and many others, saying that character and laws consist not in the order of nature, but only in either the opinion or fiction of men. This is confuted in the books *On the Republic* and in those that follow. As for what Callicles seems to bring against philosophers, understand that these things are said not against legitimate philosophers, but partly against the most idle of the sophists, and partly against those who abuse the study of philosophy: while they either pursue only logic in such a way that they abandon other parts of speculation, or they so embrace speculation alone that they neglect the philosophical precepts of character and civil institutions. Some things in Callicles's invective are said falsely, which will be refuted in the following parts. After this, however, it is commanded that all diligence must be applied in the examination and probation of our soul, and for this, one judge ought to be chosen in whom there is wisdom of the thing itself being discussed, and benevolence by which he may more willingly consult, and boldness besides, through which he may not fear to express what he thinks will be profitable. Then Socrates warns us that, since we are rational by nature, we should not live by irrational chance and fortune, but most diligently prescribe a certain end for life and choose the more convenient ways to it. Finally, while he often beseeches Callicles to refute him freely and boldly, he warns that one ought to inquire into nothing more than the medicine of the soul. These things done, Callicles concedes that by nature the same thing is both more powerful and better, and they say that natural justice wants him who is more powerful to have whatever belongs to his inferiors and to rule over them, and that his law is naturally just. To this, Socrates thus infers: If the same thing is "more powerful," "stronger," and "better," and the multitude is stronger than one, therefore it is also more powerful and better. The laws of the multitude, therefore, since they are of the more powerful and better, will be naturally just. But the laws of the multitude establish that it is just to preserve equality among all, and that it is more shameful to inflict injury than to suffer it. For which reason, it is not only by law that it is more shameful to do injury than to suffer it, and just to preserve equity, as Callicles had said in the preceding parts, but also by nature itself. Furthermore, because Callicles in the preceding parts had thought those were more powerful who surpassed others in cunning, boldness, and violence: Socrates gradually emends him, and forces him to confess that he is more powerful who is more prudent and brave for governing the republic. He signifies also among these things that he always brings the same things regarding the same matters, providing, clearly, constancy and disapproving of levity. Now indeed he tries to lead Callicles beyond prudence and fortitude to temperance also. But here, just as above he had erred regarding justice and power in imitating Thrasychamus, so now he was similarly following Aristippus <note>Aristippus was a student of Socrates who founded the Cyrenaic school, which taught that pleasure is the highest good.</note> regarding temperance, calling it the stupid idleness of a servile disposition, and asserting that virtue and happiness consist in fostering and filling the lusts of the senses. Socrates, however, soon girds himself to demonstrate that temperance consists not in human opinion, but in the order of nature. Truly, natural order requires that the inferior parts of the soul obey the superior ones, and that the whole soul be everywhere consonant and sound and beautiful, nor should it act in vain, but achieve its proposed end—which is the habit of the temperate man. On the contrary, in the intemperate man, reason (the queen of man) serves servile concupiscence; it is also discordant and languishes, and toils at an unfillable work, and follows flying pleasure with incomparable trouble. Socrates explains all this by the opinions of the Pythagoreans, especially Philolaus and Empedocles, in a twofold way: namely, through a fable and an example. In these he persuades us that the soul in this body is indeed entirely dead, and that the intemperate person is moreover assigned to the underworld, miserably agitated with vain and assiduous labor, while through a "perforated vase"—that is, a depraved and deceptive judgment—he continuously schemes to fill another "personified vase," which is unfillable concupiscence, with flowing delights. After this, because Callicles placed not only virtue but also happiness in the assiduous fulfillment of lusts, and affirmed that pleasure is the same as the good itself, and pain the same as evil, Socrates confutes this with several reasons. First: it is established that pleasure is not the good itself, since it is often most shameful and is present in the most shameful men. Second: good and evil, as contraries, cannot be in the same thing at the same time. But pleasure and pain are in the same thing at the same time, namely when someone who is thirsty drinks; for then the trouble of thirsting concurs with the pleasure of drinking. Third: good and evil, as other contraries are accustomed to do, do not depart from the same thing at the same time. Pleasure and pain, however, depart from the same thing at the same time when someone, at the same time while drinking, ceases both to thirst and to be delighted by drinking. Fourth: each one becomes good by the presence of good, but bad by the presence of evil. But men do not become good by the presence of pleasure (dissolute men), nor do upright men become bad by the presence of pain. Nay, rather, since good and bad men often equally rejoice or grieve, and sometimes bad men rejoice more and good men grieve more, certainly if pleasure were the good and pain the evil, it would follow that frequently both good and bad men would be equally good or bad, and sometimes the good would be more bad than the bad themselves, and vice versa. Among these things, notice the precept of Socrates to be observed: namely, that one must not hasten to the gravest things unless you have first achieved the lighter ones. Then several things are brought forward from which one could confirm that pleasure is not the good in itself, because many evil pleasures are found—namely, those harmful to both soul and body, and diverting us from the best things. For if pleasure were the good in itself, no pleasure would be evil. Accordingly, faculties are distinguished again: those which proceed like arts toward the good and the useful by a certain reason, and those which, like flattery, with no reason of the true good applied, catch at pleasure alone—in whose number he places poetry, music, and common oratory. But you, in the midst of the debate, note this opinion: that the virtue and health of the body consist in a certain order and ornament, and similarly the virtue and health of the soul consist in its own order and ornament. From which it happens that, just as the virtue and vice of the body are found not in opinion but in the thing itself (either agreeing with or opposed to nature), so the virtue and vice of the soul are to be judged not by human opinion, but by the law of nature. Conclude finally: as much as it is naturally better to have a healthy body than a sick one, so much is it better to possess a temperate soul than an intemperate one. Furthermore, the Pythagorean opinion is confirmed in what follows: that in all things temperance is best, which indeed is the first of all to be handed down to youths, through which the preceding intemperance of childhood may be corrected and the whole soul repaired; which he thinks the other virtues soon follow. Since the temperate man acts with decency toward god and men, he is pious and just and brave. Then it is concluded that happiness is in virtue alone, and misery in wickedness alone, and all human things are to be referred to virtue as to a certain target. Furthermore, just as virtue is necessary for beatitude, so the chastisement and punishment of vices is necessary, as if it were the medicine for the diseases of the soul. Finally, the intemperate man can be a friend neither to men, nor to god, nor to himself. Moreover, so that he may show us the natural excellence of temperance, he adds from the mind of the Pythagoreans and Orphics that the universe is contained by temperance and also by concord and justice, which are contained in temperance itself; and therefore, as Pythagoras said, intemperance in all things is to be fled with all strength as most ruinous. Since equality especially pertains to this as well as to justice, he commands equality above all to be observed, which he asserts prevails as much as possible in gods and men. Equality, I say, geometric, through which a distribution is made to each one such that it is distributed equally according to the capacity and merits of each—equally, I say, that is neither more nor less than either capacity or merit is judged to require. Geometric equality consists in a certain congruent portion. Arithmetic equality, however, in a number equal on both sides. Nor indeed are this one and that one the same. Truly, the excess of six to four, and likewise the excess of four to two, is equal to the arithmetician considering numbers: for both are completed by two. But to the geometer, the judge of the portion, it is unequal. For the number six surpasses the number four by a sesquialteral proportion <term>sesquialtera: a ratio of 3:2</term>, in which the greater number contains the smaller once whole and its half besides. But the number four surpasses two by a double proportion. By such an equality, which does not merely give as much weight to one as to another in the manner of a counter, but gives to each what is congruent to each, he says all things are preserved; for in these are contained both the justice of God in his works and the justice of man toward men. For in both, it is distributed to each according to the measure of capacity and merit. These things being said, he asserts that the theological foundations of character have been confirmed by the firmest reasons. Especially that it is worse to do injury than to suffer it; and of all things the worst, when you have done injury, not to pay the penalties, by which (as if by medicines) the soul may be freed from the greatest disease of all, injustice. For no greater detriment can be thought of than that which is inflicted on the soul by vice—so much so that, just as it is not expedient for a man to live with a sick soul in a healthy body, so it is not expedient to live with a soul sick with vices. Likewise, that life in the body is not to be valued highly, but virtue; and that it is worse to present oneself as very similar to disgraceful men because of a likeness of...

--- Page 250 ---
->232 Book Twenty-Four.<-

...likeness of character, than to be killed by them. Among these things, he warns that we should not aggregate any things to be handled of which we are ignorant, especially the graver ones, and most especially public ones. He makes little of all oratory if it can bring no safety to the soul either privately or publicly, but only consults the body and the things pertaining to it. He also derides those who, although they held the rudders of the Republic for a long time, always increased the city with external goods but neglected to form the souls of the citizens with temperance and justice—which indeed is the only duty of a legitimate governor. And he concludes that governors who look to the goods of fortune rather than the goods of the soul not only do not profit, but hinder the city the most. Furthermore, that all the power and wisdom of a man consist in this: that he preserves the soul untainted by sins against God and men. For the loss of this life is the lightest, but the loss of eternal salvation is the heaviest. Furthermore, so that you may understand what Plato affirms concerning the future rewards of virtues or punishments of vices, know that "Saturn" is understood by Plato as the supernal intelligence, in which is the universal law and providence of all things concerning the essences, lives, and orders of all things formed. Under this, however, are three principal orders of numina <term>numina: divine powers or spirits</term>, in which the Saturnian providence is distributed into three principal duties. Those spirits which properly minister to the distribution of essences, he calls by the common name of Jupiter. Those which confer to the suggestion of lives, by the name of Neptune. Those which dispose the orders of forms, he calls by the name of Pluto. Prometheus indeed is a somewhat lower rank of spirits here, who distributes the formal order of nature only to the rational, especially in this life. Finally, the three sons of Jupiter—the judges of Asia, Europe, and Africa—he wants to be understood as three spirits especially ministering to Jupiter and Pluto so that the formal order of justice may be fulfilled in souls separated from bodies. Among these things, notice that the divine law washes away the deletable stains of vices by punishing at certain times, but afflicts the indeletable ones with everlasting punishments. This indeed seems to disapprove of the everlasting transmigration of souls through bodies. But when he says that formerly the judges erred in judging the living, he signifies two things to us. First indeed, that not divine but human judgment concerning virtues and vices is deceived. Second, that divine providence foresaw in itself that judgments would be false if the living were judged by the living in this body. And therefore, not from a certain time (as the words sound) but from eternity, he decreed that judgment should happen after this life. Meanwhile, remember that the soul carries the affections and habits of vices and virtues with it. Finally, that Socrates affirms these things inwardly and fears nothing else except such detriment of the soul and the sight of the divine judge. Therefore, he concludes that we must contend in no contest more sharply than in this, so that we may offer the purest soul to the judge who inspects all things; and that all other things which men admire are to be utterly despised, and those alone of all things are to be honored which confer to the eternal salvation of the soul.
