<margin>The occasion of the dialogue. A proverb: "We have come later, after the feast."</margin> **CALLICLES:** Thus, when going to war and battle, Socrates, they say one must delay. **SOCRATES:** Have we come "after the feast," as is commonly said, and arrived late? **CALLICLES:** Indeed, after a wonderfully pleasant feast. For Gorgias just a little while ago displayed many and excellent things to us. **SOCRATES:** The cause of this lateness, Callicles, was Chaerepho here, who forced us to spend time in the forum. **CHAEREPHON:** That shall be no inconvenience, Socrates. For I provide a remedy: since Gorgias is my friend, he will demonstrate the same things to us either now, or at another time if you prefer. **CALLICLES:** What, Chaerepho? Does Socrates desire to hear Gorgias? **CHAEREPHON:** Certainly, for that very reason we were here. **CALLICLES:** Whenever you please to enter my house, it will be permitted; for Gorgias is staying with me, and he will open and explain what you desire. **SOCRATES:** You speak well, Callicles. But would he be willing to debate with us at present? For I desire to inquire from him what the power and potency of his art is, and what he himself professes and teaches. As for other things, as you say, let him bring the exposition to us at another time. **CALLICLES:** Nothing forbids asking him, Socrates. For that too was contained in his profession and proclamation. For just a little while ago, he ordered all who were inside to bring forward whatever question each wished, promising he would answer each one. <margin>Gorgias professed that he would answer any interrogation.</margin> **SOCRATES:** You tell of an excellent thing indeed. Therefore, Chaerepho, interrogate him. **CHAEREPHON:** What shall I ask? **SOCRATES:** Who he is. **CHAEREPHON:** In what way do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Just as if he were a maker of shoes, he would certainly answer that he is a tanner. Do you not yet understand what I say? **CHAEREPHON:** I certainly understand, and now I will ask. Tell me, Gorgias, does Callicles speak truly that you profess to answer all things about which anyone may inquire? **GORGIAS:** He says truly, Chaerepho. Indeed, I was just now proclaiming that very thing, and I say that for many years no one has asked me anything new. **CHAEREPHON:** Then you answer without difficulty, Gorgias. **GORGIAS:** It is permitted, Chaerepho, to make a trial of this thing. **POLUS:** It is permitted, by Jove, but more conveniently from me, if you wish, Chaerepho. For Gorgias seems to me to be already tired of speaking, as he has debated much just before. **CHAEREPHON:** What about you, Polus? Do you think you will answer more excellently than Gorgias? **POLUS:** What does it matter, as long as it satisfies you? **CHAEREPHON:** Nothing; since you wish it, answer. **POLUS:** Interrogate. **CHAEREPHON:** I ask now: if Gorgias were skilled in that art which his brother Herodicus knows, by what name would we most correctly call him? Would it not be the same as that one? **POLUS:** Entirely. **CHAEREPHON:** Therefore, calling him a physician, would we call him correctly? **POLUS:** Yes. **CHAEREPHON:** But if he had perceived that art which Aristophon the son of Aglaophon, or his brother, had, what would we correctly call him? **POLUS:** Certainly a painter. **CHAEREPHON:** But now, since Gorgias is skilled in some art, what shall we correctly call him? **POLUS:** O Chaerepho, many arts have been found for men by experience, skillfully devised. For experience causes our life to proceed through art; but inexperience causes it to wander randomly by fortune. <margin>Art follows experience; fortune follows inexperience.</margin> Of those arts, some follow others in different ways, but the best men follow the best arts, of whose number is Gorgias here, endowed with a most beautiful art. **SOCRATES:** Polus seems to be excellently instructed for speaking, Gorgias. Rather, Gorgias, you answer us what it is proper for you to be named, and of what art you are skilled. **GORGIAS:** Of rhetoric, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, we ought to call you a rhetorician? **GORGIAS:** ...

->234 The Twenty-Fourth Book.<-

Socrates continues. After these things, perhaps the physical trainer <term>pædotriba: a Greek-derived term for a gymnastics master or coach</term> <note>original: "pædotriba"</note> would greatly wonder whether you can prove there is more good in your art than in his own. If I were to ask him: "And who are you? What is your work?" He would say, "I am a physical trainer; it is the profession of my art to make the bodies of men beautiful and robust." Then, indeed, the money-changer <note>original: "nummator"</note> or merchant, looking down on the others, I suppose, would object in this way: "Consider, Socrates, whether you think there is any good more excellent than riches, whether in the view of Gorgias or anyone else." I would ask him in this manner: "Are you then the author of such a great good?" He would affirm that he is. "Who then are you?" "I am a money-changer." "What then? Do you think that riches are the highest good for men?" "Why wouldn't I think so?" he will say. I would then reply: "Yet here Gorgias contends that his art is the cause of a greater good than yours." It is certain, therefore, that he would next ask: "What is that good? Let Gorgias demonstrate it." Therefore, come, my Gorgias, imagine yourself being questioned by them and by me, and respond: what is that which you judge to be the greatest good for men, of which you profess yourself to be the author?

GORGIAS: That which is, O Socrates, truly the greatest good, and the cause both of men retaining their liberty and of each individual retaining command and power in his own city over others.

SOCRATES: What then do you say this is?

GORGIAS: To be able to persuade with words: both the judges in a court, the senators in the Senate, the listeners in a public assembly, and in any other civic gathering. Indeed, because of this faculty, the physician will be your slave, and the physical trainer will be your slave; furthermore, that very money-changer will be found to have accumulated his riches not for himself, but for another—that is, for you, who are endowed with the art of speaking and of persuading the crowd.

SOCRATES: Now you seem to me, Gorgias, to have shown very closely what art you judge rhetoric to be. And if I understand you correctly, you say that rhetoric is the producer of the art of persuasion, and that its entire labor and purpose is finished in this. Or do you have anything further that you can relate concerning the faculty of this art, than that it brings persuasion to the souls of the listeners?

<margin>Another poor definition of Rhetoric.</margin>

GORGIAS: I have nothing else, Socrates; you seem to me to have defined it sufficiently. For this is its essence.

SOCRATES: Listen, O Gorgias: be assured that if anyone else disputes with another, wishing to know the very thing which is being discussed, I also—as I am persuaded of myself—am such a person. I judge, rightly, that you are also so disposed.

GORGIAS: To what end is this?

<margin>Transition of the discussion.</margin>

SOCRATES: I will say now: I do not yet clearly enough understand what that persuasion is which you say proceeds from rhetoric, or what matters it concerns. And although I suspect which kind and concerning what things you intend to speak, nonetheless I will ask you what you mean by persuasion and on what matters it is produced by rhetoric. But I do this for the sake of the argument itself, rather than for your sake, so that the discourse may proceed in such a way that it most clearly explains the matter at hand to us. Observe, then, whether I seem to question you justly again. Just as if I had asked who Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter known for his realism.</note> the painter was, and you had replied "a painter of animals," would I not justly ask what sort of animals he paints and in what manner?

GORGIAS: Very justly.

SOCRATES: Would that not be because there are other painters who similarly paint many other animals?

GORGIAS: For that very reason.

SOCRATES: But if no one other than Zeuxis painted, you would have responded correctly in every way.

GORGIAS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Come then, say also regarding rhetoric: does this alone seem to persuade, or do other arts as well? I mean something of this sort: whoever teaches anything, does he also persuade of that which he teaches, or not?

GORGIAS: He persuades, and most of all, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Let us consider again those same arts which we mentioned a little while ago. Does not Arithmetic teach whatever pertains to number, and the arithmetician likewise?

GORGIAS: Without a doubt.

SOCRATES: And does he not also persuade?

GORGIAS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Therefore, Arithmetic also effects persuasion.

GORGIAS: It appears so.

SOCRATES: Therefore, if someone asks what kind of persuasion and concerning what it effects, we will reply: the teaching kind, namely concerning the even and the odd, and how many there are of each. We will similarly be able to show that the other arts which we were just mentioning are producers of persuasion, and of what kind and concerning what, can we not?

GORGIAS: Yes.

SOCRATES: Therefore, rhetoric is not the sole craftsman of persuasion.

GORGIAS: You speak the truth.

SOCRATES: Since, therefore, it is not the only one that does this, but other arts do as well, we might—as with the painter—rightly ask next concerning rhetoric: what kind of persuasion is it the producer of, and concerning what? Does the question not seem just to you?

GORGIAS: To me, indeed, it does.

SOCRATES: Respond then, Gorgias, since it seems so to you.

GORGIAS: I say, Socrates, that rhetoric is the mistress of that persuasion which is brought to bear in courts and other gatherings, as I said a little while ago, and concerns matters of the just and the unjust.

SOCRATES: And yet I myself suspected that you meant this persuasion. But do not wonder if I ask you something of this sort again in succession. Although it may seem clear, I will nevertheless repeat it. For as I said, I do not ask for your sake, but so that the discussion may be completed in its proper order—lest we become accustomed to snatching away by guesswork those things which ought to be discussed. But you, at your own discretion, may finish your argument as it was set out.

GORGIAS: You seem to me to act rightly.

SOCRATES: Come then, let us consider this. Do you call "to learn" something?

GORGIAS: I do.

SOCRATES: What again? "To believe" something?

GORGIAS: That also.

SOCRATES: Do you think, therefore, that "to learn" is the same as "to believe," and that knowledge <note>original: "disciplinam"</note> and belief <note>original: "credulitatem"</note> are the same, or different?

GORGIAS: I think they are different.

SOCRATES: You think correctly. You will recognize it from this: if someone should ask whether there is a certain false belief and a certain true one, you would, I think, agree.

GORGIAS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: What then? Is there true and false science <note>original: "scientia"</note>?

GORGIAS: By no means.

SOCRATES: It is certain, therefore, that they are not the same.

GORGIAS: It is certain.

SOCRATES: Nevertheless, both those who have learned and those who have believed have been persuaded.

GORGIAS: It is so.

SOCRATES: Do you wish, then, for us to posit two species of persuasion, one of which provides belief without knowledge, while the other provides knowledge?

<margin>Two kinds of persuasion.</margin>

GORGIAS: Entirely so.

SOCRATES: Which persuasion then does rhetoric bring to courts and other gatherings concerning just or unjust things? That from which men believe without knowledge, or that from which they know?

GORGIAS: It is clear: it is the one by which the listeners are led to belief.

SOCRATES: Thus, as it seems, rhetoric is the craftsman of that persuasion which provides belief rather than teaching concerning the just or the unjust.

<margin>It is concluded that Rhetoric only persuades, it does not teach.</margin>

GORGIAS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Therefore, the orator does not teach what is just and unjust in courts and other crowds, but only induces belief. For he could not teach such great matters to so large a crowd in so short a time.

GORGIAS: Certainly not.

SOCRATES: Come then, let us see what should be said about rhetoric. For I cannot yet fully understand what I am about to say. When there is a public discussion concerning the election of physicians, or the choosing of builders of ships or other things, then perhaps consulting the orator will not be relevant. For it is clear that in such elections, the most skilled person in each field...

<summary>In this dialogue, Socrates and Gorgias debate the definition of rhetoric, with Gorgias arguing that it is the most powerful art because it produces persuasion. Socrates counters by distinguishing between belief and actual knowledge, concluding that rhetoric merely creates belief about justice without truly educating the audience.</summary>

of that art should be chosen. Nor, on the other hand, when it is time to consult about building walls, or the arrangement of ports, or the equipment of ships, will it be the office of the orator to give counsel, but rather the architect. Furthermore, it will not be the orator's role when the deliberation concerns the choice of a general, or the drawing up of an army against enemies, or the seizing of locations; rather, the consultation will pertain to the leaders of the army, and not at all to the orators. What do you say to these things, Gorgias? Certainly, since you profess to be a rhetorician yourself and to be able to make others rhetoricians, it is surely better to inquire and learn from you the things which belong to your art. And indeed, consider me to be acting in your own interest now. For perhaps among those who are within, there is someone who desires to be your disciple: just as I perceive some, and indeed many, who are perhaps deterred by shame from asking these things of you. Therefore, having been asked by me, consider yourself also being interrogated by them in this manner. "What shall we report back if we hand ourselves over to your discipline? About what matters shall we be able to counsel the Republic? Only about the just and the unjust? Or also about those things which Socrates was just now bringing up?" Take care, then, Gorgias, to answer these men.

GORGIAS: I will indeed endeavor to explain the whole faculty of rhetoric to you quite clearly. For you yourself have led us to it very well. You know, surely, that these dockyards and walls of Athens, and the arrangement of the ports, were constructed partly by the counsel of Themistocles and partly by Pericles, and not by the counsel of the craftsmen. 

SOCRATES: These things are said of Themistocles, O Gorgias. As for Pericles, I myself heard him * persuading the city regarding the construction of the middle wall. 

<margin> *Regarding the wall which faces the south, Suidas <note>The "Suidas" or Suda is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>.</margin>

GORGIAS: Furthermore, whenever there is deliberation regarding the elections you just mentioned, you see that the orators themselves give counsel, and their opinions are preferred in these matters. 

SOCRATES: Indeed, marvelling at these things, I have long been inquiring of you concerning the power of rhetoric. For to me, as I consider these things, the magnitude of its power seems like something divine. 

GORGIAS: Oh, Socrates, if you had a full perspective of all the aspects of this art, you would surely see that it embraces within itself all powers and faculties, to put it briefly. I will bring you a great proof of this matter. Often now, having entered with my brother and other physicians to see some sick person—when that patient was unwilling to drink the medicine, or would not permit himself to be cut or cauterized by the doctor, and could not be persuaded by the doctor—I persuaded him by no other faculty than that of rhetoric. Wherefore I assert even more, that if a rhetorician and a doctor were to go to any city, and they were to compete in words in an assembly or any other gathering as to which of them should be chosen as the physician, the doctor would appear nowhere; rather, the one skilled in speaking would be chosen, if only he wished it. And by the same reasoning, if a rhetorician should compete against any other craftsman, he will obtain the choice for himself rather than any other, whoever he may be. For there is nothing about which a rhetorician cannot speak with greater persuasion to the common people than any of the craftsmen. The power of this art, therefore, is so great and of such a kind; yet it is necessary to use rhetoric in the same way as any other faculty of competition. For if someone has learned to fight with fists or muscles and weapons so that he can emerge superior to friends and enemies, he ought not, on that account, to fight against everyone equally, so as to strike, stab, or kill even his friends. Nor, indeed, by Jupiter, if someone exercised in the wrestling school <term>palæstræ: a Greek gymnasium for wrestling and athletics</term> <note>original: "palæstræ"</note> should acquire strength of body and then strike his parents or any other of his household or friends, should the physical trainers <term>pædotribas: gymnastics masters or coaches</term> <note>original: "pædotribas"</note> and those who teach how to fight with weapons be held in hatred and expelled from the cities. For they handed down these skills so that those who learned them might use them justly, against enemies and those who bring injury, namely for warding off harm, not for inflicting it. 

But some pervert these things and abuse their strength and art; yet those who taught them are not to be judged wicked on that account, nor is the art to be blamed and held as evil, but rather, in my judgment, those who use it perversely. The same reasoning applies to rhetoric. For an orator can speak against everyone and concerning any matter whatsoever, so that he may very easily become superior by persuading a multitude about any subject. Nevertheless, one ought not on that account to deprive doctors of their praise because they can do this, nor any other craftsmen; rather, one should use rhetoric rightly and with reason, just as with the faculty of competition. But indeed, if someone who has acquired rhetoric then uses this acquired faculty unjustly, it is not right to hate and expel from the city the one who taught him; for the teacher handed it over for just use, while the student used it for the opposite. Therefore, it is right to hate, send into exile, and even put to death the one who abuses it, but by no means the teacher. 

SOCRATES: I think, Gorgias, that you have been present at many disputes, and you have already discovered this in them: namely, that those who dispute with one another are not easily able, once they begin to differ, to depart in such a way that, by defining the matter itself, they only teach and learn from one another. Instead, if they contend about something and do not concede to one another that they are speaking either truly or clearly, they become inflamed with anger, and they think the other is speaking out of envy, competing together rather than seeking what was proposed. Sometimes, indeed, they finally depart so shamefully with quarrels and mutual insults that those listening are even pained and annoyed that they thought such men were worth hearing. But to what purpose is this? You will say it is because you do not seem to me now to be speaking things sufficiently consistent and harmonious with what you previously brought forth concerning rhetoric. Yet I fear to argue, lest you think I am contending not so much for the sake of declaring the matter, as for your sake. But if you are of that number of men to which I belong, I will gladly inquire of you about the things I have begun; if not, I will let it go. If you ask what number I am of, I will answer: of those who gladly allow themselves to be refuted if they say anything false or foolish, and who also gladly refute others if anything is said less than truly by another—for whom it is no less pleasant to be corrected than to correct. For I consider it to be so much the greater good, by as much as it is a greater good to be freed from the greatest evil than to have freed others. For I think nothing is so destructive to men as a false opinion, specifically in those matters about which our present discourse has been instituted. 

<margin>The greatest evil for men is a false opinion.</margin>

Therefore, if you also affirm that you are such a man, come, let us dispute; but if you think we should leave off, let us now dismiss and dissolve the gathering. 

GORGIAS: I say indeed, O Socrates, that I also am of that kind which you were just describing; but perhaps we must have regard for the others who are present. For long ago, before you arrived, I recounted many things to these people. And now perhaps if we proceed to dispute, the delay will be drawn out too long. Therefore, we must be careful lest we detain these men while they are intending to do something else. 

CHAEREPHON: You hear the shouting, Gorgias and Socrates, of those desiring to be present for this dissertation. Certainly, no business would be of such importance to me that I would prefer anything else over this dispute instituted by you. 

CALLICLES: By the Gods, O Chaerephon, I too, though I have been present at many disputes, do not know if I have ever been as delighted as I am now; therefore, even if you should spend the whole day disputing, it will be most pleasing to me. 

SOCRATES: And yet, O Callicles, as far as I am concerned, nothing will stand in the way, provided Gorgias is willing. 

GORGIAS: It would indeed be shameful for me hereafter, O Socrates, if I should decline the dispute, especially since from the beginning I commanded all to ask about whatever each person wished.

<summary>Gorgias argues that rhetoric is a master art capable of persuading anyone about any subject, even overstepping technical experts like doctors, but insists the teacher is not responsible if a student uses the art for evil. Socrates counters by suggesting that meaningful dialogue requires a willingness to be corrected, rather than a desire to win an argument.</summary>

Therefore, if it pleases those present, hold your discussion and ask whatever you like. **SOCRATES**: Listen now, Gorgias, to what I wonder at in your words. For perhaps, while you speak correctly, I am perceiving it differently. You say that you are able to make someone a rhetorician if they wish to learn from you. **GORGIAS**: I do indeed say that. **SOCRATES**: Not so that he is capable of teaching a crowd about all things with probability, but so that he is capable of persuading them? **GORGIAS**: Exactly so. **SOCRATES**: You were adding, moreover, that the rhetorician is more persuasive about health than the physician is. **GORGIAS**: I certainly said that, but *in a crowd*. For he would never be more persuasive than a physician about health among those who actually know. **SOCRATES**: You tell the truth. Therefore, if he is more powerful at persuading than the physician, will he not also surpass the one endowed with knowledge through his persuasion? **GORGIAS**: Entirely so. **SOCRATES**: Though he himself is not a physician? **GORGIAS**: No. **SOCRATES**: And if he is not a physician, he is therefore also ignorant of those things which the physician understands. **GORGIAS**: Without a doubt. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, the unskilled man will persuade more easily among those who do not know than the one who has knowledge, whenever the rhetorician excels the physician in the faculty of persuading. Is that how it follows? **GORGIAS**: In these cases, it certainly follows so. **SOCRATES**: Does the rhetorician and rhetoric not stand in a similar position regarding all other arts as well? So that it pertains nothing to the faculty of rhetoric to know the nature of the matter, but rather to have devised a certain art for persuading, so that among the unskilled he appears to know more than the very craftsmen of individual things? **GORGIAS**: Is this not a great faculty? Namely, that those who have never touched other arts, but this one alone, are in no way inferior to others in knowledge. **SOCRATES**: Whether the orator excels others or is surpassed himself because of this one faculty, we shall inquire a little later, if it seems to lead anywhere in our discussion. But now let us first consider this: whether the orator is prepared regarding the just and the unjust, the honorable and the base, the good and the evil, in the same way he is regarding health and other matters belonging to other arts. Specifically, whether he is ignorant of what is good or evil, beautiful or ugly, just or unjust; but instead devises a kind of persuasion about such things, so that while being ignorant himself among the unskilled, he appears to know more than those who truly know. Or is it perhaps necessary that he knows these things, and must come to you—the future orator—already having acquired this faculty? For if he does not bring the knowledge of such things with him, you, as a teacher of rhetoric, will not teach such things (for it is not your duty to teach them). However, you will make him *appear* to the common people to have knowledge of such things when he does not, and to *appear* good and excellent when he is not at all. Or will you be unable to teach him rhetoric at all unless he has first attained the truth of these matters? Or how do these things stand, Gorgias? I pray, by Jove, that just as you began a little while ago, you would finally reveal to us the power of rhetoric. **GORGIAS**: Well, if it happens that someone is ignorant of them, I believe he will learn them from me. **SOCRATES**: Stop there, for you speak rightly: if you are to make someone a rhetorician, it is necessary for him to know the just and the unjust, either before he comes to you or by learning it from you afterward. **GORGIAS**: Entirely so. **SOCRATES**: What then? Is he who has learned the things pertaining to building not a builder? **GORGIAS**: He is. **SOCRATES**: And he who has learned music, a musician? **GORGIAS**: Yes. **SOCRATES**: And he who has learned things pertaining to medicine, a physician? And in the others in the same way: whoever has learned something becomes such a person as the knowledge of each subject makes him? **GORGIAS**: Entirely. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, by this reasoning, will not anyone who has learned just things be just? **GORGIAS**: Most certainly. **SOCRATES**: But the just man does just things. **GORGIAS**: It is so. **SOCRATES**: Is it not therefore necessary that the rhetorician be just? And that the just man wishes to do just things? **GORGIAS**: It appears so. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, the just man will never wish to do an injury <note>Latin: *iniuriam*, meaning an unjust act or a wrong.</note>. **GORGIAS**: Never. **SOCRATES**: It is necessary from the preceding reasoning that the rhetorician be just. **GORGIAS**: Necessary. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, the rhetorician will never wish to do an injury. **GORGIAS**: Never. **SOCRATES**: Do you remember saying a little while ago that physical trainers <note>Latin: *paedotribas*, the instructors in gymnasia who trained youth in wrestling and athletics.</note> should not be blamed or expelled if a boxer uses his boxing art badly and inflicts an injury? And in the same way, if an orator uses rhetoric unjustly, the one who taught him should not be accused and expelled, but rather the one who does the unjust act and does not use rhetoric rightly? Was this said, or not? **GORGIAS**: It was said. **SOCRATES**: But now, the orator himself appears to be someone who would never do an injury. **GORGIAS**: Never. **SOCRATES**: And yet in the earlier parts, it was said that rhetoric is concerned with speech, not indeed about the even and the odd <note>i.e., mathematics</note>, but about the just and the unjust. **GORGIAS**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, when you were saying these things, I thought that rhetoric was never unjust, since it always spoke about justice. But when you said a little later that if an orator should use rhetoric unjustly—immediately I was struck with wonder, and thinking that the things said by you were not consistent with each other, I brought forward this discourse: so that if you thought it useful to be refuted, as I do, it would be worthwhile for us to discuss it; but if not, we should let it go. Then, upon closer inspection, as it is not hidden from you, it was admitted that it is impossible for a rhetorician to use rhetoric unjustly or to inflict an injury. To discern sufficiently in what manner these things stand, by the dog, <note>Socrates' characteristic oath, "by the dog" (per canem), was often used instead of swearing by a god.</note> Gorgias, there will be need of no small conversation and meeting. **POLUS**: What now? Do you hold this view of rhetoric as you now say, or otherwise? Or do you think Gorgias, led by a certain shame, conceded to you that the rhetorician knows the just, the honorable, and the good, and that if someone unskilled in these things comes to him, he will teach him? From which confession, perhaps, something contradictory followed in the discussion. You catch yourself in this with too much zeal, Socrates, while by questioning you lead the way to such responses. For who do you think would have denied to you that he knows just things and will teach others? Indeed, it is a great rudeness <note>Latin: *rusticitas*, implying a lack of urbanity or social grace in the way Socrates conducts the argument.</note> to lead the questioning to these things. **SOCRATES**: For this very reason, my dear Polus, we acquire friends and sons: so that if ever we should slip in our old age, you younger men being present might correct our life in both words and deeds. And now, if anything has escaped Gorgias and me in our discussion, you yourself, being present, amend it. For you ought to, and I gladly permit you, so that if you think any of the things which have been conceded were not rightly conceded, you may change it at your discretion, provided you avoid one thing for me. **POLUS**: What is that, Socrates? **SOCRATES**: That prolixity <note>Long-windedness or making long speeches instead of short answers.</note> of speech which you were beginning at the very start of the discussion. **POLUS**: Why so? Shall I not be allowed to speak as much as I wish? **SOCRATES**: You would be treated with a very grave injury, O best of men, if having come to Athens, where there is the greatest freedom of speech in all of Greece, you alone in this place did not have the power of speaking as you pleased. But on the other hand, if you spoke at length and were unwilling to respond to questions, and I were not allowed to go away and refused to hear you, would I not also be treated with a grave injury if the power to depart and to refuse to listen to your oration were not permitted to me? But if you have any care for this discussion and wish to correct it, as I was just saying, retracting what seems to you should be retracted, and questioning and answering in turn as Gorgias and I have done, refute me, and allow yourself to be refuted. Or do you also affirm that you know what Gorgias professes to know? **POLUS**: I certainly say so. **SOCRATES**: And do you bid anyone to ask of you whatever they wish, as from a man who knows how to answer? **POLUS**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: Now...

Polus interjects, accusing Socrates of being rude and manipulative, leading to a debate over the style of the dialogue and the freedom of speech in Athens.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Gorgias, with Polus now intervening. Socrates begins to define rhetoric not as an art, but as a form of "flattery" that mimics genuine care for the soul and body.</meta>

-># Gorgias, Or, On Rhetoric. 237<-

**SOCRATES**: Now then, you may do whichever you prefer: either ask me, or answer. **POLUS**: I will do the asking. And you, Socrates, tell me: since it seems to you that Gorgias is unable to speak adequately about rhetoric, <margin>It is no art.</margin> what do you say it is yourself? **SOCRATES**: Are you asking what kind of art I think it is? **POLUS**: Exactly that. **SOCRATES**: To tell you the truth, Polus, I think it is no art at all. **POLUS**: What, then, does rhetoric seem to be to you? **SOCRATES**: A thing which you say created art in that <margin>Rhetoric is a knack for producing some grace and pleasure.</margin> book I recently read. **POLUS**: What do you mean? **SOCRATES**: A certain **knack** <note>original: "peritiam"; refers to a skill gained by experience rather than theoretical knowledge</note>. **POLUS**: Does rhetoric seem to be a knack to you, then? **SOCRATES**: To me it does, unless you say otherwise. **POLUS**: A knack for what kind of thing? **SOCRATES**: For producing a certain grace and pleasure. **POLUS**: Do you not think, then, that rhetoric is something beautiful, since it can win grace among men? **SOCRATES**: What, Polus? Have you already heard from me what I say it is, that you go on to ask whether I think it is beautiful? **POLUS**: Have I not heard you say it is a certain knack? **SOCRATES**: Since you value "grace" so highly, are you willing to grant me a small grace? **POLUS**: I am. **SOCRATES**: Ask me now what kind of art I think cookery is. **POLUS**: Behold, I ask: what kind of art is cookery? **SOCRATES**: None at all. **POLUS**: What is it then? **SOCRATES**: I say it is a certain knack. **POLUS**: What kind of knack? **SOCRATES**: For producing grace and pleasure. **POLUS**: Are cookery and rhetoric the same thing, then? **SOCRATES**: By no means, but they are both parts of the same pursuit. **POLUS**: What pursuit? **SOCRATES**: I fear it may be somewhat harsh to speak the truth for Gorgias’s sake, lest he think I am disparaging his own pursuit. For I do not know if this is the rhetoric that Gorgias practices—indeed, nothing was made clear to us from this discussion just now as to what he himself thinks. But what I call rhetoric is a part of a certain thing that is not at all honorable. **GORGIAS**: <margin>A certain unartful pursuit is described.</margin> What thing, Socrates? Speak out, and do not worry on my account. **SOCRATES**: It seems to me, Gorgias, to be a certain pursuit, not at all artful, but belonging to a shrewd and daring mind, naturally clever at associating with people. I call its primary heading **flattery** <note>original: "adulatio"</note>. Of this pursuit, there seem to me to be many parts. <margin>Cookery, rhetoric, and sophistry are parts of an unartful pursuit, whose primary heading is flattery.</margin> One indeed is cookery; though it seems to be an art, in my judgment it is none, but rather a knack discovered by practice. I say that rhetoric is also a part of this same thing, as is **beautification** <note>original: "fucatoria"; the art of using dyes or makeup to create a false appearance</note>—which is also called the faking of goods—and **sophistry**. These four parts pertain to four different things. If, therefore, Polus wants to ask, let him ask. For he has not yet heard which part of flattery I say rhetoric is; <margin>Rhetoric is a phantom of a part of politics.</margin> he did not notice that I have not yet answered that. And so he asks whether I think it is beautiful or not. But I will not answer whether I think rhetoric is something beautiful or ugly until I have first revealed what it is. For that would not be right, Polus. But if you wish to hear, ask me what part of flattery I say rhetoric is. **POLUS**: I ask you now: what part is it? **SOCRATES**: Will you understand my answer? It is, in my opinion, a **phantom** <note>original: "simulacrum"; an image or shadow without substance</note> of a part of politics. **POLUS**: What then? Do you say it is something beautiful or ugly? **SOCRATES**: Ugly—if indeed I must call evil things ugly—since I must answer you as one who is not ignorant of the things I am saying. **GORGIAS**: By Jove, I do not quite understand what you are saying. **SOCRATES**: And with good reason, Gorgias, for I have not yet expressed it clearly. But this Polus here is young and sharp. **GORGIAS**: Leave him aside, and answer me instead: in what way do you say rhetoric is a phantom of a part of politics? **SOCRATES**: I will try to express what rhetoric seems to me to be. If the matter is otherwise, let Polus here refute me. You call something "body" and something "soul"? **GORGIAS**: Why wouldn't I? **SOCRATES**: And do you not think there is a good condition for each of these? **GORGIAS**: I certainly do. **SOCRATES**: Furthermore, can a condition appear to be good when it is not? I mean something like this: many people seem to have a well-conditioned body, whose poor health and condition no one would easily detect except a physician or a master of gymnastics. **GORGIAS**: You speak the truth. **SOCRATES**: I say there is something similar in both the body and the soul, which makes it seem that both body and soul are in good health when they are not. **GORGIAS**: It is so. **SOCRATES**: Come then, if I can, I will explain what I said more clearly. Since there are two things, I believe there are two arts: the art pertaining to the soul I call **politics**; the one pertaining to the body I cannot name with a single word. But of this single art which cares for the body, I set down two parts: one is gymnastics, the other is medicine. In politics, I set down **legislation** <note>original: "nomotheticam"</note>—the framer of laws—as corresponding to gymnastics, and **justice**—that is, the judicial art—corresponding in a way to medicine. They communicate with each other because they are about the same things: medicine and gymnastics on one hand, and the judicial and legal on the other. Yet they also differ from one another. Since there are these four, and they always care for what is best—these for the body, those for the soul—the faculty of flattery, sensing this (not by knowledge, but by guesswork), divides itself fourfold. It creeps under each of the parts and pretends to be that which it has crept under. It has no care for what is best, but always by means of what is most pleasant, it snares the unwary mind as if with a hook, and deceives it to such an extent that it seems to be of the greatest value. Cookery creeps under medicine and pretends to know the best foods for the body. Therefore, if a cook and a physician had to contend before children, or before men as foolish and senseless as children, as to which of them understands more about good or bad foods, the physician would die of hunger. This, then, I call flattery, and I think it is something ugly, Polus—for I say this against you. And for this reason, it pursues pleasure without any regard for what is best. <margin>That which lacks reason is not an art.</margin> I do not say it is an art, but a certain knack, because it has no rational account of the nature of the things it offers, <margin>Every art [works] with reason.</margin> and thus it cannot give the cause of any thing. Therefore, I do not call that an "art" which lacks a rational account. But if you doubt these things, I am willing to explain the reasoning to you. Thus, as I said, cookery is the flattery that creeps under medicine. <margin>Flatteries creep under arts: Cookery, Adornment, Sophistry, Rhetoric [under] Legal [and] Judicial.</margin> Similarly, **beautification** <note>cosmetics/makeup</note> creeps under gymnastics; it is a harmful, deceptive, ignoble, and illiberal thing, deceiving with shapes, colors, smoothing, and a certain sense, so that because of this external "veneer," we neglect the proper and true form that comes through gymnastics. But so I am not too long-winded, I will speak in the manner of a geometer; for perhaps thus you will follow: What beautification is to gymnastics, cookery is to medicine. Or rather: what beautification is to gymnastics, **sophistry** is to legislation; and what cookery is to medicine, **rhetoric** is to justice. Nevertheless, as I was saying, they are distinguished by nature, yet because they are kin, they are mixed together in the same field and around the same things—namely, sophists and rhetoricians. Nor do they look toward any utility that they might ever follow for themselves or for others. For if the soul did not rule the body, but the body ruled itself, and the soul did not perceive and distinguish cookery...

<summary>Socrates argues that rhetoric is not a true art but a form of "flattery" (like cookery) that provides pleasure rather than actual well-being. He presents a geometric analogy comparing the true arts of health and justice to their deceptive counterparts: sophistry, rhetoric, cookery, and cosmetics.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Polus. Socrates has just defined rhetoric as a "knack" for producing pleasure, comparing it to cookery rather than a true art like medicine. He is now explaining why this distinction matters for the soul.</meta>

-># 238 Book Twenty-Four.<-

...cookery and medicine, but the body itself had to judge these by its own grace and pleasure, then that saying of Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras was a philosopher who famously claimed that originally "all things were together" in a confused mass before Mind (Nous) organized them.</note> would surely apply, my friend Polus—for you are familiar with these things: namely, all things would be mixed indiscriminately together, and those things pertaining to medicine and health would be confused with those pertaining to cookery. You have heard now what I say rhetoric is: a thing corresponding to cookery, being in the soul what the latter is in the body. Perhaps I have acted absurdly, in that while I forbid you from being prolix <note>long-winded</note>, I have extended my own speech at length. However, I deserve some pardon: for if I had spoken more briefly, you would not have understood at all, nor would my answer have satisfied you; instead, you would have required a further explanation. If, therefore, I am unable to understand when you answer, you also may extend your speech. But if I can understand, allow me to use your answer or my own (for that is only fair) as I see fit. And now, if you can make any use of this answer, do so. **POLUS**: What then are you saying? Does rhetoric seem to be flattery to you? **SOCRATES**: I said it was a *part* of flattery. Do you not remember this, Polus, at your age? What will you do later when you are older? **POLUS**: Do good orators seem to you to be held in as little esteem in the city as flatterers? **SOCRATES**: Is this a question you are asking? Or are you starting some speech? **POLUS**: I am asking a question. **SOCRATES**: They seem to me to be held in no esteem at all. **POLUS**: How can you say "none"? Do they not have the greatest power in cities? **SOCRATES**: Not at all, if you say that power is something good for the one who possesses it. **POLUS**: I certainly say so. **SOCRATES**: Then orators seem to me to have the least power of all in a republic. **POLUS**: What are you saying? Do they not, like tyrants, kill whomever they wish, and strip them of their patrimony, and drive them from the city? **SOCRATES**: By the dog <note>A favorite oath of Socrates.</note>, I am in doubt regarding each thing you say, whether you are explaining your own opinion or asking for mine. **POLUS**: I am asking for yours. **SOCRATES**: Very well, my friend: then you are asking two things of me at once. **POLUS**: In what way two? **SOCRATES**: Did you not just say that orators kill whomever they wish in the manner of tyrants, and strip them of their goods, and even cast them into exile? **POLUS**: I did. **SOCRATES**: I tell you then, these are two questions, and I shall answer both. I assert that both orators and tyrants possess the least power in cities, just as I was saying a little while ago. For they do nothing, so to speak, of what they *will* to do, yet they do whatever seems best to them in their own opinion. **POLUS**: Is this not great power? **SOCRATES**: Not according to Polus. **POLUS**: I do not say so? I certainly do. **SOCRATES**: By Jove, you do not, since you said that great power is a good for the one who has it. **POLUS**: I do say that. **SOCRATES**: Do you then say it is a good if someone does what seems best to him while lacking sense, and do you call that great power? **POLUS**: Certainly not. **SOCRATES**: Must you not then demonstrate to me that orators have sense, and that rhetoric is an art rather than flattery, in order to convince me? Otherwise, unless you prove this and argue against me, the orators and tyrants who do whatever seems fit to them in the city will gain no good from it. If indeed having power is, as you say, a good, but doing whatever one pleases without sense is—as you yourself admit—an evil. Is it not so? **POLUS**: It is. **SOCRATES**: How then can orators or tyrants have great power in a republic, unless Socrates is convinced by Polus that they do what they *will*? **POLUS**: Look at this man! **SOCRATES**: I deny that they do what they *will*; you, however, must refute me. **POLUS**: Did you not admit a moment ago that they do what seems good to them? **SOCRATES**: And I admit it again now. **POLUS**: Do they not then do what they *will*? **SOCRATES**: Not in my opinion. **POLUS**: But they do what seems best to them? **SOCRATES**: That I grant. **POLUS**: You say troublesome and incredible things, Socrates. **SOCRATES**: Do not accuse me, excellent Polus, to call you by your own style. But if you have something to inquire, refute my error; if not, answer me. **POLUS**: I prefer to answer, so that I may understand what you are saying. **SOCRATES**: Does it seem to you then that men *will* the thing they are doing at any given time, or rather that thing for the sake of which they do it? For instance, those who drink medicines given by doctors: does it seem to you that they *will* the thing they are doing—namely, to drink the medicine and suffer its bitterness—or rather health, for the sake of which they drink? **POLUS**: It is manifest they will to be healthy, for which reason they take the potion. **SOCRATES**: And do not those who sail, or undertake any other business for the sake of profit, *not* will what they are doing? For who would *will* to sail, to undergo dangers, and to have troubles? But they will that, I believe, for the sake of which they sail: namely, wealth, for it is for wealth's sake they sail. **POLUS**: Most certainly. **SOCRATES**: Is it not similarly so in all things: whoever does something for the sake of another thing, does not *will* the thing he does, but that for the sake of which he does it? **POLUS**: So it seems. **SOCRATES**: Is there anything among all things that is not either good, or evil, or intermediate—that is, neither good nor evil? **POLUS**: Nothing at all. **SOCRATES**: Do you not call wisdom, health, wealth, and other things of that kind "good"? And their opposites "evil"? **POLUS**: I do. **SOCRATES**: And do you not say those things which are neither good nor evil are such things as sometimes participate in the good, sometimes in the evil, and sometimes in neither? Like sitting, walking, running, or sailing. Or again, like stones, wood, and other common things. Do you not say there are such things that you call neither good nor evil? **POLUS**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: Do they then do these intermediate things for the sake of the good whenever they do them? Or the good for the sake of the intermediate? **POLUS**: The intermediate for the sake of the good. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, in pursuit of the good, we walk, thinking it better to do so; and conversely we rest, whenever we rest, for the sake of that same good. Is it not so? **POLUS**: Precisely so. **SOCRATES**: Furthermore, if we kill someone, we kill for the same reason; and similarly we expel or rob them, thinking it better for us that such things be done. **POLUS**: Without a doubt. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, they do all these things, whatever they do, for the sake of the good. **POLUS**: I agree. **SOCRATES**: Have we not agreed that we do not *will* the things we do for the sake of something else, but rather that for the sake of which we do them? **POLUS**: Most certainly. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, we do not *will* simply to slaughter people, or to expel them, or to take their money; but if these things are beneficial, we *will* to do them; if they are harmful, we do not *will* them. For we *will* what is good, as you yourself say. But those things which are neither good nor evil, we do not properly *will*, nor those that are evil. Do I seem to you, Polus, to speak the truth? Or not? Why do you not answer? **POLUS**: Truth. **SOCRATES**: Wherefore, if we agree on these things, and if someone kills another, or casts him out of the city, or deprives him of his goods—whether that person be a tyrant or an orator—thinking it will be better for him, when in fact it is worse, he surely does what seems best to him, does he not? **POLUS**: Certainly. **SOCRATES**: But does he also do what he *will*, if these things happen to be evil? Why do you not answer? **POLUS**: It does not seem to me that he does what he *will*. **SOCRATES**: By what reason then does such a man have great power in the republic? If indeed great power is a good thing, as you yourself confess. **POLUS**: By no means. **SOCRATES**: I was speaking the truth then: it is possible for a man to do what seems best to him in a city and yet not have great power, nor...

[Marginalia:]
<margin>Whoever does something for the sake of someone or something, does not will what he does, but that for the sake of which he does it.</margin>
<margin>A negative disjunctive is posed, so that he may ask about something that perhaps is not in the disjunctive.</margin>

<summary>Socrates argues that tyrants and orators actually lack power because they do what "seems best" (opinion) rather than what they "will" (the good), illustrating this through the distinction between means (bitter medicine) and ends (health).</summary>

that he may do whatever he wishes. POLUS: As if you yourself would not choose to have the license to do whatever seems best to you in the city rather than not to have it, or that you do not envy those you see either killing, or stripping others of their goods, or throwing into chains whomever and whenever it seems fit to them. SOCRATES: Do you mean doing so justly, or unjustly? POLUS: However it is done, is not both to be desired? SOCRATES: Use better words, I pray, Polus. POLUS: Why so? SOCRATES: Because it is not fitting to envy those who are not at all enviable, or the miserable; rather, one should pity them. POLUS: What? Do you think those of whom I speak are in such a state? SOCRATES: Why not? POLUS: Whoever, therefore, kills whomever he thinks justly deserves death, does he seem unhappy and miserable to you? SOCRATES: Not to me, indeed, yet his condition is not to be envied. POLUS: Did you not just a little while ago call him miserable? SOCRATES: My friend, I did indeed say that the one who kills unjustly is miserable, and moreover pitiable; but that the condition of the one who kills justly is not one to be envied. POLUS: Is not the one who is killed unjustly both miserable and unhappy? SOCRATES: Less so than either his killer, or the one who is killed justly. <margin>Inflicting injustice is the greatest of evils.</margin> POLUS: How so, Socrates? SOCRATES: Because to inflict an injury is the greatest of all evils. POLUS: In what way is it the greatest? Is it not worse to suffer an injury? SOCRATES: Not at all. POLUS: You yourself, then, would you rather suffer an injury than inflict one? SOCRATES: Indeed, I would wish for neither. But if it were necessary either to do an injury or to suffer one, I would prefer to receive the injury rather than to inflict it. POLUS: You would not, therefore, choose a <term>tyranny</term> <note>original: "tyrannidem"; in this context, it refers to absolute power held by a single ruler, often seized illegally.</note>. SOCRATES: No, if you define tyranny as I do. POLUS: I say it is tyranny, as I said before: namely, to have the license in the city to do whatever seems fit, whether it pleases one to kill someone, or to expel them, and to do all other things according to one's whim. SOCRATES: But, my blessed friend, listen to what I say. If I were in the forum amidst a great crowd of men, with a dagger tucked under my arm, and I boasted to you that I had recently acquired a wonderful power and tyranny: for if it seemed to me that any of those men you see should be killed, he would be slain instantly; or if someone's head should be broken, it would be broken immediately; or if a garment should be torn, it would be torn at once—such is my power in this city. If, because you did not believe me, I showed you the dagger, you might perhaps object upon seeing it: "But Socrates, in that way everyone would have great power, and could clearly burn down any house they pleased, and the Athenian shipyards, and the <term>triremes</term> <note>Athenian warships with three banks of oars.</note>, and all the vessels, and in short, anyone could destroy both public and private property." Truly, this is not "great power," to do whatever seems fit to you in any way you like. Does it seem so to you? POLUS: Certainly I do not approve of power in that sense. SOCRATES: Can you say for what reason you do not approve of such power? POLUS: I can indeed. SOCRATES: Why then? Tell me now. POLUS: Because it is necessary that he who commits such things must pay the penalty. SOCRATES: And is it not an evil to pay the penalty? POLUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Then, O wonderful man, do you not again judge power to be great only if the one who does whatever he sees fit happens to act usefully, and thus achieves a good? Is that what it is to have great power? <margin>Cicero discusses this in the 5th Tusculan Disputation.</margin> On the contrary, is it not an evil, and a small power, otherwise? But let us also consider this: do we say it is better to do those things we just mentioned—namely to kill, expel, and plunder—at some times, and at other times not at all? POLUS: Exactly so. SOCRATES: On this point, it seems, you and I are now in agreement. In what way then do you say it is better to do these things? Come, tell me what limit you establish. POLUS: You yourself, Socrates, should define it. SOCRATES: If you would rather hear it from me, I will say: namely, when someone does these things <margin>A just and good man is happy. An unjust man is base and miserable.</margin> justly, it is better; but when unjustly, it is worse. POLUS: It is very difficult to refute you, Socrates. And yet even a child could prove you wrong and show that what you say is false. SOCRATES: I shall be very grateful to that child, and no less to you, if by refuting me you free me from such an error. I beg you, then, let it not be troublesome to you to bestow this benefit upon a friend, but refute me now. POLUS: But Socrates, there is no need for ancient examples to refute you. For from recent and even yesterday's events, it can be clearly proven that many unjust men are happy. SOCRATES: Which ones are these? POLUS: Do you see Archelaus, the son of Perdiccas, ruling Macedonia? <margin>Archelaus was born of a slave-woman of Alcetas.</margin> SOCRATES: Even if I do not see him, I at least hear of him. POLUS: Does he seem happy to you, or unhappy? SOCRATES: I do not know. For I have never spoken with him. POLUS: Can you not know it in any other way? SOCRATES: In no way. POLUS: Then you cannot even say whether the Great King of the Persians is blessed? SOCRATES: How can I, when I am ignorant of how learned he is, or how good a man? POLUS: What? Do you think a blessed life is placed in that? SOCRATES: I think exactly so: that the good are blessed, and the wicked are miserable. POLUS: Is Archelaus miserable then? SOCRATES: Certainly, if he is unjust. <margin>An unjust person cannot be happy.</margin> POLUS: But how can that be denied? For he was born of a slave-woman of Alcetas, the brother of Perdiccas; therefore, the kingdom of Macedonia which he now possesses did not belong to him at all. By right, he was the slave of Alcetas; and if he had wished to act justly, he would have served Alcetas himself, and in that way, according to your reasoning, he would be happy. But now, how wonderfully he has been reduced to misery, after he inflicted the greatest injuries. For first, he summoned this very master and uncle of his, Alcetas, to him as if he were going to restore the kingdom which Perdiccas had taken; having weighed him down with a feast and wine, he cast both him and his son Alexander—his own cousin and equal—into a wagon, carried them off by night, slaughtered them, and disposed of them. Yet even after committing these deeds, he did not recognize his misery, nor did he repent of having done it. But a little later, he did not want his legitimate brother, the son of Perdiccas, a boy of seven years to whom the kingdom belonged, to live happily, to be nourished justly, and to have the kingdom handed over to him; instead, he threw him headlong into a well and drowned him. He told the boy's mother, Cleopatra, that while the boy was chasing a goose, he had fallen into the well and met his death. After committing such great injuries, is he the most miserable of all Macedonians, or rather the most happy? Is there any Athenian, beginning with yourself, Socrates, who would not rather be any other Macedonian than Archelaus? SOCRATES: At the very beginning of this disputation, Polus, I praised you as being well-instructed in Rhetoric, but I said you had neglected the art of dialectic <note>original: "artem differendi"; the art of logical discussion or debate.</note>. Is this that reasoning by which even a child, as you said, might refute me? And have I been convicted by you, in your judgment, by this reasoning, for saying that a wrongdoer cannot be blessed? From where do you get this, my good man? I do not agree with a single thing you say. POLUS: For you do not wish to agree, even though these things seem true to you. SOCRATES: O blessed man, you strive to convict me in the manner of orators, as is done in the courts, where some think they convict others when they bring forward many famous witnesses for their cause; while the adversary produces either none or only one, although a proof of this kind is of no weight regarding the truth. For often, due to a multitude of false witnesses, even those who seem to be of some...

<summary>Socrates and Polus debate whether power and tyranny lead to happiness. Polus uses the example of the usurper Archelaus of Macedonia to argue that an unjust man can be happy, while Socrates maintains that doing injustice is the greatest misery.</summary>

...therefore dispels poverty; Medicine drives away diseases; and finally, Judicial justice removes intemperance and injustice. POLUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: Which, then, of these is the most beautiful? POLUS: Which do you mean? SOCRATES: Business, medicine, judicial justice. POLUS: Judicial justice far excels among these, Socrates. SOCRATES: Then it either brings the most pleasure, or utility, or both, if indeed it is the most beautiful. POLUS: So it is. SOCRATES: Is it then delightful to be cured by a physician? And are the sick pleased while they are being cured under the hands of the physician? POLUS: It does not appear so. SOCRATES: Yet it is beneficial, is it not? POLUS: It is. SOCRATES: Because, clearly, they are freed from a great evil. Therefore, it is useful to endure pain so that you may come out healthy. POLUS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Would he then be the most happy as far as the body is concerned—the one who, having been cured by medicine, recovers; or rather the one who was not sick from the beginning? POLUS: Certainly the one who was not sick. SOCRATES: Clearly happiness does not seem to consist in this—that we are freed from evils—but that we are safe from the very beginning. POLUS: So it is. SOCRATES: But if two are badly affected either in body or soul, which of these is more miserable: the one who is cured and freed from the evil, or the one who is not cured at all? POLUS: The one who is not cured, in my opinion. SOCRATES: Was not being punished by a judge a liberation from a certain greatest evil, that is, from wickedness? POLUS: It was indeed. SOCRATES: Since just punishment moderates and makes people more just, like a certain medicine for wickedness. POLUS: So it is. SOCRATES: Therefore, he is most happy who has no vice of the soul, since that appeared to be the greatest evil. POLUS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Next, however, is the one who is freed from such an evil. POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: And this is the one who, having been corrected and terrified, has paid the penalty. POLUS: That very one. SOCRATES: Most wretchedly, then, does he live who is unjust and is not released from his injustice. POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Is this not the one who, having committed the greatest injuries and used the greatest violence, has brought it about that he is neither corrected, nor punished, nor pays the penalty—just as you say Archelaus and other tyrants, orators, and powerful men have done? POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: For nearly such men, O best of men, act just as if someone afflicted with the most serious disease should take care that he does not receive the penalty of the vices that are in the body under a physician, and is not cured: fearing burning and cutting like a child, as if it were a troublesome thing. Does it not seem so to you as well? POLUS: It does to me. SOCRATES: Clearly because they are ignorant of how great health and the virtue of the body are. They seem, by those things we just conceded, to do such a thing, Polus—those who flee judgment: to look at the pain of it, but to be blind to the utility, and to be ignorant of how much more miserable it is to have a soul that is not healthy, but broken, unjust, and impious, than to carry about a sick body. And so they take care that they do not undergo judgment, nor are they released from the greatest evil. For that reason they pile up money, acquire friends, and study eloquence. But if we have confessed the truth to each other, do you perceive what finally follows from this disputation? Do you wish for us to collect each point in order? POLUS: Unless it seems otherwise to you. SOCRATES: Was it not established that injustice and injury are the greatest evil? POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: Moreover, that the release from this evil is to pay the penalty? POLUS: It appeared so. SOCRATES: And to escape it is the perseverance of the evil? POLUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, among evils, to inflict injury holds the second place in magnitude. But to bring it about that the penalty for injuries is not undergone is by nature the greatest of all, and the first of evils. POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: This is what we were disagreeing about, my friend. You indeed affirmed that Archelaus was happy—he who, though he committed the greatest injuries, yet paid no penalty. But I felt differently: namely, that whether it be Archelaus or any other mortal who does not bear the punishments for injuries, he is especially miserable; and that always he who has inflicted injury is more miserable than he who has sustained it; and finally, that he who does not pay the penalty is more miserable than he who does. Were these not the things I was saying? POLUS: These very things. SOCRATES: Has it not been demonstrated that these things were truly said? POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Come then, Polus, if it is established that these things are true, what use is there for rhetoric? Clearly it follows from the previous points that we ought to observe ourselves most diligently: first, so that we do not inflict injury on anyone, as we would have enough evil from that very thing; is it not so? POLUS: Certainly so. SOCRATES: Next, however, if an injury is inflicted either by ourselves or by someone else dear to us, we should of our own will offer ourselves to a judge to be punished, as if to a physician, quickly: lest the long-standing disease of injury so infect the soul as to make it incurable. In what other way shall we speak, Polus, if those previous things conceded between us remain? Do these not necessarily harmonize with them, and cannot be otherwise? POLUS: What else, then, can we say? SOCRATES: For defending or excusing our own injustice, or that of our parents, or friends, or children, or an injuring fatherland, rhetoric brings us no utility. Unless someone should judge that one ought to use rhetoric for the opposite purpose—namely, for accusation: first of ourselves, then of our household, family, and others; if any of those dear to us has committed injuries, let their crimes not be hidden, but be brought forward, so they may pay the penalty and come out healthy. Moreover, to compel oneself and others not to be sluggish, nor to be terrified: but with a brave soul and as if with closed eyes, to hand themselves over to the judge as if to a physician to be cut and burned, following the good and honorable itself, having despised the pain. Thus, if they have committed something worthy of stripes, they should offer themselves to be beaten; if of chains, to be bound; if of a fine, to be fined; if of exile, to be expelled; if of death, to be killed. <margin>Socrates wants us to accuse our friends of injury and to be exposed to the judge.</margin> In this matter, let each one be the accuser of himself and of his own; and let him use the oratory faculty for this: so that by making his injuries manifest, he may be released from the greatest evil of injustice. Is it so, Polus, or do we say otherwise? POLUS: These things seem absurd to me, Socrates. Nevertheless, perhaps they harmonize with your previous points. SOCRATES: Is it not necessary that either those previous points be torn down, or these following ones be conceded? POLUS: That is how the matter stands. SOCRATES: On the contrary, considering it further, if one must do evil to someone—whether an enemy, or someone I desire it for—it is only to be avoided that he himself does not suffer injury from the adversary; but if the enemy has done injury to others, one must provide with all study, both in words and deeds, that he does not pay the penalty, nor is he dragged to the judge; but if he is snatched away to him, perhaps one should strive so that the enemy escapes, and no punishment is taken from him. Nay, if he has stolen much gold, let it be so that he does not restore it, but possessing it, he pours it out unjustly and impiously upon himself and his own; but if he has committed something worthy of death, let him never die, if possible, but be an immortal evil man. But if that cannot be, at least let him live in that wickedness for the longest time. For these and such things, it seems to me, Polus, rhetoric is useful. But to the one who is not going to inflict injury, it seems to be of no great benefit; if indeed there is any advantage or utility in it at all. For in those things said above, nothing of the kind appeared at all. CALLICLES: Tell me, Chaerephon, is Socrates speaking seriously, or is he joking? CHAEREPHON: It seems to me, Callicles, that he speaks in a wonderfully serious way. However, it would not be out of place to ask him. CALLICLES: By the gods, Socrates, I desire to know whether we should think you are speaking seriously or joking. For if these things are serious and...

...and evil, that is, defined by harm? POLUS: It must be. SOCRATES: Whenever, therefore, one of two beautiful things is more beautiful, it is more beautiful because it exceeds the other in one of those things, or both: namely, either in delight, or utility, or both. POLUS: Precisely. SOCRATES: Again, when one of two shameful things is more shameful, it is more shameful by exceeding either in pain or in harm. Is that not necessary? POLUS: Yes. SOCRATES: Come then, what was said a little while ago about inflicting and receiving injury? Did you not say that to suffer an injury is worse, but to do one is more shameful? POLUS: I did say so. SOCRATES: If, then, to do it is more shameful than to suffer it, is it not also necessary that it is either more painful—and it is more shameful by surpassing in pain—or in harm, or in both? POLUS: Why not? SOCRATES: First, let us consider if the pain surpasses: do those who inflict injury suffer more pain than those who receive it? POLUS: In no way. SOCRATES: Therefore, it does not exceed in pain. POLUS: It does not appear so. SOCRATES: If not in pain, then not in both. POLUS: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: Therefore, in the other. POLUS: Yes. SOCRATES: In evil, then, and in harm. POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: For which reason, to do injury, exceeding in harm, will be worse than to suffer it. POLUS: It is manifest. SOCRATES: And was it not conceded by many men, and by you above, that it is more shameful to inflict an injury than to receive it? POLUS: Yes. SOCRATES: And now it has appeared to be worse? POLUS: It has. SOCRATES: Would you choose that which is worse and more shameful over that which is less so? Do not be reluctant to answer, Polus; for it will do no harm. But commit yourself to the argument as if to a physician, candidly; and by answering, either concede what I say, or deny it. POLUS: I would never choose that, Socrates. SOCRATES: Do you think any other person would accept it? POLUS: It does not seem so to me by this reasoning. SOCRATES: For which reason I spoke the truth: neither I, nor you, nor any other person would accept doing injury more than suffering it, insofar as it is worse. POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: You see then, Polus, that having compared the arguments, they differ greatly from each other. For all others besides me agree with you, but for me, you alone are sufficient by agreeing and testifying, for yours is the only vote and opinion I have asked for, letting the others go. And let it be so. <margin>Whether it is the greatest of evils for one who inflicts injuries to pay the penalty, or not to pay it.</margin> But after this, let us now consider what was doubted in the second place between us: whether for the wrongdoer to pay the penalty is the greatest of evils, as you thought; or whether not to pay it is greater, which was my opinion. Let us consider it in this way. To pay the penalty for injuries, and to be justly punished, do you call that the same thing for the one who does the injury? POLUS: The same. SOCRATES: Can it be denied that all just things, insofar as they are just, are beautiful? And see that you answer providently. POLUS: It seems so to me as much as to you. SOCRATES: Notice this as well: if someone acts upon something, is it necessary that there is something being acted upon by that agent? <margin>In whatever way the agent acts, in such a way the thing acted upon suffers.</margin> POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore, must it also suffer that which the agent does? And moreover, of such a kind as the act itself? I mean something of this sort: if someone strikes, is it necessary that something is struck? POLUS: Necessary. SOCRATES: And if he strikes violently or swiftly, that the thing struck is similarly struck? POLUS: Similarly. SOCRATES: Such a passion <note>original: "passio"; here used in the philosophical sense of "suffering an action" or being the object of an act.</note>, then, is in the thing struck, as the striker effects? POLUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: And if someone burns something, must something be burned? POLUS: It must. SOCRATES: And if he burns it violently, and so to speak, with sharp pain, that which is burned is similarly burned, just as the burner burns? POLUS: Precisely. SOCRATES: Similarly if someone cuts? Something is also cut. POLUS: Yes. SOCRATES: And if the cut is wide or deep, or painful, is it necessary that the thing being cut is cut with such a cutting as the cutter himself cuts? POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: Consider then in summary, if you confess what I just said in all cases: namely, that of whatever kind the agent's act is, such is the suffering of the one acted upon. POLUS: I confess it. SOCRATES: These things being granted, answer: is to pay the penalty to suffer something, or to do something? POLUS: To suffer. SOCRATES: And is it not from some agent? POLUS: It is established: namely, from the one who punishes. SOCRATES: But he who punishes rightly, does he not punish justly? POLUS: Justly. SOCRATES: Doing just things, or not? POLUS: Just things. SOCRATES: Therefore he who is punished, while he pays the penalty for injustice, suffers just things. POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: But just things have been said to be beautiful. POLUS: So it is. SOCRATES: Of these two, then, one does beautiful things; but the other, namely the one punished, suffers beautiful things. POLUS: So it is. SOCRATES: And if they are beautiful, they are also good. For they are either pleasant or useful. POLUS: It must be so. SOCRATES: Therefore, whoever is justly punished suffers good things. POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: This, therefore, benefits him. POLUS: It is useful. SOCRATES: Is it not so, as I judge it, that he receives a better soul, if indeed he is justly punished? POLUS: It is consistent. SOCRATES: Therefore, he who pays the penalty is freed from the wickedness of the soul. POLUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Thus he is freed from the greatest evil. In the same way, consider: in the collection of money, do you see any other evil for a man than poverty? POLUS: Only that. SOCRATES: And in the body, would you call evil weakness, disease, deformity, and other things of that kind? POLUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: And do you not think there is some evil in the soul? POLUS: Why not? SOCRATES: And do you not call that injustice, ignorance, cowardice, and others of the same kind? POLUS: Especially. SOCRATES: Since there are these three—money, body, soul—you said there are three evils belonging to them: poverty, disease, injustice. POLUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: But of these evils, which is the most shameful? Is it not injustice? And, to speak in summary, the vice of the soul? POLUS: Especially. SOCRATES: If the vice of the soul is the most shameful, then it is also the worst. POLUS: By what reasoning do you say this, Socrates? SOCRATES: By this: whatever is most shameful is so either because it brings the greatest pain, or the greatest harm, or both, as appears from what was conceded earlier. POLUS: Surely. SOCRATES: And was it not conceded by us that injustice and every vice of the soul is most shameful? POLUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, either because it is most painful—and surpassing in pain, it is therefore the most shameful of these—or because it brings harm, or because of both. POLUS: So it must be. SOCRATES: Is it more painful to be unjust, intemperate, cowardly, or ignorant than to be pressed by poverty and disease? POLUS: Certainly not, as far as can be gathered from these things. SOCRATES: Since, therefore, by some incredible and wonderful magnitude of harm and evil, the vice of the soul surpasses other evils, for that reason it is the most shameful of all; since it does not exceed in pain, as you yourself say. POLUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: Now indeed, that which exceeds by the greatest damage is the greatest of all evils. POLUS: So it is. SOCRATES: Therefore injustice, intemperance, and other wickedness of the soul is the greatest evil of all. POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: What art frees us from poverty? Is it not the art of commerce <note>original: "quaestuaria"; the art of making money or business.</note>? POLUS: This very one. SOCRATES: And what from disease? Is it not medicine? POLUS: Truly that. SOCRATES: And what from wickedness and injustice? If it does not occur to you, consider it this way: where and to whom do we primarily lead those laboring under bodily diseases? POLUS: To physicians, Socrates. SOCRATES: And where those who are unjust and dissolute? POLUS: To the judges. SOCRATES: So that, clearly, they may be punished. POLUS: I agree. SOCRATES: Do not those who punish rightly punish by relying on a certain justice? POLUS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Business...

<summary>Socrates proves to Polus that doing injustice is worse than suffering it because it causes more harm. He then argues that punishment is a "medicine" for the soul, and therefore, an unpunished wrongdoer is more miserable than one who pays the penalty.</summary>
