<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous page, where Socrates and Polus were debating whether it is worse to inflict or suffer an injury. Polus has just conceded that doing wrong is more shameful and harmful than being wronged. Here, Socrates moves to the "cure" for such harm.</meta>

242 Book Twenty-four.

...therefore [money-making] drives away poverty; Medicine, however, drives away diseases; and finally, Justice <note>original: "iudiciaria"</note> removes intemperance and injustice. POLUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: Which of these, then, is the most beautiful? POLUS: Of which do you speak? SOCRATES: Money-making, medicine, or justice? POLUS: Justice far excels the others, Socrates. SOCRATES: Then it either brings the most pleasure, or utility, or both, if indeed it is the most beautiful. POLUS: That is so. SOCRATES: Is it then delightful to be treated by a physician? And do the sick take pleasure in being in the doctor's hands while they are being cured? POLUS: It does not appear so. SOCRATES: Yet it is beneficial, is it not? POLUS: It is. SOCRATES: Because they are clearly being freed from a great evil; for which reason it is useful to endure pain so that you may emerge healthy. POLUS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Would a man then be the happiest regarding his body if he were cured through medicine and regained his health, or rather if he had never been sick from the beginning? POLUS: Certainly, the one who was never sick. SOCRATES: For happiness, it seems, does not consist in being freed from evils, but in being sound and healthy from the very start. POLUS: That is true. SOCRATES: Furthermore, if two people were ill in either body or soul, which of them would be more miserable: the one who is treated and freed from the evil, or the one who is not? POLUS: The one who is not treated, in my opinion. SOCRATES: And was not being punished by a judgment a liberation from the greatest evil, that is, from wickedness? POLUS: It certainly was. SOCRATES: Since a just penalty brings moderation and makes people more just, acting as a kind of medicine for wickedness. POLUS: That is true. SOCRATES: The happiest man, therefore, is he who has no vice in his soul, since that has appeared to be the greatest evil. POLUS: Beyond doubt. SOCRATES: And in the second place is he who is freed from such an evil. POLUS: So it appears. SOCRATES: And this is the man who, having been corrected and rebuked, has paid the penalty. POLUS: That is the one. SOCRATES: He lives worst, then, who is unjust and is not released from his injustice. POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: And is this not the man who, having committed the greatest wrongs and used the greatest violence, ensures that he is neither corrected, nor punished, nor pays the penalty—just as you say Archelaus <note>Archelaus was a King of Macedon whom Polus previously cited as a "happy" man because he committed crimes to gain power and was never punished.</note> did, along with other <term>tyrants</term> <note>In this context, a ruler who has seized power illegally and rules without the constraint of law.</note> and orators and powerful men? POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: For such men, my good friend, act almost as if someone suffering from a most grievous disease were to take care that he does not pay the penalty for the vices of his body under a doctor's care, nor be cured—fearing, like a child, the <term>cautery and surgery</term> <note>original: "vſtionẽ atq; ſectione" (burning and cutting)</note> as something painful. Does it not seem so to you as well? POLUS: It does to me. SOCRATES: Because they are clearly ignorant of how great a thing health and the virtue of the body are. It seems, Polus, from what we have just conceded, that those who flee from judgment do something similar: they look only at the pain of it, but are blind to its utility. They are ignorant of how much more miserable it is to live with a soul that is not healthy, but is broken, unjust, and impious, than to carry around a sick body. And so they do everything they can to avoid undergoing judgment and being freed from the greatest evil. For that reason, they amass wealth, acquire friends, and study the art of eloquence. But if the things we have confessed to each other are true, do you see what follows from this discussion? Or do you wish for us to gather the points in order? POLUS: Unless you think otherwise. SOCRATES: Has it not been established that injustice and doing wrong is the greatest evil? POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: And furthermore, that the cure for this evil is to pay the penalty? POLUS: That appeared to be so. SOCRATES: And that to escape the penalty is to persist in the evil? POLUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, in the scale of evils, the second place in magnitude is held by doing an injury. But to do an injury and not undergo the punishment is, by its very nature, the greatest and first of all evils. POLUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: This, then, my friend, is what we were debating. You asserted that Archelaus was happy, who, though he committed the greatest wrongs, paid no penalty. But I held the opposite view: that whether it be Archelaus or any other mortal who does not suffer punishment for his wrongs, he is uniquely miserable. And I held that he who inflicts an injury is always more miserable than he who suffers it, and he who does not pay the penalty is more miserable than he who does. Were these not the things I said? POLUS: These very things. SOCRATES: And has it not been demonstrated that these words were spoken truly? POLUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Come then, Polus, if this is established as true, of what use is <term>rhetoric</term>? <note>The art of persuasive speaking.</note> For it follows from what was said above that we must most diligently watch ourselves, first, so that we do not inflict injury on anyone, as we would have enough evil from that alone; is that not so? POLUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Secondly, if an injury is committed either by ourselves or by someone dear to us, we must go of our own accord to where we may be punished, offering ourselves to the judge as if to a physician, quickly, lest the long-standing disease of injustice so infect the soul as to make it incurable. How else can we say it, Polus, if our previous concessions remain? Do not these things necessarily harmonize with those, and can they be otherwise? POLUS: What else can we say, then? SOCRATES: Rhetoric, therefore, is of no use to us for defending or excusing our own injustice, or that of our parents, friends, children, or country. Unless, perhaps, someone thinks he should use rhetoric for the opposite purpose—that is, for accusation: first against himself, then against his family and friends, if any of those dear to him have committed a wrong. He should not hide their crimes, but bring them to light, so they may pay the penalty and emerge healthy. Furthermore, he should use it to compel himself and others not to be sluggish or fearful, but with a brave heart and as if with closed eyes, to offer themselves to the judge as to a surgeon to be "cut and burned," pursuing what is good and honest while despising the pain. Thus, if they have committed a crime worthy of stripes, let them offer themselves to be beaten; if of chains, to be bound; if a fine, to be fined; if exile, to be expelled; if death, to be killed. In this matter, let each man be the accuser of himself and his own, and let him use the oratorical faculty for this purpose: that by revealing his injustices, he may be freed from the greatest evil of injustice. Shall we say this, Polus, or something else? POLUS: These things seem absurd to me, Socrates. Yet, perhaps they are consistent with what you said before. SOCRATES: Is it not necessary either that those earlier points be overturned, or that these following points be conceded? POLUS: That is how it stands. SOCRATES: On the other hand, if one must do harm to someone—whether an enemy or anyone else—one must only take care that he himself does not suffer an injury from that adversary. But if the enemy has done an injury to others, every effort must be made, in word and deed, to ensure he does not pay the penalty, nor is he dragged before a judge. If he is hauled there, one must strive so that the enemy escapes and suffers no punishment. Indeed, if he has stolen much gold, let him not restore it, but possess it himself and spend it unjustly and impiously on himself and his own. If he has committed crimes worthy of death, let him never die, if possible, but be immortal in his wickedness. Or if that is not possible, let him at least live in that depravity for as long as possible. For these and such things, Polus, rhetoric seems useful to me. But for the man who is not going to do an injury, it seems to be of no great benefit—if indeed there is any advantage or utility in it at all. For in those things said above, nothing of the sort appeared. CALLICLES: Tell me, Chaerephon, is Socrates speaking seriously, or is he joking? CHAEREPHON: To me, Callicles, he seems to be speaking with wonderful seriousness. However, it would not be out of place to ask him himself. CALLICLES: By the gods, Socrates, I desire to know whether we should think you are speaking seriously or joking. For if these things are serious and true...

<margin>
Socrates wants us to accuse our friends of wrongdoing and be exposed to the judge.

<summary>Socrates argues that justice is a "medicine" for the soul's wickedness and that it is better to be punished than to escape penalty. He concludes that rhetoric's only virtuous use is in accusing oneself or loved ones so they may be "healed" through punishment, while it should only be used against enemies to keep them trapped in their own unpunished vice.</summary>

This is a scholarly translation of the provided Latin text, which is a Renaissance-era translation of Plato’s *Gorgias* (likely that of Marsilio Ficino). The text follows the dialogue between Socrates and Callicles regarding the nature of rhetoric, justice, and the best way to live.

### PAGE 261 [Original Page 243]

**Gorgias, Or, On Rhetoric**

...and the things you say are true: undoubtedly our life is perverse, and we do everything contrary to what is proper.

**SOCRATES:** Callicles, if there were not an affection inherent in men—one indeed in some, another in others, yet common in most—but instead some of us had a unique affection peculiar to ourselves beyond the rest, it would by no means be easy to explain to others what one feels. To what does this tend? I notice that the same thing happens to both of us: since we are two, we love two things. For I love Alcibiades and Philosophy; but you, I perceive, love the Athenian people and Pyrilampus. Therefore, it usually happens to you that, despite whatever gravity you are endowed with, nevertheless when your beloved opposes you and contends that a matter is a certain way, you cannot contradict him, but are changed up and down. For in the assembly, if the Athenian people contradict you while you are speaking, you are compelled to change your opinion and say those things which you understand please them. The same things usually happen to you when you are dealing with that beautiful youth Pyrilampus; you cannot in any way resist his will. Therefore, if someone, marveling at those things which you say for his sake or for the sake of the people, should object that they are absurd, you will perhaps respond—if you are willing to confess the truth—that unless the one you love and the people change their opinion, you will never change yours. Consider, then, that you hear such things from me, and do not wonder that I say them, but strive that Philosophy, my mistress, should cease to desire these things. For she says, O sweet friend, always what you hear from me. And to me, she is much less foolish and stubborn than a boyish lover. For this Clinias [1] speaks to me now one way, now another, but Philosophy is always the same. Moreover, she says the things you now wonder at; for you have just heard them present. Therefore, either refute what was just said, and show that to do injury and not pay the penalty is not the extreme of evils; or, if you allow this to stand, I predict to you, O Callicles, by the Dog, the god of the Egyptians, that Callicles will never agree with Callicles, but will be at odds throughout his whole life. And yet I, O best of men, judge it better that my lyre be discordant and out of tune, and that the chorus I lead and many men besides should contradict me, rather than that I, being one, should be out of harmony with and contradict myself.

**CALLICLES:** O Socrates, you seem to exult youthfully while speaking, and in truth you appear as a sort of orator. And even now you act the orator in these things, since the same thing happened to Polus that he was accusing Gorgias of a little while ago in your presence. For when Gorgias was asked by you whether, if someone came to him to learn rhetoric but was ignorant of justice, he would teach him, Polus says that Gorgias, moved by shame, affirmed that he would teach him—and this because of the customs of men, who would take it ill if one did not concede such things. Then, because of this sort of concession, Gorgias was forced to contradict himself, which was wonderfully pleasing to you. Wherefore someone rightly mocked you in judgment then, because you followed such ineptitudes. [2] Now indeed, the same things have happened to Polus: in this I least approve of him, that he conceded to you that doing injury is more shameful than suffering it; for by that concession, hindered by you, he could not explain what he had thought. You, in truth, O Socrates, lead your listeners into difficulties and oratorical traps while you profess to follow the truth. You bring into the midst things which are not beautiful by nature, but by law. For it usually happens that law and nature are contrary to each other. If anyone, therefore, suffused with shame, does not dare to express what he thinks, he is compelled to confess things contrary to himself. You, noticing this quite astutely, lay snares in words. For if someone speaks according to law, you then question according to nature. But if he speaks according to nature, you question according to law; just as you did just now concerning the infliction or the endurance of injury. For when Polus said that by law it is more shameful to inflict it, you followed the law. By nature, however, whatever is worse is also more shameful, such as suffering injury; but by law, it is to inflict it. For it is not the part of a man to suffer injuries, but of some slave, for whom it is better to be dead than alive; who, being affected by insults and injuries, can help neither himself nor his own. But, as I think, those who establish laws are the weaker ones, and the multitude itself. Therefore, consulting their own utility, they constitute laws. Furthermore, they distribute praises and censures, led by the fear of the stronger, lest they might exceed them in any matter. Therefore, they say it is shameful and unjust for others to have more, and they define doing injury as seeking to have more than others. For they think it enough for themselves if, being inferior, they have an equal portion. For this reason, then, it is called unjust and shameful by law to seek to possess more than the rest; and the common people call this "injury." Nature herself, however, as I think, demonstrates that it is just that the more excellent and powerful should have more than the rest. She shows this in many ways, both in other animals and in all states and nations, among whom it is judged just that the more powerful should rule the weaker and possess more. For by what right did Xerxes lead his army against the Greeks, or his father against the Scythians, or innumerable others whom one could mention? But these, as I judge, act according to the nature of right itself, and (by Jove) according to the law of nature itself; yet perhaps not according to these laws established by us, through which we bind the most excellent and strongest youths from the cradle like lions, and as if by certain magical charms we fascinate them and reduce them to a servile manner, saying that equality must be preserved, and that this is beautiful and just. But if some man of an excellent nature should arise, trampling underfoot and tearing apart these writings, fascinations, and incantations of yours, and subverting and treading upon all laws that depart from nature, and ruling over the rest, in him the right of nature itself would shine forth. Pindar seems to me to show these same things in a certain song: where he says law is the queen of all mortals and immortals, and that she carries out justice by violence with a most powerful hand. He says he conjectures this from the deeds done by Hercules: who (though I do not hold the poem itself well in memory) I remember him saying that Hercules drove away the oxen of Geryon without having bought or been given them: as if by natural right itself dictating that both oxen and all other things possessed by men ought to belong to him who is more excellent and stronger. The truth, therefore, is thus. And you may clearly know it if, having dismissed the care of philosophizing, you turn now to greater things. For philosophy, O Socrates, is a graceful and charming thing if one touches it moderately in youth. But if one consumes more time in it than is proper, it is the corruption of men. For no matter how good a natural talent one is endowed with, if he philosophizes too long into an advanced age, he will necessarily turn out ignorant of all those things in which a clear, good, and excellent man ought to have skill. For they are ignorant of civil laws, and of the words which it is proper to use in the custom and assembly of men both publicly and privately, and furthermore of human pleasures and desires.

*[Marginal note: "Deest in Graeco" (It is missing in the Greek)]*

### PAGE 262 [Original Page 244]

**Book Twenty-Four**

...and to comprehend briefly, they are utterly ignorant of morals. Wherefore, as often as they betake themselves to managing any affair, whether public or private, they are held as ridiculous, just as civil men are if they descend into your exercises and disputations. For that saying of Euripides happens: in whatever thing each one is famous, to that he hastens, and imparts the greatest part of the day to it, so that he may surpass himself. But where he is inferior, from there he flees and censures it; but he praises the other, thinking by a certain benevolence toward himself that he thus praises himself. Truly, I judge it better to become a participant in both: in philosophy indeed insofar as it is proper for the sake of discipline. Nor is it shameful for a youth to philosophize. But when one older in age still leans upon philosophy, the thing is, Socrates, truly ridiculous. Indeed, I am affected toward those who give effort to philosophy in the same way as toward those who stammer and play. For as often as I behold a boy, for whom it is still decorous to speak so, stammering and playing, I am delighted; it seems to me festive and liberal, and becoming to a youthful age. But as often as I hear a boy expressing words more precisely, something troublesome arises in me and offends my ears; and it seems to involve something servile. On the other hand, when one hears a man stammering or sees him playing, it appears ridiculous, and alien to men, and worthy of blows. The same, therefore, happens to me regarding those who philosophize. For when I see philosophy in a youth, I am greatly delighted, and I judge it becoming, and I consider this man to be well-bred; but he who does not philosophize, I think illiberal, and one who will never perform anything famous or noble for himself. But when I notice an older man philosophizing, and not yet deserting such studies, I judge this man, Socrates, to be in need of stripes. Because, as I was just saying, it happens to this man that even if he is well-born, nevertheless he turns out inert and cowardly. For he flees the middle of the city and the customs of the marketplace, in which the poet says the most excellent men are made; and he hides himself with three or four boys, and leads a life whispering in corners, never about to bring forth anything liberal or magnificent. Toward you, however, Socrates, I am well and kindly affected. Therefore, I think the same thing has happened to me toward you as to Zethus toward Amphion in Euripides, of whom I just made mention. For such things now come into my mind to say against you as he said against his brother. Surely, Socrates, you neglect those things which it was fitting for you to care for, and you conform the excellence of a noble mind to a certain boyish appearance, as one who could neither speak rightly in judgments and consultations, if use demanded, nor choose anything probably for anyone, nor promptly counsel others. Therefore, friend Socrates, be not angry with me. For my benevolence toward you now leads me to bring these things forth. Do you not think it shameful to be so composed as I think you and all others are who pursue philosophy too long? Truly, if someone now should seize you or anyone else from your group and drag you into prison, and accuse you of doing an injury though you did none, you certainly would not know what to do; but you would stagger and gape, being utterly ignorant of your detention. Then, being led into court, even by a cowardly and abject accuser, you would be affected by the ultimate punishment, if only it pleased him. Now, how does that pertain to wisdom, O Socrates: if an art, having found a man of a noble mind, renders him worse, so that he cannot bring help even to himself, nor save himself or anyone else from the gravest dangers, but places him at the mercy of the injuries of enemies and robbers as he lives ingloriously in the city? Truly, such a man, even if it be said somewhat rudely, may be struck upon the cheek with impunity. Wherefore, good man, hear me, and cease now to be occupied in vain subtleties; exercise the decorous duties of managing affairs, and those things from which you may seem to be wise. Leave to others those subtle things—whether they ought to be called deliriums or trifles—whence houses are to be inhabited by you that are empty. Finally, imitate not those who catch at these small things, but those to whom livelihood, glory, and many other goods accrue.

**SOCRATES:** If I had a golden soul, O Callicles, do you not think I would gladly find some of those stones by which the best gold is usually tested, to which, applying my soul, if it were approved by it as being rightly educated, I would know for certain that I have enough, and need no further proof?

**CALLICLES:** To what does this tend, O Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** I will tell you. Truly, I think that having found you, I have found this precious stone.

**CALLICLES:** For what reason?

**SOCRATES:** Because I know for certain that those things which you feel with me, in those things which my mind opines, will be undoubtedly true. For I judge that in him who is to test someone's soul, whether it has been rightly instituted or not, three things are chiefly required, all of which are in you: first, knowledge; second, opinion—namely, that of a prudent and benevolent person; third, boldness. For I find many who cannot test me with a right examination because they are not wise, as you seem to be. Others are indeed wise, but they do not wish to tell me the truth because they do not care for me as you do. These strangers, Gorgias and Polus, are indeed wise and love me, but they lack boldness and are more bashful than is proper. Indeed, how could this be doubtful? Since they proceeded so far in bashfulness that each, because of that very bashfulness, dared in the presence of many men to contradict himself regarding the greatest matters. All of which you possess, while others lack them. First, you are abundantly and liberally educated, which many Athenians, if necessary, would confirm; and you are benevolent to me. By what conjecture I understand this, I will tell you. I know indeed, Callicles, that there were four of you as associates in the study of wisdom: yourself, Tisander of Aphidnae, Andron the son of Androtion, and Nausicydes of Cholargus. And I heard that when it was once discussed among you how far one should study wisdom, a sentiment of this sort prevailed among you: that one should not strive for an exact diligence in philosophy, but must take care lest, becoming wise beyond what is proper, you should secretly deprave yourselves. When, therefore, I hear you giving me the same advice that you gave your closest friends, it is an abundantly great argument of your true love toward me. Finally, that boldness is not lacking, and that shame does not hinder you, you yourself affirm, and the speech which you just now had here testifies. Since these things are so, whatever you concede to me in dispute will have been sufficiently proven by us; nor will it be necessary to refer it to another examination. Otherwise, you would never have conceded it to me, either from a defect of wisdom, or led by bashfulness, or for the sake of deceiving. For you are my friend, as you yourself say. In truth, therefore, my confession and yours will now have the end of truth. Moreover, the consideration of these things in which you corrected me, Callicles, is the most beautiful of all: what sort of man one should be, and what, and how far...

*[Marginal notes: "Three things he ought to have who will test the soul of another: knowledge, benevolence, boldness." / "The opinion of Callicles and his friends: One should not strive for an exact diligence in philosophy." / "The consideration of which things is most beautiful."]*

### PAGE 263 [Original Page 245]

**Gorgias, Or, On Rhetoric**

...one should exercise both in youth and in old age. For if I do anything in my life less than rightly, I am certain that I err not by my own will, but rather by ignorance. Wherefore you, as you have begun to admonish me, proceed I pray, and plainly demonstrate to me what that thing is, and by what way I may attain what you judge I ought to seek. But if you find me consenting to you now, and afterward you find me failing to perform what I assented to, consider me altogether sluggish and cowardly, and do not lose any more effort in admonishing me further. Resume for me from the beginning what you and Pindar were saying: that it is just by nature for the more powerful to take away by force those things which belong to the weaker, and for the better to rule the inferior, and for him who is more excellent to have more than he who is more abject. Do you say justice is anything else? Or do I remember rightly?

**CALLICLES:** I was saying these things then, and I say them now.

**SOCRATES:** But do you call the "better" the same as the "more powerful"? For I could not then plainly understand what you were saying. Do you call the stronger "more powerful"? And must the weaker obey the stronger? As you seemed to demonstrate then, when you said that great states rise up against small ones by natural right, because they were more powerful and stronger—as if the more powerful, the stronger, and the better were the same. Or can it be that someone is indeed better, yet inferior and weaker? And similarly, that he is more powerful, yet worse? Or is the definition of the better and the more powerful the same? Explain this very thing to me more clearly, whether the more powerful, the better, and the stronger be the same or different.

**CALLICLES:** I plainly tell you they are the same.

**SOCRATES:** Is not the multitude itself by nature more powerful than one? Which indeed established laws over the one, as you yourself were just saying.

**CALLICLES:** How could it be otherwise?

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the laws of the multitude are those of the more powerful.

**CALLICLES:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** Are they not, therefore, also those of the better? For those who are more powerful, as you yourself say, are much better.

**CALLICLES:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Are not their institutions right by nature, since they are more powerful?

**CALLICLES:** I so affirm.

**SOCRATES:** Does not the multitude determine, as you yourself were just saying, that it is just that equality be preserved among all, and that it is more shameful to inflict injury than to suffer it? Is it so, or otherwise? And take care lest you also are caught here by bashfulness. Does that multitude determine or not: namely, that it is just that equality be preserved, and not that one should have more than another; and that it is more shameful to do injury than to receive it? I pray, Callicles, let no envy keep you from responding to these things; so that if you agree with me, I may be confirmed by you as by a man abundantly sufficient for judging.

**CALLICLES:** Thus indeed the multitude determines.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is not by law alone that it is more shameful to do injury than to suffer it, and that it is just to preserve equality; but also by nature itself. Wherefore you seem not to have spoken truly in the previous matters, nor to have accused me rightly; and that I, noticing these things, show myself a "veterator" [old fox/shrewd person] in disputing; and if anyone speaks according to nature, I lead him to law; but if anyone speaks according to law, I lead him to nature.

**CALLICLES:** This man will never cease dealing in trifles. Tell me, Socrates, are you not ashamed, being of such an age, to hunt for names? And if someone should exceed in a word, to catch at it greedily as if it were a gain to you? Do you think I say the more powerful are anything other than the better? Have I not long been saying that the better and the more powerful are the same? Or do you think I am saying that if a dreg of slaves and of the vilest men from all sides should flow together, these are more powerful—except perhaps by the strength of their bodies—and that what these establish are rights?

**SOCRATES:** Come now, O most wise Callicles, is it thus you speak?

**CALLICLES:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** But I, blessed man, have long been conjecturing that you call something of that sort "more powerful"; and I question you desiring to know openly what you mean. For do you not judge two to be better than one? And your slaves are not better than you because they are stronger? But say again from the beginning whom you finally mean to be the "better," when they are not the "stronger." And see, I pray, O marvelous man, that you teach me more mildly, lest I flee from your schools.

**CALLICLES:** You speak ironically.

**SOCRATES:** Not by Zethus, Callicles, upon whom you relied to use much irony against me just now. But come, tell me, whom do you call the "better"?

**CALLICLES:** The "more excellent," indeed.

**SOCRATES:** You see, therefore, that you only speak names, but show nothing. Do you not open whether you say the better and more powerful are the more prudent, or some others?

**CALLICLES:** By Jove, I say these, and most especially.

**SOCRATES:** Often, therefore, one prudent person is more powerful than many imprudent ones according to your discourse; and it is fair that he should rule, and the rest should be subject, and that he should have more than those whom he commands. For you seem to wish to say this (and I do not catch at words) if indeed one is more powerful than many.

**CALLICLES:** But these are the very things I say. For I judge this to be the right of nature: namely, that he who is better and more prudent should command, and possess more than the inferior.

**SOCRATES:** Stay a little. What would you think if in this place, as now, many of us were gathered together, and we had common food and many drinks, and we were composed of various kinds of men, some indeed strong, some weak; but one of all of us was perhaps a most prudent physician? And he would be, as is reasonable, stronger than some, but weaker than others. Would not he, being more prudent, furthermore be better and more powerful as far as these things pertain?

**CALLICLES:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** But is it fitting that he, because he is better, should take more of these foods than we? Or rather, because of his excellence, ought he to distribute all things, and not retain more for himself in distributing—otherwise he would be punished—but have more than some, and less than others? And if he were the weakest of all, should the least be attributed to himself, although he is the best, Callicles? Is it not thus the "good" must be said?

**CALLICLES:** You speak of food, and drink, and physicians and such trifles; I, however, do not speak of these.

**SOCRATES:** Do you then say the more prudent is the better, or not? Answer.

**CALLICLES:** Indeed.

**SOCRATES:** But ought not the better to receive more?

**CALLICLES:** Not of food and drink.

**SOCRATES:** I understand. Perhaps of clothes. And it is proper that he who is most skilled in making clothes should have a great cloak, and walk about adorned with many and precious garments.

**CALLICLES:** What clothes are you telling me about?

**SOCRATES:** But perhaps in shoes it is proper that he should receive more who is more prudent and better in them; and perhaps the cobbler himself ought to have the largest and most shoes, and carry many about on his feet.

**CALLICLES:** What shoes are you now raving about?

**SOCRATES:** But if not such things, at least you say something of this kind, as that a man prudent in cultivating fields, honest and good, ought to report more seeds, and use the most in his own fields.

**CALLICLES:** How you always say the same things, O Socrates!

**SOCRATES:** Not only the same things, Callicles, but also concerning the same matters.

**CALLICLES:** By the gods, you always have cobblers, shoemakers, fullers, cooks, and physicians...

### PAGE 264 [Original Page 246]

**Book Twenty-Four**

...in your mouth, as if our discussion were instituted concerning these.

**SOCRATES:** Will you not then yourself say at last in what things the more powerful and prudent ought justly to possess more? Or will you neither permit me to speak, nor speak yourself?

**CALLICLES:** But I have been saying it for a long time: first, indeed, those who are more powerful. For I do not mean cobblers, nor cooks, but those who are prudent in administering the republic; and not only prudent, but also brave, who are most fit to perfect those things they have thought out, and do not succumb to any softness of mind.

**SOCRATES:** Do you notice, Callicles, that I am not accused by you of the same thing that you are by me? For you accuse me as if I always repeat the same things; I, however, accuse you on the contrary as never bringing forward the same things concerning the same matters. For at one time you define the better and more powerful as the stronger, at another time as the more prudent. Now, furthermore, you bring forward something else. For now certain brave ones are named by you as the more powerful and better. But come, O good man, finally explain whom most especially and to what end you call the better and more powerful.

**CALLICLES:** I have already said: namely, the prudent in public affairs and the brave. For it is fitting for these to rule cities; and it is just that they have more than others, namely, as those ruling over subjects.

**SOCRATES:** But should they rule themselves in any way, or obey themselves?

**CALLICLES:** How do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** I say, should each one rule himself? Or is there no need that he should rule himself, but only others?

**CALLICLES:** In what way do you say "rule himself"?

**SOCRATES:** I say nothing obscure, but as many say: the temperate man, and one who is master of himself, ruling his own pleasures and desires.

**CALLICLES:** How festive you are, Socrates: you call stupid men "temperate."

**SOCRATES:** What do you say? There is no one who does not know that I least mean that.

**CALLICLES:** Nay, very much so, O Socrates. For how can he be blessed who serves anyone? But this is just and beautiful by nature, which I now boldly tell you: it is necessary that he who is to live rightly should permit his desires to be increased to the utmost, and not restrain them in any way; and should subminister to these, being as great as possible, whatever they seek, because of fortitude and prudence; and should utterly fulfill the affection of each of them. Which indeed, because many cannot attain it, they censure those who do attain it, hiding their own impotence through shame; and they say that intemperance is shameful, as I was saying in the earlier parts. Furthermore, they lead men of a better nature into a servile habit; and they themselves, since they cannot fulfill their own lusts, praise temperance and justice because of cowardice. But if it had happened to these from the beginning that they were either sons of kings, or their nature was sufficient for empire, or tyranny, or some power to be acquired, surely it would be more shameful and worse for them to use such temperance; for when it was permitted them to enjoy goods, and they were hindered by no one, they themselves would have set over themselves as mistress the law, discourse, and censure of the multitude. For in what way are they not miserable? Since because of a certain honesty of justice and temperance, they would distribute nothing more to friends than to enemies, even while they ruled in their city. But, O Socrates, the truth itself which you profess to follow is thus: luxury, intemperance, and liberty—provided the faculty is supplied—is virtue and happiness. All those other spectacles added contrary to nature are the deliriums of men, and trifles utterly to be condemned.

**SOCRATES:** Not ungenerously, O Callicles, do you proceed in disputing, using such boldness. Certainly those things are now openly said by you which others indeed think, but are unwilling to say. Wherefore I beseech you by no means to desist, so that in truth we may be made more certain of what manner of life one should lead. Tell me, then: you say desires are not to be coerced if one wishes to be such as he ought to be; nay, they must be permitted to be increased to the utmost, and their fulfillment must be acquired from elsewhere; and this you say is virtue.

**CALLICLES:** I so say indeed.

**SOCRATES:** If it were so, then stones and the dead would not be most happy. [3]

**CALLICLES:** Otherwise stones and the dead would be most happy.

**SOCRATES:** But nevertheless, even that life which you speak of is grave. Nor would I wonder if Euripides’ saying about this matter were true: "Who knows whether to live is to die, and to die is to live?" And now perhaps in truth we are dead. I have already heard from a certain wise man that we are now dead, and our body is a tomb for us; and that part of the soul in which the desires are is such that, by persuading and being persuaded in turn, it is agitated up and down. Therefore, a certain elegant man—a Sicilian perhaps, or an Italian—contriving in these things, called this part of the soul, because of its slippery persuasion and credulity, a "jar" [dolium]; but the foolish he called "uninitiated" and "damned." Moreover, he said that this part of the soul of those which is agitated by lust is like a leaking jar, because of its inexplebile [unfillable] incontinence. Wherefore this man shows you the contrary: that of those who are among the obscure shades, those are most miserable who are utterly uninitiated and damned, and are forced to carry water into a perforated vessel using another perforated vessel. And that this other vessel, or sieve, as he who taught me was saying, is the mind of the foolish. He likened it to a perforated vessel because, due to distrust and forgetfulness, it cannot contain anything poured in. These things seem in a certain way strange to someone; yet they demonstrate what I wish, if I may by any means persuade you to choose a moderate life, always content with present things, instead of an unfillable and incontinent one. But do I persuade you anything through these things? So that, having changed your opinion, you think those who live temperately are more blessed than those who live intemperately? Or do I profit nothing? And although I may contrive many things by a similar reasoning, are you in no way about to change your opinion?

**CALLICLES:** This, O Socrates, you have added more truly.

**SOCRATES:** Come, I will bring you some similarity from the same gymnasium. Attend whether you determine thus concerning the life of each, namely the temperate and the intemperate, as concerning two men who had many vessels; and one indeed had them whole and full, some of wine, some of honey, some of milk, and others similarly of other things; but each of these liquors was rare and difficult to find, and acquired with many and grave labors. He, therefore, to whom the vessels are full, would care to pour nothing more in; but as far as these things pertain, he would lead a quiet life. But to the other, the liquors would be as to the former—which could be acquired, but nevertheless with difficulty—yet the vessels were perforated and broken, and he would be forced to fill them continuously day and night, or be agitated by extreme miseries. Since, then, the life of each is such, which do you say is the more blessed, the temperate or the intemperate? Do I persuade you by these words to concede that the life of a moderate man is better than that of an immoderate one? Or do I not yet persuade you?

**CALLICLES:** By no means, O Socrates. For to him for whom all things are full, there is no longer any pleasure; but as I was just saying, he lives like a stone...

**Translator's Notes on OCR and Abbreviations:**
1.  **Gliniam/Clinia:** Likely a variant or OCR error for *Clinias*, the brother of Alcibiades.
2.  **Veterator:** A term used for a "shrewd person" or "old hand" at an art, here used pejoratively by Callicles to mean Socrates is a crafty sophist.
3.  **Abbreviation Tags:** The `[[abbrev: s. o. c. → SOCRATES.]]` and `[[abbrev: c. a. l. → CALLICLES.]]` tags identify the speakers in the original text, where Socrates is abbreviated as *Soc.* and Callicles as *Cal.*
4.  **Cinaedorum:** Refers to those living a life of base sensual pleasure, often used in a highly derogatory sexualized context in classical/Renaissance Latin.

# Book Twenty-Four.

**CALLICLES:** Let it be so for you, Socrates, so that you may conclude this discussion. **SOCRATES:** It seems, therefore, that a certain power and art <term>art [Greek: technē]: a specialized skill or craft</term> must be acquired for this purpose, lest we do injury to anyone. **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** What art then is there to acquire the faculty by which one suffers either no injury, or the least possible? Consider if it seems the same to you as to me. To me, it seems one must either obtain leadership in the republic, or seize a <term>tyranny [Latin: tyrannidem]: absolute rule by one person, often viewed negatively by Socrates</term>, or have close dealings with the current government. **CALLICLES:** You see, O Socrates, how ready I am to approve if you say anything rightly. Indeed, this seems to me to have been said by you very correctly. **SOCRATES:** Consider this further, if I seem to speak rightly to you. It seems to me that each person is most a friend to someone when they are most similar to them—just as the ancient sages also teach. Does it not seem so to you? **CALLICLES:** To me, indeed. **SOCRATES:** Is it not the case that where a fierce and unrefined tyrant rules, if anyone in that city is much better than him, the tyrant fears him and can never be a true friend to him? **CALLICLES:** So it happens. **SOCRATES:** Nor if the person is much worse? For the tyrant will despise him and never feel toward him as a friend. **CALLICLES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, only he can be a friend worthy of esteem in the tyrant's eyes who is similar in character, who praises and blames the same things, and is willing to be subject to the master and obey him. This man will surely have great power in that city; no one will inflict injury on him with impunity. Is this not how things stand? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** If someone in this city, even from his youth, should think by what reason he might best gain great power so that no one could bring injury upon him, this very way, it seems, is the path: to accustom himself from adolescence to rejoice and grieve at the same things as the master, and to make himself as similar to him as possible. Is it not so? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** This man then, as our current speech indicates, will achieve the ability to avoid injury and will possess great power in the city. **CALLICLES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** But will he also achieve the ability to do injury to no one? Or is he far from it? Since he will be similar to an unjust prince and have great authority under him. Truly I think such a state of life is perfectly suited for this: that he can do as many injuries as possible and entirely avoid the punishment for them. Is it not so? **CALLICLES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** And will he not be occupied by the greatest evil, since his soul is shameful and infected by his imitation of the master and the pursuit of similar power? **CALLICLES:** I do not know how you turn the argument upside down, Socrates. Do you not know that he who imitates the tyrant can kill the one who does not, if he wishes, and strip him of his fortunes? **SOCRATES:** I know indeed, O good Callicles, unless I am deaf; since I have heard the same thing frequently not only from you but also from Polus a little while ago, and from almost everyone else in the city. But listen to me: he will kill him, provided he wishes; but it will be a bad man killing an honest and good man. **CALLICLES:** But this very thing is hard to endure! **SOCRATES:** Not certainly by a man endowed with mind and reason, as your own speech indicates. Do you think a man should labor so much just to live as long as possible? Should he meditate only on those arts which can always save us from dangers—such as <term>rhetoric [the art of persuasive speaking]</term>, which you exhort me to take up because it often saves us in the law courts? **CALLICLES:** By Jove, I advise you rightly! **SOCRATES:** What then, O best of men? Does the skill of swimming seem a noble art to you? **CALLICLES:** By Jove, no. **SOCRATES:** And yet this saves men from death whenever they fall into a place where such an art is needed. But if this seems small to you, I will bring forward a greater one, namely the art of navigation, which saves not only lives but also bodies and money from extreme dangers, no differently than rhetoric. And yet this art is humble and modest, not boastful nor bombastic, as if it were performing something magnificent. But though it does the same things as rhetoric, if it saves someone by bringing them from Aegina <note>An island near Athens</note> to here, it demands only two small coins. If indeed it brings back safely from Egypt or the Black Sea those things I just mentioned—ourselves, our children, wives, and wealth—it asks for only two <term>drachmae [Greek silver coins]</term>. And the man endowed with this art, having performed these things, gets off and walks along the shore by the sea and his ship without puffing himself up or acting inflated. For he notices, I think, that it is uncertain whether he has actually benefited or harmed those whom he saved from drowning; he understands that he has brought them back no better in body or soul than they were when they first boarded the ship. He thinks, therefore, that if someone suffering from great and incurable diseases of the body does not perish in the sea, that man is actually miserable for not having died, as he received no real benefit from being saved. If someone, however, has many incurable diseases in his *soul*—which is far more precious than the body—should such a man live? Will it benefit him if someone saves him from the sea, or from a trial, or from anywhere else? Surely the pilot knows that for a shameful man, it is better not to live, for he must necessarily live badly. Therefore, there is no law by which a pilot, even though he saves lives, can boast and be held in high honor. Furthermore, O wonderful man, consider the engineer <note>original: "machinarum faber" — a maker of war machines or civil engines</note>, who can sometimes save no less than a pilot, or even a general, because he sometimes provides safety to entire cities. Does he seem to you equal to a lawyer? If he wished to boast of his business as you do, he would overwhelm you with words, urging everyone to become engineers, as if nothing else mattered. Yet you would despise him and his art regardless, calling him a "machinist" as an insult, nor would you want to give your daughter in marriage to his son. Although you praise your own faculty for certain reasons, by what right can you justly despise the engineer or the others I mentioned? I know you will say you are better, and born of better people. But if "being better" is not what I say it is, but if "virtue" is simply this: to save oneself and one's possessions regardless of character—then your mockery of the engineer, the doctor, or other arts invented for the sake of safety is ridiculous. But O blessed one, see if the noble and the good is something other than "saving and being saved." For a man who is truly a man should not desire to live for just any length of time; nor is this life to be loved above all else, but the care of it should be left to God. One should believe the women who say that no one can avoid fate. 

<margin>A saying of women: that no one can avoid fate.</margin>

Each person should consider this first: by what reason, in the time he has, he may live best. Would this not happen if he makes himself similar to the citizens with whom he lives? And must you now turn out most similar to the Athenian people if you are to be a friend to them and hold great authority? Consider therefore whether this is expedient for you and me, or not: lest that happens to us, O blessed man, which they say happens to the <note>Thessalian witches were famously said to be able to "draw down the moon" from the sky, but it was believed they paid for this power with the loss of their eyes or the lives of their children. Socrates is warning that gaining political power by mimicking the "demos" comes at a terrible price.</note> Thessalian women who draw down the moon. I wish this power to be friendly to us. If however you think any man can teach you an art of this kind...

<vocabulary>tyranny, Alcibiades, Pyrilampus, drachmae, engineering, Thessalian.</vocabulary>

<summary>Socrates argues that merely surviving or gaining power by mimicking a corrupt ruler is not a true "art" of living. He compares rhetoric to humble skills like swimming or navigation, noting that "saving a life" is only useful if the person being saved is actually good.</summary>

# Gorgias, or, On Rhetoric.

is fitting to practice in youth rather than in old age. I indeed, if I do anything in my life less than rightly, I am certain that I err not by my own will, but rather through ignorance <note>original: "inscitia"</note>. Wherefore you, just as you began to advise me, please continue, and clearly demonstrate to me what that thing is, and by what way I might be able to attain what you think I should seek. For if you find me in agreement with you now, but later you find me failing to perform what I agreed to, then consider me altogether sluggish and worthless, and do not waste any further effort in advising me. Recap for me from the beginning, just as you and Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet who wrote that "Law is king of all" and praised the "right of the stronger."</note> were saying: that it is just by nature for the more powerful to take by force what belongs to the weaker, for the better to rule the worse, and for the superior man to have more than the more lowly. Do you say that justice is anything else? Or do I remember correctly? **CALLICLES:** I was saying these things then, and I say them now. **SOCRATES:** But do you call the "better" the same thing as the "more powerful"? For even then I could not clearly understand what you were saying. Do you now call the stronger "the more powerful"? And must the weaker obey the stronger? Just as you seemed to demonstrate then, when you said that great cities rise up against small ones by natural right <term>natural right [Latin: naturali iure]: the idea that laws should be based on the inherent power dynamics of nature rather than social contracts</term>, because they were more powerful and stronger—as if "more powerful," "stronger," and "better" were the same thing. Or is it possible for someone to be better, yet inferior and weaker? And similarly, can one be more powerful, yet worse? Or is the definition of "better" and "more powerful" the same? Explain this very thing more clearly to me: whether "more powerful," "better," and "stronger" are the same or different. **CALLICLES:** I tell you plainly that they are the same. **SOCRATES:** Is not the multitude <note>the common people or the masses</note> by nature more powerful than one man? Since they are the ones who establish laws over the individual, just as you yourself were saying just now. **CALLICLES:** How could it be otherwise? **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the laws of the multitude are the laws of the "more powerful." **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Are they not, therefore, also the laws of the "better"? For those who are more powerful, as you yourself say, are much better. **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Are not their institutions right by nature, since they are more powerful? **CALLICLES:** So I affirm. **SOCRATES:** Does not the multitude establish, as you yourself were saying just now, that it is just for equality to be maintained among all, and that it is more shameful to inflict an injury than to suffer one? Is it so, or otherwise? And take care that you are not caught here out of a sense of shame. Does that multitude establish this or not: namely, that it is just for equity to be preserved, and not for one to have more than another; and that it is more shameful to do wrong than to receive it? I ask that no ill-will <note>original: "inuidia"</note> keep you from answering these things, Callicles; so that if you agree with me, I may be confirmed by you as a man who is abundantly sufficient for judging. **CALLICLES:** Indeed, the multitude establishes it so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is not by law alone, but also by nature, that it is more shameful to do wrong than to suffer it, and that it is just to preserve equality. Wherefore you seem not to have spoken truly in your earlier remarks, nor to have accused me rightly: saying that I play the "old fox" <note>original: "Veteratorem," implying a cunning or deceitful person</note> in debate, and that if someone speaks according to nature, I lead them toward the law; but if someone speaks according to the law, I lead them toward nature. **CALLICLES:** This man will never stop dealing in trifles! Tell me, Socrates, are you not ashamed, at your age, to hunt after names? <term>hunt after names [Latin: venari nomina]: to argue over the literal meanings of words rather than the concepts they represent</term> And if someone slips in a word, you catch at it greedily as if it were a prize for you? Do you think I say that "the more powerful" are anything other than "the better"? Have I not been saying for a long time that "better" and "more powerful" are the same? Or do you think I am saying that if a dreg of slaves and the most worthless of men flow together from all sides—who perhaps are "more powerful" only in their physical strength—that what they establish are laws? **SOCRATES:** Come now, O most wise Callicles, is this what you say? **CALLICLES:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** But I, blessed man, have for a long time suspected you call something else "more powerful," and I ask because I desire to know clearly what you mean. For do you not judge two men to be better than one? And you do not consider your slaves to be better than you just because they are stronger? Tell me again from the beginning, whom do you mean by "the better," if not the stronger? And please, O wonderful man, see that you teach me more gently, so that I do not flee from your school. **CALLICLES:** You speak ironically. **SOCRATES:** Not by Zethus <note>Socrates swears by the character Zethus from a play by Euripides, whom Callicles previously used to mock Socrates' philosophical life.</note>, Callicles, upon whom you relied when you used much irony against me just now. But come, tell me, whom do you call the better? **CALLICLES:** The superior, certainly. **SOCRATES:** You see, then, that you are only speaking names, but showing nothing? Will you not reveal whether by "better" and "more powerful" you mean the "more prudent" or some others? **CALLICLES:** By Jove, I mean these, and most especially! **SOCRATES:** Often, therefore, one prudent man is more powerful than many imprudent men according to your speech; and it is fitting for him to rule, and for the others to be subjects, and for him to have more than those whom he commands. For this is what you seem to want to say (and I am not catching at words) if indeed one man is more powerful than many. **CALLICLES:** But these are the very things I say. For I judge this to be natural right: that he who is better and more prudent should rule, and possess more than the inferior. **SOCRATES:** Wait a moment. What would you think if, in this place, as we are now, many of us were gathered together, and we had food and drink in common, and we were a mixed group of people—some strong, some weak—but one of us was a most prudent doctor regarding these things? He would be, as is likely, stronger than some and weaker than others. Would not this man, being more prudent, also be better and more powerful regarding these matters? **CALLICLES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Is it fitting, then, for him to take more of this food than us because he is better? Or rather, because of his excellence, should he distribute everything, and not retain more for himself in the distribution? Otherwise he would be punished. Instead, he should give more to some and less to others; and if he were the weakest of all, the least should be given to himself, even though he is the best? Is this not how it should be said, Callicles? **CALLICLES:** You speak of food, and drink, and doctors, and such trifles; I am not talking about these things. **SOCRATES:** Do you say that the more prudent man is the better, or not? Answer. **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** But should not the better receive more? **CALLICLES:** Not of food and drink. **SOCRATES:** I understand. Perhaps of clothes. And it is fitting for him who is most skilled in making clothes to have a large cloak, and to walk about adorned in many and precious garments. **CALLICLES:** What clothes are you telling me about? **SOCRATES:** Or perhaps in shoes, it is fitting for him to receive more who is more prudent and better in them; and perhaps the shoemaker himself should have the largest and most shoes, and carry many about on his feet. **CALLICLES:** What shoes are you raving about now? **SOCRATES:** If not such things, then at least something of this kind: as if a man prudent in cultivating fields, being honorable and good, should carry back more seeds, and use the most in his own fields. **CALLICLES:** How you always say the same things, Socrates! **SOCRATES:** Not only the same things, Callicles, but also about the same subjects. **CALLICLES:** By the gods, you are always talking about cobblers, shoemakers, fullers, cooks, and doc-

<summary>Socrates deconstructs Callicles' argument that the "stronger" should naturally rule, showing that if strength is merely numbers, then the laws of the masses are naturally superior. When Callicles shifts his definition to "the more prudent," Socrates uses analogies of craftsmen to mock the idea that expertise entitles one to a larger share of material goods.</summary>

# Book Twenty-Four.

You have these words in your mouth, as if our discussion were established concerning them. **SOCRATES:** Will you not then say at last, in what matters the more powerful and prudent man ought to possess more justly? Or will you neither permit me to speak, nor speak yourself? **CALLICLES:** But I have been saying this for a long time: first, who the more powerful are. For I do not mean cobblers, nor cooks, but those who are prudent in the administration of the republic; and not only prudent, but also brave, who are most fit to carry out what they have devised, and do not succumb to any softness of spirit. **SOCRATES:** Do you notice, Callicles, that I am not accusing you of the same thing as you, in turn, accuse me? For you accuse me as if I always repeat the same things; I, however, accuse you of the opposite—that you never bring forward the same definitions regarding the same matters. At one time you define the "better" and "more powerful" as the stronger, at another time as the more prudent. Now, moreover, you bring forward something else. For now certain "braver" men are named by you as the more powerful and better. But come, good man, explain at last: whom do you call the better and more powerful, and in what regard? **CALLICLES:** I have already said: those who are prudent in public affairs and brave. For it is fitting for these to rule the cities; and it is just that these rulers have more than others—the masters more than the subjects, that is. **SOCRATES:** But what about themselves? Is it fitting for them to rule themselves in any way, or to obey themselves? **CALLICLES:** What do you mean? **SOCRATES:** I mean that each man ought to rule himself; or is there no need for him to rule himself, but only others? **CALLICLES:** How do you mean "to rule oneself"? **SOCRATES:** I am saying nothing obscure, but rather what many people say: to be temperate <term>temperate [Latin: temperatum]: referring to the Greek concept of *sophrosyne*, a state of self-control and moderation</term> and master of oneself, ruling over one's own pleasures and desires. **CALLICLES:** How festive you are, Socrates: you call stupid men "temperate." **SOCRATES:** What are you saying? Everyone knows I mean no such thing. **CALLICLES:** Indeed you do, Socrates. For how could a man be happy who is a slave to anything? On the contrary, this is what is naturally just and beautiful, which I now boldly tell you: the man who is to live rightly must allow his desires to grow to the greatest extent and not restrain them in any way. He must minister to them, however great they may be, with whatever they seek, through his courage and prudence, and fully satisfy every impulse. Because many people are unable to achieve this, they find fault with those who do, hiding their own impotence behind a mask of shame. They claim that lack of restraint is disgraceful—as I said earlier. Moreover, they reduce men of a better nature to a slave-like condition; and because they themselves cannot satisfy their lusts, they praise temperance and justice out of cowardice. But if it had been the lot of these men from the beginning to be the sons of kings, or if their own nature were sufficient to acquire a kingdom, a tyranny, or some other power, surely nothing would be more disgraceful or worse than for them to practice such "temperance." While it was permitted for them to enjoy good things without being hindered by anyone, they would have set over themselves as a master the laws, talk, and criticism of the common crowd. For how are they not wretched? Indeed, because of this "honesty" of justice and temperance, they would bestow no more upon their friends than their enemies, even while they were masters in their own city. On the contrary, Socrates, the truth itself, which you claim to follow, is this: luxury, lack of restraint, and freedom—provided the means are available—constitute virtue and happiness. All those other things, those unnatural displays, are the delusions of men and utter nonsense to be held in contempt. **SOCRATES:** Not without spirit, Callicles, do you proceed with such boldness in your argument. Clearly you have now openly stated what others think but are unwilling to say. I beseech you, therefore, by no means to stop, so that we may truly be made more certain of how one ought to live. Tell me then: you say desires are not to be restrained if one wishes to be as one should be; rather, they must be permitted to grow to the utmost, and their fulfillment provided from somewhere; and you say this is virtue? **CALLICLES:** I certainly do say so. **SOCRATES:** If that were so, then stones and the dead would be the happiest of all. **SOCRATES:** <note>Note: The text repeats Socrates' name here in the original OCR transcription</note> But in that case, they would be called blessed who lack nothing. **CALLICLES:** Otherwise, as I said, stones and the dead would be the happiest. **SOCRATES:** Nevertheless, the life you describe is a heavy one. I would not be surprised if Euripides spoke truly on this matter: *Who knows whether living is actually dying, and dying is living?* <margin>Euripides on life and death.</margin> And perhaps we are actually dead right now. Indeed, I once heard from a certain wise man that we are now dead, and that our body is a tomb for us; and that part of the soul in which the desires reside is such that it is agitated up and down by persuasion and shifting beliefs. Thus, an elegant man—perhaps a Sicilian or an Italian <note>Likely a reference to the Pythagoreans or Empedocles</note>—telling a story about these things, made a play on words regarding this part of the soul because of its easy persuasion and belief, and called it a "jar" <note>original: "dolium" (a large storage jar)</note>. Those who are foolish he called "uninitiated" and "damned." He said that this part of the soul in the foolish, where the lusts are agitated, is like a leaky jar, because of its lack of self-control and its inability to be filled. Therefore, this man shows you the opposite: that among those in the dark underworld, the most wretched are those who are "uninitiated" and "damned," who are forced to carry water into a leaking vessel using another leaking vessel. Moreover, this other vessel, or sieve <note>original: "cribellum"</note>, as the one who taught me said, is the mind of the foolish. He likened it to a leaky vessel because, through its lack of faith and its forgetfulness, it is unable to hold anything in. These things seem somewhat strange to some, yet they demonstrate what I want: to persuade you, if I can, to choose a moderate life, always content with what is present, instead of a life that is insatiable and lacks restraint. But do I persuade you of anything through these words? So that you might change your mind and think those who live temperately are happier than those who live without restraint? Or do I accomplish nothing? Even if I tell many similar stories, are you not going to change your opinion in the least? **CALLICLES:** You have added this last point more truly, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Come then, let me bring you another similarity from the same school of thought. Consider whether you would judge the life of each—the temperate man and the intemperate man—as being like two men who each had many jars. For one, the jars were sound and full: some of wine, some of honey, some of milk, and others similarly of other things. But the sources of these liquids were rare and difficult to find, acquired only through many and heavy labors. Now, the one whose jars are full has no further care to pour anything in; as far as these things are concerned, he is at rest. But for the other man, the liquids are the same—attainable only with difficulty—but his jars are leaky and broken, and he is forced to fill them continually, day and night, or else suffer the most extreme distress. Since such is the life of each, do you say the life of the temperate or the intemperate man is the happier? Do I persuade you with these words to concede that the life of the moderate man is better than that of the immoderate? Or do I still not persuade you? **CALLICLES:** By no means, Socrates. For the man who has everything full no longer has any pleasure; but, as I was just saying, he lives like a stone...

<summary>In this passage, Socrates and Callicles debate the nature of happiness, with Callicles arguing that virtue consists of satisfying unrestrained desires, while Socrates uses the "leaky jar" metaphor to argue for the peace of a temperate life.</summary>

# Gorgias, or, On Rhetoric.

**SOCRATES:** ...he lives like a stone, once he has filled [his jars], and feels neither pleasure nor pain anymore. But the sweetness of life consists in a constant and continuous pouring in. **SOCRATES:** Is it not necessary, if much flows in, that much must flow out in turn? And that the holes for the outflow be wide? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** You are describing the life of a <term>charadrius</term> bird <note>original: *Charadrij auis*; a bird mentioned in ancient texts as eating and excreting at the same time, symbolizing the insatiable consumer</note>, rather than that of a dead man or a stone. But answer me: do you mean something like being hungry and eating when hungry? **CALLICLES:** I do indeed. **SOCRATES:** And being thirsty, and drinking when thirsty? **CALLICLES:** I do; and I affirm that a life is happy if one is affected by all other desires and is able to fulfill them with pleasure. **SOCRATES:** Bravo, best of men! Continue as you have started, and do not be ashamed. It seems I too must not be held back by shame. Tell me first whether a man with the itch <note>Socrates uses the example of *scabies* (an itchy skin condition) to challenge Callicles' definition of pleasure.</note> who scratches himself, and can do so continuously, should be thought to live happily? **CALLICLES:** How absurd you are, Socrates, and truly a common orator! **SOCRATES:** Indeed, Callicles, I have already confounded Polus and Gorgias and forced them to blush. But you, take care not to be frightened or hindered by shame. For you are brave; just answer. **CALLICLES:** I say that the one scratching also lives pleasurably. **SOCRATES:** And if pleasurably, also happily? **CALLICLES:** Undoubtedly. **SOCRATES:** I ask whether he scratches only his head, or something more? Consider what you will answer, Callicles, if someone follows up with what comes next. If these points are granted, would not the life of these <term>cinaedi</term> <note>original: *cinadorum*; a term used for men considered lewd, effeminate, or sexually passive, often used as a deep insult to one's honor and self-control</note> be described as anything but heavy, shameful, and unhappy? Or will you dare to call them happy if they obtain what they desire to their heart's content? **CALLICLES:** Are you not ashamed, Socrates, to lead the conversation to such things? **SOCRATES:** Do I lead it there, noble man? Or rather he who asserts so impudently that those who enjoy themselves—in whatever way they enjoy themselves—are happy, and does not distinguish which pleasures are good and which are bad? But tell me now at least, do you assert that pleasure and the good are the same? Or is there something pleasurable which is not good? **CALLICLES:** Lest my argument be inconsistent if I say they are different, I say they are the same. **SOCRATES:** You are subverting what was said before, Callicles, and you are no longer fit to investigate these matters we are searching out if you answer contrary to what you truly think. **CALLICLES:** Indeed, you do the same, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** If I do it, I do not act rightly; nor do you. But look, blessed man, whether the good is simply "to rejoice." Otherwise, many shameful things—and those we have just hinted at, and many others besides—seem to follow if this is the case. **CALLICLES:** So you think, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** But do you truly affirm this? **CALLICLES:** I do indeed. **SOCRATES:** Shall we then proceed with the discussion as if you are speaking seriously? **CALLICLES:** I certainly want that. **SOCRATES:** Come then, since you are of this opinion, answer me distinctly on these points: Do you call "knowledge" <note>original: *scientia*</note> something distinct? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And did you not say a little while ago that there was a certain "courage" <note>original: *fortitudinem*</note> along with knowledge? **CALLICLES:** I did indeed. **SOCRATES:** And did you say that courage was something other than knowledge, as if these were two different things? **CALLICLES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** And as for pleasure and knowledge, are they the same or different? **CALLICLES:** They are different, O wisest man. **SOCRATES:** And does courage also differ from pleasure? **CALLICLES:** Of course. **SOCRATES:** Let us then remember this: Callicles of Acharnae says that pleasure and the good are the same, but that knowledge and courage differ from each other and from the good. But Socrates of Alopece <note>Socrates identifies them both by their Athenian districts (demes) to emphasize the formality of their opposing positions.</note> does not concede this; or does he? **CALLICLES:** He does not. **SOCRATES:** And I think Callicles will not concede such things either, once he has properly considered himself. For tell me: do you not think the happy and the unhappy are affected in opposite ways? **CALLICLES:** I do indeed. **SOCRATES:** If these are opposites, is it not necessary that they behave like health and disease? For a person is not healthy and sick at the same time, nor do health and disease depart at once. **CALLICLES:** What do you mean by that? **SOCRATES:** Take the whole body as an example and consider this: do not a man's eyes suffer from that disease called <term>ophthalmia</term>? **CALLICLES:** Suppose they do. **SOCRATES:** Surely they are not healthy at the same time? **CALLICLES:** No. **SOCRATES:** But when someone is freed from that disease, does the health of the eyes then cease? And do health and disease finally depart at the same time? **CALLICLES:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** For that, I think, would be strange and absurd. **CALLICLES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** But, as I think, one receives and loses each in turn. **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** Is it not similar with strength and weakness? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And speed and slowness? **CALLICLES:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** Does one not also receive and lose in turn both good things and happiness, and their opposites, evils and misery? **CALLICLES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** If, therefore, we find things which a person loses and possesses at the same time, clearly these things are not the good and the evil. Do we agree on this? Consider your answer carefully. **CALLICLES:** I agree undoubtedly. **SOCRATES:** Come then, let us return to what we previously granted. Did you say hunger was pleasurable or painful? I am asking about hunger itself. **CALLICLES:** Painful, certainly. **SOCRATES:** But to eat while hungry is pleasurable? **CALLICLES:** I affirm it. **SOCRATES:** I understand. But hunger itself is painful, is it not? **CALLICLES:** Painful. **SOCRATES:** And thirst? **CALLICLES:** Vehemently so. **SOCRATES:** Do you want me to ask further, or do you concede that all want and desire are part of pain? **CALLICLES:** I concede it; ask no more. **SOCRATES:** Very well. But you say that to drink while thirsty is pleasurable? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, according to what you say, to be thirsty is painful. **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** But drinking is the fulfillment of the want and a pleasure. **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Do you say, then, that one rejoices in the act of drinking? **CALLICLES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** But suffers insofar as he is thirsty? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Do you see then what follows? Namely, that you admit a person rejoices and suffers at the same time when you say the thirsty man drinks? Does this not happen at the same time and in the same place, whether in the soul or the body? For I think it makes no difference. Is it so or not? **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** However, you said it was impossible to be happy and unhappy at the same time. **CALLICLES:** I did. **SOCRATES:** Yet you have admitted that one can rejoice and suffer at the same time. **CALLICLES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, rejoicing is not the same as being happy, nor suffering the same as being unhappy. Consequently, pleasure is something other than the good. **CALLICLES:** I don't know what you're babbling about. **SOCRATES:** You do know, but you don't want to admit it. But please, continue answering, so that you may recognize how "wise" you are in rebuking me. Does not each of us cease to be thirsty and cease to rejoice from drinking at the same time? **CALLICLES:** I don't know what you're saying. **SOCRATES:** Not so, Callicles! Answer for our sake, so the discussion may reach a conclusion. **CALLICLES:** Socrates is always like this, Gorgias. He searches out and refutes tiny, worthless points. **GORGIA:** What does it matter to you? This is not your burden; permit him to argue as he chooses. **CALLICLES:** Then ask your narrow and petty questions, Socrates, if it pleases Gorgias. **SOCRATES:** You are blessed, Callicles, for you have been initiated into the great mysteries

<margin>See Erasmus's proverb on "changing the Charadrius."</margin>

before the small ones.

<gloss>to be hungry, to be thirsty, itchy/scabious, pleasure, joy, knowledge, courage, Charadrius bird, eye-disease/ophthalmia.</gloss>

<summary>Socrates uses the physiological examples of hunger, thirst, and itching to demonstrate that pleasure (fulfillment) and pain (want) often occur simultaneously. Since he has already established that good and evil (like health and sickness) cannot coexist, he concludes that pleasure cannot be identical to the good.</summary>
