# Book Twenty-Four

<note>The heading "Liber Vigesimusquartus" likely refers to the section or volume of this specific Renaissance edition of Plato's works.</note>

**SOCRATES:** ...than before? Truly, I did not think that was right. But now, taking up from where you left off, answer: Does a person not stop being thirsty and enjoying the drink at the same time? **CALLICLES:** I grant that. **SOCRATES:** And does he not also stop being hungry and having other desires at the same time he stops feeling the pleasure of satisfying them? **CALLICLES:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** Do not pains and pleasures, then, cease at the same time? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** However, a person does not cease to be affected by good and evil at the same time, as you just admitted. Do you not admit it now? **CALLICLES:** I do. But what of it? **SOCRATES:** It follows, my friend, that "good things" are not the same as "pleasant things," and "bad things" are not the same as "painful things." For a person stops feeling the latter simultaneously, but not the former, since they are different things. By what logic, then, could pleasant things be the same as good things, or painful things the same as bad? Now, if you wish, consider it in this way instead. For I think you still do not agree. Pay attention: do you not call good men good because of the presence of good things? Just as you call those people beautiful who possess beauty? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** What then? Do you call foolish and cowardly men "good"? Certainly not a moment ago; rather, you were calling the brave and the wise "good." Do you not still call these people good? **CALLICLES:** Absolutely. **SOCRATES:** And have you ever seen a foolish child filled with pleasure? **CALLICLES:** I have. **SOCRATES:** And have you ever seen a foolish man filled with pleasure? **CALLICLES:** I believe I have. But what is the point of this? **SOCRATES:** It doesn't matter; just answer. **CALLICLES:** I have seen it. **SOCRATES:** What then? Have you seen a man of sound mind feeling both pain and joy? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Which of the two feel more joy and pain: the wise or the foolish? **CALLICLES:** I don't think they differ much. **SOCRATES:** That is enough. In war, have you ever seen a cowardly man? **CALLICLES:** Of course. **SOCRATES:** When the enemy retreated, which ones seemed to you to rejoice more: the cowards or the brave? **CALLICLES:** Both seemed to rejoice more, or at least nearly the same. **SOCRATES:** It doesn't matter. So cowards also rejoice? **CALLICLES:** Greatly. **SOCRATES:** And the foolish, as it appears. **CALLICLES:** Them too. **SOCRATES:** But when the enemy approaches, do only the cowards feel pain, or do the brave feel it as well? **CALLICLES:** Both. **SOCRATES:** Do they feel it equally? **CALLICLES:** Perhaps the cowards feel it more. **SOCRATES:** And when the enemy leaves, do they not rejoice more? **CALLICLES:** Perhaps. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, do not the foolish and the wise, the cowardly and the brave, feel pain and joy similarly, as you say—or rather, do not the cowards feel it more than the brave? **CALLICLES:** I say so. **SOCRATES:** However, the wise and the brave are good, while the cowardly and the foolish are bad. **CALLICLES:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the good and the bad feel joy and pain roughly equally. **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** Are the good and the bad, then, equally good and bad? Or rather, are only the good people good, and only the bad people bad? **CALLICLES:** By Jove <note>original: *Per Iouem*; an oath to Jupiter/Zeus</note>, I don't know what you are saying. **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that you said good people are good by the presence of good things, and that "pains" are bad things? **CALLICLES:** I did. **SOCRATES:** Then are not "good things"—that is, pleasures—present in those who are delighted? If indeed they are delighted. **CALLICLES:** What prevents it? **SOCRATES:** And are those who rejoice good because good things are present in them? **CALLICLES:** They are. **SOCRATES:** And are "bad things"—that is, pains—present in those who suffer? **CALLICLES:** They are. **SOCRATES:** And you say that the bad are bad because of the abundance of bad things. Do you not still say this? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, those who rejoice are good, and those who suffer are bad. **CALLICLES:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** And those who feel it more are "more" [good or bad], those who feel it less are "less" so, and those who feel it equally are "equally" so. **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And do you not say that the wise and the foolish, and again the cowardly and the brave, feel joy and pain similarly? Or even that cowards feel it more? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Calculate with me, then, what follows from our concessions. For they say it is a beautiful thing to say and consider "beautiful things" twice and even three times <margin>They say it is a beautiful thing to say what is beautiful twice and three times.</margin>. We said that the wise and the brave man is good, did we not? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And that the foolish and the cowardly are bad? **CALLICLES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And again, that the one who rejoices is good? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And the one who suffers is bad? **CALLICLES:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** And that the good and the bad feel joy and pain similarly, or perhaps the bad man even more? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, a person becomes good and bad in the same way as a good person, or rather the bad person himself becomes good. Does this not follow from what was said before, if one says that pleasant things are the same as good things? Do these things not necessarily follow, Callicles? **CALLICLES:** I have been listening to you for a long time, Socrates, and I grant you these points, noticing that if someone gives you even a little ground in jest, you greedily snatch it up like a child. As if you really believe that I, or any other person, do not think that some pleasures are better and others are worse. **SOCRATES:** Oh, oh, Callicles, how clever you are! You play with me as if I were a child, claiming one moment that things are one way, and another moment that they are different, trying to deceive me. And yet I did not think at the start that I would be willingly deceived by you, since you are a friend. But now you have misled me too much; and so, as the old proverb goes <margin>Proverb.</margin>, I am forced to "make the best of what is at hand" and accept what you give me. It seems that what you are now proposing is this: that some pleasures are good, and others are bad. Is that right? **CALLICLES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Are not the good ones those that are useful? And the bad ones those that are harmful? **CALLICLES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And are those useful which bring about some good, and those harmful which bring about some evil? **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** Do you mean such things as the pleasures of eating and drinking which we were just discussing? For if some of these provide health to the body, or strength, or some other physical virtue, are they good? And are those that do the opposite harmful? **CALLICLES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And in the same way, are some pains good and others bad? **CALLICLES:** Nothing prevents it. **SOCRATES:** Then we ought to choose and pursue the good pleasures and pains. **CALLICLES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And the others, not at all. **CALLICLES:** That is clear. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, Polus and I agreed that all things should be done for the sake of what is good; do you remember? And does it seem to you as well that this is the end of all actions: the good itself? And that all other things should be done for its sake, but it should not be done for the sake of other things? Do you join us as a third in this opinion? **CALLICLES:** I do. **SOCRATES:** For which reason one must pursue other things, including pleasures, for the sake of good things, and not good things for the sake of pleasures. **CALLICLES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Is it, then, the task of any ordinary man to choose which of the pleasant things are good and which are bad? Or does it require an expert? **CALLICLES:** An expert. **SOCRATES:** Let us therefore remember what I said to Polus and Gorgias. For if you recall, I said there were certain "preparatory faculties": some that only look toward pleasure, being ignorant of what is better or worse, and others that know what is good and what is evil. I placed among those concerned with pleasure the "knack" of cookery regarding the body (but not an art); while among those aimed at the good, I placed the art of medicine. And by the Jove of friendship, I beg you, Callicles, do not joke with me; do not answer whatever occurs to you against your own mind, nor take what I say as a joke. For you see that our conversation is about that subject which is nothing
more...

<summary>Socrates uses logical puzzles to force Callicles to admit that "pleasure" and "the good" cannot be identical. Callicles eventually pivots, arguing that some pleasures are better than others, allowing Socrates to reintroduce the idea that all actions must be directed toward a purposeful "Good."</summary>

# Gorgias, or, On Rhetoric.

**SOCRATES:** ...a man of sound mind should strive to know this above all: namely, how one ought to live. Should it be as you urge, by performing the duties of a "real man"—speaking before the people, practicing **Rhetoric**, and governing the state as you all do now? Or should one instead take up this **philosophical life**, and in what way does the latter differ from the former? Perhaps it is worthwhile, as I began to do a moment ago, to distinguish between them; and then, once we have agreed on the distinction, if these are indeed two different ways of life, we can consider what the difference is and which one should be lived. But perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying.

**CALLICLES:** Certainly not yet.

**SOCRATES:** Then I shall speak more plainly. Since we both confessed that there is something called "the good" and something called "the pleasant," but that the pleasant is different from the good, and that there is a certain study and preparation for attaining each of them—one being the pursuit of the good, the other the pursuit of pleasure—do you first agree with me on this point before I go further?

**CALLICLES:** I agree.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, agree also to those things I said to these others, if I seemed to you to speak the truth then. For I firmly maintained that **cookery** <note>original: "coquinariam"</note> does not seem to me to be an art, but a certain knack or experience. **Medicine**, however, is an art, because the faculty of medicine investigates both the nature of what it treats and the cause of its actions, and it can give a rational account of each of these. 

<margin>Why medicine is an art.</margin>

But the other faculty, which deals with pleasure—toward which its entire study is directed—proceeds entirely without art. It considers neither the nature of pleasure itself nor its cause. It is utterly reckless, so to speak, and has no regard for anything; rather, relying solely on a certain habit, experience, and the memory of what usually happens, it busily provides pleasures. 

<margin>See what qualities belong to a mere knack.</margin>

Consider these things first: do you think this has been sufficiently stated? Do you think there are certain similar faculties concerning the soul—some being truly "artful," taking care for what is best for the soul, but others neglecting this, thinking only of how they might delight the soul (just as we said regarding the body)? These do not consider at all whether a pleasure is better or worse; they care for nothing else than how to delight, whether for better or for worse. To me, it seems there are such faculties, and I call this entire type of service **flattery** <note>original: "adulationem," often translated in Plato as "pandering."</note>, whether it concerns the soul, the body, or anything else whose pleasure one pursues without regard for better or worse. Do you come to the same opinion as us, or do you disagree?

**CALLICLES:** Not at all; rather, I agree, so that your discussion may reach a conclusion and to gratify Gorgias here.

**SOCRATES:** Does this apply to only one soul? Or is it not also the same for two or many?

**CALLICLES:** Not just one, but for two and for many.

**SOCRATES:** Can one not also gratify many people gathered together without any regard for what is best?

**CALLICLES:** So I believe.

**SOCRATES:** Can you say which studies these are that do this? Or rather, if you prefer, as I ask about them, if one seems to be of this kind to you, concede that it is so. If not, deny it. First, let us consider **flute-playing** <note>original: "tibicinariā"</note>; does it not seem to you to be of this kind, caring for nothing other than delighting the ears?

**CALLICLES:** It seems so to me.

**SOCRATES:** And are not all others of this sort, such as the art of the harp <note>original: "citharistica"</note> as used in competitions?

**CALLICLES:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** What about the teaching of choral songs and **dithyrambic poetry**? <note>Dithyrambs were wild, rhythmic hymns sung in honor of Dionysus.</note> Does it not seem to be of this sort? Or do you think **Cinesias**, son of Meles, looks to say something that would make the listeners better? Or rather, does he look for a way to please the crowd of spectators?

**CALLICLES:** It is manifest, Socrates, that this is the case with Cinesias.

**SOCRATES:** And his father, Meles—did he seem to look toward what was best when he sang to the harp? In truth, he did not even look toward pleasure, for he was a nuisance to his listeners! But consider: do you not think the entire skill of the harp-singer and dithyrambic poetry were invented for the sake of delight?

**CALLICLES:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** And what does this noble **Tragedy**, this "admirable poetry," strive for? Is its effort and endeavor directed solely toward the pleasure of the listeners? Or if something is pleasant and agreeable but nonetheless evil, will it take care never to say it? Conversely, if something is troublesome but useful, will it speak and sing it, whether the listeners are delighted or not? Which of these do you think the poetry of tragedy works most to achieve?

**CALLICLES:** It is clear that it leans toward the pleasure and favor of the spectators.

**SOCRATES:** This is the very thing we just called "flattery."

**CALLICLES:** Plainly.

**SOCRATES:** Come now: if one were to take away from all poetry the melody, the rhythm, and the meter, would anything remain besides certain **speeches**?

<margin>Poetry without melody and meter is nothing other than popular speech.</margin>

**CALLICLES:** Only that.

**SOCRATES:** And surely these speeches are delivered to the crowd and the people.

**CALLICLES:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, **Poetry** is a certain kind of popular oratory.

**CALLICLES:** It appears so.

**SOCRATES:** And is not Rhetoric also a popular oratory? Do poets not seem to you to use Rhetoric in the theaters?

**CALLICLES:** They do.

**SOCRATES:** Now we have found a certain **Rhetoric** addressed to the people—a crowd composed of children, women, men, slaves, and free men alike. We do not highly approve of this kind, since we have admitted it is a form of flattery.

<margin>Rhetoric is shown to be flattery.</margin>

**CALLICLES:** That is certainly so.

**SOCRATES:** What should we say of the rhetoric used for the people of Athens and other cities made up of free men? What is that like? Do the orators seem to you to always direct their words toward what is best, looking only to how the citizens might become as good as possible through their speeches? Or do they, too, hunt for the favor of the listeners, seeking their own private gain while neglecting the public good? Like children, they treat the people with an eye only for their favor, caring nothing for whether they are made better or worse by it.

**CALLICLES:** That which you ask is not simple. For there are those who, in their speaking, care for the utility of the citizens; but there are others such as you describe.

**SOCRATES:** That is enough. For if this too is double-sided, one part of it will be flattery and a shameful way of addressing the assembly; the other part, however, is beautiful—striving to make the souls of the citizens as good as possible, always contending for the utility of the listeners, whether the things said please or displease them. But you have certainly never seen such oratory. If you can point out any such man among the orators, why have you not shown him to me?

**CALLICLES:** By Jove, among the orators who are now living, I have no such man to name.

**SOCRATES:** But can you point out someone among the ancients through whom the Athenians became better after he began to speak, having been worse before? For I do not know who such a person might be.

**CALLICLES:** What? Do you not hear that **Themistocles** was a good man? And **Cimon**, and **Miltiades**, and **Pericles**, who only recently passed away—whom you yourself heard speaking?

**SOCRATES:** If indeed, Callicles, "true virtue" is what you said it was earlier: namely, to satisfy one's own desires and the desires of others.

<note>Themistocles, Cimon, Miltiades, and Pericles were the most famous Athenian statesmen and generals of the 5th century BCE.</note>

He challenges Callicles to name a single Athenian statesman who actually made the citizens better people rather than just pleasing them.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the dialogue in Plato's Gorgias. Socrates has just distinguished between arts that aim at the good and "knacks" that aim only at pleasure. He is now moving to prove that the soul, like the body or a manufactured object, requires "order" and "arrangement" to be considered good.</meta>

[[original page: 250]]

# Book Twenty-fourth.

But if the case is otherwise, and as we were compelled to admit in the later part of the discussion, those desires that make a man better ought to be pursued, while the others should not, and if there exists a certain art for achieving this, can you point out any practitioner of such an art to me? **CALLICLES:** I truly do not know what to say. **SOCRATES:** But indeed, if you search rightly, you will find one. Let us look at this now, considering it calmly and quietly, to see if any such person among these men has emerged. Come then, the good man, who looks toward what is best, does just as all other craftsmen do; each of them keeps his own work in view and does not choose at random what he applies to his task, but acts so that the work may achieve some specific form according to the model he has set for himself. For example, if you care to look at painters, architects, shipbuilders, and all other craftsmen: any one of them disposes each part into a certain order, and forces one part to fit and harmonize with the others, until the whole is constructed as a thing adorned with a certain order. Therefore, all craftsmen do this, as do those whom we mentioned earlier: <term>physical trainers</term> <note>original: "pædotribæ"</note> and physicians likewise do the same regarding the body. For they adorn it and put it together. Do we admit that this is so, or not? **CALLICLES:** Let it be so. **SOCRATES:** A house, therefore, having attained adornment and order, will be good; if it lacks these, it will be bad. **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** And a ship in the same manner? **CALLICLES:** In the same manner. **SOCRATES:** And indeed, our bodies similarly? **CALLICLES:** Similarly. **SOCRATES:** What then of the soul? If it is devoid of order, will it be good? Or rather if it is composed of order and adornment? **CALLICLES:** It is necessary from what was said before to admit this also. **SOCRATES:** What then is the name for that which is produced in the body from order and adornment? <margin>Health in the ordering of the body.</margin> **CALLICLES:** You mean, perhaps, health and strength. **SOCRATES:** I do indeed. And what is the name for that which is produced in the soul from order and adornment? Try to find and express its name, just as you did for the body. **CALLICLES:** Why do you not say it yourself, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** If it pleases you, I shall say it; but if I seem to speak the truth, you must concede; if not, reject it, and do not yield at all. To me, it seems the name for the ordering of the body is "healthy," from which health and other bodily virtues arise. Is it so, or otherwise? **CALLICLES:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** But for the ordering and adornment of the soul, the names are "lawful" and "law," from which men become law-abiding and orderly; these, indeed, are **justice** and **temperance** <note>original: "iustitia atq; temperātia"</note>. Do you agree, or not? <margin>Lawfulness and law in the ordering of the soul, which is justice and temperance.</margin> **CALLICLES:** Let it be. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, will not that skilled and good rhetorician, looking to these things, apply his words to the souls of men? And will he not always direct all his actions, and whatever he grants at any time or denies, toward this end: that justice may dwell in the souls of the citizens, and injustice be absent; that temperance may be present, and intemperance be cast out, and that the other virtues may be cultivated and wickedness expelled? Do you concede this, or not? **CALLICLES:** I do concede it. **SOCRATES:** For what does it profit, O Callicles, to offer a sick and ill-affected body many and most pleasant foods, or drink, or anything else that will not be beneficial—that is, more or less or the opposite of what just reason dictates? Is this true, or not? **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** For I do not think it is profitable for a man to live in an afflicted body. For in such a state, he must necessarily live badly; is it not so? **CALLICLES:** It is. **SOCRATES:** Do not physicians generally permit a healthy man to satisfy his desires—such as eating as much as he wants when hungry, or drinking as much as he pleases when thirsty—but they never, so to speak, permit a sick man to fulfill his appetites? Do you concede this yourself? **CALLICLES:** I concede it. **SOCRATES:** Concerning the soul, is not the reasoning the same? For as long as it is wicked, mindless, intemperate, unjust, and impious, it must surely be restrained from its desires, and not be permitted to do anything other than those things by which it may turn out better. Do you agree or not? **CALLICLES:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** For this is more profitable for the soul itself. **CALLICLES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Is not "to restrain" the same as to keep it from the things it desires? **CALLICLES:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, **restraint** <note>original: "continentia"</note> is better for the soul than lack of restraint, just as you yourself were establishing a moment ago. **CALLICLES:** I do not know what you are saying, Socrates. Ask someone else. **SOCRATES:** This man cannot bear to have what is useful applied to himself, nor to attain that restraint of which we are now speaking. **CALLICLES:** I have no care at all for your words, O Socrates, and I have only responded to you this far for the sake of Gorgias. **SOCRATES:** Look at that—what shall we do then? Shall we break off the discussion in the middle? **CALLICLES:** You decide. **SOCRATES:** But they say it is a sin to leave stories incomplete; <margin>It is wrong to leave stories incomplete. A proverb.</margin> rather, a "colophon" <note>The "colophon" (Greek: kolophon) was a finishing touch or crowning stroke; Socrates is saying the argument needs a proper ending.</note> must be added, lest they wander about without a head. Answer the rest, therefore, so that our discourse may receive its head. **CALLICLES:** How violent you are, Socrates! Truly, if you take my advice, you will let go of this dispute now, or dispute with someone else. **SOCRATES:** Who else is willing, so that we do not leave the discourse imperfect? **CALLICLES:** Can you not run through the discourse yourself, either by narrating it or by answering yourself? **SOCRATES:** Lest that saying of <term>Epicharmus</term> <note>A Greek comic playwright and Pythagorean philosopher.</note> happen to me: "what two used to say, I alone shall now suffice for." Nevertheless, it seems entirely necessary. If we do this, I think we should all strive eagerly to know what is true and what is false in what we say. For it is a common good for all that this should be clear to everyone. I shall therefore proceed with the discourse as it seems to stand. If, however, I seem to any of you to concede things to myself that are not true, it will be your task to object and refute me. For I do not say these things as one who knows, but searching for the truth in common with you. Therefore, if the one who reproves me seems to say anything rightly, I shall be the first to agree. I say these things, however, with the intent that the discourse ought to be finished. If not, let us leave off now and go away. **GORGIAS:** But it does not seem to me that we should go yet; rather, the discussion should be completed by you. I think the others feel the same, and I myself greatly desire to hear the rest from you. **SOCRATES:** And yet, O Gorgias, I would have gladly disputed with Callicles until I had returned to him the speech of Zethus to Amphion <note>A reference to a lost play by Euripides, *Antiope*, where two brothers debate the active vs. the contemplative life.</note>. But since you, Callicles, refuse to finish the dispute with me, at least listen and challenge me if I seem to say anything incorrectly. If you convict me, I shall not be angry with you as you are with me, but I shall record it as the greatest benefit. **CALLICLES:** Speak yourself, good man, and finish what you have started. **SOCRATES:** Listen to me, then, repeating the discussion from the beginning. Is pleasure the same as the good? Certainly not the same, as I and Callicles have agreed. Should we pursue pleasure for the sake of the good, or the good for the sake of pleasure? **CALLICLES:** Pleasure, certainly, for the sake of the good. **SOCRATES:** Is pleasure that by which we rejoice when it is present? And the good that by which we are good when it is present? **CALLICLES:** Precisely. **SOCRATES:** But we are good, both ourselves and anything else, because of a certain present virtue. For this, O Callicles, seems necessary to me. But the virtue of anything—whether of an instrument, a body, or a soul—is not present by chance, but by the order, rectitude, and art that is given to each. Are these things not so? **CALLICLES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the virtue of each thing is that it be ordered and adorned by its own proper order.

<summary>Socrates argues that goodness in any entity—be it a house, a ship, or a soul—comes from internal order and arrangement. He equates this order in the soul with justice and temperance, eventually taking over the dialogue himself after Callicles refuses to continue.</summary>

<keywords>order, soul, health, justice, temperance, craftsmanship, colophon, Epicharmus, Gorgias, virtue</keywords>

--- Page 269 ---
->Gorgias, or, On Rhetoric. 251<-

CALLICLES: Truly, I would confess it so.

SOCRATES: Therefore, a certain proper adornment implanted in each thing makes it good.

CALLICLES: So it appears to me.

SOCRATES: For this reason, the soul that has its own proper adornment is better than the soul that is devoid of adornment.

CALLICLES: It must be so.

SOCRATES: Now, that which has adornment is "adorned" and "modest."

CALLICLES: Why not?

SOCRATES: And such a soul is also "temperate."

CALLICLES: It is altogether necessary.

SOCRATES: And the temperate soul is good. Truly, my friend Callicles, I do find no other way to speak. But if you have something else, teach me.

CALLICLES: Speak on, good man.

SOCRATES: I say, therefore, if the temperate soul is good, it follows that the one who is affected in the opposite way to the temperate is bad. And such is the intemperate and incontinent soul.

CALLICLES: So it is, entirely.

SOCRATES: Moreover, the temperate man does what is fitting toward the Gods and men. For he would not be temperate unless he observed what is decorous.

CALLICLES: It must be so.

SOCRATES: Consequently, he who does what is fitting among men acts justly; and acting similarly toward the Gods, he acts piously. But he who acts justly and piously must necessarily be just and pious.

CALLICLES: So the truth holds.

SOCRATES: Furthermore, it is perhaps necessary that he be brave. For it is not the part of a temperate man to pursue or flee what is not fitting. Rather, he ought to flee and pursue both individual things, and men themselves, and pleasures and troubles, and also to endure them when necessary. For this reason, it is altogether necessary that the temperate man—being, as we said, just, brave, and pious—be perfectly good. But the good man does well and honorably whatever he does. And he who does well is happy and blessed. But the wicked man who acts badly is miserable. Such a person is the one who is affected in the opposite way to the temperate: namely, the intemperate man whom you were praising.

I therefore establish these things thus, and I feel them to be true. For this reason, if this is the state of affairs, whoever wishes to be happy must pursue and practice temperance; but he must flee intemperance as fast as his feet can carry him. He must so prepare himself that he does not need chastisement and punishment; but if he himself or anyone else among his associates—whether a private citizen or a city—does need it, he must be restrained by the application of punishment if he is to be happy. This seems to me to be the mark toward which we should look and direct our lives, referring all things, both public and private, to this: that justice and temperance may be present in him who is to be happy. One must not permit everything to his desires: to try to fulfill them is an unquenchable evil, leading the life of a robber. For such a man will never be dear to any human being, nor to God; for there can be no fellowship with him. And for him who has no fellowship, friendship can never be established.

The wise men say that heaven and earth, Gods and men, are held together by a certain fellowship and friendship, by modest adornment, temperance, and justice; and for this reason they call the whole the **Universe** <note>Latin "mundum", from the Greek "kosmos," which means both "world" and "order/adornment."</note> and **Adornment**, not disorder or intemperance. You, although you are wise, seem to me never to have noticed these things. For it has escaped your notice that **geometrical equality** <note>Proportionate justice, where rewards are given according to merit, rather than simple numerical equality.</note> has great power among both Gods and men. But you think that <term>pleonexia</term> <note>Grasping for more than one's share; greed.</note> (that is, preeminence or taking the first part) should be practiced in all things; for you hold geometry in contempt.

Come then, either our speech must be refuted—as if people do not become happy by the possession of justice and temperance, or miserable by wickedness—or if it is true, we must consider what follows. Surely all those earlier points will follow, about which you were asking whether I was speaking seriously. I was asserting that one must accuse oneself and one's son and friend if any injustice has been committed, and that rhetoric should be used for this purpose. And what you thought **Polus** had conceded out of shame was indeed true: namely, that to do an injury is as much worse as it is more shameful than to suffer one; and that he who is to be a righteous orator must be just and know what things are just. Polus said that **Gorgias** had conceded this out of shame.

Since these things are so, let us consider what those things are for which you reproach me: whether they are said correctly or not. You say that I cannot bring help either to myself or to my friends and household, nor free them from the greatest dangers, but that I am in the power and whim of anyone—just as the most abject people are—whether someone wants to strike me on the cheek, as you boastfully said, or snatch my money, or expel me from the city, or even put me to death. You said that to be in such a state is the most shameful thing of all.

But my opinion, already stated many times and to be stated again with nothing forbidding it, is the opposite: namely, that it is not the most shameful thing to be struck on the cheek unjustly, or to have one's body or purse cut, but to strike and cut me and mine unjustly is both more shameful and worse. Likewise, to steal, to lead into slavery, to dig through walls, and in short to do any injury at all is both worse and more shameful for the one who does it than for the one who receives it.

These things, having been conceded by us above, are held and bound together—if it is not too rustic to say—by iron and adamantine reasons, by which I am led to feel this way. Unless you or someone stronger than you can dissolve them, it is impossible for it to be said correctly in any other way than I am saying it now. For to me, the speech always remains the same: that I do not know how these things are; yet no one with whom I have spoken until now, just as I have with you, has ever been able to say otherwise without appearing ridiculous. Therefore, I establish again that these things are so.

And if they are so, and if injury is the greatest of evils to the one who does it, then something even greater must be judged: namely, that the one who has done it never pays the penalty. What help, then, is that which someone cannot bring to himself and is truly to be held in contempt? Is it not that which would remove from us the greatest harm? Certainly, it must be the most shameful thing not to be able to provide such help to oneself, to one's friends, and to one's kin. The second help is against the second evil, the third against the third, and so on, according to the magnitude of each evil; so just as it is beautiful to be able to bring help, it is shameful not to be able to. Is it any other way than this, Callicles?

CALLICLES: Certainly not otherwise.

SOCRATES: Since these two things exist—doing an injury and suffering one— we say that to inflict it is the greater evil, and to suffer it the lesser. What help then, if someone were to prepare it for himself, would most effectively achieve both, so that he neither inflicts an injury nor receives one? Is it power or will? I put it this way: if he does not wish to suffer, will he not suffer injury? Or if he has prepared power for himself, will he only then not suffer?

CALLICLES: It is clear, certainly, that it is by power.

SOCRATES: What about in inflicting injury? If someone does not wish to do wrong, will that be a sufficient remedy? For then he will not inflict injury. Or must a certain power and art be prepared for this as well, which unless someone has learned and practiced it, he will do injury? Why do you not at least answer me on this, Callicles? Do I and Polus seem to you to have been rightly compelled by the previous reasons, or not, when we confessed that no one does injury willingly, but that whoever inflicts it does so against their will?

--- Page 270 ---
->Twenty-Fourth Book. 252<-

CALLICLES: Let it be so for you, Socrates, so that you may conclude this dispute.

SOCRATES: Therefore, must a certain power and art be prepared so that we do not do injury to anyone?

CALLICLES: Entirely so.

SOCRATES: What then is the art for acquiring the faculty by which one suffers either no injury or the very least? Consider whether the same thing seems right to you as to me. To me, it seems one must either obtain leadership in the republic, or seize a **tyranny**, or have commerce with the current government.

CALLICLES: You see, Socrates, how ready I am to approve if you say anything correctly. Truly, this seems to me to have been said very correctly by you.

SOCRATES: Consider this as well: whether I seem to speak correctly to you. Each person seems to me to be most a friend to the one who, as the ancient wise men say, is most like them. Does it not seem so to you?

CALLICLES: To me it does.

SOCRATES: Then where a fierce and unrefined tyrant rules, if someone in that city were much better than him, the tyrant would fear him and could never be a friend to him with his whole heart.

CALLICLES: So it happens.

SOCRATES: Nor if he were much worse? For the tyrant will despise him and never be affected toward him as toward a friend.

CALLICLES: You tell the truth.

SOCRATES: Therefore, only he can be a friend and worthy of esteem to him who, being similar in character, rejoices in, praises, and blames the same things, and is willing to be subject to the master and obey him. This man will certainly have great power in that state; no one will inflict injury on him with impunity. Is this not how it is?

CALLICLES: Yes.

SOCRATES: If someone in this city, from his very youth, were to think of the best way to acquire great power, so that no one could inflict injury on him, this is the very way: from his adolescence, he must accustom himself to rejoice and grieve at the same things as the master, and prepare himself to be as similar to him as possible. Is it not so?

CALLICLES: Yes.

SOCRATES: Then this man, as our present speech indicates, will achieve the ability not to be injured and to have great power in the city.

CALLICLES: Entirely.

SOCRATES: Will he also achieve the goal of inflicting injury on no one? Or is he far from it? Seeing as he will be like an unjust prince and have great authority with him. Indeed, I think such a state of life is most suited for him to be able to do as much injury as possible and entirely escape the penalties for those injuries. Is it not so?

CALLICLES: It appears so.

SOCRATES: And will he not be occupied by the greatest evil, since he is a scoundrel and has a soul infected by the imitation of his master and similar power?

CALLICLES: I do not know how you turn the speech upside down again, Socrates. Do you not know that he who imitates in this way can kill the one who does not imitate, if he wishes, and strip him of his fortunes?

SOCRATES: I know it indeed, good Callicles, unless I am deaf; since I have heard the same thing frequently not only from you but also from Polus a little while ago, and from almost everyone else in the city. But listen to me. He will certainly kill him if he wishes; but the bad man will kill the honorable and good man.

CALLICLES: And that is exactly what is so hard to bear.

SOCRATES: Certainly not to a man endowed with mind and reason, as even your speech indicates. Or do you think a man should labor much for the sake of living as long as possible, and meditate on those arts that can always save us from dangers—such as **rhetoric**, which you exhort me to embrace because it often saves us in the courts?

CALLICLES: By Jupiter, I am advising you rightly.

SOCRATES: What then, best of men? Does the skill of swimming seem noble to you?

CALLICLES: No, by Jupiter.

SOCRATES: Yet it saves men from death whenever they fall into a place where such an art is needed. If this seems small to you, I will bring forward a greater one: the **art of navigation** <note>Latin: "gubernatoria." The skill of a pilot or ship's captain.</note>, which saves not only lives but also bodies and money from extreme dangers, no differently than rhetoric. And yet this art is humble and modest, not boastful or pompous, as if it were performing something magnificent and excessive. But although it achieves the same things as rhetoric—if it saves one from Aegina to here—it demands only two coins. If it brings one safely back from Egypt or the Black Sea—along with the children, wives, and riches I just mentioned—it demands two drachmas. And the man himself, endowed with this art and having performed these things, steps out onto the shore and walks securely by the sea and his ship, by no means exalting or inflating himself. For he realizes, I think, that it is uncertain whether he has benefited or harmed those he saved from being submerged in the waves; knowing that he has brought them back no better in body or soul than they were when they first boarded the ship.

He thinks, therefore, that if someone pressed by great and incurable diseases of the body does not perish at sea, he is miserable for not having perished and has received no utility from him. But if someone has many incurable diseases in his soul, which is more precious than the body, should this man live? Would it bring him utility if someone saves him from the sea, or from the court, or from anywhere else? Surely he knows that it is not expedient for a scoundrel to live. For he must necessarily live badly. For this reason, no law exists by which a navigator, even if he saves someone, can boast and be held in honor.

Furthermore, you yourself, wonderful man, look at the **maker of machines** <note>An engineer or mechanic.</note>, who can sometimes save no less than a navigator, or even a general or anyone else, because he provides safety for entire cities. Does he seem to you to be comparable to a lawyer? If he wanted to extol his own work as you all do, he would surely overwhelm you with words, exhorting everyone to become makers of machines, as if everything else were of no moment. He would not lack for material. Nevertheless, you yourself would despise him and his art no less, and you would call him a "machinist" as an insult, nor would you want to give your daughter in marriage to his son, nor take his daughter for yourself.

Yet, by what reasoning do you praise your own faculty? On what grounds can you justly despise the machinist or the others I mentioned a moment ago? I know you will say you are better and born of better people. But if "better" is not what I say it is—but rather virtue is this: to save oneself and one's possessions no matter what—then your reproach against the machinist, the physician, or other arts invented for the sake of safety is ridiculous.

But, blessed man, see whether being noble and good is something other than saving and being saved. For a man who is truly a man should not wish to live for any length of time, nor should this life be so loved; rather, this care should be left to God. <margin>A saying of women, that no one can avoid fate.</margin> One should believe the women who say that no one can avoid fate; instead, one should consider primarily by what means he might live as well as possible during the time he is alive. Would it not be by showing himself to be most like the citizens with whom he lives? And should you now become most like the Athenian people if you are to be a friend to them and have great authority among them?

Consider, then, whether this is expedient for you and me; lest that happen to us which they say happens to the **Thessalian women** who "draw down the moon," <note>A reference to witches who were said to suffer great personal loss or physical harm as a price for their magic.</note> when we choose this power for ourselves at the cost of what is most dear. But if you think any man can hand down an art of such a kind...

### Translation

**[Page 253]**

# Gorgias, Or, On Rhetoric.

...that he will deliver such things to you, through which you may be made powerful in this city, although you are unlike the public government, whether for better or for worse; you do not think altogether rightly, O Callicles, as it seems to me. For it is necessary to be not merely an imitator, but by very nature truly similar to them, if you are to achieve anything great in winning the goodwill of the Athenian people, and by Jove, in addition, that of Pyrilampes. Whoever shall make you similar to these will make you, just as you desire, a statesman and a rhetorician. For indeed, all men are delighted by those words which are consistent with their own character, and are disturbed by those that differ. Unless you, O charming head [1], might offer something else. Shall we say anything to these things, Callicles?

CAL. I know not how it is, Socrates, but you seem to me to speak well. Yet that which is accustomed to happen to many others happens to me: for I do not have great faith in you.

SOC. The love of the people, O Callicles, implanted in your soul, resists me; but if we should consider these same things more often and better, they will perhaps seem probable to you. Remember, therefore, that two types of preparation were described by us, pertaining as much to the body as to the soul. One of these indeed tends toward pleasure, but the other toward that which is better, not gratifying, but resisting. Did we not define these in the previous sections?

CAL. Entirely so.

SOC. And that which declines toward pleasure is servile; and is nothing other than flattery, is it not?

CAL. Let it be so, if indeed it pleases you.

SOC. But the other strives so that whatever we care for becomes as excellent as possible, whether it be the soul or the body.

CAL. Absolutely.

SOC. Therefore, we must take up the care of the republic and its citizens in such a way that we make the citizens themselves good. Otherwise, as we discovered above, it profits nothing to confer any other benefit, unless the mind of those who are to receive it be honest and good, whether they receive much money, or power, or any other authority whatsoever. We posit it to be so, do we not?

CAL. Entirely, if it pleases you.

SOC. If, therefore, O Callicles, we were exhorting one another, while dealing publicly with civil affairs, toward the building of walls, or naval docks, or the massive edifices of temples: would it not be necessary to consider ourselves and examine: first indeed, whether we have skill in that art, and from whom we learned it? Or was it necessary that it be done so or not?

CAL. Entirely.

SOC. Secondly, however, if we ever constructed any building privately for ourselves or for our friends, whether it be beautiful or shameful. And if we find that our masters were good and excellent, and that many and distinguished buildings were built, first together with the masters, then by ourselves privately after we were released and freed from the masters, then at last it would be consistent with reason to turn ourselves to public works. But if we can show neither our master nor any buildings—or none well constructed—it would certainly be foolish to attempt public works and to exhort one another to them. Do we admit these things are rightly said, or not?

CAL. Entirely.

SOC. Similarly in all other things; if we were to exhort one another in the management of civil affairs as if we were suitable physicians, it would be fitting to examine one another in this way: "Come, by the gods, how does Socrates himself have a body disposed toward health, or who else has emerged healthy by the work of Socrates, whether slave or free?" It is also fitting for me to judge you by the same reasoning: and unless we find someone, whether of the foreigners or the citizens, whether man or woman, to have been healed by us, by Jove it would be truly ridiculous to be carried to such a point of madness that, with no private trials and no things perfected, and with the art not yet practiced, we should attempt—as it is said—to learn the potter’s craft on the [large] jar [2], both approaching the republic ourselves and provoking others to it. Would you not think that attempting that is the mark of a foolish man?

CAL. Certainly.

SOC. But, O best of men, since you have recently begun to administer the republic, and you exhort me in addition, and reproach me because I do not do it: should we not thus consider between us? Come then, Callicles, which of his citizens has he made better? Is there anyone who, though he was previously wicked and unjust and incontinent and imprudent, finally became honest and good by the work of Callicles, whether foreigner or citizen, slave or free? Tell me, if anyone should demand this from you, what would you answer? Whom will you bring forward as having at some time been made better by your company? Or does it loathe you to explain if any such work was finished by you privately before you applied yourself to the republic?

CAL. You are contentious, Socrates.

SOC. But I do not ask this for the sake of contention, but truly from a desire for learning how you think the public ought to be administered by us: whether anything else is to be cared for by those approaching the republic than that the citizens be made as good as possible? Have we not already many times confessed that this is to be done by a civil man? Have we confessed it? Answer, I pray; certainly we have confessed it, so that I may answer for you. If, therefore, it is fitting for a good man to apply himself to this in his city, I would wish you to tell me, now that you recall it to memory, whether those others whom you commemorated a little while ago—Pericles, Cimon, Miltiades, Themistocles—still seem to you to have been good citizens.

CAL. To me, indeed, they do.

SOC. If they were good, did not each of them render the citizens better from worse? Did they not?

CAL. Yes.

SOC. If it is so: therefore, when Pericles first began to speak to the people, the Athenians were worse than when he held his last speech to them.

CAL. Perhaps.

SOC. It is not for you to say "perhaps," best of men. For it follows necessarily from those things which we have granted, if indeed he was a good citizen.

CAL. What then?

SOC. Nothing; but tell me this: is it said that the Athenians were made better by the work of Pericles, or altogether on the contrary corrupted by him? Truly I hear that Pericles made the Athenians lazy, timid, loquacious, and greedy, and that he first introduced mercenary wages [stipends].

CAL. You hear these things from those who have "broken ears" [3], O Socrates.

SOC. But I no longer merely "hear" these things, but we both know them most clearly: namely, that Pericles was held in great esteem at the beginning, nor did the Athenians bring any shameful sentence against him while they were "depraved"; but after they were made honest and good by him, at the end of his life they condemned him for theft, and they were not far from punishing him with the ultimate penalty as an evil man.

CAL. What then? Did Pericles exist as an evil man because of that?

SOC. Such a caretaker of asses and horses and oxen indeed seems evil, if, when he received them, they were neither kickers, nor goring with horns, nor biting, and he made them have these vices because of their wildness. Does not he seem to you to be an evil caretaker of any animal whatsoever, who, when he received it tame, rendered it more wild than he received it? Does it seem so to you or not?

CAL. I grant it indeed, so that I may do a favor for you.

SOC. Furthermore, gratify me in this: answering whether man is one of the animals or not.

CAL. Why not?

SOC. Did not Pericles have the care of men?

CAL. He had it.

SOC. What then? Should they not, just as we just now contended, have been made justly more just from more unjust by him? If indeed he who cared for them was skilled in civil affairs.

CAL. Entirely.

SOC. Are not the just tame, as Homer says? But what do you say? Is it not similar?

CAL. I say so.

SOC. Nevertheless, he rendered them more wild than he had received them: and that against

**[Page 254]**

# Thirty-fourth Book.

himself, which indeed he would have least wanted.

CAL. Do you wish me to agree with you?

SOC. If I seem to you to speak the truth.

CAL. Let those things be.

SOC. Therefore, if they were more wild, they were more unjust and worse.

CAL. Let it be so.

SOC. Wherefore Pericles was not a good citizen for administering the republic, as this reasoning shows.

CAL. Not as you yourself say.

SOC. By Jove, nor as you say, by those things which you confess. But again, tell me about Cimon: did not those very people whom he had cared for ostracize him, so that they might not hear his voice for ten years? Furthermore, they did the same against Themistocles, and punished him with exile in addition. Miltiades, truly, who fought at Marathon, they decreed to thrust into the pit [the Barathron], and unless the magistrate had stood in the way, he would have undoubtedly fallen into it. But truly, if these had been good men, as you say, such things would never have happened to them. For indeed, good charioteers do not fall out [of the chariot] at the beginning; but after they have cared for the horses and have been more skilled in that art, do they then fall out? For that is accustomed to happen neither in chariot-driving nor in any other work; or does it seem so to you?

CAL. Not at all.

SOC. Therefore, those things were true which were said by us in the previous parts: namely, that we know no man to have existed in this city who was to be held as a good citizen in the republic. You truly confessed that none of those who are now are such; but that of those who preceded, some existed, and among them you chose these men above the rest. But these men appeared to behave no differently in this matter than the rhetoricians who are now. Wherefore, if these were orators, they used neither true rhetoric—otherwise they would never have fallen—nor the "flattery" art.

CAL. It is far off, however, O Socrates, that any of those who are now should have performed such deeds as any of those men did.

SOC. O blessed man, I do not vituperate those men as far as the administration of the city pertains; rather, in this matter they seem to me to have been more diligent than these men of ours, and more fit for finishing those things which the city desired. But in that it is necessary to chastise the desires of the citizens and not to comply with them, and by persuading and compelling to lead them to this very thing whence the citizens may be rendered better: nothing, so to speak, interests [differs] between these men and those, which indeed is the only duty of a good citizen. However, I confess to you that those were more fit than these for providing ships, naval docks, walls, and many other such things for the republic. We have therefore revolved into a ridiculous thing in disputing: if indeed in all this disputation we are continually carried around to the same point, ignorant of what I might say. For I think you have often conceded and known that this faculty is twofold concerning the work and concerning the caring soul. And one is indeed a ministering part, through which the things the body desires are provided: such as, if it hungers, food; if it thirsts, drink; if it is cold, clothes, blankets, shoes, and other things which are required for the use of the body. And truly, I speak to you with a purpose through the same images, so that you may understand more easily: that the provider of these is either a shopkeeper, or a merchant, or a craftsman of any of these: namely a baker, or a cook, or a weaver, or a shoemaker, and a dyer of hides. Nor is it a wonder that he who is such seems to the unskilled to be a caretaker of the body, as much for himself as for others—that there is, besides, a certain gymnastic art and medicine, in which the care of the body truly consists. Which it is fitting to command these types of arts, and to use their works, because it has knowledge of the good and the evil, as much as pertains to the nourishment and health of the body: which indeed is ignored by all these others. For which cause it must be said that these indeed are

**[Right Column]**

servile and ministering and illiberal [arts] concerning the cultivation of the body: but gymnastics and medicine rightly dominate these. These same things you seem to me at times to recognize also concerning the soul: and you grant to me as if you understand what I say. But a little after, you bring into the midst that there were once distinguished and good men in this city: and when I ask who those were, you seem to bring forward men very similar concerning the republic, as if, when I was inquiring who were or are good caretakers concerning the gymnastics of bodies, you should answer soon, and that seriously: Thearion the baker, and Mithaecus who wrote about the Sicilian art of cooking, and Sarambus the vintner: as if these existed as wonderful cultivators of bodies: of whom this one prepared sweet breads, that one feasts, and that one wine. Perhaps, therefore, you would take it indignantly if I should say that you do not understand gymnastics. For you bring ministers into the midst, and providers of desires: who in no way judge whatever is honest and good in these things, but as it happens, they fill the bodies of men and fatten them. These are praised by them, when nevertheless because of excessive filling they have consumed that old flesh. And afterward when diseases rush in, those who were nourished by those things accuse those who consulted [advised] them thereafter on account of ignorance: but they by no means accuse those who nourished them for lust. When, I say, such a repletion, as if immoderate, finally brings in disease, then they incriminate and reproach the present consultants, and affect them with injury besides if they can; but those prior ones who gave the cause of the disease, they extol with praises. And you now, O Callicles, do something very similar, while you praise those who nourished these and filled them with these things for which a desire had come upon them; whom they say made the city great; but they do not perceive that it is now swelling and unhealthy within on account of those ancient men. For without temperance and justice, they filled this city with ports, naval docks, walls, tributes, taxes, and such trifles. Therefore, when the disease breaks out, then those who govern the republic in the present are reproached. Themistocles himself and Cimon and Pericles, who were the cause of evils, are praised. Wherefore you perhaps, unless you beware, will be caught, and my friend Alcibiades, when besides those things which were acquired, the old things also shall have been lost, although you are not the cause of evils, but a cause along with the others. And yet I perceive a foolish thing even now, and I hear it concerning those ancient men. For I feel when the city begins to condemn any of those who are engaged in the republic for injustice, that they bear it heavily and are distressed in mind, as if they suffer unequal [unjust] things who have conferred many benefits on the republic. For they say they are condemned unjustly by it. Which is altogether false. For never is a governor of a republic condemned unjustly by that city over which he presides. It seems, however, that the same happens to those who are engaged in the republic as to the sophists. For the sophists, although wise in other things, yet in this one they behave absurdly: because although they assert that they teach virtues, they nevertheless often accuse their disciples as if ungrateful and unjust, who, when they have carried off good things from them, yet return no reward or thanks. Than which speech nothing is further from reason, because namely men made good and just, and removed from injustice by the work of the teacher, and endowed with justice, would bring injuries on their teachers by that very injustice which they do not have. Does it not seem absurd to you, O friend? In truth, you have compelled me to harangue, since you refuse to answer...

### Notes on Abbreviations and OCR Readings

1.  **"O lepidum caput"**: A Latin idiom (translating the Greek *ō phile kephalē*) meaning "O dear fellow" or "charming man."
2.  **"Figularia... in dolio discere"**: A Latin proverb (*en pithō tēn kerameian manthanein*) meaning to try to learn a craft by starting with the largest and most difficult project (learning pottery on a massive storage jar) before mastering the basics.
3.  **"Fractas habent aures"**: Literal translation of "those who have broken ears," referring to those who mimic the Spartan lifestyle (specifically boxers whose ears were battered), used here to denote a specific political/cultural faction.

**Abbreviations and Normalizations:**
*   `ꝙ` -> *quod*
*   `nēne` -> *nenne* (ne...ne)
*   `atq;` -> *atque*
*   `tā`, `tēdat`, `tū`, `cū`, `demū` etc.: These use the tilde/macron to represent a nasal 'm' or 'n' (*tam, tendat, tum, cum, demum*).
*   `definiuimꝰ` -> *definivimus* (The '9' or 'us' hook).
*   `Prouerbiū` (in margin) -> *Proverbium* (Proverb).
*   `quauis` -> *quamvis*
*   `incōtinēs` -> *incontinens*
*   `Atheniēses` -> *Athenienses*

Let it be. SOC. For which reason Pericles was not a good citizen for administering the republic, as this reasoning shows. CAL. Not as you yourself say. SOC. By Jove, nor as you say, by those things which you confess. But tell me again about Cimon: did not those very people whom he had cared for banish him so that they might not hear his voice for ten years? Furthermore, they did the same against Themistocles, and condemned him to exile besides. And Miltiades, who fought at Marathon, they decreed to thrust into the pit <term>barathrum; originally a deep pit at Athens into which criminals were thrown</term> of the prison, and if the magistrate had not stood in the way, he would undoubtedly have fallen into it. But truly, if these had been good men, as you say, such things would never have happened to them. For good charioteers do not indeed fall out at the beginning; but after they have cared for the horses and become more skilled in that art, they do not then fall out—for that is not accustomed to happen in chariot-driving, nor in any other work: or does it seem so to you? CAL. Not at all. SOCRATES. Therefore, the things that were said by us in the previous sections were true: namely, that we know of no man in this city who should be considered a good citizen in the republic. You indeed confessed that none of those who are now alive is such a person; but that among those who preceded them, some existed, and among them you chose these men above the rest. But these men appeared to behave no differently in this matter than the Rhetoricians who are now. Therefore, if these were orators, they neither used true rhetoric—otherwise they would never have fallen—nor flattery. CAL. Yet it is far from the case, O Socrates, that any of those who are now living has performed such deeds as any of those men performed. SOC. O blessed man, I do not disparage those men insofar as it pertains to the administration of the city; indeed, in this matter they seem to me to have been more diligent than these men of ours, and more fit for accomplishing those things which the city desired. But in that it is necessary to restrain the desires of the citizens, and not to comply with them, and by both persuading and compelling to lead them to this very point from which the citizens might be rendered better: in this, so to speak, there is no difference between those and these, which is indeed the only duty of a good citizen. Nevertheless, I confess to you that those men were wiser than these in providing ships, dockyards, walls, and many other such things for the republic; thus we have returned to a ridiculous thing in our disputing: since in all this disputation we are continually carried around to the same point, ignorant of what I am saying. For I think you have often conceded, and have recognized, that this faculty is twofold, concerning the work and concerning the caring for the soul. And the one part is a servant, through which those things which the body desires are provided: such as, if it is hungry, food; if it is thirsty, drink; if it is cold, clothes, blankets, shoes, and other things which are required for the use of the body. And indeed, with deliberate effort I speak to you through these images so that you may more easily understand: that there is a provider of these things, either a shopkeeper, or a merchant, or a craftsman of any of these: namely a baker, or a cook, or a weaver, or a shoemaker, and a tanner of hides; and it is no wonder that he who is such a man seems to be a caretaker of the body, both to himself and to others who are unskilled; that there is besides a certain gymnastic art and medicine, in which the care of the body truly consists. It is fitting for the gymnastic art to command such arts, and to use their works, because it has the knowledge of good and evil as far as pertains to the nourishment and health of the body: which is indeed ignored by all these others. For which reason it must be said that these arts are indeed servile, ministerial, and illiberal concerning the care of the body: but gymnastic and medicine rightly dominate them. You seem to me sometimes to recognize that these same things are also true concerning the soul: and you concede to me as if you understand what I am saying. But a little later you bring into the middle that there were once illustrious and good men in this city: and when I ask who those were, you seem to bring forward men very similar in the republic as if, when I asked who were or who are good caretakers of the bodies in gymnastic, you should answer presently, and that seriously, Thearion the baker, and Mithaecus who wrote about the Sicilian art of cooking, and Sarambus the innkeeper: as if these emerged as wonderful cultivators of bodies: of whom this one prepared sweet breads, that one feasts, and that one wine. Perhaps, therefore, you would take it indignantly if I said you did not understand gymnastic. For you bring ministers into the middle, and providers of desires: who do not at all judge what may be honorable or good in these things, but however it happens, they fill the bodies of men and fatten them. These men are praised by them, even though on account of excessive filling they have consumed that old flesh. And afterwards when diseases attack those who have been so nourished, they accuse those who advised them next on account of their ignorance: but those who nourished them for lust, they do not accuse at all. When, I say, such a repletion, as if immoderate, finally brings disease, then they complain against and reproach the present advisors, and moreover they inflict injury if they can, but those prior ones who gave the cause for the disease, they extol with praises. And you now, O Callicles, are doing something very similar, while you praise those who nourished these people and filled them with those things for which a desire had come upon them; who they say made the city great, but that it is now swelling and diseased within on account of those ancient men, they do not perceive. For without temperance and justice, they have filled this city with harbors, dockyards, walls, tributes, taxes, and trifles of this sort. Therefore, when the disease breaks out, then those who govern the republic in the present are reproached. But Themistocles himself and Cimon and Pericles, who were the cause of the evils, are praised. Wherefore you perhaps, unless you take care, will be caught, and my friend Alcibiades, when besides those things which were acquired, the old things also shall have been lost; although you are not the cause of the evils, but a cause together with the rest. Yet I see a foolish thing now, and I hear it regarding those ancients. For I perceive when the city attempts to condemn any of those who are engaged in the republic for injustice, they take it heavily and are tormented in their soul, as if they are suffering unfair things who have conferred many benefits on the republic. Indeed, they say they are unjustly condemned by it. Which is altogether false. For never is a governor of a republic unjustly condemned by the city which he precedes. It seems, however, that the same thing happens to those who are engaged in the republic as happens to the sophists. For the sophists, although wise in other things, behave absurdly in this one: that when they affirm that they teach virtues, they nevertheless often accuse their disciples as if they were ungrateful and unjust, who, when they have carried away good things from them, nevertheless return no reward or thanks. In which speech indeed nothing is further from reason: namely that men made good and just, and removed from injustice by the work of the teacher, and endowed with justice, should inflict injuries by that very injustice which they do not have upon their teachers. Or does that not seem absurd to you, O friend? In truth, you have forced me to deliver a speech, while you refuse to answer. CAL. But you cannot speak through yourself, unless someone answers you—

—responds? SOC. I seem so indeed, and now I am extending frequent speeches, while you do not deign to answer me. But, O good man, tell me by Jove the friend, does it not seem beyond reason to you that he who says he has rendered someone good, should complain about the same person, as if he who has been made good by him were also bad? CAL. It seems so to me indeed. SOC. Do you not hear those who profess to teach virtue complaining of such things? CAL. Indeed, but what can you say of men of no value? SOC. But what would you say of those who say they preside over the republic, and carefully devise how it may be the best possible: and again they accuse it, as happens, as if it were the worst? Do you think these differ from those? Truly, O blessed one, the sophist and the rhetorician are the same, or something close and similar: as I was saying to Polus. But you, on account of ignorance, think rhetoric is something illustrious, while you despise sophistry. But in truth, sophistry is more beautiful than rhetoric: by as much as the making of laws is more beautiful than the judiciary, and gymnastic than medicine. But I think it should least of all be conceded to the public speakers and sophists that they complain about that which they themselves teach, as if it were an evil to them. Otherwise, in that same accusation they would equally incriminate themselves, as if they had been of no use to those to whom they say they have brought utility; is it not so? CAL. Entirely so. SOC. And to have conferred a benefit without reward, as is consistent, was fitting for these alone, if indeed they spoke the truth. For when someone has received other benefits, such as having been made fast by a master of the gymnasium, he might perhaps not return thanks, unless precautions were taken that he pay the fee as soon as he has emerged fast enough. For not by slowness, as I think, do men do injury, but by injustice. Is it not so? CAL. So. SOC. If someone therefore should take away this very thing, namely injustice, he would then have avoided the danger of injury. But a benefit can be placed in safety by this alone, if someone is truly able to make those on whom he confers it good. Is it not so? CAL. I agree. SOC. Therefore, as it seems, in other contracts it is not shameful to take precautions for oneself, as for buildings and other crafts. CAL. It appears so. SOC. But for this faculty, namely that someone might become good, and govern his family and the republic in the best way, you think it shameful to be willing to teach nothing before precautions are taken concerning money. Is it not so? CAL. Certainly. SOC. For it is established that this is the cause: because only this among other benefits makes the one who has received it desirous of returning thanks. Wherefore it seems to be a clear argument if he who has performed a duty of this sort should receive it in turn; on the contrary, however, not at all. Do these things hold thus? CAL. So. SOC. To which care of the city, therefore, do you exhort me? Come, define for me, is it to that through which I should fight with the Athenians and contend so that they may become as good as possible, like a doctor: or to that through which I might become like a servant of pleasure, and speak for the sake of favor? And tell me the truth, O Callicles, for it befits you, just as you began, to proceed boldly, freely expressing to me what you feel. And now therefore answer well and nobly. CAL. I exhort you indeed to the service <note>original: "ministerium"; meaning a servile attendance to desires</note>. SOC. Therefore you provoke me to flattery, O most noble man. CAL. If you prefer, O Socrates, to be called a Mysian <note>original: "Mysion"; a term for the lowest or most contemptible of people</note>, you will be called that anyway, unless you believe me. SOC. Do not object to me now what you have already objected more than once, namely: "whoever wishes will kill you, O Socrates," lest I should answer thus again: "but a bad man will kill a good one"; nor say again: "anyone, if you have anything, will take it away from you, O Socrates," lest I also answer: "but he who takes it away will not know how to use those things as useful to himself, but just as he took them unjustly from me, so he himself will use them unjustly, and if unjustly, therefore also shamefully, and finally, if shamefully, badly." CAL. You seem to me to think that nothing of this sort can happen to you: just as if you lived far from here, nor do you think you could be led into judgment by any most cowardly man of no value. SOC. I would certainly be a fool, O Callicles, if I did not think that in this city anyone could suffer anything of this sort. This, however, I know for certain: if I come into judgment risking those things which you bring forward, he who accuses me will be a wicked man. <margin>No good man accuses the innocent.</margin> For no good man accuses an innocent person. Truly it would be no wonder if I were condemned to death. Do you want me to tell you for what reason I expect these things? CAL. I do indeed. SOC. I think indeed that I, together with a few Athenians—not to say alone—truly handle the civil discipline, and that I alone of all who are now living exercise civil affairs: inasmuch as I do not speak words for favor, which I do very frequently, but rather for that which may be best, rather than what is sweetest; and those things which you now by advising exhort me to do as if they were certain illustrious things, I do not accept that I will do, for indeed I do not have what I might most especially say in a judgment. And now indeed there recurs to my mind again what I had said to Polus. For I would be judged just as among children a doctor would be judged whom a cook has accused. For consider by what reasoning a doctor would defend himself, a case having been brought against him before children, if someone should accuse him with these words: "This man, O children, has brought many evils upon you. For he twists both you and the youngest among you by cutting and burning, and making you thin and suffocating you he afflicts you, moreover he offers the most bitter drinks, and urges you to hunger and thirst. But I on the contrary prepare many and various and sweet things for you." If, I say, a cook should bring this accusation, what do you think this doctor, circumvented by evil, would answer? Or perhaps he will confess the truth saying: "I did all these things, O children, for the sake of your health"? But indeed, how vehemently do you think judges of that sort would cry out against him? CAL. Vehemently, perhaps, it must be thought. SOC. Therefore do you not think he would then be held in the greatest ambiguity and poverty of his defense? CAL. Entirely. SOC. I know the same would happen to me if it happened that I were dragged into judgment: for neither could I commemorate any pleasures found by me for their lust, which they themselves consider in the place of benefit and utility: but I do not at all approve of the inventors of them, nor do I consider those more happy on account of the things which are provided to them. Furthermore, if someone should say that I either corrupt the youth by leading them into ambiguity and poverty, or that I reproach and refute the elders with certain sharp and biting words either privately or publicly, the faculty of speaking will not be given to me to seem to say: "I say all these things justly, and I look to the utility of those very people"; nor will I be able to bring forward anything else easily. For which reason perhaps there is nothing that would not be decreed against me. CAL. Does it seem to you then to be well for one who is such a person in the city, that he cannot be a protection to himself? SOC. Provided this is in him, O Callicles, which you have often agreed to: that he can provide that help to himself by which he has done or said nothing unjustly either against men or against gods. For we have often agreed now that this kind of help for oneself is the best. If someone therefore should convince me that I cannot bring help of this sort to myself or to others, I would undoubtedly blush whether I were refuted among many, or among few, or alone by one person. And so if I were to die on account of this impotence, I would take it heavily. But if indeed on account of a defect of flattering rhetoric I were to be afflicted with the ultimate punishment, I know for certain that I would bear death very easily—
