—seeing me. For no one fears to die, unless he is altogether devoid of reason and cowardly, but he fears to act unjustly. For for a soul filled with many sins to descend to the underworld is the extreme of all evils. Accordingly, if you desire to know why the matter stands thus, I will exhibit the reason to you. CAL. On the contrary, since you have completed the rest, complete this also. SOC. Hear then, as they say, a most beautiful speech, which I think you will consider a fable: but I consider it not a fable, but a speech. For as things truly spoken I will narrate to you what I am about to say. Truly as <margin>Iliad 2</margin> Homer says, Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto divided the kingdom among themselves which they received from their father. But there existed a law concerning men under Saturn, and it always existed, and now even exists among the gods: that whatever men had lived a just and pious life, when they migrated from life, having set out for the islands of the blessed, they should live in all happiness, separated far from the wicked: but those who had lived unjustly and impiously should go into the prison of punishment and just penalty, which they call Tartarus. But the judges of these under Saturn, and even under Jupiter himself when he recently began to reign, were living men judging the living, and they judged on the same day on which someone was about to die, for which reason they were judged unjustly. Therefore Pluto and the caretakers of the blessed islands, approaching Jupiter, reported that unworthy men were coming to them from both sides. To whom Jupiter said thus: "But I will apply a remedy. For now the reason it is judged iniquitously is that they are judged each clothed and surrounded, since they are judged before death. And so many carrying about wicked souls are surrounded by the form of the body, and by birth and riches. Furthermore, when the judgment is imminent, a multitude of witnesses flows together asserting that they have lived justly. By which it happens that the judges are dazed by these things. It is added that they themselves judge clothed and surrounded, having eyes and ears and the whole body as if a veil of the soul. For all these things are obstacles to them, namely both their own coverings and those of the ones who are judged. First it must be provided," he said, "that men do not foresee their own death: for now they foresee it, and it has been commanded to Prometheus that he not permit them to foresee it. Then they must be judged naked of all these things. For they must be judged after death. It is also necessary that the judge himself be naked, namely dead: and inspecting the soul itself with the mind alone immediately after the unexpected death of each, the soul, I say, deserted by all relatives, and leaving all external ornament on the earth, so that the judgment may proceed justly. I therefore, as I foresaw these things before you, have already appointed my sons as judges, two indeed from Asia, namely Minos and Rhadamanthus: and one from Europe, Aeacus. These therefore, after they have died, will judge in a certain meadow, and there in a three-way crossroad, from which two ways tend: one indeed to Tartarus, the other indeed to the islands of the blessed. And Rhadamanthus shall judge the Asians: but Aeacus shall judge those who come from Europe. To Minos I will enjoin this duty, that he himself decide if anything should be ambiguous from the others, so that it may be judged most justly and rightly concerning the transmission of souls." These are the things, O Callicles, which I have heard, and I believe them to be true, and led by these speeches I thus reflect with myself. Death indeed is, as it seems to me, nothing other than the dissolution of two things, namely the soul and the body, from each other. But when these two are disjoined from each other, it is not far off that each of them preserves the same habit which it possessed while the man was living. First the body displays both its nature and its cultivation and passions. Just as if someone had a large body either by nature, or by nourishment, or by both while he lived, it will also be large when the man is dead. Likewise if it had been thick, it will also be thick, and other things similarly. Furthermore, if the man had been studious of long hair, he will preserve the hair. Again if someone was a scoundrel, and had many marks of blows impressed on his body either from lashes or from wounds while he lived: we see the body of this man when dead also retain the same. And if it was broken or distorted in any part, these same things appear also when he is dead: and to say it briefly, of whatever sort the body of the living person was, all or most such things of the same person when dead appear for a time. The same thing also seems to me, Callicles, to be thought concerning the soul: for all things appear in the soul when it has put off the body, both those which were in it from nature, and those which were in it from affections, which on account of the pursuit of each thing the man contracted into it. When therefore they have come to the judge, the Asians indeed to Rhadamanthus. Rhadamanthus, making them stand, looks at the soul of each one, yet whose soul that might be, he does not notice. But for the most part, having contemplated the soul of the great king of the Persians or another king, or a potentate, he finds nothing healthy in it: but infected with perjuries and injustice as if with certain blows and scars, such as the action of each contracted and impressed on the soul, and all things twisted by lies and vanity and having nothing straight, because it had been educated without truth: furthermore on account of the license of sinning and petulance and soft lasciviousness and intemperance in individual actions, thoroughly disordered and base. Contemplating the soul thus affected, he ignominiously transmits it straight into custody, where it is necessary to undergo deserved punishments. But it is fitting that everyone who is rightly punished by someone either himself becomes better and perceives utility, or gives examples to others, so that others seeing his punishments might be made better on account of fear. Those who thus give penalties among gods and men that they might report some utility from it: these are they who committed sanable sins, for whom pain and torture is profitable both among men and among those below. For not otherwise can one be liberated from injustice. But those who are held by extreme injustice, and on account of such crimes are incurable, from these examples are taken, and they themselves report no further utility from it, inasmuch as they cannot be healed: but they profit only others through the example, who look upon them tortured for their outrages with the greatest, most bitter, and most terrible punishments for all time, providing as it were an example, a monument, and a spectacle among those below in the prison for all the unjust who descend to those places. One of whom I say will be Archelaus, if Polus narrates true things, and another whoever shall have emerged as such a tyrant. But I think in the number of those who hand down only examples, most are tyrants, kings, potentates, and governors of cities. Since these indeed, on account of the very license of sinning, commit the gravest and most profane sins. And <margin>Odyssey λ <note>Book 11</note></margin> Homer attests to us, who introduces kings and potentates tortured for all time among those below, such as Tantalus, Sisyphus, and Tityus. But Thersites, and if anyone else was privately evil, no one ever made him be tortured with great punishments as if incurable, for indeed he did not have the license, as I think, for which reason he was happier than those to whom the license of perpetrating a crime was given. Truly Callicles, from those who have power and license, there are those who were excessively wicked. Nevertheless—

—nothing prevents there being some good men even among these: and certainly he who has been such is wonderfully to be cherished. Indeed it is arduous, O Callicles, and worthy of great praise, that someone established in great license of sinning should lead a just life; and few such are found. Yet there were both here and elsewhere, and as I think, there will be some illustrious and good men, endowed namely with this virtue, through which they might handle justly those things of which authority was granted to them. But one of all the Greeks emerged as most approved, Aristides the son of Lysimachus. But most of the powerful men, O best man, are wicked. For which reason as I was saying, when Rhadamanthus catches someone of this sort, he knows nothing else in him, neither who he may be, nor from whom sprung, but only whether he be evil: and when he has found that, he dismisses him into Tartarus, marking whether he seems sanable or incurable. But he, transmitted thither, undergoes deserved punishments. But sometimes having looked upon another soul, either of a private person or of someone else who has lived piously and with integrity: which indeed I think happens most especially to philosophers, doing their own business and not implicating themselves in many affairs: he applauds this one, and transmits him to the islands of the blessed. Aeacus performs these same things. But each of them holds a rod while he judges. <margin>Odyssey λ <note>Book 11</note></margin> But Minos sits alone considering, having a golden scepter, just as Ulysses says about this in Homer, namely that he saw him holding a golden scepter and giving laws to the dead. I therefore, O Callicles, am moved by speeches of this sort, and I already consider by what reasoning I might be able to show a most healthy soul to the judge. Wherefore, despising the honors of all the people, and considering the truth, I will truly endeavor, as much as I will be able, to live as a good man and to die. And I exhort all others also as much as I can. You also I recall to this sort of life and contest: which indeed I assert is to be undergone by a man above all other contests in this life. Wherefore I also rebuke you who will not be able to bring help to yourself when judgment shall be passed on you, and that sentence which I was just now saying shall press upon you. But when you have come to the judge, the son of Aegina, and he, having apprehended you, shall lead you: you will gape and stagger there no less than I do here before your judges. There perhaps someone will strike you shamefully upon the cheek, and will afflict you with utter contumely and injury. These things perhaps seem to you some old woman's fable, and you despise what has been said: but truly it would be nothing wonderful to despise these things, if in any way by searching we could find better and truer things than these. But now you see, since you are three men of all the Greeks who are now living the wisest—you, namely, and Polus, and Gorgias—that you nevertheless cannot show that one ought to live by any other reasoning than that which seems to lead there also. Indeed, in so many speeches when the others have been refuted, this one alone remains firm: namely that one must take care to do injury more than to suffer it: and that this must be meditated upon by a man above all other things, not so that he might seem good indeed, but so that he might truly be good publicly and privately: but if someone has been in some way evil, he must be punished. And that this is good in the second place, after that which is to be just, namely to be made good by chastisement, and to pay the penalties of injustice: furthermore, every flattery concerning oneself and others, whether few or many, must be fled: finally, Rhetoric and every other kind of action must be used for justice alone. For which reasons believing me, follow me thither, where when you have arrived, you will be blessed both living and dead, just as your speech also signifies. And permit that someone despise you as a fool, and afflict you with injuries if he pleases, nor care if you are struck ignominiously. For you will suffer nothing grave, if you are truly honorable and good, and exercise virtue. But after we have thus been exercised together, then if it seems to you to be worthwhile, we will then bring ourselves to public business, or to whatever shall have seemed best to us deliberating then, when we will be able to deliberate better. For it is shameful since we are such as we now seem to be, to boast in words as if we were something: about which things we never judge the same about the same and indeed the greatest matters: so far have we proceeded in rudeness. Let us therefore follow this reasoning, which has now become known to us, as a leader, showing to us that this is the best way of living, so that cultivating justice and the other virtues, we may both live and die. Let us therefore obey this, and let us exhort others to this. But let us not obey that one, trusting in which you exhort me to the same. For it is of no value, O Callicles.

# COMMENTARY
# OF MARSILIO FICINO
# THE FLORENTINE ON THE
# BANQUET <term>Symposium</term>
# OF PLATO,
# CONCERNING LOVE.
*
### CHAPTER I.
PLATO, having been born more than eighty-one years, on the seventh day of November, on which he had been born, reclining at a banquet after the tables were removed, expired. But this banquet, in which both the birthday and the anniversary of Plato are equally contained, all the ancient Platonists, even up to the times of Plotinus and Porphyry, used to institute annually. But after Porphyry for one thousand and two hundred years, these solemn feasts were omitted. At last in our times that most illustrious man Lorenzo de' Medici, about to renew the Platonic banquet, appointed Francesco Bandini as the Master of the Feast. When therefore Bandini had instituted to celebrate the seventh day of November, with royal preparation in the field of Careggi he received nine Platonic guests: Antonio Agli, bishop of Fiesole; Ficino the Physician; Cristoforo Landino the poet; Bernardo Nuzzi the rhetorician; Tommaso Benci; Giovanni Cavalcanti our familiar friend, whom on account of the virtue of his mind and his egregious natural disposition the guests called "Hero"; the two Marsupini, Cristoforo and Carlo, sons of the poet Carlo. Finally, Bandini wished me to be the ninth, so that with Marsilio Ficino added to the previous ones the number of the Muses might be filled. After the tables were removed, Bernardo Nuzzi took up Plato's book, which is inscribed *The Banquet concerning Love*: and he read all the orations of this Symposium, which having been read, he prayed the remaining guests that each should explain one oration. All assented: and the lots having been cast, that first oration of Phaedrus fell to Giovanni Cavalcanti to be explained; the oration of Pausanias to Antonio the Theologian. That of Eryximachus the Physician to Ficino the Physician. That of the poet Aristophanes to Cristoforo the Poet. That of the youth Agathon to Carlo Marsupini. To Tommaso Benci was given the disputation of Socrates. But that of Alcibiades to Cristoforo Marsupini. All approved a lot of this sort. But the bishop and the physician, the one to the care of souls, the other to that of bodies, having been forced to depart, left their parts in speaking to Giovanni Cavalcanti. The others turned to him, and prepared for hearing, they fell silent. Then that hero began in this manner.

# BY WHAT RULE LOVE IS TO BE PRAISED.
# What is its dignity and magnitude.
### CHAPTER II.
THAT lot today fell to me, most excellent guests, most gratefully, <margin>What kind of man Phaedrus was.</margin> by which it was brought about that I should play the person of Phaedrus of Myrrhinus. Of that Phaedrus, I say, whose familiarity Lysias the Theban, the supreme orator, valued so much that with an oration composed in many nightly labors, he contended to conciliate him to himself: whose natural disposition Socrates so much admired that by its splendor, sometimes moved near the river Ilissus and raised higher, he sang divine mysteries—

<keywords>Aristides the Just, virtue, Socrates' defense, Marsilio Ficino, Lorenzo de' Medici, Platonic Banquet, Symposium, Careggi, Neoplatonism</keywords>

258 On the Banquet.

—he sang; who before had proclaimed himself ignorant not only of celestial things, but also of all inferior things. With whose genius Plato was so delighted that he dedicated the first-fruits of his studies to Phaedrus. To him are the epigrams, to him the elegies of Plato; to him his first book concerning beauty, which is inscribed *Phaedrus*. Since therefore the lot first, and your applause thereafter, has judged me similar to this Phaedrus—not that I indeed, for I do not arrogate so much to myself—under these happy auspices I will most willingly interpret his oration in the first place. Then I will execute the parts of Antonio and Ficino according to the strength of my genius. In every matter <margin>What is a proper praise.</margin> every best man, an imitator of the philosopher Plato, considers three things: what precedes, what accompanies, and what follows. If these be good, he praises the thing itself; if bad, he disparages it. That therefore is a perfect praise which recounts the preceding origin of the thing, narrates the present form, and shows the following events. From the antecedents each thing is praised as noble; from the present things, as great; from the following things, as useful. Wherefore from those three, these three are concluded in praises: nobility, magnitude, and utility. Therefore our Phaedrus in the first place, having contemplated the present excellence of Love, called it a "Great God"; he added, "To be wondered at by Gods and men." Nor without injury. For we admire those things which are properly great. He is indeed great, to whose empire men and gods, as they say, are all subjected. For both gods among the ancients as well as men love, which Orpheus and Hesiod signify, saying that the minds of mortals and immortals are tamed by love. Furthermore, he is said to be wonderful, because each person loves that whose beauty he admires. Gods indeed, or as our people say, Angels, admire divine beauty; Men admire and love the appearances of bodies. And this indeed is the praise of Love, deduced from the present excellence which accompanies it. Then Phaedrus praises from the antecedents, when he asserts it to be the most ancient of all the gods. In which the nobility of love shines forth, since its ancient origin is narrated. And he will praise thirdly from the following things, where its wonderful utility from the event will appear. But we will treat concerning its ancient and noble origin first; then concerning its future utility.

<margin>Orpheus on the beginning of things.</margin> Orpheus in the *Argonautica*, when he was singing concerning the beginnings of things in the presence of Chiron and the heroes, following the theology of Hermes Trismegistus, placed Chaos before the world, and before Saturn, Jupiter, and the other gods. He located Love in the very bosom of Chaos, and praised it with these words.

# THE ORIGIN OF LOVE FROM CHAOS.
### CHAPTER III.
HESIOD in the *Theogony*, and Parmenides in the book *On Nature*, and Pythagoras, and the poet Acusilaus have agreed with Orpheus and Hermes that Love is most ancient, perfect in himself, and most wise. Plato in the *Timaeus* describes Chaos similarly, and in it he locates love. And Phaedrus recounted the same in the banquet. The Platonists call the unformed world "Chaos"; but the formed world "World" <term>Mundus</term>. There are three worlds among them; likewise there will be three chaoses. The first of all is God, the author of the universes, which we call the Good itself. He first creates the angelic mind; then the soul of this world, as Plato wishes; finally the body of the world. We do not call that supreme God the "world"; because world signifies an ornament composed of many things, but He truly ought to be entirely simple: but we assert Him to be the beginning and the end of all worlds. The angelic mind is the first world made by God. The second is the soul of the universal body. The third is this whole machine which we discern. Therefore in these three worlds, three chaoses are considered. In the beginning, God creates the substance of that mind, which we also name essence. This in that first moment of its creation is unformed and obscure. But because it was born from God, it is turned toward God its beginning by a certain inborn appetite. Having turned toward God, it is illuminated by His ray. By the splendor of that ray, its own appetite is kindled. The kindled appetite adheres totally to God; by adhering, it is formed. For God, who can do all things, fashions the natures of created things in the mind adhering to Himself. In it therefore are painted in a certain spiritual way, so to speak, all things which we perceive in these bodies. From there the globes of the heavens and the elements, the stars, the natures of vapors, the forms of stones, metals, plants, and animals are begotten. We do not doubt that the species of all things of this sort, conceived by a certain nourishment of God in the supernal mind, are the "Ideas"; and that form and idea of the heavens, we often call the god Caelum <note>Uranus</note>. The form of the first planet, the god Saturn; of the second, Jupiter; and in the following planets in the same manner. Also that idea of this fire, the god Vulcan; of the air, Jupiter and Juno; of water, Neptune; of earth, Pluto. Wherefore all gods assigned to certain parts of the inferior world are the Ideas of those parts collected in that supernal mind. But that conception of ideas perfected by the forming God was preceded by that approach of the mind toward God. This was preceded by the kindling of appetite, this by the infusion of the ray, this by that first conversion of appetite, this by the essence of the unformed mind. Furthermore, we wish that essence not yet formed to be "Chaos"; the first conversion of the same toward God, the "birth of love"; the infusion of the ray, the "food of love"; the following kindling, we call the "increase of love"; the approach, the "impetus of love"; the formation, the "perfection of love." We call the complex of all forms and ideas *Mundus* in Latin, in Greek *kosmos*, that is, ornament. For the sake of this ornament is beauty. To which that love, immediately born, attracted the mind and led the mind, previously deformed, to the same mind thereafter formed. Therefore the condition of love is: that it may snatch toward beauty, and join the deformed to the beautiful. Who therefore will doubt that love immediately follows chaos, and precedes the world, and all the gods who are distributed into parts of the world? Since that appetite of the mind is before its own formation, and in the formed mind the gods and the world are born. Justly therefore Orpheus named this one most ancient. Furthermore, perfect in himself: as if he should say, perfecting himself. Since that first instinct of the mind by its own nature seems to draw its perfection from God: and to provide it to the mind which is formed therefrom, and to the gods who are begotten therefrom. He named it moreover most wise, and not without injury. For all wisdom, of which counsel is proper, was therefore given to the mind because, having turned toward God by love, it shone with His splendor. And in the same way the mind is directed toward God as the eye toward the light of the sun. For from here it looks first, then it sees the light of the sun: thirdly in the light of the sun it comprehends the colors and figures of things. Wherefore the eye, obscure at first and like chaos unformed, loves the light while it looks; it is irradiated by looking, by receiving the ray it is formed by the colors and figures of things. Just as indeed in God that mind immediately born and unformed is converted by love and formed: so the soul of the world reflects itself into the mind and God, begotten from there. And when at first it is unformed, and chaos, directed by love into the mind, with forms received from it it becomes a world: not otherwise also the matter of this world, when in the beginning it lay as unformed chaos without the ornament of forms, immediately by a love inborn to itself it directed itself into the soul, and offered itself obedient to it, and with this love reconciling, having obtained from the soul the ornament of all forms which are seen in the world, the world was fashioned out of chaos. Therefore there are three worlds, and three chaoses. Finally in all things love accompanies chaos, precedes the world, arouses the torpid, illuminates the obscure, vivifies the dead, forms the unformed, perfects the imperfect. Than which praises almost none greater can either be said or devised.

# ON THE UTILITY OF LOVE.
### CHAPTER IIII.
BUT concerning its origin and nobility thus far. Concerning its utility I think we must now discuss. To recount individual benefits of love conferred upon the human race is superfluous: especially since all can be comprehended summarily. For all things consist in this, that having avoided evils we follow good things. The bad and shameful things of a man are the same. Likewise the good and honorable things are the same. Indeed, all laws and doctrines contend for nothing else than to so institute men that they decline from shameful things and act honorably. But this very thing, which almost innumerable laws and arts scarcely at last attain in a long time, Love itself alone perfects in a short time. For shame deters from shameful things; the study of excelling provokes to honorable things. Love exhibits these two things to men more easily and more quickly than anything else. When we say love, understand the desire for beauty. For this among all philosophers is the definition of love. But beauty is a certain grace, which for the most part is born especially in harmony. It is threefold: since from the harmony of many virtues there is grace in souls. From the concord of many colors and lines, grace is born in bodies. Likewise the greatest grace in sounds is from the consonance of many voices. Therefore beauty is threefold: of souls, of bodies, and of voices. That of souls is known by the mind; that of bodies by the eyes; that of voices is perceived by the ears alone. Since therefore mind, sight, and hearing are those things by which alone we can enjoy beauty: and Love is the desire of enjoying beauty: Love is always content with Mind, Eyes, and Ears. What need is there for smell? what for taste? what for touch? These senses perceive Odors, Flavors, Heat, Cold, Softness and hardness, and similar things. None of these is human beauty, since forms are simple: but the beauty of the human body requires the concord of diverse members. Love looks upon the enjoyment of beauty as its end: these things pertain to the mind, sight, and hearing alone. Love therefore is terminated in these three. But that appetite which follows the remaining senses is not called love, but lust and madness. Furthermore, if love toward a man desires beauty itself: but the beauty of the human body [consists] in a certain harmony—

<summary>Giovanni Cavalcanti, speaking as Phaedrus, discusses the origins of Love as the first force that brings order (the World) out of disorder (Chaos), and defines Love as the desire for beauty perceived through the mind, eyes, and ears.</summary>
