consists in harmony: harmony is temperance. Love demands only those things which are temperate, modest, and decorous. Therefore, the pleasures of taste and touch—which are so vehement and furious <margin>In these there is lust, not love.</margin> that they move the mind from its state and disturb the man—love not only does not desire, but abominates and flees, since these things, due to their lack of temperance, are contrary to beauty. Venereal madness <note>Lust or sexual frenzy.</note> drags one toward intemperance, and therefore toward a lack of harmony; for this reason, it seems to entice one toward deformity, whereas Love leads toward beauty. Deformity and beauty are opposites. Therefore, movements of this kind, which seize one toward these things, appear to be contrary to one another. For this reason, lust, sexual intercourse, and love are shown to be not only not the same, but actually opposites. The ancient theologians also testify to this, having attributed the name of Love to God. Later theologians have likewise strongly confirmed this. Indeed, no name suitable for God is held in common with shameful things. Therefore, every person of sound mind must take care not to rashly transfer the name of Love, which is divine, to insane disturbances. Let Dicaearchus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who criticized Plato.</note> blush, and anyone else who does not fear to misinterpret the majesty of Plato because he indulged too much in love. For we can never indulge too much or even enough in decorous, honest, and divine affections. From this it follows that all love is honest, and every lover is just. For everything that is beautiful and decorous is loved, and love properly delights in the decorous. However, the turbulent heat by which people are seized toward lewdness is judged to be contrary to love, as it drags them toward deformity. So that we may return eventually to the utility of love: <margin>The utility of love.</margin> shame, which deters us from shameful things, and the zeal that makes us burn for honest things, proceed easily and quickly from love. First, because love, which seeks beautiful things, always desires things that are decorous and magnificent; and he who hates deformed things necessarily flees from the base and the obscene. Second, if two people love one another, they observe each other and desire to please one another mutually. Insofar as one is observed by the other—since they are never without a witness—they abstain from shameful acts. Insofar as they strive to please one another, they always undertake magnificent things with burning zeal, so that they might not be held in contempt by the beloved, but rather be thought worthy of a return of love. Phaedrus explains this reasoning most abundantly where he provides three examples of loves: one of a woman for a man, where he speaks of Alcestis, the wife of Admetus, who wished to die for her husband; another of a man for a woman, like Orpheus for Eurydice; and a third of a man for a man, like Patroclus for Achilles. In these he shows that nothing makes men braver than love. Indeed, it is not my intention at present to provide an allegory of either Alcestis or Orpheus. For these things express the power and empire of love more vehemently if they are narrated as historical events than if they are thought to be told through allegory. Therefore, let us confess without controversy that love is a great and wonderful God, noble and exceedingly useful; and let us indulge in love in such a way that we are content with its end, which is beauty itself. We enjoy that beauty with the part of us by which we know; we know with the mind, the sight, and the hearing. Therefore, we enjoy beauty with these; with the other senses, we do not use beauty (which love desires), but rather whatever else the body requires. Therefore, we shall hunt for beauty with these three: and through that beauty which shines forth in voices and bodies, as if through certain tracks, we shall investigate the decorum of the soul. We shall indeed praise the former and approve the latter as just; and we shall always strive to ensure that there is as much love as there is beauty. And where the body is beautiful but the soul is not at all, let us love it only slightly and lightly, as a shadowy and fleeting image of beauty. Where the soul alone is beautiful, let us ardently love this stable decorum of the soul. But where both beauties concur, let us admire it more vehemently; and thus we shall testify that we are truly of the Platonic family, for that family knows nothing but what is festive, joyful, celestial, and heavenly. But let these things suffice regarding the speech of Phaedrus. Let us come to Pausanias.

# THE SECOND SPEECH.
# GOD IS GOODNESS, BEAUTY, JUSTICE; THE BEGINNING, THE MIDDLE, AND THE END.

## CHAPTER I.

The Pythagorean philosophers wished the Trinity to be the measure of all things, for the reason, I believe, that God governs things by the number three, and even things themselves are terminated by the number three. Hence that saying of Virgil: "God rejoices in an odd number." <note>original: "Numero deus impare gaudet."</note> Truly, that supreme author first creates individual things; second, he draws them back; third, he perfects them. Individual things also flow out from that perennial fountain in the first place while they are being born; then they flow back into the same while they seek their origin; finally, they are perfected after they have returned to their beginning. Orpheus prophesied this, calling Jove the beginning, middle, and end of the universe: the Beginning as he produces; the Middle as he draws back what was produced to himself; the End as he perfects those who return. Hence we can name that King of the universe as Good, Beautiful, and Just, as is often said in Plato. Good, I say, when he creates; Beautiful, when he allures; Just, when he perfects according to each person’s merit. Beauty, therefore, whose property it is to allure, is located between goodness and justice: it flows from goodness and flows forth toward justice.

## HOW DIVINE BEAUTY PRODUCES LOVE.
## CHAPTER II.

This divine appearance has procreated love—that is, the desire for itself—in all things. For if God draws the world to himself, and the world is drawn, there is one continuous attraction beginning from God, passing into the world, and finally ending in God; which returns, as if in a circle, into the same place from which it flowed. Therefore, the one and the same circle from God into the world, and from the world into God, is called by three names. Insofar as it begins in God and allures, it is Beauty; insofar as it passes into the world and seizes it, it is Love; insofar as it returns to the author and joins his work to him, it is Pleasure. Love, therefore, begins from beauty and ends in pleasure. This is what that famous hymn of Hierotheus and Dionysius the Areopagite meant when these theologians sang: "Love is a good circle, perpetually revolved from good, by way of good, to good." For love is necessarily good, since being born from good it returns to good. For it is the same God whose appearance all things desire, and in whose possession all things find rest. From there, therefore, our desire is kindled; there the heat of lovers finds rest, not being extinguished, but fulfilled. Not without reason does Dionysius compare God to the sun: because just as the sun illuminates and warms the body, so God provides the clarity of truth and the heat of charity to souls. We gather this comparison from the sixth book of Plato’s *Republic* in this way: the Sun produces visible bodies and seeing eyes, infusing a lucid spirit into the eyes so they may see, and painting bodies with colors so they may be seen. Yet neither the ray proper to the eyes nor the colors proper to the bodies are sufficient to perfect vision unless the light itself—the one above the many—from which many and proper lights are distributed to eyes and bodies, arrives to illustrate, excite, and strengthen them. In the same way, that first act of all things, which is called God, granted appearance and act to individual things by producing them. This act, when it is received in a created thing and a passive subject, is weak and powerless for the execution of work. But the perpetual and invisible light of the divine sun always stands by all things, fostering, vivifying, exciting, completing, and strengthening. Concerning this divine light Orpheus said: "Fostering all things and bearing himself above all." <note>original: "Cuncta fouens atque ipse ferens super omnia sese."</note> Insofar as he is the act of all and strengthens them, he is called Good. Insofar as he vivifies, softens, soothes, and excites, he is called Beautiful. Insofar as beauty allures the three knowing powers of the soul—Mind, Sight, and Hearing—in the objects that are to be known. Insofar as it applies that beauty to the known thing in the knowing power, it is Truth. Finally, as Good, he procreates, rules, and completes; as Beautiful, he illuminates and infuses grace.

## BEAUTY IS THE SPLENDOR OF DIVINE GOODNESS, AND GOD IS THE CENTER OF FOUR CIRCLES.
## CHAPTER III.

Not without reason did the ancient theologians place Goodness in the center and Beauty in the circle. Goodness, I say, in the one center, but Beauty in four circles. The one center of all is God. The four circles continuously revolved around it are Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter. Mind is a stable circle. Soul is mobile by itself. Nature is mobile in another, but not by another. Matter is mobile by another and in another. Now I will explain why we call God the center and those four the circles. The center of a circle is a point, one, indivisible, and stable. From there, many divisible and mobile lines are led out to their similar circumference; which circumference, being divisible, is turned around the center as if around a hinge. And such is the nature of the center that, although it is one, individual, and immobile, it is found everywhere in many—indeed, in all—divisible and mobile lines. For the point is everywhere in the line. Since nothing can be touched by its opposite, the lines led from the circumference to the center must reach that middle point by a certain point of their own, one, simple, and immobile. Who denies that God is deservedly named the center of all, since he is present within all things as one, simple, and immobile; while all things produced by him are many, composite, and mobile, and just as they flow from him, so they flow back to him like lines and a circumference? Thus, mind, soul, nature, and matter, proceeding from God, strive to return to the same; and they revolve themselves around him everywhere according to their strength. And just as the center point is found everywhere in the lines and in the whole circle, and through its own point each line touches the middle point of the circle: so God, the center of all, who is the simplest unity and purest act, inserts himself into the universe; not for that reason alone because he is present to all, but also because he has placed in all things created by him some part, or internal power, most simple and most excellent, which is called the unity of things: from which and upon which, as from a center and toward its own center, the remaining parts and powers of each thing hang. Created things must first collect themselves at this, their own center, at this proper unity, before they can cling to their creator; so that through their own center, as we have often repeated, they may cling to the center of all. The mind of an angel rises to its own peak and head before it ascends into God. The soul and the rest do the same. And of those invisible circles—namely, mind, soul, nature—the circle of the visible world is the image. For bodies are the shadows and tracks of souls and minds. A shadow and a track reflect the figure of that which they are a shadow or track of. Therefore, those four are not unjustly called four circles. But the mind is an immobile orb for the reason that its operation, like its substance, always remains the same and operates similarly: it understands always in the same way, and wills similarly. However, the mind can sometimes be called mobile only because, like all other things, proceeding from God, it turns itself toward him. The soul of the world, and any other soul, is a mobile circle. For this soul knows by running through things by its nature, and it operates in the courses of time. This running through from one thing to another, and temporal operation, is without doubt called motion. If there is any stability in the soul’s cognition, it consists in the benefit of the mind rather than the soul. Nature is also a mobile circuit. When we say "nature," according to the custom of ancient theologians, we understand the power of the soul placed in reason and sense; when we say "nature," we mean the power of the soul located in generating. That power in us they properly called "man," while they called this other one the "idol" and "simulacrum" of man. This faculty of generating is said to be mobile because it executes its work in intervals of time. But in this it differs from that property of the soul: that the soul moves by itself and in itself. By itself, I say, because it exists as the principle of motion. In itself also, because the operation of reason and sense remains in the substance of the soul itself. From these, no work necessarily results in the body. But that power of generating which we call nature moves by itself, since it is a certain power of the soul moved by itself. However, it is said to move in another, because all its operation is terminated in the mass of the body. For it nourishes, increases, and generates the body. Matter and the mass of the body is an orb mobile by another and in another. By another, indeed, because it is necessarily agitated by the soul. In another, however, because the motion of the body is agitated in the space of a place. Now, therefore, we can clearly understand for what reason theologians place goodness in the center and beauty in the circle. For goodness of all things is God himself, through whom all things are good. But beauty is a ray of God, inserted into those four circles revolved in a certain way around God. A ray of this kind fashions all the species of all things in those four: those species we are accustomed to call "Ideas" in the mind, "Reasons" in the soul, "Seeds" in nature, and "Forms" in matter. Therefore, in the four circles, four splendors appear to be. The splendor of Ideas in the first; of Reasons in the second; of Seeds in the third; and of Forms in the last.

## HOW PLATO IS TO BE EXPLAINED REGARDING DIVINE MATTERS.
## CHAPTER IV.

Plato indicated this mystery in his letter to King Dionysius when he affirmed God to be the cause of all beautiful things, as if he were the principle and origin of all beauty. "Around the King of all," he says, "are all things: all things are for his sake: he is the cause of all beautiful things: second things around the second. Third things around the third. But the human soul desires to understand what those things are like, looking at those things that are related to itself, none of which is sufficient. But around the King himself and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of such a kind: but what is after this, the soul says." "Around the King," not "inside the King," signifies something outside. For in God there is no composition. What that word "Around" signifies, Plato explains when he adds: "All things are for his sake: he is the cause of all beautiful things." As if he were to say, for this reason all things are around the king, because all things are revolved toward him as toward an end according to their nature, just as all things were produced by him as the principle. "Of all beautiful things"—that is, of total beauty, which shines forth in the aforementioned circles. For the forms of bodies are reduced to God through seeds; these through reasons; these through ideas; and they are produced from God by the same steps. Properly, indeed, when he says "All things," he understands the Ideas; for in these the rest are included. "Second things around the second: Third things around the third." Zoroaster placed three princes of the world, masters of three orders: Oromasdes, Mithras, Arimanius. These Plato calls God, Mind, and Soul. He placed three orders in divine species: Ideas, Reasons, and Seeds. Therefore, the first things, that is, Ideas, are around the first, that is, around God, since they are granted to the mind by God and lead back to the same God the mind to which they are given. Second things around the second, that is, Reasons around the mind: since through the mind they pass into the soul and direct the soul toward the mind. Third things around the third, that is, the seeds of things around the soul: for through the soul they pass into nature—that is, into that power of generating—and again join nature to the soul. In the same order, forms descend from nature into matter. But Plato does not count them in the stated order because, being asked by Dionysius about divine matters, he introduced three orders pertaining to incorporeal species as being divine, but he omitted the forms of bodies. He did not wish to call God the "first King," but the "King of all," lest if he called him "first," he might perhaps seem to place him with the following leaders in some species of number and parity of condition. Nor did he say "first things around him," but "all things," lest we believe him to be the governor of one order rather than of all. "The human soul desires to understand what those things are like." Skillfully, after those three splendors of divine beauty shining in the three circles, he added the love of the soul for them. For from there the heat of the soul is kindled. Indeed, it often happens that the divine soul desires divine things, looking at those things that are related to itself. Since human cognition arises from the senses, we have often been accustomed to judge divine things through those things we see to be more excellent in bodies: through the powers of corporal things we investigate the power of God; through order, his wisdom; through utility, the goodness of God. He calls the forms of bodies related to the soul, as if born next to it. For in the following step after the soul, the forms of bodies are arranged. "None of which is sufficient." Forms of this kind are neither sufficient in themselves, nor do they sufficiently show us divine things. For the true things are Ideas, Reasons, and Seeds. But the forms of bodies appear to be shadows of things rather than true things. Just as the shadow of a body does not indicate the exact and distinct figure of the body, so bodies do not demonstrate the proper nature of divine things. "Around the King himself and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of such a kind." For in what way can mortal things be similar to immortal ones, and false things to true ones? "But what is after this, the soul says": that is, as long as the soul judges divine things through mortal ones, it speaks falsely about divine things; it does not pronounce divine things, but mortal ones.

## DIVINE BEAUTY SHINES THROUGH ALL THINGS, AND IS LOVED IN ALL THINGS.
## CHAPTER V.

Furthermore, to comprehend many things in few words: goodness is said to be the supereminent existence of God itself. Beauty is a certain act or ray penetrating from there through all things: First into the angelic mind; Second into the soul of the whole and other souls; Third into nature; Fourth into the matter of bodies. It decorates the mind with the order of Ideas; it fills the soul with the series of reasons; it supports nature with seeds; it adorns matter with forms. Just as one ray of the sun illuminates four bodies—fire, air, water, and earth—so one ray of God illuminates mind, soul, nature, and matter. And in these four elements, whoever looks at the light looks at the ray of the sun itself, and through it is turned toward contemplating the heavenly light of the sun. So whoever contemplates the decorum in these four—mind, soul, nature, body—and loves it, beholds and loves the radiance of God in these, and through this radiance God himself.

## THE PASSIONS OF LOVERS.
## CHAPTER VI.

From this it follows that the impetus of love is not extinguished by the sight or touch of any body. For love does not desire this or that body, but admires, affects, and is stunned by the splendor of the heavenly light shining through bodies. Therefore, lovers do not know what they desire or seek. For they are ignorant of God himself, whose hidden flavor has inserted a certain most sweet odor of himself into his works. By this heat, indeed, we are excited daily. We perceive the odor, but we are undoubtedly ignorant of the flavor. Since, therefore, we are enticed by the manifest odor and latently desire the flavor, we deservedly do not know what we desire and suffer. Hence it also always happens that lovers in a certain way fear and venerate the sight of the beloved. This even the stronger—I will say it indeed, even if I fear lest any of you blush hearing these things—and even wise men are accustomed to suffer in the presence of any inferior beloved. Truly, it is not a human thing that terrifies them, that breaks them, that occupies them. For human power is always more excellent in the stronger and wiser. But that radiance of divinity shining in the beautiful, like a simulacrum <note>A representation or image.</note> of God, compels lovers to be stunned, to tremble, and to venerate. For the same reason, on account of the presence of the beloved, the lover contemns riches and honors and holds them as nothing. For it is right that divine things be preferred to human things. This also happens quite often: that everyone desires to transfer himself into the person of the beloved. Nor without merit. For God desires and strives to become man. And who would not exchange a man for God? And also, those ensnared by love sigh and rejoice in turn. They sigh because they lose themselves, because they perish, because they are destroyed. They rejoice because they transfer themselves into something better. They are also hot and cold in turn, like those whom a tertian fever <note>A fever that returns every third day, often associated with malaria.</note> invades. They are deservedly cold, because they are deserted by their own heat; and they are also hot, since they are kindled by the splendors of the heavenly ray. Timidity follows coldness; audacity follows heat. Therefore, they appear timid and audacious in turn. Furthermore, even the dullest people are rendered sharper by loving. For who, with the heavenly ray breathing upon him, would not see most sharply? But concerning love itself, and beauty, and its origin, and the affections of lovers, let these things suffice.

## CONCERNING TWO KINDS OF LOVE, AND THE DOUBLE VENUS.
## CHAPTER VII.

Next, we must briefly dispute the two kinds of Loves. Pausanias asserts in Plato that Cupid is the companion of Venus. He thinks it necessary that there be as many Cupids as there are Venuses. He records two Venuses, whom likewise twin Cupids accompany. He places one Venus as Celestial, and the other as Vulgar. The Celestial one was born from Heaven without a mother; the Vulgar one was generated from Jove and Dione. The Platonists call the supreme God "Heaven" because just as this sublime body of the heavens rules and contains all bodies, so that supreme God surpasses all spirits. But they name the Mind by many names. For sometimes they call it Saturn, sometimes Jove, sometimes Venus. For that mind is, it lives, and it understands. They were accustomed to call its Essence Saturn, its Life Jove, and its Intelligence Venus. Furthermore, we call the Soul of the World similarly Saturn, Jove, and Venus: insofar as it understands heavenly things, Saturn; insofar as it moves celestial things, Jove; insofar as it generates inferior things, Venus. The first Venus, which is in the Mind, is said to be born of Heaven without a mother, since among natural philosophers "mother" is matter. But that Mind is alien to the company of corporal matter. The second Venus, which is placed in the soul of the world, is generated from Jove and Dione. From Jove—that is, from that virtue of the soul itself which moves celestial things. For that virtue created this power which generates these inferior things. They also attribute a mother to her because, being infused into the matter of the world, she is thought to have commerce with matter. Finally, to speak summarily, Venus is double. One is indeed that intelligence which we placed in the angelic mind. The other is the power of generating attributed to the soul of the world. Each has a similar companion, love. For the former is seized by an innate love to understand the beauty of God. The latter likewise by its love to procreate the same beauty in bodies. The former embraces the radiance of divinity in itself first; then it translates this into the second Venus. The latter pours the sparks of that radiance into the matter of the world. By the presence of these sparks, individual bodies of the world appear beautiful, according to the capacity of their nature. The human soul perceives the appearance of these bodies through the eyes. It again possesses twin powers. Indeed, it has the power of understanding. It also has the power of generating. These twin powers are two Venuses in us, whom twin loves also accompany. As soon as the appearance of a human body is offered to our eyes, our mind—which is the first Venus in us—venerates and delights in it as an image of divine decorum, and through this is often incited toward the divine. But the power of generating, the second Venus, desires to generate a form similar to this. Therefore, there is love on both sides: there the desire of contemplating beauty, here of generating it. Both loves are honest and to be approved. For each follows a divine image. What then does Pausanias disapprove of in love? I will say it indeed. If anyone, more greedy for generation, should desert contemplation, or pursue generation beyond measure with women, or against the order of nature with males, or prefer the form of the body to the beauty of the soul, he certainly abuses the dignity of love. Pausanias vituperates this abuse of love. He who uses it rightly praises the form of the body, but through it thinks of the more excellent appearance of the soul, the mind, and God, and admires and loves it more vehemently. He uses the office of generation and congress only so far as the natural order and the civil laws established by the prudent prescribe. Pausanias speaks more diffusely on these matters.

## EXHORTATION TO LOVE, CONCERNING SIMPLE LOVE, AND MUTUAL LOVE.
## CHAPTER VIII.

But you, friends, I exhort and beseech that you embrace love—a truly divine thing—with all your strength; nor let that deter you which they say Plato said about a certain lover. "That lover's soul," he said, "is dead in its own body, living in another's body." Nor let it disturb you what Orpheus sang about the bitter and miserable lot of lovers. For how these things are to be taken, and by what way they are to be succored, I ask you then, if it please you, to attend diligently. Plato calls love bitter; nor without reason, because whoever loves dies. Orpheus also names this bittersweet <note>original: γλυκύπικρον</note>, that is, sweet-bitter. Indeed, since love is a voluntary death. As death, it is a bitter thing. As voluntary, it is sweet. For whoever loves dies. For his thought, forgetful of himself, always dwells in the beloved. If he does not think of himself, he certainly does not think in himself. Therefore, the soul so affected does not operate in itself, since the chief operation of the soul is thought itself. He who does not operate in himself is not in himself. For these two, being and operation, are equal between themselves; neither is being without operation, nor does operation exceed being itself; nor does anyone operate where he is not; and wherever he is, he operates. Therefore, the soul of the lover is not in itself, because it does not act in itself. If it is not in itself, it does not live in itself; he who does not live is dead. Therefore, whoever loves is dead in himself. Does he live at least in another? Certainly. There are two kinds of Love: one is simple love, the other mutual. Simple love is where the beloved does not love the lover. There the lover is entirely dead; for he neither lives in himself, as we have already sufficiently demonstrated, nor in the beloved since he is rejected by him. Where then does he live? Is it in the air, or water, or fire, or earth, or some body of a brute? By no means. For the human soul does not live in any body other than a human one. Will he perhaps lead his life in some other body of a man not loved? Not even that. For if he does not live in that place where he most vehemently desires to live, in what way will he live in another? Therefore, he who loves another and is not loved by that other lives nowhere. For this reason, the unloved lover is entirely dead. Nor will he ever come back to life unless indignation rouses him. But where the beloved responds in love, there at least the lover leads his life. Here certainly a wonderful thing happens: as often as two people embrace each other with mutual benevolence, this one lives in that one, and that one in this one. Such men exchange themselves in turn, and each gives himself to the other so that they may receive the other. How they give themselves while they forget themselves, I see. But how they receive the other, I do not understand. For he who does not have himself will much less possess another. Nay, rather, each has himself, and has the other. This one indeed has himself, but in that one. That one also possesses himself, but in this one. Indeed, while I love you loving me, I find myself in you thinking of me, and I recover myself—lost by my own negligence—in you preserving me. You do the same in me. Again, this also appears wonderful. For after I have lost myself, if I redeem myself through you, I have myself through you: if I have myself through you, I have you first and more than myself; I am closer to you than to myself. Since indeed I cling to myself not otherwise than through a medium. In this, certainly, the power of Cupid differs from the violence of Mars. Indeed, empire and love differ thus. A commander possesses others through himself, but a lover embraces himself through another; and each of the lovers, farther from himself, becomes closer to the other; and being dead in himself, he comes back to life in the other. There is only one death in mutual love, but a double resurrection. For he who loves dies in himself once when he neglects himself. He comes back to life in the beloved immediately when the beloved embraces him with ardent thought. He comes back to life again when he finally recognizes himself in the beloved and does not doubt that he is loved. O happy death, which two lives follow! O wonderful commerce, by which one hands over himself for another, and neither has nor ceases to have himself! O inestimable gain, when two become one in such a way that each of the two, instead of one alone, becomes two; and as if doubled, he who had one life now has two, with one death intervening. For he who, having died once, comes back to life twice, has obtained a double life for one, and two for himself alone.

A most just vengeance certainly exists in mutual love. A homicide is to be punished with death. For who would deny that the person loved is a homicide when he separates the soul from the lover? Who again would deny that the same person dies similarly when he loves the lover similarly? This restitution is more than due: when this one returns to that one, and that one to this one, the soul which he received. Each, by loving, hands over his own, and by loving back, restores the other's through his own. Therefore, by right itself, whoever is loved ought to love. But he who does not love the lover is to be held guilty of homicide. Nay, rather, a thief, a homicide, a sacrilegious person. Money is possessed by the body, the body by the soul. He, therefore, who has seized the soul, by which both the body and money are possessed, seizes the soul, body, and money at the same time. From which it follows that as a thief, homicide, and sacrilegious person, he is liable to a triple death; and as if thoroughly infamous and profane, he can be killed by anyone with impunity, unless he himself of his own accord fulfills that law—namely, that he should love the lover back. Where, with the one dying once, he himself being about to die similarly once, comes back to life twice as the other comes back to life twice. By the superior reasons, it has been shown that the beloved ought to love the lover in turn; not only that he ought, but that he is compelled, is shown thus: Likeness procreates love. Likeness is a certain nature that is the same in many. For if I am similar to you, you are also necessarily similar to me. Therefore, the same likeness which compels me to love you also forces you to love me. Furthermore, the lover takes himself away from himself and gives himself to the beloved. Therefore, the beloved cares for him as his own thing, for his own gifts are dear to everyone. It is added that the lover carves the figure of the beloved in his own soul. Thus, the soul of the lover becomes a mirror in which the image of the beloved shines back. Therefore, the beloved, when he recognizes himself in the lover, is compelled to love him. Astrologers think the return of love between them is especially strong in whose birth there was an exchange of luminaries—that is, the sun and the moon. For instance, if at my birth the sun was in Aries and the moon in Libra; and at your birth the sun was in Libra and the moon in Aries. Or those for whom the same or a similar sign and the same or a similar planet ascended; or benign planets looked upon the angle of the orient similarly; or Venus was placed in the same house of nativity and in the same degree. The Platonists add: those whose life the same or at least a similar demon leads. But natural and moral philosophers wish the likeness of complexion, nutrition, erudition, custom, and counsel to be the cause of a similar affection. Finally, where more causes concur, there a more vehement reciprocity is found. Where all concur, there the affections of Pythias and Damon, of Pylades and Orestes, arise again.

## WHAT LOVERS SEEK.
## CHAPTER IX.

Furthermore, what do those seek when they love one another mutually? They seek beauty. For love is the desire of enjoying beauty. But beauty is a certain splendor seizing the human soul to itself. Indeed, the beauty of the body is nothing else than the splendor itself in the decorum of colors and lines. The beauty of the soul is also a radiance in the harmony of doctrine and morals. That light of the body, not the ear, not the smell, not the taste, nor the touch, but the eye perceives. If the eye alone recognizes it, the eye alone enjoys it. Therefore, the eye alone enjoys the beauty of the body. Since love is nothing else but the desire of enjoying beauty, and this is comprehended by the eyes alone, the lover of the body is content with sight alone. But the desire of touching is not a part of love, nor the affection of a lover, but a species of petulance and the disturbance of a servile man. Furthermore, we comprehend that light and beauty of the soul with the mind alone. Therefore, he who seeks the beauty of the soul is content with the intuition of the mind alone. Finally, beauty is exchanged between lovers for beauty. A man enjoys the beauty of a younger beloved with his eyes. The youth attains the beauty of the man with his mind; and he who is beautiful in body alone, by this association becomes also beautiful in soul; he who is decorous in soul alone fills the eyes of the body with the beauty of the body. It is clearly a wonderful exchange, honest, useful, and pleasant to both. Honest, indeed, for both; for it is equally honest to learn and to teach. The pleasure is greater in the elder, who is delighted by sight and intelligence. But the utility is greater in the younger; for by as much as the soul is more excellent than the body, by so much is the attainment of the beauty of the soul more precious than that of the body. Thus far Pausanias; now let us interpret the speech of Eryximachus.

# THE THIRD SPEECH.
# LOVE IS IN ALL THINGS, TOWARD ALL THINGS, THE CREATOR OF ALL, THE MASTER OF ALL.

## CHAPTER I.

Three things next seem to us to be treated from the mind of our Eryximachus. First, that love, being inserted in all things, extends through all. Second, that of all works which are according to nature, he is the effector and preserver. Third, that he is the master and lord of individual arts. Truly, three steps of things are considered in nature: Superior, Inferior, and Equal. Those which are above are the causes of the inferior; those which are below are the works of the superior. Those which are equal are endowed with the same nature among themselves. Now, causes love their own works as their parts and images. Works also seek causes as their preservers. Those things, however, which are placed in that order are affected by mutual charity toward each other as members of one and the same family. Therefore, God governs angels, and angels with God together govern souls, and souls with them together govern bodies with a certain benevolence. In this, the affection of the superior toward the inferior is clearly seen. Again, bodies are joined to their souls most greedily and are separated from them most painfully. Our souls desire the beatitude of celestial things; celestial things happily venerate the majesty of the supreme divinity; and this is the affection of love from the inferior toward the superior. Likewise, all parts of fire willingly cling together; the parts of earth, water, and air likewise; and in any species of animals, the animals of the same species always join themselves by mutual custom. Where love toward equals and family is seen. Who then will doubt that love is innate in all things toward all things? And that is what Dionysius the Areopagite in the book *On Divine Names*, from the mind of Hierotheus, indicated with these words: "Whether we speak of divine love, or angelic, or spiritual, or animal, or natural, we understand a certain infinite and mixing virtue, which moves superior things to the providence of inferior things; again, it reconciles equals to a social communion of one another; finally, it admonishes all inferior things to be turned toward better and more sublime things." These are his words.

## LOVE IS THE AUTHOR OF ALL AND THE PRESERVER.
## CHAPTER II.

But that second member of our speech, by which love was called the effector of all and the preserver, is proved thus. The desire of propagating one's own perfection is a certain love. Absolute perfection is in the supreme power of God. Divine intelligence contemplates it, and from there the same will desires to propagate it outside itself; from which love of propagating all things were created by him. Therefore, our Dionysius says: "Divine love did not permit the King of all to remain in himself without offspring." The same instinct of propagation was put into all things by that first author. Through this, those holy spirits move the heavens and grant their gifts to all following things. Through this, the stars diffuse their light into the elements. Through this, fire by the communion of its heat moves air, air moves water, water moves earth; and vice versa, earth draws water to itself, water draws air, and air draws fire. Herbs also and trees, greedy for propagating their own seed, beget their kind. Brute animals also and men are seized by the enticements of the same desire to procreate offspring. But if love makes all things, it also preserves all things. For the office of affection and conservation is always of the same. Truly, similar things are preserved by similar things. But love draws like to like. Individual parts of the earth, with mutual love coupling them, betake themselves to other parts of the earth similar to themselves. The whole earth also descends toward the center of the world, which is similar to it, by the greed of that place. Parts of water likewise are carried to each other and to the place suitable for them with the whole body of water. The parts of air and fire do the same; and even these two elements are drawn toward the supernal region suitable and similar to them by the love of that region. The heaven also, as Plato says in the book *On Kingship*, is moved by innate love. For the soul of heaven is entirely at the same time in any of the points of heaven. Heaven, therefore, greedy for enjoying its soul, runs for the reason that through all its parts it may enjoy the whole soul everywhere. But it flies most rapidly so that, as far as possible, it may be the whole at once everywhere, wherever the whole soul is at once. Furthermore, the concave surface of the larger sphere is equally compatible with any particle of the smaller sphere; any particle desires to touch all particles of the other. If it were at rest, individual parts would touch individual parts, not any part all parts. By running, it almost attains what it could not attain by being at rest. But it runs most swiftly so that any part at almost the same time, according to its strength, touches all parts. Furthermore, all things are preserved by the unity of their parts; they perish by the dispersion of parts. But mutual love of those parts effects the unity of parts. This can be seen in the humors of our bodies and the elements of the world, by whose concord—as Pythagoras and Empedocles say—both the world and our body consist, and by discord they are dissipated. But the reciprocity of peace and love provides concord for them.

Hence Orpheus: "For you alone hold the reins of all these things in the world." <note>original: μοῦνον γὰρ κόσμου πάντων ἡνιοχὰ κρατύνεις</note>

## THAT IT IS THE MASTER OF ARTS AND THE GOVERNOR.
## CHAPTER III.

It remains after these things that we explain in what way it is the master of all arts and the governor. We shall indeed understand it to be the master of arts if only we consider that no one can ever either find or learn any art unless the pleasure of investigation and the desire of finding incites them; and he who teaches loves his disciples, and the disciples most greedily thirst for that doctrine. Furthermore, it is deservedly named the governor. For he who most loves the arts themselves and the persons for whom they are made, diligently executes and exactly completes the works of art. It is added that artisans in individual arts seek and care for nothing else than love. We shall now briefly run through those arts which Eryximachus commemorates in Plato. For what else does medicine consider than how the four humors of the body may become friends to each other and remain so? What foods and drinks, and other uses of living or healing, does nature love and require? Eryximachus also found those two loves here by a certain similitude—the Celestial and the Vulgar—which Pausanias had distinguished above. For a temperate affection of the body has a moderate love and toward moderate and suitable things. An intemperate affection has the contrary and contains itself toward contrary things. The former is indeed to be indulged, the latter never to be obeyed. In gymnastic exercise also, it is to be investigated what habit of body, what modes of exercising, what gestures it loves and requires. In agriculture, what soil, what seeds, what kind of cultivation it demands; or what mode of tilling is loved by individual trees. The same is observed in music: whose artisans investigate which numbers love which numbers, either more or less. If they find the least love between one and two, and one and seven. But between one and three, four, five, six, they find a more vehement love. Between one and eight, the most vehement. If they make high and low voices, diverse by nature, more friendly to each other by certain intervals and modes. From which the composition and sweetness of harmony is born. They also temper slower and swifter motions together so that they become especially friends and exhibit rhythm and harmony. Two kinds of musical melodies are handed down. For there is a certain grave and constant kind; and there is another soft and lascivious kind. The former is useful to those who use it; the latter is noxious, as Plato judges in the books *On the Republic* and *On the Laws*. In the banquet, he placed the Muse Urania over the former, and Polymnia over the latter. Some love the first kind, others the second. Their love is to be obeyed, and those things which they seek are to be provided; the appetite of the others is to be resisted. For the love of the former is celestial; but of the latter, vulgar. There is in the stars and the four elements a certain friendship, which astronomy considers. In these, those two loves are found in a certain way. For there is a moderate love in these when they harmonize most temperately among themselves with mutual strengths. There is also an immoderate love when any one of them loves itself too much and in a certain way deserts the others. From the former comes the pleasant temperateness of the air, the tranquility of water, the fertility of lands, the health of animals; from the latter, the contrary things proceed. Finally, the one faculty of the Priests seems to be occupied chiefly in this: to teach us what offices of men are friendly to God, and by what reason men may become friends to God; what mode of love and charity toward God, toward the country, toward parents, toward others—both living and dead—is to be applied. The same can be conjectured in the other arts, and we may summarily conclude that love in all things toward all things is the author and preserver of all, and exists as the lord and master of universal arts. Deservedly, the divine Orpheus called him "Skilled, twin-natured, holding the keys of all." For how he is of a twin nature, you have heard first from Pausanias, and then from Eryximachus. Also, by what reason he is said by Orpheus to hold the keys of the world, we can sufficiently understand from the superior things: since, as we showed, this desire of propagating one's own perfection, innate in all, explains the latent and implicit fecundity of everyone; while it compels seeds to sprout into a bud, and educes the strengths of each, and conceives offspring, and as if by certain keys, by opening the conceptions, it produces them into the light: for which reason all parts of the world, because they are the works of one artisan, are members of the same machine, similar to each other in being and living. They are bound to each other by a certain mutual charity, so that it can deservedly be said that love is the perpetual knot and the bond of the world and its parts, and its immobile support and the firm foundation of the whole machine.

## NO MEMBER OF THE WORLD HATES ANOTHER MEMBER.
## CHAPTER IV.

But if this is so, no members of this work can be inimical to each other in any way. For fire does not flee water out of hatred for water, but out of love for itself; lest it be extinguished by the cold of the water. Nor does water extinguish fire out of hatred for fire; but it is drawn by a certain appetite of amplifying its own cold to procreate water similar to itself from the body of the fire. For since all natural appetite tends toward good and none toward evil: the purpose of water is not to extinguish fire, which is an evil; but to generate water similar to itself, which is a good. And if it could fulfill this without the death of the fire, it would certainly not consume the fire. The same reason is assigned for the rest of the things which appear contrary and inimical. Furthermore, the lamb does not hate the life and figure of the wolf, but it dreads its own destruction which is brought in by the wolf. Nor does the wolf tear and devour the lamb out of hatred for the lamb, but out of love for itself. Nor does man dread man, but the vices of man; nor do we envy the gifts of the more powerful or sharper out of hatred for them, but out of benevolence for ourselves, fearing lest we succumb to them entirely. Therefore, nothing prevents love from being in all things and penetrating through all. Therefore, let us without doubt fear this so great a god, because he is everywhere, he resides in the innermost parts of all, as a powerful lord whose empire we cannot escape, as a most wise judge from whom our thoughts cannot be hidden: let us venerate him as a father because he is the creator and preserver of all, let us worship him as a tutor and protection: let us follow him as a teacher because he teaches individual arts: by whose authorship we are and live: by whose preservation we remain perpetual: by whose presiding and judgment we are governed: by whose teaching we are instructed and formed for living well and blessedly.

# THE FOURTH SPEECH.
# THE TEXT OF PLATO IS NARRATED CONCERNING THE ANCIENT NATURE OF MEN.

## CHAPTER I.

When these things were said, our companion put an end to his words. Christopher Landino, a man excellent in doctrine, whom we have especially known in our times as an Orphic and Platonic poet, followed him in this manner, about to explain the obscure and implicit opinion of Aristophanes. Although Giovanni Cavalcanti has freed us by his diligence from the long ambiguities of disputations: yet the opinion of Aristophanes, involved in most obscure words, still requires some explanation and light. "Love," says Aristophanes, "is above other gods most greatly beneficial to the human race, the curator and tutor of men, and a physician. It is necessary first to notice what the nature of men once was, and what its passions were. For it was not once such as it is now, but far different. In the beginning, there were three kinds of men: not only the two which are now, male and female, but also a certain third kind was present, composed of both. Furthermore, the species of each man was whole and round, having back and sides in a circle: four hands: and pairs of legs matching the hands. Likewise two faces connected by a smooth neck and similar in every way. The masculine genus was from the sun; the Feminine from the earth. The Moon the promiscuous one. From which they were of an elated mind and robust body, wherefore they tried to fight with the gods and to ascend into heaven. Therefore, Jupiter cut each one in length: and made each from one, after the fashion of those who cut eggs in length with a hair: and again, if they should seem to go insane in their pride against the gods, he threatened that he would divide them again similarly. After the nature of men was thus divided, each desired his own half. Therefore they ran together, and with their arms thrown around each other they embraced each other, desiring to be reduced to their former habit. Therefore they would have failed by hunger and torpor, unless God had imposed a mode on the congress. Hence indeed mutual love was born in men, the reconciliator of the ancient nature, striving to make one out of two, and to heal the nature of men. For each of us is a half of a man as if cut, like the little fishes which are called flatfish and giltheads, two are made from one by being split. But each seeks his own half. Therefore, as often as someone's half occurs to him—of whatever sex he may be greedy for—he is most vehemently excited, he clings with ardent love, nor would he suffer to be separated from that person even for a moment. Therefore, the desire of restoring the whole took the name of love. Which helps us greatly in the present time, while it leads each most friendly person to his former half: and in the future it puts the highest hope in us who piously worship God, that by restoring us to the old figure and healing us, he will make us most blessed."

## THE OPINION OF PLATO IS EXPLAINED CONCERNING THE ANCIENT FIGURE OF MAN.
## CHAPTER II.

These things Aristophanes narrates, and many other things similar to monsters and portents: under which, as if under certain veils, divine things...

->260 On the Banquet<-

is forced to touch its own center at a single, simple, and immobile point. Who denies that God is rightly called the center of all things, since He is within all things—one, deeply internal, simple, and immobile? Truly, all things produced by Him are many, composite, and mobile; and just as they flow from Him, so do they flow back toward Him like lines and circumferences. Thus, the mind, the soul, nature, and matter, proceeding from God, strive to return to the same: they circle around Him from every side as much as they are able. And just as the central point is found everywhere in the lines and in the whole circle, and through its own point each individual line touches the middle point of the circle: so God, the center of all things—who is the simplest unity and the purest act <note>original: "actus purissimus"; a theological term meaning God is fully realized potential and perfect action.</note>—inserts Himself into the universe. This is not only because He is present to all things, but also because He has bestowed upon all things created by Him a certain part, or an intimate, simplest, and most excellent power, which is called the "unity of things." From this unity, and through it, as if from a center, the remaining parts and powers of each thing hang and relate to their own center. It is necessary for created things to collect themselves into this, their very own center—into this personal unity—before they can cling to their Creator, so that through their own center (as we have often repeated) they may cling to the Center of all things. The mind of an angel rises up into its own peak and head before it ascends into God. The soul and the rest do so in the same manner.

And the circle of the visible world is an image of those invisible circles—namely, of the mind, the soul, and nature. For bodies are the shadows and footprints of souls and minds. Truly, a shadow and a footprint reflect the shape of that of which they are a shadow and footprint. For this reason, those four levels are not wrongly called "four circles." But the **Mind** <note>The "Angelic Mind," the first level of creation in Neoplatonic thought.</note> is an immobile circle because its operation, as well as its substance, always remains the same and operates in a like manner: it understands always in the same way and wills similarly. The mind can only be called "mobile" at times because, like all other things, it turns toward the same God from whom it proceeded. The **Soul of the World** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, the force that animates the physical universe.</note> and any other soul is a mobile circle. For the soul, by its nature, knows through "discourse" <note>Moving from one thought to another sequentially rather than knowing all at once.</note> and operates through the courses of time. This "discourse" from one thing to another, and temporal operation, is undoubtedly called motion. If there is indeed any stability in the knowledge of the soul, it consists in the benefit of the mind rather than the soul. **Nature** is also a mobile circuit. When we say "soul," we understand (in the manner of the ancient theologians) the power placed in reason and sense; when we say "nature," we mean the power of the soul situated in generation <note>The power of biological reproduction and growth.</note>. They properly called that first power "Man" within us, and this second power the "image and phantom of man." This faculty of generation is called mobile because it carries out its work over spans of time. However, it differs from that property of the soul in this: the soul is moved by itself and in itself. "By itself," I say, because it is the principle of motion. "In itself," also, because the operation of reason and sense remains within the substance of the soul itself. No work necessarily results in the body from these. Truly, that power of generation which we call "nature" is moved by itself, since it is a certain power of the soul moved by itself. But it is said to be moved "in another" because all its operation ends in the bulk of the body. For it nourishes, increases, and generates the body. **Matter** and the bulk of the body is a circle moved by another and in another. "By another," indeed, because it is necessarily agitated by the soul. "In another," because the motion of the body is agitated within the space of a location. 

Now, therefore, we can clearly understand why the theologians place **Goodness** in the center and **Beauty** in the circle. For the Goodness of all things is God Himself, through whom all things are good. Beauty, however, is a ray of God, inserted into those four circles that revolve in a certain way around God. A ray of this kind fashions all the species of all things in those four circles: we are accustomed to calling those species **Ideas** in the mind, **Reasons** in the soul, **Seeds** in nature, and **Forms** in matter. Therefore, there appear to be four splendors in the four circles. The splendor of Ideas in the first; of Reasons in the second; of Seeds in the third; and of Forms in the last.

->HOW PLATO IS EXPLAINED REGARDING<-
->divine matters.<-
->CHAPTER IV.<-

Plato indicated this mystery in his letter to King Dionysius <note>Plato’s Second Letter, traditionally attributed to him in the Renaissance.</note> when he affirmed God to be the cause of all beautiful things, as if He were the principle and origin of all beauty. "Around the King of all things," he said, "are all things; for His sake are all things; He is the cause of all beautiful things; second things around the second; third things around the third. The human mind strives to understand what sort of things those are, looking into those things which are related to itself, none of which are sufficient. Truly, around the King Himself and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of that sort; but that which is after this, the mind speaks." <note>This is a famous, cryptic passage from Plato's Second Letter (312e) used by Neoplatonists to justify the Trinity or a hierarchy of three principles.</note> When he says "Around the King," he signifies "outside the King," not "inside." For in God there is no composition. What that word "Around" signifies, Plato explains when he adds: "For His sake are all things; He is the cause of all beautiful things." As if he were to say: all things are around the King because all things revolve toward Him as their end according to their nature, just as all things were produced by Him as their principle. "Of all beautiful things," that is, of the whole beauty which shines out in the aforementioned circles. For the forms of bodies are led back to God through seeds; these through reasons; these through ideas; and by these same steps they are produced by God. 

Properly, when he says "All things," he understands the **Ideas**; for in these, the rest are included. "Second things around the second; third things around the third." Zoroaster <note>The legendary Persian prophet, whom Renaissance thinkers believed was an ancient source of Platonic wisdom.</note> posited three princes of the world, lords of the three orders: Oromasin, Mithrin, and Arimanin <note>Ormuzd (the good god), Mithras (the mediator), and Ahriman (the destructive spirit).</note>. These Plato calls God, Mind, and Soul. He placed three orders in the divine species: Ideas, Reasons, and Seeds. Therefore, the first things—that is, the Ideas—are around the first, which is around God, since they were granted to the mind by God, and they lead back that same mind to which they were given. Second things are around the second—that is, Reasons around the Mind—since they pass through the mind into the soul, and they direct the soul into the mind. Third things are around the third—that is, the Seeds of things around the soul—for they pass through the soul into nature (namely, into that power of generation), and they join nature back to the soul. In the same order, Forms descend from nature into matter. But Plato does not count these in the established order because, having been questioned by Dionysius about divine matters, he introduced three orders pertaining to incorporeal species as if they were divine; he omitted the forms of bodies. He did not wish to call God the "first king," but the "king of all," lest if he called Him "first," he might seem to place Him in some species of number or equality of condition with the following leaders. Nor did he say "first things are around Him," but "all things," lest we believe Him to be the governor of only one order rather than of all. 

"The human mind strives to understand what sort of things those are." Wisely, after those three splendors of divine beauty shining in the three circles, he added the love of the mind toward them. For from that source the ardor of the mind is kindled. Indeed, it often happens that the divine desires divine things: "looking into those things which are related to itself." Since human knowledge arises from the senses, we are often accustomed to judge divine things through those things which we see to be more excellent in bodies: we investigate God's power through the forces of corporeal things; His wisdom through their order; and God's goodness through their utility. He calls the forms of bodies "related to the soul," as if they were "born next" to it. For in the following step after the soul, the forms of bodies are arranged. "None of which are sufficient." Forms of this kind are neither sufficiently real, nor do they sufficiently show us divine things. For the true things are Ideas, Reasons, and Seeds. Truly, the forms of bodies seem to be shadows of things rather than true things. Just as the shadow of a body does not indicate the exact and distinct figure of the body, so bodies do not demonstrate the proper nature of divine things. "Around the King Himself and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of that sort." For in what way are mortals similar to immortals, and false things to true things? "But that which is after this, the mind speaks"—that is, while the mind judges divine things through mortal things, it speaks falsely about the divine; it does not pronounce divine things, but mortal ones.

->DIVINE BEAUTY<-
->shines through all things, and is<-
->loved in all things.<-
->CHAPTER V.<-

Furthermore, to compress much into a few words: the Good is said to be the super-eminent existence of God Himself. **Beauty** is a certain act or ray penetrating from there through all things: first into the Angelic Mind; second into the Soul of the universe and the rest of the souls; third into Nature; fourth into the Matter of bodies. It graces the Mind with the order of Ideas; it fills the Soul with the series of Reasons; it supports Nature with Seeds; it adorns Matter with Forms. Just as a single ray of the sun illuminates four bodies—fire, air, water, and earth—so a single ray of God illuminates the Mind, the Soul, Nature, and Matter. And whoever looks at the light in these four elements sees a ray of the sun itself, and through that ray is turned toward perceiving the supernal light of the sun. So, whoever contemplates and loves the decorum in these four—Mind, Soul, Nature, and Body—is contemplating and loving the glow of God in them, and through a glow of this kind, he perceives and loves God Himself.

->THE PASSIONS OF LOVERS.<-
->CHAPTER VI.<-

From this it follows that the impulse of love is not extinguished by the sight or touch of any body. For love does not desire this or that body; but it admires, affects, and is stunned by the splendor of the supernal light shining through bodies. For this reason, lovers do not know what they desire or seek. For they do not know God Himself, whose hidden flavor [produces] a certain sweetest scent of Himself in His works...

...inserted into his works. We are daily aroused by this very heat. We indeed sense the scent, but we remain undoubtedly ignorant of the taste. Since we are enticed by the manifest scent and yet secretly desire the taste, we rightly do not know what we want or what we are suffering. This is also why it always happens that lovers somehow fear and revere the sight of the beloved. Indeed, I will say—though I fear some of you may blush to hear this—that even the strongest and wisest men are accustomed to suffering this in the presence of any beloved, even an inferior one. Truly, it is not something human that terrifies them, breaks them, and seizes them. For human strength is always more excellent in the stronger and wiser. Rather, it is that flash of divinity shining out in beautiful people, like an **image of God**, which compels lovers to be struck dumb, to tremble, and to show reverence. For the same reason, the lover despises riches and honors because of the presence of the beloved and considers them as nothing. For it is right that divine things be preferred to human ones.

It also frequently happens that everyone desires to transfer themselves into the person of the beloved. And not without cause. For God desires and strives to become man for the sake of man. Who, then, would not trade being a man for being a God? Furthermore, those ensnared by love sigh and rejoice in turn. They sigh because they lose themselves, because they perish, and because they are destroyed. They rejoice because they transfer themselves into something better. They are also hot and cold by turns, like those whom a **tertian fever** <note>A fever that returns every third day; here used as a medical metaphor for the erratic, fluctuating emotions of a lover.</note> invades. They are rightly cold because they are deserted by their own heat, and yet they are hot as they are set on fire by the flashes of heavenly rays. Timidity follows the coldness; audacity follows the heat. Therefore, they appear both timid and audacious by turns. Moreover, even the dullest people are rendered sharper by loving. For who, when a heavenly ray breathes upon them, would not see most sharply? Truly, let these things suffice concerning love itself, beauty, its origin, and the emotions of lovers.

### ON THE TWO KINDS OF LOVE,
### and on the dual Venus.
### CHAPTER VII.

Next, we must briefly discuss the two kinds of Love. Pausanias, in Plato's work, asserts that Cupid is the companion of Venus. He considers it necessary that there be as many Cupids as there are Venuses. He mentions two Venuses, who are likewise accompanied by twin Cupids. He places one Venus as **Celestial**, and the other as **Vulgar**. The Celestial one was born from Heaven <note>Uranus</note> without a mother; the Vulgar one was born from Jupiter and Dione. 

The Platonists call the Supreme God "Heaven" because, just as this sublime heavenly body rules and contains all bodies, so that Supreme God surpasses all spirits. They call the **Mind** <note>The "Angelic Mind," the first level of creation below God in Neoplatonic thought.</note> by many names. For they call it sometimes Saturn, sometimes Jupiter, sometimes Venus. For that Mind exists, lives, and understands. They are accustomed to call its Essence "Saturn," its Life "Jupiter," and its Intelligence "Venus." Furthermore, we call the **Soul of the World** <note>The life force that animates the physical universe.</note> similarly Saturn, Jupiter, and Venus: Saturn insofar as it understands heavenly things; Jupiter insofar as it moves the celestial bodies; and Venus insofar as it generates lower things. 

The first Venus, which is in the Mind, is said to be born of Heaven without a mother, since among **natural philosophers** <note>original: "Physicos"; meaning those who study the nature of the physical world.</note> "mother" refers to matter. But that Mind is foreign to any association with corporeal matter. The second Venus, which is placed in the Soul of the World, is born of Jupiter and Dione. From Jupiter—that is, from that power of the soul which moves the heavens. For that power created the potential which generates these lower things. They attribute a mother to her because, being infused into the matter of the world, she is thought to have commerce with matter. 

To put it briefly, Venus is twofold. One is surely that intelligence which we placed in the Angelic Mind. The other is the power of generation attributed to the Soul of the World. Each has a companion love similar to itself. For the former is drawn by its innate love to understand the beauty of God. The latter is drawn by its own love to procreate that same beauty in bodies. The former first embraces the flash of divinity within itself and then translates it to the second Venus. The latter pours the sparks of that flash into the matter of the world. Because of the presence of such sparks, the individual bodies of the world appear beautiful, according to the capacity of their nature. 

The human soul perceives the appearance of these bodies through the eyes. The soul also possesses twin powers. Indeed, it has the power of understanding and it has the power of generating. These twin powers are the two Venuses within us, which are accompanied by twin loves. When the appearance of a human body is first offered to our eyes, our mind—which is the first Venus in us—venerates and loves it as an image of divine beauty; through this, it is often incited toward that higher beauty. But the power of generation—the second Venus—desires to generate a form similar to it. Therefore, there is love in both cases: in the former, a desire to contemplate beauty; in the latter, a desire to generate it. Both loves are honorable and to be praised, for each follows a divine image. What, then, does Pausanias disapprove of in love? I will tell you. If someone, being too greedy for generation, deserts contemplation, or pursues generation beyond measure with women, or against the order of nature with males, or prefers the form of the body to the beauty of the soul, he certainly abuses the dignity of love. Pausanias censures this abuse of love. He who uses love rightly praises the form of the body, but through it, he contemplates a more excellent species of the soul, the mind, and God, and he admires and loves it more vehemently. Moreover, he uses the office of generation and intercourse only so far as the natural order and the civil laws established by the prudent prescribe. Pausanias speaks of these things more at length.

### EXHORTATION TO LOVE,
### On simple love, and on mutual love.
### CHAPTER VIII.

I exhort and beseech you, friends, to embrace love—which is truly a divine thing—with all your strength. And let it not deter you that they say Plato once spoke of a certain lover: "That lover," he said, "is a soul dead in its own body, living in another's body." Nor let it disturb you that Orpheus sang of the bitter and wretched lot of lovers. For how these things are to be understood, and by what way they are to be helped, I ask you to then attend to diligently, if you please. 

Plato calls love "bitter," and not without justice, because whoever loves dies. Orpheus also calls this **bittersweet** <note>original: "γλυκύπικρον" (glykypikron)</note>, since love is a voluntary death. Insofar as it is a death, it is a bitter thing. Insofar as it is voluntary, it is sweet. But whoever loves, dies. For his thought, forgetful of itself, always dwells in the beloved. If he does not think of himself, he certainly does not think in himself. Therefore, the soul so affected does not act within itself, since the primary operation of the soul is thought itself. He who does not act in himself, is not in himself. For these two things—being and operation—are equal to each other; there is no being without operation, nor does operation exceed being itself. No one acts where he is not, and wherever he is, he acts. Therefore, the soul of the lover is not in itself, because it does not act in itself. If it is not in itself, it does not live in itself; and he who does not live is dead. Therefore, whoever loves is dead in himself. 

Does he at least live in another? Certainly. There are two species of love: one is **simple love**, the other is **mutual**. Simple love is where the beloved does not love the lover back. There, the lover is entirely dead; for he neither lives in himself (as we have already sufficiently shown) nor does he live in the beloved, since he is rejected by them. Where, then, does he live? In the air, or water, or fire, or earth, or some body of a beast? Not at all. For the human soul lives in no body other than a human one. Or perhaps it will lead its life in some other body of a person not loved? Not that either. For if it does not live where it most vehemently desires to live, how could it live in another? Therefore, he who loves someone without being loved back lives nowhere. Thus, the unloved lover is entirely dead. Nor will he ever come back to life unless indignation rouses him. 

But where the beloved responds in love, the lover at least leads his life in them. Here, surely, a wondrous thing happens: as often as two people embrace each other with mutual goodwill, this one lives in that one, and that one lives in this one. Such people exchange themselves in turn, and each gives himself to the other so that they may receive the other. I see how they give themselves when they forget themselves. But how they receive the other, I do not understand. For he who does not have himself will much less possess another. 

Indeed, however, each has himself, and each has the other. This one has himself, but in that one. That one also possesses himself, but in this one. Truly, while I love you who love me, I find myself in you thinking of me, and I recover myself—lost by my own negligence—in you who preserve me. You do the same in me. Again, this also appears wondrous. For after I have lost myself, if I redeem myself through you, I have myself through you; if I have myself through you, I have you first and more than myself; I am closer to you than to myself. Indeed, I am joined to myself in no other way than through you as the medium. In this, certainly, the power of Cupid differs from the violence of Mars. For power and love differ in this way: a ruler possesses others through himself, but a lover embraces himself through another. And each lover, being further from himself, becomes closer to the other; and being dead in himself, he comes back to life in the other. 

In mutual love, there is only one death, but a twofold resurrection. For he who loves dies once in himself when he neglects himself. He comes back to life in the beloved immediately when the beloved embraces him with ardent thought. He comes back to life a second time when he finally recognizes himself in the beloved and does not doubt that he is loved. O happy death, which two lives follow! O wondrous exchange, by which someone gives himself for another, and yet neither lacks the other, nor ceases to have himself! O inestimable gain, when two become one in such a way that each of the two becomes two instead of only one; and as if doubled, he who had one life now has two, with one death intervening. For he who has died once and comes back to life twice has obtained a twin life for one, and two selves for one.
