<meta>This page continues the discussion of the psychological and spiritual mechanics of attraction, moving from the physical sensation of "divine flashes" in the beloved to the legal and cosmic obligations of mutual love. It transitions from the Second Speech (Pausanias) to the Third Speech (Eryximachus).</meta>

->262 On the Banquet<-

Vengeance in mutual love is certainly most just. A murderer should be punished with death. For who would deny that someone who is loved is a murderer if they separate the soul from the lover? Who, again, would deny that the same person dies in a similar way when they love their lover in return? This is a restitution that is more than owed: when one person returns to the other—and the other back to them—the soul they received. Each, by loving, gives away their own soul, and by loving in return, restores the other’s soul through their own. Therefore, by right itself, whoever is loved ought to love back. Truly, anyone who does not love their lover must be held guilty of homicide. Nay, more: they are a thief, a murderer, and a practitioner of sacrilege. Money is possessed by the body, and the body by the soul. Therefore, whoever seizes the soul—from which both the body and money are possessed—seizes the soul, body, and money all at once. Thus, like a thief, murderer, and committer of sacrilege, they are liable to a triple death. As someone utterly infamous and profane, they could be killed with impunity by anyone—unless they spontaneously fulfill that law themselves, namely, by returning love to the lover. Where once the lover dies, the beloved is about to die in the same way; yet as the lover twice revives, the beloved likewise twice returns to life.

By the previous arguments, it has been shown that the beloved ought to love the lover in return. Now it is shown that they are not only "ought" to, but are compelled to. Similarity creates love. Similarity is a certain identical nature shared among several things. For if I am similar to you, you are also necessarily similar to me. Therefore, the same similarity that compels me to love you also forces you to love me. Furthermore, a lover takes themselves away from themselves and gives themselves to the beloved. The beloved, therefore, cares for this person as if they were their own property, for each person’s own gifts <term>charisma: here meaning personal graces or gifts</term> are dear to them. Added to this is the fact that the lover carves the image of the beloved into their own soul. Thus, the lover's soul becomes a mirror in which the image of the beloved shines back. Because of this, when the beloved recognizes themselves in the lover, they are compelled to love them.

Astrologers believe that the reciprocity of love between people is especially strong when there is an exchange of "the lights" (that is, the Sun and the Moon) in their birth charts <term>genesi: a horoscope or nativity chart</term>. For example, if at my birth the Sun was in Aries and the Moon was in Libra, and at your birth the Sun was in Libra and the Moon was in Aries. Or for those whom the same or a similar sign, and the same or a similar planet, was rising; or if the benevolent planets looked upon the "corner of the east" <note>The Ascendant or Eastern Horizon</note> in a similar way, or if Venus was positioned in the same house of birth and at the same degree. The Platonists add that this happens to those whose lives are led by the same, or certainly a similar, spirit <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or tutelary deity</term>. Physicians and moral philosophers, however, maintain that similarity of physical temperament, upbringing, education, habit, and counsel is the cause of similar affection. Finally, where more causes concur, there a more vehement reciprocity is found. Where all these causes meet, there the legendary affections of Damon and Pythias, or Pylades and Orestes, are reborn.

### WHAT LOVERS SEEK
### CHAPTER IX

But what do these people seek when they love each other? They seek beauty. For love is the desire to enjoy beauty. Beauty, moreover, is a certain splendor that ravishes the human soul toward itself. Clearly, the beauty of the body is nothing other than that very splendor found in the grace of colors and lines. The beauty of the soul, likewise, is a brilliance found in the harmony of learning and character. The eye perceives that light of the body—not the ear, nor smell, nor taste, nor touch. If the eye alone recognizes it, the eye alone enjoys it. Therefore, the eye alone enjoys the beauty of the body. Since love is nothing else but the desire to enjoy beauty, and beauty is grasped by the eyes alone, the lover of the body is content with sight alone. The desire for touching is not a part of love, nor an affection of the lover, but a form of lewdness and the disturbance of a slavish man. Furthermore, we grasp that light and beauty of the soul with the mind alone. Therefore, he who seeks the beauty of the soul is content with the mind's intuition alone. Finally, among lovers, beauty is exchanged for beauty. A man enjoys the beauty of a younger beloved with his eyes; the youth attains the beauty of the man with his mind. He who is beautiful only in body becomes, through this association, beautiful also in soul; he who is handsome only in soul fills the eyes of the body with physical beauty. It is a truly miraculous exchange—honorable, useful, and pleasant to both. It is honorable because it is equal for both; for it is equally honorable to learn and to teach. The pleasure is greater in the older man, who is delighted by sight and intelligence. In the youth, the utility is greater; for as much as the soul is more excellent than the body, so the attainment of the beauty of the soul is more precious than that of the body. So much for the speech of Pausanias; now let us interpret the speech of Eryximachus.

# THE THIRD SPEECH
## LOVE IN ALL THINGS, TOWARD ALL THINGS,
## the creator of all, the master of all.
### CHAPTER I

Three things next seem to us to be treated according to the mind of our Eryximachus. First, that love is implanted in all things and extends through the whole universe. Second, that love is the maker and preserver of all works that exist according to nature. Third, that love is the master and lord of the individual arts. 

Indeed, three levels of things are considered in nature: Higher, Lower, and Equal. Those things which are above are the causes of the lower; those below are the works of the higher. Those which are equal are endowed with the same nature among themselves. Now, causes love their own works as if they were parts and images of themselves. Works, furthermore, seek their causes as their own preservers. Those things placed in the same rank are moved by mutual charity toward one another, like members of one and the same family. Thus God governs the angels, and the angels along with God govern souls, and souls along with them govern bodies with a certain benevolence. In this, the love of higher things for lower things is clearly seen. Conversely, bodies are joined most eagerly to their souls, and are separated from them most painfully. Our souls desire the blessedness of the heavenly beings; the heavenly beings happily worship the majesty of the supreme divinity—and this is the affection of love from lower things toward the higher. Likewise, all parts of fire willingly cling together; the parts of earth, water, and air do the same; and in any species of animal, the animals of that same species always join themselves together in mutual association. Here, love is seen toward equals and kin. 

Who then will doubt that love is innate in all things toward all things? And this is what Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Pseudo-Dionysius, a highly influential 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist</note> signified in his book *On Divine Names*, following the mind of Hierotheus, with these words: "Whether we speak of love as divine, angelic, spiritual, animal, or natural, we understand a certain unifying and mixing power: which moves the higher to provide for the lower; coordinates equals in social communion with each other; and finally warns all lower things to turn back toward the better and more sublime." These are his words.

### LOVE IS THE AUTHOR
### and preserver of all.
### CHAPTER II

Regarding the second part of our speech—in which love is called the maker and preserver of all—it is proved thus: The desire to propagate one's own perfection is a kind of love. Absolute perfection exists in the supreme power of God. The Divine Intelligence contemplates this, and from there the same Will desires to propagate it outside itself. From this love of propagating, all things were created by Him. Therefore, our Dionysius says, "Divine love did not permit the King of all to remain within Himself without offspring." <note>original: "regem omnium sine germine in seipso manere"</note> The same instinct for propagation was bestowed upon all things by that first Author. Through this love, those holy spirits move the heavens and bestow their gifts upon all that follow. Through this, the stars pour their light into the elements. Through this, fire moves the air by the communication of its heat, the air moves the water, and the water the earth; and conversely, the earth draws the water to itself, the water the air, and the air the fire. Plants and trees, also, desirous of propagating their own seed, give birth to their offspring. Even brute animals and humans are seized by the allurements of this same desire to procreate offspring. 

If love makes all things, it also preserves all things. For the office of creation and preservation always belongs to the same affection. Clearly, likes are preserved by likes. Love, however, draws like to like. The individual parts of the earth, coupled by mutual love, betake themselves to other parts of the earth like themselves. The entire earth also descends toward the center of the world, which is similar to it, out of a greed for that place. The parts of water are likewise carried toward each other and toward a place suitable for them along with the whole body of water. The parts of air and fire do the same; even these two elements are drawn toward the higher region that is congruent and similar to them, out of love for that region. Even the Heavens, as Plato says in his book *The Statesman* <note>original: "De regno"</note>, are moved by innate love. For the Soul of the Heavens is present in its entirety at every point of the heavens. The Heavens, therefore, desirous of enjoying that Soul, run their course so that they may enjoy the whole Soul through every one of their parts. They fly most rapidly so that, as far as possible, they might be everywhere at once, since the whole Soul is everywhere at once. 

Furthermore, all things are preserved by the unity of their parts, and they perish by the dispersion of their parts. Mutual love produces this unity of parts. This can be seen in the humors <term>humoribus: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile—that determine health</term> of our bodies and the elements of the world. As Empedocles and Pythagoras say, both the world and our bodies consist of harmony, and are dissipated by discord. Reciprocity of peace and love provides them with this harmony.

Hence...

# Arguments
[[notes: This is part of the introductory material (argumenta) written by Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Florentine translator, to accompany Plato’s Letters.]]

...he transmits [knowledge] only by means of a pact and a law: a legitimate pact, I say, established by rites duly performed and confirmed by an oath, with God himself called to witness and implored as the author and preserver of this union. I say he calls to witness and implores Him by the odd number, in which God is said to take pleasure. For here he introduces the three supreme principles of things, which he also touched upon in the first letter. For where he speaks of "the leader of all things present and future," he wishes the *anima mundi* (world-soul) to be understood, which, as the principle of motion, leads all things by temporal reason from the future into the present, and from the present into the past. But where he speaks of "the father and lord," he signifies the supreme God and the *ipsum bonum* (the Good itself). Yet he seems to insert a certain divine *mens* (mind) between these two when he repeats the term "leader" and joins to it "cause." For in the works of Plato, "king" often signifies the Good itself, "cause" signifies the mind, and "leader" signifies the soul. 

And since he refers "cause" to the mind, the Platonists in the *Timaeus* argue that the Intellect emerged as the son of the Good itself and the immediate architect of the world. Concerning this, it is written in the *Epinomis*: "The most divine Reason, or the most divine Word (*verbum*), adorned the visible world." Moreover, he calls the Good itself both "father" and "lord": so that by the first term he might designate the father of the mind, and by the second, the lord of the soul. Perhaps this is how the Platonic Number [[notes: cf. *Republic* VIII, 546b-d]] explains it. So too does the Christian Platonist, though of the Arian persuasion [[notes: Arius was a 4th-century priest who taught that the Son was subordinate to the Father; Ficino notes that this hierarchical Neoplatonic reading was sometimes used to support Arianism]]. 

Someone else might understand the "leader" as the Holy Spirit and the "mind" as the Son. For wherever Plato speaks of the "father," he likewise implies the "son." But if anyone should posit a single essence, it will seem to oppose many Platonists, yet it will not manifest any repugnance to Plato himself. Furthermore, he exhorts us toward more graceful studies of doctrine and toward certain more pleasant disciplines related to these—namely, eloquence, poetry, and music. He commands us to apply ourselves to all of these with the intention that, by investigating the "divine scent" through these traces, we may love Him alone, and through loving, attain a further taste of Him. 

He says, therefore: "if you truly wish us to philosophize life," that is, either to investigate by loving or to love by investigating. Finally, we shall all undoubtedly know Him. Indeed, the name of "philosophy" seems to imply a certain inquiry, yet "love" properly implies an amorous inquiry. Therefore Pythagoras knew, and Plato knew, that we relate to finite goods in one way, and to the infinite Good in another: finite goods are known by us before they are loved, and they must be loved so that they may be known; but the infinite must be loved before it is known, and it is investigated not so much so that it may be known, but so that it may be loved. 

But why must it be loved before it is understood? Clearly because love transfers the lover into the beloved; what was lacking in proportion, the transforming affection supplies. Is not God often called "fire" in the sacred scriptures? [[notes: cf. Hebrews 12:29]] By the same metaphorical license, an angel might be called a "diaphanous (transparent) body," while the soul is called an "opaque body" as long as it is enclosed in this blind prison. Thus, just as a transparent body—such as air or water—suddenly admits light both outside and inside when under a fire, while earthly bodies must first be heated intensely and thinned by heat into a diaphanous likeness before they can receive fiery light: so spirits separated from the body suddenly capture the divine light. However, spirits bound to earthly bodies require the transforming fire of love; once purified by this and translated into a divine likeness, they are at last divinely illuminated by the splendor of knowledge. 

Hence Porphyrius (the Neoplatonist) says: "The inquiry into divine things purifies the soul, but love deifies it." For he expresses the matter here with the proper word, and not without justice; for fire is not made from any material because it receives light, but because it receives fiery heat. It is therefore the Platonic opinion that divine things are to be investigated—that is, that they exist and what kind they are—by a certain common perception. But meanwhile, they must be loved with a charity that is not common, but singular and incomparable. For only in this way can we somewhere clearly understand what will happen and be blessed. How much these things harmonize with sacred letters, no one but the profane is ignorant of.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE SE-
#### venth letter.

**Plato's seventh** letter was written to the relatives and friends of Dion (the Syracusan statesman), after their fatherland had been liberated by Dion, and after Dion had been unjustly slain. However, so that the many things pertaining to history in this letter and others may be clearly understood, we must repeat things from a bit further back. Plato traveled to Syracuse three times. Once during the time of Dionysius the Elder (the tyrant), when he was forty years old. Twice afterward, when Dionysius the Younger held the tyranny. What he did in each journey, or for what cause he went, appears partly in the *Life of Plato* written by us, and partly in these letters. 

Dion seems to have been from the same family as Dionysius, and was further entangled with him by various affinities. For the elder Dionysius had Dion's sister, Aristomache, in marriage. Dion himself had Dionysius's daughter, named Arete, as his wife. Dionysius the Younger, however, was born not from Dion's sister, but from another wife named Doris. On the first journey, Dion became a student of Plato, converted his life to virtue, and began to desire the public good of his country. Therefore, when Dionysius the Elder died and the Younger Dionysius succeeded to the tyranny—being still a boy and governed almost entirely by Dion's counsel—Dion, wishing to turn him toward a desire for the philosophical life, called Plato to Syracuse with many prayers and induced Dionysius to summon him. 

Plato obeyed, led primarily by the hope that through his counsels he might transform the state from a tyranny into a republic or a kingdom. But about a month after Plato's arrival, Dionysius, led by false slanders, expelled Dion as if he were an invader of the tyranny. Nevertheless, he continued to embrace Plato. But Plato, indignant that the business was unfinished, returned to his fatherland. He went a third time to reconcile Dion to Dionysius, having been implored again and again by both, and also requested by Archytas and Archidemus the Pythagoreans, and many other nobles. Then Dionysius promised both the recall of Dion and that he would maintain the best form of government. But he performed none of the things he had promised. 

When Plato openly rebuked Dionysius for breaking his word—both concerning the recall of Dion and concerning his promise to Theodotus about saving Heraclides—Dionysius then became hostile to him. Thus, Plato lived in the greatest danger of being killed by the soldiers. But Archytas of Tarentum sent the orator Salmicius to Dionysius with a ship, asking that he release Plato. He released him and provided provisions. Plato returned safely to his fatherland. Shortly after, Dion secretly gathered forces, marched to Syracuse, and expelled Dionysius, restoring liberty to the Syracusans. But shortly after, he was killed through the deceit and envy of his own people. 

After this, Hipparinus (Dion's son) and Hipparinus (Dionysius's brother and Dion's nephew by his sister), holding Syracuse, were deliberating on a better form of government by the counsel of the nobles. Meanwhile, Dionysius was attempting to return to power with his allies. Plato, therefore, writes to them, exhorting and instructing them toward the best form of government—that is, a kingdom subject to laws and supported by the authority of the nobles. Various precepts of this kind are gathered from this letter. 

It is not alien to a good nature to desire the helm of the republic, especially when necessity demands it; but it is alien to a good citizen to desire to obtain this with total license. It is not the part of a prudent man to involve himself rashly in public affairs, especially where he is subjected to danger without hope of public safety. Only philosophy can discern what is good and just, and what is not, in both public and private matters. The human race will not cease to be involved in evils until either philosophers rule, or those who rule, by God's illumination, philosophize. A delicate and luxurious education depraves even divine natures. No intemperate person can be prudent. A city in which the citizens are incontinent cannot be contained by any power of laws, because it suffers frequent changes, and always for the worse. Violence must be inflicted neither upon the fatherland nor upon parents, but both must be consulted far from violence. 

The authority of the ancients is to be preferred to the speeches of the sophisticated. To a good man, nothing evil can happen. The soul, separated from this body, pays the penalties for its crimes under the sentence of divine judgment. It is better to suffer the most heavy injuries than to inflict them. The greedy and the intemperate are blind and deaf to divine things, so that they neither see for themselves, nor can they bear to hear from others, nor perceive what they have heard. Impiety is mixed with all sins, and vice versa. Impiety itself, mixed with sins, is the stimulus by which sinners are especially troubled in this life and tortured in the next. 

After this, where he writes about his association with Dionysius and about the study of philosophy, he proves that no one will progress in philosophy unless, ignited by the love of wisdom, they sustain all labors and despise all pleasures for its sake. Then, since it is the part of a wise man to contemplate divine things, he opportunely shows that divine things can never be expressed to the common people in writing or words—indeed, they ought not to be. They cannot be, because those things which are greater are entirely grasped only by the mind. They ought not to be, because those who are the lowest of the people would laugh at them like old wives' tales; and those who are slightly higher among the people, having heard these things, would either fall into false heresy or, on account of a light opinion of higher things, would become vain and contentious beyond measure. 

Plato does not say that nothing true or certain can ever be understood about divine things; rather, he says that what is understood about them cannot be expressed, and that their proper truth cannot be understood by the same reasoning as other things. Some forms are entirely joined to bodies, while others are completely separate. The former are called "natural," the latter "divine." There are also middle forms, joined in one way and separable in another—that is, rational souls, which are intermediate between divine and natural things. Insofar as they are joined to bodies, they are necessarily disjoined from divine things. For they cannot be joined to forms separated from matter except by separation. They are separated from matter in two primary ways: by moral purification and by contemplative resolution.

# On the Letters of Plato. 627
[[margin: Philosophy]]
The study of philosophy does both. Just as one who dries wet wood first by the sun and then moves it toward the fire provides the occasion for the wood to be ignited—yet it is not he, but the fire that ignites the wood—so the study of philosophy, through moral discipline and purification, prepares the soul for divine things. Then, by contemplative resolution, it moves the mind toward divine things and joins them. Yet philosophy itself does not form the mind with divine truth; rather, God himself, like a fire, illuminates with his own light the mind that has been prepared by the benefit of philosophy and is drawing near. 

Therefore, when Plato said that our inquiry into perceiving divine things does not of itself prepare and form the intellect—even though in perceiving divine things, the most purified and eminent inquiry prepares it, but does not form it—he said that for this reason there is need for long association with divine things, signifying the constancy of speculation; and likewise a "joining of life" or "communion," signifying purification perfected by moral discipline. He adds that, finally, in a mind so affected, the light of truth is ignited—not gradually by a certain human love, but suddenly. 

But from where? From the fire—that is, from God, leaping forth or sparkling. By "sparks," he designates the Ideas, the archetypes of things in the divine mind. He also designates the "formulas" of the Ideas innate in us. These, having been once lulled to sleep by sloth, are excited by the fanning of doctrine, and like rays from the eyes, they are illuminated by the Ideas as if by the rays of stars. He adds that such light is not only ignited but "produced in the soul," to show that souls were originally formed with these innate sparks and that such splendor becomes familiar to them. 

Lest the mind in that state be anxious and doubtful, he added: "It now nourishes itself." That is, this light, first ignited divinely in the mind, thereafter draws a bounty of divine rays by its own virtue and fills the mind with nourishing joy. Here the soul nourishes itself—that is, seeking nothing from without, it lives content with itself. And however blessedly it is affected within, even if it wished to, it cannot and does not know how to express it. 

Plato meditates on five degrees in this contemplation, which you may read more diligently explained by us in our *Theology*. [[notes: Ficino’s *Platonic Theology* (1482)]]. For he commands the one who is greedy for truth to proceed from the name of the thing (heard by the ear), then through sight and other senses from the accidents of the thing to its definition; through this to the formula innate in the mind; and finally through the formula to the Idea, which is the creator of both the formulas and the things themselves. 

He teaches, meanwhile, that the Idea differs far from the rest in four primary ways: because the Idea is a substance, simple, immobile, and not mixed with its contrary. The other four—namely, the name, the accidental image (*simulacrum*), the definition, and the formula/notion—degenerate from the substance, simplicity, stability, and purity of the Idea. Therefore, they do not sufficiently imprint the Idea upon us, but they accommodate us, as far as they can, to the divine impression. Finally, the mind divinely imprinted, if ever it should strive to express the characters of the Ideas in words and letters, will produce deformed images of the most beautiful things. But if it believes the Pythagoreans, it will not strive so much to depict the Ideas as to cultivate the souls of the listeners, polishing them like tablets upon which divine forms may at last be painted by the divine finger. Indeed, the soul, looking up at the celestial rays, will not attempt to describe the forms of the rays in vain to the blind; if they are incurable, it will dismiss them. If they are curable, it will only attempt to purify their sight and raise it upward, understanding that otherwise it would labor in vain.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE
#### eighth letter.

**IN** the previous letter, while instructing the Syracusan princes, he was concerned with the precepts already given and the deeds performed by himself and Dion. In this one, however, he encompasses his own specific institutions in shorter terms, always maintaining a middle course between vanity and popular government, but above all studying how citizens may be reconciled rather than expelled, and how the state of the republic may be stabilized as much as possible without injury to others. 

Immediately at the beginning, he asserts that men polluted by impious crime are incurable, and no counsel will profit them. Likewise, in all things, both in speaking and thinking, one must begin with God. Throughout the whole letter, you will observe how cautious and yet merciful a governor Plato is, and how diligent a reconciler of souls. He approves, as is his custom, a government similar to the Lacedaemonian (Spartan). In this, there should be much of the aristocracy, some royal form, and something of the people as well. He condemns extreme servitude, through which all things are subjected to human lust. He also disapproves of extreme liberty or license, in which almost anyone without selection takes the helm of the republic. But he approves the middle. Note the golden saying: "Moderate servitude is that by which one serves God; immoderate is that by which one serves men." To temperate men, the law is God; to the intemperate, it is lust.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE
#### ninth letter.

**IN** the letter to Archytas the philosopher, who was very occupied with public affairs, he gives counsel on contemplation, lest he should desert an action that is both honorable and necessary. For to benefit men both publicly and privately, he calls an action honorable and necessary. Honorable, because just as any member of the body is not for itself alone but for others too—especially for the whole—so men are for one another, and most of all for the species. Necessary, because unless you live for others, you cannot live for yourself; and unless you succor your family and fatherland, family and public affairs, destitute of governors, will either totter or, governed by worse men, will be endangered and finally shipwrecked.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE
#### tenth letter.

**Plato confirms** Aristodemus, a friend of Dion, who was philosophizing primarily through the elegance of his character, in his opinion and life. He asserts that the substance of philosophy is moral virtue—which the name itself declares—by a certain love and cultivation of its definition. He says that human speculations are either certain extrinsic ornaments of philosophy or ways to prepare that firm purity of mind which pertains to character. Once this is prepared, contemplation follows—divine rather than human, and infused from above rather than acquired. Compared to this, that prior speculation is called "a kind of play" by Plato. This is the greatest precept of Pythagoras and Socrates. 

Where we translate "ornaments," the Greek word signifies an ornament mixed with a certain subtle vanity and pride. As if to say, "Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up." [[notes: 1 Corinthians 8:1]]. Likewise, "Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul." [[notes: Wisdom of Solomon 1:4]]. He places sincerity or health in a simple and tranquil soul; faith in words; and finally, firmness in gestures and actions.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE
#### eleventh letter.

**To the prince** Laodamas, who was consulting him on the best government, he gives that accustomed counsel of his: that all laws will be vain unless, in addition, men of the highest character—through whom the laws live—hold great power in the republic; and unless there is established in the city a certain magistrate with the greatest authority, who, as a censor of character, observes the actions of individuals through spies, always intent on the goal that the daily life of citizens may lead their souls toward fortitude and temperance.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE
#### twelfth letter.

**The twelfth letter** is proof to us of how liberal and simple Plato was, seeing that he entrusted certain of his more secret commentaries, not yet finished, to Archytas. It is also proof that Archytas, philosophizing no less by character than by words, was worthy of having the most precious things entrusted to him. Perhaps these commentaries pertained to the completion of the unfinished *Critias* or to the writing of the *Hermocrates*, which was not yet composed. 

As for the letter to Dionysius which is added to these by the ignorant, we have not translated it, because both the words of the letter itself and all the learned deny it is by Plato. It is, however, worthwhile to notice in these letters with how great and constant a mind our Plato acted, especially in the affairs of his friends, and how often he underwent heavy dangers for the safety of a friend. Furthermore, how freely and kindly he often rebuked the tyrant—being more alien to adulation than anyone else, yet yielding to no one in charity and duty. Thus, no less by his life and character than by his disputations, he can lead us to live well and blessedly.

# Thirty-Sixth Book.

## THE THIRTY-SIXTH BOOK OF PLATO: THIRTEEN LETTERS.

### DION TO DIONYSIUS: MAY HE FARE WELL. LETTER I.
[[notes: Though attributed here to Dion, this letter is generally considered to be from Plato to Dionysius in the standard corpus, often numbered as Letter I.]]

**WHILE I** was among you for a long time and managed your empire so faithfully that you perceived more utility from it than others, I sustained heavy slanders. For I know that even though I was supporting you, it will nevertheless seem that a cruel deed was done. But all who were involved in that same government can be witnesses for me. I liberated many of them from no small losses with my greatest effort. Furthermore, holding office under you, I guarded your city many times. 

Finally, however, I was expelled by you more ignominiously than it is fitting for some beggar to be expelled—I, who for so long a time imparted such effort for your benefits. Therefore, hereafter I intend to lead a solitary life. You, as such a tyrant, will rule alone. As for that "excellent" money sent by you for my travel expenses, I return it to you through this Bachius together with these letters. For it is neither sufficient for travel, nor is it useful enough for the rest of my life; it brings the greatest disgrace upon you for giving it, and not much less upon me for receiving it. Therefore, I was unwilling to receive it. To you, it makes no difference whether you give or receive so much; but once it is received back, you will honor someone else of your people as you honored me. 

For I have been sufficiently "honored" by you already. And it is opportune for me now to say that line of Euripides: "In times of shifting affairs, you will wish such a man stood by you." I want you to remember, as many other tragic poets do, that when they bring on a tyrant who is perishing, they attribute to him words of this sort: "Alas, wretch, I perish supported by no friends." But no poet has yet depicted someone perishing for a lack of gold. That poetic thought is also strongly approved by those who have a mind: "Not the glitter of gold in the miserable life of mortals, which is most rare, nor adamant, nor silver tables which men hold in prize, so flash to the eyes; nor wide estates, nor cultivated rich lands avail so much for life as the mind of good men in agreement with one another." Farewell: and consider that so great an error was committed toward us, that you may bear yourself more rightly toward others.

### PLATO TO DIONYSIUS: MAY HE FARE WELL. LETTER II.

**I HEARD** from Archidemus that you think not only I, but even my associates—except for Dion alone—ought to say or do nothing evil against you. However, this exception you make concerning Dion shows that I have no power over my associates. For if I had power over others, and especially over Dion and you, many good things, as I judge, would result for both you and the rest of the Greeks. But now, I am "great" only in this: that I present myself as obedient to my own reason. 

I say these things because Cratistolus and Polyxenus reported nothing sincere to you. One of them is said to have claimed he heard many of those who were with me at the Olympics disparaging you. Perhaps he hears more acutely than I, for I heard no such thing. It seems to me that hereafter, whenever something of this sort is reported to you, you ought to do this: write to me and inquire into the matter itself. For I will neither fear nor blush to confess the truth. 

Between me and you, the matter stands thus: that neither are we (to speak freely) unknown to any of the Greeks, nor is the humanity of this age silent about our association; and hold this as certain: posterity will not be silent either. Those who know of it are of such a kind that it is neither small nor obscure. To what end is this? I will open it immediately, having started from a somewhat higher point. 

By the law of nature, wisdom and power, both being excellent, tend toward the same thing. These two always affect each other, pursue each other, and come together. Furthermore, men are greatly delighted whenever they hear or report things of this kind, whether in the songs of poets or in private conversations: as when men speak of Hiero and Pausanias the Spartan, they rejoice to commemorate the association they had with Simonides and to report what he said and did among them. Similarly, they are accustomed to celebrate together Periander the Corinthian and Thales of Miletus, Pericles and Anaxagoras, Croesus and Solon (as wise men), and Cyrus (as a powerful one). And indeed, the poets, imitating these, bring on Creon and Tiresias together; Polyidus and Minos; Agamemnon and Nestor; Ulysses and Palamedes. And as it seems to me, for the same reason the ancient men joined Prometheus to Jove (Jupiter). Of these, they bring some on as agreeing, others as disagreeing; some as sometimes in concord, others sometimes in discord. They sing of both their dissensions and their agreements. 

I have said all these things to show this: that even when we are dead, men will not be silent about us. Therefore, we must not neglect to have a care ourselves for the time that follows. For it happens by a certain nature that the most lazy men care nothing for what the future opinion of them will be; but the most excellent men do everything so that they may be well-heard among men in future ages. From this, I make the conjecture that there is some sense for those who are dead of the things that are done in life. For the best men divine this strongly, but the worst not at all. The presages of divine men are stronger than those of others. I think, indeed, that those deceased ones I speak of would take the greatest effort to amend their own association, so that they might carry around a better opinion of themselves than they do now. This we may do even now, God favoring us; and if anything was sinned in our prior association, we may amend and correct it by deeds and words. 

Indeed, I say this: there will be a true opinion (especially regarding philosophy) about us: if we are good, a good reputation; if evil, an evil one. And in caring for these things, we could do nothing more pious; and neglecting them, nothing so impious and profane. How this should be done and can be done justly, I will say. When I came to Sicily, there was a fame that I excelled far among those who were then philosophizing. I desired, when I came to Syracuse, to have you as a witness to that opinion, so that philosophy might be in honor for me even among the multitude. But that matter did not succeed prosperously enough for me. I say the cause of this was not what many would judge, but I assert this futile cause: that you did not seem to trust me enough, but in a way wished to dismiss me and call others, inquiring into what my business was—disagreeing, as it seemed to me. And concerning these things, many were saying that you indeed despised me and had turned your mind toward other things. This fame, therefore, then increased. 

Now hear what ought to be done after this, so that I may respond to that which you ask: how we should bear ourselves in-

-turn toward each other. If you indeed utterly despise philosophy, let us let it go. But if you have either heard from another or found for yourself better things than those which are transmitted by me, embrace those. But if our things please you, you ought to honor us most greatly. Now, however, as if from the beginning, you lead, and I will follow. For honored by you, I will honor you; but not honored, I will rest. 

Furthermore, if you begin to honor me first, you will seem to honor philosophy; and that, among the multitude which you especially desired, will produce glory for you as a lover of wisdom. But if I honor you when you do not honor me, I will seem to admire and follow riches; and how shameful this is judged by all, we are not ignorant. To say it summarily: if you honor me, there will be honor for both; if I honor you, infamy for both. And enough of these things. 

The little sphere (*orbiculus*) [[notes: likely a mechanical model of the heavens]] is not in a right state. Archidemus will tell you himself when he returns to you. But that more precious and divine thing, about which you inquire of me through him, must be shown to him accurately. For you say, as he reports, that it was not sufficiently demonstrated to you by me concerning the first nature. I must speak to you now through certain enigmas: so that if anything happens to this tablet either by sea or land, he who reads it may not be able to understand it. 

It is thus: "Around the King of all are all things; for his sake are all things; he is the cause of all beautiful things; around the second are second things; third things around the third." [[notes: This is the famous "Three Kings" passage, central to Neoplatonic theology and often interpreted as a precursor to the Trinity.]] The human soul affects to understand what kind of things those are, looking into those things which are related to you. Of these, nothing is sufficient. But in the King himself, and in those things I have said, there is nothing of the sort. 

As for what follows, the soul speaks. But what kind of question is this, O son of Dionysius and Doris? And how is it the cause of all evils? Rather, is it not a certain stimulus innate in our soul? Which, unless someone uproots it, he will certainly never attain the truth. You said to me in the gardens when we were under the laurels that you had thought this out, and that it was your invention. And I said, if this seemed so to you, you would have liberated me from many disputations. Nor have I ever found another inventor of this; and my greatest investigation is turned toward it. But you, perhaps having heard someone, reached that point by some divine fate. 

However, you never held firm demonstrations of that thing, but produced them now one way, now another, insofar as you were conjecturing by phantasy. This is nothing of the sort, and this does not happen to you alone. But know for certain that no one, when he first hears me, is affected otherwise. One is indeed more exhausted, another less, and they only with difficulty at last cease from labor. Nearly all labor not a little. 

Since these things are and were so, we have found, as I judge, what you sought by letter: how it is fitting for us to bear ourselves toward each other. For after you have discussed these things both by yourself and compared them with the opinions of others—provided you have performed a right examination—you will show yourself in agreement with us and our things. How, then, will these and other things we have said stand? You did rightly indeed for that reason in sending Archidemus to us. And after he has returned to you and reported my opinion to you, other doubts will perhaps seize you; you, if you counsel yourself rightly, will send Archidemus back to me; he, again like a merchant, will return not without profit. If you do this two or three times and diligently examine those things we send, I will be surprised if you do not have yourself much better than you do now toward those things you doubt. 

Act boldly, therefore. For neither you nor Archidemus can undertake any business that is either more honorable or more acceptable to God. Beware, however, lest these things ever fall into the ears of men unskilled in discipline and erudition. For there are none, as my opinion goes, which seem more ridiculous when said to the common people; nor any which, brought before the gifted, seem more wonderful and divine. Often indeed, things said and heard many times and for many years are at last purified like gold with great labor. 

For hear what is accustomed to happen in this matter that is wonderful. There are many men who have now heard these things: powerful in docility, powerful in memory, shrewd in examining and judging; now advanced in age and having heard these things for no less than thirty years; these men nevertheless affirm that those things which once seemed most incredible in the hearing now seem to them first to be very credible and clear; and what then seemed most probable now seems to them the opposite. Looking at these things, therefore, beware lest you ever repent of those things which have now fallen from you unworthily and rashly. The greatest custody of this matter is not to write anything, but to learn. For what is written cannot be contained; for this reason, I have never written anything about these things, nor is there any prescribed work of Plato, nor will there be. What is now said belongs to Socrates, who even while he was young, was famous for virtue. Farewell: and believe us. And this letter, when you have read it many times, burn it immediately. 

And enough of these things. You wonder that I did not send Polyxenus to you. But concerning Lycophron and the rest who are with you, I affirm what I did long ago and now: that you excel them as much as possible both in nature and in art; nor does any of them willingly yield to you in disputation, as some suspect, but they yield unwillingly. And yet you seem to have used them quite humanely and treated them with honorable gifts. But concerning these, one may say many such things. Use Philistion as much as possible, if it happens you can. And if it can be done, use the work of Speusippus; and send him back. Speusippus indeed needs you. Philistion promised me that if he is dismissed by you, he will seek Athens immediately. It would be laudable to release him from the stone-quarries. There is also a light petition both concerning his relatives and concerning Hegesippus, the son of Aristo. For you wrote to me: if anyone wished to inflict injury upon him or them, and you perceived it, you would not permit it. Concerning Lylichides, it is fitting to tell the truth. Truly, he alone of those who went from Sicily to Athens has changed nothing in your and my association. But daily he honors those things which were done with words as much as his strength allows.

### TO THE SAME.
### LETTER III.

**YOU ASK** whether it is more rightly placed in greetings: "Plato to Dionysius, Rejoice," or as I have been accustomed to write to friends, "Act well." You indeed, as those who were present with you at Delphi say, so blandly addressed the God himself and wrote similarly: "Rejoice, and preserve the pleasant life of the tyrant." I, however, would greet neither God nor man in this way. Not God: because I would speak against His nature. For divinity is far from trouble and pleasure. Not man: because pleasure often brings detriment and pain to him, producing dullness in the soul and forgetfulness, bringing forth foolishness and petulance. And let these things be said by me concerning the greeting. Which, after you have read them, you will take as you wish. Many report that you were accustomed to say to certain legates that when they approached you, you had in mind to restore the Greek cities in Sicily and Syracu-

[[summary: This text contains Marsilio Ficino's introductory arguments for Plato's Letters, followed by the first two letters and the start of the third. The content focuses on Neoplatonic interpretations of divine principles, the historical context of Plato's Syracusan missions, and the ethical/philosophical advice Plato gave to Dionysius.]]

[[keywords: Plato, Dionysius, Dion, Syracuse, Neoplatonism, anima mundi, Archytas, Speusippus, political philosophy, esoteric knowledge, Marsilio Ficino]]

--- Page 282 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s works, specifically transitioning from the introductory arguments of the Letters to an allegorical interpretation of the *Symposium* (The Banquet) and the nature of the soul.</meta>

# 264 On the Banquet.

One must believe that divine mysteries lie hidden here. For it was the custom of the ancient theologians to cover their sacred and pure secrets with the shadows of figures <note>original: "figurarum umbraculis"; metaphorical or allegorical language</note> so they would not be polluted by the profane and the impure. However, we do not believe that every single detail described in the figures of the ancients and others pertains exactly to the literal sense. For as Aurelius Augustine says, "all those things noted in figures are prepared to signify something else. Many things are added for the sake of order and connection to those things they signify." The earth is broken by the plowshare alone. But so that this can happen, the other parts of the plow are also joined to it. 

Therefore, this is the summary of what is proposed for us to explain: Humans once had three sexes: Male, Female, and Mixed <note>original: "Promiscuum"; referring to the Androgynous sex in Aristophanes' speech in Plato's *Symposium*</note>. They were the children of the Sun, the Earth, and the Moon, and they were whole. But because of their pride, wanting to equal themselves to God, they were split into two; if they are proud again, they are to be split into two once more. Once the cut was made, one half is drawn to the other half by love, so that a restoration of wholeness may occur, which, when completed, will make the human race happy. 

The summary of our interpretation will be as follows: "Humans," that is, the souls of humans, were "once"—that is, when they were created by God—whole. They were adorned with two lights, the innate <term>innate light (ingenito)</term> and the infused <term>infused light (infuso)</term>. With the innate light, they could see things equal to and below themselves; with the infused light, they could see things above them. They wished to equal themselves to God, so they turned themselves toward the single innate light. Here they were divided; they lost the infused splendor when they turned only toward the innate light, and they immediately fell into bodies. If those who have been made higher are divided again—that is, if they trust too much in their natural genius—that innate and natural light which remains will be extinguished in a certain way. 

They had three sexes. Males were born of the sun, females of the earth, and the mixed of the moon. Some received the radiance of God according to courage, which is masculine; others according to temperance, which is feminine; and others according to justice, which is mixed. These three virtues in us are the daughters of the other three which God possesses. But in God, those three are called Sun, Moon, and Earth; in us, they are called Male, Female, and Mixed. Once the cut was made, one half is drawn to the other by love. Souls now divided and immersed in bodies, as soon as they reach the years of adolescence, are stirred by the natural and innate light they preserved—as if by one of their halves—toward that infused and divine light (once their other half, which they lost when falling). They must receive this through the pursuit of truth. Once it is received, they will be whole again and blessed by the vision of God. This, therefore, will be the compendium of our interpretation.

### MAN IS THE SOUL ITSELF, AND THE SOUL IS IMMORTAL.
### CHAPTER III.

Since the body consists of matter and quantity, and it belongs to matter to receive and to quantity alone to be divided and extended, and thus reception and division are passive states, it follows that by its very nature the body is subject only to passivity and corruption. If any action seems to belong to the body, it does not act insofar as it is a body, but insofar as there is within it something in a way incorporeal, a quality: such as heat in the mass of fire, cold in the matter of water, or the temperament in our body. Certainly, the operations of bodies proceed from these qualities. Let us note that fire does not heat because it is long, or wide, or deep, but because it is hot. Nor does a fire that is more extended heat more—rather, it heats less due to dispersion—but the one that is hotter. 

Since, therefore, operations arise by the benefit of powers and qualities, and the powers and qualities themselves do not consist of matter and quantity (though they are *in* matter and quantity), it follows that being acted upon belongs to the body, while acting belongs to something incorporeal. These powers are indeed instruments for working. Yet on their own they are never sufficient for working, because they are not sufficient for existing. For what lies in another and cannot sustain itself certainly depends on something else. Thus it happens that qualities, because they are necessarily sustained by the body, are stood up and ruled by some superior substance which is neither a body nor lies within a body. 

The soul is of this kind; present and residing in bodies, it sustains itself, and it grants the quality of a unique temperament to bodies, through which—as if through instruments in the body and by the body—it exercises various operations. Hence, man is asserted to beget, nourish, grow, run, stand, sit, speak, manufacture arts and works, perceive, and understand. But the soul itself does all these things, and therefore the soul shall be the man. If we say a man begets, grows, and nourishes, the soul—like the father and craftsman of the body—begets, grows, and nourishes it. If he stands, sits, or speaks, the soul sustains, bends, and vibrates the limbs of the body. If he manufactures or runs, the soul stretches out the hands and twists them by its will, and moves the feet. If he perceives, the soul perceives external bodies through the instruments of the senses, as if through windows and openings. If he understands, the soul attains a variety of things through itself without any instrument of the body. Therefore, everything whatever a man is said to do, the soul itself does, and the body experiences. 

Wherefore, man is the mind alone, while the body is the work and instrument of man. This is especially true because the mind exercises its most powerful operation—namely, intelligence—without any instrument of the body, since it understands incorporeal things through intelligence, while through the body only corporeal things are known. And so, if the mind acts anything through itself, it certainly exists and lives through itself. Moreover, it lives without the body because it works without the body. If it exists through itself, it is fitting that it has a way of being proper to itself, not common to the body; therefore, it can obtain for itself the name of "man" separately from the mass of the body. Truly, this name, because it is spoken of each of us through our whole life—for everyone at every age is called a man—seems to signify something that remains stable. The body flows perpetually, by growing, by shrinking, by continuous dissolution, liquefaction, and being changed by turns of heat and cold. The soul always remains the same, which the inquiry into truth shows us clearly, along with the always-identical will for the good and the firm preservation of memory. Who, then, will be so insane as to attribute the name of "man," which is most firm in us, to the flowing body that is always and everywhere changed, rather than to the most stable mind? From these things it can be clear that when Aristophanes named "men," he meant our souls in the Platonic sense.

### THAT THE SOUL IS ADORNED WITH TWO LIGHTS, AND WHY IT DESCENDS INTO THE BODY; THE CREATION OF THE SOUL WITH TWO LIGHTS.
### CHAPTER IV.

Furthermore, the soul, immediately born from God, is turned toward God its parent by a certain natural instinct, just as fire generated on earth by the power of the higher things is immediately directed toward the higher regions by the impulse of nature. Having turned toward Him, it is illuminated by His rays. But this first radiance, received in the substance of the soul (which was previously formless in itself), becomes darker and, according to the capacity of that space, turns out as the soul's own and natural light. Therefore, through this light—as if through something equal to itself—the soul indeed sees itself and those things which are below it (that is, all bodies); but it does not see God or other higher things. 

However, having been made nearer to God through this first spark, it receives again another clearer light, by which it may also know the things above. Therefore, it has a twin light: one natural, hence "innate"; the other divine and "infused." With these joined together, as if with two wings, it may be strong enough to travel through the sublime region. And if it always used that divine light, it would always cling to divine things; the Earth would be empty of rational animals. But it was decreed by divine providence that the soul should be mistress of herself, and be able both to use both lights at once, and to use only one. From this it happens that, with nature as its guide, having turned toward its own proper light and neglected the divine, the soul notices itself and its own powers which pertain to the construction of the body; and it desires to exercise these powers in building bodies. Weighted down by this desire, as they say, it descends into the body, where it exercises the powers of generating, moving, and perceiving. By its presence, it adorns the earth—the innermost seat of the world—which therefore ought not to lack reason, nor should a part of the world be destitute of the presence of rational living things, just as the author in whose likeness the world was made is entirely Reason. Our mind fell into the body when, neglecting the divine, it used only its own light and began more often to be content with it. God alone, who lacks nothing and above whom is nothing, remains content with Himself and sufficient for Himself. Therefore, the mind made itself equal to God when it wished to be content with itself alone, as if it were no less sufficient for itself than God is for Himself.

### BY HOW MANY WAYS THE SOUL RETURNS TO GOD.
### CHAPTER V.

Aristophanes says that this was clearly the cause of pride, so that the soul which was born whole was cut—that is, it used one of the twin lights while disregarding the other, and indeed neglected the second. Here, immersed in the pit <term>pit (barathrum)</term> of the body as if in the river of forgetfulness <term>river of forgetfulness (letheum flumen)</term>, having forgotten itself for a time, it is seized by the senses and by lust, as if by guards and a tyrant. 

But when the body is mature, the instruments of the senses purged, and learning provides nourishment, the soul comes to its senses. Then the natural radiance flashes out, and by investigating the order of natural things, it perceives through this investigation that there is some noble architect of this machine. It desires both to see and to possess Him; but He is seen only by the divine splendor. Therefore, the mind, by the investigation of its own light, is most vehemently incited to recover the divine light. Such an incitement and appetite is true Love. With this as a guide, one half of the man desires the other half of the same man, because the natural light—which is one half of the soul—seeks to kindle again that divine light, which is called the other half of the same soul, once neglected.

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of Aristophanes' speech from Plato's Symposium. The previous page established that humans were originally "whole" with three sexes (Male, Female, and Mixed) corresponding to the Sun, Earth, and Moon, but were split due to pride. This page explores how the four cardinal virtues and the light of God work to restore that lost wholeness through Love.</meta>

# Commentary. 265

strives again in the soul: and this is what Plato says in the letter to Dionysius: "The human soul strives to understand what divine things are like, looking upon those things that are related to itself." <note>original: "Humanus animus affectat quaha diuina sint intelligere, aspiciēs in ea, quae sibi cognata sunt." This refers to Plato's Second Letter.</note> Truly, when God infused His light into the soul, He adapted it especially for this purpose: to lead men to the blessedness which consists in the possession of Himself. We are led to this by four virtues: Prudence, Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance. Prudence first shows us this blessedness. The remaining three virtues lead us toward blessedness like three paths. Therefore, God tempers His spark in various souls toward this end in different ways: so that with Prudence as the leader, some undergo dangers and death with a brave soul for the sake of honor or for their country through **Fortitude**. Others so establish their lives justly that they neither inflict injury on anyone nor, to the best of their power, allow it to be inflicted, through **Justice**. Others tame their lusts through vigilance, fasting, and labor, through **Temperance**. These people proceed by these three ways; but they strive to reach the same end of blessedness that Prudence shows them. Accordingly, these three virtues are also contained in God by His own Prudence. The souls of men, inflamed by the desire for these virtues, wish to reach them through their duties, to cling to them, and to possess them perpetually.

He calls the masculine strength and audacity of men **Fortitude**. He calls **Temperance** female, on account of a certain relaxed and cooler habit of desire and a mild nature. He calls **Justice** mixed <term>promiscuous (promiscuam); meaning shared or of both genders</term>: female insofar as by its innocence it inflicts injury on no one; but masculine insofar as it does not allow injury to be inflicted on others and punishes wicked men with a more severe judgment. Because it is the property of the male to give and the female to receive, we therefore call the **Sun**, which receives light from no one but provides it to all, male. The **Moon**, which receives from the sun and gives to the elements, we call mixed because of this giving and receiving. The **Earth**, since it receives from all but grants to none, we call female. For this reason, the Sun, Moon, and Earth, and Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance are deservedly designated by the names of male, mixed, and female. And, so that we may provide a more excellent name for God, we call these virtues in Him the Sun, Moon, and Earth; in us, we call them the masculine, mixed, and feminine sex. 

Whomever that divine light was infused into from the "sun of God" with the affection of fortitude at its origin, we say that masculine light was granted to them. To those from the "moon of God" with the affection of justice, mixed light. To those from the "earth of God" with the affection of temperance, female light. We neglect that infused and divine light when we turn back toward the natural light. Therefore, having neglected one, we have preserved the other; where we hold one half of ourselves, we have let go of the other half. Indeed, at a certain fixed time, led by the natural light, we all certainly desire the divine, but we proceed toward its attainment in different ways: through fortitude, those who once received it from the fortitude of God; others through justice or temperance similarly. Finally, each one seeks that half of himself as he had received it. And some, through the masculine light of God once lost and now recovered, wish to enjoy God with masculine fortitude; others through the mixed light similarly with mixed virtue; others through the female light in the same way. 

Truly, only those follow this great gift who, after the spark of natural light has shone forth in them in adulthood, judge that it is not sufficient for judging divine things. They do this so that they do not, by the judgment of the natural spark, attribute the affections of either souls or bodies to the divine majesty, or think that the divine is not more excellent than bodies and souls. In this matter many are said to have erred: those who, trusting in their natural talent in the investigation of divine things, either said there is no God, like **Diagoras**; or doubted, like **Protagoras**; or judged God to be a body, like the **Epicureans, Stoics, Cyrenaics**, and many others; or some kind of soul, like **Marcus Varro, Marcus Manilius**, and several others. These men, as if impious, not only failed to recover the divine light they once neglected, but even corrupted the natural light because of its abuse. Because it was corrupted, it is rightly thought to have been split. Therefore the souls of those who, being proud and timid in their arrogance, trust in their own strengths, are "cut again," as Aristophanes says: since they even obscure the natural light that was left to them with false opinions and extinguish it with wicked habits. 

Thus, whoever recognizes that the natural light is lame and mutilated, and considers it sufficient in some way for judging natural things, uses it rightly. But thinking that for those things which are above nature, a more sublime light is needed, they prepare themselves by a most exact purging of the soul so that the divine light may shine upon them again; by its rays they will think rightly about God and be restored to that former integrity.

**LOVE BRINGS SOULS BACK INTO**
**heaven, distributes degrees of Bliss,**
**grants eternal joy.**

### CHAPTER VI.

Distinguished guests, make this God—whom Aristophanes says is beneficial to the human race above all other gods—favorable to you with every kind of sacrifice. Invoke him with pious prayers; embrace him with your whole heart. He, by his beneficence, first leads souls to the **heavenly table**, abounding with <term>ambrosia and nectar (the food and drink of the gods)</term>. Then he assigns each to their individual seats; finally, he sweetly detains them forever. For none return to heaven except those who have pleased the King of the heavens; and they please Him who love Him most of all. 

Indeed, to know Him truly is entirely impossible in the present time. But to love Him truly, in whatever way He is known, is both possible and easy. Those who know God do not yet please Him unless they love Him as known; those who know and love Him are loved by God, not because they know, but because they love. For we do not embrace with affection those who have merely known us, but those who have loved us. For we have many enemies who know us. Therefore, it is not the knowledge of God that restores us to heaven, but Love. 

Furthermore, the order of those reclining at the heavenly table follows the different degrees of lovers. For those who have loved God more excellently enjoy more excellent feasts there. Truly, those who have worshiped the fortitude of God through works of fortitude enjoy that very thing. Those who worshiped justice truly enjoy justice, and temperance similarly. And so, various souls enjoy various ideas and reasons of the divine mind according to the various rapture of their love. Moreover, all will enjoy the whole of God, because the whole is in each individual idea. But they possess the whole of God more excellently who behold Him in a more excellent idea. Each one possesses that virtue of God which they loved. Therefore, <margin>sublime</margin> "envy," <note>original: "livor"</note> as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*, is absent from the divine choir. For since it is the most pleasant thing of all to possess the thing loved, everyone lives content and full in possessing that which they love. Indeed, if two lovers become masters of their delights, each rests in the beloved possession of his own; nor will he have any concern if the other possesses a more beautiful beloved. Therefore, by the benefit of love, it happens that in the different degrees of happiness, each is content with his portion without any envy. It also happens that the soul feeds upon the same feasts forever without any satiety. For guests to be delighted, feasts and wines are not enough unless hunger and thirst entice them to eat; and the delight lasts as long as the greed remains. But who would deny that greed is a kind of love? Therefore, the eternal love with which the soul is always affected toward God causes it to always rejoice in God as a new spectacle. The same goodness of God always kindles this love in the soul, which also makes the lover blessed. 

Therefore, to sum up briefly, we will praise three benefits of love: that by restoring us who were once divided into wholeness, it leads us back to heaven; that it places each in their own seat and makes all peaceful in that distribution; and that, with all boredom expelled, it continually kindles a new delight in the soul by its own heat, and makes the soul blessed by a charming and sweet enjoyment.

# THE FIFTH ORATION.
# LOVE IS MOST BLESSED, because it is beautiful and good.
# CHAPTER I.

**Carlo Marsuppini** <note>Marsilio Ficino's contemporary, a humanist scholar</note>, the sweet foster-son of the Muses, following the poet **Landino**, approaches the speech of Agathon in this way. Our Agathon judges Love to be the most blessed god because he is the most beautiful and the best. He diligently enumerates what things are required for him to be the most beautiful, and likewise what for him to be the best; in enumerating these, he portrays Love itself. Finally, after he has described what Love is like, he recounts the benefits granted by him to the human race; and this is the summary of that discussion. 

It is in our interest first of all to inquire for what reason he said Love was very beautiful and good in order to show him to be blessed; and what the distinction is between goodness and beauty. Plato, in the *Philebus*, wants that person to be **blessed** who lacks nothing; and that this is that which is perfect in every part. Now, there is a certain internal perfection, and also an external one. We call the internal one **Goodness**, and the external one **Beauty**. Because something is thoroughly good and beautiful, we call it most blessed as being perfect from every side. 

We certainly notice this difference in all things. In gemstones, natural philosophers claim that a certain most temperate internal mixture of the four elements produces an external brightness. Furthermore, in herbs and trees, the fertility innate in the roots and marrow clothes them with a most heavy variety of flowers and leaves. In animals, a healthy composition of humors produces a pleasant appearance of features and colors. Even the virtue of the soul is seen to display a most honorable decorum in words, gestures, and works. The heavens also
