Their sublime substance is surrounded by the clearest light. In all these things, internal perfection produces external perfection. We can call the former "goodness" and the latter "beauty." Therefore, we have argued that beauty is a certain flower of goodness; by the allurements of this flower, as if by some bait, the latent internal goodness attracts beholders. <note>Ficino uses the metaphor of a flower to explain that beauty is the visible "bloom" of an invisible inner moral goodness.</note> Since the knowledge of our mind takes its origin from the senses, we would never understand nor desire goodness itself hidden in the inner chambers of things unless we were carried toward it by the outward appearance of manifest external signs. In this matter, the utility of this beauty and its companion [Love] appears quite marvelous. Through these things, I think it has been shown sufficiently that there is as much difference between goodness and beauty as there is between a seed and a blossom. And just as the flowers of trees, having sprouted from seeds, also produce the seed itself; so this flowering beauty of goodness sprouts from the good, and thus leads lovers back to the good, which our hero here has abundantly demonstrated in the preceding sections.

### HOW LOVE IS PAINTED, and by which parts of the soul beauty is known, and love is generated.
### CHAPTER II.

After these things, Agathon enumerates more diffusely how many things are required for its shapely appearance. He says Love is young, tender, agile, graceful, and radiant. First, we must ask what these contribute to beauty. Then, since they are attributed to this god [Love], how they ought to be understood. Men possess reason and sense. Reason by itself grasps the <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Meaning "without a physical body."</note> rational principles of all things. Sense, through the five instruments of its body, reaches the images and qualities of bodies: colors through the eyes, voices through the ears. Smells through the nostrils, flavors through the tongue, and through the nerves simple qualities of the elements—namely heat, cold, and the rest. Therefore, six powers of the soul are numbered pertaining to knowledge, as far as the proposed question is concerned: Reason, Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, and Touch. 

Reason is attributed to the highest divinity, Sight to fire, Hearing to air, Smell to the scent of vapors, Taste to water, and Touch to earth. Reason indeed investigates celestial things and does not have its own seat in any member of the body, just as divinity has no fixed seat in any part of the world. Sight is located in the sublime part of the body, like fire in the highest region of the world, and by its nature perceives light, which is characteristic of fire. Hearing follows sight just as pure air follows fire and catches voices, which are born in and by broken air, and glide into the ears through the interval of air. Smell is entirely assigned to misty air and vapors mixed from air and water: because, placed between the ears and the tongue, like air and water, it easily perceives those vapors and especially loves those which come from the mixture of air and water—such as the scents of herbs, flowers, and fruits, which are most sweet to the nostrils. Who would doubt that taste is compared to the liquids of water? It follows smell like a thicker air, and being bathed in dark liquid, it is most vehemently delighted by drink and is moist with flavors. Who likewise would hesitate to ascribe touch to earth? Since it happens through all parts of the earthy body; it is perfected in the nerves, which are most earthy; it most easily touches things that have solidity and weight, which earth grants to bodies. 

From this it also happens that touch, taste, and smell only feel those things placed closest to them, and they are affected quite a bit in the process of sensing, although smell seems to grasp more remote things than taste and touch. Hearing, however, knows more remote things and is not so offended. Sight looks even further: and in a moment it does what the ears do over time: for the flash is seen before the thunder is heard. <note>Ficino notes that sight is instantaneous while sound takes time to travel.</note> Reason captures the most remote things: for it perceives not only things that are in the world and present, like the senses, but also things above the heaven, and what has been or will be. 

From these things it can be clear to anyone that of those six powers of the soul, three pertain rather to the body and matter: namely, Touch, Taste, and Smell. The other three, however—Reason, Sight, and Hearing—pertain to the spirit. Therefore, those three declining rather toward the body agree more with the body than the soul: and those things perceived by them, since they move the body suited to them, hardly reach the soul, and they please the soul the least, as being least similar to it. The three higher ones, most remote from matter, suit the soul much more; and they capture things that move the body very little, but the soul most vehemently. For Scents, Flavors, Heat, and the like, either harm the body greatly or help it a little, but what do they contribute to the soul’s wonder or judgment? They are only moderately desired by it. Reason, the incorporeal colors of truth, shapes, and voices, move the body either not at all, or hardly and minimally. But they especially sharpen the edge of the soul for investigating, and they snatch its desire to themselves. 

Truth is the food of the soul. The eyes contribute greatly to finding it, and the ears to learning it. Therefore, those things which pertain to reason, sight, and hearing, the soul affects for their own sake, as its own nourishment. But those things which move the three other senses are more necessary for the body for nourishing, or warming, or generating. Therefore, the soul seeks those things not for its own sake, but for the sake of another—that is, the body. But we are said to "love" those things which we desire for our own sake; those which we desire for the sake of something else, not at all. Deservedly, then, we want Love to pertain only to sciences, shapes, and voices; and therefore only to that grace which is found in these three: in the virtue of the soul, in shape, and in voice. 

Because it especially provokes the soul <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ καλοῦ" (apo tou kalou), meaning "from the beautiful."</note>, it is named "provocation" because the word <note>original Greek: "κάλλειν" (kallein) meaning "to call or provoke."</note> means to call, and <note>original Greek: "κάλλος" (kallos)</note> indeed means "beauty" in Greek. Indeed, the true and best habit of the soul is pleasing to us; the shapely figure of the body is pleasing; the harmony of voices is pleasing. And since the soul—as these three are related to it and in some way incorporeal—values them much more than the remaining three, it is consistent that it should look upon them more greedily, embrace them more ardently, and admire them more vehemently. And this very grace—whether of virtue, of shape, or of voices—which calls and snatches the soul to itself through reason or sight or hearing, is most rightly called "beauty." And these are those three Graces of which Orpheus speaks: <note>original Greek: "ἀγλαΐα ἠδὲ θάλια καὶ εὐφροσύνη" (Aglaia, Thalia, Euphrosyne)</note> Splendor, Greenness, and Abundant Joy. He calls "Splendor" that grace and beauty of the soul which consists in the clarity of truth and virtue. He calls "Greenness" the sweetness of shape and color, for this flourishes most in the greenness of youth. Finally, "Joy" is that pure, healthy, and perpetual delight which we feel in music.

### BEAUTY IS SOMETHING INCORPOREAL.
### CHAPTER III.

Since these things are so, it is necessary that beauty be something common to virtue, shape, and voices. For we would not call any of these three "beautiful" in the same way unless there were one definition of beauty in these three. From this it follows that the principle of beauty itself cannot be a body: because if beauty were corporeal, it would least of all suit the virtues of the soul, which are incorporeal. And yet beauty is so far from being a body that not only the beauty in the virtues of the soul, but even that which is in bodies and voices, cannot be corporeal. For although we say certain bodies are shapely, they are not shapely from their own matter. Indeed, the body of one and the same man is beautiful today, but tomorrow by some foul accident it is ugly—as if being a body were one thing, and being beautiful were another. 

Nor are they beautiful from their very quantity: since some large things and also some short things seem beautiful; and often large things are ugly, small things beautiful; and on the contrary, small things are foul, large things most pleasing. It also sometimes happens that beauty is similar in certain large and small bodies. If, therefore, while the same quantity often remains, beauty is changed by some accident, and if beauty remains even when quantity is changed, and appears similar in both large and small, then certainly these two—beauty and quantity—must be entirely different. 

Furthermore, if the shapeliness of a body were in some way corporeal in that very thickness of its body, it would not, however, please the one enjoying it insofar as it was corporeal. The appearance of some person's beauty pleases the soul not as it lies in external matter, but as its image is captured or conceived by the soul through sight. That image in sight and in the soul, since they are incorporeal, cannot be a body. For in what way would the whole heaven, so to speak, be captured by the small pupil of the eye if it received it in a corporeal way? Certainly in no way. But indeed the spirit receives the entire amplitude of the body in a point, in a spiritual manner and as an incorporeal image. Truly, only that appearance which is received by the soul pleases it. And this appearance, although it is a likeness of the external body, is nevertheless incorporeal. Therefore, an incorporeal appearance pleases. What pleases is agreeable; what is agreeable is, finally, beautiful. From this it is brought about that love is referred to something incorporeal; and beauty itself is a certain spiritual likeness of a thing rather than a corporeal appearance. 

There are, however, some who think that a certain position of all the members, or, to use their words, "commensuration and proportion" with a certain sweetness of colors, is beauty. We do not admit their opinion because, since such a disposition of parts exists only in composite things, no simple things would be beautiful. But now we see pure colors, lights, a single voice, the glitter of gold, the whiteness of silver, knowledge, and the soul—all of which are simple—to be <margin>beautiful</margin>.

<summary>This page defines beauty as the "flower" of inner goodness and argues that it is an incorporeal (spiritual) quality perceived through reason, sight, and hearing. Ficino classifies the senses by their proximity to the soul and rejects the idea that beauty is merely physical proportion or matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the nature of beauty. On the previous page, he distinguished between internal "goodness" and external "beauty." Here, he argues that beauty cannot be merely a physical property like size or color, but is instead a spiritual "splendor" emanating from God.</meta>

# Commentary. 267

...we call things beautiful; and those things delight us wonderfully as if they were truly beautiful. Added to this is the fact that proportion includes all the composite members of the body; it does not exist in the individual parts, but in the whole. Therefore, the individual members would not be beautiful by themselves. Yet, the proportion of the whole composite is born from the individual particles. From this follows something quite absurd: that things which are not beautiful by their own nature could give birth to beauty. 

It also frequently happens that while the same proportion and measure of the limbs remain, the body does not please us as much as it did before. Furthermore, the figure of your body may be the same today as it was last year, yet the grace <note>original: "gratia"—often used by Ficino to describe the "charm" or "spirit" of beauty that goes beyond physical measurements.</note> is not the same. Nothing ages more slowly than the figure, yet nothing ages more quickly than grace. From this it is clearly established that beauty and figure are not the same thing. 

We also often see a more correct disposition of parts and measure of limbs in one person than in another; yet the other, we know not for what reason, is judged by us to be more handsome and is loved more ardently. By this we seem sufficiently warned to consider beauty as something other than the disposition of parts. By the same reasoning, we are warned not to suspect beauty to be the sweetness of colors. For generally, color is brighter in an older person, yet grace is greater in a younger one. And among equals, it sometimes happens that the one who surpasses the other in color is nevertheless surpassed by that person in grace and beauty. 

Nor does anyone dare to affirm that beauty is a certain mixture of figure and colors. For if that were so, then neither knowledge nor voices (which lack color and figure), nor colors and lights themselves (which have no fixed figure), would be judged worthy of love. Furthermore, every desire flies toward and is fulfilled by its own habit. Namely, hunger and thirst are soothed by food and drink; yet love is satisfied by no sight or embrace of the body. Therefore, it does not burn for any physical nature; it certainly pursues beauty. Thus it follows that beauty cannot be something corporeal. 

From all this, it is concluded that those who are inflamed by love and thirst for beauty—provided they wish to extinguish their burning thirst by drinking this liquid—must seek the sweetest moisture of this beauty elsewhere than in the river of matter, or in quantity shaped by art, or in the streams of any colors. For these only inflame their thirst further. Where at last will you turn, you miserable lovers? Who will extinguish the sharpest flames of your heart? Who will settle such a great fire? This is the task, this the labor. <note>A literary echo of Virgil's *Aeneid* ("Hoc opus, hic labor est"), emphasizing the difficulty of the spiritual path.</note> I shall tell you immediately. But pay attention.

### BEAUTY IS THE splendor of the divine face.
### CHAP. IIII.

The divine power towers above all things. It mercifully pours into the angels and souls born directly from it that ray of its own in which the fertile power of creating all things exists, as if into its own children. In them, as they are closer to itself, it paints the disposition and order of the whole world much more exactly than in the matter of the world. For this reason, this entire picture of the world which we see shines more expressively in angels and souls. For in them are the figures of every sphere—of the sun, the moon, and the other stars; also of the elements, stones, trees, and individual animals. 

Pictures of this kind are called "Exemplars" and "Ideas" in the angels; "Reasons" and "Notions" in the souls; and "Forms" and "Images" in the matter of the world by the Platonists. They are clear in the world, clearer in the soul, and clearest in the mind of the angels. Therefore, the single face of God shines in three mirrors placed in order: the Angel, the Soul, and the Body of the world. In the first, being closer, it shines most clearly; in the second, being more remote, more obscurely; and in the third, being most remote, it is most obscure compared to the others. 

Accordingly, the holy mind of the angel, hindered by no service to a body, reflects upon itself. There it gazes upon that face of God engraved within itself; it immediately admires the sight and, once seized, it clings to it forever. We call the grace of that divine face "Beauty." We call the greed <note>original: "auiditatem"—here meaning an intense, spiritual hunger or longing.</note> of the angel, clinging deeply to the face of God, "Love." 

Oh, if only the same would happen to us! But our soul, born under the condition of being surrounded by an earthly body, declines toward the duty of generation. Weighted down by this inclination, it neglects the treasure hidden in its inner chambers. Then, wrapped in the earthly body, it serves the use of the body for a very long time; it accommodates its senses always, and its reason longer than is proper, to this work. From this it happens that it does not notice the brightness of that divine face perpetually shining within itself, until the body is mature and reason is awakened. Then it considers through thought the face of God shining in the machinery of the world and manifest to the eyes. By this consideration, it is carried forward to behold that which shines within. 

Since the face of a parent is pleasing to the children, it is necessary that the face of God the Father be most pleasing to souls. The brilliance and grace of this face—whether in the angel, the soul, or the matter of the world—must be called "Universal Beauty"; and the impulse toward it must be called "Universal Love." We do not doubt that this beauty is everywhere incorporeal. For in the angel and the soul, no one doubts that it is not a body. 

We have shown above that it is also incorporeal in bodies, and for now we understand it chiefly from the fact that the eye perceives nothing other than the light of the sun. For the figures and colors of bodies are never perceived unless illustrated by light, nor do they come to the eyes along with their own matter. Yet it seems necessary that they be in the eyes in order to be seen by the eyes. Thus, the single light of the sun, painted with the colors and figures of all the bodies illustrated by it, offers itself to the eyes. The eyes perceive the light affected in this way with the help of a certain ray of their own; having perceived it, they see the light itself and all things within it. 

Therefore, this whole order of the world which is seen is perceived not in the way it exists in the matter of bodies, but in the way it exists in the light infused into the eyes. In that light, since it is separated from matter, it is necessarily incorporeal. This is also clearly apparent from the fact that light itself cannot be a body, since in a moment it fills almost the whole world from east to west; it penetrates the "body" of air and water everywhere without any clash; and even when mixed with filth, it is never stained. These properties do not suit the nature of bodies at all. For a body is moved not in a moment, but in time; nor does one body penetrate another without a clash to itself or the other; and two bodies mixed together stain each other by mutual contagion. We see this in the confusion of water and wine, or fire and earth. Since the light of the sun is incorporeal, it receives whatever it takes up in the manner of its own nature. Therefore, it receives the colors and figures of bodies in a spiritual way; and in the same way, it is gazed upon when received by the eyes. Thus it happens that all this beauty of the world, which is the "third face of God," offers itself to the eyes as something incorporeal through the incorporeal light of the sun.

### HOW LOVE AND hatred are born, and that beauty is incorporeal.
### CHAP. V.

From all this it follows that every grace of the divine face, which is called universal beauty, is incorporeal—not only in the angel and the soul, but also in the sight of the eyes. Nor do we love this face only as a whole, but moved by admiration, we also love its parts. This is where "particular love" for "particular beauty" is born. Thus we are affected toward some human being, a member of the worldly order, especially when a spark of divine beauty shines forth clearly in them. 

An affection of this kind is born for two reasons: both because the image of the paternal face pleases us, and also because the appearance and figure of a well-composed human being fits most aptly with that "Reason" of the human race which our soul receives from the Author of all things. Whence the image of the external man, received through the senses and passing into the soul, if it disagrees with the figure of man which the soul possesses, it immediately displeases and is held in hatred as something deformed. If it harmonizes, it immediately pleases and is loved as something beautiful. 

This is why some people we meet please or displease us instantly, and we do not know the cause of such an affection. Indeed, the soul, hindered by the service of the body, does not look back at those innermost forms of its own. But it happens through a certain natural and hidden incongruity or congruity. The external form, striking the form of the same thing painted in the soul with its own image, either disagrees or harmonizes. Moved by this hidden offense or delight, the soul either hates or loves the thing itself. 

Truly, that divine power implanted the complete configuration for creating a human being in the angel and the soul. In the matter of the world, however, being most remote from that Craftsman, the constitution of a human being degenerates from that complete figure of its own. Yet in better-disposed matter, it comes out more similar; in other matter, more dissimilar. That which comes out more similar squares with and harmonizes with the soul's Reason, just as it does with the power of God and the Idea of the angel. The soul approves of this harmony. 

Beauty consists precisely in that harmony; the affection of love consists in that approval. Because the Idea and the Reason are alien to the matter of the body, the constitution of a human being is judged to be "similar" not because of matter or quantity, but rather because of something incorporeal. As something similar, it harmonizes with those internal forms; as it harmonizes, it is beautiful. Therefore, body and beauty are different things. 

If anyone should ask how the form of a body can be similar to the form and Reason of the soul and mind, let him consider, I pray, the building of an architect. In the beginning, the architect conceives the "Reason" and, as it were, the "Idea" of the building in his soul. Then, he builds the house as he has thought it out, to the best of his ability. Who would deny that the house is a body, and that it is similar to the architect's incorporeal Idea, in whose likeness it was made? Furthermore, it should be judged similar to the architect because of a certain incorporeal order, rather than because of its matter.

# 268 On the Banquet.

...and so. Come then, remove the matter if you can; however, you can remove it in thought, but leave the order. Nothing of the body will remain for you, nothing of the matter. On the contrary, that very order which comes from the Creator, and which remains in the Creator, will be exactly the same. You may do the same in any human body. You will find that the form of that soul, corresponding to reason, is simple and devoid of matter.

### WHAT IS REQUIRED FOR A THING TO BE BEAUTIFUL, AND THAT BEAUTY IS A SPIRITUAL GIFT.
### CHAPTER VI.

What, then, is the beauty of the body? It is a vitality of action <note>original: "actus vivacitas"—the lively spark or energy that makes a form appear "alive" rather than static.</note> and a certain grace shining in the body by the influence of its own Idea. A radiance of this kind does not descend into matter until it has been most aptly prepared. This preparation of a living body consists of these three: order, measure, and form. **Order** signifies the intervals of the parts; **Measure** signifies the quantity; **Form** signifies the lines and the color. First, it is necessary that the members of the body have their natural placement: that the ears, eyes, nostrils, and so on be in their proper place; that the eyes be near the nose at equal intervals; and likewise that both ears be at equal distances from the eyes. Nor does this equality of intervals pertaining to order suffice, unless there is added the **measure** of the parts, which, preserving the due proportions of the whole body, gives the proper size to each member: so that three noses placed in a line would fulfill the length of one face; the semicircles of both ears joined together would make the circle of the open mouth. The joining of the eyebrows should produce the same. The length of the nose should equal the length of the lip, and the ear similarly. The two circles of the eyes should equal the one opening of the mouth. Eight heads should encompass the height of the body. The extension of the arms to the side should show the same, as should the legs and feet likewise. Furthermore, we consider **form** necessary, so that an artistic drawing of lines and the splendor of the eyes may decorate that order and measure of the parts. 

And yet, although these three are in matter, they cannot be any "part" of the body. The order of the limbs is certainly no single limb. For order exists in all the limbs, yet no single limb is found in all the limbs. Added to this is the fact that order is nothing other than a decent interval between parts. But what else shall we call an interval but a distance between parts? Finally, distance is either nothing—a completely empty void—or it is like a certain drawing of lines. But who would call lines "bodies," since they lack the width and depth necessary for a body? Likewise, **measure** is not quantity, but the limit of quantity. Limits, truly, are surfaces, lines, and points; since these lack the thickness of depth, they are not considered bodies. **Form** also, we place in the pleasant harmony of lights, shadows, and lines, not in the matter itself. From all these things it is clear that beauty is so foreign to the mass of the body that it never communicates itself to the matter itself unless it is affected by those three incorporeal preparations we have described. 

The foundation of these is the temperate <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio"—in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the "temperament" or the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) in an individual.</note> of the four elements: so that our body may be most similar to the heavens, whose substance is balanced, and may not deviate from the formation of the soul by any excess of the humors. In this way, the celestial splendor will easily shine in a body very much like the heavens; and that perfect form of man, which the soul holds imprinted upon it, will be expressed more clearly in the obedient matter. Furthermore, to receive its own beauty, voices are similarly arranged. For their **order** is the ascent from a deep voice to a high one, and the descent from there; their **measure** is the proper progression through thirds, fourths, fifths, and sixths, as well as tones and semitones; their **form** is the ringing intention of a clear voice. By these three, as if by certain elements, bodies composed of many members—trees, animals, and the gathering of many voices—are arranged to receive beauty. Truly, simpler bodies, such as the four elements, stones, and metals, and likewise individual voices, are sufficiently fitted for the same beauty by a certain internal tempering of their nature, by fecundity, and by clarity. 

The soul, however, is most of all suited to beauty by its own nature, because it is both spirit and like a mirror nearest to God. In it, as we said in the previous sections, the image of the divine countenance shines. Therefore, just as nothing at all needs to be added to gold for it to appear beautiful, but the filth of the earth must be removed if any should cling to it; so the soul needs no additions to appear beautiful. Rather, the care of the body and such anxious solicitude must be set aside; the disturbance of desire and fear must be driven away; and immediately the natural form of the soul will shine forth. But lest the discourse wander too far, let us briefly conclude from the above: beauty is a certain vivacious and spiritual grace, first infused by a ray of God into the Angel; from there into the souls of men, the shapes of bodies, and voices; which, through reason, sight, and hearing, moves and delights our souls, and by delighting it seizes them, and by seizing them inflames them with burning love.

### ON THE PAINTING OF LOVE.
### CHAPTER VII.

Agathon the poet, in the manner of the ancient poets, clothes God himself in a human image: he paints him in the likeness of men as beautiful, young, tender, flexible or agile, well-composed, and shining. What are these? These are preparations for a beautiful nature rather than beauty itself. For out of these five parts, the first three signify the temperate complexion of the body, which is the first foundation; the remaining two indicate order, measure, and form. Physicians have shown that the sign of a temperate <term>corporation</term> <note>A healthy, balanced physical state.</note> is a tenderness of the flesh that is smooth, firm, and equal. Where heat exceeds too much, the body is dry and hairy; where cold, it is stiff; where dryness, it is hard and rough; where moisture, it is flowing, sagging, unequal, and twisted. Therefore, an equal and firm tenderness of the body indicates that its state is moderated in the four humors. For this reason, Agathon called Love soft, delicate, and tender. Why young? Because this temperament is possessed by benefit of age as well as nature. For with the length of time, the finer parts of the humors are dissolved and only the much thicker parts remain; and when fire and air have exhaled, an excess of water and earth reigns. But why agile and flexible? So that you may understand him to be fit and ready for all movements; lest by chance you think when he called him "soft," he meant a softness that was womanish, sluggish, or inept. For that is the opposite of a moderated complexion. After these things he added, "Well-composed," that is, most honorably shaped by the order and measure of parts. He also added "shining," that is, reflecting a sweet appearance of colors. 

Having described these specific preparations, Agathon kept silent about what remained. For it is our task to understand the arrival of grace following these. These five parts are understood in the figure of a man as we have said: but in the power of love they seem to be understood differently, for they show its force and quality. He is called **young** because love ensnares young men for the most part, and those ensnared by his traps desire a youthful age. **Soft**, because mild natures are more easily captured; and those who are captured, though fierce before, are rendered gentle. **Agile and flexible**, because he flows in secretly and likewise flows out. **Elegant and well-composed**, because he desires beautiful and ordered things and flees their opposites. **Shining**, because he inspires the mind of man in the flowering and shining age, and desires flowering things. Since Agathon pursues these things most copiously, let it suffice to have touched upon them briefly.

### ON THE VIRTUE OF LOVE.
### CHAPTER VIII.

Those things which are said by Agathon concerning the four virtues to signify the goodness of love are to be understood thus: he is affirmed to be **Just** because where love is whole and true, there is a reciprocity of goodwill that admits no insult or injury. So great is the power of this <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitatis"—meaning selfless, divine love or deep benevolent affection.</note> that it alone can keep the human race in tranquil peace—something which neither prudence, nor fortitude, nor the force of arms, laws, or eloquence can achieve without goodwill. Furthermore, he calls him **Temperate**, because he tames shameful desires. For since Love seeks beauty, which consists in a certain order and temperance, he spurns vile and immoderate lusts; he always shrinks from shameful acts, as you heard from the beginning from the Hero; and where this affection reigns, all other desires are held in contempt. 

He added, **Fortissimum** (Most Brave/Strong). For what is stronger than audacity? Also, who fights more daringly than a lover for the beloved? Among the other gods—that is, the other planets—Mars excels in fortitude because he makes men stronger. Venus tames him. For when Mars, positioned in the angles of the heaven, or the second house of the nativity, or the eighth, portends evils for the one being born, Venus often, by her conjunction, or opposition, or reception, or by a sextile or trine aspect, restrains the malignancy of Mars, so to speak. Again, when Mars rules in the birth of a man, he bestows greatness of soul and wrath. If Venus approaches closely, she does not hinder that virtue of greatness of soul given by Mars, but she represses the vice of wrath; whereby she is seen to make Mars more clement and to tame him. Mars, however, never tames Venus. If she is the leader, she provides the affection of love. If Mars follows, he makes the empire of Venus more burning with his heat; so that if anyone is born with Mars in a house of Venus—in Libra or Taurus—that person is burned by the sharpest loves because of the presence of Mars. Again, Mars follows Venus; Venus does not follow Mars, since the audacity of love is a follower, not a leader...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Symposium, specifically transitioning from the discussion of physical beauty as a reflection of divine Ideas to Agathon’s speech regarding the nature and sovereign power of Love.</meta>

# Commentary. 269

It is not a love of audacity. For men are not ensnared by love because they are audacious; rather, it is usually because they are wounded by love that they become most audacious in the face of any danger, fearlessly undergoing them for the sake of the beloved. Finally, the most evident proof of his all-excelling strength is that all things obey love, but love obeys none. Indeed, the heavenly beings love, as do animals and all physical bodies. So too do the brave and the wise. Even the wealthiest men and the greatest kings submit their necks to the empire of love. Yet Love is subject to none of these. For neither the gifts of the wealthy can buy love, nor can the threats and violence of the powerful force us to love or to stop loving. For Love is free, and it arises of its own accord in a free will—which even God will not compel, having decreed from the beginning that the will should be free. Thus it happens that Love, which exerts force upon all things, escapes the violence of all. So great is its liberty that while other affections of the mind, or arts and operations, usually expect some reward different from themselves, Love is content with itself as its own supreme reward, as if there were no other reward besides love that is worthy of love. For he who loves, loves love above all else. This is what he most desires from the beloved: that the beloved love the lover in return. Love is also most wise. The reason why love is the creator and preserver of all things, and the master and lord of every individual art, was sufficiently discussed in the speech of Eryximachus <note>Eryximachus was the physician in Plato's Symposium who argued that Love is a universal force found in medicine, music, and the seasons.</note>. In those arguments, the wisdom of love is shown. From all of this, it is concluded that love is therefore the most blessed, because it is the most beautiful and the best. It is established as the most beautiful because it delights in beautiful things as being like itself. It must be the best because it makes others best.

### ON THE GIFTS OF LOVE.
### CHAPTER IX.

What love is has appeared from our discourse. What kind of thing it is, is clear from the earlier words of Agathon. What gifts it bestows can easily be learned from what has been said. For love is of two types: one is simple, the other mutual. Simple love <note>Refers to unrequited love or love directed toward an object.</note>, whomever it seizes, renders that person prudent in foresight, sharp in debate, eloquent in speech, magnanimous in action, witty in jokes, ready for games, and most strong in all serious matters. Mutual love grants security from many dangers, concord by removing dissension, and happiness by driving away misery. For where there is mutual charity, there are no snares; there, all things are held in common; there, lawsuits, thefts, homicides, and battles cease. Agathon touches upon the fact that love bestows this kind of tranquility not only upon animals but also upon the heavens and the elements, and this was shown more diffusely above in the speech of Eryximachus. In Agathon’s speech, it is clearly stated that love soothes the minds of gods and men with its song. Anyone will clearly understand this who remembers it was demonstrated earlier that love is in all things and extends to all things.

### LOVE IS BOTH OLDER AND YOUNGER than the other gods.
### CHAPTER X.

But before I finish, most excellent men, I shall resolve three questions according to my ability which arise in Agathon's discussion. First, it is asked why Phaedrus said Love was older than Saturn and Jupiter, while Agathon said he was younger. Second, what the "kingdom of necessity" signifies in Plato, and what the "empire of love" signifies. Third, which gods discovered which arts while love was reigning. God, the Father of all, begot those minds that serve Him—which move Saturn, Jupiter, and the other planets—out of a certain love for propagating His own likeness and the kindness of His providence. These Minds, born in that very instant, recognize and love their parent. We say that the love by which the heavenly beings are created is older than they are; but the love by which they are drawn toward their creator is younger. Furthermore, the Angelic Mind did not receive the Ideas <note>In Neoplatonism, "Ideas" are the divine blueprints of all things.</note> of the planet Saturn and the others from its Father before it was turned toward His face by an innate love. Once it received them, it loved the gift of the parent even more ardently. Thus, the angels' love for God is partly older than the Ideas (which are called gods), and partly younger. Therefore, love is the first and last principle and end of the gods.

### LOVE REIGNS BEFORE NECESSITY.
### CHAPTER XI.

To solve the second question, Love must be said to reign before Necessity because divine love gave origin to all things born from it, and in this, no violence of necessity is placed. For since it has nothing above it, it does not act by compulsion, but does whatever it wishes spontaneously. However, the Mind that follows it sprouts necessarily as Love carries it along. Love, therefore, produces; the Mind is produced by necessity. There the domination of love begins, here the domination of necessity. Although this necessity is born from the supreme goodness of God and is therefore good, it nevertheless proceeds outside of God, and by being necessary, it "degenerates" <note>A technical term in Neoplatonism meaning to step down or diminish in perfection as a thing moves further from the Divine Source.</note> from the infinite perfection of its parent. For the effect never receives the full goodness of the cause. In this necessary procession and degeneration of the effect, the empire of necessity is established. But indeed, the Mind, once born, immediately loves its author, as we said; there, the kingdom of love rises again. For the Mind is raised toward God by love, and God illuminates it with love as it turns toward Him. But here again, the power of necessity creeps in. Since that light descending from God is not received by the Mind (which is dark by its own nature) with the same clarity with which it is given by God. For it is forced to receive it according to the capacity of its own nature. Therefore, by the violence of the receiving nature, the light becomes obscured. To this necessity, the sovereignty of love succeeds again. For the Mind, ignited by this first flash of God, is reflected back toward Him more ardently, and as if spurred on by this spark of light, it seeks the full abundance of light. Hence, God, by the kindness of His providence, bestows a divine light beyond that first natural light; and thus the powers of love and necessity succeed one another in turn. This succession occurs by the origin of nature in divine things, and by intervals of time in others; yet in such a way that love is the first and last of all. We must judge similarly regarding the soul and all other things that come from God concerning these two empires. Therefore, if one speaks absolutely, the empire of love is more ancient than that of necessity, since the power of the former begins in God, and the latter in created things. If we understand this regarding things created by God, the tyrannical kingdom of necessity precedes the kingdom of love, since things themselves first proceed by necessity and degenerate in the proceeding before they turn themselves back toward their Father through love. Orpheus sang of these two empires in two hymns. He described the empire of necessity in the *Hymn to Night* thus: <note>original: "αὐτὴ γὰρ ἀνάγκη πάντα κρατύνει"</note> *For heavy Necessity dominates all things.* But he described the kingdom of love in the *Hymn to Venus* thus: <note>original: "καὶ κρατέεις τρισσῶν μοιρῶν, γεννᾶς δὲ τὰ πάντα / ὅσσα τ’ ἐν οὐρανῷ ἐστὶ καὶ ἐν γαίῃ πολυκάρπῳ"</note> *You rule over the three Fates, and you beget all things: those in heaven, those on the earth, and those in the sea.* The divine Orpheus established two kingdoms and compared them to one another, and he placed love before necessity when he said that love rules the three Fates, in which necessity consists.

### IN WHAT MANNER, WHILE NECESSITY REIGNED, Saturn castrated Uranus, and Jupiter bound Saturn.
### CHAPTER XII.

In what manner the subsequent gods are said by Agathon to have either castrated or bound their parents while Necessity was dominating, we can easily understand from what has been said. These things are not to be taken as meaning that the angelic mind "castrates" God himself, but rather that it divides and disperses the gift bestowed upon it by God within itself. We showed a little while ago that the gifts of God in a receiving spirit necessarily fall away from the supreme perfection of God. Thus, that fecundity of nature, which is whole in God but diminished and in a way mutilated in an angel, is rightly said to have been "castrated." This is said to happen while Necessity reigns because it happens not by the will of the giver or the receiver, but by that necessity where the effect cannot equal its cause. Thus Saturn (that is, the Angelic Mind) seems to castrate Heaven (that is, the supreme God); and Jupiter (that is, the World Soul) binds Saturn—meaning he restricts the power received from the angel within the narrower limits of his own nature's defect. For the power of the former is greater than the latter. Therefore, the power which is free and unbound in the former due to its magnitude is considered bound and restricted in the latter due to its narrowness. I omit what the astrologers believe: that the malice of the planet Saturn is very often restrained by its conjunction, reception, opposition, sextile aspect, or trine aspect with Jupiter. But enough on these matters; let us descend to the third question.

### WHICH GODS BESTOW WHICH ARTS upon humanity.
### CHAPTER XIII.

Agathon believes that arts were handed down to the human race by the gods because of love. The art of ruling from Jupiter; the arts of archery, prophecy, and healing from Apollo; the craft of bronze-working from Vulcan; the craft of weaving from Minerva; and finally, music from the Muses. Twelve deities preside over the twelve signs of the Zodiac. Pallas over Aries; Venus over Taurus; Apollo over Gemini; Mercury over Cancer; Jupiter over Leo; Ceres over Virgo; Vulcan over Libra; Mars over Scorpio; Diana over Sagittarius; Vesta over Capricorn; <note>The text cuts off here, but usually Aquarius is assigned to Juno or Neptune in this system.</note>

Juno: To the fish, indeed, Neptune. From these, all the arts were handed down to our race as signs in the body: the Deities <note>In the Platonic tradition, "Deities" often refer to the governing intelligences of the planets and spheres.</note> who preside over them pour their powers into the soul for each individual art. Thus Jupiter, through the "Jupiter-man" <note>This refers to the astrological influence of the planet Jupiter on a person's constitution.</note>, makes one most fit for the governance of gods and men—that is, for the excellent management of both divine and human affairs. Therefore, from these nine sounds of the heavens, we name the nine Muses after this musical concord. Our soul was once gifted with the logic of this music. For that which has a celestial origin is rightly said to possess an innate celestial harmony. This harmony the soul later imitates with various instruments and songs. And this gift is likewise granted to us by divine providence through love. Therefore, most distinguished men, let us love this god because he is most beautiful; let us imitate him because he is best; let us venerate him because he is most blessed: so that by his clemency and bounty he may grant us the possession of his beauty, goodness, and beatitude.

# SIXTH SPEECH.
# INTRODUCTION TO THE DISPUTATION ON LOVE.
# CHAPTER I.

Thus far spoke Carolus Marsupinus. Then Thomas Benci <note>Thomas Benci (Tommaso Benci) was a member of Marsilio Ficino’s inner circle and a translator of Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, a diligent imitator of Socrates, applied himself to the commentary on Socratic words with a willing spirit and a cheerful countenance. Socrates, he said, our man judged the wisest of all Greeks by the oracle of Apollo, was accustomed to profess the art of loving above all others, as if by the expertise of this art, Socrates—or anyone else—should be judged most wise. He said he did not receive an art of this kind from the physicists Anaxagoras, Damon, or Archelaus; nor from the professors of rhetoric Prodicus of Ceos and Aspasia; nor from the musician Conon, from whom he had learned many things; but from Diotima, a woman of prophetic power inspired by a divine spirit. In my opinion, this was to show that men can understand what true beauty is, what legitimate love is, and in what manner one should love, only through the inspiration of divinity. So great is the power of the amatory faculty, so great its sublimity. Therefore, stay far away from these celestial feasts, stay far away, I say, you profane ones! You who are utterly enslaved to earthly filth and to Bacchus and Priapus <note>Bacchus and Priapus represent physical intoxication and carnal lust, contrasted here with spiritual love.</note>, you defile celestial love and, in the manner of pigs, cast yourselves down into the mud of the earth. But you, most chaste guests, and all others consecrated to Diana and Pallas—you who exult in the purest liberty of the soul and perpetual joy of the mind—attend happily: and listen diligently to the divine mysteries revealed to Socrates by Diotima. But before you hear Diotima, a certain controversy must be resolved which has arisen between those who treated love in the preceding speeches and those who are about to treat it. For the previous speakers called love a beautiful, good, and blessed god; Socrates and Diotima deny this, and they place him in the middle between the beautiful and the ugly, the good and the bad, the blessed and the wretched, and between god and man. We consider both opinions to be true, though in different ways.

### LOVE IS THE MIDDLE BETWEEN beauty and ugliness, and between God and man.
### CHAPTER II.

The lodestone <note>original: "magnes lapis"</note> inserts its own quality into iron; by which the iron, touched by the magnet, inclines toward this stone in a very similar way. This kind of inclination, insofar as it arises from the stone and tends toward the stone, is certainly called a "stony" inclination; but insofar as it is in the iron, it is both "iron-like" and "stony" at once. For it is in the matter of the iron, not in its pure state, but already formed by the quality of the stone. Therefore, it retains the property of both. To speak more clearly: fire, by its own quality (that is, heat), ignites flax <note>original: "linum"</note>. The flax, transformed by the quality of the heat, flies up toward the upper region of the fire. This kind of flight, insofar as it is stirred by the fire and tends toward the fire, we clearly call "fiery"; but insofar as it is in the flax (not pure flax, but already ignited), we call it equally "flaxen" and "fiery" from the nature of both. Frequently, because of an interior goodness happily granted by God, the figure of a man pours a ray of its splendor through the eyes of those looking on and into their soul. By this spark, the soul, drawn like a man toward something, hastens toward the one drawing it. This "pull," which is also love, we do not hesitate to call a "beautiful, good, blessed god" according to the opinion of Agathon and the others, because it depends on the beautiful, good, and happy, and is reflected back toward them. But because it is in the soul, which is already ignited by the presence of that beautiful ray, we are forced to call the affection a "middle" between the beautiful and the not-beautiful. For the soul, which does not yet perceive any image of a beautiful thing, does not yet love that thing because it is unknown; and the soul which possesses beauty in its entirety is not vexed by the stings of love. For who desires what they already have? It remains that the soul burns with ardent love only when, having obtained some beautiful likeness of a beautiful thing, it is spurred from that "pre-tasting" toward the full possession of beauty. In the lover, therefore, the soul of the lover partly has the beautiful thing and partly does not have it; not wrongly, it is partly beautiful and partly not beautiful. And so we maintain that love, from this kind of mixture, is a certain middle affection between the beautiful and the not-beautiful, participating in both. For this very reason, to come now to Diotima, she called love a *daemon* <note>In Greek philosophy, a *daemon* is an intermediary spirit, neither a god nor a mortal, but a bridge between the two.</note>; because just as daemons are in the middle between celestial and earthly things, so love holds the middle between formlessness and form. John <note>Referring to Giovanni Cavalcanti, who delivered the first and second speeches in this commentary.</note> has sufficiently revealed this middle region of his between the formless and the shapely nature in his first and second speeches.

### CONCERNING THE SOULS OF THE SPHERES AND daemons.
### CHAPTER III.

But learn how daemons inhabit the middle region between heaven and earth from the words of Diotima in the *Banquet*, of Socrates in the *Phaedrus* and *Philebus*, of the Athenian guest in the *Laws* and the *Epinomis*. Plato thinks that the entire machine of this world is ruled and moved by a certain soul. Indeed, the body of the world is a certain whole body composed of all four elements, whose parts are the bodies of all living creatures. For the small body of any animal is a particle of the worldly body. It is not composed of the whole element of fire, air, water, or earth, but of certain particles of these elements. Just as the whole is more perfect than the part, so the body of the world is more perfect than the body of individual animals. It would be absurd for an imperfect body to have a soul, while a perfect one had neither soul nor life. For who is so out of their mind that they would say the part lives but deny it to the whole? Therefore, the whole body of the world lives, since the bodies of animals, which are its parts, live. There must be one soul for the whole, just as there is one matter and one connection. Since, therefore, there are twelve spheres of the world—as it pleases the Platonists: eight of heaven and four elements under the heaven—and since these twelve spheres are distinct from each other and diverse in species, motions, and properties, it is necessary that twelve souls be present in them, diverse in species and power. There will be one soul of the first matter. There will be twelve souls for the twelve circles. Who would deny that the earth or the water lives, which grant life to the animals born from them? If even these dregs of the world <note>A common Neoplatonic way of referring to the heavy, material elements of earth and water.</note> live and are full of living things, why should air and fire, the more excellent parts of the world, not live and similarly have living things within them, and the heavens likewise? But those celestial animals, which are the stars, and the earthly and aquatic ones we see; the fiery and aerial ones we do not see. Indeed, we do not even perceive the pure element of fire or air. But there is this difference: on earth there are two kinds of living beings, the brute and the rational; and similarly in the water, since water is more excellent than the body of earth, it ought to be no less a possessor of reason. Truly, the ten upper globes, because of their sublimity, are adorned with rational beings alone. The Platonists name the Soul of the World (that is, of the first matter), the souls of the twelve spheres, and the souls of the stars "Gods," as if they were the attendants of the angelic mind and the highest God. Those animals that inhabit the region of the ethereal fire located below the moon, or of pure air, or of the misty air closest to the water, are called *daemons*. Those who inhabit the earth as rational beings are humans. The Gods are also immortal and impassible <note>Unable to suffer or be affected by external change.</note>; humans are passible and mortal. Daemons are indeed immortal, but they are passible. They do not attribute the passions of the body to daemons, but certain affections of the soul, by which they love good men in a way and hate the wicked, and they involve themselves more closely and ardently in the governing of lower things, especially human affairs; all these, from this office, are seen as good. However, some Platonists and Christian theologians have wanted there to be certain other bad daemons. But for the present, we have no dispute concerning bad daemons. Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian who adapted Neoplatonism into a hierarchy of angels; he was highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> is accustomed to call the good ones, our guardians, by the proper name of "Angels," the governors of the lower world, which deviates very little from the mind of Plato. Furthermore, those whom Plato calls Gods and the souls of the spheres and stars, we can call the Angels who are ministers of God, which also does not disagree with Plato for this reason: because he by no means binds such souls to the enclosures of the spheres in the same way as to bodies, as appears in the tenth book of the *Laws*.

It explains the hierarchy of the universe, from the World Soul and planetary "Gods" down to intermediary "daemons" (or angels) and finally to mortal humans.</summary>

# Commentary. 271

...the souls of earthly things. But he affirms that they are endowed with such great virtue by the highest God that they are able to enjoy the vision of God at the same time as they rule and move the spheres of the world without any labor or worry, according to the will of their Father; and by moving these, they easily govern the lower realms. Therefore, between Plato and Dionysius <note>original: "Dionysium"; likely referring to Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian often synthesized with Neoplatonism.</note> there is a disagreement in words rather than in sentiment.

### ON THE SEVEN GIFTS WHICH ARE GRANTED BY GOD TO HUMANS THROUGH THE INTERMEDIARY SPIRITS.
### CHAPTER 4.

Following the Ideas of all things, which the divine mind contains, the lower gods are said to serve the gifts of the gods as daemons <term>daemons: in the Platonic sense, these are not "demons" but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the divine and the human</term>. For everything passes from the highest to the lowest through intermediaries: so that those Ideas—the conceptions of the divine mind—bestow their gifts upon humans through the gods and daemons. Of these, there are seven principal ones:
1. The sharpness of contemplation.
2. The power of governing.
3. High-spiritedness <note>original: "Animositas"; here meaning courage or vital energy.</note>.
4. Clarity of the senses.
5. The ardor of love.
6. Subtlety of interpretation.
7. Fecundity of generation.

God contains the power of these first within Himself. Then He grants their power to the seven gods who move the seven planets (and are called angels within them), so that each one receives a specific power above the others. Those seven then display these powers primarily to the orders of daemons serving them. These daemons, in turn, hand them down to humans.

Indeed, God infuses these into souls immediately upon their birth from Him: as these souls glide down from the Milky Way through the sign of Cancer into the body, they are wrapped in a certain celestial and luminous body <term>luminous body: often called the "astral body," a subtle vehicle for the soul as it descends into matter</term>; surrounded by this, they are then enclosed in earthly bodies. For the order of nature requires that the purest soul cannot fall into this most impure body before it has received a certain middle and pure covering. Because this covering is thicker than the soul but purer and more subtle than the body, it is judged by the Platonists to be the most fitting bond between the soul and the earthly body.

From this, therefore, it happens that the souls of the planets confirm and strengthen the powers of those seven gifts given by God in our own souls from the very beginning, while their bodies do the same for our bodies. The same duty is overseen by as many natures of daemons, which are intermediaries between the celestials and humans. Saturn strengthens the gift of contemplation through Saturnian daemons. Jupiter, through the ministry of Jovial daemons, strengthens the power of governing and commanding. Mars, through Martial daemons, grants greatness of soul. The Sun, with the help of Solar daemons, grants clarity of sense and opinion, from which prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"</note> follows. Venus inspires love through Venereal spirits. Mercury aids the skill of speaking and interpreting with Mercurial intermediaries. Finally, the Moon fosters the duty of generation with the help of Lunar daemons.

Although they impart the faculty for these things to all humans, they do so especially to those in whose conception and birth they have the most power due to the position of the soul. Indeed, although these gifts are divine and honorable when infused, they can sometimes appear deformed in us because of abuse, which is evident in the use of governance, high-spiritedness, and the love of one's kind. Not to wander too far, we have the instinct of love from the highest God, from Venus (who is called a goddess), and from the Venereal daemons. Since it descends from God, it is a god; since it is confirmed by daemons, it must be called a daemon. Therefore, in Agathon's speech, Love was rightly called a god, and in Diotima's, a daemon. A Venereal daemon, I say.

### ON THE ORDER OF VENEREAL DAEMONS, AND HOW THEY WOUND THROUGH LOVE.
### CHAPTER 5.

Regarding the Venereal daemon, love is threefold. The first is placed by the Platonists in the "Celestial Venus"—that is, in the very intelligence of the angelic mind. The second is in the "Common Venus"—namely, that power of generating which the Soul of the World possesses. These two are called daemons because they are intermediaries between uniformity and form, as we touched on above and will explain more broadly shortly.

The third is the order of daemons accompanying the planet Venus. Of these Venereal daemons, we also set three orders. Some are assigned to the element of purest air; others to the thicker and cloudy air. All are called "Heroes" <note>original: "Heroes"; Ficino makes a linguistic connection between the Greek words "Eros" (Love) and "Heros" (Hero).</note> from the Greek word *Eros* <note>original: "ἔρως"</note>, which means love; that is, they are called "amatory." The first group hurls the stings of love into those humans in whom bile, the choleric and fiery humor, dominates. The second into those in whom blood, the airy humor, dominates. The third into those in whom phlegm and black bile (the watery and earthy humors) rule.

All people are wounded by Cupid’s arrows, but especially those four following the souls of Jupiter, Phoebus <note>Apollo/The Sun</note>, Mars, and Juno (that is, the handmaidens of Venus). Plato signifies in the *Phaedrus* that these souls are most prone to love from the very beginning of their generation, and that these humans usually love most intensely those who were born under the same stars. Hence, "Jovials" are vehemently moved by other Jovials, "Martials" by Martials, and so on for the others.

### HOW THEY ARE CAPTURED BY LOVE.
### CHAPTER 6.

Understand from one example what I say about the other three. Whichever soul glides down into an earthly body under the empire of Jupiter conceives for itself, in that very descent, a certain figure for the building of a man that matches the star of Jupiter. It expresses this most exact figure in its own ethereal body as if it were perfectly fashioned. If the soul finds a seed on earth that is similarly tempered, it paints a third figure in that seed, very similar to the first and second. But if not, the figure is not so similar.

It often happens that two souls descend while Jupiter is ruling, though at different intervals of time. One of them, finding suitable seed on earth, figures the body most correctly according to those prior Ideas. The other, however, due to the unsuitability of the matter, begins the same work but does not execute it with such great similarity to its exemplar. The first body is more beautiful than the second. Both please each other because of a certain similarity of nature. But the one who is judged more beautiful among them pleases more.

Thus it happens that people do not love just anyone who is beautiful, but "their own"—that is, those born similarly—even if they are less beautiful than many others. Therefore, those who are born under the same star (as we said) are so constituted that the image of the more beautiful one, flowing through the eyes into the soul of the other, matches and harmonizes in every way with a similar image formed since birth both in the ethereal body and in the inner recesses of the soul. Thus struck, the soul recognizes that approaching image as if it were something of its own.

Indeed, if that image is as powerful as the one the soul has long possessed within itself (and which it was unable to fully fashion in its own body even though it wished to), the soul immediately draws it to its interior. If anything is lacking in that image for the perfect likeness of a "Jovial" body, the soul restores it by reforming it. Then it loves the reformed image itself as its own work. From this, it happens that lovers are so deceived that they think the beloved is more beautiful than they actually are. For as time goes on, they do not see the beloved in the mere image received through the senses, but they gaze upon an image already reformed by the soul into the likeness of its own Idea, which is more beautiful than the body itself.

Furthermore, they desire to gaze daily upon that body from which the image first flowed. For although the soul preserves the image within itself even when the body is absent—and this is almost enough for the soul—nevertheless the "spirit" (the instrument of the soul) and the eye do not preserve it.

Therefore, three things seem to be in us: Soul, Spirit, and Body. The Soul and the Body, being very different in nature, are joined by the intermediary Spirit, which is a certain very thin and transparent vapor, generated by the heat of the heart from the subtlest part of the blood. From there, diffused through all the limbs, it receives the powers of the soul and transfers them into the body. It receives again, through the organs of the senses, the images of exterior bodies; these cannot be fixed in the soul because an incorporeal substance (which is superior to bodies) cannot be formed by them through the reception of images. But the soul, being present to the spirit, easily inspects the images of bodies shining in it as if in a mirror, and judges the bodies through them. The Platonists call this cognition "sense." While the soul inspects these, it conceives within itself, by its own power, similar images that are much purer. We call this kind of conception "imagination" or "phantasy," and these conceived images are preserved by memory. Through these, the soul's sharp gaze is often incited to contemplate the universal Ideas of things which it contains within itself.

Therefore, the soul sees one particular man by sense and conceives him by imagination. By the intellect, it contemplates the reason and definition common to all men through the innate Idea of humanity, and preserves what has been contemplated. Thus, the soul has once conceived the image of a beautiful man, reformed it within itself, and preserved it in memory; though they may let it go when the person is absent, there is a need for the constant presence of the beautiful body, so that by its illumination, they may continually shine, be fostered, and be delighted. Therefore, these people demand the presence of the body because of their need, and the soul, having mostly complied with them, is forced to affect the same.

### ON THE BIRTH OF LOVE.
### CHAPTER 7.

But now let us return to Diotima. When she had assigned Love to the number of daemons for the reasons we have narrated, she demonstrated his origin to Socrates in this manner: At the birth of Venus, while the gods were feasting, Porus (the son of Counsel), drunk with the drink of nectar, mixed with Penia <note>original: "Penia"; Poverty.</note> in the garden of Jupiter...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato's Symposium, moving from the general celestial hierarchy to the specific mythological birth of Love (Amor). It explains the dual nature of Love as the child of Abundance and Poverty, and how this manifests as different "Venuses" or levels of desire in the cosmos and the human soul.</meta>

# 272 On the Banquet.

<note>original: "In convivium"; referring to Plato’s Symposium, or "The Banquet."</note>

...mixed: from that union, Love was born. At the birth of Venus—that is, when the angelic mind and the souls of the world (which we have named "Venuses" for the reasons stated elsewhere) were arising from the supreme majesty of God—the gods were reclining at the feast. This means that Uranus <note>original: "Cælius"</note>, Saturn, and Jupiter were feasting upon their own specific goods. For when the intelligence in the angel and the power of generation in the soul of the world—which we properly call the twin Venuses—came forth into the light, that highest God whom they call Uranus already existed, as did the Essence and Life in the angel, which we call Saturn and Jupiter.

Porus and Penia <note>Greek: "Poros" (Plenty/Resource) and "Penia" (Poverty/Want)</note> signify abundance and want. Porus is the son of Counsel, which is to say, a spark of the highest God. Indeed, God is called Counsel and the fountain of counsel because He is the truth and goodness of all things. By His splendor, every counsel is made true; toward His goodness, every counsel tends. By "the Garden of Jupiter," he <note>Plato</note> understands the fecundity of the angelic life. When Porus—that is, the aforementioned ray of God—descends into this garden and is mixed with Penia (the soul's prior state of lack), Love is created. 

In the beginning, the angel exists and lives through God; in respect to these two, essence and life, he is named Saturn and Jupiter. He possesses, moreover, the power of understanding, which we judge to be Venus. This power is by its own nature formless and dark unless it is illuminated by God, just as the power of the eye is dark before the arrival of the sun. We consider this darkness to be Penia: a state of want and a defect of light. However, that power of understanding, reflected toward its parent by a certain natural instinct, receives from Him a divine ray, which is Porus, or abundance. In this ray, as if in a seed, the reasons <term>reasons: in this context, the "Logoi" or formative blueprints of all things</term> of all things are included. By the flame of this ray, that natural instinct is ignited. This fire, this ardor arising from the prior darkness and the newly lit spark, is Love: born of want and abundance, procreated in the garden of Jupiter—that is, under the shadow of life. Indeed, immediately after the vigor of life, the ardor for understanding arises. 

But why does he describe Porus as drunk with nectar? Because he overflows with the divine reason of vitality. Why is Love part wealthy and part needy? Because we are not accustomed to burn with desire for what we possess perfectly, nor for what we lack entirely. Since everyone seeks what they lack, if someone possessed the whole thing, why would they seek further? Yet, since no one desires the unknown, it is necessary that what we love was somehow known to us before. Not only known—for we often hate many things known to us—but judged to be good and pleasant. Nor does this seem enough for a burning benevolence, unless we judge that we can easily obtain what we deem pleasant. Therefore, whoever loves something does not yet possess it fully in reality. Nevertheless, the lover gazes upon it in thought, judges it pleasant, and trusts that they can attain it. Through this very knowledge and judgment, hope arises, which is a present anticipation of an absent good. One would not burn for it unless the union pleased them; and it would not please them unless it had been "pre-tasted" in some way. Therefore, since lovers partly have what they desire and partly do not, Love is not unreasonably mixed from a certain indigence and abundance. 

By this reasoning, that heavenly Venus, ignited by the first tasting of the divine ray itself, is carried toward the integral fullness of the entire light. By this effort, clinging more effectively to its parent, it immediately shines with His fullest brightness. Those "reasons" of things which were previously folded within the ray we call Porus are now unfolded, and through the inherent power of Venus, they shine forth more clearly and distinctly. Just as the angel relates to God, so the soul of the world relates to the angel and to God. Turning itself toward the higher realms, the soul likewise receives a ray from them and is ignited, begetting a love that participates in both abundance and want. From here, adorned with the forms of all things, it moves the heavens according to their model, and through the power of generation, it creates forms similar to them in the matter of the elements. 

Here again, we see the twin Venus. One is in the soul for the purpose of knowing the higher things; the other is the procreatress of the lower things. The former is not the soul's own unique property, but an imitation of angelic contemplation; the latter, however, is proper to the nature of the soul. Therefore, whenever we place one Venus in the soul, we mean its peculiar power, its own Venus. Whenever we place two, one is common with the angel, the other is proper to the soul itself. There are, therefore, two Venuses in the soul: the first is celestial, the second is truly vulgar. Both have love: the Celestial for contemplating divine beauty, the Vulgar for generating the same in the matter of the world. For whatever beauty the former sees, the latter wishes to pass on to the machine of the world as much as it is able. Indeed, both are moved to generate beauty, but each in its own way. The Celestial Venus strives to fashion within itself through intelligence the most exact beauty of higher things; the Vulgar Venus strives to give birth in the matter of the world to the beauty it has conceived divinely from the abundance of divine seeds. We sometimes call that first love a "god" because it is directed toward divine things; but more often a "daemon," because it is a mediator between want and plenty. The second love we always call a "daemon" because it seems to have an effect upon the body and is more inclined toward the lower region of the world. This is indeed foreign to God, but suits the nature of daemons.

### IN ALL SOULS THERE ARE TWO LOVES, BUT IN OURS TRULY FIVE.
### CHAPTER VIII.

These twin Venuses and twin loves are present not only in the soul of the world, but also in the souls of the spheres, the stars, the daemons, and humans. And since all souls are traced back to that first one in a natural order, it is necessary that the loves of all are also traced back to its love, so that they depend upon it in some way. For this reason, Diotima <note>The priestess and philosopher who taught Socrates about love in the Symposium.</note> was accustomed to call these "daemons" simply, but that one the "Great Daemon." Hovering over all throughout the entire world, he does not allow hearts to grow sluggish but stirs them everywhere to love. 

In us, however, not only two but five loves are found. Two are the extreme daemons; the middle three are not just daemons, but affections. Truly, in the human mind, there is an eternal love for perceiving divine beauty, for the sake of which we follow the study of philosophy and the duties of justice and piety. There is also in the power of generation a certain hidden stimulus for procreating offspring. This love is perpetual, by which we are constantly incited to fashion a likeness of that higher beauty in the image of the offspring we procreate. These two loves in us are perpetual—they are those two daemons that Plato prophesies are always present in our souls: one of which raises us to the higher, the other presses us to the lower. One is a *calodaemon* <note>Greek: "kalos" (good) + "daemon"</note>, that is, a good spirit; the other is a *cacodaemon* <note>Greek: "kakos" (bad) + "daemon"</note>, that is, an evil spirit. In truth, both are good, since both the procreation of offspring and the investigation of truth are considered necessary and honorable. But the second is called "evil" because, due to our abuse of it, it often disturbs us and turns the soul away from its principal good (which consists in the speculation of truth) and twists it toward viler mysteries. 

Between these, three loves hold the middle ground in us. Since these are not as steadfast in the soul as the others, but begin, grow, decrease, and end, they are more rightly called movements and affections than daemons. One of these is equidistant from both extremes. The remaining two lean toward one side or the other. When the shape of some body, due to the preparation of its matter, is very much like that which the divine mind contains in its Idea, it meets the eyes and penetrates through the eyes into the spirit. It immediately pleases the soul because it resonates with those "reasons" <note>ideals/patterns</note> that our mind carries as models of the thing itself. These do not seem to be in you alone: Soul, Spirit, and Body. Rather, the soul compares what it once received divinely. 

Then a triple love creeps in, as we said: for we are either ready and inclined toward a contemplative, active, or voluptuous life. If toward the contemplative, we are immediately raised from the sight of bodily form to the consideration of the spiritual and divine. If toward the voluptuous, we suddenly descend from sight to the desire of touching. If toward the active and moral, we persevere in the sole delight of seeing and conversing. Those who are so talented are carried to the highest heights; those who are so dull are depressed to the lowest depths; these others, as middle ones, remain in the middle region. Therefore, all love begins from sight. But the love of the contemplative man ascends from sight to the mind. That of the voluptuous man descends from sight to touch. That of the active man remains in sight. The love of the former turns more toward the highest daemon than the lowest; that of the latter turns toward the lowest rather than the highest; the love of the middle one is at an equal distance from both. These three loves are given three names. The love of the contemplative man is called "divine"; of the active man, "human"; and of the voluptuous man, "bestial."

### WHAT PASSIONS ARE IN LOVERS ON ACCOUNT OF LOVE'S MOTHER.
### CHAPTER IX.

We have so far declared that Love is a daemon born of abundance and want, and is divided into five species. Next, we shall treat, from the words of Diotima, what kind of affections are born in lovers from this nature of love. "Since," she says, "Love was procreated at the birth of Venus, he follows and honors Venus and is captured by the desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is most beautiful." Because he is the son of Want (Penia), he is dry, thin, and squalid, barefoot, humble, without a home, without bedding or any covering, sleeping at the doors or in the street under the open sky, and finally, always needy. Because he is the son of Abundance (Porus), he lies in wait for the beautiful and the good. He is manly, bold, and fierce.

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic origin of Love as a middle state between abundance (Porus) and poverty (Penia). It categorizes five types of love in humans, ranging from the divine/contemplative to the bestial/voluptuous, based on how the soul responds to the beauty it perceives.</summary>
