# Book Thirty-One.

Indeed, of those who came from the earth, many—because [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] they themselves had labored through calamities and had seen others [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] laboring—did not choose their next life at random. For this [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] cause, and also because of the lot of fortune, a change of good [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] and evil things happens to many souls. Furthermore, if anyone, whenever he comes into this life [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], should practice philosophy sincerely, and if the final lot of choice [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] does not fall to him, it appears from those things reported from the other side that he will not only be happy here, but his journey [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] from here to there, and his return [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] back here again, will not be earthly and rough, but gentle and celestial. 

He [Plato] used to say that this was a spectacle [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] worthy of consideration: how the individual souls chose their individual lives. It was a pitiable, ridiculous [[abbrev: -ū → -um]], and wondrous sight [[abbrev: -ū → -um]], for they made their choice [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] according to the habit of their prior life [[abbrev: -ū → -um]]. For he says [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] he saw the soul that had once belonged to Orpheus (the legendary poet) choosing the life [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] of a swan out of hatred for the female race, being unwilling [[abbrev: -ē → -en]] to be born [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] from women, by whom he had been killed. He saw the soul of Thamyris (a mythical singer) choosing the life of a nightingale [[abbrev: -ē → -en]]. He also saw a swan [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] turned toward the choice [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] of a human life, and other musical animals likewise, as is fitting [[abbrev: -ū → -um]]. 

He said that a certain [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] soul, when the lots were offered, chose the life [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] of a lion; this was the soul of Aiax Telamonius (Ajax, the Greek hero), who detested [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] human nature whenever he remembered that judgment [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] where he contended for the arms of Achilles with Vlyxes (Odysseus) [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] [[abbrev: -ō → -on]]. After him, the soul of Agamemnon (the leader of the Greeks at Troy), on account of his hardships [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], adopted the life of an eagle out of hatred for the human race. Then the soul of Atalanta (the swift-footed huntress), who had received a middle sort of lot, seeing [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] with what great honors [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] an athlete is treated, could not restrain herself [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] from choosing the life of an athlete. 

Next, the soul of Epeus of Panopeus (the builder of the Trojan horse) migrated immediately into the nature of a craftswoman [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. Far among the last, the soul of the ridiculous Thersites (the ugliest man at Troy) put on the form of an ape. By chance [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], the last lot fell to the soul of Vlysses (Odysseus) [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. Therefore, he said that he came to the choice [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] last. But through the memory of his past [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] labors [[abbrev: -ū → -um]], ceasing from ambition and going around for a long time before he chose, he sought the life [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] of a private man, one most removed from the governing of affairs. He found it lying somewhere, barely at last [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], neglected [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] by the others [[abbrev: -ē → -em]]. He said he would not have chosen any other life [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], even if he had happened to get the first lot [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]; wherefore he gladly embraced that life. He also claimed that souls pass from other wild beasts into humans [[abbrev: -ā → -an]] and are changed in turn: the unjust into savage beasts [[abbrev: -ē → -em]], while the just take up the life [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] of gentle animals, and all mixtures are made in this manner.

When all the souls had chosen their lives step by step, as the lot had given, he recounted that they approached Lachesis (the Fate of the Past) in a long line. To each, Lachesis assigned the *daemon* (guardian spirit) [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] which the soul had taken, to be the guardian [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] of its life and the executor of its chosen works. First, the daemon leads the soul to Clotho (the Fate of the Present), and under her hand and the revolution [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] and whirl of the spindle, he confirms the fortune it had chosen by lot. When he has touched this, he soon leads it to Atropos (the Fate of the Future) spinning [[abbrev: -ē → -em]], who makes the threads unchangeable [[abbrev: -ē → -em]]. 

From there, they afterwards quickly go to the throne of Necessity [[abbrev: -ū → -um]]. When all have passed through it, they proceed under a vehement heat [[abbrev: -ē → -en]] and glow into the Plain of Lethe (Forgetfulness), entirely destitute of trees [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] and all things that grow from the earth [[abbrev: -ū → -um]]. He said that as night approached, they lay down by the river Amelitas (the River of Unmindfulness) [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], whose water no vessel [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] can hold. It is necessary [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] for each to drink some of its water. Those who do not have wisdom as their guide drink more than is proper. Indeed, one who drinks [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] always forgets all things. 

When they have slept until [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] midnight, suddenly they are roused by thunder and an earthquake [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] [[abbrev: -ē → -em]], and they spring up [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] here and there, upwards toward birth, shooting forth like stars. He recounted that he himself was forbidden from drinking from that river [[abbrev: -ū → -um]]. But how [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] he returned into his body, he did not know; but when he suddenly looked around [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] at dawn, he noticed himself [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] placed upon the funeral pyre [[abbrev: -ū → -um]]. 

And so, O Glaucus, the fable was saved and did not perish, and it will save us likewise: if we obey it and cross the Lethean river, that is, the river of forgetfulness, well, and infect the soul with no stain. Wherefore, if we comply with my words, believing the soul to be immortal and such that it can sustain all evils and goods [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], we will always follow the way leading to the things above, and we will cultivate justice with wisdom by every means. Thus we may be dear to ourselves and to the gods while we lead this life [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], and after we have carried off the rewards of virtue, as if having gained victory and triumphs [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], we may fare happily both here and in the thousand-year journey of which we have spoken.

### ON THE SUBJECT OF THE BOOK.
### CHAPTER I.
[[image: Decorative initial V]] JUST AS in the *Parmenides* he grasps [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] all types of divine things according to his powers, so in the *Timaeus* he embraces [[abbrev: -ō → -om]] all natural things, and in both he is greatly Pythagori- [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] can, disputing under a Pythagorean persona. And in the *Parmenides* indeed, he imitates Parmenides and Zeno, the Eleatics and Pythagoreans who wrote [[abbrev: -ā → -ant]] about divine matters. In the *Timaeus*, however, he follows Timaeus of Locri, the Pythagorean who composed a book on the nature of the universe. He does so in such a way, however, that he adds not only eloquence to these, but mysteries [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. 

Since divine things are indeed the principles and archetypes of natural things, and natural things are the effects [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] and images of divine things, for that reason, even in the *Parmenides* while he treats divine matters, he meanwhile descends to natural ones; and in the *Timaeus*, treating nature [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], he frequently rises into divine matters. Nor does he wrongly divinize and join nature at the same time. For nature is the instrument of divinity. And thus he either treats natural things divinely, like Aristoteles, or he treats divine things naturally. He also interposes mathematics as the middle between both [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], namely the divine and the natural [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. For mathematics signifies divine things through numbers [[abbrev: -ū → -um]], but natural things through measures. Therefore, let the subject of this book be universal nature itself—that is, a certain seminal and life-giving power [[abbrev: -ū → -um]] infused into the whole world, subject to the *mundane anima* (world-soul) [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] but presiding over matter, and bringing forth individuals in the same order as the soul itself conceived them, looking up to the divine mind as much as it desires the good.

### ON THE ORDER OF THE BOOK
### and its parts
### CAP. II.
IT WILL become clear that the nature of the universe and the universe itself [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] do not consist of themselves, but depend on a superior and divine cause. It will be clear, moreover, into how many grades nature is distributed: celestial, elemental, simple, composite, rational, and those lacking [[abbrev: -ē → -es]] reason. It will be clear that the whole of generation under the moon is referred back to the rational [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] animal as its end and master. Many things besides [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] this will be treated concerning this very animal, looking both to the soul [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] and to the body [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. Many things also concerning those matters which are composed by nature below the rational animal [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. 

And to speak briefly [[abbrev: -ō → -on]], the triple world will be treated: namely the divine, the celestial [[abbrev: -ū → -um]], and the human. It will also be shown that for all things composed in the world, and for the world itself, there are two principal internal [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] elements: namely matter and form [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. There are, however, three external principles: namely the efficient, exemplary, and final cause of the world. And the efficient cause is indeed divine power [[abbrev: -ā → -am]], intelligence, and will; the exemplary cause is the Ideas conceived by divine intelligence; and finally, the final cause is the Good.

[[page number: 457]]

# On the Timaeus.

### ON THE INTRODUCTION TO
### the dialogue. CAP. III.

FURTHERMORE, to come to the disposition of the dialogue itself, Plato had destined five continuous days for the discussions. On the first day, Socrates disputed in the Piraeus together with Polemarchus, Glaucon, Adimantus, and Thrasymachus the Sophist regarding the republic [[abbrev: -ā → -am]]. On the second day, he withdrew into the city [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] with Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates, and a certain nameless fourth traveler [[abbrev: -ē → -em]], perhaps a companion of Timaeus. On the third day, they made an epilogue of these things. With this prologue having been made, Timaeus soon disputed about nature in the presence of the three: Socrates, Critias, and Hermocrates. For the fourth, who was present without a name [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] for the second narration, is now absent from the third; for it is not for just anyone to be present for the more secret matters [[abbrev: -ē → -em]]. On the fourth day, Critias held his oration [[abbrev: -ē → -em]]. Finally, the fifth day has not yet dawned. 

Quite conveniently, after the disposition and epilogue of the divine republic among men [[abbrev: -ū → -um]], the archetype [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] for this was added in the *Timaeus* concerning the celestial republic composed by God himself; and then concerning the antiquity of the world and the human race, and the wondrous things strenuously performed by the ancients.

### THE ALLEGORY OF THE HISTORY
### which is narrated in the prologue.
### CAP. IIII.

HE NARRATES, among the beginnings of this dialogue, a history of a certain war committed between the Athenians and the Atlantians. Crantor (the first commentator on Plato), therefore, first [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] [[abbrev: -ī → -in]] took this as bare history without allegory. Certain others, however [[abbrev: -ō → -on]], took it as only allegory. But the most proven of the Platonists refute these: affirming the history [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] because Plato said: "The future discourse is very wonderful, but entirely true." Besides, they think that an allegorical sense should be exhibited for Plato, who never builds anything at random [[abbrev: -ū → -um]]. 

Therefore, they think that war between the Athenians and the Atlantians bears the image of the opposition [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] of all things that are in the universe. For war—that is, opposition—is, according to Heraclitus, the father of all things. Amelius indeed brings in the opposition between the firmament and the planets, especially since it is said in the *Critias* that the Atlantic island was divided into seven [[abbrev: -ā → -am]] [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] circles. Origen, however, sees the opposition of the superior daemons to the inferior ones, with the former exceeding in power and the latter in number. 

Numenius sees the dissension of excellent souls following Pallas (Athena) against other souls following generation under Neptune (Poseidon). Porphyrius (the Neoplatonist) sees a battle between daemons leading souls into generation and souls striving for the things above [[abbrev: -ē → -en]]. He distinguishes daemons in a triple way: some are divine; others are according to a certain habit, whose number particular souls fill when they have obtained a demonic lot; others are evil and harmful to souls. These lowest daemons [[abbrev: -ō → -on]], therefore, conflict with souls in their ascent and descent; especially the western daemons, for that region is assigned by the Egyptians to the harmful daemons. 

Accordingly, Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus (later Neoplatonists) add to these that opposition itself [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] which is perpetually vigorous in the universe: between the One and the multitude; limit and infinity; the Same and the Other; rest and motion; from which all things are composed under the First. Likewise, being is either through itself or not [[abbrev: -ō → -on]] through itself. Again, essence is either incorporeal or corporeal; and the incorporeal either does not decline toward bodies [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] or it does. The corporeal is either not perishable, like the celestial, or perishable, like the elemental [[abbrev: -ē → -em]]. Finally, in the heavens there are motions opposite to each other and diverse [[abbrev: -ē → -em]] virtues. Below the heavens, however, are qualities repugnant to each other [[abbrev: -ē → -em]]. In sum [[abbrev: -ū → -um]], the discrepancy of all these things is signified through that ancient war; and everywhere the superior and more excellent things are signified through the Athenians, and the others through the westerners. Such an allegory [[abbrev: -ē → -on]] is not slightly suited to the discourse of Timaeus. It is also confirmed through those things which we comment upon in the *Critias*.

[[notes: Ficino is tracing the lineage of Neoplatonic interpretation of the Atlantis myth, moving from literal history (Crantor) to metaphysical allegory (Proclus).]]

The previous page discussed the transmigration of souls; this page shifts to the psychological and metaphysical "gifts" that Love inherits from his father, Plenty (Porus), contrasting them with those of his mother, Poverty (Penia).</meta>

274 On the Banquet.

->WHAT GIFTS LOVERS HAVE
because of the father of love.<-
### CHAPTER X.

These things follow from the poverty of love’s mother, but contrary things follow from Plenty, his father. <note>In Plato’s *Symposium*, Love is the child of Penia (Poverty) and Porus (Plenty/Resourcefulness). Ficino here interprets how these two lineages affect the lover's behavior.</note> Anyone who understands what was said above will recognize what these opposites are. Previously, Love was described as simple, incautious, lowly, and unarmed; here, the opposites of these are introduced. For he is called clever: a sagacious hunter, a schemer, a plotter, studious of wisdom, a philosopher, manly and bold, vehement, eloquent, a magician, and a sophist. This same love, which makes a lover careless and sluggish in other affairs, renders him astute and clever in matters of love, so that he might court the favor of the beloved in marvelous ways—whether he entangles them with deceits, captures them with services, soothes them with eloquence, or charms them with song. The same fury that made him gentle in service also provides him with weapons: ferocity toward those indignant at the beloved, and security and invincible strength for those fighting on the beloved's behalf. 

Love, as we have said, takes its origin from sight. Sight is positioned midway between the mind and touch; hence, the soul of the lover is always pulled apart and tossed up and down by turns. Sometimes a desire for an embrace arises; at other times, a chaste longing for celestial beauty, and now the former, now the latter, conquers and leads him. In those who are most honorably educated and possess a sharp intellect, the latter usually prevails; in others, the former. Whoever prostrates themselves in the dregs of the body is deservedly judged to be parched, naked, humble, unarmed, and sluggish. They are parched because they are always hungry and never filled. They are naked because, as reckless people, they are subject to all dangers, and as most impudent and unrefined, they are held in infamy. They are humble because they think of nothing high or magnificent. They are unarmed because they succumb to shameful desire. They are sluggish because they are so dull that they do not know where love draws them, and they stop on the way without reaching the goal. 

Conversely, the opposite type of lovers appear affected in the opposite way: for those with solid souls, feeding on good things, are more filled and love more tranquilly; they preserve modesty, neglect the shadowy appearance of the body, and are elevated higher. As if protected by armor, they drive away empty lusts and subject their senses to reason. These, being the most skillful and prudent of all, practice philosophy in such a way that they walk most providently through the shapes of bodies as if following certain "footprints" or "scents." <note>Ficino uses the metaphor of a hunter following a trail to describe the philosopher seeking divine beauty through physical forms.</note> From these, they sagaciously track down the sacred beauty of the soul and the gods; and thus, by hunting prudently, they happily attain what they desire. 

Truly, such a great gift of love proceeds from his father: since the ray of beauty, which is both "plenty" and the father of love, has this power—that it is reflected back to where it came from, drawing the lover along with it. It descends first from God; passing into the Angel and the Soul as if through glass materials, and flowing easily from the Soul into a body prepared for its reception, it shines out from that body of a younger person, especially through the eyes, the brightest windows of the soul. It flies straight through the air and, penetrating the eyes of the older person, transfixes the soul, kindles the appetite, and leads the wounded soul and the kindled appetite toward its healing and refreshment, while it carries them away to the same place from which it had descended: first to the body of the beloved, second into the Soul, third into the Angel, and finally into God, the primary origin of this splendor. 

This is the useful hunt, the happy fowling of lovers. <note>original: "aucupium" — a term for bird-catching, used here as a metaphor for winning a soul.</note> In Plato's *Protagoras*, a certain friend of our Socrates attributes this very hunt to him. He says: "From where, O Socrates? I think you are returning from that hunt to which the noble nature of Alcibiades is accustomed to provoke you." <note>original: "Vndenam inquit, ô Socrates? Arbitror equidem à venatione illa redire..." — quoted from the opening of Plato's Protagoras.</note> Furthermore, he calls Love a "Sophist" and "Great." In the dialogue *The Sophist*, Plato defines a sophist as ambitious and crafty in disputation, who by the cleverness of petty traps shows us the false as true, and forces those who dispute with him to contradict themselves in their speeches. Both lovers and beloveds sometimes suffer this. Indeed, lovers, blinded by the mists of love, often accept the false for the true, while they judge their beloveds to be more beautiful, sharper, and better than they really are. They contradict themselves because of the violence of love. For reason advises one thing, while lust follows another. They change their plans at the command of the beloved; they oppose themselves just to comply with others. Often even the beautiful are ensnared by the cunning of lovers, and those who were previously stubborn become easy. 

But why do we consider Love "great"? Because the whole power of Magic consists in Love. The work of Magic is the attraction of one thing by another through a certain kinship of nature. <note>term: <term>Magic</term> (Magica) — For Ficino, "natural magic" was not sorcery but the science of natural affinities and the "sympathy" between parts of the universe.</note> The parts of this world, like the members of a single animal, all hanging from one author, are joined together by the communion of a single nature. Therefore, just as in us the brain, lungs, heart, liver, and other members draw something from each other, help each other mutually, and suffer together when one of them suffers, so the members of this huge animal—that is, all the bodies of the world—being similarly connected, mutually exchange natures and are changed. From a common kinship, a common love is born; from love, a common attraction. This is true Magic. 

Thus, fire is drawn upward from the concavity of the moon's sphere because of a kinship of nature; air from the concavity of fire; earth is drawn to the lowest parts from the center of the world; and water is snatched from its own place. Hence the magnet turns iron, amber turns straws, sulfur turns fire, the sun turns many flowers and leaves toward itself, and the moon turns the waters. Mars is accustomed to stir the winds, and various herbs invite various kinds of animals to themselves. In human affairs, too, "his own pleasure draws each person." <note>A reference to Virgil: *Eclogue* 2.65, "trahit sua quemque voluptas."</note> The works of Magic, therefore, are works of Nature. Art is merely the servant. For where something is lacking in natural kinship, Art supplies it at opportune times through vapors, numbers, figures, and qualities; just as in agriculture, Nature produces the crops, but Art prepares them. 

The ancients attributed this art to "demons" <note>In the Platonic sense, *daemones* are intermediary spirits, not evil entities.</note> because they understand the nature of the society of natural things, what fits each thing, and how the concord of things, if it is lacking anywhere, may be restored. Some men are said to have been friends to these demons either by a certain similarity of nature, like Zoroaster and Socrates, or beloved through worship, like Apollonius of Tyana and Porphyry. Therefore, signs, voices, and portents are said to have happened to them while awake, or oracles and images from demons while asleep. Those who became magicians through the friendship of demons are seen to be like the demons themselves, who are magicians knowing the friendship of things. And all of Nature is called a "magician" because of mutual love. 

Furthermore, every beautiful person enchants us with their tender eyes. Men soothe and win them over with the power of eloquence and the measures of songs, as if with certain incantations; moreover, they appease and capture them with devotion and gifts, no differently than with potions. Therefore, no one doubts that Love is a magician, since the whole power of magic consists in love, and the work of love is fulfilled by enchantments, incantations, and potions. 

Nor is love entirely mortal, nor even immortal. It is not mortal, because two loves (those two "demons" we spoke of) are perpetually in us. It is not immortal, because three of the intermediate stages change daily, increasing and decreasing. Furthermore, an unquenchable innate fervor is born in the appetite of men from the beginning of life, which does not allow the soul to rest, but always impels it to apply itself studiously to something certain. Men have diverse natures, and one does not live by a single wish. From this, that continuous fervor of desire, which is "natural love," impels some to the study of letters; others to music or figures; others to honesty of character or a religious life; others to honors; some to accumulating money; many to the luxury of the belly; others to other things—and even the same man to different things at different ages. 

Therefore, the same fervor is called both immortal and mortal. It is immortal because it is never extinguished, and it changes its matter rather than vanishing. It is mortal because it does not always lean toward the same thing; rather, either from a change in nature or from a satiety arising from long-term frequency of the same thing, it seeks new delights. And what almost died in one thing, somehow revives in another. It is also called immortal for this reason: that a figure once loved is always loved. For as long as the same figure remains in the same man, it is loved in him; but when it has flowed away from him, the figure you loved before is no longer the same in him. You do not burn for this new figure, because you did not burn for it before, but you do not stop loving that prior one. However, there is this difference: you previously saw it in another; now you look at it only in yourself, and you always love it fixed in your memory, and as often as it occurs to the eyes of the mind, it burns you as a lover. 

Therefore, as often as we meet that person who was once most dear to us, we are moved: either the heart leaps or trembles, or the liver melts, or the eyes quiver, and the face takes on various colors in their presence. For their presence suggests to the eyes the figure of the soul lying hidden in the mind, and rouses the fires as if poking at coals sleeping under ashes. For this reason, love is called immortal. But it is also considered immortal because, although the faces remain always fixed in the breast, they do not always offer themselves equally to the eyes of the mind, whereby the benevolence seems to boil and cool by turns. 

Added to this is that both bestial and human love can never be without indignation. Who would not be indignant at the one who took away their very soul? For just as liberty is pleasing above all things, so slavery is burdensome. Therefore, you hate and love beautiful people at the same time: you hate them as thieves and murderers, yet as mirrors shining with celestial splendor, you are forced to wonder at them and love them. What should you do, wretched man? Where can you turn, alas, you lost one? While you would wish this murderer not to exist, you also would not wish to live without the blessed spectacle. Since you cannot be with the one who destroys you, who kills you—yet without them you cannot live, who with such marvelous allurements steals you from yourself and claims all of you for themselves. You desire to flee the one who burns you with their flames; yet you also desire to cling to the one who possesses you, so that you might be closest to yourself.

<summary>This page explores Marsilio Ficino’s Neoplatonic theory of Love, characterizing it as a "Magician" that connects the universe through natural affinities. It describes the "Ladder of Love" where divine beauty descends into bodies and draws the lover back up toward God, while also touching on the psychological torment of the lover who both hates and loves the person who "steals" their soul.</summary>

->Commentary. 275<-

You seek yourself outside yourself, you wretch, and you cling to your captor so that you might one day redeem yourself. You would certainly not want to love, madman, because you would not want to die; yet you would also not want not to love, since you judge that the image of celestial things must be served. Therefore, by this alteration, it happens that at every moment (so to speak) love withers and revives. 

Love is also placed by Diotima as the middle between wisdom and ignorance. Furthermore, love follows what is beautiful. Wisdom is the most beautiful of all things. Therefore, love desires wisdom. He who desires wisdom does not possess it entirely—for who seeks what is present? Nor does he lack it entirely. For in this one thing at least he is wise: that he recognizes his own ignorance. But he who does not know that he is ignorant is ignorant of both the things themselves and his own ignorance, and he does not seek knowledge, of which he does not know he is destitute. Therefore, the love of wisdom, because it is partly deprived of wisdom and partly wise, is located between wisdom and ignorance. 

This, says Diotima, is the condition of love. But the nature of the beautiful itself—that is, supreme beauty—is that it is delicate, perfect, and blessed. **Delicate**, insofar as it attracts the appetite of all things to itself by its own sweetness; **Perfect**, insofar as it illustrates and perfects those who approach it with its rays; **Blessed**, insofar as it fills those it has illustrated with eternal goods.

### WHAT THE UTILITY OF LOVE IS FROM ITS DEFINITION.
### CHAPTER XI.

After Diotima explained what the origin of love is and what kind it is, she now opens toward what it tends and for what it is useful to men. We all desire to have good things; and not only to have them, but to have them always. Each of the goods of mortals is changed and fails, and all things would quickly vanish unless they were made daily in the place of those departing. Therefore, so that good things may always endure for us in some way, we desire to recreate what is perishing. Recreation happens through generation. Hence the instinct for generation is innate in everyone. 

Moreover, since generation makes mortal things similar to divine things by continuation, it is surely a divine gift. Deformed things are contrary to divine things (inasmuch as they are beautiful); beautiful things are similar and friendly. Therefore, generation—a divine work—is consummated perfectly and easily in that which is beautiful, and the opposite in the contrary. For this reason, that effort of generation seeks beautiful things and flees their opposites. 

What do you ask human love is? To what does it lead? It is the **desire for generation in the beautiful** for the sake of preserving perpetual life in mortal things. This is the love of men living on earth; this is the end of our love. For indeed, at that very time in which each animal is said to live and be the same (as from childhood to old age), although it is called the same, it never contains the same things in itself; but it is always made new, as Plato says, and sheds old things in terms of hair, flesh, bones, blood, and the entire body. 

And this happens not only in the body, but also in the soul. Character, habits, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears are constantly changed; nor does anything from these remain the same and similar. Prior things are abolished, and new things succeed and grow. Furthermore, what is more wonderful, not only do some sciences vanish and others arise, and we are not always the same in regard to sciences, but even any one of the sciences suffers nearly the same thing. For meditation and reminiscence are, as it were, a resumption of a passing science. For forgetting seems to be the exit of a science. Meditation, however, always restoring a new memory in place of the departing one, preserves the science so that it appears to be the same. 

In this way, whatever things in the soul or body are mutable are preserved: not because they are always entirely the same (for this is the property of divine things), but because that which decays and departs leaves something new and similar to itself. By this remedy, surely, mortal things are rendered similar to immortal things. There is, therefore, in both parts of the soul—both that which looks toward cognition and that by which the body is ruled—an innate love of generation for the sake of perpetually preserving life. 

The love which is in the part accommodated to ruling the body does not immediately from the beginning impel one to take food and drink so that humors might be generated from these nourishments, by which what flows constantly from the body might be resumed. By this generation, the body is nourished and grows. When the body is adult, the seed itself is stirred and provokes the lust for procreating offspring, so that what cannot remain always in itself may remain everlasting, reserved in an offspring very similar to itself. 

Love is also attributed to the knowing part of the soul, causing the soul to desire truth, its own proper nourishment, through which it may be nourished and grow in its own way; and if anything has fallen from the mind through forgetfulness, or lies numb because of sloth and neglect, it regenerates it, as it were, by the study of recollection and meditation, and recalls into the mind what had perished through forgetfulness or had become numb through laziness. When the mind is adult, it stimulates it with a most burning desire for teaching and writing, so that science generated either in writings or in the souls of disciples—the intelligence and truth of the teacher—may remain eternal among men. And thus, by the benefit of love, both the body and soul of every man may seem able to survive always in human affairs after death. 

Both loves follow beautiful things. To be sure, he who rules and governs the body desires to nourish his own body with feasts as delicate, pleasant, and beautiful as possible, and to generate beautiful offspring with a fair woman. And he who belongs to the soul studies to imbue it with the most ornate and serious disciplines, and to produce a science most similar to his own by writing in an ornate and beautiful style, and by teaching to generate it in a most beautiful soul—I mean a pure, sharp, and excellent soul. We do not see the soul itself; therefore, we do not inspect its beauty. But we see the body, the shadow and image of the soul; thus, suspecting from its image, we conjecture that a beautiful soul exists in a beautiful body. For this reason, we more willingly educate beautiful men.

### ON THE TWO LOVES, AND THAT THE SOUL IS BORN ENDOWED WITH TRUTH.
### CHAPTER XII.

We have said enough now about the definition of love; now, however, let us declare the distinction regarding love in Plato from the fecundity of the mind or body. "Of all men," he says, "the body is pregnant and heavy, and so is the soul." The seeds of all its own things are inserted into the body from the beginning. Hence, in the established courses of time, teeth break out, hair comes forth, the beard spreads, and the seeds of procreation flow down. 

If the body is fecund and pregnant with seeds, much more the soul, being more excellent than the body, is most fertile and possesses the seeds of all its own things from the beginning. Therefore, the soul has long since been allotted the reasons of character, arts, and disciplines, and it brings forth its offspring from there at established times if it is rightly cultivated. 

Moreover, we know that it has the reasons of all its own things innate from its appetite, inquiry, invention, judgment, and comparison. Who would deny that the soul, immediately from a tender age, desires true, honorable, and useful goods? But no one desires unknown things. Therefore, some notions of these things are in the soul even before it desires them; through these, as if through their forms or reasons, it judges that they are to be desired. 

The same is proved from inquiry and invention: if Socrates seeks Alcibiades in a crowd of men, and is one day to find him, it is necessary that some figure of Alcibiades be in Socrates' mind, so that he knows which man he seeks above the rest, and having found him in a gathering of many, he is able to discern Alcibiades from the others. Thus, the soul would neither track down those four things <note>referring to Truth, Goodness, Beauty, and Utility</note>, nor ever find them, unless it had some notion of them—that is, of Truth, Goodness, Honesty, and Utility—through which it might seek them in order to find them, so that as often as it finds what it had investigated, it recognizes it and discerns it from its opposites. 

Nor is it proved only from appetite, investigation, and invention, but also from judgment. For whoever judges someone to be a friend or an enemy is not ignorant of what friendship or ill-will is. In what way, therefore, would we daily judge many things true or false, good or bad, as we are accustomed to do, and judge them rightly, unless truth and goodness were in some way foreknown to us? How again would the works of architecture, music, painting, and the other arts—and even the inventions of philosophers—be very often rightly approved or rejected by many who are not even versed in the arts, unless some form and reason of those things were attributed to them by nature? 

Comparison also shows us the same thing. For whoever, comparing honey to wine, pronounces one sweeter than the other, recognizes what a sweet taste is; and he who, conferring Speusippus and Xenocrates with Plato, judges Xenocrates more similar to Plato than Speusippus, undoubtedly knows the figure of Plato. In the same way, when from many good things we rightly think one better than another, and one appears better or worse than another by a greater or lesser participation in goodness, it is necessary not to be ignorant of goodness. Furthermore, since from many diverse opinions of philosophers or even others, we often judge very well which is more similar to truth and more probable, it must be that we do not lack some intuition of truth, so that we are not ignorant of what things are more similar to it. 

Wherefore some are said to have emerged as most learned in youth, some even without a teacher, and most from very few rudiments of doctrine demonstrated by teachers; which could never have happened unless nature, as we said, had helped much. Socrates demonstrated this abundantly to Phaedo, Theaetetus, Meno, and the boys; and he taught that boys are able to answer rightly in individual arts if someone questions them prudently; precisely because they are endowed by nature with the reasons of all arts and disciplines.

### THE LIGHT OF TRUTH IN THE SOUL.
### CHAPTER XIII.

In what way reasons of this kind are in the soul seems ambiguous in Plato. If one follows those books which the younger Plato wrote—the *Phaedrus*, *Meno*, and *Phaedo*—he will perhaps think they are painted in the substance of the souls almost like figures on a wall, which has been touched upon often by both me and you in previous discussions; for he seems to hint at it there. 

However, in the sixth book of the *Republic*, that divine man opens the whole matter and says that the light of the mind for understanding all things is God himself, by whom all things were made. For he compares the Sun and God to each other in such a way that, as the sun is to the eyes, so God is to minds. The sun generates eyes and provides them with the power of seeing. This power would be in vain and buried in everlasting darkness unless the light of the sun were present, painted with the colors and figures of bodies; in which light the eye sees the colors and figures of bodies. Nor does the eye behold anything other than light. Yet it seems to behold various things, because the light infused into it is adorned with various formulas of external bodies. The eye perceives this light reflected in bodies, but it by no means sustains the light in its source. 

In the same way, God procreates the soul and grants it a mind, a power for understanding; which would be empty and dark unless the light of God were present to it, in which it might inspect the reasons of all things. Whence it understands through the light of God, and recognizes only the divine light itself. Yet it seems to recognize diverse things, because it understands that light under diverse ideas and reasons of things. When someone, seeing a man with his eyes, fashions an image of the man in his imagination and revolves longer in judging it, he raises the sharp edge of his mind to behold the reason of man existing in the divine light. Then a spark immediately flashes in the mind; and in truth, the very nature of man is understood, and the same for all other things. 

Thus we understand all things through the light of God, but we cannot see his pure light and its source in this life. In this clearly consists the entire fecundity of the soul: that in its innermost parts shines that eternal light of God, most full of the reasons and ideas of all things, to which the soul, as often as it wishes by purity of life and supreme intention of study, is converted; and having converted, it flashes with sparks of ideas.

### FROM WHENCE LOVE TOWARD MALES, AND FROM WHENCE TOWARD FEMALES.
### CHAPTER XIV.

Thus the body of men is pregnant, as Plato wishes, and so is the soul, and both are stimulated to birth by the incitements of love. Furthermore, some are more fit for the offspring of the mind than the body, either because of nature or because of education; others, and indeed most, the opposite. The former follow celestial love, the latter vulgar love. The former naturally love males—and those indeed nearly adult—rather than females or children; because in them the sharpness of mind, which is most fit for the discipline they are about to generate, is much more vigorous on account of its more excellent beauty. 

Others, on the contrary, love because of the pleasure of venereal intercourse and the effect of corporal generation. Since, however, that genital force of the soul, being devoid of cognition, has no discrimination of sex, it is nevertheless by its own nature incited to generate as often as we judge some body beautiful. It happens frequently that those who converse with males, in order to settle the stings of the genital part, mingle with them. These are especially those in whose birth Venus was in a masculine sign and with Saturn, or in the signs of Saturn, or opposite Saturn. 

It was necessary, however, to notice that the incitements of that genital part should not affect this useless work of waste, but the office of sowing and procreating, and translate it from males to females. We think that nefarious crime <note>original: "nefarium scelus," referring to sodomy</note> arose from an error of this kind, which Plato detests most sharply in his *Laws* as a species of homicide. Surely he is to be judged no less a murderer who snatches away a man about to be born than he who removes one who is born from the midst. He who breaks off a present life is bolder, but he who envies the light to one about to be born is more cruel and kills his sons not yet born.

### THE SOUL IS ABOVE THE BODY, THE ANGEL ABOVE THE SOUL, GOD ABOVE THE ANGEL.
### CHAPTER XV.

But enough about the twin fertility of the soul and the twin loves. Next, let us discuss by what steps Diotima carries Socrates from the lowest things to the highest: from the body to the soul, from the soul to the angel, and from the angel she leads him back to God. 

One may argue that these four levels of things must be in nature in this way: Every body is moved by another; but it cannot move itself by its own nature, since it can do nothing through itself. But it seems to be moved by itself because of the presence of the soul, and to live because of the soul. And while the soul is present, it moves itself in a certain way; but when it is absent, it is moved only by another, since it does not have this nature from itself, but the soul properly possesses the power of moving itself. For to whomever it is present, it imparts the power to move itself; moreover, what it imparts to others by its own presence, it must have much earlier and more greatly. 

Therefore, the soul is above bodies, as it can move itself according to its essence, and thus it must be above those things which do not attain moving themselves from themselves, but from the presence of others. When we say the soul is moved by itself, we do not use that word transitively (as Aristotle wanted it to be taken from Plato), but we utter it absolutely, as when we assert that God stands by himself, the sun shines by itself, and fire is hot by itself. For it is not that a part of the soul moves and a part is moved; but it is moved as a whole from itself—that is, by its own nature. This means it runs from one thing to another by reason and carries out the works of nutrition, growth, and generation through intervals of time. 

This temporal discourse belongs to the soul from itself; because that which is above it does not understand things at different moments, but understands all things at once in one point of eternity. Therefore, the first motion and the first interval of time are rightly placed in the soul by Plato; from whence both motion and time pass into bodies. 

Since, however, it is necessary that rest be before motion, as rest is more perfect in reason, it is necessary that above the mobile motion of the soul some stable intelligence be found, which according to its whole self is intelligence and is always intelligence in act. For the soul does not understand with its whole self, nor always, but from a certain part of itself and sometimes; nor does it have a certain but an ambiguous power of understanding. So that what is more perfect may precede that which is less perfect, above the mind of the soul (which is mobile, partial, intermittent, and doubtful) must be placed the mind of the angel—stable, whole, continuous, and most certain. Just as the soul, moved by itself, precedes the body agitated by another, so the mind, stable by itself, precedes the soul agitated by itself. 

And just as the body has it from the soul that it moves itself (and therefore not all bodies, but only animated ones, seem to be moved of their own accord), so the soul has it from the mind that it always understands. For if the intellect were in the soul by its own nature, it would also belong to the souls of all beasts, just as the power of agitating themselves. Therefore, the intellect does not belong to the soul by itself and primarily; wherefore it is necessary that it be preceded by that which is composed of mind by itself and primarily. Such a thing is an angel, an essence more excellent than a soul. 

But indeed, that principle of things and supreme good, which Plato in the *Parmenides* calls "the One itself," necessarily towers above the mind of the angel. Surely above every multitude of a composite thing, the simple "One itself" must be placed, from which the whole composition of the mind—from diverse and simple things—is forged. For although that mind is immobile, it does not exist as the pure, simple "One itself." For it understands itself; where these three things seem to be diverse among themselves: that which understands, that which is understood, and the understanding. For its reason is one thing as it understands, another as it is understood, and another as it is the understanding. 

Furthermore, it has the potency of knowing before the act of cognition, being entirely formless in itself; it is formed by knowing, and by understanding it desires and receives the light of truth, which it seems to have lacked before it understood. It also has in itself a multitude of all ideas. See how great and how varied the multitude and composition in the angel is! Therefore, we are forced to place the pure one and simple before it. 

But we can place nothing before the one God, because the true One is devoid of all multitude and all composition. If it had anything above itself, it would surely be made by it; wherefore, depending on it, it would degenerate into this very thing from the same, as every effect is accustomed to from its cause. And therefore it would no longer be one and simple, but at least composed of two things: namely, from the gift of its cause and its own defect. Therefore, the One itself, as Plato wishes and Dionysius the Areopagite confirms, towers above all things; and the most excellent name of God, the One itself, is judged by both. 

The reason also shows us its sublimity: that the gift of the most eminent cause must be the most ample and extend itself to all things by the excellence of its power. The gift of the One propagates itself through all things. For not only is the mind one, and any soul one, and any body one, but even formless matter itself and the privation of things is said to be "one" in a certain way. For we speak of "one of those sensing," "one darkness," "one death." Yet the gifts of mind and soul do not extend as far as that. For the mind grants artistic form and order; the soul provides life and motion; but formless and primary matter of the world and the privation of things are devoid of form and life. Thus the One itself precedes the mind and the soul, since its gift is diffused more widely. By the same reason, the mind seems to exceed the soul, because life, the gift of the soul, is not given to all bodies; yet the mind attributes form and order to all of them.

### WHAT THE COMPARISON IS BETWEEN GOD, ANGEL, SOUL, BODY.
### CHAPTER XVI.

Therefore we ascend from the body into the soul, from this into the angel, from this into God. God is above eternity; the angel is entirely in eternity. Indeed, both its operation and essence remain stable. Stability, moreover, is proper to eternity. The soul is partly in eternity, partly in time. For its substance always endures the same without any change of increase or decrease. Its operation, however, as we showed a little before, runs through intervals of time. The body is entirely subject to time. For both its substance is changed, and its every operation requires a space of time. 

Therefore, the One itself exists above stability and motion; the angel is in stability; the soul is in stability and motion alike; the body is located in motion alone. Again, the One remains above number, motion, and place; the angel is in number above motion and place; the soul is in number and motion, but above place; the body is subject to number, motion, and place. Since the One itself has neither any number nor composition of parts, nor is it changed in any way from that which it is, nor is it closed in any place. The angel indeed has a number of parts or forms, but is free from motion and place. The soul has a multitude of parts and affections and is changed by the progression of reasoning and the variety of perturbations, but it is exempt from the limits of place. The body, however, is obnoxious to all these.

### WHAT THE COMPARISON IS BETWEEN THE BEAUTIES OF GOD, ANGEL, SOUL, BODY.
### CHAPTER XVII.

There is the same comparison between these four and their forms. Truly the form of the body consists in the composition of many parts, is constrained by place, and glides away in time. The form <note>original: "species"</note> of the soul suffers indeed the vicissitudes of time and contains a multitude of parts, but it is absolute from the boundaries of place. The form of the angel has number only and exists immune from the other two. But the form of God suffers none of those things. 

You see the form of the body. Do you wish also to behold the form of the soul? Take away from the corporal form the weight of the nature itself and the limits of places; leave the rest: you now have the form of the soul. Do you wish that of the angel also? Take away, I pray, not only the spaces of place but also the progress of time; retain the manifold composition; you will immediately obtain it. Do you also desire to discern the beauty of God? Take away, in addition, that manifold composition of forms; leave a completely simple form; you will have immediately followed after the form of God. 

But what, finally, would remain for me after these things are subtracted? Do you think that being anything other than light is beauty? Furthermore, the beauty of all bodies is that light of the sun which you see, infected by those three things: by the multitude of forms (for you see it painted with many figures and colors), by the space of place, and by temporal change. Take away its seat in matter, so that it retains the other two besides place: the beauty of the soul is exactly of this kind. Take away from here, if it pleases you, the change of time; let go the rest: light remains without place and without motion, most clear; but engraved with all the reasons of all things. That is the angel, that is the beauty of the angel. Finally, take away that number of diverse ideas; leave one simple and pure light: like that light which remains in the globe of the sun itself and is not dispersed through the air; now you understand the beauty of God in a certain way. It exceeds the other forms at least as much as that pure, one, inviolate light of the sun in itself surpasses the splendor of the sun scattered, divided, infected, and obscured through the cloudy air. 

Therefore, God is the source of all beauty. Therefore, God is the source of all love. Furthermore, the light of the sun in water is a certain shadow compared to the clearer light of the same in the air. The splendor in the air is likewise a shadow compared to the glow of the same in fire. The glow in fire is a shadow to the light of the sun shining in that very sun. The same is the comparison between those four beauties: of the body, soul, angel, and God. 

God is never so deceived that he loves the shadow of his own form in the angel but neglects his own true beauty. Nor is the angel so captured by the form of the soul, which is its shadow, that it deserts its own proper figure for a worse shadow. Yet our soul—which is greatly to be grieved, for this is the origin of our entire unhappiness—the soul, I say, alone is so soothed by the allurements of corporal form that it holds its own form second; and having forgotten, it follows the form of the body, which is its shadow, more submissively. 

Hence that most cruel fate of Narcissus in Orpheus. Hence the miserable calamity of men. Narcissus indeed, a youth—that is, the soul of a rash and inexperienced man—does not behold his own face; he by no means notices his own substance and virtue. But he follows its shadow in the water and tries to embrace it; that is, he admires beauty in a fragile body and one like flowing water, which is the shadow of the soul itself. He deserts his own figure; he never attains the shadow. For the soul, by following the body, neglects itself and is not filled by the use of the body. For it does not truly desire the body itself; but like Narcissus, it affects its own form, attracted by the corporal form which is the image of its own form. And since it does not notice this at all, while it desires one thing but follows another, it cannot fulfill its desire. Therefore, resolved into tears, it is consumed—that is, the soul, thus placed outside itself and fallen into the body, is tortured by pernicious perturbations. Infected with the filth of the body, it as if dies, since it seems now to be the body rather than the soul. So that Socrates might avoid this death, Diotima led him back from the body to the soul, from this to the angel, and from that to God.

### HOW THE SOUL IS ELEVATED FROM THE BEAUTY OF THE BODY TO THE BEAUTY OF GOD.
### CHAPTER XVIII.

Come, most dear guests, imagine Diotima thus addressing Socrates: "No body, O Socrates, is beautiful in every part. For it is either beautiful in this part and deformed in that; or beautiful today and not at all at another time; or judged beautiful by one and ugly by another. Therefore, the beauty of the body, polluted by the contagion of ugliness, cannot be pure, true, and primary beauty. Furthermore, no one ever suspects beauty to be ugly, just as no one suspects wisdom to be foolish. But we think the disposition of bodies is sometimes beautiful and sometimes ugly; and at the same time, different people feel differently about it. Therefore, primary and true beauty is not in bodies. 

Add that many bodies are called by the one name of beauty. Therefore, there is one common nature of beauty in many bodies, through which they are similarly denominated beautiful. But judge one nature of this kind—just as it is in another, that is, in matter—so to depend on another. For what cannot be sustained in itself can much less depend on itself. Will it depend on matter? Not at all. For nothing deformed and imperfect can adorn and perfect itself. What is one must arise from one. For this reason, the one beauty of many bodies depends on some one incorporeal artisan. The one artisan of all is God, who daily renders all the matter of the world through angels and souls into beauty. Therefore, one must think that the true reason of beauty is found in God and his ministers rather than in the body of the world. 

To this beauty, you will ascend easily, I think, O Socrates, by these steps. If nature had given you Lyncean eyes, my Socrates, so that you could penetrate anything you met with your sight, that most beautiful body of your Alcibiades would seem most ugly to you on the outside. How much is it that you love, friend? Only the surface—rather, color snatches you; rather, a certain reflection of lights and a very light shadow. Or a vain imagination deceives you; so you love what you dream rather than what you see. 

But so that I do not seem to oppose you completely, let this Alcibiades be beautiful. But in what part is he beautiful? Surely in all his members except for his snub nose and eyebrows higher than they should be. Yet these are beautiful in Phaedrus. But the thickness of the legs in him does not please. These are comely in Charmides, unless a slender neck would offend you. Thus, if you observe individual men, you will praise none in every part. Whatever is right anywhere, you will collect; you will forge a complete figure in yourself from the observation of all; so that the absolute beauty of the human race, which is found scattered in many bodies, may be collected in your mind by the thought of one image. 

You will value the figure of each man little, O Socrates, if you compare it to this one. Moreover, you possess this one not so much by the benefit of bodies as by your soul. Therefore, love this image which your soul has forged and the soul itself, its artisan, rather than that exterior, maimed, and dispersed beauty. 

What, however, do I command you to love in the soul? The beauty of the soul. Light is the beauty of bodies; light is also the beauty of the soul. The light of the soul is truth; which alone your friend Plato seems to ask from God in his prayers. 'Grant me, O God,' he says, 'that my soul may be made beautiful, and that those things which pertain to the body may not impede the beauty of the soul; may I judge only the wise man to be rich.' In these words, Plato declares that the beauty of the soul consists in truth and wisdom, and that it is given to men by God. 

Truth is one and the same, given to us by God; in its various affections, it receives the names of various virtues: as it demonstrates divine things, it is called **Wisdom**, which Plato asked from God before the rest; as it demonstrates natural things, **Science**; as human things, **Prudence**; as it makes men just, **Justice**; as invincible, **Fortitude**; as tranquil,

--- Page 296 ---
->278 On the Symposium<-

**Temperance**. From these, two kinds of virtues are numbered: moral virtues, and intellectual virtues which are more excellent than they. The intellectual virtues are Wisdom, Science, and Prudence; the moral are Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance. The moral virtues are better known on account of their operations and civil duties; the intellectual are more hidden because of their recondite truth. Furthermore, he who is educated in honorable character, being purer than others, is easily raised to the intellectual virtues. 

Therefore, I command you to consider first the beauty of the soul which consists in character, so that you may understand that there is one reason for all characters, through which they are similarly called honorable—namely, the one truth of a most pure life, which leads us to true happiness through the actions of Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance. Therefore, love first this one truth of character and most fair light of the soul. 

Know also that you will immediately ascend above character to the most lucid truth of wisdom, science, and prudence, if you will consider that these are granted to a soul educated with the best character, and that in them the most correct norm of moral life is contained. Although you may behold various doctrines of Wisdom, Science, and Prudence, nevertheless think that in all of them there is only one light of truth, through which all are similarly called beautiful. I charge you to love this as the supreme beauty of the soul. 

But indeed, this one truth in many doctrines cannot be the primary truth, since it is in another, being distributed in many doctrines. Whatever lies in another certainly depends on another. Nor, however, is the one truth born from a multitude of doctrines. For what is one must arise from one. Therefore, it is necessary that there be some one wisdom above the soul of man, which is not divided through diverse doctrines, but is one wisdom; from whose unique truth the manifold truth of men arises. 

Remember, O Socrates, that unique light of the unique wisdom is the beauty of the angel, which you must worship above the form of the soul. As we showed in the previous sections, it excels the form of bodies because it is neither constrained by place, nor divided according to the parts of matter, nor corrupted. It also excels the form of the soul because it is entirely eternal and is not moved by temporal discourse. Since, however, the light of the angel flashes into a series of many ideas, and above every multitude there must be a unity which is the origin of the whole number, it is necessary that it flow from the one principle of all things, which we call "the One itself." 

Therefore, the light of the One itself is entirely simple, infinite beauty; because it is not polluted by the filth of matter like the form of the body, nor is it changed by temporal progression like the form of the soul, nor is it dissipated by multitude like the form of the angel. Moreover, every quality secreted from an extraneous addition is called "infinite" by the physicists. If heat were in itself, not impeded by cold and moisture, not weighted by the gravity of matter, it would be called infinite heat, because its power is free and is not narrowed by any additional limits. Similarly, light free from every body is infinite; for it shines without mode or limit, which shines by its own nature when it is least terminated by it. 

Therefore, the light and beauty of God, which is pure and absolutely free from all others, is called without doubt infinite beauty. Infinite beauty, moreover, also requires immense love. Therefore, I beseech you, Socrates, to love other things with a certain measure and limit; but love God with infinite love, nor let any measure be present for divine love."

### HOW GOD IS TO BE LOVED.
### CHAPTER XXI. <note>original: CAP. XXI, though following XVIII</note>

These things Diotima said to Socrates. We, however, most illustrious men, will not only love God without measure, as Diotima is imagined to command, but we will love God alone. For the mind is toward God as the sharp edge of the eyes is toward the sun. The eye, however, does not desire light above the rest, but it desires light alone. If we love bodies, if we love souls, if we love angels, we will not love these, but God in them. In bodies indeed the shadow of God; in souls the similarity of God; in angels the image of the same. 

Thus we will love God in all things for the present, so that we may finally love all things in God. For living thus we will proceed so that we see both God and all things in God; and we love both him and all things which are in him. And whoever at this time devotes himself to God with charity will finally recover himself in God. Surely he will return to his own idea, through which he was created; there again, if anything was lacking to him, he will be reformed; he will cling perpetually to his idea. 

The true man and the idea of man are the same. Therefore, each of us on earth, separated from God, is not a true man, since he is disjoined from his own idea and form; divine love and piety will lead us to it, since here we are dispersed and mutilated. Then, joined by loving our ideas, we will emerge as whole men; so that we may seem to have worshiped God first in things, in order that we may then worship things in God, and to venerate things in God so that we may embrace ourselves above the rest, and by loving God we may seem to have loved ourselves.

->SEVENTH SPEECH.<-

### CONCLUSION OF THE ABOVE, AND THE OPINION OF GUIDO CAVALCANTI THE PHILOSOPHER.
### CHAPTER I.

Finally, Christopher Marsupinus, a most refined man, about to play the persona of Alcibiades, turned to me with these words: "I congratulate indeed, Marsilio, your family of Giovanni <note>original: "Ioannis," likely Giovanni Cavalcanti, Ficino's friend</note> most greatly; which among many knights most illustrious for both doctrine and deeds, produced the philosopher Guido, well-deserving of the republic and excelling everyone in his age in all the stings of dialectic. He, imitating this Socratic love in both character and songs, briefly touched upon whatever has been said by you. 

For Phaedrus touched upon the origin of love emanating from the bowels of chaos. Pausanias divided love, now born, into two species—namely, celestial and vulgar. Eryximachus opened its amplitude while he showed it to be present in all things distributed into two parts. Aristophanes declared what he does in individuals by the presence of so great a God, showing that broken men are mended by him. Agathon treated how great his virtue and power is, when he disputed that men are made blessed by him alone. Finally, Socrates, taught by Diotima, explained in summary what love is, and what kind, and from whence it arose, how many parts it has, where it tends, and how much it is worth. 

Guido Cavalcanti the philosopher <note>original: "Guido Cavalcantes," the medieval Italian poet and friend of Dante</note> seems to have inserted all these things most artificially into his songs. Just as a mirror, struck in a certain way by a ray of the sun, shines again and inflames the wool placed next to it by that reflection of splendor: so he judges that the part of the soul which they call the 'dark imagination' <note>original: "obscuram phantasiam"</note> and memory is struck by the image of that beauty which holds the place of the sun (swallowed through the eyes like a ray), so that it fashions another image for itself from that one, as if a splendor of the first image; by which the power of desiring is kindled no differently than wool and loves. 

He adds that this first love, kindled in the appetite of sense, is created from the form of the body inspected through the eyes; but that form is not impressed in the imagination in the way it is in the matter of the body, but without matter; yet it is an image of a certain certain man placed in a designated place and time. Again, he says some form of an image of this kind immediately shines in the mind: which no longer appears to be the similarity of one certain human body as it was in the imagination, but the common reason and definition of the whole human race. 

Therefore, just as from the image of the imagination taken from the body, a love prone to sense arises in the sensory appetite dedicated to the body; so from this form and common reason of the mind, as if most remote from the body, another love is born in the will, most alien from the commerce of the body. He placed the former in pleasure, the latter in contemplation. He thinks the former revolves around the particular form of one body, the latter around the universal beauty of the whole human race. He says these loves fight against each other in man: the former drives downward to the bestial and voluptuous life; the latter raises upward to the angelic and contemplative life. He wishes the latter to be without perturbation and found in few; the former to be anxious with many passions and occupy the most. 

Therefore, he finished the latter with few words and was more prolix in explaining the passions of the other. Since indeed he explains here the very same things most clearly which you also narrated above, I did not think it necessary to review them at present. But let it suffice to have known that this philosopher mixed some chaos-like formlessness (such as you placed above) into the procreation of love when he said that the dark imagination is illuminated; and from the mixture of that darkness and this light, love takes its origin. Furthermore, who does not see that twin love—the celestial and vulgar—in his words? He places the first origin of the former in the beauty of divine things, and the second in the beauty of bodies. For he understands the sun as the light of God, the ray as the form of bodies. Finally, he wishes his end to respond to the same principle: while the instigation of love carries some as far as the form of the body, and others as far as the form of God.

### SOCRATES WAS A TRUE LOVER AND SIMILAR TO CUPID.
### CHAPTER II.

Enough about love thus far. Let us come to Alcibiades and Socrates. After the guests had praised the paths of lovers enough, it remained for the legitimate worshipers of this god to be praised. Socrates is presented by everyone as the most legitimate lover of all. When he had campaigned openly throughout his whole life in the camps of Cupid without any dissimulation at all, he was never noted by anyone as if he had loved someone dishonorably. The severity of life and the correction of others' crimes...

His frequent corrections had made many powerful men hostile to him, as truth often does, especially Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon—citizens of great influence in the republic—as well as the orators Thrasymachus, Polus, and Callias. Furthermore, he had the comic poet Aristophanes as a most bitter persecutor. Yet those citizens, in the accusation with which they dragged Socrates to judgment, did not charge him with dishonorable loves; nor did his enemies among the orators object to any such thing; nor did Aristophanes the Comic poet, although he collected many other absurd slanders against Socrates at the Dionysia <note>The Great Dionysia was the major Athenian festival where comedies and tragedies were performed.</note>. Do you think that if he had been defiled by such a foul stain—or rather, if he had not been farthest removed from even the suspicion of this crime—he would have escaped the poisonous tongues of such detractors? 

Did you notice, excellent men, in the preceding sections, that while Plato describes the figure of Love itself, he paints a complete image of Socrates? He describes the figure of that deity from the person of Socrates, as if true love and Socrates are most similar, and therefore he, above all others, is the true and legitimate lover. Come now, recall the picture of Love in your mind. You will see Socrates figured within it. Place the person of Socrates before your eyes. You will see a man thin, withered, and squalid; a man naturally melancholic, as it is said, and hairy. Weakened by fasting. Unkempt in the assembly. Naked, moreover—that is, covered only by a simple and old little cloak <note>The *tribon*, a humble philosopher’s cloak.</note>. Walking without shoes. Phaedrus shows in Plato’s works that Socrates was always accustomed to walk in this way. Humble and flying through the lowest places. Socrates’ gaze was always fixed on the ground, as Phaedo says. Furthermore, he frequented common places: he was found either in the shops of Simon the cobbler or in the workshops of sculptors. He used rustic and unpolished words, as Callicles objects to him in the *Gorgias*. Moreover, he was so mild that, though provoked by many injuries and even frequently struck, he is recorded as never having been moved in his spirit. Without a home. When Socrates was asked what country he was from, he said: "A citizen of the world." For there is one's fatherland, where there is good. But he had no private hearth, no soft bed, no delicate food, no fine furniture. Sleeping at the doors in the street under the open sky. In our Socrates, these things signify an open breast and a heart accessible to all. 

Furthermore, because he was delighted by sight and hearing, which are the doors of the soul; because he also walked secure and intrepid, and would lie down anywhere wrapped in his cloak if necessary. Always needy. Who does not know that Socrates was the son of a sculptor and a midwife? And that until his old age he sought his living by his own hand in carving stones, and never had enough to feed himself and his sons? He confessed the poverty of his own mind everywhere, questioning everyone and declaring that he knew nothing. Manly: for he was of a constant mind and invincible opinion, who even looked down upon Archelaus of Macedon, Scopas of Cranon, and Eurylochus of Larissa with a high spirit, as he would not accept the money they sent, nor did he wish to travel to them. Bold and fierce. Alcibiades explains most copiously in the banquet how great his fortitude was in military matters, where Socrates, though he had won at Potidaea, is said to have voluntarily yielded the victory. Vehement: he was indeed, as Zopyrus the Physiognomist <note>A specialist in judging character from facial features.</note> had rightly judged, most excitable. Indeed, while speaking, he often used to toss his fingers and pull his hair because of the vehemence of his oration. Eloquent. Reasons were available to him to carry weight on either side while he discussed. Although he used common words, as Alcibiades says in the banquet, he nevertheless moved the minds of his listeners more than Themistocles, Pericles, and all other orators. 

He lies in wait for the beautiful and the good. Alcibiades says that Socrates was always lying in wait for him. Captured by the love of those who seemed endowed with an honorable nature, Socrates captured them for the study of philosophy with his reasoning. A clever and sagacious Hunter. It has been sufficiently stated above that Socrates was accustomed to hunt for the divine appearance from the form of the body, and Plato testifies to this in the *Protagoras*. A contriver: In many ways, as Plato’s dialogues indicate, he refuted the sophists, exhorted the youth, and educated modest men. Studious and prudent. For there was such prudence in him, and he was so sharp-sighted in foreseeing the future, that whoever dared anything against his advice was ruined, as narrated by Plato in the *Theages*. Philosophizing through his whole life. In his famous defense before the judges, he declared that if they should acquit him of death on the condition that he never philosophize thereafter, he would prefer to die than to cease philosophizing. Enchanter, fascinator, sorcerer, and sophist. For Alcibiades says he is soothed more by Socratic words than by the melody of Marsyas and Olympus, the excellent musicians. Truly, both his accusers and friends testify that a "daemon" <note>A personal tutelary spirit or divine voice.</note> was familiar to him. Aristophanes the comic poet also called Socrates a sophist, as did his accusers. Indeed, he had an equal faculty for exhorting and dehorting. Between wisdom and ignorance. "While all men are ignorant," says Socrates, "I differ from the others only in this: that I am not ignorant of my own ignorance, whereas others are altogether ignorant." Thus he will be in the middle between wisdom and ignorance: because although he did not know the things themselves, he nevertheless knew his own ignorance. For these reasons, 

<margin>Eulogy of Socrates</margin>

Alcibiades judged Socrates to be most similar to Love and therefore the truest lover to be praised after Love itself, so that in his praise we may understand that all who love similarly are praised. You have heard here what the praises of Socrates are, and they are clear in Plato’s words through the mouth of Alcibiades; also in what manner Socrates loved. He who remembers the doctrine of Diotima can know this. For Socrates loved just as Diotima taught above.
