**ON BESTIAL LOVE,**
**which is a species of madness.**
### CHAPTER III

But perhaps someone asks: What does this Socratic love benefit the human race? Why should it be celebrated with such great praises? What harm does its opposite do? I shall indeed speak, having started from a somewhat deeper point. Our Plato defines "fury" in the *Phaedrus* as an alienation of the mind. He teaches that there are two kinds of alienation. One he considers to result from human diseases, the other from God. He calls the former "insanity," and the latter "divine fury." By the disease of insanity, a man is cast down below the human species and is turned into a brute after a fashion. There are two kinds of insanity. One arises from a defect of the brain, the other from the heart. The brain is often occupied by burnt bile <note>Melancholy or "black bile," associated with depression and madness.</note>, often by burnt blood, and sometimes by too much black bile; hence men are sometimes rendered demented. Those who are vexed by burnt bile are most vehemently angered even when provoked by no one; they shout loudly, rush at those in their way, and strike themselves and others. Those who suffer from burnt blood break out into excessive laughter; they boast beyond everyone's custom, promise wonderful things about themselves, and delight in song and dance. Those who are pressed by black bile grieve perpetually; they fashion dreams for themselves, so that they dread present things or fear future ones. And these three species of insanity occur through a defect of the brain. For when those humors are retained in the heart, they produce anguish and anxiety, not dementia; but they produce madness when they have oppressed the head, and so they are said to happen by a defect of the brain. But we judge that that insanity by which those who love ruinously are afflicted is properly caused by a disease of the heart. To these, the most sacred name of "love" is falsely attributed. Yet, lest we seem to be wise against too many people, we shall also use the name for them for the sake of arrangement.

---

**COMMON LOVE**
**is a kind of fascination.**
### CHAPTER IIII

Apply the attention of your ears and mind to what is to be said. Blood in youth is subtle, clear, hot, and sweet. For as age proceeds and the subtler parts are dissolved, it becomes thicker; therefore it also becomes darker. To be sure, what is thin and rare is pure and translucent; the contrary is true for the opposite. Why hot and sweet? Because life and the beginning of living—that is, generation itself—consist in heat and moisture, and seed, the first generation of living things, is hot and moist; such a nature flourishes in childhood and youth. In subsequent ages, it is necessarily changed little by little into the contrary qualities of dryness and coldness. Therefore blood in a youth is subtle, clear, hot, and sweet: because it is subtle, it is clear; because it is fresh, it is hot and moist; because it is hot and moist, it therefore seems sweet. For sweetness occurs in the mixture of the hot and the moist. To what end is this? So that you may understand that the spirits <term>spiritus: the subtle vapors believed to bridge the soul and body</term> in this age are subtle, clear, hot, and sweet. For since these are generated from the heart’s heat out of the purer blood, they are always in us such as the humor of the blood is. Just as the vapor of the spirits is created from the blood in this way, so it emits rays like itself through the eyes as if through glass windows. And just as the sun, the heart of the world, sends down light and through light its virtues to the lower things by its circuit, so the heart of our body, by its own perpetual motion, agitates the blood closest to it and from it diffuses spirits through the whole body, and through them sparks of light, through each limb indeed, but through the eyes most of all. For since the spirit is lightest, it flies out especially to the highest parts of the body; and its light shines out more abundantly through the eyes since they are transparent and the brightest of all parts. That some light, however small, is present in the eyes and brain can be testified by many animals that see at night, whose eyes sparkle in the darkness. And also, if one presses and twists the corner of the eye with a finger in a certain way, one seems to perceive a certain lucid circle within oneself. It is said that the divine Augustus had eyes so clear and bright that when he looked at anyone more sharply, he compelled him to lower his gaze as if before the glare of the sun. Tiberius also is recorded to have had very large eyes, which—what is wonderful—could see even at night and in the dark, but only for a short time and when they first opened from sleep; then they grew dim again. Now, that the ray emitted from the eyes draws...

--- Page 298 ---
280
On the Banquet.

...spiritual vapor with it, and blood with the vapor, we perceive from the fact that bleary and reddened eyes <note>Original: *lippi et rubentes oculi*. "Lippitude" was a common term for eye inflammation believed to be contagious through the gaze.</note> compel the eyes of a nearby person looking at them to suffer from a similar disease by the emission of their ray. Here it appears both that the ray is extended as far as the person met, and that together with the ray, the vapor of corrupted blood flows out, by the contagion of which the eye of the spectator is infected. Aristotle writes that women, when menstrual blood flows down, often foul a mirror with bloody drops by their gaze. I think this happens because the spirit, which is the vapor of the blood, seems to be a kind of thinnest blood, so much so that it escapes the sight of the eyes; but having become thicker on the surface of the mirror, it is clearly perceived. If this should fall upon some more porous material like cloth or linen, it is not seen because it does not remain on the surface of that thing but penetrates it. If it falls upon something dense but rough, such as stones, bricks, and similar things, it is dissipated and broken by the inequality of that body. But a mirror, on account of its hardness, stops the spirit on its surface; on account of its equality and smoothness, it keeps it unbroken; on account of its brightness, it aids and increases the ray of the spirit itself; on account of its coldness, it forces that very thin mist into little drops. By the same logic of speech, as often as we breathe hard with open mouths onto glass, we sprinkle its face with a certain thinnest dew of saliva, since the breath flying out from the saliva, being compressed in that material, falls back into saliva. Therefore, is it a wonder if an eye, opened and intent upon someone, hurls the stings of its rays into the eyes of a bystander? And also, with those stings, which are the vehicles of the spirit, directs that bloody vapor which we call spirit? Hence a poisonous sting pierces through the eyes; and since it is sent from the heart of the striker, it seeks the breast of the struck man as its own proper region; it wounds the heart, and grows dull on its harder back, and returns into blood. This foreign blood, being in some way alien to the nature of the wounded man, infects his own blood; the infected blood becomes sick. From this follows a double fascination. The sight of a foul old man, and of a woman suffering her menses, fascinates a boy. The sight of a youth fascinates an elder. But since the humor of the elder is cold and very slow, it hardly reaches the back of the heart in the child; and being unfit for passage, it moves the heart very little unless it be most soft on account of infancy. This, therefore, is a light fascination; but that other is most grave, through which the younger transfixes the breast of the elder. This is that thing, best friends, of which the Platonic Apuleius complains: "The cause," he says, "and origin of all this present pain, and even the remedy itself and only salvation for me, is you yourself. For those eyes of yours, having slipped through my eyes to my innermost heart, stir up a most sharp fire in my marrow. Therefore have mercy on one perishing for your sake." 

Place before your eyes, I pray, Phaedrus of Myrrhinus and that Theban orator Lysias captured by his love. Lysias gapes at the face of Phaedrus; Phaedrus fixes the sparks of his eyes into the eyes of Lysias. Together with the sparks, he also transmits spirit. The ray of Phaedrus is easily coupled with the ray of Lysias; spirit is also easily joined to spirit. A vapor of this kind, generated from the heart of Phaedrus, immediately seeks the breast of Lysias; by their dullness, it becomes more compact and falls back into the former blood of Phaedrus, so that—what is wonderful—the blood of Phaedrus is now in the heart of Lysias. Hence both break out immediately into a cry: Lysias to Phaedrus, "My heart, Phaedrus, my dearest viscera!" Phaedrus to Lysias, "O my spirit, O my blood, Lysias!" Lysias follows Phaedrus because his heart demands its humor. Lysias pursues Phaedrus because the bloody humor requires its own vessel and demands its own seat. But Lysias pursues Phaedrus more ardently. For a heart lives more easily without a tiny particle of its humor than the humor itself lives without its own heart. A stream needs the fountain more than the fountain needs the streamlet. Therefore, just as iron, having received the quality of a magnet, is indeed drawn to this stone, but does not attract the stone; so Lysias follows Phaedrus more than Phaedrus follows Lysias.

---

**HOW EASILY WE ARE**
**ensnared by love.**
### CHAPTER V

Could someone say: can a thin ray, a most light spirit, a little bit of Phaedrus's blood, so quickly, so vehemently, so perniciously infect the whole of Lysias? This will certainly not seem wonderful if you consider other diseases that arise by contagion—if you consider an itch, the scabies, leprosy, pleurisy, consumption, dysentery, blear-eyedness, or an epidemic. But the amatory contagion happens easily and turns out to be the most serious plague of all. Indeed, that spiritual vapor and blood of the youth, injected entirely into the elder, has four qualities, as we said above. It is clear, subtle, hot, and sweet. Because it is clear, it accords most with the clarity of the eyes and spirits in the elder, it flatters and entices, which causes it to be greedily drunk in by them. Because it is subtle, it flies most quickly into the breast; from there it easily flows through the veins and arteries into the entire body. Because it is hot, it acts and moves vehemently, and more strongly infects the blood of the elder, turning it into its own nature, which Lucretius touches upon thus:
*Hence first into the heart the drop of Venus's sweetness*
*Distilled, and cold care followed after.*
Furthermore, because it is sweet, it somehow cherishes the viscera, feeds them, and delights them. Hence it happens that the whole blood of the man, changed into the nature of the youthful blood, desires the body of that youth, so that it may inhabit its veins, and the humor of fresh blood may glide into veins that are also fresh and tender. It also happens that this sick man is touched by pleasure and pain at the same time. By pleasure, on account of the clarity and sweetness of that vapor and blood; for the former entices, the latter delights. By pain, on account of its subtlety and heat. For the former divides and tears the viscera; the latter takes away from the man what is his own and changes him into the nature of another. By this very change, it does not permit him to rest in himself, but always draws him toward the one by whom he was infected. Lucretius hints at this thus:
*And the mind seeks that body from which it is wounded by love.*
*For mostly all fall toward the wound, and the blood*
*Gushes out toward that part from which we are struck.*
*And if the enemy is near, the red humor reaches him.*
In these verses, Lucretius means that the blood of a man wounded by the ray of eyes flows toward the wounder in the same way that the blood of a man cut by a sword flows toward the striker. If you ask for the reason for this miracle, so to speak, I shall bring it forth. Hector wounds Patroclus and kills him. Patroclus looks at the wounding Hector. Whence his thought judges that he must be avenged—immediately bile is kindled for vengeance; by it, the blood is inflamed and hastens on the spot to the wound, both to cherish that part of the body and also for vengeance. The spirits also run to the same place; because they are light, flying all the way to Hector, they migrate into him; they are preserved by his heat for a time, say for seven hours. At that very time, if Hector should look closely at the wound of the corpse, the wound ejects gore toward Hector; for the gore can flow out toward the enemy in a certain way, both because all heat is not yet extinct and the internal agitation has not yet rested, and because a little before it had been stirred toward him, and finally because the blood seeks its own spirits, and also the spirits attract their own blood. In a similar way, Lucretius hinted that the blood of a man wounded by love hastens into the striker, and we most strongly approve of this.

---

**ON A CERTAIN MARVELOUS**
**effect of common love.**
### CHAPTER VI

Shall I say, most chaste men, what follows, or rather pass it over? I shall certainly say it since the matter itself demands it, even if it seems absurd to say. But who could say shameful things in a non-shameful way? Such a great change of the older man pressing toward the likeness of the younger makes him strive to transfer his whole body into the other and to pour the other's whole body into himself, so that either the fresh humor may follow fresh vessels, or the tenderer vessels may follow the tenderer humor. Hence they are compelled to do many most shameful things among themselves. For since the genital seed flows down from the whole body, they trust that by the mere casting or touch of this, they can hand over the whole body and receive the whole. That Epicurean philosopher Lucretius, the most unhappy of all lovers, felt this in himself:
*Thus, therefore, he who receives strokes from the weapons of Venus,*
*Whether a boy hurls this at him with womanly limbs*
*Or a woman casting love from her whole body,*
*He tends toward the source of the blow and longs to join,*
*And to cast the humor drawn from his body into the other's body.*
*Greedily they press body to body, and join the saliva*
*Of the mouth, and breathe into each other, pressing faces with teeth,*
*In vain: since they can scrape nothing from there,*
*Nor penetrate and go into the other body with the whole body.*
*For they seem at times to want to do this and to struggle.*
*To such an extent they cling greedily in the bonds of Venus,*
*While the limbs of pleasure melt, weakened by force.*
Thus says Lucretius the Epicurean. That lovers also desire to take the whole beloved into themselves, Artemisia, the wife of King Mausolus of Caria, showed; she is said to have loved her husband beyond the belief of human affection, and to have reduced his deceased body to powder and drunk it mixed in water.

---

**COMMON LOVE IS**
**a disturbance of the blood.**
### CHAPTER VII

That this passion is indeed in the blood is proven by the fact that such heat lacks alternating rest. For a continuous fever...

Commentary.
281

...is placed by physicians in the blood; but that which leaves six hours for rest is in the phlegm; that which leaves one day, in the bile; that which leaves two, in the humor of black bile. In the blood, therefore, we rightly place this. Specifically in melancholic blood: as you heard in the speech of Socrates, a fixation always accompanies this contagion of the blood.
