**HOW LOVERS**
**become like the beloved.**
### CHAPTER VIII

Therefore let none of you wonder if you hear that some lover has contracted some likeness or figure of his beloved into his own body. Pregnant women often desire one thing most greedily and think of it vehemently; the vehement thought moves the internal spirits and paints the image of the thought thing upon them. These move the blood similarly and express the image of the thing upon the softest material of the fetus. But the lover desires his delights more ardently than pregnant women; he also thinks more vehemently and firmly. What wonder if faces so clinging and fixed in the breast are purged from thought itself into the spirit, and from the spirit are immediately fixed in the blood, so that daily, when the most soft blood of Phaedrus is generated in the veins of Lysias, the face of Phaedrus can most easily shine back in his own blood? But since the limbs of the body are dried by blood daily, so they revive daily when the dew of nourishment is taken; it follows that every day the body of each man, which has dried out bit by bit, is gradually restored. Moreover, the limbs are restored by blood flowing out from the streamlets of the veins. Therefore, will you wonder if blood painted with a certain likeness has impressed the same upon the limbs? So that Lysias finally seems to have turned out similar to Phaedrus in some colors or features, or dispositions, or gestures.

---

**BY WHOM WE ARE CHIEFLY**
**ensnared.** 
### CHAPTER IX

Perhaps someone will ask: by whom chiefly and in what manner are lovers ensnared, and how are they set free? Women certainly capture men easily; but those who show a certain masculine disposition capture them more easily; and males capture men all the more easily as they are more similar to men than to women, and have a blood and spirit that is clearer, hotter, and subtler: in which thing the amatory ensnarement consists. But among males, those who are most powerful in blood and in some part choleric, having large, gray-blue, and shining eyes, capture men—or rather, the better men—most quickly; especially if they live chastely and have not fouled their serene faces by exhausting the clear juice of their humors through coitus. For these things are properly required to emit those very arrows which wound the heart, as we touched upon above. They are quickly ensnared, moreover, for whom at birth Venus was in Leo, or the Moon looked upon Venus vehemently, and who are endowed with the same complexion <term>complexio: the balance of the four bodily humors</term>. Phlegmatic people, in whom phlegm dominates, are never captured; Melancholic people, in whom black bile dominates, are captured with difficulty; but once captured, they are never released thereafter. When a sanguine person binds a sanguine person, it is a light yoke; a sweet bond, for a similar complexion creates mutual love. Furthermore, the sweetness of this habit offers hope and confidence to the lover. When a choleric binds a choleric, it is a more intolerable slavery. Likeness of complexion creates some mutual benevolence in this case, but that fiery humor of bile disturbs their brains with anger. When a sanguine binds a choleric, or vice versa, on account of the mixture of sweet and sharp humor, a certain alternation of anger and grace, pleasure and pain, arises. When a sanguine binds a melancholic, it is a perpetual but not most miserable knot. For the sweetness of the blood tempers the bitterness of the melancholy. But when a choleric ensnares a melancholic, it is the most destructive plague of all. The most sharp humor of the youth glides everywhere into the viscera of the elder. A soft flame eats the marrow. The unhappy lover is burned. Cholera provokes to anger and slaughter; Melancholy to grief and perpetual complaint. For these, there is often the same end of love as for Phyllis, Dido, and Lucretia. But a phlegmatic or melancholic youth captures no one on account of the thickness of his blood and spirits.

---

**THE MANNER OF ENSNAREMENT.**
### CHAPTER X

In what manner lovers are fascinated, we seem to have said enough above, provided we add this: mortals are then most greatly fascinated when, directing the sharpness of sight to the sharpness of sight with a most frequent gaze, they join lights with lights and drink in a long and miserable love. Of this disease, as Musaeus <note>A legendary pre-Homeric poet.</note> pleases, the eye is the whole cause and origin. Therefore, if someone excels in the brightness of the eyes, even if he is less well-formed in the rest of his limbs, he compels those looking at him to go mad by that logic which we have said. He who is disposed to the contrary invites a certain moderate benevolence rather than ardor. The harmony of the rest of the limbs besides the eyes seems to have not the force of a cause for a sickness of this kind, but the weight of an opportunity. For such a composition encourages one looking from a distance to approach closer; then it holds the one looking closely for a very long time in consideration of itself; but the gaze alone strikes the one lingering. But for that moderate love, the participant of divinity, about which there is the most dispute in this banquet: not the eye alone, but the concord and pleasantness of all parts run together.

---

**THE CURE OF LOVE.**
### CHAPTER XI

Hitherto we have treated how and by whom we are ensnared; it remains for us to teach in a few words how we are set free. The solution is double: one indeed of nature, the other of diligence. Nature is that which is perfected in certain intervals of time. This pertains not only to this disease, but to all. Indeed, an itch remains in the skin as long as the filth of tainted blood flourishes in the veins or the saltiness of phlegm in the limbs. When the blood is purified and the phlegm softened, the itch ceases, and the foul spots of the skin are abolished. Nevertheless, mature diligence in evacuation confers much. Sudden evacuation or anointing is judged most dangerous. The unrest of lovers also necessarily perseveres as long as that infection of the blood, injected into the viscera through fascination, remains and presses the heart with grave care. It feeds the wound in the veins; it burns the limbs with hidden flames. For from the heart into the veins, and from the veins into the limbs, there is a passage. Finally, when this is purged away, the unrest of the lovers—or rather, the madmen—ceases. This requires a long space of time in all; but in melancholics, the longest; especially if they were ensnared by the influence of Saturn. Add that it is most bitter if they are subject to Saturn retrograde, or joined to Mars, or opposite the Sun. Those also are sick for a very long time in whose nativity Venus was in the house of Saturn, or looked upon Saturn and the Moon vehemently. To this natural purgation must be added the industry of most diligent art. We must take care first not to attempt to pluck out or cut off immature things; nor should we divide with the greatest danger what we can more safely wash away; there must be an intermission of habit. Most of all, care must be taken lest the lights of the eyes be joined to the lights of the eyes. If there is any vice in the soul or body of the beloved, it must be revolved diligently in the mind. The mind must be applied to many, various, and grave businesses; the blood must often be reduced; clear wine should be used, and sometimes even drunkenness, so that when the old blood is emptied, new blood may come, and new spirit. It is best to use exercise often until sweat, through which the passages of the body are opened for making purgation. Furthermore, all those things which physicians apply to the defense of the heart and the nourishment of the brain are as helpful as possible. Lucretius also prescribes frequent coitus.
*But it is fitting to flee images, and to scare away*
*The fodder of love from oneself and turn the mind elsewhere,*
*And to cast the humor gathered into any bodies,*
*Nor to retain seed turned by the love of one.*

---

**HOW HARMFUL IS COMMON**
**love.**
### CHAPTER XII

But lest by speaking longer of madness we ourselves go mad, let us conclude in short. That anxious anxiety by which common lovers are vexed day and night is a species of madness; those who, while love lasts, are afflicted first by the fire of bile, then by the burning of black bile, rush into furies and fire; and as if blind, they are ignorant of where they are being thrown headlong. How ruinous this adulterous love is to both the beloved and the lovers, Lysias the Theban and Socrates demonstrate in Plato’s *Phaedrus*. By this fury, therefore, man is rolled down into the nature of beasts.

---

**HOW USEFUL IS DIVINE**
**love, and on its four species.**
### CHAPTER XIII

By divine fury, however, man is raised above human nature and passes into God. Divine fury is the illumination of the rational soul, through which God draws back the soul, which had fallen from the upper things to the lower, back from the lower to the upper. The fall of the soul from the one principle of all things into bodies is effected through four steps: through mind, reason, opinion, and nature. For since in every order of things six steps exist, of...

--- Page 300 ---
282
On the Banquet.

...the highest of which the One itself holds, and the lowest is the body, while the four we have already mentioned are in the middle: it is necessary that whatever falls from the first to the last must fall through the four middle steps. The One itself is the end and measure of all things, free from confusion and multitude. The Angelic Mind is indeed a multitude of ideas, but stable and eternal. The Reason of the soul is a multitude of notions and arguments, mobile but ordered. Opinion, however, is an unordered and mobile multitude of images, but united in substance and points; since the soul itself, in which opinion resides, is one substance occupying no place. Nature—that is, the power of nourishing from the soul—and the complexion of the animal are similar, except that they are diffused through the points of the body. The Body, moreover, is an indeterminate multitude of parts and accidents subject to motion, and a substance divided by points and moments. Our soul regards all these; through these it descends, and through these it ascends. For as it is produced by the One itself, which is the principle of all, it has obtained a certain unity which unites all its essence, powers, and operations; to which and from which the other things in the soul are related, just as the lines of a circle are to and from the center. It unites not only the parts of the soul to each other and to the whole soul, but the whole soul to the One itself, the cause of all things. But as it shines by the ray of the divine mind, it contemplates the ideas of all things through the mind in a stable act. As it regards itself, it thinks the universal reasons of things and runs from principles to conclusions by reasoning. As it regards bodies, it ponders the particular forms and images of mobile things accepted through the senses by opinion. As it touches matter, it uses nature as an instrument with which it unites, moves, and forms matter. From this, generations, increases, and their contraries proceed. You see, therefore, that from the One, which is above eternity, it falls into eternal multitude; from eternity into time; from time into place and matter. It falls, I say, when it departs further from that purity in which it was born by embracing the body.

---

**BY WHAT STEPS DIVINE**
**furies lift up the soul.**
### CHAPTER XIIII

Therefore, just as it descends through four steps, it must necessarily ascend through four. Divine fury is that which lifts one to the upper things, as stands in its definition. There are, then, four species of divine fury. The first is the poetic fury. The second is the mystery fury. The third is prophecy. The amatory affection is the fourth. Poetry is from the Muses, Mystery from Dionysus, Prophecy from Apollo, and Love from Venus. Indeed, the soul cannot return to the One unless it itself is made one. But it has become many, because it has fallen into the body, distributed into various operations, and it regards an infinite multitude of corporal things. From this, its superior parts almost fall asleep, while its inferior parts dominate the others. The former are affected by torpor, the latter by perturbation. The whole soul is filled with discord and lack of harmony. Therefore, the poetic fury is first necessary, which through musical tones may rouse what is torpid; through harmonic sweetness may soothe what is disturbed; and finally, through the consonance of diverse things, may drive out dissonant discord and temper the various parts of the soul. Nor is this enough. For multitude and diversity still remain in the soul. Therefore, there comes the mystery pertaining to Dionysus, which through expiations, sacrifices, and all divine worship directs the intention of all parts to the mind by which God is worshiped. Whence, when the individual parts of the soul have been reduced to one mind, the soul has now become a certain whole one out of many. But in the third place, there is need for this fury which may reduce the mind to unity itself, the head of the soul. Apollo effects this through prophecy. For when the soul rises above the mind into unity, it foretells the future. Finally, when the soul has become one—one, I say, which is in the very nature and essence of the soul—it remains that it immediately recall itself to the One which is above essence, that is, God. The celestial Venus completes this through love—that is, the desire for divine beauty and the ardor for the good. Thus the first fury tempers the unharmonious and dissonant. The second makes the tempered parts into a whole one. The third makes the whole one above the parts. The fourth leads into the One which is above essence and above the whole. 

Plato in the *Phaedrus* calls the mind dedicated to divine things the "charioteer" in the soul of man; the unity of the soul, the "charioteer’s head"; Reason and Opinion running through natural things, the "good horse"; confused Phantasy and the appetite of the senses, the "bad horse"; the nature of the whole soul, the "chariot," because its motion is as if circular, beginning from itself and finally returning to itself when it notices its own nature. Where its consideration, having proceeded from the soul, returns into the same. He gives wings to the soul by which it may be carried into the heights; one of which we think is that investigation by which the mind assidiously strives for truth; the other, the desire for the good, by which our will is always affected. These parts of the soul lose their order when they are confused by the disturbing body. Therefore, the first fury distinguishes the good horse—that is, reason and opinion—from the bad horse—that is, from confused phantasy and the appetite of the senses. The second subjects the bad horse to the good, and the good to the charioteer—that is, the mind. The third directs the charioteer into his own head—that is, into the unity of the apex of the mind. The last turns the head of the charioteer into the head of all things. There the charioteer is blessed, and standing the horses at the manger—that is, at divine beauty, accommodating all the parts of the soul subject to him—he offers them ambrosia, and nectar to drink above that—that is, the vision of beauty and joy from the vision. These are the works of the four furies. About which he disputes generally in the *Phaedrus*, but properly about the poetic fury in the *Ion*, and about the amatory in the *Symposium*. The books of Orpheus can be testimony that he was occupied by all these furies; we have received that Sappho, Anacreon, and Socrates were especially seized by the amatory fury.

---

**OF ALL THESE FURIES,**
**love is more excellent.**
### CHAPTER XV

The amatory fury is the most powerful and excellent of all. Most powerful, I say, because all others necessarily need it; for we do not attain poetry, nor mysteries, nor prophecy without great study, flaming piety, and sedulous worship of divinity. But what else do we call study, piety, and worship but love? Therefore, all loves consist in power. It is also the most excellent because the others are referred to this as to an end. Moreover, this brings us closest to God who saves us. These four furies, to be sure, four adulterous affections seem falsely to imitate. Poetic fury is imitated by that common music which only flatters the ears. Mystery fury by the vain superstition of many men. Prophetic fury by the fallacious conjecture of human skill. Amatory fury by the impulse of lust. For true love is nothing other than a certain effort of flying to divine beauty, excited by the sight of corporal beauty. But adulterous love is a precipitation from sight into touch.

---

**HOW USEFUL IS SOCRATIC**
**love.**
### CHAPTER XVI

You ask what Socratic love confers? First indeed, it confers much on Socrates himself for recovering those wings by which he may fly back to his fatherland. Then, it confers much on his city for living honorably and happily. For men, not stones, make a city. But men must be cared for from a tender age just as trees are from their younger stages, and directed to the best fruit. Parents and pedagogues have the care of boys. But youths do not cross the boundaries of parents and pedagogues before they are depraved by the wicked custom of the common people. They would indeed follow the higher rule of living inbred by their masters, were they not deflected from it by the use and custom of wicked men, especially those who flatter them. What then will Socrates do? Will he permit the youth, who are the seed of the future republic, to be corrupted by the contagion of the shameful? But where is the love of fatherland? Socrates will therefore succumb to his fatherland, and he will free its sons—his own brothers—from this destruction. Perhaps he will write laws by which he will segregate lascivious men from the company of youth. But we cannot all be Lycurguses or Solons. The authority for establishing laws is given to few; very few obey the laws of the hearth. What then? Will he use force, and having laid on a hand, drive away the elders from the youth? But only Hercules is said to have fought with monsters; for others, violence of this kind is most dangerous. Perhaps he will warn, rebuke, and scold wicked men. But the disturbed mind despises the words of a warner, and what is worse, it rages against the monitor. For which reason Socrates was struck by one with a fist and by another with a heel while he was attempting that. Only one way of salvation remains for the youth: the company of Socrates. Therefore that wisest of the Greeks, bound by charity, mixes himself everywhere, and a great crowd of youth follows with him in conviviality. Thus the true lover, as a shepherd, protects the flock of lambs from the whirlpool and plague of false lovers, as if from wolves. But since equals most easily congregate with equals, he makes himself equal to the younger by purity of life, simplicity of words, games, jokes, and witticisms. And he makes himself a boy from an old man, first so that he may eventually render the boys old in wisdom through domestic and pleasant familiarity. Youth prone to pleasure is held by pleasure alone and flees rigid teachers. Hence the tutor of our youth, having neglected the administration of his own affairs for the safety of his fatherland, takes up the care of the younger, and first catches them with the sweetness of pleasant company. Thus having ensnared them, he then warns them more severely. Finally, he chastises them with a more rigid censure.

--- Page 301 ---
# Axiochus.

...and the perpetual labors of contests. From this point, a deceptive old age creeps in, where everything weak and fragile in nature converges. Unless one quickly returns life as if it were a debt, nature—standing over one's head like a moneylender—demands its interest. Sight is taken from one, hearing from another, and very often both; but if someone lingers too long, nature torments him with debility and afflicts his limbs with disease. Thus, some people in deep old age return to childhood, and in their spirit (*animo*), the elderly become boys twice over. 

On account of this very thing, the gods (since human affairs are most known to them) remove those whom they value most from life. Thus Agamedes and Trophonius [[notes: legendary architects of the temple at Delphi]], when they had built the temple of Pythian Apollo and prayed that what was best for them be given, never rose again once they had fallen asleep. So too the priests of Argive Juno [[notes: Kleobis and Biton, cf. Herodotus I.31]]: when their mother prayed that Juno would return some grace to them for their piety—for when the oxen were late, they themselves took the place of the draft animals and pulled the vehicle to the temple—they died that night after their prayers. 

It would be long to recount the sayings of the poets, who in their more divine poems chant of the things pertaining to our life as if from an oracle, lamenting it. I am satisfied to remember the words of one most worthy of mention, who said: "How the gods above have spun a wretched state for mortals' age, so that as they live, they endure through all things that must pass away." [[notes: cf. Homer, Iliad 24.525-526]]. And again: "For all the race of men, the worst lot of life stands, for whoever breathe and move upon the earth." [[notes: cf. Homer, Iliad 17.446-447]]. 

And what does he say about Amphiaraus? "Jupiter loves him with all his heart, and great Apollo loves him, yet he did not reach the goals of a just age." [[notes: cf. Homer, Odyssey 15.245]]. Regarding him who commands: "Let the newborn weep, who enters such great evils of life," what does it seem to you? 

But let me make an end of commemorating others, lest I lead the matter further than I intended. For what way of life or what art shall anyone choose, so that he does not complain of it and find offense in present circumstances? Let us review the craftsmen and the mercenary arts: working from night until night, barely enduring the necessary expenses of life, lamenting themselves and filling their every waking moment with sorrow and tears. 

Or should we speak of the sailor, penetrating through such great dangers, who (as Bias [[notes: one of the Seven Sages of Greece]] says) is neither among the dead nor among the living? For as a man of the land, as if of an ambiguous genus, he has cast himself into the sea and made himself entirely a subject to the judgment of fortune. 

"But agriculture is sweet," you say. It is indeed, but is it not entirely, as they say, a wound? Always having a ready cause for pain—now complaining of drought, now rains, now blight, now rust, now untimely heat or cold? 

And that most honored care for the Republic—for I pass over many things—through what great anxieties is it snatched? What joys it has are always trembling like a small boil and full of stings, while its rejections are bitter and a thousand times worse than death. For who could be happy living by the judgment of the common crowd? Even if he is favored and applauded, he is tossed about as the plaything of the people, hissed at, condemned, dead—and you, a pitiable living soul. 

For where, Axiochus, you who are involved in the republic—where is Miltiades? Where did Themistocles go? Where Ephialtes? Where also those who were recently kings and leaders? For I myself was not asked for my opinion (nor did it seem honorable to me to become a partner in power with a maddened people). But Theramenes and Callixenus, having then appointed the governing magistrates, brought it about that men were killed without trial. You and Euryptolemus stood against them, alone out of thirty thousand gathered in the assembly. 

**AXIOCHUS:** These things are as you say, Socrates; and therefore a satiety of that platform has seized me, and nothing has seemed more bitter to me than the republic. 

**SOCRATES:** That is indeed clear to those who have been involved in the business itself. For you say these things like one who has looked on from a sublime height; but we who have faced the danger, how much more exactly do we know it? For the people, dearest Socrates, are ungrateful, peevish, cruel, envious, and ignorant—as they are collected from the dregs of the crowd and from the foolish and insolent. He who flatters them is himself much more miserable. 

Since therefore, Axiochus, you think this art, which is the most liberal of all, to be the most abominable of all, what of the remaining kinds of life? Shall we not think they should be entirely fled? I even heard Prodicus [[notes: a Sophist and contemporary of Socrates]] saying at one time that death pertains neither to the living nor to the dead. 

**AXIOCHUS:** How do you say such things, Socrates? 

**SOCRATES:** Because it is not around the living; while those who have died are no longer. Therefore, it is not with you, for you have not yet died; nor, if anything should happen to you, will it be around you in the future, for you will not exist. Foolish, therefore, is the grief concerning Axiochus; just as he is not, nor will be, for Axiochus to be tortured in mind. It would be similar to someone fearing Scylla or a Centaur, which neither threaten you now nor will ever be present for your destruction. For fear belongs to existing things; but of things which are not, there is no one who is terrified. 

**AXIOCHUS:** You have indeed brought forth these learned words from that talkativeness which is now sprouting up. For from that source come these ineptitudes of words, prepared for enticing the youth. But the loss of the good things in life makes me sad—even if, Socrates, you should rattle off a speech more probable than the one you just gave. For the wandering mind is not led aptly by coherent words, nor do those things reach the mind; rather, prepared for the ostentation and splendor of oratory, they are far from the truth. But sickness of the soul is by no means halted by captive words; it rests only on those which are strong enough to penetrate all the way to the mind. 

**SOCRATES:** You are joining things together imprudently, Axiochus; you are substituting a sense of evils for the deprivation of goods, forgetting that you will then be dead. For the one who loses goods is hurt by the contrary evils he suffers; but for the one who does not exist, nothing takes the place of that which he is deprived of. How, then, could there be any pain in him who will exhibit no notice of things that hurt? 

If you did not from the beginning, Axiochus, through your imprudence, combine some sense with death, you would not fear it at all. Now you subvert yourself, fearing the soul will be lost, and you surround that loss with another soul. You are disturbed that you will be without sensation, and you think that you will perceive this very "not-sensing" with another sense. 

To this, there are many very beautiful reasons concerning the immortality of the soul (*animi immortalitate*). For mortal nature could not raise itself to such varied things as to despise the strength of huge beasts, cross the seas, build cities, establish republics, look even into the heavens, and see the revolutions of the stars and the courses of the sun and moon—their risings and settings, eclipses, speed, distances, equinoxes, and double conversions, the Pleiades, the winds of winter and summer, the falling of rains and the horrendous snatching of whirlwinds—so that it might hand down the apprehended labors of the world to the ages, unless some divine spirit (*diuinus spiritus*) was within our minds, by which it might reach the embrace and knowledge of such great things. 

[[page number: 647]]

# Axiochus. 647

Therefore, Axiochus, you pass not into death, but into immortality; not into the loss of goods, but into a purer perception of them. You do not go to pleasures confused with a mortal body, but to those purged entirely of all troubles. For you will depart from this prison to that place where all things are restful and happy, where there is no failing old age. You will spend a tranquil life there, free from all inconveniences, placid with serene quiet, contemplating the nature of things, and devoted to philosophy—not for the crowd, nor for appearance, but for pure and genuine truth. 

**AXIOCHUS:** You have moved me to the opposite by this speech, Socrates. For no longer does fear hold me, but a longing (*desiderium*) for death. And so that I, imitating the rhetoricians, may say something more grand: I have for some time been conceiving of things with a higher mind, and I am reviewing that immense and divine course. I have collected myself from my weakness and have become, as it were, new again. 

**SOCRATES:** If you wish, take another account which Gobryas the Magus [[notes: a Persian priest/sage]] related to me. He said that during the passage of Xerxes into Greece, his grandfather of the same name was sent to Delos to protect that island in which two deities were born [[notes: Apollo and Artemis]]. There he learned from certain bronze tablets, which Opis and Hecaergus had brought from the Hyperboreans, that after the soul is released from the body, it departs to a certain unknown place in a subterranean recess, in which is the palace of Pluto, no less than the court of Jupiter. 

For while the Earth holds the middle of the world, its circuit is a sphere, of which the upper gods have received one hemisphere, and the lower gods the other—these being the brothers of the former, and those the sons of brothers. The vestibules that provide entry to Pluto's kingdom are fortified with iron bars and keys. For him who opens them, the river Acheron receives him, after which is Cocytus. When one has crossed these, it is necessary to approach Minos and Rhadamanthus. They call this the Plain of Truth, and in it the judges sit, reviewing the life of each person who arrives, and by what reason each, inhabiting a body, finished his span of age. 

There is no opportunity for lying there. But for whomever a better *daemon* (spirit/guiding genius) breathed during life, they inhabit the seats of the pious (*sedes piorum*). There, all the hours overflow with every kind of fertile fruit, springs glide with pure water, and meadows of all sorts bloom with various flowers. There are gatherings of philosophers, theaters of poets, circles of dancers, and musical harmonies. Added to this are carefully prepared banquets, and an abundance of food supplying itself; there is immortal joy, hilarity, and the most pleasant way of life. For they have neither cold nor heavy heat, but a temperate air illuminated by the rays of the sun. Here also is a certain dignity for the initiated, and they perform religious rites in that same place. 

How, then, will honor not be held for you, a kinsman of the gods? For the ancient story is that Hercules and Father Liber [[notes: Dionysus]], descending to the underworld, were initiated here, and that they conceived the confidence to go there from Eleusis [[notes: site of the Eleusinian Mysteries]]. 

But those whose lives were spent in crime are snatched through Tartarus by the Furies to the chaos of Erebus, where the place of the impious is. There are the unfillable urns of the daughters of Danaus, the thirst of Tantalus, the entrails of Tityus, and Sisyphus's unending stone, the end of which begins again with another labor. There, with beasts licking around them, they are endlessly scorched by torches and afflicted by the torture of all punishments, mangled by immense torments. 

I heard these things from Gobryas; but the judgment concerning them will be yours, Axiochus. For by reason alone I know this one thing constantly: that every soul is immortal which is transferred from this place, and entirely devoid of pain. Whether you go upward or downward, Axiochus, you must be happy, you who have lived uprightly and piously. 

**AXIOCHUS:** I am ashamed, Socrates, to say something to you. I am so far from fearing death that I am now held by a love of it, so much has this—and that other—almost celestial speech persuaded me. I even despise life, as one who is about to transition to a better domicile. Now, little by little, I will review these things that have been said with myself. But you, Socrates, make sure you are with me at noon. 

**SOCRATES:** I will do as you said. I too am returning to my walk at Cynosarges [[notes: a gymnasium outside Athens]], from where I was called here.

-> The End of the Axiochus of Plato <-

[[page number: 648]]

# SIX DIALOGUES OF PLATO, WHICH, AS IF SPURIOUS, HAD NOT YET BEEN RECEIVED INTO THIS VOLUME: NOW CONVERTED FROM GREEK INTO LATIN FOR THE FIRST TIME BY SEBASTIANUS CORRADUS.

-> **SEBASTIANUS CORRADUS SENDS HEARTY GREETINGS TO SYLVESTRO MAUROCENO, SON OF IOANNES.** <-

[[notes: This is a dedicatory letter from the translator, Sebastianus Corradus, to his patron Sylvestro Mauroceno. Corradus was an Italian humanist and scholar (c. 1510–1556).]]

**W**hen six dialogues are circulated with the works of Plato—which, if they were not written by Plato as many think, were nevertheless so polished by the author (whoever he was) in Platonic sentiments and words that they may now deservedly be called Platonic, and ought to be transcribed with the Platonic works, as has been done until now. I, judging them worthy to be read even by our people who do not know Greek letters, converted them from Greek into Latin in previous years while I was with you in Venice. I did this both so that I might consume that leisure, which was then given to me, chiefly in these writings, and so that I might dedicate them to you; by which I might return some gratitude to you for your so many benefits toward me—if not equal to what I should owe, then at least what I could, until a more convenient occasion might be given. 

But afterward, recalled by the letters of our Senate, and indeed by the voice of almost our entire Republic, I was put in charge of a business in which, though there is much honor, I alone have always sustained such a burden in it that I have never been able to attend to this interpretation nor any private matter in all this time. Now the *Accensi* [[notes: likely a literary academy]], who are the academics of Reggio, young men truly "inflamed" by the love of virtue and no less of me, you, and your many virtues than of all letters and doctrines, when they had learned of these dialogues in some way and greatly desired to read them, they took pains, and indeed diligently, so that the entire month of August might be granted to me by the Senate as vacant; and I was able to see and consider them a little more accurately. 

I, however, although I was away for the greater part of the month after this vacation was obtained, having set out for the countryside and Bologna, nevertheless saw to it that, as far as was possible in such a short time, I sent them to you written by my own hand as studiously and diligently as I could: so that, if they seem worthy to you to appear in your name, you might see to their publishing there, and love me and all the *Accensi* who venerate you and who desire to be in your debt as much as possible. Farewell. August 30, 1542. Reggio Emilia.

### ON THE JUST.
### I.
### SOCRATES, THE GUEST.

**SOCRATES:** Can you tell us what is "The Just" (*Iustum*)? Or does it seem to you a thing unworthy of speaking about? 

**GUEST:** To me indeed it seems worthy, and very much so. 

**SOCRATES:** What is it then? 

**GUEST:** What else should I say it is, except all those things which are judged just? 

**SOCRATES:** I would not want you to answer me that way. But just as, if you were to ask me what an Eye is: I would say to you, it is that by which we see. And if you should command me further, I would show something else. And if you ask me of what thing "Mind" (*Animus*) is the name: I would tell you, it is that by which we know something. If you should ask what "Voice" is: I would respond that it is that by which we differ. I would wish you also to speak thus: that "The Just" is that which we use for doing something, as was said concerning those things I just asked about. 

**GUEST:** I certainly cannot answer you so easily. 

**SOCRATES:** Since therefore you cannot answer so easily, we will be able to find it more easily by this reasoning. Come, considering what, chiefly, do we discern Great things and Small things? Is it not by measurement (*mensura*)? 

**GUEST:** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** But besides measurement, by what art then? Is it not the art of measuring? 

**GUEST:** Quite so. 

**SOCRATES:** What of Light and Heavy things? Is it not the scale (*statera*)? 

**GUEST:** Yes. 

**SOCRATES:** And after the scale, by what art then? Is it not the art of weighing? 

**GUEST:** Most of all. 

**SOCRATES:** What then? By what instrument, I pray, and by what art besides do we discern Just and Unjust things? Or is that not yet manifest to you? 

**GUEST:** Not by Hercules. 

**SOCRATES:** But again in this way. When we disagree about Larger and Smaller things, who among us judges that matter? Is it not those skilled in the art of measuring? 

**GUEST:** So it is. 

**SOCRATES:** When we contend about Many and Few, who judges? Is it not the Reckoners (*Ratiocinatores*)? 

**GUEST:** True. 

**SOCRATES:** But when we litigate among ourselves concerning Just and Unjust things: tell me, I pray, to whom should we go, so that they may bear a sentence on the matter under dispute? 

**GUEST:** Would you mean judges (*iudices*), O Socrates? 

**SOCRATES:** You have found it correctly. Come now, 

[[page number: 649]]

# On the Just. 649

tell me this also: what do those skilled in the art of measuring do when they discern Great and Small? Do they not measure? 

**GUEST:** Surely. 

**SOCRATES:** What? Those who judge concerning Heavy and Light, do they not weigh? 

**GUEST:** They weigh. 

**SOCRATES:** What now will you say of these who pronounce concerning Just and Unjust? Answer. 

**GUEST:** I certainly cannot. 

**SOCRATES:** Would you not say they reason (*ratiocinari*) correctly? 

**GUEST:** I suppose so. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore the judges, who bear sentence between us, certainly reason when they judge concerning Just and Unjust. 

**GUEST:** I agree. 

**SOCRATES:** But those who practice the art of measuring measure small and large things. For we said that measurement is that by which such things are judged. 

**GUEST:** We said so. 

**SOCRATES:** But again, those weigh heavy and light things who have been able to put their study into the art of weighing. For the scale was for us that very thing by which those things are accustomed to be discerned. 

**GUEST:** It was indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** But those who are held by the study of numbering count Many and Few. For we posited that Number is that by which things of this sort are distinguished. 

**GUEST:** We did. 

**SOCRATES:** But judges, as we just agreed, reason when they judge between us concerning Just and Unjust. For Reason (*Ratio*) is that by which those things are separated. 

**GUEST:** O! You speak well, Socrates. 

**SOCRATES:** And truly indeed. Therefore Reason seems to be entirely that by which Just and Unjust things are judged. 

**GUEST:** It seems so. 

**SOCRATES:** Now indeed Just and Unjust must be defined: so that, if someone should ask us: "Since measurement, the art of measuring, and the man skilled in that art discern the Great itself and the Small, what then is Great and Small?" We would say surely that Great is that which exceeds, and Small that which is exceeded. Likewise, if he should ask: "When the scale, the art of weighing, and the man studious of that art discern the Heavy and Light, what is Heavy and Light?" We would respond that Heavy is that which, placed in the balance, sinks; while Light is that which is carried upward. 

So now, if someone asks us: "Since Reason and the judicial art and the judge discern Just and Unjust, what is Just and Unjust?" Will we have something to answer him, or will we still have nothing? 

**GUEST:** Nothing. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you think men endowed with injustice are so voluntarily, or against their will? I say it this way: Do you believe men act unjustly and are unjust voluntarily, or against their will? 

**GUEST:** O, voluntarily, Socrates: for they are wicked. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore you judge wicked and unjust men to be so voluntarily? 

**GUEST:** I certainly judge so. Do you not? 

**SOCRATES:** Not I, if only one ought to believe the Poet. 

**GUEST:** Which poet? 

**SOCRATES:** He who said, "No one is evil by choice, nor good against his will." [[notes: a common Socratic paradox, often attributed to Solon or Evenus]]. 

**GUEST:** But Socrates, the old proverb holds it right: "Poets lie in many things." 

**SOCRATES:** It would be a wonder indeed if this poet lied in this matter. Therefore, if you have leisure, let us see whether he spoke false or true. 

**GUEST:** There is leisure. 

**SOCRATES:** Come now, which do you lead to be just: to Lie, or to speak Truth? 

**GUEST:** To speak Truth. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore to Lie is unjust? 

**GUEST:** Unjust. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you think to Deceive is just, or Not to deceive? 

**GUEST:** Not to deceive, certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** To Deceive, then, is unjust? 

**GUEST:** Unjust. 

**SOCRATES:** What indeed of Harming: is it just, or is Benefiting? 

**GUEST:** Benefiting. 

**SOCRATES:** To Harm—is that not unjust? 

**GUEST:** Unjust. 

**SOCRATES:** Certainly to speak truth, and Not to deceive, and to Benefit is just; but to Lie, and to Deceive, and to Harm is unjust. 

**GUEST:** By Hercules, it is so. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you feel the same concerning enemies? 

**GUEST:** By no means, Socrates. But to Harm enemies is just, while to Benefit them is unjust. 

**SOCRATES:** Is it therefore just for us to harm enemies even by deceiving them? 

**GUEST:** Why not? 

**SOCRATES:** What then of Lying, so that we may deceive and offend enemies: is it not just? 

**GUEST:** Just. 

**SOCRATES:** What? Do you not lead it to be just for us to benefit friends? 

**GUEST:** I do indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** By Not deceiving them, or for the sake of some utility for them, by Deceiving them? 

**GUEST:** Even by Deceiving them. 

**SOCRATES:** But while deceiving them it is just to benefit them: yet is it by not lying, or also by Lying? 

**GUEST:** Even by Lying. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore to Lie and to speak Truth—does it not seem that both are both just and unjust? 

**GUEST:** It seems so. 

**SOCRATES:** And to Deceive, both just and unjust? 

**GUEST:** It seems so. 

**SOCRATES:** And to Harm, both just and unjust? 

**GUEST:** That also. 

**SOCRATES:** All these things, since they are of this sort, are they not both just and unjust? 

**GUEST:** They are, as it appears. 

**SOCRATES:** Hear the rest: I have a right eye and a left one, just as other men do? 

**GUEST:** You have. 

**SOCRATES:** A right nostril and a left one? 

**GUEST:** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES:** And a right hand and a left one? 

**GUEST:** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** Since therefore you, naming these same things, say that some of mine are Right and some are Left: if I should ask you which they are, could you say that these indeed on this side are Right, and those on that side are Left? 

**GUEST:** I could. 

**SOCRATES:** Now go there also. Since naming these same things, you said some were Just and some were Unjust, can you say which are just and which are unjust? 

**GUEST:** Each of these, done appropriately and in its time, seems to me to be just; but the contrary, unjust. 

**SOCRATES:** They seem correctly. Therefore, each of these things which one does opportunely, he does Justly; he who does the contrary, Unjustly. 

**GUEST:** So the matter holds. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, he who does just things is just; he who does unjust things, Unjust. 

**GUEST:** No one denies it. 

**SOCRATES:** Who, therefore, can at the opportune time Cut, Burn, and Thresh? 

**GUEST:** The doctor (*Medicus*). 

**SOCRATES:** Because he knows, or for some other reason? 

**GUEST:** Because he knows. 

**SOCRATES:** Who can opportunely Dig, Plow, and Sow? 

**GUEST:** The farmer (*Agricola*). 

**SOCRATES:** Because he knows, or because he does not know? 

**GUEST:** Because he knows. 

**SOCRATES:** In other things also in the same way, he who knows can do opportune things, and when it is necessary, and in his own time; he who does not know, the contrary? 

**GUEST:** He can. 

**SOCRATES:** He who knows how to Lie, and Deceive, and Benefit, can do each of these things both when it is necessary and in his own time; but he who does not know, cannot. 

**GUEST:** You speak the truth. 

**SOCRATES:** He who does these things opportunely, is he not called just? 

**GUEST:** He is called so. 

**SOCRATES:** Does he do these things through knowledge (*scientiam*)? 

**GUEST:** He does. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore the just man is just through knowledge? 

**GUEST:** He is. 

**SOCRATES:** The unjust man, through the contrary, is unjust? 

**GUEST:** It is evident. 

**SOCRATES:** The just man is just through wisdom (*sapientiam*)? 

**GUEST:** Doubtless. 

**SOCRATES:** And the unjust man is unjust through ignorance (*in fcientiam*)? [[notes: OCR 'f' for 's'; read *inscientiam*]]. 

**GUEST:** It follows. 

**SOCRATES:** It seems from these things that that very thing which our ancestors left to us under the name of Wisdom is called Justice; while that which is called Ignorance may deservedly be called Injustice. 

**GUEST:** It seems so. 

**SOCRATES:** But men—are they ignorant by choice, or unwillingly? 

**GUEST:** Unwillingly. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore they are also Unjust unwillingly? 

**GUEST:** It appears so. 

**SOCRATES:** But unjust men—are they Wicked? 

**GUEST:** They are. 

**SOCRATES:** Are they not wicked and unjust unwillingly? 

**SOCRATES:** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES:** But through injustice they act unjustly? 

**GUEST:** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** Through that which they do unwillingly? 

**GUEST:** Through that very thing. 

**SOCRATES:** But through that which they do unwillingly, that cannot be done which is called Voluntary. 

**GUEST:** Certainly not. 

[[page number: 650]]

# On Virtue.

**SOCRATES:** But through injustice is born that which we called acting unjustly. 

**GUEST:** It is born. 

**SOCRATES:** But we said Injustice is that which they do unwillingly. 

**GUEST:** We said so. 

**SOCRATES:** Unwillingly, therefore, they act unjustly, and are unjust, and are wicked. 

**GUEST:** Unwillingly, as it appears. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore the Poet did not lie in that matter. 

**GUEST:** It does not seem so.

### ON VIRTUE,
### WHETHER IT CAN BE HANDED DOWN BY TEACHING.
### II.
### SOCRATES, A FRIEND.

**SOCRATES:** Can virtue (*Virtus*) be handed down by teaching, or is it rather something that cannot be acquired? Do men become good by nature, or by some other way? 

**FRIEND:** I do not have anything to answer you now, Socrates. 

**SOCRATES:** But let us consider this very thing thus. Come, if someone wished to become good in that faculty by which cooks are good, who are considered the best, from where would he become so? 

**FRIEND:** Clearly from there, if he learned from good cooks. 

**SOCRATES:** What if he wished to become a good Doctor? By setting out to whom would he become a good doctor? 

**FRIEND:** To some one of those who are good doctors. 

**SOCRATES:** But if he desired to be good in that art by which Smiths are good? 

**FRIEND:** To some one of the smiths. 

**SOCRATES:** But if he strongly desired to turn out good in that virtue by which men are both Good and Wise, where should we say he must set out? 

**FRIEND:** I judge to some one of those who are good men, provided that he who desires to learn is fit for thoroughly learning that virtue; for where else could he set out? 

**SOCRATES:** Come, what good men have there been in our city, so that we may weigh whether men of this sort likewise make others good? 

**FRIEND:** Thucydides, Themistocles, Aristides, and Pericles. 

**SOCRATES:** Can we refer to the teacher of each of these? 

**FRIEND:** We cannot; for it is not said. 

**SOCRATES:** What? Can we name a disciple, either foreign or citizen, free or slave, who can affirm that he was made both Good and Wise through their company? 

**FRIEND:** Neither is this said. 

**SOCRATES:** Were they perhaps envious, such that they did not want to impart virtue to others? 

**FRIEND:** Perhaps. 

**SOCRATES:** Was it for this reason: that they feared lest others become their rivals, just as Cooks, Doctors, and Smiths do? For they do not think it useful for themselves if many become adversaries to them in their art; nor convenient if they themselves live among many like themselves. Is it therefore in the same way also inconvenient for good men to live with those like themselves? 

**FRIEND:** It can happen. 

**SOCRATES:** Are not the same men both Good and Just? 

**FRIEND:** They are. 

**SOCRATES:** Is there anyone to whom it can be useful to associate not with the good, but with the wicked? 

**FRIEND:** I cannot say. 

**SOCRATES:** Can you therefore not even say this: whether it is the part of the good to harm, but of the wicked to benefit; or the contrary? 

**FRIEND:** The contrary. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you assert that the good help, but the wicked hurt? 

**FRIEND:** I assert it. 

**SOCRATES:** Is there therefore anyone who prefers to be hurt rather than helped? 

**FRIEND:** Certainly none. 

**SOCRATES:** No one, therefore, prefers to live among those who harm, rather than among those who are useful. 

**FRIEND:** The matter is as you say. 

**SOCRATES:** No one therefore among good men takes it badly if another becomes good and similar to himself. 

**FRIEND:** No one, as it appears from this reasoning. 

**SOCRATES:** Have you heard that Cleophantus was the son of Themistocles? 

**FRIEND:** I have heard. 

**SOCRATES:** Surely Themistocles, who envied no one for their goodness, if only he was good (as he truly was and as is said by us), would never have prohibited his son from becoming as good as possible through envy. 

**FRIEND:** Never. 

**SOCRATES:** On account of this, he wished his son to be taught the art of riding, so that he might be skilled and good in it. For he mounted the horse upright, and upright he threw javelins from horses, and he did many other and wonderful things. He also took care that he was instructed and taught in many other things besides, whatever things are handed down by good preceptors. Have you not heard these things from your elders? 

**FRIEND:** Indeed often. 

**SOCRATES:** No one therefore can accuse the nature of this son as being bad. 

**FRIEND:** No one indeed justly, as is manifest from these things which you say. 

**SOCRATES:** But concerning Cleophantus himself, the son of Themistocles, in those things in which the father was wise, have you ever heard from any young man or old man that he was a man both good and wise? 

**FRIEND:** Never. 

**SOCRATES:** Is it therefore to be thought that Themistocles had his son instructed in these things which we mentioned, but in Wisdom, by which he himself was wise, he wished him to become no better than any neighbor, if Virtue could be acquired? 

**FRIEND:** Hardly likely. 

**SOCRATES:** Such a teacher of virtue indeed was he whom you proposed. But let us look at Aristides: he educated Lysimachus, and gave effort so that he might be erudite most beautifully of all Athenians in all these things which are in the faculty of teachers; yet he made him a man better than no one. For both I and you have not only seen him, but even met him. 

**FRIEND:** True. 

**SOCRATES:** Now indeed you know Paralus and Xanthippus, of whom you seem to me to have loved one, so raised and instructed by Pericles that they yielded to no one of the Athenians in the art of riding; in Music besides, and other kinds of contests, and even in all other things which are handed down by art, he labored vehemently so that they were no less erudite than others. But did the father not want them to become good men? 

**FRIEND:** Perhaps they would have become so, Socrates, had the young men not died. 

**SOCRATES:** You indeed rightly succor your loved ones; but Pericles, nevertheless, if virtue were obtainable and he himself were able to make them good, would have made them wise in his own virtue much rather than in Music and the study of contests. But that cannot be compared. For even Thucydides raised two sons, Melesias and Stephanus, for whom you could not say those things which you just said for the sons of Pericles. For both you and I knew one of them even into old age, and the other indeed beyond. And these the father wished to be taught so that they might know other things well, but especially so that they might wrestle most beautifully of all the Athenians. For he handed them over to be instructed, one indeed to Xanthias and the other to Eudorus. These masters themselves then seemed to excel all in the art of wrestling. 

**FRIEND:** It is known. 

**SOCRATES:** Clearly then, where he ought to have spent much on those who taught, he wished his sons to be taught these things; but where nothing had to be spent expensively on him who would make them good men, would he not have taught them this, if indeed it could be handed down? 

**FRIEND:** You say no wonder. 

**SOCRATES:** But perhaps Thucydides was ignoble, nor had many friends among the citizens or allies. He was from an ample family and was most powerful both among the citizens and among other Greeks. Therefore, if this very thing could be acquired, he surely would have found someone, either among the citizens or among foreigners, who would have made his sons good, if he himself was not permitted through the administration of the Republic. But indeed, Friend, virtue cannot be acquired. 

**FRIEND:** It is perhaps so. 

**SOCRATES:** But if virtue cannot be acquired, are men born good by nature? And let us contemplate this very thing by this reasoning; perhaps we will find it. Say then: are the natures of good horses known to us? 

**FRIEND:** They are. 

**SOCRATES:** Are there therefore men who hold the art by which they know the natures of good horses, and thus understand which horses are strong in body for running and in spirit, and which on the contrary are lazy? 

**FRIEND:** There are. 

**SOCRATES:** What then is that art? What is its name? 

**FRIEND:** Equestrian. 

**SOCRATES:** And concerning dogs in the same way, is there an art by which they discern good and bad natures of dogs? 

**FRIEND:** There is. 

**SOCRATES:** What is it? 

**FRIEND:** Canina (Cynological/Hunting). 

**SOCRATES:** But of gold and silver, must the same be said: that there are assayers who, by inspection, indicate what is better and what is worse? 

**FRIEND:** It must be said. 

**SOCRATES:** What then do you call them? 

**FRIEND:** Argentarii (Bankers/Assayers). 

**SOCRATES:** But these masters who are in charge of exercising bodies, do they not, when they contemplate the natures of bodies, recognize which are fit for enduring labors and which on the contrary are inept? And they notice, of both the old and the young, which bodies will be worthy of praise, and in which there is hope that they will do all the works which are of the body best? 

**FRIEND:** These things are so. 

**SOCRATES:** Is it therefore a greater care to Republics that there be good horses and dogs and other things of this sort, or good men? 

**FRIEND:** Good men. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you not therefore think that if the natures of men were good toward virtue, men themselves would have thought out everything to recognize them? 

**FRIEND:** I think so, and it is consistent. 

**SOCRATES:** Can you therefore name any art which shows the natures of good men, in such a way that we might be able to judge them? 

**FRIEND:** I cannot. 

**SOCRATES:** And yet that art would have been most practiced, and those who would have known it would have been many. For they would have indicated to us the young men themselves who would have become good, even as boys; whom we would have taken care to be guarded in the citadel no differently than silver, and even much more diligently, so that they might suffer nothing bad in battle nor in any other danger; but they would be deposited for the Republic as saviors and benefactors when they reached age. But virtue seems to be present to men neither by nature nor by discipline. 

**FRIEND:** In what way, then, Socrates, do they seem to you to become good? For if it is neither by nature nor by discipline, by what other way then do they become good? 

**SOCRATES:** I judge indeed that this very thing cannot be so easily declared; since I suspect the possession of this thing to be something most divine, and that men become good similarly to how divine Prophets (*Vates*) and Soothsayers (*Fatidici*) become so. For they become such neither by nature nor by art, but by the spirit by which they are divinely inspired (*afflantur*). So also good men often predict things that will happen to Republics much more clearly and manifestly than soothsayers, from a certain divine inspiration. Hence even women say such a man is "divine." And indeed the Lacedaemonians [[notes: Spartans]], when they wish to praise someone magnificently, call that man "divine." This is the same as what Homer and the rest of the poets frequently employ. Therefore, when God wishes to benefit some Republic most, he generates good men in it; but when he wishes to harm it, he takes those same men, if there are any, away from it. Thus Virtue seems to be compared neither to discipline nor to nature: but to be in those who are endowed with it by a divine lot (*diuina sorte*).
*

# DEMODOCUS, OR, ON CONSULTING. III.

[[notes: This dialogue discusses the nature of advice and deliberation in a political or communal setting.]]

**Y**ou command me indeed, O Demodocus, to bring some counsel to you concerning these things about which you have met to consult: but it has come to my mind to consider what your council, and the study of those who think they can give you counsel, and the vote which each of you thinks to cast, can effect. For how is this not ridiculous: if it is not permitted to you to give counsel rightly and skillfully concerning these things about which you have met to consult, that you have met to consult about things about which it is not permitted to give counsel rightly? 

Indeed, how is it not also absurd that you have met to consult, if it is indeed permitted to give counsel rightly and skillfully concerning things of this kind, but there is no knowledge (*scientia*) from which anyone can rightly give counsel concerning these? But if there is some knowledge by which it is permitted to give counsel rightly in these, is it not necessary that there also be some who know how to give counsel rightly concerning these things? Since there are some who know how to give counsel concerning these things about which you are to consult, is it not necessary that you also either know how to give counsel concerning these, or that part of you knows and part indeed does not know? 

If therefore all of you know, why do you need to meet further for consulting? For each of you is fit for giving counsel. But if on the contrary you all do not know, how can you consult? Or what utility can this counsel bring to you, who cannot even deliberate? But if part of you indeed knows and part does not, and he lacks counsel, and if it can indeed happen that one prudent man gives counsel to the unlearned, one man can also give counsel to you who do not know. Or do not all who know give the same counsel? Wherefore you, having heard this, should depart from here. Now, however, you do not do this, but you wish to hear many of those who give counsel. For you do not believe those who set out to give counsel to you know those things about which they give counsel. For if you had believed those who give counsel know, it would have been enough for you to hear one. 

Therefore, that you meet to hear those who do not know, as if you were about to do something worthwhile, how can it not be absurd? And concerning your counsel, I doubt thus; but concerning the study of those who think they can give counsel to you, I am in doubt of this: for if those who give counsel concerning the same things do not respond with the same things, how can they all give counsel beautifully when they do not respond with the same things as he who gives counsel rightly? Or how is the study of those not inept who bring their mind to give counsel concerning things of which they are unskilled? For the skilled will never so determine for themselves that they wish to give counsel not rightly. 

If on the contrary they respond with the same things, why is it necessary for them all to give counsel? For one of them, who responds with the same thing, will be able to suffice. Who therefore would not laugh at those who desire to do things which bring no utility? Neither therefore can the study of the unskilled be anything but inept, when it is of this sort; nor should the prudent ever undertake to do such things, since they know that even any one of them who gives counsel, as is proper, can provide that very thing. 

Wherefore I can think of no reason by which the study of those who think they can give counsel to you does not seem ridiculous. But concerning the vote which you think to cast, what that can do, I am vehemently in suspense of mind. For will you decree that those who know should give counsel? But they will not give counsel more than once, nor differently concerning the same thing. Or will it be necessary that from these you should not cast a vote? Or will you appoint the unskilled, and those who do not give counsel as is proper, to give counsel? But these are no more to be consulted than the insane. 

But if you bear a sentence neither concerning the skilled nor the unskilled, whom from the beginning will you judge fit for giving counsel? How does it entirely fit that others give counsel to you, if indeed you can judge these things? But if you cannot judge, how can votes benefit you? Or in what way is it not ridiculous that you, as if lacking counsel and not fit for finding it, have met: but after you have met, you judge that a sentence must be born by you, as if you could judge? 

For it must not be said that you indeed individually were rude, but after you met in one place, you were made prudent: nor besides that you privately indeed doubted, but as soon as you came here, you no longer doubt, but have been made fit for perceiving those things which are to be done by you; when you have learned these from no one, nor have you yourselves found them, which is far the most difficult of all things. For unless you can know those things which are to be done by you, you will never be able to judge concerning him who gives counsel to you whether he does it rightly. 

Nor besides will any one man who gives counsel to you say that he will so teach you what is to be done by you that you can judge both those who give counsel to you badly and those who give it well; and that very thing in so short a time, and to so many: especially since this seems no less difficult than that. But if neither the council nor he who gives counsel to you makes you fit for judging, what need do you have of votes? Or how does your council not most disagree with the votes, and the votes with the study of those who give counsel to you? 

For your council is held just as if you were not fit for determining something, but needed the counsel of others: but the votes are cast just as if you not only do not need counsel, but can even judge and give counsel to others. Then the study of those who give counsel is present, as if they know how to do it: but the votes are cast by you as if they do not know. 

But if someone should ask you who cast votes, and him who has given counsel to you concerning these things which you decree by vote: "Do you know that which is to come, for the sake of which you think to do those things which you have decreed?" I do not believe you would say so. What then, if that should be for the sake of which you think to do these things, do you know this will be useful to you? Neither do I think you would say this, nor he who gives counsel to you. If someone besides should ask of you: "Do you judge there to be any one of all mortals who knows any one of these things?" Neither do I judge you would concede this. 

Since therefore those things which come into consultation are of such a sort that they cannot be manifest to you: and since those who cast votes and those who give counsel are unskilled: you will say it happens by right that both we do not believe, and they themselves often repent of those things about which they consult, and about which they cast a vote: which it is not consistent to happen to the most excellent men. 

For they know what sort of things those are about which they give counsel: nor are they ignorant of those things for the sake of which they give counsel, those things being certain for those who have been persuaded by them, and that it will be that neither they themselves nor those who were persuaded will ever repent. Concerning these things therefore I judged it worthy that those who are prudent should give counsel, but not concerning these things about which you command me to give counsel. For from their consultation happiness, but from these trifles unhappiness is born. 

I happened to be present when a certain man reprimanded his friend because he believed a certain accuser, when he had not yet heard the defender, but only the accuser himself. He said therefore that he was doing an unworthy thing, who condemned a man whose matters he himself had not seen present, nor had he heard from friends who had seen, and whom it was proper to believe when they reported about him: since, with the cause of neither having been heard, he so rashly believed the accuser. And he said it was just that the defender should be heard by him no less than the accuser, before he absolved or condemned. 

For how can someone judge either a cause well or men uprightly, unless he has first heard both litigants? For causes and reasons compared are much better judged like purple cloth and gold. Why indeed would the Legislator have commanded both that time be given to each of the adversaries, or that the judges swear they would hear both sides equally, unless he judged causes would be judged more justly and better by judges in this way? 

But you seem to me not even to have heard that which is said by many. "What?" he said. "Never decide, unless you have first heard both." [[notes: a common legal maxim: *Audi alteram partem*]]. This surely would not have been so divulged unless men judged the saying was well and properly said. Give to yourself therefore, he said, that counsel: that you never hereafter so rashly either condemn or absolve men. 

The other responded that it seemed absurd to him if indeed, with one speaking, it could not be known whether he spoke true or false, but with two, it could: and as if from him who speaks the truth men could not learn, but from the same and another together who lies, they could be taught: likewise if one indeed, who speaks rightly and truly, could not show what he says: but two, of whom one lies and speaks nothing rightly, could indicate that which he who speaks rightly cannot. 

Here, he said, I am stuck. And that besides, in what way then will they declare it, by being silent or by speaking? For if by being silent they show it, it will not be necessary to hear either one or both. But if both by speaking show it, and both confusedly (for they want to speak both, separately), in what way then can it happen that both together manifest the matter? For if they both demonstrate together, and they speak then together, they will never allow this to happen. Wherefore it remains (if indeed they show it by speaking) that each speaking demonstrates: and when each speaks, then both will demonstrate. 

Therefore, if each will show the same in turn, why will it be necessary besides to hear the second? For by him who spoke first, the matter will have already been declared. Added is also that, he said. If both will show, in what way will not also one of them show? For how will both show, of whom one cannot show? But if each will indicate, it is manifest that he who speaks first will also indicate first. Wherefore, he who hears him alone, how can it be that he does not know the matter? 

Hearing these things therefore, I was in doubt, nor had I what I should judge. Others indeed, who were present, affirmed that the former spoke truly. I ask therefore, if you have anything which you may bring forth into the middle concerning these things, whether it is permitted, with one speaking, to know that which he says: or whether there is need of another who responds, if it is to be entirely that someone can know whether it is said rightly: or rather he would not have wished either to accommodate or to believe you. 

A little before he was accusing another certain person because he would not either lend or trust him with silver. And he indeed, who was accused, defended himself: but another certain person from those who were present asked the accuser thus: "Did this one indeed, who did not believe you nor lend to you, err? But you, who did not persuade him to lend, did you not err?" "What indeed," said he, "did I err?" "Which," he said, "seems to you to err, he who is rejected from those things which he sought, or he who is not?" "He who is rejected," he said. "Do you say therefore that you indeed were rejected by him whom you desired to use: but this one, who was unwilling to impart, was not rejected by him?" "I say so," he responded: "but what did I err, if he did not give to me?" 

"If indeed," he said, "you were asking from him those things which were least proper, what cause can there be why you do not think you erred, and that he who did not give did rightly? But if you were seeking things which were proper, and you were rejected from these, by what reason can it happen that you did not necessarily go astray?" "Perhaps," he said, "I erred: but how did he, who did not believe, not err?" 

"Do you not," he said, "also say this, that you would not have erred if you had dealt with him as was proper?" "I say so." "Now you have dealt with him not as was proper." "I seem to have," he said. "If therefore he did not yield to you dealing not as was proper, what is there for which you can justly accuse him?" "I cannot say." "Nor can you say that one should not lend to those using things badly?" "On the contrary, I can," he said, "and indeed easily." "But," he said, "do they not seem to you to use things badly who do not deal as is proper?" "They seem so to me," he said. "What therefore did he err if he did not lend to you using things badly?" "Nothing," he responded, "as it seems." 

"Why therefore do men criminate each other concerning these things: and they are angry with these indeed, whom they themselves have not persuaded, because they did not obey: but they themselves, who did not persuade, do not accuse themselves at all?" Then another, who was present, said: "When someone uses another well, and is of great use to him, or because he thereafter thinks himself to be worthy that he should use him similarly, yet does not follow that, why can he not justly be indignant?" 

"He certainly," he said, "whom he thinks should use himself similarly, either can use him well, or cannot: and if indeed he cannot, in what way does he think he will use him well, who cannot? But if he can, why did he not persuade such a man: or rather what can be brought why those who say such things seem to speak well? But this by Hercules," he said, "it is proper to vituperate, so that he and other friends who hear the one vituperating may thereafter use him better." 

"But did it not seem to you that he judged rightly that it was worthy to use someone better?" "It seemed so," he said. "In what way therefore will those who hear a man vituperating these things use him better?" "By no way," he said. "Why therefore does someone vituperate these things?" He responded that he could not find it. 

A certain person was arguing against the ignorance of a man because he believed quickly, and to any men saying anything. For to believe citizens and domestics saying things was equitable: but to these men whom he neither knew nor had ever heard before, to give faith, especially since he knew most men to be deceptive and versatile, was a sign of no small folly. 

But a certain one of those who were present said: "But I thought you were he who judged it much more to be valued that someone perceived anything quickly rather than slowly." "Indeed I judge so," said he. "Why therefore do you accuse him if he has faith quickly and to any people saying true things?" "But this," he said, "I do not accuse, but that he quickly believes those saying false things." 

"But if after a long time and not to any people he had believed and had been offended, would you not have accused him more?" "Entirely," he said. "Is it because he believed slowly, and not to any people?" "By no means," he said. "For I do not think," said the other, "that you can be led to judge a man to be worthy of accusation because of this: but because he believes those who say incredible things." "So indeed," he said. 

"Do you therefore judge him indeed unworthy to be accused when he believes slowly and not to any people: but worthy when he believes quickly and to any people?" "Not I," he said. "Why therefore do you accuse him? Because he errs, before he weighs the matter, believing quickly and any people." "But if he had believed slowly before he considered, would he not have erred?" "Without doubt," he said. "Indeed he would have erred no less. But I judge one should not believe any people." 

"If you judge one should not believe any people, how is it proper quickly to give faith to unknown people? Do you not judge first it must be considered whether they say true things?" "I judge so indeed," he said. "But if they are domestics and familiars, is it not proper to examine whether they say true things?" "I indeed," he said, "would say it is proper. For perhaps even some of these say incredible things." "And very much so," he said. 

"Why therefore should it be more equitable to believe domestics and familiars than any people?" "I cannot say," he said. "What? If it is more to be believed to domestics than to any people, should we not judge them indeed less unworthy of faith than any people?" "Why not?" he said. "If therefore these are domestics to them, but unknown to those, how will it be that it is not proper to judge the same more worthy of faith to the same people? For it does not please you to affirm that domestics and unknown are equally and with the same faith worthy." 

"It does not please me," he said. "But those things which are said similarly and in the same way by the same people, these indeed will believe, but those will judge them least credible, and neither will err?" "It would be absurd also this," he said. "Then, if domestics and any people say the same things, in what way are those things which are said not similarly credible, or similarly incredible?" "It is necessary," he said. 

"Therefore to those saying the same things it must be believed equally, since they say the same things." "It is probable," he said. While they said these things, I was in doubt, nor could I determine whom I should believe and whom I should not believe it was proper: and whether to those worthy of faith and those who knew those things about which they spoke, or to domestics and known people it was to be believed. But you, what do you judge concerning these things?
