# Sisyphus.

### SISYPHUS,
### OR,
### ON DELIBERATING.
### IIII.
### SOCRATES, & SISYPHUS.

**W**e indeed, SISYPHUS, expected you yesterday even after a long space at Stratonicus's exhibition, so that you might hear with us a wise man showing many and beautiful things in word and work: and after we judged you were no longer about to come, we ourselves heard the man. 

**SISYPHUS:** By Hercules, I could not be present. For I had a certain business more necessary than that I could neglect it. For our magistrates were consulting yesterday, and therefore they compelled me to be an advisor to them. For us Pharsalians [[notes: people of Pharsalus in Thessaly]], the law is that it commands us to obey the magistrates if they wish someone to give counsel to them. 

**SOCRATES:** But it is honorable both to obey the law and especially to be judged a good counselor by one's citizens, just as you alone of the Pharsalians were judged. But O Sisyphus (for I could not have a speech with you about deliberating well, thinking with myself that for that there is need of much leisure and a long speech), I would wish to ask you what "To Deliberate" is. Can you therefore say to me what Deliberating itself is—I do not say either well or badly, or honorably—but only what Deliberating itself is? Or can you rather, who are so good a counselor, do that very easily and with no trouble, such that I act too curiously who ask you concerning this matter? 

**SISYPHUS:** Is what "To Deliberate" is unknown to you? 

**SOCRATES:** To me indeed, Sisyphus, if it is anything other than what he who does not know those things of which it is proper to do something proposes, as if prophesying and pronouncing unexpectedly and rashly, and indeed accommodating whatever occurs to be said, no differently than those who play "Even or Odd" [[notes: *Par impar*]], who, when they do not know whether they have even or odd things compressed in their hands, nevertheless enounce by chance, and say true things concerning these. Thus therefore Deliberating often seems to be that which he who knows nothing of those things about which someone deliberates says by case, but nevertheless attains that he brings forth true things. If indeed therefore it is of this sort, I now understand what deliberating is; but if it is not of this sort, I certainly do not know what it is. 

**SISYPHUS:** Not indeed that which you bring into the middle, he who knows entirely nothing: but that which he refers who knows the matters in part already, but in part has not yet been able to know. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you say, by the immortal gods, that deliberating is such a thing as if someone (for I too seem to myself as if prophesying what your sentiment about Deliberating is) should ask and give effort so that he may find those things which are best for him to do, yet does not yet manifestly know, but thinks that entire thing to be in another? Do you not say so? 

**SISYPHUS:** I say so indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** Which do men seek: things they know, or things they do not know? 

**SISYPHUS:** Both. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you also say this: that men seek both what they know and what they do not know, similarly as if someone who knows Callistratus and knows who Callistratus is, yet does not know where he is, should seek not indeed that he may find who Callistratus is? Is it thus indeed you say it is, to seek both? 

**SISYPHUS:** I say so. 

**SOCRATES:** That therefore certainly he does not seek, so that he may know Callistratus, whom he already long ago knew. 

**SISYPHUS:** Certainly not. 

**SOCRATES:** But where he is, he seeks. 

**SISYPHUS:** It seems so to me. 

**SOCRATES:** Indeed he would not even have sought this, that he might find where he was, if he had first known: but he would have found him immediately. 

**SISYPHUS:** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** These things therefore which they know, men do not seek, but those things which they do not know, as it appears. But if this reason seems litigious to you, Sisyphus, and said not for the proposed matter but for the sake of disputation, you ought to consider whether it seems to you to hold thus as it is now said. Do you not know this is accustomed to happen in Geometry: that Geometers are ignorant of the Line which is called the *diameter* (*διάμετρος*), not indeed whether it is a diameter or not (for this is not sought by them), but how long it is and what proportion it has with the sides of the areas which it cuts? Is it not this which is sought concerning it? 

**SISYPHUS:** It certainly seems so to me. 

**SOCRATES:** And what is unknown, is it not? 

**SISYPHUS:** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES:** What? Do you not know that of that square which is called a *cube* (*κύϐος*), the double is sought by Geometers so that how much it is can be found by reason: but by the same it is least sought whether it is a cube or not, because they know that certainly? 

**SISYPHUS:** I know. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you not know also about the air: that Anaxagoras, Empedocles, and all others who scrutinized sublime things sought whether it is infinite or has an end? 

**SISYPHUS:** I know this also. 

**SOCRATES:** But they did not seek whether there was air or not. 

**SISYPHUS:** Certainly not. 

**SOCRATES:** Would you now therefore concede to me all other things to hold thus, such that it is the part of no man to seek what he knows, but those things which he does not know? 

**SISYPHUS:** I would certainly concede. 

**SOCRATES:** But Deliberating seemed to us to be similar to if someone seeks and gives effort so that he may find the best from these things which he thinks it convenient for him to do? 

**SISYPHUS:** It seemed so. 

**SOCRATES:** To seek concerning matters was the same as to Deliberate, was it not? 

**SISYPHUS:** It was indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** For us therefore it must now be considered what can be an impediment to those seeking for finding those things about which they seek. 

**SISYPHUS:** So indeed it seems to me it should be done. 

**SOCRATES:** Shall we therefore say anything else but ignorance (*inscitiam*) to be an impediment? With greatest study therefore, all rudeness explained and every voice (as it is said) sent, let us consider: and this first do you now already weigh with me. Do you judge it can happen that a man deliberates about music who is unskilled in Music, nor knows in what way he should play the cithara or anything else which pertains to Music? 

**SISYPHUS:** I certainly do not judge so. 

**SOCRATES:** What do you say of the military or nautical art? Do you judge him who knows neither of these can deliberate whether one of two things should be done by him: should soldiers be led, or a ship be governed, when he knows neither how to lead soldiers nor how to govern a ship? 

**SISYPHUS:** Least of all. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you judge the same of all other things: that what someone does not know, he never entirely understands, nor can it ever happen that what someone does not know, he deliberates concerning those things? 

**SISYPHUS:** I indeed judge so. 

**SOCRATES:** But to seek is concerning these things which someone does not know, we said, did we not? 

**SISYPHUS:** We said so indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** To seek is indeed no longer the same as to Deliberate. 

**SISYPHUS:** What? 

**SOCRATES:** Because seeking is in these things which someone does not know: but Deliberating does not seem to be able to be around those things which someone does not know: was it not thus said? 

**SISYPHUS:** Said indeed, Socrates. You therefore yesterday were seeking indeed so that you might find what were best for the Republic, but you did not know those very things. For if you knew, you would not have sought the same things further, just as of those things which we know, we seek nothing: is it not thus? 

**SISYPHUS:** It is thus. 

[[page number: 655]]

# On Deliberating. 655

**SOCRATES:** Which therefore seems to you to be done, Sisyphus: if someone does not know, should he seek or should he learn? 

**SISYPHUS:** Learn, by Hercules. 

**SOCRATES:** It seems correctly to you indeed. But do you think one should learn on account of this, rather than seek, because someone can find more quickly and easily if he learns from those who know, than if he himself unskilled seeks? Or something else? 

**SISYPHUS:** No, but on account of this. 

**SOCRATES:** Why therefore did you yesterday, both you and the leaders of the city, not—spurning the counsel of deliberating concerning those things which you did not know and seeking what were best for the Republic to do—learn from some of those who know by what reason you could do what were best for the Republic: but (as it seems to me indeed) you sat the entire day yesterday mixing things and prophesying about those things which you did not know, neglecting entirely the study of learning? 

These things perhaps you will say were said by me to you only for the sake of disputation as a joke, not demonstrated seriously: but do you, I pray, Sisyphus, now diligently attend to this. If it be conceded that Deliberating is something, and that which we now say is not true—that it seems to be nothing other than knowledge, conjecture, and a device, or any weightier name, but only that and nothing else besides: do you think men in deliberating well and exhibiting themselves as good counselors differ some from others, as in all other disciplines some differ from others—Smiths from Smiths, Doctors from Doctors, and Flute-players from Flute-players—and all other artisans are themselves dissimilar among themselves? Do you think in deliberating also some differ from others? 

**SISYPHUS:** I indeed think so. 

**SOCRATES:** Tell me: do not all who deliberate well and badly deliberate about future things? 

**SISYPHUS:** Most of all. 

**SOCRATES:** What else should we say here but that future things are not yet? 

**SISYPHUS:** Nothing else. 

**SOCRATES:** For if they were, they would no longer be future things, but would already be: would they not? 

**SISYPHUS:** No. 

**SOCRATES:** If therefore in no way they are, by the same reason they have not been made, since they do not exist. 

**SISYPHUS:** Not by Hercules. 

**SOCRATES:** If therefore they have not yet been made, they have as yet no nature which is proper to them. 

**SISYPHUS:** None at all. 

**SOCRATES:** Do not all deliberating well or badly therefore deliberate about things which neither are, nor were, nor have any nature, when they deliberate about future things? 

**SISYPHUS:** They seem so indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** Does it therefore seem it can happen that someone attains that which is nowhere, either well or badly? 

**SISYPHUS:** By what reason do you say this? 

**SOCRATES:** I will explain to you what I wish to say: you apply diligence. From many archers, in what way do you know who is skilled and who on the contrary is unskilled? And this indeed seems to be not difficult to know. Perhaps indeed you would command them all to seek the arrows [[notes: i.e., aim at a target]]: would you not? 

**SISYPHUS:** Certainly indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** You indeed therefore would decree him who more often so sends the arrows that he aims correctly to be the victor. 

**SISYPHUS:** I would decree so indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** But if among them no target is proposed into which they may direct the arrows, but each throws where he wishes, in what way could you know who throws well or badly? 

**SISYPHUS:** By no way. 

**SOCRATES:** Thus also those deliberating well or badly, if they do not know about what they deliberate, you would not know how to discern. 

**SISYPHUS:** True. 

**SOCRATES:** True indeed: for if those deliberating deliberate about future things, do they not deliberate about those things which are not? 

**SISYPHUS:** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES:** But it cannot happen that someone attains that which is nowhere. For by what reason could it seem to you someone could attain what is nowhere? 

**SISYPHUS:** By none, Socrates. Since therefore it cannot happen that someone attains what is not, there will no longer be anyone who deliberates about these things which are not. For Fortune is numbered among those things which are not: does the matter not hold thus? 

**SISYPHUS:** It seems to me to hold. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore no one who does not attain future things can be either a good or a bad counselor. 

**SISYPHUS:** It does not seem so. 

**SOCRATES:** Indeed neither can one be a better counselor than another, nor can one be worse, unless he either more happily attains that which is not, or more unhappily goes astray from it. 

**SISYPHUS:** He cannot. 

**SOCRATES:** To what therefore do men look when they call certain men good and bad counselors? Is this worthy to you, Sisyphus, that we think about it again and again?

# ERYXIAS, OR, ON WEALTH. V.
### OTHERWISE.
### ERASISTRATUS, SOCRATES.

**W**hen by chance I and Eryxias of Stiria were walking in the portico of Jupiter the Liberator, Critias and Erasistratus the son of Phaeacus Erasistratus's brother came to us: of whom Erasistratus, who then was fresh from Sicily and those places, approaching nearer, said, "Hail, O Socrates." 

"And you," said I, "hail: what news do you bring to us from Sicily? Do you have anything beautiful to report?" 

"Most of all: but do you wish," he said, "that we sit? For I am still weary from the road, having set out yesterday from Megara." 

"So be it, if it seems good." 

"What therefore," he said, "do you wish first to hear from these things which are there? Whether what the Sicilians practice, or in what way they are affected toward our Republic? For they seem to me to be affected toward us no differently than wasps: which if slightly irritated they are provoked, they become invincible until someone attacking them entirely extinguishes them. Thus therefore the Syracusans are affected. For unless someone about to wage war and indeed a huge one should set out there with a greatest fleet, never will that city come into our jurisdiction and power: but rather it will be irritated by these small fleets such that it will be most troublesome to us. Now indeed they have sent legates to us, for that reason indeed (as it seems to me) so that they may deceive our city." 

In the meantime, while we so talked, the Syracusan legates themselves by chance arrived. Wherefore Erasistratus, showing one of them to us, said: "That one, O Socrates, is the wealthiest of all the Sicilians and Italians. And how," he said, "is he not the wealthiest, to whom there is a field so wide that it could give faculty if someone wished to practice agriculture far and wide: and that field of such a sort as another in all Greece could not so easily be found: and to whom other things which pertain to wealth are separately: slaves, horses, gold, and silver?" 

Seeing him already led to this, that he seemed about to say more about the man's wealth, I asked thus: "What Erasistratus? What sort of man then does he seem to be in Sicily?" 

"Of all the Sicilians," he said, "and of the Italians he seems by so much the most wicked, as he is also the wealthiest: such that if you ask any of the Sicilians whom he thinks most wicked and wealthiest..."

As you say, but as Homer describes it—the "shabbier man" <note>original: "vilis homunculus"; a reference to a proverb based on Homer's Iliad</note> coming to the banquet of the wise man—I will seem to come uninvited. Since you are leading me, see what reason you give for my arrival. For I will not admit to coming uninvited, but I will say I was invited by you.

On the way itself, he said, being two, we will perhaps consult on what we should say; but let us go now. When they had discussed such things among themselves, he said he was ordered; and when he had waited for Socrates, who was walking with a slow pace, lost in thought, and left behind, he finally ordered him to go ahead. But when he approached Agathon's house, he found the door open, and something ridiculous happened: right on the threshold, a certain servant met him and led him to where the others were reclining, whom he found already about to dine. As soon as Agathon saw him, he said, "O Aristodemus, you have come at the right time to dine with us. But if you want anything else, put it off to another time. Indeed, I saw you nowhere yesterday when I was looking for you to invite you. But why do you not lead Socrates to us?" And I, he said, turning around, saw Socrates nowhere. I replied to Agathon: "Indeed, I came with him, having been called here to dinner by him." "You did well," he said, "but where is Socrates?"

"He was walking just behind me. Therefore, I also wonder where he is and do not know." "Search for Socrates," Agathon said to a boy, "and bring him in to us. You, Aristodemus, recline next to Eryximachus." "Hey you, give water for his feet so he may sit now." Then another boy entered and reported, according to Aristodemus, that Socrates himself had withdrawn into the nearest vestibule and refused to enter when summoned. "You tell of something absurd," he said. "Call him again, and do not let him go until he comes." "Not so, O Agathon," Aristodemus said he replied, "but let him be; for that is Socrates's habit. Sometimes he stops and is accustomed to stand still wherever he happens to be. He will come quickly, I think. Do not disturb him, but permit him to come at his own will." "If it seems so to you," Agathon said, "it must be done. But you, boys, bring food for the others and set out whatever pleases you. Since no one presides over us—I have never done that—imagine now that I and the others are being received at a banquet by you, and attend to everything diligently, so that we may approve of your work." After this, Aristodemus added that they began to dine, and Socrates, though often called by Agathon's order, did not enter until he had exercised himself somewhat in his usual way, arriving in the middle of the dinner. To him, Agathon, who was sitting last and alone, said, "Here, O Socrates, recline near me, so that by touching you I may enjoy that wise thought which you discovered in the vestibules. For it is clear that you have found it and possess it; for you would not have stopped before." Socrates sat down and said: "It would be well for us, Agathon, if wisdom were such that it flowed from the fuller man into the emptier one through contact, just as water flows from a full cup into an empty one through a piece of wool. For if wisdom is so, I value very much that I sit near you. For I think I will be filled by you with most abundant and excellent wisdom. For mine is thin and ambiguous, like a certain dream; yours, however, is very bright and powerful, as it shone forth and flashed so clearly yesterday in your youth in the sight of more than thirty thousand Greeks." "You are insulting, O Socrates," Agathon said. "But we two will judge these things about wisdom later with Dionysus <note>The god of wine and theater; here acting as a judge of their relative wisdom</note> as judge; but now, dine." After this, Aristodemus said, when Socrates had reclined and dined, and the others had also finished dining, they began to offer libations and taste the wines in the ritual of those sacrificing, and to sing to the god, and doing other such things as is the custom, they turned to drinking. Whereupon Pausanias began to speak: "It must be seen, O men, by what means we may drink most lightly and pleasantly. For to confess the truth about myself first, I feel myself still burdened by yesterday's pure wine, and I need a certain intermission. I think most of you are similarly affected, for you were present yesterday. Consider, therefore, how we may drink most lightly and healthfully." To him, Aristophanes immediately replied: "You speak wisely, Pausanias; a certain moderation in drinking must be applied. For I too am one of those who gorged themselves yesterday." When Eryximachus, the son of Acumenus, heard this, he said: "You speak rightly. And I desire to hear this further from you, Agathon: how much strength do you have for drinking?" "Not at all," Agathon said. "It certainly benefits us—I mean myself, Aristodemus, and Phaedrus, and these others—that you who have the most strength for drinking now refrain as if exhausted by drinking. For we are always weak, except for Socrates, who is fit for either. Therefore, whatever we do, it will be the same." Here Eryximachus said: "Since none of those present seems to want to gorge themselves, perhaps if I speak the truth about drunkenness, I will be less troublesome. For from the skill of medicine, it is clear to me that drunkenness is a heavy thing for men. For I would never willingly want to drink excessively, nor would I advise another, especially if one suffers from yesterday's hangover." To him, Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian said, as Aristodemus relates: "Indeed, I have always had faith in you, especially in medicine. Now similarly, provided the others also agree." When they all heard this, he said, they agreed that they should drink in the present banquet not to drunkenness, but for pleasure. Then Eryximachus: "Since it has seemed best that it will be in each person's judgment how much he drinks, and no one is to be forced beyond what he wishes, I will explain what remains. I think the flute-girl who just entered should be sent away, let her play the flute for herself or, if she wishes, for the women who are inside. But I judge that we should converse with one another today. What our speeches should be, I will reveal if you wish." At this, all said it pleased them and ordered him to explain. Eryximachus then said: "The beginning of my speech will be according to Euripides's *Melanippe*. For the story I am about to begin is not mine, but Phaedrus's. Phaedrus here often complains to me, asserting something absurd: that while poets have fashioned songs and hymns for the other gods, yet no one among so many poets has ever written any praise for Love, such a great god. And yet if you wish to search, O Eryximachus," he said, "you will surely find eloquent Sophists <note>Professional teachers or philosophers in ancient Greece</note> have praised Hercules and others in prose, just as the most skilled Prodicus did; although this should seem less wonderful to anyone. But I even read once a book by a wise man in which salt was extolled with wonderful praises for its utility to life; and one can find many other things of this kind celebrated with praise. Is it not unworthy then that men deal with these things so studiously, but no man until this day has dared to praise Love worthily, but he is even despised, although he is such a great God? Indeed, this speech of Phaedrus seems true to me. Therefore, I desire to confer this gift upon him and gratify him, and I think it is decent that this god be honored by us. If it also seems so to you, a suitable discussion will arise among us. I think Love should be praised by each one of us as skillfully and excellently as possible. Let Phaedrus begin, since he both sits first and is the inventor of this discussion." Then Socrates said: "No one would oppose you, O Eryximachus. For I, who..."

# Phaedrus, or, On Beauty. 303

"Not at all, Socrates; but tell the truth, by Zeus <note>original: "Iovem"</note>, the god who presides over friendship: do you really think any other Greek could speak more or greater things on this very subject?" **SOCRATES:** "What indeed? Do we think the writer is to be praised only because he said what was necessary? Should we not also praise him because he placed each word clearly, precisely, and elegantly? If you wish, I must concede this for your sake, for my own sluggishness and ignorance meant it escaped me. I was attending only to the rhetorical style of the speaker. As for the content, I did not think even Lysias himself considered it sufficient. In fact, Phaedrus, unless you disagree, he seemed to me to repeat the same things two or three times, as if he lacked the abundance to say many things on the same topic, or perhaps he simply didn't care. He seemed to me to be showing off—demonstrating that he could say the same thing in different ways, and both times excellently." **PHAEDRUS:** "You say nothing of the sort, Socrates! For that is the best thing about the speech. Of all the points in the matter that could be discussed fittingly, he omitted nothing; so much so, that besides what he has said, no one could say more or more convincingly on the same subject." **SOCRATES:** "I can no longer agree with that. The ancient wise men and women who spoke and wrote of these things will refute me if I concede this for your sake." **PHAEDRUS:** "Who are they? And where have you heard better things?" **SOCRATES:** "At the moment, I do not quite remember. But I certainly heard them somewhere—perhaps from the beautiful Sappho, or the wise Anacreon, or other writers. Why do I suspect this? Because, my dear friend, I feel my chest is full of the ideas of others, and they are not inferior to these. Yet, being conscious of my own ignorance, I know I have realized none of this by myself. It remains, then, that like a vessel, I have drawn these things from the fountains of others; but again, because of my clumsiness, I have forgotten both how and from whom I received them." **PHAEDRUS:** "Nobly spoken! Do not tell me from whom or how you received them, even if I command you. But do tell me what you promised: that you have more and better things to say than those written by Lysias. If you do this while avoiding his points, I promise you a golden statue at Delphi <note>original: "in Delphis"</note>, of equal weight to yourself, just as the nine archons <note>original: "novem illi principes"</note> are accustomed to dedicate—not just of myself, but of you as well." **SOCRATES:** "You are most kind, and truly golden yourself, Phaedrus, if you think I meant Lysias missed everything and that better things could be said in every respect. I don't think that happens even to the worst writer. For instance, regarding the topic of our talk: do you think anyone wishing to prove that one should gratify a non-lover rather than a lover could do so without first proving that the non-lover is sane and the lover is mad? These are necessary points—one to be praised, the other blamed. What else would he have to say? I believe such points should be allowed and forgiven in writers; they should be praised not for the *invention* <note>original: "inventione"; the rhetorical term for finding arguments</note> of these points, but for their *disposition* <note>original: "dispositione"; the arrangement of the arguments</note>. But for those things that are not strictly necessary and are difficult to find, I think both the invention and the disposition should be praised." **PHAEDRUS:** "I concede your point; you seem to have spoken reasonably. I will do the same: I will allow you to presuppose that the lover is more 'unwell' than the non-lover. For the rest, if you say more and better things than Lysias, you shall stand in Olympia, skillfully fashioned in gold, alongside the offerings of the Cypselids <note>original: "Cypselidas"; a powerful family of tyrants from Corinth who dedicated famous golden statues</note>." **SOCRATES:** "Are you taking this seriously, Phaedrus, because I poked fun at your beloved friend? Do you really think I would attempt to say something more ornate and abundant than that man’s wisdom?" **PHAEDRUS:** "On this matter, my friend, you have fallen into your own trap. You must speak, however you can. And so that we are not compelled to play that tiresome game of actors—repeatedly answering one another—take care, and do not force me to say: 'Socrates, if I do not know Socrates, I have forgotten myself.' He wanted to speak, but pretended to be reluctant. Finally, consider this: we are not leaving this spot until you speak those better things you said you held in your chest. We are alone, in a deserted place, and I am younger and stronger. Understand what I am saying from all this, and do not choose to speak by force rather than by your own will." **SOCRATES:** "But, blessed Phaedrus, I will look ridiculous if I, an amateur, try to compete with that excellent writer and dispute these same matters on the spot." **PHAEDRUS:** "You know how things stand: stop boasting to me. I have found the very thing to compel you." **SOCRATES:** "Please, do not say it." **PHAEDRUS:** "Not say it? On the contrary, I am saying it now. I will turn to an oath. I swear to you by some god—or if you prefer, by this plane tree <note>The plane tree is a significant setting in the Phaedrus, providing shade for their philosophical discussion</note>—that unless you speak here in its presence, I will never again show you or tell you another person's speech!" **SOCRATES:** "Aha! You rogue! How beautifully you have discovered the art to compel a man who is a lover of conversation to do whatever you wish." **PHAEDRUS:** "Why then do you hesitate, since you are such a man?" **SOCRATES:** "Not at all, since you have sworn such an oath. For who could abstain from such a feast of words?" **PHAEDRUS:** "Speak, then." **SOCRATES:** "Do you know what I will do?" **PHAEDRUS:** "About what?" **SOCRATES:** "I will speak with my head covered <note>original: "obvolutus"; Socrates covers his head out of shame for the "shameful" arguments he is about to make against love</note>, so that I may run through the speech quickly and not be hindered by shame looking at you." **PHAEDRUS:** "Just speak. Do the rest as you wish." **SOCRATES:** "Come then, O sweet Muses—whether you have this name because of the beauty of your song, or because of that musical race of 'sweet and shrill' singers—assist my speech, which this excellent man compels me to give, so that his companion, who seemed wise to him before, may seem even more so now. There was once a boy, or rather a youth, of extraordinary character. He had many lovers, but one of them was a truly cunning man who, although he loved the boy no less than the others, persuaded the boy that he did *not* love him. And when he was once making his suit, he persuaded him that he should gratify the non-lover rather than the lover. And this is what he said: 'In all things, O boy, there is one principle for those who wish to deliberate well: they must understand what it is they are deliberating about, or they will necessarily miss the mark entirely. Most people do not realize they are ignorant of the true substance of the matter. Therefore, as if they already knew, they do not define it at the start of their inquiry. As they proceed, the logical consequence is that they agree neither with themselves nor with others. Let it not happen to you and me, then, what we condemn in others. Since our disagreement is whether friendship should be entered into with the lover or the non-lover, let us establish a definition by consensus of what Love itself is and what power it has. Then, looking back to that definition and referring to it, let us consider whether it brings benefit or harm. Now, that love is a kind of desire <note>original: "cupiditas"</note> is manifest to all; and we know that even those who do not "love" still desire beautiful or good things. To distinguish the one who loves from the one who does not, we must understand that there are two ruling and leading ideas within each of us, which we follow wherever they lead. One is an innate desire for pleasures. The other is an acquired opinion that strives for what is best. These two sometimes agree within us, but sometimes they are in a state of faction and discord, and now one, now the other prevails. When opinion leads by reason to what is best and triumphs, this very power of living..."

Socrates, though claiming he only remembers the ideas of others, is coerced by Phaedrus into delivering his own superior speech on love, beginning with a formal definition of love as a conflict between desire and reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of Plato's Phaedrus. In the previous section, Socrates began a speech defining the nature of love to compete with a speech by Lysias. Here, he defines Love (Eros) as a form of irrational desire and begins to list the harms an "in-love" lover inflicts upon the beloved youth.</meta>

# 304 Book Twenty-six.

...the power to rule [oneself] is called **temperance** <note>Latin: temperantia; the virtue of self-control and moderation</note>. However, when a desire without reason drags us toward pleasures and rules over us, this rule is called **lust** <note>Latin: libido</note>. Now, since lust is multifaceted and has many parts, it certainly has many names; and whichever of these forms most overflows in someone, that person is named after that specific calling. It does not grant any honorable or worthy title. For instance, regarding food, the desire that overcomes reason and what is right and good—and indeed all other desires—is called **gluttony** <note>Latin: ingluvies</note>. Furthermore, that which exercises a tyranny over drunkenness and leads the one it possesses, it is clear what name that will have <note>i.e., Drunkenness</note>. It is also clear how we should name other sibling desires, related to these, wherever one of them happens to dominate. 

The reason why we have said all the things above is now almost clear; yet whether it is spoken or not, it will be more apparent than if it were left out. For the desire without reason, which overcomes the opinion tending toward what is right, and which is snatched away toward the pleasure of beauty—and is violently reinforced by its kindred desires toward bodily beauty—wins out and conquers <gloss>from the rush</gloss> <note>original Greek: "apo tes rumes"</note>, that is, by strength and vehemence, and is called **Eros**, which is love. Now, my friend Phaedrus, do I seem to you, as I do to myself, to have experienced something divine? 

**PHAEDRUS:** Indeed, Socrates, a certain unusual abundance of speech has taken hold of you. 

**SOCRATES:** Listen to me then in silence. For truly, this place seems divine. Therefore, if I am seized by the nymphs <note>spirits of the woods and waters</note> as my speech proceeds, do not be surprised. Certainly, what I was just singing is not far from dithyrambs <note>passionate, wild choral hymns usually dedicated to Dionysus</note>. 

**PHAEDRUS:** You speak the absolute truth. 

**SOCRATES:** You are the cause of these things. But hear the rest, lest the inspiration that has come upon me should depart. These matters will be the care of God; let us return in our discussion to the boy. Come then, most excellent one: what the subject is upon which we deliberate has been stated and defined. Looking back, therefore, to this definition, let us see what advantage or harm is likely to come from the lover, and from the non-lover, to the one who complies with them. 

It is necessary for a man enslaved to lust and serving pleasures to make his beloved as pleasant to himself as possible. To a sick man, whatever does not resist him is pleasant, but what is better or equal is annoying. Therefore, a lover will never willingly endure his beloved being superior or even an equal. He will always make the beloved inferior and more needy as much as he can. Now, the ignorant is inferior to the wise, the timid to the brave, the one unskilled in speaking to the rhetorician, and the dull to the sharp. Since these and many more evils of the soul are either present by nature or created in the beloved, the lover rejoices, and he even tries to introduce more. Otherwise, he is deprived of his pleasure. 

Therefore, the lover must necessarily be envious of the beloved and, by removing him from every association and pursuit from which he might emerge as an excellent man, the lover does him great harm. But the greatest harm comes from depriving him of that which would make him most wise. Now, divine philosophy makes one most wise, and the lover is compelled to lead his beloved far away from it, fearing that if the youth becomes wiser, he will be held in contempt by him. In short, the lover does everything to ensure the youth remains ignorant of all things and looks only to the lover in admiration. Such a state will be most pleasant for the lover, but most ruinous for the youth himself. And so, in those matters pertaining to the intellect, association with a lover is harmful. 

Next, we must see how he who is forced to prefer the sweet over the good will care for the body of the one he loves, if it is entrusted to him. Surely he will desire a body that is not solid, but soft and delicate; one not nourished under the sun, but in the shade; one that, far from dangers and labors and dry sweat, has been brought up on a womanly and delicate diet, adorned with artificial colors and external ornaments for lack of its own natural beauty, and accustomed to all other such things. Since it would be unworthy to review all these things in detail, we will conclude briefly for the present so that we may proceed to the rest: in battles and any other great necessity, enemies certainly invade such a body with boldness, while friends and the lovers themselves fear for it greatly. 

But let this now be dismissed as obvious. Next, we must see what advantage or harm the familiarity and guardianship of a lover provides us in external matters. Now, this is clear to everyone, especially to the lover: he desires the beloved to be bereaved of his most friendly, most dear, and most divine possessions. For he hopes the youth will be deprived of parents, relatives, and friends, thinking they would be obstacles to the very sweet association he has with the beloved. Furthermore, if the boy is very rich in gold or any other possession, the lover thinks he will not be easily captured, or if captured, not easily held. Wherefore, it is necessary for the lover, like an envious man, to grieve at the beloved’s prosperity and rejoice in his adversity. Moreover, he desires the youth to live for a long time without a wife, without children, and without a home, wishing to enjoy his own sweetness for as long as possible. 

There are also other evils, but to most of them some deity has mixed a pleasure at the very beginning; just as nature has inserted some clumsy delight into the flatterer, a most grievous beast and a great calamity. Someone might also find fault with a prostitute as being harmful, and other such creatures and pursuits, which nevertheless are accustomed to delighting us daily. But a lover, besides being harmful, is also the most annoying of all in his daily company. For "equals congregate most pleasantly with equals," as the old proverb says. [[margin: Proverb]] For equality of age, as it draws people toward equal pleasures because of similarity, gives birth to friendship. Nevertheless, even these bring a certain excessive satiety. Indeed, necessity is heavy for everyone in all things, and this is especially true in the relationship of a lover to his beloved due to their dissimilarity. 

For an older man clinging to a younger one does not leave him willingly by day or night but is snatched away by necessity and madness, which drags him with the allurements of pleasures—seeing, hearing, touching, and altogether perceiving the beloved with every sense—so that he follows him constantly with great pleasure. But as for the beloved, what pleasure or what consolation will keep him for an equal amount of time so that he is not vexed by extreme annoyance? When he sees a face deformed by old age and other similar things which are not only unpleasant to experience but even to hear about; when he is constantly under the eye of a certain necessity to be captured by him, while being observed always and everywhere by suspicious guards; and when he hears untimely and immoderate praises and reproaches with which the lover pursues him. These are intolerable when the lover is sober, but when he is drunk, they are not only intolerable but also most shameful in their excessive and openly disgusting license of speech. 

Furthermore, while he loves, he is ruinous and troublesome. But when he stops loving, he becomes unfaithful for the future toward the one whom he had barely managed to persuade with many oaths, prayers, and promises to endure his troublesome company in the hope of rewards. At last, when it is time to pay back, he receives another master into himself—he receives faith, mind, and temperance instead of love and insanity—and having now become another man, he deceives the beloved. Then the beloved, [recalling] those things which were once said and done...

[[vocabulary: **Temperance**, **Lust**, **Gluttony**, **Love (Eros)**, **Proverb**, **Drunkenness**, **Philosophy**]]

<summary>Socrates defines Love as a form of irrational lust for beauty that overpowers reason, comparing it to other gluttonous desires. He argues that a lover is fundamentally harmful to a youth because he seeks to keep the beloved weak, ignorant, and isolated to maintain control and pleasure.</summary>

# Phaedrus, or, on Beauty. 305

...they are, and unmindful of past favors he demands gratitude, thinking he is speaking to the same person. But the other, out of shame, neither dares to admit that he has changed, nor does he find a way to fulfill the oaths and promises of that former insane rule, now that he has regained his mind and self-control. He fears that if he acts as he did before, he will become again what he was. From this, it follows that the one who previously loved now flees, departing as a changed man—just like a shell falling on the opposite side <note>Original Latin: "testa in aduersum cadente." This refers to an ancient Greek game "ostrakinda" where a shell was flipped to determine who would chase and who would flee.</note>. The other is forced to pursue him, taking it poorly and turning to curses. Truly, he was deceived from the beginning, not knowing that he should never have gratified a lover—who is necessarily out of his mind—but rather a man who is free from love and possesses his reason. Otherwise, it would be necessary to entrust oneself to an unfaithful, peevish, envious, troublesome man, one ruinous to one's possessions, ruinous to the condition of the body, and far more ruinous to the discipline of the soul—than which nothing is or ever will be more venerable among gods and men. These things, O boy, must be considered, and it must be further noted that the friendship of a lover does not consist of any goodwill, but of a certain greed for satisfaction, like hunger.

*As the wolf loves the lamb, so the lover burns for the boy.* <note>Original Latin: "Ut lupus ipse agnum, puerum sic ardet amator." This is a proverbial comparison used to show the predatory nature of a lover driven by lust.</note>

This is what I predicted, O Phaedrus. You will not hear me speaking further; let the discourse have its end here.

**PHAE.** But I thought half of the discussion was finished, and that just as much remained to be said about the non-lover—how it is more fitting to indulge him, and to enumerate the good things he offers. Why do you stop now, O Socrates?

**SOC.** Have you noticed, Phaedrus, that I am no longer just singing dithyrambs <note>Dithyrambs were wild, passionate hymns; Socrates is noting that his speech has become poetic and frenzied</note> but even more, even though my speech was focused on criticism? If I proceed to praise the other, what do you think I will do? Do you not perceive that I am being clearly inspired by the nymphs—both through your doing and by divine providence? Therefore, I say in summary: as many good things exist in the one, as we have numbered evils in the other. Why is there a need for many words? Enough has been said about both. And so, let the story suffer the fate it deserves. I am now crossing the river and leaving, before I am compelled by you toward something even greater.

**PHAE.** Not yet, O Socrates, not before the heat recedes. Do you not see that it is now plainly midday, which is called "Constant and Steady"? But let us stay a while and talk about what we have said, and as soon as it cools down, then let us go.

**SOC.** You are divine when it comes to speeches, O Phaedrus, and truly wonderful. I think, indeed, that of all the orations delivered in these times, no one has been the author or cause of more than you—whether by speaking them yourself or by compelling others in some way. I except Simmias the Theban, but you far surpass others. And now you seem to be the cause of yet another speech being delivered by me.

**PHAE.** You aren't declaring war, surely? But in what way, and what speech?

**SOC.** When I was about to cross the river, my "spirit" <note>The "daimonion," a divine inner voice Socrates claimed warned him against making mistakes.</note> and the sign that usually comes to me appeared. Whenever it happens, it forbids me from doing what I was about to do. Thus, I seemed to hear a voice that forbade me from leaving before I had made an expiation, as if I had committed some offense against God. I am therefore a prophet—not a very good one, perhaps, but like those who write poorly, I am sufficient for myself. So now I clearly understand my offense. Indeed, my friend, there is even a kind of prophetic power in the soul. It troubled me even while I was speaking earlier, and I was somewhat afraid lest, as Ibycus <note>A Greek lyric poet</note> says, "by sinning against the gods, I might gain glory among men." Now I realize where I sinned.

**PHAE.** What is it?

**SOC.** A grave, O Phaedrus, a grave speech, I say, both you brought here and you forced me to say.

**PHAE.** How so?

**SOC.** It was foolish and somewhat impious; what could be more grave than that?

**PHAE.** Nothing, if what you say is true.

**SOC.** What about Love? Do you not think he is the son of Venus and some kind of God?

**PHAE.** So it is said.

**SOC.** But not by Lysias, nor by your speech, which was brought forth through my mouth as if drawn out by your prompting. If Love is, as he surely is, a God or something divine, he could not be evil. Yet our speeches were held about him as if he were evil. In this, therefore, we have sinned against Love. Indeed, these discussions of ours seem very foolish, however clever; for while they contain nothing sincere or true, they boast as if they were of great value, if they can deceive and win the approval of some little men. Therefore, my friend, it is necessary for me to be purified. For those who sin in their storytelling, there is an ancient purification, which Homer did not know, but Stesichorus did. When he was deprived of his sight for slandering Helen <note>Helen of Troy; legend says the poet Stesichorus was blinded for writing that she caused the Trojan War.</note>, he was not ignorant of the cause of his blindness as Homer was, but being a man of the Muses, he recognized it. Thus, he immediately wrote those verses:

*That story was not true; you did not go*
*On the well-decked ships, nor did you reach the towers of Troy.* <note>Stesichorus's famous "Palinode" or recantation, claiming Helen never actually went to Troy.</note>

And so, having published the poem which they call a *palinodia*—that is, a recantation—he immediately recovered his lost sight. I, however, will be wiser than both of them in this: before any harm happens to me for slandering Love, I will try to offer him a recantation, and indeed with my head uncovered, not veiled out of shame as I was before.

**PHAE.** Nothing you could do, Socrates, would be more pleasing to me.

**SOC.** For you remember, O Phaedrus, how shamelessly the book was read, and what was said by me about the lover. If some noble and modest man, who loves or has loved another like himself, should hear us saying that lovers stir up the greatest enmities for the smallest reasons and are envious and harmful to the beloved, he would think he was hearing men raised on ships <note>Metaphor for unrefined, rough people who have never known true "liberal" or noble love.</note> who had never seen a noble love; he would by no means agree with the things we brought against Love.

**PHAE.** Perhaps, by Jove, O Socrates.

**SOC.** Revering this man and fearing Love himself, I desire, as if with a drinkable speech <note>A metaphor for a speech that "washes away" the salty/bitter taste of the previous slanderous one.</note>, to wash away that false and harmful discourse from our ears. I even advise Lysias to write as soon as possible that the lover, rather than the non-lover, should be indulged under similar circumstances.

**PHAE.** Know for certain it will be so. For after you have praised the lover, it will be necessary for Lysias to be compelled by me to write the same.

**SOC.** I believe that, as long as you are who you are.

**PHAE.** Speak then, with a brave heart.

**SOC.** Well, where is that boy I spoke to in the previous discourse? Let him hear this one too, so that he does not rashly obey a non-lover for lack of hearing it.

**PHAE.** He is always right here next to you, as long as you wish.

**SOC.** Thus, O noble boy, consider that the previous speech was by Phaedrus, son of Pythocles of Myrrhinus; but the one following will be by Stesichorus, son of Euphemus, a man of love. This will be its beginning:

"That story is not true, which says that when a lover is present, one should rather gratify a non-lover because the lover is mad and the non-lover is sane. For if it were simply true that madness is an evil, it would have been rightly said by us. But now, the greatest of goods come to us through madness, granted by a certain divine gift. For the prophetess at Delphi and the priests at Dodona, while mad, have provided many and great benefits..." <margin>The greatest goods come through a madness granted by the gods.</margin>

He begins a new speech, arguing that madness is often a gift from the gods that leads to great benefits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Socrates' second speech in Plato's Phaedrus, where he recants his previous criticism of love. He begins to argue that "madness" (mania), when sent by the gods, is actually a great blessing rather than a literal mental illness, shifting the dialogue from a cynical view of romance to a profound philosophical exploration of the soul.</meta>

# 306 Book Twenty-Sixth.

...they have brought both privately and publicly to the Greeks; indeed, while they are sane, they bring little or none. If we were to recount the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses inspired by the gods (usually Apollo) to give oracles.</note> and others who have used divine prophecy, and how many things they foretold that benefited the future, we would extend this discourse far too long, bringing forth a matter manifest to all. Yet it is worthy to testify that the ancients who gave names to things did not think madness <note>Original: "furorem," referring to the Greek *mania*.</note> was something shameful or disgraceful. For they would not have given such a name to the most noble of arts, when it happens by divine chance, if they had not considered it an honorable art. But now, these younger people have inserted the letter *tau* <note>Original Latin: "tau litera." This refers to the word *manike* (madness/inspired frenzy) being changed into *mantike* (divination/prophecy) by later generations.</note> and, quite unskillfully, called it <term>divination</term> <note>original: "mantike"; the art of foretelling the future.</note>. Indeed, the investigations of the future by sane men through birds and other signs—proceeding as they do from the conjecture of human intelligence—they named the "mental and augural history." This term later generations, turning a small thing into a large one, adorned with a more honorable name. 

Therefore, just as divine prophecy is more perfect and excellent than the guesswork of <term>augury</term> <note>The practice of interpreting the will of the gods from the flight of birds.</note>—and as the name is to the name, and the work to the work—so the ancients testify that the madness proceeding from God is more noble than human prudence. Furthermore, against the greatest diseases and hardships that sometimes hang over mortals due to ancient crimes and divine indignation, a certain madness arriving from somewhere for certain peoples has found remedies, foretelling what was necessary and taking refuge in the prayers and worship of the gods. From this, having obtained expiations and rituals of atonement, it has rendered the one possessed safe for the present and the future, attaining a release from present evils for the person who is rightly frenzied and occupied by this spirit. 

A third type of occupation and madness comes from the Muses; taking hold of a tender and untouched soul, it awakens and inspires it. Thus, through songs and other poetry, it adorns the infinite deeds of the ancients and instructs posterity. But he who approaches the gates of poetry without the madness of the Muses, trusting that he will become a good poet by some technical skill, is himself empty, and his poetry is eclipsed by that which proceeds from madness; indeed, the poetry produced by mere prudence vanishes before it. 

I can recount so many, and even more, noble works of divine madness. Therefore, let us not fear this very thing, nor let any reasoning frighten us away by showing that a prudent and sane friend is to be loved rather than a stirred one. But let him further show, if he can—and report a victory—that love was not granted by the gods for the benefit of the lover and the beloved. We, however, must now show the opposite: that such madness is given by the gods to men for the greatest happiness. 

The demonstration will be incredible to the contentious, but credible to the wise. However, we must first know the truth concerning the nature of the divine and human soul by looking at its passions and works. Let this be the principle of this demonstration: Every soul is immortal. For that which is always moved is eternal. But that which brings motion to another, and is itself moved from elsewhere, must necessarily have an end to living when it has an end to motion. 

<margin>On the immortality of the soul. This is word-for-word from Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations.</margin> 

Only that which moves itself, because it is never deserted by itself, never ceases to move. Indeed, for all other things that are moved, this is the source and the principle of moving. There is no origin for a principle, for all things arise from a principle, but the principle itself cannot be born from anything. For it would not be a principle if it were generated from elsewhere. And if it never arises, it never dies; for a principle, once extinguished, will neither be reborn from another nor create another from itself, since it is necessary that all things arise from a principle. 

Thus it happens that the principle of motion comes from that which is moved by itself; this can neither be born nor die. Otherwise, the whole heaven and all nature would necessarily collapse and stand still, nor find any force by which they might be moved by a first impulse. Since, therefore, it appears that what moves itself is immortal, one will not blush to say that this is the very substance and definition of the soul. For every body that receives motion from the outside is inanimate (soulless). But that which has motion within itself and from itself is animate (endowed with a soul), as if this were the very nature of the soul. If this is so—that there is nothing else which moves itself except the soul—then the soul is necessarily unbegotten and immortal. 

Enough has been said about the immortality of the soul. Regarding its <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" or "Form" refers to the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing.</note>, however, we must speak in this way: To describe what it is entirely would be a task for a divine and very long narration, but to describe a likeness of it is a human task and a shorter one. Therefore, I shall speak in this manner. 

<margin>On the Idea of the soul.</margin> 

Let the soul be likened to the combined power of a winged chariot and a charioteer. Now, the horses and charioteers of the gods are all good and of good stock, but those of others are mixed. In our case, the ruler first guides a pair of horses; then, one of the horses is good and beautiful and of such stock, while the other is the opposite and of opposite stock. Thus, our driving is necessarily difficult and troublesome. 

<margin>In what way a living creature is made.</margin> 

We must try to say how an animal is called mortal and immortal. Every soul has care for all that is inanimate and traverses the whole heaven, sometimes taking on different forms. When it is perfect and winged, it walks on high and governs the whole world. But when its wings have fallen off, it is carried along until it takes hold of something solid, where it finds a dwelling place and takes on an earthly body, appearing to move itself because of the soul's power. The whole is called a "living creature"—soul and body joined together—and is named a mortal animal. 

As for the "immortal," this is not perceived by any rational discourse, but is something we imagine; for we have neither seen nor sufficiently understood God, whom we imagine as an immortal living being having a soul and also a body naturally joined for all time. But let these things be and be spoken of as it pleases God. Now, let us state the cause by which the wings are cast off and fall from the soul. 

It is something like this: The natural power of a wing is to lift what is heavy into the heights where the race of the gods dwells. Of all things concerning the body, the soul is most a participant in the divine. The divine is beauty, wisdom, goodness, and whatever else can be called such. By these, the "winging" of the soul is most nourished and increased, but by the foul, the evil, and the opposites of these, it wastes away and perishes. 

The great leader in heaven, Jupiter <note>Original: "Iupiter," referring to Zeus.</note>, driving a winged chariot, goes first, adorning all things and disposing them with providence. He is followed by an army of gods and spirits, ordered into eleven parts. Vesta <note>Original: "Vesta," referring to Hestia.</note> alone remains in the house of the gods. Of the other gods, whoever is counted in the number of the twelve, each presides over his own function as he has been ordered. Thus, many blessed sights and paths exist within the heaven, where the race of the blessed gods directs their attention, each performing his own duty. He who wishes and is able follows, for envy is far removed from the divine choir. 

But when they go to the banquet and the feast, they travel upward to the highest summit of heaven. The vehicles of the gods, well-balanced and easy to steer, proceed easily, but the others struggle. For the horse that partakes of wickedness is heavy, weighing down and pulling toward the earth if the charioteer has not nourished him well. Here, finally, the ultimate labor and contest is proposed to the soul. For those called immortal, when they reach the...

# Phaedrus, or, on the Beautiful. 307

...when they have reached the summit, having moved outside, they stand upon the back of heaven. Once positioned there, the very rotation of the sphere carries them around, and they behold those things which are outside of heaven. <margin>Note how Plato places certain things outside of heaven.</margin> As for the super-celestial place, no one among our poets has yet praised it as it deserves, nor will any ever do so. It is, however, of this nature. For one must dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about the Truth itself. Without color, without shape, without touch, the truly existing essence <note>original: *essentia vere existens*—referring to Plato's Theory of Forms, the perfect "blueprints" of reality</note> is perceived only by the intellect, the pilot of the soul; the category of true knowledge occupies the region around this essence. <margin>The intellect is the pilot of the soul.</margin> Therefore, since the thought of God is nourished by intellect and pure knowledge, just as the thought of every soul that is about to receive its proper condition, it rejoices when it beholds that which truly *is* over time. Nourished and gladdened by the contemplation of truth, it is carried around by the revolution until the circle returns it to the same point. In this circuit, the soul perceives Justice itself, it perceives Temperance, it perceives Knowledge—not the kind of knowledge that is subject to change, nor that which differs according to the various things we now call "beings," but that which is true Knowledge in that which truly *is*. And having contemplated the other things that truly exist in the same way and being nourished by them, the soul sinks back inside the heaven and returns home. When it has returned, the charioteer stops the horses at the manger and sets before them ambrosia, and after that, nectar to drink. This is the life of the gods.

As for the other souls, that which best follows God and has become most like Him raises the head of the charioteer into the super-celestial place and is carried along with the rotation; yet it is troubled by the horses and barely beholds the things that truly exist. Another soul sometimes raises its head and sometimes sinks down: because of the violence of the horses, it sees some things but fails to see others. The rest of the souls, though all desiring the higher place, follow along; but being unable to reach it, they are submerged and carried around, trampling one another and colliding, each striving to precede the other. Thus, there is a great tumult and contest and extreme sweat. Here, through the fault of the charioteers, many are crippled, and many have their wings broken; all of them, entangled in great labor, depart without having shared in the vision of that which truly is. After their departure, they make use of the "food of opinion" <note>This refers to mere belief or appearances, rather than certain knowledge.</note>. The reason there is so much effort to see where the "Field of Truth" is located is that the best part of the soul receives its proper nourishment from that meadow, and the nature of the wings by which the soul is lifted is fed by this.

The decree of the goddess Adrastea <note>A name for Nemesis or Necessity; the law of fate.</note>—that is, the inescapable divine power—is this: whichever soul, following a god, has glimpsed any of the truths, shall be free from harm until the next circuit; and if it can always do this, it shall remain forever unharmed. But if, being unable to follow, it fails to see, and by some misfortune is filled with forgetfulness and vice and grows heavy, and having grown heavy it breaks its wings and falls to the earth, then the law forbids this soul to enter into a brutal nature <note>i.e., the body of an animal</note> in its first generation. Instead, it commands that the soul which has seen the most should enter the birth of a man who will be a philosopher, a lover of beauty, or a man of the Muses and of love. The soul that holds the second place shall descend into a lawful king, or a man of war and command. <margin>Nine conditions of souls.</margin> The third into a governor of a republic, or a manager of a household or a financier. The fourth into a hardworking gymnast, or someone concerned with the healing and care of the body. The fifth into those who will be prophets or involved in certain mysteries. The sixth into a poet, or some other person occupied with the art of imitation. The seventh into a craftsman or a *farmer*. <margin>Greek: Geometrician.</margin> <note>The Latin text says "farmer" (*agricolam*), but the marginal note corrects this to "Geometrician" based on the original Greek text.</note> The eighth into a sophist and a panderer to the crowd. The ninth into a tyrant.

In all these states, whoever lives his life justly afterwards obtains a better fate; but he who lives unjustly, a worse one. For no soul returns to the same place from which it set out for ten thousand years. <margin>The soul returns to the same place after ten thousand years.</margin> For it does not recover its wings before that space of time, except for the soul of one who has practiced philosophy without guile, or who has loved youths alongside the study of wisdom. These souls, in the third thousand-year circuit, if they have chosen this same life three times in a row, thus recover their wings and fly away after three thousand years. The other souls, having reached the end of their first life, are judged. Having been judged, some go into a place of judgment under the earth and endure their deserved punishments there. Others, lifted by judgment into a certain place in heaven, live in a manner worthy of the life they led in human form. In the thousandth year, both groups return to receive the lot and choice of a second life; each chooses the life it wants. Here, a human soul can pass into the life of a beast, and from a beast back into a man, provided that the soul was once that of a human. <margin>The transmutation of the human soul.</margin> For a soul that has never glimpsed the truth will not be able to come into this human form. 

Indeed, a man must understand according to "species" <note>or "Form"</note>, which proceeds from many sensations into a single concept reached by reasoning. This is the recollection <term>Anamnesis: the Platonic idea that learning is actually the soul remembering truths it knew before birth</term> of those things which our soul once saw when it was with God, looking down upon the things we now say *are*, and looking up toward that which truly *is*. Therefore, it is right that only the thought of the philosopher recovers its wings. For as much as is possible, his memory dwells upon those things in which God dwells, making him divine. He who uses such memories rightly, and is always initiated into the perfect mysteries, alone becomes truly perfect. Withdrawn from human pursuits and clinging to the divine, he is rebuked by the multitude as if he were out of his mind; but the fact that he is full of God is hidden from the multitude.

The whole discourse tends toward this: the fourth kind of madness <note>Plato identifies four divine "manias": prophecy, ritual, poetry, and love.</note>, which occurs when someone, seeing beauty here on earth and truly remembering that heavenly beauty, recovers his wings. Having received them, he strives to fly away. But since he cannot do so, looking upward like a bird and despising the things below, he is accused of being possessed by madness. Therefore, this divine alienation is the best of all alienations, and it arises from the best things, both for the one who possesses it and the one who participates in it. He who is gripped by this madness, because he loves beautiful things, is called a lover. As has been said, every human soul has beheld the things that truly are; otherwise, it would not have entered into this living being. To remember those things from the things that are here is not easy for everyone—neither for those who only glimpsed that place for a short time, nor for those who were unfortunate in their descent here and were corrupted by certain associations, so that they forgot the sacred things they once saw. Consequently, few remain who have enough memory left. These, when they behold some likeness here of the things they saw there, are struck with awe and are, as it were, taken out of themselves. Yet they do not know what this affection is, because they do not perceive it clearly enough. In these images, we see no splendor of Justice, Temperance, or any of the other things precious to souls; but through certain obscure instruments, barely and very few, approaching their images, perceive the nature of that which is represented. But Beauty was then to be seen most clearly, when, following that blessed choir in happy vision and contemplation—we following with Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, and others with some other god—they saw and were initiated into mysteries which it is right to call the most blessed of all. These we performed while we were still whole and untouched by the evils...

# 308 Book Twenty-Six.

...how many visions remained for the future, whole, simple, unchanging, and blessed; we, as initiates, gazed upon them in pure light, being ourselves pure and unstained, and released from this thing we now carry around and call a "body," to which we are bound like an oyster to its shell. <note>original: *in modum ostree huic alligati*—a famous Platonic metaphor for the soul being trapped in the physical body</note> These things must be credited to memory, for the sake of which we now extend our discourse out of a longing for those sights we once beheld. Beauty, however, as we have said, shone brightly among those celestial visions, and since we have come here, we have perceived it most clearly through the keenest of our senses. <margin>The words of Cicero from Book 1 of *On Ends*.</margin> For the sense of sight is the sharpest in us, though through it we do not see Wisdom. <note>Cicero famously paraphrased this passage, noting that if we could see Wisdom with our eyes, she would arouse incredible love.</note> What burning love would Wisdom excite for herself if she were visible? The same logic applies to all other things that are lovable. But Beauty alone has had this fortune: to be the most visible and the most lovable of all. <margin>Beauty alone is lovable.</margin> Therefore, he who was not recently initiated into the mysteries, or rather has become corrupted, is not quickly moved from this world to that absolute Beauty when he looks upon its namesake here. Thus, he does not feel reverence when he sees it, but, after the fashion of a four-legged beast, is intent on pleasure and strives to mate and procreate; joining together petulantly, he neither fears nor blushes to pursue pleasure against nature. But he who was recently purified through the sacred rites, or who once contemplated many things, when he sees a face of divine form that gracefully imitates Beauty itself, or some incorporeal appearance, first he shudders, and some ancient fear returns to him. Then, gazing upon it, he reveres it as a god; and unless he feared the charge of extreme madness, he would offer sacrifices to his beloved no differently than to the statues of the gods. As he gazes, he is seized by a change, a sweat, and an unusual heat following the shuddering. For when he receives the influx of beauty through his eyes, he becomes warm, and by this, the nature of his wings is irrigated. Once he has warmed up, the parts that relate to the budding of the wings melt—those parts which, long compacted by hardness, had blocked the growth of the germ. When the nourishment flows in, the seeds of the wings swell from their very roots and strive to break out through the whole form of the soul. For once, the soul was entirely supported by wings. Therefore, the whole soul seethes and leaps forward; just as infants when they are cutting teeth feel a stinging and pain in the gums, so too the soul of one growing wings seethes and is affected by a tickling sensation and distress. Thus, when the soul gazes at the beauty of a boy and, drinking in the desire flowing from it, is irrigated and warmed, it is relieved of its pain and rejoices. But when it is far away and the channels where the wing strives to sprout have dried up, they become parched and constricted, blocking the seed of the wings. This seed, shut inside along with that influx of desire, leaps like a pulsing vein and pricks its own channels from all sides. Thus, the whole soul, wounded on every side, is goaded and anguished, yet again, remembering beauty, it feels delight. From both these mixed feelings, it is vexed by the intensity and novelty of this passion, and in its anxiety, it rages and goes mad. Thus affected, it can neither sleep by night due to the frenzy, nor stay still by day, but runs everywhere, struck by the longing to see the beautiful one. Upon seeing him and drinking in that influx of desire, those things which were previously obstructed and closed are now opened and released. When the soul finally breathes again, it is freed from stings and pains. It is so soothed by this most sweet pleasure in the present moment that it never willingly departs from these charms, nor does it value anyone more than the beloved. It consigns parents, brothers, and all friends to oblivion, and is not moved at all by the loss of its estate through neglect; it utterly despises the ancestral customs and honors in which it used to glory, and is prepared to be a slave and to lie down wherever it is permitted, as long as it is near the object of its desire. For it not only worships and reveres the beautiful one, but has also found in him the only physician for its most grievous ailments. This is the state, O noble youth to whom I speak, which men call **Eros**, that is, Love. But what the gods call it, if you heard it, you would likely laugh because of your youth. Some followers of Homer, I believe, report from hidden poems two verses on love, the second of which is quite petulant and not very harmonious. They say: "Mortals call him **Eros**, that is, fleeting love; but the Immortals call him 'The Winged One' (*Pteros*), because of the necessity of flight." One may believe these things in part, or not. Yet the cause and the affection of lovers is exactly this. Those who were followers of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> can bear the burden of the "winged one" with more gravity and constancy. But those who worshiped Mars, and traveled in his circle, when they are ensnared by love and think they have been wronged by the beloved, are easily moved to slaughter and are carried headlong into killing both themselves and their loved ones. And so, according to which of the gods each person followed in the celestial choir, he honors and imitates that same god as long as he lives and remains uncorrupted; in this way, he conducts his first life here and presents himself to his beloved and others. Each person chooses a love from among the beautiful according to his own character, and treats that person as his god, crafting and adorning him like a statue, as if to honor and sacrifice to him. Those who follow Jove seek a beloved whose soul is Jovial <note>meaning kingly or philosophical, like Zeus</note>. Therefore, they consider whether his nature is suited for philosophy and command; and when they have found such a person and love him, they strive with all their might that he may become so. If they have not previously entered upon what they desire, they now strive with great zeal, learning from wherever they can and progressing in this work themselves. Investigating the nature of their god from within themselves, they finally achieve their prayer because they are compelled to fix the sight of their mind upon the God with the greatest attention. Then, when they touch him through memory, they are inspired by divinity, and from him they take their customs and pursuits, as far as it is possible for a human to participate in God. Since they attribute the cause of all these things to the beloved, they are even more ardently inflamed with affection. And if they draw inspiration from Jove, like Bacchic priests, they pour it into the soul of the beloved, making him as similar as possible to their own God. Those who followed Juno <note>Hera</note> seek a royal person, and having found him, they act in the same way toward him. Likewise, the followers of Apollo and each of the other gods, imitating their respective deities, seek a youth of a nature corresponding to that god; and having found him, they themselves imitate the god and persuade the youth, leading him into the pursuits and the very "Idea" of that deity to the best of their power. They use no envy or ill-will toward their youths, but with all their effort they try to form them into a perfect likeness of themselves and the God they worship. This, then, is the care and the goal of true lovers: if they achieve what they desire, it is as we have described; and a great and happy blessing comes from the friend who is "mad" with love to the one he loves, if the beloved is won over. But how the beloved is won, happens in this way. Every soul from the beginning...

<meta>This page continues the Latin translation of Plato’s *Phaedrus*, specifically the famous Allegory of the Charioteer.
