# Phaedrus, or, On Beauty. 309

At the beginning of this story, we divided the soul into three parts: we established two forms of horses, and the charioteer as the third part. Let those same divisions remain for us in the present discussion. Of the horses, one is good, and the other is not. However, we have not yet fully described what constitutes the virtue of the good horse or the wickedness of the bad one, so we must speak of it now. The good horse is of an excellent disposition, upright in form, well-defined in its limbs, with a high neck, a slightly aquiline nose <note>original: *naribus modice aquilinis*—a hooked or "eagle-like" nose was often considered a sign of noble character</note>, a bright color, and black eyes. It is a lover of honor, a participant in temperance and modesty, and a friend of true opinion. It requires no whip, but is guided by encouragement and reason alone. The other horse is crooked and bulky, clumsily driven, sprawling and confusedly put together, with a stiff and thick neck, a low-hanging throat, a flat face, a dark color, and grey eyes shot with blood. It is moody and insolent, with shaggy and deaf ears, barely obeying the lash and the goads. Therefore, when the charioteer looks upon a lovely face and his whole soul is inflamed with the sensations of tickling and the stings of desire, that horse which is obedient to the charioteer—as is its custom—is restrained by shame and holds itself back from leaping upon the beloved. But the other horse can be restrained neither by goads nor by lashes; it leaps forward and, carried away by violence, troubles its fellow horse and the charioteer, dragging them toward the pleasures of Venus <note>original: *Veneris voluptate*—meaning physical or sexual pleasure</note>. At first, the others resist, indignant that they are being dragged toward such heavy and lawless acts. At last, when that evil horse will not cease, they are compelled to move forward, and they finally yield and agree to do what is commanded. From here, they draw near to the "little fire" <note>original: *igniculo*—a metaphor for the beloved child or the spark of beauty</note> and behold his flashing face. Looking upon him, the charioteer’s memory returns to the nature of Beauty itself, and he sees it again standing with Temperance upon a holy pedestal. Seeing this, he is afraid and, out of reverence, falls backward. In doing so, he is forced to pull the reins back so hard that both horses sit back on their haunches—the one willingly, because it does not struggle, but the wanton horse entirely against its will. As they move further away, the good horse is so overcome by shame and wonder that it drenches the entire soul with sweat. The bad horse, once freed from the pain of the bit and the fall, barely catches its breath before it begins to rage, reproaching the charioteer and its yoke-mate with indignation, claiming they have deserted their post out of cowardice and laziness. Again, it forces them to approach against their will, and only with difficulty does it grant their plea to delay until another time. When the appointed time comes, which the others pretend to have forgotten, the bad horse reminds them, neighing and dragging them, compelling them again to approach the beloved with the same words. Once they are close, it lowers its head, stiffens its tail, bites the bit, and shamelessly pulls. But the charioteer, suffering even more than before and falling back as if from a starting gate, pulls the reins even more violently, jerking the teeth of the wicked horse, drenching its foul tongue and jaws with blood, and forcing its legs and muzzle to the ground, compelling it to pay the penalty. After that wicked horse has suffered this many times, it ceases its wantonness and, now humbled, obeys the charioteer’s foresight. Thus, when it sees the beautiful youth, it trembles with fear, so that the soul of the lover follows the footsteps of the youth with a certain reverence and awe. Therefore, as the youth is observed by the lover with all devotion as if he were equal to a God—not by a lover who is pretending, but one truly so affected—and since the youth himself is naturally a friend to the one who honors him, he eventually joins in friendship with the lover. Even if he had previously been deceived by the slander of his companions and classmates saying it is shameful to associate with a lover, and had therefore rejected him, eventually, as time passes, his age and the natural order of things lead him into the lover's company. For it is never decreed by fate that an evil man should be a friend to the evil, or that a good man should not be a friend to the good. Thus, when the youth has received the lover into conversation and companionship, the benevolence of that lover becomes more intimate, and it compels the beloved to wonder. He notices that the goodwill of all his other relatives and friends, when compared to this divinely inspired friend, is of no weight at all. If the older man continues this for a long time, remaining close and touching him in the gymnasiums and other such places, then the fountain of that flowing liquid—which Jupiter, when captured by love for Ganymede, called **Desire** <note>original: *imeron*</note>—flows abundantly into the lover. Part of it flows into him, and part of it flows out when he is overflowing. And just as air or an Echo is reflected back from smooth and solid bodies to the place from which they came, so that flow of beauty reflects back into the beautiful youth through his eyes—the way it usually penetrates the soul—and it so waters the passages of the feathers that they are now able to, and begin to, sprout <note>Referencing the "regrowth of wings" mentioned on the previous page</note>. Thus, it fills the soul of the beloved with mutual love. He loves, yet he is uncertain what he loves; he neither knows his own feeling nor can he explain it. But just as if he had caught a disease of the eyes from looking at someone with sore eyes, he cannot name the cause of his illness, nor does he realize that he sees himself in the lover as if in a mirror. Therefore, when the lover is present, his pain ceases just as the lover's does; when the lover is absent, he longs just as he is longed for, possessing a mutual love that is like an image of love, though he calls it and thinks of it not as love, but as friendship. He desires, almost as much as the lover (though more moderately), to see, touch, love, kiss, and trust him; and as is expected, he soon does these things. In their intimacy, the intemperate horse of the lover speaks to the charioteer, demanding a brief pleasure in exchange for many labors. But the horse of the youth does not know what to say; instead, bursting with longing and anxiety, it returns the lover's goodwill, rejoicing in his most loving friend, and in their familiarity, it is prepared to obey the lover’s desire to the best of its ability. However, the yoke-mate and the charioteer oppose these things with shame and reason. Therefore, if the better parts of the mind prevail according to a right way of life and the study of philosophy, they lead a blessed and harmonious life here, being masters of themselves and modest, having subdued that part in which the soul's vice dwells and having liberated that part to which virtue belongs. At the end of this life, having regained their wings, they fly away, having won one of the three truly Olympic contests. No greater good can either human temperance or divine madness bring to men. But if they have followed a more base life, devoid of philosophy though otherwise ambitious, perhaps in a state of drunkenness or some other careless license, their intemperate horses invade their unguarded souls. Bringing them together into that kind of delight which the common people judge to be most blessed, they compel them to pursue it and spend their time fulfilling that desire. However, they perform this act only rarely, because the whole thought of the mind does not consent to it. These men are also friends, though less so than the others...

...father. Is it not so?" "Certainly," Agathon said. "And is a mother not the mother of someone?" And he agreed to that. "Answer further," Socrates said, "to a few things, so that you may better understand what I mean. A brother, in the very thing he is, is he the brother of someone?" He said yes. "Is he not the brother of a brother or a sister?" "Certainly of those." "Try similarly to show us about love: is love the love of something or of nothing?" "Of something, certainly." "Keep this in mind, then, of what he is the love. And answer this: does Love desire that very thing of which he is the love, or not?" "And most especially so." "Does he possess this very thing within himself, and yet desire and love what he has? Or rather, does he love and desire it because he does *not* have it?" "It is likely that he does not have it." "Consider further whether, instead of it being merely 'likely,' it is *necessary* that whatever desires something, desires that which it lacks; and if it does not lack it, it does not desire it. This pleases me wonderfully as being necessary. But how does it seem to you, Agathon?" Socrates asked. "The same as to you," Agathon replied. "You speak well. Would someone who is big want to be big, or someone who is strong want to be strong?" "From what we have granted above, it seems to me impossible. For he would not be in need of those things which he already contained in himself." "You speak the truth. For if he who is strong wanted to be strong, and he who is swift to be swift, and finally he who is healthy to be healthy, perhaps someone might believe that these, and any others, desire the things they already have. I say this so that we are not deceived here. If you consider this diligently, Agathon, you will see it as necessary that whatever these people have in the present time, they must have it in that same time, whether they want to or not; and who would desire that? But when someone adds: 'But I, while I am healthy, want to be healthy; and while I am rich, I want to be rich; and therefore I desire what I have,' we immediately answer him: 'O good man, you who have obtained riches, health, and strength, want to possess these also in the future; for in the present, you have them whether you want to or not. You see then, when you say "I desire what is present to me," do you mean anything other than this: "what is present to me now, I long to be present in the future"?' Do you think this man would answer this or something else, Agathon?" "Nothing else," Agathon said. "Love, surely, of this kind looks to that which is not yet at hand nor possessed, namely that those things may be present and preserved in the time that follows." "That is entirely so." "And here, then, as well as anyone else who desires, he desires what is not yet ready or provided, or what is not present, or what he does not have, or what he himself is not, or what he lacks. Such are the things of which there is desire and love." "Undoubtedly such." "Come," Socrates said, "let us repeat what has been said above. First, Love was said to be the love of certain things; second, of those things especially which he lacks." "Certainly," he answered. "Remember, furthermore, of what things you asserted Love to be. I will reduce it to your memory if you wish. I believe you spoke thus: that all the affairs of the gods were arranged through the love of beautiful things. For of ugly things, there is no love at all. Did you not say so?" "I did indeed." "You speak probably, my friend. And if it is so, Love is certainly the love of beauty, and not at all of ugliness." "I agree." "Has it not been granted that one loves that which one lacks and does not have?" "Plainly granted." "Therefore Love lacks beauty, and does not have it." "Necessary." "What then? Do you call that beautiful which lacks beauty and does not have it?" "Not at all." "Furthermore, if these things are so, do you still assert that Love is beautiful?" "I seem to have understood nothing of the things I said above." "You spoke rightly. But answer a little further: do not good things themselves seem to be beautiful?" "To me they do." "If, therefore, Love lacks beautiful things, and good things are beautiful, he also lacks good things." "I could in no way resist you, O Socrates. Let it be, then, as you say." "You could never oppose the truth, O beloved Agathon, though you can very easily oppose Socrates."

[Initials: Ornamental V]
"But I will now let Agathon go, and I will relate to you, O guests, a speech about Love which I once received from a prophetic woman, Diotima, who was...

<margin>Diotima the prophetess.</margin>

...skilled in these matters and understood many other things wisely; she once, when the Athenians had performed sacrifices ten years before the plague, gave them a postponement of the disease. She instructed me in the faculty of love. What she said, I will try to express to you from myself, according to those things on which Agathon and I have agreed. It is necessary first, O Agathon, as you also set forth, to show what and of what kind Love is, and then to enumerate his works. It is better, as it seems to me, to relate it to you now in the same order in which that stranger examined me. For I said almost the same things to her that Agathon said to me: that Love was a great god and looked toward beautiful things. And she refuted me with the same arguments by which I refuted him: that Love was neither beautiful, as I said, nor good. To which I then said: 'What are you saying, O Diotima? Is Love then ugly and bad?' and she said: 'Hush, I pray. Or do you think it is necessary that whatever is not beautiful must be ugly?' 'Most certainly.' 'And that what is not wise is ignorant? Have you not noticed that there is a certain middle ground between wisdom and ignorance?' 'What is that?' 'To have a right opinion: that is, to participate in the truth without a certain reason. For this is neither science (for science is never without reason) nor, on the other hand, ignorance.'

<margin>Right opinion is the middle ground between wisdom and ignorance.</margin>

'For that which hits upon the truth is not called ignorance. Right opinion is something of this kind, a middle between wisdom and ignorance.' 'You were telling the truth,' I said. 'Do not force, then,' she said, 'that which is not beautiful to be...

<margin>What right opinion is like.</margin>

...ugly; or that which is not good to be bad. By the same reasoning, although you may grant that Love is neither beautiful nor good...

<margin>Love is the middle between the ugly and the beautiful.</margin>

...you nevertheless should not think he is necessarily ugly or bad, but a middle between them.' 'But surely,' I said, 'all agree on this: that Love is a great god.' 'Do you mean all those who are ignorant,' she said, 'or those who know?' 'Everyone,' I said. 'How,' she said laughing, 'could those confess him to be a great god who do not even want him to be a god at all?' 'Who are they?' I asked. 'You are one,' she said, 'and I am another.' 'How do you assert that I said this?' 'I will easily show you. Come, tell me: do you not affirm all gods to be beautiful and blessed? Would you dare to say any of the gods is not beautiful or blessed?' 'Not by Jupiter.' 'But do you not call those blessed who possess good and beautiful things?' 'Them only.' 'Yet you admitted in what came before that Love, because of his lack of beautiful and good things, desires those very things he lacks.' 'I admitted it indeed.' 'How then is he a God,' she said, 'who is devoid of beautiful and good things?' 'In no way, it seems,' I said. 'Do you see that you yourself do not think Love is a God?' 'What then? Is Love mortal?' 'Not at all.' 'What then?' 'Like the things above, a middle between mortal and immortal.' 'What is he, O Diotima?' 'A great daemon, O Socrates. For the whole nature of daemons...

<margin>The nature of spirits (daemons).</margin>

...is a middle between mortals and gods.' 'What power does it have?'

<margin>The duties and offices of spirits (daemons).</margin>

'It interprets,' she said, 'and conveys human things to the gods, and divine things to humans: the prayers and sacrifices of the former, and the commands, sacred rites, institutions, and order of the latter. Constituted in the middle of both, it fills up the whole, so that the universe is connected with itself by such a link.'

<summary>Socrates uses logic to prove that Love must be a "middle" state, neither beautiful nor good itself, but a desire for those things. He introduces the mysterious priestess Diotima, who explains that Love is a "daemon" or mediating spirit.</summary>

# On Riches.

[[notes: This text is a Latin translation of the *Eryxias*, a dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato but likely written by a member of the early Academy. It features Socrates debating the nature of wealth.]]

...thinks that it is the most important thing: let no one say it is anything other than that. Believing that I was speaking not of small matters, but of those things which seem most important—*virtus* (virtue) and *divitiae* (riches)—I asked: whether he thought a man who had two talents of silver was wealthier, or a man who possessed a field valued at two talents.

"The one who has the field, I think," he said.

"By this reasoning, then," I said, "if someone has cloaks, or rugs, or other garments that are worth more than what that foreigner possesses, he would also be wealthier." He agreed to this as well.

"But if someone gave you a choice of these, which would you want?"

"Whichever is worth the most," he said.

"In which way do you believe you would be wealthier?"

"In that way."

"Now, it seems to me that just as someone possesses things of the greatest value, so he must be considered the wealthiest."

"It seems so," he replied.

"Therefore," I said, "the healthy are wealthier than the sick, if indeed health is worth more than the money of the sick. For there is no one who would not prefer to be in good health while possessing a small amount of silver, rather than to be ill while having the riches of a Great King; clearly indicating that health is estimated as having more value to him. For he would not prefer it unless he judged it to be of greater price than money."

"Certainly not."

"If indeed it is established that there is something else which is worth more than health, would he who possesses that very thing be the wealthiest?"

"Indeed he would."

"But if someone approaching us right now should ask: 'O Socrates, Eryxias, and Erasistratus, can you tell me what is of the greatest value to a human being? Is it that possession by which the owner might best deliberate on how to most conveniently manage his own affairs and those of his friends?' What shall we say this is?"

"To me, Socrates, *felicitas* (happiness) seems to be of the greatest value to a man."

"And not wrongly so," I said. "But can we not consider those men the happiest who act in the best possible way?"

"We can, in my judgment."

"Do not those men act best who sin the least against themselves and against other men, and who carry out the most things rightly?"

"Most certainly."

"Do not those who know good and evil, and what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—cannot they manage things most rightly and sin the least?" He conceded this as well.

"Now it seems altogether that the same men are the wisest, those who act best, the happiest, and the wealthiest—if indeed *sapientia* (wisdom) is seen to be of the greatest value."

"Let it be so," said Erasistratus, interrupting, "but what utility is there for a man, O Socrates, even if he were wiser than Nestor, if he does not have the things necessary for living—food, drink, clothing, and other things of this sort? How could wisdom profit him here? Or in what way is he 'wealthiest' whom nothing prevents from begging, and to whom none of the necessary things are supplied?"

He seemed to be saying something significant here. But I said: "Would he who possesses wisdom, if he were lacking these things, suffer what you say? Whereas if someone possessed the house of Pulytion [[notes: a famously wealthy Athenian]], and the house were full of gold and silver, would he lack nothing?"

"Nothing prevents that man," he said, "from holding an auction as soon as possible, so that in exchange for what he possesses, he might have either those very things needed for food, or coins with which he can acquire the same for himself, and thus immediately abound in all things."

"That is true," I said, "if it should happen that there are men who would rather have a house of that sort than the other's wisdom. But if there are those who value wisdom and the things that proceed from it more highly, would he not be able to 'auction' it much more conveniently if he lacked something and wished to sell his wisdom and its works for that reason? For while the use of a house is great and necessary, and the comforts pertaining to life are great if one lives in such a house rather than a small, vile hut; yet the utility of wisdom might not seem so great, and its benefits appear small—whether a man be wise or unskilled in the greatest matters—because men not only do not want to buy it, but even despise it. Yet many people, as if in need, desire and willingly buy cypress wood to ornament a house, and Pentelic stones [[notes: marble from Mount Pentelicus]].

If someone is a skilled pilot, yet cannot practice medicine or any other such art well and beautifully, will he not be more precious and 'saleable' than any of these things held as great riches? And he who can deliberate well for himself and for another, and determine in what way he might do the best things—will he not be able to sell this very thing when he wishes?"

But Eryxias, interrupting, etc., as if he had been offended, looking on angrily, said: "You, Socrates, if you had to tell the truth, would you say you are wealthier than Callias son of Hipponicus? [[notes: Callias was one of the richest men in Athens]]. Yet although you would claim to be less ignorant and wiser in the greatest matters, you would be no wealthier for that reason."

"Perhaps," I said, "you think these discourses we are now sharing are jokes, because you do not truly believe things are as they are said to be. Rather, you think they are like those games which, if someone plays them well, he can easily defeat his fellow players so that they have nothing more to object. Perhaps you think the same about the wealthy: that the reality is not as it is said, but that these are certain speeches no more true than they are false—speeches by which a man circumscribes his adversaries to persuade them that the wisest are also the wealthiest, even though he is lying and they are speaking the truth. 

Indeed, perhaps it is no wonder, as if two people were disputing about letters: one contending that 'S' is the first letter in 'Socrates,' and the other contending it is 'A'. Whose speech has more reason? His who says 'A', or his who wants 'S' to be the beginning?"

Then, laughing and blushing at the same time, Eryxias looked around at those present as if he himself had not been part of what was said, and said: "I do not think, Socrates, that we should hold those speeches among us which benefit no one and persuade no one present. For what mortal who is even slightly sane could be persuaded that the wisest are the wealthiest? Instead, we should hear speeches that show, when we speak of acquiring riches, from where it may be done honestly, and whether it is a good or an evil thing."

"Let it be as you say," I replied. "We shall act more cautiously hereafter. And by Hercules, you do well to warn us. But you yourself, who put on this new discourse and think that what was said before is irrelevant, why do you not proceed to say whether acquiring riches seems to be a good or an evil?"

"To me, certainly," he said, "acquiring riches seems to be a good thing."

While he still wanted to say something else, Critias (the Athenian politician and philosopher) interrupted and asked: "Tell me, Eryxias, do you think acquiring riches is a good thing?"

"I would be mad indeed," he said, "if I thought otherwise. I believe there is no one who would not affirm the same."

"I also believe," said the other, "that there is no one I could not induce to agree with me that for some men, acquiring riches is an evil. For if it were entirely a good thing, it would clearly never appear to be an evil to any of us."

Then I said to them: "If...

[[page number: 657]]

# On Riches.

...if you were disagreeing about this—which of you spoke more truly about the study of horsemanship, that is, in what way one rides best—and if I were skilled in this matter, I would ask you to put an end to the disagreement. For I would be ashamed if, being present, I did not prevent your contention according to my ability; or if, contending about some other matter, you were to depart having become enemies instead of friends because you did not agree. 

But now, since you contend over a matter that is necessary for use in one's whole life, and it matters greatly whether it should be cared for as useful or useless—and these are not small things, but seen by the Greeks as the greatest of all; for fathers command this first to their sons: that as soon as they reach the age where they seem to understand for themselves, they should look around to see how they can become rich. For if you have something, you thrive; if nothing, you lie low. Since these things are so strongly sought, and you disagree on so great a matter—and disagree specifically on the acquisition of riches—not whether acquiring riches is black or white, light or heavy, but whether it is an evil or a good: it seems you will take up enmities between you if you persist in contending over goods and evils, even though you are the best of friends and kinsmen. 

I, therefore, as much as is in me, would not neglect this, nor permit you to be discordant, if I could speak of the matter as it is to recall you from disagreement. Now, since I cannot provide that myself, and each of you thinks he can induce the other to agree, I am ready to help as much as I can, so that at last you may agree on how the matter stands. You, therefore, Critias, proceed as you promised to make us agree."

"Gladly," he said. "I would ask this Eryxias, just as I began: whether men seem to him to be just and unjust."

"They certainly do," he said, "and very much so."

"And what about acting unjustly? Does it seem to you to be an evil or a good?"

"An evil."

"Does a man who corrupts and seduces the wives of his neighbors with silver, and does so against the customs and laws of the city—does he seem to you to act unjustly or not?"

"He acts unjustly."

"Therefore," he said, "the unjust and covetous man, if he is rich and can spend silver, easily sins. But if he is not rich and has nothing to spend, he cannot so easily fulfill what he desires, and for that reason he sins less. Thus it happens that it is more expedient for a man not to be rich if he will accomplish less of what he desires, especially when he desires shameful things. 

Furthermore, would you say being sick is an evil or a good?"

"An evil."

"What? Do some men seem to be intemperate?"

"They do."

"If it is better for such a man, for the sake of his health, to abstain from food, drink, and other things thought to be sweet, yet because of his intemperance he cannot, would it not be more useful for him not to have the means to supply these things than to have a great abundance of necessities? For thus he would have no faculty for sinning, even if he greatly wished to. Thus it was said well and beautifully by **Critias**."

Wherefore **Eryxias**, had those present not been feared, could have been restrained by nothing from rising up and striking Critias, so much did he think himself deprived of a great thing once he clearly perceived that he had not previously thought rightly about acquiring riches. 

But I, having recognized that Eryxias was so affected, and guarding against a greater reproach and contention: "This discourse," I said, "Prodicus of Ceos, a wise man, was holding a little while ago in the Lyceum. To those present, he seemed to be talking such nonsense that none of them could be induced to believe he was telling the truth. Indeed, a certain young and witty man approached him, and sitting nearby, began to deride and mock him, and soon to rouse him, wanting to receive a rational account of what he was saying. In this matter, he received much more praise from the listeners than Prodicus did."

"Can you relate that discourse to us?" asked Erasistratus.

"I can, if I recall it from memory. The matter went like this, I believe. The youth asked him in what way he thought acquiring riches was both an evil and a good. Then he, answering in the same way you did just now, said: 'For honest and good men, and those who know where it is necessary to use coins, it is a good; but for the wicked and those who do not know how to use them, it is an evil.' 

'Things are also like this in other matters,' he said. 'For whatever the nature of those who use them, such must the things themselves be.' Archilochus seems to me to have sung that beautifully:

> Such things they think, as are the peaks they hold.

'Now,' said the youth, 'if someone were to make me wise with that wisdom by which good men are wise, it would be necessary that at the same time he handed over other good things to me, even though he had no business in them. Because he would have made me wise from being foolish, just as if someone made me a grammarian, it would be necessary that he simultaneously taught me grammatical things; and if a musician, musical things. And even so, if someone made me good, it is necessary that he prepared good things for me at the same time.' 

Prodicus did not agree with these things, but affirmed his previous points. Therefore the youth said: 'Does it seem to you that just as building a house is a man's work, so is making things good? Or is it necessary that whatever things are from the beginning, they remain so perpetually?' 

But Prodicus, cleverly (as it seems to me) suspecting where the speech would fall, lest he should seem refuted before all who were present (for if he suffered it alone, he would have thought nothing of it), replied that it was far from being a man's work. 

'For tell me,' he said, 'does virtue seem to you to be able to be handed over by teaching, or is it innate in men?' 

'Handed over by teaching.' 

'Would not he seem a fool to you,' he said, 'who, praying to the Gods, thinks he can become a grammarian or a musician, or attain any other science, when it is necessary to acquire it either by learning from another or by finding it for oneself?' 

The youth agreed, and soon said: 'You, Prodicus, when you pray to the Gods that you may act well and that things may be good for you, then you ask for nothing else than that you become honest and good; if indeed things are good for honest and good men, but evil for the wicked. Therefore, if indeed virtue can be acquired, you seem to pray for nothing else than to be taught what you do not know.' 

Then I said to Prodicus that he seemed to commit no small fault if he offended in this matter—if he thought that what we ask for is done for us by the Gods at the same time. 'For even if,' I said, 'often coming hastily into the city, you make vows and ask the Gods to give you good things, you do not know whether they can give what you ask; just as if, going to the grammarian's door, you were to ask him to hand over grammatical science to you, when you have previously worked at nothing in that matter, but wish, learning it immediately, to be able to perform what belongs to a grammarian.'"

When I had said these things, Prodicus...

[[page number: 658]]

# On Riches.

...Prodicus attacked the young man to avenge himself, demonstrating the same things you do now, and taking it badly that it seemed vain to say one must pray to the Gods. And meanwhile, the overseer of the gymnasium approaching, ordered him to leave the gymnasium, on the grounds that he was disputing things that were not suitable for the youth, and if not suitable, then clearly harmful. 

I have run through these things for you for this reason: so that you may know how men are disposed toward Philosophy. For Prodicus, saying these things, seemed so insane to those present that he was ejected from the gymnasium. 

You, on the contrary, now seem to dispute so well that you not only persuade those present but even induce your adversary to agree with you. As in the forum, if two men give testimony about the same matter, one of whom seems honest and upright, and the other wicked, the judges are certainly not moved by the testimony of the wicked one, but would rather do anything else or the opposite; but if he who seems honest and upright says these things, they are believed to be most true. 

Perhaps in that way, those present were disposed toward you and Prodicus: they thought him a sophist and too arrogant, but you a *politicon* (statesman) and a man of great value. Whence they later think that one should look not at what kind of speech it is, but what kind of people they are who say it. 

"And if you are mocking, Socrates," said Erasistratus, "nevertheless Critias seems to me to be saying something."

"By Hercules, I am not mocking," I said. "But why did you arrive at this point by discussing so well and beautifully, and yet not finish the rest of the speech? For it seems to me something still remains for you to consider. After it was conceded that acquiring riches is a good for some and an evil for others, it remains to consider what that thing itself is. For unless you first know this, you will never be able to agree whether it is an evil or a good. I, as much as I can, am ready to weigh the matter with you. Therefore, let him tell us, who thinks acquiring riches is a good thing, how he defines it."

"But I, Socrates," he said, "will bring forward nothing unheard of, nothing new to other men. For I say that possessing much money [[margin: What it is to acquire riches.]] is to acquire riches, and thus to be rich; nor do I think Critias is one who thinks acquiring riches is anything else."

"By this reasoning," I said, "it still remains to be observed what kinds of money there are, lest a little later you disagree about this matter again. For at first, they seemed different to you. For the Carthaginians use a coin of this sort: something is tied in a small piece of leather, and it is only as large as a very large *stater* (coin). What is tied inside, no one knows except those who make it. They use it thus sealed, and he who has the most of these coins seems to have the most money and to be the wealthiest. But if someone among us possessed many coins of this sort, he would be no more rich than if he had many pebbles from the mountains. 

The Lacedaemonians (Spartans), however, use a coin made of that iron which is useless; and he who possesses a great weight of this iron seems to be rich, though elsewhere it is of no price. In Ethiopia, they use engraved stones, which a Spartan could use for nothing. But among the Scythians who are called Nomads, if someone had Pulytion’s house, he would seem no wealthier than if he possessed Mount Lycabettus among us. 

It is clear, then, that each of these things should not be numbered among riches, since it is established that some who possess them are no wealthier because of it. Truly," I said, "each of these things is money to some, and those who hold them are rich; but to others they are neither money, nor are the owners wealthier because of them—just as honorable and shameful things are not the same for everyone, but different for different people. 

If we wish to inquire why the houses that are precious to us are not counted among riches by the Scythians, and why we conversely value less the skins that are money to the Carthaginians, or the iron the Spartans use as a coin—could we not find it easily and immediately? If someone at Athens possessed a thousand pounds of those stones in the forum which we use for nothing, would he be considered any wealthier than you for that reason?"

"Not to me, certainly."

"But if he had a thousand pounds of Lychnite stone [[notes: Parian marble]], we would say he was very rich."

"Precisely."

"For this reason especially," I said, "that this one is useful, and those are useless to us."

"Indeed."

"For among the Scythians, too, houses are not held among their wealth because there is no utility in a house for them. Nor would a Scythian man value a beautiful house more than a garment made of goat skins, which is called a [[Greek: σίσυρα]] (*sisyra*); because he thinks there is much utility for him in the latter, but none in the former. Nor do we put Carthaginian coins in our money. For we cannot, as with silver, import or export the things we need with it. Therefore it must be useless to us."

"It seems so."

"Therefore, whatever things are useful to us are to be called money, having been prepared for the necessary uses of life; [[margin: What is money?]] but whatever things are not for use, they are certainly not to be called money."

"How can this be, Socrates?" said Eryxias, interrupting. "Do we not sometimes use disputation, and offense, and many other such things among us? Are these too—since there clearly seems to be a use—money to us?"

"Therefore," I said, "by this reasoning, it has not been declared to us what is properly money. For it is almost universally conceded by all that it must be useful if it is to be money; but which things among those we use are money—since they are not all money—has not yet been sufficiently said. 

Wherefore, let us now first see this. Will what we seek be more easily found if we pursue it again and inquire: what is that for which we use money, and for what was the possession of money invented, as Medicine was invented for driving away diseases? Thus perhaps the matter will become more manifest to us. 

Since, therefore, it appears necessary that all things which are money must also be useful; and among things that are useful, there is a certain genus of things we call money: it remains to perceive in what matter money is most useful. For all things which we use for some work are equally useful—just as all things that have a soul are animals, but we call a certain genus of animals 'Man'. 

If someone now asked us: 'If what thing were removed from us, would we need neither Medicine nor its instruments?' we could say: 'If diseases were removed from bodies and never born at all; or if they were born, but immediately departed.' For Medicine is, it seems, the science that is useful to us for driving away diseases. 

If he asked us again: 'If what were taken from us, would we not need money?' could we say?"

[[page number: 659]]

# On Riches.

"If we cannot say, let us consider it thus: Come, if a man could live without food and drink so that he never hungered nor thirsted, would he sometimes not need these very things, or silver, or any other thing to acquire them for himself?"

"It certainly seems so to me."

"Therefore," I said, "the same would happen in other things, if we did not need those things for the care of the body for which we are now in need—sometimes heat and cold, and other things which the body, being born in need, must necessarily require. For those things called money would not be useful to us if a man lacked none of those things for whose sake we desire to have money—so that we can supply the desires and necessities of the body with those things we frequently lack. 

But if a man is in need, the possession of money is useful for the care of the body for those who are needy. If this were driven away from the midst of us, as we say, we would not need money, and perhaps there would be no money at all."

"It appears so."

"It also appears, it seems, that the things useful for the same business are money to us."

But this little reasoning greatly disturbed him. Wherefore I said: "What? Can we say it is possible for the same thing to be useful at one time and useless at another for the same action?"

"I would not say so," he said, "but if we need something for a certain action, it seems useful to me; if we do not need it, it is useless."

"If indeed," I said, "we could make a bronze statue without fire, we would not need fire to make it; and if we did not need it, it would not be useful. The same reasoning can be applied to other things."

"It is established."

"Nothing, therefore, without which something can be done, seems to be useful to us for that thing."

"Nothing."

"If we, therefore, without silver and gold and other such things—which we do not use for the care of the body in the same way as food, drink, clothing, rugs, and houses—could so soothe the desires and necessities of the body that it required nothing more, then neither silver, nor gold, nor other things of this sort would seem to be money to us, since this could be done without them."

"They would not seem so."

"Certainly," I said, "if these are not useful, they cannot seem to be money to us; but those things must be money by which we can acquire the things that are useful. Never, Socrates," he said, "could I be induced to believe that gold and silver and other things of that kind are not money to us. I am certainly very persuaded that what is useless to us is not money; and conversely, that what is useful should be numbered among those riches that profit most. But I will never allow myself to be persuaded that these things we just mentioned are not useful for the uses of life, since we acquire the things necessary for living with them."

"Come now, what shall we say of these matters? Are there men who teach Music or literature, or hand over some other science, and who, demanding a fee for these things, prepare for themselves the things necessary for life?"

"There are."

"Do not these men acquire the necessary things for themselves through science, exchanging it just as we exchange gold and silver?"

"I think so."

"If indeed they prepare for themselves by this very thing those things which they use for life, then this itself must be useful for life. For we said silver was useful for that reason: because with it we can acquire the things necessary for life."

"We said so."

"Since, therefore, sciences themselves seem useful to us for this, for the same reason that gold and silver are money, it is manifest that those who hold them are also wealthier—even if a little while ago we did not so easily allow them to be the wealthiest. Indeed, from what has now been conceded, it must follow that those who are more endowed with science are sometimes also wealthier. 

For if someone asked us whether we think a horse is useful to any man, would you say 'yes,' or rather this: 'to those who know how to use a horse, it is useful; but to those who do not, it is useless'?"

"I would say the latter."

"By the same reasoning," I said, "you would say Medicine is not useful to any man, but only to him who knows how it ought to be used."

"I would."

"Does it not seem the same should be said of other things—indeed, all things?"

"It seems so."

"Gold and silver, and other things that seem to be money—would they not be useful only to him who knows how they are to be used?"

"They would."

"But a little while ago, did it not seem to be the part of honest and good men to know where and in what way each of these is to be used?"

"It seemed so."

"To honest and good men, therefore, and thus to them alone, must these things be useful, since they must be used scientifically. But if they are useful to them alone, they must also seem to be money to them alone. Therefore, it seems, if someone makes a man who is unskilled in the art of horsemanship, yet possesses horses that are useless to him, skilled in that art, he also makes him wealthier at the same time; if indeed he makes the things that were previously useless useful to him. For handing over some science to a man, he makes him rich at the same time. 

I seem to be able to swear, however, that Critias can in no way be induced to believe these reasons are true."

"You may swear," he said, "for I would be entirely insane if I believed these things to be true. But why did you not complete that reasoning: that gold and silver and other things of that kind, though they seem so, are not money—so that hearing these speeches, and those you now run through, I might wonder much more?"

I said therefore: "You seem to me, Critias, hearing me, to be affected by joy no differently than when you hear reciters who sing the verses of Homer, since none of these reasons seem true to you. Come, however, let us consider such things: I say gold, and silver, and the rest. Would you say these are useful to architects for building a house?"

"I would certainly say so."

"Therefore, shall we say those things are useful which they use for building the house—stones, bricks, wood, and other such things? Or also the instruments with which they build the house, and with which these woods, stones, and instruments are prepared?"

"All these," he said, "seem useful to me for those things."

"Is it not therefore," I said, "that in other crafts, not only these things which we use for each work are useful, but also those things by which we acquire these, and without which these could not be made?"

"They certainly are."

"Are not those things also useful by which we prepare these, and whatever is above them, and by which we further prepare those and much higher things—so that all these things, falling into some infinite number, must seem useful for the crafts themselves?"

"Nothing," he said, "prevents things from being so."

"What if a man has food, drink, clothing, and other things for his body? Does he need gold, or silver, or any other of these things by which those things he already has are acquired?"

"It does not seem so to me."

"Is it now established for us that a man sometimes needs none of these for the necessity of the body?"

"It is established."

"If indeed these appear useless for the same work, would it not be...

[[page number: 660]]

# On Riches.

...necessary on the contrary that they never seem useful? For it has been supposed that it is impossible for the same things to be useful at one time and useless at another for the same work."

"But," he said, "this reasoning should be established between you and me: if indeed the same things are sometimes useful for the same work, it can never conversely happen that they are useless. Now, furthermore, we would say some actions of evil things are, and some are of good things. Is it possible for an evil thing to be useful for the action of some good thing?"

"It seems impossible to me."

"But good things—do we not say these are what a man does through virtue?"

"We do."

"Is it possible for a man to learn any of these things that are handed over by speech if he is entirely deprived of hearing or some other sense?"

"By Hercules, it does not seem so to me."

"Does it not therefore appear that hearing is useful to us for virtue, if indeed virtue is acquired by hearing, and we use it for learning?"

"It appears so."

"If Medicine can free a sick man from disease, would Medicine sometimes also seem useful to us for virtue, if indeed hearing is often recovered through Medicine?"

"Nothing prevents it."

"Furthermore, if we acquire Medicine with money, would money also seem useful to us for virtue?"

"It would seem so."

"Is the same to be said of that by which we acquire money?"

"The same must be said of all these things."

"Does a man seem to you to acquire silver from evil and shameful things, with which he may attain the science of Medicine, or by which he can hear what he previously could not—yet be able to abuse that very thing for virtue or for other such things?"

"It certainly seems so to me."

"Therefore, an evil thing would not be useful for virtue?"

"It would not."

"Because it is not necessary that those things by which we acquire useful things are themselves useful for those same things. For evil things would thus sometimes seem to be useful for something good. But in this they will be even more caught. For if these things are useful for each, without which they would not be made unless these were first present, come, see what you say about such things. 

Would you say it is possible for ignorance to be useful for science, or disease for health, or vice for virtue?"

"I would certainly not say so."

"But we affirm this: science cannot be in him in whom ignorance was not first present; nor health in him in whom disease was not; nor virtue in him in whom vice was not."

"It is so, as it seems to me," he said.

"Does it not necessarily follow that those things without which something cannot be made are also useful to it? For thus ignorance could seem useful for science, disease for health, and vice for virtue."

He had no faith at all in these reasons, as if all these things were not useful. But I, recognizing that persuading him was like 'boiling a stone,' as they say, said: "Let us dismiss these speeches, since we can neither agree nor affirm whether these are useful and money or not. 

But what shall we say of that? Do we think a man is happier and more powerful if he needs the most things for clothing and food, or if he needs the fewest and the smallest?"

"This perhaps can be best observed in this way: if someone, contemplating man in man himself, considers which state is better: when he is sick, or when he is well."

"That," he said, "does not require much contemplation."

"For perhaps," I said, "any man understands what is at hand: that the state of a healthy man is far better than that of a sick man. But do we need more and more varied things when we are sick, or when we are well?"

"When we are worse affected within ourselves, are not desires and wants, as far as the pleasures of the body are concerned, both more vehement and more numerous?"

"They are."

"The same must be said if there are two people. For as one man seems to be better off when he needs the fewest things, so it will be if there are two men: and this one needs few things, nor are they vehement—those things which gamblers, wine-bibbers, and gluttons practice, all of which are nothing other than desires."

"Nothing."

"Furthermore, all desires are nothing other than wants of certain things. Men, therefore, who are affected by most of these are in a worse state than those who are affected by none, or the fewest."

"Certainly."

"Men of this sort, therefore, I think are either very evil, and the more they are of this sort, the worse they are. Does it not therefore seem to us that it is impossible for these to be useful to us unless we also need them for this purpose?"

"I think so."

"It is necessary, if indeed these are going to be useful to us for the care of the body among those things which are needed, that we also simultaneously need them for this. So it seems to me. Does it not therefore follow that he for whom the most things are useful for this purpose also needs the most things himself, if indeed it is necessary to need all these things which are useful?"

"It is established, as I judge."

"It is also established as necessary from this reasoning that those who have much money also need many necessary things for the care of the body. For it appeared to us that those things which are useful for this are money. Wherefore it is necessary that the wealthiest, since they need the most things, seem to us to be the worst affected."
