# DEFINITIONS.
# VI.

[[notes: These definitions are attributed to the Pseudo-Platonic collection of *Definitiones*.]]

**ETERNITY** (*Aeternitas*) is that which was before all time, nor is it finished in the present. **God** (*Deus*) is an immortal animal, content in himself for living blessedly; an everlasting force and the cause of a good nature. 

**Origin** (*Ortus*), a motion toward that nature which is called [[Greek: θεῖον]] (*theion*, divine): the attainment of nature; proceeding to where it is possible to be. **The Sun** (*Sol*), a celestial fire which alone can be seen to be the same from rising until setting; an eternal and animate animal; the greatest star shining by day. 

**Time** (*Tempus*), the motion of the sun; the measure of celestial conversion. **Day** (*Dies*), the journey of the sun from east to west. **Light** (*Lux*), that which is contrary to night. **Dawn** (*Aurora*), the beginning of the day; the first light proceeding from the sun. **Midday** (*Meridies*), the time in which the shadows of bodies are smallest. **Setting** (*Occasus*), the end of the day. **Night** (*Nox*), darkness contrary to the day; the privation of the sun. 

**Fortune** (*Fortuna*), a transition from the uncertain to the uncertain, and the fortuitous cause of a happy action. **Old Age** (*Senectus*), the failing of a living being caused by time. **Spirit** (*Spiritus*), the motion of air around the earth. **Air** (*Aer*), an element whose motions, made in place, are according to nature. **Heaven** (*Coelum*), a body embracing all things perceived by sense, except for the highest air itself. 

**Soul** (*Animus*), that which moves itself; the cause of vital motion in animals. **Power** (*Potentia*), that which makes itself by itself. **Sight** (*Aspectus*), the habit of discerning bodies. **Bone** (*Os*), marrow thickened by heat. **Element** (*Elementum*), that which composes and dissolves composites. **Virtue** (*Virtus*), an affection of the soul, or the best habit of a mortal animal, praiseworthy by its own nature.

[[page number: 661]]

# Definitions.

...habit, which he who holds is called good. **Community** (*Communitas*), a just disposition of laws, which whoever has attained, if only he be best affected, is called honest; a habit effecting good legislation. **Prudence** (*Prudentia*), a force which by itself prepares happiness for a man; the science of good and evil things; the science which gives happiness; the habit by which we judge what is to be done and what is to be avoided. 

**Justice** (*Iustitia*), a concord of the soul within itself, and in the parts of the soul itself giving to each its dignity; a habit which he who has attained chooses and does willingly those things that seem just to him; a habit in life obeying the law; equity communicating; a habit obeying right laws. 

**Temperance** (*Temperantia*), a moderation of the soul accommodated to moderating those desires and pleasures that arise in it by nature; a congruent mode and right order of the soul to soothe natural pleasures and pains; a certain harmony of the soul and a consensus for commanding and obeying; an action acting according to nature of its own accord; the right order of the soul; the soul as if reasoning about honest and shameful things; a habit which he who is endowed with it chooses what is to be chosen and avoids what is to be avoided. 

**Fortitude** (*Fortitudo*), a habit of the soul which can be moved by no fear; warlike magnanimity; science of warlike matters; constancy and firmness of the soul in undergoing those things which are formidable and grave; confidence obeying prudence; a superior strength of the soul in the expectation of death; a habit preserving right thoughts in dangers; strength equal to danger; strength constantly tending toward virtue; tranquility of the soul in those things which are rightly seen as grave and horrible; liberation from uncertain opinions about adverse things, and experience of war; a stable habit obeying the law. 

**Constancy** (*Constantia*), a force sustaining pain; the rule of right reason; an invincible force of that which has been grasped by right thought. **Happiness** (*Beatitudo*), the perfection of the possession of goods; a habit which those who have it command themselves. **Equity** (*Aequitas*), the reduction of things just and useful; moderation in commerce; the right order of the soul using reason toward honest and shameful things. 

**Tolerance** (*Tolerantia*), the enduring of evils for the sake of honesty; a habit of enduring labors for the sake of honesty. **Confidence** (*Fidentia*), the expectation of no evil; firmness in a present evil. **Cheerfulness** (*Hilaritas*), a habit which prevents us from falling into sorrow. **Zeal for Labor** (*Studium laborandi*), a habit completing what you first undertook to do; voluntary enduring; a habit never reproaching labor. 

**Modesty** (*Pudor*), a voluntary ceding of audacity, giving place justly to that which seems best; a voluntary grasp of the best; the avoidance of just reproach. **Liberty** (*Libertas*), the principality of life; the highest power in oneself of any matter; the power placed in each one to live as he wishes; the free faculty of enjoying resources in use and possession. **Liberality** (*Liberalitas*), the affection and study of gaining as is fitting; the just addition or possession of riches. 

**Gentleness** (*Mansuetudo*), the soothing of the motion that is usually excited by anger; a moderate tempering of the soul. **Grace** (*Venustas*), a voluntary access to that which seems best; modesty in the motion of the body. **Felicity** (*Felicitas*), a good composed of all goods; a force content in itself for living well; perfection proceeding from virtue; an aid sufficiently suitable for oneself. 

**Magnificence** (*Magnificentia*), an amplitude proceeding from the gravest agitation and proposition of the mind. **Industry** (*Industria*), a good natural disposition of the soul, which he who has is skillful at devising...

...everything that is necessary; sharpness of mind. **Goodness** (*Bonitas*), integrity of character with beneficence; an ardent study of character. **Honesty** (*Honestas*), a habit which he who has it does eagerly and willingly what is honest. **Magnanimity** (*Magnitudo animi*), civil use in those things which happen; magnificence of the soul with reason. **Humanity** (*Humanitas*), a habit of character very inclined toward friendship with man; a habit conferring benefits upon men. 

**Piety** (*Pietas*), justice toward the Gods; virtue worshipping the Gods; voluntary undertaking of the religion of the Gods; right science of the worship of the Gods; a good that is desired for its own sake. **Security** (*Securitas*), a habit keeping us from fear. **Freedom from Disturbance** (*Vacuitas perturbationum*), a habit acting so that we do not fall into disturbances. **Peace** (*Pax*), rest from hostile contentions. **Leisure** (*Desidia*), the right of the soul's rest; freedom from the soul's impulse. 

**Shrewdness** (*Solertia*), a habit which he who has is suitable for attaining his proper end by conjecture. **Friendship** (*Amicitia*), a consensus of wills about honest and just things; a considered choice of the same life; a consensus of opinions about choosing and doing; a conjunction of wills toward the community of life with benevolence; a community of giving and receiving benefits. 

**Nobility** (*Generositas*), the virtue of a noble character; an easy induction of the soul toward reasons and actions. **Heresy** (*Haeresis*), [[notes: here meaning "choice" or "sect"]] right approval. **Benevolence** (*Beneuolentia*), choice; an embrace coupling man with man. **Kinship** (*Cognatio*), a communion of the same kind. **Concord** (*Concordia*), a community of all things which truly are; a harmony as it were of sentiments and opinions. 

**Courtesy** (*Comitas*), a perfect demonstration. **Civil Science** (*Ciuilis scientia*), the science of honest and useful things; the science establishing justice in the city. **Companionship** (*Sodalitas*), friendship among equals reconciled by custom. **Good Counsel** (*Consilium bonum*), an innate force of thought. **Faith** (*Fides*), a right opinion that a matter is as it seems; a certain grasp of the truth. 

**Truth** (*Veritas*), a habit which is occupied with affirmation and negation; science of true things. **Will** (*Voluntas*), desire with right reason; an appetite congruent with reason; a natural appetite with reason. **Counsel-giving** (*Consiliū datio*), an admonition before an action, prescribing to another how he ought to act. **Opportunity** (*Occasio*), a prescription of time in which one ought to suffer or act. 

**Caution** (*Cautio*), the declination of evil; the care of preserving oneself. **Order** (*Ordo*), the similarity of action of all things that are connected among themselves; the proportion of community; the cause of all things compared among themselves; a proportion suitable for learning. **Attention** (*Attentio*), the contention of the soul for learning. **Natural Disposition** (*Indole bona*), speed of learning; a good procreation of nature; natural virtue. **Docility** (*Docilitas*), the soul's disposition for speed of learning. 

**Judgment** (*Iudicium*), the ratified outcome of a matter that was doubted. **Law** (*Lex*), a dispute about just or unjust matters. **Right institution of laws**, obedience to honest laws. **Joy** (*Laetitia*), gladness in temperate works. **Honor** (*Honor*), the donation of goods given in actions of virtue; dignity prepared from virtue; a species of gravity; preservation of authority. 

**Alacrity** (*Alacritas*), a sign of the will inclined toward acting. **Grace** (*Gratia*), voluntary beneficence; the remuneration of a good at the time an office is conferred. **Consensus** (*Consensio*), the opinion of those commanding and obeying that one must command and obey. **Republic** (*Respublica*), a community of a multitude of men content in itself for living well; a community of a multitude constituted by laws. **Providence** (*Prouidentia*), preparation for certain future things. **Counsel** (*Consilium*), consideration about future things as is expedient. **Victory** (*Victoria*), a force overcoming in a contest. **Perspicacity** (*Perspicientia*), the faculty of...

[[page number: 662]]

# Definitions.

...attaining what is thought. **Gift** (*Donum*), a commerce of grace. **Maturity** (*Maturitas*), an opportunity of time for a useful matter; time helping at once to complete something good. **Memory** (*Memoria*), an affection of the soul guarding the truth that is in it. **Consideration** (*Consideratio*), the contention of thought. **Intelligence** (*Intelligentia*), the principle of science. 

**Chastity** (*Castimonia*), caution against vices which offend the Gods; natural care for the worship of the Gods. **Prophecy** (*Vaticinatio*), science without demonstration, signifying beforehand what is to be done. **Divination** (*Diuinatio*), science perceiving what is present and what will happen to a mortal animal. **Wisdom** (*Sapientia*), science not assumed; science of divine things; science contemplating the cause of things. 

**Philosophy** (*Philosophia*), the desire for the science of divine things; contemplation of truth as it is; care of the soul with right reason. **Science** (*Scientia*), a perception of the soul which cannot be refuted by reason; a force receiving something thus so that it can in no way let go; true reason in thought, immutable. **Opinion** (*Opinio*), a suspicion which can be refuted by reason; the impulse of reasoning; thought falling into false and true through reason. 

**Sense** (*Sensus*), an impulse of the soul; a motion of the mind; a messenger of the soul proceeding through the body to the outermost parts of men, by which the force of the soul devoid of reason, yet a participant in cognition, is effected through the body. **Habit** (*Habitus*), an affection of the soul by which we are said to be such as we are. 

**Voice** (*Vox*), a flux exiting from thought through the mouth. **Speech** (*Sermo*), a voice which can be written and explains each thing; a diction composed of nouns and verbs without song. **Noun** (*Nomen*), a simple diction which signifies both what is said of that power they call [[Greek: θεῖον]] (*theion*) and everything that is not said by itself. **Diction** (*Dictio*), a human voice which can be written and declares a thing as a common sign without song. **Syllable** (*Syllaba*), an article of human voice which can be written. 

**Definition** (*Definitio*), a reason composed of difference and genus. **Indication** (*Indiciū*), the demonstration of a hidden thing. **Conclusion of an argument**, a reason which collects truth by arguing; a reason demonstrating something from things previously perceived. **Element** (*Elementum*), a simple voice of voice; the cause for other voices that they may be voices. **Useful** (*Vtile*), that which is the cause that we are affected by some convenience; the cause of good. 

**Conducive** (*Conducens*), that which leads to good. **Honest** (*Honestum*), good. **Good** (*Bonum*), the cause that those things which are may be preserved; the cause of every thing that looks toward itself, from which all things proceed that are to be chosen. **Temperance**, moderation of the soul. **Just**, an institution of law exercising justice. **Voluntary**, that which insinuates itself; which is chosen by itself perfected by thought. **Free**, that which dominates itself. 

**Moderate** (*Mediocre*), that which is the medium between excess and deficiency, and what is sufficient in art. **Mediocrity**, the middle of excess and deficiency. **The Palm** (*Palma*), the prize of virtue; that which is desirable for its own sake. **Immortalitas**, a nature which is called [[Greek: θεῖον]] (*theion*), animate and perpetual staying. **Sanctity** (*Sanctitas*), the worship of God; a thing pleasing to God. 

**Feast day** (*Dies festus*), a sacred time, proclaimed according to the laws. **Man** (*Homo*), a featherless animal, bipedal, having broad nails, which alone apprehends the science of things handed over by reason. **Sacrifice** (*Sacrificium*), a gift dedicated to a sacred thing for God. **Vow** (*Votum*), a petition by which men ask good things from the Gods, or what seem good. 

**King** (*Rex*), he who commands free from rendering an account according to the laws; the prince of civil institution. **Magistrate** (*Magistratus*), care of the whole; power; the procurement of law. **Law-giver** (*Legum lator*), the effector of laws by which the Republic ought to be administered. **Law** (*Lex*), a civil decree of a multitude defined for no time. **Argument** (*Argumentum*), a principle, not a perfect demonstration: a collection of reason made summarily.

**Decree** (*Decretum*), a civil edict defined for some time. **Politician** (*Politicus*), one skilled in constituting a Republic. **City** (*Ciuitas*), the domicile of a multitude of men who use common decrees; a multitude of men who are under the same law. **Virtue of the city**, the constitution of the best Republic. **Warlike virtue**, the science of waging war. **Warlike society**, community of war. 

**Safety** (*Salus*), the preparation of a secure state. **Tyrant** (*Tyrānus*), a master governing a city according to his own will. **Sophist** (*Sophistes*), one who hunts and captures rich and glorious youths for the sake of a fee. **Riches** (*Diuitiæ*), a possession moderated for living well; a copy of money which at the same time looks toward living well. **Deposit** (*Depofitū*), a thing given with trust. 

**Purgation** (*Purgatio*), the secretion of the worst things from the best. **To Conquer**, to overcome by contending. **Good man**, such a one who deserves well of men. **Temperate**, he who has moderate desires. **Continent**, he who overcomes parts of the soul opposing right thought. **Honest**, he who is perfectly good; who has his own virtue. 

**Conscience** (*Conscientia*), a silent thought with sorrow. **Difficulty of departing**, slowness in perceiving discipline. **Principality**, a just lordship free from rendering an account. **Contempt of Philosophy**, a habit which he who has it hates reason. **Fear** (*Timor*), a disturbance of the soul in the expectation of evil. **Irascibility** (*Iracūdia*), a vehement and violent appetite without thought; a sign that the order in the soul is being disturbed. 

**Perturbation** (*Conturbatio*), fear in the expectation of evil. **Flattery** (*Assentatio*), a colloquy which is made for pleasure, fallacious and wicked; a habit exceeding the mediocrity of talking for pleasure. **Anger** (*Ira*), the exhortation of irascibility for avenging. **Injury** (*Iniuria*), injustice leading to ignominy. **Intemperance**, a habit violent beyond reason, drawing toward those things which seem pleasant. 

**Sloth** (*Pigritia*), the flight from the beginning of labors. **Cowardice** (*Ignaula*), a cause silently repressing the first appetite for a matter. **Disputation** (*Disputatio*), the disagreement of friends in speech. **Maturity**, the time in which each matter is suitable for suffering or doing. **Injustice**, a habit despising the laws. **Want** (*Indigentiā*), the deficiency of goods. 

**Shame** (*Verecūdia*), fear in the expectation of ignominy. **Arrogance** (*Arrogātia*), a habit arrogating a good or goods which are not. **Sin** (*Peccatū*), an action beyond right reason. **Envy** (*Inuidentia*), sorrow from the goods of friends, which either are or will be in the future. **Impudence** (*Impudentia*), a habit of the soul enduring ignominy for the sake of gain. 

**Audacity** (*Audacia*), confidence in fears for which there is no need, an abundance. **Ambition** (*Ambitio*), a habit of the soul inclined toward every expense, and liberal without thought. **Native evil**, vice in nature and natural sin; a disease implanted in nature. **Hope** (*Spes*), the expectation of good. **Insanity** (*Insania*), a habit corrupting true perception. 

**Loquacity** (*Loquacitas*), inconsiderate intemperance of speech. **Contrariety**, the maximum distance of things that fall under the same genus according to some difference. **Involuntary thing**, a thing which is completed beyond thought. **Institution**, a force caring for the soul. **Erudition**, the handing over of discipline. **Legislation**, science constituting a firm city. 

**Admonition**, a speech made from the soul with reproach; a speech instituted for the sake of noticing a sin. **Aid**, the driving away of a present or imminent evil. **Chastisement**, the soul's cure in a fault that is committed. **Power**, excellence in action or in speech: a habit which he who has is powerful; a force naturally preserving or making a man safe.

[[page number: 663]]

# On the Universe.

### A FRAGMENT OF PLATO’S TIMAEUS TRANSLATED BY M. TULLIUS CICERO, CORRESPONDING TO THE PLACES NOTED IN THE MARGIN.

[[notes: This is the Latin version of Plato’s *Timaeus* as translated by Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC). It reflects the Roman effort to adapt Greek cosmology into Latin philosophy.]]

**WHAT** is that which always is, and has no origin? And what is that which is born, and never is? One of these is grasped by intelligence and reason, being that which is always one and the same; the other is what the sense-opinion brings, devoid of reason—that which is entirely opinable—it is born and perishes, nor can it ever truly be. 

Everything, however, that is born, must necessarily be born from some cause. For with the cause removed, the origin of nothing can be found. Wherefore if he who strives to effect some gift looks upon that species which is always the same, and proposes that for himself as an exemplar (pattern), he must necessarily effect a brilliant work. But if he follows that which is born, he will never attain that beauty which he seeks. 

The whole heaven, therefore, or the world—or by whatever other name it rejoices to be called by us: concerning this let us first consider what must be considered at the beginning of every inquiry—whether it has always been, generated with no origin, or whether it arose from some beginning of time. 

Since it is seen, and touched, and is corporeal on all sides. All such things move the sense: those things which move the sense rely upon opinion, which we said have an origin and are born. Nothing, however, can be born without causes. And to find that parent of this universe [[margin: [[Greek: * ἀρχὴν]] (Origin/Principle)]] is difficult, and when you have found him, it is a crime to indicate him to the common crowd. 

Again, therefore, it must be seen: whether that fabricator of so great a work imitated an exemplar—that which is always one and the same and similar to itself, or that which we say is generated and born. But if this world is beautiful, if its artificer is upright, surely he preferred to imitate the species of eternity. If otherwise—which is a crime even to say—he followed a generated example instead of the eternal. 

There is no doubt, then, that he preferred to follow eternity [[margin: [[Greek: * ἔκδοσιν]] (Edition/Version)]], since neither is anything more beautiful than the world, nor anyone more excellent than its builder. If therefore it was generated, it was effected according to that which is grasped by reason and wisdom, and is contained by immutable eternity. 

From which it follows that it is necessary that this world which we see is an eternal image of something eternal. The beginning, however, is the most difficult part in every investigation of reason. Concerning those things we have said, therefore, this be the first distinction: in every speech, a kinship explained with those things about which it seems to be. 

And so, when it is disputed about the stable and immutable, let the speech be such as that which can neither be refuted nor convinced. But when it enters into imitated and effected images, it thinks it does well if it attains a likeness of the truth. For as much as eternity is worth compared to that which is born, so much is truth worth to faith. 

Wherefore if perhaps, differing concerning the nature of the gods and the origin of the world, we do not attain with our mind that which we have—so that the whole speech, clearly and plainly adorned, consists with itself and in every part agrees with itself—it will not be a wonder; and you ought to be content if probable things are said. For it is fair to remember that both I who speak am a man, and you who judge are men, so that if probable things are said, you should require nothing further. 

Let us seek, therefore, the cause that impelled him who engineered these things to seek a new origin and construction of things: he excelled in uprightness, and the upright envies no one. And so he generated all things similar to himself. This is truly the most just cause for the birth of the world. 

For when God had determined to fill the world with all good things, and to mix in no evil as far as nature would permit, whatever there was that fell into the sense of seeing, he took it to himself—not tranquil and quiet, but immoderately agitated and fluctuating. And therefore he brought it from disorder into order. For he judged this to be more excellent. 

It is not right, nor ever was it right, for him who was best to make anything except the most beautiful. When he had taken account, therefore, he found that nothing of those things which were seen by nature, not intelligent, was more excellent than the intelligent in its whole genus: intelligence, however, can be found in no other nature except in the soul. Wherefore he enclosed intelligence in the soul, and the soul in the body. Thus he thought that work was effected most beautifully. 

For which cause there must be no delay in professing—if only some conjecture can be investigated—that this world is an animal, and an intelligent one, and constituted by divine providence. 

This being posed, what follows must be seen: the likeness of which of the living beings did God follow in fashioning the world? Surely none of those living beings known to us. For they are all partitioned into certain genera, or are inchoate, perfect in no part. But nothing can be beautiful that is similar to the imperfect or the non-absolute. 

Let us say the world is similar to that of which every animal is as it were a certain particle, whether seen in individuals or in a different genus. For all living beings which are seen by the mind and understood by reason are comprehended by the embrace of reason and intelligence—just as men in this world, and cattle, and all things which fall under sight. 

For what can be understood as most beautiful in the nature of things, and what is most absolute from every part—when God wished to effect a similar world, he made one visible animal, in which all animals are contained. 

Did we therefore rightly say one world, or are there many and innumerable, which would be truer and better to say? One surely, if indeed it was made according to the exemplar. For that which embraces all living beings which are understood by reason cannot exist with another. 

For again, there would have to be another living being which contained it, of which the superior living beings would be parts. And this heaven would be an image of that ultimate one, not the proximate. Lest any of these things should happen, and so that this world might be most similar to the absolute living being in this very fact—that it was alone and one—for that reason God procreated this world singular and only-begotten. 

Everything, however, that is born, must necessarily be corporeal and visible and likewise tangible. Furthermore, nothing can be seen void of fire, nor indeed touched which lacks solidity, and nothing is solid which is void of earth. Wherefore God, striving to effect the world, first joined earth and fire. 

But all two things require some third thing for cohering, and desire a certain knot and bond as it were. But of bonds, that is the most fit and beautiful which makes itself and those things which it binds most entirely one. This is best attained by what the Greeks call [[Greek: ἀναλογία]] (*analogia*), and in Latin—for one must be daring, since these things are first being innovated by us—can be called *proportio* (proportion) or *comparatio* (comparison).

[[page number: 664]]

# On the Universe.

...proportion. For when of three either numbers, or figures, or of whatever kind, it happens that as the middle is to the first in proportion, so it is compared to the last; and conversely, as the last is to the middle, so the middle is conferred with the first: that which is middle then becomes first and last; and the last and first become middle. 

[[margin: * Or bound.]] Thus necessity compels that those things be the same which were [[margin: *]] disjoined. Since they have been made the same, it is effected that all things are one. 

But if the body of the universe were explained as a plane and equal surface, and nothing was required in it, one interposed middle would bind both itself and those things to which it was interposed. But when solidity was sought for the world—and all solid things are never coupled by one middle but always by two—it so happened that God placed air and water between fire and earth, and compared them among themselves and joined them by proportion: so that as fire is to air, so air is to water; and as air is to water, so water is to earth in proportion. 

From which conjunction the heaven was thus driven that it falls under sight and touch. And so, for that reason and from those things four in number, the body of the world was effected, constructed by that proportion which I said. From which it embraces itself in a certain concordant friendship and charity, and thus aptly coheres so that it can in no way be dissolved except by the same one by whom it was bound. 

Of those four things which I said above, all parts are thus placed in the whole world so that no part of this genus exceeded outside, and those universal genera were in this universe. This was for these causes: first, so that the living world might be perfect from perfect parts. Second, so that it might be one, no part being left from which another could be born. Finally, lest any disease or old age could afflict it. 

For every joining of a body is weakened and broken either by heat or cold or some vehement impulse, and is driven to diseases and old age. Therefore the God who effected and engineered the world had this reason: that one work, whole and perfect, should be absolved from all things whole and perfect, which would lack every disease and age. 

He gave it a form, moreover, which was most akin and decorous to it. For by which living being he wished all the remaining living beings to be contained, he figured it with that form by which alone all other forms are concluded. Therefore it was fabricated globose (spherical), which the Greeks call [[Greek: σφαιροειδὲς]] (*sphairoeides*), of which every extremity is bound by rays from the middle. 

And he turned it thus, so that nothing could be made more round, so that it had no roughness, no offense, nothing enclosed in angles, nothing in windings, nothing protruding, nothing hollowed; and all parts were most similar to all others, for in his judgment similarity was better than dissimilarity. 

And he surrounded the whole world with a smoothness of form. Nor did it need eyes, because nothing was left outside which could be seen; nor ears, because there was nothing to be heard; nor were the extremities of the world surrounded by air so that it required respiration. Nor indeed did it desire the auxiliary members of the body for nourishment or the detraction of finished and consumed food; for neither could any departure occur, nor any access, nor indeed was there a source for it. 

Thus it nourished itself by its own consumption and age, since it suffered and did all things by itself and through itself. For thus he thought, who joined and founded those things, that the world was content in itself and did not need another. And so he did not affix hands, because nothing was to be taken, nor anything repelled; nor feet nor other members by which it might sustain the body in progress. 

For he gave the heaven that motion which is most fit for its form—which one of the seven motions contains the mind and intelligence. Therefore by one greatest conversion and the same, it is twisted and turned around itself. But he separated the six remaining motions from it. Thus he freed it from all error. 

For this conversion, God—who was, thinking of the god that would one day be—did not give members; he made him smooth and equal on all sides, and from the middle to the highest point equal and perfect and absolute from the absolute and perfect. 

As he placed the soul in its middle, so he extended it through the whole. Then when he surrounded it with a body and clothed it outwardly, and embraced it with the sun-wandering, revolving, and incited heaven in a circle, so that it could easily be with itself on account of virtue and not desire another—known to itself and familiar enough. Thus that eternal God procreated this perfectly blessed God. 

But the soul—not as we have just spoken, only then when he had effected a body for it—did he begin. For it would not be right for the greater to obey the lesser. But we say many things inconsiderately and rashly. God, however, generated the soul as more ancient both in origin and virtue, and placed it as master and commander over the obedient body, and engineered it in such a certain way. 

From the matter which is indivisible and which is always of one mode and similar to itself, and from that which is born divisible in bodies, he mixed a third genus of matter from the two in the middle, which was of the same nature and that of the other; and he interposed it between the indivisible and that which was divisible in the body. 

And when he had taken three, he tempered them into one species, and that nature which we said was of the other, when he joined it with the same—mixing the fleeing and alienated part of that coupling with the matter—when he had made one from three, he partitioned that itself into the members which were fitting. Now he tempered the single parts from the same, and from the other, and from the matter. 

Such, however, was that partition. First he took away one part from the whole; then a second double the first; then a third which was a sesquialter (one and a half) of the second and triple the first; then a fourth which was double the second; then a fifth triple the third; then a sixth eight times the first; finally a seventh, which preceded the first by twenty-seven parts. 

Then he determined to fill the double and triple intervals, cutting off parts again from the whole: which he placed in the intervals thus, so that in each there were two middles. (For I scarcely dare to say 'medieties,' which the Greeks call [[Greek: μεσότητας]] (*mesotetas*), but if I should speak thus let him understand, for it will be plain). One of these exceeded the extremes by the same part as it was exceeded by them, the other exceeding the extremes by an equal number and being exceeded by an equal number. 

By sesquialter intervals and sesquitertians (four-thirds), and sesquioctaves (nine-eighths) taken from these bindings, in the first intervals he filled all the sesquitertians with a sesquioctave interval, while leaving a small particle of each. With the interval of that particle left, the number had the same proportion and comparison to the number in the extremes as 256 have to 243. 

And thus he had consumed all that mixture from which he had made these things. This whole conjunction he split double in length, and accommodating the middle to the middle, he cross-cut it as it were [[notes: like the Greek letter Chi, Χ]]; then he twisted it into a circle, so that they joined themselves and each other from the commissure which was opposite, and...

[[page number: 665]]

# On the Universe.

...and by that motion which was always in the same place and moved in the same way, he embraced them on all sides. And thus since one had embraced the exterior circle, he marked that one of the nature of the same, and this of the other; and that which was of the same he turned from the side into the right part, but this nearest one from the middle line he directed to the left. 

But he gave the principality to the superior, which alone he left indivisible. But the interior, when he had divided it into six parts of heaven, he ordered seven disparate circles to be moved by double and triple intervals, with contrary courses among themselves; of these he made the speeds of three equal, but four disparate both among themselves and from the three remaining. 

Therefore when that procreator of the world, God, had generated the soul from his mind and divinity, then at last he placed everything that was concrete and corporeal under the soul, and made it interior, and thus accommodating the middle to the middle, he coupled them. 

Thus the soul, proceeding from the middle, threw around the extremity of heaven from the supreme region in a round circuit, and turning itself, led in the beginning of a divine, everlasting, and wise life. And the body of the heaven was effected visible, but the soul escaped the gaze of the eyes. 

The soul, however, is a participant and partaker of all contentions of reason ([[Greek: λογισμῶν]] *logismon* in Greek) of everlasting things and those falling under intelligence, than which nothing better was procreated by the best and most excellent parent. 

Indeed, bound from the same and the other nature, with matter added by the tempering of three parts and compacted by proportion, revolving itself, when it had seized the mutable matter and again the indivisible and simple through which everything is moved: it discerns what is of the same genus and what is of the other, and judges the rest—what is most fit for each thing, what happens in each place or mode or time, and what distinction there is between those things which are born and those which are always the same. 

But the true reason which is occupied in those things which are always the same, and is moved in the same and in the other by itself without voice and without any sound, when it touches that part by which the sense can be moved: and the circle of that other genus, immutable and right, announces all things to the soul and mind; then firm and true opinions and assents are born. 

But when it is turned in those things which, remaining always the same, are contained not by sense but by intelligence—so that the course of the Moon proximately circles the earth, and above the earth the proximity of the Sun’s circumvection. Lucifer (Venus) then and the holy star of Mercury (Mercury) have a course equal to the speed of the Sun, but a certain contrary force; by the meeting they have among themselves, Lucifer, Mercury, and the Sun sometimes overcome some and are in turn overcome. 

The cause for placing the remaining stars, and what the placement of each is, must be deferred to another speech, lest a greater speech be placed in that which was to be touched upon than in that for whose cause we touched it. 

Therefore when each of those stars attained its decorous course, by which the motion of time was to be marked, and with the bodies bound by animal bonds, when the animals were born and they learned to obey command, then from the transverse motion of the nature of the other into the motion of the nature of the same, running into them and being stuck and impeded in them: some traversed a greater circle, others a smaller; more slowly the greater, and more swiftly the smaller, by the motion of one and the same nature. Those which were moved most swiftly seemed to be overcome in speed by the slower ones, and though they surpassed they seemed surpassed. 

For every circle of them was turned as if by a spiral [[Greek: ἕλιξ]] (*helix*) inflection, because proceeding twofold contrarily at the same time they effected that what was slowest became proximate to the swiftest. And so that there might be some evident measure which in those eight courses declared speeds and slownesses, God himself lit the sun like a light for the second circuit above the earth, so that the nature and force of numbers might be most known. 

Night and day therefore were generated in this way and for these causes, effecting one circuit of the circle, most wise and best. A month occurs when the moon, having traversed its course, has followed the sun. A year when the sun has finished its whole circle and wandered through it. 

The circuits of the other stars, however, men being ignorant except for very few, neither call by name nor measure among themselves by number. Therefore they do not know that these errors of the stars are that very thing which is rightly called time—endowed with an infinite multitude and admirable variety. 

Yet this is perceived and can be understood: that with the absolute and perfect number of time, the absolute and perfect year is finally completed when the eight circuits, having finished their courses, have returned to the same head, and when the same and always similar circle has measured them. 

For these causes the stars were born, which penetrating through the heaven turned themselves by the solstitial and brumal revocation, so that this whole animal which we see might be most similar to the animate being which we perceive, in imitation of eternity. 

And indeed the other things until the birth of time had been fashioned impressed by those things it imitated, but because it had not yet included every animal inside the world, from that part the similitude of the image failed the proposed exemplar. 

Therefore as many and such forms of animals as the mind, looking into the species of things, could discern—so many and such he thought to fashion in this world with himself. There were, however, four genera of living beings, one of which was divine and celestial, another winged and aerial, the third terrestrial, the fourth of divine animation. 

He made the species chiefly from fire, so that it was most splendid and most beautiful to the sight. And when he wished to effect a nature similar to the universe, he rounded it for volubility, and made it accompany that wisdom of the best possible mind, and distributed it equally around the heaven, so that this, distinguished by variety, the Greeks rightly call [[Greek: κόσμον]] (*kosmon*), and we call the 'shining world'. 

He gave to the divine two genera of motion: one which was always in the same way equally, and the same in all, and sped in one mode; the other, which moved forward, into which part it was driven by the conversion of the same and the similar. 

But with the five remaining motions he wished that circle to be immobile and standing, from which genus are those stars which, fixed in the heaven, are not moved in place—which are living beings, and those divine ones, and for that cause they remain in their seats and stay perpetually. But those which glide by a wandering and mutable reason were generated as we said above. 

Now truly the earth, our nourisher, which is sustained by the traversed axis, the effector of day and night and the same the most ancient guardian of the Gods, he wished to be of those who were born within the heaven. The fusions of the Gods and the meetings among the Gods themselves, and what conversions and antecessions happen in their circles, and how those who are coupled in a contrary region or glide behind or before nearly touch those who are near...

In this section, Socrates and Phaedrus discuss the technical requirements of rhetoric and the nature of madness.</meta>

# 312 Twenty-Sixth Book.

**SOCRATES.** When someone pronounces the name of iron or silver, we all immediately understand the same thing, do we not? **PHAEDRUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** But what when the name of "the just" or "the good" is spoken? Is not one person carried in one direction and another elsewhere? Do we not disagree with others and even with ourselves? **PHAEDRUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** In some things, then, we agree, while in others we disagree. **PHAEDRUS.** That is how it is. **SOCRATES.** In which of these are we more easily deceived? And in which of them does <term>rhetoric</term> <note>the art of persuasive speaking</note> have the most power? **PHAEDRUS.** Clearly, it is in those things about which we disagree. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who intends to pursue the art of rhetoric must first have distinguished these things in order, and perceived what the characteristics of each species are—where the multitude can most easily be deceived by ambiguity, and where they cannot. **PHAEDRUS.** He who could grasp that in his mind, Socrates, would recognize a truly magnificent principle. **SOCRATES.** Next, I believe, nothing should escape him when he comes to individual cases; he must keenly perceive to which genus the subject he is about to speak on belongs. **PHAEDRUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** What then of Love? Shall we say it belongs to the ambiguous genus, or the other? **PHAEDRUS.** To the ambiguous, certainly. **SOCRATES.** Or do you think Love would allow you to say those things about it which you said before? Namely, that he is ruinous both to the beloved and the lover, and yet again that he is the greatest of all goods? **PHAEDRUS.** You speak cleverly. **SOCRATES.** But since I was under that divine inspiration, I do not quite remember whether I defined Love at the beginning of the dispute. **PHAEDRUS.** By Jupiter, you did so marvelously. **SOCRATES.** Oh, how much more skillful you show the nymphs of <term>Achelous</term> <note>a river god; Socrates suggests the local spirits inspired him</note> and Pan, the son of Mercury, to be at composing speeches than Lysias, the son of Cephalus! Or did Lysias, in the beginning of his discourse on love, fail to force us to understand Love as some certain thing that he himself intended, and then, referring all subsequent things to that, complete his entire speech? Would you like us to read the beginning again? **PHAEDRUS.** As you wish, though what you seek is likely not there. **SOCRATES.** Read it, so that I may hear the man himself. **PHAEDRUS.** *My situation is as you have understood; and since it is so, you have heard how I think it would benefit us. I believe I should achieve what I ask of you no less because I am not captured by love for you. For lovers, as soon as they cease to love, regret the benefits they have bestowed.* **SOCRATES.** He seems to be very far from doing what we seek. For he does not strive to finish the speech from the beginning, but from the end, in a reversed and backward manner, and he begins with those things which a lover objects to in a youth after his love has been extinguished. Or have I said nothing of value, my charming friend Phaedrus? **PHAEDRUS.** It is indeed the end of the matter, Socrates, of which he speaks. **SOCRATES.** What else? Does it not seem that all the parts are scattered and dissected? Or do you think that what is placed in the second position is joined there by some necessity? Or any other of the things spoken? For to me, as one ignorant of all things, it seems the writer simply set down whatever came to mind with some nobility. Do you have any rule of writing by which he arranged those things in that specific order? **PHAEDRUS.** You are too kind, Socrates, to think I can judge his writings with such subtlety. **SOCRATES.** But I think you would agree that every speech ought to be constructed like a <note>This is the famous "Organic Unity" theory of composition.</note> living creature, so that it has its own body, which is neither without a head nor lacking feet, but has a middle and extremities consistent with each other and with the whole. **PHAEDRUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Consider, I pray, whether your friend's speech is like that or otherwise. You will find it differs in no way from that epigram which some say was inscribed for Midas the Phrygian. **PHAEDRUS.** What is that, and of what sort? **SOCRATES.** Listen.
*I am the bronze maiden, placed upon the tomb of King Midas,*
*And as long as fountains flow and the tall tree turns green,*
*Remaining here on this mournful monument for eternity,*
*I tell the traveler that Midas is buried here.*
That it makes no difference which part of it is placed first or last, you yourself see. **PHAEDRUS.** You are mocking our speech, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Let us leave this one, then, lest you become angry with us, though it seems many examples could be found in it which might be useful to inspect so that we do not imitate them. But let us turn to other speeches; for they contained something, I believe, that should be observed by those eager for the art of speaking. **PHAEDRUS.** What was that? **SOCRATES.** They were certainly contrary to one another. One asserted that one should yield to the lover, the other to the non-lover. **PHAEDRUS.** And quite vigorously. **SOCRATES.** I thought you were going to answer more truly: "and quite madly." For that is the very thing I was seeking. We called Love a kind of madness, did we not? **PHAEDRUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Now, we posit two species of madness. [[margin: Species of madness.]] One arising from human diseases. The other from a divine alienation, where one is snatched away from the customary constitution of life. **PHAEDRUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Of the divine madness, there are four parts, just as four gods preside over them. [[margin: The four divine madnesses.]] We attribute the inspiration of prophecy to Apollo, the mysteries to Dionysus, poetry to the Muses, and the madness of love to Venus and Amor <note>Aphrodite and Eros</note>, which we call the best of all. And I know not how, while we were sketching the affection of love through certain images, we perhaps touched upon some truth, or perhaps were carried elsewhere. Therefore, mixing a speech that was not entirely improbable, we composed a kind of mythical hymn, and as if playing, Phaedrus, we modestly praised your lord and mine, Love, the guardian of beautiful boys. **PHAEDRUS.** This is not unpleasant for me to hear. **SOCRATES.** Let us take this from it: how the dispute passed from blame to praise. **PHAEDRUS.** In what way do you mean? **SOCRATES.** It seems to me we were playing at other things. But if anyone could grasp the power of the two species we have just encountered by art, he would have achieved a worthwhile work. **PHAEDRUS.** Which species do you mean? **SOCRATES.** That by looking toward a single Idea, one brings together things scattered everywhere; so that by defining each thing, he makes clear whatever he has set out to teach. Just as we just now defined what Love is, whether it was done well or ill. Certainly, our dispute gained clarity and a consistent harmony from this. **PHAEDRUS.** And what is the other species you speak of, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** That one may again cut it back into species according to its joints, following the nature of things, and not, after the manner of an unskilled cook, break any limbs; but rather do as our previous speeches did, which took one common species through the agitation of the mind. Just as in one body, twin members are called by the same name, one right and one left, so those speeches considered the species of mental agitation within us to be one by nature. And the first speech, dividing the left part and again partitioning it, did not stop until it found a certain "left-handed" love there, which it rightly condemned. The following speech led us to the right-hand part of madness, where finding a Love similar in name to the first but divine, and magnifying it, it praised it as the cause of our greatest goods. **PHAEDRUS.** You speak most truly. **SOCRATES.** These divisions and collections, O Pha—

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Phaedrus. # Phaedrus, or, On Beauty. 313

O Phaedrus, I am a lover of these things, so that I may be capable of both understanding and speaking. And if I think anyone else is able to perceive the "one and the many" according to the nature of things, I follow in his footsteps as if following a god. Whether I name those who can do this correctly or not, God knows; but until now, I have called them <term>dialecticians</term> <note>those skilled in logical division and synthesis</note>. But now, I pray you, tell me by what name your friend Lysias’s opinion should be called. Or is this the "art of speaking" which Thrasymachus and others used to become wise in speaking themselves, and which they passed on to others who were willing to bring them gifts as if to kings? **PHAE.** Those men were indeed "royal," yet they were not experts in the things you are asking about. **SOC.** But you seem to rightly call this specific form <term>dialectic</term>; however, <term>rhetoric</term> still escapes us. **PHAE.** How do you mean? **SOC.** Is there anything beautiful which, though separate from these things, is nonetheless grasped by art? This is by no means to be despised by you or me, but we must state what remains in rhetoric. **PHAE.** Very many things, Socrates, are passed down in the books written on the art of speaking. **SOC.** You have reminded me opportunely. I believe the <term>prologue</term> <note>original: *prooemium*</note> must be called the first part of a speech. Is it these sorts of elegant "ornaments of the art" that you mean? **PHAE.** Indeed. **SOC.** Second follows the **narration** and the assertion of witnesses. Third, **conjecture**. Fourth, **probabilities**. And, as I believe, that excellent "maker of speeches" from Byzantium introduced **proof** and **confirmation**. **PHAE.** You mean the eminent Theodorus? **SOC.** Exactly. He also discovered how **refutation** and **counter-refutation** can be used and doubled in both accusation and defense. And why do we not bring the distinguished Evenus of Paros into our discussion? He was the first to discover **sub-declarations** and **praises**; and some say he even wove **reproaches** into poems to aid the memory. For he is a wise man. But we shall let Lysias and Gorgias sleep, who preferred **probabilities** over truths, and who use the power of speech to make small things seem large and large things small, new things seem old and old things new. They also discovered a concise way of speaking and, conversely, an infinite wordiness. When Prodicus once heard this from me, he laughed, and asserted that you alone had discovered what words that art requires: namely, that it needs neither few nor many, but a moderate amount. **PHAE.** You have answered most wisely, Prodicus! **SOC.** But we are by no means mentioning Hippias. For I believe the guest from Elis <note>Hippias of Elis</note> would agree with him. **PHAE.** Why wouldn't he? **SOC.** Furthermore, what shall we say of Polus’s "musical elegance"? He introduced the doubling of words, famous maxims, metaphors, and similes, and the use of names for the splendor of speech, just as he learned from Licymnius. **PHAE.** But weren't the writings of Protagoras something like that, Socrates? **SOC.** The eloquence of Protagoras, my boy, was indeed correct and appropriate, with much that was excellent in his style. But in moving **compassion** regarding old age and poverty, the orator from Chalcedon <note>Thrasymachus of Chalcedon</note> excelled; he was also powerful in stirring up and then soothing anger, as if he were charming it with an incantation, as they say—a master at creating and dissolving **calumnies** <note>false and defamatory statements</note> wherever necessary. Regarding the **conclusion** of a speech, all seem to agree, though some call it a **recapitulation** <note>original: *epanodon*, that is, repetition</note> and others name it differently. **PHAE.** You mean to recall all the aforementioned points to the audience's memory at the very heel of the speech? **SOC.** That is what I say—unless you have something else to say about this art. **PHAE.** I have only small things, not worthy of mention. **SOC.** Let us set aside small things and bring these others into the light instead, so we can see what power of art they have and when. **PHAE.** They have the greatest power, Socrates, in the assemblies of men. **SOC.** Indeed they do. But, my blessed friend, look and see if the fabric of these things seems to you, as it does to me, to be thin and loosely woven. **PHAE.** Only show me how. **SOC.** Tell me then: if someone said to your friend Eryximachus, or to his father Acumenus, in this manner: "I know how to apply those things to the body by which it may become warm or cold at my will; I can also induce vomiting and purging, and other such cleansings, and I know many other such things; having learned these, I profess myself to be a doctor, and that I can make anyone else a doctor"—what do you think they would respond? **PHAE.** What else could they do but ask him if he also knows to **whom**, **when**, and **to what extent** each of these things should be applied? **SOC.** And if he were to say that he understands that in no way, but that whoever learns from him ought to be able to do such things, what will they respond? **PHAE.** Certainly, that such a man is insane; having heard something from some medical book and stumbled upon a few remedies, he thinks he has become a doctor without understanding anything of the art. **SOC.** What if someone said to Sophocles and Euripides that he knew how to give a long speech on a small matter and a very short one on a large matter, and how to move pity whenever he wished, or its opposite, to strike horror and threats, and other similar things? And by teaching these, he thought he was teaching the art of tragedy? **PHAE.** They too, Socrates, I think, would laugh at him, for thinking that tragedy is anything other than the composition of these parts, in harmony with each other and with the whole. **SOC.** Yet they would not, I think, rebuke him rudely, but would act just as a musician would when meeting a man who believes himself a musician because he knows how to produce the lowest and highest strings. The musician would not say harshly, "You are insane, you wretch," but being a musician, would advise him more gently: "O best of men, it is entirely necessary for one who is to be a musician to know these things. However, nothing prevents one who is in your state from understanding nothing at all of **harmony**. For you recognize the things necessary *before* harmony, yet you are utterly ignorant of harmony itself." **PHAE.** Most correctly. **SOC.** Thus Sophocles would say to that man he met that he possesses the "preliminaries" of tragedy rather than tragedy itself; and Acumenus the doctor would say the same regarding the preliminaries of medicine, not medicine itself. **PHAE.** Exactly so. **SOC.** What if "honey-tongued" Adrastus or Pericles heard of these "splendid word-tricks" we were just recounting—brevity, similes, and the rest which we thought should be brought to light—would they, like us, be harshly angry out of rudeness toward those who wrote and taught such things as the "faculty of rhetoric"? Or would they, being wiser than us, rebuke us thus: "O Phaedrus and Socrates, we must not be angry but forgiving, if some who are ignorant of **dialectic** are unable to define what rhetoric is; and being thus affected, while they possess the rudimentary preliminaries of the art, they boast that they have 'found' rhetoric, and by teaching these things, they profess to pass on the complete art of oratory. But they expect their students to acquire for themselves, through their own industry, the ability to arrange each of these points persuasively and to weave the whole speech together, as if a teacher were not needed for these things." **PHAE.** Such indeed, Socrates, seems to be the art which those men teach and write about as "rhetoric." And it seems to me <margin>He who can divide nature according to its nature is a dialectician—that is, a philosopher of ultimate reality.</margin> <margin>On the power of speech and timing.</margin>

For it is not easy for a man so affected to enumerate your wonderful manners eloquently and in a certain order. I will try to praise Socrates, O guests, through images. He perhaps will suspect that I turn the discourse to ridiculous things. But the image will be taken for the sake of truth, not of the ridiculous."

### ALCIBIADES PRAISING SOCRATES.

"I assert that SOCRATES is most similar to those **Silenes** <note>Silenus was a companion of Dionysus, often depicted as a fat, drunken satyr. Alcibiades is referring to hollow statues of Silenus that opened up to reveal divine images inside.</note> who are figured by sculptors sitting among other images, so that they hold pipes or flutes. Which, if they are divided in two, are found to have the image of the Gods inside. I say also that he is similar to the Satyr Marsyas. <margin>See the proverb in Erasmus: *The Sileni of Alcibiades*.</margin> And that you are indeed most similar to these in appearance, not even you, Socrates, will deny. But that you also have the similarity of them in other things, listen now. You are provocative and contumelious, are you not? If you do not confess it, I will bring witnesses. Are you not a flute-player? And indeed a flute-player far more excellent than Marsyas. For he used to soothe men with certain instruments by the power of his mouth, and even now if anyone uses his modulation. For those things which Olympus modulated, I say were modulated by Marsyas who taught him. His harmony, therefore, whether a man uses it well or a woman badly, alone attracts souls,

attracts, and because it is divine, it shows who has need of the gods and the mysteries. But you differ from him in this only, that without any instrument you effect this same thing with naked words. We certainly, whenever we have heard another relating the words of another, even if of a very good orator, yet we make those of no account, so to speak. But when someone hears you, or your words related by any other, even if he who relates is inept, and whether a man or woman or adolescent hears, we are indeed stupefied and seized in mind. Indeed, unless I suspected lest perhaps I seem too drunk, I would affirm with an oath interposed what things have happened to me at other times from this man’s words, and happen even now. For whenever I hear him, much more than those who are carried away in the manner of the <term>Corybants<note>Priests of the goddess Cybele who performed wild, ecstatic dances.</note></term>, my heart is incited within me at his words, and I shed tears, and I see this same thing happening to many others. And when I heard Pericles and other good orators, they indeed seemed to me to speak nobly, but no such thing happened to me, nor was my soul incited, nor did it condemn itself as living almost like a slave. But I am often so bent by this Marsyas of ours that I think I should by no means live in this state of life. Do not deny these things, Socrates. Furthermore, I know for certain, if I should wish to lend my ears to him at present, I would by no means tolerate it, but those same things would happen to me. For he forces me to confess that while I myself fail in many things, yet I neglect myself and care for the affairs of the Athenian people. Therefore, by force, as if stopping my ears against the Sirens, I flee and avoid him, lest I grow old sitting near him. But I suffer toward him alone what no one would believe, or I am detained by the shame and modesty of anyone. And yet I fear him alone. For I am conscious within myself that I cannot defend myself against doing the things he commands: but when I depart from him, I am overcome by popular ambition. I flee him therefore and avoid him, and whenever I behold him, shame takes me because I have not kept my promises, so that I often desire him to depart from life: but again if that should happen, I know I would tolerate it far more unfairly. Therefore, I do not know where to turn or how to use this. And from the modulations of this Satyr such things have happened to me and to many others. But hear the rest, how he is similar to those to whom I said he was similar, and behold what a wonderful power he has. Know that none of you knows Socrates. But I will show you, since I have already begun to speak. Do you see how vehemently Socrates is affected toward the beautiful? And is always among them and is stupefied? And is ignorant of everything, knows nothing. This figure is surely most similar to the Silenes. Know therefore that he is clothed on the outside with this form of habit, like a certain sculpted Silenus. But inside, if he is opened, O guests, there is wonderful chastity and integrity within. Nor does he value the beauty of anyone’s body at all, nor riches, nor honors, nor other things which the common people admire, but he despises all those things far beyond what can be thought, and counts them as nothing. Therefore I assert to you that we are of no account in his eyes: yet he, being <term>ironic<note>This refers to 'Socratic irony,' where Socrates would pretend to be ignorant to lead others to the truth.</note></term>, feigns otherwise and never ceases to joke openly about these things. But when he is acting seriously and is opened within, I do not know whether any of you has ever inspected the divine images that lie hidden inside. I certainly once saw them, and they seemed to me so divine, and golden, and beautiful, and wonderful, that I judged it by no means lawful to act otherwise than as Socrates prescribes. I once indeed, O guests, 

thinking that Socrates was truly delighted by my appearance, thought that I had found this wonderful and happy occasion for what I was affecting. Indeed, I decided to gratify Socrates, so that whatever he knew, he might communicate with me. For I thought my beauty something great and wonderful, and I trusted in it most of all. And when I had never been accustomed to speak with him without a companion before, once, having dismissed the companion, I remained alone with him. All the truth must be opened to you. Attend, I pray. If I lie, Socrates, you yourself refute it. I remained indeed, O guests, alone with him alone, hoping he would say the same things to me that lovers are accustomed to say to their loved ones when they are alone. In which hope I rejoiced greatly; but none of these things was done, but as he was accustomed, when he had discoursed until evening, he went away. After this I invited him to the gymnasium and exercised with him, as if about to achieve something in this. Often therefore we alone exercised gymnastics together. What need is there of many words? Nothing succeeded for me. But after it had by no means succeeded in this way, I decided to approach this man with harder machinations, nor to desist from what I had begun. Hear how vehemently I ambushed him. I invited him to dinner as a lover ambushing his loved one. He did not easily nor at first obey, but at last he complied. He came therefore: but having taken food, he immediately rose up to go away. Then I, detained by shame, permitted him to go. But stretching other more vehement ambushes, after dinner I protracted the discourse until late at night: and when he wanted to depart, objecting that it was late at night, I forced him to stay. He rested therefore in the next bed, on which he had sat and dined, nor did any other besides us sleep there that night. What has been said so far can be brought forth everywhere without a blush. But what follows you will not hear before I have recounted that proverb: <margin>Proverb.</margin> **Wine is truthful, both with childhood and without childhood.** Furthermore, it seems unjust that he who praises Socrates should pass over his proud and unconquered deed in silence. Moreover, I am affected no differently than he who is bitten by a viper. For they say that he who is bitten does not wish to open what his passion is like except to those who are similarly sick, as if these alone, being not ignorant of the evil, might forgive if someone, compelled by torture, does not hesitate both to speak and to do everything. I therefore, above the rest, constrained by a more vehement bite of philosophy—which is the sharpest of all, whether it be the heart, or the soul, or whatever it should be called, wounded by desire in the discourses of philosophy, which bite more sharply than a viper, and occupy when they have touched a youthful soul which is not entirely lazy, and compel it to whatever finally happens, to do and to say—and beholding the Phaedruses, Agathons, Eryximachuses, Pausaniases, Aristodemuses, Aristophaneses, and finally Socrates himself, and the others. (For you all have been seized together with me by the fury and bacchic revelry of philosophy) therefore hear all of you. Indeed you will give me pardon for these things which were then done by me, and are now said. But the servants, and if any other profane and rustic person is present, let them stop their ears. When the lamp was extinguished and the servants were absent, it seemed to me, O guests, no longer to be dissembled or deferred, but candidly to open what I felt. Therefore I touched him, saying: "Socrates, are you sleeping?" "Not yet," he said. "Do you know what has seemed best to me so far?" I said. "About what matter, and what do you ask?" he said. These things I know you will not deny, Socrates. He however entirely despised the form in which I trusted most, as if it were ridiculous, and proudly contemned it. I call all the gods and goddesses to witness, O judges—for you are the judges of Socratic pride—that I rose up no differently than if I had lain with my father or an older brother. What mind do you think I had after these things, when I considered myself indeed despised, but admired his genius, temperance, and fortitude, having found such a man as I had believed no one to be found by me in prudence and tolerance? For which reason I did not find a way to be angry with him, nor to depart from him, nor again by what allurements I might reconcile him to myself. I knew indeed that he could be conquered more difficultly by money than Ajax by iron, and that by which I had hoped to have easily ensnared him had failed me. Ambiguous therefore, and enslaved to this man more than anyone else to another, I wandered about. All these things were done by me then. After this, as time proceeded, military service fell to him and to me together against Potidaea, and Socrates and I were tent-mates and mess-mates in that army. First indeed, in patience of labors he far surpassed not only me, but all others: and if in any place, as is accustomed to happen in war, provisions failed, none were found equal to him in bearing hunger and thirst. Conversely, in the abundance of things and in revelry and the military table, he alone seemed to be able to enjoy it. And although he did not want to drink, yet if he was forced, he far surpassed everyone in drinking: and what is most wonderful of all, no one ever saw him drunk. But this seems to be able to be refuted nothing yet for the future. Against the winters and colds, which are very harsh in those places, 

he did wonderful things. For whenever a very great and intolerable frost occurred, so that no others dared to go out from the tents, and if any did go out, they were only very much bundled up, and their feet and legs diligently wrapped in skins and woolen cloths: Socrates during this very time went out with the other soldiers such that he added nothing to that garment which he had been accustomed to wear before. But with naked feet he walked more easily through the ice than others with shoes. The soldiers indeed beholding these things suspected they were despised by him. And in these things indeed such was Socrates. But what this most tolerant man did in the same army is worth hearing: for when once a certain thought had fallen upon him, he stood thinking in the same spot from the morning time: and when it was not given to explain that which he was thinking, he persisted thinking, nor did he let go: and it was already midday, and the soldiers had noticed it, and were wondering, and one was telling another that Socrates had been standing thinking since dawn. Finally however, some soldiers from Ionia, when night was already imminent, having dined before—for it was then summer—placed their mats around him, and lay in the cold, observing him, whether he would also persevere through the night. Socrates indeed stood until the following dawn and the rising of the sun. Afterward however he went away, when he had already greeted the rising sun. In battles also what kind of man he was must not be passed over in silence. For when that battle was from which the leaders of the army gave me prizes as the best fighter, no one else saved me but Socrates. For seeing me heavily wounded, he by no means deserted me, but leaping forward before me, he protected me and my arms, and saved me from the enemies. And I then preaching those things tried to have those gifts handed over not to me, but to this Socrates, by whom I had been saved. Nor would you refute those things, nor deny them as false, Socrates. Then indeed the leaders, looking to my dignity, preferred to give to me, you especially, O Socrates, beseeching that the honor should be exhibited to me, not to you. But it was noble, O men, to see Socrates when our army was fleeing from Delium. For I was also present at this battle, and indeed fighting from a horse, when Socrates himself was on foot. Our men having been routed, and the flight of everyone now made, Socrates and Laches together were retreating. And when I had fallen upon these by chance, I told them to be of good heart, and said I would never desert them. Here therefore I was better able to behold Socrates than at Potidaea, because I myself, trusting in the horse, was less afraid. First therefore it was permitted to behold with how much caution and presence of mind he surpassed Laches. Then he seemed to me, O Aristophanes, what you say he does here: to walk proudly, and surveying everything quietly with his eyes, and cautiously examining each thing. Indeed he looked at enemies and citizens in turn, showing by his eyes and look, and demonstrating even to those farther away, that if anyone should attack him, he would not do it with impunity. Therefore he himself and the other went away safely. For almost no one attacks those who walk thus, but those who are carried away in headlong flight. In many other things indeed Socrates can be wonderfully praised, but they are such that perhaps some others also might deserve the same praise: but those things are chief in this, through which he is found to be similar to none of other men, neither of the ancients, nor of the moderns. For what kind of man Achilles was, someone might perhaps guess that Brasidas and some others were such: and what kind of man Pericles was, such were Antenor and Nestor. There are others also who can be compared in this way to each other. But such as Socrates is, and of what sort...

and such is his marvelous way of speaking, that almost no one comes close to his likeness, neither among the ancients, nor among those who live now, except as I have just said and compared him. For he is like no other man, but is himself like the **Silenuses** and **Satyrs**, as are his speeches. <note>Silenuses and Satyrs were mythological companions of Dionysus, often depicted as grotesque or snub-nosed on the outside but possessing hidden wisdom.</note> For this also I had omitted before: that his speeches are very much like opened Silenuses. For if anyone were to hear his speeches, they seem at first, as is said, to be excessively absurd on the surface. Indeed, the names and words present the outward appearance of some insulting Satyr. For he always has donkeys, and blacksmiths, and shoemakers, and tanners in his mouth, and he seems to always say the same things about the same subjects, so that almost all who are less experienced or skilled might mock his words. But if anyone looks inside his speeches, he will find first that they alone of all others possess a depth of meaning, and moreover that they are most divine, containing many most beautiful images of the virtues, and extending themselves to many things—or rather, embracing all the precepts by which he who is to live honorably and well ought to be instructed.

These are the things, O fellow guests, for which I praise Socrates, and also of which I complain. For you have heard meanwhile what injuries he has inflicted upon me. Nor has he behaved this way toward me alone, but also toward Charmides the son of Glaucon, and toward Euthydemus the son of Diocles, and many others, whom he deceived under the guise of a lover; for instead of the lover, he turned out to be the beloved. <note>In the Greek social structure of "paiderasteia," Socrates frequently inverted the roles, making his young followers pursue him for his wisdom rather than him pursuing them for their beauty.</note> Therefore I warn you also, Agathon, to beware of his simulations and dissimulations, and knowing him from what I have suffered, look to your own interest, and do not, according to the proverb, "become wise like fools after receiving a misfortune."

When Alcibiades had said these things, Aristodemus related that laughter was stirred in everyone at his audacity and freedom of speech, since he seemed to be captured by the love of Socrates. "You seem to me to be sober, O Alcibiades," Socrates said. "Otherwise you would never have so craftily made such a long circuit of words to hide the purpose for which you said everything else: which at the heel of your speech, as if you seemed to bring it forth unintentionally, you finally added—as if you did not say all those things for the sake of separating me from Agathon. You think that I ought to love no one except you alone, and that Agathon should be loved by no one but you. But your **Satyric and Silenic fiction** did not escape us. But, O friend Agathon, effort must be made so that his machinations do not succeed, and so that no disagreement caused by any slander thrown between me and you may occur."

"Truly, O Socrates," Agathon responded, "you seem to speak the truth. I gather this from the fact that he placed himself in the middle between you and me in order to separate us. But this will profit him nothing; for rising from here, I will sit near you." "It must certainly be done so," said Socrates. "Sit here below me." "By Jupiter!" Alcibiades exclaimed. "What things this man forces me to endure! He wishes to overcome me in everything. But if nothing else, O wonderful man, at least permit Agathon to sit here in the middle." "By no means is it fitting," Socrates responded. "For you have praised me. But it is necessary that I now praise this man sitting to my right. If therefore Agathon remains after you, he will hardly praise me again before he is praised by me. But let him be, happy man, and do not envy this youth my praises. Indeed, I desire to praise him vehemently." "Alas, alas, Alcibiades!" Agathon said there. "Why do I stay here? I am leaving now so that Socrates may praise me." "That is the custom of Socrates," Alcibiades responded, "that while he is present, it is permitted to no one else to win over the beautiful. See now, I pray, how easily and by what probable reason he has drawn this man to himself."

Agathon therefore rose to rest near Socrates. Then suddenly many revelers, finding the doors open—for someone had gone out against them a little before—entered and sat down around them. By their noise everything was thrown into confusion, and after this no moderation in drinking was observed. Aristodemus recounted that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others departed, and that he himself slept for a long time—for the nights were long then—and rose around dawn as the roosters were already crowing. Having been waked from sleep, he found that some of the others were sleeping, and some had departed. Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates alone were still awake, and were drinking from a certain large bowl, passing it to the right in succession. Socrates, however, was disputing with them. Aristodemus said he did not remember the rest of the discussion, for he had not been present from the beginning and was heavy with sleep. But the sum of that dispute was this: that Socrates was forcing them to admit that it is the office of the same man to compose both tragedy and comedy, and that he who is a tragic poet by art is also a comic poet. <note>A famous and debated conclusion where Socrates argues for the unity of the dramatic arts.</note> When they had conceded these things, being forced rather than persuaded, Aristophanes first gave himself to sleep, and then Agathon as light was already arising. But Socrates, with the others sleeping, set out for the **Lyceum** <note>A gymnasium and public meeting place in Athens where Socrates often taught.</note>, with Aristodemus himself following him as he was accustomed; and having bathed in his usual manner, he spent the whole day as he was wont, and finally rested at home in the evening.
