# PHAEDRUS,
# OR, ON BEAUTY.
*
### THE ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.
*

Our Plato, pregnant with the frenzy of the poetic muse—which he followed from a tender age, or rather from his Apolline birth—first gave birth to a book that is almost entirely poetic. And being most radiant, he wrote a most radiant work; and being most beautiful, and most worthy of the love of all, he wrote of beauty and love together. Thus he deservedly published his other books thereafter full of charm and grace, having made a happy beginning from the Venerean Muse; and he alone of all men joined charm with dignity everywhere.

Since, however, we have explained many mysteries of this book in our *Theology* and in our *Book on Love*, we shall touch upon its argument very briefly. The *Banquet* indeed treats primarily of Love, and consequently of beauty. But the *Phaedrus*, for the sake of Beauty, disputes concerning Love. Nor is the speech of Lysias and the oratorical dispute inserted entirely without reason. For Beauty pertains to the mind, to sight, and to hearing. Thus it happens that where the beauty of souls and names is treated, and likewise the beauty of the body, the beauty of speech is deservedly disputed.

Immediately in the very opening, Socrates, while joking, hands down very serious precepts: that all things must be utterly despised for the sake of the study of wisdom; and that the primary study of wisdom is to consider oneself. Among these things, the most artificial description of the place signifies the **Academy** allegorically: the **Plane tree** signifies Plato; the **Chaste tree** (shrub) signifies the chastity of Platonic and Socratic love; the **Fountain** signifies the bounty in communicating wisdom; and the other ornaments signify the oratorical and poetic flowers in which the Academy of Plato abounds. Lysias is rightly reproved because he inquires into what the affection of love is like, yet neither defined nor distinguished love itself beforehand. Consider among these things the modesty of Socratic love, for some things less honorable...

300 Twenty-sixth Book.

...he begins with his head covered, being about to speak of things less than honorable. Soon he invokes the Muses, so that they might at least honor a less honorable matter with their own splendor of speech. But before he censures the shameful lover, so as not to fall into the same fault as Lysias, he defines shameful love as a certain desire or lust rebelling against reason, which overcomes the opinion tending toward right and snatches one toward the pleasure of form. But while he proceeds to define it, he gives us two leaders: one, the innate appetite for pleasure; the other, a certain legitimate opinion acquired gradually through discipline and leading toward honorable things. Truly, two extrinsic leaders move these intrinsic ones: a certain **aerial demon** <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "demons" were intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</note> moves opinion, while a **watery one** moves lust. 

After he has defined it, he separates the youths from shameful lovers with many reasons. Then, meanwhile, note a wonderful mystery, similar to the **Mosaic mystery** <note>Ficino often sought to harmonize Plato with the "mysteries" of Moses and the Old Testament.</note>. Into the very beginning of most evils, some demon immediately mixed pleasure. Since he acts not so much a philosophical persona as a poetic one, he adds that he was seized by a demon because he criticized the name of Love, which is a God. He does this so that, when he goes to distinguish Love, he may do so in a poetic rather than a dialectical manner. In this, you will notice that it is a most grave sin to offend against the name of God. Again, there is a presage in the soul. 

Then, through certain poetic ambiguities, he separates art from frenzy. He divides frenzy into divine and human. The divine into four types: namely, prophecy, mystery, poetry, and love. He confirms providence and religion. He places wisdom infused by divine frenzy far above human wisdom. Before he proceeds to the treatment of particular souls, he brings forward the common souls into the midst, namely the **Soul of the World**, which he names **Jupiter**, and under it the twelve souls of the twelve mundane spheres, to which he subjects as many orders of demons and as many particular souls. He assigns a chariot to each, that is, celestial and eternal bodies. 

He disputes about rational souls, both divine and human, about the circuit of both, and by what means the souls of men in heaven might accompany the contemplation of the celestial souls and follow the intuition above the angelic heaven. What indeed the Chariot vehicle, the wings, the charioteer, the horses, Fate, and the fall into the body mean, and what again the great Jupiter in heaven and the other following Gods signify, we explain in our *Theology*. It will be enough for you at present to understand that the twin wings are the twin instinct innate to the mind, lifting the soul to the heights: in the intellect, the instinct toward divine truth; in the will, the instinct turning toward divine good according to its strength. When these are relaxed, however, and the vegetal inclination of nature is stretched toward governing bodies, the Pythagoreans think that the souls, their wings now broken, descend into the elements. 

After this, he distributes the soul falling from heaven into nine ranks. In all these, he uses poetic license and relates Pythagorean tales rather than his own. Meanwhile, notice that a similar fall of souls is described by the Pythagoreans, and of demons by the prophets. I would also have you know that the number fits both the angelic choirs and the demons fallen from there. I pass over now that **Pherecydes of Syros** <note>A 6th-century BC Greek thinker often cited as a teacher of Pythagoras.</note> relates a certain similar fall happening to demons. And he adds that **Ophion**, that is, the demonic serpent, was the head of the army rebelling against the divine mind. To this is also similar what is contained in the divine mysteries: namely, that Jupiter cast down the lower demons to the underworld. 

But let us return to the dialogue. Finally, the man with a purified mind, devoted to God, is filled thereafter with all good things and is the only wise man, even if, being as it were placed outside himself, he is mocked by the common people as if insane. After this, he descends to the divine frenzy of legitimate love, which he thinks is kindled in the soul when, looking upon the beautiful form of a body, it easily remembers the divine beauty which it had once contemplated, and is inflamed with the desire of recovering it, and rages. But he describes a frenzy contrary to this, like a beastly one, not ascending from the form of the body to divine intuition, but shamefully descending to venereal union. 

He describes again a certain human frenzy between the divine and the beastly, kindled in the soul of him who, occupied by admiration of the bodily form, neither completely consigns the divine to oblivion nor fully remembers it. Thus it happens that he is neither entirely intemperate nor entirely temperate, but appears now as it were incontinent, now continent. Seeking afterward the causes for which some love others more or less, he flees to the stars, whose companions the souls were from the beginning. For he arranges as many orders of human souls in the *Timaeus* as there are stars in heaven. 

From here he returns again to dividing the powers of the soul: and indeed he calls reason the **charioteer**, and the twin appetites the twin horses: the rational appetite the good horse, the irrational appetite the bad horse. But in this category, he considers the appetite verging toward anger less evil, and that declining toward...

...lust, more evil. Then he depicts the passions of lovers, both the continent and the incontinent, and mutual love, like a poet. Thus it happens that these are to be indulged in allegorically no differently than the **Songs of Solomon** <note>The Song of Songs in the Bible, often interpreted allegorically as the soul's love for God.</note>. 

These things done, when he had treated beauty pertaining to the mind and to sight, he now proceeds to examine the speech of Lysias and to demonstrate the office of the orator, so that it may be clear what the beauty of speech is, which pertains to hearing. He places the beauty of speech in order: namely, that it should have a head differing from the end, and have a middle, necessarily coupled to the head and the end and to each other. He commanded such an order to be observed by the orator first of all. Moreover, he proves that no one can be an orator of things unless he has a knowledge of things, especially human things and souls. 

So that the orator might achieve this, he commands him to learn the **dialectical faculty** of dividing and composing, which he wants to be the principal instrument for searching out and finding the truth, and in the *Philebus* he calls it a gift of god, because just as it is the perpetual office of God in the world to divide and compose, so it is of the dialectician in art. Therefore, he judges the perfected dialectician—that is, the metaphysician—as someone to be worshiped like a god. After this, he compares orators in turn and censures those who, preferring the probable to the true, deceive the people and themselves, and foolishly trust that they can know what is most like the truth even without knowledge of the truth itself. 

Soon he notes some best precepts. Three things are first necessary to the orator: Talent, Doctrine, and Practice. Philosophy is needed for the very perfection of every art. From dialectical practice and the contemplation of sublime things, a sublimity of mind and an effective force for action are finally acquired. These two are greatly necessary in the perfection of the greatest arts. Then he compares the illegitimate orator to cooks and flatterers, as in the *Gorgias*; but the legitimate one to a physician. Hence he delivers the rule by which the nature of both the soul and the body—indeed, of every thing—is to be known, and immediately returns to the office of the orator. 

He adds that, because of the office of writing itself, letters were invented in Egypt by a certain demon, **Teuth** <note>Thoth, the Egyptian god of writing.</note>, together with the other disciplines. Furthermore, he mocks the zeal for writing, namely in him who trusts that he can reveal undoubted truth to posterity through letters. And in the manner of the Pythagoreans, he proves that the contemplation and tradition of truth should be in souls rather than in books. He confirms this also in his letters. Finally, he praises only the orator who is a philosopher by talent and study. He concludes the dialogue with a prayer and vows seeking beauty of the soul from God. In this, consider that Socrates, having entirely spurned all other things, is content with the beauty of the soul alone—that is, wisdom—yet indicates that this itself is acquired not so much by human study as by divine gift.

He was heading now outside the walls to meditate on those very things. Meeting a man with an insane love for speeches, he rejoiced at seeing him, because he would have a fellow-rejoicer and fellow-exulter, and he commanded him to go along. Then, when asked by that same man greedy for speeches to speak, he pretended to be burdened, as if he did not want to relate it; but finally, even if no one wanted to hear it voluntarily, he was going to force it to be heard. Therefore, if someone does not believe these things are as they are told, but wants to bring each one to a convenient meaning, relying on a certain boorish wisdom, he will need too much leisure. 

But I have no leisure for these things, O friend, for this reason: because I am not yet able, according to the **Delphic precept** <note>The famous inscription at the Temple of Apollo: "Know thyself."</note>, to know myself. It seems ridiculous to me, therefore, while I am ignorant of my own things, to want to search into the things of others. A most clear spring also flows under the Plane tree with very cold water, as can be guessed by the touch of the foot; which I judge to be sacred to the nymphs and **Achelous** <note>A river god.</note> from those figurines and statues. Do you not notice, moreover, how pleasant and sweet a breeze breathes here? Above all, something summery and musical resounds from the choir of **cicadas**. But the most ornate of all is to look at the grass itself, how it is suited to gently receive the head of a man reclining on the sloping meadow. Thus you have led me out very well, like a guest, O friend Phaedrus." 

PHAE. "O admirable man, you seem most absurd indeed: and truly, as you say, you are like some guest being led, not like a local; so you appear never to have crossed our borders, nor even to have stepped outside the walls themselves." You, however, seem to me to have found an inducement for my going out. For just as they lead hungry animals by stretching out leaves or fruit, so you, stretching out a book to me, could lead me through all of Attica and anywhere else you wish. Now therefore, since we have arrived here, it pleases me to lie down. You, however, in whatever posture it seems you can read most comfortably, take it and read."

302 Twenty-sixth Book.

...carelessly they have administered their affairs because of love, and what benefits they have conferred to their own loss, or what labors they have undergone; therefore, they think they have returned a worthy grace to their beloveds. But these who are not deceived by love do not complain that they have incurred either negligence of domestic affairs, or past labors, or discords with relatives for the sake of the beloved. Wherefore, such great evils being removed, nothing else remains except that they be ready to perform all things which they think will be pleasing to them. 

Most people say that lovers ought to be valued more for this reason: because they are bound by the greatest charity toward the beloved, and are always ready, both in words and deeds, to obey the beloved, even if they offend all others by this. We easily guess that their opinion is not true from this: because, their benevolence being transferred from some to others, they prefer later beloveds to the prior ones; and if the more recent ones command it, they treat the former ones with evils. 

And yet, by what reason is it right to concede such a thing to him who is afflicted by that calamity which no one who has experienced it would ever concede? Indeed, they themselves confess that they are insane rather than wise, and they know moreover their own insanity, but they cannot contain themselves at all. But truly, those who are wise, in what way will they approve the counsels and wills of those who are so affected? 

Moreover, if you wish to choose the best from among lovers, your choice will be given from a few; but if you seek the most convenient companion for yourself from among others, it will surely be possible to choose from many. There is a greater hope that a man worthy of your friendship will be found among many than among few. 

If, therefore, you fear public infamy from the constitution of the laws, you ought to remember that lovers, who judge themselves so worthy of being loved just as they love others, are accustomed to boast openly that they have not kept watch in vain. But those who do not love, because they can contain themselves, are accustomed to seek what is best rather than the rumor of the multitude. 

Add that the common people, when they perceive lovers following beloveds assiduously and think this worth the effort, suspect lest a shameful desire has seized them, or perhaps is seizing them now. But they do not dare to disapprove of the familiarity of non-lovers: for they know it is necessary for men to be together often, either for the sake of friendship or some convenience. 

Furthermore, if fear invades you, thinking that it will be difficult for friendship to remain—indeed, that if a grudge arises, a common loss to both will happen, and that you will be most harmed if you concede those things you value highly—you will not without reason fear lovers greatly. For many things offend them, and they judge everything to happen to their own detriment. For which reason they prohibit beloveds from being among others, fearing lest wealthy men surpass them in riches, or learned men excel them in intelligence; and they try to keep the beloved far away from anyone who seems to have anything remarkable in themselves. Thus, persuading them to abstain from these, they deprive them of all friends. But you, if you have deliberated better than they by taking account of your own affairs, you will disagree with them and depart. 

But those who are not captured by love of you, but perform what is right because of virtue, will by no means envy you the familiarity of others; but rather they will hate those who wish to cling to you, judging that you are despised by those, but helped by your familiars. Wherefore, there is a much greater hope that friendships will come from this commerce than enmities. 

Added to these things is that most lovers desire the body before they have known either the manners or anything else pertaining to the beloved. Thus it happens that it is doubtful whether they will persevere in friendship when their desire is extinguished. But for non-lovers, who even when they were friends before did not do everything for the sake of pleasure, it is consistent that not such an ardent benevolence is kindled, but that their offices are received as monuments of things to come. 

Moreover, you will turn out better if you believe me than if you offer your ears to a lover. For lovers extol your words and deeds with praises beyond measure, partly because they fear they might offend you, and partly because they are deceived in judging due to the heat of desire. For love designates certain such things: it compels the unfortunate ones to think even those things which offer no annoyance to others are sad; but it forces the fortunate ones and those who have obtained their wish to praise things not worthy of joy as if they were pleasant. 

Wherefore, it is more appropriate to pity them than to love them. But if you believe me, first I will be there for you not for the sake of present pleasure but for future utility, not enslaved to love but commanding myself; nor for the smallest reasons will I ever stir up grave enmities—indeed, for the greatest ones, having been moved at last with difficulty, I will forgive involuntary errors, and I will try to correct and avoid voluntary ones. These are the arguments for a friendship that will last for a long time. 

But if it seems to you that a firm friendship cannot be born except through love, you ought to notice that, by this reasoning, we would not value our sons much, nor our parents, nor would we have those faithful friends who became friends not from the heat of this love but from any other studies. 

To these things, if the needy are to be gratified most, it is altogether appropriate to help not the better men but the poorest; for having been freed from the greatest evils, they will have huge thanks. In your own and private expenses, too, friends will not be those to be called together, but the hungry and the supplicants. For these will value the benefit most, they will follow you, they will wait at your doors, they will applaud, they will give huge thanks, they will pour out vows for you. 

Furthermore, it is perhaps fitting to indulge not the needy most, but rather those who can return the favor; nor lovers alone, but those worthy of the benefit; nor those who are delighted by your beauty, but those who will be of use to you even when you are old; nor those who, having obtained their wish, will boast of themselves openly, but those who will be silent out of modesty; nor those who will court you for a short time, but those who will love you similarly through all your life; nor those who, their heat of desire extinguished, will seek occasions for enmities, but those who, when your beauty fades, will show their virtue and constancy. 

You therefore remember what I have said, and think of this: that lovers are rebuked by their friends as if love were something shameful. But no familiar censures those who do not love for that reason, as if they were consulting ill for themselves by this. 

Perhaps you will ask me whether I advise you to obey all non-lovers. But I think that not even a lover would command you to have this same mind toward all lovers. For that is not worthy of an equal grace to the one receiving it, nor similarly easy for you who wish to remain hidden from others. It is appropriate, however, that no loss come from this, but some utility come to both. I judge what has been said already to be enough; if, however, anything seems to be added by you, ask." 

"What does it seem to you, O Socrates? Does this speech not seem wonderfully composed, both in other things and in its words?" SOC. "In a wonderful way, O friend, so that I was stunned. And I was so affected because of you, O Phaedrus, while I was looking at you, because you seemed to me to be exulting in reading the speech. Thinking, therefore, that you know such things more than I, following you, O divine head, I myself also joined in the revelry with you." PHAE. "Does it seem to you that you should joke thus?" SOC. "Do I seem to you to be joking? Or not to be speaking seriously?" PHAE. "By no..."

<summary>Phaedrus finishes reading the speech of Lysias, which argues that non-lovers are more stable, less jealous, and more likely to offer lasting friendship than those blinded by the madness of passion; Socrates responds with playful, mock admiration.</summary>
<keywords>Lysias, speech on love, lovers vs. non-lovers, jealousy, social reputation, stability, Socratic irony, Phaedrus</keywords>

### On the Universe
[[notes: This is the conclusion of Cicero’s *De Universitate*, his Latin translation and adaptation of Plato’s *Timaeus*.]]

...should they be hidden from our sight by their orbits, and emerging again, strike fear into those unskilled in reason—if we were to attempt to explain these things in words without placing a physical model of them before the eyes, our labor would be undertaken in vain. But enough has been said of these things. Let this be the conclusion of what we have prefaced concerning the nature of the Gods who are perceived and those who have been born.

As for the others, whom the Greeks call [[abbrev: δαίμονας → daimones]] (*daimones* or spirits), and our people (in my opinion) call the *Lares* [[notes: household gods in Roman religion]]—if indeed this can be seen as a correct translation—to know and to announce their origin is a task greater than what we would dare to profess or write. One must surely believe the men of old and the ancients, as they say, who claimed to be the offspring of the Gods and thus handed down their names to us; for they were best able to know their own progenitors. It is very difficult to withhold belief from those born of the Gods, even if their speech is confirmed neither by arguments nor certain reasons. Because they seem to be speaking of things known to them, we must obey the ancient law and custom. 

Thus, as it has been handed down by them, let the origin of these Gods be held and described as follows: let us remember that Oceanus and Salacia [[notes: Cicero uses Roman equivalents; Salacia is the goddess of salt water, roughly corresponding to Tethys]] were generated and brought forth by the breath of the Heavens and the conception of the Earth. From them were born Saturn and Ops, and thereafter we are accustomed to name and call upon Jupiter and Juno, and the rest of the brothers born of the same kin, and their *prosapia* (lineage)—to use an ancient word. 

When, therefore, all the gods—both those who move and show themselves openly, and those who reveal themselves to us only insofar as they wish—were created, then that God who begot all things [[notes: the Demiurge]] spoke these words to them: 

"Pay attention, you who were born from the breath of the Gods. Of these works, I am the parent and the maker; these things are indissoluble because I will it so, although everything that is bound together can be loosed. But it is by no means the part of a good being to wish to dissolve that which is bound by reason. Since you have been born, you are not indeed immortal and indissoluble in your own right. Yet you shall never be dissolved, nor shall any fates of death destroy you; nor is any deceit more powerful than my counsel, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those by which you were bound when you were being born. 

Hear now what I think. Three species remain for us to create, and these are mortal; if these are omitted, the completion of the heavens will not be perfect. For the heavens will not contain all classes of living things. But it is necessary that it should contain them, so that those things which are made by me might be able to equal the life of the Gods. Therefore, so that they may be generated in a mortal condition, you yourselves undertake the task; imitate, in producing them, the power that I used, which you remember me using in your own origin. 

Among these, those who are created such that they ought to be like kinsmen of the immortal Gods shall be called of a divine race; they shall hold the leadership over all living things and shall obey you willingly by right and by law. Their beginning and status is handed over to you by me. You, however, shall weave a mortal part onto that which will be immortal. Thus shall arise living beings whom you may nourish while living, and whom you may receive back into your bosom when they are consumed."

He said these things, and then returned to the previous mixing-bowl. In it, he mixed the soul of the entire universe, pouring in and equalizing the remaining parts with the previous mixtures in nearly the same way, except that these were not as incorruptible as those which are always the same, but he took from them a second and even a third degree of purity. 

When the whole was constituted, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars and assigned each soul to an individual star, and placed them, as it were, into the chariot of the universe. He showed them the fatal and necessary laws, and demonstrated that the first birth for each would be the same for all, moderated and constant, and diminished by no one. It would be enough, as if the souls were scattered, that at certain intervals of time a living creature should be born who was most fit for the worship of the Gods. 

But since the nature of the human race was twofold, things were so arranged that the more excellent gender would be those who were to be men. When he had sown souls into bodies by necessity, and when by necessity an addition to the bodies was made, and then a withdrawal [[notes: birth and death]], it was necessary that there exist one sense, common to all, excited by a more vehement motion and joined to nature; then love mixed with pleasure and distress, after that anger and fear, and the other motions of the soul, companions to the former, and even those contrary and dissenting. He who rules these by reason will have lived justly; he who gives himself up to them, unjustly. 

And he who has rightly and honestly completed the course of living given by nature shall return to that star to which he was suited. But he who lives immoderately and intemperately shall be transferred in a second birth into a feminine form. And if even then he does not make an end to his vices, he shall be tossed about even more severely and shall be transferred into the forms of beasts and wild animals most similar to his own habits. Nor shall he see the limit of his evils until he begins to follow that rotation which he had within himself, innate and implanted. This will finally happen when he has driven away by reason those things from fire, air, water, and earth which have settled within him—turbulent and devoid of reason—and reaches the first and best state of his soul.

When he had designated these things, so that he might place himself beyond all blame and cause if any fraud or vice should happen afterward, he sowed them—scattering some into the earth, others into the moon, and others into the remaining parts of the world which are established as signs for the marking of the spaces of time. After that sowing, he permitted the "younger Gods," so to speak, to fashion mortal bodies, and to polish and complete whatever remained of the human soul that ought to be added, along with all subsequent parts. Furthermore, he commanded them to provide themselves as leader and guide to this living being, and to rule and govern its life most beautifully, except insofar as the being might seek some misery for itself through its own fault.

And indeed, he who composed all things remained constantly in his own state; but those who were created by him, when they had recognized their parent’s order, followed it. Therefore, having received the immortal principle of a mortal living being, imitating their progenitor and maker, they borrowed particles of fire, earth, water, and air from the world—which they were to return later—and joined them together, not with the same bonds by which they themselves were bound, but with such as could not be seen because of their smallness. By driving in frequent little wedges, as it were, they made one body out of all the parts; likewise, they bound the circuits of the divine soul into that body as it flowed in and out. 

Thus, those souls, immersed in a river, neither held nor were held, but with great force they were now carried along, and now were being carried. Thus the whole animal was moved indeed, but immoderately and by chance, so that it was carried in six motions: for it went forward and backward, to the left and to the right, and upward and downward, now here, now there... 

But if it settles in brilliance, then either the same appearance or sometimes an altered one is returned, when the fire of the eyes has mingled and combined itself with that fire which is poured out before the face. Things which are on the left appear on the right, because they touch contrary parts of the eyes with contrary parts of the object.

[[page number: 667]]

### On the Universe

...on the right. But right things correspond to right, and left to left by the conversion of the lights, when they do not cohere among themselves. This happens when the smoothness of mirrors assumes depth on this side and that, and thus pushes the right into the left part of the eyes, and the left into the right. Even faces turned upward are perceived by the repulsion of the lights, which, by turning, makes the lower parts appear to be the upper. 

Now all these things are of that kind which assist the causes of things; God uses them as ministers when he effects the appearance of the best insofar as it can be done. But most people estimate that these are not assisting causes, but are the primary causes of all things—things which have the power of cold and heat, of solidity and liquidity. However, they lack all intelligence and reason, which are found nowhere else in nature except in the soul. The soul, however, escapes all the perception of the eyes. But fire, water, earth, and air are bodies, and they are seen. 

But he who professes himself a lover of intelligence and wisdom must first seek the primary causes of an intelligent and wise nature; then the secondary causes of those things which necessarily move others, while being moved themselves by others. Wherefore it seems to me that we must act in such a way that we speak of both kinds of causes separately: both of those which, with intelligence, are the producers of the most beautiful and best things, and of those which, lacking wisdom, produce inconstant and perturbed effects. 

Regarding the causes of the eyes, and why they have the power they now possess, I think enough has been said. Next, let the greatest utility of them given to the human race by the gift of the gods be explained. For the eyes have brought us the knowledge of the best things. For this discourse which we have held concerning the Universe would never have been discovered if neither the stars, nor the sun, nor the heaven could have fallen under the gaze of our eyes. But now, days and nights known to the eyes, then the revolutions of months and years have devised number, and measured the space of time, and we have attained philosophy through these things. Than this good, no more desirable or more excellent thing has been given to the mortal race by the grant and gift of the gods, nor shall it ever be given.

[[summary: This text contains the concluding portion of Cicero's Latin translation of Plato's *Timaeus*, describing the Demiurge's speech to the lesser gods and the creation of mortal souls, followed by a comprehensive index of Platonic themes.]]
[[keywords: Plato, Cicero, Timaeus, De Universitate, Demiurge, reincarnation, anima mundi, elements, vision, philosophy, index]]

--- Page 322 ---
->304 Book Twenty-Six<-

...the power of choosing is called temperance <term>temperantia: self-control or moderation</term>. But when desire draws us toward pleasures without reason and rules over us, this rule is called lust. Lust, since it is multiform and has many parts, certainly has many names; and of these forms, the one that most overflows in someone gives him its own name, and does not grant any honorable or worthy title to its own. For regarding food, that desire which overcomes reason and what is fair and good is called gluttony; and it gives this very name to the one who possesses it. Again, the desire that exercises a tyranny over drunkenness and leads the one it possesses toward it—it is clear what name it will have. And it is manifest how other names of this kind, sister desires, should be assigned where one especially dominates.

The reason for which we have said all the things above is now almost clear; yet whether it is stated or not, it will be clearer than if it were omitted. For the desire without reason which overcomes the opinion tending toward what is right, and which is snatched toward the pleasure of beauty, and is vehemently strengthened by its kindred desires toward the beauty of the body, it prevails and overcomes, **by this very strength** <note>original: "ἀπ' αὐτῆ τῆς ῥώμης", meaning by force or violence</note>, and is called **Love** <note>original: "ἔρως" (Eros)</note>. Now to you, O friend Phaedrus, do I seem, as I do to myself, to have suffered something divine? 

PHAEDRUS. Certainly, O Socrates, a certain unusual flowing abundance has seized you. 

SOCRATES. Listen to me then in silence. For truly this place seems divine. Therefore, if as the speech proceeds I am seized by the nymphs <note>In Greek mythology, nymphs were spirits of nature who could cause "nympholepsy," a state of divine possession or inspiration.</note>, do not be surprised. Certainly the things I was just chanting are not far from dithyrambs <note>Wild, passionate hymns usually dedicated to Dionysus.</note>. 

PHAEDRUS. You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES. You are indeed the cause of these things. But hear the rest, lest that which has come upon me should depart. These things will be a care to God. Let us return in our discussion to the boy. Come then, O best of men, what the subject of our consultation is has been stated and defined. Looking back then to this which remains, let us see what benefit or harm is likely to come from the lover and the non-lover to the one who complies. 

It is necessary for a man enslaved to lust and serving pleasures to make his beloved as pleasant to himself as possible. To a sick man, whatever does not resist is pleasant; but what is better or equal is troublesome. Therefore, the lover will never willingly allow his beloved to be either superior or equal. He will always make him inferior and more needy as much as he can. The ignorant is inferior to the wise, the timid to the brave, the unskilled in speaking to the rhetorical, the dull to the sharp. Since these and more mental evils are naturally present or develop in the beloved, the lover rejoices and tries to introduce even more. Otherwise, he is deprived of pleasure. 

Therefore, the lover must necessarily envy the beloved and, by removing him from every association and study from which he might emerge as an excellent man, do him great harm. Yet he does the most harm by depriving him of that which makes him most prudent. Truly, divine philosophy makes one most prudent, and the lover is compelled to lead the beloved far away from it, fearing lest he be despised by him if he becomes wiser. Finally, he does everything to make the youth ignorant of all things and an admirer of the lover. When he is such a person, he will be most pleasant to the lover, but most ruinous to himself. And so in those things which pertain to the intelligence, association with a lover is harmful. 

After this, it must be seen how he who is compelled to prefer the sweet to the good will care for the body of the one he loves, if it is committed to him. He will surely desire a body that is not solid, but soft and delicate, nourished not under the sun but in the shade, which has been brought up far from dangers and labors and the dry sweats of exercise, educated with a feminine and delicate lifestyle, adorned with artificial colors and external ornaments for lack of its own, and accustomed to other things like these. Since it would be unworthy to recount all these things at greater length, we will conclude them briefly for the present, so that we may follow up the rest. Such a condition of the body in battles and any other great necessity is one which enemies indeed invade boldly, but friends and the lovers themselves fear for most of all. 

But let this be dismissed now as something manifest. Next, it must be said what benefit or harm the lover's familiarity and guardianship provides us in external matters. Yet this is manifest to everyone, especially to the lover: that he desires the beloved to be robbed of his most friendly, dearest, and most divine possession. For he wishes him to be deprived of parents, relatives, and friends, thinking they will be an impediment to his sweetest association with the beloved. Furthermore, he thinks a boy very rich in gold or any other possession cannot be easily captured, nor, if captured, held. For which reason it is necessary for the lover, like an envious man, to grieve at the beloved's prosperity and rejoice in his adversity. Moreover, he desires the youth to live for a long time without a wife, without children, without a home, wishing to enjoy his own sweetness for the greatest amount of time. 

There are also other evils, but to most of these some spirit has mixed pleasure at the very beginning: just as nature has inserted some unseemly delight into a flatterer, a most heavy beast and a great calamity. Someone will also disparage a harlot as harmful, and other such animals and pursuits which are accustomed to delight us daily. But a lover, besides being harmful, is also the most troublesome of all in his association. For "like with like," according to the old proverb, gather most pleasantly <margin>Proverb</margin>. For equality of age, since it draws toward equal pleasures because of similarity, produces friendship. Nevertheless, even these bring too much satiety. Moreover, necessity is heavy to everyone in all things, which is indeed greatest in the lover toward the beloved along with their dissimilarity. For the older man clinging to the younger does not willingly leave him by day or night, but is snatched away by necessity and madness. This leads him indeed with the allurements of pleasures when he sees, hears, touches, and in any way reaches the beloved with any sense, so that he follows him continually with great pleasure. 

But with what pleasure or what consolation will he keep the beloved for an equal time, so that he is not vexed by extreme annoyance? When he sees the aged and deformed face, and other things similarly which are not only unpleasant to do, but even to hear, with a certain necessity always set before him to capture him, while he is observed always and everywhere by ill-suspicious guards, and hears untimely and immoderate praises and reproaches with which the lover pursues him; which are indeed intolerable in sobriety, but in drunkenness are not only intolerable but also most shameful because of the excessive and satiating license of speaking. 

Furthermore, while he loves, he is ruinous and troublesome. But when he ceases to love, he is thereafter a deceiver against the one whom he had finally induced with many oaths, prayers, and promises to endure his hostile association in the hope of rewards. At last, when it is time to repay, he accepts another prince and ruler within himself, mind and temperance instead of love and madness, and having now become someone else, he deceives the beloved. Then the beloved, remembering those things which were once said and done...

--- Page 323 ---
->Phaedrus, Or, on Beauty. 305<-

...remembering the benefits, he demands gratitude, thinking he is speaking with the same man. But the other, out of shame, neither dares to confess that he has changed, nor finds by what means he might fulfill the oaths and promises of that former mad rule, having now become a master of his mind and temperance, lest if he did the same things as before, he should again become similar and the same as he had been before. Hence it happens that he who loved before now flees, and having changed, departs, just as if a shell had fallen on the other side <note>A reference to "ostrakinda," an ancient Greek game where a shell was thrown to decide which side would chase the other.</note>; but the other is compelled to pursue, taking it heavily and turning to imprecation. 

He was surely deceived from the beginning, since he did not know it was not right to gratify a lover who was necessarily out of his mind, but rather a man much more free from love and possessing his mind. Otherwise it would be necessary to commit oneself to an unfaithful, morose, envious, troublesome man, ruinous to the possession of things, ruinous to the habit of the body, and by far most ruinous to the discipline of the soul, than which nothing is or ever will be more venerable among gods and men. These things, O boy, must be considered, and that must be noticed besides: that the friendship of a lover consists not in any goodwill, but in a certain greed for fulfillment, like hunger.

"As the wolf loves the lamb, so the lover burns for the boy."

This is what I had predicted, O Phaedrus. You will not hear me speaking further, but let the speech have its end now. 

PHAEDRUS. And yet I thought half the discussion was finished, and an equal amount remained to be said about the non-lover, that it is more fitting to indulge him, and all the good things in him should be enumerated; but why do you stop now, O Socrates? 

SOCRATES. Did you notice, Phaedrus, that I am no longer singing dithyrambic poems, even though my speech is spent in disparagement? If I should proceed to praise the other, what do you think I would do? Do you not feel that I am manifestly inspired by the nymphs, both by your work and by divine providence? Therefore I say briefly: as many good things are in the other as there are evils we have numbered in the first. But what need is there for many words? For enough has been said about both. And thus the story will have what is fitting. I am going away now, having crossed the river, before I am compelled by you to something greater. 

PHAEDRUS. Not yet, O Socrates, not until the heat departs. Do you not see that it is now plainly noon, which is called the "Constant and Steady"? But let us stay in the meantime and talk about these things we have said, and when it first cools down, then let us depart. 

SOCRATES. You are divine regarding speeches, O Phaedrus, and truly wonderful: I think indeed that of the speeches made in these times, no one has been the author and cause of more than you, whether by speaking yourself or by compelling others in some way. I except Simmias the Theban. But you far excel the others. And now you seem to have been the cause for some speech to be made by me. 

PHAEDRUS. You certainly do not declare war, but in what way, and what speech? 

SOCRATES. When he is about to cross the river: which indeed as often as it happens, prohibits me from doing what I was going to do. Hence I seemed to hear a voice which forbids me to depart before I have performed an expiation, as if I had committed some offense against God. I am therefore a prophet indeed, but by no means a good one, but like those who know letters poorly, sufficient for myself. Therefore I now understand my offense. Since, O friend, there is even something of a presage in the soul. For it moved me even before while I was speaking. Whence I was somewhat afraid lest, as perhaps according to Ibycus <note>A Greek lyric poet who feared offending the gods while seeking fame among men.</note> I had offended against the gods, I might achieve glory among men. Now I feel in what I have offended. 

PHAEDRUS. What is it? 

SOCRATES. A grave, O Phaedrus, a grave speech, I say, you both brought forward and compelled me to say. 

PHAEDRUS. In what way? 

SOCRATES. Foolish and in a way impious; than which what can be more grave? 

PHAEDRUS. Nothing, if you tell the truth. 

SOCRATES. What about Love? Do you not think him the son of Venus and some God? 

PHAEDRUS. So it is said. 

SOCRATES. Not however by Lysias, nor by your speech, which was brought forth through my mouth by you, as if drawn out by a certain agitation. But if Love is, as he certainly is, a God or something divine, he could not be evil. But the speeches about him were held as if he were evil. In this therefore we have offended against Love. And yet these discussions of ours seem very foolish, although polite: which since they contain nothing sincere or true, nevertheless boast as if they were of great value if they should be approved by some deceived little men. Therefore I, O friend, must be expiated. But there is a certain ancient expiation for those who sin in speaking myths, which Homer did not know, but Stesichorus did. For being deprived of his eyes because of his disparagement of Helen, he was not ignorant of the cause of his blindness as Homer was, but being a musician he recognized it. And so he immediately made those poems:

"That story was not true, nor in the high ships
Did you depart fleeing, nor did you go to the towers of Troy."

And thus having published the poem, which they call a **palinode** <note>original: "παλινωδίαν", a recantation or retraction</note>, he immediately recovered his lost sight. I however will be wiser than both in this, that before anything evil happens to me because of the disparagement of Love, I will try to return a palinode to him, and indeed with my head uncovered, not as above, veiled out of shame. 

PHAEDRUS. In this, O Socrates, you could do nothing more pleasing to me. 

SOCRATES. For you remember, O Phaedrus, how shamelessly it was read from the book, and said by me too about the lover. But if some noble and modest man, who loves or has loved another like himself, should hear us when we say that lovers often stir up the greatest enmities for the smallest causes, and that they are envious and ruinous men to the beloved, he will think he is hearing men brought up on ships <note>Socrates implies that sailors were considered unrefined or only familiar with coarse, transactional love.</note>, who have never looked upon any liberal love; nor will he in any way concede to us the things we bring forward in the disparagement of Love. 

PHAEDRUS. Perhaps by Jupiter, O Socrates. 

SOCRATES. Fearing this man, and fearing Love himself, I desire as if with a drinkable speech to wash away that false and harmful speech from our ears. I even advise Lysias that he should write as soon as possible that the lover rather than the non-lover should be indulged from similar motives. 

PHAEDRUS. Know for certain it will be so. For after you have praised the lover, it will be necessary for Lysias to be compelled by me to write the same. 

SOCRATES. I believe that indeed, as long as you are who you are now. 

PHAEDRUS. Speak then with a brave spirit. 

SOCRATES. Where is that boy for me, to whom I held the former speech, so that he may also hear this one; lest if he hears less, he should rashly obey the non-lover. 

PHAEDRUS. He always stays very close to you, as long as you wish. 

SOCRATES. Think then, O excellent boy, that the former speech was by Phaedrus the son of Pythocles of Myrrhinus; but the following will be by Stesichorus the son of Euphemus, an amiable man. This will be its beginning. 

"The speech is not true which says that while the lover is present, one should rather gratify the non-lover, because the lover is mad, while the non-lover is sane." 

For if it were simply true that madness is an evil, it would have been rightly said by us. But now the greatest of goods come to us through madness granted by a certain divine gift. For the prophetess at Delphi and the priests at Dodona, while mad indeed, have brought many and great benefits <margin>The greatest goods come through madness divinely granted.</margin> privately and publicly to the Greeks;

--- Page 324 ---
->306 Book Twenty-Six<-

...but while they are sane, they bring few or none. And if we mention the Sibyl and others whoever have used divine prophecy, how many things they have predicted that profited the future, we would extend the speech too far, and we would bring forth a matter manifest to all. Nevertheless, it is worthy to testify that the ancients who imposed names on things did not think madness a shameful or disgraceful thing. For they would not have attached this name to the most noble art by which the future is discerned, calling it **prophecy** <note>original: "μαντικήν" (mantike), which Socrates links to "mania" or madness</note>, but as if madness were something good when it comes by divine lot, they gave such a name to the honorable art. But now those younger people, interjecting the letter **t**, too ignorantly called it **the art of the whip** <note>original: "μαστικὴν" (mastike), a pun on seeking things through harsh human effort rather than divine inspiration</note>. Indeed, investigations of the future by sane men through birds and other omens, as proceeding from the conjecture of human intelligence, they named the augural history of the mind. Which then later people, turning the small **o** into a great one, adorned with a more honorable term. 

As much therefore as prophecy is more perfect and excellent than augural conjecture, and name than name, and work than work, so much do the ancients testify that madness proceeding from God is more noble than human prudence. And yet against the greatest diseases and labors looming over mortal nations at some time because of divine indignation for ancient offenses, a madness coming from somewhere for certain people, and predicting what was needed, found remedies, fleeing to prayers and the worship of the gods: whence having achieved expiations and propitiations, it rendered the possessor safe; and for the present time and for the future, he achieved an absolution of present evils by being rightly mad and occupied. 

The third occupation and madness is from the Muses, which, receiving a tender and untouched soul, rouses and inspires it. Whence, adorning infinite deeds of the ancients through songs and other poetry, it instructs posterity. But he who approaches the poetic gates without the madness of the Muses, trusting that by some art he will turn out to be a good poet, is himself empty and his poetry is nothing compared to that which proceeds from madness; for that which comes from prudence vanishes. I can indeed recount so many and even more noble works of divine madness. 

Therefore let us not fear this very thing, nor let any reason frighten us away, showing that the prudent and sane friend should be loved rather than the agitated one. But let him besides show if he can, and carry off the victory, that love was not granted by the gods for the utility of the lover and the beloved. We however must now show on the contrary that such madness was given by the gods to men for the greatest happiness. The demonstration will be incredible to the contentious indeed, but the opposite to the wise. But we must first know the truth about the nature of the divine and human soul, by looking at its affections and works. And let this be the principle of this demonstration. 

Every soul is immortal <margin>On the immortality of the soul.</margin>. For that which is always moved is eternal. But that which brings motion to something else, and which is itself moved from elsewhere, when it has an end of motion, must necessarily have an end of living. Only that, therefore, which moves itself, because it is never deserted by itself, never even ceases to be moved. Moreover, for other things that are moved, this is the fountain, this is the principle of moving. But there is no origin of a principle: for all things arise from a principle, but the principle itself can be born from no thing. For it would not be a principle if it were generated from elsewhere. 

And if it never arises, it never even dies: for if the principle is extinguished, it will neither be reborn from another, nor will it create another from itself, since it is necessary for all things to arise from a principle. Thus it happens that the principle of motion is from that which is moved by itself; that however can neither be born nor die. Or else all heaven would collapse and all nature must stand still, nor would it find any force by which it might be moved by a first impulse. <margin>These words are from Cicero's book Tusculans II, word for word.</margin>

Since therefore it appears that what moves itself is immortal, he who says this very thing is the substance and reason of the soul will not blush. For every body which receives motion from the outside is inanimate. But that which has this within from itself is animate, as if this were the nature of the soul. But if it is so, that there is nothing else whatever that moves itself besides the soul, then the soul is necessarily unbegotten and immortal. 

Enough has been said about the immortality of the soul. But about its **Idea** <note>The essential form or nature</note> <margin>On the idea of the soul.</margin> it must be said in this way. What it is entirely would be a matter of a purely divine and long narration; but to describe its likeness is a matter of a human and shorter one. In this very way I will speak. 

Let it be like the joined power of a winged chariot and a charioteer. The horses and charioteers of the gods are all good and from good stock, but those of others are mixed. In the first place, our leader governs a pair of horses with reins: then of the horses, one is good and beautiful and from such ancestors, the other is the contrary and from contrary ones. Wherefore our driving is necessarily hard and difficult. 

By what reason an animal is called mortal and immortal must be tried to be said. <margin>In what way it becomes an animal.</margin> Every soul has care of all that is inanimate, and traverses the whole heaven, having allotted different forms at different times. When it is perfect indeed and winged, it walks on high and governs the whole world. but that from which the wings have flowed away is carried until it has seized something solid, where having allotted a dwelling, it takes up an earthly body, appearing to move itself because of its power; and the whole is called an animal, soul and body joined together, and it is named a mortal animal. 

Immortal however is not perceived by any reason of discourse, but is imagined: since we have neither seen nor sufficiently understood God, an immortal animal indeed having a soul, and having also a body naturally joined for all time. But let these things be and be said as it pleases God. But through what cause the wings are cast away and fall from the soul, let us now say. It is such a thing as this. 

The natural power of wings is to raise what is heavy into the sublime, where the genus of the gods dwells; but of all things that are around the body, the mind is especially a participant in the divine. The divine is beautiful, wise, good, and whatever such thing can be said. By these indeed the flight of the mind is especially nourished and increased; but by the foul and evil and things contrary to these, it fails and perishes. 

The great leader in heaven, Jupiter, driving a winged chariot, goes first, adorning all things and disposing them with providence. Him follows an army of gods and spirits ordered through eleven parts. But Vesta remains alone in the house of the gods. Of the other gods, whoever are counted in the number of twelve, each presides over his own function, as each is ordered. Many and blessed spectacles therefore and circuits exist within heaven, to which the genus of the blessed gods directs itself, each performing his own duty. He follows always willing and able. For envy is far from the divine choir. 

But when they go to the banquet and feasts, they go sublime to the highest peak of heaven. The vehicles of the gods indeed, fit for the reins and equally balanced, go easily, but those of others with difficulty. For the horse that participates in depravity is weighed down, leaning toward the earth and dragging, for whichever of the charioteers the horse has not been well nourished. There already the labor and extreme contest is proposed to the soul. For those which are called immortal, when they have come to the highest...

->Phaedrus, Or, on Beauty. 307<-

...when they have reached the summit, having gone outside, they stand upon the back of heaven. There, as they stand, the revolution itself carries them around, and they behold the things that are outside of heaven. <margin>Note how Plato places some things outside of heaven.</margin> 

But the supracelestial place, neither has any of our poets praised it yet, nor will anyone ever praise it according to its dignity. It is indeed in this way. For one must dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about truth. Without color, without figure, without touch, the truly existing essence uses the mind alone as the governor of the soul for contemplation, around which the genus of true science has this place. <margin>The mind is the governor of the soul.</margin> 

Since therefore the thought of God turns itself to mind and immaculate science, every thought of the soul also, whichever is about to receive its convenient condition, having looked through time at that which is, is content and nourished and rejoices in the contemplation of truth, until the revolution brings it back in a circle to the same point. But in this circuit, it beholds justice itself, it beholds temperance, it beholds science—not that to which generation is present, nor that which is somehow different in another, such as are the ones of those things we now call "beings"—but that which is science in that which is truly being; and having seen other things in the same way which truly are, and having been nourished by these, entering again within heaven, it returns home. 

But when it has returned, the charioteer, standing the horses at the manger, throws ambrosia to them, and after that nectar to drink. And this is the life of the gods. 

But of the other souls, one, having followed God best and being similarly affected, raised the head of the charioteer into the supracelestial place, and was carried around together with the revolution itself, but was disturbed by the horses, and with difficulty beheld those things which truly are. Another indeed sometimes raised its head, sometimes lowered it; and because of the violence of the horses, it saw some things indeed, but did not see others. But all the other souls, desiring indeed the higher place, follow; but when they are unable, they are carried around submerged, trampling each other and leaning on one another, each striving to go before the other. A tumult therefore and contest and extreme sweat occurs. 

Where indeed by the fault of the charioteers many are crippled, many break many feathers, and all, involved in great labor, depart without having beheld that which truly is; but after departure they use the food of opinion. For which reason there is much effort to behold where the field of truth is. For from such a meadow the best power of the soul receives convenient nourishment, and the nature of the wings by which the soul is elevated is nourished by this. 

And the rule of the goddess Adrasteia <term>Adrasteia: a goddess of inescapable destiny or necessity</term>, that is, of the inevitable divinity, is this: that whichever soul, having accompanied God, has inspected any of the true things, it shall be unharmed until another circuit; and if it can always do this, it shall be always unhurt. But if, being unable to follow, it has not inspected, and having used some chance, and being filled with oblivion and depravity, it is weighed down, and having been weighed down it has broken its feathers and fallen to the earth, then the law prohibits this soul in its first generation from going into any brutal nature; but it commands that the one which has seen the most should go into the birth of a man who is a philosopher, or a lover of beauty, or a musician, and a lover; <margin>Nine conditions of souls.</margin> but the one which is in the second place, into a legitimate king, or a warlike and imperial man. 

Third, into a governor of a republic or a dispenser of household affairs or a businessman. Fourth, into a laborious gymnast, or one who will be occupied with medicine and the care of the body. Fifth, into those who will be prophets, and concerned with certain mysteries. Sixth, into a poet, or any other of those who are aptly occupied in imitation. Seventh, into a craftsman or **farmer** <note>original: "agricolam", corresponding to the Greek "geometricum" (one who works the earth)</note> <margin>*Gr. Geometric.</margin>. Eighth, into a sophist and a demagogue. Ninth, into a tyrant. 

In all these, whoever has led a just life afterwards obtains a better lot; but whoever has led an unjust one, a worse one. For the soul of each does not return to the same place from which it set out for ten thousand years. <margin>The soul returns to the same after ten thousand years.</margin> For it does not recover its wings before this space of time, except the soul of him who has philosophized without guile, or who together with the study of wisdom has loved boys. These indeed in the third circuit of a thousand years, if they have chosen this very life three times in succession, having thus recovered their wings, fly away departing after three thousand years. 

But the other souls, having reached the end of their first life, are judged. Having been judged, some going under the earth into the place of judgment, suffer the punishments they deserve there. Others elevated into a certain place of heaven by judgment, live in a way worthy of that life which they lived in human figure. In the thousandth year both return and take up the lot and election of a second life; each one chooses that life which it wishes. <margin>Transmutation of the human soul.</margin> Here even a human soul passes into the life of a beast, and from a beast back into a man, if only the soul had once been a man’s before. For that which has never inspected the truth will not be able to come into this figure. 

But it is necessary for a man to understand according to species, proceeding from many senses into one concept by reasoning. But this is the recollection of those things which our soul once saw when perfected with God, and looking down on those things which we now say are, and reflecting back to that which truly is above. Wherefore the thought of the philosopher alone deservedly recovers its wings. For memory always clings to those things, as much as possible, in which God in-dwelling is divine. 

By such meditations, he who uses them rightly, and is always imbued with perfect mysteries, alone truly becomes perfect. But segregated from human studies, and clinging to the divine, he is reproached by the multitude as if he were out of his mind, but he, being full of God, is hidden from the multitude. The whole speech therefore tends here, which is about the fourth madness, by which when someone, having seen some beauty here, remembering that true beauty, receives wings, and having received them strives to fly away. But when he is unable to do so, like a bird looking upward and despising lower things, he reports a crime, as if seized by madness. 

Therefore this divine alienation is the best of all alienations, and is from the best things, both for the one having it and the one participating in it: and he who is held by this madness, since he loves beautiful things, is called a lover. For as has been said, every soul of man has beheld those things which truly are, otherwise it would not have come into this animal. But to remember those things from these which are here is not easy for all, nor for those who looked there for a short time, nor for those who, descending here, were unfortunate, so that having been depraved by certain associations, they received oblivion of the sacred things they had once inspected. 

Wherefore few remain to whom enough memory survives. These indeed, when they behold here some likeness of those things which they had inspected there, are amazed, and are placed as it were outside themselves: yet they do not know what this affection is, because they do not perceive it entirely enough. Of justice indeed and temperance, and whatever other things are precious in souls, we discern no splendor in these images, but through certain obscure instruments, with difficulty and very few approaching their images, behold the genus of that which is represented. But then it was allowed to see beauty most clearly, when with that blessed choir they followed the happy vision and contemplation—we with Jupiter indeed, but others with some other of the gods—and they were initiated into mysteries which it is right to call the most blessed of all mysteries: which we performed being ourselves whole and free from evils...

->308 Book Twenty-Six<-

...as many as remained for the future, and being initiated, we were spectators of whole and simple and immovable and blessed sights in pure light, being pure and immaculate, and freed from this which we now carry about and call the body, bound to it in the manner of an oyster. These things must be credited to memory, for the sake of which, through desire for those things we once saw, we now extend the speech. 

But beauty, as we said, was both shining out as it moved with those things then, and having come here, we perceived it through our sense most clearly refulgent. For the sense of the eyes is the sharpest in us, by which we do not see wisdom. How burning a love she would excite for herself if she were seen? The same is the reason concerning other things that are lovable. But truly beauty alone has had this lot, so that it is the most perspicuous and most lovable of all. <margin>Words of Cicero from book 1 of *On Ends*.</margin> <margin>Beauty alone is most lovable of all.</margin>

He therefore who was not recently initiated into the mysteries, or rather is depraved, is not quickly excited from here to there toward beauty itself, beholding here a certain likeness which is named after it. Wherefore he does not venerate it when he beholds it, but given over to the manner of a four-footed beast, he strives to attack and lie with it for pleasure; and coming together petulantly, he neither fears nor blushes to follow pleasure against nature. 

But he who was recently expiated by the mysteries, or who once contemplated the most things, when he sees a face decorated with divine form, aptly imitating beauty itself, or some incorporeal species, first indeed he shudders, and some old fear rolls back into him: then looking at it, he worships it as a god: and unless he feared the crime of vehement insanity, he would perform sacrifices to the beloved no differently than to the statue of a god. But as he looks at it, a change, sweat, and unusual heat occupy him as if from the shudder. For when he receives the influx of beauty through the eyes, he becomes warm, by which the nature of the feathers is irrigated: but after he has become warm, the things which pertain to budding melt, which for a long time because of hardness, being compacted, prohibited the exit of the germ. 

But when the nourishment has flowed in, the germs of the feathers now swelling from the very roots strive to break out with a certain impetus through the whole species of the soul. For the whole soul was once supported by feathers. It boils therefore then all over and leaps forth: and as infants when they produce teeth are vexed by the itching and pain of the gums; so also the soul of the one producing feathers boils, and is affected by titillation and annoyance. Therefore when it beholds the beauty of the boy, and drinking the desire flowing from there is irrigated and becomes warm, it now ceases from pain and rejoices. 

But when it has been far away, and the passages have dried up where the wing strives to gush forth, being dry and constricted, they prohibit the germ of the feathers. This, closed in within together with that influx of desire and leaping back in the manner of those that swell, pricks its own passages everywhere and stings them. The whole soul therefore, wounded on all sides, is stirred by the goad and is anguished, and again, remembering beauty, it is delighted. 

But from both mixed together, it is vexed by the vehemence and novelty of such a passion, and being anxious it rages and is mad. Thus affected, because of madness it can neither sleep by night, nor stand anywhere by day, but runs about everywhere struck by the desire of seeing the beautiful. But seeing it and drinking that influx of desire, it now opens and releases what was previously hidden and concluded. 

But when it has now breathed again, it is freed from the goads and pains. In this sweetest pleasure it is so far soothed in the present that it never departs from its allurements of its own accord, nor does it value anyone more than the beloved, but gives parents, brothers, and all friends to oblivion, and is not at all moved by the dissipation of its patrimony through neglect; it also utterly despises the fatherland's customs and dignities in which it used to glory, and is ready to serve and lie wherever it is permitted, as long as it is closest to its desire. For it not only worships and venerates the beautiful one, but even finds this person to be the only doctor of its most grave diseases. 

This affection indeed, O noble youth to whom my speech is directed, men call **Love** <note>original: "Erota", corresponding to the Greek "Eros"</note>, but what the gods call him, if you hear it, you will deservedly laugh because of your youth. Certain Homeric writers report, I think, from recondite poems, two poems on love, of which one is very petulant and not very elegant. But they say: "This one mortals call **volatile** <note>original: "pterota" (winged) or volatile</note>, that is love; but the immortals call him **winged** <note>original: "erota" (Eros)</note>, because of the necessity of flying." To these things one may partly believe and partly not believe. 

Yet the cause and affection of lovers is this very thing. Whichever of the followers of Jupiter have been captured can carry the burden of that winged one more gravely and constantly. But those who worshiped Mars, and were carried around with him, being ensnared by love, if they think any injury is brought upon them by the beloved, they easily rush into slaughter, and are carried headlong both to killing themselves and their beloveds. 

And thus according to each of the gods with whom anyone led a choir, he honors and imitates the same as long as he can live, and as long as he remains uncorrupted, and in this way he leads the first generation of life here, and exhibits himself such to the beloveds and others. Each therefore chooses a love of beautiful ones from his own custom, and as if that one were a God to him, he fashions and adorns him like a statue, as one who will honor and sacrifice to him. 

The worshipers of Jupiter therefore seek for themselves to love him whose soul is Jovial <note>Meaning having the qualities of Zeus: wise, regal, and authoritative.</note>. Wherefore they consider whether he is apt by nature for philosophy and command: and when they love him having been found, they strive with all work that he may turn out to be such. And unless they have previously entered upon what they desire by their own study, they then strive altogether, and learn from wherever they can anything, and they themselves also proceed to this work. 

Investigating from themselves the nature of their god, they are at last masters of their wish, because they are compelled to raise the sharp edge of the mind to the God with a certain supreme attention: then when they touch him through memory, they are inspired by divinity, and from him they take customs and studies, as far as it is allowed for a man to become a participant in God. Since indeed they refer the causes of all these things to the beloved, they are more ardently kindled with affection. And if they draw from Jupiter, in the manner of Bacchic priests, pouring into the soul of the beloved, they render him as similar as possible to their own God. 

Whichever indeed followed Juno seek a royal one, who being found, they being similarly affected, do all the same things toward him. Furthermore, the individual worshipers of Apollo or the rest of the gods, imitating individual gods, seek a youth of a similar nature, and having obtained him and themselves imitating, and persuading and moderating the youths into the study and idea of the divinity itself, they act according to their strength. They do not use envy or illiberal malevolence toward their youths, but with all study they try to form them to the perfect likeness of both themselves and the God whom they worship. The care and end therefore of true lovers, if only they have attained what they desire, is such indeed as we have described...

<summary>In these pages, Socrates delivers his "Palinode," a recantation in which he argues that love is a form of divine madness that leads the soul to remember the true beauty it saw in the supracelestial realm. He explains the nature of the soul using the allegory of the winged chariot and describes the intense psychological and physical symptoms of falling in love as the "regrowing" of the soul's wings.</summary>
