At the beginning of this fable, we divided the soul into three parts: we established two forms of horses as two specific types, and the charioteer as the third type; let these remain for us at present. Of the horses, one is good, the other is not. We have not yet plainly stated what the virtue of the good horse or the depravity of the bad horse consists of, but now it must be said. The good horse is of an excellent habit, upright in form, well-defined in its limbs, with a high neck, slightly aquiline nostrils, a shining color, and black eyes. It is a lover of honor, a participant in temperance and modesty, and a friend of true opinion. It needs no lash, but is guided by encouragement and reason alone. 

The other horse is twisted and massive, moving recklessly; it is sprawling and confusedly put together, with a stiff and hard neck, a lowered head, a flat face, a dark color, and grey eyes shot with blood. It is moody and insolent, with shaggy and deaf ears, scarcely obeying the whip and the spurs. Therefore, when the charioteer beholds a face of love, and his whole soul is inflamed through his senses and incited by the stings of tickling and desire, the horse that is obedient to the charioteer—restrained as usual by shame—contains itself so as not to leap upon the beloved. But the other horse can be coerced neither by spurs nor lashes, but exults, and being carried away by violence, it disturbs its yoke-mate and the charioteer, dragging them toward the pleasure of Venus <note>original: "Veneris voluptatẽ" - referring to sexual pleasure</note>. 

At first, they resist, indignant that they are being dragged toward shameful and lawless things. At last, when this evil does not cease, they are driven along, yielding now and consenting to do what they are commanded. Thus they cling to the little fire and behold the flashing sight of the beloved. Looking upon it, the charioteer’s memory recalls the very nature of beauty, and sees it again standing with Temperance upon a chaste pedestal. Seeing this, he fears and falls back in reverence; at the same time, he is forced to pull back the reins so far that both horses sit back on their haunches on the ground—one willingly, because it does not struggle, but the wanton horse entirely against its will. 

Moving further away, the good horse, out of shame and wonder, wets the whole soul with the sweat of modesty. But the other horse, freed from the pain it felt from the bit and the fall, scarcely catches its breath; then, regaining its senses and moved by indignation, it rebukes the charioteer and its yoke-mate, saying they have deserted their station out of cowardice and lack of spirit. Again, forcing them to approach against their will, it scarcely yields to them when they beg for it to be deferred to a later time. When the appointed time comes, which they pretend to have forgotten, the bad horse reminds them, urging and neighing and dragging them, compelling them to approach the beloved again with the same words. After they have come near, it bends its head, extends its tail, bites the bit, and drags them most impudently. 

But the charioteer, suffering the same thing much more intensely, and as if falling back from the starting line of a race, pulls the reins back even more vehemently, and jerks back the teeth of the wicked horse, pinning its foul tongue and bloody jaws, its legs and haunches to the ground, and compels it to pay the penalty. When that depraved horse has suffered this often, it ceases its wantonness and, now humbled, obeys the foresight of the charioteer. And when it sees the beautiful one, it trembles with dread, so that it eventually happens that the lover’s soul follows the footsteps of the youth with reverence and fear. 

The youth, being observed by the lover with all devotion as if he were equal to a god—not by a lover who is pretending, but one truly so affected—and being himself naturally a friend to the one who honors him, eventually conspires in the same love. And even if he was previously deceived by the slanders of his family, classmates, or others saying it is shameful to stick to a lover, and therefore rejected the lover, as time proceeds, his age and the natural order of things lead him into the lover's company. For it was never decreed by fate that the evil should be a friend to the evil, or the good not a friend to the good. 

Therefore, when the youth has received the lover into his conversation and company, then the benevolence of that lover, having become more intimate, compels the beloved to wonder at it, noticing that the goodwill of all other relatives and friends is of no weight compared to the friend who is divinely inspired. And if the elder continues thus for a long time, clinging to him and touching him in the gymnasia and other such places, then that fountain of flowing liquid, which Jupiter called "Desire" <note>original: "cupidinem"</note> when he was captured by love for Ganymede, flows abundantly into the lover; part of it is infused into him, and part flows out when it overflows. And just as air and an echo are repelled by light and solid bodies and reflected back to where they came from, so that flow of beauty, flowing back into the beautiful youth through the eyes—by which it is accustomed to penetrate the soul—so irrigates the passages of the feathers <note>The "wings" of the soul described earlier in the Phaedrus</note> that they can now begin to sprout, and thus it fills the soul of the beloved with mutual love. 

He loves, therefore, but he is uncertain what he loves; he neither knows his own affection nor can he explain it. But just as if he had been infected by the eyes of one who has sore eyes, he does not know the cause of his present disease, nor does he notice that he beholds himself in the lover as if in a mirror. Thus, when the lover is present, his pain ceases just as the lover's does; but when the lover is absent, he desires in turn as he is desired, possessing a mutual love as a reflection of love—though he calls it not love, but friendship, and thinks it so. He desires almost as the other does, though more moderately, to see, touch, love, kiss, and trust, and as is natural, he soon does these things. 

In the lover’s company, the intemperate horse, speaking to the charioteer, demands a brief pleasure in return for many labors. The youth's horse, however, does not know what to say, but being excited and anxious, it follows the lover with mutual goodwill, congratulating its most loving friend, and in their intimacy is prepared to obey the lover’s desire to the best of its power. But the yoke-mate and the charioteer oppose this with shame and reason. Therefore, if the better parts of thought prevail according to a right institution of life and the study of philosophy, they lead a blessed and harmonious life here, being masters of themselves and modest, having subjected that part in which the vice of the soul resides and having liberated that to which probity belongs. 

At the end of this life, having recovered their wings, they fly away, having won one of the three truly Olympic contests. No greater good than this can either human temperance or divine madness bestow upon men. But if they have followed a more base life, devoid of philosophy but otherwise ambitious, perhaps in drunkenness or some other idle license, their intemperate horses invade their unwary souls, and leading them into that same kind of pleasure which is commonly judged most blessed, they compel them to pursue it, and henceforth they spend their time in the fulfillment of that desire. Yet they use this rarely, because the whole thought of the mind does not consent to this. These two are also friends, though less so than the former, both during their heat...

Therefore, for many reasons, something must be said, and we must not sleep at midday. PHAE. It must certainly be said. SOC. Therefore, what we just established must now be considered: namely, by what reasoning someone speaks and writes either rightly or not rightly. PHAE. Beyond doubt. SOC. Is it not necessary that he who is to speak rightly have a true understanding of the matter about which he speaks? PHAE. I have heard, my friend Socrates, that it is not necessary for a future orator to learn what things are truly just, but what things *seem* so to the multitude who will judge; and not what is truly good or honorable, but what appears so. For persuasion comes from these things rather than from the truth. 

SOC. The sayings of the wise are never to be despised, Phaedrus; rather, what they mean must be diligently considered. Therefore, I do not think that what you just said should be passed over. PHAE. You speak well. SOC. Let us consider it in this way. PHAE. In what way? SOC. If I were to persuade you to fight enemies using a horse, but we were both ignorant of what a horse was, yet I only knew this about you: that Phaedrus thinks a horse is that animal which, of all domestic creatures, has the largest ears. PHAE. That would be ridiculous, Socrates. 

SOC. Not yet; but suppose I earnestly tried to persuade you by a speech composed in praise of an ass, calling it a horse and affirming it to be a most excellent animal, useful at home and abroad, most prompt for war, fit for carrying baggage, and most convenient for many other things. PHAE. That would be very absurd. SOCR. Is it not better to be a ridiculous friend than a grave enemy? PHAE. So it seems. 

SOCR. When, therefore, an orator ignorant of good and evil persuades a city in a similar state—not by a speech composed in praise of the shadow of an ass as if it were a horse, but discussing evil as if it were good—and having caught the opinions of the crowd, leads them to do evil instead of good, what kind of harvest do you think an orator of this sort will reap from the seeds he has sown? PHAE. Hardly a good one. 

SOC. Have we, my good man, disparaged the art of speaking more rudely than is fitting? Perhaps the Art itself might say: "Why do you marvels of men talk such nonsense? For I compel no one who is ignorant of the truth to learn to speak; but if anyone, using my counsel, grasps the truth, let him take me. I truly affirm this: that without me, even if someone knows the facts, he will have no more power of persuasion." Would she not be right to say this? 

PHAE. I confess it, provided that the following arguments testify that it is an art. For I seem to hear some arguments asserting that it lies, and that it is not an art, but a certain practice without art. "The true art of speaking without truth," says the Spartan <note>original: "Laco" - referring to a Spartan/Laconian proverb</note>, "neither exists nor ever will exist." Bring these arguments here, Socrates, and discuss what they say and how. 

SOC. Come forth, noble creatures, and persuade Phaedrus, that handsome youth, that unless he philosophizes sufficiently, he will never be able to speak sufficiently about anything. Let Phaedrus answer Socrates’ questions. Will not rhetoric be an art that allures the soul through words, not only in courts and other public assemblies, but also in private meetings, the same regarding great things and small? For nothing is more honorable than to conduct oneself according to the right reasoning of art in great things as in small. Have you heard these things? 

PHAE. Not exactly, by Jove. This art is said and written about chiefly regarding courts and assemblies, but I have not heard it extended beyond that. SOC. Have you heard of the art of speaking which Nestor and Ulysses used at Troy? And that which Palamedes used—have you never heard of it? PHAE. By Jove, I have heard of Nestor’s speeches—unless perhaps you are pretending that Gorgias is Nestor, or Thrasymachus and Theodorus are Ulysses. 

SOC. Perhaps, but let us leave them. You, however, answer. What do adversaries do in courts? Do they not contradict one another? Or shall we say something else? PHAE. Exactly that. SOC. Is it not about the just and the unjust? PHAE. Yes. SOCR. Will not he who does this by art make the same thing appear now just, now unjust? PHAE. What is to prevent it? SOC. And in the assembly, so that the same things seem to the city now good, now the opposite? PHAE. Certainly. 

SOCR. Indeed, we have heard that the Palamedes of Elea <note>likely Zeno of Elea</note> was accustomed by his skill to make the same things seem to his listeners both similar and dissimilar, one and many, standing still and flowing. PHAE. Very much so. SOCR. Therefore, the faculty of contradiction is not only in courts and assemblies, but as it appears, it is one single art used in everything that is said. By it, one is able to make all things similar to all others, as far as possible, and to bring things to light while another hides those similarities. 

PHAE. How do you mean that? SOC. This, indeed. Does deception occur in things that differ much, or in things that differ little? PHAE. In those that differ little. SOC. But if you shift ground little by little, you will remain hidden more while coming to the opposite than if you leaped across suddenly. PHAE. Why not? SOC. Therefore, whoever is to deceive another without being deceived himself must exquisitely distinguish the similarity and dissimilarity of things. PHAE. It is necessary. 

SOCR. Can someone, then, who is ignorant of the truth of individual things, judge the small or great similarity of that which he ignores in the universe? PHAE. That is impossible. SOC. Therefore, let it be established that those who hold opinions contrary to the nature of things and are deceived have been so affected because of certain similarities. PHAE. So it happens. SOC. Can anyone, then, if he is ignorant of a thing, skillfully lead someone step by step from the truth to the opposite through certain specific similarities? Or can he avoid this error in himself? PHAE. Never. 

SOCR. Therefore, my friend, whoever ignores the truth and is led by opinions exhibits a faculty of speaking that is, as it seems, clumsy and ridiculous. PHAE. So it seems. SOC. Do you want to see in the speech of Lysias, which you have in your hands, and in our own discussion, where it is handled skillfully and where without art? PHAE. Most of all. For we are speaking plainly at present, as we lack suitable examples. 

SOCR. By some fortune, arguments have been spoken, as it seems, showing by example that a man who possesses the truth can draw his listeners even while he is joking with words. And I, Phaedrus, think the local gods are the causes of this. Perhaps even the singers, the prophets of the Muses above our heads, have inspired this gift in us. For I myself have no art of speaking. PHAE. Let it be as you say. Just show me what you mean. SOC. Come then, read the introduction of Lysias’ speech. 

PHAE. "The state of my affairs is as you have understood; and since it is so, you have heard how I think it would be to our advantage. I think I should not fail to obtain what I ask from you for the reason that I am not captured by love for you. For lovers repent of the benefits they have bestowed as soon as they cease to love." SOC. Stop. We must say where he fails and what he does without art. Must we not? PHAE. Indeed. SOC. Is it not clear to everyone that in some things we all feel the same when we speak, but in others we do not? PHAE. Although I seem to understand what you say, I desire you to say it more plainly.

SOC. When someone pronounces the name of "iron" or "silver," we all immediately understand the same thing. PHAE. Exactly. SOC. What about when he says the name of "just" or "good"? Does not one person go one way and another another? And do we not disagree with others and with our own selves? PHAE. Greatly. SOCR. Therefore, in some things we agree, and in others we disagree. PHAE. That is so. SOC. In which of these can we be more easily deceived? And in which of these does rhetoric have the most power? PHAE. It is clear: in those about which we are ambiguous. 

SOC. Therefore, he who is to practice rhetoric must first have distinguished these in order, and perceived the forms of both species: where the multitude can most be deceived by ambiguity, and where they cannot. PHAE. He would recognize a most noble form, Socrates, who could grasp that in thought. SOC. Then, I think, it is necessary that nothing be hidden from him when he comes to individual cases, but that he acutely perceive to which genus the thing he is about to speak of belongs. PHAE. Why not? 

SOC. What then about love? Shall we say it belongs to the ambiguous genus or the other? PHAE. To the ambiguous, certainly. SOCR. Do you think it would allow you to say those things about itself which you said before—namely, that it is ruinous both to the beloved and to the lover, and again that it is the greatest of all goods? PHAE. You speak cleverly. 

SOC. But say this too—for because of that divine inspiration I do not quite remember—whether I defined love at the beginning of our discussion. PHAE. By Jove, most wonderfully. SOC. O, how much more skillful you show the nymphs of Achelous and Pan the son of Mercury to be at composing speeches than Lysias the son of Cephalus. Or am I saying nothing? But did Lysias also, in the beginning of his lover's discourse, compel us to understand Love as some certain thing which he himself wanted, and then finish his whole speech by referring everything that followed to that? Do you want us to read the beginning again? 

PHAE. As you like, although what you seek is not there. SOC. Read it, so that I may hear the man himself. PHAE. "The state of my affairs is as you have understood; and since it is so, you have heard how I think it would be to our advantage. I think I should not fail to obtain what I ask from you for the reason that I am not captured by love for you. For lovers repent of the benefits they have bestowed as soon as they cease to love." 

SOC. He seems to be very far from doing what we seek. For he strives to carry through his discourse not from the beginning, but from the end, in a certain inverted and backwards manner, and he begins with those things which a lover objects to a youth after his love is extinguished. Or have I said nothing, my delightful friend Phaedrus? PHAE. It is certainly the end of the matter he is talking about, Socrates. 

SOC. What about the rest? Do not all the parts seem scattered about? Do you think that what is placed in the second position is joined there by some necessity? Or any other part of what he said? For to me, as one ignorant of everything, it seems that whatever occurred to the writer was said without any noble order. Do you have some necessity for his writing, by which he arranged those things in that sequence? PHAE. You are a good man, Socrates, if you think I can judge his writings so subtly. 

SOC. But I think you would say this: that every speech ought to be constructed like a living animal, so that it has its own body, which is neither without a head nor lacking feet, but has a middle and extremities fitting to each other and to the whole. PHAE. Why not? SOC. Consider, I pray, whether your friend’s speech is like that or otherwise. You will find it differs in no way from that epigram which some say was inscribed for Midas the Phrygian. PHAE. What is that, and of what sort? SOC. Listen:

I am a bronze maiden, placed upon the tomb of King Midas,
And while fountains flow, and the tall tree grows green,
Remaining forever on this mournful monument,
I tell the traveler that Midas is buried here.

That it makes no difference which of its parts is placed as first or last, you yourself see, I believe. PHAE. You are biting our speech, Socrates. 

SOC. Let us dismiss this one, then, so you do not get angry, although many examples can be found in it which, if inspected, would be useful for us so that we do not imitate such things. But let us descend to other speeches; they had something, I think, that should be observed by those studious of speaking. PHAE. What was that? SOC. They were indeed opposites. For one asserted that one should cling to the lover, the other to the non-lover. PHAE. And vigorously so. 

SOC. I thought you would answer with what is more true—namely, "and furiously so." But what I was seeking is this. We called Love a certain madness, did we not? PHAE. Certainly. SOC. Of madness, we establish two species: one from human diseases, the other from a divine alienation by which someone is snatched out of the customary constitution of life. PHAE. Entirely. 

SOCR. Of the divine madness, there are four parts, just as four gods preside over them. We attribute the inspiration of prophecy to Apollo, the mysteries to Dionysus, poetry to the Muses, and the madness of love to Venus and Love, the best of all. And somehow, while we were sketching the affection of love through certain images, we perhaps touched upon some truth, and perhaps also wandered elsewhere. And so, mixing a discourse that was not entirely improbable, we composed a certain fabulous hymn and, as if playing, we modestly praised my and your master, Phaedrus—Love, the guardian of beautiful boys. PHAE. This was not unpleasant for me to hear. 

SOC. Let us take this from it, then: how the discussion transitioned from rebuke to praise. PHAE. How do you mean? SOC. It seems to me that we were playing at the rest. But if someone could grasp by art the power of the two species which we just happened upon, he would have achieved a not ungrateful work. PHAE. Which species do you mean? 

SOC. That one should look upon one idea and bring together things scattered everywhere, so that by defining each thing, he makes clear whatever he has set out to teach. Just as we at present defined what Love is, whether it was done well or ill. Certainly, from this, our discussion had clarity in itself and a constant harmony with itself. PHAE. And what is the other species you mean, Socrates? 

SOC. That one should again divide into species according to the joints of the nature of things, and not break any members like an unskilled cook, but do as our previous discourses did, which took the agitation of the mind as one common species. Just as in one body, twin members are called by the same name, one right and the other left, so those discourses considered the species of mental agitation in us as one nature. 

And the first discourse, dividing the left part and then partitioning this again, did not stop until it found a certain "left-handed" love there, and quite rightly condemned it. The second discourse led us into the right-hand part of madness, where finding a Love similar in name to the first, but divine, it praised it and amplified it as the cause of our greatest goods. PHAE. You speak the most true things. SOC. Such divisions and collections, Phaedrus...

...O Phaedrus, I love these, so that I may be capable of both understanding and speaking. And if I think anyone else is able to perceive the "One and the Many" <note>original: "vnũ & multa" - a key Platonic concept of unity and diversity</note> according to the nature of things, I follow his footsteps as if those of some divinity. And whether I name those who can do this correctly or otherwise, God knows. Hitherto I call them "dialecticians." But now tell me, I pray, by what name your and Lysias's opinion should be called. Is this that art of speaking which Thrasymachus and others used, who were themselves wise in speaking and made others such, whoever wished to offer them gifts as if to kings? 

PHAE. Those men were indeed kingly, yet they were not skilled in those things about which you ask. SOC. But you seem to rightly call this form "dialectic"; but the form of rhetoric still escapes us. PHAE. How do you say that? SOC. Can there be anything beautiful which, being separate from these, is nevertheless grasped by art? It is by no means to be despised by you or me, but we must say what remains in rhetoric. PHAE. Very many things, Socrates, are handed down in the books composed on the art of speaking. 

SOC. You have reminded me opportunely. I think the "preamble" <note>original: "Procœmiũ"</note> should be called the first part of a speech. Do you call such things those outstanding ornaments of the art? PHAE. Indeed. SOC. There follows in the second place the "narrative," and the assertion of "testimonies." Third, "conjecture." Fourth, "probabilities." Also "proof" and "confirmation," as I think the excellent maker of speeches from Byzantium <note>Theodorus of Byzantium</note> introduced. PHAE. You mean the eminent Theodorus? 

SOC. Indeed. He also found out how to perform "refutation" and "double refutation" in accusation and defense. And why do we not bring the excellent Evenus of Paros into our midst? He first found "sub-declarations" and also "praises"; and there are those who say he inserted certain "reproaches" of this kind into poems for the sake of memory. For he is a wise man. But we shall let Lysias and Gorgias sleep, who preferred probabilities to truths, and by the power of speech make small things seem great, and great things in turn seem small, likewise old things new, and new things old. 

They also discovered a concise brevity of speaking, and again an infinite prolixity of words. When Prodicus once heard these things from me, he laughed and asserted that he alone had found what words that art needs. He said it needs neither few nor many, but a moderate amount. PHAE. You answered most wisely, Prodicus. SOC. And we shall by no means forget Hippias. For I think the guest from Elis <note>Hippias</note> also agrees with him. PHAE. Why not? 

SOC. What then shall we say of the musical elegance of Polus? Who introduced the "doubling of words," "notable maxims," "comparisons," and "similarities," and the use of names for the splendor of a speech, just as he learned from Licymnius. PHAE. And were not the writings of Protagoras of such a kind, Socrates? SOC. The eloquence of Protagoras, my boy, was indeed correct and proper, and there were many excellent things in his style. The orator from Chalcedon <note>Thrasymachus</note> excelled in moving the audience, and was powerful in inciting and calming anger, as if he were soothing them with an incantation, as he said; he was supreme in creating and dissolving slanders from wherever necessary. 

Concerning the end of a speech, all seem to agree, but some call this "recapitulation" <note>original: [unclear Greek term], likely "anakaleiosis" or "epanodos"</note>, and others by other names. PHAE. You mean the "end" which summarizes all the aforementioned things at the heel of the speech to bring them back to the listeners' memory? SOC. That is what I mean, and anything else you have to say about this art. PHAE. I have only small things, not worthy of mention. SOC. Let us dismiss the small things, but let us rather bring these into the light, so that we may see what power of art they have and when. 

PHAE. They have indeed the greatest power, Socrates, in the assemblies of men. SOC. They do indeed. But, blessed man, you also see whether the garment of these things seems to you, as it does to me, to be thin and coming apart at the seams. PHAE. Just show me. SOC. Tell me then: if someone should say to your friend Eryximachus, or to his father Acumenus, in this way: "I indeed know how to apply those things to the body by which it may grow warm, and I know many other such things, having learned which, I profess myself to be a doctor, and able to make anyone else a doctor"—what do you think they would answer? 

PHAE. What else than to ask whether he also knows to whom, when, and to what extent each of these should be applied? SOC. Therefore, if he should say that he in no way understands that, but that it is necessary that he who has learned from him be able to do such things, what will they answer? PHAE. Certainly that such a man is insane, who having heard something from some book of doctors and having happened upon some remedies, thinks he has become a doctor though he understands nothing of the art. 

SOC. What if someone said to Sophocles and Euripides that he knew how to make a long speech about a small matter, and conversely a very short one about a great matter, and whenever he wished to move someone to pity, or its opposite, to strike horror and threats, and other such things, and by teaching these he thought he was teaching the art of tragic poetry? PHAE. And they too, Socrates, I think, would laugh at him who thought tragedy was anything other than the composition of these parts, fitting to each other and to the whole. 

SOC. Yet they would not rebuke him rudely, I think, but would act just as a musician would who happens upon a man believing himself to be a musician because he knows how to produce the highest and lowest notes on the strings. For he would not say harshly, "You are a miserable madman," but as a musician, he would advise him more gently: "O best of men, it is absolutely necessary for one who is to be a musician to know these things. But nothing prevents one who is in your condition from understanding nothing at all of harmony. For you recognize the things necessary *before* harmony, but you are entirely ignorant of harmony itself." 

PHAE. Most correctly. SOC. So also Sophocles would say that the man he met had the things that *precede* tragedy rather than tragedy itself; and Acumenus the doctor would say he had the preliminaries of medicine, not medicine. PHAE. Exactly so. SOC. But what if the honey-tongued Adrastus, or Pericles, heard of those excellent word-crafts we were just relating—the brief sayings, the similarities, and those other things which we thought should be brought to light for consideration—do we think they would be harshly angry at those who wrote and taught such things as the "faculty of rhetoric," as we were out of our rusticity? 

Or rather, being wiser than we are, would they rebuke us thus: "O Phaedrus and Socrates, one should not be angry, but should forgive, if some people, being ignorant of dialectic, are unable to define what rhetoric is; and being thus affected, while they possess the rudimentary elements that precede the art, they boast that they have found rhetoric, and by teaching these they profess to hand down the absolute art of oratory. But they say the disciples must acquire for themselves by their own industry the ability to arrange each of these for persuasion and to weave the whole speech together, as if a teacher were not needed for these things." PHAE. Such indeed, Socrates, seems to be that art which these men teach and write about as rhetoric. And you seem to me...

# Phaedrus, Or, On Beauty. 315

<margin>On the propriety of writing.</margin>

[Text Column 1]
...rather, it is the art of persuasion that usually concerns them. They claim that one who intends to speak according to the rules of art must focus his mind on what is likely <note>original: "verisimile" - literally "truth-like" or probable</note>. Indeed, they say that sometimes facts should not be told if it is not probable that they happened; instead, in both accusation and defense, one should always introduce things that are likely. In short, the speaker should pursue what is likely, and though he says much, he may neglect the truth. For if this is observed in every speech, it supposedly demonstrates a perfect art of oratory. 

PHAE. You have related, O Socrates, exactly what those who profess the art of rhetoric say. For I remember that we touched on this briefly in our previous discussions. This seems to be a matter of great importance to those who dwell upon this art. But you have also severely criticized Tisias himself <note>Tisias was a legendary founder of Greek rhetoric, credited with developing the logic of probability</note>. 

SOC. Let Tisias then tell us this: does he define the "probable" and the "likely" as anything other than that which seems so to the common crowd? PHAE. What else could it be? 

SOC. He seems to have discovered and written this clever and artificial example: that if a weak but bold man, having beaten and robbed a strong but timid man, is brought to court, neither of them should confess the truth. Instead, the timid man should say he was not beaten by the bold man alone, while the bold man should refute this, showing they were alone, and take refuge in this argument: "How could I, being so weak, have attacked this strong man?" The other will not admit his own cowardice, but by devising some other lie, he will perhaps try to convict his adversary. And there are other such things said to be "according to the art." Is it not so, O Phaedrus? 

PHAE. Exactly so. SOC. O, how cleverly Tisias—or whoever else it may have been, by whatever other name he delights to be called—seems to have discovered this hidden art! But shall we say this to him, my friend, or not? PHAE. What is that? 

SOC. O Tisias, long before you arrived, we were affirming that this "probable" and "likely" thing arises among the crowd only through a likeness to the truth. We were asserting that these likenesses of the truth can be most aptly discovered by one who actually knows the truth. Therefore, if you have anything else to say about this art, we shall listen; if not, we shall stand by what we said a little while ago: that unless a man knows the natural dispositions of his listeners and can distinguish them, and can divide things into their specific kinds and then gather them back under a single idea <note>the process of dialectic: collection and division</note>, he will never acquire the art of speaking as far as it is possible for a human. 

This, however, can never be achieved without long study. A prudent man will not labor in this just so he can speak and act among men, but rather so that he may be able to speak and do what is pleasing to the gods to the best of his ability. For those wiser than us, O Tisias, say that a man of sound mind ought not to meditate on how to gratify his fellow slaves—except in passing—but how to obey masters who are good and of good origin. Therefore, if the circuit is long, do not wonder at it. For we must go the long way around, not for the reasons you think, but for the sake of great matters. Yet, as reason dictates, these will be most beautifully accomplished from those efforts, should anyone wish it. 

PHAE. This seems to be very beautifully said, Socrates, if only one could achieve it. SOC. But it is noble to always strive for noble things, and to endure whatever happens. PHAE. Very much so. SOC. Let this much be said regarding the art and the ignorance of speech. PHAE. Sufficiently, indeed. 

SOC. It remains for us to speak of what is fitting and unfitting in writing. PHAE. Clearly. SOC. Do you know how you can best please God by speaking or acting regarding discourses? PHAE. Not at all. Do you? SOC. I have heard some things handed down by the ancients; whether they are true, they themselves know. But if we were to find the truth ourselves, would we then care at all for human opinions? [Text Column 2] PHAE. A ridiculous question, indeed; but recount what you say you have heard. 

SOC. I heard that near Naucratis in Egypt, there was one of the ancient gods, to whom the bird they call the Ibis was sacred; the name of the spirit <note>original: "daemoni" - refers to a divine being or deity</note> himself was Theuth. He was the first to discover number and calculation, geometry and astronomy, and also the games of dice and lots, and letters. At that time, Thamus was king of all Egypt, living in the great city of the high district which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and they call the god himself Ammon. Theuth went to him and showed his arts, saying they ought to be distributed to the rest of the Egyptians. Thamus asked what the utility of each was; as Theuth explained, the king praised what seemed well said and criticized what seemed otherwise. Thamus is said to have shown Theuth many points for and against each art, which would take a long speech to recount in detail. 

But when they came to letters, Theuth said, "This discipline, O King, will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memory. For it is a medicine <note>original: "remedium" - translating the Greek 'pharmakon', which can mean medicine, charm, or poison</note> discovered for memory and wisdom." But Thamus replied, "O most ingenious Theuth, one man is fit to give birth to the works of art, but another is more ready to judge what measure of harm or profit they will bring to those who use them. And now you, the father of letters, out of benevolence, have claimed the opposite of what they can actually do. For their use will produce forgetfulness in the souls of learners through the neglect of memory; since they will rely on external marks and monuments of letters, they will not revolve the things themselves within their own minds. Therefore, you have discovered a medicine not for memory, but for reminding. You hand down to your disciples the appearance of wisdom rather than the truth. For when they have read much without the teaching of a master, they will seem to be experts in many things while they are mostly ignorant. They will be burdensome to be around, as they are not endowed with true wisdom, but merely adorned with the opinion of wisdom." 

PHAE. You easily make up stories about the Egyptians, Socrates, or about any nation you please. SOC. But, my friend, those who dwell in the temple of Dodonian Zeus say that the first prophetic words broke forth from an oak tree. To those ancients, since they were not "wise" in the way you younger people are, it was enough in their simplicity to listen to rocks and oaks, provided they told the truth. You, perhaps, think it matters who the speaker is and what country he is from. For you do not consider only this: whether what is said is true or false. 

PHAE. You have rebuked me rightly, and it seems to me that it happens with letters just as the Theban king said. SOC. Therefore, anyone who thinks he can hand down an art through writing, or receive one so handed down, as if something certain and firm will come from the letters, is quite foolish and truly ignores the prophecy of Ammon, believing that there is something more in written words than a reminder to the one who already knows the things the letters signify. PHAE. Most right. 

SOC. Writing has this grave quality, O Phaedrus, and it is truly very similar to painting. For the works of painting stand there as if they were alive; but if you ask them something, they keep a very modest silence. You might think written discourses speak as if they understood something. But if, eager to learn, you question them about what they say, they always signify the same one thing. And every discourse, once it is written, is rolled about everywhere equally among those who understand and those for whom it is not at all fitting; it does not know to whom it ought to speak and to whom not. And when it is mistreated and unworthily insulted, it always needs its father's protection. For it can neither fight back against an adversary nor help itself. PHAE. These things also seem rightly said by you. 

D ij <note>Printer's signature mark</note>

--- Page 333 ---
# 316 Book Twenty-Six.

[Text Column 1]
SOC. What then? Do we see another discourse, the brother of this one, how it is legitimate, and how much better and more powerful it is than the one that is born [written]? PHAE. What is this, and how do you say it comes to be? SOC. It is the one, I say, that is written with knowledge in the soul of the learner, which can help itself and understands to whom it should speak and before whom it should be silent. PHAE. You speak of the living and animated word of the one who knows, of which the written word may not unjustly be called a certain image <note>original: "simulacrum"</note>. 

SOC. Entirely so. But tell me this as well: Would a farmer of sound mind take the seeds he most cherishes, from which he expects fruit, and in the heat of summer sow them with great zeal and diligence in the "Gardens of Adonis" <note>small pots of quick-growing but short-lived plants used in festivals</note>, and rejoice to see them become beautiful within eight days? Or would he rather, if he ever did such a thing, do it for the sake of a festival or a game? But when acting in earnest and applying the study of agriculture, would he not sow where it is fitting, and think himself successful if his sowing reached its harvest after an interval of eight months? PHAE. Exactly so, Socrates; he would do the one as a joke, as you say, and the other in earnest. 

SOC. And shall we think the man who possesses knowledge of the just, the noble, and the good is less skilled than the farmer in sowing his own seeds? PHAE. Not at all. SOC. He will not, then, zealously sow them in black water [ink] with a pen along with discourses, since he cannot help them when they are in danger, nor can he sufficiently show the truth through them. PHAE. Certainly that is not reasonable. 

SOC. Indeed not. Instead, he will sow and write in the gardens of letters, as it seems, for the sake of play; and when he has written them as monuments and treasures against the forgetfulness of future old age, both for himself and for others who follow the same tracks, he will surely rejoice when he sees his tender fruits growing. And while other men follow other games, celebrating banquets and similar things, he instead will spend his life in the delight of these discourses, omitting those other things. PHAE. You describe a most noble game compared to the base games of others, Socrates—the play of one who can play with discourses and converse about justice and the other things you mention. 

SOC. It is so indeed, friend Phaedrus. But in my opinion, the study is much more noble when one, using the dialectic art and finding a suitable soul, plants and sows discourses with knowledge; these can help both themselves and their sower, produce fruit, and yield seeds. From these, others born in different characters can always preserve that immortal gift and make the one who possesses them as happy as is possible for a human. PHAE. That is also much more noble. 

SOC. Now then, Phaedrus, since these things are granted, we can distinguish those other matters. PHAE. Which ones? SOC. Those for the sake of which we came down to this point: so that we might examine the reproach against Lysias regarding the art of writing itself, and the discourses themselves, whether they are written with art or without it. I believe it has been sufficiently declared what is artificial and what is devoid of art. PHAE. So it appears. 

SOC. One must remember again that a person cannot master the art of speaking to the highest degree for the purpose of persuasion and teaching—as the superior reasoning has shown us—until he knows the truth of those things he says or writes, and knows how to define the whole matter, and having set the definition, knows how to divide it again according to species down to the [Text Column 2] individuals. And having contemplated the soul in this way, and having caught what is congruent to each nature, he thus disposes and adorns the discourse, accommodating various discourses to various souls—complex ones to complex and harmonious souls, and simple ones to simple souls. 

PHAE. That is exactly how it appeared. SOC. But what shall we say about that question we touched on above? Whether it is honorable or shameful to deliver and write speeches, and how this study can be rightly blamed or not? Have our previous points declared this sufficiently? PHAE. Which points? 

SOC. Namely, that if Lysias or anyone else ever wrote or writes, and shall write anything privately or publicly—such as civil constitutions—in such a way that he thinks there is in his writings a certain great stability and certainty, that should be considered shameful for the writer, whether it is said by anyone or not. For to be ignorant of what is true and what is false regarding the just and unjust, the good and the bad, even if the whole crowd praises it, can never happen without being truly most shameful. PHAE. Most shameful. 

SOC. On the contrary, consider the man who thinks that in a written discourse on any subject there is a necessary element of play and jest, and that no discourse, whether in prose or verse, is worthy of great study in its composition—like those who, without judgment or teaching, are accustomed to recite poems only for the sake of persuasion. Suppose he believes that the best of those discourses were composed for the sake of reminding those who already know, but that in those discourses spoken for the sake of teaching and learning—and truly written in the soul about justice, nobility, and goodness—there is at last clarity and perfection, and that these alone are worthy of study. Suppose he judges that discourses of this kind should be called his legitimate sons: first the one within himself, if it be found, and then whatever children and brothers of this offspring have been born as they ought in his own or in the minds of others. Such a man as this, Phaedrus, seems to be the kind we should pray to become. 

PHAE. I certainly desire and pray for it, just as you say. SOC. But these things have been said by us about the art of speaking as if in play. Therefore, you may tell Lysias that we went to the spring of the Nymphs and the Muses and heard certain discourses, which commanded us to tell Lysias and the other writers of speeches—and Homer too, and whoever else composed bare poetry or poetry adorned with song, and finally Solon and all who committed civil institutions to writing—that if they composed such things knowing the truth, and can defend their works when brought into discussion, and can show by speaking that their writings are cheap compared to their spoken words, they should be named not from the things they played with using a pen, but rather from those they seriously thought out. 

PHAE. What names do you assign, and in what way? SOC. To call someone "Wise," Phaedrus, seems to me a great thing and one that fits God alone. But to call such men as we have described "Philosophers" <note>literally "Lovers of Wisdom"</note> or something similar would be more fitting and more modest. PHAE. That certainly is not unbecoming. SOC. Therefore, will you not rightly call a poet or a writer of speeches or laws the one who has nothing in himself more excellent than what he has written, and who has composed by twisting things up and down, adding and subtracting in long-lasting emendation? PHAE. Why not? SOC.

# The Apology. 317

<margin>Cicero says this in 'The Orator' in these words.</margin>

[Text Column 1]
SOC. You should report these things to your friend. PHAE. But what will you do? For your friend must not be passed over. SOC. Who is that? PHAE. I speak of the upright Isocrates. What will you announce to him, Socrates? What shall we say he is? 

SOC. Isocrates is still a young man, Phaedrus. But I am pleased to say what I augur for him. PHAE. What then? SOC. He seems to me to be of a greater genius than to be compared with the speeches of Lysias. Moreover, he has a greater natural disposition toward virtue, so that it would be no wonder if, as he advances in age, he should excel all who have ever touched oratory in this very genre of speeches he now studies; or if, not content with these, he should desire greater things by some divine movement of the mind. For a certain philosophy is in this man's mind by nature. This message, received from these gods, I bring to my beloved Isocrates. You bring yours to your dear Lysias. 

PHAE. So it shall be. But let us depart, now that the heat has cooled somewhat. SOC. We must offer prayers to these gods before we go. PHAE. Why not? SOC. O dear Pan, and all you other gods who inhabit this place, grant that I may become beautiful within; and that whatever I have outwardly may be friendly to what is within. May I count the wise man alone to be rich. And may I have as much gold as no one else can carry or drive, except a temperate man. Is there anything else we should pray for, Phaedrus? For me, the prayer is enough. PHAE. Pray the same for me too. For all things are common among friends. SOC. Let us depart. 

# THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATES.
*
## THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO. <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator of Plato into Latin during the Renaissance; his "Arguments" or introductions reflect his Neoplatonic and Christian synthesis</note>
*
Ancient theologians were divided into three opinions. Some sacrificed only to spirits <note>original: "daemonibus"</note>, doubting that human prayers could reach celestial beings. Others worshiped celestial beings too, thinking they not only lived and understood but also saw and heard everything with their rays; thus, rites of sacrifice were offered to them, judging that although all effects proceed from the causes of things, the prayers of those living in bodies could not reach those gods who have no commerce with bodies. Finally, others venerated these gods themselves above all, judging that from the highest causes of things, all effects—including human ones—are perfectly contained by both knowledge and power. 

They called "gods" both the visible (the celestial bodies) and the invisible (the super-celestial), whom our people call angels, and the gods themselves, as it were, the closest contemplators and ministers of the Supreme God. Furthermore, they thought there was a triple providence: a Universal one in God, by which He foresees and provides all things to all; a less Universal one in the gods, by which they consult for all, yet provide not all gifts but certain ones to all; and finally, a Particular one in the spirits, by which certain things are bestowed upon certain people. 

These spirits are distributed into as many orders as there are stars in the sky, so that some are of Saturn, others of Jove, and so on. They place all these orders in fire (in a fiery way), in pure air (in an airy way), and in thick air (in a watery way). They think these "watery" ones preside over different species of living things and favor the sensual and vegetal nature everywhere. Plato says these, right from the beginning, mixed pleasure into most evils. The "airy" spirits favor the rational power, separating it from the vegetal and sensual nature. The "fiery" ones turn the discourse of reason toward the contemplation of higher things. 

In this way, the watery spirits rule the voluptuous life, the airy spirits the active life, and the fiery spirits the contemplative life. While they judge the gods to be immortal and impassive <note>not subject to suffering or change</note>, and humans to be mortal and passive, they believe all spirits are passive in their affections, with the higher and middle ones being immortal, and the lowest ones being long-lived. [Text Column 2] Moreover, they place in all of them an affection toward corporeal things: in the first, according to a certain tranquil providence; in the second, human-like but moderated; in the third, declining toward our disturbances. 

Likewise, some spirits are natural, established from the beginning; others are foreign—namely, the souls of men translated into airy bodies, caring for men with the same reason as they did before. Some spirits preside over larger regions of the earth, others over smaller cities. Some govern individual men, whom souls falling into bodies have drawn by lot according to their choice of life—thereafter the leaders, observers, and judges of the chosen life. Accordingly, some souls are accommodated to the natures of Saturnian spirits, others to Jovian, and others to different stars and spirits. The complexions of our bodies are distinguished by a similar reasoning. Animals, plants, metals, and stones are also naturally discerned according to the variety of stars and spirits, so that some are solar, others lunar, and so on. 

In these things, the Platonists think all the power of sacrifices, oracles, and divinations consists. Indeed, Plato himself, imitating the older theologians, and all the Platonists accept the history of oracles as true and confirm them with reasons. I pass over how much faith he places in these in the *Phaedrus* and in the *Timaeus*: in the *Phaedrus*, weighing human wisdom as nothing compared to that which is held by oracles and divine furies; and in the *Timaeus*, saying that a philosopher should only affirm things about divine matters insofar as they are confirmed by divine oracles. I pass over many similar things in Plato. Certainly, in the *Apology*, he begins the whole defense of his Socrates from oracles and prophecies; indeed, what is greatest, he asserts that the whole life of Socrates—the wisest and most just of men—was instituted both according to the oracle of Apollo and according to the prophecy of a certain spirit <note>Socrates' "daimonion" or divine sign</note> of his own. 

If you ask what kind of spirit Socrates had, the answer is fiery, because it raised him to the contemplation of sublime things. Also Saturnian, because it abstracted the intention of his mind from the body daily in a wonderful way. It was attributed from the beginning, not acquired. For he says it inspired him from childhood. It never provoked him to action, because it was not Martian, but often recalled him from actions, because it was Saturnian. It did not apply spurs to a man already sufficiently prone to honorable things, but held him back with a bridle when he seemed likely to be deceived in choosing paths to his end due to the fallacy of conjectures. It breathed into his mind, showed signs to his eyes, and suggested voices to his ears. But with what eyes and ears? Namely, the sight and hearing that are issued through the entire ethereal body lurking beneath this manifest body. 

Socrates could perceive through these ethereal senses, easily recalling himself from the elemental senses. He saw what was shown through these same senses, both while dreaming and while awake. Similarly, Avicenna proves that prophets see the forms of angels and hear their voices. But why do Socrates and a few like him notice their spirit? Because few are "spiritual" <note>original: "daemonici"</note> by birth or discipline; more are human, and most are bestial. Why, then, does he call it sometimes a spirit and sometimes God? Because the sublime spirit breathed upon Socrates as an interpreter and messenger of God. 

But can we call Socrates' own intellect his spirit? We certainly can. For Timaeus says God gave us the highest part of the soul as a spirit. Again, in the *Symposium*, the very love of the mind for contemplating divine beauty is named a spirit. But besides these, it is necessary that a superior substance of a spirit preside over us, because—as is proved in the *Symposium* and the *Laws*—the human race, being most distant from divine things, needs a middle nature, such as the spiritual one, as a reconciler. Nor did divine providence unjustly set closer spirits over us as shepherds (as in the *Statesman* and *Protagoras*) or as governors (as in the *Critias*). For man, placed in this darkness of ignorance and agitated by countless evils or distracted by the allurements of fortune, cannot reach the end set for him by God without God's perpetual help. 

Hence he proves that God committed us to purer spirits as rulers, who would help with prophecies, auguries, dreams, oracles, voices, sacrifices, and inspirations. He wants the familiar spirit of Socrates to be from this number, differing from the Socratic mind. For the mind often provokes Socrates, but the spirit never does. Also, the mind cannot teach unless it speaks or writes. But the spirit, as proved in the *Theages*, taught many even by silence. Furthermore, that it corrects Socrates by voice and signs signifies that this spirit is something besides the mind. If it pleases you less to call the familiar leader of a man a "spirit," then at least call it a "good angel," as our people do. After this, the *Apology* forces us to treat somewhat of oracles and their status. First, if you ask why spirits do not perform those accustomed miracles in our ages, the answer is that Christ deprived evil spirits of their empire and took away both the worship of spirits and the spiritual art from men. 

D iij <note>Printer's signature mark</note>

--- Page 335 ---
# 318 Book Twenty-Seventh.

[Text Column 1]
...both the worship of spirits and the spiritual art. If you ask again by what reasoning the influences of spirits are drawn into statues or into men, listen carefully. Something natural is drawn daily: as often as they either smear wood with oil (which could not be lit by a thin flame due to its density) or infect it with sulfur, they catch the flame in a tinder. And something divine is daily drawn through nature, when a tender fetus in the womb, affected and figured in a certain way, so draws a human soul from God through nature, just as a statue through magic receives a spirit from the world. Hence the Egyptians also called nature a magician, placing magic itself in the attraction of like things by like, or at least of convenient things by convenience. 

Daily you emit a voice; you also emit the image of your face. But your voice and image are not reflected back to you everywhere. Only parts disposed and opposed in such a way reflect the voice through an echo, and a mirroring body returns your image to you. Let those parts then be mirroring, and suddenly the whole of you, so to speak, will be in that; for there you will be seen, heard, and understood, almost like a spirit in a statue. If you consult Hermes Trismegistus, he will say that a statue duly composed of the world's own materials congruent to a certain spirit is immediately animated by that congruent spirit—either by a spirit, he says, or by an angel. Understand that it is accustomed to be breathed upon either by an impure or a pure spirit. 

You will also hear this Mercury condemning most of the ancients because, doubting either that there were deities above the heaven or that the prayers of earthly beings reached the celestial and superior ones, they fabricated statues as habitations for spirits, whom they would worship as familiar gods. He thought, indeed, that although sometimes salutary spirits were called into temples, often noxious ones descended. You have heard briefly of the drawing of spirits into the bodies of statues. Hear also briefly of their capture into the bodies of men. When, either through black bile <note>melancholy</note> or something similar, or by vice, the whole mind is turned toward imagination, it easily becomes a domicile for inferior spirits, by whose presence it may be insane and vexed in both mind and body. 

When, through philosophical purgation, the whole mind is transferred into reason, it becomes a house for middle spirits, from whom it receives wonderful reasons for human affairs more often, and sometimes even for natural things. When, through piety, the whole mind is raised up, it becomes a breathing hole for sublime spirits, or rather for angels, by whose leadership it penetrates the secrets of divine things in a wonderful way. 

I see you wish to understand which oracles Plato trusts most, whether those issued through statues or through men. Know it is only those which it is found by certain reasoning were promised not through deceptive spirits, but through truthful ones, or rather through angels. For he had received from the Egyptian mysteries that Jove cast down the more wicked spirits to the lower world, who also strive to twist men toward the depths as much as they can; and from Pherecydes of Syros, that many spirits rebelled against Jove, whose army the serpentine Ophioneus led. He judged one must guard most diligently against these evildoers. 

Socrates, led by his own reasons and individual cases, committed himself to a certain oracle and his own spirit to be led at its will. Finally, however it may be, he so instituted his life toward these things that he always preferred eternal things to temporal ones: he feared injustice more than death; for the sake of truth, piety, and charity, he did not hesitate to undergo labors, poverty, insults, injuries, beatings, and death. Truth produced false calumnies against him among men, charity produced hatred, and piety an impious accusation and death. But he weighed all these as little—indeed, as nothing—hoping to merit good things before the divine judge for his good deeds. Therefore, relying on this hope and confidence, he went willingly to the judges and did not excuse himself, but accused the judges. And like a seer, predicting what he says happens to those near death, he foretold their repentance and punishment following their false judgment, while he meanwhile migrated to the eternal judge with wonderful joy of mind and alacrity of face. 

I had decided to end this honorable argument or rather little commentary here. But two doubts delay me for a moment. First, that Socratic saying repeated both here and often elsewhere: "This one thing I know, that I know nothing." Yet he affirms many things both here and elsewhere as if knowing them. But this is similar to: "I said in my excess, every man is a liar." Thus Socrates says: "I, abstracted from the body, rapt by a spirit, illustrated by God, know indeed in the divine light this one thing—namely, that otherwise joined to the body, I know nothing in the natural light." I do not know, I say, the things themselves by the natural light through that very mode of affirmation. For such knowledge is proper to God, who comprehends both the natures themselves and the causes of natures, since He Himself made them. 

Yet I know many things through a certain mode of negation. For instance, that God is not a body, rather than what He is. Likewise, that the soul [Text Column 2] is not mortal, rather than what it is. Again, that absolute good is not this or that good, rather than what it is. And in this way Socrates both knows and teaches many things. Furthermore, this is why the spirit recalls him and does not provoke him—that is, it invites him to negation rather than affirmation. Sometimes, however, he affirms certain things, and great ones at that, as if not only rapt by a spirit but already full of God. He also affirms where he brings the testimonies of holy ancients, or cites the souls of men rising from the dead as testimony. 

A second doubt follows: why Socrates, although he never usually doubts that the soul is immortal, uses this disjunction at the end of the *Apology*: "Either no sense remains after death, or some sense remains." Answer first: he does not doubt all sense (that is, all knowledge), but our sense of our own affairs, or a sense similar to ours. This is signified by the things added in the second part of the disjunction, where he says the same as in the *Republic*: namely, that separated souls will recognize each other there in the same way they were accustomed to here. Consider this said against those who say souls migrate from bodies into other bodies. 

Then, answer more safely this way: Socrates uses this disjunction in the present case not because he thinks one should doubt what he holds most constantly through negative science and divine inspiration, but because he respects the persons of his adversaries, who, while they were studying to harm him in every way, were inflicting death on him as an undoubted evil. Socrates, therefore, counters that it is in no way evil, whether our affairs be this way or that. That which appears ambiguous about mortality is added for the sake of those who, as tyrants in the Epicurean manner, could have mocked Socrates: as if he could easily be deceived if he affirmed death was not evil only on the grounds that after this life other good things remain. Those eternal goods, though they were certain to Socrates, were in no way certain to them, nor could they be demonstrated in that short span of time—things which are demonstrated in the *Phaedo* and often elsewhere. 

But you, note the certain confidence of our Socrates, saying to his friends near the end of the *Apology*: "You ought to hope well regarding death. For nothing evil can happen to a good man, whether living or dead. For the affairs of a man who is in some way similar to God are not neglected by God." As for his shouting with his final voice to the judges, "I indeed go from here to die, you to live; which of us goes to the better is certain only to God," understand that he does not doubt what he affirmed a little before, but says that it is certain to God alone by the way of affirmation; yet it can become certain to a man through God himself and the way of negation. Add that he does not dare to affirm that he migrates with such a purged soul that his soul will immediately be returned to the celestial fatherland. 

[Text following Ficino's Argument]
In what way, O men of Athens, you have been affected by my accusers, I do not know; certainly, they affected me so that I almost forgot myself, so persuasively did they speak. Although they brought nothing true to you, so to speak. But of the many things they falsely asserted, I wondered most at this: that they warned you to beware lest you be deceived by me as if I were eloquent. For they were not at all ashamed to assert that which I would soon refute by my very work, since in your presence I appear far from eloquent; this, I say, seemed most impudent of all to me, unless perhaps they call one who speaks the truth "eloquent." For if they say that, I certainly admit that I am a rhetorician, though not after their fashion. Since these, as I say, said nothing true, but from me you will hear all true things. 

Neither indeed, by Jove, O men of Athens, will you hear from me a painted speech like theirs, adorned with elegance of words and names, or otherwise decorated; but you will hear one woven with words that occur by chance and fortune. For I trust I shall say just things, and let none of you hope I shall speak otherwise. Otherwise, it would not befit this age, O men, to enter here before you like [Page 5] little boys with words studiously formed.

...like little boys with words studiously formed. Rather, O men of Athens, I earnestly ask and beseech this: that if you hear me using the same words in my defense that I use in the forum at the tables of the money-changers (where many of you have sometimes heard me) and elsewhere, do not wonder or be annoyed. For this is how it is: I come now for the first time into a court, being more than seventy years old, from which it follows that I am truly a stranger to the kind of speaking used here. And indeed, just as if I had come to Athens as a foreigner, you would certainly forgive me if I spoke in a foreign voice and manner, according to the custom of my upbringing; so also now I pray you—and not unjustly—that you pay little attention to the form of my speaking, which may be better or worse as it happens, but consider this alone, and apply your mind to whether I speak just things or unjust. For this is the duty of a judge, but the duty of a rhetorician is to speak the truth. 

It is just, O men of Athens, that I first respond to the first accusation falsely fashioned and to the first accusers, and then to the newest. For many have already accused me falsely to you for many years, whom I fear more than the supporters of Anytus <note>Anytus was one of the three primary accusers in the trial of 399 BCE</note>, although these too are powerful in persuasion. But those are more powerful, O men, who have occupied most of you from childhood, accusing me far from the truth and persuading you: namely, that there is a certain wise man named Socrates, a searcher into things above the air and under the earth, who is accustomed to make the weaker cause the stronger by arguing. These, O men of Athens, who spread this rumor are my most powerful accusers. For those who hear these things think that searchers into such matters do not believe the gods exist. 

Indeed, such accusers are many, and they have been accusing me for a long time, and they persuaded you at that age when many of you were boys or certainly young men and very easily believed, in a deserted cause with no one defending me. And what is most alien to the reasoning of defense, it is not even possible to know or tell their names, except perhaps if one of them is a writer of comedies <note>referring to Aristophanes, who satirized Socrates in 'The Clouds'</note>. As many as have persuaded you through envy and calumny, or those who, being persuaded themselves, persuaded others—all these are infinite in number, and it is not possible to bring any of them into court or refute them. Instead, it is necessary to fight against them as if in the dark while defending myself, and to refute with no one responding. 

Consider then that my accusers have appeared in two forms, as I was saying: those who accused me recently, and those of old, whom I was just describing. And judge that I must respond first to those whom you yourselves heard first and much more often. Come then, I must respond, O men of Athens, to those crimes and try in this so brief time to remove that opinion which you, deceived by calumnies, have conceived against me for so long. I wish to refute my adversaries and succeed, if that would be better for you and me. Although I think it will be difficult. Nor is it hidden from me what kind of task this is. But as it pleases God, so let it succeed. We must obey the law and bring our defense for ourselves. 

Let us repeat then from the beginning what the accusation is, from which was born that calumny against me, relying on which Meletus brought this day against me. What then do my accusers say? As if they were present in court, let their accusation be recited, in which they swore about the calumny: "Socrates acts unjustly and too curiously inquires into things under the earth and in heaven, and makes the weaker cause the stronger. Moreover, he teaches the same to others." Such is the accusation. Indeed, you saw such things in the comedy of Aristophanes: for the persona of Socrates is carried about there, [Text Column 2] asserting that he wanders through the air, and many such trifles. Of these things, I know nothing, neither much nor little. 

Nor do I say this as if I make little of the science of such things, if anyone is wise in such matters, lest I be accused of so great a crime by Meletus; but because in truth, O men of Athens, I know none of these. I bring most of you as witnesses. I ask that you be willing to teach and explain to one another, as many of you as have ever heard me conversing—and most of you have heard me. Recount then to one another whether any of you ever heard me disputing about such things, either much or little; and from this you will finally know that the other things many spread about me are of the same kind. 

But none of these things is true. Furthermore, if you have heard from anyone that I teach men and make money from it, that is not true either. Although that seems a noble thing to me, if someone could teach men, like Gorgias of Leontini, and Prodicus of Chios, and Hippias of Elis. Each of these, O men, has that faculty by which, going to individual cities, they persuade young men (who could commend themselves for free to the discipline of their own citizens in their homeland) to follow them instead, leaving behind the discipline of others, and to pay money and be grateful besides. 

There is another wise man here, a Parian, whom I heard had come here; for it happened that I once ran into a man who has spent more money on Sophists <note>professional teachers of rhetoric and virtue who charged high fees</note> than all the rest, Callias, son of Hipponicus. I questioned him, for he has two sons: "O Callias," I said, "if your sons were colts or calves, we would have someone to hire and set over them who would make them beautiful and excellent in their respective kinds, and such a man would be someone skilled in horses or farming. But now, since your sons are humans, whom do you think of setting over them? And who has the science of this human and civil virtue? I think you have thought about this since you have sons. Is there such a person," I asked, "or not?" "There is indeed," he said. "Who is he?" I asked, "and from where? and for how much does he teach?" "Evenus," he said, "O Socrates, from Paros, and the fee is five minae." And I judged Evenus happy if he truly has this art and teaches it so diligently. For I also, if I knew such things, would be quite proud and think highly of myself. 

But certainly, O men of Athens, I do not know these things. Someone might perhaps ask: "Then what is your work, Socrates? And from where have these calumnies against you arisen? For unless you were doing something outside the custom of others, so great a rumor would never have been raised about you. For from where comes such frequent talk, unless you had done something different from the rest? Tell us then what it is, lest we judge anything rashly about you." This seems a just question to me; and I shall try to show you what it is that brought me both this name and this calumny. But hear now, and though I fear perhaps some of you...
