->I might seem to be joking, but nevertheless, believe that I am going to tell you the absolute truth. Indeed, O men of Athens, I have gained this name for no other reason than a certain kind of wisdom. But what kind of wisdom? Perhaps that which is human wisdom. For in this matter, I truly seem to be wise. But those whom I was mentioning a little while ago perhaps have some wisdom greater than human, or I do not know what to call it—for I am certainly not endowed with it. But if anyone says that I possess it, he lies, and says this to slander me. But let it not be troublesome to you, O men of Athens, nor be disturbed if I seem to say something great to you; for I will not speak from myself alone, but I will bring to you a witness worthy of trust. Truly, if there is any wisdom in me, and of what sort it might be, I will offer the Delphic god <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Delphi, the most prestigious religious site in ancient Greece</note> as a witness for you. You certainly know Chærephon. He was a familiar friend to me from my youth, and a friend to the Athenian people, and he fled with you and returned with you at the same time. You clearly know what kind of man Chærephon was, and how vehement he was in whatever thing he turned himself to. Once, therefore, having set out for Delphi, he dared to test this prophecy. Do not take it poorly, O men, what I am about to say in your presence. He asked if there was anyone wiser than me. The Pythia <note>The high priestess of Apollo who delivered the oracles</note> responded that no one was wiser. Indeed, his brother here will testify to these things for you, for Chærephon himself has passed away. Consider, then, for what reason I say these things. For I must open to you from where this slander against me has arisen. Truly, when I had heard these things, I thought to myself: "What does the God say? Or what does he mean? For I am conscious within myself that I am wise neither in great things nor in small. What then does he mean when he asserts that I am the wisest? Surely the God is not to be believed to lie, for that is not lawful for God." And so for a long time, I searched in ambiguity for what the oracle intended. At last, with difficulty after long wandering, I found a way of this sort: I approached one of those who seem to be wise, hoping that, if anywhere, the prophecy could be refuted in him, and it could be shown to the oracle that I was not the one it preferred, but that he was to be preferred in wisdom. While I was examining him—his name it is not necessary to reveal, but he was one of those involved in public affairs—while, I say, I was examining him and discussing with him, O men of Athens, I was affected in this way: that man seemed to be wise both to many others and especially to himself, but he was not. Then I tried to show him that he thought himself wise, but was not so at all. Consequently, he became hostile toward me, and many who were present took it poorly. And so, having returned to myself, I reasoned thus: "I am indeed wiser than this man. For it appears that neither of us knows anything beautiful and good. But there is this difference: that while he knows nothing, he thinks he knows something; I, however, just as I do not know, so I do not think I know. I seem, therefore, in this tiny matter to be wiser than this man, because what I do not know, I do not even think I know." After this, I went to another of those who are held to be wiser still, and in considering him I judged entirely the same, and I made him and many others hostile toward me. Henceforth, I proceeded to others in like manner, not unaware of how much hatred I was exciting against myself, and therefore I proceeded not without some pain and fear. Nevertheless, it seemed necessary to me to put the divine oracle before all things, and to go everywhere to investigate what the oracle meant, and for its sake to approach everyone who seemed to know something. And by the Dog <note>original: "per Canem" — a signature oath of Socrates</note>, O men of Athens—for it is necessary to tell you the truth—something of this sort happened to me while inquiring into these things from the divine oracle: that those who were most approved by the opinion of men, I found to be almost the most ignorant of all; while those who were held to be inferior, they conducted themselves more reasonably as far as prudence is concerned. It is worthwhile to relate to you my errors and labors, which I sustained so that the oracle might be so proven that it could not thereafter be refuted. After the men involved in public affairs, I turned to the poets, the authors of tragedies and dithyrambs and other poems, thinking that here I would clearly be caught as more ignorant than they. Therefore, taking their books in which they seemed to have labored the most, I inquired into their meanings so that I might learn something from them. I am ashamed, O men, to reveal the truth here to you, yet it must be said. Almost everyone else present, so to speak, could speak better about the things about which they themselves had written poems. I discovered soon, therefore, regarding the poets, that they do not do by wisdom what they do, but by a certain nature and from a divine agitation of the mind, just like those who prophesy when inspired by divine frenzy. For these too say many and excellent things, but they understand nothing of what they say. The poets seem to me to have been affected in the same way, and at the same time, I noticed that because of their poetry, they judged themselves to be the wisest of all men in other things in which they were not wise. I left, therefore, from there with the same opinion that I had of the political men. At last, however, I turned to the craftsmen, being well conscious of how I knew nothing there, so to speak, but I knew that they knew many and beautiful things, and in this I was not deceived. For they knew what I myself did not know, and in this part they were wiser than me. But, O men of Athens, I found the skilled craftsmen in the same error as the poets. For because they performed their own craft properly, each one of them thought himself to be the wisest in other things as well, even the greatest matters. And yet this error obscured even that wisdom which was in them. Therefore, I asked myself on behalf of the oracle whether I would choose to be as I am, neither knowing what they know nor ignoring my own ignorance, or having both as they have them; I answered clearly to myself and to the oracle that it is better for me to be as I am. Because of this inquiry of mine, O men of Athens, many very difficult and heavy enmities have arisen against me, from which many slanders have followed. The name of "wise" has arisen for me because those present think that I know the things in which I refute others. But it seems, O men of Athens, that in truth only God is wise, and in this oracle he means this: that human wisdom is to be valued at little or nothing. But that he names Socrates as wise, he does so because he uses my name as an example, as if he said: "He, O men, is wisest who, like Socrates, knows in truth that his wisdom is to be valued at nothing." These things I continue to seek everywhere, obeying the God, and I do not cease to investigate whether I consider anyone—either citizen or foreigner—to be wise. And if ever he does not seem so to me, then aiding and obeying the God, I demonstrate that he is not wise. And because of occupations of this sort, almost no leisure is left to me either for public...<-

But lest they seem to lack material, they flee to those things which are commonly and easily thrown against those who philosophize: <margin>Thus we translate from the *Apology*.</margin> namely, that he meddles with things in the air and under the earth, that he does not believe in the gods, and that he persuades the worse cause to be the better. Since, therefore, they are ambitious and vehement and many, and as if by arrangement and with the study of persistent persuasion they are accusing me, they have filled your ears, both for a long time and recently, with slanders diligently fashioned against me. From among these, Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon have risen against me: Meletus indeed hostile to me on account of the poets, Anytus on account of the craftsmen and the governors of the republic, and finally Lycon for the sake of the rhetoricians. These things, O men of Athens, I speak truly to you, and I do not hide or subtract anything great or small, although I know well enough that in saying these things I will be troublesome to them. This very argument is proof to you that I speak the truth, and that this is the slander that has arisen against me, and its causes are of this sort. And whether you investigate this now or in the future, you will find it to be so. Therefore, to those things which the first accusers brought forward, let this be my sufficient defense before you. Next, I will attempt to respond to the good Meletus—and as he says, the lover of his country—and to the remaining accusers. And again, as if they were other accusers, let us bring forward the accusation taken up under oath for the sake of avoiding slander. It is roughly of this sort: "Socrates acts unjustly, depraving the youth, and not believing in the Gods whom the city believes in, but in certain other new divine things." Such indeed is the accusation; let us discuss each part of this accusation. He charges me with depraving the youth and in this doing injury; but I, O men of Athens, say on the contrary that Meletus does injury, because he deliberately mocks and jokes, so easily dragging men into court, pretending that he is concerned with serious things and has a care for those matters for which he never had a care. I will attempt to show you also that this is so. "Hey Meletus, answer me: do you not care most of all that the youth should turn out as well as possible?" "I do indeed." "Come then, tell these men now who makes the young better. For it is certain that you know, since it is a care to you. You have already caught me, as you say, as their corrupter; you have accused me before these men and dragged me to court. Therefore, come and tell them who makes them better, and show who he is. Why, O Meletus, are you silent? Do you see...<-

...that you have nothing to say? And yet does that not seem shameful to you, and a sufficient argument for what I say: that you have never cared about these things? But speak now, good man. Who makes them good?" "The laws." "But I am not asking that, O best of men, but what person, who first knows this very thing, namely the laws, by which they might become better." "These judges, O Socrates." "What then, O Meletus? Can these men educate the youth and make them good?" "Most certainly." "All of them? Or can some indeed, while others cannot?" "All of them." "By Juno, you speak well, and of a great abundance of those who are useful to the youth. But what about these who are listening? Do they also make them better, or not?" "They also." "What of the senators?" "The senators as well." "But then, O Meletus, we must take care lest the public speakers perhaps corrupt the adolescents. Or do they also all similarly make them better?" "They also." "All the Athenians, therefore, as it seems, make them honorable and good except me alone. I alone corrupt them. Do you say so?" "I say so certainly, and indeed vehemently." "You condemn me indeed with a great misfortune. Answer me further: do you think the same about horses—that all men make horses good, while there is only one who corrupts them? Or is it entirely the contrary: that there is one, or certainly very few skilled in riding, who make horses better, while the vast majority of people, if they are involved with horses and use them, deprave them? Is it not so, Meletus, both regarding horses and all other living creatures? Entirely so, whether you and Anytus deny it or confess it. For the youth would have gained a very great happiness if only one person could pervert them, while all others were beneficial. But, O Meletus, you demonstrate sufficiently that you have never had any care for the youth, and you clearly declare your negligence, and that you have never meditated on those things of which you accuse me. Furthermore, I beseech you by Jove, O Meletus, answer us: is it better for us to live among good citizens or among bad ones? Answer, friend. For I ask you nothing difficult: do not the bad always do something bad to those with whom they associate? And the good do good?" "Without a doubt." "Is there anyone who wishes to receive harm rather than benefit from those whom he uses familiarly? Answer, O good man. For the law commands you to answer. Is there anyone who wishes to suffer damage?" "No one." "Come then, you call me here into court as a corrupter of the youth. Do you say I do it willingly or unwillingly?" "I say willingly." "Is it so, Meletus, that you, being so much younger, are so much wiser than I, an older man, that you clearly know that the bad harm their associates and the good benefit them? While I have fallen into such madness that I do not even know that if I make one of my associates worse, I risk suffering some evil from him, and that I would willingly bring such a great evil upon myself, as you say? I do not believe you in this, Meletus. I think also that no one else will grant it to you. But either I do not deprave the youth, or if I do deprave them, I do it unwillingly. Therefore, you lie in either case. But if I corrupt them unwillingly, the law does not command that involuntary offenses be dragged into court, but that one be privately taught and admonished. For it is certain that if I learn, I will no longer do that which I did through ignorance. You, however, did not wish to correct me familiarly, but you drag me into court, where the law commands those to be dragged who need punishment rather than instruction. Already, then, it is manifest from these things, O men of Athens, what I was just...<-

--- Page 339 ---
322                                **Book Twenty-Seventh.**

->...saying: that this Meletus never had any care, great or small, for educating the youth. Nevertheless, tell us in what way you assert, O Meletus, that I pervert the youth. Is it clearly as you wrote in the accusation: because I teach them not to believe in the Gods whom the city believes in, but in certain other new divine things? Do you not affirm that I corrupt the youth in teaching these things?" "I assert this entirely and vehemently." "By those very Gods, O Meletus, of whom our speech now concerns, speak more clearly both to me and to these men. For I indeed do not yet plainly understand whether you say that I teach the youth to believe that there are some Gods—and if that is so, I believe there are Gods, and I am not entirely without God, nor is that in which I act unjustly, although I teach that they are not those whom the city holds, but others. Whether, I say, this is what you charge me with, that I clearly introduce other Gods? Or do you say that I entirely deny the Gods, and teach others to deny them as well?" "I assert indeed that you entirely deny the Gods." "O admirable Meletus, why do you say such things? Do I not even believe the sun or the moon to be Gods, as other men do?" "By Jove, no, O judges! For he says the sun is a stone and the moon is earth." "You seem to yourself to be accusing Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras was a philosopher who was also charged with impiety for his scientific theories about the cosmos</note>, O friend Meletus, and thus you think so little of these men, thinking them ignorant of letters, as if they did not know that the books of Anaxagoras of Clazomenae are full of opinions of this sort. Shall the youth learn these things from me? When they could buy them from the orchestra <note>The space in the theater where books were sometimes sold or performances held</note> for a drachma at most, and then laugh at Socrates if he pretended they were his own, especially since they are so absurd. But by God, O Meletus, do you think in truth that I believe in no God?" "In none, by Jove. Not even one." "What you say is incredible, Meletus, and indeed, as it seems to me, even to yourself. For it appears to me, O men of Athens, that this man is excessively insolent and petulant, and that he has written this accusation with a certain insolence and petulance and youthful rashness. For he seems to compose a kind of riddle, testing whether Socrates, the wise man, will catch him mocking and joking pleasantly and proposing contradictions to himself, or whether Socrates, along with his audience, will be deceived. For he seems to me to contradict himself in the very words of the accusation, as if he said: 'Socrates acts against the laws by not believing in Gods, but by believing in Gods.' Which things seem to be the trifles of one joking and wittily mocking. Notice, O men, in what way Meletus seems to me to say these things. You, answer us, O Meletus. But you, as I asked from the beginning, do not be annoyed if I speak in my accustomed manner. Is there anyone, O Meletus, who thinks there are human things, but not humans? Let him answer me, O men, and let him not make a disturbance now in these things, now in those. Is there anyone who does not think horses exist, but things pertaining to horses? Or that flute-players do not exist, but things pertaining to the flute? There is no one, O best of men. I answer for you to both yourself and these others, since you yourself do not wish to answer. But at least answer this, which pertains more to the matter: Is there anyone who thinks there are works of spirits <note>original: "dæmonum" — referring to *daimones*, intermediary beings</note>, but no spirits?" "No one." "How slowly and with difficulty you answered when compelled by these men! Do you not therefore confess that I both believe in and teach works of spirits, whether they be new or ancient? For entirely, as you confess, I assert spiritual things, and indeed I will swear to this in my response. But if I believe in spiritual things, it is entirely necessary that I also believe that spirits exist. Is it not so?" "Certainly so." "I take you as confessing, since you do not wish to answer. But spirits—do we not think they are either Gods or the children of Gods? Do you confess this or not?" "Entirely." "Is it not true that if I think spirits exist, as you yourself grant, and spirits are certain Gods, then what I just said happens? That you propose a riddle and play and talk nonsense by saying that I do not believe in Gods, yet again believe in Gods, since I hold that spirits exist? Again, if spirits are the children of Gods, certain bastards indeed, either from nymphs or from some others as is said, who among men would think children of Gods exist, but deny the Gods? For that would be just as absurd as if someone should think the offspring of horses or donkeys—mules—exist, but did not think horses and donkeys exist. But, O Meletus, you seem without a doubt to have instituted this accusation either to test our wits, or because you had nothing of a true crime to accuse me of. By what reason could you persuade anyone having even the smallest amount of mind that it is not the part of the same man to believe in spiritual and divine things, and yet the part of the same man to believe in neither spirits, nor Gods, nor heroes? It can be shown by no certain reason to be otherwise. Furthermore, O men of Athens, that I have not committed a crime as Meletus accuses, I think does not require a great defense, but I judge that what has been said is sufficient. But what I said from the beginning—that much ill-will has been stirred up against me among many—that is indeed most true, and this is what will destroy me, if indeed I am destroyed: not Meletus, nor Anytus, but the slander and envy of many. Which things indeed have destroyed many other good men until now, and as I think, will destroy them. For it is nothing grave or strange if it does not cease to be harmful in my case. But perhaps someone will ask me: 'Are you not ashamed, Socrates, to practice such a thing from which you immediately come into the danger of dying?' Indeed, I will give this just response to this objection. You do not speak rightly, O man, if you think that a great account of either life or death ought to be held by a man in whom there is even some small utility; and not rather this alone to be considered, whenever he does anything: whether he acts justly or unjustly, and whether his works are those of a good man or a bad one. Otherwise, by this reasoning of yours, all the demigods who fell at Troy would have to be despised, and others, and especially the son of Thetis himself <note>Achilles</note>: who so despised the danger of death lest he should undergo shameful infamy, that when his mother the Goddess predicted to him as he was hastening to kill Hector—in these words, I think: <margin>Iliad book 18</margin> 'O son, if you kill Hector for the sake of avenging your friend Patroclus killed by Hector, you yourself will perish.' For she said, 'Immediately after Hector an unhappy fate awaits you.' When, I say, he had heard these things from her, he so despised the danger and death that he much more feared a shameful life with his friends' injuries unavenged than death; and immediately he responded that he preferred to die for the just vengeance of his friend than to live as a laughingstock lingering by the ships, a useless burden on the earth. Who then would say that he had a care for the danger of death? And indeed the matter stands thus, O men of Athens. In whatever place a person has stationed himself, judging it to be the best, or is ordered to stand by a superior, in that place, as it seems to me, he ought to remain and undergo danger, fearing neither death nor anything else more than disgrace. Indeed, O men of Athens, I would err gravely if, when I obeyed those commanders whom you placed over me at Potidaea, and at Amphipolis, and at Delium—for then where they ordered me to stand, I stood...<-

--- Page 340 ---
**Apology.**                                       **323**

->...there I stood like anyone else, and I underwent the risk of death. But where God has placed me and wished me to remain, as I have thought and judged—namely, that I should live philosophizing and searching into myself and others—if there I should desert my post because of the fear of death or any other thing, that, I say, would be a very grave offense. And then indeed someone would justly drag me into court as one not believing in the Gods, clearly not obeying the oracle, and fearing death, and thinking myself to be wise when I am not wise at all. For to fear death, O men, is nothing other than to seem wise when one is not wise. Since it is to seem to know what one does not know. For no one knows whether death might be the greatest of all goods for a man; yet they fear it as if they knew it to be the greatest of evils. To whom then should it be a doubt that this very ignorance is most to be blamed, through which someone thinks he knows what he does not know? I, however, O men, perhaps differ in this from many men: and if in any matter I should say that I am wiser than someone, it would be in this, that since I do not sufficiently know the things that are among those below <note>In the underworld or after death</note>, I likewise recognize that I do not know them. But to do injuries and not to obey a superior, whether God or man, I know to be an evil and shameful thing. Therefore, those things which I do not know, whether they be good, I will never fear and flee more than those things which I know to be evil. Wherefore, if you should now acquit me, not believing Anytus, who said that either I should not have been called into court from the beginning, or having been called, it was necessary that I be condemned—for if I were acquitted by you, he said your sons, following the discipline of Socrates, would all be entirely corrupted. If, I say, you should say to this: 'O Socrates, we do not believe Anytus, and we acquit you by our votes, but on this condition: that you never hereafter engage in this inquiry and philosophy; and if you are caught doing so, you shall die.' If, therefore, as I said, you wished to dismiss me on these conditions, I would certainly respond to you: O men of Athens, I indeed esteem and love you, yet I prefer to obey God rather than you. And as long as I shall breathe and my strength suffices, I will not cease to philosophize, exhorting and teaching whoever I shall meet, as I am accustomed, in this way: 'How is it, O best of men, that since you are a citizen of Athens, the greatest city and most excellent in wisdom and power, you are not ashamed to put all your effort into that by which you may have as much money and glory and honor as possible; but as for prudence and truth and the best habit of the soul in you, you neither think of nor care for them?' And if any of you should contend with me, asserting that he does care for them, I will not immediately let him go nor depart, but I will question, examine, and refute him. And if he does not seem to me to possess virtue, though he professes it, I will reproach him because he values at nothing those things which are of the greatest price, while he makes the vilest things of the most value. This duty I will perform for the younger and the older, whomever I meet, and again for the foreigner and the citizen, but more for the citizens, by as much as you are closer to me in race. For God himself commands this. And I think that which also ought not to be hidden from you: that no greater good has yet happened to you in this city than this ministry of mine, which I exhibit obeying God. For I go about doing nothing else than persuading the younger and the older among you that a care should be held neither for bodies nor for money nor for any other things at all more vehemently than for the soul, so that it may be as good as possible, teaching that virtue does not come from money, but money and all other goods for men, both privately and publicly, come from virtue. If, therefore, by teaching these things I pervert the youth, they would certainly be pernicious. But if anyone says that I teach other things than these, he says nothing. For the sake of these things, O men of Athens, I profess indeed, whether you believe Anytus or not, whether you dismiss me or not, I profess that I will do nothing else, not even if I must die many times. Do not be disturbed, O men of Athens. But as I asked from the beginning, listen to me with an equal mind; for it will be, as I think, useful to you if you hear the things I am about to say. Indeed, I am going to say some other things to you which, upon hearing, you might perhaps be provoked to a clamor in the present; but do not do this. Know that if you kill me, being such as I was just telling you, you will not harm me more than yourselves. Me indeed neither Meletus nor Anytus will ever harm. For it could not be. Since it is not lawful, as I think, for a better man to be harmed by a worse. He can kill, however, or expel, or affect with some disgrace. And indeed he and some other might think these to be great evils; but I do not think so, but rather that it is a much worse thing to do what he now does, attempting to kill a man unjustly. Wherefore, O men of Athens, it is not so much my need now to meditate on a defense for myself, as someone might think, as for you, lest in condemning me you commit some offense against that gift which God has granted to you. For if you kill me, you will not easily find another such man—truly, even if perhaps it is a ridiculous thing to say—given to your city by God, as if to a certain large and noble horse, but sluggish because of its very mass, and needing to be stirred up by spurs <note>Socrates' famous "gadfly" metaphor—a fly that bites a horse to keep it moving</note>: such a one God seems to have added me to the city, I who, exciting and advising and reproaching each one, do not cease all day long to be present with you everywhere. You will not easily find another such, O men of Athens. Therefore, if you believe me, you will acquit me by your votes. But if perhaps, in the manner of those sleeping, being annoyed that you are being awakened, you should rashly and lightly kill me as Anytus wishes, you will sleep for all the remaining time, unless perhaps God, looking out for you, should send someone else. That I am such a one as to seem to have been granted to the city by God, you can notice from this. It certainly does not seem human that I should have entirely neglected all my own affairs and have persevered for so many years now in this negligence of domestic property, always intent on your good, while advising each one like a father or an older brother to have a care for virtue. And if I had received any reward for my duty, that would have some human reason. Now, however, as you also plainly see, although these accusers of mine have most impudently piled up all other things against me, in this one thing they have by no means dared with their usual impudence to try and bring forward witnesses who might prove that I ever exacted or asked for any reward for these things. For of this matter I bring to you, as I think, a sufficient witness: my poverty. But perhaps it might seem absurd to someone that I consult these things privately for each person, going around too anxiously, but publicly in assemblies I have not dared to give this same advice to the city. The cause of this is that which you have often and everywhere heard me saying: that a certain divine and spiritual voice <note>original: "dæmonicū vocem" — Socrates' *daimonion*, a divine sign or voice that warned him away from certain actions</note> is present with me. Which indeed Meletus mocked in the accusation. But for me, from my very childhood, this has been present: a certain voice, which as often as it happens, prohibits me from doing what I was about to do, but never provokes me. <margin>Cicero, On Divination, book 1.</margin> This, I say, is what resists me from turning to public affairs. And very...<-

# Apology. 325

...begging you in that way to be acquitted. Why then do I do none of these things? Not out of any stubbornness, nor out of contempt for you, O men of Athens: whether I am bold in the face of death or not is another matter. However, for the sake of my reputation, yours, and that of the entire city, I do not think it appropriate for me to do these things at my age, and with the name <note>Socrates refers here to his reputation for wisdom</note> I have acquired, whether that reputation be true or false. For it is already a common opinion among men that Socrates excels above many others in some particular way. If, therefore, those among you who are thought to excel in wisdom, or courage, or any other virtue, were to act as I have often seen some act when they were being judged, it would be a great shame. These men, though thought to be of some value, nevertheless behaved in a wonderful manner during their trial to stir up pity, as if they were about to suffer something terrible if they should depart from this life—as if they would be immortal if only you did not kill them. Indeed, these men seem to me to bring disgrace upon the city, because some foreigner might think that those Athenians who excel in virtue, and who are held in higher regard for offices and other honors, are no different from women. These things, O men of Athens, you who appear to have some authority ought not to do; nor, if we wished to do them, should you permit it. Instead, you should show that you will much more readily condemn the man who introduces such pathetic displays and makes the city look ridiculous, than the man who waits for the verdict in silence.

Furthermore, O men of Athens, in addition to what has been said about the city's reputation, it does not seem just to me to beg a judge, nor to be acquitted by begging, but rather to teach and persuade. For a judge does not sit for this purpose: to grant justice as a favor, but to judge according to the laws. He has promised by oath that he will not grant favors to whomever he pleases, but will judge according to the laws. Therefore, it is not right for us to accustom you to swear falsely, nor for you to become accustomed to it. For in that way, neither of us would be observing our religious duty. Do not, therefore, O men of Athens, demand that I do such things before you which I consider neither honorable, nor just, nor holy—especially, by Jove <note>original: "per Iovem"; Socrates refers to Zeus</note>, when I am accused of impiety against God by this man Meletus. Truly, if I were to proceed to persuade you and bend your will by begging when you have sworn an oath, I would certainly be teaching you to believe that there are no gods, and in truth, while preparing a defense for myself, I would meanwhile be accusing myself of not believing in the gods at all. But far from it being so: for I believe that there are gods, O men of Athens, more than any of my accusers do, and I entrust to you and to God to judge concerning me, in whatever way will be most beneficial for both me and you.

As to the fact that I am not distressed, O men of Athens, that I have been condemned by you, many other things contribute to this, and especially this: that it did not happen contrary to my expectation. Truly, I much more admire the number of the votes on both sides. For I did not think I would be away from acquittal by such a small number of votes. Now, however, as it appears, if only three votes had fallen otherwise, I would have escaped. Certainly, I seem to have escaped Meletus now; and not only escaped, but it is clear to everyone that if Anytus and Lycon had not risen to accuse me, he would have had to pay a thousand <term>drachmas</term> <note>A significant fine imposed on accusers who failed to receive at least one-fifth of the jury's votes</note>, since he would not have received a fifth part of the votes.

This man, then, proposes the penalty of death for me. So be it. But I, O men of Athens, what counter-penalty should I propose for myself? Is it not clearly that which I am worthy of? What then? What am I worthy to suffer or pay, because I did not remain silent about what I learned, but neglected those things which the crowd values highly: profit, household affairs, military commands, powers, and other magistracies? Furthermore, I avoided the conspiracies and factions that occurred in the republic, thinking myself in truth born for more equitable duties than to think my safety depended on these things. To these things, I say, I did not apply myself, for in them I would have been of no use either to you or to myself. Instead, I devoted myself to this one duty alone: that by applying myself privately to each one of you, I might bring the greatest benefit (as I truly believe), persuading each of you not to care for his own things before he cares for himself—that he may become as good and as prudent as possible—nor to care for the affairs of the city before caring for the city itself, and that the care for all other things should be held in the same way.

What then, being such a man, am I worthy to receive from you? Something good, surely, O men of Athens, if you are to value me truly according to my merit, and indeed such a good as would befit me. What, then, befits a poor man who is a benefactor, for whom it is helpful to be free from other occupations so that he may encourage you toward virtue? There is surely no other reward, O men of Athens, that more befits such a man than to be fed in the <term>Prytaneum</term> <note>The seat of government in Athens where distinguished citizens and Olympic victors were fed at public expense</note> at public expense; and much more so than if one of you had won at Olympia with a horse, or a two-horse chariot, or a four-horse chariot. For that man indeed makes you *seem* happy, but I make you *be* so. Furthermore, he does not lack nourishment, but I do. Therefore, if I must be valued according to merit and justice, I judge myself worthy of this: namely, that food be provided for me publicly in the Prytaneum.

Perhaps in saying these things to you, I seem as arrogant as I did before when I was detesting pity and supplications. But it is not so, O men of Athens; it is rather in this way. For I am persuaded that I do not voluntarily do injury to anyone. I do not persuade you of this because we have had only a short time to talk. Truly, if there were such a law among you as there is among others, that where death is the penalty, the trial is discussed not for one day but for many, I would have persuaded you, I think. But now it was not easy to dissolve great slanders in so short a time. Since, therefore, I am persuaded that I should do injury to no one, I am far from doing injury to myself and saying that I am worthy of evil, and judging that I myself deserve something of this kind. What then? Should I, fearing lest I undergo that which Meletus thinks I am worthy of—which I say I do not know whether it be good or evil—should I, to avoid this, choose something of those things which I clearly know to be evil, and judge myself worthy of that? Should it be chains? And why should I live my life in prison, always serving the <term>Eleven</term> <note>The board of officials in charge of the prison and executions</note>? Should I pay a fine, and remain in chains until it is paid? But that is the same as what I said above, since I lack the means to pay. Should it perhaps be exile? For perhaps I will be judged worthy of this. Yet a great desire for life would possess me, O men of Athens, if I were so foolish as to think that if you, my fellow citizens, could not bear my way of life and my speeches—but my conversation and speech were so heavy and hateful to you that you have now decided to free yourselves from it—others would easily tolerate me. Far from it, O men of Athens. A fine life it would be for me at this age, living in exile, wandering from one city to another, and living in continual rejection. For I know clearly that wherever I go, the young men will listen to me just as they do here; and if I drive them away, they themselves will in turn persuade their elders to drive me away. If I do not drive them away, their fathers and relatives will drive me out on their account.

Perhaps someone will say: "Can you not, O Socrates, live in silence and quiet in exile?" But this is the most difficult thing of all to persuade some of you. For if I should answer that this would be to disobey God, and that therefore I cannot keep quiet, you will not believe me, thinking I am speaking with irony. Or if I say that it is the greatest good to happen to a man—namely, to speak every day about virtue and about the other things you hear me talking about daily, and thus to examine myself and others, and that the unexamined life is not worth living—you will believe me even less in these things. These things are as I say, O men of Athens, but it is not easy for people to be persuaded. And at the same time, I have never been accustomed to think myself worthy of evil. If I had money, I would have proposed a fine as large as I could pay, for it would not have harmed me to lose it. But now I have none, unless perhaps you wish to value the fine at as much as I am able to pay. I can pay perhaps a <term>mina</term> <note>A unit of currency; roughly 100 drachmas</note> of silver. Therefore, I value the fine at that much. But Plato here, O men of Athens, and Crito, and Critobulus, and Apollodorus, bid me to offer thirty minas. They themselves will be the guarantors for such a sum. Therefore, I value it at that much; and these men will be sufficient guarantors of this silver for you.

--- Page 343 ---
# 326 Book Twenty-Second.

For the sake of a short time, O men of Athens, you will acquire a bad reputation and provide material for those wishing to criticize the city, because you have killed Socrates, a wise man. For those who wish to criticize you will say that I am wise, even if I am not. If you had waited only a short time, death would have come to me on its own. Look at my age, how far it is from life and how near to death. I do not say these things to all of you, but only to those who condemned me to death. I say these things also to them: Perhaps you think, O men of Athens, that I have fallen in court because of a lack of such words by which I might have persuaded you, if I had thought I should do and say everything to be acquitted by you. Far from it. Certainly, I was condemned for a lack, not of words, but of audacity and impudence, and because I was unwilling to say to you such things as would have been most pleasant for you to hear—namely, hearing me weeping and lamenting, and doing and saying many other things, as I said, unworthy of me, such as you are accustomed to hear from others. But I did not think from the beginning that I should do anything illiberal <note>meaning "unworthy of a free man"</note> to avoid danger, nor do I now repent of having used this method of defense. I would much rather die having defended myself in such a way, than live by the opposite way. For neither in court nor in war should I or anyone else do everything possible to avoid death. In battles, it is often clear that death could be avoided if one were to throw down his arms and turn as a suppliant to his pursuers. There are other devices in every danger by which one might escape death, if he were not ashamed to do or say anything at all. But consider, O men of Athens: it is not difficult to escape death, but it is much more difficult to escape wickedness. For it runs faster than death. And now I, being slow because of old age, have been caught by the slower one; but my accusers, being vigorous and swift, have been caught by that which is swifter: wickedness. And now I go away, condemned by you to undergo death; they go away condemned by Truth herself, liable for wickedness and injustice. I acquiesce to my penalty, and so do they. These things perhaps had to be so, and I think they are handled appropriately.

After this, I desire to prophesy to you who condemned me. For I have now reached that point where men are accustomed to prophesy: namely, when they are near death. I predict to you, O men of Athens, that if you kill me, a punishment will come to you immediately after my death, and by Jove, much harder than the one you have inflicted on me. For now you have done this thinking to free yourselves from being compelled to give an account of your lives to any critic. But the opposite will happen to you. For I think there will be more people to rebuke you, whom I was holding back though you did not perceive it; and they will be all the more troublesome the younger they are, and therefore you will take it more heavily. Truly, if you think that by killing men you can free yourselves from criticism, you are very much mistaken. For this is not a liberation that is either effective or honorable. But that other way is both easiest and best: not to suppress others, but to prepare oneself to be as good as possible. Having prophesied these things to you who condemned me, I make an end.

But to you who acquitted me, I would gladly speak about this matter that has happened, as long as the magistrates are busy and I have not yet gone to the place where I must die. But, O men, stay with me for this time. For nothing prevents us from talking with one another (while it is permitted). Indeed, I want to show you, as friends, what has just happened to me, and what it signifies for my mind. To me, O judges—for I can rightly call you judges—a marvelous thing has happened. <margin>These things Cicero [discusses] in his book *On Divination*, Book 1.</margin> For that prophetic voice of the <term>daemon</term> <note>Socrates' "divine sign" or inner voice that warned him against certain actions</note> has always been accustomed to present itself to me very frequently in the past, opposing me even in very small matters if I were about to do something not quite right. But now, these things you see have happened to me, which someone might surely think and judge to be the extreme of evils. Yet the sign of God did not oppose me when I left my house this morning, nor when I ascended this platform to speak, nor in any part of my speech while I was talking, although at other times it frequently used to stop me in the middle of a sentence. But now in this matter, it has nowhere opposed me in either action or speech. I will reveal to you what I think the cause of this is. It appears to me that what has happened is a good thing. And we do not judge correctly in any way, those of us who think death is an evil. Of this thing, this is a great proof to me: that the sign would have opposed me as it usually does, unless I were about to do something good.

We can think of it in this way: there is much hope that it is a good. For death must be one of two things: either death entirely removes all sensation, or as it is said, one migrates by death from these places to some other place. <margin>Almost all these things are described from Cicero's *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 1.</margin> Therefore, if sensations are extinguished and death is like a sleep which sometimes, even without the visions of dreams, brings the most peaceful rest: good gods, what a gain it is to die! I think indeed, if someone had to compare that night which he passed with such quiet that he saw not even a dream, with the other nights and days of his whole life, and say how many nights and days in his life he had spent better and more sweetly: I think, I say, that not only a private person, but not even a Great King could count many. If, therefore, death is such a thing, I say it is a gain. For the whole of time seems to be no more than a single night. But if the things said are true, that death is a migration to those shores which those who have departed from life inhabit, then it is a much more blessed thing for you, when you have escaped from those who wish to be considered among the number of judges, to come to those who are truly called judges—Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and as many other demigods as lived justly—can this journey seem mediocre to you? Or to be allowed to speak with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer, at what price would you value that? Indeed, I would be willing to die often, if it were possible, so that I might find those things I am talking about.

--- Page 344 ---
# Crito, Or, Concerning What Must Be Done. 327

Truly, that habitation and society will be wonderfully pleasing to me, since I will be together with Palamedes, and Ajax the son of Telamon, and others of the ancients whoever died by being circumvented by a [false] judgment; among whom it would not be unpleasant, I think, to compare my misfortunes with theirs. Besides, the greatest thing would be to spend time there searching and examining each person as I did here, to see which of them is wise, and who, though he is not, yet thinks himself to be wise. Furthermore, at what price should it be valued, O judges, to test the prudence of the great king who led the greatest forces to Troy, and Ulysses, Sisyphus, and many other men and women whom one could mention, with whom to speak and live in examination would be an altogether inestimable happiness? For those who live there do not die anymore, and they are both more blessed than we are in other matters, and additionally in this, that for the remaining time they remain immortal, if indeed the things said are true.

You too, O judges who acquitted me, should not fear death. Think of this one thing as true: that nothing evil can happen to a good man, whether living or dead, and his affairs are never neglected by the immortal gods. Nor has this happened to me by chance; rather it is clear to me that to die now and be freed from labors was better for me. And for this reason, that divine sign did not stop me. Nor indeed do I hold a grudge against those by whom I was accused, or those by whom I was condemned, although they did not accuse and condemn me with this mind, but because they believed they were harming me. For this, they are certainly to be blamed. (But now having returned to those same men, I speak to them thus). Yet I pray you for this much, O men: that when my sons have grown up, if they are as troublesome to you as I was, you punish them in the same way, especially if they seem to you to care more for money or anything else than for virtue; and if they wish to seem to be of some value when they are worth nothing, rebuke them as I rebuked you, because they do not apply themselves to what they should, and they think they are something when they are of no value. If you do this, I and my sons will have suffered justly from you. But it is time to depart hence, I to die, you to live your lives. Which of us has the better part, the immortal gods know; I think no human being knows.

->CRITO, OR, CONCERNING WHAT MUST BE DONE.<-

->*<-

->MARSILIO FICINO’S ARGUMENT.<-

->*<-

Just as in the *Apology*, the arrangement of the *Crito* is so orderly and plain that it does not need an argument <note>In this context, an "argument" means a formal summary or structural analysis</note>. Notice first, however: just as Socrates prophesied while awake in the *Apology*, so in the *Crito* he prophesies while sleeping, so that you may know that God is always present to a wise and pious man, both waking and sleeping. From all these things, collect the confirmation of evangelical doctrine: the approval of martyrdom, the exemplar of justice, incomparable fortitude, contempt for mortal things, the desire for eternal things, and finally the foundation of religion. Why should I mention that the opinion of the crowd is to be despised, and only the opinion of the wise man—indeed, Truth itself—is to be honored? Again, that not merely living, but living *well* is to be sought? Likewise, that one must never do evil to enemies, nor avenge injuries? Again, that the danger of death and destruction must be undergone rather than sinning? Why should I report his singular observance of the laws and his inestimable love for his country? Which he undoubtedly prefers even to parents and to life, for this reason (as he himself says), so that when he has set out for the other life, he may be able to give a fair account of his past life to the eternal judge, and not be compelled to fear the laws that rule there, which are the sisters of human laws. Finally, he concludes that the reasons favoring justice ring so loudly in the ears of his mind that he cannot hear anything else, and whoever tries to dissuade him will labor in vain. He adds that one must go only by that way where God—that is, the reason divinely infused—leads.

->SOCRATES, CRITO.<-

SOCRATES: Why have you come at this hour, O Crito? Is it not still very early? CRITO: Very early indeed. SOCRATES: How early, then? CRITO: Just before dawn. SOCRATES: I wonder how the prison guard was willing to listen to you. CRITO: He is already familiar to me, O Socrates, because I come here often. Besides, he has received some benefit from me. SOCRATES: Have you just arrived? Or some time ago? CRITO: Quite some time ago. SOCRATES: Why then did you not wake me immediately, but sat by in silence? CRITO: By Jove, Socrates, I would never have woken you. For I myself would not wish to remain in such wakefulness and sorrow for so long. But I have been admiring you for some time, as I watch how sweetly you sleep. And I deliberately did not wake you, so that you might pass the time as peacefully as possible. Indeed, both often before and truly throughout your whole past life, I have judged you blessed because of your character, but especially in your present calamity, because you bear it so easily and calmly. SOCRATES: But it would be very absurd, O Crito, if someone of such an age should take imminent death poorly. CRITO: Nevertheless, O Socrates, others just as old are overwhelmed by similar calamities; yet their age does not so help them that they do not bear their present fortune heavily and with distress. SOCRATES: That is so. But why have you come so early? CRITO: I bring bitter news, O Socrates—not to you, as it seems to me, but to me rather and to all your friends, both bitter and heavy. Which I indeed, if anything else, would bear heavily and with distress, as I think. SOCRATES: What is this news? Has the ship from Delos returned? After which I must die. CRITO: It has not yet returned, but it seems it will return today, from what some reporting from Sunium say, who left it there. It is clear, therefore, from these reports, that it will arrive today, and therefore it will be necessary for you tomorrow, O Socrates, to depart from life. SOCRATES: Good fortune, O Crito. If it so pleases the gods, let it be so. Yet I do not think it will return today. CRITO: From where do you conjecture that? SOCRATES: I will tell you. For on the day after, or on the very day the ship returns, I must die. CRITO: So they say, who have power over this matter. SOCRATES: Therefore I do not think it will arrive *on this day*, but on the next. <gloss>Greek: by chance.</gloss> I take this conjecture from a certain dream which appeared to me a little while ago this very night; and you seem opportunely not to have disturbed my sleep. CRITO: But what was the dream? SOCRATES: There seemed to me a certain woman approaching, beautiful and pleasing in appearance, wearing white garments, calling me and saying: "O Socrates, on the third day from here you will reach fertile Phthia." <margin>Iliad 9.</margin> <note>A quote from the Iliad; Achilles says this when threatening to leave Troy. Here, Phthia represents the "home" of the soul</note> CRITO: What an absurd dream, Socrates! SOCRATES: Yet it is manifest, as it seems to me, O Crito. CRITO: Manifest indeed. But, O blessed Socrates, even now listen to me and save yourself. For to me, if you die, <gloss>namely</gloss> not just one calamity looms: but besides being deprived of you, such a friend as I will never find another, I will appear to many who do not know either of us well, when I could have saved you if I had been willing to spend money, to have neglected it. And yet, what reputation could be more shameful than to appear to value money more than friends? For they will not be able to be persua...

# Crito, Or, Concerning What Must Be Done. 329

...but is that evil, and where does it lead, and into what part of the one who is disobedient? CRITO: Into the body, obviously, for this it corrupts. SOCRATES: You speak rightly. And is it not the same regarding other things, O Crito, if we run through them all? Concerning things just and unjust, shameful and honorable, good and evil, about which our consultation is presently concerned: whether we ought to follow and fear the opinion of the many, or rather of the one who understands, whom it befits us to both respect and fear more than all others combined. Unless we obey him, we will be harmed and corrupted in that which is made better by justice, but is accustomed to be corrupted by injustice. Or is that nothing? CRITO: I think it is so, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Come then, if we corrupt that which is made better by what is healthy but corrupted by what is unhealthy, by not following the judgments of the experts, will we have to live after it is destroyed? That is the body, is it not? CRITO: That very thing. SOCRATES: Then should we live with a vicious and corrupted body? CRITO: In no way. SOCRATES: Or perhaps should we live with that part of us corrupted which is harmed by injustice but helped by justice? Or do we think that part of us, whatever it is, which is concerned with justice and injustice, is viler than the body? CRITO: In no way. SOCRATES: But more precious? CRITO: Much more. SOCRATES: Therefore, O best of men, we must not care much at all what the many say of us, but what that one says who understands the just and the unjust, and Truth herself. Therefore, first of all, you did not lead correctly in saying that the common opinion concerning just and honorable and good things (and their opposites) ought to be valued. But someone might say, "Can the crowd kill us? This is certainly manifest." CRITO: That can certainly be said, O Socrates. SOCRATES: You speak the truth. But, O admirable one, this reasoning we have run through seems to be similar to the previous one. And consider this again, whether it remains for us or not: namely, that we should not value living highly, but living *well*. CRITO: It remains. SOCRATES: And does this also remain: that to live well, honorably, and justly is the same thing? CRITO: It remains. SOCRATES: Therefore, from these things we have confessed, we must consider this: whether it is just for me to try to go out from here when the Athenians do not dismiss me, or unjust; and if it appears just, let us try; if not, let us omit it. As for the considerations you bring concerning the spending of money, reputation, and the education of children: we must be careful, O Crito, lest these be the considerations in truth of those "many" who easily kill people and, if they could, would bring them back to life, and that without any reason. But for us, since reason so demands, nothing else is to be attended to than what we were just saying: whether we will be doing justly by paying money and giving thanks to those who lead me out from here; whether, I say, we will be doing justly in this—we who are led out, and they who lead—or rather, if it appears that we are acting iniquitously, then we must not even think of it, but it befits us to submissively undergo death and any other punishment rather than do anything iniquitously. CRITO: You seem to speak rightly, Socrates. Consider, however, what we should do. SOCRATES: Let us consider together, O good man. And if in any part you can refute what I am saying, refute it and I will agree. If not, I pray you, O blessed man, cease now to repeat the same words so many times: that I ought to go away from here against the will of the Athenians. Indeed, I value highly having been persuaded by you to do these things, but not against your will. Attend, therefore, to whether the beginning of our consideration seems to you to be stated appropriately, and try to answer what is asked in the way you most think it should be answered. CRITO: I will try. SOCRATES: Do we say that in no way should one voluntarily do injury, or perhaps in some way injury should be done, and in another way not at all? Or is it in no way either good or honorable to do injury, as we often confessed in the past? Which indeed was recently confirmed. Or have all those past agreements of ours vanished in these few days, and has it escaped us for so long—we who are such old men, O Crito, and who have disputed so studiously among ourselves—that we differ in no way from children? Or rather does the matter stand exactly as we were saying for so long: whether the multitude affirms it or denies it, and whether we are compelled to undergo things more heavy than the present ones or lighter? Nevertheless, do we confess that to do injury is altogether evil and shameful for the one who does it, or not? CRITO: We certainly confess it. SOCRATES: Therefore, in no way should injury be done? CRITO: In no way. SOCRATES: Nor, if you have suffered injury, should you take revenge, as the crowd thinks, since in no way should injury be done? CRITO: So it seems. SOCRATES: What then? Is it right to do evil to anyone, O Crito, or not? CRITO: Certainly not, O Socrates. SOCRATES: What about this: is it right for one who suffers evil to return evil in turn to the one who inflicted it? Would that be just, as the crowd says, or unjust? CRITO: Unjust. SOCRATES: Namely, to inflict evil on men does not differ from doing injury. CRITO: You speak truly. SOCRATES: Therefore, it is neither right to take revenge nor to do evil to any man, whatever you yourself have suffered from others. And see, O Crito, lest while you concede these things, you are agreeing with us against your own opinion. For I know that to very few does it appear so, or will it appear so. But for those to whom it appears so, and those to whom it appears otherwise, there is no common deliberation; rather, it is necessary for them, when they look at each other's counsels back and forth, to despise one another. Consider, therefore, diligently, whether this opinion is common to you and me, and whether you feel with me. And let us deliberate starting from this principle: that it is never right either to do injury, or to take revenge for injury, or for one who has been affected by evil to return evil to him who inflicted it. Or do you depart from us here, not consenting to this principle? To me indeed it seemed so for a long time, and it seems so now. If it appears otherwise to you, speak and teach me. But if you remain in the previous conclusions, hear now what follows. CRITO: I agree indeed and I remain: speak then. SOCRATES: I say then next, or rather I ask: whether those things which someone confesses to another to be just, he ought to do, or to deceive? CRITO: To do them. SOCRATES: From these things, now consider this. If we go away from here without the consent of the city, will we be doing evil to some people, and indeed to those whom it is least fitting, or not? And will we be remaining in those things which we agreed were unjust, or the opposite? CRITO: I cannot answer these things, O Socrates. For I do not understand. SOCRATES: But consider it in this way, as if we were wanting to either flee from here or however this must be called, and the Laws and the Republic of this city were to come and, standing by, were to ask thus: "Tell us, O Socrates, what do you intend to do? Do you not understand that by this thing you are attempting, you are plotting destruction for us, the Laws, and the entire city, as far as it lies in you? Or do you think any city can stand any longer and not be subverted, in which public judgments have no force, but are made void and rescinded by private men?" What then will we say to these things, O Crito, and other things of this kind? For someone could bring many things to this effect, especially an orator declaiming on behalf of a law thus violated, which...

...indeed orders that sentences passed by public judgment be held valid. Or shall we answer them that the city brought an injury upon us by not judging correctly? Thus, or otherwise? CRITO: Thus, by Jove, O Socrates. SOCRATES: But indeed the Laws themselves would answer thus: "O Socrates, was this not agreed between us and you: that you must stand by the judgments which the city has passed?" And if we were to marvel at the Laws speaking thus, perhaps they would say: "Do not marvel, Socrates, at what we have just said; rather answer, since you are accustomed to both asking and answering. Tell us, what do you accuse in us and the city that you strive to dissolve us? First, did we not give you birth? And through us your father took your mother and brought you forth? Tell us, therefore, do you find fault with those of us which are the laws concerning marriage, and are you angry with them in some part as being less than right?" "I find no fault," I would say. "But [what about] those laws which provide for the education and instruction of children, in which you yourself were instructed? Did these laws, established for this duty, not dispose correctly when they ordered your father to instruct you in music and gymnastics?" I would concede they disposed correctly. "Well then, since you were born through us, and nurtured and educated: first of all, can you deny that you are our offspring and servant, both yourself and your ancestors? Then, since that is so, do you think justice is on an equal footing for you and for us, and that whatever we attempt to do to you, you judge it just to return the same in turn to us? Whereas you do not have justice on an equal footing with your father, or with a master if you had one, so that you could return what you suffered from them—neither if they provoked you with a quarrel could you quarrel back, nor if they struck you could you strike in turn, nor attempt other such things against them—will it be permitted to you against your country and the laws? To such an extent that if we, judging it to be just, wish to kill you, you in turn would strive to destroy us, the Laws, and your country, to the best of your strength, and say that by doing these things you act justly, you who profess to truly have a care for virtue? Or are you so wise that it has escaped you that your country is to be preferred to your father and mother and all your ancestors; and that the country is something more venerable and holy and in a higher place, and that the country is to be placed in higher regard both among the gods and among men of sound mind, and that it ought to be cherished more and obeyed, and when it behaves more harshly and severely, one must be more submissive to it than to a father; and if it should order anything, either one must persuade it otherwise or do it, and suffer most patiently whatever it orders to be suffered; and whether it commands you to be struck, or to be cast into chains, or if it sends you into battle to receive wounds and undergo death, it must be obeyed altogether. For justice so dictates, and one must neither hesitate, nor flee, nor desert the rank. But both in war, and in court, and absolutely everywhere, those things must be done which the republic and country command; or certainly, one must persuade and show it wherein [what it commands] is just. To use force is a sin, whether against a mother or against a father, and most of all against one's country." What shall we say to these things, Crito? Do the laws speak the truth, or not? CRITO: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: Furthermore, the laws will perhaps say: "Consider, O Socrates, whether we speak the truth, that you are attempting unjust things against us. For we, who brought you forth, nurtured you, and instructed you, have made you and all other citizens participants in all good things as far as we were able; nevertheless, we permit any of the Athenians, once he has recognized and approved the customs and laws of this city and the form of governing the Republic, if we do not please him, to take his things and go wherever he pleases. None of us laws impedes or prohibits if any of you, whom we and the city do not please, wishes to depart for some colony, or transfer his habitation elsewhere, from doing so according to his will and taking his things with him. But whoever of you remains, after he has seen how we exercise judgments and rule the city in all other matters, we assert that he has now agreed with us in fact that he will do whatever we command. And we say that he who does not obey does injury in three ways: both because he does not obey us who are his parents, and because he does not obey his nurturers, and because having promised to obey us, he neither obeys nor strives to persuade us if we seem to be doing anything not quite right. And although we propose our precepts freely, and do not command rigidly but permit one of two things—either to be persuaded by words or to fulfill the commands—he does neither of these. We judge that you, O Socrates, will be liable to these crimes if you do what you intend; and indeed no less than the other Athenians, but most of all. And if I were to ask the reason why I am liable more than the others, they would perhaps justly rebuke me, saying that I most of all the Athenians have consented to the laws of the city. For they would say thus: 'Great are the arguments for us, O Socrates, that we and the city pleased you. For you would never have inhabited it most of all the Athenians unless it had pleased you wonderfully. Therefore, you never went out from the city for the sake of a spectacle, except once to the Isthmus, nor anywhere else except on military service, nor did you ever make another journey as others are accustomed to do, nor did a desire for another city or for knowing other laws take you; but we and our city are sufficient for you—to such a degree did you vehemently approve us and agree that you would live by our customs—then, to omit other things, you even procreated children in it, inasmuch as it pleased you. Furthermore, it was permitted to you in the trial itself to be punished with exile if you had wished, and what you now attempt against the city's will, you could have done then with its consent. But you then boasted in words, as if you would not take it heavily if it were necessary for you to die. Indeed you chose death itself, as you said, rather than exile. Now, however, you neither blush at those words of yours, nor do you respect us, the Laws, but you plot destruction for us. You are doing what the worst slave would do, attempting to take flight against the pacts and conventions in which you agreed with us to provide yourself to be governed by our institutions. First, therefore, answer us this very thing: whether we speak truly by affirming that you agreed not in words, but in fact, to be governed by our customs. Or are these things not true?'" What shall we say to these things, Crito? Shall we not confess? CRITO: It is necessary, O Socrates. SOCRATES: "What then," (the laws will say) "are you doing other than transgressing the conventions and pacts made with us? Which you were neither coerced to enter into with us, nor deceived, nor compelled to deliberate in a short time, but for seventy years; in which time it was permitted to you to go away, if we had not pleased you and the conventions had not seemed just to you. But you preferred neither Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> nor Crete to us—which cities you yourself frequently preach are governed correctly—nor any other city, either Greek or Barbarian. Indeed, you have gone on journeys from here more rarely than the lame and the blind and others who are maimed. To such a degree did the city please you more than the other Athenians, and we [laws] as well..."

namely the laws. For to whom can a city be pleasing, whose laws do not please? But now you do not abide by those things in which for a long time we and you were in agreement. If you believe us, you will not commit the error of letting everyone laugh at you as you leave the city. Consider again: if you transgress these things and fail in any of them, what good will it do for you or your kin? For it is almost certain that your relatives will be in danger of being driven into exile themselves, deprived of their citizenship, and stripped of their inheritance. As for you, if you betake yourself to some neighboring city, such as Thebes or Megara (for both are well-governed), you will arrive there as an enemy of their political order; all those who care for their homeland will look at you with sideways eyes <note>original: "limis... oculis," meaning with suspicion or disapproval</note>, regarding you as a corrupter of the laws. You will also confirm the opinion the judges have of you, so that they will seem to have passed their sentence against you rightly. For whoever is a corrupter of the laws will most certainly seem to be a corrupter of the young and the ignorant. What then? Will you avoid those cities that are well-governed and the most decent of men? If you do that, will your life be worth living? Or will you perhaps unwisely mingle with them, and feel no shame in discussing among them the same things you were accustomed to discuss among us? That is, that virtue and justice, and laws and institutions, are to be valued above all else? Do you not think such an act by Socrates would appear unseemly and hardly honorable? It must certainly be thought so. But perhaps, declining these cities, you will go off to Thessaly to Crito’s hosts. For life there is quite disorderly and intemperate. Perhaps they will listen to you gladly as you tell the story of how ridiculously you fled from prison: how you threw some bundle over yourself, or put on a leather cloak, or wrapped yourself in other things, as those who take flight are accustomed to do, changing your habit and appearance. But do you think no one will say that an old man, with so little time left to live, as is likely, dared to live in such wretched poverty out of a greedy desire for life, having transgressed the greatest laws? Perhaps indeed—if you do not offend anyone. Otherwise, O Socrates, you will hear many things unworthy of you. You will live as one beholden to all men and serving them. What will you do in Thessaly? Will you frequent banquets, as if you had traveled to Thessaly for a dinner party? Where will those famous dialogues of ours concerning justice and the other virtues be? But surely you wish to live for the sake of your children, to nurture and educate them. Will you then lead them into Thessaly to nurture and educate them there, making them strangers to their own land, so they might carry off this additional "benefit" from you? Or will you not do that, but rather, if they are left here while you are alive, will they be better nourished and educated by your relatives in your absence? Will they care for them if you go to Thessaly, but not care for them if you pass into the other life? Surely, if there is any help in those who call themselves your relatives, one must believe they will care for them. But, O Socrates, trust in us who nurtured you; do not value your children, or your life, or anything else more than justice, so that when you have migrated into the other life, you may be able to give an account of all these things to those who preside there. Truly, if you do these things by transgressing the laws, it will happen neither better, nor more justly, nor more holily for you or your own, nor will it profit you there. Rather, you depart having suffered an injury—if you do depart—not from us laws, but from men. But if you flee so basely, returning injuries and evils, transgressing the agreements and promises made with us, and harming those whom you least ought to harm—namely yourself, your friends, your country, and us—then we shall be angry with you while you live, and in the other life, the laws there (which are our sisters) will by no means receive you kindly, knowing that you attempted to destroy us to the best of your power. Therefore, take care that Crito does not persuade you to do otherwise than we say." These things indeed, O sweet friend Crito, I seem to hear, just as the Corybantes <note>Ecstatic priests of the goddess Cybele who, in their religious frenzy, believed they heard the constant sound of flutes.</note> think they hear flutes. And the sound of these words echoes so loudly within me that I am unable to hear anything else. You see how it seems to me at present; if you attempt to say anything to the contrary, you will labor in vain. Nevertheless, if you are confident you will achieve something, speak.

CRITO: I have nothing to say, O Socrates.

SOCRATES: Then let it be, Crito, and let us proceed this way, since God himself leads us this way.

->**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.**<-

OUR book on religion proves a thing sufficiently known in itself: that the life of Christ is the idea of all virtue. Moreover, the eighth book of our letters demonstrates that the life of Socrates is a certain image, or at least a shadow, of the Christian life; and it confirms the Old Testament through Plato, and the New through Socrates. <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a Renaissance philosopher who sought to harmonize Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> As for this Socratic similarity, if anyone doubts it, let him read Xenophon and Plato, and the others who wrote down the words and deeds of Socrates, especially Plato's *Gorgias*, *Apology*, *Crito*, and *Phaedo*. We shall therefore run through the argument of this *Phaedo* with a swift pace, or rather a leap. For we seem to have explained its mysteries sufficiently in [our] theology. One thing we shall advise first: let no one wonder that Socrates, among the arguments pertaining to the immortality of the soul, omitted here that one in which he places sole confidence in the *Phaedrus* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue *Phaedrus*, which argues the soul is a self-moving principle.</note>—namely, that the Soul is the principle of motion, from which it follows that it is moved by itself and perpetually, and lives forever. This was done by Socrates because that kind of reasoning is common not only to our souls, but also to celestial and demonic souls. In the *Phaedo*, however, arguments more specific to us are required. But let us now come to the briefest arrangement of the dialogue. First, it must be observed how wonderfully Socrates consoles his friends, who greeted him in prison on the very day he was to drink the poison, as if they were the ones to console him. Second, how religiously he observes even the precepts of dreams, as if they were certain oracles; and how exceptionally cautious he is in this, lest he fail in even the slightest way regarding divine commands. Third, it must be committed to memory that men are under the constant guardianship of God, and it is not permitted to depart from here unless God wills it. Fourth, one should carefully note what he intends when he says he hopes that in death he will go to good men and other good gods; but he affirms more strongly that he will go to good gods than to good men. First, when he speaks of other and very good gods, he understands that besides the souls of the spheres <note>In the medieval and Renaissance cosmos, the planets were moved by "spheres" which were thought to have guiding intelligences or souls.</note> there are angelic minds higher than the spheres. He hopes that our souls may one day be admitted into familiarity with these; yet he does not dare to assert it, because it seems to many wise men that the soul's goal would be sufficiently met if it were eventually received into the company of celestial souls. Indeed, his doubt properly falls upon that part which calls them "good men." For he does not dare to affirm that the souls of men are good in the same sense as he spoke of the gods. After this, intending to console himself and his friends at the same time under the persona of a philosopher, he says:
