<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the "Crito" into Marsilio Ficino’s detailed commentary and summary of the "Phaedo," Plato's famous dialogue on the immortality of the soul and the final hours of Socrates.</meta>

332 Book Twenty-Nine.

He says: Since the whole endeavor of one practicing philosophy is a kind of separation from the body, and is perfected daily through that very separation, he should not only not fear the separation from the body that occurs through death, but should expect it with the best hope and joy. Soon, he shows in two ways how the philosopher separates the soul from the body. First, indeed, from disturbances through the purification of moral discipline; then from the senses and from imagination itself through the focus of contemplation. Wise physicians use <note>original: "vruntur," likely a typo for "utuntur"</note> purgation in two ways. First by soothing; second by dissolving: knowing that it is neither sufficient to soothe, nor safe to dissolve before you soothe. Similarly, among philosophers, moral purification comes first, acting as a soothing agent. For it does not uproot the internal diseases of the imagination—that is, its deceptions. There follows the speculative <note>meaning theoretical or contemplative</note> purification of the imagination, which eventually clears away the clouds according to one's strength. However, it is not safe to approach the duty of speculation before moral purification, lest anyone infected with the diseases of vice should abuse the sharpness of speculation itself to defend injustice and impiety. From these things, he concludes that to the extent the philosopher separates the mind by its sharpness from bodily things, to that extent he joins it to incorporeal reasons and Ideas. 

But when he had enumerated the many inconveniences brought upon the soul by the body, he added that the last and greatest of evils is that fallacy by which the imagination, while the mind is raising itself toward the incorporeal, often distracts it toward certain images of bodies and forces it to think in a certain bodily manner. After this, he also suggests that because the soul cannot attain the truth of things which it naturally desires while joined to the body, it must follow that it either never attains it, or attains it after death. But to never attain it is not reasonable, since it is perpetually desired by every mind. 

Furthermore, he disapproves of those who think temperance consists of abstaining from smaller bodily pleasures in order to subsequently attain greater bodily pleasures; and again, those who define courage as overcoming certain fears for the sake of other fears that have already overcome us. For he wants the entire duty of moral virtue to consist in a certain purification of the soul for the sake of wisdom. Otherwise, there is no virtue. Indeed, he even calls human wisdom a kind of purification, as if he thinks we attain nothing else by the meditation of our wisdom than a certain purity, which divine illumination—which is properly called wisdom—soon follows. He signifies, moreover, that it is not so much a habit acquired by our labors as the purification itself that joins us to God. 

These things being done, intending to prove the immortality of the soul, he says that a progression occurs from one kind of opposites to the other, and conversely, a regression. Therefore, just as the dead come from the living, so from the dead the living must one day rise again. Here he seems to prophesy the resurrection of the dead, which he also confirms in the *Politicus*. Furthermore, through long detours he hints that just as the substance of the heaven and the matter of the elements are infinitely arranged and pass one into another in turn, so also the rational soul—which is the principle of motion, life, and generation—can be infinitely joined to the body and separated in turn. For indeed, many substances of nature change qualities in a long-lasting cycle, and everywhere an eternal circuit occurs by the power of the soul. In the following sections, with a certain immense confidence, he asserts the resurrection which he had hinted at. 

He then approaches the argument concerning reminiscence <term>Reminiscence: The Platonic theory that "learning" is actually the soul recovering knowledge it possessed before birth</term>, proving the same thing as a little before: that the soul lives both before the body and after the body. You should understand such arguments to be Pythagorean. And from them, choose what leads more toward the truth. He says, therefore, if learning is reminiscence, souls lived before the body. He proves that it is reminiscence in two main ways. First, because to one questioning correctly, we often answer truths about things we never learned. Second, because from the knowledge of things that are sensed, by a certain sudden abstraction, we ascend to the knowledge of Ideas—as in recognizing these "equal" things, we come to the knowledge of Equality itself. Here we recognize how difficult it is for these things to become like those Ideas, and how much they approach them, and which more or which less. Since we do this throughout our whole life, it is necessary that we had the knowledge of the thing itself before birth. For we did not suddenly receive the knowledge of a perfect thing from imperfect ones. 

He shows, moreover, that Ideas exist in two ways. First: any subject called "equal" can, while remaining the same in substance, both become and appear "unequal." But Equality can never either become or appear to be Inequality. Furthermore, these equal things, being imperfect, participate in inequality, but Equality itself does not. In the following parts, note with what great assertiveness he affirms the Ideas, and adds that the essence of the Ideas is our own essence. And since our soul refers individual things to the Ideas, it shows itself to be eternal along with the essence of the Ideas, and recognizes that essence as its own. 

Note, moreover, that in no matter should we labor more than to expel the fear of death, like a most serious disease, through the demonstration of immortality. Immediately he approaches another argument drawn from the proportion of the intellect to the "intelligible" <note>that which can be understood by the mind alone, as opposed to the senses</note>. He calls the intelligible itself the incorporeal and eternal Idea itself. And since the intellect agrees with it as its own proper object, he concludes that the intellect is incorporeal and eternal, especially since it rules the body and resists mortal things. He confirms the proportion of the mind with the Idea from the fact that as often as it is not hindered, it brings itself to the Idea, enjoys its commerce, and is perfected. 

But where, after he said the soul is altogether indissoluble, he added "or close to an altogether indissoluble thing," understand this addition because it is proved in the *Timaeus* that God alone is altogether indissoluble; while other things, if compared to God, are judged in some way dissoluble because they are in some way composite—even though those things that are best composed (that is, apart from elemental matter) are never dissolved. Therefore, both our souls and divine souls are close to the indissoluble God; they are in a certain way dissoluble, but never to be dissolved. Furthermore, he calls "altogether indissoluble" that in which no parts of essence or action are scattered. The soul, therefore, though it is not scattered according to the parts of its essence, is nevertheless diffused through the parts of its action. For it acts in time and through motion. 

Accordingly, he adds that after death the pure soul returns to pure and eternal things, but the soul that is impure and infected by earthly things is dragged to wretched and earthly places, and is often seen. Truly, the affection toward bodies remaining in the soul does not properly make the soul visible by itself, since affection is not visible; yet it causes the soul to drag something visible with it—that is, a certain envelope, either airy or composed of the spirits of its own body, as Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the "vehicle" of the soul</note> wishes, or recently gathered from the surrounding air. Certainly here Plato signifies what Proclus wishes: namely, that between the ethereal body (which is both immaterial, simple, and eternal) and the earthly body (which is material, composite, and short-lived), there is an airy body, material indeed, but in a certain way simple and of longer duration, in which souls dwell for a long time even after departure. When this is dissolved, they put on a composite body again, provided they are not purified; but if they are purified, they seek heaven with only the ethereal body. 

What he tells of the passage of souls into beasts is Pythagorean. Understand it this way: namely, that our souls do not so much animate the bodies of beasts, as that for the sake of purgatory they are in a certain way mixed with the imagination of brutes through their own irrational imagination, just as they say impure demons are often mixed with the imagination of the insane. This is how most of the Platonists, except Plotinus, explain it. This is evident from the fact that he does not say the soul "becomes" a beast, but "puts on," "enters," or "passes into." He concludes that only those who depart purified through true philosophy are received into God. 

Hear, besides these things, that the bond of the soul with the body is nothing other than love—that is, naturally providing for it. Likewise, as often as the soul acts through an instrument regarding forms lying in a subject, it knows nothing purely; but only when it turns through itself to the forms existing simply in themselves. Learn here also that the soul, from the fact that it is delighted and nourished by the things of the body, becomes "bodily"; and from this it is so far deceived that it judges only bodily things to be true, when it is entirely the opposite; and that a fallacy of this kind is the most serious of all evils. It follows that the soul, having now become bodily, even after death slips around bodily things, away from the incorporeal. Conclude that the mind, restored entirely to its purity, in no way distrusts its own immortality. 

The fable of the swan is Pythagorean and allegorical. Pythagorean, indeed, where it says the swan's soul survives. It is understood allegorically that the swan is contained in the number of solar animals, and that Socrates is "solar"—both because he was approved by the oracle of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, and because he healed the minds of men. Add that prophecy is fourfold: divine, demonic, human, and natural. And that the last occurs in beasts by a certain instinct of nature. Understand also the innocent swans to be men without philosophy: who, since they often do not fear death in the least, signify that absolute philosophers ought to fear it in no way. 

Notice then that it is very difficult in this life to understand the substance of the soul, because we behold it under a bodily appearance. Therefore, the safest method for comprehending the soul is both moral purification and metaphysical abstraction. But where that may be insufficient, there is need of a certain "divine word"—that is, revelations and miracles made by God. We truly ought to consider here the mystery of the Divine Word signified by Plato. 

He then hands down two precepts for debating. First, that we should not believe any reasons without long examination. But after we have believed a certain reason through sufficient examination, we should not be easily moved from it by any objections or similarities. Second, that we should not consider either our own or another's persona in debating, but only the reason consonant with the truth. There follow doubts against the soul, lest perhaps...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the "Phaedo," specifically addressing the arguments against the "soul as a harmony" theory and transitioning into the metaphysical "Theory of Forms" and the geography of the afterlife.</meta>

# Phædo, Or, On the Soul. 333

...[supposing that the soul] might be a certain harmony of humors, and thus either dissolve before the body, or together with it, or shortly thereafter. Socrates solves these certain doubts in this way: If learning is recollection <note>This refers to the Platonic doctrine of *anamnesis*, where the soul "remembers" truths it knew before birth</note>, and therefore the soul lived before the body, the soul cannot be a harmony of the body. This is because a harmony does not precede the parts from whose union it arises, but rather follows them. If the nature of harmony and the soul were the same, then just as one soul is no more a "soul" than another, one soul would not be more "harmonious" than another. Thus, a temperate soul would be no more a harmony than an intemperate one. Furthermore, if harmony necessarily follows and is led by the elements from which it is composed, the soul cannot be a harmony of the body, because the soul daily leads the body and often resists it. 

However, before he resolves these doubts and fully perfects the arguments for immortality, he uses a long discourse to condemn those who, in assigning causes to things, flee to certain materials and instruments. He argues that the entire study of natural history is insufficiently proven through these same natural things, since all these things and the movements of everyone depend entirely on divine causes—efficient, final, and ideal. He desires, above all, the final cause of each thing and of the universe; that is, the good of each thing and the good of the whole, the power of which good he calls the efficient cause. But since he cannot grasp the full magnitude of the Good itself, he chooses in the second place the "Ideal" reasons of divine intelligence, according to whose likeness all things in the matter of the world are expressed. Among these things, note the confirmation of the Mosaic mystery <note>Ficino often sought to prove that Plato's philosophy aligned with the "mysteries" of Moses and the Bible</note>, just as in the *Timaeus*. God saw that individual things were good, and indeed all things were very good. Thus, all things are connected to the Good itself. Again, he notes that the soul, while looking at corporeal things, is meanwhile blinded to incorporeal vision. The truth of things cannot be grasped unless we take refuge in the Ideas <note>The "Forms" or eternal archetypes of reality</note>. 

Furthermore, the formulas of these Ideas are present in our minds; by their agreement or disagreement, individual things are judged to be true or false. Socrates was never accustomed to ceasing the certain contemplation of Ideas, and he used to affirm them alone. The certain cause of things is situated in the Ideas; likewise, the immortality of the soul is demonstrated most powerfully through the Ideas. The process among Ideas moves from the less common, through intermediate ones, to the most common, as well as descending from the Ideas to their effects. Finally, he arranges the argument for immortality based on the fact that the rational soul provides life to the body, not as an "accidental form" <note>A temporary quality, like "being tan"</note> inherent in the body, but as a "substantial form" <note>The core essence of a thing</note> remaining in itself, living formally from itself like a certain "Idea" of bodily life, and vivifying the body through efficient power. Therefore, he concludes that the soul cannot receive death, since death is the opposite of life; the soul truly has its own life and remains in itself, so that it is able to receive death neither through itself properly, nor through another subject.

After this, because the soul is immortal, he exhorts everyone to moral and speculative discipline, so that the soul, purified and perfected through both the will and the intellect, may fly back to the heavenly homeland on these two wings. Meanwhile, he confirms that the soul is immortal because virtue should not ultimately be a disadvantage, nor should vice be a benefit. The laborious path of virtue would be harmful to the good, and conversely, the voluptuous life would benefit the wicked, unless the soul were immortal. And lest someone perhaps deny that vice can harm or virtue can benefit after this life, he adds that the soul carries with it the gathered affections and habits of both the will and the intelligence—whether good or bad—which will suddenly either harm or benefit. For a *daemon* <note>A guiding spirit or guardian</note> as a leader suddenly conducts everyone to the divine judge of life, to a place designated for common judgment: those who are less pure into the air, and those who are purer into the ether. There, judged by another *daemon* again, they are drawn through a "three-way crossroad" to their own places—that is, to those places similar to themselves. I say "through a three-way crossroad" because some are sent to heaven, others to Tartarus, and others to the middle regions. The *daemon* leads them, moving the intelligence in the good, but disturbing the imagination and the emotions in the evil. When he says the wicked wander without a leader, understand this as being without a *beneficial* leader. Add to this that they do not recognize where they are being dragged, and are snatched away by violence.

Furthermore, before he distributes the fates of the souls, he describes the orb of the earth, saying that there are certain regions of the earth—and those indeed most vast—which are so high that they are not struck by winds or rains. There, the air is most temperate, under which the most precious things are born, people have the sharpest senses, and they are long-lived. There are those who believe that both the people and other things born there are composed as much as possible from ether and air, and as little as possible from the thicker elements: so that the bodies of the men are as if made of air, and they are nourished by mostly airy fruits. Lest anyone deny this as impossible, Olympiodorus <note>A later Neoplatonic commentator</note> brings up a story from Aristotle, in which Aristotle says he had played with <note>original: "ludisse," perhaps meaning "joked about" or "studied"</note> a man who was nourished by air alone and by the sun. As for his dividing the face of the sublime earth into twelve regions, this arises because twelve corresponds to the signs of the zodiac, it is ruled by the souls of the twelve spheres, and the twelfth is the sphere of the world; and just as it is the foundation of the whole, it takes for itself that dodecahedron shape <note>A twelve-sided geometric solid</note> which the *Timaeus* attributes to the world. But regarding this very figure and other questions proper to the earth, we shall speak in the *Timaeus*. You, however, remember that a habitation of the earth of this kind is similar to the terrestrial Paradise of Moses.

Next, he describes the rivers beneath the earth, by which the souls are nourished. Whoever explains these according to the humors of our body and the disturbances of the soul afflicting us in this life brings forth something similar to the truth, yet does not attain the whole truth. For Plato, both here and in the *Republic*, signifies that the rewards of virtues and the punishments of vices pertain most especially to the other life. **Acheron**, therefore, the river beneath the earth, is a place of purgatory; it pertains to care and sorrow, and it also corresponds to the Air and the southern part of the world. **Phlegethon** corresponds to Fire and the East; it contains the power of punishing through heat, and it punishes the fervor of anger and desire. **Styx** and **Cocytus** correspond to the Earth and the West; they punish through mourning, hate, and weeping. They differ between themselves only in this: that Styx is the name for the river rising, and Cocytus for it proceeding. He wishes **Tartarus** to hold the lowest place of the underworld, in which the most wicked are fixed, not for the sake of medicine <note>i.e., healing/correction</note>, but for the sake of example, as is read here and in the *Republic* and *Gorgias*. Some add that the **Ocean** also pertains to these rivers in some way, corresponding to Water and the North, in which the power of distinguishing and defining is understood. You, however, should understand what is said about the rivers as pertaining most especially to the *daemons* and divinities who punish the shameful in such an order. 

Truly, sins that are easily curable are those which have not yet been turned into a habit. Those which have already generated a habit are cured with difficulty; nevertheless, they are committed together with a certain resistance of reason, and they affect those committing them with repentance. The incurable ones are those whose habit puts both resistance and repentance far to flight. The first are purged in Acheron. The second, if they lean toward the first, are punished in Phlegethon; if toward the third, in Styx and Cocytus. The third are afflicted in Tartarus, from which, as Plato says, they never depart. In what way others might explain this differently, I prefer to omit for the present. The souls can be afflicted not only through the imagination unhappily agitated by *daemons*, but through certain "airy bodies" which are designated by the names "vehicle" and "skiff." <note>Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic concept of the *pneuma* or "astral body" that carries the soul</note> 

Rewards, however, Plato distinguishes in this way: Souls that have lived justly and holily without philosophy, ascending to the heights of the earth such as we described above, dwell there in very thin and spiritual bodies. Those who have philosophized for "civil" <note>political/social</note> reasons dwell in heaven with splendid and celestial bodies. But those who have been perfectly purified through exact philosophy fly out into the "supracelestial" place, where they live through all time entirely without bodies, as Plato says here. By what reasoning some explain this, I will deliberately not recount. Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Famous Neoplatonist philosophers</note> certainly hand down that souls perfectly restored to God never fall back. This indeed corresponds appropriately to the opposite: those who are judged never to emerge from Tartarus. If this is indeed so, the infinite cycles [of reincarnation] will now be removed. Temporal cycles will be seen to be applied for the sake of a certain purgation. 

Finally, Socrates confesses that he owes a cock to **Asclepius** <note>The god of healing</note>, and he orders it to be returned most diligently. The ancients used to sacrifice a cock—the messenger of the day and the sun—to the physician Asclepius, son of Apollo; that is, they confessed they owed the light of day (which is the light of life) to the divine benevolence that cures all diseases, which is called the daughter of divine providence. He had ordered them to seek such a physician for the diseases of the soul in the higher realms. And as if they have now been liberated from every fear of doubt and the sign of disease [life in the body], he orders thanks and a victim to be returned to God. Furthermore, the oracles of the ancients hand down that souls returning to heaven sing a *paean*—that is, a triumphal song—to Apollo. He therefore returns his vow to God, so that, singing the *paean* eagerly, he may seek again his heavenly homeland.

->ECHECRATES, PHAEDO, APOLLODORVS, SOCRATES, CEBES, SIMMIAS, CRITO, THE SERVANT OF THE ELEVEN.<-

**ECHE.** Were you present, O Phaedo, on that day when Socrates drank the poison in prison? Or did you hear it from another? **PHAE.** I was present there, O Echecrates. **ECHE.** What were those things which that man spoke before he died? And how did he depart from life? For I would gladly hear. For neither does any of our Phliasian citizens frequently travel now to Athens...

# 334 Book Twenty-Nine

...to Athens, and for a long time now no traveler from there has come to us who could report anything certain about that matter, except that he departed from life after drinking poison. Regarding the rest, he had nothing to report. **PHAEDO.** Have you then not heard how the matters pertaining to the trial were handled? **ECHECRATES.** We did hear; for someone reported these things to us. And we were certainly amazed that, although the trial was already finished, he seems to have died a long time afterward. What was the cause of this, O Phaedo? **PHAEDO.** By a certain stroke of fate, O Echecrates, it happened to Socrates. For on the day before he was judged, it happened that the stern of the ship was decorated—the one which the Athenians send every year to Delos. **ECHEC.** What does that signify? **PHAEDO.** This is that ship, as the Athenians say, in which Theseus once carried those "twice-seven" <note>The fourteen youths (seven boys and seven girls) sent as tribute to the Minotaur in Crete.</note> with him to Crete; he saved them, and he himself was saved. They had vowed, it is said, to Apollo that if they were saved, they would send a certain procession to Delos every year. Which indeed even now, and always from that time, they send every year to the God. Therefore, when the start of the procession is underway, they purify the city according to law, and they kill no one publicly during that time, until the ship reaches Delos and returns again to Athens. This is sometimes completed over a long period of time when the winds hold them back. The beginning of the procession is after the priest of Apollo has crowned the stern of that ship. That, as I was just saying, had been done the day before he was judged. For this reason, Socrates was in prison for a long time between the judgment and his death. **ECHEC.** But concerning the death itself, O Phaedo, what things were said by him, what was done, and which of his companions were present? Or did the magistrates <note>Specifically the "Eleven," the officials in charge of the prison and executions in Athens.</note> not permit them to be present? And so did he depart, destitute of friends? **PHAEDO.** Not at all; some were present, and indeed many. **ECHEC.** Prepare yourself then to report all these things to us as clearly as possible, unless some business hinders you. **PHAEDO.** I am at leisure indeed, and I will try to narrate it to you. For to remember Socrates, whether I speak myself or hear others speaking, is always the sweetest of all things to me. **ECHEC.** Likewise, O Phaedo, you will find those who are about to hear you are of the same mind. Therefore, try with all your strength to recount everything most diligently.

**PHAEDO.** Indeed, O Echecrates, I was affected there by a certain wonderful feeling. For no pity seized me, as one present at the death of a most intimate friend. For that man seemed blessed to me, O Echecrates, when I considered both the habit of his mind and his speech: so intrepidly and nobly did he depart from life, that he seemed to me to migrate into the other life not without a divine fate, but that there too he would be blessed, if ever any other man was. For this reason, I was not excessively moved (as would seem natural for a man present at a mournful event), nor on the other hand was I affected by joy, as we were accustomed to be at other times when we were engaged in philosophy. For the discourses were indeed of that kind, but in truth a certain strange feeling and an unusual mixture of pleasure and pain had invaded me, considering that he was to die a little later. And all of us who were present were affected almost similarly, sometimes indeed laughing, but at other times weeping. One among us especially, Apollodorus: for you know the man and his ways. **ECHEC.** Why not? **PHAEDO.** He therefore was thoroughly affected in that way, and I myself and the others had our minds similarly distracted by agitation. **ECHEC.** But who happened to be present, O Phaedo? **PHAEDO.** Of citizens and locals there were present: Apollodorus himself, and Critobulus, and his father Crito; also Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines, and Antisthenes. Ctesippus of Paeania was there too, and Menexenus, and certain other locals. But Plato, I believe, was ill. **ECHEC.** But were any foreigners present? **PHAEDO.** Foreigners were also present: Simmias the Theban, and Cebes, and Phaeondondes; and from Megara, Euclid and Terpsion. **ECHEC.** Were Aristippus and Cleombrotus present? **PHAEDO.** No: for they were said to be in Aegina. **ECHEC.** Were any others there besides? **PHAEDO.** I think these whom I have named were those who were present.

**ECHEC.** Tell me then, what kind of discourses were there? **PHAEDO.** I will indeed try to narrate everything to you from the beginning. We were accustomed to go to Socrates every day in the preceding days, myself and others, meeting in the morning in that court where the trial had been held: for it was very close to the prison. Talking among ourselves, therefore, we always waited there until the prison was opened; for it was opened not very early. But when it was opened, we went in to Socrates, and often spent the whole day with him. Then, however, we met earlier than usual. For on the day before, when we had left the prison in the evening, we heard that the ship from Delos had returned. Therefore, we told one another to return to the usual place at the very break of dawn. When we had returned, the gatekeeper who was accustomed to admit us came out to meet us and ordered us to wait, and not to enter until he himself summoned us. "For," he said, "the Eleven are releasing Socrates and announcing to him that he must die today." Not long after, he returned to us and ordered us to enter. Entering, we found Socrates just recently released from his shackles; and Xanthippe, our friend's wife, sitting nearby and holding his boy in her arms. When she saw us, she began to wail and say the kinds of things women are accustomed to cry out: "O Socrates," she said, "now for the last time your friends speak to you, and you to them." But Socrates, looking at Crito, said, "O Crito, let someone lead her home." And certain of Crito's servants led her away, as she was shouting and lamenting. Socrates, sitting on the bed, drew his leg toward himself and rubbed it with his hand, and while rubbing it, he spoke thus: "How strange this thing seems to be, O men, which people call pleasure, and in what a wonderful way it relates by nature to pain itself, which seems to be its opposite. Inasmuch as they are unwilling to be present in a person at the same time. Yet if someone pursues and catches one, he is almost always compelled to take the other as well, as if both were joined together from the same peak. I think indeed that Aesop, if he had noticed these things, would have made a fable: namely, that when God himself wanted to reconcile these things that were fighting among themselves and could not do it, he joined their heads into one, and therefore to whomsoever one is present, the other will also soon be present; which indeed has happened to me at this moment. For just now my leg was affected by pain because of the chains, but now pleasure seems to follow it." To this Cebes said, "By Jove, O Socrates, you have opportunely recalled that to my memory. For since you have composed poems—first a song in praise of Apollo, then also the fables of Aesop set to verse—many others have asked me, and Evenus just recently, with what intention you did these things after you came into prison, which you had never done before. If therefore you care for me to have something to answer to Evenus when he asks me again, which I know for certain..."

<summary>Phaedo begins his eyewitness account of Socrates' final day, explaining the delay caused by the sacred ship to Delos and listing the friends present. The scene opens with Socrates being unshackled and reflecting on the paradoxical link between pleasure and pain.</summary>
