### Book Thirty-Four.
[[notes: This heading refers to the division within this specific edition of Ficino’s *Opera Omnia*; the content actually concludes Book II of Plato’s *Laws* and begins Book III.]]

The proper education and instruction of children is that which leads them toward the way of life dictated by right law, which the most equitable of the elders have confirmed through their own experience. To ensure the soul of a child follows the law—not experiencing joy in things contrary to it, but in the same things the law and the elders teach—the lawgiver shall use persuasion. If necessary, he will compel the poet to describe the deeds of temperate, brave, and entirely good men in noble words. The poet must depict their forms through rhythm and their accents through harmonies as is fitting, using those songs which we call *Odas* (Odes). In truth, these are *incantationes* (incantations) for the soul, intentionally composed so that the souls of men may obey the laws through their experiences of pain and joy. 

Because the tender souls of children cannot yet undertake serious studies, let these lessons be spoken and performed as games and songs. In these, the same effect is achieved as by a physician treating a sick body: he smears healthy food with pleasant sweeteners but infuses harmful things with bitter flavors, so that the patient becomes accustomed to accepting the one and rejecting the other. 

**CLINIAS.** Do you believe, Guest, that these practices are observed in other cities? As far as I know, the things you prescribe are done nowhere except among us and the Lacedaemonians (Spartans). For new things are always being devised in dances and other music—not changed by laws, but by certain wandering pleasures that are never the same or permanent. They are always varied, contrary to those Egyptian customs you described.

**ATHENIAN.** Well said, Clinias. If it seemed to you that I said these things are currently done everywhere, do not wonder if I explained my thoughts unclearly. I was describing what I *wish* were done in music, and I seemed to you to speak as if it were already happening. Indeed, it is never pleasant to criticize an incurable matter that has wandered far into error, but sometimes it is necessary. But since we agree on these points, do you not assert that these things are done more among you and the Lacedaemonians than among other Greeks?

**CLINIAS.** Why should we not assert that?

**ATHENIAN.** If they were done similarly among the others, would things not be better than they are now?

**CLINIAS.** Much better certainly, if they were arranged as they are with us, and as you just now prescribed.

**ATHENIAN.** Come, let us see if these are the things preached among you in every discipline and music. You compel poets to say in their verses that the good man—because he is temperate and just—is happy and blessed, whether he is large and robust, or small and weak, whether poor or rich. But the unjust man, even if he were wealthier than Cinyras or Midas (kings of legendary wealth), is miserable and leads a life of sorrow. If the poet speaks rightly, he will say to us: "Shall I mention or call him a man who does not possess and manage with justice all those things called good?" Such a man, adorned with justice, would delight in fighting the enemy hand-to-hand. But the unjust man would not dare to look upon bloody slaughter, nor could he outrun the Thracian North Wind; nor would he ever possess anything truly good. For those things commonly called "good" are not correctly named. People say the best thing is health, the second is beauty, *the third is strength* [[margin: In Greek, wealth is third]], and the fourth is riches. Innumerable other such "goods" are recounted: sharp sight and hearing, the integrity of the other senses, and the power to do whatever you desire with tyrannical license. They say the height of all happiness is to become immortal immediately upon possessing all these things. 

However, you and I agree that for just and holy men, the possession of all these things is best, but for the unjust, it is the worst—starting with health. For to be healthy, to see, to hear, to feel everything easily, and to live forever as an immortal is the worst of all if one lives always devoid of justice and the other virtues. It would be a lesser evil if a person so affected ended their life as quickly as possible. These are the things you will urge and compel your poets to say, and you will educate your youth through rhythms and harmonies consistent with these truths. Do you notice this yourselves? For I assert that what are commonly called "evils" are good for the just, but for the unjust, they are evil. And those things called "goods" are truly good for the good, but evil for the wicked. Do we agree on this thus far, or not?

**CLINIAS.** In part we seem to agree, and in part not at all.

**ATHENIAN.** Perhaps I have not persuaded you that the man who is unjust and insolent is not blessed, but miserable—even if he possesses health, riches, perpetual tyranny, invincible physical strength, and immortality, and suffers none of those things commonly called "evils."

**CLINIAS.** You speak the truth.

**ATHENIAN.** Very well, but what should be said next? If he is strong, beautiful, and rich, and does whatever he desires throughout his life, does it not seem to you that if he is unjust and insolent, he necessarily lives "basely" (*turpiter*)? Do you concede he lives basely?

**CLINIAS.** Entirely.

**ATHENIAN.** What then? Does he not also live "badly" (*male*)?

**CLINIAS.** Not quite in the same way.

**ATHENIAN.** And do you not concede that he lives unpleasantly and disadvantageously?

**CLINIAS.** How can we concede that?

**ATHENIAN.** How? If some god, my friends, were to grant us a harmony of mind [[notes: consensus of opinion]], for now we disagree. To me, Clinias, these points seem more necessary than the fact that Crete is an island. If I were the legislator for the Cretans, I would compel poets and all citizens to speak this way. I would threaten almost the greatest punishment if anyone in that region dared to say that there are wicked men who live pleasantly, or that some things are useful and profitable while others are more just. I would persuade my citizens to speak against what is currently said by the Cretans, the Spartans, and indeed by all other men. 

Come then, by Jupiter and Apollo, best of men, if we asked those very gods who gave us our laws: "Is the most pleasant life also the most just? Or are there two lives—one the most pleasant, the other the most just?" If they replied that there are two, we might ask them again: "Which should be called more blessed: those living most justly, or those living most pleasantly?" If they replied "those living most pleasantly," their answer would be shameful. I would prefer such a thing to be said by human fathers and legislators rather than by gods. Therefore, consider that I have asked these questions of a father and legislator, and he has replied to me that the most blessed man is the one who lives most pleasantly. I would then oppose him: "O Father, did you not want me to live as blessedly as possible?" "Certainly." "But you never ceased commanding me to live as justly as possible!" Whoever grants both these points—whether a legislator or a father—speaks absurdly and is inconsistent with himself. But if he responds that the most just life is the most blessed, then anyone who hears this will ask, I believe: "What good and beautiful thing does the law praise in that life that is better than pleasure?" For what good can be present in the just man that is not surpassed by pleasure?

Tell me, I pray: are praise and glory among both men and gods good and honorable, but unpleasant? And infamy the opposite? "Not at all," we shall say, O legislator. But is it pleasant not to inflict or suffer injustice, yet not good or honorable? And are other things pleasant but base and evil?

**CLINIAS.** How so?

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the reasoning that does not separate the pleasant from the just, nor the good from the honorable, is persuasive. Even if it serves no other purpose, it is highly conducive to making someone want to live a holy and just life. Thus, it would be a most shameful and contrary speech for a legislator to deny this. For no one will willingly do that which does not contain more joy than pain. Whatever is seen from a distance brings a foggy dizziness to everyone—even children, so to speak. Therefore, having removed the dizziness and darkness, the legislator will lead the opinions of the citizens toward the opposite. Through praise, custom, and reason, he will persuade them that both just and unjust things are shaded, and that unjust things appear opposite to the just. To the unjust and wicked man, unjust things seem pleasant and just things most unpleasant; but to the just man, both appear entirely the opposite.

**CLINIAS.** So it appears.

**ATHENIAN.** But in truth, which judgment shall we consider superior? That of the better soul or the worse?

**CLINIAS.** Of the better soul, necessarily.

**ATHENIAN.** It is necessary, therefore, that the unjust life is not only baser and worse than the just and holy life, but also more unpleasant.

**CLINIAS.** So it certainly seems, my friend, according to this logic.

**ATHENIAN.** Even if the matter were not as we have just said, a legislator of any weight would still consider it useful for the benefit of youth to tell a "productive lie" (*falsum aliquid*)—if indeed a lie must ever be told—for no lie could be more useful than this one, which leads the listeners to embrace justice not by force, but by their own will.

**CLINIAS.** Truth is a beautiful and stable thing, Guest, but it often seems difficult to persuade people of it.

**ATHENIAN.** Be that as it may. But the Sidonian fable [[notes: the myth of Cadmus]], though it had no probability, was easily believed, as were many others.

**CLINIAS.** Which ones?

**ATHENIAN.** That armed soldiers were once born from sown teeth. This is a great example for a legislator: he can persuade the minds of the young of whatever he wishes. Therefore, he should seek nothing else but how to bring the greatest good to the city through the acceptance of these persuasions. He must apply every effort so that the entire city sings one and the same thing regarding these matters, always and as much as possible, in songs, fables, and every speech. This is my view. If you feel otherwise, feel free to contradict me.

**CLINIAS.** Neither of us seems able to doubt these things.

**ATHENIAN.** I shall proceed then, asserting that all three choruses—the children, the youths, and the elders—should instill these "good things" we mentioned into the tender and soft minds of boys through a kind of *incantatio* (incantation). The main point is this: if we assert that the gods judge the same life to be both the best and the most pleasant, we will speak the truth and be more persuasive to those who need it.

**CLINIAS.** What you say must be conceded.

**ATHENIAN.** First, then, the childish "Chorus of the Muses" should enter to sing this to the whole city. The second chorus, those up to thirty years old, shall invoke the *Paeana* (Paean/Hymn to Apollo) as a witness of truth and supplicate for favor toward the younger ones. The third shall be composed of those between thirty and sixty years old. As for those older than sixty, since they can no longer sing fables regarding these same morals, we shall consider them dismissed to a divine oracle.

**CLINIAS.** Guest, who are these third choruses you speak of? We do not clearly grasp who you mean.

**ATHENIAN.** These are the very people for whose sake most of the previous discussion was introduced.

**CLINIAS.** We still do not understand. Try to speak more plainly.

**ATHENIAN.** It was said at the beginning of our dispute, if we remember, that the nature of all young people is so burning that they cannot keep body or voice quiet; they are always shouting and leaping without order. No other animal but man has a sense of order in these two things. The name of the order seen in motion is *Rhythmus* (Rhythm/Number), while that in the voice—tempering high and low notes—is *Harmonia* (Harmony/Concord). Together, they are called *Chorea* (Choral Dance). We also said that the gods, pitying us, gave us Apollo, the Muses, and—if we remember—Dionysus as leaders and companions in these dances.

**CLINIAS.** Why should we not remember?

**ATHENIAN.** The choruses of Apollo and the Muses have already been mentioned. The third, which remains, must necessarily be attributed to Dionysus.

**CLINIAS.** How? Explain further. At first hearing, a "Dionysian chorus of elders" seems quite absurd if men over thirty, or fifty, or sixty are to use it.

**ATHENIAN.** You speak the truth. But I think reason is needed here to show how this can be done appropriately.

**CLINIAS.** Why not?

**ATHENIAN.** Are the previous points agreed upon between us?

**CLINIAS.** Which ones?

**ATHENIAN.** That all men and boys, freemen and slaves, males and females—indeed the entire city—should daily sing what we have described to the whole city in various modes and poems, so that through an innumerable variety of hymns, they may be affected by an insatiable pleasure in singing together.

**CLINIAS.** Nothing prevents us from conceding that it should be so.

**ATHENIAN.** But how shall the best part of the city—those who possess the highest authority to persuade because of their age and prudence—be the cause of the greatest goods by singing the best songs? Or shall we foolishly omit the very group in which the power of the best and most useful songs resides?

**CLINIAS.** We must not omit it, provided it can be made clear.

**ATHENIAN.** How then can it be done decently? See if it might be this way: Each elder, already satiated with songs, takes little delight in them. When asked to sing, the older and more modest he is, the more he is ashamed to do so. Is it not so?

**CLINIAS.** Exactly.

**ATHENIAN.** But he will much less tolerate singing in a theater before a multitude out of shame—especially if the choruses of elders are forced to sing with thin and hungry voices like those competing for a victory. They would sing with distress and shame and would be slow to begin.

**CLINIAS.** You speak of necessary facts.

**ATHENIAN.** How then shall we make them ready to sing? First, we shall establish by law that boys up to the age of eighteen shall entirely ignore the use of wine [[margin: Wine forbidden to boys]]. We shall warn them not to add "fire to fire" in the body and soul before they reach adulthood and begin their labors. One must guard the habits of youth. Then, they may use wine moderately until the age of thirty. But young men must entirely abstain from drunkenness and over-filling themselves with wine. When they reach forty, however, they may recline more freely at banquets and invoke Dionysus to the sacred rites and games of the elders. For Dionysus gave wine to men as a *remedium* (remedy) against the rigors of old age [[margin: Wine as a remedy for the hardness of old age]], so that we might seem to grow young again. Through wine, the oblivion of sorrow takes hold of us, and the very disposition of the soul, like iron in a fire, is brought from hardness into softness and becomes more flexible. 

Affected in this way, each man—having gained confidence—will be less ashamed to sing among his peers (though not among many strangers) and to "enchant" the soul, as we have repeated.

**CLINIAS.** Very much so.

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, this will be a decent way to induce them to take part in the songs.

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** But with what voice and what muse shall these men sing? Surely that which is most suitable for them?

**CLINIAS.** And which is suitable for divine men? Is it not the one the choruses sing?

**CLINIAS.** Guest, we and they cannot sing anything other than what we learned in the chorus. We are accustomed to that song.

**ATHENIAN.** That is reasonable. For you have not learned the *best* song; you have a Republic that is more like a military camp than a city. You keep your young men like a brood of chicks feeding in a flock. None of you takes a young man aside to handle him gently and tame him like a master of horses, educating him not only to be a stout soldier but also a fit governor of cities—who, as we said at the beginning, would be better than the soldiers of Tyrtaeus (the Spartan poet), honoring virtue not only in the private and public duty of fortitude, but everywhere.

**CLINIAS.** Guest, I do not know why you keep disparaging our legislators.

**ATHENIAN.** I do not do it from the heart, good man, if I do it at all. But let us go where reason leads, if you wish. If we have a muse superior to the common muse of choruses and theaters, let us try to offer it to those who, as we said, are ashamed of the common one and seek something better.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely.

**ATHENIAN.** In everything followed by a certain grace (pleasure), that grace alone must entice, or its correctness, or its utility. Let me explain by example. Food and drink have a grace we call pleasure; their correctness and utility lie in whether they contribute to health.

**CLINIAS.** Exactly.

**ATHENIAN.** So also in learning, there is a grace called pleasure. Its correctness, utility, and good habit are produced by truth itself.

**CLINIAS.** Indeed.

**ATHENIAN.** What then of the arts that produce imitations? Do we not look for the same thing? A pleasure surely comes from them, which it is right to call grace.

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** But the correctness of such things—to speak generally—is produced by their "equality" (proportion) in being such and so great, rather than by pleasure.

**CLINIAS.** Excellent.

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, that which produces neither utility, nor truth, nor likeness, nor harm—but exists solely for the sake of that grace called pleasure—should be judged by pleasure alone when none of those other things follow it.

**CLINIAS.** You mean pleasure alone that does no harm?

**ATHENIAN.** Exactly. And I call that same thing "jest" or "play" when it brings neither harm nor utility worthy of esteem.

**CLINIAS.** You speak the truth.

**ATHENIAN.** From this, it follows that no *imitatio* (imitation) should be judged by pleasure or false opinion. Similarly, no "equality." For something is not equal or commensurable because it *seems* so to someone, or because someone *rejoices* in it; it is equal only by truth.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely so.

**ATHENIAN.** But we say all music is imitative and a producer of likenesses.

**CLINIAS.** Who doubts it?

**ATHENIAN.** When someone asserts that music should be judged by pleasure alone, he must not be heard. Rather, we must seek that music which possesses a likeness through the imitation of the good.

**CLINIAS.** These are true words.

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, those who seek the best species of song and muse should look for that which is correct, not that which is merely pleasant. For the correctness of imitation consists in this: that it expresses something as it truly is in itself.

**CLINIAS.** Who doubts it?

**ATHENIAN.** Everyone will concede that all poems in music are an imitation and a kind of assimilation. All poets, listeners, and actors would agree.

**CLINIAS.** Greatly so.

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, one who wishes not to err in judging a poem or fiction must know what it is that is being depicted. For if he does not know the essence of the thing or what it is an image of, he will never understand its correctness or its error.

**CLINIAS.** Never, certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** And if he does not understand the correctness of the work, can he know if it is well or poorly made? I speak obscurely; perhaps I can make it clearer.

**CLINIAS.** How?

**ATHENIAN.** Many likenesses pertain to sight. If someone does not know the form of a depicted body, will they ever know if it is painted correctly? For example, whether it has the proper joints and parts, their number, quality, and location—or whether it is all painted in a confused way? Do you think anyone could know this if they did not know the animal being painted?

**CLINIAS.** Not at all.

**ATHENIAN.** But if someone *does* know it is a man being painted, and that all the parts, figures, and colors have been received from art, will he not necessarily recognize if there is some defect of beauty in it?

**CLINIAS.** We would almost all recognize what is beautiful in animals in this way.

**ATHENIAN.** You speak rightly. In every image—whether through painting, music, or otherwise—should not a prudent judge have these three things? [[margin: What belongs to a prudent judge.]] First, that he knows *what* is being imitated; second, *how correctly*; third, *how well* the likeness has been produced in words, harmonies, and rhythms.

**CLINIAS.** So it seems.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us not be reluctant to explain the difficulty in music. Since music is celebrated more than other likenesses, it requires greater diligence. For he who errs in this is harmed the most, as he drinks in bad morals through the sweetness of the pleasure. This is difficult to know because poets do not possess the poetic art as the Muses do. The Muses would never err so much as to give the words of men a feminine harmony, or combine the rhythms of slaves with the melodies of freemen. They would never mix the voices of wild beasts with those of humans, or confuse the sounds of instruments as if they were all imitating one thing.

But human poets confuse many such things and mix them without reason, provoking laughter in men like Orpheus, whom they follow for the sake of delight. They see all things in confusion; the poets themselves tear apart rhythm and figure from harmony, composing naked speeches in meter without melody, or adapting harmony and rhythm without words to the sound of the lyre or flute alone. In this, it is very difficult to know what rhythm and harmony without words signify, or what imitation they resemble that is worthy of reason. One must consider it full of great crudeness if a poet uses the flute or lyre for anything other than dance or song—to use either "nakedly" (without words) is an abuse similar to a magician’s show, and far removed from the Muses. 

But this is the reason for these things. We were considering that those aged thirty or fifty and above should not use our muses, but let us see when they *should*. Our speech suggests that those who have reached fifty—who must sing—ought to possess the "Muse of the Chorus" better than others. For they must acutely feel and know harmonies and rhythms. How else can anyone know the correctness of a song—whether the Dorian mode fits it, or if the rhythm the poet joined to it was joined correctly?

**CLINIAS.** By no means.

**ATHENIAN.** The common people are laughable when they think they sufficiently know what is a good or bad composition of harmony and rhythm. I speak of those who were once forced to sing and dance to rhythms. But they do not realize they are ignorant of these particulars: that any song is correct only if it contains all the things fitting to it.

**CLINIAS.** That is necessarily so.

**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, if someone does not understand the reason for a thing, will he ever know how it is "correct"?

**CLINIAS.** How could that be?

**ATHENIAN.** Thus we have found this: those elder singers—whom we previously had to provoke but who now sing willingly—must have learned these things so that they can follow both the weight of the rhythms and the harmonic sounds of the strings. By understanding harmony and rhythm, they can choose those which ought to be sung by people of such a kind. Thus, while singing, they will immediately perceive innocent pleasures and lead the youth toward upright morals through songs and delights. Having been so taught, they will possess a more exquisite discipline than the common people or the poets. 

The poet need not know if an imitation is good or bad, only the harmony and rhythm. But these elders must know all three so they can choose the best. Otherwise, they will never be able to entice the souls of the young to virtue through "incantations." Our speech has done its best to offer aid to the Dionysian chorus. 

But let us consider if this has been done correctly. Such a harmony of men necessarily becomes more turbulent as the drinking progresses. We supposed at the start that this must happen in current practices.

**CLINIAS.** It must.

**ATHENIAN.** Where surely everyone, having become lighter in spirit, is uplifted and exults, filled with audacity; he does not listen to his neighbor but considers himself a sufficient leader of both himself and others.

**CLINIAS.** Without a doubt.

**ATHENIAN.** Did we not say that whenever this happens, the souls of the drinkers, like iron in fire, become softer and younger when heated by wine? [[margin: Just as iron by fire, so bodies of elders are softened by wine.]] They are thus more easily led, as when they were young—if someone has the power and knowledge to educate and mold them. And that "painter" (educator) is the one we call a good legislator. In his laws, a mode of drinking must be prescribed, so that these laws may restrain the man who has become bold, audacious, and more impudent than is fitting—who refuses to observe the order of silence, speech, drinking, and music in turn. The law should instruct him to act contrary to his base confidence, applying a "good fear" combined with justice—which we have called divine fear, shame, and modesty.

**CLINIAS.** It is as you say.

**ATHENIAN.** The authors and guardians of these laws—the leaders of the drinkers—must be removed from perturbation and drunkenness. Without them, fighting against drunkenness is harder than fighting enemies without prudent and considerate commanders. If anyone refuses to obey these "Dionysian leaders" over sixty years of age, let him bear a disgrace equal to or even greater than one who disobeys the commanders of Mars (war).

**CLINIAS.** Correct.

**ATHENIAN.** If such drunkenness and such play were employed, would not the drinkers gain great utility from it? They would leave more joined in mutual benevolence than before—not as enemies, as often happens now. For they would have conversed legitimately and, while intoxicated, obeyed the laws under sober leaders.

**CLINIAS.** Certainly, if the drinking were such as you described.

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, let us not simply criticize the gift of Father Liber (Bacchus/Dionysus) as if it were an evil or unworthy to be received in a city. More could be said on this point, although I fear to praise the greatest good that Dionysus grants to many, for when men hear of it, they may not receive it rightly or understand it.

**CLINIAS.** What is that?

**ATHENIAN.** A certain rumor and fame has reached us that this god was once disturbed in his mind by the goddess Juno, and therefore, for the sake of vengeance, he introduced the Bacchic chorus and all madness, and gave wine for this very purpose. I leave such talk to those who think it safe to speak such things of the gods. I know this much: no animal is born with as much intelligence as it will need when grown. During the time before it possesses prudence, it is mad; it cries out without order, and when it gains strength, it exults in a disorderly way. We should remember that we called these the principles of music and gymnastics.

**CLINIAS.** We remember.

**ATHENIAN.** Did we not also say that the sense of rhythm and harmony was given to us alone from this principle? And that Apollo, the Muses, and Dionysus were given to us as leaders?

**CLINIAS.** Indeed.

**ATHENIAN.** Wine, then—though many say it was given to humans for vengeance to make them mad—is, according to our speech, a remedy and a medicine to the contrary: so that the soul may gain shame, and the body health and strength. [[margin: Why wine was given to men.]]

**CLINIAS.** Guest, you have commemorated the previous discourse excellently.

**ATHENIAN.** Half of what pertains to the *chorea* has now been said. Shall we complete the rest, or leave it?

**CLINIAS.** What parts do you mean, and how do you divide them?

**ATHENIAN.** The whole *chorea* was described by us as a universal discipline. One part of it is in the voice, through rhythm and harmony. [[margin: The whole chorus and its parts.]]

**CLINIAS.** So it is.

**ATHENIAN.** The other is in the motion of the body, through rhythm and figure. Rhythm is common to both the voice and the motion, but figure is proper to the body. In the first part, song is the motion of the voice.

**CLINIAS.** True.

**ATHENIAN.** But the habit of the voice that reaches the discipline of the soul's virtue, we have somehow named "Music."

**CLINIAS.** Very rightly.

**ATHENIAN.** If the motion of the body in play—which we call "Dance"—reaches the virtue of the body, let us call this skillful deduction of the body "Gymnastics."

**CLINIAS.** Most correctly.

**ATHENIAN.** Regarding Music, which we called the middle part of the *chorea*, we think enough has been said. Now let us speak of the rest.

**CLINIAS.** O best of men, you who converse with Cretans and Spartans! When Music has been sufficiently treated but Gymnastics not at all, what do you think either of us would respond?

**ATHENIAN.** I would affirm that you have already answered clearly by asking this. I understand that your question is both a response and a command to proceed with the matters pertaining to Gymnastics.

**CLINIAS.** You understood perfectly; please do so.

**ATHENIAN.** It must be done. It is not difficult to explain what is well known to both of you. You are much more skilled in this art than in the other.

**CLINIAS.** That is mostly true.

**ATHENIAN.** Is there not a principle for this play as well? Every animal by nature is accustomed to leap. But man, as we touched upon, having received a sense of rhythm, generated the Dance. Song likewise excites rhythm. The two joined together gave birth to the *chorea* and play.

**CLINIAS.** So it is.

**ATHENIAN.** We have completed one part; now we shall tackle the other.

**CLINIAS.** Entirely.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us conclude the discourse on the "Dionysian chorus" of drinking with this thought: If a city uses drinking parties as a serious matter and with the order of laws—for the sake of exercising temperance—and does not flee other pleasures but exercises so as to overcome them, then drinking should be used in this way. But if a city uses drinking merely as play, and allows anyone to drink whenever and with whomever they wish, I would not be of the opinion that such a city or man should ever indulge in drunkenness. I would much rather approve the law of the Carthaginians over the customs of the Cretans or Spartans: that no one in a military camp should ever taste wine, but only drink water. In the city, I would never allow a slave—male or female—to use wine; nor magistrates during their year of office; nor pilots and judges about to perform their duties; nor those deliberating on important matters. I would allow no wine during the day unless for physical exercise or sickness, nor at night for a man or woman intending to conceive children. 

Many other instances could be cited where men of right mind and law should abstain from wine. According to this reasoning, a city would not need many vineyards. Agriculture and the whole standard of living would maintain its order, and the use of wine would be the most moderate and spare. Thus, guests, let this be the *Colophon* (finishing stroke) to our discourse on wine.

**CLINIAS.** Well said. We agree.

---

# THE THIRD DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, OR, ON LEGISLATION.

### ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.

Just as a physician looks to the health of the body, so the author of laws looks to the health of the soul. Since it is more desirable for everyone to retain a prosperous health than to recover it once lost, the primary purpose of both the statesman and the physician is to preserve health—whether of body or soul. Their secondary counsel is to restore that health if it has been lost. For this reason, both in Plato’s view and in truth, those writers of laws are to be held in contempt who only determine how crimes already committed should be punished, but do not provide for how men should be born, nourished, and educated so that they have no desire to commit crimes. 

Therefore, let no one wonder that our Plato—zealous for the firmest health of the soul—dwells so accurately on many things in the *Laws* and the *Republic* that seem trivial, such as the education of boys and youths. It is fitting for the most diligent physician of souls to compose those newly born in such a way that they seem either born with firm health or, at least, that the health of the soul grows together with their youth. Hence that preceding diligence in the first and second books regarding every kind of music, play, and banquet. In discussing the office of the legislator, his primary concern is the study of children and adolescents. 

Remember with what caution he judged that the drinking of wine should be approached: that it is not permitted to drink every day, nor for everyone, nor according to anyone's lust, but only at solemn banquets—and then only for men, moderately, and under a judge. Remember also how much he approves that soldiers in camp, slaves in the city, magistrates, pilots, and judges should not taste wine during their service, nor men about to deliberate on great matters, nor a man or woman at the hour they intend to conceive children. 

Now let us proceed to the proper argument of the Third Book. Since the law of the city is the form of civil discipline, and the city itself is the form of the state, it is not out of place to discuss the beginning of the city and civilization. Plato wonders whether the human race has existed from eternity, and similarly the world. When he calls time "infinite," he does not necessarily mean without beginning or end in a strict sense, but rather infinite relative to our computation; he often calls time "inestimable" rather than "immense." In the sixth book, he remains ambiguous: either the generation of men never began, or it began an inestimable length of time before us. For a Christian, it is enough that the philosopher did not affirm the eternity of the world. 

Let us return to the matter of laws—the city and civilization. Four figures (stages) of civilization are counted. The first is immediately after a calamity of the human race, when a few seeds of it were saved by the benefit of high mountains or divine providence. Then, it is probable that sons and grandsons obeyed the power of the father of the family—a power consisting solely in the law of nature. The second figure is among several families gathered together by mutual need or fear of wild beasts. From this assembly, various forms of governing arose. Because of mutual injuries, they were forced to appoint common arbiters, judges, and rulers. Thus arose the third figure of civil discipline, drawing its origin from preceding injustice. These rulers likely prescribed common laws for the city after considering the most honorable laws of each household. The fourth figure is a kingdom of nations, where multiple cities agree on a common will and law.

Between these, poets are exhorted to sing divine things. The race of poets is said to be divine and moved by God. Authors of laws are also warned not to pass laws that are arduous or violent, but light and pleasant. Through a historical example, the main purpose of this dispute is followed: the best way to establish laws. This begins with the author looking toward the universal virtue of the citizens, especially the leader of all virtues—Prudence (Wisdom). No one doubts that other virtues are led by Prudence like limbs by a head. That all humans desire their affairs to succeed according to their wishes, and they think the one whose desires are met is most blessed. Plato, however, argues the opposite: the man whose desires are met daily will be most miserable unless he is endowed with prudence and moderation, so that he discerns true goods. 

He warns that we should not pray that all things follow our desire, but that our desire follows reason. He touches on the comparison of a son to a father and a father to God. A boy prays for many things he thinks are good, while his father prays they do not happen because they are harmful. Similarly, the Heavenly Father detests the vain and harmful prayers of men. There is no refuge from deceptive prayers except through Prudence. Therefore, the lawgiver must primarily focus on propagating prudence through civil souls. The perfection of prudence is such that it teaches what to wish for and how to use it profitably. In this lies the total happiness of the city. 

Just as prudence preserves a city, imprudence (which he calls ignorance) destroys it. Not ignorance of letters or arts, but ignorance of the Good. This is the most ruinous ignorance: when a man does not know how to temper his soul so that his senses obey the laws of his reason. Those blinded by such ignorance, even if they are brilliant and literate, are judged "ignorant" by Plato. But those who are temperate are judged "prudent" and "knowing," even if they are illiterate. He then forbids any magistrate from being given power if he does not know how to govern himself due to incontinence. He counts seven reasons for the dignity of command: Paternity, Nobility, Mastery, Power, Age, Prudence, and the Lot (chance). He chooses Prudence above all, saying it is the proper reason for the dignity of a ruler: that the more prudent should command and the less prudent obey. 

The law will provide that beyond childhood education, degrees of public office should be distributed according to degrees of prudence. To prevent the reckless exercise of power, he subjects everyone to the laws and joins kings with a senate. He will guard against "proud luxury" that desires power beyond the laws. He will strive to keep the body of the city free, prudent, and friendly. Free so it can consult for its country; prudent so it knows how; friendly so it wants to. This is best achieved in a city that holds a middle ground between the power of one and the power of the people—not entirely under one ruler or a few, nor accepting every person as a consultant, but combining the best of royal and popular governance. 

He notes that the ruin of cities often proceeds from the delicious and luxurious life of youth. Temperance must be honored above all. He forbids fortitude from being held without temperance, as it is dangerous. Finally, he teaches that the first degree of honor belongs to the soul (when mixed with temperance), the second to the goods of the body, and the third to external goods. He prohibits both excessive liberty and excessive slavery. Too much slavery removes the benevolence of the people toward the prince; too much liberty produces insolence, contempt for laws, sedition, and finally extreme slavery. No one should wonder that Plato makes much of music and games, as they have great power over the soul, just as air has over the body. He concludes with an epilogue regarding whether these discussions have contributed anything.

---

[[margin: The beginning of civil discipline.]]
Let these things be as they are. But what shall we say was the beginning of civil discipline? Can one not see it most easily and best from this point?

**CLINIAS.** From where?

**ATHENIAN.** From where the growth of cities toward both virtue and vice can be observed.

**CLINIAS.** And from where do you say that is?

**ATHENIAN.** I believe it is from the length and infinity of time, and the mutations of things within it.

**CLINIAS.** How so?

**ATHENIAN.** Come, tell me: since cities and civil institutions of men began, how much time has passed?

**CLINIAS.** That is not easy to say.

**ATHENIAN.** It is infinite and impossible to think.

**CLINIAS.** Quite so.

**ATHENIAN.** Have not innumerable cities been built and destroyed in this time? Have they not used every condition of civil life—becoming larger from smaller, smaller from larger, worse from better, and better from worse?

**CLINIAS.** That is necessary.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us think of the cause of this mutation, if we can. Perhaps it will show us the first cause and change of civil life.

**CLINIAS.** You speak well. You should explain your thoughts on this, and we shall listen attentively.

**ATHENIAN.** Do the ancient stories seem to have any truth in them?

**CLINIAS.** Which ones?

**ATHENIAN.** That many destructions of men have occurred from deluges, diseases, and many other things, from which few men survived.

**CLINIAS.** That also is very probable.

**ATHENIAN.** Come, let us look at one of these destructions caused by a flood.

**CLINIAS.** What should we think about this?

**ATHENIAN.** Surely those who escaped the slaughter were certain mountain shepherds, saved on the peaks of mountains—a few seeds preserved to propagate the human race.

**CLINIAS.** That is clear.

**ATHENIAN.** But they must have been unskilled in other arts and ignorant of the studies of avarice and contention among citizens, and of other deceits used against one another.

**CLINIAS.** That is consistent.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us assume that the cities in the plains and by the sea perished entirely at that time.

**CLINIAS.** Let us assume it.

**ATHENIAN.** We shall assert then that all instruments and whatever inventions of the arts—whether for civil discipline or any other faculty—collapsed at those times.

**CLINIAS.** For how, best of men, if these things had remained forever as they are now, could anything new be invented by anyone? For an incalculable multitude of years was unknown to them. Only a thousand or two thousand years have passed since anything was said to have been invented by Daedalus, or Orpheus, or Palamedes. Or music by Marsyas and Olympus, and the lyre by Amphion; and many other things were invented, so to speak, "yesterday and the day before."

**ATHENIAN.** Do you see, Clinias, that you have omitted a friend who was truly "of yesterday"?

**CLINIAS.** Do you mean Epimenides?

**ATHENIAN.** Him indeed. For he excelled everyone among you in the invention of new things. What Hesiod once divined in words, Epimenides himself perfected in fact, as you assert.

**CLINIAS.** We plainly assert it.

**ATHENIAN.** We believe a great and terrible desolation in human affairs occurred after that devastation. A vast magnitude of fertile fields was deserted, other animals were destroyed, and barely the kind of goats and cattle remained—and those were rare—upon which men lived by herding.

**CLINIAS.** Who doubts it?

**ATHENIAN.** Regarding the city, civil discipline, and laws—of which we are now speaking—do we think there was even any memory of them?

**CLINIAS.** None at all.

**ATHENIAN.** Is it not from those conditions that all these things came to us: cities, civil disciplines, arts, laws, and a great supply of both vice and virtue?

**CLINIAS.** How do you mean?

**ATHENIAN.** Do we think, wonderful man, that those humans—ignorant of many things considered honorable or shameful among citizens—existed at the height of virtue or vice?

**CLINIAS.** You have spoken well, and we understand what you mean.

**ATHENIAN.** As time progressed and the human race multiplied, everything advanced to the state we see now.

**CLINIAS.** Very correctly.

**ATHENIAN.** Yet not suddenly, but gradually over a long period of time.

**CLINIAS.** That is very fitting.

**ATHENIAN.** For a fresh fear prevented them from descending from the mountain peaks into the plains.

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** And because of their scarcity in those times, did they not rejoice at the sight of one another? Especially since travel by land or sea was not easy; almost all instruments for travel had been destroyed along with the arts. Therefore, I think they could not easily meet. For iron, bronze, and all metals had perished in confusion, so they could not be found or brought into the light. Thus there were no workers of wood. Even if some instrument had been left on the mountains, it quickly wore away and vanished; others could not be made until the art of metallurgy was rediscovered by men.

**CLINIAS.** For how else could it have happened?

**ATHENIAN.** How many generations later do we think that occurred?

**CLINIAS.** Surely many.

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, all arts that use iron, bronze, and such materials were buried in the darkness of ignorance for the same long period.

**CLINIAS.** That is certain.

**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, there was neither sedition nor war at that time.

**CLINIAS.** For what reason?

**ATHENIAN.** First, because they embraced each other with burning benevolence due to their solitude. Second, because food did not incite war. There was no lack of pasture, except perhaps for a few at the very beginning. They lived mostly on pasturage in those times. There was no lack of milk and meat. Hunting provided food, and not bad food at that. They also had a supply of clothing, bedding, housing, and vessels—both those needing fire and those not. For the arts of molding and weaving do not require iron; by the nod of God, we possess these so that if men ever fall into such calamity, they can propagate the human race. For this reason, they were not very poor, nor were they compelled to war by poverty. They could not become rich either, since they had neither gold nor silver. 

In any gathering of men where there is neither poverty nor riches, the most just morals will be present. For there, neither insolence nor injury has a place. Rivalry and envy are also far away. They were good for these reasons, and especially because of their simplicity. Whatever they heard was honorable or shameful, they believed to be true because of their simplicity and obeyed the warnings. No one, out of an opinion of their own wisdom (as happens now), suspected a lie; but believing what was said of gods and men to be true, they quietly ordered their lives. They were entirely such as we described just now.

**CLINIAS.** I and my companion agree with you on this.

**ATHENIAN.** We said that many generations living this way had less skill than those before the flood or those today—both in other arts and in the military arts practiced today on land and sea. They also lacked the knowledge of trials and seditions that strive to inflict injury on others by word and deed. They were simpler, braver, more modest, and more just in all things. We have already stated the cause of this.

**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly.

**ATHENIAN.** Let these things be said, and let what follows be explained so we may understand why they needed laws and who established them.

**CLINIAS.** Well said.

**ATHENIAN.** Did they not need legislators, nor had it yet become customary to have them? For the men of that time did not yet have letters, but lived following the customs and morals of their ancestors.

**CLINIAS.** That is likely. But what was their mode of civil discipline?

**ATHENIAN.** This.

**CLINIAS.** Which?

**ATHENIAN.** It seems to me everyone calls the civil discipline of that time *δυνάστειαν* (dynasteian), that is, autocracy or the power of chiefs, which even now flourishes in many places among both Greeks and Barbarians. Homer testifies that this existed in the habitation of the Cyclopes: [[margin: Odyssey i.]] "They never meet for public counsel, nor to hold trials; but inhabit hollow caves on high mountains, and each gives laws privately to his wives and children, disregarding public matters."

**CLINIAS.** This poet seems charming to you. We have seen some of his other works, which are quite sophisticated, though not many. We Cretans do not use foreign poetry much.

**MEGILLUS.** But we Spartans use it. This poet seems to excel, although he mostly explains an Ionian life rather than a Laconic (Spartan) one. He seems to testify well to your words here, having reduced the antiquity of men to a wild way of living through his fables.

**CLINIAS.** Indeed.

**ATHENIAN.** He certainly testifies. Therefore, induced by his testimony, let us believe that such governments once occurred.

**MEGILLUS.** Correct.

**ATHENIAN.** Do these governments not arise from those men who live dispersed in individual habitations and families because of the need created by the devastations? In these, the eldest always rules, because the principle of authority comes from the father and mother. Following them like a flock of birds, they form a single group, using the paternal will for law and governed by the most just of all kingships.

**MEGILLUS.** Exactly.

**ATHENIAN.** Afterward, many flowing together in common establish larger cities. They turn first to agriculture at the foot of the mountains and build enclosures like the walls of cities to protect against wild beasts, building one large and common house.

**MEGILLUS.** That seems likely.

**ATHENIAN.** And what of this? Is it not also likely?

**MEGILLUS.** What?

**ATHENIAN.** When these larger habitations are made from the smaller ones, each of the small ones brings with it its own senior prince and its own customs—because they lived separately and therefore received different customs from different parents and educators. They were accustomed to their own ways of honoring the gods and managing themselves—the more modest from the modest, the braver from the brave—according to how each had educated their sons and grandsons. They brought these rites like their own laws to the larger habitation.

**MEGILLUS.** What prevents it?

**ATHENIAN.** And it is necessary that each person's own laws please them most, while the laws of others are secondary.

**MEGILLUS.** So it is.

**ATHENIAN.** But we seem now to have entered into the very cradle and beginning of laws.

**MEGILLUS.** Indeed.

**ATHENIAN.** After this, it is necessary that those who meet should choose some among themselves to commonly oversee the institutions of all. They would present those they most approved of to the common leaders of the people, like kings. Those who established these approved laws will be called "legislators." By establishing an aristocracy or some kind of kingdom from these powers, they will agree on this change of civil discipline.

**MEGILLUS.** That will certainly happen in a natural succession.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us now name the third figure of civil discipline, in which all species and conditions of republics and cities are found.

**MEGILLUS.** Which is that?

**ATHENIAN.** It is surely the one Homer signified after the second became third: [[margin: Iliad. v.]] "He then built the Dardanian land. For the sacred walls of Ilium (Troy) were not yet erected on the plains to be a city of many nations; but they inhabited the foot of Mount Ida of many springs." Surely these verses and those about the Cyclopes were written divinely and according to nature itself. For the race of poets is divine; it is moved by God and sings sacred hymns. Thus, with the Muses and Graces, they often touch upon the truth.

**MEGILLUS.** Greatly so.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us follow the preceding fable then. Perhaps something will become clear from it regarding what we want. Should we not do so?

**MEGILLUS.** By all means.

**ATHENIAN.** We were saying that Troy was built from higher places in a large and beautiful plain, on a hill that was not high, where many rivers flowed down from Ida.

**MEGILLUS.** So it is handed down.

**ATHENIAN.** Do we not think this was done a long time after the flood?

**MEGILLUS.** Who would not think so?

**ATHENIAN.** A great oblivion of that devastation seems to have seized them when they built a city near many rivers flowing from high places and trusted themselves to small hills.

**MEGILLUS.** Thus it is clear they were many centuries after the destruction of the flood.

**ATHENIAN.** Many other cities were inhabited then, as the human race had already spread further.

**MEGILLUS.** Why not?

**ATHENIAN.** Those which, of course, also fought against Troy—perhaps even by sea, as if everyone then used it fearlessly.

**MEGILLUS.** It appears so.

**ATHENIAN.** The Achaeans, besieging Troy for ten years, overthrew it.

**MEGILLUS.** Plainly.

**ATHENIAN.** In those ten years while Troy was besieged, many things happened at home to the Achaeans because of the seditions of the youth. They did not receive the returning soldiers honorably or justly; many were killed and many sent into exile. Those who were expelled returned [[margin: Origin of the Dorians]] and were called Dorians instead of Achaeans, named after a certain Dorus by whom the exiles were gathered and restored. You Lacedaemonians tell all these stories.

**MEGILLUS.** Without a doubt.

**ATHENIAN.** When we began this discourse on laws, we digressed into a dispute about music and drinking. Now, finally, as if by divine guidance, our speech has returned to the same point and given us a handle. It has fallen upon that civil discipline which you assert was established in Sparta and Crete as if by brotherly laws. We have gained this much from the digression: while we passed through the civil disciplines and habitations of cities, we observed the first, second, and third cities, one depending on the other over a very long span of time. Now this fourth city comes to us—or if you wish, this fourth race of men—which once inhabited some place and still inhabits it now. If from all this we can understand what was well established or otherwise, and what laws preserve them and what corruptions destroy them, and what kind of change in civil institutions makes a city blessed, then we shall consider our task done. All these things, I say, must be treated again as if from the beginning, unless perhaps we reject what has been said.

**MEGILLUS.** Guest, if some god promised us that if we tackle the dispute on the laying down of laws again, we would hear no fewer or worse things than what has been said, I would make a long journey for this cause. This day would seem short to me, though the days are now turning from the summer solstice toward winter.

**ATHENIAN.** Should these things be considered then?

**MEGILLUS.** Most certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us grasp in our thought those times in which Lacedaemon, Argos, and Messene, and all things joined to them, were subject to your ancestors, Megillus. For then it was decided—as it is said in the story—that the army being divided into three parts, they would inhabit three cities: Argos, Messene, and Lacedaemon.

**MEGILLUS.** So it was done.

**ATHENIAN.** And Temenus was made king of Argos, Cresphontes of Messene, and Eurysthenes and Procles of Lacedaemon.

**MEGILLUS.** Yes.

**ATHENIAN.** They all swore that they would be an enemy to anyone who attempted to devastate the kingdom of any of them.

**MEGILLUS.** Plainly.

**ATHENIAN.** Tell me, by Jupiter, are kingdoms or powers ever overthrown by others, or by themselves? When we fell into this speech earlier, did we think that was the case, and now we have forgotten?

**MEGILLUS.** Not at all.

**ATHENIAN.** Shall we not confirm the same thing now? We are reminded of it by the history of the deeds we have encountered. We shall not revolve our speech around something vain, since we speak of a true and performed deed. These three kingdoms and three cities governed by kings swore together to laws regarding commanding and obeying: the kings swore that they would not rule more violently as time and lineage progressed, and the people swore that if the kings kept their oath, they would never undermine the kingdoms, but would defend them if anyone attacked. Kings also swore to kings and peoples, and peoples to peoples and kings, binding themselves by oath to repel mutual injuries. Was it not so?

**MEGILLUS.** Entirely.

**ATHENIAN.** And what is greatest in establishing civil discipline was present to those three cities, whether kings or others brought the laws.

**MEGILLUS.** What was that?

**ATHENIAN.** That two should rise up together against the one that transgressed the established laws.

**MEGILLUS.** That is manifest.

**ATHENIAN.** Many also prescribe to legislators that they should bring laws such as the multitude and the people will freely receive—as if one were to command gymnastic masters or physicians to treat bodies with pleasure and heal them pleasantly.

**MEGILLUS.** Exactly so.

**ATHENIAN.** Yet it often goes beautifully if one restores good habit and health to bodies with a little distress.

**MEGILLUS.** Why not?

**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, this was no small aid to them in the ease of making laws.

**MEGILLUS.** What was that?

**ATHENIAN.** Those legislators who were creating an equality of honors did not face that greatest difficulty which usually happens to many cities when they meet to form a law: the desire to disturb the possession of fields and introduce "new tables" (the cancellation of debts). They see that equality cannot be achieved without these. Against anyone who tries to move such things, everyone cries out "not to move the unmovable." They curse the one dividing fields and introducing new tables so that he does not know where to turn. But the Dorians did not have this difficulty or turmoil. They possessed the fields abundantly without controversy, and their debts were not already old or great.

**MEGILLUS.** You tell the truth.

**ATHENIAN.** Why then, best of men, did that constitution and legislation fail them so badly?

**MEGILLUS.** How so? What was the fault?

**ATHENIAN.** Because of the three city constitutions, two quickly lost both their civil discipline and their laws, and only your city was left.

**MEGILLUS.** Your question is not easy to answer.

**ATHENIAN.** Yet we must consider it now, playing a certain "elderly and modest game" of laws, so that we may complete this journey without distress.

**MEGILLUS.** It must be done as you say.

**ATHENIAN.** Can we have a more beautiful consideration of laws than of these laws that adorned such cities? Or think of more honorable and greater city institutions than these?

**MEGILLUS.** One would not easily prefer others to these.

**ATHENIAN.** No one will doubt that they, being so joined, believed they could defend not only the Peloponnesus but indeed all Greece if any Barbarian brought injury, excited by the example of the Trojans who, relying on the Assyrian power that took its origin from Ninus, stirred up war against them. For the power of that principality was still not to be held in contempt. Just as we now fear the Great King (of Persia), so everyone then dreaded the power of those nations conspiring into one. The second destruction of Troy brought great envy upon them. For Troy's power was a certain part of the Assyrian principality. Therefore, against that power, the army divided into three cities by the brothers, the sons of Hercules then reigning, seemed to be excellently and most formally arranged—much better equipped than the one that besieged Troy. First, they believed they had better leaders in the Heraclidae than the Pelopidae (the house of Agamemnon); then, they believed this army was superior in virtue to the one that sought Troy. For these had conquered, while the others had been surpassed—the Achaeans by the Dorians. Do we not believe they thought this, and for that reason prepared themselves?

**MEGILLUS.** Entirely.

**ATHENIAN.** It is likely they thought this constitution of theirs would be firm and last a long time, especially since they had undergone many dangers and labors together and were governed by brother kings. Moreover, they had used many prophets, including the Delphic Apollo.

**MEGILLUS.** Very likely.

**ATHENIAN.** But these things, which they thought would be greatest, soon vanished, as it seems, except for the small part that inhabits your region. This part has never ceased to be at war against the other two parts down to this day. For if the constitution then made had remained in concord, it would surely have been invincible in war.

**MEGILLUS.** Why not?

**ATHENIAN.** How then and for what reason was it dissolved? Does it not appear worthy of consideration what fortune overthrew such a great constitution?

**MEGILLUS.** Surely no one, neglecting these things, will ever be able to understand other laws or republics by which great and beautiful things are preserved or, on the contrary, lost.

**ATHENIAN.** We seem to have luckily fallen upon this most suitable consideration.

**MEGILLUS.** Greatly so.

**ATHENIAN.** Is it not then, wonderful man, that our error remains hidden from us all, especially in the present, while we think we have perceived a singular thing, and what marvelous outcomes will follow if one knows how to use it in the proper way? But we perhaps do not feel correctly or according to nature about this; and all others err in everything they think about in a similar way.

**MEGILLUS.** What are you saying? And about what do you say this most?

**ATHENIAN.** I just laughed at myself, good man. For when I considered that army of which we just spoke, it seemed truly excellent and wonderful, destined to perform noble deeds for the Greeks if someone had used it well.

**MEGILLUS.** Did you not speak prudently, and did we not praise you rightly?

**ATHENIAN.** Perhaps. But I think everyone who sees something great and endowed with immense power immediately feels that if the one who possesses it knew how to use such a great thing, he would be happy for the many noble deeds done through it.

**MEGILLUS.** Is that not correct? Or what do you say?

**ATHENIAN.** Consider now toward what the person who so praises individual things is looking, so that he may speak correctly. First, regarding what we were saying, how if those who then presided had known how to order the army correctly, they would have happily used the occasion: if they had established a safer one then, they would have always preserved it, so that they themselves would be free and could subjugate others as they wished. They and their descendants would have obtained whatever they desired among both Greeks and Barbarians. Did they not desire everything for the sake of this?

**MEGILLUS.** Indeed, very much so.

**ATHENIAN.** Whoever then looks upon vast riches, or the excellent honors of a high birth, or anything of the sort, would say the same—looking toward this, as if through these things everything he desires, or the most and greatest, would come to him.

**MEGILLUS.** So it seems.

**ATHENIAN.** There is surely one common desire of all men, which our present speech has signified.

**MEGILLUS.** Which?

**ATHENIAN.** That all things, or at least human things, be carried out according to the desire of one's own soul. [[margin: One should not pray that all things follow our will, but that our will follows our prudence.]]

**MEGILLUS.** Who doubts it?

**ATHENIAN.** Since we all always want this—in childhood, adulthood, and old age—we surely pray diligently to have it.

**MEGILLUS.** Indeed.

**ATHENIAN.** We also pray for these things for our friends, which they would pray for themselves.

**MEGILLUS.** And this too.

**ATHENIAN.** A friend is a son to his father, a boy to a man.

**MEGILLUS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** But of those things which the boy prays will happen to him, the father prays to the gods that many will not happen.

**MEGILLUS.** Do you say that happens when the son who prays is young and senseless?

**ATHENIAN.** Yes, and even when the father—whether old or quite young—knows nothing of what is honorable or just, and is so affected as Theseus was toward the unhappy Hippolytus, he prays intensely, while the son knows better. Do you think the son will then pray for the same things as his father?

**MEGILLUS.** I understand what you mean. You seem to be saying that one should not pray or strive for all things to follow our will, but for our will to follow our prudence. Both the city and individuals should pray and strive for this: to have a mind.

**ATHENIAN.** That is exactly what I say. Moreover, a statesman who is a legislator should always look toward this in making laws. I have remembered this, and I want you to remember it now. In the beginning of our dispute, you said that a good legislator should refer everything to war. I, however, said that he should refer to only one virtue—though there are four—not only to one, but to all: especially to the first, which is the leader of all others. This is Prudence (Wisdom), and intellect, and opinion, along with the love and desire following it. 

Our speech returns to the same point. And I who then said those things, say the same now, whether in jest or in earnest. I assert that it is not safe to use a prayer and to obtain what you pray for if you do not have a mind; rather, it is better for the opposite of what you ask to happen. If you want to think these things are spoken in earnest, think so. For I hope to persuade you of what we proposed just before: that the cause of the destruction of kings and of the dissolution of that whole constitution was not cowardice, nor ignorance of military matters by the princes or subjects, but all other wickedness—and especially ignorance regarding the greatest human affairs. That these things so happened then, and if they happen anywhere now or in the future, they will occur in no other way, I shall try—as reason will show hereafter—to find out and explain to you as friends.

**CLINIAS.** To praise you with words, Guest, would be troublesome; we shall praise you by our actions, by listening to what you say—for in this, the liberal and true praiser is most clearly seen.

**ATHENIAN.** Excellent, Clinias. Therefore, let us do what you say.

**CLINIAS.** It shall be so, if God wills. You speak now.

**ATHENIAN.** We judge then, proceeding along the path of this dispute, that the greatest ignorance was the cause of that power being destroyed, and similar outcomes of affairs now proceed from the same cause. Therefore, if this is so, the legislator should strive to give prudence to the citizens as much as possible, and take away ignorance.

**CLINIAS.** That is manifest.

**ATHENIAN.** What then shall rightly be called the "greatest ignorance"? Consider if you agree with me. I judge it to be this. [[margin: What is the greatest ignorance of citizens]]

**CLINIAS.** What?

**ATHENIAN.** When someone does not love what seems honorable or good to him, but hates it; and what is evil and unjust, he loves and embraces. I assert that this dissension of pleasure and pain against the opinion that follows reason is the *extreme ignorance*. I also call it the "greatest" because it is in the multitude (lower part) of the soul. For that part in it which is enslaved to pains and pleasures is like the common people and the multitude of a city. Therefore, when the soul is adverse to the science, or opinion, or reason that by nature should rule, I call this "ignorance." This applies to a city when the multitude does not obey the princes and laws, and also to an individual man when—even if there are good reasons in the soul—nothing is carried out according to them, but everything is done to the contrary. I assert that these ignorances are the most ruinous to a city and to any citizen—not the ignorance of craftsmen, if you understand what I say, guests.

**CLINIAS.** We understand these things, friend, and we concede them.

**ATHENIAN.** Let it be held as settled, then: nothing pertaining to rule should be committed to those citizens who are ignorant in this way. Rather, they should be rebuked as ignorant, even if they are most sharp and eloquent, and have grasped everything pertaining to the ornament and sharpness of the mind. Those who are affected in the opposite way are to be held as wise—even if they do not know their letters (as it is said), [[margin: A proverb]] nor know how to swim. Rule should be committed to them as to the prudent. For how, my friends, can even the smallest species of prudence consist without concord?

**CLINIAS.** In no way.

**ATHENIAN.** But the most beautiful and greatest of all concords shall rightly be called the "greatest wisdom." He who must live according to reason must be a participant in this. Whoever is devoid of it is the overthrower of his own house and never the preserver of a city, but on the contrary, he will always seem ignorant of these things. Let these points be as we have just said.

**CLINIAS.** Quite so.

**ATHENIAN.** Should there not be rulers and subjects in cities?

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** Very well. What and how many are the reasons for the dignity of commanding and obeying, both in large and small cities and in private homes? [[margin: Seven dignities of commanding.]] Is not the first right reason of dignity that father and mother—and parents generally—should command their offspring everywhere?

**CLINIAS.** Most especially.

**ATHENIAN.** Second, that the noble rule over the ignoble? Third, that the older rule over the younger?

**CLINIAS.** And this.

**ATHENIAN.** Fourth, that masters rule over slaves?

**CLINIAS.** Without a doubt.

**ATHENIAN.** Fifth, that the more powerful should dominate and the weaker should serve?

**CLINIAS.** You have just described a very necessary kind of rule.

**ATHENIAN.** Indeed, and one that—as the Theban Pindar says—is found most abundantly and according to nature in all animals. But the greatest dignity...
