336 Book Twenty-Ninth.

...I think it is right. Furthermore, you will only have cleared yourself before us if you can also persuade us of what you say." "I will certainly try," he said. "But let us listen to Crito first. For he has seemed to want to say something for a long time." "What else do you think it is, Socrates," said Crito, "except what the man who is to give you the poison has been telling me for a while? He says you should be warned to speak as little as possible. He claims that those who engage in debate become too heated, and that such heat is not good for those about to drink the poison <note>The executioner is concerned that the physiological effects of an intense argument might interfere with the hemlock's efficacy</note>. Otherwise, those who do so are sometimes forced to drink the poison twice, or even three times." Then Socrates said, "Let him be. Just let him prepare his task as if he were to provide it twice, or if necessary, three times." "I knew that would be your answer," Crito said, "but he has been bothering me about it for a while." "Let him be," he said.

"Now, O judges, I wish to give you my account of why it seems to me that a man who has devoted himself to philosophy throughout his life is right to face imminent death with great confidence and good hope, believing that he will obtain the greatest blessings there after he has departed from here. How this is so, O Simmias and Cebes, I will try to explain.

Whoever handles philosophy correctly seems to prove to others that they are doing nothing else but practicing how to die, and how to be dead <note>Original: "nihil aliud ipsi commentarentur quàm mori, atq; esse mortuos." This is the famous Socratic definition of philosophy as a 'preparation for death.'</note>. If this is true, it would be absurd if they were to grieve when that very thing arrives which they have been studying and practicing for their whole lives." Here Simmias smiled and said, "By Jove, Socrates, you made me laugh when I had little desire to do so. For I think many people, upon hearing this, would think it a very fitting description of philosophers; and our own people would heartily agree that philosophers truly are dying, and that they are not unaware that philosophers deserve to suffer this very thing."

"They might be right, Simmias, except for the part about them not being 'unaware.' For it escapes them in what way true philosophers both strive to die and are worthy of death. But let us leave those people aside and speak to ourselves. Do we think death is something?" "Certainly something," said Simmias. "Is it anything else," he asked, "than the release of the soul from the body? And that to be dead is this: the body, released from the soul, exists by itself separately? And the soul, released from the body, exists by itself separately? Is death anything other than this?" "Nothing else," said Simmias. "Consider, then, good man, if you and I see this the same way; for from this I think we will more clearly understand what we are investigating. Does it seem to you to be the duty of a philosopher to pursue those things called pleasures, such as those of food and drink?" "Not at all, Socrates," he said. "What about the pleasures of love <note>Refers to sexual pleasures</note>?" "In no way," he said.

"What about the rest of the body's care? Do you think a philosopher makes much of it? For instance, having fine clothes, shoes, and other ornaments for the body—do you think he values them highly, or ignores them, except as far as great necessity forces their use?" "It seems to me," Simmias said, "the true philosopher holds these all of little account." "Does it not seem to you," he asked, "that such a man's focus is not on the body at all, but as much as possible, he turns away from it and toward the soul?" "It does to me," said Simmias. "Is it not clear, then, that in such matters the philosopher, more than other men, manifests the separation of the soul as much as possible from communion with the body?" "It appears so," he said. "Yet most people, Simmias, think that a man who finds no sweetness in such things and does not enjoy them does not truly live; they consider him almost dead, since he does not care for the pleasures of the body." "You speak the truth," he said.

"But what about the acquisition of wisdom itself? Is the body an obstacle if one takes it along as a partner in the search, or not? What I mean is this: Do sight and hearing have any truth for humans? Or is it as the poets always sing, that we hear nothing and see nothing accurately? <note>Socrates is questioning whether human senses provide true knowledge or just distorted perceptions.</note> And if these bodily senses are not accurate or certain, then neither are the others, for they are all somewhat inferior to these. Do you not think so?" "Entirely," he said. "When then," he asked, "does the soul grasp the truth? For whenever it tries to investigate something with the body, it is clearly deceived by the body." "You speak truly," he said. "Is it not in reasoning, if anywhere at all, that some of the things that truly exist become manifest to it?" "Yes," he said. "But it reasons best when none of these things disturb it—neither hearing, nor sight, nor pain, nor pleasure—but when it retires as much as possible into itself, leaving the body behind and, as far as possible, neither communicating with it nor touching it, it reaches out for that which truly is." "That is so," he said. "In this, then, Simmias, the soul of the philosopher most despises the body, flees from it, and seeks to live by itself?" "It appears so," he said.

"What about these things, Simmias? Do we say that Justice itself is something, or nothing?" "Something, by Jove!" he said. "And Beauty itself and Goodness itself?" "Why not?" "Have you ever perceived any of these with your eyes?" "Never," he said. "Or have you touched them with any other bodily sense? I am speaking of all such things—like Greatness itself, Health, Strength, and in short, the essence of all other things—that is, what each thing is. Is their truest nature perceived through the body? Or is it that whoever among us prepares himself to think most deeply and accurately about the thing he is investigating will come closest to knowing it?" "Entirely so." "Would he not do this most purely who approaches each thing with thought alone, neither using sight in his thinking nor dragging any other sense into his reasoning? Instead, using pure thought by itself, he would strive to hunt down each pure reality by itself, as much as possible free from eyes, ears, and in short, the whole body, as it disturbs the soul and does not permit it to attain truth and wisdom when it is in communion with it? Is it not this person, Simmias, if anyone, who will reach that which truly is?" "You speak wonderfully, Socrates," said Simmias.

"Does it not necessarily follow from all this that a certain opinion must remain with true philosophers, so that they say such things among themselves? 'A sort of path of reason seems to lead us to this consideration: as long as we have the body, and our soul is mixed with such an evil, we will never abundantly possess what we desire. For the body provides almost innumerable obstacles because of its necessary nourishment. Furthermore, diseases falling upon us from it hinder the investigation of truth; it fills us with loves, desires, fears, and various images, and many trifles, so that it is truly said that it never permits us to be wise in anything. For nothing else but the body and its desires incite wars, seditions, and battles...

--- Page 353 ---
Phædo, or, On the Soul. 337.

...incite them. For all wars arise for the sake of money. And we are forced to seek money for the sake of the body, being slaves to its care. Thus it happens that because of all these things we are distracted from the study of philosophy. The final blow of all is that, if we happen to get any leisure from it and turn ourselves to considering something, it constantly throws itself in our way as we investigate, disturbing us with a certain tumult and, as if striking us, it renders us stunned, so that hindered by this obstacle, we cannot perceive the truth. But it has truly been demonstrated to us that if we are ever to know anything purely, we must withdraw from the body and consider the things themselves with the soul itself. And then, as it appears, we shall obtain what we desire and of which we profess ourselves lovers—namely, wisdom—only when we are dead, as our argument indicates, but not while we live.

For if nothing can be purely discerned with the body, one of two things must be: either we can never attain knowledge, or only after death. For then the soul itself will be by itself, separate from the body, but not before. And while we live, it seems we shall come closest to knowledge if we have the minimum possible commerce with the body, and do not communicate with it except as far as extreme necessity requires. We must not be filled with its nature, but guard against its contagion until God himself releases us. And thus being pure and liberated from the foolishness of the body, we shall likely be with others like ourselves, and we shall know through ourselves everything that is pure—which is perhaps the truth itself. For it is not permitted for the impure to touch the pure. Such things, Simmias, I think all who truly desire to learn must say to one another and believe. Do you not think so?" "Most definitely of all things, Socrates."

"If these things are true, my friend, there is great hope that for him who reaches the place where I am now going, if anywhere else, he will abundantly obtain that for which we have undertaken so much trouble in this present life. Therefore, I undertake this migration imposed on me at present with good hope; and so will any other man who believes his mind is prepared, as if purified." "Quite so," said Simmias. "And does not purification," he said, "consist in what we were saying a while ago: namely, to separate the soul from the body as much as possible? And to accustom it to gather and collect itself from every part of the body, and so (as much as it can) to dwell alone by itself both in the present time and in the future, as if released from the chains of the body?" "Exactly," he said. "Is this not called death: the release and separation of the soul from the body?" "Entirely," he said. "And to release it, as we agree, is the constant and primary aim of those who practice philosophy. This very thing is the meditation of philosophers: to release and separate the soul from the body. Is it not so?" "So it seems."

"Therefore, as I was saying at the beginning, would it not be ridiculous if a man who so prepared himself in life that he lived as close to death as possible, were then to be indignant when death arrived? Would that not be ridiculous?" "How could it not be?" "In truth then, Simmias, those who philosophize correctly practice dying, and death is to them the least terrifying of all things. Consider it this way: If they everywhere despise the body and desire to have the soul itself by itself, would it not be the height of absurdity if, when this happens, they were to be terrified and bear it poorly, rather than going gladly to the place where there is hope of obtaining what they loved in life—and they loved wisdom—and of being liberated from that which they bore with annoyance? Many have been willing to go to the underworld of their own accord when their boyfriends, wives, or children died, hoping to see them there and be with those they loved. Shall a true lover of wisdom, who has been strongly led by this very hope that he will find it nowhere worthily except in the underworld, be grieved at death and not migrate there gladly? One must believe, my friend, that if he is truly a philosopher, this opinion will be very strong in him: that he will find pure wisdom nowhere else but there. If this is so, would it not be, as I just said, entirely against reason if such a man feared death?" "By Jove," said Simmias, "it would be against reason."

"Sufficient proof then," he said, "if you see someone grieving at death, will be that he is not a philosopher but a <term>philosomaton</term> <note>original Greek: φιλοσώματον — a lover of the body</note>, and likely also a <term>philochrematon</term> <note>original Greek: φιλοχρήματον — a lover of money</note> and a <term>philotimon</term> <note>original Greek: φιλότιμον — a lover of honor</note>, or someone who pursues one or both of these." "It is exactly as you say," he said. "Therefore, Simmias, what is called 'fortitude'—does it not especially belong to such men?" "Most certainly," he said. "And 'temperance' (which even the many say consists in not being a slave to desires, but despising them and keeping oneself modest)—does this not belong only to those who despise the body most and live in philosophy?" "It must be so," he said.

"For if you were to consider the fortitude and temperance of others, it would seem very absurd to you." "In what way, Socrates?" "You know that everyone else considers death one of the greatest evils." "Very much so," he said. "Is it not, then, out of fear of greater evils that those among them who are 'brave' endure death, when they do endure it?" "Indeed." "So everyone except philosophers is brave through fear and dread—though it is absurd for someone to be brave through fear or cowardice." "Certainly." "And what about those among them called 'moderate'? Is it not the same? Are they not temperate through a kind of intemperance? Though we say that is impossible, a similar state happens to them in their foolish temperance. Fearing they will be deprived of other pleasures which they desire, they abstain from some because they are overcome by others. Even though they call it 'intemperance' to be overcome by pleasures, it happens to them that by being overcome by pleasures, they overcome other pleasures. Now this is similar to what was just said: that they become temperate in a way through intemperance." "It is indeed similar."

"But look, blessed Simmias, whether this is the right path to virtue: to trade pleasures for pleasures, pains for pains, and fear for fear, the greater for the smaller, as if they were coins. Perhaps the only right 'coin' for which all these things should be exchanged is wisdom <note>original: "prudentia" - often used for the Greek "phronesis" (practical wisdom)</note>. In this, and with this, all things are truly bought and sold: fortitude, temperance, justice, and in short, true virtue exists with wisdom, whether pleasures and fears are present or absent. But if they are exchanged for one another apart from wisdom, such virtue is a mere shadow-painting, truly slavish, possessing nothing healthy or true. True virtue is actually a purification from all these things: temperance, justice, fortitude, and wisdom itself is a kind of purification. Therefore, those who established the Mysteries <note>Refers to ancient religious initiations, like the Eleusinian Mysteries</note> for us seem not to be contemptible, but have long been secretly warning us that whoever goes to the underworld unexpiated and uninitiated...

--- Page 354 ---
338 Book Twenty-Ninth.

...shall lie in the mud; but he who arrives there purified and initiated shall dwell with the gods. For as they say in the mysteries: 'Many are the thyrse-bearers, but few are the Bacchants.' <note>A 'thyrse' was a wand carried by followers of Bacchus/Dionysus. This proverb means that many people participate in the outward rituals, but few truly achieve the spiritual state of the god.</note> These Bacchants, in my opinion, are none other than those who have philosophized correctly. To be numbered among them, I have left nothing undone in my life, as much as was in my power, but have striven in every way. Whether I have striven correctly or achieved anything, we shall know for certain once we arrive there, if God wills, in a little while, as it seems to me.

This, then, is the defense I offer, Simmias and Cebes, as to why I do not take it hard or feel indignant to leave you and my masters here. For I hope that there, no less than here, I shall find good masters and friends. Most people do not believe this. If, therefore, my defense has been more persuasive to you than to the Athenian judges, it is well."

When Socrates had said this, Cebes took up the conversation and said: "Socrates, the rest of what you said seems correct to me. But regarding the soul itself, men have great doubts. They fear that when the soul is separated from the body, it may no longer exist anywhere, but may perish on the very day a man dies. They fear that as soon as it is separated from the body, it is dissolved and vanishes like wind or smoke, and is no longer anything at all. Certainly, if it were collected somewhere into itself, and liberated from those evils you just described, there would be great and beautiful hope, Socrates, that what you said is true. But perhaps it requires no small persuasion and faith to believe that the soul survives after the death of the man, and that it possesses some power and intelligence."

"You speak the truth, Cebes," said Socrates. "But what do you think should be done? Shall we talk about these very things—whether it is probable that it is so, or otherwise?" "I would gladly hear," said Cebes, "what you think about these matters." "I do not think," said Socrates, "that anyone hearing this, even a comic poet, would say that I am talking nonsense or speaking of things I should not. If it pleases you, we should consider it in this way: whether the souls of the dead are in the underworld or not.

There is an ancient discourse <note>Often referred to as the 'Ancient Argument' or 'Palaios Logos,' suggesting a traditional or Orphic belief in reincarnation</note> that we remember, stating that souls which depart from here exist there, and return here again, and are born from the dead. And if this is true—that the living are born again from the dead—then our souls must be there. For they could not be born again if they did not exist. This is a sufficient proof that it is so, if it is clearly established that the living are produced from nowhere else but from the dead. But if that is not the case, another argument will be needed." "Entirely," said Cebes.

"If you want to understand this more clearly," he said, "do not consider it only in humans, but in all animals and plants, and in short, in everything that is born. Let us see if everything is produced in this way: opposites from their opposites, wherever such a thing occurs. For instance, 'beautiful' is somewhat opposite to 'ugly,' and 'just' to 'unjust,' and we see many other such things. Let us consider whether it is necessary that whatever has an opposite is produced from nowhere else but its own opposite. For example, when something becomes greater, must it not have been smaller before it became greater?" "Yes." "And if it becomes smaller, was it not greater before?" "Certainly." "Furthermore, does the weaker not come from the stronger, and the swifter from the slower?" "Entirely." "And if something becomes worse, does it not come from the better? And the more just from the more unjust?" "Why not?"

"In all things, then, we have explored this enough: that all things are produced this way, opposites from opposites." "Entirely." "Now, is there also something like this between the two opposites? Are there two 'generations' or progressions, from one to the other, and back again? Between 'greater' and 'smaller,' there is 'increase' and 'decrease'; we say one grows and the other shrinks." "Yes," he said. "And is it not similar for 'separating' and 'mixing,' 'cooling' and 'heating,' and all such things? Even if we lack names for them sometimes, it must necessarily happen this way in reality: that all things come from their opposites in turn, and there is a process of generation from each into the other?" "Entirely," he said.

"What then? Is there something opposite to living, just as sleeping is opposite to being awake?" "Certainly," he said. "What is it?" "Dying," he said. "And do these not come from one another, since they are opposites? And since there are two of them, are there not two processes of generation between them?" "Nothing prevents it." "I will tell you one pair of these that I just mentioned," said Socrates, "both the state and the generation. You tell me the other. I say that one is 'sleeping' and the other 'waking,' and from sleep comes waking, and from waking comes sleep; and the processes are 'falling asleep' and 'waking up.' Does that satisfy you or not?" "It certainly does." "Now you tell me similarly about life and death. Do you not say that living is opposite to dying?" "I do." "And they come from each other?" "Yes." "Then what comes from the living?" "The dead." "And what from the dead?" "One must confess: the living." "Therefore, Cebes, from the dead come living things and living people." "It appears so." "Are our souls, then, in the underworld?" "It seems so." "And of the two processes of generation, is one not manifest? For dying is manifest, is it not?" "Quite so." "What then shall we do? Shall we not grant the opposite process? Is nature to be defective in this one part? Or must we grant a process of generation opposite to dying?" "Entirely." "What process is that?" "Coming back to life." "Then if there is a coming back to life, is this not a progression from the dead to the living?" "It is indeed." "So we agree on this further reason: that the living are produced from the dead no less than the dead from the living. Since this is so, it provides sufficient evidence that the souls of the dead must necessarily be somewhere from which they return again." "It seems to me, Socrates, that this necessarily follows from what has been granted."

"Consider then, Cebes, that we did not grant these things without reason. For if one set of opposites did not constantly replace the other, as if moving in a circle, but instead there was only a straight progression from one to its opposite and no return, believe me, all things would eventually have the same form and state, and would cease to be produced." "How do you mean?" he asked. "It is not difficult to understand," he said. "Just as if everyone fell asleep but no one ever woke up again, you can see that eventually everything would make the story of Endymion <note>A mythological figure granted eternal sleep</note> look ridiculous, because everything else would be overwhelmed by sleep just like him. Furthermore, if everything were mixed together and never separated, Anaxagoras's saying <note>Anaxagoras was a philosopher who taught that 'all things were together' in a primordial chaos</note> would suddenly come true: 'all things are together.' By the same reasoning, friend Cebes, if everything that received life were to die, and having died, remained dead and never came back to life, is it not absolutely necessary that everything would eventually be dead and nothing would live? For if living things were produced from other things, and then died, what would prevent all things from being consumed by death?" "Nothing at all, Socrates," said Cebes, "you seem to me to speak the absolute truth." "It is certainly so, Cebes, most of all, as it seems to me. We have not been deceived in making these concessions, but in reality there is a coming back to life, and the living are produced from the dead, and the souls of the dead survive. And it is better for the good and worse for the evil."

"And also, Socrates," said Cebes, "according to that doctrine you frequently mention—if it is true—that our learning is nothing other than recollection <note>Refers to the Theory of Reminiscence (Anamnesis): that the soul 'remembers' knowledge it had before birth</note>, it follows that we must have learned in some previous time the things we now remember. This would be impossible unless our soul had been somewhere before it came into this human form. Therefore, by this reasoning too, the soul seems to be something immortal."

"But what are the proofs of this, Cebes?" said Simmias. "Bring them back to my memory, for I do not remember them well at present." "One very beautiful proof," said Cebes, "is that when men are questioned, if someone questions them correctly, they themselves answer everything as it is. Yet they could never do this unless knowledge and correct reason were already in them. Furthermore, if someone directs them to geometric figures and diagrams or something similar, he will clearly find that this is the case."

"If this proof does not satisfy you, Simmias," said Socrates, "see if you find the same thing we do when considering it this way. For you doubt how what they call 'learning' can be 'recollection.'" "I do not exactly doubt it," said Simmias, "but I need to do the very thing we are talking about: to remember. From what Cebes began to say, I am already remembering and believing. Nevertheless, I would gladly hear from you how you were just about to prove it."

"In this way," said Socrates. "We agree, surely, that if someone remembers something, he must have known it at some time before." "Certainly," he said. "Do we then also agree that whenever knowledge comes in this way, it is recollection? I mean it like this: if someone sees, hears, or perceives something with another sense, and not only knows that thing but also recognizes something else, of which the knowledge is not the same but different—do we not rightly say he remembers that thing which came into his mind?" "How do you mean?" asked Simmias. "Like this," said Socrates. "The knowledge of a man is one thing, and the knowledge of a lyre is another." "Why not?" said Simmias. "Well, you know what happens to lovers when they see a lyre, a cloak, or anything else their beloved boys are accustomed to use? They recognize the lyre, and at the same time, the image of the boy who owned the lyre forms in their mind. This is recollection. Just as someone seeing Simmias often remembers Cebes, and infinite other such examples." "Infinite, by Jove!" said Simmias. "Is such a thing not a kind of remembering? Especially when it happens with things we have already forgotten through length of time and neglect?"

"Certainly," said Simmias. "What then?" said Socrates. "Can it happen that someone who sees a painted horse or a painted lyre remembers a man? Or seeing a painting of Simmias, remembers Cebes?" "Quite so," he said. "Does it not also happen that someone who looks at a painting of Simmias remembers Simmias himself?" "It certainly does." "According to all these examples, does recollection not happen from similar things? And must one not furthermore consider whether this recollection from similarity falls short, or not, of the thing remembered?" "It must."

"Now see if this is how it stands. We say there is something 'Equal.' I do not mean one piece of wood equal to another piece of wood, nor one stone to another stone, nor anything else of that kind, but beyond all these, we say Equality itself is something—do we say it is something, or nothing?" "We say it is something, by Jove, and wonderfully so!" "And do we know what this Equality itself is?" "Entirely." "Where did we get the knowledge of it? Was it not from the things we just mentioned—seeing equal woods or stones or other equal things, from these we conceived that Equality, which is different from them? Does it not seem different to you? Consider it this way: Do not stones or woods, while remaining the same, sometimes appear equal to us and sometimes unequal?" "Absolutely." "But what about 'the Equals' themselves? Can they ever appear unequal to you? Or can Equality appear to be Inequality?" "Never, Socrates." "Therefore, these 'equal things' and 'Equality itself' are not the same." "In no way do they appear the same to me, Socrates." "Nevertheless, from these equal things, which are different from that Equality itself, you have conceived and perceived the knowledge of it?" "You speak most truly." "Whether it be similar to them or dissimilar?" "Entirely." "It matters not; as long as by seeing one thing, you have understood another from that very sight—whether similar or dissimilar—it must necessarily be a case of recollection." "Most certainly."

"What about this? Does it happen to us regarding those things we just mentioned, the woods and such? Do they seem as equal to us as Equality itself? Or do they fall short of being such as Equality itself is?" "They fall short by a great deal." "Do we not agree that whenever someone, looking at a thing, realizes: 'This thing I see wants to be like some other reality, but it falls short and cannot be equal like that other, but is inferior'—must he not have known beforehand that other thing which he says this resembles, but does not fully achieve?" "He must." "Does such a thing happen to us or not, regarding equal things and Equality itself?" "In the highest degree." "It is necessary, then, that we had knowledge of Equality itself before that time when we first saw equal things and recognized that they all strive to be like it, but fall short of its perfection." "That is so."

"But we also agree that we did not recognize it, nor could we recognize it, from anywhere else but from sight, or touch, or some other sense. I judge all these senses to be the same in this regard." "They are the same, Socrates, for showing what we are discussing." "But from the senses, one must understand that all things perceived by the senses strive for that Equality, yet do not reach it. Or do we say otherwise?" "Not otherwise." "Before we began to see, or hear, or use other senses, we must have possessed the knowledge of Equality itself—namely, what it is—if we were to refer these equal things from the senses to it, judging that they all aim to be like it, but are left as inferior." "Did we not see and hear and use our other senses immediately upon being born?" "Entirely." "But we must, as we said, have had the knowledge of Equality itself before these." "Yes." "If we obtained it before birth and were born possessing it, then we knew it both before we were born and immediately at birth—not only Equality itself, but also the Greater, the Smaller, and all such things? For our discussion now is no more about Equality than it is about the Beautiful itself, the Good itself, the Just, the Holy, and as I say, about all those things to which we assign the name 'What It Is' <note>This refers to the 'Essence' or 'Form' of a thing</note> in our questions and answers. So it is necessary that we had knowledge of all these before we were born." "It is so."

"And if, having once obtained these knowledges, we did not always forget them, we would always be born with them and always know them through our whole life. For to know is to retain knowledge once received and not to have lost it. Do we not call the loss of knowledge 'forgetting,' Socrates?" "Certainly, Socrates." "But if, having obtained knowledge before birth, we lost it at birth, and then by using our senses upon those things, we recover those knowledges we had before—is not what we call 'learning' the recovery of our own knowledge? And in calling this 'Recollection,' would we not be naming it correctly?" "Correctly. For it appeared possible that someone, having perceived something by seeing or hearing or some other sense, should recognize from this something else he had forgotten, to which this thing was somewhat related, whether it be similar or dissimilar. So as I have been saying, one of two things must be: either we were born knowing them and we all know them through our whole life; or those we say are 'learning' are only remembering, and 'discipline' is 'recollection.'"

"It is entirely so, Socrates." "Which then do you choose, Simmias? That we were born with knowledge, or that we remember later the things we once knew?" "I am unsure which to choose at the moment, Socrates." "What about this? Can you choose what you think about this: Can a man who knows give an account of the things he knows, or not?" "He must be able to, Socrates." "And do you think everyone can give an account of these things we were just discussing?" "I would wish so," said Simmias, "but I much more fear that by tomorrow there will be no man here who can do so worthily." "So you do not think, Simmias, that everyone understands these things?" "In no way." "Then they remember what they once learned?" "It must be so."

"When did our souls receive this knowledge? For it was not after we were born as men." "Certainly not." "So it was before." "Yes." "Unless, Socrates, we receive these knowledges at the very moment we are born. For that time remains as a possibility." "Be it so, friend. But at what other time do we lose them? For we are not born possessing them, as we just agreed. Or do we lose them in the very same moment we receive them? Or can you suggest another time?" "In no way, Socrates; I did not realize I was saying nothing."

"Does it stand like this for us, Simmias? If those things we are always talking about exist—namely, the Beautiful and the Good and every such essence...

...to which we refer all things perceived by the senses, which was ours before, and which we find again as our own, and if we refer these things to that exemplar, it is necessary that just as those things exist, so also our soul existed even before we were born. But if these things do not exist, this argument would have been treated in vain. "Wonderfully, Socrates," said Simmias, "it seems to me to be the same necessity. And the argument leads us beautifully to this point: we must confess that our soul existed before we were born, just like that Essence <note>This refers to the Platonic 'Idea' or 'Form'</note> you just mentioned. For I hold nothing so certain as that all such things exist in the highest degree—namely, the Beautiful itself, and the Good, and all the others you just mentioned. As far as I am concerned, it has been sufficiently demonstrated."

"But what does it seem to Cebes?" asked Socrates. "For he too must be persuaded." "I think he is sufficiently persuaded," said Simmias, "even though he is the most resistant of all men and the slowest to believe. Yet I think it has been sufficiently proved to him that the soul existed before our birth. But whether it will still exist after our death does not yet seem to me, Socrates, to have been shown. For that doubt of the many which Cebes brought forward still remains: whether when a man dies, the soul is at the same time dissipated and thus ceases to be. For what prevents it from being produced and constituted somewhere else, and existing even before it entered a human body, but then after it has departed from it, it then perishes?"

"You speak rightly, Simmias," said Cebes. "For it seems as if only half of what is necessary has been proved: namely, that our soul existed before we were born. It is necessary to show also that after we have died, it will exist no less than it did before we were born, if the demonstration is to reach its end."

"It has already been demonstrated even now, Simmias and Cebes," said Socrates, "if you are willing to connect this proof with the one we agreed on before—namely, that every living thing comes from the dead. For if the soul exists before, and when it comes into this life and becomes a man it must necessarily proceed from nowhere else but from the dead, why is it not necessary that it also remains after death, since it must return to this life again? So what you asked has been demonstrated even now. Nevertheless, you and Simmias seem to desire to have this same point treated more diligently again; and perhaps like children you fear that when the soul leaves the body, the wind will truly dissolve and scatter it, especially if someone dies not in calm weather but when the winds are blowing strongly."

At this, Cebes smiled and said, "As if we were afraid, Socrates, try to persuade us—or rather, not as if we were afraid, but perhaps there is a child within us who fears such things. Let us strive to persuade him not to fear death like <term>larvae</term> <note>original: 'larvas' - refers to scary masks, ghosts, or boogeymen used to frighten children</note>." "One must indeed," said Socrates, "cure him with charms every day until he is made healthy." "But where, Socrates," asked Cebes, "shall we find such a charmer, now that you are leaving us?"

"Greece is wide, Cebes," he said, "and in it are many good men, and there are many barbarian nations besides. Among all these, you must search for such a doctor, sparing neither money nor labor. For there is nothing on which you could more profitably spend your money. You must also search among yourselves, for perhaps you will not easily find anyone who can do it better than you." "It shall be done," said Cebes.

As long as the soul and body are in the same place, nature commands the latter to serve and be subject, but the former to rule and dominate. Do you not think the divine is such by nature that it rules and leads, while the mortal is such that it is subjected and serves? I think so indeed. To which of these is the soul similar? It is certain, O Socrates, that the soul is similar to the divine, and the body to the mortal. Notice now, O Cebes, whether these things follow from everything we have said. Namely, that the soul is most similar to the divine, immortal, intelligible, uniform, indissoluble, and that which is always the same and remains in the same state; whereas the body is most similar to the human, mortal, unintelligible, multiform, dissoluble, and that which never remains in the same state. Since these things are so, is it not fitting for the body to be quickly dissolved, but for the soul to be entirely indissoluble, or at least something very close to it? Why not? You see, therefore, after a man has died, that the visible part of him, the body, placed in a visible place, which we call a corpse—which is fated to be dissolved, to fall apart, and flow away—does not suffer any of these things immediately, but remains for a quite a long time, especially if someone dies with the body in a healthy state, and even remains in that very beauty. For the body, dried out and preserved <margin>*Embalming, from Herodotus Book 2</margin> <note>Socrates refers to Egyptian mummification, which Herodotus famously described.</note> as they do in Egypt, remains almost whole for an incredible amount of time. Even if it should rot, nonetheless some parts of the body, namely the bones and sinews and such, remain immortal, so to speak. Is it not so? Yes. But the soul, which is something invisible, migrating to some similar and different place, excellent, pure, and invisible—<margin>*to Hades</margin> <note>original: "eis hadou" — to the place of the unseen.</note> *hidden from us, truly to the good and wise God, where, if God wills, my own soul must also migrate shortly—I say, such a soul, endowed with such a nature, will it be dissipated and perish as soon as it is freed from the body, as many people think? These, O Socrates, said Cebes, are never in the same state. And these indeed can be touched, seen, and attained by the other senses. 342                               Book Twenty-Ninth.

...being thus affected, does it not go to that which is like itself, the divine? Divine, and immortal, and wise? Where, when it arrives, it becomes happy, being liberated from error, ignorance, fears, and fierce loves, and the other human evils; and as is often said of the initiated, it truly spends the rest of time living with the gods? Shall we say it is so, Cebes, or otherwise?" "So it is, by Jove," said Cebes. 

"But if it should depart polluted and impure from the body, as one that always embraced the body and served and loved it, and was soothed by its pleasures and desires as if by certain spells, and was so captured by it that it thought nothing else was true except what is corporeal—what can be touched, seen, drunk, eaten, and used for sexual pleasures—but had grown accustomed to hating, fearing, and fleeing that which is obscure and invisible to the eyes, yet intelligible and to be grasped by philosophy: do you think a soul so disciplined will escape by itself in its purity?" "In no way," he said. "But it will be infected and entangled, I think, by the corporeal contagion, which the habit of communion and association with the body, through constant familiarity and great attention to it, has made almost innate?" "So we think." 

"We must think, O friend, that this is ponderous, heavy, earthy, and visible, which such a soul trails with it; therefore it is weighed down by it, and is drawn back to the visible place through fear of the invisible and hidden. And, as it is said, it wanders around monuments and tombs, around which some shadowy phantasms of souls have appeared, such as the images which souls of that kind project—souls that did not depart pure from the body, but still trail something visible, which is why they can be seen." "That is consistent, Socrates." "Consistent indeed, O Cebes, that these are not the souls of the good, but of the wicked, which are compelled to wander about such places, paying the penalty for their wickedly lived life. And so they wander about for so long until, with the desire for their corporeal nature accompanying them, they again put on a body." 

"And they put on, as is fitting, such characters as they practiced in life." "What kind of characters do you mean, Socrates?" "For instance, those who lived a life devoted to gluttony, insolence, and drunkenness, and had no regard for shame, it is fitting that they should enter the forms of donkeys and such brutes. Do you not think so?" "You speak consistently." "But those who preferred injustices, tyrannies, and robberies, it is right that they should pass into the genera of wolves, hawks, and kites. Or where else should we say they migrate?" "To such places most of all," said Cebes. 

"Similarly," he said, "concerning the rest, they go into whatever genera they contracted similar habits to in life." "That is manifest," he said. "Why not?" "Are not the happiest among these, who go to the best place, those who have practiced the popular and social virtue, which they call temperance and justice, acquired without philosophy and intellect, but from habit and practice?" "In what way are these the happiest?" "Because it is fitting that these should migrate again into some such social and mild genus, either of bees, or wasps, or ants, or even back into the same human genus, and that modest men should be born from them." "So it is fitting." 

"But into the genus of the gods, it is not permitted for any to arrive, except those who, burning with the desire for learning, both philosophized and departed entirely pure. For the sake of these things, O friends Simmias and Cebes, those who philosophize rightly abstain from all bodily desires, and so they persevere and never surrender themselves to them, nor do they fear the loss of family or poverty, like those many who are fond of money; nor again do they fear contempt and ignominy, like those who seek magistracies and honors and then abstain from these things." "For that would not be becoming, O Socrates," said Cebes. 

"Not by Jove," he said. "Wherefore those who care for their soul, and do not serve the cultivation of the body, despising all these things, by no means walk in that path where those others go whom we mentioned, because they do not know where they are going. But they, thinking that they must not resist philosophy and its liberation and purification, follow this way wherever it leads them." "In what way, O Socrates?" 

"I will tell you," he said. "Men fond of learning recognize that philosophy receives their soul truly bound in the body and entangled, forced to consider things through the body as through a prison, and not through itself, being involved in utter ignorance. They recognize, moreover, how philosophy, seeing how severely the corporeal bond constricts the soul—since it happens through desire, by which the bound soul becomes a helper in its own binding—recognize, I say, men fond of knowledge, that philosophy, receiving their soul thus disposed, gradually instructs it and attempts to set it free, showing how deceitful is the judgment of the eyes, how deceitful that of the ears and the other senses, persuading them to withdraw from these insofar as necessity does not force them to cling to them, and to recall and collect itself into itself, and to believe nothing except itself, insofar as it understands through itself each of those things which exist by themselves. But that which it considers through other things, being in other things, it considers to be nothing true; and that such things are sensible and visible, whereas what it considers by itself is intelligible and invisible. 

Therefore, thinking it must not resist this liberation, the soul of the true philosopher abstains from pleasures, desires, sorrows, and fears as much as possible, judging that whenever one is vehemently delighted, or fears, or grieves, or desires, one suffers not only such evil from these as one might think—namely, if someone should fall sick or spend money because of his desires—but the greatest and extreme of all evils, yet does not notice it." "What is this, Socrates?" said Cebes. "That the soul of every man is compelled at the same time to be delighted or to grieve vehemently about something, and to think that that about which it suffers this most is the most manifest and most true, when it is far otherwise. And these are mostly the visible things, are they not?" "Entirely." "Is not the soul most bound by the body in this passion?" "In what way?" 

"Because every pleasure and pain, as if holding a nail, fastens the soul to the body and connects it, and makes it so corporeal that it now thinks those things are true which the body says. For from the fact that it shares opinions with the body and delights in the same things, it is compelled, I think, to become of the same character and the same nourishment, so that it can never depart pure into the other life, but always goes out full of the stain of the body. Therefore it quickly falls again into another body, and is sown again as if by fate, and thereby becomes entirely alienated from communion with the divine, pure, and uniform essence." "What you say is most true, Socrates," said Cebes. "For the sake of these things, then, O Cebes, those who are justly fond of learning follow temperance and fortitude, and not for those reasons for which the common people do. Or do you think so?" "Not at all." "Certainly not."

->Phædo, Or, On the Soul. 343<-

...so the soul of a true philosopher would think, and would not at all suppose that, once philosophy had set it free, it should give itself back again to pleasures and pains to be bound once more, and thus perform an endless task, like Penelope unweaving her web. Rather, seeking a calm from these things, following reason, and always remaining in it, contemplating that which is true, divine, and beyond mere opinion, it migrates from human evils. From such an education and exercise, there is no reason to fear, Simmias and Cebes, that when it departs from the body, it will be torn apart and dissipated, and vanish into the winds, and nothing of it will remain."

When Socrates had said these things, a long silence followed. And Socrates himself, as it seemed, was repeating the things that had been said to himself, and most of us were doing the same. But Cebes and Simmias talked with each other for a little while. Socrates, seeing them, said, "What do you think of the things that have been said? Do you perhaps feel that something has been left out? For many doubts and objections still remain, if one is to treat them sufficiently. If you are discussing something else among yourselves, I say nothing. But if you are hesitating about the things we have said, do not fear to speak and go over them, if you think they could be said better in some part. And take me as a partner, if you think it can be done more conveniently with me." 

"Truly, Socrates," said Simmias, "I will confess to you. For some time, each of us in doubt has been pushing the other and urging him to ask, because of our desire to hear. But we were afraid lest it be unpleasant to you because of your present misfortune." Socrates, hearing this, smiled gently and said, "Aha, Simmias! How difficult it would be for me to persuade others that I do not consider this fortune to be at all adverse, when I cannot even persuade you of it. For you fear that I am more difficult and more mournful at present than I was in my past life. And, it seems, I appear to you inferior to the swans in divination. 

They, when they perceive that they must shortly die, then sing much more sweetly and loudly than they were accustomed to before, rejoicing because they are about to migrate to the God whose servants they are. But men, because they themselves dread death, also falsely accuse the swans, saying that they sing out of grief, lamenting their death because of pain. They do not consider that no bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or afflicted by any other pain. Not the nightingale itself, nor the swallow, nor the hoopoe, which they say sing lamenting out of sorrow. But to me, neither do these birds seem to sing out of pain, nor do the swans. 

But because they are sacred to Apollo, I think, being endowed with divination, they foresee the goods of the other life; therefore they sing more eagerly and rejoice on that day more than in time past. And I too think myself to be a fellow-servant of the swans, and sacred to the same God, and to have no worse prophecy from the same Lord than they do, and to depart from life with no less courage. Therefore you may speak and ask whatever you like, as long as the Eleven of the Athenians <note>The officials in charge of prisoners and executions</note> permit." 

"You speak nobly," said Simmias. "And so I will open to you that in which I doubt, and Cebes here will say what he does not admit from the previous discussion. For it seems to me, Socrates, as perhaps it does to you, that to know the manifest truth about such things in the present life is either impossible or extremely difficult. But as for the things that are said about them, not to explore them in every way, and not to stop until one has exhausted oneself examining everything, I judge to be the mark of a very soft man. For one must do one of two things: either learn and find out how things are, or if this is impossible, choose the best and most secure of human reasons, on which one may be carried as if on a raft, and so pass through the storms of this life, unless one could cross more safely and with less danger on a firmer vessel, or some divine word. 

And now I will not be afraid to ask, especially since you yourself exhort us to this: lest perhaps I should blame myself hereafter for not having said what I think now. Truly to me, Socrates, when I reflect on your words together with Cebes, they do not seem sufficiently confirmed." "Perhaps," said Socrates, "you think truly, my friend. But say in what part you judge them to have been spoken insufficiently." 

"In this part," said Simmias. "Namely, someone could say the same thing about a harmony, a lyre, and its strings: that harmony is something invisible, incorporeal, and very beautiful and divine in a rightly tuned lyre; but the lyre itself and its strings are bodies, and corporeal, composite, and earthy, and related to the mortal. When, therefore, someone has broken the lyre, or cut or snapped the strings, one could affirm by the same reason you used that it is necessary for that harmony to survive and not be destroyed. For it could in no way be that the lyre and the strings of a mortal nature still exist when the strings are broken, but the harmony, which was related to the divine and immortal, has perished before that mortal thing. He would say that the harmony must still be somewhere, and that the wood and strings would rot before the harmony suffered anything. 

For I think, Socrates, that you have noticed that we think the soul to be something of this kind. Namely, that there is in our body a certain tension and composition of the hot, the cold, the dry, the moist, and other such things, and that our soul is the tempering and consonance of these, resulting in our body after these have been well and moderately tempered with each other. If therefore the soul is a kind of harmony, whenever our body is either relaxed or strained immoderately because of diseases and other evils, it is necessary for the soul, although most divine, to perish suddenly, just as other consonances do, whether in voices or in other works of craftsmen; while the remains of each body stay for a long time, until they are either burned or rot. Consider, then, what should be answered to this reason, if someone should judge the soul to be a certain temperament of the things in the body, and that it is the first to perish in death." 

Then Socrates, as he often used to do, looking sharply and smiling, said, "You speak justly, Simmias. If any of you has a better faculty for answering than I do, why does he not answer these things? For he seems to have touched on the argument not badly. I judge, however, that before we answer, we should hear what Cebes also finds fault with, so that we may have time to deliberate. Then having heard these things, we must either concede to them, if they seem to assert things consistent with the truth, or if not, the previous argument must be defended and maintained. Therefore, come, Cebes, say what it is that most troubles you, so that you do not assent." 

"I will tell you," said Cebes. "It seems to me that the argument has revolved back to the same point, and is liable to the same charge we mentioned before. For I do not withdraw the claim that our soul existed before it descended into human form, which was very beautifully said; and unless it were so, I would say it had been sufficiently demonstrated. But that it survives us when we are dead does not seem to me to have been proved. And yet I do not concede to Simmias' objection that the soul is not stronger and more lasting than the body. For the soul seems to me to surpass all these things by far. Why then, the previous argument (turning to me) will say, do you still doubt? When you see that after a man is dead, the weaker part survives, does it not seem to you that the more lasting part is also preserved at that time? Observe, then, if I answer anything to this. I also need a simile, just as Simmias did. 

Truly it seems to me these things are said just as if someone were to say of an old weaver who had died, that he had not perished, but was perhaps surviving somewhere; and as a conjecture, he would bring forward the garment which the weaver himself had woven and wore, and assert that it was still safe and had not perished. And if someone did not believe it, he would ask whether the race of men or the garment which one uses daily is more lasting. And if the answer were that the human race is more lasting, then he would think it demonstrated that therefore the man is much more safe, since that which was more fragile in him has not yet perished. But I do not think this is so, O Simmias. Consider also what I say. For anyone would understand that this is brought forward foolishly. For this weaver, who wore out many garments and wove many, died after many of them, since there were many, but he died before the last one; yet it does not follow that a man is viler and weaker than a garment. 

I think the same similarity can be made of the soul to the body; and if someone should bring forward these same things about them, he would seem to speak congruously: namely, that the soul is more lasting, but the body weaker and less lasting. But he would say that each soul wears out many bodies, especially if they live many years. For if the body flows, and is dissolved even while the man lives, but the soul continually re-weaves what is consumed, it will nonetheless be necessary, when the soul perishes, that it has its last garment, and that it perishes before that one alone. But when the soul has perished, then at last the body shows the weakness of its nature, quickly rotting and vanishing. So that by this reasoning, we cannot yet be confident, even when we have died, that our soul survives. 

For if someone should grant to the speaker even more than what you say, and confess not only that the soul existed before our birth, but even that nothing prevents some souls from remaining even after death, and frequently entering and leaving bodies—for the soul is so strong that it often preserves itself and the body it is in—yet even if these things were granted, it would not yet follow that the soul does not grow weary in many generations, but finally in some one of many deaths it is entirely destroyed. And he would add that no one can know that death and dissolution of the body which also brings destruction to the soul: for it is impossible for any of us to perceive it. If this be the case, no one is not foolish to be confident in death, unless he can demonstrate that the soul is altogether immortal and indissoluble. Otherwise it is necessary that he who is about to die should fear for his soul, and always be anxious lest in the very next disjunction of the body it should utterly perish." 

When we all had heard them saying these things, we were disturbed, as we later opened to each other; for after we had been greatly persuaded by the previous discussion, they seemed to have perturbed us again, and to have cast us down to such a point that we would no longer give any credit not only to the reasons already brought forward, but also to those yet to be said, fearing lest either we were no good judges, or the things themselves were unworthy of belief. 

ECHECRATES: By the gods, Phædo, I grant you pardon. For to me also, hearing you just now, such a thing came into my mind. To what reason shall I finally trust? Since that reason of Socrates, which was so probable a little while ago, has now lost its credit. For it is wonderful how much that reason which proves our soul to be a kind of harmony has always had power over me, and still does; and now when I heard it, it suddenly recalled to my memory that the same thing had also seemed so to me before. Wherefore I need, as if from the very beginning, some other reason which may persuade me that the soul does not perish with the body. Tell me, therefore, I pray by Jove, in what way Socrates finished the discussion, and whether he also, as you confess of yourselves, seemed to be troubled by it, or on the contrary, benignly defended his reason; and whether he protected it sufficiently or not: relate all these things to us as diligently as you can. 

PHÆDO: Truly, Echecrates, I have often admired Socrates, but never with greater pleasure than then was I present and admired him. That he had something to answer to the objections is perhaps not surprising; but I especially admired these things in him: first, how pleasantly, benignly, and kindly he received the words of the young men; then how sagaciously he sensed that we were moved by their arguments; and finally how opportunely he applied a medicine to us, and as if we were fleeing and conquered, he recalled us and turned us back to following and considering the discourse together. 

ECHECRATES: In what way? 

PHÆDO: I will tell you. I happened to be sitting at his right hand on a certain low stool, next to the bed. But he was sitting much higher. Stroking my head, then, and pressing my hair over my neck (for he was accustomed sometimes, when the occasion arose, to play with my hair), he said, "Tomorrow, perhaps, Phædo, you will cut off these beautiful locks." "So I think, Socrates," I said. "Not so, if you will listen to me," he said. "What is this?" I asked. "Indeed today both I will cut mine and you yours, if our argument dies and we cannot raise it up again. And if I were you, and the argument fled from me, I would swear an oath like the Argives, not to grow my hair until I had conquered and overcome the arguments of Simmias and Cebes." 

"But," I said, "against two, even Hercules is said not to have been enough." "Then call me as your Iolaus," <note>Iolaus was the nephew and helper of Hercules</note> he said, "while it is still light." "I call you indeed," I said, "but not as Hercules called Iolaus, but rather as Iolaus called Hercules." "It makes no difference," he said. "But first we must beware lest something happen to us." "What is that?" I asked. "Lest we become haters of arguments," he said, "just as some become haters of men. For no greater evil than this could happen to us, namely, if we should hate arguments. 

Hating arguments arises in the same way as hating men. Hatred against men especially enters when we trust someone too much without art, <note>Without critical skill or judgment</note> and think him to be altogether true, sincere, and faithful, but then soon find him to be wicked and unfaithful, and again another in the same way. And when this has happened to someone often, especially from those whom he considered his most familiar and dearest friends...

<summary>Simmias and Cebes present powerful objections to Socrates' arguments: Simmias compares the soul to a harmony that vanishes when the lyre is broken, and Cebes compares it to a weaver who outlives many cloaks but eventually dies. ...he considered them so, and finally, being often offended, he hates everyone, and thinks that nothing at all is sincere in anyone. Has it escaped you that this usually happens in this way?" "I have certainly noticed it," I said. "Is it not shameful," he said, "and is it not without the art of human affairs that this man attempts to deal with men? For if he studied to deal with them by art, he would think that the matter itself is as it is: namely, that very good or very bad men are very few, but those in the middle are the most numerous."

"In what way do you say this?" I asked. "Just as it happens in things that are very small or very large," he said. "Do you think anything is rarer than to find a man, or a dog, or anything else that is very large or very small? Or again, the swiftest and the slowest, the most beautiful and the ugliest, the whitest and the blackest? Do you not know that in all these, the extremes are rare and few, but the middle ones are frequent and many?" "I think so," I said. "Do you not then think," he said, "that if a contest of wickedness were proposed, very few would be found to be at the top of this kind?" "It is consistent," I said. 

"Consistent indeed," he said. "But in this way arguments are not like men, but I am following you now as you lead. Rather, the similarity consists in this: when someone, without the art of arguments, believes a certain argument is true, but a little later it appears false—sometimes being so, sometimes not—and again another and another. Especially this happens to those who spend most of their time on contradictory arguments. For you know that these people think they have finally become the wisest, and that they alone have noticed that there is nothing sound or firm either in things or in arguments, but that all things are truly tossed up and down as if in the Euripus, <note>A strait in Greece famous for its violent and changing currents</note> and remain in no state for any time." 

"Truly, you speak the truth," I said. "Would it not then be a miserable affliction, Phædo," he said, "if when some argument is true and firm and can be grasped, yet after hearing such arguments as appear sometimes true and sometimes false, one should not blame oneself or one's own lack of skill, but finally, out of pain, should gladly transfer all the blame from oneself onto the arguments themselves, and for the rest of his life hate and revile them, being deprived of the truth and knowledge of things themselves?" "By Jove, a miserable affliction," I said. 

"First of all, then," he said, "let us carefully beware of this, lest we persuade ourselves that there is nothing sound in arguments, but much more that we are not yet sound ourselves. Therefore, we must strive with all our strength to become sound: you and the others for the sake of your whole remaining life, and I for the sake of death itself. For I am in danger, at this very time, of behaving in this matter not like a philosopher, but like a contentious and stubborn man, as some who are most alienated from learning are accustomed to do. For when something is in doubt, they do not care how the matter itself stands, but they strive stubbornly that what they have posited may appear true to those present. And I seem to myself to differ from them in this alone at present: that I shall not strive to prove what I say to those present—unless it should happen by chance—but that it may appear as true as possible to myself. 

For thus I think, sweet friend, and see how much gain there is in my reasoning. If what I say is true, it is worthwhile to believe it; but if nothing remains after death, yet in this time that remains to me of life, I shall be less troublesome to those present by my lamenting. And this ignorance will not remain with me—for that would be an evil—but it will be destroyed shortly. Thus prepared, O Simmias and Cebes, I return to the discussion. You, however, if you would listen to me, should have no regard for Socrates, but most of all for the truth; if I seem to speak the truth to you, assent to it; if not, contradict it entirely, carefully guarding lest I, in my excessive zeal, deceive both myself and you at once, and like a bee depart leaving my sting behind. 

But now we must proceed. First, recall to my memory what you were saying, if I seem to remember it poorly. Simmias, I think, distrusts and fears lest the soul, although more divine and more beautiful than the body, should nonetheless perish first, as it is a species of harmony. Cebes, however, seemed to me to grant that the soul is more lasting than the body, but that no one can know whether, after it has often worn out many bodies, finally when it leaves the last body, it also perishes, and that such a death is the destruction of the soul, since the body never ceases perishing. Are these not the things, Simmias and Cebes, which we must consider?" Both confessed they were. 

"But do you deny all the things that were said in the previous parts? Or do you deny some, but grant others?" "Some," they said, "and not others." "What then," he said, "of that which we said, that learning is recollection, and if it is so, it necessarily follows that the soul was somewhere before it was enclosed in the body?" "To me indeed," said Cebes, "that was wonderfully pleasing when you said it, and now if ever I remained in any opinion, I remain in this one most of all." "I too am similarly affected," said Simmias, "and I would be vehemently surprised if I ever thought otherwise about this matter." 

"But it is necessary," said the Theban guest, <note>Referring to Simmias</note> "for you to think otherwise if you persist in this opinion: namely, that harmony is a certain composite thing, and the soul is a certain harmony constituted from those things which are stretched through the body. For you will never admit that a composite consonance exists before those things from which it was necessary for the consonance to be composed. Or will you admit it?" "In no way, Socrates," he said. 

"Do you notice then," he said, "that you do not happen to say the same things when you say that the soul existed before it came into human form and the body, but that it is constituted from things that do not yet exist? For your harmony is not like that to which you say it is similar. Rather, first there is the lyre itself, and the strings, and the untempered sounds; and finally, the consonance is composed last of all, and is destroyed first. How then will this discourse harmonize with that other one of yours?" "In no way," said Simmias. "But yet," he said, "if any words should preserve harmony, it is especially fitting that they should be harmonious when treating of harmony." "It is indeed fitting," said Simmias. 

"Therefore this discourse of yours is out of tune," he said. "But see which of these two you choose: that learning is recollection, or rather that the soul is a consonance?" "I choose the first rather, Socrates," he said. "For I admitted that other one without demonstration, from a certain likely consistency, whence it seems the same also to many. But I have always judged those words which make demonstrations through likelihoods to be vain; and unless one is careful, they deceive greatly, both in geometry and in all other things. But the reason concerning recollection and learning rests on a foundation worthy of belief. For it was said that our soul was somewhere thus, even before it fell into the body, so that its essence has the name of that which truly is. And I, as I persuade myself, have admitted this sufficiently and rightly. For these reasons (as it seems to me) it is necessary that neither I nor another should affirm..."

...affirming that it must be admitted, he says that the soul is a <term>harmony</term><note>Latin: *harmonia*. In this context, it refers to the "attunement" or musical balance of the body's physical elements.</note>. But what of you, Simmias? Does it seem to you that either a harmony, or any other composition, should be in any state other than that of the elements from which it is composed? In no way. Nor even, as I think, should it be acted upon or act in any way other than how those elements act or are acted upon. He agreed. It is therefore not fitting for a harmony to precede those things from which it is composed, but rather to follow them. So it seems. Wherefore it is very far from the case that a harmony is moved in an opposite direction, or sounds, or produces anything else contrary to its own parts. Very far indeed, he said. But what of consonance? Is it not a consonance according to its nature, insofar as it is <term>tempered</term><note>Latin: *temperatur*. This refers to the specific "tuning" or mixing of elements.</note>? I do not quite understand. Is it not the case that if it were more and more greatly tempered, provided it allows for this, it would be more and more a consonance? But if less and very little, would it not be similarly less and very little a consonance? Entirely so. Can this be said of the soul? That even in the smallest thing one soul might be more or more greatly a soul, or the opposite, than another? Not at all. Come now, by Jove, do we not say that one soul has mind and virtue and is good, while another has folly and wickedness and is evil? Are these things, I ask, truly said? Truly indeed. Therefore, among those who assert that the soul is a harmony, what will anyone say these things in the souls are—namely, vice and virtue? Will they say they are another harmony and dissonance? And that a good soul is consonant, and while being a harmony itself, possesses another harmony within itself; but a bad soul is dissonant and possesses no other harmony within it? I have no answer to give, said Simmias. It is certain, however, that he who proposed the soul as a consonance would answer something of that sort. But it has already been conceded that one soul is no more or less a soul than another. And the nature of that concession is this: that one consonance is neither more, nor more greatly, nor less, nor by fewer degrees a consonance than another. Is it not so? Exactly. And that which is neither more nor less a consonance is, of course, neither more nor less tempered. Is that so? It is. But can that which is neither more nor less tempered participate in consonance by more or fewer degrees? Or rather equally? Equally, rather. Therefore the soul, if indeed one is no more or less a soul than another according to the nature of a soul, is consequently neither more nor less tempered. It is as you say. But since it is so affected, it participates no more in consonance or dissonance. No more indeed.

Furthermore, since it is so constituted, does one soul possess any more wickedness or virtue than another? If indeed wickedness is dissonance, and virtue is consonance. Certainly nothing more. Rather, Simmias, according to right reason, no soul anywhere will be affected by wickedness if it were a harmony. Since a true harmony, according to what a harmony is, would never participate in dissonance. Never, certainly. Therefore neither will the soul, which is entirely a soul, be infected by wickedness. For in what way, by what has been said, could that happen? By this reasoning, therefore, all souls of all living beings will be equally good, if they are equally souls according to the nature of the soul itself. To me, Socrates, it seems so. Does it not seem to you that this is rightly said, and that these conclusions follow, if that position were true—that the soul is a harmony? In no way.

But what then? Of all things that are in man, do you assert that anything else rules except the soul, especially the wise soul? Nothing else. Does it rule by indulging the disturbances of the body, or rather by resisting them? I mean something like this: as if when under heat and thirst, the soul nonetheless opposes it and pulls back, so that he does not drink; and similarly if hunger presses, so that he does not eat; and in many other instances, we see the soul resisting the affections of the body. Is it not so? Most certainly.

Did we not confess in the previous points that the soul, if it were a harmony, would never be dissonant with those things by which it is stretched, or relaxed, or vibrated, or whatever else those things from which it is composed might suffer; but rather that it would follow them, and never lead them? We did confess it; why not? But what now? Does it not seem to act entirely to the contrary, since it leads all those things from which someone might say it is constituted? And it resists almost all of them throughout life, and dominates them in every way, sometimes punishing them more rigidly and with pain through gymnastics and medicine, and sometimes chastising more mildly by threatening or advising against desires, angers, and fears, as if one thing were disputing with another, just as Homer handed down in the *Odyssey*:

By Jove, Socrates, it does not seem so to me.
Therefore, my excellent man, we would not rightly say that the soul is a harmony. For so, as it appears, we would agree neither with Homer the divine poet, nor with ourselves. It is so. But you say that to show the soul is something strong and similar to the divine, even before we were born, is no hindrance to all these things signifying not immortality, but only that the soul is more long-lived than the body, and existed for many ages before us, and knew and did many things; yet it is not to be thought any more immortal because of this. Furthermore, whether it is blood by which we think, or air, or fire; or whether it be none of these, but the brain, which provides the senses of hearing, seeing, and smelling; and from these memory and opinion are made, and from memory and opinion coming to rest, through these knowledge arises.
