For I thought it was previously manifest to anyone that a man is increased through food and drink. For when, through these, flesh is added to flesh, and bone to bone, and in the same way in other things when their own parts are applied to each, then surely the mass, first small, then becomes large, and thus the small man is made large. So I then thought; do I not seem to you to have thought well enough?" "To me indeed," said Cebes. "Note these things in addition. For I thought it seemed right enough to me whenever I judged a large man or horse near a small one, that the one was larger than the other by the head itself. And even more evidently, ten seemed more to me than eight, because ten contained two more than the eight. Furthermore, a two-cubit length seemed greater than a cubit length because it exceeded it by half." "Now indeed," said Cebes, "what do you judge of these things?" "By Jove, I seem to myself far from thinking I understand the cause of any of these things, I who cannot yet persuade myself that when one adds one to one, then either that one to which one is added becomes two, or both the added one and that to which it was added become two because of the addition of the one to the other. For I wonder if, when each of these was separate, each was one, and they were not then two; but after they were joined to each other, this very thing was the cause of their becoming two, namely the meeting by which they were placed closer together. Nor even if someone divides one, can I yet be persuaded that this very division is the cause of their becoming two. For then the cause of becoming two would be the opposite of the previous one. For then it was because they were joined closer together and one was moved to the other; now indeed because one is removed from the other and separated. Nor do I yet think I know why one is made, nor, to speak summarily, do I profess to know any other thing through this path, why it is made, or perishes, or exists; but I myself fruitlessly mix some other way, and I by no means admit this one. But once, having heard someone reading from a book of Anaxagoras (as he said), and reading this opinion of Anaxagoras himself: namely, that Mind orders all things and is the cause of all; I was greatly delighted by this kind of cause, thinking it somehow fitting that Mind is the cause of all. And I thought that if it were so, that Mind ordered all things, individual things were so disposed by it as they could best be disposed. Therefore, if anyone wished to find the cause by which individual things are made, and perish, or exist, this very thing must be found: namely, by what reason it is best for each thing either to exist, or to suffer anything else, or to act. And by this pact, nothing else is to be considered by a man, either about himself or about others, except what is most excellent and best. And it is necessary that he who knows this should also know that which is worse, since the knowledge of these things is the same. Thinking these things over with myself, I was glad, thinking I had found in Anaxagoras a master who would teach me the causes of things which I so greatly desired, and would tell me first whether the earth is flat or round. And when he had said this, he would add for me the cause and necessity, bringing forward namely that very thing which is better, and that it was better for the cause to be such. Furthermore, if he said the earth was in the middle of the world, he would soon explain that it was better that it be in the middle. If he showed these things, I so prepared myself as if I were to seek no further kind of causes. Furthermore, concerning the sun and moon and the other stars, and their velocity relative to each other and their revolutions, and other things that usually happen to them, I had prepared myself similarly to ask and hear, namely how and by what reason it is better for each of these either to act or to suffer, whatever they do or suffer. For I did not think that since he said from the beginning that they were ordered by Mind, he would later assign any other cause to things except that it is best for them to be as they are. Thus I thought that in rendering the causes of individuals and of all things in common, he would assign to individuals what is best for each, and to all the common good. Nor did I set small store by my hopes, but with a certain greatest zeal I read the books I had received as quickly as I could, so that I might know as soon as possible what was best or what was worst. Led by this wonderful hope, when I proceeded to read, I saw a man using Mind in no way, nor referring any cause to the ordering of things itself, but assigning airy natures, and ethereal and watery ones, and many other such incredible things as the causes of things. In which matter he seemed to me to act just as if someone should say that Socrates does whatever he does by Mind; then, wishing to explain the causes of each thing I do, should say first that I sit here now because my body is composed of bones and sinews; and the bones are solid and have intervals of joints between them; but the sinews are of such a kind that they can be stretched and relaxed, and they embrace the bones with flesh and skin which contains them. Therefore, with the bones lifted in their joints, the sinews which both stretch and relax conveniently make it so that I have the faculty of bending each limb, and for this cause I sit here bent. And again, concerning my disputation, he would assign some other such causes—voices and air and hearing and very many other things of the same kind, neglecting the truest causes: namely, because it seemed better to the Athenians

to condemn me, and therefore it also seemed better to me to sit here, and I judged it more just to remain and pay the penalties they might order. Since, by the Dog <note>A common oath of Socrates.</note>, I think these sinews and these bones would have been long ago among the Megarians or Boeotians, carried there by the opinion of what is best, had I not thought it more just and honorable to pay the city whatever penalties it might exact from me, rather than to flee and live as an exile. But to call such things causes is furthest from reason. If someone says that without bones and sinews and such things I could not fulfill what seems to me necessary to do, he will speak truly. Nevertheless, to assert that because of these things I do whatever I do, while I act with Mind, and not by the choice of what is best, would be a great and many-fold laziness of speech. For he who is so affected cannot discern that the true cause of a thing is one thing, and that without which the cause cannot be a cause is another. Which indeed many seem to me, as if groping in the dark, to call by a foreign name when they name the cause. Wherefore some, placing a vortex around the earth, make it stable under the heaven. Others, as if it were a broad vessel in which bread is kneaded, support it with air as a base. But the power itself, by which it is now so disposed as it could best be disposed, they neither seek, nor do they think it has a certain divine force; but they think they have found a certain Atlas, stronger and more immortal, and containing all things more, than this. But they do not believe that the Good and the Fitting truly connect and contain anything. I, therefore, would most gladly be the disciple of anyone to learn how this very cause is. But after I was deprived of this, and could neither find it myself nor learn it from another, I set out on a "second sailing" <note>original: "secundã nauigationé" - a Greek proverb meaning the next best way, like using oars when the wind (the first sailing) fails.</note> to investigate the cause. Do you wish, O Cebes, that this be demonstrated to you by me?" "I desire it wonderfully," said Cebes. "I finally thought, when I was already weary in considering things, that I should beware lest the same thing happen to me that usually happens to those who fix their gaze on the sun during an eclipse. For they are sometimes robbed of sight, unless they look at its image in water or in some such thing. I thought of such a thing, and feared lest my soul be entirely blinded if I looked at things with my eyes and attempted to touch them with any sense. Therefore, I judged it worthwhile to flee to reasons <note>Logoi, or arguments/definitions.</note> and in them consider the truth of things. Perhaps this comparison of ours does not agree in every part. For I do not entirely agree that he who contemplates things in reasons looks at them in images rather than looking at them in works. Nevertheless, I directed my journey by this way, and assuming the reason which I judge to be strongest, whatever things seem to harmonize with this, I set down as true, and I do this both concerning the causes of things and concerning all other things; but whatever things are dissonant, I deny to be true. I wish to explain more clearly to you what I say. For I think you do not yet understand." "By Jove, not much," said Cebes. "But I bring forward nothing new, but what I have never ceased to say often elsewhere and in the previous disputation. I proceed now, therefore, to demonstrate to you the kind of cause which I have treated continually, and I return to those things now often repeated, and I begin from them, assuming that there is something that is Beauty itself, and Goodness, and Greatness, and all the rest. Which indeed, if you give them to me and concede that they exist, I hope from these to demonstrate the cause itself to you, and likewise to find that the soul is immortal." "But indeed," said Cebes, "as if I have already conceded it to you, you must not be hindered from concluding now." "Consider now," he said, "what follows in order, whether you agree with me in these. For I think, if there is anything else beautiful besides Beauty itself, it is beautiful for no other reason than because it participates in Beauty itself. And I say all things in this manner. Do you receive this cause?" "I receive it indeed," he said. "Therefore I do not yet perceive further, nor can I know those 'clever' causes. If someone tells me why anything is beautiful, namely because it has a florid color, or a shape, or any other such thing, I let those others go; for in all those others I am usually confused. But I hold this one thing simply and truly and perhaps unskilfully in my possession: that there is nothing else that makes a thing beautiful except either the presence, or the communion, or in whatever way and in whatever manner it happens, of Beauty itself. For I would not yet affirm that; but that by Beauty all beautiful things are beautiful, that seems to me the safest thing to answer, both to myself and to others. And leaning on this foundation, I think I shall never fall, but that both I and anyone else can safely answer that whatever things are beautiful, they become beautiful by Beauty itself. Do you not also agree?" "I agree indeed." "Therefore, those things that are great are great by Greatness itself; and those that are greater are similarly greater; and those that are smaller are smaller by Smallness." "So it is." "Therefore, you will not agree if someone says one person is larger than another by a head, and that he who is smaller is smaller by the same head; but you will testify that you will say nothing else than that every larger thing is larger than another by no other thing than by Greatness, and is larger because of this, namely because of Greatness itself; and the smaller is similarly smaller by nothing else than Smallness, and is smaller because of this, namely because of Smallness itself. Fearing, I think, lest if you say someone is larger or smaller by a head, someone might object to you: first, that by the same thing both the larger is larger and the smaller is smaller; second, that you affirm the larger is larger by the head, which is a small thing. But he will say this is very like a monster, that you should say something is large because of something small. Would you not fear these things?" Then Cebes, smiling, said, "Indeed I would." "Would you not similarly fear to say that ten is more than eight by two, and exceeds for this cause rather than by Multitude and because of Multitude? And similarly that a two-cubit length is larger than a cubit length by a half rather than by Greatness? For that is similarly to be feared." "Entirely," he said. "What then if one is added to one, would you not fear to say the addition itself is the cause of their becoming two, or if it is divided, the division itself is the cause of the two? And you would cry out more loudly that you do not know in what other way anything is made, except by participation in the essence proper to each thing, of which it is a participant? And in these, you have no other cause why they become two except the participation in Duality itself; and it is necessary for those things which are to be two to be participants of this; and similarly of Unity, whatever is to be one? But you would let go of these divisions and additions and other such subtleties, leaving them to those wiser than you to answer as they please. But you, as is often said, fearing your own shadow and unskilfulness, and leaning on that safest position, would answer thus? "It is necessary." "In the same way, it is necessary we speak concerning the immortal. For if that which is immortal cannot perish, it is impossible for the soul to perish when death is imminent. For it will not receive death, as is clear from the previous points, nor will it have perished; just as three will never be even, as we said, nor again will the odd be even, nor fire cold, nor the heat which is in fire ever be coldness. "Therefore, when death is imminent for a man, that which is mortal in him perishes, as it appears; but that which is immortal withdraws from death incorrupt and safe." "It is manifest." He ends with a solemn warning that because the soul is immortal, its moral state is of eternal consequence, as death is not an escape for the wicked.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue of the Phaedo, shifting from the logical proofs of the soul's immortality to a "mythic" description of the soul's journey after death and the true geography of the universe. This follows the conclusion that the soul must be indestructible and therefore requires moral care.</meta>

...salvation, unless it becomes as good and as wise as possible. For when the soul migrates to the world of the spirits <note>original: "manes"; the souls of the departed</note>, it carries nothing else with it except its own education and cultivation. These things, indeed, are said to greatly benefit or harm the deceased right at the very beginning of that migration. For they say that each person who departs from here is led by that guardian spirit <note>term: "daemon" (a personal guiding spirit assigned to each soul at birth)</note> which had been allotted to them in life, to a certain place where all must be gathered together to be judged, and then proceed to the underworld under the guidance of that leader whose task it was to bring those departing from this world to those places. Having received there what was their lot to receive, and having remained for the required time, they are brought back here again by another guide after many long circuits of time.

However, the journey is not such as Telephus describes in Aeschylus <note>Aeschylus was a famous Greek tragedian; Telephus is a character in a lost play</note>. For he says that a simple path leads to the underworld. But I think it is neither simple nor one. Otherwise, there would be no need for guides, since no one could wander off a single path. As it is, the way seems to have many tracks and many windings. This can indeed be conjectured from our sacrifices and religious rites. Therefore, the soul that is moderate and wise follows its guide willingly and is not ignorant of its surroundings. But the soul that is infected by the desires of the body—as I said before—passionately clings to the body for a long time; and having struggled in many ways and suffered much around the visible realm, it is finally led away by force and with great difficulty by the guardian spirit to whom its care was assigned. 

When it arrives at the place where the other souls are, if it is utterly impure and guilty of such crimes as being contaminated by unjust killings, or having perpetrated other similar deeds of kindred souls, everyone flees and turns away from it. No one is found who is willing to be its companion or its guide. Thus, destitute of all help, it wanders until certain cycles of time are completed. When these are finally fulfilled, it is carried by necessity itself into a dwelling suitable for it. But the soul that has passed through life in a pure and moderate way, having found gods for companions and guides, dwells in the place that is appropriate for each. 

There are indeed many wonderful places on the earth, and the earth itself is neither of such a kind nor of such a size as those who usually discuss the earth believe, as I have been persuaded by someone. Then Simmias said, "In what way do you say this, O Socrates? I have certainly heard many things about the orb of the earth, but not these things which you say you have accepted as true. I would gladly hear them from you." 

"Indeed, O Simmias, it does not seem to me to require the art of Glaucus <note>term: "Art of Glaucus" (a proverbial expression for a very difficult or nearly impossible task)</note> to tell what these things are; but to prove they are true seems to exceed the capacity of the art of Glaucus. Furthermore, I perhaps would not be sufficient for the task. Even if I did know it, my remaining life, O Simmias, would by no means be enough for such a long narration. However, there is nothing prohibiting me from describing the form of the orb of the earth and its regions as I believe them to be." 

"That will be enough," said Simmias. 

"I am persuaded, first, that if the earth is round in the middle of the heavens, it has no need of air or any other such necessity to prevent it from falling. But for its support, it is enough that the earth is completely uniform with itself in every direction, and that the heaven is always in equilibrium. For a thing in equilibrium, placed in the middle of something uniform, cannot tilt more or less in any direction. Since it is in a similar state, it remains free from inclination. This is the first thing I am persuaded of." 

"And rightly so," said Simmias. 

"Furthermore, I believe the orb of the earth is immense, and that we inhabit a small portion of it—from the Phasis <note>The Rioni River in Georgia, the eastern limit of the Greek world</note> to the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, the western limit</note>—living like ants and frogs around a pond or the sea. I believe there are many other inhabitants in many similar places. For everywhere across the earth there are many and varied hollows, differing in form and size, into which water, mist, and air flow. But the pure earth itself lies in the pure heaven where the stars are, which most of those who treat these matters call the 'ether.' These things [the water and air] are like sediment that always flows into the hollow parts of the earth. We, therefore, dwelling in these hollows, are so deceived that we believe we live upon the high surface of the earth. It is as if someone dwelling in the middle of the deep sea thought they lived on the upper surface of the ocean; and looking at the sun and the other stars through the water, they would think the sea itself was the heaven. Because of their slowness and weakness, they would never have emerged to the top of the sea, nor raised their head above the waves to see clearly how much purer and more beautiful this place is than that depth; nor would they have heard it from anyone who had seen it. 

This same thing happens to us: living in a certain hollow of the terrestrial orb, we think we inhabit the high surface, and we call the air 'heaven,' as if we were looking at the movements of the stars through it as though it were the true heaven. This happens to us because, due to our weakness and slowness, we are unable to transcend to the uppermost air. But if someone were to escape to the top, or fly there on wings, then—just as fish emerging from the sea see our world—so they would see the things that are there. And if their nature were sufficient for the sight, they would immediately recognize that that is the true heaven, the true light, and the true earth. For this earth we inhabit, and these stones, and this whole place, are eaten away and corrupted, just as things in the sea are by the saltiness. Nothing worthy of esteem grows in the sea; there is, so to speak, nothing perfect in it, but only caverns, sand, incredible mud, and filth wherever there is earth. These are in no way to be compared to our beauties. But the beauty of that place will appear to exceed our own by far. Therefore, if it is appropriate to tell a beautiful myth, it is worth the effort, Simmias, to hear what those regions of the earth are like that lie beneath the heaven." 

"Indeed," said Simmias, "we would very gladly hear this myth." 

"They say, then, my friend," he said, "that the face of that earth, if one were to look down from above, appears first of all like those balls sewn together from twelve pieces of leather, distinguished by various colors. Our colors here, which painters use, are like faint likenesses of them. But there, the whole earth consists of such colors, and much more brilliant and pure than these: part of it is purple, endowed with wonderful beauty; part is golden; part is whiter than chalk or snow. Furthermore, it is composed of other colors similarly, even more numerous and more beautiful than any that have come to our knowledge. Indeed, these very hollows of the earth, filled with water and air, present a certain splendid appearance of color amidst the variety of the other colors, so that its single appearance always seems varied. In such a earth, trees, flowers, and fruits grow in a corresponding way. Furthermore, the mountains and stones there have a similar perfection, transparency, and more beautiful colors. Certain small parts of these are the little stones we prize here—Sardian stones, Jaspers, Emeralds, and others of that kind. But there, there is nothing that is not of such a kind, or even more beautiful. The reason for this is that those stones are pure...

they are, and not, like ours, eaten away and corrupted by rot and saltiness, which, flowing together in this place, infect the stones, soil, animals, and plants, and force them to be diseased. But the earth itself is adorned with all these things, and even with gold and silver and other similar things. These shining things are born there, many and large, and throughout the whole earth, so that to see it is a spectacle for happy spectators. 

Furthermore, there are many animals there, and humans, some inhabiting the inland region, some living near the air, as we live near the shores of the sea, and some even on islands situated not far from the mainland which are surrounded by air. But to say it briefly, what water and the sea are to us for our use, the air is the same there; and what air is to us, the ether is to them. The seasons there have such a temperate quality that the inhabitants live without disease and much longer than we do. Also, in sight, hearing, wisdom, and other such things, they surpass us as much as air surpasses water and ether surpasses air in purity. Furthermore, there are temples and groves of the gods there, in which the gods truly dwell familiarly, and there are oracles and divinations, and perceptions of the gods and familiarities of that kind for men with the gods. The sun also, and the moon and other stars, are seen by them as they truly are; in other matters, they possess a happiness matching these things. 

Such then is the nature of the whole earth and the things around it. There are, moreover, many places in the earth through its hollows in a circle, some indeed deeper and wider than the region inhabited by us, others deeper but having a narrower opening than this region of ours; and there are some elsewhere less deep, but wider than ours. All these, beneath the earth, meet one another and break through in many ways from all sides, both through narrower and wider passages, having channels and exits by which a great abundance of waters flows from some into others as if into mixing bowls. Also, there are incredible magnitudes of underground waters of perennial rivers, both hot and cold, and much fire, and great rivers of fire; many also of muddy liquid, some indeed purer, some dirtier, like the torrent of mud in Sicily, and the muddy rivers flowing from it. With these, each place is filled wherever it happens that they flow through. All these things are moved up and down as if by a certain hanging vessel placed in the earth (and so balanced that it inclines and lifts on each side in turn). This hanging vessel is of such a nature due to a certain cause. One of the chasms of the earth is certainly the largest, pierced through the entire earth and open, of which <margin>Iliad, Book 8</margin> Homer says: "Far, far beneath the earth the deep pit lies." This, both he elsewhere and many of the poets have called Tartarus. Into this chasm all the rivers flow together, and from there they flow out again. Each of them is such as the lands through which they glide. The cause of all of them flowing out from here and back again is that this liquid has neither a bottom nor a foundation. Therefore, it is lifted and fluctuates up and down. And the air and breath that surround it do the same. For they follow it, both when it glides to the upper parts of the earth and when it glides to these of ours. And just as in breathing animals the breath continually expires and respires, so there the breath, lifted together with the liquid, stirs up certain violent and incredible winds, whether it flows in or flows out. Therefore, when the water glides down into the place they call the lower region, it flows through the passages of the earth near such rivers, *and overflows everywhere through them, * and fills them like those who draw water. But when it breaks out from there to here, it fills these places again in turn. When they are full, the water flows through the rivers and the passages of the earth. And when each of the liquids has flowed to that place toward which it flows more suitably, they create seas, lakes, rivers, and springs. 

Then, receding again from here through the earth, some indeed through more regions and windings, but others through fewer and shorter ones, they flow back into Tartarus: some certainly much deeper than they were drawn from, others only a little, but all flow in lower than they flowed out. Some glide out on the opposite side from where they glided in, others on the same side. But some, flowing around everywhere once or more often, and winding around the world like snakes, glide back as far down as possible and are mixed again; they are allowed to flow down in either direction as far as the middle, but by no means further, for the further fall on either side would be an uphill climb. 

There are many other large and varied streams, but there are four principal ones. The largest and outermost of these, surrounding the earth, is called Oceanus. From the region opposite to this flows Acheron, which, flowing through other desert places and through underground places, flows down into the Acherusian marsh. To this place the souls of most of the dead come, and having stayed there through certain fated cycles of time—some indeed longer, some shorter—they are sent back again into the generations of animals. A third river flows between these two. Not having gone very far, it falls into a vast place, blazing with much fire, and creates a marsh larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. From here, turbid and muddy, it flows around the earth, and among other places, it reaches the edge of the Acherusian marsh, yet does not mix with its water, but having revolved many times under the earth and been swallowed up, it flows down below Tartarus. They call this river Pyriphlegethon, whose streams, like fragments torn from it, flow wherever they happen upon the earth. From the region opposite to this, a fourth river first breaks out into a wild and rugged place, as they say; the whole place has such a color as is dark blue <note>cyaneus</note>: they call this the Stygian place. This river, falling down, creates the Stygian marsh. Falling into this place and taking on violent powers in the water, it hides itself under the earth, and winding around, it glides opposite to Pyriphlegethon and meets it in the Acherusian marsh from the opposite side. Nor is any of its water mixed, but having revolved in a circle against Pyriphlegethon, it breaks into Tartarus. The poets call this Cocytus. 

When these things have been so arranged by nature, when the dead have arrived in that place to which the daemon leads each one, they are first judged there, both those who have lived honorably and holily, and those who have lived otherwise. Therefore, whoever are found in life to have held a certain middle way, having set out for Acheron and embarked on the vehicles available to each, they arrive at the Acherusian marsh, and there they dwell and are purged, paying the penalties for their injustices. And having been purified, they are absolved, and each receives rewards for their good deeds according to their merit. But those who, because of the magnitude of their crimes, seem to be incurable—namely, those who have committed many and great sacrileges, or unjust killings, or other things similar to these—a fitting fate plunges all these into Tartarus, from which they never come out. But those who have committed curable sins, though great ones—such as if they have done something by force against

After they have been carried by these rivers and arrive at the Acherusian marsh, they shout there and call upon those whom they either killed or afflicted with injuries, and they beg and pray as suppliants that they be allowed to enter the marsh and be received there. And if they obtain their request, they enter there and find an end to their evils; if not, they are carried back into Tartarus, and from there back into the rivers, and they do not cease to be carried through these evils until they have obtained their request from those they injured. For this penalty was imposed on them by the judges. 

But those who are found to have lived more piously than the rest, these are the ones who, being released and freed from these earthly places as if from a prison, transcend to the higher places and inhabit a pure region above the earth. Among these, whoever have been sufficiently purified by philosophy live entirely without bodies for the whole of time and obtain habitations even more beautiful than these. The beauty of these is neither easy to tell, nor would the present time suffice for telling it. But for the sake of these things which have been narrated, Simmias, one must strive with all effort to attain virtue, prudence, and wisdom in this life. For the reward is beautiful, and the hope is great. 

To assert that these things are exactly as I have set them out does not become a man of sound mind; yet that either these or some such things exist concerning our souls and their habitations, since the soul itself appears immortal, seems to me to be both fitting and worth the risk to believe. For the risk is noble, and it is necessary to pour these things into our minds like certain charms <note>incantations</note> in the manner of the Magi; for which reason I have been drawing out the story for a long time. But for the sake of these things, he ought to have good hope for his soul, whoever has neglected the pleasures and ornaments of the body as if they were alien, thinking he would do something more, and has studiously followed the pleasures perceived in learning, and has decorated his soul not with an alien ornament, but with its own: with temperance, justice, fortitude, liberty, and truth. Thus he awaits the migration from this life, ready to migrate whenever fate calls. 

You indeed, Simmias and Cebes, and the rest here, will each migrate at some time in the future. But now, as some tragic poet would say, fate already calls me. And it is almost time that I go to wash. For it is better, I think, to drink the poison after the bath, so that we do not cause trouble to the women in washing a corpse." 

When Socrates had said these things, Crito said: "Come tell us, Socrates, what do you command these men or me to do, either concerning your sons or concerning other matters? Or by doing what would we most gratify you?" 

"I command nothing new," he said, "but what I always tell you: namely, if you take care of yourselves, whatever you do will be pleasing to me and mine and to yourselves, even if you do not promise it now. but if you neglect yourselves, not wishing to direct your life according to the footsteps of what has been said now and in the past, you will accomplish nothing at all, even if you promise many things to us now." 

"Those things," said Crito, "will be our care. But how do you order us to bury you?" 

"As you please," he said, "if indeed you catch me, and unless I escape you." And at the same time, smiling and turning to us, he said, "I cannot persuade Crito that I am this Socrates who is now disputing and arranging each of my words. But he thinks that I am that which he will see as a corpse a little later. And so he asks how he should bury me. But what I have been contending for a long time with many words—that after I drink the poison, I shall no longer be among you, but shall go to the happiness of the blessed—this I seem to have said in vain to Crito, comforting both you and myself at the same time. Therefore, give a guarantee for me to Crito, a guarantee opposite to that which he gave to the judges. For he guaranteed that I would stay at the trial; but you, guarantee that I will not stay after I die, but will depart, so that Crito may bear my death more easily, and not, seeing my body either burned or buried, bewail me as if I were suffering something terrible. Nor let him say at the funeral that Socrates is laid out, or carried out, or buried under the earth. For know this well, best Crito, that not to speak correctly is not only a fault in itself, but it also does some harm to souls. But one must be confident and say that my body is being buried, and buried in such a way as will please you and as you judge to be most just." 

Having said these things, he rose and entered a certain room as if to wash. Crito followed him. But he ordered us to wait. We were waiting, therefore, talking among ourselves about the things that had been said and considering them again. Furthermore, we were recounting how great a calamity had befallen us: as if we, deprived of a father, were to be orphans for the rest of our time. When Socrates had washed, his children were brought to him. For he had two small sons, and one already grown. The women of his household also came. When Socrates had spoken to them in Crito's presence and had commanded what he wished, he ordered the women and children to leave, and he returned to us, now around sunset; for he had stayed inside for a very long time. When he came to us having washed, he sat down. He had not spoken much after this when the officer of the Eleven <term>the Athenian officials in charge of executions</term> came. Standing near him, he said, "Socrates, I do not notice in you what I do in others. For they are angry with me and curse me when I announce to them that they must drink the poison, with the magistrates so compelling. But I have known you especially in this time to be the most generous, gentlest, and best man of all who have ever come to this place. And now I certainly know that you are by no means angry with me, but with those whom you know are the cause of this matter. Now, therefore, you know what message I bring to you. Farewell and strive to bear what is necessary as easily as you can." And at the same time, having said these things, he went away weeping. 

Socrates, looking at him, said, "And you farewell, and we shall do so." And turning to us, he said, "How polite this man is! Not only in this, but in the past also, he used to greet me and talk with me sometimes, and he was always the best of men. And now how nobly he bewails me! But come, Crito, let us obey him, and if the poison is already ground, let someone bring it here. If it is not yet ground, let him grind it." 

"But I think, Socrates," said Crito, "the sun has not yet left the mountains nor set. And I know others who, after it was announced to them, used to drink it very late, having dined and drunk plentifully, and sometimes even having enjoyed those they loved. Therefore, do not hurry so, for there is still time." 

Then Socrates said, "Rightly, Crito, do they do those things. For they think that by doing these things they gain something.

He, having gone out and stayed for a little while, returned, bringing with him the man who was to give the poison, who carried it ground in a cup. Seeing him, Socrates said, "Tell me, good man, for you have experience in these matters, what must I do?" 

"Nothing else," he said, "than walk about after the drink until you feel your legs become heavy, and after that, lie down; and so you will do it." Saying these things, he handed the cup to Socrates. 

Socrates took it very cheerfully, O Echecrates, not at all disturbed, with neither his color nor his countenance changed. But as he was accustomed, looking at him with a bull-like gaze, he said, "What do you say? Is it permitted to sacrifice by pouring some of this drink?" 

"We have ground only so much, Socrates," he said, "as we thought would be enough." 

"I understand," he said. "But it is both permitted and necessary to pray to the gods that our migration may be happy. Which indeed I pray for, and may it be so." And at the same time, having said these words, he took the cup and drank it very easily and readily. 

Most of us had been able to hold back our tears somehow until then. But after we saw him drinking and having drunk, we could no longer do so, but grief so overcame me that tears flowed abundantly from me. Therefore, covering myself, I bewailed, not him indeed, but my own fortune, that I should be deprived of such a friend. Crito, even before me, since he could not contain his tears, rose up. But Apollodorus had never ceased weeping even in the previous time; then, especially, crying out and afflicting himself, he left no one of those present whose heart he did not break, except for Socrates alone. 

He, noticing these things, said, "What are you doing, O wonderful men? Indeed, I sent the women away mostly for this reason, that they might not do such things. For I had heard that one should migrate from this life with blessing and applause. Be quiet, therefore, and endure." 

We, hearing these things, were ashamed and stopped from tears. But he, when he felt his legs grow heavy during his walking, lay on his back; for so the one who provided the poison had ordered. A little later, touching him, he examined his feet and legs. Then, pressing his foot harder, he asked if he felt it. Socrates said no. He pressed the shins again, and gradually moving his hand upward, he showed us that they were cold and stiff. And he himself touched him again and said that when it reached the heart, then he would depart. 

Now his belly had already grown cold, when uncovering himself—for he was covered—he said, which were his last words: "O Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius <term>The god of healing; Socrates implies death is a cure for the illness of life</term>; pay it, and do not neglect it." 

"It shall be done," said Crito, "as you command. But see if you want anything else." To this question, he answered nothing further. But when he had rested for a short time, he was moved. And the minister uncovered him, and his eyes were fixed. When Crito saw this, he composed his mouth and eyes. 

This was the end of our friend, O Echecrates, a man in our judgment, of all whom we have known, the best, and supremely the wisest and most just.

->**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.**<-

The purpose of Plato in the *Menexenus* is to exhort everyone to the highest love of their country; and he does the same, although differently, in the *Crito*, the *Laws*, and the *Republic*. Here, however, he accomplishes it in two principal ways: First, while he praises those who intrepidly undergo dangers and death for the safety of their country. Second, while he extols the antiquity and virtues of his own country with wonderful praises. 

But you, right from the beginning, note that moral philosophy is supremely necessary for a man who is to govern a republic. Soon, that it is noble to fall in war, namely for the safety of one's country, and that this is confirmed by the fact that this is honored above all else among all nations. Then, taking the opportunity from oratorical praises, notice how pernicious flattery is. Indeed, he judges common oratory in the *Gorgias* to be a form of flattery. In the *Phaedrus*, however, he calls a flatterer a beast pestilential to the human race. And he affirms it is similar to an impure daemon, continually polluting incautious souls with the bait of harmful pleasure and the filth of the body. Here, moreover, he judges the flatterer, both private and public, to be very similar to sorcerers and poisoners: for he is worse and more unjust than a thief and a murderer, as he takes away from us not just money, nor only the life of the body, but truly, like a sacrilegious person, he steals and withdraws a sacred thing—namely, the judgment of reason—under the appearance of good. 

And see how greatly he deceives. For not only in hidden matters, but what is wonderful, he fails most skillfully in the most manifest things. For to whom is his ancestral and paternal origin not most evident? Likewise the very size and form of his body? Nevertheless, in these things also, poisonous flatterers circumvent us, more cruel than Circe as they inflict more serious damage. For she is said to have transformed the exteriors of men into beasts with her cups; but these transform the interiors with their allurements. Therefore, Socrates derides the orators because they hunt for popular favor with every machine, and praise others beyond measure so that they themselves may be praised, and treat such a light matter with serious study and long premeditation. 

He proceeds, moreover, to what he had established from the beginning: namely, to exhort everyone to defend their country by praising those who have fallen for their country. For this was an old custom of the Athenians, to praise them every year in a public assembly and, in addition, to celebrate funeral rites. But lest he attribute more to the oratorical faculty than is proper, he asserts that he received such an oration from another, and indeed from a woman, Aspasia; especially since it is not of the Socratic spirit to harangue in the manner of orators. In what order it is mostly to be praised, especially in a funeral oration, he clearly declares. 

As for his saying that from the beginning in the Attic region, humans alone and only from the earth were spontaneously born; but from other regions, similarly from the earth, only beasts: accept it however you please, whether as from a philosopher or rather an orator. Know, however, that it is a Platonic opinion that after vast floods of the earth, from the abundant moisture and heat following after the deluge, the earth is rendered so fertile that from it not only small animals, such as now, but even large ones, and humans themselves moreover, are born spontaneously. Which indeed he confirms both here and elsewhere often. And most of the Egyptians and Greeks felt this, and many Arabs, and finally, Algazeles and Avicenna especially confirmed it. Which opinion Aristotle used in natural questions from the mind of the ancients, saying: "Just as in small changes of time certain small animals sprout from the earth, so in larger changes, larger ones, and finally in the greatest, the largest and most perfect." 

Plato, however, wherever he draws living things from the very bowels of the earth, employs the artisan gods as ministers of the mundane architect. Gods, I say, that is, the Ideas and special reasons consisting in the life of the world and the divine intelligence: through which both immediately after deluges, and daily, the species of living things are formed, wherever the bodily seed of the same species would seem to be absent. Which indeed we proved sufficiently yesterday in our theology. But where man is born, not only as with others does he employ the hands of the gods, but also a certain breath of the supreme God and a more express image. Then, for those immediately born, he appoints the gods themselves, at least in the first centuries, as leaders and teachers. 

But you, from all these things, choose prudently those which are more consonant with Mosaic wisdom. Truly, it most agrees with Moses that here, and in the *Protagoras*, and in the *Statesman*, and the *Critias*,

**Menexenus, Or, the Funeral Oration.**

...[The text] wishes that man was at some time brought forth from the earth or from God to the likeness of God himself. But what kind of illusions these are, and when, and for what cause, we shall teach in the *Timaeus*. After these things, a man distinguished by piety interweaves the praises of his own fatherland, which he pursues with as much charity as skill, from its first origin, from the very form of the republic, from daily discipline, and from deeds outstandingly performed, which are very manifest both here and elsewhere from other writers. Wherefore, let us conclude our argument in a few words, noting sentences of this kind:

All things obey virtue. Prosperity first gives birth to emulation, then to envy, and finally to dissensions and battles. Every possession without moral virtue is not only useless, but harmful. Knowledge separate from moral virtue is to be judged not wisdom, but a certain craftiness. The splendor of ancestors becomes obscure in their sons when it is not poured into their descendants through their own sloth. It is not to be wished that all things should turn out according to one’s prayer. In all things, the old proverb must be observed: "Nothing in excess." He who has so prepared himself that everything which contributes to happiness depends on himself, or comes as close as possible to this, has instituted his life best. Do not exult with joy, nor be cast down by grief. Parents ought to judge that they have begotten sons not as immortals, but so that they might be good men. The mournful lamentations of the household are troublesome to the deceased, if indeed they hear them. It is fitting to follow those who have conducted themselves strenuously in war for the safety of the fatherland with a certain perpetual and solemn honor; their children are to be educated by public care, and their parents are also to be cherished. Lest the things themselves be unjust to us, they are to be endured with an even mind.

**SOCRATES, MENEXENUS.**

**SOCRATES:** Does Menexenus come from the forum? Or from where?
**MENEXENUS:** From the forum, O Socrates, and from the Senate.
**SOC.** Why were you at the Senate? Is it perhaps because you think you have already attained the line [limit] of discipline and philosophy and have profited enough, and you study to undertake greater things hereafter, and you, though younger, wish to preside over us elders, so that your family might always, as it is accustomed, provide us with someone as a counselor?
**MEN.** If you yourself permit it, O Socrates, and counsel that I preside, I shall give my effort; but if on the contrary, by no means. But now, I set out to the Senate for this reason: because I had heard someone was to be chosen who might adorn the deceased with praises. For, as you know, they are about to perform the funeral rites.
**SOC.** I have heard indeed, but whom have they chosen especially?
**MEN.** No one. For they deferred it until tomorrow. I think, however, that Archinus or Dion will be chosen.
**SOC.** It seems, Menexenus, that among many nations it is a noble thing to fall in war. For he who migrates from life here is honored with a most magnificent funeral and sepulcher. And even if some poor man dies thus, he does not lack a panegyric; even if someone is base or cowardly, he is again extolled by wise men, who—not at random, but with a speech composed and prepared over much time—praise him so excellently that, while they declare of someone both what is and what is not there, they deceive the minds of the listeners with the elegance of their words as if by some charms or sorceries. Meanwhile, they adorn the city in every way, and they weave anew the origin of our ancestors and those who fell in arms. They even extol us who are still living. Wherefore, Menexenus, being praised by them, I conceive I know not what noble thing about myself; and when I give my ears to them everywhere, I am soothed by a wonderful sweetness, and immediately I repute myself greater, nobler, and more beautiful than before. And frequently some strangers hear these things with me, and I am rendered more excellent in their estimation than before; for indeed it seems to happen to them just as it does to me, both toward me and toward the rest of the city. For, persuaded by the orator, they think the city more wonderful than before. And yet this glorious beauty remains with me for more than three days; so much does the harmonious speech and the melodious voice of the orator flowing from his mouth pour into [OCR: *infundif* for *infundit*] my ears, that only at last on the fourth or fifth day do I remember myself and recognize where on earth I am. At that time, I think myself all but inhabiting the Islands of the Blessed—so great is the dexterity with which our rhetoricians are endowed.
**MEN.** You always mock the rhetoricians, O Socrates. But now I fear lest any faculty of speaking be lacking to him who is chosen. For the choice happened suddenly. Wherefore, perhaps whoever is to speak will be compelled to make words in a way from the unexpected [extemporaneously].
**SOC.** Why so, O good man? For there are speeches for each of them composed long ago for this purpose. Then, it is not arduous to learn about these things without meditation. For if it were necessary to praise Athenians in the Peloponnese, or Peloponnesians at Athens, then there would be need of an eloquent orator who might both persuade and be approved. But when one exercises oneself among those same people whom he also praises, it is surely not difficult to speak well.
**MEN.** Do you think that is easy, Socrates?
**SOC.** Indeed, by Jove.
**MEN.** Do you hope that you could speak, if it were necessary and you were chosen by a decree of the Senate?
**SOC.** What wonder is it, Menexenus, that I am sufficient for speaking—I who have obtained a mistress [teacher] by no means unskilled in rhetoric, who has both rendered many others eloquent orators, and one most excellent of all the Greeks, the son of Xanthippus, Pericles?
**MEN.** Who is she? Surely you do not mean Aspasia?
**SOC.** I mean her, and also the son of Metrobius, Connus. For these two are my teachers: Connus indeed of music, but Aspasia of rhetoric. Thus, therefore, it is no wonder that an educated man is eloquent in these matters. Nay, even if someone were less learned than I, having been taught music by Lamprus and rhetoric by Antiphon of Rhamnus, he could nevertheless, by praising Athenians among the Athenians themselves, speak in such a way that his speech would be approved by the listeners.
**MEN.** What indeed do you have that you could bring forward if it were necessary for you to speak?
**SOC.** From myself indeed, perhaps nothing. But yesterday I heard Aspasia herself dictating a funeral oration concerning these men. For she had heard what you yourself were saying—that the Athenians would choose someone to have a speech about these things. Then, partly from the unexpected, and partly setting forth things premeditated in my judgment, she wove together a funeral oration (which Pericles said), composing certain remains from it.
**MEN.** Could you not remember what Aspasia said?
**SOC.** Indeed, unless I be unjust [to her]. For I learned it from her, and I was nearly beaten with blows by her on account of my forgetfulness.
**MEN.** Why then do you not report it?
**SOC.** I fear lest my mistress be somewhat angry with me if I publish her speech.
**MEN.** By no means, Socrates. But gratify me; whether you please to say the speech of Aspasia or of anyone else, only speak.
**SOC.** Perhaps you will laugh at me, if I, an old man, still seem to you to joke.
**MEN.** In no way, O Socrates; but speak by all means.
**SOC.** Your whim must be indulged. For almost even if you ordered me to dance naked, since we are alone, I would comply. But listen now. For in this manner, as I think, she began to speak, taking the exordium from the deceased themselves.

**THE SPEECH:** In deed itself, just things have been done for these men among us, who, having now attained them, perform their fatal journey, dismissed as much publicly by the city as privately by their own with magnificent expense and a crowded gathering. But the law commands that a praise be returned to them in words, and indeed it is fitting. For when deeds have been well done, through the very adornment of words, a perennial memory and splendor proceeds to those who performed them among the listeners. But there is need of that speech which might sufficiently praise the deceased...

**THE REPUBLIC OF PLATO, OR, THE FIRST DIALOGUE ON JUSTICE.**

**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.**

As much as the eye surpasses the hands, the head the feet, reason the senses, the soul the body, the end all things which are directed to the end, stability [surpasses] motion, and eternity time; so much the contemplative life seems to surpass the active. For contemplation is both the principle and the end of action, and commanding that [action] be led at its will and institution, it finally orders the inferior motions and external action to cease, so that an intrinsic and stable action might at last be possessed more freely. Thus indeed, from contemplation of God himself, the celestial and natural motions and all actions are led as if from a principle, and are led back [to it] as if to an end. Wherefore our Plato is at least more excellent than the other founders of cities and laws in this: that certain others instituted a city more toward human action, but he, being as it were divine, leads all action of the city, both public and private, especially toward contemplating; and he constitutes a city more to be looked up to than as a mistress of the world—not so much to be feared by many as to be venerated by all nations—a celestial Jerusalem, as it were, expressed on earth according to one’s powers. In this city, the grace of private possession having been removed, all things are common to all for the sake of the law of nature itself; there is common plenty, firm concord, one will of all, and therefore a tranquility always ready for contemplating. He composes, moreover, an absolute and entire Republic in the number of ten books, the most whole of all numbers...

# Book Thirty. 356

...survivors or to kindly advise them, to exhort their sons and brothers to the imitation of their virtue, and to console the parents and any other elders who remain. What sort of speech will this be for us? Or from where shall we best begin to praise these illustrious men, who while living delighted their own people wonderfully with their own virtue, and did not hesitate to offer themselves to death for the safety of the living? It seems to me, therefore, appropriate to praise them according to their nature, just as they became good men; and they became good because they drew their origin from good people. Therefore, let us first praise their noble lineage. Then their education and discipline. Finally, let us recount how their deeds were performed in a manner most becoming to those who were sprung from such ancestors and thus educated afterward. 

The first praise of their race is that the origin of their ancestors was not foreign, nor did it leave these successors here as if they were new residents or people born from foreigners. Instead, they were indigenous and truly dwelling in their fatherland, living and nourished not by a stepmother, as others are, but by their mother herself—the very region in which they lived. In this land they are now buried having finished their lives; they rest in the womb of her who bore them, nourished them, and received them. For it is right to honor the mother herself before all things; for in this way, their race is most greatly adorned. Moreover, this region is to be celebrated not only by us, but by all men, for many other reasons, but especially because it is most dear to the Gods. The contest and judgment of the Gods concerning this land <note>referring to the myth of the contest between Athena and Poseidon for the patronage of Athens</note> bears witness to this. Why should that which has been praised by the Gods not be praised by all men? 

The second praise will be this: that at the time when the earth produced all kinds of animals, wild beasts and all herds, our land alone was sterile of such things and void of wild animals. Specifically, out of all living things, it gave birth to man, who surpasses the rest in intelligence and alone honors justice and the Gods. That this region brought forth both those whom we celebrate in this assembly and our ancestors is most clearly recognized from this: every being that gives birth contains the nourishment suitable for its offspring. By this, a woman who has given birth is clearly discerned from one who has substituted a child; for she who gave birth abounds in milk for the nourishment of the one born, while the other does not. Thus, our mother earth provides a clear argument that she procreated men. For she alone and first then produced human food—the fruits of wheat and barley—by which the human race is most conveniently nourished, as she truly produced that living being. It is more likely to conclude this about the earth than about a woman. For the earth does not imitate woman in conception and birth, but woman imitates the earth. She distributed fruit of this kind not sparingly, but bestowed it on other men as well. After this, she supplied oil as a help for the labors of her children. When her sons were nourished and grown, she introduced the Gods as princes and teachers. Their names must be omitted now. For we are not unaware of those who fortified our life, as much by the invention of arts looking toward daily livelihood as by the tradition and skill of arms for the protection of the region itself. 

Thus the ancestors of these men, having been born and educated, instituted the Republic. Regarding this, it is right if we speak in a few words. For the Republic is the education of men—good for the good, and the opposite for the evil. Therefore, it must be declared that our ancestors were nurtured in an excellent Republic, through which both they and these good men, among whom are those who have departed from life, became good. For the same Republic existed once as exists now: a government of the best <term>optimatum gubernatio: an aristocracy based on merit</term>, under which we live in these times and nearly always since that time. Some call it popular <note>democracy</note>, others call it otherwise, however it pleases them. But in truth, this is a government of the best with a certain dignity of the people. For we always have kings, sometimes created by succession of lineage, other times by election; but the greatest power in the city rests with the people, who always impart the magistracy and power to those who are judged to be the best. In this city, no one is rejected because of the weakness, poverty, or ignobility of their parents, nor is anyone honored for the opposite reasons, as is accustomed to happen in other cities. But this is the rule: whoever is held to be wise or good, dominates and commands. 

The cause of this kind of government for us is the equality of our origin. For other cities are constituted from various and dissimilar races; because of this, their governments are unequal—tyrannies and the powers of the few. In those places, men live in such a way that they consider one another partly as masters and partly as slaves. But we, all born as brothers from one mother, do not think ourselves to be masters and slaves to each other; rather, the equality of our race leads us to seek equality of law, nor do we yield to anything at all except the reputation for virtue and wisdom. Wherefore both our parents and the parents of these men, being honorably born and nurtured in all liberty, performed many and noble deeds most well-known among all nations, both privately and publicly, thinking that for the sake of liberty they must fight as much against Greeks for other Greeks as against barbarians for all Greeks. Indeed, in what way they once aided the Argives in war against the Cadmeans, and the Heraclidae against the Argives—since Eumolpus and the Amazons, and those even before them, invaded the region—time is too narrow to relate according to their dignity; and the poets, elegantly celebrating their virtue with Music, have spread their fame among all nations. Therefore, if we were to attempt to repeat the same things in naked speech now, perhaps we would seem second to them. 

These things, for this reason, I think should be omitted, since they seem already sufficiently celebrated according to their dignity. But those things which have not yet been sung by any of the poets as the dignity of the matter requires, and which no one has yet vindicated from oblivion—these I think must be proclaimed by us now, so that we may praise and help them, and provoke others to adorn the same with odes and other songs as is fitting. Of the things I speak of, these are the first that stand out. When the Persians commanded Asia and were becoming masters of Europe, the men of this region, our progenitors, were the first to stop them; whose virtue it is especially necessary and becoming to remember and praise. It is necessary indeed, if anyone is to rightly praise the deeds done by them at that time, when all Asia already served a third king. Of these, Cyrus was the first, who with a certain greatness of soul restored his Persian citizens to liberty, and at the same time subjected the Medes, their masters, and ruled all Asia as far as Egypt. His son then ruled Egypt and Libya as far as it was possible to go. The third, Darius, extended his empire by land battle as far as the Scythians. By naval force, he dominated the sea and the islands. Thus it happened that no one dared to resist him. Indeed, all the minds of men were cast down by a certain servile fear; so many great and warlike nations were held under the empire of the Persians. Darius, however, accusing us and the Eretrians as if we were plotting against Sardis, and having found this occasion for war, sent five hundred thousand men in fleets...

# Menexenus, Or, The Funeral Oration. 357

...and three hundred ships, and he placed Datis in charge of these, commanding him to lead the Eretrians and Athenians to him as captives if he wished his own head to remain safe. Having arrived by ship at Eretria, where there were not a few men—and moreover they were numbered among the most illustrious of the Greeks of those times in matters of war—he made them captives within three days. He explored the whole region so that there would be no place of escape; he did it in this manner: his soldiers, extending themselves from sea to sea and running about with joined hands, traversed the entire region so that they could report to the king that no one had escaped them. With the same plan, they descended from Eretria to Marathon, as it was most suitable for them to lead the Athenians as captives under the same yoke with the Eretrians. 

With some of these things thus completed and others attempted, none of the Greeks except the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> came to the aid of the Eretrians and Athenians. And they arrived on the day following the battle. All the others were terrified and, thinking they were doing well if they escaped the present danger, remained quiet. From this, one can see how great the virtue of those men was who sustained the attack of the barbarians at Marathon and subdued the pride of all Asia. They were the first to triumph over the barbarians and showed by example to the rest that the force of the Persians was not invincible; indeed, that all the multitude and the abundance of riches yield to virtue. I think those men were not only the fathers of our bodies, but also the authors of our liberty and the liberty of all who dwell in this region. For provoked by these examples, the later Greeks did not hesitate to undergo all dangers for their safety in the following wars, becoming the disciples of those who routed the Persians at Marathon. 

Therefore, it is fitting to grant the first prize in speech to them, and the second to those who defeated the enemy in naval battle near Salamis and Artemisium. Indeed, we could tell of many things done by these men—how great were the dangers they sustained and overcame by land and sea—but what I think is outstanding above the rest, I will now relate. For they completed what remained after the Marathonian war. While those who fought at Marathon demonstrated to the Greeks that a few Greeks could break the attack of many barbarians in a land battle, the matter of victory at sea was still uncertain. The Persians were thought to be invincible in maritime battles due to their number, riches, skill, and strength. Therefore, this is worthy of praise in those who then fought with ships: that they utterly drove away the fear instilled in the Greeks and ensured they would no longer dread the number of ships and men. By both these groups—those fighting on land at Marathon and those later at sea near Salamis—the remaining Greeks were both taught and accustomed, by the former on land and by the latter at sea, not to fear the barbarians. 

I assert that the third thing, which was done at Plataea, was the cause of the safety of Greece, both in number and in virtue. That achievement is now common to the Lacedaemonians and the Athenians; they performed the greatest and most difficult deed. Because of that virtue, they are praised by us now and will be by those who follow and by posterity. After this, many cities of the Greeks were still under the barbarians. It was reported that the King was about to invade the Greeks again. It is surely fitting to commemorate those who placed the final hand of safety upon the works of their predecessors when they drove all barbarism from the sea. These were the men who fought with the fleet near Eurymedon, and those who set out to fight in Cyprus, and likewise those who sailed to Egypt and traversed many other coasts of the lands. These men must be remembered and thanks must be given to them, because they compelled the terrified king to think of his own safety rather than to lay snares for the destruction of the Greeks. In this war, all cities were liberated while the Greeks defended themselves and all men of the same language against the barbarians. 

Finally, when peace was made and the city was in honor, there arose against it what usually arises among men toward those for whom things succeed prosperously: first emulation, and then from emulation, envy, which dragged this city against its will into a war to be waged with the Greeks. After this, the war having begun, they met at Tanagra, fighting for the liberty of the Boeotians against the Lacedaemonians. Though the outcome of the battle was uncertain, what followed afterward made the matter clear. For many fled, deserting the Boeotians whom they were aiding. But our men, having gained victory on the third day at Oenophyta, justly restored those who were unjustly exiled. These were the first after the Persian War to aid the Greeks for the sake of liberty against other Greeks; they were noble men and authors of liberty for those to whom they brought help, and they were the first placed to be honored by the city in these monuments. 

After these things were done, as the war increased and all the Greeks took up arms and devastated the region, returning an unworthy thanks to the city, our men overcame them in a naval battle and captured their leaders, the Lacedaemonians. Although it was permitted to slaughter them, they released them and confirmed a peace, thinking that against men of the same race one must fight only until victory, and that the communion of the Greeks should not be utterly dissolved because of the city's own indignation, but that against barbarians one must fight to the death. It is fitting, therefore, to praise these men who lie here after this war was finished, because they showed that the suspicion of those was vain who, distrusting the virtue of the Athenians, might think that in the first war against the barbarians some others were more outstanding than the Athenians. For these men, when all Greece was shaken by seditions and they had captured men more outstanding than the rest of the Greeks in war, declared that they could conquer separately those with whom they had collectively defeated the barbarians. 

After this, a third unforeseen and grave war arose, in which many brave men fell and are buried here. Many of these won many victories near Sicily for the safety of the Leontines, to whom they were bound by oath to bring help, under which treaty they had sailed to those places. But because the voyage was long and in the meantime the city was pressed by a crisis of affairs and poverty and could not help them, their affairs did not succeed prosperously because subsidies were denied. Their enemies and adversaries in war have a greater praise for moderation and virtue than the friends of others have. Moreover, many in a naval battle throughout the Hellespont captured all the ships of the adversaries in one day and overcame many others. I called that war unexpected and hard because no one would have thought that all the remaining Greeks would be kindled against the city with such sharp zeal of contention that they would not hesitate to provoke that most hateful barbarian king, whom they had driven out together with us, through legates to bring war upon the Greeks again, and to collect all Greeks and barbarians to besiege this city. There, especially, the power and virtue of this city shone forth.

--- Page 374 ---
# Book Thirty. 358

For when they thought the city had already succumbed, and the ships were besieged near Mitylene, they themselves, about to bring help, entered sixty ships and—men who were brave without controversy—routed the enemy and liberated their friends; but having been surrounded by an unworthy misfortune, and not having been killed by the sea, they lie here. It is fitting always to remember them with praise. For by their virtue, we reported victory not only then from the naval contest, but also in the rest of the battle. Indeed, because of them our city attained such glory that it was believed it could never be conquered, not even by all men. And surely that seemed to be true. For we were not oppressed by the strength of others but by our own dissensions. Indeed, even now we are undefeated by foreigners. But we conquered ourselves; we brought offense upon ourselves. 

After these times, all things being pacified and peace being made with others, internal sedition arose among us, in which the fighting was such that if it were altogether decreed that men should be shaken by seditions, no one would seem to wish his country to suffer otherwise. For from the Piraeus and the city, how kindly and domestically, contrary to the opinion of other Greeks, did the citizens conflict with each other? And the war stirred up against those who were at Eleusis—how moderately did they conduct and settle it? Surely there is no other cause for all these things except true kinship itself, which provides firm and twin friendship not in speech, but in deed. 

It is necessary also to honor the memory of those who fell in this war by mutual wounds, and as much as we can, to reconcile them among themselves with prayers and sacrifices performed for those who survived, since we too have been reconciled. For they did not join hands together because of wickedness or enmity, but by a certain misfortune. We who survive are witnesses of these things. For since we are joined to them by race, we mutually give and receive pardon if we either brought anything upon another or suffered it from another. 

Then, when the city rested in the greatest tranquility of affairs, it forgave the barbarians because, having been attacked by it, they had fought back bravely enough. But it was indignant with the Greeks because, for benefits received, they sometimes returned injury, while entering into society with the barbarians and plundering the ships by which they had been saved, and tearing down the walls by which we had once defended their own walls lest they collapse. Therefore, the city decided no longer to protect the Greeks if ever they were oppressed either by Greeks or by barbarians. While we were of this opinion, and the Lacedaemonians thought we, the defenders of liberty, had fallen and that it would be their task hereafter to subjugate others, they acted accordingly. 

What need is there for many words? For I would not speak of old things or things done many centuries ago that followed. Nor is it hidden from us that the first of the terrified Greeks—the Argives, Boeotians, and Corinthians—implored the help of this city. And what is most divine of all, the King himself was in such difficulty that he considered his safety could come from nowhere else than from this city, which he had attempted to destroy with all his zeal. Indeed, if anyone wished to accuse this city rightly, he could only object to this: that it is always moved too much by mercy and too diligently relieves the one who is failing. At that time, it could not endure or continue to observe what it had instituted. It had surely decreed never to bring help to those from whom it had received injury when they were failing. Yet it changed its purpose and provided help. From which it liberated the Greeks by its aid from slavery, so that they lived as free men until they subjugated each other. 

But it dared not help the King at all. For it feared the triumphs formerly reported from Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea. But because it favored him with sincere exiles and voluntary helpers, without controversy it saved him also. Having built walls and fabricated ships and undertaken war when it was compelled to wage war, it fought for the safety of the Parians against the Lacedaemonians. But the King, fearing the city after he had seen the Lacedaemonians refuse naval war, and for that reason wishing to abandon it, demanded the Greeks who were on the continent—whom the Lacedaemonians themselves had previously surrendered—thinking this would be denied to him, whereby he might find an occasion to abandon us. There he was deceived by the other allies. For the Corinthians, Argives, Boeotians, and other allies in war were willing to surrender them and agreed with an oath that if he gave money, they would hand over those Greeks who were on the continent to him. We alone, however, dared neither to surrender them nor to swear then; so noble, free, constant, and upright is the custom of this city, and its nature is hostile to barbarians because these men are pure and upright Greeks without any mixture of barbarians. For Pelopes, or Cadmuses, or Egyptians, or Danaans, and many others who are barbarians by nature and Greeks only by law, are not mixed with us; but we ourselves, being only Greeks and not infected by any confusion of barbarians at all, persevere. 

This purity produced in this city a hatred against a foreign race. We alone, being pure, persevered in this: that we were unwilling to perpetrate a shameful and profane deed and surrender Greeks to the hands of barbarians. Coming down to these things, from which we were first overcome, with God favoring us, we were able to end the war more happily than then. For retaining our ships, walls, and colonies, we were liberated from war; so willingly did even the enemies themselves desist. Yet we lost brave men in this war too, partly intercepted at Corinth by the roughness and narrowness of the region, partly routed by treachery at Lechaeum. There were also notable men who both liberated the King and drove the Lacedaemonians from the sea. These I indeed bring back to your memory. It is fitting for you to praise and celebrate men of this kind. 

And indeed these works of the men lying here, and of all others who died for their country, as they have been related, are many and noble; but those which remain are far more and more excellent. Indeed, many days and nights would scarcely suffice if anyone wished to embrace them all. These things being recalled to memory, it is necessary for each man to assiduously exhort the sons of these men that, as if in war, they should keep the rank of their ancestors and not flee through laziness. Indeed, O sons of excellent men, I myself both exhort you in the present and will always advise and cohort you, whomever of you I find in the future, to strive to turn out as well as possible. Now also it is right to relate to you what your fathers commanded us to proclaim to posterity if anything should happen when there was a risk to be taken. I will therefore recount to you in the present what I heard from them themselves, or what they themselves would now willingly prescribe to you if the opportunity were given, as much as I can conjecture from what they once said. Consider that those themselves are now hearing the things I relate as I speak. They began in this manner: 

"That you are born from noble parents, O sons, the present circumstances testify; surely when it was permitted to us to live basely, we preferred to die honorably rather than subject you and the rest of posterity to any infamy, and to be a disgrace to our parents and ancestors..."
