...a disgrace; thinking that a man who disgraces his own people should not live. For to him, neither in life nor after death is anyone a friend, whether of men or of gods. It is necessary, therefore, that you be mindful of our words; if you practice anything else, practice it with virtue, knowing that without virtue all exercises and possessions are shameful and evil. For riches bring no splendor to the one possessing them with laziness; for he prepares and possesses riches not for himself, but for another. Nor do beauty of body and strength, when they are in a timid and wicked man, provide decorum. For they befit him not; they make him more notorious and reveal his laziness. 

<margin>Cicero, On Duties, Book 1.</margin> 
Moreover, science <note>original: "scientia"; here meaning knowledge or skill</note> which is remote from justice and other virtue is seen to be not wisdom, but craftiness. For the sake of these things, both first and last, and through all things, contend with all zeal and diligence that you may surpass both us and our ancestors in the glory of virtue. Otherwise, know that if we surpass you in virtue, this victory will bring us disgrace; but if we are surpassed by you, it will bring happiness. We will indeed be most greatly surpassed, and you will surpass us, if you institute your life in such a way that you do not abuse the glory of your ancestors, nor, so to speak, squander it; knowing that to a man thinking himself to be something, nothing more shameful can happen than to offer himself to be honored not for his own virtue, but because of the glory of his superiors. For the glory of parents is a noble and magnificent treasure for their children. But to use a treasure of money and honors and not to transfuse this to posterity, through a lack of one's own possession and glory, is shameful and utterly foreign to the nobility of a man. If, therefore, you practice these things, you will come to us as dear children to dear parents when your lives are finished. But if you neglect these things and turn out wicked, no one will willingly receive you. 

Let these things be said to our children. Our fathers and mothers, if any of ours remain and need consolation, must be consoled because it is becoming to bear easily whatever happens; nor is the case to be deplored together with them. For they will not need the lamentations of others; for fate will bring enough sadness to them. It is surely necessary to heal and soothe them, and first of all to commemorate that the gods have already granted them the greatest of the things they were accustomed to pray for. For they did not pray that immortal sons be given to them, but good and illustrious ones. They have become partakers of this vow, which must be considered the greatest good. For all things to succeed according to one's prayer in life is not easy for a mortal man. And yet, if they will tolerate brave things with a brave mind, they will seem to be truly the parents of brave sons and themselves brave. But if they succumb to grief, they will bring suspicion to men, lest perhaps either they are not our parents at all, or those who extol us with praises are lying. But neither of these should happen; indeed, let our praisers be especially those who show by their deeds that they are truly parents who are men of men. 

Indeed, that old proverb, *Nothing in excess* <note>original: "Ne quid nimis"</note>, seems wisely said. 
<margin>Cicero translates this thus in the Tusculan Disputations, Book 5.</margin> 
For he to whom all things which lead to living well are truly fitted from himself, and do not depend on others hanging either on good or contrary chance, nor are compelled to wander from the outcomes of another—from this the best way of living is prepared. This is that moderate man, this the brave, this the wise; he will obey and follow that old precept, both when things are born and when they fall, with other comforts and especially with children. Nor will he ever rejoice too much, nor grieve too much, who always places all hope in himself. We judge and wish our people to be such. And yet in the present, we exhibit ourselves as such, certainly not perturbed or terrified by too much fear if it is necessary for us to depart from life now. 

We also pray our fathers and mothers that they lead their future life similarly affected, knowing that they will not gratify us most by lamentations and wailing; but if there is any sense of the living to those who are deceased, they will be most troublesome to us if they lose themselves and bear their fate unjustly. But if they bear it moderately and lightly, they will follow us most greatly; moreover, our affairs now have an end which is most beautiful for men. Wherefore they are to be praised rather than deflated. Surely if they protect and nourish our wives and children and devote themselves to these, they will most greatly consign our fall to oblivion, and lead a life more beautiful, more right, and more pleasing to us. Let these things suffice on our behalf to our people. 

To the city, however, we command that it take care of our parents and children, and that it educate the latter honorably and cherish the old age of the former worthily. We know that you will take excellent care, even if we do not prescribe these things at all. Therefore, O children of the deceased and parents, they commanded that we advise these things. I indeed, as much as I can, most diligently advise you, and in their name I beseech the younger ones to imitate the noble deeds of their own; and the elders to hope for the best for themselves. Indeed, we will nourish your old age privately and publicly; and whomever of their progeny we find, we will embrace with the greatest benevolence. You yourselves are not unaware of the providence of the city, which, having established laws, protects the parents and children of those who died in war, and commits the care of such to the highest magistrate before other citizens, lest the parents of these be affected by any injury at all. 

It educates the sons itself and strives that their orphanhood be unknown to them. For it acts in the place of a parent both while they are boys, and when they have come to mature age, it sends them to their duties, adorns them with all armor, shows and records the interests of the father while it grants the instruments of paternal virtue. And at the same time, for the sake of a good omen, it commands the son then for the first time to enter the paternal house as if about to command, and adorned with arms and strength. Moreover, it honors those who have departed from life, renewing every year the ceremonies decreed by law commonly for all, which are accustomed to be performed specifically for each individual privately. It likewise institutes gymnastic and equestrian contests, and various musical games. And surely as far as it looks toward the deceased, it takes up the condition of heir and son; as far as toward the sons, of a father; as far as toward parents and others of this kind, of a guardian, always providing for all with all diligence. By the thought of these things, you ought to bear adverse things with an equal mind. For in this way, you will be more pleasing both to the dead and the living, and you will easily take care and easily be cared for. Now you and all the rest who have already followed with mournful expiations those who have yielded to nature commonly according to the law, depart." 

This, O Menexenus, is the speech of Aspasia of Miletus.

->**PLATO'S REPUBLIC, OR, DIALOGUE I ON THE JUST.**<-

**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.**

AS MUCH as the eye surpasses the hands, the head the feet, reason the senses, the soul the body, the end all things directed toward the end, status motion, and eternity time, so much the contemplative life seems to surpass the active life. For contemplation is both the beginning and the end of action, and it leads and stops it at will, commanding at last the inferior motions and external action to cease, so that an intrinsic and stable action may finally be possessed more freely. Thus indeed from the very contemplation of God, celestial and natural motions and all actions are led as from a beginning and reduced as to an end. 

Wherefore our Plato is at least more excellent than the other founders of cities and laws, in that others indeed, like humans, instituted the city more for action, but he, as if divine, leads all action of the city, both public and private, especially toward contemplating, and constitutes the city as mistress of itself before being mistress of the world, not so much to be feared by many as to be revered by all nations, a celestial Jerusalem as it were expressed on earth according to its strength, in which, contentions having been removed for the sake of one's own possession, all things may be common to all for the sake of the law of nature itself, there may be common abundance, firm concord, one will of all, and therefore tranquility always ready for contemplating. 

He composes the entire form of an absolute Republic in a denary <note>ten-fold</note> number of books, the most whole of all numbers, both containing the numbers numbered within itself and replicating innumerable ones from itself. And as he often declares in these books, especially in the second, he prefers the whole disputation to be inscribed *On Justice* by us, rather than *On the Republic*: teaching, as I judge, that every thing and action, both public and private, is not to be referred to abundance, nor to power, nor to victory, but thoroughly to justice itself. Which justice, all perturbation having been removed and the impediments of contentions expelled, finally renders the citizens most ready for investigating the true and worshipping God. Our Plato judges such contemplation and worship to be the chief end of the republic: so that what neither one, if he lived alone, nor many if they lived together, can effect without law, at least many citizens gathered by a common law into one assembly of a city may perfect. 

Furthermore, Timaeus and Critias teach us that before the great inundation of lands, other Athens existed, both among the Greeks and among the Egyptians, governed by similar laws among themselves, which the goddess Pallas founded, educated, and taught. And she delivered to them that form of a republic which Plato writes in these books. But in the books *On Laws*, he composes a republic from the Cretan, Lacedaemonian, and new Attic government, and begins the composition itself from God, the author of all laws. But to return to the present things, he begins this republic also with happy auspices from the very rites of divine wisdom, from the custom and counsel of the elders, and from religious justice and sanctity. 

For from the fact that he had said both vows to God and things due to each must be returned, he begins now to dispute about a certain private justice, through which he will opportunely pass to public justice in its own place. But you, remember that in these things it is signified by Plato that without divine and human justice, and the counsel of elders, and the favor of divine wisdom, a city cannot be successfully established from the beginning, or happily governed once established. Next, touching upon the argument of the first book, I will excerpt certain necessary things from many and grave precepts. 

Moderate youth easily makes old age; immoderate makes it difficult. He who obeys the lusts of the body undoubtedly serves insane tyrants. The soul in old age, with the perturbations which youth brings with it having been settled, and being segregated from the body, inspects divine things more closely and more openly. Innocence alone provides the best hope for the soul in the future, the unique solace of life. A man of sound mind will judge money to be useful especially for this: that whatever he has either vowed to God or promised to man, or owed otherwise, he may fulfill, nor be led because of poverty either to lie to anyone or to defraud in any matter. For money is to be referred to justice, but justice to the reward of the other life. 

But before we pursue the disputation about justice, I advise that it be considered that individual things are disposed under a certain allegory by Plato. First indeed, Cephalus the old man—that is, the head <note>Latin "caput"</note>—provides the head for the disputation. Then Polemarchus—which his name also signifies, prince—that is, the first, moderately approaches the battle. Then Thrasymachus—that is, the fierce fighter—acts more harshly. Socrates, however—that is, the savior—powerful everywhere, saves all from error and injustice. 

But leaving the allegory to the commentaries, let us now proceed to the definition of justice. They say Simonides, Pittacus, and Bias said that justice is to confess the truth and to return to each what is owed. Which indeed some interpret thus: simply to open the truth to anyone, and to restore what you have received. But Socrates disapproves of that, because to an insane man neither should every truth be revealed, nor should arms be returned which he had deposited with you while he was sane. 

Others explain it thus: to give to each what is suitable for him, as emolument to friends, but harm to enemies; to benefit the good, but to injure the evil. That again is disapproved, because it is never becoming to injure anyone. For whoever injures anything makes that very thing worse and more inept for its own work and proper virtue; as he who injures a dog renders it inept for the proper virtue of a dog. But justice is the virtue of a man. Whoever therefore injures a man makes him worse regarding justice. But justice never diminishes justice, just as the work of music does not destroy the work of music. Wherefore it is not just to injure anyone. 

Among these things, Thrasymachus, as many others do at other times, objects to Socrates that he never wishes to answer, but always to interrogate. But it should not be hidden from you that for many reasons Socrates was accustomed always to seek rather than to teach. First, to advise the arrogant that in every age one must learn rather than teach. Second, to signify that truth is immediately infused by divinity into minds segregated from the body and errors through opportune inquiry. Which Avicenna also greatly approves. Third, to show that the forms of things are innate in our souls, through which the truth of things itself may sometimes be refined in souls through interrogation turned toward them. Fourth, to declare that human science consists at least in a certain negation rather than in the affirmation of truth. 

Then a definition of justice is brought forward by Thrasymachus, such as also by Callicles in the *Gorgias*: that the just is that which is useful to the more powerful. For the more powerful always dominate and bring laws to their own utility and govern subjects. Then indeed subjects act justly when they obey those laws which are constituted for the utility of the governors. Socrates draws him into a contradiction. Since a prince could command through ignorance things which will be detrimental to himself. If a private person observes these, then he will be just, because he obeys the dominant one; and then unjust, because he acts against the utility of the dominant one. 

He adds that any absolute art, and therefore one least in need, in handling materials and men, consults not its own utility but the utility of the things commended to it, like a tutor to wards, a doctor to the sick, a pilot to sailors; and similarly the legitimate magistrate looks forward to the utility of the subjects. If any art such as medicine exacts a reward, it makes a gain not insofar as it is medicine—whose end is the cure of disease—but insofar as it is mixed with a certain mercenary and gain-making art. It is clear that the civil art, the most perfect of all and therefore least needy and servile, governs much less for the sake of utility. 

I omit what Thrasymachus rashly and with a certain repugnance of himself brings against justice. But you, note that it is not becoming for anyone to seek the principate and to solicit magistracies. Likewise, if ever a city of good men exists, they will fight for the sake of not commanding, just as they now contend with the desire for commanding. 

Now notice three things. First, the evil are not to be admitted to the magistracy. Second, citizens who are not evil, so that they may willingly undertake the grave burden of governing, are to be invited by an imposed reward of stipend and honor. Third, honest men who are moved neither by avarice nor by ambition, ought to be provoked to the republic only by that discrimination and fear: namely, lest they themselves be subjected to the unjust government of the worse. 

The divine Plato understands, if anyone ever did, that the duty of governing the fatherland, if it is just, ought to be voluntary. But by the example of the most approved citizen, he wishes to disprove the wicked arrogance of those who always solicit magistracies by any way and hunt for dignities. But in what way they themselves may become worthy of dignities, they do not care at all. He wishes, therefore, that duty to be voluntary as well as necessary, so that a most approved man may most willingly undertake the rudders of his fatherland, but do it only then when necessity demands; meanwhile, however, he should prefer contemplation to action: but sometimes, when affairs are urgent, he should prefer action concerning the public good for a time to his own contemplation. All this can be most clearly understood from the letter of Plato to Archytas of Tarentum.

### Dialogue I. On the Republic, or, On the Just. 361

[Column 1]

...placing [justice] in the category of wisdom and the good. This is shown to be false because any art is a form of wisdom, and whatever a person is wise in, they are also good in. A man who is learned in any art does not seek to do more than another learned person in a skillful action, but rather to perform the action equally and in a similar fashion. Although he only wishes to equal the learned, he nevertheless wishes to surpass the unlearned. But the unlearned person sometimes rashly attempts to take more for himself than both the learned and the unlearned. The just man is very similar to the learned man, desiring to have nothing more than another just man, but yet having something more—namely virtue—than the unjust man. The unjust man, however, like the unlearned, strives to have more than both the just and the unjust. He <note>Socrates</note> concludes, therefore, against Thrasymachus, that justice must be referred to the category of wisdom and the good, while injustice must be referred to the category of ignorance and evil. 

He adds that injustice is the cause of weakness in all things. For in any group, by producing hatred and discord, it first makes the group very weak and then dissolves it. A group can only hold together to the extent that some degree of just distribution is maintained. Therefore, it stands through justice but is dissolved through injustice. Through justice, they are friends both to one another and to others; through injustice, they are enemies on all sides. Furthermore, justice and injustice perform the same function in any individual soul as they do in any gathering, so that the just man is in harmony with himself and is a friend to himself, to men, and to the gods. For the gods are most just, so it is no wonder that the just man, being like them, is also their friend. The unjust man, in all these matters, is the complete opposite. 

Moreover, every thing has its own proper function. It also requires its own proper virtue—that is, a certain faculty through which it may most aptly fulfill its proper work, and without which it cannot do so. Since, therefore, the soul has a certain proper work, such as deliberating and governing, and even more importantly, living, it also demands its own proper virtue through which it may perform these things most conveniently, and if this is taken away, the soul suffers. The virtue of the soul is justice; its vice is injustice. Therefore, through justice, the soul deliberates and governs perfectly and lives happily. But if justice is removed, the opposite occurs. With these things said, the first book is concluded with a certain correction. Specifically, since it should have been said what justice *is* before discussing what its *qualities* are, the reverse has been done so far, while Socrates partly followed those disputing, and partly disputed through better-known principles, both indulging the intellect of his listeners and consulting their capacity.

->SOCRATES, GLAUCON, POLEMARCHUS, THRASYMACHUS, ADEIMANTUS, CEPHALUS.<-

I WENT DOWN YESTERDAY to the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens, about five miles from the city center</note> along with Glaucon, the son of Ariston, both so that I might pray to the Goddess and to observe the festival, to see in what manner they would conduct it, as they were doing so then for the first time. The procession of our fellow citizens seemed beautiful to me, but nonetheless, the one sent by the Thracians <note>The festival was likely for the Thracian goddess Bendis</note> appeared equally fitting. When we had finished our prayers and observed the spectacle, we began to return toward the city. 

Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, saw us from a distance as we were heading home and sent his servant, running ahead, to tell us to wait for him. Catching me by my cloak from behind, the servant said, "Polemarchus bids you to wait." I turned to him and asked where his master was. "He is following behind you," he said, "just wait." "We will wait," replied Glaucon. 

And a little while later, Polemarchus arrived, together with Adeimantus, Glaucon’s brother, and Niceratus, the son of Nicias, and several others who seemed to be coming from the procession. Then Polemarchus said, "O Socrates, you seem to me to be hurrying toward the city as if you are about to leave." "You have guessed not badly," I said. "Do you see how many of us there are?" he asked. "Of course." "Then either you must be stronger than all these, or you must stay here." "There is one other option," I said, "which is that you might allow us to go if we can persuade you that we should be let go." "Could you persuade us," he said, "if we refuse to listen?" "By no means," said Glaucon. "Then deliberate as if we are not going to listen," he replied. 

Then Adeimantus said, "Do you not know that there will be a torch race on horseback this evening in honor of the Goddess?" "A race on horseback?" I asked. "That is certainly new. 

[Column 2]

Will they carry torches and pass them to one another while racing on horses? Is that what you mean?" "Exactly so," said Polemarchus <margin>* Missing in the Greek manuscripts.</margin> (wherefore it is necessary that you either be more powerful or stay here). "Furthermore, they will perform nocturnal rites that are certainly worth seeing. For we shall rise after dinner and watch those rites, and we will be there among many young men and we shall converse. So stay, and do not do otherwise." And Glaucon said, "It seems we must stay." "Well, if it seems so," I said, "then so it must be done."

So we went to the house of Polemarchus, and there we found both Euthydemus and Lysias, the brothers of Polemarchus, Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Charmantides of Paeania, and Cleitophon, the son of Aristonymus. Inside was also Cephalus, the father of Polemarchus, who seemed to me quite old; I had not seen him for a long time. He was sitting crowned <note>Wearing a ceremonial wreath</note> on a certain cushion and seat. For he had been sacrificing in the courtyard. We sat down next to him, as many seats were arranged in a circle. 

As soon as Cephalus saw me, he greeted me and said: "O Socrates, you come to us only very rarely, descending to the Piraeus; you do not do right. For if I were still able to come to the city easily, there would be no need for you to come here to us, but we would come to you. But now it is right for you to come here more frequently; for truly, the more the other pleasures of the body fail me, the more the desire for conversation and the pleasure I take from it increases. Therefore, do this: come here to us and spend time with these young men as if with very close friends." 

"And yet," I said, "O Cephalus, I am very much delighted by conversations with the elderly. For it seems to me that we ought to hear from those who have already completed a journey upon which we too must enter—whether it be rough and difficult, or easy and passable. And I would gladly hear from you what you think of this matter, now that you have reached this age which the poets call 'on the threshold of old age' <note>A common Homeric expression for the very end of life</note>: whether you find it a difficult part of life, or how you would describe it." 

"By Jupiter, I will tell you, Socrates," he said, "how it seems to me. Many of us who are roughly the same age often meet, keeping that old proverb <note>The proverb 'like joins with like' or 'birds of a feather'</note>. Most of us in that gathering lament, feeling a longing for the pleasures we enjoyed in youth, recalling sex, drinking parties, and other things of that kind which you now enjoy; they take it heavily, as if they were deprived of the greatest things. They claim they lived well then, but now they are not even truly living. Some even deplore the insults and outrages of their relatives, and in this they especially blame old age as the cause of their greatest evils. <margin>Cicero, *On Old Age*.</margin> But they did not seem to me to be blaming what should be blamed. For if that happened because of the fault of old age, the same things would happen to me and to all others of greater age. <margin>Cicero, in the book *On Old Age*.</margin> 

But I have found many who are not affected this way, and I was once with the poet Sophocles when someone asked him if he still enjoyed sexual things. 'God forbid!' he said, 'I have gladly escaped from that, as if from a wild and raving master.' He seemed to me then to have answered very well, and no less so now. For in old age there is altogether much peace and freedom from things of this sort. For when the lusts have cooled and ceased, exactly what Sophocles described happens: we are freed from many masters, and mad ones at that. But the fault for all these complaints lies in a person’s character, not in their age. For moderate and easy-going old men, who are not inhumane, lead a tolerable old age. But the difficulties and inhumanity..."

...and inhumanity are troublesome at every age." Then I, being wonderfully delighted by these things he said and desiring to hear more, provoked him further: "I think indeed, O Cephalus, that many, when you say these things, do not accept them; they think rather that you bear old age easily because of your riches rather than because of your character; for they say many comforts are available to the rich." "You speak the truth," he said. "For they do not accept it, and there is indeed something to that, but by no means is everything in that. Just as they say Themistocles answered a certain man from Seriphus <note>A small, insignificant island</note> in a quarrel, when that man said Themistocles' fame came not from himself but from the glory of his city: 'By Hercules,' he said, 'if I were a Seriphian I would not be noble; but if you were an Athenian, you would never have been famous.' The same can be said of those who, not being rich, bear old age heavily. For old age cannot be light in extreme poverty, not even for a wise man; nor can it be anything but heavy for a foolish man in extreme poverty." "But," I said, "of the things you possess, were more left to you by your ancestors than you acquired yourself?" "I have acquired some," he said, "O Socrates: I have stood midway in wealth between my father and my grandfather. My grandfather Cephalus, receiving almost as much as I have now, accumulated much on top of it. But my father Lysanias made those riches even less than they are now. I am satisfied if I leave these things not less, but a little greater than I received." "I asked this," I said, "because you did not seem to me to admire riches very much, which is what those usually do who have not made them for themselves. But those who have prepared them love them twice as much as others. For just as poets love their poems and fathers love their sons, in the same way those who have acquired money are devoted to it as their own work, not merely for use and necessity as others are. From this their company is difficult, since they wish to praise nothing else besides riches." "You tell the truth," he said. "And very much so," I said. "But tell me this also: What is the greatest good you think you have gained from the possession of riches?" "Something," he said, "which I might not easily persuade many of if I were to say it. Know for certain, O Socrates, that after someone reaches the point where he thinks he is soon to die, fear and a certain care fall upon him concerning those things which he neglected in his earlier life. For the stories that are told about the dead—how those who acted unjustly must pay the penalty there—which have been laughed at until now, then move the soul, lest perhaps they be true; and the soul itself, either because of the weakness of old age or because it sees those things more acutely as it is closer to the other life, is filled with anxiety and fear, and it reckons and examines whether it has treated anyone with injury. He who finds many iniquities in his life is frequently awakened from sleep like a child and is terrified, living in wretched hope. But to him who is conscious of no injury to himself, a pleasant hope is always present, the best nurse of old age, as Pindar says. For he sang that skillfully, O Socrates: 'Whoever spends his life justly and holily, sweet hope accompanies him, nourishing his heart and fostering his old age, which most of all governs the fickle mind of mortals.' He speaks well and most admirably. To this I think the possession of money is to be valued most, not for just any man, but for a moderate and fair one; the possession of money contributes much to this: that one may depart there without fear, having neither circumvented anyone against their will, nor lied, nor owing either victims vowed to God or money to a man. It has, besides, other uses, and indeed very many. But if one were to compare one thing with another, O Socrates, I would not place this as the least thing for a man having a mind; rather, money contributes very much to this." "You speak excellently," I said, "O Cephalus. But as for this very thing, namely justice: shall we say it is simply telling the truth and returning what one has received? Or is doing these very same things sometimes just and sometimes unjust? For example: everyone would say that if someone in his right mind deposited a sword with you, and then demanded it back while in a state of madness, it would be a sin to return it, and he who returned it would not be just; nor again should one tell the whole truth to a man in such a state." "You speak rightly," he said. "Therefore this is not the definition of justice: to speak the truth and to return deposits." "You speak quite rightly, O Socrates," said Polemarchus, taking up the conversation, "if we are to believe Simonides <note>A famous Greek lyric poet</note> at all." Here Cephalus said, "I hand the conversation over to you. For I must go attend to the sacred rites." "Is Polemarchus not your heir?" I asked. And he, smiling, said, "He is indeed," and at the same time he departed for the sacrifice. "Tell me then," I said, "heir of the conversation, what do you assert was rightly said about justice by Simonides?" "That," he said, "he says it is just for what is owed to be returned to each. And saying this, he seems to speak rightly." "And yet it is not easy," I said, "to deny faith to Simonides. For he is a wise and divine man. But what he means, you perhaps understand, O Polemarchus, but I do not know. For it is manifest that he does not mean what we were saying just now, namely returning a deposit to someone who is not sane when they demand it back. And yet a deposit is in a sense something 'owed.' Is it not?" "Certainly," he said. "But it must not be returned then, when someone who is not sane demands it." "You speak the truth," he said. "Simonides, therefore, means something other than this when he asserts that it is just to return what is owed."

"Something else, by Jove," he said. "For he thinks friends owe it to friends to do good, but not evil. I understand indeed that he who would return gold to the one from whom he received the deposit would by no means be returning what is owed, if the return and the receipt were to be harmful, and if the one who receives and the one who returns are friends. Do you not affirm that Simonides speaks thus?" "Exactly so." "But what then? Must what is owed be returned to enemies?" "Altogether what is owed to them. And there is owed to an enemy, I think, by an enemy what is fitting—namely, something evil." <margin>Cicero discusses this in Book 3 of On Duties.</margin> "Simonides, therefore, signified poetically what justice is. For he judged, as it appears, that it is just to attribute to each what is fitting. And this he called 'what is owed.' But what do you think he would say if someone asked him: 'O Simonides, what faculty, and to whom, and giving what that is owed and fitting, is called medicine?' What do you think he would answer us?" "Surely, that which gives medicines, foods, and drinks to bodies." "And what art, and to whom, and providing what that is owed and fitting, is named cookery?" "That which gives sweet seasonings to dishes." "Come then, what art, and to whom, and giving what, shall be named Justice?" "If the previous things are to be followed, O Socrates, that is justice which returns benefits to friends and harms to enemies." "Therefore, he calls it justice to treat friends well and enemies ill?" "So it seems to me." "Who is most able to treat friends who are laboring under disease well, and enemies the opposite, both for good health and for bad?" "The doctor." "And who can do so for those sailing through the danger of the sea?" "The pilot." "In what action, then, and for what work is the just man most able to benefit friends and harm enemies?" "By fighting against and fighting for, as it seems to me." "But for those who are not sick, friend Polemarchus..."

Dialogue I. On the Republic. Or, On the Just. 363

"...the doctor is useless." "True." "And for those not sailing, the pilot." "Certainly." "Will the just man then be useless to those not at war?" "I do not at all admit this." "Justice is therefore useful in peace?" "Useful." "Agriculture is also useful in peace, is it not?" "It is." "For the harvesting of fruits?" "Yes." "And shoemaking?" "Certainly." "For providing shoes, that is?" "Clearly." "What about justice? For what use or gain will you say it is useful in peace?" "For commerce, Socrates." "By commerce do you mean partnerships, or something else?" "That very thing." "Is the just man, then, a good and useful partner in throwing dice? Or is he who plays dice?" "He who plays, surely." "But in the building of bricks or stones, will the just man be a better and more useful partner than the architect himself?" "Not at all." "In what partnership, then, will the just man be better than the lyre-player, as the lyre-player is more useful than the just man in striking strings?" "In money matters, as it seems to me." "But not, O Polemarchus, in using money, such as when horses must be sold or bought for money. Then surely a horse-dealer would be more useful. Would he not?" "It appears so." "And when a ship is needed, the shipbuilder or the sailor?" "So it seems." "For what common use of gold or silver, then, is the just man more useful than others?" "When we wish to deposit it and have it be safe, O Socrates." "Do you mean when there is no need to use it, but to set it aside?" "Exactly." "When money is useless, then, justice is useful in regard to it?" "It appears so." "And when a pruning-hook must be kept safe, justice is useful both privately and publicly; but when it must be used, the art of vine-cultivation is useful?" "It is clear." "Will you say further that when a shield and a lyre need to be kept safe, but not brought into use, justice is useful? But when we wish to use these, then the discipline of arms and music is useful?" "It must be so." "And must the same be said of all other things: that justice is useless in the use of things, but useful when we do not use them?" "It appears so." "Justice is not, then, a thing of great worth, my friend, if it is only useful for useless things. But let us consider this. Is not he who is most apt at striking in a fight, whether with fists or any other way, also the same who is best at guarding against it?" "Certainly." "Is it not also the case that whoever can avoid and hide a disease, can also inflict it?" "So it seems to me." "But the same person is the best guardian of an army who can steal the plans and other actions of the enemy." "It is so, indeed." "Therefore, of whatever thing one is an apt guardian, of that same thing he is an apt thief." "It appears so." "If, then, the just man is most able to keep money safe, he is also most able to steal it." "So the logic indicates," he said. "Therefore, the just man has been shown to be a kind of thief, as it appears, and you seem to have learned this from Homer. For he admires Autolycus <margin>Odyssey, Book 19</margin>, the maternal grandfather of Ulysses, and affirms that he surpassed others in both theft and the swearing of oaths. It seems, therefore, according to you and according to Homer and Simonides, that justice is a certain thieving faculty for the benefit of friends and the harm of enemies. Did you not say so?" "By Jove, no," he said, "but I no longer know what I said. For this still seems to me: that justice benefits friends and harms enemies." "By friends do you mean those who seem to each person to be good and useful, or those who are so, even if they do not seem so? And enemies in the same way?" "It is fitting to love those whom one thinks are good and useful, and to hate those whom one judges to be bad and useless." "Do not men err in this? So that many seem to them to be good and useful when they are bad and useless; and many the opposite?" "They certainly err." "To such people, then, the good are enemies, and the bad are friends." "Very much so." "Yet it is then just for them to help the bad and harm the good." "It appears so." "But the good are indeed just, and such as do nothing unjustly." "You speak the truth." "According to your argument, then, it is just to harm those who do no injury." "Not at all, Socrates; for this seems a wicked speech." "It is just, then, to harm the unjust and help the just." "This speech is more probable than the previous one." "It will happen then, O Polemarchus, to many of those who have erred in judging their friends, that it is just for them to harm their friends; for their friends are sometimes bad; and likewise to benefit their enemies, since they are sometimes good. And so we shall say the opposite of those things we said were brought forth by Simonides." "So it will happen, indeed. But let us reconsider. For we seem not to have correctly defined 'friend' and 'enemy'." "How did we define them, Polemarchus?" "That we said a friend is he who seems good and useful." "How shall we correct it for the present?" "We shall call a friend him who both seems and is good and useful. But him who seems so, but is not, we shall say seems a friend, but is not one. And the same logic will apply to the enemy." "A friend, therefore, by this logic will be a good man, and an enemy a bad man." "Exactly." "Do you bid us add something to the unjust besides what I was saying? We were saying further that it is just to benefit a friend and harm an enemy. But now do you want us to say it is just to help a friend who is good, and on the contrary to harm an enemy who is bad?" "This seems to me perfectly well said." "Is it, then, the part of a just man to harm any human being?" "One ought surely to harm the wicked and enemies." "If horses are harmed, do they become better or worse?" "Worse." "Is it in the virtue of dogs, or rather of horses?" "Of horses." "And are not dogs, when harmed, rendered worse in the virtue of dogs, not of horses?" "Necessarily." "Therefore, my friend, shall we not judge men who are harmed to become worse in human virtue?" "Altogether." "And is not justice a human virtue?" "Clearly." "It must be, then, that men who are harmed become more unjust." "It seems so." "Can musicians, by music itself, make anyone unmusical?" "By no means." "Can horsemen, by horsemanship, make men unpracticed in horsemanship?" "It is not possible." "Can just men, by justice itself, make men unjust? And in short, can good men, by virtue itself, make men bad?" "Certainly not." "For I do not think it is the work of heat to make anything cold, but of its opposite." "It is so." "Nor of dryness to make anything wet, but of its opposite." "Very much so." "Therefore, it is not the part of the good man to harm, but of his opposite." "It seems so." "And the just man is good?" "Altogether." "It is not, then, the work of the just man, O Polemarchus, to harm either a friend or anyone else, but of his opposite, the unjust man." "You seem to speak the truest things, O Socrates." "If anyone, therefore, says that justice is giving each his due, and understands by this that harm is owed to enemies by a just man, and benefit to friends, he is by no means to be judged wise who said this. For these things are not true. For it has been established that it is in no way just to harm anyone." "I confess it indeed," he said. "We shall fight together, then, you and I, if anyone asserts that Simonides said this, or Bias, or Pittacus, or any other of the wise and blessed men." "I am indeed ready to fight with you against him." "But do you know whose opinion I think this is, that justice is benefiting friends and harming enemies?" "Whose?" he said. "I think it is Periander's, or Perdiccas', or Xerxes', or Ismenias the Theban's, or some other wealthy man who thinks he can do the greatest things." "You speak the truth," he said. "After this, since it appears that neither this nor justice itself is what someone would say it is, what else might it be?" Thrasymachus...

<summary>Socrates deconstructs the idea that justice is "helping friends and harming enemies" by showing that justice, as a virtue, cannot be used to make people worse or more unjust. He concludes that a truly just person never harms anyone.</summary>

364 Book Thirty-One.

...Thrasymachus, however, had several times desired to interrupt our discussion, but had been prevented by those present who wished to hear us. But after we finished speaking, and I said these things, he could no longer contain himself; but gathering himself like a wild beast, he launched himself at us as if he were about to tear us to pieces. And so we were both terrified, Polemarchus and I. But he cried out, "What nonsense has occupied you for so long, Socrates? Why do you play the fool among yourselves, yielding to each other? If you truly wish to know what the just is, do not only ask, nor seek to conquer by refuting after an answer has been given to you, observing that it is easier to ask than to answer. But you yourself answer what you think justice to be: and do not tell me that it is what is fitting, or what is useful, or what is profitable, or what is gainful, or what is conducive: but tell me plainly and clearly what you mean. For I will not accept it if you bring forth such nonsense." Hearing these things, I was terrified, and looking at him, I was afraid; and as I think, if I had not looked at him before he looked at me, I would have become completely mute. But when he began to be exasperated by the speech itself, I looked at him first, and therefore I was able to answer him, and said, trembling slightly: "O Thrasymachus, do not be fierce with us. For if we have slipped in the examination of these arguments, both I and this man, know for certain that we have erred unwillingly; truly, if we were searching for gold, we would never willingly yield to each other in searching so as to impede the finding. Therefore, do not think that while we search for justice, a thing far more precious than gold, we would so foolishly yield to each other, but that we strive with all zeal to find it clearly. But, as I think, we are not able to attain it. Wherefore it is much more fitting for you wise men to pity us than to be harsh." Then he, hearing this, laughed very Sardonically and loudly, and said, "O Hercules, this is that usual irony of Socrates! Indeed, I knew this and predicted it to these people: that you would not be willing to answer, but would rather use irony, and finally do everything rather than answer anyone who asked you." "You are wise, Thrasymachus," I said, "and you know well that if you asked someone how much twelve is, and while asking you predicted: 'Do not tell me, friend, that twelve is twice six, nor three times four, nor six times two, nor four times three, otherwise I will by no means accept such nonsense'—no one would answer you if you asked thus. But if he said to you, 'How do you mean, Thrasymachus? Should I not answer any of the things you predicted? What, O wonderful man, even if it is one of those things but something different from the truth? Or in what way do you say it?' What would you say to him in return?" "So be it," he said. "But how is this similar to that?" "Nothing prevents it," I said. "For even if it is not similar, if it seems similar to the one asked, do you think he will answer any less according to what seems to him, whether we forbid it or not?" "Is that what you will do?" he said. "Will you answer one of the things I forbade?" "What wonder would it be," I said, "if it seemed so to me as I searched?" "But what if I demonstrate another answer about justice besides all these, and better than these; what penalty will you think yourself worthy of?" "What other," I said, "than that which is fitting for one who is ignorant? It is fitting that he learn from the learned. And I therefore judge myself worthy to suffer this." "How witty you are," he said. "But besides what you say, you shall also pay money." "When it is available, of course," I said. "Indeed it is available," said Glaucon, "the money. Speak now, Thrasymachus, for money will not be lacking. Moreover, all of us answer on behalf of Socrates here." "I think exactly so," he said, "that Socrates, keeping his habit, will answer nothing, but taking up the speech of the one answering, will refute it." "In what way," I said, "most excellent man, could anyone answer? First indeed, one who neither knows nor claims to know; then, if he thinks something about these things, he is nonetheless forbidden by a man of no small authority from saying what he thinks? But it is more fair for you to speak, for you profess to know and to be able to tell. Therefore, grant me this favor, and do not grudge teaching Glaucon here and the others." When I said this, Glaucon and the others also begged for this same thing. And it was manifest that Thrasymachus was affected by a great desire to speak, that he might show himself off. For he thought he had the best answers, but he pretended to struggle with me so that I might answer. Finally, however, he yielded. "This," he said, "is the wisdom of Socrates: himself being unwilling to teach, but learning from others, and returning no thanks for it." "That I learn from others," I said, "you speak the truth; but that I do not return thanks is far from the truth. For I pay as much as I am able; but I am able only to praise. For I have no money. But how readily I do that with a willing heart, if someone seems to me to speak well, you will soon understand when you have answered. For I think you will speak well." "Listen then," he said. "For I affirm that the just is nothing other than what is useful to the stronger. Why do you not praise? I know you will not." "Provided I first learn," I said, "what you are saying. "You are too villainous, Socrates," he said, "and you take my words in the way you can most deprave the speech." "Not at all, most excellent man," I said. "But explain this more clearly." "Do you not know," he said, "that of cities, some are governed by tyrants, some by the people, and some by the aristocrats?" "I know indeed." "Is it not the case that in any city, that which rules is most powerful?" "Why not?" "Each government, moreover, makes laws for its own utility: the popular government makes popular laws, the tyrannical makes tyrannical ones, and similarly in the others. But in making the laws, they show that what is useful for themselves is just for those who are subjects, and they punish anyone who transgresses this as one acting unjustly and against the laws. This, therefore, most excellent man, is what I say: that in all cities the same thing is just, namely what is beneficial to that government; but the government everywhere rules because it is more powerful. Wherefore it is clear to one who collects the facts correctly, that everywhere this same thing is just: what is conducive to the stronger." "Now at last," I said, "I understand what you are saying. But whether it is true, I will try to learn. You have also answered, Thrasymachus, that the just is something useful, although you had forbidden me from answering that. But there is added to it: 'to the stronger'." "A small addition, perhaps," he said. "It is not yet manifest," I said, "whether it is large or small. But that this must be investigated to see if you speak the truth is clear. Since I also confess that the just is something useful, and you add 'useful to the stronger,' I, however, do not know; it must be considered." "Consider," he said. "I will," I said. "And tell me, do you assert that it is just to obey the rulers?" "I do." "Are those who rule in any cities whatever always without error, or do they err sometimes?" "They can err sometimes." "Is it not the case, then, that when they set out to make laws, they make some correctly and some not correctly?" "So I think." "But they make them correctly when they establish what is useful for themselves; and not correctly, when the opposite?" "Is it so, or do you say otherwise?" "Exactly so." "And what they have made must be observed by the subjects. And that is justice." "Why not?" "Not only...
