...inquires and prescribes what is beneficial to the pilot himself, but rather what is beneficial to the sailors who are ruled by him. This, too, he conceded reluctantly. And here I said: Nor does any other person, Thrasymachus, in any position of command or power, insofar as he is a ruler, think of or prescribe what is beneficial to himself, but rather what is conducive to the subject; and everything he says and does, he says and does for that person's utility and fittingness. When we had reached this point, and it was clear to everyone that the definition of the just had been turned into its opposite, Thrasymachus did not respond as he should have, but said, "Tell me, Socrates, do you have a nurse?" "What?" I said, "Should you not rather answer than ask such things?" "Because," he said, "she neglects you and does not wipe your runny nose <note>original: "oppletas tibi nares nó emūgit" - a crude ancient insult implying Socrates is acting like a foolish child</note> even though you need it, since you know neither the duty of the sheep nor the shepherd." "Why is that?" I asked. "Because," he said, "you think that shepherds or cattle-herders consider the good of the sheep and oxen, and feed and tend them, looking toward anything other than the utility of their masters and themselves. And those who rule in cities as they should, you think they look upon those under them in any other way than a shepherd looks at his sheep: and think of anything else night and day than from where utility might come to themselves. You are so far removed from the just and justice, and likewise the unjust and injustice, that you ignore that justice and the just are someone else’s good—in truth, the advantage of the ruler and the stronger—but the personal detriment of the one who obeys and serves. Injustice, on the contrary, rules over the simple-minded and the just; those who obey do what is conducive to the stronger ruler, and by their service make him happy, but do not consult their own interest. You must consider it thus, O most simple Socrates, that a just man always has less than an unjust one. First, in mutual dealings where the just and the unjust enter into a contract, when the partnership is dissolved, you will always find the just man reporting less than the unjust. Then, in public affairs, when taxes must be paid, the just man pays more than his equals, while the unjust man pays less. But when something is to be received, the just man gets nothing, while the unjust man reports much. Indeed, if they ever hold some office, if no other loss happens to the just man, this at least does not fail him: that his domestic affairs are worse disposed through neglect, while he gains nothing from the public because he is just. Added to this, he makes his domestic relations and friends hostile to him, since he will not comply with them in anything beyond what is just. To the unjust man, however, everything happens the opposite, namely what I said before: that he gains everywhere above all others. Consider this, therefore, if you wish to judge how much more it benefits him privately to be unjust than just. You will learn it most easily if you reach the extreme of injustice, which makes the one acting unjustly most happy, and those who suffer the injury and wish to harm no one unjustly, most unhappy. This is tyranny, which usurps the property of others not little by little, but all at once: by stealth and force, things sacred and holy, private and public. If anyone fails in some part of these and is caught, he is punished and subjected to the greatest disgrace. For the sacrilegious, thieves, robbers, kidnappers, and those sinning in individual parts of these crimes are named according to such crimes. But after someone, beyond these robberies of money, has also reduced the citizens themselves into his slavery, he is no longer branded with such shameful names, but is called both blessed and happy, not only by his citizens, but by all who hear that he has fulfilled all wickedness. For those who blame injustice do not blame it because they fear doing unjustly, but because they fear suffering it. In this way, Socrates, injustice when perfected in all its parts is something stronger, more liberal, and more kingly than justice; as I said from the beginning, that which is conducive to the stronger is just: but the unjust is useful and conducive to itself." When Thrasymachus had said these things, he had already intended in his mind to depart, after he had poured this long speech into our ears with great force, like a bath-attendant. <note>Socrates compares Thrasymachus's overwhelming speech to a bathman pouring water over someone all at once.</note> Yet those present did not permit this, but compelled him to remain and provide a reason for what he had said; and I especially begged him vehemently: "O blessed Thrasymachus, having cast such a speech, are you hurrying to leave before you either fully teach or learn whether this is as you say, or otherwise? Or do you think you have undertaken to define a small matter, and not rather the conduct of life, by which each of us might live the best life?" "Do I," he said, "think this is otherwise?" "You seem," I said, "to have no care for us, nor to think whether we live better or worse, being ignorant of what you affirm you know. But, O good man, gladly show this to us. For you will not have poorly placed a benefit which you confer on so many of us. I will say what I feel. You do not persuade me at all that injustice brings a greater gain than justice, even if it is granted every license to do whatever it desires. But, O good man, let someone be unjust, and let him be able to do injury either by stealth or force, yet you do not persuade me that there is greater gain in injustice itself. In this opinion, perhaps, I am not alone, but someone else among us is too. Persuade us, then, blessed man, that we have not rightly valued justice more than injustice." "How," he said, "shall I further persuade you, if you are not persuaded by what I just said? What more shall I do? Shall I pound the speech into your soul?" "By no means," I said, "by Jove! But first I would like you to stand by what you have said; or if you wish to change anything, make this clear, and do not deceive us. Now you see, Thrasymachus, to resume what was said before, that when you first defined the true doctor as a healer of the sick, you then did not think the shepherd should be defined so sincerely, as if he should only guard the sheep insofar as he is a shepherd. Rather, you think he feeds the sheep insofar as he is a shepherd not for the utility of the sheep, but rather for gluttony, not as a shepherd, but as a guest who must eat, or as a greedy person who is going to sell them. Surely the pastoral art has no other care than that which it guards should be in the best state. For as far as the true pastoral faculty is concerned, nothing is lacking for it to be sufficient and best. Thus I thought it necessary for us to confess that every rule, in that it is a rule, looks to the good of nothing else except that which is under it and cared for by it, whether it be private or public. But do you think the rulers in cities, who are truly rulers, take up their offices willingly?" "By no means," he said, "I think, but I know for certain." "What then," I said, "of other commands? Do you not know that no one is willing to take them, but they demand a reward from them, as if no utility will come to themselves from such a command, but rather to the subjects? Come tell me, do we not say that any diverse arts are different from each other because they have a different power? And do not, O blessed one, answer contrary to your opinion, so that we may accomplish something. By this very thing, namely, one from another. Does not each one provide us some particular utility, and not one common with another? Just as medicine provides health, pilotage provides safety in sailing, and others similarly?" "Entirely so." "And does not the mercenary art provide a price? <note>Socrates distinguishes between the professional skill (like medicine) and the "wage-earning art" (making money).</note> For this is its power; or do you call medicine and pilotage the same? Or if you wish to define and distinguish more absolutely as you proposed, even if someone steering a ship...

...steering a ship were to become healthy because sailing was beneficial to him, you would not for this reason call pilotage itself "medicine"? "Certainly not." "Nor even, I think, 'mercenary' if someone who is a mercenary becomes healthy through that service." "Nor that." "What then? Medicine 'mercenary' if someone practicing medicine makes a profit?" "By no means." "Is it not then clear that we have conceded that all other craftsmen share this in common?" "So be it." "If, therefore, some utility is obtained commonly by all craftsmen, it is clear that they obtain such utility by using one and the same thing." "It seems so." "But we say that craftsmen receiving wages obtain utility from using the mercenary art." He barely assented. "Therefore, this utility—the receiving of a reward—does not come to each from his own art. But if we wish to inquire diligently, medicine produces health, the mercenary art produces profit; and architecture produces a building, while the wage-earning art following this produces a reward; and all others similarly. Each performs its own work and benefits that for which it was invented. But if no reward is given to him, does the craftsman now receive any utility from the art?" "None." "Does it then not even benefit him when he works for free?" "I think so." "Is it not then, Thrasymachus, as is already manifest, that no art and no office produces utility for itself, but as we were saying earlier, it produces and commands what is beneficial for the subject, looking always to the advantage of that inferior, not the superior? For these reasons, therefore, dear Thrasymachus, I said just now that no one is willing to undertake command and to voluntarily tackle the correction of others' evils, but they seek a reward, since he who acts rightly according to the art never acts for his own advantage according to the command of that art, but for the utility of the inferior. For which reason, it seems, a reward must be placed for those who are going to rule willingly, whether money, or honor, or a penalty if they do not take up the command." "How do you say this, Socrates?" asked Glaucon. "I know of two rewards, but the penalty you speak of, and how you place it in the category of a reward, I do not know." "Then," I said, "you are ignorant of the reward of the best men, for the sake of which the best men rule whenever they wish to rule. Are you unaware that to be ambitious and greedy is considered a disgrace and indeed is one?" "I know," said Glaucon. "For this reason, then, neither led by money nor honor do good men wish to rule. For they do not wish to be called mercenaries by openly receiving the reward of office, nor thieves by taking it secretly. Nor again for the sake of honor, for they are not ambitious. It is necessary, therefore, that necessity and a penalty be imposed on them, if they are to be willing to take up office. For which reason it is considered shameful for someone to approach command voluntarily and not wait for necessity. But the greatest of penalties is to be ruled by someone worse, unless one is willing to rule himself. Fearing this very punishment, good men seem to me to take up offices when they do; and then they approach them not as if toward some benefit, nor as if taking some pleasure from them, but as a necessary thing, since they can commit themselves neither to better men nor to their equals. Indeed, if a city of good men existed, in it, I think, there would be a struggle not to rule, just as now there is a contest out of the desire to rule; and there it would be clear that a truly legitimate prince looks to the advantage not of himself, but of him who is under him. Therefore every man who is not insane would rather choose to have another benefit him than to involve himself in troubles while he consults for others. Therefore, I in no way concede to Thrasymachus that the just is what is useful to the stronger. But this should be considered next; it seems to me a much greater thing that Thrasymachus now says, when he affirms that the life of the unjust is better than the life of the just. You therefore, Glaucon, which of these do you choose as truer?" "I think the life of the just is better," said Glaucon. "Did you hear," I said, "how many goods of the unjust life Thrasymachus was numbering a little while ago?" "I heard," he said, "but I do not agree." "Do you want us to show him, if we can in some way, that he is by no means saying the truth?" "Why wouldn't I?" he said. "If we oppose his speech with a contrary speech, as if by a comparison, enumerating how many additional goods he who is just achieves, and he in turn compares his own, it will be necessary for some third person to enumerate again and measure the goods, however many we have collected for both in both; and thus there will be need for some judges to decide this altercation. But if, as we recently began, the matter is discussed by bringing forward alternate concessions, we ourselves will be both speakers and judges." "So it is," he said. "Which way pleases you more?" "This one," he said. "Come then, Thrasymachus, answer us from the beginning. Do you affirm that extreme injustice is more useful than extreme justice?" "I certainly do affirm it," he said, "and I have given the reason." "What about this? Do you call one of these virtue and the other vice?" "Why not?" "Is justice then virtue, and injustice vice?" "Is it fitting for me to confess that, O witty man, I who say injustice is profitable and justice is not?" "What then?" "The opposite," he said. "Do you perhaps call justice a vice?" "No, but a very noble stupidity." "Do you then call injustice wickedness?" "Not even that. But good counsel and sagacity." "Do unjust men, Thrasymachus, seem to you to be prudent and good?" "Those who are able to inflict injury on cities and subject nations to themselves. But you perhaps think I am speaking of those who cut purses in secret; these too are profitable if they remain hidden, but they are not worthy of estimation. Rather, what I was saying a little while ago." "Indeed, I understand what you want. But I wonder greatly if you place injustice in the category of virtue and wisdom, and justice in the opposite." "I certainly do place them so." "This is now more solid, my friend, and no longer easy to find what one might say. For if you had placed injustice as profitable, yet confessed it to be a vice or something shameful, as some others do, we could say something to these things according to what they think. Now, however, it is clear that you are going to say that injustice is something both beautiful and strong, and you will give it all other things that we attribute to justice, since you did not hesitate to place it in both virtue and wisdom." "You prophesy most truly." "Yet I must not desist from inquiring through disputation, as long as I think you are saying what you think. For you seem to me, Thrasymachus, at present to be by no means joking, but to be bringing forward what seems true to you." "What does it matter to you whether it seems so to me or not, when you do not refute my reasoning?" "Nothing, certainly. But answer me this besides: Does it seem to you that a just man wants to have more than another just man?" "By no means. For he would not be refined and simple as he is now." "What then? More than a just action?" "Not even more than a just action." "But of an unjust man, would he think it worthy to have more, and consider that just, or the contrary?" "He would consider it so, and think it worthy, but he would not be able." "But I am not asking that, but whether the just man neither thinks it worthy nor wants to have more than a just man: but contrary to an unjust...

...contrary. "It is so indeed." "What about the unjust man? Does he think it fair to have more than both the just man and a just action?" "Why not? Since he thinks himself worthy to have more than everyone." "Will then the unjust man also have more than an unjust man and an unjust action, and will he strive to surpass all in having?" "These things are true." "So we say: The just man does not want to have more than his like, but more than his unlike; the unjust man wants to take more than both. "You have said correctly." "But the prudent and good is the unjust man himself; the just man, however, is neither." "Correct also." "Therefore the unjust man is like the prudent and good, but the just man not at all." "What prevents it," he said, "that he who is such should also be like such people; but he who is not such, should not be like?" "You say it well. Therefore each of them is such as those to whom he is like." "What then?" he said. "Let it be so, indeed, but tell me Thrasymachus, whether you call someone musical, and another not musical." "I do." "Which of these is prudent, and which imprudent?" "The musical man is certainly prudent, the one unskilled in music is imprudent." "Are they not good in the same things they are prudent in, and bad in the things they are imprudent in?" "Certainly." "And shall we say the same of the doctor?" "The same." "Does it seem to you, best of men, when a musical man tunes a lyre, he wants to surpass another musical man in the tension and loosening of the strings, or thinks it worthy to achieve more than he?" "By no means." "But does he strive to surpass the one unskilled in music?" "Necessarily." "What about the doctor? In food or drink would you say he wants to achieve more than either another doctor, or what the thing itself requires?" "By no means." "But more than one unskilled in the medical art?" "Undoubtedly." "Finally, contemplate all sciences and ignorances, if someone seems to you, who indeed has knowledge, to want to take more either in saying or doing than another knowing man, and not rather the same things for the same action as he who is like him." "Perhaps it is so, it must be." "What about the unlearned man? Would he not want to assume more for himself than the learned man, and also than the unlearned?" "Perhaps." "But is the learned man not wise?" "I concede." "And is the wise man not good?" "That also." "Therefore the good and wise will not want to claim more for himself than his like: but he will want more than his unlike and contrary." "It seems so." "But the bad and unlearned will claim more for himself both than his like and unlike." "It appears so." "Does not the unjust man, Thrasymachus, strive to usurp more than either his like or unlike? Or were you saying so?" "I was indeed saying so." "But the just man will not want more than his like, but more than his unlike." "I confess." "The just man is therefore like the wise and good, but the unjust man is like the bad and ignorant." "It appears so." "But we conceded that each is such as he is whom he is like." "We plainly conceded." "Therefore the just man appeared to us to be good and wise: the unjust man unlearned and bad." Thrasymachus conceded all these things, though not with the facility with which I now report them, but hardly and dragged along with much sweat; for it was then summer. And I then saw for the first time what I had never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. When therefore it was established that justice is both virtue and wisdom, but injustice is vice and ignorance: "Let this," I said, "remain so for us. But we were saying that injustice is something strong and powerful. Do you not remember, Thrasymachus?" "I remember indeed," he said. "But what you say now does not please me; and I have things to say against them, which if I were to bring forward, I know for certain you would say I was making a speech. Therefore either let me say what I want: or if you wish to ask, ask. I will assent to you, as to old women telling fables, and I will nod and shake my head." "By no means contrary to your own opinion." "To please you in all things, since you do not allow me to speak, do you want anything else?" "Nothing, by Jove, if you do that, then do it: I will ask questions." "Ask then." "I ask this now as I did a little while ago, so that we may consider in the following speech in its order how justice stands against injustice. For it was said that injustice is more powerful and robust than justice. Now what news do you bring? If indeed justice is wisdom and virtue, it will easily appear, I think, to be more robust than injustice, since injustice is ignorance, and no one would be ignorant of this. But I do not wish to act so simply, but to consider in this way. Would you affirm some city to be unjust? and that other cities want to unjustly reduce it to slavery, and have many slaves under them?" "Why not? Indeed, that one will do this most especially which will be most excellent, and which has reached the extreme of injustice." "I understand indeed that this was your speech. But I consider this about it, whether this city which is more excellent than another city will have this power without justice, or if it is necessary that it have it with justice." "If indeed, as you were saying a little while ago, justice itself is wisdom, it is necessary with justice. But if as I say, without justice." "I am greatly delighted by your answers, O Thrasymachus, since you not only nod and shake your head, but also answer excellently." "I am doing you a favor," he said. "You are doing well indeed. But favor me in this too, and tell me: Do you think any city or army, whether robbers or thieves, or any other group of men attacking something together unjustly, could accomplish anything if they injured each other in turn?" "By no means." "But what if they abstained from injury? Would they not accomplish more?" "Certainly." "For seditions, Thrasymachus, injustice, enmities, and contentions are produced among them; but justice produces concord and friendship. Does it not?" "Let it be so, that we may not dissent from you." "You are doing well, best of men. But tell me this also: If this is the work of injustice, to beget hatred wherever it is, will it not, if it is among free men and slaves, cause them to exercise hatreds and contentions among themselves; and in no way can they do anything from common concord?" "Entirely." "What then? If it be among two, will they not dissent between themselves, and pursue each other with hatreds, and be enemies both to themselves and to the just?" "They will indeed." "But if injustice be in one, O wonderful man, will its power dissipate? Or will it have nothing less?" "Let it have nothing less." "Does it not seem to have some such power, that to whomever it is in, whether city, or nation, or army, or any other, it first renders it impotent to act because of dissension and discord: then it makes it an enemy both to itself and to any contrary, and to the just? Is it not so?" "It is." "And if it be in one, it will do all these same things which it does by its nature. First it will render him impotent to act, when he dissents with himself and is not consistent with himself. Then it will make him an enemy both to himself and to the just. Will it not?" "Certainly." "But the just, O friend, are also gods?" "Let them be." "Therefore the unjust man will be an enemy to the gods, Thrasymachus; but the just man, a friend." "Satiate yourself, Socrates, according to your whim, with the feast of the speech. For I will not oppose you, lest I make these people hostile to me." "Come then, provide the rest of the banquet, just as before in responding. It is indeed established that the just are wiser, better, and more powerful for acting: but the unjust cannot even handle anything among themselves. But what we say most strongly, that those who are altogether unjust can together accomplish something in common, is not altogether true...

...is not true. For they would not abstain from mutually inflicting injury if they were altogether unjust. But it is clear that there is in them a certain justice which affects them so that they do not want to hurt each other nor others with whom they deal: and through which they do whatever they do. But they are impelled to act unjustly by injustice, since they were semi-evil. For those who have reached the peak of wickedness and injustice can accomplish nothing at all. I understand that these things are so, and not as you proposed above. But whether the just also live better than the unjust and are happier (which indeed we had proposed to consider later) must be considered. And, as it seems to me, this follows from what we have said. But yet it must be better considered. For the speech is not about some vile and contemptible thing, but in what way one must live. Consider now." "Behold, I consider." "Tell me then, does it seem to you that a horse has some function?" "To me indeed." "Would you say this is the function of a horse and of anything else, which one could do either only with that, or most of all with that?" "I do not understand." "But in this way: do you see with anything other than eyes?" "By no means." "What then? would you hear with anything other than ears?" "Not at all." "Therefore we would rightly call these the functions of those." "Rightly." "Could you prune the shoots of a vine with a sword, and a small knife, and many other things?" "Why not?" "However, not as conveniently as with a sickle made for this use." "It is as you say." "Therefore shall we not say this is its function?" "We shall indeed." "I think you now hold better what I was saying a little while ago, when I asked whether that was each thing's function, which is performed either only by it, or better than by others." "I understand now. And that seems to me to be each thing's function." "Come," I said. "Does it not seem to you that there is also a virtue assigned to that to which some function is assigned? Let us return then to the previous things. We say there is some function of the eyes?" "Certainly." "Therefore is there not also a virtue of the eyes?" "A virtue too." "What then? is there some function of the ears?" "There is." "Is there then also a virtue?" "There is." "Should not the same be said of all the rest?" "The same." "Would the eyes ever perform their function beautifully, not having their own virtue, but a vice instead of virtue?" "But how? For you perhaps speak of blindness instead of sight." "Whatever their virtue may be, for at present I do not ask that, but whether it performs its function rightly by its own virtue, but not rightly by vice." "You speak the truth." "And will the ears perform their own function poorly by being deprived of their private virtue?" "Poorly." "Do we feel the same about all the rest?" "The same." "Come and contemplate these things besides. Is there some function of the soul which you would do with nothing else, such as to care, to command, to consult, and others of the same kind? Could we rightly attribute these to anything other than the soul, and would we say they are its own?" "To no other." "What then about living itself? Shall we not say it is the function of the soul?" "Most of all." "And do we not also say there is a certain virtue of the soul?" "We do." "Will the soul ever, O Thrasymachus, deprived of its own virtue, fulfill its functions well? Or will it be able in no way?" "It will not be able." "It is necessary therefore that a bad soul command and care badly, but a good soul do all these things well." "Necessary." "Did we concede that the virtue of the soul is justice, and injustice is vice?" "We conceded." "Therefore the just soul and the just man will live well, but the unjust man badly." "So it appears according to your reasoning." "But he who lives well is blessed and happy. He who lives badly, the opposite." "Why not?" "Therefore the just man is happy, but the unjust man miserable." "But to be miserable is not profitable, but it is profitable to be happy." "Undoubtedly." "Never therefore, O blessed Thrasymachus, will injustice be more useful than justice." "You have been fattened on these feasts at the * Dionysia, O Socrates." <margin>* At the feast of Diana, from Strabo.</margin> "By your leave I have eaten, Thrasymachus, after you became milder to me and ceased to be difficult. I did not however happen to eat abundantly, and that rather for my own sake than yours. For just as men more greedy for feasts and incontinent always snatch whatever is brought out in the banquet, and taste it before they are sufficiently fed by the prior dishes: so also I, as I seem to myself, before I found what was originally proposed, namely what the just itself is, having skipped that, turned myself to considering whether it is wickedness and ignorance, or wisdom and virtue. And finally, that speech falling in which brought forward that injustice is a utility over justice, I did not restrain myself from descending from that to this. Wherefore it happens to me at present from this dispute that I know nothing. For when I am ignorant of what the just is, I shall in no way know whether it is a virtue or otherwise, and whether he who possesses it is blessed or not blessed."

## THE SECOND DIALOGUE ON THE REPUBLIC. OR, ON THE JUST.
**MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT.**

The second dialogue begins from a three-fold division of goods. Good is indeed the same as that which is desirable. But we desire something for its own sake only, like pleasures and joy. Something for the sake of another only, such as whatever things are laborious. Something both for its own sake and for the sake of others which follow from it, as knowledge for prosperous health. But he says justice is to be desired both for the sake of others following from it, and most especially for its own sake. But before anything is perfectly defined concerning justice, Glaucon pursues more copiously and elegantly those things which were omitted by Thrasymachus on behalf of injustice, and add also more modestly. For he says, not because he thinks so, but so that he may provoke Socrates to defend justice more sharply, that he will praise injustice. We have similar things also in the *Gorgias*. After him Adeimantus, and first speaks for justice, attributing to it both human and divine rewards, where you will note certain religious mysteries of the poets. Then he brings some things forward for injustice, namely representing the person of Socrates and Thrasymachus, adding also that he does not want to disparage justice, but in a way to irritate Socrates. But he wishes to hear praises of justice which are drawn not from external things, but from the intrinsic nature of justice, such as are not accustomed to be brought by others. But you should notice that Plato has not rashly placed here many things again pertaining to poets and priests; for he shows that in these often from poets and more often from bad priests, the license of sinning is provided. Where he mocks the superstitions of the nations. Furthermore, not without reason in these books most dear to him, he inserted the persons most dear to him, his brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus, and his father Ariston. Again, Socrates contemplated nothing in all his life more inclinedly than what justice itself is and what it does, and vice in the soul, with external affections removed. Which indeed both voluntarily and provoked he will henceforth demonstrate concerning justice and injustice. But I here have unjustly omitted too much that wonderful reward of justice brought forward from the mind of Musaeus, I mean perpetual drunkenness. Which indeed Musaeus received from Orpheus, signifying the same through the rites of Dionysus. This is similar to that prophetic saying: *I shall be inebriated from the fatness of your house.* Drunkenness therefore is twofold. One below the moon, brought on by the Lethean drink: through which the soul placed outside itself and placed below itself forgets divine things, raving about earthly things. The other however above the moon proceeding from a nectarean drink, through which the soul placed outside itself placed above itself forgets mortal diseases, and looking up at divine things as if by their first splendor it grows dark: or rather tasting by a savor it changes from its prior habit with a certain new heat. Soon however it clearly perceives and tastes healthily, indeed it is nourished. Truly the divine idea through which the soul was made glides into the returning soul, like a flavor to the taste. From it first it sweetly washes away anything that is alien. Then it fills it inwardly, and by filling it more it delights. Third it brings it back...

--- Page 386 ---
370 Book Thirty-One.

...into itself, pouring over it an inestimable pleasure. Where the soul from being a soul is first made intellect, and finally from intellect, God. Neither does it savor further as before, nor what before, but it savors otherwise and other things. And just as among us a vehement imagination moves and forms the body, there also the body subject to the soul and its senses is moved and formed immediately by the most powerful thought of the mind, so that by the ineffable sweetness of the mind the sense also grows wonderfully sweet and the body. But let us now return to justice. Socrates, seeking this as the end and object of his dispute through individual things, because it would be difficult to find in the soul, first seeks it in the city, as if in it it would be more manifest, so that through this finally he may manifestly define the justice of the soul. But so that he may be able to consider justice in the city, he constitutes the city from the beginning, saying first what is its origin, namely mutual need, then what is the material, namely necessary things and arts, finally what is the form, namely the rule of life and legitimate governance. And see how much he praises a sober life, and how much he blames a delicate and luxurious one. The former indeed is healthy and sufficient, the latter however is insane and needy of many things. Finally, since because of this war is born, there is need for soldiers in such a city. Wherefore descending to the diligent institution of the military art, he accurately pursues how many things are necessary for a strenuous soldier and guardian of the fatherland. In all things however remember, no one can be born most fit for diverse things. And therefore no one should exercise diverse arts. Especially since from the work of one, the work of the other is hindered. It is necessary that each one exercise his art immediately from a boy and continuously through all his life. Furthermore, the soldier guardian of the fatherland should be both born and educated such that like a dog he is mild toward those known, and fierce toward those unknown. Always watchful and sagacious. Therefore Socrates asserts that the beginning of any work is something greatest, especially in tender age easily formable in both directions. Therefore he rightly forms future soldiers from tender fingernails <note>an ancient idiom meaning "from early childhood"</note> both according to the soul first through music, and according to the body then through gymnastics, comprising under music poetic fables also. Which he prescribes to be applied assiduously to the ears of boys. But only such as provoke and educate for military study as if some preludes. And similarly he orders others to be accustomed from childhood to these fables, which especially may be conducive to future study. The contrary however he keeps far away. That indeed is the greatest precept. He soon detests poetic impiety feigning shameful things about the gods. And he prohibits such fables to be heard. He joins twofold figures of theology. First, that God is altogether good, and the cause only of good things. But of no evil is God the cause. Likewise if God punishes someone, he punishes for the sake of good. Second however, that God is inwardly immutable, from the fact that he is most simple, most powerful, best, most wise. By which it happens that he denies God ever deceives anyone, either by feigned images, or signs and words. For neither is he changed into various forms, nor since he is not changed, does he pretend to be changed. Conclude the book with a certain golden sentence. A lie is most of all hateful to both gods and men. But if a lie in speech is hateful, and that is an image of the lie itself which is in the soul, surely the lie which is in the soul is very hateful to both gods and men. Such a lie indeed is ignorance, through which the soul itself lies to itself concerning the truth of things. Since however truth looks to that which is said to be, and therefore the false declines to not being, deservedly as far as it falls into the false, so far it also falls into nothingness.

[Large initial H] AVING said these things, I thought I was freed from the dispute: but this, as it seems, was only a prologue. For Glaucon, both always in other things certainly a most brave man for all things, and then indeed did not approve of Thrasymachus's exhaustion, but said: "Do you, O Socrates, wish to seem to have persuaded us, or truly to persuade us, that it is altogether better to be just than unjust?" "I indeed, if it were in my choice, would rather truly persuade you." "Then you are not doing," he said, "what you want. For tell me, does something of this kind seem to you to be a good, which we would choose, certainly not desiring what follows from it, but loving it for its own sake? Just as to rejoice, and pleasures which are without harm, and which in the future are going to bring nothing besides joy to him having them." "To me indeed it seems," I said, "to be something of such a kind." "What then? Is there something which we love both for its own sake and for the sake of those things which flow from it? Just as to be wise, to see, to be healthy, for we embrace these of such a kind for both reasons." "Certainly," I said. "And do you see a third," he said, "kind of good, in which is to be exercised, to be cured when sick, and to practice medicine and making money? These at least we confess to be laborious, but to benefit us. And for their own sake we would never seek them, but for the sake of profit and others which proceed from them." "This is plainly," I said, "the third kind. What then?" "In which of these," he said, "do you place justice?" "In my opinion in the most beautiful, which both for its own sake and for the sake of those things which it produces, is sought by him who is going to be blessed." "It does not seem so to many, but to be of the laborious kind, which indeed should be sought for the sake of rewards and honors and glory, but for its own sake should be fled as difficult." "I know indeed that it seems so to many, wherefore for a long time by Thrasymachus as if it were such a thing, it is disparaged: but justice is praised. But I am dull, as I seem." "Come then and hear me," he said, "if these things also seem so to you. For Thrasymachus seems to have been charmed by you before it was proper, like a serpent by songs. But to me not yet has both been demonstrated according to my opinion. For I desire to hear what both are and what power each has existing in the soul by itself: but rewards and what proceed from them, to let go. So therefore I will do, if it also pleases you. I will indeed renew the speech of Thrasymachus, and first I will say of what kind they say justice is, and whence they wish it to have arisen. Second however in place, that all whoever cultivate justice, follow it in a way unwillingly, as a necessary thing, but not a good one. Third, that they do this deservedly. For the life of the unjust is much better than that of the just, as they hand down. To me indeed, O Socrates, it does not seem so. I hesitate however often, because I am stunned daily hearing Thrasymachus and countless others. But a speech for justice itself, that it is better than injustice, I have heard from no one yet as I would wish. I would desire indeed to hear justice itself praised according to itself, and most especially I think I shall hear this from you. Wherefore I will speak more broadly praising the unjust life, and by speaking I will show you in what way I most want to hear you, disparaging indeed injustice, but praising justice. But see if this pleases you." "Most of all," I said: "for about what thing would anyone of sound mind more gladly both hear and speak?" "Excellently," he said, "you speak. Indeed, what I first promised to speak about this, hear now what kind it is, and whence justice has arisen. By nature indeed they say it is good to do injury, but bad to be affected by injury, but that there is far more evil in suffering injury than good in inflicting it. Wherefore after they have both inflicted and received injury in turn, and have tasted both, those who cannot avoid the former and achieve the latter think it would be worthwhile to so bargain among themselves that injury can neither be inflicted nor received: and hence they want laws to have had their origin, and their decrees, and the precepts of the laws called legitimate and just. This therefore they want to be the origin and substance of justice, which becomes a middle way between the best and the worst. Since it is best to inflict injury and not give penalties: but worst to suffer it and not be able to take revenge. Just therefore, constituted in the middle of these, is loved not as a good: but from the weakness of injury in...

<summary>This section concludes Book I of Plato's Republic, with Socrates arguing that the soul's function is living well through the virtue of justice. It then begins Book II, where Glaucon challenges Socrates to prove that justice is desirable for its own sake, not just for its consequences, and recounts the "social contract" theory of the origin of laws.</summary>

## Dialogue II. On the Republic, Or, On Justice. 371
<note>original: "de rep." (de republica). This refers to Plato’s "Republic," his famous work on the ideal state and the nature of the soul.</note>

as if to create an obstacle against the inflicting of injuries. Surely a person who is truly a man and capable of doing as he pleases would never agree to such a pact to avoid doing or receiving harm; to do so would be insane. This, Socrates, is the nature of justice, and this is its origin according to the common view. We would clearly see that those who practice justice do so unwillingly—only because they lack the power to do wrong—if we were to imagine something like this: suppose we granted both the just and the unjust person the license to do whatever they desired. If we then followed them closely, watching where their desires led them, we would surely catch the "just" man being driven by the same greed for "having more" <note>original: "plus habendi auiditate" refers to the Greek concept of *pleonexia*, or over-reaching greed.</note> as the unjust man. Every nature naturally pursues this as a good, though by law and force it is led to respect equality. This "license" I speak of would be like the power once given to the ancestor of Gyges the Lydian <margin>Cicero says the same in the third book of his *On Duties*.</margin> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman who later used this same story to discuss ethics.</note>. They say he was a hired shepherd for the man then ruling Lydia. After a great storm of rain arose and the earth was shaken, they say the ground opened up with a chasm in the region where he was grazing his herds. Seeing this, he descended into the chasm in wonder; he saw many marvelous things told of in fables, including a hollow bronze horse with doors in its sides. When he opened them, he saw the body of a dead man of unusual size, wearing nothing but a gold ring on his finger. He took the ring and left, returning to the assembly of shepherds. It was their custom to meet every month to report to the king on the status of his flocks. As he sat with the others, he happened to turn the collet <note>The "palam" or face of the ring.</note> of the ring toward the palm of his hand. When he did so, he became invisible to everyone, and they began to speak of him as if he were absent. Marvelling at this, he felt the ring again and turned the collet back to the outside; immediately he became visible again. Noticing this, he tested the ring's power more carefully to see if it really worked this way: and so he found that when the gemstone was turned toward him, he was seen by no one, but when turned outward, he was conspicuous. Having proven this, he arranged to be sent as a messenger to the king along with the others. Once there, he seduced the king's wife and plotted with her to kill the king. Having slain him, he seized the kingdom. Now, if there were two such rings, and the just man possessed one while the unjust man possessed the other, no one, it seems, would be so "adamantine" <note>Unbreakably firm or hard like a diamond.</note> as to remain steadfast in justice and keep his hands off what belongs to others. He could boldly take whatever he wanted from the market, enter any house he pleased, sleep with whomever he desired, kill anyone, and release whomever he liked from prison—acting among men as if he were a god. In doing these things, the "just" man would act no differently than the "unjust" man; both would head toward the same goal. This is a great proof that no one is just willingly, but only by constraint, as if justice were not a private good. For wherever someone believes they can act unjustly with impunity, they do so. Every person believes in their heart that injustice is far more profitable than justice. And according to those who argue this way, such a person is right. If someone with such a power were to refuse to act unjustly or touch the property of others, he would be thought most miserable and foolish by those who knew the truth, though they would praise him to one another's faces, deceiving each other out of fear of being victims of injustice themselves. So much for that. But we will truly judge the lives of the just and the unjust man if we set the most just man and the most unjust man apart from one another; otherwise, we cannot. Let the distinction be this: we shall take nothing of injustice away from the unjust man, nor anything of justice from the just man, but let each be perfect in his own pursuit. First, let the unjust man act like a master craftsman: just as a great navigator or physician knows what is possible and impossible in his art—attempting the former and leaving the latter—and can correct any mistake he makes, so too let the unjust man be subtle in his crimes, remaining hidden if he is to be truly "perfectly" unjust. If he is caught, he must be considered unskilled. For the height of injustice is to *seem* just when one is not. Therefore, we must grant the "perfectly" unjust man the most complete injustice without taking anything away: he must be allowed to maintain a reputation for justice among all while committing the greatest wrongs. If he slips up, he must be able to correct it, being persuasive enough to talk his way out of accusations, or using force if necessary through his courage, strength, and abundance of wealth and friends. Having imagined such a man, let us place beside him the just man—a simple and noble person who, as Aeschylus wrote, "desires not to seem, but to be good." <note>Aeschylus was a Greek tragic poet. This quote is from his play *Seven Against Thebes*.</note> Indeed, we must strip away every reputation for justice from him, lest he be thought just by anyone. For if he is seen as just, he will receive honors and rewards. It would then be uncertain whether he is just for the sake of justice itself, or for the sake of the honors and gifts. He must be stripped of everything except his justice and placed in a position exactly opposite the first man. Though doing no wrong, let him be believed to be the most unjust man imaginable, so that his justice may be tested as if by fire, to see if he remains unmoved by infamy and its consequences. Let him persevere, unchanging, until death, being thought unjust throughout his whole life while actually being just. Thus, when both have reached the absolute extremes—one of justice, the other of injustice—we may judge which of them is the happier. "My word!" I said, "my dear Glaucon, how vigorously you polish each of these two men for our judgment, just like a pair of statues!" "As much as I am able," he replied. "Since they are such as I have described, it is not difficult, I think, to tell what kind of life awaits each of them. It must be said, then: and if the words seem harsh, Socrates, do not think they are mine, but rather the words of those who praise injustice over justice. They will say that the just man, so disposed, will be scourged, tortured, and bound in chains. His eyes will be burned out, and finally, after suffering every kind of evil, he will be impaled <note>The Latin *suspendetur* here refers to a form of agonizing public execution, often equated with the Greek term for being "crucified" or "impaled."</note>, and he will realize that one should not desire to *be* just, but only to *seem* just. Aeschylus’s poem could be more rightly applied to the unjust man. For they will say that the unjust man, because he pursues a course in harmony with reality and does not live according to the opinions of men, does not wish to *seem* unjust, but to *be* so: 'Harvesting the deep and fertile furrow in his mind, from which noble counsels sprout.' <note>Another quote from Aeschylus regarding the character Amphiaraus, here applied ironically to the unjust man.</note> First, he holds the offices of the city because he appears just; then he marries whom he wants and gives his children in marriage to whom he wants; he associates and enters into business with whomever he chooses. In all these things, he gains an advantage and makes a profit because he is not afraid to do wrong. In contests, both public and private, he comes out on top and gains more than his adversaries. He becomes wealthy, benefits his friends, and harms his enemies. He honors the gods with gifts and sacrifices abundantly and magnificently, and he is much better than the just man at winning favor..."

<summary>Glaucon presents the "Ring of Gyges" thought experiment to argue that people are only just because they fear punishment. He challenges Socrates to prove that justice is better than injustice even if the just man is tortured and hated while the unjust man is honored and wealthy.</summary>

# Book Thirty-One. 372

...any god or man much better than the just man can. From this, they argue it is likely that he is dearer to the gods than the just man is. In this way, Socrates, they say that both gods and men have provided a better life for the unjust than for the just."

When Glaucon had said this, and I was thinking of how to respond, his brother Adeimantus said, "Do you think, Socrates, that enough has been said on this matter?"

"What more is there?" I asked.

"The most important point," he said, "has not yet been mentioned."

"Then, brother," I said, "stand by your brother, as the proverb goes. If he has left anything out, help him—though what he has already said is enough to overwhelm me and make me unable to defend justice."

"Nonsense," he replied. "Listen to this as well. For we should also bring forward the arguments opposite to those he gave—the ones that praise justice and criticize injustice—so that what Glaucon wants may become even clearer. Fathers tell their sons, and all who have care of others, that one must be just—not praising justice itself, but the reputation that comes from it. They want a man who is thought to be just to obtain high offices, good marriages, and all the things Glaucon just listed. And they go even further with this talk of reputation; for by mentioning the goodwill of the gods, they can point to the immense benefits the gods are said to bestow on holy men. 

The noble Hesiod and Homer <margin>In Book 1 of Works and Days.</margin> testify to this. Hesiod says that for just men, the gods make the oaks bear acorns at the top and bees in the middle, and make the sheep heavy with wool, along with many other such goods. The other poet says much the same: 'Like a good king who, fearing the gods, upholds justice, the black earth bears wheat and barley, the trees are weighed down with fruit, the flocks are fertile, and the sea provides fish.' <note>This is a paraphrase of Homer's Odyssey, Book 19.</note> 

Musaeus and his son <note>The son is Eumolpus, legendary figures associated with Orphic mysteries.</note> promise even more excellent goods from the gods for the just. They take them down to the underworld, seat them at a banquet of the holy, and make them live forever in great pleasure, wearing crowns and being perpetually drunk—thinking that the most beautiful reward for virtue is eternal intoxication. Others extend these rewards from the gods even further, saying that the children and descendants of a just and faithful man carry on his lineage for generations. 

With these and similar things they praise justice. But they bury the profane and unjust in a kind of mud in the underworld and force them to carry water in a sieve. Even while they are alive, they brand them with infamy. In short, all the punishments that Glaucon described for the just-who-seem-unjust, these people say befall the unjust; they have no others to tell of. This, then, is the praise and blame given to each.

Besides this, Socrates, consider another way of speaking about justice and injustice used by both private citizens and poets. With one voice, they all sing that temperance and justice are good, but difficult and full of labor; whereas intemperance and injustice are pleasant and easy to acquire, and are shameful only by opinion and law. They say that unjust things are more profitable than just ones. They are quick to honor wicked men if they are rich and powerful, and call them happy in public and private; but they despise those who are weak and poor, even while admitting they are better people. 

But the most amazing of all are the stories they tell about the gods and virtue: that the gods have given many good men a miserable life, while giving the wicked the opposite. Furthermore, wandering priests and soothsayers <note>Plato uses the term 'circulatores' or peddlers to describe these itinerant ritual experts.</note> go to the doors of the rich and persuade them that they have power from the gods, through sacrifices and chants performed at festivals, to expiate any crime committed by the man or his ancestors. They claim they can harm any enemy, whether just or unjust, at little cost. They say that with their spells and "bindings" they can persuade the gods to serve them. 

To all this they bring the testimony of poets, partly to show how easily one falls into vice. (For 'to reach vice is easy' <margin>Hesiod, Book 1 of Works and Days.</margin>; 'the path is smooth and it lives very near. But before virtue the gods have placed sweat: the way is long and steep.') And partly to show that the gods can be turned by our prayers and gifts, they cite Homer as a witness, since he said, 'The gods themselves can be turned' <margin>Iliad, Book 9.</margin>, and men turn them with sacrifices, vows, libations, and incense when someone has sinned. 

They also circulate books by Musaeus and Orpheus, the sons of the Moon and the Muses (as they say), according to which they perform their rituals. They persuade not only individuals but entire cities that there are 'releases' and 'purifications' for crimes through sacrifices and pleasurable games, both for the living and the dead. These they call 'Teletae' <note>Initiation rites or mystery ceremonies.</note>, or expiations, which free us from the evils of the afterlife; but if we neglect the sacrifices, terrifying things await us.

All these things, Socrates—so many and of such a kind—are said about the rewards of virtue and vice regarding gods and men. What do we think they do to the minds of young men who are clever by nature and able to flit through these various arguments, reasoning out what kind of person one should be and what path one should take to live the best life? A young man would likely turn over in his mind that line from Pindar: 'Shall I climb the high wall of justice, or walk the crooked paths of guile, and so fortify my life?' 

For people say that if I am just, but do not seem so, there is no profit, only certain labors and penalties. But for the unjust man who has acquired the reputation of justice, they say a divine life awaits. Therefore, since 'appearance' (as the wise men say) 'masters the truth' and is the lord of happiness, must I not turn entirely toward it? I must put on a facade and present a painted image of virtue, while dragging behind me the 'cunning and versatile fox' of the wise Archilochus. <note>Archilochus was a Greek lyric poet; the fox is a symbol of deception.</note>

But perhaps someone will say it is not easy for a wicked man to always stay hidden. We shall reply that nothing great is easy. Nevertheless, if we want to be happy, we must go where the tracks of the arguments lead. To keep our wickedness secret, we will form conspiracies and secret societies. There are also masters of persuasion who teach the wisdom of the assembly and the courtroom; through them, we will partly persuade and partly use force, so that while we take more than our share, we pay no penalty. 

'But the gods,' someone says, 'cannot be hidden from or forced.' Well, if they do not exist, or do not care about human affairs, we need not care about hiding from them. But if they do exist and do care, we only know of them through stories and the genealogies written by poets. And these very same poets say that the gods can be turned by sacrifices, sweet prayers, and gifts. We must either believe both these things or neither. If we believe them, then we should act unjustly and then offer sacrifices to the gods from the spoils. For if we are just, we will be unharmed by the gods, but we will lose the profits of injustice. If we are unjust, we will get the wealth...

# Dialogue II on the Republic. Or, on Justice. 373

...and by offering prayers after our crimes, we shall be freed from punishment. 'But we will pay the penalty in the underworld for what we did unjustly here, either ourselves or our children's children.' But, my friend, as the reasoning goes, 'the expiations for committed sins are very powerful, and the gods are merciful,' as the greatest cities say. And the poets, the sons of the gods, and the prophets born of the gods, testify that this is so. 

What reason, then, is left to us to prefer justice over the height of injustice? For if we hide our injustice under a false appearance of honesty, everything will go according to our wishes with both gods and men, in life and in death, as the speech of many excellent men testifies. After all that has been said, Socrates, who could believe that a man would want to cultivate justice if he has any power—of fortune, wealth, body, or birth—and would not instead laugh when he hears it praised? 

Indeed, if anyone can show that what we have said is false, and truly knows that justice is best, he will be very forgiving and not angry at the unjust, understanding that—unless someone has a divine nature that hates iniquity, or has learned through knowledge to abstain from injustice—no one is just of his own accord. Rather, it is through cowardice, or old age, or some other weakness that people criticize injustice, because they lack the power to practice it. This is clear from the fact that as soon as someone acquires that power, he is the first to act unjustly to the extent he can.

The only cause of all this is the very reason why my brother and I, Socrates, have addressed you. For of all of you, wonderful Socrates, who profess to praise justice—from those ancient heroes of old whose memory survives down to the men of our own time—no one has ever praised justice or criticized injustice in any other way than by looking at the reputation, honors, and rewards that come from them. But what each of them does by its own nature in the soul of the possessor, hidden from gods and men, no one has ever sufficiently explained, either in poetry or in prose: namely, that injustice is the greatest of all evils the soul can contain, and justice is the greatest good. 

If this had been said by all of you from the beginning, and we had been persuaded of it from our childhood, we would not be guarding each other against injury, but each man would be his own guardian, fearing that by acting unjustly, he would be living with the greatest evil. 

This, Socrates, and perhaps even more, Thrasymachus or someone else might say about justice and injustice, perverting the power of each—quite inappropriately, it seems to me. But I, wishing to hide nothing from you and desiring to hear the opposite from you, have drawn out this argument. Do not, then, merely show us that justice is superior to injustice, but show how each of them, by itself, affects the soul, the one being an evil and the other a good. 

And strip away the reputations, as Glaucon ordered. For if you do not strip away the true reputations and add false ones, we will say you are not praising justice, but the *appearance* of it; and that you are not criticizing being unjust, but *appearing* unjust. We would say you are telling the unjust man to stay hidden and that you agree with Thrasymachus: that justice is another's good, serving the more powerful, while injustice is profitable to oneself but useless to the weaker. 

Since you have agreed that justice is among the greatest goods—those that are desirable both for their consequences and, much more so, for themselves (such as sight, hearing, wisdom, health, and whatever other goods are fertile by their own nature and not just by reputation)—praise this very thing in justice: how it benefits the one who has it by itself, while injustice harms him. Leave the reputations and rewards for others to praise. For I could tolerate others praising justice or blaming injustice in that way, by focusing on opinions and rewards. But from you, I cannot, unless you command it; for you have spent your whole life in no other pursuit than this very speculation. Therefore, do not merely show us by your argument that justice is better than injustice, but show how each of them affects its possessor—whether it is hidden or not from gods and men—the one being a good and the other an evil."

When I had heard this—though I had always admired the character of Glaucon and Adeimantus—I was then truly struck with wonder, and I said: "It was not a bad start to those elegiac poems written by Glaucon's admirer to you, the sons of that great man, after you fought bravely at the Battle of Megara: 'Sons of Ariston, divine lineage of a famous man.' That seems well said, my friends. For you must be affected by something divine if you are not persuaded that injustice is better than justice, even though you can speak so well on its behalf. 

I do believe you are not persuaded. I gather this from your character, for if I judged only by your words, I would not have believed you. But the more I believe you, the more I am at a loss as to what to do. I do not know how I can help. I seem to lack the power. The proof is that you did not accept the arguments I thought were sufficient to show Thrasymachus that justice is better than injustice. Yet I do not find how I can now refuse to help, for I fear it may be an impiety to stand by while justice is slandered and not come to its defense as long as I have breath and speech. It is better, then, to support it as best I can."

Then Glaucon and all the others asked me to help with all my might and not abandon the discussion, but to search out what each was and what the true utility of each was. I said, therefore, what my opinion was: that this investigation we are starting is no small matter, but requires a man with keen sight, as it seems to me. And since we are not that capable, we should investigate justice just as if someone had ordered people who were not keen-sighted to read small letters from a distance, and then someone noticed that the same letters existed elsewhere in a larger place and in a larger size; it would then be seen as a godsend to read the large ones first and then consider the smaller ones to see if they are the same.

"Exactly," said Adeimantus. "But what do you see in the inquiry into justice that is like that, Socrates?"

"I will tell you," I said. "Do we not say there is a justice of a single man, and also of a whole city?"

"Certainly," he said.

"And is not a city larger than one man?"

"It is larger," he replied.

"Perhaps, then, justice exists in larger form in the larger thing, and is easier to recognize. Therefore, if you wish, let us first seek what it is in cities. Then we will consider it in individuals, looking for the likeness of the larger thing in the form of the smaller."

"You seem to speak wisely," he said.

"If we were to watch a city being built in our speech, we would also see its justice and injustice arise."

"Perhaps," he said.

"Once that is done, there will be hope of more easily finding...

# Book Thirty-One. 374

...what we are looking for."

"Very much so."

"Then we must try to do this. For it is no small task, I think. Consider it, then."

"It has already been considered," said Adeimantus. "Do not do otherwise."

"A city comes to be, I believe," I said, "since none of us is self-sufficient, but we all have many needs. Or do you think there is any other beginning for the founding of cities?"

"None other," he said.

"So then, one man takes on another for one use, and another for another use, and since we have many needs, we gather many partners and helpers into one settlement. And this collective we call a 'city,' do we not?"

"Entirely so."

"They share their goods with one another, then, and receive from others in turn, believing this exchange to be to their advantage."

"Exactly."

"Come then, let us build a city in our speech from the beginning. It will be created, it seems, by our needs."

"How could it be otherwise?"

"The first and greatest of all needs is the provision of food, so that we may exist and live."

"Certainly."

"The second is housing. The third is clothing and such things."

"It is as you say."

"Now then, how will the city be sufficient for this preparation? Will not one be a farmer, another a builder, and another a weaver? <margin>Note: Aristotle, Politics Book 4, Chapter 4.</margin> Shall we not also add a shoemaker there, or someone else to care for the things pertaining to the body's use?"

"By all means."

"So the city itself would consist of at least four or five men."

"It appears so."

"What then? Must each of them share his work with the others? For instance, must the one farmer prepare food for four men, and spend four times the time and labor in farming to share it with the others? Or should he neglect the care of the others and prepare only a fourth part of the food for himself in a fourth of the time? And should he spend the other three parts of his time building his house, making his clothes, and making his shoes—not taking the trouble to share his work with others, but providing for himself by himself?"

"Perhaps, Socrates," said Adeimantus, "the first way would be easier than the second."

"By Jove, it would not be strange," I said. "For as you were speaking, I was considering that we are not born all alike, but different from each other; each of us is produced by nature suited for a particular task. Don't you think so?"

"I do."

"Well then, would someone do better practicing many arts at once, or one man practicing one art?"

"One man, one art."

"And I think this is also clear: that if someone misses the proper moment for a task, the work is ruined."

"It is clear."

"For the thing to be done does not want to wait for the leisure of the doer, but necessity forces the doer to follow the work, always observing the opportunity."

"It is necessary."

"From this it follows that more things are produced, and better, and more easily, when each person does one thing according to his nature, at the right time, and is free from other tasks."

"That is exactly right."

"We need more citizens than four, then, Adeimantus, to provide the things we mentioned. For the farmer, it seems, will not make his own plow if it is to be a good one, nor his hoes and rakes, nor the other tools needed for farming. Nor will the builder. For he also needs many tools. The same will be said for the weaver and the shoemaker. Right?"

"The same."

"So carpenters and smiths, and many other such craftsmen, becoming fellow citizens in our little town, will make it more crowded."

"True."

"But it would still not be large enough unless we added cowherds, shepherds, and other herdsmen, so that the farmers would have oxen for plowing, and the builders could use beasts of burden to haul materials with the farmers, and the weavers and shoemakers would have hides and wool. It would be no small city that had all these."

"Indeed. But to found a city in a place where it will not need imports is almost impossible."

"Impossible."

"It will need others, then, to bring in from another city what this one lacks."

"It will."

"But a distributor who brings nothing that those people need—from whom he gets what his own city lacks—would be going on a useless errand. He would return empty-handed, wouldn't he?"

"So it seems."

"Therefore, they must produce not only enough for their own city, but the kind and quantity of things needed by those from whom they get their supplies."

"They certainly must."

"We need more farmers and other craftsmen in our city, then."

"More indeed."

"And we need other distributors who will import and export the various goods. These are 'merchants,' are they not?"

"They are."

"So we will need merchants."

"Certainly. And if the trade is by sea, we will also need many who are skilled in things pertaining to navigation."

"Many, clearly."

"What about in the city itself? How will they share the things they each produce? It was for the sake of this sharing that we formed our partnership and built the city."

"It is clear," he said, "that it is by buying and selling."

"A marketplace, then, and a currency for exchange will be established for us for the sake of this trade?"

"Entirely so."

"Now, if a farmer or some other craftsman brings something he has made to the market, but does not arrive at the same time as those who want to trade with him, will he sit idle in the market, away from his work?"

"Not at all," he said. "There are people who, seeing this, prepare themselves for this service. In well-ordered cities, these are people who are somewhat weak in body and useless for other work. They stay there in the market to exchange money for the goods of those who have something to sell, and then give the goods for money to those who want to buy. This necessity creates a class of 'shopkeepers' in our city. Do we not call those who stay in the market for buying and selling 'shopkeepers,' and those who travel between cities 'merchants'?"

"Without a doubt."

"There are others as well, I think—servants who have little to offer in terms of mental strength, but have enough physical strength for labor. These people, selling the use of their strength and calling the price of it 'wages,' are named 'wage-earners.' Is that not so?"

"Exactly. So wage-earners are the final piece of the city."

"It seems so. Now, Adeimantus, is our city already so enlarged that it is perfect?"

"Perhaps."

"Where then, in this city, will justice and injustice be? And with which of the things we have discussed did they come in?"

"I don't know, Socrates," he said, "unless perhaps they consist in some mutual use of these things we have mentioned."

"You may be right," I said. "We must consider it and not give up. First, then, let us look at how those who are so settled will live. Will they not produce food, wine, clothes, shoes, and houses? In summer they will work mostly without clothes and shoes, but in winter they will be sufficiently dressed and shod. They will be fed on barley-meal and wheat-flour, making noble cakes and loaves, serving them on reeds or clean leaves. They will lie on beds of bryony and myrtle and feast with their children, drinking wine with crowns on their heads and praising the gods, living pleasantly together...

...they will live together, nor will they beget children beyond their means, guarding against both poverty and war. To this **Glauco** [Glaucon] responding, said: "You have made a feast, it seems, without relish." "You speak the truth," I said. "For I had forgotten this: that they were to have relish—namely salt, and olives, and cheese, and bulbs; furthermore, they will cook vegetables as the pottage of the fields. And we shall set before them desserts of figs, chickpeas, and beans; and they will roast myrtle berries and beech-nuts [1] in the embers, drinking in moderation. And so, living a quiet and healthy life as is fitting, and having reached old age, they will leave a similar life to their descendants."

"If, O **Socrates**, you were establishing a city of pigs, what other fodder would you have prepared for them?" "What then must be done, O **Glauco**?" "That which many are accustomed to," he said: "they must recline upon couches, unless we wish to live wretchedly, and eat from a table, with the feasts and relishes which men use in these times." "So be it, **Glauco**," I said. "I understand: for it seems we are not only considering how a city is made, but a delicate [luxurious] city. Perhaps, therefore, it will not be a bad thing. For by observing this, we may perhaps discover where justice and injustice are born in cities. The city we have described seems to me to be the true city, as if it were a healthy one; but if you wish, let us also consider the 'turgid' [swollen/feverish] city. For nothing prevents it."

"Truly, for some people, it seems these things will by no means be sufficient, and this way of life will not please them; but couches will be added, and tables, and other furnishings, and vessels, and relishes, and perfumes, and incense, courtesans, spices, condiments, and delights—and every kind of each of these. Nor must we only posit those things which we recounted above as necessary—houses, clothes, and shoes—but again painting must be added, and the arts of variety, gold and ivory, and all other things of that kind. Is it not so?" "Entirely," he said. "Must not the city, therefore, be made larger? For that healthy one is no longer sufficient, but it must be filled with a certain mass and multitude of those who are no longer in cities for the sake of necessity: such as all hunters, and mimes, and imitators—partly concerning figures and colors, partly concerning music—namely poets, and their ministers the rhapsodes, reciters of poems, actors, singers, dancers, contractors [2], and the craftsmen of various equipment and instruments; then of other things, including those which pertain to women's adornment. Furthermore, we shall require many more servants. Does it not seem to you that there is a need for tutors, nurses, educators, hairdressers, barbers, and those who prepare relishes and the kitchen? Moreover, we shall need swineherds. For these were not with us in the former city: for there was no need. But in this one, we shall require both these and many other foods from the flesh of animals, if anyone eats them; shall we not?" "Why not?" "And shall we not need doctors much more, living in this way, than we did before?" "Very much so, indeed."

"And yet the region, which then nourished those men quite conveniently, will become small instead of ample. Or how do we say it?" "It is as you say." "Must we not therefore usurp something from the region of our neighbors, so that we may have enough land for grazing and plowing? And will the neighbors not do the same from ours, if they too should devote themselves to the infinite accumulation of riches, exceeding the boundaries of necessity?" "It will be quite necessary, O **Socrates**." "Shall we fight then? Or what shall we do?" "We shall fight." "And yet we do not yet say whether war brings anything of evil or of good: but only this, that we have found the origin of wars—from which, when they occur, great calamities invade the city [3], both publicly and privately." "It happens exactly so." "Therefore, there is need of an even larger city to provide a very great army, which, because of the things already said, may go out to meet attacking enemies."

"Are those whom we have described not sufficient for fighting?" "No, if indeed you and we all rightly granted the previous points when, in constituting the city, we agreed that it is impossible for one man to practice many arts well." "You speak the truth." "Is the contest of war not an artful faculty?" "It is, and most especially so." "Is there then more care to be given to shoemaking than to the art of war?" "Not at all." "But we forbade a shoemaker from attempting the work of a farmer, or a weaver, or an architect at the same time, and we commanded him to dwell only in his own art, so that his work might be finished for us as well as possible; and to each of the others we assigned one thing according to each one's nature, so that each..."

### Translator's Notes and Observations:

*   **[1] *phaginas glandes***: Literally "beech acorns" or beech-nuts. The Latin *fagus* refers to the beech tree.
*   **[2] *redemptores***: In a classical or Renaissance context, these are contractors or purveyors who undertake public works or the supply of goods.
*   **[3] *vrbē***: The OCR reads *vrbē* (urbem, accusative). In the phrase *magnę vrbē calamitates inuadunt*, one would grammatically expect *urbem* (the calamities invade the city) or *urbi* (calamities fall upon the city). Given the context, "invade the city" is the intended meaning.

**Abbreviation/OCR Clarifications:**
*   *cauiua*: Likely a mis-reading of *convivia* (feasts/banquets).
*   *scililicet*: A typo in the original text or OCR for *scilicet* (namely/to wit).
*   *vpantea*: Likely a mis-reading of *ut antea* (as before).
*   *iuperiora*: Likely a mis-reading of *superiora* (the aforementioned things).
*   *tribuim'*: A standard abbreviation for *tribuimus* (we assigned/allotted).
