<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Socrates and Glaucon (now joined by his brother Adeimantus) are discussing the requirements for the "guardians" of their expanding, luxurious city. They have just concluded that a guardian must be both fierce and gentle, a combination that seems contradictory until Socrates finds a parallel in nature.</meta>

376 Book Thirty-One. <note>This heading likely refers to the sequence of books in a larger Renaissance collection of philosophical works, rather than the specific book number of Plato's Republic.</note>

...did we find that there are certain natures of such a kind as we least expected, possessing these contrary qualities at the same time? Where? In other animals this may certainly be seen, and not least in that guardian with whom we shall compare our own guardian. For you know that this is the natural character of a **noble dog**: to be most gentle toward his house-mates and acquaintances, but the opposite toward those he does not know. I know it certainly. Therefore, what we are seeking is neither impossible nor against nature—namely, that a guardian should be such a person. So it appears. Does it further seem to you that the future guardian needs to add this to his ferocity: that he be a **philosopher** by nature? How do you mean? For I do not understand. And yet, this too can be observed in dogs, which is indeed a thing worthy of admiration in a beast. What sort of thing? Because if he sees someone unknown, he is angry, even if he has suffered no ill from him. But he fawns upon one he knows, even if he has received no benefit from him. Have you not wondered at this before? I have not noticed it much until now, but that he does this is manifest. Yet this seems to be an innate effect of his nature, and truly philosophical. By what reasoning? Because he distinguishes a friendly sight from an enemy by no other means than that he **knows** the one and is **ignorant** of the other. Should we not, then, rightly call him a lover of learning and a seeker of wisdom, since he distinguishes the domestic from the foreign by knowledge and ignorance? It would be so. Why not? Furthermore, the seeker of learning and the philosopher are the same. The same. Why then should we not boldly propose that in a man, too, if he is to be gentle toward his friends and acquaintances, he must be a philosopher and a lover of learning? Let us propose it. He who is to be the best guardian of the city will therefore be, by nature, a philosopher, high-spirited, swift, and strong. This is entirely so.

Let such, then, be the guardian. But in what way shall these guardians be nourished and educated by us? And will this consideration help us find that for the sake of which we are considering everything: namely, how **justice** and **unjustice** arise in a city? We must certainly think on this, lest we either omit what is necessary or pursue what is superfluous. I think indeed, said the brother of Glaucon <note>Adeimantus</note>, that this discussion contributes greatly to what has been proposed to us. By Jove, friend Adeimantus, I think so too. Therefore we must not desist, even if the discussion should be somewhat long. Certainly not, he said. Come then, as if we were telling stories in our leisure, let us instruct these men in our discourse. That is indeed fitting. What then shall be the discipline? Will it be difficult to find a better one than that which was found long ago? This consists of **gymnastics** for the body and **music** for the soul. <term>Music: In the classical sense, 'mousike' referred to all the arts overseen by the Muses, including poetry, storytelling, and history, not just melody.</term> It is clearly so. Should not this education begin with music before gymnastics? Certainly. When you say music, do you include speeches/stories or not? I do. There are two kinds of speech: the true and the false. It is so. The future guardian must be educated in both, and first in the false. I do not understand what you are saying, he said. Do you not know that we first tell fables to children? These, to speak simply, are false, yet they contain some truths. We use fables for children before gymnastics. It is as you say. This is what I meant when I said we must touch upon music before gymnastics. Rightly so. Do you not know that in every task the beginning is the greatest part? Especially for the young and tender. For then the form is most easily molded and takes on whatever impression one wishes to imprint upon each. Entirely so. Shall we then so easily permit children to hear just any fables fashioned by anyone, and to drink into their souls opinions that are for the most part contrary to those we think they should have when they have grown up? We shall by no means permit it.

First, therefore, as it seems, we must oversee the fashioners of fables; if they make a good fable, let it be chosen, but let the rest be rejected. Those we choose we shall take care to have told to the children by nurses and mothers, so that their souls may be formed by fables much more than their bodies are shaped by hands. But of those stories they now recount, many must be cast out. Which ones? he asked. In the greater ones, I said, we shall clearly see the lesser. For there must be the same form and the same power in both the greater and the lesser. Do you not think so? I do indeed. But I do not at all understand which ones you call the "greater." Those which **Hesiod** and **Homer** and the rest of the poets wrote. For these men fashioned false fables for mankind, which are still circulated daily. Which fables do you mean? And what do you condemn in them? That which ought to be condemned first and foremost, especially when someone does not lie well. What is that? When someone portrays badly in words what the gods and heroes are like—just like a painter who paints things not at all similar to the subjects he is trying to imitate. Such things are rightly censured. But how and what do we mean? First and greatest is the lie about the greatest things, which Hesiod lied about unskillfully when he imagined those deeds done by **Uranus**, <note>original: "Cęlo" (Caelus), the Latin name for Uranus, the primordial sky god.</note> and added how **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnus" (Cronus)</note> punished him, and recounted what Saturn did and what he suffered from his son <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. Even if these things were true, I would not think they should be so openly brought before the minds of the helpless and the young; they should rather be kept silent. But if there were a necessity to speak, they should be heard in secret by a few, who have sacrificed not a mere pig, but some precious and rare victim, so that it happens that as few as possible hear them. Truly, these are harsh stories. Nor are they to be told, O Adeimantus, in our city. Nor should it be said to a young listener that he who commits the most wicked crimes does nothing strange; or that he who punishes a father for his sins is not straying much, but is doing what the first and greatest of the gods did. By Jove, he said, these things do not seem to me worthy to be told. Nor should it be told at all that gods wage war with gods, or plot, or fight. For these things are not true—if indeed our future guardians of the city are to think it shameful to quarrel among themselves. Therefore, by no means should the **war of the Giants** be narrated to them, nor many other battles of gods and heroes against their own kin and neighbors. Rather, if we are to persuade them that no citizen was ever an enemy to another, and that this is not holy, such things should be told to children and youths immediately by the elders and old women, and the poets must be compelled to direct their fables toward this. But the chains cast upon **Juno** <note>Hera</note> by her son, and **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus</note> being cast out of heaven by his father when he wanted to help his beaten mother, or whatever battles of the gods Homer wrote, must by no means be received into the city, whether they are spoken through **allegory** or without allegory. For a youth cannot distinguish these things, and the opinions accepted at that age are usually very difficult to wash away or uproot. For this reason, perhaps, every effort must be made so that these first stories they hear are the best possible ones for the cultivation of virtue. What you say is not far from reason. But if someone should ask what these are, and what kind of fables, what shall we say? Then I said, O Adeimantus, we are now poets...

Dialogue II on the Republic. Or, on Justice. 377

...at present, neither I nor you are poets, but the founders of a city. It is necessary for founders to know the forms in which poets must fashion their stories; if they exceed these, such stories are not to be permitted. Yet it does not belong to the founders of a city to fashion stories themselves. Rightly said, he replied. But declare this to me: what are these forms concerning theology? They are such as this, I said: that God must always be described as He truly is, whether he is described in epic poems, or songs, or even in tragedy. So it is fitting. And is not God himself good, and must he not be called so? Undoubtedly. And yet nothing good is harmful. Is it not so? Nothing, I think. Does that which is harmless ever cause injury? In no way. Does that which does not injure do any evil? Not that either. And that which does no evil is the cause of no evil. None. Likewise, is not the good beneficial? Entirely. Therefore, it is the cause of doing well and happily. Certainly. And so the good is not the cause of all things, but the cause of those things that are in a good state; but of those things that are in an evil state, it is in no way the cause. It is exactly so. Therefore God, since He is good, is not the cause of all things, as many say, but He is the cause of a few things for men, and of many things He is not the cause. For our good things are far fewer than our evils. And of the good things, God alone must be called the cause. But for evil things, one must seek any other cause besides God. You seem to me to speak most truly. 

<margin>Iliad book 24</margin> Therefore we must not admit the error of Homer, or any other poet, who speaks foolishly about the gods, saying that on Jupiter’s threshold lie two jars full of fates, one of good and the other of evil. And when Jupiter imparts these to someone in a mixture, at one time things go well for him, and at another, poorly. But to whomsoever he gives from the second jar alone, him a ravenous hunger drives over the earth. Nor indeed must we admit that Jupiter is for us the dispenser of both good and evil. 

<margin>Iliad book 4</margin> And if anyone says that the violation of oaths and treaties was done by Pandarus through Jupiter and Minerva, we shall by no means praise it, 

<margin>Iliad book 20</margin> nor the controversy and dissension of the gods, and the judgment through Themis and Jupiter. Nor should the young hear what Aeschylus says, that God provides a cause for mortals when he wishes to utterly overturn a house. But if someone introduces iambic verses in which the sufferings of Niobe <note>original: "Nicobę"</note> are recounted, or of the Pelopidae, or the Trojans, or anything of this kind, he must either not be allowed to say these are the works of God, or if they are of God, the reason we are now seeking must be found in them: it must be said that God did what was good and just, and that He helped them by punishing them. But the poet must not be permitted to say that those who pay the penalty are miserable and that it is God who thus afflicts them. But if he says that wicked men, being miserable, needed punishment and that by paying it they were helped by God, that may be permitted. But to say that God, who is good, is the cause of evil to anyone, must be rejected entirely; nor should anyone be permitted to say this in his city, if the city is to be established with good laws. Furthermore, no one should hear this, whether he be younger or older, whether it be brought in through poems or told in prose, as these things are neither holy to say, nor useful to us, nor consistent with themselves. I agree with you in the passing of this law; these things please me. Let this then be one law and form among those regarding the gods: in which everyone is compelled both to say and to represent God not as the cause of all things, but only of the good. It is sufficient. 

But what of this second form? Do you think God is a sorcerer, appearing now in one form and now in another as if from an ambush? That He changes His form into many shapes, now altering His own appearance and now deceiving us, offering us false images of Himself? Or is He rather simple and least of all likely to depart from His own form? I do not know what to say about this at present. Well, what about this? If anything departs from its own form, is it not necessary that it be changed either by itself or by another? Necessary. But things that are in the best condition are least of all changed or moved by another—just as the body is affected by food, drink, and labor, and all plants by heat and storms of wind, and similar passions; yet that which is most sound and robust is least altered. Certainly. And would not an external disturbance least of all alter a soul that is most brave and wise? Truly. Furthermore, all composite things—vessels, buildings, clothes—when well-constructed and in good condition, are similarly least changed either by time or by other accidents. It is as you say. Therefore, whatever is in a good state, whether by nature, or art, or both, undergoes the least change from another. It seems so. But indeed God Himself, and what belongs to God, are in every way in the best possible state. Why not? For this reason, then, God would least of all take on many forms. Least of all. But would He turn and change Himself by Himself? It would be manifest that He would, if indeed He were changed. Would He then change Himself into something better and more beautiful, or into something worse and uglier than Himself? It must be into something worse, if indeed He changes. For we do not say that God is lacking in beauty or virtue. You speak most rightly. But since this is so, does it seem to you, Adeimantus, that anyone—whether God or man—would voluntarily make himself worse? That is certainly impossible. It is impossible, therefore, for God to wish to change Himself. But as it seems, since each of the gods is most beautiful and best, He remains as far as possible eternally and simply in His own form. I think this is entirely necessary. Therefore, let no poet tell us, O best of men, that the gods visit cities in various forms, looking like strangers. 

<margin>Odyssey book 3</margin> Nor let anyone lie similarly about Proteus and Thetis. Nor in tragedies or other poems should anyone introduce Hera changed into the appearance of a priestess of Inachus, the Argive river, collecting gifts for the sons who were granted life; and let no one dare to fashion other such tales. Nor let mothers terrify their children with these vain stories, saying that certain gods wander by night in various forms, looking like strangers, lest they both speak ill of the gods and make the children more timid. In no way. 

But are the gods themselves immutable, yet by some sorcery they deceive us and seem to change into various forms? Perhaps so. But what of this? Does God wish to lie, either in word or by presenting a false image in deed? I do not know. Do you not know that the true lie itself—if it can be called so—is hated by all men and gods? What do you mean by that? Thus, I said: No one willingly wishes to lie in the most principal and excellent part of himself, and about the most principal and excellent things, but he fears that lie there most of all. Even now I do not understand. You think I am saying something profound. But I am saying that no one would ever want his soul to lie about reality, to have lied, to be deceived by ignorance, and to have accepted and held a lie there. Indeed, all men hate having a lie in their soul most of all. Most of all. And yet, what I was just saying would rightly be called the true lie: the ignorance in the soul of the one who is deceived. For the lie in speech is a certain imitation...

...an imitation of that passion which is in the soul, a later-arising image, and not an altogether pure lie. Is it not so? Exactly so. Therefore, the true lie itself is hateful not only to gods but also to men. It seems so to me. But what about the lie in words? When and for whom is it so useful that it is not worthy of hatred? Is it not against enemies, or those called friends when, due to madness or some ignorance, they attempt to commit some evil deed? Then, for the sake of turning them away, it is useful as a kind of medicine. And in those stories we were just discussing, because we do not know where the truth of ancient things lies, we make the lie resemble the truth, for in this way we make it most useful. It is exactly so. According to which of these, then, is a lie useful to God? Is it because He does not know ancient things that He lies under the image of truth? That would be ridiculous. Therefore, there is no lying poet in God. It does not seem so to me. Will He lie out of fear of enemies? Far from it. Or because of the folly and madness of His familiars? Thus, the nature of gods and spirits <term>spirits (daemones): In the Platonic sense, intermediary beings between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</term> is entirely without lies. Entirely. It seems so to me as you say it. Do you grant then that this is the second form in which one must speak of the gods and fashion stories: as beings who are neither sorcerers nor change themselves, nor seduce us with lies, either in word or in deed? I grant it. 

<margin>Iliad book 2</margin> Therefore, while praising many things said by Homer, we shall by no means praise the dream sent by Jupiter to Agamemnon. Nor shall we praise Aeschylus when he introduces Thetis saying that Apollo sang at her wedding, saying that Thetis’ noble offspring would be long-lived and untouched by disease. He said my fortunes would be beloved by God, and he filled me with joy by his praises. And I hoped the mouth of Phoebus was divine, truthful, and prophetic. But he himself who was praising, who was himself present at the table, who himself spoke these things—it was he himself who killed my son. Whenever such things are said about the gods, we shall immediately protest and hiss them off, nor shall we permit teachers to use them for the education of youth, if our guardians are to be pious and divine, as far as is possible for a man. I accept this form, he said, and I shall use it everywhere as law.

->**THIRD DIALOGUE ON THE REPUBLIC, OR, ON JUSTICE.**<-
->**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO**<-

<meta>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator of Plato into Latin during the Renaissance. His "Arguments" are interpretive summaries intended to guide the reader through the philosophical text.</meta>

The third dialogue continues the education of the guardians begun in the second. And just as in the second he forbade them to hear false and shameful things about the gods, so here he forbids hearing tragic tales about the underworld, which might make them more timid. Likewise, comic tales, which provoke immoderate laughter. For one who is daily dissolved into profuse laughter becomes just as soft as one who is compelled to tears by grief. Since the guardians must be kept not only from timidity but also from intemperance, greed, and injustice, he again forbids the hearing of poems by which the lusts, thefts, and iniquities of the gods, heroes, and great men are fashioned. This military education is common to almost all citizens. Among these things, pay attention to what he says about the lie. A lie is a calamity to the city—specifically when private individuals lie to one another, and most of all if they lie to the magistrates. It is just as if a sick person lies to a doctor, or a sailor to a pilot. However, it is permitted for rulers to use a lie sometimes for the sake of public safety, and sometimes for a private individual toward another private individual, solely for the sake of avoiding some very grave evil. It is also permitted to tell stories moderately about ancient things whose truth is unknown, and as if through certain images to fashion those things of which we hardly have a certain form. 

Furthermore, he distinguishes speech into three species. For it is either simple narration, or simple imitation, or a mixture of both. But he rejects all speech that recounts the vilest things without discrimination and portrays a disturbed man. For whoever studiously imitates something for a long time passes into its nature. Therefore, he commands the poet who imitates disturbed souls too sharply to either change his style to imitate a constant character or to depart far from the city, as he is harmful to youth. He also says that he who manages too many things, whether by imitating or by doing, eventually fails in each one so that he becomes excellent in none. 

He then proceeds from the first music—that is, poetry—to the next, and divides it into three species: Speech, Harmony, and Rhythm. At the start, musicians call the "phthongus" the harmonic voice, that is, one suited for consonance, which is neither so deep that it cannot be made deeper by the same singer, nor so high that a higher one cannot be uttered. From these "phthongi" he then constitutes harmony, namely a suitable measure in the excess and defect of deep, high, and middle voices. Here there are four voices: deep, high, rising to high, and declining to deep. Likewise, there are four primary proportions: the double (2:1), the sesquialtera (3:2), the sesquitertia (4:3), and the sesquioctave (9:8). From the double proportion follows the consonance of the octave; from the sesquialtera, the fifth; from the sesquitertia, the fourth; and from the sesquioctave, the tone. But of these things more diligently elsewhere. 

He approaches rhythm in the third place, that is, a certain order of motion and time, as perceived from the second book of the *Laws*. For after you have reconciled the voices by a certain harmonic measure of excess and defect through tension and relaxation, there is need for rhythm, by which you measure the motions and times of the high, deep, and middle voices, both in individuals and between individuals. I mean the gentler, the more severe, and the middle motions. I mean the longer, the shorter, and the equal times, through long, short, and middle accents. In these things, note that "base" <term>base: Ficino is likely referring to the musical 'basis' or ground-note.</term> is a diverse word: for as the matter requires, it signifies foundation, seat, weight, progress, and terminus. 

Besides these, nine degrees of the most common consonances and dissonances must be considered. First, in reason—that is, an opinion consenting with the truth of the thing itself: whose contrary is a false opinion dissenting from the truth. Second, in imagination: whose consonance is the following of reason, but whose dissonance is the pursuit of external things. Third, in effect: either following temperate reason or intemperate imagination. Fourth, in decorous or indecorous speech, insofar as it follows either right reason or tumultuous imagination. Fifth, in song: whose consonance is to imitate decorous speech, and dissonance indecorous. Sixth, in sound imitating the song in one way or another. Seventh, in harmonious or inharmonious jumping pertaining to dance. Eighth, in a certain composition of the limbs and the whole body, as much pleasing to the sight as ready for gymnastic exercise. Ninth, in the artificial works of any art, composed with a certain musical proportion. Let these nine degrees represent the nine Muses to you. 

Remember, however, that the best harmony of all is the temperance of the soul. Which the others follow and imitate, and in turn, when they are practiced, they increase. For this reason, he commands that only those consonances be practiced, heard, and watched which represent a constant habit of mind—not one elated by pride, nor hardened by anger, nor softened and dissolved by pleasure, nor broken by grief, nor complaining from pity or want. He approves therefore of a deep and constant concert, but disapproves of the extremes—that is, the agitated and the soft; he also condemns the complex and praises the simple above others. He judges that harmony has the greatest power over the soul. Indeed, the soul is a certain divine harmony and was once accustomed, as I might say in a Platonic way, to celestial harmony. Again, the body consists of a certain harmony, and the spirit is also compounded. Furthermore, the consonance of voices, being air that penetrates the airy spirit with motion and carries the affect and mind of the singer with it, moves the affect of the listener by affect and affects the soul by the soul, and gradually instills habits. In all things, notice how Plato educates his city with not only civil but also very religious observance, and always what he also teaches...

Dialogue III on the Republic. Or, on Justice. 379

...in the *Statesman*, he mixes temperance with fortitude. Finally, how shameful, how dissonant he considers venereal <note>pertaining to sexual desire</note> pleasure to be, and therefore he separates it far from legitimate love, which always desires only what is beautiful and harmonious. He treats many things concerning music and gymnastics; for they were of the greatest importance: everyone applied themselves to these, and they ought to apply themselves. For the former shapes and composes the soul and spirit, while the latter does so for the body for the sake of the soul. He adds that a good soul does not come from a good body, but a good body is made from a good soul. He adds that simple music benefits the soul and a simple diet benefits the health of the body, while complexity harms both, and that men, as long as they lived soberly, did not need the help of natural physicians. He condemns superstitious observations of the body regarding diet and medicines. He says a principal sign of a poorly established city is if it requires the diligent work of doctors and judges. He describes the duty of the doctor and the judge, and he chooses a judge who is good in nature, prudent, old, and experienced with many men, both good and bad. He asserts that depravity, like a certain privation, knows neither itself nor virtue. But virtue, like a habit, knows itself through itself alone, and also judges vices through its own use of things. One must always remember that Plato confirms not only here, but also in the *Laws*, the *Statesman*, and the *Protagoras*, that nothing is more necessary for every man—especially the civil and philosophical man—than a bond forged equally from fortitude and temperance: so that through the former high things are sought, and through the latter humble things are not despised; and on both sides, you may never dare or fear too much. Through the former you repel private and public injuries; through the latter you abstain from injury. Through the former you are called to honest things; through the latter you are restrained from shameful things. Thus it is that he ultimately refers gymnastics and music to these two things: so that through the former fortitude—not so much of the body as of the soul—and through the latter temperance may be gained. He commands that both be rightly mixed with each other. For gymnastics alone produces ferocity, and music alone produces softness; but both together produce fortitude and temperance. Finally, from the number of those so educated, he chooses both the guardians (that is, the magistrates) and the defenders (that is, the soldiers). To the magistracy he wishes to appoint old men, prudent, brave, lovers of the public good, and proven in this very thing through experience. He also commands that the young be tested in the midst of pleasures and pains, to discern whether they are temperate and brave, or the opposite: and whether they will ever easily change their opinion of preserving the public good due to deceits, threats, or allurements. Finally, he says that the natures of men are similar to metals: one fit for governing is gold, one fit for military service is silver, and one for craftsmanship and agriculture is iron and bronze. He commands that individual natures be turned toward those things for which they are fit: thus the sons of rulers are sometimes moved to viler tasks according to their nature, and conversely the sons of inferiors to more noble duties. He also forbids soldiers from possessing anything of their own, lest through greed they be turned from dogs into wolves.

->**[THE DIALOGUE RESUMES]**<-

These things, then, as it seems to me, are what should or should not be heard about the gods from earliest childhood by those who are to honor the gods and their parents, and who will not make light of common friendship. I think, said Adeimantus, that this seems right to us. But what of those who are to be brave? Must they not be told those things which will make them least afraid of death? Or do you think anyone can ever be brave who fears this? Not at all, by Jove, he said. And he who believes what is said about the underworld and thinks it is terrifying—do you think he will be intrepid in the face of death, and in battle itself prefer death to slavery and captivity? In no way. Therefore we must, as it seems, give commands to those who tell stories about these things and pray that they do not simply disparage what is in the underworld, but rather praise it—as they neither tell the truth nor say what is useful to those who are to be warriors. It is indeed necessary. We shall therefore delete all such things, beginning from this verse: 

<margin>Iliad book 11</margin> *I would rather serve as a poor hired laborer in the countryside than rule over all the dead.* 

And this: *Indeed, let the houses appear horrible, vast, and foul to mortals and immortals alike, which even the gods hold in hatred.* 

And this: *O miserable ones, is there indeed a soul and an image in the underworld? But no mind is present.* 

<margin>Iliad book 23</margin> And this: *He alone has wisdom; the rest flit about as shadows.* 

Likewise: <margin>Iliad book 23</margin> *The soul, released from the limbs, flies to the underworld, bewailing its calamity, since it has left both a brave and tender age.* 

<margin>Iliad book 23 / Odyssey book 24</margin> Likewise: *The soul went beneath the earth like smoke, wailing.* 

Likewise: *As bats fly wailing in a vast cave, after some have fallen from the line from the rock where they hung together, so they went together shrieking.* 

These and other such things, by the good leave of Homer and the rest of the poets, we shall cast out—not because they are not poetic and pleasant for many to hear, but because the more poetic they are, the less they should be heard by boys and men, who ought to be free, fearing slavery more than death. It is entirely so. Furthermore, must we not cast out the horrid and terrifying names given to these things? 

I mean Cocytus <note>River of Wailing</note>, and Styx <note>River of Hatred</note>, and the underworld, and the dead, and other names of the same kind. They vehemently terrify all who hear them, and perhaps they serve some other purpose; but for our guardians, we greatly fear such names, lest from this fear they be made softer than is fitting. And we rightly dread it. They are therefore to be removed. Removed. And a form contrary to these must be spoken and introduced. Clearly. 

Therefore, we shall remove the lamentations and pities of illustrious men. It is necessary, if we also remove what went before. Consider then, whether we do this rightly or wrongly. Do we not say that a moderate man will not think death a grave thing for another moderate man who is his friend? We do indeed. Therefore, he will not lament his death as if he had suffered something grave. No. For we also assert that such a man is self-sufficient for living well, and least of all needs another. You tell the truth. Therefore, he will least of all take it hard to be deprived of children, or brothers, or riches, and other such things. Least of all, certainly. And so he will not lament, but will bear it most moderately when he falls into any such calamity. Certainly. Rightly then would we remove the wailings of famous men and leave them to women—and not even to good women—and to cowardly men besides, so that those whom we educate for the guardianship of the region may disdain to do such things. Rightly so. 

<margin>Iliad book 24</margin> Again, we will pray to Homer and the rest of the poets not to make Achilles, the son of a goddess, now lying on his side, now on his back, <margin>Iliad book 18</margin> now also prone; or rising to wander, afflicted with sadness, on the shore of the sea; or with both hands taking burning dust and pouring it on his head; nor wailing and lamenting in other ways, as many and of such kind as he did. 

<margin>Iliad book 24</margin> Nor should they show Priam, who was near to the gods, supplicating and rolling himself in dung, calling each man by name. And much more shall we pray the same Homer not to introduce them wailing in this manner: 

<margin>Iliad book 22</margin> *Woe is me, miserable; woe is me, how unhappily I bore the best of sons.* 

But if he must show gods, let him at least not dare to imitate the greatest of the gods in such a dissimilar form as to introduce him saying: 

<margin>Iliad book 16</margin> *Alas, what a dear man I see being routed around the city with my own eyes. My heart grieves for him.* 

And likewise: <margin>Iliad book 24</margin> *Woe is me, since fate compels Sarpedon, the most beloved of all to me, to be tamed by Patroclus, son of Menoetius.* 

For if, friend Adeimantus, the young were to hear these things studiously and not think them ridiculous or unworthy of being said, they would never—knowing themselves to be men—think those things unworthy of them, or restrain themselves when it came into their minds to say or do something of the kind. Rather, without any shame or endurance...

...even in the smallest losses, they would break out into the greatest wailings and shrieks. You speak the truth, he said. Nor indeed is that fitting, as our reason was telling us just now; and we must trust it unless we find something better in the meantime. It is indeed not fitting. 

But neither should we be given to excessive laughter. For a violent change follows profuse laughter. So it seems to me also. Therefore, it is not to be admitted when someone introduces men of the highest authority dissolved in laughter, and much less so the gods. Much less, certainly. Therefore, we shall not hear such things about the gods from Homer as: 

<margin>Iliad book 1</margin> *Inextinguishable laughter was stirred up among the gods when they saw Vulcan bustling through the house, since he was lame.* 

This must not be admitted, according to your word. If you wish to attribute this word to me (it certainly should not be admitted). 

Furthermore, truth is to be valued more highly. For if we were saying rightly just now that a lie is truly useless to gods, but for men it is useful as a medicine, then it must be granted to public "doctors" <note>meaning the rulers</note>, but private men must not touch it. It is clear. Therefore, it is fitting for those who administer the republic, if for anyone else, to lie, whether for the sake of enemies or citizens for the utility of the city. But the rest must abstain from lying. But for a private person to lie against such princes is the same as, or a greater sin than, a sick person lying to a doctor, or an athlete to his trainer about his bodily faults, or a sailor not telling the truth to the pilot of a ship about the ship and the sailors, or how his own affairs or those of his comrades stand. You tell the truth. If, therefore, you catch someone else in the city lying, from the class of those who are craftsmen—namely a prophet, or a doctor of evils, or a carpenter—punish him as one who introduces a thing from which the overturning and ruin of the city itself, like a ship, follows. So it must clearly be done, since deeds are accomplished by speech. 

What else? Will not our youths have need of temperance <term>temperance (temperantia): here meaning self-control and moderation</term>? Without doubt. And of temperance, are not these things the greatest for subjects: namely, that they obey the magistrates; and for the rulers themselves, that they be continent in the use of venereal matters, feasts, and drinking? It certainly seems so to me. Therefore, we shall assert that such things are well said as when Diomedes says in Homer: 

<margin>Iliad book 4</margin> *Come now, sit in silence and obey my words.* 

<margin>Iliad book 3</margin> and other similar things: *The Achaeans went breathing strength in silence, fearing their leaders.* And whatever else is said to this effect. Rightly so. 

But what of this? <margin>Iliad book 1</margin> *Heavy with wine, having the eyes of a dog but the heart of a deer*—and the rest that follows, and other such things said proudly and youthfully by private persons to their superiors, whether one brings them into prose or poetry—are they rightly said? In no way. For I do not think hearing these things contributes to the temperance of the young; it is no wonder, however, if they delight some people. How does it seem to you? Thus. 

What then? Does it seem to you suitable for a youth to achieve continence when he hears a most wise man in a poem speaking thus: 

<margin>Odyssey book 9</margin> *It seems to me to be the most beautiful of all things when the tables are full of feasts and meats, and the cupbearer, drawing wine from the bowl, pours it into cups and carries it around?* 

<margin>Odyssey book 12</margin> Or that: *It is most miserable to perish by hunger and undergo an adverse fate?* 

<margin>Iliad book 14</margin> Or when it is said that Jupiter, while other gods and men were sleeping, forgot all that he had planned while waking because of a rare desire for venereal pleasure, and was so struck at the sight of Hera that he would not even wait to go into the house, but wished to couple there on the ground immediately, saying he was inflamed with a more vehement desire than when they first coupled in secret from their parents? 

<margin>Odyssey book 8</margin> Or when it is told that Mars and Venus were bound by Vulcan? And other things of this kind: by Jove, it does not seem suitable to me. 

But wherever the deeds or words of excellent men are told modestly and constantly, these are the things to be noticed and heard. As when it is said: 

<margin>Odyssey book 20</margin> *Striking his breast, he rebuked his heart, saying: Endure, O heart, for you have borne far more grievous things elsewhere.* 

Entirely so it must be done. Nor must the citizens be permitted to be corrupted by gifts, nor to be greedy. In no way. Therefore, it must not be sung to them: *Gifts, believe me, please both men and gods.* Nor is Phoenix, Achilles' teacher, to be praised as if he had spoken rightly when he advised him to help the Achaeans if he received gifts, <margin>Iliad book 9</margin> but not to withdraw from his anger if he did not receive them. 

<margin>Iliad book 19</margin> Nor again shall we think Achilles himself worthy, <margin>Iliad book 24</margin> nor shall we agree that he ought to be so greedy for money that he would receive gifts from Agamemnon, or that he would not return the corpse of Hector without a price. Certainly, it is not fitting to praise such things, he said. 

I am indeed afraid, I said, to speak because of Homer; for it is not right to have asserted these things about Achilles, or to believe others asserting them. And that he said again against Apollo: 

<margin>Iliad book 22</margin> *You have ruined me, Apollo, most pernicious of all gods, whom I would certainly take vengeance upon if the power were mine.* 

<margin>Iliad book 21</margin> And how stubbornly he behaved toward the river god, even being ready to fight. Again, he says to the other river Spercheius regarding his consecrated hair: 

<margin>Iliad book 23</margin> *To the hero Patroclus, now dead, I shall give my hair to be carried.* 

Nor is it to be believed that he did this. And the dragging of Hector <margin>Iliad book 23</margin> around the tomb of Patroclus, and the slaughter of the captives upon the pyre, and all such things, we shall neither affirm to be true, nor shall we allow our people to be persuaded that Achilles—the son of a goddess and of Peleus, a most temperate man and third from Jupiter, educated by Chiron the most wise—was full of such great disturbance that he labored under two contrary diseases of the soul: illiberality combined with greed, and likewise contempt for gods and men. 

You speak very rightly. Again, let us neither believe nor allow it to be said that Theseus, son of Neptune, and Pirithous, son of Jupiter, rushed into such great thefts, nor that any other son of a god or hero ever dared to perpetrate such grave and impious deeds as they daily lie about. Rather, let us force the poets either to deny that these are their works, or not to affirm that they are the sons of gods; but in no way to assert both at once, nor to take pains to persuade our youths that evils arise from the gods, or that heroes are in no way better than men. Since, as has been said, these things are neither holy nor true. For we have shown that evils cannot proceed from the gods. We have shown it clearly. 

Furthermore, these things harm the listeners. For everyone will forgive his own depravity, being persuaded that such things are done and have been done even by those who were born nearest to the race of gods, close to Jupiter, whose altar to ancestral Jupiter exists in the ether on the peak of Ida, and in whom the blood of the gods has not yet vanished. For which reason such stories must be repressed, lest they offer an easy occasion for wickedness to our young people. Thus it must be done entirely. 

What species then remains next for us?

...of speeches, distinguishing which kinds are to be told to whom, or which are not to be told? For it has already been said how one ought to speak concerning the gods. Likewise concerning the spirits <note>original: "dæmonibus," referring to intermediary beings between gods and humans</note> and heroes, and those things which are in the underworld. Sufficiently and abundantly. Would it perhaps remain for us to speak about men? Certainly. It is impossible to establish that at present, oh friend. Why so? Because I think we shall say that poets and orators speak wrongly about men concerning things of the greatest importance: that many unjust men are happy, while the just are miserable; and that it is profitable to act unjustly if it remains hidden. Therefore, if you confess that I speak rightly, shall I say that you have granted the very things we have been seeking for a long time? You judge correctly, he said. Shall we not also grant that one ought to use such speeches about men then, when we have discovered what sort of thing justice is, and how it is naturally profitable to the one who has it, whether he seems to be just or does not seem so? You speak the truth. Concerning those things which are to be said, therefore, there has been enough dispute; next, as I think, we must discuss the **method of speaking**; and thus both what is to be said and how it is to be said will be discovered by us. I do not quite understand what you are saying, Adeimantus replied. Yet it is necessary for you to understand it, I said, and perhaps thus you will understand this more clearly. Do we not say that everything said by poets or creators of fables is a narration of things past, present, or future? What else? he said. And in the rest he always explains things thus, both in the deeds done at Troy and at Ithaca, and those things which happened in the *Odyssey*. It is entirely so. Why should we not say so? Is it not to imitate the one to whom he makes himself similar, whether in appearance or in voice? Without a doubt. In this, therefore, as it seems, both he and the rest of the poets narrate through imitation. I agree. But where the poet does not hide himself, that whole poetry and narration is without imitation. It would have stood thus—for I shall speak without verse since I am not poetic: *The priest, having set out, prayed that the gods might grant to them that they themselves might capture Troy in safety, and restore his daughter to him after receiving the gifts. Venerating the God Apollo. When he had said these things, the rest approved the words of the priest. Therefore he ordered him to depart and not provoke him, so that he might depart safe. When the old man heard these things, he was terrified and departed in silence. I understand now what you wished to say then. This, therefore, was what I was saying ought to be agreed upon between us: whether we should permit the poets to use imitation perpetually, or to imitate in part and not at all in others, and what sort of things each are, or to imitate nothing at all. I divine indeed that you will consider whether comedy and tragedy are to be received into the city, or not. Perhaps, I said, and even more than these. It would happen exactly so. Does not the same reasoning apply to imitation, that someone cannot imitate many things as well as he can one? Certainly not. Hardly, therefore, will anyone simultaneously apply himself to any pursuit worthy of esteem and imitate many things, or be a suitable imitator, since the same men could not even handle well two imitations which seem to differ little from each other, such as comedy and tragedy together. ...the imitations themselves are certain likenesses. It is as you say. # Dialogue III. On the Republic. Or, On Justice. 383

...expressed in the same formulas about which we were speaking a little while ago, and in the same way? You speak the truth. Yet harmony and rhythm ought to follow the speech. Why not? Furthermore, we were saying that we have very little need of lamentation and mourning in speeches. Not at all. What then are the plaintive harmonies? Tell me, for you are a musician. The Mixed Lydian, the Sharp Lydian, and others of this sort. Must these not be removed? For they are useless even for women, at least good ones, let alone for men. Very much so. Besides, drunkenness, softness, and laziness are least fitting for guardians. Least of all. What then are the soft and convivial harmonies? The Ionian and the Lydian, as many as are called "relaxed" and "remiss." Will you then use these, oh friend, in any way for the utility of the soldiers? In no way. But it seems to you that the Dorian and Phrygian harmonies are left. Not indeed, I said, do I know the harmonies; but leave that harmony which, as is fitting, imitates the voices and accents of one going bravely into battle and behaving manfully in any violent task, and of one in danger, whether rushing into wounds or death, or falling into any other calamity, in all these things repelling fortune constantly and manfully. And leave again the other harmony which imitates the voices and accents of a man engaged in a tranquil and least violent voluntary action, either persuading or supplicating someone, whether in prayers to God, or in teaching and admonishing a man, or on the contrary, offering himself easily to another supplicating, teaching, or dissuading him, and who, because he has been made master of his wish, is not then carried away by pride, but in all these things behaves temperately and modestly, and bravely bears every fortune; leave these two harmonies, the violent and the voluntary, of the unfortunate and the fortunate, of the temperate and the brave: and entirely whichever most beautifully imitate their accents, leave all these harmonies. But indeed you command no others to be chosen than those which I was saying above. Will we then have need in songs and melodies of a harmony which consists of many strings and of all modes? Not, as it seems to me. Therefore, we shall not nourish the builders of Trigons, Pactides <note>ancient stringed instruments</note>, and of all instruments which consist of many strings and many consonances. No, as we seem. What then? Will you leave the makers of flutes and flute-players in the city? Or do not instruments of many strings and of all harmonies imitate the flute? It is clear, he said. Therefore the Lyre remains, and the Cithara useful in the city, and the pipe convenient for shepherds in the fields. So the reasoning shows us. We introduce nothing strange, oh friend, when we prefer Apollo and the instruments of Apollo to Marsyas himself and his organs <note>referring to the myth where Apollo defeated the satyr Marsyas in a musical contest</note>. Not by Jove, as it seems to me. By the Dog <note>a favorite oath of Socrates</note>, we have begun gradually and secretly to purge the city, which we said above was given over to excessive delicacies. And wisely indeed. Come, let us purge the rest also. It follows those things said about harmonies that we should pursue rhythms in the same way, lest we wander through too many varieties or through just any movements, but let us distinguish which rhythms belong to a brave and temperate life. Which having been recognized, let us compel the foot and the song to follow such speech, not the speech to follow the foot and the song. But which rhythms are such, it is your part to declare, just as you explained the harmonies. By Jove, he said, I do not know what to say. For that there are three certain species from which these movements are woven, just as in voices there are four from which all harmonies are finished, I have observed and could say. But what kind of imitations they are of what kind of life, I am unable to open. But concerning these things we shall deliberate with Damon <note>a famous Athenian music theorist</note>, which movements of the feet are fit for illiberality, petulance, madness, and other vices, and which rhythms agree with their opposites. But I think I have heard, although not clearly enough, when he named a certain warlike composite dactyl and a heroic one, which in I know not what way he adorned when he placed it equal both above and below, ending in short and long; and as I think, he called another an iamb, and a certain other a trochee. He applied lengths and brevities. And in some of these I think he blamed or praised the movements of the foot no less than the rhythms themselves, or something mixed from both. For I cannot declare these things sufficiently. But let these things, as I was saying, be referred to Damon himself. For indeed a long speech would be needed to distinguish these. Do you think so? Long, by Jove. But you can discern this thus: that grace and ineptitude follow the congruity and incongruity of rhythm. Why not? But congruity follows beautiful speech and imitates it as a likeness; while incongruity follows the opposite. Furthermore, the consonant itself and the dissonant in the same way: since rhythm and harmony, as was said a little while ago, follow the speech, not the speech follow the rhythm and harmony. Certainly these ought to follow the speech. But what of the manner of speaking and the speech itself, does it not follow the affection of the mind? Without a doubt. And do the rest also follow the speech? Namely. Therefore, the decor of discourse, consonance, beauty, and the congruity of rhythm follow a moderated affection of the mind, which they call [unclear: ευήθειαν] <note>original: euetheian, meaning "good-natured simplicity" or "guilelessness"</note>. I do not mean that which is often when there is a certain ignorance, and we call it [unclear: ευήθειαν] by a certain bland mockery; rather, I mean that [unclear: ευήθειαν], I say, which in truth signifies a thought endowed with the best character. It is entirely so. Ought not young men to follow these everywhere, therefore, if they want to do their own business? They certainly ought. But the whole art of painting is full of these, and every such craftsmanship; the faculty of weaving is also full, and of variegating and building, and moreover the production of all other furniture and instruments; and even the nature of bodies and plants. Furthermore, in all these, there is either a certain decency or indecency. And indecency and the incongruity of rhythm and dissonance are sisters of shameful and wicked character; but the opposites are the kin of the opposite, temperate and good character, and are certain imitations of it. It is as you say. Must only the poets be urged and compelled to express the image of good character in their poems, or else not write among us? Or shall we besides prescribe to other craftsmen and forbid them to make any image of bad character in a work not well-chastened—whether illiberal, indecent, in the figures of animals, in buildings, or in any other craft? Or if someone cannot perform this, is he to be prohibited from doing anything among us, lest our guardians, nurtured on images of depravity as if on noxious grass, and daily plucking and grazing little by little on many things, should unknowingly contract one single greatest evil in their soul? For which reason those craftsmen are to be sought who by a certain natural industry can express the nature of the beautiful and the decent as if by footsteps, so that the young men, living as if in a healthy place, may be helped from all sides: since from beautiful and honest works, whether to their eyes or to their ears, something honest arrives, like a sweet breeze bringing health from healthy places; which indeed, beginning to blow immediately from the first years, gradually...

# 384 Book Thirty-One.

...animos of men into a likeness, friendship, and concord with honest speech and reason. They would be nurtured exceedingly well in that way. For this reason, therefore, I said, oh Glaucon, from the primary education in music, rhythm and harmony enter the interior of the soul and move the soul most vehemently, bringing a certain decent figure, through which he who is rightly instructed (in music) is made decent and beautiful; but on the contrary, if someone has been educated otherwise. And because he who has been nurtured there as is fitting will most acutely perceive things that are again imperfect, or not rightly fabricated, or not well-sprung, he will rightly bear these things with difficulty, and will praise beautiful things, and loving them and greedily seizing them, he will be nourished by them and become good and beautiful from them. But shameful things he will rightly blame and hate, even at that age in which he has not yet received reason. Finally, when reason arrives, he who has been thus nurtured will gladly embrace it, recognizing it from its very proximity and familiarity. For the sake of these things, it seems to me, they are to be nurtured in music. Just as then we surely know letters correctly enough when the elements do not escape us, which are few in whatever things they are turned, and we have not despised them in small or in large things as if it were not necessary to understand them, but everywhere we have tried to know them, as those who are not going to be grammarians until we have so prepared ourselves. You speak the truth. Furthermore, if the images of letters should appear anywhere, whether in water or in mirrors, we shall not know them before we know the letters themselves. For this is a matter of the same art and exercise. Entirely. Whether therefore (by the gods) is it as I say? Neither shall we be musicians before, neither we nor those themselves whom we are instructing for the guardianship of the city, until we have known the species of temperance, and of fortitude, liberality, and magnificence, and whatever are the sisters of these, and their opposites, wherever they may be: so that we may perceive both these and the images of them in whatever things they are in, and not despise them in small or in large things, but think them to belong to the same art and study? It is entirely necessary. Therefore, if these things should concur in some man, so that beautiful characters are in his soul, and in the appearance of his body individual things respond and agree with them, receiving the same form, will this not be the most beautiful spectacle for him who is able to behold it? Very much so. And yet what is most beautiful is also most lovable. Truly. A musical man would most of all love such men; but if he should perceive something dissonant, not at all. Not surely if something were lacking in the soul; but if something were merely lacking in the body, he would endure it so far as to wish to love and embrace him. Otherwise, let him undergo ignominy, as one who knows nothing at all of music or the beautiful. Exactly so. Does it not seem to you that the speech concerning music has now followed its end? For it has now arrived where it ought to be finished. For music ought to be finished in the love of the beautiful. I agree indeed. After music, however, the young men are to be exercised in gymnastics <note>physical training</note>. Why not? Entirely. Therefore, we said they must abstain from drunkenness.
