This text is a Latin translation and commentary by **Marsilio Ficino** (1433–1499) of Plato’s *Republic* (*De Republica*). It covers the end of Book III and the majority of Book IV.

### Dialogue III. on the Republic, Or, on Justice.

[Page 385]
...according to gymnastics, health in the bodies. You speak most truly. But when intemperance and diseases are multiplied in a city, both the courtrooms and the doctors’ workshops are opened. From this, the judicial and medical arts are held in high esteem, since many free men study them with the greatest zeal. Why not? Therefore, you can take no greater conjecture of a bad and shameful discipline in a city than when the highest judges and doctors are needed—not only by abject and mechanical men, but even by those who boast that they have been educated in the liberal disciplines. Does it not seem shameful, and a great conjecture of bad institution, that we are compelled, due to a lack of our own virtue, to use the eternal justice of others, namely as if they were lords and judges? Truly, the most shameful of all. Or do you not think this is even more shameful: when someone not only wastes much of their life’s time in courts, now accusing, now defending, but—elated by a certain crude boasting—glories in the very fact that he is powerful at inflicting injury, and is able to shuffle so far with his own craftiness and find such refuges that he pays no penalties, and this for the sake of the smallest and vilest things, ignorant of how much more noble and better it would be so to prepare himself that he should not need a drowsy judge? Certainly, this is more shameful than that.

Furthermore, it must be considered absurd that men need doctors not merely to heal wounds and cure diseases occurring differently according to the intemperance of the air and the season of the year, but because of sloth and that luxury which we condemned above in our way of life; so that men, like marshes, being overflowing with water and stagnant air, have forced the noble successors of **Aesculapius** to call certain diseases by new names, such as "flatus" and "catarrhs." These names of diseases, he said, are indeed new and quite absurd. These, I believe, did not exist in the time of **Aesculapius**.

[Margin: Iliad. 2.] Which I conjecture from this: that his sons at **Troia** did not disapprove of the cup offered by a woman to the wounded **Eurypylus** at the command of **Patroclus**, even though there was mixed in it **Pramnian** wine, meal, and grated cheese, which increase phlegm. Surely that cup was absurd, and least of all suitable for one so affected. No. Because if you notice, I said, the followers of **Aesculapius** before **Herodicus**, as it is said, made very little use of this pedagogical faculty of ours for curing diseases. But **Herodicus**, since he was a master of exercising youths and was himself sickly, mixing gymnastics with medicine, first afflicted himself and then many others with weariness. In what way? Indeed, he provided a long death for himself. For while he followed the disease which was lethal, he could not, as I think, cure himself; and occupied with the study of medicine, having omitted all other things, he wasted his life in this indulgence of the body, being badly affected if he departed even a little from his accustomed diet; dying with difficulty, he reached old age through this wisdom. A remarkable palm, he said, he reported from his art. Namely, I said, that which it was fitting for him to report, who was ignorant that **Aesculapius** did not fail to show this form of medicine to his successors out of ignorance or lack of skill; but because he saw that in a city best instituted, his own work was assigned to each, which it is necessary to complete, nor does leisure remain for anyone to be occupied throughout his entire life as a sickly person in caring for his body. This indeed we notice in a certain ridiculous way among craftsmen; but in those who are considered wealthy and happy, not at all. How so? A carpenter, if he ever falls into disease, demands a cure from the doctor, either through vomiting, or purging of the belly, or cauterization, or incision. But if anyone prescribes for him a long observation of diet, and wrappings for the head, and other things of this sort, he immediately objects that he has no leisure to be sick, nor is it profitable for him thus to drag out his life brooding over continuous cures and neglecting his craft. Then, saying goodbye to the doctor, returning to his accustomed diet, if he recovers, he executes his work; but if his body cannot sustain the disease, having finished his life, he is freed from his troubles. Thus indeed it seems fitting for a craftsman to use medicines. And therefore I said a work was proposed for him, which unless he completes it, it is not expedient for him to live. It is agreed. But the rich man, as we said, is urged by no work, from which if he were ever forcibly restrained, he would no longer have to live. Not at all, as it is said. Perhaps you do not hear **Phocylides** saying that one must exercise virtue while the means of living are supplied. I think even before. Let us not oppose him in this, but let us teach ourselves whether the rich man ought to meditate on this in this way: or if he wastes less time in nourishing diseases, he must not live. Since it is an impediment to the carpenter’s art and others. For it diverts the mind from work. But the precept of **Phocylides** hinders nothing. By **Jove**, he said, almost most of all, since this superfluous care of time occupies us more than gymnastics. For it is a great obstacle to domestic and military affairs, and to all urban magistracies; but what is greatest, it hinders the study of learning and all diligence of understanding and meditating, while one always suspects headaches and dizziness; and one blames the study of wisdom, as if those things arise from it. For which reason, it is entirely an impediment to us for the exercise and testing of virtue. For it makes it so that we always think we are sick, nor do we ever cease to complain about the habit of the body. It is consistent. I think **Aesculapius**, seeing these things, showed medicine to men who were healthy by nature and education, but then became sick with some external and sudden disease, by which medicine the infirmity might be removed by drugs and incisions, while maintaining their accustomed diet, so that civil affairs should not be disturbed. But he in no way attempted to lead into life bodies thoroughly sickly with internal corruption, by exhausting and infusing through diligence of a slow diet, so that he might generate sickly children, which follows from that. Nor indeed did he think one should be cured who could not live in the established and usual diet and rule, as it was thought to be of no benefit to him or to others, nor that the art should be exercised around them, nor that they should be cured, even if they were wealthier than **Midas**. You claim the sons of **Aesculapius** were very clever men. It is fitting indeed. Though the tragic poets and **Pindarus** agree with us little. For they say that **Aesculapius**...

[Page 386]
...was the son of **Apollo**, and that he was induced by gold to cure a wealthy man when he was being oppressed by extreme sickness leading to death. Whence he was also struck by lightning. But we, because of those things which we said above, do not concede both of these things to them. Rather, if he was the son of a god, he was not greedy for shameful gain; if he was greedy for shameful gain, we reject that he was the son of a god. These things are indeed said rightly. But what do you say about this, O **Socrates**? Ought we not to have good doctors in the city? Such would be especially those who had conversed with very many healthy people and very many sick people. Likewise judges similarly, who had experienced the various dispositions of men. And I call them very good indeed. But do you understand whom I think to be such? If you say. I will try indeed. However, you were not asking about a similar thing in the same discourse. By what reason? Doctors would indeed turn out most excellent if from an early age, besides the study of learning their art, they conversed among very many people affected badly in body, and were themselves labored with every kind of disease and were weak by nature. For they do not, I believe, cure body with body. For that would be impossible, for them ever to have been or to be healthy themselves; but the soul cures the body. Can it not happen that a soul which was and is bad might cure something well? Rightly indeed. But a judge, O friend, governs the soul with the soul itself. Is it not possible for some soul, conversant from childhood with evil souls and having performed every unjust deed, finally to conjecture acutely from itself the crimes of others, just as from its own body it conjectures diseases? Must he not himself have been innocent and ignorant of evil manners when he was young, if, being good and honest, he is to judge just things sincerely? For which reason, modest men, while they are young, seem to be dull-witted and those who can easily be deceived by the unjust, as they do not have in themselves the same examples of evil affections that the wicked have. Entirely, certainly, that happens to them. But indeed, it is not a youth, but an old man who ought to be a good judge, who has learned late what kind of thing injustice is; as one who did not feel it in his own soul as his own, but knew it as foreign in foreign souls over a long time, and therefore discerns what kind of evil it is, judging by knowledge rather than by his own experience. Certainly, a most noble judge seems to be of this kind. And good besides, which you yourself were seeking. For he who has a good soul is good. But that crafty and suspicious man, who has done many things unjustly, is considered sagacious and wise when he converses with those like himself; he appears cautious and cunning when, directing his mind to the examples which he has in himself, he takes enough care for himself. But when he adheres to good and elder men, he seems a fool; since he distrusts out of season and is ignorant of healthy and sincere manners, as he does not have examples of that. But when he converses more frequently with the wicked than with the wise, he also seems more often wiser than foolish to himself and others. You speak the truth without doubt. Therefore, one ought not to seek such a man as a judge as if he were good and wise, but such a one as I was saying a little before. For wickedness would never know itself or virtue. But virtue, with discipline added to nature over time, will understand both itself and wickedness at the same time. Therefore not the bad man, as my opinion goes, but this one turns out wise. It seems so to me as well. Therefore, will you not establish medicine such as we have said, together with this kind of judicial equity in the city, which indeed will cure those citizens who are well-disposed by nature, both in soul and body? But those who are not of this sort, endowed with a [sickly] body, let them die; and those who, produced with a bad disposition, are incurable, let them be punished with death? This indeed seems to be for the benefit of both those who suffer such things and for the city. It is agreed, moreover, that they will take care that the youths do not come into judicial use, using that simple music, from which we said temperance is born. Why not? And will not the musician, following these same footsteps into gymnastics, if he wishes, achieve and attain that he needs no medicine unless necessity compels? I assent indeed. He will exercise his body in gymnastics, looking more to the spiritedness (*animositatem*) of his nature and exciting it, rather than to strength; nor will he, as other athletes do, establish a diet and apply labors for the sake of strength. Quite rightly. Therefore, those who decide, O **Glauco**, to educate men in music and gymnastics, do not approach these studies for the cause which many think—that they may cure the body with the one and the soul with the other. Why not? For both seem to exercise primarily for the sake of the soul. In what way? Do you not see how it affects the soul of those who exercise gymnastics throughout their whole life and do not touch music, or those who are affected otherwise? Of which kind do you speak? Of rustic hardness and ferocity, I said, and likewise of softness and mildness. I know indeed, he said, that those who use only gymnastics turn out more savage than is fitting. But those who use only music turn out softer than becomes them. Yet the very force, I said, of the savage pertains to the spiritedness of a wrathful nature; which if it is nourished rightly, turns out brave; but if it is exercised beyond what is fitting, it becomes, as is consistent, fierce and hard. I assent. But what of the mild and gentle force itself? Does not the philosopher have it by nature? Which if it is relaxed too much, becomes softer than is fitting; but if it is well nourished, it becomes mild and modest? It is as you say. But we were saying it is necessary for the guardians themselves to have both natures. It is necessary indeed. And must they not agree and harmonize among themselves? Why not? And is his soul in which these harmonize temperate and brave? Entirely. But is his soul in which they disagree tumid and savage? And most greatly indeed. Whoever permits music to occupy and soothe his soul with constant surrounding sound, and pours through his ears, as if through a funnel, the harmonies we mentioned above—sweet, bland, soft, and mournful—and spends his age in songs that charm the soul, he first indeed, if he had anything wrathful, softens it like iron and makes it useful from the useless and hard. But when he dwells on it longer, it soothes him more; after this it now liquefies the soul and dissolves it, until it liquefies all spiritedness and cuts it out like nerves from the soul; from which it makes the soul like a soft fighter. It is entirely so. And if he had such a nature from the beginning without strength of soul, he quickly perfects this. But if he was spirited, by breaking the strengths of the soul it renders him headlong toward anger, so that he is moved by the smallest offenses and easily extinguished again. Whence, instead of spirited men, they become wrathful and morose, full of trouble and loathing. It happens exactly so. But if one should give himself over much to gymnastics and banquets, neglecting music and philosophy, first indeed he attains a firm habit of body and his soul is filled with strengths and magnitude, and he turns out braver than he was. Very much so. Then if he should so persevere in this that he does nothing else and does not touch music at all, surely if there was any instinct in his soul burning with the desire of learning, it becomes weak, deaf, and blind; as one who has tasted no doctrine, nor any investigation of things, nor any reason at all, nor any other music from which his sense could be awakened, coalesced, and purged. So plainly...

[Page 387]
...from reason, I believe, a man of this kind is made a stranger to the Muses, and he uses no persuasion or reasons of another; but by force and rustic cruelty, like some beast, he is carried toward all things; and in ignorance and rudeness, he lives without harmony and grace. The matter stands entirely so. To these two things, therefore, as it appears, I would assert some god gave two arts to men, music and gymnastics, for the spiritedness and the philosophical nature, not for the soul and body (unless by accident), but for that [soul], so that they might harmonize among themselves, being tightened and relaxed to the extent that is fitting. So it appears. He therefore who most beautifully mixes gymnastics with music, and most moderately applies these to the soul, we would rightly call the most absolute musician and composed with the highest harmony, much more than him who tunes strings. And rightly indeed, O **Socrates**. Therefore, will we not always need some such president in the city, O **Glauco**, if the republic is to be safe? We will surely, most greatly. These, then, would be the modes of discipline and education. For one might rightly say that dances of this kind, and huntings, both other types and those done with hands, and finally gymnastic and equestrian contests, are of this sort. For it is almost certain that these should follow those things, nor are they difficult to find. Perhaps they are not difficult. Come, I said. What else must we distinguish? Must we not distinguish which of all these ought to command and which obey? Why not? It is certain that the elders ought to command, the younger to obey. It is surely certain. And this is clear: that the best from these are to be chosen. That too is clear. Are not the best of the farmers those who have the greatest skill in cultivating fields? Entirely. Now, since the best must be chosen from the guardians, is it not fitting to choose those who have the greatest skill in guarding the city? Plainly them. Therefore, they must be prudent for this, and powerful, and those who have care for the Republic. It is so. But each cares most for that which he loves most. It is necessary. But he loves this most, for whom he thinks the same things are conferred by himself upon himself, and upon whose happiness he thinks his own happiness or unhappiness depends. It is so. Therefore, from all the guardians, those are most to be chosen who, as we consider them, seem to do throughout their whole life with the greatest zeal those things which they lead to be for the republic, and to avoid the contrary. Surely these are the most suitable. Therefore, they must be observed, I believe, in each age, whether they keep this precept, and neither as if deceived by certain tricks, nor compelled by any force, forgetting themselves, they cast out that opinion by which those things alone are judged to be done which are best for the republic. What "casting out" do you mean? I will tell you: it seems to me that an opinion departs from the mind either voluntarily or involuntarily. Voluntarily, indeed, a false one, in him who has unlearned it; but involuntarily, every true opinion. What you say about the voluntary departure, I understand; but about the involuntary, I desire to learn. Do you not think men are deprived of good things involuntarily, and of bad things voluntarily? Is it not a bad thing to lie and not to know the truth, but a good thing to judge truly? Does it not seem to you that to think things as they are is to think truly? You speak rightly, and it seems to me men are deprived of a true opinion involuntarily. Do they not suffer this either by theft, or by deception, or by force? I do not understand that either. I seem to speak tragically. For I say opinions are stolen from those who change their mind, either gradually obliterated by time, or secretly subtracted by an adverse reason. Now do you understand? I understand indeed. But that force is brought upon them whom pain or torture compels to think otherwise. That I understand indeed, and you speak rightly. But those who are led away as if by tricks, I think you too would say are those who lay down a prior opinion either soothed by pleasure or terrified by fear. Surely all things that deceive seem to seduce us by tricks. Therefore, what I was saying just now, we must seek who they are who constantly keep that sentiment which is among them, namely that that must always be done which they think benefits the republic. They must therefore be observed immediately from childhood, and those works proposed to them from which one might most forget that precept and be deceived. And he who keeps it in memory and is not deceived is to be chosen; the contrary is to be rejected, is he not? Certainly. Therefore, both labors and pains and contests are to be opposed to them, and these same things observed in them. Skillfully. Must we not fight according to that third species, of tricks? And just as those who desire to see whether colts are fearful or not lead them into noise and tumult, so the younger must be pushed into certain terrible things, and likewise into delights, and in these much more than gold is examined by fire; so that we may find if anyone exists among them who is not easily ensnared, and is composed in all things, a very good guardian of himself and a preserver of that music which he learned, and shows himself harmonious and consonant in all these things. Such a man would be most useful both to himself and his country. And he who has been tested always in childhood, youth, and mature age, and exists uncorrupted, is to be established as the guardian and prince of the city. Honors are to be given to him both living and dead, receiving the greatest gifts of tombs and other monuments. But he who is not such is to be rejected. Such, therefore, O **Glauco**, the selection and institution of princes and guardians seems to me it ought to be, to speak summarily rather than accurately. It seems so to me as well. Therefore, most truly will these be called guardians in every part, both of external enemies and internal friends, so that those should not wish, and these should not be able, to plot anything evil. But the youths whom we were calling guardians a little before will rightly be called auxiliaries and defenders of the institutions of the princes themselves. Thus I also think. What therefore will be the mode for those lies which are sometimes fitting, just as we were saying before: to persuade first the princes by lying about something noble? If not them, at least the remaining citizens? What kind of thing is this you say? Nothing good indeed, but something **Phoenician**: which formerly was done among many, as the poets have said and persuaded, but in our times not at all; nor do I know if it will ever be persuaded; it is certainly difficult. How sluggishly, he said, you seem to approach speaking. I will seem to you, after I have spoken, not without reason sluggish. Speak, and do not fear. Behold, I say it now, though I do not know with what audacity and with what words relying I shall speak; and I will first attempt to persuade the princes themselves and the soldiers, and then also the remaining citizens, that those things in which we nourished and educated them seemed to have all those things around them like dreams. But they were then in truth under the earth, formed and nourished within, they themselves and their arms and all their furniture. But after they were entirely perfected, the earth like a mother brought them forth. And now indeed, as to a mother and nurse, they ought to consult for and succor this region in which they are, if anyone invades it, and think of the other citizens as of brothers born from the earth. Not without reason, he said, were you ashamed before to tell this lie. Quite rightly I said, but hear now the rest of the fable. You are all in the city as brothers (for so we shall say to them fabled), but when God formed you, whoever of you were born fit to command...

[Page 388]
...He mixed gold in their generation, because of which they are most honored. But for those who are to help, silver. Finally, iron and bronze for the farmers and other craftsmen. Therefore, as all of the same kind, you generate for the most part those similar to yourselves. But it happens sometimes that from a golden one is born a silver one, and from a silver one likewise a golden one, and the rest so in turn. Wherefore God commands the princes themselves first and foremost that they take no greater care and guard of anything than of their children, to discern what (of these four) is mixed in their souls: and if anyone is born among them with bronze or iron, they should in no way have mercy, but giving the honor suitable to that nature, they should transfer him to the craftsmen or farmers. [Margin: Aristotle notes this place in Pol. Book 2, Ch. 2.] And again if from those is born anyone golden or silver, honoring them they should extol them, the former to the guardians, the latter to the auxiliaries: as if it were an oracle that the republic will then perish when either a bronze or an iron guardian governs it. Do you have a way for them to believe this fable? In no way, he said, for these men; but in what way their sons and the rest of posterity might, I have a way. And this would be good for having greater care for themselves and the city. I understand almost what you say. And this indeed will tend thither where the oracle leads. But let us bring forth these earth-born men, armed, with the princes leading. And indeed let them explore where in the city it is best to place a camp, from where they might most restrain those who are within if anyone refuses to obey the laws themselves; and repel those who are without if an enemy like a wolf invades the sheepfold. When they have placed the camp and sacrificed to whom they ought, let them build tents. So? Or otherwise? So certainly. But of such a kind as suffice against winters and heat? Why not? For you seem to me to mean habitations. I say so, but military ones, not opulent ones. How do you assert this differs from that? I will indeed try to declare it. For it would be the most grave of all and most shameful for shepherds if they so nourished dogs to be guardians of the flock that from intemperance, or from hunger, or from some other bad habit, the dogs themselves should attempt to hurt the cattle, and instead of dogs become like wolves. Grave, he said. Entirely, therefore, we must take care lest they do anything such against the citizens, who are employed as defenders, since they are more powerful than they, lest instead of benevolent allies they show themselves like savage masters. We must surely take care. Would not the greatest caution be applied if they were truly nobly educated? But they were indeed already, he said. This, O friend **Glauco**, it is not fitting to assert; but what we were saying just now is surely fitting: that they ought to attain the right discipline, if there is any, if they are to attain what is greatest for exercising mildness both toward themselves and those they guard. And rightly indeed. Toward this and the remaining furniture it should be so applied that it should not prohibit them from being the best men, nor impel them to hurt the other citizens. And truly indeed. Inspect therefore whether it is necessary for them to live and dwell in such a way, if they are to be such. First, indeed, let no one possess anything of his own, except insofar as the greatest necessity compels. Then let them have neither a house nor a storeroom to which access is not open to all. But those things which pertain to food, let there be as much among them as temperate and brave military athletes need: let them receive as much reward as is established from the other citizens for the sake of their guard, so that from annual expenses nothing is lacking nor anything remains. Bringing themselves together to meals, just as in camps, let them eat a common banquet. And it must be said to them that they have gold, nor do they need human gold, nor is it holy to pollute that possession with the admixture of mortal gold. Namely, from the money of the common people many impious things have come; but the gold that is in them is entirely uncorrupted. Indeed, for them alone of all who are in the city, it is a crime to touch gold or silver, or to receive it under their roof, or to carry it about, or to drink from that material. In this way, therefore, they would prepare safety for themselves and the city. But if ever they possess a house or field or money privately for themselves, they will be household managers and farmers instead of guardians, and in place of those who help the citizens, they will become hostile masters: and they themselves being hated, and hating others, and preparing plots in turn and suffering them, will spend their whole life. Where they will fear the citizens much more than external enemies, and they and the rest of the city will then come very close to ruin. For the sake of all these things, therefore, I say the guardians themselves ought to be so instructed concerning the house and all other things. This is the law to be passed, is it not? Let it be so, said **Glaucon**.

---

### DIALOGUE FOUR ON JUSTICE.
#### ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.

In the fourth book is delivered the mode of possession and of the city, so that the citizens are neither too rich nor too poor. For he thinks that from both excessive abundance and lack, sedition arises and the city is divided. He judges, moreover, that that city is not one, but many, in which some are poor and others rich: and as usually happens, the rich despise the poor, while the latter are affected by envy and hatred toward the former. Whence he gradually descends to his mystery, that all things should be common, lest some have less and others more, and thence envy, conspiracies, thefts, and hence luxury, pride, and sloth be born. Add that the possession of things, whether exceeding or deficient, is an obstacle not only to morals and concord, but also to genius and the arts. He teaches that a city is preserved not by riches but by virtue, and performs great things. Likewise, any part of the city is not to be so disposed that it seems to be as well as possible in itself, but that it confers to all and benefits the common tone of the city's good. Otherwise neither the city itself nor any parts can stand. He adds, moreover, the mode of increasing the city, namely insofar as the city remains one. But as soon as the unity seems able to be lost, it is not to be increased further. He commands therefore that the city be neither small nor vast, but moderate, equal, and concordant, by which its unity is preserved. But since he who was negligent in sowing hopes for honey in the troughs, he therefore judges that all study should be applied around childhood and youth, as if around the sowing of an urban harvest; so that a diligent account even of single words, smells, and gestures should be held around boys and youths. Otherwise if this age is neglected, one will labor in vain around daily laws, no differently than if someone tried to cure with drugs daily him who wishes to keep no mode of temperance in diet. Among these consider that games are gradually converted into studies and morals; he inspects that for a man both robust by nature and prudent and temperate in diet, almost no medicines are ever needed: so for a city both best constituted from the beginning and persevering in that form, neither many laws from the beginning nor daily constitutions thereafter are needed. But bad republics are occupied in daily care through new laws, but never well. Wherefore in this republic as the best, **Plato** applied no study to laws, hoping that prudent and good men are living laws. But what of sacred laws? Certainly he thought much less should be labored in these. For no one understands in what way God is to be worshipped unless he first understands God. But the divine sun, unless by the divine...

[Page 389]
...sun itself showing itself, we cannot see. He judges, therefore, that the laws of religion are to be sought from **Apollo**, that is, divine light: sought, I say, not by the tongue but by a purged and serene mind. I pass over what he touches here regarding the history of oracles. For these are very well known. But allegorically he signifies that **Apollo**, that is, divine light, sits (that is, is firmly present) in the middle of the earth (that is, everywhere in the inner recesses of all things). To rest in the navel—that is, in the mind segregated from the senses, and reflected into itself in the likeness of a spherical figure and motion. Furthermore, that **Apollo** is the ancestral one (*patrius*) to all, that is, present and familiar; and a proper father indeed to those being born, and finally the fatherland to those returning.

The republic having been constituted, he thereafter recognizes four virtues in it. **Prudence** in the princes, that is, the science of rightly guarding and consulting. **Fortitude** in the soldiers, that is, a firm opinion against both allurements and threats against dangers for the country, as far as the laws and magistrates command. **Temperance** in the princes together with the soldiers and craftsmen—that is, a certain consensus by which all freely agree that some should command and others obey: and among those who obey, some in war and others in craftsmanship; nor should such consensus be hindered by any pleasures; rather, the desires of the inferiors should obey the command and counsel of the superiors. **Justice** also in all, through which each one performs his own work and duty—that is, that to which he is most fit by nature and study—both publicly and privately for the sake of common benefit, nor does anyone claim what belongs to another.

But that he called temperance the **Diapason** harmony, understand: the **Diapason** resonance resulting from the double proportion of tension, velocity, and vehemence to that which is twice as relaxed, slower, and gentler. From which double proportion indeed arises the excess of the sharp (that is, the eighth) voice to the heavy, and not by a little. For the first double proportion is between two and one. In which proportion indeed the binary number, while it seems to surpass, recreates the one and doubles the one. The binary thereafter while it is moved and revolved into itself produces the solid number eight. For twice two twice makes eight. But it is called **Diapason**, that is, "through all things," for such a resonance both contains all within itself and is replicated in all. Not without reason **Plato** says temperance, like a **Diapason**, is extended through the highest, lowest, and middle citizens. For in the octave there is a heavy voice and a most sharp one, and there are middle ones.

But to return to justice, just as in the diapason resonance the eighth voice so harmonizes with the heavy that what is a double voice appears to be one: so in a well-composed city the gravity of temperance so aptly agrees with the strength of justice that these two virtues are scarcely discerned from one another. And see how opportunely from the diapason resonance of the eighth voice **Socrates** betakes himself to justice, designated by the **Pythagoreans** by the number eight. For while justice is an entirely equal distribution according to each one's merits, and the solid foundation of the city, it is justly described by the octenary number. For this number is both the first of solids, and the first of all is so resolved into even-even numbers, that is into twice four, that nevertheless the division itself is resolved into equally even-even numbers, that is, twice two. And again by what equality they are resolved, by the same it is woven together. For twice two twice constitutes eight, the image of just equality. Wherefore **Orpheus**, wishing everywhere to attest to divine justice, swore by eight deities: fire, water, earth, heaven, moon, sun, the planet, and night. In the **Egyptian** column also placed as a sign of justice, eight deities were noted in writing, as **Eusider** [likely a corruption or specific reference] testifies: **Saturn**, **Rhea**, **Osiris**, spirit, heaven, earth, night, day. Finally, all antiquity thought that by the order of celestial justice it was digested into eight spheres.

**Socrates**, after these things, considers justice to be the sudden destruction of the city when individuals usurping what belongs to others disturb and confound all things. But justice is the order and safety of the city. Accordingly, from this more manifest justice of the city, he passes to the more occult one in the soul as if latent. And he divides the powers of the soul into three: reason in the place of the prince, and the power of anger (*ira*) in place of the soldiers, and the nature of desiring (*concupiscendi*) similar to the craftsman. And he proves that there is one soul in us, whose three powers these are, not distinct by place within themselves, but by property. Which indeed both refutes certain **Peripatetic** barkers and can be made manifest to any diligent reader. Here indeed he brings a distinction, that it may be clear how the soul and the city, and the justice of the one and the other, are very similar. He says therefore: since the soul cannot through its same power do opposite things at once regarding the same thing, it is necessary to have at least those three powers. Since at the same time through lust it is snatched toward pleasure, and through reason in the meantime is called back. Likewise through lust it is retracted from battle, through wrath provoked to fight. From which it is clear that reason is different from lust, and that the vigor of anger differs also from it. It is also clear that this [anger] differs from reason, both in children...

[Dialogue translation begins:]
...HERE **Adimantus** responding, What, O **Socrates**, will you say, he said, if someone teaches you that you do not make these men very blessed, when nevertheless they are those whose city it truly is, yet they receive nothing from the goods of the city, like others, who possess both fields and magnificent houses and furniture suitable for such houses, and perform private sacrifices to the gods, receive guests, which things you were just saying, having attained gold and silver, and whatever are thought to confer to happiness: but these sit in the city like certain auxiliaries hired for pay, doing nothing else than guarding? Certainly, I said, as those who receive food only besides, nor a reward beyond food, like others. Wherefore neither if they wish to set out privately elsewhere will it be permitted to them, nor to bestow anything on [prostitutes/courtesans], or to spend money on any other things after the manner of those who are thought blessed. Which things you and many other such things worthy of reproach omit.

But, said **Adimantus**, let those things also be included in the accusation. What then? do you say we must respond? Surely. Entering, I said, that same way, we shall find, as I believe, what things are to be said. We shall say, furthermore, that it would be no wonder if these were thus most happy. However, we did not constitute the city looking to this, that one certain class among us should be happy in a greater way, but that the entire city should be as happy as possible. For we hope to find justice most in such a city: and on the contrary, in that which was worst instituted, injustice. Which having been inspected, we thought we would easily judge what we have long sought. Now surely, as we think, we fashion it blessed, not so that a few indeed in it are blessed, but that the whole city is. Thereafter we shall contemplate the contrary: just as if someone, as we were painting the figure of a man, should reproach us because we do not apply the most beautiful colors to the most beautiful parts of the animal: for the eyes, the most beautiful member, were painted not with purple but with black color: we might seem to respond decently, O wonderful man, it is not fitting for us to paint eyes so beautiful that they do not even...

[Page 390]
...seem to be eyes, nor the other members: but consider if, attributing to each its own decorum, we render the whole beautiful. So do not now compel us to affect the guardians with that happiness which would make them anything rather than guardians. For we could also exhort the farmers to cultivate the earth only for the sake of the soul, adorned with the most precious clothing and gold; and the potters that, reclining at the right and drinking at the hearth and celebrating a banquet, having dismissed the wheel, they should exercise pottery as much as they please; and make all others blessed in this way, by which the universal city would be happy. But do not so advise us. Furthermore, if we obey you, neither will the farmer be a farmer, nor the potter a potter, nor will any other have the form of those from whom a city is made. But the reason of the others is lighter. For shoemakers made worse and depraved, and simulating that which they are not, bring nothing grave to the city. But if the guardians of the laws and the city are not so, but only appear so, do you see how they destroy the whole city at once, since they alone have the opportunity of constituting it well and rendering it blessed? Wherefore if we seek true guardians of the city, we least of all ought to choose those who would harm the city. But he who says that and makes the farmers happy not as in a city but as if reclining in some festive celebrity, says something other than a city. We must see, therefore, whether looking to this we constitute guardians, that they should abound as much as possible in happiness: or rather we should have regard for the whole city, that it should be happy as a whole: and it should be fitting to compel and persuade these auxiliaries and guardians to do those things by which each should be the best craftsman of his own work, and all others similarly. And thus, the city having been increased and rightly instituted as a whole, to allow individuals to participate in blessedness insofar as each one's nature is capable.

Rightly, he said, you seem to me to speak. And what is next to this, I said, will I seem to you to speak rightly? What most of all? Contemplate whether these things also so corrupt the other craftsmen that they are bad. Which things? Riches, namely, and poverty. By what reason? Thus: does a potter made rich seem to you even then to have care for his art? Not at all. He will certainly be rendered more lazy and negligent. Very much so. Wherefore he also becomes a worse potter. That too. But again, if because of want he lacks instruments and the rest which the art needs, he will both make the works themselves worse, and will teach his sons and whoever else, rendering them worse craftsmen. Why not? From both, therefore, both opulence and poverty, both the works of the arts become worse and the craftsmen themselves become worse. So it appears. Other things therefore we shall find for our guardians to observe, lest they creep into the city unnoticed. Which things? Opulence, I say, and want. For the former produces luxury, sloth, and the study of new things. But the latter produces illiberalism and malice along with the innovation of things. It is entirely so.

Nevertheless, O **Socrates**, notice I pray, in what way this city of ours, since it lacks money, will be able to wage war, especially if ever it is compelled to take up arms against a large and opulent city. It is certain, I said, that against one it is difficult, but against two such, certainly easier. In what way, he said, do you say that? First, if a fight is to be joined, will not these, exercised in warlike things, fight against the rich? I confess that indeed. What then, **Adimantus**? Does not one pugilist best instructed for this seem to you likely to fight easily against two non-pugilists, especially rich and fat ones? Perhaps not at the same time. Or perhaps not even if it were permitted to avoid the blows of him who first invades by dodging, then hitting him with a sudden turn? Why, if he does that often in the sun and heat, he will subdue many such men by virtue. Indeed, no wonder. Do you not think the rich have attained more use and notice of the pugilist's art than of the warlike one? Indeed. Therefore our athletes will easily, as is consistent, contend with double and triple of them. I will admit that too. For you seem to speak rightly. What if, a legation being sent into another city, they should say the truth: that we indeed do not use gold and silver, nor is it lawful for us as for you. Wherefore you who have contracted a society of war with us, have the things which others possess: do you think any, hearing these things, would prefer to fight against hard and lean dogs rather than together with such dogs against fat and soft sheep? Not at all, it seems to me. But if in one city the money of the others is accumulated, take care lest it bring danger to the less moneyed one. You are blessed, since you think it is decent to call another city such as that which we ourselves have constituted. Why does it prohibit? Other cities require a more ample appellation. For each of those is many cities, not a city, as is usually said by those who joke. For at least two they are to be. One of the poor, the other of the rich. And again in each of those very many: at which, if you aim as one, you will entirely miss: but if as many, giving the things of others to others, both money and powers, you will always use many allies and auxiliaries, but few enemies. And insofar as the city is thus ordered as just now, it will exist as the greatest; and that not by opinion, but truly greatest, even if it consists of only a thousand defenders. For you will not easily find one city so great either among **Greeks** or among **Barbarians**: yet many you will find that seem much greater than this kind of city. Or do you think otherwise? Not otherwise, by **Jove**. Will not this, therefore, be the most beautiful limit for our princes for increasing the city: to which, when it has become so great, it is fitting to allot such a region, but to dismiss the rest? What limit? I think indeed, as long as the increased city remains one, it is to be increased to that point, not beyond. Nobly. This precept besides we shall command the guardians to keep: that by every reason they provide that it should not seem to be either a small city or a great one, but one and sufficient. But perhaps we shall command them something light. And that lighter thing besides, of which we made mention in the preceding things, when we were saying it is necessary if any guardian is born lazy, to send him to others; if from others an honest one, to the guardians themselves. In which we plainly wished to show that it also becomes each of the other citizens to be led to that one work only for which he is fit by nature, so that each following the study of his own nature, should exist not many, but one, and thus the whole city should become one, not many. This, he said, is even less than that. Not at all, O good man **Adimantus**, we do not command them these many and great things, as someone might think, but all light and small things, if they keep one "great thing" as is said, or rather for a great thing, a sufficient one. What is that? Education, I say, and erudition. For if well educated, they turn out moderate men, they will easily discern all those things, both others however many we omit in the present, and...

[Page 391]
...the unions of women and husbands, and the procreations of children, that namely it is necessary that all these things of friends be as common as possible according to the proverb. Most rightly indeed would it thus be. For the republic if it once begins well, proceeds like a circle always increasing. Since education and good erudition being kept, also makes good geniuses. Again, good geniuses having attained such education turn out even better than before, both for other things and for generating children, just as in other animals. That is consistent indeed. Finally, that I may speak summarily, this is to be observed diligently by the tutors of the city, lest it be corrupted secretly without them knowing. Rather let them care for this in the first place, lest anything be innovated contrary to the order given by us regarding gymnastics and music, but that everyone follow that as much as possible. And when someone has said that poetic thing, namely that "men are greatly delighted by new songs," these guardians ought to fear lest many times one think the poet says not new songs, but new modes of singing, and praise them. But it is necessary neither to praise anything such nor to receive it. We must surely take care not to induce a new species of music, as if a shipwreck in the whole. For nowhere are the modes of music changed without the greatest change of civil laws, as **Damon** says, with whom I also agree. Know that I also, O **Socrates**, agree. A certain citadel, therefore, as it seems, for the sake of guarding, must be built by these guardians around music. Namely, a sin of this kind creeps in secretly and easily. Certainly in the likeness of a certain joke, and so that it seems to hurt nothing. For it does nothing else (he said) than that having affected the familiar, it gradually creeps into morals and studies: from these then it emerges more into commerce: finally from commerce it breaks out into laws and republics, O **Socrates**, with great petulance and lasciviousness, until finally privately and publicly it overturns all things. The matter stands so, I said. Surely, he said, as it seems to me indeed. Therefore as we said from the beginning, immediately from the first years boys must be accustomed to honest jokes. For if they should become accustomed to less decent jokes, they will never be able to turn out legitimate and honest men. Why not? When therefore boys beginning well joke and play, they imbibe a legitimate manner through music; music tends entirely in the contrary to these and superior things, and increases, erecting whatever lay before in the city. You speak true. Those things therefore which seem to be small institutions of the city, as I said, these men will find, all of which the superiors were perturbing. What kind? These namely: in what way the younger ought to be silent before the elders, give place to them and rise up, and honor parents: what mode of hair is to be kept by each, what clothes or shoes are to be used, and entirely what ornament of the body is fitting, and the rest of that kind. Do you not think so? Indeed. But to prescribe these by laws, I think it is inept. For neither does it happen anywhere, nor would these things consist commanded by words and letters. Why not? It appears therefore, O **Adimantus**, of what kind the beginning of each one's boyish education was, such will be those things also which follow. Does not like always provoke like? Why not? And finally, I think, it must be said to end in one certain highest and valid thing, whether good or bad. What prohibits? By this reason I would never contend to establish these by laws. And rightly indeed. Tell by the gods, I said, whether the business itself of the market and mutual commerce and pacts in mechanical arts, likewise insults and blows, the lots of lawsuits, the constitutions of judges, and whatever are either to be imposed or exacted as taxes around the forum or ports, or entirely all forensic laws, or urban ones, or of ports and the rest of that genus—whether these, I say, or any of them we shall attempt to constitute by laws? It in no way becomes to command good and noble men. For very many of these, what and in what way they are to be established, they themselves will easily find. Namely, O friend, if God grants them the safety of those laws which we placed above. If not, they will so pass their life that they establish many such things by laws, and always correct and innovate, thinking thus they will attain what is best. You say these will live exactly like those who, when they are sick, because of intemperance are unwilling to change their unhealthy diet. So entirely. And indeed in a certain ridiculous way these seem to persevere in diseases, and by their cures attain nothing else than that they make more various and more vehement diseases, and always confound, if anyone should advise drugs to be used, that they will be well. Entirely such are the diseases of those so laboring. What then? is not this most pleasing in them: that they think him the most hostile of all who warns truly, and says that neither drugs, nor cauterizations, nor incisions, nor incantations, nor those things which are applied from without, or anything of that kind will profit, until one ceases to indulge in drunkenness, gluttony, lust, and sloth? That is not very pleasing. For to be indignant against him who advises useful things has no grace. Therefore a man of this kind, as you seem, you in no way approve. Not at all, by **Jove**. Nor also if the whole city does that which we were just saying, will you praise it. Does it not seem to you that cities do the same as those men—whatever cities, being badly instituted, interdict the citizens from moving the whole state of the republic itself, otherwise whoever innovate things should be condemned to death? On the contrary, whoever thus honors the one administering the Republic, and gratifies him, and creeps in, and assents to their will, and carries out their manner, this one finally will be a good man, he wise in the greatest things, he will be affected with honor by them. They seem to me to do exactly the same, nor do I praise them in any way. But what? do you not wonder at their fortitude and more prone affection, who contend to cure these cities? I wonder indeed, those excepted who are deceived by them and think they are truly civil because they are praised by the common people. What do you say? Do you not forgive those? Do you think he who is ignorant of measuring, if ever many others of such a size proclaim him to be four cubits, can escape thinking the same of himself? Not that indeed. Do not therefore be angry. For these are indeed most ridiculous of all, who bring laws in those things we said, and always emend, trusting they will find some end around those things which are committed iniquitously in commerce, and around those which I said a little before, ignorant that they are truly cutting a hydra. Certainly they do nothing else. Indeed I believe this species of institutions around laws and republics the true founder of laws ought to treat neither in a badly disposed nor in a well-constituted city: in the former indeed, because they are useless, such institutions, nor do they profit anything; in the latter, because some each will find, some by its own nature proceeds from superior studies. What besides remains for us concerning the constitution of laws? To us indeed nothing. But to the **Delphic Apollo** the greatest, noblest, first institutions. What are those? The constitutions of temples and sacrifices, and other cults of gods and demons and heroes, tombs besides and funerals of the defunct, and whatever...

[Page 392]
...ministrations are to be undergone for pleasing them. Such things indeed we do not know, and in ordering the city we will believe no other, if we are wise, and we will use no other interpreter than the ancestral (God). For this God in things of this kind is to all men the ancestral interpreter, sitting in the middle of the earth upon the navel, he explains. You speak skillfully, and so it must be done.

Therefore let the city now be constituted for you, O son of **Aristo**. Thereafter also, a great light being brought from elsewhere, through it also you yourself look around, and call your brother, and **Polemarchus**, and others besides, that we may try if by any way we can see where justice and injury are: or how they differ among themselves, and which of these he ought to attain who is to live blessedly, whether he lies hidden or does not lie hidden from all gods and men. You are doing nothing, said **Glauco**. For you promised to investigate, as if it were to be impious if you did not bring help to justice according to your powers. You admonish truly, I said, and so certainly it must be done. However, you also must be present with me. So we shall do, he said.

I hope therefore in this way to find it. Namely, I think the city, if it has been rightly constituted by us, exists as absolutely good. It is necessary. It is certain surely that it is wise, brave, and temperate, and just. It is certain. Whatever of these is found in the city, the remainder will be that not yet found. Why not? he said: If from some other four things, we were seeking one certain thing in some subject, and that first was open, enough was done for us: but if we found the three remaining first, from this very thing we would know the sought one, because it would be certain that it was nothing else than what remained. You speak rightly. Must we not seek concerning these also in the same way since they are four? Plainly. And from all these, first wisdom seems to shine forth in the city, or something wonderful around it appears. What? Truly wise the city which we have described seems to me to be. For it is well-advised (*consulta*). Is it not? It is surely. For this very faculty of consulting is a certain science. For not by ignorance but by science rather do men advise well. That is perspicuous indeed.

But many and varied sciences are in the city. They are. Is the city to be called wise and well-advised because of the science of carpenters? In no way because of that, but "carpenter-like." Therefore the city is not to be called wise from the fact that it advises well in what way wooden works may be performed as well as possible. Not surely. Is it perhaps because of the science which fashions bronze works? or another such? Certainly because of none of this kind. Nor also because of the science of producing fruits from the earth, but the skill of agriculture. So I think. What then? Is there any science in the city just now founded by us, among any citizens, by which one deliberates not about some private thing in the city, but about the whole city rather, in what way both it and itself should bear itself as well as possible toward other cities? There is indeed. Which is this, and in whom? The very diligence of guarding, and in these princes whom just now we were calling perfect guardians. Because of this science, by what name do you call the city? Perspicacious in consulting and truly wise. Do you think more blacksmiths in the city or more of these true guardians? Surely many more blacksmiths. And will not these be the fewest of all other craftsmen, whoever are said to be some? The fewest indeed. Therefore from a certain smallest nation and part of itself, and from the science which is in the presiding and prince part, the whole city instituted according to nature will be wise: and that, as it seems, a nature the fewest and rarest genus, to whom it is fitting to be a participant of this science, which alone of all others it is fitting to call wisdom. You tell most true things. This one therefore of the four, I know not by what reason we have found both what it is and in what part of the city it is located. To me indeed it seems sufficiently said.

But truly it is not difficult to find what fortitude is, or in what part of the city it is located, because of which the city is called brave. In what way? Who, looking to anything else, names a city either timid or brave, than to that part which fights and militates for it? Surely none. Nor indeed do others in it existing either timid or brave have authority by which they render it either timid or brave. Not surely. Therefore the city will be brave from its part, because in it it has such a force which keeps a rated opinion in all things, that those things only are to be feared, and such, which and what kind the legislator pronounced in the institution. Do you not call this fortitude? I did not sufficiently perceive what you said; say it again. A certain conservation I say fortitude is. What conservation? Of the opinion namely conceived through education by law, by which it is judged what are terrible things, and of what kind. But I said that conservation was in all things, that is, so that it should be kept rated always and everywhere, whether one be affected by pains or pleasures, or desires, or fears, nor in any way should anyone be moved away from it because of these. To what I think it is similar, if you wish, I will open to you. I desire indeed. Do you not know that fullers, as often as they wish to dye wools with purple color, first indeed from so many colors choose white, then prepare it with no mediocre work so that they may most receive the flower, and so finally they dye? What is thus dyed remains indelible, nor can that flower of color be diluted by water alone, nor abolished even with these purgations added which pertain to wiping away. But what things are not so prepared, do you know what kind they turn out, whether one dyes with other colors or with these, when one has cultivated it less before? Surely they are deformed, and their colors are easily diluted. Think us to have studied to do something such according to our powers when we were choosing the soldiers themselves, and were educating them both in music and gymnastics: and think we thought out nothing else than that they should imbibe the laws like a certain color being most optimally persuaded: so that their opinion about terrible things and about all other things should persevere immovable, because they were born of the best nature and nourished by decent education, nor should those purgations most vehement for diluting be able to delete their dye: namely pleasure the bitterness of all nitre, and sharper than lime for expurging, likewise pain, fear, and desire more powerful for wiping away than any other purgation. This force indeed everywhere of the right and legitimate opinion the preserver around terrible things and their contraries, I call fortitude indeed and assert it, unless you perhaps say something else. But I say nothing else. For you seem not at all to judge a right opinion about those same things conceived without discipline, namely beastly and servile, to be legitimate, but to call it something other than fortitude. You speak most true things, I said. I admit therefore this to be fortitude. Admit besides and "civil" [fortitude], and so you will receive it rightly. Thereafter about this, if you wish, we will treat more diligently elsewhere. But in the present we were seeking not that, but justice. For the investigation of which, enough has been said of this, I believe.

[Page 393]
You speak nobly. Two things remain besides to be considered in the city: temperance namely, and for the sake of which we investigate all things, justice. Entirely. Can we now by any means find justice itself, lest we labor again in investigating temperance? Indeed I do not know, nor would I wish justice to become known to us before we have considered temperance. Wherefore if you wish to do a favor to me, investigate this before that. I wish indeed, unless I am unjust. Inquire now. Behold I inquire, and as one can see from here, it is more similar to resonance and harmony than the superior things. In what way? Temperance is a certain ornament, and an abstinence from certain pleasures and desires, as they say. And they affirm that to be superior to oneself and some other similar things, I know not in what way, are as if certain footsteps of temperance itself. Is it not? Most of all. Does not that which is named "more powerful than oneself" appear in a ridiculous way? For whoever is more powerful than himself will also be weaker than himself: and again he who is weaker and more powerful. For the same person is named in all these. Why not? But this discourse seems to me to mean this: that in the soul of a man there are certain two things. One indeed better, the other truly worse. And when that which is better by nature dominates the worse, then someone is said to be more powerful than himself, and is praised by this discourse. But as often as because of improper education or some habit, that which is better (since it is less itself) is overcome by the multitude of the worse, this is reproached with a certain opprobrium and said to be weaker than itself: and he who is thus affected is called intemperate. So it appears. Contemplate this city recently founded by us, and you will find the one or the other of these to be in it. For you will confess it to be called more powerful than itself by right. For if the better in it commands the worse, it is to be called temperate, and better than itself. I contemplate indeed, and you speak true things. Indeed, anyone will be able to find most numerous and varied desires, pleasures, and pains in all these, in women and servants, and in those who are said to be free among the plebeian and abject men. Entirely indeed. But the simple and moderate ones which are led with the mind and right opinion, by the very ratiocination, you will find surely in few, and these indeed born best and best educated. These things are true. Do you not see these in this city, and here the desires of the common people and vile persons overcome by the desires and prudence of the few and modest men? I discern indeed. If any city therefore is more powerful than desires and pleasures, and likewise than itself, this is most to be called such. Entirely. Therefore will you not say temperance is in it, as often as they have held so? in the princes? or in the subjects? In both in a certain way. Do you see therefore how aptly we prophesied a little before, that temperance is similar to a certain harmony? Why so? Because not in the way that wisdom and fortitude existing in certain parts, the former makes the city wise, the latter brave, so temperance also: but in the likeness of the harmony which is called diapason, it is diffused through the whole city, making it so that in the same the weaker men and stronger and middle ones, by prudence, power, multitude, money likewise, or any other such thing should harmonize. Wherefore we could most rightly call this temperance concord, the consensus namely of the worse and better according to nature, which teaches who it is fitting to dominate either in the city or in each one. I assent indeed. Since it is so, three things are now found by us in the city, as appears from these. But the remaining species, because of which besides the city would be a participant of virtue, what will it be? It is certain this is justice.

It is plainly certain. Is it not now necessary for us, O **Glauco**, as hunters to surround this thicket, looking around lest justice escape from any part and, vanishing from eyes, hide itself? For it is clear it is here. Fix therefore your intuition everywhere, and strive if in any way you can see it before me, and show it to me. I wish I could. But rather use me as such a companion who can look forward to the demonstrated things. Follow therefore, having first prayed to God with me. I will do what you advise. Lead only. This place, I said, seems to be arduous and shadowy, certainly dark and inscrutable. Nevertheless we must proceed. We must plainly proceed. Here I, looking at **Glaucon**, "Hui hui," I said, "my **Glauco**, we seem to have found certain footsteps of that which we seek, it appears that it will not escape us for long." A surely auspicious message. Indeed, I said, we are soft and dull. What is that? Long ago from the very beginning, blessed man, what we seek has been rolling before our feet, nor did we inspect it, but are equally to be laughed at as those who often seek what they have in their hands. We also were seeking far away what was near us, or perhaps it lay hidden from us. In what way do you say that? Thus. Namely we seem to me saying this long ago and hearing it, not at all to have noticed that we were saying it in some way. A surely long proem for one desiring to hear. Attend if I say anything. For what we placed everywhere to be done at the beginning, when we founded the city, that is, as I believe, or a certain species of it, justice. For we said many times, if you remember, that each one ought to exercise one certain thing of those which benefit the city, for which his nature was most fit. We said without doubt. Indeed, that to do one's own things, and not to be curiously occupied in foreign ones, is justice, we both heard from many others and often said ourselves. We said plainly. This surely which appears, friend, since it is so, in some way is justice, to do namely one's own things. Do you know whence I conjecture that? Not at all, but tell me. It seems to me that what remains to us in the city, besides those things which we considered—temperance, fortitude, prudence—is this which provided force to all those so that they should be born, and being born should persevere, as long as it is present. But we said justice would be what remained if three were found by us. That is necessary indeed. Nevertheless if it is to be judged which of these most of all when it is in, makes the city good, it will be difficult to judge whether it is the conservation of opinion in the soldiers, judging according to law what are to be thought terrible or not: or in the princes themselves prudence and guard. Or whether that rather makes it good before others when it is in boys, women, servants, free men, craftsmen, magistrates, and private persons, that namely each one being one did one thing, nor is involved in foreign business. Difficult certainly. Why not? Therefore the force itself, as it seems, by which each in the city does his own things, contends for the virtue of the city itself on equal terms with wisdom, temperance, and fortitude. Very much. Will you not therefore place justice as that which contends with those on equal terms for the virtue of the city? Entirely indeed.

[Page 394]
Consider besides also by this reason, whether it seems so to you. Will you command the princes in the city to give sentence justly? Why not? Will they judge of anything else more greedily than of this very thing, that individuals neither usurp foreign things nor be deprived of their own? Of nothing else certainly, but of that, as if it were just. Namely. And by this reason also it is asserted that the possession and action of each one's and proper work is justice. It is so.

See whether the same seems to you as to me: If a carpenter should approach the works of a tanner, or a tanner of a carpenter, or they should exchange instruments among themselves or rewards, or if the same should contend to exercise both, and all such were changed among themselves, do you think this change would affect the city with some great loss? Not certainly, he said. But as often as some craftsman or other by nature a seeker of gain, elated by riches, or by multitude and abundance, or another such by some other thing, attempts to pass into the order of a military man, or a soldier since he is unworthy, to ascend to the dignity of a counselor, nurse, and guardian, and they exchange instruments and rewards in turn, or the same someone attempts to perform all these at once, then I think the change and the handling of such things seems to you the ruin of the whole city. And most greatly indeed. When therefore there are three genera in the city, the handling of many things and the change of the one into the other is the extreme calamity of the city, and will most rightly be called destruction. It is so. But the highest destruction of your city, will you not say it is injustice? Why not? This therefore is injustice. Again we say so: the proper action of the genre of gain-seekers, auxiliaries, and guardians, each one performing his own work in the city, contrary to that superior consulting, will both be justice and render the city just. It seems to stand not otherwise than so.

We ought not yet to assert that entirely. But if in the soul of each man also the same species is asserted to be justice as we consider it, then finally we shall agree. For what else shall we say? otherwise then we shall think out something else. But now let us impose an end to this discussion, according to which we thought that if of many having justice in some larger thing we first contemplated it, then more easily in one man we would inspect what kind of thing this is. And it seemed to us the greater itself to be a city, and so as well as we could we founded it, knowing that in a good republic justice is in. Wherefore what appeared to us in that, let us refer to the one: and if the same consists for itself, it will be enough done for us. But if something else appears in the one, returning again to the city, we shall examine these: and perhaps considering them compared among themselves and striking them together like flints, we shall strike out justice, and when it has now clearly shone, we shall establish it among ourselves. You speak skillfully, and so it must be done. Is that which we call the same both greater and smaller, dissimilar insofar as it is called the same, or similar? Similar certainly. Therefore a just man differs in nothing from a just city as far as pertains to the species of justice, but will be similar. Similar. But a just city then seemed to be, when in it three genera of men for the nature of each did their own work. Temperate again and brave and wise, because of the affections and habits of these same genera, not because of others. These things are true. We shall judge each one thus, O friend, having the same species of this in the soul, because of the same affections, to merit the same names with the city. It is necessary entirely.

Have we fallen again, O wonderful man, into a light thought about the soul, whether it has these three species in itself or not? Not at all do we seem to me to have fallen into a light discussion. For perhaps what is said is true, O **Socrates**, that beautiful things are difficult. It appears surely. And certainly know, O **Glauco**, as my opinion goes, we shall never exactly comprehend it from such discourses as we use in the present disputation; furthermore, the way is longer which leads thither. Perhaps however according to those things which were said and considered above, it would be discussed for its dignity. Should not that seem enough? To me surely the present things will suffice. To me also very sufficient. Therefore let it not weary you, but consider. Truly it is necessary for us to confess that the same species and morals are in us as are in the city. For they did not come from elsewhere into the city. For it would be ridiculous if someone should think wrathful spiritedness was in no way brought into cities from private men, whose temperament was the same, which is also of the **Thracians**, **Scythians**, and superior nations: or the study of wisdom, not from such a private instinct as is by nature attributed to our men: or the greed of gain, not from the desire of individual men, with which the **Phoenicians** and **Egyptians** not a little are said to be affected. And most greatly indeed. This indeed is so, nor difficult to know. Not surely difficult. But that is difficult now: whether with one and the same we do each of these things, or rather we have three certain things in us, by each of which we work each: by one indeed we learn, we are angry with another, with the third we desire those pleasures which pertain to nutrition and generation, and the rest such: or with the whole soul we fulfill each of them, when we approach a stirred thing. These will not easily be discerned for the dignity of the matter. To me also the same seems. Thus however let us approach to define these, whether they are the same among themselves, or diverse. By what way? It is plainly certain that the same cannot do or suffer contrary things according to the same and toward the same at once. Wherefore if ever we find these happening in them, we shall understand they are not one and the same, but many. Be it so. Notice what I say. Say it. Can the same at once stand and be moved according to the same? In no way. Furthermore, let us confirm these more diligently, lest as we proceed some ambiguity perhaps should arise. For if someone says a man standing indeed, but moving his hands and head, the same stands at once and is moved, we shall judge it should in no way be said so, but that part of him stands, and part is moved? Is it not so? So entirely. But if that person should play more artificially and acutely, asserting that a spinning top (*turbinem*) or a hoop (*trochum*) is moved as a whole and stands at once, when fixing the center and point in the same point it is revolved: or anything else, saying it does the same when it is carried around fixed to the same hinge: we shall in no way assent, because those things are not then moved and remain according to the same part of themselves. For one has to say they have the straight and the round in them: and according to the straight indeed they stand, when they decline from no part: but according to the round, they are moved in an orb. But as often as while something is revolved, it [leans] into the straight either forward or backward, then it remains nowhere. Quite rightly. Wherefore none of these objections will perturb us, or persuade us that the same sometimes at once according to the same and toward the same, contrary things either acts or suffers. Me indeed those things will move least of all. Nevertheless, lest in all those controversies in pursuing and discussing which are false, we be compelled to insist longer, these having now been as if conceded and placed, let us proceed further, a promise being made between us that if ever they appear to be otherwise than so, whatever are effected from these should be void.
