386 Thirty-First Book. <note>In this Renaissance edition, the "Thirty-First Book" refers to the sequence of works in the complete collection, though the text itself is Plato’s Republic, Dialogue III (Book 3).</note>

They say that he <note>Referring to Asclepius, the god of medicine.</note> was the son of Apollo, and that he was bribed with gold to cure a wealthy man who was already at the point of death. For this, they say, he was struck by a lightning bolt. But based on what we said before, we do not grant them either of these points. Rather, if he was the son of a god, we shall deny that he was greedily seeking shameful profit; but if he was greedily seeking shameful profit, we shall reject the idea that he was a son of a god. These things are rightly said. But what do you say to this, O Socrates? Is it not necessary to have good doctors in the city? Those would be especially good who had dealt with the greatest number of healthy people and the greatest number of sick people. Likewise, the judges would be those who had experience with various human characters. I say they should be very good indeed. But do you understand whom I consider to be such men? Only if you tell me. I shall try. However, you were not asking about similar things in the same argument. How so? Doctors, indeed, would become most excellent if, from an early age, besides studying their art, they interacted with a great many people with diseased bodies, and if they themselves had suffered from every kind of disease and were of a weak nature. For they do not cure the body, I think, with the body. For it would be impossible for their own bodies to have ever been or to be sick. Instead, the soul cures the body. Is it not possible that a soul that was and is bad could not cure anything well? Rightly so. But the judge, my friend, governs the soul with his own soul. Is it not possible for a soul, from childhood, to have associated with bad souls, to have committed every kind of unjust deed, and finally to sharply infer the crimes of others from its own self, just as one might infer diseases from one's own body? Should he not rather have been innocent and inexperienced in bad character while he was young, if he is to be a good and honorable man who judges just things sincerely? For this reason, modest men, while they are young, appear to be foolish and easily deceived by the unjust, as they do not have within themselves the same examples of evil passions that the wicked possess. This certainly happens to them. Truly, a good judge ought not to be a young man, but an old one, who has learned late in life what sort of thing injustice is; as one who has not sensed it as his own in his soul, but has recognized it as something foreign in the souls of others over a long time, and therefore discerns what kind of evil it is, judging by knowledge rather than by his own experience. Such a man seems to be a most noble judge. And he is good, moreover, which is what you were seeking. For he who has a good soul is good. But that crafty man, suspicious of evil, who has committed much injustice and is considered shrewd and wise, appears cautious and clever when he deals with his own kind, for he looks to the examples within himself and is on his guard. But when he associates with good and older men, he appears a fool, since he is unseasonably distrustful and does not recognize a healthy and sincere character, having no example of it within himself. But since he associates more frequently with the wicked than with the wise, he often appears wiser than foolish to himself and others. You speak the truth, without a doubt. Therefore, one should not seek such a man to be a judge, as if he were good and wise, but rather the kind I described a moment ago. For depravity would never know either itself or virtue. But virtue, when added to nature by time and discipline, will understand both itself and depravity at once. Therefore, not the bad man, as I see it, but this wise man becomes the judge. It seems so to me as well. Will you not, therefore, establish such medicine as we have described, along with this kind of judicial equity in the city, which will care for those citizens who are well-disposed in both mind and body? But as for those who are not of this kind in their bodies, they shall let them die; and those who are of a bad nature and are incurable in soul, they shall put to death? This seems to be beneficial both for those who suffer such things and for the city. It is also clear that young men will take care not to fall into the use of the courts, by using that simple music from which we said temperance is born. Why not? And by these same footsteps, will not the musician who follows gymnastics, if he wishes, act so that he needs no medicine unless necessity compels it? I certainly agree. He will exercise his body in the gymnasiums, looking more toward the spiritedness <note>The "thumos" or spirited part of the soul, associated with courage and anger.</note> of his nature and arousing it, rather than toward mere strength; nor will he regulate his diet and labor for the sake of strength like other athletes. Quite right. Therefore, O Glaucon, those who set out to educate men in music and gymnastics do not do so for the reason many think—that the latter should care for the body and the former for the soul. Why not? It seems that both are practiced mostly for the sake of the soul. In what way? Do you not see how the soul is affected by those who practice gymnastics throughout their lives but do not touch music, or by those who are affected in the opposite way? Of which are you speaking? Of boorish hardness and ferocity, I say, and likewise of softness and gentleness. I know, he said, that those who use gymnastics alone become more savage than they ought to be. And those who use music alone become softer than is becoming for them. Yet that savage force, I said, belongs to the spiritedness of a quick-tempered nature; which, if nourished rightly, becomes brave; but if it grows beyond what is proper, it becomes fierce and hard, as is consistent. I agree. But what of the mild and gentle force? Does not the philosopher have this by nature? If it is relaxed too much, it becomes softer than is proper; but if well nourished, it is gentle and modest? It is as you say. We were saying that the guardians themselves must have both natures. They must indeed. And must they not harmonize and be in tune with each other? Why not? And the soul in which these things are in harmony is temperate and brave? Entirely so. But the soul in which they are dissonant is timid and boorish? Most certainly. Whoever permits music to surround his soul, occupying and soothing it, pouring harmonies through his ears as if through a funnel—those sweet, pleasant, soft, and mournful ones we mentioned above—and spends his life in songs that soften the soul, he first softens whatever was quick-tempered in him, like iron, and makes it useful from something useless and hard. But when he persists longer and is soothed more, he then liquefies the soul and dissolves it, until he has melted away all spiritedness and cut away, as it were, the nerves from the soul. From this, he makes the soul into a soft warrior. It is entirely so. And if he had a nature without strength of soul from the beginning, he accomplishes this quickly. But if he was spirited, by breaking the strength of the soul he makes it prone to anger, so that it is offended by every little thing and easily extinguished again. Thus, instead of being spirited, they become irritable and peevish, full of distress and loathing. That is exactly what happens. But if someone gives himself to gymnastics and feasts, neglecting music and philosophy, at first he gains a firm habit of body and is filled with strength and greatness of soul, becoming braver than he was. Very much so. Then, if he continues in this so that he does nothing else and does not touch music at all, surely if there was any instinct for learning in his soul, burning with desire, it becomes weak, deaf, and blind; seeing as it has tasted no doctrine, no investigation of things, nor any reason at all, nor any other music from which his senses could be awakened, grow, and be purged. Thus plainly...

<summary>Socrates explains that a good judge must be an old man who knows evil by observation rather than personal experience, and argues that a balance of gymnastics and music is necessary to prevent the soul from becoming either too savage or too soft.</summary>

Dialogue III. On the Republic. Or, On Justice. 387

...plainly. By this reasoning, I think, such a man is rendered a stranger to reason and the Muses, and he uses no persuasion of others induced by reasons; but with force and boorish cruelty, like some wild beast, he is carried toward all things, and lives in ignorance and rudeness, without harmony and grace. The matter is entirely so. For these two things, then, it appears that some god has granted two arts to men, music and gymnastics, for the spiritedness and the philosophical nature respectively—not for the soul and body, except by accident—but for the purpose of making them harmonize with each other, tightened and loosened to the proper degree. So it appears. Therefore, we would rightly call him the most perfect musician and the one composed of the greatest harmony who most beautifully mixes gymnastics with music and applies these to the soul in the most moderate way, much more than the one who tunes strings. And rightly so, O Socrates. Shall we not always need some such presiding officer in our city, Glaucon, if the republic is to be safe? We shall certainly need one most greatly. These, then, would be the modes of discipline and education. For one might rightly say that dances are of this kind, and hunts, both others and those done with the hands, and finally gymnastic and equestrian contests. For it is almost certain that these should follow those others, and they are not difficult to find. Perhaps they are not difficult. Come then, I said. What else must we distinguish? Is it not which of all these should rule, and which should obey? Why not? It is clear that the elders should rule and the younger should obey. It is clear indeed. And this is also evident, that the best among them must be chosen. That too is clear. Are not the best of the farmers those who have the greatest skill in cultivating fields? Exactly. Now then, since the best of the guardians must be chosen, should we not choose those who have the greatest skill in guarding the city? Those, plainly. They must therefore be prudent for this task, and powerful, and those who have a care for the Republic. It is so. But everyone cares most for that which he most loves. It must be so. And he loves that most which he considers to have the same interests as himself, and upon whose happiness he thinks his own happiness or unhappiness depends. That is so. Therefore, from all the guardians, those must be chosen who appear to us, upon consideration, to do with the greatest zeal throughout their whole lives those things which they lead to be for the republic; and to avoid those things which are contrary. These are certainly the most suitable. They must be observed, therefore, I think, in every age, to see whether they keep this precept, neither being deceived by any charms, nor compelled by any force, nor forgetting themselves and casting away that opinion by which they judge that only those things which are best for the republic should be done. What casting away do you mean? I will tell you: it seems to me that an opinion leaves the mind either voluntarily or involuntarily. Voluntarily, a false one in him who unlearns it. Involuntarily, every true opinion. What you say about the voluntary departure, I understand; but as for the involuntary, I desire to learn. Do you not think that men are deprived of good things against their will, but of bad things voluntarily? Is it not a bad thing to be deceived and not to know the truth, but a good thing to judge truly? Does it not seem to you that to have an opinion of things as they are is to think truly? You speak well, and it seems to me that men are deprived of a true opinion against their will. Do they not suffer this either by theft, or by deception, or by force? I do not understand that either. I seem to be speaking like a tragic poet. For I say opinions are stolen from those who change their mind, either gradually obliterated by time, or secretly withdrawn by a contrary argument. Now do you understand? I understand indeed. But force is brought upon those whom pain or torture compels to think otherwise. That I understand, and you speak rightly. And those who are led away by charms, I think, you also would say are those who abandon their former opinion, either soothed by pleasure or terrified by fear. It seems that whatever deceives us seduces us by charms. What I was saying just now, then, must be sought: who are they who constantly keep that opinion within themselves, namely that they must always do what they think is beneficial to the republic. They must be observed, therefore, from childhood, and those tasks set before them in which one might most easily forget that precept and be deceived. And he who keeps it in his memory and is not deceived should be chosen; the one who is not should be rejected. Should he not? Certainly. Therefore, labors and pains and contests must be set before them, and in these the same things must be observed. Wisely said. Must we not also contend against that third type, the charms? And just as those who wish to see whether colts are fearful or not lead them into noise and tumult, so young men must be pushed into certain terrors, and likewise into delights, examining them in these much more than gold in fire; so that we may discover if there is anyone among them who is not easily ensnared, and is composed in all things, a most excellent guardian of himself, and a preserver of the music he has learned, showing himself harmonious and in tune in all these things. Such a man would be most useful both to himself and to his country. And he who has always been proven in childhood, youth, and mature age, and exists uncorrupted, must be appointed as a guardian and prince of the city. Honors must be given to him both in life and in death, receiving the greatest gifts of tombs and other monuments. But he who is not such a man must be rejected. Such, O Glaucon, it seems to me the choice and institution of the princes and guardians ought to be, stated summarily rather than with precision. It seems so to me as well. Therefore, these will most truly be called guardians in every respect, as much against external enemies as internal friends, so that the latter do not wish to, and the former are unable to, plot any evil. But the young men whom we called guardians a little while ago will be rightly called auxiliaries and defenders of the institutions of the princes themselves. I feel the same way. What then will be the method by which we can use those lies which are sometimes becoming—as we were saying before—to persuade first the princes, or if not, at least the rest of the citizens, by lying about something noble? What sort of thing do you mean? Nothing good indeed, but something Phoenician <note>Socrates refers to the "Noble Lie" or the Myth of the Metals as a "Phoenician tale," referencing the legends of Cadmus and the dragon's teeth.</note>: which has been done before among many, as the poets have said and persuaded people of, but in our times not at all; nor do I know if it will ever happen, though it is certainly hard to persuade. How reluctantly, he said, you seem to approach the speaking of it. I will seem to you to be reluctant with good reason after I have spoken. Speak, then, and do not fear. Behold, I speak now, although I do not know with what boldness or with what words I shall speak; and I shall attempt first to persuade the princes themselves and the soldiers, and then the rest of the citizens, that those things with which we nourished and educated them were all like dreams they had about themselves. In reality, they were then underground, being formed and nourished within, they and their weapons and all their equipment. But after they were entirely finished, the earth, like a mother, brought them forth. And now indeed, they ought to consult for and help this region in which they are, as if it were their mother and nurse, if anyone should invade it, and to think of the rest of the citizens as brothers born from the earth. Not without reason, he said, were you ashamed to tell this lie before. Quite right, I said, but hear now the rest of the fable. You are all indeed in the city like brothers (for so we shall say while telling them the fable), but when the god was forming you, those of you who were born fit to rule,

he mixed gold into their generation, for which reason they are most honored. Into those who are to be auxiliaries, he mixed silver. Finally, iron and bronze for the farmers and other craftsmen. Since you are all of the same kind, you will for the most part produce offspring similar to yourselves. But it happens sometimes that from a golden parent a silver child is born, and from a silver parent a golden one, and so on for the others in turn. Therefore, the god commands the princes first and most greatly that they should take no greater care or guard over anything than over the children, to discern which of these (four) metals is mixed into their souls: and if anyone is born among them with a bit of bronze or iron, they should show no mercy at all, but assigning the honor suitable to that nature, they should transfer him to the craftsmen or farmers. <margin>Aristotle notes this place in Politics Book 2, Chapter 2.</margin> Conversely, if someone is born from those classes who is golden or silver, they should exalt them with honor, leading the former to the guardians and the latter to the auxiliaries; for there is an oracle that the republic will perish when either a bronze or an iron guardian shall govern it. Do you have a way for them to give credit to this fable? In no way for these men themselves, he said; but in what way their sons and later descendants might, I do have. But this would be good for having greater care for themselves and the city. I almost understand what you are saying. And this indeed will tend where the oracle leads. But let us bring forth these earth-born men, armed, with the princes leading them. And indeed let them explore where in the city it is best to place a camp, from which they might best restrain those who are within, if anyone refuses to obey the laws themselves; and repel those who are without, if an enemy should invade the fold like a wolf. When they have placed the camp and sacrificed to whom they ought, let them build tents. Is it so? Or otherwise? So indeed. Should they be of the kind that suffice against winters and heats? Why not? For you seem to me to be speaking of dwellings. I say so, but military ones, not opulent ones. How do you say this differs from that? I will try indeed to declare it. For it would be the most serious of all things, and most shameful for shepherds, if they were to nourish the dogs who are to be guardians of the flock in such a way that, from intemperance or hunger or some other bad habit, the dogs themselves should attempt to harm the livestock, and become like wolves instead of dogs. Serious indeed, he said. We must therefore take every precaution lest they do any such thing against the citizens who use them as defenders, since they are stronger than them, and instead of being benevolent allies, they show themselves like savage masters. We must indeed take care. Will not the greatest caution be applied if they are truly well educated? But they are already, he said. That, my friend Glaucon, is not becoming to assert; but what we were saying just now is certainly becoming, that they must obtain the right discipline, whatever it is, if they are to exercise what is most important for gentleness both toward themselves and toward those they guard. And rightly so. Toward this discipline, therefore, any person of sound mind would say that the dwelling and the rest of the equipment should be so provided that it does not prevent them from being the best men, nor impel them to harm the rest of the citizens. And truly so. See then if they ought to live and dwell in such a manner, if they are to be such men. First, indeed, let no one possess anything of his own, except insofar as the greatest necessity compels. Then, let them have neither a house nor a storeroom to which access is not open to all. As for what pertains to food, let there be only as much among them as temperate and brave military athletes require: and let them receive from the other citizens as a reward for their guarding just as much as will neither be lacking nor remain over from the annual expenses. Gathering themselves for meals, as if in a camp, let them eat at a common table. It must be told to them that they possess gold and silver from the gods in their souls, and do not need human gold, nor is it holy to pollute that possession by mixing it with the gold of mortals. For indeed many impious things have come from the money of the common people; but the gold that is in them is entirely uncorrupted. Truly, for them alone of all who are in the city, it is a crime to touch gold or silver, or to receive it under their roof, or to carry it about, or to drink from that material. In this way, they would provide safety both for themselves and for the city. But if ever they possess a house or land or money privately, they will be house-managers and farmers instead of guardians, and instead of being those who help the citizens, they will become their hateful masters; and being hated themselves, and hating others, and preparing snares and in turn suffering them, they will lead their entire lives. Whereupon they will fear the citizens much more than external enemies, and they will then come very close to ruin, both themselves and the rest of the city. For all these reasons, then, I say the guardians themselves ought to be so provided concerning their house and all other things. And let this be a law, shall it not? Let it be so, said Glaucon.

**FOURTH DIALOGUE ON JUSTICE.**
*
**ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.**

IN the fourth book is handed down the mode of possession and of the city, so that the citizens are neither too rich nor too poor. For he thinks that seditions arise as much from excessive abundance as from lack, and the city is dissipated. He judges, moreover, that a city is not one, but many, in which some indeed are poor, and others rich; and as usually happens, the rich despise the poor, and the poor are affected with both envy and hatred toward them. Whence he descends gradually to his mystery, namely that all things should be common, lest some have less and others more, and thence envy, lies, thefts, and from here luxury, pride, and laziness be born. Add that the possession of things both exceeding and deficient is a hindrance not only to morals and concord, but even to talent and the arts. He teaches that a city is preserved not by riches, but by virtue, and does great things. Likewise, that any part of the city should not be so disposed that it appears to be as well off as possible in itself, but <margin>Aristotle notes this in Politics Book 2, Chapter 3.</margin> so that it contributes to the whole and leads to the common good of the entire city. Otherwise neither the city itself nor any of its parts can stand. He adds, moreover, the mode of increasing the city, namely insofar as the city remains one. But as soon as unity seems able to be lost, it is not to be increased further. He commands, therefore, that the city be neither tiny nor vast, but moderate, equal, and concordant, whereby its unity may be preserved. Since indeed he who has been negligent in sowing hopes for a harvest in vain, therefore he judges that all zeal should be applied toward childhood and youth, as if toward the sowing of the urban harvest. So much so that even a diligent account of individual words, games, and gestures should be kept regarding boys and youths. Otherwise, if this age is neglected, there will be labor in vain concerning daily laws, no differently than if one should contend to cure a man daily with medicines who refuses to observe any mode of temperance in his diet. Among these things, consider that games are gradually turned into studies and morals. Likewise, just as a man both robust by nature and prudent and temperate in diet has need of almost no medicines; so a city both best constituted from the beginning and persisting in that form has need neither of many laws from the beginning, nor of daily constitutions thereafter. But bad republics are occupied in daily curing through new laws, yet never truly enjoy good health. Wherefore in this republic as the best, Plato applied no study toward laws, hoping that prudent and good men would be living laws. But what of sacred laws? He certainly thought that one should labor much less in these. For no one ever understands by what reason god is to be worshiped, unless he first understands god. But the divine sun, unless the divine sun itself...

Dialogue IV. On the Republic. Or, On Justice. 389

...shows itself, we cannot see. He judges, therefore, that the laws of religion are to be sought from Apollo, that is, divine light: to be sought, I say, not with the tongue, but with a purged and serene mind. I pass over what he touches upon here regarding the history of oracles. For these things are most well known. Allegorically indeed, he signifies Apollo, that is, divine light; to sit, that is, to be firmly present; in the middle of the earth, that is, everywhere in the innermost parts of all things. To rest in the navel, that is, in the mind separated from the senses, and reflected into itself like a spherical figure and motion. Moreover, that Apollo is ancestral to all, that is, present and familiar; and a propitious father indeed to those being born, and a homeland finally to those returning. When the republic is constituted, he recognizes thereafter four virtues in it. Prudence in the princes, that is, the science of rightly guarding and consulting. Fortitude in the soldiers, that is, a firm opinion in the face of both allurements and threats of coming to the aid of the country in dangers, insofar as the laws and magistrates command. Temperance in the princes and soldiers together, and the craftsmen; that is, a certain consensus by which all willingly agree that some indeed should rule, and others obey: and among those who obey, some in war, others in duty; nor is such consensus impeded by any pleasures, rather the desires of the inferiors should obey the command and counsel of the superiors. Justice also in all, through which each one executes his own work and task—that for which he is most fit by nature and study—both publicly and privately for the sake of the common advantage, nor does anyone claim for himself what belongs to another. But as for his calling temperance the "Diapason harmony," <note>Diapason is the Greek term for the musical octave.</note> understand this: the Diapason is the consonance resulting from the double proportion of tension, speed, and vehemence to that which is twice as relaxed, slower, and gentler. From which double proportion indeed arises the excess of the high, that is, the eighth voice to the low, and not without merit. For the first double proportion is between two and one. In which proportion indeed, while the number two seems to surpass, it recreates and doubles the one. The number two then, while it is moved and revolved into itself, produces eight, a solid number. For twice two twice make eight. It is called Diapason, that is, "through all." For such a consonance both contains all within itself and is replicated in all. Not without reason, Plato says, is temperance extended like a Diapason through the highest, the weakest, and the middle citizens. For in the octave there is both a low voice and a very high one; there are also middle ones. But to return to justice, just as in the diapason consonance the eighth voice so harmonizes with the low one that what is a double voice appears as one; so in a well-composed city the gravity of temperance so aptly agrees with the strength of justice that these two virtues are scarcely discerned from each other. And see how opportunely from the diapason consonance of the eighth voice Socrates betakes himself to justice, designated among the Pythagoreans by the number eight. For while justice becomes an entirely equal distribution according to each one’s merits, and the solid foundation of the city, it is justly described by the number eight. For this number is the first of the solids, and the first of all is so dissolved into equally even numbers, that is into twice four, that nevertheless the division itself is also dissolved into equally even numbers, that is into twice two. Again, by whatever equality it is resolved, by the same it is also woven together. For twice two twice constitute eight, the likeness, as I said, of just equality. Wherefore Orpheus, wherever he wished to call upon divine justice, swore by eight powers: fire, water, earth, heaven, moon, sun, the planet, and night. In the Egyptian column also, placed as a sign of justice, eight deities were noted in writing, as Evader testifies: Saturn, Rhea, Osiris, spirit, heaven, earth, night, day. Finally, all antiquity thinks that the order of celestial justice is digested into eight spheres. Socrates, after these things, shows that injustice is the sudden destruction of a city, when individuals usurping what belongs to others disturb and confound all things. Justice, truly, is the order and safety of the city. Then, from this more manifest justice of the city, he passes to the more hidden one in the soul, as if latent. He divides the powers of the soul threefold: into reason in the place of the prince; and the force of anger <note>Spiritedness or Thumos.</note> in the place of the soldiers; and the nature of desiring similar to the craftsman. He proves that there is one soul in us, whose three powers these are, not distinct by place within themselves, but by property. Which indeed both refutes certain Peripatetic barkers, and can become manifest to anyone reading diligently. But he brings in this distinction so that it may be clear how very similar the soul and the city, and the justice of the former and the latter, are to each other. He says, therefore: Since the soul cannot through its same power do opposite things at the same time regarding the same thing, it is necessary that it have at least three powers. Indeed, since at the same time it is carried by lust toward pleasure, and by reason meanwhile is called back. Likewise, by lust it is drawn away from battle, and by anger it is provoked to the fight. From which it is clear that reason is different from lust, and that the vigor of anger also differs from the same. That this also differs from reason is clear, both in children not yet using reason, yet very much burning with anger, and in others doing many things through anger contrary to the law of reason. <unclear>...</unclear>

(Right column)
But he proves that the vigor of anger is closer to reason by this: that indignation often helps reason against lust. He concludes thereafter that justice together with temperance is a certain legitimate consensus, both in anyone's soul among the three parts we mentioned, and in the city among the three parts similar to these. A consensus, I say, in governing, executing, obeying, and in performing their own duties, and not usurping those of others. Not without merit here he calls justice, the sister of temperance, harmony: consisting of high and low and middle voices; the voices, I say, referring to the princes and the money-makers and the middle soldiers of these. Then, to respond to the question long ago brought in, seeking what justice and injustice produce in the soul, he says that virtue is the health and beauty and strength of the soul; vice, truly, is disease, foulness, and weakness. Since indeed virtue disposes and preserves all parts of the soul as nature has ordained. Vice, truly, on the contrary, confounds and disturbs the order of nature. Since indeed when the nature of the body is entirely depraved, it is better to die than to live, even if external things are supplied to us in abundance, therefore he concludes that his life, as if miserable, is to be fled by all, in whom the soul through which we live is depraved through vice. Finally, at the very end of this book, he asserts that such a soul and city as he has described is the best and most happy. A royal soul and city, disposed by the queen, namely human reason. He adds that such a government is called royal when some one person among many good men is manifestly the most excellent of all; and the republic of the optimates, <note>Aristocracy, or rule by the best.</note> when several seem equally to excel. But he thinks it is to be considered entirely the same government. He agrees also that in the following book he will distinguish in order the four remaining affections of both souls and republics.

HERE Adimantus, responding, said: What, O Socrates, will you offer if someone says that you do not make these men very happy, although they are the ones to whom the city truly belongs, yet they receive nothing from the goods of the city, like others, who possess both fields and magnificent houses and equipment suitable for such houses, and perform private sacrifices to the gods, and receive guests, and those things you were just now saying, having obtained gold and silver, and whatever things are thought to contribute to happiness: but these men sit in the city like certain hired auxiliaries, doing nothing other than guarding? Certainly, I said, as those who receive only their food besides, nor any reward beyond food, like others. Wherefore, not even if they wish to set out privately elsewhere will it be permitted to them, nor to bestow anything on * courtesans, <margin note: * The Greek codex says "to others." He seems, however, to have read differently.</margin> or to spend money on any other things, in the manner of those who are thought happy. These and many other such things worthy of reproach you omit. But, said Adimantus, let these also be included in the accusation. What then? Do you say an answer must be given? Certainly. Entering upon that same path, I think, we shall find what things are to be said. We shall say, furthermore, that it would be no wonder if these men were most happy in this way. Nevertheless, we did not constitute the city looking to this, that any one race among us should be happy in a greater measure, but that the entire city should be as happy as possible. For we hope to find justice most of all in such a city; and on the contrary, in that which was worst instituted, injustice. Having inspected these, we thought we should easily judge what we have long been seeking. Now indeed, as we think, we are fashioning a happy city, not so that a few indeed in it should be happy, but so that the whole city is. Thereafter, however, we shall contemplate the contrary: for just as if someone should blame us while we were painting a figure of a man, because we did not apply the most beautiful colors even to the most beautiful parts of the animal; for the eyes, the most beautiful member, were not depicted with purple, but with a black color: we might seem to answer fittingly, O wonderful man, it is not necessary for us to paint eyes so beautiful that they are not even eyes, nor the other members; but consider whether, by attributing to each its own decorum, we make the whole beautiful. So now do not force us to affect the guardians with that happiness which would make them anything rather than guardians. For we could also exhort the farmers to cultivate the earth only for the sake of the mind, adorned with the most precious bodily dress and gold: and the potters, so that reclining on the right and drinking at the fire and celebrating a banquet, having sent away the wheel, they might practice pottery as much as they pleased in their minds: and all others in this way to make them happy, by which the entire city would be happy. But do not advise us so. Furthermore, if we obey you, neither will the farmer be a farmer, nor the potter a potter, nor will any other have the form of those from whom the city is made. But the reason for the others is lighter. For shoemakers, having become worse and depraved, and pretending to be what they are not, bring nothing serious upon the city. But the guardians of the laws and the city, if they are not such but only appear to be, do you see how they destroy the whole city at once, since they alone have the opportunity of constituting it well and rendering it happy? Wherefore, if we seek true guardians of the city, we least of all ought to choose those who would harm the city. But he who says that, and makes the farmers happy not as in a city, but as in some festive celebration reclining, certainly says something else other than a city. We must see, therefore, whether we constitute guardians looking to this, that they should abound as much as possible in happiness: or whether we should rather have a reason for the entire city, so that the whole is happy: and it should be becoming to compel and persuade those auxiliaries and guardians to do those things from which each one should be the best artisan of his own work, and all others likewise. And so, the city having been increased and rightly instituted, it must be allowed that individuals be participants in happiness insofar as each one's nature is capable. Rightly, he said, you seem to me to speak. Shall I not also, I said, seem to you to speak rightly regarding what is closest to this? What most of all? Contemplate whether these things also corrupt the other artisans, so that they are bad. What are those? Wealth, plainly, and poverty. By what reason? Thus: does a potter become rich seem to you to still have a care for his art? Least of all. He will certainly be rendered more lazy and negligent. Very much so. Wherefore he also becomes a worse potter. And that too. Again, however, if because of want he lacks tools and the rest of the things which the art needs, he will both make the works themselves worse, and he will teach his sons and whoever else, rendering them worse artisans. Why not? From both, therefore, as much from opulence as from poverty, both the works of the arts become worse, and the artisans themselves become worse. So it appears. Other things, therefore, we have found to be observed by our guardians, lest they creep into the city without their knowledge. What are those? Opulence, I say, and want. For the former breeds luxury, idleness, and a desire for new things. The latter, however, with the innovation of things, generates illiberalism and malice. It is exactly so. Nevertheless, O Socrates, consider, I pray, in what way this city of ours, since it lacks money, will be able to wage war, especially if ever it is compelled to take up arms against a large and opulent city. It is clear, he said, that against one it is difficult, but against two such, it is certainly easier. How, he said, do you say that? First, if a fight is to be joined, will not these men exercised in military affairs fight against rich men? I confess that indeed. What then, Adimantus? One boxer most excellently instructed for this, does he not seem to you likely to fight easily against two non-boxers, especially rich and fat ones? Perhaps not at the same time. What if it were possible by fleeing to avoid the blow of the one who first invades, then by a sudden turning to strike him? If he should do that often in the sun and heat, such a man would subdue several such men. Indeed, it is no wonder. Do you not think the rich have obtained more by use and knowledge of the art of boxing than of the military? I do. Easily, therefore, our athletes, as is consistent, will contend with double and triple their number. I will admit that too. For you seem to speak rightly. What if, an embassy having been sent to another city, they should say the truth: that we indeed do not use gold and silver, nor is it lawful for us as it is for you. Wherefore you, who have contracted a society of war with us, have those things which others possess: do you think anyone, having heard these things, would prefer to fight against hard and lean dogs, rather than along with such dogs against fat and soft sheep? In no way does it seem so to me. But if in one city the money of the rest is accumulated, take care lest it bring danger to the less moneyed one. You are blessed, since indeed you think it is becoming to call another city anything but such a one as we have ourselves constituted. Why is it prohibited? The others require a more ample appellation. For each of them is many cities, not a city, as is usually said by those who jest. For there are at least two, and those dissenting among themselves. One indeed of the poor, the other of the rich. And again in each of those, very many: to which, if you intend as to one, you will go entirely astray: but if as to many, giving those things which belong to some to others, both money and powers, or also themselves, you will always use many auxiliary allies, but few enemies. And insofar as the city is so ordained as it was just now, it will exist temperate, it will be greatest; and that not indeed in opinion, but in reality greatest, even if it consists of only a thousand defenders. For such a great city as one you will not easily find either among the Greeks or among the Barbarians: yet you will find many which appear much greater than a city of this kind. Or do you feel otherwise? Not otherwise, by Jove. <margin note: Aristotle notes this in Politics Book 2, Chapter 1.> Will not this, then, be the most beautiful limit for our princes for increasing the city, to which, when it has become so great, it is becoming to assign so much region, but to let the rest go? What limit? I think indeed, as far as the city remains one when increased, it should be increased so far, but no further. Most excellently. This precept furthermore we shall command the guardians to keep, that they provide by every reason that neither a small city nor a great one appears to be, but one and sufficient. And yet perhaps we shall command them something light. And that is lighter furthermore, of which we made mention in the upper parts, when we were saying it is necessary if any sluggish guardian is born, to send him to others: if from others a thorooughbred, to the guardians themselves. In which I plainly wished to show that of the other citizens also, each one should be led to that one work alone for which he is fit by nature, so that each one following the study of his own nature, should exist not as many, but as one, and so the whole city should become one, not many. This, he said, is even less than that. By no means, O good man Adimantus, do we command them these many and great things, as someone might think, but all light and small things, if they keep one thing, as is usually said, great—no, rather instead of great, sufficient. What is that? Education, I say, and erudition. For if well educated, they become moderate men, they will easily discern all those things, both as many others as we omit in the present, and the...

...indeed they may seem to be, nor the other members: but consider, if by attributing to each part its own proper grace, we render the whole beautiful. Thus, you should not now compel us to bestow such a "happiness" upon the guardians that would make them anything rather than guardians. For we could also urge the farmers to dress in the most precious clothing and gold, and to cultivate the land only for the sake of their own pleasure; and we could tell the potters to recline at their ease, drinking by the fire and celebrating feasts, having cast aside the wheel to practice their craft only as much as they feel like; and we could make all others "blessed" in this way, so that the entire city might be happy. But you must not advise us so. Furthermore, if we follow your suggestion, the farmer will not be a farmer, nor the potter a potter, nor will any other retain the form of those parts out of which a city is made. However, the concern for these others is of less weight. For if shoemakers become worse and corrupted, pretending to be what they are not, they bring nothing grave upon the city. But if the <term>Guardians</term> <note>The 'Guardians' (custodes) are the ruling philosopher-class in Plato's ideal state.</note> of the laws and the city are not truly so, but only appear to be, you see how they utterly destroy the whole city, since they alone have the opportunity to establish it well and render it blessed.

Therefore, if we seek true guardians of the city, we must by no means choose those who would harm the city. But he who speaks of making farmers happy, not as if they were in a city but as if they were at some festive celebration reclining at ease, is certainly speaking of something other than a city. We must see, then, whether we should appoint guardians with a view to making them as abundant in happiness as possible, or whether we should rather consider the reason of the whole city, so that the whole may be happy. It is proper to compel and persuade these <term>auxiliaries</term> <note>The 'auxiliaries' (auxiliarios) are the warrior class who support the rulers.</note> and guardians to do those things which make each the best craftsman of his own work, and all others likewise. And so, as the entire city grows and is rightly established, we must allow the individual parts to participate in happiness insofar as the nature of each is capable. "You seem to me," he said, "to speak rightly." "And," I said, "will I seem to speak rightly on the point that is closest to this?" "What especially?" "Contemplate whether these two things corrupt the other craftsmen as well, making them wicked." "Which things are those?" "Wealth and poverty, evidently." "In what way?" "In this way: does a potter who has become wealthy seem to you to still have any care for his art?" "Not at all." "He will surely become lazier and more negligent." "Very much so." "And thus he becomes a worse potter." "That is true." "Again, if through want he lacks the tools and other things his art requires, he will produce worse works, and he will teach his sons and others to be worse craftsmen." "How could he not?" "From both, therefore—from opulence as well as poverty—the works of the arts become worse, and the craftsmen themselves become worse." "So it appears." "We have therefore found other things that our guardians must watch against, lest they creep into the city without their knowledge." "Which things are those?" "Wealth," I said, "and want. For the former breeds luxury, idleness, and a desire for revolution; the latter breeds illiberality and malice along with the desire for innovation." "That is exactly right. Nevertheless, O Socrates, consider, I pray, how our city, since it lacks money, will be able to wage war, especially if it is ever forced to take up arms against a large and wealthy city." "It is clear," he said, "that against one it is difficult, but against two such cities, it is certainly easier." "How can you say that?" he asked. "First, if a battle must be joined, will not our men, trained in the affairs of war, fight against rich men?" "I grant that." "What then, Adimantus? Does it not seem to you that one boxer perfectly trained for this purpose would easily fight against two non-boxers who were, moreover, rich and fat?"

(Right column)

"Perhaps not both at once." "Not even if he were allowed to avoid the blows of the first attacker by retreating, and then, by a sudden turn, strike him? If he did this repeatedly in the sun and heat, would such a man not subdue many men of that sort? Certainly, it would be no wonder." "Do you not think the rich have more experience and knowledge of the art of boxing than of the art of war?" "I do indeed." "Therefore, our athletes, as is reasonable, will easily contend with double or triple their own number." "I will admit that too, for you seem to speak rightly." "What if, having sent an embassy to another city, they told the truth: that we indeed do not use gold or silver, nor is it lawful for us as it is for you. Therefore, you who have joined in a war-alliance with us, take the possessions of others. Do you think anyone hearing this would prefer to fight against hard and lean dogs, rather than to fight alongside such dogs against fat and soft sheep?" "Not at all, it seems to me. But if the money of everyone else is accumulated in a single city, beware lest it bring danger to the less wealthy one." "You are blessed, since you think it proper to call any other a 'city' except for such a one as we have established." "What forbids it?" "The others require a grander title. For each of them is many cities, not one city, as those who joke are accustomed to say. For there are at least two: those two being at odds with one another. One is the city of the poor, the other of the rich. And again, within each of these there are very many; if you treat them as one, you will utterly fail. But if you treat them as many, handing over the things of one to the others—both money and power—you will always have many allies and helpers, but few enemies. And as long as the city is ordered as it was recently, it will be the greatest; not merely in reputation, but truly the greatest, even if it consists of only a thousand defenders. For you will not easily find one city so great even among the Greeks or the Barbarians, though you will find many that seem many times larger than such a city. Or do you think otherwise?" "Not otherwise, by Jupiter." "Will this not, therefore, be the best limit for our princes for the increasing of the city: <margin>Aristotle notes this in Politics, Book 2, chapter 1.</margin> that while it is of such a size, they should allot it that much territory, but let the rest go?" "What is that limit?" "I think indeed that as long as the city remains one as it grows, it should be increased, but not beyond that." "Excellent." "Furthermore, we will command the guardians to observe this precept: to provide by every means that the city appears neither small nor large, but one and sufficient. And yet, perhaps we shall prescribe a light thing to them. And this is even lighter: that which we mentioned previously, when we said it was necessary that if a guardian is born base, he should be sent to others; but if a noble child is born among the others, he should be sent to the guardians. In this we plainly wished to show that each of the other citizens ought to be led to that one work alone for which he is fit by nature, so that each, following the study of his own nature, might not be many, but one; and thus the whole city might become one, not many." "This," he said, "is even less than that other." "By no means, O good Adimantus; we do not prescribe many and great things to them, as someone might think, but all are light and small, if they preserve the 'one big thing,' as it is called—or rather, instead of 'big,' let us say 'sufficient.'" "What is that?" "Education," I said, "and instruction. For if they are well educated and turn out to be moderate men, they will easily discern all these things, as well as whatever else we are omitting for the present, such as the matter of women..."

### Fourth Dialogue on the Republic, or, on Justice. 391

...the unions of women and men, and the procreation of children; it is evident that all these things should be held as common as possible among friends, according to the proverb <note>original: "amicorum omnia... communia," referring to the Pythagorean saying that friends hold all things in common</note>. This would indeed be the most correct way to proceed. For a republic, if it once begins well, advances like a circle that is always expanding. Truly, if good education and training are preserved, they produce good natures. In turn, good natures, having received such an education, turn out even better than the previous ones—both in other respects and in the generation of children, just as is seen in other animals. That is certainly likely.

Finally, to speak briefly, the guardians of the city must diligently observe this: that it does not become corrupted without their knowledge. Rather, they should take care above all that nothing is innovated in gymnastic and music contrary to the order we have established, but that everyone follows that order as much as possible. And when someone quotes that poetic line, that men <margin>Odyssey, Book 1</margin> are most delighted by "new songs," <note>original: "cantibus... delectari"</note> these guardians ought to fear that someone might think the poet is speaking not of new songs, but of *new modes of singing*, and praise them. One must neither praise nor accept such a thing. We must be truly careful about introducing a new style of music, as it risks a total shipwreck of the state. For musical modes are never changed without the changing of the greatest civil laws, as Damon says, and I myself agree with him. Know, Socrates, that I also agree.

It seems, then, that we must build a kind of fortress for the sake of protection, with these very guardians, centered around music. Indeed, such a sin creeps in secretly and easily. It starts out like a kind of game, and in such a way that it seems to do no harm. It does nothing else, he said, than creep slowly into habits and pursuits through the influence of those we are familiar with; from these it then emerges further into commerce; finally, from commerce it breaks out into the laws and republics, O Socrates, with great insolence and wantonness, until it finally subverts everything both privately and publicly. That is how things stand, I said. Indeed, he said, so it seems to me.

Therefore, as we said from the beginning, boys must be accustomed to honorable games right from their earliest years. For if they grow accustomed to games that are less decent, they will never turn out to be law-abiding and upright men. Why not? When, therefore, children begin well—playing and joking—they drink in the lawful character through music. This music tends toward the opposite of those earlier influences and grows, raising up whatever was previously lying low in the city. You speak the truth. These things, then, which seem to be the small institutions of the city, will be discovered by those who disturbed all previous things. What sort of things? Namely, these: that the younger should keep silent before their elders, give place to them, and stand up for them; how they should honor their parents; what style of haircut each should keep, what clothes or shoes should be used, and generally what bodily ornament is fitting, and other things of that kind. Do you not think so? I do. Yet to prescribe these things by law, I think, is foolish. For it is never done anywhere, nor would these things hold fast if committed to words and letters. Why not? It appears, then, Adimantus, that whatever the beginning of each person's childhood education was, such will be the things that follow. Does not like always call to like? Why not? And finally, I think, we must say that it ends in one supreme and powerful thing, whether good or evil. What prevents it? For this reason, I would never contend to establish these things by laws. And rightly so.

Tell me, by the gods, I said, shall we attempt to establish by law the matters of the marketplace itself, and mutual commerce, and contracts in the mechanical arts, or insults and blows, the casting of lots for lawsuits, the appointments of judges, and whatever pertains to the marketplace or ports,

(Right column)

or the taxes that must be imposed or collected, or any forensic rights, or urban or port laws, and the rest of that kind? It is not at all fitting to command good and noble men on these points. For they will easily discover for themselves most of these things, such as they are and how they should be established. Truly, O friend, if God grants them the safety of those laws we laid down above. Otherwise, they will spend their lives establishing many such things by laws, always correcting and innovating, thinking they will thus achieve what is best. You mean those people will live just like those who, though they are sick, refuse to change their unhealthy lifestyle because of their lack of self-control. Exactly.

Indeed, in a ridiculous way, those people seem to persevere in their diseases, and through their cures they achieve nothing other than making their illnesses more varied and more violent; and they always trust that if anyone suggests a remedy, they will be well. Such are the diseases of those who struggle in that way. What then? Is this not charming in them: that they think the man who tells the truth is their greatest enemy, and tells them that no medicines, cauterizations, incisions, incantations, or things applied from the outside will be of use until they stop indulging in drunkenness, gluttony, lust, and idleness? That is not very charming. For there is no grace in being angry at someone who gives useful advice. Therefore, you do not at all approve of such men, it seems. Not at all, by Jupiter. Nor will you praise the city if it does what we were just saying. Don't those cities seem to you to be doing the same thing—whatever ill-governed cities forbid the citizens from moving the state's constitution, otherwise those who innovate are condemned to death? On the contrary, whoever thus honors those administering the Republic, and gratifies them, and creeps into their favor, and agrees with their will, and follows their ways—this man finally will be the "good man," the "wise man" in great affairs, and will be treated with honor by them. They seem exactly the same to me, and I do not praise them in any way.

But what? Do you not admire the courage and the ready affection of those who strive to care for these cities? I do admire them, except for those who are deceived by the cities themselves and think they are truly statesmen because they are praised by the crowd. What are you saying? Do you not forgive them? Do you think that a man who is ignorant of measurement, if everyone else tells him he is four cubits tall, can escape thinking the same of himself? Not that man, certainly. Therefore, do not be annoyed. For these are the most ridiculous of all, who bring laws in the matters we spoke of and are always amending them, trusting they will find some end to the injustices committed in commerce and those things I mentioned a little while ago—ignorant that they are, in truth, <note>original: "hydram secare," an allusion to the Lernean Hydra whose heads grew back when cut off</note> cutting a Hydra. Certainly, they do nothing else. Indeed, I believe a true founder of laws should not deal with these things, whether in an ill-disposed or a well-constituted city: in the former, because such institutions are useless and achieve nothing; in the latter, because someone will find part of them for themselves, and part will proceed by their own nature from their earlier studies.

What else remains for us concerning the constitution of laws? For us, nothing. But for the Delphic Apollo, the greatest, noblest, and first institutions. Which ones are those? The building of temples and sacrifices, and the other cults of gods, spirits, and heroes; furthermore, the tombs and funerals of the dead, and whatever

...ministries must be undertaken to appease them. Such things we do not know ourselves, and in ordering the city, we will trust no one else, if we are wise, nor will we use any other interpreter than the ancestral God. For this God is the ancestral interpreter for all men in such matters, sitting at the center of the earth upon the navel <note>original: "vmbilicū," referring to the Omphalos at Delphi, believed to be the center of the world</note>, he explains them. Let the city, then, O son of Ariston, be established for you. Next, bring a great light from elsewhere, and look around through it yourself, and call your brother, and Polemarchus, and others besides, so that we may try to see if we can find in what place justice and injustice are; and how they differ from each other, and which of them he who is to live happily ought to possess, whether it is hidden from all gods and men or not. You are doing nothing, Glaucon said. For you promised to investigate, as it would be a sin if you did not help justice with all your strength. You remind me of the truth, I said, and we must certainly act so. However, you must also assist me. We will do so, he said.

I hope, therefore, in this way to find it. I think the city, if it has been rightly established by us, exists as something absolutely good. It must be so. It is clear, then, that it is wise, brave, temperate, and just. It is clear. Whichever of these is found in the city, the remainder will be that which has not yet been found. Why not? he said. If from some other four things we were seeking one in a certain subject, and that one appeared first, we would be satisfied; but if we found the three remaining ones first, by this very fact we would recognize the one sought, because it would be clear that it was nothing other than what remained. You speak well. Should we not seek these in the same way, since there are four? Clearly.

And yet, out of all these, wisdom seems to shine first in the city, and something wonderful appears concerning it. What is it? The city we have described seems to me to be truly wise, for it is well-advised. Is it not? It is indeed. And this very faculty of advising is a kind of knowledge. For men do not advise well through ignorance, but rather through knowledge. That is evident. But there are many and various kinds of knowledge in the city. There are. Should the city be called wise and well-advised because of the knowledge of smiths? In no way because of that, but rather "skilled in smithing." Therefore, the city should not be called wise because it advises well on how wooden works may be best performed. Certainly not. Is it perhaps because of the knowledge that shapes bronze works? Or another such thing? Certainly not because of any of these. Nor even because of the knowledge of producing fruits from the earth, which is the skill of agriculture. So I think.

What then? Is there some knowledge in the city recently founded by us, among any citizens, by which one deliberates not about some private matter in the city, but rather about the whole city, in what way it may best conduct itself toward itself and other cities? There is indeed. What is this, and in whom? Namely, the very diligence of guarding, and it is in those leaders whom we just now called perfect guardians. Because of this knowledge, then, what name do you give the city? Sharp in deliberation and truly wise. Do you think there are more blacksmiths in the city than these true guardians? Many more blacksmiths, certainly. And will these guardians not be the fewest of all the other craftsmen, whoever they are said to be? Very few indeed. Therefore, from a very small class and part of itself, and from the knowledge that is in the presiding and leading part, the whole city established according to nature will be wise: and that, it seems,

(Right column)

is by nature the fewest and rarest kind, to whom it belongs to be a participant in this knowledge, which alone of all others is fitting to call wisdom. You speak the truest things. This one of the four, then, I know not how, we have found—both what it is and in what part of the city it is located. To me, it seems sufficiently stated.

But indeed, it is not difficult to find what courage is, and in what part of the city it is located, because of which the city is called brave. In what way? Who, looking at anything else, calls a city either cowardly or brave, except toward that part which fights and campaigns for it? Certainly no one. For the others in it, being either cowardly or brave, do not have the authority to make it either cowardly or brave. Certainly not. The city will be brave, then, because of a part of itself, from the fact that it has in it such a power which preserves a fixed opinion in all things, that only those things are terrible, and such as they are, which the legislator pronounced in their training. Do you not call this courage? I did not quite grasp what you said; say it again. I say that courage is a kind of preservation. What preservation? Namely, of the opinion conceived through education according to the law, by which it is judged what things are terrible, and of what kind. And I said that this preservation is in all things—that is, so that it is kept fixed always and everywhere, whether someone is affected by pains, or pleasures, or desires, or fears, and is in no way moved from it because of these. To what I think this is similar, if you wish, I will reveal to you. I certainly desire it.

Do you not know that dyers <note>original: "fullones," referring to cleaners or dyers of cloth</note>, whenever they want to dye wool with a purple color, first choose the white from so many colors, then prepare it with no small labor so that it may receive the bloom as much as possible, and only then do they dye it? And what is dyed in this way remains indelible, and the bloom of that color cannot be washed away by water alone, nor even by adding those cleansers that pertain to scouring. But those that are not so prepared, you know what they turn out like—whether someone dyes them with other colors or these, when they have been less refined beforehand? Certainly, they are ugly, and their colors are easily washed away. Think of us as having studied to do something similar to the best of our power, when we were choosing the soldiers themselves and educating them in music and gymnastics: and believe that we devised nothing else than that they might drink in the laws like a kind of color, so that they might be best persuaded: so that their opinion about terrible things, and about all other things, remains immovable, because they were born of the best nature and nourished with a fitting education; nor can those cleansers, however powerful for washing away, erase their "dye": namely, pleasure, which is sharper than any stinging salt or lime for purging; likewise pain, fear, and desire, more powerful for scouring than any other cleanser. This power, which everywhere preserves the right and lawful opinion concerning terrible things and their opposites, I call courage and I assert it to be so, unless you perhaps say something else.

I say nothing else. For you seem to think that a right opinion about the same things conceived without discipline—namely, the wild or slavish kind—is not at all lawful, but you call it something other than courage. You speak most truly, I said. I admit, therefore, that this is courage. Admit further that it is *civil* courage, and so you will receive it rightly. Next, concerning this, if you wish, we will treat it more diligently at another time. For the present, however, we were not seeking that, but justice. For the investigation of that, enough has been said about this, I think.

<meta>The dialogue moves to the definition of Temperance, described as a harmony across the whole city, and then finally identifies Justice as "minding one's own business."</meta>

### Fourth Dialogue on the Republic, or, on Justice. 393

You speak excellently. Two things remain besides to be considered in the city: namely, temperance, and that for the sake of which we investigate all things, justice. Exactly. Could we somehow find justice itself now, so that we do not labor again in investigating temperance? I neither know that, nor would I wish justice to become known to us before we have considered temperance. Therefore, if you wish to do me a favor, investigate the latter before the former. I certainly wish to, unless I am being unfair. Investigate now. Behold, I am searching; and as far as can be seen from here, it is more like a kind of consonance and harmony than the previous ones. In what way?

Temperance is a kind of order, and an abstinence from certain pleasures and desires, as they say. They affirm that being "master of oneself" <note>original: "Seipso... superiorem," literally 'superior to oneself'</note> and other similar things are, in some way, traces of temperance itself. Is it not so? Most of all. Does not that which is called "being stronger than oneself" appear somewhat ridiculous? For whoever is stronger than himself will also be weaker than himself; again, he who is weaker is also stronger. For the same person is named in all these. Why not? But it seems to me this speech means that there are two things in a man's soul. One indeed is better, and the other worse. And when that which is better by nature rules over the worse, then someone is said to be "master of himself," and is praised by this speech. But whenever, because of bad education or some habit, that which is better (being smaller) is overcome by the multitude of the worse, this is blamed as a reproach and he is said to be "weaker than himself": and he who is so affected is called intemperate. So it appears.

Contemplate this city recently founded by us, and you will find one of these present in it. For you will confess that it is rightly called more powerful than itself. For if the better rules the worse in it, it must be called temperate and "better than itself." I am contemplating it, and you speak the truth. Indeed, anyone could find the most numerous and varied desires, pleasures, and pains in all these: in women, in servants, and in those who are called free among the common and abject men. Entirely so. But the simple and moderate ones, which are led by reason and right opinion with the mind, you will find in only a few—and these born of the best nature and best educated. These things are true. Do you not see these in this city, and that here the desires of the common crowd and of vile persons are overcome by the desires and wisdom of the few and modest men? I see it indeed. If any city, therefore, is more powerful than desires and pleasures, and also than itself, this one especially must be so called. Exactly.

Therefore, are not all these things just and temperate? Most of all. And if in any other city there is an opinion among both the subjects and the rulers as to whom it is most fitting to grant the command, it must be especially present in this one; or do you not think so? Very much so. In which citizens, then, will you say temperance resides when they are so disposed? In the rulers? Or in the subjects? In both, in a way. You see, then, how aptly we predicted a little while ago that temperance is similar to a kind of harmony? Why? Because unlike wisdom and courage, which, existing in certain parts, make the city wise and brave respectively, temperance does not act so: but like the harmony which is called the *octave* <note>original: "diapason"</note>, it is diffused through the whole city, making the weaker and the stronger and those in the middle—in wisdom, power, multitude, money, or anything else of the kind—consonant in the same thing.

(Right column)

Wherefore we could most rightly call this temperance a concord—namely, a consensus of the worse and the better according to nature; which teaches who should rule, whether in the city or in each individual. I certainly agree. Since this is so, three things have now been found by us in the city, so it appears from these. But what will be the remaining species, by which the city further participates in virtue? It is clear that this is justice. It is entirely clear.

Is it not necessary for us now, O Glaucon, to surround this thicket like hunters, looking around lest justice escape somehow and, vanishing from our eyes, hide itself? For it is clear it is here. Fix your gaze everywhere, then, and strive if somehow you can see it before me, and show it to me. I wish I could. But you will use me better as a companion who can look at what is demonstrated. Follow me, then, having first prayed to God. I will do what you advise. Lead on. Arduous, I said, this place seems to be, and shadowy; it is certainly dark and impenetrable. Nevertheless, we must proceed. Clearly, we must proceed. Here, I looking at Glaucon, cried out: "Hui hui!" <note>an exclamation of discovery</note> my Glaucon, we seem to have found some tracks of what we are seeking, and it appears it will not escape us for long. Certainly, a happy message. Indeed, I said, we are soft and dull. Why is that?

For a long time, from the very beginning, O blessed man, what we seek has been rolling before our feet, and we did not see it, but were equally worthy of being laughed at, like those who often search for what they have in their hands. We too were seeking far away what was near us, or perhaps it was hidden from us. How do you say that? In this way. We seem to me to have been saying and hearing it for a long time, without at all noticing that we were saying it in some way. A long prologue for one desiring to hear! Listen, then, if I say anything. For what we established as necessary to be done everywhere from the beginning, when we founded the city—that is, I think, or some species of it, is justice. For we said many times, if you remember, that each person ought to practice one thing of those that contribute to the city, for which his nature was most fit. We said so, without a doubt. And indeed, that *doing one's own business* <note>original: "sua agere," the core Platonic definition of justice</note>, and not being curiously occupied in other people's affairs, is justice, we have both heard from many others and often said ourselves. We said so, clearly. This, then, my friend, seems to be justice in some way: doing one's own business. Do you know from where I conjecture this? Not at all, but tell me.

It seems to me that what is left for us in the city, besides those things we have considered—temperance, courage, and wisdom—is this: that which gave them all the power both to be born and to be preserved once born, as long as it was present. And yet we said that justice would be what remained if three were found by us. That is necessary. Nevertheless, if it were to be judged which of these, when present, most makes the city good, it would be difficult to judge: whether it is the preservation of opinion in the soldiers, judging according to the law what is to be deemed terrible and what is not; or wisdom and guardianship in the rulers themselves. Or whether this rather makes it good above the rest when it is present in children, women, slaves, free men, craftsmen, magistrates, and private citizens: namely, that each one does his one work, and is not entangled in other people's affairs. Difficult, certainly. Why not? Therefore, the power itself, as it seems, by which each person in the city does his own things, contends for the virtue of the city equally with its wisdom, temperance, and courage. Very much so. Will you not then place justice as that which contends equally with those for the virtue of the city? Entirely.

--- Page 410 ---
<meta>This page applies the definition of justice found in the state to the individual human soul, beginning the analysis of the tripartite soul.</meta>

394 Thirty-First Book.

Consider it also in this way, to see if it seems so to you. Will you command the rulers in the city to give judgment justly? Why not? And will they judge with any other aim than this: that individuals should neither seize what belongs to others nor be deprived of their own? No other aim, certainly, but this, as it is just. Clearly. And in this way also, it is asserted that the possession and action of one's own and proper work is justice. It is so.

See if you think the same as I do. If a carpenter should attempt the work of a shoemaker, or a shoemaker that of a carpenter, or if they exchange their tools or rewards, or if the same person attempts to practice both, and all such things are exchanged between them, do you think this exchange would affect the city with a great loss? Not at all, he said. But whenever some craftsman or someone who is by nature a money-maker, puffed up by wealth, or by the multitude and abundance of his means, or by strength, or some other such thing, tries to pass into the rank of a military man; or a soldier, though unworthy, tries to ascend to the dignity of a counselor and guardian; and they exchange their tools and rewards in turn, or when the same person tries to perform all these things at once—then I think such an exchange and the handling of many things would appear to you to be the destruction of the whole city. And most especially so.

Since, therefore, there are three classes in the city, the meddling in many things and the exchange of one for another is the extreme calamity of the city, and will most rightly be called its ruin. It is so. And the greatest ruin of your city—will you not say it is injustice? Why not? This, then, is injustice. Again, we say this: the proper action of the money-makers, the helpers, and the guardians, with each one performing his own work in the city—contrary to that confusion mentioned above—will be justice, and will make the city just. It seems to be no other way than this.

We ought not yet to assert this absolutely. But if the same species of justice is found to exist in the soul of each individual man when we consider it, then finally we will agree. For what else could we say? Otherwise, we will then devise something else. But now let us put an end to this discussion, according to which we thought that if we first contemplated justice in something larger that possessed it, we would then more easily inspect what it is like in one man. And it seemed to us that this larger thing was the city, and so we founded it as best as we could, knowing that justice exists in a good republic. Therefore, what appeared to us in that, let us refer to the individual: and if the same is established there, we shall be satisfied. But if something else appears in the one, returning again to the city, we will examine these things; and perhaps by considering them together and striking them against each other like flints, we will strike out justice, and once it shines clearly, we will establish it among ourselves. You speak skillfully, and we must act so.

Is that which we call the same, whether it be larger or smaller, dissimilar insofar as it is called the same, or similar? Similar, certainly. Therefore, a just man, as far as the species of justice is concerned, differs in no way from a just city, but will be similar. Similar. And yet the city seemed to be just when the three classes of men in it each did their own work according to their nature. It was temperate, brave, and wise because of the affections and habits of these same classes, and not because of others. These things are true. We shall likewise judge each individual, my friend—that having these same species in his soul, because of the same affections, he deserves to share the same names with the city. It is absolutely necessary.

Have we fallen again, O wonderful man, into a slight thought about the soul—whether it has these three species in itself, or not? It does not seem to me that we have fallen into a slight discussion.
