For perhaps what is said is true, O Socrates, that "beautiful things are difficult." <note>original: "pulchra difficilia esse," a common Greek proverb (chalepa ta kala)</note> It appears so. And indeed know, O Glaucon, that in my opinion we will never exactly comprehend this from the kinds of discourse we are using in the present dispute; for the way that leads there is longer. Perhaps, however, it could be discussed worthily according to those things that were said and considered above. Should that not seem enough? To me, for the present, it will suffice. To me also it is very sufficient. Therefore, do not be weary, but consider.

Indeed, it is necessary for us to confess that the same species and habits are in us as are in the city. For they did not come into the city from elsewhere. It would be ridiculous if someone thought that spirited anger <note>original: "iracundam animositatem"</note> was not brought into cities from private men, whose nature is the same—such as the Thracians, Scythians, and the northern nations; or the love of wisdom, not from such an instinct of private men, such as is naturally attributed to our people; or the greed for gain, not from that desire of individual men, with which the Phoenicians and Egyptians are said to be especially affected. And most especially so. This is how it is, and it is not difficult to know. Not difficult, certainly.

But this is difficult: whether we do each of these things with one and the same part of us, or rather we have three things in us, by each of which we perform each action: we learn with one, we are angry with another, and with a third we desire those pleasures which pertain to nutrition and generation, and other things of this kind; or whether we fulfill each of them with the whole soul when we set about something. These things would not be easily discerned according to the dignity of the matter. It seems the same to me. Let us attempt to define them in this way, whether they are the same among themselves or different. In what way? It is clearly established that the same thing cannot do or suffer opposites according to the same part and toward the same thing at the same time. Wherefore, if we ever find these things happening in them, we will understand they are not one and the same, but several. Let it be so. Notice what I say. Speak.

Can the same thing stand still and be moved at the same time according to the same part? In no way. Furthermore, let us confirm this more diligently, lest any ambiguity should perhaps arise as we proceed. For if someone says that a man standing still, but moving his hands and head, both stands and is moved at the same time, we shall not think it should be said so, but rather that a part of him stands and a part is moved? Is it not so? Exactly. But if that person should play more artfully and cleverly, asserting that a spinning top <note>original: "turbinem trochumque"</note> is moved and stands still as a whole at the same time, when, fixing its center and point in the same spot, it revolves; or anything else, you will say it does the same when it is carried around fixed to the same axis: we shall not at all agree, because it is not according to the same part of itself that it then moves and remains. For it must be said that they have in themselves a "straight" and a "round" part: and according to the straight, they stand, since they do not lean in any direction; but according to the round, they move in a circle. But whenever, while it revolves, it is also carried in a straight line, whether to the right or to the left, or forward or backward, then it stays nowhere. Quite right. Therefore, none of these objections will disturb us, nor persuade us that the same thing sometimes, simultaneously, according to the same part and toward the same thing, either acts or suffers opposites. These things will not move me, at least. Nevertheless, lest we be forced to stay longer in following and discussing all these controversies which are false, let us proceed further with these things already granted and laid down, having made a promise between us that if these things should ever appear to be otherwise than so, whatever follows from them shall be void.

--- Page 411 ---
### Fourth Dialogue on the Republic; Or, On Justice

It is surely fitting in this way. Would you not posit that assenting and refusing, desiring to receive something and rejecting it, embracing and repelling, are contraries [abbrev: *cōtraria*] among themselves, whether they be actions or passions? For it makes no difference. They are contraries. What then? To hunger, to thirst, and in general to desire, to will, to choose—will you not refer these to those species which we just mentioned [abbrev: *diximꝰ*]? Just as you would say the soul of one who always desires is either inclined toward that which it appetites, or embraces what it wishes to be present for itself, or insofar as it wants something to be offered to it, it assents and draws it to itself, affecting it in the manner of a lover so that it may come to pass. Indeed. But what of nilling, being averse, not desiring—shall we not refer these to the species [abbrev: *ſpeciem*] of rejecting and repelling, and into all things contrary to the former? Why not? Since [abbrev: *hæc*] this is so, shall we say that there is some species of desires, and of these the most manifest are those which we call thirst and hunger? We shall certainly say so. And one is for drink, the other for food [abbrev: *eſta* is likely a misreading for *esca* (food)]. Now, insofar as it is thirst, is there a desire for anything else in the soul? Plainly. Is it for a hot drink, or a cold one, or much, or little [abbrev: *paucæ*]? Or for a specific kind of cup? Or rather, if heat is in the thirsty one, it induces an appetite for the cold; but if cold, for the hot? And if it be vehement and copious, it will provide a great thirst, an avidity for much; but if little, for little? But thirsting itself is never the appetition of anything other than that which is its own nature, namely drink itself; and likewise [abbrev: *rursusq;*] hungering, for food? Thus certainly each desire itself is of that thing itself which it is, only that which is according to its nature. But when it is called "such or such," it is by addition. We must take care, however, lest someone disturb us unawares, suggesting that no one desires drink, but good drink, or food, but good food, since all desire good things. Wherefore if thirst is an appetition, it is of the good, whether of drink or of any other avidity. And similarly [abbrev: *Similiterq;*] regarding the rest. Perhaps, he said, he who says such things will seem to achieve something. Nevertheless, as many as are of such a kind that they belong to something, they are such of some specific thing, as I think. But the things themselves belong only to the thing itself. Indeed, I do not understand. Do you not understand that "greater" is of such a kind that it always exists as greater than something? Plainly. Is it not greater than a lesser? Than a lesser. And the much greater than the much lesser, is it not so? It is so. And the once greater than the once lesser, and the future greater than the future lesser? Nothing prohibits it. And also the more to the fewer, the double to the half, and all such things, likewise the heavier to the lighter, and the swifter to the slower, and the hot likewise to the cold, and all [abbrev: *omniaq;*] similar things of these behave in the same way. Certainly. And is not the same reason regarding those things which pertain to the sciences? Science itself is the science of the thing itself which is known, or of whatever else science must be said to be. But indeed, a certain science, and a science of such a thing, is said to be of a certain and such a kind. I mean something of this sort. After the science of building houses arose, it was distinguished from other sciences, so that it was called architecture. Why not? Is it not from the fact that it is of such a kind as none of the others? Truly. Therefore, because it is of a certain thing, it was made into such a kind. And in the same way the other arts and [abbrev: *atq;*] sciences. It is so. Say then that I wished to infer this, if only you have now understood, that whatever things are of such a kind that they belong to something, they themselves are only of those things themselves, but such things are of certain such things. Nor indeed do I say that of what kind they are, they are also such, as if the science of the sick and the well were itself well or sick; or that of good and [abbrev: *atq;*] evil were good and evil; but since it has become not a science of that thing itself of which it is science, but rather of a certain kind, and this is the healthy and the unhealthy, it too has become a certain kind of science. From which it happened that it is no longer called science simply, but with a certain quality added, medical science. I grasp it now, and it seems to me to be so. But thirst—will you not number it among those things which, as what they are, exist as of something? And is there thirst? I number it indeed, and I say thirst is of drink. Is it not that a certain kind of thirst is for a certain kind of drink? And therefore thirst itself is neither of much, nor [abbrev: *neq;*] of little, nor of good, nor of evil, nor, to embrace it in one word, of any certain kind, but thirst is by its nature only of drink itself. It is entirely so. Therefore the soul of the thirsty one, insofar as it is thirst, appetites nothing else than to drink, and affects that, and is carried toward it. It is agreed. If, therefore, something sometimes draws back the thirsty soul, it will be something else in it, different from that part which thirsts and impels it like a beast to drink. For we say it cannot be that the same thing acts in contrary ways at the same time with the same part of itself concerning the same thing. Certainly not. Just as it is absurd to say of the same archer that his hands at once propel the bow and draw it back [abbrev: *atq;*] and contract it. Rather, it must be said that it is one hand that propels and another [abbrev: *alterā*] that draws back. Exactly so. Do we confess that there are some who, though they thirst, sometimes do not wish to drink? Many, and often. What shall one say of these? Is there not in their soul something that allures them to drink, and something contrary that prohibits it? Which is indeed something else, and it dominates that which allures. It seems so to me. Is it not therefore that what prohibits these things is in them from reason whenever it operates? But those things which bind and [abbrev: *atq;*] draw, are they from affections and perturbations? It appears so. Deservedly, therefore, shall we judge these two to be diverse from each other, and that by which the mind reasons, we shall name the rational [part] of it. But that by which it loves, hungers, and thirsts, and falls more prone to other lusts, we shall call the irrational, and the greedy companion of certain repletions and pleasures. Diverse indeed, he said. And deservedly shall we so judge. These two species now in the soul, I said, let them be distinct. But that which pertains to anger, or by which we are angered—is it a third thing? Or is it kindred to one of these? Perhaps, he said, it is kindred to that which desires pleasures. Yet I believe this from what I once heard: that [abbrev: *ꝙ*] Leontius the son of Aglaion, ascending from the Piraeus under the northern wall (to the city), perceived dead bodies lying in the city's pit and public sewer; at once he desired to see them, and yet he was horrified, and turned away [abbrev: *auersabaturq;*], and covered his face, fighting with himself. Finally, overcome by desire [abbrev: *cupiditate deniq; q;*], he ran to the corpses with eyes intent, saying: "Behold now you may, O wretched ones, fill your desire with this beautiful spectacle." I too have heard this. And so the speech testifies that anger often fights against concupiscence, as if these were diverse among themselves. It certainly signifies that. And do we not frequently observe elsewhere, when desires bring force upon someone contrary to reason, that they rebuke themselves, and are indignant against that part of themselves which brings the force? And as if between two dissenters, anger runs as an ally to reason? But as for being joined to desires, I do not think you have ever asserted, either in yourself or in another, that such a thing has been perceived, that spirit works anything contrary to the will of reason. Never, by Jove. What then, I said. When someone thinks he is inflicting an injury, is it not that the more noble he is, the less he is angered, though he hungers and freezes, and suffers anything else from him whom he deems to act justly? And as I said, his anger is not excited against him? You speak the truth.

[[page number: 396]]
### Thirty-First Book

...you speak. What then? When someone thinks he suffers an injury, does he not then boil and rage, and offer aid to that which seems just, enduring hunger, cold, and other such things? And he contends for victory, nor [abbrev: *neq;*] does he cease from his noble work until he has either finished it, or died, or finally, like a dog by a shepherd, he is called back by the reason within him and grows mild? Entirely so, this power is similar to that to which you compare it. For in our city we placed the auxiliaries themselves like dogs, obeying the princes as if they were certain shepherds of the city. You have understood excellently what I wished to say. But do you notice this one thing further? What is that? That at present we judge concerning anger contrary to what we did above. For then we referred the power of being angered to the nature of concupiscence. But now we say it differs much, and we assert much more that anger takes up arms for reason when the parts of the soul are in discord. Exactly so. Is the power of being angered also diverse from reason, or a certain species of reason, so that there are not three species in the soul, but two: the rational and the concupiscent? Or rather, just as three classes contained the city—the mercantile, the auxiliary, and the consultative—so also in the soul there is a third power, namely irascibility [anger], which by its very nature protects the parts of reason, unless it has been depraved by wicked education? It must be that it is a third. Truly, even if it appeared as something other than reason, as was seen above, differing from concupiscence. But indeed, this can easily be made clear. For anyone may understand this in small children, who are full of anger as soon as they are born. But of reason, some never, and many seem to me to become composed late. By Jove, I say, you speak excellently. Moreover, anyone will find it to be so in beasts, as you yourself say [[margin: *Odyssey*]]. Homer also testifies to this, in that which we cited above: "Striking his breast, he addressed it with bitter warnings." For here Homer clearly made one of these rebuke the other, namely reason itself consulting about better and worse, [rebuking] the irrational impulse of anger. You speak very rightly. In these things, therefore, we have finally agreed, and it is sufficiently established between us that there are the same classes in the city and the same and equal in number in the soul of each. So certainly. And is this not now necessary, that just as and by what the city was wise, so also by the same the individual is wise? Plainly. Likewise, by what a certain individual is brave and how, by that same thing the city is brave, and in all other things both behave similarly toward virtue. It is necessary. And yet, O Glauco, we shall call a man just by the same reason by which we call the city [just]. That is entirely necessary. But we have not yet forgotten that [abbrev: *ꝙ*] the city appeared just from this, that while there are three classes of men in it, each fulfills his own office. We certainly do not seem to have forgotten. Therefore it must be remembered that each of us, whose individual parts of the soul do what is their own, will both be just and performing his own [affairs]. To remember entirely. Does it not befit the rational power to command, since it is wise and carries the providence of the whole soul? And for the nature of anger to be obedient to reason, and to fight for it? Inwardly. Did not the mixture and temperance of music and gymnastics, as we treated above, effect this so that these might be in concord? Stretching and increasing and nourishing one with noble speeches and disciplines; but relaxing, soothing, and taming the other through harmony and [abbrev: *atq;*] rhythm? Especially. And since these have been so nourished, and have truly learned what is their own, and have been excellently erudite, they will preside over the heat of concupiscence: which part of the soul is the most in everyone, nor [abbrev: *neq;*] can its nature ever be filled with money: and they will take care lest, increased by the filling of corporeal pleasures, it should escape as greater and more robust. And it should not wish only to perform its own office, but contend to subject to itself those things which it ought not to command by nature, and thus subvert the universal life of all. Exactly so. Nay even, it guards the whole soul and body from external enemies, while the former consults prudently, and the latter fights, obeys the prince, and follows with fortitude what has been consulted. These are true. Indeed we call each man brave in this part, when the vigor of anger in him observes, in the midst of pleasures and pains, that which reason has prescribed, whether it be harsh or not. Rightly. But wise by that small part which commanded in him and dictated those things, having in itself the science by which it discerns what is most useful both for each part and for the whole assembly of these three. Certainly. We call someone temperate, again, by the friendship and concord of these very parts, when both that which presides and that which is commanded agree in the same opinion, namely that reason ought to command, and it must not be deserted by the others. Temperance therefore, he said, is nothing else whether it be of the city or the individual. Finally, each will be just from that which we have often said, and as we have exposed. It is necessary, he said, entirely. What then, never? Is there anything that might disturb this our opinion to the point that justice appears to be something else to us than what was established in the city? It does not seem so to me, he said. So then, I said, entirely, if anything is still in controversy among us, we shall debate it, proposing those things which might seem to be said against it. Of what kind? As if we had to deliberate concerning that city, and concerning a man born and nourished in the same manner with it, whether such a man, when he has received a deposit of gold or silver, would seem likely to devise a fraud; do you think anyone would judge such a man would commit a fraud rather than men otherwise affected? No one at all. Will he not abstain from sacrilege, theft, and betrayals, both privately against companions and publicly against the republic? Surely. And he is not perfidious either in an oath or in any [abbrev: *quibuicunq;*] dealings. By no means. Adulteries, contempt for parents, impiety toward the Gods—these befit anyone else rather than him. Exactly so. And is not the cause of all these things this, that whatever is in him executes its own work, whether by commanding or by obeying? Certainly no other. What else do you seek justice to be than this very power, which makes such men and such cities? I, he said, [seek] nothing else. At last that dream has been fulfilled for us, which we said we had guessed: namely that [abbrev: *ꝙ*] soon after beginning to found the city, with some God favoring us, we seemed to have entered into some principle and image of justice. Entirely so. But this, O Glauco, was that on account of which a certain likeness of justice is conferred. Namely, that he who is by nature a tanner ought to execute this art and do nothing else, and he who is a smith, to forge. And similarly in the rest. It appears so. Truly such is justice, but not concerning exterior action, but rather concerning the interior action of its parts truly toward the soul itself and its own: while it permits nothing of its own to attempt alien things, nor does it allow the species of the soul to handle works mutually confounding each other: but in truth it rightly digests its own affairs, and is master of itself, adorns itself, and is a friend to itself...

[[page number: 397]]
### Fourth Dialogue on the Republic; Or, On Justice

...having become a friend to himself, tempering those three parts in himself like three terms of harmony—the lowest, the highest, and the middle, or whatever other middle there may be. Thus binding all these together, he becomes entirely one out of many, tempered and [abbrev: *atq;*] composed, and thus finally he acts if he acts at all, whether concerning the acquisition of money, or the care of the body, or even concerning civil or private dealings, in all these considering and calling that action just and noble which performs and preserves this habit. And [calling] wisdom the science presiding over this operation; but the unjust operation that which dissolves this; and ignorance the leader of this operation, opinion. You speak the truth, O Socrates. If therefore we say we have found the just man, and the just city, and what justice is in both, we shall not, I think, be seen to be measuring much [wrong]. Not by Jove. Is it to be asserted then? Without doubt. Let it be so then. Indeed, next we must consider injustice. Plainly. It is fitting to call injustice a certain sedition of these three, a meddlesome and varied usurpation of another's work, and an insolent prevarication of a certain part rebelling against the whole soul, and rising up to command the royal kind of the soul, which nature commands it to serve. Such things, as I think, and the perturbation and error of these, we shall say is injustice, and intemperance, cowardice, ignorance, and finally universal depravity. These things are exactly so. Does it not now appear clearly enough what it is to do unjust things and to inflict injury, and again what it is to do just things, since justice and injustice are clear? In what way? Because they differ nothing from healthy things. Truly, as these are regarding the body, so those are regarding the soul. By what reason? Healthy things induce health, unhealthy things disease. Plainly. Similarly also to act justly begets justice in the soul; to do unjust things, injustice. It is necessary. But to bring health is so to dispose the things in the body that according to the order of its nature they are mastered and master among themselves. Disease, however, is for one to command and another to obey contrary to nature. It is so. By the same reason, to provide justice to anyone is nothing else than [abbrev: *ꝙ*] to digest the parts of the soul into their own order, so that they obey and command according to the norm of nature. Injustice, however, is so that one commands and obeys another contrary to nature. Exactly. Virtue therefore, as it appears, is a certain health, and beauty, and good constitution of the soul. Depravity, on the contrary, is disease, baseness, and weakness. It is as you say. Is it not therefore that honorable exercises lead to the acquisition of virtue, and base ones to depravity? It is necessary. It remains to be seen and discussed whether it profits to act justly, to cultivate honorable things, to be just, whether it be hidden or not: or to inflict injury and be unjust, provided one does not pay the penalty, nor becomes better through chastisement. To me, O Socrates, this debate seems ridiculous. If indeed, the nature of the body being corrupted, it seems life is not to be lived, even in the greatest abundance of feasts and drinks, all riches, and the empire of the whole world. But the nature of that by which we live [the soul] being perturbed and corrupted, shall life be lived, if one does whatever he pleases, other than this one thing, whence he may be liberated from improbity and iniquity, and acquire justice and probity, after both these have appeared such as we have described. Ridiculous indeed, I said. But since we have come to the point that it can be made most manifest that these things are so, we must not be weary. By Jove, least of all. Come then, I said, step here, that you may see how many species vice has, as it seems to me. Attend now. Truly these are worthy of being seen. I follow indeed, only speak. And yet, as if from a watchtower, after we have ascended here by reasoning, one species of virtue occurs to me, but of depravity innumerable. Of which there are four certain ones which must be remembered. How do you say that? Just as there are modes of republics having their own species, so many also appear to be of the soul itself. How many? Five of republics, and again five of the soul. Say which ones. I assert this one mode of republic to be that which we have polished. But it can be called by two names. For if among the princes of the city one certain man is most excellent of all, it will be called a kingdom. But if many, it will be the government of the optimates [aristocracy]. You tell the truth. I say this is one species because whether many govern, or one, no one who has been thus educated and erudite as we said, will change anything worthy of estimation in the laws of the republic. For it would not be consistent, he said.

### FIFTH DIALOGUE ON THE REPUBLIC; OR, ON JUSTICE.
\*
#### ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.

I AM NOT unaware that there will be some who expect an Apology from us, by which we might defend this fifth dialogue, positing the community of all things in the city, against the calumnies of both the malicious and even the ignorant. But let them read Plato himself, I pray, let them read diligently, and judge without envy; an Apology (I know what I say) they will not desire. Plato therefore, the Phoebus [shining healer] of the human race, who noticed that individual men and families and cities are always and everywhere gravely ill, nor have they yet been liberated from the disease by any medicines of civil physicians curing in vain for so many centuries, or at least relieved a little... he prudently and piously turned to that chief law among physicians... if one does not recover by such medicines, say cold ones long applied, one must finally cross over to hot ones. Knowing therefore that the human race profits nothing through laws distributing private property for so many centuries, but rather falls daily into worse, not unjustly he transferred the laws to friendship, commanding all things to be common among friends... [Ficino continues to cite historical and philosophical precedents like the Bohemians, Diodorus's island, the Garamantes, Brahmans, Gymnosophists, Essenes, Pythagoreans, and early Christians].

[[page number: 398]]
### Thirty-First Book

...note first the Socratic providence, deeming it worse to err in constituting laws than to kill a man. For an error of this kind kills many souls and bodies together through many centuries. Then [note] the modesty of one approaching difficult things with diffidence... [Ficino notes the invocation of the goddess Adrasteia]. Next, he proceeds gradually to the common discipline, namely from the institution of men to the institution of women likewise. He commands all private and public studies, both of peace and war, to be common to women with men, lest the human race be maimed...

[The Dialogue Begins]

I CALL THE GOOD city of this kind and a right Republic, and such a man I say is good. And if this republic is right, others I call depraved, insofar as they wander concerning the government of the city itself and the discipline of private citizens, which are indeed in four species of depravity. Which are those? he said. Then I proceeded to tell by what reason each seemed to me to depend upon the other in turn. But Polemarchus—for he sat a little further from me than Adimantus—sitting behind Adimantus's back, extended his hand, and catching Adimantus's cloak from above around the shoulders, he drew him to himself, and moved his mouth to his ear. Of those things which he said, we perceived nothing except this one thing: "Shall we permit it? Or what shall we do?" To which Adimantus, responding more loudly, said: "By no means." At this I said: "What is it that you do not wish to permit?" "You," he said. "Why so?" I said. "You seem to us to be declining," he said, "and to be keeping silent and stealing away from us a whole part of this dispute, and not a small one: and you think it escapes us that you spoke poorly regarding wives and children, that it is established for all that all things ought to be common among friends." "Was it not rightly said, O Adimantus?" I asked. "Rightly indeed," he said, "but just as in other things, so in this it must be explained by what reason it is rightly so, and what is the mode of the community. For there can be many. Do not therefore omit to open to us which one you especially mean. For we have long been waiting, hoping you would expose both concerning the procreation of children... and concerning nutrition... and the community of wives and children."

[[page number: 399]]
### Fifth Dialogue on the Republic; Or, On Justice

...everyone, O Socrates, think [that we agree]. "What are you doing, I pray, why do you call me back thus? What a grave dispute about the Republic you raise again as if from the beginning! Truly I was rejoicing as if I had already finished this, thinking it sufficient if anyone accepted these things in the part they were said. Which you now demanding, do not know what a swarm of disputes you incite. Which I, foreseeing then, omitted lest it excite many disturbances for us." "What indeed," said Thrasymachus, "do you think these have come here, O Socrates, to smelt gold, or rather to hear discourses?" "To hear discourses," I said, "but moderate ones." "The measure and term of hearing these discourses, O Socrates," said Glauco, "is the whole of life for men having a mind. But dismiss us; do not be burdened, if it seems good to you, to declare what we seek: what shall be the community of our guardians regarding women and children... strive to open these to us." "It cannot easily be explained, O blessed man," I said, "for in these there are more ambiguities than in the former things. First, whether these can be done would be doubted. Furthermore, if they can, whether they are the best, and how, will be doubted. Wherefore this difficulty discourages me, fearing, O most joined friend, lest this my speech should seem to be a certain wish [vow]." "Do not be reluctant," he said, "I pray, for you do not have ungrateful, or incredulous, or malevolent auditors." "O best man," I said, "do you bring these things to exhort me?" "Indeed." "On the contrary," I said, "you do the opposite. For if I persuaded myself that I knew these things which I say, this exhortation would be timely. For it is safe and daring to pronounce the truths which one knows about the greatest and most precious things among prudent friends. But to speak words with diffidence and ambiguity, as I myself do, is to be avoided and dangerous, lest I move the auditors to laughter: for that is childish indeed: but lest wandering far from the truth, I myself succumb to falsehood, and draw my friends with me into ruin... I adore therefore suppliant Adrasteia [Nemesis] for those things which I am about to say, Glauco. For I reckon him to offend less who kills someone unintentionally than he who deceives concerning the constitutions of honorable, good, and just things. It is better to undergo this risk among enemy men than friends. Wherefore, O Glauco, better confirm me." "But indeed, O Socrates," said Glauco, "if by any means it happens that we err from this dispute, we absolve you as if from a homicide, and we shall pronounce you innocent of this deception. Therefore enter the dispute boldly." "Furthermore, he who is absolved there is innocent, as the laws teach," I said. "Therefore he who is absolved here is innocent. Speak therefore, on this account." "It is necessary to speak now again," I said, "things which perhaps ought to have been said next. Perhaps it is worthwhile, after those things pertaining to men have had their act, next to refer to those which are of women, especially since you yourself exhort me to this. To men born and erudite as we described above, as my opinion goes, there is no other right acquisition and use of children and women than by walking that way which we ourselves entered from the beginning. For we attempted to set men over the flock as guardians in our speech. Indeed," he said. "Let us follow then, applying a most similar generation and nutrition, and let us consider whether it is fitting so, or not?" "In what way?" he said. "Thus: do we think that among guardian dogs, the females themselves ought to guard together the same things which the males do, and hunt together, and do all other things in common? Or do we keep the females inside for domestic affairs, as being weak because of the birth and nutrition of the pups; but the males undergo the labors and carry the whole care of the herd?" "We attribute all things commonly to them," he said, "except that we use the females as weaker, and the males as more robust." "Can it be that you use any animal for the same things unless you have nourished and erudite it in the same reason?" "In no way." "If therefore we use the females for the same things as the men, it is fitting to erudite them in the same. Certainly. But we attributed music and gymnastics to the men. Surely. Therefore these arts and bellicose affairs are to be attributed to women similarly, and it is fitting to use them for the same. That is consistent indeed from what you say. Perhaps many things contrary to custom will seem ridiculous if they are done as they are said. And especially indeed. What do you see most ridiculous in these? Or is it because you are to see naked women in the wrestling grounds [palaestra] contending with men, not only young ones, but even old women, just as old men in the gymnasia when they exercise together, though they are now wrinkled and not pleasant to the sight?" "So by Jove," he said. "For that would seem ridiculous as things now are. We therefore, after we began to speak, ought not to fear at all the ridicule of facetious men... regarding music and gymnastics, nor less regarding equestrian armor and power. You speak rightly. Therefore after we began, let us proceed to the severity of the law, asking those not to act in their usual way, but to think serious things, admonishing [abbrev: *q;*] them that it was not long ago when it seemed base and ridiculous to the Greeks what today seems ridiculous to most of the barbarians, namely to see naked men: and when they first approached exercises of this kind—first indeed the Cretans, then also the Lacedaemonians—it was certainly permitted to urban and facetious men who then were to carp at all these things, or do you not think so? Indeed. But after, as I think, it seemed more commodious to those using it to exercise with the body naked than covered, it happened that because the best thing had been indicated by speech, it did not seem ridiculous to the eyes. From which it is manifest that he is vain who thinks anything ridiculous except what is evil... It is entirely so. Ought we not first to agree on this, whether these things can be done, or not? To grant to anyone to doubt against these at will, whether in jest or in earnest, whether in the nature of humans the female can communicate with the male in all works, or in none, or be strong in some but in others not at all, and in which of these kinds military service is? Will not whoever has thus rightly begun, as is decent, also rightly finish? Especially. Do you wish that we ourselves, for the sake of others, oppose ourselves to the doubts, lest those things which belong to another reason be attacked without defense? Nothing prohibits it. Let us say therefore in their person in this manner.

[[page number: 400]]
### Thirty-First Book

"There is no need, O Socrates and Glauco, for others to oppose us. For among us from the very beginning of founding the city it was established that it is necessary for each one to perform one certain thing which is his own according to nature. It was established, why not? Is it not then that the woman herself does not differ far in nature from the man? Why should she not differ? Therefore, must not a different work be attributed to each according to the nature of each? Without doubt. What remains then, but that you wander now and contradict yourselves, since you assert that men and women ought to work at the same things, though they differ greatly in nature? Will you have, O wonderful man, what you may respond to these for our defense?" "At present indeed," he said, "not easily enough, but I pray you and I beg that you expose what can most especially be brought in defense of our speech." "These things indeed, O Glauco," I said, "and many others of the same kind, I have long foreseen, timid and unwilling to descend to this law concerning the acquisition and nutrition of women and children." "Truly," he said, "it does not appear light." "Certainly not. But the matter is thus. Whether someone has fallen into a small pond or the deep sea, nevertheless he swims in the middle of the water. Exactly. And must we not also swim, and strive, that we may escape the waves of the dispute unharmed, hoping either some dolphin will receive us or some other unhoped-for and repentant cause of safety will be for us? So it seems. Look around I pray, if we might find any exit. For it is agreed between us that a different nature ought to handle a different work; but the nature of woman and man is different. Now we command these diverse natures to study the same things. In this we are accused by you. Greatly. How noble, O Glauco, is the power of the contradictory art? Why, he said? Because it seems to me that many fall into it even unwillingly, thinking they are not at all litigating but discoursing, from the fact that they cannot perceive what is said according to the dividing species, but rather they pursue the contradiction by the name itself of the thing proposed, contending rather than disputing. For it happens to many; but does the same now happen to us? And especially indeed, I said. We seem to touch upon a contradiction unwillingly. By what reason? Because we contend very strongly and contentiously, if you look at the words, that the same nature ought not to handle the same works. But we have considered in no way what species of another or the same nature it may be, and where looking then we described different studies for different natures, and the same for the same. Certainly we did not consider that. But it is permitted to us, it seems, to inquire of ourselves: is the nature of the bald and the long-haired the same, or rather contrary? And after we have confessed it to be contrary, if the bald cut leather and make shoes, we should by no means allow the long-haired to do the same; but if the long-haired do it, we should not allow [abbrev: *nequaꝙ*] the bald. But that would be worthy of laughter," he said. "Is it for anything else that this is laughable than that we could not then consider entirely the same and different nature, but we observed only that species of dissimilitude and similitude which pertained to those same studies? Just as we said a physician and a man having a soul apt for the studies of medicine have the same nature, or do you not think so? Indeed. But one apt for medicine, and another man prompt for building. Entirely. Is it not, I say, that the genus of men and women, if they differ nothing among themselves in some art or study, we shall say this must be assigned to them? But if they seem to differ in this alone, that the female [abbrev: *fœmina*] bears and the male begets, we shall by no means admit it has been shown that a woman differs from a man regarding that of which we now speak, but we shall still judge that both guardians and women ought to exercise the same things among us? Rightly indeed. Do we not next command him who says the contrary to teach us this very thing: for what art, or what office of those which lead to the institution of the city, is the nature of man and woman not the same, but diverse? So certainly it is fitting. Perhaps what you said a little before, another also would say: it may be enough to say suddenly that it is not easy; but if it be thought upon, not very difficult. He would say so. Shall we pray him who opposes us to lend his ears to us, and attend, if by any reason we might show him that there is no study pertaining to the government of the city peculiar to a woman? By all means. Come then, let us say to him: Respond, did you not say that one is endowed by nature with an apt or inapt [abbrev: *ineptoue*] disposition for a certain work based on this: that he perceives anything easily, the other with difficulty; and the former, if he has learned some small thing from anyone, finds much from it himself; but the latter, though he has learned and thought out many things, does not even preserve those which he learned... Are there other things besides these by which you distinguish a man well-instituted by nature for something from one poorly instituted? No one will say others. Do you know of anything practiced by men in which the genus of men does not have all things the same and more excellently than the genus of women? Or shall we wander in words, commemorating the art of weaving, and the confection of cakes and dishes, in which the genus of women seems to be something, where it appears very ridiculous when it is surpassed? You speak the truth," he said, "because by far in all things, as I might say, genus is surpassed by genus. But many women are more excellent than many men at many things. But the whole itself is as you say. There is therefore no office, O friend, among those who administer the city that is peculiar to a woman insofar as she is a woman, or peculiar to a man insofar as he is a man, but the natures of both are equally dispersed in living things: and the female is a participant by nature in all duties, and the man in all: but in all the female is weaker than the man. It is entirely so. Shall we then prescribe all things to men, and nothing to a woman? But how? There is indeed, I think, as we shall bring forth, among women also one apt for medicine, another not; one musical, another by nature alienated from music. Why not? And one indeed prompt for gymnastic exercises and military affairs, another inapt for these. So I think. Is not one also studious of wisdom, another despises wisdom; and one high-spirited, another low-spirited? I assert this too. There is therefore among females one fit for guarding, another not at all. Did we not choose a certain nature of this kind of men apt for guarding? Surely of that kind. The nature of woman and man is therefore the same for guarding the city, except that women are to be used as weaker, men as more robust. It appears so. Therefore such women are to be chosen to dwell with and guard the city together with the men, since they are fit and kindred to them by nature. Exactly. But are not the same studies to be attributed to the same natures? The same. At last, by a long circuit, we have returned to those prior things, and we have granted that it is not against nature for the women of the guardians to be exercised in music and gymnastics. Most greatly. Wherefore we have established by law neither impossible things, nor things similar to a wish, since...

[[page number: 401]]
### Fifth Dialogue on the Republic; Or, On Justice

...those things which are done against these in these times are much more against nature, as it seems. It seems so. Was it not for us to debate whether we were saying things possible and best, or not? It was. That they are possible, was established. Plainly. That they are best, must be asserted after this. It is manifest. To this end, that women might escape as sufficient for guarding, no other discipline is needed than that by which we instruct men for the same, especially since the same is found in the nature of both. No other. Furthermore, what do you think of this? Of what? Whether you think some men are better and others worse, or all similar. By no means. In the city which we have founded, do you think more excellent men are made guardians, having obtained the discipline we gave, than tanners imbued with the tanning skill? You ask a ridiculous thing, he said. I understand indeed. What then? Are not these the best of the rest of the citizens? And of the rest. Furthermore, will such women be the best of women? Greatly. Is there anything better for a city than that men [abbrev: *ꝙ*] and women be made as best as possible? There is not. But music and gymnastics, if they are present as we related above, can perfect this. Without doubt. Therefore it is not only possible, but also a best thing for the city, established by law. It is so. The body of the women guardians will therefore have to be stripped, since they will put on virtue instead of clothes. And they must communicate in war and other guardianship of the city, nor do anything else. Nevertheless, the lighter of these offices are to be attributed to women rather than men because of the weakness of the genus. But he who laughs at naked women exercising themselves for the sake of some best thing, carps at a fruit of wisdom in vain regarding ridiculous trifles, nor does he understand what he laughs at, nor what he does. For it is elegantly said and will be said: that what is useful is honorable; but what is noxious is base. And especially indeed. Let us say therefore that we have swum out from this one wave, as it were, treating of the law of women, so that we were not entirely submerged while we affirmed that all things ought to be exercised commonly by the guardians among us, both men and women. Yea rather, our speech agreed with itself, namely that it brought things both possible and useful. You have escaped no small wave. You will say it is not huge when you see what follows next. Speak now that I may see. This law, as I think, and the others prior, this also follows. Which one? That these women of these men be all common to all, and that no one dwell privately with any, and again common children, nor [abbrev: *neq;*] should the father know his son, nor the son recognize his father. Certainly it is believed much more difficultly that this is either possible or useful. I do not indeed think it will be doubtful to anyone that it would be useful and a greatest good for women to be common and children common, if only it could be done. But I think the greatest controversy will be in this: whether it can be done, or not. Regarding both, surely, he said, it will be greatly doubted. You say, I said, a conspiracy of both speeches. But I thought I would be liberated from one if it seemed useful to you. For it would remain for me to inquire whether it is possible or not. But you could not be hidden while you fled, he said. Give the reason for both. A penalty must certainly be sustained by me, I said, but indulge me in this. Let me refresh myself like a festive man, as those who are lazy in mind are wont to feed themselves with thought whenever they walk alone. For such men, before they have found out by what means what they seek can be done, omitting this care lest they be burdened by too much labor, while they deliberate about the possible and the impossible, as if that were already so which they affect, they persuade themselves: and next they digest the rest, and are delighted while they think what kind of things they will do with that present, and thus they render the torpid mind even more languid. Not otherwise do I myself grow lazy, and I desire to differ that debate to another time, whether these things are possible or not. At present, however, admitting them as possible, I shall inquire if you permit, by what reason the princes themselves will dispose these existing things, and how these will be the most useful of all if they are done, both for the guardians and for the city. These things I shall strive to consider with you first, but those later, if you grant it. I grant it indeed, consider now. I think therefore, I said, if only the princes will be worthy of this name, and in the same way their ministers, these will wish to execute what is commanded, but those will command, partly obeying the laws themselves, partly imitating them insofar as we have permitted them. That is probable. You therefore, the lawgiver, as you chose the men, so also choosing the women, will provide them as similar to each other as possible in nature. But these, as having houses and meals in common, and possessing nothing of such things as their own, will dwell together, and congregating among themselves in the gymnasia and the rest of their living, they will be drawn from innate necessity, as I think, to mutual commingling. Do I not seem to you to say necessary things? By no means [physically] necessary, but by a certain geometric necessity, or rather an amatory one, which is much sharper than that for persuading the common people and drawing them. Surely vehement, I said. But after this, O Glauco, to be denuded among themselves without order, or to do anything else, is neither holy in a city of blessed men, nor will the magistrates permit it. Nor would it be just, he said. It is established indeed that [abbrev: *ꝙ*] we shall next institute marriages as sacred as possible. But they would be sacred as they are most useful. Most greatly. In what way will they be most useful? Tell me this, O Glauco. I see indeed in your house both hunting dogs and many noble birds. Now, have you ever noticed anything regarding their coitus and generation? To what purpose is that? First among these themselves, although noble, are there not some most excellent ones? There are. Whether, therefore, do you permit generation to happen from any equally? Or do you take care rather that they be generated from the best? From the best. From the very young, or those finished by age? Or rather those constituted in the flower of age? From these themselves rather. And unless generation happens in this manner, do you think the genus of dogs and birds will be far worse? Indeed. Do you think it happens otherwise in horses and other animals? That would be absurd. Pope! [Alas/Wow!], O most joined friend, how we have need of the highest princes, if indeed it is the same in the human race. It is so, what then? Because it is necessary, I said, that they use many medicines. For when bodies do not need medicines, but only require the institution of diet, we judge a cheaper physician to suffice. But when it must be acted with medicines, we know there will be need of a more excellent physician. You tell the truth. But to what purpose are these things? Truly it will seem necessary for the princes to use frequent lying and deception for the utility of the subjects. We said above that all such things are useful in the place of pharmacy and medicine. And rightly indeed. In marriages therefore and the procreation of children, it seems this is done rightly, not moderately. In what way? It is fitting surely according to those things we granted above, that the best men congregate with the best women as much as possible...

[[page number: 402]]
### Thirty-First Book

...as much as possible; but the worst, on the contrary, with the worst. And to nourish the offspring of the former indeed, but not of the latter, if the herd is to be most excellent. And while all these things are done, they should be ignored by all except the princes, if the herd of guardians is to be free of sedition. Very rightly. Therefore certain festivals will have to be designated by laws, in which we shall congregate the grooms and brides, sacred rites will be performed, and hymns by our poets, befitting the celebrated marriages. But the number of marriages we shall concede to the judgment of the princes, so that looking toward enemies and diseases and other such things, they may preserve as much as possible the same number of citizens, lest the city be too populous insofar as possible, nor empty. You speak rightly. Therefore certain lots of such a kind of artifice are to be instituted, so that that worse man in any coupling may blame fortune, not the princes. And especially indeed. Furthermore, next, among the more excellent young men in affairs either military or others, gifts and prizes are to be given, and many such: nay even, more abundant license of congregating with women, so that from this occasion at once more children than from others might be borne from these. Rightly. Thus the children who are born from these, those magistrates will receive who preside over such things, whether of men, or of females, or of both, for the magistrates are common to men and women. It is so. Receiving surely the offspring of excellent men, they will carry them to the fold, to certain nurses dwelling apart in some part of the city. But those who are born from the worse, or even from any others but maimed in some limb, they will hide in hidden places as is decent, since the genus of guardians is to be pure. Furthermore, these will care for the nutrition. For they will transmit mothers to the fold when they abound with milk, taking care lest any be able to recognize her own. And if these are not sufficient, they will add others besides full of milk. They will also provide that a moderate time be kept in sucking milk. Likewise they will command vigils and other labors to the nurses. Much power you attribute to the women of the guardians for procrearing offspring, he said. So it is decent. But come next, let us run through what we especially intended. We said clearly that it is fitting for children to be procreated from those who are in the flower of age. We said so. Does it not seem to you also that a moderate time of ripe age is twenty years for a woman, but thirty for a man? What is the mode of these? Namely, that a woman beginning from the twentieth year of age should bear until the fortieth: but a man after he has passed the highest flower of his course (namely thirty years) should procreate until fifty-five years. Surely, he said, in these ages the vigor of mind and body consists. If therefore one older than these, or younger, touches generation in common, we shall deem this a profane and iniquitous crime, as if a fetus were brought into the city which, if it be hidden, will arise not under sacrifices and vows which the priests, both men and women, and the whole city will perform in individual marriages, praying that from good better may be born, from useful more useful: but rather under the darkness from a certain grave incontinence. You speak rightly. The same reason will also be had regarding him who, when he is still in the age for generating, but has not been coupled by the prince, touches a woman of legitimate age. Truly we shall assert this man generates a spurious, incestuous, and profane boy. Elegantly indeed. When therefore the women and men have already passed the age apt for generation, we shall say it is permitted to the men to be commingled with whomever they wish, except for the daughter and mother, and the children of daughters, and the elders of the mother: and it is permitted to women to be coupled with anyone, except for the son and father, and the elders and inferiors of the same. But when we have commanded these things, we shall interdict such a fetus (if it happens) from being brought into the light. If anything forces the mother to bear, we shall command it to be so exposed, as if there were no nutrition for it. These things also are rightly said. But the fathers and daughters and (other kinsmen) whom you mentioned, how will they discern each other in turn? In no way, but all who are born in the tenth month, or the seventh from that day on which someone worked for children, the males from this will be named sons, the females daughters. But those born will call him father, and similarly he will say the sons of those born are grandsons, and they will name the superiors grandfathers and grandmothers: and those who were born at that time when their fathers and mothers were generating, brothers and sisters. And thus what I just said, they would in no way touch each other. But to brothers and sisters the law will concede cohabitation, if the lot gives it, and Pythia [the oracle] confirms it through responses. Very rightly. Such indeed, O Glauco, will be the community of women and children among the guardians of the city; but that it agrees with the rest of the order of the city, and thus is by far the best, must next be confirmed by reason: or what shall we do? This by Jove, he said. Is not the principle of this agreement that we ask of ourselves, what maximum good we might find for the constitution of the city, looking toward which the legislator ought to establish laws, and what is the maximum evil? Let us consider then, whether those things which we just related agree with the investigation of the good itself, and dissent from the track of evil. Especially of all. Have we any more pernicious evil for a city than that which divides it and makes many out of one? Or anything better than that which conquers it at once as one, and makes it one? We have not. Does not the community of pleasure and pain unite, when all citizens rejoice and grieve together especially from the same access or decease of things? And especially indeed. But the diversity of these dissolves it, when at the same events of the city and of those who are in the city some grieve vehemently, others exult. Why not? From this however something such proceeds, when these words are not said at the same time in the city, namely "Mine" and "Not mine," and concerning the alien in the same way. Greatly. In whatever city therefore most say this same thing toward the same thing according to the same—"Mine" and "not mine"—that city is best governed. Exactly. And whichever is affected as most similarly to one man, as whenever the finger of any of us is struck, the whole community of the body reaching to the soul, feels at once in one coordination of that which dominates in the soul itself, and at once the whole grieves with the afflicted part. And therefore we say the man has a pain in his finger. And the reason is the same concerning any other part of the man: both that which is affected by pain, and that which is recreated by pleasure. The same reason certainly: and what you ask, the city which is best ruled, approaches most closely to this. Whenever, as I think, anything of good or evil happens to any of the citizens, such a city will cry out that he who is thus affected is its own, and therefore the whole will either rejoice together, or grieve. It must be that it happens so in a city governed by the best laws. But it is now time that we return to our city, and inquire whether those things which they have now established among us agree most with this city, or rather with another. It is permitted entirely. Are there not also in other cities princes and people, and similarly in this one? There are. And will all those call each other citizens? Why not? But beyond the name of citizen, how does the people call the princes in other cities? In most indeed lords [masters], but in a popular government, princes. But how will the people of our city call the princes beyond the name of citizen? Saviors and auxiliaries, he said. But in what way will those call the people? Tributaries of reward and nourishers. But those who preside in others, [how do they call] the people? Slaves. The princes themselves each other? Co-princes. But ours? Co-guardians. Have you anyone whom you may name among the princes of other cities, who calls one of his colleagues his kinsman, another an outsider? Indeed many. Therefore he both thinks and calls the kinsman his own: but the outsider as not his own. Plainly. But of your guardians, is there any who would judge and call any of his colleagues an outsider? None. For to whomever anyone meets, whether brother, or sister, or father, or mother, or son, or daughter, or their offspring, or elders, he will think he meets his own. You speak excellently: but respond also to this. Will you only impose the names of kinship on your citizens by law, or furthermore the duties of proximity, namely that they bear themselves so as the dignity of the appellation itself demands, and preserve toward parents whatever the law prescribes to be exhibited to them—reverence, care, obedience: otherwise they would have both the gods and men hostile, as those who do neither holy nor just things if they do the contrary? Will not other speeches than these, from all citizens, immediately resound to the ears of boys, both concerning parents (whomever anyone indicates to them) and concerning others close in genus? These certainly themselves. For it would be absurd if the names of kinship were uttered only by the mouth, without duty. In this city therefore especially of all, one being well or poorly affected, all will cry with one mouth what we were just saying: "Mine is well," or "Mine is poorly." You tell the truth. With this opinion and such words we said it followed that both pleasures are common and pains. And rightly indeed. In this therefore our citizens will communicate most with each other, that they say "Mine": from which communion it will follow that they have common pleasures and pains. Inwardly. But the cause of these, together with the rest of the constitution of the city, is the community itself of the guardians regarding women and children. It is entirely so. Indeed we confessed this to be the highest good for the city, when we said the city rightly governed was similar to a body, communicating with its individual parts concerning pleasure and pain in whatever way. And we deservedly conceded. Therefore the cause of the greatest good for the city has appeared to us to be that community of women and children among the auxiliaries. Greatly. And yet these are consonant with the prior things. For we said that neither private houses ought to be for these, nor fields, nor any possession, but they should receive nutrients as the reward of guardianship from others, and consume them commonly all, if they are to be true guardians. Rightly. Does not what I say, and the things said above and now, especially make it so that these escape as true guardians, nor [abbrev: *neq;*] do they distract the city, while they say "Mine" not as the same for all, but different for some than others, and one draws into his private house whatever he wishes to usurp apart from others, another into his own house diverse from others: and from private women and children, diverse ones rejoice and grieve for diverse reasons: but rather so that from one private same opinion of all, all tending toward the same thing insofar as possible, they are affected by similar pleasures and the same pains, if anything should happen? Especially. What then? Will not the controversies of judgments and mutual accusations all cease, since no one will have anything private except his body, but the rest will be common? Whence it follows that they will be without sedition, as far as pertains to those lawsuits which are wont to arise for the sake of money, or children, or kinsmen. It is entirely necessary that these be absent. Nay, nor will there be contention anywhere concerning force inflicted. For we shall assert it is honorable and equitable that an equal should ward off an equal from injury, imposing the province of protecting bodies. Rightly. And yet this law contains this right, that if anyone is angered with another, and contends to fill his anger, he will excite fewer toward greater seditions. It is entirely so. For our law will constitute the elder to preside over all younger ones, and to correct them. That is manifest indeed. It is established furthermore that [abbrev: *ꝙ*] the younger will never attempt to violate the elder unless by order of the princes or in another way, nor to strike him, as is decent, nor to affect him with any ignominy. For fear and shame are guardians sufficient to prohibit these things. Shame indeed will not permit those whom they suspect to be parents to be violated. But fear will deter each from injury, fearing namely lest all the rest, partly as sons, partly as brothers, partly as fathers, should succumb to the oppressed. Thus it entirely happens. Entirely therefore from these laws the citizens will lead a life in peace with each other. Most greatly. But with these not dissenting among themselves, it is not to be feared lest sometimes another city should fight against these, or they among themselves, and move seditions. Certainly not. I am ashamed to mention, because it is less decent, all the very small evils from which the citizens will be free. Adulations will certainly be absent, which the poor are wont to use against the rich. Likewise the anxieties of the indigent and the pains by which they are vexed in nourishing children, and in seeking money on account of the necessary nutrition of domestics, while they both give attention to usuries, and deny what they received, and study gain from everywhere. They put away furthermore among women and ministers, and very many things are hidden for a time. For how many things, and of what kind men suffer in these, O friend, are both servile and illiberal, and unworthy of being told. They are manifest even to a blind man. Furthermore they will be free from all these, and they will lead a life more blessed than that most blessed life of those who have won at Olympia. By what reason? Truly those are thought blessed for a small part of those things which these possess. For the victory of these is more noble, and their alimony from the public more perfect: and the victory of these is the safety of the whole city. Nutrients furthermore and whatever is necessary for diet they and their children receive in the place of a coronation. Honors moreover and prizes they follow from the republic itself while living, and when dead they have monuments of their sepulchres worthy of their virtues. These are certainly quite egregious. Do you remember that in the prior things some speech objected to us, as if we were making the guardians not at all blessed? since they have nothing, though it was permitted to them to possess all things of the citizens. But we responded then, that we would consider in the future if it should happen: for at present we were making guardians truly guardians, and the city as blessed as we could: nor looking to one certain part of it, but to the whole republic, seeking that beatitude. I remember indeed. Now certainly the life of the auxiliaries, since it appears by far more noble and better than of those who win at Olympia, in no way seems similar to the life of tanners, or other artisans, or farmers. Certainly not, as I too judge. Nevertheless what I also said above, it is fair that I repeat here: that if thus a guardian should study to be blessed so that he is not a guardian, nor does a life so moderate and stable and as we assert best suffice him: but an insane and childish opinion of happiness arisen, should snatch him on account of power itself to vindicate to himself all things which are in the city: [[margin: *Lib. 1. iγγν.*]] he will know that Hesiod wisely said, "The half is more than the whole." If he uses me as a counselor, he will remain in this life. Do you therefore approve the community which we attributed to women with men, as to discipline, the reception of children, the guardianship of other citizens so that they remain in the city together with men, militate in war, guard together, and hunt after the manner of dogs, and be participants in all offices entirely insofar as possible. And while they do these things, you concede they do the best, nor against the nature of the female, by which she was instituted to communicate with the male. I approve indeed. Does it not remain next that we declare whether this community can be among men just as in the rest of animals, and in what way it can. You have occupied what I was about to ask. Regarding the military matter indeed, I judge it is manifest in what way they will handle it. In what way? They will certainly militate commonly, and they will lead adult children with them to the battle: so that just as the sons of other craftsmen, these also may discern the works of their fathers, which they themselves also when they have reached mature age are to perform, and furthermore so that they may be an aid to parents, and minister all things which look to war, and the fathers and mothers may care for them. Or have you not noticed what happens in the arts, namely while the sons of potters watch their fathers shaping, and minister to them, before they bring their hand to the work? Especially. Should they erudite their sons more diligently than the guardians with the skill and inspection of works befitting each? That would be ridiculous indeed. Nay even, every kind of living thing fights more ardently when their young are present. It is so, but the danger is very great, O Socrates, lest if by chance, as happens in war, adverse fortune should occur, they lose their sons together with themselves, from which another city could not be restored. You speak the truth. But perhaps you judge that first each one ought to so prepare himself that he never undergoes any danger. In no way. What? Is it not then that one must come into risk, so that there those who have conducted themselves egregiously escape more excellent? It is manifest. Do you think it makes little difference, or is unworthy of being undertaken for the sake of danger, whether the boys who are to be soldiers see or do not see military affairs? Nay rather, it refers to what you say. Labor must therefore be given so that the boys watch the war, and it must be thought out by what reason they may be safe, and thus it will be rightly. Truly. At the start their parents will not be ignorant, but as far as is conceded to men, they will be perspicacious in discerning which camps have danger in them, which have no danger. That is very likely. Therefore they will lead them to the safer ones, to others not at all. Rightly. Then they will set rectors over them, not the most lazy ones, but men both by experience of things and by age fit as leaders and pedagogues. So it is decent. But we shall say many things happen beyond the opinion of many men. And especially indeed. For the sake of these, O friend, immediately from tender years certain wings are to be applied to the little boys, so that if ever there is need, they may immediately fly away. How do you say that? They must be placed on horses, so that immediately from boyhood they learn to ride, and they must be led to the spectacle of horses not fierce ones indeed, or too bellicose, but as swift as possible, and easily obeying the reins, and thus they will most commodiously discern their work, and they will escape most securely if anything adverse happens, following the elder leaders. You seem to me to speak very elegantly. What must be said of those things which pertain to war? What things are to be preserved by soldiers among themselves and against enemies? Do I think rightly, or not? What then? I judge that he who has deserted the order in the line, or cast away his arms, or committed any such thing on account of timidity, must be transmitted to the order of craftsmen or farmers. So it is decent. But he who has been captured alive by enemies, even if they wish to return him for free, must be left so that they may use the prey in whatever way they please. Entirely. But he who, conducting himself egregiously, has excelled, first indeed in the expedition itself he is to be crowned individually by any of the adolescents and boys who militate together, does it not seem so to you? Indeed to me. What: must they not also join right hands with him? This too. But this furthermore perhaps does not seem so to you? What? That he ought to receive and give kisses from anyone. Nay rather, most of all. But I judge it must be added to this law, that as long as they are in that expedition, it is permitted to no one to refuse whomever he himself desires to kiss, so that if anyone is captured by the love of anyone, whether male or female, he may be sharper to achieve victory. Elegantly, for it has already been said that marriages are more easily prepared for strenuous men than for others, and cooptions will be more frequent, so that as many as possible are born from these. We said so certainly. For according to Homer it is most just to honor such young men. For he said Ajax, excelling in war, was honored by continuous shoulders, as if this were an honor befitting a pubescent and brave man, from which at once honor and strength might be increased. Very rightly. In these things therefore we shall obey Homer. For we in the sacrifices and other such things will honor good men more, the more they appear good, both by hymns and by those things which we just said, likewise by seats and meats, and full bowls, so that we may both honor together the excellent men and women, and exercise them. You speak most beautifully. But him who has died in the militia when he has conducted himself strenuously, we shall say is of the first golden genus. Most of all. Then, faith being applied to Hesiod, we shall assert that whoever of this genus departs from life, they become holy terrestrial demons, the best expellers of evils, and guardians of mortals. So certainly we shall believe. Therefore we shall consult the oracle, in what way it is decent to bury blessed and divine men, and with what insignia especially to decorate them, and thus we shall bury them as it [the oracle] has ordered. Without doubt. For the remaining time we shall worship their sepulchres as of demons, and we shall adore them. The same we shall also preserve toward those who, though they have been judged to excel in life with exceptional probity, have ceased from life by old age or in some other way. It is decent surely. But how will our soldiers conduct themselves against enemies? In what matter? First indeed I ask about slavery, whether you judge it just that Greeks should reduce Greek cities to slavery: or rather, that they should not permit that to be done by others, and should resist according to their strength, and should accustom themselves to spare the genus of Greeks, taking care lest they be forced to serve barbarians themselves. It is altogether and in all ways better to spare (the Greeks), nor [abbrev: *neq;*] ought our men to make any Greek a slave: but also to counsel other Greeks rather to beware of this. Exactly. For thus more easily and more strongly against the barbarians...

[[vocabulary: Plato's Republic, Marsilio Ficino, Socrates, Glauco, Thrasymachus, justice (iustitia), state (republica), community of wives/children, guardian (custos), Greek vs. Barbarian warfare]]

--- Page 412 ---
396 Book Thirty-One <note>Likely referring to the volume number in this specific edition of the collected works.</note>.

...you speak. But what of this? When someone thinks they are suffering an injustice, does their spirit not boil and rage? Do they not stand as an ally to what they see as just, enduring hunger, cold, and all such hardships? They strive for victory and do not cease their noble effort until they either succeed or die—or, finally, like a dog called back by a shepherd, they are calmed by the reason within them. This power is entirely similar to the one you compare it to. Indeed, in our city, we placed the auxiliaries <note>The soldier class in Plato’s ideal state.</note> as dogs, obedient to the rulers as if to the shepherds of the city. You have understood perfectly what I meant to say. 

But do you notice this one thing further? What is that? That we are now judging the spirited part <note>Latin: *iracundia*, referring to the 'thumos' or the emotional, spirited part of the soul.</note> in a way opposite to how we did before. For then, we referred the power of anger to the nature of desire. But now, we say there is a great difference, and we assert much more strongly that when the parts of the soul are at odds, anger takes up arms on the side of reason. Exactly so. Is the power of anger something different from reason, or a species of reason, so that there are not three parts in the soul but only two: the rational and the desiring? Or rather, just as there were three classes that held the city together—the laborers, the auxiliaries, and the councilors—so too in the soul is there a third power, namely spiritedness, which by its nature protects the rational parts, unless it has been corrupted by bad education? It must be a third part. Indeed, it appears to be something other than reason, just as it was previously seen to be different from desire. 

Truly, this can be easily seen. For anyone can understand this in small children, who are full of anger as soon as they are born. Yet some, it seems to me, never become masters of reason, and many do so only late in life. By Jove, I say, you speak excellently. Furthermore, one may find it is the same in beasts, just as you say. <margin>Odyssey, Book 20</margin> Homer also bears witness to this, in the passage we quoted earlier: *Beating his breast, he rebuked his heart with bitter words.* For here, Homer clearly made one of these parts rebuke the other—namely, reason itself, consulting on the better and the worse, rebuking the irrational impulse of anger. You speak very correctly. 

In these matters, then, we have at last reached an agreement, and it is sufficiently established between us that the same classes exist in the city and in the soul of each individual, and they are equal in number. Certainly. Is it not then necessary that, just as the city was wise, so too is the individual wise in the same way? Plainly. Likewise, in the way a particular individual is brave, the city is brave in that same way; and in all other matters concerning virtue, both have the same relationship. It must be so. And so, Glaucon, we shall call a man just by the same rule by which we call a city just. That is entirely necessary. But we have not yet forgotten that the city appeared just because, while there are three classes of men within it, each one performs its own duty. We certainly have not forgotten that. We must remember, then, that each of us, whose individual parts of the soul do what is theirs to do, will be both just and a performer of his own duty. We must remember that indeed. 

Is it not fitting for the rational power to rule, since it is wise and carries the providence of the whole soul? And for the spirited nature to obey reason and fight for it? Entirely. As we discussed earlier, does not the mixture and tempering of music and gymnastics <note>Referring to the balance of intellectual and physical education.</note> make these parts concordant? It stretches and nourishes one with noble speeches and disciplines, while it relaxes, soothes, and tames the other through harmony and rhythm. Most certainly. And when these parts have been so nourished, and have truly learned what is theirs, and have been perfectly educated, they will preside over the heat of desire.
