This part of the soul is the most abundant in everyone and by its nature can never be satisfied with money. They will watch lest it becomes too large and robust from the fulfillment of bodily pleasures, and refuses to perform its own duty, but instead strives to subject those things to itself which by nature it ought not to rule, thereby overturning the entire life of all. 

Exactly so. Furthermore, this part protects the whole soul and body from external enemies; while one part consults with providence, the other fights, obeys the ruler, and carries out what has been decided with courage. These things are true. We certainly call an individual brave for this reason: when the vigor of his spirit observes, in the midst of pleasures and pains, that which reason has prescribed, whether it be harsh or not. Rightly. And we call him wise because of that small part which ruled within him and dictated these things, possessing within itself the knowledge by which it discerns what is most useful for each part and for the whole community of these three. Certainly. Again, we call someone temperate because of the friendship and concord of these very parts: when both the ruler and the ruled agree in the same opinion—namely, that reason ought to rule and should not be rebelled against. Temperance, therefore, he said, is nothing else, whether in the city or the individual. Finally, each person will be just for the reason we have now often stated, and in the manner we have explained. 

It is absolutely necessary, he said. What further, I asked? Is there anything that so disturbs our opinion that justice appears to us to be something other than what was established in the city? It does not seem so to me, he said. In this way, then, I say, we shall settle it entirely: if anything still remains in controversy between us, we shall discuss it by proposing what might be said against it. What sort of things? For instance, if we had to deliberate about that city, and about a man born and raised in the same way, whether such a man, if he received a deposit of gold or silver, might at some point devise a fraud—do you think anyone would judge such a man more likely to commit a fraud than those who are differently affected? No one at all. Will he not abstain from sacrilege, theft, and betrayals, both privately against companions and publicly against the republic? Surely. And he will not be unfaithful to an oath or to any other agreements. In no way. Adultery, contempt for parents, and impiety toward the Gods fit anyone else rather than him. Exactly. And is the cause of all these things not this: that whatever is within him performs its own work, whether by ruling or by obeying? Certainly no other. What else do you seek justice to be than this very power, which makes such men and such cities? I, he said, seek nothing else. At last, that dream of ours is fulfilled, which we said we had guessed: namely, that as soon as we began to build the city, with some God favoring us, we seemed to have entered upon a certain principle and image of justice. Entirely so. 

And this, Glaucon, was the reason why there is a certain image of justice: namely, that he who is by nature a leather-worker must perform this craft and do nothing else; and he who is a smith, must work as a smith. Similarly in other matters. It appears so. In truth, such is justice—but not concerning external action; rather, concerning the internal action of its parts, truly directed toward the soul itself and its own concerns. It permits nothing of its own to attempt what belongs to another, nor does it allow the classes of the soul to handle tasks that confuse one another. Instead, it rightly arranges its own affairs, becomes master of itself, adorns itself, and becomes a friend to itself...

--- Page 413 ---
Dialogue IV on the Republic, or, on Justice. 397

...having become a friend to itself, and tempering those three parts within itself like the three intervals of a harmony—the low, the high, and the middle—or any other intermediates there may be. Thus, binding all these together and having become entirely one out of many, temperate and composed, he only then acts, if he acts at all, whether regarding the acquisition of money, the care of the body, or even civil or private business. In all these things, he considers and calls that action "just and noble" which achieves and preserves this habit. He calls "wisdom" the science presiding over this operation; "unjust" the operation which dissolves this state; and "folly" the leader of this operation, which is mere opinion. 

You speak the absolute truth, Socrates. If we were to say, then, that we have found the just man and the just city, and what justice is in both, we would not, I think, be lying much. Not by Jove. Shall we assert it then? Without a doubt. So be it. 

Next, it seems we must consider injustice. Plainly. It is fitting to call injustice a certain "sedition" of these three parts, a meddlesome and varied usurpation of another's work, and an insolent rebellion of a certain part against the whole soul, rising up to rule over the sovereign class of the mind, which nature commands it to serve. We shall say that such things, I think, and their disturbance and error, are injustice, and intemperance, cowardice, folly, and, in short, all wickedness. This is exactly how it is. Is it not now clear enough what it is to do unjust things and to commit injury, and again what it is to do just things, since justice and injustice are clear? In what way? Because they differ in no way from things that are healthy. Just as those are to the body, so these are to the soul. In what way? Healthy things induce health, and unhealthy things induce disease. Plainly. Similarly, acting justly produces justice in the soul; acting unjustly produces injustice. But it is necessary to bring about health by so disposing the things in the body that they are mastered and master one another according to the order of nature itself. Disease, however, is for one thing to rule or obey another contrary to nature. It is so. By the same logic, to provide justice to someone is nothing other than to arrange the parts of the soul into their own order, so that they obey and rule according to the norm of nature. Injustice, however, is for one to rule or obey another contrary to nature. Exactly. Virtue, therefore, as it appears, is a certain health, beauty, and good constitution of the soul. Wickedness, on the contrary, is disease, ugliness, and weakness. It is as you say. 

Do not noble exercises, then, lead to the acquisition of virtue, and shameful ones to wickedness? It must be so. It remains, it seems, to be discussed whether it is profitable to act justly, to cultivate noble things, and to be just, whether that be hidden or not; or to commit injury and be unjust, provided one does not pay the penalty and does not become better through punishment. To me, Socrates, this discussion seems ridiculous. If the nature of the body is corrupted, it seems that life is not worth living, even in the greatest abundance of feasts and drinks, all riches, and the empire of the whole world. But when the nature of that by which we live <note>The soul.</note> is disturbed and corrupted, will life be worth living if someone does whatever he pleases, other than this one thing—by which he may be freed from wickedness and inequity, and attain justice and goodness—after both have appeared as we have described them? Ridiculous indeed, I said. But since we have come to the point where we can see as clearly as possible that these things are so, we must not grow weary. By Jove, least of all. 

Come then, I say, step here, so that you may see how many species vice has, as it seems to me. Pay attention now. For these are worthy of being seen. I am following; just speak. And yet, as if from a watchtower, after we have climbed here by reasoning, one species of virtue meets me, but of wickedness, they are innumerable. Of these, there are four which we ought to remember. How do you say that? As many modes of republics as there are having their own species, so many also appear for the soul itself. How many? Five of republics, and five again of the soul. Tell me which they are. I assert that one mode of the republic is this one which we have explained. But it can be called by two names. For if among the rulers of the city there is one who is the most excellent of all, it will be called a Kingdom. But if there are more, it will be an Aristocracy <note>Latin: *gubernatio optimatum*, "the government of the best men."</note>. You tell the truth. I say this is one species because whether many govern or one, no one who has been educated and instructed as we have said will change anything worthy of regard in the laws of the republic. For that would not be reasonable, he said.

# THE FIFTH DIALOGUE ON THE JUST.
*
### THE ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.
*

I am not unaware that there will be some who expect an apology from us, in which we defend this fifth dialogue—which proposes the communion of all things in the city—against the slanders of both the malicious and the ignorant. But let them read Plato himself, I pray; let them read diligently and judge without envy, and they will (I know what I am saying) desire no apology. Plato, therefore, the Phoebaean <note>A follower of Apollo; a healer or divinely inspired person.</note> physician of the human race, because he noticed that individuals, families, and cities are always and everywhere gravely ill, and have not yet been freed from disease or even relieved a little by the medicines of civil physicians who have been treating them in vain for so many centuries, he turned as prudently as piously to that primary law among physicians: which the authors of medicine sanction, that if someone does not recover by using such medicines (say, cold ones) for a long time, one must finally transition properly to hot ones. 

Recognizing, therefore, that the human race gains nothing through laws that distribute private property for so many centuries—but rather falls daily into worse states—he transitioned, not without reason, to laws of friendship, commanding that all things be common among friends, so that by removing the cause of division and misery, we might attain concord, union, and happiness. But let us begin again differently. Socrates, at the beginning of the fourth, placing the discipline of educating youth above all laws, touched briefly on the idea that the best discipline would be if there were a communion of wives, children, and property. But because this matter is new to many and unheard of by many more, he is called back at the very beginning of the fifth to declare it more clearly and prove it more firmly. Now, even if you have learned from Critias and Timaeus that a similar discipline once existed in the Greek and Egyptian Athens, you will not wonder at it too much as something new, nor hear it with distrust as something entirely difficult, nor admit it unwillingly as if it were not good. I pass over the fact that many report that the city of Prague in Bohemia <note>Ficino likely refers to the radical Hussites or Taborites who practiced communal living.</note> was once governed similarly. Moreover, Diodorus describes an island in the Southern Ocean in which, among other things, wives are common, and the men are very studious of philosophy and astrology. Pomponius Mela also witnesses that the Garamantes in the furthest parts of Africa have all things common in their republic. Furthermore, we have found that there was a similar communion of goods among the Brahman philosophers, the Gymnosophists, the Essenes <note>Ficino writes *Ephecos*, likely meaning the Essenes.</note>, the Pythagoreans, and finally among the holy founders of the Christian republic. We see also in our own times that only those religious orders approach virtue and happiness among whom nothing is private property. But if the communion of wives disturbs you, first allow it to be done properly according to the law in Plato, which is done in common by sacrilege among adulterous priests. Then hear Plato himself speaking more deeply in his own cause before you judge. In the following...

--- Page 414 ---
398 Book Thirty-One.

...note first the Socratic providence, which judges it worse to err in establishing laws than to kill a man. For an error of this kind kills many souls and bodies simultaneously through many centuries. Then, note his modesty as he approaches difficult things distrustfully, as if unwilling and compelled. Third, his piety as he invokes divine aid, according to his custom, in grave matters. And lest he err in making laws, he seeks help from the goddess Adrasteia <note>A goddess of inevitable fate or necessity, often associated with Nemesis.</note>, whom he also mentioned in the *Phaedrus*. This Adrasteia, among ancient theologians, is the most powerful queen of inevitable laws—laws, I say, both Saturnian, pertaining to minds, and Jovial, pertaining to natures. I call Adrasteia divine providence, insofar as nothing can escape her eyes or flee her hand. 

It is not without reason that he wishes to establish the firmest laws, which neither oblivion may delete, nor cunning defraud, nor violence break, and which absolutely no one may avoid. Let Adrasteia keep everyone away as he sanctions the inevitable things which no one can escape. Next, he proceeds gradually to the common discipline: from the institution of the men to the institution of the women. He commands that all studies, private and public, both of peace and of war, be made common to women and men, lest the human race be crippled; yet in such a way that in individual tasks, the heavier ones are committed to the men, the lighter to the women. Similarly, he teaches elsewhere that arms must be so accustomed that each person is dextrous with both, whom he calls "ambidextrous," and shows that this will be useful and possible, and how it ought to be done. 

Then he brings in another communion, namely of wives and children. And there, notice how the providence of order establishes Magistrates, the presidents of marriages, and the rites, and times, and ages, guarding lest anything be done intemperately or uselessly for the city. And after the generation, how diligently he thinks about the nursing of the newborn, yet in such a way that neither man nor woman recognizes their own child, nor the child their own parents, nor others each other; but the elders are compelled to think that almost all the younger ones are their children or grandchildren, and the younger ones in turn suspect all the elders to be their progenitors, and equals to be brothers. 

Among these things, where he scorns the nursing of one who was born either against the law or from the unfit, or who is himself unfit, understand that he is not to be destroyed, but is to be raised more cheaply in a more hidden place or in the suburbs, outside that most exact rule by which those are raised who are judged fit to be taken for guardianship. But the one who falls below the rule is to be sent at the proper time to the more menial ministries of the city or field, or perhaps transferred to other cities as soon as born. Soon after, recognize the invention of common charity, where he so disposes each thing that each individual, seeing the same thing or person shown to their eyes, judges it equally and says, "this is mine." Since his own things are most dear to each, all will care for everything, especially when they are led to such care by the laws and the magistrates. 

Hence, our carelessness and negligence, such as exists in everyone regarding many things as if they were alien to us, will be removed. Also removed will be the daily fallacy by which our judgment is foolishly deceived in cultivating that which we think is our own property. Finally, the extreme disturbance, anxiety, and misery which angers us from the insane love of private things will be removed. I pass over the fact that with the cause of discord removed, charity will be both common and whole. 

Furthermore, notice how diligent, how just, and how mild he makes the laws of war, and what rewards await the victors—namely, a certain divinity. For he says they are transferred into the blessed demons, the caretakers of men, and are to be rightly worshipped as dear gods. As for what is said about the kissing of boys, it is a certain joke of Glaucon's, said for the sake of relieving boredom. Add also something triumphal and festive. 

It remained to be proven that this communion could be done, after it had been affirmed to be the best. First, therefore, even if it cannot be done, he shows he has not brought this forward in vain, but rather as an exemplar to be imitated as much as possible in forming cities. Then he demonstrates that it can only then be done when philosophers rule, and not before will there be any rest from evils. Wherefore, he opportunely descends to the forming of philosophers as future governors of the city, teaching what the character of a civil philosopher is, and what his effect and discipline are. 

At the start, just as the common people are greedy and curious about perceiving these lower sensible things, so the philosophical genius is greedy and prone to finding the ideal reasons for all these things, and is a sagacious hunter of truth itself. But because these things are truly residual, and natural forms are images of ideas, he says not without reason that the common people are dreaming, thinking that the images are true things; but the philosopher alone is awake among others. 

And because he places a middle between being and non-being, remember that all things are thought of in five grades. And "pure non-being" is said to be whatever is imagined below matter. "Pure being" is the pure mind and the idea. The soul and the heaven are called "being" and simultaneously "non-being," namely on account of motion, yet they "are" more than they "are not." Matter, on the contrary, in a certain way "is not" more than it "is." But things which are composed by nature under the moon both "are" and "are not." Knowledge itself is concerned with those things which truly are. Ignorance with those things which truly are not. Opinion revolves around those things which equally are and are not. He attributes ignorance and opinion both to the common people and the Sophists; but knowledge (that is, science) only to philosophers. 

As for his calling science and opinion a certain "power," understand power not as unformed, but as endowed partly with natural form and partly with habit. Furthermore, where he deals with ideas to which the philosopher's science is referred, he says in his custom: the Good, the Beautiful, the Just. This ternary number is explained in three ways. First, the Good is God; the Beautiful is the multiform angelic mind; the Just is the celestial soul distributing the world justly. Second, the Good is the very form and act of divine nature; the Beautiful is the intelligence of the same; the Just is the will of the same. Third, the Good among ideas is the exemplar of the form and act of each thing and nature; the Beautiful is the exemplar of the order which results from any form within itself; the Just is the exemplar of the order which is referred from any form and thing to others. 

When, however, he subjects evil to the good, the ugly to the beautiful, and the unjust to the just, beware of placing these three opposites in the ideas. Rather, place these both in the very informity and deformity of matter (which in the book *On Science* he calls the "exemplar devoid of divinity," and in the *Statesman* the "place of dissimilarity") and also in the soul now depraved and turned entirely toward matter. Finally, as for the childish riddle of the eunuch he touches upon, it is of this sort: *A man who is not a man, seeing and not seeing, struck and did not strike, with a stone that is not a stone, a bird that is not a bird, upon a tree that is not a tree.* That is: a one-eyed eunuch struck a bat's wing with a pumice stone upon an Elder tree. But you will laugh at this, I know. It was added for the sake of the ridiculous.

I call a good city a "rectified Republic" of this kind, and I say such a man is good. And if this republic is right, I call the others depraved, inasmuch as they wander from the government of the city and the discipline of private individuals; these are indeed in four species of depravity. Which are they? he asked. Then I was proceeding to tell in what way each seemed to me to depend upon the other. But Polemarchus—for he was sitting a little further from me than Adeimantus—sitting behind Adeimantus's back, extended his hand and, grabbing Adeimantus's cloak from above around the shoulders, drew him toward himself and moved his mouth to his ear. Of the things he said, we perceived nothing except this one thing: "Shall we permit it? Or what shall we do?" To which Adeimantus, responding more loudly, said: "By no means." 

At this I said: What is it that you do not wish to permit? You, he said. Why so? I asked. Because you seem to us to be declining, he said, and to be keeping silent and stealing away an entire part of this discussion—and not the smallest one—so as not to explain it to us. You think it escapes us what you said poorly: that concerning wives and children, it is surely clear to everyone that all things among friends ought to be common. Did I not say it correctly, Adeimantus? I asked. Correctly indeed, he said, but just as in other things, so in this it must be explained in what way it is right, and what the mode of communion is. For there can be many. Do not then omit to open to us which one you mean most of all. For we have long been waiting, hoping you would explain both the condition of generation regarding the procreation of children, and the ratio of education regarding their nursing; and what this whole thing ought to be that you call the communion of wives and children. For we consider this to refer very much—indeed, entirely—to the republic, whether it be done rightly or not. Now, therefore, since you are approaching another republic before you have sufficiently treated these things, it seemed right to us, as you yourself heard, not to permit you to approach anything else until you have explained all these things just as you have the rest. 

Glaucon said: Consider me to feel the same as they do. Indeed, Thrasymachus said: In this, Socrates, think that we all agree...

...all of us, Socrates, believe me. What are you doing, I pray? Why do you call me back like this? What a heavy discussion about the Republic you are reviving, as if from the beginning! Indeed, I was rejoicing as if I had already finished it, thinking it was enough if anyone accepted these things insofar as they were said. But now you, demanding these things, do not know what a swarm of discussions you are stirring up. Foreseeing this then, I passed over it lest it excite many troubles for us. 

But what, said Thrasymachus, do you think these men have come here for, Socrates? To melt gold, or to hear speeches? To hear speeches, I said, but moderate ones. The "measure" and "end" of hearing such speeches, Socrates, said Glaucon, is the whole of life for men who have a mind. But let us be; do not be burdened, if it seems right to you, to declare the things we seek: what will be the communion of our guardians concerning women and children, and what ratio of nursing children should be applied at that very time that falls between birth and education, which certainly seems to be the most laborious; try to open these things to us. 

It cannot easily be explained, I said, O blessed man; for more ambiguities are in these things than in the previous ones. First, it might be doubted whether these things can be done. Furthermore, if they can, whether those very things are the best, and how, will be doubted. Therefore, this difficulty discourages me, fearing, O most close friend, lest this speech of mine seem to be a mere wish. 

Do not be reluctant, I pray, he said, for you do not have ungrateful, or incredulous, or malevolent listeners. O best of men, I said, do you bring this to exhort me? Indeed. On the contrary, I said, you do the opposite. For if I were persuaded that I knew what I am saying, this exhortation would be timely. For it is safe and daring to pronounce the truths one knows about the greatest and most precious things among wise and friendly men. But to speak words with distrust and ambiguity, as I am doing, is something to be guarded against and is dangerous, lest I move the listeners to laughter—for that is indeed childish—but worse, lest wandering far from the truth, I fall into falsehood and drag my friends down into ruin with me, and we be deceived together in those things in which it is least of all fitting to err. 

Therefore, as a suppliant, I adore Adrasteia <note>Invoking the goddess to avoid the sin of pride or intellectual error.</note> for the things I am about to say, Glaucon. For I think he sins less who kills someone unintentionally than he who deceives concerning the constitutions of honest, good, and just things. It is better to undergo this risk among enemies than friends. Therefore, O Glaucon, confirm me better. But, O Socrates, said Glaucon, if by any chance it happens that we err from this discussion, we absolve you as if from a homicide, and we shall pronounce you innocent of this deception. Therefore, enter the discussion boldly. 

Furthermore, I said, he is innocent who is absolved there, as the laws teach. Therefore, he who is absolved here is also innocent. Speak then, he said, for this reason. I must speak now again, I said, the things that perhaps ought to have been said next. But perhaps it is worthwhile, after the things pertaining to men have had their "act" as it were, to report next the things that are of women, especially since you yourself exhort me to this. 

For men born and educated as we described above, in my opinion, there is no other right acquisition and use of children and women than by walking that path which we entered upon from the beginning. For we tried to set the men, as guardians, over the flock in our speech. Indeed, he said. Let it follow the generation then, applying a most similar nursing, and let us consider whether it is fitting or not. In what way? he asked. In this: whether among guardian dogs, we think the females themselves ought to guard together the same things that the males do, and hunt together, and do all other things in common. Or should the females remain inside to look after domestic affairs, as being weak because of the birth and nursing of the pups, while the males undergo the labors and have the whole care of the herd? 

We attribute all things to them in common, he said, except that we use the females as the weaker and the males as the more robust. Can you use any animal for the same tasks unless you have nourished and educated it in the same way? In no way. If therefore we use the females for the same tasks as the men, it is fitting to educate them in the same things. Certainly. We attributed music and gymnastics to the men. Surely. Therefore, these arts and matters of war must be similarly attributed to the women, and it is fitting to use them for these things. That is consistent with what you say. 

Perhaps many things will seem ridiculous contrary to custom among the things now said, if they are done as they are said. And very much so. What do you see as most ridiculous in these things? Is it because you are going to see naked women in the wrestling pits competing with men—not only the young, but also the old women, just as the old men in the gymnasiums, when they exercise together, even though they are already wrinkled and not pleasant to look at? Yes, by Jove. For that would seem ridiculous as things are now. 

But we, after we have begun to speak, ought in no way to fear the "jokes" of witty men, however many and of whatever kind they may hurl against such a mutation which we are inducing regarding music and gymnastics, and no less regarding armor and equestrian skill. You speak well. Therefore, since we have begun to speak, let us proceed to the severity of the law, asking those men not to act in their usual way, but to think serious thoughts, and reminding them that not a long time has passed since it seemed shameful and ridiculous to the Greeks—as it seems today to most of the barbarians to be laughed at—to see naked men. And when they first approached exercises of this kind (first the Cretans, and then also the Spartans), it was certainly permitted for the urban and witty men who were then alive to carp at all these things, do you not think? Indeed. 

But after, I think, it appeared more convenient to those who used it that men should exercise with a naked body rather than a covered one, it happened that because it had been shown by reason to be the best, it did not look ridiculous to the eyes. From which it is clear that that man is vain who thinks anything is to be derided except what is bad, and who approaches derision by proposing some other cause of laughter to himself than what is insipid and bad, or who thinks anything is honest and worthy of study while looking elsewhere than to the good. It is entirely so. 

Must we not first agree on this: whether these things can be done or not? And to grant anyone who wishes to doubt against these things, whether in jest or in earnest, whether in the nature of humans the female is able to communicate with the male in all works, or in none, or whether she is strong in some but in others by no means; and in which category of these does military service lie? Will not whoever has started so correctly, as is fitting, also finish correctly? Most of all. Do you wish then that we, for the sake of others, oppose ourselves to our own doubts, lest the arguments of the other side be attacked without a defense? Nothing prohibits it. Let us speak therefore in their person in this way:

...to oppose us. For it was agreed among us immediately from the beginning of building the city that each one must perform according to nature one thing which was his own. It was agreed; why not? Is it not true, then, that the woman herself by nature differs not a little from the man? Why would she not differ? Therefore, must not a different work be attributed to each according to the nature of each? Without a doubt. What remains, then, except for you to wander now and contradict yourselves, since you assert that men and women ought to perform the same works, even though they differ greatly in nature?" 

Will you have, O wonderful man, anything to respond to those things for our defense? At the moment, he said, not easily enough; but I ask you and beg you to explain what can most of all be asserted in defense of our speech. These things, Glaucon, I said, and many others of the same kind, I foresaw long ago; and fearful and unwilling I descended to this law concerning the acquisition and nursing of women and children. Truly, he said, it appears not light. 

Certainly not. But thus the matter stands. Whether someone has fallen into a shallow pond or into the deep sea, he nevertheless swims in the middle of the water. Exactly. Must we not also swim, and try to escape the waves of the discussion unharmed, hoping either that some dolphin will pick us up or some other unhoped-for and sudden cause of safety will be ours? So it seems. Look around, I pray, if we may find an exit. It was agreed between us that a different nature ought to handle a different work; but the nature of a woman and a man is different. Now we command different natures to study the same things. In this we are accused by you. Strongly. 

How noble, Glaucon, is the power of the contradictory art! Why? he asked. Because it seems to me many fall into it even unwillingly, and think they are not litigating but discoursing, because they are unable to perceive what is said according to the dividing species; instead, they pursue the contrariety of the proposal according to the name itself, contending with each other rather than discussing. For this happens to many, but has the same now happened to us? And very much so, I said. We seem indeed to touch upon contradiction unwillingly. By what reason? Because we are contending very strongly and contentiously—if you look at the words—that a nature not the same should not handle the same works. 

But we have in no way considered what species of "different" or "same" nature it is, and what we were looking toward then when we described it, when we attributed different studies to different natures and the same to the same. Certainly we did not consider that. But it is permitted for us, as it seems, to ask of ourselves: is the nature of bald men and hairy men the same, or rather contrary? And after we have granted it is contrary, if bald men cut leather and make shoes, should we by no means permit hairy men to do the same? Or if the hairy do it, not permit the bald? But that would be worthy of laughter, he said. 

Is it for any other reason that this is laughable, except that then we did not posit an entirely "same" and "different" nature, but observed only that species of dissimilarity and similarity which pertained to those same studies? Just as we said a physician and a man having a mind fit for the studies of medicine have the same nature; do you not think so? Indeed. But one fit for medicine is different from another man prompt for building. Entirely. 

Is it not then, I said, that the race of men and the race of women, if they differ in no art or study <gloss>It is missing in the Greek; read "provided that it is."</gloss>, must be assigned this very thing? But if they appear to differ in this very thing alone—namely, that the female bears and the male begets—we shall no more admit it has been shown that a woman differs from a man regarding that which we are now speaking of; but we shall still judge that both the guardians and their wives ought to exercise the same things among us. Rightly indeed. 

Must we not next command him who says the contrary to teach us this very thing: for which art, or which duty from those that lead to the institution of the city, is the nature of a man and a woman not the same, but different? So it is indeed fitting. Perhaps what you were saying a little before, another would also say: that to say enough suddenly is not easy; but if it is thought upon, it is not very difficult. He would say that. Do you wish then that we ask him who opposes these things to us to lend us his ears and pay attention, to see if in any way we can show him that no study regarding the government of the city is proper to a woman? Entirely. 

Come then, let us say to him: Respond: did you say that someone is endowed by nature with a fit or unfit genius for some work based on this—that he perceives something easily, while another with difficulty? And the one, if he learns a little something from anyone, finds much out from it himself; but the other, when he has learned and thought upon more things, does not even preserve those things he learned? And for the one, the members of the body sufficiently serve the mind, but for the other they rebel? Are there other things besides these by which you distinguish a man well-instituted by nature for some things from one ill-instituted? No one will say anything else. 

Do you know of anything practiced by humans in which the race of men does not have all the same things and more excellently than the race of women? Or shall we wander far in words, mentioning the art of weaving, and the making of cakes and side-dishes, in which the race of women seems to be something, where it certainly appears very ridiculous when it is beaten? You speak the truth, he said, because in all things, so to speak, the one race is far surpassed by the other. But many women are more excellent than many men at many things. But the whole matter itself is as you say. 

There is therefore, O friend, no duty among those who administer the city that is proper to a woman insofar as she is a woman, or to a man insofar as he is a man; but the natures of both are equally dispersed in living beings. And the female is by nature a participant in all duties, and the man in all; but in all things the female is weaker than the man. So it is entirely. Shall we prescribe all things to men, but to a woman nothing? But how? There is indeed, I think, as we shall assert, among women also one fit for medicine, another not; one by nature musical, another alien to music. Why not? And one prompt for gymnastic exercises and military affairs, but another unfit for these. So I think. 

Is not one a lover of wisdom, while another scorns wisdom? And one with a high spirit, another with a lowly one? I assert this also. There is therefore among women a certain one fit for guarding, another not. Did we not choose a certain nature of this kind for men fit for guarding? Certainly of that kind. Therefore, the nature of a woman and a man for guarding the city is the same, except that we must use women as the weaker and men as the more robust. It appears so. 

Women of such a kind are therefore to be chosen to inhabit and guard the city together with the men, since they are fit and are by nature related to them. Exactly. And must not the same studies be attributed to the same natures? The same. We have at last returned by a long circuit to those prior things, and we have granted that it is not against nature for the wives of the guardians to be exercised in music and gymnastics. Very much so. Wherefore, we have established by law things that are neither impossible nor similar to a mere wish, since...

...as for the things that are done nowadays against these principles, they are done much more against nature, as it seems. It seems so. Was it not necessary for us to agree whether we were speaking of things that are possible and best, or not? It was. It was established that they are indeed possible. Plainly. That they are also the best must be asserted after this. It is clear. To the end that women might turn out to be sufficient for guardianship, no other education is needed than that by which we instruct the men for the same task, especially since the same nature is found in both. Not another. What further do you think of this? Concerning what? Whether you judge that among men some are better and others worse, or are they all alike? Not at all. In the city we have founded, do you think more excellent men are made into guardians—having obtained the education we gave them—than leatherworkers <term>coriarios</term> <note>Latin: coriarios. Someone who works with hides or leather.</note> who are imbued with the skill of leatherworking? You ask a ridiculous thing, he said. I understand indeed. What then? Are these not the best of all the remaining citizens? Of the rest as well. And will such women also be the best of women? Very much so. Is there anything better for a city than that the best possible men and the best possible women be produced? There is not. Now music and gymnastics, if they are present as we described above, can accomplish this. Without a doubt. Therefore, we have established by law something not only possible, but also the best for the city. So it is. 

The bodies of the female guardians must therefore be bared, since they will put on virtue instead of clothes. They must share in war and all other guardianship of the city, and do nothing else. However, the lighter of these duties should be assigned to the women rather than the men because of the weakness of the sex. But he who laughs at naked women exercising themselves for the sake of what is best, plucking the fruit of "wisdom" from ridiculous trifles, understands neither what he laughs at nor what he does. For it is said and will be said quite rightly: that which is useful is honorable, and that which is harmful is shameful. Most certainly. Let us say then that we have escaped this one "wave" <note>Socrates uses the metaphor of "waves" to describe the increasingly difficult challenges or controversial arguments he must overcome.</note> while treating the law concerning women, so that we were not entirely submerged while asserting that all things ought to be practiced in common by our guardians, both men and women. Indeed, our speech has agreed with itself, showing that it proposed things both possible and useful. You have certainly escaped no small wave. 

You will say it is not huge when you see what follows next, I said. Speak now, so that I may see. I think this law follows that one and all the previous ones. Which one? That these women are to be common to all these men, and no one is to live privately with anyone; and again, that the children are common, and neither shall a father know his own son, nor a son recognize his own father. This is certainly much harder to believe is either possible or useful. I do not think there would be any doubt for anyone that it would be useful, and the greatest good for women and children to be common, if only it could be done. But I think the greatest controversy will be over whether it can be done or not. Concerning both points, he said, there will be the greatest doubt. You speak, I said, of a conspiracy of arguments. I thought I would be freed from one if it seemed useful to you, for then it would remain for me only to inquire whether it is possible or not. But you could not escape unnoticed while fleeing, he said. Give an account of both. 

I must certainly endure the penalty, I said, but grant me this. Let me refresh myself as if I were on holiday, just as those who are lazy in mind are accustomed to feast themselves on thought whenever they walk alone. For men of this kind, before they have discovered how it might be possible for what they desire to happen, set aside that care (so as not to be burdened by too much labor) while they deliberate on the possible and impossible; as if what they affect were already so, they persuade themselves; and thereafter they arrange the rest, delighting themselves while they think what they will do when it is present, and thus they make a sluggish mind even more languid. I myself am growing lazy in the same way, and I desire to defer that discussion—whether these things are possible or not—to another time. For the present, however, assuming they are possible, I will inquire (if you permit) in what manner the rulers themselves will arrange these things, and how they will be the most useful of all things if they happen, both for the guardians and the city. These things I will try to consider with you first, and the others later, if you allow. I allow it indeed; consider it now. 

I think, therefore, I said, if the rulers are to be worthy of this name, and in the same way their assistants, the latter will be willing to execute what is commanded, while the former will command, partly obeying the laws themselves and partly imitating them, insofar as we have permitted them. That is probable. You, therefore, as the lawgiver, having chosen the men, will also choose the women and provide them to be as similar in nature as possible. Since these people will have common houses and common meals, and will possess nothing of the sort as their own, they will live together; and mingling with one another in the gymnasia and in the rest of their lifestyle, they will be drawn to mutual union by an innate necessity, as I think. Do I not seem to you to speak of necessary things? 

Not by a geometric necessity, he said, but by an erotic one, which is much sharper than the other for persuading and drawing the common people. Vehemently so, I said. 

But after this, O Glaucon, to be bared among one another without order, or to do anything else, is neither holy in a city of blessed men, nor will the magistrates permit it. For it would not be just, he said. It is established that we shall thereafter institute marriages as sacred as possible. They would be sacred if they were as useful as possible. Extremely so. In what way will they be the most useful? Tell me this, O Glaucon. I see in your house both hunting dogs and noble birds in great numbers. Have you ever noticed anything concerning their mating and procreation? To what end? First, among these noble creatures themselves, are there not some who are and become the most excellent? There are. Do you then permit procreation from just any of them equally? Or do you take care that it happens from the best? From the best. From the youngest, or from those consumed by old age? Or rather from those established in the flower of their age? From these rather. And unless procreation happens in this way, do you think the race of dogs and birds would be far worse? I do indeed. Do you think it happens differently with horses and other animals? That would be absurd. 

Great Heavens! <note>Latin: Papæ. An exclamation of surprise or wonder.</note> O my dearest friend, what a great need we have for the highest rulers, if indeed the matter stands similarly in the human race. It does indeed; what then? Because it is necessary, I said, for them to use many medicines. For when bodies do not need medicines but require only the institution of diet, we think a common doctor suffices. But when we must act with medicines, we know a more excellent doctor will be needed. You speak truly. But to what end is this? Because it seems it will be necessary for the rulers to use frequent lies and deception for the utility of their subjects. <margin>Aristotle sharply criticizes this opinion of Plato in the *Politics* Book 2, Chapter 1.</margin> Now we said above that all such things are useful in the place of a drug or medicine. And rightly so. In marriages, therefore, and the procreation of children, it seems this is done quite correctly. In what way? It is necessary, according to what we granted above, that the best men should mate with the best women as often as possible...
