...as much as possible; but the worst, on the contrary, with the worst. And the offspring of the former should be nourished, but of the latter not at all, if the flock is to be most excellent. And while all these things are being done, they should be unknown by all except the rulers, if indeed the flock of guardians is to be free from sedition. Quite right. Therefore, certain festivals will be designated by law in which we will bring together the grooms and brides; sacred rites will be performed, and hymns composed by our poets suitable for the celebrated marriages. We will leave the number of marriages to the discretion of the rulers, so that, looking toward wars and diseases and other such things, they may preserve the same number of citizens as much as possible, so that the city does not become too populous or empty. You speak rightly. Therefore, certain lots must be instituted with such craft that the inferior man, in any coupling, blames fortune and not the rulers. Most definitely. Indeed, to those among the young who are more excellent in military matters or other things, gifts and rewards must be given, and many such things; and even a more abundant license for consorting with women, so that from this occasion more children than from others may be sown from them. 

Excellent. Therefore, the children who are born from these will be taken up by the magistrates presiding over such things, whether men or women or both—for the magistracies are common to men and women. It is so. Taking the offspring of the excellent men, they will carry them to the fold, to certain nurses dwelling separately in some part of the city. But those born from the inferior parents, or even from any others but who are defective in some limb, they will hide in secret places as is fitting, since the race of guardians is to be pure. They will also take care of the nourishment. Mothers, when they are overflowing with milk, will be sent to the fold, the rulers taking care that no one is able to recognize her own. And if these are insufficient, they will bring in others besides who are full of milk. They will also provide that a moderate time be kept for suckling. Likewise, they will command watches and other labors to the nurses. You grant much power to the women of the guardians for procreating offspring, he said. So it is fitting. 

But come now, let us run through what we intended most of all. We clearly said that children ought to be procreated by those who are in the flower of their age. We did. Does it not also seem to you that the moderate time for a full age is twenty years for a woman and thirty for a man? What is the measure of these? That a woman, beginning from her twentieth year of age, should bear children until her fortieth; but a man, after he has passed the highest bloom of his course (namely thirty years), should procreate until fifty-five years. Indeed, he said, the vigor of mind and body consists in those ages. If therefore someone older than these, or younger, should touch procreation in common, we shall judge this to be a profane and unjust crime, as if a fetus were sown in the city which, if it remained hidden, would be born not under sacrifices and vows (which the priests, both men and women, will perform at each marriage so that from useful parents more useful children may be born), but rather under the darkness of a grave incontinence. You speak rightly. 

The same reasoning must be held concerning one who, though still in the age for procreating, has not yet been coupled from the beginning and touches a woman of legitimate age. For we shall assert that this man generates a spurious, incestuous, and profane child. Quite rightly. Therefore, when both women and men have passed the age fit for procreation, we shall say it is permitted for the men to be mingled with whomever they wish, except for a daughter and a mother, and the children of daughters, or the elders of a mother; and it is permitted for women to be coupled with anyone, except for a son and a father, and the superiors and inferiors of the same. But when we have commanded all these things, we shall forbid such a fetus (if it should happen) to be brought forth into the light. And if anything should force a mother to give birth, we shall command her to expose it as if there were no nourishment for it. These things are also rightly said. 

But the fathers and daughters and other kinsmen you mentioned, how will they distinguish each other? Not at all; but all who are born in the tenth month, or the seventh, from the day on which someone applied himself to procreating, the males shall be called sons by him, and the females daughters. And those born shall call him father, and similarly he will say the sons of those born are his grandsons, and they will call those above them grandfathers and grandmothers; but those who are born at that time in which their fathers and mothers were procreating, they shall call brothers and sisters. And thus, as I was just saying, they shall in no way touch each other. But the law will grant cohabitation to brothers and sisters if chance gives it and the Pythia <note>The priestess of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> confirms it through her responses. Quite rightly. 

Such, O Glaucon, will be the community of women and children among the guardians of the city; but that it is consistent with the rest of the city's order, and that it is by far the best, must next be confirmed by reason. Or what shall we do? This, by Jove, he said. Is not the beginning of this agreement that we ask ourselves what we find to be the greatest good for the constitution of a city, looking toward which the legislator ought to establish laws, and what is the greatest evil? Let us then consider whether the things we have just described agree with our investigation of the good and differ from the trace of the evil. Most of all. 

Have we any more pernicious evil for a city than that which divides it and makes many out of one? Or anything better than that which binds it together and makes it one? We have not. Does not the community of pleasure and pain unite them, when all citizens rejoice and grieve equally at the gain or loss of the same things? Most certainly. <margin>Aristotle notes this in the *Politics* Book 2, Chapter 2.</margin> But the diversity of these things dissolves it, when some grieve vehemently and others exult at the same accidents of the city and of those who are in the city. Why not? And from this something of this sort arises: when these words are not said together in the city, namely "Mine" and "Not mine," and concerning the property of another in the same way. Exactly. In whatever city, therefore, the greatest number say "Mine" and "Not mine" regarding the same thing in the same way, that city is best governed. Entirely. And whichever is affected as nearly as possible like a single man; so that whenever the finger of one of us is struck, the whole community of the body reaching to the soul perceives it immediately in a single coordination of that which rules in the soul itself, and the whole is afflicted and feels pain with the part. And therefore we say that the *man* has a pain in his finger. And the same reasoning applies to any other part of a man, both when it is afflicted by pain and when it is refreshed by pleasure. The same reasoning certainly; and as for what you ask, the city which is best ruled comes nearest to this. Whenever, I think, anything good or evil happens to any of the citizens, such a city will cry out that the one so affected is its own, and therefore the whole will either rejoice together or grieve. It is necessary that it happen so in a city governed by the best laws. 

But it is now time for us to return to our city, and let us inquire whether the things we have now established among ourselves agree most with this city or rather with another. <margin>Ficino seems to have had another codex than the Aldine, in which as in others this place is corrupted.</margin> It is altogether permitted. There are rulers and people in other cities, and similarly in this one? There are. And all these citizens will call each other mutually...? Why not? But besides the name of citizen, how does the people in other cities call the rulers? In most indeed "Lords," but in a popular government "Rulers." But the people of our city, how will they call the rulers beyond the name of citizen? Saviors and Helpers, he said. And in what way will the rulers call the people? Pay-givers and Nourishers. And those who lead in other cities, the people? Slaves. The rulers themselves each other? Co-rulers. But ours? Co-guardians.

--- Page 419 ---
->Dialogue V. On the Republic. Or, on Justice. 403<-

Do you have anyone you can name among the rulers of other cities who calls one of his colleagues his kinsman and another a stranger? Indeed, many. He thinks of and speaks of the kinsman as his own, but the stranger as not his own. Plainly. But among your guardians, is there any who would think of or call any of his colleagues a stranger? None. For whomever anyone meets, he will think he meets either a brother, or a sister, or a father, or a mother, or a son, or a daughter, or their offspring, or their elders. You speak excellently; but answer this as well. Will you impose only the names of kinship on your citizens by law? Or also the duties of proximity, so that they behave in such a way as the dignity of the name itself demands, and preserve toward parents whatever the law prescribes—reverence, care, and obedience; otherwise, they may have both gods and men hostile to them, as those who do neither holy nor just things if they act otherwise? Will any other speeches than these, from all the citizens, immediately resound in the ears of children, both concerning parents (whomever anyone indicates to them) and concerning others close in kind? These certainly. For it would be absurd if the names of kinship were uttered only by mouth without the duty. 

In this city, therefore, most of all, when one is well or ill affected, all will cry with one voice what we were just saying: "Mine is doing well," or "Mine is doing poorly." You speak truly. We were saying that with this opinion and words of this kind it follows that pleasures and pains are common. And rightly so. In this, therefore, our citizens will most of all communicate with each other, in that which they call "Mine"; and from this community it will follow that they have common pleasures and pains. Completely. And the cause of these, along with the rest of the city's constitution, is the community of the guardians concerning women and children. It is so entirely. Indeed, we confessed this to be the highest good for the city when we said the rightly governed city is similar to a body, communicating with all its parts concerning pleasure and pain in every way. And we rightly conceded it. 

The cause of the greatest good for the city has therefore appeared to us to be the community of women and children among the helpers. Greatly so. And these things are consistent with what was said before. For we said that they ought to have neither private houses, nor fields, nor any possession, but should receive nourishment from others as the wage for their guardianship, and all consume it in common, if they are to be true guardians. Excellent. Do not both what I say, and what was said above, and what is said now, work most toward making these people true guardians, so that they do not distract the city by calling "mine" not the same thing for all, but one thing for some and another for others, and one man draws into his private house whatever he wishes to use apart from others, and another into his own house separate from the rest; and from private women and children, different people rejoice and grieve at different things? Rather, from one private and identical opinion of all, all tending toward the same thing as much as possible, they may be affected by similar pleasures and the same pains if anything happens. 

Most certainly. What then? Will not the controversies of judgments and mutual accusations all cease, since no one will have anything private except his body, and the rest will be common? Whence it follows that they will be without sedition, as far as those lawsuits are concerned which are accustomed to arise for the sake of money, or children, or kinsmen? It is altogether necessary that these be absent. Nor will there ever be a contention concerning violence offered. For we shall assert that it is honorable and equitable for an equal to ward off injury from an equal, imposing the province of protecting bodies. Excellent. And this law contains something else that is right: that if anyone is angry with someone and seeks to satisfy his anger, he will excite fewer major seditions. It is so entirely. For the law will establish that the elder shall rule over all the younger and correct them. That is clear. It is also established that a younger man will never attempt to violate an elder, unless commanded by the rulers, nor to strike him (as is decent), nor to affect him with any ignominy. For fear and shame are guardians sufficient to prohibit these things. Shame indeed will not permit them to violate those whom they suspect to be parents. Fear, however, will deter everyone from injury, fearing namely lest all the others—partly as sons, partly as brothers, partly as fathers—should come to the aid of the oppressed. So it happens entirely. 

Therefore, from these laws, the citizens will lead their lives in peace with one another. Greatly so. Since these least of all disagree among themselves, it is not to be feared that another city might ever fight against them, or they among themselves, and move seditions. Certainly not. I am ashamed to mention, because it is less becoming, every tiny evil from which free citizens will be delivered. Flatteries will certainly be absent, which the poor are accustomed to use toward the rich. Also the anxieties and pains of the indigent, with which they are vexed in nourishing children and seeking money for the necessary nourishment of the household, while they give effort to usury, and deny what they have received, and study profit from everywhere. They set aside, moreover, with women and servants many things to be stored for a time. For how many and what kind of things men suffer in these, O friend, are both servile and illiberal, and unworthy of narration. They are plain even to a blind man. Furthermore, they will be free from all these, and lead a life more blessed than that most blessed life of those who have conquered at Olympia. 

In what way? Because those are thought blessed for a small part of what these possess. For the victory of these is more noble, and their nourishment from the public is more perfect; the victory of these is the safety of the whole city. Furthermore, they and their children receive nourishment and whatever is necessary for life as a place of coronation. In addition, they obtain honors and rewards from the republic itself while living, and when they have departed life, tombs worthy of the monuments of their virtues. These are certainly quite extraordinary. Do you remember what someone's speech objected to us in the earlier parts, as if we were making the guardians not at all blessed, since they had nothing, though they were permitted to possess everything of the citizens? But we responded that, if it happened later, we would consider it; for in the present we were making guardians truly guardians, and the city as blessed as possible, not looking to any one part of it, but seeking that blessedness for the whole. I remember indeed. Now certainly the life of the helpers, since it appears far more noble and better than that of those who...

--- Page 420 ---
404 Book Thirty-One.

...conquer at Olympia, in no way seems similar to the lives of leatherworkers, or other artisans, or farmers. Certainly not, as I myself judge. Nevertheless, what I said above, it is right that I repeat here: that if a guardian should study to become so blessed that he is not a guardian, nor does a life so moderate and stable—and, as we assert, the best—suffice for him, but an insane and childish opinion of happiness arising should seize him by that power to claim for himself everything in the city, he will learn that Hesiod spoke wisely when he said, "The half is more than the whole." <note>A famous Greek proverb from Hesiod's *Works and Days*, suggesting that moderation is better than greedy excess.</note> If he uses me as a counselor, he will remain in this life. 

Do you then approve of the community which we grant to women with men, regarding education, the taking up of children, and the guardianship of other citizens, so that they remain in the city together with the men, serve in war, guard together, and hunt like dogs, and participate in all duties entirely as much as possible? And while they do these things, you grant that they do the best things, and not against the nature of the female, by which she was instituted to communicate with the male. I approve indeed. Does it not remain next that we declare whether this community can exist among men as it does in other animals, and in what way it can? You have anticipated what I was about to ask. 

Concerning military matters, I think it is manifest in what way they will handle them. In what way? They will certainly serve in war in common, and will lead the adult children with them to the battle; so that, just as the children of other craftsmen see the works of their fathers, which they themselves will also do when they come to mature age, and furthermore so that they may be a help to their parents and minister to everything which pertains to war, and take care of their fathers and mothers. Have you not noticed what happens in the arts, such as as long as the sons of potters watch their fathers molding and minister to them before they put their hand to the work? Most certainly. Should those potters be more diligent than guardians to instruct their children by the skill and inspection of the works suitable to each? That would be ridiculous indeed. Furthermore, every kind of living creature fights more ardently when its offspring are present. 

It is so, but there is a very great danger, O Socrates, lest if by chance (as happens in war) an adverse fortune should occur, they may also lose their children with them, from which another city could not be restored. You speak truly. But do you perhaps think that one ought primarily to arrange things so that he never undergoes any danger? By no means. What then? Must not danger be entered then, so that those who behave excellently there may turn out more outstanding? It is clear. Do you think it makes little difference, or is unworthy to be undertaken because of danger, whether the children who are to be soldiers see or do not see military matters? Rather, it matters for what you say. Therefore, effort must be given so that children see war, and we must devise a way for them to be safe, and thus it will be rightly done. Certainly. 

In the first place, their parents will by no means be ignorant, but insofar as it is granted to men, they will be sharp-sighted to discern in which camps there is danger and in which there is not. That is likely. Therefore, they will lead them to the safer ones, and to the others not at all. Rightly so. Then they will set rulers over them, not the most idle, but men suitable as leaders and pedagogues both by experience of things and by age. So it is fitting. But we shall say that many things have happened contrary to the opinion of many men. Most certainly. For the sake of these, O friend, certain wings must be applied to the little children from their tender years, so that if ever there is a need, they may fly away immediately. 

What do you mean by that? They must be put on horses, so that from childhood they may learn to ride; and they should be led to the spectacle on horses that are not fierce or too warlike, but the swiftest possible and easily obedient to the reins; and thus they will most conveniently behold their work and escape most safely if any adversity happens, following the elder leaders. You seem to me to speak quite rightly. What is to be said of those things which pertain to war? What things should be preserved by soldiers among themselves and against enemies? Do I judge rightly or not? What is it? I think that he who deserts his rank in the battle line, or throws away his arms, or commits any such thing because of timidity, ought to be transferred to the rank of artisans or farmers. So it is fitting. But him who is captured alive by the enemies should be left to them, even if they wish to return him for free, so that they may use their prey however they wish. Altogether. 

But he who has excelled by behaving excellently, first indeed in the expedition itself, should he not be crowned individually by each of the youths and boys who serve with him? It seems so to me. What? Should they not also join right hands with him? And this too. But this besides perhaps does not seem right to you? What? That he should receive and give kisses from anyone. Rather, most of all. And I think this should be added to the law: that as long as they are in that expedition, it shall be permitted to no one to refuse whomever he himself desires to kiss, so that if anyone is seized by love of anyone, whether male or female, he may be sharper to attain victory. 

Excellent; for it has already been said that marriages for strenuous men will be more easily prepared than for others, and co-options more frequent, so that as many as possible may be born from these. We certainly said so. For according to Homer it is just to honor such young men most of all. For he said that Ajax, excelling in war, was honored with a "continuous back," <note>A Homeric reference to giving the best cut of meat—the long chine—to a hero.</note> as if this honor were suitable for a young and brave man, from which at the same time as the honor, his strength might also increase. Quite rightly. In these things, therefore, we will obey Homer. For in sacrifices and other such things, the more good men appear, the more we will honor them with hymns and those things we just said, and likewise with seats and meats and full cups, so that we may both honor outstanding men and women and exercise them together. 

You speak most beautifully. But him who has died in service having behaved strenuously, we shall say first that he is of the golden race. Most of all. Then, placing faith in Hesiod, we shall assert that whoever of this race departs from life becomes "holy terrestrial demons, excellent expellers of evils, and guardians of mortals." <note>Plato is quoting Hesiod's description of the "Golden Age" souls who watch over humanity.</note> We shall certainly believe so. We shall therefore consult the oracle as to how it is fitting to bury blessed and divine men, and with what insignia especially to decorate them, and thus we shall bury them as it commands. Without a doubt. Therefore, for the remaining time, we shall cherish and adore their tombs as those of demons. We shall also preserve the same things toward those who, having been judged to excel in life with exceptional probity, have departed life from old age or some other way. It is certainly fitting. 

But how will our soldiers behave against enemies? In what matter? First, I ask about slavery: whether you think it just that Greeks should reduce Greek cities to slavery? Or rather, that they should not permit this to be done by others, and should resist according to their strength, and accustom themselves to spare the Greek race, taking care lest they themselves be forced to serve the barbarians. It matters altogether and in all things to spare Greeks, and our people ought not to make any Greek a slave; but also to consult other Greeks rather, so that they themselves may beware of this. Entirely. For thus they will more easily and strongly rise up against the barbarians...

--- Page 421 ---
This text is a Latin translation and commentary on Plato’s *Republic* by the Renaissance humanist and Neoplatonist **Marsilio Ficino**. It covers the end of Book V and the beginning of Book VI.

### Dialogue V: On the Republic, or On Justice

[Page 405]

They will rise up against barbarians and restrain themselves from one another. But what then? Is it honorable to despoil the dead of anything besides their arms after they have conquered, or not? Does this not offer an occasion for cowards to avoid facing the enemy, as if they were performing some magnificent deed when they are merely wallowing among corpses? For indeed, many armies have perished through a greed for plundering. Most certainly. Does it not seem a matter of illiberality, of a greedy, womanish, and base mind to strip a corpse, and to consider the body of the dead an enemy when the adversary himself has flown away, leaving behind that with which he fought? Do we think those who do this differ at all from dogs who are angry at the stones thrown at them, letting the one who threw them go? I think they differ not at all. Therefore, one must abstain from such plunderings, for they hinder victory. They must be avoided entirely. Nor shall we carry arms into a temple to dedicate them to God—especially the arms of Greeks—if indeed we care for goodwill with other Greeks. Rather, we shall greatly fear lest it be an impious crime to transfer such things from one’s own people into a sacred place, unless the god should say otherwise. Quite right. Will your soldiers depopulate the fields of the Greeks with whom they fight, and burn their houses? I would gladly hear what you think of this. To me, it seems nothing of the sort should be done, but only that the annual fruits should be taken. Shall I tell you the reason? By all means. It seems to me that just as these two names exist, "War" and "Sedition" [Faction], so also two distinct things underlie these two differences. I say these two: one is internal and kin, the other foreign and strange. The enmity between us [Greeks] is called sedition; that between foreigners is called war. What you say is not beside the point. Observe whether I might say this to the point as well: I say indeed that all Greeks are near [**ꝑ** - *propinquos*] and kin to one another, but distinct and foreign to barbarians. You speak excellently. Whenever, therefore, Greece fights against barbarians, or barbarians against Greeks, we shall say they wage war and are enemies by nature, and we shall call these enmities "war." But when Greeks rise against Greeks, we shall say they are friends by nature, but that Greece is laboring under a disease and is agitated by seditions, and we shall call these enmities "sedition." I agree entirely. If, in a seditious city, the men of both factions were to ravage the fields of their adversaries and burn their houses, do you see how destructive that sedition would be, neither side being lovers of their own fatherland? For if they loved it, they would certainly never dare to devastate their nurse and mother, but would think it sufficient if the victors took the fruits of the others, thinking they would not always fight one another but would eventually be reconciled. Indeed, this is the sentiment of refined men. This city you are founding, is it not Greek? It should be. Therefore, the citizens in it will be equitable and mild. Most certainly. And thus friends of the Greeks. They will surely consider all Greece joined to themselves, and they will hold the sacred rites in common with others. Exceedingly so. Thus, they will consider a contention arisen against other Greeks as if conducted with their own people, and will call it sedition, not war. They will act exactly so. Therefore, they will contend as those who must one day be reconciled. Certainly so. They will conduct the matter with a benevolent and temperate mind, looking not toward slavery or slaughter, as those who are by no means enemies. In this way, surely. They will not, therefore, destroy Greece, being Greeks themselves, nor burn houses, nor believe that in individual cities everyone is their adversary—men, women, and children—but only the few who were the authors of the discord. For this reason, they will not devastate the region of those who are mostly friends, nor subvert houses, but will contend only so far as those who gave cause for the discord pay the penalty to the innocent. I agree that one must fight against Greeks in this way, but toward barbarians one ought to be minded as Greeks are now affected toward Greeks. Let us then establish this law for the guardians: that they neither ravage fields nor consume dwellings with fire. Let us establish it indeed, he said, and let us assert that these things, along with the previous ones, are correct. But it seems to me, O Socrates, if one allows you to speak of other things, you will never remember that which you passed over in the previous parts to bring all these matters into the midst: namely, that it is possible for this republic to exist, and in what way it can exist. For if it should exist, I do not doubt that all good things would come to the city itself; and even those things you pass over, that [**ꝙ** - *quod*] these citizens will fight strenuously against enemies because they will by no means desert each other, knowing themselves to be kin, calling each other by these names: brothers, fathers, sons. And if the women should also serve in war, whether in the same rank or in the following line, both to terrify the enemies and to bring aid to the men when necessity demands, I know surely they would be invincible; and I understand how many good things would follow them at home, even if all have not been mentioned. But as if I were conceding all these things and many others that would come to pass if this republic were to exist, do not speak more of it, but let us now try to persuade ourselves of this very thing: that it is possible, and by what reasoning it is possible for this republic to exist. Let us leave the rest. By a sudden incursion, you have again invaded my speech, nor do you forgive me for struggling, nor do you perhaps notice that I have scarcely emerged from two waves, and now you push me back into a third, the greatest and most difficult. After you have seen and heard it, you will surely give me pardon, recognizing that not without cause did I fear to enter into a discourse so abhorrent to the opinions of men. The more you pile up arguments in this sentiment, he said, the less you will be released by us from showing in what way this republic can exist. Therefore, speak now, and do not delay. First, I said, it is necessary to remember that we arrived here while inquiring into the nature of Justice and Injustice. We must indeed, but to what end is this? Surely if we have seen the nature of justice, shall we judge that a just man ought to differ not at all from it, but be entirely such as justice itself is? Or shall we think it sufficient if he approaches it as closely as possible and partakes of it more than anyone else? We shall think it quite sufficient. For the sake of an example, then, we sought the nature of justice and what a perfectly just man would be like if he existed; and again, what injustice is like and the most unjust man: so that, seeing what they were like in terms of happiness and misery, we would be compelled to confess concerning ourselves that our lot would be similar to whoever showed himself most like them. We did not, however, search these things out to show that they could happen. These things are true. Do you think someone would be a less good painter because, after he had produced an absolute exemplar of human beauty and omitted nothing of its appearance, he could not demonstrate that such a man could be found? By no means. And have we not also shaped the exemplar of a most excellent city in speech? Entirely. Do you then think we speak less correctly if we cannot show that such a city can exist as we have depicted in speech? Not at all. Such is the truth of it. But if, for your sake, this must also be demonstrated—how and according to what it can most effectively be achieved—you must again confess these same things to me for this demonstration. Which things? Can anything be done exactly as it is said, or is it so arranged by nature that action attains truth less than speech, even if it does not seem so to some? Do you confess this or not? I do indeed confess it. Do not compel me then to demonstrate that those things we have run through in words must be made entirely so in reality. But if we are able to find by what reasoning a republic's institution may come as close as possible to these things, it must be confessed that we have discovered how those things you command can be achieved. Will you not lead us to think it sufficient if you achieve these things? For I indeed would be satisfied. I too. Let us then try to declare hereafter what that thing is on account of which things go badly in cities, preventing them from being so ruled, and whether by the change of some one small thing a city might be instituted in this form; and what that might be: and whether it happens most by the change of one thing, or at least two, or more, but of as few as possible and the least in power. Exactly so. By changing one certain thing, we can show that the form will be changed; which is not a small matter, nor easy, but possible nevertheless. What is that? I return to that which we compared to a great wave. It shall be said, although I suspect it may be entirely overwhelmed by the flooding laughter of the stubborn. Consider what I am about to say. Speak now.

[Page 406]

Unless either philosophers rule in cities, or those who are now called kings and potentates legitimately and sufficiently philosophize [**phulofopheni** - *philosophari*], and these two concur in the same power and philosophy, and (which happens now) these two are not handled by diverse natures, there will be no rest from evils for the city or, in my opinion, for the human race; nor will this republic which we have set forth in words arise as much as it is able and behold the light of the sun. This is what I have long feared to say, as it is incredible to hear. For it is not easily persuaded that no other government, privately or publicly, will be happy. From this speech of yours, O Socrates, expect that many men—and not base ones—will cast off their clothes and, having seized whatever weapons they happen upon, will make an assault upon you and attempt something great. Unless you meet them with speech and defend yourself, you will truly pay the penalty, torn by many insults. Are you not the cause of these things for me? And rightly so. But I will not betray you; rather, I will defend you with whatever I can. I can certainly respond with benevolence and exhortations, and perhaps more diligently than anyone else. Therefore, aided by this defender, try to demonstrate to these incredulous ones that it is as you say. I must indeed strive, since you also seem ready to fight sharply. It seems necessary to me, if we wish to escape those you mention, to declare to them first what kind of men we think philosophers are when we affirm they ought to command: so that these things being made clear, someone might bring help, showing that it befits these men by their very nature both to touch upon the study of philosophy and the administration of the republic; and that it befits others by no means, but rather to obey those leaders. It must be declared now. Come, follow me this way, if in any way we may be able to set forth what is sufficient. Lead on. Is it necessary to remind you? Or do you remember well enough that when we say someone loves something, it must appear, if it is truly said, that he does not love part of it and not another, but is affected toward the whole? I indeed need a reminder. For I do not quite grasp it. It would have befitted anyone else rather than you, O Glauco, to speak thus. But it does not befit a man very indulgent in love to be ignorant that all those established in the flower of age stimulate and incite a lover of boys in some way, since they seem worthy of care and choice. Are you not thus affected toward shapely youths? One, because he is snub-nosed, is judged gracious by us and praised; another with a hooked nose you call "royal." Another who is between these seems to you very well-proportioned. You call the dark ones "manly," the fair ones "sons of the gods." And as for a pale youth, who, unless he is a lover himself, uses a soothing name and calls it "sallow," easily bearing the pallor in ephebes? And, to speak briefly, you catch whatever excuses you can and say everything so that you reject no youth of a flourishing age. If you wish to show in me how lovers are affected, I accept this for the sake of the dispute. What of those greedy for wine? Do you not see them similarly affected? Seeking any wine whatever on any occasion? Greatly. Moreover, I think you have observed that ambitious men, if they cannot obtain the prefecture of a whole army, at least wish to be made tribunes; and unless they are honored by great and venerable men, they receive honor from the ignoble, as those who utterly affect honor. Greatly. Will you confess this or not? When we say someone loves anything, shall we say he burns for that whole thing? Or shall we confess he desires part and not part? The whole. Shall we not therefore say the philosopher is a studier of wisdom, not greedy for this part and not that, but rather for all wisdom? You speak truly. He, therefore, who hates any doctrine, especially while he is young and does not yet have a choice dictated by reason discerning what is useful and what is not, we shall by no means assert to be a seeker of learning or a lover of wisdom: just as we do not say he who loathes feasts is hungry or desires feasts or is a lover of food, but we call him a despiser. And rightly so. But the man who is more prone to tasting any doctrine, most ready for learning, and gapes for it insatiably, we shall rightly name a philosopher. Shall we not? Here Glauco assented. But indeed, he said, many and absurd men will be found to be such. For those greedy for spectacles all seem to be lovers of learning; and it is absurd to call curious men who listen to everything "philosophers," who do not willingly approach the reason of speaking and disputing; but as if their ears were hired for pay, they run about at all the choruses in the festivals of Bacchus, so great is their desire to hear everyone, whether in the city or the villages. Shall we name all these and others greedy for perceiving such things, and those brooding over the vilest arts, philosophers? By no means, but similar to philosophers. But the true philosophers—whom do you call so? Those greedy for beholding the truth. That is right, but how do you say it? I would not easily say it to another. But I think you will grant me this. What especially? Since the beautiful is the contrary of the ugly, these are two. Why not? And since they are two, each will be one. This also. And concerning the just and the unjust, the good and the bad, and all species, the same reason holds. For each of these is one itself; but by the common communion of actions and bodies and alternatives appearing everywhere, they seem to be many. You speak skillfully. By this reasoning indeed I distinguish: on one side those you just mentioned, greedy for seeing and for arts

[Page 407]

and for actions, and on the other side those of whom we speak, whom alone one will rightly call philosophers. How do you say this? Men greedy for hearing and seeing are greatly delighted by beautiful voices, colors, and figures, and all things that consist of such; but their thought cannot touch the nature of the beautiful itself. So it is. But those who are able to ascend to the beautiful itself and inspect it according to itself, are they not rare? Very rare. He who thinks these beautiful things exist, but does not think beauty itself exists, nor can he attain the perception of it if someone leads him—does he seem to you truly to be wise, or to be played with in dreams? Consider then: is not dreaming this—when either sleeping or waking, one thinks that which is similar to something is not similar, but is the thing itself which it resembles? I would say this man sees dreams. But what of him who is affected the opposite way, and understands what the beautiful itself is, and can discern both it and the things that participate in it, so that he thinks neither it is those things nor those things are it—does he live waking or dreaming? Surely wide awake. Therefore, we shall rightly call the thought of this man "knowledge" [*cognitionem*] as one who knows; and the other's "opinion" [*opinionem*] as one who opines. Entirely. If he whom we say opines and does not know is angry with us and denies that we speak the truth, by what reasoning shall we mitigate him and gently persuade him that he is not of sound mind? We must indeed. Observe what [**margin note: * vel. Non / magnopere / laboramus.** - *Or: We do not labor greatly.*] we shall say to him. If you wish, we shall inquire of him in this manner, saying that if he knows anything, it is with no envy: but it will be pleasing to us for him to know something, and for us to have known what he knows. But tell me this. Does whoever knows, know something or nothing? You answer in his place. Something, certainly. Is it that which is, or that which is not? That which is. For how could that which is not be known? This will be sufficiently established if it is investigated under various reasons: namely, that what is entirely "being" [*ens*] can be entirely known; what is in no way "being" can in no way be known. Most sufficiently. Come, if anything is so that it both is and is not, will it not be a medium between that which is entirely and that which is in no way? A medium. Knowledge itself is turned toward that which is. Ignorance of necessity toward that which is not. Concerning the medium of these, some medium must be investigated between science and ignorance, if anything of this kind is found. Exactly. Do we say opinion is something? Why not? Is it the same power as science, or a different one? A different one. Therefore opinion is turned toward one thing, science toward another, either according to the same power or according to the different power of each itself. It is so. Does not science indeed know that which is, by that reason in which it is being? Rather indeed, I think [**margin note: * censeo*] it necessary that I first distinguish these. How? We shall say that powers are a certain genus of things that are, by which we can do whatever we can, and another can do whatever it can. Just as I call sight and hearing certain powers, if you understand what I speak. I do indeed understand. Hear what seems to me concerning these. For I indeed see neither any color of power itself, nor figure, nor any such things as of many of the rest, looking at which I distinguish some things among myself, that these are some and those are others. But in power, I look only to that toward which it is and what it does: and by this reason, I have named the power of any of them; and that which tends toward the same thing and does the same, I call the same; but the other which looks to another thing and works another. What do you do in these? The same as you. Come again to these, O best of men: do you say science is a certain power? Or do you refer it to another genus? A power, and surely the strongest of all. And opinion—shall we say it is a power or something else? A power, certainly. For that by which we can opine is nothing other than opinion. But a little while ago you confessed that science and opinion are not the same. In what way would anyone having a mind assert that what can be deceived is the same as what cannot? Very well indeed. It is established then that science is something else for us than opinion. Clearly another. Therefore each is able by its own nature to work toward something else. It is necessary. Science indeed, toward that which is, to know being itself as it is. Surely. But opinion is to opine. This also. Does it know the same thing as science? And will that which is perceived by opinion be the same as that which is by science? Or is it rather impossible? Impossible certainly from those things we granted, if indeed a different power is turned by nature toward a different thing; and both are powers, namely science and opinion; and each is another, as was said. From these, then, it cannot be that what is comprehended by science and what is conceived by opinion are the same. Therefore, if being itself is perceived by knowledge, must not that which is conceived by opinion be said to be something else besides being itself? Something else. Does one opine "non-being"? Or is it impossible to opine "non-being"? Think thus. Does not whoever opines direct his opinion toward something? Or is it possible to opine indeed, but to opine nothing? Impossible. But whoever opines, opines some one thing? Without doubt. But that which is not is not one thing, but should rather be called nothing. Entirely. To non-being indeed we of necessity attribute ignorance, but to being knowledge. Quite right. Therefore, one opines neither being nor non-being. It is so. Wherefore neither ignorance nor knowledge will be opinion. Not, it seems. Is it outside these, exceeding knowledge in clarity or ignorance in obscurity? Neither of these. Or perhaps opinion seems to you more obscure than knowledge but clearer than ignorance? Greatly. Therefore it lies between both? Surely. Therefore opinion will be the medium of these? The medium. Did we not say above, if anything appeared such that it simultaneously was and was not, that thing was to be placed between truly being and entirely not being; and neither science nor ignorance pertains to it, but that which appears to be a medium between ignorance and science? Skilfully. But now the medium of these appeared to be that which we call opinion. Clearly. That therefore, as I think, remains for us to find: that which partakes of both, namely of being and not being, and should be said to be neither of them sincerely: so that if it is open to us, we might rightly name it the "opinable," attributing extremes to extremes and mediums to mediums. Is it not so? Exactly so. These being thus placed, I shall inquire of him who denies that the beautiful itself and the idea of beauty are one, always being in the same way according to the same things; but thinks there are many beautiful things, and being dedicated to looking at beautiful things, in no way admits that there is one beautiful, one just: and similarly concerning the rest, I shall inquire in this manner: Is there anything of these many beautiful things, best of men, which might not also seem ugly? And likewise of the just, which might not seem unjust? And of the holy, which might not seem profane? No, but it is necessary that the beautiful things themselves also appear ugly, and whatever else you ask. What of many doubles? Do they seem less halves than doubles? By no means. And great

[Page 408]

moreover and small, likewise light and heavy—will they be called such any more than their contraries? No, but each will always partake of both. Is each of the many more that which one says it is than it is not? This is similar to those things which are often said in banquets on both sides, and to the riddle of children about the eunuch and the striking of the bat, how and in what they argue he struck it. For these are ambiguous, and none of them can be firmly understood as being, or not being, or both, or neither. Do you have a reason how to use these? Or can you induce a more convenient position for them than the medium between essence and non-being? For it will not appear more obscure than non-being so that it is less, nor clearer than being so that it is more. You speak truly. We have found, then, as it seems, that those many things which are thought by many to be beautiful or other things in any way whatever, are rolled in the medium between entirely being and entirely not being. We have found it clearly. But we had confessed before that if any such thing appeared, it should be said to be perceived not by knowledge but by opinion, the medium being comprehended by the medium power. It was conceded. Therefore those who behold these many beautiful things, but do not see the beautiful itself, nor can follow him who leads to it, and look upon many just things but the just itself not at all, and other things similarly—we shall say they opine all things, but know nothing of those things they opine. It is necessary. What of those who contemplate each thing itself, always in the same way according to the same things—do they not know rather than opine? This also is necessary. Shall we not say these love and admire those things in which knowledge is turned, but the others those in which opinion is? Do we not remember that we said these men love and look upon beautiful voices and colors and such things, but do not admit that the beautiful itself is anything? We remember. Wherefore we shall not err if we call them *philodoxos*, that is, friends of opinion, rather than philosophers; although they will be sharply angry with us if we say so. Not if they obey me. For it is a crime to be angry with the truth. Therefore those who admire and love each thing that is by itself, we shall call philosophers, not *philodoxos*. So it is fitting, he said.

### DIALOGUE SIX ON JUSTICE.
**ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.**

Since all laws, even the best, are dead without most approved magistrates, and the best magistrates even without written laws are themselves divine laws, our Plato—as we have explained elsewhere—rightly labors in an excellent republic not in founding laws, but with all diligence in forming magistrates... Since he calls these "guardians," and it is most proper to a guardian to look forward and look around, he therefore chooses the philosophical nature, the most perspicacious of all without controversy, for guarding the human flock...

[Summary of Ficino’s Argument: Ficino explains that the philosopher is the only one who can see the exemplar of the Good and Justice. He discusses the corruption of great natures by the "Great Beast" (the public) and the necessity of the "Idea of the Good" as the sun of the intelligible world. He mentions the mystical parallels between Plato’s "Father and Son" and Christian theology, citing Hermes Trismegistus and Iamblichus.]

[Page 409]

...What kind of men philosophers are, I said, and what kind those are who are foreign to philosophy, O Glauco, has finally been established by a long discourse. It was perhaps, he said, not easy to explain in fewer words. No, as it appears. But this would shine forth more clearly, I think, if it had been necessary to narrate only this, and not to wander through many other things, if one wished to show how much a just life differs from an unjust one. What remains for us to do hereafter? What else than what follows in order? Since philosophers are those who can touch that which always is in the same way according to the same things, and those who cannot are not philosophers but wander through many mutable things: which of these should be leaders of the city? How can we rightly answer this? Those who can guard the laws and the offices of the city, to these the rudders of the republic must be committed. Correctly. But it is clear whether it ought to be a blind man or one who sees sharply to whom we entrust something to be kept. Why not clear? Do those who lack knowledge in each thing of that which truly is, seem to you to differ from the blind? They have no perspicuous exemplar in their mind, nor can they, like painters looking toward the truest exemplar and referring to it and beholding it most accurately, thus finally bring laws here concerning the beautiful, just, and good, if it is necessary, and guard and preserve the laws once brought? Indeed, they do not differ much. Shall we choose these for guardianship rather than those who know each thing that truly is, and in experience or any other part of virtue are in no way inferior? It would be absurd to choose others, especially if other things are not lacking. They surely surpass in this greatest thing. Shall we not say how they can have those and these simultaneously? Entirely. Therefore, what we said at the beginning of this dispute, we must first learn their nature; and I think, if we sufficiently agree on that, we shall also agree that it is possible for the same men to attain these things, and that none besides these should be leaders of the city. In what way? Let this first be established among us concerning the natures of philosophers: that they always love that discipline by which that nature which always is—and is not changed by generation and corruption—becomes better known to them. Let it be established. Moreover, that they affect all of it, and do not willingly scorn any part of it, neither small nor great, neither honorable nor base, as we said above concerning the ambitious and those captured by love. Rightly. Moreover, observe this: is it not necessary that there be in the nature of those who will be such as we have described? What sort of thing? That they be free of all falsehood, and never willingly lie, but hate all falsity and love truth. It is probable. It is not only probable, O friend, but entirely necessary, that he who is affected by love toward anything by nature should love whatever is cognate and familiar to the beloved. Skillfully. Is anything found more familiar to wisdom than truth? Nothing. Is it then possible for the same nature to be philosophical and lying? In no way. Therefore, it is necessary for a true lover of learning to affect all truth immediately from childhood. Entirely. But when desires violently carry someone toward one certain thing, his desires for other things are more relaxed, as if flowing elsewhere like rivulets. No doubt. Whoever, therefore, burns with all desire for disciplines and such things, seeks the pure pleasure of the soul itself, but despises the delights of the body—unless he be a feigned and not a true philosopher. This is exceedingly necessary. Such a man will be temperate and in no way greedy for money. For to gape after piling up money belongs to anyone rather than to him for whose sake others sweat to seek money with the greatest loss. It is so. Moreover, that must be considered whenever you wish to discern the nature of him who is a philosopher and him who is not. What? Lest perhaps some latent illiberality be in him. For pusillanimity is entirely adverse to a mind about to investigate the whole divine and human universe. You speak truly. Surely, to one who possesses magnificence of thought and the contemplation of all time and all substance, human life cannot seem anything great. Not indeed. Will he think death terrible? Least of all. Therefore, true philosophy does not befit a timid and illiberal nature. Not, as it seems to me. But a modest man, not dedicated to gain, not illiberal, not proud, not timid—will he be difficult in dealings or unjust? By no means. Moreover, when you wish to discern which mind is philosophical or not, you will observe this from tender years:

[Page 410]

whether it is just and mild, or inequitable and fierce. Most certainly. Nor will you pass this over, I think. What? Whether he is swift or slow at perceiving. Do you think anyone would ever love that which he does with the greatest difficulty when he approaches it, and scarcely achieves a little? Never indeed. What if he should forget everything he learns, would he not be void of science? Void. When truly all his labor is undertaken in vain, will he not finally be compelled to hate himself and such action? Nothing prevents it. Let us therefore never think a forgetful mind befits the natures of legitimate philosophers, but a very mindful one. Exactly so. Moreover, a discordant and unharmonious nature always draws toward immoderation. Always. But do you think truth agrees with immoderation and lack of measure, or rather with measure? With measure. Therefore, let us attribute a composed and graceful thought to this nature, which we want to be prone by its own nature to inspecting the idea of each thing that truly is. Surely. Does it not seem to you that we have run through each thing which it is necessary should belong in a continued series to the mind of him who is to perfectly attain the truth of things? Exactly so. Can you in any way damn that study which no one can sufficiently execute unless he is by nature perspicacious, mindful, magnificent, graceful, a friend and familiar of truth, justice, fortitude, and temperance? Not even Momus [the god of mockery] could carp at that. Will you not commit the administration of the republic to these alone, finally advanced in erudition and age? To this Adimantus replied: No one, O Socrates, could contradict you. But thus are they affected who hear those things you narrate everywhere. For they think that through inexperience in questioning and answering they are led away a little from reason in each thing they are asked, and small errors being finally collected, they assert an immense error and something contrary to what they first asserted... just as those who are unskilled at playing checkers are finally coerced and closed in by those skilled in that game so they have nowhere to move... so they think they are finally coerced and closed in, having nothing to say, circumscribed by words as if by checkers... they see those who approach the study of philosophy not for the sake of education as youths but remaining longer, to turn out mostly very absurd and alienated from human affairs, not to say most wicked. And those who seem more excellent are so defiled by the study you praise that they turn out useless for governing the republic. When I had heard this, I said: Do you think those who say these things lie? I do not know, he said, but I would gladly hear what you feel. You will hear it certainly: I think they speak the truth. By what reasoning then is it rightly said that there will be no rest from evils in cities until philosophers rule in them, whom we confess are useless to the republic? What you ask requires a response introduced through a certain image. But you are not accustomed, I think, to speaking through similitudes. So be it, I said, do you mock me when you have driven me into a discourse so difficult to demonstrate? Hear then the similitude... It is so hard what excellent men in philosophy suffer in governing the republic... Just as when painters depict goat-stags [*tragelaphos*] and other mixed fictions. Imagine some pilot of a ship or fleet such as this: exceeding the rest of the sailors in magnitude and strength of body, but deaf and with dim eyes and ignorant of navigation; and the sailors contending among themselves about the government, while each thinks himself worthy of command, although he never learned the art nor can show any teacher in that matter, nor assign at what time he learned... denying even that the art can be taught... Imagine them crowding around that pilot, beseeching, contending that he hand over the rudders to them. Where, if they do not persuade him, but others do, they either kill the others or cast them from the ship; and finally, having occupied that noble prince of the ship with mandragora or wine, they seize the government of the ship, use the present things, indulge in wine and feasts, and govern as is likely for such men. Moreover, all praise him, call him a sailor and a pilot... and whoever can help them in usurping the princedom of the ship... they praise, but him who cannot, they vituperate as useless: not even thinking of the office of the true pilot; namely, that it belongs to him to have reason of the year, seasons, sky, stars, and winds, and all things that pertain to that art, if he is truly to be a pilot of the ship... If these things were thus in a ship, do you not think the true pilot would be called by those who sail in such ships a vain and curious inspector of sublime things, and useless to the ship? Most certainly, said Adimantus.

[Page 411]

I do not think it necessary, I said, to explain to you more broadly how, according to the image of the proposed comparison, the citizens in cities are affected toward true philosophers... First, then, to him who wonders why philosophers are not honored in cities, expose this image and try to persuade him it would be much more wonderful if they were honored. I will do so. Add this also: that those speak the truth who say those who are the best philosophers are useless to the crowd. But that they are useless, say that they themselves are not the cause. For it is not according to nature that the pilot should pray to the sailors that they commit themselves to his government, or that the wise should go to the doors of the rich. But whoever first threw this out, lied. In truth, it is naturally so: whether rich or poor be held by adverse health, he necessarily seeks the doors of doctors; and all who need the government of a superior should go to the houses of men potent at governing... But if you compare those who in these times administer republics with those sailors we just mentioned, you will not err; and if you compare those who are called useless and vain and superstitious inquirers of recondite things by them, to true pilots, you will act rightly. Very rightly, he said. For these reasons, it is not easy for an honest study to be approved by those who are affected by contrary morals. But the greatest and most vehement calumny of philosophy arises on account of the morals of those who profess the studies of philosophy... those who criminate philosophy say that most of those who go to philosophy are very wicked; and if some of them excel the rest, they are useless; and I have conceded these things to you, have I not? Certainly. But have we not exposed the cause on account of which the best philosophers seem useless? Surely. But why most are wicked, do you want us to open up next? And declare that the fault is not philosophy's? I do indeed. Let us proceed, repeating what we said above: what kind of nature he must have who is to be honest and good. His leader first of all, if you hold it in memory, was Truth, which he must follow entirely and everywhere; or if he be a vain man, he is truly void of philosophy. So it was said. This one thing then is entirely foreign to what they now think of him. Most foreign. Shall we not decently defend his cause in this way? Saying that a man greedy for science is so instituted by nature that he always contends toward that which truly is, nor does he draw delays in those individual and many things about which opinion is turned, but proceeding further is not fatigued and does not cease to desire until he has touched the proper nature of each thing with that power of the mind by which it is fitting to apprehend it. It is fitting by a certain cognate power. Which, when it has adhered and mixed itself with that which truly is, and thence truly generated intelligence and truth, he will know truly, and live truly and be nourished. From this birth finally his whole trouble will cease, but not before. Very appropriately said. Will he in any way love a lie? Or rather hate it entirely? He will hate it certainly. Surely where truth is the leader, we shall not say a chorus of evils follows. How so? Rather we shall say a sincere and just moral follows. Shall we say temperance also follows? Skilfully. Moreover, what need is there to recount from the beginning the rest of the chorus of the philosophical nature? For you remember that with these agree, as we said, fortitude, magnificence, sharpness of wit, and memory... [Discussion of how great philosophical natures are corrupted].

[Page 412]

...Do you not see that they note with infamy, loss of money, and the penalty of death the man not obeying them? Exceedingly. What other sophist then do you think, or what other private discourses could oppose these and resist? None certainly. Indeed, to resist these is the greatest folly. For there never was, nor is, nor will be another moral, a human one at least, instituted toward virtue besides the discipline of these, O friend. For a divine one, as the proverb says, let us except. For know this for certain: whatever remains immaculate and integer from this constitution of republics, has remained so by divine aid. It seems no different to me. Moreover, this ought to appear to you. What? Each of those who privately receive pay to instruct men, whom they call sophists and rivals of the arts, thinks nothing else should be taught than the opinions of the many in which they agree whenever they are gathered, and this he calls wisdom: just as if someone had observed the rages and desires of some vast, robust, and nurtured brute animal, and by what reasoning it is fitting to approach it, how to touch it, when it is either fiercer or milder, and from what causes it becomes such. And the voices which each is accustomed to express. Moreover, by what voices of others that animal is either excited or placated. After he has perceived each thing through long habit, he calls this experience "wisdom," and as if it were an art collected for teaching he goes to it, in truth ignorant of which of these opinions and desires is honest or base, good or bad, just or unjust. But he names each thing according to the opinion of that huge beast: good things those by which it is delighted, bad those by which it is offended; nor does he bring any other reason for these, but calls necessary things "just" and "honest": but how much the nature of the good itself and the necessary differ, he has neither perceived himself nor can he show to others. If someone, I said, were thus affected, would he not seem an absurd teacher to you? To me indeed. Does he seem to differ from this who thinks it is wisdom to know the rage and pleasures of many and various men coming together, whether in painting, or music, or the discipline of administering the republic? It is clear that if someone deals with these and shows them either the work of a poet or another art, or a ministry pertaining to the republic, and exhibits the authority of the work to the crowd to be judged, he will be compelled by a "Diomedean necessity," as they say, beyond what is necessary, to do those things they approve. But have you ever heard any of them assigning a reason that was not ridiculous why these are truly good and honest? I have not heard, and I do not think I shall. Thinking on all these things, remember also this: Can the crowd, either by another's speaking or of itself, admit or touch the beautiful itself? Or the nature of each thing itself? By no means. Therefore, the crowd cannot be a philosopher. No. Moreover, it is necessary that those philosophizing be vituperated by it. Necessary. And by all those wishing to please the people. It is clear. From these things, then, do you see how to preserve the philosophical nature so that it may reach the end of philosophizing? ... [Discussion of the rare philosopher].

[Page 413]

...Those who see the insanity of the many... seeing that no one acts rightly in republics, nor is there any ally or helper to be found... but like a man fallen among beasts, since he neither wishes to act unjustly with them nor can he alone resist all the wild beasts, he perishes before he can help either the city or friends; and thus he is useless both to himself and others. All these things, I say, whoever diligently observes, they keep quiet and care only for their own: and as if in a storm, while both a whirlwind is agitated and winds blow, and the sky is covered in dust, they remain safe within walls: and beholding others involved in wickedness, they think they will have enough if they themselves have lived pure from injustice and iniquitous deeds, and having finished the course of life, depart cheerful and pious with good hope. Certainly he will have done no small thing who thus spends his life. But not the greatest thing, if he has not found a republic convenient to himself. For in it he himself will profit and increase more, and preserve both private and public things. Thus far why philosophy underwent calumny, and that the calumny is unjust, I think has been sufficiently said, unless you perhaps add something else. I would say nothing else. But of the republics that now exist, which do you think most fits philosophers? None at all, and therefore I complain, because I see no institution of republics among those that now exist worthy of the nature of a philosopher. Wherefore it is necessary that this nature be changed and turned... [Discussion of the "foreign seed" and how the philosopher's nature only thrives in the ideal state]. ...The beautiful things are difficult... Now what follows is not easy to say at all: By what reasoning especially the city ought to undertake philosophy so that it is not destroyed... For anything great is wont to be deceptive... [Socrates proposes that the young should do light philosophy and exercise, and as they grow older, increase the study, and when they are old and "emeriti," live for philosophy]. You seem to speak quite promptly, O Socrates. But I think most when they hear these things will repugn even more promptly, not at all persuaded by you. And first I think Thrasymachus will do that. Do not, I say, plot against the benevolence between me and Thrasymachus. For we have recently become friends, nor were we enemies before... [Socrates explains that the reason people don't believe is they have never seen a true philosopher-king].

[Page 414]

...Wherefore, since we foresaw and feared these things, compelled by truth we said that neither any city, nor republic, nor perfect man will exist until a certain necessity by chance falls upon these few philosophers—who are neither wicked nor useless as is commonly thought—so that whether they wish it or not, they take up the care of the city... or that in those who rule, or their sons, by some divine inspiration, a true love of true philosophy should be instilled. But that either of these or both are impossible, I think cannot be demonstrated... If therefore at some time in the infinite past... or in the future... we affirm that the republic described above has been, is, and will be. When this Muse is present to a city, it can certainly be done, nor do we imagine impossible things. But that these are difficult was also conceded by us. It seems so to me too. You will add perhaps that it does not seem so to the crowd. Perhaps. Do not blame the crowd so much, O blessed man. But what do you think they will opine if not out of the study of contention but by friendly warnings... you show them whom especially you call philosophers... do you think anyone is irritated against a mild man? Or that a man without envy envies a man who is not envious? ... I think that for why the multitude bears philosophy with an iniquitous mind, the cause is those who, being inept for philosophy, professing it, harass men with insults... and always speak ill of men, doing a thing least fitting for philosophy. Entirely. For indeed, O Adimantus, to that man who has directed all the edge of his mind toward those things that truly are, there is no leisure to look back at the inferior affairs of men and, fighting with them, to contract the dust of envy and malevolence. But he contemplates those things that always keep the same order, which neither inflict injury on each other nor suffer it: but all are ornate and disposed according to reason. And he imitates these and makes himself as similar to them as possible... [The philosopher, by communing with the divine, becomes as divine and orderly as a man can be]. ...If therefore some necessity leads him to transfer those things he beholds there to the morals of men privately and publicly... do you think he will be an inert artisan of temperance, justice, and all popular virtue? Least of all. If the crowd feels we speak the truth of this, will they be angry with philosophers? Or will they not believe us when we say the city will not otherwise be happy than if those who use a divine exemplar, like painters, form it? They will by no means be angry, he said, if they feel it. But what manner of painting do you mean? When these painters, I say, have taken the city and the morals of men like a certain tablet, they will first purge it, which is in no way easy. Do you not know that philosophers differ from others especially in this, that they do not attempt to touch either a private person or a city, nor to found laws, before they have either received them purged or have purged them themselves? And rightly so. Do you not think they will describe the form of the republic after this? Why not? Then doing these things, I think, they will frequently look toward both: toward that which is naturally just, honest, and temperate, and such things; and again toward human things: and they will dispose the human according to the exemplar of that superior thing... Part will they erase, part again will they paint, until they have joined human morals, as much as can be, to God in love. Most beautiful, he said, is this painting. Do we persuade those, I said, who you said were carried away against us, that such is the painter of republics? ... Now in what part do they oppose us? ... [The opponents are finally silenced and persuaded]. ...Therefore let these now be persuaded of this. But who will doubt this, that sons of kings and potent men will not be born philosophers? No one. But one might add that even if they are born such, it is necessary they be defiled. For that they should be preserved pure from stains is arduous, as we also concede. But who will add this further: that in all time of all men not even one was ever preserved? No one would say this. But one nature thus instituted, and having found an obedient city, is sufficient for perfecting all these things which now lack faith. Sufficient indeed. I place it thus: if some prince commands the laws and offices which we have narrated, it is not impossible that the citizens should wish to obey them. Surely not. But that others should feel the same as we feel, is that wonderful or impossible? Not, I think. And that these are best, if indeed possible, has been sufficiently disputed above. Sufficiently. Wherefore from those things said, it follows that those things we predicted concerning founding laws will be best if they are done: likewise difficult to do, but not impossible. It follows clearly. Since we have finally imposed an end on these things, we must now proceed to the rest...

--- Page 422 ---
