remains to be demonstrated: in what way, and according to what principle, it can most especially be brought about. Returning to this demonstration, you must grant me these very things. Which things? Whether it is possible for anything to be done exactly as it is said, or whether it is the nature of things that action attains less of the truth than speech, even if it does not seem so to some? Do you agree to this, or not? I certainly agree. Therefore, do not compel me to demonstrate that these things we have run through in words must be realized exactly in every detail. But if we are able to find by what means the institution of the Republic may come as close as possible to these ideals, it must be admitted that we have discovered how these things you command can be achieved. Or will you not be satisfied if you obtain these results? For I, indeed, would be satisfied. I would too. Let us endeavor, then, to declare after this what it is that is currently done badly in cities, preventing them from being governed in this way, and whether by the change of one small thing a city might be established in this form—and what that thing might be. And whether this is best done by the change of one person, or at least two, or more, but as few as possible and with the least power. Entirely so. By changing one thing, we can show that the form will be changed, which is indeed no small thing, nor easy, yet possible. What is it? I return to that which we compared to a massive wave. It shall be said, though I suspect it may be entirely overwhelmed by the overflowing laughter of the persistent. Consider what I am about to say. Speak now. **Unless either philosophers rule in cities, or those who are now called kings and potentates philosophize legitimately and sufficiently, and civil power and philosophy concur in the same person—and while (as happens now) these two are treated by diverse natures—there will be no rest from evils for the city, or, in my opinion, for the human race. Nor will this republic, which we have set forth in words, arise to its full strength and see the light of the sun.** This is what I have long feared to say, as if it were incredible to hear. For it is not easily persuaded that no other governance, privately or publicly, will be happy. From this speech of yours, O Socrates, expect that many—and not lowly men at that—will cast off their cloaks and, seizing whatever weapons they happen upon, will rush at you to attempt something great. Unless you meet them with speech and defend yourself, you will truly suffer the penalty, torn apart by many insults. Are you not the cause of these things for me? And rightly so. But I will not betray you; rather, I will certainly defend you with whatever means I can. I can certainly help with goodwill and exhortations, and perhaps I will respond more carefully than anyone else. Therefore, having been aided by such a defender, try to demonstrate to these skeptics that it is as you say. I must certainly strive, since you also seem ready to fight so sharply. It seems necessary to me, if we wish to escape those you mention, to declare to them first what kind of men we think philosophers are when we affirm they ought to rule. Thus, when these things are made clear, someone may be able to help by showing that it is fitting for these men, by their very nature, to touch upon both the study of philosophy and the administration of the republic, while others should not touch them at all, but should obey those who lead. It must be declared now. Come, follow me this way, so we may somehow explain what is sufficient. Lead on. Do you need to be reminded, or do you remember well enough, that when we say someone loves something, it must be seen—if it is truly said—that he does not love one part of it and not another, but is moved toward the whole? I indeed need a reminder, for I do not grasp it sufficiently. It would have been more fitting for anyone else to speak so, O Glaucon. But it does not befit a man so deeply indulgent in love to be ignorant of the fact that all those in the flower of their age stimulate and move a lover of boys in some way, since they seem worthy of care and affection. Are you not affected this way toward beautiful youths? One, because he has a snub nose <note>Latin: *simus*</note>, is judged by us to be charming and is praised; but a hooked nose you call "royal." Another, because he is in the middle of these, seems very well-proportioned to you; the dark-skinned you call "manly," the fair ones "children of the gods." And as for the pale youth, who but a flattering lover would call him "honey-colored" <note>Latin: *suffici* from the Greek *melichloros*</note>, easily tolerating the pallor in the youths? And to speak summarily, you seize upon any pretext and say anything so that you do not reject any youth who is in the bloom of his age. If you wish to show in me how lovers are affected, I accept this for the sake of the discussion. What of those greedy for wine? Do you not see them similarly affected? That they seek out any wine whatsoever, seizing any occasion? Greatly. Furthermore, I think you have noticed that ambitious men, if they cannot obtain the leadership of a whole army, at least wish to be made tribunes. And if they are not honored by great and venerable men, they accept honor from the ignoble, as those who are entirely affected by honor. Most certainly. Will you admit this or not? That he whom we say loves something, we shall say burns for that entire thing? Or shall we say he desires one part and not the other? The whole. Shall we not therefore say that the philosopher is a lover of wisdom <term>philosophos: literally "lover of wisdom"</term>, not greedy for one part and not another, but for all wisdom? You speak the truth. Therefore, he who hates any learning—especially while he is young and does not yet have a choice dictated by reason of what is useful or not—we shall by no means assert to be a lover of learning or a lover of wisdom. Just as we say he who is disgusted by feasts is neither hungry nor desires the feast, nor is he a lover of food, but we call him a despiser. And rightly so. But the man who is inclined to taste every kind of learning, and is most ready to learn, and gapes for it insatiably, we shall rightly name a philosopher. Shall we not? Here Glaucon assented. But truly, he said, many and indeed absurd men will be found to be such. For those who are greedy for spectacles seem all to be lovers of learning; and as for people curious for hearing, it is absurd to call them philosophers, for they do not willingly approach the practice of speaking and debating. Instead, as if they had hired out their ears for a fee, they run about the festivals of Bacchus to hear every chorus, whether they are held in the city or in the villages. Shall we name all these, and others greedy for perceiving such things and devoted to the lowliest arts, philosophers? By no means, but they are *similar* to philosophers. But whom do you call true philosophers? Those who are lovers of seeing the truth. That is right, but how do you mean it? I would not easily say this to another. But I think you will grant me this. What especially? Since the beautiful is the opposite of the ugly, these are two. Why not? And since they are two, each will be one. That too. And concerning the just and the unjust, the good and the evil, and all forms, the same logic applies. For each of these is one itself; but because of their communion with actions and bodies and each other, appearing everywhere, each seems to be many. You speak skillfully. By this reasoning I distinguish, setting apart those you just mentioned, the lovers of seeing and of the arts...

...and of the arts and actions, and setting apart also those of whom we speak, whom alone one will rightly call philosophers. How do you say that? Men greedy for hearing and seeing are greatly delighted by beautiful voices, colors, and shapes, and all things composed of such, but their thought cannot reach the nature of the beautiful itself. So it is. But those who are able to ascend to the beautiful itself, and to behold it according to itself, are they not rare? Very rare indeed. He who considers these beautiful things, but does not believe in beauty itself, nor if someone should lead him to the perception of it, can he reach it—does he seem to you to be truly wise, or to be playing in dreams? Consider, then: is not dreaming this, when whether sleeping or awake, one thinks that which is similar to something is not similar, but is the very thing itself to which it is similar? I would say this man is seeing dreams. What then? He who is affected in the opposite way, and understands what the beautiful itself is, and is able to discern both it and the things that participate in it, so that he thinks neither that it is those things, nor those things are it—does he live awake or dreaming? Certainly awake. Therefore, we shall rightly call the thought of this man "knowledge," as of one who knows; but the thought of the other "opinion," as of one who opines. Entirely so. If he whom we say opines and does not know is angry with us and denies that we speak the truth, by what means shall we pacify him and gently and mildly persuade him that he is not of sound mind? We certainly must. Observe what we shall say to him. If you wish, let us inquire of him in this way *<margin>or: we labor with no envy</margin>* saying that if he knows anything, we do not grudge him; but we will be grateful if he knows something, and to have known what he knows. But tell me this: does he who knows, know something or nothing? You answer in his place. Something, certainly. Is it that which is, or that which is not? That which is. For how could that which is not be known? This will be sufficiently established if it is investigated under various reasons: namely, that what is entirely "being" is also entirely able to be known; what is in no way "being" is in no way able to be known. Most sufficiently. Come, if something is such that it both is and is not, will it not be a medium between that which is entirely and that which is in no way? A medium. Around that which is, knowledge itself revolves. Ignorance, of necessity, revolves around that which is not. Around the medium of these, some medium must be investigated between science and ignorance, if anything of this kind is found. Exactly. Do we say that opinion is something? Why not? Is it the same power as science, or a different one? A different one. Therefore, opinion revolves around one thing, and science around another, either according to the same power, or each according to its own power. It is so. Does not science indeed know that which is, by that reason by which it is being? Rather, I think it is necessary that I first distinguish these things. How? We shall say that "powers" are a certain genus of those things which are, by which we are able to do whatever we can, and another does whatever it can. For example, I call sight and hearing certain powers, if you understand what I say. I do understand. Hear what seems to me concerning these. For I do not see any color of the power itself, nor any shape, nor any such thing as in many other things, looking at which I distinguish some things as being one thing and others another. But in a power I look only to that toward which it is directed and what it does; and by this reasoning, I have called each of them a power. And that which tends toward the same thing and does the same thing, I call the same; but another which looks toward another thing and operates differently, I call different. What do you do in these matters? The same as you. Come back again to these things, O best of men: do you say that science is a certain power? Or do you refer it to another genus? A power, and certainly the most valid of all. And opinion—shall we say it is a power, or something else? A power, certainly. For that by which we can opine is nothing other than opinion. But a little while ago you confessed that science and opinion were not the same. How could any man in his right mind assert that that which can be deceived is the same as that which cannot? Very well indeed. It is established, therefore, that science is something different for us from opinion. Plainly different. Each, therefore, can by its own nature operate around different things. It must be so. Science, indeed, around that which is, to know the being itself as it is. Certainly. But opinion is to opine. That too. Does it know the same thing that science knows? And will that which is perceived by opinion be the same as that which is known by science? Or is it rather impossible? Impossible certainly from those things we have granted, if indeed a different power revolves around a different thing by its very nature. Both are powers, namely science and opinion, and both are different, as was said. From these things, it cannot be that what is comprehended by science is the same as what is conceived by opinion. Is it not, therefore, that if being itself is perceived by knowledge, that which is conceived by opinion must be said to be something else besides being itself? Something else. Does it opine that which is not? Or is it impossible to opine that which is not? Think of it this way. Does not whoever opines direct his opinion toward something? Or is it possible to opine indeed, but to opine nothing? Impossible. But whoever opines, opines some one thing? Without a doubt. But that which is not is not "some one thing," but rather should be called "nothing." Exactly. To non-being, indeed, we necessarily attribute ignorance; but to being, we attribute knowledge. Quite rightly. Therefore, one opines neither being nor non-being. That is so. Wherefore opinion will be neither ignorance nor knowledge. Not, as it seems. Is it something outside these, surpassing knowledge in clarity or ignorance in obscurity? Neither of these. Or does it perhaps seem to you that opinion is more obscure than knowledge, but clearer than ignorance? Greatly. Therefore it lies between both? Certainly. Therefore opinion will be the medium of these? The medium. Did we not say above that if something appeared such that it was simultaneously being and not being, it should be placed between true being and entirely not being? And that neither science nor ignorance pertains to it, but that which appears again as the medium between ignorance and science? Skillfully said. And now it has appeared that the medium of these is what we call opinion. Plainly. That, therefore, remains for us to find, I think: that which participates in both—namely, in being and non-being—and which ought to be called purely neither of those. So that if it is revealed to us, we may rightly name it the "opinable" <note>Latin: *opinabile*</note>, attributing extremes to extremes and mediums to mediums. Is it not so? Exactly so. These things being so placed, I will question him who denies that the beautiful itself and the one idea of beauty exist, always being in the same way according to the same things. He who thinks there are many beautiful things and, being devoted to looking at beautiful things, in no way admits that the beautiful is one, or the just is one; similarly concerning the rest, I will question him in this way: "Is there anything among these many beautiful things, O best of men, which may not also appear ugly? And among the just, what may not appear unjust? And among the holy, what not profane?" No, but it is necessary that those beautiful things also appear ugly, and whatever else you ask. What of many doubles? Do they seem any less halves than doubles? Not at all. And great...

...and moreover great and small, light and heavy: will they be called these things any more than their opposites? No, but each will always participate in both. Is each of the many things any more that which someone says it is than it is not? This is similar to those things which are usually said at banquets on both sides, and to the children's riddle about the eunuch and the striking of the bat—how and on what they argue he struck it. For these things are ambiguous; it cannot be firmly understood that any of them either are or are not, nor both, nor neither. Do you have a way to use these? Therefore, those who behold these many beautiful things, but do not see the beautiful itself, nor can they follow him who leads to it; and who behold many just things, but the just itself not at all, and other things similarly—we shall say that they *opine* all things, but *know* nothing of those things which they opine. It must be so. What of those who contemplate the things themselves, always being in the same way according to the same things? Do they not know rather than opine? That too is necessary. Shall we not say these men love and admire those things in which knowledge is involved, but those others in which opinion is involved? Do we not remember that we said these men love and behold beautiful voices and colors and such things, but do not admit that the beautiful itself is anything? We remember. Wherefore we shall not err if we call them *philodoxous* <note>original: *φιλοδόξους*</note>, that is, lovers of opinion, rather than philosophers. Although they will be sharply angry with us if we say so. Not if they obey me. For it is a crime to be angry with the truth. Therefore, those who admire and love each thing that is being in itself, we shall call philosophers, not *philodoxous*. So it is fitting, he said.

**DIALOGUE SIX**
**ON THE JUST.**
**ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.**

Since all laws, even the best, are dead without the most approved magistrates, and since the best magistrates are themselves living laws even without written laws, our Plato rightly—as we have explained elsewhere—labors with all diligence in his excellent republic not in the composing of laws, but in the forming of magistrates. And indeed he contends for this studiously not only from a tender age, but even from the very birth, so that from chosen seeds and continuous cultivation, the best fruit may be reached. Because he calls these men "guardians," and because it is most proper for guardians to look forward and look around, he therefore chooses the philosophical nature—without controversy the most perspicacious of all—for guarding the human flock. Indeed, since to the eye of this man alone lies open the exemplar of the Good itself and of justice, toward whose image the city is to be painted well, justly, and blessedly. Furthermore, it pertains to a guardian to be truthful, liberal, temperate, brave, just, magnanimous, and mild. He will also prove these same qualities to be proper to the philosopher, so that he may finally conclude that the office of guarding is to be committed to the philosopher above all others. Wherefore, that the nature of the philosopher is of such a kind, he first treats by a probable argument. And because a noble nature, otherwise right, may be useless or even most often harmful without culture, he hands down the discipline for cultivating this genius. Meanwhile, he treats of the spurious and adulterous philosopher who simulates the legitimate philosopher. Also of a certain abuse of philosophizing. Again, of the form of philosophizing pertaining to him above all others who is someday to rule the republic. He teaches that it is most proper to the philosopher to have a perpetual love of truth itself concerning eternal things. And therefore, both the love of temporal things and lying are most alien of all to the philosopher. He shows, moreover, that the philosopher's mind in the very investigation of truth is separated from the body and, from a certain divine kinship of its own, is joined to the mind, and through the formulas of ideas implanted in it from the beginning, it reaches the ideas themselves, and from them by that very contact strikes out a light, by which—having soon been made more fecund—it conceives, or rather, having been made more valid, it gives birth to truth; that is, through its own conceptions it agrees in every way with the ideas. You, however, notice here that the act of understanding—just as in the *Symposium*—is called "generation and birth." This indeed agrees with Christian theology and shows that there is in the mind not only an imaginary but even a certain natural form and truth. Accordingly, he thinks such a genius is born very rarely and in few men, and even then it is indulged by many conditions and hindered by obstacles. Especially, it is depraved by the speech and opinion of the common people, and much more by the works of that same crowd. Again, by vulgar teachers who themselves accommodate their life and speech to the crowd like flatterers and hand down a similar discipline to their listeners. And see how fittingly Plato compares the crowd to a vast beast. Likewise all cities to ships steered by some chance by sailors entirely ignorant of governing, who mock the man endowed with the skill of governing. Note that all best things, whether gifts of nature or fortune, if they have been even slightly neglected in cultivation, turn out bad; or if poorly cultivated, turn out worst in the end. Furthermore, it seems to be judged that although it is very rare, if any great and most approved man appears in a badly disposed city (as he judges all to be), it is to be attributed not to art or nature, but to divinity alone. Where he mentions Momus, the god of reprehension, understand that Momus is the divine care looking forward to what could have been rebuked in individuals if they had been made otherwise than they were, and therefore disposing each thing so that it cannot be rightly rebuked. He assigns accordingly the causes from which calumnies against philosophers have arisen, as if they are either evil or useless to the republic. First, indeed, many daily invade and seize upon philosophy who are most inept for the study of it, as much by a depraved nature as by little judgment, yet with no small ambition or avarice; and from their commerce they procreate adulterous and ridiculous opinions, and moreover disgrace the philosophical faculty with evil morals. Then, if any are born for that study, they are either immediately depraved by wicked education and custom, or if they persist with integrity of morals, they are nevertheless not instructed in the suitable grades of disciplines; or if instructed, they are not admitted to the republic, or they rather refuse to immerse themselves in public waves, fearing certain dangers and despairing that they can benefit the city with sound counsels among men who are everywhere corrupt. Among these things, observe the storms of the active life, the tranquility of the contemplative life, the exalted mind of the philosopher, the contempt for mortals, the study of divine things, and a certain formula of doctrines according to the stages of age. In every way he educates the philosopher and the citizen by a similar reason, and not without justice. For he asserts in the *Statesman* and the *Sophist* that the royal man, the citizen, and the philosopher are the same. But he proves it is necessary for two kinds to concur in this man which very rarely concur in men: namely, a nature sharp in intellect, fit for contemplation, burning with greed for truth, together with a grave nature, strenuous in acting, and provident for the public good. He leads such a genius through all the grades of discipline, as will be clear in the seventh book. He also orders him to be exercised in civil actions, and among pleasures, pains, labors, and dangers, to be diligently examined and proven like gold in the fire, before the rudders of the city are trusted to him. In the first place, however, he judges the science of the Good itself, the most excellent of all, to be necessary for him, affirming that just as all things are possessed uselessly without the possession of the good, so also the knowledge of all things and arts without the understanding of the good itself is entirely useless. Nor can anyone rightly direct either private or public affairs toward the good unless he knows by reason what is good. Although the science of this divine good may seem superfluous to an Aristotelian for governing the republic by human morals, it is nevertheless necessary for this very governance, through which Plato says in the above passages that one must strive to render the citizens like God and his friends. He added, furthermore, that a governor is both blind and moved by some chance in disposing individual goods toward the good itself, unless he has perceived the first form of the good itself, the exemplar and cause of all goods. But so that you may notice Aristotle in the *Ethics* playing against Plato concerning the Idea of the Good, read Plato's words most diligently and you will clearly...

--- Page 425 ---
Dialogue VI. on the Republic. Or, on Justice. 409

...perceive that the Idea of the Good is not this species or that, here or there, but the very fecundity of the most eminent divinity, propagating itself powerfully, sweetly, and healthfully through all things. He wishes the visible sun to be a certain image of this in the visible world, diffusing its powers similarly through all things. But before this sun which we see, Plato thinks of another in the invisible world, the first image of God the Father, and the true Son. Therefore he called them "sons of the good," so that above this visible and imaginary son, you could contemplate the invisible and archetypal one. Concerning this Father and Son, we read in the letter to Hermias. Concerning this, the Platonic Philo says in the *Book of Causes*: "One must strive in the first place to ascend to being itself, that is, of whom it is said, 'I am who I am.' Or at least to his image and most sacred reason and first-born word." Through such reason and word, all things are made according to Heraclitus and Plato, as Amelius the Platonic asserts, and he uses the testimony of John the Evangelist. Plato also testifies to this in the *Epinomis*. And although some of the Platonists distinguish the Son of God the Father by substance from the Father, in the manner of the Arians—especially Julian in his book *On the Sun*—nevertheless Julian's teacher Iamblichus brings forward the mysteries of the Egyptians, in which the reason of the Father and the Son is indeed diverse, but the substance seems to be the same. But hear the mystery: "The first God and one is of the first father god, whom he begets remaining in the solitary unity of himself. But he is the exemplar of the Son who is named the son of himself, his own parent and father of the one, God truly good. For he is the fountain of ideas: from which one indeed, God, sufficient through himself, unfolded himself into the light. Therefore he is named sufficient through himself and his own father. For he is the principle here, God of gods, one from one, above all essence, and the principle of essence." Iamblichus testifies that this mystery is of Hermes <note>Original: *Mercurij*</note>. Indeed, how the good itself is above pleasure, and morals, and wisdom, Plato signifies here briefly. Above pleasure indeed, because if pleasure itself were the good itself, no pleasure would be evil and harmful. Likewise above morals, because many think they have enough concerning morals if they seem to have honest morals. But that which they judge to be the true good, they do not seek by opinion, but to have entirely in the thing itself. Furthermore, above science, because you do not especially desire to know in just any way, nor just anything, but rather well and good things. Otherwise, you either reject or neglect science. Nor should you say that the good itself is the science of the good, lest you foolishly define the same thing through the same thing. Again, above the intellect: for this assiduously seeks the good. But the good itself does not seek the good. Add also above truth. For what you judge more good, you also choose more. But a lesser true illness and loss you choose rather than a more true one. Finally, above being. For you desire to be so that you may be well. But concerning these, and how by the light of the good itself the intellect understands all true things, we dispute more widely in the *Theology*. There follows a distinction of things into two genera: visible and invisible, and of each into two, namely the antecedent and the following, and a similar distinction of human perception. In these he follows Brontinus and Archytas; but he explains it more elegantly and more widely at the same time.

WHO ARE the philosophers, I said, and who are those alien to philosophy, O Glaucon, has finally been established after a long speech. It was perhaps, he said, not easy to explain it in fewer words. No, as it appears. But I think it would shine forth more clearly if it had been necessary to narrate only this, and not to wander through many other things, if one wishes to show in what way the just life differs from the unjust. What remains for us to do after this? What else but that which follows in order? Since philosophers are those who are able to reach that which always behaves in the same way according to the same things, while those who cannot do so, but always wander through many and mutable things, are not philosophers: which of these should be the leaders of the city? How can we rightly respond to this? Those who are able to guard the laws and the duties of the city, to them the rudders of the republic are to be committed. Well said. But it is clear whether he to whom we entrust something to be guarded ought to be blind or sharp-sighted. Why not clear? Do they not seem to you to differ from the blind, who lack the knowledge in each thing of that which truly is, and have no clear exemplar in their soul? Nor can they, like painters looking toward a most true exemplar and referring to it and beholding it as accurately as possible, thus finally carry laws here concerning beautiful, just, and good things, if it is necessary, and guard and preserve the laws once carried? Indeed, they do not differ much. Shall we choose those rather than these for guardianship, who know each thing that truly is, and are also in no way inferior in experience or any other part of virtue? It would certainly be absurd if any others were chosen, especially if they are not lacking in other respects. In this they certainly excel most. Shall we not say this now: in what way will they be able to have those things and these things at the same time? Entirely. Therefore, what we said at the beginning of this dispute, it is necessary first to perceive their nature; and I think, if we agree sufficiently among ourselves concerning that, we will also agree that it is possible for them to attain these things, and that no others besides these should be the leaders of the city. In what way? Let this first be established between us concerning the geniuses of philosophers: that they always love that discipline by which that nature which always is—and is changed neither by generation nor corruption—becomes better known to them. Let it be established. Furthermore, that they desire it all, and do not willingly spurn any part of it, neither small nor great, neither honorable nor lowly, just as we said above concerning the ambitious and those captured by love. Rightly. Besides, consider this: whether it is necessary for it to be in the nature of those who are to be such as we have narrated. What is that? That they be devoid of the nature of all lying, and never lie willingly, but hate all falsehood and love the truth. It is probable. It is not only probable, O friend, but entirely necessary, that he who is affected by love for something by nature, should love whatever is kindred and familiar to the beloved. Skillfully said. Is anything found more familiar to wisdom than truth? Nothing. Therefore, is it possible for the same nature to be both philosophical and lying? In no way. Therefore, it is necessary for a true lover of learning, immediately from childhood, to desire all truth above all else. Exactly. But those whose desires are carried ardently toward something certain, their desires for other things are more relaxed, since they flow elsewhere like streams. No doubt. Whoever, therefore, burns with all desire for disciplines and such things, seeks the pure pleasure of the soul itself, but despises the delights of the body—unless he is a feigned and by no means true philosopher. That is most necessary. Therefore, such a man will be temperate and not greedy for money. For to gasp after accumulating money pertains to anyone rather than to him for whose sake the rest sweat to seek money with the greatest loss. It is so. Furthermore, that must be considered whenever you desire to discern the nature of him who becomes a philosopher and him who does not. What? Lest perhaps some latent illiberality be in him. For pusillanimity <note>small-mindedness</note> is entirely adverse to a mind that is always to investigate the whole itself, both divine and human. You speak the truth. Surely, to him whom there is magnificence of thought and the contemplation of all time and all substance, human life cannot seem to be anything great. Certainly not. Will he think death is a terrible thing here? Not at all. Therefore, true philosophy does not suit a timid and illiberal nature. Not, as it seems to me. But a modest man, not dedicated to gain, not illiberal, not proud, not timid: will he be difficult or unjust in his dealings? In no way. Furthermore, when you desire to discern which mind is a philosopher or not, immediately from tender...

--- Page 426 ---
410 Thirty-First Book.

...years you will observe this: whether he is just and mild, or unjust and savage. Especially. Nor, I think, will you overlook this. What? Whether he is quick to perceive, or slow. Do you think anyone will ever love that which he does with the greatest difficulty when he approaches it, and after much effort barely accomplishes anything? Never, surely. What if he should preserve nothing of what he learns, but forgets everything? Will he not be empty of knowledge? Empty. But when all his labor is undertaken in vain, will he not finally be forced to hate both himself and such an action? Nothing prevents it. Therefore, let us by no means think that a forgetful soul suits the geniuses of legitimate philosophers, but rather one that is very mindful. Exactly so. Furthermore, a discordant and ungraceful nature always draws toward excess. Always. But do you think the truth agrees with excess and immoderation, or rather with moderation? With moderation. Therefore, let us attribute a composed and graceful thought to this genius beyond others, which we want to be inclined by its own nature to beholding the idea of each thing that truly is. Surely. Do we not seem to you to have run through each of the things which must necessarily belong in a continuous series of successions to the mind of him who is to perfectly follow the truth of things? Exactly so. Can you in any way damn that study which no one can sufficiently execute unless his nature is perspicacious, mindful, magnificent, graceful, a friend and intimate of truth, justice, fortitude, and temperance? Not even Momus <note>The Greek god of mockery and criticism</note> could pluck at it. Will you not commit the administration of the republic to these alone, when they are finally advanced in erudition and age? To these things Adimantus said: "No one, O Socrates, could contradict you. But truly, those who hear these things you narrate everywhere are affected in this way: they think that through inexperience in questioning and answering, they are led a little away from the path of reason in each of the things asked, and having finally collected many small errors, they assert a great error and the opposite of what they previously asserted. And just as those who do not know how to play at calculatory games <note>Latin: *calculis*, a board game like checkers</note> are finally so constrained and cornered by those skilled in that game that they have no move to make, so they also think themselves finally forced and cornered, and have nothing to say, hemmed in by words as if by pebbles—since the truth is no more here than there. I speak of what pertains to our present purpose. For someone would say to you that he cannot oppose these words being proposed; but in the thing itself, he has discovered that as many as have approached the study of philosophy, they do not spend time in it for the sake of education, tasting the precepts of philosophy while still young and then departing, but they linger longer. They say that most of them turn out quite absurd and alien to the affairs of men, not to say most wicked. And if some seem more excellent, they are nevertheless so stained by this study which you yourself praise, that they turn out useless for governing the republic." When I had heard this, I said: "Do you think those who say these things are lying?" "I do not know," he said, "but I would gladly hear what you yourself feel." "You shall certainly hear, if you ask it, that they seem to me to speak the truth." "By what reasoning then is it rightly said that there will be no rest from evils for cities before philosophers rule in them, whom we admit are useless to the republic?" "What you seek requires a response introduced through a certain image <note>Socrates begins the famous 'Ship of State' analogy</note>. But you, I think, are not accustomed to speaking by similitude." "Be it so," I said. "Are you snapping at me, when you have driven me into a speech so difficult to demonstrate? Hear then the similitude, so you may more clearly know how slippery I am in using similitudes." So hard is that which those who excel in philosophy suffer in governing a republic, that there is nothing else that suffers this one thing. Therefore it is necessary to collect this from many sources to compare it, and finally to give a reason for them. Just as when painters depict goat-stags <note>Latin: *tragelaphos*, a mythical hybrid beast</note> and other such mixed figments. "Imagine in your mind a certain governor of a ship or a fleet of this kind: exceeding the rest of the sailors in the size and strength of his body, but deaf, and with dim eyes, and with a mind ignorant of governing. But imagine the sailors quarreling among themselves about the governing, while each thinks himself worthy of the command, although he never learned the art, nor can he show any teacher in that matter, nor can he assign at what time he learned it. They even deny that the art can be taught, and they attack with the sword anyone who contends it can be taught. Think of them flocking around that governor, beseeching him, contending with all their might that he should hand the rudders to them. If they themselves do not persuade him, but others do, they either kill the others or cast them out of the ship. And finally, having occupied that noble prince of the ship with mandragora or pure wine, they seize the governing of the ship, use the things present, indulge in wine and feasts, and govern in such a way as is likely for such men. Furthermore, they all praise him, calling him a sailor and a governor, and say he is skilled in what pertains to ruling a ship—whoever can help them in usurping the princedom of the ship by moving the governor either by persuasion or force. But him who cannot do so, they vituperate as useless. But the duty of a true governor they do not even think of: namely, that it pertains to him to have a calculation of the year, and the seasons, the sky, the stars, and the winds, and all things that pertain to that art, if he is truly to be the governor of the ship. But as for how he may govern, whether some are willing or unwilling, they think no art can be accepted for this along with the governing faculty. If these things are so in a ship, do you not think the true governor would be called an empty and curious inspector of sublime things and useless to the ship itself by those who are carried in such ships?" "Very much so indeed," said Adimantus. "I do not think there is any need," I said, "to explain to you more widely how the citizens in cities are affected toward true philosophers according to the image of the proposed comparison, as the sailors in such ships are toward the true governor. For I think you understand what I say." "Extremely well." "First, therefore, to him who wonders that philosophers are not honored in cities, explain this image and try to persuade him that it would be much more wonderful if they were honored." "I shall indeed." "Add also this besides: that those who say the best philosophers are useless to the crowd speak the truth. But tell him that it is not they themselves who are the cause of being useless, but rather those who do not use these philosophers. For it is not according to nature that the governor should beg the sailors to commit themselves to his governing, or that the wise should approach the doors of the wealthy. But whoever first boasted of this surely lied. For the truth is naturally arranged thus: whether a rich man or a poor man is held by an adverse health, he must necessarily seek the doors of physicians; and all who need the governing of a superior must go to the houses of men capable of governing, not the governors—if indeed they are of any value—should beg that the inferiors be governed by them. But if you compare those who in these times administer Republics..."

<summary>This section contains the climax of Socrates' argument for the Philosopher-King, defining the philosopher as a lover of the whole of truth and being. It introduces the "Ship of State" parable to explain why true philosophers are often viewed as useless or strange by the general public.</summary>

...administers, if you compare him with those sailors whom we were just mentioning, you will not go astray. And if you compare those whom they call useless, vain, and superstitious searchers of hidden things to the true pilots, you will indeed be doing it correctly. "Very correctly," he said. For these reasons, therefore, it is not easy for an honorable study to be approved by those who are accustomed to contrary ways of life. But truly, the greatest and most vehement slander of philosophy arises because of the character of those who profess the study of philosophy. For indeed, those who cry out against philosophy say, as you yourself say, that most of those who betake themselves to philosophy are quite wicked; and if any of them excel the others, they are useless. And I granted these things to you, did I not? "Certainly." Have we not explained the cause for which the best philosophers seem to be useless? "Indeed." Do you wish for us to next reveal why the majority are wicked, and declare as best we can that the fault is not philosophy's? "I certainly do." Let us proceed to these things, repeating what we pointed out above: what kind of nature he must have who is to be honorable and good. His leader above all, if you have committed it to memory, was truth, which he must follow entirely and everywhere; otherwise, if he were a pretender, he would have no share of true philosophy. "So it is, indeed." This one thing, therefore, is entirely foreign to those things which are now thought about him. "Most foreign." Shall we not decently defend his cause in this way, saying that a man greedy for knowledge is so constituted by nature that he always strives toward that which truly is, nor does he linger among those individual and manifold things about which opinion wanders? Instead, progressing further, he is not fatigued nor does he cease from his desire until he reaches the proper nature of each thing with that power of the mind which it is fitting to apprehend it. And it is fitting for a certain kindred power. When he has clung to this, and mixed himself with that which truly is, and from there truly generated intelligence and truth, he will surely know the truth, and truly live and be nourished. Finally, from this birth, all his distress will cease, but not before. "Those things are said very well." Will such a man in any way love a lie? Or rather, will he hate it entirely? "He will certainly hate it." Surely, where truth is the leader, we will not say that a chorus of evils follows, I think. "For how could it?" Rather, we will say that a sincere and just character follows. Shall we say that temperance also follows this? "Cleverly put." Furthermore, what need is there to recount from the beginning the rest of the chorus of the philosophical nature? For you remember that with these agree, as we were saying, fortitude, magnificence, sharpness of wit, and memory. But when you objected that anyone would necessarily be forced to admit what we were saying, yet, setting aside our words and turning to those of whom the talk was, said that he saw them to be partly useless and partly corrupted by every wickedness: now indeed we have begun to examine the cause of this slander, and why many of them are evil. For this reason we have again repeated the nature of legitimate philosophers and necessarily defined it. "It is so." Next, we must seek the reason why the nature of the philosopher is corrupted in many (though one small point escaped us): namely, we must also observe those whom they call not evil, but useless. Then also, what kind of human geniuses these are who imitate this nature and usurp its work; approaching a study unworthy of themselves and beyond their strength, they often fail, and spread everywhere that opinion of philosophy which you were narrating. But what corruptions do you mean? "I will show you if I can." Truly, I think anyone will 

concede to us that a genius such as we have described, and endowed with all these things which a future perfect philosopher needs, arises rarely and in few people. Do you not think so? "Exceedingly so." And even of these few, see how many and how great are the destructions. "Which ones?" For what is marvelous to hear beyond the rest is that each of those things which we lately approved in the philosopher’s genius stains the soul that has it, and mostly twists it away from philosophy: I mean fortitude, and temperance, and the others we recounted. "This is indeed absurd to hear." Furthermore, whatever things are commonly called good corrupt and hinder the soul: beauty, riches, bodily strength, a powerful family in the city, and other things of that same kind. For you have, as it were, a formula of the things I am saying. "I do indeed, and I would gladly hear more exactly what you say." Grasp the whole matter correctly, and it will appear clear to you; nor will the things said about these seem absurd to you. "How do you prescribe that?" For we know that every seed, whether of plants or of animals, which has not obtained the nutrition fitting for each, nor the right time or place, the more noble and vigorous it is, the more it lacks many advantages. For is not evil more contrary to the good than to the non-good? "Why not?" It is therefore, I think, consistent that the best nature, if nourished with diverse food, turns out worse than a cowardly one. "Certainly." In this way, therefore, we say, Adimantus, that souls endowed with the most excellent genius, if they have been poorly educated, become the worst. Or do you think unspeakable crimes and extreme wickedness proceed from a cowardly genius rather than from a noble one corrupted by education? Will a weak nature ever be the cause of either great goods or great evils? "Certainly not." If, therefore, the nature of the philosopher itself obtains a fitting discipline, it is necessary that it always arrive at every virtue by progressing. But if it has been sown and born perversely, and so nourished, it slides back into all the opposites, unless perhaps some of the gods should help it. Do you also think, as many do, that it is true as they say, that certain adolescents are corrupted by Sophists <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece often criticized by Plato for prioritizing rhetoric over truth</note>, and that the corrupters of them are certain private Sophists? Should we not rather believe that those who speak thus are themselves the greatest Sophists, who teach and render every single one, both old and young, men and women, exactly as they want? "When is that most of all?" he asked. When, I say, many people crowded together either in assemblies, or trials, or theaters, or camps, or some other huge gathering of men, boldly disparage some things that were said or done and praise others, being carried away more sharply toward both with a huge tumult, while they hiss and applaud with a certain extreme noise and shouting. Whence the walls also and the places in which they are, resonating, give out a double tumult compared to those who praise and disparage. At that time, in what state of mind (as it is said) do you think that adolescent is in this crowd? Or what private discipline do you think can resist these acclamations, so that it is not overwhelmed by such disparagements and praises and immediately carried off to where this wave brings it? So that he will approve as honorable the same things as they do, and likewise reject the same as base. Furthermore, he will apply himself to the same studies as they do, and turn out just like them. "That is entirely necessary, O Socrates." However, we have not yet introduced the greatest necessity. "Although they insert it into their works, not persuading with words, those teachers

and those Sophists. Do you not see that they mark a man not obeying them with infamy? They damn him with the loss of money and the punishment of death? "Very much so." What other Sophist, therefore, do you think, or what other private discourses could oppose these and be able to resist? "Certainly the speech of no one," he said. "Truly none." Indeed, to resist these is the height of folly. For there never was, nor is, nor will there be another character—a human one, that is—instructed in virtue, besides the discipline of these people, my friend. For the divine indeed, according to the proverb, let us except. For know this for certain: whatever emerges immaculate and whole from this constitution of public affairs must have emerged so by divine help. "It seems no different to me." Furthermore, this ought to seem so to you. "What is that?" Each of those who, having privately received a fee, instruct men—whom they indeed call Sophists and rivals of the arts—thinks nothing else should be taught than the opinions of the many in which they agree whenever they are gathered together, and he calls this wisdom. It is just as if someone had observed the individual rages and desires of a certain large, powerful, and (by man) nourished brute animal: in what way it is right to approach it, how to touch it, also when it is either more fierce or milder, and from what causes it becomes so. Likewise, the voices which each is accustomed to express in individual cases. Furthermore, by what voices of others that animal is either stirred up or calmed. After he has perceived these individual things through long habit, he might call such experience wisdom, and as if having collected it into a certain art, he betakes himself to teaching, truly ignorant of which of these opinions and desires is especially honorable or base, good or evil, just or unjust. But he names each thing according to the opinion of that huge beast: namely, "good" things are those in which it delights, "evil" those by which it is offended. Nor does he bring any other reason at all concerning these, but calls those things which are necessary "just" and "honorable." But how much the nature of the good itself and the necessary differ, he has neither ever perceived himself, nor can he show to others. If someone, I say, were so affected, would he not, by Jove, seem to you an absurd teacher? "To me indeed." Does he seem to differ from this who considers it wisdom to have learned the anger and pleasures of many and various men coming together into one, whether in painting, or in music, or in the discipline of administering the republic? For it is clear that if anyone associates with these, and shows them either a work of poetry or another art, or a service pertaining to the republic, and exhibits to the crowd the authority of judging the work, he will be forced by a Diomedean necessity <note>A Greek idiom for an unavoidable or overwhelming necessity</note>, as they say, to do those things which they approve. But have you ever heard any of them assigning a non-ridiculous reason for why these things are truly good and honorable? "I have never heard one, nor, I think, will I hear one." Therefore, imagining all these things in your mind, remember also this: Is it possible for the crowd, either by another speaking or touching it by itself, to admit the "beautiful itself" <note>The Platonic Idea of Beauty</note>, and not instead these many beautiful things? And in the same way concerning other things—not indeed these individuals which are many and open to view, but the one nature itself of each? "By no means." Therefore, the crowd cannot be a philosopher. "No." Furthermore, it is necessary for those practicing philosophy to be disparaged by it. "Necessary." And by whoever wishes to please the people. "That is clear." From these things, therefore, what way do you see of preserving the philosophical genius, so that by persevering in its study, it may arrive at the end of philosophizing? Think thus from these things which have been said. It was granted that sharpness of learning, memory, fortitude, and magnificence belong to this genius. "Clearly." Will such a person not immediately be first among all in all things, especially if he has obtained a body by nature conforming to his soul? "Nothing prevents it." Therefore, both all his household and the citizens will want to use him for conducting their business when he has grown up. "So it certainly happens." Wherefore with prayers, supplications, honors, and flatteries they will preoccupy his future virtue and power. "So it is accustomed to happen." What do you think such a man will do then? Especially if he was born in a great city, and is distinguished in riches and family, and is moreover of honorable form and tall. Do you not think he will be elated with immense hope? Thinking himself sufficient for conducting the affairs of both Greeks and Barbarians. Whence also he extols himself, playing about with a disdainful habit, and inflated with empty pride and insane arrogance. "Vehemently." If someone should amically warn a man so affected, saying that he has no mind at all, yet he needs it; but it can be acquired by no one unless he subjects himself to its attainment, do you think that one occupied with such evils will easily lend his ears to the one warning? "Far from it." But if, led by the goodness of his nature and a certain innate affection toward reason, someone should listen and be turned, and be drawn to philosophy, what do we think those will do who think that the adolescent is being corrupted by the use and custom of that warner? Will they not strive with all zeal, both in speaking and acting, so that the adolescent does not obey the warnings, nor the exhorter persuade him of anything, pursuing him with both private snares and public accusations? "It is very necessary." Will there remain to this man any faculty for philosophizing? "Plainly a small one." Do you see that we said above not without reason: that the parts of the philosophical nature, if a perverse education is applied, are in a way the causes for someone to be turned away from that study? Indeed, even those things which are commonly thought good are an impediment, namely riches, and all such furniture? "Rightly indeed was it said." This, O wonderful man, is the destruction and corruption of such and so great a nature for the excellent office of the best, which indeed is found very rarely, as we said. And of this genius are those men who commit unspeakable crimes, both privately and publicly; and likewise those who are authors of great goods for both private individuals and cities. But a meager genius never effects anything great, either privately or publicly. "You truly speak the truth." Since most of those naturally fit for philosophizing are twisted away from this study, and leave philosophy imperfect and desolate, they lead a life neither decent nor true. But philosophy, as if orphaned of her kin, others indeed unworthy of her approaching, disgrace her too much, and affect her with that infamy with which you recounted she was marked by those detractors, objecting that many of them are worthy of many evils. "These things were certainly said." And rightly said. Seeing this, indeed, many other little men <note>original: "homunculi," a diminutive suggesting people of small spirit or character</note>, seeing this seat empty indeed, yet distinguished by noble titles and dignity, like those who flee from prison to temples, gladly leap from the arts into philosophy, especially whoever excel in their own little art. For surely philosophy, although she is in such a state, yet excels the other arts in dignity and magnificence. Which many affect, being indeed naturally imperfect, and just as their bodies are damaged by arts and trades, so also their souls are depressed and broken by mechanical services. Is it not necessary? "Exceedingly." Or do you think they differ at all in appearance from a copper-smith, rich, poor, and bald, who has come out of chains, washed himself in the baths, and

dressed himself in a new garment like a bridegroom, and is about to marry the daughter of his master who is pressed by poverty and has no one else to whom he might give her? "I think they do not differ much." What kind of offspring must be thought to be born from these? Surely a bastard and abject one? "It is entirely necessary." But men unworthy of discipline, whenever they themselves cling to it beyond their dignity, what kind of thoughts and opinions do we say they produce? Is it not, as is fitting to name them, sophisms? And nothing legitimate, nothing worthy, nothing fitting for true prudence? "So it must entirely be said." Therefore very few men remain, Adimantus, who are worthily engaged in philosophy: and these are those who, born with a good disposition and well-nourished, either caught by exile obtain leisure for philosophy, whence free from adverse occupations they persevere in their studies under nature's lead; or when a certain magnificent soul born in a small city, having spurned the duties of the republic itself, and much more having contemned the trades of the rest of the arts, betakes himself to philosophizing according to the gifts of nature. There would also be the "bridle of our friend Theages" <note>A reference to a contemporary whose poor health kept him from politics, forcing him into philosophy</note> enough to restrain him. For our Theages is so constituted that he is excluded from philosophizing [by others]. But the weakness of his body prohibits him from civil affairs. But to mention the sign of our spirit <note>original: "daemonis nostri signum," referring to Socrates' "daimonion" or inner voice</note> is not fitting now. For it has happened to either one other at most, or to none of our predecessors. But whoever of these few taste and have tasted how sweet and blessed this possession is, and perceive the insanity of the majority: because indeed no one, to speak so briefly and simply, acts rightly in anything in republics, nor is any companion and helper found, so that if someone undertakes the care of defending justice he might emerge safe. But like a man falling among wild beasts, since he neither wants to act unjustly alone nor can he himself alone resist all the beasts, he perishes before he can help either the city or his friends; and thus he becomes useless both to himself and to others. All these things, I say, whoever diligently observe, they keep quiet and care only for their own affairs; and as if in a storm, while the whirlwind is stirred and the winds blow through, and the sky is covered with dust, they remain safe within walls. And looking at others involved in wickedness, they think they will have enough if they themselves have lived pure from injustice and iniquitous deeds, and having finished the courses of life depart cheerful and pious with good hope. "He would certainly have done no small thing who so passes his life." Yet not the greatest, if he has not found a republic fitting for himself. For in it he himself will progress, and increase more, and preserve both private and public things at the same time. Thus far, for what reason philosophy has undergone slander, and that that slander is unjust, I think has been sufficiently said, unless you perhaps add something else. "I would say nothing further to these things. But of those republics which now exist, which one do you think especially suits philosophers?" None at all; and for that reason I complain, because I see none of those republics which now exist worthy of the genius of a philosopher by its institution. Wherefore it is necessary for this nature to be changed and turned. Just as a foreign seed cast into an alien soil is weakened, and degenerating turns toward the nature of the place and the local seed, so also this kind, having now lost its own virtue, is transformed into an alien species. But if it should obtain the best republic, just as it is itself the best, then finally it will declare itself to be something divine, and all the rest to be human, both geniuses and studies. But you seem to me about to ask immediately what that republic is. "You have not presaged correctly. For I did not desire this from you, but whether it be this very one which we introduced in founding the city, or another?" As to other things, this very one. But this was also said then, that there must always be something in the city which has the same reason for the republic as you the legislator had while you were founding the laws. "It was plainly said." Yet not sufficiently explained. For your speech deterred us, objecting that this would be a long and arduous demonstration. For what follows is not easy to say at all. "What is that?" In what way especially the city ought to undertake philosophy, so that it is not destroyed. For any great things are accustomed to be deceptive, and, as is truly said in the proverb, "fine things are difficult." Nevertheless, since this is agreed between us, let the demonstration now take its end. "Faculty will perhaps fail me, but will certainly never." But you will understand my present zeal. Observe even now how promptly and intrepidly I am about to say that, contrary to what is done now, the city ought to touch this study. "In what way?" Indeed at this time, young men, when immediately from tender years among domestic and profit-making business they approach the most difficult part of this study, a little later they depart, even those who are thought to be especially studious of wisdom. But I call the most difficult part the experience of disputing. Afterward, indeed, if called by others doing it they allow themselves to be hearers, they think something great and think it must be executed in passing. In old age, indeed, with a few exceptions, much more than the Sun of Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus famously said the sun is new every day; Socrates suggests these men are extinguished forever</note> they are extinguished, since they are never again rekindled. "What then must be done?" Entirely the contrary. For it is fitting for youths and boys to handle boyish discipline and philosophy, and to take care of their bodies, insofar as they grow and are strengthened for the service of philosophy. As age proceeds, in which the soul now begins to be perfected, they should increase their exercises. But when their strength has failed from old age, then free from civil and military labors, as if retired and immune, let them live according to their wish, and be bound by no certain duty, whoever are to live happily, and after the migration of the soul, to receive a lot conforming to their past life. "You seem to me to speak quite promptly indeed, O Socrates. I think, however, most people when they have heard these things will also more promptly resist, being by no means persuaded by you. And especially I think Thrasymachus <note>A Sophist who appears as an antagonist in Book I of the Republic</note> will do that." "Do not plot against the mutual benevolence between me and Thrasymachus," I said. "For we have lately been made friends, nor were we enemies before. Nor indeed will we stop before we persuade him and others, or at least do something contributing to that life in which, when they have arrived, they will find these things said." "You have spoken for a short time." "Rather for none, if it be compared to the whole. But that many do not offer faith to these things which have been said is no wonder. For they have never seen happen what has just been said, but rather such words purposely composed into a certain likeness, not occurring by chance as now. But a man as perfect as possible in virtue, and exceedingly powerful in deeds and words in such a city, they have never looked upon, either one or many. Do you think so?" "In no way." "Nor ever, O blessed one, have they applied their ears to honorable and free discourses, by which truth is sought with all zeal for the sake of knowing; but these things full of tricks and contentious, seeking nothing else than opinion and contention, both in trials and private colloquies, are omitted." "Certainly not."

"Certainly not. Wherefore, since we ourselves foresaw and feared these things, forced by the truth we said that neither any city, nor republic, nor man will be perfect before a certain necessity happens by chance to these few philosophers, who are neither evil nor useless as they are commonly thought, so that whether they want to or not, they undertake the care of the city, or are heard by the citizens, or at least in those who rule, or their sons, a true love of true philosophy has been instilled by a certain divine inspiration. But that either one of these, or both, are impossible, I think cannot be demonstrated. Otherwise we would justly be laughed at, as if fashioning things according to the wish of the mind. Is it not so?" "Entirely so." "If, therefore, at some time in the infinite past time, men outstanding in philosophy, impelled by necessity, governed the republic, or in these times rule in some barbarian region very remote from our sight, or will administer in the future, in this state of affairs we certainly assert without doubt that the republic described above has been, is, and will be. When this Muse presides over a city, this can certainly happen, nor are we fashioning impossibilities. Yet that these things are difficult was conceded by us also." "It seems so to me too." "You will perhaps add that it does not seem so to the crowd." "Perhaps." "Do not so thoroughly blame the crowd, O blessed man. But what do you think they will think if, not from a zeal for contention but with friendly warnings, the dissolved slander adverse to philosophy being shown, you show what men you especially call philosophers, and as you were lately distinguishing, both their genius and study, so they do not suspect you of speaking of those whom they themselves imagine? Or if they have so begun to understand, would you say they are deceived in opinion, nor respond to the things proposed? Or do you think," I say, "anyone is irritated against a mild man? Or a man without envy and malice envies a man who is not envious? Indeed I respond for you, that not in the multitude of men, but in very few, is there such a harsh nature."
"I think the same myself." "Do you also think this? The cause for which the multitude bears philosophy with an unfair mind is those who, since they are inept for philosophy, having professed it, provoke men everywhere with insults, and as if delighted by enmities, always speak ill of men, doing a thing least fitting for philosophy."
"Entirely." "For to that man, O Adimantus, who has directed all the sharpness of his mind to those things which truly are, no leisure remains to look back at the inferior business of men, and fighting with them, to stir up envy and malevolence for himself. But he contemplates those things which always keep the same order, which neither inflict injury on each other nor suffer it; but all things are arranged ornately and according to reason. And these he imitates, and makes himself as similar to them as possible. Or do you think it can happen that someone does not imitate that to which he clings with admiring love?" "In no way." "Wherefore since the philosopher frequently clings to the divine and the decorous, he himself becomes divine and decorous as far as is possible for a man. But slander is great in all things." "So it is entirely." "If, therefore, he is led by some necessity to transfer those things which he contemplates there to the character of men privately and publicly, and not only forms himself but also others, do you think he will be an inert maker of temperance, justice, and every popular virtue?" "By no means." "If the crowd should feel that we are reporting true things about this, will it be angry with philosophers? And will it not believe us saying that a city will not otherwise be happy than if painters who use a divine example form it?" "By no means will it be angry," he said, "if it should feel it. But what mode of painting do you mean?" "When these painters," I say, "have received the city and the characters of men like a certain tablet, they will first of all purge it, which is by no means easy. Or do you not know that this especially distinguishes philosophers from others, that they attempt neither to touch a private person nor a city, nor to establish laws, before they have either received these purged or have purged them themselves?" "And rightly indeed." "Do you not think they would describe the form of the republic after these things?" "Why not?" "Then doing these things, I think, they will frequently look back to both, namely to that which exists by nature as just, honorable, and temperate, and other things of this kind, and again to human things: and they will dispose human things according to the exemplar of that superior thing, contemplating human nature from human duties, according to the figure of that which Homer also, when it is in men, called the 'form and image and likeness of God'." <note>Homer often uses epithets like "god-like" for heroes</note> "Cleverly." "In part, therefore, the philosophers will erase, in part again they will paint, until they have joined human characters as much as possible to God in love." "Truly this is a most beautiful painting," he said. "Do we persuade those," I say, "whom you said were attacking us, that such a painter of republics is that man whom we lately praised among them, on account of whom they were indignant that we would commit the governing of the city to him, but now they hear this with a fairer mind?" "And most of all indeed, if they are wise." "In what part will they now oppose us? Will they assert that philosophers are not lovers of those things which truly are, and of truth itself?" "That would indeed be absurd." "Or will they perhaps deny that the nature of philosophers which we narrated is familiar with the best itself?" "Not even this." "What then? Will they refuse that this nature, instructed with congruent duties, will be absolutely good, and beyond others closest to wisdom? Or will they approve more those whom we ourselves set apart?" "By no means." "Will they still be angry with us saying that unless the kind of philosophers takes up the rudders of the city, there will be no rest from evils for either the city or the citizens? Nor will the republic which we describe in speech arise into the light?" "Perhaps less so." "Do you wish, then," I say, "that we say they were not a little, but altogether, made mild and persuaded? Lest perhaps being ashamed they should confess something else." "Without doubt." "Let them then be persuaded of this now. But who will doubt this, that the sons of kings and powerful men will not be born philosophers?" "No one." "But someone could add that even if such are born, they must necessarily be stained. For that it is arduous to be preserved (pure from spots) we also concede. But who will add this further? That in all time from all men not even one was ever preserved?" "No one would say this." "But indeed one so instituted by nature, and having found an obedient city, is sufficient for perfecting all these things which now have no faith." "Sufficient indeed." "I posit, if some prince should command the laws and duties which we recounted, it is not impossible that the citizens should be willing to obey these." "Certainly not." "And is it a wonder or impossible that others should feel the same things which we ourselves feel?" "I think not." "That these things are the best, if indeed they are possible, I think has been sufficiently disputed above." "Sufficiently." "Wherefore from these things which have been said, it follows that the things which we predicted about establishing laws will be the best if they are done: likewise difficult to do, but not impossible." "It plainly follows." "Since we have finally put an end to these things, we must now proceed to the rest: namely, in what way, and with what disciplines and studies
