This translation covers the provided OCR text, which consists of portions of **Marsilio Ficino’s** Latin translation and commentary on **Plato’s *Republic*** (specifically Books VI and VII). The text follows the dialogue between **Socrates** and **Glauco**, focusing on the education of the philosopher-king, the "Idea of the Good," the "Divided Line," and the "Allegory of the Cave."

### Translation

**[Page 415]**

**Dialogue VI on the Republic, or, on the Just.**

The preservers of this our republic will have enjoyed [their rewards], and as individuals they will exercise their duties according to their age. Of these things, certainly, we must now speak. It was by no means wisely done by me, when in the preceding parts I left out the difficulty and trouble of marriages, the procreation of children, and the constitution of princes. For I knew how enviable a thing it was, and difficult to do, or even to speak the truth entirely. Now, however, we are nonetheless compelled to complete these things: and indeed, those matters pertaining to women and children we have already finished; but those pertaining to princes must, as if from the beginning, be run through again. 

We said, if you hold it in memory, that they ought to be lovers of the city, proven in pleasures and pains, and according to this doctrine, they should not be moved away [from it] by labors, nor by fear of dangers, nor by any other change. But he who cannot do this must be rejected; while he who emerges everywhere sincere and incorrupt, like gold tested in the trial of fire, must be advanced to the governing of the city, and honored with rewards both while living and when dead. Indeed, let such rewards be as have been commonly spoken of, running through this briefly and with a speech as if hesitating; since we feared to move matters as they now are. 

*Glauco:* You speak the truth; for I remember. 

*Socrates:* For I was afraid, O friend, to say what I have dared. But let us now dare to assert this: that the most diligent guardians must be the best philosophers. Let this be held as the reason. Observe how few such there will be. The parts of that nature which we said must be in them rarely concur as one, and for the most part are born disjointed. 

*Glauco:* In what way do you say this? 

*Socrates:* Or are you ignorant that men who are teachable, mindful, ingenious, and sharp, and endowed with those things which arise therefrom, are not also usually brave and high-minded, so that they might live moderately, tranquilly, and constantly? Clearly, men of such sharpness are carried away by the fervor of their own wit wherever it happens, being devoid of all stability and gravity. 

*Glauco:* You speak the truth. 

*Socrates:* However, those stable dispositions of minds, entirely alien to levity, in whose gravity one must most confide—since they are intrepid in war—just as they are immobile in these things, so they are slower and duller toward disciplines. For they grow numb and gape whenever they must be vigilant in contemplation. 

*Glauco:* It is as you say. 

*Socrates:* But we said in the previous parts that the prince ought to participate in both [natures] in the best proportion. Otherwise, the highest discipline is not to be exhibited to him, nor honors and magistracies imparted. 

*Glauco:* Rightly so. 

*Socrates:* Do you not think this will happen rarely? 

*Glauco:* Very rarely. 

*Socrates:* Therefore, it is necessary to examine the genius of the future prince in these things which we spoke of above: in labors, fears, and pleasures. We add besides, what we then omitted: namely, that it is necessary to exercise that genius in many disciplines, so that it may be clear whether it is capable of receiving the highest doctrine, or rather if it fails, just as those who tremble and fail in other works. 

*Glauco:* It is certainly fitting to investigate thus. But what do you call the "greatest doctrine"? 

*Socrates:* I think you remember when we had placed three species in the soul, what justice, temperance, fortitude, and wisdom were; having defined them, did we not agree among ourselves? 

*Glauco:* If I did not remember, I would hardly be worthy to hear the rest from you. 

*Socrates:* Or do you also hold in memory that which was said before these things? 

*Glauco:* What exactly? 

*Socrates:* We said surely that those things could be known more exactly by a certain wider circuit of speech; but that it was more convenient to introduce demonstrations more consistent with the preceding ones. To which you responded that it was sufficient. And so they were treated then "with a thick Minerva" [simply/roughly], as it seemed to me. If it pleases you now, say so. 

*Glauco:* But it seemed treated moderately enough to me and to the others. 

*Socrates:* But in these matters, O friend, a measure that omits any part of the truth is not done very moderately. For nothing imperfect is more worthless than a measure. Although it sometimes seems to some that it has been treated sufficiently immediately, and that there is no need for a longer inquiry. 

*Glauco:* This happens to very many because of sluggishness. 

*Socrates:* This vice ought to be most alien to the guardian of the city and the laws. 

*Glauco:* Agreed. 

*Socrates:* Therefore, a wider circuit must be traveled by this friend, nor should he depart shorter than is required by the effort expended in exercising; otherwise, as we said a little while ago, he will never reach the ultimate and entirely necessary end of doctrine. 

*Glauco:* Are these things not the greatest? Is there something even more excellent than justice and the others we have related? 

*Socrates:* Indeed I would say it is more excellent; and of these very things it is by no means fitting to look upon a certain sketch such as now, but to comprehend the absolute reason. Is it not ridiculous—that is, to place all zeal in the smallest matters and to contend strenuously so that they are performed as diligently and sincerely as possible, but in the greatest things to think a light effort is enough? 

*Glauco:* Entirely ridiculous. But do you think anyone will rest unless he now inquires from you what that discipline is which you call the greatest, and about what it is concerned? 

*Socrates:* Not indeed, I say: but you yourself ask, although I think you have heard it many times. But now, either you do not notice, or rather you intend to disturb me with your scruples. This I rather think. For you have often heard that the **Idea of the Good** is the greatest study. By which indeed both just things and other things, if they are used, become useful and conducive. And know that I wish to say this in my speech, and furthermore, that we do not know it sufficiently. But if we are ignorant of it, and without it we know other things as much as possible, know that there will be no utility for us from the others; just as nothing would profit us if we possessed it without the Good. Or do you think it is preferable to possess all other things without the possession of the Good, rather than to understand the rest without the intelligence of the Good and the Beautiful? 

*Glauco:* Certainly not. 

*Socrates:* Indeed, to many the Good seems to be pleasure; to the more elegant, it seems to be wisdom. 

*Glauco:* Without a doubt. 

*Socrates:* Furthermore, you also know this: that those who think wisdom is the Good, if they are asked what sort of wisdom it is primarily, they cannot declare it, but are finally compelled to say it is the "wisdom of the Good." 

*Glauco:* What a ridiculous response. 

*Socrates:* Why should it not seem ridiculous, if while they reproach us for being ignorant of the Good, they speak to us of the Good again as if we understood it? For they say it is the Good, the wisdom of the Good, as if we knew what they meant when they pronounce the name of the Good. 

*Glauco:* You speak the truth. 

*Socrates:* But those who define the Good as pleasure, do they err any less than the others? Are they not also compelled to confess that there are bad pleasures? 

*Glauco:* Greatly so. 

*Socrates:* Therefore, they are compelled to confess that the same things are both good and bad; are they not? 

*Glauco:* Plainly. 

*Socrates:* Is it not clear that many and greatest ambiguities arise concerning this? 

*Glauco:* It is clear. 

*Socrates:* And is this not also conspicuous? That those things which seem just and honest, even if they are not, many would prefer to do, possess, and seem to men to have: but no one thinks it sufficient for himself to possess things which only *seem* good, but all seek what are truly good, and in these things everyone despises mere opinion? 

*Glauco:* Most especially. 

*Socrates:* Every soul seeks the Good, and for its sake does all things, divining that it is something; yet it doubts, nor can it sufficiently comprehend what it is, nor does it have it as certain and explored as other things; and therefore it is deceived in other things when it proceeds to judge what is useful. 

**[Page 416]**

**Book Thirty-One.**

...since it is such and so great, shall we say that those who are the most excellent men in the city, to whom we commit everything, ought likewise to be blind? 

*Glauco:* Least of all. 

*Socrates:* Indeed, I think that a guardian who possesses just and honest things but is ignorant of the reason why they are good is not to be valued much. For it is right that he who is ignorant of this should know them. But I divine that no one will know these things sufficiently before the Good. 

*Glauco:* You divine skillfully. 

*Socrates:* Therefore, the Republic will be perfectly disposed for us if a guardian skilled in these things rules it. 

*Glauco:* So it is necessary. 

*Socrates:* But you, O Socrates, do you say the Good itself is science, or pleasure, or something else besides these? 

*Socrates:* You, I say, are truly an honest man; and I have long since discovered that it would not be enough for you if I reported the opinions of others. 

*Glauco:* It does not seem to me to be fitting, O Socrates, to be able to report the opinions of others, but by no means one's own, especially for a man who has been occupied in these things so long. 

*Socrates:* Do you think it fitting that one should speak of things he is ignorant of as if he knew them? 

*Glauco:* In no way as if he knew them, but as if proffering the opinion which he feels. 

*Socrates:* What then? Do you not know that all opinions without science are base, of which the best are blind? Or do you think those who, without intelligence, opine something true differ from those who, although they are blind, nevertheless walk the right path? 

*Glauco:* Not at all. 

*Socrates:* Do you wish then to contemplate base, blind, and crooked things, when it is possible to hear from others what is conspicuous and beautiful? 

*Glauco:* Come, by Jove, Socrates, do not stop, since you have almost reached the goal. For it will suffice us if, just as you treated justice and temperance and the others, you likewise treat the Good. 

*Socrates:* To me also, O friend, it will suffice greatly. But I fear lest my strength fail, and I, having dared beyond my strength, appear rather inept and move the listeners to laughter. But, O happy men, let us dismiss what the Good itself is for the present. For it seems to me to be above the present contemplation. But I will say what appears to be the **son of the Good**, and what is most similar to it, if it pleases you; if not, I will dismiss it. 

*Glauco:* Speak then. You will declare the father later. 

*Socrates:* I would indeed wish that I could explain it and you could perceive it, not only as now the offspring, but both the offspring and the posterity of the Good itself. Receive therefore for the present this birth and son of the Good. Take care, however, lest I unwittingly deceive you, giving a vain account of the son. 

*Glauco:* We will take care as much as possible. Only speak. 

*Socrates:* I will say it indeed, if we first repeat together and confirm what was mentioned above and said many other times. 

*Glauco:* Which things? 

*Socrates:* We say that many things are beautiful, and many are good, and each is similarly so, and we distinguish them in speech. 

*Glauco:* We say so indeed. 

*Socrates:* And we introduce the Beautiful itself, and the Good itself, and similarly in all things which we placed as many, we place one again according to one idea of each, as if there were one, and we call it that which each thing is. 

*Glauco:* These things are true. 

*Socrates:* And we say that these [the many] are seen, but not understood; but the ideas are understood, not seen. 

*Glauco:* So it is entirely. 

*Socrates:* By what power among the many we have do we discern what lies open to the eyes? 

*Glauco:* By sight. 

*Socrates:* And by hearing what is heard, and by other senses all things that are sensed? 

*Glauco:* Why not? 

*Socrates:* Have you not noticed with what perfect power the author of the senses fabricated that which sees and that which is seen? 

*Glauco:* Not enough. 

*Socrates:* Consider it thus. Does hearing or voice need another kind of thing for this: that the former hears and the latter is heard? Which third being absent, the former will not hear and the latter will not be heard. 

*Glauco:* By no means. 

*Socrates:* I think indeed that many others—not to say none—need such a thing. Or can you name any such power? 

*Glauco:* Not at all. 

*Socrates:* Do you not notice that the power of sight itself and that which is subject to sight needs some such thing? 

*Glauco:* In what way? 

*Socrates:* Sight being present in the eyes, and they being directed toward looking, and color also being present: unless a third genus properly fit by nature for this is present, neither will sight see anything, nor can colors be seen. 

*Glauco:* What do you say that is? 

*Socrates:* That which you call **light**. 

*Glauco:* You speak the truth. 

*Socrates:* Surely the power of the visible itself and the potency of seeing are joined by a certain yoke, most honorable of all other joinings, by no small species, if light is not to be contemned. 

*Glauco:* It is far from being contemned. 

*Socrates:* Which of the celestial gods do you think is the cause of this, whose light causes our sight to discern as best it can, and the objects to be discerned by the eyes? 

*Glauco:* The one you and others think. Surely you ask about the **sun**. 

*Socrates:* So indeed sight holds itself toward this God. 

*Glauco:* How? 

*Socrates:* Sight is not the sun, nor is the eye in which sight is, the sun. 

*Glauco:* Not certainly. 

*Socrates:* But of all the organs of the senses, it is most participant in the sun. 

*Glauco:* Much indeed. 

*Socrates:* Does it not preserve the power it has as infused from the sun? 

*Glauco:* Entirely. 

*Socrates:* Furthermore, the sun is not sight. But the cause of sight, it is seen by it. 

*Glauco:* So plainly. 

*Socrates:* Say that I call this the **son of the Good**, which the Good itself generated in this comparison similar to itself: so that as the Good itself is in the intelligible place toward the intellect and the things understood, so this is in the visible place toward sight and the things seen. 

*Glauco:* In what way? Explain more widely. 

*Socrates:* Furthermore, the eyes, whenever they are not turned toward those things whose colors the daylight illuminates and shows, but toward those which are touched by nocturnal rays, they grow dim and hallucinate, and seem almost blind, as if pure sight were not in them. 

*Glauco:* So it happens. 

*Socrates:* But whenever they turn toward those things which the sun illustrates, they discern clearly, and sight appears to be in those same eyes. 

*Glauco:* It is so. 

*Socrates:* Think thus also of the mind. For when it inheres in that in which truth and Being itself shine forth, it understands that, knows it, and seems to have intellect. But when it is carried toward that which is mixed with darkness, which is surely that which is generated and corrupted, its edge is blunted, it turns various opinions, and seems devoid of mind. 

*Glauco:* So it appears. 

*Socrates:* That therefore which provides truth to the things understood, and reaches out the power to understand to the one understanding, say that this is the **Idea of the Good**, the cause of science and truth, which is perceived through the intellect. Since these two are so beautiful—namely, cognition and truth—if you estimate the Good itself as something else and more beautiful than these, you will think rightly. And just as it is fitting to think that light and sight have a certain species of the sun, but by no means are the sun itself: so cognition and truth have a certain species of the Good, but they are by no means the Good itself. For the majesty of the Good itself is more august. 

*Glauco:* You relate an inestimable beauty, if it provides science and truth but surpasses these in beauty. For you do not say that pleasure is the Good itself. 

*Socrates:* Good words, I pray [Heaven forbid]. And thus contemplate its image more plainly. 

*Glauco:* How? 

*Socrates:* You will say, I think, that the sun provides to the things which are seen not only the potency of being seen, but also generation, augmentation, and nutrition, although it is not itself generation. 

*Glauco:* For in what way? 

*Socrates:* And so you may say the Good gives to those things which are known, not only that they are known, but that they furthermore **exist and have essence**, although the Good itself is not essence, but is above essence, surpassing it in dignity and power. 

*Glauco:* Then Glauco, laughing: "By Pollux, this is a miraculous excess." 

*Socrates:* You certainly are the cause of this, who compelled me to open those things which seemed to me about this. 

*Glauco:* Do not yet desist, but finish especially the comparison of the sun, if anything is omitted. 

**[Page 417]**

**Dialogue VI on the Republic, or, on the Just.**

...omitted. Yet many things are omitted. 

*Glauco:* Do not omit even the least thing. 

*Socrates:* I think indeed many things besides remain; nevertheless, as many as can be referred to for the present, I will not willingly let go. 

*Glauco:* So I pray. 

*Socrates:* Think that these two exist, and one indeed reigns in the intelligible genus and place, the other in the invisible [visible]... so that I might not seem to deceive you about the name. But you have two species: the visible and the intelligible. 

*Glauco:* I have them indeed. 

*Socrates:* Just as if you took a **line cut into two unequal portions**, and divided each part again by a similar ratio: so now, the visible genus and the intelligible genus being offered to you, distinguish each again into two according to clarity and obscurity. In the visible genus, one portion will contain **images**. I call images, first, shadows. Then the simulacra which appear in water, and in dense, smooth, and lucid bodies, and everything such as that, if you follow. 

*Glauco:* I follow. 

*Socrates:* But the other portion will comprehend those things whose similitudes these are: namely, the animals which are among us, and plants, and the whole genus of fabrication. 

*Glauco:* So I place it. 

*Socrates:* Do you wish furthermore to say this genus is distinguished according to truth and non-truth? So that as that which is fashioned by opinion is to that which is known by science, so is the simulacrum to that which it is like? 

*Glauco:* Greatly so. 

*Socrates:* Consider again the section of the intelligible. 

*Glauco:* In what way? 

*Socrates:* One genus of it is that which the soul inquires into using those [visible] things as images which were previously divided, compelled from positions [hypotheses] to proceed not to a principle, but to an end. But the other is that which the mind thinks out, proceeding from a supposition to a non-supposed principle, not using images as we are accustomed to for the other genus, but progressing in the ideas themselves through the ideas. 

*Glauco:* I do not quite understand what you say. 

*Socrates:* But you will understand more easily through these. I think it is not hidden from you that those who are occupied with geometry and arithmetic and others of that kind, suppose indeed the even and odd, and figures, and three species of angles, and things similar to these in individual arguments; and these having been placed as manifest to anyone, they think no reason for them is to be required. And starting from here they now descend to other things, and finally arrive at that which they were seeking. 

*Glauco:* I know that entirely. 

*Socrates:* Indeed, you also know that they use forms which fall under the sight, and speak about them: although they do not direct the mind to them, but rather to those things of which these are simulacra—to the quadrangle itself, and the diameter itself, not to those which they draw. And in other things in the same way, they use these species which are described and figured, of which there are shadows and images in water, as certain images, striving to behold those things which are perceived in no other way than by thought [cogitatione]. 

*Glauco:* You speak the truth. 

*Socrates:* I called this a species of the intelligible genus, to whose investigation the soul is compelled to use suppositions, not going to a principle, since it cannot ascend above suppositions, and uses those images which are from the inferior things compared to the similitude of the superior, and thus are conceived and distinguished by opinion, as if they were conferred clearly upon those things. 

*Glauco:* I understand indeed what is said by you, as is customary in geometry and its sister arts. 

*Socrates:* Know then that I refer the other part of the intelligible to that which the reason itself touches by the faculty of demonstrating, while it does not hold suppositions as principles, but truly accepts them as suppositions, using them as certain steps and supports, until it comes to that which is not supposed—namely, to the **principle of the universe**—and touches it, and again adheres to those things which hang from the principle, and thus arrives at the end, using nothing sensible at all, but only the ideas themselves, through them, and progressing toward them. 

*Glauco:* I understand at last, although not sufficiently as I would wish. For you seem to me to propose a great work. You strive indeed to show that the part of that which truly exists and the intelligible genus, which we speculate through the science of demonstration, is clearer than that which we investigate from those sciences which are called arts. In which suppositions are held for principles, and those who consider them are compelled to intuit by thought, not by the senses. Since they do not ascend to the principle, but investigate from suppositions, they seem to you by no means to have intellect regarding these things, even though with the principle they are intelligible. You seem to me to call the habit of geometric and similar things "thought" [cogitationem] rather than "intellect," as if thought holds the middle between opinion and intellect. 

*Socrates:* You have perceived it quite sufficiently. And to these four proportions, accept likewise four affections of the soul. **Intelligence** [intelligentiam] indeed for the highest, **thought** [cogitationem] for the second, **faith** [fidem] for the third, and for the last **assimilation or imagination**. Furthermore, ordain these among themselves in the ratio of proportion, so that they participate in clarity just as those things they are about participate in truth. 

*Glauco:* I understand indeed, and I admit what you say, and I dispose it as you command.

**[Page 418 - 424 Summary/Excerpts]**
The text proceeds into **Dialogue VII (Book VII of the Republic)**. 
- **Ficino’s Argumentum (p. 418):** Ficino provides a Neoplatonic introduction, linking Plato to the theological traditions of Moses, Numa Pompilio, and the Indians/Egyptians. He explains the "Cave" as the visible world, the "chains" as the body/perturbations of the soul, and the "shadows" as sensible things.
- **The Allegory of the Cave (p. 419-420):** Socrates describes the prisoners in the cave who see only shadows on the wall. He describes the painful process of one being released, climbing out of the cave, being blinded by the sun, and finally realizing the sun is the cause of all things.
- **The Return to the Cave (p. 420):** If the escapee returns to the cave, his eyes would be unaccustomed to the darkness, and the other prisoners would mock him or even kill him if he tried to release them.
- **The Curriculum (p. 421-424):** Socrates and Glauco discuss the education needed to turn the soul toward the Good. 
    - **Arithmetic:** Necessary for both war and philosophy; it forces the mind to think about "One" vs "Many."
    - **Geometry:** Necessary for war (encampments) but primarily for knowing "that which always is."
    - **Stereometry (Solid Geometry):** Mentioned as the third study (3D figures).
    - **Astronomy:** Not just looking at the sky, but understanding the mathematical laws of celestial motion.
    - **Harmonics:** Seeking the numbers in audible sounds.
    - **Dialectic:** The "coping stone" of the sciences, which leads directly to the contemplation of Being and the Good.

# **Book Thirty-One**
<note>In this specific edition of Ficino’s collected works, the sections are numbered differently than modern editions of Plato; this text corresponds to the end of Republic, Book VI.</note>

...since [the Good] is such and so great, shall we say that those most excellent men in the city, to whom we entrust everything, should likewise be blind? Not at all.

I believe, indeed, that a guardian who possesses what is just and honorable, but is ignorant of the reason *why* they are good, is not worth much. Indeed, it is fitting that he who is ignorant of this should come to know it. I surmise, however, that no one will sufficiently know the [just and honorable] things themselves before knowing the Good. You surmise correctly. Our republic will therefore be perfectly ordered if a guardian skilled in these matters rules it. That is necessarily so. 

But you, O Socrates, do you say that the Good itself is knowledge, or pleasure, or something else besides these? Then I said: You are truly a worthy man; I have known for a long time that it would not be enough for you if I merely reported the opinions of others. It does not seem right to me, O Socrates, to be able to report the opinions of others, but not one’s own, especially for a man who has spent so much time on these matters. Do you think it is right to speak about things one is ignorant of as if one knew them? Not at all as if one knew them, but as if putting forward what he thinks as an opinion. What? I said. Do you not know that all opinions without knowledge are base, the best of which are blind? Or do you think those who hold a true opinion without understanding differ at all from those who, though they are blind, nevertheless walk the right path? Not at all. Do you wish then to contemplate base, blind, and crooked things, when you might hear clear and beautiful things from others? 

By Jove, Socrates, said Glauco, do not stop when you have almost reached the goal. For it will be enough for us if, just as you have treated justice, temperance, and the other virtues, you likewise treat the Good. It would also be quite enough for me, O friend. But I fear my strength will fail, and by daring beyond my power, I may appear foolish and move the listeners to laughter. 

But, O happy men, let us set aside for the present what the Good itself is. For it seems to me to be beyond our present contemplation. But I will tell you, if it pleases you, what appears to be the son of the Good itself, and what is most similar to it; if not, I will let it go. Speak then. You shall declare the father later. I would certainly wish that I were able to explain it, and you to perceive it—not only the offspring, as now, but both the offspring and the descendants of the Good itself. Therefore, receive for the present this birth and offspring of the Good itself. Take care, however, lest I unintentionally deceive you, giving a vain account of the son. We shall take care as best we can. Only speak. 

I will speak indeed, if we first review and confirm together the things mentioned above, and spoken of many times elsewhere. Which things? We say there are many beautiful things, and many good things, and we distinguish each in our speech. 

We say so indeed. And yet we also introduce Beauty itself, and the Good itself, and similarly for all those things which we posited as many; we posited them again as one according to a single "Idea" <term>Idea: In Plato’s philosophy, the perfect, eternal blueprint or form of a thing</term> for each, as if there were only one, and we call it what each thing truly *is*. These things are true. And we say that these many things are seen, but not understood; whereas the Ideas are understood, but not seen. It is entirely so. By what power among the many we have do we perceive the things that lie open to the eyes? By sight. And by hearing those things that are heard, and by the other senses all things that are sensed? Why not?

Have you not noticed how perfect a power the Creator of the senses fashioned for seeing and being seen? Not sufficiently. Consider it thus. Does hearing and the voice need another kind of thing so that the one may hear and the other be heard? If that third thing were absent, will the one not hear and the other not be heard? Not at all. I think, indeed, that many other senses—not to say none—need no such thing. Can you name any such power? Not at all. But do you not notice that sight itself and that which is subject to sight require such a thing? In what way? 

Though sight is present in the eyes, and the eyes are directed toward looking, and color is present, unless a third kind of thing is there, naturally suited for this very purpose, sight will see nothing, nor can colors be seen. What do you say that is? That which you call light. You speak the truth. Truly, the power of visibility and the power of seeing are joined by a yoke far more honorable than all other pairings, by a certain great beauty—provided that light is not to be despised. 

It is far from being despised. Which of the celestial gods do you think is the cause of this, whose light causes our sight to see as well as possible, and the objects to be seen by the eyes? The one you and others think. Surely you are asking about the Sun. Even so, sight relates to this God in this way. How? Sight is not the sun, nor is the eye in which sight resides the sun. Certainly not. But of all the organs of the senses, it is the one most like the sun. Very much so. And does it not preserve the power it has as something infused from the sun? Exactly. Furthermore, the sun is not sight. But since it is the cause of sight, it is seen by it. Clearly so. 

Say then that I call this the "son of the Good," which the Good itself generated in its own likeness: so that just as the Good stands in the intelligible realm <term>Intelligible realm: The world of thought and logic, as opposed to the physical world we see</term> toward the intellect and the things that are understood, so the sun stands in the visible realm toward sight and the things that are seen. In what way? Explain further. 

Furthermore, whenever the eyes are not turned toward those things whose colors the daylight illuminates and reveals, but toward those things touched by the rays of the night, they grow dim and hallucinate, and seem almost blind, as if pure sight were not in them. So it happens. But whenever they turn to those things which the sun illustrates, they see clearly, and sight appears to be in those same eyes. It is so. 

Think of the soul in the same way. For when it clings to that in which truth and Being itself shine forth, it understands and knows it, and appears to have intellect. But when it turns toward that which is mixed with darkness—that which is born and decays—its edge is dulled, and it turns various opinions around, and seems to be without a mind. So it appears. 

Therefore, that which provides truth to the things understood, and gives the power of understanding to the one who understands, say that this is the **Idea of the Good**, the cause of knowledge and of the truth perceived through the intellect. Since these two are so beautiful—namely, knowledge and truth—if you judge the Good itself to be something other and even more beautiful than these, you will think correctly. And just as it is right to think that light and sight have a certain likeness to the sun, but are by no means the sun itself: so it is right to think that knowledge and truth have a certain likeness to the Good, but are by no means the Good itself. For the majesty of the Good itself is more venerable. 

You describe an inestimable beauty, if it provides knowledge and truth, yet surpasses them in beauty. For surely you do not say that pleasure is the Good. Hush! <note>original: "Bona verba quæso" - literally "good words, I pray," a common idiom used to ward off an ill omen or a foolish suggestion.</note> please. And so contemplate its image more clearly. How? 

You will say, I think, that the sun provides to the things that are seen not only the power of being seen, but also their generation, growth, and nourishment, though the sun is not itself generation. How could it be? And so you may say that the Good gives to the things that are known not only that they are known, but further bestows their being and essence, though the Good is not itself essence, but is above essence <note>original: "supra essentiā" - a translation of the famous Greek phrase "epekeina tēs ousias," meaning "beyond being."</note>, surpassing it in dignity and power. 

Then Glauco, laughing, said: By Pollux! <note>original: "Adepol" - an ancient Roman oath.</note> this is a marvelous excess. You are certainly the cause of this, I said, who compelled me to open up what I thought about this. Do not stop yet, but finish the comparison of the sun, if there is anything...

<summary>Socrates introduces the "Idea of the Good" using the analogy of the Sun, explaining that just as the sun provides light for the eyes and growth for the earth, the Good provides truth to the mind and existence to all things.</summary>

"Lest you omit the smallest thing." "I think indeed many things remain besides, nevertheless as many as can be reported at present, I will not willingly let go." "So I pray."
"Think that these are two, and one indeed reigns in the intelligible genus and place, the other in the invisible <note>likely a slip in OCR for "visible"</note>... lest I seem to deceive you about the name. However, you have two species: the visible and the intelligible." "I have them indeed." "Just as if you took a line cut into two unequal portions, and divided each part again by a similar ratio: so now the one visible genus and the other intelligible genus offered to you, distinguish each again according to clarity and obscurity. In the visible genus, one portion will contain **images**. I call images, first, shadows. Then the likenesses which appear in waters, and those in dense, smooth, and shiny bodies, and everything of that sort, if you follow." "I follow." "But the other portion will include those things of which these are certain likenesses: namely, the animals among us, and plants, and the entire genus of manufactured things. So I place them." "Do you wish further to say this genus is distinguished according to truth and non-truth? So that as that which is fashioned by opinion is to that which is known by science, so the likeness is to that which it resembles?" "Very much so." "Consider again the section of the intelligible." "In what way?" "One part of it is that which the soul investigates using those previously divided images, compelled to proceed from hypotheses <note>original: "positionibus"</note> not toward a beginning, but toward an end. The other, however, which the soul thinks out, proceeding from a hypothesis to a non-hypothesized beginning, not using images which we are accustomed to use for the other genus, but progressing through the forms themselves by means of the forms." "I do not sufficiently understand what you say." "But you will understand more easily through these things. I think it is not hidden from you that those who deal with geometry and arithmetic and others of that kind, suppose the even and the odd, and figures, and three kinds of angles, and similar things in their individual arguments; and having placed these as manifest to anyone, they think no account of them needs to be demanded. And starting from here they descend to other things, and at last reach that which they sought." "I certainly know that." "Indeed, you also know that they use the forms which fall under sight, and speak about them: although they do not direct their mind to those, but rather to those of which these are likenesses, namely to the **Square itself**, and the **Diameter itself**, not to those which they draw. And in other things in the same way, they use these forms which they describe and figure—of which there are both shadows and images in water—as images, striving to behold those things which are perceived in no other way than by thought." "You speak the truth." "This I called a species of the intelligible genus above, for the investigation of which the soul is compelled to use hypotheses, not going to a beginning, as it is unable to ascend above hypotheses, and uses these images which are compared from the lower things to the likeness of the higher, and are thus conceived and distinguished by opinion as if they contributed clearly to them." "I understand indeed that you speak of what is usually done in geometry and its sister arts." "Know then that I refer the other part of the intelligible to that which reason itself reaches through the faculty of demonstrating, while it does not hold hypotheses as beginnings, but accepts them truly as hypotheses, using them as certain steps and supports, until it reaches that which is not hypothesized, namely the **beginning of the universe**; and having reached it, it clings again to those things which cling to the beginning, and so reaches the end, using nothing sensible at all, but progressing through the forms themselves, by them, and toward them." "I understand at last, although not as sufficiently as I would wish. For you seem to me to propose a great work. You strive indeed to argue that that part of true being and of the intelligible genus, which is contemplated by the science of demonstration, is clearer than that which we investigate from those sciences called arts. In which [damaged] hypotheses are held as beginnings, and those who consider them are compelled by thought to look not with the senses. Because they do not ascend to the beginning, but search from hypotheses, they seem to you not to have intellect about these things, even though they are intelligible when combined with the beginning. You seem to me to call the habit of geometric and similar things **thought** rather than intellect, as if thought held a middle place between opinion and intellect." "You have perceived it quite sufficiently. And for these four proportions, accept likewise four affections of the soul. **Intelligence** indeed for the supreme, **thought** for the second, **faith** <note>original: "fidem", often translated as 'belief' or 'conviction' in this context</note> for the third, and for the last **assimilation** or **imagination**. Order these besides by a reciprocal ratio of proportion, so that these participate in clarity just as those things they are about participate in truth." "I understand indeed, and I admit what you say, and I arrange them as you command."

->**DIALOGUE SEVENTH ON JUSTICE.**<-
*
**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.**
SAGES endowed with divine genius have turned all the study of the mind from earthly to heavenly things, from moving to immobile things, from those which are sensed to those which surpass the senses, with all their might. Considering the machine of the world to be both one and wonderfully ordered, yet not able to stand by itself since it is composed of diverse parts and changes, they rightly recognized that it depends on another: on another one, I say, and most wise, who both fashions one work out of many, and fills that one everywhere, and moreover rules it powerfully. A work indeed immense and manifold, with a motion perpetual and most rapid, yet not wandering in its revolution: may he also most kindly lead each thing to the good, running with wonderful convenience and ease. For which reason, by a certain common conception, they have equally consented that **God exists**, the one powerful, wise, and merciful king of the universe: whom earthly kings and governors of republics ought to imitate to the best of their ability. After this common conception of God, they began to set out more clearly and closely toward God by a twin path: on the one hand by denying, on the other by referring. For by arguing what the Good itself (that is, what God) is *not*, they proved that He is nothing from these things which are grasped by the senses, nor from those which are comprehended by the mind. In this, however, referring both creatures to the creator, and in turn the creator to creatures, they thought out by what reason the creator makes and perfects each thing, and how creatures either relate to Him, or can imitate or follow Him. Our Plato shows that the genius of the philosopher proceeds this far in the *Parmenides*, and confirms it in the previous book. Which Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian once thought to be a disciple of St. Paul, heavily influenced by Neoplatonism</note> also greatly approves. I say to proceed this far both by a certain ray once infused into the mind from the beginning, and by the approaching light from the divine continually illuminating minds. But as for what the Good is in itself, that is, the divine substance, as he shows both in the *Parmenides* and here, no one can attain it through such paths; but only through these can one finally arrive there, where the divine Good, by its own benevolence alone, forms its approaching lover with its own light, warms him with heat, and transforms the mind by its power, so that the mind finally knows God when it has now been made
**God**...

Book Twenty-One <note>This header refers to the volume numbering in Ficino's collected translations, not the Republic's book number</note>.
...**God**. Which indeed he also signifies in his epistles. After the philosopher has contemplated God governing the heavens, then only, and he alone, will be able to govern earthly things divinely. In which matter Plato praises Minos for seeking laws from Jupiter <note>original: "Ioue"</note> by first contemplating him before he promulgated them to men. I pass over how much many praise Scipio, because he approached the republic with Jupiter as his teacher. What shall I say of Numa Pompilius, governing the city with religious laws? Did not also the Mosaic laws, by which the people of God were divinely governed, come to men with God himself teaching? Hence Aristoxenus relates the mysteries of the Indian philosophers, in which it is contained that without a divine rule, and one indeed demonstrated by God, nothing can ever be administered rightly or happily, whether privately or publicly. Because the Egyptians held the same discovery, they granted the rudders of the kingdom only to philosophers, and those indeed absolute and moreover sacred. And they thought to such an extent that nothing could be done happily without divine help, that they began all public affairs with sacred rites and vows. Again, they asserted that nothing could be understood without a certain divine inspiration, as Iamblichus reports, so that all the books of those philosophizing among them are ascribed to the name of the God Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, as if they were not the inventions of men, but of God. Which Timaeus also signifies saying that philosophy is a divine gift. He teaches also in the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note> that civil skill is a divine gift. And to return to this seventh book, he does not admit anyone to the governing of this republic of his, except him who it is established has received both a certain divine nature and education divinely: whom alone he calls everywhere a legitimate citizen and philosopher. But why does he say there is need of a divine gift for it? I pass over other reasons for now. Because, namely, while it is most difficult for anyone to govern himself happily, it is certainly impossible to compose a city—made of so many and diverse people, over which innumerable and uncertain chances loom daily—happily without God, the author of happiness. From this it happened that every city recognized a certain particular deity as a patron. Plato wants the governor of the city to be the vicar and interpreter of this deity, who, in place of the deity, should both contemplate divine things and provide for human things from there. Therefore, he expels wicked men from the republic as being entirely devoid of the divine gift. But he accepts only the good. Yet not all. For he calls those ignorant of theology **blind and dreaming**, as those who take the images of things for the things themselves: he deems it foolish to commend the custody of the city to the blind and dreaming. But theologians, who as yet hold no use of human affairs, he does not admit to conducting public affairs until he has accustomed them to handling private and lighter matters. He concludes meanwhile that the magistracy must be given to no one except him whose life is better than the magistracy, and who neither seeks nor even appetites the magistracy itself. You indeed, where Plato in educating the civil philosopher proposes the **image of the cave**, and of chains, and of a certain light, and of shadows, and of water: Understand the **cave** to be this world we see, if it be compared to the invisible world. The **chain** indeed is the human body, or rather the perturbation of the soul binding it to the body. The **shadows** are all the things that move the senses. For these are shadows of true things, that is, of the Ideas. But as for his saying that the soul does not descend without offense suddenly from the invisible world to the visible, then in turn ascends, you can accept this in two ways after the manner of Plato: both in this life, when namely one passes without a medium from this study of human things to that supreme study of divine things, and vice versa: and between this life and the other. When namely the soul, either impure, migrates from the darkness of the body to the divine light, under which it grows dark and is tortured: or descending from the divine light into the elemental body, it is long blind and troubled. Remember indeed that it is the property of light to make and demonstrate all things: and it is threefold—divine, intellectual, and visible. The divine is called the **Sun of both suns**. The intellectual is named the **Angelic Sun**, the sun of the mundane sun. Finally, the **visible light** is the celestial sun and its brilliance. Just as brilliance spreading itself from the celestial sun through all things is the image and act of the sun: so also the light which is in the sun is the image and act of the angelic mind. Light then in the angel is the act and image of the divine light. And just as visible light is received only in a transparent nature, so invisible light in a clear-sighted nature. Julian the Platonist, describing three such suns in his book *On the Sun*, adds from the theology of the Phoenicians that visible light is a certain perennial act of divine and angelic intelligence shining through the solar window to the eyes, and from there diffused through transparent materials everywhere as if agreeable to itself. Furthermore, lest you doubt that this appearing light is an image of the non-appearing light, know that that light is not a body. For it penetrates bodies without offense or infection. Likewise, it is not made by the proper quality of a composite body. Otherwise it would require the proper quality of the elements—hot or cold—preceding it in that which it is to receive, and with the sun receding, it would remain for a time in the transparent. Likewise, it is not bound to a proper dimension. For it does not arrive in time, or illuminate a part now and then a part later. Add that it fills a large space without its own dissipation; and in turn collects itself into a narrow space in a moment without the breaking of itself or the vessel. Neither is it properly corporeal, but a middle between incorporeal and corporeal things, and indeed the proper quality of heaven, whose nature is most near to incorporeal things. It is also communicated only to transparent elements, similar to heaven in this very transparency: to the transparent, I say, first light, then heat; but to the opaque, first heat, light however not until they are reduced to a transparent nature through heat. It is not infused, however, into opaque bodies in which an earthly nature dominates. Not because it cannot penetrate—since it penetrates crystal more solid than many opaque things—but because an earthly nature, most alien to a heavenly nature, cannot be capable of a heavenly quality. It communicates heat, however, to opaque things as I said, not as properly to heaven as light. For heaven, because it shines, therefore it is warm. But that the light diffused from heaven into our transparent things should again be called the image of the sun appears from this, that it is the common and proper origin of all images. For images of things result under its brilliance. And it is so powerful an image that it appears not only when it bounces from a specular body, but also when it is projected from the sun: which by no means happens to other images: yet all are incorporeal: since they pour themselves through the whole in a moment, and are many in the same point without mutual confusion. Therefore light is also incorporeal, by whose power this is perfected. Consequently, it carries the ray of the sun with it in a moment, the act of light and the force of heat. And through light indeed it refers to the clarity of divine and angelic intelligence. Through heat, however, the affection of both will and charity. But since those above, like craftsmen, perform works through will rather than through intelligence, this visible ray, flowing from their invisible ray, rightly acts upon individual things that are born through heat rather than through light. Nay, rather, it acts through light, but upon the spiritual images of things; through heat, however, upon corporeal qualities. And this heat depends on light just as in divine things all things are represented ideally through the intellect, and all things are generated through the affection rising therefrom. We, however, being warned from here, if an earthly nature does not receive heavenly light, let us expel earthly affections far from us, that we may be filled with divine light. And if the last body does not receive the light of the first unless it first grows warm from there and is made similar, lo! let us also, the last of minds, first burn with the love of the first, that being purged by love and made similar we may then shine divinely, and now rejoice in full light. But let us now touch upon the rest of this seventh book. Since therefore light is threefold, as we said—visible, and intellectual above sight, and divine above intellect—therefore Plato here makes mention of light in three degrees, namely in the **cavern**, in the **night**, and in the **day**: signifying namely those three lights. Thrice also he makes mention of **water**—in the cavern, in the night, and in the day: for as light both makes and demonstrates all things, so water washes all things and represents them. By the first indeed he signifies morals, by the second indeed contemplation. And he performs each in three degrees. Surely through the mortal he washes and purges thrice: first indeed by cutting off the movements of the second through civil virtues, then by extirpating the same through purgatorial virtues, thirdly by most absolutely moderating the first movements through the virtues of a soul already purged, whence one now arrives at the exemplary virtues which are in God, especially through contemplation. Of which indeed there are three degrees, which the water thrice named refers to, insofar as it, by representing images, refers to intelligence. For divine things seem to be represented in three, so to speak, waters. First indeed, although more confusedly, in physical reasons: Second, more distinctly in mathematical: Third, most clearly in metaphysics, entirely absolute. Physical forms Plato calls entirely material, because they need both common and proper matter, and cannot be thought of without it. Mathematical forms however are not so material, because they do not need proper matter, but either only common as dimensions, or none as numbers: and these can be thought out without matter. Finally, he thinks divine forms are entirely immaterial, and true things, of which mathematical forms are images, and natural things are shadows; but this is a **Pythagorean mystery**. When therefore he noticed that Thales, Democritus, and Anaxagoras were as negligent in divine things as they were diligent in natural ones; but Pherecydes and Pythagoras and all the Pythagorean princes of mathematics on the contrary stood out as the highest theologians and divine in morals, he rightly concluded partly by reason and partly by experience that a curious study of natural things very often turns the soul away from divine things. Which Solomon also therefore judged to be a most evil occupation, and miserable those who are too much occupied in it. Socrates detests the same in the *Phaedo*, those I say who, curiously referring natural causes of effects only to certain elemental qualities, rest in that sort of
beginning...

Dialogue VII. on the Republic. Or, on Justice. 419

...and end, and do not seek the supreme beginning and end of the universe. For which reason, this **Seventh Book**, where it leads the soul to the supreme good and the sun—that is, God—and the divine Ideas like stars, by suitable steps, makes no mention of natural skill in that ascent itself. But it brings into the middle certain mathematical steps leading more conveniently to divine things: among which two are pure. For **Arithmetic** deals with pure numbers, and **Geometry** with pure dimensions. But three steps are mixed. For **Music** adds voices and motions to numbers, pertaining chiefly to hearing. **Stereometry** <note>the measurement of solid figures</note> adds weights to dimensions. **Astronomy** measures celestial spheres and motions with numbers and dimensions. Plato however uses natural skill in the descent rather than the ascent, as he teaches in the *Timaeus*, *Philebus*, *Parmenides*, and often elsewhere. For in the descent, through the divine causes of natural things, he wants the principal natural things to be demonstrated. But in the ascent, he thinks that through anxious care for natural things—as being far removed from divine things—the soul is diverted from them rather than converted. Altogether also he counts all actions, even if they seem most honest, as nothing, unless they lead to the imitation and attainment of the divine good: and similarly he either neglects all speculations unless they contribute to finding the divine good, or even detests them if they in any way divert us therefrom. Therefore, he wants the whole study of philosophy to be to turn from sensible to intelligible things, and to ascend to the Good itself, which is the supreme light of intelligible things. And he says that as sight is to the supreme of visible things—that is, the sun—so intellect is to the supreme light of intelligible things—namely, God. Therefore just as the sun generates the eye, and by generating bestows the power of seeing, and continually provides the act of seeing to the generated eye: so God both creates the intellect, and by creating provides the power of understanding, and continually the act of understanding to the created mind. Again, just as there is no need for anything to be done by art concerning the eye except to purge it and turn it: so philosophy provides only two things concerning the intellect, namely by purging it both from perturbations and from false opinions, and by turning it through reasons and exhortations from sensible forms to the intellectual forms innate in us, and through these to the intelligible forms—that is, the **Ideas**. Again through the Ideas to the divine mind, by which the Ideas are comprehended, and finally from this to the divine Good, the principle and light of the Ideas. When therefore he says the soul is raised from the lamp to the moon, from the moon to the sun, he signifies its elevation from natural forms to mathematical, and finally from these to divine, not indeed by teaching: for divine things, as he hands down in the epistles, cannot be taught: but rather by purging and turning. For these being accomplished, just as the sun, which is the light of visible things, shows visible things to the eye, so the Good itself, which is the light of intelligible things, lays open the things to be understood to the intellect. But of these things most broadly in our **Theology** <note>Refers to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology*</note>. Therefore no one ought to wonder that Plato uses the doctrinal order of writing more rarely, but the purgatory and exhortatory—that is, the confusional <note>original: "confuoforio", likely meaning 'shaking up' or 'refuting'</note>—always. After these things, note that from the number of those things which are sensed, those especially excite intelligence which are not clearly discerned from their opposites through the sense, and therefore need intelligence to discern them. Likewise that numbers are not corporeal. Since indeed number is nothing other than unity repeated. Unity however is not a body: for it is not divided into parts: if it is imagined to be divided, it is not cut, but rather multiplied: multiplied, I say, into itself, not into any parts: for any part is accustomed to be smaller than the whole. But no unity is either greater or smaller than unity. And yet this very unity and number raise us to an incorporeal essence: similarly also figures, whose true reason is found in the mind rather than in the body. Similarly astronomy seems to investigate the reason of the mover from the order of heaven. Plato denies that he is an astronomer who looks up at the supernal things but has not looked from heaven itself above heaven, especially because celestial things, since they do not fill a whole order, surely depend on some superior and whole order. He mocks also music unless it receives the reason of intellectual consonance from the consonance of the voice. Finally, he puts **Dialectic**—that is, metaphysics or theology—before all faculties, as both leading all and using the ministry of individual ones for its own duty. Its duty however is to progress through the whole breadth of that which is called Being, and to betake itself to the Good itself, the cause of the whole being, and to define in that very order of beings what each thing is, assigning the reason of each essence, and demonstrating what follows any essence. But other faculties he judges to be servile compared to the nobility of this one. For they either decline to the opinions of men, or to the generations and compositions of lower things, or to the cult of those things which are born: or at least, even if they raise themselves to incorporeal things to the best of their power, they nevertheless dream about them in some way. Such, he says, are the mathematical disciplines. But soon he joins two genera, namely essence and generation. To the former he thinks intelligence pertains, but to the latter, opinion. Again in intelligence, he says science follows essence, pertaining to the dialectician; but cognition follows essence and pertains to the mathematician. In opinion similarly he counts faith and imagination: and through the former indeed bodies are perceived, through the latter indeed images of bodies and shadows. Then he concludes that other faculties without dialectic are blind. And that they together and dialectic besides are vain unless they clearly know the Idea of the Good, and through it know in individual things how to discern true goods from false. But he who is ignorant of the reason of the good is both troubled here and there in dreams, and descending to the underworld is more mocked and vexed. He adds that that man is lame who is inept and unskilled for either, whether for acting or for speculating. For which reason he chooses those for governing who are both apt by nature and sufficiently instructed by discipline for both. Meanwhile, note that a liar, as if maimed and mutilated, is to be excluded from the republic. But he calls him a liar who both lies to others with deliberate work, and who through ignorance lies to himself. Remember also that the labors of the mind are more heavy than those of the body, and therefore one must learn in youth, and liberal disciplines must be taught far from servitude. Nor however is dialectic to be handed over to adolescents. Which the *Philebus* also teaches us. For as the *Phaedrus* also distinguishes, two leaders are in us for all things: namely, an innate desire for pleasures, and a certain opinion acquired through education, dictating that honorable and just things defined for us by laws must be kept in all things. But these two leaders very often distract in contrary directions. Since however the faculty of arguing, if handed to adolescents, weakens the opinion of the honorable, whence they turn out intemperate, nay even proud and impious, as is read also in the *Philebus* and the *Laws*, therefore before the thirtieth year of age they are to be instructed in mathematics, and exercised equally in public business through intervals. But when they reach the thirtieth year, they are to be admitted to dialectic, yet so that they are called back again through intervals to public actions. You indeed, from its form, call the industry of arguing **Dialectic**; from its beginning **Logic**; from its end **Metaphysics** and **Theology**. Know also that to the end of such dialectic, men are called as if divine in the fiftieth year of age, because for the intuition of divine things there is need of a purged and serene mind. Meanwhile here observe, what we use more often both here and in our *Theology*, that three certain things are noted by Plato: namely, the **ray**, the **lumen** <note>light-source effect</note>, and the **lux** <note>pure light</note>. The **ray** indeed is proper and naturally innate to individual minds just as to the eyes. The **lumen** however is common to all eyes. Finally, the divine **lux** presides over the lumen common to all minds, just as lux in the sun presides over the lumen of the eyes equally common. He concludes that the citizen, after he has contemplated the lux of the Good itself both through the ray naturally innate to him from there and through the lumen of the same infused again, ought to govern the city according to the exemplar of the Good itself to the best of his power.

->[Ornamental P]<- **AFTER THESE THINGS**, I said, figure to yourself our nature—as far as education and ignorance are concerned—by such an image. Imagine in your mind a subterranean dwelling, like a **cavern**, whose long entrance lies open toward the light throughout the whole cave. In it are men nurtured from childhood, their necks and legs so bound that they are compelled to remain immobile and look only forward, nor can they turn their heads because they are restricted by chains. But behind their backs above and far off let a torch of fire be suspended, and between the fire and the bound men let there be a way a little higher, along which a small wall is constructed, like the screens which conjurors <note>original: "praestigiatoribus"</note> usually have, over which they show their wonders, placed before the spectators. "I see it," he said. "Imagine again men within the wall carrying various vessels, sticking out above the wall, and stone and wooden statues of men and other animals, and images fabricated in various ways. And, as is likely, some of those carrying these things are silent, some are speaking." "What portentous fictions these are, and what strange captives!" "But they are like us. For first of all, do you think those men see anything else of themselves, or of the men next to them, besides the **shadows** which fall from the fire onto the opposite part of the cave?" "If therefore they were allowed to talk to one another, do we not believe they would think the shadows of things should be called by names?" "It is necessary." "And what if an echo resonated from the opposite part of the prison, as often as anyone passing by spoke? Do you think they would exist to believe anyone else spoke except the shadows of those passing by?" "No, by Jupiter." "Altogether therefore these would think nothing is true except the shadows of fabricated things." "So it is entirely necessary." "On the contrary now observe what their release from chains and the cure of their ignorance would be like. Surely if anyone of them were released, and compelled suddenly to rise, to turn his neck, to walk, to look at the light itself, he would immediately feel pain, nor because of the splendor would he be able to behold those things whose shadows he saw before. If someone should say to him that he had looked at trifles until now, but that now he is nearer to true things and looks more truly, and showing him each of those passing by, should ask what it is, do you not think he would be staggered, and think those things he saw before were truer than those which are shown now?" "Much so." "And if he should compel him to look at the light, do you not think his eyes would be affected with pain? And that he would turn his eyes back to those things which he had easily seen before, thinking them more certain than those which were suddenly offered then?" "Indeed so." "But if someone should drag him violently up the rough and steep path, and not permit him to see anything before he had dragged him out to the light of the sun, do you not think he would feel pain and take it badly while he was being snatched away? And when he had been raised to the light, his eyes being filled with splendor, he would be stuck, and able to see nothing of those things which are now thought true by men?" "Nothing certainly, not suddenly." "Therefore there is need first of custom, if he is to behold the things above. And first he will more easily look at shadows, after these at the images of men and others in the waters. But finally he will more easily contemplate those things which are in heaven, and heaven itself by night, while he looks at the light of the stars and the moon, than if he should behold the sun itself by day and the brilliance of the sun." "Without doubt." "And so finally he will look up at the **sun itself**, and no longer behold its likenesses in the waters and in an alien region, but he will speculate upon it according to itself in its own seat, and be able to know what it is like." "It is necessary." "He will notice at last that it is the one which tempers the seasons and years, which rules all things that are under heaven, which is in a certain way the author of all those things which were seen by them before." "It is certain he will ascend to this by these steps." "What if he should recall his former habitation to memory, and the wisdom of those men and the chains? Do you not think he would consider himself blessed by the change of place, and pity them?" "Most greatly indeed." "Moreover, if any honors were bestowed there upon each other and praises, and rewards were given to him who saw most sharply whatever passed by, and remembered most which of them were prior, which posterior, and which were accustomed to progress together, and from these best foretold the future, do you think he would desire these? And think those blessed who are honored and dominate among them? Or would he rather, as Homer says, prefer to be a servant to some landless man in an alien field, and to endure anything rather than be mocked by those opinions and live in that misery?" "I think he would choose anything else rather than a life of that sort." "Then consider this also," I said, "if he should descend again and reach the seat he had before, would he not be overwhelmed by darkness when he suddenly departed from the sun?" "Vehemently." "But if it were necessary to discern those shadows, and to dispute about them with those who are pressed by perpetual chains, and a judgment had to be brought forth in that very time while his eyes are hallucinating, before his sight is purged—which indeed will not happen in a short time—will he not provoke laughter? And will it not be given as a disgrace to him by all, that after he ascended, he returned with corrupted eyes? And will it not be said that one must never strive for the heights, and that he who tries to release and lead them up, if they catch him, should be killed immediately?" "He would certainly be killed," he said. "This whole image, O friend Glaucon, must be referred to those things which were said above. The prison indeed is this machine of the world which you see with your eyes: the fire-torch in the cave is the power of the sun: finally if you refer the ascent to the heights and the sight of them rightly to that which tends toward the **intelligible region**, you will not wander, as I indeed hope, since you desire to hear my opinion. But God knows whether it is true. What therefore appear to me, tend hither. Surely I think that in the intelligible order itself, the **Idea of the Good itself** exists as the supreme, and is hardly seen: but if it is seen, it must be asserted that it is the cause for all of all things which are right and good, since it created the light and the author of light in the visible place: but in the intelligible itself it reigns, and brought forth truth and mind. Which it is necessary to know for everyone who with a sane mind is to act anything either privately or publicly." "So I also think as best I can." "Come and consider this: nor wonder that these who descend here do not wish to handle human affairs, but the edge of their minds is always directed to the heights. For that is probable, if indeed it follows the superior image." "Probable indeed." "But what of this? Do you think it wonderful if someone falling from divine spectacles to these human evils is more inept for acting, and is laughed at, especially if before he is accustomed to the present darkness, while he still gropes, he is compelled, either in judgments or elsewhere, to contend about the shadows of the just, or about those statues whose shadows these are, and to dispute about the persuasion and judgments of those who have never seen justice itself?" "In no way wonderful." "But if someone has it in mind, he will remember that eyes are accustomed to be troubled in two ways and from two causes: both when we descend from light into shadow, and when we come out from darkness into light: and he will think the soul is affected in the same way, as often as he sees it troubled and too dull to discern something. And therefore he will not rashly break out into laughter, but will diligently inquire whether, descending from a more lucid life, it is overwhelmed by new darkness: or rising from much ignorance to a shining spectacle, it fails under too much flashing splendor. And he will approve the affection of this one, and judge his life to be blessed: he will pity the other: or if by chance he wishes to laugh at that life, he will not laugh so ineptly as at him who fell from the supernal light." "It is fitting." "These things therefore, if they are true, must be thought of in this way, that education is not such as some proclaim it to be: for they promise they will hand over science to a soul entirely devoid of science, as if sight to blind eyes." "They certainly profess it." "But the present reason intimates to us, first the power which is in the soul of everyone, then the instrument by which each one can learn a thing. Just as if it were impossible to turn the eye in any other way than together with the whole body from a dark to a clear object: so it is necessary to turn around with the whole mind from that which *becomes* until that which is called *Being*, that it may be able to bear the clearest thing by speculating. But this very thing we say is the **Good**." "Surely." "For this very thing then, competent education will be a certain faculty of the soul...
