of directing the soul. In what way? So that its own eye may be turned as easily and effectively as possible. It will not give sharpness of sight to this eye, but rather, since it already possesses sight but is not correctly turned nor looking where it should, it will strive to turn it by every possible device. So it seems. Therefore, the other things which are called virtues of the soul seem to be similar to the virtues of the body. For since they are not present by nature, they seem to be acquired gradually through habit and practice. But **Wisdom** truly exists as a certain more divine virtue than all others, which indeed never loses its power, but from its very turning it becomes useful and beneficial, or again useless and harmful. Have you not yet noticed how sharply the little soul of those who, though they are evil, are yet considered wise, sees and how quickly it discerns the things to which it is turned, as if it had a sight by no means dull, but were compelled to serve wickedness? And therefore, the more sharply it gazes, the more evils it performs. Entirely so. If from this nature, immediately from childhood, there were pruned away the things that are kindred to the world of becoming, like leaden weights, which—clinging to the soul through gluttony and such pleasures and lusts and refinements—twist the sight of the mind toward lower things; if it were freed from these, its gaze would be turned toward those things which are true, and indeed that same sight in those same men would discern those truths as sharply as it now discerns the things upon which it is presently intent. It is probable. What of this? Is it not probable and necessary from what has been said, that neither uneducated men and those ignorant of the truth can sufficiently administer the republic, nor those who have spent their whole lives in literary studies? Because the former have no certain goal proposed for themselves in life, looking toward which they ought to do whatever they do both privately and publicly. The latter, however, will not willingly handle civil affairs, thinking that even in this life they inhabit the **Islands of the Blessed** <note>In Greek mythology, a paradise for the souls of the righteous; Plato uses it here to describe the philosopher's desire for isolated contemplation</note>, far removed from human business. You speak the truth. It will therefore be our duty, we who have founded the city, to compel the best natures of men toward that greatest discipline which we mentioned above—to know the Good—so that they may both ascend upward, and after they have ascended and seen enough, we must not permit them what is now allowed. What is that? That they remain in that study, and be unwilling to descend again to those men shut in the prison, nor to be partakers of those labors and honors, whether they be of lesser or greater value. Shall we then do them an injury, and compel them to undergo a worse life, when they could enjoy a better one? You have forgotten, O friend, that it is not the legislator's concern that any one class in the city be especially happy, but that the whole city be so. Indeed, he reconciles the citizens themselves to this by persuasion and force, and makes them help one another, and cultivate a common utility according to their strength. For the legislator gathers men into a civil assembly, not to allow each one to be carried wherever he pleases, but that he may use them for the binding together of the city. You speak the truth. That had escaped me. Consider then, Glaucon, how we shall do no injury to the philosophers who are found among us. But when we compel them to care for others, we shall say with justice in this manner: that those who are found to be philosophers in other cities deservedly flee the labors of administering the Republic, because they grow up on their own in whatever city they are, without the Republic caring for them. It is fair that what is born of itself, since it is indebted to no one for the nourishment it received, should pay the price of nourishment to no one. But we have created you, both for yourselves and for the rest of the citizens, like leaders and kings in a hive of bees, educated better and more perfectly than the kings of bees, and more fit to undertake both cares <note>The "two cares" are the life of contemplation and the life of action/governance</note>. Each of you must therefore descend in turn into the assembly of other men, and become accustomed to looking at obscure things. For when you have become accustomed, you will see those things much more sharply than those who live among them daily, and you will recognize what any images are and of what things they are, as those who truly know what is honorable, just, and good. And so for us and for you, the city will be inhabited by those who are truly awake and thinking rightly, and not by those who are dreaming, as many are now inhabited—namely by those who fight among themselves over shadows, and contend for leadership as if it were the greatest good. But the truth is this. Surely the city in which the citizens are least ambitious to seek magistracies remains best and furthest from seditions; but the city that has citizens otherwise affected is the opposite. It is exactly so. Will our pupils refuse our advice when they hear these things? And will they be unwilling to take their turn in the administration of the city, but rather dwell longer in the leisure of contemplation? Not at all. For we shall command just things of just men. But each of them will approach the magistracy entirely as a necessary thing, unlike those who now rule in individual cities. For the matter stands thus, O friend. If you find a life for those who are to be in charge of magistracies that is better than the magistracies themselves, then for the first time a best-instituted city will shine forth for you. In that city alone will the truly rich rule: I do not mean rich in gold, but in that which a blessed man ought to be rich in—a life of integrity and prudence. But if those who are poor and void of their own goods approach the Republic, desiring to snatch goods from there, that city cannot be happy. For where leadership is contended for, since this is a personal and internal war, it destroys both those who fight thus and the rest of the city. You speak the truth. Do you have any who despise civil honors, except true philosophers? No, by Jupiter. But indeed, magistracies must be given to men who are least desirous of power; otherwise, a grudge will arise among rivals. Certainly. Whom then will you lead to the guardianship of the city, other than those who best understand these things through which the city is rightly cultivated, and who possess both other honors and a life superior to the civil life? No others indeed. Do you wish then that we now inquire in what way such men may emerge in the city? And by what reason someone may lead them out into the light? Just as some are said to have ascended from the underworld to the gods. Why should I not wish it? This, as it seems, will not be the mere "turning of a shell" <note>A reference to a Greek game of chance (ostrakinda); Socrates means education is more than luck</note>, but the turning of the soul, from a certain night-like day to the contemplation of that which truly is. Which ascent indeed we shall say is true philosophy. Entirely so. Must we not investigate which discipline especially has this power? Why not? What then, O Glaucon, will be the discipline through which the soul is led back from those things which flow to those things which truly are? Now while I speak, I am thinking. For it considers the growth and decrease of the body. It appears so. This therefore will not be the discipline we seek. No. Or perhaps the kind...

The tragedies everywhere show Palamedes to have been a ridiculous leader of Agamemnon <note>In Greek legend, Palamedes was credited with inventing counting and the alphabet; here Socrates mocks the idea that Agamemnon was a "great" leader if he couldn't count his own troops</note>. What kind of leader then do you think he was then? Absurd indeed, if these things were true. We shall say therefore that the knowledge of numbers is necessary to a soldier, so that he may be able both to number and to calculate. Most of all, if indeed he ought not to be entirely raw at organizing battle lines. Nay, rather if he is to be a man. Does the same thing occur to you in this discipline that has come into my mind? What? It seems by nature to be from the number of those things which raise men to intelligence, such as we seek. And since it is such that it can altogether lift the mind to essence, no one seems to use this knowledge as is fitting. In what way do you say that? I will try indeed to explain my opinion to you. Notice, I pray, how I distinguish the kinds of things with myself, so that some lead to intelligence, such as we say, and some by no means: and confirm what I say, or deny it, so that we may more clearly discern whether this is such as I prophesy. Show me now. Behold I show you: if indeed you see that the things which move the senses are partly such as by no means provoke intelligence to consideration, as being sufficiently judged by the senses; and partly such as provoke it, as if the sense judges nothing in them purely. You speak of those things which are seen from a great distance, and those which are in some way shadowed. You have not quite guessed which ones I mean. Which ones then? Those indeed, I say, do not provoke the mind which do not fall into a contrary sense at the same time. But those which fall into a contrary sense provoke it, whenever the sense shows this no more than its contrary, whether it looks from far off or near. Thus what I say will be more open to you. We say these are three fingers: the thumb, the index, and the middle. Plainly. Think of me speaking thus, as if they were seen closely. And consider this in them. What? Each of them appears similarly to be a finger, and in this it makes no difference whether the middle one is offered, or the last, white or black, thick or thin, and whatever of the same kind. For in all things of this sort the soul is not compelled to provoke intelligence to a debate as to what among many things a finger is. For the sight itself did not signify at the same time that the finger was anything other than a finger. Certainly not. Deservedly therefore that which is such will neither move nor excite the mind. Deservedly. But does the sight sufficiently discern the magnitude and smallness of the finger itself? And does it matter nothing to it whether some of them lie in the middle or in the extremes? And in the same way, does the touch discern thick, thin, or softness and hardness? Or do the other senses not declare such things imperfectly? Or does each of them act thus? For first indeed the sense which pertains to the hard is compelled also to reach the soft, and it reports to the soul as if it sensed the same thing to be both soft and hard. So indeed. Is it not necessary in things of this kind for the soul to doubt what this sense of the hard signifies, if indeed it asserts the same thing to be soft as well? Likewise, the sense of the heavy and the light—what is heavy and light, if it signifies that the light is heavy and the heavy is light? Truly these interpretations reach the soul absurdly and stand in need of consideration. Deservedly therefore in these things the soul first strives, provoking reason and intelligence, to consider whether each of the things reported are one or two. Why not? If they are two, they appear as two, and each appears as one? So. If therefore each is one, and both together are two, the soul will understand two separate things. For if it perceived them indistinctly, it would understand not two, but one. Correct. We say the sight sees large and small, not as something discrete, but as something confused. Is it not so? Plainly. But for the sake of the declaration of this, the intelligence is compelled to look again at the large and the small, not as confused, but rather as distinct, contrary to the sense. You speak the truth. Hence we are immediately incited to ask what is the large, and what is the small. Most especially. And so we have called one intelligible and the other visible. Very skillfully. These are the things which I recently began to discuss: namely, that some things raise the soul to intelligence, and some do not; and those raise it which fall into the senses together with their contraries; but those which do not so, do not rouse the mind. I understand now, and it seems so to me. What then about number and the "one"? In which genus do they seem to you to be? I do not understand. But notice from the things said above. For if "the one" is sufficiently inspected by itself, or is apprehended by some other sense, it by no means leads the mind to essence, as we said of the finger. But if something always arises contrary to it at the same time, so that nothing seems more "one" than its contrary, it then stands in need of a debater and a judge, and the soul is compelled to doubt and investigate in it, and moving intelligence within itself, to ask what "the one" itself is. And in this way the discipline and knowledge of the one will be from the number of those things which lift the soul and turn it to the contemplation of that which truly is. But indeed, the inspection of "the one" has something of this kind. For at the same time we see it as one and as an infinite multitude. If "the one" suffers this, all number will suffer the same. Without a doubt. Indeed, every science of calculating and numbering is about number. Most especially.

And these seem to contribute toward truth. In a wonderful way. This discipline therefore will be of the kind we seek: most necessary for a soldier to know for organizing battle lines, and for a philosopher so that he may emerge from the waves of becoming and touch upon essence, without which discipline they will not be able to calculate and reason. It is so. But our guardian is both a soldier and a philosopher. Indeed. It will certainly be a fitting institution, O Glaucon, to persuade those who have performed the greatest duties of the city to apply themselves to the science of calculation, and not to touch upon it lightly, but to pursue it until they reach by the mind itself the contemplation of the nature of numbers; not for the sake of buying and selling, like merchants or innkeepers, but so that they may be equipped for war, and easily turn the soul from becoming toward truth and essence. You speak excellently. But since these things have been said about the discipline of reasoning, I indeed think within myself how graceful and useful the knowledge of numbers is to us everywhere for what we want, if someone follows it for the sake of knowing, not for the sake of "innkeeping" <note>Socrates uses "innkeeping" as a metaphor for using mathematics only for trade and profit</note>. By what reason? This very thing, I say, which we just mentioned: that namely it vehemently lifts up the soul and compels it to debate about numbers themselves, in no way admitting it if someone in the dispute introduces for numbers bodies which are both seen and handled. For you know how those who are skilled in these things, as often as someone strives to divide "the one" itself in words, they laugh immediately and do not tolerate this. But if you cut it, they multiply it, taking care lest "the one" itself should ever appear not to be one, but many small parts. You speak the truth. What then do you think, O Glaucon, if someone should ask them: "O wonderful men, what kind of numbers are you disputing about, in which there is such a 'one' as you describe, where each unit is equal, and every one entirely equal to every other, differing in not even the slightest way, yet containing no part within itself?" what do you think they would answer to these things? I think indeed they would answer that they are speaking of numbers themselves, which can only be thought of, but can by no means be handled otherwise. You see then, O friend, that this skill of this discipline is truly necessary to us? Since as it appears it leads the soul to this, that it uses intelligence itself for perceiving truth itself. It effects that vehemently. What then? Have you also noticed this, that men who are by nature arithmetical seem sharp, so to speak, in all doctrines? Moreover, if any who are slower in talent give themselves to this study, even if they receive no other utility, they yet achieve this, that they are sharper than they were before. It is so. But indeed you will not easily find many things, I think, which are learned with greater difficulty than these. Certainly not. Because of all the reasons we have brought forward, these must by no means be neglected, but in these especially those who have the best talents are to be educated. I certainly agree. Let this then be established for us: after this, let us consider what is next to it, whether it may be of use to us. What is that? Do you mean Geometry? This very thing. For as far as it contributes to the matter of war, so far certainly it is fitting for us. For in pitching camps, occupying a region, gathering troops, or even scattering them, and in every reason for arranging an army both in the fight itself and on the march, it makes a great difference whether someone is a geometrician or not. For these things indeed a certain small portion of Geometry and Arithmetic suffices. But it must be investigated whether a more lasting study and more abundant perception contributes toward easily discerning the **Idea of the Good** <note>The "Idea of the Good" is the highest point of Plato's philosophy, the source of all truth and knowledge</note>. All things contribute toward this which turn the soul to that place where the most blessed essence is, which must be thoroughly known by it. Rightly. Therefore if the study of Geometry compels one to look at essence, it is fitting; but if it compels one to look at "becoming," it is not fitting. So we say. Surely those who have tasted even a little bit of Geometry will not deny this to us, that this science is entirely the opposite of how those who work in it speak of it. In what way? Because they often speak quite ridiculously and as if compelled. For like certain laborers and for the sake of work they speak, while they say both "to square," and "to produce," and "to add," and other things similarly. But this whole doctrine is sought for the sake of knowledge. It is entirely so. Must this also not be conceded to us? What? That what is sought is for the sake of knowing that which always is, not that which both arises at some time and perishes. It must be conceded plainly: for Geometry is the knowledge of that which is always. It will therefore lift the soul toward truth, O noble man, and thus prepare the thought for philosophizing, so that we may turn toward higher things what we now, contrary to what is fitting, cast down to lower things. As much as is possible. As much as possible therefore, it must be commanded that those who inhabit this most distinguished city in no way despise Geometry: for those things which seem in some way to be outside its purpose are not small. What kind? Those which you were mentioning concerning the matter of war. We know moreover that for learning all disciplines more easily, it makes all the difference whether someone has touched upon Geometry or not. Entirely. Let us then propose this doctrine to be learned in the second place by the youths. Or shall we put Astronomy in the third place? What do you think? It should certainly be put there. For to sense the opportunities of months and years is no less fitting for military affairs than for agriculture and navigation. How pleasing you are to me. For you seem to fear lest many think you are introducing useless disciplines. But it is not a light thing, but very difficult to persuade people, that from disciplines of this kind a certain instrument of each soul is purged and revived, which before had been infected and blinded by other studies, when it ought rather to be preserved than ten thousand eyes of the body. For by this alone is truth inspected. Therefore, to those who feel this same way, you will seem to speak wonderfully well. But those who have never thought of it will deservedly think you say nothing. For they see no other utility worthy of esteem from them. Here then you see with which of the two you will especially dispute. Or perhaps with neither, but you speak the words especially for your own sake, yet you are not held by any envy if someone should take some utility from these. I choose this rather, namely to dispute by asking and answering primarily for my own sake. Come then, I say, go back: for just now we did not rightly take what follows Geometry. Why? Because after the plane, we immediately took that solid which is moved in a circle before we apprehended the solid itself by itself. It is fitting, however, immediately after the second increase to take the third <note>This refers to moving from 1D (points) to 2D (planes/Geometry) to 3D (solids/Stereometry) before moving to 4D (solids in motion/Astronomy)</note>: and this is about the increase of cubes, and that which partakes of depth. It is certainly so. But these things, O Socrates, do not yet seem to have been discovered. Of this there are two causes: because namely these are honored in no city; and since they are difficult to find, they are not ardently sought; and those who search into them stand in need of a leader, without whom they would by no means find them. Whom it is first...

--- Page 440 ---
# 424 Book Thirty-One.

...difficult to find: then even if he were found, as matters now stand, those who investigate these things, being puffed up with pride, would by no means obey. But if the whole city should preside over this work, leading it honorifically, these would indeed obey, and these things, being discussed assiduously and with the greatest contention, would be clearer. For even now, although both <margin>* Ficinus seems to have read **poikilmata** <note>Ficino, the translator, notes a variant in the Greek text referring to "decorations" or "ornaments" (poikilmata) rather than "contaminations"</note></margin> the common people despise and contaminate these things, and those who investigate them are ignorant of the reason why they are useful, yet they prevail by the force of a certain grace. Nor is it a wonder if these things have appeared so. Indeed, what is pleasing is the chief thing. But explain to me more openly what you were just saying. The study which turns around the plane you called Geometry. I did indeed. After Geometry you immediately placed Astronomy. But a little after you retreated your step. Indeed, the more I hurry, the later I arrive. For since that faculty which deals with the increase in depth should have followed, because the investigation of it is held to be ridiculous, I passed over it and immediately touched upon Astronomy after Geometry, which consists in the agitation of depth itself. You speak well. Therefore let us place Astronomy in the fourth place, as if that faculty which had just been passed over were present, if only it were undertaken in the city. So it is fitting. And that praise of Astronomy, O Socrates, in which you interrupted me, as if I were extolling it importunely, I now pursue because you agree with me. For I think it is clear to everyone that this directs the eyes of the soul to higher things, and leads it from here to that place. Perhaps this is clear to everyone except me. Since to me indeed it does not seem so. But in what way? As they now treat it, those who join it to philosophy, they seem to me to cast the eyes of the soul toward lower things. By what reason do you say that? You seem to me to define the intelligence of higher things within yourself not ungenerously. For it is established that if someone looking up at ceilings painted with various colors should perceive anything, you think he does not look with his eyes, but understands. And perhaps you feel rightly, and I foolishly. I think indeed no other discipline excites the soul to the inspection of higher things, except that which turns around essence and that which cannot be seen. But if someone, gaping upward or turned downward, strives to perceive something sensible, I assert that he by no means learns. For I deny that he attains knowledge, and I judge his soul to be looking not upward but downward, even if he perceived something while lying on his back on the shore of the earth or the level of the sea. You have corrected me not without cause. But what is the reason for learning Astronomy besides that which those people follow, if the knowledge of it is to be profitable to us for those things we speak of? This indeed. It must be estimated that these varieties which are in the heaven, since they are in a visible place, if they are compared with other things of that kind, are arranged most excellently and purely: but regarding true things, they fall far short. I mean the true varieties and motions, with which the very velocity which truly is, and the very slowness which truly is in true number, and in all true figures, are both carried in turn, and carry the things that are within. All of which things indeed can be apprehended by reason and thought, but by sight not at all: do you think so? Exactly so. Must we not therefore use the celestial variety like a certain example for the contemplation of higher things? Just as if someone should see figures composed and elaborated excellently by Daedalus <note>The mythical master craftsman and inventor</note>, or some other artist or painter. Indeed, if he were one who sees them and is skilled in Geometry, he would praise the craftsmanship itself, yet he would judge it ridiculous if anyone should consider such things more attentively, as if he were going to find in them the truth of equals, or doubles, or of some other proportion. Why should it not seem absurd? We ought to think that the true Astronomer will do the same when he looks at the motions of the stars: thinking, namely, that as far as is possible in works of this kind, both the heaven itself and the things that are in it were fabricated most beautifully by the creator of the heaven himself: yet he will think it absurd if anyone thinks that the comparison of the night to the day, and of these to the month, and of the month to the year, and of the other stars to one another and to these, always happens similarly, and never in any way changes their tenor, since they both have a body and are seen, and that he should seek the truth in these with all study. To me certainly, listening to you at present, the same thing seems so. Therefore we shall use propositions as in Geometry, so also in Astronomy itself: and we shall dismiss the things that are in the heaven, if we are to perceive Astronomy in such a way that what exists in us as a nature partaking of wisdom may be made useful from useless. How much more of labors you impose on the astronomer than is spent by the common people today! But I think we ought to command other things in the same way, if any utility is to come from us as builders of laws. But what will you now mention from the fitting disciplines? I have none at present to mention, he said. And yet not only one, I said, but more species of motion does it offer us. Everyone indeed who is wise will be able to bring them forth. But those which occur to me are two. What kind? One indeed similar to Astronomy and of equal power. What kind, I say? Just as the eyes are for Astronomy, so the ears seem to be fabricated for harmonic motion. Whence also the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that the universe was ordered according to mathematical and musical principles</note> think these are sister sciences, and we, O Glaucon, agree. Or what shall we do, I say? Exactly so, he said. Is it not because this is a great work that we shall ask them how they speak of these things, and whether there is anything else besides these, but in all these things we shall preserve our own rule? What is that? Lest they ever take pains to teach our pupils anything less than perfect from these things, which does not always tend toward where all things ought to proceed, as we just now related concerning Astronomy. Or are you ignorant that they do something of the same kind regarding harmony? For while they measure and compare the concords and tones which are perceived by the ears, they waste their time in vain labor just like the Astronomers. By the gods, those people very ridiculously frequent and redouble the sounds more often, and move their ears closer, as if to hunt the sound itself from a closer place. And some of them say they still hear some sound in the middle, and that this is the smallest interval by which one ought to measure: but others doubt, as if a similar sound were now heard. And both prefer the ears to the mind. But you, I say, do you call those musicians useful who both twist and vex the strings, and extend them violently with pegs (now by tightening, now by loosening)? But lest the similarity be carried further into the striking which is done with the plectrum <note>A small tool used to pluck the strings of an instrument like a lyre</note>, and that boasting and obstinacy of the strings be accused, I will put an end to this image? I say that not these, but those rather, are to be asked to speak about harmony. For they do the same thing as those who are engaged in Astronomy. Namely, they pursue those numbers which are in the concords pertaining to the ears. But from there they do not pass over to investigating which numbers are consonant, which are not, and for what cause both...

This translation covers the provided OCR text of Marsilio Ficino’s Latin translation and commentary on Plato’s *Republic* (specifically the end of Book VII and the beginning of Book VIII).

### General Notes on the Text and Translation:
*   **Source:** Marsilio Ficino, *Opera Omnia* (Translation of Plato’s *Republic*).
*   **Proper Nouns:** Socrates, Glauco, Iuppiter (Jove), Homerus, Hesiodus, Adimantus, Polemarchus, etc., are preserved.
*   **Abbreviations:** The text uses standard Renaissance conventions: `q;` for *-que* (and), tildes for omitted ‘m’ or ‘n’ (e.g., `quã` for *quam*), and `vtpote` or `nõ` for *non*. These have been expanded for the English translation.
*   **Technical Terms:** "Dialectic" refers to the highest form of philosophical reasoning. The "Platonic Number" passage (p. 429) is a notoriously difficult mathematical allegory regarding the decline of states.

[[page number: 425]]

# Dialogue VII. on the Republic. Or, on Justice.

...are such. You relate a distinguished thing. Add also that it is useful for the investigation of the good and beautiful itself, which, if sought otherwise, would be altogether useless. This is indeed probable. I consider, moreover, that the treatment of all the aforementioned things, if it touches upon their mutual communion and kinship, and investigates in what way they cohere with one another, will lead toward those things we seek, and men will not labor in these things in vain, but quite usefully; however, uselessly if it is done otherwise. And indeed, I divine so, but what you command is a great thing, O Socrates. What? The beginning, you say, or something else? Or are we ignorant that all these things are the beginning of the law itself, which it is fitting to learn? For the dialecticians do not yet seem to you to be able to discourse on these matters. No, by Jove, except for a very few of all those whom I have ever known. But unless someone, I said, is able both to receive and to give a reason [ratio], he will never know anything of those things which we say must be known. Never at all. 

Is it not now the law, O Glauco, I said, which is shown through the art of discoursing [dialectic], which, since it is intelligible, that power imitates the sight, which we said above, turns itself toward animals, and toward the stars, and finally toward the sun itself? Not otherwise, when someone applies himself to discourse without any senses, he strives by reason alone toward that which is, whatever it may be; if he does not stop until he has perceived by intelligence itself that which is the good, then finally he arrives at the end of the intelligible itself, just as that other ascended to the end of the visible. It happens exactly so. 

Do you not call this progression "dialectic"? What forbids it? And just as that release from chains, and the conversion from shadows to likenesses and light, and the exit from the cave to the light of the sun, and there the inspection of animals and plants, and the intuition of the sun and stars in water because of the weakness of the eyes, turn the brightest thing in bodies toward that which is the most shining in the corporal and visible region: So the study of all the aforementioned arts leads the soul through the shadows, not of likenesses, but rather of those things which truly are: and it makes the soul judge them toward another light as if toward the sun, and has a certain power of exalting that which is most excellent in the soul to the contemplation of that which is best in the order of things. Indeed, I accept it so: although such things seem to me to be such that they can neither easily be admitted nor easily rejected. 

Nevertheless, since they must be heard not only at present, but repeated more often hereafter, with these things established as they have now been handed down, let us now come to the law itself, and let us run through it as we have now completed the prelude. Therefore, tell me, I pray, what is the mode of the power of discourse, and into what species is it distributed, and what are the ways, for these are, as it seems, those which lead there where whoever arrives will finally rest as if at the end of a journey. You will not yet be able to attain it, O friend Glauco. Truly, as far as is in me, no zeal will be lacking to you, by which you may become a master of your wish. You shall no longer look upon an image of that which we are treating, but the true thing itself as it appears to me. Whether, however, it is truly so or not, it is not at all fitting to affirm. But only this must be assured: that such a thing is to be known. Is it not so? Nothing forbids it. Furthermore, only the faculty of discourse will show it to a man learned in those things we have said. Otherwise, it is altogether impossible to be known. This too must be assured.

[[column 2]]

No one, moreover, will oppose us when we say that the faculty of discourse alone attempts, in a certain order, to find what each thing itself is. Since the other arts look either to the opinions and desires of men, or to generations and compositions, or to the cultivation of those things which are generated and composed. But as for the rest which we said are in some way partakers of true things—namely Geometry and its companions—they dream in a certain way about essence itself, but it is impossible for anything to be discerned clearly by them so long as they use suppositions and keep them so fixed and immobile that they cannot give a reason for them. For where the principle is placed as that which is unknown, and the end and means are drawn from the unknown and connected to each other: by what agreement shall we call the assertion collected therefrom "science"? By none. 

But Dialectic alone, having removed all suppositions, proceeds to the principle itself so that it may have it as found, and truly draws the eye of the soul, buried in a barbaric slough [*coeno barbarico*], gradually upward and leads it, using these arts which we have related as certain helpers and ministers. Furthermore, we have often called these "sciences" because of custom. But they need another name, clearer than "opinion," but more obscure than "science." Certainly, we named their notion "Thought" [*Cogitatio*] in the previous parts. Nor is there a controversy about the name among those for whom there is a controversy regarding such great matters as those before us at present. Certainly not. For they only require the expression of internal concepts for the condition of things. 

It pleases us, therefore, as before, to call the first part "Science" [*Scientia*], the second "Thought" [*Cogitatio*], the third "Faith" [*Fides*], and the last "Imagination" [*Imaginationem*] or "Assimilation" [*Assimilationem*]. And both of these together [the first two] are "Intelligence" [*Intelligentia*], and both of those together [the last two] are "Opinion." And Opinion, indeed, is concerned with generation, but Intelligence with essence. What essence is to generation, Intelligence is to Opinion. And what Intelligence is to Opinion, Science is to Faith, and Thought to Imagination. But the comparison of those things in which these are engaged, and the twofold division of each—namely the opinable and the intelligible—let us omit, O Glauco, lest a longer discourse be held about these than about the previous things. Indeed, as far as my mind is able, I wish to follow the rest. 

Do you not call him a "dialectician" who grasps the reason of the essence of anything? But him who does not have this reason, insofar as he can give no reason to himself or another, to that extent will you deny that he has intelligence concerning this? Certainly, it is not to be said otherwise. Concerning the Good also, it must be judged similarly. For whoever cannot define the idea of the good by reason, distinguishing it from all other things, and as if in a battle penetrating through all things, rejecting all other things, arguing and refuting not according to opinion but according to substance, and proceeding through all these with a stable and unshaken reason: you will say that this man, so affected, knows neither the good itself nor any other good; but if perchance he touches upon some likeness, he touches it by opinion rather than by science, and while dreaming he is mocked in sleep, and before he wakes up, descending to the underworld, he is finally occupied by the final slumber. By Jove, I will assure all these things altogether. Furthermore, your children whom you now nourish and instruct by discourse, if you were ever to educate them in reality, you would not, I think, permit them to have power over the greatest things in the city while, like lines [*linearum instar*], they could not give a reason for each thing.

[[page number: 426]]

# Thirty-First Book [of the Republic].

...give a reason for each thing. Certainly not. Therefore, you will pass a law by which they are commanded to embrace that discipline especially, from which they may be most fit for questioning and answering as befits science. I shall enjoin that together with you. Does it then seem to you that dialectic is placed as a summit, as it were, over all doctrines, and that no doctrine is found further or higher, but that here now is the end of all doctrines? It seems so to me. It remains, therefore, next to disclose to whom these disciplines must be distributed, and how. Clearly. Do you remember in that first selection what kind of leaders we chose? Why should I not remember? 

Regarding other things, consider that those natures are to be chosen. For it is fitting to choose the most grave and the strongest men, and as far as possible the most handsome; nor are noble and terrible men alone to be sought, but those who in addition have those gifts of nature which this discipline requires. Which? Sharpness, I say, and ease of intellect must be present for the perception of doctrines. For difficulty of disciplines deters the soul more than difficulty of bodily exercises. Since that labor is more the soul's own, which belongs to it alone, than that which is common also to the body. You speak the truth. A man must also be sought who is strong in memory, most upright, and most enduring. For whom else do you think will willingly undergo the labors of the body and pursue such an arduous study of doctrine and meditation until the end? No one at all, unless he is endowed with the best nature. From that error, as I was saying above, infamy has arisen against philosophy, because they do not touch it with dignity. For it is to be handled not by bastards, but by legitimate [sons]. 

In what way? In the first place, whoever is to be initiated into the sacred rites of philosophy must not be a cripple in undertaking labors, so that he approaches some but refuses others. But this happens whenever someone given to gymnasiums and hunting and other bodily exercises flees the study of disciplines, and is neither delighted by hearing nor by inquiring, but hates all this care. Furthermore, he is also a cripple who, delighted by exercises of the mind, despises others. You tell the truth. Shall we not also similarly place that soul as maimed regarding truth, which hates a voluntary lie and bears it ill in itself, and is indignant at others lying, but easily tolerates an involuntary lie; and if it is caught being ignorant of something, it does not bear it heavily, but willingly wallows in the filth of ignorance like a pig? Altogether indeed. 

Furthermore, concerning temperance and fortitude and magnificence, and the other parts of virtue, it must be no less observed who is legitimate and who is a bastard. For when these things are considered less, both private men and the city use the maimed and bastards for whatever of these things happens, private men using them as friends, and the Republic as leaders. It happens exactly so. All these things must be guarded against by us. For if we lead and educate men most upright in the habit of body and mind to such great doctrine and exercise, justice itself will not be angry with us, and we shall preserve the city and the Republic. But if we lead men otherwise affected to these things, we shall do all the contrary, and we shall disgrace philosophy much more. That would indeed be shameful. 

In a wondrous way. However, nothing seems to me to have happened in the present so worthy. What is that? It escaped me, surely, that we were joking, wherefore I acted more sharply than was fitting. For while speaking...

[[column 2]]

...turning toward philosophy itself, I saw her unworthily affected by disgrace. I seem to have suffered this heavily, and as if indignant at those who are in fault, to have said these things more severely. Not by Jove, as it seems to me listening. Yet to me speaking, it appears so. But let this not escape us: that in the prior election we chose old men, but in this it will not be permitted at all. Nor is Solon to be believed when he says that an aging man can learn very many things daily, who can do that less than he can run. For many and the greatest labors befit the young. It is necessary. 

Therefore, those things which pertain to arithmetic and Geometry, and all that doctrine which ought to precede dialectic, must be handed over to boys, and that mode of teaching must be adopted for them in which they seem least forced to learn. Why so? Because it is not fitting for a free man to learn any discipline with servitude. Indeed, the immense labors of the body undertaken by force make the body no worse. But no violent discipline of the soul is stable. You speak the truth. Therefore, O best of men, nourish the boys in disciplines not as if forced, but as if playing, so that you may also better recognize for what each is fit by nature. What you say is consistent. 

Do you not remember what was said by us in the previous parts, that boys must be led into camps on horses for the sake of watching, and if it can be attempted safely, they must be moved closer, so that like whelps they may begin to taste blood? I remember indeed. Whoever, therefore, appears more prompt and sharper for these labors, disciplines, and dangers, must be selected into a certain number. At what age? When they are released from necessary businesses and exercises. In this clear time, whether it be two or three years, they can do nothing else. For labor and sleep are adverse to disciplines. And at the same time, this examination of others will not be the least, as to how each will appear in the gymnasiums themselves. Why not? 

After that time, whoever from twenty years of age shall have been chosen as more excellent than the others, let them be affected by greater honors than the others: and those disciplines which were shown to them dispersedly in boyhood, let them be offered to them again as one, for the sake of beholding the kinship of the disciplines among themselves, and the nature of that which truly is. This knowledge alone, to whomever it is handed, remains stable. And indeed, by this experience it is known most who is best instituted by nature for dialectic, and who is not. For whoever is perspicacious in discerning this is a dialectician; but whoever is dull is not at all. I grasp it indeed. 

Having noticed these things, therefore, it will be necessary to establish those who are found to be especially such in these matters—stable in disciplines, constant in war, persevering in other legitimate duties—after they have completed their thirtieth year, as pre-selected from the elect into greater honors, and to examine them diligently by the faculty of discourse itself, as to which of them can transcend to that which truly exists with truth, without the ministry of the eyes and other senses. In which, O friend, there is need of the greatest caution. Why? he says. Do you not notice, I said, how much evil now happens concerning the skill of discourse? Of what kind? they are altogether abundant in iniquity, I say. Very much so, he says. Do you think they suffer something strange, and do you not forgive them? By what reason especially? If some supposititious boy is nourished in many delights by a noble family among very many flatterers, but when grown up he perceives that he was not born from those whom he considers parents, yet finds his true parents nowhere: can you...

---

[[page number: 427]]

# Dialogue VII on the Republic. Or, on Justice.

...can you divine what his state of mind will be toward the flatterers, and toward those who substituted him, both at the time when he suspected nothing of the substitution, and after he recognized the fact itself? Or do you wish to hear my presage? I wish it indeed. I divine, therefore, that while he is entirely ignorant of the substitution, he will honor those whom he thinks are his parents and kinsmen more than the flatterers; and he will less neglect them if they are in need, and he will be slower to inflict injury upon them or to speak an insult, and he will be more obedient to them in grave matters than to the flatterers. It is indeed likely. 

But if he perceives it, he will certainly honor and care for these [the foster parents] less, but he will cultivate the flatterers more than before, obey them more readily, institute his life according to their example, and converse with them openly and freely. But of those whom he had thought were his parents and kinsmen, unless he is of a naturally good disposition, he will care nothing at all. All would happen exactly as you relate. But what does this similitude have to do with those who follow disputations? You shall hear presently. There are for us from boyhood opinions about honest and just duties, under which, as if under parents, we have been educated: we obey these, we honor these above others. There are plainly. 

Pleasures also offer themselves to us, which allure us to the contrary: and while they flatter our souls, they twist us toward those things. Yet they are not turned by these, who are even a little more moderate than the others, but they cultivate those paternal [opinions] and obey them. So it happens. If the power of dialectic, having attacked someone so affected, asks what is honest, and the reason refutes his answer which he had perceived from the legislator, and by frequent and various refutations leads him out so that he opines that thing to be no more honest than base, and argues similarly about the just and the good, and about the rest which he held before in the highest honor: do you think he will thereafter pursue them with the same honor and observance? It is necessary, he says, neither to honor nor to obey in that way. 

When, therefore, one considers these things no longer domestic as before, nor honors them, nor finds true ones, he falls into a flattering life rather than another, as is consistent. It is indeed likely. From being just, therefore, he becomes unjust. It is necessary. Is it not rightly, as I said recently, that the affection of those who prepare themselves for discourse in this way is such that it deserves the greatest pardon? And mercy besides. Therefore, so that this miserable event may be avoided, let those thirty years of age only, very cautiously, taste dialectical argumentations. Exactly so. 

Is this not a prudent caution, that younger men should not touch them? For it is not hidden, I think, that when adolescents first taste the artifice of disputation, they use it immediately as if for a certain play for refuting, and zealously following those who refute others, they themselves also refute others, tearing and mangling them after a fashion. But when they have convicted many, and have been convicted themselves by many, they fall immediately into this, that they have no rare one of their former opinions. And from these, both they and all philosophy have brought back calumny among others. You report true things. 

But a man older in age will more diligently decline from this insanity, and will rather imitate a man discoursing for the sake of investigating the truth, than one who for the sake of joking indulges in craftiness and petty catches. Nay, he himself will carry himself more modestly, and render the study of disputing illustrious instead of infamous. Very skillfully: moreover, all the previous sayings were for the sake of caution: namely, that those who are admitted to the study of disputation should be moderate and grave, and that it should not be communicated to inept men, and as it is now, to everyone whom chance offers. Very much so. 

If anyone gives work diligently and assiduously to disputation, or does nothing else except that he exercises his body in gymnasiums in turn, double the years of the previous [studies] will be sufficient for this perception. Do you say six? or four? You may apply five. Then they are to be led back again into that cave, and forced to assume those leaderships which pertain to war, and whatever leaderships of the young there are, lest they be surpassed by others in the use of things. And in these also they must be examined, whether they remain constant while they are drawn in every direction, or whether they waver. But how many years do you assign to these? Fifteen. 

When, however, they have arrived at the fiftieth year, whoever among them appear whole and excelling in deeds and sciences, are now to be led to the end, and forced to direct the ray of the soul to the things above, and to look up at that which provides light for all: and when they have known the good itself, relying on its example, let them adorn the city, private men, and themselves through all the subsequent life, and each in turn. And they shall indeed be occupied mostly in philosophy: but when they are summoned to the magistracy, let them keep watch in civil businesses and govern individually for the sake of the republic, so that they seem to perform a necessary ministry rather than something good and desirable. And so when they themselves have similarly instructed others, they shall leave them in turn as guardians of the republic, and they themselves shall pass over to the islands of the blessed. 

Monuments and sacred rites shall be dedicated to them publicly as to daemons, if the Pythia confirms it by oracle; if not, at least as to the blessed and divine. You seem, O Socrates, to have figured wonderful leaders like a sculptor. What I have said of men is to be understood also of women. Nor should you think, O Glauco, that I have spoken more of men than of women, specifically those who are by nature fit for these duties. It holds itself rightly, if indeed they shall communicate equally in all things with men, as we related. 

Do you not grant that we have spoken of all things concerning the republic not as if we fashioned them by desire, but according to truth—difficult indeed to do, but possible nevertheless, only by that reason which we said? Namely, when men who are truly philosophers, either one or more, having obtained power in the city, shall despise the present honors and judge them illiberal and of no value: but they shall value most that which is right, and the honors which proceed from it, and they shall value most of all and as most necessary that which is just: and ministering to this and increasing it, they shall rightly dispose their city. 

In what way? All who have completed ten years in the city, they shall send out into the fields: but receiving their children, far from these customs which the parents use today, they shall educate them in their own customs and laws, such as we have related. And so most quickly and easily that city and republic will arise which we said above, if it ever exists, will be blessed, and will greatly benefit the race of men in which it was founded. Most greatly indeed. And you seem to have found, O Socrates, how such a city might be established, if it ever be established. 

Is it not then abundantly said by us now, both about this city and about the man very similar to it? For it is clear what kind of person we shall say his likeness ought to be. It is clearly clear, and what you seek seems to me now to have its end.

N iiij [Signature mark]
