[[page number: 428]]

# Thirty-First Book.

# EIGHTH DIALOGUE ON THE REPUBLIC OR, ON JUSTICE.

### ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.

**SOCRATES** has completed the perfect form of the republic in seven dialogues, consecrated to the septenary number of Pallas. He calls it both a royal and an aristocracy [government of the best]. Aristocracy indeed, because in it many men distinguished by virtue perform public duties and constitute the Senate. Royal indeed, because there is one will of all for the public good, one mind as if queen, and if someone among them is singular in probity, he is singularly honored. Nor yet is so much attributed to him that without the Senate—that is, the number of all the approved—he can change public affairs. It remained, after the best and blessed form of the republic, to bring forward the inferior ones. He counts four of these. 

The first indeed he wishes to be that into which the best soon degenerates, which he names ambitious [Timocracy]. The second indeed the power of the few [Oligarchy], born from the ambitious. The third the popular [Democracy], proceeding from this. The fourth and last the tyranny, springing up chiefly from the popular. But because the forms of republics proceed from the forms of souls, he thereafter describes with a certain wondrous art five affections and habits of souls, and just as many of cities and similar ones similarly named, and concludes that the aristocratic and royal mind is the best and most blessed, and similarly the city similar to it. But the Tyrannical is the worst and most miserable. Similarly the cities oppressed by tyrants are the worst and most miserable. But the middle ones and middle governments he concludes to be in a certain middle way. 

From all these, it appears how pernicious injustice is both in the city and in the soul, and how salutary justice is in both. Everywhere, however, he explains with wonderful diligence the permutations both of souls and of cities from other forms into others. Especially, however, the change of the blessed republic—and as I might say, the golden one—into the ambitious or silver or iron one, he draws from a higher beginning, and feigns that the Muses are pouring forth this as if an oracle, or rather confounding it. 

Truly, if the blessed republic cannot fall into a worse one by its own defect, and yet it sometimes falls, it falls by some common defect and cause. In which matter, one may laugh at the Aristotelian calumnies. For Aristotle ought not, in the fifth book of the *Politics*, to have demanded from his Plato—nay, ever his own—the proper cause of changing the blessed republic, since there is no proper one, but he ought to have been content with the common one. For just as a man both very strong and very temperate, so also such a city labors from a disease not so much from a proper as from a common cause—that is, by a certain fatal order, perpetually revolving through the celestial circuits which are below the moon, so that those things which were composed by certain configurations of the spheres and courses of times, are sometimes dissolved. 

But because the assignment of such a cause far exceeds the limits of the present civil faculty, Socrates therefore uses the prophecy of the Muses, and indeed he uses it so that for us also to interpret these things there is need of the prophecy of Apollo. Nor undeservedly did Cicero, where he wishes briefly to express that a matter is most obscure, say: "It is more obscure than the number of Plato." Nor do I wonder that Theon of Smyrna, a mathematician among the first of the Platonic professors, astutely passed over such a mystery as if inexplicable. Which indeed Iamblichus the Chalcidian, while he wished to explain it, seems to have entangled. What if there is more difficulty than weight in such words? Indeed, since he himself feigns that the Muses are trifling with a certain tragic tumidity, terrifying the childish and simple mind and bringing about stupor. Finally, whatever that may be, you will more opportunely receive our exposition from the commentaries on the *Timaeus*. 

Otherwise, consider these mortal precepts: It is impossible for riches to be honored in a city together with virtue. Likewise, to hand over the rudders of the republic to those of longer standing is just as if a ship were handed over to be governed not by one skilled in navigating, but by one more wealthy. For both this and that will be endangered. Again, the safest guardian against all vices is science. Furthermore, the extreme of one contrary is the beginning of the other; thus, the extreme license of liberty is the beginning of extreme servitude. Just as in any quality, every excess of things and times is accustomed to be turned immediately into its contrary. The same in his letters, or approving a moderate liberty before all.

[[column 2]]

**LET IT BE**, I said, it was indeed agreed between us, O Glauco, that in a city best instituted, women and children ought to be common. Every education also common. Similarly all duties, both of war and of peace, common. But that their kings ought to be men most excellent in the study of philosophy and the military art. It was clearly agreed. Nay, we also granted this, that when such leaders have now been established, going on an expedition, they shall assign habitations for the soldiers such as we predicted—namely, common to all—in which nothing is the property of anyone. Not only concerning habitation, but also concerning furniture and possessions, if you remember what kind they ought to be, we agreed. 

I remember indeed, he says, that we judged that none of those things which others now possess should be possessed by anyone, but that like athletes of war and guardians, they ought to receive sustenance from others as an annual wage for their guardianship, and to protect both themselves and the city. Rightly, I say. But after we have completed these things, let us now repeat from where we digressed to here, so that we may proceed again through the same things. That is not at all difficult; for almost just as now, as if you had done enough concerning the city, you added that you would call such a city "good," such as you had described, and a good man whoever was very similar to it, since you could still, as it appeared, refer to a better city and man. 

You said, moreover, if this is a right republic, that the others err. But of the other republics, as I remember, there are four species, about which it was necessary to speak, and to inspect their defects, and to declare men similar to them: so that intuiting all of them, and declaring who is the best man and who is the worst, we might consider whether the best man is the most happy, and the worst the most miserable, or whether the matter holds itself otherwise. When, however, I asked you which four republics you meant, then surely Polemarchus and Adimantus interrupted my speech: from where you, taking up the discourse, finally arrived here. 

You remembered quite rightly. Therefore, again as a wrestler, provide the same handle, and with me asking the same thing, try now to say those things which you were now about to declare. If indeed I can. Indeed, I greatly desire to hear which four republics you spoke of above. You shall hear that without difficulty. For they are those I speak of, those which also have names: namely that which is praised by many, the Cretan and Laconian [Timocracy]. The second indeed and praised in the second place, that which is named the power of the few [Oligarchy], a republic full of many evils. Likewise, that which differs most from this and follows it, the popular government [Democracy]. Furthermore, the noble tyranny, differing from all these, the fourth and extreme disease of the city. Do you have another form of republic, which is situated in some clear and distinct reason? For also certain lesser leaderships, and venal kingdoms, and such civil powers obtain a certain middle way between these. Of which not fewer are found among the Barbarians than among the Greeks. Many certainly, and absurd ones are related. 

There are also just as many species and characters of men. Or do you perhaps think that republics are made from an oak, or rather from the characters of the citizens, which, wherever they have flowed, drag the rest with them? From the characters, without doubt. Wherefore, if the species of governments are five, the affections and habits of private souls will also be five. Nothing hinders it. Certainly, we saw the man similar to the government of the best [Aristocracy], whom we rightly asserted to be good and just.

---

[[page number: 429]]

# Dialogue VIII. on the Republic. Or, on Justice.

...we saw him. Next, it is fitting to relate the worse ones: the contentious and ambitious man according to the Lacedaemonian institution of the republic; furthermore, the one greedy for the empire of the few [Oligarchy], and the popular man [Democracy], and the tyrannical: so that discerning the most unjust, we may compare him with the most just, and perfectly recognize how the supreme and pure justice holds itself to the supreme and pure injustice, as pertains to the beatitude or misery of the just or unjust man: so that, persuaded by those present reasons, we may follow justice. Exactly so must it be done. 

Shall we not, as we began before, observe characters in republics rather than in private persons, because they are more open there: so first must be considered the ambitious republic, for which I have no name except ambitious power and leadership: after it, we shall consider such a man: then the power of the few, and such a man: afterwards the government of the multitude, and the popular man: finally, considering the city oppressed by tyranny, and recognizing thence the tyrannical mind, we shall try to judge sufficiently those things which we proposed? Rightly in this way shall the inspection and judgment proceed. 

Come then, let us try to explain in what way the ambitious empire [Timocracy] is born from the government of the best [Aristocracy]. Is this not simply true, that every republic is changed from that which dominates, when sedition arises in it: but while it agrees with itself, even if it is very small, it is impossible to be changed? It is so. But in what way, O Glauco, shall this city of ours be moved from its state? Shall the leaders and defenders disagree with one another and among themselves? Or do you wish that, imitating Homer, we ask the Muses to explain to us by what reason sedition first falls in? And let us say that they, in the rite of tragedians, joking and trifling with us as if children, speak so that while they trifle, they act seriously, and speak something great? 

In what way? Almost so. It is difficult indeed for a city so constituted to be moved from its state. But since everything which is generated is subject to corruption, such a constitution also will not be able to remain forever, but will be dissolved. But this dissolution is this: not only concerning plants, but also terrestrial animals, fertility and sterility of soul and bodies happen, when the revolutions have joined the circuits of the circles for each: for those which are of brief age, shorter circuits, but for the contrary ones, contrary. 

But those whom you have educated for the government of the city, although they were wise, will none the more attain the fertile or sterile generation of your race by reason together with sense, but the opportunity of generating will escape them, and often when it is not opportune, they will give work to begetting children. But that which is generated divinely is a circuit which a perfect number contains. But for human generation it is indeed that in which first the super-proportionate and super-proportioned augmentations, receiving three distances and four terms, of the similar and dissimilar, and of the increasing and decreasing, made all things corresponding and comparable to one another, of which the sesquiterian root joined to the quinary provides two harmonies thrice increased. One indeed equal equally, a hundred a hundred times. The other indeed equal in length, but more oblong, a hundred of the numbers from the comparable diameters of the quinary, needing one from each, but two of those which cannot be spoken, a hundred indeed of the cubes of the trinity itself. 

But this entire geometric number, having such authority, has power over the better and worse generation. Which if the guardians of your city should be ignorant of, and should not join the brides in the opportune time, children not at all ingenious or happy will be born from there. And although the elders themselves establish those as leaders who were more excellent among them: nevertheless, because they will be unworthy of the succession of the parents, in the magistracies themselves they will neglect the subjects, and they will not have care for music as is fitting, nor for gymnastics, whence the youths will be in their minds alien to music. From these, moreover, leaders will be established more negligent than is fitting for examining those races which are related in Hesiod and by us—namely, the golden race, the silver, the bronze, and the iron. 

But when iron is mixed with silver, and bronze with gold, dissimilarity and discordant inequality will arise. Which wherever they are born, always produce war and enmities. But a race of such men, wherever it is present, is always agitated by seditions. We shall say they respond quite rightly. For it is necessary, since they are Muses. But what will the Muses say thereafter? After sedition has arisen, both races will be carried away—the iron indeed and bronze toward gain, and the possession of fields and houses, and a copy of gold and silver. But that which is in them golden and silver, as if not of a poor but of an opulent nature, toward virtue and the prior state. But fighting with one another and dragging toward contraries, they will finally come together in the middle, so that the fields and houses being divided, they are also possessed privately: but those who were before saved by them as free men, friends, and nourishers, are reduced into servitude, and as subjects and slaves, they are compelled to bear the care of war and their guardianship. 

Hence also it certainly seems to me this change happens. This government indeed will be in the middle between the aristocracy and the power of the few. It will certainly be. It will be changed so. But when it has been permuted into that, what mode of government will it especially preserve? Or is it clear that it will partly imitate the prior republic, partly the power of the few, as that which is located in the middle, and partly also obtain something of its own? Exactly so. And it will imitate the prior one in that the leaders will be honored, and the soldiers will abstain from agriculture, mechanical arts, and other gains; and they have common banquets, and gymnastics, games, and contests of war will be frequented. 

Truly. But it will have certain things of its own, such as that it will fear to admit wise men to leadership, because it possesses men not simple, nor most upright, but mixed: and it will take up for governing rather more spirited and simpler men, who seem born for war rather than for peace? Will it also value most the deceits and machinations of war, and always fight? Certainly. But they will be greedy for money, just as those who lead their life in the power of the few, and overwhelmed by darkness they will more rustically honor gold and silver, as those who have treasuries and their own storehouses in which to hide these, and also the enclosures of houses like their own nests, in which they will expend much with women and others for their pleasure. You speak the truth. Will they not also be more parsimonious in their own affairs than is fitting? Since they value money, and do not acquire it openly: but in others' affairs more profuse because of pleasure, and they will secretly indulge in pleasures, not otherwise fleeing the law everywhere than boys the sight of a father, educated not by persuasion but by force, from the fact that they neglected true music which is joined with discourse and philosophy, and...

---

[[page number: 430]]

# Thirty-First Book.

...neglected it, and honored gymnastics much more and before music? You refer to a republic mixed from bad and good. It is mixed indeed: but before the others in it, on account of the empire of spiritedness and anger, the studies of contention and ambition prevail. Vehemently. 

Will not this republic so coalesce, and be such, as much as it is permitted to figure the republic in discourse not with the greatest diligence, because it suffices from the description itself to discern the most just and the most unjust man, and it would be an inextricable work if someone were to attempt to relate all republics and all characters with nothing at all omitted. Rightly. Who then is the man according to this republic? How is he made? What is he like? I think indeed, says Adimantus, he is similar to Glauco here, for the sake of contention. 

Perhaps, I said, in this he is similar. But in these he seems not at all similar in nature. In what? He must surely be more contumacious, and somewhat more alien to music, yet greedy for music: and studious of hearing indeed, but not at all rhetorical. And toward slaves he will be rustic, such a man, not despising slaves as a man moderately learned does: but toward free men he will be mild: toward leaders indeed especially obedient, but also a hearer of leadership and honors, thinking it necessary to excel and preside over others not by the art of speaking or any other similar faculty, but by warlike and civil things, since he is quite studious of gymnastics and hunting. It is certainly, he says, the character of that republic. 

Will not such a one despise money in youth? But as he grows older, he will love money more, from the fact that he is a partaker of an avaricious nature, nor is he whole toward virtue, because he lacks the best guardian? Which? says Adimantus. Reason and operation, I say, mixed with music, which alone when it is present, preserves virtue in him over whom it presides through all life. You speak excellently, he says. Such an adolescent is indeed greedy for ambitious empire, similar to such a city. Altogether. 

But he is made such in this way sometimes: namely when some youth is the son of a good father living in a city not well governed, fleeing honors, leaderships, and judgments, and the rest of the care of such businesses, and willingly subjecting himself so that he may avoid labors. In what way is he made? When namely he hears his mother bearing it ill that her husband does not at all perform magistracies, and for that reason she is held in contempt among other women: then indignant as often as she sees the man not at all studying to accumulate money, nor solicitous contending for others either privately or in judgments and publicly: but rather negligent toward all these, and such that he lives with himself for the most part, but does not indeed despise his wife, nor does he cultivate her much. 

From which things the mother often tells the son that the father is idle and remiss in spirit, and other things, whatever women have been accustomed to chatter about such men. Many such things indeed, says Adimantus, and similar ones, women are accustomed to speak ill. Nor is it hidden from you that also servants and domestics, especially those who seem most benevolent, often whisper such things into the ears of boys. And if they see anyone, either owing money to the father, whom he does not at all call into court, or in some other thing committing injury, they tell the boy that when he turns out a man, he should avenge all such things, and be more of a man than the father turned out. 

That same son, having gone out from home, hears and sees many other similar things: namely that men who in the city are busybodies are called fools and little valued: but those dissimilar to these are...

[[column 2]]

...honored and praised. When the adolescent hears and sees these things, and again hears the speeches of his father, and sees his studies close to the studies of the others, he is attracted by both: by the father indeed his rational power is fostered and increased, but by the others the nature of desiring and being angry. Wherefore, since he is born with a not bad disposition, but using the bad custom of others, and drawn by these into the middle, he subjects himself to a certain middle power, contentious and angry, and becomes a man of exalted spirit and greedier for glory. You seem to me to have related the nature of this man sufficiently. We have then the second republic and the second man. We have indeed. 

Do we not after these say that of Aeschylus: "Another man corresponding to another city"? Nay, rather according to that superior supposition, another city congruent to another? Exactly so. But that which follows such a republic is the power of the few [Oligarchy], as I think. What institution of a republic do you especially call the power of the few? That in which magistracies are given to citizens from the estimation of the census, and in which the rich dominate, but for the poor there is no communion of the republic. I understand indeed. Should it not be said in what way the transgression from the ambitious government into this is made? It must certainly be said. 

Or is it even clear to a blind man in what way the transgression is made. In what way? That treasury of each full of gold destroys such a republic. For first indeed they find new expenditures and lead them to laws, which neither they nor their women obey. It is consistent indeed. Then one incited by the example and emulation of the other, many finally turn out such. Likely. Hence, therefore, having fallen away more profusely to accumulating money, as much as they value it more precious, so much they consider virtue cheaper. Does not virtue so differ from riches, as if both were placed in the scales of a balance, and always decline to the contrary part? Exactly so. 

When therefore in the city riches and the rich are honored, virtue and good men are despised. It is clear. And all are inflamed to those studies which are in honor, and they frequent them: but those which are held in no honor are accustomed to lie neglected by everyone. So it is. Thus from being greedy for victory and honor, they finally become greedy for gain and money. And they praise and admire rich men indeed, and exalt them to magistracies, but despise the poor. It happens altogether so. Do they not also establish by law the limits of leadership, while they establish that where there is a greater copy of money, there such a leadership is greater: where less, on the contrary less: and they prohibit anyone from commanding who has not arrived at a certain hundred [census]? 

But these things they perform either by force and arms: or after they have struck fear, they established such a republic. Is it not so? Exactly so. The constitution indeed, so to speak, is this. It is certainly. But what is the mode of the republic? Or what are the defects which we said that republic has? First, see what kind of prescribed limit is in it. If someone in the government of a ship should choose governors from the estimation of the census, but should not at all admit a poor man although more skilled in governing, what do you think would follow from this? That they would lead the ship badly. Is it not by the same pact in any other leadership? So I indeed think. Is it so in all except in the city? Or also in the city besides? Much more indeed, since this is the gravest and greatest government. 

One indeed and so great a defect the power of the few suffers. It appears. What then of this? Is it lighter? Of what kind is that? Because it is necessary that this be not one, but two republics—one indeed of the poor, another of the rich, and...

---

[[page number: 431]]

# Dialogue VIII. on the Republic. Or, on Justice.

...and men living within the same walls always insidiously plotting against one another. Certainly that is not lighter. But neither is this beautiful, to be unable to wage war: because they are compelled, if they use the armed people, to fear them more than the enemies; if they do not use them, to appear in the battle itself truly studious of the power of the few: and they will also refuse to expend money for that use, as avaricious men—this, I say, is it not unseemly? Not certainly. 

Do you not think that that is rightly done which we criticized above, that in such a city the same men are occupied in diverse duties at once, they cultivate the earth, accumulate money, and soldier? By no means rightly. See surely if this first among all these evils suffers this most grave thing. Of what kind is it? That it is permitted to each to alienate all his own; but to another to acquire all those things: and for him who alienated them, to live in the city, while no part of the city exists, neither a money-changer, nor a craftsman, nor a knight, nor an arm-bearer, but called everywhere poor and needy. 

This is certainly the first. This indeed in the cities which are subjected to the empire of the few is least prohibited; for otherwise some would not be more opulent than is fitting, others altogether beggars. You speak rightly. But consider this, whether when such a rich man was spending, he was contributing more to the city for those things which we were saying a little before: or did he seem indeed to be of the number of the leaders, but in truth was neither a leader nor a minister, but a consumer of his own faculties? So indeed it appeared. But he was nothing else than a consumer. Or do we wish to say, just as a drone born in a hive is a disease of the swarm of bees, so also a man born at home in this way is a pest of the republic? Altogether, he says, O Socrates. 

Has not God made all the flying drones without stings? But these terrestrial ones we discern partly without stings, partly armed with dire stings. And from those who do not have stings, they finally become indigent in old age: but those instructed with stings are those who are called malefactors. You speak true things. It is clear therefore in a city where you see beggars, that there also thieves are hidden, and cutpurses, and sacrilegious men, and architects of all these crimes. It is clearly clear. Do you not see that in cities which are governed by the few, needy ones are in them? Almost all, except for the leaders. 

Do we not therefore think that there are many malefactors in it armed with stings themselves, whom the leaders detain by diligence and force? We think so plainly. Shall we not assert that on account of bad education, and defect of discipline, and inequitable disposition of the republic, men turn out such there? We shall assert it. Such will be the city subjected to a few leaders, and it will be entirely pressed by evils, perhaps even more. So it will be. 

Let that republic be now established for us which they call the power of the few, choosing leaders from the estimation of the census: after this, however, let us investigate in what way some man similar to them is made, and after he has been made similar, what he is like. Exactly so. Does he not by this reason especially pass from an ambitious man into one greedy for the empire of the few? By what? When there some adolescent first indeed imitates his father and follows his footsteps: then he sees him, who has struck against the city as if against a rock, suddenly fallen from the summit of dignity, destroying himself and all his own, whether after being a commander and leader, or in the dignity of another greatest magistracy, drawn into judgment by plotters, circumvented by calumniators, oppressed, ejected, spoiled of honors and patrimony. Consistent indeed. 

He, O friend, having intuited and suffered these things, his patrimony lost, because of fear, immediately casts down from the throne of his mind that ambition and audacity, and made humbler on account of poverty, he converts himself to gain, and with a very narrow mind, dryly and parsimoniously living: and vexing himself in conducting business, he gathers money. Do you not then think that such a man locates avarice and greed for lucre in that seat of the mind? And fashions for himself some great king? and adorns him with royal ornaments, crowns, a belt, fibulae, fringes, and a Persian sword? Indeed. 

And here indeed he compels the rational power and the heat of spiritedness, deposited on the ground here and there, to serve this, and permits them to inquire into nothing else, and to consider nothing else, than from where from fewer monies more may be gathered: and to admire and cultivate nothing else than riches and the rich, nor to seek dignity from any other thing than from money, and if anything else confers to it. Certainly no other change is so quick and vehement from an ambitious youth into one greedy for money. 

Is not this man therefore studious of the empire of the few? The change of him indeed from a man is similar to that Republic from which the power of the few stood out. Let us consider surely whether he is similar. Let us consider. First, in that he values money much, he will be similar. Why not? Furthermore, also in that he is more parsimonious and more intent on work, and satisfies only necessary desires, but does not at all indulge in other expenditures, but restrains other appetites as superfluous. Greatly. He lives therefore drier and more squalid, everywhere increasing his family substance with the highest parsimony, intent on a treasure to be coacervated [piled up], which men the vulgar indeed approve. Will not this be such a man, similar to that Republic? 

It seems so to me. Money therefore is especially honored both by every city and by him. For neither has this man, I think, applied his mind to discipline. No, as I opine. For he would not have placed a blind man as his leader. Very best indeed. But notice this. Do we not say that desires similar to the nature of drones are in him on account of defect of discipline, partly beggarly, partly maleficent, detained by force from another diligence? And especially indeed. Do you know where looking, you shall discern their maleficence? Where? At the guardianships of orphans, and if anything such happens to them, by which they obtain the most license for injury. You relate true things. 

Is it not clear that in other commerces such a man, in which he is held honest, since he seems just, by a certain equity of life restrains the other small desires which are in him: not for that reason obeying because it is better, nor softening them by reason, but by necessity and fear trembling about the rest of his substance? Greatly. Indeed, O friend, you will find in many of them, when it behooves them to spend others' things, desires very similar to the drone. Especially. 

He will not therefore lack internal sedition, nor will he be one certain thing, but double, and he will have in himself desires for the most part dominating over desires—the better ones namely over the worse. It is so. Wherefore this man was more modest than many others. True virtue, however, of a consenting and composed mind will flee far from him. It seems so to me. Furthermore, the parsimonious man will be slower for a contest, as often as there is to be a private contention in the city about some honest victory and magnificence, since he is unwilling to spend money for the sake of honor and such contentions, fearing to sustain prodigal lusts and to provoke them to defending and contending. Fighting with few of those things which are around him, in the rite of the aristocracy, for the most part he permits himself to be conquered, and increases his riches. Greatly. Do we yet disagree that the parsimonious and avaricious man is instituted according to the example of that city which is governed by the few? By no means.

---

[[page number: 432]]

# Thirty-First Book.

...restrains whatever [desires] allure to expenditures, not to lucre, which desires are indeed called "not necessary." It is manifest. Does it please you, lest we be in ambiguity, that we first discern which are necessary desires and which are not necessary? It pleases me indeed. Those indeed would be rightly called "necessary" which we cannot remove, and which when they are perceived, help us, for it is necessary for our nature to seek both of these. Is it not so? Greatly. 

Rightly, therefore, we shall call them necessary. Rightly. Shall we not rightly deny those to be necessary which can be removed, if someone is accustomed from tender [years], and which when they are present, bring nothing good, nay for the most part they harm? Quite excellently. Let us take an exemplar of them, so that we may know what each are, and let us inspect them by a certain figure. So it is fitting. The desire of eating indeed, and of food and seasoning up to health and good bodily habit, is necessary. I think so. Certainly the use of food is necessary for a double cause: both because without it life does not suffice, and because it is useful. It is so. But of other seasonings, insofar as it confers to a good bodily habit. Altogether. 

But if the appetite for these or others, being superfluous, confers nothing either to these or to others, then it can also be restrained from tender years, and it stands in the way of both body and mind toward prudence and temperance; it will be rightly named "not necessary." Rightly. Therefore, we shall call these "sumptuous desires," but those "dedicated to gain," because they contribute to acting. Why not? And we shall say the same of venereal and other things. The same. 

Truly, whom we named the "drone" a little before, we were saying that this is he who is full of such pleasures and lusts and is enslaved to non-necessary desires: but him who is dedicated to necessary ones, parsimonious and greedy for the power of the few. Without doubt. Let us say again in what way from one greedy for the power of the few a "popular" man is made. But it seems to me to happen in this way, for the most part. In what way? 

When a youth, as we just said, nourished rudely and too dryly, tastes the honey of the drones, and adheres to burning and vehement animals, which can compare all-formed and various pleasures from everywhere: from here indeed consider that change to arise, by which this man passes from the power of the few which is in him into the popular. It is necessary. Just as the city was changed while external aid was provided to either of the parts, from similar to similar: is not the character of the adolescent changed while again a kindred and similar species of external desires supports one species of those desires which are in him? Exactly indeed. 

But if some help is given to his character studious of the power of the few, whether it be brought by the father or by other domestics, advising and rebuking, then sedition and reluctance and battle arise in him toward himself. Why not? And sometimes, I think, the popular condition yields to the state of the few, and some desires partly perish, partly fall away, some shame having arisen in the youthful mind, whence it is again cultivated. It happens sometimes. Again, besides those desires which fell away, others coalescing kindred ones on account of the ignorance of the paternal education turn out many and vehement. So certainly it is accustomed to happen. 

Furthermore, they drag to themselves familiarities and customs, and while they creep secretly, they grow out into a great number. What forbids it? Finally, they occupy the citadel of the youthful mind, perceiving it to be empty of doctrines and honest duties, and of true reasons besides. Which indeed are the best guardians and saviors of all in the minds of pious men. 

[[column 2]]

...they exist. Greatly. False and proud and petulant reasons and opinions succeed into their place and occupy the same place of such a man. Especially. Does he not again approaching those Lotophagi, manifestly dwell there? And if some aid is sent from friends to the laboring better part of his soul, the proud and petulant reasons, closing the gates of the royal walls in him, neither admit the aid itself nor receive the advice of private elders as ambassadors, but they themselves overcome in battle: and calling shame "fatuity," they expel it basely into exile; but calling temperance "cowardice" and insulting it, they eject it; modesty also in character, and moderation in expenditures, they detest and flee as rusticity and illiberality, and they themselves together with many futile desires grow strong? 

Greatly. When they have driven these out of his mind who occupied and purged it, now initiated with great expenses, after these they lead down petulance, license, prodigality, and impudence, crowned in a great band, extolling and applauding them: while calling petulance "noble education"; license indeed and liberty "prodigality" and "magnificence"; impudence "fortitude." Does not the youth in some way pass from an innately nurtured affection of necessary desires into a dissolute license of non-necessary and futile pleasures? 

That is plainly clear, he says. Thereafter such a one lives, I think, spending money, labors, and exercises for the sake of non-necessary pleasures no more than superfluous ones. But if he is so fortunate that he does not rave beyond measure, but having become older, and with a great crowd of pleasures approaching, he admits some but not all, the rest being excluded in the meantime: and when they have entered, he does not give himself entirely to them, but lives so that he imparts himself equally to each: committing the empire of himself to whichever perchance then fell in, as to a supreme magistrate, until it is filled, and again to another with none neglected, while he nourishes each equally with himself. 

So it happens. This man indeed does not accept true reason, nor does he admit it into the citadel of his guardianship, if someone should say that pleasures are partly of good and honest desires, but partly of bad ones, and the former are to be exercised and honored: but the latter, on the contrary, are to be moderated and restrained. But to all these he nods, and affirms all to be similar, and to be honored equally. Truly whoever is so affected, does that. 

Does he not live so in the days, that he obeys the always occurring and present desires? while namely at times he indulges in drunkenness and modulations, at times he is content with the drinking of water and fasting: sometimes indeed he exercises himself in studies of gymnastics, sometimes he is torpid with a remiss and sluggish mind: sometimes he touches the studies of philosophy, often also he betakes himself to the republic, and steps forth into the middle; whatever chance offered, he will both say and do; and if sometimes he admires soldiers, he is carried to them; if merchants, he arrives at these in turn, nor does he direct his life by any order or necessity, but calling this life "pleasant" and "liberal" and "blessed," he assiduously cultivates it. 

You have skillfully related the life of a popular man having no selection. I think indeed that this man is full of diverse and very many characters, beautiful and varied, just as that city appeared, which many men and many women would judge to live happily, since it contains in itself many examples of republics and characters. So it is surely. Let such a man be for us similar to the popular republic, as one who is deservedly called "popular." Let it be. It remains that we speak of that "noble" republic and "noble" man, about tyranny and the tyrant. Altogether. Come...

...and to give an account. Certainly not. Therefore, you will establish a law by which they are commanded to especially take up that discipline from which they may become most fit for questioning and answering, as befits scientific knowledge. Together with you, I will prescribe that very thing. Does it then seem to you that **dialectic** <note>The art of logical discussion and the highest branch of Platonic philosophy</note> is placed like a pinnacle atop all sciences, and that no other science is found further or more eminent, but that this is now the end of all studies? It seems so to me. It remains, then, to reveal to whom these disciplines are to be distributed, and in what manner. Clearly. Do you remember in that first selection what kind of leaders we chose? How could I not remember? Regarding other things, indeed, consider that those natures are to be chosen: for it befits us to choose the most serious and the strongest men, and as far as possible, the most handsome. Not only are noble and formidable men to be sought, but those who moreover possess those natural gifts which this discipline requires. Which ones? Acumen, I say, and a facility of wit must be present for the perception of teachings. For the difficulty of studies terrifies the soul more than the exercises of the body. Since that labor is more its own, belonging to it alone, rather than that which is common also to the body. You speak the truth. A man must also be sought who is strong in memory, of great integrity, and most enduring. For who else do you think will willingly undergo the labors of the body and pursue such an arduous study of doctrine and meditation even to the end? No one at all, unless he be endowed with the best nature. From that error, as I was saying above, infamy has arisen against philosophy: that men do not touch it according to its dignity. For it is not to be handled by the spurious, but by the legitimate. In what way? First, anyone who is to be initiated into the sacred mysteries of philosophy must not be "lame" <note>Plato uses the metaphor of "lameness" to describe someone who exercises their body but neglects their mind, or vice versa</note> in undertaking labors, such that he approaches some but refuses others. This happens whenever someone, devoted to gymnasiums, hunting, and other bodily exercises, flees from the study of disciplines; he is neither delighted by hearing nor by inquiring, but hates all this care. Furthermore, he is also "lame" who, delighted by the exercises of the mind, despises the others. You tell the truth. Shall we not similarly place that soul as maimed in regard to truth, which hates a voluntary lie and bears it poorly in itself, and is indignant at others lying, but easily tolerates an involuntary lie? And if it is caught being ignorant of something, it does not take it heavily, but willingly wallows in the filth of its own ignorance, like a pig? Entirely so. Furthermore, regarding temperance, fortitude, magnificence, and the other parts of virtue, it must no less be observed who is legitimate and who is spurious. For when these things are less considered, both by private individuals and the city, they ignorantly use the maimed and spurious for whatever of these tasks may happen—private men use them as friends, and the Republic as leaders. It happens exactly so. We must take precaution against all these things. For if we lead and erude men who are most upright in both bodily and mental habits to such great doctrine and exercise, even Justice herself will not be angry with us, and we shall preserve the city and the Republic. But if we lead men otherwise affected to these things, we shall do all the contrary, and we shall bring much more disgrace upon philosophy. That would indeed be shameful. In a marvelous way. But nothing seems to have happened to me at present worthy of laughter. What is that? It escaped me, surely, that we were joking; wherefore I acted more sharply than was decent. For while speaking, having turned toward philosophy herself, I saw her affected by unworthy disgrace. Which I seem to have suffered heavily, and I spoke these things more severely against those who are at fault, as if indignant. Not by Jove <note>original: "per Iouem"</note>, as it seems to me while listening. To me, however, while speaking, it appears so. But let this not escape us: that in the prior selection we chose old men, but in this one it will by no means be permitted. Nor is Solon to be believed when he says that an aging man can learn many things daily, for he can do that less than he can run. For many and very great labors befit the young. It must be so. Therefore, those things which pertain to arithmetic, geometry, and all that doctrine which ought to precede dialectic, must be handed to children, and that mode of teaching must be adopted by which they may seem least compelled to learn. Why is that? Because it does not befit a free man to learn any discipline with slavery. Indeed, great labors of the body undertaken by force make the body no worse. But no violent discipline of the soul is lasting. You speak the truth. Therefore, O best of men, do not nurture children in disciplines as if they were compelled, but as if they were playing, so that you may better recognize for what each is naturally suited. What you say is reasonable. Do you not remember that it was said by us in the previous parts that children are to be led into the camps on horses for the sake of watching, and if it can be tried safely, they should be moved closer, so that like puppies <note>original: "catulorum"</note> they may begin to taste blood? I do remember. Whoever appears more prompt and sharper in these labors, disciplines, and dangers, are to be selected into a certain number. At what age? When they are released from necessary business and exercises. In this time, whether it be two or three years, they can do nothing else. For labor and sleep are adverse to disciplines. And at the same time, this examination of the others seems not the least: namely, how each will appear in the gymnasiums themselves. Why not? After that time, whoever shall have been chosen from the age of twenty as more outstanding than the rest shall be treated with greater honors than the others: and those disciplines which were shown to them dispersedly in childhood shall be offered to them again together, for the sake of contemplating the kinship of the disciplines with one another, and the nature of that which truly is. Only this knowledge, to whomever it is handed, remains stable. And indeed, by this experience it is most known who is best instituted by nature for dialectic, and who is not. Surely, whoever is sharp-sighted for discerning this is a dialectician; but he who is dull, by no means. I understand. These things having been observed, it will be necessary to appoint those who are found to be especially such—stable in disciplines, constant in war, persevering in other legitimate duties—after they have completed their thirtieth year, as pre-selected from the selected ones to be placed in greater honors, and to examine them diligently by the very faculty of disputing, to see which of them can transcend to that which truly exists with truth, without the ministry of the eyes and other senses. In which, O friend, there is need of the greatest caution. Why? he says. Do you not notice, I say, how much evil currently happens concerning the skill of disputing? What sort of thing? he says. They abound in iniquity, I say. Very much so, he says. Do you think they suffer something marvelous, and do you not forgive them? For what reason especially? If some supposititious <note>A child substituted secretly for another, i.e., not the true heir</note> child were nurtured in many delights by a noble family, among very many flatterers: but as an adult he perceives that he was not born from those whom he considers parents, yet finds his true parents nowhere: would...

--- Page 443 ---
Dialogus VII. on the Republic. Or, on Justice. 427

...you be able to prophesy what the affection of his soul would be toward the flatterers, and toward those who substituted him, both at that time when he suspected nothing of the substitution, and after he knew the matter itself? Or do you wish to hear my presage? I wish it indeed. I prophesy, therefore, that as long as he is entirely ignorant of the substitution, he will honor those whom he thinks are his parents and relatives more than the sycophants; and he will be less likely to neglect them if they are ever in need, and slower to bring injury upon them or speak an insult, and will obey them in serious matters more than the flatterers. It is likely. But if he perceives the truth, he will certainly honor these less, and will cultivate the sycophants more than before; he will obey them more readily, he will model his life after their example, and will converse with them openly and freely. Concerning those whom he had thought were parents and relatives, unless he be of an otherwise honest natural disposition, he will care nothing at all. Everything would happen exactly as you relate. But what does this similarity have to do with those who pursue disputations? You shall hear presently. We have had opinions from childhood about honorable and just duties, under which we were educated as if under parents: we obey these, we honor these above others. There are such, clearly. Pleasures also offer themselves to us, which allure us to the contrary: and while they coax our souls, they twist us toward those things. Yet they do not turn those who are even a little more moderate than the rest, but they cultivate those paternal things and obey them. So it happens. If the power of dialectic, having approached someone so affected, asks what is honorable, and as he answers what he had perceived from the legislator, reason refutes him, and by frequent and varied redargutions <note>Logical refutations</note> leads him to the point where he thinks that thing is no more honorable than it is base; and if it argues similarly about the just and the good, and about the rest which he previously held in highest honor, do you think he will pursue them hereafter with equal honor and observance? It is necessary, he says, that he neither honor nor obey them in that way. When, therefore, he no longer thinks those things are "domestic" <note>Familiar or traditional</note> to be honored as before, nor finds true ones, he falls into a life of coaxing rather than into another, as is consistent. That is likely. From a just man, therefore, he will become unjust. It must be so. Is it not deservedly, as I was just saying, that the affection of those who so prepare themselves for disputing is such that it earns much forgiveness? And mercy besides. Therefore, so that this miserable outcome may be avoided, only those thirty years of age should cautiously taste dialectical argumentations. Entirely so. Is this not a prudent caution, namely that younger men should not touch them? For it is not hidden, I think, that when young men first taste the art of disputation, they immediately use it like a kind of play for refuting; and zealously imitating those who confute others, they themselves also refute others, and are continually delighted in distracting and tearing their neighbors apart like puppies <note>original: "catulorum"</note>. In a marvelous way. But when they have convicted many, and have been convicted themselves by many, they quickly come to the point where they hold none of their former opinions as valid. And from these things, both they themselves and all philosophy have brought back a bad reputation among others. You report the truth. But a man older in age will diligently decline this insanity, and will rather imitate a man disputing for the sake of investigating truth than one who, for the sake of joking, occupies himself with shifty tricks and sophistries. Moreover, he will conduct himself more modestly, and will make the study of disputing more illustrious instead of infamous. For the sake of such caution, furthermore, all the previous things were said: namely, that those who are admitted to the study of disputation ought to be moderate and grave, and that it should not be communicated to inept men, and as happens now, to everyone whom chance offers. Most certainly. If someone gives diligent and assiduous work to disputation, and does nothing else except that he occasionally exercises his body in gymnasiums, twice the number of previous years <note>Refers to the two or three years mentioned earlier, thus five years total</note> will be sufficient for him for perception of this kind. Do you say six? or four? You should apply five. Then they are to be led down again into that cave <note>The Allegory of the Cave</note>, and compelled to assume those commands which pertain to war, and whatever commands are for the youth, lest they be surpassed by others in the experience of things. And in these also they must be examined, whether they remain constant while they are pulled in every direction, or whether they falter. But how many years do you assign to these? Fifteen. But when they have reached the fiftieth year, whoever among them appear whole and excellent in deeds and sciences are now to be led to the end, and compelled to direct the ray of their soul toward the higher things, that they may look up at that which provides light to all: and when they have known the Good itself, relying on its example, they may adorn the city, private citizens, and themselves through all the following life, and each in turn. And they should be occupied mostly in philosophy: but when they are called to the magistracy, they should keep watch in civil business, and govern individually for the sake of the republic, so that they seem to perform it not as some good and desirable ministry, but rather as a necessity. And thus when they themselves have similarly instructed others, they will leave them in turn as guardians of the republic, and they themselves will pass over to the Isles of the Blessed. Monuments and sacrifices shall be publicly dedicated to them as to divine beings <note>original: "daemonibus"</note>, if the Pythian oracle confirms it; if not, at least as to the blessed and divine. You seem, O Socrates, like a sculptor to have figured wonderful leaders. What I said of men is to be understood also of women. Do not think, O Glaucon, that I have spoken more of men than of women, namely those who are naturally fit for these duties. It is well. Since they will communicate equally in all things with the men, as we have related. Do you not grant that we have not fashioned all things about the republic as if by desire, but spoke in favor of truth—things difficult to do indeed, but possible, in that way alone which we have said? Namely, when men who are truly philosophers, either one or more, having obtained power in the city, will despise present honors, and will think them illiberal and of no value: but they will make most of that which is right, and the honors which proceed from it, and they will consider justice as the greatest and most necessary thing: and serving this, and increasing it, they will duly dispose their city. In what way? All who have completed ten years in the city, they will send into the fields: but taking up their children, far from these customs which the parents use today, they will educate them in their own customs and laws, which we have described. And thus most quickly and easily that city and republic will arise, which we said above would be blessed if it ever existed, and would greatly help the race of men in which it was founded. Especially indeed. And so that a city of this kind might be established, if it ever be established, O Socrates, you seem to have found the way. Have we not then spoken abundantly, both of this city and of the man most similar to it? For it is clear what kind of man we shall say he ought to be. It is clearly clear, and what you seek seems to me now to have its end.

-> MARSILIO FICINO'S <-
-> ARGUMENT. <-

SOCRATES has now completed the perfect form of the republic in seven dialogues, consecrated to the sevenfold number of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom; the number seven was associated with her because it is "virgin" (not a product or factor of other numbers under ten)</note>. And he calls it both a royal and an aristocratic government. Aristocratic <note>original: "optimatum"</note> indeed, because in it many men distinguished by virtue perform public duties and constitute the Senate. Royal, however, because there is also one will of all toward the public good, one mind as if a queen, and if someone among them is singular in probity, he is singularly honored. Yet not so much is attributed to this one that he can change public affairs without the Senate, that is, the number of all those approved. It remained, after the best and blessed form of the republic, to bring the inferior ones into the midst. These he counts as four. The first indeed he wishes to be that into which the best soon degenerates, which he names **Ambitious** <note>Also known as Timocracy, based on honor and competition</note>. The second, the power of a few <note>Oligarchy</note> born from the ambitious. The third, the **Popular** <note>Democracy</note> proceeding from this. The fourth and last, **Tyranny** sprouting especially from the popular. But because the forms of republics proceed from the forms of souls, he describes with a certain marvelous art five affections and habits of souls, and as many and similarly named ones of cities; and in summary he concludes that the royal mind is the best and most blessed, and the similar city similarly. But the tyrannical is the worst and most miserable. Also, cities oppressed by tyrants are similarly the worst and most miserable. But he concludes that the middle souls and middle governments are in a certain middle state. From all these it appears how pernicious injustice is both in the city and in the soul, and how salutary justice is in both. Everywhere, however, he explains with marvelous diligence the permutations both of souls and of cities from some forms into others. Especially indeed, he draws the change of the blessed republic—and, so to speak, the golden one—into the ambitious or silver or iron one, from a higher beginning, and he feigns the Muses pouring this out as an oracle, or rather confusing it. Certainly, if the blessed republic cannot slide into a worse one by its own defect, and yet it sometimes slides, it slides by some common defect and cause. In which matter, one may laugh at the Aristotelian slanders. For Aristotle ought not, in the fifth book of his *Politics*, to have demanded from his Plato—or rather, never his—a proper cause for changing the blessed republic, since there is no proper cause, but he should have been content with the common one. For just as a man who is both very strong and very temperate, so also a city of this kind suffers from disease not so much from a proper as from a common cause—that is, by a certain fatal order, revolving perpetually through the celestial circuits below the moon—so that those things which are composed by certain configurations of the spheres and courses of times, are dissolved when the time arrives. But because the assignment of a cause of this kind far exceeds the terms of the present civil faculty, therefore Socrates uses the prophecy of the Muses; and indeed he uses it so that we too have need of the prophecy of Apollo to interpret these things. And not undeservedly did Tully <note>Cicero</note>, when he wished to briefly express that a matter was most obscure, say it was "more obscure than the number of Plato" <note>Referring to the "Platonic Number," a notoriously difficult mathematical riddle in Book VIII of the Republic concerning the timing of births and the decay of the State</note>. Nor do I marvel that Theon of Smyrna, a mathematician among the first professors of Platonism, astutely passed over a mystery of this kind as if inexplicable. Which indeed Iamblichus of Chalcis seems to have entangled while he wished to explain it. But what if there is more difficulty in such words than weight? Since he himself feigns the Muses babbling with a certain tragic swelling and terrifying the childish and simple soul, and bringing on stupor. Finally, whatever that may be, you will receive our exposition more opportunely from the commentaries on the *Timaeus*. Moreover, consider these mortal precepts. It is impossible for riches to be honored in a city at the same time as virtue. Likewise, to hand over the rudders of the republic to the wealthier is the same as if a ship were handed to be steered not to the more skilled in navigating, but to the richer. Surely both this and that will be endangered. Again, the safest guardian against all vices is knowledge. Furthermore, the summit of one contrary is the beginning of the other. Thus extreme license of liberty is the beginning of extreme slavery. Just as in any quality, every excess of things and times is accustomed to be turned immediately into the contrary. He says the same in his epistles, approving moderate liberty before all things.

I SAID, it has indeed been agreed among us, O Glaucon, that in a city optimally instituted, women and children ought to be common. All education also common. Similarly all duties, both of war and of peace, common. But their kings ought to be men most outstanding in the study of philosophy and military affairs. It was clearly agreed. Indeed we also granted these things: that when such leaders have now been established, going into an expedition, they will assign habitations to the soldiers such as we have said, common to all, in which nothing is the property of anyone. Not only about the habitation, but also about the furniture and possessions, if you remember what kind they ought to be, we agreed. I remember indeed, he says, that we judged that none of those things which others now possess should be possessed by anyone, but as athletes of war and guardians receiving annual food from others as the wage of their guardianship, they ought to protect both themselves and the city. Well said, I say. But after we have finished these things, let us now repeat from where we digressed to here, so that we may travel again through the same things. That is not at all difficult. For almost as now, as if you had treated the city enough, you added that you called such a city good, as you had described, and the man good whoever was most similar to it, when you could still, as it appeared, report a better city and man. You said besides that if this is the right republic, the others err. But of the remaining republics, as I remember, there are four species, about which it is necessary to speak, and to inspect their defects, and to declare the men similar to them: so that having looked at them all, and declaring who is the best man and who the worst, we may consider whether the best man is the happiest and the worst the most miserable, or whether the matter stands otherwise. But when I asked you which four republics you especially meant, then surely Polemarchus and Adeimantus interrupted my speech: from where you, taking up the discourse, have finally arrived here. You remember quite correctly. Therefore, like a wrestler, offer the same hold again, and as I ask the same thing, try now to say those things which you were now about to declare. If indeed I can. I truly desire to hear which four republics you were speaking of above. You shall hear that without difficulty. For those which I speak of are those which also have names: namely, that which is praised by many, the Cretan and Laconian <note>The Spartan system</note>. The second indeed, and praised in the second place, is that which is named the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>, a republic full of many evils. Likewise that which differs most from this and follows it, the popular government <note>Democracy</note>. Furthermore, the noble **Tyranny**, differing from all these, the fourth and extreme disease of the city. Or do you have another form of republic, which is situated in some clear and distinct ratio? For some minor principalities, and venal kingdoms, and such certain civil powers hold a middle place among these. Of which no fewer are found among the Barbarians than among the Greeks. Many certainly, and absurd ones are mentioned. There are also just as many species and characters of men. Or do you think perhaps that republics are made from an oak or a rock, rather than from the characters of the citizens, which, wherever they have flowed, drag the rest with them? From characters, without doubt. Therefore if there are five species of governments, there will also be five affections of private souls. Nothing prevents it. We have certainly seen the man similar to the aristocratic government, whom we correctly asserted to be good and just.

--- Page 445 ---
Dialogus VIII. on the Republic. Or, on Justice. 429

We have seen him. Next it befits us to relate the worse ones: the contentious and ambitious man according to the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> republic's institution; besides the one greedy for the empire of the few, and the popular man, and the tyrannical man: so that discerning the most unjust, we may compare him with the most just, and perfectly distinguish how the highest and pure justice stands toward the highest and pure injustice, as far as pertains to the happiness or misery of the just or unjust man: so that either obeying Thrasymachus we may pursue injustice, or persuaded by present reasons, justice. Thus it must entirely be done. For just as we began to notice characters in republics before in private persons, because there they are more open: so also now in the first place must the **Ambitious** republic be considered, for which I have no name except "ambitious power" and "principality": after it we shall consider such a man: then the power of the few, and such a man: afterward the government of the multitude, and the popular man: finally, considering the city pressed by tyranny, and knowing from there the tyrannical soul, we shall try to judge sufficiently those things which we proposed. In this way the inspection and judgment will correctly proceed. Come then, let us try to explain in what way the ambitious empire is born from the aristocratic government. Surely this is simply true: that every republic is changed from that which dominates, when sedition arises in it; but while it agrees with itself, even if it be very small, it is impossible for it to be changed. It is so. But in what way, O Glaucon, will this city of ours be moved from its state? Will the leaders and defenders disagree with one another and among themselves? Or do you wish that, imitating Homer, we pray to the Muses to explain to us in what way sedition first falls in? And let us say that they, in the manner of tragic poets, playing and babbling with us as if with children, speak in such a way that while they babble, they act seriously and speak something great? In what way? Almost thus. It is difficult indeed for a city so constituted to be moved from its state. But since everything that is born is subject to corruption, even such a constitution cannot remain forever, but will be dissolved. But this is the solution: not only regarding plants, but also earthly animals, fertility and sterility of soul and bodies happens when the revolutions have joined the circuits of the individual circles: for those which are of short life, shorter circuits; but for the contrary, contrary ones. But those whom you have educated for the government of the city, although they were wise, will no more attain by reason combined with sense either the fruitful or sterile generation of your race, but the opportunity of generating will lie hidden from them, and they will often give work to begetting children when it was not opportune. But there is a circuit for that which is to be divinely generated, which a perfect number contains. But for human birth, it is that in which first the augmentations, overcoming and overcome, accepting three distances and four terms, of the similar and dissimilar, and increasing and decreasing, have made all things corresponding and comparable to one another; of which the sesquitertian root <note>A mathematical ratio of 4:3</note> joined to the fivefold provides two harmonies when tripled. One indeed equal by equal, a hundred a hundred times. But the other of equal length, but more oblong, a hundred indeed of numbers from comparable diameters of the fivefold, needing one from each, but two which cannot be said in turn, a hundred indeed of cubes of the trinity itself. But this whole geometric number, having such authority, has power toward better and worse generation. Which if the guardians of your city shall be ignorant of, and shall not join spouses to spouses in the opportune time, by no means ingenious or happy children will be born from there. And although the elders themselves may appoint those as leaders who are more outstanding among them: yet because they will be unworthy of the succession of parents, they will neglect the subjects in the magistracies themselves, and will neither have care of music as befits, nor of gymnastics, whence the young will be too alien from music. But from these, leaders will be appointed more negligent than is fitting for examining those races which are related in Hesiod and among us—namely the golden race, the silver, <margin>Book 7. page 2.</margin> and the bronze and iron. But when iron is mixed with silver, and bronze with gold, dissimilarity and discordant inequality will arise. Which wherever they are born, always give birth to war and enmities. But a race of men of this kind, wherever it is present, is always agitated by seditions. We shall say they answer quite correctly. For it is necessary, since they are Muses. But what will the Muses say hereafter? After sedition has arisen, both races will be carried away: the iron and bronze indeed to gain, and the possession of fields and houses, and the abundance of gold and silver. But that which is in the golden and silver, as if not of a needy but an opulent nature, to virtue and the former state. But fighting with one another and pulling in contrary directions, they will finally come together in the midst, so that having divided the fields and houses, they may possess each privately: but those who before were kept by them as free men, friends, and nurturers, are reduced into slavery, and as subjects and slaves, are compelled to bear the care of war and their guardianship. From here indeed it certainly seems to me this change happens. Surely this government will be in the middle between the aristocratic and the power of the few. It will be certainly. It will be changed thus. But when it has been changed into that, what mode of government will it especially preserve? Or is it clear that partly it will imitate the prior republic, partly the power of the few, inasmuch as it is located in the middle, and partly also it will obtain something of its own? Exactly so. And indeed it will imitate the prior in that the leaders will be honored, and the soldiers will abstain from agriculture, mechanical arts, and other gains, and common banquets will be made, and gymnastic games and the contests of war will be frequented. Certainly. But it will have some such things proper to itself: that it will fear to admit the wise to the principality, because it possesses men of this kind not simple nor most upright, but mixed: and it will rather admit more spirited and simpler men to govern, who seem born for war rather than for peace? Will it also make much of deceits and machinations of war, and always fight? Certainly. And yet they will be greedy for money, just as those who lead their life in the power of the few, and overwhelmed by shadows they will honor gold and silver more rustically, inasmuch as they have treasuries and their own storehouses in which to hide those things, and also walled enclosures of houses as their own nests, in which they will spend much with women and others according to their pleasure. You speak the truth. Will they not also be more sparing in their own things than is fitting? Inasmuch as they make much of money and do not acquire it openly: but in the things of others, because of pleasure, they will be more profuse, and will secretly indulge in pleasures, fleeing the law everywhere, just as children flee the sight of a father, having been educated not by persuasion but by force, from the fact that they neglected true music which is joined with discourse and philosophy, and...
