...neglected it, and honored gymnastics much more and before music? You describe a republic mixed from bad and good. It is mixed indeed: but because of the empire of spiritedness and anger in it, the studies of contention and ambition prevail above the rest. Vehemently. Will not this republic so coalesce, and be such, as far as it is permitted in discourse to describe the figure of the republic not with absolute diligence, because it suffices from the description itself to discern the most just and the most unjust man, and it would be almost an inextricable work if someone were to attempt to narrate all republics and all characters with none omitted? Well said. Who then is the man according to this republic? how is he made? what sort is he? I think indeed, says Adeimantus, he is similar to this Glaucon, for the sake of contention. Perhaps, I say, he is similar in this. But in these things he seems by no means similar in nature. In which things? He must certainly be more stubborn, and somewhat more alien from music, yet greedy for music: and studious of hearing indeed, but by no means a rhetorician. And yet toward slaves, a man of this kind will be rustic, not despising slaves as a man moderately educated does; but toward free men he will be mild: toward leaders indeed especially obedient, but also more greedy for principality and honors, thinking it necessary to excel and lead others not by the art of speaking or any other similar faculty, but by warlike and civil things, since he is also quite studious of gymnastics and hunting. That is certainly the character of that republic, he says. Will not he also despise money in his youth? but the more he ages, the more he will love money, from the fact that he is a participant in a greedy nature, and is not whole toward virtue, because he lacks the best guardian? Which one? says Adeimantus. Reason, I say, and the operation of music mixed with it, which alone when it is present, preserves virtue throughout all life in him whom it presides over. You speak excellently, he says. Such a youth is surely greedy for ambitious empire, similar to such a city. Entirely. But he is sometimes made such in this way: namely, when some youth is the son of a good father living in a city not well governed, fleeing honors, principalities, and judgments, and the rest of the care of such business, and willingly subjecting himself so that he may avoid labors. In what way is he made? Namely, when he hears his mother bearing it poorly that her husband by no means performs magistracies, and for that reason she is held in contempt among other women: then becoming indignant whenever she sees the man by no means studious in accumulating money, nor contending and anxious for those things either privately or in judgments and publicly: but more negligent toward all these things, and such that he lives mostly with himself, and neither despises his wife nor especially cultivates her. From which things the mother often predicts to the son that his father is lazy and too remiss, and other things, whatever women are accustomed to chatter about such men. Many such things indeed, says Adeimantus, and things similar to themselves, women are accustomed to say reproachfully. Nor does it escape you that even slaves and domestics, especially those who seem to be most benevolent, often whisper such certain things into the ears of boys. And if they see someone either owing money to the father, whom he by no means calls into court, or affecting him with some other injury, they tell the boy that when he becomes a man, he should avenge all such things, and be more of a man than his father was. That same son, having gone out of the house, hears many other similar things and sees them: namely, that men who in the city mind their own business are called fools and little valued: but those dissimilar to them are honored and praised. When the youth hears and sees these things, and again hears his father's discourses and sees his studies closely compared to the studies of the others, he is pulled by both: by the father indeed his rational power is nurtured and increased, but by the others the nature of desiring and angering. Therefore, since he was born with not a bad disposition, yet having used the bad custom of the others, and being pulled into the midst by these, he subjects himself to a certain middle power, contentious and angry, and becomes a man with an elate mind, and more greedy for glory. You seem to me to have sufficiently narrated his nature. We have therefore the second republic and the second man. We have indeed. After these things do we not say that of Aeschylus: "Another man suitable for another city"? Or rather, according to that previous supposition, another city congruent to the other? Exactly so. But that which follows a republic of this kind is, as I think, the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>. What institution of the republic do you especially call the power of the few? That in which magistracies are given to citizens based on a wealth rating <note>original: "censūs"</note>, and in which the rich dominate, but for the poor there is no communion in the republic. I understand indeed. Must it not be said in what way the transgression from the ambitious government into this one happens? It must certainly be said. Even to a blind man it is clear in what way the transgression happens. In what way? That treasury of each man full of gold destroys such a republic. For first indeed they find new expenses and lead them to laws which neither they nor their women obey. Consistent indeed. Then each one, moved by the example and emulation of the other, many finally become such. Likely. From here therefore, having slipped more profusely into accumulating money, the more preciously they value it, the more they think virtue is vile. Does not virtue so differ from riches, as if both were placed in the scales of a balance, and always decline to the contrary part? Exactly so. Therefore when in a city riches and the rich are honored, virtue and good men are despised. It is clear. And all are inflamed to those studies which are in honor, which they frequent: but those which are held in no honor are accustomed to lie neglected among all. It is so. Thus from being greedy for victory and honor, they finally become greedy for gain and money. And they praise and admire rich men and elevate them to magistracies, but despise the poor. It entirely happens so. Do they not also establish by law the limits of the principality, when they establish that where there is a greater abundance of money, there such a principality is greater; where less, on the contrary less; and they prohibit anyone from commanding who has not reached a certain rating? But they effect these things either by force and arms, or after they have struck fear, they established such a republic. Is it not so? Exactly so. This is, so to speak, the constitution. It is indeed. But what is the mode of the republic? or what are the defects which we said that republic had? First, look at what kind of prescribed limit is in it. If someone were to choose pilots, but by no means admitted a poor man although he were more skilled in steering, what do you think would follow from this? That they would steer the ship poorly. Is it not in the same way in any other principality? So I think indeed. Is it so in all things except in the city? Or in the city besides? Much more so, since this is the gravest and greatest government. One indeed, and so great a defect the power of the few suffers. It appears. But what of this? Is it not lighter? What sort of thing? That it is necessary for this to be not one, but two republics: one indeed of the poor, the other of the rich; and men...

## Dialogue VIII. On the Republic, Or, On Justice. 431

men living within the same walls are always plotting against one another. Certainly, that is no light matter. But neither is this a beautiful thing: namely, that they are unable to wage war. This is because they are forced to either use an armed populace—whom they fear more than the enemy—or, if they do not use them, they appear in the heat of battle to be truly "the few" <note>This is a pun on the word "Oligarchy," which literally means "rule of the few."</note> in their pursuit of power. Furthermore, they will refuse to pay out money for the use of war, being greedy men. I ask you: is this proper? Certainly not. And do you think it is right, as we criticized above, that in this kind of state the same men are occupied with diverse duties at once—tilling the soil, accumulating money, and serving as soldiers? In no way is it right. See if this is the first and most serious of all these evils. What is that? That it is permitted for anyone to alienate all their property, and for another to acquire all that belonged to them; and for the one who has sold it all to live in the city while being no part of the state at all—neither a money-changer, nor a craftsman, nor a knight, nor a soldier—but only a <term>pauper</term> <note>original: "pauper & egenus"; literally a poor and destitute person without a functional role in the community.</note>. This is certainly the first. Indeed, in states subjected to the rule of the few, this is by no means prohibited; for if it were, some would not be excessively wealthy while others are outright beggars. You speak correctly. But consider this: when such a wealthy man was spending his money, was he of more use to the city for the purposes we spoke of earlier? Or did he only seem to be of the number of the leaders, while in truth he was neither a leader nor a servant, but a consumer of his own resources? So it seemed. He was nothing else but a consumer. Shall we say that, just as a drone <note>original: "fucus"; a male bee that does not work, used here as a metaphor for an idle person living off others.</note> is born in a hive as a disease to the swarm, so also a man of this kind, born in a home, is a pest to the republic? Entirely so, Socrates. Has God not made all the flying drones without stings? But we see that these terrestrial drones are some without stings, and some armed with terrible stings. And from those who have no stings, they eventually become beggars in their old age; but those who are equipped with stings are the ones called criminals. You speak the truth. It is clear then that in a city where you see beggars, there are also hidden thieves, cutpurses, temple-robbers, and architects of all such crimes. It is certainly clear. Do you not see that in cities governed by the few, there are destitute people? Almost everyone, except the leaders. Do we not therefore think that there are many criminals in those cities, armed with stings, whom the diligence and force of the leadership hold back? We plainly think so. And shall we assert that such men emerge there because of a perverse education, a lack of discipline, and an unfair disposition of the republic? We shall. Such then will be the city subject to a few leaders, and it will be entirely oppressed by evils, and perhaps even more. So it is. Let us now consider as established that republic which they call <term>Oligarchy</term> <note>original: "paucorum potentiam"; rule based on the estimation of property.</note>, which chooses its leaders by the assessment of wealth. After this, let us investigate how a man becomes similar to it, and once he has become so, what sort of man he is. Certainly. Does he not pass from being an ambitious man to one greedy for the rule of the few by this reasoning? By what? When a young man there first imitates his father and follows in his footsteps, but then sees him crash into the state as if against a reef—suddenly fallen from the height of dignity, scattering himself and all his property, perhaps after leading an army or holding some other great office—dragged into court by plotters, circumvented by accusers, oppressed, exiled, and despoiled of his honors and patrimony. That is likely. That young man, my friend, having witnessed and suffered these things, and having lost his patrimony, is driven by fear; he immediately casts down from the throne of his soul that ambition and boldness, and having become humble because of poverty, he turns himself to profit-seeking; and in a very narrow and stingy manner, living sparingly and exhausting himself in business, he gathers money. Do you not think that such a man then places on that seat of the soul avarice and the desire for gain? And that he creates within himself a sort of Great King, adorning him with royal ornaments, crowns, belts, buckles, fringes, and a Persian sword? I do. And here he forces his rational power and the fire of his spirit to lie on the ground on either side and serve this king, permitting them to inquire into or consider nothing else except how the most money can be gathered from the least; to admire and worship nothing but wealth and the wealthy, and to seek dignity from no other thing than money and whatever contributes to it. Certainly, no other change is quite so swift and vehement as that from an ambitious youth to a seeker of money. Is he not therefore a devotee of the rule of the few? Indeed, his transformation is similar to that of the Republic from which the power of the few arose. Let us consider whether he is similar. Let us. First, in the fact that he values money above all, he will be similar. Why not? Furthermore, he is similar in that he is more stingy and intent on work, satisfying only his necessary desires, but by no means indulging in other expenses; rather, he restrains other appetites as if they were superfluous. Greatly so. Thus he lives a drier and more squalid life, increasing his family estate everywhere with the highest parsimony, intent on hoarding a treasure—the kind of man the common crowd approves of. Will not such a man be similar to that Republic? So it seems to me. Money is therefore most honored by every such city, and by this man. For he has not, I think, applied his soul to discipline. No, I suppose not. For he would not have appointed a blind guide <note>A reference to Plutus, the god of wealth, who was traditionally depicted as blind.</note> over himself. Very well. But observe this: do we not say that desires similar to the nature of drones exist in him because of a lack of discipline—some of them beggarly, others criminal—restrained by force and other diligence? Most especially. Do you know where to look to see their crimes? Where? To the guardianship of orphans, and if any such thing happens to them, where they might obtain the greatest license for injury. You tell the truth. Is it not clear that in other dealings where such a man is considered upright, because he seems to be just, he restrains the other small desires within himself through a certain equity of life—not because it is better to do so, nor by taming them with reason, but out of necessity and fear, trembling for the rest of his substance? Most certainly. Indeed, my friend, you will find in many of them, whenever they have the opportunity to spend what belongs to others, desires very much like drones. Especially. Therefore, he will not be free from internal discord; he will not be a single man, but a double one, having within him desires that are for the most part masters over other desires—the better over the worse. It is so. For this reason, he will be more modest than many others. Yet the true virtue of a harmonious and composed mind will flee far from him. So it seems to me. Furthermore, the stingy man will be slower toward any contest, whenever there is a struggle in the city for some honorable victory or magnificence; he is unwilling to spend money for the sake of such honors and contentions, fearing to rouse prodigal lusts and provoke them to fighting and striving. Fighting with only a few of his resources, in the manner of the <term>optimates</term> <note>original: "optimatū ritu"; referring here to the "best" or the wealthy few who fight sparingly to preserve their capital.</note>, he usually allows himself to be conquered and increases his wealth. Most certainly. Shall we disagree any further that the stingy and avaricious man is fashioned after the example of the city governed by the few? In no way.

## Dialogue VIII. On the Republic, Or, On Justice. 433

...he restrains whatever entices him to spending rather than profit, which pleasures are indeed called unnecessary. That is manifest. Should we, so as not to wander in ambiguity, first distinguish which desires are necessary and which are not? I would like that. Those should rightly be called necessary which we cannot turn away, and which, when they are satisfied, help us; for it is necessary for our nature to seek both of these. Is it not? Most certainly. We shall therefore rightly call them necessary. Rightly. And shall we not correctly deny those to be necessary which can be removed if one is accustomed to it from a tender age, and which, while they are present, bring no good—or rather, for the most part, do harm? Excellent indeed. Let us take an example of them so that we may know what each are, and behold them through a certain figure. So it must be. Surely the desire for eating—for food and relish—up to the point of health and good physical condition, is necessary. I think so. Certainly, the use of food is necessary for two reasons: because without it life is not sufficient, and because it is useful. So it is. And the use of other seasonings is necessary insofar as it contributes to a good habit of the body. Entirely. But if the appetite for these or other things is superfluous and contributes nothing, and can be restrained from a tender age, and stands in the way of both the body and the mind toward prudence and temperance, it will rightly be called unnecessary. Rightly. We shall therefore call these "spending desires," but those others "profit-seeking," because they contribute to action. Why not? And we shall say the same of sexual and other desires. The same. Indeed, the one we called a "drone" a little while ago—we were saying he is the one who is full of such pleasures and lusts, and is enslaved to unnecessary desires. But the one who is enslaved to necessary ones we called stingy and greedy for the power of the few. Without a doubt. Let us say again how the "popular" <note>This refers to the Democratic man.</note> man is made from the one who desires the power of the few. It seems to me that it happens mostly in this way. How? When a young man—as we just said, raised unrefinedly and too dryly—tastes the honey of the drones and joins with ardent and vehement animals who can procure all-formed and various pleasures from every side: from this, you must think, arises that transformation by which he passes from the "power of the few" that is in him into the "popular" state. It is necessary. Just as the city was changed when outside aid was provided to one of the parts—like to like—so is the youth's character changed when an external form of desires, related and similar, supports one of the forms of desires already within him? Entirely. But if some assistance is brought to the part of his character that favors the rule of the few—either by his father or other household members, admonishing and rebuking him—then sedition, and resistance, and a fight within himself against himself arises. Why not? And sometimes, I think, the popular condition yields to the state of the few, and some desires partly perish and partly fall away, as some shame arises in the youthful soul, from which it is again refined. That happens sometimes. Again, besides those desires that fell away, other related ones coalesce because of the ignorance of the father's education, becoming many and vehement. So it is certainly accustomed to happen. They further draw him to familiarities and customs, and while they creep in secretly, they grow into a great number. What forbids it? At last, they occupy the citadel of the youthful soul, perceiving it to be empty of teachings, honorable duties, and true reasons. These are surely the best guardians and saviors in the minds of pious men. Most certainly. But false, arrogant, and petulant reasons and opinions succeed in their place, occupying the same position in such a man. Most especially. Does he not then return to those Lotus-eaters <note>A reference to the Odyssey; those who eat the lotus forget their home and duties.</note> and openly dwell there? And if any aid is sent by friends to the laboring better part of his soul, those arrogant and petulant reasons close the gates of the royal wall within him; they neither admit the aid itself nor receive the embassies of the warnings of private elders, but they themselves conquer in battle. Calling shame "foolishness," they shamefully expel it into exile; calling temperance "cowardice" and insulting it, they cast it out; and moderation in character and moderation in spending they utterly detest and put to flight as if it were "rusticity" and "illiberality," while they themselves thrive along with many futile desires. Greatly so. When they have driven these from the soul which they occupied and purged—having initiated him with great expense—they then lead in petulance, license, prodigality, and impudence, shining in a huge crowd and crowned with garlands, extolling and applauding them. They call petulance "noble education"; license they call "liberty"; prodigality they call "magnificence"; and impudence they call "fortitude." Does the youth not in this way transition from the nurtured affection of necessary desires into the dissolved license of unnecessary and futile pleasures? That is plainly clear, he said. Such a man lives thereafter, I think, spending money, labor, and exercise for the sake of unnecessary pleasures no less than for necessary ones. But if he is so fortunate that he does not rave beyond measure, but having become older and the huge crowd of pleasures having arrived, he does not admit all but only some, having excluded the rest for a time; and once they have entered he does not give himself entirely to them, but lives so that he imparts himself equally to each. To the one that happens to fall to him, as if committing the command of himself to a supreme magistrate until it is satisfied, and then again to another, neglecting none, while he nurtures each one equally. So it happens. This man does not receive true reason, nor does he admit into the citadel of his guard anyone who might say that pleasures are partly of good and honorable desires, and partly of evil ones, and that the former should be exercised and honored, while the latter should be moderated and restrained. Rather, he nods to all these things, affirming that all are similar and to be honored equally. Certainly, whoever is so disposed does that. Does he not live day by day, obeying whatever desires happen to be present? At one time indulging in drunkenness and music, at another time content with drinking water and fasting; sometimes exercising in the studies of gymnastics, sometimes sluggish in slackness and sloth; sometimes touching on the studies of philosophy, and often throwing himself into the republic, saying and doing whatever chance offers. If he sometimes admires soldiers, he is carried toward them; if merchants, he comes to them again. He directs his life by no order or necessity, but calling this life pleasant, free, and blessed, he cultivates it assiduously. You have skillfully described the life of a popular man who has no choice in how he lives. I think indeed that he is full of very many diverse characters, beautiful and varied, just like that city; many men and women would judge him to live happily, since he contains within himself many examples of republics and characters. So it is, undoubtedly. Let such a man be for us the one similar to the democratic republic, who is rightly named "popular." Let it be so. It remains for us to speak of that famous republic and that famous man: tyranny and the tyrant. By all means. Come, ...

## Book Thirty-One. 434

...let us see, sweet friend, what is the manner of tyranny itself. That it arises from the popular state is almost clear. Manifest. Does tyranny then arise from the popular state in the same way that the popular state arose from the power of the few? How? Because they proposed to themselves as the "good" in the power of the few—by which that power grew—the abundance of wealth. Did they not? That very thing. An insatiable thirst for wealth and the neglect of other duties for the sake of profit itself destroys it. That is true indeed. Furthermore, an insatiable desire for that which is considered "good" in the popular state also perverts it. What do you say is considered the greatest good in it? Liberty. For you will hear that in a popular city, this is considered the most beautiful thing. Therefore, it is said that only in this city is it fit for a man to dwell who is free by nature. Certainly, that name "liberty" is preached most frequently in this city. Does not, as I was about to say, an insatiable desire for this very thing and the neglect of other things change this republic and force it to need a tyranny? In what way? When, evidently, a popular city thirsting for liberty finds bad cupbearers presiding over it, and gorges itself on it more profusely than is proper, becoming drunk, and punishes its leaders as if they were rigid and seekers of the "dominion of the few," unless they are very mild and grant much license. So it entirely happens. And it rebukes those who obey the leaders as if they were servile and men of no worth; but it praises and honors privately and publicly those leaders who are like subjects, and subjects who are like leaders. Is it not necessary in such a city for men to arrive at the highest liberty? Without a doubt. And does not this innate license, impatient of obedience, my friend, creep into private homes and extend itself even to the beasts? How do we say this? For example, if a father becomes like his son and fears his sons, and the son becomes like his father, and neither reveres nor fears his parents, so that he may be as free as possible; and the resident alien is equal to the citizen, and the citizen to the resident alien, and the stranger likewise. So it happens. These things and other similar smaller things occur. Surely in such a city the teacher fears his students and fawns on them, and the students despise their teachers and likewise their tutors; and to sum it up, the younger people make themselves equal to the elders. The elders, sitting with the younger ones and placing themselves on the same level, oppose them with words and deeds, and like jesters they delight them with witticisms, lest they appear severe or imperious. Most certainly. And the extreme liberty of the crowd, my friend, in such a city—how great is it, since the purchased slaves are no less free than those who bought them? And we almost forgot to say how much equality and liberty there is for women toward men, and men toward women. Shall we not say, according to Aeschylus, whatever now comes to our lips? Entirely so, I said; and I indeed say this: truly, the beasts that are fed by men—how much freer they are in this city than elsewhere, no one would believe unless they experienced it. For even the little dogs, as the proverb goes, are like their mistresses. And the horses and donkeys are made such that they have become accustomed to walk very freely and haughtily through the streets, so that they run into anyone they meet unless he yields. And everything else is conducted with the highest license. You are telling me my own dream. For such things frequently happen to me when I go out into the countryside. Do you see where the sum of all these things mentioned above tends? Indeed, the delicate mind of the citizens is rendered such that if anyone brings even a little bit of servitude, they are annoyed and cannot tolerate it. At last, they despise all laws, both written and unwritten, so that no one may be master over them. That is indeed manifest. This, my friend, is that excellent and elegant republic from which, as it seems to me, tyranny is born. Elegant certainly, but to what end? Furthermore, the disease which, creeping into the power of the few, weakened it, also sprouts and grows in this one from excessive license, and subjects the popular city to the yoke of servitude. And to sum it up, every excess is usually turned into its opposite—in the weather, in trees, in animals, and especially in republics. Not without cause. For excessive liberty seems to turn into nothing else but excessive servitude, both privately and publicly. Certainly, that is consistent. Therefore it was not without reason that I said tyranny rises from no other republic than the popular one: from extreme liberty, the gravest and most savage servitude. So reason shows. But you will not, I think, ask this, but rather what is that same disease born in the power of the few and in popular government that reduces it to servitude. You tell the truth. I was saying that the genus of idle and prodigal men is partly stronger and more manly, and partly more sluggish: the former lead, the latter follow. We compared these men to drones in the previous sections: the former to drones with stings, the latter to drones without stings. And rightly so. These men disturb whatever city they are in, just as phlegm and bile disturb the body. A good doctor and founder of laws, no less than a skillful beekeeper, must take precautions from afar—first that they do not arise in the city; and if they do arise, that they be cut out immediately along with the honeycombs. So it must entirely be done. Let us then take it this way, so that what we seek may be more clearly known. In what way? Let us divide the popular city into three parts, as it is in reality. One genus is this which is born in it because of license, no less than in the power of the few. It is so. But it is much more acute in this one than in that. By what reason? There, because it is held in contempt and driven away from the magistracies, it becomes weak because of idleness. But in the popular state, this whole genus—with a few exceptions—presides, and the fiercest part of it speaks and acts. Another part, clinging to the tribunals, whispers and does not tolerate it if anyone says otherwise. Therefore, everything in such a city is administered by this genus, with a few exceptions. Most certainly. Another such group is always distinguished from the multitude. Which one? Since all are seeking profit, those who are most elegant by nature usually become the wealthiest. That is consistent. From here, a great and easy abundance of "honey" is squeezed out for the drones. For how could honey be squeezed out of those who possess little? The wealthy, I think, are called the "pasture of the drones." So it is. The people will be the third genus—those who care only for their own affairs and do not involve themselves in others', having little money. This genus is both the most numerous and the most powerful in a popular city whenever it is gathered. It is indeed, but it does not often wish to do so unless it is made a participant in the honey. Is it not always a participant, insofar as those who preside despoil the wealthy and distribute to the people, though they themselves take the most for their own use? Indeed, it becomes a participant in that way. Therefore, those who have been despoiled are forced to fight back, speaking and acting for their lives before the people. Why not? Thus they receive the occasion from others—though they themselves did not desire it—for innovating things; namely, so that they might plot against the people and intend their minds toward the rule of the few. Why not? Finally, after they see that the people, not of their own accord but through the ignorance sown by accusers, are trying to do them injury, then—willingly or not—they truly become seekers of the power of the few, not voluntarily, but because that drone goads and stings them.

--- Page 450 ---
## Dialogue VIII. On the Republic, Or, On Justice. 435

...very much so. Therefore, accusations, litigations, and mutual contentions arise. Most of all. And so the people are accustomed to create one certain person as their defender, and to nurture him and foster him so that he may become great. They are certainly accustomed to do so. From this, it is clear that the tyrant springs from the root of a "protector" <note>original: "ex radice pretoria"; Ficino uses the term for a magistrate or leader of the people who eventually seizes power.</note>, and from nowhere else. That is certain. What is the origin of the transformation from a protector—that is, one who leads—into a tyrant? Is it not after he begins to do that which the fable tells about the temple of Lycaean Jupiter in Arcadia? What is that? That whoever tastes human flesh cut up with the flesh of other victims is forced to become a wolf. Have you not heard the fable? I have. In the same way, this man—to whose <margin>A wolf from a man.</margin> command the crowd entirely obeys—does not abstain from kindred blood; but with false accusations, as is their custom, he drags those he fears into court and stains himself with unjust slaughter, extinguishing a man’s life, tasting with an impure tongue and profane mouth the blood of his closest kin. He drives some away, kills others, and presents himself as a promiser of the cancellation of debts and the distribution of lands. Therefore, it is necessary for a man of this kind either to be killed by his enemies or to exercise a tyranny, and to become a wolf from a man. It is entirely necessary. This man, then, is the one who becomes seditious against the wealthy. Certainly. Does not danger threaten him from the power of his enemies? If he is expelled and returns against the will of his enemies, he returns having become a tyrant. It is clear. And if they cannot expel him by public accusations, or kill him, they intend a violent death for him and plot against him in secret. So it is certainly accustomed to happen. From this follows that usual request of tyrants: namely, all who have ascended to this point ask the people for some bodyguards for their person, so that the "helper of the people" may be safe. Most of all. The people give them to him, being too anxious for him but too secure about themselves. Greatly so. When a man of money notices this—one who is an enemy to the people because of his wealth—then indeed, according to the oracle given to Croesus, he flees to the pebbly Hermus; he does not delay, nor is he ashamed to be called a coward. He certainly would not fear it a second time. Indeed, whoever is caught is put to the ultimate punishment. Necessary. But that "protector" of the state does not behave magnificently at all, but prostrates many others and stands himself in the chariot of the city—a tyrant made from a protector and a curator. What forbids it? Do you want us to describe the happiness of this man, and of the city in which such a man is born? Entirely so. At first, he greets everyone, smiling at whomever he meets, and refuses the name of tyrant; he promises many things, both privately and publicly, frees people from debt, distributes lands to the people and his familiars, and finally pretends to be mild and gentle to everyone. It is necessary. But when he has first reconciled some external enemies to himself and extinguished others, and matters are now peaceful, he immediately always stirs up some war so that the people may be in need of a leader. It is consistent. In this, he furthermore effects that those under him, exhausted by many expenses, are forced to turn to daily sustenance and meditate less on plots against the tyrant. It is clear. Furthermore, if he knows any who are endowed with a noble spirit and appear likely to refuse his command, he throws them to the enemy so that he may have an occasion to extinguish them. For these reasons, it is necessary for a tyrant always to move new wars. Necessary. On account of which he renders the citizens hostile to himself. Greatly so. It is likely that some of those who supported the tyranny and have the most power with the tyrant will boldly disapprove of what is being done, both among themselves and with him—especially those of a higher spirit. Likely. It is consistent that the tyrant must take all these away from the midst if he is to remain ruler, until he leaves no one among friends or enemies who is of any importance. That is indeed manifest. He must therefore look acutely at who is brave, who is magnanimous, who is prudent or wealthy. Indeed, he is so "blessed" that, whether he wants to or not, he must be an enemy to these and plot against them until he has purged the city. You describe a remarkable "purge" indeed. Entirely contrary to the purge of doctors. For doctors wash away from the body what is worst and leave what is best; the tyrant does the opposite. He is forced to do so if he is to remain ruler. He is bound by a "blessed" necessity which commands him either to live a life with many wicked people and be hated by them, or not to live at all. Such is indeed his condition. Is it not true that the more hostile his citizens are while he does these things, the more and more faithful satellites <note>original: "satellitibus"; bodyguards or henchmen.</note> he needs? What forbids it? Who then are most faithful to him? From where will he summon them? Many will fly to him of their own accord from everywhere, enticed by pay. You seem to be speaking of drones again, like some from the Cerne <note>Possibly a reference to a distant African tribe or a general term for foreign mercenaries.</note>, flowing together from external and various nations. You seem to be right. But who from the natives? Will there not be some, if he wishes? How? Namely, if having taken away the citizens, he grants liberty to their slaves and enlists them into his bodyguard for his services. Most especially, since these are most faithful to him. What a "noble" possession of the tyrant you describe, if indeed he uses such friends and faithful men after he has destroyed those former ones. Yet he uses such as these. And such friends admire him, and new citizens converse with him, but good men hate and flee him. What prevents it? It is not without reason then that tragedy seems to be a wise art, and Euripides seems to excel in it. For what reason? Because he sang this with a profound mind: "Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise," and he said those who converse with them are wise. Furthermore, he extols tyranny as if it were a divine thing; and many other such things he and other poets say. The tragic poets, being wise, will forgive us, I think, and those who administer the republic as we do, if we do not admit them into our republic—being, as they are, praisers of tyranny. They will forgive us, I think, whoever among them are more elegant men. But they go around other cities, gathering a crowd with noble, grand, and probable voices that do not lack a price, and they draw republics toward tyranny and the popular state. Vehemently. Do they not receive a price for this, and are they not honored first by tyrants, as is likely, and then also by that popular republic? But the higher they ascend into the steep peak of republics, the more their honor fails, as if it were exhausted and could not proceed further because of frequent panting. So it is indeed. But lest we proceed further after having digressed here, let us say from where the tyrant feeds that noble, numerous, and various army of his, which is always changing. It is clear first that if there are any sacred riches in the city, he will seize them and consume them as long as those things suffice which are sold, while he demands lighter tributes from the people. What if these riches fail? It is clear that he and his colleagues, his messmates, his harlots, both boys and women, will be fed from the paternal estate. I understand that the people who begat the tyrant will feed him and his friends. So it compels. But what if the people should be angry and say that it is not right for an adult son to be fed by his father any longer, but rather the father by the son; and that they did not create him for this...

This text is a Latin translation and commentary of Plato's *Republic* (specifically the end of Book VIII, all of Book IX, and the beginning of Book X) by the renowned Renaissance Neoplatonist **Marsilio Ficino**. 

The text follows Ficino’s standard pedagogical structure: a concluding passage from the previous book, an "Argumentum" (a philosophical summary and interpretation), and then the translated dialogue itself.

***

### Book Thirty-One [End of Book VIII]

...that he created this, so that with the son now grown, the father himself, serving his [the son's] servants, might nourish both him and his servants, and all others besides who flock from every side as his supporters; but that he [the son] might be liberated by this leader from those rich men who are considered distinguished and good in the city. And thus should the people order him to depart from the city, along with his friends, just as a father driving a son from the house together with a crowd of revelers? Then at last, by Jove, will the people recognize what sort of thing they are, and by what kind of beast they were delighted while they generated and nourished it, and how much weaker they are when they attempt to cast out one more powerful than themselves. What do you say? Will the tyrant dare to bring force against his father, and beat him if he does not comply? Most certainly, for he will take away his arms. You say, then, that the tyrant is a parricide and a harsh nurturer of old age. And so it seems, this is properly a tyranny; and as it is said, the people, fleeing the smoke of the ferocity of free men, fall into the flame of the rods of domination, undergoing the harshest and most bitter servitude of slaves in place of that immense and unseasonable liberty. So indeed it happens. Shall we not, therefore, have spoken rightly if we say it has been sufficiently discussed in what manner tyranny is born from popular government [democracy], and having been born, what sort of thing it is? Sufficiently indeed.

# DIALOGUE NINE
## CONCERNING
### THE JUST.
#### *
#### ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.

SOCRATES, having treated very many things concerning the kingly life of the best men, also disputes much concerning its contrary, tyranny, so that we may approve the former as most blessed and reject the latter as most miserable. This is not only dealt with in the eighth book, but furthermore, it treats tyranny—namely, by what reason it chiefly arises from the popular state, what kind of thing it is, how harmful and how unhappy: so that we may avoid with all our strength the primary tyranny which occurs in the soul, and in turn embrace the kingship inward to the soul. Through these things, he returns immediately to the first proposition of the entire disputation. In this, he certainly establishes to demonstrate that justice is not only laudable by human opinion, but also by its own nature, it is wonderfully honorable and, above all things, to be venerated as salutary. Likewise, that injustice is to be censured not only out of fear of laws or infamy, but is to be fled far away because of the poison of its own malignant nature. 

When he names Justice, at times he designates legal and common justice—namely, the universal virtue established under the providence of laws; at other times he means justice more proper or distributive, through which honors, rewards, and punishments are distributed in the city according to merit, and actions and duties are attributed to the parts of the soul according to the dignity of nature; or commutative justice, through which things are exchanged for things or money at a fair and lawful price in the city, and in the soul duties are exchanged in a similar way, so that as much as the reason consults the inferior parts, so much do the inferior powers supply necessities for the command of reason. 

Among these things, note that the tyrannical soul is so disturbed that it is properly judged lost in lust, drunken, furious, and monstrous. Indeed, it is snatched away by those lusts like monstrous wild beasts, the ferocity of which others experience only occasionally while dreaming. What pertains here to the falsehood and truth and the reasoning of dreams, we treat abundantly in our theology. Consider how diligently he enumerates all the evils by which a city oppressed by tyranny is weighed down, and how aptly he numbers just as many evils, and even more, in the soul of the tyrant, so that nothing more miserable can be imagined [OCR: *etlingi* → *effingi*]. Soon he directs the whole disputation to this end: that the wise and just life be preferred to the contrary life, which he gathers into three heads. He wishes the first to be that which has been treated thus far, namely from the comparison of the foolish and unjust man to a certain city governed by no wisdom or justice. Where indeed it appears that both that city and that man are, by equal reasoning, in the worst and unhappiest state. He now approaches the second head, repeating that distinction of the parts of the soul into the natures of reasoning, anger [spiritedness], and desiring...

(Right column)

...to which he also accommodates three lives: the philosophical, the ambitious, and the covetous; covetous, I say, for the sake of pecuniary pleasures, and therefore it is also named "greedy." He disposes three limits or parts in the city: magistrates, soldiers, and money-makers. He proves then that a life of the aforementioned virtue is more to be chosen than a vicious one, and furthermore that it is in truth sweeter. Truly, since any one of those people prefers his own pleasure to the others, only the philosopher can rightly judge this. For there is need of experience, prudence, and reason for judgment. In the first place, as far as pertains to experience, the philosopher has experienced both his own pleasure and that of others, by which it happens that he can easily know which is to be preferred. Others, however, have never tasted the joys of the one philosophizing; therefore their pleasures cannot be compared with the joy of the philosopher. Furthermore, the philosopher alone is powerful in perfect prudence and in the industry of assigned reasons, which two things are necessary for the remainder of the judgment. Therefore, since the wise and just philosopher prefers the joys of his life to the delights of the ambitious and lustful life, we ought rightly to prefer the direct life of virtue to the dissolved life of vice by his own judgment. 

Finally, in the third head, he chiefly begins [to show] that true pleasure can be found in the wise and just man alone. In others, however, it is established that pleasure is false and shadowy. This is indeed proved thus: pleasures are for the most part vehement repletions of some indigence. And where both that which is filled and that which fills is truer and more perfect, the mode of filling is purer and more effective, where there is truer pleasure, and more perfect, and more innate. Since therefore the truth of the intellect in things to be understood has a more perfect truth and nature than sense and the sensible, and interior truth penetrates the intellect more than the sensible does the sense, and it approaches without the mixture of pain, it follows that the pleasure of the intelligence is truer and more perfect. 

Among these things, by a certain chance, he intersperses some mathematical matter, the declaration of which you will receive opportunely from the commentaries on the *Timaeus*. Attend thereafter to that figure of the nature of the soul, in which under the name of a manifold beast he understands the nature of desiring; under the figure of a lion, the vigor of anger; under the form of a man, reason. And see how expressly he depicts the life—nay, the foul servitude—of the ambitious soul and the lustful man. Likewise, receive there the formula by which the passage of souls into beasts can be so interpreted that they are said to migrate into the affections and habits of beasts rather than into their bodies. Furthermore, remember how in the body the perspicacity of sense, health, strength, and beauty are good not by opinion but by nature, and their contraries similarly evil; so in the soul, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice are naturally good, and their contraries naturally evil. Finally, receive the form of the whole life, through which you may so dispose all corporeal things that they harmonize with the temperance of the soul. And to that extent choose each thing, insofar as they contribute to the health of the soul; and on the contrary, flee far from those things which hinder this; dwell always in the citadel of fear, and permit yourself to be precipitated from it by no allurements... suspended [at the end]... suspended finally to form yourself and others, look up at the clear exemplar of this in the heaven: in the heaven, I say, that is in the order of the celestial motions, and higher still in the divine mind; so that from there at last, according to its image, you may compose first yourself, then your family, and thirdly the city, justly and happily.

***

[[margin: Concerning distinct pleasures.]]

**I**T remains next to be considered, I said, by what reasoning the tyrannical man arises from the popular [democratic] one, and what he is like, and whether he leads a miserable or a blessed life. Certainly that remains, he said. Do you know what I still desire? What? We do not yet seem to have sufficiently distinguished how many and of what sort the desires are. And unless that is established, the inquiry into that which we seek will be more obscure. It will still be opportune. Entirely indeed; and see what I wish to know in them; it is such: of those pleasures and desires which are not necessary, some seem to me to be repugnant to the laws, and to be in everyone indeed; but being chastened by the laws and by better desires together with reason, in some men they either altogether wither away or are so repressed that they are rendered very rare and thin; but in others they turn out more vehement and frequent. Which ones do you chiefly call these? Those which are more often excited in sleep. When in those sleeping that part of the soul which is partaker of mind and reason lies dormant and faint, that part, however, in which there is a certain ferocity and rustic monstrosity...

[[page number: 437]]

### Dialogue IX. on the Republic, or, on the Just.

[[margin: These things from Cicero, On Divination, book I.]]
...since it is stupified by immoderate drink and food, it exults in sleep and is immoderately tossed about, and all things are presented to its vision being void of mind and reason: so that we seem either to mingle the body with a mother, or with anyone else, whether man, or god, or often a beast; and even to slay someone and be impiously bloodied, and to do many things impure and foul, with rashness and impudence. But he who gives himself to rest with healthy and moderate cultivation and diet, with that part of the soul which is of mind and counsel agitated and erect and saturated with the feasts of good thoughts, and that part of the soul which is nourished by pleasure being neither killed by want nor overflowing with satiety—both of which are accustomed to graze the edge of the mind, whether something is lacking to nature or it abounds and overflows—and that third part of the soul in which the heat of anger exists being calmed and extinguished: then it will happen, with the two rash parts of the soul compressed, that the third part of reason and mind shines forth, and provides itself vigorous and sharp for dreaming; then tranquil and true visions of rest occur to him. I think exactly so. What more? This we wish to know summarily: that there is in everyone a certain dire, rustic, and iniquitous species of desires, even in those who seem most moderate among men. Which becomes manifest in sleep. Should I say anything further, and you will see whether you agree. I agree indeed. Remember what sort of man we said the popular [democratic] man was. He was he who from his early age was nourished under a parsimonious father, who indulged only in the desire for profit, but the other non-necessary ones, the companions of play and ornament, he despised. Was it not so? Exactly so. Having then conversed with more elevated men full of those lusts which we just narrated, he began to decline toward all petulance and their customs, out of hatred for his father's parsimony. But since he was of a better nature than his corrupters, being distracted on both sides, he found a middle affection of both loves, affected moderately by each as he himself thinks, leading neither an illiberal nor a dissolved life, changed from the power of the few [oligarchy] into a popular man. This was the opinion concerning such a man. Suppose again the son of this man, now great in age, imbued from his first years with his father's customs. I suppose it. Suppose again that the same things happen to him as happened to his father, that he is drawn toward every disgrace and the license of a wanton life, which those who live it call "liberty"; but the father and other domestics support those desires which we said were in a certain middle; while others suggest help. When those vehement enchanters and nourishers of tyranny have already hoped that they can contain the youth in no other way, they excite in him a certain love by some machinations, as a leader and tutor of idle desires and those supplying him with lust—a winged and surely huge drone. Do you think such love is anything else? Nothing else. But when other desires, filled with the scent of ointments, crowns, and unmixed wine, buzz around him, and being resolved in the custom of such pleasures, they altogether goad and nourish that desire, and thus add a sting to the drone: then already this leader of the soul rages altogether and burns with madness; and being thronged then by satellites and goaded by a sting, if he finds within himself any frugal and modest opinions and desires, he immediately extirpates and expels them, until he casts out all temperance from the soul and fills himself with new insanity. You relate excellently the origin of the tyrannical man. Was it not for this reason that love was once called a tyrant? It seems plainly so. And a drunken man, O friend, does he not bear a tyrannical soul? Certainly. Furthermore, one who is furious and positioned outside himself contends to command not only men but even gods, and hopes he will attain it. Vehemently. A tyrannical man, O blessed one, becomes so in truth when, either by nature or by studies or by both, he becomes drunken, obnoxious to love, and furious. Thus the matter stands. Thus then such a man, as it appears, is made. But how does he live? That, as they say who joke, you will tell me. I tell you indeed. After these things, as I think, they indulge in feasts, revelries, circles, and meetings of harlots, and all other things of this kind, those in whom the tyrant love, inhabiting the inner shrines of the soul, rules all things. It is necessary. And so many indeed, days and nights, vehement desires sprout up needing many things. Many indeed. Quickly then if any profits exist, they are consumed. Why not? After these things certainly come interest [usury] and the dissipation of the patrimony. Without doubt. But when all things fail, it is necessary for the desires to cry out and complain, which indeed lurk frequent and burning in the nest of the soul; and they, goaded as if by certain stings—namely by other lusts, and especially with love as the leader of all others as if of satellites—are tossed and carried away to explore if anyone possesses anything which can be snatched by fraud or seized by force. Most of all. Wherefore he is compelled either to usurp from everywhere, or to be tortured by huge stings and pains. They are plainly compelled. Now, just as his new and adult pleasures surpassed the former ones and usurped what was theirs: so will he also judge it to be just that he, being younger, should have more than his parents and take from them, and if he consumes his own portion, he should expend the paternal one besides? Why not? But if those parents by no means permit it, at first he will begin to steal and deceive them. Altogether. But if he cannot do that, he will now seize, and bring force to his parents. So I think. And if the father and mother are old, O wonderful man, will he not revere them, and so contain himself that he does nothing tyrannical? I fear for the father and mother of a man so affected. By Jove, O Adeimantus, I said, for the sake of some recently loved concubine who is not necessary, will such a man seem to you to be about to strike with blows a mother who was already for a long time necessary and a friend, or for the sake of some handsome recently armed youth who is not necessary, an old father who is deformed and necessary and the oldest of all friends, and subject them to those people if he introduces them into the same house? By Jove, altogether. How "blessed" it seems to have begotten a tyrannical son. Not much. What then? When the parents' resources fail him, and there is in him a most crowded swarm of pleasures, will he not first dig through the wall of some house, or snatch the cloak of someone going late at night? Then also he will despoil some temple? And in all these things, those opinions which he once had from childhood concerning the honorable and the base, as if certain laws by which he was judged, those which recently left servitude, thronging around love as satellites, will now overcome along with him: those which formerly, while he slept, were loosed only through dreams, when he was still established in a popular condition under laws and paternal precepts? At last, truly ensnared by the tyranny of love, such as he rarely was in dreams, such will he always be awake? For he will abstain from no impious slaughter...

(Catchword: *nebit* → *abstinebit*)

[[page number: 438]]

### Book Thirty-One [Actually continued IX]

...nor from gluttony, nor from crime: but tyrannically love, living in him with all license and transgression, as he who is sole master, will impudently snatch the man subject to him like a city toward all things: whence he will nourish both himself and the crowd of his satellites, partly entered from without from a certain wicked custom, partly from within from the same customs loosed and manumitted by him. Is this not the life of such a man? This exactly. And if there be few such in the city, but all the rest of the multitude is modest, because there is no place for them there, having departed, they will throng another tyrant: and having accepted pay, if he has war anywhere, they help; but if they can be in peace and quiet, they commit many small evils there in the same city. Of what sort? They will steal, dig through walls, cut purses, despoil and plunder, snatch sacred things, compel captured men to serve, and sometimes also they will bring false accusations if they are strong in speaking, and give false testimonies, and judges will be corrupted by gifts. You call these "small" evils, if there are few such? These indeed, if compared to greater ones, are called slight. And all these things compared to the malice and misery of a city under a tyrant are by no means, as the proverb goes, "near the mark." For whenever many such are found in a city, and many others follow them, and they perceive the huge number of their own, they procreate a tyrant through the ignorance of the plebs, him especially who among them is so affected that he has the most powerful tyrant in his own soul. That is consistent indeed. Such a one will certainly be the chief tyrant. Will it not be easy if all yield? But if the city resists this tyrant, then surely he, just as in the previous cases he violated his father and mother, so again he will violate his fatherland according to his power, bringing in other youths, and will compel the fatherland and mother, once dear to him, to serve them, to speak in the Cretan manner, both by education and habit: and that will be the end of that man's desire. Exactly so. Do not these such men become thus privately before they dominate? In the beginning they converse mostly with those who flatter and assent to them, and obey them in all things, and serve them. And if they need anything, they themselves do the same, they submit themselves, and bear whatever persona as if domestics. But when they have become masters of their wish, they declare themselves to be strangers. Most certainly. They spend their whole age thus. Friends to no one ever, but always dominating someone or serving someone. But true liberty and friendship the tyrannical nature never tastes. Most certainly. Shall we not rightly call such men unfaithful? Rightly. Furthermore, as unjust as can possibly be, if only we correctly conceded among ourselves in the previous parts what sort of thing justice is. Correctly indeed. Let us conclude then who is the worst man. He is he who is such while awake as we figured above while dreaming. Altogether. Such indeed becomes he who, being most tyrannical by nature, attains sole dominion; and the longer he lives in tyranny, the more he is such. It is necessary so, said Glauco, having taken up the part of responding. Whoever appears most iniquitous will also appear most miserable: and he who for the longest time and most greatly possesses tyranny, is in truth most greatly and for the longest time most iniquitous and miserable. But to many, many things will seem otherwise. It is necessary that these things be so. The tyrannical man is most similar to a city oppressed by tyranny. The popular man to the popular city, and others similarly. Why not? As city stands to city in virtue and happiness, so also man stands to man. Nothing prevents it. How does a city subject to a tyrant stand to that which obeys a king, such as we first described? Altogether contrary. For one is the best, the other the worst. I will not ask which you mean. For it is established. But concerning blessedness and misery, do you judge in the same way or another? Let us not wonder at the species of the tyrannical city, looking only at the tyrant, or at those few who possess power with him, but as is fitting, having entered entirely into the whole city, let us survey each thing, and with eyes turned to all things let us bring forth our sentence. You advise rightly, and surely it is established among all that no city is more miserable than one pressed by tyranny, and none more blessed than one governed by a king. If I ordered the same to be observed concerning men, would I prescribe rightly? namely if I thought judgment should be permitted to him who can creep into the mind of the tyrant by thought, and look thoroughly into his customs, nor like boys are accustomed, looking at external things be stupified while he beholds that tyrannical pomp and the appearance which they fashion for themselves among those who look at external things, but judges perspicaciously. If I say we should listen to him who is able to discern, and who has both lived with him and was present at domestic actions, and then who has known in what way he is affected toward each of his familiars. For in these things especially someone, stripped of all tragic apparatus, is perceived; and again in popular dangers, if I should order one discerning these things to declare in what way the tyrant stands to others, as pertains to blessedness and misery, would I order rightly? Very rightly you would order that. Do you wish that we also feign ourselves to be of the number of those who can judge, and have adhered to them, so that we may have someone to respond to those things which we ask? I wish it indeed. Come then, consider the similarity thus, repeating the memory of both the city and the man, and so specifically and in turn observe the affections of each. Tell me of what sort. In the beginning, will you call the tyrannical city free, or a slave? Most of all a slave. Yet in it you behold masters and free men. Plainly, but that is a small part; the whole indeed, so to speak, in itself and the most excellent genus, is basely and miserably a slave. If therefore the man is similar to the city, it is necessary that the same order be in him, and his soul be oppressed by much illiberality and servitude, and those parts of the soul serve which are most excellent: but the thin part, most cowardly and most demented, dominates. Necessary. What further? Will you call such a soul slave or free? Slave. Yet a city that is a slave and subject to a tyrant does least what it wishes. Truly. Therefore the tyrannical soul will least do what it wishes, to speak thus of the whole soul: but always goaded by a violent sting, it will overflow with perturbation and repentance. Why not? Is it necessary for a tyrannical city to be rich or poor? Poor. Is it necessary for a tyrannical soul also to be always a beggar and inexplebile [insatiable]? It is as you say. But is it not necessary for such a city and such a man to be solicited by fear? Greatly. Lamentations furthermore, sighs, weeping, anguishes—do you think you will find them more frequent in another city? By no means. Furthermore, do you think such things are more in any other man than in this tyrannical one, who rages with desires and loves? How so? Surely looking at all these things and others of the same genus, you judged the tyrannical city to be the most miserable of all cities. Was it not rightly? Highly so. But concerning the man...

- *Socatras* is a clear OCR error for *Socrates*.
- *tesplum* is an OCR error for *templum*.
- *etlingi* is an OCR error for *effingi*.
- *inexplebilem* (insatiable) is used frequently to describe the tyrannical appetite.
- Ficino's "Argumentum" is a critical Renaissance synthesis of Plato's text with Christian/Neoplatonic ethics.

<meta>This page continues the translation of Book IX of Plato's Republic. The previous page concluded Book VIII, discussing how democracy devolves into tyranny. Here, the dialogue explores the internal psychology of the tyrannical man, beginning with the nature of lawless desires that emerge in dreams.</meta>

# Dialogue IX. Concerning the Republic, or, Concerning Justice. 437

When the wildness <note>The "immanitas" or bestial nature of the soul.</note> is immoderately stunned by drink, food, or sexual indulgence, it leaps up in sleep and is tossed about immoderately. Thus, all things are presented to its vision while the mind and reason are absent. We might seem to have intercourse with a mother, or anyone else—whether human, god, or even a beast; or even to slaughter someone and be impiously bloodied, and do many foul and grim things with recklessness and shamelessness. 

But whoever goes to rest with a healthy and moderate way of life, having stirred and raised that part of the soul which belongs to mind and counsel, and having feasted it on a banquet of good thoughts—and having neither starved nor overstuffed that part of the soul nourished by pleasure (either of which usually blunts the sharp edge of the mind, whether nature lacks something or overflows)—and having calmed and extinguished that third part of the soul where the fire of anger resides; then it will happen, with the two reckless parts of the soul suppressed, that the third part of reason and mind shines forth. It shows itself vigorous and sharp for dreaming, and then peaceful and true visions occur to it. I think exactly so. 

Why say more? This is what we wish to understand in summary: that in every person there exists a certain species of desires—dreadful, wild, and lawless—even in those who seem most moderate among men. This becomes manifest in dreams. Now, see if you agree with what I say. I certainly agree.

Record, then, what sort of man we called the "democratic" <note>original: *popularem*; a man whose soul is governed by the "rule of the people," meaning all desires have an equal vote.</note> man. He was the one who, from an early age, was raised under a thrifty father who indulged only the desire for profit, but despised the others that were not necessary but were companions of play and ornament. Is that not so? Exactly. Then, having associated with more exalted men full of the lusts we just described, he began to decline into every kind of insolence and their habits, out of hatred for his father's parsimony. But since his nature was better than that of his corrupters, being pulled from both sides, he reached a middle ground between the two types of affection. He pursued both moderately (as he thought), leading a life neither illiberal nor dissolute, changed from a lover of the power of the few <note>An "oligarchic" man, focused on wealth.</note> into a democratic man. This was and is the opinion regarding such a man. 

Now, again, imagine the son of this man, now grown, imbued from his earliest years with his father's habits. I imagine it. Imagine again that the same things happen to him as happened to his father: that he is drawn toward every disgrace and the license of a decadent life—which those who live it nevertheless call "total liberty." The father and other household members support those desires which we said were in the middle ground, while others offer help to the extremes. When those powerful enchanters and nurturers of tyranny have despaired of being able to restrain the young man in any other way, they excite in him a certain "Love" <note>In the Platonic sense, *Eros* is a powerful, driving desire that can become a "tyrant" over the soul.</note> through various machinations—a protector and guardian of idle desires that minister to lust, a winged and truly giant drone. Do you think Love of such things is anything else? Nothing else. 

But when other desires, filled with the smell of incense, ointments, crowns, and unmixed wine, and the pleasures released from such habits, buzz around him, they thoroughly thicken and nourish that longing, and thus add a sting to the drone. Then this leader of the soul rages entirely and seethes with madness. Thronged by his satellites and driven by the sting, if he finds any frugal and modest opinions or desires within himself, he immediately uproots and expels them, until he casts out all temperance from his soul and fills himself with a new insanity. You describe the origin of the tyrannical man excellently. 

<margin>These things are from Cicero, *On Divination*, Book 1.</margin> And was it not for this reason that, long ago, Love was called a tyrant? It certainly seems so. And a drunk man, my friend, does he not possess a tyrannical mind? Indeed. Furthermore, one who is mad and out of his mind strives to command not only men but even the gods, and hopes he will achieve it. Strongly so. 

A tyrannical man, O blessed one, truly becomes such when, either by nature or by habits or by both, he becomes intoxicated, subject to Love, and driven mad. That is exactly how the matter stands. This, then, is how such a man is made. But how does he live? As those who joke say: you will tell me. 

I will tell you indeed. After this, I think, they indulge in feasts, revelries, social circles, and meetings with courtesans, and all other such things, those over whom Love the tyrant dwells within the inner chambers of the soul and rules everything. It must be so. Therefore, many violent desires, in need of many things, sprout up every day and night. Many indeed. Thus, whatever income exists is quickly consumed. Why not? After this come loans and the dissipation of the father’s estate. Without a doubt. 

But when all things fail, the desires—which hide in the "nest" of the soul, frequent and burning—must cry out and complain. Driven as if by stings, namely by other lusts, and especially with Love as the leader of all the others like a bodyguard, they are tossed about and carried away to scout if anyone possesses anything that can be snatched by fraud or taken by force. Most certainly. Therefore, he is compelled either to seize from every side or to be tortured by immense stings and pains. They are certainly compelled. 

Just as his new, full-grown pleasures surpassed the old ones and seized what belonged to them, will he not also judge it "just" that he, being younger, should have more than his parents and take from them? And if he has consumed his own portion, will he not spend his father's as well? Why not? But if his parents will not permit it, will he not first attempt to steal from them and deceive them? Entirely. If he cannot do that, he will then snatch it and use force against his parents. So I think. But if his father and mother are old, O wonderful man, and they resist and fight back, will he fear them and restrain himself from acting tyrannically? I fear for the father and mother of a man so affected. 

By Jove, Adeimantus, I said, for the sake of a newly beloved and unnecessary mistress, do you think such a man would strike his mother—his long-time, necessary friend—or for the sake of some beautiful, newly-armed, and unnecessary youth, would he strike his deformed and necessary old father, the oldest of all his friends, and subject them to those others if he brought them into the same house? By Jove, absolutely. How "blessed" it seems to have fathered a tyrannical son! Not very. 

What then? When his parents' resources fail him, and there is already a thick swarm of pleasures within him, will he not first break through the wall of someone’s house, or snatch the cloak of someone walking late at night? Then he will even despoil some temple. And in all these acts, those opinions which he held since childhood regarding what is honorable and shameful—which were like the laws by which he judged—will now be overcome by those desires that recently escaped from servitude. Acting as satellites surrounding Love, they will conquer together with him. These were once released only during sleep through dreams, while he was still living under the laws and his father’s instructions in a democratic condition within himself. But finally, irritated by the tyranny of Love, he will always be while awake such as he rarely was in his sleep. For he will abstain from no impious murder...

<summary>This page discusses the psychological transition from the democratic man to the tyrannical man, focusing on how lawless desires—usually confined to dreams—take control of the waking mind through the influence of an internal "Love" (Eros) that acts as a tyrant. The tyrannical man eventually turns to theft, sacrilege, and even the physical abuse of his parents to satisfy his bottomless lusts.</summary>
