nor from gluttony, nor from any crime. But love, living tyrannically within him with all license and transgression—as if it were the sole master—will impudently drag the man subjected to it, like a city, toward everything. From this, he will nourish himself and the crowd of his henchmen, partly those who entered from without through some wicked habit, and partly those released and manumitted by him from within due to the same character. Is this not the life of such a man? Exactly so. And if there are a few such men in a city, while the rest of the multitude departs in all modesty because there is no place for them there, they will surround another tyrant. Having received pay, if there is a war anywhere, they will help; but if they can be at peace and quiet, they will commit many "minor" evils right there in the city. What kind? They will steal, dig through walls, cut purses, despoil and plunder, snatch sacred objects, force captured men into slavery, and even bring false accusations if they are powerful in speaking, and give false testimony, and corrupt judges with gifts. You call these "minor" evils if there are few such men? These are indeed called small if compared to greater ones. And all these things, compared to the malice and misery of a city under a tyrant, do not at all "hit the mark," as the proverb says. For whenever many such men are found in a city, and many others follow them, and they sense the great number of their own kind, they create a tyrant through the ignorance of the common people—specifically the one among them who is so affected that he has the most powerful tyrant within his own soul. That is certainly consistent. For he will be the most powerful tyrant. Does this not happen easily if everyone yields? But if the city resists this tyrant, then just as he violated his father and mother previously, he will again violate his fatherland with all his strength, bringing in other youths, and he will force his once-dear fatherland and "motherland" (to speak in the Cretan manner) into slavery through both education and habit; and that will be the end of that man's desire. Exactly so. Are these not the sort of men they are in private before they rule? At first, they associate mostly with those who flatter and fawn over them and obey them in all things and serve them. And if they lack anything, they do the same themselves: they submit, and they play whatever role is necessary as if they were household servants. But once they have achieved their wish, they declare themselves to be strangers. Very much so. Thus they spend their whole lives. Friends to no one ever, but always either ruling over someone or serving someone. The tyrannical nature never tastes true liberty or friendship. Most certainly. Shall we not rightly call such men unfaithful? Rightly. And also as unjust as possible, if we correctly agreed earlier on what sort of thing justice is among us. Correctly indeed. Let us conclude then who is the worst man. He is the one who is such while awake as we described the dreamer to be above. Entirely. Such a man he becomes, whoever is most tyrannical by nature and achieves sole dominion; and the longer he lives in tyranny, the more he is so. It must be so, said Glaucon, having taken up the role of responding. Whoever appears most unjust will also appear most miserable; and he who for the longest time and most greatly possesses a tyranny is in truth the most unjust and most miserable for the longest time. But many things will seem so to many people. It must be so. A tyrannical man is very similar to a city oppressed by tyranny. A popular man to a popular city, and others similarly. Why not? As city stands to city in virtue and happiness, so also man stands to man. Nothing forbids it. How does a city subject to a tyrant stand in relation to one that obeys a king, such as we first described? Entirely the opposite. For one is the best, the other the worst. I shall not ask which you mean. For it is clear. But concerning happiness and misery, do you judge in the same way or another? Let us not wonder at the appearance of the tyrannical city by looking only at the tyrant alone, or at those few who hold power with him, but as is fitting, having entered deeply into the whole city, let us survey every part, and having turned our eyes to everything, let us bring forth a judgment. You advise well; and indeed it is agreed among all that no city is more miserable than one pressed by tyranny, and none more blessed than one governed by a king. If I ordered the same to be observed regarding men, would I be commanding correctly? That is, if I think the judgment should be permitted to one who can creep into the tyrant's mind by thought and look thoroughly into his character—not, as a child might, staring in amazement at the exterior while looking at that tyrannical pomp and the appearance which they fashion for those who look from the outside, but judging with insight. If, I say, I think we should listen to him who is able to discern, who has both lived with him and been present for his domestic actions, and who knows how he is affected toward each of his family members. For it is in these things that one is seen most clearly, stripped of all tragic apparatus, and again in popular dangers, he will distinguish all these things. If I order him to declare how the tyrant stands toward others regarding happiness and misery, would I not be ordering correctly? Very correctly you would order those things. Do you want us to pretend that we are among those who can judge and have been close to them, so that we may have someone to answer what we ask? I certainly do. Come then, consider the similarity thus, calling to memory both the city and the man, and so observe the affections of each individually and in turn. Tell me which ones. First, will you call the tyrannical city free or enslaved? Most of all, enslaved. Yet you see masters and free men in it. Clearly, but that is a tiny part; the whole, so to speak, and the most excellent part in it is basely and miserably enslaved. If therefore the man is like the city, it is necessary that the same order be in him, and his soul be oppressed by much illiberality and servitude, and those parts of the soul serve which are most excellent, while a small, most cowardly, and most insane part rules. Necessary. Furthermore, will you call such a soul enslaved or free? Enslaved. Yet a city that is enslaved and subject to a tyrant least of all does what it wants. Surely. Therefore, a tyrannical soul will least of all do what it wants (to speak thus of the whole soul); but always pierced by a violent sting, it will overflow with disturbance and repentance. Why not? Is it necessary for a tyrannical city to be wealthy or poor? Poor. Is it also necessary for a tyrannical soul always to be a beggar and insatiable? It is as you say. Is it not necessary for such a city and such a man to be troubled by fear? Very much so. Furthermore, do you think you will find lamentations, sighs, weeping, and distress more frequent in any other city? In no way. Do you think more such things exist in any other man than in that tyrannical one, who is insane with desires and loves? How could it be otherwise? Surely, looking at all these things and others of the same kind, you have judged the tyrannical city to be the most miserable of all cities. Is it not correctly so? Most definitely. But regarding

the tyrannical man again, what do you say when you observe these same things? I say this man is by far the most miserable of all. You do not say this correctly. Why? This man is not yet, I think, the most miserable. Who then? This one perhaps will seem more miserable to you. Who, I say? He who, being tyrannical by nature, does not lead a private life but is unhappy, and by some chance is led to the point where he actually obtains a tyranny. From what has been said, I guess you are speaking the truth. It is so. But one ought not to merely opine about such things, but rather investigate them most diligently with such reason: for our dispute is about a very great matter, namely, the good life and the bad life. Wisely said. Attend then to what I say. For it seems to me that we must consider this from these things. From what? From each of the private citizens, as many as abound in wealth so that they have many slaves. For these have this similarity to tyrants: they rule over many. The difference is that the tyrant rules over more. There is a difference indeed. You know that these live securely with their household and do not fear their servants? For what would they fear? Nothing. But do you understand the reason? I do, since clearly the whole city assists each of the private citizens. You speak excellently. But what if some god were to take one man who has fifty or more slaves out of the city, along with his wife and children, and place him in a desert with all his things and slaves, where no free man could bring him help? With what and how much fear do you think he would be vexed, lest perhaps the slaves should kill him and his children and wife? The greatest, I think. Would he not be forced to flatter certain slaves and promise many things and set them free, even when he has no need to do so? From which he himself would become a flatterer to his own servants. He would be entirely forced either to do so or to perish. What if God had placed others near him in that region who would by no means tolerate one man ruling over another, and if they caught anyone claiming dominion for himself, they would afflict him with extreme punishments? I think his condition would be much worse if he were enclosed by a wall of enemies. Is not the tyrant closed in such a prison—being such by nature as we explained above—agitated by many and diverse fears and loves? But since his nature is especially greedy, he alone is permitted neither to go out anywhere nor to look at what is pleasing to free men; but within the walls of his house, he remains fearful like a woman, envying other citizens if anyone walks outside the walls and sees anything good. Exactly so. Does not that man incur even more from such evils, who, governing himself badly (the one whom you just judged the most miserable tyrannical man), by no means lives as a private citizen, but by some force of fortune is compelled to exercise tyranny? And since he cannot command himself, he strives to command others—just as if someone with a weak body, not sustaining himself by his own strength, were forced never to take rest with himself, but to contend and fight against other bodies. You bring in very similar and very true things, O Socrates. Is not this condition, O friend Glaucon, entirely miserable, and is not the life of a man who has obtained a tyranny harsher than that life which you previously judged to be the harshest? Very much so. But he is in reality, although it may not seem so to someone, truly a tyrant and truly a slave, bound to extreme flattery and servitude, a flatterer of the most wicked men. He never fills his appetites but always lacks most things, and he appears truly poor 

<margin>Why the father of the family fears nothing from a multitude of servants.</margin>

<margin>A tyrant who has obtained tyranny is a most miserable thing.</margin>

if someone looks into the inner chambers of his soul. He is also terrified by perpetual dread and vexed by anxiety and distress, provided he is similar to the state of the city over which he presides. And he is similar. Is he not? Especially so. In addition to these things, we shall also attribute to this man those things we mentioned before: that it is necessary for him both to be such before, and much more so after he has obtained the tyranny—envious, unfaithful, unjust, devoid of benevolence, impious, and to become the sink and fuel of all wickedness, and because of all these things to be the most miserable, and to make others who adhere to him similar. No one of sound mind would contradict this. Come, just as a judge looking around at all things judges each one, so you in the present should bring forth who in your judgment is first in happiness, who is second, and tell the others gradually who are five in number: the Kingly, the Timocratic <note>Ficino uses "studiosum" for the honor-seeker in the city where magistrates are created from property census.</note>, the Oligarchic <note>The one desiring the power of the few.</note>, the Popular, and the Tyrannical. And that judgment is easy. For as if I had entered, I compare these as if they were choruses in virtue and depravity, in happiness and its opposite, and I judge them. Shall we hire a herald? Or shall I rather pronounce these things? That the son of Ariston <note>Glaucon.</note> has judged the best and most just man to be the most blessed, and has said that he is the man who is most of all kingly and ruling himself; but the worst and most unjust man to be the most miserable, and that such a man is the one who becomes most of all a tyrant and presses both himself and the city with tyranny? Let it be so proclaimed. Shall I add, whether such men remain hidden or not hidden to men and gods alike? Add it. Let it be so then. For this demonstration is made as one; but the second, if it seems right, it is fitting to look at in this way. Which one is that? After the city was divided into three species, so also the soul of each will be divided in three ways, as I think; and from here the second demonstration will be born. Which one? This: since there are three parts of the soul, there also seem to be three pleasures, each proper to its own part. Desires also as many, and kinds of rule. In what way? One part we say is that by which a man learns. The second, by which he is angered. The third, because of its variety, we could not name with one proper word of its own, but we called it "concupiscible" <note>The appetitive part.</note> from that which it contains as greatest and most vehement, because of the vehemence of those desires that snatch toward food, drink, sex, and those things that follow them; we also called it "money-loving," since such desires are most of all satisfied by money. Correct. And if we say its pleasure and affection is for gain, we shall reduce it to one greatest sum of reason, so that we may signify something certain to ourselves whenever we speak of this part of the soul. And if we call this whole part greedy for money and gain, we shall name it very correctly. So it seems to me. What then? Does not the nature of anger draw the whole man toward power, victory, and glory? Greatly. If therefore we call it "contentious" and "ambitious," shall we do so correctly? Most correctly. But it is clear that the part by which we learn always strives toward investigating every truth and has the least care for money and glory. Entirely. If we name this third part "desirous of learning" and "philosophical," the name will not be ill-imposed. It is as you say. Do we not say that in the souls of some men one of those parts dominates, in others another, whichever happens to be? We do. Therefore we say there are three primary kinds of men:

the philosopher, the contentious, and the greedy. Exactly. Also three species of pleasures subject to these, one for each. Entirely. If you ask each of these separately which life of theirs is sweetest, each will prefer his own to the others. The greedy man, in comparison to gain itself, will consider the delights of honors or learning as nothing, unless perhaps they contribute something to money. You speak the truth. The ambitious man, however, thinks the pleasure perceived from money is heavy and troublesome, and again that which is perceived by learning—because doctrine brings no honor—he thinks is smoke and trifles. That is how it is. Let us also suppose the philosopher thinks the other pleasures are worth a lock of wool when he compares them to the constant joy of learning in which he himself delights while investigating truth; he calls the others "unnecessary" because he would not pursue them unless necessity forced him. It is important to know that well. When, therefore, the pleasures of each life and the life itself come into contention—not about which is more honorable or base to live, or better or worse, but about the sweeter and more peaceful state of life—by what reasoning shall we discern whose opinion is truer? I do not have enough of an answer. But consider it thus: By what thing ought one to judge whatever is to be correctly decided? Is it not by experience, prudence, and reason? Does anyone have other things by which he might judge better? In no way. Attend then: since there are three, who among these is most experienced in all the pleasures we described? Does the greedy man, by saying what the truth is, seem to you more experienced in the sweetness of learning than the philosopher is in gain, or rather the opposite? There is a great difference. For it is necessary for the philosopher to have tasted the pleasure of the other since childhood. But it is by no means necessary for the greedy man to have perceived how great a delight there is in the investigation of truth, and to have been experienced in it. In fact, even if he strives, he does not easily achieve it. Therefore the philosopher far surpasses both in the experience of pleasures. By far. But is the ambitious man any more unacquainted with the pleasure perceived from honor than the philosopher is with that from prudence? Honor indeed follows all of them if they perform the duty set before them. For the wealthy man is honored by the multitude, as is the brave and the wise. Therefore everyone understands by experience how great a pleasure comes from honor. But how great the sweetness is in the contemplation of truth, only the philosopher feels. Therefore, as far as experience is concerned, the philosopher judges best among all. Greatly so. Furthermore, he alone will be experienced along with prudence. Nothing prevents it. Moreover, that organ through which judgment must be made is not the instrument of the greedy or ambitious man, but of the philosopher. What sort is that? For we said judgment must be made through reasons. We did. But reasons are especially the instruments of the philosopher. It is clear. If everything were best judged by riches and gain, what the man devoted to profit praised or disapproved of would necessarily be the truest. Entirely. But if by honor, victory, and courage, it would be what the ambitious man, most ardent for victory, judged. It is clear. But since it is by experience, prudence, and reason: It is necessary that what the philosopher and the man studious of reasons praise are the truest. Therefore, since there are three pleasures, the pleasure of that part by which we learn will surely be the sweetest, and the life in which this part dominates will be the most delightful. Nothing stands in the way. Surely the philosopher, in whom is the authority for true judging, praises his own life. But what life would that judge place second, or what pleasure second? It is clear: that of the warlike and ambitious man. For this is closer to him 

<margin>Proverb.</margin>

than that of the greedy man. Therefore he seems to place the life of the one greedy for gain last. Why not? These two follow each other thus, and the just man has already twice conquered the unjust. 

<margin>On the middle state between pleasure and pain.</margin>

But the third time, in the manner of the Olympics, attributing it to the Savior and Olympic Jove <note>Zeus the Savior. Ficino notes this "third" victory as the ultimate one.</note>, consider that no pleasure except that of the prudent man is truly real or pure, but rather shadow-like and empty, as I seem to have heard from some wise man; and this will be the heaviest fall and ruin of the unjust man. Truly marvelous. But in what way do you say this? I shall certainly find out by inquiring through your answers. Inquire. Tell me, please, do we not say pleasure is the opposite of pain? We do. Do we also place a certain middle state, which is neither to rejoice nor to feel pain? We do. And when it is a middle state, is it a quiet and vacation of the soul from both? Is that not how you say it? Exactly so. Do you remember what sort the words of the sick usually are while they labor under a disease? What sort do you mean? That nothing is sweeter than health, but they say it escaped them how sweet it was before they were sick. I remember indeed. You also hear men vexed by the sharpest pains exclaiming that nothing is sweeter than to be free from that affliction. I hear it. Moreover, you hear men tortured by many other such afflictions, while they are being tortured, shouting and asserting that it is sweetest to be afflicted by no pain and to be free from present trouble; they do not say it is sweetest to rejoice. Surely this "quiet" is then perhaps most pleasing to them. But when someone stops rejoicing, will he think that cessation of pleasure is troublesome? Perhaps. Therefore that "quiet" which we said a little while ago was the middle of both will sometimes be both: now pain, now pleasure. It seems so. Can it be that what is neither becomes both? I think not. Yet when pleasure or pain is in the soul, are they not both certain motions? Yes. But that third thing which is neither pain nor pleasure, did it not just appear to be a certain quiet and a middle state of those? Clearly. How then shall we correctly think that not feeling pain is sweet, and not rejoicing is bitter? In no way. Therefore that is not so, but it appears so: if you compare it to something troublesome, it seems pleasant; if to something pleasant, it seems troublesome; and it is then a middle and a quiet. Nor do such things offer us any truth about pleasure, but they come about through certain enchantments. So reason shows. Look therefore at the pleasures that follow no pain, lest you think too often in this present discussion that it is so naturally ordained that pleasure is the privation of pain, or pain the privation of pleasure. Of which ones, he asked, and what pleasures do you mean? There are many others, but especially, if you wish to observe, the pleasures that occur regarding smell; for these, with no prior pain preceding, suddenly come forth as great; and when they cease, no pain follows them. You tell very true things. Let us not believe, therefore, that the cessation of pain is pure pleasure, nor that pain is the absence of pleasure. No. But of those things that enter into the soul through the body and are called pleasures, almost the greatest and most numerous are of such a kind that they are liberations from pains. They are indeed. And those things regarding the future that are born from expectation—certain pre-tastes of pleasure and pain—stand in the same way. The same. Do you know what sort these pleasures are, and what they are most similar to? To what? Do you think there is in nature a highest, a lowest, and a middle? I do. Do you think someone, when he is carried from the lowest to the middle, thinks anything else than that he is ascending to the highest? And while he stands in the middle and turns his eyes back toward where he had come from,

Dialogue IX. On the Republic. Or, On Justice. 441

does he think he is anywhere else than in the highest, since he does not see that which is truly highest? By Jupiter, I think such a man would think no differently. If he were carried down again, would he think he was being carried downward, and would he think so truly? Why not? Do not all these things happen to him for this reason: because he has not yet experienced what is truly highest, what is middle, or what is lowest? It is manifest. Will you then wonder if men unacquainted with the truth, as they feel incorrectly about many other things, are also so affected regarding pleasure and pain and their middle state, that whenever they fall into pain, they judge truly and truly suffer; but whenever they rise from pain into the middle, they think they have achieved both fulfillment and pleasure? And just as those who, next to black, only look at gray because they do not see white, think that gray is the brightest thing: so also those who compare the vacancy of pain with pain, but have not experienced true pleasure, are deceived in judging? By Jupiter, I will not wonder at that. Indeed, if the opposite happened, I would rather wonder. But consider it thus: Are not hunger and thirst and others of the same kind certain vacancies of the body's own habit? Why not? Ignorance and imprudence are a certain vacancy of the soul's habit. Most of all. But the one is filled when it takes food, and the other when it takes intelligence. Why not? Which fulfillment is truer? That which is through things that are more and truer, or through others? That which is through things that "are" more. Which kinds do you think are of a purer substance? Is it the kinds of food, drink, meat, and any nourishments? Or the species of true opinion, science, and mind, and in summary, of all virtue? Judge in this way: Does that which always adheres to the similar, the immortal, and the truth—and even exists as such and occurs in such a thing—seem to you to "be" more? Or that rather which never adheres to the similar and the mortal, and is not such, and is produced in such a thing? That which is always related to the similar far excels. Does the essence of a thing that is always similar participate more in essence than in science? No. Or in truth? Not this either. But if it participates less in truth, does it not also less in essence? It is necessary. Do not all the kinds regarding the care of the body participate less in truth and essence than these kinds which are concerned with the care of the soul? Less. And is not the body similarly less than the soul? The body too. Is not that which is filled with these things that exist more and more truly, and which itself exists more and more truly, also more filled than that which is filled with these things that "are" less and is itself less? What forbids it? If therefore to be filled with things agreeable to nature is pleasant, then that which is truly filled with more real things naturally and more truly affects one with true pleasure. But that which receives things that are both less and less true is less truly or firmly filled, and becomes a participant in a more fallacious and false pleasure. It is entirely necessary. Therefore, men unacquainted with prudence and virtue, and devoted to feasts and similar things, are carried downward, and again reach as far as the middle, and wander around these things through their whole life. They never emerge above these things, and they never look up at what is truly highest, nor are they ever carried to the upper things, nor do they ever enjoy any true thing, nor do they taste stable and pure pleasure. But like cattle, they look downward toward the ground, and obedient to their bellies, they spend their lives feeding and coupling; and for the sake of possessing these things more abundantly, they fight among themselves with heels and iron horns and hooves, 

<margin>That which is best for each is most "one's own."</margin>

slaughtering each other because of an insatiable lust, as those who fill neither the true and firm part of themselves nor with true fodder. Entirely, replied Glaucon, O Socrates, you reveal the life of the common people as if by some oracle. These men must pursue pleasures mixed with pains, which are images of true pleasure and shadows, contaminated to such a degree by mutual comparison with pain that both the pleasures and the pains appear more vehement from that comparison, and the loves of such pleasures produce rabid desires in the foolish and inflame them to fight. Just as Stesichorus <note>A Greek lyric poet who claimed Helen never went to Troy, but only her phantom did.</note> says the Trojans, ignorant of the true Helen, fought over her image. It is entirely necessary that it be so. What then regarding the nature of anger? Must not other similar things happen when someone acts upon it—either envy because of ambition, or violence because of a desire for contention, or anger because of a difficulty of character—following the fulfillment of honor, victory, and anger without reason and mind? Such things must happen here as well. Let us dare to assert, therefore, that regarding the part greedy for gain, and the other studious of victory, whatever appetites are such that they obey science and reason: if they follow and take those pleasures which reason itself permits, they will attain the truest pleasures insofar as their nature is capable of true pleasures, because they obey the truth, and moreover they perceive pleasures proper to themselves—if indeed what is best for each is also most "its own." Most proper. When therefore the whole soul conspires with that part in which philosophy is, far from all sedition, then it happens that each part performs its own office, and is just, and attains its own pleasures and the best, and moreover as far as possible the truest. Greatly so. But when any of the remaining parts prevails, it immediately happens that it neither finds its own proper pleasure, and it forces the other parts to follow an alien and least true pleasure. So it happens. Do not those things which are furthest from philosophy and reason most especially produce such things? Entirely. But what is furthest from reason is also furthest from law and order. Clearly. And those desires burning with love and tyrannical appeared to be separated by the longest interval. Entirely. But the kingly and moderate appetites appeared to differ the least. Yes. Therefore the tyrant will be very far from true and proper pleasure; but the King will be closest to it. Necessary. Therefore the tyrant will lead the most bitter life, and the King the sweetest. It is entirely necessary. Do you know how much more sadly the tyrant lives than the king? I will certainly know if you tell me. Since there are three desires, and one is indeed legitimate, while two are adulterous and spurious: the tyrant, having attained the highest peaks of the adulterous ones while he flees law and reason and mingles with certain slave and henchman pleasures—how long an interval he is separated from legitimate pleasure can hardly be expressed otherwise, unless perhaps in this way. In what way? From the man greedy for the power of the few, the tyrant appeared to be third. For the popular man was the middle of these. It is so. With the third image of pleasure, therefore, as far as truth is concerned, he meets after that one, if we said true things above. It must be said so. Furthermore, the one devoted to the power of the few is third from the king, if we place the aristocrat and the king in the same category. Third indeed. Therefore the tyrant is distant from true pleasure by triple the triple in number. So it appears. Thus the image of the tyrant is plain according to the number of length...

of tyrannical pleasure. Indeed, according to the second power and the third increase <note>Plato is using a mathematical metaphor here, cubing the distance between the king and the tyrant ($9^3 = 729$) to represent a three-dimensional "volume" of happiness.</note>, it is manifest how great an interval separates them. It is manifest, at least, to a calculator. If someone, reversing the order, asks how much the king surpasses the tyrant in the truth of pleasure, once the multiplication is completed, he will find that the king surpasses the tyrant in the sweetness of life—and the tyrant the king in the bitterness of life—by **seven hundred and twenty-nine degrees**. You have piled up a truly wondrous interval here between the life of the just and the unjust man in regards to pleasure and pain. This is certainly a true and fitting number for the lives of men, since days, nights, months, and years are fitting to them. <note>Ancient Greek astronomers often used 729 as a significant number related to the solar and lunar cycles (roughly the number of half-days and half-nights in a year).</note> They are indeed fitting. But if the good and just man so greatly exceeds the evil and unjust man in pleasure, it is surely even more wondrous how much more he will exceed him in the refinement, beauty, and virtue of his life. 

Wondrous indeed. But now that we have reached this point in the dispute, let us recall what was said at the beginning, which led us to these conclusions. It was said at one point that it profits a man to act unjustly if, while being entirely unjust, he is nevertheless thought to be just. Was it not said so? It was. To this, therefore, let us now respond, since we have agreed upon what power the operation of justice and injustice possesses. How? Let us **fashion an image of the soul in words**, so that he who spoke those things may recognize what sort of things he said. What kind of image? One like those creatures of old that are said to have existed in nature: the Chimera, Scylla, and Cerberus, and many others in which various forms are said to have grown together into one. They are indeed so described. 

Fashion, therefore, a single figure of a very diverse beast, having many heads in a circle—heads, I say, partly of domestic beasts and partly of wild ones—which is able to change and produce all these things from itself. You describe the skill of a strange painter, yet since speech is easier to mold than wax, let it be fashioned. Add to these, moreover, one form of a lion from above, and one form of a man above that. Let the first be the largest, the second narrower, and the third the narrowest. These are easy enough to fashion. Now join these three together so that they grow into one another to form a single being. They are joined. Around them, on the outside, place the image of a single man, so that to those who cannot look inside, but only see the outer covering, it appears to be one animal: a human being. 

I have placed it around them. Let us say, then, to him who asserts that it profits this man to act unjustly, and that living justly does not profit him at all: he is asserting nothing other than that it profits the man to feed that multi-headed beast and the lion, making the lion stronger, while allowing the human within to perish of hunger and become weak, to the point that he is dragged wherever those other parts lead him. Nor does he make one part familiar with the other or reconcile them, but rather lets them tear each other with bites and devour one another as they fight. Anyone who praises injustice would surely be saying this. 

Therefore, if someone says that just duties are profitable, he will advise that these things be done and said by which that "inner man" <note>This refers to the rational part of the soul, which Plato believes should govern the other parts.</note> might obtain the greatest power over the whole animal. Like a farmer, he should take care of that multi-headed beast, nourishing and tending to the domestic heads while immediately cutting away the wild ones, all while taking the nature of the lion as his helper. He cares for all parts in common, making them friendly to one another and to himself. Truly, this is what the man who praises justice says. Thus, by every reasoning, he who praises justice speaks the truth; he who praises injustice lies. For whether in regard to pleasure, or to beauty, or to profit, the praiser of the just pronounces the truth. The censurer, however, offers nothing of the truth, nor does he know what he disapproves of. 

In no way, at least it seems so to me. Let us therefore persuade him with gentle words, for he does not err of his own free will, asking him: "O blessed man, do we not say that honorable and shameful institutions of life exist for such reasons?" The honorable are those that subject the bestial part of our nature to the human—or perhaps rather to the **divine**—while the shameful are those that enslave the gentle part to the wild master. Will he agree, or not? He will agree, if he believes me. Is there anyone then whom it profits, by this reasoning, to take gold unjustly, if it happens that while he receives the gold, he compels the most excellent part of himself to serve the most ignoble? For if by receiving gold he made his son or daughter a slave to wild and wicked men, it would by no means profit him to have received it, not even if he took a great deal. If, then, he forces his most divine part to serve the most profane and wicked part, and is not touched by pity, is he not miserable? Has he not been corrupted by gifts of gold to his own much more grave destruction than **Eriphyle**, who accepted that necklace to betray her husband’s life? <note>original: "Eriphyle". In myth, she was bribed with the Necklace of Harmonia to convince her husband Amphiaraus to join the expedition of the Seven Against Thebes, knowing he would die there.</note> Very much so, I will answer for him. 

And do you not think that **intemperance** was of old called so for such a reason, because in it that dire, huge, and multi-headed beast wanders further than is fitting? It is clear. And are not **stubbornness** and **insolence** blamed when that lion-like and snake-like nature grows so strong that it becomes powerful beyond all moderation? Exactly. And is not **delicate luxury** blamed for the excessive loosening and relaxation of this same part, when it breeds cowardice and laziness within? Why not? Furthermore, are not **flattery** and **meanness** blamed when someone subjects this very vigor of spirit to the turbulent and multi-headed beast, and for the sake of money and its insatiable greed, casts it down and accustoms it from its earliest years to turn from a lion into a monkey? Greatly so. 

And why is the **mechanical and mercenary art** held in low esteem? Surely these things are infamous in us only when someone has been allotted a nature where the best part is so weak that he cannot dominate the beasts within him, but is only able and eager to tend to them and know their flatteries. It seems so. Therefore, so that such a man may be ruled by a leader similar to the one who rules the best of men, do we not say he ought to be the servant of that best man, who has a divine commander within himself? We do not think he should be a servant to the detriment of the subject (as **Thrasymachus** thought regarding all subjects), but because it is better for everyone to be subjected to a divine and wise prince—ideally having such a prince within himself, but if not, then at least to this external prince—so that we may all be, as far as possible, similar and friends, being subjects of the same ruler? 

Rightly so. It is clear from the law that this is its very purpose, since it provides for all citizens equally. This is also shown by the authority over children, who are not permitted to be their own masters until we have established a "republic" within them as if in a city. By tending to the best part of them, we create a similar guardian in them to take the place of our own best part—an inner ruler—and only then do we permit them to be free. This is clearly established. 

By what reasoning, then, O Glaucon, shall we assert that it profits anyone to act unjustly, or intemperately, or shamefully, from which deeds he will become worse, even while he acquires more money or any other power? None. In what way could it profit the wrongdoer...

And so governing, both in increasing and in spending money, he will act according to his strength. Greatly. Moreover, he will refer honors to the same place. For he will taste only those from which he hopes he will emerge better; but he will flee those, both privately and publicly, by which he might be disturbed, whenever he fears for the present state of his soul. Then he will never wish to administer public affairs, if he cares for that. Indeed, by the dog, I say, but in the city of himself. And most especially. Yet perhaps not in his fatherland, unless some divine chance should occur. I understand, indeed, that you speak of that city which we have founded for the present, which exists only in words, but nowhere on earth, as I think. But perhaps a pattern of it exists in heaven, conspicuous to him who wishes both to look upon it and, having looked, to institute himself according to it. It matters nothing, however, whether it is anywhere or will be. For he will do the duties of that city alone; those of another he will not. It is consistent.

**DIALOGUE TEN ON JUSTICE**
*
**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO**
*
HITHERTO Socrates, that most diligent pedagogue <note>A "pedagogue" was a teacher or guide of youth.</note> of the human race, has provoked the race of men to legal justice—that is, universal virtue—through the very beauty of justice. Similarly, he has called them back from injustice through the ugliness of injustice. Next, however, he will exhort them to the former through its everlasting fruit and reward, and he will keep them from the latter through its everlasting detriment and punishment; and that is the primary duty of this tenth book. But before he performs this chief duty, he uses a certain preface, in which he diligently finishes what he had touched upon in earlier dialogues and had not left at the end, which is very necessary for public safety. Truly, this physician of our human diseases is more diligent in curing that kind of disease which others not only treat negligently, but never even treat at all; indeed, what is worse, they love it as a most healthy thing and embrace it with all study: I mean poetic imitation, by which ingenious poets, while they express disturbed minds more sharply, more vehemently and deeply print similar disturbances into the minds of those listening and reading. And they infect everyone all the more because they are praised and pleasing. Truly, such a preface does not follow the end inconsistently: for there the soul is distributed into reason and into lower parts agitated by disturbances, the rule of which in the soul first, and then in the city, is called "tyrannical." But since poetic imitation arouses, cherishes, and increases parts of this kind—irritating anger, tickling lust, dissolving into laughter, pouring out tears and complaints—it therefore seems to undermine the kingdom of reason and to bring in the tyranny of disturbance. Wherefore Socrates destroys such a pest, pleasant otherwise but most poisonous, lest it destroy us. And see with what great charity our Plato everywhere consults the human race, namely searching out and looking around for those dangers which no one else at all would suspect: add moreover that he strongly fights for public safety, even though it is very repugnant to his own nature and education, that is, to poetry. Wherefore it should seem a wonder to no one that Plato here, for the love of truth, does not spare even his own Homer, since for the cult of justice he does not even indulge his own genius. He especially detracts from Homer so that, through him as the prince of imitators, we may consider the others much more condemned. And since he says that neither divine nor human things are taught by Homer, understand the praises attributed to Homer by Plato in the *Philebus* not as Plato's own opinion, but as deduced from common opinion. But he proves that the skill of imitators is, as we have narrated, very dangerous, and furthermore slavish and most vile. Since imitators neither understand the things themselves nor make them, but following the forms of things appearing to the senses, and catching at common opinions about them, they both report certain images and obey the senses and disturbances, having no regard for reason. However much he disapproves of poets where they disturb, so much does he approve if they exhort toward virtue and piety through the honorable praises of heroes and divine hymns. But so that he may express how vile all imitation is, he divides the genus of arts into three species: using, fabricating, and imitating. And indeed he says the one who uses the lyre—that is, music—surpasses the art of the lyre-maker, since by a certain prescribed end, he proposes to him the form of the work to be fabricated. But the fabricator surpasses the painter, who imitates the lyre with colors. Such he judges the poet also to be, thus reporting images of things to the ears just as the painter does to the eyes. If among these certain theological mysteries about the Ideas are inserted, which because we have opened them more widely in theology, we will touch upon briefly for the present. Come now, Platonic contemplator, ascend from those forms which you perceive in the matter of the world to the nature that is the mother of such forms. Which, if you do not perceive it, yet think of it as infused into the matter of the world like a vital spirit and full of seeds, and artistically disposing each thing through the seeds. Know that this nature in the world is such as you know the vegetal power to be in yourself. Therefore, just as you understand the power of sensing to preside over the vegetal nature in yourself, so also in the world, reduce the similar but most common nature into a source of sensing that is, as it were, similar but most common. Then also in yourself, reduce sense into reason, and reason into intellect, and in the world similarly reduce the genus of sensing into rational nature, and this into the intellectual genus. Furthermore, when you perceive in your own intellect that it desires that which is intelligible as something more perfect, and is formed by it as by something more powerful, place the intelligible nature before the intellectual nature, both in the world and in yourself. Call the intelligible itself the same thing as Being itself. Finally, place the Good itself before that which you have called both intelligible and Being. For you desire to exist so that you may be well, and you desire the intelligible for the sake of the Good itself. After you have ascended here, you will perceive the universe designated by a certain sacred sevenfold, rising from the lowest matter through sensible qualities, through nature, through sense, reason, intellect, the intelligible, to the Good itself. Furthermore, that the good spirit perfected all things under the number six, as on the sixth day, and in the seventh degree, as on the seventh day—that is, in himself—he rested. For the end of all other things is the Good itself. Of the Good, therefore, no end outside itself can either exist or be imagined. If all things desire the Good by which they may be perfected, conclude that all things are made by the Good. Likewise, if he makes all things by an intrinsic and proper virtue, understand that he embraces the universe in himself. But since he is the first and therefore simplest nature, remember that the forms of all things in him are one form of his own, which Plato calls the Idea of the Good itself, in which Timaeus said God the maker of the world rested when he had created the world, saying that the maker of the world received himself back into his own circumspection. Hence the Idea of the Good itself generates ideas—that is, special forms of all things, distinct among themselves only by species—in the intelligible nature, by which the universal being is comprehended in a certain intelligible way, and all intelligence also by a certain wonderful reason above intelligence. All intellects look up to this intelligible nature, and from it they receive stable formulas of the Ideas. The reasons of the soul also receive them, whence they have accepted formulas, though in some way mobile. After these formulas of the reasons of the souls, the images of the Ideas descend also to the sensual virtue. Thence into the vegetal nature as seeds, and finally through qualities into matter. When...

<meta>Ficino continues his philosophical exploration of the "Ideas" (Forms), explaining how God creates the ultimate pattern of species and why the soul's immortality is necessary for true justice to be rewarded.</meta>

444 Book Thirty-two.
When therefore Plato says that God makes Ideas in nature, understand this as being in the nature and the intelligible world of the angelic captains. But when he spoke of the bed and the table, let it be said for the sake of example, so that through these artifacts you may understand natural things—that is, by the bed and the table, understand the man who uses them. Furthermore, an example in art seemed more suited to the proposed question. Perhaps indeed he does not think that forms necessary for the rules of the arts are absent from the Ideas. Nor should it seem a wonder that man has the forms of the arts from the divine, since imaginations of the arts are not lacking even to beasts. And if forms of this kind are made divinely in the soul, they will be said to be made in nature for this reason, because they are naturally implanted. But if someone seems rather inept at certain artifacts, the Platonists will say he has either been distracted by various things or has turned himself entirely to opposites. Note the words of Plato saying that God not only understands, but also wills, signifying that God conceives within himself by understanding, and fabricates outside himself by willing. Note again that God has expressed only one Idea in species for one natural species in the intelligible world itself—for instance, one ideal humanity for the human species. For if in matter, where there is innumerable and mobile variety, a certain union of common nature is preserved in individual men, much more in a simple and stable nature is a single Idea sufficient for one natural species. Indeed, these diverse and unstable things cannot have a union of nature in themselves from anywhere else than from the unity of that sublime nature. Again, if two "humanities" were posited, certainly by the reasoning that each is humanity, they do not differ between themselves; indeed, they are one. Therefore, if they were to differ, surely they would disagree with each other through certain additions joined to each. Thus neither would be the absolute humanity itself, but a certain humanity and such-and-such, and something human rather than humanity. And each, as a participant in the same humanity, would similarly be called human: and besides these, there will be humanity in itself, one before it is taken up by many subjects. Rightly God, since he is simply the cause, is not to be called the author of a certain man, or of a certain horse, but the author of Man and Horse. Therefore he procreated one absolute Idea for each species of things. But when among us here this man generates that one, this man is by no means to be called the author of Man simply, but the author of something of a certain man. For neither is man alone the cause, but he is in the cause, namely in the number of causes: nor does he make the whole: for he does not give the first matter, or the soul, or the principle to the man himself: for before this one, Man was everywhere, and without the work of this man, Man exists and will exist everywhere. But where Plato says God procreated one Idea because he either did not want there to be more, or some necessity was in it that there be no more, understand that in God necessity is turned with will, so that it is necessary to be so because God wills it to be so. Since in the highest simplicity of divinity, necessity is nothing other than will. Therefore if you say, "it is necessary for God so to will or to do," I will similarly turn it: "God wills it to be so necessary." Rightly where the highest goodness concurs with the highest power, there the highest liberty conspires with the highest necessity. Among these, certain separate things are to be considered, yet very useful. Such as this: Reading or doctrine, unless it leads to the best reason of life, is useless. In which matter the life and discipline of Pythagoras was admirable, and rightly of the greatest authority among all, even in Plato's time. Likewise poems, if the harmonic composition of words is taken away, come to nothing for the mourner. Furthermore, virtue, whether of a man or of a thing, consists in a certain faculty contributing chiefly to that end for whose sake both the thing itself was made and the man was born. Meanwhile, a certain distinction appears between sense and reason, because the senses are mostly deceived about magnitude and figure and number and weight: yet meanwhile reason, through the faculty itself of measuring and numbering and weighing, corrects the judgment of the sense. It is established, moreover, that the soul cannot at the same time through the same power judge the same thing in a contrary way. It also appears that diverse powers of desiring are in us. For we may desire and reject the same thing at once. Note that it is not to be demanded of a good citizen that he should feel no pain at all, but that he should console such rising pain with reasons. Where it appears that there is one part of the soul which, as if sick, needs medicine, and another which, as if healthy, heals. These reasons against pain are chiefly four. First, because it is uncertain whether that which happened is good or evil. Second, that whatever it may be, it is certainly to be weighed lightly. For nothing among all human things is to be weighed as great. Third, that we profit nothing at all by grieving. Fourth, because pain always hinders that which could be a sudden help to us. He confirms these from the fact that it is most shameful to be overcome, and most beautiful to overcome. He who is pressed by pain or any other disturbance is already most shamefully overcome. Therefore he commands that in adversities and disturbances we should chiefly use the office of a physician, who does not grieve with the grieving, but heals them.

He compares the daily lots of life to the throws of dice, which he wants to be corrected by reasons, just as the throws of dice seem to be corrected by a certain skill of the game. But the preceding precepts are as it were certain preludes to those which follow. Most of all of these, let that contest be proposed to us in life by which we may overcome vice and follow virtue, and all things whatsoever which are held as good among men, so that we ourselves may be good, let us hold for nothing. Since the proper reward of justice is greater than all the rewards that can be reported among men: since even the splendor of justice itself surpasses all these things beyond measure, and in mobile, brief, and shadowy things, a reward fitting for immobile, everlasting, and most true justice cannot be found. From these it is concluded that the immobile habit of justice ought to be desired because of the immobile reward. Which indeed remains after the racecourse of the present life for the labors of justice. Otherwise justice itself, which is judged the most excellent good, would be an evil for just men continually laboring for the love of justice, and often affected by injury, and not avenging the injury; add also those despising present goods for the desire of eternal ones, and not reporting the reward of justice among men—indeed, often reporting unjust punishment instead of justice. Wherefore, lest the good should harm, and justice lack a reward, and God either provide too little or not repay according to merits, it must be judged that souls will be immortal. Especially so that both the unjust, who while living did not pay the penalties of injustice, may at least pay them when dead, and the just, entirely despised among mortals, may be crowned among those above. Hence he hands down a noble precept: The immortal soul ought not to be solicitous for this brief time, but for all time. Plato shows the immortality of the soul in the *Phaedrus* and *Phaedo*, and elsewhere. And he shows that reasons of this kind are certain demonstrations in the book *On Science* <note>Referring to the *Theaetetus* or similar works on epistemology.</note>, saying that the words of those who think contrary things, when examined, finally turn out to be ridiculous. Likewise in the *Gorgias*, affirming that these mysteries have been proved by adamantine reasons. Furthermore, in this tenth book, where after the argumentation he adds that we are forced to confess it both by such argumentation and by many others. I think indeed that in Plato's words a certain wonderful force lies hidden, understood by very few, so that it is no wonder if through Platonic argumentations some think it is demonstrated, but others think it is not yet demonstrated. Certainly Demosthenes, a hearer of Plato, was persuaded with such efficacy by the living voice that he said he preferred to die honorably than to live basely, after he had heard Plato and Xenocrates debating on the immortality of souls. Cleombrotus perceived the same force in the Platonic writings, as did many hearers of Hegesias at Cyrene, who liberated themselves from the prison of the body because of the desire for another life. The Platonic Boethius perceived the same, conceding with philosophy as witness that this was demonstrated to him by certain reasons. Aurelius Augustine seems to have felt the same, where he says he never doubted this matter. These things are confirmed by Avicenna, saying that certain reasons for these are demonstrations. Nor does Plato say here only that it can be demonstrated, but even that it is easily demonstrated among those, as I think, who, since they themselves have a mind purged and segregated from the body, rightly do not distrust that the soul, once segregated from the body, can live. Since they themselves experience that their mind, separated from the senses, lives better than when conjoined. They also have discovered that the souls of others, immersed in bodies and thus vicious, do not perish from their own vice and disease, and therefore much less can they be corrupted by an external disease, that is, of the body. Since even the body itself is not destroyed by an external evil before an intrinsic evil is brought in from it, by which it is most closely destroyed. For the rest, lest anyone distrust the divinity of his soul, he commands him to purge it thoroughly from the filth contracted from corporeal love, and once purged, to perceive how pure, how simple, how greedy for divine things (as if kindred to divinity), how quickly, and how well it is capable of divine light. But as for his saying that souls do not become more in number day by day, understand this as meaning they do not so become as to arise and be composed from bodies. Which indeed the following reason makes manifest, saying: if divine things were composed from bodies, finally since divine things are never resolved back into bodies, there would be nothing left of bodies in nature. Again, note what he adds, that the soul is not composite: otherwise it might not be indissoluble. And understand that for an essence not to be able to be dissolved, it must either be composed of nothing, or if it is composed, yet not be composed of any matters, and so be fused again that in its composition multitude does not surpass unity; indeed, unity through harmonic union must surpass multitude, and state must surpass motion. Conclude the mystery, pertaining partly to providence, partly to immortality and the reward of justice. The just man indeed turns out similar to God, the unjust dissimilar. And since it is not hidden from God that this one is similar to himself, but that one dissimilar, it is consistent with reason that the just man is dear and a friend to God, the unjust the opposite. Therefore, God by no means neglects the just as friends, but always looks forward to them in such a way...

<meta>Ficino delves into the "Myth of Er" from the end of Book X, explaining the allegorical significance of the numbers, the afterlife "Meadow," and the celestial mechanics of the Fates.</meta>

Dialogue X. On the Republic. Or, on Justice. 445

...that even if individual things seem adverse to them, they finally turn out prosperous, whether for the living or the dead. But why did he assert the mystery of immortality here with a certain historical example rather than with the diligence of argumentations? Because citizens are to be provoked to justice not so much by the skill of words as by example and work. Furthermore, why does he bring into the middle, to confirm it, a man rising from the dead? Because even if immortality is established by reasons, and a certain common execution of justice, yet the place, form, and disposition of either reward or punishment must be received from one who has been present there. Which is signified to us near the end of the *Phaedo*. Nor is it without cause that he testifies that Er the Pamphylian rose again, having died in battle for the safety of his country, to signify that those who die for the public good will rise again to true life, although out of many, one rose for our sake. But is this history, or a fable? Justin the Platonic, a Christian martyr, wants it to be history. Which I indeed will not refute. But where Plato calls it an apologue and a fable, it can be explained that history can be called a fable whenever, beyond the things done, it has a narrower allegory. For which cause Olympiodorus also says that Plato often called histories and reasons "fables." And since he disposes the shades and the places and figures of justice differently in the *Phaedrus*, the *Gorgias*, the *Phaedo*, and here and elsewhere, it is clearly evident that these contain an allegorical sense besides the form of the place. Moreover, he uses the number twelve here regarding the resurrection, which among the ancients is the number of the worldly spheres, they thinking that there are eight heavens above the four elements: as if he would say that there is need of divine virtue, the mistress of the universe, to rouse the dead, and that this sometimes happens for the teaching of men by divine providence. There are also those who say that the "Great Year," in which the soul of man completes its circuit through which it returns to the same state, is comprised of twelve thousand years, and that such a year of the world is equaled by three such years, in which the soul of the world through the motion of the firmament completes its ambit, to be completed in thirty-six thousand years. Indeed, they want the circuit of our soul to be driven through twelve thousand years because it must run through all the spheres, and the choruses of demons and gods, which in the *Phaedrus* are distributed through twelve orders. But what do the two openings in the earth mean, and as many in heaven? So that you may understand that souls descend to earthly things by one way, namely by a certain corporeal habit; but ascend from the earth by another, namely by the purgation of that habit. Similarly, they fall from heaven into the elements of the body through the love of the elemental, and in turn rise into celestial things, this love being extinguished and a celestial one kindled. Hence Orpheus says that Love has the keys of all things, both of those above and those below. He places the judges of souls in the air and the ether as angels, ministers of divine providence. After the sentence, the just seek heaven, carrying before them both their works and judgments: because namely they have known themselves, they shine both for themselves and for others: the unjust on the contrary descend, carrying their deeds behind their backs. For they neither knew themselves, nor did they profit themselves, but are an example to others rather than a help to themselves. The Meadow in which the souls, both ascending and descending, rest for a time, is a certain middle region between the lower and celestial parts, and a disposition between a good habit and an evil one, and a state between beatitude and misery, designated like a limbo in the air. Here notice that souls which had mutual knowledge in the previous life recognize each other in turn in the other. Likewise, in such a meadow, souls reside for a very long time according to the Platonists—those of children who died in infancy: of whom Er recounted certain things little worthy of memory. Because since they declined to neither part by choosing, nor brought on a habit, the Platonists leave them in natural light only. But they think the blessed are placed above natural light, and the wretched below that light. Furthermore, the matter of purgatorial punishments is treated here. But why is fault abolished by pains? Namely because it grew in through pleasures. Do not physicians also cure diseases mostly by their contrary? Notice that Plato not without reason uses the number ten to delete fault, and a hundred besides, and a thousand. Truly, for any degree of pleasure, he applies ten degrees of punishment. First, it is asked for what cause more degrees of punishment are paid than degrees of pleasure were perceived. It is answered that it is so owed because of the crime of injured divine majesty. Furthermore, just as the joys of beatitude exceed the pains of human justice, so do the tortures of misery exceed the pleasures of injustice. Finally, marks are not so easily deleted as they are easily printed: nor would he who confirmed the habit of sin have ceased to transgress if he had lived longer. Then it is asked, why ten degrees? What if Plato imitated the Mosaic Decalogue? And since he thought that he who altogether neglected any one of the ten acted in some way against the precepts of the divine law, he rightly judges him to be tortured ten times? Therefore the number ten is called universal. For it either implies all numbers within itself, or explains them through itself and its own by replicating. Moreover, the universal number is opportunely accommodated for purging souls, so that by this it may be signified that the universal stain of the body must be laid down before you come to the prince of the universe, with whom nothing corporeal can exist. It is asked after this, why besides the ten degrees of punishments, a hundred years are attached to the unjust. I answer: because if they had lived up to a hundred years, by which term the life of man is in some way designated, they would have sinned continually. But to each of the ten degrees, the number hundred is attributed, from which the number thousand is made. Hence that saying: "They wander for a hundred years." Also: "They rolled the wheel for a thousand years." Furthermore, you shall receive a hundred for one. For Plato uses these numbers not only in punishment, but also in certain rewards. Truly, if ten is led into itself by multiplying ten times ten, from it is born a hundred. Then if it is reduced into itself, by computing ten times ten times ten, a thousand is procreated. Therefore both ten is a universal number, and a hundred and a thousand are universal numbers. Also if you proceed from one into ten, a linear number is born. If from ten into a hundred, it becomes a superficial number. If from ten into a thousand, it becomes solid. So that we may explain allegorically: the soul of the unjust man has departed from itself into the body and is infected with a corporeal stain. It is surely to purge this universal stain through ten, which is a universal number. But that it is necessary for ten to be led into itself creating a hundred, signifies that the soul ought to emerge from the body to itself through reason. Then that there is need to reduce ten into itself generating a thousand, allegorically teaches that the soul ought not only to be turned toward itself through reason, but also to be converted into itself through intelligence, and thus be reduced into its own unity, by which finally it can enjoy God, the highest unity of all. Moreover, the linear number and superficial and solid mystically teach that to purify the mind, not only the external surface of works, words, and thoughts, but also all the most profound inner parts must be most diligently searched. After limbo and purgatory, he descends to the lower world. But know that the Platonists want punishments in purgatory to be temporal, and also temporal joys in a certain celestial region, so that each responds to the other equally. For they distinguish thus: either the sense in life entirely obeyed reason, or reason entirely obeyed sense, or they always fought each other: and in that fight either sense mostly or reason prevailed. Souls therefore in which sense has entirely complied with reason through a confirmed habit, obtain an everlasting reward. On the contrary, those affected otherwise are condemned to everlasting punishments. But the middle ones, if reason prevailed, are transferred to temporal rewards; if however sense prevailed, to temporal punishments. But to those to whom no time for consulting was given, limbo is kept among the Platonists as a place for choosing, designated here under the name of the "Meadow." And if the Platonists sometimes call meadows celestial, especially the highest ones, here nevertheless the meadows signify the airy region. For in what way would he signify the sublime heaven here through meadows, when he says that some souls descend to these from the heavens, and others arrive suddenly from the bowels of the earth? Let such meadows then be certain sublime tracts of air, contiguous to those sublime tracts of the earth which he describes in the *Phaedo* in the form of an earthly paradise, having happy cultivators under a perpetual spring. In the same place they also place the Elysian fields, earthly ones I say. For the eighth heaven has the celestial Elysium. Hence that saying:
"The stars hold the celestial floor, and the forms of the gods."
I pass over for the present Proclus and Plotinus, who where Plato says "everlasting," explain it as the universal time of the "Great Year," in which the circuits of individual times are completed. I approve more of Porphyry in part on this, and Iamblichus, so that eternal things may be understood from this. For where Plato calls the soul "incurable," and such that it can never be purged, he sufficiently indicates eternal punishments, and in turn infinite joys. But in what way certain others explain these, I have not judged worthy of memory. Furthermore, if you consider the words of Plato, you will recognize that Gospel: "With hands and feet bound, cast him into the outer darkness." But he adds here, "with the head bound." The bond of the head signifies the impediment of reason and the loss of light. The knot of the hands, the privation of action and progress. Finally, the bound feet do not lead, do not progress, do not arrive, but are snatched away by force applied. You will also recognize under the figure of fiery men the avenging demons and corporeal punishments, and you will perceive the same from many conjectures. You will note also the proper word for "outer." Furthermore, darkness, where the openings are closed. Also under the name of "lowing," the gnashing of teeth and weeping. But after he has disposed the places and punishments, and signified the joys through the opposite form, and touched upon the middle things, he now returns to those souls which flowed into the meadow, partly from heaven after a temporal reward, and partly from the earth after a temporal...
