### [Page 446]
### Thirty-First Book [of Ficino's Commentary]

...they flowed together to the [places of] punishments. He says it is necessary for these to return again into elemental generation, and to progress through it until they earn a firmer state, or eventually the firmest state. He says these souls rested for seven days in the meadow. Here, you might interpret the sevenfold number through the seven planets; likewise through the seven-day periods of seven weeks in which the fetus rests in the womb before birth, and even through every seven days in which the forms are changed step-by-step in the uterus—perhaps you will seem to contribute something by this. But what does that have to do with souls? For they are no longer in the planets, as they have descended; and they are not yet enclosed in the womb, for they are about to descend into the uterus after they have come to the three fates. Meanwhile, in an aerial body, they inhabit the aerial region. But let it be so, if it pleases. Perhaps also because they live in a certain sterile way in the meantime, they are assigned to a certain sterile number. And since the sevenfold number is neither produced from any number found [multiplied] by another, nor does it produce any [square] within ten, it most aptly fits souls still vacant from generation on both sides. The Pythagoreans attribute this same number to Pallas [Athena], because she was neither born from a mother nor did she give birth. They wish this to agree also with souls still removed from an earthly mother and contemplating the universe under the wisdom of Pallas. 

But as soon as they rise from such a vacation, they undergo the eightfold number, which is both produced and is the first among solid numbers. Therefore, it is fitting for a soul almost about to approach a solid body. We call the eightfold a "solid" because it is created from the two-fold repeated three times by itself and returning into itself, signifying a triple dimension. For two times two times two completes eight. Add to this that in celestial music, the seventh voice is entirely dissonant, but the eighth is the most consonant of all. Moreover, it is necessary for the body to harmonize with the soul as much as both harmonize with fate, so that the celestial soul may enter into commerce with the terrestrial body. Of this harmony, once the numbers are finally completed, the soul now dissonates from the earth itself and harmonizes with heaven, if only it is to be happy. 

Furthermore, regarding the fact that Plato subjoins four days to the eight days for the progress of generation: understand that in the nature of the vegetable soul, a certain power and effect now reigns in a way to form a body constituted from the four elements. Likewise, under the eighth consonance, there is need for a fourth, approaching consonance in a way, and a fifth, which is now a true consonance. For five is made if you wish to compute the following four together with the preceding one. Furthermore, you will see assigned here the twelve-fold number, by which souls approach the beginnings of generation. For to that work, there is need of the help of the twelve spheres and the divine and demonic orders. Moreover, the twelfth voice and consonance is most perfect, resulting from the *diapason* [octave] and *diapente* [fifth], resulting from the eighth and fifth, fitting by its own grace for the affairs of a lover, and also suitable for weddings. Indeed, such souls, led now by a certain Venus-like love, so to speak, are to be reconciled to earthly weddings. 

But why, when Plato was to compute the twelve-fold, and after seven there was a remainder to be added, did he not immediately say "five"? Namely, so that through "eight" and through "four" he might hint at the mysteries you have heard; and again, through the journey of one day added to complete the twelve-fold, you might notice that a body composed of four elements cannot be prepared for the soul before it has been tempered into a single five-fold form, as if similar to heaven, and the soul easily imprints upon the figured body a single vital act from itself. 

Because, however, souls declining toward composite bodies are largely subjected to the laws of fate, and in turn glide toward them with fate as their guide, therefore he says these souls proceed into the sight of fate. First, therefore, he depicts nature itself under a columnar light, which is the bond of the universe. By "nature," he understands the vital and feminine power infused into the matter of the world by the World Soul itself. This is called "light" because it is penetrating and vital. Likewise, it is called a "straight column" because it penetrates the whole of matter everywhere, as if along its length, and produces many grades of forms differing in species and genus. It is also said to be extended through every part and to bind heaven on all sides, because it is present and contains everything everywhere, and propagates many things as if through certain sides equal and similar to each other—yet in such a way that from length, one arrives at breadth, because by penetrating it is also diffused, and insofar as it is diffused, it fills and rules by filling. Hence that saying: *The spirit nourishes within.* 

The variety of colors declares the variety of the feminine power. In this nature, surely, lies the fatal spindle: according to the imagination, it is the axis of the spheres itself, adorned at both ends with twin poles; according to reason, however, it is a certain image of the mundane soul, and its vegetable power presiding over nature, moving it like an instrument to manufacture natural things not only skillfully but also inevitably—so that there is not only order from nature in the world, but also an inevitable order from fate. Hence that saying in the *Politicus*: *The world is led by natural desire and fate.* But the kinship of such nature with fate is so great that they are scarcely distinguished by philosophers. To express the immutable nature of fate, he said its spindle was made of **Adamant**. The whorl—that is, the head—is again from Adamant and other materials, namely the stars, not only fixed but also mobile and common, with a manifold variety of forms. 

Next, he evidently depicts the eight spheres, which are indeed agitated by nature, but are immutably agitated by fate presiding over nature, and are said to be the instruments of fate. Among these, many things are insisted upon pertaining to the measurements, depths, intervals, motions, harmonies, forms, and powers of the celestial spheres, which we shall explain more opportunely in the commentaries on the *Timaeus*. Briefly, however, imagine that from the swiftest and most orderly motion of the heavens and the most powerful contact, a huge, varied, and sweetest melody is created: deeper voices from the slower motions, sharper ones from the swifter, and middle ones from the middle. But because the elemental sense of hearing lacks proportion to the celestial melody, such a sound is not heard. Here we think of the nine Muses and the Sirens, the tones of the eight spheres, and the harmonic concert from the tones. 

Hence he says the fatal spindle, that is, the **erasum** [the worked object], turns between the knees of the goddess Necessity. She has three daughters: **Lachesis**, **Clotho**, and **Atropos**, who along with their mother will the celestial things. I pass over what Proclus thinks of these, placing not only one universal Jupiter as the maker of the whole world, but three particular Jupiters as makers under him. Next, by equal proportion, there is one goddess Necessity in that order guarding all things, in which the common Jupiter composed everything. Furthermore, there are three fates, that is, three goddesses, daughters of this Necessity, of whom some under the mother’s empire preserve certain things far from transgression. And he places the goddess Necessity entirely above the world, but the daughters partly removed from the world and partly declining toward the world. 

To me, however, as to most other Platonists, it is more pleasing that Necessity is the World Soul. The three daughters are three powers of this soul pertaining to fatal matters. He calls her Necessity, not because she brings violence either to nature or to reason, but because she preserves everything in its own order instituted by the Maker of things, nor does she permit anything to transcend those laws so far that it does not soon return to the laws. She turns the heavens with her knees, that is, with the lowest part of herself, with such ease that she meanwhile most expeditiously enjoys the joy of contemplation. 

But he calls this vegetable part of her by three names: **Lachesis**, because she is the mistress of the seeds of things, and of the lots and forms of lives which she infuses into the souls about to descend. **Clotho**, next, because she evolves the internal lots of life in their order into the act of living, and unfolds them into effect. Finally, **Atropos**, because she confers and guards life, already evolved into act by an undeclinable progress, unto an inevitable end. Some name the first Vesta, the second Minerva, and the third Mars or Martia. 

Next, what he says about the Parcae singing to the harmonic motions of the Sirens: take this to mean that fatal lives proceed to effect through celestial motions and influences. The seats of Necessity and her daughters show the firmness of the fatal order, as if it were necessary for the progression of mobile things to be ruled and ordered by the immobility of the mover. The equal intervals of the seats evidently show that a just distribution is made both among the fates and through the fates. The white robes show the nature of the fates to be inviolate and innocent. For the universe does not do evil, which depends on the best guide of the universe. The crown describes the empire. To sing is to arrange through intervals of time individual things, which the divine mind prescribes in a moment to be arranged in times. Hence it happens that the Parcae all sing of temporal things. 

And why does Lachesis sing of the past, Clotho of the present, and Atropos of the future? Proclus responds that in the past, three times are thought of: for it is said to be "past," and once to have been "present," and before it was present, to have been "future." In the present, the "present" itself is thought of, which previously had been "future." In the future, finally, only the "future" is recognized. After these things, he declares that Lachesis is the chief. In the second place of dignity is Clotho. In the third, Atropos. 

But why do the Parcae handle the globes with their hands, but the mother not at all? Because the lowest powers of that soul are more closely related to the globes than the substance of the soul itself. Why likewise does Lachesis touch with both hands? Because in the beginning both the middle and the end are contained. Why then does Clotho touch the larger circuit from the outside and with her right hand? While Atropos touches the narrower from the inside and with her left? Because the evolution of life through the middle begins from an external cause, and is broader, and happens more prosperously. The inevitable end, however, already proceeds from an internal conceived property, and defines itself into a narrow space. Add that it creeps in secretly, and mostly against one's wish. 

As for what he says about the Parcae...
*[Margin: Parcas]*

### [Page 447]
### Dialogue X on the Republic, or, on Justice.

...touching the heaven with a certain intermission of time, do not think that the fatal powers of the mundane soul sometimes rule mundane things and sometimes do not. For if there were mutability in fate, whose property is immutability itself, nothing could be imagined as not mutable. Plato, therefore, depicts divine offices in a human manner and speech, wishing to hint that the fates partly handle the things themselves, and partly not: both because the virtue of the mundane soul, consisting in the dignity of integrity itself, accommodates its action to governing things, and in turn while it accommodates, it is not mixed; and because they exhibit a temporal change in works, and the intermission they are said to have in their operation they demonstrate not in themselves, but in the effect; and also because it handles natural things, but does not touch supernatural things. For those things which pertain to pure and free reason, or to divine intelligence superior to fate, it touches not at all. Such things are reduced to the sublime providence of God, superior to celestial fate, in a certain wondrous order. Similarly, it is written in the *Politicus* that mundane things are ruled sometimes by fate, sometimes by providence: not because such a commutation happens through an intermittent change of times, but because daily some things happen under fate, and some are disposed through the laws of providence above the fatal series. 

To these things is added that our souls are sometimes entirely in providence, sometimes entirely in fate, sometimes in both at once. For when they live only with an unfettered contemplative mind, they live in providence alone, and entirely free. But when the inclination toward this body becomes strong in the vegetable part, and such an inclination is propagated as far as the imagination, declining now toward fate, they degenerate equally from liberty. But while they are joined to the composite body, they now merge themselves into the fate of their own body, and retain much less of their pristine liberty. Finally, after they have contracted bodily affections into a habit, they are now thoroughly overwhelmed by fate, deprived of all liberty. 

It is asked for what reason the souls here seem to approach Lachesis by a certain natural instinct. Truly, in the general nature of the corporeal machine are the seeds of all species, certain to sprout not only in forms and modes but also in times. Furthermore, in any proper nature of any species, there is a similar order of seeds, but pertaining to the propagation and preservation of its own species. Similarly, in any individual under a species, there is a property of forms and times to be produced in their own modes and times. These three natures are subsequently so disposed that the individual follows the specific, and the specific follows the general; so that for the most part, what is of the nature of one is likewise from the others, and the particular nature consents with the universal. 

Almost in the same way stands fate—that is, a certain prefiguration of things to be explained—both in the world soul itself, and in the souls of the twelve spheres and stars, and also in the souls that are now as if particular, in whose number are the human ones. In the vegetable virtue of our soul, therefore, there is a certain proper fate, and an involved series of future things, consenting in form, mode, and time together with the fates of the celestial souls and the world soul. Just as the germ of any plant, sprouting in its own certain figures and its own time, seems of its own accord to concur with the universal nature of the springtime provoking it to the same; so also souls by their own nature and fate opportunely bring forth certain lives then, when the universal fate similarly calls them to the same. Thus the chorus of souls, by their own certain figures to be danced and the diversity of various dancers at once, imitates the fatal song and sound. By "song" I would rather understand the celestial souls; by "sound," the spheres; and finally in us, fate. By such an instinct, souls in the auspices of life come to Lachesis to have their lots confirmed through the lots of Lachesis. 

It is confirmed, therefore, through a certain prophet. This "prophet" signifies two things: both the universal and primary influence of providence upon the soul, and the opportunity under which such a concurrence occurs, so that souls are carried to that which universal fate also carries. That he says the prophet disposes the souls in order and transfers the lots from Lachesis to them: this signifies that all these things are confirmed, both through the favor of divine providence and through the opportunity of that concurrence. 

Nor is it said without reason that the Parcae govern the universe with their hands, but the lots of souls are received from the knees of Lachesis. For since the government of the universe is more excellent than the disposition of souls, the former is rightly judged to be performed by the hands, and the latter by the knees. To sit upon a tribunal expresses authority and judgment. Among the "lots" of lives and the "examples," there seems to be this kind of distinction: that lots pertain to the vegetable powers, but examples to the imaginations, superior to the vegetable power but near to it. Surely, as soon as in this power such seeds of a future life have grown strong above the rest, at the same time in the imagination also the figures and machinations of a similar life arise, and the affections glow: just as among us, a cheerful imagination follows a sanguine affection of the body, a wrathful one follows a choleric, a sad one a melancholic, and a lustful one follows the [appropriate] one. 

Thus far proceeds fatal necessity. But indeed, reason is superior to imagination—to which belongs reasoning, counsel, and choice, and therefore motion toward either side is free—perceiving the figures and affections of the imagination, it can approve as well as disapprove of the description of such a life. For which reason, he says that virtue is free from fate, and the fault in the choice of a worse life belongs to the chooser, not to fate. For although it is by fate, both in common and in particular, to choose a new life now as before, yet it is by counsel to choose such a one specifically, or such. Indeed, if reason, by examining, rejects the first form of living offered by the imagination to the eyes of reason, another better one will not be lacking immediately, and then another. Hence that inspiration of providence is called a "prophet." For it pre-shows to reason, by a certain light of judgment, that it has a free faculty of consulting and choosing, [warning] what follows most of all from a rash choice. The prophet is also said to pour out the lots and propose examples of living: not only because the influx of divine providence in a way sanctions fatal things, but because he brings forward fatal lots and fatal examples to the examination and judgment of reason. 

As for his announcing in the proclamation that the souls are "ephemeral" [of a day], he expresses that they are both there in perpetual day, and that the life they value so much is but one day, and a nocturnal one at that. He adds "the beginning of another circuit," to open the mystery of souls returning from heaven to earth and back again. He calls the human race not only "mortal," but as souls propagate their own evils, he adds "death-bearing," as if to say the life of the body is the death of the soul. He then pronounces that even if reason is free from the beginning in choosing a life, nevertheless after it has chosen, it will no longer be free in rejecting it, although at some time it will be free in composing or tempering it in various ways, whatever it may be. 

If you ask why some souls of men choose some lives and others choose others: some will respond that there are certain differences of species in the natures of souls, others that they are individual and proper; and they will add many differences deduced from the diversity of a superior life. Plotinus strongly confirms this, and it most harmonizes with what follows. Furthermore, souls choosing a life simultaneously obtain a *daemon* as a guide of the chosen life. About this, we have said many things elsewhere. Here distinguish thus: 

The Platonists think of some gods outside the world, namely minds separated from the body like intellectual spheres, worshipping one God as the firmest center and most stable unity of the spheres. Others they call mundane, namely accommodated to revolving the spheres of the world beyond divine worship. Under these are the daemons, as if ministers to dispose and compose those things which happen either in species or in the spheres or from the spheres. They count just as many genera of daemons as there are powers found in the mundane gods, the leaders of the daemons. 

But truly, in any mundane God, unity itself is the supreme part of its substance, by which it reflects divine unity. After it is the intellect, containing all things at once, through which it represents the angelic minds. Likewise, reason, running through forms by a certain progression, proper to such souls. Furthermore, a certain imagination, entering through particular forms insofar as reason itself progresses through universal ones. Next follows the vegetable nature of the sphere, both vivifying and moving. According to these five powers, five genera of daemons are computed. Among these, the celestial daemons follow the unity of the mundane gods accommodately; the ethereal daemons (that is, the fiery ones), follow the intelligence of those same gods; the aerial daemons follow reason; the aquatic, imagination; and the terrestrial, the nature which we have called vegetable in the gods. Under these, the Orphic [tradition] places subterranean daemons, reflecting the bodies of the mundane gods in a lowest order, and avengers of crimes. Plato seems to have made mention of these here. 

If you ask what kind of daemons are primarily the leaders of souls descending into bodies, the answer will be: not the celestial, not the fiery. For these, being more sublime, lead souls back up, they do not lead them down. Likewise, neither the aquatic nor the terrestrial. For these, as the craftsmen of the lowest generation, do not so much lead the soul in the fatal journey as they precipitate it into the precipices of fate. Therefore, the aerial daemons remain—the middle leaders through middle things—who, as companions of divine reason, lead human reason in this journey. From this genus of daemons, some lead some souls [and others lead others]. Saturnian ones lead Saturnian souls, Martian ones lead Martian, and others similarly, each most accommodated to each, both from the soul's own proper affection and from common providence and fate, and primarily according to the form of the chosen life. With this leader of life, the souls now undergo the three fates, which they had only seen before...

---

### [Page 448]
### Thirty-First Book [of Ficino's Commentary]

...namely with the daemon thus decreeing as the executor of the whole order, and the corporeal affection now gradually prevailing. Finally, after the three Parcae, they pass to the mother of the Parcae: Necessity herself, whose impulses they now experience. 

Next, that the souls go under a vehement heat can signify three things: namely, that corporeal loves grow burning, and at the same time care and anxiety increase. Likewise, to descend through the sphere of fire from heaven. Furthermore, the ministry of natural heat for vivifying the terrestrial body. But because through excessive care for earthly things, celestial things are consigned to oblivion, and through oblivion sterility happens from fertility, therefore they soon descend into the Lethean field, that is, the field of forgetfulness, which is entirely sterile. And because of diligent care for mortals, eternal things are neglected, whence both oblivion is born and loss, and difficulty of reminiscence; he says the souls in the Lethean field descend all the way to the river Amelita [Ameles], that is, the bottom of negligence, and there they lie down under the night, that is, they are prostrated under the privation of divine light. 

But what does it signify that the water of Amelita can never be contained in any vessel? This is a poetic metaphor, signifying the lower matter, which is called a river, flowing constantly through forms and fluctuating. Likewise, the vice of oblivion, which is to retain nothing but immediately to pour it out. Add that no extrinsic support preserves a soul perishing by its own negligence. Furthermore, that it is necessary to drink from the river of oblivion is clear, because it is thus instituted from proper nature and common fate and providence. To drink either more water or less results from the effect upon the body more or less extensively: and the same is the cause of greater or lesser oblivion, or rather of a greater or lesser faculty for reminiscence. 

Surely, the soul experiences these passions in a way in a certain body composed of thicker air in the superior field, before it is enclosed in the womb of the terrestrial mother. For from celestial bodies to terrestrial ones, the descent happens not only through the element, but through an aerial body. He adds that the souls in this aerial body sleep until the middle of the night, showing that soon under the terrestrial body there will be not half but a whole night of ignorance. Sleep bears witness both to the impediment of reason and the fallaciousness of judgment. 

Finally, he says the souls are insinuated into the terrestrial womb under a certain thunder and earthquake, for nearly two reasons: both indicating that they enter this prison with unhappy auspices, and showing that both celestial and terrestrial motion, and indeed a vehement one, must concur to coerce the divine soul in such a foul prison. That the souls leaped forth to generation like stars: beyond the poetic figure, he hints that souls are in a way stellar, and will finally return to the stars. 

Regarding the fact that Plato tells such a ridiculous fable about the migration of souls into the bodies of beasts, differing not at all from the tales of old women: surely he warns us that the whole thing is to be explained allegorically: namely, that rational souls do not migrate into the life of a brute, but into a "brute-like" life, that is, in a way similar to a brute and vice-versa. This was pleasing to almost all Platonists except Plotinus. And Origen in his books against Celsus seems to confirm the same. 

But you, do not neglect the moral precept: that the skill of right choice is to be preferred to all things and arts. Furthermore, so many things about the beauty and power of the spheres were brought in here, so that we might think that justice and a huge reward will follow in heaven, and will greatly lead to the best choice of living. But you will say now, great-hearted **Laurentius** [Lorenzo de' Medici], that you have received a commentary from Marsilio Ficino here rather than a mere summary (*argumentum*). Let it be so; I think it was and will be worthwhile that I promised a summary, but provided a commentary.

***

**I**ndeed, as I was thinking to myself (I said) about this city which we have recently established in words, while we seem to have established many other things quite rightly, then most especially those which were brought forward concerning poetry. 
Which are those? he asked. 
Namely, that no part of poetry which consists in imitation should be received. For it is now, as it seems to me, transparent above all else that nothing of that sort is to be received by us, after the individual species of the soul have been separately distinguished. 
How do you say this? 
So that I may say among you what I feel (for you will not accuse me in the presence of the tragic poets and other imitators), all these things seem to be a certain corruption of the mind for those who, when they hear these imitations, do not have that remedy of the mind by which they may most effectively discern what sort of fables these are. 
To what purpose is this? 
It must be said, although a certain friendship and reverence contracted from my boyhood for **Homer** holds me back. For he seems to have been the first leader and teacher of all those distinguished tragic poets. But I do not think a man should be preferred to the truth. Therefore, what I have begun must be said. 
By all means. 
Listen then. Or rather, respond. 
Ask. 
Can you explain to me at all what imitation is? For I do not sufficiently understand what it is. 
And shall I then understand? 
That is no wonder. For it often happens that those with a duller edge perceive some things before those who see more sharply. 
It is as you say. But in your presence, I would never dare to express what seems to me. But you yourself see. Do you wish us to begin from here, considering by our usual method? We are accustomed to posit a single species for any plurality to which we give the same name. Do you not understand? 
I understand indeed. 
Let us posit now any one from many. For example, there are many beds and tables. 
Why not? 
Yet the Ideas of these things are two. One of the bed, the other of the table. 
So it is. 
We are accustomed to say that the craftsman of either furniture thus absolves his work, so that he looks toward that Idea, one for beds, the other for tables, which we ourselves use, and other things similarly. For no craftsman makes the Idea itself. 
For in what way could he? 
In none. 
See further whether you would call someone such a craftsman? 
What kind? 
One who makes all things whatsoever that every single craftsman of those who work with their hands makes. 
You speak of a powerful and wonderful man. 
I have not yet expressed his whole power. Perhaps you will wonder much more if I express it. For this same craftsman is not only able to manufacture all furniture, but he also makes whatever grows from the earth, and all animals and himself. He also completes the earth, heaven, and gods, and whatever is in heaven, and under the earth among the dead. 
You speak of a wonderful Sophist. 
Do you distrust it? Tell me, I pray, does it seem to you in no way that there is such a craftsman? Or that in a certain way he is the maker of all these things, but in a certain way he is not? Do you not notice that you can do all these things in a certain way? 
What is this way? 
It is not difficult; for you can make all things everywhere and quickly. Take a mirror and carry it around everywhere. You will immediately make the sun, and what is in heaven, the earth as soon as possible, yourself most swiftly, and other animals similarly, furniture, plants, and all things we recently commemorated. 
Images of them indeed, but the things themselves not at all. 
Opportune (I said), you have responded too much. Such a maker is the painter himself. Is he not? 
He is. 
But you will say that he by no means makes the true things which he makes, although in some way the painter also makes a bed. Does he not? 
He makes it indeed, but an appearing one. 
Did you not say that the maker of the bed does not make the species itself, which we say is that which is "bed-ness," but some bed? 
I said it indeed. 
If he does not make that which *is*, he surely does not make what truly is, but something such as that which truly is, yet not that which it is in reality. If someone says that the work of the carpenter, or of the bed-makers, or of other crafts is "perfectly being," will he err? 
Not as it seems to those who are versed in these disputations. 
It is no wonder then, if this too is thin compared to the truth. 
Certainly not. 
Do you wish us to investigate in these also...

---

### [Page 449]
### Dialogue X on the Republic, or, on Justice.

...who this **Imitator** is? 
*[Margin: Imitator]*
If it pleases. 
Are there not these three beds? One indeed existing in nature itself, which we shall say God made, as I think. Or any other? 
None. 
The second which the carpenter makes. 
Plainly. 
The third indeed which the painter makes. Is it not? 
It is. 
Thus the painter, the bed-maker, and God are three, presiding over three species of beds. 
Three indeed. 
God, therefore, whether because he was unwilling, or because some necessity was inherent, made no more than one bed in nature from himself. Thus he made only that one bed, which surely is "that which a bed is." But two such, or more, were neither then generated by God, nor will be generated. 
By what reason? 
Because if he made only two, one would appear again whose species both would have: and it would be "that which a bed is," but those two would not be it. 
Clever. 
Since God understood these things, and willed to be the true author of the true bed, but not a certain author of a certain bed, he produced only one by nature. 
It seems so. 
Do you wish us then to call him the "planter" of this, or something of the sort? 
It is fair, since nature made both this and all other things. 
The carpenter, however, do we not call the "maker" of the bed? 
And this. 
And the painter too, the maker and craftsman of this work? 
In no way. 
But how will you say he stands in relation to the bed? 
It seems to me most aptly said that he is the *imitator* of that which those others are the craftsmen. 
Therefore you call him an "imitator" who makes the third from nature? 
Greatly. 
Such then will also be the **Tragic Poet**: if indeed he is an imitator, a certain third from the king and the truth: and similarly all other imitators. 
*[Margin: Tragici carpuntur (Tragedians are criticized)]*
It appears so. 
About the imitator we have agreed. But I would like you to tell me about the painter, whether he strives to imitate each thing that is in nature, or the works of craftsmen? 
The works of craftsmen. 
Whether as they are, or as they appear to us? Distinguish this for me further. 
How do you say? 
Thus. A bed, whether it is seen from the side, or from the front, or in any other way, does it differ from itself? Or does it differ not at all? But it seems disposed in one way to those looking, and in another similarly? 
So it appears indeed, but it differs [not]. 
Notice also this: what does the painter’s industry intend in each thing? Whether to imitate each thing as they are? Or what appears rather, as it appears? Is it an imitation of an appearing image or of the truth rather? 
Of an appearing image. 
Imitation, therefore, is far from the truth: and as it seems, for that reason it can make all things, because it touches a tiny thing of each, namely a simulacrum. Just as the painter will paint for us a cobbler, a carpenter, and other craftsmen, when he understands nothing in these arts: nevertheless if he is a skilled painter, and has expressed the image of the carpenter himself, when he shows it from afar, he will deceive boys and foolish men so that the true carpenter appears to them. 
Why not? 
But, O friend, this must be thought of in all such things. Whenever someone announces to us about this very thing, that he has met a man learned in all arts, and most perfectly understanding beyond others whatever anyone else understands: to him it must immediately be responded that he is a fool, and has fallen in with a certain magical juggler, by whose imitations he has been deceived because he himself cannot discern between ignorance and imitation of the thing itself. 
You speak most true things. 
Does it not follow after this to discuss Tragedy, and its leader Homer? Since we have received from some that tragic poets understand all arts, and all human things pertaining both to virtue and to vice, and even...

---

### [Page 450]
### Dialogue X on the Republic, or, on Justice.

...divine things: for a good poet ought, if he is to treat what he composes rightly, to have knowledge of them, or else be able to compose nothing. Therefore we ought to weigh whether those who praise them have been deceived by the imitative industry of the poets, and while they look at their works, do not clearly perceive that they stand at a third grade from the truth, and are easy to do even for a man ignorant of the truth. Indeed they make shadows, not true things. Or perhaps they say something [worthwhile], and in truth good poets understand those things about which they seem to speak well to the common people? 

It must be discerned entirely. If someone could perform both—both that which falls into imitation and its simulacrum—do you think he would linger in fashioning simulacra? And propose that work to himself in life as the best? 
By no means. 
Surely if he has a true skill of those things he imitates, he will much more incumbently apply himself to the works themselves than to their imitations: and he will try to leave many and distinguished works as monuments of himself to posterity, and will judge it better that he himself be praised by others, than that he always be a praiser of others' works. 
So I think indeed. For there is not equal honor or equal advantage. 

But concerning others let us not demand an account, asking Homer or any other of the poets if any of them were truly a physician, not only an imitator of words looking toward a physician—whom of the ancients or moderns did the poet restore to health, just as Aesculapius did, or what disciples of the medical art did he leave, just as he left posterity? But neither let us ask them about other arts: for let us let go of the rest. But truly about those greatest and most distinguished things which Homer attempts—wars, empires, republics, and the disciplines of men—it is fair to ask him thus: "O friend Homer, if you are not third from the truth, and you do not fashion an image of virtue, which we defined as an 'imitator' above, but you are second, and you can tell what studies make men either better or worse privately and publicly, tell me, I pray, what city has been better disposed through you? Just as Lacedaemon through Lycurgus, and many other cities great and small through many others. Of what city especially do men preach you as the best founder of laws, and commemorate your benefits toward them? Italy and Sicily celebrate Charondas. We celebrate Solon. But who will preach you, and of what kind?" 

"None, as I think," said **Glaucon**, "commemorates his benefits. Nay, not even the Homerists themselves dare to testify this." 
What war specifically in Homer's times is commemorated as having been happily dispatched by him as a counselor or leader? 
"None." 
Furthermore, what inventions of this man as if wise in these things are referred to as most apt for the duties of life and art? As of Thales of Miletus, and Anacharsis the Scythian. 
"Nothing of the sort." 
If not publicly, then at least privately, as a leader of what discipline is Homer himself said to have stood out while he lived, who delighted in his company and handed down to posterity some Homeric way of life? Just as Pythagoras lived with the highest authority in this, and posterity even in these times celebrating the Pythagorean life are held as illustrious among the rest. 
"Neither is any such thing told of Homer. For **Creophilus**, O Socrates, perhaps the familiar of Homer, will appear more ridiculous in discipline than in name, if indeed the things told of Homer are true. For he is said to have been quite negligent toward him while he lived under him." 

"He is said so indeed. But, O Glaucon, if Homer truly could instruct men and make them better, as one who was not only an effect of imitation in these things but also composed of intelligence, why did he not acquire many friends for himself? Why was he not honored while living? Why not loved? Indeed Protagoras of Abdera and Prodicus of Chios and many others can persuade men of their time, approaching individuals privately, that they will never govern domestic and public affairs rightly unless they themselves educate them: and they are loved so ardently for this wisdom that their followers can scarcely contain themselves from carrying them about on their heads. If indeed those poets could help them toward virtue, would the men of those times have permitted Homer or Hesiod to wander about chanting their songs everywhere? Would they not rather have embraced these more than gold, and brought them into domestic and familiar social life? And if they did not persuade them, they would have followed them everywhere until they were sufficiently imbued with those same studies." 

"You seem to me to speak very true things, O Socrates." 

"Let us posit therefore all poetic men starting from Homer as imitators of the images of virtue, and of other things similarly which they sing, but never touching the truth. But as we said a little before, the painter will paint a visible image of a cobbler, although he understands nothing of cobbling, and that image appears to be the cobbler himself to those who do not understand the thing itself, but look at colors and figures." 

"Entirely." 

"In no other way shall we say the poet expresses certain colors of the individual arts with names and words, though he himself understands nothing of these, but imitates only, so that to those who judge these things from words, he seems to speak well, whether of cobbling by verse, rhythm, and harmony, or of military affairs, or of anything else. So much do those poetic things soothe the ears by a certain nature. But I think you know how these works of poets appear when they are considered stripped of musical colors. Have you ever noticed?" 

"I have noticed." 

"Do they not behave just like the faces of those who are handsome rather than beautiful because of youth: what they are in aspect after the bloom itself has left them?" 

"Entirely." 

"Age, then, and notice this. The imitator, the author of the simulacrum, understands the thing not at all, but only the appearing image of the thing. Is it so?" 

"So it is." 

"Let us not then leave it imperfect, but complete it as much as is sufficient." 

"Speak." 

"A painter will paint reins and a bit." 

"Plainly." 

"But the cobbler and the blacksmith will make them." 

"Greatly." 

"Will the painter understand what kind the reins ought to be, or what kind the bit? Or not even the maker himself, whether the blacksmith or the cobbler, but only he who knows how to use them, the horseman?" 

"You speak true things." 

"Shall we not say it is thus about everything?" 

"How?" 

"That around everything there are these three arts: the using, the making, and the imitating?" 

"Certainly." 

"The virtue, therefore, beauty, and rectitude of any instrument, animal, or action is referred to nothing else than to the use, for whose sake each thing is both made and generated." 

"So it is." 

"It is necessary then that he who uses something be most skilled, and signify to the maker of the work what good or bad things he makes in the use of that which he uses. Just as the flute-player shows the flute-maker what flutes are most apt for use, and orders what kind it is necessary to make: he however offers himself as a minister, and does not prescribe it." 

"Why not?" 

"Does not this one, understanding, pronounce about apt and inept flutes to the other? And he, believing, makes them?" 

"Plainly." 

"Therefore about the same..."

---

### [Page 451]
### Dialogue X on the Republic, or, on Justice.

"...instrument, the maker indeed has a right faith about beauty and depravity, adhering to the one who understands and being compelled to hear from the understanding one: but the user has knowledge." 

"Certainly." 

"But the imitator, will he have knowledge from the use of those things which he paints, whether they are beautiful and right, or otherwise? Or a right opinion, from the fact that he necessarily adheres to the one who understands and is instructed by him what kind each thing to be painted should be?" 

"Neither." 

"Therefore the imitator will neither understand nor have right opinion about the beauty or the contrary of those things he imitates?" 

"It does not seem so." 

"The imitator will be 'fine' in his production as far as wisdom is concerned regarding what he makes?" 

"Not much." 

"Nevertheless he will imitate, not understanding in what way each thing is either rightly held or otherwise. But as it appears, what he believes is beautiful to the many and the ignorant, this he will imitate." 

"What else indeed?" 

"These things seem sufficiently agreed upon by us: namely that imitators understand nothing worthy of estimation about these things which they imitate: but that imitation is a certain play rather than a serious matter: and that all those who treat tragic poetry in iambics and heroic verses are imitators above all others." 

"And especially indeed." 

"By Jove (I said), this imitation stands at a third grade from the truth. Does it not?" 

"It is as you say." 

"To which of those things which are in man does it pertain, insofar as it has such power?" 

"About what are you asking?" 

"About such a thing: the same magnitude seen from afar and from near does not seem equal." 

"No." 

"The same thing also appears crooked and straight in water to us looking, and out of water, and again concave and prominent because of the error of sight regarding colors. Every such disturbance is found in our soul. Which debility of our nature the faculty of adumbration, the ingenuity of jugglers, and other machinations attack, leaving nothing of magical seduction unattempted." 

"You speak true things." 

"Are not the disciplines of measuring, numbering, and weighing opportune aids to man against these, so that what appears larger or smaller, or more or heavier, may not prevail in us, but that which is apprehended by number, measure, and scale?" 

"Why not?" 

"And yet this is the office of the rational part of the soul." 

"Of this very part." 

"When this part oftentimes measures and indicates that some things are larger or smaller than others, or equal, contrary things appear to us about these same things at the same time; so it happens. Did we not say yesterday that it is not possible for the same parts of the soul to have contrary opinions about the same things at the same time?" 

"And we said it rightly." 

"The power of the soul, therefore, which opines beside measure, will not be the same as that which opines with measure." 

"Certainly not." 

"But indeed that which trusts in measure, reasoning, and computation is the best part of the soul." 

"Nothing stands in the way." 

"That which therefore repugns this will be some ignoble part of ours." 

"Necessarily." 

"Wishing to express that confession, I said above that painting and every faculty of imitating performs its work far removed from the truth: and again it joins with some part of ours, entirely devoid of prudence, and contracts a friendship: for nothing sincere or true." 

"Mostly." 

"Therefore a vile faculty of imitating, mixing itself with a vile thing, procreates vile things." 

"It appears so." 

"Is such a thing only that which pertains to sight? Or also that which pertains to hearing? Which we call poetry." 

"It is probable that this also is such." 

"Let us not then only believe that which appears likely to us from painting, but let us come to that very nature of thought to which poetic imitation solely accommodates itself, and let us see whether it is something vile or precious."

---

### [Page 452]
### Dialogue X on the Republic, or, on Justice.

"Precious. We ought thus." 

"Let us propose then in this way. Poetry indeed imitates men acting either by force or spontaneously, and thinking from their actions that either some good happens to them or some evil, and for that reason affected either by pain or by pleasure. Is it anything else?" 

"Nothing else." 

"In all these, does a man consent with himself? Or rather just as he distrusts according to sight, as we narrated, and has contrary opinions in himself at the same time about the same thing, so also in acting does he dissent and fight with himself? But now it comes to my mind that nothing about this needs to be discussed by us in the present. For in the superior disputation we sufficiently agreed on these together, namely that our soul, by the confession of many such varied contentions, is agitated by things opposing themselves at the same time." 

"Rightly. Rightly indeed." 

"But what was then omitted by us, now seems to me necessarily to be expedited." 

"What sort of thing?" 

"A good man, and endowed with such a mind, if he loses a son or anything else very dear to him, will bear it more easily than others, as we said." 

"Plainly." 

"Now however let us also consider this, whether he will not grieve at all. Or is this indeed impossible, but he will moderate his grief in some way." 

"This certainly is truer." 

"Tell me this about him in the present, whether you think this man will more repugn his grief when he is seen by similar men, or when he is alone, destitute of the consort of others." 

"It makes a great difference if he is in the sight of others. Furthermore, when he is alone, he will dare to say many things which he would be ashamed to emit before others. He will do many things which he would never wish to be seen by others." 

"It is so. That which bids him to resist is reason and law: that which drags him to pains is perturbation." 

"You speak true things." 

"When a man is agitated around the same thing by contrary motions at the same time, we necessarily say those are two things." 

"Without doubt." 

"One indeed is ready to obey the law, however it enjoins. In what way? The law surely dictates it is best in adversities, as much as can be done, to keep quiet and not to complain: because it is uncertain whether that which happened is good or bad, and because pain contributes nothing to subsequent things, nor is any human affair to be greatly valued, and pain is an impediment to that which can be a sudden protection." 

"To what, do you ask?" 

"I say it is necessary in the first place to consult about those things which happened, and just as in a throw of dice, as it fell, however reason says it is better to have the affair, to dispose of businesses. Nor truly if any adversity has fallen upon us, ought we to prostrate ourselves, and as boys are accustomed to do when they strike a stone, falling down around that which hurt them, to draw out delays by wailing: but to accustom the soul so that it is present to heal, and whatever is sick, let it correct with lamentations dismissed." 

"This is an opportune remedy against the blows of fortune." 

"That which surely is best, willingly obeys this reason." 

"It stands." 

"That which truly drags us to the record of perturbation and mourning, and detains us in them longer, is irrational, languid, and fearful." 

"So it must be said." 

"That which is plaintive admits of very much and varied imitation. But the prudent and peaceful character, always similar to itself, we cannot easily imitate: nor if we imitate it, will it be easily perceived, especially by a crowd flowing together into the theater from various nations. For the imitation of an alien affect happens. It is so entirely." 

"But the imitation of the poet does not intend this, so that it may please this nature of the soul with its wisdom, if it is to please the common people, but it observes the plaintive character of the soul and the varied one, which can be easily fashioned by imitation." 

"It is clear." 

"Rightly therefore we shall reprehend poetic imitation, and we shall say it corresponds to painting in its imitation. First indeed, because both, if you look at the truth, produce vile things. Then also because they similarly support the part of the soul devoid of reason, and desert the best. And for that reason we shall by no means receive it in a city to be legitimately governed, since it rouses and nourishes this part of the soul: which while it corroborates, it destroys the power of reason. And just as he who in a city, making those who have the most power into wicked men, would betray the city and destroy the good: so also the imitator poet induces a perverse republic into the soul of each, while he soothes that part of the soul which is without mind, nor discerns larger or smaller things, but thinks the same things are sometimes small and sometimes great, and fashions simulacra for this part, far removed from the truth." 

"Far indeed." 

"We have not yet narrated what greatest evil comes from it. This must be thought of as the greatest detriment, that it can corrupt even good men with very few excepted." 

"Why can it not? if indeed it does that." 

"Listen, I say, and see. Do not even the best of us, when we hear Homer or any other tragic poet who imitates some hero involved in grief, vociferating and bewailing his fortune with plaintive modulations and beating his chest with his fists, delight in a certain way, and gaping after those things follow them, and are affected together with him, and seriously and studiously praise him as a good poet who so vehemently moves us?" 

"I have noticed." 

"Whenever however a domestic and true sorrow invades any of us, you know how we glory in the contrary: namely if in any way we can keep quiet and tolerate the pain: as if this indeed were the part of a man, and that which we praised before were of a woman." 

"Plainly." 

"Is this praise distinguished? Nay, it is absurd, that he who looks at such a man as he would by no means wish to be himself, and would be most ashamed, does not abominate it but delights and praises." 

"Abominable indeed." 

"Certainly, if you also notice it in this way." 

"In what way?" 

"That namely which in our own calamities is forcibly restrained, and prohibited from breaking into tears and weeping, and from indulging its nature greedy for tears, that very thing is what the poets fill, to which they entirely flatter. Then certainly, that which is best in us, as one neither sufficiently instructed by reason nor by use, ceases to guard that plaintive thing, as if it looks at alien perturbations, and nothing is a disgrace to it if, while another man who preaches that he excels in virtue wails immoderately, he himself praises and pities him. Nay, he thinks he gains that pleasure, nor would he wish to lack that poetry from contempt of reason. Few indeed notice, as I think, that it is necessary to transfer something from alien things into one's own. For if you nourish that tearful talent in alien miseries and make it stronger, you will not easily stay it in your own." 

"You speak too much truth." 

"Is not the same reason about laughter? For that which you would be most ashamed to do for the sake of moving laughter, when you hear it in a comedy or private imitation as something ridiculous, you listen to it most willingly, and you do the same here as we said happens in the tearful imitation. For that talent of yours more prone to laughter, which you yourself contained in you from fear of the crime of scurrility, here you now release into jokes, and you gradually make the affect of laughter more vehement, so that even in your own gestures you begin to be carried away in laughter beyond what is decent, and you turn out to be a ridiculous buffoon excited by the jokes of comedy." 

"Vehemently indeed." 

"We say the same also about venereal things and anger, and about all desires and affects of the soul, sad and joyful, which we said follow us in every action in the superior parts, and that poetic imitation fashions such things in us: for it nourishes those things while it cherishes and waters them, which rather ought to be thinned by aridity: and it makes these dominate in us, which rather ought to be subject, so that we may turn out better and more blessed from worse and more miserable." 

"I cannot say otherwise." 

"Therefore whenever, Glaucon, you show the praisers of Homer, and you hear them saying that Homer instructed all Greece, and that for the government and discipline of human affairs this poet is to be adopted, and all life is to be instructed according to his institutes, remember that they are to be borne and loved as men best according to their faculty, and it is to be conceded that Homer is primarily poetic and the chief of tragic poets. But know that only hymns to the gods and laudations of good men are to be admitted from poetry into the city. But if you receive the voluptuous muse in songs and poems, pleasure and pain will dominate in the city instead of the law and that which has always seemed best—namely, reason." 

"You speak true things." 

"These things then let be said by us in that opinion, that we rightly expelled poetry from the city, since it is such. For so reason compelled. Let us also add this, lest it accuse us of rigidity and rusticity, that a certain old dissension exists between poetry and philosophy. (Of which contention certainly these things which I subjoin can be arguments, and many others). Namely, 'that barking dog at the ears of the master.' And, 'that great one in the vain talk of the insane.' And, 'the crowd of superstitious wise men surpassing.' Likewise, 'those who meditate on minute and thin things, are pressed by poverty.' And innumerable other signs of that ancient enmity. Nevertheless let it be said, that if the minister of pleasure, poetry and imitation, can bring forward anything to that reason so that it ought to be received in a rightly instituted city, we shall receive it willingly, so that we may enjoy its delights. For so we are conscious to ourselves. And indeed what seems true, it is a crime to betray. For even you, O friend, are you not soothed by it? Especially the Homeric." 

"Greatly." 

"Is it not fair that it should come forward into the middle defending itself, either in song or in any other meter?" 

"Entirely." 

"Let us concede then to its defenders, who are not poets themselves but friends of poets, that they may defend it without song, asserting it to be not only pleasant but useful for the republic and the institution of human life. Which defense we shall listen to with an equal mind. For we think that will be a gain to us if it appears not only sweet but also useful to us." 

"What stands in the way of it being a gain?" 

"Otherwise, O sweet friend, just as those who once loved something, if they then judge that love will be useless to them, although they cease to love with difficulty, they nevertheless cease: so also we, because of the love of such poetry engrafted in us from the education of beautiful republics, shall wait benignly indeed for it to appear best and truest. Until however it cannot bring forward a defense for itself, so shall we hear it, so that with the speech set forth by us above we may fortify ourselves as if by a certain incantation against imminent dangers, taking care lest we be again entangled in amatory delights and the loves of the common people. We shall also feel that one must not so study such poetry as if it were true or serious: but it must be guarded against by every listener, fearing for the republic of his own interior soul. And what we have narrated about poetry, is entirely to be thought about it. A contention indeed." 

"A huge one furthermore, O friend Glaucon, huge, and not as small as it seems, is the contest to be made good or bad. Wherefore neither for the sake of money, nor of honor, nor of power, nor of any poetic delight, is it decent to neglect justice and the other virtues." 

"I assent from these reasons which we narrated. But I think any other would confess the same." 

"And yet the huge rewards and wages of virtue proposed to it, we have by no means narrated." 

"Immense rewards you say, if there are any larger than these which we have reported." 

"What can be great in a brief time? Namely, all this time from boyhood to the end of old age is a tiny thing compared to the universe." 

"Nay, it is nothing." 

"Do you think an immortal thing for this brief time indeed, but for the universe by no means, ought to be solicitous?" 

"For all time certainly. But to what purpose is this?" 

"Do you not know that the soul of man is immortal and free from destruction?" 

Then suddenly turning to me Glaucon, and wondering, he said: 
"By Jove, I indeed do not know. But can you show it?" 
"Certainly, unless I wished to be injurious. But I think you also can do it, nor is it difficult." 
"To me indeed it is difficult. But I would willingly hear you declaring that which you deny is difficult." 
"You shall hear now." 
"Speak." 
"Do you call something good? and something evil?" 
"I do." 
"Do you have the same opinion about these as I do?" 
"What?" 
"I think all that which dissolves and corrupts is evil. That however which preserves and helps is good." 
"And I." 
"Do you say there is some good for each thing, and some evil? As for the eyes bleariness, and for the whole body disease, for crops and food blight, for wood rot and putridity, for brass and iron rust, and as I say, almost in all things a proper evil and disease according to nature?" 
"Indeed." 
"Whenever any such thing happens to anything, does it make that to which it happened worse, and finally dissolve and lose the whole?" 
"Why not?" 
"The proper evil of each then, and its own depravity, corrupts anything. And unless that corrupts it, nothing else will ever corrupt it. For that which is good does not destroy anything: nor again that which is neither good nor evil. For in what way?" 
"If therefore there is anything such that there is some evil for it which makes it worse, yet it is not able to dissolve it, certainly for a thing so naturally affected there can be no destruction." 

"It is consonant." 

"Is there anything that makes the soul depraved?" 

"And most of all indeed those which we commemorated: injustice, intemperance, timidity, and ignorance." 

"Does any of these lose the soul? But notice, lest we be deceived, thinking that an unjust and insane man, when he is caught in a flagrant crime, is then corrupted by injustice which is a vice of the soul. Come, tell me. Does not its own proper vice, disease, liquefy and resolve the body, and lead it to this, that it is not a body? And all those things which we said a little before, by their own evil insofar as it inheres, tainting them, do they cease to be? Do they not?" 

"So entirely." 

"Does not also the soul in the same way by injustice and the rest of depravity, when it is in it by its very presence, dissipate and waste away, until dragging it into death it separates it from the body?" 

"In no way." 

"But indeed that is absurd, that an alien vice should kill something to which its own vice does not bring destruction." 

"Beyond reason indeed." 

"Attend (I said), O Glaucon. From the proper depravity of foods themselves, by which either corrupted by age or putrid, or in any other way they are said to be compared, we do not think the body can perish. But if the vice of foods...

---

### [Page 453]
### Dialogue X on the Republic, or, on Justice.

...brings its own proper vice to the body, we shall say that through those the body is lost by its own vice, namely disease. But the body itself since it is another thing, by the alien defect of foods whose nature is another, unless it has induced its own defect, we shall never think it can be dissipated. 

"You speak rightly indeed." 

"By the same reason, unless the detriment of the body brings detriment to the soul itself, we ought by no means to think that from an alien evil without proper depravity, the soul perishes, nor is one thing dissipated by the evil of another." 

"So reason advises." 

"Either then let us redargue these as if they are not rightly said, or while these remain whole, let us not concede that the soul is dissipated either from fever or any other disease, nor by throat-cutting, nor even if someone cuts the body into the tiniest pieces, before someone has shown that because of these passions of the body the soul itself becomes more unjust and more profane. Insofar however as an alien evil is present to another, and its own proper evil does not adhere to each, let us by no means concede that anything can be corrupted." 

"But indeed," he said, "no one will ever show that the souls of the dying become more unjust because of death." 

"If someone," I said, "dares to object to us that he who dies becomes worse and more unjust, so that he may not be compelled to confess that souls are immortal, we shall say it is necessary, if he has spoken true things, that injustice is lethal to an unjust man just like a disease, and by this very thing perishing everywhere are those who are most [unjust], but less so those who are less: nor does it happen only what happens now, that the unjust die then because of injustice when they afflict them with other punishments." 

"By Jove, injustice will seem to be not at all a most grave evil if it will be lethal to an unjust man. For it will be a liberation from evils. I think on the contrary it is entirely כך, that it kills others according to its powers, and makes the man who participates in it most vivacious, and supremely wakeful: so far is it from being lethal." 

"You speak skillfully. For when its own depravity and its own evil cannot lose the soul, never will an evil from the destruction of another and instituted for another thing, beyond that to which it properly happens, dissolve either the soul or anything else." 

"Never, as it is probable." 

"Since it is killed by no evil at all, whether proper or alien, it is clear that it always is, and necessarily is. If it always is, it also exists as immortal." 

"Necessary." 

"Let this then be כך. And if it is so, you should notice that the same souls will always be. For they will never be fewer, since none at all perishes. Nor again more. For if anything immortal is made more, it will be made from the mortal, and all things would finally be immortal." 

"You speak true things." 

"But indeed we by no means think that, for reason prohibits it. Nor again do we think the soul in its truest nature is such that it is varied, dissimilar, and differing in itself." 

"How do you say this?" 

"It is not easy for that to be sempiternal which is constituted from several things, and has not obtained the best composition, as has appeared to us now about the soul." 

"It is consonant." 

"That the soul is immortal, therefore, both the present reason and others besides can convince. But if someone truly wishes to inspect what kind it is in reality, he ought by no means to behold it as tainted by communion of the body and other evils, as we now behold it, but what kind it is when it is pure, he must diligently discern with reason. Where certainly it will appear much more beautiful, and will more clearly judge when it is such what is just and what not, and the other things we said above. Now indeed we have said true things about it, such as it appears in the present. But we have seen it no otherwise than many would inspect the marine Glaucus. For they cannot easily consider the ancient nature of Glaucus, because the ancient parts of the body are partly broken, partly worn away, and entirely dissipated by the waves, and other shells, seaweed, and stones adhere to him, from which he much more presents the image of a beast than the countenance of his prior nature. So also we always see the soul tainted by innumerable evils. 

But indeed it is decent to turn the eyes thither, O Glaucon." 

"Whither?" 

"To its philosophy (I said), and about that it is necessary to notice what things the soul touches, and with what things it strives to enter into custom and strives for, as one which is cognate to the divine, immortal, and sempiternal. And what kind it will be hereafter, if ever it follows a nature of this sort entirely, led out by this affect and effort from the sea in which it is presently merged, and emerging naked with the sand and oysters shaken off, which now adhere to it as if nourished from the earth—earthy, stony, and many rustic things—because of that nourishment which many think is blessed. Then finally we shall contemplate the true nature of the soul itself, and we shall recognize whether it is varied or simple, or what kind is its whole condition. Now however we have sufficiently, as I think, declared the affects and forms of the soul in human life." 

"Quite indeed." 

"Have we not explained the rest in this disputation? But the rewards and honors of justice we have by no means brought in, just as you were saying Homer and Hesiod brought them in: but we have found that justice itself is the best reward for the soul itself, and we have shown that one must act justly, whether one has the ring of Gyges or even the helmet of Pluto?" 

"You speak true things." 

"But now also besides these no envy prohibits us from attributing to justice and to universal virtue those rewards which it prepares for the soul as much among men as among gods, for a man both living and dead." 

"Greatly." 

"Will you then restore to me what you borrowed in the speech?" 

"What especially?" 

"I gave to you that a just man should seem unjust, and an unjust one just. For you had asked, although it could not be yesterday so that these should be hidden from men and gods, yet it pleased to concede this for the sake of the disputation, so that justice itself compared to injustice itself might be judged. Do you not remember?" 

"I would be injurious unless I remembered." 

"After the judgment has been performed, I now again ask that you explain what wages justice refers from gods and men, so that it may also carry off the palm from opinion and manifest estimation, by which it also decorates its worshippers, after it has been openly seen that even its presence confers benefits on us, and does not deceive those who truly possess it." 

"You ask fair things." 

"First indeed you restore this to me, that what kind each of them is, both the just and the unjust, is not hidden from the gods." 

"We shall restore it." 

"If that is not hidden from the gods, this one indeed will be loved by God, and that one will be held in hatred, that which we confessed in the beginning." 

"So it is." 

"But to the friend of the gods, all things as far as can be done by the gods are given as best, unless some evil from a prior fault hangs over him by a certain necessity." 

"Entirely." 

"Thus therefore it must be thought of a just man, whether he is obnoxious to poverty, or diseases, or any other of those which seem to be evils, that finally these conduce to some good for him either living or dead. For he is never neglected by the gods, whoever will strive to turn out just by the duties of virtue, as much as is allowed to man to become similar to God. It is decent that such a man should not be contemplated by one similar. About the unjust man however it is to be felt entirely on the contrary." 

"Vehemently." 

"Among the gods therefore this palm will be given to the just man." 

"So I think." 

"Among men however does it not thus happen, if we ought to confess true things? For cunning and iniquitous men do just like those runners who run well from the lower parts, but from the superior parts not at all. For at first they leap forth quickly: but finally they bring back laughter, with ears drooping, and depart without a crown. But the men runners reach the end, and having obtained the reward are crowned. To just men similarly the same thing, for the most part, happens. Namely in the end of each action and custom and life, they are approved, and receive gifts from men." 

"Greatly." 

"Will you sustain that I, about these things which you [said] about the unjust, should bring in? For I shall say that just men, when they have arrived at mature age, perform the duties of the city according to their judgment: they enter into marriages with whom they will, both by giving and receiving in turn: and in sum whatever you [said] of those, I now affirm of these: and again I assert of unjust men. For most of them, however much for a time they hide their vices: finally in the heel of the course, what kind they are is apprehended: they turn out entirely ridiculous: and in old age, miserable, they are rebuked by foreigners and citizens, they are beaten, they suffer all things which you truly said were harsh: for they will be tortured and branded. Furthermore, whatever things you were commemorating, think that they are heard again from me. But as I was saying, see whether you are going to tolerate these." 

"I shall bear them indeed: for you say what is decent." 

"These then are the rewards, wages, and gifts which are given to a just man besides those goods which justice itself contains inherent in itself, from gods and men." 

"These are very distinguished and certain." 

"But indeed these in number and magnitude are nothing, if they are compared to those which remain for each after death. But these also must be heard, so that all things which fit either may be sufficiently apprehended." 

"Speak indeed, not indeed as too many things already, but as to one who will listen most willingly." 

"Indeed I shall not relate to you the apology of Alcinous, but of a most excellent man, **Er the son of Armenius**, by genus a Pamphylian. Who when he had fallen in battle, and the other corpses already corrupted were taken up on the tenth day, he was found indeed whole with an uncorrupted body: and carried home so that he might be buried, on the twelfth day from his death, while he was placed upon the pyre, he revived: and what he had seen in the meantime, he related. He said therefore that after the soul had been separated from the body, it came with many into a certain place of daemons. In which he saw two proximate hiatuses of the earth: and two other similar ones he saw from the sight above in the celestial region: and between these hiatuses judges were sitting: who after they judged the souls, the just indeed they bid to ascend to the right upward through heaven, suspending on the front part of them signs of those things which they had judged: the unjust on the contrary to the left downward, carrying on their back signs of all things they had done in life. When he also had approached the judges, they said to him to respond: that he must return as a messenger to men about these things which he had seen there, and they ordered him to hear and behold whatever things happened in those places, diligently. 

He had seen therefore there through either gate of heaven and earth the souls departing with the sentence passed: through the other two, from the earth indeed ascending souls confected with dust, squalor, and thinness: from heaven however others descending bright. And it seemed (he said) that souls from everywhere coming as if from a long pilgrimage, willingly reclined in the meadow which is there, as if in a celebrated assembly: and they saluted each other, whoever had mutual acquaintance: and they all, both those who came from the earth and those who came from heaven, asked each other about those things which they saw in their places. And they responded in turn to each thing: these indeed grieving and weeping at the memory of the evils which they suffered and saw in the past journey under the earth. Moreover, that journey is of a thousand years. But those which had descended from heaven narrated delights and spectacles of immense beauty. Many indeed were those things which he related, which he recited in a long order, of an excessively prolix narration, O Glaucon. 

But this he said was the sum. Whomever it was certain they had brought injuries to others, they paid penalties individually for each tenfold, that is in the space of a hundred years: as if this is the goal of human life, so that souls gave a decuple penalty for injury. Therefore if any were the cause of the slaughter of many, and betrayed cities and armies, or led men into servitude, or were conscious of any other flagitious crime and wickedness, in all these for each crime they paid decuple penalties. And again if any conferred certain benefits, and worshipped justice and piety, in the same reason they reported rewards. 

About those indeed who died immediately as they were born, or lived a brief time, he recited some things little worthy of memory. Toward the gods however and parents, the pious or impious, and homicides who polluted their own hands with slaughter, he narrated they were affected with greater rewards and penalties. For he said he was present when someone else asked where the great **Ardiaeus** was: this one had been a tyrant in a certain city of Pamphylia, a thousand years already exacted from that time: who had killed his old father and his elder brother: and had perpetrated many other impious crimes. And he said that he, having been asked, responded: 'He does not come, Ardiaeus, nor will he come. For we saw among other dire things this spectacle. For when we sought the hiatus to depart, all other things having been suffered, we saw him suddenly and others with him, almost all tyrants: among whom were also some private individuals who had perpetrated great crimes: whom that hiatus by no means permitted to ascend when they already dared nearly to ascend: but it bellowed horribly whenever any of those who were either incurable or not yet purged strove to go out. Therefore there were present there fierce men of fiery aspect: who when they heard the bellowing suddenly, seized these separately, Ardiaeus namely and those like him: and their hands and feet and neck being bound, they prostrated them, and excruciated them: and along a certain way to the exterior part being dragged, they lacerated them with thorns: indicating to those passing by for what cause they suffered such things, or that they were being driven to be cast into Tartarus.' Where when many and various things terrified them, this fear most vehemently vexed them: when in the ascent a bellowing was excited: which being silent, each most willingly seemed to ascend. And penalties indeed and such supplications he recited: on the contrary however benefits of this sort. 

When truly those souls of which we spoke above had rested in the meadow for seven days, he said it was necessary that they, rising on the eighth day, should depart thence: and on the fourth day finally arrive at a certain place: whence from above through the whole heaven and earth extended there is seen a light like a column most similar to **Iris** [a rainbow], yet clearer and purer. Into that in a journey of one day he came and saw that there in the middle of the light...
