### [Page 455]
### Dialogue X on the Republic, or, on Justice.

...in the middle of the light were the extremes of the celestial bindings held from heaven. For that light is the bond of heaven: just as the **succincturae** [undergirding cables] of triremes. And thus the whole circumference is contained. From the apices truly is suspended the spindle of the goddess Necessity: through which all circuits are performed. Of which spindle indeed and point is from **Adamant**: but the whorl is mixed from this and other kinds. Whose nature is of this sort according to figure, such as is discerned among us. It must be noticed however from his speech, that it behaves just as if in one certain broad and concave whorl, and engraved through the whole, another smaller and similar one lay inserted: so congruous, that they mostly fall together, which are inserted in turn: and thus a third and a fourth: and four others. For those eight whorls are, circles inserted in turn, showing lips from above: but the back of one whorl making a continuous whorl around the spindle. But that spindle through the middle of the eighth, and through the whole is traversed. 

The first therefore and outmost whorl has the broadest circle of the lip. Of the sixth however the second. The third of the fourth. The fourth of the eighth. The fifth of the seventh. Of the fifth the sixth. Of the third the seventh. The eighth truly of the second. The circle of the first and greatest similarly is varied. Of the seventh most lucid. But the circle of the eighth whorl receives the color from the seventh irradiating it. Of the second truly and the fifth similar to each other, somewhat yellower than those. The third surely possesses the most white color. The fourth, sub-red. The second truly exceeds the sixth in whiteness. And the whole spindle is carried around with a similar rotation: when however the whole is revolved, the seven interior circles are turned around with a motion contrary to the whole and slower. From these plainly the eighth is agitated with the most rapid motion: the second truly one after the other consequently: the seventh, the sixth, and the fifth. With such a motion truly the third is carried, that it seems to revolve the fourth. The fourth however the third, and the fifth the second. 

But the spindle is revolved in the knees of Necessity. Above furthermore to each circle adheres a **Siren** carried together with the globe, emitting one voice, one tone namely. Yet one harmony concords from all eight. But three others, the daughters of Necessity, sit in a throne with equal interval from each other: the Parcae in white robes, with a crowned head: **Lachesis**, **Clotho**, **Atropos**. Who sing to the harmony of the Siren. Lachesis indeed of the past. Clotho of the present. Atropos truly of the future. And Clotho indeed with the mother together with a certain intermission of time, with her right hand touching the outmost circumference of the spindle revolves it. Atropos truly with her left again the interior ones similarly. Lachesis finally in turn with either hand touches from either side. 

Thither therefore when the souls have come, immediately they must approach Lachesis: where some prophet first disposes them in order: after when from the knees of Lachesis he has received the lots, and the examples of lives, ascending some sublime tribunal he thus speaks: 'Oratio of Lachesis the most beautiful girl, daughter of Necessity. O souls of one day, beginning of another circuit, of a mortal and death-bearing genus, a daemon will not obtain you by lot, but you will choose a daemon. He who first by lot has taken, let him first choose a life: to which he will necessarily adhere. Virtue is in-violable and free. As each honors it, or neglects it, so more or less he will possess from it: The fault of the choosing is entirely of the chooser: God however is outside fault.' 

Having said these things, he pours out the lots upon all: from which anyone seizes that which fell upon him. Nor is it allowed to know what order of place it is, unless he who took it. Then indeed he disposes the examples of lives before them in the pavement: much more than what appear here at present. For he was saying that there are omniform lives of men and of all animals. For tyrannies exist among them: partly perpetual, partly for a time: which in the middle of the space collapse, fallen into poverty, exile, and want. There are also the lives of distinguished men, partly in species, beauty, virtue, and contests excelling: partly in the ancestry and virtue of ancestors noble. And the lives of women in the same way. But the order and condition of the soul is not in them: because it is necessary, that one choosing another life is made of another condition. But the rest are mixed with each other, partly with riches and poverties: partly with diseases and health: partly obtaining the middle of these. 

Where certainly, O Glaucon, consists every danger of man. Wherefore with every study work must be given: so that each of us, omitting the other disciplines, should seek this one, and follow it for his powers, through which he both can and knows how to discern a good life from a bad one: and as far as can be done, from all choose the better: noticing all those things which we have now said, what things joined together or disjoined lead to the virtue of life. Nor let him ignore what beauty joined with poverty or riches and with what habit of soul, operates evil or good: what nobility or ignobility: private life and empire: strength and imbecility: swift genius and slow: and other such things which are around the soul by nature and which are acquired, coupled in turn they do: so that from all these he may be able to consider the nature of individual things looking back to the nature of the soul: and to discern the better life from the worse: calling the worse that which makes the soul more unjust, the better however, which makes it more just: but the rest let him despise. For we have seen both for the living and for the dead this choice is best. 

With this opinion therefore, like a firm and rare adamant, it is necessary to proceed to the dead, lest anyone there should admire riches and such evils: nor falling into tyrannies and other such actions, should perpetrate many and incurable crimes: and he himself again suffer worse. Nay truly let him know always to choose the middle life from all these with the extremes dismissed: and in this life and in the future. For thus each becomes most blessed. And indeed when then the messenger returned thence, he was showing that in this way the prophet added in the edict: 'If anyone even last approaches, let him only choose prudently, live constantly, a life will occur to be sought not bad. Let the first not choose drowsily, let the last not despair.' 

When he had said these things, he said that he to whom the lot had first come, immediately hastening chose the greatest tyranny: and because of ignorance and greed did not sufficiently examine individual things first: and for that reason ignored, that in that life it was decreed by fate, that he should devour his own sons, and suffer many other evils. But afterwards when by leisure he had considered the chosen life, he wailed, deploring the harmful choice, that he had not heeded what the prophet had predicted, nor condemning himself as the cause of the evils, but fortune and the daemons and all other things rather than himself. But he was from those who had descended from heaven, who surely in a superior life, had lived in some moderate city, and had exercised virtue by a certain use, without the studies of philosophy nevertheless. Nor fewer from those who fall from the high, than from others, as if ignorant of evils are deceived in choosing.

--- Page 462 ---
-> Dialogue X on the Republic. Or, on the Just. 447 <-

He says that the Fates touch the heavens at a certain interval of time, so that you do not think the fatal powers of the world-soul rule the worldly things at one moment and not at another. For if there were mutability in Fate, whose very property is immutability itself, nothing could be imagined that is not changeable. Plato, therefore, painting divine offices in a certain human manner and speech, wants to hint that the Fates handle some things directly, and other things not at all. This is partly because the power of the world-soul, consisting in the dignity of its own integrity, accommodates its action to governing things, and in turn, while it accommodates, it is not mixed with them. It is also because they exhibit a temporal change in their works, and the "intermission" they are said to have in their operation is shown not in themselves, but in the effect. Finally, it is because Fate handles natural things but does not touch supernatural things. For those things which pertain to pure and free reason, or to the divine intelligence superior to fate, it does not touch at all. Such things are reduced by a certain marvelous order to the sublime providence of God, which is superior to celestial fate. Similarly, in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note> it is written that worldly things are ruled sometimes by fate, sometimes by providence: not because such a change happens through an intermittent succession of times, but because daily certain things happen under fate, while others are disposed through the laws of providence above the fatal series. Added to this is the fact that our souls are sometimes entirely in providence, sometimes entirely in fate, and sometimes in both at once. For when they live only by the unhindered contemplative mind, they live in providence alone, and live entirely free. But when the inclination toward this body grows strong in the vegetative part, and such an inclination is propagated even to the imagination, they are already declining toward fate and degenerate from liberty in equal measure. But while they are joined to the composite body, they now plunge themselves into the very fate of their body, and retain far less of their former liberty. Finally, after they have contracted bodily affections into a habit, they are now thoroughly overwhelmed by fate, deprived of all liberty.

It is asked for what reason the souls here seem to approach Lachesis <note>one of the three Fates, who measures the thread of life</note> by a certain natural instinct. Surely, in the general nature of the bodily machine are the seeds of all species, destined to sprout not only in certain forms and modes, but also at certain times. Furthermore, in any specific nature of any species there is a similar seminal order, but pertaining to the propagation and preservation of its own species. A similar spark and tendency exists in any individual under a species to produce individual things in their own modes and times. These three natures are disposed in succession so that the individual follows the specific, and the specific follows the general, so that for the most part what is from the nature of one is likewise from the others, and the particular nature agrees with the universal. Fate holds almost the same logic; that is, it is a certain prefiguration of things to be unfolded, both in the soul of the world itself, and in the souls of the twelve spheres and stars, and also in souls that are now, as it were, particular: in whose number are the human souls. Therefore, in the vegetative power of our soul there is a certain proper fate, and an involved series of future things, agreeing in form, mode, and time together with the fates of the celestial souls and the world-soul. Just as the sprout of any plant, budding with certain proper figures and in its own time, seems to run together spontaneously with the universal nature of springtime provoking it to the same: so also souls, by their own nature and their own fate, opportunely bring forth certain lives then, when the universal fate similarly summons them to the same. Thus, the chorus of souls, with certain figures of dancing and with the diversity of various dancers at once, imitates the fatal song and sound. I would prefer "song" to be understood in the celestial souls, "sound" in the spheres, and finally "dance" in us. By such an instinct, at the start of life, souls come to Lachesis to have their lots confirmed by the lots of Lachesis.

They are confirmed, therefore, through a certain prophet. This "prophet" <note>the messenger or spokesman for the Fates in the myth</note> signifies two things: both the universal and primary influx of providence into the soul, and the opportunity under which such a concurrence happens, so that souls are carried to that place where universal fate also carries them. Therefore, when he says the prophet disposes the souls in order and transfers the lots from Lachesis into them, he means all these things are confirmed, both by the favor of divine providence and by the opportunity of that concurrence. Nor is it said without reason that the Fates govern the universe with their hands, but the lots of souls are taken from the knees of Lachesis. For since the government of the universe is more excellent than the disposition of souls, the former is deservedly judged to be perfected by the hands, and the latter by the knees. Sitting on a tribunal, moreover, expresses authority and judgment. Among the lots of lives and the models, there seems to be such a distinction: that the lots pertain to the vegetative powers, but the models pertain to the imaginations, which are superior to the vegetative power but close to it. Surely, when first in this power certain seeds of a future life grow strong above the rest, at the same time figures and mechanisms of a similar life rise up into the imagination, and the affections grow hot: just as among us a cheerful imagination follows a sanguine affection of the body, an angry one follows a choleric, a sad one follows a melancholic, and a lustful one follows a fertile one.

Thus far fatal necessity proceeds. But reason, superior to imagination—to which belongs reasoning, counsel, and choice, and therefore a movement free toward either side—perceiving the figures and affections of the imagination, can equally approve or disapprove of such a description. For this reason, he says that virtue is free from fate, and the blame for the choice of a worse life belongs to the one choosing, not to fate. For even if it is from fate, both in common and in private, to choose a new life now and then as before: nevertheless, it is from counsel to choose specifically such a life or such a one. Indeed, if reason, by examining, rejects the first form of living offered to the eyes of the mind by the imagination, another better one will not be lacking immediately, and again another. Hence that inspiration of providence is called a "prophet." For it shows to reason, by a certain light of judgment, that it has a free faculty of consulting and choosing, and what follows specifically from a rash choice. The prophet is also said to pour out the lots and propose models of living: not only because the influx of divine providence in a way sanctions fatal things, but because it brings fatal lots and fatal models into the examination and judgment of reason.

In announcing that the souls are "creatures of a day" <note>original: "diurnas"</note>, he expresses that they are both there in perpetual day, and that the life they value so much is but one day, and a nocturnal one at that. He adds that there will be the "beginning of another circuit," to open the mystery of souls returning from heaven to earth and back again. He calls the human race not only mortal, but so that souls may presage their own evils, he adds "death-bringing," as if to say the life of the body is the death of the soul. He pronounces then that even if reason is free from the beginning in choosing a life, yet after it has chosen, it will no longer be free in rejecting this thing, although it may be free in it at some future time, however it may be, to be composed or tempered in one way or another. If you ask why some souls of men choose some lives and others choose others, some will answer that there are certain specific differences in the natures of souls, others that they are individual and proper, and they will add many differences deduced from the diversity of a previous life. Plotinus confirms this strongly, and it agrees most with what follows. Therefore, souls choosing a life at the same time obtain a daemon <note>a guardian spirit or guiding genius</note> as the leader of the chosen life. We have said much about this elsewhere. Here distinguish it thus: the Platonists think of some Gods outside the world, namely minds separate from the body like intellectual spheres, worshipping one God as their most firm center and stable unity. Others they call "worldly," namely accommodated to the revolving spheres of the world beyond divine worship. Under these are the daemons, as ministers to dispose and compose those things which happen either in species or in the spheres or from the spheres. Therefore, they count as many genera of daemons as there are powers found in the worldly Gods, the leaders of the daemons. But in any worldly God, unity itself is the supreme part of his substance, by which he reflects divine unity. After that is the intellect, beholding all things at once, through which he represents the angelic minds. Likewise, reason running through certain forms by progression, which is proper to such souls. Furthermore, a certain imagination meeting through particular forms to the extent that reason itself progresses through universal ones. Next follows the vegetative nature, both the life-giver and the mover of the sphere. According to these five powers, five genera of daemons are computed. From whose number the celestial daemons follow the unity of the worldly gods appropriately: the ethereal daemons, that is the fiery ones, follow the intelligence of those same gods: the aerial daemons follow reason: the aquatic follow imagination: the terrestrial follow nature, which we called vegetative in the gods. Under these the Orphic followers place subterranean daemons, reflecting the bodies of the worldly gods in a certain lowest order, and the avengers of crimes. Plato seems to have made mention of these here.

If you ask what kind of daemons are especially the leaders of souls descending into bodies, the answer will be: not the celestial, not the fiery. For these, being more sublime, lead souls back, they do not lead them down. Likewise, not the aquatic nor the terrestrial. For these, being the artisans of the lowest generation, do not so much lead the soul on the fatal journey as they hurl it into the precipices of fate. Therefore, the aerial daemons remain as the middle leaders through the middle regions, who, as companions of divine reason, lead human reason on this journey. From this genus of daemons, some lead some souls: Saturnian daemons lead Saturnian souls, Martial daemons lead Martial ones, and others similarly lead others, each one especially accommodated to each soul, both from the soul's own affection and from common providence and fate, but most especially according to the form of the chosen life. With this leader of life, the souls now undergo the three fates, which they had only seen be- <margin>P ii</margin> -fore...

--- Page 463 ---
-> 448 Book Thirty-one. <-

...fore, namely with the daemon, the executor of the whole order, so decreeing, and with the bodily affection now gradually outweighing. Finally, after the three Fates <note>Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos</note>, they pass to the mother of the Fates: Necessity herself, whose impulses they now experience. Then, that souls go under a vehement heat can signify three things: namely, that the ardor of bodily love grows, and at the same time care and anxiety are increased. Also, to descend from heaven through the sphere of fire. Furthermore, the ministry of natural heat to vivify the earthly body. But because through excessive care for earthly things, celestial things are consigned to oblivion, and through oblivion sterility happens from fertility, therefore they soon descend into the Lethean, that is, the "forgetful" plain, which is entirely sterile. And because on account of diligent care for mortal things, eternal things are neglected—whence both oblivion is born and loss, and difficulty of remembrance—he says the souls descend in the plain of Lethe even to the river Ameles, that is, the "bottom of negligence," and there they lie down under the night, that is, they are prostrated under the privation of divine light.

But what does it mean that the water of Ameles <note>Greek: 'careless' or 'negligent'</note> can never be contained in any vessel? This is indeed a poetic metaphor, signifying the lower matter, which is called a river, constantly flowing and fluctuating through forms. Also the vice of oblivion, which is to retain nothing, but immediately to pour it out. Add that no external support saves a soul perishing through its own negligence. That it is furthermore necessary to drink from the river of oblivion is clear, because it is so established by its own nature and common fate and providence. To drink either more water or less comes from the effect of being more or less prone to the body: and that same thing is the cause of greater or lesser oblivion, or rather of greater or lesser faculty for remembrance. The soul experiences these passions in a way in a certain body composed of thicker air in the upper plain, before it is enclosed in the womb of the earthly mother. For from celestial bodies to earthly ones, the descent happens not only through the elements, but through an aerial body. He adds that souls sleep in this aerial body even until midnight, showing that soon under the earthly body there will be not a half, but an entire night of ignorance. Sleep testifies to both the hindrance of reason and the falsity of judgment.

Finally, he says that souls are insinuated into the earthly fetus under a certain thunder and earthquake, for two reasons as I think: both indicating that they enter this prison under unhappy auspices, and showing that both celestial and terrestrial motion, and indeed a vehement one, must concur to coerce the divine soul in such a foul prison. That the souls leaped forth to generation like stars, beyond the poetic figure, sub-hints that souls are in a way stellar, and will finally return to the stars. As for the fact that Plato brings forward such a ridiculous fable about the migration of souls into the bodies of beasts, differing in no way from the stories of old women, it surely admonishes us that the whole thing must be explained allegorically: namely, that rational souls migrate in turn not into the life of a brute, but into a "brutish" life, that is, one in some way similar to a brute. This indeed pleased almost all Platonists except Plotinus. And Origen seems to confirm the same in his books against Celsus. You, however, do not neglect the moral precept: that the skill of right choice is to be preferred to all things and arts. Furthermore, so many things were brought in here concerning the beauty and power of the spheres so that we might think that justice and a huge reward will follow in heaven, and will greatly lead toward the best choice of living.

But you will say now, magnanimous Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, that you have received a commentary here from Marsilio Ficino rather than a summary. So be it indeed; I think it was and will be worth the effort that I promised a summary but provided a commentary.

***

**I** indeed, I said, thinking about this city which we have recently established in words, it seems we have established many other things quite rightly, and especially those things which were brought forward concerning poetry. "What are those?" he asked. Namely, that no part of poetry which consists in imitation should be received. For it is now more clear than the rest, as it seems to me, that nothing of the sort is to be received by us, after the individual species of the soul have been separately distinguished. "How do you say that?" To say what I feel among you (for you will not accuse me before the tragic poets and other imitators), all these things seem to be a certain corruption of the mind for those who, when they hear these imitations, do not have that remedy of the mind by which they can especially discern what kind of fables these are. "To what end is this?" It must be said, although a certain friendship and reverence contracted from childhood toward Homer holds me back. For he seems to have been the first leader and teacher of all those distinguished tragic poets. But I do not think a man should be preferred to the truth. Therefore, what I have started must be said. "By all means."

Listen then. "Rather, answer." "Ask." Can you explain to me at all what imitation is? For I do not sufficiently understand what it is. "And should I understand then?" That would be no wonder. For it often happens that those with a duller edge perceive some things sooner than those who see more sharply. "It is as you say. But in your presence, I would never dare to express what seems to me. But you yourself look into it. Do you want us to begin from here, considering by our usual method? We are accustomed to posit a single species for any group of many things to which we give the same name. Do you not understand?" "I understand indeed." "Let us posit now any one from many. As, look, there are many beds and tables. Why not? Yet the Ideas of these things are two. One is of the bed, the other of the table. It is so. We are accustomed to say that the artisan of each piece of furniture thus completes his work if he looks into that Idea; one indeed makes beds, the other tables, which we ourselves use, and other things similarly. For no artisan fabricates the Idea itself. For by what means?" "By none."

"See further whether you would call someone such an artisan?" "What kind?" "Who makes everything, as many things as every single artisan of those who work with their hands makes." "You describe a powerful and marvelous man." "I have not yet expressed his full power. Perhaps indeed you will marvel much more if I express it. For this same artisan not only can fabricate all furniture, but also makes everything that grows from the earth, and all animals and himself. He also carries out the earth, the heaven, and the gods, and whatever is in heaven, and under the earth among those in the lower world." "You describe a marvelous Sophist." "You distrust? Tell me, I pray, does it seem to you in no way that such an artisan exists? Or that in a certain way he is the maker of all these things, but in a certain way he is not? Do you not notice that you can do all these things in a certain way?" "What is this way?" "It is not difficult, for you can make everything everywhere and quickly. Take a mirror, and carry it around everywhere. You will immediately make the sun, and the things that are in heaven, the earth as soon as possible, yourself very quickly, and other animals, furniture, plants, and whatever we just mentioned." "The images of these things indeed, but the things themselves not at all." "Opportune," I said, "you have answered too well. For such a maker is even the painter himself. Is he not?" "He is." "But you will say that he by no means makes true the things he makes, although in some way the painter also makes a bed. Does he not?" "He makes one indeed, but an appearing one." "Did you not say that the maker of the bed does not make the species itself, which we say is that which a bed is, but some particular bed?" "I said so indeed." "If he does not make that which is, he surely does not make what truly is, but something such as that which truly is, yet not that which is in reality. But if someone should say that the work of the carpenter, or of the beds, or of other artifices is perfectly 'being,' will he wander from the truth?" "Not as it seems to those who are engaged in these disputes." "It is no wonder then if even this is thin in relation to the truth." "Certainly not." "Do you wish that we investigate in these things also who...

...who this imitator is?" "If you please." "Are there not these three beds? One indeed existing in nature itself, which we will say God, as I think, made. Or anyone else?" "None." "The second which the carpenter makes." "Plainly." "The third indeed which the painter makes. Is it not?" "It is." "Therefore the painter, the carpenter of the bed, and God, are three, presiding over three species of beds." "Three indeed." "God therefore, whether because he did not want to, or because some necessity was in it, made not more, but one bed in nature by himself. Thus he made only that one bed, which surely is that which the bed is. Two such, or more, were neither then generated by God, nor will be generated." "By what reasoning?" "Because if he made only two, one would appear again of which both would have the species: and that one would be that which the bed is, but those two would not be it." "Skilfully put." "Since God understood these things, and wanted to be the true author of a true bed, but not a certain author of a certain bed, he produced only one by nature." "It seems so." "Do you wish then that we call him the planter of this, or something of the sort?" "It is fair, since he made both this and all other things by nature." "The carpenter indeed, is he not the worker of the bed?" "That also." "Is not the painter also the maker and worker of this work?" "In no way." "But how will you say he is related to the bed?" "It seems to me it can most aptly be said: he is the <margin>Imitator.</margin> imitator of that of which those others are called workers." "Therefore you call him an imitator who makes the third thing from nature?" "Very much so." "Such then will be even the tragic poet: since he is an imitator, a certain third from the king and the truth: and similarly all other imitators." "It appears so." "We have agreed about the imitator.

But I would like you to tell me about the painter, whether he strives to imitate each thing that is in nature, or the works of artisans." "The works of artisans." "Whether as they are? Or as they appear to us? Distinguish this for me further." "How do you mean?" "Thus. A bed indeed, whether it is seen from the side, or from the front, or in any other way, does it differ from itself? Or does it differ nothing? But it seems disposed in one way or another to those looking, and other things similarly." "It appears so indeed, but it does not differ." "Notice this also: what does the industry of the painter intend in each thing? Whether to imitate each thing as it is? Or rather that which appears, as it appears? Is it an imitation of an appearing image or of truth?" "Of an appearing image." "Therefore imitation is far from the truth: and as it seems, it can do all things for this reason, because it touches a tiny bit of each thing—certainly a ghost <note>original: "simulacrum"; an image or likeness</note>. Just as the painter will paint for us a cobbler, a carpenter, and other workers, although he understands nothing in these arts: nevertheless if he is a skilled painter, and has expressed the image of the carpenter himself, showing it from afar, he will deceive boys and mindless men so that he appears to them to be a true carpenter. Why not?

But, O friend, this must be considered in all such things. Whenever someone tells us about this very thing, that he has met a man learned in all arts, and understanding everything more perfectly than all others that anyone else understands: to this man it must be immediately answered that he is a fool, and has fallen into a certain sorcerer and trickster, by whose imitations he was deceived: for that reason he thought that man most wise because he himself was unable to discern science from ignorance, and imitation from the thing itself." <margin>Tragic poets are plucked.</margin> "You speak most truly." "Is it not proper after this to discuss tragedy, and its leader Homer? Since we have received from some that tragic poets understand all arts, and all human things pertaining both to virtue and to vice, and also divine things: for it is necessary for a good poet, if he is to treat rightly what he composes, to have knowledge of them, or he can compose nothing. Therefore we ought to weigh whether those who praise them have been deceived by the imitative industry of poets, and while they look at their works, they do not plainly perceive that they are distant in the third degree from the truth, and are easy to do even for a man ignorant of the truth. They make shadows, almost, not true things. Or perhaps they say something, and in reality good poets understand those things about which they seem to speak well to the common people?" "It must be discerned entirely." "If someone could perfect both, both that which falls into imitation and its ghost, do you think he would linger in fashioning ghosts? And would propose that work for himself in life as the best?" "Least of all." "Surely if he should have true skill in those things which he imitates, he will much more attend to the works themselves than to their imitations: and he will strive to leave many and distinguished works as monuments of himself to posterity, and he will think it better that he himself be praised by others, than that he always be the praiser of others' works." "I think so indeed. For there is not equal honor or equal advantage."

"But let us not demand a reason concerning other things, asking Homer or any other of the poets: if any of them was in reality a physician, and not only an imitator of words looking toward a physician, which of the ancients or moderns did the poet make healthy, as Aesculapius did, or what disciples of the medical art did he leave, as he left his posterity? But let us not ask them about other arts: let us dismiss the rest. But about those greatest and most distinguished things which Homer attempts—wars, commands, republics, and the disciplines of men—it is fair to ask him thus: 'O friend Homer, if you are not third from the truth, and you do not fashion an image of virtue, which we defined as an imitator in the things above, but you are second, and you can tell what studies make men either better or worse privately and publicly, tell me, I pray, what city was more rightly disposed through you? Just as Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> through Lycurgus, and many other cities small and large through many others. Of what city especially do men preach you as the best founder of laws, and commemorate your benefits toward them? Italy and Sicily celebrate Charondas. We celebrate Solon. But who will preach you, and as what kind of man?'" "None, I think," said Glaucon, "commemorates his benefits. Indeed, not even the Homerids themselves dare to testify to this." "What war especially in Homer's times is commemorated as having been successfully dispatched with him as consultant or leader?" "None." "Furthermore, what inventions of this man as one wise in these things existed, who were both delighted by his company, and handed down to posterity some Homeric way of life? Just as Pythagoras lived with the highest authority in this, and even his posterity in these times, celebrating the Pythagorean life, are held as illustrious among the rest. Nor is anything such told again of Homer. For Creophilus, O Socrates, <margin>Loving the flesh.</margin> perhaps the familiar of Homer, will appear ridiculous in discipline even more than in name, if indeed the things told about Homer are true. For he is said to have been rather negligent toward him while he lived under him." <margin>P iiii</margin> "It is said...

...It is said indeed. But surely, O Glaucon, if Homer were truly able to instruct men and make them better, as one who in these things was possessed not only of imitation but also of intelligence, why did he not acquire many friends for himself? Why was he not honored while living? Why not loved? Surely Protagoras of Abdera, and Prodicus of Chios, and very many others can persuade men of their time, approaching individuals privately, that they will never govern family and public affairs rightly unless they themselves erudite them: and on account of this wisdom they are so ardently loved, that their followers can scarcely restrain themselves from carrying them around on their heads. If indeed those poets were able to help them toward virtue, would the men of those times have permitted Homer or even Hesiod to wander about everywhere singing their poems for so long? Would they not rather have embraced these more than gold, and led them to domestic and familiar living? And if they had not persuaded them, they would have followed them everywhere, until they were sufficiently imbued with those same studies. "You seem to me to speak quite truly, O Socrates."

"Let us posit then that all poetic men, beginning from Homer, are imitators of images of virtue, and similarly of the other things they sing, but they do not touch the truth at all. But as we said a little before, the painter will paint a visible image of a cobbler, although he himself understands nothing of cobbling, and that image appears to be the cobbler himself to those who do not understand the thing itself, but look from colors and figures." "Entirely." "Not otherwise will we say the poet expresses certain colors of the individual arts with names and words, though he himself understands nothing of these, but only imitates, so that to those who judge these things from words, he seems to speak well, whether he speaks of cobbling with verse, rhythm, and harmony, or of military affairs, or of any other things. To such an extent do those poetic things soothe the ears by a certain nature. But I think you know what kind of things these works of the poets seem like when they are considered stripped of the colors of music. Have you ever noticed?" "I have noticed." "Are they not just like the faces of those who, on account of youth, are 'well-formed' rather than beautiful: such as they are in appearance after the bloom itself has left them?" "Entirely."

"Come then and notice this also. An imitator, an author of a ghost, understands the thing itself by no means, but only the appearing image of the thing." "It is so." "Let us not leave that imperfect, but let it be completed as much as is enough." "Say on." "The painter will paint reins and a bit." "Plainly." "But the cobbler and the blacksmith will make them." "Greatly." "Will the painter understand what kind the reins ought to be, what kind the bit? Or not even the maker himself, whether the blacksmith or the cobbler, but only he who knows how to use them, the horseman?" "You speak truly." "Shall we not say it is thus concerning all things?" "How?" "That around everything there are these three arts: the using, the making, and the imitating?" "Certainly." "Therefore the virtue, beauty, and rectitude of any instrument, animal, and action is referred to nothing else than to the use, for whose sake each thing is both made and generated." "It is so." "It is necessary then that he who uses something be most skilled, and signify to the maker of the work what good or bad things he makes in the use of that which he uses. Just as the flute-player shows to the maker of flutes which flutes are most fit for use, and ordains what kind he ought to make: the maker, however, offers himself as a minister, and does not prescribe. Why not? Is not the one here, being intelligent, pronouncing to the other about fit and unfit flutes? And the other, believing him, makes them?" "Plainly."

"Concerning the same instrument, therefore, the maker indeed has right faith about beauty and depravity, adhering to the intelligent one, and being compelled to hear from the intelligent one: but the user has science <note>knowledge</note>." "Entirely." "But will the imitator have science from the use of those things he paints, whether they are beautiful and right, or the contrary? Or right opinion, from the fact that he necessarily adheres to the intelligent one, and is instructed by him what kind of things are to be painted?" "Neither." "Therefore the imitator will neither understand, nor will he have right opinion, concerning the beauty or contrary of those things he imitates?" "It does not seem so." "The imitator will be fine in his fashioning, as far as wisdom is concerned, in the things he makes?" "Not much." "Nevertheless he will imitate, not understanding in what way each thing is either rightly held or the contrary. But as it appears, that which he believes to be beautiful to the many and the ignorant, this he will imitate." "What else indeed?" "These things seem sufficiently confessed by us: that imitators understand nothing worthy of esteem about these things which they imitate; but that imitation is a certain joke rather than a serious thing: and that all those who treat tragic poetry in iambics and heroic verses are imitators above the rest." "And especially indeed."

"By Jove," I said. "This imitation is distant in the third degree from the truth. Is it not?" "It is as you say." "To which of those things that are in man does it pertain, insofar as it has power of such a kind?" "About what are you asking?" "About such a thing. The same magnitude seen from afar and near does not seem equal." "No." "The same thing also seen crooked and straight in water and out of water by us looking, and again hollow and protruding on account of the error of sight around colors, is seen. And every such turbulence in our soul is found. Which weakness of our nature the faculty of shadow-painting and the ingenuity of tricks, and other machinations having attacked, leave nothing of magical seduction unattempted." "You speak truly." "Are not the disciplines of measuring, numbering, and weighing opportune helps for man against these things, lest that should prevail in us which appears greater or smaller, or more, or heavier, but should be grasped by number, measure, and scale?" "Why not?" "And yet this is the office of the rational part of the soul." "Of this very part." "But when this part frequently measures and indicates that some things are greater or smaller than others, or equal, contraries appear to us at once about these same things." "So it happens." "Did we not say elsewhere that it is impossible that we should think contraries at once about the same things with the same part of the soul?" "And we said so deservedly." "Therefore the part of the soul which thinks outside of measure will not be the same as that which thinks with measure." "Certainly not." "But indeed, that which believes in the computation of measure and reasoning is the best part of the soul." "Nothing hinders." "That therefore which opposes this will be some ignoble part of ours." "It must be."

"Wishing to express that confession, I was saying above that painting and every faculty of imitating performs its work far from the truth: and again it meets with some part of ours, entirely devoid of prudence, and contracts a friendship: toward the sincere and true, it contributes nothing." "Especially." "Therefore a base faculty of imitating, mixing itself with something base, procreates base things." "It appears so." "Is such only that which looks to sight? Or also that which looks to hearing? Which we call poetry." "It is probable that this is also such." "Let us not then believe only what appears probable to us from painting, but let us come to that very nature of thought to which poetic imitation accommodates itself, and let us see whether it is something base, or precious...

...precious." "So it must be." "In this way then let us propose it. Poetry indeed imitates men acting either by force or spontaneously, and thinking from their actions that either some good or some evil is to them, and therefore affected either by pain or by pleasure. Is it anything else?" "Nothing else." "Does a man in all these things agree with himself? Or rather, just as he dissents according to sight, as we related, and has contrary opinions in himself at once about the same thing, so also in acting does he dissent and fight with himself? But now it comes to my mind that there is no need for us to dispute about this at present. For in the previous discussion we sufficiently agreed together about these things: having confessed, namely, that our soul is agitated by many and various contentions of this kind opposing themselves at the same time." "A good man, and one endowed with such a mind, if he loses a son or something else most dear to him, will bear it more easily than others, as we said." "Plainly." "But now let us consider this also, whether he will not grieve at all. Or is this indeed impossible, but he will moderate his grief in some way?" "This certainly is truer." "Tell me this about him at present: whether you think he will resist grief more when he is seen by men like himself, or when he is alone, destitute of the company of others?" "It matters very much if it be in the sight of others." "Furthermore, when he is alone, he will dare to say many things which he would be ashamed to utter before others. He will do many things which he would never want to be seen by others." "It is so." "That which commands him to resist is reason and law: but that which drags him to griefs is perturbation." "You speak truly." "When a man is agitated at once about the same thing by contrary movements, we necessarily say those two things are present." "Undoubtedly." "One indeed is ready to obey the law, however it shall have enjoined." "In what way?" "The law surely dictates that it is best in adversities, as much as can be done, to keep quiet and not to complain: because it is uncertain whether that which happens be good or evil, and because grief contributes nothing to what follows, nor is any of human affairs to be greatly valued, and grief is a hindrance to that which can be a sudden protection." "To what, you ask?" "To consulting, I say, about those things which have happened; it is necessary above all, and as in a cast of dice, as it has fallen, however reason says the matter may be better held, to dispose of business. Nor indeed if any adversity has fallen, ought we to prostrate ourselves and, as boys are accustomed when they stumble on a stone, falling down around that which hurt them, draw out a delay by wailing: but we must accustom the soul to be present for healing, and whatever is sick, to correct it with lamentations dismissed." "This is indeed an opportune remedy against the blows of fortune." "What is certainly best, gladly obeys this reason." "It is clear." "But that which drags one to the record of perturbation and to mourning, and detains one longer in them, is irrational, sluggish, and fearful." "So it must be said."

"That which is complaining receives a very great and varied imitation. But a prudent and peaceful character, always similar to itself, we cannot easily imitate: nor if we imitate it, will it be easily perceived, especially by a crowd flowing together into the theater from various nations. For an imitation of alien affections becomes their own." "It is entirely so." "But the imitation of the poet does not intend this, that it please this nature of the soul with its wisdom, if it is to please the common people, but it observes the complaining and varied character of the soul, which can easily be fashioned by imitation." "It is evident." "Deservedly then shall we reprehend poetic imitation, and we shall say it corresponds to pictorial imitation from the opposite side. First indeed, because both, if you look at the truth, produce base things. Then also because they similarly support a part of the soul void of reason, and desert the best part. And therefore we shall by no means receive it in a city to be legitimately governed, since it excites and nourishes this part of the soul: which while it corroborates, it destroys the power possessed of reason. And just as he who, in a city, making those who can do most wicked, would betray the city and destroy the honest: so also the imitative poet induces a perverse republic into the soul of each one, while he fawns upon that part of the soul which is without mind, and does not discern greater or smaller things, but thinks the same things now small, now large, and fashions ghosts for this part, being vehemently alien from the truth." "Far indeed."

"We have not yet narrated what greatest evil comes from it. This must be considered the greatest detriment, that it can corrupt even honest men, with very few excepted." "Why could it not? If indeed it does that." "Listen, I say, and see. Do not even the best of us, when we hear Homer or any other tragic poet, who imitates some one of the heroes being in mourning, vociferating, and bewailing his fortune in complaining measures, and beating his breast with his fists, do we not delight in a way, and gaping we follow those things, and are affected together, and seriously and studiously we praise him as a good poet, who so vehemently moves us?" "I have noticed it." "But whenever a true and domestic sorrow invades any one of us, you know how we glory in the contrary: namely, if by any way we can keep quiet and tolerate the pain: as if this indeed be of a man, and that which we were praising before be of a woman." "Plainly." "How distinguished is this praise? Indeed it is absurd that he who looks at such a man as he would by no means want himself to be, and would be most ashamed of, does not abominate it, but is delighted and praises it." "Absurd entirely." "Certainly, if you notice it also in this way." "In what way?" "Because namely that which is scarcely restrained in one's own calamities, and is prohibited from bursting into tears and weeping, and from indulging its nature greedy for tears, that is the very thing which the poets fill, and which they thoroughly fawn upon. Then certainly, and that which is best in us by nature, as being instructed neither by reason nor by use sufficiently, ceases to guard that complaining part, as if it looks at alien perturbations, and nothing be a disgrace to itself if, while another man who preaches that he excels in virtue wails more immoderately, he himself praises and pities him. Nay, he thinks he gains that pleasure, and by no reason would he want to be without it from contempt of that poetry. Few indeed notice, as I think, that it is necessary to transfer something from alien things into one's own. Surely if you have nourished that mournful character in alien miseries, and have rendered it more vehement, you will not easily stop it in your own." "You speak too truly." "Is there not the same reason concerning laughter? For that which you would be most ashamed to do for the sake of moving laughter, when you hear it in a comedy or a private imitation as something ridiculous, you listen most willingly, and you do the same thing here that we said happens in a mournful imitation. For that character of yours more prone to laughter, which you yourself were containing in yourself for fear of the crime of scurrility, here you already release into jokes, and gradually you render the affection of laughter itself more vehement, so that even in your own gestures you begin to be carried away into laughter beyond what is decent, and <margin>ridiculous</margin> a ridiculous buffoon...

# 452 Book Thirty-One. <note>original: "Liber trigesimusprimus" — In this Renaissance edition of Plato's collected works, the books are numbered consecutively across the entire volume rather than resetting for each dialogue.</note>

...you may end up being made ridiculous by the jokes of comedy. This is very true. We say the same regarding sexual desires and anger, and all the cravings and passions of the soul—both the sorrowful and the pleasant—which we previously said follow us in every action. Poetic imitation shapes such things within us: for it nourishes them by fostering and watering them, when they ought instead to be withered by dryness. It causes these passions to rule over us, when they ought rather to be subordinates, so that we might become better and more blessed rather than worse and more miserable. I cannot say otherwise. Whenever, therefore, Glaucon, you encounter the praisers of **Homer**, and you hear them saying that Homer educated all of Greece, and that for the governance and discipline of human affairs this poet should be taken up, and one's whole life should be arranged according to his instructions—remember that they are to be tolerated and loved as men who are the best they can be according to their capacity. Grant them that Homer is the greatest of poets and the leader of the tragic writers. But know this: only hymns to the gods and praises of good men should be admitted from poetry into the city. If, however, you accept the "pleasurable muse" in songs and verses, then pleasure and pain will rule in the city instead of law and that which has always seemed best to reason. You speak the truth. Let these things be said by us to support the view that we quite rightly expelled poetry from the city, being the kind of thing it is. For reason compelled us. Let us also add this, lest poetry accuse us of harshness and rusticity: there is an ancient disagreement between philosophy and poetry. (The following sayings, and many others, can be seen as evidence of this contention): "The yelping hound barking at her master's ears," and "The great man in the empty talk of fools," and "The crowd of over-wise superstitions," and "Those who meditate on tiny and thin things, being pressed by poverty." <note>These are likely fragments of lost Greek poems or common proverbs cited by Plato to show how poets traditionally mocked philosophers.</note> And there are countless other signs of this old feud. Nevertheless, let it be said that if poetry, the minister of pleasure and imitation, can bring any argument to show that she ought to be received into a well-ordered city, we will gladly receive her, so that we may enjoy her delights. For we are conscious of her charm ourselves. Truly, it is a sin to betray what seems to be the truth. For you too, my friend—are you not charmed by her? Especially by the Homeric sort? Greatly. Is it not then fair that she should come forward to defend herself, either in song or in any other meter? Entirely. Let us certainly grant her defenders—those who are not poets themselves but friends of poets—the chance to defend her in prose, asserting that she is not only pleasant but also useful for the state and for the conduct of human life. We shall listen to such a defense with a fair mind, for we consider it our gain if she appears not only sweet but truly useful to us. What stands in the way of it being a gain? Otherwise, my dear friend, just as those who have once loved something, if they later judge that love to be useless to them, they stop loving it, even if they do so with difficulty; so we, because of the innate love for such poetry bred into us by our education in beautiful republics, will kindly wait for her to appear as the best and truest thing. Yet, until she can bring such a defense for herself, we will listen to her while protecting ourselves with the argument we have set forth, like an incantation against imminent dangers, taking care lest we be ensnared again by the amorous delights and loves of the common crowd. We shall also feel that one must not be devoted to this kind of poetry as if it were true or serious; rather, every listener must be wary of it, fearing for the "republic" within his own soul. <note>The "inner republic" is Plato's metaphor for the self-governed and balanced soul.</note> And what we have narrated about poetry is exactly how it should be regarded. I certainly agree. Furthermore, my friend Glaucon, this is a great contest—greater than it seems—to become either good or evil. Therefore, neither for the sake of money, nor honor, nor power, nor any poetic delight, is it fitting to neglect justice and the other virtues. I agree based on these reasons we have discussed, and I think anyone else would confess the same. And yet, we have by no means narrated the greatest rewards and prizes proposed for virtue. You speak of immense rewards, if there are any greater than those we have already related. What can be "great" in a short span of time? For this whole time from childhood to the end of old age is but a tiny thing compared to the whole of eternity. Indeed, it is nothing. Do you think an immortal thing should be concerned with happiness only for this brief time, and not for the whole of eternity? Certainly for the whole. But what is the point of this? Do you not know that the human soul is immortal, and free from destruction? Then Glaucon, suddenly turning toward me in wonder, said: By Jove, I do not know it. Can you truly show this? Certainly, unless I wish to be unjust. I think you can do it too, for it is not difficult. To me, it seems difficult. But I would gladly hear you explaining that which you say is not difficult. You shall hear it now. Speak. Do you call something "good"? And something "evil"? I do. Is your view of these the same as mine? What is that? I think "evil" is everything that dissolves and corrupts. But that which preserves and helps is "good." I agree. Do you say there is a specific good and a specific evil for each thing? For example, bleariness for the eyes, disease for the whole body, blight for grain, rot and decay for wood, rust for brass and iron—and as I say, almost everything has its own specific evil and disease according to its nature? Indeed. Whenever any of these happens to something, does it not make the thing it touches worse, and finally dissolve and destroy the whole? How could it not? Therefore, a thing's own evil and its own depravity is what corrupts it. And if that does not corrupt it, nothing else ever will. For that which is good will never destroy anything, nor will that which is neither good nor evil. How could it? If, therefore, there is something that has an evil which makes it worse, yet is unable to dissolve it, surely a thing so naturally constituted can have no destruction. That is consistent. Is there anything that makes the soul depraved? Most certainly those things we mentioned: injustice, intemperance, cowardice, and ignorance. Does any of these destroy the soul? But take care that we are not deceived into thinking that an unjust and foolish man, when he is caught in a crime, is then corrupted by injustice, which is the soul's vice. Think about it. Does not a disease—the body's own vice—melt and dissolve the body, leading it to the point where it is no longer a body? And do not all the things we just mentioned cease to exist when their own specific evil, insofar as it inheres in them, defiles them? Do they not? Entirely so. Does injustice and other depravity, when present, in the same way dissipate and waste away the soul by its very presence, until leading it toward death it separates it from the body? Not at all. But it is absurd that a foreign vice should kill something, when its own specific vice does not bring about its destruction. That is indeed contrary to reason. Pay attention, I said, O Glaucon. We do not think the body can perish from the specific depravity of food—whether it be corrupted by age, or rotten, or prepared in any other way. But if the vice of the food brings into the body...

<summary>Socrates argues that poetry can be dangerous if it nourishes emotions over reason, and he challenges poetry's defenders to prove its utility. He then begins a logical proof for the soul's immortality, arguing that the soul is not destroyed by its own vices (like injustice) in the way physical objects are destroyed by their specific defects.</summary>

# Dialogue X on the Republic. Or, on the Just. 453

...the body's own specific vice, we will say that the body is destroyed by its vice—namely, disease—through the food. But since the body itself is different from the food, we will never believe it can be dissipated by a foreign defect (the food's nature being different) unless it induces its own specific defect. You speak quite correctly. By the same reasoning, unless a detriment of the body induces a detriment in the soul itself, we ought by no means to believe that the soul perishes from a foreign evil without its own depravity; nor is one thing dissipated by the evil of another. Reason advises this. Therefore, let us either refute these points as being incorrectly stated, or as long as they remain unshaken, let us not concede that the soul is dissipated by fever or any other disease, nor by the cutting of the throat, nor even if someone cuts the body into the smallest pieces—not until someone demonstrates that the soul itself becomes more unjust and more unholy because of these sufferings of the body. As long as a foreign evil is present to another thing, but no specific evil attaches to it, let us not concede that anything can be corrupted. But, he said, no one will ever show that the souls of the dying are made more unjust because of death. If anyone, I said, should dare to object to us that the one who dies becomes worse and more unjust (so as not to be forced to confess that souls are immortal), we shall say that if it is true that injustice is lethal to the unjust man just like a disease—and that those who receive it are destroyed by this very thing which kills by its own nature—then those who are most unjust would be destroyed quickly, and those who are less so would be destroyed later. It would not be as it is now, where the unjust only die because others inflict punishments on them. By Jove, he said, injustice will not seem to be a very grave evil if it is lethal to the wicked man, for it would be a liberation from evils. But I think it is entirely the opposite: it kills others as much as it can, but it makes the man who possesses it very much alive and especially vigilant. It is that far from being lethal! You speak skillfully. For when a thing's own depravity and its own evil cannot kill the soul, an evil arising from the destruction of another thing will never dissolve the soul or anything else beyond that which it specifically affects. Never, as is probable. Since it is destroyed by no evil at all, whether its own or foreign, it is clear that it must always exist. If it always exists, it is immortal. Necessarily. Let this then be so. And if it is so, you should notice that the souls will always be the same. For they will never become fewer, since none perish. Nor again will they become more; for if anything among the immortals were to increase, it would be from the mortal, and eventually everything would be immortal. You speak the truth. But we do not believe that at all, for reason forbids it. Nor again do we think the soul in its truest nature is such that it is varied, dissimilar, and differing within itself. How do you mean? It is not easy for something to be eternal if it is composed of many parts and has not obtained the best composition, as the soul now appears to us. That is consistent. Therefore, both the present reasoning and others besides can convince us that the soul is immortal. But if one desires to see what it is truly like, he must by no means look at it as we do now, defiled by its association with the body and other evils, but he must diligently discern by reason what it is like when it is pure. There, certainly, it will appear much more beautiful, and when it is in such a state, it will judge more clearly what is just and what is not, and the other things we discussed above. For now, we have spoken the truth about it as it appears in the present. But we have looked at it in no other way than many might look at the sea-god **Glaucus**. <note>Glaucus was a mortal fisherman who became a sea-god. Over time, his body was covered in seaweed, shells, and stones, making him look more like a monster than a god.</note> They cannot easily see Glaucus's ancient nature because the old parts of his body are partly broken, partly worn away, and entirely dissipated by the waves, while other things have grown onto him—shells, seaweed, and stones—so that he presents the image of a beast rather than his original form. In this way, we always look upon the soul defiled by innumerable evils. But one must turn one's eyes elsewhere, O Glaucon. Where? Toward its **philosophy**, I say; and one should observe what the mind touches and what company it seeks and strives for, as it is kindred to the divine, the immortal, and the eternal. What it would become if it followed such a nature entirely, being led out of the sea in which it is presently submerged—emerging naked and shaking off the sand and oysters which now cling to it. For many earthly, stony, and wild things cling to it because it is nourished by the earth, according to that sustenance which most people think is "blessed." Then at last we shall contemplate the true nature of the soul and recognize whether it is multiform or simple, and what its whole condition is. But for now, I think we have sufficiently declared the passions and forms of the soul in human life. Entirely so. Have we not set forth the other things in this discussion? We did not bring up the rewards and honors of justice, as you said Homer and Hesiod did; rather, we found that justice itself is the best reward for the soul, and we showed that one must act justly, whether one has the **Ring of Gyges** <note>A mythical ring mentioned earlier in the Republic that makes the wearer invisible, allowing them to commit crimes without being caught.</note> or even the **Helmet of Pluto** <note>A helmet of invisibility.</note>. You speak the truth. But now, besides these things, no envy prevents us from attributing to justice and all virtue those rewards which justice itself prepares for the soul among both men and gods, both while a man is living and after he is dead. Greatly so. Have you then restored to me what you borrowed in our conversation? What specifically? I granted to you that the just man should appear unjust, and the unjust man just. For you had requested it. Although it is impossible for these things to be hidden from gods and men, it pleased us to concede this for the sake of the argument, so that justice itself compared to injustice itself might be judged. Do you not remember? I would be unjust if I did not remember. After the judgment has been performed, I now demand back that you explain what reward justice receives from gods and men, so that it may also carry off the palm <note>A symbol of victory.</note> of reputation and manifest esteem, with which it also decorates its practitioners, since it has been clearly seen to bestow benefits by its very presence and does not deceive those who truly possess it. You demand what is fair. First, then, you grant me this: that the true nature of each—the just and the unjust—is not hidden from the gods. We grant it. If it is not hidden from the gods, then the one will be loved by God and the other hated, as we confessed at the beginning. It is so. And to the friend of the gods, all things that can be given by the gods are given in the best way, unless some evil hangs over him from a prior offense by some necessity. Entirely. Thus it must be thought regarding the just man, that whether he be subject to poverty, or diseases, or any other things that seem to be evils, these will ultimately turn out...

...to some good for him, whether living or dead. For he is never neglected by the gods, whoever strives to become just and, by the duties of virtue as far as is possible for a man, to become like God. It is fitting that such a man should not be despised by one who is like him. But regarding the unjust man, the opposite must be felt entirely. Vehemently so. Among the gods, then, the just man shall be given this palm of victory. So I think. But among men, does it not happen thus, if we must speak the truth? Clever and unjust men do just like those runners who run well from the starting line but not at the finish. For at first they leap out quickly, but in the end they bring back only laughter, departing with drooping ears and without a crown. But the true runners reach the finish, obtain the prize, and are crowned. The same thing, for the most part, happens to just men. Namely, at the end of every action, social interaction, and life, they are approved and receive gifts from men. Greatly so. Will you tolerate it if I bring up for them the things you said of the unjust? For I shall say that when just men reach a mature age, they hold the offices of the city as they choose; they enter into marriages with whomever they wish, both giving and receiving; and in short, whatever you said of them, I now affirm of these. And again, I say of the unjust: many of them, though they hide their vices for a time, are caught at the end of the race and made ridiculous. In old age they are miserably insulted by foreigners and citizens alike, they are beaten, and they suffer all those harsh things which you said were truly harsh: for they will be tortured and burned. Furthermore, consider all those things you mentioned as being said again by me. But as I was saying, see if you will tolerate this. I will certainly endure it, for you say what is fitting. These then are the prizes, rewards, and gifts which are given to the just man by gods and men, besides those goods which justice itself contains within itself. These are very excellent and certain. And yet these things are nothing in number and magnitude if compared to those things which await each after death. These too must be heard, so that all the things that belong to each may be sufficiently understood. Speak then, not as if you have already said too much, but as if to one who will listen most gladly. I shall not relate to you an "Apologue of Alcinous," <note>original: "Alcini apologū" — A reference to the long stories told by Odysseus in Homer's Odyssey, often used as a proverb for a long-winded tale.</note> but the story of a most excellent man, **Er the son of Armenius**, a Pamphylian by race. He had fallen in battle, and when the other corpses were taken up on the tenth day already decayed, he was found whole with an uncorrupted body. Carried home to be buried, on the twelfth day after his death, while placed upon the pyre, he came back to life and related what he had seen in the meantime. He said that after his soul had been separated from his body, it went along with many others to a certain demonic place. There he saw two nearby openings in the earth, and two others opposite them above in the region of heaven. Between these openings sat judges. After they had judged the souls, they ordered the just to ascend to the right through heaven, hanging on their front side the tokens of the judgment passed on them. The unjust, on the contrary, they ordered to the left and downward, bearing behind their backs the signs of all they had done in life. When he himself approached the judges, they told him that he must return as a messenger to men regarding the things he saw there, and they ordered him to listen to and look at everything that happened in those places diligently. He saw there souls departing through each gate of heaven and earth after the sentence was passed. Through the other two, he saw souls ascending from the earth, covered in dust, squalor, and thinness; while from heaven, others descended shining and clean. The souls coming from everywhere seemed to have come as if from a long journey, and they went gladly into a meadow that is there, as if to a famous assembly, to rest. They greeted one another, whoever had mutual acquaintance. Those who came from the earth and those from heaven questioned one another about what they had seen in their respective places. They answered one another in turn: some wailing and weeping at the memory of the evils they had suffered and seen on their journey under the earth (for that journey is a thousand years long); while those who had descended from heaven told of delights and sights of immense beauty. To relate all the things he recited in long order would be a too-lengthy narration, O Glaucon. But the summary, he said, was this: Whatever injuries they were found to have inflicted on others, they paid the penalty ten times over for each—that is, in a space of a hundred years (taking this to be the limit of human life), so that the souls might pay a tenfold penalty for an injury. Thus, if any were the cause of many deaths, or betrayed cities and armies, or drove men into slavery, or were conscious of any other atrocities and crimes, they paid tenfold penalties for all these for every deed. And again, if any had conferred certain benefits and cultivated justice and piety, they received rewards in the same proportion. Regarding those who died immediately after being born or lived only a short time, he recounted things hardly worth remembering. But regarding the pious or impious toward gods and parents, and those who had polluted their hands with murder, he said they were affected by even greater rewards and penalties. For he said he was present when someone asked another where **Ardiaeus the Great** was. This man had been a tyrant in a certain city of Pamphylia a thousand years before that time; he had killed his aged father and his elder brother, and had committed many other impious crimes. He said the one questioned replied: "Ardiaeus has not come, nor will he come. For we saw this among other dire sights: When we were about to exit the opening, having suffered all other things, we suddenly saw him and others with him, almost all of them tyrants; among whom were also some private individuals who had committed great crimes. When they dared to ascend, that opening would not permit them, but it roared horribly whenever anyone tried to go out who was either incurable or not yet purged." There stood nearby certain fierce men, fiery in appearance, who, when they heard the roar, seized them apart—Ardiaeus and those like him—and binding their hands, feet, and necks, they threw them down and flayed them. They dragged them along a path on the outside, tearing them against thorns, indicating to those passing by for what cause they suffered such things, and that they were being led away to be cast into Tartarus. There, though many various things terrified them, this fear most vehemently vexed them: lest the roar should be raised as they ascended. When it was silent, each seemed to ascend most gladly. And he recounted punishments and supplications of this kind; and on the other hand, benefits of a similar sort. When those souls of which we spoke have rested for seven days in the meadow, he said they must rise on the eighth day and depart from there, and on the fourth day after that reach a certain place from which a light is seen extending from above through the whole heaven and earth like a standing pillar, most like a rainbow, yet clearer and purer. They came to it after one day's journey, and saw there in the middle...
