# Dialogue X on the Republic. Or, on the Just. 455

...of the light, the extremities of the celestial bonds stretched from heaven. For that light is the bond of heaven, like the under-girding of triremes <note>The ropes used to reinforce the hull of an ancient Greek warship.</note>; and thus the whole circumference is held together. From the apexes is suspended the **Spindle of Necessity**, by which all the revolutions are carried out. The shaft and the hook are of adamant, but the whorl is mixed from this and other kinds of materials. The nature of the whorl is like this: in its shape, it is like those seen among us. However, one must understand from his description that it is as if one large, hollow whorl, carved throughout, had another smaller and similar one lying inside it, fitting together like those vessels that fit inside one another; and so a third and a fourth, and four others. For there are eight whorls in all, being circles inserted into one another, showing their rims above, while the back of each whorl forms a continuous surface around the shaft. That shaft is driven through the middle of the eighth and through the whole. The first and outermost whorl has the widest circular rim. The sixth has the second widest. The third the third. The fourth the fourth. The eighth the fifth. The seventh the sixth. The fifth the seventh. And the second the eighth. The circle of the first and greatest is variegated. The seventh is the most brilliant. The circle of the eighth whorl receives its color from the seventh shining upon it. The second and fifth are similar to each other, somewhat yellower than the others. The third possesses the whitest color. The fourth is reddish. The sixth exceeds the second in whiteness. The whole spindle is carried around with a similar rotation; but as the whole revolves, the seven inner circles turn more slowly in a motion contrary to the whole. Of these, the eighth is clearly moved with the swiftest motion; the second, seventh, sixth, and fifth follow one another in speed. The third is carried with such a motion that it seems to revolve the fourth. The fourth the third, and the fifth the second. The spindle turns on the knees of **Necessity**. Above each circle sits a **Siren**, carried around with the sphere, uttering a single voice, namely a single tone. From all eight, a single harmony rings out. Three others, the daughters of Necessity, sit on thrones at equal intervals: the **Fates**, in white robes with crowns on their heads—**Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos**. <margin>The Fates.</margin> They sing in harmony with the Sirens: Lachesis of the past, Clotho of the present, and Atropos of the future. Clotho, with her right hand, touches the outermost circumference of the spindle at intervals to help it turn. Atropos, with her left hand, does the same for the inner ones. Lachesis, in turn, touches both with either hand. Therefore, when the souls arrived, they had to go immediately to Lachesis. There, first, a certain prophet arranged them in order. Then, having taken lots and patterns of lives from the knees of Lachesis, he ascended a high platform and spoke thus: "The word of the maiden Lachesis, daughter of Necessity. O souls of a single day, the beginning of another cycle of a mortal and lethal race! A daemon <note>A guardian spirit or destiny.</note> shall not choose you by lot, but you shall choose a daemon. Let the one who draws the first lot choose the life to which he will be bound by necessity. Virtue is without a master; as each honors or neglects it, so shall he possess more or less of it. The fault is in the chooser; God is blameless." Having said this, he cast the lots among them all, and each snatched up the one that fell near him. Nor was anyone allowed to know his place in the order until he had taken it. Then he knew what number he had drawn. After this, he laid the patterns of lives before them on the ground—many more than those present. He said there were lives of all kinds of men and animals. For there were tyrannies among them, some lasting, others for a time, which collapsed in the middle into poverty, exile, and want. There were also the lives of famous men, some famous for appearance, beauty, strength, and athletic contests; others for their ancestry and the virtue of their noble forebears. There were lives of women in the same way. But there was no fixed order or condition of the soul in them, because it is necessary that by choosing another life, the soul's condition becomes different. Other things were mixed together: some with riches and poverty, others with diseases and health, and some occupying a middle ground. There, truly, O Glaucon, is the whole danger for a man. For this reason, every effort must be given so that each of us, neglecting other studies, seeks and pursues this study with all his strength: by which he may be able and know how to discern a good life from a bad one, and choose the better from among all as far as is possible. He must consider all the things we have now said, what they contribute to the virtue of life when joined together or separated. He should understand what beauty joined with poverty or riches does, and with what habit of the soul it works evil or good; and what nobility or ignobility, private life or power, strength or weakness, quickness of wit or slowness, and all such things that are in the soul by nature or acquired, do when coupled together. So from all these, he may be able to consider the nature of each, looking toward the soul, and discern the better life from the worse—calling "worse" that which makes the soul more unjust, and "better" that which makes it more just—and let him despise the rest. For we have seen that this choice is best both for the living and the dead. With this opinion, one must go to the underworld firm and resolved as if with adamant, lest anyone there be dazzled by riches and such evils, and falling into tyrannies and other such actions, commit many and incurable crimes and himself suffer worse things. Indeed, let him know always to choose the middle life, letting go of the extremes, both in this life and the future. For thus each becomes most blessed. Indeed, the messenger who returned from there showed that the prophet had added this to the edict: "Even for the one who comes last, if he chooses prudently and lives consistently, a desirable life will meet him, not a bad one. Let not the first choose carelessly, nor the last despair." When he had said this, he said that the one who had drawn the first lot immediately rushed forward and chose the greatest tyranny; because of his ignorance and greed, he had not examined everything sufficiently beforehand, and thus he did not know that in that life it was decreed by fate that he should devour his own children and suffer many other evils. Afterward, when he had considered the chosen life at leisure, he wailed and deplored the harmful choice, not having heeded what the prophet foretold; nor did he blame himself as the cause of his evils, but rather fortune, the daemons, and everything else rather than himself. He was one of those who had descended from heaven, who had lived in his former life in some well-ordered city, having practiced virtue by habit but without the study of philosophy. Not fewer of those who fall from above are deceived in their choosing than others, as they are ignorant of evils.

<summary>Socrates describes the Spindle of Necessity and the celestial mechanics governing the universe, then moves to the central moment of the Myth of Er: the choosing of new lives. He emphasizes that the individual is responsible for their choice of life, while God is blameless, and that a philosophical life is the best preparation for this choice.</summary>

This text is a significant Neoplatonic commentary by Marsilio Ficino on Plato’s *Timaeus*. The translation below follows your requirements, preserving the scholarly tone and structural formatting.

***

[[page number: 456]]

# Thirty-First Book.

Truly, of those who came from the earth, most—because they themselves have labored under calamities and have seen others laboring—choose a life not at random. For which reason, and also because of the lot of fortune, a change of good and evil things happens to many souls. Furthermore, if anyone, whenever he comes into this life, should practice philosophy sincerely, and the final lot of choice does not fall to him, it appears from those things which are reported from that place, that he will not only be happy here, but also that he will undergo a departure from here to there and a return back here again that is by no means earthly and harsh, but gentle and celestial. He [Er] said also that this was a spectacle worthy of consideration: in what manner the individual souls chose their individual lives. For it was a miserable, ridiculous, and wonderful sight; namely, that they made their choice for the most part according to the habit of their prior life. 

For he says that he saw the soul which had once belonged to Orpheus choosing the life of a swan out of hatred for the female race, being unwilling, naturally, to be born from women by whom he had been killed. Truly, the soul of Thamyris chose the life of a nightingale. He also saw a swan turned toward the choice of a human life, and other musical animals likewise, as is consistent. He said also that a certain soul, when the lots were offered, chose the life of a lion; this was the soul of Ajax Telamon, detesting human nature whenever the memory of that judgment came to mind, where he contended with Ulysses for the arms. After this, the soul of Agamemnon, on account of his hardships, through hatred of the human race, took up the life of an eagle. He said that the soul of Atalanta, to whom a certain middle lot had fallen, having gazed upon the great honors with which an athlete is endowed, could not restrain herself from choosing the life of an athlete. Then the soul of Epeus of Panopeus passed immediately into the nature of a skillful woman. Truly, far among the last, the soul of the ridiculous Thersites put on the form of an ape. 

By chance, however, the last lot of all fell to the soul of Ulysses. Wherefore he said that he came to the choice last. But through the memory of his past labors, ceasing from ambition and wandering about for a long time before he chose, he sought the life of a private man, and one most removed from the management of affairs. He found it at last lying somewhere and neglected by others; and he said that he would not have chosen another life even if he had happened to obtain the first lot; wherefore he gladly embraced that life. He asserted likewise that souls pass from other wild beasts into men and are changed in turn: the unjust indeed into savage beasts, but the just take up the life of gentle animals, and in this manner all mixtures are completed. 

When all the souls had chosen their lives step by step, as the lot had given, he recounted that they approached Lachesis in a long line. Truly, to each soul Lachesis assigned the *daemon* it had taken as the guardian of its life and the executor of its chosen works. This daemon first leads the soul to Clotho, and under her hand and the revolution and whirling of the spindle, it approves the fortune which the soul had chosen by lot. When the soul has touched this, it soon moves from here to the spinning Atropos, who renders the threads immutable. From there, it afterwards hastens to the throne of Necessity; through which when all have passed, they go forth under a vehement heat and glow into the Plain of Lethe, which is utterly destitute of trees and everything that grows from the earth. 

He said, therefore, that as night approached, they reclined next to the river Amelites, whose water no vessel can contain. And it is necessary for each to drink a certain amount of this water. Those, however, who do not have prudence as a leader, drink more than is proper. Truly, he who drinks always forgets all things. When they have slept until midnight, suddenly, awakened by thunder and an earthquake, they rise up suddenly, one here, another there, upward toward generation, leaping forward like stars. But he [Er] recounted that he was prohibited from drinking from that river. In what manner, however, he returned into the body, he did not know; but when he suddenly looked around at dawn, he noticed himself placed upon the funeral pyre. 

And so, O Glaucon, the fable was saved and did not perish, and it will save us likewise: if we obey it, and pass well over the Lethean river (that is, the river of oblivion), and infect the soul with no stain. Wherefore, if we comply with my words, believing the soul to be immortal and of such a kind that it can sustain all things both evil and good, we shall always follow the way leading to higher things and cultivate justice with prudence by every reason: so that we may be friends both to ourselves and to the gods while we lead this life, and after we have carried off the rewards of virtue, as if having obtained victory and triumphs, we may fare happily both here and in the thousand-year journey of which we have spoken.

## COMPENDIUM OF MARSILIO FICINO ON THE TIMAEUS.

### ON THE SUBJECT OF THE BOOK.
### CHAPTER I.

[[image: Decorative initial V]] JUST AS in the *Parmenides* he [Plato] encompasses all kinds of divine things according to his ability, so in the *Timaeus* he embraces all natural things; and in both he is greatly Pythagorean, disputing under a Pythagorean persona. And in the *Parmenides* indeed, he imitates Parmenides and Zeno, the Eleatic Pythagoreans who wrote on divine matters. In the *Timaeus*, however, he follows Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean who composed a book on the nature of the universe. Yet he does so in such a way that he joins not only eloquence to these things, but mysteries. 

Since, truly, divine things are the principles and exemplars of the natural, and natural things are the effects and images of the divine; for that reason, even in the *Parmenides* while he treats of divine things, he occasionally descends to the natural; and in the *Timaeus* while treating of nature, he rises more often into the divine. Nor does he wrongly divinize and couple nature at the same time. For nature is the instrument of divinity. And thus he either treats of natural things divinely, as Aristotle does, or he treats of divine things naturally. He also intersperses mathematics as a medium between both—namely, between the divine and the natural. These, evidently, signify divine things through numbers, but natural things through measures. Let the subject of this book, therefore, be the whole of nature itself—that is, a certain seminal and vivifying power infused into the whole world, subject indeed to the world soul, but presiding over matter, and bringing forth individual things in the same order in which the soul itself conceived them, looking as much toward the divine mind as it desires the good.

### ON THE ORDER OF THE BOOK
### and its parts.
### CAP. II.

It will be clear, moreover, that the nature of the universe and the universe itself do not consist of themselves, but depend on a superior and divine cause. It will be clear, furthermore, into how many grades nature is distributed: celestial, elemental, simple, composite, rational, and lacking reason. It will be clear that the whole generation under the moon is referred to the rational animal as to its end and master. Many things besides these will be treated concerning this very animal, pertaining both to the soul and to the body. Many things also concerning the things which are composed by nature below the rational animal. 

And to speak summarily, the triple world will be treated—namely, the divine, the celestial, and the human. It will also be shown that for all things which are composed in the world, and for the world itself, there are two certain principal intrinsic elements: namely, matter and form; but there are three extrinsic principles: namely, the efficient cause of the world, the exemplar, and the final. And the efficient cause is indeed divine power, intelligence, and will; the Exemplar, truly, is the ideas conceived by the divine intelligence; and the Final, finally, is the good.

[[page number: 457]]

# On the Timaeus.

### ON THE INTRODUCTION TO
### the dialogue. CAP. III.

FURTHERMORE, to come to the arrangement of the dialogue itself, Plato had destined five continuous days for the disputations. On the first day, indeed, Socrates disputed in the Piraeus together with Polemarchus, Glaucon, Adeimantus, and Thrasymachus the Sophist concerning the Republic. On the second day, however, he retired into the city with the same Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates, and a certain fourth unnamed stranger, perhaps a companion of Timaeus. On the third day, they make an epilogue of these things. With this made as a sort of preamble, Timaeus soon disputed concerning nature, in the presence of the three: Socrates, Critias, and Hermocrates. For the fourth, who was present at the second narration without a name, is now absent from the third; for it is not for just anyone to be present at more secret matters. On the fourth day, however, Critias held a discourse. Finally, the fifth day has not yet dawned. Quite conveniently, after the disposition and epilogue of the divine republic among men, the exemplar of this approached in the *Timaeus* in the form of the celestial republic composed by God himself; then to the antiquity of the world and the human race, and the wonderful things strenuously performed by the ancients.

### THE ALLEGORY OF THE HISTORY
### which is narrated in the prologue.
### CAP. IIII.

He narrates, moreover, among the beginnings of this dialogue, a history concerning a certain war waged between the Athenians and the Atlantians. Accordingly, Crantor, the first interpreter of Plato in his time, took this as a bare history without allegory. Certain others, on the contrary, took it as allegory alone. But all the most esteemed of the Platonists refute these, affirming indeed that it is history because Plato said it. The discourse to follow is exceedingly wonderful, but entirely true. 

Furthermore, they think that an allegorical sense must be shown for Plato, who never constructs anything at random. Therefore, they think that the war between the Athenians and the Atlantians bears an image of the opposition of all things which are in the universe. For war, that is, opposition, is the father of all things according to Heraclitus. Amelius indeed brings forward the opposition between the firmament and the planets, especially since in the *Critias* it is said that the Atlantic island was divided into seven circles. 

Origen, truly, brings forward the opposition of the superior daemons to the inferior, with the former exceeding in power and the latter in number. Numenius, however, brings forward the dissension of excellent souls following Pallas against other souls following generation under Neptune. Porphyry brings forward the battle between daemons leading into generation and souls striving toward the higher regions. He distinguishes daemons in a threefold way: some are divine; others are according to a certain habit, whose number particular souls fill when they have obtained a daemonic lot; others are evil and harmful to souls. These lowest daemons, therefore, conflict with souls always in their ascent and descent: especially the western daemons, for that region is assigned by the Egyptians to harmful daemons. 

Furthermore, Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus add to these the opposition itself prevailing perpetually in the universe: between the one and the multitude; limit and infinity; the same and the other; rest and motion; from which all things are composed under the first. Likewise, being is either through itself or not through itself. Again, essence is either incorporeal or corporeal; and the incorporeal indeed either does not decline toward bodies or it does. The corporeal, truly, is either not perishable, like the celestial, or perishable, like the elemental. Finally, in heaven indeed, there are motions opposed to each other and diverse powers. Under heaven, however, there are qualities repugnant to each other. Summarily, the discrepancy of all these things is signified by that ancient war: and everywhere the superior and more excellent things are signified by the Athenians, and others by the westerners. Such an allegory indeed fits the disputation of Timaeus not in a mediocre way. It is also confirmed through those things which we comment upon in the *Critias*.

### THE FALL OF PHAETHON. FLOODS,
### Fires, and the Description of Minerva.
### CHAPTER V.

HERE again, I advise you to remember that nine thousand years are computed by Eudoxus as nine thousand months. Likewise, that Phaethon, the son of the sun, struck by lightning, burned the earth, signifies according to some that a vast comet of a solar nature, being finally dissolved, stirred up intolerable heats. Perhaps also the fires which Moses narrates are not unlike these. 

When, truly, he comes to the floods, remember that fire is indeed the most effective of all; but water is more effective than earth, and less passive than air. Likewise, fire powerfully divides and penetrates; water everywhere strikes forcefully. Therefore, through these two elements, vaster calamities occur. Add also the final cause: namely, because through the destruction made by these two, there follows a greater good—that is, a more fecund regeneration of things—than through the plagues of the air and the chasms of the earth. Therefore, providence uses these two especially for the most ample destruction. To which the celestial wheels rightly obey: so that in whatever intervals of time God has instituted that there be destruction or rather reformation, at those same times all the planets concur in the signs either of fire or water, with the fixed stars also leading to the same end in due order. 

Remember, furthermore, that Neptune signifies natural providence, but Pallas signifies intellectual providence. And this Pallas herself is described by the Platonists as a wise and at the same time powerful divinity, both adorning celestial things and building those which occur under heaven: among the stars, presiding especially over Aries, and the leader of the equinoctial circle, where they think the moving power of the universe most thrives. Mandalus mentions a golden epigram which Proclus read in the histories of the Egyptians, inscribed in the temples of Minerva: *I am what is, what will be, and what has been. My veil no one has revealed. The fruit which I have brought forth is the born sun.*

### MOST SELECT PRECEPTS ON VOWS AND
### prayers. CAP. VI.

WHEN, truly, Plato comes to the point where God is to be suppliantly adored, listen to Porphyry thus proving divine supplications. Since God provides for us, and our affairs can be otherwise, certainly we adore usefully for the utility of our affairs: provided that we are good; for thus, having been made similar, we shall be joined more closely to God. In which conjunction, indeed, the virtue of adoration consists. Truly, since we are sons of God, but separated from him as if in exile and prison, it is fitting to adore suppliantly, so that, liberated from here, we may return to the Father. Otherwise, we shall be like those who are deprived of the patronage of their parents. 

Certainly, since we are parts of the universe, we undoubtedly need the universe. For it provides health to the parts through a conversion to the whole. If, therefore, you follow virtue, he must be adored who contains all virtue. For to love the Good itself will be the cause for you also of that good which is expedient for you. If you desire corporeal good, there exists in the universe a virtue containing all bodies. Thence, therefore, it is necessary that health come to whichever parts. 

Truly, we have discovered that the most excellent men of wisdom among all nations have applied themselves especially to divine vows: particularly the Brahmans of the Indians, the Magi of the Persians, and the theologians of the Greeks. The Chaldeans, however, adored something else also; for calling the power of the superior beings itself "God," they venerated it by this one name. These things says Porphyry. 

After him, let us hear his disciple, the divine Iamblichus, approved in this matter especially by Proclus. All things are from God in such a way that nowhere is even the smallest thing deserted by God. For everywhere divine unity thrives, through which each thing consists; and by a certain perpetual and intimate circle, they are wonderfully revolved back to God himself, from whom and in whom they are; otherwise, they would suddenly collapse into nothing. All things proceed from the divine unity, and having been produced, they retain a certain unity impressed upon them as an image of the divine unity, by which they are called back into it, and being called back, are perfected. This itself snatches souls to vows, by which union with God may be fully accomplished in us. 

But if nature, flowing from God, inserts into certain things properties agreeing with the superior beings, through which they may turn themselves in some way to the superior beings—as solar things to the sun, and lunar things to the moon—much more has the Father of souls impressed upon them powers snatching them to himself. Which indeed are seen to be situated first in a certain divine unity in the superior intellect, as well as in the intellectual reflection itself. 

Truly, suppliant adoration arising from here absolutely completes our restitution into God, drawing divine beneficence into us by natural congruity, coupling the adorers with the Adored, fitting the prayers of those vowing to the intelligence of the superior beings, moving the will of those who embrace all good things in themselves to impart good things to us according to our vow, being the effectress of divine persuasion, and stabilizing all our things in the firm stability of the superior beings. 

To the perfection of the vow, five principal things pertain. The first, indeed, is a certain notion of that which is to be adored and by what reason it is to be worshipped. The second, truly, is a certain assimilation of our life to the divine life, progressing in purity, chastity, holiness, discipline, and order, capturing divine benevolence and subjecting souls to divine bounty. The third is a certain contact, through which we almost already touch the divine essence, and we incline toward it with a certain summit of the soul. The fourth is a certain entry into the vestibule of divine light. Fifth, finally, is union, introducing the unity of the soul into the property of the divine unity intimately and connecting them, and now fusing one and the same action of the soul and of God, so that we are no longer under our own law but are of God, overwhelmed and surrounded by divine splendor. 

Truly, of this adoration which is to be performed without intermission, the supreme end is this: namely, that it may join the conversion of the soul with its own permanence, and whatever has proceeded from the divine unity, it may firmly restore that same thing to unity, and surround our light with celestial light. Therefore, right adoration alone restores souls to their blessed

[[page number: 458]]

# Compendium.

homeland. Holiness alone is full virtue. Only the good man, as Plato writes in the *Laws*, prays to God decently and happily. Constant association with the superior beings alone makes them blessed. From this, the wicked are entirely absent, and as profane persons, they are to be separated from prayers and sacrifices. Truly, the pure approach for supplication decently, leading with them especially three companions: faith, truth, and love, by which they may conceive a firm hope of good things; and beyond other things... they may merge themselves into the divine... [Note: The text here, *ipsos potiti diuinę ſēpsit ſoci lori fus immergāt*, is unclear and likely contains extreme abbreviations or printing errors]. For in vain is God sought by one who does not present himself alone to the Alone, immobile to the Stable, and simple to the most Simple. For just as we cannot join being through non-being, so neither can we join unity through multitude, stability through motion, or simplicity through mixture, but we fall back rather into the opposite. 

Thus say Iamblichus and Proclus. To these the great Theodorus adds: If anyone explores the natures of things more diligently, he will find that not only souls and minds, but in some way all things except the First, adore and vow.

### THE WORLD HAS THREE CAUSES
### above it: and depends upon an
### incorporeal cause.
### CHAPTER VII.

AFTER these things, the prayers having been performed, Timaeus—because he thinks the world was made, and therefore made by another—investigates its triple cause: first indeed the efficient, that is, the divine mind; second the exemplar, that is, the series of ideas conceived in the divine mind; third the final, that is, the good. 

Truly, that the world is from another, he indicates from this: that although it is most perfect for a corporeal nature, yet for an absolute nature it is not entirely perfect; since on account of matter it undergoes formless or deformed things; on account of dimension it undergoes a defect of powers and expects division if a divider approaches; on account of composition it is subject to dissolution; on account of the repugnance of parts it contrives evil; on account of motion it shows indigence and undergoes an admixed privation; finally, on account of the very congress from diverse things, it needs a certain superior connecting principle which exists most perfectly because it is from itself; just as the world, because it is not most perfect, is known not to be from itself. 

Absolutely all kinds of composite things are reduced to something which is not composite in that kind: just as dimensions are reduced to a point, which is not composed of dimensions; numbers to unity, which is not from numbers; elements to that which is not mixed from elements; therefore also the whole continuous order is reduced to Being, which does not consist of beings. That, however, will be a substance mixed with no accidents. Therefore, it will be neither "how much" nor "of what kind," but a total and impartible substance. Nor does it have any accidents that come upon it beyond substance, except from that which is one and the simplest. For those things which in following things are accidents, in the Supreme must be substance, and those the best. 

Truly, the more things you add to the Best, the further you compel it to depart from unity itself. Since from the admixture of new things there, quality results, and you degenerate. Not only, therefore, this world—because it is entirely composite—but also if there is any superior world, and yet in some way composite, it depends on a superior simplicity. Which also exists above eternity, from which in divine minds there is an integral eternity; and in rational animals, an eternity mixed with time; and in the spheres of the world, a temporal sempiternity. In these things, however, which are made by the motion and virtue of the spheres, there is a certain portion of time. 

Those things, therefore, which are thought of above the soul, always *are* and never *become*. The soul itself both *is* and *becomes* always. The world is indeed never, but becomes always. Those things which are born in the world are also never, but sometimes become. Truly, we say that "becoming" is transacted in time. Since, truly, the world is completed by perpetual motion and time, therefore it is judged to become always. Insofar as it is eternal, it is thus said to be "never," just as an image in a torrent is made continually, always indeed brought into becoming in it, yet never established in being. 

Truly, the Platonists think that this differs between the soul and the world: that the heaven continues to become not only through action but even through essence. Truly, the soul becomes through action, but through essence it *is* from God rather than *becomes* from God; since the essence is impartible, let it have a certain power that is in some way productively taken, through which it may produce in itself its own life and motion. Truly, the heaven depends entirely from elsewhere. Summarily, just as from the same rock, between a pond and a running torrent, an image is steadily in the pond, but in the torrent it *becomes* and being evanescent is continually recreated; so both always depend on God, but in one way and another. For from him the soul indeed always *is*, but the world always *becomes*. But let us begin again from another principle.

### THE GOOD ITSELF IS THE CAUSE
### of all things more than following causes, nor has it
### any proportion with the rest.
### CAP. VIII.

THAT this universe has all things from the supreme God—both action and virtue equally, and essence—all Platonists maintain without controversy. For they accept this from Plato out of all his books. They hear him confirming the same in his letters. Where indeed, with a vast mystery, he referred the third effect to the third cause, the second effects to the second, and all indeed to the one cause of all. Nor did he say that the first effects are to be reduced to the first cause, lest by pronouncing only "firsts" we should suspect that those alone depend on God, and by naming God the "first cause," we should suspect that he himself agrees in a certain genus with the other causes, and agrees with the effects in a certain property of domination. 

And so, he showed at once that all things proceed from him, and that he meanwhile is entirely absolute from any communion with those proceeding. And on account of absolute simplicity, he names him the One itself; on account of exuberant beneficence—through which, as a productive principle, he effects all things, and as an end, he perfects the same by leading them back—he names him the Good itself. He thinks, however, that whatever things are made, depend more on him than on the other causes. Since he himself in any work both acts earlier, and longer, and more vehemently than the other causes; and the others, whatever they are, are because he makes them; and whatever they act, they act with him leading. 

Truly, to show that individual things emanate more from him than from other causes, he replicated that he himself is the principle of all. Seeking "about the king of all, all things." Likewise, "for his sake, all things." Again, "he himself is the cause of all things," so that we might understand both that all things arise especially from there, and that God is the Guardian, the Effector, the Exemplar, and the End. Furthermore, that the One itself and the Good is above all essence and intellect, and is the cause of both, he evidently showed in the sixth book of the *Republic* and in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. 

It is established, moreover, that the One and the Good are the same, lest if they were diverse, there should be compelled to be two supreme principles. Truly, the principle must be both most simple and best. Nothing, however, is either simpler than unity or better than goodness. Nor is unity better than goodness, nor goodness simpler than unity. One, therefore, is both, and the supreme God. And that he is entirely above essence and mind, we have sufficiently confirmed in the *Theologia* and elsewhere.

### ON THE DEPENDENCE OF MATTER
### on the Good itself: and on the action of mind and soul
### on matter: and on the intelligible
### world. CAP. IX.

FROM this One and Good, therefore, which is eminent above all essence, Plato in the *Parmenides* and *Sophist* derives all grades of beings: both those which truly are, that is, separate forms; and those which are not truly, that is, forms inherent in matter; and then the lowest grade of matter. Which is so much "not truly" that it is closest to that which is now imagined not truly to be. This matter, derived in the *Parmenides* from the Good itself in the ultimate grade of things, he accepts in the *Timaeus* as if already generated, and subjected to the architect of the world for the effect of the mundane work. 

But is God the author of the world also the effector of matter? The school of Ammonius and Origen will answer that he is the same. And in the *Parmenides* indeed it is treated how matter accepts being from God; in the *Timaeus*, truly, by what reason it accepts "well-being" from the same, but it is thought to be in some way "to be" before it is "to be well." 

The common school of the Platonists will answer otherwise: that it is not the same God who makes matter and who next formats it. Rather, matter is from the supreme Good; but it is formed by the intellect; and finally moved by the soul. Nay, rather all these are from the First; but being is from the First alone. Being formed is from the First through the intellect; being moved, and through moving being formed movably, is from the First through the intellect and soul together. 

For the sake of example, let us imagine a certain potter who makes the clay with his own hand, and forms the made clay through a wheel; and in forming, distinguishes and figures it with a certain wooden comb. No one would say that the vessel is made more by the comb and the wheel than by the potter, although it is made by the potter through the wheel and the comb. They judge this universe similarly to proceed from the Good itself through a certain divine intellect and the soul of the universe. Merely from him, the world is next made most one, and from the Good itself, most good. 

But since this visible world—on account of the multiple distance of parts, the repugnance of qualities, the diversity of effects, and the deformity of materials—is neither most one nor most good, therefore they think that before this world, from the divine unity and goodness itself, another world next emanates, and as much as nature permits, as great as possible, not visible indeed, but intelligible and intellectual, having the exemplars of all things which are born in this world. Which divine intellect indeed they name not the Good itself,

[[page number: 459]]

# On the Timaeus.

but the best son of the Good. If we understand this to be of one substance with the First, we shall reconcile Plato more to Christian theology. But the interpreters of Plato will cry out against this.

### SUN, LIGHT, LUMEN, SPLENDOR,
### Heat, Generation; similarly Unity, Goodness,
### Intellect, Soul, Nature, the Body
### of the world, an image of the
### superior worlds.
### CAP. X.

LET Christian and Mosaic truth, therefore, remain. And meanwhile, if it pleases many, perhaps this was the opinion of the interpreters or of Plato or of Pythagoras: that the intelligible world is a medium between the visible world and the Good itself: an image indeed of the Good, but an exemplar of the corporeal world: thus depending on the Good, just as lumen outside the sun depends on the lux within the sun. 

Furthermore, producing from itself next the soul of the world, just as light pours out from itself splendor; through which soul it generates individual things daily, just as splendor through heat generates corporeal things. Just as, therefore, these six grades are arranged in order: First, any substance itself. Second, a substantial and intimate light (*lux*). Third, the light (*lumen*) flowing from there. Fourth, the splendor resulting from the light. Fifth, the heat ignited by the splendor. Sixth, the generation coalescing from the glow of heat: so let six others be arranged. 

First indeed Unity, then Goodness; yet these two are not two in the thing itself, but are distinguished in some way by reason. For it is the same divinity: and because it surpasses all things, it is called Unity; and because it overflows back through all things, it is called Goodness. This exuberant virtue indeed Plato in the sixth book of the *Republic* calls the idea of the Good. Truly in the letters, "of good things," and "of the good"—that is, of the Supreme, and of the good things which proceed from him. 

In the third grade, let there be placed a certain divine mind, as light (*lumen*) flowing from light (*lux*), conceiving in itself multiform ideas by a double fosterage of the supernal light and the divine idea of unity: not otherwise than in light (*lumen*) many rays are now derived from one ray of light (*lux*). Truly, not only are the ideas of things grasped in this mind as if sources; but also to this multitude of minds, armies are reduced as if by a leader from the same divine light, from which they also equally proceed. 

Truly, that whole genus is named the superior world: but as far as it looks to following minds, the intellectual world; but as far as it looks to the leader, the intelligible world. But the mind itself is named two minds, partly indeed intellect, and partly intelligible. Intellect indeed insofar as it applies itself to discerning the reasons of things. Intelligible, truly, insofar as such reasons are contained in its ideas. Finally, the idea of the Good reigns not only over the intellect, but even over the intelligible. 

After this archetypal world, in the fourth grade let there follow the soul of the corporeal world: the world now rational, begotten from the intellectual world, just as splendor from light. And just as splendor is already mixed with motion, so the soul touches and traverses the reasons of immobile ideas in a certain mobile manner. 

To this let the fifth grade succeed, namely nature itself, the world now seminal, from the rational world of the soul, just as heat resulting from splendor. Finally, in the sixth grade, let this corporeal world be placed, thus derived next from the seminal, just as the generation of things from heat. 

But if you wish to compare it more aptly by other things, you will think of a certain most wise architect: first, the power and natural goodness; then the geometric and contemplative intellect, having the common reasons of measures; third, the practical reason, so they say, now consulting about the artifice through those very reasons; fourth, the imagination figuring the shapes and modes leading to the work; fifth, the affect; sixth, the power of moving. In such comparisons, you will see effects made much more by the antecedent things than by the following.

### INDIVIDUAL ORDERS ARE REDUCED TO INDIVIDUAL
### heads, the whole order to a universal
### head, from which all things are com-
### posed from act and
### potentiality.
### CHAPTER XI.

NOR truly ought it to escape us that the proper genera of things must be referred to proper heads, and the whole genus to a universal head. For all the bodies of the world are referred to one body; all natures to one nature; souls to the Soul; minds to the Mind; and finally, good things to the Good. And because they are good, therefore all things. 

Thus indeed all things by a certain natural conversion desire the Good as an end: since they have come forth from the Good itself as a common procession from a principle: and therefore all things desire it. So that the lowest matter desires it with no low desire. Perpetually indeed in all things generated there is a certain similarity to the Good, so that it may appear that this world depends on the Good. 

On the Good, I say, rather than on the mind. For since the action of the mind, which is made through ideal forms, is terminated at forms; truly, the action of the Good, as it is most ample, descends beyond forms even into matter, and makes it both a sort of good and capable of good. But what I now call matter, Plato in the *Philebus* calls by a broader name, "infinity," saying that the Good itself next begat infinity and limit; and immediately mixed them together, and from this mixture composed all things. That is, from a certain formable potentiality and an approaching form. 

For he calls the formable potentiality, as if not yet defined by itself nor perfect, "infinity." Truly, the form applied to this he names "limit": because evidently it defines the undefined potentiality and perfects the work now in species. From these two, therefore, they wish the intelligible world to be fused next from God: and then the sensible world to be constituted from the intelligible world out of the same or similar things. 

So that that intellect, the next architect of the visible world, accepted matter from the Good itself, in some way spiritual; but already under itself degenerating into the dimension of a mass, formless and void: as if perhaps it might be moved from itself, changing without order: but through the order of ideas received from the same Good, he formed it and reduced it into order, before it might wander outside of order. Especially since he first introduced into it a rational soul, the mistress of most orderly motion. Truly, not only will matter be formless by itself, but he says that the soul also will be formless, unless God forms both. What indeed in matter is the corporeal species, that in the soul is the reason and intelligence: which if they lack, they will move matter inordinately. But to express this, he considered matter without form and the rational soul; and he overcame the motion that would proceed from there without order.

### MATTER WAS NOT INOR-
### dinate before the world in time, but by a certain
### reason of order.
### CHAPTER XII.

FROM all these things, we can gather that matter is not equal to the maker of the world. It is not before the world by any interval of time, although by a certain origin and order: it was not tossed inordinately before order, but was about to wander far from order, as much as is in itself, unless it had been immediately ordered from above. 

Lest anyone should disapprove of this mode of speaking in Plato, imagining matter tossed inordinately before the world, let him hear also Moses, saying before the distinction of the world that the earth was void and composite, and darkness was over the face of the abyss. I omit for the present the poetic chaos. 

It is pleasing to bring forward Philo the Jew, expounding the Genesis of Moses with similar words. If anyone wishes to seek the cause why this universe was created, he will not err in my judgment if he thinks what a certain one of the ancients brought forth: that the creator himself and progenitor and author of the universe is good: and for the sake of his goodness, he envied no substance which by its own nature had nothing of good, and yet could become all things. For its own nature was inordinate, formless, inanimate, altogether varied, incongruous, inharmonious, inconstant, fit to be changed into the contrary, and to receive the reason of the best things, namely, of form, animation, similarity, congruity, harmony: finally, of the idea of every better thing. 

Likewise in the second volume of the same book, he says: When the creator had begun to form into order from inordination, and into discretion from confusion, the substance which was inordinate and confused by its nature: he situated the earth and water in the middle place. These things says Philo. Furthermore, if you consider the six grades of things brought forward above, you will perceive perhaps how similar Plato is to Moses, absolving the Genesis of the world in six days: how similar also to Pythagoras, proving that the number six is altogether accommodated to Genesis and marriages; whence also he calls it *Gamon*, for the reason that its parts placed together beget itself, and render the begotten similar to the progenitor.

### DOUBLE OPINION ON THE ORIGIN
### of the world. CAP. XIII.

IF anyone should ask whether according to Plato the world was sempiternal: I answer indeed to the interpreters Severus and Atticus and Plutarch and many others, as Proclus recounts, that it was not always. But to the interpreters Crantor, Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, and most others, that it always was, and was always from God, nay rather, flowed. For they say that God always *is*. Truly, the world always *becomes* and flows. 

And if you consider it lacking a beginning of time, it is said to be unbegotten; but if you consider the perpetual efflux of the world from God, it is said to be assiduously generated: nor does it depend any less on God if it always depends and flows, than if it began sometimes to depend or ceases. Just as light no less draws its origin from the sun, nor less serves the sun, if it always produced and flowed from the sun than if it did so sometimes.

[[page number: 460]]

# Compendium.

### TRIPLE CONJECTURE OF THE PLA-tonic
### opinion concerning the world, and what is the cer-
### tainty of the Platonic sentiment concerning the world.
### CAP. XIIII.

FURTHERMORE, in Platonic matters, we proceed either by conjecture or by science. As far as conjecture looks: he himself thus speaks, and his followers thus dispute, so that his opinion on the origin of the world may be gathered into three heads. 

For either he thought that matter was sometimes created from nothing by God, and at the same time formed in time. Although in this work which is composed from matter, according to a certain order of production, matter itself is thought to become before it is formed: and for matter to be before being formatted: and before the work made from matter, matter as if alone out of which the work was to be made. 

Or, that God did not sometimes produce new matter, but from eternity, and similarly adorned it: although it is imagined inordinate before being ordered. Since by its nature it lacks order, which it expects from another. And since anything is thought first according to what it is, rather than according to what it receives, it can rightly be thought of by itself apart from order, as being itself devoid of order. 

Or, as I said, that matter was always from God, and continuously: but not continuously ordered, nay rather through intervals of times: so that it is for God to order stably: but for matter to receive order movably: and let it receive the temporal tempering of its order, not otherwise than a clock receives it from a craftsman: and having completed it according to its nature in certain intervals of times, let it lose its order gradually and finally entirely, and return into Chaos: but let God, not at all tolerating the sudden extreme confusion, re-temper it into its prior disposition by a single nod, and let that be done infinitely in turn, with God never changed, and matter infinitely reformed. 

Thus far human conjectures have preceded in Platonic matters. As far, truly, as we have science, we affirm that our Plato affirmed that the World does not exist from itself, but from a cause: not indeed by chance, but from a certain one: not from a natural cause only, but from an intellectual one: not from an intellect determined by the mode of nature, but rather voluntary, with the will not compelled by a certain natural instinct, but free. For nothing is more free than that which is through itself, and acts through itself entirely: yet not by any contingent will. For nothing is contingent where will and necessity are the same. Again, nothing is violent where necessity and will are the same in turn. 

Truly, to open that up, he replicated the name of divine intelligence no less than that of divine will in fabricating the world. And he added that the will of the good itself is the highest cause and the most certain of causes. Which he shows to be free from this: that he often says the architect God consulted in the manner of a deliberation, and deliberated about constructing the work. By which words he wants not an ambiguous God to be understood, but a free one choosing. Furthermore, he says that the mundane work did not proceed from God only once, but proceeds and is preserved assiduously. Since the supreme deities of the world together with the world would be dissoluble by their nature, unless they were ruled by the divine will. 

It will be sufficient, therefore, and that indeed as great as possible, to have affirmed such things about the philosopher. For these being granted, you will easily be able to say that God, when he effects by a providing and free will, composed the world new without any novelty of himself. And thus hearing that it was not sometimes produced new, but rather from an age: you will be able to preserve at once his majesty for God, on whose will, and this indeed free, the world no less needs and depends, if it always needs and depends, than if it proceeded at some time. 

Since, truly, Plato often says that asseverations must be made about divine things as far as they are proved by divine oracles: we also ought to assent to sacred letters rather than to our conjectures.

### THE WORLD PROCREATED FOR THE SAKE OF THE GOOD
### according to the similarity of the divine reason and the
### divine word.
### CAP. XV.

HE made the world, therefore, by his will, that is, by his goodness. As much by will as naturally overflowing on account of immense fecundity, which first indeed rejoices in itself: and on account of that, it is then delighted by this its image: yet in such a way that it constitutes the end of this delight not in this image, but in the exemplar itself and principle. 

Since, therefore, he made the world by goodness: therefore he made it for the sake of the good. For he did not procreate it simply that it might be, live, and understand: but that it might both be well, live well, and understand and compare the good. That is very consonant with the Mosaic: "God saw this and that were good: and all things were very good." 

And because beauty is the splendor of goodness, therefore he adds that the world was procreated most beautiful by the best God: temporal indeed, but to the image of the eternal exemplar. He will also say often, that as many species as are in the archetype—that is, the principal world, that is, intelligible and imitable—he disposed just as many forms of things in this world, and thus made it similar to himself: as one who understands the ideas of things not among the clouds, as certain materialists calumniate, but to consist in the mind of the mundane architect. 

When, truly, he says that the ideas are in the Life itself, he seems to prophesy that evangelical saying: "That which was made was life in him." And where he says and repeats often that the world was constituted by divine providence, he confirms the whole religion. When Theophrastus had observed this as something wonderful in a philosopher, he said: "Plato alone, or certainly most of all, assigned the causes of things to divine providence." But, O Theophrastus, with whatever mind you say that about Plato, undoubtedly you will confess that Plato alone or of all most of all is providing and divine.

### WHY THE WORLD IS ONE
### and spherical, and moved in
### a sphere.
### CAP. XVI.

TRULY, he shows next that the divine exemplar of the world—which the evangelist, but in a more divine sense, calls the divine Word—is unique: because that which contains all things, leaves nothing outside itself: and therefore it is necessarily unique. But on this itself more diffusely in the *Theologia*. 

Since, however, this world in the rest, as far as could be done, refers to the divine world and intellect: so that he who perceives forms in this matter, as if beholds the divine countenance in a mirror: certainly it represents that one in the very unity itself, the effector and preserver of all: so that the work of one architect may be one. One, therefore, is the world of the one God. 

Certainly, if a human architect could dominate matter, after he had made several buildings, of which any one in itself is one, he would finally circumvallate all with one certain wall. God, however, can entirely, since he is the master of matter. Nor is it permitted to imagine many worlds as if balls, some outside others. For thus the divine work would be dissipated: and there would be empty spaces between the worlds. 

You will judge it more probable, if for as many orbs as he imagines scattered through a vacuum, you think of spheres rather within spheres, so that any sphere is a world in a world: and the whole work is one, and thus ordered in turn: and nothing is found empty or devoid of unity and order. 

But if the figure of the world is spherical, thus indeed it is most uniform, capable, indissoluble, agile, and thus and not otherwise can a mass be placed in a mass and without vacuum, and moved without offence: that is, if not squares into squares or circles, but orbs into orbs are inserted. Finally, the principal cause of this mundane sphere is: that the nature of the divine world is also orbiculate: which reflects upon itself in understanding and loving. Truly, the reason of spherical motion is both the figure itself which receives motion and the intimate revolution through intellectual species of the mundane soul which moves it.

### WHY THE WORLD IS DIVIDED EITHER
### into five or into six regions: and how the
### septenary and circular number agree with it: and
### how it is distributed according to the
### similarity of the intelligible world.
### CAP. XVII.

WHEREFORE, to the mundane division numbers are not wrongly accommodated: in which the first roots are of circular numbers: Five, namely, from the odds; and from the evens, six. 

Truly, we say that the number twenty-five is multiplied from five in the manner of a circle: since one returns in some way to the same point when five times five are computed as twenty-five. Likewise in a similar circle the number one hundred twenty-five. For five times twenty-five make so many. 

The same is the reason of the circular six for thirty-six, and likewise for two hundred sixteen. Also the superior numbers, they name some square by reason of their origin, others oblong; yet they call them circular by reason of their fall and state. And so, by five and six, the first roots of circular numbers, we divide the circular body of the world. 

First indeed into five parts, namely the celestial fire: the ethereal fire under the moon, air, water, earth. Which division indeed is proved in the *Epinomis*. Then we distribute through the senary: where we divide the celestial fire into the non-wandering and the wandering. Which partition is frequently used by Plato. 

But we shall derive the sensible distribution of the world from the exemplary distribution of itself more commodiously in this Platonic manner. God indeed imagines in the world within himself, in the intelligible, one power as formable and another as formative. That one, as I said, they call infinity; this one, limit, the Pythagoreans and Platonists name. He imagines also the mutual mixture of these things: and understands that a third form from this mixture immediately coalesces. 

But he also notices this form itself as if triple: having something of infinity, something of limit,

[[page number: 461]]

# On the Timaeus.

and something of its own. Whence it happens, that after the number two—namely of infinity and limit—the number three arises immediately, with the third form added to these. Let the number four also arise, with such a form distributed triply. Finally, the number six is born, where that world of that world is extended to produce inferior things. The number seven is also born, where that world as an image is referred back to the father. In which grade, as on the seventh day, let him rest. 

Truly, if you render individual things to individuals: you will notice that this corporeal world has fire as form from that limit of the supernal world: but from infinity as matter it has earth. Truly, from the middle form of that world, it has the moisture as a conciliator of fire and earth: which both glues together the earth, by its nature dissipable; and nourishes the fire, easily resolvable from itself. And it possesses three certain things in itself: here indeed something igneous, there truly something earthy; but something of its own and pure in the middle, something aerial: while on one side through the high it verges toward fire, and on the other through the low it verges toward earth. After this fivefold division of the world, let there be a sixfold: if you imagine the common form of all things. Let it become sevenfold: if you reform this very form of the world by the exemplar: in which seventh day let him rest.

### WHY THERE ARE DISTINCT PARTS IN THE WORLD
### and why they are contrary, and concerning
### the four elements.
### CAP. XVIII.

NOT only indeed do we see the distinction of forms, but also repugnance in the world. For it proceeds from the first, and in proceeding it degenerates. Procession indeed makes distinction: degeneration makes repugnance. 

The origin of that division itself is the fecundity of the cause overflowing outward: propagating into the ample. Truly, with the procession through many grades of division, one arrives finally at repugnance: especially since the matter of the world, on account of imbecility, cannot thus in turn reconcile forms, as that superior world reconciles them in itself. Whence it happened, that God preceded matter with dimension, so that he might receive forms that would be repugnant to each other in diverse hostings. 

Finally, since we call those things contrary which in the same genus are most distant; and those things diverse which are separated from each other in genera: from that indeed that they are contraries in the world, it appears that any genus has as many species as possible: from that however that they are diverse, it is established that the universe possesses many genera. 

Since, truly, both all species are reduced to genera, and genera to the universe and finally to its common form, it is concluded that just as the superior world is uniform and omniform, so this one is omniform and uniform. Truly, the contrary quality and figure of elements and heavens lead to generating new forms daily: with motion contributing evidently. For if there were only one element, nothing would be generated: which Hippocrates also asserts. If many were similar to each other, nothing new would be effected: which Heraclitus proves. 

It is necessary, however, that this world, by the perpetual generation of new forms, imitate the eternal action of the superior omniform world according to its ability. Let there be, therefore, as Empedocles sings to the poets, elements contrary to each other. Let there be also a medium between contraries: since contraries both are most distant, and without a medium they least agree. 

But this medium cannot be indivisible. Otherwise contraries will not be distant through it. Therefore it has dimension. But by that part with which it touches one, it does not touch the other. And it has moreover a necessarily middle part, through which it may also be discrete from the extremes. Therefore Plato always interposes at least two mediums between contraries: as appears evidently from his words. He interposes also a third: where he says that the medium has a power through which it may guard the union not only of the extremes but also its own. But let him place two manifestly—nor indeed do we contend that now—namely between fire and earth, two certain things: namely air and water. 

Truly, that there is need of at least two mediums between entirely contrary bodies, he shows from numbers and dimensions, which in some way precede natural bodies.

### LINEAR, PLANE, AND SOLID NUMBERS,
### and why one medium suffices between planes: but
### between solids it does not satisfy. And how
### mathematical reasons are referred
### to Physical things.
### CAP. XIX.

THAT numbers are triple among the Pythagoreans we have declared elsewhere: Linear, Plane, Solid. Linear indeed which only unity measures as a point: as Two, Three, Five, Seven, and similar ones. 

Truly, Plane numbers are those which are multiplied from numbers as if from sides. Just as six from twice three is made... Truly from the number of planes we call those "quadrangular" and "equilateral" which are completed from the multiplication of some number into itself. As four from twice two, and nine from thrice three: and sixteen from four times four. 

"Inequilateral," however, are those which are from the multiplication of a smaller number into a larger: such as six from the deduction of two into three. We call them also "oblong": which are completed from the multiplication of a much smaller number into a far larger number: such as ten resulting from the deduction of two into five. Since from twice five comes ten. This, if in the tenth book of the *Republic* we called it "oblong" in some way linear, we wanted "oblong" to be understood. 

Besides these, we called those "solid" which are effected from the deduction and reduction of some number into itself, like a solid mass into three as if produced dimensions: as twice two twice is eight. Thrice three thrice is twenty-seven. Four times four four times is sixty-four. 

Take the first two planes: those namely which are procreated from the first linears: as for instance here four from two; and there nine from three. These two planes, namely nine and four, you can bind to each other by a single competent medium: that is, six. For what proportion nine is to six, the same six will be to four, for in both it is the sesquialter proportion [3:2]. Since nine contains six and besides its other part, that is, three. Similarly, six comprehends four, and besides two, the other, that is, the half part of four. 

Truly, that six is the competent medium is evident from this, that it is composed from both. For the side of four is two; truly of nine is three. Truly from the multiplication of two into three comes six. Similarly if you take beyond nine the square sixteen, the middle will be twelve: which is born from the sides of these. For the side of nine is three; of sixteen, four. But if you lead three into four, you will report twelve: which being the middle of these connects both by an equal reason, namely by a sesquialter reason. For sixteen comprehends twelve, and besides its third part. Similarly twelve beyond nine includes the third portion of nine. You see therefore what Plato says: that plane numbers can be bound together by a single medium. 

Take besides the first solid numbers, those I say which are first made from the first linears in being led out and reduced: here eight from two; and there twenty-seven from three. These certainly you cannot couple to each other by a single medium: but you are compelled to accept at least two mediums, namely twelve, and eighteen. For you will accept twelve from twice two thrice; truly eighteen from thrice three twice: and through these numbers you will reconcile the extremes in a sesquialter ratio. 

Truly the number twenty-seven embraces eighteen and again its other part, that is, nine; similarly eighteen exceeds twelve. Likewise twelve equally exceeds eight. Through these things it is clear: that solid numbers always need more mediums by which they may be congruously coupled. 

What however we have explained in numbers, we can demonstrate the same in dimensions both plane and solid, showing that between comparable planes one medium often suffices: but between comparable solids, more true mediums must be placed. Which indeed would be both too long, and is already sufficiently shown by Iamblichus, and Proclus, and Chalcidius. 

Since, truly, Plato accepted these mathematical things not for their own sake, but for the sake of natural things here: these being passed over, let us consider briefly why he especially understands the mysteries of nature through mathematical images. 

Beginning with what is read in sacred letters, that God perfected all things in "number, measure, and weight," it is manifestly touched upon by Plato, bringing forward numbers, measures, and solids. For through solids he comprehends also weights, which he also signifies where after dimensions he commemorates the powers of inclinations, as if the causes of weights. 

By numbers indeed he wants to be understood certain instrumental figures, or magnitudes... also Aristotle compared to numbers. By measures, however, certain instrumental figures, or magnitudes accommodated to certain species. Finally by solids and powers, he signifies qualities, and those things which are extended intimately with the masses, and provide momentum to motions and actions. 

Truly all in the universe indicate both the species of things, and the figures and magnitudes of species, and qualities, composed by a geometric and mutual proportion to each other: so that by whatever reason the lowest are exceeded by the middle, by the same the middle are exceeded by the superior. 

Likewise through numbers he designates the arithmetic medium, which consists in the parity of numbers. Through dimensions and measures, the geometric medium, which is located in the identity of ratio and proportion. Through weights and powers, the musical medium: which in the equality of portion or similarity of powers, comprehends by its virtue the velocity and tardiness of motions, and the sharpness and gravity of voices.

[[page number: 462]]

# Compendium.

### FIRST DISCUSSION, WHY THE
### quaternary number of elements
### agrees with the world.
### CAP. XX.

BUT concerning these more broadly elsewhere. Now indeed let us return to the partition of the mundane parts, so that we may be able to behold their harmonic composition. In the superior parts indeed we said that five and six agree with the circular figure of the world. Now moreover we say that the quaternary agrees with the same plenitude. 

Certainly the first quaternary fills all difference of numbers: embracing in itself the first even and the first odd. It fills also the simple progression of numbers, since four terms complete the denary: one, two, three, four; perfectly consummating the denary [10]. It fills also the procession of dimensions, attaining by four terms the point, length, width, and depth. It fills musical consonance. Namely, within the limits of the quaternary, the double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter, sesquitertia, diapason, disdiapason, diapente, diatessaron, are coerced. 

It fills nature proceeding up to four terms: substance, quantity, quality, motion. Finally it fills the universe, whether what is in nature, or what is above nature: essence, being, virtue, and action. Rightly therefore the Pythagoreans designated the plenitude of the mundane, both of the body and of the soul, by the quaternarity, and they testified to it by swearing that the quaternary is the fountain of ever-flowing nature. 

From this fountain surely flows the quaternary number of elements. Hence the quadruplicity in the heaven is fourfold. Hence under the heaven are four times [seasons]. Hence under time, four humors, complexions, affects. Hence above time four virtues arise. Hence in eternity four examples of virtues.

### SECOND DISCUSSION FOR PROVING
### the same.
### CAP. XXI.

FURTHERMORE, unless I feared partly prolixity, partly also... I would recount certain wonderful comments of Iamblichus and Syrianus and Proclus, constituting four grades above the world... namely one, limit, infinity, mixture. Furthermore placing after them the world of the superior beings—that is, the first and intelligible mind—the mind and the world partly intelligible, partly also intellectual: after this the simply intellectual mind and world. Truly in the fourth place the now animal mind and world, the leader of the sensible world. 

Likewise that the supreme mind both looks toward those four—namely the One and the limit, and infinity and the mixture—and has four by its own nature: namely here indeed unity, there truly essence. Again substantial unity, and uniform essence, and all ideas of things entirely partaking of a similarly fourfold nature. 

Likewise that the intellectual and Jovial mind, the maker of the world, in fabricating the world, looks toward the intelligible and supreme mind as an exemplar, and toward the good as an end. And because by reason in the intelligible world—which they also name "being itself" and "living itself"—it receives principles and ideas of a fourfold nature, it similarly distributes the world into four regions. 

Of which the first may extend from the first heaven, and after the heaven through the sphere of fire up to the beginning of the air: the second from there up to the middle of the air: the third from there to the earth: truly the fourth may be the earth: and to such a partition let four armies of rational inhabitants in any region respond, namely of mundane gods, likewise of angels, then of daemons, and finally of particular souls. But these being omitted, let us return to our purpose.

### THIRD DISCUSSION FOR CON-
### firming the same.
### CAP. XXII.

THERE are four elements with the metaphysician: essence, being, virtue, and action. Four with the mathematician: point, line, plane, and depth. Four with the physicist: the seminal virtue of nature, natural sprouting, and the adult form and the composite. 

Render truly individual things to individuals. To essence indeed the fold and the seed; to being itself the line and the sprouting; to virtue the plane and the form; to action the depth and the composite; and everywhere extremes as if solids by two continuous mediums. 

Manifestly truly what in mathematics is the point, he thinks is in the physicist the seminal virtue, individual and stable. Truly what in mathematics is the linear production in length, he thinks is in physics the sprouting of the germinating form, so to speak. Likewise what is there the plane, here properly form: for as a plane terminates a body, so form terminates matter. 

Finally what is there depth, here is the composite; a double composite indeed, both formal—that is, a certain complexion from many forms similar to a solid sphere—and material—that is, from form and matter, more similar to a cube. 

What therefore he says: that one medium suffices between two planes, understand that between two forms one unique medium satisfies, that is, the formal. For forms with forms successively, where they touch each other by their extremes, agree by a certain one formal medium, on both sides partly indeed agreeing, and partly also differing. 

But truly what he says: that solids are coupled to solids by a double medium, signifies that between two natural composites of diverse nature, twin mediums are interposed. Of which one indeed may be formal, truly the other material. For in any composite, here the principal form is considered, there the subject accommodated to the form. From this it is effected, that between diverse composites a double discrepancy arises: one indeed more by reason of form, truly the other more by reason of the subject.

### FOURTH DISCUSSION ON THE SAME,
### and concerning the powers and proportions
### of elements.
### CAP. XXIII.

THESE same things are corroborated besides by another reason, if from the quaternities just described, you descend to the quaternity of the sphere, in this certainly both the nature of the medium is considered, and the nature of the circumference is considered, most distant from each other as much in property as in situation. Furthermore here indeed space is considered, insofar as the proper virtue of the center is extended: truly there space, insofar as the proper virtue of the circumference is more extended. Hence four regions of the world are computed, and four similarly elements.

| | From substance | From virtue | From action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fire** | subtle | acute | mobile |
| **Air** | subtle | obtuse | mobile |
| **Water** | thick | obtuse | mobile |
| **Earth** | thick | obtuse | immobile |

| Another position of the same | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fire** | acute | subtle | mobile |
| **Air** | obtuse | subtle | mobile |
| **Water** | obtuse | thick | mobile |
| **Earth** | obtuse | thick | immobile |

Of which, that which is placed in the circumference following its nature, is the most ample, and therefore the most subtle of all through substance; through virtue truly the most acute, and most fit for penetration; through action finally it is the most prompt for motion. 

That however which is situated in the middle, also following the nature of the middle, is the narrowest and most dense through substance; through virtue truly obtuse; through action finally it is the most inept for motion. 

Truly two mediums in these behave in a middle way. Furthermore just as the ambit and the center are most distant in a sphere, so by situation and nature fire and earth most disagree. For that one so possesses the ambit, that it is never naturally the medium: this one so the center that it is never naturally the ambit. 

And truly sometimes it descends, if namely the region of fire is placed in the high. Water also ascends, if it is confined under the earth. Just as truly in fire and earth three things are considered—namely substance, virtue, action—so also three properties especially: namely in fire indeed through substance thinness [subtlety], through virtue sharpness [acumen], through action mobility. 

Truly in the earth the opposites: through substance thickness, through virtue obtuseness, through action immobility. Truly their natures are called solids among Plato, because in the manner of a triple dimension, they possess triple qualities: which if they had only in the manner of planes, one medium would suffice: which namely in one quality indeed would agree with the extremes, in another truly would differ. 

And since they have three opposed to each other, so that they may be bound, there is need of two mediums: of which both may agree with the next indeed, both with the extreme and with the double middle quality, and may disagree in one; truly with the remote extreme, it may agree in one indeed, but differ in two. 

Thus surely air follows fire, in subtlety and mobility very similar to fire: but dissimilar in a certain obtuseness of virtue, in which also it agrees in some way with the earth; truly with water in two, namely obtuseness and mobility. Water follows air, similar to air in these two; but similar to fire in one, namely in mobility only: but dissimilar to fire in two, in thickness and obtuseness at the same time: dissimilar to the earth in a certain mobility, but similar in thickness and obtuseness. 

Certainly that fire is comparable to the earth by a certain analogy—that is, by a similarity of reason and proportion—is apparent. For just as the subtlety of fire behaves to the thickness of earth: so the sharpness of fire to the obtuseness of the earth: so again the mobility of fire to the immobility of the earth. 

That it is also comparable, but by some more powerful reason, fire to air: air to water: water to earth: is manifest from the agreement of qualities. Truly it seems that the agreement of the next element to the next is double to the discrepancy: truly to the remote on the contrary, the discrepancy is double to the agreement.
