# On the Timaeus.

Fire seems twice as subtle as air, thrice as mobile, truly four times as acute. Likewise air twice as acute as water, thrice as mobile, and four times as subtle. Again water twice as acute as earth, thrice as subtle, and four times more prepared for motion. 

Truly to proceed among cognates up to a quadruple proportion only is granted among musicians. For by a further progression ears are offended. Since in these perfect musical reasons are contained. In these surely through three qualities as if through three dimensions, and certain solids, thrice also and solidly we arrive at solids. 

For through the double at the fourth grade we arrive at eight [2, 4, 8]: whence reasons, finally in the fourth place at sixty-four, which holds the third place among solid numbers [4, 16, 64]; for eight from two is solidly—that is, accepted, or led; twenty-seven from three led thrice; sixty-four from four similarly multiplied into itself three times is created. 

Furthermore so that it may be better known how much congruity in Plato is in mathematical things to physics, those two mediums of the first solids must be repeated. For we placed between eight and twenty-seven two competent mediums, namely twelve and eighteen. 

The number twelve indeed is born from both eight and twenty-seven. Since the side from which eight is multiplied is two; truly the side from which twenty-seven is three. But from two and three, twelve thus becomes, if you do twice two thrice: where twelve arising accepts two sides from eight; truly one from twenty-seven. Likewise from two and three thus becomes eighteen, if you do thrice three twice: where...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from the discussion of the soul's choices in the Republic to the specific structural and allegorical introduction of the Timaeus dialogue.</meta>

# On the Timaeus. 457

-> ON THE INTRODUCTION TO THE <-
-> dialogue. CHAPTER III. <-

Furthermore, to come to the very arrangement of the dialogue, Plato had designated five continuous days for these disputations. On the first day, Socrates disputed in the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens where the *Republic* is set.</note> together with Polemarchus, Glaucon, Adeimantus, and Thrasymachus the Sophist concerning the republic. On the second day, in the city, he recounted these same things to Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates, and to a certain fourth person, a nameless stranger, perhaps a companion of Timaeus. On the third day, these men make an epilogue <note>A summary or concluding statement.</note> of those matters. Once this introduction was made, Timaeus immediately disputed concerning nature, with three others present: Socrates, Critias, and Hermocrates. For the fourth person, who was unnamed and present for the second narration, is now absent from the third; for it is not within the capacity of just anyone to be present for the more secret matters. <note>Ficino suggests the "missing guest" represents someone not spiritually ready for the deep physical and metaphysical mysteries of the *Timaeus*.</note> On the fourth day, Critias held his oration. Finally, the fifth day has not yet dawned. Very appropriately, after the arrangement and summary of the divine republic among men, the model of this republic was added in the *Timaeus*—composed by God himself—moving then to the antiquity of the world and the human race, and the wondrous deeds performed by the men of old.

-> ALLEGORY OF THE HISTORY, <-
-> which is narrated in the prologue. <-
-> CHAPTER IV. <-

Among the beginnings of this dialogue, he narrates a history of a certain war waged between the Athenians and the Atlanteans. Crantor, the first interpreter of Plato in his time, accepts this as a bare history without allegory. Others, on the contrary, take it as a pure allegory. But the most esteemed Platonists refute both, asserting it is indeed history—because Plato said: *The discourse will be very wonderful, but entirely true*—yet they also think an allegorical sense should be shown, as the mind of Plato never labored on anything in vain. Therefore, they think that war between the Athenians and the Atlanteans carries an image of all the oppositions that exist in the universe. For "war"—that is, opposition—is the "father of all things" according to Heraclitus. <note>original: "Bellum enim, id est oppositionem apud Heraclitum esse omnium patrem." A reference to Heraclitus's famous fragment on strife as the driving force of the world.</note> Amelius brings up the opposition between the firmament <note>The sphere of fixed stars.</note> and the planets, especially since it is said in the *Critias* that the Atlantic island was divided into seven circles. Origen, however, suggests the opposition of the higher <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> to the lower ones, and their victory; the former exceeding in power, the latter in number. Numenius suggests the dissent of the excellent souls who follow Pallas <note>Athena</note> against other souls who follow Neptune into the realm of generation <note>Physical birth and becoming.</note>. Porphyry suggests the battle between spirits leading souls into generation and souls striving for the things above. He distinguishes spirits in three ways: some are divine; others are "according to a certain habit," a number filled by particular souls who have obtained a spirit-like lot; others are evil and harmful to souls. These lowest spirits, therefore, conflict with souls in their ascent and descent—especially the western spirits, for that region is assigned by the Egyptians to harmful spirits. Furthermore, Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus add to these the opposition itself which is perpetually vigorous in all things: between the One and the Many, Limit and Infinity, Same and Other, Rest and Motion—from which all things are composed under the First. Likewise, being is either "through itself" or "not through itself." Again, essence is either incorporeal or corporeal; and the incorporeal either does not decline toward the corporeal, or it does. The corporeal is either not subject to decay (like the celestial) or subject to decay (like the elemental). Finally, in heaven, motions and various powers are opposed to one another; while below heaven, qualities are repugnant to one another. In short, the discrepancy of all these things is signified by that ancient war: and everywhere the higher and more excellent things are signified by the Athenians, and the others by the westerners. Such an allegory is not moderately suited to the disputation of Timaeus. This is also confirmed by those things which we comment upon in the *Critias*.

-> THE FALL OF PHAETHON. <-
-> Floods, Fires, and the description of Minerva. <-
-> CHAPTER V. <-

Here again I advise you to remember that nine thousand years were computed by Eudoxus <note>A famous Greek astronomer and mathematician.</note> as nine thousand months. Likewise, that Phaethon, the son of the Sun, struck by lightning and burning the earth, signifies according to some a vast comet of a solar nature which, finally dissolving, stirred up intolerable heats. Perhaps it even refers to the fires sent by divine power that Moses narrates. When he comes to the floods, remember that fire is the most effective of all things; but water is more effective than earth, and less passive than air. Also, fire divides powerfully and penetrates, while water strikes very hard from every side. Therefore, through these two elements, more vast calamities occur. Add also the final cause: namely, that through the destruction caused by these two, a greater good follows—that is, a more fruitful regeneration of things—than through plagues of the air or chasms of the earth. Therefore, Providence uses these two especially for the most extensive destruction. Thus the celestial wheels obey correctly from that point: so that in whatever intervals of time God has ordained there should be destruction or rather reformation, all the planets concur in due order toward either fiery or watery stars, with the fixed stars also leading to the same end. Remember, moreover, that Neptune signifies natural providence, while Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva</note> signifies intellectual providence. This same Pallas is described by the Platonists as the divinity who, wisely and powerfully, both adorns celestial things and builds those things which occur below heaven. Among the stars, she presides especially over Aries, and is the leader of the equinoctial circle, where they think the moving power of the universe is most vigorous. You shall commit to memory the golden epigram which Proclus read in the histories of the Egyptians, inscribed in the temples of Minerva: *I am the things that are, the things that will be, and the things that have been. My veil no one has revealed. The fruit I have brought forth is the born sun.* <note>Ficino identifies the goddess at Sais with Athena/Minerva and links the sun to the Neoplatonic "Intellect" or "Logos."</note>

-> SELECT PRECEPTS CONCERNING <-
-> VOWS AND prayers. CHAPTER VI. <-

When Plato comes to the point where God must be suppliantly adored, hear Porphyry thus proving divine supplications. Since God provides for us, and our affairs can be otherwise, we certainly adore usefully for the utility of our affairs—provided, of course, that we are good. For thus, having been made similar to God, we shall be more closely joined to Him. In this conjunction, the whole force of adoration consists. Indeed, since we are children of God, but separated from Him as if in exile and prison, it is fitting to adore suppliantly, so that having been liberated from here, we may return to the Father. Otherwise, we shall be like those who are orphaned of their parents' protection. Truly, since we are parts of the universe, we undoubtedly have need of the whole. For the very turning toward the whole provides salvation to the parts. Therefore, whether you pursue virtue, you must adore Him who contains all virtue. For to love the Good itself will be the cause for you also of that good which is expedient for you. Whether you desire a corporeal good, there exists in the universe a virtue containing all bodies. Thence, therefore, salvation must proceed to whatever parts. We have found that the most excellent men of wisdom among all nations have applied themselves especially to divine vows: particularly the Brahmans of the Indians, the Magi of the Persians, and the theologians of the Greeks. The Chaldeans, however, also adored something else. For calling the very power of the higher beings "God," they worshipped it by this one name. These are the words of Porphyry. After him, let us hear his disciple, the divine Iamblichus, who is foremost in being approved by Proclus in this matter. All things are from God in such a way that nowhere is even the smallest thing forsaken by God. For everywhere divine unity flourishes, through which each thing subsists; and by a certain perpetual and intimate circle, they are wondrously revolved back to God Himself from whom and in whom they are—otherwise, they would suddenly fall into nothingness. All things proceed from the divine unity, and in proceeding, they retain a certain unity impressed upon them, an image of the divine unity; by which they are called back into it, and having been called back, they are perfected. This very thing snatches souls toward vows, by which our union with God may be fully completed. For if nature, flowing from God, has inserted into certain things properties corresponding to certain higher beings—through which they turn themselves in a way toward those higher beings, such as sun-plants <note>original: "solaria"</note> toward the sun, and moon-plants <note>original: "lunaria"</note> toward the moon—how much more has the Father of souls impressed upon them powers that snatch them toward Himself. These seem to be situated primarily in a certain divine unity in the higher intellect, as well as in intellectual reflection itself. Suppliant adoration arising from here absolutely completes our very restoration into God: drawing divine beneficence into us by a natural congruence, coupling the adorers with the Adored, co-adapting the prayers of those making vows to the intelligence of the higher beings, moving the will of those who embrace all good things in themselves to impart good things to us according to our vow—the effecter of divine persuasion, stabilizing all our affairs in the stable firmness of the higher beings. Five primary things pertain to the perfection of a vow. The first is a certain notion of that which is to be adored, and by what reason it should be worshipped. The second is a certain assimilation of our life to the divine life, proceeding through purity, chastity, sanctity, discipline, and order, capturing divine benevolence and subjecting souls to divine bounty. The third is a certain contact, through which we almost touch the divine essence and verge into it with the very summit of the soul. The fourth is a certain entry into the vestibule of divine light. The fifth, finally, is union, insinuating the soul's own unity deeply into the divine unity and connecting them, fusing the action of the soul and of God into one and the same—so much so that we are no longer our own, but belong to God, overwhelmed and surrounded by divine splendor. Of this adoration, which must be performed without intermission, the supreme end is that it may join the turning of the soul with its very permanence, and firmly restore back to unity whatever has proceeded from the divine unity, and surround our light with the celestial light. Therefore, right adoration alone makes souls blessed.

# On the Timaeus. 459

...the Good, but the best son of the Good. If we understand this "Son" to be of one substance with the First, we shall better reconcile Plato with Christian theology. But the other interpreters of Plato will protest.

## THE SUN, LIGHT, BRIGHTNESS, HEAT, GENERATION, AND LIKEWISE UNITY, GOODNESS, INTELLECT, SOUL, NATURE, AND THE BODY OF THE WORLD. The image of the higher worlds. CHAPTER X.

Let Christian and Mosaic truth remain. And meanwhile, if it pleases the majority of the interpreters, perhaps this was either the opinion of Plato or of **Pythagoras**: that the **Intelligible World** is the medium between the **Visible World** and the **Good** itself. It is the image of the Good, but the model for the corporeal world—depending on the Good just as light outside the sun depends on the light within the sun. Furthermore, it produces from itself the Soul of the World as its closest neighbor, just as light pours out brightness from itself; through this Soul, it generates individual things daily, just as brightness produces corporeal things through heat. 

Therefore, just as these six grades are arranged in order: First, indeed, is **Unity**, then **Goodness**; yet these two are not distinct in the thing itself, but are distinguished in some way by reason. For it is the same divinity: and because it transcends all, it is called Unity; and because it overflows back through all, it is called Goodness. This power of overflowing, at any rate, Plato calls the "Idea of the Good" in the sixth book of the *Republic*. In his *Epistles*, however, he calls it the "Good of goods"—that is, of itself, and also of the goods that proceed from it.

In the third grade, let there be placed a certain **Divine Mind**, like light flowing from light, conceiving in itself multiform Ideas, so to speak, by a certain double nourishment of the supernal light and of the unique divine Ideas—not otherwise than in light many rays are now derived from a single ray of light. In this Mind, the Ideas of things are not only comprehended as if in a fountain, but also many armies of minds are reduced to this as if to a leader, namely springing equally from the same divine light as the Mind itself. That entire genus is named the "Higher World"; but as far as it regards the minds that follow, it is the "Intellectual World"; as far as it regards the leader, it is the "Intelligible." But the Mind itself, the leader of minds, is named partly **Intellect** and partly **Intelligible**. It is Intellect insofar as it applies itself to discerning the reasons of things. It is Intelligible insofar as it is contained in its own Ideas. 

Finally, the **Idea of the Good** reigns not only over the Intellect but also over the Intelligible. After this archetypal world, let the **Soul of the Corporeal World** follow in the fourth grade: a rational world already begotten from the intellectual world, like brightness from light. And just as brightness is already mixed with motion, so the Soul touches and traverses the reasons of immobile Ideas by a certain mobile agreement.

Let the fifth grade succeed this, namely **Nature** itself, the "Seminal World," resulting from the rational world of the soul like heat from brightness. In the sixth grade, finally, let this **Corporeal World** be placed, led most closely from the seminal world, just as the generation of things comes from heat. But if you wish to compare them more aptly, omitting the rest, think of a most wise **Architect**: first, his natural power and goodness; second, his geometric and contemplative intellect, having the common ratios of measures; third, his "practical reason," as they say, already consulting about the craftsmanship through those same ratios; fourth, his imagination, shaping the figures and modes conducive to the work; fifth, his affection/drive; sixth, his power of moving. In comparisons of this kind, you will see that effects are produced much more by what comes before than by what follows.

## INDIVIDUAL ORDERS ARE REDUCED TO INDIVIDUAL HEADS. The universal order to the universal head, by which all things are composed from act and potency. CHAPTER XI.

Nor should it escape us that the proper kinds of things must be referred to their proper heads, and the universal kind to the universal head. For all the bodies of the world are referred to one Body; all Natures to one Nature; all Souls to one Soul; all Minds to one Mind; and finally, all good things to the Good. And because they are good, therefore they are all. Thus, certainly, all things by a certain natural conversion desire the Good as their end, because they have proceeded from the Good itself by a certain common procession as from a principle; and so all things desire it, so that the lowest matter desires it with no low desire. Indeed, in all things to be generated, it perpetually verges toward the very likeness of the Good, so that it appears to depend on the Good. On the Good, I say, rather than on the Mind. For whereas the action of the Mind, which happens through ideal forms, is terminated at the forms, the action of the Good, being the most ample, descends beyond the forms even into matter, making it greedy for and capable of good things. 

But what I now call matter, Plato in the *Philebus* calls by a broader name, **Infinity** <term>infinitudinem</term>, saying that the Good itself brought forth Infinity and **Limit** <term>terminum</term> as its closest offspring, and immediately mixed them together, and from this mixture composed all things—that is, from a certain formable potency and an approaching form. For he calls the formable potency "Infinity," as if not yet defined or perfected from itself. The form applied to this, however, he names "Limit," because it namely defines the indefinite potency and perfects it in the now desired species. From these two, therefore, they want the Intelligible World to be fused most closely by God, and the sensible world then to be constituted from the intelligible world out of the same or similar things. 

So it is that the Intellect, that closest architect of the visible world, received matter from the Good that was in some way spiritual—but which was already, right under it, degenerating into the dimension of mass and was shapeless and void. And if perhaps it should be moved of itself, it would change without order; but through the order of Ideas received from the same Good, he formed it and reduced it to order before it could wander out of order. Especially since he first infused into it a rational soul, the mistress of the most orderly motion. He says that not only would matter be shapeless through itself, but the soul also would be shapeless, unless God formed both. That which is corporeal species in matter is "Reason" in the intelligence of the soul; if it lacks this, it will move matter inordinately. To express this, he considered matter without form and without a rational soul, and saw that motion would proceed from there without order.

## THAT MATTER WAS NOT DISORDERED BEFORE THE WORLD IN TIME, but by a certain reason of order. CHAPTER XII.

From all these things we can gather that matter is not equal to the Craftsman of the world; it is not before the world by any interval of time, though it is by a certain origin and order; it was not tossed about inordinately before order, but would have wandered far from order, as far as it is in itself, unless it had been immediately ordered from above. And lest anyone should disapprove of this mode of speaking in Plato—feigning matter tossed inordinately before the world—let him hear also **Moses** saying before the distinction of the world that the "earth was void and unformed, and darkness was upon the face of the abyss." I pass over for now the poetic "Chaos." It is helpful to bring into the open **Philo the Jew**, explaining the Genesis of Moses in similar words: "If anyone wishes to seek the cause why this universe was created, he will not err, in my judgment, if he thinks what one of the ancients brought forth: that the Creator himself and father and author of the universe is Good; and for the sake of his goodness, he envied no substance which by its own nature had nothing of good, and yet all things could be made. For its own nature was inordinate, shapeless, inanimate, entirely varied, incongruous, unharmonious, inconstant, fit to be changed into the contrary and to receive the ratio of the best things—namely of form, animation, likeness, congruence, harmony, and finally of the better idea of all things." 

Likewise in the second volume of the same book, he says: "When the Creator had begun to form the substance, inordinate and confused by its own nature, translated into order from inordinancy and into discretion from confusion, he established the earth and water in the middle place." These are the words of Philo. Accordingly, if you consider the six grades of things brought forward above, you will perhaps perceive how similar Plato is to Moses, finishing the Genesis of the world in six days; and how similar also is Pythagoras, proving that the number six is thoroughly accommodated to Genesis and "marriages"—whence he also calls it **Gamon** <note>From the Greek 'gamos' for marriage.</note>, because its parts placed next to each other beget it and render the begotten similar to the begetter.

## A DOUBLE OPINION CONCERNING THE ORIGIN OF THE WORLD. CHAPTER XIII.

If anyone asks whether for Plato the world was everlasting: I answer, following the interpreters **Severus, Atticus,** and **Plutarch**, and many others as Proclus recounts, that it was not always. But following the interpreters **Crantor, Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus,** and most others, it was indeed always, and was always from God—rather, it flowed from Him. For they say God is always. But the world is always being made and flowing. And if you consider it as lacking a beginning in time, the world is called "unbegotten"; but if you consider its perpetual efflux from God, it is "continually begotten." Nor does it depend any less on God if it has depended and depends always than if it began at some time to depend or should cease. Just as light draws its origin no less from the sun, and serves the sun no less if it flowed always than if it flowed forth and flowed out from the sun at some time.

## A THREEFOLD CONJECTURE OF THE PLATONIC OPINION CONCERNING THE WORLD, and what is the certainty of the Platonic sentiment concerning the world. CHAPTER XIV.

Furthermore, in Platonic matters, we proceed either by conjecture or by knowledge. As far as conjecture is concerned, he himself speaks and his followers dispute in such a way that his opinion on the origin of the world can be collected into three heads. For either he thought that matter was at some time created out of nothing by God and formed simultaneously in time (although in this work which is composed of matter, according to a certain order of production, matter itself is thought to be made before it is formed, and to be matter before it is formed; and before the work made from matter, matter is usually sought from which the work was to be finished). Or, that God did not at some time beget matter as something new, but from eternity, and similarly adorned it—although it is imagined as inordinate before it is ordered, since by its nature it lacks order, which it expects from another; and since any thing is thought of first according to what it is, rather than according to what it receives, it can rightly be thought of in itself as devoid of order, separately from order. 

Or, as I said, that matter was always from God and continually; but not continually ordered, rather by intervals of time; so that it belongs to God to order it stably, but to matter to be ordered movably; and it receives a temporal tempering of its order, not otherwise than a clock receives it from a craftsman; and after certain intervals of time are completed according to its nature, it loses order gradually and finally entirely, and returns into Chaos; but God, suddenly by no means tolerating extreme confusion, retempers it into its prior disposition by a single nod, and this happens infinitely in turn, with God never changed, and matter infinitely reformed. Thus far has human conjecture preceded in Platonic matters.

But as far as we have knowledge, we affirm that our Plato affirmed that the World does not exist from itself, but from a cause: not indeed a fortuitous one, but from a certain one; not from a natural cause only, but an intellectual one; not from an intellect determined by the mode of nature, but rather voluntary; not from a will compelled by some natural instinct, but a free one. For nothing is more free than that which is through itself and acts entirely through itself; yet not by some contingent will. For nothing is contingent where will and necessity are the same. Again, nothing is violent where necessity and will are the same in turn. But that he might open this, he repeated the name of the divine **Will** no less than the name of **Intelligence** in fabricating the world. And he added that the Will of the Good itself is the highest cause and the most certain of causes. He shows this to be free from the fact that he often says God the Architect consulted and deliberated in the manner of a craftsman about the work to be constructed; in which words he does not want God to be understood as doubting, but as freely choosing. 

Accordingly, he says that the mundane work did not proceed only once from God, but proceeds and is preserved assiduously. Furthermore, the supreme deities of the world together with the world would be dissolvable of themselves, unless they were ruled by the divine will. It will be enough, then, and that indeed a very great thing, to have affirmed such things about the affirming philosopher. For once these are granted, you will easily be able to say that God, when he acts by a provident and free will, composed the world as new without any novelty in himself. And thus you will hear that he produced it not "at some time new," but rather "from eternity"; and nevertheless you can preserve his majesty for God, on whose will—and this a free one—the world no less needs and depends, if it always needs and depends, than if it at some time proceeded. But because Plato often says that divine things are to be asserted only so far as they are proven by divine oracles, we also ought to assent to the sacred scriptures rather than to our conjectures.

## THE WORLD PROCREATED FOR THE SAKE OF THE GOOD, according to the likeness of the divine reason and the divine Word. CHAPTER XV.

He made the world, therefore, by his will—that is, by his goodness—overflowing as much voluntarily as naturally because of his immense fecundity. This goodness first indeed rejoices in itself; because of this, it next delights in this image of itself; yet in such a way that it constitutes the end of this delight not in this image, but in the model itself and the principle. Since, therefore, he made the world by goodness, for that reason he made it for the sake of the Good. For he did not procreate it simply that it might be, live, and understand; but that it might both be well, and live well, and understand and acquire the good. This is very consonant with that Mosaic saying: "God saw this and that, that it was good; and all things were very good." And because beauty is the splendor of goodness, therefore he adds that the most beautiful world was procreated by the best God: temporal indeed, but according to the image of the eternal model. 

He will also say often that as many species as are in the archetype—that is, the principal world, which is to say, the intelligible and imitable ones—so many forms of things did he arrange in this world, and thus made it like himself: namely, as one who understands that the Ideas of things do not consist among the clouds (as some slanderers maliciously claim) but in the mind of the mundane architect. Where he says that Ideas are in life itself, he seems to prophesy that evangelical saying: "That which was made was life in him." And where he says and repeats often that the world was constituted by divine providence, he confirms the whole of religion. When **Theophrastus** had observed this as something wonderful in a philosopher, he said: "Plato alone, or certainly most of all, assigned the causes of things from divine providence." But, O Theophrastus, with whatever mind you say that about Plato, you will undoubtedly confess that Plato alone or of all men is most provident and divine.

## WHY THE WORLD IS ONE and spherical, and moved in a sphere. CHAPTER XVI.

He next shows that the divine model of the world itself—which the Evangelist, but in a more divine sense, calls the divine **Word** <term>verbum</term>—is unique: because that which contains all things leaves nothing outside itself; and therefore it is necessarily unique. But of this matter, more diffusely in the *Theology*. Since, however, this world in other respects as far as was possible reflects the divine world and intellect—so much so that he who beholds the forms in this matter looks as if at the divine face in a mirror—certainly it represents that model even in the very unity that is effective and preservative of all things: so that the work of one architect may be one. One, therefore, is the world of the one God. 

Surely, if a human architect could master matter, after he had made several buildings, each of which was one in itself, he would finally surround them all with a certain single wall. God, however, can do this entirely, since he is the master of matter. Nor is it permitted to dream of many worlds like balls, some outside others. For thus the divine work would be dissipated, and there would be empty spaces between the worlds. You will think it more probable that as many spheres as you imagine scattered through a vacuum, you should instead think of spheres within spheres, so that any sphere is a world within a world; and the entire work is one, and thus ordered in turn; and nothing is found either empty or devoid of order and union. 

If the figure of the world is spherical, it is because it is most capable of being uniform, indissoluble, and agile; and thus, and in no other way, can mass be placed in mass without a vacuum, and be moved without offense: that is, if not squares are fitted to squares or circles, but spheres are inserted into spheres. Finally, the chief cause of this mundane sphere is that the nature of the divine world is also orbicular: which reflects into itself by understanding and loving. The reason for the spherical motion is both the figure itself which receives the motion, and the intimate revolution of the mundane soul itself which moves through intellectual species.

## WHY THE WORLD IS DIVIDED either into five or into six regions: and how the seven and the circular number suit it: and how it is distributed according to the likeness of the intelligible world. CHAPTER XVII.

Wherefore numbers are not wrongly accommodated to the mundane division: in which the first roots are of **circular numbers**: namely, the **Five** <term>quinarius</term> from the odd numbers, and the **Six** <term>senarius</term> from the even ones. We say that the number twenty-five is multiplied from five in the manner of a circle, because in some way one returns from the same to the same: while five times five are computed as twenty-five. Likewise, by a similar circle, the number one hundred twenty-five; for five times twenty-five makes that many. The same is the ratio of the circular number six to thirty-six, and likewise to two hundred sixteen. For six times six fills thirty-six. Likewise, six times thirty-six fills two hundred sixteen. And if they name the higher numbers, by reason of their origin, some "square" and others "oblong," yet by reason of their fall and end they call them "circular." 

Therefore, by the numbers five and six, the first roots of circular numbers, we divide the circular body of the world. First indeed into five parts: namely, the **celestial fire**, the **ethereal fire** under the moon, **air**, **water**, and **earth**. This division is confirmed in the *Epinomis*. Then we distribute it by the number six: where we divide the celestial fire into the **non-wandering** <note>Fixed stars.</note> and the **wandering** <note>Planets.</note>. This partition is used more frequently by Plato. But we shall more conveniently deduce the distribution of the sensible world from the distribution of its model in this manner after the Platonic fashion. God indeed devises in the world as it is in the intelligible realm two powers: one formable, the other formative. The former, as I said, the Pythagoreans and Platonists call **Infinity**; the latter, **Limit**. He also devises a mutual mixture of these powers; and he understands that a third form immediately coalesces from this mixture. But he also observes this same form as being, as it were, threefold: for it has something of Infinity, something of Limit...

### CHAPTER XIV.

Furthermore, in Platonic matters, we proceed either by conjecture or by knowledge. As far as conjecture is concerned, he himself speaks and his followers dispute in such a way that his opinion on the origin of the world can be collected into three heads. For either he thought that matter was at some time created out of nothing by God and formed simultaneously in time—although in this work which is composed of matter, according to a certain order of production, matter itself is thought to be made before it is formed, and to be matter before it is formed; and before the work made from matter, matter is usually sought from which the work was to be finished. Or, that God did not at some time beget matter as something new, but from eternity, and similarly adorned it—although it is imagined as inordinate before it is ordered, since by its nature it lacks order, which it expects from another; and since any thing is thought of first according to what it is, rather than according to what it receives, it can rightly be thought of in itself as devoid of order, separately from order. Or, as I said, that matter was always from God and continually; but not continually ordered, rather by intervals of time; so that it belongs to God to order it stably, but to matter to be ordered movably; and it receives a temporal tempering of its order, not otherwise than a clock <note>original: *horologium*; here referring to a mechanical or water-regulated device for measuring time</note> receives it from a craftsman; and after certain intervals of time are completed according to its nature, it loses order gradually and finally entirely, and returns into Chaos; but God, suddenly by no means tolerating extreme confusion, retempers it into its former disposition by a single nod, and this happens infinitely in turn, with God never changed, and matter infinitely reformed. Thus far has human conjecture proceeded in Platonic matters. 

As far as we have certain knowledge, however, we affirm that our Plato asserted the World does not exist from itself, but from a cause: not indeed a fortuitous one, but a certain one; not from a natural cause alone, but an intellectual one; not from an intellect determined by the manner of nature, but rather a voluntary one; not by a will compelled by a certain natural instinct, but a free one. For nothing is more free than that which is through itself, and acts entirely through itself; yet not by any "contingent" <term>contingens: something that could happen or not happen by chance</term> will. For nothing is contingent where the will and necessity are the same. Again, nothing is violent where necessity and will are in turn the same. Moreover, so that he might open this up, he repeated the name of divine will no less than that of intelligence in the fabrication of the world. And he added that this very will of the good is the highest cause, and the most certain of causes. He shows it to be free from the fact that he often says God the architect consulted and deliberated, after the manner of a craftsman, concerning the construction of the work. In these words, he does not want an uncertain God to be understood, but one who chooses freely. Consequently, he says the mundane work did not proceed from God only once, but proceeds and is preserved continually. Furthermore, the supreme powers of the world, together with the world itself, would be dissolvable from themselves unless they were ruled by the divine will. It shall be enough, therefore—and that indeed a very great thing—to have affirmed such things about the philosopher who affirmed them. For once these things are granted, you will easily be able to say that God, since he acts with a provident and free will, composed a "new" world without any newness in Himself. And thus you will hear that he produced it not "at some time new," but rather from eternity; you will be able to preserve at the same time the majesty of God, on whose will (and this indeed a free one) the world no less lacks and depends—if it always lacks and depends—than if it had proceeded at some point in time. Since indeed Plato often says that one must assert concerning divine things only so far as is approved by divine oracles, we also ought to assent to the Sacred Scriptures rather than to our own conjectures.

### CHAPTER XV.

He made the world, therefore, by his will, that is, by his goodness, as much voluntarily as naturally, overflowing with immense fecundity. This goodness first indeed rejoices in itself; and therefore next is delighted by this, its own image—yet in such a way that it establishes the end of this delight not in this image, but in the archetype <note>original: *exemplari*; the perfect original model</note> itself and the principle of this delight. Since therefore he made the world by goodness, for that reason he made it for the sake of the good. For he did not procreate it simply so that it might be, live, and understand; but so that it might be well, live well, and understand and obtain the good. This is very much in harmony with that Mosaic saying: *God saw this and that to be good, and all things to be very good.* <note>Reference to Genesis 1</note> And because beauty is the splendor of goodness, he therefore adds that the most beautiful world was procreated by the best God: temporal indeed, but after the image of the eternal archetype. He will also often say that as many species as there are in the archetype (that is, the primary world, which is to say, the intelligible and imitable ones), just so many forms of things has he disposed in this world, and thus made it like himself:

### CHAPTER XVI.

He shows next that the divine archetype of the world itself—which the Evangelist, but with a more divine sense, calls the divine "Word" <note>original: *verbum*; the Greek *Logos*</note>—is unique: because that which contains all things can leave nothing outside itself, and therefore it is necessarily unique. But of this same matter, we speak more diffusely in the *Theology*. Since, however, this world refers back to the divine world and intellect in other respects as far as possible—so much so that he who perceives the forms in this matter beholds, as it were, the divine face in a mirror—it certainly represents that Word also in its very unity, which effects and preserves all things: so that there is one work of one architect. One world, therefore, belongs to one God. Surely if a human architect could dominate matter, after he had made several buildings, each of which was one in itself, he would finally surround them all with a single wall. God, however, is altogether able, since he is the master of matter. Nor is it permitted to dream of "many worlds" as if they were some here and others there, one outside another. The reason for spherical motion is partly the figure itself which receives the motion, and partly the intimate revolution of the mundane soul itself which moves through intellectual species <term>species: here meaning the mental forms or Ideas</term>.

limits: some are general and some are specific. Thus it happens that after the binary number <note>The number two, representing duality or the first step away from unity</note>—namely of infinity and limit—the ternary <note>The number three</note> arises immediately, with a third form added to these. The quaternary <note>The number four</note> also arises, with a form of this kind distributed threefold. Finally, the senary <note>The number six</note> is born, when the duty of that world is extended to produce lower things. The septenary <note>The number seven</note> is also born, when that world is reflected back to the father like an image. In this seventh degree, it rests as if on the seventh day. But if you assign each thing to its proper place, you will notice that this corporeal world takes fire as its form from the limit of the supernal world, but takes earth as its matter from infinity. From the middle form of that world, it takes a moisture <note>original: *humorem*; here meaning a binding fluid or "spirit" that connects extremes</note> that reconciles fire and earth. This moisture glues together the earth (which is naturally prone to dissipating) and nourishes the fire (which is easily dissolved by itself). It possesses three qualities within itself: on one side it is fiery, on the other it is earthy, but in the middle it has its own pure, airy quality. From one side, it tends upward toward the fire; from the other, it tends downward toward the earth. After this fivefold division of the world, the senary is made, if you conceive of the common form of all things. The septenary is made again, if you reshape this very form of the world according to the archetype; in which seventh day, indeed, it may rest.

### WHY THERE ARE DISTINCT PARTS
### IN THE WORLD, AND WHY THEY ARE CONTRARY, AND CONCERNING
### THE FOUR ELEMENTS.
### CHAPTER XVIII.

**W**e see in the world not only a distinction of forms, but also a repugnance <note>Opposition or conflict between elements</note>. For the world proceeds from the First, and in proceeding, it degenerates. The proceeding creates distinction; the degeneration creates repugnance. Indeed, the origin of division itself is the fertility of the Cause, which overflows outward and propagates itself into the vastness. But as the division proceeds through many steps, it finally arrives at repugnance—especially since the matter of the world, due to its weakness, cannot reconcile forms with one another in the same way that the higher world reconciles them within itself. Because of this, God extended matter by dimension, so that it might receive forms that would otherwise clash in different dwellings. Finally, since we call those things "contraries" which are most distant within the same genus, and those things "diverse" which are separated by their genera: from the fact that there are contraries in the world, it appears that every genus has as many species as possible; and from the fact that they are diverse, it is clear that the universe possesses very many genera. Since, indeed, all species are reduced to genera, and all genera to the universe and its common form, it is concluded that just as the higher world is uniform and "all-form" <note>original: *omniformis*; containing all possible forms</note>, so this world is "all-form" and uniform. Moreover, the contrary quality and shape of the elements and heavens lead to the daily generation of new forms, with motion contributing to the process. For if there were only a single element, nothing would ever be generated, as Hippocrates asserts. If there were many things similar to one another, nothing would be achieved in the world, as Heraclitus proves. It is necessary, however, for this world to imitate the eternal action of the higher and all-form world to the best of its ability through the perpetual generation of new forms. Therefore, let there be contrary elements, as the poetry of Empedocles sings. And let there be a medium between contraries, since contraries are both most distant and least compatible without a middle ground. But this medium cannot be indivisible; otherwise, the contraries would not be distant through it. It must, therefore, have dimension. But where it touches one side, it does not touch the other. It must necessarily have a middle part through which it is equally distant from the extremes. For this reason, Plato always inserts at least two media <note>Middle terms or elements</note> between contraries, as is clearly apparent from his words. He even inserts a third, where he says the medium has a power by which it preserves not only the union of the extremes, but also its own. But let him clearly place two—for we are not arguing that now—as if between fire and earth there were two things: namely, air and water. He shows from numbers and dimensions, which in a way precede natural bodies, that at least two media are absolutely necessary between contrary bodies.

### LINEAR, PLANE, AND SOLID NUMBERS,
### AND WHY ONE MEDIUM SUFFICES BETWEEN PLANES, BUT
### IT IS NOT ENOUGH BETWEEN SOLIDS. AND HOW MA-
### THEMATICAL RATIOS ARE
### REFERRED TO PHYSICAL ONES.
### CHAPTER XIX.

**W**e have explained elsewhere that among the Pythagoreans there are three types of numbers: Linear, Plane, and Solid. Linear numbers are those measured only by unity, like a point: such as Two, Three, Five, Seven, and the like. Plane numbers, however,

<column-break/>

are those multiplied from numbers as if from sides. For example, six is made from twice three, or three times two. Among plane numbers, we call those "quadrangles" and "equilaterals" <note>Square numbers</note> which are made from multiplying a number by itself. For example, four comes from twice two, nine from three times three, and sixteen from four times four. "Inequilaterals" <note>Rectangular numbers</note> are those made from multiplying a smaller number by a larger one, such as six, which comes from multiplying two by three. We also call them "oblongs" when they are made from multiplying a much smaller number by a much larger one, such as ten, resulting from multiplying two by five. (Indeed, if we called this a linear number in the tenth book of the *Republic*, we intended it to be understood as an oblong). Besides these, we called those "solids" which are made from multiplying and reducing a number into itself, like a solid mass in three dimensions: such as two times two, twice <note>2 x 2 x 2 = 8</note>, which is eight; three times three, thrice, which is twenty-seven; four times four, four times, which is sixty-four. Take the first two planes, which are procreated from the first linear numbers: for example, four from two on one side, and nine from three on the other. You can bind these two planes, nine and four, to each other with a single fitting medium: that is, six. For whatever the proportion of nine is to six, the same is six to four—in both cases it is a *sesquialter* ratio <note>A ratio of 1.5 or 3:2, which in music forms a perfect fifth</note>. For nine contains six plus another half of it (three). Similarly, six contains four plus another half of it (two). That six is the fitting medium is evident because it is composed of both. For the side of four is two, and the side of nine is three. From the multiplication of two by three, six is made. Similarly, if you take the square beyond nine, which is sixteen, the medium will be twelve, which is born from their sides. For the side of nine is three, and of sixteen is four. If you multiply three by four, you get twelve, which connects them both by an equal ratio, namely the *sesquialter* ratio. For sixteen contains twelve plus a third part of it. Similarly, twelve includes nine plus a third part of nine. You see, therefore, what Plato says: that plane numbers can be bound by a single medium. Take, furthermore, the first solid numbers: I mean those first made from the first linear numbers multiplied into themselves: on one side eight (from two), and on the other twenty-seven (from three). You certainly cannot join these together with a single medium, but you are forced to take at least two media: namely twelve and eighteen. For you will get twelve from "twice two, thrice," and eighteen from "thrice three, twice." Through these numbers you will reconcile the extremes by a *sesquialter* ratio. For the number twenty-seven encompasses eighteen plus another half (nine); similarly, eighteen exceeds twelve by half; and twelve equally exceeds eight by half. Through this it is clear: solid numbers always need more media to be joined appropriately. What we have explained in numbers can be demonstrated in dimensions, both plane and solid, showing that between comparable planes one medium often suffices, but between comparable solids, several true media must be placed. This would be too long to explain, and has already been sufficiently shown by Iamblichus, Proclus, and Chalcidius. Since, however, Plato accepted these mathematical things here not for their own sake, but for the sake of natural things, let us set these aside and briefly consider what mysteries of nature he primarily understands through these mathematical images. First, what is read in the Holy Scriptures—that God perfected all things in "number, measure, and weight"—is clearly touched upon by Plato, who brings numbers, measures, and solids into the discussion. By "solids," he also understands "weights," which he signifies when, after dimensions, he mentions the forces of inclinations <note>Gravity or natural tendency</note> as the causes of weights. By "numbers," he wants the species and substantial forms of natural things themselves to be understood (which Aristotle also compared to numbers). By "measures," he means the certain instrumental shapes or magnitudes adapted to specific species. Finally, by "solids" and "forces," he signifies qualities, which are fully extended within the masses and provide momentum to motions and actions. All people judge that in the universe, the species of things, the shapes and magnitudes of those species, and the qualities are composed by a geometric and mutual proportion: so that by the same ratio the lowest things are exceeded by the middle, and the middle by the higher. Likewise, by "numbers" he designates the arithmetic mean, which consists in the equality of numbers. By "dimensions and measures," he designates the geometric mean, which is placed in the identity of ratio and proportion. By "weights and forces," he designates the musical mean, which is situated in the equality or similarity of portions, and encompasses the speed and slowness of motions, and the high and low pitch of voices by its power.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from the conceptual origins of matter to the specific mathematical and elemental structure of the physical universe. It explores how numerical ratios—specifically the progression from linear to solid numbers—dictate the relationship between the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth.</meta>

### FIRST DISCUSSION: WHY THE
### fourfold number of elements 
### suits the world.
### CHAPTER XX.

But of these matters we speak more at length elsewhere. Now, however, let us return to the division of the world’s parts, so that we may behold their harmonic composition. In the preceding sections, we said that the fivefold and sixfold numbers <note>original: *quinarium & senarium*</note> were fitting for the circular shape of the world. Now, moreover, we say that the fourfold <note>original: *quaternarius*; the number four</note> suits its fullness. Indeed, the fourfold is the first to fulfill every distinction of numbers: embracing within itself the first even and the first odd number. It also fulfills the simple progression of numbers, since in four terms it completes the ten—perfectly finishing the ten by adding one, two, three, and four <note>This refers to the Pythagorean *Tetractys*: 1+2+3+4=10, which was considered the foundation of the universe</note>. It also fulfills the progression of dimensions, attaining them in four terms: the point, length, width, and depth. It fulfills musical consonance. Indeed, within the limits of the fourfold are contained the double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter <note>a 3:2 ratio</note>, and sesquitertian <note>a 4:3 ratio</note> ratios, as well as the octave, double octave, the fifth, and the fourth <note>original: *diapason, disdiapason, diapente, diatessaron*</note>. It fulfills nature as it proceeds through four terms: substance, quantity, quality, and motion. Finally, it fulfills the universe, whether in nature or above nature: through essence, being, power, and action. Justly, therefore, did the Pythagoreans designate the fullness of the worldly body and soul by the fourfold <note>original: *quatrinita*</note>, and they swore an oath that it was the fourfold fountain of ever-flowing nature. From this very fountain flows the fourfold number of the elements. From here comes the fourfold nature in the heavens. From here come the four seasons beneath the heavens. From here, beneath time, come the four humors, complexions, and passions. From here, above time, rise the four virtues. From here, in eternity, are the four archetypes of the virtues.

### SECOND DISCUSSION FOR 
### proving the same.
### CHAPTER XXI.

Furthermore, if I did not fear being partly tedious and partly too novel, I would recount certain wonderful commentaries of Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus <note>Famous Neoplatonist philosophers who blended Plato’s logic with mystical theology</note>, who establish four grades above the celestial world: namely, the "One," "Limit," "Infinity," and "Mixture." Furthermore, they place the supernal world—that is, the first and intelligible mind—and after it the worldly mind, which is partly intelligible and partly intellectual; after this, the intellectual mind and world simply. In the fourth place, they put the animate mind and world, the leader of the sensible world. Likewise, they say the supreme mind looks up to those four—namely the One, Limit, Infinity, and Mixture—and possesses four things by its own nature: namely, unity on one side and essence on the other. Again, it possesses essential unity and uniform essence, and all the "Ideas" <note>Plato’s eternal forms or blueprints for reality</note> of things are similarly partakers of a fourfold nature. Likewise, the intellectual and "Jovial" <note>pertaining to Jupiter, often associated by Neoplatonists with the Demiurge or world-maker</note> mind, the craftsman of the world, in fabricating the world looks toward the intelligible and supreme mind as a model, and toward the Good as an end. And because in the intelligible world (which they call "being itself" and "living itself") it perceives the principles and Ideas of a fourfold nature, it arranges the world into four similar regions. The first of these extends from the first heaven, and after the heaven through the sphere of fire to the beginning of the air; the second from there to the middle of the air; the third from there to the earth; and the fourth is the earth itself. To such a division, four armies of rational inhabitants respond in each region: namely, the worldly gods, then the angels, then the demons, and finally the particular animals. But leaving these things aside, let us return to our purpose.

### THIRD DISCUSSION FOR 
### confirming the same.
### CHAPTER XXII.

According to the metaphysician, there are four elements: essence, being, power, and action. According to the mathematician, four: the point, line, plane, and depth. According to the physicist, four: the seminal power of nature, the natural budding, the adult form, and the composite. Match these one to one: to essence belongs the womb and the seed; to being, the line and the budding; to power, the plane and the form; to action, the depth and the composite. Everywhere the extremes are like solids joined by two intermediate means. Truly, what is a point in mathematics, Plato considers in physics to be the seminal power, indivisible and stable. What is the production of a line in length in mathematics, he considers in physics to be the "budding" (if I may call it that) of the germinating form. Likewise, what is a plane there, is properly the form here; for just as a plane terminates a body, so form terminates matter. Finally, what is depth there, is the "composite" here—a composite that is twofold: both formal—that is, a certain complexity of several forms similar to a 

<column-break/>

solid sphere—and material—that is, made of form and matter, more similar to a cube. Therefore, when he says that one mean <note>an intermediate value in a mathematical ratio</note> suffices between two planes, understand that one intermediate mean satisfies two forms: the formal mean. For when forms follow one another where they touch at their extremes, they agree by one formal mean, being partly in agreement and partly different on both sides. But when he says that solids are coupled to solids by a double mean, he signifies that between two natural composites of different natures, two twin means are interposed. One of these is formal, the other material. For in any composite, the principal form is considered on one side, and the subject suited to the form on the other. From this it follows that between different composites a double discrepancy arises: one more by reason of the form, the other more by reason of the subject.

### FOURTH DISCUSSION ON THE SAME, 
### and on the powers and proportions 
### of the elements.
### CHAPTER XXIII.

These same things are corroborated by another reason, if you descend from the fourfolds just described to the fourfold of the sphere. In this, one considers the nature of the center and the nature of the circumference, which are furthest apart from each other both in property and in position. Furthermore, one considers the space on one side insofar as the proper power of the center is extended, and the space on the other insofar as the proper power of the circumference is stretched out. Hence the four regions of the world are counted, and similarly the four elements.

| | By substance, | By power, | By action. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fire, | subtle, | acute, | mobile. |
| Air, | subtle, | obtuse, | mobile. |
| Water, | thick, | obtuse, | mobile. |
| Earth, | thick, | obtuse, | immobile. |

->Another arrangement of the same.<-

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fire, | acute, | subtle, | mobile. |
| Air, | obtuse, | subtle, | mobile. |
| Water, | obtuse, | thick, | mobile. |
| Earth, | obtuse, | thick, | immobile. |

Of these, the one placed at the circumference (following its nature) is the most ample, and therefore the most subtle of all in substance; in power it is the most acute and suited for penetration; and in action it is the most prompt for motion. However, that which is situated in the middle (following the nature of the center) is the narrowest and densest in substance; in power it is obtuse; and in action it is most unsuited for motion. The two means <note>air and water</note> are positioned intermediate between these. Accordingly, just as the circumference and center are furthest apart in a sphere, so fire and earth differ most by position and nature. For fire so seeks the circumference that it never naturally seeks the center; earth so seeks the center that it never naturally seeks the circumference. Air sometimes descends, namely if it is placed in the high region of fire. Water also ascends, if it is confined beneath the earth. Just as three things are considered in fire and earth—namely substance, power, and action—so also there are three primary properties: namely, in fire, fineness by substance, sharpness by power, and mobility by action. In earth, the opposites: thickness by substance, bluntness by power, and immobility by action. Their natures are called "solid" in Plato because, like a triple dimension, they possess triple qualities. If they had only the nature of planes, one mean would suffice; that is, it would agree with the extremes in one quality but differ in another. But because they have three mutually opposite qualities, they need two means to be bound together. Each of these means must agree with its neighbor (both the extreme and the other mean) in two qualities and differ in only one. Conversely, it must agree with the remote extreme in one quality but differ in two. Thus, air follows fire, being very similar to fire in subtlety and mobility, but dissimilar in a certain bluntness <note>original: *obtusitate*</note> of power—in which single quality it somehow agrees with earth. It agrees with water in two qualities: bluntness and mobility. Water follows air, similar to air in these two; but it is similar to fire in only one, namely mobility; and dissimilar to fire in two: thickness and bluntness together. It is dissimilar to earth in mobility, but similar in thickness and bluntness. Indeed, it is clear that fire is comparable to earth by a certain analogy—that is, a similarity of reason and proportion. For as the subtlety of fire is to the thickness of earth, so is the sharpness of fire to the bluntness of earth, and so again is the mobility of fire to the immobility of earth. That fire is also comparable—but by a stronger logic—to air, air to water, and water to earth, is manifest from the agreement of their qualities. It seems that the agreement of one element to its neighbor is double its disagreement; but to a remote element, the disagreement is double its agreement.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, transitioning from the mathematical ratios that define the elements to the metaphysical presence of those elements within the celestial spheres. It argues that the four elements exist in the heavens not in their gross, earthly forms, but as refined "virtues" or "powers."</meta>

# On the Timaeus.

Fire appears to be twice as subtle as air, three times more mobile, and four times sharper. Likewise, air is twice as sharp as water, three times more mobile, and four times as subtle. Again, water is twice as sharp as earth, three times more subtle, and four times more <term>stable<note>original: *pastatior*, likely a variant of *pactatior*, meaning more compact or stable</note></term> in its character. Musicians only allow for a progression among related things up to a quadruple proportion <note>a 4:1 ratio</note>, for the ears are offended by a longer progression. Furthermore, the perfect ratios of music are contained within these. In these elements, through three qualities—as if through three dimensions—we proceed toward solid things. For through the double ratio, at the fourth step, we arrive at eight: which is the first solid number <note>2 x 2 x 2 = 8. In Pythagorean thought, "solid" refers to a cubed number</note>. Likewise, through triple ratios, at the fourth step, we arrive at twenty-seven: which is the second solid number <note>3 x 3 x 3 = 27</note>. Again, through quadruple ratios, in the fourth place, we reach sixty-four, which holds the third place among solid numbers. For eight is created from two taken solidly—that is, three times or multiplied—twenty-seven from three multiplied three times, and sixty-four from four similarly multiplied by itself three times. 

But so that it may be better known how much consistency there is in Plato between mathematics and physics, those two means of the first solids must be repeated. For we placed two fitting means between eight and twenty-seven: namely twelve and eighteen. The number twelve is born from both eight and twenty-seven. For the "side" <note>the root or factor</note> from which eight is multiplied is two; the side from which twenty-seven is multiplied is three. But twelve is made from two and three if you multiply two twice, then by three <note>2 x 2 x 3 = 12</note>; here the emerging twelve takes two "sides" from the eight and one from the twenty-seven. Likewise, eighteen is made from two and three if you multiply three three times, then by two <note>3 x 3 x 2 = 18</note>; here the number eighteen takes one side from the distant eight (where it is said "by two") but two sides from the number twenty-seven (where it is said "three times three"). Similarly, the two elements that are intermediate between fire and earth, while they are tempered from the extremes, carry back a double nature from the nearest element and borrow a single nature from the distant one.

### THAT THE WHOLE WORLD IS COM-
### posed of four elements: and how these are in 
### one way in heaven, and another way below the moon.
#### CHAPTER XXIV.

The Pythagoreans and all Platonists believe the entire world is composed of these four elements, joined by geometric and musical ratios. However, they believe the consonance of these in heaven never suffers any dissonance; but below heaven, some dissonance may occasionally seem to arise, yet it is immediately and wonderfully reduced back into a consonant form by the influence of the higher realm. No one will deny that these elements exist below the moon. But some physical philosophers will deny they exist in heaven. I pray these men would listen to the metaphysicians, who prove that elements exist through their "Ideas" in the Maker of the world himself; then in the Soul of the World through their "Reasons"; and in nature through their "Seeds." Therefore, they are also in heaven through their "Virtues" <note>or powers</note>, and below heaven through their "Forms." For in what way could the natures of the elements pass from causes higher than heaven to the regions below heaven, and be nourished there, unless their moderating virtues were meanwhile poured into heaven? 

Indeed, just as a farmer does not rule an architect because he possesses no principles of architecture, but a geometer, possessing these principles, does rule him; so heaven could never govern these elements unless it encompassed the powers of the elements and elemental things. In governing them, it embraces them; rather, it governs them by embracing them. Let the astronomer also listen, as he identifies the natures of the elements in the signs of the zodiac and the planets, and proves this by their effects. Finally, let them listen to Sacred Scripture, which often places "waters" in the heavens and also speaks of a "land of the living." If these two things, which are most unlike the heavens, are placed there, how much more would fire and air, which are more similar to the celestial realm, be placed there by the Sacred Scriptures? 

Some will respond, I think, that the most excellent powers of the elements should be placed there as causes; but in the spheres below the moon, their natures exist according to form; and finally in composite things through a certain participation. But they will deny that the natures of the elements themselves are in heaven. To this, the Platonists would argue that proper virtues are everywhere founded in a proper nature. Therefore, if the virtues of these elements are in heaven, their natures must also be there. But just as the virtues there exist in a genus far more excellent than these, so the natures exist in a more excellent—nay, to speak more correctly, the most excellent—way. That most eminent nature of fire provides the heavens with sensible light, life-giving heat, and the swiftest motion. The nature of earth grants solid and firm stability; likewise, it gives the stars the density by which they can be seen, and the moon the density by which it reflects solar rays. The nature of air provides that transparent quality which they call "translucent." The nature of water brings a most delicate and uniform smoothness. And what is greatest of all, it inserts into the very "lips" or edges of the spheres where they touch each other that virtue of cold and moisture, so that even though they touch each other most rapidly and vehemently due to their swift motion, no burning or dissolution occurs there. 

<column-break/>

The Hebrews will strongly approve of these "waters" in the heavens. They will also approve, I think, if they hear that by the nature of the "land of the living" there, it happens that otherwise very thin matter is not dissipated by such great motion. One must remember that there is such great virtue in celestial substance, so effective for reconciling opposites, that qualities and motions which fight among themselves here on earth do not fight there. Likewise, just as the remaining elements there were, from the first birth of the world, reduced into the form of the most excellent element—that is, fire—so, through celestial motion, the four elements among us are reduced into a single form of a mixture in any generation. 

Nor should you wonder that the elements are fused into one there, if you consider that even below the moon they are compacted into one mass, and that fire participates in earthly solidity so that it is not immediately dispersed due to its extremely thin and mobile nature. Earth also, which is sluggish by itself, gains action and life through its fellowship with fire. If the extremes are mixed, then surely the intermediates are mixed with the other intermediates and extremes. Likewise, if there is such great union below the moon, it is much greater above the moon; but the solidity or stability of earth reigns there without grossness, in a sort of vaporous form. Again, the uniformity and smoothness of water is far from falling; the agility of air is separate from flowing away; and the efficacy of fire dominates in light and healthy heat, very similar to intelligence and life. This is separate from that combustion which fire is forced to perform here among us—where light is reflected between hollows and fiery heat is trapped in rough and biting matter. Certainly, to the extent that fire is freed from earthly grossness, it shines more purely and warms more healthfully. 

Therefore, together with Heraclitus and Empedocles, we shall say that of the fire which is in the "Idea" <note>the perfect, conceptual form of fire</note>, there is an intellectual light; in heaven, a visible light shines out to the eyes; below heaven in the ether, its pure and harmless flame thrives; but on earth, it is a coal burning in rough matter. We shall say finally with Orpheus that there are, moreover, four elements in the underworld: Pyriphlegethon, Acheron, Oceanus, and Cocytus <note>These are the four rivers of the Greek underworld, here equated with the elements</note>. We shall say with Plato: just as in the Archetypal world all things are in all things, so in this world of images all things are in all things. But according to the nature of the recipients, each thing is received differently: so that celestial things in the elements are "elemental," and elements in heaven are "celestial." Indeed, the excellence of the celestial region over others is so great that celestial fire, besides being the elemental fire and the other three elements, can be called a "fifth element" <note>The Quintessence</note>. 

Hence, he says five worlds can be named, since all kinds of things are in any of these five according to their own nature. We shall conclude, finally, with the concord between Moses and Plato—whom Numenius calls "another Moses." For what Moses says—"In the beginning God made heaven and earth"—Plato says: "God first made fire and earth," understanding "fire" primarily as heaven. For in the beginning, he considered the center and the circumference in the sphere of the world, and placed the rest between them for their sake.

### EVERY CIRCULAR MOTION IS
### proper to an ever-moving sphere. Likewise, light 
### is most proper to fire.
#### CHAPTER XXV.

But let those not disturb us who doubt that heaven is fiery because the motion of heaven is circular, while the motion of fire is straight. For even any portion of heaven, if it were by chance placed in the center, would immediately ascend in a straight line, seeking its homeland by the shortest path; and yet the proper motion of heaven is a circuit. And earth, if separated from the center, will descend, yet its proper state is to rest. Surely any mobile sphere, whether elemental or celestial, moves naturally in a circle according to its shape, so that it may enjoy its place more fully. Straight motion, wherever it exists, is not so much "natural" as it is a "return to nature." 

If a circuit suits any body, it suits fire most of all. Since fire is naturally furthest from the earth, just as the earth is always immobile, so fire is always mobile. If it is always mobile, then it moves in a circle. For that which moves in a straight line finishes its motion when the finite distance is completed. That both fire and air move in a circle is shown by the circuit of comets. The circuit of water is also witnessed by its perpetual ebb and flow. It was necessary for the earth to remain still, so that it might be more like an indivisible and stable center and enjoy it more conveniently. But it was necessary for the higher things to move, so that they might always produce varied things according to the variety of their motion. 

Nor should anyone deny that heaven is hot, but rather deny that it is "scorching." Nor should they say the light of the sun warms only by reflection, but rather that it only *burns* by reflection. For the rays of the moon, when reflected, do not warm at all, since a watery virtue dominates in her. But the rays of the sun warm healthfully because of the fiery and life-giving nature of the sun. Nor should they object that the rays of the moon fail to warm because of its slower motion. For even if it is said to be slower, it is so much closer to men than the sun that it ought to warm at least somewhat if warming occurred only through reflection. Nor should they argue that "scorching heat" is the property of fire. Indeed, the less it is mixed with foreign matter, the less it burns. But let the light...
