<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, moving from the physical construction of the world's body to the metaphysical composition of the World Soul (Anima Mundi). It establishes a hierarchy of spirit—Intellect, Soul, Intelligence, and Nature—and links them to the four elements.</meta>

...light is the property of fire. For the purer it is, the more lucid it is—though perhaps not more manifest to certain eyes. It shines further than it heats; it illuminates first and in an instant, and it bestows heat, with the warmed object retaining the heat for a time after the fire is gone. Light, however, it bestows on nothing <note>meaning light is not "absorbed" and kept by objects like heat is</note>, as light is its own property. Indeed, when the fire departs, the light departs with it.

### ON THE SPIRIT OF THE WORLD, THAT IS,
### on intellect, soul, intelligence,
### and nature.
### CHAPTER XXVI.

After he treated how God constructed the world’s body, he next proceeds to discuss how He tempered the world-soul. He shows, meanwhile, that he placed before our eyes the unformed mass before the formed, and soon after, the formed mass before the animated. This was not because unformed matter existed before formation, or corporal formation before the soul, but so that we might understand that formable nature was divinely instituted for the sake of corporal formation, just as corporal formation exists for the sake of the soul as its end. Therefore, wishing to make a perfect work, God made the world living and intellectual. And so that a single living being might be more conveniently connected from the spirit and the matter of the world, He distinguished the matter into four elements, as we have said—like the humors of this animal—because He also willed its spirit to be distinguished into four parts.

For four things pertain to the spirit of the world. First is the **Intellect**, remaining immobile within itself, the ruler of the sphere's motion without being moved, so instituted by the author of all things to rule the spheres. Second is the **Soul** of the sphere, a "moved mover," mobile indeed, but mobile through itself <note>original: *motor mobilis... per se ipsum*; a reference to the Platonic definition of the soul as that which moves itself</note>. Third is a certain **Intelligence**, divinely implanted in this soul by God and the higher Intellect. Fourth is **Nature**, that is, the vital seminal virtue, infused everywhere into matter by the soul. Intellect and Soul are substances; Intelligence and Nature, however, are qualities—the former of the soul, the latter of matter.

The four elements are images of these four. For **Fire** reflects the Intellect, **Earth** reflects Nature, **Air** reflects Intelligence, and **Water** reflects the Soul. And just as three properties belong to fire and three opposites to earth, and the middle elements agree in a certain middle way, so three properties belong to the Intellect, their opposites to Nature, and the middle properties to the middle states. For the Intellect is indivisible, uniform, and eternal. Nature is divisible, multiform, and temporal. The Soul, however, is the middle between these; through Intelligence it becomes more a participant in the Intellect itself than in Nature, but through its animal power, it accords more with Nature than with the Intellect. For this reason, it is called partly indivisible and partly divisible. Likewise, it is similarly uniform and multiform. Again, it is partly eternal and partly temporal.

Furthermore, four "lives" are numbered according to the fourfold spirit of the world. The **Saturnian** life is in the Intellect, looking up to its father, the Heavens—that is, God, the craftsman of the heavens. The **Jovial** life is in the Intelligence, already declining toward mobile action. The **Venereal** life is in the animal virtue, now loving matter. The **Dionysiac** life is in Nature, as if drunk—that is, immersed in matter <note>These names refer to planetary archetypes: Saturn for contemplation, Jupiter for governance, Venus for desire/vitality, and Dionysus for the "intoxication" of physical existence</note>.

Moreover, four senses are counted in the universe by a similar logic. The first sense is in the world-soul—I mean the **common sense**, and it is one; that is, a certain imaginary power accompanying its intelligence and touching the particular forms of things, just as intelligence touches the universal ones. It touches them from within; therefore, it needs no instruments, nor does it proceed outside anywhere, nor does it suffer. The second sense is in the souls of the spheres and the stars; it is certainly common and similarly impassive, but it proceeds outward. The third is in particular souls <note>such as human souls</note>, distributed through individual instruments beyond the common power, extending itself outside, and arising from "passion" <note>in the sense of being acted upon by external stimuli</note>, but ending in judgment. Finally, the Pythagoreans grant a fourth sense to plants—or rather a phantom of a sense—and a dull one at that, having no judgment of quality, but placed only in the "passion" of a certain pleasure and pain.

The first sense represents the Intellect; the second, Intelligence; the third, the animal power; and the fourth, the natural. It is necessary to remember that the matter of the world does not receive the soul except through Nature, nor Intelligence except through the Soul, nor Intellect except through Intelligence. Just as the earth receives water, and through water the air, and through air the fire. Take note of what follows next, which is similar to these things. For he says: *God placed the soul in the center, and from there extended it through the whole, and finally protected the exterior of the world through it.* First, he signifies that the soul both fills the entire mass of the world—moderating different parts of the world with different virtues—and that it surpasses the world by its highest virtue, that is, its intellectual providence. That the virtue of the soul is extended from the center itself through the universe is explained twice through four steps. First,

<column-break/>

from the middle of the **Earth**, it extends the power of connecting everywhere; from the middle of the **Water**, it diffuses vital power; from the **Air**, similarly, sensual power; and from the **Fire**, rational power. Then, from the middle of the world-sphere <note>the center of the cosmos</note>, it extends the power of connecting; from the sphere of the **Moon** (the middle point between the generable and ingenerable), it extends vital power; from the **Sun** (the heart of the world), sensual power; and from the middle **Zodiac** of the firmament, rational power.

Since there is a double order of things toward God—one by which they proceed from Him, the other by which, having proceeded, they are turned back toward Him—Plato followed the order of procession when he said: *God located the intellect in the soul, and the soul in the body.* Considering also the order of conversion <note>the return to the divine source</note>, he said: *God extended the soul, placed in the center, from there through the whole, and meanwhile led something of it out beyond the world,* so that, while it provided for the world, it might be turned back toward God.

### ON THE COMPOSITION OF THE SOUL,
### and that it is appropriately proceeded 
### through the number five in its composition.
### CHAPTER XXVII.

Since we have explained many things regarding the souls of the spheres, their motions, and the composition of the soul in our *Theology* <note>likely referring to Ficino's *Platonic Theology*</note>, we have been and will be briefer in explaining them here. For we are now hurrying toward some more specific matters.

In the beginning, we believe the number **five** <term>quinarius<note>The Quinary; the number 5, considered by Pythagoreans to be the number of "marriage" or balance</note></term> is suited to the composition and partitioning of the soul for three reasons. First, because just as five consists of the first even and the first odd number <note>2 + 3 = 5; 1 was not considered a number but the source of numbers</note>, so the soul consists of divisible and indivisible nature. You know, moreover, that an even number is called "divisible," while an odd number is called "indivisible," since it cannot be divided into equal parts. Second, because the genera from which all things are composed by God are distributed through five: they are **Essence, the Same, the Different, Rest, and Motion**. They believe the soul, as the middle of all things, is composed from these five genera of all things by a certain primary logic. Third, because since the soul is the middle of the universe, it naturally receives the number five, which is the middle of the universal number <note>10</note>. For five is the perfect middle of ten. For when we

-> 1 <-
-> 2 --- 3 <-
-> 4 ----- 9 <-
-> 8 ------- 27 <-
-> 5 - 5 - 5 - 5 - 5 <-

<image-desc>This diagram illustrates the Platonic Lambda, a pyramid of numbers used in the Timaeus to describe the harmonic proportions of the world-soul. It features the "double" series (1, 2, 4, 8) and the "triple" series (1, 3, 9, 27). The row of fives below represents the soul as the mediating "Quinary."</image-desc>

rightly divide ten five times, the number five is the middle, equally distant in any division. First, if you divide ten into nine and one, you will see that five is the middle between one and nine, equally distant from both. Second, if you wish to part ten into eight and two, you will again find five as the equal middle between these. If thirdly into seven and three, or fourthly into six and four, you will again receive five as the true middle between the extremes. In every case, we call this the **Arithmetic Mean**. That you have five as the middle when ten is divided a fifth time into five and five is unnecessary to say.

For these reasons, Plato, in the distribution of the universe—both of the "animable" body, so to speak, and of the soul—brings forward five main heads into the middle. For in both cases, he first treats the **subsistence** and foundation of the thing itself, whether of the body or the soul. Second, the **concord** of both parts. Third, the **species** resulting from the concord of parts. Fourth, the **virtues** of the species. Fifth, the **actions** that arise from the virtues.

The Platonists wish for those first three—subsistence, concord, and species—to pertain to the essence of the soul; through these follow virtue and action. By concord, I mean a fitting temperament, and this is fivefold: namely of genera, parts, reasons, powers, and actions. For the soul consists of those five genera of things, through which its own parts are also assigned. It receives, in turn, the "reasons" of all things from God. From this, it has many and specific powers, through which it also performs actions.

But where he calls the soul a "concord" or "harmony," remember that Plato in the *Phaedo* denies that the soul is a harmony—specifically, a harmony of corporal parts made from them and lying within them. In the *Timaeus*, however, he affirms the soul is a harmony—specifically, a harmony of its own parts, remaining within itself and tempering the body from itself. Furthermore, where he says: *God composed from the indivisible essence, always existing in the same way, and likewise from that which is around bodies...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the composition of the World Soul. It transitions from a general definition of the soul as a "mean" between the divine and the physical to a detailed analysis of its mathematical and musical structure.</meta>

becomes divisible, the middle species of essence—that is, the soul—explain these things through what he says elsewhere: God made the world living, animated, and intellectual. Where he says "living," he designates a certain natural life scattered through the bodies of the world, extended together with the body of the world and acting in a mobile way. But where he says "intellectual," he understands the angelic intellects, which are properly appointed to rule the spheres; they are indivisible according to place and immutable according to time, existing in a manner opposite to natural life and the divisible and mutable bodily form. But where he says "animated," he signifies the very substance of the world-soul, whose essence is indeed both indivisible and immutable, like the intellect. However, it can be called in a certain way divisible and mobile, because it is the proper source of certain powers that decline toward divisible and mobile things. Its power and action are partly individual and immobile, insofar as it agrees with divine things and acts stably; yet it is also partly divisible in a way, both because it is manifold and because it declines toward the manifold and divided body; and it is mobile, because it operates within time. Therefore, he calls this soul the third species of essence, a mean between the individual and eternal things, and again the divided and temporal things. 

That he intends to signify angelic intellects when he names the world "intellectual" is proved by this: that the body of the world is prepared for intellect through life. Therefore, as it relates to life, so it relates to intellect. Thus, just as it does not only have natural life lying within the matter of the world, but also animal life beyond that—that is, the soul existing in itself—so it does not only have an intellectual quality infused into the soul, but also an intellectual substance remaining in itself. For everywhere certain qualities are reduced to certain substances; just as a vital quality refers to a vital substance, so an intellectual quality is also referred to an intellectual substance. 

He composes the soul in five ways especially. First, from the five genera <note>The "Five Greatest Kinds" from Plato's Sophist: Being, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion.</note> of things. Second, from numbers. Third, from numerous harmonies. Fourth, from the beginnings of figures <note>Geometric shapes</note>. Fifth, from the principles of motions; namely, so that possessing the accounts of metaphysics and mathematics, it may thus know all things: essences, numbers, harmonies, figures, and motions. Likewise, insofar as the soul is kindred to divine things, he says it is composed of the genera of things that are primarily in divine things. Insofar as it is kindred to natural things, he mixes it with figures and motions. But insofar as it obtains the middle between both, he tempers it with numerous harmonies and proportions. 

Those five—namely Essence, the Same, the Other, Rest, and Motion—he names the "genera of things," because all things (except the First) are composed from them. **Essence** clearly signifies the formal account of each thing; it also hints at "being" as the proper act of essence. **The Same** is so called because anything agrees first with itself and then with others. Again, **the Other** is added because it has a certain difference both within itself and toward other things. Furthermore, **Rest** <note>original: "status"</note>, since it retains its own unity for some time. Finally, **Motion** in this place signifies a certain exit from potentiality into act: whether by being, or in any way acting intrinsically or extrinsically. 

But above these five genera are placed **One**, **Limit**, **Infinity**, and **Mixture**. Above these three is placed the **One itself**. Essence follows the divine One itself. The Same and Rest follow Limit. But the Other and Motion accompany Infinity. Finally, just as we have placed the four elements of the world in the highest degree in the celestial regions, in the middle degree under the moon, and in the lowest degree under the earth; so we place the five genera by a certain highest account in divine things, a middle account in the soul, and the lowest account under the soul. For in divine things, unity surpasses multitude, and limit surpasses infinity, and the same exceeds the other, and rest prevails over motion. But in lower things it is entirely the opposite: those which surpassed there are now surpassed here in turn. In the soul especially, an equal tempering of each to each emerges, so that they rightly wish this to be both the "mean" of things and tempered by musical proportions. 

Both types of mathematics suit the soul, for both are judged as means between divine and natural things. Musical numbers suit the soul most of all. For they are mobile, and for that reason they rightly signify the soul, which is the principle of motion. The soul is described not only through numbers but also through figures: so that through numbers it may be thought of as incorporeal, but through figures it may be known to decline naturally toward bodies. 

The **Triangle** suits the soul. Because just as a triangle is extended from one angle into two, so the soul, flowing from an individual and divine substance, falls into the entirely divisible nature of the body; and if it is compared with divine things, it appears divided. For while those divine things act through a single and stable power and do so suddenly, the soul performs through many and mutable powers and actions, and through intervals of time. But if it is compared with natural things, it is judged undivided. For it does not have different parts in different places like they do, but it is in

<column-break/>

any part of the whole as a whole; nor does it pursue all things with mobility and time as they do, but it also attains something suddenly and possesses something eternal. Furthermore, one may compare the soul with the triangle in this: that the triangle is the first figure among those consisting of multiple lines produced in a straight line. Similarly, the soul is the first of all to be distributed into multiple powers, which are brought under intelligence within it; and it seems to be produced in a straight line while it falls from divinity into nature. In this descent from the highest intelligence, it flows into three lower powers: that is, into a certain rational discourse, into sense, and into the vegetative power. Just as the triangle, produced from a point, is drawn into three angles. He says the soul is the first of every genus, and is mixed from several powers in a way, and falls—if I may put it thus—in a straight line. 

For the **Angelic Mind** above the soul needs no lower powers within itself, but is pure mind, a whole and sufficient mind. Likewise, it does not turn toward lower things, but toward divinity alone, from whence it is; it turns back in the manner of a circle. Therefore, its action is compared to a circle. For it is one and equal action: just as a circle is from one and equal line, and there is a certain marvelous capacity in both. Furthermore, the circle is the first and last of figures. First, because it is contained by one line. Last, because figures composed of many lines, the more faces they take on, the more they seem to approach gradually toward the form of the circle as if to an end. Similarly, the intellect is the first of all procreated by God, and the intellectual "vultus" <note>face or countenance</note>—that is, the absolute order of things—shines last of all in the mirror of nature, toward which natural forms approach more and more by degrees as if to an end. But concerning the intellect, another time. Now let us return to the soul.

### WHY THE SOUL IS COMPARED TO A COMPOSITE
->thing; why to musical harmonies.<-
->CHAPTER XXVIII.<-

**W**e seek three things especially concerning the Soul at present. First, why Plato fashions the soul similar to a composite thing. Second, why to a thing composed by a certain concord. Third, why to musical harmonies. 

In the first place, the soul, even if it is indissolubly composed, is nevertheless composed of such great multiplicity that by a certain natural inclination it turns toward those things which are entirely composite. Therefore, it is figured as somewhat similar to composite things, with which it agrees by a certain natural—I do not say blood-relation, but affinity. 

Secondly, because it is the "mean" of things, it is deservedly composed of all things and binds all things together concordantly; and therefore it is compared either to a certain concord or to something concordantly composed: especially since the soul reconciles those things which in nature fight among themselves, connects the reconciled, and preserves the connected. Thus, not wrongly is the soul judged to be a certain substantial concord, or a substance most concordant and indissoluble. 

But since those things which are apprehended by the other senses are also very often concordantly composed, it was asked thirdly: why Plato expressed the soul as being especially similar to **musical concord**. The answer to this is: musical harmony occurs in the medium of all things (the air), and through motion, and this reaches the ears in a circular way, so that it is no wonder that it suits the soul, which is both the mean of things and the principle of motion revolving in a circuit. 

Add to this that harmony, especially among those things which are sensed, is as if "animated"; it carries the affection and thought of the soul—whether of the singer or the player—into the souls of the listeners; therefore, it agrees with the soul in the highest degree. Furthermore, things pertaining to sight, even if they are pure in a way, are nevertheless often apprehended without the efficacy of motion and through an image alone without the nature of the thing: therefore, they are accustomed to move souls very little. But things pertaining to smell, taste, and touch, being as if very material, tickle the instruments of the senses rather than penetrating the depths of the soul. 

Harmony, however, moves the body through the nature of air set in motion; through purified air, it excites the aereal spirit, the knot of the soul and body; through affection, it affects the sense and the soul simultaneously; through significance, it acts upon the mind; finally, through the motion of the subtle air itself, it penetrates vehemently; through contemplation, it licks sweetly; through its conforming quality, it pours in a certain marvelous pleasure; through its nature—both spiritual and material—it seizes and claims the whole man at once. 

And truly, if one were to observe harmonies with as much art and diligence of the Muses for the hearing, as the care of nature or art offers flavors to the taste or soft things to the touch, we would undoubtedly know that **Apollo** seizes the soul with melody much more than either **Bacchus** is accustomed to occupy the taste with wine, or **Venus** the touch with itching. It happens, in addition, that where Plato introduces the world-maker speaking—both reasoning with himself and commanding the rest—he thinks that the speech itself, being as if an Apollonian song and supremely musical, is the origin of both the world-soul and body, and that the soul, born in a similarly musical account, strikes the celestial lyre. And indeed, because in the celestial me...

[Me]lody is: just as a low tone arises from a slower motion, and a high tone from a swifter motion, so in the heavens there is gravity and levity; likewise cold and heat, and again the moisture and dryness of the elements. The same is true in the generation of things: there is matter and form. The same is true in human dispositions: gentleness and magnanimity, temperance and fortitude. And just as from the low and high voice, so from all these pairs of natures which we have recounted, a "one" is produced everywhere. Since, therefore, musical consonance is, as it were, living, rational, and effective—likewise, because it is most similar [to the soul], it is most pleasing to the soul—and since it claims the whole man for itself, and (what is greater) since the soul was made through it, and all things were made and are preserved and moved through it: not without reason did our Plato describe the soul, as the maker, preserver, and mover of all natural things, chiefly by musical numbers and ratios; constituted, I say, not by accidental mathematical numbers, as some falsely claim, but by the ideal and metaphysical ratios of numbers.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically Chapter 31, which discusses the mathematical properties of musical ratios. It follows the previous page's introduction to Pythagorean and Platonic proportions.</meta>

-> On the Timaeus. 467 <-

Suppose, for instance, that between two and sixteen you placed four and eight. For all these numbers in sequence look toward their neighbor in a double ratio <note>A 1:2 ratio, where each number is twice the previous one (2, 4, 8, 16). This creates a geometric progression.</note>. If, therefore, you multiply two by sixteen, you will return the same result as if you had multiplied four by eight <note>Both 2 × 16 and 4 × 8 equal 32. Ficino is demonstrating a property of geometric means.</note>. The same occurs in other ratios, both among **multiples** and **superparticulars** <term>superparticular: A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one equal part of it, such as 3:2 (a whole plus a half) or 4:3 (a whole plus a third).</term>. In **superpartients** <term>superpartient: A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part of it, such as 5:3 (a whole plus two-thirds).</term>, however, it is not the same. Arrange three, five, and seven. Just as there is a "super-two-part" <note>original: *superbipartiens*</note> relationship from seven to five, so there is from five to three. For in both cases, two specific parts are added on top of the whole. If you multiply three by seven, you will not produce the same number as if you multiplied five by itself <note>3 × 7 = 21, whereas 5 × 5 = 25. Unlike the "pure" musical ratios, these do not share the same geometric symmetry.</note>. In the first rank, therefore, are the **multiples**: because, besides what we were just saying, through them all numbers also look back toward unity <note>The number 1, which for Platonists represents the source of all being.</note> even as they regard the numbers themselves. In the second rank are the **superparticulars**: because although they do not look at unity itself, they always look at one specific part fitted to a whole unit. In the third rank are the **superpartients**: because they seem to see neither of these...

<summary>Ficino explains the mathematical hierarchy of musical ratios, arguing that multiples and superparticulars are superior to superpartients because of their geometric symmetry and their closer relationship to "Unity" (the number one).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, focusing on the mathematical derivation of musical intervals and their application to the structure of the cosmic soul. # Compendium.

...stretched twice as much, while both were struck, it returned to its original tension twice as forcefully and quickly. It gave back a voice far sharper than the much deeper one, yet so harmonious that it appeared as a single sound—narrower on one side, broader on the other. Where this sharper sound occurred, he measured it by a scale at the eighth degree of height from the deep note, counting the deep note itself as the first. He found it consisted of eight sounds, seven intervals, and nearly six whole tones. Furthermore, where the ratio of tension and slackness between the strings was **one-and-a-third** <term>sesquitertia: The 4:3 ratio, which produces the musical interval of a fourth.</term>, he found the harmony of the **fourth** <term>diatessaron: A musical interval spanning four letter-notes.</term>, encompassing two tones and a minor semitone, four sounds, and three intervals. But in the **one-and-a-half** ratio <term>sesquialtera: The 3:2 ratio, which produces the musical interval of a fifth.</term>, he discovered the **fifth** <term>diapente: A musical interval spanning five letter-notes.</term>; in this, he perceived three tones and a minor semitone, five sounds, and four intervals. 

He then noticed that the **octave** <term>diapason: From the Greek "through all [strings]," the interval where a note repeats at a higher or lower pitch.</term> is composed of the fourth and the fifth. This is because the double ratio <note>The 2:1 ratio.</note> which produces the octave is constituted of the one-and-a-third and one-and-a-half ratios, from which those intervals are made. For the first double ratio having a middle term is two to four <note>2 : 3 : 4</note>, composed of the one-and-a-half between three and two, and the one-and-a-third between four and three. But in the triple ratio <note>3:1</note>, he considered the **octave-plus-fifth** <note>original: "diapason diapente"</note>, having twelve sounds but eleven intervals. For the octave has its seat in the double ratio, and the fifth in the one-and-a-half. But a one-and-a-half ratio joined to a double ratio creates a triple ratio. For six against three is double; add nine (from which a one-and-a-half ratio is born relative to six), and you will immediately have a triple ratio from nine to three. 

However, a triple ratio is not made if you add a one-and-a-third to a double; for instance, if you joined an eight to that six. It lacks the **one-and-eighth** ratio <term>sesquioctaua: The 9:8 ratio, which defines a single whole tone in music.</term>, namely nine to eight. And since a one-and-a-third added to a double becomes a **superpartient** <note>original: "superpartiens" — a complex ratio like 8:3.</note>, Pythagoras forbade continuing suddenly from the octave via a one-and-a-third fourth, although Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist.</note> admits this addition in some places. 

But it is convenient to add a one-and-a-third to a triple ratio. From this comes the quadruple ratio, and through the quadruple harmony, the **double octave** <term>disdiapason: An interval spanning two full octaves (4:1 ratio).</term>, having fifteen sounds and fourteen intervals. If you place a triple ratio between nine and three and add twelve (which is one-and-a-third compared to nine), you suddenly acquire the quadruple ratio arising from twelve to three. 

For the sake of melody, he forbids progressing beyond the quadruple ratio, not only because the violence to the senses arises from the more vehement motion and breaking of the air, but also because as soon as a five-fold ratio <note>5:1</note> is born between five and four beyond the first quadruple, a ratio of five to three arises simultaneously, which mixes in a dissonance. 

But to return to the narrower side of the quadruple, he also forbids descending often below the one-and-a-third ratio to avoid "sluggishness" <note>original: "torporis gratia" — referring to the lack of musical tension in very small intervals.</note>. He forbids continuing two one-and-a-third ratios in a row, both because they are otherwise displeasing and because they do not fill out the double ratio or the octave. If you arrange 9, 12, and 16, you have two one-and-a-third ratios, but by no means a double ratio; for it lacks the one-and-eighth ratio—namely 18 to 16—to make a double ratio from 18 to 9. Nor does he gladly continue twin one-and-a-half ratios, for these together exceed the double ratio by a one-and-eighth tone. You can detect this if you write down 4, 6, and 9. Here are two adjacent one-and-a-half ratios from four to nine. But nine exceeds eight (which is the double of four) by a one-and-eighth portion. 

From this it appears that the power of the one-and-a-half ratio is greater than half of a double ratio. From this it is also clear that the power of the one-and-a-third ratio is just as much less than half; since a double ratio is created from both together. Indeed, the one-and-a-third is exceeded by the one-and-a-half by a single one-eighth portion. For from eight to six you have a one-and-a-third, but from nine to six you have a one-and-a-half. And from nine to eight you have a one-and-eighth. By this very one-and-eighth part, you understand that the one-and-a-third is surpassed by the one-and-a-half. 

It is necessary to remember that the fourth—that is, the harmony of four sounds ascending to the fourth height—is not approved by the hearing on its own, yet it is gladly received because, with a tone added, it easily becomes the fifth, the most pleasing concord of the fifth voice. Likewise, if it is connected to the fifth, it completes the octave, the most perfect of all. Nor should it trouble anyone that although we said the fourth has four sounds and the fifth has five, the octave composed of both is said to have no more than eight. For when we deal with composite harmonies, we arrange the strings in joined tetrachords and continue the sounds such that the last sound of the first harmony is the first sound of the following harmony in that composition. 

From this, the matter suggests we return to the seven-stringed lyre of Terpander <note>A famous Greek poet and musician of the 7th century BCE who added strings to the lyre.</note>, in which the fourth string is struck twice, so that it somehow becomes an eight-stringed instrument. I believe Terpander followed this joining because the multiplication of voices clearly differing from one another increases up to the seventh sound. But the eighth sound now returns to the first with a certain wonderful 

<column-break/>

similarity. Just as the double ratio through which it is created restores the smaller number which it surpasses, while it exceeds that same number by the same amount. The ninth returns to the second, and is dissonant like the second. The tenth to the third, and is consonant like the third. The eleventh to the fourth. The twelfth to the fifth. The thirteenth to the sixth. But the fourteenth returns to the seventh. Finally, the fifteenth returns to the eighth, and with the eighth simultaneously to the first. 

The first and deepest sound they name **Hypate** <note>The strings of the Greek lyre were named for their physical position. Hypate was the "highest" physically but the lowest in pitch.</note>; the following, **Parypate**; the third, **Lichanos**; the fourth, **Mese**; the fifth, **Paramese** or **Trite**; the sixth, **Paranete**; and the seventh sound, **Nete**. 

Furthermore, if a comparison is made in quality and lasting motion, we shall compare **Hypate** with Saturn, and the following strings with the following planets in order. But if the comparison is in daily motion and its speed or slowness, we shall instead compare **Hypate** with the Moon, and the following ones in turn with the higher planets. We shall find deep sounds in the heavens mixed with sharp ones, and those same spheres emitting a sharp tone with one motion and a deep one with another. Likewise, from immense globes come immense sounds; from divine ones, divine; from multiple revolutions, in the same way, multiple sounds. And just as the revolution returns to the same after the seventh sound, so above the seven distinct spheres of the planets, all things revolve into one sphere, marvelously embracing such a sevenfold nature within itself. 

But of these things elsewhere. Let us return to the harmonies and conclude them now with a proper end. Three were numbered among the ancients. 

First is the **Diatonic**, in which any four-stringed scale proceeds through a minor semitone, then a tone and a tone. Other wise men, and Plato especially, approve this before others as the most natural of all. Since it proceeds from the minor semitone as if from a soft material, by the custom of nature, toward the stronger material of the tone, it has a form that is simple and gentle yet robust at the same time. Add that it most fits the four-stringed scale, in which the fourth is produced from twin tones and a semitone. 

The second harmony is called the **Chromatic**, which used to run through a minor semitone, a major semitone, and a **trihemitone** <term>trihemitone: An interval of three semitones, also known as a minor third.</term>. But the philosophers reject this as being too soft. 

The third is named the **Harmonic** <note>Often called "Enharmonic" in other texts.</note>, proceeding through roughly a quarter-part of a tone, again through a similar quarter, and then a **ditone** <term>ditone: An interval of two whole tones, a major third.</term>. This too they do not approve because of the superstitious difficulty of perceiving and using it. Many things pertaining to these matters that we omit for the present, we treat more diligently in the eighth book of our *Letters*.

***

### ON THE HARMONIC
### composition of the soul.
### CHAPTER XXXII.

When God was about to create the Soul of the World, He fashioned it from **indivisible and divisible** essence. This first division in Plato—namely into essence, the indivisible property, and the divisible—is the most universal. For what he calls "indivisible" contains within itself that which is neither cut into part-outside-part according to place, nor flows from a prior to a posterior according to time. By the first it is called the **Same**; by the second, **State** and **Stability**. Similarly, what is called "divisible" embraces within itself both what is spread out in place and what glides in time. By the first it is called the **Other**; by the second, **Motion** and **Mobile**—motion, I say, in natural things. 

Therefore, under that division which said the soul was gathered from indivisible and divisible essence, five kinds of things are in a way contained: **Essence, Same, Other, Rest, and Motion**. Plato, for the sake of brevity, does not repeat five, but three. He repeats Essence, Same, and Other, as if they were sufficient. For Rest follows the Same, while Motion follows the Other. And conversely, the Same follows Rest, and the Other follows Motion. 

He says that God fashioned one nature out of Essence, the Same, and the Other with such an exact mixing that the Same and the Other were present everywhere in its Essence; and conversely, in its Same, the Other and Essence were present; and again, in its Other, both Essence and the Same lay hidden. For Essence, through the Same, has the quality of agreeing with itself and others; through the Other, it is in a way distinguished within itself, and much more so from others. The Same and the Other both obtain their existence from Essence. But the Same possesses agreement from itself, and difference from the Other. The Other itself possesses difference from itself, but agreement and order from the Same. 

Plato thinks this heap of "kinds" serves the soul for both judging all things and performing all tasks. Certainly, because it consists of **Essence**, it defines what each thing is; because of the **Same**, it knows what is simple, and if composite, by what union it is joined, and how it agrees with itself and others; because of the **Other**, it knows what diversity is in anything, and by what condition it is either arranged in itself or separated from others; because of **Rest** <note>original: "statu"</note>, it knows in what way and of what sort anything remains in itself; because it consists of **Motion**, it recognizes from what source each thing depends and by what reason, and likewise what kind and in what way...

how he acts. Furthermore, through essence, he gives being to things: through this same essence, he joins things to himself and to others; through difference, however, he separates them; through stability, he confirms them in their own nature and order; through motion, he moves them and causes them to be moved and to act. For this reason, it was not without merit that Plato, in the fabrication of the soul, joined together all kinds of things according to a certain ratio. He says these are mixed with one another by a **harmonic ratio**, not an arithmetic one, for otherwise the distribution would be unjust in some places; nor by a geometric proportion alone, for otherwise the equality in the mixture would be so great that it could not closely harmonize with the extreme diversity of bodies. But the harmonic ratio, consisting of the likeness of various things, both makes dissimilar things similar and connects unequal things by a certain common equality. Such is the quality and office of the soul, both toward itself and toward bodies. For whether it acts within itself, it mixes a certain "otherness" with the identities of the intelligence (if I may speak thus), and a certain "identity" with the otherness of reason. Similarly, it does this in imagination and sense. Whether it acts upon the body, it produces the otherness of motion in a certain stable order, as if by identity: this is apparent in the heavens, and likewise below the heavens in the very "otherness" of generation <note>The world of changing, physical things.</note>, it preserves identity through a continuous order; and in both places, it preserves and restores essence. Therefore, the God composing the soul of the world uses harmonic ratio, both in mixing the kinds of things with each other, and in the portions themselves which he took from them to compose the soul, and in the powers of the soul immediately accompanying its origin, and in the spheres of the world that correspond to the soul. Plato did not only investigate such a mixture of the soul through reasoning, but also carefully envisioned it by taking clues from the world itself. For when he contemplated the body of the world—placed under the soul, made for its sake, and ruled, moved, and shaped by it—he judged it consistent with nature that we might conjecture a certain form of its soul as a model from the figure of the world as an image. Therefore, by whatever proportions he suspected the spheres of the world were composed, arranged, and moved, he divined that its soul was tempered by nearly those same ones—that is, harmonic ratios. Just as among musicians, harmony flows from the skill of the mind into the voice, so from the harmony of the celestial soul, harmony passes into the world. But let us now hear Plato himself. First, he took one portion from the whole. Second, a portion double the first. Then a third, which was one-and-a-half times the second, but triple the first. Afterwards a fourth, double the second. A fifth thereafter, triple the third. A sixth, eight times the first. Finally a seventh, which exceeded the first by twenty-six parts. These are his words. Let us therefore establish a triangle at whose apex is placed unity, and from which the numbers flow out on both sides: here the even parts, there similarly the odd. Specifically in this ratio: on one side after unity, first two, then four, finally eight; on the other side under unity, first three, then nine, finally twenty-seven.

The first portion, therefore, which God took from the "ferment" of the genres themselves (if I may say so) to fashion the soul, is unity. The second is the **dyad** <note>the number two</note>, double the first. The third is the **triad** <note>the number three</note>, whose ratio is triple the first (that is, unity), but **one-and-a-half** <note>sesquialtera</note> the second (that is, the dyad). The fourth portion is the **tetrad** <note>the number four</note>, double the second (that is, the dyad). The fifth is the **ennead** <note>the number nine</note>, whose ratio is triple the third (that is, the triad). The sixth is the **octad** <note>the number eight</note>, whose proportion is eightfold to the first (that is, unity). The seventh is **twenty-seven**, a ratio indeed triple to the nine, but exceeding unity by twenty-six parts. In these numbers, he certainly encompasses all harmonic ratios. For in the **one-and-an-eighth** ratio <note>sesquioctava</note> between nine and eight, he brought forth the **tone** <note>tonum</note> which obeys the nine Muses. In the **one-and-a-half** ratio <note>sesquialtera</note> between three and two, he created the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The interval of a musical fifth</note>, the Venus-like grace of the fifth voice. In the **one-and-a-third** ratio <note>sesquitertia</note> between four and three, he created the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The interval of a musical fourth</note>, the Mercurial nature of the fourth voice, adapting itself to consonances. In the **double** ratio between two and one, and likewise between four and two, and again between eight and four, he brought forth the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave</note>, that is, the universal and absolute melody of the eighth voice dedicated to Apollo. In the **triple** ratio between three and one, likewise between nine and three, and again between twenty-seven and nine, he composed the <term>Diapason Diapente</term> <note>An octave plus a fifth; a twelfth</note>, that is, the Jovial symphony of the eighth and fifth together. In the **quadruple** ratio between four and one, and eight and two, he wove the symphony of the <term>Disdiapason</term> <note>A double octave</note>, again harmonizing for Apollo through fifteen sounds. Moreover, he inserted the beauty of the third voice into the beginnings as a <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>Fourth</note>, and then subjoined the beauty of the sixth voice to the ends as a <term>Diapente</term> <note>Fifth</note>, so that by the more delicate softness of both voices, the harshness of the second voice on one side and the seventh on the other might be softened. For thus the third and sixth voices are similar in softness, just as the second falling from the

<column-break/>

first, and likewise the seventh degenerating from the eighth, are very similar in harshness. In the beginning, where he says God took seven portions, he touched upon a mystery, both in music and also in nature. In music, certainly: because all variance of voices proceeds up to the seventh degree, after which there is a revolution back to the same. In nature, however, both because many things are transacted through the number seven in natural affairs (about which other Platonists have said enough), and because the number seven possesses unity as a bond of the twin trinities; and from these twins and itself, it again unfolds a trinity. Such is the likeness of the universe. For it is divided into three at the beginning. Hence Plato here commended the **triad**. It is divided, I say, into the eternal, the temporal, and the middle between them. The eternal things, under the property of the trinity, possess simplicity in essence, stability in power, and reflection in action. The temporal things, in turn, have a composition of essence in triple dimension, then mobility of power, and finally the transition of action. Between these trinities of eternal and temporal things, the soul, holding the middle ground, effects the **seventh degree**. It also effects the **ninth**, also praised here by Plato. Not unjustly, since the soul itself has three faces: for it is turned toward itself, toward higher things, and toward lower things. It is helpful here, before I return to the number seven, to commend the triad together with the nine for a little while longer. The first trinity of numbers seems to contain the beginning, middle, and end of things, and alone among numbers to contain them by a certain indivisible ratio. For it signifies each of these with individual unities. Furthermore, should one wish to run through the causes of things, one finds a triple property in the causes. For causes are in themselves, they produce effects, and they perfect the effects by leading them back. Or if you descend to consider the effects, you will similarly discover a trinity. For effects are in their causes, they proceed from them, and they are turned back to them. If you turn yourself to the soul, which connects the sublime causes with the lowest effects, you will see it remaining in itself, declining toward effects, and ascending toward causes. And indeed, this soul rules the world by a triple set of seven. First, indeed, by certain hidden seven powers of the planets dominating in the firmament through causes. Second, by the seven forms of the planets in the seven globes subject to the firmament. Third, by the seven gifts of the planets ruling generation below the Moon. Since below the Moon, the Sun provides life-giving light, while Mars provides burning heat; the varied surface of the earth is subject to Mercury, but the whole mass to Saturn. Yet, in the middle regions, moisture reigns: the airy moisture obeys Jupiter, the watery obeys the Moon, and finally the mixed moisture obeys Venus. Likewise, the acting causes follow the Sun; matters follow the Moon; the fruitfulness of acting causes follows Jupiter; the fruitfulness of matters follows Venus; the swift dispatch to an effect follows Mars and Mercury—the former because of vehemence, the latter because of dexterity and multiform virtue. The permanent continuation of all things is dedicated most of all to Saturn. Furthermore, the order of the seven parts here proceeds from groups of seven, which are distributed according to the three powers of the worldly soul. For in this intelligence, there is a stable circle. A circle indeed, because it reflects back to that place from which it came. Stable, because it does so suddenly. Under the intelligence, as if under the firmament, there are three powers: namely, universal reason, imagination, and vegetation <note>The "vegetative soul" responsible for growth and biological life.</note>. In reason, there are three circles that are in a way mobile and temporal. The first is from the soul toward loving the cause, and vice versa, occurring secretly by a certain natural instinct. The second is from the causes of things toward considering the effects, and vice versa. The third is from the more universal forms and Ideas toward the less universal, a descent and in turn a recursion. In the remaining two powers of the soul, there are altogether four circles, similarly temporal: two in each. The first is a natural reflection toward its own cause. The second is a certain and perpetual revolution from those same forms at certain intervals, through which both the temporal and certain revolution of configurations in the heaven and of transformations below the heaven occurs. Thus, the circuit of generation necessarily follows the circuit of the heaven, and this in turn follows the circuit of the soul. The revolution of the soul accompanies the orb of intelligence. Indeed, if the motion of the soul were entirely deserted by intelligence, it would immediately pass only in a straight line, both in perceiving and in acting. That it seeks itself again and gathers similar gyrations through other things, it receives from a certain higher intellect, which, both remaining in itself and suddenly turned toward the cause, bestows intelligence upon the soul; by which, as if by an outstretched hand, it stops the soul which is by its own nature wandering, and twists back its restless motion—naturally more prone to a straight line outside itself—into a middle orb between straight motion and rest. Hence my soul, about to return into itself, circles the profound mind and turns the heaven in a similar image. But of these things, more diffusely in the *Theology*. Let us return to the numbers.

On the *Timaeus*. 471

We shall explain the present matters: unless perhaps, while he places several—or at least two—means <note>In mathematics, "means" are the intermediate values in a sequence or ratio.</note> between the extreme terms, he wants it to be understood that the types of things and elements in the soul (which regard each other in an opposite way) give back two qualities to one another. For example, where a boundary touches infinity, let it carry back the indefinite quality of the boundary; and conversely, where infinity touches a boundary, let it undergo the determined passion of infinity. Furthermore, let there be in the boundary a certain "terminal infinity," and conversely, in infinity itself, a boundary progressing indefinitely. To these points is added that certain such means can be thought of even among the very powers of the soul, and the soul is accustomed to insert at least two means between those things that are far apart, according to its own examples in the world. A **Tone** <note>original: "Tonus"; in musical terms, a whole step, representing a full vibration or movement.</note> moreover signifies the full motion and pulse of the soul both in itself and in the heavens. But a **semitone** signifies a weaker motion in the elements, falling away from the first to such an extent that it receives a portion smaller than half of its perfection. Finally, the whole preceding treatise on harmony seems to signify a triple concord: namely, between the soul and the body, between the parts of the soul themselves, and between the parts of the body themselves.

### THE DIVISION OF THE SOUL, MOTION AND TIME. CHAPTER XXXVI.

When he says that the very mixture of the types was consumed in the completion of the soul, understand that the soul proceeded from God as perfect, so that it nearly fulfilled its own Idea. Furthermore, the long division shows that the soul's own movement is naturally straight—specifically toward the senses, and the nature of growth or movement. Likewise, for this reason, he cuts it into two to show both that there is a double straight motion in the soul (namely, for sensing and for moving), and that there is a similar twin motion from the soul in the body: namely, the uniform and the multiform. He intersects two lines to figure the soul <note>Plato describes the soul being shaped like the Greek letter Chi (X), representing the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic.</note>, and then he bends them into a circle, indicating that the nature of the soul—though naturally inclined toward straight motion—is adapted by God through the gift of intelligence entirely to circular motion. I say "twin circles": namely, the firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> which does not wander, and after the firmament, the orbits of the wandering planets. The circuit of the firmament properly reflects the very nature of Identity and Intelligence. But the multiple windings of the planets properly represent the nature of Difference and the lower parts of the soul. But from that very internal motion of the soul, time follows in the world together with motion. Among these things, he touches upon a few common points pertaining to Astronomy; but anyone even moderately learned easily understands these, and certain Platonists, both Greek and Latin, treat them at too great length. Soon a question arises concerning the **Ideas** and the types of worldly animals, which we have treated most extensively in our *Theology*. Furthermore, what he recounts concerning the genealogy of certain gods and daemons has a certain probability, as is declared similarly in the *Theology* and elsewhere.

### WHAT IS MADE DIRECTLY BY GOD AND WHAT THROUGH INTERMEDIARIES. CHAPTER XXXVII.

Hitherto it can be clear to anyone that the souls, the worldly gods, the daemons, all the spheres of the world, and the species of things themselves have proceeded from the Divine Intellect, the Craftsman of the world, without intermediate causes. However, regarding the ambiguity among Platonists concerning prime matter, we have spoken from the beginning. Therefore, the Architect of the world thereafter commands his "sons"—that is, the souls of the spheres and stars and the daemons, or even the lower angels—that in imitation of him, they should undertake the mixing of things below the moon, and subject all things to man. They are to reconcile man's rational soul (received from God himself) to a decaying body through a certain irrational life, depending partly on them and partly on the soul of man. You will note, however, in the very words of God, that whatever is made directly by God is eternal; and whatever is composed by any reason is, insofar as it is composed, also dissolvable. But insofar as certain composed things are so established through the divine will that in them unity overcomes multitude, they are preserved undissolved. You will note, moreover, where he says that God remains in his own state while he gives the command, but the ministers follow, that there is no mutability in God while he rules and moves mobile things; but in his ministers, providence is closer to a certain change. Finally, in all these things, you will recognize that Mosaic saying, *I am who I am* <note>original: "Ego sum qui sum"; a reference to Exodus 3:14.</note>, to be wonderfully confirmed.

### ON MAN AS IT PERTAINS TO THE SOUL AND BODY. CHAPTER XXXVIll.

He says that the rational soul of man was forged by God from the same types of things, mixed in the same bowl <note>original: "crater"; the "mixing bowl" of the Demiurge.</note>, as the World

<column-break/>

Soul. The Bowl signifies the very Idea of rational life. But he adds that it was made from the "remnants" of the superior mixture, signifying that particular lives are lower than the universal life. Then indeed God adapts the souls—that is, the individual orders of souls—to individual stars. He also applies **vehicles** <note>original: "vehicula"; the "astral bodies" or subtle envelopes that carry the soul from the heavens down to the physical body.</note>, that is, ethereal bodies. He also teaches the "fatal laws" while he pours into the souls the formulas of the Ideas, through which the souls, having at some time turned into themselves, may be able to recognize the reasons of things. What he says concerning the fated descent and circuit of the soul has been explained elsewhere. After these things, the ministers of God pursue the fabrication of the human body, connecting it with hidden bonds. By these "hidden bonds," he understands the temperament of man to be so balanced and so similar to heaven that the excess of elemental qualities hardly appears in it. He then adds that the circuits of the soul are hindered in the mass of the body. Here, remember above all else that our soul was woven by a similar reason as the World Soul, and possesses similar circuits. Therefore, he says that the circuit of intelligence is hindered, and the circuit of reason is distracted, for two primary reasons: first, because before the body is grown, the soul is entirely occupied in the fabrication of the body; and second, because things that move the senses from the outside strike more vehemently in a tender age, and because of the novelty of things, they make the soul full of wonder regarding bodily matters. For these reasons, the intelligence is long vacant from its divine office, and the rational discourse itself, distracted around lower things, is troubled and deceived as if insane. Thus, the whole mind undergoes a perverted shape and leads a laborious life while reason yields to the senses—just as if someone were to fix their head on the ground instead of their feet, and lift their feet high instead of their head. Now, the things he brings forward concerning the disposition of the limbs of the body are treated sufficiently by physicians. Among these, you will observe this most of all: that the head is called not only the principal part, but even the *whole* in the body; for the rest were added only to serve the head. From this, you may gather that man was born for the sake of contemplation. There follows the discussion of the instruments of the senses. What is said in these matters concerning sight is explained sufficiently by Chalcidius <note>A 4th-century commentator on the *Timaeus*.</note>, and what concerns dreams is explained sufficiently by us elsewhere. You will soon consider the firm opinion of our Plato concerning causes: that bodily things and qualities—which are not moved by themselves, but rather by an incorporeal cause, and are directed toward an end—ought not truly to be called "causes," but instruments of a hidden providence. The primary cause is the will of providence, disposing all things according to its own model in the way it judges and decrees to be best. Therefore, Plato asserts that the **final cause** prescribed in providence is the highest of causes. Then he confirms again that man was born to contemplate celestial things—indeed, to imitate the very Mover of the heavens according to his strength. And just as he had spoken of sight, so also hearing was granted to us for the sake of contemplation and discipline: likewise so that through sensible harmony we might also harmoniously compose the movements of the soul. But the other senses besides sight and hearing, he thinks of as nothing, as they contribute less to speculation <note>In the sense of "looking" or "contemplating."</note>.

### HOW THE WORLD IS COMPOSED OF MIND AND NECESSITY. CHAPTER XXXIX.

After he has treated the formal order of the world—which he therefore calls "intellect" because it is a likeness of the divine intelligence—he now treats the matter of the world. This he names **Necessity** <note>original: "necessitatem"; matter is "necessary" because the forms need a medium to exist in, but it also provides a "necessary" resistance to the divine plan.</note>, because it was introduced not for its own sake, but as necessary for the ultimate forms. Also because the world, on account of its admixture, necessarily suffers something deformed. Hence that saying: *The world is composed of intellect and necessity*; that is, from the order of forms itself and from matter. We can also understand under the name of "necessity" not only matter, but also the soul of the world in the first stage of its procession, considered as if it were formless like matter. For both, as much the soul as matter, are indeed without forms in the first stage of their origin, but are easily formable through the gift of intelligence. Whence the "seeded reasons" <note>The *logoi spermatikoi*; the formative principles.</note> of natural forms are poured into the soul itself, and qualities and forms into matter. When he says that before the disposition of the world the elements existed in a certain way, understand certain powers of the elements: both formative in the soul and formable in matter. Likewise, when he says that matter was tossed without order before the world, explain it as the motive power of the soul being able to agitate matter even before the gifts of intelligence, but far from order. Furthermore, where he says that the world was adorned by God after "Necessity" had been persuaded, take it thus: that although that first nature of matter and soul is thought of as formless, nevertheless it received from the beginning such a "formable" preparation for forms from God that it could not have been more ready. Among these things, that distinction must be observed, by which it is said that at the beginning of the book the universe was divided into two—that is, Model and Image—but now it must be distinguished into three: that is, **Model**, **Image**, and **Matter**. Here...

But concerning this very liver, you will note a wondrous opinion of the Pythagoreans <note>The followers of Pythagoras, whose mystical and mathematical philosophy deeply influenced Plato and, subsequently, Ficino.</note>: namely, that this organ is so tempered by a certain solidity and an equally clear smoothness that, in the manner of a mirror, it very easily receives and reflects the images of things. Truly, just as the vehement imagination of a pregnant woman often expresses the marks of a desired thing upon the most tender fetus <note>Ficino refers to the historical theory of "maternal impression," the belief that a mother's intense thoughts or cravings could physically mark her unborn child.</note>; so a vehement notion of the mind, or an imagination of the senses, very easily shapes the mirror-like nature of the liver. 

In this very mirror, daimons <note>original: "demones"; in the Platonic tradition, these are intermediary spirits that convey messages between the divine realm and the human world, rather than "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and higher beings fashion images of future things, provided that when the soul is entirely peaceful, no other images are painted there from elsewhere. And so, the marks of future events infused into this mirror immediately reflect back into the mind and imagination; but there they are often so confused with other images that they are unable to portend the future. This happens, specifically, when either the mind, occupied with the duties of prudence <note>original: "prudentiae"; refers here to practical wisdom or the active management of earthly affairs and governance.</note>, is distracted by matters of governance, or the imagination is occupied with similar business. But where the prudent, continuous, and laborious discourse of reason and imagination is absent, often images of the future from...

<summary>Ficino explains the Pythagorean theory of the liver as a "mirror" of the soul, capable of receiving prophetic visions from spiritual intermediaries (daimons) when the mind is at rest.</summary>
<keywords>liver, divination, Pythagoreans, daimons, imagination, prophecy, Timaeus, physiology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the liver's role in divination and introduces the function of the spleen as a secondary organ that maintains the liver’s clarity, following Ficino’s analysis of the irrational soul's physiology.</meta>

474

...earthly affairs, or when the spirit is shaken by some passion of the soul. For this reason, divination through the liver, or through the entrails, requires a quiet mind. This is why such foresight flourishes especially during sleep, in the midst of illness, or when the soul is seized by a divine frenzy <note>original: "enthusiasmo"; in the Platonic sense, this is a state of being "filled with God," where the rational mind steps aside to allow for divine inspiration.</note>. 

Plato asserts that the Creator placed the power of divination in the liver so that even the most irrational part of our nature—the part driven by appetites—might somehow participate in truth. Because this lower soul cannot comprehend rational arguments, it is instead moved by images and "likenesses." The liver, being smooth and polished like a mirror, is the perfect vessel for these reflections. 

However, this mirror is not always clear. When the rational mind, employing the "bitterness" of the bile, sends harsh or threatening thoughts to the lower soul, the liver becomes wrinkled, dark, and contracted, causing physical pain and spiritual distress. Conversely, when the mind sends "sweet" thoughts, the liver becomes smooth, bright, and calm. In this state of tranquility, the liver provides the soul with peaceful dreams and prophetic visions.

### The Function of the Spleen

To the left of the liver lies the spleen <note>original: "splenem"</note>. Its nature is porous, hollow, and bloodless. Its primary duty is to act as a servant to the liver, much like a sponge or a napkin used to wipe a mirror. 

<margin>The spleen as a cleanser of the soul's mirror</margin>

The spleen draws away the impurities and dense vapors that arise from the stomach during the process of digestion. By absorbing these "dregs," it prevents them from clouding the liver's reflective surface. When the liver is thus cleansed and polished by the spleen's action, it remains capable of reflecting divine images clearly. If the spleen fails in this duty, the liver becomes obscured, and the individual may suffer from melancholy or be plagued by dark and confused visions.

<summary>Ficino explains how the liver acts as a physiological mirror for divine visions during sleep or illness and describes the spleen's role in "cleaning" the liver to ensure these visions remain clear.</summary>

<keywords>divination, liver, spleen, divine frenzy, enthusiasm, physiology of the soul, prophetic dreams, Marsilio Ficino, Timaeus</keywords>

**Timaeus, Or, On Nature.** **475**

[Left Column]
...many of the poets' songs were recited from memory, and the verses of Solon were sung by many of the children, who marveled at the novelty of the poetry. Then a certain member of the tribe—whether because he truly judged it so, or because he wished to flatter Critias—remarked that it seemed to him that Solon was not only the wisest in other matters but also the most noble of all poets in his songs. At these words, as I rightly remember, the old man was greatly delighted, and smiling, he said: "If only Solon, O Amynander, had followed poetry seriously and with dedicated effort like others, rather than merely for the sake of relaxing his mind—or if he had finished the history <note>This refers to the lost account of Atlantis which Solon allegedly began writing after his travels.</note> which he had undertaken after returning from Egypt, from which he was turned away by the seditions and other turmoils of the city, he would have been inferior, I believe, to neither Homer nor Hesiod, nor any other poet." To this, the other replied: "What subject, O Critias, did Solon intend to treat?" "Concerning the greatest deeds," he said, "once performed by this city, the memory of which has been extinguished among us by the length of time and the death of men." "Tell us, I pray," he said, "O Critias, what was that work, how did it happen, and from whom did Solon hear it as a true account?" 

He said: "There is a region of Egypt called the Delta, at the summit of which the streams of the Nile are divided. Its fields are called the Saite district. In these lands is a very great city called Sais, from which King Amasis came. The foundress of the city was a goddess whom the Egyptians call Neith <note>original: "Neithen"</note> and the Greeks call Athena. Furthermore, the people there are friends of the Athenians and claim to be joined to them by a certain kinship. Solon related that when he traveled there, he was received with great honor. And when he inquired about the memory of antiquity from those priests who were the most skilled in this matter, he said he discovered that neither he himself nor any other Greek possessed any real knowledge of antiquity. On one occasion, in the presence of the priests, in order to provoke them into telling their own stories, he began to speak of the most ancient events of Athens: of Phoroneus <note>In Greek myth, the first man or a culture-hero of Argos.</note> the first, and Niobe, and after the great flood of the world, of Pyrrha and Deucalion and their descendants, and of the times in which each of these events occurred. 

Then one of the priests, a man of great age, said: 'O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old man from Greece.' When Solon asked why he said this, the priest replied: 'Because your souls are always young; in them is no ancient opinion derived from the commemoration of antiquity, no gray-haired knowledge. This happens to you because there have been, and will be, many and varied destructions of men. The greatest of these must occur either by a conflagration of fire or by floods of water; the lesser ones by innumerable other calamities. For that story which is told among you—that Phaethon <note>original: "Phaëthontē"</note>, the son of the Sun, once ascended his father’s chariot but, failing to keep to his father’s path, burned the earth and was himself consumed by celestial flames—though it sounds like a fable, it is to be understood as true in a certain way. For at long intervals of time, a certain shifting of the celestial bodies occurs, which is necessarily followed by a vast inflammation. Then those who inhabit high and arid places perish in greater numbers than those near the sea and rivers. But to us, the Nile is a savior in many things, and it wards off this kind of destruction. On the other hand, when the gods cleanse the filth of the earth with a deluge of water, the shepherds and herdsmen who inhabit the mountain ridges escape that danger, but your cities situated in the plains are swept away to the sea by the force of the rivers. But in this our region...

<column-break/>

[Right Column]
...neither then, nor at any other time, does water descend upon the fields from above; on the contrary, it gushes upward from the bowels of the earth. For this reason, the monuments of the most ancient things are preserved among us. Therefore, wherever neither an excessive storm of rain nor a great fire occurs, men are always present, though sometimes fewer and sometimes more. Whatever has been done, either by our people or by yours or by other nations, that is worthy of memory—if only it has reached our ears—is found described and preserved in our temples. Among you and other nations, deeds are only recently being recorded in writing and monuments; but at certain cycles of time, a deluge sent from heaven devastates everything. Thus, those who survive are left bereft of both letters and the Muses. The result is that you become like children again, young and unrefined, utterly ignorant of all past things. For even those things which you were just now recounting from your histories, Solon, are little better than children's fables...
