### Thirty-Second Book.

[[page number: 476]]

[[margin: Concerning the ancient Athenian and Egyptian histories.]]

[The nature of the creator] was such that he was to bring forth men similar to himself. Thus, shaped by these laws, or even by more honorable institutions, the ancient Athenians excelled all others in every kind of virtue, as was fitting for those who were begotten and brought forth by gods. Indeed, many and wonderful deeds of your city are read in our records, but one exploit surpasses the rest in magnitude and virtue. For it is handed down that your city once resisted countless forces of enemies, which, having set out from the Atlantic Sea, had already besieged nearly all of Europe and Asia. For at that time that strait was navigable, having at its mouth and, as it were, its vestibule, an island which you call the Pillars of Hercules; and that island is said to have been larger than Libya and Asia together, through which an approach lay open to other nearby islands, and from those islands to the whole continent lying in sight, truly neighboring that sea. But within the mouth of the harbor itself, it is said to have been a very narrow bay. That sea was a true sea, and that land was truly a continent. In this island of Atlantis, there existed a great and marvelous power of kings, who ruled over that whole island, and many others, and a great part of the continent, and furthermore over these parts which are near us. Indeed, they ruled over the third part of the world which is called Libya, as far as Egypt, and Europe as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea. All their power, gathered into one, invaded our region, O Solon, and yours, and whatever was contained within the pillars of Hercules. Then the virtue of your city shone forth among all nations. Since it excelled all in magnanimity and the arts of war, partly together with other Greeks, and partly alone when the others deserted, it underwent extreme perils and conquered the enemies; it prevented those who had not yet come into their dominion and power from doing so, and others—namely us, as many as dwell on this side of the pillars of Hercules—it liberated and saved altogether. After this, by a huge earthquake and a continuous flood of one day and night, it happened that the earth gapped open and absorbed all those warlike men of yours together, and the island of Atlantis was merged beneath the vast whirlpool. For which reason that sea became unnavigable on account of the mud left by the absorbed island. This, O Socrates, is the sum of those things which the elder Critias related as received from Solon. But while you were discoursing yesterday concerning the republic and your citizens, a certain wonder from recollection came upon me, thinking namely that it happened by a certain divine chance that you handed down certain things very similar to the history of Solon, not without relevance. For that reason, I brought forward nothing then, since from long negligence I did not sufficiently remember it. Therefore, I myself judged it better that before I began to relate it to you, I should repeat it with myself. For this reason, I immediately consented to your command, because I was confident that, as is most fitting in matters of this kind, I would find something that would suit the present matter. So yesterday, as he says, immediately after our departure, I reviewed these things according as I then remembered them. Then, from nocturnal vigils, I recovered nearly everything. Indeed, what we learn in childhood, we are accustomed to remember longer and more firmly, as it is said. And I do not know whether I could now relate from memory all that I heard yesterday; but as for what I received as a boy, I would truly wonder if any of it should escape my memory. For I heard those things with pleasure and jest, since that old man taught me willingly, and I asked and inquired of him repeatedly. Wherefore, like certain indelibly branded marks of letters, all those things remained fixed in my memory. And I narrated these things even before the rising of the sun today, so that they might be more ready for this oration along with me. But to bring myself to that which all these things look toward, I am ready, O Socrates, to recount everything not only in summary, but in detail just as I heard it. We shall set down the city and the citizens whom you fashioned, as if through a fable in yesterday's disputation, as a true thing. Indeed, [we shall say] that city is this city of Athens. We shall also judge that the citizens whom you yourself were thinking of were those true ancestors of ours related by the priest. Surely these things will entirely agree, nor will it be out of place if we say that your citizens were truly those ancient ones. Wherefore, partitioning the matter among us in common, we shall all endeavor to satisfy the duty imposed on us by you according to our strength. But see, O Socrates, whether we should approve this discourse, or require another. **SOCRATES:** But indeed, O Critias, what discourse shall we approve more than this? Which, on the present sacred days of the goddess, wonderfully agrees on account of a certain proximity. But the greatest thing is that it is not a fable fashioned by us, but a true history being reviewed. In what way then, and from where, if this is rejected, shall we begin another disputation? Certainly it is not permitted. Therefore, with the good auspices of fortune, it is now necessary for you to discourse, as it is for me to hear you in silence today in return for yesterday's narration. **CRITIAS:** Consider, Socrates, whether we have conveniently arranged a mutual banquet for you. It seemed to us that Timaeus, as being the most skilled of us all in Astronomy, and especially versed in knowing the nature of things, should discourse first, so that, beginning from the generation of the world, he may descend to the nature of the human race. And I then, taking up the men generated by Timaeus, but instructed greatly by Critias, shall bring them into your judgment according to the discourse and law of Solon, and I shall make the citizens of that city of yours those who were the ancient Athenians, whom the sacred letters of the Egyptians have now brought out of darkness into light, so that henceforth words may be spoken of them as if of the ancient Athenians. **SOCRATES:** You seem to me to have prepared a copious and splendid table of disputation. It is your duty then, O Timaeus, having invoked the gods according to the law, to begin the disputation now. **TIMAEUS:** You advise well, Socrates. For since all who are in any way composed in mind are accustomed to invoke God in the beginning of any work, whether great or small, how much more just is it for us, who are about to dispute concerning the universe, whether it be generated or ungenerated (unless perhaps we are foolish), to invoke divine aid? Therefore, we pray to all the gods and goddesses, first indeed, that those things may be said by us which please them; and then that we may be consistent with ourselves. As far as pertains to the gods, let our prayer be so made. But as for what looks to us, it must be asked that you may easily follow, and that I, according to the purpose of my mind, may pierce the very matter of which we treat. In the beginning, it seems to me that it must be distinguished thus: what is that which always is, lacking generation; and what is that which is indeed born, but never truly is. The former can be perceived by the intellect through the investigation of reason, since it is always the same. The latter is reached by opinion through irrational sense, since it is born and perishes, and never truly exists. Moreover, whatever is born, is necessarily born from some cause. Truly, for anything to arise without a cause is impossible. Therefore, when the craftsman (*opifex*) in the construction of some work looks to that which always holds itself in the same way, and using an example of this kind brings forth the idea and power into the work, it is necessary then that every such work becomes beautiful; but when he looks to that which is made [a created model], it is least beautiful. This whole Universe, then—whether we call it Heaven, or World, or by whatever other name it rejoices—

[[page number: 477]]

### Timaeus, Or, Concerning Nature.

[[margin: Definition of the world.]]

let us name it. Concerning which, let us first consider that which must be investigated before all else in every question: whether it has always been without any beginning of generation, or whether it was generated, taking its beginning from some principle. Indeed, it is seen and touched, and it has a body. Moreover, all things of this kind move the senses. Those things which move the senses are perceived by opinion through sense. And it is certain that such things are of the kind that they are born and have been generated. Moreover, we have asserted that whatever is born is necessarily born from some cause. To find the Maker and Father of the world is difficult, and when you have found him, it is forbidden to proclaim him to the common crowd. Again, it must be considered which model the builder of the world imitated: whether that which is always the same and similar, or that which had been generated. And yet, if this world is beautiful, and the craftsman of the world is good, he surely preferred to imitate the eternal model. But if otherwise—which is not lawful even to say—he followed a generated model instead of the eternal one. Since, however, the world is the most beautiful of all generated things, and its author the best of all causes, there is no doubt that he followed an eternal model. Thus, being generated, it was fashioned after that which can be comprehended by reason and wisdom alone, and remains immutable. From which it follows that it is necessary for this world to be the image (*simulacrum*) of something. Moreover, to explain the reason of its origin naturally is most difficult. Therefore, let us distinguish thus between the image and the model. Surely, orations seem to have a certain kinship with those things which they express. Therefore, when one discourses about a firm and stable thing which is to be comprehended by the mind, the orations ought similarly to be stable, immutable, and as far as possible, unassailable. But when one disputes concerning the image of the firm and stable thing itself, likely reasons suffice, which hold themselves to the higher reasons just as the image holds itself to the model. For what essence is to generation, that truth is to faith [or conviction]. Since therefore, O Socrates, many things concerning the gods and the generation of the world have been said by many, do not wonder, I pray, if I cannot bring forward the most proven and exact reasons concerning them. For you ought to consider it sufficient if I bring forward reasons no less probable than anyone else. It is right to remember that both I who shall speak, and you who will judge, are men; so that if probable things are said, you should require nothing further. **SOCRATES:** You speak skillfully, O Timaeus. Wherefore we think it must be done as you command. We have wonderfully approved this beginning of your oration. But come, proceed with the disputation. **TIMAEUS:** Let us say, then, for what cause that author of things constituted generation and this universe. He was good. And the good is never touched by any envy concerning any matter. Therefore, since malice was most foreign to him, he willed all things to become as similar to himself as they could be. If anyone receives this as the chief cause of the generation of the world from prudent men, he will receive it most correctly. And so, since God willed that all things should be good, and nothing evil so far as nature allowed, he took up whatever was of the kind that could fall into the sense of sight—not tranquil and quiet, but recklessly agitated and fluctuating—and from that inordinate tossing he reduced it into order. For he judged this to be more excellent. Moreover, it was not, nor is it, lawful for him who is best to do anything except the most beautiful. When therefore he had deliberated, he found that of those things which according to nature are subject to sight, if it lacks intelligence, it would never be more beautiful as a whole than that which is intelligent, and that intellect cannot be given to anything without a soul. By this reasoning, he gave mind to the soul, and the soul to the body, and so constituted the whole world, so that it might be the most beautiful and best work of nature. Wherefore, as this probable reasoning persuades us, it must be said that this world is a living being (*animal*), and an intelligent one, truly constituted by divine providence. This being placed, let us see what follows: according to the likeness of which living being did God constitute the world? Let us not think he made it similar to any one specific species of animals. For if it were made similar to an imperfect animal, it would certainly not be beautiful. Rather, let us say that it is most similar to that animal of which the other animals, both individually and generically, are parts. For that [intelligible] animal embraces in itself all living things which are perceived by the mind alone, just as this world contains us and the other animals which are seen. Wishing, therefore, to make this world most similar to the most beautiful and everywhere absolute of all things that can be understood, God made it one single living thing, subject to sight, containing within its own limit the animals that are by their nature convenient to it. Furthermore, did we rightly say the world is one? Or would it have been more right to say there are many and innumerable? One surely, if indeed it was formed after the likeness of the One. For that which contains all living things whatsoever that are understood cannot have a second companion. Otherwise, there would have to be another animal which contained these two, of which these two would be parts, and this world would more rightly be called the image not of those, but of this third one. Therefore, so that this world might be most similar to the absolute animal, in that it was alone and one, for that reason neither two nor innumerable worlds were procreated, but one only-begotten world was made and shall be. Since, however, it was going to be corporeal, visible, and tangible, and nothing can be seen without fire, and nothing touched without something solid, and nothing is solid without earth, therefore in the beginning of this work God first created fire and earth. But two things alone cannot conveniently cohere without a third, and they require some middle bond of both. Moreover, that bond is most apt and beautiful which makes itself and those things which it binds together as much as possible into one. This, proportion and the ratio of alternate comparison especially achieve. For when in three numbers or masses or powers, the middle is so related to the last as the first is to the middle, and conversely, as the last is to the middle, so the middle agrees with the first, then that which is middle becomes both first and last, and the last and first also become middle. Thus necessity compels that all things which have been so bound together shall be the same among themselves. And since they have been made the same, it follows that all are one. But if the body of the universe ought to have had latitude but no depth, one middle term interjected would have sufficed to bind itself and the extremes. But since the world required solidity, and solid things are always coupled not by one, but by two means, God placed air and water between fire and earth, and so compared them among themselves that they might be as congruent as possible. From which conjunction the world was so constituted that it can be seen and touched. Therefore, from things of this kind, four in number, the body of the world was fused together, connected by that comparison which I have said. From which it embraces itself in a concordant friendship, and so aptly coheres that it cannot be dissolved in any way, except by the same one by whom it was bound together.

[[page number: 478]]

### Thirty-Second Book.

[[margin: The world consists of the whole of matter.]]

The world therefore received each of those four things in its entirety. For from all fire, air, water, and earth, its craftsman so composed it that he left no part or power of any of them outside. And he did this for this reason: first, indeed, that this whole living being might be as perfect as possible from perfect parts. Then, that it might be one, since nothing was left outside from which another might be generated. Finally, lest any disease or old age should touch it. For he saw that such was the nature of a body, that it is harmed by the importunate accession of heat or cold and other things too vehement, and being driven into diseases and old age, it fails. For which cause and reason, God constituted the world as one whole, perfect from all things whole and perfect, free from disease and old age. To which he gave a figure most congruent and decorous. For this living being, which was to contain within its circuit all animals, especially required that figure in which all figures are contained. Wherefore he made it spherical, in which every extremity is reached by equal rays from the middle; and he so turned it that nothing can be made more round, and all parts were most similar to all. For he thought that the similar was much more beautiful than the dissimilar. Furthermore, he polished this globe everywhere smooth on the outside. Nor did it undeservedly lack eyes, since nothing was left outside that could be seen. Nor ears, since nothing remained outside that it might hear. Nor were the external parts of the world surrounded by air, so that they required respiration. Nor indeed was there need of such members through which it might receive new nourishment, or emit the excrements of digested food: no decrease could occur, no increase. For there was neither where nor whence such things might happen. For it nourishes itself by the consumption and age of itself. Indeed, the world was fabricated by divine art so that it might suffer and act all things in itself and by itself. For that author judged that the world, if it were self-sufficient, would be more excellent than if it required the assistance of others. Nor did he deem hands necessary to it, because nothing was to be taken, nor anything to be repelled. Nor was there need of feet or other members for progress or standing. For he attributed to it a movement congruent to its body, which of the seven movements is the one that especially pertains to the mind and intelligence. And therefore, when he had led it around through the same things, and in the same thing, and in itself, he caused it to be moved in a circular conversion. But the six remaining movements he separated from it, and entirely freed it from their error and wandering. For this conversion then, which did not need feet, he did not give legs and feet. Since therefore that God who always is thought concerning a God who was to be at some time, he made him smooth and equal, and from the middle to the top everywhere equal, and a body whole and perfect from bodies whole and perfect. But he placed the Soul in its middle, and stretched it through the whole, and even covered the body itself with it from the outside, and [made] this world one and alone and solitary; and he established it to revolve in a circle, which on account of virtue can easily restrain itself with itself, needing no other, and being sufficiently known and a friend to itself. Therefore, for all these causes, its craftsman made the world a blessed God; but the soul not in such a way as we have just begun to say—that he procreated it only then when he had made the body for it. For he who joined these would not have permitted the older to obey the younger. But we, as being partakers of chance, speak many things inconsiderately and recklessly. He, however, constituted the soul prior and older than the body both in generation and virtue, as that which was to rule over the obedient body, namely from these things, and in this way. From that substance

[[margin: Old age and disease from external causes; from which see that the world is eternal from a lack of cause [of decay], not from matter.]]
[[margin: Seven species of local motion.]]
[[margin: The parts of the substance of the soul.]]

[[Diagrams: A Lambda diagram showing the harmonic intervals (1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27); a triangular numeric grid; and a circular celestial diagram showing the zodiac and elements.]]

which is individual [indivisible] and always the same and similar, and from that again which is divisible around bodies, he mixed a third middle species of substance, which again would be partaker of the nature of the same and the nature of the other, and he constituted it as a middle through these between the individual substance and those things which are divided around the body. When he had taken these three, he tempered them all into one species. Where he reconciled by a certain force the nature of that which we call the "Other" and "Diverse," which was repugnant to mixing, with that which is called the "Same." Moreover, after he mixed those two with substance, and made one from the three, he again partitioned that whole into those members which were fitting, each of which consisted of the three—the same, the other, and substance. Moreover, that partition was such: In the beginning he took one portion from the universe. The second moreover double the first part. Then the third, which was one-and-a-half times the second, and triple the first. After that the fourth, double the second. Then the fifth, triple the third. The sixth, eight times the first. Finally the seventh, which exceeded the first by twenty-six parts. After these he filled the double and triple intervals, cutting away parts from the whole again, which he so placed in the intervals that there were two means in each, or as I might say, medietates: one of which exceeds one of the extremes by the same part as it is exceeded by the other. The other medietate exceeds one extreme by an equal number, and is exceeded by an equal number by the other. Moreover, when he had taken sesquialteral [3:2], sesquitertial [4:3], and sesquioctave [9:8] intervals, from these bonds in the first spaces, he filled all the sesquiquartial things with a sesquioctave interval, a small part of each being left. Moreover, the interval of this particle being left, there was held from it that comparison of number to number in terms, which is between two hundred fifty-six and two hundred forty-three. Now truly that mixture from which he was discerning those things was entirely consumed by the section of such parts. Then he cut this whole series lengthwise, and from one he made two, and adapted the middle of the middle into the species of the Greek letter X [Chi]. Then he bent them into a circle, until the heads met each other in such a way that the lines themselves were joined both with themselves and with each other from the region of their intersection: and he surrounded them everywhere with that motion which is always revolved in the same thing and similarly: and he made one of the circles exterior, the other interior. The exterior motion indeed he named of the nature of the "Same," but the interior of the "Other." And that which was of the nature of the "Same"...

<margin>The world consists of the whole of matter.</margin>
Therefore, the world received each of those four elements in its entirety. Indeed, from all fire, air, water, and earth, its Craftsman <term>Faber: The divine artisan or Demiurge</term> composed it in such a way that he left no part or power of any of them outside. He did this for several reasons: first, so that this entire living creature might be as perfect as possible, made from perfect parts. Second, so that it might be unique, since nothing would be left outside from which another world could be generated. Finally, so that no disease or old age could touch it. For he saw that it is the nature of a body to be harmed by the untimely approach of heat or cold and other such powerful forces, <margin>Old age and disease come from external causes: from which see that the world is eternal from the absence of an external cause, not from its matter.</margin> and to fail when driven into disease and old age. For this cause and reason, God constituted the world as one whole, made of all wholes, perfect, and free from disease and old age. To this world he gave a shape that was most suitable and becoming. Indeed, for this living creature, which was to contain all other living creatures within its scope, he required that specific shape in which all other shapes are contained. Therefore, he made it spherical, in which every extremity is reached by equal rays from the middle. He turned it on a lathe so that nothing could be made more round, and all its parts were most similar to one another. For he thought that what is similar is much more beautiful than what is dissimilar. Furthermore, he polished this globe smoothly on the outside everywhere. And not without reason. For it had no need for eyes, since nothing was left outside that could be seen. Nor did it need ears, since there was nothing remaining outside to be heard. Nor was the exterior of the world surrounded by air so as to require respiration. Nor did it have need of such members through which it might receive new nourishment or discharge the waste of digested food; no loss could occur, and no addition was possible. For there was nothing from which or to which such things could happen. For it nourishes itself by its own consumption and aging. Indeed, the world was fabricated by divine art in such a way that it experiences and does all things within itself and by itself. For that Author judged that the world would be more excellent if it were self-sufficient than if it required the assistance of others. Nor did he think hands were necessary to it, because there was nothing to be grasped nor anything to be repelled. Nor was there any need for feet or other <margin>Seven species of local motion.</margin> limbs for movement or standing. For he granted it a motion suitable to its body, which, out of the seven motions, is the one that most pertains to the mind and intelligence. Therefore, when he had led it around through the same path, and in the same way, and within itself, he caused it to move in a circular rotation. However, he separated the other six motions from it, and freed it entirely from their wandering and straying. For this rotation, which did not require feet, he gave it neither legs nor feet. Therefore, when that God who always is was thinking about the God who was to be, he made it smooth and equal, and everywhere equidistant from the center to the surface, a whole and perfect body made of whole and perfect bodies. Moreover, he placed the Soul in its center, and stretched it through the whole, and even covered the body itself on the outside with it; and he established this world to be one, alone, solitary, and revolving in a circle, which by its own virtue could easily sustain itself, needing no other, being sufficiently known and a friend to itself. Therefore, for all these reasons, its Creator made the world a blessed god. But he did not create the soul in the way we have just begun to describe—that is, only after he had made the body for it. For he who joined these would not have permitted the older to obey the younger. But we, as participants in chance, often speak inconsiderately and rashly. He, however, <margin>Parts of the substance of the soul.</margin> established the soul as prior to and older than the body, both in generation and in virtue, as that which was to rule over the obedient body, from these elements and in this manner. From that substance

which is indivisible and always the same and similar, and from that again which becomes divisible around bodies, he mixed a third type of substance in the middle, which would participate in the nature of the "Same" and the nature of the "Other," and he established it as a mean between the indivisible substance and that which is divided around the body. Next, he filled the double and triple intervals, cutting off parts again from the whole. The other mediation exceeds one extreme by the same number as it is exceeded by the other. <note>These refer to the geometric and arithmetic means used to create a musical/mathematical scale for the universe.</note> When he had taken the intervals of one-and-a-half <note>3:2 ratio</note>, one-and-a-third <note>4:3 ratio</note>, and one-and-an-eighth <note>9:8 ratio</note>, he filled all the one-and-a-third intervals with the one-and-an-eighth intervals, leaving a small portion of each. The interval of this remaining portion had the numerical ratio of 256 to 243. <note>This is the "Pythagorean limma," a small musical interval similar to a half-step.</note> By now, the whole mixture from which he was cutting these parts was exhausted. Then he cut this whole composition along its length and made two strips from the one, and he joined them at their centers in the shape of the Greek letter Chi (X). He then encompassed them with that motion which revolves always in the same way and in the same place. He made one of the circles the outer and the other the inner. The outer motion he named the nature of the "Same," and the inner he named the nature of the "Other." And that which belonged to the nature of the "Same"...

On the contrary, he who lived badly would be compelled at his second birth to change his sex and become a woman. And he who even then does not make an end to sinning, insofar as he is depraved, would be transformed into a nature of brutes similar to his own character: nor would he cease from changes and labors until, following that revolution of the nature of the Same and similar implanted in him, and subjecting the turbulent and manifold affections later contracted from fire, water, air, and earth to reason, he should return to the first and best state of his habit. When he had designated these things to them, so that no cause of future wickedness should rest with him, he scattered some into the earth, some into the moon, and others into other established markers for the signification of periods of time, as if he were sowing them. After this kind of sowing, he mandated that what remained was to be done by the <term>younger gods</term><note>The celestial deities created by the Demiurge</note>, so that they might fashion mortal bodies, and whatever remained of the human soul that ought to be added to this, they should join and rule all that followed, and govern the nature of the mortal living being as well and as beautifully as possible, unless it should be the cause of evils to itself. And he, indeed, who disposed all these things, remained properly in his own state. While he remained so, his children, having recognized the order of their parent, immediately followed it. Thus, having received from him the immortal principle of a mortal living thing, imitating their own maker, they borrowed from the world particles of fire, air, water, and earth, which they were to return later: and they coupled them together, not with those same indissoluble bonds by which they themselves had been bound, but with such as could not be seen because of their smallness: and by joining many such "nails" together, they made one body out of all, and into this very body, which was now flowing in and now flowing out, they bound the circuits of the divine soul. Therefore, these circuits, immersed in a deep river, neither held nor were held, but were carried by force and did carry. From which it happened that the whole animal moved, yet without order, and by a certain fortuitous tossing. It happened to wander in six motions everywhere through the six differences of place by proceeding: namely, forward and backward, to the right and left, upward and downward. But while a great flood surged in and flowed out from where the animal was nourished, an even greater turmoil followed from passions brought in from the outside, whenever a body encountered the assault of external fire, or was harmed by the solidity of earth, or the moisture of water, or the blast of air. Furthermore, from all these, motions pass through the body to the soul, which for that reason were called "senses" both from the beginning and now. These indeed from the beginning continuously stir many and great motions, in that manner of constant flowing, and they violently shake the circuits of the soul with these floods. And they utterly impede that circuit of the nature of the Same and similar in its very course: but they distract the circuit of the Other, to such an extent that those three double and triple intervals arranged on both sides, and the medians and connections interposed in the ratios of 4/3, 3/2, and 9/8—which can be dissolved by no one except him who joined them—they twist with every kind of revolution, and they induce as many turnings and varieties of circles as can possibly occur: so that the circuits themselves, scarcely connected to one another, are indeed carried along, but they are carried without reason, sometimes in reverse, sometimes obliquely, sometimes in a certain upside-down disposition. Just as if someone should fix their head to the ground instead of their feet, and lift their feet high instead of their head. Then I think both for him who is so affected, and for those who look on, the right parts seem to be left, and conversely the left parts seem to be right. Therefore, when the circuits of the soul also suffer this very thing or other things of this kind, if they then encounter something external of the genus of the Same or the Other, they judge falsely what is "the same" for someone or what is "other." And for that reason, they are then liars and senseless, nor is there then any prince or leader circuit among them. And when senses from the outside strike the soul more violently and possess it entirely, then those circuits, though subjugated and serving, seem to dominate. For these reasons, from the beginning, when the soul is enclosed in the bonds of a mortal body, it is made senseless. But after the river of nourishment and growth flows more gently and less abundantly, and the circuits of the soul perform their journey with a more tranquil motion, and in the process of time a settling occurs, and they are restored to the shape suitable to their nature: then the direct revolutions of the individual circles properly discern the nature of the Same and the Other, and they make the person so established prudent. But if someone adds to right education and nourishment a convenient discipline and erudition, having avoided a most grave disease, he will emerge entirely healthy and whole: but if he neglects it, having entered the limping path of life, he falls back to the underworld as if maimed and altogether useless. But these things indeed happen after birth. Now, however, we must discuss more exactly the first composition of man, and show by a probable reason for what cause and providence of the gods the individual members of the body were accommodated to the individual offices of the soul. In the beginning, the gods fashioned the shape of the head after the roundness of the world, and in it they placed those two divine circuits of the soul. Moreover, the head is the most divine member of the body, and the prince of the other members: to which the gods commanded the whole connected body to be subject and to obey. For they devised that it would be capable of all motions, however many they might be. <margin>Why the elders are prudent.</margin> <margin>The head is the most divine member.</margin> <margin>Tallness.</margin> <margin>Many things about the eyes.</margin> <margin>Cicero's interpretation of these things does not exist.</margin> Since, however, the earth is unequal and rough, and partly ascending and partly descending, if the head were to crawl on the ground and be rolled along the surface of the earth, it could not pass through these turnings without injury. They annexed to the body four long and flexible members, by which divine providence might easily be moved, namely to grasp whatever objects it might, to stand, and to stay, and through all these things the head might travel, staying above as the habitation of the most divine and most sacred part. Furthermore, it was necessary for the anterior parts to be distinct and dissimilar. Therefore, they first added a face to the globe of the head, and they assigned to the face instruments which would assist all the providence of the soul, and they decreed that the natural command of man should consist in this anterior and prior part. Therefore, this whole, having obtained the same quality due to its similarity, whenever it touches anything else or is itself touched by another, diffuses this motion through the entire body until it reaches the soul, producing that sensation which is called sight. But after the related fire has departed into the night, the ray of vision vanishes. For this reason, it ceases to see and induces sleep. Indeed, the gods engineered the healthy covering of the eyelids; when these are drawn shut, that internal consistency of fire is restrained by the covering, and being compressed, it spreads through and soothes the internal motions, and when these are relaxed and softened, rest creeps in. If a deep slumber occupies us because of the great stillness of these motions, few dreams follow. But if some more violent motions are left behind as remnants of our waking state, depending on what kind they are and from what places these remnants are drawn, such images of dreams are born, and their memory remains with us even after we have woken up. 

<margin>You will find the interpretation of these passages from Cicero all the way through.</margin> 

But truly, the understanding of images that arise either in mirrors or are seen in a clear and smooth surface is easy to grasp. For from the communion of both fires—the internal and the external—and from their meeting and congruence, which is adapted everywhere to a polished and smooth body, all these things necessarily arise, when the fire of the eyes has blended itself with that fire which has flowed from the object in view upon the smooth and shining body. Indeed, things which are on the left appear on the right, because we touch the opposite parts of the eyes with the opposite parts of the object in an unusual manner. However, right corresponds to right and left to left when the light, mixed with that which it is blended, leaps across. This occurs when the smoothness of the mirrors takes on depth on both sides, and thus twists the right part of the eyes into the special left, and the left into the right. But if the mirror is turned to the length of the face, it renders the face upside down, as the upper part of the light is turned to the lower, and the lower to the upper. 

<margin>Why eyes were given to men.</margin>

And all these things are of that class of things which serve as supporting causes <note>secondary or material causes</note>, which God uses as ministers to perfect the idea of the "Best" as far as is possible. But most people think these are not the helpers of the principal causes, but that these are themselves the causes of all things—having the nature of cold and heat, of rare and dense, and other similar things—yet they possess no reason or mind. For it is fitting that Mind is possessed by nothing else except the soul; and this soul escapes the sight of the eyes. But fire, water, air, and earth are bodies and are seen. It is necessary for a lover of mind and knowledge to seek the primary causes of a wise nature; and to consider as secondary causes those which are necessarily moved by others, but which in turn move other things. 

Wherefore, we must act in such a way that we distinguish between both types of causes: separately concerning those which, with intelligence, are the creators of beautiful and good things; and again concerning those which, lacking wisdom <note>original: "prudētia" (prudence/practical wisdom)</note>, produce anything at random and without order. And regarding the secondary causes of the eyes contributing to that power which they possess, I think enough has been said. 

But the greatest work for the sake of which the eyes were usefully given to us by God must next be explained. For the knowledge of the best things, I believe, has been brought to us by our eyes. For these discussions about the universe would never have been discovered if neither the stars, nor the sun, nor the heavens could have been looked upon. Indeed, the knowledge of day and night, arising from the eyes, has made it possible for us to measure the circuits of months and years by a kind of counting, to know time, and to scrutinize the order of the whole of nature. From these things, we have attained philosophy. No greater good than this has ever been given to the mortal race as a gift of the gods, nor will it ever be given. This, therefore, I say is the greatest benefit of the eyes. 

<margin>On voice and hearing.</margin>

I pass over other lesser benefits. If those who are strangers to philosophy should complain about being deprived of these, they would complain in vain. But we must assert that for this reason above all God fathered the eyes: so that, having observed the circuits of the Mind that are performed in heaven, we might apply them to the use of our own mind; and that we might recall the wanderings of our own thought—which are related to those heavenly circuits, but are in some way disturbed—to the stability of those others. And once we have recognized them, and having been endowed with right reason according to nature, and perceived the order of each, we should imitate the revolutions of God which are performed without any error, and according to their example, compose the wandering and erratic movements of our own thought. 

I believe the gods gave us voice and hearing for the sake of the same thing. For speech pertains to these very things and contributes greatly, and every use of the musical voice is granted for the sake of harmony. And yet harmony, which has motions related and akin to the wanderings of our soul, is useful to a person using the Muses wisely—not for a pleasure devoid of reason, as it now seems—but was given by the Muses so that through it we might compose the discordant circuit of the soul and lead it back to a concert agreeable to itself. Rhythm also seems to have been granted for this: so that we may most aptly temper a habit in us that is immoderate and lacking in grace. 

<margin>The generation of the world.</margin>

Thus far, with few exceptions, we have treated the works of the Mind. But it is necessary to speak also of those things which Necessity introduces. For the generation of this world is mixed, resulting from the union of Necessity and Mind. For when Mind dominated Necessity—because by persuading it, Mind led it to the best outcomes for most things—and Necessity, yielding in this way, obeyed the wise persuasion, the beginnings of this world were established. Therefore, he who would truly narrate the constitution of the world must also mix in the species of the "erratic cause" <note>This refers to 'Ananke' or Necessity, the material constraints that reason must work with</note> according to the instinct of nature itself. This will be done most conveniently if, having taken a suitable principle for these very things, we discourse about them just as we did about the higher things, starting again from their very origin. 

Let us therefore consider the nature and the affections of fire, water, air, and earth, which preceded the generation of the heavens. No one indeed up to this time has shown their generation, but as if it were known what fire and the rest are, we speak about them and establish them as the "elements" of the world, though they ought not to hold the place even of syllables, much less of elements, among men who are in any way composed of mind. But we think that at present, nothing should be said about the beginning of all things, or the principles, or whatever else it may be called. Indeed, nothing else hinders this discussion except that it is difficult to express what seems true about these things in our current mode of disputing. Therefore, you shall not expect it, nor will I persuade myself that I can rightly undertake such a great work. But what I said from the beginning: we shall preserve the force of probability, and we will strive in assigning probable reasons concerning these things to yield to no one. And so we shall explain both the individual parts and the whole from the beginning. Therefore, even now, we call upon God as the preserver of our discussion...

For two were sufficient in the previous parts. One, indeed, in the place of the <term>Model</term><note>The eternal Forms or Ideas</note>, always the same, to be comprehended by intelligence alone. The other a <term>likeness</term><note>The physical world</note> derived from this model, subject to generation and the eyes. While we thought these two were sufficient, we did not add a third. But now reason seems to compel us to try to declare a difficult and obscure species. What power, then, or what nature should it be thought to have? This one above all: to be the receptacle and, as it were, the nurse of all generation. Although this is said truly, it must be stated a little more clearly. This is indeed arduous, especially because for the demonstration of this thing, it is necessary first to doubt and inquire concerning fire and the rest which are called elements—which of these ought rather to be called water than fire, or air rather than earth, or to call something one certain thing rather than all of them. It is certainly difficult to assert something certain and firm about them. In what way, then, and by what reason, and what probable thing shall we say in an inquiry of this kind? 

In the first place, that body which we just now named "water," when it congeals into a solid matter, seems to become stone and earth; but when it melts and flows away, it becomes spirit and air. Likewise, scorched air becomes fire. Extinguished and more corpulent fire creates air. Again, air made thicker congeals into mists and clouds. When these are even more compressed, rains flow down. From water, again, earth and stones are born. And thus we see all these things, in a certain circuit, giving to one another in turn the powers and nourishments of generation. Since these things never appear to remain the same, who can, without the blush and suspicion of being refuted, call one of these something certain and firm rather than another? Surely no one. Therefore, the safest mode of speaking in these matters will be this: that which always appears formed differently at different times, and mostly according to the image of fire, is not "this" fire, but is "of such a quality," that is, something fiery; nor is water "this," but something "of such a quality," that is, watery; nor is anything else as if it had any stability. Finally, these things should not even be designated by pronouns, which we are accustomed to use in the demonstration of any thing when we say "this" or "that": for they flee, and do not wait for that demonstration which designates "this" and "of this" and "to this," nor for the naming which would regard them as existing and stable. Therefore, all such things we ought to call neither "this" nor "that," but rather "of such a quality," or "such" because of some similarity. And we should call fire everywhere "such," and likewise for the others that are generated. 

But that in which each of these is seen to become, and then to dissolve, I think should be called alone by those pronouns by which we signify "this" or "that." But that which is "of such a quality" in a certain way—namely hot or white, or any such of the opposites, or from opposites—that should by no means be called by those names. But let us explain what we mean more clearly. For if someone were to continuously reshape all figures made from one and the same material of gold into others and still others, and if someone present were to ask of one of those what it is, we could most truly and safely answer that it is gold; but as for the triangle or any other figure of those which are impressed upon it and are continuously changed, it is not permitted to speak as if they truly exist. Indeed, we ought to be content with that one response as being the safest. The same reason applies to that nature which receives all bodies: it must always be said to be the same. 

<margin>Matter never departs from its potentiality.</margin>
<margin>The things that happen in matter are likenesses of true things.</margin>
For it never departs from its own power. It always receives all things, and never in any way contracts any form similar to them for itself. Surely every nature is subject to the fashioning, and being moved by the things entering it and figured in some way, it appears to be different at different times. But the things that enter and exit are likenesses of the true and always existing things, figured in a wondrous and scarcely explicable way from the things themselves that truly exist, as we shall narrate next. Three kinds are to be taken at present: One which is generated; another in which it is generated; another from which that which is born draws its similarity. 

<margin>See how matter is formless.</margin>
<margin>That fire and others are not truly "this"; they can only be shown by names.</margin>
Therefore, it is fitting to compare these thus: That which receives, to a mother; that from which it receives, to a father; and the nature between these, to the offspring. But it must be understood thus: since it ought to be the effigy of things distinct with every variety of forms, that very bosom of this formation will never be well prepared unless it is formless and by its own nature lacks all the forms which it is about to receive. For if it were similar to any of those things which it receives into itself, when it received a nature contrary to that to which it is similar, or something else entirely, it would by no means express its similarity and effigy, since it would display its own. Whereby it happens that it has no species proper to itself, since it is about to receive all kinds. 

<margin>See how matter is shown by analogy.</margin>
<margin>He proves briefly that the Ideas exist.</margin>
Just as those who are about to compose sweet-smelling ointments prepare the liquid matter—which they wish to season with a certain scent—so that it has no scent of its own; and those who wish to impress some figures into soft materials that yield to impression allow no prior figure at all to appear in them, but polish them with a certain most exact smoothing: so that which is to be rightly figured in all the likenesses of all eternal things everywhere must by its own nature lack all these forms. For which reason, let us say that the mother and receptacle of the universe—which is both generated and manifest to all senses—is neither earth, nor air, nor fire, nor water, nor again anything constituted from these, nor any things from which these themselves properly subsist; but rather let us call it a certain invisible species and formless, capable of all things, which in a certain ambiguous and scarcely explicable way participates in the divine and intelligible nature. It cannot be comprehended by itself in any way; but as far as its nature can be reached from what has been said above, we can rightly say this: the part of it that is ignited appears as fire; the moistened part as water; and earth and air similarly, insofar as it receives their likenesses. 

But distinguishing about these things, we ought to consider by reason whether there is some fire by itself, remaining itself in itself apart from matter, and the other things which we often say remain by themselves; or are these only the things which we perceive by the sense of the body, and contain such truth in themselves, and there are none besides these anywhere at all, and we vainly posit some intelligible species for each thing, these being nothing but words? This must not be asserted rashly and without examination, nor should another long discussion be added to the present one, which is lengthy by nature. But that circumscription which encompasses great things in brief will seem very opportune. Thus, then, I shall give my own opinion on this matter.

<summary>Plato introduces the concept of "Prime Matter" or the "Receptacle," describing it as a formless "nurse" or "mother" that receives all physical forms without having any of its own, while explaining that physical elements are in constant flux and cannot be called "this" or "that."</summary>

484 Book Thirty-Two.

...if Intellect and True Opinion are two distinct kinds, it is necessary that there be species of this sort that exist by themselves and are comprehended by intelligence rather than by the senses. But if, as it seems to some, true opinion differs in no way from intellect, then all things which the sense of the body touches must be held as certain. But I think they must be called two, because they were made separately and are dissimilar. For doctrine instills one in us, and persuasion the other; the former is always with true reason, the latter without reason; the former is unchangeable by any persuasion, the latter is subject to this change. Every man is a participant in true opinion; but of intelligence, all the gods indeed, but very few men are participants. 

Since these things are so, it must be confessed that there is a species which is always the same, without beginning or end, which neither receives anything else from elsewhere into itself, nor itself proceeds into anything else, and is perceived by no sense of the body—and this is what pertains to intelligence alone and is proper to its intent. But there is something after this which agrees with it not in reason but in name, and bears its likeness, generated and manifest to the senses, which is always carried and supported by something else, and is born in some place, and again departs from there, to be comprehended by opinion through the senses. 

<margin>Few men are participants in intelligence.</margin>
<margin>That matter is Space (Place).</margin>
The third kind is <term>Space</term><note>Plato’s "Chora"</note>, which never perishes, but provides a seat for all things that are generated. This is touched without the sense of touch, by a certain bastard reason, scarcely believable. Finally, when we look back at this with the mind, we dream in a certain way and think it necessary that whatever exists must be placed in some location and occupy some region; and that what is neither on earth nor in heaven simply does not exist. And because of this "dreaming," we are unable to distinguish all these and similar states from the vigilant and truly existing nature. Therefore, we cannot even discern that for an image—since the very thing in which it is made does not belong to it, but it is always carried as the likeness of another—it appropriately fits that it should be in something else, and so in a way participate in essence, otherwise it could not exist at all. But for that which truly exists, this true and exquisite reason supports it, teaching that as long as things are such that one is one thing and the other another, neither will ever be made one in the other so as to be simultaneously one and two. 

This, finally, is the summary of my mind's opinion: that there exist, and were three things even before the origin of heaven in a triple ratio: Existence, Space, and Generation. As for the nurse of generation, being ignited and moistened, and receiving the forms of earth and air, and suffering the accompanying passions of these, she appears to be of every form in her affection. But because she is filled with powers that are neither similar nor equalized in weight, she is in no part in equilibrium, but swaying unequally in every direction and declining, she is agitated by those things we have mentioned, and in turn, she herself, being moved, agitates them. 

By this pulse, they are driven and separated in different directions, just as we see those things which are tossed and shaken by the tools of the grain-cleaner in the purging of wheat are separated, and the solid and heavy things are carried one way, the rare and light another. Thus those four kinds then, being moved by their very receptacle—which was tumultuous and discerning like that grain-cleaning instrument—dissimilar things were separated far from dissimilar things, and similar things again came together. And for this reason, even before the adornment of the world, they were divided in their seats, but there was neither reason nor measure in them. 

But when it pleased God that all things should be brought together, he first adorned with distinct figures, species, and numbers the fire, earth, air, and water, which indeed bore some traces of elements, but were in such a state as is proper for those from which God is absent. Let that opinion always be held as fixed and indubitable among us above all others: that God, when they were not such, ordered them as beautifully and excellently as they could possibly be made. 

<margin>Dispositions and generations of the elements.</margin>
Now it is appropriate to demonstrate their disposition and generation individually, by a new and unusual kind of demonstration, but one plain and clear to you who have traversed all the paths of noble learning. In the first place, that fire, earth, water, and air are bodies, no one will doubt. But every species of body has depth. And it is necessary to connect depth with planes. Furthermore, the straightness of a plane base is constituted from triangles, and all triangles have their beginning from two, both having one right angle and two acute angles. One of these occupies a part of the right angle on both sides, being distinguished by equal sides; but in the other, unequal things are distributed to unequal sides. Therefore, proceeding through probable reasons joined to necessity, let us posit the beginning of fire and the other bodies of this kind. But the higher principles of these are known to God, and to him who is a friend of God. 

Let us see, then, by what most powerful reason four most beautiful bodies may be made, dissimilar indeed among themselves, but such as are dissolved into one another and generated from one another. If we comprehend this, we will hold the truth itself about the generation of earth and water, and those things which are made in between them while preserving the competent ratio. For then we will yield to no one saying that there are anywhere bodies more beautiful than these, manifest to the eyes, of which each is made according to one kind. We must therefore attempt to constitute the four kinds of bodies excelling in beauty, and thus assert that we have sufficiently comprehended their nature. 

Of the two triangles, the <term>Isosceles</term><note>A triangle with two equal sides</note>, that is, the one consisting of equal sides, has a single nature; but the one that is longer in another part has infinite natures. Therefore, if we wish to begin rightly, we must pre-select the most beautiful from the infinite ones. And if anyone wishes to assert that a more beautiful one has been chosen by him for the constitution of these, his opinion should be preferred, not as an adversary's but as a friend's. We therefore, setting aside the rest, posit one most beautiful among the many triangles, from which an equilateral triangle is constituted from a third. The reason why this is so would be too lengthy. But for him who finds it to be so by diligent discussion, a sweet prize of victory awaits. 

Let there be proposed to us two triangles out of many, from which fire and the other bodies are composed. One of these is the Isosceles triangle consisting of equal sides. The other is that which always has its longer side three times greater in power than its shorter side. But what we followed and said too much of in the previous parts must now be more distinguished. It seemed to us, and not quite rightly, that all four kinds were generated from each other. In truth, the four kinds are generated from the triangles we have chosen. Three indeed from one, having unequal sides. But the fourth alone is composed from the Isosceles triangle. Therefore, not all can be thus resolved into one another and changed, so that from many small ones a few huge ones are made, or vice versa. Three certainly can. For since all these are made from one, when the larger are dissolved, many small ones are constituted from them, having obtained small and congruent figures for themselves. Again, when many are dispersed through triangles...

Timaeus, Or, On Nature. 485

...they make one number of one mass, and perfect another single great species. Let these things be said thus far regarding their mutual generation. It remains for us to say what kind of species each of them became, and from what concurrent numbers they were heaped together. 

The first species will be that which is composed from the fewest elements, whose longer side is twice as large as its shorter side. When two of this kind are composed according to the diagonal, and that is done three times, and the shorter sides of the diagonal are drawn to the same center, as it were, one equilateral triangle is made from triangles numbering six.

[Diagram: Four triangles forming a tetrahedron and an octahedron]

But four equilateral triangles composed according to three plane angles make one solid angle; which angle follows next in birth after the most obtuse of all plane angles. And once four such triangles are born, the first solid species <note>The tetrahedron or pyramid, representing fire</note>, distributive of the entire circumference into equal and similar parts, arises. 

The second <note>The octahedron, representing air</note> is indeed from the same triangles, but constituted according to eight equilateral triangles, making one solid angle from four planes, and once six of this kind are made, the second body is completed. 

But the third <note>The icosahedron, representing water</note> is born from one hundred and twenty elements joined together, and twelve solid angles, each of which is contained by five plane equilateral triangles, having twenty equilateral bases. 

Now, therefore, the one element has thus far generated these. But the isosceles triangle generated the nature of the fourth kind <note>The cube, representing earth</note>, being constituted according to four, and gathering right angles to the center, making one equilateral quadrangle. Six of these joined together produced eight solid angles, each of which is fitted together by three plane right angles. And the figure of the body thus constituted was made cubic, having obtained six plane equilateral quadrangle bases. 

There is also a certain fifth composition <note>The dodecahedron, representing the universe/quintessence</note>, which God used for the constitution of the universe, and he described and figured it, which someone having contemplated might not absurdly doubt whether infinite worlds or finite ones should be thought to exist. To say they are infinite, he would think proper to one who has no skill in the knowledge of things worthy of being known. But whether one world or five have truly been born, he would think less absurd to inquire. Our reason indeed asserts by a probable proof that one itself was born. But someone else looking at other things will think differently. But these things are to be dismissed. 

And now let us distribute the four kinds we digested a little while ago into fire, earth, water, and air. To earth let us assign the cubic species. For of all four, earth is the most immobile, and the most compact of all corporeal things. And it is necessary that such a thing be made primarily from that which possesses the firmest and safest bases. Furthermore, among the triangles polished from the beginning, those which are equilateral possess a firmer and safer base than the scalene ones. And that which is a plane composed from both, an equilateral quadrangle from an equilateral, certainly comes forth necessarily more stable than a triangle, both as to the whole and as to the parts. Wherefore, if we wish to follow a convenient and probable reason, let us attribute this to earth; then to water, that which is more immobile than the remaining three; to fire, that which is most mobile; and to air, the medium. 

And indeed the smallest body to fire, the largest to water, and the medium to air; also the sharpest to fire, the second from this to air, the third to water. Among all these, it is necessary that that which has the fewest bases be the swiftest. For it is the most prompt for penetrating, since it is indeed the sharpest of all. It is also the lightest, since it consists of the fewest of the same parts. That which is second should have these qualities in the second place. The third in the third. 

Therefore, according to right and probable reason, let the first solid species be the element and seed of fire. Let us attribute the second species in generation to air, and the third to water. Concerning all these so small things, it must be thought that if individual ones of the individual kinds are taken, none of them can be seen by us because of their smallness; but if many are gathered together, their masses and magnitudes are seen. Moreover, all these things were connected by God everywhere according to their multitudes, motions, and powers in an exactly absolute proportion, as much as the nature of Necessity, willing and persuaded, could receive. 

From all those whose kinds we narrated above, the matter seems to hold itself thus by merit. Earth, when it falls into fire, being dissolved by its sharpness, is carried along resolved into fire, or air, or water, until its parts meeting again and joined to each other, recreate earth. For it would never transmigrate into another species. Water, moreover, divided into parts by fire or air, once its parts are reconciled, makes one body of fire and two of air; and portions of air from one dissolved part make two bodies of fire. Again, when fire is occupied by some air or water or earth, and being few moves in many, and fights among those agitated, and being tossed is distracted, the bodies of fire congeal into one species of air; then when the air is overcome and dispersed, from two whole parts and a half, one whole species of water coalesces. 

Finally, let us consider them again thus: as often as some kind of the others is comprehended by fire and is cut by the sharpness of its angles and sides, it then finally ceases to be torn apart when it has passed into the nature of fire. For any similar and same kind suffers least from a similar and same thing; but as long as it is changed into another, and the weaker struggles with the more powerful, it does not cease to be dissolved. Again, when smaller things are surrounded by many larger ones, and a few torn apart are extinguished, when they wish to be constituted in the idea of the victor, they cease to be extinguished, and air is made from fire, and water from air. 

But if there is a transition into these, and it attacks some other kind, the agitated things do not cease to be dissolved until either, since they are dissolvable, they are driven off and flee to their kindred, or being conquered, they finally emerge as one thing from many similar to the one that overcame them, and remain familiarly with the victor. Indeed, through these passions, all things change their seats in turn. For the multitudes of any kind are distinguished by their own place, because of the agitation of the seat itself. But those which have been made dissimilar to each other are carried by the flow and concussion to the place of those to which they have become similar. 

Therefore, the unmixed and primary bodies were fabricated from causes of this kind. But that other kinds were also born in their species is due to the constitution of each element: which not only from the beginning produced one triangle with magnitude, but also larger and smaller ones, as many in number as there are kinds in the species. Wherefore, these mixed in themselves and with each other have an infinite variety: in which those who are to render a probable reason about nature must be skilled. Therefore, unless one certainly comprehends in what way and with what things together the motion...

# Book Thirty-Two

If a constitution should certainly be established, [it is likely that] it has comprehended many things; however, many matters seem likely to hinder the disputation that remains behind. Regarding these, some things have indeed been said, but the rest remains to be spoken. In a nature that is perfectly smooth and flat, motion is never accustomed to exist. For it is difficult, or rather impossible, to find that which is shaken without a shaker, or a shaker without that which is shaken. Motion is the least of all these; and these smooth and flat things can never truly be. Thus, we shall place rest in smoothness and flatness, but motion always in the contrary nature. Furthermore, inequality is the cause of this nature, which is contrary to the smooth and flat. Now, we have already treated the generation of inequality. But in what way individuals, according to their types, do not cease to be moved and carried toward one another, we have by no means explained. Therefore, we shall explain it next in this way. 

Since the circuit of universal nature, with its circular compass, has embraced the genera and strives to meet with itself, it constrains all things and suffers no empty space to be left anywhere. Wherefore fire has penetrated all things most of all, then air, as it is closest to it in thinness, and other things by a similar reasoning thereafter. For those things which are composed of the largest parts leave also the largest void in their constitution, while the smallest leave the least. The narrowness of this compression thrusts the small things into the voids of the great. Therefore, when the small are insinuated into the great, and the small ones themselves discern those which are great, while the greater coerce the smaller, all things are carried upward or downward into their own places. For whatever has changed in magnitude changes its seat. Thus, for these reasons, the generation of the nature contrary to smoothness is always preserved, exhibiting a perpetual motion of these things both in the present and the future. 

**[Margin: Many kinds of fire.]**
After this, it must be known that there are many kinds of fire: namely, flame; and that which is kindled by it, which indeed burns but brings no light to the eyes; and that which remains within those things which had been kindled once the flame is extinguished. 

**[Margin: Many kinds of air.]**
Similarly, there is one kind of air that is most pure and agile, which they call ether; another most turbulent, obscure with darkness and clouds; and it must be thought that there are other species without a name, because of the inequality of the triangles themselves. 

There are two principal kinds of water: one liquid (*humidum*), the other fusible (*fusile*). The liquid kind indeed, because it consists of small and unequal types of water, is easily moved by itself and by others due to the condition of its inequality and the appearance of its figure. But that which is composed of larger, equal, and smooth parts is more stable than the former. And it is compacted heavily because of its smooth equality, but due to the force of penetrating and dissolving fire, having lost its equality, it becomes a participant in motion; and having become agile and mobile, pushed by the neighboring air and extended through the earth, it suffers two things: for it both liquefies and falls into the earth. The first is called the purging of the mass, the second is called flux. Again, with fire flying out from here (since no exit is made into a vacuum), the neighboring air, having been pushed, impels the still-mobile liquid mass into the seats of the fire and mixes it with itself. Finally, the mass being driven together and having again attained smooth equality—since the fire, the artisan of inequality, has now departed—assembles into the same state with itself. We call the departure of fire "cooling," but the joining and meeting that occurs when the fire goes away, we call "conglutination" and "frosty rigidity." 

**[Margin: Generations of metals and of the diamond.]**
Indeed, from these which we have called fusible waters, that which is most dense, uniform, splendid, and yellow, being made of the thinnest and smoothest parts, is a most precious thing: gold, flowering and compacted through rock. But a branch of gold, most hard because of its density and moreover suffused with a black color, is called *adamas* [diamond/hardest metal]. But that which has parts close to it, and contains more than one species, denser even than gold, and a participant in a small and thin earthly part so that it is rougher and harder—but because it has great intervals within, it is lighter—this is one kind of shining and concreted waters, and it is named *æs* [bronze/copper]. But when the earthly part mixed into this is separated from its other parts due to age, and being sent out to the extreme surface becomes visible to the sight by itself, rust is then born. 

It is by no means laborious to attain the rest of this kind by similar reasons. For if anyone, for the sake of relaxing his study, should consider the probable proofs concerning generation—having intermitted the reasons of those things which exist forever—and should be delighted by such consideration without the addition of regret, he will attain a moderate and prudent play in life. These things being thus granted now, the probable things which seem to follow concerning them must be run through. Often a thin part of water is mixed with fire, both liquid and fluid, so named because it flows around slippery earth; it is soft also for this reason: because its bases are less firm and stable than those of earth, and they easily yield and slip. 

**[Margin: On hail, ice, snow, frost.]**
When this is destitute of fire and is also deserted by air, it becomes smoother, and other things being squeezed out, it is forced into itself. And thus compacted, if this happens above the earth, it becomes hail; if on the earth, ice. These things indeed happen when it freezes and coheres most greatly by frost. But when it is less congealed, if it happens above the earth, it is snow; but if on the earth, having been made thicker from dew, it is frost. 

Truly, when many species of water are mixed together, another universal kind trickling through trees from the earth is called *liquor* or *humor*. Indeed, individual liquors, having obtained many other unnamed kinds because of the dissimilarity of their mixture, have four fiery species that are most evident and clear, which have received names. That which warms the soul together with the body is called wine. That which is smooth and discerns the sight, and thus appears splendid, shining, and oily to us, is the anointed and oily species: pitch, gum, oil, and others of that kind. 

**[Margin: Various liquors.]**
But that which drenches the narrow passages of the mouth even to the inner parts of nature, applying sweetness by this power, is commonly called honey. Finally, that which dissolves and burns the flesh and is foamy, secreted from all liquors, is called *succus* [sap/juice]. 

The species of earth emerging through waters becomes stone in this way. For when the congealed water fails in the mixture, it passes into the species of air; this air recurs to its own place, but nothing of them is vacuum; therefore it pushes the nearest air. If that pushed air be heavy and wound around the soft earthly mass, it strikes it vehemently and conducts itself into those seats from whence the new air had ascended. Finally, the earth, being indissolubly driven by the air together with water, creates stones; those more beautiful which shine transparently from equal and smooth parts, but those more deformed which are the opposite. 

But where all moisture is resolved by the sharpness of fire, and the body is rendered drier by it, that species remains which is called solid and "fusible earth." 

**[Margin: On stone, nitre, salt, glass, and the rest.]**
Sometimes also, the moisture being left behind and the earth being made fusible through fire, and then frost approaching, it becomes black stone. But when that same thing is similarly deprived of much moisture from the mixture, but consists of thinner parts of earth, and is salty, and becomes semi-congealed, and emerges through water—partly indeed it is the purging kind of oil and earth, called nitre; partly it is most convenient for daily sustenance according to law: salt, a body dear to God. But common things from both, which are not soluble by water, are thus glued together by fire because of something of the sort. Fire and air do not liquefy the masses of earth. 

[[Page 487]]

Since these two are most thin and smaller than the voids of the earth, they remain through its most capacious passages without any violence, so that they neither dissolve it nor liquefy it. But the parts [of water], because they are larger, liquefy it by a violent flux. Thus water alone dissolves poorly compacted earth, but fire alone dissolves that which is compacted; for nothing except fire penetrates this. Again, both fire and air diffuse the weaker part of water: air through the voids, fire even through the triangles. Air indeed, when constricted by force, is dissolved by nothing except through an element; fire alone resolves it when it coheres without force. Bodies composed of water and earth in such a way that the water obstructs the voids of the earth constricted by force, behave in this way: that exterior water cannot flow in through them and therefore does not liquefy them; but fire, penetrating the passages of the water (just as water does the voids of the earth), and affecting the water as fire does the air, provides the cause of liquefaction for the common body. Some of these have less water than earth, such as the kind of glass and those stones which are called "fusible"; others, on the contrary, have more water, such as all things which are glued together, turn waxy, and emit vapors. 

Thus far we have almost demonstrated those species which vary in figures and changes among themselves; next, we shall attempt to demonstrate for what reasons their passions [sensations/affects] are born. In the beginning, it is always necessary that sense be present for these things which have been said. But the generation of flesh and those things which pertain to flesh, and also as much of the soul as is mortal, we have not yet declared. For these things are by no means separated from the passions which occur with sense, and those cannot be sufficiently explained without these, yet they can hardly be fulfilled together. First, therefore, other things must be placed; finally, the things that follow must be expedited. So that the passions themselves may follow the genera in the discussion, let those things which pertain to the body and soul stand first for us.
