**[Margin: Why fire is hot, and on heat.]**
First, let us see by what reason fire is called hot: which we shall perceive only if we consider the discretion and division made by it in our body. For it is manifest to almost everyone that this passion is a certain sharpness. Truly, we ought to consider the thinness of the angles, the subtlety of the sides, the smallness of the particles, and the velocity of motion—by all of which it is vehement and penetrating, and always quickly divides and dissipates what it meets—recalling the generation of its figure to memory. For that nature, and no other, dividing our bodies and parting them into tiny pieces, deservedly induces that passion which is legitimately called heat. 

**[Margin: On cold.]**
But the contrary passion to this, though manifest to everyone, should not lack its own explanation. For the liquid parts of bodies, being larger than our liquid parts, when they flow into our body, indeed thrust out the smaller parts, but cannot insinuate themselves into their seats; they instead coagulate our moisture, and from the unequal and agitated, they make it immobile because of equality and coagulation, and drive it into a narrow space. But that which is forced contrary to nature resists according to nature and recalls itself to the contrary. In this reluctance and quaking consists trembling and rigor, and every passion of this kind is called "cold," and that which brings it, "frigid." 

**[Margin: On the hard and soft.]**
We call that "hard" to which our flesh yields, and "soft" which yields to the flesh; and we call things themselves hard and soft among each other by the same reason. Whatever leans with a small force yields. But that which is of triangular bases and firmaments, as if leaning vehemently on a plane, resists most of all; and that which is supremely dense vehemently repels things coming against it. 

Furthermore, "heavy" and "light" will be most conveniently declared together with that nature which is called upward or downward. But it is absurd to say that there are two places distinct from each other by a long interval by nature: 

**[Margin: Upward and downward.]**
and that one indeed is called "downward," to which place all things are carried which have a certain mass of body; but the other "upward," to which all things are moved by force. For since the whole heaven is round, whatever extremes are made equidistant from the center, they must similarly be extremes. The center also, being equidistant on all sides from the extremes by equal lines, looks back upon all things equally from its region. Since, therefore, the world is כך disposed, if anyone should say that any of the things said are "upward" or "downward," he will seem to err not without cause. For the middle place in it should be called neither upward nor downward, but middle. That which again circles around on all sides is neither middle, nor has it one part in itself differing from another toward the center itself, nor indeed whatever may be located in that region. Truly, to that which is similar to itself, no one will rightly attribute contrary names. For if anything solid and equilibrated were in the center of the universe, it would decline to no part of the extremes because of their perfect similarity; but if anyone should walk around it, he would often stand with his feet opposite to himself, and would call the same part of it now upward, now downward. Therefore, since the universe is round, as we said a little before, a wise man will by no means affirm it has a superior or inferior place. 

But from whence are those names, and in what things having viewed them have we transferred them from those to the whole world? Let us investigate, placing certain things of this kind first. If anyone should sit in that region of the world which fire has obtained for the most part, and to which it is carried from everywhere, and should obtain some force by which he might seize and weigh the parts of fire—or where he has placed them in the scales of a balance to twist them downward into the dissimilar air—it is plainly established that a smaller portion of fire will be more easily forced than a larger. For where two things are suspended together by one strength, the smaller yields more to the one bringing force, the larger less. And one indeed is said to be carried heavily and "downward," but the other "upward" and lightly. The same thing happens to us inhabiting the earth. For leaning on the earth, by which walking upon it we separate and distinguish earthly genera from each other, and often violently throw earth into the dissimilar air contrary to nature—often both parts being participants in a kindred nature—here the smaller portion, thrown more easily than the larger to a dissimilar place, yields first to the violence, and we have named it "light"; and the place to which we compel it, "upward." The contrary affection to these is something "heavy" and "downward." It is necessary that these differ from each other, because the multitudes of the genera obtain a place contrary to others. For what is light in one place is light compared to that which is in the contrary place; and heavy similarly to heavy; and to that which is called downward, that which is downward; and to that which is upward, that which is called upward: for all these will be found to be and to become transversely opposite and contrary and thoroughly different. Yet one thing must be thought concerning all these: that the way and progress of individual things carrying toward the similar and kindred makes that which is carried "heavy"; but the place into which such a thing is carried, "downward." Those which behave otherwise, it effects otherwise. Therefore, let certain causes of this kind be said for these passions. 

**[Margin: On the smooth and rough.]**
Anyone, by looking, will be able to reveal to others the cause of the smooth and rough passion. For hardness mixed with inequality exhibits the latter, but equality exhibits the former to density. But of those passions which occur commonly around the whole body, 

**[Margin: On pleasure and pain.]**
the greatest remains, which is the cause of pleasure and pain in those things we have discussed. Similarly, whatever things are open to the senses through the parts of the body move both pains and pleasures. Thus, let us take the causes of every passion, both sensible and insensible, first recalling to memory what we distinguished above concerning that nature which is easily moved and that which is moved with difficulty. For in this manner we ought to pursue all those things which we desire to comprehend. 

When some passion, even a brief one, falls upon that which is accustomed to be easily moved, any part of it transfuses the passion itself to the following parts on all sides, until it arrives at the seat of prudence [the brain]: where, through these messengers as it were, the power of that which brought the passion is known. But that which is affected to the contrary and remains in a way immobile does not have that circular transfusion: and it alone suffers, but moves the neighboring parts not at all. Wherefore, since the other parts do not impart the first passion to each other, and the whole animal is not agitated from here, that which it suffers stands forth void of sense. This indeed happens around the bones, the hair, and the remaining parts which are for the most part earthly in us. Truly, the instruments of sight and hearing are affected entirely otherwise, because the greatest force of fire and air is in them. 

Furthermore, as it pertains to pleasure and pain, let it be considered thus. A passion violently and contrary to nature brought upon us abundantly and at once is painful. Again, that which returns into nature abundantly and at once is sweet; that which happens to the contrary is the contrary. Truly, a great passion brought with ease is indeed sensed greatly, but is a participant in pleasure and pain the least. Such are those things which proceed from sight. We have narrated above that our body is made kindred to this [the light] in the day; to this, burns or cuts and whatever passions of this kind do not bring pain, nor even when the restitution into its own species occurs, do they bring pleasure. Yet vehement and very clear senses belong to it insofar as it suffers something, and runs into something, and touches. Indeed, no violence is in this discretion or concretion at all. 

But bodies constituted from larger parts, and yielding with difficulty to the agent, when they transfer the motions brought into the whole body, contain pleasures and pains: namely, when they are moved from their state, pains; when they return, pleasures. Whatever things experience departures and evacuations of themselves little by little, but repletions at once and abundantly—since it has no sense of evacuation, but has a sense of repletion—bring no pains to the mortality of its power, but the greatest pleasures. This is known from the perception of sweet odors. But those things which are driven from their nature at once and abundantly, but are restored into it little by little and with difficulty, are accustomed to be affected contrary to the former. This plainly appears in limbs that are cut or burned. 

Now we have almost treated the common passions of the whole body and the names of those things bringing them. Now, therefore, let us explain according to our strength those which happen to certain parts of our body, and from whence they proceed, or by what causes they are brought. First, those things which we left when we were dealing with humors, since they are passions of the tongue, let us declare if we are able. It seems indeed that this, like many other things, occurs by certain discretions and concretions, and moreover uses smoothness and roughness more than the rest. Veins are tended from the tongue to the seat of the heart, the messengers of flavors: 

**[Margin: Flavors.]**
into which if things should so fall that, penetrating the liquid softness of the flesh and being moderately liquefied by their earthly nature, they contract and dry the veins themselves, they produce flavors of this kind. Namely, if they are rougher, they produce bitter and sharp ones; but if less rough, austere ones. Those which also purge them, and if anything adheres to the tongue, wash it away—if they do this beyond measure, and liquefy not a little of that nature itself, such as is the power in nitre—they are all named bitter. But if they have a more temperate power than nitre, and wipe away more smoothly, they appear salty to us without the roughness of bitterness, and more friendly. 

But those things which, applied to the heat of the mouth, and being softened and made to boil by it, in turn make it boil, and by their own smoothness are elevated upward to the senses of the head, and by their own attraction divide individual things, are called "acute" [sharp] because of such powers. But sometimes these same things, attenuated by putrefaction, enter the narrow veins and force the interior parts—both the earthly and those which are in a way aerial—to be mixed together by being tossed about, and being mixed, some to flow around and others to enter; and by their entrance to penetrate and make them concave and tense. Where a concave and blistered humor is poured around the air, and that humor is sometimes earthy in whatever way, sometimes pure, a liquid and clear vessel of air is made from the water. But that which is born from pure water shines through on all sides and is called a "bubble" (*ampulla*). But that which is composed of a more turbid humor together with agitation and being raised up and tensed around, is called "ebullition," "bubble," and "fermentation." The cause of all these passions is called the "acid" quality. 

To all these things which have been said of them, the contrary passion proceeds from a contrary cause. But when the quality of the ingredients is liquid, naturally concordant and consenting to the quality of the tongue, it smooths and softens it, and soothes the contracted roughness, and relaxes or collects those things which were contracted or scattered in us contrary to nature, and in sum restores the natural habit to individuals—everything of this kind is sweet and friendly to all, a medicine and remedy for violent passions, and is called "sweet." 

**[Margin: On smell.]**
Around the power of the nostrils, there are no species. For the nature of odors is of a "half-kind" [imperfect]. For it belongs to no species to have any odor. But our veins around these are too narrow for the kinds of earth and water, but too wide for the kinds of fire and air. Wherefore no one ever sensed any odor of those things. But odors are begotten in the moistening of certain things, or putrefaction, or liquefaction, or evaporation. For when water passes into air or air into water, odors occur in the middle of these, and every odor is either smoke or fog. But of these, that which is changed from air into water is fog; but that which is from water into air is smoke. Hence it happens that odors are thinner than water, but thicker than air. Which becomes most manifest when someone vehemently draws breath into himself when a certain thing is meeting the nostrils. Then surely no odor flows in at once, but the breath alone follows, naked of odor. Therefore these two varieties in these things are without a name, neither from many nor from simple species: but only two names are manifest there, namely "sweet" and "troublesome." This indeed disturbs and violates all that capacity which is extended from the top of the crown of the head to the navel. But the former soothes it, and by a friendly entrance preserves its natural habit. Furthermore, the third power of sensing, 

**[Margin: On hearing.]**
namely hearing, we ought to consider thus: that we may explain from what causes its passions proceed. 

[[Page 489]]

In short, let us posit voice as a certain pulsation from the air, penetrating through the ears, the brain, and the blood even to the soul. Let us call the motion born from it, beginning from the head and ending in the seat of the liver, "hearing." A fast motion indeed proceeds as acute; a slow one, as grave. One that is equal and smooth [is harmonious], but the contrary is rough. Great is that which is much, small that which is little. We shall declare the concord and consonance of these voices in the following things. 

Next, the fourth kind of sensing must be explained, which contains the most variety in itself: and all things that are under it 

**[Margin: On colors.]**
are called "colors." Color is like a certain small flame and splendor emanating from individual bodies, having parts accommodated to the sight for sensing. We have treated the causes from which sight is begotten above. Now, concerning colors, it seems probable things should be said in this manner. Those things which are carried from other parts and fall into the sight are partly smaller, partly larger, and partly equal to the parts of the sight itself. Those which are equal cannot be sensed, which are named "diaphanous," that is, transparent on both sides. But those which are smaller or larger we say partly discern and partly contract the sight, just as those things which by heat or cold contract or discern the flesh, or those which by acrimony or sharpness or heat contract or discern the tongue. And those things which כך affect the sight we call white or black, which passions are indeed kindred to those I just narrated, and in a way the same as them, but they seem to be different in another genus for these reasons. Thus they are to be named: that which disintegrates the sight, "white"; but that which congregates it, "black." 

Indeed, fire of a sharper and different kind, falling upon and dispersing the sight even to the eyes, and by force striking and liquefying the passages and the very globes of the eyes, is said to be fire meeting from the opposite; by whose meeting the tear, a body mixed from fire and water, is poured out. And with one fire leaping out as if from a certain lightning, but the other penetrating and being extinguished by the humor, various colors are created from such a mixture: and we call the passion itself splendor and lightning; and that which does it, "splendid" and "flashing." The middle kind of fire between these, arriving at the humor of the eyes and mixing itself there—by no means indeed flashing, but from the very admixture of the fiery ray to the humor creating a bloody color—we name "red." Splendid and white mixed with red produces "yellow." 

But in what way of measure individuals are mixed with each other, even if someone should know, it is not the part of a wise man to tell, especially since he could by no means bring a necessary or probable reason for these things. Red with white and black generates "purple." A slightly darker and "burnt" and yellowish color is made when blackness is more joined to these having been blown together and parched among themselves. "Tawny" [fulvus] is produced from the tempering of yellow and [red]. "Brown" (*fuscus*) from the confusion of white and black. The coupling of white and yellow generates "paleness." Splendid joined to white and much dulled by blackness effects "blue" (*cæruleum*). Blue with white creates "glaucous" [grey-blue]. From the tempering of tawny and black, the color "green" is born. Almost all other things become manifest from these. For if anyone, imitating the superior mixtures, pursues the remaining colors, he will dispute with probable reasons. 

But if anyone should attempt the discussion and proof of these things by work itself, he will seem to be ignorant of what lies between human and divine nature. For God is sufficient to collect many into one, and again to produce one into many: for He knows and is able at once. But no man is able to do either, nor is now, nor ever shall be. 

All these things, thus naturally affected by necessity, that fabricator of the most beautiful and best work assumed in these things which were being begotten, when He was generating a God sufficient in Himself and most perfect: using indeed causes as ministers to these things, but Himself acting in individuals what was well-disposed. 

**[Margin: Two species of causes.]**
For it is fitting to distinguish two species of causes: one indeed "necessary," the other "divine." And to seek the divine in all things, that we may attain a blessed life as far as is possible for our nature. To search out the necessary cause also for the sake of those things. For one ought to think that without these, those things in which we place our study cannot be understood, or comprehended, or perceived in any other way. 

Since, however, the material lies before us in the present as if for craftsmen—namely, the genera of causes obtaining the place of almost prepared material, from which the following discussion must be woven—let us return briefly to the beginning: and let us go back quickly thither from whence we have arrived thus far, and thus finally let us impose the end and apex of the discussion, such as the superior things require. 

As we said from the beginning, when these things lacked order, God bestowed a mode and reason of proportion upon individuals, both toward themselves and toward each other, as far as each was able to receive. Then surely there was nothing of order, except perhaps by some chance, a participant: nor then was water or fire or any other of those things which are now named among us rightly to be called. But He first adorned all these, then from them He constituted this universe, one animal, containing in itself all mortal and immortal animals. And of the divine things He Himself is the author, but the generation of the mortal He delivered to His own offspring [the lesser gods] to be absolved. They, therefore, receiving from their parent an immortal principle of the soul, enclosed that soul in a mortal body, and subjected the whole body to the soul as if a vehicle, and in it they fabricated another mortal species of the soul, which was affected by heavy and necessary perturbations. 

**[Margin: Perturbations.]**
The first of these would be pleasure, the greatest bait of evil; then pain, the flight and impediment of good things; furthermore, audacity and fear, the counselors of madness; and implacable anger would be added; and hope, the seductive and conciliating, with irrational sense, and love the innovator of all things. They, therefore, mixing these things, necessarily composed the mortal genus. 

Furthermore, lest the divine should be polluted by any mortal contagion, except as much as supreme necessity compelled, they placed the mortal soul separately from it in another seat of the body: and they separated the head from the breast, with the neck and throat interposed. In the breast, therefore, and the thorax, they placed the mortal genus of the soul: and since it was naturally part better, part worse, they disposed the capacity of the thorax again, distinguishing the seat as if of men and women. For they interposed a certain cartilage called the "diaphragm" (which they also call *phrenas*) as a middle between these. 

**[Margin: Diaphragm.]**
They made the part of the soul participant in fortitude and anger and contention nearer to the head, in the middle between the diaphragm and the neck, so that this, obeying reason, might coerce the genus of desires together with it by force, if ever desire should reject the commands of reason dwelling in the citadel of the head. 

**[Margin: The heart is the origin of veins and font of blood.]**
They wished to suspend the heart, the origin of veins and font of blood flowing through every body with a certain impetus, in the region of the bodyguards: so that when the force of anger blazes up, reason announcing if anything is done unjustly from without, or within—

[[Page 490]]

—if any concupiscence should disturb within, then it might quickly perceive the commands and threats through any narrow passages whatever in the body that is a participant in sense, and thus obey and follow altogether, and tolerate in all things the empire of that most excellent one. 

But when they knew that the heart would tremble at the object of terrible things, and would more often blaze with anger, and that all that work would be through fire, for the sake of tempering such heat, they applied the covering of the lungs to the heart— 

**[Margin: The lung.]**
soft first and bloodless, then distinguished with hollow tubes on the outside like a sponge, so that having drawn in breath and drink, it might cool the heat of the heart by such respiration and refreshment. For which reason they derived the arteries like aqueducts through the substance of the lungs, and they surrounded the heart with it as if a soft leap [cushion]: so that when too much anger boils, it may cool down to easier obedience, and the tumult being settled, it may be able to serve and obey reason more easily with anger as a minister. 

Finally, they applied that part of the soul which desires food and drink, and concupiscences all things entirely which the body needs, to the middle region between the diaphragm and the navel: where they wished a certain manger as it were to stand for the nourishment of the whole body, and there they bound that part of the soul like a wild animal. Here surely it is necessary for it to nourish its body, if indeed the mortal genus is to be at some time. That it might always feed and dwell at the manger, far from the counselor, and therefore might not disturb him with its clamor and noise, but permit the principal leader of us to consult in tranquil leisure for the common utility of all, the gods seem to have given it the inferior region to inhabit. 

Since truly God saw that that part of the soul would be such that it would not hear reason; and if it should be struck by any sense, it would by no means obey reasons, but would be most seized by images and sight by night and day: therefore He procreated the nature of the liver and disposed it in its habitation, a nature dense, smooth, clear, sweet, and not void of bitterness: so that the power of thoughts descending from the mind might be received in the liver itself as if in a mirror receiving figures and returning images to the sight. And that it might terrify it when received, whenever using the kindred part of bitterness, and intending threats, and suddenly suffused over the whole liver, it shows felleous [bilious] and terrible colors: contracting it, moreover, it renders it all wrinkled and rough, and so affects its fibers, the bile and its ventricle, and the veins which are called the *portae* [portal veins], that partaking from the right habit it deflects and contorts, partly obstructing and closing, and provides pains and detriment. 

But again, when the inspiration of gentleness from the mind fashions contrary visions, soothing the bitterness because it wishes neither to move nor touch a nature adverse to itself, using the sweetness innate to it, and directing all things straight, smooth, and free in it: then surely it makes the pacified and gentle part of the soul dwelling in the liver, so that even in sleep it is moderately affected and uses divination, when it is void of reason and prudence. For those who composed us, mindful of that paternal mandate by which he had commanded the mortal genus to be made as good as possible according to their strength, כך instituted the worse part of us, that it itself might also be in some way a participant in truth, and indeed they established divination to be fulfilled in it. 

That God gave the power of divining to human madness can be an argument to us, that no one while he is of sound mind attains any divine and true divination, but only when either the power of prudence is impeded by sleep, or oppressed by disease, or moved from its state by some long rapture, is divination accustomed to occur. Truly, it is the office only of the prudent man to understand those things which are pronounced by a soothsaying and raging nature while sleeping or waking: and to discern whatever visions have shone forth by reasoning, כך that he may explain by what reason and to whom some future thing, or past, or present good or evil seems to portend. 

But of him who was and still remains in fury, it is not the office to judge what he saw or brought forth. 

**[Margin: The work of prudence.]**
That ancient saying is surely wise: To do one's own business, and to know oneself, is the work only of a prudent man. Hence the law commands prophets to preside as judges over divine divinations, whom they indeed call vates [seers], being altogether ignorant that they are interpreters of those oracles and visions which are involved in obscure volumes, and not vates themselves. Wherefore those who judge divinations are not to be called vates, but prophets, that is, interpreters and announcers of divinations. 

**[Margin: Liver.]**
And the nature of the liver was made such for this cause, and placed in that seat which we said, namely for the sake of divination. And also while each one is living, such signs are accustomed to be expressed more clearly: but when deprived of life, blindness occurs, nor does any sign of divination become evident. 

Placed next to this on the left is a member for the sake of this [the spleen], that it might always render the liver pure and clear, and shining and transparent like a mirror, and accommodated for expressing images. Wherefore when the liver abounds with filth because of a disease of the body, the rarity of the spleen purging it drinks those things up, since this member is hollow and bloodless. 

**[Margin: Delirium.]**
Whence filled with purgings, it grows and swells with gore. And again when the body is cleansed, it subsides, restricted into itself. What the soul has of mortal, what of divine, and where, and with what, and why these are distinct among themselves, we have said. But that it is really כך as we have said, we shall affirm only if a divine oracle should confirm it: but that it is probable it is כך, both now and hereafter by investigating more diligently we do not hesitate to assert, and let it be thus asserted by us in the present. 

What follows this must be treated similarly. For it remains to narrate by what reason the remaining members of the body are digested. Therefore, it is fitting that these consist by this reason most of all. Those fabricators of our genus certainly knew that we would be intemperate toward food and drink, and because of gluttony we would take from these more than measure or necessity required. 

**[Margin: On the intestines and their spirit.]**
Therefore, lest a sudden death should proceed because of diseases, and כך the mortal genus soon fail as imperfect, they fabricated the inferior belly to receive the superabundance of food and drink. They moreover wound it around with the coils of the intestines, lest the nourishment assumed by us should suddenly flow out, and again the necessity of new nourishment should immediately hang over us. For because of that insatiable and perpetual whirlpool, our genus would have been left void of all philosophy and music and moderation, and would have been least obedient to that part which is most divine in us. 

The nature of bones and flesh and other things of this kind is thus composed. To all these, the generation of the marrow provided the beginning. 

**[Margin: On bones and flesh.]**
For the bonds of that life by which the soul leads, joined to the body, being applied to the marrow and deduced from it through every part, bind and support the construction of our body. Truly the marrow itself is generated from others. There are certain first and inflexible triangles, smooth and most accommodated for the most exact generation of fire, air, water, and earth, 

[[Page 491]]

from whose individual genera God, severing individuals and mixing them together in mutual temperance, constituted the seed and fuel of the whole generation of mortals, while He procreated the substance of the marrow from these. Afterward, sowing in it, He bound the genera of souls. Furthermore, whatever figures and of whatever kind it was fitting for marrow to have from individual species, He distinguished so many entirely and such immediately in that first distribution. 

And that part of the marrow indeed in which, as if in a field, the divine seed was to be cast, He fashioned globular and round on all sides: and He wished it to be named *encephalos* [brain], because once each animal was finally absolved, the vessel capable of the brain was to be called the *cephale* [head]. But that which was to contain the remaining and mortal powers of the soul, He adorned with both round and oblong figures, and wished the whole to be named marrow: and from these as if from certain anchors cast, the bonds of the whole soul, He then absolved our entire body around those, and He supported them from the outside with the texture of bones. 

He כך composed the bone itself: rubbing pure and smooth earth, He mixed it and moistened it with marrow. Afterward He threw it into fire, then merged it in water, again in fire, and again in water. And thus often transferring it into both, He rendered it such that it could be liquefied by neither. Using this therefore, as if by a lathe, He fashioned a bony sphere and surrounded the brain. Here He left narrow passages, and around the marrow of the neck and back alike, fashioning rotulas and vortices from it, He added them as if hinges, so that it might extend from the head through the whole. Thus indeed He preserved all the seed, while He walled it around with a stony circuit. 

He added joints moreover, using another nature of its own in them as a certain middle power existing for the sake of motion and flexion. 

**[Margin: On nerves.]**
But thinking that the nature of bones would be drier and more rigid than it ought to be, and when it became ignited and also cooled, it would quickly corrupt and destroy the internal seed, He fashioned the genus of nerves and flesh: so that with the nerves indeed binding the remaining members, being tensed and relaxed around the hinges themselves, He might render the whole body prompt and agile for flexion or tension: but the flesh would be a covering against cold and heat, and as external supports of the body are accustomed to be, a protection against various falls: especially because it was to be such that it would softly and smoothly yield to bodies. 

To which He gave hot moisture for this reason: so that in summer indeed, being dewy and moist on the outside, it might provide a domestic refreshment to the whole body, but in winter again, by its own fire, it might moderately repel the exterior ice. When that maker of our body thought these things, with a certain mixture tempered from water, fire, and earth, and with a sharp and salty ferment applied to them, He fashioned the full and soft flesh: but He tempered the nature of nerves from bone and unfermented flesh as one middle power from both, and He dyed it with a yellow color. Hence it happens that the substance of nerves is more tense and drier than flesh, but more agile and softer than bones. 

With these God bound both the marrow and the bones, and He covered all these with flesh. Therefore, those bones which were most animated, He covered with very little flesh; but those which were least, on the contrary, with most and thickest. Furthermore, at the junctions of the bones, except where necessity and reason demanded otherwise, He added little flesh, lest it should be an impediment to flexions, and make the bodies slow to motion, or lest by its own solid thickness and dull mass it should blunt the edge of the senses, impede memory, and dull the sharpness of wit. 

Wherefore the bones of the groin, the shins, the loins, the arms, the shoulders, and all others which lack joints, or those bones which lie hidden within because of the paucity of the soul in the marrow, are void of prudence and covered with much flesh. But with fewer, those which have prudence, unless perhaps a certain fleshy mass is properly adapted to some sense, such as is the tongue. In the rest, it is as we said. For nature generated and nourished from necessity by no means admits compacted bone and much flesh together with acute sense. For most of all, that composition of the head would have had it, if it had wished to concur: and the genus of men, being fat, nervous, and having a robust head, would have been able to have a double and even much more lasting, stronger, and more placid life than we. 

But it seemed to those fabricators of ours, consulting concerning our genus whether they should make it more lasting indeed but worse, or of shorter life but better, that a short and better life was altogether to be preferred to a long and worse one. Therefore, they wove the head with rare bone, but they did not support it with flesh and nerves because it was not to have flexions. For all these causes, the head is constituted more acute for sensing and more prudent than all members, but weaker. 

For this reason and in this way, God placing nerves around the extreme part of the head, wound them around the spine of the back with a certain similarity, and He bound the highest jaws to them under the face, and He disseminated the rest through all members, connecting joint to joint. 

Furthermore, those adorners of ours adorned the nature of the mouth with teeth, the tongue, and lips, just as we now see, for the sake of necessary and best things together. For they thought out the entrance for the sake of necessary things, but the exit for the sake of the best. Namely, whatever is admitted into the body for nourishment is necessary. But the outflow of words, the minister of prudence, is the best and most beautiful of all outflows. 

Furthermore, the head could not be left with naked bone destitute of all other covering, because of the excess of heat and cold: nor again, being weighed down by the weight of flesh, was it to be rendered void of sense and dull. Therefore, the flesh not being entirely dried up, the greater residue which remained was segregated, and the skin itself, joined to itself around the humor of the brain and germinating, sowed the head around. But the humidity springing up under the junctions irrigated it, and compacted it at the crown. 

The species of the junctions indeed was made various because of the power of the circuits and nourishment: and to these indeed more pugnacious ones, more; but to less, fewer. God pricked and struck all this skin on all sides with fire. Then as if from the wounds of the pricks, moisture flowed out: 

**[Margin: On hair.]**
and whatever of liquid and hot was pure there, departed: but that which was mixed from the same things as the skin, being produced outward by the impetus of emanation, was extended in length, having a thinness equal to that puncturing and penetration. But because of slowness, being blunted by the surrounding breath, and revolving back under the skin, it took roots. For these causes surely, hair was born in the skin, kindred to the skin according to the similarity of the hide and leather, but harder than the skin and denser because of the coagulation made by cold. 

Namely, hair produced outside the skin stiffened by cold. In this way God instituted for us a constricted and hairy head, using indeed those causes which we said: but He wished the covering itself for the protection of the brain to be not ponderous with flesh, but light, which would suffice to repel the intemperance of cold or heat, and would least impede the sharpness of sense. 

[[Page 492]]

But that complexion of nerve, skin, and bone which is in the fingers, being made drier, is covered by one common and harder covering than the skin. Whose accessory and ministerial causes indeed consist in those things which we have said: but the principal cause is in that intelligence which He fabricated for the sake of future convenience. For those workers of ours were not ignorant that from men women and other animals would at some time be. Moreover, they understood that many beasts also would have a certain use of nails for many works. Wherefore they armed men immediately born with nails. By this reason surely, and for these causes, they covered the extreme members with skin, hair, and nails. 

Truly, since all parts and members of a mortal animal were generated in a certain mutual kinship, and they necessarily possessed life in fire and breath, lest the animal itself should quickly fail, being resolved and exhausted by these, the gods provided by this counsel. Namely, mixing a certain kindred nature of the human genus with other forms and senses, they planted as it were another certain animal. Such are domestic trees, plants, and seeds, which being sown and now cultivated by the art of husbandry are ours: formerly indeed without culture, they were wild. For whatever is a participant in life will be rightly named an animal. 

But what we now say, it is a participant in the third species of the soul, which we placed between the diaphragm and the navel. In which no opinion, reason, or mind is present at all. But sweet and sad sense together with desires agrees with it. It continually suffers all things clearly. But since it is converted to itself in itself, and rejects external motion, and uses its own domestic motion, therefore nature did not grant to it that, having any thought, it should consider any of its own things. Wherefore it indeed performs life, nor is it different from an animal. But because it was deprived of that force by which anything transfers itself, it stood stiff, and remained fixed by roots. 

When those superior ones of ours had supplied all these things to us inferiors for nourishment, they derived various passages as if aqueducts in our body like a certain garden, so that it might be irrigated by the derivation of liquid. First, they divided two veins in the back, hidden passages under the constitution of skin and flesh, according to the twin figure of the body itself, to the right and left. These surely they sent down to the spine, and they comprehended the middle genital marrow, so that this also might flourish and sprout as much as possible, and a more abundant effusion from here to other things as if from a slope might provide an equable irrigation. 

After these, they dispersed veins around the head, and those in turn implicated from the opposite, part from the right to the left, part from the left to the right of the body, so that the head might have a connection to the rest of the body together with the skin, after it was not comprehended and distinguished by a certain circle according to the crown by nerves: and also that the force of sensing might flow from both parts through the whole body on all sides. 

But from here they derived this aqueduct in this order: which we shall plainly perceive, if we first assert this among us. Whatever things are composed of smaller parts detain the larger: but those from larger parts cannot contain the smaller. Fire indeed, before other genera, consists of the smallest particles. Therefore it penetrates water, air, earth, and all things composed of these, and passes through so far that nothing is able to contain it. The same also must be thought of our womb [stomach]. Namely, they retain the food and drink cast in. But breath and fire, because they are thinner than its composition, it cannot delay. These therefore God used for the perfecting of irrigation from the womb into the veins. 

For they weave a certain net from air and fire like a gibbous [bulging] seine. Where there are two connected bulges at the entrance itself: one of which He implicated again by a double sprout, and from the connected bulges themselves He tended cords like ropes through the whole body even to the extremes of that texture. Therefore He composed all its interior intricacies from fire, and assuming the connected parts in the formed animal, He disposed them in this way. 

He indeed sent the convex parts into the mouth. But since the convex and gibbous is twofold, He threw one through the arteries into the lung, the other around the arteries into the womb. But parting the other, He led each part of it commonly to the tubes of the nostrils, so that when the one does not reach the mouth, all its flux and passages may be filled from this. 

But He wished the other capacity of the bulge and net to be around all the concave parts of the body. And He effected all that sometimes to flow together softly into the convex and curved parts, as if air were there; but sometimes to flow back from the convex and curved parts: but the net, since it be rare, to penetrate the body through itself, and again to emerge. 

But the interior rays of fire follow in continuous succession, with air passing through into each part. And that, as long as the mortal animal consists, never ceases to happen. We think such agitation is rightly named expiration and respiration. Truly, all this work and all this passion of ours occurs in the body by a certain irrigation and refreshment for life and nourishment. 

For when, in the habit of expiring and respiring, the interior fire follows at the same time, being diffused through the womb it meets the drink and food, it immediately liquefies them, parts them into smallest pieces, and leads them out through the exits where the progression is open as if from a certain fountain: namely, it throws into the passages of the veins whatever it has exhausted, and conducts the fluids of the nourishments through the body as if a valley of veins. 

But let us see again by what causes respiration was instituted in this manner which we now see. Of which thing surely such will be the consideration. Since there is vacuum nowhere, into which any of those things which are carried might enter, but the breath flies out from us, it is established to anyone that this breath indeed flies out into a vacuum [not], but repels the nearest from its seat, and that repelled one always thrusts out its neighbor, and according to such necessity whatever is struck and impelled into that seat from whence the habit was excluded, entering thither and filling the habit itself, follows. And all that together by a certain revolution, by which there is vacuum nowhere, happens. 

Wherefore when the breast and lungs have blown out the breath, immediately they are filled by air poured around the body penetrating the passages of the body. And again, the air flying from the body and the emitted breath forces the inspiration to be drawn back within through the passages of the mouth and nostrils. 

But the causes which give a beginning to these we posit in this manner. Every animal of this universe possesses heat in the veins and blood as a certain fountain of fire. And we compared that to a seine net, extended through the middle, and all contexted from fire, since all exterior things are from air. Surely the heat must be thought by its nature to emanate outward into its own region toward that which is kindred to it. 

But since there are two discourses, one through the body outward, the other again through the mouth and nostrils, when the breath makes an impetus toward other things and thrusts them out, it draws back and repels others to the contrary. But that which is drawn back, running into the fire, grows hot: that which it exhaled is cold. Therefore while the heat is changed, and those which use another passage grow hot, and again that which boils emigrates to its own nature, and by this emigration repels another into another journey, and these do the same things perpetually and always, certainly this breath, fluctuating hither and thither continually in a circle, contains expiration and inspiration. 

[[Page 493]]

Furthermore, the causes of the passions which happen from the attraction of cupping glasses from the body by physicians, and also of drinking, and moreover of those things which are thrown, whether they are emitted on high or carried on the ground, seem to be treated by this reason. 

Voices moreover, whatever fast and slow, acute and grave are accustomed to be heard, are sometimes dissonant because of the dissimilarity of the motion which is made in us by them, sometimes consonant because of similarity. For the ceasing motions of the prior and faster ones, and those already progressed to a certain similarity, the slower voices themselves succeeding them and moving them, occupy: but they do not perturb by injecting another motion, but induce the beginning of the slower motion according to the principle of the faster. But while they accommodate to themselves a certain similarity of the ending motion, they temper one concert from the acute and grave. Whence they attribute pleasure to the foolish, but to the wise joy because of the imitation of divine harmony found in mortal motions. 

The reason is the same concerning the fluxes of waters, the impetus of lightnings, and that miraculous attraction of amber, or of that stone which is named Heraclean [magnet]. Truly, no attraction of these happens: but since vacuum is nowhere, and these push and repel each other, and being concreted and discretized individual things demand their own place, to a diligent investigator of these things those miraculous events will seem to happen from these mutual passions. 

And yet respiration, from whence we digressed hither, proceeds from these causes and in this manner as we said above. Namely, while the fire divides the food and is elevated, having attained the breath within, it fills the veins from the belly by such common elevation, because it hauls from there the ground things, and for this reason the liquors of nourishments are thoroughly diffused through the whole body of all animals. 

Immediately the ground things, being taken from their kindred by fruits or grasses, which God produced for the nourishment of our body, have altogether various colors because of the mixture: but the red color prevails most in these, whose nature proceeds from the portion of fire and the scouring made in the liquid. Therefore the color of that which permeates into the whole body is such in appearance as we said. We have named it blood, the fodder of the flesh and the universal body: from whence the irrigation distributed everywhere, being exhausted, fills all things. 

But the mode of repletion or evacuation is such as the motion of anything in the universe, through which anything kindred confers itself to itself. For those things which are poured around us on the outside resolve us assiduously, and emit individual portions of us outward to their own species. But the bloody things ground in us and enclosed in the viscera, as is fitting to happen in any animal constituted under heaven, are forced to imitate the motion of the whole. Therefore when any ground things in us demand their kindred, they fill whatever is exhausted. 

Furthermore, when more departs than has accessed, the animal decreases; when the contrary happens, it is increased. Therefore the recent composition of any animal, since it has new triangles as if from a certain wooden contexture, possesses a valid structure of them: but its whole mass has grown together more tenderly: for it grew together recently from more recent marrow, and was nourished by milk. Therefore it overcomes and grinds with the force of the younger those triangles incident from the outside from which food and drink consist, which are older and weaker, and renders the animal itself large, while it nourishes it from many similar things. 

But when it relaxes the root and compage of its triangles, because it has been fatigued and tamed by great labors for a long time by striving against many things, then surely it cannot reduce the assumed nourishments into its similarity by grinding, but its own members are easily dissipated by the ingredients. Hence now every animal begins to be diminished and to fail, and that detriment is called old age. 

But the end then happens, when the bonds of those triangles from which the marrow is made, formerly coadapted, bind nothing further, but the nexus of the soul being now relaxed by fatigue, they desert it. But the soul secretly according to nature immediately flies out with pleasure. For whatever is against nature is troublesome: but what is according to the nature of the thing is pleasant. Similarly also, death which diseases and wounds have brought is violent and troublesome: but that which old age, leading little by little to the end, naturally steals away, is the lightest among all kinds of death, and happens with pleasure rather than pain. 

But from whence diseases are born, who would doubt? For since those four are those from which the body is compacted—Earth, Fire, Water, Air—their abundance contrary to nature, and defect, and translation from their own place into a foreign one, through which they do not hold what is convenient for themselves, bring a certain intestine sedition and diseases. For when everything is contrary to nature or is transferred, those things surely grow hot which were formerly cold, the dry grow moist, the light grow heavy, and all other things are similarly permuted. 

But only something the same approaching or departing to itself according to the same, and similarly and with the due proportion preserved, will permit itself to remain the same to itself, safe and whole. But that which errs, whether by approaching or departing, induces various mutations, diseases, and infinite corruptions. From the second compositions also, constituted according to nature, a second conjecture of good or bad health will be given to anyone seeking it. For since marrow has consisted from those, and bone and flesh and nerves, and blood moreover has grown together from them although in another way, many other events indeed happen just as the superior things, but the greatest and gravest diseases are born in this way. Namely, when these are made from each other in reverse order, they are undoubtedly corrupted. 

For according to nature, flesh and nerves are generated from blood: nerves indeed from the fibers and ligaments because of kinship, but flesh from a certain coagulation of that which was secreted from the fibers and ligaments. That which again emanates from nerves and flesh, glutinous and oily, at the same time increases the flesh, for the most part toward the nature of bones, and also the bone itself surrounding the marrow by nourishing it. That which again trickles through the thickness of the bones, the purest kind of triangles, smoothest and most abounding in fat, while it flows down from the bones and slips away, irrigates the marrow. 

Insofar therefore as individual things are made in this manner, good health is preserved. But bad health follows when it happens to the contrary. For as often as the melted flesh transmits rot again into the veins, the blood together with the breath becomes much 

[[Page 494]]

and various in the veins, infected with different colors and bitterness and acid and salty flavors; it begets bile, gore, and phlegm as much as possible. All of which being again כך begotten and corrupted, infect the blood itself in the first place, and they themselves, administering no nourishment to the body, are carried everywhere through the veins with no order of natural circuit observed. 

These things are surely enemies among themselves, because they provide no use of themselves to each other. Furthermore, they are most adverse to the natural habit of the body and that which perseveres in its own state, by dissolving and liquefying it. For a very old portion of flesh when it liquefies, being most inept for digestion and concoction, grows black because of old burning: and because it wasted away and was thoroughly eaten away, it contracts bitterness, adverse to all other parts of the body not yet contaminated: and then indeed for bitterness that black color itself has acerbity and acrimony, that which had been bitter being now more attenuated: but then bitterness again dyed with the color of blood has red, but with this black mixed in, a felleous [bilious] color. 

Furthermore, a yellow color meets with bitterness when new flesh liquefies because of the flame of fire. And indeed a common name was imposed on all these, "bile," either by some physician or certainly by someone of that wit who could discern many and dissimilar things, and again look upon one genus in many worthy of one name. But those which are called species of bile have received a proper reason for individuals according to the variety of colors. 

Gore moreover, which is the residue and flux of blood, is smooth and mild: but that which is of black bile and air is wild, when because of heat it is mixed with a salty flavor, something of this kind is called acid phlegm. Often indeed some portion of thinner and recent flesh liquefies together with air, then is inflated by the enclosed wind, with moisture immediately poured around: and from this are made bubbles (*ampullae*), which individually cannot be seen because of their depravity; but joined together and swollen into a larger mass, they are conspicuous, and they have a white color because of the generation of foam. 

All this liquefaction of thinner flesh made together with breath, which swells from wind poured around with moisture, we call white phlegm: likewise the residue and flux of recent phlegm we call tears and sweat, and whatever other things into which the body is resolved daily. And all these are instruments of diseases, namely when blood increases not by food and drink according to nature, but from contraries against the laws of nature. 

Therefore when any flesh is cut around, and its root remains, it is a certain half power of calamity. For it is easily restored. But when that which binds flesh to bones is sick, and blood flowing from them and the nerves no longer nourishes the bones or binds the flesh, but has become rough, salty, dry, and squalid from the oily and glutinous by iniquity of food, then surely that which suffers all those things, being cut off from the bones under the flesh, again stiffens. The flesh also falling from the roots leaves the nerves naked and covered with salty humor, and permeating the influence of blood, renders the diseases which we said above even more numerous. 

These are indeed grave passions for bodies. But those which precede these are much graver. Namely, when because of the thickness of the flesh it does not have sufficient respiration, and therefore vexed and restricted by the heat of putrefaction, it does not receive nourishment, and it again falls back into that to the contrary, having been cooled. That indeed into flesh, and flesh into blood again falls down. Whence sharper diseases than the superior ones are born. 

But the extreme of all is when the nature of the marrow is sick because of some defect or excess, for from here the most vehement and most dangerous diseases to death proceed, for then every compage of the body is necessarily dissipated. 

After these, we divide the third species of diseases into three parts. For one is created by breath, another by phlegm, another by bile. For when the lung, the guardian and as it were the storehouse of the breath itself, is closed up by distillation and does not exhibit free and expedited spiracles to us, and from here indeed no breath is sent, but from there more than is fitting is received, then those things which lack respiration and refreshment wither. 

But that which is received too much, being conducted through the veins, contorts them, and liquefies the body in the middle of the diaphragm; occupying the middle interposed, from here diseases admodum troublesome with much sweat and innumerable arise. Often also, with the flesh being discrete and rarefied within the body, breath is born: which since it cannot go out, affects with the same pains as the entrance of breath from elsewhere. But then it afflicts with huge pains when poured around the nerves and neighboring venules it inflates these, and intends and detorts the ligaments and continuous nerves from the back. Which diseases surely from the intending and inflating passion are named tensions, and from the back contortions, of which the remedy is difficult. For fevers arising most of all solve these. 

White phlegm indeed is difficult, being enclosed within because of the breath of the bubbles: but having slipped down to the exterior event, it is milder, but it sprinkles the body with various filths and infects it with white spots, and generates other diseases of this kind. But mixed with black bile, when it glides into the most divine passages of the head, it is accustomed to dissipate and disturb them. If that happens to those sleeping, it is milder: but if to those waking, it is more difficult of expulsion. Since truly this is a sacred languor of nature, not without cause it was called the sacred disease [epilepsy]. 

Hence acid and likewise salty phlegm is the origin of all languors which happen by distillation, since truly it glides into many places, it begets many bad healths. But whatever parts of the body are said to swell are vexed by the fire of bile and by burning, which when it expires, produces various tumors on the outside by its heat: but within being held back, it procreates many burning and eating diseases. 

But it is then worst when mixed with pus and blood it moves the threads of the fibers and ligaments from their order, which are therefore deduced and scattered in the blood, so that it may attain a moderate habit of thinness and thickness: and neither because of heat be slippery with it, and rarely flow out from the body, nor if thick flow and reflow. For this utility of nature, ligaments of this kind are very opportune, which if anyone even in a dead man and in blood stiffened because of cold should conduct and contract among each other, all the remaining blood is diffused. But when they have been [melted?], they are immediately restricted with the preceding cold. 

Since truly these fibers have this force in the blood, when by the nature of bile the blood has become old, and again has been resolved from the flesh into this, hot 

[[Page 495]]

and liquid, gradually falling upon the first force of those fibers, being compressed it is restricted. Compressed truly and extinguished violently, it moves a storm and trembling within. 

Furthermore, when it flows more abundantly, overcoming the ligaments by its own heat, and parching beyond measure, it indeed preserves, and if it be fit for victory continuously even to the end, it penetrates into the marrows, and the roots being burned there, it resolves and amputates the bonds of the soul like the ropes of a ship, and dismisses it free. 

But when the inferior is present, and the body being liquefied resists it, that being bound either falls out through the whole body, or being thrust into the inferior or superior belly through the veins as if a fugitive from a seditious city, it thus escapes from the body, and induces those diseases which they call 

**[Margin: Diarrhea and Dysentery.]**
Diarrheas and Dysenteries, that is, slippery fluxes of the belly and gnawing fluxes, and also brings many other troubles of the same kind. 

**[Margin: On fevers.]**
Therefore when the body languishes by an excess of fire most of all, it labors with a continuous fever: but when of air, a discrete daily one. Of water, a tertian, because water is slower than fire and air. Finally, by an excess of earth, a quartan. Since earth is the slowest of all, being in the fourth degree, it boils and cools in the fourth circuit of time: hence it brings in quartan fevers, which are healed with difficulty and late. 

And in this way indeed the diseases of the body happen. But the diseases of the soul proceed in this way because of the habit of the body. We judge that the disease of the soul is madness (*dementia*). We posit its two genera, Insanity and Ignorance. 

**[Margin: Vehement pleasures and pains are the gravest diseases of the soul.]**
Whatever passion therefore induces either of these is to be named an ailment of the soul. Therefore admodum vehement pleasures and pains are to be judged the gravest of all diseases of the soul. For whoever either exults with too much joy, or is depressed by too much pain, while he strives more greedily and importunately to receive the former, and to avoid the latter with effort, he can neither discern nor hear anything rightly, but he rages with madness, and being constituted in that habit, he is least of all master of reason. 

But he who abounds with fluid and stupid seed around the marrow, like a tree heavy with more fruits than are convenient and luxuriating with too much fertility, he surely affected with many pains everywhere, and likewise with many pleasures in the lusts themselves and their offspring and fruits, through almost his whole life rages and is mad because of huge pleasures and pains: and since the mind of this man is sick and unwise because of the body, yet by the vulgar he is thought not sick, but as if affected freely by his own will. But the truth has it thus. 

Namely, the intemperance of venereal things is for the most part an infirmity of the soul because of the habit of one genus, by the rarity of the bones in the body, being slippery and moist. And almost all incontinence of pleasures, which is accustomed to be vituperated just as if we were wicked by our own will, is not rightly כך vituperated. For no one is wicked by his own will, but because of a certain depraved habit of the body and a rude education, every wicked man becomes wicked. But these are adverse and inimical to all, and bad and noxious things happen. 

Again, the mind afflicted by pain similarly falls into much depravity because of the body. For sharp and hostile phlegm, and likewise bitter and felleous humors, when wandering through the body they do not exhale, but being revolved through the viscera they infuse their vapor into the inner parts of the soul itself, they effect various languors of the soul both more and less, now many, now few. To the three seats of the soul humors and vapors of this kind are carried, and according to the diversity of the place each generates various species of difficulty and trouble, and again of audacity and timidity, and furthermore of oblivion and hebetude. 

Often also to this depraved habit of corporature and affection access the iniquitous customs of a city, and speeches both private and public not a little noxious entirely, nor are any remedies of doctrine for such great evils learned from a tender age. And thus whoever of us are depraved, are depraved for two causes happening most of all beyond our will, such causes of evils being attributed rather to the sowers than the sown, to the educators than the educated. 

Yet one must strive according to his strength to reject impropriety and attain propriety by the diligence of education, studies, and doctrines. But the treatment of these consists in another mode of differing. Now it is fitting to explain by what culture and by what causes we may attain the health of body and soul. For it is more just to make words about good things than about bad. 

Everything good is beautiful: but the beautiful cannot be without measure and moderation. And therefore the animal which is to be such ought to be moderate with convenient measure. But of that number of those which are called commensurate and moderate, we perceive and judge some small things, but the principal and greatest we ignore. 

Furthermore, to good and bad health, to virtues and vices, no moderation or immoderation seems to be of greater moment than that of the soul to the body itself. We consider none of these, nor do we notice that when a species more weak and inferior carries a robust and great soul, or when to the contrary these are joined, the whole animal itself cannot be beautiful, for it lacks the greatest measure and moderation. But that which is affected to the contrary, to him who is able to intuit it, appears the most beautiful and most amiable of all spectacles. 

A body indeed which dissents with itself by larger or unequal legs, or any other member exceeding measure, is both deformed, and in bearing labors is contorted, vacillates, is fatigued, and falls and provides the cause of innumerable evils to itself. The same must also be judged of that composed of soul and body, which we call an animal. 

For when the soul is admodum more powerful than the body, it exults in it and is carried away, shaking the whole within and filling it with languors. When also it incumbents vehemently with collected forces in one for the sake of learning and investigating, it immediately liquefies the body and makes it totter. Finally, when it contends with a certain ambitious concertation for teaching and disputing privately and publicly, it inflames the body and resolves it. Sometimes also commoving distillations and fluxes it deceives most of the physicians, and forces them to judge contrary causes. 

Again, when a large body and super-exceeding with a slower mass is coupled to a small and exiguous thought of the mind—since there are twin desires in man according to nature, one indeed through the body for nourishments, but the other through that which is most divine in us for prudence—then surely the prevailing agitations of that more powerful one increase what is their own, but render what is of the mind dull, unteachable, and oblivious, and כך generate the greatest infirmity, namely ignorance. There is finally one safety and conservation for both: that we move neither the soul without the body, nor the body without the soul, so that in mutual contention with forces mutually equated, rising together they may protect the good health of the whole. Wherefore...

--- Page 502 ---
-># Timaeus, or, on Nature. 487<-

it makes. For since these two <note>Referring to fire and air</note> are the thinnest, and smaller than the voids of the earth, they flow through its most capacious passages without any violence, such that they neither dissolve nor liquefy it. But the parts of water, because they are larger, liquefy it through a violent flow. Thus, water alone dissolves poorly compacted earth; but when it is compacted, only fire can do so, for nothing except fire penetrates it. <margin>Why fire is hot, and concerning heat.</margin> Again, as for the thickening of water, fire alone diffuses the most violent kind, but both fire and air diffuse the weaker kind; air, I say, through the voids, and fire also through the <term>triangles</term> <note>Plato’s "geometrical atomism" posits that the elements are composed of tiny triangles.</note>. Air that is constricted by force is dissolved by nothing except an element; but fire alone resolves that which coheres without force. Bodies composed of water and earth in such a way that the water obstructs the voids of the earth by being squeezed in by force, are in such a state that external water cannot flow through them and thus does not liquefy them; but fire, penetrating the passages of the water—just as water does the voids of the earth—and affecting the water as fire affects air, provides the cause of liquefaction for the combined body. These things partly have less water than earth, such as the genus of glass and those stones called <term>fusible</term>; partly, on the contrary, they have more water, such as all things that are glued together, turn out waxy, and emit vapors. 

Thus far, we have almost demonstrated those species which vary by their shapes and mutual exchanges; next, we shall attempt to demonstrate for what causes their <term>passions</term> <note>In this context, "passions" refers to sensations or how a body is acted upon.</note> are born. In the beginning, it is always necessary that sensation be present in those things that have been mentioned. <margin>Concerning cold.</margin> But we have not yet declared the generation of the flesh and those things pertaining to the flesh, nor of the soul insofar as it is mortal. For these are by no means separated from the passions that involve sensation, and those cannot be sufficiently explained without these, yet they can hardly be fulfilled at the same time. Therefore, some things must be placed first, and finally, those that follow must be explained. So that the kinds of passions may follow next in the discussion, let those things which pertain to the body and soul stand first for us. First, let us see by what reason fire is called hot; which we shall finally perceive if we consider the separation and division made by it in our body. For it is manifest to almost everyone that this passion is a certain sharpness. We ought to consider the thinness of its angles, the subtlety of its sides, the smallness of its particles, and the velocity of its motion—by all of which it is vehement and penetrating, and quickly divides and always dissipates whatever it encounters—recalling to memory the generation of its figure. For that nature, and no other, by dividing our bodies and partitioning them into tiny parts, rightly induces that passion which is legitimately named heat. 

<margin>Concerning the hard and soft.</margin> The contrary passion to this, though manifest to anyone, should not lack its own explanation. For the moist parts of bodies, being larger than our own moist parts, when they flow into our body, push out the smaller parts but cannot insinuate themselves into their seats; they coagulate our humor, and from the unequal and agitated, they make it immobile because of equality and coagulation, and drive it into a narrow space. But that which is forced contrary to nature resists according to nature and pulls itself back in the opposite direction. In this struggle and shaking, trembling and shivering consist, and every passion of this kind is called cold, or that which brings it, "the cold." We call that "hard" to which our flesh yields, and "soft" that which yields to the flesh; and we call things themselves mutually hard and soft by the same reasoning. Whatever yields is that which is supported by a small base. But that which is from triangular bases and foundations, being vehemently supported by a plane, resists and withstands most greatly; and that which is most densely packed strongly repels things coming against it. 

<margin>Up and down.</margin> Furthermore, "heavy" and "light" will be most conveniently declared along with that nature which is called "up" or "down." But it is absurd to say that there are two places by nature distinct from each other by a long interval: and that one indeed is called "down," to which all things are carried that have a certain mass of body; and the other truly "up," toward which all things are moved by force. For since the whole heaven is round, whatever extremes are made equally distant from the center must be similarly extremes. The center also, being distant by equal lines from the extremes on all sides, looks upon all things equally from its region. Since, therefore, the world is so disposed, if someone should say any of these things are "up" or "down," he will be seen to err, and not without reason. For the middle place in it should be called neither up nor down, but "middle." That which again circuits on all sides is neither middle, nor has it one part in itself differing from another toward the middle itself. To that which is most similar to itself, no one will rightly attribute contrary names. For if anything solid and equilibrated exists in the middle of the universe, it will decline toward no part of the extremes because of their perfect similarity; but if someone should walk around it, he will often stand with his feet opposite to himself, and will call the same part of it now "up" and now "down." Therefore the universe, as we said a little before, since it is round, a wise man will by no means affirm to have a superior or inferior place. 

But let us investigate whence those names come, and in what things we beheld them before we transferred them to the whole world. If someone were to sit in that region of the world which fire has obtained for the most part, and to which it is carried from everywhere, and if he should obtain some force by which he might seize parts of the fire and weigh them, or when he has placed them in the scales of a balance, so as to twist them downward into the dissimilar air, it is clearly established that a smaller portion of fire will be more easily forced than a larger one. For where two things are suspended together by one strength, the lesser yields more to the force, and the greater yields less. And one is indeed said to be "heavy" and carried "downward," and the other truly "upward" and "light." The same happens to us inhabiting the earth. For standing upon the earth, and walking upon it, we separate and distinguish earthly kinds from one another, and often throw earth into the dissimilar air violently and contrary to nature. Here the smaller portion, being thrown more easily than the larger into the dissimilar place, yields sooner to the violence, and we have named it "lightness," and the place toward which we compel it, "up." The contrary affection to these is something "heavy" and "down." It is necessary for these to differ from each other because the multitudes of kinds occupy a place contrary to others. For what is light in one place is contrary to the light in a contrary place; and similarly the heavy to the heavy: and to that which is called "down," that which is "down"; and to that which is "up," that which is called "up." For all these will be found to be and to become mutually transverse and contrary and thoroughly different. Yet one thing must be thought concerning all these: that the path and passage of each thing leading toward its like and kin makes that which is carried "heavy," and the place into which such a thing is carried, "down." What is otherwise makes it otherwise. Let these be said as the causes of such passions. <margin>Concerning the smooth and rough.</margin> Anyone, upon inspection, will be able to reveal to others the cause of the "smooth" and "rough" passion.

S iiii Hardness

--- Page 503 ---
-># Book Thirty-Two. 483<-

For hardness mixed with inequality exhibits the latter, while equality exhibits the former to density. But of those passions which happen commonly around the whole body, there remains the greatest, which is the cause of pleasure and pain in those things we have discussed. Similarly, whatever things are open to the senses through parts of the body will know pains and pleasures. Thus, then, let us grasp the causes of every passion, both sensible and insensible, first recalling to memory what we distinguished above concerning that nature which is easily moved and that which is moved with difficulty. For in this way we ought to pursue all things we desire to comprehend. <margin>Concerning pleasure and pain.</margin> When some passion, even a brief one, falls upon that which is accustomed to be easily moved, any part of it transfers the passion itself to the following parts on all sides, until they reach the seat of prudence <note>Referring to the brain or the rational part of the soul.</note>; where through these, as if through messengers, the power of that which brought the passion is known. But that which is affected in the contrary way, and remains in a way immobile, does not have that circular transfusion; and it alone suffers, but does not move the neighboring parts. Wherefore, since the parts do not impart the first passion to one other, and the whole animal is least agitated by this, that which suffers remains devoid of sensation. This indeed happens around the bones and hair and other parts which are for the most part earthy in us. But the instruments of sight and hearing are affected in an entirely different way, because the greatest force of fire and air is in them. 

Furthermore, as pertains to pleasure and pain, let it be considered thus. A passion brought upon us violently, contrary to nature, and abundantly all at once, becomes troublesome. Again, that which returns into nature abundantly and all at once is sweet; and that which is done in the contrary way is contrary. But a passion brought with great ease is indeed sensed most greatly, but is least a participant in pleasure and pain. Of such a kind are those which proceed from sight. We have related above that our body becomes kindred to this <note>The light of the eyes</note> during the day; for this, burns and cuts and whatever passions of this kind do not insert pain, nor do they bring pleasure when restoration to its own species occurs. Nevertheless, vehement and most clear sensations belong to them insofar as they suffer something, encounter something, and touch it. For there is absolutely no violence in this separation or thickening. But bodies constituted from larger parts, and yielding with difficulty to an agent, when they transmit the motions brought into the whole body, contain pleasures and pains: namely, when they are moved from their state, pains; when they return, pleasures. Whatever things suffer gradual departures and evacuations of themselves, but repletions all at once and abundantly, since they have no sensation of evacuation but do have it of repletion, they bring no pains to the mortality of that power, but the greatest pleasures. This is known from the perception of sweet odors. But when they are driven out of their nature all at once and abundantly, and are restored to it gradually and with difficulty, they are accustomed to be affected in the opposite way to the above.
