This is clearly apparent in the cutting and burning of limbs. 

Now we have treated almost all the passions common to the whole body and the names of those things inserting them. Now, therefore, let us explain as far as our strength allows those which happen to certain parts of our body, and whence they proceed, or by what causes they are brought. <margin>tastes.</margin> First, let us declare if we can the things we left above when we were dealing with humors, since they are passions of the tongue. It seems that these, like many other things, happen by certain separations and thickenings, and moreover use smoothness and roughness more than others. Veins are stretched from the tongue to the seat of the heart, the messengers of flavors: if anything falls into these such that, penetrating the moist softness of the flesh and being moderately liquefied by its earthly nature, it contracts and dries the veins themselves, it produces flavors of this kind. Clearly, if they are rougher, they produce bitter and sharp tastes; but if less rough, austere ones. Those things which both purge them and wash away whatever sticks to the tongue—if they do this beyond measure and liquefy something of nature itself, as is the power in nitre—are all called "bitter." But if they have a power more tempered than nitre, and wipe away more gently, they are "salty" without the roughness of bitterness, and appear more friendly to us. Those things which, applied to the heat of the mouth and softened and heated by it, heat it in turn, and by their own lightness are elevated upward to the senses of the head, and by their attraction divide individual things—because of such powers they are called "sharp" <note>or pungent/spicy</note>. 

Sometimes truly these same things, thinned by putrefaction, enter narrow veins and compel the interior parts, both earthy and in a way airy, to be tossed about and mixed together, and being mixed to flow around some and enter others, and by their entry to make the penetrated parts hollow and tense, where a hollow and blister-like humor is poured around the air; and that humor is sometimes earthy in whatever way, and sometimes pure, and a moist and clear vessel of air is made from the hollow water. But that which is born from pure water shines through on all sides and is called a "bubble." But that which is made from a more muddy humor, agitated and raised and stretched around at the same time, is called an ebullition, a bubble, or fermentation. The cause of all these passions is called "acid" quality. To all these things that have been said, a contrary passion is produced by a contrary cause. But when the moist quality of things entering is naturally concordant and agreeable to the quality of the tongue, and it smoothes and softens it, and soothes the contracted roughness, and relaxes or collects those things which in us were contracted or scattered contrary to nature, and in short restores the natural habit to each—everything of this kind is sweet and friendly to all, a medicine and remedy for violent passions, and is called "sweet." 

<margin>Concerning smell.</margin> Concerning the power of the nostrils, there are no "species" <note>specific types or forms</note>. For the nature of odors is half-formed. It is not suitable for any species to have any odor. But our veins around these are too narrow for the kinds of earth and water, but too wide for the kinds of fire and air. Wherefore no one ever sensed any odor of those things. But odors are begotten in the moistening of certain things, or in putrefaction, or liquefaction, or evaporation. For when water passes into air or air into water, odors are made in the middle of these, and every odor is either smoke or mist. But of these, that which is changed from air into water is mist; but that which from water into air is smoke. Hence it happens that odors are thinner than water, but thicker than air. This becomes most clear when someone, encountering a certain thing with his nostrils, vehemently draws his breath into himself. Then surely no odor flows in at the same time, but the breath alone follows, stripped of odor. Therefore these two varieties in them are without a name, neither from several nor from simple species: but two names only are manifest there, namely "sweet" and "troublesome." This latter indeed disturbs and violates that whole capacity which extends from the top of the crown of the head to the navel. But the former soothes the same, and by a certain friendly entry preserves its natural habit. <margin>Concerning hearing.</margin> Furthermore, we must consider the third power of sensing, namely hearing, so that we may explain from what causes its passions proceed.

--- Page 504 ---
-># Timaeus, or, on Nature. 489<-

Therefore, let us define voice entirely as a certain pulsation by the air, penetrating through the ears, the brain, and the blood all the way to the soul. And let us call the motion born from it, beginning from the head and ending in the seat of the liver, "hearing." A fast motion produces a "sharp" <note>high-pitched</note> sound; a slow one, "heavy" <note>low-pitched</note>. One that is equal and smooth is the contrary of the rough. A large one is composed of many, a small one of few. We shall declare the concord and harmonies of these voices in the following sections. Next, the fourth kind of sensing must be explained, which contains in itself the most variety: and all things under it are called "colors." Color is like a certain little flame and brightness emanating from individual bodies, having parts accommodated to the sight for sensing. <margin>Concerning colors.</margin> We have treated the causes from which sight is begotten above. Now it seems we must speak probable things about colors in this manner. Those things which, carried from other parts, fall into the sight are partly smaller, partly larger, and partly equal to the parts of the sight itself. Those that are equal indeed cannot be sensed, and are called "diaphanous," that is, transparent on both sides. But we say that the smaller or larger parts either dilate or contract the sight: just as those things which by heat or cold contract or dilate the flesh, or those things which by sharpness or pungency or heat do the same to the tongue. And those things which affect the sight thus we call "white" and "black," which are indeed passions of those things just narrated, and are in a way kindred and the same, but in another genus, yet they seem to be different because of these causes. Thus they must be named: that which breaks up the sight, "white"; but that which congregates it, "black." 

We say that a sharper motion of another kind of fire, falling upon and dispersing the sight all the way to the eyes, and by force beating through the very circles of the eyes and the passages, liquefying the fire, is what produces the effect. Coming from the opposite direction, and meeting it, a tear flows out, a body mixed from fire and water. And while one fire leaps out as if from a certain flashing, and the other truly penetrates and is extinguished by the humor, various colors are created from such a mixture: and we call the passion itself "brightness" and "flashing"; and that which does it, "splendid" and "glittering." A middle kind of fire between these, reaching the humor of the eyes and mixing itself with it—not indeed glittering, but from the very admixture of the fiery ray to the humor, creating a blood-like color—we have named "red." The splendid and white mixed with red procreates "yellow." But in what measure individual things are mixed with one another, even if someone knew, it is not the part of a wise man to tell, especially since he could in no way bring forth any necessary or even likely reason concerning these. Red with white and black generates "purple." A slightly darker, mulberry and yellowish color is made when blackness is more joined to these being fused together and burned. "Tawny" is produced by a tempering of yellow and brown. "Brown" truly from a confusion of white and black. The coupling of white and yellow generates "pallor." Splendid added to white and besieged by much blackness produces "blue." Blue with white creates "glaucous" <note>grey-blue</note>. From a tempering of tawny and black, the color "green" is born. Almost all other colors become manifest from these. For if someone, imitating the above mixtures, pursues the remaining colors, he will dispute with probable reasons. But if anyone approaches the discussion and proof of these by actual work, he will seem to be ignorant of what lies between human and divine nature. For God is sufficient to collect many things into one, and again to produce one into many: for He knows and is able at the same time. But no man exists now, or ever will be, who is capable of either. 

<margin>Two types of causes.</margin> Surely all these things, then naturally affected by necessity, that fabricator of the most beautiful and best work assumed in those things that were being begotten, when he generated God sufficient unto Himself and most perfect: using indeed causes as ministers to these things, but He Himself acting in each thing that was well-off. For it is fitting to distinguish two species of causes. One indeed is "Necessary," the other truly "Divine." And we must seek the Divine in all things, so that we may obtain a blessed life as far as is possible for our nature. We must also investigate the Necessary cause for the sake of those things. For we must think that without these, those things in which we place our study cannot be understood, or comprehended, or perceived in any other way. Since indeed the matter lies beneath us at present as if for craftsmen—namely, the kinds of causes holding almost the place of already prepared matter from which the following discussion must be woven—let us return briefly to the beginning: and let us quickly go back there, whence we have proceeded to this point, and so finally place a finish and peak upon the discussion, such as the previous parts require. 

As we said from the beginning, since these things lacked order, God bestowed upon each a mode and reason of proportion, both to themselves and to one other, insofar as each was able to receive it. Then surely there was nothing of order, except perhaps by some chance; nor was anything then rightly to be called water or fire or any of those things which are now named among us. But He first adorned all these things, then from them He constituted this universe, one animal, containing in itself all animals, mortal and immortal. And of divine things He Himself is the author, but He handed over the generation of mortals to His own offspring to be completed. They, therefore, imitating their parent, and receiving the immortal principle of the soul, enclosed the soul itself in a mortal body, and subjected the whole body to the soul as if as a vehicle, and in it fabricated another mortal species of soul, which would be affected by heavy and necessary perturbations. <margin>The greatest perturbation of evil.</margin> The first of these would be Pleasure, the greatest bait of evil; then Pain, a flight from and impediment to goods; furthermore Audacity and Fear, foolish counselors; and there would be added implacable Anger, and Hope, a bland and conciliating thing, with irrational sense and all-invading Love. Mixing these, they necessarily composed the mortal race. But lest the divine be polluted by any mortal contagion, except as much as supreme necessity compelled, they placed the mortal soul separately from it in another seat of the body: and they separated the head from the breast, with the neck and throat placed between. Therefore, they placed the mortal kind of soul in the breast and thorax: and since that was naturally partly better and partly worse, they again disposed the capacity of the thorax, distinguishing the seats as if one for men and the other for women. <margin>Diaphragm.</margin> For they interjected a certain cartilage between these in the middle, named the "diaphragm," which they also call the <term>phrenes</term>. They made the part of the soul participating in fortitude and anger and contention nearer to the head, between the diaphragm and the neck, so that being obedient to reason, it might together with it coerce the kind of desires by force, if ever the desire should spurn the orders of reason dwelling in the citadel of the head. <margin>The heart is the origin of veins and the fountain of blood.</margin> They wished to suspend the heart—the origin of the veins and the fountain of the blood flowing through the whole body with a certain impetus—in the region of the attendants: so that when the force of anger flares up, reason announcing if anything is done unjustly from without, or

--- Page 505 ---
-># Book Thirty-Two. 490<-

if some concupiscence disturbs from within, then quickly through any narrow passages, whatever in the body is a participant in sensation may perceive the commands and threats, and thus obey and follow entirely, and tolerate in all things the empire of that most excellent part. But when they knew that the heart would tremble at the object of terrifying things, and would more often burn with anger, and that all such work would be through fire, for the sake of tempering such heat, they applied the covering of the <margin>Lungs.</margin> lungs to the heart—first soft and bloodless, then distinguished by hollow tubes on the outside like a sponge—so that by drawing in breath and drink, it might cool the heat of the heart with such respiration and refreshment. For this reason they derived the arteries like aqueducts through the substance of the lungs, and surrounded the heart with them as if with a soft leap: so that when too much anger boils, it may cool down to a more easy obedience, and with the tumult sedated, it may more easily serve and obey reason along with anger. 

Lastly, they applied that part of the soul which desires food and drink, and desires all other things that the body needs, to the middle region between the diaphragm and the navel: where they wanted a certain manger, as it were, to exist for the nourishment of the whole body, and there they tied that power of the soul like a wild animal. Here surely it is necessary for it to nourish its body, if indeed the mortal race is ever to be. So that it may always feed at the manger, and live far from the counselor <note>Reason</note>, and therefore disturb him least with its clamor and noise, but permit our chief leader to consult for the common utility of all in tranquil leisure, the gods seem therefore to have given it the inferior region to inhabit. 

But because God saw that that part of the soul would be such that it would not listen to reason; and if it were struck by any sensation, it would in no way obey reasons, but would be most greatly carried away by images and visions night and day: for this reason He procreated the nature of the <margin>Liver.</margin> liver, and disposed it in its habitation—a dense nature, I say, smooth, clear, sweet, and not devoid of bitterness: so that the power of thoughts descending from the mind might be received in the liver itself as if in a mirror receiving figures and returning images to the sight. When received, it might terrify the liver itself, whenever using its kindred part of bitterness and intending threats, and suddenly suffusing the whole liver, it shows gall-like and terrifying colors: moreover, contracting it, it renders it all wrinkled and rough, and so affects its fibers, its bile, its ventricle, and the veins which are called the "gate" <note>the portal vein</note>, that it provides pains and detriments, partly deflecting and twisting it from its right habit, and partly obstructing and closing it. But again, when the inspiration of gentleness from the mind fashions contrary visions, soothing the bitterness because it wishes neither to stir up nor touch a nature adverse to itself, and using the sweetness innate to it, and arranging all things right, smooth, and free within it: then surely it makes the pacified and gentle part of the soul dwelling in the liver, so that even in sleep it is moderately affected and uses prophecy, since it is devoid of reason and prudence. For those who composed us, mindful of that paternal command by which he had ordered the mortal race to be made as good as possible according to their strength, so instituted the worse part of us that it too might be in some way a participant in truth. Indeed, they ordained that prophecy be fulfilled in it. 

<margin>The work of Prudence.</margin> That God gave the power of divining to human madness can be an argument for us: that no one while he is of sound mind attains any divine and true prophecy, but when either the power of prudence is impeded by sleep, or oppressed by disease, or moved from its state by some long-lasting rapture, divination is accustomed to happen. But it is the duty of the prudent man alone to understand those things which have been pronounced by a prophetic and frenzied nature while sleeping or waking: and to discern whatever visions have shone forth by reasoning, so as to explain by what reason and to whom some future, past, or present good or evil seems to be portended. But it is not the duty of him who remained and still remains in frenzy to judge what he saw or brought forth. Truly, that ancient saying is wise: "To do one's own business, and to know oneself," is the work of the prudent man alone. Hence the law orders that prophets preside as judges over divine prophecies, whom some call "seers," being entirely ignorant that they are interpreters of oracles and visions which are involved in obscure volumes, and not seers. Wherefore those who judge prophecy are not to be called seers, but prophets, that is, interpreters and announcers of prophecies. 

And the nature of the liver was made such for this cause, and placed in that seat which we said, namely for the sake of divination. And while each one is living, signs of such things are accustomed to be expressed more clearly: but when deprived of life, blindness happens, and no evident sign of prophecy is made. <margin>Concerning the spleen.</margin> Located next to this on the left is a member for this purpose, to keep this [the liver] always pure and clear, and like a mirror, shining and transparent, and accommodated to expressing images. Wherefore when the liver abounds with filth because of a disease of the body, the rarity <note>porosity</note> of the spleen, purging it, drinks those things up, whence this member becomes hollow and bloodless. From which, filled with purgings, it grows and swells with corruption. And again when the body is cleansed, it sinks back into itself. What therefore the soul has that is mortal, and what divine, and where, and with what, and why these are divided among themselves, we have said. But that it is really so as we have said, we shall only assert if a divine oracle should confirm it: but that it is likely to be so, we do not hesitate to assert both now and hereafter by investigating even more diligently, and for the present let it be כך asserted by us. 

What follows these must be treated similarly. For it remains to narrate by what reason the other members of the body are arranged. Therefore, it is fitting that these consist by this reason most of all. <margin>Concerning the intestines and their coils.</margin> Those fabricators of our race certainly knew that we would be intemperate toward food and drink, and because of gluttony would take from these more than measure or necessity demanded. Lest sudden death should occur because of diseases, and so the imperfect mortal race soon end, they fabricated the lower belly for receiving the superabundance of foods or drinks. Furthermore, they wound it with coils of intestines, lest the nourishment assumed by us should flow down suddenly, and again the necessity of new nourishment immediately hang over us. For because of that insatiable and perpetual whirlpool, our race would have been left devoid of philosophy and music and all moderation, by no means obeying that part in us which is most divine. <margin>Concerning bones and flesh.</margin> The nature of the bones and flesh and other such things is composed thus. For all these, the generation of the marrow provided the beginning. For the chains of that life which the soul leads joined to the body, applied to the marrow and drawn from it through all, bind and support the construction of our body. But the marrow itself is generated from others. There are indeed certain first triangles, both unbent and smooth, most accommodated for the most exact generation of fire, air, water, and earth.

For this reason and for these causes, they covered the extremities of the limbs with skin, hair, and nails. 

Since all parts and limbs of a mortal living being were created in a certain mutual kinship, and necessarily possessed life through fire and spirit, the gods provided a counsel lest the animal itself, being dissolved and exhausted by these elements, should quickly fail. Indeed, mixing a certain nature related to the human race with other forms and senses, they planted, as it were, another kind of living creature. Such are domestic trees, plants, and seeds, which, being sown and cultivated by art, are now mild to us; but once, without cultivation, they were wild. 

For whatever partakes in life shall rightly be named a living creature <note>original: *animal*. In this context, it refers to any being with *anima* (soul/breath), including plants.</note>. But that which we are speaking of now partakes of the third species of soul, which we located between the diaphragm and the navel <note>In Platonic philosophy, this is the "appetitive soul," responsible for nutrition and growth, shared by both humans and plants.</note>. is changed, and those things which use another passage are heated, and again that which is hot migrates back toward its own nature, and by this migration it strikes other things into another path; and as these things continually suffer and perform the same actions, surely this breath <note>original: "anhelitus"</note>, flowing back and forth in a certain circle, contains both expiration and inspiration. Furthermore, the causes of those effects produced by physicians through the suction of cupping glasses <note>original: "ampullarū"; refers to the medical practice of bloodletting or "cupping" to draw out humors</note> upon the body, and also the causes of drinking, and moreover of those things which are thrown—whether they are cast upward or fall to the ground—must be treated by this same reasoning. Additionally, all voices, whether fast or slow, high-pitched or deep, are usually heard as discordant at times, due to the dissimilarity of the motion they produce within us; at other times, they are heard as harmonious because of their similarity. For the slower voices that follow occupy the movements of the earlier and faster voices which are already fading and have progressed to something similar, and by moving them, they take hold of them. In taking hold, they do not cause a disturbance by injecting a different motion, but rather introduce the beginning of a slower motion according to the principle of the faster one. While they adapt a certain similarity of the ending motion to themselves, they temper a single harmony <note>original: "concentum"</note> out of the high and the deep. From this, they grant pleasure to the foolish, but joy to the wise, because of the imitation of divine harmony found in mortal movements. The same reasoning applies to the flow of waters, the force of thunderbolts, and that wondrous attraction of amber or of that stone which is called "Heraclean" <note>original: "Heraclius"; this refers to the lodestone or magnet, named after the city of Heraclea</note>. In truth, there is no "attraction" in any of these; but since there is nowhere a vacuum <note>Plato’s "plenum" theory: the universe is entirely full of matter, so motion happens by things pushing each other into empty spaces created by other movements</note>, and these things push and repel one another, and as they are joined or separated they each seek their own place, these wondrous events will seem to occur from these mutual interactions to a diligent investigator of such matters. Yet respiration, from which we digressed to this point, arises from these causes and in this manner, as we said above. Namely, while fire divides food, and being elevated internally it follows the breath, it fills the veins from the common belly by such an elevation, because it draws the ground-up nutrients from there; and for this reason, the liquids of nourishment are spread deep through the whole body of all living creatures. Immediately, these ground-up materials—taken partly from fruits and partly from grains which God produced for the nourishment of our body—possess entirely various colors because of their mixture. But among these, a red color prevails most, whose nature arises from a portion of fire and the cleansing made in the moisture. Therefore, the color of that which flows through the whole body is such as we have described in appearance. We have named this "blood," the food of the flesh and the entire body; from it, a distributed irrigation, being exhausted, refills everything. Moreover, the manner of filling and emptying is such as the motion of everything in the universe, through which every kinship-group gathers toward itself. For those things which surround us from the outside continually dissolve us, and send out individual portions of us to their own species. But the bloody parts within us, ground up and enclosed in the viscera—as is proper to happen in any living creature established under the heavens—are compelled to imitate the motion of the whole. Therefore, when any ground-up parts within us seek their kin, they fill whatever has been exhausted. Furthermore, when more departs than has entered, the animal decreases; when the opposite occurs, it grows. The recent composition of any animal, having new triangles as if from a wooden framework <note>Plato’s theory that the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) are composed of microscopic geometric triangles</note>, possesses a strong structure; however, its entire mass is more tender, since it

<column-break/>

[Column 2]
was recently hardened from younger marrow and nourished by milk. Therefore, it overcomes and grinds down those triangles arriving from the outside—from which food and drink are composed—which are older and weaker than its own triangles, with the strength of its younger ones, and it makes the animal itself large while it nourishes it from many similar parts. But when the root and bond of its own triangles are relaxed—because they have been exhausted and tamed by great labors over a long time of struggling against many things—then indeed it cannot reduce the received nourishment into its own likeness by grinding it down; rather, its own members are easily dissipated by the incoming elements. From this point, every animal begins to diminish and fail when it is overcome, and this decay is called old age. But the end then arrives when those bonds of the triangles from which the marrow is composed, once joined together, can bind nothing further, but now from exhaustion...

And the moisture, gradually falling upon those first fibers <note>original: "villorum"; refers to the small, hair-like structures or filaments in the body's tissues</note>, is compressed and restricted by their force. **Book Thirty-Two.**

...and whoever devotes effort to mathematical doctrines, or studies any investigation of the mind more vehemently, must also employ the movement of the body and engage in gymnastic exercise. And again, he who forms and strengthens the body with the greatest diligence must, in turn, join to it the movements of the soul, making use of music and all the studies of philosophy, if indeed one is to be rightly called both "good and beautiful" [*kalos kagathos*] at the same time. Similarly, we ought to care for the parts by imitating the form of the whole. For since the body is attacked from within by those things that enter it, and becomes cold, and again is rendered dry or moist by external things, and suffers those things which subsequently follow these, whenever someone leading a life of leisure commits his body to these motions, he is overcome by them and dissolved. 

But if someone, in caring for the body, imitates that nature which we shall call the "Nourisher of the Universe," so that he never permits it to be sluggish, but always moves it and, with a constant agitation, resists internal and external movements everywhere according to nature; and if, by a certain moderate motion, he brings back into order and adorns the wandering passions and parts of the body—preserving the ratio of their kinship [to the whole] according to that superior discourse which we held concerning the universe—he by no means permits enemy to stir up battles and diseases against enemy within the body, but will rather ensure that, by friend adhering to friend, he maintains the health of the body.

**[Margin: What movement is best.]**
Truly, of all movements, that is best which occurs in itself from itself. For it is most akin to the motion of both the mind and the universe itself. But that which is caused by another is inferior. The worst movement, however, is when the body, lying still and acting quietly, is moved by other things according to its parts. For this reason, of all the purifications and constitutions of the body, that which is done through gymnastic exercise is the most healthful.

**[Margin: Concerning purifications.]**
The next closest to these is easy transport, whether it be performed by ship or any other vehicle. A third species of commotion is to be undertaken then only when the greatest necessity compels it; otherwise, it is useful in no way and should be taken up by no man of sound mind. That is the "purgation of physicians," which is usually done by "pharmacs"—that is, by loosening remedies. For unless diseases are most dangerous, they are not to be provoked by drugs...

### Notes on the Text and Translation:
*   **Proper Nouns:** All names (Socrates, Jupiter/Iuppiter, Lorenzo [de' Medici], etc.) have been retained as requested.
*   **Abbreviations:** The OCR-noted abbreviations (e.g., *q;* for *que*, *vbiq;* for *ubique*, and tildes for omitted 'n' or 'm') have been expanded to their full Latin forms in the reading process to ensure an accurate English rendering.
*   **"Nourisher of the Universe" (*altricem universi*):** Ficino is translating Plato’s term *tithenē* (nurse/receptacle), often associated with the material world or the *chora* in the *Timaeus*.
*   **"Good and beautiful" (*bonus simul & pulcher*):** A translation of the Greek ideal *kalokagathia*.
*   **Gadirum/Eumelum:** Refers to the twin brother of Atlas in the Atlantis myth; "Gadiric" refers to the region of Gades (modern Cádiz).
*   **Missing End:** The *Critias* ends abruptly in mid-sentence in all known manuscripts; Ficino correctly notes this with "*Deest finis dialogi*."

By this design, the organ <note>original: "animal auidum generandi" – literally 'an animal greedy for generating,' referring to the Renaissance medical view of the womb as a semi-autonomous entity</note> for procreation, when it is kept for too long beyond its prime and away from bearing fruit, bears the delay with difficulty and becomes greatly indignant. Wandering everywhere through the body, it blocks the passages of breath, does not allow for respiration, vexes the person with extreme distress, and finally weighs them down with all sorts of diseases, until the desire and love of both sexes—like picking fruit from trees—produces a child. They then pluck this fruit and sow it into the womb as if into a field. From this, they conceive animals that are at first so small they cannot be seen and are not yet formed; soon, they unfold what they had gathered, nourishing them to a great size within, and finally lead them out into the light, thus completing the generation of animals. In this manner, women and all females were created. 

The race of birds was formed from men in such a way that they received feathers instead of hair. Into this state those men pass who, though they are simple and innocent, are yet light-minded and curious about high things in vain; they are so foolish that, relying on the judgment of their eyes, they do not doubt that these highest things can be firmly demonstrated through sight alone. 

The race of walking wild beasts, however, was born from those men who were entirely alienated from philosophy and never lifted their eyes to the heavens, because they never used those revolutions of thought which are performed in the head, but followed those parts of the soul that dominate in the belly and the chest. Because of these pursuits, they fixed their front limbs and their heads entirely on the ground due to their lack of knowledge; they held the top of the body in a long and varied extension. For there, because of the laziness of each, the circuits of the soul were crushed and broken; and for this reason, the form of four feet and even more was established, so that God might provide a greater occasion for the more foolish—through many feet and their forward movement—to be deflected even more toward the earth. 

As for those who were the most foolish of all and prostrated their bodies entirely to the earth, as if they had no further need for feet, they were changed into bodies lacking feet and creeping upon the ground. 

The fourth kind is the aquatic race, born from those who were the most dull and ignorant, whom our creators did not judge worthy of pure respiration because, due to the magnitude of their extreme transgression, they possessed an utterly impure soul. Therefore, from that thin and pure respiration of air, they were moved into the deep and turbid respiration of water. From this arose the multitude of fish and oysters and, finally, all water creatures; in this change, they certainly pay the penalty of extreme ignorance by inhabiting the furthest depths. 

In this manner, both in the past and now, animals migrate into one another, changing through the loss or acquisition of intellect and madness. Now, therefore, let our discussion of the universe have its end. For having received mortal and immortal living things, and being filled by them, this world has finally been made: a visible animal containing visible things, the image of the intelligible God, a sensible god <note>meaning a god that can be perceived by the senses</note>, the greatest, the boundless, the most beautiful, the most perfect—this one and only-begotten heaven.

## CRITIAS, OR,
## THE ATLANTIC.

### THE ARGUMENT OF 
### MARSILIO FICINO.

[Right Column]

Our Plato, a most dutiful son of his fatherland, praised it in the *Menexenus* for its deeds against the Easterners, and praises it again in the *Critias* for its deeds strenuously performed against the Westerners. In both places, he commends it for many gifts of God, nature, and art; at the same time, he warns everyone not to be ungrateful to their fatherland. While he recounts how Attic virtue <note>referring to the excellence of the Athenians</note> surpassed both the rising and the setting regions, he teaches that all things are tamed by virtue, and that men endowed with virtue behave rightly and happily both in "Western" matters (that is, adversity) and in "Eastern" matters (that is, prosperity). 

Nor is it without reason that he wishes the *Critias*, concerning the antiquity of the world, to be read after the *Timaeus*, which concerns the generation of the world. It seems, however, that he neither put an end to this history, nor composed the subsequent history promised under the title of *Hermocrates*. Nevertheless, it is certain that this was not a fictional story, but a true history. First, because whenever he invents something, he is accustomed to calling it a myth; here, however, he dares to assert it as history. Next, he asserts the very same thing in the *Timaeus*, calling the matter wonderful indeed, but entirely true. He also carefully recounts from whom it was received in both places—namely, from his ancestors and kinsmen. For this Critias heard it from his grandfather Critias, and he from his kinsman Solon (who also committed it to writing), and Solon from the Egyptian priests. 

Furthermore, Proclus brings forward the histories of a certain Marcellus concerning the affairs of the Ethiopians, in which these things are most clearly confirmed, inserted among the deeds of the Ethiopians. And even if none of the Platonists denies the history, Porphyry, Proclus, and before them Origen, nevertheless wish it to contain a physical allegory. I fear that if they try to accommodate every detail perfectly to an allegory, they might be mocked by Plato himself, who, in the beginning of the *Phaedrus*, ridicules through the persona of Socrates those who are too curious about allegories in such matters. 

However, lest we seem to entirely neglect the Anagogical sense <note>the spiritual or "upward-leading" interpretation</note>—without which no one truly becomes a Platonist—let Pallas Athena be the divinity presiding over the intellectual life, and Neptune the divinity nourishing and governing generation. Let the Athenians be the figures of souls living by intellect alone, and of similar divinities. Let the Atlanteans be the figures of divinities favoring generation, and of souls joined to bodies for the duty of generation and the adornment of the whole. 

Most appropriately, the very matter and diverse mobility of generation is signified by the West, the sea, the islands, and the various partitions of places. Furthermore, let the war be the studious contention through which the higher divinities continually turn the lower ones back, and segregate souls from matter and motion as if by fire and sword. 

Accordingly, when you hear that Neptune procreated sons from a woman, understand that he either generated them from the earth, or regenerated them from a prior form of living into another form by a certain inspiration. The five births are the five forms of bodies which he composes in this sea of matter by perpetual agitation: namely, stones, metals, plants, animals lacking reason, and animals endowed with reason. There are ten sons, for in each birth twins are created. Truly, in any composite thing, an elemental power grows together, and simultaneously a certain celestial power is infused, which physicians call a "specific virtue." From the five twin births, ten sons are counted. 

The five zones or coils surrounding the citadel of Neptune are the natures of the five spheres: celestial, fiery, airy, watery, and earthy. He says some are of earth and some of water to signify stability and motion in things. The common passage through all signifies the mutual generation of things between themselves. He also mentions metals, so that through the seven metals we may understand the influences of the seven planets governing the generation of all things. The Platonists attribute gold to the Sun, silver to the Moon, lead to Saturn, electrum <note>a natural alloy of gold and silver</note> to Jupiter, iron and bronze to Mars, orichalcum <note>a legendary reddish gold-like metal, often associated with brass</note> to Venus, and tin to Mercury. 

Let the measures and their numbers be drawn partly from history and partly from the logic of architecture. Something must be attributed to the grace and beauty of the work and the eloquence. But enough now concerning the allegory. 

Let us now confirm the mysteries of this book in this way. The Platonists think that some gods are—to use their words—super-celestial, others celestial, and others sub-celestial. They call the first the sons of God, and all the following ones the sons of the gods. Again, they place the most ample providence in the first, less ample in the second, and in the third a providence reduced to narrower limits, as they preside over certain regions of the earth and kinds of things by divine distribution: just as some celestial beings are placed over certain parts of heaven and stars. 

These sub-celestial gods, therefore, in a certain order, took up the governing of various nations from the beginning. I say from the beginning, either of the generated world or of the regenerated human race. For after the great floods of the earth, Plato thinks that such men are generated by divine power from the earth itself as if from a mother, through the works of these gods. For they are able to beget—namely, through the "Human Idea" acting as a seed. And the earth is able to give birth, when it is infused with moisture and made fertile by approaching heat, whether warm suns follow after the collisions of waters, or...

The transformers of their bodies <note>Refers to the "lesser gods" or demiurges who, in Plato's system, shaped the physical bodies of mortals</note> did not think them worthy of even pure respiration, because their souls were polluted by all sorts of errors. Instead of the subtle and pure air, they were pushed into the murky and profound moisture of the sea. From these come fish, oysters, and all other water-dwelling creatures, who have received the lowest habitations as a reward for their extreme ignorance. 

In this way, both then and now, all living creatures are transformed into one another, changing as they lose or gain intelligence and folly.

# Marsilio Ficino’s Introduction to Plato’s Critias

Since in the *Timaeus* Plato has discussed the generation of the world and of man, in this book, which is called the *Critias*, he describes the civil life of men. But because a person is first born as a natural being before they are formed into a citizen, the *Timaeus* rightly precedes the *Critias*. Just as the World and Man are the works of God, so the State is the work of men who imitate God.

<margin>The war of the Athenians against the Atlanteans</margin>
The summary of the story is this: Long ago, the island of Atlantis was larger than Libya and Asia combined. Its kings, having subjugated many nations, eventually attempted to conquer the Athenians. But the Athenians, through their singular courage and wisdom, defeated them. Soon after, a great flood and earthquake occurred; Atlantis was swallowed by the sea, and the Athenian warriors were likewise consumed by the earth. 

<note>Plato’s *Critias* is famously unfinished, ending mid-sentence during a speech by Zeus. Ficino treats it as a historical/allegorical sequel to the *Republic*.</note>

Plato uses this narrative to show that the ideal Republic he described elsewhere is not merely a theoretical dream, but a practical reality that once existed in ancient Athens. He compares the "Ideal State" to a body that has been given life and movement through history. He describes the power of the Atlantic people <note>original: "Atlanticorum potentiam"</note> and their defeat by the Athenians to prove that even the greatest material power falls before a small, virtuous state.

<summary>This page concludes the Timaeus with the creation of land and sea animals as a consequence of intellectual neglect and begins the Critias with Marsilio Ficino's framing of the Atlantis myth as a historical validation of Plato's political philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>Timaeus, Critias, Atlantis, Marsilio Ficino, transmigration of souls, Ancient Athens, cosmology, political philosophy</keywords>

# Critias, Or, The Atlantic. 499

->Regarding heavenly and divine things, if anything, or even just a small amount that is suitable, is brought forward, it is often accepted. But we are accustomed to examine mortal and human works with far too much exactness. Therefore, if we handle the things that are to be said with less dignity than the subject deserves, it is only right to forgive us. For it should not be thought easy—indeed, it is certainly difficult—to represent mortal things through imitation <note>original: "imitatione" – referring to the concept of mimesis, the artistic or rhetorical representation of reality. Critias is arguing that since we know humans better than gods, we are more critical of stories about them.</note> in a way that satisfies human opinion. I have said all these things, O Socrates, desiring to remind you and to seek from you a greater indulgence for the remaining parts of my discourse. If I seem to ask for what is just, I hope you will grant this indulgence freely.<-

**SOCRATES:** Why should we not grant it to you, O Critias? Furthermore, let this same indulgence be granted by us to Hermocrates <note>The third member of the dialogue's group, who was intended to speak in a third book that Plato likely never wrote or completed.</note> as well. For it is clear that when he is about to speak a little later, he will pray for these same things. Therefore, so that he may begin his speech differently and not be forced to repeat these same requests, let him know that indulgence has already been granted to him; and treating that as settled, let him immediately prepare himself to speak.

# Critias, Or, Atlanticus. 501

[Column 1]

Indeed, he named the eldest Atlas, king of the whole island. From him, the sea is also named the Atlantic. The twin brother who followed him in birth he called Gadirum in his native tongue, whom we in Greek call Eumelum. He was allotted the furthest parts of the island toward the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, considered the edge of the known world in antiquity.</note> and named the place Gadiricus after his own name. Of the second birth, he named one Ampherus and the other Eudæmon. Of the third, the first-born was Mneseus, the second Autochthon. Of the fourth, Elasippus was the elder and Mestor the younger. Finally, of the fifth, the first was Azaes and the second Diaprepes. All these and their descendants inhabited that place for many ages, ruling over many other islands throughout the sea, even as far as Egypt and Tyrrhenia <note>The region of Etruria in central Italy.</note>, as we said before. In the greatest generation was the entire race of Atlas, and the elder king always left the kingdom to the firstborn; they preserved this empire for many centuries.

Indeed, they possessed such a store of wealth as no kings had ever held before, nor will any in the future easily match. Everything needed for use was built and arranged within the city and throughout the whole kingdom. Many things came to them from abroad because of their empire, but the island itself produced most things necessary for all life's uses. First, all things dug from the bowels of the earth, both solid metals and those that are melted; and what is now only a name, but was then most abundant, was <term>Orichalcum</term> <note>original: "Orichalcū" — a legendary golden-colored metal, likely a high-quality brass or copper alloy.</note>, a noble metal dug from many places on the island, then held as the most precious among them except for gold. And whatever the forest produces for architects, it bore in abundance. It even provided pastures for animals, both wild and domestic.

Furthermore, there was a huge abundance of <term>elephants</term> <note>original: "Elephantū" — Plato includes these to emphasize the island's vast size and tropical fertility.</note> there. It supported sufficiently whatever lives in marshes, lakes, and rivers, or feeds on mountains or fields; even this vast and most voracious kind of animal. Then there was whatever the earth now nourishes that is fragrant: roots, grasses, woods, flowing juices, flowers, and fruits. Also the sweet juice of the vine and the solid food by which we are nourished <note>Referring to grain or bread.</note>. Also those things we use for food and seasoning, which we call legumes. Likewise, liquids from trees and food to quench thirst and hunger. Nor were ointments lacking. There were also the most copious fruits of various trees for the sake of delight. There were even <term>desserts</term> <note>original: "bellaria" — sweetmeats or dainties served after a meal for pleasure.</note>, a comfort for satiety, pleasant to those who have labored. All these things that island, which once existed, produced: sacred, beautiful, wondrous, and most fertile.

Collecting these things from the earth, they built temples, royal palaces, harbors, docks, and the whole region in this manner, arranging those rings of sea which surrounded the ancient metropolis. First, by constructing bridges, they provided a crossing to the outer parts and to the royal seat, where, in the home of the god and his ancestors, they had built the palace from the very beginning. Each successor, receiving the decorated palace from the one before, surpassed his predecessor in adornment according to his strength, until they fashioned works wondrous in size and beauty. Furthermore, they led a trench from the sea to the outermost circle, which extended three <term>acres</term> <note>original: "iugera" — here used as a measure of width, roughly 300 feet.</note> in width, one hundred feet deep, and fifty <term>stadia</term> <note>original: "stadia" — a Greek unit of distance; 50 stadia is roughly 6 miles.</note> in length. And so that ships could approach from the sea to that circle as if to a port, they made the opening wide enough to hold the largest ships. Likewise, they cut through the zones of land that separated the rings of water with bridges, so that one <term>trireme</term> <note>original: "triremi" — an ancient warship with three banks of oars.</note> could sail from one to another;

[Column 2]

but they covered them above, so that the passage was made by boat beneath. For the banks of the land zones were high and towered over the sea. The largest circuit through which the sea flowed was three stadia wide; the next ring of land was exactly equal to it. Of the next two, the water ring was two stadia, and the land ring was again equal to the preceding water one; finally, the last ring was one stadium wide, which surrounded the island itself placed in the middle. The diameter of the island where the palace stood was five stadia. This island, the rings, and the bridge, which was a <term>plethron</term> <note>original: "plethri" — about 100 feet.</note> wide, they enclosed on both sides with a stone wall, building towers and gates on each bridge at the water passages.

Stone was quarried from beneath the island all around—black, white, and red—both for the central buildings and for those rings inside and out; in the process, they created two excellent docks from the rock of the city. The buildings were partly simple, and partly made of stones of various colors, seeking pleasure through variety itself. Moreover, they coated the entire surface of the wall that enclosed the outermost ring with thin bronze; that of the inner wall with tin; and finally, the wall surrounding the citadel with orichalcum that sparkled with a fiery brilliance.

The palace itself within the citadel was built in this way. In the middle was the sacred and inaccessible temple of Clito and Neptune, surrounded by a golden enclosure. There, having come together from the beginning, they begot the race of the ten kings, and there every year, gathered from the ten regions, they performed solemn sacrifices for each of them. The temple of Neptune was one stadium long, three acres wide, and as high as its length and width seemed to require; its appearance was <term>barbaric</term> <note>original: "barbarica" — used here in the classical sense to mean exotic or foreign rather than crude.</note>. They decorated all the exterior, except the highest peaks, with silver; the gables and peaks themselves with gold. Inside, however, the entire ceiling was seen to be ivory, variously carved with gold, silver, and orichalcum. But the walls, columns, and floors they decorated with orichalcum. They even erected statues of gold: the God himself standing in a chariot, holding the reins of winged horses, his head touching the high ceiling. Around him were a hundred Nereids sitting on dolphins; for that was how many were thought to exist then. There were also many statues and votive offerings from private individuals. Outside stood golden images of all the royal women and of all the men who had descended from the ten lineages, along with many other large statues and offerings from both kings and private citizens, from the city and from other lands subject to their empire. There was also an altar, fitting in size and craftsmanship to the rest of the display. In the same way, the palace was suitable both to the magnitude of the kingdom and to the sacred ornaments.

They used springs, both hot and cold, overflowing with a constant flow, in which there was a wonderful healthfulness and pleasantness for both uses. Furthermore, dwellings were built around the springs, and trees planted; water basins were also placed around, some open to the sky, others under cover for warm baths in the winter time—some for the royalty, others for private citizens, some for women, and others for horses and other beasts of burden. A fitting and useful arrangement was maintained for each. They led the flowing and irrigating water into the grove of Neptune, which, due to the fertility of the soil, was filled with various trees of wonderful height and beauty. And from there they diverted it into the outer circuit through aqueducts alongside the bridges. Where there were many temples and shrines of the gods, gardens, and gymnasiums—some for men, some for horses, separately...

There were many other specific laws concerning sacred matters that governed each of the kings individually, but these were the most important: That they should never take up arms against one another, but rather that all should come to the rescue if anyone in any city should attempt to destroy their royal lineage. <note>The "royal lineage" refers to the descendants of the ten sons of Poseidon who founded the Atlantean dynasties.</note> And when they deliberated in common, just as their ancestors had done, regarding war and other public actions, they granted the right of supreme command to the lineage of Atlas. <note>Atlas was the eldest of the ten brothers and his line held the high kingship over the others.</note> However, they did not grant the king the authority of life and death over any of his kinsmen unless more than five out of the ten kings had reached the same judgment.

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation, Dialogue I. [space] 505

[Left Column]

...is better, and what is worse. Truly, a judgment of this kind in each individual is a **private law**, and in the state, it is **public law**. 

Since he had already said that a single living creature was composed of such diverse elements <note>referring to the "puppets" of the soul—the conflicting pulls of pleasure, pain, and reason discussed in Plato's Laws</note>, he adds, not without reason, that man is a **divine miracle** among animals. In this, he imitates Hermes <note>original: "Mercurium" — referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the text *Asclepius*</note> who said that **man is a great miracle**. 

There are three kinds of living beings: 
1. They are either immortal in both body and soul, 
2. or mortal in both, 
3. or indeed immortal in soul but perishable <note>original: "caduca" — literally "falling" or "fading"</note> in body. 

In the first kind are the celestial, ethereal, and aerial beings, whether they be called **gods** or <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "daemons" are not evil spirits but intermediary beings that bridge the gap between the divine and the human.</note>. In the last kind, truly, are the **brute animals**. 

But in the middle are **men** and the daemons of water and earth. For since the bodies of these daemons, just like human bodies, are composed of opposites, they can at some point be dissolved; and they bring about certain disturbances <note>original: "perturbationes" — referring to emotional or physical agitations that cloud the mind</note>. 

But leaving the rest aside for now, why then is man a miracle? Because, while he is divine, it is a wonder that he is infected by mortal things; and while he is mortal, it is a wonder to what [degree he participates in the divine]...

<summary>This page defines the unique status of humanity as a "divine miracle" that stands between the immortal gods and the mortal brutes. It classifies living beings into three categories based on the mortality of their souls and bodies, positioning humans and certain "daemons" in the middle.</summary>

### Page 506
**Thirty-fourth Book.**

Shall we say that he himself is like an enemy prepared and plotting against an enemy? Or otherwise? **Clinias:** Athenian guest—for I do not wish to call you an Attic inhabitant. For you seem to me to be more worthy of the name of the Goddess herself, Athens, that is, of Pallas. Indeed, you have made this whole reasoning plain by reducing it to the principle, whereby it may more easily be found to have been rightly said: namely, that all are enemies to all, both publicly and privately, and individuals are enemies to themselves. **Athenian:** How say you this, O wondrous man? **Clinias:** I say, O guest, that the first and best victory is for one to conquer oneself. But the most shameful and worst thing is to be conquered by oneself. And all these things signify that there is a war in individuals against themselves. **Athenian:** Let us therefore resume that discourse. For since each of us is either superior to himself or inferior, must it be said that a house, a village, and a city have themselves in the same way? **Clinias:** Or otherwise? **Athenian:** Do you say that some are superior to themselves, and some inferior? **Athenian:** That very thing. **Clinias:** You have questioned this rightly also. For this happens no less to cities; indeed, they perceive this most of all in them. For where the better overcome the multitude and the worse, that city is rightly called superior to itself, and will be praised for this victory not without justice. But on the contrary, where the opposite occurs. **Athenian:** But whether that which is prior might sometimes be superior and more powerful than the better, let that be permitted for the present. For it requires a longer discourse. But what was said by you, I understand thus: that citizens, even kinsmen and many of the same city, being wicked, will conspire against the few just ones and bring force to bear to subject them. And if they conquer, that city is called inferior to itself and depraved; but if they are conquered, it is superior and upright. **Clinias:** It is a marvel, guest, what is said. Yet it is necessary to confess it so. **Athenian:** Come now, and let us consider this again. Many brothers may be born from one father and mother; nor is it a marvel if many of them be unjust, and the just be fewer. **Clinias:** Nothing of a marvel. **Athenian:** Nor does it become me, I think, or you to strive for this point: namely, that a house and a whole kinship seem inferior to themselves if the wicked prevail, and superior if they are conquered. For we do not act thus to observe elegance or rudeness of words, as many are accustomed to do, but to track down what the right reason is according to nature in laws, and what the error is. **Clinias:** You speak the truth, guest. **Megillus:** Truly, thus far it seems to me also to have been spoken well. **Athenian:** Let us consider this further. Could some judge be set over the aforementioned brothers? **Clinias:** Without doubt. **Athenian:** Which, therefore, will be the better judge? He who destroys the wicked and brings it about that the upright command themselves? Or he who makes the upright command, but allows the wicked to live after he has persuaded them to undergo command voluntarily? Let us add a third judge in virtue to these, if such a one be found, who holds a dissenting kinship so commended to him that he destroys no one, but writes laws for those reconciled, by which they may be friends to each other forever. **Clinias:** Far better would such a judge and law-giver be. **Athenian:** And yet, he will write laws for them looking toward the opposite of war. **Clinias:** You speak the truth. **Athenian:** What then? He who, looking toward war, constitutes a city—will he look toward external wars and refer the life of the citizens to those? Or toward internal wars, which are called seditions? Which he would least of all wish to be in his city, and if they are there, would wish to abolish as quickly as possible? **Clinias:** Plainly toward these. **Athenian:** Would anyone prefer to follow peace out of sedition by the destruction of a part of the citizens, when the other part has obtained victory? Or rather, through reconciliation, with peace made and friendship strengthened, to turn the mind of the whole city toward external wars? **Clinias:** Indeed, everyone will choose that this latter rather than that former should happen to his city. **Athenian:** And would not the legislator do likewise? **Clinias:** Likewise. **Athenian:** Are not all laws to be passed for the sake of the best thing itself? **Clinias:** For that, surely. **Athenian:** And yet neither war nor sedition is the best; for all pray that nothing of these might fall upon them; but peace and mutual benevolence are. But neither is that victory by which the city overcomes itself the best thing, but rather a necessary one. To think, however, that the best state of a city consists in fighting and conquering is similar to thinking that someone is faring best with a sick person while he is being cured, but never thinking of him who has never been sick. And if anyone thinks similarly regarding the habit or happiness of a city or a private person, he will never truly be a civil man while he looks only and primarily toward external wars, nor a refined law-giver, unless he writes laws concerning war for the sake of peace rather than laws concerning peace for the sake of war. **Clinias:** These things, guest, seem to have been said rightly. Yet I would wonder if perhaps someone should contend that both our laws and those of the Lacedaemonians were not diligently placed for the sake of war. **Athenian:** Perhaps it is so. But it is necessary to inquire into the matter not contentiously, but quietly, with the greatest zeal applied by you as well as by them to such matters. Attend, therefore, I pray. Let us begin from Tyrtæus, an Athenian by nature but afterwards a citizen of the Lacedæmonians, who beyond other men applied himself most to matters of this kind. *Not if he excels in wealth as a guardian, and alone possesses most goods (for he counts almost all things), will a man depart more worthy of the name in my eyes, unless he is suited for handling arms.* Perhaps you also have heard these verses. **Megillus:** These are very common among us. **Clinias:** These have also reached us, brought from Lacedæmon. **Athenian:** Let us therefore interrogate the poet in common in this way: O most divine poet Tyrtæe, you certainly seem to us to be wise and good, you who have extolled with excellent praises those who have excelled in war. Concerning which I and Clinias the Gnosian now seem to agree with you strongly. But whether we speak about the same men or not, I would plainly wish to know. Therefore explain to us, do you also, like us, think there are two kinds of war, or otherwise? To this I think not only Tyrtæus, but even anyone far inferior to him, would immediately answer: two. One which we call sedition, and which we just now conceded is the gravest of all. And the other kind of war, which we all place as much milder than that, which we use against outsiders and foreigners. **Clinias:** Who could doubt it? **Athenian:** Say then to us, which men in which kind of war have you so greatly praised, and whom have you so far disparaged? For you seem to have praised those who wage external wars with a great mind. For thus you have said in your songs: *Whoever dares not behold the same bloody things, and provoke harsh Mars face to face with his hands, him I despise.* From this we, O Tyrtæe, conclude that you praise those who are eminent beyond others in waging external wars. Would Tyrtæus concede those things? **Clinias:** Why not? **Athenian:** But we, though these be excellent, think those far more excellent who excel in the greatest war. And we too have a poet as a witness, Theognis, a citizen of Megara in Sicily, who says: *A faithful man staying in insane sedition should be equated to silver and refined gold.* Thus we say that in the gravest war, he is so much better, as justice, temperance, and wisdom joined with fortitude are better than fortitude alone. For no one can be found upright and faithful in seditions without the full number of all virtues.

### Page 507
**On the Laws, or, Of Lawgiving, Dialogue I.**

But many mercenaries, which Tyrtæus will not deny, are found who fight intrepidly in an external war: of whom the majority are fierce, unjust, insolent, and with very few exceptions, the most foolish of all. To what purpose is this? What did he wish to be declared from these things when he said this? Namely, that altogether both he who gave laws here from Jove [Jupiter], and every other legislator if he is to be of any profit, will so establish laws that he looks to nothing other than always to the fullest virtue. But that is, as Theognis says, that faith which shines most in dangers. Which one will name perfect justice. But that which Tyrtæus just now praised in his work, although it is beautiful and opportunely praised by the poet, is nevertheless to be honored in the fourth place in rank and number among the honorable virtues. **Clinias:** Then, guest, shall we reject the founder of our laws among the last founders of laws? **Athenian:** Not him, O best man, but we reject ourselves, if indeed we think that both here and among the Lacedaemonians Lycurgus and Minos established laws looking toward war. **Clinias:** How then ought we to speak of this? **Athenian:** As truth and justice demand: to say that those who discourse concerning a divine republic must be thought to have looked not to a portion of virtue, and especially to a lower one, but to universal virtue itself, and to have sought laws through each of their species, and not to have investigated those species which many now proposing them seek. For each man is accustomed to seek most that which he most lacks: one concerning inheritance and women left as sole heirs to be taken in marriage, another concerning injury, another concerning many other such things. But we think the inquiry concerning laws is well made when it is sought in the way we have just begun. And I certainly highly approve your entrance into explaining the laws. For since you made the beginning from virtue, saying that laws were established for the sake of virtue, you seem indeed to have approached it rightly; but because you asserted that the founder of laws looked toward a portion of virtue and that the smallest, you seemed to me not to speak rightly, and therefore I later used a longer discourse. How I would have wished you to distinguish it for us, if you wish, I shall tell you. **Clinias:** I certainly wish it. **Athenian:** It was necessary to speak in this manner, O guest. The laws of the Cretans are not without reason praised among all Greeks in the first place. For they are rightly placed, since they make those who use them happy.
