| Justice | Strengths |
| Fortitude | Riches |

For they extend all goods to these. But goods are twofold: some human, others divine; and human goods depend upon the divine. If any city has received the greater, it possesses the lesser also; but if it lacks those, it is deprived of both. Of the lesser, the first is health, the second beauty, the third strengths for running and other bodily motions, the fourth riches, which are not blind but see sharply if they follow prudence. Which prudence indeed exists as the first leader of divine goods. Then, after the mind, the tempered habit of the soul. From these two mixed with fortitude, justice emerges in the third place. Fortitude holds the fourth place. All of which are naturally placed before those human ones. Wherefore it is necessary that the lawgiver himself follow this order, and command all that they always work in individuals looking toward these very things; for human things are to be referred to the divine, and divine things to the mind as the principle. Furthermore, he ought to care for marriages among the citizens, and the generations and educations of children, males and females alike, of the young as well as of those advanced in age: and those who conduct themselves rightly in these, as is fitting, he should honor; but on the contrary, he should disparage pains, pleasures, and desires in all social interaction. He shall also consider and observe diligently toward which studies love carries each person, and he shall praise right duties through laws, and disparage the contrary. He shall also teach and define what is honorable in each person's affection, what is shameful, namely concerning anger and fear, and whatever other perturbations happen either in adverse things or delights in favorable things, and finally concerning all motions which vex men from disease, war, poverty, or their opposites. After these things, it is necessary that the legislator diligently observe the gains and expenses of the citizens, and recognize how they are made, and further the societies and their dissolutions which they make either voluntarily or involuntarily: whatever of these they have contracted among themselves, let him observe where justice is present and where it is absent: and he should establish honors for parents, and due penalties for those not parents. Finally, all these things having been brought into the handling of the Republic, let him observe and establish as necessary how they should build monuments for the dead, or what honors ought to be paid to each of the defunct. These things finally declared, the legislator shall set guardians over all these, some administering the matter with prudence, others with true opinion: so that the mind, gathering all these into one, may lead it thither, that it may follow temperance and justice rather than riches or ambition. Thus indeed, guests, I would have wished, and still wish to be explained by you, in what way in the laws of Jove and Pythian Apollo, which Minos and Lycurgus wrote, all these things are present, and in what order they appear plain to him who has skill in laws by art or some force, but to us others are in no way plain. **Clinias:** In what way then, guest, are the things which follow to be treated? **Athenian:** From the beginning again, as we began above, those things seem to me primarily to be treated which pertain to fortitude, then we shall pass through one and another species of virtue, if it so pleases you also, and let us now treat the first, and to its exemplar the rest, so that our conversation may bring us relief on our journey; and finally when we have treated universal virtue, we shall show, if God wills, that the things we just now related look thither. **Clinias:** You say rightly; and first try to examine for us this praiser of Jove. **Athenian:** I will try, both for you and for myself. For this discourse pertains to both me and you. Say therefore: did we say that those banquets which are held in common and gymnasia were invented by the lawgiver for war? **Clinias:** Yes. **Athenian:** Should a third or fourth thing be said to be invented for the same? For perhaps it is necessary to enumerate them thus, both in this kind of virtue and in the other parts of the virtues, or in whatever other way it may be decent to name them for the sake of declaration. **Megillus:** I would say the third myself, and no one of the Lacedæmonians would deny that hunting was devised. But let us try to find a fourth and fifth. I therefore place the fourth as a principal thing among my people, namely, the endurance of pain: which thing is practiced daily with fights among themselves and certain plunderings, with many wounds. In addition to these, a certain wondrous and strong concealment for endurance is related of those wandering day and night through the whole region with bare feet in winter, and often with the rest of the body bare, without attendants. Furthermore, in the exercises of naked youths there is a wondrous endurance among us, when the force of intense heat must be resisted. There are many other things of this kind among us which someone would not easily enumerate. **Athenian:** You speak uprightly, Lacedæmonian guest, but is the battle of fortitude only against fears and pains, or also against desires and pleasures...

### Page 508
**Thirty-fourth Book.**

...and certain vehement blandishments, which bend the minds even of those who seem honorable, and make them as if blind? **Megillus:** Against all these. **Athenian:** If we remember the things said above, here he said that some city was inferior to itself, and some man inferior to himself. Is it so, Gnosian guest? **Clinias:** Entirely so. **Athenian:** Which therefore ought to be called the worse: he who is broken by pain, or he who is overcome by pleasure? **Clinias:** I think it is he who is overcome by pleasure: and everyone thinks that a man ensnared by pleasure is more inferior to himself, and indeed with reproach, than one demolished by pain. **Athenian:** Did therefore the legislators of Jove and Apollo establish a "lame" fortitude, which can resist on the left against adverse things, but on the right succumbs to favorable, joyful, and flattering things? Or rather one sufficient for both? **Clinias:** I think for both. **Athenian:** Let us therefore explain similarly what duties are in your cities, which taste pleasures as I wish, and do not flee them entirely, just as they do not flee pains, but just as in pains, let them be led into the midst of pleasures, and to overcome them let men partly be impelled by force, and partly invited by honors. Where in your laws is that seen which makes men strong against pleasures just as against pains? And shows them victors over those things they ought, and in no way allows them to be overcome by those closest to them within themselves, their gravest enemies? Tell me, I beseech you, what such thing is among you? **Megillus:** It is not so easy, guest; just as I could produce many laws opposed to pain, so I could for pleasure: I do not have great and conspicuous parts against pleasures, but perhaps I shall find small ones. **Clinias:** Nor would I be able to show this similarly in the laws of the Cretans. **Athenian:** Nor is it a marvel, best guests. But if someone among us, a diligent investigator of the true and the best, should find something to blame in the laws of each of our homelands, we ought to bear it in turn not with a heavy but with an equal mind. **Clinias:** You speak rightly, Athenian guest. Wherefore I judge you must be obeyed. **Athenian:** Certainly, Clinias, it does not become men of this age and condition as you are to do otherwise. **Clinias:** Certainly not. **Athenian:** Whether someone can rightly or not blame the Laconic and Cretan Republic is another question. But what is said by many, perhaps I can relate more than either of you. To you indeed, whether the laws were constituted rightly or not, there is certainly one best law, which commands that no one of the youth should dare to ask whether the laws are right or contrary, but with one mouth of all and one voice it prescribes that they be conceded to be rightly placed as if by the gods, and in no way to allow anything else to be said by anyone; but if an old man has thought of something, to relate it to the princes and equals, no one of the youth hearing. **Clinias:** You speak rightly, guest, and although you were absent then from the mind of the founder, yet like a seer you seem to have cleverly guessed those things now, and to speak deeply true things. **Athenian:** Therefore, for the present, no youths are present with us, but we ourselves on account of old age are permitted by the legislator to discourse alone among ourselves concerning these things without sin. **Clinias:** It is as you say. Wherefore do not spare, but freely blame our laws. For it is not unseemly to know if something does not hold itself rightly. For from this, if someone accepts it not with envy but with a benevolent mind, a remedy is found. **Athenian:** You speak excellently. I indeed shall not blame before I have considered diligently according to my strength, but rather I shall speak by doubting. For to you alone of all the Greeks and barbarians of whom we have knowledge, the legislator prescribes to beware of the greatest pleasures and most pleasant games, and not to taste anything of these. Concerning pains and fears, what we just now said, he thus judged: if anyone from his first years becomes accustomed to decline them, it happens that as often as it is necessary to undergo pains, fears, and labors, he flees those who are exercised in these and serves them. This very thing, as I think, it was necessary for him to think concerning pleasure also, and to think this with himself: if from a tender age citizens be devoid of the greatest pleasures, nor taught to contain themselves in pleasure, and to do nothing shameful for the sake of voluptuous pleasantness, they will so succumb just as those who are conquered by fear, and will serve in another and more shameful way than those who are accustomed to contain themselves in the midst of pleasures; and those who, conversing among pleasures, can supply themselves with delights, will perhaps be the worst of men. And thus they will have a mind partly slave, partly free, nor ought they to be called entirely brave and free. Consider therefore if anything from what has been said seems to be spoken rightly to you. **Clinias:** It seems so indeed. For thus the discourse is. But it would be the part of youth, or rather of those entirely insane, to assent immediately and easily to such great matters. **Athenian:** What then? Shall we now pursue what we proposed, O Clinias and Lacedæmonian guest? For after fortitude I shall speak of moderation; what the difference is between these and other Republics, or those which seem to be governed by chance not law, as now concerning war. **Megillus:** That is not easily done. **Clinias:** Yet common banquets and gymnastic contests seem to have been commodiously invented for both. **Athenian:** It seems indeed, O guests, to be arduous in Republics, as in words so in the matter itself, to introduce something safe and certain on all sides. For just as in bodies it cannot happen that some one study is accommodated to one body which is not seen to profit some and harm others; so also in a city. Indeed, gymnasia and sodalities profit cities in some places, but in seditions they are entirely harmful. Of which thing the Milesians, and Boeotians, and Thurians are examples to us. And yet these ancient studies seem to have perverted the old and natural pleasures concerning venereal matters not only in men, but also in beasts. In which matter your first cities could be accused, and all others which have the greatest care for gymnastic exercises. And whether one must think in jest or in earnest, it must be thought that when a female and a male come together for generating, pleasure of this kind seems to have been attributed to them according to nature. But that males are joined with males or females with females, that pleasure is contrary to nature. And those who first dared such a deed did it through the incontinence of pleasure. Furthermore, we all vehemently blame the Cretans' fable concerning Ganymede, because it was feigned against Jove: so that when the laws of themselves are believed to have had their origin from him, imitating that god who handed down the laws, they might also enjoy this pleasure. But let the fable be gone; but the thought of those who consider concerning laws ought to be almost entirely concerning pleasures and pains both in public and in private morals of each person. For these two sources flow from nature: from which he who draws whence, when, and as much as he ought, is happy—namely, the private person, and the city, and every animal; but he who lives foolishly and contrary to opportunity, is unhappy. **Megillus:** Those things are spoken rightly, O guest, nor do we see what can be said against them. But it seems to me that the founder of the Lacedæmonian laws rightly commanded that pleasures be fled...

### Page 509
**On the Laws, or, Of Lawgiving, Dialogue I.**

...Clinias here, if he wishes, will help the Gnosian laws. For among the Spartans, I judge that those things which pertain to pleasures are best disposed of all. For where all men fall most greatly into the most vehement pleasures, and petulance and insanity, our law has exterminated that from the entire region; neither in the fields nor in the cities which the Spartans govern will you see drinking bouts, nor those things joined to drinking bouts by which we are moved to all pleasures. Nor is there anyone who, having met some person wanton from drunkenness, does not immediately affect him with the greatest punishment, nor does the time of the Bacchanals itself free him. Just as I saw among you in carriages, and among the Tarentines who are our colonists, the whole city drunk in the Bacchanals. But among us, no such thing is seen. **Athenian:** All these things are to be praised, O Lacedæmonian guest, where there is a certain continence; but where they are entirely permitted, they soften. For quickly someone defending our ways might blame you, if he should show the license among your women. One answer certainly frees both the Tarentines and us, or rather you also, in all these things: that these are held rightly, not wrongly. For each person will be able to answer a stranger wondering because he sees unusual things: Do not wonder, O guest, this law exists among us. But among you perhaps concerning the same things there is another law. But to us at present, O most beloved men, the speech is not about other men, but about the virtue and vice of the founders themselves. But let us speak more broadly about universal drunkenness. For it is no small matter, nor does its judgment look to some common object. I do not say whether wine should be drunk or not, but I say we must inquire concerning drunkenness, whether it should be used thus, as the Scythians and Persians use it, and the Carthaginians besides, and the Gauls, and Spaniards, and Thracians, all of which nations are most warlike; or as you, who as you say abstain entirely. But the Scythians and Thracians use unmixed wine entirely, both men and women, and they drench their clothes with unmixed wine, thinking this a noble and happy kind of life. But the Persians also use other delights, which you spurn, very much, although more moderately than those, O best man. **Megillus:** But all those we rout and put to flight whenever we take up arms. **Athenian:** Do not say these things, O best man. For many both flights and pursuits have been made and will be, of which a certain cause of this kind cannot be rendered. Wherefore we shall take not a certain, but an ambiguous argument and sign concerning honest duties and their contraries in life if we look to the victory or flight of war, especially since smaller cities are reduced to servitude by greater ones through fighting, as the Locrians by the Syracusans, who used the best laws among those nations, and the Ceans by the Athenians, and many such things may be observed. Therefore, passing over victory and the offense of war, let us try to persuade ourselves by considering concerning each duty according to itself, what is true in each. Let us speak, however, in what way this indeed is such, and good; but that is such, and not good. But first hear me, in what way in matters of this kind good and evil ought to be considered. **Megillus:** In what way do you say that? **Athenian:** Whoever immediately in a dispute disparages or praises some matter proposed seems to me to fail, and to do the same as if someone should immediately disparage a cereal food praised by another as good, before he perceives its effect, and by what reason, to whom, with whom, how prepared, and to what kind of affected bodies it ought to be offered. Which we now seem to be doing in disputing. For as soon as mention of drunkenness was made, some of us immediately disparage it, others indeed praise it, and very absurdly indeed. For using witnesses and assertors on both sides, some of us think we bring something worthy of faith because we have more, and others because those abstaining from wine conquer in battle, which however is ambiguous to us. If therefore we proceed in this way also in other things, we shall do nothing in my opinion. But as it seems to me, I shall try, if I can, by the example of drunkenness itself, to open for us a way and right reason in all such matters, especially since innumerable nations doubting about these things contend with your two cities. **Megillus:** It must be heard entirely if any right consideration is found concerning these. **Athenian:** Let us therefore consider it thus. If someone should approve the care of goats and that kind of animal to be kept and possessed; and another should disparage it, when he has seen them feeding through the fields without a shepherd and doing damage, and has observed every flock either without a shepherd or governed by bad shepherds: shall we judge his disparagement just? **Megillus:** In no way. **Athenian:** But a pilot of a ship—will he be called good if he has only the art of steering, or if he be tossed by seasickness or not? Or finally in what way will he be called good? **Megillus:** Seasickness does nothing to the art. **Athenian:** What then of a leader of an army? If he holds the art of warring rightly, is he to be thought a sufficient leader from this, even if he be fearful, and in dangers be sick with a certain drunkenness of fear itself? **Megillus:** In what way? **Athenian:** What further, if he neither has the art, and is fearful? **Megillus:** You describe him as entirely cowardly and useless, and a leader not of men, but of some base women. **Athenian:** But he who praises or disparages some society, of which some leader can be, and the society is useful whenever it has obtained its pilot, but he has never seen it rightly governed, but always either without princes or with wicked ones—will he ever be able to disparage or praise it rightly? **Megillus:** In what way will he do that who has never seen the society rightly governed? **Athenian:** Come now, attend. Shall we call drinkers and drinking bouts one society out of many? **Megillus:** Most greatly. **Athenian:** But has anyone ever seen this rightly governed? But it is very easy for you to answer, that you have never observed it. For that is not customary to you from your ancestral laws. I indeed have been present at many here and there, and have diligently inquired about all, to speak briefly, and I have never seen or heard of almost any being governed entirely rightly, but small portions in some way, and those few. But many, so to speak, I have known to err entirely. **Clinias:** By what reason do you say these things, O guest? Explain more clearly. For we, as you were saying, since we have no skill in this matter, cannot immediately know what is done rightly and what less so in it. **Athenian:** That is indeed reasonable, but try to perceive me as I speak. In every assembly and community of whatever things are to be done, you confess that there ought to be a prince? **Clinias:** Without doubt. **Athenian:** And yet a little while ago we were saying that the prince of those fighting ought to be brave. **Clinias:** We were saying so. **Athenian:** But a brave man is less perturbed by fear than a fearful one. **Clinias:** It is so. **Athenian:** If some way could be found so that we might set a leader over an army who was altogether intrepid, would we not strive for it with all zeal? **Clinias:** Most greatly.

**Thirty-fourth Book.**

**Athenian:** Now, however, we speak not of an army, nor of one to command against enemies in war, but of one to govern in peace the pleasant custom of friends among themselves. **Clinias:** It is so. **Athenian:** That society, if indeed drunkenness be present—will it lack tumult? Will it not? **Clinias:** How could it? I think the contrary. **Athenian:** First therefore even these have need of a leader. **Clinias:** Most of all. **Athenian:** It is necessary that this prince be skilled in reconciling society; for it ought to be his office both to preserve the present friendship for them, and to procure that more besides be made from that fellowship. **Clinias:** You speak true things. **Athenian:** Ought not therefore a sober and wise prince be appointed for the drunkards, and not the opposite? For even if he be young, and not wise, but drunk, or a prince of drunkards, it will be imputed to good fortune, not to counsel, if by his rashness he does not overturn all things. **Clinias:** Most excellently indeed. **Athenian:** If someone therefore should accuse drinking bouts while they were, as far as could be, rightly disposed in a city, accusing the thing itself, he would perhaps act rightly. But if because of one turbulent drinking bout which he saw, he should disparage all drinking, first it is plain that he is ignorant that it was not rightly disposed; then it is certain that all things would appear wicked in the same way, even if they were done by a sober master and prince. Do you not notice that a drunken pilot of a ship or of any other thing overturns all things, whether ships, or carriages, or an army, or whatever else is ruled by him? **Clinias:** You have said that entirely truly, guest, but also explain this for us. What will these drinking bouts, if they are rightly done, confer upon us? As we were just saying, a rightly led army would bring victory in war, a certainly not small good. And the same must be judged concerning the rest. But from a rightly governed drinking bout, what great thing would reach either the city or private persons? **Athenian:** What great thing, however, will the city obtain from one boy, or one certain assembly rightly instituted? But indeed, if we were interrogated thus we would answer, that a small utility reaches the city from the education of only one. But if you should ask in general about the erudition of well-instituted youth, what it most especially confers upon the republic, it will not be difficult to say. For those well-erudite will turn out to be upright men. But having been made upright, they will both do other things well, and also conquer enemies by fighting. Discipline affords victory to both; victory sometimes begets negligence and rudeness. For many elated in victory have contracted many other vices through insolence. And certainly no discipline was ever Cadmean. But many victories of this kind have been and will be. **Clinias:** You seem, O friend, as if you praise the common custom in the drinking of wine, if it be done rightly, as a great part of discipline. **Athenian:** Certainly. **Clinias:** Will you be able therefore henceforth to show that that is true? **Athenian:** To approve these things as true, O guest, when many doubt concerning them, belongs to God alone; yet if I say what I feel, I think no envy will stand in the way, for we have determined to speak at present concerning laws and the republic. **Clinias:** Come, let us try to learn thoroughly what seems to you concerning these ambiguities. **Athenian:** Thus it is fitting. But it is necessary that you turn your whole discourse to learning, and I to teaching. And first hear this. All Greeks judge our city to be both fond of words and wordy. But Lacedæmon and Crete, the one as brief in speech, the other as zealous for intelligence more than for words. I fear therefore lest I seem to you like a wordy man to speak many things about a small matter, while I use too long a discourse about drunkenness, a small matter indeed. But the right constitution of a drinking bout itself according to nature can never be treated openly and sufficiently in discourse without the right rule of music, nor music without universal discipline. All of which indeed require many words. See therefore what is to be done. Whether, these being passed over for the present, we must now cross over to another question of laws? **Megillus:** You are perhaps ignorant, Athenian guest, that our family is a common guest of your city. And what I judge happens to all boys, that when they hear they are guests of some city, a certain benevolence toward it flows into them from their tender years as if toward a second homeland, happened to me also. For I used to hear Lacedæmonian boys, as often as they either were angry with the Athenians or praised them, say thus: "Your city, O Megille, has brought this evil or good upon us." And hearing these things, I used to fight against those who disparaged you, with a great affection of benevolence toward you. And to me indeed your voice is now very pleasant, and what is commonly said, "Good Athenians are especially good," seems to me to be said truly. For they alone are upright of their own nature, by a certain divine lot, not forced nor feigned. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, freely relate whatever you wish. **Clinias:** If you will hear me also, guest, you will bring forth whatever comes into your mind with the greatest confidence. For perhaps you have heard that Epimenides was a divine man: who was from our family, and ten years before the Persian war, warned by an oracle of the god, came to you and performed certain sacrifices given by the oracle of the god, and predicted to the Athenians fearing the Persian fleet that the Persians would by no means come for a decade: and also after they had come, they would depart with the business unfinished, having suffered more evils than they did. Then indeed our ancestors embraced yours with hospitable affection, and from that time our parents and I have been benevolent to you. **Athenian:** You are therefore ready to hear, as you seem. I however am ready to speak by will rather than prepared by faculty. I shall try, however, as I can. But first, let us define what discipline [education] is, and what force it has, in relation to this sermon. For through this the discourse must go for us in the institution presently begun, until it reaches God himself. **Clinias:** Thus certainly it must be done, if it pleases you. **Athenian:** While I say what discipline is, consider whether my opinion pleases you. **Clinias:** Say it. **Athenian:** I bring forth indeed that those who are to turn out to be excellent men in something, ought to meditate on that very thing from their very entrance into childhood as much by playing as by studying in each thing suitable to that business. Indeed if someone is to be a skilled farmer or builder, it is necessary for him while playing from his first age either to till the earth or to build certain boyish houses: and he who educates both, should prepare for each certain small instruments, images of true instruments. From doctrines also they ought to learn thoroughly those things which make for their own business. For instance, the future smith should measure and use a rule; the future horseman should ride while playing, or do something of this kind. For in all things we ought to try by playing so that we may turn the pleasures and desires of boys thither...

### Page 511
**On the Laws, or, Of Lawgiving, Dialogue I.**

...where we finally desire them to arrive. But we call the head of discipline right education, which leads the mind of the player especially into love of that which, having perfectly prepared virtue in his manly age, it will then be necessary for him to do. But consider now, as I was saying, if what has been said thus far is approved by you. **Clinias:** What prevents it? **Athenian:** Yet it ought not to be left indeterminate what we say discipline most especially is. For when we disparage or praise the educations of individuals, we are accustomed to say, this one is instructed in discipline, that one is an expert in no discipline, although he may be most skilled in the tavern-keeper’s and navigator’s art and other such things. Indeed we do not think this is discipline, but that which from childhood makes virtue desired and loved: and indeed that by which someone having been made a perfect citizen, knows how to rule and to obey with justice. This sermon teaches that this education alone is to be called discipline. But that which tends toward collecting money, or toward increasing bodily strength, or toward some other skill without mind and justice, it judges to be mechanical and illiberal, and unworthy of the name of discipline. But let us not contend about the word: but let this, asserted a little while ago, be agreed among us, that those who have obtained right discipline, almost all turn out upright: but on the contrary, the wicked. Wherefore in no matter is discipline to be neglected, which is present to excellent men as the first of most noble things. And if anyone fails in some matter, and can be corrected, let him amend himself, and let him do that through his whole life according to his strength. **Clinias:** You speak rightly, therefore what you say must be conceded. **Athenian:** And yet long ago we conceded that those are good who can rule themselves, but bad who cannot. **Clinias:** Quite skillfully. **Athenian:** Let us resume therefore that very thing, so that what we say may become more clearly known. And may you receive it through an image so that it may be clear, if in any way I can open this matter to you. **Clinias:** Say it now. **Athenian:** Do we not think each of us is one? **Clinias:** One. **Athenian:** Having namely in himself two counselors, contrary and insane, which we call pleasure and pain. **Clinias:** This also. **Athenian:** To these let the opinions of future things be added, for which the common name is hope: but properly that which is hope before pain is fear: that which is before the contrary is confidence. To all these, the judgment of reason, dictating what of these is better, what worse. If this is made the common decree of the city, it is named law. **Clinias:** I follow you with difficulty. Say however what remains, just as if I followed. **Athenian:** The same happens to me also. **Athenian:** But let us think of these things thus, that we should think each of us is a certain divine miracle [puppet] in the genus of living things, whether in jest or in earnest (for we do not know this) constituted by the higher ones. This however we do not ignore, that these affections in us are like nerves or ropes implanted that pull us in turn and pull us back to contrary actions, where virtue and vice are separately handled. For reason declares that one traction must always be followed and never left, but that by this one all others must be resisted, and that that drawing of reason is golden and sacred, which is called the common law of the city. And that the rest are hard and iron, but this one soft because it is golden: and uniform besides, the rest multiform. It is necessary therefore that we always follow the most beautiful drawing of the law, and favor it. For since the judgment of reason is an honorable thing, and indeed mild rather than violent, it needs ministers for its own drawing, so that the golden genus in us may overcome the other genera. And thus the fable, by which man is related to be a wondrous thing, will be preserved by virtue: and by what reason one is said to be superior and in some way inferior to himself, will be more plainly known: and that it is necessary that each one, having perceived the truth in himself concerning these treatments by reason, should direct his whole life to that very thing: and that a city, having received reason either from some of the gods or from this very person who has known this, should have it for law, and institute its duties with itself and with other cities according to its norm; and thus virtue and vice will appear more clearly distinct to us. Having plainly perceived which things, both discipline and the rest of the studies will perhaps shine more. And that custom now received in drinking bouts, concerning which it will perhaps be thought base if I speak with more words. **Clinias:** Perhaps it will not be seen unworthy of a long discourse. **Athenian:** You speak rightly, wherefore let us say what in it seems most worthy. **Clinias:** Proceed now. **Athenian:** If we add drunkenness to this wondrous thing, what kind shall we make it? **Clinias:** To what purpose do you ask that? **Athenian:** I do not yet say. But if this wondrous thing mixes itself with that, of what kind is it rendered? But I shall try to say even more openly what I wish. I ask something such as this. Does the use of wine excite pleasures, pains, angers, loves, more vehemently? **Clinias:** Most greatly indeed. **Athenian:** Does it also make senses, memory, opinion, intelligence similarly more vehement? Or does it altogether extinguish them if someone has been occupied by drunkenness? **Clinias:** It certainly extinguishes them altogether. **Athenian:** He returns therefore to that habit of soul which the boy had from his first years. **Clinias:** Certainly. **Athenian:** Wherefore he will then be least composed of himself. **Clinias:** Least. **Athenian:** He will therefore be worst. **Clinias:** Very much so. **Athenian:** Not only therefore will the old man, as it seems, be a boy twice, but also the drunken man himself. **Clinias:** That was said most excellently, guest. **Athenian:** Can any reason persuade us that this thing must be tasted in some way? And must not be fled with all strength? **Clinias:** It will perhaps be able, as you say, and just now you were showing yourself prepared to speak. **Athenian:** You have remembered most excellently. Indeed even now I am prepared, since both of you promised to hear not unwillingly. **Clinias:** Why should we not hear, even if for no other reason, yet because it seems a wondrous and absurd thing, if it shall sometimes be necessary for a man voluntarily to cast himself away into every depravity? **Athenian:** Do you say of the soul? **Clinias:** Of the soul. **Athenian:** But shall we wonder, O friend, if someone should come voluntarily into depravity of the body, I say leanness, deformity, weakness? **Clinias:** Why not? **Athenian:** Do we think therefore that those who take the medicines of physicians are ignorant that they will shortly have their body so affected for several days, that if they were to have it similarly affected perpetually, they would not wish to live? Or do we also ignore that those who undergo gymnasia and labors become weak from weariness immediately? **Clinias:** We have known all these things. **Athenian:** And yet this too, that all tend toward these voluntarily for the sake of future utility. **Clinias:** Excellently. **Athenian:** Must it not be thought in the same way concerning other things? **Clinias:** Entirely in the same way. **Athenian:** Not otherwise also must it be thought concerning the drinking of wine, if it is given that this be rightly considered in those matters. **Clinias:** Thus certainly. **Athenian:** If it shall be perceived to have some utility in no way inferior to that which is in corporal exercise, then indeed—yet in the beginning it surpasses the exercise of the body in this, that this has pain, but that has not. **Clinias:** That is indeed right. But I would wonder indeed if we could perceive any such thing in it. **Athenian:** This very thing must now be tried to be explained. Wherefore tell me. Can we think of two species of fear almost contrary to each other? **Clinias:** Which do you mean? **Athenian:** I mean these: we fear indeed evils, when they are frequent in the future; and we also fear estimation [reputation], when we dread lest by saying or doing something less honorable we appear evil. Which fear indeed we, or rather all as I think, call shame (*pudor*). **Clinias:** Who could doubt it? **Athenian:** I was saying these were two fears. One of which is indeed contrary to pains and other fears, and is contrary also to very many and huge pleasures. **Clinias:** Quite rightly. **Athenian:** Ought not therefore both the legislator, and anyone else who can profit men in any way, honor this fear with the greatest honor and call it shame? And name the confidence contrary to this as impudence, and judge it the greatest private and public evil for men? **Clinias:** Rightly said. **Athenian:** That fear indeed both preserves us most greatly in many other huge things, and in war, if one is compared to one, this certainly more than all grants us victory and safety. For there are two things which beget victory: audacity against enemies, and fear of shameful infamy before friends. **Clinias:** It is so. **Athenian:** It is necessary therefore that each of us become both intrepid and fearful. For what reason however it is necessary for both, we have already distinguished. **Clinias:** Altogether. **Athenian:** And yet as often as we wish to render someone intrepid, being driven by the law into the terror of many dreads, we make him such. **Clinias:** So it seems. **Athenian:** But him whom we wish to lead to fear what things are to be feared, we ought indeed to test him with things declining toward impudence, to exercise him in the fight against domestic pleasures, or in the institution of his former life, and to exhort him to victory, and thus to render him truly brave when conquering. But he who has neither made any peril of himself, nor been exercised in these contests, will not have even the middle part of his virtues toward virtue. But how will he be perfectly tempered, unless he has bravely resisted many pleasures and desires compelling him to impudence and injury, and has conquered by reason, work, and art both in jocular and serious things? Or will he be tempered, I ask, who has suffered nothing of this kind? **Clinias:** It is by no means likely. **Athenian:** But say I pray, has some god given some medicine to men for inducing fear, so that the more someone drinks of it, so much the more unhappy he thinks himself to become from any drinking, since he fears all things both present and future for himself, and arrives finally at all dread even if he be the bravest of all: and when he has slept, and been freed from a potion of this kind, the same happens to him daily again? **Clinias:** And what potion of this kind, O friend, shall we say has ever been in the life of men? **Athenian:** None indeed. Yet if this potion were found, would it be suitable for fortitude for a founder of laws, so that we could say something of this kind concerning it to the lawgiver? Come first, say O lawgiver, whether you are writing laws for the Cretans or any others, would you wish to be able to make a trial of fortitude and cowardice from your citizens? **Clinias:** Anyone would certainly answer that he wishes to. **Athenian:** Then whether safely, and with no great imminent danger, or on the contrary? **Clinias:** Safely namely and securely anyone will confess. **Athenian:** Will you not therefore use this potion thus, to compel them to terrors, and in those very perturbations argue by your admonition and command, or make your citizens undaunted, honoring some, but disparaging others if they do not obey your admonitions? And those who have conducted themselves by exercising strenuously, you leave unpunished: but those who do otherwise, you affect with punishment? Or will you use it in no way, although you have nothing else which you may accuse in that potion? **Clinias:** Why should he not use it, guest? **Athenian:** Exercise indeed, O friend, beyond the usual is of wondrous facility, by which either one or a few can exercise either as many as you wish. And whether someone in a solitary place alone, placing ignominy before his eyes because he does not wish to be seen before he has progressed, thus exercises himself against dread, with this potion alone prepared instead of many other things, he will certainly achieve something uprightly: or whether someone trusting in his nature and being sufficiently instructed by use, does not fear to be exercised with many drinkers, and to show himself in exhausting and losing the wine in the cup necessarily so prevailing and surpassing, that he errs in no great matter through impudence, and on account of virtue is not moved from his state, and departs next to the last drink before drunkenness, especially avoiding violence toward all men. **Clinias:** Certainly even here, O guest, conducting himself thus, he will turn out moderate. **Athenian:** Again let us say thus to the founder of laws: O law-giver, neither has a god yet given such a medicine of fear to men, nor have we devised it. For I do not count the poisoners themselves among the guests. But it is necessary to trust very much, and intrepidly, besides daring in whatever things, whether it is some potion or none, which does it. **Clinias:** He will say it is wine. **Athenian:** Furthermore it does the contrary to that potion of which mention was just made. For when someone has drunk, first he becomes more cheerful than he was before: then the more he drinks, by so much he is in greater and better hope, and feels more strongly about himself. Finally like a wise man, that man is filled with confidence, liberty, and audacity, so that he intrepidly both says and does whatever pleases him. **Clinias:** I think indeed all will concede that. **Megillus:** Certainly all. **Athenian:** Let us therefore now remember that there are two certain things which we said above must be cared for in our souls. One that we may trust most greatly, the other that we may fear most greatly. **Clinias:** We judge these things said concerning shame (*pudor*). **Athenian:** You hold them rightly. But since it is necessary to learn fortitude and the habit of an undaunted mind in fears, let us consider whether it is convenient to learn the contrary in contraries. **Clinias:** That is consequent. **Athenian:** In those things therefore in which we are accustomed by nature to become especially confident and audacious having suffered them, it seems we must think that we should be as little as possible impudent and audacious, but on the contrary fearful of saying, or suffering, or doing anything shameful. **Clinias:** So it seems. **Athenian:** Are not these things thus, in which we are such—anger, love, petulance, ignorance, avarice, sloth, and to these those things: riches, beauty, strength, and whatever things make men insane with a certain drunkenness of pleasure? For making a light and innocent peril of all these, and for inducing exercise, we have no pleasure more commodious than that which examines morals by a potion, if only a prudent caution be applied. For let us see. Of a hard and rustic soul, from which a thousand injuries sprout, where is it safer to take an experiment—in commerce...

### Page 513
**On the Laws, or, Of Lawgiving, Dialogue II.**

...which seem most to declare what is innate, or in the spectacles of Dionysus, or in a venereal matter when the soul succumbs, so that you prove someone's morals with the modesty of either a daughter or a son, or a wife exposed to danger? Indeed if you recount infinite things, you will never find in what you can behold natures as if in play, without any absolute danger, as is allowed in wine. Wherefore we think neither the Cretans, nor any other of men will ever doubt but that a trial of morals of this kind is convenient, and easy, safe, and brief beyond the rest. **Clinias:** That is indeed true. **Athenian:** This therefore will be something most useful: to know the natures and habits of souls by that art, by which those things are to be cured. But this is, as I judge, the office of civil faculty. Is it not? **Clinias:** It is so altogether.

**SECOND DIALOGUE CONCERNING THE LAWS, OR, CONCERNING THE GIVING OF LAWS.**
*
**ARGUMENT BY MARSILIO FICINO.**
*

OUR PLATO, with wondrous charity toward the human race, leaves nothing unattempted in his disputes which seems to lead by any reason to human safety. And while he contends for that studiously, he prefers to undergo the crime of being either too prolix or even most curious, rather than negligent. Therefore he pursues refined discipline of tender age even in the second book. For noticing that boys almost like beasts, as if they have nothing of weight but burst forth wherever pleasure pulls, and immediately flee from wherever pain pulls back—not without justice, before the proclivity of following evil or fleeing it grows into a habit, he places a charioteer over the horses of childhood, namely holding the reins of pleasure and pain in his hand. Which charioteer he names discipline, namely virtue, which first comes to boys, by which pleasure, and love, and pain and hatred flow rightly into their souls through another's reason, before they are moved by their own reason: then with reason present, they additionally consent to their own reason, on account of the higher custom of good morals. This very consent he wishes to be universal virtue. But that decent habituation concerning pleasures and pains, through which from the beginning until the end of life men hate what they ought to hate, and love what is to be loved, as long as it is ruled under the reason of another, he names discipline. Then indeed, when it now consents to its own awakened reason, he calls it by the name of virtue. That the foundation of moral life is of such great moment, even Aristotle himself in the Ethics greatly approves. But since the nature of boys is restless, and desirous of delights through all things, and therefore does not receive severe discipline, he rightly commands that boys be educated under the honest pleasure of that most common music bearing the traces of virtue: or rather also the elders sometimes, to whom for the solace of a laborious life certain honest delights are to be applied. For this cause he says that the gods instituted festivals and sacred holiday remissions for them. He brought in the Muses, and Apollo, and Bacchus as leaders to celebrate these things, who should amend the wantonness of morals, and moderate the nature greedy for motion through the music of the reason of motions, and delight it honestly. These words not only praise the use of music divinely commended and granted, but also allegorically teach that man would be more miserable than brutes for many reasons unless he had received divine worship and religion by divine providence and kinship. In which indeed the Muses signify the divine invention of truth granted to religious men by God: but Apollo the grateful expression and prophecy of that invention. Bacchus finally both the abstraction of the mind, and the admirable works of religious men. Observe that harmonic reason was primarily attributed to us by divine providence, through which we might harmonize all motions of a restless nature which by their own nature would be inharmonious. But from the Muses we have the consonance of the motion of the soul, from Apollo moreover the harmony in the movement of speech and song, from Bacchus finally the festive harmony in the motion of the limbs. While he disputes most diligently about this discipline through music, pertaining both to boys entirely and also to elders, and he repeats the institutes placed in the Republic, by which license should never be granted to poets, musicians, painters to imitate whatever they wish, but let them imitate only honest and grave things for the safety of those watching and hearing. But he wishes the judges of imitation to be skilled and most grave men, and commands that through honest imitation frequented daily he should accustom the youth in all games and studies alike always to the same things in which both the laws and the elders rejoice and grieve. Which habituation indeed he judges to contain the whole foundation of virtue. Among these he commends some things to memory very much leading to precepts of morals. An unjust man, even if he possesses all things which are held as goods among men, is unhappy: and he who lives thus, it must be said that it is better for him to die than to live. Likewise whoever separates the honorable, the useful, and the pleasant in turn while speaking, is not to be heard. And although an honorable and just life may sometimes seem laborious, that must never be said to boys, but rather that the most just life will be the most pleasant of all. Which Plato asserts will finally be necessary, although perhaps to those with whom he disputes it seems otherwise. And he commands silence on that. Yet truth is something beautiful and stable. He descends after this to the use of wine, which he wishes to be entirely ignored by youths before the eighteenth year of age. Otherwise he says fire is poured upon fire both into the soul and into the body. after this age he permits wine to be drunk moderately. After the fortieth year indeed he concedes in banquets among the hymns of the gods to drink wine more freely, as a remedy against the hardness of old age, through which we may seem to rejuvenate, and oblivion of sadness may take us, and that affection of the soul, like iron in fire, being led from hardness into softness may become more flexible. By which he wishes it to be brought about that elders who otherwise would not wish to sing, having been made more cheerful in banquets, would wish to sing to the ears of the juniors, and together to incite their souls, so to speak. Which incitation indeed through melody gravely harmonizing, the souls of the juniors are tempered. In these laws, for the sake of nobility, they name beauty in the things themselves, but pleasure in cognition. You will note that no animal except man has a sense of rhythm and harmony. And that rhythm is order in time and motion; but Harmony is order in the voices themselves through the tempering of high and low. What we often call harmony, in Latin we properly call *concentus* (concert/agreement). But what is rhythm, we can commodiously call *numerus* (number), provided you understand number in time and motion. You will note in what matter the utility of wine consists, and with what caution it must be drunk, namely with the founders of laws or guardians present at the banquet, sober indeed and observing and correcting the morals of the drinkers, and then opportunely when they have been made softer through wine, reforming them. He concludes finally let citizens use unmixed wine in banquets with cautions of this kind, as something to be granted useful for the things which have been said; but its use for each one's own libido is to be kept far from his citizens. Indeed since it most impudently strikes the sacred citadels of Pallas, which before all things are to be cultivated.

NEXT however we must consider concerning these, whether they have only that good, that we may perceive in what way we have our natures, or whether there is also great utility worthy of much study in the drinking of wine, if it be done rightly. What therefore do we say? It is in it indeed, as this reason seems to insinuate. Where however, and how, attend I beseech you, and let us not be impeded by that matter. **Clinias:** Say it then. **Athenian:** I desire therefore to repeat in memory what we say right discipline is. For of this, as I conjecture at present, is safety in this office when it is rightly instituted. **Clinias:** You say a great thing. **Athenian:** First indeed I say the sense of boys is of pleasure and pain: and these are the two in which virtue and vice are first born in the soul. But happy is he to whom it has happened in old age that he can attain wisdom and true opinions. Furthermore, he is a perfect man who possesses these and all the goods which are in these. I call discipline the virtue which first comes to boys. If pleasure, and love, and pain, and hatred flow rightly into their souls before they are moved by reason, and then with reason present, they consent to reason on account of the higher custom...

### Page 514
**Thirty-fourth Book.**

...of good morals, this very consensus is indeed universal virtue. But that decent habituation concerning pleasures and pains, through which from the beginning until the end of life men hate what they ought to hate, and love what they ought to love, if you call it discipline separately considered by reason, you will call it rightly, as I think. **Clinias:** For indeed what you guest formerly and what you have now discoursed concerning discipline seem to have been spoken rightly. **Athenian:** It is well then. But of such a kind of right institution of pleasures and pains, which is called discipline, men overstep it in life, and often pervert it. But the Gods, having pitied the human race pressed by nature with labors, established remissions of their labors, providing solemn festivals in turn instituted in honor of the gods themselves. They brought in the Muses moreover, and Apollo the leader of the Muses, and Bacchus as co-celebrators, and as emenders of morals among the solemnities in the council of the gods. It must be considered therefore whether this sermon is natural and true for us, which says: that all of a tenderer age, to embrace it in one word, cannot be quiet either in body or in voice, but always wish to be moved and to speak, some exulting and gesturing, and as if dancing and playing with pleasure, others shouting with various voices, and that the rest of the animals do not at all advert to order or the defect of order, which order is surely seen in morals, and is called rhythm and harmony of voices. But to us by those gods whom we said were given to us as co-celebrators, a sense participant in rhythm and harmony was attributed, and they move us with pleasure, and lead the choir for us, coupling us in turn with songs and dances: which choir they named from *chara* [χαρά], that is, joy. First however it must be considered, whether we concede that the first discipline is through the Muses and Apollo. Or in what way? **Clinias:** Thus altogether. **Athenian:** Therefore he who has never used a dance is to be called devoid of discipline. But on the contrary, he who has done it enough is possessed of discipline. **Clinias:** So we place it. **Athenian:** But every dance is at the same time a tripudium [measured step] and a concert [concentus]. **Clinias:** It is necessary. **Athenian:** When therefore someone is well instructed in discipline, he can both dance and sing well. **Clinias:** It seems so. **Athenian:** But let us see what it is that we just now said. **Clinias:** What is that? **Athenian:** When we say someone sings well, and dances well, must it be added whether he sings good things, and dances good things, or not? **Clinias:** It must be added. **Athenian:** What further if someone thinks honest things, as they are, so to be honest, and shameful things similarly shameful, and thus uses these, will he hold the choir and music better than he who in body and voice is able to execute sufficiently what he thinks is honest, yet neither rejoices in honest things nor hates shameful ones? Or he who in any voice and body cannot follow as is fitting, yet follows with pleasure and pain, so that he rejoices in good things, but hates depraved ones? **Clinias:** You relate a great difference of discipline, O guest. **Athenian:** If therefore we three do not ignore a good song and tripudium, we certainly know both him who has rightly obtained discipline, and him who has not. But if we ignore this, we shall never be able to know if there is any conservation of itself, and where it is. Is it not so? **Clinias:** Entirely so. **Athenian:** Next therefore like dogs through footprints let us investigate the decent figure, melody, song, and dance. For if these flee us, in vain shall we dispute concerning right discipline, whether Greek or barbarian. **Clinias:** So I judge. **Athenian:** What figure, therefore, and melody is it fitting to call good? Are the similar figures and voices of a brave soul and a fearful one in the same and equal labors? **Clinias:** How similar, when neither are the colors? **Athenian:** Skillfully, O friend, but in Music, there are both figures and concerts, since it turns around rhythm and harmony. Wherefore it is allowed to say the figure and song of good rhythm and harmony: but of good color we cannot speak rightly, imagining in the same way as masters of the choir are accustomed to do. But of a cowardly and a brave man there is a certain figure or song: and these are rightly named honest in brave men, and shameful in cowardly ones. But lest I be longer in these, all figures and concerts adhering simply to the virtue of the soul or body, or to the image of virtue, are honest: but the contrary ones, shameful. **Clinias:** Rightly indeed, and thus we judge it to hold itself at present. **Athenian:** Furthermore this also must be thought, whether we are all similarly delighted by all dances, or whether there is much difference. **Clinias:** Much altogether. **Athenian:** What therefore shall we say it is, which impels us into error? Whether the same things are not honest and good for all of us? Or are they indeed the same, yet do not seem to be the same? Nor indeed will anyone dare to say that a vicious dance participant in virtue is better. Nor will anyone ever confess that he indeed is delighted by depraved figures, but others by some contrary muse. Although many proclaim that the right reason of music consists in a certain force which brings pleasure to friends. Which is neither to be held nor said at all, for it is nefarious. This however is rather the cause of error. **Clinias:** What kind? **Athenian:** Since in a dance there are imitations of various morals, and of various things done in various fortunes and morals, by which those things which are said are either declared or expressed under the species of dancing, they are approved either by nature, or by custom, or by both, and they agree with the mind of those whom it is necessary to rejoice in them, to praise them, and to call them honest. But to those for whom these things happen contrary to nature or habit or some custom, these can neither rejoice in them, nor praise them, but rather it is necessary to call them shameful. But indeed to those for whom these things happen rightly by nature, but on the contrary by custom, or by custom indeed rightly, but on the contrary by nature, these bring forth praises contrary to their pleasures. For they assert each of these to be pleasant: but they also concede them to be depraved. And therefore in the presence of others, whom they think are composed of mind, they fear to move the body in that way: they fear also to sing those things, and to assert them honest and worthy of study. But they themselves are delighted by all those things in private. **Clinias:** You speak very true things. **Athenian:** Is any damage brought upon him who is delighted by depraved figures or songs: or utility to those who take pleasures in contraries? **Clinias:** That is indeed likely. **Athenian:** Whether is it only likely, or even necessary that it should so hold itself: just as when someone is in conflict with wicked men, and does not hate their morals, but is rather delighted by these and indulges them: and yet in place of a jest he disparages them, as if through a dream perceiving their depravity in himself. Then indeed it is necessary that he be made similar to those in whom he rejoices, even if he fears to praise them. By which thing indeed what greater thing, either good or evil, should we think reaches us out of all necessity? **Clinias:** I think nothing. **Athenian:** Do we think that where laws are well constituted, or will be so in the future, in the disciplines and jests of the poetic muses there will be such license that whatever delights the poet either in rhythm, or song, or poetic word, the same is also permitted for him to teach? and to bend the boys and adolescents of well-instituted citizens in choirs toward whatever happens, whether to virtue or to vice? **Clinias:** That is against reason. **Megillus:** Certainly. **Athenian:** But that, to speak briefly, is allowed almost everywhere except in Egypt. **Clinias:** But in what way do you say this law was sanctioned in Egypt? **Athenian:** This is indeed wondrous to hear. For they long ago, as it seems to me, knew that it was necessary (what we just now said) for youths in cities to become accustomed to good figures and good songs. What kind and of what quality such are, was instituted by them in sacred things, and beyond those it was allowed neither to painters nor to other makers of figures or of whatever handiworks to introduce any new things, nor even to devise others beyond the ancestral ones, nor today is it allowed either in these or in universal music. And so if you observe, you will find there things which were depicted or formatted in whatever way ten thousand years ago, as if they were not so ancient, so to speak, neither more beautiful nor more shameful than those which are depicted today, but finished with the same art. **Clinias:** Wondrous to hear is what you say. **Athenian:** Indeed it is civil in the highest degree and especially convenient to the positioning of laws. You will find there certain other light things: but this concerning music is true, and worthy of animadversion: namely that it was possible to take caution concerning matters of this kind by a certain and stable law, and that the mind of the legislator was to introduce such concerts as exhibited rectitude of nature. Which indeed is the work either of a god or of some divine man. Just as they say there that those most ancient concerts among them are the poems of Isis. Wherefore, as I was saying, if someone can in any way understand the rectitude of those things, he must dare to reduce these to order and law. For a new affection of appetite itself always around pleasure and pain, which indeed always studies to use new music, has perhaps no great force to corrupt those dances by the accusation of antiquity, which are constituted by sacred laws. Indeed it seems to have been possible for the dances of the Egyptians to be corrupted in no way by so much time, but on the contrary altogether. **Clinias:** The matter holds itself thus, as is gathered from your words. **Athenian:** Let us therefore say confidently, that the dance coheres rightly with games and music. We rejoice as often as we judge ourselves to live happily: and as often as we rejoice we again judge ourselves to live happily. Is it not so? **Clinias:** Entirely so. **Athenian:** And while we rejoice, we are not able to be quiet. **Clinias:** It is as you say. **Athenian:** Are not therefore those who are youths among us apt for dancing? But we who are elders think it fitting to be occupied decently in watching these, while we rejoice in their games and celebrity, since the lightness of body has left us, from the desire of which we place contests for those who can most greatly recall that youthful age in memory for us. **Clinias:** You relate true things. **Athenian:** Do we think therefore that it was said in vain by many concerning those performing sacred games for the human race, that he is to be judged the wisest and the master of victory especially, who makes us rejoice and be glad as much as possible? For after it is permitted to play in those things, it seems to be convenient that we especially honor him who provokes as many as possible and most greatly to joy, and as I was just saying, say that he is the victor. Is that said rightly? and would it be done rightly if it were so done? **Clinias:** Perhaps. **Athenian:** But, O blessed one, let us not bring forth a sentence so precipitately, but let us consider this very thing by distinguishing it into parts in this way. If someone should sometimes propose a contest of whatever kind, but should add neither gymnastic, nor musical, nor equestrian, but with all citizens congregated, for the sake of pleasure should institute a contest only, and propose a prize for him who should most delight the spectators, and be judged to have done it best of all, when no mode of delighting is expressed, what do we think would happen from the herald's proclamation? **Clinias:** Concerning what matter do you speak? **Athenian:** It is likely that one like Homer would show a Rhapsody, another a Cithara, another Tragedy, another indeed Comedy. Nor will there be lacking one who thinks he will obtain victory by showing a marvel. When such and others of the same kind of contestants have flocked together, can we say who would go away as the victor by rite? **Clinias:** You ask an absurd thing. For who will be able to answer that skillfully before he himself present has heard the individual contestants? **Athenian:** Do you wish therefore that I myself answer to that absurd thing? **Clinias:** Why not? **Athenian:** If very small boys should give a sentence, they will judge the juggler to have conquered the rest. Will they not? **Clinias:** What stands in the way? **Athenian:** But older boys will prefer the comedian to the rest. But erudite women and adolescents, and almost the whole multitude, will perhaps praise Tragedy. **Clinias:** Perhaps it will so happen. **Athenian:** But we elders will perhaps hear most pleasantly a Rhapsode who has sung some Homeric thing well, the Iliad or Odyssey, or something Hesiodic, and we shall proclaim him the victor of all. Which therefore rightly becomes the victor—does it not remain to be declared? **Clinias:** Certainly. **Athenian:** It is indeed plain, as it seems to me also, and it is necessary for you to concede, that he is truly the victor who shall be judged to have conquered by our equals. For the use of things which we have from age is everywhere a certain great thing and the best in all civil matters. **Clinias:** Without doubt. **Athenian:** I concede therefore this to many, that Music is to be judged by pleasure, yet not by the pleasure of any men whatever, but I say that that Muse is almost the most beautiful which delights the best and sufficiently erudite, especially indeed, which delights the man outstanding in virtue and discipline. On which account we affirm that the judges of these things lack virtue. For it is necessary that they be participants both in prudence and in fortitude. In prudence indeed, because the true judge ought not to learn from another what things are to be determined by judgment, and as if stupefied by the clamor of many as well as by his own ignorance, thus bring forth a sentence. But in fortitude, because he ought not, even if he understands through himself, on account of cowardice and fear from the same mouth by which he invoked the gods as he was about to judge, cowardly promulgate an iniquitous judgment. For not as a disciple, but as a master of the spectators, as is fitting, the judge sits, opposed to the inept pleasures of the spectators. **[Note: The phrase "sed vt magister spectantorum, ficut par est, iudex sedet, ineptis spectantium voluptatibus aduerfus" is repeated four times in the OCR, likely a printer's error.]** It was allowed by ancient and Greek law, just as now by Sicilian and Italian: which permitting the matter to the multitude of spectators, and declaring the victor by raised hands, has indeed depraved the poets themselves, who compose all things for the judgment of the vulgar for a depraved pleasure, so that the spectators themselves educate the poets and themselves. It has also corrupted the pleasures of the spectacle itself. For since it is necessary that those who are present always hear better things for their morals, and thus follow a better pleasure, now the contrary happens to them from the theater. What therefore do these things so spoken wish for themselves? For long ago, it seems to me, they recognized what we have just now said: that in cities, the young must be accustomed to beautiful forms <note>original: "bonis figuris." This refers to both visual art and the "postures" or gestures used in dance.</note> and beautiful melodies. What these are, and of what kind, was established by them in their sacred rites; and beyond these, it is permitted neither for painters, nor for any others who create forms, or wh... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the Athenian is about to explain that Egyptian artists were forbidden from innovating or changing the traditional "correct" styles of art and music.</note>

<summary>The Athenian Guest argues that poets should not have total freedom to teach whatever they please, praising ancient Egypt for legally fixing the standards of "beautiful" art and music to prevent moral decay.</summary>
