### [Page 516]

### Book Two [continued]

...education is the training of boys which leads them to that manner of living which right law dictates as correct, and which men of outstanding equity and elders, through the experience of things, have approved as right. Therefore, so that the mind of boys may follow the law in such a way that it does not rejoice in contrary things, but in those same things which the law and the elder teach, the lawgiver shall altogether persuade—and if necessary, compel—the poetic man to describe the deeds of temperate, brave, and entirely good men in noble words, portraying their forms in rhythms and their accents in harmonies as is fitting, through those songs which we call Odes, which are in truth incantations; that is, they are incantations regarding souls, composed for this purpose with industry so that the souls of men, through grieving and rejoicing, may obey the laws. But because younger souls do not take up serious studies, let these things be said and done as jests and songs; and in these the same thing is effected which he who heals men sick in body is accustomed to do. For they smear suitable foods with pleasant seasonings, but they infect harmful things with bitter ones, so that they may grow accustomed to accept the former and reject the latter.

**CLIN.** Do you think, O Guest, that these things are now preserved in other cities? For as far as I know, the things you prescribe are done nowhere except among us and the Lacedaemonians. For new things are always being devised both in dances and in other music, changed not by laws, but by certain wandering pleasures, which are by no means the same, nor do they remain in the same way, but are always made varied against those customs of the Egyptians which you narrated.

**ATHEN.** Rightly so, O Clinias. If, however, I seemed to you to have said above that the things you now mention are done everywhere, do not wonder if I explained what I feel less clearly. I said indeed what I wished to happen in music, and I seemed to you to speak of them as if they were happening. For it is in no way pleasant to vituperate a thing that is incurable and has proceeded far in error, though sometimes it is necessary. But since we agree on these things, do I not ask whether you assert that these things are done more among you and those [the Spartans] than among other Greeks?

**CLIN.** Why should we not assert it?

**ATHEN.** If they were done similarly among the others, would they not be conducted better than they are now?

**CLIN.** Certainly much more excellently, if they were arranged in the same way as they are among those and among us, and as you prescribed a little before.

**ATHEN.** Come then, let us see whether these are the things which are preached among you in every discipline and music. You compel poets to say in their songs that the good man, because he is temperate and just, is happy and blessed, whether he be great and robust, or small and weak, whether he be poor or rich. But that the unjust man, even if he be richer than Cinyras or Midas, is wretched and leads his life in sorrow. Thus, the poet will say to us, if he speaks rightly: "Should I make mention of that man, or call him a man, who does not possess and dispose of all things called good with justice?" Let him, therefore, adorned with justice, delight to fight hand-to-hand with enemies. But let the unjust man not dare to see bloody slaughter, nor be able to surpass the Thracian Boreas in running; nor let any of those things called good ever be present to him. For those things which are commonly called good are not rightly called good. For they say that the best is health...

[Margin: Ficinus here inverts some things, perhaps following another codex.]
[Margin: What poets ought to sing.]
[Margin: *In Greek, riches are third.]

...next to it, beauty; strength as the third good, and riches as the fourth. Almost innumerable other goods of this kind are recounted. For both sharp seeing and hearing, and the integrity of the other senses, seem to be goods, and to be able to do whatever you desire with tyrannical license added to all these. And they say the sum of all happiness is if, with the possession of all these, you should immediately become immortal. But I and you together agree that for just and holy men the possession of all just things is best, but for the unjust, the possession of all is worst, beginning from health. For to be healthy, and to see and hear, and to perceive all things easily, and altogether to live as an immortal, is worst if you have lived forever possessing all these but devoid of justice and the other virtues. It is, however, a lesser evil if you end your life in such a state in the shortest possible time. These things, certainly, you will both exhort your own to say and compel the poets to say, and through numbers and harmonies consistent with these, to erudite the youth. Do you yourselves notice this? For I assert that those things called evils by the common people are good for the just, but evil for the [un]just. But those things called good are truly good for the good, but evil for the evil. Do we agree thus far in what I was seeking, or not?

**CLIN.** In part we seem to agree, in part not at all.

**ATHEN.** Perhaps I do not persuade you that he is not happy, but wretched, who is unjust and insolent, even if he has health, and riches, and perpetual tyranny, and moreover possesses invincible bodily strength and courage and immortality, and suffers nothing of those things which are commonly called evils.

**CLIN.** You speak the truth.

**ATHEN.** Let it be so; but what must be said next? If he is strong in strength, and beautiful and rich, and does throughout his whole life all that he desires, does it not seem to you that if he be unjust and insolent, he necessarily lives basely because of this alone? Do you grant at least that he lives basely?

**CLIN.** Entirely.

**ATHEN.** What then? Does he not also live badly?

**CLIN.** That is not so similar.

**ATHEN.** Do you not grant to him that he lives unpleasantly and disadvantageously?

**CLIN.** How shall we grant these things?

**ATHEN.** How? If some god...

[Margin: To the unjust, even if all other things which are called good remain, he is unhappy, or for that reason, because he is unjust.]

...O friends, should grant us a consensus of mind (as it seems); for now we disagree among ourselves. For these things seem to me more necessary, O friend Clinias, than that Crete is an island; and if I were giving laws to the Cretans myself, I would compel both poets and all other citizens to speak thus; and I would threaten almost the greatest of all punishments if anyone in that region should assert that there are sometimes some wicked men who live pleasantly, or that some things are useful and conducive, and others more just. And I would indeed persuade my citizens to say many things against those which now seem to be said by the Cretans and Lacedaemonians, and indeed by other men as well. Come then, by Jove and Apollo, O best of men, if we should ask these gods who gave us laws: "Is the most pleasant life the most just? Or are there two certain lives, one the most pleasant, the other the most just?" And if they themselves, to us so inquiring, should respond that there are two, we might perhaps ask them again, if we wished to inquire rightly, which of them ought to be called more blessed: those living most justly, or those living most pleasantly? And if they should respond "those living most pleasantly," the response will be base. I would wish, however, that such a thing be said by the fathers and bearers of laws rather than by the gods. Therefore, consider that what I asked, I asked of the father and lawgiver, and that it was responded to me that he is most blessed who lives most pleasantly. Then I would oppose him thus: "O father, did you not wish me to live as blessedly as possible?" "Certainly." "But you never ceased commanding me to live as justly as possible." Whoever grants these things together, whether a legislator or a father, speaks absurdly and is not consistent with himself. But if he should respond that the most just life is the most blessed, whoever hears it will ask, I think, what good and beautiful thing in that life, as if better than pleasure, does the law itself praise? For what of good...

### [Page 517]

...can be present to the just man that is surpassed by pleasure? Tell me, I pray, is praise and glory, both among men and among gods, a certain good and honorable thing, but unpleasant? And infamy, on the contrary? "By no means," we shall say, O legislator. But to neither inflict nor suffer injustice, is this pleasant indeed, but good and honorable; while other things are pleasant indeed, but base and evil?

**ATHEN.** In what way?

**CLIN.** Therefore, the reasoning which separates neither the pleasant from the just, nor the good from the honorable, is probable; and if for nothing else, yet for this, that one might wish to live holily and justly, it conduces much. Wherefore it is a most base speech for a legislator, and very contrary, if he should deny that these things are so. For no one will do that willingly in which there is not more of joy than of pain. But that which is seen from afar brings, so to speak, to everyone—even to children—a murky dizziness. Wherefore, with the dizziness and darkness removed, the legislator will lead the opinions of the citizens to the contrary, and he will persuade them by praises, by custom, and by reasons, that both just and unjust things are overshadowed, and that unjust things appear contrary to the just. For to the unjust and wicked man, pleasant things seem to be those which to the just seem most unpleasant. But to the just man, both seem entirely the contrary.

**CLIN.** So it appears.

**ATHEN.** But in truth, which opinion shall we think better? That of the better or the worse mind?

**CLIN.** Necessarily of the better.

**ATHEN.** It is necessary, therefore, that the unjust life is not only baser and worse than the just and holy life, but also more unpleasant.

**CLIN.** So it certainly seems, O friend, from this reasoning.

**ATHEN.** Therefore, a lawgiver for whom a small utility might come forth, even if it were not so as we just said, nevertheless would not think it foreign to his gravity for the utility of the youth to say something false, if ever anything else ought to be said falsely; especially since he could devise no lie more useful than this falsehood, namely, that he might be able to draw the listeners so that, not by force but willingly, they might wish to embrace justice.

**CLIN.** Truth, O Guest, is indeed something beautiful and stable. But it seems for the most part not to persuade easily.

**ATHEN.** Be it so. But indeed that Sidonian fable, even if it had no likelihood, nevertheless persuaded easily, and many others similarly.

**CLIN.** Which ones?

**ATHEN.** That once from [sown] teeth armed soldiers were born. For that is a great example for a lawgiver, that he can persuade the minds of the youth of whatever he wishes. Therefore, he ought to search for nothing other than by what things, once persuasion is accepted, he may confer the greatest good upon the city; and to lean upon this with all study, so that the whole city may sing one and the same thing about these matters as much as possible and always, in songs, fables, and every discourse. I indeed feel thus. If you feel otherwise, let there be no envy in contradicting.

**CLIN.** Neither of us seems able ever to doubt these things.

**ATHEN.** I shall proceed, therefore, asserting that all choruses, which are three, ought to instill into the still tender and soft minds of boys both the other goods which we mentioned, and whatever we can narrate, as if by a certain incantation. Let that be the chief point: namely, if we shall assert that the same life is judged by the gods to be the best and most pleasant, we shall both speak the truth and persuade those for whom there is need more than if we spoke otherwise.

**CLIN.** Your words must be granted.

**ATHEN.** Let the first, the childish chorus of the Muses, enter to sing these things studiously to the whole city. Let the second chorus of those who have advanced up to thirty years invoke Paean as the witness of truth of the gods, and suppliantly pray that he be propitious to the younger ones. Let the third be the chorus...

[Margin: He follows a codex different from the common one.]
[Margin: What things pertain to a prudent judge.]

...of those who spend their age between thirty and sixty years. But the elders beyond these, because they can no longer sing fables about the same customs, let us judge that they should be dismissed by a divine oracle.

**CLIN.** Which third choruses do you mean, Guest? For we do not clearly grasp whom you wish to speak of.

**ATHEN.** These are surely they for whose sake most of the things above were introduced.

**CLIN.** We do not yet understand. Wherefore try to speak more clearly.

**ATHEN.** It was said at the beginning of the discussion, if we remember, that the nature of all youth is so ardent that it can rest neither in body nor in voice, but always shouts and leaps without order; and that no other animal except the nature of man alone has a sense of the order of both these things. But the name of the order which is seen in motion can be Rhythm, that is, number; but of that which is in the voice, the sharp and grave tempered together, Harmony, that is, concord. But both together, it called the Dance (*Chorea*). We also said the gods, pitying us, gave us Apollo and the Muses as fellow-celebrants and leaders of the dance. And if we remember, we numbered Dionysus as the third.

**CLIN.** Why should we not remember?

**ATHEN.** And yet the choruses of Apollo and the Muses have already been mentioned. But the third, which remains, will necessarily be attributed to Dionysus.

**CLIN.** In what way? Explain more broadly. For at first hearing, a Dionysian chorus of elders seems very absurd, if those advanced beyond the thirtieth year, and now up to the fiftieth, and even to the sixtieth, should use it.

**ATHEN.** You speak the truth. But I think there is need of a reason for these things, so that it may appear in what way it might happen opportunely.

**CLIN.** Why not?

**ATHEN.** Do those former things remain agreed between us?

**CLIN.** Which ones?

**ATHEN.** That it is necessary for all men and boys, free and slaves, males and females, and the entire city to sing to the whole city daily in various ways and songs the things we have said, so that from an innumerable variety of hymns, they may be affected by singing together with a certain insatiable pleasure.

**CLIN.** Nothing prevents it being granted that it ought to be so.

**ATHEN.** But whereby shall this best part of the city, in which there is the greatest authority for persuading because of age and prudence, be the cause of the greatest goods by singing the best things? Or shall we foolishly omit that in which the power of the best and most useful songs chiefly resides?

**CLIN.** It is not permitted to omit it, so long as it soon appears.

**ATHEN.** How then will it be done decently? See, I pray, whether thus.

**CLIN.** In what way?

**ATHEN.** Every elder, being already affected by satiety regarding songs, is least delighted by them; and when the matter requires singing, the older and more modest he is, the more he fears to sing. Is it not so?

**CLIN.** Entirely so.

**ATHEN.** But much more indeed will he not tolerate singing out of shame in the theater before a multitude, especially if choruses of elders, like those who contend for victory, and they indeed so that the voice may be clearer, should be compelled to sing thin and fasting. For thus they will sing not without trouble and shame, and they will approach those things more slowly.

**CLIN.** You narrate necessary things.

**ATHEN.** In what way then shall we render them ready for...

[Margin: Wine is forbidden to boys.]
[Margin: Wine is a remedy against the hardness of old age.]

...singing? First, we shall sanction by law that boys up to the eighteenth year should altogether ignore the use of wine. Namely, we shall warn them that it is not fitting to suggest fire upon fire into the body and soul before, having become men, they begin to undergo labors. For again, one must beware of the habit of youth. Then let them use wine moderately up to the thirtieth year of age. But from drunkenness and repletion of wine, let the youth altogether abstain. But when they have arrived at the fortieth, then...

### [Page 518]

...reclining more freely in banquets, let them invoke both the other gods and Dionysus to the sacred rites and games of the elders, who has bestowed wine upon all as a remedy against the hardness of old age, so that we may seem to grow young again, and forgetfulness of sorrow may take us, and the very affection of the mind, just as iron in fire, may become more flexible, led from hardness into softness. First, indeed, everyone thus affected, having taken confidence, will less fear to sing among some and his own—though not many and strangers—and to sing together what we have now repeated many times, to incant.

**CLIN.** And especially indeed.

**ATHEN.** For the purpose of inducing us to be willing to participate in songs, this method will not be indecent.

**CLIN.** Certainly not.

**ATHEN.** But with what voice and with what muse shall these men sing? Will it be that which is more suitable to them? That only.

**CLIN.** What then will be suitable for divine men? Is it not that which the choruses sing?

**CLIN.** [Corrected: **ATHEN.**] We indeed, Guest, and they cannot sing anything other than what we learned in the chorus. For we are accustomed to this song.

**ATHEN.** It is equal. For you have not learned the best song; for you have a Republic that is rather like a military camp than an urban one. Therefore, like many chicks feeding in a flock, you have amatory youths. Whence no one of you takes his wildness, and to restrain its ferocity, commits it to someone like a master of horses, who might erudite him, treating him gently and making him tame, and performing other things which are suitable for education, and whereby he might be made not only a good soldier, but also a suitable governor of cities and towns; whom indeed we said at the beginning would be more heroic than Tyrtaeus’s soldiers, inasmuch as he would cultivate the gift of fortitude not always as the first place of virtue, and everywhere privately and publicly.

**CLIN.** I know not how, Guest, you again disparage our lawgivers.

**ATHEN.** I do not do it from my soul, good man, if indeed I do it. But let us proceed where reason leads, if you wish. For if we have a muse of the choruses and theater better than the common muse, let us try to exhibit it to those whom we said fear that one and seek another better one.

**CLIN.** Altogether.

**ATHEN.** In all things whatsoever a certain grace follows, it is necessary that it be in them, so that either that grace alone attracts in them and is the chief thing, or rectitude, or utility. I will explain by an example what I say. Food and drink and all nourishment have grace, which we call pleasure; but rectitude and utility, if it confers to health.

**CLIN.** Entirely.

**ATHEN.** So also in learning, grace is in it, which is called pleasure. Rectitude also and utility and a good and beautiful habit, which are effected by truth itself.

**CLIN.** Thus it is.

**ATHEN.** What further in the arts, by which similar things are effected? Shall we not look into that same thing? Pleasure surely sometimes proceeds from them, which it is equal to call grace.

**CLIN.** Certainly.

**ATHEN.** But by the rectitude of such things, to speak in general, equality itself of so much and such a kind effects it rather than pleasure.

**CLIN.** Excellently.

**ATHEN.** By pleasure alone, therefore, that will be deservedly judged which effects neither utility, nor truth, nor similitude, nor again damage, but is only the cause of that grace which accompanies other things, which we can rightly name pleasure, when namely nothing of those things follows it.

**CLIN.** Do you mean pleasure alone, which does not harm?

**ATHEN.** Namely, and I call it again jest and play, when it brings nothing of harm or utility worthy of estimation.

**CLIN.** You speak the truth.

**ATHEN.** It follows from these things we have said, that no imitation is to be judged by pleasure and untrue opinion. Similarly also no equality. For not because it seems so to this person, or because this person rejoices, is equality therefore equal itself, or the commensurable itself commensurable, but by nothing else than truth alone.

**CLIN.** It is altogether so.

**ATHEN.** And yet we say all music is imitative and an effecter of similar things.

**CLIN.** Who doubts it?

**ATHEN.** When therefore anyone says music is judged by pleasure alone, he is by no means to be heard; but such music is to be sought, if it is cultivated anywhere, but that which through imitation possesses the similitude of the good.

**CLIN.** These are true.

**ATHEN.** Those therefore who seek the best species of song and muse should seek not that which is pleasant, but that which is right. For rectitude of imitation consists in this, as we were saying, if so much and such a thing is made which is expressed by imitation, as much and such as it is in itself.

**CLIN.** Who doubts?

**ATHEN.** And yet everyone will grant this about music, that all its poems are an imitation and a kind of assimilation. Which all poets, and listeners, and actors would grant.

**CLIN.** Greatly.

**ATHEN.** It is necessary, therefore, regarding every poem and figment, as it seems, that he who is not going to err in it should know what it is that is being portrayed. For he who does not know what its essence intends, nor of what it is an image, will never understand its rectitude and error.

**CLIN.** Never certainly.

**ATHEN.** But he who does not understand the rectitude of the work, will he know whether it is well or ill done? I speak somewhat obscurely. Perhaps, however, it will be said more plainly to me thus.

**CLIN.** In what way?

**ATHEN.** Many things pertaining to sight happen by similitude.

**CLIN.** Certainly.

**ATHEN.** If anyone does not hold the manner of a depicted body, will he ever know whether it is rightly painted? As, for instance, whether it has the joints of the body and individual particles, and the number, and the quality, and the location of each as is fitting for each, colors moreover and figures; or on the contrary whether all these are painted confusedly? Or do you think anyone will know these things, who does not know the animal that is being painted?

**CLIN.** In no way.

**ATHEN.** But if someone knows that what is painted, or in whatever way formed, is a man, and has received all its parts and figures and colors from art, will he not necessarily immediately recognize if any defect of beauty is in it?

**CLIN.** Almost all of us, Guest, would in this way recognize those things which are beautifully held in animals.

**ATHEN.** You speak rightly. Is it not necessary, therefore, in every image whether through painting, or through music, or in whatever way else it may be made, that a prudent judge have these three things? First, that he know what it is that falls into imitation; second, that he know whether it is done rightly; third, whether any similitude is well effected by words, harmonies, and numbers?

**CLIN.** It seems so.

**ATHEN.** Let it not be a burden, therefore, to explain the difficulty which is in music. Furthermore, because these similitudes are celebrated more than others, there is need of greater diligence than in the others. For he who errs in this is most harmed, since he drinks in bad customs by the sweetness of lust. But it is difficult to know, because poets do not hold the poetic art as the Muses do. For they could never err so much that in portraying the words of men, they would render the color and harmonies of women, or in harmonies and figures of children, render the numbers of slaves and illiberal people, or in numbers and figures of free people, render a harmony or speech contrary to the numbers. Never, moreover, would they confound the voices of wild beasts and men, and of instruments to be struck, and all noises as if they were imitating one thing, into one.

### [Page 519]

...Human poets indeed perturb many such things and mix them without reason, and move men to laughter: whom Orpheus called those who had attained the grace of delight. For they see all things confused, and the poets themselves also distract them, separating the number and the figures from the harmony, composing naked orations without harmony metrically, and also accommodating harmonies and numbers without words to the naked striking of the cithara and the sound of the pipe. In which matter it is most difficult to know what the number and harmony which is without words intends, and to what imitation it is similar of those which are worthy of reason. But one must think that everything whatever is filled with much rudeness, whether it follows velocity or slowness, and the voice of wild beasts closely, so that you use the pipe and cithara otherwise than is necessary for the dance and song. But to use both nakedly is an abuse very similar to a prestigiatory display, and very foreign to the Muses. But of these things, this is the reason. We, however, were not considering this, that those born thirty and fifty years and beyond ought not to use our Muses, but let us see when they ought to use them. From those things, however, this speech seems to signify to us that those advanced to the fiftieth year whom it behooves to sing, it behooves to hold the Muse of the chorus better than the others. For it is necessary that they acutely perceive and know harmonies and numbers. For how else will anyone know the rectitude of a song, whether the Doric fits it or not, and the number which the poet joined to it, whether he joined it rightly or not?

**CLIN.** In no way certainly.

**ATHEN.** But the common people are to be laughed at, when they think that they sufficiently know what is of good harmony and number, and what is the contrary. These, I say, who were long ago compelled to sing and dance to numbers; but that they ignore the particulars of those things, they do not so consider among themselves, that any song, if it contains all things suitable to it, is rightly held; if it does not contain them, the contrary.

**CLIN.** So it is altogether necessary.

**ATHEN.** What further? If anyone does not understand the reason of it, or what it has, will he ever know in what way it is rightly held in anything, which we have said?

**CLIN.** How could that happen?

**ATHEN.** This, therefore, we now seem to have found in these things, that those senior singers, whom we first provoke unwillingly so that they may sing in a certain way willingly, must have learned these things to such an extent that any of them may follow the weights of the progress of numbers as well as the harmonic sounds of strings: so that understanding harmonies and numbers, they may be able to choose those which ought to be sung by such and so great persons, and thus singing, they themselves may immediately perceive innocent pleasures, and lead the youth to honest customs by songs and delights. To that extent, however, being taught, they will have a more exquisite discipline there than the common people and the poets. That third thing indeed, whether it be a good or bad imitation, it is not necessary that the poet know, but harmony and number it is necessary. But these [the elders] ought to know all three, so that they may be able to choose the best and second. Otherwise they will never be able sufficiently, as if by certain incantations, to allure the souls of the youth to virtue. Truly, what we wished from the beginning, that namely our speech should bring right aid to the chorus of Dionysus, has been said according to our strength. But let us consider whether this has been so done. Such a harmony of men necessarily is rendered more turbulent as the drinking-party progresses. Which we also supposed from the beginning, in those things which happen today, must necessarily happen.

**CLIN.** Necessarily.

**ATHEN.** Where certainly everyone, having become lighter than himself, is extolled and exults, and is filled with audacity, nor hears his neighbor, but thinks himself a sufficient leader both of himself and of all others.

**CLIN.** Without doubt.

**ATHEN.** Have we not said, as often as these things happen, that the souls of the drinkers, just as iron in fire, so fermenting with wine, become softer and younger, and therefore are more easily led, just as when they were young: if anyone both can and knows how to erudite and mold them. But the painter is the same who was then called the upright legislator. In whose laws the manner of the drinking-party is to be prescribed, so that these laws may be able to restrain that confident and audacious one, made more impudent than is fitting, who does not wish to keep order in turn by silence, speech, drinking, and music, and so instruct him that he may wish to do in all things the contrary of what he does, moving against that rising and base confidence the best fear with justice, which fear indeed we have called divine, shame and modesty.

[Margin: Just as iron by fire, so the bodies of elders are softened by wine.]

**CLIN.** It is as you say.

**ATHEN.** The authors and guardians of these laws ought to be removed from perturbation and drunkenness, the leaders of the wine-bibbers. Without whom to fight against drunkenness is harder than to contend with enemies without prudent and considerate leaders. If anyone, however, does not wish to obey, let him bear a disgrace equal to or even greater than he who does not obey the leaders of Mars, especially here to the leaders of Dionysus born beyond sixty years.

**CLIN.** Rightly.

**ATHEN.** Would not, if such drunkenness and such play were applied, the drinkers gain great utility therefrom, and joined to one another with greater benevolence than before, would they not depart enemies as now: when they had conversed together legitimately, and the drunken also had obeyed the laws with sober leaders?

**CLIN.** So certainly, if such were the drunkenness as you just narrated.

**ATHEN.** Let us not therefore simply vituperate the gift of Father Liber [Dionysus] as if it were evil, nor unworthy to be received into the city. And yet more could be referred to this opinion, although I fear to extol into many that greatest good which Dionysus grants, since men, when they have heard, may not receive it rightly, nor understand.

**CLIN.** What is that?

**ATHEN.** A certain rumor and fame has flowed down to us, that this god was once disturbed in mind by the Goddess Juno; and that therefore for the sake of vengeance he introduced the whole chorus of bacchants and all insanity, and bestowed wine for this very purpose. I, however, permit those to say these things who think it safe to say such things of the gods. That, however, I know: that no animal is born with as much and such intelligence as and of what kind suits it when it has advanced. Furthermore, in this time, in which prudence does not yet possess its own, everything rages and shouts without order, and when anyone has killed it [quenched its rage], again it exults incomposedly and without order. Let us remember, however, that we said these were the principles of music and gymnastics.

**CLIN.** We remember.

**ATHEN.** Have we not also said that the sense of number and harmony is given to us alone, from this principle? And that Apollo and the Muses and Dionysus were given to us as leaders for these things?

**CLIN.** Indeed.

**ATHEN.** But wine, as many say, was given to men for vengeance, so that they might be insane. But as our speech holds, it is a remedy and medicine to the contrary, so that the soul indeed may obtain shame, and the body health and strength.

[Margin: Why wine was given to men.]

**CLIN.** Excellently, Guest, you have commemorated the former speech.

**ATHEN.** But already the middle part of those things which pertain to the dance has been said. But the rest, as it seems, shall we finish? Or shall we pass over it?

**CLIN.** What parts do you mean, and how do you divide both?

### [Page 520]

**ATHEN.** Since the whole dance was called by us universal discipline, one part of the dance is in the voice through numbers and harmonies.

**CLIN.** So it is.

**ATHEN.** The other is in the movement of the body through number and figure. But it has number in common with the movement of the voice, but figure as its own. In that first part, however, the song itself is the movement of the voice.

**CLIN.** You narrate true things.

**ATHEN.** But the habit of the voice, which arrives at the discipline of the virtue of the soul, we have named music, I know not in what way.

**CLIN.** Very rightly.

**ATHEN.** If, however, the movement of the body in play, which we have called dancing, reaches to the virtue of the body, let us name this artificial leading of it thereto gymnastics.

**CLIN.** Most rightly.

**ATHEN.** Regarding music, which we called the middle part of the dance, we thought it enough has been done; and let it be so said of it. Wherefore let us now speak of the rest, or what is to be done?

**CLIN.** O best of men, you who discourse with Cretans and Lacedaemonians, since enough has already been treated of music, but of gymnastics thus far not at all, what do you think either of us would respond to an interrogation of this kind?

**ATHEN.** I shall indeed affirm that you, when you have asked these things, have already responded openly. For I understand that this interrogation of yours is a certain response, as a command at the same time, that those things which pertain to gymnastics be transacted.

**CLIN.** You have understood excellently, and so you should do.

**ATHEN.** It must be done; nor indeed is it difficult to transact those things which are most known to both of you. Namely, you are much more skilled in this art than in that one.

**CLIN.** You say almost true things.

**ATHEN.** Is not the principle of this play also that every animal is accustomed by nature to leap? But man, as we touched upon, when he received the sense of number, generated and brought forth dancing. Song likewise excites number. Which both, coupled together, brought forth the dance and play.

**CLIN.** It is so.

**ATHEN.** We have already finished one part of this; we shall next approach the other.

**CLIN.** Altogether.

**ATHEN.** Let us first conclude the discourse about the dance of drunkenness with this sentiment, if it pleases.

**CLIN.** In what way?

**ATHEN.** If any city should use drinking-parties as a serious matter and with the order of laws, for the sake of a certain exercise unto temperance, and should not flee other pleasures, but should be exercised in the same way so as to overcome them, in this way all these things are to be used. But if the city should use drinking-parties as a play, and it should be permitted to everyone to drink when he wishes and with whom he wishes, and to exercise other things according to lust, I would not be of this opinion, that it is fitting for that city or this man to indulge in drunkenness at any time. But much more than the use of the Cretans and Lacedaemonians, I would approve the law of the Carthaginians: that no one in camp should ever dare to taste wine, but that water should be drunk in all that time; and in the city I would never grant the use of wine to a male or female slave; nor even to magistrates in all that year in which they perform their magistracy. I would also entirely prohibit governors and judges about to perform their duty from wine. Also those about to deliberate on matters not to be neglected. And I would grant wine to no one at all by day, unless for the sake of bodily exercise or diseases this drink was needed; nor even at night to a man or woman when they wish to give attention to children. Many more things could also be referred to, in which men possessing right law and mind would abstain from wine. Wherefore according to this reason, there would be no need for many vineyards for the cities. And indeed the rest of agriculture, and every norm of living, would hold its own order, and the use of wine would be almost the most moderate and sparing of all. To this discourse about wine, Guests, if it also seems so to you, let the colophon be imposed.

**CLIN.** Well said. Wherefore it also seems so to us.

---

### THIRD DIALOGUE ON LAWS, OR, ON LEGISLATION.

### Argument of Marsilio Ficino.

Just as a physician looks to the health of the body, so the author of laws looks to the health of the soul. Since indeed it is more desirable for all to retain prosperous health lest it perish, than to receive it back when perishing, therefore the chief institute of both, the civil and the medical, is to preserve the health either of body or soul...

[Ficino’s long argument continues, summarizing the transition to Book III, focusing on the origin of cities after a cataclysm, the development of four stages of civil discipline—from patriarchal rule to city-states—and the vital importance of prudence over ignorance in governance.]

### [Page 521]

...Prudence, therefore, is so great that it teaches both to desire and to acquire things to be desired, and to use those acquired things chiefly by the reason through which they may profit. In these things the whole happiness of the city consists...

[Margin: Beginning of civil discipline.]

**ATHEN.** Let these things indeed be so. But what shall we say was the beginning of civil discipline? Or will not someone most easily and best inspect it from here?

**CLIN.** From where?

**ATHEN.** From where the increase of cities both toward virtue and toward vice may be inspected.

**CLIN.** From where do you say?

**ATHEN.** I think indeed from the length and infinity of time, and the mutations of things in it.

**CLIN.** In what way do you say that?

**ATHEN.** Come then, if you can, tell me how great a multitude of time has passed since cities and the civil institutions of men began.

**CLIN.** That is by no means easy.

**ATHEN.** It is surely infinite and impossible to think.

**CLIN.** It is altogether so.

**ATHEN.** Have not innumerable cities been built in this time, and as many destroyed, which have used every condition of civil life everywhere, and become now greater from smaller, now smaller from greater, worse also from better, and on the contrary, better from worse?

**CLIN.** That is indeed necessary.

**ATHEN.** Let us therefore devise the cause of this mutation, if we can. For perhaps it will show us the first cause and mutation of civil life.

**CLIN.** You speak rightly. Wherefore it behooves you to explain diligently what you feel about this matter, and us to listen attentively.

**ATHEN.** Do the ancient discourses seem to have some truth?

**CLIN.** Which ones?

**ATHEN.** Namely, that many destructions of men from floods, diseases, and many other things happened long ago, from which few men were survivors.

**CLIN.** That also is very likely.

**ATHEN.** Come now, from the many, let us perceive this one destruction which was made by flood.

**CLIN.** What do you bid us think in this?

**ATHEN.** Namely, that those who then escaped the slaughter were certain mountain shepherds, a few seeds preserved in the peaks of mountains for propagating the race of men.

**CLIN.** It is clear.

**ATHEN.** And yet it is necessary that they were both unskilled in other arts, and ignored the studies of avarice and contention among citizens, and the other astuteness against others.

**CLIN.** That is indeed consistent.

**ATHEN.** Let us also assume that the cities of the plains and the maritime cities perished fundamentally at that time.

**CLIN.** Let us assume it.

**ATHEN.** Shall we assert therefore that all instruments and whatever of the arts belonged to either civil discipline or another faculty which were existing as inventions, fell away in those times?

**CLIN.** For how, O best of men, if these things had remained for eternity as they are now, would anything new have been invented by anyone? Namely, because an innumerable multitude of years was ignored by them. But a thousand years or two thousand have intervened since anything is said to have been invented, partly by Daedalus, partly by Orpheus, partly by Palamedes. Just as those things which pertain to music are attributed to Marsyas and Olympus; those to the lyre, to Amphion; and many other things to others, invented, so to speak, yesterday and the day before yesterday.

**ATHEN.** Do you see, Clinias, that a friend has been omitted by you, who was truly of yesterday?

**CLIN.** Do you mean Epimenides?

**ATHEN.** Him indeed. For he excelled everyone among you by far in the thinking out of new things, O friend. Which truly Hesiod once divined in words, but Epimenides himself perfected in fact, as you assert.

**CLIN.** We assert it plainly.

**ATHEN.** We think then that from that devastation a great and terrible desolation happened in human affairs. The magnitude of fertile fields deserted, and the other animals corrupted, only a few of the breed of goats and sheep were left, and those rare, by pasturing which men then lived.

**CLIN.** Who doubts?

**ATHEN.** But of the city and civil discipline and laws about which the present discourse is held by us, do we think there was even any memory, so to speak?

**CLIN.** None at all.

**ATHEN.** Did not all these things proceed to us from those so disposed—cities, and civil disciplines, arts, laws, and no small abundance of vices and virtue?

**CLIN.** In what way do you say that?

**ATHEN.** Do we think, O wonderful man, that those men, since they were ignorant of many things which among citizens are held honest or base, emerged as supreme either in virtue or in vice?

**CLIN.** You have spoken well, and we understand what you wish.

**ATHEN.** Therefore, as time progressed, and the race of men was multiplied, all things advanced to that habit which we now see.

**CLIN.** Very rightly.

**ATHEN.** Nor yet suddenly, as is likely, but gradually and in a long time.

**CLIN.** So it is very fitting.

**ATHEN.** For fear forbade them to descend into the plains from the peaks of the mountains.

**CLIN.** Certainly.

**ATHEN.** Did they not also congratulate one another because of the paucity of their mutual sight in those times, especially since neither by land nor by sea was passage to others easy, almost all instruments for passage having been destroyed together with the arts? Wherefore they could not come together much, as I think. For iron and bronze and all metals had perished in confusion, so that they could not be found and brought into the light; whence also there were no workers of wood. For even if some instrument remained sometimes in the mountains, yet it soon vanished, worn away; nor could others be made before the metallic art was found again by men.

**CLIN.** For in what way could it have been done otherwise?

**ATHEN.** But by how many generations afterward do we think that was done?

**CLIN.** Surely by many.

**ATHEN.** Therefore the arts which use iron and bronze and all other such things were ignored at the same time, or even covered by the darkness of greater ignorance.

**CLIN.** That is certain.

**ATHEN.** Furthermore, there was neither sedition at that time, nor war.

**CLIN.** For what reason?

**ATHEN.** First, because on account of solitude they embraced one another with ardent benevolence. Then, because food did not incite war; for there was no lack of pasturage, except perhaps for some few at the beginning. But they lived for the most part in those times by pastures. Likewise, an abundance of milk and meats was not lacking. And hunting supplied easily food, and that not bad. Clothing moreover, bedding, dwellings, and vessels, both fired and not fired, they had in abundance. For the arts of molding and weaving do not need iron, by which we obtain all these by the nod of God, so that if ever men fall into such a calamity, they may be able to propagate the human race. For this reason they were not very needy, nor were they compelled by need to wars. They could by no means become rich either, since they had neither gold nor silver. But in whatever gathering of men there are neither need nor riches, the most just customs will be present to it. For there neither insolence nor injury has a place. Emulation also and envy are far away. For these causes, therefore, they were good, and especially because of simplicity. For whatever they heard to be honest or base, believing them to be true because of simplicity, they obeyed the warnings. Nor did anyone, because of an opinion of wisdom as happens now, suspect a lie, but thinking those things which were said of gods and men to be true, they instituted their life quietly according to these. Wherefore they were altogether such as we narrated a little before.

**CLIN.** I indeed and he here agree with you in these things.

**ATHEN.** We said furthermore that many generations so living had less skill than those who were before the flood, as well as today’s men, both in other arts and in military ones which are exercised today by land or sea; in judgments also and seditions which in the city contend diligently both in words and deeds to inflict injury on others. But they were simpler and stronger, and at the same time more modest, and more just in all things. But the cause of these we have already said.

**CLIN.** You speak rightly.

**ATHEN.** Therefore let these things be so said by us, and let all the things that follow be explained, so that we may understand why they had need of laws, and who founded laws for them.

**CLIN.** You have spoken well.

**ATHEN.** Did they then not need lawgivers, nor had it yet become customary in those times for that to happen? For the men of that time did not yet have letters, but they lived following the custom and manners of their ancestors.

**CLIN.** It is likely. But what was the mode of civil discipline?

**ATHEN.** This.

**CLIN.** What?

**ATHEN.** All seem to me to call the civil discipline of living of that time *dynasteian*, that is, lordship [potentate], which even now flourishes in many places both among Greeks and among Barbarians, which indeed Homer testifies to have existed in the habitation of the Cyclopes: "They never come together publicly for consulting, nor to exercise judgments; but they inhabit hollow caves in high mountains, and with public things despised, each gives laws to his wives and children." [Odyssey IX]

**CLIN.** This poet seems to have been charming to you. And yet we have seen some other things of his, very urban indeed, but not many. For we Cretans use foreign poetry little.

**MEG.** But we use it. And this poet seems to us to have excelled, although he explains everywhere not the Laconic, but rather the Ionic life. But he seems to attest well here to your words, since he reduced the antiquity of men through fables to a sylvan way of living.

**CLIN.** Indeed.

**ATHEN.** He certainly attests. Wherefore, induced by his testimony, let us believe that such governments sometimes happen.

**MEG.** Rightly.

**ATHEN.** Do not these governments happen from those same men who live dispersed through individual habitations and individual families because of the need made from devastations? In which always the elder dominates, from the fact that they took their beginning from father and mother: whom indeed, following like birds, they finish one flock, using paternal wills for law, and governed by the most just kingship of all.

**MEG.** Entirely so.

**ATHEN.** But afterward, coming together commonly and in greater numbers, they constitute larger cities, and first turned to agricultures at the roots of mountains, they build circuits like the walls of cities from hedges for the sake of wild beasts, building one large and common house.

**MEG.** That seems likely.

**ATHEN.** What about this? Is it not also likely?

**MEG.** What then?

**ATHEN.** When these larger habitations are made from the smaller and first ones, each of the small ones is present, of which each brings an elder prince and its own manners, from the fact that they lived separately, and therefore they received some manners from some parents and educators, to which they were accustomed—each for worshipping gods, and caring for themselves—the more modest from the modest, the stronger from the stronger, and in all other things just as each erudited his sons or grandsons, whose rites they carry like their own laws to the larger habitation.

**MEG.** What forbids it?

**ATHEN.** And yet it is necessary that his own laws please each in the first place, but the laws of others in the second place.

**MEG.** It is so.

**ATHEN.** But we seem now to have entered into the very cradle and beginning of laws without knowing it.

**MEG.** Indeed.

**ATHEN.** After these things, it is necessary that they who come together choose some from themselves commonly, who might know the institutes of all, and which they most approve from these, they should bring to certain common leaders of the people as if kings. But they themselves will be named the bearers of those laws which shall have been approved; and constituting a government of the best [aristocracy] from powers, or some kingdom, they will agree in this mutation of civil discipline.

**MEG.** So certainly it will happen by a suitable succession.

**ATHEN.** Let us now say the third figure of civil discipline, in which all species and affections of republics and cities are found.

**MEG.** Which is that?

**ATHEN.** It is surely that which Homer, after the second was made into the third, thus signified: "He then built the city of Dardania. For not yet were the sacred walls of Ilium [Troy] erected and standing in the plains, a city of many nations. But they inhabited at the roots of Mount Ida of many springs." [Iliad XX] Surely these verses and those former ones about the Cyclopes were written divinely and according to nature itself. For the race of poets is divine: it is moved by god, and sings sacred hymns. Whence they are accustomed to touch true things everywhere with the Muses and Graces.

**MEG.** Altogether.

**ATHEN.** Let us therefore proceed with the preceding fable. For perhaps something will be clear from it of those things we wish. Is it not so necessary?

**MEG.** Entirely so.

**ATHEN.** We were saying therefore that Ilium was built from higher places into a great and beautiful plain, on a certain hill not high, where many rivers flowed down from above from Ida.

**MEG.** So it is handed down.

**ATHEN.** Do we not think that was done a long time after the flood?

**MEG.** Who would not so think?

**ATHEN.** A great forgetfulness of that devastation therefore seems to have taken them, when they built a city near many rivers, and those flowing from higher places, and trusted themselves to small hills.

**MEG.** Then it is clear that they were many centuries after the vastation of the flood.

**ATHEN.** Many other cities besides were then already inhabited, the race of men being propagated further.

**MEG.** Why not?

**ATHEN.** Which namely also campaigned against Ilium. And perhaps by sea, as if all were now using it intrepidly.

**MEG.** It appears so.

**ATHEN.** But the Achivi, besieging Troy for ten years, overturned it.

**MEG.** Plainly.

**ATHEN.** In that decade therefore in which Troy was besieged, many things happened at home to the besieging Achivi because of the seditions of the youth, who received the returning soldiers neither honestly nor justly, but so that many were affected by death, many by exile. Who again being expelled were led back, to be called Dorians instead of Achivi with the name changed, because of a certain Dorieus by whom the exiles were gathered and restored. And all these things you, O Lacedaemonians, narrate from here.

**MEG.** Without doubt.

**ATHEN.** When our discourse about laws had been instituted, we digressed into a discussion about music and drunkenness. Now at last as if divinely the speech has returned for us to the same, and has provided us with handles in a certain way. For it has slipped down to that civil discipline which you assert was rightly instituted as if by fraternal laws both in Lacedaemon and in Crete. But we have gained this much from this digression of speech: that while we were carried across through civil disciplines and habitations of cities, we perceived the first and second and third city, depending one from the other in a certain very long tract of time, as our opinion holds. But now this fourth city comes to us, or if you wish this fourth race of men, which both will inhabit somewhere sometime, and already inhabits now. From all of which if we can understand what was instituted well or on the contrary in the habitation, and which laws of theirs preserve those things which are preserved, and which corrupted things corrupt, and what kind of mutation of civil institutions makes a city blessed, O Megillus and Clinias, we shall think enough has been done by us. All these things, I say, must be treated by us again as if from the beginning, unless perhaps in some way we should reject those things which have been said.

**MEG.** If some guest god should promise us: if we again approach the discussion about the bearing of laws, that we are to hear things neither fewer nor worse than these which have been said: I would make a long journey for this cause, and this day would seem short to me, although from the summer solstice to the winter ones, the day is now turned.

**ATHEN.** Do these things therefore seem to be considered?

**MEG.** Greatly.

**ATHEN.** Let us therefore embrace in thought those times in which Lacedaemon, Argos, and Messene and all things joined to them were subject to your ancestors, Megillus. For then that itself, as is said in the fable, pleased: that with the army divided into three parts, they should inhabit three cities, Argos, Messene, Lacedaemon.

**MEG.** So it was done.

**ATHEN.** And of Argos indeed Temenus was made king, of Messene indeed Cresphontes, and of Lacedaemon together Eurysthenes and Procles.

**MEG.** So indeed.

**ATHEN.** They all likewise swore that he would be an enemy who should attempt to devastate the kingdom of any of them.

**MEG.** Plainly.

**ATHEN.** Tell me then by Jove, are any kingdom or principality overturned, or to be overturned sometime by others, or by themselves? Or when a little before we fell into this speech, did we think it to be so, but now have we altogether forgotten?

**MEG.** By no means.

**ATHEN.** Shall we not more confirm the same now? For from the history of things done into which we fell, we are warned to affirm this. Wherefore we shall not revolve the speech about something vain, since we say a thing done and true. These things were done. Three kingdoms, and three cities governed by a kingdom, swore together with laws placed about commanding and obeying in turn—the kings indeed lest as they progressed in race and time they should rule more violently; the peoples however, if the kings should preserve the oath, that they would never undermine the kingdoms, but indeed defend them if anyone should ever attack. The kings also to the kings and peoples, and also the peoples to the peoples and kings, bound themselves by oath to repelling mutual injuries inflicted. Is it not so?

**MEG.** Entirely so.

**ATHEN.** But that which in constituting a civil discipline is greatest, that was present to those three cities, whether the kings or others bore the laws.

**MEG.** What was that?

**ATHEN.** That two together should rise up against the one which should transgress the placed laws.

**MEG.** That is indeed manifest.

**ATHEN.** Many also prescribe this to legislators: that they bear such laws as the multitude and people may freely receive, just as if someone should prescribe to masters of the gymnasium or physicians that they cure bodies with pleasure, and heal them pleasantly.

**MEG.** Entirely so.

**ATHEN.** Yet it often holds beautifully, if someone with small trouble restores a good habit and health to bodies.

**MEG.** Why not?

**ATHEN.** This besides was present to them as no small thing for the facility of federated laws.

**MEG.** What then?

**ATHEN.** There was not for the bearers of those laws effecting equality of honors that greatest difficulty which is accustomed to happen to many cities agreeing in one law, if they seek to disturb the possession of fields, and to introduce new tablets [cancellation of debts], since they see that equality cannot sufficiently be made without these. For against him who attempts to move anything from these, everyone clamors, lest he move things not to be moved. For to one dividing fields, and introducing new tablets, all openly speak evil, so that each knows not where to turn himself. For the Dorians, however, there was not this difficulty and perturbation. For they possessed fields abundantly without controversy, and debts to others already long ago contracted were not great.

**MEG.** You narrate true things.

**ATHEN.** For what reason then, O best of men, was that constitution and legislation so badly lacking to them?

**MEG.** In what way? Or what fault?

**ATHEN.** Because from the three constitutions of cities, two quickly lost both civil discipline and laws, and your city alone was left.

**MEG.** It is not easy what you ask.

**ATHEN.** And yet there is need that considering it now, and discoursing about laws with a certain senile and modest jest, we should finish this journey, as we said when we began to make the journey, without trouble.

**MEG.** Without doubt it must be done, as you say.

**ATHEN.** Can we have a more beautiful consideration of laws than of these laws which adorned such cities? Or even think of more honest and greater cities, villas, and institutions than these?

**MEG.** Not easily would anyone prefer others to these.

**ATHEN.** No one, however, will doubt but that they so joined believed they could defend not only the Peloponnese, but also the whole of Greece, if any Barbarian should inflict injury, excited by the example of the Trojans, who, relying on the power of the Assyrians which drew its origin from Ninus, stirred up war against themselves. For the power of that principality was still not to be despised. Wherefore just as we now dread the great king, so all then dreaded the power of those nations conspiring into one. But the second overthrow of Troy stirred up great envy for them. For the power of Troy was a certain small part of the Assyrian principality. Against that power therefore, the army divided into three cities by the brothers, the sons of Hercules then reigning, seemed to have been best and most adorned, and much better instructed than that very one which besieged Troy. For first they thought themselves to have more excellent leaders, the Heraclidae, than the Pelopidae; then they thought this army to excel in virtue that which sought Troy. For these had conquered, those were surpassed by these, the Dorians over the Achivi. Do we not believe they so thought, and for that cause so prepared themselves?

**MEG.** Altogether.

**ATHEN.** It is likely therefore that they also thought this constitution of theirs would be firm and last for a long time, especially since they underwent many dangers and labors together, and were governed by brother kings. And they used many seers, both others and the Delphic Apollo.

**MEG.** Very likely.

**ATHEN.** But these things which they thought would be greatest, quickly then, as it seems, vanished, except for the small part, as we just said, which inhabits your region. This never until this day, war being undertaken against two parts, has rested. For if the constitution then made had remained concordant, it would surely have been invincible in war.

**MEG.** Why not?

**ATHEN.** How therefore and by what reason was it dissolved? Does it not appear worthy of consideration what fortune overturned so great and such a constitution?

**MEG.** Never surely would anyone, considering anything else, be able to understand either laws or other republics, by which beautiful and great things are preserved, or on the contrary lost, if he neglects those things.

**ATHEN.** Happily therefore we seem to have fallen into this so accommodated consideration.

**MEG.** Greatly.

**ATHEN.** Is not then, O wonderful man, our error hidden from all of us, and especially in the present, while we think we have perceived a singular thing, and what wonderful events will follow, if someone will not be ignorant of how to use those things in the due way? But we perhaps now think of this same thing neither rightly nor according to nature: and all others err in all things about which they think similarly.

**MEG.** What do you say? And about what matter do you say that especially?

**ATHEN.** I myself, O good man, certainly laughed now. For when I had considered that army, about which the discourse was just held, it seemed to me surely excellent and wonderful, and about to design famous deeds for the Greeks, if anyone had then used it well.

**MEG.** Did not you also say all things prudently, and we praised them rightly?

**ATHEN.** Perhaps; I think, however, all who have seen something great and endowed with huge power are immediately so affected that they think, if he who possesses it knew how to use such and so great a thing, he would be happy with many and famous deeds done therefrom.

**MEG.** Is not this also right? Or how do you say?

**ATHEN.** Consider now where he who so praises each thing, looking back, might speak rightly. And first about what we were saying, in what way if those who then presided had known how to order the army rightly, they would have happily used the occasion: would they not, if they had then constituted it more safely, have preserved it always, so that they themselves also would be free, and others whom they wished, they would subjugate? and altogether both they and their posterity, both among Greeks and among Barbarians, would obtain whatever they desired? Did they not desire all things for the sake of this?

**MEG.** Indeed very much.

**ATHEN.** Whoever therefore, when he has looked upon huge riches, or excellent honors of birth, or anything of that kind, should say the same things, will say it looking to this, as if through this all things which he desires, or very many and most powerful, are to be for him.

**MEG.** So it seems.

**ATHEN.** There is surely one common desire of all men, which the present discourse has signified.

**MEG.** What is it?

**ATHEN.** That according to the desire of their own mind all things, or at least human things, be conducted.

**MEG.** Who doubts?

**ATHEN.** Since we always all wish this, both in childhood and adult age and old age, we proculdubio pray to have it.

**MEG.** Indeed.

**ATHEN.** We also pray for these things for friends, which they also would pray for themselves.

**MEG.** And this.

**ATHEN.** But a friend is a son to his father, a boy to a man.

**MEG.** Surely.

**ATHEN.** And yet of those things which the boy prays may happen to him, the father prays the gods that many may not happen.

**MEG.** Do you say that happens when the son who prays is young and mindless?

**ATHEN.** Nay, even when the father, whether old or very young, since he knows nothing either of honest or just things, being so affected as Theseus toward the unhappy Hippolytus, imprecates more intensely, but the son knows; do you think the son will then pray the same things with the father?

**MEG.** I understand what you say. For you seem to me to say that it is not to be prayed and attempted that all things follow our will, but that our will follow prudence. And that both for the city and for individuals, it must be sought by prayers and studied that they have a mind.

[Margin: One must not pray that all things follow our will, but that our will follow our prudence.]

**ATHEN.** And I say that entirely. Furthermore, that a civil man, a lawgiver, always looking to these things ought to bear laws, I also have remembered, and I wish you now to remember. Namely, you were saying at the beginning of the discussion that a good lawgiver ought to refer all things to war. But I was saying that he ought to look and respect not only to one virtue, although there be four, but to all: especially indeed to the first, which is also the leader of all others; but this is prudence, and intellect, and opinion, together with the love and desire following those same things. Our speech now returns to the same. And I who was then saying those things, say those same things also now, whether you wish it in jest or seriously. I assert indeed that it is not safe to use a vow, and to obtain a vow, if you do not have a mind, but that it is better for the contrary of those things which you seek to happen. If you wish to think these things said seriously, think so. For I hope now to persuade you of what we proposed a little before: that the cause of the destruction of the kings and of the dissolving of that whole constitution was not timidity, nor ignorance of military affairs either of the princes or of the subjects, but the universal remaining depravity, and especially ignorance about the greatest of human affairs. That these things so happened then, and now if they happen anywhere, or are to happen sometime, they may not come out otherwise, if you wish, I shall try—as reason will next show—to find out, and to explain to you as friends, according to my strength.

**CLIN.** To praise you in words, Guest, is troublesome; but in fact we shall praise you greatly, by hearing what you say of your own accord, in which matter a liberal and true praiser is most especially clear.

**ATHEN.** Excellent of you indeed, Clinias. Wherefore let us effect what you say.

**CLIN.** It shall be so, if God wills. You only speak.

**ATHEN.** We judge therefore, proceeding next through the following way of this discussion, that by the greatest ignorance then that power was lost, and that similar events of things proceed from the same cause also now. Wherefore if this is so, the legislator ought to try to give prudence, as much as can happen, to the citizens, and to take away ignorance as much as possible.

**CLIN.** That is indeed manifest.

**ATHEN.** What then will be called the greatest ignorance by right? Consider if you agree with me. For I judge this.

**CLIN.** What?

**ATHEN.** When someone does not love what seems honest or good to him, but hates it; but what is evil and unjust, that he loves and embraces: this dissension of pleasure and pain against that opinion which follows reason, I assert to be the extreme ignorance, which I also call the greatest, because it is in the multitude of the mind. For that in it which is enslaved to pains and pleasures is like the common people of the city and the multitude. Therefore when the mind is adverse to the sciences, or to opinion, or to reason which dominate by nature, this I call ignorance: both of the city, when the multitude does not obey the princes and laws; and also of one man, when although there be good reasons in the mind, nevertheless nothing is performed according to them, but all things on the contrary. These ignorances I assert to be the most pernicious to the city, and to any citizen, but not the ignorances of craftsmen, if only you understand what I say, Guests.

**CLIN.** We both understand, O friend, these things, and we grant them.

**ATHEN.** Let this therefore be held as ratum [settled], that to citizens who are ignorant in this way, nothing pertaining to the principality is to be committed: nay rather, as being ignorant, they are to be rebuked, even if they be most acute and eloquent, and have embraced all things which look to the ornament and acumen of the mind. But those who are affected on the contrary are to be held as wise even if they know neither letters, as is said, nor how to swim. Magistracies also are to be committed to these as if to the prudent. For how, O friends, will even the smallest species of prudence be able to consist without consensus?

[Margin: Proverb.]

**CLIN.** In no way.

**ATHEN.** But indeed the most beautiful and greatest of all consensuses will be said by right to be the greatest wisdom. Of which indeed he must be a participant who ought to live according to reason. But whoever is devoid of it, is both the overturner of his own house, and never the preserver of the city, but on the contrary altogether will always seem ignorant for these things. Let these things therefore, as we said a little before, be so held.

**CLIN.** Entirely so.

**ATHEN.** But ought there not to be rulers and subjects in cities?

**CLIN.** Indeed.

**ATHEN.** Be it so. But the reasons for the dignity of ruling and obeying, both in cities whether great or small, and privately in houses, of what kind and how many are they? Will not the first right reason of dignity be that father and mother, and altogether parents, everywhere rule over their offspring?

[Margin: Seven dignities of ruling.]

**CLIN.** Greatly.

**ATHEN.** The second, that the noble over the ignoble? The third, that the elders over the younger?

**CLIN.** And this.

**ATHEN.** The fourth, that masters over slaves?

**CLIN.** Without doubt.

**ATHEN.** The fifth, that the more powerful dominate, the weaker serve?

**CLIN.** You have just mentioned a principality very necessary.

**ATHEN.** Nay rather, one which is most frequent, and according to nature, as Theban Pindarus says, is found in all animals. But the greatest dignity...

...then reclining more freely at banquets, they may invoke other gods and especially Dionysus <note>Dionysus (or Bacchus) is the god of wine and theater. **On Laws, Or, On Legislation. Dialogue II. 519**

[Left Column]

...lest they should confuse them. But human poets disturb many things of this kind and mix them together without reason, provoking laughter in men; these poets, Orpheus <note>A legendary hero and musician in Greek myth, credited with the power to charm all living things with his music.</note> says, have merely obtained the grace of providing delight. For these poets see everything in a confused way and they themselves tear music apart, separating the rhythms and figures from the harmony, composing naked speeches in meter without melody, and even adapting harmonies and rhythms without words, suiting them to the bare plucking of the lyre or the sound of the flute. In this matter, it is very difficult to know what rhythm and harmony without words actually mean, or what worthy imitation they resemble. One must believe that any music is full of great crudeness if it merely follows the speed, slowness, or the voices of wild beasts—as if you were to use the flute or lyre for something other than the requirements of rhythmic dance and song. Indeed, to use either instrument alone is a misuse very similar to the display of a conjurer, and is quite alien to the Muses. But this is the reasoning behind these things. We, however, were not considering whether those who are thirty or fifty years old and beyond should use our Muses, but rather *when* they should use them. From these points, our discourse seems to signify that those advanced toward their fiftieth year, who are required to sing, ought to hold the Muse of the chorus better than others. For it is necessary that they acutely perceive and recognize harmonies and rhythms. How else will someone recognize the correctness of a song—whether the Dorian mode <note>A musical mode in ancient Greece considered to be solemn, stable, and manly; Plato often favored it for education.</note> is appropriate or not, and whether the rhythm which the poet added to it was joined correctly or not? 

**CLINIAS:** Certainly in no other way. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** But the common people are to be laughed at when they think they can sufficiently recognize what constitutes a good composition of harmony and rhythm, and what does not. These are the people, I say, who have long been compelled to sing and dance to rhythms. But they do not consider within themselves that they are ignorant of the particulars of these things; they think that any song is "right" if it contains everything that happens to suit their own taste, and "wrong" if it does not. 

**CLINIAS:** That must be so. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** What further? If someone does not understand the reason for a thing, or what qualities it possesses, will they ever recognize how it may be "right" in any way, as we have said? 

**CLINIAS:** How could that be possible? 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** We seem to have discovered this now: that those older singers, whom we previously provoked against their will so that they might sing with some pleasure, must necessarily have learned these things to such a degree that each of them can follow the weight of rhythmic progressions as well as the harmonic sounds of the strings. This is so that, understanding the harmonies and rhythms, they may choose those which ought to be sung by such men as themselves; and thus, while singing, they may immediately perceive innocent pleasures and lead the youth toward upright morals through songs and delights. Having been taught to this extent, they will possess a discipline in these matters more exquisite than that of the common people or even the poets. For a poet does not necessarily need to know that third thing—whether an imitation is good or bad—but he must know harmony and rhythm. However, these elders must know all three so that they can choose the best and the second best. Otherwise, they will never be able to sufficiently allure the souls of the young toward virtue, as if by certain incantations <note>original: "incantationibus." Here, Plato refers to the use of music as a psychological tool to "charm" or "enchant" the soul into a virtuous state.</note>. Truly, what we intended from the beginning—namely, that our discourse might bring proper help to the Chorus of Dionysus—has been stated according to our ability. But let us consider whether this has been achieved. Such a harmony of men necessarily becomes more turbulent as the drinking party progresses. This is what we supposed from the beginning must necessarily happen in those things that occur today. 

**CLINIAS:** Necessarily. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** 

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

Where certainly each person, having become lighter than himself, is lifted up and exults, filled with boldness; he does not listen to his neighbor, but considers himself a sufficient leader both of himself and of everyone else. 

**CLINIAS:** Without a doubt. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Did we not say that whenever these things happen, the souls of the drinkers—just as iron in the fire—become hotter, softer, and younger because of the wine, and are therefore more easily led, just as when they were young? If, that is, someone is both able and knows how to instruct and mold them. And that this "molder" is the same one who was then called a good legislator. A limit to the drinking party must be prescribed in his laws, so that these laws may restrain the man who has become confident, bold, and more impudent than is fitting—the man who refuses to take his turn in observing order in silence, speech, drinking, and music. The laws should instruct him so that he wishes to do the opposite of what he is doing, moving him against that rising and base confidence by applying the "best fear" along with justice. This divine fear we have named "shame" and "modesty." 

**CLINIAS:** It is as you say. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** The authors and guardians of these laws must themselves be removed from disturbance and drunkenness; they are the leaders of the wine-drinkers. Without them, it is harder to fight against drunkenness than it is to fight against enemies without prudent and considerate generals. If anyone refuses to obey these leaders of Dionysus who are over sixty years old, he should suffer a disgrace equal to or even greater than one who does not obey the generals of Mars <note>Mars is the Roman name for Ares, the god of war. Plato is comparing the discipline of a social gathering to the discipline of the battlefield.</note>. 

**CLINIAS:** Correct. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** If such drunkenness and such play were employed, would not the drinkers obtain great utility from it? Would they not depart joined in greater mutual benevolence than before, rather than as enemies, as they do now? For they would have conversed with one another according to the law, and while intoxicated, they would have obeyed the laws under the guidance of sober leaders. 

**CLINIAS:** Certainly, if such a drunkenness were as you have just described. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Therefore, let us not simply disparage the gift of Father Liber <note>original: "Liberi patris." Liber was an Italian god of fertility and wine, often identified with the Greek Dionysus.</note> as if it were an evil or unworthy to be received into the city. Indeed, more could be said on this point, although I fear to extol that greatest good which Dionysus bestows before many people, since men might not receive it correctly or understand it when they hear it. 

**CLINIAS:** What is that? 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** A certain rumor and fame has flowed down to us that this god was once driven out of his mind by the goddess Juno <note>The Roman name for Hera. In myth, Hera drove Dionysus mad because he was the son of her husband Zeus by another woman.</note>; and that for the sake of vengeance, he introduced the dance of the Bacchants and all madness, and gave wine for this very purpose. I, however, permit those to say such things who think it is safe to speak this way about the gods. But this much I know: no animal is born with as much intelligence as it will suit him to have when he is grown. Furthermore, in that time when he does not yet possess his own prudence, every creature rages and cries out without order, and when it has exerted itself, it exults again in a disjointed and disorderly way. Let us remember that we said these are the principles of music and gymnastics. 

**CLINIAS:** We remember. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Did we not also say that the sense of rhythm and harmony was given to us alone, and that this arose from this principle? And that Apollo, the Muses, and Dionysus were given to us as leaders for these things? 

**CLINIAS:** Certainly. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Wine, indeed—as many say—was given to men for vengeance, to make them go mad. But as our discourse has it, it was given as a remedy and a medicine for the opposite purpose: so that the soul might gain modesty, and the body might gain health and strength. 

**CLINIAS:** Stranger, you have excellently recalled the previous discourse. 

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** But now the middle part of what pertains to the chorus has been said. The remainder, it seems...
