### On the Laws, or the Giving of Laws, Dialogue III, 521

...matters, I say, prompted then by mutual need as well as the fear of wild beasts. But from the very beginning of this gathering, it is likely that there were as many forms of governing as there were households, differing greatly among themselves in both opinions and impulses. Because of this diversity, when mutual injuries arose between them, they were forced to establish certain common arbitrators, judges, and rulers. From this, a third form <note>Original: "figura." Here, the author uses "figure" to describe a stage or model of political development.</note> of civil discipline has now arisen, evidently drawing its origin from the preceding injustice <note>The author suggests that laws were not created in a vacuum but as a necessary response to the conflicts and "injustice" that arose when different families began to interact.</note>. 

It is probable, indeed, that such rulers of the city prescribed common laws for the state after they had considered the most honorable laws of each household; through these, they transferred the management of domestic affairs <term>rei familiaris: the private governance of a home or family estate</term> to the governance of the Republic <note>Original: "Reipublicae." While we often think of a "Republic" as a specific type of democracy, here it refers more broadly to the "commonwealth" or public state affairs.</note>. 

Finally, there is a fourth form, found in a kingdom of nations: where several cities agree among themselves upon the same will and common law, just as [individuals once agreed] within a single city...

# On the Laws, or, on Legislation. Dialogue III. 523

...and public laws, while individually they give laws to their wives and children. 

**CLEINIAS.** This poet <note>The "poet" referred to here is Homer. In the preceding lines, the Athenian quoted Homer’s description of the Cyclopes to illustrate primitive, lawless society.</note> seems to have been quite charming to you. Indeed, we have seen some other works of his which are certainly very witty, though they are not many. For we Cretans do not make much use of foreign poetry. 

**MEGILLUS.** We Spartans, however, do use it. It seems to us that this poet has surpassed others, although he depicts an Ionian way of life everywhere rather than a Laconian <note>Megillus is noting that Homer’s style is more "Ionian"—luxurious and flowing—rather than the "Laconian" (Spartan) style, which was famously brief and disciplined.</note> one. Yet he seems to support your argument well here, since he traced the ancient history of men through myths back to a wild way of living. 

**CLEINIAS.** Quite right. 

**ATHENIAN.** He does indeed support it. Therefore, led by his testimony, let us believe that such forms of government once existed. 

**MEGILLUS.** Correct. 

**ATHENIAN.** Do not these governments arise from the people themselves, who live dispersed in individual households and families because of the scarcity caused by the vastations? In these groups, the eldest always rules <term>Patriarchy: literally "rule of the father," describing a society where the head of the family holds total authority</term>, because they took their beginning from a father and mother. Following them like birds, they form a single flock, using the father's will as their law, and are governed most justly by a total kingship. 

**MEGILLUS.** Exactly so. 

**ATHENIAN.** But later, many people flow together in common and establish larger cities. Turning first to agriculture at the foothills of the mountains, they build enclosures made of hedges like city walls to protect themselves against wild beasts, creating one large and common household. 

**MEGILLUS.** That seems very likely. 

**ATHENIAN.** And what about this? Is it not also likely? 

**MEGILLUS.** What? 

**ATHENIAN.** Since these larger settlements were made from the smaller, original ones, each of the small groups would arrive with its own elder leader and its own particular customs. This happened because they lived apart and therefore received different customs from different parents and teachers. These customs included how they were accustomed to worshiping the gods and caring for themselves—the more orderly groups coming from orderly elders, the braver from the brave, and so on, just as each had educated their children or grandchildren. They bring these rituals, which are like their own private laws, into the larger settlement. 

**MEGILLUS.** What is to prevent that? 

**ATHENIAN.** And yet, it is inevitable that each person's own laws please them most, while the laws of others are only second. 

**MEGILLUS.** That is true. 

**ATHENIAN.** But it seems we have now entered, without realizing it, into the very cradle and beginning of legislation. 

**MEGILLUS.** Certainly. 

**ATHENIAN.** After this, it is necessary that those who have come together choose some from among themselves who know the customs of all. These men, having selected the customs they most approve of, present them to the common leaders of the people—who are like kings. These men will be named the "law-givers" <term>Legislators: those who "carry" or "propose" the laws</term> of those rules which were approved. By establishing an aristocracy <note>Original: "optimatum gubernationem," the government of the best or elite.</note> or some form of kingship from these powers, they come together in this transition of civil discipline. 

**MEGILLUS.** It will certainly follow in that orderly succession. 

**ATHENIAN.** Let us now speak of the third form of civil discipline, in which all the types and characteristics of republics and cities are found. 

**MEGILLUS.** What form is that? 

**ATHENIAN.** <margin>Iliad, Book 20</margin> It is certainly the one which Homer signified as having been made third, after the second stage. He said: "He then built the land of Dardania. For not yet were the sacred walls of Ilium <note>Ilium is the ancient name for Troy.</note> erected and standing in the plains, a city of many peoples. But they still dwelt at the roots of Mount Ida, rich in springs." <note>Original: "Dardaniam verò tunc terram ille ædificauit..." This is a translation of Homer, Iliad XX, 216-218.</note> Truly, these verses and those earlier ones about the Cyclopes were written by divine inspiration and according to nature itself. For the race of poets is divine; it is moved by the gods and sings sacred hymns. Thus, with the help of the Muses and the Graces, it often touches upon the truth. 

**MEGILLUS.** Most certainly. 

**ATHENIAN.** Let us therefore follow the preceding story. For perhaps it will reveal something of what we desire. Should we not do so? 

**MEGILLUS.** By all means. 

**ATHENIAN.** We were saying, then, that Ilium was built by moving from the higher places down into a large and beautiful plain, on a certain hill that was not very high, where many rivers flowed down from Mount Ida. 

**MEGILLUS.** So it has been handed down. 

**ATHENIAN.** Do we not think this happened a long time after the flood? 

**MEGILLUS.** Who would not think so? 

**ATHENIAN.** A great forgetfulness of that devastation seems to have taken hold of them, when they built a city near many rivers flowing from higher places and trusted themselves to such small hills. 

**MEGILLUS.** It is clear, then, that they lived many centuries after the disaster of the flood. 

**ATHENIAN.** Many other cities besides were being inhabited by then, as the human race had spread further. 

**MEGILLUS.** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN.** These are the cities, of course, which also went to war against Ilium. And perhaps they traveled by sea, as if everyone were now using it without fear. 

**MEGILLUS.** It appears so. 

**ATHENIAN.** And the Achaeans <note>The Achaeans were one of the primary names for the Greeks who fought in the Trojan War.</note>, attacking for ten years, overthrew Troy. 

**MEGILLUS.** Clearly. 

**ATHENIAN.** In those ten years while Troy was being besieged, many troubles occurred at home for the besieging Achaeans because of the rebellions of the young men. When the soldiers returned to their own lands, these youths did not receive them honorably or justly, but treated them such that many were put to death and many were sent into exile. Those who were expelled were later led back, and their name was changed from Achaeans to <margin>Origin of the Dorians.</margin> Dorians, because of a certain man named Dorieus who gathered and restored the exiles. And all these things, you Lacedaemonians <note>Lacedaemonian is the formal name for a Spartan.</note>, tell as your own history. 

**MEGILLUS.** Without a doubt. 

**ATHENIAN.** Although our conversation was intended to be about laws, we wandered off into a dispute about music and drunkenness. Now at last, as if by divine providence, the speech has returned to the same point and has, in a way, given us a handle to grasp. For it has drifted down to that very civil discipline which you assert was rightly established with brotherly laws in both Lacedaemon and Crete. We have gained this much from this digression: that while we were traveling through the civil disciplines and the settlements of cities, we have observed the first, second, and third city, depending one upon the other across a very long stretch of time, as is our opinion. Now, this fourth city comes to us—or if you prefer, this fourth race of men—which once lived somewhere and still lives today. If from all these we can understand what was established well or poorly in these settlements, and which laws preserve the things that are preserved, and which corrupt things destroy them, and what kind of change in civil institutions makes a city happy, O Megillus and Cleinias, we shall consider our task done. All these things, I say, must be treated by us again as if from the beginning, unless perhaps we reject what has already been said. 

**MEGILLUS.** If some guest god were to promise us that if we take up the discussion of law-giving again, we would hear things no fewer or worse than what has been said, I would make a long journey for this cause, and this day would seem short to me, even if the day were now turning from the summer solstice toward the winter ones <note>The Spartan is saying he would talk all day and night, even through the longest day of the year.</note>. 

**ATHENIAN.** It seems, then, these things must be considered? 

**MEGILLUS.** Very much so. 

**ATHENIAN.** Finally, let us embrace in our thoughts those times in which Lacedaemon, Argos, and Messene, and all the things joined to them, were subject to your ancestors, Megillus. For then it pleased them—as is said in the myth—to divide the army into three parts and inhabit three cities: Argos, Messene, and Lacedaemon. 

**MEGILLUS.** So it was done. 

**ATHENIAN.** And Temenus became the king of Argos, while Cresphontes became the king of Messene...

These, in truth, are the facts: three kingdoms, and three cities governed by kings, swore to one another under laws established in common regarding ruling and obeying. ### On the Laws. Or, Latin Dialogue on the Laws, Book III. Page 525

[Left Column]

...looking back at the outcome, he who thus praises each particular thing might speak correctly. And first, concerning what we were saying: in what way, if those who were then in charge had known how to correctly organize an army, would they have successfully used that opportunity? If they had established a safer state at that time, would they not have preserved it forever, so that they themselves would be free and could subjugate others as they wished? And altogether, both they and their descendants, among both the Greeks and the Barbarians, could have done whatever they desired? Was it not for the sake of this that they desired all things? **MEGILLUS.** Indeed, very much so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, whoever perceives vast riches, or the excellent honors of noble birth, or anything of that sort, and speaks of them in this way, will say so looking to this: as if through these things all that he desires will come to pass, or at least the most and greatest of them. **MEGILLUS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** There is certainly one common desire of all men, which our present discourse has indicated. **MEGILLUS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** That all things, or at least human affairs, should be conducted according to the desire of one’s own soul. **MEGILLUS.** Who could doubt it? **ATHENIAN.** Since we all always wish for this, in childhood, adulthood, and old age, we undoubtedly pray earnestly to have it. **MEGILLUS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** We also pray for these things for our friends, which they also pray for themselves. **MEGILLUS.** This too. **ATHENIAN.** Now, a son is a friend to his father—a boy to a man. **MEGILLUS.** Assuredly. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, of those things which the boy prays may happen to him, the father prays to the gods that many may *not* happen. **MEGILLUS.** Do you say that happens when the son who prays is young and foolish? **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, and even when the father—whether old or quite young—knows nothing of what is honorable or just, and is moved as Theseus was toward the unhappy Hippolytus <note>In Greek mythology, Theseus cursed his son Hippolytus based on a false accusation, leading to the youth's death. This is cited here as an example of a father’s prayer being granted to his own later regret.</note>, he prays more vehemently. But if the son knows better, do you think the son will then pray for the same things as the father? **MEGILLUS.** I understand what you are saying. For you seem to me to be saying that we should not pray or strive for all things to follow our *will*, but rather that our *will* should follow our *prudence*. Both the city and the individual should seek this through prayer, and study so that they may possess a mind. **ATHENIAN.** Precisely so, I say. Furthermore, I have remembered, and I want you now to remember, that a statesman and lawmaker must always look to these things when passing laws. You said at the beginning of our discussion that a good lawmaker ought to refer everything to war. I, however, said that he should look to only one virtue, even though there are four <note>The four "cardinal virtues" are Prudence (Wisdom), Justice, Fortitude (Courage), and Temperance.</note>. He must look not to one only, but to all: and especially to the first, which is the leader of all the others; and this is **prudence**, and intellect, and opinion, joined with the love and desire that follow them. Our discourse now returns to the same point. And I, who said those things then, say the same things now—whether you wish it in jest or in earnest. I assert, indeed, that it is not safe to use a prayer, or to obtain what is prayed for, if you do not have a mind; rather, it is better that the opposite of what you ask for should happen. If you wish to consider these words spoken in earnest, then do so. For I hope now to persuade you of what we proposed a little while ago: that the cause of the destruction of kings, and of the dissolution of that entire constitution, was not cowardice, nor ignorance of military affairs by either the rulers or the subjects, but all the rest of vice, and especially **ignorance** concerning the greatest of human affairs. That these things happened this way then—and if they happen anywhere now, or shall happen in the future, they will not turn out otherwise—I will endeavor to find out (as the logic follows) and explain to you as friends, to the best of my ability. **CLINIAS.** It is troublesome to praise you with words, Stranger, but we shall praise you greatly in deed, 

[Left Margin]

<margin>One should not pray that all things follow our will, but rather that our will follows our prudence.</margin>

[Right Column]

by willingly listening to what you say, in which matter a liberal and true praiser is most clearly seen. **ATHENIAN.** Most excellent, Clinias. Therefore, let us do as you say. **CLINIAS.** It shall be so, if God wills. You just speak. **ATHENIAN.** We think, then, proceeding further along this path of discussion, that that great power was destroyed by the greatest **ignorance**, and similar outcomes of events even now proceed from that same cause. Therefore, if this is the case, the legislator ought to strive to give prudence to the citizens as much as possible, and to take away ignorance to the greatest extent. **CLINIAS.** That is certainly manifest. **ATHENIAN.** What then may rightly be called the "greatest ignorance"? Consider if you agree with me. For I judge it to be this. **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** When someone does not love, but hates, what seems honorable or good to him; but loves and embraces what is evil and unjust. I assert that this discord of pleasure and pain against that opinion which follows reason is the **extreme ignorance**, which I also call the greatest, because it resides in the mass of the soul. For that part in it which is enslaved to pains and pleasures is like the common people <note>original: "plebs." The Athenian compares the irrational parts of the human soul to the uneducated "mob" or "masses" of a city.</note> and the multitude of a city. Therefore, when the soul is set against science, or opinion, or reason (which by nature should rule), I call this ignorance: both in a city, when the multitude does not obey the rulers and the laws; and also in a single man, when although there are good reasons in the soul, nothing is done according to them, but everything is carried out to the contrary. I assert that these types of ignorance are the most ruinous for a city and for any citizen—not the ignorance of craftsmen, if you understand what I am saying, friends. **CLINIAS.** We understand these things, O friend, and we concede them. **ATHENIAN.** Let it therefore be established that for those citizens who are ignorant in this way, nothing pertaining to leadership should be entrusted to them; rather, as ignorant people, they are to be rebuked, even if they are the most acute and eloquent of men, and have mastered everything regarding the ornament and sharpness of genius. But those who are the opposite should be considered wise, even if (as the saying goes) they "know neither their letters nor how to swim." <note>original: "neq; literas... nouerint, neq; natare ſciant." A Greek proverb for total incompetence; here, Plato reverses it to say that moral harmony is more important than basic literacy or physical skills.</note> Magistrates should be entrusted to these men as being prudent. For how, O friends, could even the smallest species of prudence exist without such harmony? **CLINIAS.** In no way. **ATHENIAN.** But truly the most beautiful and greatest of all harmonies will rightly be called the greatest wisdom. He who is to live according to reason must necessarily participate in this. But whoever is devoid of it will be the overturner of his own house, and never the preserver of a city, but the opposite in all things. **ATHENIAN.** Must there not be rulers and parents in cities? **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Very well. But what are the claims <note>original: "rationes." In the context of the *Laws*, these are the 'titles' or 'claims' to authority (axiomata).</note> of dignity for ruling and obeying, in cities both great and small, and similarly in private homes? How many are they, and of what kind? Is not the first "right claim" of dignity that the father and mother, and generally parents everywhere, should rule over their children? **CLINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** The second: that the noble rule over the ignoble? The third: that the elders rule over the younger? **CLINIAS.** This also. **ATHENIAN.** The fourth: that masters rule over slaves? **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** The fifth: that the stronger rule, and the weaker serve? **CLINIAS.** You have just described a most necessary form of rule. **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, it is the most common and is found in all animals according to nature, as Pindar of Thebes says <note>Pindar (c. 518–438 BC) was a Greek lyric poet. The Athenian refers to Pindar's idea that "might makes right" is a law of nature.</note>. But the greatest claim...

**[Page 526]**
# Thirty-fourth Book.

...dignity is to be placed sixth, by which the ignorant are commanded to follow, while the prudent are to lead and dominate. This indeed is the command, O most wise Pindar, which I would affirm to be not against nature, but according to the nature of law and undertaken by choice, not by violence. **CLINIAS:** Well said. **ATHENIAN:** Let us bring forth the seventh [form of] sovereignty by a certain lot, asserting that it falls to one by the grace of God and a certain good fortune: and let us consider it most just that he whom the lot has chosen should rule, and he whom it has rejected should obey. **CLINIAS:** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN:** We shall speak, therefore, in a certain place to one of those who undertake the duty of easily passing laws. Do you see, O legislator, how many ranks of dignity there are concerning those who rule? And how they are opposed to one another? Truly, we have now found a certain source of seditions, against which you must be cautious. First, consider carefully with us what and in what manner those kings at Argos and Messene, by acting wrongly in these matters, overturned both themselves and the power of the Greeks, which was then wondrous. [Margin: *How it is to be understood that the half is more than the whole.*] Was it not because they were ignorant of that most rightly said [maxim] by Hesiod, that "the half is sometimes more than the whole"? Namely, when to grasp the whole is harmful, but the half is a moderate amount, then surely he judged the moderate to be more than the immoderate, inasmuch as the better is more than the worse. **CLINIAS:** Most rightly. **ATHENIAN:** Shall we believe this was ruinous to the kings before it was to the people? **CLINIAS:** It is probable that this disease belongs especially to kings, who live haughtily on account of luxuries. **ATHENIAN:** It is clear, therefore, that those kings first possessed this: that they wished to be able to strive for more than the laws [allowed], nor did they remain in concord in that which they had praised by words and by oath. But a disagreement, as it seems to you—which, though it is the greatest ignorance, appears to be wisdom—overturned all those things through error and bitter rudeness. **CLINIAS:** It seems so. **ATHENIAN:** So be it. What, therefore, ought the legislator, fearing this disease, to have guarded against? By the gods, does the recognition of this now require neither the praise of wisdom nor is it difficult to say? But if anyone had foreseen it then, he would certainly have appeared wiser to us. **MEGILLUS:** What is it that you say? **ATHENIAN:** It is permitted now, Megillus, to observe what was done by you [Spartans] long ago, and from there to know the matter itself, and thus to say more easily what could have been done then. **MEGILLUS:** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN:** In this way it shall certainly become most evident. **MEGILLUS:** By what means? **ATHENIAN:** If anyone commits a greater power to lesser things, neglecting moderation—sails to ships, food to bodies, sovereignty to souls—all things will be perverted. For things raised beyond measure become insolent: and some fall into diseases, others into the daughter of haughty insolence, which is injustice. What therefore do we say? Is it not this? That there is no human nature at all, O my dearest men, which, if it be both youthful and subject to no one, could so bear the greatest power that it would not be filled with the greatest disease of madness in its mind, and incur the envy even of its closest friends; when this happens, it immediately loses its soul and obscures all its power. To guard against this by the observation of moderation itself is the work of excellent legislators. What was done then is now easy to perceive: it seems to be this. **MEGILLUS:** What? **ATHENIAN:** Some God, as I believe, had care for you; who, since he foresaw the future, established for you a twin generation of kings from a single one, and so contracted it more toward moderation. Furthermore, a certain human [prudence] joined with divine powers, perceiving your sovereignty to be swelling, joined the moderate power of those who are engaged in the judicial forum to the power of the haughty nobility, making the opinion of the twenty-eight elders equal to the power of the kings in the greatest matters. To these, a third savior was present, who, observing the sovereignty still luxuriating and raging, applied a bridle to it, so to speak, by the census of the Ephors, brought near to a power chosen by lot. By this reasoning, therefore, your kingdom, composed of those elements which were fitting and constituted moderately, was itself preserved and was the cause of the safety of others. Since under Temenus and Cresphontes and the others who established laws for them, whoever they were, not even the faction of Aristodemus itself would have been preserved. For they were not sufficiently skilled in passing laws. Since, if they had been, they never would have thought that a youthful soul, having accepted a sovereignty from which a tyranny could arise, would be restrained by an oath. But now God has shown of what sort the sovereignty ought to have been, and ought to be, most chiefly constituted. That this is understood by us after it has happened, as I said before, is nothing wondrous. For it is not difficult to see if you are warned by an example. But if anyone had foreseen it then, and could have moderated the sovereignties and made one out of three, he would have preserved all their magnificent thoughts, and neither the Persian fleet nor any other would have ever sailed into Greece, despising us as worthy of nothing. **CLINIAS:** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN:** They resisted them basely, therefore, O Clinias. I say "basely" not because those who then conquered by land and sea did not carry themselves with decent bravery in fighting: but I call it base because only one of those three cities fought for Greece: the other two were so depraved that one [Messene] even prevented Lacedaemon from bringing aid by waging a not-insignificant war against it; the other, that of the Argives, although it was the first in Greece in those times of distribution, yet when summoned to repel the Barbarian, would neither hear those entreating nor defend them. I could relate many things that were done in Greece at that time which could be accused as base. Nor do those who say they defended Greece speak truly. For unless the common counsel and power of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians had repelled the imminent servitude, almost all things would now be confused: Greeks with Greeks in turn, likewise Barbarians with Greeks, and Greeks with Barbarians. Just as those Greek [cities] which are now subject to the tyrants of the Persians are confused among themselves without any order, and even badly scattered. We have these things, O Clinias and Megillus, to oppose both to the ancient statesmen and legislators and to the younger ones, so that searching out their causes, we may find what else besides these things ought to have been done: such as what we have now set forth, namely that it is not fitting to establish great [Margin: *That the state ought to be wealthy, free, and prudent, and a friend to itself.*] and unmixed sovereignties, always keeping in memory that a city ought to be always free, prudent, and a friend to itself. To this the one who is to pass laws must look. Do not wonder, moreover, if we have already proposed certain other things to which the legislator must look, which indeed do not appear to be the same as these. But it is necessary to consider, when we say one must look to temperance, or prudence, or friendship, that our intention is not different, but the same: and if we use many other words of this kind, do not be disturbed. **CLINIAS:** We shall endeavor to do so, repeating the words in order. But now set forth what you were going to say, when you said the legislator ought to look to friendship, liberty, and prudence. [Margin: *Two mothers of civil governments.*] **ATHENIAN:** Listen then.

**[Page 527]**
# On the Laws, or, Dialogue III on the Legislator.

There are, as it were, two mothers of civil governments, from which if anyone says the others derive their origin, he will certainly speak rightly. It is fitting to call one of these "monarchy," that is, the rule of one, and the other "democracy," that is, of the people. The race of the Persians holds the height of the one, and it is not to be thought that any other [holds the height] of the other. All other forms are indeed composed of these in various ways, as I said. It is necessary, moreover, that a city be a participant in both of these, if there is to be liberty and friendship with prudence in it. Which indeed the discourse wishes to command us when it says that a city devoid of these can never be well governed. **CLINIAS:** By what means? **ATHENIAN:** Since, therefore, the one embraced Monarchy (namely, the rule of one) and the other liberty more than was fitting, neither has preserved the moderation of servitude and liberty. But yours—I mean the Laconian and Cretan [constitutions]—do so more. The Athenians and Persians did so formerly in almost this way, but now less so. But shall we also state the causes? [Margin: *Many things concerning the government of Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius.*] **CLINIAS:** Entirely, if only we desire to complete what has been proposed. **ATHENIAN:** Let us hear, then. The Persians, when in the time of Cyrus they possessed more of the moderation of servitude and liberty, were first themselves free: then they subjected many others. For when the princes themselves imparted liberty to their subjects and reduced the matter more toward equality, the soldiers were more friendly to their leaders and showed themselves ready in dangers. And if there was anyone more prudent among them and strong in counsel, since the king was not envious but gave the faculty of speaking freely to all and honored those capable of counsel, he brought the faculty of prudence into the common midst. All things, therefore, were rendered easy for them at that time by liberty, friendship, and the communion of the mind. **CLINIAS:** These things seem to have happened just as they are told. **ATHENIAN:** By what means, therefore, did that kingdom almost fall in the time of Cambyses, and was restored again in the time of Darius? Do you wish that we speak as if using divination? **CLINIAS:** Why should we not? For this contributes to that toward which we tend. **ATHENIAN:** Thus, then, I prophesy concerning Cyrus: that in other matters he was both a good leader and a friend of civil life, but he never touched upon right discipline in any way, nor did he ever apply his mind to the administration of the household. **CLINIAS:** Why so? **ATHENIAN:** Occupied with military service through his whole life from his youth, he handed over his sons to women to be educated; who educated them as if they were already happy and blessed boys, in no need of anything, so that they prohibited anyone from opposing them in any matter as being blessed, forcing all to praise whatever they themselves said or did. Thus they educated them to be such. **CLINIAS:** You seem to have described a fine education indeed. **ATHENIAN:** A feminine one, to be sure, which the royal women introduced, being puffed up by new riches and deserted by their husbands who were occupied with war and dangers. **CLINIAS:** That is consistent. **ATHENIAN:** Their father, indeed, had many herds [OCR: *muigreges* for *multos greges*] of sheep and men: but he was ignorant that his sons, to whom he was to leave these things, were not taught the paternal and Persian art itself; for the Persians were shepherds born in a harsh region, and the Persian art itself was hard, and sufficient to produce robust shepherds who could both keep guard and stay awake and serve in the military if the matter demanded. He permitted, however, that women and eunuchs should nourish his sons according to the rite of the Medes: whose education was corrupted by that which is commonly thought to be happiness. Whence they turned out such as it was fitting for those to become who had been nourished in the greatest license of things. When, therefore, at the death of Cyrus they took possession of affairs, being full of luxuries, impunity, and license, first one, not bearing equality, kills the other; then he himself, raging with ignorance and drunkenness, lost the sovereignty. For the Medes and a certain one then called a Eunuch despised him as if he were out of his mind. **CLINIAS:** So it is said, and so it seems to have happened. **ATHENIAN:** And yet this is also said, that through Darius and those seven men the sovereignty returned again to the Persians. **CLINIAS:** Plainly. **ATHENIAN:** Let us inspect it, therefore, following the reason. Darius was not the son of a king, nor was he nourished in luxuries. When he had come to the sovereignty, and as the seventh had received it, he divided it into seven parts, of which today certain small dreams still remain; and he judged that they must live under laws contributing toward a certain common equality: and he sanctioned it thus, and that distribution which Cyrus had promised to the Persians he embraced by law, providing friendship and community to all Persians, and attracting the Persian people with money and gifts. Thus, being loved by the soldiers, he himself subjugated no fewer regions than Cyrus had left. After Darius came Xerxes, who was educated in the luxuries of a king. But now I rightly call upon you, O Darius, who were not warned by the evil of Cyrus, but educated Xerxes in the same habits in which Cyrus had nourished Cambyses. He himself, therefore, being educated in the same way, suffered similar things likewise. From that time, almost no king of the Persians was great except in name. Nor do I judge this to be cautious fortune, but a bad life, such as many children of very wealthy men and tyrants live. For never can a boy, a man, and an old man emerge from such a life as excellent in virtue. These things are to be considered by the legislator and observed by us in the present. And yet it is also fair for you, O Lacedaemonians, to attribute this [to your system]: that you do not commit any excellent magistracy to poverty, nor to riches, nor to kingship, nor to private citizens, which the voice of some god has not already commanded from the beginning. For it is not fitting in a city to confer excellent honors upon anyone because he excels in riches, or because he is swift, or handsome, or robust, if he lacks virtue. But not even if he should have some other virtue, but does not have temperance. **MEGILLUS:** In what way do you say that, stranger? **ATHENIAN:** Is not fortitude one certain part of virtue? **MEGILLUS:** It is. **ATHENIAN:** You yourself, therefore, when you have heard, judge. Would you wish to have any neighbor or domestic servant who is indeed exceedingly brave, but least temperate, but rather wanton and one who pours himself into every vice? **MEGILLUS:** May the gods grant better. **ATHENIAN:** Or indeed one skilled in many arts and wise in them, but unjust? **MEGILLUS:** By no means. **ATHENIAN:** But indeed, justice can have no origin without temperance. **MEGILLUS:** For how otherwise? **ATHENIAN:** But neither even that man, who was just now called wise by us, who has his pleasures and pains in concord with and obedient to right reason. **MEGILLUS:** Certainly not. **ATHENIAN:** Let us further consider this, so that we may inspect how honors are distributed among citizens rightly or not rightly. **MEGILLUS:** What [honor]? **ATHENIAN:** If temperance should be destitute of every other kind of virtue in someone's soul, is it rightly to be honored, or the opposite? **MEGILLUS:** I do not have what to answer. **ATHENIAN:** You have answered modestly and sufficiently. For if either of those had been granted, you would have answered, I believe, incongruously. **MEGILLUS:** It is well done, then. **ATHENIAN:** So be it. Truly, the accession itself and honor...

    *   **muigreges:** (Page 527) A clear OCR error for *multos greges* ("many herds") or possibly *mutos greges* ("dumb/silent herds," a common classical trope for sheep), though "many" fits the context of Cyrus's vast holdings better.
    *   **vtrariuq;:** (Page 527) OCR for *utriusque* ("of both").
    *   **cōponunf:** (Page 527) Expanded to *componuntur* ("are composed").
    *   **-q;:** This standard abbreviation for *-que* ("and") appears throughout (e.g., *Meſſenamq;*, *faciliùsq;*).
    *   **Dimidium plus esse quam totum:** A citation of Hesiod, *Works and Days*, line 40.
    *   **Mediocritas:** In this context, it is the Latin rendering of the Greek *meson* (the mean/moderation), a central theme in Platonic and Aristotelian ethics.
    *   **Proper Nouns:** All names (Pindar, Hesiod, Argos, Messene, Megillus, Clinias, Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius, Xerxes, Temenus, Cresphontes, Aristodemus) have been preserved in their Latinate or standard English forms as requested.
    *   **The "Two Mothers":** Plato's Athenian Stranger identifies Monarchy and Democracy as the two primary sources of all other constitutions.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book III of Plato’s Laws, translated here from the Latin version by Marsilio Ficino. The previous page discussed the various claims to authority (such as wisdom, age, and the lot). This page introduces the fundamental theory of the "two mothers" of all constitutions—Monarchy and Democracy—and the necessity of blending them to achieve a stable state.</meta>

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation: Dialogue III. 527

[Left Column]

There are two "mothers," as it were, of civil governments, from which if anyone were to say the others derive their origin, he would certainly speak correctly. Of these, it is fitting to call one **monarchy**, that is, the rule of one; the other, **democracy**, that is, the rule of the people. One might say that the Persian race holds the highest form of the former, while we should consider [the Athenians] <note>The text implies the Athenians here as the counter-example to the Persians.</note> for the latter. Indeed, all other forms of government are composed of these two in various ways, as I have said. However, it is necessary for a state to participate in both of these if liberty, friendship, and wisdom <note>original: *prudentia*, often translated as practical wisdom or foresight</note> are to exist within it. This is exactly what our discourse intends to teach us when it says that a city lacking these can never be well governed.

**CLINIAS:** In what way, then? 

**ATHENIAN:** Since, therefore, the one embraced **Monarchy**—that is, the rule of one—and the other embraced liberty alone more than was fitting, neither maintained the proper balance <note>original: *mediocritatem*, referring to the "golden mean" or a moderate middle ground</note> between servitude and liberty. Your constitutions, however—I mean the Spartan <note>original: *Laconica*</note> and the Cretan—did so more than others. But the Athenians and the Persians, once...

<column-break/>

<summary>The Athenian Stranger identifies Monarchy and Democracy as the two primary "mother" constitutions, arguing that a successful state must find a moderate balance between the two to ensure liberty and social harmony.</summary>

Having introduced the idea that a successful state must blend both, the dialogue now examines how the Persian Empire failed by leaning too far into absolute monarchy, and how Athens must avoid the opposite extreme of total license. 528 [space] Book Thirty-Four <note>This heading refers to the volume's internal numbering in the early modern edition; the text itself is Book III of Plato's *Laws*.</note>

[Column 1]

...matters and reproaches will be worthy of silence rather than an irrational response. MEGILLUS: You seem to me to be speaking of **Temperance** <note>original: *temperantia*, meaning moderation or self-control</note>. ATHENIAN: That is exactly what I mean. Therefore, that which profits us most among other things, if it is honored with the greatest distinction, will be honored most rightly; and that which profits us in the second degree should be honored second. And so, according to the logic of succession, if each thing attains the honors that follow in due order, it will surely attain them rightly. MEGILLUS: And so it is. ATHENIAN: We say, therefore, that a city which is to be safe and happy as far as human strength allows, must distribute honors and disgraces rightly. MEGILLUS: That is true. ATHENIAN: The right distribution is this: the **goods of the soul** should be considered primary and most honorable, provided that temperance is joined to them. In the second rank of dignity, the **goods of the body** should be placed. In the third, **external possessions and money**. If any legislator or city transgresses this—either by honoring money above all else, or by placing something of lower honor before a higher one—they act neither piously nor as a citizen should. Shall we hold this as settled, or how shall we proceed? MEGILLUS: Entirely so. ATHENIAN: Our consideration of the Persian government led us to speak of these things at greater length. We find that they have become even worse. We say the cause is that they took away too much of the people's liberty and increased the power of lordship more than was fitting, thereby destroying society and friendship within the state. When these are corrupted, the rulers no longer look out for their subjects and the people, but only for their own empire. Furthermore, for the sake of a tiny advantage for themselves, they do not care if they utterly overturn cities and allow friendly nations to be consumed by fire. Thus, they hate with hostility and without mercy, and they are held in hatred in return. And if ever there is a need for the people to fight for them, they find no common consensus among them, nor a willingness to undergo dangers from the heart and fight for their rulers. Instead, although they rule over almost countless men, they find them all useless for war; as if lacking men of their own, they hire others for pay, thinking they will be saved by mercenaries and foreign soldiers. Moreover, they are forced to act foolishly, since by their very deeds they proclaim that the things said to be honorable and worthy in a city are mere trifles when compared to silver and gold. MEGILLUS: So it is. ATHENIAN: But regarding the affairs of the Persians—how they are not managed rightly due to excessive domination and servitude—let enough have been said. MEGILLUS: <margin>Attic de- / mocracy.</margin> Absolutely. ATHENIAN: Next, it is fitting to run through the Attic government in the same way, so that it may be clear how a liberty subject to no magistrate is not a little worse than a liberty that follows a moderate rule of magistrates. For at the time when the Persians were attacking Greece—indeed, almost all of Europe—we had an ancient Republic, and there were magistrates chosen from a four-fold division of wealth <note>referring to the Solonian census classes</note>. In us there was a **sense of shame** <note>original: *pudor*, translating the Greek *aidos*</note>, like a master, for whose sake we were willing to live as subjects to the laws. Moreover, the magnitude of the forces on land and sea so terrified us that it forced us to obey and serve the laws and magistrates with even greater observance. For these reasons, a greater benevolence arose among us. For almost ten years before

[Column 2]

the naval battle at Salamis was fought, Datis was sent by Darius leading a Persian fleet against the Athenians and Eretrians. Death was decreed for Datis by Darius unless he brought these nations under his sway. Datis, therefore, quickly conquered the Eretrians with a countless multitude of soldiers, and a terrible rumor reached our city: that not a single Eretrian had escaped, but that the soldiers had joined hands with one another and, by surrounding the entire region of Eretria, had captured every last person <note>This refers to the "netting" technique mentioned by Herodotus, where soldiers formed a line across an island to sweep up all inhabitants.</note>. This rumor, whether true or false, terrified both the other Greeks and especially the Athenians. Though they sent embassies everywhere to all of Greece to urge them to bring aid, no one wished to help except the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>. And they, either hindered by the war they were waging against Messene, or for some other reason—for we do not know—arrived to help on the day after the Battle of Marathon. After this, it was said that the king was preparing great things and making many threats. Meanwhile, Darius is reported to have yielded to nature <note>i.e., died</note>, and his son, a fierce youth <note>Xerxes</note>, received the empire and did not wish to desist from his father's undertakings. The Athenians believed all his preparations were turned against them because of the slaughter at Marathon. Furthermore, hearing that Mount Athos was being dug through, the Hellespont joined by a bridge, and an immense fleet being gathered, they thought there would be safety for them neither by sea nor by land. They especially lacked confidence in anyone's protection, for they remembered that when the Eretrians were first captured, no one had brought them aid or wished to undergo danger for their safety. They expected the same thing would happen to them on land. And at sea, they found no safety at all, as more than a thousand ships were being brought against them. They saw only one hope of safety, however thin and doubtful: for looking back at what had been done before, and how they had conquered despite having despaired of safety, they were carried away by this hope and found their refuge only in themselves and the gods. All these things, therefore, bound them together with a greater benevolence toward one another—I mean the present fear, and the fear which had long been within them from the laws, which they acquired by serving the laws. This **sense of shame** <note>original: *pudor*</note> we have often named in the preceding passages; we said that everyone who is to be good must serve it, and whoever is affected by it is free and intrepid. And unless that present fear had been joined to this sense of shame, they never would have been provoked by such a clash or come together to defend the temples of the gods, the tombs of their ancestors, their fatherland itself, and their other family and friends as they are said to have done; instead, they would have scattered, each going his own way. MEGILLUS: Well said, stranger, and you have spoken as befits yourself and your fatherland. ATHENIAN: These things are true, O Megillus. For it is fitting to recount the things done then with you, who preserve the nature of your parents. But both you and Clinias consider carefully whether what we say pertains to the making of laws. For I do not narrate these things for the sake of mere storytelling. See for what purpose I say these things: so that we may understand that the same thing happened to us as to the Persians, in a way—while they dragged the common people into total servitude, we, on the contrary, dragged them into sheer liberty. How and what we should say next, the words already spoken and appropriately said demonstrate in a certain way. MEGILLUS: You speak well. But try to express what you were just saying more clearly. ATHENIAN: I shall do so. My friends, under the ancient laws, the common people were not masters of anything among us, but rather were in a sense servants to the laws by their own will. MEGILLUS: To which laws? ATHENIAN: To those, I say, which were established concerning **music**...

He recounts the terror of the Persian invasions to illustrate how shared fear and legal discipline united the Athenian people before they moved toward excessive liberty.</summary>

On the Laws, Or, Dialogue III on Lawmaking. 529

[Column 1]

...so that we may recount how this excessive liberty has gradually increased. For at that time, music was divided by us into specific types and forms. One type was a song of prayer to the gods, which they called **hymns**. Opposite to this was another type of song, which one might most accurately call **plaintive songs** <note>original: *querulos*, likely referring to "threnoi" or laments</note>. Another type was the **Paean** <note>A song of praise or healing, usually dedicated to Apollo</note>. Yet another was the "birth of Dionysus," which I believe was called the **Dithyramb**. There was also another type of song which they named **citharoedic laws** <note>Fixed standards or "rules" for singing to the lyre</note>. Therefore, it was not permitted to misuse one type of song for another, according to these and other established laws. The authority to recognize, judge, and condemn anyone who acted to the contrary was not granted to the hissing or the foolish shouts of the multitude, as is the fashion now; nor was the license to praise given to the clapping and noisy crowd. Instead, it was granted to men distinguished by their learning, and they were permitted to listen in great silence until the end. Children, their tutors <note>original: *pædagogi*, the slaves who supervised children</note>, and the common people were kept in order by the threat of the rod. Since these things were done in an orderly fashion, the multitude of citizens willingly obeyed and did not dare to judge anything in a tumultuous way. 

As time went on, however, the authors of a lawlessness foreign to music were the poets themselves. They were men of talent, but they did not sufficiently observe what was just and lawful in music. They acted like rioters <note>original: *debacchātes*, acting like followers of Bacchus/Dionysus</note> and indulged in pleasure more than was proper. These poets mixed laments with hymns, and paeans with dithyrambs; they imitated the sounds and songs of the pipes on the lyre, mixing everything with everything else. Out of ignorance, they unintentionally lied about music, claiming that it possessed no inherent standard of rightness, but that it should be judged most correctly by the pleasure of the listener, whether that person be a good man or the opposite. By composing such poems and saying such things to the common people, they rendered the masses so wicked and bold regarding music that they believed themselves fully capable of passing judgment on it. 

Hence the theaters, which used to be silent, began to shout frequently, as if the crowd keenly perceived what was beautiful in the Muses and what was not. And so, the matter fell away from the rule of the best men <note>original: *optimatum potestate*, referring to aristocracy or meritocracy</note> into the base power of the theater <term>theatrocracy|The rule of the audience; a situation where public taste and popular opinion dictate artistic and legal standards.</term>. For if a "popular power" of free men alone had existed, it would not have been a great misfortune. But now, from music began our general opinion that everyone is wise in everything, followed by lawlessness and a false sense of liberty. For they became fearless, as if they knew the truth; this license gave birth to impudence. Indeed, if the opinion of a better person is not feared because of one's own audacity, that itself is a most ruinous impudence, which proceeds from a certain reckless liberty. 

MEGILLUS: You speak the absolute truth. 

ATHENIAN: This liberty is followed by that license which makes us unwilling to be subject to magistrates. From this originates the tendency to despise the service and commands of father, mother, and elders. And as we reach the extreme of this transgression, we even refuse to obey the laws. At the very edge of this decline, we neglect oaths, our word, and the gods themselves. Whence, having returned to that ancient and tyrannical nature, we shall suffer those same old evils again and live through hard ages once more, finding no end to our troubles. But why have these things been said by us? It seems to me that our discourse must be pulled back like a horse from every side, lest having an unbridled mouth and being carried away by its own momentum, it "falls off the ass," as the proverb says <note>original: *ab asino... excidat*, a Greek proverb meaning to make a fool of oneself or fail through lack of skill</note>. We must ask, therefore, for what purpose these things were said. 

MEGILLUS: Indeed we must. 

ATHENIAN: We have said these things, then, for the sake of those matters. 

MEGILLUS: Which matters? 

ATHENIAN: We said—surely—that three things must be 

<column-break/>

[Column 2]

regarded by the lawgiver: so that the city established by laws may be free, at peace with itself, and possess wisdom. Were these things not said? 

MEGILLUS: Precisely so. 

ATHENIAN: For this reason, we brought forward two types of government: one in which there is the strictest servitude, and the other in which there is unrestrained liberty. We considered which of these was governed rightly. We perceived that when a middle ground was added—some authority to the one and some liberty to the other—both states fared exceptionally well. But they fared poorly when servitude in one and liberty in the other were pushed to the extreme. 

MEGILLUS: You tell the truth. 

ATHENIAN: Moreover, it was for this same reason that we considered the constitution of the Dorian army, the roots of the Dardanian mountains, and the seaside habitation; furthermore, those first people who were left behind after the desolation of the flood. It was for their sake that we held our discourse on music, on drunkenness, and on the things that came before. All these things were said for the purpose of understanding how a city might best be governed, and how an individual might best arrange his own life. If we have indeed achieved anything worthwhile, what proof or refutation of ourselves will there be for us, O Megillus and Clinias? 

CLINIAS: Stranger, I seem to see something for myself. All the preceding words seem to have been spoken by us quite opportunely. For in a way, I was in need of them. Both of you—you and Megillus here—have found me at just the right moment. I will not hide from you what has happened to me. For I have been confirmed by these speeches as if by an omen. The greater part of the Cretans is thinking of leading out a certain colony, and they have entrusted the care of that matter to the Gnossians. The city of the Gnossians, in turn, has mandated that I and nine other men should take charge of it. It orders us to establish laws, both from those of the Cretans that please us, and from those that can be gathered from elsewhere. It commands us not to be afraid of foreign laws, provided they are proven good. Now, therefore, let us grant this favor both to me and to yourselves. Having collected laws from everywhere, let us build a city in speech from the beginning. In this way, that which we seek will be more diligently considered, and perhaps this dispute will contribute to the future constitution of my city. 

ATHENIAN: You are not declaring war, Clinias! Therefore, unless it is inconvenient for Megillus, my efforts are prepared for you to the best of my ability. 

CLINIAS: You speak well. 

MEGILLUS: I also am ready. 

CLINIAS: You have both spoken excellently. Therefore, we must first attempt to found the city in speech.

### THE FOURTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, OR, ON LAWMAKING.

*

**THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO** <note>Ficino was the 15th-century priest and scholar who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin, making them accessible to the Renaissance world.</note>

*

**T**his fourth dialogue, just like the three preceding ones and also the first part of the fifth, is concerned with the counsel and duty of the founder of laws. His counsel concerns the "matter" and the "form" of the city. By **matter**, I mean the site, the composition, and the layout of the town. By **form**, I mean the manner and order of public government. But since this form can never be beautiful unless the souls of the citizens are beautiful, the lawgiver is therefore ordered to watch over the forming of the souls of his citizens from a tender age and throughout their whole lives. The "matter" of the city is thus explained in few words, but he treats the "form" and the "formation of souls" most accurately; for in view of the dignity of the soul, he considers all external things—no matter how grand they may seem—to be of no value. Truly, if our Plato were a doctor of bodies, he would labor more diligently in choosing the healthiest air to contribute to a firm and strong condition of the body. But he who...

### On the Laws. Or, On the Fourth Dialogue of the Laws. 531

Immediately after the flood, divine providence ruled more
unrefined men through the service of **angels**, or better **daemons** <note>original: *daemonum*; in the Platonic tradition, these are intermediary spirits or guardian intellects that bridge the gap between the divine and the human, rather than evil beings</note>,

Furthermore, it is explained in a third way in this manner: that
every day, whoever chooses a way of life somewhat set apart
from others and has been rightly educated, is said to immediately migrate into the contemplative
and blessed **kingdom of Saturn** <note>The "Kingdom of Saturn" refers to the mythological Golden Age, which Ficino interprets here as a state of spiritual contemplation and divine order</note>. But insofar as
they are distinguished into various rites under the duty of contemplation, to that
extent they also seem to be separated into many flocks, and to be inspired and ruled by different
divine powers according to the likeness of their life. For the present, I pass

wonderfully like flocks under **Saturn as their shepherd**. Under Saturn,
I say, in three principal ways: first, under the divine and angelic mind;

...if it were deprived of this very thing? **Clinias**: It is almost impossible. However, guest, we Cretans believe that the naval battle of the Greeks at Salamis against the Barbarians <note>original: *Barbaros*; referring to the Persian Empire</note> saved all of Greece. **The Athenian Stranger**: And yet many of the Greeks as well as the Barbarians affirm that. But I, my friend, and Megillus here, say that the land-based battle at *Marathon* and at *Plataea*, the one was the beginning of salvation, the other the end: and by these battles the Greeks were made better, but by the others <note>meaning the naval battles</note> they were not made better—if we may speak this way of the battles by which we were equally saved at that time. For to the war waged at *Salamis*, I add that maritime one fought at *Artemisium*. But looking now at the virtue of civil discipline, we are considering the nature of the region and the order of the laws. For we do not think that merely to be saved and to exist is to be held in the highest value for men, as the common people <note>original: *vulgus*</note> think: but that as long as they exist, they should be the best. This was also said by us in our previous discussions, I believe. **Clinias**: Quite clearly said. **The Athenian Stranger**: Let us therefore only observe if we are following the same path which is best for cities in establishing a dwelling and in enacting laws. **Clinias**: In a wonderful way. **The Athenian Stranger**: Tell me then what follows: what multitude will inhabit the colony? Will it be whoever wishes from all of *Crete*, as if a great crowd overflows from the individual cities? Or will they be chosen for the strength and fertility of the land itself? For you do not gather all who are willing from the Greeks, although I see some from *Argos* and *Aegina* and other parts of Greece inhabit this region. But tell me at present, from where will the multitude of these current citizens come to you? **Clinias**: I think they will come from all of *Crete*; and among other Greeks, it will, I think, most readily receive those who come from the *Peloponnese*. And what you were saying is true, that those indeed are from *Argos*. For the clan that is most praised here at present is the *Gortynian*, which migrated here from *Gortyn* in the Peloponnese itself. **The Athenian Stranger**: But that migration into one city is not usually so easy for cities when it is not done in the manner of swarms <note>original: *examinum more*; a metaphor comparing human colonists to a swarm of bees leaving a hive</note>, as when one friendly clan coming from among friends from a certain region—either pressed by the narrowness of the land or forced by some other necessity of this kind—migrates into a foreign land. Sometimes it happens that in a city agitated by civil strife, one part of the citizens secedes. An entire city conquered in war is also found to have fled together at times. All these situations are partly easy, in that they may be arranged in a new habitation and governed by laws newly established; but they are also partly difficult. For a race that is one, of one language and of the same laws, since it has a communion of sacred rites and all such things, is bound by a certain friendship among themselves, but [finds it hard to accept] other laws and a mode of government from the ancient...

The dialogue then turns to the logistical and social challenges of settling a new colony with a diverse or displaced population.</summary>

### On Laws, or, on the Passing of Laws, Dialogue IV. 535

[Left Column]

...with our own ease, he took care of our affairs, providing peace and modesty, liberty and an abundance of justice; he kept us far from civil strife and made the human race happy. This discourse, relying on the truth, asserts that for all cities where not a God, but some mortal dominates, there will never be any rest from evils and hardships. 

But it commands us to strive with all our effort to imitate the life that existed under Saturn <note>original: *Saturno*; referring to the Greek god Cronus and the mythical "Golden Age" where gods ruled over men</note>; and, obeying whatever spark of immortality exists within us, to govern both homes and cities privately and publicly, calling the very distribution of the mind <note>original: *mentis... dispensationem*; a play on the Greek words *nomos* (law) and *nous* (mind), suggesting that law is the outward expression of reason</note> in every matter "Law." 

For if a single man, or the power of a few, or even that of the people, possesses a soul devoted to pleasure and desire, and longs to be filled with these things—and since he cannot achieve satisfaction, is tormented by an unquenchable, inextinguishable fire and an incurable disease—and yet he dominates either a city or certain private individuals, immediately...

<column-break/>

<summary>The Athenian Stranger uses the myth of Saturn’s Golden Age to argue that human rulers are naturally prone to corruption. He concludes that "Law" should be the "distribution of the mind" to mirror divine governance and avoid the "incurable disease" of unrestrained desire.</summary>

# Book Seventeen.

...it is, it must be, that it is both an art and a *scientia* (knowledge). PROTAGORAS: They will admit this.
SOCRATES: As for what specifically this *scientia* may be, we will consider that at another time. For now, it is enough that it is a form of knowledge, insofar as it relates to the demonstration that I and Protagoras were going to give in response to your question. Now, if you recall, this was the question: We agreed that nothing is more powerful than *scientia*; indeed, that wherever it is present, it always dominates pleasure and all other things. But you objects that pleasure and pain often dominate one's choice. Since we did not grant you this at all, you immediately asked: "If this—being overcome by pleasures—is not what it seems, O Protagoras and Socrates, then declare what else it might be." At this, if we had answered right then that it is *inscitia* (ignorance), you would have laughed at us. But now, if you mock us, you will also be mocking yourselves. For you yourselves confessed a little while ago that those who err in their choice regarding pleasure and pain do so through a defect of *scientia*—that is, a lack of knowledge of things that are good and bad. And you did not merely say it was a defect of knowledge, but you added that it was specifically a defect of the "science of measurement" (*scientia metiendi*). 

[[notes: Socrates is referencing the "hedonic calculus" or the art of measuring pleasure and pain over time to make rational choices. Cf. Protagoras 357a.]]

Moreover, an action that goes astray and which *scientia* does not govern—as you well know—proceeds from *inscitia*. 

[[margin: To be overcome by pleasures is extreme ignorance.]]

Therefore, being overcome by pleasures is extreme ignorance. Of this disease, Protagoras here, along with Prodicus and Hippias (the sophists), profess themselves to be the physicians. But because you think this is something other than ignorance, you do not send yourselves or your sons to these sophists—the teachers of these matters—to be cured, as if virtue could not be taught. Instead, by hoarding your money uselessly and not applying it to these instructors, you fail both in private and public life. This is plainly what we would have responded to the common people. But now I ask you as well, O Prodicus and Hippias, together with Protagoras—for let this discourse be shared with you: Does it seem to you that I speak the truth, or what is false? It seemed to everyone that what was said was very true indeed. 

"Do you concede then," I asked, "that what is pleasant is good, and what is painful is bad?" I reject that distinction of names which Prodicus here is accustomed to introduce, and I ask for his judgment. For whether you call it "pleasurable," or "delightful," or "joyful," or by whatever name you finally choose, O excellent Prodicus, answer me now on this point which I seek. Prodicus smiled and gave his assent, and the others likewise agreed.

Then I said: "What of this, O men? Are not all actions that pertain to living pleasantly and without distress honorable and useful? And is not an honorable work both good and useful?" They agreed. "If therefore the pleasant is the good," I said, "no one—knowing or believing that other things are better than those he is doing, and being capable of doing them—then does those [lesser] things when better ones are possible. Indeed, what is called 'being overcome by the passions' is nothing other than *inscitia* (ignorance), and to dominate the passions is nothing other than *sapientia* (wisdom)." 

[[margin: Ignorance.]]

This pleased everyone. "Furthermore, do you not say that ignorance is something like this: when someone is deceived by a false opinion concerning matters of great importance?" They granted this too. "No one," I continued, "willingly descends toward evils, or toward those things he considers evil. Nor, as it seems, is it in the nature of man to wish to decline toward those things he deems bad in place of the good. And when he is forced to choose one of two evils, no one chooses the worse when it is permitted to choose the lesser evil." All these points seemed to us to be firmly established. 

"What then," I asked, "do you call fear and terror? Is it not what I say to you, Prodicus? I call it a certain expectation of evil, whether you call it fear or terror." It seemed to Protagoras and Hippias that fear and terror were this, but to Prodicus, fear was this indeed, while terror was not. 

[[notes: Prodicus was famous for "orthoepeia" or the precise use of words; he likely distinguished between fear and a more sudden or intense dread.]]

"That matters not at all, O Prodicus," I said, "but rather this: whether what was said above remains true. For what mortal will want to proceed toward those things he fears, when he is permitted to go toward what he does not fear? Or is it impossible, according to what we have already conceded? For it is established that what someone fears, he thinks to be evil; and no one of his own will descends toward, or takes up, what he believes to be evil." 

These things also pleased everyone. "With these things established," I said, "O Prodicus and Hippias, let Protagoras now defend what he first answered—or rather, not quite what he said at the very beginning. For he said that among the five parts of virtue, no one was like another, but each had its own private power. I do not press this now, but what followed. For he said in what followed that four parts of virtue were closely related to one another, but one of them—namely *fortitudo* (courage)—differed greatly from the rest. He said this could be inferred from the fact that many men are found to be most brave, yet are most profane, most unjust, most intemperate, and most ignorant. By this, he wished to show that courage differs greatly from all other parts of virtue. I was immediately and vehemently amazed by his answer, and even more so after I discussed these matters with you. Therefore I asked him whether he called the courageous 'bold.' He replied that they were 'daring' as well. Do you remember, Protagoras, that you answered this?" 

PROTAGORAS: I remember. 
SOCRATES: Tell us, I pray, for what reason do you call daring men courageous? Is it for those things which the timid approach? 
PROTAGORAS: No. 
SOCRATES: Then for other things? 
PROTAGORAS: Certainly. 
SOCRATES: Do the timid approach things that are to be dared? And the courageous approach things that are to be feared? 
PROTAGORAS: So it is said, O Socrates. 
SOCRATES: You speak the truth. But I do not ask this; rather, for what reason do you call daring men courageous? Is it because they approach evils, knowing them to be evil and destructive, or rather things that are not such? 
PROTAGORAS: That this is impossible has been shown by your previous arguments. 
SOCRATES: In this too you speak truly. Therefore, if this was correctly demonstrated, no one approaches things he judges to be evil and destructive, since it is established that 'being overcome by the passions' is actually ignorance. 
PROTAGORAS: Clearly. 
SOCRATES: Yet everyone approaches the things they dare, the timid as well as the courageous. And in this sense, the timid and the courageous approach the same things. 
PROTAGORAS: On the contrary, O Socrates, the things toward which the courageous and the timid strive are completely opposite. For the brave are willing to go to war, but the timid are not. 
SOCRATES: Is going to war honorable, or base? 
PROTAGORAS: Honorable. 
SOCRATES: And if it is honorable, did we not agree above that it is also good? For all honorable and beautiful actions are agreed to be good. 
PROTAGORAS: You speak the truth, and it always seems so to me. 
SOCRATES: Rightly so. But whom do you say are unwilling to go into battle, though that path is beautiful and good? 
PROTAGORAS: The timid. 
SOCRATES: And if it is beautiful and good, is it not also pleasant? 
PROTAGORAS: That was conceded. 
SOCRATES: Then is it with knowledge that the timid are unwilling to proceed toward that which is beautiful, better, and more pleasant? 
PROTAGORAS: But if we admit this, we shall overturn what was agreed upon before. 
SOCRATES: What then? Does the brave man not tend toward that which is beautiful, better, and more pleasant? 
PROTAGORAS: It is necessary to confess it. 
SOCRATES: Entirely, then, brave men do not fear basely, if ever they fear, nor are they daring in a base way. 
PROTAGORAS: That is so. 
SOCRATES: If not basely, then honorably and beautifully. 
PROTAGORAS: Certainly. 
SOCRATES: If honorably, then also well. 
PROTAGORAS: Indeed. 
SOCRATES: And do not the timid,
