# Protagoras, Or, the Sophists.

...the timid, the fierce, and the furious, on the contrary, dare basely and fear basely? 
PROTAGORAS: That is true. 
SOCRATES: And for what other reason do they dare basely and badly, if not because of ignorance and *inscitia*? 
PROTAGORAS: For that very reason. 
SOCRATES: That which makes the timid what they are—do you call it timidity, or courage? 
PROTAGORAS: Timidity. 
SOCRATES: And have not the timid appeared to be such because of their ignorance of what is to be feared? 
PROTAGORAS: Indeed. 
SOCRATES: They are timid, then, because of this ignorance? 
PROTAGORAS: Yes. 
SOCRATES: And you asserted that being timid is timidity. 
PROTAGORAS: I did. 
SOCRATES: Is it not then the case that the ignorance of what is to be feared and what is not to be feared is timidity? 
PROTAGORAS: It is. 
SOCRATES: Yet courage is the opposite of timidity. 
PROTAGORAS: Without a doubt. 
SOCRATES: And is not *sapientia* (wisdom) regarding what is to be feared and not feared the opposite of that ignorance? 
PROTAGORAS: Entirely. 
SOCRATES: And the ignorance of these things is timidity. 
PROTAGORAS: Most certainly. 
SOCRATES: Therefore, wisdom regarding what is to be feared and what is not to be feared is *fortitudo* (courage), being the opposite of the ignorance of these same things. 

Protagoras did not assent further, but remained silent. Then I said: "Why are you silent, Protagoras? Why do you neither agree nor refuse?" He said, "Finish the matter yourself." I said, "I will conclude immediately, if I may ask only this one thing: whether it still seems to you now, as it did before, that there are some who are most ignorant, yet who are nevertheless most brave." 

He replied, "You seem to contend stubbornly, Socrates, that I should be the one to answer; therefore I will comply with you. I say that it seems impossible, based on those things which were conceded above."

"I ask you about all these things for no other reason," I said, "than that I desire to know what kind of things pertain to virtue, and what virtue itself is. I know that once this is declared, that which you and I have spent so many words upon will immediately become known: namely, my claim that virtue cannot be taught, and your assertion that it can. Yet I think the outcome of our dispute, if it could take the voice of a man, would mock us and rebuke us in this way: 'How absurd you are, O Socrates and Protagoras! You, Socrates, said from the beginning that virtue could not be taught, yet now you contend against yourself to show that all these things—justice, temperance, and courage—are *scientia* (knowledge). By this reasoning, it is most clear that virtue *can* be taught. For if virtue were anything other than knowledge, as Protagoras first asserted, it clearly could not be taught. But now if it appears to be knowledge, as you, Socrates, are trying to infer, it would be a wonder if virtue could not be acquired through doctrine. Protagoras, on the other hand, at first wanted virtue to be taught; but now he seems to strive for the opposite—that virtue should appear to be anything rather than knowledge, by which means it would be the least teachable of all things.'" 

"Truly, O Protagoras, seeing all these things so heavily tossed upside down, I apply myself vehemently so that they may come into the light. I would wish that, having run through these matters between us, we might show what virtue is, and likewise consider whether it can be taught or not. Let that Epimetheus (Afterthought) not deceive us too often in our dispute, just as he neglected us in the distribution of gifts in the story you told. For Prometheus (Forethought) in the fable pleases me more than Epimetheus; using his example and being *promethumenus*—that is, looking forward—in my own life, I treat all these matters. And if you are willing, as I said from the beginning, I would most gladly deliberate on these things with you." 

Then Protagoras said: "I praise this zeal of yours, O Socrates, and the course of your discourse. For although other vices are absent from me, if I am not mistaken in my opinion, envy is certainly most absent of all. And I have already said of you to many people that I admire you more than anyone I have met—certainly more than any of your peers. I add, moreover, that it will be no wonder to me if you become famous in the study of wisdom. As for these things, we shall discuss them at another time whenever you wish. For now, it is time for me to attend to other business." 

"So it must be done," I said, "if it so seems to you; since for some time now, as I said, it was time for me to depart. However, to comply with the honorable young man Callias, I remained." These things having been said and heard, we departed.

# PLATO'S EUTHYDEMUS, OR, THE LITIGIOUS.

-> **THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.** <-

[[notes: Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator and commentator on Plato during the Renaissance. His "Arguments" provide a Neoplatonic and moral framework for understanding the dialogues.]]

PLATO, a man of signal charity, strives in the *Euthydemus*, as he often does elsewhere, to turn minds born for serious matters away from the vain trifles of the sophists. He shows that even when they deal with the gravest subjects, they are merely playing, and he mocks their audacity everywhere. He describes them here as elsewhere as curious and vain contestants in the altercation of words, ready to repel any statement whether it be true or false. 

First, he shows how greedy the character of the sophists is, since Euthydemus and his brother Dionysodorus, being sophists, are ready to teach for a fee the military art in which they boast—an art which no one ever sold before. Second, he shows how ambitious they are, since they profess judicial skill together with military skill, and both together with sophistry, though these differ most widely from one another. Third, how vain they are; for now that they are old men, they turn from things to words, and from the study of truth to lies. Fourth, how contemptible they are, for anyone can attain this faculty of quibbling in a short time—at most two years. Fifth, how dangerous they are. For who should wonder that simple adolescents are easily ensnared by the painted subtleties of the sophists, and are imbued with false opinions and pernicious morals? Even Socrates himself, portrayed as the oldest and wisest of men, is shown as if ensnared by the same bait, hurrying in wonder to the gymnasia of the sophists. Note that even that Socratic *daemon*, which seems to be able to be taught by no one, is imagined to be deceived by the sophistic tricks of these rascals.

Meanwhile, Socrates, even in his old age, frequenting the schools of boys, the music games, and the rudiments of words, admonishes us: first, that we should not contemptuously overlook even the smallest thing regarding the perfection of the disciplines. Second, that we should not, as often happens, be kept from the study of discipline by a certain rustic shame or blushing. Third, that according to the custom of Solon, we should judge that we must learn for as long as we must live. 

Furthermore, the fact that the sophists never notice the Socratic irony directed against them—indeed, there is nothing so magnificent said in their praise that they do not most easily believe and openly accept—declares two things to us especially: first, that nothing more empty than these rascals can be found; second, that because they study so intensely to deceive others, they are most easily deceived by their own fallacy. 

Moreover, that such charlatans never provide the virtue they promise, nor ever exhort anyone toward it, but everywhere take refuge in their accustomed word-quibbling—treating these as serious matters above other studies—signifies three things to us. First, those who are not themselves adorned with virtue can never teach it, either by reason or example. Second, men too curious about words never follow or establish good things. Third, those who most easily promise the most, keep their promises least of all. 

Added to this is that Socrates lures the sophists to teach virtue by using the crowd of wealthy disciples, appealing to them as if they were overly ambitious and greedy. But there, under the persona of Crito, we are warned not to rashly commit the care of the soul to anyone. That Socrates, while the sophists promise virtue, meanwhile beseeches them as if they were gods, clearly declares that virtue is to be sought from God himself, and that men endowed with virtue are to be held as divine. Likewise, that he considers them happier than kings because of their study of virtue plainly signifies that a man endowed with virtue is, first, a king of himself, and then of a kingdom. Socrates further teaches, in caring for Clinias, with how much...

# CRITO, SOCRATES, EUTHYDEMUS, DIONYSODORUS, CLINIAS, CTESIPPUS.

[[notes: The dialogue begins with Crito asking Socrates about a conversation he witnessed at the Lyceum gymnasium.]]

**CRITO:** Who was that man, O Socrates, with whom you were disputing yesterday in the Lyceum? A large crowd was surrounding you. Although I wanted to get closer to hear the matter, I could not perceive anything clearly. But when I stood on my tiptoes to look, it seemed to me to be a certain stranger with whom you were discoursing. Who was he? 

SOCRATES: Which one are you asking about, Crito? For there was not just one, but two. 

CRITO: The one I mean was sitting third to your right. Between you was that youth, the son of Axiochus (Clinias), who seemed to me to have made quite a bit of progress. He is nearly the age of Critobulus. But while Critobulus has a leaner physical habit, this youth seems to have the appearance of one more mature, and of an honorable and excellent nature. 

SOCRATES: That is Euthydemus whom you seek, O Crito. The one sitting to my left was Dionysodorus, his brother, who also took part in the dispute. 

CRITO: I know neither of them, Socrates. 

SOCRATES: They are new, as it seems—they are sophists. 

CRITO: What is their country? What is their wisdom? 

SOCRATES: They are from Chios, I believe, by birth; but they migrated to Thurii. Fleeing from there, they have lived in these parts for many years now. As for your question about their wisdom, O Crito, they are plainly the wisest. Indeed, until now I did not know they were perfect athletes. For they are instructed in every kind of combat—not like the Acarnanian brothers who are athletes only of the body. These men, however, are primarily strong in speech, and in that kind of fighting by which everything is overcome. They are most skilled in the art of arms, and can make others skilled in arms if someone pays them a fee. Then they can handle and explain judicial combat, and instruct anyone in both writing and delivering legal cases. Until now they were only skilled in these things, but now they have put the finishing touch on their "athleticism." For they have recently attained that kind of combat that was lacking, so that no one can resist them; they are so strong in speaking, and so prompt to repel any statement, whether true or false. Therefore, O Crito, I am thinking of handing myself over to these men. For they promise they will make anyone else a master of the same things in a short time. 

CRITO: Does not your advanced age deter you, O Socrates? 

[[margin: That advanced age ought not to deter one from discipline.]]

SOCRATES: Not at all, Crito. There is something that consoles me and does not let me despair. For even these men, being old (so to speak), have dedicated themselves with great effort to this faculty which I now affect—namely, verbal contention. For a year ago, or certainly three years ago, they did not yet possess this skill. I only fear one thing: that I might be a disgrace to these strangers, just like Connus the son of Metrobius, the harp-player, who is even now teaching me the strings. The boys who are my fellow students laugh at me every day and call Connus "the teacher of old men." I fear someone might object to these strangers in the same way, and they, deterred by that, might reject me. I have therefore exhorted some other older men to go there with me for the sake of learning, and I will try to persuade some here as well. Why don't you go along too? Indeed, let us bring your sons as an "attraction." For when they hope for the attendance of your sons, they will more willingly accept us to be educated, led by these attractions. 

CRITO: Nothing prevents it, Socrates, if it seems good to you. But first, tell me what their wisdom is, so that I may know what we are about to receive. 

SOCRATES: You wait in vain for me to say I cannot tell you, as if I had not listened enough; on the contrary, I listened diligently and I remember, and I will try to relate everything to you from the beginning. By a certain divine luck, I was sitting alone in the place where the athletes undress—where you saw me—and I was already thinking of leaving, when as I rose, that accustomed sign of the *daemon* (divine voice) suddenly stopped me. So I stayed, and a little later Euthydemus and Dionysodorus entered, and with them many others who seemed to be their disciples. Having entered, they began to walk in the covered track. They had scarcely completed two or three laps when Clinias arrived—the one you say has made great progress, and you speak truly. He was followed by many friends and others besides, including a certain youth, Ctesippus the Paeanian, a good and beautiful boy by nature, but quite wanton in his youth. 

Clinias, seeing me sitting alone from the entrance, came over and sat at my right, as you also said. Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, having seen him, at first stood apart and discussed something with each other, turning their eyes toward us from time to time. For I was observing them most diligently. Then, coming closer, they sat down: Euthydemus next to the youth himself, and Dionysodorus next to me on my left; others sat where there was room. I congratulated them, as I had not seen them for a long time. 

After this, turning to Clinias, I said: "These men, O Clinias—Euthydemus and Dionysodorus—are wise not in small matters, but in the greatest. They know everything that pertains to military affairs: whatever is necessary for one who would be a strenuous commander, and the arrangements of the battle line and the army. Moreover, they can teach how one may defend oneself from injury in a court of law." 

They, however, looked down upon my speaking so, and looking at each other, they both laughed. And Euthydemus said: "We no longer treat these things seriously, Socrates, but only in passing." 

But I, being amazed, said: "Your studies must be excellent indeed, if your 'pastimes' are so great! Tell me, I pray, what is this most remarkable work of yours?" 

EUTHYDEMUS: We persuade ourselves, O Socrates, that virtue can be taught by us most easily and better than by anyone else. 

SOCRATES: By Jove, what a precious thing you promise! By what stroke of luck did this profit come to you? Until now, as I said, I thought of you as men outstanding in the military art, and I spoke of you as such. For I remember when you first came here, that was the only thing you professed. But if you have now truly attained this *scientia* (knowledge), be propitious! Indeed, I greet you just as I would gods, beseeching you to forgive what I said before. But see, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, whether you speak the truth. For it would be a wonder...

<meta>This page transitions from the Protagoras in the previous section to Plato's Laws (De Legibus), specifically Book IV. The discussion shifts from the nature of knowledge to the methodology of lawmaking, using the analogy of medical practice.</meta>

# On Laws, or On Legislation, Dialogue IV. 537

[Left Column]

...doctors who are slaves flit from slave to slave. In this way, they truly provide the masters with ease in caring for the sick. However, a free doctor <note>In ancient Greek society, Plato distinguishes between 'slave doctors' who treated slaves with brute efficiency and 'free doctors' who treated citizens through dialogue and education.</note> mostly treats and examines the diseases of free people, so that he investigates the nature of the disease from its beginning and consults both with the patient and his friends, both by learning something from them and by teaching them as much as possible; he does not issue any command until he has persuaded them. And thus, by always persuading gently, he tries to lead the sick toward health. Which is the better doctor and trainer—the one who heals and trains in this way, or the one who uses the other method? That is, the one who accomplishes the same result in two ways, or the one who uses only one way, and that the harsher and more violent of the two? 

<note>CLI: Cleinias, a Cretan politician and one of the three speakers in this dialogue.</note> 
CLI. The one who performs it in two ways, stranger, is much better. 

<note>ATH: The Athenian Stranger, the primary philosopher in the Laws, often considered a mouthpiece for Plato's later thought.</note> 
ATH. Shall we then consider how this double and single method might be applied to the making of laws? 
CLI. I certainly wish to. 
ATH. Tell me then, by the gods, which law will the lawgiver write first? Will he not, according to nature, first of all adorn with laws the very beginning of generation in the city? 
CLI. Clearly. 
ATH. But the beginning of generation for all cities is the union and community of marriage. 
CLI. Indeed. 
ATH. Therefore, if laws concerning marriage are set down first, they will seem correctly placed for the proper establishment of the entire city. 
CLI. That is absolutely correct. 
ATH. Let us then first state the "simple" version, which might go like this: A man shall marry between his thirtieth year and his thirty-fifth year. If he does not, he shall be punished with a fine and dishonor: a fine of a certain amount, and a dishonor of a certain kind. And let that be the simple law concerning marriage. But the "double" version would be like this: Every man ought to marry when he is thirty years old, considering that by a certain law of nature the human race achieves a kind of immortality. 

<margin>Man becomes eternal through generation.</margin> 

Every person is by nature most desirous of this thing. For there is no one who does not desire to have a perpetual name among posterity. Thus the human race, being immortal, lasts forever in this way: by leaving behind children's children, it always attains immortality as one and the same through generation. It is a sin, however, to willingly deprive oneself of immortality. But he truly deprives himself of this in his soul who neglects children and a wife. Whoever obeys this law shall be free from penalty. But he who does not obey, and reaches thirty-five years of age without marrying—lest he think his solitary life will bring him profit or pleasure—shall be fined a certain sum of money every year, and he shall have no share in those honors which the younger men in the city daily show to the elders. When these two laws are compared, one can judge which is better: whether they should be written with a double length, being as brief as possible while interposing persuasion alongside threats; or whether one should use only threats and establish simple laws in their length. 

<note>MEG: Megillus, a Spartan participant in the dialogue.</note> 
MEG. It is the Spartan custom, stranger, always to choose the shorter way. But if someone made me the judge of these, so that I could choose which of these laws I wanted in the city, I would choose the longer one; and in all other laws, if these two options were proposed, I would do the same according to this very model. However, these present laws must also be approved by Cleinias here, for it is his city for which these laws are being established. 
CLIN. You speak well, Megillus. 
ATH. To care too much about the length or brevity of writing is quite foolish. For I believe the best things, not the shortest or longest, should be chosen. And yet, in the laws proposed just now, it is not only that the double version contributes more to virtue than the other; rather, what was said about the

<column-break/>

two kinds of doctors is most correctly applied here. It seems that no legislator has ever considered this. For while it is possible for those making laws to use two methods—force and persuasion—when dealing with a crowd lacking in discipline, they use only one as far as they are able. They do not join persuasion to threats, but only apply pure force. I, however, O blessed man, see a third thing that ought to be done in laws, which we never see done. 
CLI. What is that? 
ATH. That which, by some divine inspiration, has happened to us through the things we have discussed. For we began to dispute about laws in the morning, and now it is noon, and we are resting most comfortably in this pleasant place, doing nothing but disputing about laws. 

<margin>Concerning Preambles.</margin> 

And now for the first time we seem to be making a beginning of the laws we must treat. All the previous things, however, were "preambles" <note>original: "exordia," also called "prooemia." These are the introductory arguments meant to persuade citizens before the law commands them.</note> to the laws. Why say this? Because I wanted to say that for all speeches and other things involving vocal imitation, there are preambles—a kind of prelude—which contain a skillful and useful treatment for the matter at hand. Indeed, for those songs called "citharodic laws" <note>The Greek word 'nomos' meant both a 'musical mode' and a 'statutory law.' Plato is playing on this double meaning.</note> and for other musical works, wonderfully invented preludes are prefixed. But for the true laws, which we call civil laws, no one has ever pronounced a preamble, nor brought one to light in writing, as if none existed by nature. To us, however, this delay and our discussion seem to signify that such a thing exists. The laws which were just now called "double" are not simply double, but consist of two parts: the law itself and the preamble to the law. That which we compared to the tyrannical and slave-like command of the doctors is the "pure law." But that which was placed before it, which we called the "persuasive" part, truly aims at persuasion, yet it has the force of a preamble. For the purpose of that entire speech, introduced to persuade, is that the citizens might hear the legislator’s command (which is the law) more benevolently and, because of this, accept it more easily. Therefore, in my opinion, all of this will rightly be called not the "reason of the law," but the "preamble." Beyond this, what more do I desire to add? This: that the legislator should always place a preamble before every law, and distinguish how they differ from one another in each case, just as those two examples we related differed. 
CLI. I, for one, would never wish for a man skilled in these matters to enact laws in any other way. 
ATHEN. You seem to me, Cleinias, to have spoken rightly in saying that a preamble should precede all laws, and that at the beginning of every legal composition, an introduction suited to each individual law should be placed before the whole discourse. For what is said afterward is no small matter, nor is it of little consequence whether such things are mentioned clearly or obscurely. But if we should order that preambles be composed in the same way for both great and small laws, we would not be ordering correctly. For that is not to be done in every song or every speech. For although it can be found in all, it should not be used in all. This choice must always be granted to the orator, the singer, and the lawmaker himself. 
CLIN. You speak the truth, stranger. But let us linger no further; rather, let us return to the proposed discourse and begin, if you please, with those things which you said above, though not using them as a preamble. Therefore, let us take up the second part from the beginning, as they say in the games, "better things from the start," treating it as a certain preamble and not just any discourse as we did lately. Let us begin, then, and profess to make an opening. And concerning the honor of the gods and ancestors...

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Stranger introduces the concept of the "preamble" to a law, arguing that a good legislator should persuade the citizens to obey through reason (the "double law") rather than merely commanding them through force (the "simple law").</summary>
<keywords>legislation, persuasion vs. force, physician analogy, preambles, prooemia, marriage laws, immortality, Athenian Stranger, Cleinias, Megillus</keywords>

538 Book Thirty-Four.

...and the care of our friends, enough has been said. Let us strive to push through the rest, until you feel you have sufficiently completed the whole preamble <note>Plato argues that laws should not merely be commands, but should include a 'prooemium' or preamble to persuade the citizen of the law's wisdom.</note>. Finally, after the preamble, you shall approach the laws themselves.

ATH. Since we have said enough in the introduction about the gods and those who follow the gods <note>original: "dijs deófque sequentibus". This refers to the hierarchy of divine beings, including daemons and heroes, who were thought to bridge the gap between gods and men.</note>, and about parents, whether living or dead—as we now affirm—what remains must be brought into the light, as you seem to command.

CLIN. Indeed, precisely.

ATH. After those things, however, which pertain to souls, to bodies, and to possessions—by discussing together with what zeal they should be cultivated—we ought to determine them in such a way that both those speaking and those listening may follow the instruction to the best of our ability. These things, therefore, are truly what we must speak and hear next.

CLIN. You speak quite rightly.

### 544 . V . Book Thirty-Four.

[margin] That the very wealthy are not good men. [/margin]

...things which are honorable, and are honorably spent. Therefore, a man who acquires twice as much and spends half as much will never be wealthier than one who does the opposite. One of these is virtuous, the other is not necessarily evil, provided he is merely frugal; but sometimes he is entirely bad; however, a truly good man, as we have just said, can never be exceedingly rich. For he who accumulates money both justly and unjustly, and spends it neither justly nor unjustly, becomes rich when he is frugal. But he who is entirely bad, since he is for the most part a spendthrift and a prodigal, becomes very poor. Yet he who spends honorably and acquires only justly will never easily excel in riches, nor will he be pressed by poverty. Therefore, our discourse rightly asserts that the very wealthy are not good men; and if they are not good, they will not be happy either. 

Our purpose in establishing laws looks toward this: that the citizens may be most happy and, above all, friends to one another. Indeed, they will never be friends if, vexed by many mutual injuries, they are forced to use the courts for litigation; rather, they should be friends if these disputes are as small and as few as possible. For this reason, we say that there ought to be neither gold nor silver in the city, nor moreover much profit from mechanical crafts, innkeeping, or usury <term>usury: "foenore," the practice of lending money at interest, which Plato and many Renaissance thinkers viewed as a "sterile" and exploitative way to grow wealth</term>, nor from cattle-rearing in a shameful manner; but rather from those things which agriculture offers and provides. And this should be so that the pursuit of profit does not force one to neglect those things for which money is sought—namely, the soul and the body, which without gymnastics and other discipline <note>original: "disciplina," referring here to the structured education of the mind and character</note> will never be of any value. 

[margin] Three things in which men place their zeal: goods of the soul, goods of the body, and money. [/margin]

Therefore, the care for money, as has been said many times already, should hold the last place of honor. Since there are three things in total upon which men set their zeal, the last and third—if held correctly—is the zeal for money; the middle is for the body; and the first is for the soul. Furthermore, if the republic we are now founding distributes honors in this way, it is rightly disposed. But if any law established within it prefers riches to either the health of the body through temperance, or prefers riches to both health and temperance, it is seen as not rightly established. Often, therefore, the legislator ought to proclaim what he intends; if this is achieved, things will go well. If not, the hope of his institution will frustrate him. And thus perhaps he will deliver himself and others from the burden of bearing laws; otherwise, it is in no way possible. 

Therefore, let him who has received his allotted portion <term>allotted portion: "partem suam sortitus est," referring to the "kleros" or ancestral plot of land given to each citizen to ensure they have a stake in the land</term> possess it under the condition we have stated. It would be ideal if all other things coming into the colony were possessed equally. But since that cannot happen—as one man arriving will have more money and another less—for the sake of many opportunities and times of equality in the city, it is necessary that unequal census classes be established. This is so that magistrates, taxes, and distributions may be assigned according to dignity—not only for the virtue, beauty, or physical strength of oneself or one's ancestors, but also according to the use of wealth and poverty as equally as possible. That is to say, by receiving an unequal portion, but one easily made proportionate, they shall not contend with one another. 

For these reasons, four classes of property <note>original: "census," the Roman term for a property-based classification used to determine social status and military/tax obligations</note> differing in size ought to be created: First, Second, Third, and Fourth (or called by any other names), so that some may remain in the same class, while others who have become richer or poorer may move into the class that fits them. To this, I shall add the following form of law: Indeed, we say that in a city that is to be free from the greatest disease—which I would more rightly call discord or sedition—there should be neither extreme poverty among some citizens nor immense wealth. For both of those conditions are produced by each other. 

Therefore, the legislator must establish a limit for both. If, then, the limit of poverty is the original allotment, which must remain stable and which no magistrate or anyone else who cares for virtue will allow to be less for anyone; once the legislator has prescribed this measure, he shall permit one to hold double, triple, or quadruple this amount. But if anyone has more—whether found, or given, or gained through trade, or acquired by any other such fortune—if he gives all that remains above the limit to the city and the gods who are the city's guardians, let him be exempt from penalty and worthy of praise. But if he does not obey the law, whoever reports this shall receive half. The man himself shall be fined an equal part of his own goods, and let the other half belong to the gods. Whatever they possess beyond their allotment should be openly recorded with the magistrate appointed by law as their guardian, so that all judgments concerning money may be easy and very clear. 

[margin] On the site of the city. [/margin]

# Eighteenth Book

"Now at last, Dionyſodorus," I said, "you seem to me to be speaking seriously, and I have finally prevailed upon you to act with gravity. Do you truly know all things? Even the craft of the carpenter and the tanner?" 
"Every single thing," he replied. 
"Do you even know the number of the stars and the grains of sand?" 
"Indeed," he said. 
"Do you think we will grant you these things?" I asked. 
Here Cteſippus interrupted: "Show us some proof, ô Dionyſodore, by which we might infer that you are telling the truth." 
"What sort of proof?" he asked. 
"Do you know," Cteſippus said, "how many teeth Euthydemus has? And does Euthydemus know how many you have?" 
"Is it not enough for you," he replied, "to hear that we know all things?" 
"Not at all," said Cteſippus, "but show us just this one thing, that you speak the truth. For if you tell us how many teeth each has, and we count them afterward and find you have spoken correctly, we will believe you in everything else." 

They, however, thinking that Cteſippus was trying to bait them, refused to answer anything except that they knew all things. When questioned by Cteſippus about individual matters—even the smallest and most sordid things—they boldly insisted they understood everything, like boars charging against a blow. 

Consequently, I too, ô Crito, was finally compelled to ask Euthydemus whether Dionyſodorus also knew how to dance. He agreed that he did. 
"But surely," I said, "he does not jump over swords with his head tilted toward the ground, or tumble on a wheel at such an advanced age? Has he progressed that far in wisdom?" 
"There is nothing," he said, "that he does not know." 
Then I asked: "Is it only *now* that you know all things? Or have you *always* known them?" 
"Always." 
"Did you know all things from a tender age, immediately from birth?" 
"Everything," they both replied together. 

To us, this seemed an incredible matter. Then Euthydemus said, "Do you not believe it, ô Socrates?" 
"Except for the fact," I replied, "that it is likely you are wise men. If you will answer me, show me that I too possess these wonders." 
"It would be most pleasing if you could convince me of this," I said. "For if I was wise and did not know it until now, and you show me that I know all things and have always known them, what a gain I could find in my life!" 
"Answer now," he said. 
"Ask away," I replied, "and I shall answer." 

"Are you knowing (*scius*) of something, ô Socrates, or of nothing?" 
"Of something," I said. 
"Do you know by that very thing through which you are knowing, or by something else?" 
"By that which makes me knowing. For I think you mean the *anima* (soul). Is this what you understand?" 
"Are you not ashamed, ô Socrates," he said, "to ask a question in return when you are being questioned?" 
"But what should I do?" I asked. "I will do whatever you command, though I do not know what you are seeking. You order me to answer, not to question." 
"Do you not grasp in some way," he said, "what I am asking?" 
"Indeed, I do," I said. 
"Then answer according to what you grasp." 
"But what," I said, "if you ask with one meaning in mind and I answer with another? If I conceive of the matter differently than you, will you be satisfied if I answer nothing to the point?" 
"It will be enough for me," he said, "though not for you, I suppose." 
"Then by Jove," I said, "I will not answer until I hear more." 
"You do not answer according to what you conceive," he said, "because you are a trifler, Socrates, and more boorish than you ought to be." 

I realized then that he was angry with me because I was distinguishing the words with which he sought to ensnare me. I was reminded of Connus (Socrates' music teacher), who often becomes indignant with me when I do not yield to him, and then scorns me as a novice. Since I had decided to give myself over to their teaching, I thought it best to be obedient, lest one of them reject me as inept and unteachable. Therefore, I said, "If it seems best to you to act this way, Euthydeme, then let it be done. For you understand the method of *disputandi* (disputation) much better than I, since you possess this art, while I am a novice. Therefore, ask again from the beginning." 

[[margin: Hercules against the sophistical hydra and the sophist crab.]]
[[notes: cf. Plato, Euthydemus 297c regarding the Hydra of sophistry.]]

"Answer again," he said. "Do you know by something through which you know, or by nothing?" 
"By the soul," I said. 
At this, he cried out, "He answers more than he was asked! I am not asking *by what* you know, but *whether* you know by something or not." 
"I answered more than was fitting," I said, "on account of my lack of skill. But forgive me, I pray. I will answer simply now: I always know whatever I know by something." 
"Do you always know by this *same* thing," he asked, "or sometimes by this and sometimes by another?" 
"Always," I said, "when I know, I know by this." 
"Are you not yet done answering beside the point?" he asked. 
"I answered thus," I said, "lest the word 'always' should deceive us." 
"Do not say 'us,'" he said, "but 'you.' But answer: do you always know by this?" 
"Always," I said, "once the 'when' is removed." 
"Do you not then always know? And knowing always, do you know some things by this through which you know, and other things by another, or all things by this very same thing?" 
"All things," I said, "whatever I know, I know by this." 
"Here you transgress again, Socrates." 
"Let it be excepted," I said, "that I mean 'whatever I know.'" 
"I ask for no exceptions," he said. "Rather, answer: could you know all things unless you knew all things?" 
"That would be a monster," I said. 
"Now add whatever you please," he said, "for you confess that you know all things." 
"So it seems," I said, "since my saying 'I know all' is of no weight if I do indeed know all." 
"And did you not confess that you always know by this by which you know, whether *when* you know, or however else you please? For you confessed that you always know, and all things at once. It follows, therefore, that you knew as a boy, and when you were conceived, and when you were born—indeed, even before you were born, and before the rising of heaven and earth, you knew all things, if indeed you always know. And by Jove, you shall always know all things, if I so will it." 

"But you *will* so will it, most honored Euthydeme," I said, "if indeed you speak the truth. But I have little confidence you can do it unless your brother Dionyſodorus here wills it with you. Tell me further: how can I not grant you the rest, endowed as you are with such wonderful and new wisdom? How could I not know all things when you assert it? But by what reason should I say I know such things as this: that good men are unjust? Tell me, do I know this or not?" 
"You certainly know it," he said. 
"What?" I asked. 
"That good men are *not* unjust." 
"I knew that long ago," I said. "But that is not what I am asking. Where did I learn that good men *are* unjust?" 
"Nowhere," said Dionyſodorus. 
"Then I do not know this," I said. 

Then Euthydemus turned to Dionyſodorus and said, "You are destroying the argument! It will appear that he both knows and does not know at the same time." Dionyſodorus blushed. But I said, "What do you say, Euthydeme? Does it not seem to you that your brother speaks the truth, since he knows all things?" 
"I am the brother of Euthydemus," Dionyſodorus said. 
"Leave that aside, good man," I said, "until Euthydemus teaches me that I know good men are unjust; do not envy me this lesson." 
"You are fleeing, Socrates," Dionyſodorus said, "and you refuse to answer." 
"I flee not without cause," I said. "For since I am weaker than either one of you, why should I not flee the two of you? I am far weaker than Hercules, who was not able to fight at once against the sophistical hydra—who, on account of its wisdom, sprouted many heads of discourse for every one cut off—nor against a certain sophistical Crab coming from the sea. When Hercules was being distressed by the crab on the left and bitten sharply by its words, he called for the help of his nephew Iolaus, who came to his aid. But if my 'Iolaus,' Patrocles, should come, he would do quite differently." 

"Answer then," said Dionyſodorus, "since you proclaim these things: was Iolaus more the son of Hercules' brother than yours?" 
"It would be worth the effort to answer you, Dionyſodore. For you would not stop asking, out of a certain envy to disturb the argument, lest Euthydemus teach me that piece of wisdom." 
"Answer then," he said. 
"I answer," I said, "that Iolaus was the son of Hercules' brother, but in no way mine. For his father Patrocles was not my brother, but Iphicles was the brother of Hercules. Was Patrocles yours?" 
"Certainly," I said, "but from the same mother, not the same father." 
"Therefore he is your brother and not your brother." 
"Not from the same father, best of men," I said. "His father was Chaeredemus, but mine was Sophronicus." 
"Were Sophronicus and Chaeredemus fathers?" 
"Entirely—the one mine, the other his." 
"Was Chaeredemus other than a father?" 
"Other than *my* father, certainly." 
"Was he a father while being other than a father? Are you the same as a stone?" 
"I fear," I said, "lest I seem so by your assertion, though I do not seem so to myself." 
"Are you not then other than a stone?" 
"Other, surely." 
"If you are other than a stone, you are not a stone. And if you are other than gold, you are not gold." 
"That is so," I said. 
"By the same reason, since Chaeredemus is other than a father, he will not be a father?" 
"It seems," I said, "that he is not a father." 

At this, Euthydemus added: "Chaeredemus is hardly a father. And again, since Sophronicus is other than a father, he is not a father. Therefore, Socrates, you are without a father." 
Taking up the discourse, Cteſippus brought in: "But since the same thing applies to your father, is he not other than my father?" 
"Far from it," Euthydemus said. 
"Is he the same?" 
"The same, indeed." 
"I would not agree. But Euthydeme, is he only my father, or also the father of all other men?" 
"Of all others as well." 
"Do you think the same man, being a father, is not a father?" 
"I would have thought so," Cteſippus said. 
"Is gold, being gold, not gold? And a man, being a man, not a man?" 

Then Cteſippus said, "As the proverb goes, Euthydeme, you are joining 'linen to linen' (matching like with like). You say a grave thing if your father is the father of all." 
"He is, however," he said. 
"Of humans only," asked Cteſippus, "or also of horses and all other animals?" 
"Of all of them." 
"And is your mother the mother of all?" 
"She is." 
"Therefore your mother is the mother of sea urchins." 
"And yours," he said. 
"And you are the brother of gudgeons, puppies, and piglets." 
"And you are," he said. 
"Furthermore, your father is a dog." 
"And yours as well." 

[[margin: Proverb.]]

Here Dionyſodorus said, "If you will answer me, Cteſippe, I will make you concede these things. Tell me, do you have a dog?" 
"A very bad one," Cteſippus said. 
"Does he have puppies?" 
"He has many." 
"Is the dog not their father?" 
"Entirely; I saw him mating with the mother dog." 
"Is the dog not yours?" 
"He is." 
"Therefore, since he is a father and he is yours, your father is a dog, and you are the brother of puppies." 

Lest Cteſippus object, Dionyſodorus quickly added: "Answer a little more. Do you beat this dog?" 
Laughing, Cteſippus said, "I beat him, but I cannot beat you." 
"Do you not then beat your own father?" 
"It would be far more just," he replied, "if I beat *your* father, who, having acquired such a 'discipline,' begat such wise sons. But Euthydeme, has your father and the father of puppies gained many good things from your wisdom?" 
"He needs neither many good things, Cteſippe, nor do you." 
"Neither do you, Euthydeme, nor any other man," he said. "For tell me, Cteſippe, do you think it is a good thing for a sick man to drink medicine when he needs it, or not? Or is it good for a man about to fight to go out armed or unarmed?" 
"I think so indeed," he said, "and I expect something excellent from you." 
"You shall see," he said. "But answer: since you confessed it is good to drink medicine when the situation requires, should one drink as much as possible? Will it be best if someone grinds up and pours into the cup as much hellebore as a chariot could carry?" 
"Certainly," Cteſippus said, "if the one drinking is as big as the Delphic statue." 
"Likewise in war," he said, "if it is good to be clothed in arms, should one have as many arms as possible? Should a whole burden of spears and shields be carried around, since it is a good thing?" 
"Very much so," said Cteſippus. "But do you not think, Euthydeme, that only one spear should be carried?" 
"Indeed," he said. 
"Would you thus arm Geryon and Briareus? I thought you were stronger, and this companion of yours as well, being men of arms." 

Euthydemus was silent. But Dionyſodorus, countering what Cteſippus had first answered, said: "Does it seem good to you to have gold?" 
"Very much so," Cteſippus replied. 
"And to have money always and everywhere?" 
"Most of all," he said. 
"Do you not confess that gold is good?" 
"We have already confessed it." 
"Should one always have it, and everywhere, and as much as possible within oneself? Would he not be most blessed who had three talents of gold in his belly, one talent under his skull, and a stater—that is, a certain coin and weight of gold—in each eye?" 

Cteſippus said, "They say, ô Euthydeme, that among the Scythians those are the happiest and best men who contain much gold in their own skulls—just as you said a moment ago that a dog was a father. And what is more marvelous, they drink from their own gilded skulls and look into them, lifting their own scalps and foreheads with their hands." 

To this Euthydemus asked, "Do the Scythians and other men see what they *can* see, or what they cannot?" 
"What they can, clearly." 
"And you?" 
"I likewise." 
"Do you see our clothes?" 
"I see them." 
"Can these then be seen?" 
"Wonderfully," Cteſippus said. 
"What further?" he asked. 
"Nothing. Do you not think these clothes see?" 
"What a pleasant fellow you are," Euthydemus said. 
"You seem to me, Euthydeme, to have fallen asleep with your eyes open, and I think that in speaking, you say nothing." 
"And you seem to do the same," he replied. 
"Is it not impossible," Dionyſodorus said, "for the silent to speak?" 
"Impossible," Cteſippus said. 
"And for the speaking to be silent?" 
"Much less possible." 
"When you say 'stone,' do you not speak of the silent? And likewise for wood and iron?" 
"I will not grant you that iron is silent," Cteſippus said, "for if one strikes it, it is said to ring and echo. Therefore, you have not noticed how much you say nothing on account of your wisdom. But show me what remains: that it is possible for the speaking to be silent." 
It seemed to me then that Cteſippus was contending vehemently on account of his friend. 
"When you are silent," Euthydemus said, "are you not silent about all things?" 
"Indeed." 
"Are you not then silent about any speaking thing? Since speaking things are counted among the number of all things." 
"What?" asked Cteſippus, "are all things not silent?" 
"No," said Euthydemus. 
"Do all things speak, then, best of men?" 
"Yes, those that speak." 
"I was not asking that," he said, "but whether all things are silent or speak." 

Then Dionyſodorus, snatching up the discourse, said: "Neither and both. For I know for certain you will not know how to object to this answer." 
Immediately Cteſippus, as is his wont, burst into laughter and cried out, "O Euthydeme, your brother has been conquered!" Clinias also laughed, greatly delighted. Cteſippus, exulting, grew ten times larger with joy. It seemed to me that Cteſippus, like an old hand, had wrung these things from them by cunning. For such wisdom is not found among other men of our time. 

After this I said, "Why do you laugh, ô Clinias, at things so serious and so beautiful?" 
But Dionyſodorus turned to me: "Have you ever seen a beautiful thing, Socrates?" 
"Many indeed, Dionyſodore." 
"Are they other than 'the Beautiful itself,' or are they the same?" 
I was hesitant, and thought I deserved it for not being able to keep silent longer. I answered, however, that they were other than the Beautiful itself, yet a certain beauty was present in each. 
"If an ox is present to you," he asked, "will you be an ox? And because I am present to you now, are you Dionyſodorus?" 
"Heaven forbid!" I said. 
"How can one thing be present to another when they are different?" 
"Do you doubt this?" I asked. (I was already striving to imitate their wisdom, being inflamed with desire for it). 
"Why should I and everyone else not doubt that which in no way exists?" 
"What do you say, Dionyſodore? Is the beautiful not beautiful, and the ugly not ugly?" 
"If it seems so to me," he said. 
"Does it not seem so?" 
"Entirely," he said. 
"Is the same not the same," I asked, "and the other similarly other? Not that the other is the same?" 
"I did not think even a child would suspect that the other is anything but the other. But, ô Dionyſodore, you have omitted this on purpose. You seem to me like craftsmen who complete each task; you conclude and hand over the method of disputation with grace. Do you know what each craftsman ought to complete? First, do you know who should strike bronze?" 
"The blacksmith," I said. 
"Who should mold clay?" 
"The potter." 
"Who should slaughter, skin, and roast or boil the cut meat?" 
"The cook." 
"Does whoever does what is fitting do it correctly?" 
"Greatly so," I said. 
"And it is fitting, as you say, for the cook to cut and skin. Did you agree to this or not?" 
"I agreed," I said, "but please forgive me." 
"It follows then," he said, "that if someone, slaughtering and cutting the cook, boils or roasts him, he does what is fitting. Furthermore, if someone strikes the blacksmith with bronze or molds the potter, he will likewise be operating with decorum." 
"O Neptune!" I said, "now you have put the *colophon* (the finishing touch) on your wisdom. Will this ever be present to me and become my own?" 
"Would you recognize it, ô Socrates, once it became your own?" 
"If you wish it," I said, "I would." 
"What further," he asked, "do you think you know your own things?" 
"Indeed," I said, "unless you say otherwise. For it must begin with you and end with Euthydemus here." 
"Do you not think those things are yours," he asked, "of which you are the master? And which you may use as you please, like oxen and sheep? Do you consider those things yours which you can sell, give away, or vow to any of the gods? And those you cannot, are not yours?" 

I, thinking some noble question was about to arise and inflamed with eagerness to hear it, said: "It is exactly so. Such things are mine." 
"Do you call those things 'animals' which have a soul?" 
"Those very ones," I said. 
"Do you admit then that only those animals are yours which you can do all these things to—sell, give, sacrifice?" 
"I admit it," I said. 
Here he paused ironically, as if contemplating something great, and then said: "Tell me, ô Socrates, do you have a 'paternal Jove' (father Zeus)?" 

Suspecting the discourse was returning to where it had been, and escaping by an ambiguous detour the net in which I was already entangled, I answered: "I do not, ô Dionyſodore." 
"Wretched man!" he said. "You are not even an Athenian, if you have no paternal gods, no sacrifices, nor anything else noble and magnificent." 
"Stop this, Dionyſodore," I said, "lest you speak ill omens or teach me too harshly. For I have altars, domestic and paternal sacrifices, and all other such things that belong to the Athenians." 
"Do the other Athenians have a paternal Jove?" 
"The Ionians do not have such a kinship," I said, "nor those who flowed out from this city, nor do we. But we have a paternal Apollo because of the birth of Ion. Jove is not called our paternal god, yet he is called the Protector of the City and the Guardian of the Tribe, and Minerva is the Guardianess of the Tribe." 
"That is enough," said Dionyſodorus. "For you have, as it seems, Apollo, Jove, and Minerva." 
"Entirely." 
"Will these not be your gods—ancestors and masters?" 
"Are they not yours? Have you not confessed they are yours?" 
"I confessed it," I said. "What then?" 
"Are these gods not animals?" he asked. "For you confessed that whatever has a soul is an animal. Do these gods not have souls?" 
"They certainly do," I said. 
"Are they then animals?" 
"They are, surely." 
"And you said those animals were yours over which you had power to sell, give away, or dedicate to the gods at your will." 
I could not refute Euthydemus on these points. He immediately brought in: "Since you confess Jove is yours, and the other gods are yours, is it permitted for you to sell them and give them away, and treat them as you please like the other animals that are yours?" 

I, Crito, was struck by this discourse and became silent. Cteſippus, however, tried to help me and said, "Bah! By Hercules, what a noble speech!" 
To which Dionyſodorus replied: "Is Hercules a 'Bah,' or is a 'Bah' Hercules?" 
Then Cteſippus said, "By Neptune, what twisted and hard words. I give up now. Both are invincible." 

At this point, my friend Crito, no one present could contain themselves from praising their speech with the highest acclaim. Those guests, Dionyſodorus and Euthydemus, exulting with laughter, applause, and joy, were almost undone by their own merriment. In earlier parts, only their followers would applaud; here, it seemed almost the columns of the Lyceum themselves were shouting, clapping, and exulting. I was so affected that I asserted I had never seen any men of such wisdom. Bound to their wisdom, I began to praise and celebrate them. 

"O men," I said, "blessed by the wondrous gifts of nature! For you have completed such a great matter so easily and in so short a time. Many other things in your speeches are noble, Euthydeme and Dionyſodore, but this is especially magnificent: that you have no concern for the common people, nor even for illustrious men or those held in high esteem, but only for those like yourselves. I know for certain there are few who love this kind of discourse, and they are like you. Others are so ignorant of it and scorn it that they would blush more deeply to convince others with such arguments than to be convinced themselves. Furthermore, your speeches have this popular and gentle quality: when you say nothing is good or bad, nor white, nor anything else of that kind, and that nothing is different from anything else, you truly shut the mouths of men, as you boast. Because you shut not only the mouths of others, but your own as well, it is a graceful thing; you avoid the hatred of the speech and the offense of the listeners. 

But the greatest thing is that these things are so skillfully prepared and established by you that you can hand them over to anyone in a short time. I recognized this, and observing Cteſippus, I saw how suddenly he began to imitate you. It is a noble thing to be able to teach the mystery of this matter so quickly, yet it does not seem worthwhile to discuss it before many people. Rather, if you believe me, take care not to speak in a large assembly, lest people perceive these things too quickly and give you no thanks. Communicate these things only among yourselves, and let no one else hear them unless they have put down money. If you are wise, advise your disciples likewise—never to speak of these things with anyone but themselves and you. For what is rare, Euthydeme, is honored. Water is bought at a very cheap price, though it is the most precious thing by nature, as Pindar says. But come," I said, "take up Clinias and me." 

After we had discussed these and a few other things, ô Crito, we departed. Deliberate then whether you will come with me to these men. For they promise to teach anyone who is prepared to give money, excluding no talent or age. And what is most useful for you to hear: they say that no study of accumulating money prevents anyone from easily perceiving their wisdom.

**CRITO**: Indeed, ô Socrates, I am eager to hear and would most willingly learn. Yet I seem to be one of those who are not like Euthydemus, but rather those you mentioned earlier who would rather be refuted by such sophistries than refute others. Truly, it would be ridiculous if I proceeded to advise you. Yet nothing prevents me from relating what I heard from one who left your assembly. As I was walking, I met one of those who are esteemed as most excellent in legal cases. "O Crito," he said, "have you heard nothing from these wise men?" "Nothing, by Jove," I said. "The crowd and the tumult prevented me when I tried to listen." "The matter, however," he said, "was worth hearing." "Why?" I asked. "So that you might hear those men disputing who excel others in this kind of discourse." To which I replied: "What did it seem to you?" "What else," he said, "than what is always heard from such men when they trifle? They argue with unworthy zeal about matters of no moment." Then I said, "Nevertheless, philosophy is a graceful thing." "How graceful, ô blessed man," he said, "when it is of no value? If you had been present, you would have blushed, I think, for your friend, who was so inept that he desired to give himself over to men who have no care for what they say, but catch at every word and object to names, though they excel other such men of our age." Truly, ô Crito, this study is most vile, and those who engage in it are ridiculous. 

To me, ô Socrates, it seems he was not right to disparage the matter itself. But that someone should strive to dispute with such men in a large assembly—that, it seems to me, he rightly blamed.

**SOCRATES**: O Crito, these men are worthy of admiration. But I do not yet know what I am about to say. From which group was the man who disparaged philosophy to you? Was he one of the orators who prevail in legal contests, or one of those who compose the speeches with which orators contend in court? 

**CRITO**: By no means an orator, nor do I think he has ever pleaded in court; but they say he understands legal matters very well and composes elegant speeches.

**SOCRATES**: I understand now. Indeed, these are the ones, ô Crito, whom Prodicus placed between the philosopher and the statesman. These men think they are the wisest of all and appear so to many. They believe that only philosophers are an impediment to their being equally approved by everyone. They think that if they spread this common opinion against philosophers—that they are of no value—they will carry off the highest glory of wisdom among all without controversy. For they believe they are truly the wisest, but are hindered in private discourses when the followers of Euthydemus oppose them. They want it to seem consistent that they are wise because they have enough of philosophy and enough of civil skill, participating in each as much as they ought, and being placed outside the turbulent tumults of civil business, they enjoy the fruits of wisdom pleasantly.

**CRITO**: Does it seem to you, ô Socrates, that these men say anything?

**SOCRATES**: By no means.

**CRITO**: Nevertheless, their speech has something plausible.

**SOCRATES**: It has plausibility, ô Crito, rather than truth. Nor can they easily be persuaded that men, and all other things that are intermediate between two things and participate in both, are such that those made of bad and good become better than the bad but worse than the good. But those made of two goods not leading to the same end are worse than both for achieving the work toward which each of those components is aimed. Only those composed of two evils not tending toward the same end are better than both. If philosophy is good and civil action is good, but each contributes to a different thing, and these men participate in both and are placed in the middle, they conclude nothing—for they are worse than both. If one is good and the other bad, they are better than the bad but worse than the good. If both are bad, only then would they speak the truth; otherwise, in no way. Nor do I think they would confess that both are bad, or even one good and the other bad. But truly, these participants in both are more inept for that toward which philosophy and civil action pertain; and though they hold the third place, they do not hesitate to usurp the first. Their desire should be forgiven and not resented, but they should be judged as they are. For we ought to love every man who, participating in prudence, says something and acts manfully.

**CRITO**: Indeed, ô Socrates, as I often speak with you, I am in doubt as to how I should educate my sons. The younger is still more tender than discipline requires, but Critobolus is already grown and needs someone whose work may help him progress. Whenever I speak with you, I am affected such that I think it madness to be occupied with other things for the sake of sons—such as marriage, so they may be born from the most noble mother, or leaving them an ample patrimony—and yet neglect their education. But when I look at those who profess to educate men, I am deterred; each of them seems to me far from what he proclaims. To tell you the truth, I do not know how to exhort and provoke my son to philosophy.

**SOCRATES**: O friend Crito, do you not know that in every study, vile and worthless men are very many, while the upright are few and to be held in the highest esteem? Does it not seem to you that gymnastics, commerce, rhetoric, and military affairs are noble things?

**CRITO**: To me, certainly.

**SOCRATES**: Do you not see in each of these arts many who are inept for every work and worthy of derision?

**CRITO**: It is so, and you speak only too truly.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore, because of this, will you flee all studies and dissuade your son from them?

**CRITO**: That would not be right, ô Socrates.

**SOCRATES**: Take care then, ô Crito, lest you do what is unbecoming. Cease this worry about whether men devoted to philosophy are good or bad. Examine the matter itself diligently. If it seems a wicked thing upon inquiry, deter not only your sons but all men from it. But if it appears to you as it does to me, follow it manfully and practice it, and exhort your sons to the same study.

[[summary: This section covers the conclusion of the Euthydemus, where Socrates satirizes sophistical logic and its empty claims to omniscience, and transitions into a discussion with Crito on the value of true philosophy versus the "middle-way" of the rhetoricians.]]
[[keywords: Socrates, Crito, Euthydemus, Dionyſodorus, Sophistry, Education, Philosophy, Fallacy]]
