[[page number: 186]]
# HIPPIAS MINOR,
## OR, ON LYING.
### BY MARSILIO FICINO
### ARGUMENT

The wonderful goodness of our Socrates and Plato most diligently provides in many ways that credulous youth be not captured and destroyed by the subtle snares of the sophists. Thus, he rightly agitates Hippias of Elis—the most unlearned and deceitful of sophists—in two dialogues: the *Greater* and the *Lesser*. In the *Greater*, he demonstrates that Hippias, a professor of the most beautiful things, is entirely ignorant of what beauty itself is. In the *Lesser*, he shows that the same man, boasting that he can distinguish a liar from a truthful person above others, errs entirely in the definition of both. Thus it appears that as Hippias is the most arrogant of all, so he is the most ignorant and inept. 

Socrates depicts him here as boastful, rash, and greedy, as is the custom of sophists. Although Hippias promises everything, he gives only words and performs nothing. While he boasts of being the greatest, he falters even in the smallest things. But to return to the definition of the liar and the truthful: a liar should be described as one who most desires and knows how to lie in whatever way possible. The truthful man, conversely, is one who most desires and knows how to speak the truth. 

But Hippias, the most inert master of all arts and most confused in distinguishing the truthful from the liar, begins with the opposite order. He calls him a liar who is most able and knows how to lie whenever he wishes; and truthful, he who can and knows how to speak the truth whenever he wishes. From this he is first forced to confess that liars are powerful, knowing, prudent, and wise. Second, he is forced to admit they are "good" at those things in which they are powerful and wise. Third, by leading him through individual arts, Socrates compels him to admit that in any matter or art, the same person is both truthful and a liar. For in any field, he who is most skilled is also most able and knows how to speak the truth or lie at his will. Fourth, he is led to concede that the truthful person is no better than the liar, since both appear equally "sufficient" and "good" for their respective ends.

After this, Socrates leads the sophist into an ambiguity: who sins more gravely, he who lies willingly or he who lies unwillingly? The sophist does not know how to solve this, nor does Socrates wish to solve it for him. It should be solved thus: in matters pertaining to the intellect, those who lie on purpose err less; but in matters of morals, they err more. Then, he who says a lie willingly is in a worse state. 

Next, it is doubted whether they err more who sin by deliberate effort or by lack of skill and ignorance. It is proven through long inductions that in matters of nature, art, and their instruments, a fault committed through impotence or ignorance is graver than one perpetrated by malice. For the good of nature consists in power, and the good of art in power and knowledge. Evil, therefore, is in the opposite. From these, Socrates transfers the point to morals (though out of context), concluding the same for morals as for nature and art. Although Socrates understands this should not be done, he strives to show that the sophist does not notice. Truly, in matters of will and morals, malice (a certain will to sin) is a graver offense than if one sins through impotence or ignorance. Finally, Socrates says justice is either power, or knowledge, or both. He knew how to add the third—will—but did not wish to. For justice consists especially in the will. He wanted to show that this escapes the sophist. But let us conclude the argument: Teach without envy. Learn without shame. Always give thanks to the teacher. Do not usurp the youth of another.

# EUDICUS, SOCRATES, HIPPIAS.

[[notes: Eudicus was a disciple of Hippias.]]

**EUDICUS**: Why are you silent, Socrates, when Hippias has shown so many things? Why do you not either approve of something said or refute it if it seems incorrectly stated? Especially since we, who claim no small study of philosophy, are left behind?

**SOCRATES**: There are some things, Eudicus, among those Hippias said about Homer, which I desire to ask about. I heard from your father Apemantus that the *Iliad* of Homer is a more noble poem than the *Odyssey* insofar as Achilles is more excellent than Ulysses. For he said one poem was composed for Achilles, the other for Ulysses. I desire to ask Hippias, if it pleases him, which of these men he asserts is more excellent, since many other various things about Homer and other poets have been shown to us.

**EUDICUS**: No envy will prevent Hippias from answering if he is asked. Will you answer, Hippias, if Socrates asks something?

**HIPPIAS**: I would hardly be acting rightly, Eudicus, if I fled Socrates' questioning now. I am accustomed always to go from my home in Elis to the Olympic festival, where the Greeks flow from all sides for the common celebration. There I offer myself at the temple to anyone, declaring whatever one desires to be demonstrated and answering every question.

**SOCRATES**: O what a happy lot has fallen to you, Hippias, if you arrive at every Olympiad so confident in the wisdom of your mind! I would truly wonder if any athlete confident in his bodily strength would go there to compete as much as you are confident in the subtlety of your mind.

**HIPPIAS**: I am rightly affected this way, Socrates. For from the time I began to exercise in the Olympics, I have found no one yet superior to me in any matter.

**SOCRATES**: Noble is what you say, Hippias, and this glory of yours will be a monument of wisdom for the city of the Eleans and your parents. But what do you judge of Achilles and Ulysses? Which of these is more excellent, and in what way? Furthermore, while we were inside and many were present and you were discoursing, some words escaped me. I was reluctant to ask then, both because the crowd was large and lest I be an impediment to your speech. But now, since we are fewer and Eudicus here bids me ask, show us more clearly what you were saying of these men, and how you judged them.

**HIPPIAS**: I wish, Socrates, to relate more openly than I did then what I feel about these and others. I assert that Homer fashioned Achilles as the best man of all who went to Troy, Nestor as the wisest, and Ulysses as the most crafty (*versutum*) and "many-formed" (*multiformem*). 

[[notes: *Multiformem* refers to the Greek *polytropos*, "of many turns" or "wily."]]

**SOCRATES**: Bah, ô Hippia! Will you grant me this: that you will not laugh at me if I am slow to perceive and ask too often? Deign to answer me freely and easily.

**HIPPIAS**: It would be shameful, ô Socrates, when I teach others and take money for it, if I did not indulge you when you ask, and answer with a glad heart.

**SOCRATES**: You speak most nobly. Indeed, when you said Achilles was fashioned as the best man and Nestor the wisest, I seemed to understand. But when you called Ulysses crafty and many-formed, to tell the truth, I did not understand what you meant. Tell me—for perhaps from this I may perceive it better—was Achilles not also induced by Homer as many-formed and crafty, or not?

**HIPPIAS**: Not at all, ô Socrates, but entirely simple. For in the supplications themselves, when he induces them debating, he makes Achilles speak thus against Ulysses:

[[margin: Iliad.]]
[[notes: cf. Iliad IX.308-314. Ficino provides a verse translation.]]

"O most noble fabricator of guile, Ulysses, 
It behooves me to refell your words intrepidly, 
As I think must be done, lest you sitting here 
Stun me from this side and that with deceits. 
For he is more hateful to me than the gate of black Dis 
Who hides one thing in his heart and speaks another."

In these verses, he declares the character of both: Achilles is truthful and simple, Ulysses crafty and lying. These things Achilles inserts against Ulysses.

**SOCRATES**: I seem to understand now what you say, ô Hippia. For you call the crafty man a liar, as it appears.

**HIPPIAS**: Most certainly, ô Socrates. Homer fashions Ulysses as such often in both the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore Homer thought that one man was truthful and another was a liar, and that both were not the same?

**HIPPIAS**: What prevents it, Socrates?

**SOCRATES**: And do you think the same, Hippia?

**HIPPIAS**: Most of all. For I would err too much if I thought otherwise.

**SOCRATES**: Let us leave Homer aside, then, since it is not permitted to ask him what his intention was in composing these poems. But since you take up the cause, and those things seem so to you which you assert Homer said, answer for Homer and yourself at once.

**HIPPIAS**: Let it be so. Ask in few words what you please.

**SOCRATES**: Do you call those liars who are unable to do something—like the weak or the weary—or those who *can* do something?

**HIPPIAS**: The powerful, and most especially so in many other things, as well as in deceiving men.

**SOCRATES**: They are powerful then, according to your speech, and crafty, are they not?

**HIPPIAS**: Certainly.

**SOCRATES**: Are they crafty and subtle out of a certain stupidity and imprudence, or rather out of astuteness and prudence?

**HIPPIAS**: Most of all out of astuteness and prudence.

**SOCRATES**: They are prudent then, it seems.

**HIPPIAS**: Greatly so, by Jove.

**SOCRATES**: Being prudent, do they not know what they do, or do they know?

**HIPPIAS**: Indeed, they know most of all. For this is why they seduce others.

**SOCRATES**: Since they are knowing in those things they know, are they foolish, or rather wise?

**HIPPIAS**: Wise, clearly, in these very things for deceiving.

**SOCRATES**: Stop, I pray. Let us repeat what has been said, so we may see what you mean. You say liars are powerful and prudent, knowing and wise concerning those things about which they lie?

**HIPPIAS**: I do.

**SOCRATES**: And you say others are truthful, and others conversely are liars, and these are far contrary to each other?

**HIPPIAS**: I say that too.

**SOCRATES**: From this it follows that liars are among the number of the powerful and wise.

**HIPPIAS**: Most certainly.

**SOCRATES**: When you say liars are powerful and wise at these same things, do you mean they are powerful to lie if they wish, or powerless at those things about which they lie?

**HIPPIAS**: Powerful, indeed.

**SOCRATES**: To sum up: liars are those who are powerful and wise at lying.

**HIPPIAS**: Plainly.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore, a man who cannot lie and knows nothing will not be a liar.

**HIPPIAS**: So it is.

**SOCRATES**: A powerful man is one who is not hindered by certain things. I ask you, just as you can write my name whenever you wish, do you not call a man thus affected "powerful"?

**HIPPIAS**: Surely.

**SOCRATES**: Tell me, ô Hippia, are you not skilled in numbering and counting?

**HIPPIAS**: Most of all.

**SOCRATES**: If someone asks you how much three times seven hundred makes, will you not, if you wish, answer most quickly and most excellently about these things?

**HIPPIAS**: Entirely.

**SOCRATES**: Is it not because you are most powerful and wise in these matters?

**HIPPIAS**: Indeed.

**SOCRATES**: Are you only most wise and powerful? Or are you also the "best" in these same things in which you excel in wisdom and power—that is, in counting numbers?

**HIPPIAS**: And the best besides, Socrates.

**SOCRATES**: You could speak the truth about these things above others, could you not?

**HIPPIAS**: I believe so.

**SOCRATES**: And could you also speak false things about them? Answer now, Hippia, generously and magnificently as before. If someone asks what three times seven hundred is, will you lie more about these things—always pronouncing false things according to the same, wishing to lie and never bring forth the truth? Or can he who is ignorant of numbers lie more than you, even if you wish to lie? Or conversely, will the ignorant man often bring forth the truth by chance even when he wants to speak falsely, because he is ignorant of the matter? Whereas you, since you are wise, will always lie in the same way when you wish to lie?

**HIPPIAS**: It is as you say.

**SOCRATES**: Is the liar then a liar about other things, but not about numbers? And will he not lie about number?

**HIPPIAS**: Indeed, he will lie also about numbers.

**SOCRATES**: Let us establish this then, Hippia: that there is a certain liar about counting and number.

**HIPPIAS**: Certainly.

**SOCRATES**: Who will this be? It must be one who can lie, as you said, if he is to be a liar. For you said—if you remember—that he who cannot lie is not a liar.

**HIPPIAS**: I remember indeed; it was so stated.

**SOCRATES**: Did it not just now consist that you were most powerful at lying in counting numbers?

**HIPPIAS**: That was stated as well.

**SOCRATES**: Are you not also most powerful at bringing forth the truth about those same numbers?

**HIPPIAS**: Greatly so.

**SOCRATES**: The same person then is most able in counting both to speak the truth and to lie. And that person is he who is good at numbers—namely, the *computator* (calculator).

**HIPPIAS**: Entirely so.

**SOCRATES**: Who then, Hippia, can be a liar in counting except he who is good at it? For this man is powerful, and this man is also truthful.

**HIPPIAS**: It appears so.

**SOCRATES**: You see that the same person is truthful in these things and also a liar, and the truthful is no better than the liar. For they are the same, and not far contrary as you recently thought.

**HIPPIAS**: It certainly does not appear so now in these things.

**SOCRATES**: Do you wish to consider this in other matters?

**HIPPIAS**: As you please.

**SOCRATES**: Are you not skilled in geometry?

**HIPPIAS**: I am.

**SOCRATES**: Does not the same thing happen in geometry? The same person can pronounce false things about figures as can pronounce true things. And that man is the geometer.

**HIPPIAS**: Indeed.

**SOCRATES**: Is any other good at these things besides him?

**HIPPIAS**: No other.

**SOCRATES**: Can the good and wise geometer do both? If anyone else is a liar in figures, it is most of all he who is good in them. For he is powerful, but the bad man is powerless at lying. And one who is powerless at lying can never be a liar, as was conceded.

**HIPPIAS**: These things are so.

**SOCRATES**: Let us look at a third: the astronomer. You are accustomed, Hippia, to profess this art even more than the previous ones, are you not?

**HIPPIAS**: Certainly.

**SOCRATES**: Do not the same things happen in Astronomy?

**HIPPIAS**: It is consistent, ô Socrates.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore, if anyone else is a liar in astronomy, it will be most of all he who is a good astronomer. For he can lie most excellently. He who is powerless is also ignorant.

**HIPPIAS**: So it appears.

**SOCRATES**: The same man then in astronomy will be both truthful and a liar.

**HIPPIAS**: It seems so.

**SOCRATES**: Come, Hippia, think thus through all the sciences, whether it is so or otherwise. For you are adorned with more arts than all others. I once heard you boasting that you abounded in wisdom more than others—disputing in the forum among the tables—saying that you once went to Olympia and all the ornaments you had on your body you had made with your own hands. 

[[margin: Cicero, De Oratore III, also says the same.]]

First, your ring was your own work (for you began there), as if you were skilled in engraving. Furthermore, a certain seal was your work, and a strigil, and an oil-flask was similarly your work; shoes also sewn by your hands, a cloak, and a tunic woven by you. And what seemed most marvelous and a sign of singular wisdom: you said you showed a girdle you made, similar to the Persian and precious ones. Also your poems—epic verses, tragedies, dithyrambs, and many orations composed in various free measures. Besides, you claimed to hold all those things I mentioned earlier above all others, and to excel in rhythms, harmonies, and the correct ratio of letters, and in very many other things of this kind, if I remember correctly. But I had forgotten your art of memory, in which you seem to me most polished. Perhaps I have forgotten many other things as well. 

But as I said: looking into your arts (which are too many) and the arts of others, tell me if you have ever found, among those things conceded between us, that the truthful man is different from the liar, and that they are not the same. Search in any wisdom or craftiness, or whatever you wish to call it. But ô friend, you will never find it, for it is nowhere. If it is anywhere, tell me.

**HIPPIAS**: I do not find it at present, Socrates.

**SOCRATES**: Nor will you find it hereafter, I think. If I speak the truth, remember, Hippia, what follows from our previous points.

**HIPPIAS**: I do not sufficiently follow what you are saying, Socrates.

**SOCRATES**: There is no need for your art of memory at present. It is clear enough, even if you do not think so, but I will bring it to your memory. You remember saying Achilles was truthful and Odysseus a liar and crafty?

**HIPPIAS**: Certainly.

**SOCRATES**: But now you feel that the same man appeared to be both truthful and a liar. Therefore, if Ulysses was a liar, he was also truthful. Likewise, if Achilles was truthful, he was also a liar. These two were neither different from each other nor contrary, but similar.

**HIPPIAS**: You always weave such little traps (*captiunculas*), Socrates. Occupying what is most troublesome in discourse, you insist on this and handle the smallest points, but you do not contend against the whole matter of which we are speaking. For if you wish, I will now show you by many arguments and sufficient reason that Homer fashioned Achilles as better than Ulysses and truthful, but Ulysses as subtle, lying in many things, and worse than Achilles. If you please, compare your speech to mine, and let those present judge which of us spoke more correctly.

**SOCRATES**: I do not doubt, Hippia, that you seem wiser than me. But I am accustomed always to attend diligently when someone disputes a matter, especially when the speaker seems wise to me. Then I am eager to understand what he says; I inquire, weigh, and estimate, so I may perceive his words clearly. But if I value the speaker little, I neither ask him anything nor attend to what he says. By this very conjecture, you will grasp whom I esteem as wise. For you will see me listening most accurately to their words and inquiring from them so I may profit in my life by learning something. 

And now, when I noted your words by which you show from the testimony of those poems that Achilles speaks against Ulysses as a boaster, it seemed a marvelous thing to me, if you spoke the truth. For Ulysses himself, being crafty, cannot be refuted by any lie; but Achilles seems to be crafty and varied according to your speech, for he lies. For when he pronounced those verses you just recited:

[[margin: Iliads.]]

"He is more hateful to me than the gate of black Dis 
Who hides one thing in his heart and speaks another..."

A little later he adds what will not be persuaded by Ulysses or Agamemnon: that he will not remain at Troy.

"But tomorrow, when I have made sacrifice to Jove 
And all the celestials, and drawn the ships to the shore, 
You shall see them at first light 
Sailing the Hellespont..."

In which you shall see, if you wish, strong men leaning on their oars. For if Neptune fills the sails with favorable winds, on the third day we shall be in the fertile shores of Phthia. Likewise, earlier, quarreling with Agamemnon, he says:

"Behold, I shall go home in the black ships to Phthia, 
Since it is better; nor does my mind wish to stay here 
And fill you with wealth while I remain inglorious in arms."

Having said these things, now before the whole army, now to his friends, he never appears to gird himself for the work or draw the ships as if to return home. He cares very little whether his words are true. 

Hippia, I asked you from the beginning because I doubted which of these two is held as more excellent by the poet. I thought both were very good men, and it was difficult to know which excelled more in lying, truth, and other virtue. Both are very close in this.

**HIPPIAS**: You do not discern rightly, ô Socrates. For what Achilles lies about, he does not do out of insidious intent, but unwillingly on account of the state of the army, being compelled to remain and help. But Ulysses lies willingly and by guile.

**SOCRATES**: You deceive me, dearest Hippia, and you yourself imitate Ulysses.

**HIPPIAS**: Not at all, Socrates. What are you saying? By what reason?

**SOCRATES**: Because you say Achilles does not lie out of insidious intent, though he was such a seducer and plotter beyond his very boasting—as Homer fashions him—that he was so much craftier than Ulysses. He hid his own vanity while daring to speak contraries to himself before Ulysses, thus deceiving him. Therefore Ulysses seems to bring nothing against him, since he did not notice the lie.

**HIPPIAS**: What are these things you say, ô Socrates?

**SOCRATES**: Do you not know that afterward he said to Ulysses that he would depart at first light, but to Ajax not so, but otherwise?

**HIPPIAS**: Where?

[[margin: Iliad.]]

**SOCRATES**: In these verses:

"No care of the war will hold me 
Until I hear that Hector, son of Priam, has come to the ships 
And long tents of the Myrmidons..."

Did you think, Hippia, that the son of Thetis, educated by the most wise Chiron, was so forgetful that having just before attacked those vain boasters with a most vehement oration, he would immediately say to Ulysses (as if forgetful of himself) that he would sail, but tell Ajax he would stay? Or did he plot this because he knew Ulysses was older and far more powerful in fictitious machinations and guile?

**HIPPIAS**: It does not seem to me that Achilles said those things by guile, but rather persuaded by his own simplicity; he spoke differently to Ajax than to Ulysses. Ulysses, however, whether he speaks truth or falsehood, always weaves snares.

**SOCRATES**: Ulysses then is better than Achilles, it seems.

**HIPPIAS**: Not at all, ô Socrates.

**SOCRATES**: Did it not appear above that those who speak a lie willingly are better than those who do not?

**HIPPIAS**: In what way, Socrates, can those who do injury knowingly, plot willingly, and do harm, be better than those who do these things outside their intention? For much is forgiven to him who does injury, speaks a lie, or commits some evil through ignorance. The laws act more severely against those who do evil and lie willingly than against those who do so unwillingly.

**SOCRATES**: You see, Hippia, that I speak the truth when I say I am accurate in the questioning of wise men. Although I fail in other things, I have this one good thing: I do not know what the nature of things is. This can be conjectured most of all because whenever I speak with one of you who excel in the opinion of wisdom and have all the Greeks as witnesses of your doctrine, I appear to know nothing. For never does the same thing seem to me as to you. 

[[margin: Disagreeing with the wise is a sign of ignorance. The duties of teaching and learning.]]

What is a more evident argument of ignorance than if one disagrees with wise men? Yet I have this small good thing which helps me: I prepare myself for learning without the blush of shame. I ask and inquire, and I give great thanks to the one who answers. I am never ungrateful to anyone, nor do I ever claim for myself the inventions of others before an audience, but I always extol the teacher with praises and attribute to him before all what is his. 

And now what you say, I do not admit in the least. I disagree entirely, and I know certainly this happens by my own fault. For I confess myself to be such as I am, lest I extol myself. To me, Hippia, it seems entirely contrary to what it seems to you. I think those who willingly harm men, do injury, lie, deceive, and sin are better than those who do so not of their own will. Sometimes, however, I judge the opposite and wander about these things, being ignorant of the matter itself. 

Behold now, a certain sickness of mind has invaded me, and those who sin by purpose seem better to me than those who err besides their intention. I take the previous discourses as the cause of this evil, whereby it happens that at present I think those who sin not of their own will are worse than those who sin willingly. Therefore you will forgive me, and let no envy detain you from curing my mind. You will confer a much greater benefit on me if you free my mind of ignorance than if you free my body of sickness. 

If you wish to do this with many words, I foretell that you will not cure me thus—I would not follow. But if you wish to answer as before, you will profit me greatly. I hope this will not be harmful to you. I will rightly invoke you now, son of Apemantus. For you induced me to dispute with Hippias. Therefore, if Hippias will not answer now, intercede for me yourself.

**EUDICUS**: I think there is no need for my prayers to Hippias, Socrates. For he did not propose to answer only under compulsion; rather, he promised to answer everyone willingly. Were these not your words, Hippia?

**HIPPIAS**: I said them indeed. But Socrates here, ô Eudice, always disturbs speakers and seems to be a certain juggler.

**SOCRATES**: O best of men, Hippia, I do not do these things willingly. I would then be wise according to your speech and astute. But I act besides my intention, wherefore forgive me. For you say that he who sins not of his own will should be forgiven.

**EUDICUS**: Do not do otherwise, Hippia, but for our sake and because of what you said before, answer what Socrates asks.

**HIPPIAS**: I will answer since you ask. Seek what you please.

**SOCRATES**: I vehemently desire to consider, Hippia, what was just said: which are better—those who sin willingly and by purpose, or those who do not? I hope it can be considered most correctly in this way. Answer now: do you call a certain runner "good"?

[[margin: Whether those who sin willingly by choice are better, or those who do not.]]

**HIPPIAS**: Indeed.

**SOCRATES**: And "bad"?

**HIPPIAS**: Yes.

**SOCRATES**: Is the one who runs well good, and the one who runs badly bad?

**HIPPIAS**: Certainly.

**SOCRATES**: Does he who runs slowly not run badly? And he who runs quickly, well?

**HIPPIAS**: Without doubt.

**SOCRATES**: In running, then, speed is a good and slowness an evil.

**HIPPIAS**: What of it?

**SOCRATES**: Which runner is better? He who runs slowly by choice, or he who does so otherwise?

**HIPPIAS**: He who does so by choice.

**SOCRATES**: Is running not doing something?

**HIPPIAS**: Doing indeed.

**SOCRATES**: Doing something is operating.

**HIPPIAS**: Truly.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore he who runs badly operates this evil and shameful thing in running.

**HIPPIAS**: Evil, why not?

**SOCRATES**: But he runs badly who runs slowly.

**HIPPIAS**: Surely.

**SOCRATES**: Does the good runner not operate this evil and shame by industry, while the bad runner does so besides his purpose?

**HIPPIAS**: It seems so.

**SOCRATES**: In running, then, he is worse who acts badly besides his will than he who acts so willingly.

**HIPPIAS**: In running, clearly.

**SOCRATES**: What about wrestling? Which wrestler is better? He who falls by deliberate effort, or he who falls unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS**: He who falls by deliberate effort.

**SOCRATES**: So it seems. Is it worse and more shameful in wrestling to fall or to throw?

**HIPPIAS**: To fall.

**SOCRATES**: In wrestling, then, he who acts badly and shamefully by study is a better wrestler than he who does so by weakness and inertia.

**HIPPIAS**: It seems so.

**SOCRATES**: What of every other use of the body? Is he who is more robust and fit in body not able to do both at his will—the things of a strong man and those of a weak man, both beautiful and shameful? Therefore, he who excels in the habit of the body, whenever he acts badly according to the body, does so willingly; the weak man, however, unwillingly.

**HIPPIAS**: It seems the same happens regarding strength.

**SOCRATES**: What should be said of the grace of the figure itself? Is it not the part of a more beautiful and better body to put together shameful figures by deliberate work, but the part of the deformed to do so otherwise? What does it seem to you?

**HIPPIAS**: As it seems to you.

**SOCRATES**: The voluntary grace of figure pertains to the virtue of the body, but the contrary to vice.

**HIPPIAS**: It appears so.

**SOCRATES**: What of the voice? Which do you call better? That which is dissonant by the will of the mind, or that which is so from inertia?

**HIPPIAS**: By the will of the mind.

**SOCRATES**: And the other is worse.

**HIPPIAS**: Without doubt.

**SOCRATES**: Do you wish to have good things or bad?

**HIPPIAS**: Good.

**SOCRATES**: Would you choose to have feet that limped by deliberate effort, or unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS**: Those that do so by industry.

**SOCRATES**: Is the limping of feet not a vice and a deformity?

**HIPPIAS**: It is.

**SOCRATES**: Is dullness not a vice of the eyes?

**HIPPIAS**: A vice.

**SOCRATES**: Which eyes would you rather choose: those by which one sees confusedly or looks perversely by choice, or conversely those by which one sees badly unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS**: Those by which one does so willingly.

**SOCRATES**: From your own things, then, you judge those better which act badly by choice than those which do so unwillingly.

**HIPPIAS**: Such things, evidently.

**SOCRATES**: Does one reason not comprehend all other things—ears, nose, mouth, and all senses—teaching that senses which sin besides their purpose are never to be chosen, being depraved, but those which do so by design are to be chosen as better?

**HIPPIAS**: It seems so to me.

**SOCRATES**: Of which instruments is the use better? Those by which someone errs willingly, or those by which one errs unwillingly? Like a rudder: is that one better by which someone steers badly by industry, or that by which one does so unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS**: That by which one does so by industry.

**SOCRATES**: And likewise for a bow, a lyre, pipes, and all other things.

**HIPPIAS**: You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES**: Which soul of a horse is better to possess: that by which one rides badly willingly, or that by which one does so unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS**: That by which one does so willingly.

**SOCRATES**: It is therefore better.

**HIPPIAS**: It is.

**SOCRATES**: To the better soul of a horse, then, one will do the bad works of this soul willingly, but the contrary otherwise.

**HIPPIAS**: Entirely.

**SOCRATES**: Is the reason not the same for the soul of a dog and all other animals?

**HIPPIAS**: The same.

**SOCRATES**: Which soul of an archer would you choose as better: his who misses the mark willingly, or his who misses unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS**: His who does so by choice.

**SOCRATES**: Is this soul not better at the art of archery?

**HIPPIAS**: Better.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore, the soul that misses unknowingly is worse than that which misses knowingly.

**HIPPIAS**: In the faculty of archery, clearly.

**SOCRATES**: What about the study of medicine? Is not the soul that inflicts certain evils on bodies by deliberate work more skilled in the art of medicine than that which sins through ignorance?

**HIPPIAS**: Plainly.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore this soul is better in the art of medicine.

**HIPPIAS**: Better.

**SOCRATES**: Is the soul not more instructed for playing the cithara or blowing pipes—and all works of every art or science—and thus better? And if it ever acts badly beside the art, it does so by industry; but the worse soul does so besides its intention?

**HIPPIAS**: It appears so.

**SOCRATES**: We choose servants who sin knowingly about their service rather than those who sin unknowingly, as if they were better for these works.

**HIPPIAS**: Surely.

**SOCRATES**: And do we not desire to have our own soul as good as possible?

**HIPPIAS**: Indeed.

**SOCRATES**: Will it not be better if it does bad things and sins willingly rather than unknowingly?

**HIPPIAS**: That would be a grave thing, ô Socrates, if those who do injury willingly were better than those who do so unwillingly.

**SOCRATES**: Yet from what has been said above, it seems to follow.

**HIPPIAS**: Not to me, however.

**SOCRATES**: I thought, Hippia, that it seemed the same to you. Answer again: is justice not either a certain power, or science, or both? Must justice not be one of these?

**HIPPIAS**: It must.

**SOCRATES**: If justice is a certain power of the soul, will the more powerful soul be more just? For such a soul appeared better to us, ô best of men.

**HIPPIAS**: It appeared so.

**SOCRATES**: What if justice is science? Will the wiser soul be more just? And the more foolish, conversely, more unjust?

**HIPPIAS**: So it is.

**SOCRATES**: What if it is both? Will not the soul that has both—science and power—be more just? And that which does not have science, more unjust? Is it not necessary for the matter to be so?

**HIPPIAS**: It appears so.

**SOCRATES**: The soul that is more powerful and wiser appeared to be better and more ready for performing both beautiful and shameful things in any action.

**HIPPIAS**: Certainly.

**SOCRATES**: Whenever it does shameful things, it does them willingly on account of its art and power. These things—either both or one—pertain to justice.

**HIPPIAS**: It seems so.

**SOCRATES**: Truly, to do injury is to do bad things; not to do injury is to do good things.

**HIPPIAS**: So it is.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore, will the more powerful and better soul not act willingly whenever it acts unjustly? But the bad soul conversely?

**HIPPIAS**: It appears so.

**SOCRATES**: Is the good man not he who has a good soul? And the bad man conversely?

**HIPPIAS**: Without doubt.

**SOCRATES**: Therefore, it is the part of a good man to do injury willingly, but the part of a bad man to do so unwillingly, since a good man has a good soul.

**HIPPIAS**: He has one indeed.

**SOCRATES**: If there is any man, then, ô Hippia, who errs willingly and commits shameful and unjust things, he is none other than the good man.

**HIPPIAS**: I cannot concede these things to you, ô Socrates.

**SOCRATES**: Nor can I concede them to myself, Hippia; nevertheless, from our previous discourse, it is necessary that it seem so to us at present. Truly, as I was saying, I wander up and down about these things and do not persist in the same opinion. It is no wonder that I and similar unlearned men wander into contraries, if even you wise men wander. It is a grave evil for us if, even after coming to you, we do not cease to err.

[[summary: In the Hippias Minor, Socrates uses an eristic (argumentative) method to lead the sophist Hippias to the paradoxical conclusion that he who lies or sins on purpose is "better" than he who does so out of ignorance. This serves to expose the sophist's lack of a true moral foundation for his definitions.]]
[[keywords: Socrates, Hippias, Lying, Virtue, Knowledge, Homer, Achilles, Ulysses]]

# CHARMIDES, OR,
## ON TEMPERANCE.
### BY MARSILIO FICINO
### ARGUMENT

[[notes: Ficino's introduction to the Charmides, where he frames the dialogue through the lens of *Sophrosyne* (Temperance).]]

Socrates' study in this dialogue is to exhort all to *temperantia* (temperance); three groups especially: youth, the noble, and the beautiful. Youth, because medicine must be applied quickly to diseases: "Oppose beginnings; medicine is prepared too late when evils have grown strong through long delays." Nobles also, both to show that true nobility is placed in virtue, and because nobles are usually an example to others and are admitted daily to the republic—to the gravest detriment of the human race if they be bad. Finally, the beautiful: for these are most of all depraved by the company of the flagitious; thus they need medicine more. Furthermore, the beautiful ought to study so that, just as nature gave a brief beauty to the body, they in turn might restore a perpetual beauty of the soul to God, the author of nature. 

Nor should it be permitted that while our exterior parts please many with their beauty, our interior parts meanwhile displease with their deformity. Although all things in this dialogue have a wonderful allegory—especially the amatory ones, not unlike the *Song of Solomon*—I have changed some things and omitted some. For what was suited to the most chaste ears of the Athenians might perhaps not suit ruder ears. Therefore, a certain Aristarchus of Homer—or rather of Plato—might say some things are not by Plato but by Chronus. 

Three things are to be noted in the beginning: first, those that transfer love from this form of the body to incorporeal beauty. First, Socrates says he discerns nothing between this beautiful one and that; all beautiful ones please him equally. As if to say, one should not fix one's foot in the form of one body, but ascend to the common beauty of the whole species. Since this is one in many, it refers back to one idea of beauty over the many. Just as we transcend from the individual to the species and from the species to the idea by thinking, so we are admonished to go from the love of this form to the love of the common form first, and then to the love of the ideal form. 

To these Socrates added that the beauty of the body should not be loved for itself, but should be considered by us as an image of divine beauty. Finally, he bids us strip the soul, and having set aside the form of the body, behold the natural decorum of the soul and more diligently apply the study of acquiring it. Meanwhile, he rebukes Chaerephon who said something about the nakedness of the body in the gymnasium. 

Not without cause does he begin the exhortation to temperance from the beauty of the body. For this is the temperance of lines and colors. But from this he passes next to the health of the body, which is also a certain temperance and moderation; and in cognition there is similarly a certain temperance, consisting in a certain harmony between the intelligence and the things understood—so that Pythagoras not undeservedly said temperance was the most healthful of all virtues, the preserver of human society both publicly and privately. Especially since justice is also a certain temperance, that is, a fitting moderation in exchanging and distributing. 

Indeed, although temperance properly deals with restraining vehement lusts and pleasures, it is transferred by a certain similarity to cutting off all desires and moderating every act—so that the duty of fortitude consists in the moderation of audacity and fear, similarly justice in the measure of rewards and punishments, liberality in the manner of spending, and finally the health of the whole life: "nothing in excess" (*ne quid nimis*). Hence that Pythagorean saying: "Measure is the best of all things." 

But remember those in the *Phaedo* who are denied to be temperate who abstain from pleasures for the sake of bodily pleasures. For he bids mortal actions be referred to the purging of the mind for the sake of attaining wisdom and divine likeness. Such is the excellence of temperance that all elegant craftsmen observe it in their works, and by its virtue not only every body under the moon, but even the whole heaven itself is preserved. This is confirmed by the testimony of wise men in the *Gorgias*. Similar is this: "God disposes all things sweetly"; also, "He disposes all things in number, weight, and measure." 

But now let us return to the dialogue. While Socrates, according to the opinion of the Magi, forbids the body to be cured before the soul is cured, he manifestly reproves those who, caring for the smallest things, neglect the greatest—like those who seek remedies for sick horses and dogs, but do not consult physicians for the diseases of their own bodies and souls. They arrange every smallest piece of furniture rightly, while they themselves remain uncomposed in soul and body. With an intemperate soul, they act temperately. Daily they curiously handle the affairs of others, but desert their own. Truly, all things except the soul itself are alien to us. Therefore, he called the medicine of the body a "leaf," a light, fragile, and entirely mutable thing, and to be utterly contemned. 

He signifies also that many inconveniences of both body and fortune frequently happen to us on account of intemperance, and conversely many good things proceed from temperance. Likewise, to a perfectly composed soul, whatever happens is so prudently disposed and equally tolerated that nothing at last results in evil. But to an uncomposed soul, nothing can be well composed in the body or outside it. 

He explains in the *Cratylus* the Greek name for temperance, *Sophrosyne*, as a certain health and preservation of prudence. For he thinks that the lights of all truths were innate in the soul; therefore, if it looks into itself, it will behold the truth in all things. But the cause of its not looking in is immoderate affection toward the body and bodily things. Wherefore there is need of temperance first: when the darkness of perturbations is expelled, the mind is made more serene and is abundantly surrounded by the light of the divine sun, from which it first recovers wisdom and then attains prudence. 

Since therefore wisdom and prudence accompany temperance, Plato often elsewhere, and in this dialogue under the very name of temperance, wants wisdom and prudence to be contained. Socrates advises Charmides to look into himself when he is about to speak of temperance. For this conversion into oneself is the duty of this virtue; and he who is turned into himself will understand human temperance through the innate idea of temperance, and recognizing moderation itself (by which God tempered the parts of the soul from the beginning), he will know how the affected soul is to be tempered. 

Add to this that in this precept he signifies that no one except the temperate ought to or can speak of temperance for the sake of persuading. Furthermore, it is handed down in the *Timaeus* that from a certain consonance of the soul both to itself and to the body, all prosperous things happen to us. Moreover, the Pythagoreans—whom the Roman Censorinus follows in this—promise perpetual and true health and a long life to the body if the mind prudently moderates each motion of its own and of the body. Both Censorinus and we have found this to be true for many wise and holy men. Some refer the long lives of the ancients to this same or a similar cause. 

But something marvelous is added: the Magi promise immortality to bodies with their incantations. The magic of Zoroaster, as Plato says in the *Alcibiades*, is nothing else than divine worship. Here he added besides that not only by magical incantations, but also by philosophical reasons, the soul is tempered and the body is preserved either forever or at least for a long time far from death. Truly, that oration which is to persuade listeners entirely of temperance, and furthermore affect them, requires two things especially: power infused by God and reasons prepared by philosophy. And Plato calls an oration composed of these two a "magical incantation," by which Apollo first, and then the Pythagoreans, wonderfully expelled diseases from the soul and body. 

Nor should it be thought false that a body under a soul perfectly tempered could be immortal, and under an intemperate one fall into diseases and evils. For that Mosaic mystery contains this concerning the state and fall of our first parents. And Avicenna, following the Platonists and Hippocrates, proves that the soul by its very nature so exceeds all matter that as soon as it is restored to itself, it can move the elements of the world by a certain wonderful virtue and have empire over bodies—wherefore it can much more so over its own. Which indeed Adam could experience from the beginning, and some think Enoch and Elijah, and some suspect the Evangelist (John) still lives by a similar reason. But we dispute most widely of all these things in our *Theologia* (Platonic Theology). 

Finally, to sum up, the marvel of the virtue of temperance is declared in that it restores to itself, happily, that which had fallen into worse things. The marvelous power of the soul is declared, from which all things both good and bad flow into the body, and by whose will the body can be preserved incorrupt. Which indeed is entirely consonant with the Mosaic mysteries. 

After this follows the inquiry into what temperance is, which neither Charmides nor Critias ever fully explains. The former does not bring forth temperance properly, but the things that accompany it; the latter pertains more to prudence, and that always ineptly—namely, to show that it is not for everyone to discourse on such a noble virtue. 

Meanwhile, note that the ancient priests were accustomed to consecrate the third goblet of libations to Jove the Savior, declaring that the beginnings, middles, and ends of all things (as Plato relates in the *Laws*) are disposed and preserved under the providence of Jove. But let us return to Critias' ineptitudes: saying there is a certain science which knows both itself and all other sciences, but is ignorant of the realities themselves of which they are sciences. Which is indeed absurd, because the truth and reason of science consists in a certain contact and congruence with the things known. Furthermore, science cannot be perfectly known unless what science is is discerned; but that cannot be had unless the object of the science is had. 

Likewise, Critias confesses that someone who in no way knows can meanwhile know that he does not know. But Socrates did not receive this, because what is in no way known cannot meanwhile be known in any way. For whoever notices that he is ignorant of something, by that very fact knows he lacks it. If he knows he lacks it, then he already has a certain notion of that which he says he lacks, by which he judges that he lacks it and what it is he lacks. Wherefore, whoever knows himself to be ignorant of a thing does not meanwhile entirely ignore it, but describes it with a certain general adumbration—general, I say, because in the special distinction of things science consists perfectly, which Plato seeks in all his disputations. 

Where he induces Socrates acknowledging that he "knows nothing," he judged that although he lacked special knowledge, he had general descriptions of things; otherwise he could not recognize his own ignorance. Therefore, while he knew nothing, he in a certain way knew all things. 

Because Critias had transferred the discourse from temperance to prudence—and that with a certain Platonic license—Socrates asserts prudence (that is, the science of good and evil) to hold the highest authority for beatitude; both because it demonstrates the good itself and the means to that good, and because all things and arts, insofar as they are ruled by it, are conducive to our good—but otherwise not at all. Finally, Socrates teaches that nothing is more difficult than to define or acquire temperance. The difficulty of the definition proceeds from the fact that it can hardly be distinguished from the other virtues of which it is a certain consonance. Add that it is understood and expressed in words with as much difficulty as it is possessed within. 

Indeed, since from the very commerce with the body we are mostly inclined toward pleasure and intemperance, we are drawn away from justice; thus we attain temperance with the greatest difficulty. Furthermore, the first affections of the senses seem to some to lead either toward fortitude through anger and audacity, or toward prudence through fear, or toward patience through pain, or toward justice and liberality through love. Temperance, however, is always opposed to every impetus. For since it can be placed in a certain tranquility of the soul, it is hindered from every side by every affection. The difficulty is also increased because just as in the body we seek an entirely consonant temperament of humors and members, so in the soul we must find a harmony of its own motions.

[[summary: This introduction to the Charmides frames temperance (*Sophrosyne*) not merely as self-control, but as a metaphysical harmony between soul and body. Ficino links the Socratic "cure of the soul" to Pythagorean and Mosaic traditions, emphasizing that physical health follows spiritual order.]]
[[keywords: Charmides, Sophrosyne, Temperance, Marsilio Ficino, Socratic Method, Neoplatonism, Soul-Body relation]]

...ways. But for a little while before we elect the magistrates, let us pause and declare some things pertaining to their election. CLIN. What things? ATHEN. These. Listen now. No one doubts that since lawgiving is a great matter, if one appoints unfit magistrates for a city well-prepared by laws—even if the laws themselves are well-placed—not only will it be of no use and provoke laughter, but it will also bring the greatest losses and calamities upon the cities. CLIN. Plainly so. ATHEN. Therefore, friend, we must consider how this happens in your city and republic. For you see that those who are to rightly receive magistracies <term>magistracies - high-ranking public offices or positions of leadership</term> ought first to have been sufficiently tested from their youth, both themselves and their families, up until the election itself. Next, even those who are to cast their votes must have been educated in lawful customs, so they can easily recognize those who should be admitted or rejected, and conduct themselves toward both according to their dignity. But as for those who have recently gathered, since they neither know each other well enough nor are yet educated, how will they ever be able to choose magistrates correctly? CLIN. Almost never in any way. ATHEN. But indeed, a contest (as they say) does not easily accept excuses. This must be done by me now, and by you: since you have willingly undertaken the duty of establishing a city for the Cretans, and you are the tenth man in this work, as you say; and I promised to bring you help by this present conversation. Therefore, I will not allow this speech of ours to be headless and mutilated. For if it were to wander, it would appear ugly to everyone. CLIN. You have spoken very well, guest. ATHENIEN. Indeed, I will do so according to my strength. CLIN. Let us do exactly as we say. ATHEN. We will certainly do so, if God wills, so that we may even overcome old age in this part. CLIN. But it must be believed that God wills it. ATHEN. Certainly, it must be believed. Therefore, following Him, let us also say this. CLIN. What exactly? ATHEN. How boldly and at the same time dangerously the city is being established by us at this time. CLIN. To what end is this? ATHENNIEN. Because we give laws to unrefined men easily and fearlessly, and we command them to accept them; when it is clear to almost everyone, O Clinias, even those not very wise, that no one will easily accept new laws. If we were to wait long enough until boys educated by the laws, having lived together for a long time under those same laws, could cast their votes with the whole city, and if that were done rightly according to our strength, certainly both then and in the future, a city so instructed would remain far from error. CLIN. Reason advises so. ATHEN. Let us see, then, if we can find some suitable way for these things. It is necessary for the Knossians <note>original: "Gnosios" - inhabitants of the city of Knossos on Crete</note>, O Clinias, above the other Cretans, not only to begin this republic you are now founding as if by a tasting; but to provide with all zeal that the first magistrates are appointed as safely and as well as possible. In appointing others, the work is shorter; but it is necessary to create the guardians of the laws <term>guardians of the laws (nomophylakes) - high-ranking officials responsible for overseeing the administration of the laws and protecting the constitution</term> before others with the greatest diligence. CLIN. By what way and reason shall we do this? ATHEN. This, O Cretans, I say. It is necessary that the Knossians, since they are leaders of many cities, together with those who have come together into the same colony, should choose thirty-seven men from themselves and from them. Nineteen indeed from the number of those who will inhabit the colony, and the rest from Knossos itself. Let the Knossians give these to your city, and you yourself too, as a citizen of this colony and one of the eighteen men. Let them do these things either by persuading or by compelling with moderate force. CLIN. What then? Do not you, guest, and Megillus here, participate in this Republic with us? ATHEN. The Athenians claim much for themselves, O Clinias, and the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> claim much too, and both live far away. But for you, all things are conveniently situated: and for the other inhabitants similarly, according to those things that were just said about you, and what can most fittingly be done for you and them at this time, as explained. In the progress of time, however, and while the republic remains, let the designation of magistrates be done in this way. Whoever can bear arms, whether cavalry or infantry, and has taken part in wars when age allowed, shall enter the vote, and the assembly shall be held in the temple which the city considers most excellent. Each person, wherever he comes from, shall place his name, his father's name, his tribe, and his clan written on a tablet upon the altar. Let it be permitted for anyone who wishes, if he suspects any tablet is not correctly written, to take it away and place it in a public location, where it shall remain for no less than thirty days. Let the magistrates show three hundred tablets thus approved to the entire city, which may again accept or reject those it wishes from these. And the hundred thus selected a second time shall be shown again to everyone. For the third time, anyone may nominate whoever he wants from the hundred men. And the thirty-seven men who are selected by the most votes, let them declare them magistrates. Who then, O Clinias and Megillus, will establish all these things about the magistrates and their testing in the city? Do we understand that in cities thus joined from the beginning, there must be certain people? Those who are chosen from all the magistrates are not found among them at all. Since, however, they ought to be there, not just any common men, but the highest and most excellent men. For it is said in a proverb: the beginning is half of the whole <margin>Proverb.</margin> work; and we all everywhere praise him who has begun well. To me, however, this seems more than half, and a right beginning has never been sufficiently praised by anyone. CLIN. You speak rightly. ATHEN. Therefore, since this is not hidden from us, let us not pass it over in silence: but let us clearly declare how it may be done, although I have nothing to say at present except this one necessary and very useful thing. CLIN. What is it? ATHEN. Indeed, I say that there is no father or mother of this city we are about to found, except that city which sends the colony. Nor am I ignorant that there have been and will be many colonies distracted by discord from the cities that sent them. But just as a son conducts himself toward his parents, who, although he may sometimes oppose them, nevertheless loves his parents in the need of childhood and is loved in turn, and always fleeing to his own, finds protection only in them: so also I think the new city is affected toward its curators the Knossians, and the Knossians toward the new city. I repeat, therefore, what I just said. For it does not <margin>It does not hurt to repeat what is well said.</margin> hurt to say twice what is well said. It is necessary that the Knossians take up the care of all these things, and I say it is necessary for those who have set out as colonists into the new city to give their effort so that the magistrates are appointed according to the laws, and once appointed, they are approved. Once these things are done, let the Knossians return to Knossos: let the new city, however, strive to preserve itself and live happily. Those who are counted in the number of the thirty-seven men, let them care for these matters both now and always hereafter. First, let them have the guardianship of the laws: then also of the tablets, where each person has written the magnitude of his census <term>census - a registration of a citizen's property and wealth used to determine their social class and responsibilities</term>. <margin>The maximum census of citizens, which Plato wants.</margin> And let the maximum census be four minae <note>original: "minae" - an ancient Greek unit of weight and currency</note>: the second three: the third two: the fourth...

But both the beginning and the end of this trial <note>original: "iudicij"</note> ought to be referred to the people; the examination and approval, however, should be referred to the three highest magistrates, whom the litigants shall agree upon. If they cannot agree in this way, the council itself shall investigate and decide the selection for both parties. Furthermore, it is necessary that all citizens participate in private judgments to the best of their ability. For anyone who is entirely excluded from the power of judging considers himself to be a complete stranger to the state. For these reasons, it is necessary that trials also be held within the tribes themselves, and that the judges, chosen by lot <note>original: "forte"</note>, should immediately deliver a verdict uncorrupted by pleas <note>original: "precibus"; literally "prayers" or "entreaties," implying that the judges should be immune to lobbying or emotional appeals</note>. Finally, that court should settle all matters—the one we said must be as pure as possible in human affairs—to determine those lawsuits that could not be resolved by neighbors or fellow tribesmen <note>original: "contribules"; members of the same "phylē" or civic division</note>. Truly, concerning the courts—which one can neither easily affirm nor deny are <term>magistrates—officials holding executive or judicial power</term> without controversy...

<column-break/>

# On the Laws; Or, On Legislation. Dialogue VI. 553

[Left Column]

...if two parts have approached the other side of the house. A speech by no means lengthy would demonstrate these things to be true during leisure. Trusting, therefore, the present discourse and reason, let us distribute it, and invoking a god or a son of the gods for each part, let us dedicate altars and other such things; in the sacrifices, let us hold two assemblies each month, so that twelve may be adapted to the singular tribes and twelve to the distribution of the city. 

These things should first be done for the sake of the gods and for honoring divine matters; then also for the sake of friendship, mutual acquaintance, and finally common custom, which is highly necessary for concluding marriages. For once ignorance is removed, no one may be deceived in these matters as far as possible, but each may know to whom he gives <note>a daughter in marriage</note>, and whom and from whom he takes <note>a wife</note>. For the sake of this very thing, it is absolutely necessary that games and dances for boys and girls <note>the original uses "puellorū & puellarū", likely a scribe's error for "puerorum" (boys) and "puellarum" (girls)</note> should also be held together, with their bodies unclothed as far as modest shame allows, so that with reason and at a suitable age, they may behold one another and be beheld. 

The leaders of the choirs, along with the founders and guardians of the laws, should care for and arrange all these things, so that they may supply what we have left behind. For it is necessary, as we have said—especially in these matters which are numerous and small—that some things be omitted in the first positioning of the laws, which the succeeding magistrates, reminded by the practical use of things, will change and correct every year, until that time arrives when these institutions seem to have been sufficiently discussed and approved. 

A decade will be a moderate and sufficient time for making this trial <note>original: "periculum"</note> concerning the sacred rites, the dances, and finally all and singular things. Indeed, let this emendation through experience be done commonly with the legislator while he is living. If he should die, the individual magistrates shall refer the defects of their office to the guardians of the laws, and they shall emend them until each thing is seen to have reached its final point of approval. Only then shall they hold these laws as ratified, and use them along with the others which the legislator wrote from the beginning. In these, they shall never change anything of their own accord. If, however, some necessity should ever seem to press, let all the magistrates and the entire people consult together on this, and let all the oracles of the gods be sought. If there is a single consensus of all these, let them make the change; otherwise, never, but let the one who prohibits it prevail according to the law. 

Therefore, whenever anyone has reached twenty-five years of age, looking at others and being looked at by others, and believes he has found for himself a society suitable to his soul and decent for the communion and generation of children, let him take a wife within thirty-five years of age. But first, let him hear in what way that which is decorous and fit ought to be sought. For it is necessary, as Clinias says, to place a proper preamble <note>original: "exordiū"; an introductory explanation of the law's intent</note> for each individual before the laws. 

**CLINIAS.** You have remembered opportunely, stranger, and you have taken a favorable time for your speech. 

**ATHENIAN.** You speak well. Let us say it thus: O son, who is born of good parents, you ought to contract those marriages which wise men consider honorable. They would certainly advise that one should not flee the affinity of the poor, nor especially pursue that of the rich; but, other things being equal, one should always honor the poorer person and enter into society with them. For this is beneficial both to the city and to the families that are joined. Indeed, that which is moderate and middling is wonderfully superior to the immoderate and excessive in regard to virtue. Therefore, whoever is conscious that his soul is more fierce or swift in action than it ought to be, must take care to marry the daughter of the quietest possible parents; and he who is affected by the opposite nature should take to himself an opposite affinity.

<margin>Which marriages should be contracted.</margin>

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

But let there finally be one common reason for marriages: that each person should enter into a marriage not that is most pleasant to himself, but that is useful to the city. For individuals are always carried by nature toward those most like themselves. From this, the entire city is rendered as unequal as possible in both wealth and character, from which those things we would least wish to happen to us occur most frequently in many cities. But if we were to sanction these things by law through reason—that the rich should not admit the society of the rich, or the powerful of the powerful—and if we were to force the swifter souls to be joined with the slower, and the slower conversely with the swifter, our speech would not only seem ridiculous, but it would also stir up anger in many people. 

For it is not easy to understand that a city ought to be like a mixing bowl <note>original: "pateræ"</note>, in which the pure wine <note>original: "merum"</note> that first boils when poured in, is immediately chastened by the sobriety of another god <note>the "other god" is water, which "sobers" the wine of Dionysus; this is a metaphor for mixing fiery and calm temperaments</note> and, being perfectly tempered, becomes a good and moderate drink. But how this happens in the mixed procreation of children, no one, to speak briefly, is able to see. Therefore, we must not compel the citizens by law, but induce them by persuasion to value an equal and tempered generation of their children more than the equality of a most wealthy affinity. And him who gasps for money in marriage, we ought not to bar by written law, but deter with reproaches and rebukes. 

Therefore, both these exhortations and those things we said in previous sections encourage the proper celebration of marriages, asserting that by leaving behind children's children—our successors, namely, in divine service—we attain eternal nature. All these things and even more, one might rightly say as a preamble to entering into marriage. 

If, however, anyone does not obey of his own accord, and lives in the city as a stranger to this fellowship, and passes thirty-five years without marriage, let him be fined each year: if he is of the highest census <note>the wealthiest class</note>, one hundred drachmas; if of the second, seventy; if of the third, sixty; if of the fourth, thirty. This money is to be consecrated to the goddess Juno. If anyone does not pay in individual years, he shall owe tenfold. The collector of this money shall be the treasurer <note>original: "quæstor"</note> of the goddess herself; and unless he collects it, he himself shall owe it, and each must render an account of this. But let him who refuses to take a wife be fined in money in this way, but in honor thus: First, let him obtain no honors from the younger men, and let none of the youth obey him in any matter of their own accord. Then, if he dares to strike anyone, let anyone rise up against him and bring help to the one who received the injury. If anyone present does not do this, let him be held by the laws as a cowardly and bad citizen. 

Concerning the dowry <note>original: "dote"</note>, it was spoken of before, and now let it be said again: that equals should be for equals, since neither he who receives nor he who gives will grow old in a lack of money. For the necessities in this city are abundantly available to all. Furthermore, there will be less insulting pride in women, and less humble and illiberal servitude in men. He who obeys will surely do this one thing excellently. But he who does not obey, but either gives or receives what exceeds fifty drachmas for the sake of clothing—one a mina, another three minas, another two minas—and he who has the highest census shall pay just as much again to the treasury, and whatever was given or received shall be consecrated to Jupiter and Juno. We wish the treasurers of these gods to be the collectors of this money, just as was said recently when we were speaking of those who flee marriage, that what is owed by them must be collected by the treasurers of Juno. If they neglect this, let them pay it from their own funds. The first and firmest guarantee <note>original: "fideiussio"</note> shall be that of the father, or then, thirdly, of the brothers by the same father...

...by the father of the children. If none of these survive, then a similar guarantee should be valid from the mother’s side. But if an unusual desolation <note>Meaning a total lack of immediate family members</note> occurs, the closer agnates <term>agnati: relatives traced through the male line</term> and clansmen should stand as guarantors together with the guardians. If, however, any sacred initiation or other divine ritual of atonement seems necessary for the future, past, or present during the wedding ceremonies, they should consult the interpreters of divine matters; they should believe that if they obey them, they have performed each task with moderation.

<margin>The wedding feast.</margin>
For the wedding feast, let no more than five male friends and five female friends be invited from the father’s side, and the same number from the relatives and kin. Let the expense be no greater than is appropriate to one's wealth. The wealthiest man should spend a mina <term>mina: an ancient Greek unit of currency or weight; here representing a significant but capped sum</term>, another a half-mina, and so on, maintaining a proportion so that as the property assessment decreases, the expense decreases likewise. Let the one who obeys the law be praised by all. But let the guardians of the laws condemn the one who does not comply, as one estranged from what is proper and utterly ignorant of the law of the Muses' wedding songs.

It is never proper, nor safe, to drink to the point of drunkenness anywhere, except during the festivals of that god who bestowed wine <note>original: "eius dei qui largitus est vinum" — referring to Dionysus/Bacchus</note>. But especially the bridegroom and bride, joined in marriage, ought to be in control of their minds at that time when they are entering upon a significant change in their lives, and especially so that procreation may always result from those who are as temperate as possible. For it is almost uncertain which night or day, with God's help, will accomplish the conception itself. Therefore, so that the conception may be firm, stable, and peaceful, children should not be conceived when bodies are bloated with drunkenness. 

<margin>Drunkenness must be avoided.</margin>
He who is stuffed with wine is stirred by a madness of both soul and body; he is dragged and drags himself in every direction. Therefore, a drunkard, as if out of his mind, is useless for sowing <note>The text uses the agricultural metaphor of "sowing" for procreation</note>. Indeed, it is likely that he will procreate offspring who are uneven, unstable, and crooked, both in their limbs and in their characters. For this reason, throughout one's whole life, and especially as long as one is dedicated to procreation, everyone shall abstain and take care not to do those things which by their own nature and of their own accord induce diseases, or which lead toward insolence and injustice. For these things are necessarily transferred and imprinted upon the souls and bodies of those being born, and worse people are born as a result. But one must especially abstain from such things on that day and night. ...they ought to yield, O Clinias. # Book Twenty.

...is the most difficult of all. For this reason, Socrates says in the epilogue—just as he did in the introduction—that to achieve a temperance similar to celestial harmony, one requires a celestial and divine virtue, which is then poured into the reasonings and words of the soul. Indeed, he warns everywhere that we should strive to become temperate under the legitimate institutions of the law, rather than merely disputing about temperance using dialectical arguments. For temperance is recognized with extreme difficulty; and once recognized, it is not only of no use without practice, but is even quite harmful. Furthermore—and this is a greater point—it cannot be perfectly known unless it is possessed in reality. For it is not permitted for the impure to touch the purest of all things.

## SOCRATES, CHAEREPHO, CRITIAS, CHARMIDES.

**Y**esterday evening, when I had returned from the army at Potidaea [[notes: An ancient Greek colony where Socrates served as a hoplite]], I immediately returned with great pleasure to my usual exercises, from which I had been away for a long time. I entered the palaestra of Taureas, which is opposite the royal temple. There I found many people, some unknown to me and some familiar—and those indeed the most prominent. When they saw me entering unexpectedly from a distance, they immediately congratulated me, running up from various directions. Chaerepho especially, acting as if he were mad, immediately leapt forward from the center and ran to me. Grasping my hand, he said, "O Socrates, how did you escape surviving the battle? For shortly before we left, a battle took place at Potidaea, which these men here have recently heard about." I replied to them, "Just as you see." He said, "It was reported that the battle was very fierce, and that many men known to us fell in it." I said, "The reports you received were true." He asked, "Were you present in the battle?" "I was present." "Sit here then," he said, "and tell us the story, for we do not yet fully understand everything." Having said this, he ordered me to sit near Critias, the son of Callaeschrus.

So, sitting down, I first greeted Critias and the others, and then I recounted what had happened on the military expedition, answering what each man asked (for one asked one thing, and another another). But when we had spoken enough about these matters, I in turn asked them what the condition of philosophy was in these times, and which of the youths were distinguished for either wisdom, or natural talent, or both. Then Critias, looking toward the doors and seeing some youths entering and arguing with one another—with another crowd following them—said, "Socrates, regarding the noble youths you were asking about, you will soon know. For those who are entering now are the precursors and lovers of a certain youth who is judged the most noble and beautiful of all in this time. It seems he himself is just about to enter." "Who is he," I asked, "and whose son?" "Perhaps you know him too," he said. "But when you left, he had not yet grown up. Did you know Charmides, the son of our uncle Glaucon, my cousin?" "I knew him indeed," I said, "and even then as a boy he was not to be overlooked. But now I suppose he is already a young man." "You will immediately understand," he said, "how great and of what sort he has turned out to be."

While he was saying this, Charmides entered. As for me, my friend, I am of no account in these matters; for I am toward those distinguished by a noble nature just like a white leveling line on a white stone [[margin: Proverb.]]. For almost all men of that age seem beautiful to me. But especially then, he appeared marvelous both for the height of his body and his outstanding natural character. All the others seemed captured by love for him, to such an extent were they stunned and disturbed by his entrance. Many lovers, moreover, followed after him. Regarding the men, it was no wonder; but I also noticed the boys, none of whom—even the smallest—looked at anyone else, but all gazed at him alone as if at a certain statue. 

Then Chaerepho, turning to me, said, "How does the youth seem to you, Socrates? Is he not of a beautiful countenance?" "Wondrously so," I said. "And yet," he said, "if he were willing to strip, you would say his face is deformed compared to that beauty which lies hidden within." All the others agreed with Chaerepho. "By Hercules," I said, "you describe an insuperable man, if only one little thing more is present in him." "What is that?" asked Critias. "If," I said, "he were beautiful by nature in the best habit of the soul—which it is fitting for one born from your stock to be, Critias." "Indeed," he replied, "as far as genius is concerned, he is both most beautiful and best." "Why then," I asked, "do we not strip the soul first, and contemplate the interior form instead? For since he is now of such an age, I think he will be happy to discourse." "Certainly," said Critias. "For he is a student of wisdom, and as it seems to himself and others, he is quite poetic." "My friend Critias," I said, "you draw this nobility from a long line of the family of Solon (the Athenian lawgiver). But why do you not show me the youth now, summoning him here? For it is not unseemly, even if he were younger, to discourse with him, since you, his cousin and guardian, are present." "Well said," he replied. "He must be called now."

And having said this, turning to the one following behind him, he said, "Call Charmides. But hey, tell him that I wish to commit him to a certain physician on account of the illness he recently complained of." Critias then said to me, "Recently, when Charmides rose in the morning, he complained of a headache. What prevents you, then, from pretending you have a remedy against the heaviness of the head?" "Nothing prevents it," I said, "provided he comes." And so it happened: for he came, and he provoked a great laugh in everyone. For each of us sitting together, wishing to yield a place for Charmides to sit, intentionally pushed his neighbor. The result was that of those sitting at either end, we forced one to stand up and the other we knocked flat onto the ground.

He came and sat between me and Critias. Then I, my friend, was already stuck; and the confidence I had just a moment ago—that I would easily dispute with him—deserted me. But after Critias said that I was the one who knew the medicine, he looked at me with his eyes as if at some marvel, and he approached us as if to ask a question. Everyone in the palaestra immediately flocked to us and surrounded us in a circle. Then indeed, O noble one, when I saw what lay hidden under his cloak, I was all on fire, and I was no longer master of myself. I judged Critias to be most wise in matters of love, who, speaking of a beautiful boy but using the likeness of another thing, warned me again and again to watch out, lest a fawn coming into the sight of a lion should have a piece of flesh snatched away. Indeed, I seemed to myself to have been captured by that bait. But when he himself asked whether I knew the cure for a head, I finally and with difficulty replied that I did. "What sort of thing is it?" he asked. "A certain leaf," I said. "But an incantation (*incantatio*) must be added to it. If someone applies the incantation and uses the leaf, health is restored. Without the incantation, the leaf confers nothing." To this he replied, "I will indeed write down this incantation at your dictation." "Whether you have persuaded me," I asked, "or even if you have not?" He smiled and said, "If I have persuaded you, Socrates." "Aha," I said, "you clearly even know my name." "I do indeed," he said, "unless I am mistaken. For there is frequent talk about you among those of my age. I even remember when I was still a boy, you used to spend time with Critias here." "You are right," I said. "I will show you the manner of the incantation more boldly now. A little while ago I did not know how to show you its power. It is such, O [[margin: Certain precepts of medicine.]] Charmides, that it cannot cure the head alone. Just as you have often heard from skilled physicians, who, whenever someone consults them for pain of the eyes, say they cannot heal the eyes unless the head is healed first, nor...

[[page number: 193]]

# Charmides, Or, On Temperance.

...can the head be cured without the medicine of the whole body. For this reason, they use certain rules that benefit the whole, and they pass from the whole to the part that is to be restored. Have you not heard them speak thus, and that it is so?" "Precisely," he said. "Do they seem to you to speak rightly?" I asked. "And do you approve of this discourse?" "Most of all," he said. Indeed, when I heard him approve of these things, I recovered my confidence, and my spirit was gradually excited and refreshed again. "Such, Charmides," I said, "is the power of this incantation as well.
