I learned it there in the army from one of the Thracian physicians, followers of Zamolxis (the Thracian god-king), who are said even to bestow immortality. That Thracian physician added, moreover, that the Greek physicians also preach the things told above. But Zamolxis, our king and god, hands down this: just as it is not fitting to cure eyes without the head, nor the head without the rest of the body, so neither the body without the soul (*anima*). And that is the reason why many diseases of the body escape Greek physicians: because they are ignorant of the whole itself, which ought to be cured first. If the whole is in a bad state, it is impossible for any part to be well. For all things, whether good or evil, flow from the soul into the body and the whole man, and from there they flow out just as from the head into the eyes. He orders that the soul, therefore, be cured first and most of all, if the head and the entire body are to be well.

He teaches, O blessed one, that the remedies for the soul are certain incantations. He says these are contained in noble reasonings, by which temperance (*temperantia*) is granted to the soul. Once temperance is inserted and present, it is easy to provide health to the head and the whole body. Therefore, when he taught the medicine and the incantations, he ordered that I should not be moved by any prayers to apply the remedy against headache to anyone unless they had first committed their soul to be purged by those very incantations. He said that this is surely the error of our times: that most people strive to be physicians without a study of temperance and health. Thus he warned me in a marvelous way, and commanded me to take care lest any rich or noble or beautiful person should ever persuade me to do otherwise. I bound myself to him with an oath; therefore, I must obey, and I will obey. If you wish, according to the stranger’s precepts, to subject your soul first to all the incantations of that Thracian, I will apply the remedy to your head. If not, I will not be able to help you, my friend Charmides."

When Critias heard this, he said, "This heaviness of the head will be a gain for the youth if he is forced to become better in mind and soul because of it. But let me assure you that this Charmides excels all his peers not only in appearance, but also stands out in that very thing for which you said you had an incantation. Did you not speak of temperance above?" "Of that very thing," I said. "Know then," he said, "that of all the youths of his age, this one seems the most temperate, and in all other things, according to the growth of his age, he is inferior to none." "It is fitting, Charmides," I said, "that in these things Critias has said, you should excel the others. For no one can easily report, I think, a marriage of two families among the Athenians from which it would be more likely for a beautiful and noble offspring to be born than from the marriage of your ancestors. For the paternal line of this Critias and Dropides has been illustrated by Anacreon, Solon, and many other poets, as excelling in beauty, virtue, and other happiness. The glory of your maternal line is the same. No one seemed more beautiful or greater among all who inhabit the continent than your uncle Pyrilampes, whenever he approached the Great King or another inhabitant of the continent as an ambassador. In short, this entire house is inferior to no other in any respect. Therefore, it is probable that you, created from such stock, would hold the first parts in all things. 

As far as that beauty which is perceived by the eyes is concerned, O sweet son of Glaucon, you seem to me to have degenerated not at one bit from your superiors. If you are also naturally inclined toward temperance and other virtues, as Critias here testifies, then your mother bore you a blessed man, dear Charmides. So the matter stands: if temperance is in you, as Critias says, and you are sufficiently temperate, you need neither the incantations of Zamolxis nor of Abaris the Hyperborean [[notes: A legendary sage and healer]], but the medicine of the head should be applied to you now. But if temperance is lacking in you, the incantation must precede the medicine. Respond, therefore, to me yourself: do you agree with Critias and assert that you have enough temperance, or do you recognize that something is lacking?"

Then Charmides' cheeks, suffused with a blush, showed a more graceful appearance. [[margin: Modesty becomes a youth.]] For shame (*pudor*) becomes that age. Then he responded quite nobly: "It is by no means easy to either admit or deny the things that have been asked at present. For if I deny that I am temperate, it will first seem base because I would be disparaging myself; and second, I would be proving false the opinion of Critias and many others to whom I seem temperate. But if I affirm it, this boasting about myself will be hateful. Therefore, I do not know where to turn." "You seem to speak well, Charmides," I said. "And so I think we should investigate together whether you possess what I seek, or not; lest you be forced to speak otherwise than you wish, or I hasten to heal rashly. If, then, it will be pleasing to you, I desire to investigate with you. If not, I think we should let it be." "On the contrary," he said, "it is most pleasing of all. Therefore, search it out as you think best."

"In this way," I said, "the investigation seems likely to be more convenient. It is certainly established that if temperance is in you, you have some opinion about what it is. For it is necessary that, if it is inherent in you, it should offer some sense of itself, from which some opinion about it might arise, by which you might guess what and of what sort temperance is. Don't you think so?" "I think so indeed." "Don't you believe this: namely, that since you know how to speak Greek, you could certainly say what that thing seems to you to be?" "Perhaps," he said. "In order, then, to guess whether temperance is in you or not, come, tell me: what do you say temperance is, in your opinion?"

He was hesitant at first and did not come willingly to respond. Finally, he replied thus: "Temperance consists of two things: doing each thing decorously, and walking along the way quietly and calmly, speaking quietly, and doing all things quietly; and to embrace what you seek briefly, it seems to me to be a certain quietness (*quietudo*) and sedation (*sedatio*)." "Well," I said. "They certainly say that quiet and placid men are temperate. But let us see if you speak the truth. Tell me, then, is temperance something beautiful?" "It is, absolutely," he said. "In the skill of a grammarian, is it more beautiful to write the same letters quickly or slowly?" "Quickly." "And to read: quickly or slowly?" "Quickly." "Furthermore, is it more beautiful to strike the lyre quickly, and to compete promptly," I asked, "than quietly and slowly?" "It is," he said. "What about in games of fists and arms? Is not speed itself praised?" "Certainly." "And running and jumping, and other acts of the body—if they are done hurriedly and promptly, do they not look toward the beautiful? And if slowly, with difficulty, placidly and calmly, toward the base?" "It appears so," he said. "It is clear, then, as far as the body is concerned, that not what is slow and calm, but what is swiftest and fast, is most beautiful. Is it not?" I asked. "Entirely so," he said. "And it was agreed that temperance is something beautiful?" "It was." "Therefore, regarding the body, not quietness...

[[page number: 194]]

# Book Twenty.

...but rather speed will pertain to temperance, provided that temperance is something beautiful." "It seems so," he said. "And is not teachability (*docilitas*) more beautiful than dullness?" "Certainly more beautiful." "But teachability," I said, "is to learn quickly, and dullness is to learn late and slowly." "Indeed," he said. "Is not teaching another as quickly as possible more beautiful than doing so hesitantly and slowly?" "Without a doubt." "Likewise, to recall and remember late and slowly—is that more beautiful, or easily and promptly?" "Promptly," he said. "And is not cleverness (*solertia*) a certain speed of the soul," I asked, "rather than slowness?" "It is," he said. "And yet to understand what grammarians and lyre-players say in their games, and in all other things, not as slowly as possible, but as quickly as possible, is most beautiful." "This too," he said. "Furthermore, in investigations and consultations of the soul, is it not the man who gives counsel and thinks things out quietly and with difficulty who is to be praised, I think, but rather the one who does so briefly and most easily?" "These things are true," he said. "From this it is concluded, Charmides," I said, "that both in things pertaining to the body and those pertaining to the soul, fast and prompt things seem more beautiful than slow and quiet ones." "So it appears," he said. "Therefore, quietness will not be temperance," I said, "nor is a quiet life temperate, as is guessed by this reasoning, since what is temperate must also be beautiful. For it is one of two things: either never, or only very rarely, have quiet actions appeared more beautiful to us in life than fast and vehement ones. But if, my friend, quiet actions were found to excel fast and vehement ones in beauty no less frequently, even by this reasoning it would not follow that temperance is to act quietly rather than vehemently and quickly, neither in walking, nor in speech, nor in anything else. Nor would a quiet life be more decorous and temperate than an unquiet one; since in the previous discourse it was supposed that temperance is something beautiful, and beautiful things have been established to be no less fast than quiet." "You seem to me to have spoken rightly, Socrates," he said.

"Therefore, Charmides," I said, "look at yourself more attentively again, and think what sort of person the presence of temperance makes you, and what sort of thing temperance itself is while it makes you such. Observing all these things, answer well and manfully what it seems to you to be." He immediately collected himself and, having contemplated more diligently, said: "It seems to me that temperance induces a certain modest blush (*verecundum ruborem*), and makes a man modest; and I think that temperance is modesty (*pudor*)." "What are you saying?" I asked. "Did you not say a little while ago that temperance is something beautiful?" "I did indeed," he said. "Are not good men themselves temperate?" I asked. "They are," he said. "Do you think that is good which does not make men good?" "By no means," he said. "Therefore," I said, "it is not only beautiful, but also good." "So it seems to me," he said. "Do you not believe," I asked, "that Homer speaks rightly when he says, 'shame is not good for a needy man'?" [[notes: Odyssey 17.347]] "I believe it indeed," he said. "Therefore, as it appears," I said, "shame is both not good and good." "It appears so," he said. "But temperance is only good, since it makes those in whom it is present good, and never bad." "It seems to me to be as you say," he said. "Therefore, temperance will not be modesty, since temperance is only good, while modesty is no more good than evil." "This seems to me to be said rightly, Socrates," he said. 

"But pay attention, I pray, to what I bring forward next. For I just remembered what was handed down to me by someone saying that temperance is for each person to 'do his own business' (*sua agere*). Consider whether he who says this seems to you to speak rightly." "O you rogue," I said, "did you hear that from Critias here, or from some other wise man?" "It seems indeed," said Critias, "from another; for he never heard it from me." "What does it matter," said Charmides, "Socrates, from whom I heard it?" "Nothing at all," I said, "for we should not consider who said it, but whether it is said truly or not." "Now you speak well," he said. "Rightly, by Jove," I said. "Yet I will wonder if we find out how this is, for it is very much like a certain riddle (*aenigma*)." "Why?" he asked. "Because I do not think that man meant it as the words sound," I said, "namely, that temperance is for each person to do his own business. Do you think a grammarian does nothing when he writes or reads?" "I think he does something," he said. "Does a grammarian seem to you to write and read his own name only? Or also to instruct you boys? For you were writing the names of enemies no less than your own and your friends'." "Certainly no less," he said. "And when you were doing this," I asked, "were you more meddlesome than is fitting, and departing from the law of temperance?" "Not at all," he said. "But you were not doing only your own things, if writing and reading is doing something." "It is indeed," he said. "Furthermore, my friend, to heal, to build, to weave, and to complete the work of any art—is that doing something, or nothing?" "Something, certainly," he said. "Would that city seem to you to be well-ordered," I asked, "in which the laws ordered that each person should weave his own garment, and wash it, and make his own shoes, and his own strigil [[notes: a scraper for cleaning the skin]] and oil flasks or ointment jars, and all furniture? That he should never touch someone else's things, but perform and finish his own himself?" "By no means," he said. "But yet if a city is temperately disposed, it is well-ordered," I said. "Why not?" he said. "Therefore, temperance will not be to do such things, and in this way to do one's own business?" "No, as it appears," he said. 

"Therefore, he who declared that 'doing one's own business' is temperance was speaking in riddles," I said, "as I said above. For he is not to be thought so foolish that his meaning was the same as the sound of the words. Did some foolish person, Charmides, hand this down to you?" "By no means," he said, "not at all. Rather, he was in my judgment most wise." "Entirely so, then; he wrapped his meaning in obscure words," I said, "so that it would be hard to know what it is to 'do one's own business'." "Perhaps," he said. "Can you open for us what 'doing one's own' is?" I asked. "I don't know," he said. "Perhaps even he who said this did not fully understand what he meant."

While he was speaking thus, Charmides smiled and looked at Critias. But Critias, although he had previously been spurred by a desire for glory to dispute against Charmides and others, had held himself back until now; but he could no longer contain himself. And it seemed to me that what I had suspected was true: namely, that Charmides had received that previous opinion about temperance from Critias. Therefore, Charmides, not wanting to defend the response himself and desiring to throw this labor onto Critias, showed him as if he had been refuted. Critias did not tolerate this at all; indeed, he seemed to be no less indignant toward him than a poet toward an actor ineptly reciting his poems. And so, looking at him, he said: "Do you think, Charmides, that if you by no means understand what his meaning was who asserted that 'doing one's own' is temperance, that he himself did not understand it either?" 

"O best of men, Critias," I said, "it is no wonder this young lad does not understand. But it is fitting for you to know these things, both because of your age and your study. If, therefore, you yourself also affirm that temperance is what he said, and you take up this discourse, I will more willingly investigate with you whether it is true or not." "I do indeed affirm and take it up," he said. "You do well," I said. "But tell me, I pray: ...

[[page number: 195]]

# Charmides, Or, On Temperance.

...do you admit what I was asking just now? Namely, that all artisans do something?" "I do," he said. "Do they seem to you to do only their own business, or also that of others?" "That of others too," he said. "Do they act temperately, then, who do not do only their own things?" I asked. "What prevents it?" he said. "As far as I am concerned," I said, "nothing. But see if anything prevents it for him who, having supposed that temperance is to do one's own business, then nevertheless says that nothing stands in the way of those who do the business of others being temperate." "I did indeed concede," he said, "that those who do the business of others are temperate; but did I concede that those who 'make' do so?" [[notes: Critias makes a distinction here between *facere* (making/producing) and *agere* (doing/acting).]]

"Tell me, Critias," I said, "do you not call acting and making the same thing?" "Certainly not," he said, "nor 'operating' and 'making'. For I learned that from Hesiod, who said, 'No work is a disgrace.' Do you think he would have said that no work is a disgrace to anyone—whether cutting leather, or selling seasonings and food as an innkeeper, or sitting in a shop—if he had named such works 'operating' and 'acting' as you were describing above? One must not think so, Socrates. On the contrary, he, in my judgment, considered 'effecting' (*effectio*) to be something different from 'acting' (*actio*) and 'operation' (*operatio*). He thought that effecting is sometimes a reproach, when we do something besides what is noble; but that no 'work' (*opus*) is ever a disgrace to us. For those things which are done nobly and usefully, he called 'works', and 'operations' and 'actions' are effects of this kind. One should further think that he considered only these things to be 'one's own'; but all harmful things to be entirely 'alien'. Therefore, one ought to believe that both Hesiod and every other man of sane mind calls a man temperate who thus does his own business."

"When you first began to speak, Critias," I said, "I perceived that you call each person's own business 'good things', and you call the effects of good things 'actions'. For I have very often heard Prodicus [[notes: a famous Sophist known for linguistic precision]] distinguishing names in this way. I certainly allow you to use names as you please, provided you declare what you wish to signify by each name. Now, therefore, define again more clearly from the beginning: do you say that temperance is the action or effecting of good things, or however else you wish to name it?" "This very thing," he said. "Therefore, he who does evil things does not act temperately," I said, "but rather he who does good things. But does it seem so to you, my good man?" he asked. "Let that be for the moment," I said. "We are not yet considering what seems to me, but what you are saying now." "Indeed," he said, "I would never say that he acts temperately who acts not well but evilly. For I clearly define temperance as the action of good things itself."

"Perhaps there is nothing preventing you from speaking the truth," I said. "However, I wonder at this: if you think men acting temperately are ignorant that they are acting temperately." "I do not think so at all," he said. "Was it not said by you a little while ago," I asked, "that nothing prevents artisans, even when they do things for others, from living temperately?" "It was indeed said," he replied, "but what of it?" "Nothing else," I said. "But say whether any physician seems to you, while he makes someone healthy, to effect things useful to himself and to the one he cures?" "He does to me," he said. "Does he not act decorously," I asked, "whoever acts thus?" "Certainly," he said. "And he who acts decorously," I asked, "does he not also act temperately?" "And temperately," he said. "Must a physician understand when he cures usefully and when not? And must every artisan understand when the work he effects is going to be profitable for him, and when not profitable?" "Perhaps not," he said. "Sometimes, therefore," I said, "when a physician has operated usefully or otherwise, he does not know himself as he has operated, even if he has operated usefully; yet you were saying he acts temperately. Was that not so?" "Indeed," he said. "Therefore," I said, "as it appears, sometimes he who has operated usefully acts indeed temperately, and is temperate, but he himself is ignorant that he acts temperately, and yet is temperate?" 

"That cannot happen, Socrates," he said. "But if anything was said in the previous points from which this necessarily follows, I would rather retract that than be forced to admit I spoke incorrectly elsewhere, or to agree that he who is ignorant of himself is temperate. For I almost think this very thing is temperance: to know oneself (*seipsum cognoscere*). And I agree with him who inscribed that precept in the temple of Apollo itself. Yet that inscription seems to be a certain salutation of the God to men who enter the temple, in place of that which bids one 'rejoice'; as if it were not properly said, 'rejoice', nor were it fitting to command this to one another, but rather to live temperately. Thus the God addresses men entering the temple with a singular sentiment, and salutes us differently than men do—as he felt, in my judgment, who inscribed it. And he prescribes nothing to the one entering other than to live temperately. But he inserted this precept in obscure words, like a prophet. For 'Know thyself' is the same as 'Live temperately', as the letters testify and I interpret. Perhaps someone else will think it is something else; which I think happened to those who added the following: 'Nothing in excess' and 'Misery is the companion of a pledge'. For they thought 'Know thyself' was a piece of advice, not the God's own admonition to those entering. Then, so that they might also hang up no worse advice themselves, they added the rest besides. Therefore, Socrates, all these things have been said by me because I will concede all the previous points to you without controversy. For perhaps you said something more correctly about them, or perhaps I did; but nothing from what we have said is manifest. Next, however, I want to give you the reason for this, if you will not concede that temperance is to know oneself."

"You deal with me, Critias," I said, "as if I affirmed that I knew the things I ask, and as if I would concede to you if I wished; but it is not so. For I always seek with you concerning that which is brought into the middle, precisely because I am ignorant of it. I will see, further, whether I should concede it or not. Just stay while I consider those things." "Consider," he said. "Behold, I am considering," I said. "If temperance is to know something, it is established that it is a certain science (*scientia*) and of something. Is it not?" "It is indeed," he said, "namely, of oneself." "Is not medicine the science of the healthy?" "Precisely," he said. "If therefore you were to ask: since medicine is the science of the healthy, what does it confer on us? or what does it effect? I would certainly answer that it profits us as much as possible, and further, health is a beautiful work it perfects for us. Do you accept this?" "I accept it," he said. "And if you were to ask again, since architecture is the science of building, what work it constructs, I would answer 'houses'; and I would give a response for the other arts by the same reasoning. Since, therefore, you say temperance is the science of itself, it is your concern to answer if someone should inquire in this way: 'O Critia, since temperance is the science of itself, what beautiful and name-worthy work does it effect for us?' Tell me, I pray." 

"You do not ask rightly, Socrates," he said. "For this is not similar to other sciences, nor are the others similar to each other; but you ask as if they were similar. For tell me, I pray: what is such a work of the science of computation or geometry as a house is of architecture, or a garment of the weaving art, and many other things of that kind which one can attribute to many arts? Can you show me any such work of these?" "You speak truly," I said. "However, I can show you this: of what thing each of these sciences is a science, which is something other than the science itself. Just as the skill of computing is the science of the even and odd multitude, and how they relate to themselves and each other. Is it not?" "Certainly," he said. "Is not the even and odd something other than the science of computing itself?" "It is," he said. "Furthermore, the faculty of weighing is the balancing of heavier and lighter weight. But the heavy itself and the light are something else than the art of weighing itself. Do you agree?" "I agree," he said. "Say then: of what especially is temperance the science, such that it is something other than temperance itself?" 

"This is precisely," he said, "what you are asking now, the very thing by which temperance differs from all other sciences. But you demand some similarity of this to others. But the matter stands otherwise. For all the others are of some other science, but by no means of themselves. This alone is the science both of other sciences and of itself." "You are far from being ignorant of this," I said, "if I think you are doing what you were denying a moment ago: for you are trying to refute me, and you pass over that which is the subject of the discourse." "What are you doing?" I asked. "Do you think that if I refute you, I do it for any other reason than that for which I would examine myself—fearing lest, while I think I know what I do not know, my own ignorance should deceive me? And now I assert that I am doing this most of all: namely, weighing and examining the discourse for my own sake first, and perhaps also for the sake of my friends. Do you not think this is a common good for all men, that the condition of each thing should become known to all?" "Most of all, Socrates." "Boldly then, O blessed one," I said, "answering what is asked according to your opinion, do not care whether it is Critias or Socrates who is being refuted, but pay attention to the discourse itself, to see where it ends when refuted." "I will do so," he said, "for you seem to speak well." 

"Concerning temperance, then," I said, "repeat what you say." "I say indeed," he said, "that of all other sciences, this alone is the science of both itself and the remaining sciences." "Is it not also the science of ignorance (*inscientia*)," I asked, "since it is the science of science?" "Entirely." "Only the temperate man, therefore," I said, "will know himself, and will be able to examine what he knows and what he is ignorant of. He will be able, moreover, to judge of other men what each one knows and thinks he knows (if indeed he knows it), and what he is ignorant of and thinks he knows. But no one else will be able to do this. And this is to be temperate, and temperance, and to know oneself: namely, to understand what one knows and what one does not [[margin: Proverb.]] know. Are these the things you say?" "They are," he said. "Thirdly, then," I said, "as they say, let us consider it as if from the beginning for the Savior. First, whether this is possible or not, that what each person knows and what he does not know, he can also know and know that he does not know. Second, if that can happen, what utility will there be for those who understand it?" "It must be asked," he said. 

"Notice, Critias," I said, "whether you have anything certain in these matters; for I have nothing, and what I doubt, I will open to you if you wish." "I do wish," he said. "These things will follow," I said, "if what you were just saying stands: namely, a certain single science which is the science of nothing other than itself and other sciences; and again the same science of ignorance." "Precisely," he said. "See, my friend," I said, "how absurd this discourse of ours is. For if you were to consider this same thing in any other matters, I think it will seem impossible to you." "In what way?" he asked, "and where?" "Right here," I said. "Think whether it seems to you that there is a certain sight (*visus*) which is not the sight of those things which other visions see, but the sight of itself and other visions, and likewise of non-vision; and it sees no color although it is vision, but only inspects itself and other visions. Does any such vision seem to you to exist?" "None," he said. "Can you trust that any power of hearing is found," I asked, "which hears no voice, but perceives itself and other hearings and non-hearings?" "That is not possible either," he said. "In short, consider all the senses and whether any sense can be found which perceives itself and the other senses, yet feels none of those things which the other senses feel." "I think this is impossible too," he said. "Is there perhaps any desire (*cupiditas*) which affects no pleasure, but is a desire for itself and other lusts?" "By no means," he said. "Nor a will (*voluntas*), I suppose," I said, "which desires no good, but seeks itself and other wills." "Not at all," he said. "Will you also say that some love is such that it is the love of no beauty, but is the ardor for itself and other loves?" "I will not." "Have you ever thought of any fear which dreads itself and other fears, but is not terrified by anything terrible or dangerous?" "Never at all," he said. "Furthermore, an opinion such that it is the opinion of other opinions and of itself, but opines none of those things which other opinions suspect?" "In no way." 

"Nevertheless, we said there is a certain science of this kind, which is the science of no doctrine, but the science of itself and other sciences." "We did indeed say so," he said. "Is it not a wondrous thing, if it exists?" I asked. "Let us not yet contend that it does not exist, but let us consider whether it does." "You speak wisely," he said. "Say then, is this science of some science? And does it have a certain power of this kind, that it is of something?" "Precisely," he said. "Likewise, do we say it has a greater power, by which it is greater than something?" "It surely does," he said. "Is it not greater than some lesser thing, if it is greater?" "It is necessary," he said. "If we find something greater, which exists as greater than other greater things and itself, but yet was not greater than any of those things than which other things are greater, would it not entirely follow that just as it is greater than itself, so it is also less?" "It is absolutely necessary, Socrates." 

"Furthermore, if something is double toward other doubles and toward itself," I said, "certainly toward itself it will be the half of the double, and toward other halves it will be double. For whatever is double is the double of nothing other than the half." "That is true," he said. "Furthermore, that which is more than itself, is it not also fewer? and that which is heavier, also lighter? or that which is older, also younger? and in all other things in the same way, whatever has the power of itself toward itself, will it not also have that essence toward which its power is? I mean something like this. We say hearing is the hearing of nothing else but the voice?" "Precisely," he said. "If it hears itself," I said, "will it not hear itself having a voice? For it could not hear otherwise." "It necessarily follows," he said. "Vision also, O best of men," I said, "if it sees itself, it will be necessary for it to have some color. For without color, vision can discern nothing." "It can discern nothing," he said. 

"You see, Critias," I said, "that the things we have recounted seem partly impossible to us, and partly it is to be strongly doubted whether they have their power toward themselves. For that every magnitude and multitude and other things of this kind should have their power toward themselves is entirely impossible, is it not?" "It is entirely so," he said. "But that vision and hearing perceive themselves, that motion moves itself, and heat heats itself, and other such things—some do not believe it, and perhaps it seems to be believed by some. A great man is needed, my friend, who can sufficiently distinguish through all things whether nothing at all can have its power toward itself except science, but only toward another; or whether some can and others cannot; and if there are some that have power toward themselves, whether this science which we call temperance is among their number. As for me, I by no means trust that I am sufficient to discern these things. Wherefore I cannot even assert whether it is possible that science is of science. Even if that were granted, I would not yet agree that temperance is of this kind until I have investigated whether such a temperance being thus would profit us at all, or not profit us. For I prophesy that temperance is something useful and good. You then, son of Callaeschrus, since you posit temperance as science in science and of science, show first that this is possible which you were saying above; and then, besides its being possible, that it is also beneficial; and so you will perhaps satisfy me concerning the definition of temperance itself."

Critias, having heard these things and seeing me doubting—like those who, seeing others yawning, yawn themselves—seemed to be forced by my hesitation to hesitate similarly. But being a man who loves glory, he was afraid of those present, and did not want to confess to me that he was not sufficient to discern the things I had offered. He brought forth nothing clearly, and hid his hesitation. But I, so that our dispute might proceed, said: "If it seems good to you, Critias, we will grant for now that there can be a science of science. Whether it is possible or not, we will investigate at another time. However, even if it were possible to the highest degree, what more is it possible to know than what someone knows and what he does not know? We said that this indeed is to know oneself and to be temperate. Is it not?" 

"Most of all," he said, "and it follows in a way, Socrates. For if someone has that science which knows itself, such would he himself be as that which he has: just as when someone has speed, he is fast; and when beauty, beautiful; and when knowledge, knowing. Wherefore when someone has the knowledge itself of himself, he is then made knowing of himself." "I do not doubt that at all," I said, "that if someone has something in himself knowing itself, he himself would also know himself. But what necessity forces a man thus affected to know what he knows or what he does not know?" "This one: that this and that are the same." "Perhaps it is so," I said, "but I always seem to be similar to myself, and I do not in turn understand how it is the same to know what one knows and to know what one does not know." "How can you say that?" he asked. "In this way," I said: "since science itself is science, can it discern anything further than that of these things, this one indeed is science, and that one is ignorance?" "Not further, but to that extent," he said. "Is it then the same," I said, "to have the science and ignorance of the healthy, and likewise the science and ignorance of the just?" "In no way," he said. 

"But this indeed is the skill of medicine, and that is civil skill; but if someone should know not the healthy and the just, but only science—having, as it were, the science of this alone—then he will recognize both in himself and in others that indeed he knows, or that he has a certain science. Is it not so?" "But by what reasoning will he understand *what* this science knows? For medicine knows the healthy and the wholesome, not temperance; music knows the harmonic, not temperance; architecture knows the building, not temperance; and similarly all things, is it not so?" "It appears so," he said. "But temperance," I said, "if it is only the science of sciences, how will it understand what medicine knows as healthy and wholesome, or what architecture knows as a building?" "In no way," he said. "Therefore he will not understand *what* he knows, being ignorant of this, but only *that* he knows." "It seems so," he said. 

"Therefore to be temperate will not be this, nor will it be temperance to understand what one knows or what one does not know, but—as it seems—only *that* one knows and *that* one does not know." "It appears so," he said. "Nor will he be able even here to examine another's science who professes some knowledge, to see whether he knows what he promises or does not know. Rather, he will only recognize, as it seems," I said, "that he has a certain science; but of what thing it is the science, temperance will not show." "It does not seem so," he said. "Therefore he will not discern a feigned physician from a true one, nor anyone else knowing from one not knowing. But let us consider it this way: if a temperate man, or anyone else, is to judge between a true and a false physician, will he not do it thus? Concerning the art of healing, he will not differ from him at all. For the physician understands nothing else, as we were saying, than the healthy and the sick, and the wholesome and the harmful. Is it not so?" "Precisely so," he said. "Furthermore, concerning science he knows nothing," I said, "for we will attribute this to temperance alone." "So it is," he said. "Neither, therefore, does the physician know anything about medicine," I said, "since medicine is a certain science." "You speak the truth," he said. "The temperate man will recognize that he indeed has some science, but someone else will consider the physician's skill, what it is and of what things. Which is then clear when it is known of what things it is the science. Is not every science determined, not by this alone—that it is a science—but by *which* science it is, and what science it is, which is recognized when those things of which it is the science are recognized?" "Precisely so," he said. "The science of medicine," I said, "is distinguished from other sciences by the fact that it is the skill of the wholesome and unwholesome?" "Indeed," he said. "Must he not consider these things," I asked, "whoever comes to consider medicine—namely, those things in which medicine itself is engaged? For it seems it should not be sought in extraneous things in which it is not present." "Certainly not," he said. "In the wholesome and their opposites, therefore, he will consider the physician insofar as he is a physician, whoever examines him rightly." "It seems so," he said. "Will he not notice in these things—whether said or done—which things are truly said and which are rightly done?" "It is necessary." "Can anyone follow these things without a skill in medicine?" "No one," he said. "Nor anyone else, as it seems, besides the physician; therefore not even the temperate man. For besides being temperate, he would also have to be a physician." "These things are true." 

"Entirely then, temperance, if it is the science of science and ignorance, will be able to discern neither the physician skilled in healing—and likewise the one feigning a skill in medicine or thinking he has it—nor anyone else among those who know something, except for a man of the same profession, just as other artisans do." "So it appears." "What further utility, Critias, is going to come to us from temperance when it is such?" I asked. "For if, as we supposed in the beginning, the temperate man knew what he knows and what he does not know—the former because he knows it, and the latter because he is ignorant of it—and could judge another thus affected, we would report a huge profit from being endowed with temperance: for we would lead a life without sin, both we ourselves who share in temperance and all others who were ruled by our command. For we would not undertake to do the things we are ignorant of, but having sought out knowing men, we would certainly yield to them. Nor would we concede to others subject to our governance to do anything else than what they would do rightly having undertaken it...

[[page number: 199]]

# Charmides, Or, On Temperance.

...that is, they would be artisans of nothing? In no way does it seem so, Socrates." "Do you see, Critias, that I was not wrong to fear above, and to blame myself, because I did not perceive anything great and useful about temperance? For what is conceded by all to be the most beautiful of things would never have appeared useless to us if I myself were useful for inquiring rightly. But now we succumb everywhere, and we are unable to find to signify what especially the author of names himself established the name of temperance; although we have conceded many things that are entirely abhorrent to reason. Furthermore, we agreed that it is the science of science, with reason struggling and immediately repelling it. Moreover, we conceded that the works of the remaining sciences are known by this very science, with reason similarly repugnant, so that the temperate man would be such that he would know that he knows what he knows, and would in turn understand that he is ignorant of what he does not know. This indeed we conceded too magnificently and freely, not noticing that it is impossible for someone to know in some way what he in no way knows. In this, however, we agreed: namely, that someone ignorant of something should know by science that he does not know it; even if there is nothing, in my opinion, that seems more absurd than this. 

Nevertheless, this investigation, having found us inept rather than hard and stubborn, can find the truth no more; but it has mocked itself to such an extent that what we have for a long time fashioned by common consent and posited to be temperance, this finally appeared to be something useless, quite insolent and insulting. On your account rather than mine, Charmides, I take it hard if you, endowed with such an excellent appearance and temperance of soul, are not helped by so great a virtue, and it profits you nothing in life itself. I also take it harder for the sake of the incantation which I learned from that Thracian, if I have placed so much study in perceiving a thing of no value. I do not quite believe that these things are so; on the contrary, I think I am a sluggish investigator, since I judge temperance to be a certain great good: which if you have, you are blessed. But think whether you possess it and do not need the incantation. For if you have it, I would advise you to think me delirious and incapable of investigating the truth, but yourself to be more blessed the more temperate you are."

And Charmides said, "I do not know, by Jove, Socrates, whether I have it or not. For how should I understand that, which you—as you say yourself—cannot yet find out what it is? Indeed, I do not believe you much, Socrates. Rather, I think I do need the incantation, and as far as I am concerned, nothing prevents you from healing me with incantations every day until you think I have enough." "So be it," said Critias. "But Charmides, if you do this, it will be an argument to me that you are temperate, because you subject yourself to the incantations of Socrates and never leave his side." "Consider me as one who will obey and follow everywhere," he said. "Indeed, I would sin gravely if I did not obey you, my guardian, and execute what you command." "I do indeed command it," said Critias. "I will do it diligently," he said, "and I will begin today." "What are these men deliberating?" I asked. "Nothing more," said Charmides. "Indeed, it is decreed." "Will you use force?" I asked. "And will you leave no power of consultation to me in turn?" "Think that I will entirely use force," he said, "since he commands it. Consult for yourself also what you are going to do about this." "There remains no place for consultation," I said, "for no one will be able to resist you when you are affecting and forcing something." "Do not resist then," he said. "I will certainly not oppose you," I said.

# LACHES BY PLATO, OR, ON FORTITUDE.

### MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT.

PLATO often places the best magistrates above laws, because laws without them seem entirely useless: for no one will keep them. But the best magistrates are themselves the laws. But he says magistrates cannot be made best unless the citizens are best men; nor will men be such unless the youths and boys are also such. Wherefore in almost all dialogues he exhorts parents first to educate their sons rightly, knowing that the human race cannot either live honestly or be governed happily without the best governors. Furthermore, there will never be good princes in a republic unless they are most approved men, diligently cultivated immediately from a tender age. Since childhood is usually already governed under the providence of those at home, but youth, having found license, wanders everywhere without bridles, our Plato rightly treats very much the correcting and bridling of youths. He complains gravely that that age—which, petulant with softness and wantonness, already joins pride with it, and is therefore placed in the greatest danger—is too little observed by those at home and is unhappily neglected by laws and magistrates. Especially since they stain the youth so much while he is young as he is pursued by the older men everywhere. 

Therefore, in the *Laws* and the *Republic*, he places a magistrate of his own over youth. Who like—if I may speak כך—a bishop or scout should wonder through the whole city every day and night, observing the manners, words, and gestures of each of the youths, and faithfully report each of their deeds and words to the magistrate as to a shepherd and father. Nor was the necessary diligence toward youth the care of Plato alone among all, for in this matter not even Aristotle himself could fail to highly approve of Plato. 

But let us come to the dialogue. Lysimachus and Melesias are thinking about educating their sons, having complained about their own parents—that, treating public affairs too carefully, they neglected domestic ones and their sons. Yet the first care of a republic consists in caring for the youth. And although they are already old men, yet so that they might deliberate more rightly about that matter, they similarly call together Nicias and Laches—also old men who have sons—to consult. And so that nothing should be less provided for, they bring Socrates into the council, not only as a companion but also as a judge—Socrates, I say, who treated nothing else in his whole life than both every age and especially how to rightly care for youth. You indeed will consider meanwhile the wondrous praises of Socrates' life, likewise that they are true praises which proceed from a man worthy of praise. 

But truly, since in some cities the institution of laws inclines more to gentleness than to boldness, and in others on the contrary, Plato, judging both to be dangerous, orders both gentleness to boldness and in turn boldness to gentleness to be mixed together in the *Statesman*. If someone should join *Charmides* to *Laches*, and the exhortation there to temperance and here to fortitude together, he will rightly temper the souls of youths. I pass over that in this present exhortation of the dialogue to fortitude, both Nicias and Laches admire military fortitude more than is fitting; and Nicias, besides the games of arms as if they were very necessary preludes to military service, extols them with praises beyond measure. But Laches corrects him. 

After these things, the opinion is transferred to Socrates. Where you should notice that no consonance delights more than what is made in a wise man from the concord of the soul and the discourse itself. And on the contrary, no dissonance shows more than where the tongue and the mind are dissonant. Then, that a skilled man, even if he speaks beautifully, is not to be heard; nor is it permitted to speak of morals except by one who is moralized. Furthermore, Socrates was always accustomed, about whatever thing was being disputed, to lead the companion of the dispute to give an account of his whole life—as if you would know alien things in vain unless you knew yourself. It is added that it is necessary first of all to subject oneself to someone examining, to whom accounts of a passed life are often given. Which indeed strongly confirms the annual confession instituted by Christians. It is added that one must learn as long as one must live. 

Socrates, however, the most cautious of all, would have the judgment of the book be invincible or transferred to the elders. But meanwhile, entreated by the council, he approaches the matter itself, approving diligence in educating sons and disapproving negligence. He adds that it cannot happen...

[[page number: 200]]

# Book Twenty-One.

...that someone should exhort someone to fortitude unless he knows how to express what fortitude itself is. Soon asked by Laches what fortitude is, he responds more confidently that it is the virtue through which someone, not deserting his rank, defeats the enemy. Which is refuted for this reason, because someone can defeat the enemy in the Scythian manner no less by fleeing than by staying, and be equally brave. And therefore Homer calls him brave who dares to fear and be troubled opportunely. A little later, the victory of fortitude is drawn to any matter whatever, as if it becomes a brave man to overcome not only fears but also pains, lusts, and pleasures. Hence this definition of all fortitude is sought commonly. To this Laches responds that this is a certain endurance (*tolerantia*) of the soul. But since it is defined less sufficiently, Socrates forces him to add that the endurance itself must be noble and beneficial. Such a thing will not be unless it is done prudently. And therefore he compels Laches to say that fortitude is properly a prudent endurance. Since fortitude is something beautiful and good. 

Then it is asked what endurance, and for what prudent—that is, around what matter and what duty. But Laches slips when he is asked generally whether where boldness is greater, there fortitude is greater; and he concedes that, and in turn necessarily admits that boldness is greater in him who, without skill of the thing itself yet knowing the danger, approaches the thing itself, than in him who proceeds instructed by skill. For he acts more cautiously and safely. Laches finally receives that where there is more boldness or less skill and prudence, fortitude is greater. In which concession he both repugns himself and admits a falsehood. For fortitude is something beautiful and beneficial, but boldness is imprudent, base, and harmful. 

Among these things, note the worn sentiment of Socrates and Plato: each one is good at those things at which he is wise; bad at those at which he is ignorant. Indeed, just as all errors—both of the hand in grasping and of the foot in walking—proceed from the defect of seeing itself, so Socrates thinks all the errors of men—both in choosing and in acting—proceed from a defect of intelligence. Where the two eyes of the soul are either blind or blinking, all things fall headlong. After Laches, Nicias defines fortitude as the science of things to be feared and not to be feared—by what reasoning and how far things are to be feared and attacked. He calls fortitude a certain habit constant with prudence around things to be feared and not to be feared. But he calls rash boldness without prudence ferocity. 

Socrates argues against Nicias thus: whatever things there is some science of, there is not one science of past things as they were done, another of present things as they are done, and another of future things as they can best be done; but it is of the same science to understand all these. If therefore fortitude is the science of daring and fearing around goods and evils (namely as they are future), it is surely also the science of those same things as they are present and past—therefore of all things simply. It is therefore universal virtue. But we from the beginning were seeking fortitude as some part of virtue. This objection was made not so much to refute as for the sake of testing Nicias. But Nicias does not know how to defend his definition. 

Socrates, however, among the elders not wanting to act as a teacher on account of modesty, simulates that he similarly is ignorant of the definition; and he exhorts them that they should first seek out teachers of virtues for themselves together before they profess the faculty of educating youth, showing that in every age moral discipline is greatly necessary, and that one must always learn without shame or bashfulness. 

The definitions which he seeks either about fortitude or in *Charmides* about temperance are not finished here or there, where the plan is only to exhort and admonish, but in the *Republic* and the *Laws*. But so that I may speak about fortitude and temperance together as if they were twins: Plato in the *Phaedrus* and *Symposium* compares this life of ours to a certain journey. In which indeed reason, in directing, represents the charioteer; but the affections—partly superior, partly inferior—represent the twin horses, the white and the black. And so that we may distinguish more conveniently as far as pertains to the proposed question: he says divine providence recalls our reason to its courses; it provokes us to noble things. And therefore he says it has ingrained in us modesty and friendship more, so that our charioteer might restrain our affections like horses from base although sweet things with a certain shame as if with a bridle; but should stimulate with the spurs of magnanimity to noble things however arduous. Since a certain evil demon entices with flatteries to base pleasures; but deters from noble things with the bitterness of pain. Wherefore both temperance, using the bridles of shame, effects that we always abstain from base things against pleasure; and fortitude, relying on magnanimity with spurs, takes care that we strive manfully for noble things, having spurned the fear of difficulty and pain. And as much as it is more difficult to overcome pains than to abstain from pleasures, so much perhaps can fortitude seem to someone to be placed before temperance. Finally, temperance indeed makes us not be thrown headlong from man into beasts; but fortitude provides that we are even in a way transferred into God, who overcomes all things. On account of this virtue especially, all antiquity referred Hercules into the number of the gods—Hercules, I say, while as a victor on earth he climbed the celestial steps, shouting thus: 

"Go now, brave ones, where the high way
Of great example leads: why do you, inert,
Barer your backs? The overcome earth
Gives the stars."

## LYSIMACHUS, MELESIAS, NICIAS, LACHES, THE SONS OF NICIAS AND LACHES, SOCRATES.

**Y**ou have watched a man fighting in polished arms, Nicias and Laches. But for what cause Melesias and I ordered you to watch this here together with us, we did not declare then. Now, however, we will open it: for we think we must speak freely with you. For there are some who mock these things; and if someone consults them, they do not express their opinion; but thinking that they hold both the thing about which is consulted and the mind of the one consulting, they bring forth things other than what they feel. But since we think you are sufficient for understanding and will simply explain what you recognize, we have invited you as associates for the deliberation of the things we will report. The matter about which I have begun is of this kind. These are our sons: this one who is the son of this man, called Thucydides by his grandfather's name; and my other son, similarly keeping the name of his grandfather—for we call him Aristides. It seems to us that the most diligent care of these must be undertaken; nor do we think we should do what many are accustomed to do—who, as soon as their sons have grown up, allow them to live according to their own lust—but indeed now we must begin to have care for them, as far as we can do so. 

Since therefore we see that you have sons, we judged that you especially had thought by what reasoning they are to be educated so that they might become best. If you have not noticed it much, we admonish you in the present that you ought not to neglect it, and we exhort you to deliberate together with us about the education of our sons. But for what cause these things seem so to us, O Nicias and Laches, it is fitting to hear, although the things that follow are a little longer. For Melesias and I live together here, and these youths feast with us and are present at our consultation. Whence, as I signified in the beginning of the discourse, we speak freely and boldly with you. Surely each of us can tell these boys many noble deeds of his own father, done in peace and in war, by which they profited either their republic or their allies; but we can report no deeds done by ourselves. Wherefore we are both ashamed of these things, and we often blame our parents' negligence, because after we grew up, they permitted us to live in a certain softness and delights, being meanwhile intent on the affairs of others. And showing these same things to these youths, we declare that if they neglect themselves and despise our precepts, they will be ignoble; but if they have known this in turn by names, they will turn out famous. They indeed respond to us that they will obey. 

But as we were consulting together by what discipline or custom they can most of all become best, someone explained that it is a thing of value that they should learn to fight in arms; and he praised that man whom you just watched competing, and told us to turn our attention to it. It seemed best therefore that we should come to this spectacle, and should call you together both to watch and also, if you wish, to deliberate by common counsel about the education of the youths. These are the things we desired to confer with you about: it is now your concern both concerning this...

[[page number: 201]]

# Laches, Or, On Fortitude.

...thing—whether it is to be learned or not—to consult, as well as about other matters, if you have any discipline or study worthy of praise for a youth; then to say what you are going to do about the counsel. 

NIC. I indeed approve your sentiment, Lysimachus and Melesias, and I am ready to investigate together with you, and I think Laches here is affected similarly. LAC. You think rightly, Nicias: for indeed what Lysimachus was reporting just now about his and Melesias's father seems most aptly said against those who, like us, handle civil affairs; for, as Lysimachus complained, they neglect their sons no less than other domestic matters. In these things, therefore, Lysimachus, you speak well. But that you call us to consult about the institution of the youths but do not invite this Socrates, I wonder: first indeed a fellow citizen, then frequently occupied in that which either has discipline or a liberal study of youth, such as you require. 

LYS. What are you saying, Laches? Has this Socrates ever cared for such things? LAC. Most of all indeed, Lysimachus. NIC. I also can be a witness of this matter no worse than Laches. For recently he led a guest to me for the sake of educating my son—Damon, a disciple of Agathocles, a teacher of music, a refined man indeed beyond others, and skilled not only in music but also in other faculties, for which he is certainly worthy that youths of this kind be committed to his discipline and company. 

LYS. No longer, Socrates, Nicias, and Laches, do Melesias and I and those of my age recognize the younger men, since we mostly keep ourselves at home on account of our age. But if you can advise anything good, son of Sophroniscus, to this fellow citizen of yours, advise him. For it is fitting: for your father is a friend to us. For your father and I were always familiar and friends, and he died before any quarrel arose between us. Also the name of Socrates somehow still rings in my ears, which these boys frequently use while arguing at home and celebrate highly; I had not yet asked them whether they meant Socrates the son of Sophroniscus or another. But O boys, tell me: is this that Socrates whom you are so often accustomed to commemorate? 

BOYS. That is he, father, without a doubt. LYS. It is well indeed, by Juno, Socrates, that you extol and decorate your father, the best of men, and that our things will be yours, and yours ours. LAC. Do not let this man go, Lysimachus: for I noticed him elsewhere also, decorating not only his father but also his fatherland; furthermore, in the flight at Delium itself, he retreated together with me, and I affirm this to you, that if the others had behaved similarly, our city would stand and would not have suffered such a great ruin. 

LYS. This is the best praise, Socrates, which is now granted to you by men worthy of trust, who are themselves to be praised in the same things in which they praise you. Know therefore that I rejoice in your estimation, and think me bound to you with the highest benevolence. It is proper therefore for you to approach us first, and to think us domestic and familiar, as is fitting. Wherefore hereafter, after we have recognized each other, do not do otherwise; indeed embrace us and these younger men with a certain domestic benevolence, so that mutual friendship might be kept between us on both sides. These things you indeed will do, and we hereafter will recall them again to memory. But as for what we began to inquire, what do you say? Do you think it is beneficial to youths this discipline, that they should learn to fight in arms? 

[[margin: Boys ought to learn the discipline of arms.]]

SOC. I will indeed try, Lysimachus, if I can do anything to advise about these things, and to do all the things you ask. But it seems to me fitting that, since I am both younger than these men and more unskillful in these matters myself, I should first hear what they think, and learn; and if I have anything besides their sentiments, I will then open it to you and these men. And why do you not speak first, Nicias? 

NIC. Nothing prevents it, Socrates. It seems to me that this skill profits youths everywhere, and one should not linger in those things to which youths are accustomed to give themselves when they have found leisure; but it is better to acquire that faculty through which a robust habit of the body is acquired. For this exercise is inferior to no other, nor less laborious. Furthermore, such an exercise and equestrian skill especially becomes a free man. For in that contest of which we are athletes, and in those things for which the contest is proposed to us, those alone fight who exercise themselves in such instruments of war. Furthermore, this skill will confer in the battle itself, whenever one must fight in a rank and order with many others. But most of all it will profit then when the ranks are dissolved, and it will be necessary to either pursue a resisting enemy or repel an invading one in flight in a single contest. Surely one who is instructed in this faculty will never succumb to one, and perhaps not even to many; indeed, he will everywhere excel by this. 

Furthermore, this faculty brings a desire for a certain other noble discipline; for whoever has learned to fight in arms will affect the discipline about ordering battle lines, which follows immediately. Having obtained this, and being inflamed with a desire for glory about these things, he will take himself to the command of armies, and in short to all the noble institutions and studies around these things and worthy of knowledge and use, he will turn himself, with that first one leading him. We will also add something not to be despised: that this faculty would render each person more daring and stronger in battle in a wondrous way. Nor is that to be kept silent—although it may seem lighter—that you will make a more fit and more able man there, where it is most fitting to be seen as fit and prompt. There certainly he will appear more terrible to the enemies on account of his dexterity and ability itself. It seems to me, Lysimachus, that it is a thing of value that youths should perceive these things; and I have explained for what cause I think so. However, I will gladly hear if Laches wants to bring anything besides these. 

[[margin: The discipline of arms is depressed by reasonings.]]

LAC. Surely a discourse would be thought absurd, Nicias, if someone said some discipline is by no means to be acquired. For it seems better to know all things. Indeed, this faculty about arms, if it is a discipline as those say who teach it, and further such as Nicias predicts, it is to be learned. But if it is not a discipline, but they deceive us who promise this—or if it is a discipline indeed, but of not much value—why is it necessary to learn this? That I say these things happens because, as I think, if this were of any value, it would never have escaped the Lacedaemonians (Spartans), whose only care in all of life is to thus prepare themselves in all things so that they might excel all others in war. If by chance this escapes them, it would not have escaped the masters of this thing—that the Spartans study arms most of all, and that he who is in value because of his art would easily pile up money both among them and among others, just as a poet of tragedies is honored among us. For he who trusts in his tragedies does not wander outside Attica, showing them through other cities, but immediately arrives here and shows his things to these men, not without reason. But those who are engaged in the exercise of arms, I see, think Lacedaemon (Sparta) as if it were some inaccessible temple, and do not even dare to ascend with the top of their foot. Indeed, they wander around and boast themselves rather among others, especially among those who themselves would confess themselves inferior to many others in military matters. 

[[page number: 202]]

# Book Twenty-One.

...they confessed. Furthermore, Lysimachus, I have been present with not a few men of this kind while they were fighting, and I know what they are like. Although it is permitted to everyone to guess the matter by himself. For as if by deliberate effort, no one of those who brooded over these games ever turned out illustrious in war, whereas in all other arts those who exercise themselves frequently turn out clear and celebrated; only these alone, more than others, appear incapable of their vow. You have watched that man making a show of himself [[margin: Stesilaus the gladiator.]] and promising marvelous things; I have inspected him elsewhere when he was demonstrating himself more certainly, albeit unwillingly, to the spectators. For on the ship on which he was being carried, while it was attacking a certain transport ship, he was fighting with a hooked scythe, a very great man indeed, and a very great scythe. The other deeds of this man are not worthy of hearing, but this however must not be passed over in silence: what happened from so marvelous a machine of this man who added a scythe to his spear. For while he was fighting, the scythe got tangled in the rigging of the ship. Stesilaus pulled so that he might disentangle it, and he could not. But the ship was passing by; meanwhile he accompanied the ship in its course holding the spear. But when the ship was now passing the other ship, and he, holding the spear, was being pulled along, he finally came to the end of the spear by hand. Therefore a laugh and a noise were raised in the transport ship on account of the figure of Stesilaus's face, and on account of that besides—that someone, having thrown a stone onto the boards near his feet, forced him to let go of the spear. Then indeed those who were carried in the trireme could no longer contain their laughter, as they beheld that hooked scythe hanging from the ship. 

Perhaps these things are of some value, as Nicias asserts, however those things at which I was present were such. Wherefore as I said already from the beginning, if this is a discipline, it profits little; if it is not, but they who profess this pretend it is, the thing does not seem worthy of study. For I think thus: if some timid man follows this faculty, having been made more daring because of it, he will be more clearly a coward than he was. But if some brave man follows it, if he should err even a little, he will undergo great calumnies observed by all. For the profession of this science is an invidious one; wherefore unless he who claims this science for himself excels others in virtue in a wondrous way, he will not be able to avoid being held ridiculous. Such seems to me, Lysimachus, the study of this discipline. But we ought, as I was saying from the beginning, to beseech this Socrates most of all, that he should consult on the proposed question with his own opinion. 

LYS. I do indeed ask, Socrates: for the deliberation of this kind requires the opinion of some judge. For if these men had agreed with each other, there would be less need of a deliberation of this kind; now, however, after Laches and Nicias—as you see—disagree, it is better to hear now to whose opinion you rather would give your vote. 

SOC. What indeed, Lysimachus? Will you follow this, if more of us praise it? LYS. What else should anyone do, Socrates? SOC. Would you also, Melesias, do similarly? MEL. I would, Socrates, deservedly. SOC. Would you then give more trust to one who has science than to us four? MEL. Perhaps. SOC. For one should judge what is to be judged rightly by science, not by multitude. MEL. Without a doubt. SOC. Is it not first to be considered if someone among us is an artisan in that matter about which we are now deliberating? And if someone such is found, is he to be believed, with the opinion of the others set aside? If none, is some other person to be sought out by us? Or do you think you are risking a small matter now—you and Lysimachus—rather than about the most precious of all your possessions? [[margin: As the sons are, so is the government of the house.]] For when sons are instituted well or badly, the entire paternal house will be governed in the same way in which the sons are affected. MEL. You speak the truth. SOC. Therefore we must watch over this thing diligently. MEL. Greatly. 

SOC. By what way therefore would we have considered what I was saying just now, if the purpose was to find which of us is most skilled in fighting? Would we not have examined who both learned and practiced? And who had suitable teachers of this thing? MEL. I think so indeed. SOC. Would I not also first seek out what that thing is of which I would seek the teachers? MEL. What are you saying? SOC. Perhaps you will perceive it more clearly thus: it does not seem to have been established among us from the beginning what that thing is about which we are seeking—who among us excels most in it, and for the sake of this had teachers, and who did not. 

NIC. Were we not seeking, Socrates, whether it is proper for youths to learn to fight in arms, or not? SOC. Entirely so, Nicias. But when someone seeks about a remedy for the eyes whether it should be applied or not, then do you think the consultation is about the remedy or about the eyes? NIC. About the eyes. SOC. And when it is asked whether a bridle is to be applied to a horse or not, and when, then the consultation is not about the bridle, but about the horse? NIC. True. [[margin: A beautiful rule in recognizing things about which one acts.]] SOC. To comprehend it in a few words: as often as someone seeks something for the sake of something else, the consultation is about that very thing for the sake of which the other thing is sought, not about that which is sought for the sake of the other. NIC. Necessary. SOC. It is proper therefore for a consultant to consider whether he is skilled for caring for that thing for the sake of which we are deliberating at present. NIC. Entirely. 

SOC. Was it not said that we are inquiring about the discipline for the sake of the youths' souls? NIC. It was said. SOC. Therefore we must inquire whether any of us is powerful in the art of those same souls, and is able sufficiently to cultivate them and had learned teachers. NIC. Have you never seen, Socrates, some people who became more skilled in a certain thing without teachers than those who employed teachers? SOC. I have seen them indeed, Laches; but you yourself would not believe them if they preached themselves the best artisans, unless they showed some work of their art rightly perfected and elaborated—both one and several. NIC. What you say is true. 

SOC. It becomes us therefore, Laches and Nicias—after Lysimachus and Melesias called us to consult about their sons, desiring to make their souls best—if we confess that we have had teachers, to show those who were both themselves first best, and educated the souls of many youths, and then taught us. Or if someone of us denies having had a teacher, he ought to show his works, and bring into the middle which of the Athenians or guests, either slave or free, became good through their diligence without controversy. But if we can show neither, we ought to order them to go to other consultants, and not undergo the danger of depraving the sons of friends, for which we would deserve the greatest accusation among the youths' families. I indeed assert first about myself that no master has existed for me in this matter, although from a tender age I have always affected this thing. Nevertheless, I am not able to pay the fee to the Sophists, who alone promised to make me good and noble. But I myself by my own genius can even now by no means find this art; which if Nicias here or Laches found...
