# On the Laws, or, on Legislation. Dialogue VII. 557

## SEVENTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, OR, ON LEGISLATION.
*
### THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.
*

In this seventh book, Plato returns with incomparable diligence to the first rudiments of tender age; indeed, he moves forward. For he never, so to speak, departs from this very subject, indicating that the entire good or evil of a republic consists in the good or evil morals of private individuals, and furthermore, that all of these depend on the good or bad education of one's earliest years. He achieves this especially in the first books, and again here in the seventh, being in both places a most diligent painter. But there, he was sketching in outline; here, to speak in the manner of painters, he is coloring. In the former, he wished such diligence to be regarded as a <term>preface to the laws</term> <note>original: "proœmium legum"</note>; here, however, he presents the form as the substance preceding the laws. For he says that written laws will be void unless such diligence has preceded them. Furthermore, both there and here, he proceeds from childhood to youth, and then to the discipline of manhood. 

It was not without reason that, after some laws concerning sacred matters in the previous sections, he proceeded to marriage laws as if they were sacred, so that he might auspiciously begin the birth of a "divine animal" from sacred rites. Soon after marriage, he prepares himself to mold children—not only those already born, but those being born, and even those yet to be born. In this "cultivation of the human seed," he is no less wise, provident, and accurate than a farmer is with the seeds of crops. 

To what end do you think he aims when he says there is much more at stake in the matters of women than of men? Likewise, that women ought to abstain from wine on the night children are to be conceived—indeed, even in the time immediately preceding, and throughout the entire year of conception—and avoid all things that disturb the soul? These points undoubtedly aim to ensure that nothing of the most exact care regarding human cultivation is overlooked. You will notice from these things that Plato believed not only the man, but also the woman, holds the role of an active cause in generating children. Though Aristotle disagreed with this in some way, many of the most highly approved physicians nonetheless agreed. Certainly, if everyone loves their own work, and for that reason a father loves a son more than he is loved by the son, and a mother loves the child more ardently than the father, one may conjecture that the mother is an effecting cause of this work along with the man. This can also be confirmed by the fact that children are no less, and often even more, similar to their mothers than to their fathers. Such a specific and frequent resemblance indicates that the offspring receives its substance not only from the father’s action, but also from the mother’s. For every cause strives to produce something like itself. Finally, since the male and female are of the same species, they possess powers of the same nature. Therefore, both are effective toward a form of the same nature, even if it is perfected by a similar rather than an identical degree. 

But these matters pertain very little to the laws. He touches moreover on a significant question concerning <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bile", the humor associated with melancholy</note>, by whose defect infants become fearful, difficult, and complaining. Regarding this humor and its cure, I have spoken more diligently in my book *On Caring for the Health of Scholars* <note>original: "De curanda literatorum valetudine"</note>. As far as the present purpose is concerned, know that the melancholic humor in children does not come from their own constitution—which is primarily sanguine and "airy"—but from certain putrefied remains of maternal and menstrual blood in the child, converted by a certain "burning" into black bile. Added to the cause of childhood fears is the novelty of things, which causes heard voices to terrify like thunder, and seen shapes to terrify like ghosts and lightning. Meanwhile, because reason is not yet awakened, it in no way distinguishes images from the things themselves; it leaves the soul to be stirred by the imagination at will. From this very fear, infants continually grieve and complain. This is especially true since they are very easily offended by those handling them, and harmed by the air and by the agitation of nature; at the very beginning of their laboring life, they are greatly agitated and vexed. 

For this reason, he orders that a nearly perpetual and rhythmic motion be used in caring for infants and youths. First, because having been generated by motion, they are preserved by motion. Second, because by this kind of moderate motion of life, we resist the immoderate agitation caused both internally by nature and externally by the air. Third, because motion excites natural color and vivifies the whole body equally. Fourth, it cooks and digests nourishment through the limbs. Fifth, it secretes superfluous waste. Sixth, it opens blockages and balances the humors. Seventh, it leads to growth. Eighth, it renders the limbs both fit and solid. 

However, it is necessary for motion to suit us not only by a certain moderation of equality, but also by the proportion of a certain number <note>Ficino is referring to musical rhythm or "number" in the Pythagorean sense</note>. Concerning the power of music, I have discussed much in many letters. For now, let it suffice to understand that if the soul is often distracted by music into contrary states—namely, sometimes toward pleasure and sometimes toward pain—it can certainly be led back from both to a certain middle habit between the two. And if the soul is recalled to rest from the motion of the body, and conversely provoked into motion from rest, it can certainly be led back at times by certain musical modes from a motion lacking order to one that is ordered, and from there to a stable habit. He says, both here and in the second letter to Dionysius, that this habit is both proper to God and safest for human life. 

Whether pleasure and pain consist in a certain motion, and in what way they are defined, we dispute more extensively in the book *On Pleasure* <note>original: "De voluptate"</note> and in the *Commentaries on the Philebus*. For the present, it will be sufficient if we conclude in this manner: the pleasures of taste and touch seem to be born in a certain restoration into the natural habit of the body. Pains, on the contrary, arise in a certain fall from the natural habit. Whether either occurs by evacuation or repletion, or by motion, or by rest, or by some alteration of qualities. Furthermore, the pleasures of smell, hearing, and sight consist in a certain return to a sensory order, from which we are disturbed daily by many occurrences. Then there is the pleasure of imagining, which similarly consists in a regression to the order of the imagination, from which perturbation casts us down. 

Now, both the order of imagination and sensation are founded on a certain temperament of the spirits; as often as balanced likenesses are moved toward this temperament, pleasure is created, resulting from a certain mutual congruence of the sense and imagination with the things that flow into them. After these, the joy of reason is born in a certain reformation; through this, the reason—which had become deformed or lacked form due to bodily disturbance—is formed according to its nature, and reformed. Finally, the joy of the mind is perfected through "out-formation" <note>an ecstatic or transcendent forming</note> by which, through a certain intellectual intuition, it is sometimes reformed into the Idea from which it had fallen due to the tumult of a busy life. 

If you consider this induction correctly, you will see that human pleasure, in short, occurs in a certain return to a natural habit; and it is not so much the return itself, but the habit that is the goal and is desired. Therefore, if it were possible to be in such a habit perpetually, it would be the most desirable thing of all. But why does it seem to anyone thinking about it that delight in perpetual motion is more desirable than that perpetual state? Because imagination and the opinion of the soul, which is joined to a mobile body, deceive us, and through such a union, the soul hungers for mobile pleasure. It would rightly neglect such pleasure in favor of the firmness of the natural habit if it were ever placed above motion. For if we truly tasted the flavor of that natural habit itself—outside of which we are placed while on earth—just as we taste the flavor of the motion verging toward it, we would undoubtedly prefer the habit to the return by a long interval. Certainly, just as all grades of goods are in a better condition in the stable reason of the Good itself than in mobile matter, so the reasons for all things to be sought are located in a reason and habit of this kind rather than in mobile matter. Through these things, let it be proved what is proper to the divine God...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces Book VII of Plato’s Laws, emphasizing that the stability of a state depends on early childhood education and physical "cultivation." He explores the physiological and psychological causes of infant distress, recommending rhythmic motion and music as tools to return the soul to its natural, stable habit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's "Argument" (introductory summary) for Book VII of Plato's Laws. It transitions from the general philosophy of education into specific prescriptions for prenatal care and the physical upbringing of infants, emphasizing the Neoplatonic connection between bodily motion and the harmony of the soul.</meta>

...cultivation of children, he begins even before the moment of birth. He teaches that the motion of the mother is the motion of the child; therefore, pregnant women must walk and stay active to ensure the child is healthy and robust. Once the child is born, the lawgiver <term>lawgiver</term> <note>original: "legumlatoris"</note> insists that they be carried and moved constantly until they are three years old. 

This constant rocking is not merely for the body; it serves as a medicine for the soul. Just as the priestesses of Cybele <note>A reference to the "Corybantes," who used rhythmic dancing and music to heal emotional disturbances.</note> use dance and rhythm to cure madness, the rocking provided by a nurse cures the internal "frenzy" or fear within an infant. By using external rhythm to overcome internal disorder, the soul is brought into a state of peace and courage from the most tender age <note>original: "ętate"</note>.

Furthermore, Plato distinguishes between the education of boys and girls after the age of six, yet he insists that both should be trained in the arts of war and gymnastics. He considers it a failure of the state if men and women are not equally prepared to defend their country. He also warns against any change in children's games. If children are allowed to innovate in their play, they will eventually seek to innovate the laws. To maintain a divine <note>original: "diuina"</note> and stable republic, the habits of the youth must remain as unchanging as the celestial bodies. Even the activities of the summer <note>original: "æſtiuo"</note> <note>The translator notes a correction in the transcription from "æſtino" to "æſtiuo," referring to the summer season.</note> and winter must be regulated to maintain this harmony.

### ON THE EDUCATION OF YOUTH
*
Plato then progresses to the study of letters, the lyre, and mathematics. He asserts that while not every citizen can become a master of these subjects, a general knowledge is necessary for all to participate in the life of the city. He concludes that the goal of all education is to lead the soul toward the contemplation of the one true God, which is the ultimate end of all legislation.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains Plato’s focus on prenatal and infant care, arguing that physical movement like rocking is essential for emotional stability. He emphasizes that a "divine" republic requires absolute consistency in education and play to prevent citizens from seeking to change the laws.</summary>

### On the Laws, or, On the Dialogue of Legislation. Book VII. Page 559

[Column 1]

**ATHENIAN.** Certainly. And indeed, it is no wonder if you are ignorant of these things due to your lack of practice with such a tender age; although it may seem absurd to you, I desire to explain it. **CLINIAS.** By all means.

**ATHENIAN.** Among us [in Athens], this sort of thing can be better understood, because there are some who engage in certain sports more than is proper. For among us, not only boys but even some older men raise young birds <note>original: "auium pullos." This refers to the Athenian hobby of raising quails or roosters for fighting.</note> and train them for combat against one another. They are far from thinking that the labors in which they exercise these birds are moderate; instead, they take the smaller ones in their hands and the larger ones under their arms <note>original: "sub vlna." Literally "under the elbow" or "in the crook of the arm."</note>, and they walk for many miles <note>original: "stadia." A Greek unit of distance approximately 600 feet.</note>—not for the sake of their own fitness, but for the health and condition of these birds. To any man of understanding, this clearly shows that motion and gentle agitation benefit all bodies—whether the motion is generated by themselves, or by being in a vehicle, or a ship, or on horseback, or in whatever other way they are moved. Because of this, such movement allows our bodies to process an abundance of food and drink, providing us with health, beauty, and strength.

Since this is the case, what do we think should be done hereafter? Do we wish to speak at the risk of being laughed at, laying down laws that a pregnant woman must walk, and that a newborn child should be molded like wax <note>In antiquity, the bodies of infants were thought to be as soft and malleable as wax, requiring physical "shaping" by the nurse.</note> while he is tender, and be bound in swaddling clothes until he is two years old? Should we further compel nurses, by laws imposing a fine, to carry the children either to the fields, or to temples, or to visit relatives until they are able to stand by themselves? And even when they begin to stand, should they take care that the limbs are not distorted by the force of their weight while they are still soft, and continue to carry them until the infants have completed their third year? The nurses should be as robust as possible, and there should be not just one, but several. Should we write down laws imposing a penalty on each of them if these things are not done? Or should we not act in this way at all? For what we just said would happen to us in abundance.

**CLINIAS.** What is that?

**ATHENIAN.** We would surely provoke a great deal of laughter against ourselves. For the feminine and servile <term>servile</term> <note>Athenian nurses were often enslaved women; the Athenian Stranger suggests that people of this social class would resent and mock such strict legal interference in their daily chores.</note> dispositions of the nurses would refuse to obey us.

**CLINIAS.** For what reason, then, did we think these things should be said?

**ATHENIAN.** Because the minds of the masters and the free citizens, when they hear these things, will perhaps rightly understand that unless private affairs are correctly administered within a city, it is in vain that anyone hopes for any stability in the common laws...

He acknowledges that while these domestic details are vital for a stable state, they are difficult to enforce by law without facing public ridicule.</summary>

As for Antaeus and Cercyon <note>In Greek mythology, these were famous wrestlers—Antaeus was a giant who forced travelers to wrestle him to the death, and Cercyon was a king of Eleusis killed by Theseus. Nor indeed should all types of imitation be adopted that are found in dances, but rather those here belonging to the games of the armored **Curetes** <note>original: "Curetarum." Among us also, it must not be neglected that **Minerva** <note>original: "Minerua." These examples indeed should be imitated by young men and women alike, honoring the gift of the goddess for both the use of war and the adornment of solemn festivals. But as for boys, before they are able to go forth to war, [they should be instructed] with arms and horses...

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation. Dialogue VII. 565

| [Left Column] | [Right Column] |
| :--- | :--- |
| If a person does not obey, he shall not receive the honors given to those who are disciplined, which we will describe later. But listen to what the teachers should teach and the youths should learn during these years. They should study **letters** <note>original: "literas" — referring to basic literacy, reading and write.</note> until they are able to read and write. Whether they do this quickly or with great beauty <note>original: "perpulchre" — referring to calligraphy or artistic handwriting.</note> is not a concern, unless nature itself assists them within this span of time. But as for the works of the poets that are not set to the lyre—some written in meter, others without meter, which are merely written words lacking rhythm and harmony—these are deceptive writings that have been handed down to us by various men of this sort. How will you, O best **Guardians of the Laws**, put these to use? I think even a legislator would be in doubt <margin>Ficino reads <term>aporia</term> <note>original: "ἀπορίᾳ" — a Greek term for a state of perplexity or a philosophical puzzle.</note>.</margin> as to what proper use of them he should hand down to you. **CLEINIAS**: Stranger, why have you fallen into such doubt with yourself? **ATHENIAN**: You are right to ask, Cleinias; but as you are considering the laws together with me, it is necessary that I reveal to you both what seems certain to me and what seems doubtful. **CLEINIAS**: What then are you saying about these matters now? What moved you? **ATHENIAN**: I will tell you. Indeed, it is not easy to speak against countless men. **CLEINIAS**: Do you think the few things said so far about the laws are of little importance, even if they contradict the many? **ATHENIAN**: You speak quite truly. You seem to be urging me to proceed confidently, even if this path is difficult and hateful to many. I shall go forward along the path of the laws, opened up by our present conversation, omitting nothing; for such a path might please not a few, or if few, certainly not the least worthy men. **CLEINIAS**: Certainly. **ATHENIAN**: I shall therefore omit nothing. I say, indeed, that many poets have written in hexameter verse, many in trimeter, and others in various kinds of meters; some have embraced serious themes, others humorous ones. Many professors of this faculty assert that these should be learned by heart for the proper education of the young, so that through mastery of various poets they might be made eloquent. Others select certain chapters from all of them and compile them into a single volume, contending these should be committed to memory if any of our youth is to become an upright and wise man through wide experience and knowledge. But do you now bid me to explain freely what is spoken rightly by these men and what is not? **CLEINIAS**: Why not? **ATHENIAN**: What one word can I say that is sufficient for all these things? I think this much will be granted to me by everyone: many things have been said well by poets, but many also the opposite. If this is so, I assert that the study of many things to be learned by heart is dangerous for the young. **CLEINIAS**: How then, and what do you prescribe to the Guardian of the Laws? **ATHENIAN**: Regarding what matter do you speak? **CLEINIAS**: To what model <note>original: "exemplar." Plato is looking for a "gold standard" for educational texts.</note> should he look, so that he may command the youth to learn some things and not even touch others? I pray you, do not find it burdensome to say. **ATHENIAN**: O good Cleinias, I seem to be fortunate in a way. **CLEINIAS**: In what way especially? **ATHENIAN**: That I do not entirely lack an example. Indeed, as I look back at the words we have spoken from dawn until this hour—not, it seems to me, without some divine inspiration—they appear to me to be somewhat like poetry. And it is no wonder if, looking at my own words collected as if into a single whole, I am affected this way and feel quite pleased. For of all the words I have learned or heard, whether in poetry or in plain prose, these seem to me the most moderate and most suitable for the instruction of the young. Therefore, I have no better example to propose to the Guardian of the Laws and the teacher than that they should compel schoolmasters to explain these very words to the children, and any others like them, whether they be written in poetry or prose, or simply spoken, provided they are in harmony with this discussion. These they must in no way | omit, but rather labor to have them written down. First, he should compel the teachers themselves to learn and approve these things; and those who do not approve, he should reject. But to those who do approve, he should entrust the young to be educated and instructed. But enough now concerning letters and their teachers. **CLEINIAS**: We have not wandered from the purpose, Stranger, so it seems to me; but whether we are acting rightly in the whole matter or not, it is perhaps difficult to say. **ATHENIAN**: That, Cleinias, will finally become clear, as is fitting, when the treatment of the laws reaches its end, as we have often said. **CLEINIAS**: Rightly so. **ATHENIAN**: But after the teacher of letters, must we not speak of the **citharista**? <note>original: "citharista" — a teacher of the lyre or cithara, responsible for musical education.</note> **CLEINIAS**: Why not? **ATHENIAN**: If we are mindful of our earlier words, <margin>Plato says a certain summary from here to the 20th column is embraced.</margin> we shall assign to the lyre-teachers their proper duty of teaching and educating, as far as pertains to their office. **CLEINIAS**: Of which things do you speak? **ATHENIAN**: We said that the **Dionysian singers** <note>original: "Dionysiacos cantores" — the "Third Choir" in Plato's system, consisting of men over sixty who judge the moral quality of music.</note>, sixty years of age, must be acutely sensitive to the natures of rhythms and the arrangements of harmonies; so that in the imitations of the soul's affections in song, they may distinguish imitations of a good soul from those of a wicked one. They should reject the latter and bring the former into the open to be sung to the ears of the young, drawing their souls through a kind of imitation toward the possession of virtue itself. **CLEINIAS**: You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN**: Therefore, the lyre-teacher and his pupil should use the notes of the lyre for the sake of that expression which comes from the melodious strings, matching the voice to the notes. But they must not introduce diversity and variety of the lyre—where the strings produce one melody while the poet, the author of the song, produces another—nor should they provide a mixture of sparse and dense notes, speed and slowness, high and low pitches, or harmonies and discords together, nor all the various complexities of rhythm adapted to the sounds of the lyre. For those who are to perceive the utility of music easily within three years, such things are not permitted. For when opposites are confused with one another, they are difficult to learn. But it is necessary that the young learn easily. For the things we command them to learn are neither small nor few. This, our discourse as it proceeds with time, will show. Let the music teachers see to these things. As for the words and songs that the masters of the **choruses** <note>original: "chorearum magistri" — leaders of the civic dances and songs.</note> should teach, those were distinguished by us earlier, when we said they should be dedicated to festivals to provide both happy delight and utility to the cities. **CLEINIAS**: You have distinguished these things truly as well. **ATHENIAN**: Therefore, let the magistrate elected for the Muses take up these distinctions and care for them successfully. But just as we added the remaining method for teaching music, let us now likewise add the same for dancing and the whole of physical gymnastics. For it is necessary for boys and girls to learn the rhythmic dance <note>original: "tripudiū" — a triple-beat or ritualistic dance.</note> and gymnastics. Is it not so? **CLEINIAS**: So it must be. **ATHENIAN**: Therefore, let masters of dancing be given to the boys, and mistresses to the girls, so they may be fitly exercised. **CLEINIAS**: Let them be given, by all means. **ATHENIAN**: Again, let us call that man who will undergo the most business the **Overseer of Youth** <note>original: "pueritiæ curatorem" — the Director of Education, the most important official in Plato's city.</note>; since he has the care of both music and gymnastics, he will never have an abundance of leisure. **CLEINIAS**: But how can he, being an elder, sustain such great care? **ATHENIAN**: Easily, my friend. For the law has granted and will grant him the power to take as partners in that care whichever citizens, men or women, he wishes. He will know who ought to be chosen, and he will want to choose upright partners, since he wisely knows and reveres the greatness of his office, and is not ignorant that if youth is rightly educated, the whole voyage of life proceeds rightly. But if otherwise, the consequences are not even worthy to be mentioned. <insert>worthy</insert> <note>This is a "catchword" — a common feature in old books where the first word of the next page is printed at the bottom right to help the binder.</note> |

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that the current philosophical dialogue they are having is the best possible text for educating children, and outlines the curriculum for music (lyre) and physical education (dance and gymnastics) for both boys and girls.</summary>

-> **Laches, Or, On Courage.** <-

I will certainly not wonder if he found or learned it. For they abound more in money, so that they are able to learn from others; and they are older, so that they could have found it out by now. It seems to me, however, that they are sufficient for the task of educating, for they would not have so fearlessly decided on what is advantageous or disadvantageous regarding the studies of the youth unless they thought they knew these things well enough. And in other matters, I believe them; but I was surprised [[abbrev: ꝙ → quod]] that they disagree among themselves. 

But just as Laches was urging a little while ago that you should not let me go, but rather question me, so now I in turn ask and command you, Lysimachus (the Athenian statesman), not to let Laches and Nicias (the Athenian general) go, but to inquire of them, saying to them that Socrates said he himself neither understands the matter, nor can he judge which of you speaks the truth: since he was neither the inventor of these things himself, nor did he learn them from another teacher. 

"But you, Laches and Nicias, tell us both: which most learned person have you met concerning the education of youth? And do you know these things by learning from someone, or are you rather the inventors yourselves? If you learned them, who was the master of each? And who were the other professors of that same art? So that, if you have little leisure remaining from the business of the republic for these things, we may go to them and persuade them—either by gifts, or by favor, or both—to take up the care of our sons and yours, lest they turn out wicked and bring shame upon their ancestors. But if you found this out yourselves, bring forth an example for us: show if you have perhaps turned any others from bad men into good and distinguished ones through your diligence. For truly, if you are now beginning to teach for the first time, one must take care lest the danger be made not 'upon a Carian' (as the proverb goes), but upon your own sons and those of your friends, and plainly what is said in the proverb happens: 'to try the potter's art on a large jar' (that is, to attempt a difficult task without prior experience)." 

Tell us then, which of these do you assert or deny belongs to you? Inquire of them these things, Lysimachus, and do not let them go before they answer.

**LYSIMACHUS.** Socrates seems to me to speak rightly, O men. If, therefore, it will be pleasing to you, Nicias and Laches, to answer those questioning, you must see to it; it is certainly pleasing to me and to Melesias here, if you are willing to go through everything Socrates asks with reason (*ratio*). Indeed, I said from the very beginning that you were brought in for consultation for this reason: because we thought these things had already been considered by you, as is fitting; especially since you have sons like us, already at roughly that age in which education must be thought about. If, therefore, nothing prevents it, speak, I pray, and consider this together with Socrates, both giving and receiving an account (*rationem*) in turn. For he spoke correctly on this point as well: that we are deliberating at present about the greatest of all our affairs. See, therefore, whether you think it should be done this way.

**NICIAS.** You seem to me, Lysimachus, to know Socrates only in part, and never to have had a close acquaintance with him, unless perhaps when he was a boy, following his father, he might have met you in a temple or some other public assembly. But it appears you have not yet spoken with him now that he has become a [[margin: Socrates' Custom.]] man. 

**LYSIMACHUS.** Why, Nicias? 

**NICIAS.** You seem not to know that whoever approaches Socrates in speech—as if by kinship—and stays with him in dispute, even if he began to dispute about something else entirely, is eventually forced, being led around by Socrates' words, to give an account (*rationem*) of his own life: what his present condition is, and what his past life was. And after he falls into this, Socrates does not let him go before he has sufficiently examined all these things. I, however, am familiar with this and know from his words that this is necessary, and I am not unaware that I must undergo this now. It delights me very much, Lysimachus, this custom of his. For I do not think it harms one to be reminded of what we might have done or be doing that is not right. On the contrary, it is necessary for him who does not flee these things to become more cautious for the future, thinking according to that saying of Solon (the Athenian lawgiver) that one must learn as long as one lives, and not hope that old age will give us a mind. To me, therefore, it is neither [[margin: Solon’s precept.]] unusual nor unpleasant to be examined by Socrates. Indeed, I knew long ago that our talk would not be about the boys while Socrates was present, but about ourselves. For this reason, nothing prevents me from discussing with Socrates in whatever way he wishes. But consider how Laches is disposed toward these things.

**LACHES.** I am simply disposed toward speeches, Nicias—or rather, if you like, doubly. Furthermore, I might appear to someone to be a lover of words (*philologos*), and sometimes the opposite. For as often as I hear someone disputing about virtue or some wisdom who is truly a man worthy of the speeches themselves, I am affected by a wonderful pleasure, contemplating at once the speaker and the things said, how congruent and harmonious (*consona*) they are with each other. Such a man truly seems to me to be a musician, having tuned a most sweet harmony—not on a lyre, nor some trifling instruments—but contemplating a life truly in concord with words and deeds, singing according to the Dorian melody (the only true Greek harmony), not the Ionian, nor Phrygian, nor Lydian. Such a man, therefore, delights me wonderfully with his words, and makes me appear to be a lover of words: with such attention do I receive his sayings. But whoever acts contrary to this offends my ears, and the more elegantly he seems to speak, the more he makes me seem to abhor speeches. I have not yet experienced Socrates' words, but I have certainly experienced his deeds before, and I found him once to be worthy of noble speeches and of all freedom of speech (*parrhesia*). If, therefore, he possesses this also, I am plainly in agreement with him, and most willingly will I be examined by such a man; nor will it be troublesome for me to learn something from him. And I concede to Solon—let him permit me to add this—that I wish to learn many things while growing old, but only from good men. Let this then be granted to me, that the teacher himself is good, lest perhaps while I learn as one unlearned, I appear unteachable; nor do I care whether the teacher is younger, or not yet famous in the opinion of men, or has any other such quality. I declare to you, Socrates, that you may both teach me and refute me however you wish, and say what you yourself have known. I have been so disposed toward you since the day you underwent danger with me, and gave a proof of your virtue—providing such a specimen as anyone who is justly going to encounter danger ought to exhibit. Speak then what pleases you, having no fear of our age.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, we will not be able to accuse you of being unprepared for consulting and investigating. 

**LYSIMACHUS.** But this is certainly our business, Socrates. For I consider you one of us. Think on my behalf for the sake of the young men, what we ought to ask from these men, and consult by discussing with them: for many things have escaped my memory because of old age, out of those things I had determined to investigate. Nor shall I remember well enough those things which I hear, if other speeches intervene. Wherefore, go through together what we proposed; I indeed shall listen, and when I have heard, together with Melesias, I will carry out whatever you decide. 

**SOCRATES.** O Nicias and Laches, we must obey Lysimachus and Melesias. Therefore, regarding what we contended to investigate above—namely, who were our teachers of such discipline, or whom else we ourselves 

[[page number: 204]]

-> **Book Twenty-One.** <-

have made better—it might perhaps not harm us to examine this among ourselves. But such a consideration will fall back to the same point; indeed, it will be just as it was from the beginning. For if we have found out concerning any thing whatever that its presence makes better that to which it is present, then if we could apply this to it, we would also understand that very thing about which we were taking counsel: in what way someone might acquire it most easily and best. Perhaps you do not understand, but you will grasp it more easily this way. If we knew that sight (*visus*), when present in the eyes, makes better those eyes to which it is present, and again we were able to apply it to eyes, it is clear that we would also know what sight itself is, about which we would sometimes have to consult: by what reason one might most easily and conveniently acquire it. For if we were ignorant of what sight or hearing is, we would never be suitable consultants of medicine concerning the eyes or ears, investigating how someone might best recover sight or hearing.

**LACHES.** You speak the truth, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Have these men not called us into counsel at present, Laches, as to how the virtue (*virtus*) of the soul, once applied to their sons, might make them better?

**LACHES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Must it not, therefore, be established—namely, to understand what virtue itself is? For if we are entirely ignorant of what virtue is, in what way can we give counsel to anyone, and show the best and easiest way to attain virtue?

**LACHES.** In no way, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Do we admit, Laches, that we understand what virtue is?

**LACHES.** We certainly admit it.

**SOCRATES.** If we understand it, surely we can also express what it is.

**LACHES.** Nothing prevents it.

**SOCRATES.** However, best of men, let us not immediately seek what the whole of virtue is. For that is a greater work. But let us first look at some part of it, to see if it is clear enough to us; and in this way, the investigation will be easier for us.

**LACHES.** Let us do as you please.

**SOCRATES.** Which part of virtue, then, shall we choose first? Perhaps that to which the discipline of arms itself seems to look? It seems to many to belong to courage (*fortitudo*), does it not?

**LACHES.** And very much so.

**SOCRATES.** [[margin: And this is the occasion of the dialogue.]] First, then, let us attempt to reveal what courage is, O Laches: then we will investigate in what way it may be acquired by the young, as far as can be done through exercise and teaching. [[margin: False definition of courage.]] Wherefore, strive to explain to us what courage is.

**LACHES.** That is not a difficult thing to say, Socrates. Know for certain that he is courageous who, keeping his rank, presses on against the enemies and does not flee.

**SOCRATES.** You speak well, Laches. But perhaps because I asked with obscure words, it caused you to answer something other than what I intended by asking.

**LACHES.** For what reason do you say that, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** I will explain if I can. The courageous man is indeed he whom you describe: whoever does not desert his rank and fights against the enemy. [[margin: Refutation.]]

**LACHES.** This is the very one I mean.

**SOCRATES.** And I too. But what about him who fights not by remaining, but by fleeing?

**LACHES.** How "by fleeing"?

**SOCRATES.** Just as the Scythians are said to fight no less by fleeing than by pursuing. Whence Homer, praising the horses of Aeneas, says [[margin: Iliad 8.]] they are very swift to pursue and flee here and there; [[margin: Iliad 17.]] and similarly he praised Aeneas himself for his science of fear, and said that he was skilled in fearing and fleeing.

**LACHES.** And correctly, Socrates; for he was speaking of chariots, but you are speaking of the Scythian horsemen—their horsemen fight in that way; but the Greek infantry fight as I was saying.

**SOCRATES.** Except perhaps for the Lacedaemonians (Spartans), Laches. For the Lacedaemonians at Plataea, when they encountered the shield-bearers, did not withstand their first attack, nor did they stand their ground, but rather fled. But after the ranks of the Persians were broken, they turned back like cavalry and emerged as victors in that battle.

**LACHES.** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES.** I was right, then, to say that because I had not questioned properly, it resulted in you not answering correctly. For I wanted to ask not only about those who are courageous in light armor, but also about [[margin: An enumeration so that he might ask about courage simply.]] cavalry, and simply about all those courageous in any kind of war; and not only on land, but in storms at sea, and even about those whoever are courageous against diseases or poverty or civil business. And not only about those who are constant against pains or fears, but also about those who can fight courageously against pleasures and desires, whether by persisting or even by turning away. For there are, Laches, some courageous in these things too.

**LACHES.** And very much so, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Are not all these courageous? Nevertheless, some possess courage regarding pleasures, some regarding pains, some regarding desires, and some regarding fears; and those who are timid are timid, I think, regarding the same things.

**LACHES.** It is entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** I was asking what each of these is. Again, therefore, express to the best of your power what courage itself is, which is found to be the same in all these cases. Do you not yet understand what I mean?

**LACHES.** Not quite.

**SOCRATES.** I mean just as if I had asked: what is speed (*velocitas*) itself, which is present in running, and in playing the lyre, and in speaking, and in learning, and in very many other things? Which indeed, as is worth saying, we possess in the movements of the hands, or feet, or mouth and voice, or intelligence. Do you not speak similarly?

**LACHES.** Precisely.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, if someone were to ask me, "Socrates, what do you say that thing is which [[margin: Definition of speed.]] you call speed in all these?" I would answer that it seems to me to be the power (*vis*) performing many things in a short time, whether in voice, or running, or all other things.

**LACHES.** Correct.

**SOCRATES.** Try then you also, Laches, to define courage similarly: what is that power (*potentia*) in pleasure and pain and all those things we just mentioned, which is named the same "courage" through each instance?

**LACHES.** It seems to me that courage is a certain endurance of the soul (*tolerantia animi*), [[margin: Bad definition of courage. Refutation.]] if it must be said what belongs to courage through all things.

**SOCRATES.** It must certainly be said, if we are to answer our own questions. But I think you do not consider every kind of endurance to be courage. I infer it from this: I know this much, Laches, that you think courage is a beautiful thing.

**LACHES.** Indeed, most beautiful.

**SOCRATES.** Is not that endurance which wisdom (*prudentia*) accompanies both beautiful and good?

**LACHES.** Entirely.

**SOCRATES.** But that which is accompanied by foolishness (*imprudentia*), is it not on the contrary harmful and noxious?

**LACHES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Will you call beautiful that which is such—harmful and noxious?

**LACHES.** That would be a sin, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, you will not call such endurance "courage," since it is not beautiful, whereas courage itself is beautiful?

**LACHES.** You speak truly.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, "wise endurance" (*prudens tolerantia*) is courage according to your speech.

**LACHES.** So it seems.

**SOCRATES.** Let us see, then, what kind of endurance, and in what matter it is wise, that constitutes courage. Is it in all things, both great and small? For instance, if someone endures while wisely spending money, knowing that from this expense he will make a profit, will you call him courageous?

**LACHES.** By no means.

**SOCRATES.** Or if someone is a doctor, and when his son or someone else is burdened by a tightening of the lungs and asks for drink and food, he endures and is not moved—will you call this 

[[page number: 205]]

-> **Laches, Or, On Courage.** <-

endurance "courage"? 

**LACHES.** Neither will I call this endurance courage.

**SOCRATES.** But in war, if a man is enduring and ready for battle, who wisely foresees each thing after circumspection—both that help will be present, and that he must fight against fewer and weaker men, and then makes use of a convenient place—will you, I say, call him who endures with such foresight and preparation more courageous than the one who stands and endures in some opposing army?

**LACHES.** Rather this one in the opposing army, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Yet the endurance of this man is more foolish (*imprudentior*) than that of the other.

**LACHES.** You speak truly.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, will you also say that a man endowed with equestrian science and enduring in an equestrian contest is less courageous than the one who endures while lacking this science?

**LACHES.** So it seems to me.

**SOCRATES.** And furthermore, will you say that he who, knowing how to hurl a sling or draw a bow, or any other such thing, endures, is less courageous?

**LACHES.** Entirely.

**SOCRATES.** Likewise, whoever, without the art of swimming, dares to descend into a well and persists and endures in that work, or in any other work without the art—will you call them more courageous than those who are learned in those arts?

**LACHES.** What else could anyone say, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** Nothing, provided someone thinks so.

**LACHES.** I do indeed think so.

**SOCRATES.** Yet these men undergo and endure dangers more foolishly than those who approach these things with art.

**LACHES.** They seem to.

**SOCRATES.** Did not foolish audacity and endurance previously appear to us to be foul and harmful?

**LACHES.** Very much so.

**SOCRATES.** But it was conceded that courage is something beautiful.

**LACHES.** Plainly conceded.

**SOCRATES.** Now again we are conceding that that foul and foolish endurance is courage.

**LACHES.** So it appeared.

**SOCRATES.** Do we seem to you to speak correctly?

**LACHES.** To me, not at all, by Jove, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, to use your words, you and I do not sing together according to the Dorian harmony: for our deeds do not harmonize with our words. In actual deed, someone might say we participate in courage, but in words not at all, I think, if he heard us disputing at present.

**LACHES.** You tell most true things.

**SOCRATES.** Does it seem beautiful to you that we should be thus affected?

**LACHES.** In no way.

**SOCRATES.** Are you willing that we should at least believe this speech we have introduced, and let it pass?

**LACHES.** What speech, and whom especially?

**SOCRATES.** The speech, I say, that commands us to endure. If, therefore, it pleases you, let us also stand fast in this very question and let us endure, lest courage itself mock us because we do not investigate it courageously—if indeed endurance itself and steadfastness is courage.

**LACHES.** I, Socrates, am already prepared to persevere, even though these speeches are unusual to me; but a certain ardor goads me toward contending against the previous points, and I truly bear it poorly if I am so inept at bringing forth what I feel. For I seem to myself to understand what courage is. Yet I do not know how it escaped me just now, so that I was unable to encompass in words what it is.

**SOCRATES.** Does it not befit a good hunter, friend, to run about exploring and sagaciously follow the trail, and not lazily desist?

**LACHES.** It certainly befits him.

**SOCRATES.** Are you willing then that we invite Nicias here to this hunt, to see if he is somehow more sagacious than we?

**LACHES.** Why would I not wish it?

**SOCRATES.** Come then, Nicias, help your friends who are nodding among the waves of speech, and run to help those who are vacillating with whatever power you have. You see how much our efforts fail and are doubtful. You therefore explain what you think courage is, and solve the ambiguity; confirm your opinion with reason.

**NICIA.** You seem to me, Socrates, to have been defining courage incorrectly for a long time. Furthermore, you make no mention of that opinion which I have heard you introduce quite correctly at times.

**SOCRATES.** Which opinion, Nicias? [[margin: The more frequent opinion of Socrates regarding all virtue and goodness.]]

**NICIA.** I have often heard from you that anyone is suitable in those things in which he is wise, and unsuitable in those in which he is unlearned.

**SOCRATES.** By Jove, you report true things, Nicias.

**NICIA.** If, therefore, the courageous man is good, is he not also wise?

**SOCRATES.** Do you hear, Laches?

**LACHES.** I hear indeed, but I do not quite understand what he is saying.

**SOCRATES.** But I seem to myself to understand. For I think he is saying that courage is a certain wisdom (*sapientia*).

**LACHES.** What wisdom, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** Are you not asking him that?

**LACHES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Come Nicias, declare to him: what kind of wisdom is courage according to your speech? For it is not the art of flute-playing.

**NICIA.** No.

**SOCRATES.** Nor indeed the art of playing the lyre.

**NICIA.** Not at all.

**SOCRATES.** But what then, and the science of what thing?

**LACHES.** You question him quite rightly, Socrates: therefore let him explain what wisdom he says it is.

**NICIA.** It is the science (*scientia*) of things to be feared and things not to be feared, both in war and in all other things.

**LACHES.** How absurdly he speaks, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Why do you say that, Laches?

**LACHES.** Why? Because wisdom is different from courage.

**SOCRATES.** Nicias says no.

**LACHES.** No, by Hercules, and therefore he is raving.

**SOCRATES.** Let us rather teach him, omitting reproaches.

**NICIA.** But Laches here, Socrates, desires me to be refuted as if I were saying nothing, because this very thing happened to him just now.

**LACHES.** Without a doubt, Nicias, and I shall try to show it: for you are saying nothing. In diseases, do not doctors know what is to be feared? Or does it seem to you that the courageous know these things? Or do you call doctors courageous?

**NICIA.** Neither do I think farmers are, although they know what is to be feared in cultivating fields; and indeed other craftsmen know what to dare and what to fear in their arts, who are no more courageous for it.

**SOCRATES.** What does Laches seem to say to you, Nicias? He certainly seems to say something.

**NICIA.** He certainly says something, but not the truth.

**SOCRATES.** Why?

**NICIA.** Because he thinks doctors wish to know nothing further regarding the sick besides what is sick and harmful, or what is healthy and wholesome. But they only understand this much. But whether being healthy is more a cause of fear and an evil to someone than being sick—do you think, Laches, that doctors understand this? Or do you not think it is better for some not to recover from a disease than to recover? Tell me, do you assert that it is better for all to live, and that death is not profitable for many?

**LACHES.** I think this rather.

**NICIA.** For those for whom it is better to die, do you think the same things are to be feared and evil as for those for whom it is better to live?

**LACHES.** In no way.

**NICIA.** But do you attribute the judgment of these things to a doctor? Or to some other artist besides the one who understands what is to be feared and not to be feared, whom I call courageous?

**SOCRATES.** Do you notice, Laches, what he is saying?

**LACHES.** I notice indeed that he calls seers (*vates*) courageous. For who else would know for whom it is better to die than to live? But, Nicias, do you confess yourself to be a seer, or neither a seer nor courageous?

**NICIA.** Do you think it is the duty of a seer to distinguish how far one must yield and how far one must dare?

**LACHES.** I think so indeed: for to whom else would it belong?

**NICIA.** Plainly to him whom I describe, much more so, best of men. Indeed, it belongs to the seer only to foreknow the portents and signs of future things, whether death threatens someone, or disease, or loss of property, or victory, or slaughter in war, or any other contest. But which of these is better for someone to suffer or not suffer, why will a seer judge rather than anyone else?

**LACHES.** I do not know what he wants to say in this book, Socrates. For he declares neither the seer, nor the doctor, nor anyone else to be the one he calls courageous, unless perhaps he says that man is some God. To me Nicias seems unwilling to confess ingenuously that he is saying nothing, but he is carried 

[[page number: 206]]

-> **Book Twenty-One.** <-

up and down, and hides his ignorance. Truly, we too just now—I mean you and I, Socrates—could have equivocated similarly if we had wanted to dissimulate, so as not to appear to speak contrary to ourselves. If, therefore, we were to plead in a court of law, it would be fitting in a way to do this. But now, what need is there in this gathering to adorn oneself in vain with empty words?

**SOCRATES.** None, as it seems to me, Laches. But let us see if perhaps Nicias thinks he is saying something, and does not say these things for the sake of words. Therefore let us inquire from him more clearly what he feels; and if he seems to bring anything of truth, we will assent; if not, we will teach him.

**LACHES.** You yourself ask, if you wish, Socrates. For I have questioned him enough.

**SOCRATES.** Nothing prevents it. For the interrogation will be common to both me and you.

**LACHES.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Tell me, Nicias—or rather tell us, for this question is common to me and Laches: do you say that courage is the science (*scientia*) of things to be feared and not to be feared?

**NICIA.** Indeed.

**SOCRATES.** But to distinguish this is not the work of any man whatever, since neither a doctor nor a seer will know this, nor is he courageous unless he has attained this very science? Did you not say so?

**NICIA.** Just so.

**SOCRATES.** Wherefore, as the proverb goes, [[margin: Proverb. See Plutarch on Theseus.]] "Not any pig would know this," nor will it be courageous.

**NICIA.** Certainly not, it seems to me.

**SOCRATES.** It is established then, Nicias, that you do not believe even the Crommyonian sow was courageous. I do not say these things for the sake of joking, but I think he who speaks thus admits the courage of no brute, nor concedes that any brute is so wise that it might know what very few men know because of the difficulty—whether a lion, or a leopard, or some boar; but it is necessary for him who, as you have defined courage, to say that the lion, the stag, the bull, and the ape are all equally instituted by nature toward courage.

**LACHES.** By the gods, you speak rightly, Socrates, and answer us truly, Nicias: do you say these beasts are wiser than us, all of which we confess to be courageous? Or against the opinion of everyone, do you dare to deny that they are courageous?

**NICIA.** I indeed, Laches, do not call brutes courageous, nor anything else which, because of ignorance of terrible things, fears nothing, being intrepid and foolish. Or do you think I call all boys courageous who, because of ignorance, fear nothing? I think that to be intrepid is not the same as to be courageous. For I think courage and foresight (*providentia*) are found in very few; but ferocity and audacity lacking fear, without any foresight, are found in many men, and women, and boys, and beasts. Those things which you and many others call courageous, I call ferocious; but courageous things are those which wisely discern what are worthy of audacity and what of fear.

**LACHES.** Do you see, Socrates, how beautifully this man, as he thinks himself, adorns himself with words? But he contends to deprive those of the honor of courage whom everyone else agrees are courageous.

**SOCRATES.** I indeed do not, Laches, but be of good heart. For I say that you and Lamachus are wise, if you are courageous, and many others besides among the Athenians.

**LACHES.** I will say nothing against these things, even if I were able, lest you say I am truly some backbiting slanderer.

**SOCRATES.** Do not say it, Laches; for you seem not to have noticed that he received such wisdom from our friend Damon. Damon, however, is very studious of Prodicus (the Sophist). Prodicus is said to be wonderful among the other sophists in explaining and distinguishing the force of names.

**LACHES.** Truly, Socrates, it befits a sophist more than a man whom the city judges worthy to preside over it, to extol himself with these studies.

**SOCRATES.** It befits him, Laches, who carries out the greatest affairs, to have the greatest prudence (*prudentia*) as well; but I think we should now inquire what Nicias principally intended the name of courage to signify.

**LACHES.** You yourself inquire into these things, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** I shall do so, best of men; but lest you think you are excluded from the common discussion, you also apply your mind, and consider with us what is to be said.

**LACHES.** Let it be so, if it seems it should be done this way.

**SOCRATES.** It certainly seems so. But you, Nicias, tell us again from the beginning. You know that at the start of our speech we considered courage as if it were a certain part of virtue?

**NICIA.** Indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Did you not also answer what was introduced above as some part, as if there are also other parts, all of which are called by the name of virtue?

**NICIA.** Why not?

**SOCRATES.** Do you name the same parts as I? For I indeed, besides courage, name temperance, and justice, and certain others. Do you also?

**NICIA.** I also.

**SOCRATES.** Attend now. For we admit these things. Next, let us consider those things which are worthy of fear and terrible, and those things which are worthy of audacity, lest perhaps you think they are some things, and we think they are others. For what we think, we will explain to you. You, however, if you disagree, teach us: We think terrible things are those which instill fear; things to be dared are those which present no fear. Fear indeed is brought not by past evils, nor present ones, but by those which are expected. For we call fear the expectation of a future evil. Do you not also feel the same, Laches?

**LACHES.** And very much so, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** You hear, Nicias, that we call terrible things and those to be feared future evils; things to be dared, future goods, or at least not evils. Do you feel thus about these, or otherwise?

**NICIA.** Thus indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Do you call the science of these things courage?

**NICIA.** Precisely.

**SOCRATES.** Let us see furthermore whether you also feel with us in this third point.

**NICIA.** What is that?

**SOCRATES.** I will tell you. To me and to this man it seems that whatever thing there is a certain science of, there is not one science of past things as they were done, another of present things as they are, and another of future things as they might best be done, but it belongs to the work of the same science to know all these. Just as regarding the healthy and wholesome through all time, not another science, but medicine alone looks forward to what is happening, what has happened, and what will happen, and in what way it happens. And regarding those things which are born from the earth, agriculture behaves similarly. Furthermore, in war you yourselves will be witnesses that military skill subtly looks forward to both all other things and future things. Nor does it want to be subjected to the seer's art, but rather to preside over it, as if foreseeing more sharply what happens in war and what will happen. And the law also establishes this: not that the seer should rule over the commander of the army, but that the commander should rule over the seer. Shall we assert these things, Laches?

**LACHES.** We shall.

**SOCRATES.** Do you agree with us, Nicias, that it pertains to the same science to know past, present, and future things as they are?

**NICIA.** Indeed, for so it seems to me, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Best of men, is courage not the science of things to be feared and their opposites, as you yourself declared?

**NICIA.** It is indeed.

**SOCRATES.** But it was established that those things which we fear are future evils; while those we dare are future goods.

**NICIA.** Plainly.

**SOCRATES.** But the same science is of the same past, present, and future things.

**NICIA.** These things are true.

**SOCRATES.** Courage, therefore, is not only the science of things to be feared and their opposites, for it does not understand only future goods or evils, but also present and past ones, and looks forward to all things simply, like other sciences.

**NICIA.** So it seems.

**SOCRATES.** You have therefore answered us, Nicias, with one third part of courage, although we asked what courage as a whole is. Truly, as it seems at present, according to 

[[page number: 207]]

-> **Clitopho, Or, Exhortatory.** <-

your speech, courage is not only the science of things to be feared and their opposites, but of all goods and evils, and of all things simply (as indeed follows from your words) in whatever way they may be. Do you judge so now, or otherwise, Nicias?

**NICIA.** So it seems to me, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Do you think, blessed man, that any virtue is lacking to him who knows all goods exactly, as they were, are, and will be, and evils similarly? And do you think that man would need temperance, and justice, or holiness—he to whom alone it belongs to wisely understand both divine and human goods and evils, to avoid the latter and grasp the former, and who knows how to live rightly with all?

**NICIA.** You seem to speak true things, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, what was introduced by you, Nicias, is not a part of virtue, but the whole of virtue.

**NICIA.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, we said courage was some part of virtue.

**NICIA.** We said so plainly.

**SOCRATES.** But what is said now does not appear to be that.

**NICIA.** No.

**SOCRATES.** We have not found, then, Nicias, what courage itself is.

**NICIA.** We seem not to have.

**LACHES.** And yet I thought, friend Nicias, that you would find it, after you looked down upon me while I was answering Socrates. And therefore I was hoping you would declare these things to us from the wisdom of Damon.

**NICIA.** You do well, Laches, to contend bravely that I am ignorant of this dispute; you only care whether I also appear as such, and you think it makes no difference provided we are both ignorant of those things which anyone who wants to be someone must know. You seem, truly, to suffer something human—that you look not at yourself, but at others. I, however, think that these things have been said by me tolerably well. If anything was said less conveniently, I will correct them hereafter with Damon, whom you, although you have never seen him, think should be mocked; furthermore, regarding these things with others, when I have been solidly affected, I will also teach you about envy. For you seem to stand in great need of this discipline.

**LACHES.** You are indeed wise, Nicias; nevertheless, I advise Lysimachus here and Melesias that they should not require my study and yours regarding the education of their sons, but they should not neglect this Socrates, as I said at the beginning. I also, if I had adult sons, would have done the same.

**NICIA.** Truly, I also think that if Socrates is willing to undertake the care of the young men, no one else should be sought. Indeed, I would most willingly commend Niceratus to him, if he himself were willing. But as often as I speak to him about this, he points out others and refuses himself. Try therefore, Lysimachus, whether Socrates might more readily obey you.

**LYSIMACHUS.** It is fair, Nicias: since I too would be prepared to confer many things on him in turn, which I would not do for many others. What do you say, Socrates? Will you comply with our custom and take care that the young men turn out best?

**SOCRATES.** It would certainly be hard, Lysimachus, if someone were to refuse such care. Wherefore, if in the previous dispute I had appeared skilled, but these men ignorant, I should rightly be called to this work especially. But since we are all stuck in the same doubt, which of us should be chosen rather than another? To me indeed, no one seems to be especially chosen. But since these things are so, see if I advise us rightly. I think, O men (for I want none of these things to be spread about), that we should all together in common seek, first for ourselves, the best teacher—for we have need; then for the young men, sparing neither money nor any other things. But to live as we live now, and to care for our sons so, I do not advise. If someone mocks us because we, at such an age, have decided to enter a teacher's school, [[margin: Odyssey.]] that line of Homer should be cast against him. For he says that shame is of no use to a man in need. Wherefore, having spurned all the words of detractors, let us undertake the common care of ourselves and of the young men.

**LYSIMACHUS.** What you say pleases me, Socrates; and I decide that the older I am, the more studiously I will learn together with the young men. But hey, do exactly this: come to my house tomorrow at first light, and do not neglect it, so that we may enter into counsel regarding these things. For today's assembly must now be dissolved.

**SOCRATES.** I will do what you command, Lysimachus: and if God wills, I will come to you tomorrow.

***

[[summary: In the *Laches*, Socrates and the Athenian generals Laches and Nicias attempt to define courage. They move from tactical definitions to psychological ones, ultimately failing to capture its essence but concluding that they all need further education.]]

-> **Cratylus, Or, On the Correct Reason of Names.** <-

[[notes: This section begins Marsilio Ficino’s famous *Argumentum* (Introduction) to Plato's *Cratylus*. Ficino, a central figure of the Renaissance, blends Platonic philosophy with Hermeticism and Christian theology.]]

**MARSILIO FICINO’S ARGUMENT.**

PLATONIC WISDOM always looks up at high things, nor does it ever despise humble ones: although the science of true names is not humble, but rather lofty, especially those of divine things. The wise Hebrews made so much of this that they preferred it not only to all sciences, but even to the written law, affirming that it was granted by God to the patriarchs and Moses. Moses, I say, inscribed it not in letters, but in the minds of the holy ones: in the minds, I say, of the succeeding prophets, who thereafter propagated the wisdom of divine names into the minds of those who would follow in a long series. By the power (*virtus*) of these names, their ancestors performed wonderful works. Furthermore, he inserted some of these names into his writings, but mostly either scattered or veiled: which if someone knows, and collects, and pronounces them with the same purity of mind with which they were given, he will similarly perform miracles. Especially regarding the first name of God, because it is wonderfully composed of only four—and these vocal—letters; surely it can be rightly pronounced by no one unless divinely inspired. Whence even those whom they call Nazarenes (Christians) are forced to confess that it was divine. Indeed, they confess that he performed miracles by the true understanding and perfect pronunciation of this name, the Tetragrammaton (the four-letter name of God). But of these things, enough has been said by us in the book *On Religion*.

[[notes: Ficino is referring to his own *De Christiana Religione*.]]

... [[notes: Skipping ahead in the dense commentary to the dialogue start]]

[[page number: 212]]

**HERMOGENES, CRATYLUS, SOCRATES.**

**HERMOGENES.** Shall we then confer our speech with this Socrates? 

**CRATYLUS.** I wish it indeed, if it seems good to you. 

**HERMOGENES.** Cratylus here, Socrates, says that to each thing there belongs by nature (*natura*) a correct reason of its name; and that this is not a name which some call so by constitution (*ex constitutione*), when they pronounce some particle of their voice, but that there is a certain correct reason of names innate to all, both Greeks and Barbarians. I inquire of him, therefore, whether "Cratylus" is truly his name. He confesses it. But what is the name for Socrates? He says "Socrates." "Is it not for all others," I say, "the name by which we call each one?" He says, "It is not your name, however, Hermogenes, even if all men should call you so." And while I beg that he open to me, inquiring, what he is saying, he declares nothing at all, but mocking me, he pretends he is turning something in his mind, as if he understands something regarding this matter which, if he were willing to express it, would force me to confess it and to say the same things he says. Wherefore, I would gladly hear from you if you can guess the prophecy of Cratylus in any way; but I would more gladly hear your opinion about the correctness of names, if it pleases you.

**SOCRATES.** O Hermogenes, son of Hipponicus, an old proverb [[abbrev: ꝑuerbio → prouerbio]] says: "Beautiful things are difficult to know." And yet that knowledge of names is no small thing. Indeed, if I had already heard from Prodicus that fifty-drachma demonstration, in the tradition of which these things were also included (as he himself testifies), nothing would prevent you from immediately understanding the truth about the correctness of names. But I never heard that one, but only the one-drachma version. Wherefore, what may be true in these things, I do not know; but I am ready to investigate together with you and with Cratylus. But as for his saying that your name is not truly "Hermogenes" (which is said to come from Hermes/gain), he is biting you, I think, as if you were greedy for money and lacking your wish. But, as I just said, these things are difficult to know. It is necessary to search by bringing forth the reasons on both sides: whether it is as you yourself say, or rather as Cratylus says.

**HERMOGENES.** Truly, Socrates, although I have already disputed frequently with him and many others, I cannot yet be persuaded that the correctness of a name is anything other than convention (*conuentio*) and consensus (*consensio*). To me indeed, it seems that whatever name anyone imposes on anything, that is the correct one. And if again he changes it, and imposes another, the succeeding name exists no less correctly than the first, just as we are accustomed to change the names of slaves: for no name belongs to any thing by nature, but by law (*lege*) and the use (*usu*) of those who have become accustomed so to call it. If this is otherwise, I am ready to learn and hear it not only from Cratylus, but from anyone else.

**SOCRATES.** Perhaps you are saying something, Hermogenes. Let us consider then: do you assert that whatever name anyone imposes and calls anything, that is its name?

**HERMOGENES.** It certainly seems so to me.

**SOCRATES.** And whether a private person calls it so, or the city?

**HERMOGENES.** I assert it.

**SOCRATES.** What then if I myself call some thing—as if what we now call a "man," I should name a "horse," or what we call a "horse," a "man"? Publicly it will be a "man" to the same thing, privately a "horse"; and privately again a "man," publicly a "horse." Do you speak so?

**HERMOGENES.** So it seems.

**SOCRATES.** Tell me again, do you call anything "speaking truly," and something "speaking falsely"?

**HERMOGENES.** Indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Will not that speech be true, and the other speech false?

**HERMOGENES.** Precisely.

**SOCRATES.** Is that speech which says of existing things that they exist, true; and that which says they exist as they do not exist, false?

**HERMOGENES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Is this it: to say in speech those things which are, and those which are not?

**HERMOGENES.** That very thing.

**SOCRATES.** Regarding speech which is true: is it true as a whole, while the parts are not true?

**HERMOGENES.** Rather, the parts are also true.

**SOCRATES.** Are the large parts true, but the tiny particles false, or are they all true?

**HERMOGENES.** I think all.

**SOCRATES.** Have you any part of speech smaller than a name?

**HERMOGENES.** By no means, for this is the minimum part.

**SOCRATES.** And this name is a part of true speech?

**HERMOGENES.** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES.** A true part, as you say yourself?

**HERMOGENES.** True.

**SOCRATES.** And a false part?

**HERMOGENES.** I say so.

**SOCRATES.** Is it permitted, then, to say a name is true and a name is false, if indeed one can say so of speech?

**HERMOGENES.** What prevents it?

**SOCRATES.** Whatever name anyone says is for a thing, is that its name?

**HERMOGENES.** That very thing.

**SOCRATES.** And however many names anyone attributes to it, will there be that many? And also whenever he attributes them?

**HERMOGENES.** I have no other correctness of names, Socrates, except this: that it is permitted to me to call a thing by one name which I have imposed, and to you by another which you have imposed. I see that cities have certain proper names of their own, and Greeks have them relative to other Greeks, and Greeks relative to Barbarians.

**SOCRATES.** Let us observe, Hermogenes, whether the things themselves seem to you to behave thus: whether the essence of things is proper to each individual, as Protagoras taught? Saying that man is the measure of all things, so that such as each thing appears to me, such it is to me; and such as it appears to you, so it is to you. Or rather do you think there are some things which have a certain firmness of their own essence?

**HERMOGENES.** Sometimes, Socrates, I have been led to these doubts by what Protagoras teaches. Yet I am not sufficiently persuaded that it is so.

**SOCRATES.** Have you ever been led to this: that it never seemed to you that any man was entirely bad?

**HERMOGENES.** No, by Jove, rather I have often been so affected as to think some men were entirely bad, and indeed very many.

**SOCRATES.** And have no good men yet appeared to you?

**HERMOGENES.** Very few.

**SOCRATES.** Do some exist then?

**HERMOGENES.** I say so.

**SOCRATES.** By what reason do you judge this? This one? That some are entirely good and entirely wise (*prudentes*); and others are entirely wicked and entirely foolish (*imprudentes*)?

**HERMOGENES.** So it seems to me.

**SOCRATES.** If Protagoras spoke truly, and this is the truth itself—that as each thing appears to each, such it is—is it possible that some of men are wise, and others foolish?

**HERMOGENES.** In no way.

**SOCRATES.** But since these things, I think, seem entirely so to you—namely that there is a certain wisdom and foolishness—it follows that Protagoras cannot be entirely speaking truly. For one will not truly be wiser than another if what appears to each is true to each.

**HERMOGENES.** It is so.

***

[[summary: This portion of the *Cratylus* introduces the debate between naturalism (names have an essential link to the thing) and conventionalism (names are arbitrary labels). Socrates begins by refuting the relativism of Protagoras to argue that things have a stable essence.]]
