How shall we rightly answer these men? For to me, at least, it seems thus: "We ourselves, O best of men, are the poets of a tragedy that is as beautiful and excellent as possible. Indeed, our entire republic is an imitation of the most beautiful and excellent life, which we certainly judge to be the truest tragedy. You, therefore, are poets, and we also are poets of the same poem, and as it were, rivals in the most beautiful work of tragedy, which only the true law, as we hope, can bring to perfection. But do not believe that it is easily allowed by us for you to set up stages in the forum and bring out loud-voiced actors who cry out louder than we do, and thus speak to our children, our wives, and the whole crowd of the city about the same matters—not the same things as we do, but often the opposite. For we would be entirely insane, as would the whole state, if we allowed you to perform before the magistrates have seen what you have composed and judged whether it should be spoken to the people. Now therefore, O children of the soft Muses, we shall compare those songs of yours with ours before the leaders; and if what is said seems to be the same as or better than ours, we will give you a chorus. But if otherwise, O friends, we can never give it."

Let these things be thus established concerning all dance and its instruction, and the laws and customs—and for servants, indeed, separately from the duties of masters—if it also seems right to you. 

CLINIAS: It certainly seems so. 

ATHENIAN: But for free men, three subjects of study still remain. One is the **calculation of numbers**. The second is the **measurement of length, width, and depth**. The third is the **knowledge of the circuit of the stars**. Not many will learn all these things exactly, but only a few, whom we shall designate as we progress toward the end. For so it is fitting. 

<margin>It is shameful not to know what is necessary.</margin>

But for the multitude, it is most rightly said that it is shameful not to know what is necessary. However, to search out everything exquisitely is neither easy nor entirely possible. What is necessary among these things cannot be rejected. Indeed, he seems to have looked toward this very thing who first spoke thus of God in a proverb: 

<margin>God will never fight with necessity.</margin>

"Not even God will ever fight with necessity," which I think should certainly be understood regarding divine necessities. For if this were said of human necessities—to which many look when they say such a thing—the speech would be by far the most foolish of all. 

CLINIAS: What then, Guest, are the necessities of learning that are not human, but divine? 

ATHENIAN: I think they are those which, if a person has not learned or experienced in any way, he could never be a god, nor a demon, nor a hero among men, such that he could studiously take care of humans. He will also be far from becoming a divine man if he cannot know one, or two, or three, or even/odd numbers at all, or if he does not know how to count, nor to number days and nights, nor has he grasped the revolutions of the sun and moon and the other stars. If anyone denies that any of these most beautiful teachings are necessary for a man who is to perceive anything, he will be thinking most foolishly. But what each of these is, and how many, and when they should be learned, and what should be learned with another, and what alone without others, and what the entire mixture of these is—all this must be learned rightly before everything else. Then, with these teachings as guides, one must proceed to the others. For so nature and necessity itself have obtained, by which we say no god either fights now or will ever fight.

CLINIAS: You speak rightly, Guest, and what you say seems to be spoken according to nature. 

ATHENIAN: So the matter stands, O Clinias. But it is difficult to bring forward laws concerning these things in an orderly fashion. Therefore, if it seems right, we will defer this to another time and handle it more diligently in the laws. 

CLINIAS: You seem, Guest, to fear our lack of skill in these matters. And not without reason. Nevertheless, try to explain them, fearing nothing on that account. 

ATHENIAN: I do indeed fear what 

[Right Column]

you say, but I dread much more those who have tasted these teachings, but tasted them badly. For it is not an altogether grave or hard thing to be ignorant of all things, nor is it the greatest evil; but a poorly acquired skill and knowledge of many things is much more ruinous. 

CLINIAS: You speak the truth. 

ATHENIAN: It is necessary, therefore, that free men learn those things which a great crowd of children in Egypt learn along with their letters. First, the teaching of calculation has been devised for the child's mind so that it is perceived with play and pleasure. A distribution of many or fewer apples and crowns is made using the same fitting numbers. The seating of boxers and wrestlers, and the alternating and following order of their association, is arranged as is customary. Furthermore, mixing gold, bronze, and silver bowls <note>original: "phialas"</note>, and others like them, while playing, or passing them all from one to another, they adapt the necessary numbers to the games, as I said. And thus they provide utility to the learners for leading armies, arranging camps, for household management, and for all other things, and they make them more alert. Then, since a shameful and ridiculous natural ignorance concerning the measurement of length, width, and depth holds all men, 

<margin>analysis and logic of [unclear] genius</margin>

they lead them far away from this. 

CLINIAS: What and what kind of ignorance do you mean? 

ATHENIAN: O friend Clinias, even I, when I had heard of it, finally wondered at this ignorance of ours; it seemed to me to be the consideration not of men, but of swine and cattle. And therefore I blushed vehemently, not only for my own sake, but for the sake of all Greeks. 

CLINIAS: Speak more clearly, Guest, as to what this is. 

ATHENIAN: I will indeed speak. Or rather, I will reveal it by questioning. Answer, I pray. Do you know length? 

CLINIAS: Why not? 

ATHENIAN: What about width? 

CLINIAS: Certainly. 

ATHENIAN: And that these are two, and depth is the third? 

CLINIAS: That too. 

ATHENIAN: Do all these seem to you to be able to be measured against each other <note>i.e., to be "commensurable" or have a common ratio</note>? 

CLINIAS: Surely. 

ATHENIAN: I mean that length can be measured against length, width against width, and depth similarly, by nature. 

CLINIAS: Most vehemently so. 

ATHENIAN: But if some things can do this neither vehemently nor weakly—but some can, and others not at all—and you, however, think that all things can, how do you feel about this? 

CLINIAS: Badly. 

ATHENIAN: Again, what of length and width and depth, or width and length against each other? Do not all Greeks think they can be measured against each other in some way? 

CLINIAS: Entirely so. 

ATHENIAN: But if they can by no means be measured, yet all Greeks, as I was saying, think they can: is it not right that we, moved by shame for all of them, should say to them: "This is one of those things, O best of Greeks, which we were saying it is shameful to be ignorant of; but to know it is necessary, though not altogether a glorious thing." 

CLINIAS: Why not? 

ATHENIAN: Moreover, there are certain other things related to these, in which we for the most part err similarly. 

CLINIAS: What are they? 

ATHENIAN: By what nature it has come to pass that some things can be measured against each other, while others cannot; it is certainly necessary to know these, or else the one who is ignorant is entirely useless. In these matters, therefore, we ought to linger for the sake of the mind. For this "old man's game" will be much more pleasant than dice and gaming tables, and more worthy of a free man. 

CLINIAS: Perhaps. For these games and these teachings seem to differ greatly from one another.

### THE DIALOGUE OF PLATO

**ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Following what has been said, we must now arrange the festivals with the advice of the Delphic oracles. We must determine by law which sacrifices and which gods are better and more profitable for the city to honor, and at what times they should be celebrated. There should be nearly <note>original: *ferme*</note> three hundred and sixty-five such gatherings, so that at least one magistrate is always performing a sacrifice on behalf of the city, its people, and their property.

**CLINIAS:** That seems appropriate.

**ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, we must consider the contests of the musicians <note>original: *musicos*</note> and the athletes. We should not grant the right to compose poetry or songs to everyone. Even if a man is more skilled in music than Thamyris <note>A mythical Thracian singer who was so arrogant about his talent that he challenged the Muses to a contest; he was defeated, blinded, and stripped of his musical memory</note> or more melodious than Orpheus, he shall not be permitted to perform unless his life is seen to be honorable. We must prioritize those poets who are themselves good men and held in high honor within the city, specifically those who have performed noble deeds. This includes those who have conducted <note>original: *gesserunt*</note> themselves bravely in the business of war <note>original: *belli*</note> or other civic duties. Their songs shall be performed, even if they lack the polished technique of the professional poets.

**CLINIAS:** This is a most excellent standard for our city.

**ATHENIAN:** Truly, the legislator should ensure that the youth are trained not just in the arts, but in the imitation of those who have lived well. For in this way, the entire city remains harmonious.

...we shall set the course at two-thirds of the distance for boys: for children, half of that. These shall compete with the archers and other armed participants. For the females, however, we shall set a stadium race for girls not yet reached puberty, who will compete naked in the *diaulos* <note>original: δίαυλον; a double-lap race where runners turn around a post</note>, the equestrian course, and the *dolichos* <note>original: δολιχόν; a long-distance race of several kilometers</note>. But after the thirteenth year of age, until they are married, they shall enter the running contests from no later than their twentieth year and no earlier than their eighteenth. These, however, must wear appropriate clothing. Let this be what is said concerning the races for both men and women.

To increase physical strength, in place of wrestling and similar sports as they are now practiced, more serious forms should be desired. Contests should be held one-on-one, two-on-two, and up to ten-on-ten. What a victor ought to do or not endure—just as was recently determined for the wrestling school by the masters of wrestling regarding what constitutes good or bad technique—so too in these contests of love <note>The Latin *amorum certaminibus* here likely refers to "contests of passion" or high-spirited rivalry</note>, experts must be brought in to establish by law what an athlete wins by doing or refusing to endure, and what order determines the loser. These same laws shall be understood to apply to females as well, until they reach a marriageable age.

Furthermore, all peltastic <note>Fighting style of the *peltast*, a light-infantry soldier carrying a small shield</note> combat should be set against the pancratiac <note>A "no-holds-barred" ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling</note> contest: they shall compete with the bow, the light shield, spears, hand-thrown stones, and the sling. To whoever conducts himself best in these things, honors for victory shall be granted by law.

Now let us look at the horse-racing contests. The use of horses is not great in Crete. Therefore, the effort put into breeding horses and competing with them must necessarily be of less concern to the Cretans. For none of you keeps chariots, nor do you consider it noble to spend effort on such a thing. Since this is not customary, to establish laws for such competitors would seem the work of a madman. However, for individual horses—both those that have not yet shed their foal teeth (colts), and those of middle age or full-grown—it is permitted to grant equestrian games according to the nature of the region. Let such a contest be according to the law, and in it, the judgment shall be jointly granted to the masters of the horse and the tribunes, both for the general horse racing and for those who compete in armor. For those not in armor, we impose no contest or prize, neither in the gymnastic games nor here. But a man who can shoot an arrow or throw a javelin from a horse is not useless to Crete. Therefore, for the sake of sport, a competition and contest should be held in this as well.

To these things, however, women are not to be compelled by laws. But if, through prior training and custom, their nature rouses girls and virgins toward these things and makes them not shrink from them, they are to be admitted. 

But of the exercise and gymnastic discipline—whether what we perform in contests or what we practice daily under masters—we have now said enough. Of music also, for the most part. But concerning the rhapsodes (that is, the singers of poems) and those who follow them, and concerning the competition of choruses—however many are necessarily established for the solemnities of the gods and spirits on fixed days, months, and years—how all these things are to be arranged, and if they should occur every three or even every five years, these things will be understood and acted upon by the counsel of the gods. Then indeed, the musical contests will take place in turn, just as the athletes themselves—the declarers of prizes, the teacher of youth, and the guardians of the law who have the authority to bring forward these laws—have gathered together and ordained. For these men shall ordain when, who, and with whom each contest in all choruses and dances ought to be practiced. But what each of these should be like regarding the speech, the songs, or the harmonies mixed with rhythms and dances, has been said many times by

**[Right Column]**

the first legislator. Those who follow him, as is fitting for each sacred time, will distribute each contest and establish feast days for the city. These and other such matters are not difficult to understand in terms of how they should be ordered by laws; nor, if they are changed in one way or another, do they greatly benefit or harm the city.

However, there are some matters to be valued most highly, which are so difficult to persuade people of that they seem to be the work of a god, if they could be established by him. But now they require the work of some bold man who, relying greatly on freedom of speech, may establish what he deems best for the city and the citizens. He must do this so as to recall the corrupted souls of the citizens to a decent habit and the observation of the laws, while opposing their most burning desires, and following reason alone even when lacking any help.

**CLINIAS:** What are you saying, Guest? For we do not understand this.

**ATHENIAN:** It is likely so. But I will try to speak more clearly. For when I considered the discipline of life itself and saw young men and women conversing kindly with one another, I feared—as is right—considering how someone might behave in a city where the young men and women are delicate, and have not been tamed by great and very hard labors by which lust and petulance are extinguished; but rather where everyone spends much time on feast days, sacrifices, and choruses. How, then, in this city will they abstain from those desires that have led many to the extreme, so that the reason which commands them to abstain becomes law?

Certainly, if the higher laws drive many desires away from us, it is no wonder. For that institution by which excessive wealth is prohibited contributes not a little to temperance, and all that discipline we set out above has laws suitable for these things. Furthermore, the eyes of the leaders, compelled to look nowhere else but to always observe the youth, apply a limit to other human desires. But as for the loves of young men and women against nature, and the abuse of men for females and women for males <note>A discussion of same-sex relations and the regulation of sexual conduct to ensure it aligns with "nature" and the production of offspring</note>, from which innumerable evils have followed for men both privately and publicly—how shall someone avoid these? And what remedy will he find in the dangers of individuals? 

It is altogether difficult, O Clinias. For in many other things, all of Crete and Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> help us greatly in setting down laws different from the customs of many, but as far as it pertains to loves, they are entirely opposed and in disagreement. Since if someone, following that nature which existed before the time of Laius <note>In Greek mythology, Laius (father of Oedipus) was said to have introduced pederasty by kidnapping Pelops' son</note>, should set a law not permitting males to abuse others as they would females, and should cite the nature of beasts as a witness—among whom males do not have sexual relations with one another because it is not at all according to nature—he will perhaps use a plausible reason, but it will not harmonize with your cities. To this is added that he will by no means achieve what must always be observed by a legislator. For it must always be observed what the law decrees that leads to virtue, and what does not. 

Come then, if we agree that this is honorable or not shameful by law, what will it profit toward virtue? Will it generate a habit of fortitude in the soul of the one who was persuaded to admit a shameful thing into himself, or a likeness of temperance in the one who persuaded him? Or will no one ever believe these things, but rather the contrary? Indeed, everyone will blame the softness of one serving pleasures. In the case of one who imitates females, will not everyone disapprove of that very womanly image? Who then...

...of men, since it is such a thing, will he sanction it by laws? Hardly anyone who has the true law in his mind. How, then, do we say this is true? Certainly, it is necessary to consider the nature of friendship, of desire, and of loves, if anyone is to perceive these matters rightly. For since there are two distinct types, and a third species arising from both, all encompassed by a single name, they create total doubt and darkness. **CLINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** For we assert that a friend is one who is similar to another in virtue, and equal to an equal. Again, we call the needy man a friend to the rich man, even though they are of a contrary kind. But when either of these becomes more vehement, we call it "love." **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** Friendship, therefore, which proceeds from contraries, is harsh and rough, and often lacks a reciprocal feeling within us. But that which comes from similarities is peaceful and shared throughout life. However, when benevolence is composed of both, it is first not easily recognized what the person who loves with this "third love" intends for himself; then, pulled by both directions into contraries, he himself doubts what he should do, since he is urged by one side to enjoy the bloom of youth, while by the other he is prohibited. For he who loves the body, and hungrily seeks its beauty as if it were a kind of fruit, seeks only to be satisfied, and offers no honor to the soul of the beloved. But he who cares less for the body, and considers the soul rather than desiring the flesh—since he loves the soul itself as is proper—considers the use of the body to be insolence and an outrage. Because he reveres and cultivates temperance, courage, magnificence, and prudence, he will wish to live chastely with a chaste friend. Now, the love composed of both of these is the very one we just placed in the third position. Since there are three loves, are all to be driven out by law? Or shall we clearly accept into the city the one that looks toward virtue and desires the youth to become as good as possible, while we repel the other two, if it can be done? Does it seem otherwise to you, my friend Megillus? **MEGILLUS.** You have spoken quite excellently on these matters just now, Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** It was not in vain, my friend, that I guessed you would agree with me. It is not necessary for me now to inquire what your law feels about these things, but to accept what you admit. I will try to persuade Clinias of this later. Let what has been granted by you be accepted for now, and let us consider the laws diligently. **MEGILLUS.** You speak most rightly. **ATHENIAN.** I have a certain art <note>The "art" referred to here is the rhetorical skill of the legislator to make difficult laws seem natural or divinely ordained.</note> in bringing forth this law, which is partly easy and partly entirely difficult. **MEGILLUS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** It is well known even now that many men, though they may be unjust, well and diligently—and not unwillingly, but quite spontaneously—abstain from the union with beautiful people. **MEGILLUS.** When does that happen? **ATHENIAN.** When a brother or a sister possesses extraordinary beauty for someone. The same law, although it is not written, sufficiently repels a son from a daughter, and prohibits both manifest and secret intercourse of that kind. Indeed, it ensures that not even any desire for this thing approaches the common people. **MEGILLUS.** You tell the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, a single and very brief word has extinguished all pleasures of this sort. **MEGILLUS.** What word is that? **ATHENIAN.** That it is said that none of these things is "divinely right" <note>original: *fas*; refers to what is permissible under divine law</note>, but they are held in hatred by God, and are the most shameful of all shameful things. And is this not the cause? Because no one speaks otherwise, but immediately from a tender age, heard both in jest and in earnest, and very often in tragedies, these same things are told—whenever a Thyestes, or an Oedipus, or certain Macareuses who had secret affairs with their sisters, are seen to have immediately brought death upon themselves as the deserved penalty for their crime. **MEGILLUS.** That is rightly said. For we know the wonderful power of "fame" <note>original: *famae*; here meaning public reputation or common report</note>,

**[Column 2]**

when no one dares to even breathe otherwise than the law commands. **ATHENIAN.** Is it not rightly proclaimed by us, that for a legislator wishing to subject to reason any of those desires that vehemently subdue men, the method is easy to recognize? For if he dedicates a "fame" of this sort among all—slaves and free, males and females, and the entire city—as if it were something sacred, he will make this law most firm. **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. But by what means can he achieve it, so that everyone willingly says the same thing? **ATHENIAN.** You have raised a good objection. For this reason I said I have an art for this law: so that men may use love according to nature for procreation. Therefore, I command that they abstain from males. For those who use those ways deliberately destroy the human race, "sowing upon stone" <note>A metaphor for non-procreative sex, where the "seed" cannot take root</note> where what is sown can never take root. One must also abstain from that "feminine field" where the seed would not wish to produce sprouts. If this law is preserved perpetually in other matters just as in the intercourse of parents, it will be the cause of innumerable goods. For first, it will be established according to nature. Then it will repel men from all the rage and madness of loves, from adulteries, and from excessive luxury in drink and food. It will also reconcile husbands to their wives, and bring forth many other goods, if it remains stable in everyone. But perhaps if some vehement young man, full of "much seed" <note>original: *multo spermate plenus*; a Renaissance medical view that an excess of seminal fluid caused uncontrollable sexual urges</note>, hears this law being proposed, he will immediately disapprove and cry out with a loud voice that impossible and foolish things are being sanctioned by us in law. Considering this, I said I had an art that was in one way very easy, and in another way very difficult, for observing this law. For it is easy to understand how it is possible. Since, when this legitimate opinion has been dedicated among all, it will tame all minds and ensure that they obey the established laws through fear. But matters have now reached a point where it seems it can never be achieved—just as the practice of the "common meal" <note>original: *convivii*; referring to the Spartan *syssitia*, or public mess halls</note> was once believed to be impossible for an entire city to observe perpetually. And yet among us <note>The Athenian is likely referring to the Cretan or Spartan systems where public meals were successfully implemented</note> it is seen to happen in reality, which among women, and indeed in your own cities, is thought impossible to occur. For this reason, because of the power of this disbelief, I said it was most difficult for both of these to be preserved by law. **MEGILLUS.** And rightly so. **ATHENIAN.** But since they are not beyond human strength, but can be done, do you want me to explain a certain plausible reason to you? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Whether will someone more easily abstain from sexual matters, and wish to moderately preserve the order imposed on them, when the body has been well-affected by some prudent diligence, or when it is the contrary? **CLINIAS.** Much more so when it is done well and skillfully. **ATHENIAN.** Have we not, then, heard of Iccus of Tarentum? Shall our young men not be able to do so for the sake of a far more excellent victory? Which we in songs and fables...

...he shall restore double the damage to his neighbor. Let there be a common sharing of the fruits of autumn in this manner. God grants us two gifts of grace here: one from Dionysus <note>Dionysus is the ancient Greek god of wine, theater, and ecstasy; his "gift" here refers to grapes used for winemaking.</note>, which cannot be stored away; the other, however, is suitable for being kept <note>This likely refers to "table grapes" or fruits like figs that can be dried and preserved for later use.</note>. Therefore, let this law be established concerning fruits: Whoever tastes grapes or figs from the rustic fruits before the time of the vintage—which coincides with the rising of Arcturus <note>Arcturus is a bright star in the constellation Boötes; its appearance in the dawn sky in mid-September traditionally signaled the start of the grape harvest in the ancient Mediterranean.</note>—if he gathers them from his own field, let him pay fifty drachmas <term>drachma</term> <note>A standard silver coin in ancient Greece. Fifty drachmas was a significant fine, roughly equivalent to two months' wages for a skilled laborer.</note> to be dedicated to Dionysus. If he takes them from his neighbors, he shall pay a mina <term>mina</term> <note>A unit of currency equal to 100 drachmas.</note>; and if from others, two-thirds of a mina. 

However, as for grapes and figs of the "noble" kind, which we have named and which cannot be conveniently stored away, he may gather them how and when he wishes if they are his own property. But if they belong to another, unless he has obtained permission—since the law is that no one should move what he did not put down <note>original: "nemo moueat quæ non depoſuit" — a fundamental legal maxim in the ancient world regarding theft and property rights.</note>—he who takes them shall be fined. But if any slave takes them, without having persuaded the master of the field, for every single fig and grape seed, equal...

-> SOCRATES: And is speaking not one of these operations? HERMOGENES: It certainly is. SOCRATES: Will a person speak correctly if they speak however they see fit? Or rather, if they speak as the very nature of things requires them to speak and be spoken of? If they speak in the way nature demands, they will succeed in saying something; but if they do otherwise, they will err and accomplish nothing. HERMOGENES: I think it is exactly as you say. SOCRATES: [[abbrev: Is naming not a certain part of speaking?]] And do those who name not speak, in a certain way? HERMOGENES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And naming is a certain action, since speaking is a certain action concerning things. HERMOGENES: Precisely. SOCRATES: Actions, however, have shown us that they do not depend on us, but possess a certain nature of their own. HERMOGENES: That is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, we must name according to the reason by which the nature of things demands they be named and be spoken of, and in the way it demands—not according to the whim of our own will, if we are to stand by what has been said. HERMOGENES: With something. SOCRATES: And that which is to be woven must be woven with something, and that which is to be bored must be bored with something. HERMOGENES: Clearly. SOCRATES: Likewise, that which is to be named must be named with something. HERMOGENES: So it must be. SOCRATES: What is that with which one must bore something? HERMOGENES: A drill (*terebra*). SOCRATES: What with which one must weave? HERMOGENES: A shuttle (*radius*) and a comb (*pecten*). SOCRATES: What with which one must name? HERMOGENES: A name (*nomen*). SOCRATES: You speak well; therefore, a name is a kind of instrument. [[abbrev: HERMOGENES: It is.]] SOCRATES: If I asked what kind of instrument a shuttle or comb is, would you answer "that with which we weave"? HERMOGENES: Nothing else. SOCRATES: When we weave, what do we do? Do we not use the shuttle to separate the warp and the woof which were confused? HERMOGENES: Exactly that. SOCRATES: You would answer the same regarding the drill and the rest? HERMOGENES: The same. SOCRATES: Can you likewise declare concerning the name: what do we do when we name something with the name itself, which is the instrument? HERMOGENES: I cannot. SOCRATES: Do we not teach one another something, and distinguish things as they are?
[[margin: A name is an instrument for teaching and distinguishing the essences of things.]]
HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: A name, then, is an instrument for teaching and distinguishing the essences (*substantiae*) of things, just as the comb and shuttle are for the web. HERMOGENES: So it must be said. SOCRATES: Furthermore, the shuttle is the instrument of weavers. HERMOGENES: Why not? SOCRATES: A weaver, then, will use the shuttle and comb correctly—correctly, I say, according to the logic of weaving. But will the one who teaches use the name correctly—correctly, obviously, according to the proper logic of teaching? HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Whose work does the weaver use well when he employs the shuttle and comb? HERMOGENES: The carpenter’s (*faber lignarius*). SOCRATES: Any carpenter at all, or rather the one who possesses the craft? HERMOGENES: The one who has the craft. SOCRATES: Likewise, whose work does the borer use correctly when he uses the drill? HERMOGENES: The blacksmith’s (*faber aerarius*). SOCRATES: Is every blacksmith a craftsman, or rather the one who has the skill? HERMOGENES: The one with the skill. SOCRATES: Come then, tell me: whose work does the teacher use whenever he uses a name? HERMOGENES: I do not know. SOCRATES: Can you not even assign this? Who hands down to us the names we use? HERMOGENES: I am ignorant of this too. SOCRATES: Does it not seem to you that the law has established names for us? HERMOGENES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore, the teacher will use the work of the legislator (*legislator*) when he uses the name. HERMOGENES: I think so. SOCRATES: Does any law-setter seem to you to be equal, or rather the one who is endowed with the craft? HERMOGENES: The one endowed with the craft. SOCRATES: Therefore, Hermogenes, it is not for any man to impose a name, as if anyone were an author of names; but here also, as it seems, it is the *nominũ inſtitutor* (setter of names),
[[margin: * In Greek, the legislator. Ficino [[notes: Latin "Ficanus" is a typo for Marsilio Ficino, the Platonist translator]] calls him the ὀνομαθοθετης (*onomatothetes* / name-giver).]]
who is found to be rarer than any other craftsman among men. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Observe, I pray, where the setter of names looks when he imposes names on things. Rather, judge from the previous examples: where does the carpenter look when he makes the shuttle and the comb? Is it not toward something that is by nature fit for weaving? HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: If this shuttle breaks during the work, will he make another according to the image of the broken one? Or will he rather look toward the "form" (*species*) itself, according to which exemplar he had made the one that broke? HERMOGENES: Toward the form itself, I believe. SOCRATES: Would we not rightly call that form itself the "logic of the shuttle," and the "shuttle itself" in the highest sense? HERMOGENES: I think so. SOCRATES: If it ever becomes necessary to prepare a shuttle for a fine garment or a thicker one, whether of linen or wool or anything else, every single shuttle must have the "form" of the shuttle itself; but whichever kind is naturally most suited to each thing, that kind must be applied to finish the work as nature demands. HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: The same logic applies to other instruments. For whatever tool naturally fits each thing must be found and assigned to it, so that the craftsman produces not just whatever he wants, but what nature itself requires. For one must know how to perfect in iron the drill suited for each task. HERMOGENES: It is clear. SOCRATES: And also the shuttle appropriate for each type of wood. HERMOGENES: These things are true. SOCRATES: Indeed, by the very logic of nature, one shuttle is suited for one web and another for another, and similarly in other cases. HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES:
[[margin: How one will name and correctly name.]]
It is also necessary, my good man, that the setter of names express in voices and syllables the name that is by nature suited to each thing. Looking toward that which is the name itself, he should fashion and assign each name, if he is truly to be an author of names. [[abbrev: Because]] if every founder of names does not express the name in the same syllables, we must notice that not even all blacksmiths use the same iron whenever they make the same instrument for the same purpose. HERMOGENES: I agree. SOCRATES: Who is going to recognize whether the suitable form of the shuttle has been impressed upon any given wood? Is it the carpenter who makes it? Is it not the one who can instruct the maker, and judge whether the work has been done correctly or otherwise? HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Who then? HERMOGENES: The lyre-player (*citharista*). SOCRATES: And is he not the one who knows how to ask questions? HERMOGENES: That is the one. SOCRATES: And also how to answer? HERMOGENES: Of course. SOCRATES: But do you call the one who knows how to ask and answer anything other than a *dialecticus* (dialectician)? HERMOGENES: A dialectician, surely. SOCRATES: It is the carpenter's job to make a tiller at the pilot’s instruction, if the tiller is to be good. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: So too, the author of names must establish the name with the dialectician advising him, if the names are to be correctly placed.
[[margin: The Dialectician knows whether names are correctly imposed on things or not.]]
HERMOGENES: These things are true. SOCRATES: It appears then, Hermogenes, that the imposition of a name is not a trivial matter, as you think, nor is it the work of unskilled or random men. Indeed, Cratylus

speaks the truth when he says that names belong to things by nature, and that not just anyone is an author of names, but only that one who looks to the name that naturally fits each thing, and who can then interpret that "form" (*species*) into letters and syllables. HERMOGENES: I do not know, Socrates, by what logic I should fight against what you have said. Perhaps it is not easy to be persuaded so suddenly. But I think I would rather agree with you in this way, if you would show me what you say the "natural right reason of a name" is. SOCRATES: Indeed, blessed Hermogenes, I am learning none yet; for the discourse I spoke of above has slipped from my memory—namely, that I am ignorant of this and am searching for it together with you. But now, as we investigate together, this much at least has been found beyond what was said before: that a name has a certain natural correctness, and not just anyone can accommodate a name to things. Is it not so? HERMOGENES: Highly so. SOCRATES: It remains to be considered, if you desire to know, what exactly the correctness of the name itself is—that is, its right reason. HERMOGENES: I do indeed desire it. SOCRATES: Observe, then. HERMOGENES: By what path do you advise we investigate? SOCRATES: The most correct way, my friend, is to seek these things from those who know, having offered money and given thanks besides. HERMOGENES: How absurd this petition would be, Socrates, if, since I in no way accept that "Truth" of Protagoras, I were to value things said from that truth as being of any price!
[[margin: The title of the book "Truth," or an irony. [[notes: Referring to Protagoras's book *Truth*.]]]]
SOCRATES: But if these things do not please you, we must learn from Homerus and the other poets. HERMOGENES: What does Homerus teach about names, and where? SOCRATES: In many places throughout, but the greatest and most beautiful are those in which he distinguishes between the names used by men and those introduced by the gods themselves. Do you not think he teaches something magnificent and wonderful about the right reason of names in these passages? For it is clear that the gods use those names according to their actual correctness, which consist in nature. Do you not think so? HERMOGENES: I certainly know that if the gods call things something, they name them very correctly. But what are those names? SOCRATES:
[[margin: Iliad, Book 20 [[notes: Latin "υ" is the 20th letter]]]]
Do you not know what he says of the Trojan river that fought in single combat with Vulcanus (Hephaestus)? That the gods call it Xanthus, but men call it Scamandrus. HERMOGENES: I know. SOCRATES: Do you not think it is a magnificent thing to know this—by what logic it is more correct to name that river Xanthus than Scamandrus? Or if you wish, observe this too: that he says the same bird is called
[[margin: Iliad, Book 14 [[notes: Latin "ξ" is 14th]]]]
*Chalcis* by the gods, but *Cymindis* by men. Do you think this is trivial knowledge, to know how much more correct it is to call the same bird Chalcis rather than Cymindis, or Batieia and Myrine, and many others, both in this poet and in others? But the discovery of these things requires a sharper wit than ours. However, *Scamandrius* and *Astyanax* (the names of Hector’s son) can, as it seems to me, be comprehended by human wit and easily perceived—what Homerus wants the correctness in these names to be. Do you know the verses in which these are found? HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Which of these names do you think Homerus thought more suitable for the boy: *Astyanax* or *Scamandrius*? HERMOGENES: I do not know. SOCRATES: Consider it this way: if someone asked you whether you think the wiser or the less wise impose names on things more correctly? HERMOGENES: I would answer the wiser. SOCRATES: Do women in cities seem wiser to you, or men? As far as the gender is concerned. HERMOGENES: Men. SOCRATES:
[[margin: Homer says Scamandrius was named by Hector. Astyanax by the city.]]
Do you not know what Homerus says: that Hector’s son was called *Astyanax* by the Trojans, but *Scamandrius* by the women? Since the men were accustomed to call him Astyanax. HERMOGENES: So it seems. SOCRATES: Did Homerus not think the Trojan men were wiser than their women? HERMOGENES: I think so. SOCRATES: He judged, therefore, that he was more correctly named *Astyanax* than *Scamandrius*. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Let us observe what reason he himself brings for this denomination. "For he alone," he says, "protected the city and the wide walls for them." For this reason, it is fitting, as it seems, to name the son of the Preserver *Astyanax*—that is, the king of the city—of that city, I say, which his father saved, as Homerus says. HERMOGENES: The same seems true to me as well. SOCRATES: But as for why this is especially so, I myself do not yet sufficiently understand, Hermogenes. Do you perceive it? HERMOGENES: Not by Jupiter! SOCRATES: And yet, my good man, Homerus himself imposed the name on Hector. HERMOGENES: Why? SOCRATES: Because it seems to me that the name *Hector* is very close to *Astyanax*; for they signify almost the same thing, and the Greeks think both these are royal names. For of whatever thing one is the *anax* (that is, king), he is also the *hektor* (that is, possessor). For it is clear that he rules it, possesses it, and has it. Or perhaps I seem to be saying nothing? And am I deceived by the opinion by which I trusted I was reaching Homerus’s knowledge concerning the correctness of names, as if by certain tracks? HERMOGENES: Not at all, I think; for perhaps you are onto something. SOCRATES: It is fitting, as it seems to me, to similarly name the son of a lion a lion, and the son of a horse a horse. I certainly do not mean if some monster is born from a horse as something other than a horse; but I mean that which is born according to the nature of its genus. For if the son of a bull naturally produces a horse, it is not a calf that is born, but it must be called a horse-colt. And if a horse, contrary to nature, begets a calf, it must not be called a horse-colt, but a calf. Nor if from a human some offspring other than human is produced, should that which is born be called a human. The same is to be judged of trees and all other things. Do you approve of these things? HERMOGENES: I do indeed. SOCRATES: Watch me, lest I defraud you of anything. For by the same logic, if someone is born from a king, he must be named a king. Whether the same thing is signified in different syllables matters nothing; it does not matter if some letter is added or even subtracted, so long as the essence (*essentia*) of the thing signified shines forth as dominant in the name itself. HERMOGENES: What do you mean by that? SOCRATES: I am saying nothing strange or new, but just as you see happen in the elements (letters). For you know that we say the "names" of the elements, but not the elements themselves, except for four [[notes: possibly referring to the vowels alpha, epsilon, etc., which can stand alone as names]]. For we say *alpha, beta, epsilon, gamma, delta, mu, lambda,* and *alla*. But for the others, both vowels and non-vowels, we establish names by adding other letters, and thus we pronounce them. But as long as we insert the shining power of the element itself, it is appropriate to call it by that name which signifies the element to us. This is apparent in *Beta*, where, although *e, t, a* are added, nothing prevented the nature of that element from being shown in the whole name, as the author of names intended. To such an extent did he skillfully give names to the letters. HERMOGENES: You seem to me to speak the truth. SOCRATES: Will the same logic not apply to a king? From a king will come a king, from a good man a good man, from a beautiful thing a beautiful thing, and in all other cases; similarly, from any genus another such thing will come, unless a monster is created, and they must be called by the same names.

[[summary: Socrates argues that names are not arbitrary conventions but instruments designed to reflect the natural essence of things. He uses analogies from craftsmanship and Homeric poetry to demonstrate that a "correct" name is one that captures the internal logic of the object, as judged by a dialectician.]]

# On the Laws, or, On Legislation: Dialogue IX, 577

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a description of a virtuous legislator or physician of the state.</note> ...he consoles with the kindest [words]: and he strives with words, as if with **magical incantations**, to make them healthy before he applies the medical hand. <note>original: "magicis carminibus." Plato often compared the persuasive "preambles" of laws to medical charms meant to win the patient's consent.</note> He then applies it in such a way that the ailing person hardly feels it, and conceives much more hope than pain, and gains not destruction from the pain, but salvation. 

A man of remarkable mercy punishes no one without consolation; he destroys no one he punishes; he preserves everyone to the best of his ability. Even those he punishes with death, he claims to liberate from <term>diseases of the soul</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, vice is viewed as a "disease" (morbus) of the soul that requires treatment just as the body requires medicine.</note>; thus, by the minor evil of death, he halts a soul-sickness that is otherwise immense and growing day by day. 

Indeed, he asserts it is better to depart from this life than to live with an incurable disease of either the soul or the body. Yet he deprives no one of this life unless he knows them to be incurable; nor does he wish any punishment inflicted by a law—which is good—to lead toward evil. In fact, he argues that punishment itself is good for many reasons: first, because it is just,

**On the Laws, or on Legislation, Dialogue IX.** [Page number] **579**

[Column 1]

...in that [lot] which must always remain the same and equal. <note>In Plato’s *Laws*, the state is divided into 5,040 fixed "lots" of land (*sortes*) which were meant to remain within families to ensure economic stability and equality.</note> But when someone has committed acts that must be paid for by a monetary fine, whatever is possessed above the value of the lot should be paid out, so that the lot itself remains intact. The **Guardians of the Laws** <term>Guardians of the Laws</term> <note>The *Nomophylakes*, a high council of thirty-seven officials responsible for overseeing the administration of the laws and the conduct of citizens.</note> shall always report the exact truth of this matter to the judges based on the recorded census, so that no one may ever be deprived of their lot due to a lack of money. 

If someone is deemed worthy of a greater penalty and is not freed by the guarantee or generosity of friends, let them be punished with visible and long-lasting chains and other shames. No sin should go unpunished, nor should any fugitive escape without penalty; rather, let them pay the penalty either by being struck with death, or by chains, or by lashings, or by sitting or standing ignobly in sacred places led to the borders of the region, or by being fined in money according to the method we stated. 

The judges for a <term>capital crime</term> <note>Refers to a crime involving the loss of "caput" (status or life), essentially the most serious offenses.</note> shall be the Guardians of the Laws, along with the best among those who served as magistrates in the year immediately preceding. In what manner the accusations, summons, and similar things ought to be done, let later legislators determine. However, it is our duty to prescribe by law the manner of voting and sentencing. Let these things, therefore, be conducted openly. 

But before this, let the judges sit as close as possible before the accuser and the defendant, while preserving their dignity. Let all citizens who have abundant leisure be present and listen diligently to such trials. In these trials, once the first speech has been delivered by the accuser, let the defender speak second. Then let the eldest of the judges sufficiently examine what has been said with all possible diligence; after him, let all the others consider whatever each thinks should be investigated from what was said—or not said—by the adversaries. Anyone who deems nothing worthy of their own discussion should leave the examination to another. 

At length, let the writings that were then concluded be deposited in the **sanctuary of Vesta** <note>Vesta (Hestia) was the goddess of the hearth; her sanctuary served as the symbolic and administrative center of the Greek city-state, where important documents were kept for safety and sanctity.</note>, with the seals of all the judges included. On the following day, having gathered again in the same place, let them examine and judge in the same manner; and having applied their seals to all that was said, let them deposit the records. And when they have done this similarly a third time, with sufficient seals and witnesses having been gathered, let each judge—carrying his sacred vote and swearing by Vesta that he will judge truly and justly to the best of his power—bring an end to this trial. 

After sins committed against the gods, let those be discussed which are committed to the ruin of the republic. He who reduces the leadership to the will of a man and subjects the laws to him, thereby subjecting the state to factions and filling it with sedition by using force against the laws—this man is to be judged the greatest enemy of the whole state. The second enemy is he who, although not a participant in this crime, yet while performing the highest magistracies in that republic, does not notice these conspiracies, or if he does notice, does not aid his country due to a certain timidity. Therefore, let every man who strives to be a citizen of any value report these things to the judges and drag into court the man who, having plotted against his country, tries to turn it toward an unjust government by force. 

Let the judges of this crime be those who are judges of sacrilege, and let the whole trial be conducted similarly; and let the votes which win by majority condemn him to death. And to speak briefly, let children not pay for the sins of the father, unless the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have been successively guilty of a capital offense. These children the city shall send back to their ancestral homeland with their goods, the lot always excepted. And from the sons of citizens of whom there are more than one, being no less than ten years old, let them choose by lot those whom their fathers or grandfathers...

# On Laws, or on Lawmaking, Dialogue IX. 583

[Left Column]

...shall be purified <note>original: "purgatur"; this refers to "catharsis," a ritual cleansing required to remove the spiritual "miasma" or pollution caused by killing.</note> in a similar manner, and shall remain in exile for three full years. When he has returned, he shall neither share in the sacred rites with his children, nor share a table with them. If the parent or the son does not observe this, he may be accused of impiety <note>original: "impietatis"; a serious charge in Greek law involving the neglect of duties toward the gods or family.</note> by anyone who wishes to do so.

If a brother kills a brother or sister, or a sister kills a brother or sister in a fit of anger, they shall be purified and exiled in the same way as parents who have killed their children. After their return, they must not share in the sacred rites or the table of those whom they have deprived of brothers, sisters, or children. Whoever transgresses this law shall be rightfully condemned as impious.

But if someone is so overcome by anger that they kill a parent in an insane fury of wrath—if the parents, before they die, have voluntarily freed the killer from the charge of murder, then the killer shall be clean, provided they have been purified and performed the other required acts, just as those who commit an involuntary killing. But if they have not been freed, the one who killed is guilty under many laws. For they shall be subject to the ultimate punishments for murder, impiety, and sacrilege <note>original: "sacrilegij"; the logic here is that a parent's life is a sacred thing given by the gods.</note>, because they have taken the soul of the one who gave them life. Therefore, if it were possible for someone to die more than once, it would be most just for a parricide <note>term: parricide - the act of killing one's father, mother, or close relative.</note> to be killed multiple times. 

For to whom does any law grant the right to kill the parents from whom they were brought into the light, even if they see they are about to be killed by those parents in self-defense? Instead, the law commands them to endure all things rather than commit any such act. How else would it be possible to punish such a person justly? Therefore, the law decrees death for one who, provoked by anger, commits parricide. 

If, during an uprising or in any other way, a brother kills a brother who is attacking him in self-defense, let him be pure, as if he had killed an enemy. Furthermore, if a citizen kills a citizen, or a foreigner kills a foreigner, or a citizen a foreigner, or vice versa, in self-defense, let them similarly be clean. In the same way, if a slave kills a slave. But if a slave kills a free man in self-defense, he shall be subject to the same laws as a parricide <note>Plato’s code treats a slave's self-defense against a free citizen with extreme severity, equating it to the betrayal of a parent.</note>. 

What we have said regarding the release from the charge of killing a parent should also be understood as applying to all such releases. Therefore, if anyone voluntarily forgives any of the others, the killer shall be purified as if the murder were involuntary, and shall remain in exile for one year. 

Now, the matters regarding killings committed through violence, involuntarily, or through anger have been moderately explained. Next, let us speak of those acts committed voluntarily through total injustice, by treachery, because of the tyranny of pleasures, desires, and envy.

**CLEINIAS.** You speak rightly.

**ATHENIAN.** First, then, let us declare as best we can how many causes there are for voluntary murder. The greatest cause of this is the desire of a soul driven by lusts, which consists mostly of that heat which violently inflames the minds of many. This is surely that force which, because of nature and an ignorance of wealth, breeds an insatiable greed. The cause of this ignorance is that wealth is not rightly praised. For both Greeks and barbarians alike, though wealth holds only the third place among good things, they place it in the first; and by this opinion, they destroy both themselves and their descendants. We would live most excellently and beautifully if the true opinion about wealth were preached everywhere: that wealth exists for the sake of the body, and the body for the sake of the soul. Therefore, since those things for which wealth is possessed are good, wealth will hold the third rank, after the virtue of the soul and the body. This reasoning, therefore, will teach us like a schoolmistress that a man who intends to be happy should not seek wealth by any means, but only with justice and temperance. In this way, no murders that must be punished by more murders would be committed in cities. 

Now, however, as we said at the beginning of this discussion, this is the first and greatest thing that causes the greatest punishments for voluntary murder.

<margin>Those acts committed by those willing and knowing.</margin>

[Right Column]

The second cause is the habit of an ambitious soul, from which envies are born—first, a cruel envy toward the envious person themselves, and then toward the leading men of the city. 

The third place is held by great and unjust fears, which give birth to many murders when someone has done something, or is currently doing something, that they would wish no one to know about. Therefore, they remove by death those who seem likely to reveal such things, if it cannot be avoided otherwise. 

To all these things, let what we have said serve as preambles <note>original: "proœmia"; introductory explanations that provide the moral justification for a law before the penalty is stated.</note>. Moreover, there is a discourse which many who study the sacred solemnities hear and believe: that murderers are punished in the underworld, and having returned here again, they necessarily pay the penalties owed according to nature. For they are forced to suffer from others the very things they did to others in this life, by a similar fate. 

If anyone is persuaded by this and fears such punishments after being warned by this preamble, there is no need to set a law for him. But for a man of the opposite disposition, let this law be written: 

Whoever shall intentionally kill his fellow citizen with his own hand by injury, first, let him be far removed from the temples, the marketplace, the harbors, and every common assembly, so that he does not defile these by his presence, whether or not someone has forbidden him to be present. For the law itself forbids him, and prohibits it in such a way that it seems to always forbid and will continue to forbid him on behalf of the entire city. 

Next, for whoever does not prosecute him as is fitting, or does not keep him away—from the relatives of the slain man down to the cousins and second cousins—let the crime and the hatred of the gods first be turned upon them, just as the common curse and malediction of the law dictates. Then...

<meta>This page continues the legal codes regarding homicide, transitioning from accidental or anger-motivated killings discussed on the previous page to premeditated murder, parricide (killing of kin), suicide, and deaths caused by animals or objects.</meta>

584 Book Thirty-Four <note>While labeled "Book 34" in this specific Renaissance edition (likely by Marsilio Ficino), this text corresponds to Book IX of Plato's *Laws*.</note>

[Left Column]

...just as we judge those who kill with their own hand. If a slave voluntarily kills a free man, either by his own hand or by plotting, and has been condemned, let him be dragged by the public lictor <note>A public officer or executioner.</note> and avenger to the monument of the slain man, or to a place where he can see it, and let him be beaten as much as the judge who convicted him orders; if he survives the beating, let him be beaten until he dies. If anyone kills a slave who has done no wrong, fearing that the slave might reveal some disgraceful deed or for some other similar reason, let the killer be punished as if he had killed a citizen. 

Sometimes things happen about which it is difficult and troublesome to make laws, yet impossible not to. Of this kind are the voluntary and unjust killings of kinsmen, whether by one's own hand or by plot and treachery, which are committed most often in poorly governed cities, but sometimes even occur where no one would expect them. To avoid these crimes, let the previous discourse be repeated. For perhaps, having heard these things, someone will voluntarily abstain from such a wicked slaughter. 

For a story or a speech—or whatever other name this discourse should be called—was clearly spoken by ancient priests: that Justice is the observer and avenger of all things for the purpose of avenging kindred blood, using the law we just mentioned. Indeed, they say she decreed that whoever has perpetrated such a deed must necessarily suffer the same. Thus, if someone has put his father to death, he himself shall later, at a certain time, be violently killed by his sons; but if he has killed his mother, he himself shall later, having become a participant in the female nature <note>original: "particeps naturae muliebris effectus"; this refers to the ancient Greek concept of reincarnation, where a soul would be reborn as a woman to experience the same fate they inflicted.</note>, necessarily be slain at last by his own children. For when common blood is stained, there is no other purification, nor can the stain be wiped away in any other way, except when a wicked soul has atoned for the killing with a similar killing, and has appeased the anger of the whole family line. Therefore, men must be restrained from these crimes by the fear of such punishments which are sent by the gods. 

But if any should fall into such a miserable calamity that they dare to deprive a father or mother, brother, or son of life voluntarily and with foresight, the mortal legislator shall decree concerning such a crime: that once the proclamation is made, they shall be barred from public and sacred places, as was said above, and sureties shall likewise be required. And he who has been condemned for such a killing shall be put to death both by the officers of the judges and by the magistrates, and shall be dragged outside the city to a designated crossroads <note>original: "triuium"; a place where three roads meet, traditionally significant for religious purification.</note> naked, where each of the magistrates, on behalf of the entire city, shall throw a stone at the head of the dead man, and thus purify the whole city. Finally, having been carried beyond the borders of the region, let them cast him out unburied according to the laws. 

But what should be judged of him who has destroyed his closest and dearest friend with slaughter? I mean the one who deprives himself of life and his share of fate by a wicked force; not by the judgment of the city, nor forced by some sad and inevitable accident of fortune, nor compelled by some extreme shame, but through laziness and the weakness of a fearful soul, has unjustly inflicted death upon himself? What purifications and what burial are appropriate for such a man according to the law, God himself knows. Nevertheless, those closest to him by birth should seek this from the interpreters <note>original: "interpretibus"; legal or religious experts, known as exegetes, who interpreted sacred law.</note> and from the laws concerning these matters, and as it has been established by them, so let them do. Let there be a solitary burial for such people, where no one else is buried; then let them be buried in those places which are the last, deserted, and unnamed of the twelve parts of the region: so obscure that the graves are marked neither by a statue nor an inscribed name. 

If a beast of burden or another animal kills a man, unless it did so in a public contest, let the relatives of the slain man bring the matter before the judges. And let those caretakers of the fields to whom the relative himself has entrusted the matter judge it, and let them kill the condemned beast of burden outside the borders of the region. 

But if an inanimate thing, except for a lightning bolt or another weapon sent by the gods, has deprived a man of life, either by the man falling on it...

[Right Column]

...or by the object itself striking him: let the relative closest to the slain man appoint the nearest neighbor as a judge for this purpose, and let these and other matters be handled as is appropriate toward the dead man himself...

# On the Laws, or Latin Dialogues on the Laws. Book IX. 585

[Left Column]

...and that it is right for [intellect] to rule over all things. But now, this is nowhere found: but only a small trace of it appears. Therefore, we must choose what holds the second place: order and law, from which many things are indeed clearly seen, but all things cannot be seen. <note>original: "quod secundo loco est" — Plato famously argues that a perfectly wise ruler is best, but since such a person is rare, "the second best" option is a system of fixed laws.</note> But with these things proposed for their sake, let us now establish what the one who has wounded another, or otherwise harmed them, ought to suffer or pay. For it is easy for anyone to correctly understand individual cases of this kind: namely, whether someone has wounded another or not: whom, in what part, and in what manner. For these individual details are almost innumerable, and differ greatly among themselves. However, to leave all these things to a court’s judgment, or to leave none of them, is impossible. Indeed, it is necessary to commit this one thing to the court in all cases: whether each of these acts was committed or not. It is also nearly impossible to leave nothing to the court regarding the <term>fine</term><note>original: "mulcta" — a financial penalty or forfeit.</note> for the offender, but to determine all things, great and small, by law. 

CLINIAS: How then should we speak after this? 

ATHENIAN: Thus indeed: that the legislator should grant some things to the judgment of the court, and some things he should not, but must determine them himself. 

CLINIAS: 

<margin>Which things are from the laws, and which from equity and goodness.</margin>

But what things are to be left to the discretion and wisdom of the judges, and what are to be determined by the lawgiver himself? 

ATHENIAN: We shall next set these matters out in the following way. A more serious plague, and one common to the whole state, is born where the courts are sluggish and silent; where the opinions of the judges remain hidden from one another, and they cast their votes in secret. <note>The Athenian Stranger is criticizing judicial systems where judges don't deliberate openly or where the process is opaque.</note> Furthermore, it is even harsher when it is not conducted in silence, but like theaters, everything rings with noise, and the <term>rhetoricians</term><note>Public speakers or lawyers who used persuasive, often emotional, speech.</note> now praise and now blame, and thus they judge one after another. To such courts, if one is forced by necessity, we consider it a misfortune to give laws. But one who is forced to give them should commit only the smallest fines to such judges, but should himself declare the most and the greatest matters when making the laws. 

But where the courts are rightly established according to their powers, and the judges are well-educated and approved with all diligence, it is most correct to commit many things to the judges regarding the punishment and the status of those condemned. Therefore, let no one accuse us if we do not now ordain many and great things by these laws—things which even less-educated judges could manage—and if we do not fit a specific fine and punishment to every single crime. Since we hope that those for whom we are writing these laws will be competent judges of these matters, we believe many things should be committed to them. 

However, as we have often said and done in the previous sections, thinking that by the description and form of the punishments spoken...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger explains that while law is "second-best" to perfect wisdom, it is necessary to balance fixed statutes with judicial discretion, especially when judges are well-trained and the courts are not chaotic like theaters.</summary>

### Cratylus, or, On the Correctness of Names

...but he burns for the absent one. Whence [[abbrev: πόθος → pothos]] (longing) is said, as if it were [[abbrev: ἀπόθος → apothos]], that is, the concupiscence for what is absent. Similarly, that which is mixed into the soul's own self toward what is pleasing is called [[abbrev: ἵμερος → himeros]] (desire) when the thing desired is present; however, it is named [[abbrev: πόθος → pothos]] (longing) when the object is absent. 

Furthermore, [[abbrev: ἔρως → erōs]], that is, love, is so called because it [[abbrev: εἰσρῶ → eisrō]] (flows in) from the outside. This [[abbrev: ῥοή → rhoē]] (flux) is not inherent to the possessor, but is infused through the eyes. For this reason, [[abbrev: ἔρως → erōs]], that is, "influxion," was called "love" by our ancestors from the word [[abbrev: εἰσρῶ → eisrō]] (to flow in). For they used to use the letter [[abbrev: ο → o]] (omicron) in place of [[abbrev: ω → ō]] (omega). Now, however, it is spoken with an [[abbrev: η → ē]] (eta) in place of [[abbrev: ο → o]], with an [[abbrev: ω → ō]] (omega) having been placed between them. 

But what should we consider next? Chiefly [[abbrev: δόξα → doxa]] (opinion), and certain such things—from where do they take their name? 

**SOCRATES.** It is derived either from [[abbrev: δίωξις → diōxis]] (pursuit), or from [[abbrev: διώκειν → diōkein]], that is, from the "persecution" or "chase" by which the soul proceeds and follows after, investigating the condition of things. Or it may come from [[abbrev: τόξου → toxou]] [[abbrev: βολή → bolē]], that is, the "shot of a bow." It seems to depend more likely on this latter. 

The term [[abbrev: οἴησις → oiēsis]] (estimation) agrees with this. Indeed, it shows [[abbrev: οἴσις → oisis]], that is, the "entry" of the soul into each thing to be considered, [[abbrev: οἷον → oion]], that is, "of what quality" it might be. In the same way, [[abbrev: βουλή → boulē]] (counsel/will) is named from [[abbrev: βολή → bolē]] (a shot or cast). And [[abbrev: βούλεσθαι → boulesthai]] (to wish) signifies "to desire" because of that very effort of reaching out, as does [[abbrev: ἔφεσις → ephesis]] (aiming/desire) and [[abbrev: βούλεσθαι → boulesthai]] (to deliberate). 

All these things following after "opinion" seem to be images of that [[abbrev: βολῆς → bolēs]] (shot), that is, of the cast and the effort. Just as the contrary, [[abbrev: ἀτυχία → atychia]] (misfortune/failure), appears as a privation of the will—a certain failure of the one unable to attain—as if they do not struggle, nor do they obtain what they intend, wish, desire, or investigate. 

**HERMOGENES.** You seem to be heaping these up quite frequently, O Socrates. Therefore, let there be an end now, God willing. I still wish, however, for [[abbrev: ἀναγκαῖον → anankaion]] and [[abbrev: ἑκούσιον → hekousion]]—that is, the "necessary" and the "voluntary"—to be explained. For surely these follow the previous terms. 

**SOCRATES.** [[abbrev: ἑκούσιον → hekousion]] (voluntary) is indeed [[abbrev: εἶκον → eikon]], that is, "yielding" and not resisting. By this name is declared [[abbrev: ἄγον → agon]] [[abbrev: τῷ → tō]] [[abbrev: ἰόντι → ionti]], that is, "yielding to that which goes," or whatever is perfected by the will. 

But [[abbrev: ἀναγκαῖον → anankaion]] (necessary), that is, the "necessary and resisting," since it is contrary to the will, will be concerned with error and ignorance. It is derived from a movement according to necessity, because [[notes: Socrates implies a literal path]] in a rough way, thickets [[notes: *desa* likely a corruption of *dasea*, meaning "thickets" or "rough places"]] prohibit passage. Whence [[abbrev: ἀναγκαῖον → anankaion]] was said, as if it were [[abbrev: ἄν᾿ → an']] [[abbrev: ἄγκη → ankē]] [[abbrev: ἰόν → ion]], that is, "going through a valley" [[notes: Plato’s etymology here plays on the word *ankos* (mountain glen/valley) to suggest difficulty or constraint]]. 

As long as our strength lasts, let us not give up. Therefore, ask on, I pray, and do not stop. 

**HERMOGENES.** Behold, I ask about those things which are greatest and most beautiful: [[abbrev: ἀλήθειαν → alētheian]] (truth), [[abbrev: ψεῦδος → pseudos]] (falsehood), and [[abbrev: τὸ → to]] [[abbrev: ὄν → on]] (being), and why that which we are dealing with here is called [[abbrev: ὄνομα → onoma]] (a name). 

**SOCRATES.** What do you mean by [[abbrev: μαίεσθαι → maiesthai]]? 

**HERMOGENES.** I mean "to inquire." 

**SOCRATES.** This word "name" (*nomen*) seems to be composed from that speech by which it is said [[abbrev: ὄν → on]], that is, that "being is," of which the "name" is the inquiry. You will certainly understand this more clearly in what we call [[abbrev: ὀνομαστόν → onomaston]], that is, "that which is to be named." For here it is expressed what a name is: namely, an inquiry into being (*entis inquisitio*). 

[[abbrev: ἀλήθεια → alētheia]] (truth), just like other words, seems to be contracted and forged together. For the divine motion of being is included in this name, [[abbrev: ἀλήθεια → alētheia]], as if it were an existing [[abbrev: θεία → theia]] [[abbrev: ἄλη → alē]], that is, a "divine wandering" or "motion." 

But [[abbrev: ψεῦδος → pseudos]] (falsehood) is the opposite of motion. Here again, the obstacle to agitation is used—that which forces a stop. For it is said from [[abbrev: καθεύδειν → katheudein]], that is, "I sleep." The added letter [[abbrev: ψ → ps]] (psi) hides the sense of the name. 

Furthermore, [[abbrev: τὸ → to]] [[abbrev: ὄν → on]] (being) and *essentia* (essence/being) agree with [[abbrev: δέον → deon]] (the binding/obligatory) and [[abbrev: διόν → dion]] (the divine/passing through), if the letter [[abbrev: ι → i]] (iota) is added. For it signifies [[abbrev: ἰόν → ion]], that is, "going." But [[abbrev: οὐκ → ouk]] [[abbrev: ὄν → on]] (non-being), some name [[abbrev: οὐκ → ouk]] [[abbrev: ἰόν → ion]], that is, "not going." 

**HERMOGENES.** You seem to me, O Socrates, to have discussed these things quite vigorously. But if someone were to ask you what the correct interpretation is of those things which are called [[abbrev: δίκαιον → dikaion]] (just/right), that is, "going"; [[abbrev: δέον → deon]] (fitting/necessary), that is, "flowing"; and [[abbrev: βλαβερόν → blaberon]] (harmful), that is, "binding and detaining," what would we best answer him? Do you have an answer?

**SOCRATES.** I certainly have...
