### Book Twenty-Three.

...certainly so. 

**SOCRATES.** Since we wished to declare things by voice, tongue, and mouth, will not a showing then finally occur through these, if an imitation is made through them concerning any given thing? 

**HERMOGENES.** I think it necessary. 

**SOCRATES.** A name, therefore, is as it appears: an imitation of the voice, by which whoever imitates something, imitates and names it through the voice. 

**HERMOGENES.** It seems the same to me as well. 

**SOCRATES.** And yet, by Jupiter, I do not yet think it has been correctly stated, O friend. 

**HERMOGENES.** For what reason? 

**SOCRATES.** Because we would be forced to admit that those who imitate sheep and roosters and other animals are "naming" the very things they imitate. 

**HERMOGENES.** You speak the truth. 

**SOCRATES.** Does that deter you? 

**HERMOGENES.** Not at all. But then, Socrates, what kind of imitation will a name be? 

**SOCRATES.** Not such an imitation as occurs through music, although that is done with the voice; nor even an imitation of the same things that music imitates, for we do not seem to "name" by means of musical imitation. I speak of it this way: voice, figure, and color are present in many things. 

**HERMOGENES.** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES.** It seems to me that if someone were to imitate these, the faculty of "naming" would not consist in those imitations. For these are partly the domain of music and partly of painting, are they not? 

**HERMOGENES.** Clearly. 

**SOCRATES.** What of this? Do you not think there is an *essentia* (essence) for each thing, just as there is for color and the other things we mentioned above? Is there not an essence in color and voice, and in all other things that are worthy of the name of "being" (*essendi appellatione*)? 

**HERMOGENES.** So it seems to me. 

**SOCRATES.** If someone were able to imitate the essence of each thing with letters and syllables, would he not declare "what" each thing is? 

**HERMOGENES.** Most certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** What would you call such a person? The former ones you called partly "musician" and partly "painter"; but what will you call this one? 

**HERMOGENES.** This, Socrates, seems to me to be the "author of naming" (the lawgiver/onomaturge) whom we have been seeking for a long time. 

**SOCRATES.** If this is true, we must now consider those names you were demanding: [[abbrev: ῥοή → rhoē]], that is, "flux"; [[abbrev: ἰόν → ion]], that is, "to go"; [[abbrev: σχέσις → schesis]], that is, "detention"; and whether or not they truly imitate the essence through their letters and syllables. 

**HERMOGENES.** Exactly. 

**SOCRATES.** Come, let us see whether these are the only "first names" (primary words), or whether there are others besides these. 

**HERMOGENES.** I think there are others. 

**SOCRATES.** That is likely. But what is the method of distinguishing where the imitator begins to imitate? Since the imitation of essence is made through letters and syllables, is it not best first to distinguish the "elements" (the letters)? Just as those who study rhythms first distinguish the powers of the elements, then of the syllables, and finally they approach the rhythms themselves, but never before that. 

**HERMOGENES.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** Must we not also first distinguish the vocal letters (vowels), and afterwards the rest according to their kinds—the mutes and the semivowels? For this is how learned men speak of them. And again, they distinguish the vowels, but not the semivowels, and the species of the vowels themselves as they differ from one another. 

And after we have distinguished all these well, we must again bring in the names and consider if there are things to which all names refer, just like the elements, from which one can know the names themselves, and whether species are contained within them in the same way as in the elements. 

With all these things carefully considered, one must know how to apply each thing according to its similarity—whether one thing is applied to one in that manner, or many are to be mixed together. Just as painters, wishing to express a likeness, sometimes apply only a purple color, sometimes any other color, and sometimes mix many—as when they wish to fashion a most similar image of a man, or something else of this kind—insofar as each image requires certain colors. In no other way do we also apply elements...

...

[[page number: 229]]

->centered<-
### Critias, or, Atlanticus.

[[notes: This section actually concludes the *Cratylus*. The heading refers to the next dialogue in Ficino's collection.]]

...agreed between us that things are to be learned and sought not from names, but rather from the things themselves. 

**CRATYLUS.** So it appears, O Socrates. 

**SOCRATES.** Let us observe this further, lest these many names tending toward the same thing deceive us—as if those who imposed them thought that all things were always running and flowing, and established them with that consideration. Indeed, it seems to me they thought so: but in truth, they themselves, as if fallen into a certain dizziness, waver and are tossed about, and they pull us in and submerge us in the same whirlpool. 

Consider, wonderful Cratylus, what I often dream about: whether we should say there is something that is "the Beautiful" itself and "the Good" itself, and each of the existing things likewise, or not. 

**CRATYLUS.** It seems to me, O Socrates, that there is. 

**SOCRATES.** Let us therefore consider that very thing: not whether a certain face or something of the kind is beautiful (since all these things flow), but rather "the Beautiful" itself—do we not say it always perseveres as such as it is? 

**CRATYLUS.** It is necessary. 

**SOCRATES.** Is it possible to correctly name it if it always flees—first to say "what" it is, and then "of what quality" it is? Or is it necessary that, while we are speaking, it immediately becomes something else and continually flows away, and is no longer such? 

**CRATYLUS.** It is necessary. 

**SOCRATES.** In what way will that be "something," which never stays in the same state? For if it ever stays in the same state, it is clear that in the time it is so, it is not changed at all. But if it always stays in the same state and exists as the same thing, how does it pass away or move, since it does not depart from its own "idea"? 

**CRATYLUS.** In no way. 

**SOCRATES.** Furthermore, it would be known by no one. For while the power of knowing approached it, it would become something else and different. Therefore, "what" it is or "of what quality" it is could not be known. For no knowledge perceives a thing in such a way that it perceives it as being in no certain state. 

**CRATYLUS.** It is as you say. 

**SOCRATES.** But neither should we affirm that knowledge itself exists, O Cratylus, if all things fall away and nothing remains. For if knowledge does not fall away from being knowledge, it will remain always, and always there will be knowledge. But if the species of knowledge itself departs, it will simultaneously fall into another species of knowledge, and there will be no knowledge. If it perpetually migrates, there will never be knowledge. And by this reasoning, neither that which is to know, nor that which is to be known, will ever exist. 

But if that which knows always exists, and that which is known exists, and the Beautiful exists, and the Good exists, and finally each of the existing things exists, then these things of which we are currently speaking do not seem to me to be like flux or motion. 

Whether these things are so, or as the followers of Heraclitus (the philosopher of change) and many others used to say, is not easily discerned. Nor is it the part of a man of quite sound mind to entrust himself and his soul to names, and to assert that the author of names was wise, and thus to think poorly of himself and all things—believing that nothing exists whole or firm, but that all things flow and collapse like earthenware, and judging that things themselves are affected just as men suffering from "catarrhs" (head colds), so that all things are gripped by "distillation" and flux. 

Perhaps, O Cratylus, it is so; perhaps also it is otherwise. Therefore, the matter must be investigated with a brave spirit and diligent study. For one should not assent easily. You are still young, and your age is sufficient. And if you find anything by searching, you ought to share it with me as well. 

**CRATYLUS.** I will do my best, Socrates. And know certainly that even now I am not idle; rather, to me as I think and revolve many things in my mind, things seem to be much more as you were saying than as Heraclitus says. 

[[page number: 229 continued]]

**SOCRATES.** Hereafter, friend, after you return, teach me. But now, as you have decided, go into the country. And Hermogenes here will accompany you. 

**CRATYLUS.** It shall be as you advise, Socrates. But you too, think now on these things.

### On the Laws, or, on Legislation. Dialogue 10. Page 587

...they shall hand him over to the one he injured. That person may hold him in shackles and strike him with lashes as he wishes, provided he causes no financial loss to the slave's owner; thereafter, he must return him to the owner to be held according to the law. The law shall be this: if a slave strikes a free man without the orders of the magistrates, the master shall receive him back from the victim bound, on the condition that he does not release him until he has persuaded the victim that he is now worthy of being set free by a just payment. These same laws ought to be common to all: for women toward men, and for men toward women.

# THE TENTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE MAKING OF LAWS.

#### THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.

**THE INTRODUCTION** to the tenth summary completes the ninth, reminding us that we must now treat judgments concerning violence committed against property, following the judgments on violence against persons arranged in the ninth book. Since no violence is more harsh and intolerable than that which is committed out of a certain disdain—namely, insults and injuries either against a person or a thing born specifically of contempt—he decrees that these should be selected for their own specific chapters. These are divided into five heads: offenses committed against public sacred things, against private sacred rites, against the reverence due to parents, against the excellence of a magistrate, or against the civil and ancestral dignity of any citizen. These matters, therefore, he leaves to be judged most strictly by other lawmakers, magistrates, and judges. 

After this, he distinguishes from the rest those offenses committed in contempt of the gods, which are more serious than can be described. The entire focus of this tenth book is occupied with these. But first, he suggests the difference between sacrilege <note>original: *sacrilegium*</note> and impiety <note>original: *impietatem*</note>. He defines sacrilege as a form of theft, whether a thing or a person consecrated to the powers above is snatched away. This is contained as a specific species under the general category of impiety. For beyond sacrilege, many other things are included under impiety: whatever is thought, said, done, committed, permitted, or even omitted in contempt of the gods. And lest anything be hidden from us, impiety also includes all intimacy and fellowship—whether in food or conversation—entered into with those who are barred from sacred rites because of their wicked crimes; for being defiled, they contaminate others by their very proximity. Regarding this matter, he treats it at the end of the ninth book in such a way that he seems to have prophesied the excommunications <note>original: *exccrationes* (execrations/excommunications)</note> performed daily by our own people <note>Ficino refers to the Catholic Church of his time.</note>, driving the profane away from the communion of the church.

Accordingly, our "physician" <note>Plato is often described as a physician of the soul.</note>, intending to most diligently cleanse minds languishing with the disease of impiety, first investigates the causes of this sickness. While inquiring, he delivers an Evangelical sentiment. For he says: "Whoever believes in God according to the laws will be religious, and will never either do or say anything profane." How rightly he begins here with faith, considering that such great faith must be applied to the laws! But let the number of gods not disturb anyone, since the number of angels does not disturb us. For many gods in Plato's view can do no more than many angels and many blessed souls can in ours. 

Furthermore, since the sacred and most ancient laws concerning the gods—that is, concerning God and the angels serving God—what do they say? Truly, three things. First, that these gods exist. Second, that they provide for all things. Third, that they justly repay rewards and punishments according to the merits of the mind. All piety consists in the faith and observance of this sentiment. Who, then, is impious? Clearly, the one who either denies that gods of this kind exist; or, if they exist, denies that they provide; or, if they provide, denies that they repay justly. This last error is to think that the powers above, in the manner of human judges, can be easily appeased by gifts alone, even when offered by an unjust person. 

Plato, therefore, intending to drive out the three causes of the impious disease, proves that gods exist: both those who are the governors of the spheres in the world, and the contemplators of the supreme God who are above the world. He will prove that the gods provide for all things, even the smallest. He will prove that the constant balance and scale of justice weighs not the external gifts of the hands, but the innermost merits of the soul. Finally, with this doctrine as a sort of preface to the law, he will discourage all people from every contempt of divine things and exhort them toward piety. Moreover, he will terrify the impious with the threats and whips of the law, and he will torment them.

In the beginning, he indicates that the gods exist by two common arguments. The first is drawn from the universal nature of things; the second is deduced from the human species. The first is of this sort: we have found that order everywhere proceeds from reason, and that order is never and nowhere interrupted by a powerful reason; the most beneficial order comes from the best reason. Since, therefore, both the arrangement and the progression of the universe are most orderly, and are such always and everywhere—and not without a certain wonderful benefit—it is necessary that the world be arranged and moved by the best and most powerful reason. And since the universe is one, and a single universe cannot come except from one source, it follows that there is one supreme Reason of this kind. 

Furthermore, there are many divine beings under the supreme divine Reason, just as in a single, rationally ordered work of the world, there are many spheres distinct in species and virtue, yet all rationally ordered—so much so that in a certain way, many worlds seem to be contained within the most ample circumference of the one world. Thus, similarly, many governors of these narrower worlds, arranged in succession, are comprised under the one most ample governor of the world. He, who is surely not only the arranger but is himself, so to speak, "immense order," rejoices much more in being an arranger than in the thing arranged. Therefore, if he is undoubtedly delighted by the many things ordered in the universe, he is also much pleased by the many arrangers. Indeed, the most excellent majesty of the most high King consists in this: that he has beneath him not only humble servants, but also many great kings. 

The second argument for the same point, deduced from the human species, is of this kind: the natural instinct of any species cannot be in vain. The natural judgment of the most perfect species of animals likewise ought not to be entirely false. Since the human species, the most perfect of animals, is moved toward religion everywhere and always by a natural instinct and immutable judgment, it is necessary that there be powers above who are worshipped through religion, and that souls survive their bodies—which is the primary foundation of religion. 

Pay attention to Plato’s statement: though the reasons concerning divinity are sometimes not overly clever, they are nonetheless true. He notes two occasions for impiety: namely, intemperance (the lust for bodily pleasures) and, more rarely, ignorance arising from the absurd opinions of certain poets and physicists <note>term: *physici* — natural philosophers who studied the physical world without spiritual causes.</note>. He says the poets erred in three ways regarding the gods: First, because they sang that the gods burst forth from the confusion they call "Chaos." Second, because they asserted that some were born from others without right reason, as if through human intercourse. Third, because they transferred all human disturbances, errors, and outrages to the gods with wicked impiety. Those physicists also sinned in religion who either, with Democritus, dream that the universe, though arranged with marvelous reason, was composed by some reckless chance rather than divine reason; or who, with Anaxagoras and Archelaus, believe that the heavenly bodies have nothing more divine in them than the elements. Furthermore, they say that the forms of things that are born, which are clearly directed toward a goal everywhere, arise from elemental force rather than from the art of a mind directing each thing toward a certain end. 

Since we have been rather long in our books of theology in refuting these men and in confirming those things which we have just proven, and which we shall hereafter bring forth from the mind of Plato in this summary, we shall run through them briefly for the present. Consider how great our religion is in Plato, and how certain he is that God exists; for when disputing against those who deny God, he can scarcely contain himself—though his reason is mild and he is most gentle in the investigation of truth. In these matters, he certainly warns that those who deny God are not to be tolerated. Note that Plato approves of those who, at the rising and setting of the sun and moon, adore not the sun and moon themselves, but rather the divine beneficence; he commands that thanks be given daily for the gift of such light, and he judges that man to be a sort of monster who, against natural instinct, education, and common custom, denies that the powers above exist. 

Shortly thereafter, he warns young men, into whose minds certain absurd opinions heard against God might have crept, that as long as they are young, they should abstain from judgment on divine matters; they should believe their elders and the laws until age, experience, and reason teach them otherwise. He brings into the open the opinions of certain men who were held to be wise, through which people easily decline toward impiety and injustice. I mean those opinions asserting that the natures of the four elements, flowing together by a certain fortuitous motion, heaped all things together. Furthermore, they claim that religion and justice differ from the truth and are based only on human opinion. For this reason, he concludes that these ideas, being most ruinous to all both privately and publicly, must be refuted with reasons. Men should not be compelled to the obedience and observation of the laws by threats and rashness alone, but also by persuasions and reasons. Otherwise, since man is a rational animal and therefore free, unless you bind him with the bond of reason, he neither ought to be nor can be bound in any other way. We must, therefore, point out the reason within the laws; its power is so great for recognizing God that after a rational investigation, it becomes certain that reason exists in nature more than in itself—and it is more certain the more it sees that natural effects are more orderly than human ones. Whence also one notices that art in nature is much more perfect than in man. From this again, one notices that the art excelling in natural works, since it is more perfect than the human, is not only human but also a participant in life and intelligence; it is surely a living and intelligent thing; indeed, to the efficient cause, add life and intellect...

He presents the cosmological argument for a creator based on the rational order of the universe and defends religion as a natural human instinct.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's commentary on the tenth book of Plato’s *Laws*. The previous page introduced the legal and moral arguments against impiety; here, Ficino transitions into the metaphysical proofs for the existence of God and the nature of the soul as the primary cause of motion in the universe.</meta>

[[original page: 588]]

### Book Thirty-Four.
<note>This heading follows Ficino’s own numbering system in his *Compendium* or *Theologia*, though it comments on Book 10 of Plato’s *Laws*.</note>

...of and will. For since He manifestly directs individual things to their own proper ends, it is certain that He has foreseen the end and willed it; indeed, He always provides and wills, just as the order in individual things is always preserved whole, or where it seems interrupted, it is restored more quickly than can be said. We do not doubt that this is divine providence. I say "Providence," which is not negligent of the smallest things—for these are no less ordered than the greatest—nor does it labor in the greatest. For the things closest to the Orderer do not resist His ordering; they are diligently ordered by the same nod of His will by which they are made, and they are kept far from any transgression. Hence that saying: *He dwells on high and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth* <note>original: "In altis habitat: & humilia respicit in cælo & in terra"; a reference to Psalm 113:5-6</note>, just as heaven itself, while it completes its course within itself without labor, meanwhile without negligence surrounds the earth with the most abundant gift of its rays.

Between these points, when he says that law and art consist of nature—or no less than nature—it is because he understands them to be the offspring of the mind. He understands that forms no less true than those of nature exist and are birthed from the divine intellect as from a father, and from the human mind as from a mother. And observe the accustomed piety of our Plato, invoking God to confirm the gods. I say one God, so that he may teach that all the gods are to be referred back to the One. He proceeds, relying on the help of the highest God, to dispute most safely concerning divine matters.

In the beginning, he disapproves of those natural philosophers <term>physicos; early Greek thinkers who sought material causes for the universe</term> who placed the highest principles of things in physical bodies, from which life and intelligence would then proceed; whereas they ought rather to have said that physical bodies depend on intellectual life. He professes that he will prove this to be so, not—I say—by a new opinion, but by reason. For an opinion of this sort belongs to the ancient theologians before Plato, but the argumentation which will be made here from motion is proper to Plato.

He distinguishes the genus of motion itself into ten species: namely, **Revolution**, **Local Transition**, **Condensation**, **Rarefaction**, **Increase**, **Decrease**, **Generation**, **Corruption**, **Alteration** (or change made in one thing by another), and **Self-Motion** (change made from itself, whether in itself or in another). He admires circular motion, since in it the indivisible center stands still while the rest is moved; likewise, in a deep sphere, many circles are designated, some subsequently larger than others. And what is wonderful is that at the same moment the narrowest and widest circles complete their circuit; so much so that both the slowness of the one in a continuous body and the velocity of the other are equally to be admired. The middle circles, according to their dimension and motion, hold a middle way according to certain proportions. We have treated much of these things in our expositions of theology.

He also speaks of that which changes place: that it "changes its center," that is, the center of its location, to which the circumference of the moving body is compared. Sometimes, however, besides changing its center, it also preserves in a way the same center: namely, when it is not fixed, but is moved through a certain equal circumference. Furthermore, where he speaks of **generation**, he says the principle—that is, the motive and seminal nature—when it proceeds through alteration, goes through three steps: that is, into length, breadth, and depth. Likewise, it reaches as far as quantity and quality, and the substantial form through its effects manifest to the senses; again, it reaches toward formal, vital, and sensory being.

He thinks that in these motions the physical mass is moved, but does not move; physical forms both move the masses and are moved by the soul. The Soul moves these two, but is not moved by another; rather, it is moved from itself. But it moves in such a way that it is meanwhile moved in its own manner along with the changed things. Therefore, he considers the divine and angelic minds to be more excellent than souls, for they move internal things while remaining entirely unchanged themselves. Finally, he judges the Good itself to be eminent above minds, for all things seek truth for the sake of the Good. In these points, he touches on many things pertaining to the nature of that which is "mobile through itself," as if to the proper principle of motion and generation. In this, a certain formal motion and spiritual generation flourishes by its own nature, the exemplar of all motions and generations.

Above all, he confirms that whatever is moved by another is by nature "movable from itself," lest we proceed into infinity. Indeed, just as beyond those things which shine or grow warm through another, one arrives at something which is shiny or warm through itself; so, beyond things movable by another, one comes to a thing movable through itself. For if all things were now at rest, and a little later something had to move before the others, what would move first? Certainly not the divine substance, which is altogether immobile. Nor any physical thing, which borrows its motion from another. Only that which is movable from itself, therefore, will move first, and exercising its motion in itself, will translate it into others. For it grants to bodies that they are moved, just as the immobile principle of things grants to things that they move.

That the soul is a nature movable through itself is evident both internally—when by its own nature it freely discourses through reasoning and consultation—and externally, as long as its presence grants to the body that it be moved, in a sense, through itself. But concerning all these things, and further, that it is necessary for angels and God to be above the souls that rule the spheres, we treat abundantly in our theology. When Plato calls the soul "motion and generation," understand this by way of cause—that is, the proper principle of motion and generation. And where he says the soul "is moved by itself," that is the "account" <note>original: "rationem"</note> of the soul. Note in the same place it is also said that the account of the soul is that it *can* move itself; you should not understand the *act* of motion to be the soul, but rather the *power*—and not an accidental power, I say, for he calls the soul a "substance" in that same place. Thus you shall define it: **The Soul is a substance having its own power, by which it is both moved from itself and moves other things.**

Just as a thing movable from itself precedes a thing movable by another, so he thinks the rational soul precedes the entire physical machine, since no body is able to be moved from itself. The Platonists say it precedes both in dignity and in time. If someone wishes Plato to dissent less from the Christians, let him explain that our soul precedes either by a certain moment of time, or at least in the dignity and intention of the Creator. From the fact that the substance of the soul is prior to the substance of the body, he concludes that the affections, motions, and familiar gifts of the soul are prior to the passions of the body. When he seeks what is "proper" to the soul, remember that those things which signify *action* are common to our soul and the higher ones. Those which signify *passion* <term>passio; here meaning 'being acted upon' or suffering change</term> are proper to ours, or shared only with the lowest demons. Yet the natural motion which is in the passive body is an *action* in the soul. And what in the body is length, breadth, depth, quality, and motion, in the soul is sharpness, judgment, memory, habit, and affection. You have other such things disputed in our theology.

He says also that even the sun is a cause of evils, namely by accident, and because our soul has free will. Beware when he says the world is governed by a soul—namely its own—and adds that the soul is "twin," one beneficent and the other contrary; do not take this to mean a twin *substance*, but a twin *power*. Since in the soul of the world and the celestial soul, one power is the mover of bodies, and the other is intellectual. The intellectual is certainly beneficent, disposing all things in order. The motive power is beneficent—that is, an orderer—only insofar as it is subject to the other. If it were not subject, the more effective it is at motion, the more it would cast the universe headlong with art and confound it.

He proves that the celestial soul possesses a mind <note>original: "mente"</note> from the order it always observes in every motion and generation. Indeed, we see that the "mindless" <note>original: "amentes"</note> are alienated from order to the same extent they are alienated from mind. By "order" in this context, we mean the mutual connection between things and actions disposed in a fitting succession, and directed toward a certain end by a specific reason; and in the whole, as far as possible, preserving the similar, the equal, and the same. We see such order preserved only by those who are masters of their minds, and fully realized in the progression of the universe itself. I say it is realized as commodiously as it is beautifully, from which it appears to be governed by a soul that possesses a most artistic and excellent mind.

Nor was it without reason that he said "revolution" <note>original: "circuitum"</note> is proper to the mind. For in a revolution, the indivisible center remains while the circumference returns to the same point, and equality is preserved in both figure and motion. Similarly in the mind, a simple and direct intuition toward the truth itself remains, while causes are unfolded into effects through intermediaries, and in turn, effects are similarly folded back into causes. Meanwhile, the attention of the mind returns into itself to be considered, and it proceeds in understanding, willing, acting, intention, rule, and progression by the similar, the equal, and the same.

After he has proved both that the celestial spheres have Souls, and that the souls are endowed with excellent minds, and signifies both that the universe is moved by one soul and the many spheres by many, he now distinguishes in a few words the three modes by which souls are joined to celestial bodies: saying the soul is either in the globe just as our soul is in the body, so that one "animal" <term>a living, animated being</term> is made from them; or it is present in such a way that it does not vivify the globe but only moves and rules it, whether by some miraculous power of moving alone, or by some further intermediary. And if from these three proposed modes he does not manifestly choose one over the others here, all Platonists nevertheless choose the first without controversy, and they consider that Aristotle and Theophrastus felt entirely the same. For they think Plato held that one as more probable. For the very argumentation by which he here makes the heaven animated implies that the soul itself is moved together with the motion of the heaven. Unless one animal were made from the soul and the globe, surely it would not be a "movable mover," but an "immobile mover." He confirms the same in the *Phaedrus*, and the same in the *Timaeus*, saying: when the Architect of the world wished to make the world an intellectual animal, and since intellect could not be present to a body without a medium, he joined the intellect to the soul, and the soul to the body, and even infused it into the middle of the world, and from there diffused it through all things.

But why does Plato here manifestly confirm only the celestial gods? Because the contemplation of higher things is quite foreign to the matter of laws; and through the celestial gods who are moved and assigned to their own offices, he sufficiently warns that a Superior must be sought, who, being himself unmoved, moves all others, and as a common leader assigns offices to each individual. What more? He clearly demonstrated that above the celestial souls there is a divine Mind and angelic minds, where he says the celestial soul, inasmuch as it is from itself...

[[vocabulary: substance, soul, motion, will, intellect, providence, revolution/circuit, sphere]]

<summary>Marsilio Ficino provides a metaphysical commentary on Plato’s Laws, arguing that the soul is the self-moving principle that precedes the body and governs the universe through divine providence. He details ten types of motion and explains how the World Soul and celestial minds maintain the perfect order of the cosmos.</summary>

### On the Laws, or on Legislation, Dialogue X. 589

...it does not have this of itself, if it has always received divine understanding: to lead all things rightly, just as they are held to be right and happy among the gods; otherwise, it wanders completely. Therefore, Plato, where he proceeds from the soul to the mind—like one who ascends from the eye to a higher light—greatly fears lest he be forced into darkness. After he has shown that gods exist, he demonstrates that they provide, beginning from a certain singular opinion thus: "A certain nature kindred to divinity <note>original: "Natura quædā diuinitati cognata"</note> leads men who are not entirely degenerate from the human species to affirm that God exists, although sometimes the prosperity of the wicked—which is a false prosperity and which will pay the price at the appointed time—might cause us to doubt concerning God’s providence." 

Truly, God acts in understanding; consequently, He understands what He does, and if He makes the whole, He also understands the whole. If He knows the whole, He knows also the parts of which the whole necessarily consists; if the parts, then the particles of which the parts necessarily consist. He is able, therefore, and knows how to rule the universe: He who is able and knows how to provide. He also wills and wishes to govern His entire work. But a whole can never be governed well if the parts are not governed. Thus, neither a physician nor an architect cares for the whole work optimally without the parts that are necessarily conducive to it. God does not neglect to govern the smallest things, since He did not neglect to make the smallest things. Nor is governance difficult for God, for whom procreation is easy. Nor is He slower to care because of softness, He who is the strongest of all, who governs all things more accurately than either art or nature which are from art or nature. For by as much as the works of God depend more on God than the works of art or nature depend on art or nature, so much more diligently does God provide for His works: through whose providence other things also have this quality, that each provides for its own in like manner. 

Since art is more perfect the more easily it handles small and great things at once, and in God art is immense, He surely governs the smallest and greatest together with the greatest ease. In dispensing these things, He does not dispose the whole for the sake of the parts, but the parts for the sake of the whole, and He relates the proper good of each to the universal good. Among all things under the moon, He has the greatest diligence concerning the human species, both because it is most perfect and because it worships God—as if it uniquely begins from God. In these things you will note that by the highest God, divine governors <note>original: "rectores"; referring to celestial or angelic beings tasked with management</note> are distributed through the individual genera and species of things, as curators of even the smallest actions and passions. Although they are able through His power to do whatever they can, so through His providence, the manager of even the smallest things, they manage every smallest thing. 

You will note that there are senses in the stars, and as Plotinus and Hermes <note>A reference to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of the Hermetic tradition.</note> argue, specifically sight and hearing, but of another kind and far more excellent than the senses of terrestrial animals. You will note also that the human soul is always joined to a body—assiduously indeed to an ethereal body <note>term: ethereal body — a subtle, "star-like" envelope that carries the soul between incarnations.</note>, but through succession to a terrestrial body, then to an aerial body. Likewise, the motion of the soul, which is primary and from itself and therefore free, can be diverted into various forms: to such an extent that the soul is sometimes converted into a habit lower than man, and sometimes into one higher than man: and indeed, by the former it descends as if by a certain gravity to lower places, but by the latter it seeks the heights by levity. From this it appears that the habits conceived from their own motions concur with the law of the divine will. For just as that law dictates that celestial things suit good souls, but terrestrial things suit evil ones, so with no one impelling from without, and as if by a certain natural instinct, the habits of the good spontaneously seek higher things, while those of the bad slip toward lower ones. 

[[margin: On all power.]]
[[margin: On contempt of the divinity.]]

Here indeed, if I were permitted to comment at greater length, I would explain that most obscurely stated point where he introduces someone attempting to transmute fire into "animated water" <note>original: "ignem in aquam animatam"</note>, as if striving for the most difficult things. For since water is contrary to fire, and a soul cannot be created from fire, he surely attempts the impossible who strives to transmute fire into animated water. Nor is it less obscurely said that this must be explained regarding dialectical resolution and division. Namely, if someone proceeds by dividing through three steps—namely, from a certain most general genus to subaltern species, and from these to the most specific species—finally he easily divides the species; similarly, he who resolves through the same steps, from the most specific species to the subaltern genus, and thence to the most general, also resolves easily. But truly, he who wishes to wander through individual things infinite in number will undertake a useless task. But concerning these, see the commentaries on the *Philebus*. 

Among these, he will note how similar the words of Plato are to the oracle of the prophet David: that the divine judgment can be avoided neither by ascent into heaven nor by descent into hell <note>original: "neque ascensu in cælum neque descensu in infernum"; a parallel to Psalm 139:8.</note>. After this, he shows that God cannot be unjustly appeased by the gifts of the wicked. Here you will consider God to be the most diligent curator of the human race, more than shepherds of sheep, pilots of ships, leaders of an army, rustic workers of fields, charioteers of horses, or physicians of the sick. Furthermore, all things under heaven are full of evils, and there is a perpetual war concerning souls. In this, vices drag from the gods, but the gods and demons pull back. You will consider that there are living virtues in God—nay, rather lives—by certain sparks of which, kindled in the soul from there, the soul is raised to the sublime. 

But after the proems, he notices the impious with a severer censure, and he diligently explores not only nefarious actions, but also the impudence of words, and indeed the thoughts themselves against divine dignity: and the three species of impiety set down previously, he deduces into six: namely, by dividing each into two. For those three consist in a false opinion against God. However, iniquity of morals can also concur with a false opinion; or a more tolerable equity can exist. You will recognize here also the punishments of evildoers, heretics, the superstitious, and furthermore those who are called "False Prophets." Again, how much he condemns plebeian superstition. He also condemns the poetic kind, by which plebeian superstition is also confirmed. Everywhere, indeed, Plato disapproves of both poetic and plebeian superstition, and before all human duties, he venerates philosophical piety.

[[vocabulary: providence, divinity, contemplation, demon, idolatry, false prophet, superstition]]

<summary>Ficino explains Plato’s argument that God governs both the cosmic whole and its smallest parts with ease, and that the soul’s moral choices naturally align it with either celestial or terrestrial realms. He contrasts philosophical piety with the "false prosperity" of the wicked and the errors of poetic superstition.</summary>

is to show this truth: that the gods exist. **ATHENIAN.** In what way? **CLINIAS.** First, indeed, the earth, the sun, the stars, and the universe itself, as well as the most orderly variety of the seasons, distinguished by years and months, show this; furthermore, there is the consensus of all—both Greeks and barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples, such as Persians or Egyptians, rather than "uncivilized" people.</note>—who confess that gods exist. **ATHENIAN.** I fear, O blessed man, wicked men; I say I fear them—I do not blush, nor am I afraid to say it—lest they perhaps despise you. For you are ignorant of the cause of their disagreement, and you think that their minds fall away into an impious life only because of an incontinence of pleasures and desires. **CLINIAS.** But what other cause is there for them besides those, Guest? **ATHENIAN.** Something which completely escapes you, being unskilled in it. **CLINIAS.** What is this? **ATHENIAN.** A certain most grave ignorance, which nevertheless appears to be the greatest prudence <note>A classic Platonic theme: the most dangerous form of ignorance is "double ignorance"—not knowing, and thinking that one knows.</note>. **CLINIAS.** In what way, he asks? **ATHENIAN.** There are certain discourses among us, written partly in meter and partly in prose, which, as I hear, are not found among you because of the excellence of your civic discipline. The most ancient of these affirm that the first nature of the heavens and of the other gods was created, and having progressed not much further, they narrate the generation of the gods and how they lived with one another. Since these stories are ancient, it is not easy to criticize whether they are told rightly or wrongly; however, regarding the worship and honor of one's progenitors, I will confess that these stories are neither useful nor true. Let us therefore dismiss the ancient things; let us speak of them as it pleases the gods. But wherever the words of younger "wise men" bring evil to men, let us strike against them. Indeed, the result of the words of those men is this: when you and I bring forward these very signs—the sun, the moon, the stars, and the earth—to show that gods exist, and bring them into the middle as if they were gods and divine things, then the young men, persuaded otherwise by those "wise men," would say that these are merely earth and stones, and are unable to have any care for human affairs; they would say that the discourse concerning these things was merely composed with ornate words to seem likely. **CLINIAS.** You have shared a grave and dangerous discourse, Guest, even if there had been only one such person. But now it is even more grave and troublesome, since there are many. **ATHENIAN.** What, then, should we say, or what should we do? Should we prepare our defense as if we were accused before impious men of falsely affirming in our laws that gods exist? Or should we set these things aside and return again to the treatment of the laws, lest this "prelude" <term>prooemium: an introductory persuasive speech intended to convince citizens to obey the law willingly rather than through fear</term> to the laws grow too long for us? For the speech will not be brief if we wish to show sufficiently to those men prone to impiety what they require, and also to remove them from crime by terror, and finally, as is fitting, to pass the laws. **CLINIAS.** Frequently in this short time, Guest, it has been said by us that brevity is not to be preferred over length. For nothing, as they say, presses us. Therefore, it would be both ridiculous and wicked if we preferred shorter things to better things. For it will contribute much if our discourse shows by a likely reason that gods exist, and that they are good, and that they honor justice much more than men do; for this will be almost the best and most beautiful opening of all laws. For this reason, without any trouble or haste, let us omit nothing within our power that pertains to persuading them of this matter. **ATHENIAN.** This speech of yours shows you to be so prepared and ready that it seems to provoke a prayer and a vow, and admits no further delay. But how can someone speak about the gods without offense? Especially since it is necessary to take it hard and to hate those who have provided the cause for these words of ours. These people, certainly from childhood, could have been most led to affirm the gods, because while they were being nourished on milk, they heard from their nurses and mothers many things said and chanted about them in stories, both in jest and in earnest; and they saw in sacrifices things done consistent with them, which children most sweetly see and hear, while they saw their parents with the greatest zeal sacrificing for themselves and their children, and praying as suppliants to the gods as if they were most truly gods; moreover, they saw every day at the rising and setting of the sun and moon all Greeks and barbarians, in both adversity and prosperity, prostrating in worship; and from this, they did not bring forth a suspicion that the gods do not exist, but rather provided testimony that they exist without controversy. But those who, moved by no reason—as any person in their right mind would say—despise all these things, and for that reason compel us to say these things: in what way can we now correct them with gentle words, and first teach them that the gods exist? Let us dare, nevertheless; for it is not fitting that, while they are destroyed by pleasure, we also should be corrupted by anger against them. Therefore, with all agitation of the mind extinguished, let us approach the prelude for those whose minds are thus corrupted; and let us gently turn our speech to them, as if to one of them. "O son, you are still young: I do not doubt that the passage of time will make you feel differently about many things than you do now. Wait, therefore, I pray, so that you may then judge concerning the greatest matters. But the greatest matter is that which you now think is nothing: that we might live well by thinking rightly about the gods. But if I certify this one great thing to you, I shall not lie. Neither you alone nor your friends are the first to have this opinion about the gods, but some people always—sometimes more, sometimes fewer—labor under this disease. But what happened to most of them, I will tell you. Truly, no one of them has persevered in this opinion that gods do not exist from youth through to old age. The other two diseases, however, have remained in some, though not many: that gods exist indeed, but they care nothing for human affairs. Or that they do care, but are easily appeased by prayers and sacrifices. You, therefore, if you believe me, will wait until it becomes plain to you, according to your strength, what should be judged concerning these things. And so that you may attain that, you will consider diligently whether the matter is thus or otherwise; and you will inquire from all others, and especially from the legislator. Meanwhile, do not be so rash as to think impiously about the gods. For he who sets the laws for you will attempt to teach you, both now and later, how these things stand." **CLINIAS.** Most excellently has it been spoken by us so far, Guest. **ATHENIAN.** It is exactly so, O Megillus and Clinias. But we have fallen, without knowing it, into a certain wonderful discourse. **CLINIAS.** Which one? **ATHENIAN.** That which is thought by many to be the wisest. **CLINIAS.** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** Some say that all things which are made, which will be, and which have been made, are made either by nature, by chance, or by art. **CLINIAS.** And they speak rightly indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Certainly, it is not absurd that wise men have spoken rightly. Therefore, let us follow them; and let us inquire what they understood. **CLINIAS.** By all means. **ATHENIAN.** They say the greatest and most beautiful things are made by nature and chance; but smaller things are made by art; and they say that art, having been received from nature for the generation of the first and great works, fashions and fabricates all the smaller things which are called "artificial" by everyone. **CLINIAS.** How do you say that? **ATHENIAN.** I will speak more plainly thus. Fire, water, earth, air—they say all these exist not by art, but by nature and chance. Also the bodies which are after these: they say that the things of the earth, the sun, the moon, and all the stars, were made from those things which are entirely lacking a soul; and that chance—wherever the force of each one drove it—cast them together, fitting individual things to one another: cold things with hot, dry with moist, soft with hard, and all opposites with opposites; they were necessarily blended together by the guidance of chance. In this way, the heaven...

### On the Laws. Or, Dialogue X on Lawgiving. 591

the whole heaven, and all things that are in it—animals also, and plants, and the seasons of the year—were produced: not through intellect, nor through any god, nor through <term>art: here meaning "craft" or "intentional design" (Latin: *ars*)</term>, but by nature, as we said, and by fortune. They claim that from these, a mortal "art" was later created by mortals, which generated certain subsequent things that do not fully participate in truth, but are merely images related to the arts themselves—such as what painting, music, and other similar arts produce. If any arts do produce something serious, they are those which share their power with nature: such as medicine, agriculture, and gymnastics. Furthermore, they say that political skill shares a small part with nature, but a large part with art; and thus the entire establishment of laws is consistent not with nature, but with art, whose positions are not true. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** They wish to claim, O blessed man, that the gods exist not by nature, but by art and certain laws, and that they differ from one another according to how each group has harmoniously established them by law. They say that things that are "beautiful" or "honorable" are one thing by nature and another by law. But they claim that justice does not exist by nature at all; rather, men are always arguing with one another about these things and establishing new ones daily. They say that whatever they have recently established is just for as long as it pleases them, being established not by nature, but by art and laws. These are the things, O friends, which "wise" men—both poets and prose writers—have passed down to the younger generation, saying that "just possession" is that which is acquired by force and victory <note>This is a reference to the Sophistic "might makes right" argument, famously associated with figures like Thrasymachus or Callicles.</note>. From this, impiety is born in the young, so that they believe there are no gods such as the laws command them to believe. From this also arise seditions, through which men are drawn toward a life that is supposedly "right according to nature"—which is to live in such a way that they conquer others, rather than serving others according to the laws. **CLINIAS.** Oh, Guest, what a thing you have described! What a plague brought upon the youth, both publicly to cities and privately to their own homes! **ATHENIAN.** You speak the truth, O Clinias. But since this is how things stand, what do you think the legislator should do? Should he only threaten all men, telling them they will certainly be punished unless they believe the gods exist—and believe them to be such as the laws hand down—and that they must think and act regarding honorable, just, and all the greatest things (as well as virtue and vice) exactly as the legislator has prescribed? And if they do not obey, should some be punished with the death penalty, others with lashes and chains, others with disgrace, and others with exile and poverty? Shall the legislator only threaten in this way, or will he take no care to add the power of persuasion to his lawmaking, so that he might soften their minds? **CLINIAS.** Not at all, Guest. If any persuasion, even a modest amount, can be found in such matters, a legislator who is worth anything at all should not be deterred by the labor. Rather, as they say, he should shout with the greatest possible voice to come to the aid of the ancient law and show by reasoning that the gods exist, and all those things you were just saying. He should support law and art themselves, affirming that they exist either by nature or certainly no less than nature, since they are the offspring of Mind itself, as right reason shows—which is what you seem to me to be saying now, and which I believe. **ATHENIAN.** O most ready-minded Clinias, is it not an arduous task to pursue with reasons those things which are so widely spread among everyone, and which are themselves so lengthy that they do not suffer brevity? **CLINIAS.** What, Guest? When so many things were said about drunkenness and music <note>Referring to the lengthy discussions in Books I and II of the *Laws*.</note>, we bore that length with a calm mind; shall we not listen to one who speaks at greater length about the gods and such matters? Indeed, this will be a great defense for a prudently arranged system of laws, since the mandates of the laws—committed to writing, which are usually subject to refutation for all future time—will remain at rest once they have been thus proven. Therefore, we ought not to be terrified if the arguments are difficult to hear at first; even men of slow wit will be able to understand them by repeating them often. These things, therefore, although lengthy, should not be cast aside if they are useful. **MEGILLUS.** And most especially, O Megillus <note>The text here has the Athenian addressing Megillus, or perhaps affirming his presence.</note>, it must be done as he says. Surely, unless those [materialist] discourses were spread among almost all men, so to speak, there would be no need to demonstrate the existence of the gods through reasoning. But now it is necessary. Since the greatest laws are being corrupted by wicked men, whose duty is it more than the legislator's to bring aid? **CLINIAS.** Certainly no one's. **ATHENIAN.** But tell me, Clinias—for you must be a partner in this reasoning—does not the person who says these things seem to think that fire, earth, water, and air are the first of all things? And does he not call these "nature," and think that the soul is something born later from them? Indeed, he does not just "seem" to; he truly signifies this to us by his speech. **CLINIAS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** By Jupiter, have we not found the very fountainhead of the foolish opinion of those who have never touched upon the investigation of natural things? Consider, I pray, and scrutinize every reason. For it is of no small importance if we can show that those who rely on impious arguments, and draw others toward impiety, do not reason correctly, but perversely. This is how it seems to me. **CLINIAS.** You speak well, but try to demonstrate those points. **ATHENIAN.** But I will seem to use unusual arguments. **CLINIAS.** Do not fear, Guest. For I understand that you thought you were going far away from the purpose of making laws if we entered this dispute. But if we cannot otherwise convince people that what is said about the gods according to the law is correct, it must be said entirely. **ATHENIAN.** I will now state this new and almost unheard-of reasoning: that which is the first cause of the generation and corruption of all things <note>The Athenian is referring to the Soul.</note>—these discourses which have made minds impious affirm that it was not made first, but later. And that which is later, they claim is first. This is why they were ignorant of the true substance of the gods. **CLINIAS.** I do not yet understand. **ATHENIAN.** It seems to me that almost everyone has been ignorant of what the soul is and what power it has—both regarding other things and regarding its own generation—specifically that it was born before all bodies, and that it is the primary leader of the transformation and ordering of bodies. If these things are so, will not those things which are proper to the soul itself necessarily be prior to those which pertain to the body, since the soul itself is older than the body? **CLINIAS.** It must be so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, opinion, care, intellect, art, and law are prior to hard and soft, heavy and light. Consequently, the great and first works and operations of art will be among the primary things; whereas those things which are "by nature"—and nature itself, which they do not correctly name—are posterior and follow after art and intellect. **CLINIAS.** Why? **ATHENIAN.** They incorrectly wish to call "nature" the generation concerning the first things, and they put bodies first. But if it appears that not fire, nor air, but the soul exists first, then the soul itself will most rightly be affirmed to be older than the body. And this will be established as being "by nature" only if it is established that the soul is older than bodies; otherwise, not at all. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we then proceed with this in order? **CLINIAS.** By all means. **ATHENIAN.** Let us flee the fallacious reasoning of the <term>quibbler: a "cavillator," or one who uses deceptive arguments to mock the truth</term>, lest by chance it deceives us old men and makes us look ridiculous—appearing to have attempted great things without having achieved even small ones. If a deep river...

### Book Thirty-Four.
<note>original: "Liber trigesimusquartus." While the heading says Book 34, this text is part of Book 10 of Plato’s *Laws* in this specific edition's layout.</note>

...and if the three of us wished to cross a rushing river, and I, being younger than you both and more experienced with the currents, were to say that it is necessary for me to first make a trial of the crossing while you remain in safety—to see if the river can be crossed by you through the fords <note>original: "fenoribus," likely a variation of "vadis," referring to shallow crossing points</note> or not—and then, once the danger has been tested, I would either encourage you to cross or, if it cannot be crossed, I alone would have undergone the danger, I would seem to speak with modesty. But now, when we must enter into a deeper discourse and reasoning, which is almost inaccessible to your strength, lest it cause a dizziness <note>The Athenian warns that abstract philosophical reasoning can cause a kind of intellectual vertigo for those unaccustomed to it</note> to those who are not used to it, and in this way bring about disgrace and sadness, I think I should first take the risk upon myself. Thus, I will both question myself and answer myself, and in this way, while you listen in safety, I shall traverse this entire disputation concerning the soul, by which it may be shown that the soul is prior to the body. **CLINIAS.** You seem to speak most excellently, Stranger; do as you say. **ATHENIAN.** Come then, let us now more than ever invoke God with all zeal, as we attempt to demonstrate diligently that the gods exist, and let us enter into the argument as if with the safest ropes pulled taut. In this disputation, I think I can most securely respond to questions of this kind: if someone were to ask, "O Stranger, do all things stand still and nothing move? Or on the contrary, does nothing stand still and everything move? Or do some things move and others remain still?" To this I would certainly respond that some things remain and others move. And do they not stand and move in some place? **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** Some do this in one seat <note>meaning a fixed position or axis</note>, and some in several. Do you say that those which take their power from standing in the center move in one place? Just as things are said to revolve, even though their circumference turns? Yes, exactly. We understand that in this circumference, since this kind of motion brings around both the largest and smallest circle at the same time according to proportion, it distributes itself into larger and smaller parts; and it itself, with the proportion preserved, is both larger and smaller. Therefore, it has become the source of all wonders. For together with large and small circles, it carries out matching speeds and slownesses in such a way that it seems to proceed as something incredible. You speak truly. But as for moving in many places, you seem to me to speak of whatever things always pass from one place into another: and sometimes they maintain the base <note>original: "batim," referring to the Greek "basis" or foundation</note> of one center, and sometimes more, because they are rolled around. And when individual things happen to meet one another everywhere, if they encounter things that are standing and resisting, they are split apart; but if they encounter things moving from the opposite direction, they become one as these intermediate things are joined together and condensed. I admit these things are just as you say. And yet, things joined and condensed are increased, while things separated and thinned out are diminished—provided that the prior condition <note>original: "habitus"</note> of each remains; but when it does not remain, destruction follows because of both. Therefore, the generation <term>generation: the process of coming-into-being (Greek: *genesis*)</term> of all things occurs when a certain passion <note>here meaning "influence" or "action acting upon something"</note> takes place: namely, when the beginning, having taken an increase, reaches a second transition, and from this to the next; and when it has reached as far as three, it possesses perception in those who can perceive. Thus, by this transmutation and transition, everything is born; and it truly exists when it remains. But if it is changed into another state, it is then utterly destroyed. We have now spoken, O friends, of all species of motion except two. **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** Those motions, O good man, we have not yet spoken of, for the sake of which nearly this entire consideration exists. **CLINIAS.** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** We have undertaken this disputation for the sake of the soul. **CLINIAS.** Indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Let one motion be that by which something is always able to move other things, but cannot move itself. Let the other be that by which something can always move both itself and other things—by joining, separating, increasing, and the opposite; moreover, by generating and destroying. This motion is distinct from all the others. **CLINIAS.** Let it be as you wish. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we not place that motion as the ninth: that by which something is moved by another and moves others? And the tenth we shall place as that which moves both itself and others: which certainly accommodates itself to all actions and passions, and is called the source of all things. **CLINIAS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** Which of these ten motions shall we prefer above all others as the most robust and effective? **CLINIAS.** It is necessary that the one by which a thing can move both itself and others precedes by a very long interval, while all the others follow far behind. **ATHENIAN.** You speak rightly. But if one or two are not correctly placed, should they be positioned differently? **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** What we said about the tenth motion was not said correctly. **CLINIAS.** Why? **ATHENIAN.** Because the one which was numbered as the tenth is, according to reason, the first in both generation and strength. And the second is the one which we absurdly numbered in the ninth place. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean this? **ATHENIAN.** Thus: when something is moved by another, and that again is always moved by another, will there be among such things anything that is moved first? But how can that which is moved by something else be the first of those things that are moved? Certainly, that is impossible. But when something moving itself also moves another, and that moves another, and so many things are moved in sequence, will there be any other beginning of the whole motion than the change of that which moves itself? **CLINIAS.** That is excellently said and must be granted. **ATHENIAN.** Moreover, let us ask ourselves this way, and answer ourselves. If in some way the universe were to stand still together—as many of these "wise" men dare to say—which motion would we assert to be the first to occur among them? Surely that by which a thing moves itself. For motion depending on another will not happen before some other change has happened to them first. Therefore, it is necessary to confess that the beginning of all motions and the first motion—which occurs both in things standing still and is present in those things which are moved—is that by which a thing moves itself. And this is the most ancient and powerful change of all. The second is that by which a thing is changed by another and moves others. **CLINIAS.** You speak most truly. **ATHENIAN.** Since we have come this far in our disputation, let us also answer this. **CLINIAS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** If we see the first motion in an earthy, or watery, or fiery body—whether simple or mixed—what would we say is present within it? **CLINIAS.** Are you asking if it should be said to be "living" because it is moved by itself? **ATHENIAN.** Precisely. **CLINIAS.** Living, certainly. **ATHENIAN.** What then? When we see the soul to be in something, shall we think it lives for any other reason than this? **CLINIAS.** For this very reason. **ATHENIAN.** Pay attention, by Jove, I beseech you—do you not wish to understand three things in any given matter? **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** One is the substance itself. One is the definition <note>original: "rationem"</note> of the substance. And one is the name itself. And that there are also two questions about everything? **CLINIAS.** How two? **ATHENIAN.** Namely, that sometimes when a name is proposed to us, we seek the definition itself; and sometimes, having attained the definition, we then investigate the name. But do we wish to say this again? **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** A twofold distinction is found in other things and in numbers. And in a number so divided, the name is "even," but the definition...

<summary>The Athenian Guest uses an analogy of a river crossing to lead Clinias through a complex proof that self-motion is the first of all motions and the defining characteristic of the soul. By establishing the soul as the source of movement and therefore "prior" to physical matter, he begins to dismantle the materialist claim that gods and laws are merely secondary human inventions.</summary>

### On Laws. Or, Dialogue on Legislation. Book 10. 593

But the definition <note>original: "ratio," here meaning the logical explanation of a thing's nature</note> is: a number divisible into two equal parts. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** I am saying something like this. Do we not mean the same thing in both cases, whether we give the name when the definition is asked, or give the definition when the name is asked? Since we call one and the same thing "even" by name, but by its definition we call it "a number divisible into two equal parts." **CLINIAS.** Entirely the same. **ATHENIAN.** Now, for that thing whose name is "soul," what is the definition? Do we have any other definition besides the one we just stated—namely, that it is the thing that can move itself? <margin>What the soul can do.</margin> <margin>That the soul can move itself.</margin> **CLINIAS.** Do you assert that "to be moved by oneself" is the definition of that substance which everyone calls by the name "soul"? <margin>What the names of the soul are.</margin> **ATHENIAN.** I do indeed assert it. And if this is so, do we still require a more sufficient proof that the soul is the same as the first generation <note>original: "generationem," referring to the origin or birth of things</note> and motion of things that are, have been, and shall be, and of all their opposites as well? Since it has appeared to be the cause of all change and motion in everything. **CLINIAS.** Not at all. For it has been most sufficiently shown that the soul is more ancient than all things, since it is the principle of motion. **ATHENIAN.** Is it not true, then, that the motion which is produced by one thing in another—by which nothing ever moves itself—is secondary? And by whatever number of intervals one wishes, it must be ranked after the superior motion? For it is the change belonging to a truly inanimate body. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** We have said rightly, then, and properly, and truly, and absolutely, that the soul was made prior to the body; and the body is posterior and second, subject to the soul which rules it according to nature. **CLINIAS.** These things are most true. **ATHENIAN.** Do we remember that we conceded in the earlier parts that if the soul is shown to be more ancient than the body, then the things belonging to the soul must also be declared prior to those that are properties of the body? **CLINIAS.** Greatly so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, dispositions, characters, wills, thoughts, true opinions, cares, and memories—all these were made prior to the length, width, depth, and strength of bodies, just as the soul was made before the body. **CLINIAS.** It must be so. **ATHENIAN.** Are we not also compelled to concede that the soul is the cause of good and evil, of the honorable and the shameful, of the just and the unjust, and of all other opposites? Since we assert it is the cause of all things. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Since the soul governs all things and dwells in all things that move, must we not necessarily confess that it also governs the heavens? **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** One soul or many? Many, certainly—let me answer for you. Nor should we pose fewer than two: one beneficent, and the other its opposite. <note>This is a famous and debated passage where Plato suggests the existence of a "bad" soul to account for disorder or evil in the universe.</note> **CLINIAS.** Quite right. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the soul leads all things in the heavens, on the earth, and in the sea by its motions. The names of these motions are: to will, to consider, to care, to consult, to judge rightly and not rightly, to rejoice, to grieve, to dare, to fear, to hate, and to love. And by all other primary motions akin to these, which receive the secondary motions of bodies and lead all things into growth and decay, into combination or condensation, and separation or rarefaction. And into the qualities that follow these: heat, cold, heaviness, lightness, hardness, softness, white, black, sour, sweet, and bitter. And finally, if the soul, being a goddess, <margin>The soul joined to the intellect produces all things rightly.</margin> takes up a divine intellect <note>original: "intellectum," the highest form of reason</note> as its guide, it leads all things rightly to what is correct and happy; but if it is joined to folly, it produces all things contrary to these. Do we grant that these things are so? Or are we still in doubt? **CLINIAS.** We are in no way in doubt. **ATHENIAN.** Which kind of soul, then, do we think rules the heavens, the earth, and the whole circuit? That which is full of mind and virtue, or that which lacks both? **CLINIAS.** Do you wish us to answer in this way? **ATHENIAN.** In what way? **CLINIAS.** Let us say this, O wonderful man: if the whole circuit of the heaven and the progression of all things in it has a nature similar to the motion, circulation, and reason of the mind, and is carried out in a similar fashion, it must be conceded that the "best soul" has care for the whole world, directing it in such a manner. **CLINIAS.** Rightly said. **ATHENIAN.** But if it is moved furiously and without order, then an evil soul rules it. **CLINIAS.** This too is correct. **ATHENIAN.** What nature, then, does the motion of the mind have? But to answer this question, my friends, is difficult to do with prudence. Therefore, it is right that I should answer it with you. **CLINIAS.** You speak well. **ATHENIAN.** We must take care, then, lest as if we were turned toward the sun from the opposite side and making night at noon, we answer as if the mind could be sufficiently seen and known with mortal eyes. For we shall see more safely if we look at its image. <margin>How reverently God is to be worshipped. Transition of the discussion.</margin> **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Let us see which of those ten motions the intellect is most similar to, so that we may use it as an image. I will bring it back to your memory and answer for everyone. **CLINIAS.** Very well. **ATHENIAN.** We must remember what was said earlier by us, that of all things that are, some stand still and others move. **CLINIAS.** So it was said. **ATHENIAN.** Moreover, of those that move, some move in one place, and some in many. **CLINIAS.** That too. **ATHENIAN.** But the motion that always occurs in one place is necessarily moved around a center, similar to a circle made on a lathe; and thus it imitates the circuit of the mind as much as possible. **CLINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** I assert that both are carried through the same things, in the same way, in the same place, around the same things, toward the same things, by one reason and one order. Surely, if we say that the mind and the motion that occurs in one place are similar to the revolutions of a sphere made on a lathe, we will never be unskillful makers of good images. **CLINIAS.** Quite right. **ATHENIAN.** Conversely, the motion that is never carried out similarly, nor through the same things, nor in the same place, nor around the same things, nor toward the same things, nor in one place, nor with any order or ornament or reason, is surely related to all folly. **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** Now, then, we can openly proclaim that since all things are led around by the soul, the circuit of the heaven must necessarily be led around by a soul that cares for and adorns it—whether it be that best soul or its opposite. **CLINIAS.** But Guest, from what has been said, it now appears a sacrilege to say otherwise than that all these things are moved by a soul full of all virtue, whether one or many. **ATHENIAN.** You have understood these things well and quickly, Clinias. But add this. **CLINIAS.** What is it? **ATHENIAN.** If a soul leads the sun, moon, and all other stars, does it not lead each one individually? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Let us speak of one, then, in words that can be applied to all the stars. **CLINIAS.** Which one? **ATHENIAN.** All men see the body of the sun, but no one sees the soul; nor can the soul of any other animal be perceived by the senses of the body; it is grasped by the mind alone. Therefore, let us grasp this about the sun through intelligence alone. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** Since the soul moves the sun, <margin>The soul moves the sun.</margin> if we assert that this is done by it in one of three ways, perhaps we shall not go astray. **CLINIAS.** Which ways do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Either that it is inside this round body and carries it wherever it pleases, just as our soul leads us wherever it pleases. Or that it is outside, and having obtained a body of fire or air (as some say), it pushes body with body by force. Or thirdly, although it is itself bare of any body...

<summary>The Athenian Guest defines the soul as the source of self-motion and argues it is the primary cause of all things, being older than physical matter. He concludes that the orderly motions of the heavens must be directed by a virtuous, intelligent soul, using the sun's motion as a primary example.</summary>
