<meta>This page continues the Athenian Guest’s argument for the divine. Having established that the soul is the primary source of all motion, he now argues that these souls are gods and that they actively supervise human affairs (divine providence), rather than being indifferent or lazy.</meta>

### Book Thirty-Four.

<note>original: "Liber trigesimusquartus." This likely refers to a chapter or section division in this specific Renaissance edition of Plato's works, rather than the Book number of the Laws itself, which is Book 10.</note>

it happens that, because it possesses other powers that are wonderful beyond measure, it leads easily. **CLINIAS.** Certainly, it is necessary that all things are moved by the soul in one of these ways. **ATHENIAN.** It is better, then, that whether that soul holds the body from within like a carriage and thus pours light into all things, or whether it is outside, or in whatever way one may imagine it, we should all judge it to be a god. **CLINIAS.** Certainly so, unless someone is possessed by extreme madness. **ATHENIAN.** Moreover, concerning all the stars and the moon, the years, the months, and all the seasons, what else shall we say than this very thing? Since the soul, or souls endowed with every virtue, have been demonstrated to be the causes of all these things, we shall affirm that they are gods; whether they exist within bodies and, as living beings, adorn the whole heaven, or in whatever other way they are said to act. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** With these points granted, could anyone deny that all things are full of gods? <note>This is a famous philosophical sentiment attributed to Thales of Miletus, which Plato adopts here.</note> **CLINIAS.** No one is so out of his mind, Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** To the man who denies that the gods exist, then, having set the boundaries, O Clinias and Megillus, let us now leave the conversation. **CLINIAS.** What boundaries shall we impose? **ATHENIAN.** That he must either teach us that we do not think correctly when we say the soul is the first generation of all things—and that the other things we said consequently are not true—or, if he can say nothing better than we can, let him believe us, and live in the future in such a way that he does not doubt the gods. But let us now consider whether we have sufficiently shown that gods exist against those who deny them, or not. **CLINIAS.** It has been sufficiently stated, Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** The dispute against those men, therefore, shall have an end. But that man who, although he says the gods exist, nevertheless denies that they have care for human affairs: he must be persuaded by us in this way. "O excellent man," let us say, "a certain nature related to divinity leads you to affirm and honor the thing joined to you, when you assert that the gods exist. But the success of wicked and unjust men in public and private—which, although they are not truly happy, are nevertheless commonly held to be happy, and are extolled in poems <note>original: "carminibus," referring to epic or lyric poetry</note> and other discourses—rashly drives you headlong toward impiety. Or even when you see wicked men reach old age and leave their children and grandchildren in the greatest honors, you are greatly disturbed. You have perhaps heard, or even seen yourself, some who, although they committed many unjust and impious acts, nevertheless arrived from a small thing to a great one, and from the lowest rank to a tyranny, because of those very crimes. <term>Tyranny: in the Greek context, this refers to absolute rule seized by force rather than inherited or elected.</term> Therefore, since you do not wish to accuse the gods of being the authors of these things because of your connection to them, and yet you cannot bring yourself to be angry with the gods themselves, you have finally fallen into this: that although you think the gods exist, you believe human affairs are neglected by them." Therefore, lest this opinion push you toward a more serious disease of impiety, let us apply a remedy to the best of our ability by refuting this opinion. Wherefore, we shall join the following dispute with that preceding reasoning which we used against those who denied the gods existed. But you, Clinias and Megillus, answer on behalf of the young man, as you have done so far. And I, if any difficult point arises, taking you up, will lead you across the river as I have just done. **CLINIAS.** You speak rightly; do so, and we also will do so to the best of our power. **ATHENIAN.** It will perhaps not be difficult to demonstrate that the gods have no less care for the smallest things than for the greatest; especially since it was said a little while ago that they, being full of every virtue, claim the providence of all things as their own. <margin>That the gods have care for human affairs.</margin> **CLINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us investigate together what follows: what is that virtue of theirs by which they are conceded to be good? Come, are not being temperate <note>original: "temperatum," meaning possessing self-control</note> and having a mind granted to virtue, and their opposites to vice? **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** What further? Is not courage also granted to virtue, and cowardice to vice? **CLINIAS.** Greatly. **ATHENIAN.** And some of these will be called shameful, others honorable. **CLINIAS.** It must be so. **ATHENIAN.** And those things which are vices among these, we might say are able to be in us; but shall we say the gods are in no way participants in them? **CLINIAS.** Anyone would grant this. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we think that negligence, luxury, or idleness are virtues of the soul? Or otherwise? **CLINIAS.** How could it be? **ATHENIAN.** Do they belong to the opposite? **CLINIAS.** Yes, indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore the opposites of these belong to the opposite quality. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** He who is given to luxury, negligence, and idleness—whom Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet; the Athenian is likely referring to Hesiod's "Works and Days," where he compares the idle man to a drone bee.</note> says is most like the lazy drones—is he not held in hatred by us? **CLINIAS.** Most rightly indeed did that poet sing. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the god must not be said to have those characters which he hates, nor must anyone be permitted to say so. **CLINIAS.** In no way. **ATHENIAN.** Or will he, to whom the effect and care of some work especially pertains, care for the great things in that work but despise the small? How shall we not err if we praise this opinion? But let us consider it this way. Does not either a man or a god neglect for two reasons? **CLINIAS.** For which reasons? **ATHENIAN.** Either because he thinks it makes no difference to the whole if small things are neglected, or because, although he thinks it does make a difference, he nevertheless neglects it, held back by laziness and softness. For otherwise, negligence does not happen. For when someone cannot manage the care of all things, great and small, and therefore does not care because he is hindered by weakness, it is not then said that negligence is in him, whether he is an impotent man or a god imagined not to be able. **CLINIAS.** Certainly not. **ATHENIAN.** But now let those two answer the three of us—those who, although they grant that the gods exist, one thinks they are easily appeased, and the other thinks they are negligent in small things—and first they are asked thus: "Do you both affirm that the gods know, see, and hear all things, and that nothing can escape them of those things which are perceived either by sense or by intellect? Do you say these things are so, or otherwise?" **CLINIAS.** So. **ATHENIAN.** "Next, that they can do all things whatsoever mortals and immortals can do?" **CLINIAS.** Without doubt they will grant it is so. **ATHENIAN.** "We have also confessed that they are good, even the best." **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** It is therefore impossible for them to be seized by any laziness or any softness, since they are such as we have confessed them to be. For idleness is born in us from cowardice, and laziness from idleness and softness. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, no one of the gods, corrupted by idleness and laziness, neglects anything. For a god is a participant in no cowardice. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** It remains then, if they neglect small and few things, that they either neglect them because they know those things are to be despised, or what else is left but the opposite of this? **CLINIAS.** Nothing at all. **ATHENIAN.** "Which then, O excellent man, shall we affirm that you say? That they do not provide because of ignorance, when they ought to provide? Or just as we say of wicked men, that they see the better things, but, broken by pleasure or pain, they follow the worse; do the gods likewise fail to provide although they know they should provide?" **CLINIAS.** How could that be? **ATHENIAN.** "Furthermore, human affairs are partakers of a living nature, and man himself, above all other animals, is the most diligent worshiper of god." **CLINIAS.** It appears so. **ATHENIAN.** "Moreover, we say that all mortal living things are made and possessed by the gods, just as the entire heaven is."

<summary>The Athenian Guest argues that since gods are perfectly virtuous and all-knowing, they cannot be lazy or neglectful, and thus they must exercise providence over even the smallest human affairs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Guest’s dialogue with Clinias. Having previously argued that the gods exist, the Athenian now addresses the second common error: the belief that the gods exist but are indifferent to human affairs. He uses the analogy of craftsmen and doctors to show that a "whole" cannot be cared for if its "parts" are neglected.</meta>

### On the Laws, or the Dialogue on Legislation, Book 10. Page 595

we say. **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** Now then, whether someone says these things are small or great to the gods, in no way—since they are most provident and best—should their own possession be neglected by them. But let us consider this further. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** Whether the senses and powers of nature relate to ease and difficulty in opposite ways. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Small things, for instance, are more difficult to see and hear than large ones. But all small and few things are more easily held, carried, and governed by providence than their opposites. **CLINIAS.** Certainly, much more easily. **ATHENIAN.** What indeed? When a physician <note>original: "medicus"</note> wishes and is able to cure the whole body, if he provides for the large parts but ignores the small ones, will the whole ever be well for him? **CLINIAS.** Never. **ATHENIAN.** But neither pilots, nor generals, nor heads of households, nor rulers of cities, nor any such people at all, will rightly govern many and great things if small and few things are neglected. For even architects say that large stones cannot be well-laid without small ones. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us beware, then, lest we think God to be more worthless than mortal craftsmen <note>original: "opificibus"</note>. Indeed, the more skilled they are, the more they perform both small and large tasks with a single art in their own works, more exquisitely and perfectly. Shall God, who is most wise, and who is both able and willing to care, provide only for the great things, while neglecting the small ones—which are more easily governed—on account of laziness and sloth? **CLINIAS.** In no way, Guest, do we think this opinion of the gods should be admitted. For this thought is wicked and entirely false. **ATHENIAN.** We seem to have disputed enough now against him who accuses the gods of the crime of negligence. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** But so far, we have in a way compelled him by reason to confess that he holds a false opinion. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** I think he also needs persuasion, which might capture him as if by a certain song. **CLINIAS.** What is this persuasion? **ATHENIAN.** Let us persuade this young man that He who provides for the whole ordains all things toward the virtue and safety of the whole, of which each part acts and suffers what is fitting for it according to its powers. Over these individual parts, leaders are appointed who have care over even the smallest actions and passions, distributed through the individual and outermost particles of the universe, carried out to the very end. One of these particles is yours, O wretched one, which always looks toward the whole, however small it may be. You, however, are ignorant that every generation of individuals happens for the sake of the whole, so that the life of the universe itself may be blessed. Its substance is not for your sake, but you were made for its sake. For every physician and every skilled craftsman <note>original: "artificiosus opifex"</note> does individual things for the sake of the whole, and directs all things toward common perfection: not referring the whole to the part, but referring the individual parts to the whole. But you are annoyed because you do not know how that which is best for you is at the same time fitting for the universe and for you, according to the powers of our common generation. Since a soul is always joined with a body—now with one, then with another—and is changed by various mutations either because of itself or because of another soul, nothing else remains for the Ordainer of these things than to rearrange them, like one throwing dice <note>original: "talos iacienti"—this refers to knucklebones or dice, a metaphor for God shifting souls into different positions based on their merit</note>, so that by transposing them, He may move better characters into a better place, and worse characters into a worse place, as is fitting for each, so that each may obtain the lot that is congruent with them. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean that? **ATHENIAN.** I seem to speak of that method by which the gods most easily provide for all things. For if someone shapes each thing while always looking at the whole, and transforms everything toward it—as if making animated water out of fire, and not many things at once from one or one from many, participating in a first, second, or third generation—there would be an infinite multitude of these transposed ornaments. But now, there is a wonderful ease in the work of Him who provides for the whole. **CLINIAS.** How do you say that again? **ATHENIAN.** Since that King of ours perceived that all the actions of men are animated, and that they have much virtue in them and also much depravity, and since soul and body were made not to suffer destruction (yet not to be eternal, as the gods are—for if either of these were destroyed, all generation of living beings would cease)—and since he saw, moreover, that what is good in the soul helps, and what is evil, on the contrary, harms—having perceived all this, I say, He therefore devised where each part should be located most greatly, best, and most easily, so that virtue might have victory in the universe and vice might be hindered from winning. He invented, therefore, for this universe, how any deed should be done, and what kind of seat and habitation and what kind of places each should be allotted. But He left the causes of generating this or that to our wills. For wherever one desires, and whatever kind of soul one has, there he almost always lives, and such he becomes for the most part. **CLINIAS.** Fittingly. **ATHENIAN.** All things, therefore, that have a soul are changed; for they have the cause of change within themselves. Having been changed, they are carried according to the order and law of the fates. And those that have sinned less, wander less deeply and on the surface of the region; those that have sinned more and more atrociously, fall into the depths and sink into the lower region, which they call by the name of the "infernal regions" and similar names, which both the living and those released from bodies dream of and dread. But the soul that is possessed of greater virtue or vice, when it has been more vehemently changed by its own will and constant habit and has adhered to divine virtue, becoming especially like it, is transferred to a similarly far better and holy place. But that which is affected in the opposite way is transferred to the opposite place and carries out its life there. This is the judgment of the gods who inhabit heaven, O boy and young man who think you are neglected by the gods: that he who becomes worse goes toward worse souls, and he who becomes better goes toward better souls, both in life and in every death, and suffers and does what is fitting for like to be done to like. Therefore, neither you nor any other should hope or trust that you will be so lucky as to escape and overcome this judgment of the gods. For those who decreed this established it more firmly than all other things, so that it must be entirely guarded against. For you will never be neglected by Him, neither if you are so small that you enter into the depths of the earth, nor if you become so high that you fly on wings into heaven; but you will pay the fitting penalties, whether staying here, or having departed to the lower regions, or having been transferred to some more remote and inaccessible place. The same reasoning applies to those whom you have seen rise from small to great men through wicked crimes, and whom you thought had reached happiness from misery. In their actions, as if in a mirror, you thought you perceived the negligence of the gods toward all things, because you were evidently ignorant of how their progress contributes to the whole. It is not right to be ignorant of this, O most excellent man; for he who does not know it will never perceive the form of living, nor be able to speak words about the happiness or misery of life. Therefore, if Clinias here and this entire assembly of elders has persuaded you that you are entirely ignorant of what you say about the gods, God favors you; but if you still desire some reason, hear what we shall say to that third man, if you are in any way a partaker of mind. Indeed, I think it has been sufficiently demonstrated that the gods exist and that they provide for humans.

...and that Vulcan and Mars preside over the arts, as you may gather from many of Plato’s <note>Plato was an ancient Greek philosopher whose works often used myths to explain complex spiritual truths.</note> mysteries handed down in various places: a certain trinity of deities, which in the Platonic manner we call <term>demiurgic</term> <note>original: *opificiam* – relating to the work of a master craftsman or creator</note>, always stands beside Jove, the supreme architect of the world. In this trinity, Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> is first, Vulcan is second, and Mars is third.

But just as the whole trinity refers back to Jove himself, from whom it originates, so Vulcan and Mars are generally referred back to Pallas. I will set aside for now the fact that he <note>Likely referring to Plato or a commentator like Proclus.</note> seems to have envisioned power in Mars, wisdom in Pallas, and a fiery spirit in Vulcan. Certainly, three things are required for that "art" of Jove by which he perfects the universe:

First, the <term>reason</term> <note>original: *ratio* – here meaning the structural logic or blueprint</note> itself through which he intends to make individual things.

Second, the effective <term>execution</term> <note>original: *expeditio* – the process of bringing a mental concept into physical reality</note> of those things which he had conceived through reason.

Third, the safety and defense of those things which have been brought into being.

He names the Idea of the first "Pallas," the second "Vulcan," and the third "Mars." And because both—namely, the conservation or defense as well as the execution or expression of things—require reason...

...[a freedman] can [be recalled to slavery], if he does not honor his former master, or if he does not honor him sufficiently. This **honor** <note>original: "cultus," referring to the social and legal duties a freedman owed his former owner.</note> consists, first, of coming to the master's house three times during each harvest, and showing himself ready to do whatever is honorable and possible for him; secondly, that regarding marriage, he should do whatever seems right to the master. Nor shall he be allowed to acquire greater wealth for himself than is possessed by the one who freed him; instead, whatever surplus he has shall be given to the master. 

Furthermore, a freedman, like a foreigner, shall not remain in the city beyond twenty years; but after that time, having taken his goods, he must depart, unless he has persuaded his former master and the magistrates otherwise. If, however, the goods of any freedman or foreigner exceed the **third census** <note>Property in Plato's "Laws" was divided into four classes based on value. If anyone is convicted of not obeying this law, he shall be punished by death, and his goods shall be confiscated for the public treasury. The judges of the tribes shall take notice of these matters, unless the litigants have first been reconciled through neighbors and arbitrators. 

If anyone claims an animal or any other thing to be his own, the one who possesses it shall refer back to the person who either sold it, or legitimately and sufficiently gave it, or in whatever other way he validly and firmly handed it over. If he refers the matter to a citizen or a resident of the city, the truth shall be found within thirty days; but if he refers to foreigners, it shall be found within five months, the middle of which shall be the month in which the sun returns from the summer circle to the winter one <note>This refers to the period around the autumnal equinox.</note>. 

Whatever things are exchanged by buying and selling shall be exchanged in the designated place of the forum, by giving and receiving the item and the price of the item immediately on the spot, and nowhere else. No buying or selling shall be done **on credit** <note>original: "ad terminum," literally "at a term" or fixed future date.</note>. But if an exchange is made otherwise or in other places, there shall be no legal judgment concerning it according to the law. Nor shall any judgment be rendered concerning **contributions and banquets** <note>Private social clubs or shared meals where members pooled resources.</note>, even when several people contribute money or anything else among themselves to accomplish something. 

A seller who has received a price for a sold item of no less than fifty **drachmas** <note>An ancient Greek unit of currency.</note> must necessarily wait ten days in the city, and the buyer must not be ignorant of his lodging. We wish this to be done for the sake of complaints and **legal returns** <note>original: "redditionum," the right to return defective goods for a refund.</note> which are accustomed to happen in these matters. 

A legal return is distinguished from a non-legal one as follows: When someone has sold a slave suffering from **frenzy** <note>original: "phrenesi," referring to delirium or mental instability.</note>, or kidney stones, or **strangury** <note>A condition causing painful or difficult urination.</note>, or that disease which they call **sacred** <note>original: "sacrum," the common ancient term for epilepsy.</note>, or any other illness of body or mind that is hidden from most people, long-lasting, and difficult to cure—if a physician or a **physical trainer** <note>original: "gymnasticus," an expert in health and bodily mechanics.</note> buys him, he shall not be allowed to return the slave. ...they strive. But let us consider what the cause of the slander against this matter is, and why it does not seem honorable, so that even if we cannot fix the whole thing, we may at least regulate part of it by law.
CLINIAS: This matter, it seems, is neither a small thing, nor does it require a small amount of virtue.
ATHENIAN: How do you mean, Clinias? Very few men by nature, even those endowed with the best education, are able to restrain themselves when they are affected by poverty and a desire for certain things, so as to behave with moderation. When they have the chance to take a great deal of money, they are instead content with a modest amount and prefer moderation to excess. The common people, however, do the exact opposite. For they desire without limit; and when they might make a moderate profit, they are tormented by an insatiable greed for gain. For this reason, all classes of men who are involved in **retail trade** <term>cauponatione: the practice of keeping an inn or selling goods at retail, often viewed with suspicion in antiquity as a source of greed.</term>, commerce, and innkeeping are subject to slander and reproach. 

For if someone—may it never happen and far be it from us—but if someone were to compel (for I will say it, even if it sounds ridiculous to say) the best men everywhere to oversee inns for a time, or to engage in retail trade, or to do anything of this sort; and if most holy women were similarly forced by some necessity of fate to take up these tasks, we would clearly recognize that all these things are honorable and to be approved. Indeed, if they were performed without corruption, those who do these things would be thought of, not unfairly, as performing the roles of mothers and nurses. But as it is, men build houses in deserted places where many long roads lead, for the sake of innkeeping. They receive those driven by storms into a welcome lodging and refresh those oppressed by heat; yet they do not then send them away like friends gifted with **hospitality** <note>original: "hospitalibus muneribus," referring to the ancient Greek custom of "Xenia," or sacred guest-friendship.</note>, but instead, like enemies and captives, they cruelly force them to ransom themselves and strip them of all their possessions. These and other shameful acts committed in all these matters cause these pursuits—which actually provide help to those in need—to be subject to slander. A remedy for these things must be devised by the lawgiver. Therefore, that old proverb is correct and has long been celebrated:
<margin>Proverb: It is hard to fight against two things.</margin>
That it is hard to fight against two contrary things at once. This happens in this case, just as it does in many other diseases. For a struggle now looms for us against two things: wealth and poverty. One of these corrupts the souls of men with luxury and softness; the other drives them to impudence through suffering. What remedy, therefore, shall we devise in a wisely instituted city to drive out this disease? 
We must first endeavor to employ the smallest possible class of innkeepers in the city. Second, these trades of innkeeping must be entrusted to those people whose corruption would not cause the city great harm. Third, a way and a method must be found so that the minds of these men are not easily filled with impudence and a lack of refinement. Having said these things, let this law regarding such matters be passed for the **Magnesians** <note>The fictional citizens of the "ideal city" Plato is designing in this dialogue.</note> with good fortune, whose city the god is raising up and causing to be inhabited again. 

None of those who belong to the forty-five thousand households <note>original: "quadraginta & quinque millibus." In the standard Greek text of Plato's Laws, the number of households is 5,040. Nor shall any citizen become the servant of a private person who is not his equal in status, except for his father and mother, and others of his ancestral line, and other elders who are free and live freely. However, the distinction between a free person and one who is not free cannot be easily and precisely defined by laws. Nevertheless, let them be distinguished by the leading men, and let them be judged by their hatred or love for them. 

Truly, let anyone who wishes accuse a citizen who has devoted himself to the undignified trade of innkeeping before the leading men—those first in virtue—as if he were a disgrace to his own family. And if he is caught having stained his father’s house with an unworthy pursuit, he shall be barred from this work and held in chains for a year. If he should fall again,

he shall be bound for two years. And thereafter, as often as he is found to have sinned, the time he is detained shall always be doubled. 

The second law commands that only foreigners and **aliens** <note>original: "advenæ," referring to resident foreigners or "metecs" who lived in the city but lacked citizenship rights.</note> shall follow the arts of innkeeping. 

The third law warns that care must be taken that the foreigner or resident be either as good as possible or as little evil as possible. The Guardians of the Laws must not be ignorant that they are observers not only of those whom it is not difficult to keep from iniquity and wickedness—those who are well-born and well-educated—but even much more of those who are not so, and who are engaged in these trades by which they are more easily driven toward dishonesty. 

Since, indeed, innkeeping is manifold and varied, the Guardians of the Laws should meet with experts in each of these types. In this way, the arts of innkeeping will benefit individuals and cause the least harm. ->**The Complaints of the Dying**<-

For a man at the point of death might cry out: "By the gods, is it not a cruel thing that I am not permitted to bestow my own goods upon whomever I wish? I, as your legislator, declare that you do not belong to yourself, nor does this property you possess belong to you; rather, you belong to your whole family—both those who lived before you and those yet to be born—and even more truly, your entire family and its estate belong to the **State**."

<margin>The State’s claim over the individual</margin>

"Therefore, I will not permit you to be swayed by the flatteries of those who attend you in your sickness, nor by your own sudden impulses, to make a will that is unjust or harmful to the City or to your lineage. 604 Book Thirty-Four <note>While the header reads "Liber trigesimusquartus" (Book 34), this text actually corresponds to Book 11 of Plato's *Laws* (sections 930e–935c), as organized in traditional editions. The numbering here likely refers to a specific Renaissance chaptering system.</note>

...not ignoring that many have often been helped or harmed. If anyone in this city cares for their parents less than is fitting, or does not love them more than their own children, grandchildren, or even themselves—failing to be obedient to their will in all things above others—the person thus neglected may report the matter, either personally or through another, to the three most senior **Guardians of the Laws** <term>nomophylakes</term> <note>The highest administrative officials in Plato's ideal city, responsible for ensuring the laws are followed.</note> and likewise to the three overseers of marriages. Having investigated the matter, these officials shall punish those who committed the injury: men, if they have not yet passed their thirtieth year, and women, if they have not passed their fortieth, with imprisonment and beatings. 

However, if they are older than the ages we have mentioned and do not cease neglecting their parents—or even go so far as to afflict them—they shall be compelled to go to trial. Let those citizens who most exceed all others in age serve as judges. The condemned shall pay or suffer whatever the court decides, so that nothing is omitted that a human being might be capable of giving or suffering. If anyone is so afflicted that they cannot report it themselves, let any free person who hears of it notify the magistrates, or else be held as a wicked person himself and be liable to accusation for the damage caused by anyone who wishes to sue. 

If a slave reports the abuse, let him be free. If he was the slave of the abuser or the abused, let the magistrates grant him his liberty; if he belonged to another citizen, the price shall be paid to his master from public funds. Let the magistrates take care that no one harms the person who brought the report. 

As for the harm people do to others through poisoning <term>veneficium</term> <note>original: "veneno." In Latin, this word covers both medicinal drugs, lethal poisons, and magical potions.</note>, those that are lethal have already been categorized. But as for the rest—whether administered through drink, food, or ointment, done intentionally and with a plan—we have not yet distinguished them. For poisons harm the human race in two ways. First, as we just said, by bodies naturally harming other bodies. Second, through magical sorceries, incantations, and certain "knots" <note>An ancient magical practice of "binding" a victim by tying knots in cords while reciting spells.</note>, by which those who seek to do harm are convinced they can achieve it, and the victims are easily persuaded that they are being harmed by such sorcery. 

It is not easy to know the true nature of these and other such things, nor if one did know, could others be easily persuaded of it. But since the minds of men are troubled and suspicious toward one another regarding these matters, it is not worth trying to persuade them that they should utterly despise such things if they see **wax figures** <note>original: "cerea simulacra." Small effigies used in "sympathetic magic" to represent the target of a curse.</note> at their doors, at a crossroads, or at the monuments of their ancestors—even though they have no certain knowledge of them. 

Therefore, dividing the law on poisoning into two parts, we first exhort, warn, and advise that they do not do such things, nor terrify the many like children, nor force the legislator and judge to seek a remedy for the fears of such people. Indeed, he who strives to harm by poison, if he intends to inflict it upon bodies, does not know what he is doing unless he is skilled in medicine. Similarly, he who attempts it with magical incantations is ignorant unless he is a diviner <term>aruspex</term> <note>Traditionally a Roman priest who read omens in entrails, but used here generally for a seer or interpreter of portents.</note> or an interpreter of wonders. 

But let this law now be enacted concerning such poisons: If anyone uses poison not to kill a human, but to harm livestock or beehives—whether to kill them or otherwise harm them—if he is a physician and is judged guilty of poisoning, let him suffer the penalty of death. If he is ignorant of medicine, let the court decide what he must suffer or pay. When, however, anyone is caught prepared to do harm

[Right Column]

with knots, spells, incantations, and similar sorceries, if he is a diviner or an interpreter of wonders, let him be put to death. If he is not such a person, let the court likewise decide what he must pay or suffer. He who has caused harm secretly or otherwise shall pay great damages if he harmed in great things, and lesser in minor things; and in all cases, he shall pay enough to equal the loss. 

Furthermore, for each injury, let a fine be imposed so that he may become thoroughly more moderate: a lighter one if he was driven by another’s malice due to the imprudence of youth, but a heavier one if he acted out of his own madness, or immoderate pleasures and pains, or fear, or envy, or incurable anger. 

<margin>Why the wicked are troubled by punishments.</margin> Indeed, the wicked are troubled with punishments, not because they have sinned—for what has been done cannot be undone—but so that hereafter both the sinners themselves and those who have seen the iniquities punished might hate injustice, or at least sin less in similar vices. 

For the sake of all these things, the laws ought to look to this end, and like good archers, they should aim at this mark, considering the magnitude of punishment in each case and what is deserved. It befits the judge to act as the minister of the legislator: when the law commits it to him, he himself shall decide what the condemned ought to pay or suffer. He should certainly execute the remainder by imitating the previous standards, just as a painter paints so that he carefully follows his models. 

This, I believe, O **Clinias** and **Megillus** <note>The Cretan and Spartan characters who are debating these laws with an "Athenian Stranger."</note>, we must do as beautifully and excellently as possible: we must state what the penalties should be for those things done by theft and secrecy, as well as those done by force, insofar as the gods and the sons of gods permit us to lay down laws. 

Let no insane person <term>furiosus</term> be seen openly in the city. Instead, let the relatives guard the insane person at home in whatever way they can. If they fail to do this, let them be fined: those of the highest wealth class shall pay one hundred drachmae, whether they guard a slave or a free person with insufficient care. Those of the second class shall pay four-fifths of that; those of the third, three-fifths; and those of the fourth, two-fifths. 

Now, men are driven by madness in many ways. Some by disease, like those we just mentioned. Others through the anger of a depraved nature and a vicious education; these, moved by small enmities, shout loudly and insult one another shamefully. In a city established with good laws, it is not fitting for any such thing to happen. Regarding slander, therefore, let this one law be placed for all: 

Let no one slander anyone. Instead, whoever disputes with another about any matter, let him rather learn and teach, both for the one disputing and those present, so that he abstains entirely from all slander. For when they curse one another with foul words, they are considered womanish; and especially from words—which are certainly a very light thing—very heavy hatreds and enmities are often born. Indeed, he who gives in to anger (a truly unpleasant thing) and fills it up with noxious "food," as it were, becomes embittered; as much as he had been previously cultivated by discipline, he then makes the angry part of his soul wild, makes his way of living difficult for himself, and receives this bitter "favor" from his anger. 

From this, almost all tend to reach the point where they say something ridiculous about their adversary; in which habit, whoever accustoms himself either loses good character entirely or loses his magnanimity for the most part. For this reason, let no one ever use these reproaches in a temple, nor where public sacrifices or games are performed, nor in the marketplace of goods for sale, nor in a court, or any other common gathering. Let the presiding magistrate of these matters freely punish the one who offends in this; but if he does not, he shall be considered a traitor to the laws and a despiser of the legislator’s precepts...

<meta>This page continues the legal and social regulations for the ideal city of Magnesia, transitioning from familial duties to public conduct, the regulation of speech and theater, and the procedures for the judicial system.</meta>

# On the Laws, or, on the Passage of Laws. Dialogue XI. 605

...he should never ascend to the contest of any public office as if he were about to compete for the sake of virtue. If, however, anyone in other places uses insults, whether by provoking or responding, whoever of the elders is present should strike this man in defense of the laws; and he should restrain those who have been stirred up by anger at another's wrongdoing. Otherwise, as we have said before, let him be punished. Furthermore, we consider that no one engages in these insults and witty mockeries who does not often speak some ridicule. And this is precisely what we condemn: when it is done with anger. 

What then? Shall we admit the wit and ridiculous insults of comic poets and satirists which they use against citizens, if they bite in this way without anger? Or shall we distinguish it in two ways, into playful and serious speech? And let it be permitted in jest, so that a joke is told without anger; but with a soul stirred by anger, let it be permitted to no one, as we said before, to say such a thing. This, therefore, must in no way be admitted. To whom it may be permitted, and to whom not, must now be declared by law. It shall not be permitted to a comic poet, or a writer of iambic verse or musical melody, to disparage any citizen either by word or by image, whether he does so with anger or without it. And if anyone acts to the contrary, those who are in charge of awarding prizes <note>The judges of the theatrical festivals.</note> shall expel him on that very day; otherwise, they shall be fined three minae <term>minae</term> <note>A Greek unit of currency; three minae was a significant sum, roughly equivalent to several months' wages for a laborer.</note>, to be consecrated to the God in whose honor the contest had been held. 

To others, however, of whom we spoke above, it shall be permitted to say something ridiculous without anger and in jest; but in seriousness and with anger, by no means. The judgment of this matter shall be committed to the curator of the common education of youth. And what he approves, it is permitted to bring into the public; but what he rejects, he himself shall never show to anyone, nor teach it to another, whether slave or free. If he acts to the contrary, let him be considered wicked and a despiser of the laws.

A man is to be considered "miserable"—that is, worthy of mercy—not if he is oppressed by hunger or some other such thing, but one who, while being temperate and endowed with some other virtue or part of virtue, is perhaps afflicted by some calamity in these matters. Therefore, it will indeed be a wonder if such a man is so neglected that, whether free or slave, he falls into extreme poverty in a moderately governed city. Therefore, the legislator may safely establish such a law regarding this matter without injustice: **Let there be no beggar in our city.** Whoever attempts it and begins to collect a living with insatiable prayers, let him be driven from the market by the curators of trade, let him be ejected from the city by the magistrate of buildings <term>aedilis</term> <note>Originally a Roman office, used here to describe the city official in charge of public infrastructure and order.</note>, and finally let him be expelled from the entire region by the magistrate of the fields, so that the whole region may be entirely clean of such a creature.

If a male or female slave harms another's property, whether through ignorance or some immoderate use, and the one who suffered the loss did not provide the cause, the owner must either make satisfaction or hand over the slave to the one who suffered the loss. But if the owner of the slave contends, through some common cunning of the offender and the sufferer, that the slave is being taken from him, let him bring a charge of malice against the one complaining about the slave. And if he convicts him, let him receive double the price of the slave as determined by the court from the condemned man. But if he is convicted, let him both restore the loss and hand over the slave in addition. 

If a beast of burden, or a horse, or a dog, or any other domestic animal grinds down <note>original: "attriuerit", meaning to wear down, damage, or trample.</note> the property of a neighbor, the owner of the animal shall similarly restore the loss. 

If anyone is unwilling to bear witness voluntarily, let him be summoned by the one in need, and once summoned, let him be present at the proper time; and let him offer testimony according to what he knows. But if he says he does not know, let him affirm that he does not know by swearing an oath naming three gods—Jupiter, Apollo, and Themis—and then let him depart. He who is summoned to bear witness and does not come, let him pay the loss to the one who summoned him according to the law. If any judge is summoned as a witness, once the testimony is given, he shall not give any sentence in that same case. 

A free woman, if she has exceeded forty years of age, may be permitted to be present in court both for testifying and for speaking; indeed, she may even bring a suit if she is not under a husband. But while her husband is living, let it be permitted for her only to provide testimony. To a male and female slave and to children, let it be permitted to speak and testify only regarding homicide, provided they give a suitable guarantor that they will remain until the sentence is passed, in case they are accused of false testimony. 

If anyone wishes to act against false testimony, which is permitted both for the whole and for a part of the testimony and to both adversaries, let him object that the witnesses were false before the judges pass sentence. The accusations of false testimony brought by both parties shall be kept in writing by the magistrates themselves and later referred to the court concerning false testimony. If anyone is found to have given false testimony twice, let him be compelled by no law to testify a third time. But if three times, let it be permitted to him in no way to give testimony thereafter. But if, having been caught in falsehood three times, he dares to testify further, let him be brought to the magistrate by anyone who wishes, and let him be handed over to the court by the magistrate; and if he is convicted, let him die. When, in a lawsuit, false testimonies have intervened through which someone could be seen to have overcome his adversary, if more than half of the witnesses are condemned, no judgment shall proceed according to those testimonies. It is proper to debate whether anything was judged according to those testimonies or not, so that however it was judged, the dispute may reach a just end by this agreement.

<margin>Against rabble-rousers and lawyers corrupted by greed.</margin>

Truly, while there are many good things in the life of men, certain dire calamities settle upon most of them, which stain and defile them. Why is judicial debate and judgment not a good thing for man, which has tamed all human affairs? Yet, since such debate is a good thing, why should it not also be good to assist someone in a lawsuit and to favor a just cause? Since these things are so, a perverse calumny <note>The art of legal manipulation or sophistry.</note> has taken the good name of an "art," which asserts it has discovered a skill in lawsuits by which anyone can easily overcome what must be done and said, whether the cause be honorable or foul; and to make victors of those whom it favors with its own reasons, if money is given for the benefit of the art itself. 

Whether this is an art or some practice devoid of art, effort must be made so that it has no entrance into our city; but the creator of the truth of the laws should bring forth nothing against the laws, and having departed elsewhere, let it show its strength. If anyone does not obey, let him be deterred by this law: If anyone tries to turn the strength of justice in the minds of the judges to the contrary, and moves many litigations beyond what is appropriate, or assists those who move them, let whoever wishes bring a charge against him for the crime of acting badly or, finally, for defending, and let a judgment of this kind be conducted before elected judges. And if he is condemned, let it be discussed whether he did it out of avarice or out of some ambitious contention. And if out of contention, let the judges themselves prescribe a certain time for him in which he may plead or speak no cause for himself nor for another. But if out of avarice, let a foreigner depart from the region never to return, and if he returns, let him die. But a citizen, if he is caught having done this out of avarice, since he valued money so much, let him die altogether. But if he is judged to have done such a thing twice out of ambitious contention, let him undergo that same punishment.

Ee iiii Dialogue <note>Signature mark for the printer/binder.</note>

This is a scholarly translation of the provided Latin text, which contains Marsilio Ficinus’s *Argumentum* (Introduction) and his translation of the twelfth book of Plato’s *Laws* (*Leges*).

### Book Thirty-Four

## THE TWELFTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS,
### OR, ON THE LEGISLATION.

#### MARSILIO FICINO
#### ARGUMENT

Divine **P**lato, in all the dialogues on the laws, by a likeness to the divine work, was so delighted by the number twelve that he surely wished the twelfth dialogue to be the shared secret of the laws, just as the twelfth circle of the world is the common firmament of the stars. And just as he who penetrates that twelfth circle will immediately find, or rather even attain, the soul in perfection and happiness: so Plato, proceeding beyond the twelfth book, will demonstrate in the *Epinomis* not so much the laws as the blessed perfection of the soul acquired through the laws. Indeed, in the earlier books, he treated the law as it pertains partly to public offices, partly to private business, partly to urban affairs, and partly to external ones, whether in peace or in war. In the twelfth [book], however, all are in a certain way gathered together as pertaining to all things; not individual laws, but several singular ones from every kind. 

To the laws is added that which is greatest: namely, the reason that is both the preserver and the emender of the laws. To the magistrates is added that which is greatest: namely, the system of returning accounts and recovering property [*repetundarum*], placed over the public offices of magistrates no differently than the examination of conscience itself is placed over the private actions of souls. Indeed, by this examination, both the entire salvation of souls in private and the universal safety of the city in public consist. And that is the summary argument of the twelfth [book]. 

But since, right at the beginning, and in what follows, and often in the preceding parts, he commemorates the vengeance of the gods, and calls some gods the sons of others, and calls men the sons of the gods, it is necessary to remember that in Plato there are two ways in which gods are the sons of gods, and two ways in which men are the sons of the gods. First indeed, as the *Timaeus* teaches, all the rulers of the spheres of the world—whether the souls of the spheres themselves, or the demons within the spheres, or the angelic intellects beyond the spheres—are sons of the almighty God, created as benefits by His will. Secondly, in any of these three kinds, the inferiors are called sons of the superiors because, continuously receiving rays and forms from the superiors, they are in a certain way formed from them, and seem to obey them as if they were fathers. 

Men are similarly said to be begotten by the celestials, either because from the beginning of things they were brought forth into the light from the bowels of the earth by the nourishment of the superiors, or because some daily, vehemently inspired by the breath of the superiors, are soon transferred by divine power—as if reborn—from their human and accustomed affection into a certain divine state of life. In which rank he frequently places both pious philosophers and philosophical princes. 

Furthermore, when right at the beginning of the book he places *Iuppiter* and *Mercurius* over legates and messengers, it must be understood first, by *Iuppiter*, God the architect of the world, and by *Mercurius*, the entire number of angels; then again by *Iuppiter*, the significance of the second of the planets regarding emperors and laws, and by *Mercurius* the planet, the significance of all interpretation and expedition. I call the planets "significators." Since, as the *Timaeus* testifies and *Plotinus* discusses, the planets and all celestial things signify and announce to each person what the superiors are about to do, or what we ourselves are sometimes about to do, but often about to suffer. 

He soon detests the poets who, transferring the crimes of men onto the celestials, both impiously sinned against divinity and gravely harmed men by the evil example of the gods. Furthermore, he thinks thefts and other crimes should be judged more from the intention and habit of the sinner—whether curable or incurable—than from the [mere] effect. 

Among the laws of the military, he prescribes what he judges best of all in every life: that no one should know what it is to live for himself alone or to do anything apart from others, but that each should direct individual actions to the nod of a prudent superior and toward common use. He teaches judges not to deliver a sentence contrary to the law, whether voluntarily or under compulsion. For judgment itself, according to the opinion of the ancients, especially *Orpheus* and *Hesiod*, is a certain modest virgin; and to Modesty and Judgment, a lie is especially hateful. Indeed, he thinks the divine providence that presides over judgment is a goddess to be venerated by human judges. 

After these things, where he condemns those who shamefully threw away their arms, and moreover those leaders of war who receive them back to serve again under their standards: the number of ten *minae* [of fine] is translated by us here, though the laws elsewhere mention a thousand. A little later, he asserts that the knot of the republic is the judgment of returning accounts: so that no judge in the republic is without a judge. Otherwise, through the loose license of judging, first justice would perish, then the city, having lost justice, would die as if its soul were gone. 

By the temple of *Sol* and *Apollo*, he understands a shrine dedicated not only to the planet and the solar soul, but much more to the light of the Highest Good, of which the sun is the image. You will hear that sins are committed through a lack of religion. But of all the impious, the worst are those who trust they will so appease God with prayers and sacrifices that, because of this confidence, they may extort great wealth with impunity. 

After this, he hands down very cautious laws concerning the reception of foreigners and the travel of citizens: lest the customs of the city be confounded by alien and ill-considered habit, or lest the republic lack the skill of foreigners. You will note here that in a few people there is a certain divine power through which they discern the capacity of intellects. This shows that a certain divinity is inborn in us, not only acquired by us, so to speak. 

He prescribes that it must not be considered a small matter whether you seem upright or wicked. But the reputation for virtue must also be sought, and sought only through virtue itself. He commemorates that divine men sometimes exist even among the common people and in ill-governed cities. 

After these things, he treats many matters concerning the pleading of causes, accusation, defense, appeal, surety, proscription, and others of this sort. He also mixes with these, by a certain opportunity, various things to be dedicated as images to the divinities. This is a tradition of symbolic Pythagorean ritual. He says that the Earth and *Vesta* exist as the sacred habitation of all the gods. By adding "Vesta," he signified that under the name of this earth, it ought to be understood more deeply: both this elemental earth, and the lunar earth, and finally the starry earth. Likewise, three souls of the three earths, and three angels. 

Remember, however, that among the ancients, whatever in the universe is effective for forming and moving is metaphorically called "fire." Likewise, whatever is most easily formable anywhere is called "air." That which is purgative is "water"; that which is solid or stable and consistent, they name "earth." Such a nature, on account of its dense or consistent quality, is called "earth" by the Platonists both here and in the moon and in the firmament. To whom, then, would it be a wonder that the Earth exists as the sacred habitation of all the gods, if the universe is comprised within the three boundaries of the three earths? 

And since he said the gods are consecrated by the soul, he forbids them to be consecrated again, warning that you should not trust that you can offer anything to God that was not first God's own. He also forbids statues to be made of gold or silver, lest we trust that by their great price we might purge great crimes. Again, he prohibits ivory, since it has been destitute of its sensory soul: lest without sense—that is, vigilance and attention—we work in sacred matters. He rejects bronze and iron, blaming of course the instruments of war. For when the soul is at odds within itself and with others, we work our sacrifices in vain. 

Finally, he looks to wood and stone, from which the images of the gods are made. In stone, he commends the aptitude of the mind in sacred things. In wood, the fuel for fire—that is, the ardor of the soul, which is easily kindled in divine matters. He orders whole images to be fabricated from a single stone or piece of wood, commending simplicity and integrity above all. 

Nor must it be passed over in silence that legates were sent in the previous parts to four oracles, so that we might know that the God who is the author of all provides for all parts of the world equally: which are designated by the four "corners," as it were, under the names of East, West, North, and South; and by whatever rite God is worshipped, provided He is worshipped with a pure mind and by His own grace, it is in some way accepted. But of these things, [we speak] more diligently elsewhere. 

Among these things, he forbids those who serve the father in any matter to receive gifts. He also deals with tributes. He says nothing better can be learned by anyone than that by which he himself becomes better. He says the law is a wonderful and divine thing, having its name among the Greeks from "Mind" [*nous* / *nomos*] itself: from Mind, I say, both divine as the father, and human as the mother. He wishes judgment to follow the law. Which two are the greatest of human goods. 

But here it comes to mind that, at the end of the eleventh [book], he says our goods are for the most part defiled by certain calamities of their own. And he says the calamity of the law elsewhere is the wickedness of the magistrate himself. The calamity of judgment and judicial dispute he called there a certain legalistic skill: which, having no regard for the law, but through the study of avarice and ambition, accepts every case without distinction to be defended. Which, like a plague of the republic, he detests above all others. 

After this, where he imposes laws upon funerals, he especially wishes that the man himself be held to be the substance of the rational soul; but the body of this man is an image, and as he names it elsewhere, a shadow. What "man" is in us, and what "animal" is, is known from the *Timaeus*, and *Alcibiades*, and *Plotinus*: which indeed we discuss more broadly in the *Theologia*. Where he concludes that "man" is the substance of the rational soul, beyond reason, having also a certain intimate, impassible, and common sense. But "animal" is a certain composite from a figured body and from a certain vestige of life impressed by the soul. In which vestige is also impressed this [other] sense, second from the first sense, now distributed through various instruments and passible. That indeed seems to some to be most consonant with certain sayings of the Apostle Paul. 

When he says that the soul goes away to other gods to give an account of its deeds, he names "other gods" the angelic minds outside of bodies, who are called other gods beyond the souls of the spheres. For our souls, while joined to these bodies, are surely placed under the reign of the superior souls; but when separated, they are transferred to the judgment of the separated ones. 

Hitherto indeed he has established laws; but he says it is in vain to establish laws unless one thinks about the safety and stability of the laws. Therefore, for their stability, he will devise a certain wonderful [council] of magistrates. But before the creation of such a thing, he touches somewhat upon the power of the Fates, as one who understands that human prudence is not sufficient for the salvation of an acting man if the fatal power is utterly opposed. In these things, he certainly seems to approve of those who, in building cities, establishing laws, creating magistrates, and even in planting men, diligently beware the contrary disposition of the stars. 

Regarding Fate, [we have said] much elsewhere: with which these things are brought in here as opportunely as they are briefly. Fate is a certain immovable disposition of mobile things in the Soul of the World. The instrument of Fate is the celestial nature. But the matter in which it acts through the instrument is the mass of the elements. 

He accepts three names, *Lachesis*, *Clotho*, and *Atropos*: both as they pertain to the instrument and to the matter. For we can name *Lachesis* the firmament, in whose stars the strong powers of all inferiors are contained. *Clotho* is the assembly of the planets, ministering from the firmament in unfolding the lots of things. Finally, *Atropos* is especially *Saturn*, inevitably confirming the lots unfolded into effect by his stability. 

In the matter, we also count the three Fates for this reason: because the fatal power, infused into the elements through the celestial instrument, acts in the matter and the form and the composite. Likewise, in the essence and the virtue and the action. Likewise, in the beginning, the middle, and the end. Since, however, it acts not only upon bodies, but also upon souls insofar as they are afflicted by bodies or use them, therefore Plato says here that the Fates can preserve the prosperity of both bodies and souls, and of the laws. 

And since the Mind by its nature—relying sometimes upon the providence of the divine mind—either overcomes Fate or uses Fate happily, he added that for the safety of life, both public and private, sense must be joined with Mind, so that sense obeys and serves Mind. Similarly, this coupling, which is composed of Mind and sight and hearing, procreates a certain assembly of magistrates in the republic looking forward to the stability of the laws, who may first look to the end itself of the republic, then what power especially leads to that end; and may study entirely how each thing in the city, whether done privately or publicly, may by one and the same reason lead to the goal: directing all things to virtue, and the other virtues to prudence. This, finally, to wisdom: which he often signifies under the name of Mind. By whose reason, all virtues are judged to be approved: namely, insofar as they lead to wisdom, which he also approves for the reason that it is a participant in the one Divine Good. 

He asserts that the most exquisite consideration of things is that which not only sees many things insofar as they are many, but also what the one common nature is in all. Likewise, from what one principle they have this. Again, to what end they can lead to the one through this. Without such contemplation, no one can govern a life perfectly, whether private or public. Since, however, this speculation pertains to the philosopher, especially the divine one, not without justice does he judge that the sum of things ought to be referred to the divine philosophers among the citizens gathered in that most elect assembly. "Divine," I say, inspectors and worshippers of divine things. 

Therefore, those who are dull for inspecting divine things, or lazy for worshipping them, or inept for teaching them, he drives far away from the most ample offices of the republic. But soon he proves that two things are especially necessary for a firm faith in the highest divinity. First, that we know that the genus of rational souls is divine and older than bodies, by which the spheres of the world are moved; and within the spheres, all things are generated. Second, that we think that the genus of minds (namely, the angelic) is more excellent than the genus of souls. And that souls, because of their participation in Mind, move the spheres in an orderly way. 

For if anyone knows these two, he will easily recognize that, just as Mind is the form and order of the soul, so the Divine Good is the life and light of both Mind and soul. These three, namely the Divine Good, the Mind, and the Soul, Plato undoubtedly either demonstrates or hints are the principles of all things in almost all his writings. Which indeed he wrapped in obscure words in the epistle to *Dionysius*. 

That our soul is older than the body, he does not wish to say it is older in time, but in dignity more excellent, and prior for the reason that it has its origin from a principle superior to bodies: therefore, he placed motion in the soul from itself, but in the body from the soul. And because mutability exists in the body from the mutable soul, the body changes not only in action, but also in substance...

### Notes on the Translation:
*   **Abbreviations:** The original text uses standard Renaissance Latin abbreviations (e.g., *q;* for *que*, *nō* for *non*, *atq;* for *atque*). These have been silently expanded for readability.
*   **Proper Nouns:** Names such as *Marsilius Ficinus*, *Plato*, *Timaeus*, *Plotinus*, and the various deities and Fates have been kept in their Latin or standard scholarly English forms as requested.
*   **Terminology:** The term *repetundae* (recovery of property/extortion) in this context refers to the judicial audit of a magistrate's term, a key theme in Book 12 of Plato's *Laws*.
*   **Structure:** The paragraph structure of the original print has been maintained, including the distinction between Ficinus's *Argumentum* and the beginning of the translated dialogue.

Likewise, upon essence, power, and action. Likewise, upon the beginning, the middle, and the end. Since it acts not only on bodies but also on minds to the extent that they are affected by or use bodies, Plato says here that the Fates can preserve the prosperity of both bodies and minds, as well as the laws. And since the mind, by its own nature—resting as it does upon the providence of the divine mind—sometimes overcomes fate or uses fate happily, he added that for the safety of life, both public and private, **sense** must be joined with the **mind**, so that sense obeys and serves the mind. Similar to this union, which is composed of mind, sight, and hearing, he creates a certain assembly of magistrates in the republic to look out for the stability of the laws. This assembly should first look to the goal of the republic itself, and then to which paths most effectively lead to that goal. It should strive entirely so that every single thing done in the city, whether privately or publicly, leads by one single reason toward the one; directing all things toward virtue, and the other virtues toward **prudence**. This, finally, toward **wisdom**, which he often signifies under the name of "mind." By the single reason of this wisdom, all virtues are judged worthy of approval: namely, insofar as they lead to wisdom. He also approves of wisdom for the reason that it is a participant in the one Divine Good. He asserts that the most exquisite consideration of things is that which sees not only many things insofar as they are many, but also what is the **one common nature** in all of them. Likewise, from what one principle they have this nature, and again, to what one end they can be led through it. Without this kind of contemplation, no one can perfectly govern either a private or public life. Since this speculation belongs to the philosopher, especially the "divine" one, he judges—not without justice—that the supreme management of affairs should be referred to the **divine philosophers** gathered in that most select assembly among the citizens. I say "divine" observers and cultivators of divine things. Therefore, those who are dull in observing divine things, or lazy in cultivating them, or inept in teaching them, he keeps far away from the most ample offices of the republic. Soon, however, he proves that two things are primarily necessary for a firm faith in the supreme divinity. First, that we know the genus of rational souls itself is divine and older than bodies, by which the spheres of the world are moved and all things within the spheres are generated. Second, that we consider the genus of minds—namely, the **angelic** ones—to be more excellent than the genus of souls; and that souls, because of their participation in mind, move the spheres in an orderly way. For if anyone knows these two things, he will easily recognize that just as the mind is the form and order of the soul, so the Divine Good is the life and light of both the mind and the soul. These three—namely, the Divine Good, the mind, and the soul—Plato undoubtedly demonstrates or hints at as the principles of all things in almost all his writings. This he indeed wrapped in more obscure words in his letter to Dionysius. That our soul is older than the body—if it does not please you to say older in time—say at least it is more excellent in dignity; and prior because it has its origin from a principle superior to bodies. Therefore, he placed motion in the soul from itself, but in the body from the soul. And because mutability increases in the body, he says the body depends upon the mutable part of the soul, not only in action but even in its mutable substance.

[Column 2]

He also reproaches Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously posited "Mind" (Nous) as the cause of order in the universe.</note> because, since he did not place the soul between the mind and bodies, he was forced to conclude that natural effects are not disposed by intelligence through the soul as a part, but rather happen by elemental nature. He asserts here, as in the *Timaeus* and *Phaedo*, that all things—whether said to be done by angelic minds, but through souls, or through bodies—are done chiefly by the **divine will** for the sake of the **Good**.

**[T]** **I**F AN AMBASSADOR or a herald should falsely report the things committed to him, or remain silent about what should be said, or again, returning from enemies or friends, should be found to have reported what he received differently than he received it, let him be brought to judgment as if he had despised the mandates and embassies of Mercury and Jupiter <note>Mercury (Hermes) was the god of messengers/heralds.</note> against the law. And let the judges determine, according to the magnitude of the matter, what he ought to suffer or pay if he is convicted. The theft of money is indeed ungenerous, but robbery is most shameful. None of the sons of Jupiter, delighted by either force or guile, ever did anything of this kind. Therefore, let no one be so deceived by poets or other fabulists as to believe that if he uses theft or force, he has committed nothing shameful, but rather something that the gods also did. For that is neither true nor likely. And he who does either of these things against the law is neither a god nor a son of the gods. These things must be known by the legislator more than by all the poets. Therefore, whoever obeys this our discourse is happy and will always be so in the future. He who does the opposite will be restrained by this law: If anyone steals anything public, whether it be small or great, let him be punished with an equal penalty. For he who took a small thing, even if with less force than he who seized a great one, nevertheless stole with an equal desire. And he who removed something great from a place where he himself had not deposited it is altogether unjust. The law, therefore, does not judge that one should be punished less than the other because of the smallness of the theft, but perhaps it considers it important that one is **incurable** and the other **curable**. If a slave or a foreigner is accused and convicted of public theft, as he might seem in some way able to be cured, let it be determined by judgment what he should suffer or what fine he should pay. However, if any citizen—educated as we have instituted—is convicted of stealing or violating something public, whether caught in the very theft and crime or discovered in any other way, we condemn him to the punishment of death as one who is **incurable**. 

For the sake of military service, great deliberations are deservedly held and many laws established. But this is the greatest of all: that no one, male or female, should do anything without a commander and a leader; nor should the mind of any citizen, whether in jest or in earnest, become accustomed to doing anything alone and at his own discretion. Rather, in every war as well as in every peace, he should always look toward the leader and magistrate and follow him wherever he goes. And thus he should institute his life at his nod, so that he does even the smallest things under his guidance: he stands when ordered, and again, when ordered, he sets out, exercises, washes, eats, rises at night, keeps watch, gives signals, and in turn receives them. And in battle itself, let him never pursue nor retreat unless the leader and commander has signaled. And to say it briefly, let no one at all know what it is to act separately from others; but let there always be a common life for everyone as much as possible. For nothing will ever be better, nothing more excellent, nothing more skillful for acquiring safety and victory in war than this. This very thing should be practiced even in peace from childhood; let them grow accustomed to leading others and being led by others. But loose license should be utterly expelled from life, not only that of men, but even of beasts...
