**On the Laws, or on Legislation. Dialogue 12. Page 609**

[Column 1]

...to excel wonderfully in every kind of virtue. Therefore, let us devise the selection of these men in this way. Every year, after the summer solstice, the entire city shall gather at the place jointly dedicated to the Sun and Apollo. They shall choose three men, whom each person judges to be the best (excluding himself), and who must be at least fifty years of age. From those elected, they shall take the half who received the most votes; if the numbers are equal, they shall prefer the elders. If the number is odd, they shall set aside the one with the fewest votes and take the half of the remainder, judging by the number of votes. If many receive an equal number of votes and exceed the required half, the younger candidates shall be set aside. After selecting the others, they shall vote again until three unequal candidates remain. But if two or all of these have equal votes, the matter shall be committed to good fortune; they shall be distinguished by lot. 

The one who wins by votes, and those declared in the second and third place, shall be crowned with a wreath woven from evergreen leaves. After the prizes are given, a herald shall proclaim that the city of the Magnesians, having again found safety under God's guidance, consecrates three of its best citizens to the Sun and Apollo as the "first-fruits" <note>original: "primitias" — a sacrificial term referring to the best part of a harvest offered to the gods. Here, the best citizens are the "offering."</note> of the ancient law, insofar as they are to follow its judgment. In the first year, these men shall appoint twelve examiners of financial conduct and public accounts <term>repetundarum rationum examinatores</term> <note>These "examiners" or *euthunoi* were essential in Greek democracy to ensure officials did not steal public funds or abuse their power.</note>. They shall do this until each man has completed his seventy-fifth year; thereafter, three more shall be added every year. These officials shall divide the administration into twelve parts and, judging with full freedom of examination, shall observe everything diligently. 

During the time when accounts are being rendered to them, they shall live in the place dedicated to the Sun and Apollo where they were elected. There, both individually and collectively, after diligent investigation, they shall publicly record concerning each magistrate what penalty they should suffer or what reward they should receive according to the sentence of the accountability judges. If any magistrate complains that he was unjustly condemned by their judgment, he may bring his case before a select court of accountability judges. If he is acquitted, he may accuse the examiners if he wishes. But if he is condemned there as well, and had previously been sentenced to death by the examiners, he shall die as necessity requires. If he was condemned to a fine that he is able to pay twofold, he shall pay it twofold.

But now we must hear what the honors for these examiners should be and how they are to be granted. To those who have been placed over everyone by the consensus of the entire city, the first seats at all festivals shall be provided as long as they live. Whenever it is necessary for the city to send judges or leaders to the common Greek spectacles and sacrifices, they shall be sent from among these men. They alone in the city shall be crowned with a laurel wreath; they shall be the priests of the Sun and Apollo. Furthermore, the High Priest <term>Pontifex summus</term> for each year shall be the one from among them who is judged to have excelled the other priests in the previous year. Times shall be distinguished by their names for as long as the city is inhabited. 

When they die, their funerals and tombs shall be more excellent than those of other citizens. All their burial garments shall be white. Mourning and wailing shall be absent. Instead, two choirs—one of fifteen girls and the other of fifteen boys—shall stand around the bier and, in turn, praise the priest with songs, chanting of his happiness throughout the entire day. In the morning, the younger men who attend the gymnasia, chosen by the relatives of the deceased, shall carry the bier to the monument. First, the celibate youths shall lead the way, armed as if for battle <note>This "battle" formation at a funeral honors the deceased as a hero of the state.</note>, with cavalry on horses, infantry with light arms, and others in similar fashion. Boys shall sing ancestral songs before the bier, followed by girls and then by women past childbearing age. 

[Column 2]

Finally, the priests of both genders may come to this tomb—even if they are barred from other monuments—provided the Pythian oracle <note>The oracle of Apollo at Delphi.</note> confirms it, as if the place were entirely pure. The monument itself shall be an underground vault, quite long and made of the hardest and most beautiful stones, with stone couches on either side. Here they shall bury that blessed man, and they shall plant trees in a circle around it, except for one part so that the tomb may be expanded. Every year, they shall honor these men with musical, gymnastic, and equestrian contests. These rewards shall be granted to those whose judgments on the reported accounts have not been overturned.

However, if any of these men, trusting in the high rank to which he was preferred, should reveal the fragile condition of human nature <note>This is a poetic way of describing corruption or a fall from grace.</note>—that is, if he falls into error after being held in such high esteem—it shall be sanctioned by law that he may be accused by anyone who wishes. The judgment against him shall be conducted as follows: first, the Guardians of the Laws <term>legum custodes</term> shall be present, then the colleagues of the accused himself, and furthermore, judges from the select court. The accuser shall state in writing that the accused is unworthy of both his office and the rewards of office.

Furthermore, the guardians of the laws <note>The "Nomophylakes," a group of high-ranking officials in Plato’s ideal city responsible for overseeing the administration of justice.</note> must take care of many things, but especially this: that boys and men—and to speak summarily, people of every sex and age—should live well under their constant observation. It is unseemly for a lawgiver to compel people whether or not to honor the dead with tears; however, wailing and crying out loud outside the house must be prohibited. It shall not be permitted to carry a corpse openly through the busier streets of the city, nor to wail in public, or to afflict oneself with lamentations outside the city before daybreak. Let these statutes regarding such matters remain fixed. Whoever obeys them shall be free from penalty. But whoever does not obey a single guardian of the laws shall be punished by all of them together, as they see fit. 

Other matters pertaining either to the monuments of the dead or to those who are unworthy of burial due to parricide or sacrilege have been covered in the preceding laws. Therefore, the laying down of the laws is nearly at an end. But the end of all things is not in the fact that they have been made, or possessed, or inhabited, but rather in the fact that just as they were made rightly, they are also firmly established. For in such preservation, we must consider that as much as was necessary has been done; otherwise, it is not done at all. 

**CLINIAS.** You speak well, Stranger, but tell us more clearly: what is the purpose of these things? 

**ATHENIAN.** Many excellent sayings of the ancients are praised, Clinias; not least the names of the Fates <note>The *Parcae* or *Moirai*: the three goddesses who determine the span and nature of human life.</note>. 

**CLINIAS.** Which ones? 

**ATHENIAN.** That Lachesis is the first, Clotho the second, and Atropos the third—she who brings "salvation" or stability to what has been spoken before. These are compared to things twisted in a fire, because they contain a power that is irreversible <note>Atropos means "the one who cannot be turned." In this context, Plato uses the metaphor of the Fates to argue that laws must be made unchangeable to ensure the state's survival.</note>. In a city and a Republic, it is necessary to bring about not only a stable health of the body, but also a devotion to the laws in the mind—or rather, the salvation of the laws. But it seems to me that something is still lacking in our business until it is explained how an irreversible power can exist in those laws according to nature. 

**CLINIAS.** It is no small thing you say, if it is possible to find a way in which this might be done rightly in every case. 

**ATHENIAN.** It is indeed possible, as it seems to me for the present. 

**CLINIAS.** Then I beg you, let us not depart from here before we grant this to our laws. For it is ridiculous to have taken pains in any matter in vain, without having founded something stable. 

**MEGILLUS.** You advise rightly; you will find me in agreement as well. 

**CLINIAS.** You speak well. What, then, is this "salvation," and in what way will it be present in our Republic and its laws? 

**ATHENIAN.** Did we not say that an assembly of this kind should be established in the city, where ten of the guardians of the laws, always the seniors, should meet? To these should be added all those who have been honored with offices and prizes. Furthermore, those who have traveled through many cities to find anything contributing to the preservation of their country's laws should be included; but these shall not be received into such an assembly unless they are proven to have returned uncorrupted and upright from their travels, and are deemed worthy of the assembly. And each of these elders shall choose one younger man for himself, no less than thirty years old, who seems to the one who chooses him—and then to the whole assembly—to be worthy by nature and education. If anyone unworthy is admitted, the judgment of the group shall be of no weight. We said that this assembly ought to meet before light, when people are free from other private and

public business. Did we not say something of this kind in the previous sections? 

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** We will speak of it in due time, and we will apply ourselves with all our strength.

...they water them, they do not have them. **CLINIAS.** We, therefore, Guest, have for a long time rightly thought that our laws should look toward one thing, and we agreed that this is called virtue. **ATHENIAN.** It is so. **CLINIAS.** And we established that virtue consists of four parts. **ATHENIAN.** Certainly. **CLINIAS.** **I.** And that Mind <note>original: "Mentem," referring to *Nous* or reason</note> is the leader of all these, toward which both the other things and those three virtues ought to look. **ATHENIAN.** You follow most beautifully, O Clinias. Now follow similarly in the other matters. We were saying that the mind of a pilot, a doctor, and a general must look toward a certain specific goal. But, refuting the statesman, we have proceeded to this point, and now let us question this "statesmanlike mind" as if it were a man. "O extraordinary man, where are you aiming? What is that one thing which a doctor can clearly identify in his own art, but you, who say you excel all other wise men, cannot identify in your own faculty?" Or can you, Clinias and Megillus, answer for him what this thing is, as I have often done for others in your presence? **CLINIAS.** Not at all, Guest. **ATHENIAN.** Do you not think it should be sought, what it is, and in what things it exists? **CLINIAS.** Speak plainly. **ATHENIAN.** Since we have established four species of virtue, it is clear that each of them is one, if the four together make up a whole. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** We also call all these by one name. For we say that courage is a virtue, and wisdom <note>original: "prudentiam," translating the Greek *phronesis*</note> is a virtue, and the other two similarly, as if in truth they were not many, but only that one thing which is virtue. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** It is not difficult to say how these two differ from each other and received two names, and the other two similarly. But to say how we have placed "one" in both, and called it "virtue," and similarly in the remaining two, is not so easy. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean that? **ATHENIAN.** What I am saying is not hard to explain. Come then, let us divide the duty of questioning and answering among ourselves. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** You ask me why, when we call virtue "one," we have again called the two parts by different names: one "courage" and the other "wisdom." I will give you the reason: that one of them is concerned with fears. From this, even beasts partake in courage, and the minds of infants. For a brave soul is produced naturally and without reason, but a wise and rational soul never has been, is not, and never will be without reason. Therefore, this is one thing and that is another. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Thus you have heard from me how these two are different in their reasoning. Now, in turn, you must teach me how they are one and the same, so that you might think to say how they are one despite being four; and afterwards, I will declare to you how they are four. Next, let us consider whether he who is to sufficiently understand any things that have both a name and a definition <note>original: "rationem," often used to translate the Greek *logos*</note> ought to know the name only, and the definition not at all. Or rather, if it is of any value, is it not shameful for someone to be ignorant of the definitions as well as the names of things excellent in magnitude and beauty? **CLINIAS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** But for a founder and guardian of laws, <margin>The foundations of all laws.</margin> and for him who thinks himself to excel others in virtue and has received rewards for these things, is there any greater thing than courage, temperance, justice, and wisdom? **CLINIAS.** How could there be anything else? **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, regarding these things, should not the interpreters, teachers, lawgivers, and guardians of others teach the rest who desire to know—or who need punishment and rebuke—what power virtue has and what power vice has, and excel others by declaring these things? Or shall some poet or teacher of youth

[Column 2]

who has recently entered the city be judged more excellent than he who professes to excel in every virtue? And then, will it seem a wonder if that city, where the guardians do not hold the name and definition of virtue, suffers the same things that many other cities suffer today, like a place deserted by its protector? **CLINIAS.** Certainly no wonder. **ATHENIAN.** Let us, therefore, apply ourselves to this. How then shall we make the guardians more exquisite than others in virtue, both in deed and in word? Or in what way shall our city become like the head and senses of the wise because of this kind of guardianship? **CLINIAS.** In what way, O Guest, shall we make this comparison? **ATHENIAN.** It is clear that the city will be like the capacity of the head, while the guardians—young men who are keen and clever—will be placed at the very summit. From there, they will look around the whole city, and by guarding what they perceive, they will commit it to memory and report everything to the elders. The elders, who are very much like the "mind" because of their knowledge of many things, will take counsel for the city using the service of the youth. And thus both together will preserve the whole city. Should we think they are to be prepared in this way or otherwise? Or do we think all should be held as equals? And do we not want some to be educated and instructed with a more exquisite reason, and these to be placed before the others? **CLINIAS.** But that, O extraordinary man, is impossible. **ATHENIAN.** Let us come, then, to a discipline that is more exquisite than that previous one. **CLINIAS.** Almost certainly. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, perhaps that which we just touched upon is this very thing we seek. **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** We were saying that the chief craftsman and guardian in each thing must not only be able to see many things, but must also tend toward the "one," and know that one thing, and when he has known it, direct everything he perceives toward it. **CLINIAS.** Correctly. **ATHENIAN.** Is there, then, any more exquisite consideration of things than to be able to look toward one "Idea" <note>original: "ideam," referring to the Platonic Form</note> arising out of many and dissimilar things? **CLINIAS.** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN.** Do not say "perhaps," but "in truth," O blessed man; no one will ever have a more certain way and reason than this. **CLINIAS.** Persuaded by your reasons, Guest, I concede; let us therefore proceed. **ATHENIAN.** We must, therefore, compel the guardians of our divine Republic to inspect exactly, first, what is the same in all four [virtues]; which, since it exists in courage, temperance, justice, and wisdom, we rightly wish to call by the single name of virtue. This, O friends, if you are willing, let us hold fast to: let us not let go before it is sufficiently clear what that thing is—whether it is as one, or as a whole, or as both, or however it may be—toward which we must look. Or do we think that if this escapes us, the things pertaining to virtue will be sufficiently clear to us, about which we could not explain whether it is many, or four, or one? Either, then, if you trust our counsel, we shall try to find a way by which this will be present to us in the city, or if you prefer... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the logic of the Athenian Stranger.</note> ...for you seem to say this quite rightly. But how will anyone find this? **ATHENIAN.** We are not yet saying how it must be done; but first, let us agree among ourselves whether or not it is necessary. **CLINIAS.** It is certainly necessary, if it is possible. **ATHENIAN.** What then of the Honorable and the Good? Shall our guardians know only that they are "many"? Or shall they also know how they are "one"? **CLINIAS.** It seems necessary that they also understand how they are one. **ATHENIAN.** What then? Should they only understand it, but be unable to declare in speech what they understand? **CLINIAS.** How could that be? [servile...]

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that the guardians of the ideal city must understand the underlying unity of the four virtues (courage, wisdom, temperance, and justice) rather than just knowing their names. He introduces the concept of the "Nocturnal Council," where young, keen observers serve as the city's "senses" and elders serve as its "mind" to preserve the state through philosophical knowledge of the Good.</summary>

Namely, that those who are to be true guardians <note>term: "guardians" (custodes). These are the high-ranking officials responsible for the preservation of the state's constitution and moral character.</note> must understand the truth of the laws as perfectly as possible, and be able to explain them sufficiently in speech, and follow them in their actions, judging what is done rightly and what is not, according to nature? <note>term: "according to nature" (secundum naturam). # Gorgias, Or, on Rhetoric.
[[page number: 253]]

O Callicles, you do not seem to me to think rightly when you suggest that a man should be handed over to such a path that he might become powerful in this city, regardless of whether he is unlike the public government—be he better or worse. For one must not merely be an imitator, but by very nature be truly similar to those people, if you are to achieve anything great in winning the goodwill of the Athenian people, and by Jove, the goodwill of Pyrilampes [[notes: Pyrilampes was the stepfather of Plato and a prominent figure in the circle of Pericles]] as well. Whoever makes you most like them will make you exactly what you desire: a statesman and a rhetorician. 

Naturally, all people are delighted by words that harmonize with their own characters, and they are troubled by those that differ. Unless you, O charming head [[notes: *lepidum caput*, a colloquial Latin expression of address]], have something else to suggest. Shall we say something to this, Callicles? 

**CALLICLES.** I do not know how it is, Socrates, but you seem to speak well. However, the same thing happens to me that happens to many others: I do not have great faith in you. 

**SOCRATES.** The love of the people (*demos*), O Callicles, which is implanted in your soul, resists me. But if we consider these same things more often and more deeply, perhaps they will seem probable to you. Remember, then, that we described two kinds of preparations: one pertaining to the body and the other to the soul. One of these tends toward pleasure, while the other tends toward what is best—not gratifying the subject, but often opposing it. Did we not define these things previously? 

**CALLICLES.** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES.** And the one that declines toward pleasure is servile; it is nothing other than *adulatio* (flattery), is it not? 

**CALLICLES.** Let it be so, if that pleases you. 

**SOCRATES.** But the other strives to make the subject as excellent as possible, whether it be the soul or the body that we are caring for. 

**CALLICLES.** Absolutely. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must take up the care of the *respublica* (state) and its citizens in such a way that we make the citizens themselves good. Otherwise, as we found earlier, it is of no use to confer any other benefit unless the mind of those who are to receive it—be it great wealth, or command, or any other power—is honorable and good. Shall we set it down that this is so, or not? 

**CALLICLES.** Entirely so, if it pleases you. 

**SOCRATES.** If, therefore, O Callicles, we were encouraging each other to handle public civil works—such as the massive construction of walls, or naval docks, or temples—would it not be necessary to consider ourselves and examine, first of all, whether we possess the skill of that art, and from whom we learned it? Would it not be necessary to do so? 

**CALLICLES.** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES.** Second, we should ask whether we have ever constructed any building privately for ourselves or for our friends, and whether that building was beautiful or shameful. For if we found that we had good and excellent masters, and that many noble buildings were built by us—both while with our masters and later by ourselves privately after we were freed from them—then it would be consistent with reason to turn ourselves toward public works. But if we could show neither our master nor any buildings of our own, or only buildings poorly constructed, it would certainly be foolish to attempt public works and to encourage each other toward them. Do we admit this is rightly said, or not? 

**CALLICLES.** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES.** Is it not the same in all other matters? If we were encouraging each other to manage *civilium rerum* (civil affairs) as if we were suitable physicians, it would be appropriate to examine one another in this way: "Come now, by the gods, how has Socrates himself fared in regard to health? Or who else has emerged free from disease through the work of Socrates, be they slave or free man?" 

It is fitting that I should judge the same concerning you. And unless we find someone—be they a foreigner or a citizen, man or woman—who was healed by us, then by Jove, it would be truly ridiculous to be driven to such madness that we would attempt to learn the "potter's art on the large jar," as the proverb says [[notes: *figularia in dolio discere*; a Greek proverb meaning to attempt a large, difficult task before mastering the basics]]. It is absurd to approach the republic and provoke others to it without having tested ourselves in private matters or perfected anything, nor even practiced the art. Would you not think such an attempt belongs to a foolish man? 

**CALLICLES.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** But, O best of men, since you have recently begun to administer the republic and even urge me to do so—reproaching me because I do not—should we not consider this among ourselves? Come now, Callicles, which of his citizens has he made better? Is there anyone who, though he was previously wicked, unjust, incontinent, and imprudent, finally emerged honorable and good through the work of Callicles—be they foreigner or citizen, slave or free? Tell me, if someone were to demand this of you, what would you answer? Whom will you bring forward as having finally become better through your company? Or does it loathe you to explain if there is any such work completed by you privately before you turned to the republic? 

**CALLICLES.** You are being contentious, Socrates. 

**SOCRATES.** But I do not ask this for the sake of contention, but truly out of a desire for learning how you think the public should be administered by us. Should those approaching the state care for anything other than that the citizens be made as good as possible? Have we not already confessed many times that this is what a civil man must do? Have we confessed it? Answer, I pray; certainly we have confessed it, so I shall answer for you. 

If, therefore, it is fitting for a good man to exert himself toward this in his city, I would like you to tell me, calling it to memory: do those others whom you mentioned a little while ago still seem to you to have been good citizens—Pericles, Cimon, Miltiades, and Themistocles? 

**CALLICLES.** To me, certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** If they were good, did not each of them make the citizens better from being worse? Did they not? 

**CALLICLES.** Yes. 

**SOCRATES.** If this is so, then when Pericles first began to speak to the people, the Athenians were worse than when he held his last speech to them. 

**CALLICLES.** Perhaps. 

**SOCRATES.** It is not for you to say "perhaps," best of men. For it follows necessarily from what we have granted, if indeed he was a good citizen. 

**CALLICLES.** What then? 

**SOCRATES.** Nothing, except tell me this: are the Athenians said to have been made better by the work of Pericles, or on the contrary, were they corrupted by him? For I hear that Pericles made the Athenians lazy, timid, talkative, and greedy, having first introduced the payment of public wages [[notes: Pericles introduced pay for jury service, which critics argued led to a litigious and idle populace]]. 

**CALLICLES.** You hear these things from those who have "broken ears," O Socrates [[notes: *fractas habent aures*; an idiom referring to those who adopt Spartan customs, like boxers with battered ears, who were often critics of Athenian democracy]]. 

**SOCRATES.** But I no longer just "hear" these things; rather, we both know them very clearly. We know that Pericles was held in great esteem at the beginning, and the Athenians never passed any shameful sentence against him while they were "wicked." But after they were made "honorable and good" by him, at the end of his life, they condemned him for theft [[notes: Pericles was prosecuted and fined late in his career during the Peloponnesian War]]. They were very nearly ready to punish him with the ultimate penalty as if he were an evil man. 

**CALLICLES.** What then? Was Pericles an evil man because of that? 

**SOCRATES.** Such a caretaker of donkeys, horses, and oxen would certainly seem evil if, when he received them, they were neither kickers, nor prone to goring, nor biters, but he made them have these vices due to his wildness. Does it not seem to you that any caretaker of any animal is evil if, having received it tame, he makes it wilder than he received it? Does it seem so to you or not? 

**CALLICLES.** I grant it, simply to gratify you. 

**SOCRATES.** Furthermore, gratify me in this by answering whether man is one of the animals or not. 

**CALLICLES.** Why not? 

**SOCRATES.** And did Pericles not have the care of men? 

**CALLICLES.** He did. 

**SOCRATES.** What then? Ought they not, as we just contended, to have been made more just by him from being unjust—if indeed he who cared for them was skilled in civil affairs? 

**CALLICLES.** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES.** Are not the just "tame" (mild), as Homer says? And what do you say? Is it not similar? 

**CALLICLES.** I say so. 

**SOCRATES.** However, he rendered them more wild than he had received them, and that too against 

# Book Thirty-Four.
[[page number: 254]]

himself, which is something he certainly would not have wanted. 

**CALLICLES.** Do you want me to agree with you? 

**SOCRATES.** If I seem to you to speak the truth. 

**CALLICLES.** Let those things be so. 

**SOCRATES.** Accordingly, if he made them more wild, then he made them more unjust and worse. 

**CALLICLES.** So be it. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, Pericles was not a good citizen for administering the republic, as this reasoning shows. 

**CALLICLES.** Not as *you* say. 

**SOCRATES.** By Jove, nor as *you* say, according to the things you have confessed. But tell me again about Cimon: did not those whom he cared for ostracize him so that they might not hear his voice for ten years? Furthermore, they did the same against Themistocles, and punished him with exile besides. As for Miltiades, who fought at Marathon, they decreed he should be cast into the pit of the prison [[notes: the *barathrum*, a deep pit in Athens for executed criminals]], and had the magistrate not obstructed it, he would have undoubtedly fallen into it. But if these had been good men, as you say, such things would never have happened to them. For good charioteers do not fall out of their chariots at the beginning; nor do they fall out after they have cared for their horses and become more skilled in that art. This does not happen in chariot-driving, nor in any other work. Or does it seem so to you? 

**CALLICLES.** Not at all. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, what was said by us earlier was true: that we know of no man who has existed in this city who was to be considered a good citizen in the republic. You yourself confessed that none of those who are here now are such; but you claimed that some had existed among those who came before, and among them you chose these men above the rest. But these men have appeared to be no different in this matter than the rhetoricians who are here now. Therefore, if these were orators, they used neither the true rhetoric (for otherwise they would never have fallen) nor the flattering kind. 

**CALLICLES.** Yet it is a far cry, O Socrates, to say that any of those who are here now have performed such deeds as any of those men performed. 

**SOCRATES.** O blessed one, I do not disparage those men as far as the administration of the city is concerned; indeed, in this matter, they seem to me to have been more diligent than our contemporaries, and more fit for completing those things which the city desired. But in that duty which requires the chastening of the citizens' desires rather than following them—using both persuasion and compulsion to lead them to the point where they are made better citizens—there is, so to speak, no difference between these men and those. Yet that alone is the office of a good citizen. 

Nevertheless, I confess to you that those men were more fit than these for providing the state with ships, naval docks, walls, and many other such things. Thus we have revolved back into a ridiculous argument: in all this disputation, we are constantly circling back to the same point, ignorant of what we are saying. For I think you have often conceded and recognized that this is a twofold faculty regarding the care of work and the care of the soul. 

One is the ministerial part, through which the things the body desires are provided: such as food if it is hungry, drink if it is thirsty, clothes, blankets, shoes, and other things required for the body's use. And indeed, I deliberately speak to you through these images so you may understand more easily. The provider of these is either a shopkeeper, a merchant, or a craftsman of some such thing—namely a baker, a cook, a weaver, a shoemaker, or a tanner. It is no wonder that someone of that sort seems to be a caretaker of the body, both to himself and to other unskilled people—as if there were not also a certain art of gymnastics and medicine, in which the care of the body truly consists. 

It is fitting that these higher arts should command such ministerial arts and use their works, because they possess the knowledge of good and evil regarding the body's nourishment and health—something which is ignored by all these others. For this reason, it must be said that these 

[Right column:]

ministerial arts are servile and illiberal [[notes: *illiberales*; unbefitting a free man]] regarding the cultivation of the body, while gymnastics and medicine rightly dominate them. 

You seem to me sometimes to recognize that these same principles apply to the soul. You grant it to me as if you understand what I am saying. But a little later, you bring into the discussion men who were once "noble and good" in this city. And when I ask who they were, you seem to bring forward men involved in the republic just as if—were I to ask who were or are good caretakers of the bodies in gymnastics—you were to answer seriously: Thearion the baker, and Mithaecus who wrote on the Sicilian art of cookery, and Sarambus the shopkeeper. You would speak as if these men were wonderful cultivators of bodies, because one prepared sweet breads, another feasts, and another wine. 

Perhaps, then, you would take it indignantly if I were to say you do not understand gymnastics. For you bring forward ministers and providers of desires—men who do not at all judge what is honorable and good in these matters, but in whatever way it happens, they fill the bodies of men and fatten them. These men are praised by the people themselves, even though through that excessive filling they have consumed the old flesh. And later, when diseases attack those who were nourished by these things, the people accuse those who gave them counsel afterwards (out of ignorance), but they do not at all accuse those who nourished them for the sake of lust. 

When, I say, such overfilling—being immoderate—finally brings on disease, then they criminalize and reproach the present counselors and even treat them with injury if they can, while they extol with praises those earlier men who provided the cause of the disease. 

And you now, O Callicles, are doing something very similar. You praise those who nourished these citizens and filled them with the things they lusted for. They say these men made the city great; but they do not perceive that the city is now swollen and internally diseased because of those ancient leaders. For without temperance and justice, they have filled this city with ports, naval docks, walls, tributes, taxes, and such trifles. 

When, therefore, the disease breaks out, those who are governing the republic in the present are reproached. But Themistocles himself, and Cimon, and Pericles, who were the cause of the evils, are praised. For this reason, you perhaps, unless you are careful, will be seized—along with my friend Alcibiades—when the old possessions are lost in addition to those that were newly acquired, even though you are not the primary cause of the evils, but only a cause alongside the others. 

And yet I see a foolish thing happening now, just as I hear it happened regarding those ancient men. For I perceive that when the city attempts to condemn someone involved in the republic for injustice, they bear it heavily and complain in their souls, as if they were suffering an injustice after having conferred many benefits on the republic. Indeed, they say they are being condemned by the state unjustly. But this is entirely false. For a governor of a republic is never condemned unjustly by the city over which he presides. 

It seems that the same thing happens to those involved in the republic as happens to the sophists. For the sophists, although they are wise in other things, behave absurdly in this one thing: although they claim to teach virtues, they often accuse their disciples of being ungrateful and unjust—people who, although they received good things from them, return no payment or thanks. Nothing is more alien to reason than this talk: that men who have been made good and just, and removed from injustice by the work of their teacher, and endowed with justice, should commit injuries against their teachers with that very injustice which they no longer have. 

Does that not seem absurd to you, my friend? Truly, you have compelled me to deliver a public speech because you refuse to answer. 

**SOCRATES.** But you yourself cannot speak unless someone responds to you...

[[summary: Socrates argues that famous Athenian leaders like Pericles failed as statesmen because they merely indulged the people's desires instead of improving their virtue, ultimately leading the citizens to turn against them. He compares these leaders to cooks who fatten a body but cause long-term disease, contrasting them with true "physicians" of the soul.]]

<meta>The previous page concluded the commentary on Plato’s "Gorgias." This page transitions to the "Epinomis" (or "The Philosopher"), a dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato or his pupil Philip of Opus, which serves as an appendix to the "Laws." The text focuses on the hierarchy of souls and the divine nature of the cosmos.</meta>

# Epinomis, Or, The Philosopher. 617

For he <note>Likely referring to Plato or the Athenian Stranger in the dialogue</note> maintains that beyond the one soul of the whole world, there are twelve souls for the twelve spheres; furthermore, within each sphere, there are twelve orders of souls. In the heavens, these orders are the constellations and the stars; on earth, they are men; in the ether, the air, and the water—specifically the higher regions of it—they are the demons. In each of these living beings, he says that the rational soul, joined to its own body, procreates a "living creature"—that is, a certain composite of its own body and a life that is entirely infused into that body. This life, having now become corporeal, depends upon a threefold soul: from its own soul, from the soul of its sphere, and from the soul of the whole world. Moreover, Plato argues that celestial bodies possess souls based on the divinity of celestial substance, the magnitude of their size, the life-giving power of their quality over all things, and the velocity and efficacy of their motion. Furthermore, he concludes that celestial souls possess a mind <term>mind: "mens," often used in Neoplatonic texts to refer to the higher intellect or "Nous"</term> because of the unchanging perseverance of their order and course.

He adds that the necessity of a soul possessing a mind is as great as possible, understanding this in two ways. First, because natural necessity—for instance, in this or that part of fire to burn and ascend—acts as if led from elsewhere. But the nature of an intellectual soul, insofar as it participates in the intellect, is the mistress of its own action. Secondly, because the motion of the soul, since it is free by nature, can easily go astray and wander about unless it is ruled by the mind as if by a charioteer <note>original: "velut auriga," a famous Platonic metaphor from the "Phaedrus"</note>—by a perfect mind, I say, providing both the best end for action and the most chosen path from the beginning. When this best mind is present in the best soul, such as exists in the stars, it necessarily achieves its prescribed work. For bodies do not resist the best (that is, the most powerful) souls, and the best mind does not change its counsel. Hence, he says that the three Fates <note>The Parcae: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos</note> preserve as perfect whatever the celestial gods have deliberated with certain counsel. He mentions three Fates, a single destiny disposing three principles according to the nod of the divine minds: namely, the beginnings, the middles, and the ends of things.

In a higher book, he said that things established by the fates are similar to materials worked by fire, whether they are straightened or twisted. For just as these materials cannot be bent back in the opposite direction, neither can things of fate. Nor did he mention things "twisted by fire" without reason, for the fiery spheres of the heavens are the instruments of fate. Furthermore, when he says that the stars are either eternal or long-lived, he sufficiently touches upon the Orphic and perhaps the Mercurial <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> opinion: namely, that after many ages, the world will be resolved into fire. For that which is composite is ultimately dissoluble, and fire, as the greatest and most powerful of all things, will at last wonderfully assume everything into itself. Yet the divine mind, the craftsman of this work, will reform a similar work from the fire once more, by a similar fate and an easy nod of the reformed things. This was the opinion confirmed by Anaxagoras, Empedocles, Heraclitus, and most of the Stoics, confessing that a truly omnipotent God can always preserve his work in the order once handed down; but the work itself, because it is of a finite nature and internally conflicting, cannot be so preserved—God, however, repays through reformation what is lacking in the original formation. But let them see to these matters.

You, however, will note here that Plato rebukes those who deny that celestial bodies are alive simply because they are always moved in the same way. Indeed, this should have been an argument to everyone not of an absent life, but of present sufficiency and wisdom. Remember, moreover, that the soul is considered so different from the body that there is nothing common to both—that is, no common matter. Likewise, because the soul does not depend on matter, and again because corporeal nature is judged to be neither true substance nor true essence, he calls the souls of the stars "gods," but their bodies the "images of the gods" <note>original: "simulacra"</note>. Accordingly, among the celestial gods, he assigns to Jupiter the office of providence, and to Juno the "animal power" <note>the vitalizing force</note> subject to that providence.

He says also that the stars perceive individual things acutely, namely through a sense far different from ours. He also describes the nature of demons as powerful in prudence, sense, memory, and motion: a medium between gods and men; to be honored for the sake of intercession and interpretation; knowing our thoughts—namely from our figures, motions, and affections; loving the good and hostile to the wicked. He seems here to consider all demons good, namely those he teaches should be worshipped; but elsewhere he signifies that some are evil. The ethereal and aerial ones are invisible; the aqueous ones, which he calls "demigods," he says are sometimes seen, though barely—that is, by an internal rather than an external sight. He adds that souls are warned by demons through dreams, voices, prophecies, and omens, especially at the time when the soul departs from the body. He says that many things have been added to religion through these warnings. He says, furthermore, that it is not permitted for mortal nature to change those things which are established in religion by laws. "Mortal," he says, for it is permitted to the divine. Learn this divine saying:

-> The most divine Reason of all constituted the visible world, which the happy man, admiring, is inflamed with the love of finding divinity, whence he escapes as happy both here and in the other life, and becomes truly one through truly one wisdom: translated to places congruent with virtue, he is destined to contemplate divine things for all time to come. <-

Soon where it is translated, *For divine things*, and what follows, is read elsewhere: *For it is not the part of a prudent man to honor some divine things while neglecting others.* Amidst these things, he relates certain very well-known astronomical facts. He praises the tempered quality of the air for the virtue of the intellect. Then, where he says that motion tending toward the good proceeds from a good soul, but that which ends in evil behaves in the opposite way: do not think that one soul of the world is good and another evil; rather, good things proceed from the world soul itself insofar as it partakes of mind. Otherwise, evil things would come from it—that is, things entirely lacking the order of numbers. For in the higher realms, he called "evil" those things that lack harmonious number and beauty; but "good" those things that are joined by consenting numbers. He adds that evils—that is, the privation of order—were conquered by the goods—that is, from the beginning of things by the very ideas of the divine mind. Likewise, they must be conquered, provided the world endures. These things were said according to the judgment punishing the impious: because, clearly, the divine judgment punishing the wicked conquers the evil of injustice with the good of justice. You will note that the greatest virtue is religion, and the negligence of religion has stood as the cause of unhappy ignorance for men. Likewise, the best nature is that which is mixed from temperance and fortitude, docile, mindful, and inclined toward divine things. And when natures of this kind are rightly educated, the truest worship of religion proceeds from them to others, and is most useful to the entire city. And wisdom cannot be learned except with God’s help—but from him who does not observe moderation in teaching...

the same steps, the double, the one-and-a-half <note>original: "sesquialtera" (ratio of 3:2)</note>, and the one-and-a-third <note>original: "sesquitertia" (ratio of 4:3)</note> proportions are found. But let the physicians see to these things. Here, Plato introduces one, two, four, six, eight, twelve. From four to two, the ratio is double; from eight to four, it is also double: these two differences are equal in proportion, for both are created by doubling; however, they are not equal in number, for the number eight exceeds four by four, whereas four exceeds two by only two. Again, compare the number six, on one hand to four, and on the other hand to eight. From six to four arises the one-and-a-half proportion; from six to eight arises the one-and-a-third. Therefore, these differences are unequal in proportion, but equal in number. For in both cases, the difference is two. Again, compare six to twelve in a double proportion, and between these two, compare the number eight. Certainly, from twelve to eight, a one-and-a-half proportion is born. From eight to six, a one-and-a-third arises; from these, the double proportion between six and twelve is composed. In this, those two differences appear clearly unequal both in proportion and in number. All these matters are treated more conveniently in the commentaries on the *Timaeus*.

->CLINIAS, THE ATHENIAN GUEST, MEGILLUS.<-

I AM, as we had commonly agreed, finally arriving here correctly with all three of us, O Guest—I, you, and Megillus here—to inquire about prudence <note>original: "prudentia," referring to practical wisdom or foresight</note>, and by what reasoning we might be able to attain that thing which, once understood, allows the human disposition to best possess prudence, so far as nature allows. For we have already dealt with the other matters pertaining to the making of laws. But that which is greatest to find and to say—namely, what a man must learn to become truly wise—we have neither found nor stated. Truly, I believe this must by no means be omitted, lest we leave imperfect that very thing for whose revelation we have traveled this far. ATHENIAN. You speak skillfully, O friend Clinias. I think you are about to hear a discourse that is in one way marvelous, and yet in another way not marvelous at all. For many, tossed by the waves of this life, proclaim that the human race cannot be happy or blessed. Pay attention, then, and consider whether I myself seem to speak correctly on this matter. I think it is impossible for men in this life, except for a very few, to attain happiness and blessedness. Yet there is good hope that after death one may fully achieve those things which, inflamed by desire, he lived and completed his life for to the best of his strength. I am not bringing forward anything unheard of or new, but something that all Barbarians <note>In the Greek sense, "Barbarians" referred to anyone who did not speak Greek</note> and Greeks recognize in a certain way. For no one is ignorant of how great the difficulty is in the first generation of animals: first in conception and the womb, then in birth and labor, and afterwards in nutrition and education. For we know well that these things happen through a thousand labors. Our time is brief, not only in respect to the long duration of evils, but in whatever way one considers it; it is as if we are allowed to breathe only for a moment around the middle of human life. But quickly, grim old age comes upon us and ensures that no one would wish to return to life again, when he considers past troubles—unless he is carried away by a childish opinion. All these things being so, it serves as an argument for me for what is now being sought. For we ask in what way we can become wise, as if some power of this kind were present in individuals. This power indeed <margin>Which arts do not make a man wise.</margin> escapes us when one turns to any of those faculties commonly called by the name of art, prudence, or science <note>original: "scientia," meaning structured knowledge</note>, as if none of those things in such human affairs were worthy to be called by the name of wisdom. Yet the soul is very confident and prophesies that some such power exists within itself according to nature, but it cannot easily find what it is, or when and how it is present. Does not this doubt and inquiry of ours concerning wisdom look chiefly to this? It is certainly full of hope for those individuals who can prudently and harmoniously examine both themselves and others in every kind of speech and disputation. Shall we say things are thus, or otherwise? CLINIAS. We indeed concede this, Guest, hoping that together with you we shall eventually reach the truest opinion on these matters. ATHENIAN. Let us first run through the other arts which, though they are called sciences, do not make a man wise, so that once they are removed, we may bring forward and compare those which we need, and learn through that comparison. And let us look first at those which the human race needs most. For truly these are the first and most necessary of all. Although the practitioners of these arts were not wise from the beginning, they are not considered wise now, and are even blamed because of these arts. We must say, then, what these are, and that all who wish to appear as the best men flee from the study of such arts. The first is that which commanded us to abstain from eating human flesh—which, as the fables say, once grew common among men in the manner of wild beasts—and called us back to a more modest diet. In this, the ancient men certainly consulted for us gently and humanely; nevertheless, let them go their way, nor let them usurp the name of wisdom. Next, the art of grain-based food is indeed useful and beautiful, but it will never make a man absolutely wise. For it brings difficulty and trouble rather than wisdom. Nor will agriculture do it. For we seem to have approached the cultivation of the earth not by art, but by nature and a certain favor of God. But neither the construction of houses, nor all other building, nor the making of furniture, nor the work of the smith, the carpenter, the potter, or the weaver, nor the crafting of all tools which, being suited to the common people, bring nothing to virtue. Even the whole art of hunting, although it be varied and ingenious, does not bestow magnificence or wisdom. Nor does divination or interpretation of any kind. For even if the diviner knows what is said, he does not understand whether it be true or not. After it is established that none of those arts by which necessities are provided makes a man wise, there remains a certain imitative faculty that is least serious. For imitation is often done with instruments, or frequently with the ugly gestures and figures of bodies. There is also imitation in eloquence and in music <note>original: "mulis," likely a typo for "musicis" or "musa"</note>, and in sculpting and painting, where many and various things are expressed in bodies both hard and soft. None of these things makes a man devoted to imitation wise. If imitation is removed, other arts remain which seem to be concerned with bringing aid. These are indeed many and various, but the art of war—which they call generalship—excels them all. This is highly approved because of its utility, but it stands in greatest need of luck, and is perfected more by natural courage than by wisdom. Medicine also brings us help against the onset of immoderate cold and heat, and other such things by which the nature of animals is harmed. But none of these leads to true wisdom, for they proceed by uncertain conjectures and opinions. We shall not deny that sailors and pilots also bring aid. Yet we will not permit any of them to be called wise by anyone. For none of them knows the anger or the friendship of the winds, which...

620 **The Thirty-Fifth Book.**

<margin>What that faculty is, by which we think there is wisdom.</margin>

...everyone confesses. Also, if anyone were asked how someone is to become "good," they would answer: if they are just, moderate, and brave, and other things of this sort. Who would deny that the soul ought also to be wise? But as for what kind of wisdom is to be acquired—as we recently discussed—we have found that no two people out of many agree. Now, therefore, besides all the types of wisdom we have described above, we have found a certain one, by no means common, for this very purpose: so that he who has learned what has already been said may *seem* wise. Whether the one who has learned these things is *truly* wise and good, however, must be sought through reason. 

**CLINIAS:** You have spoken quite skillfully, Guest, since you affirmed that you would speak of great things concerning great matters. 

**ATHENIAN:** Certainly these are not small things, O Clinias; and, what is more, they are deeply true. 

**CLINIAS:** Quite so, O Guest. Do not yield to the labor, but continue as you have begun. 

**ATHENIAN:** I will give my effort; but you two must also not yield to the labor of listening. 

**CLINIAS:** We shall certainly do so; I speak for both of us. 

**ATHENIAN:** Excellent. Therefore, we must trace the matter back more deeply: and first, if we can in some way, it seems we must grasp under a single name what that faculty is which we think is wisdom. If that cannot be done, we must at least declare another thing: what and how many are the arts which, once possessed, lead us to call a man "wise" according to our custom. 

**CLINIAS:** Speak now. 

**ATHENIAN:** A law-giver will be free from all blame if he thinks better of the gods than the ancients did, and, having employed the best discipline, worships the gods with hymns and extols their blessedness, and so passes his life. 

**CLINIAS:** You speak rightly, Guest, since this end of the laws is proposed to you: that through the worship of God and purity of life, you may attain the best and most beautiful conclusion. 

**ATHENIAN:** How then shall we speak, Clinias? Shall we greatly honor the gods with hymns? And shall we pray that we may conduct the following discussion about them in the best and most beautiful way? Do you think we should act this way, or otherwise? 

**CLINIAS:** Exactly so. But, O happy man, having placed your faith in the gods and sent forth your prayers, speak well of the gods and goddesses. 

**ATHENIAN:** So it shall be, if God himself leads us. Only pray with me. 

**CLINIAS:** Pray proceed then. 

**ATHENIAN:** In the beginning, concerning the lineage of the gods and living beings—since our ancestors handed down accounts of the gods poorly—it is now worthwhile to take up the matter more effectively, so that we may resume the higher dispute we held against the impious. <note>The Athenian refers back to the arguments in Book X of Plato's *Laws*, where he argues against atheists and those who believe the gods can be bribed.</note> In that discussion, it was asserted that the gods exist, that they have care for all things, both the greatest and the smallest simultaneously, and that they cannot be appeased by any prayers or gifts in violation of justice. Do you remember that these things were said, O Clinias? Surely you accepted them then such that you ought to remember them, especially because it was established that they are most true. Indeed, this was held to be the greatest point of all: **that every soul is older than every body.** <note>A core Platonic doctrine: the "Soul" (the animating principle) precedes material "Body" in the order of existence and importance.</note> Do you now remember? 

**CLINIAS:** Most certainly. For that which is better, and older, and more divine, is prior to that which is lower and more base. And similarly, a leader is prior by nature to the led, and a prince to the subject. 

**ATHENIAN:** Let us then admit that the soul is older than the body. But if this is the case, it is surely probable that what is first in the order of generation came first. Therefore, let us posit that the leadership and the beginning of the beginning are held more fittingly [by the soul], and thus we most rightly enter into wisdom through the "generation" of the gods. 

**CLINIAS:** Let those things remain affirmed according to human strength. 

**ATHENIAN:** Come then, do we not most truly affirm that a living being is "according to nature" when a single constitution of soul and body, by their meeting, produces a single form? 

**CLINIAS:** Correct. 

**ATHENIAN:** Such a thing is therefore deservedly called a living being. 

**CLINIAS:** Certainly. 

**ATHENIAN:** Now, we can fittingly say there are five solid bodies, from which the most beautiful and best things are fashioned. <note>original: "quinque solida corpora," referring to the five elements: fire, water, air, earth, and ether.</note> But the other entire genus possesses a single form. For there is nothing else that can be incorporeal and entirely devoid of color, except that most divine genus in which the soul exists. To this genus alone it belongs to shape and fabricate; but to the body, it belongs to be shaped, to be born, and to be perceived by the eyes. But to the genus of the soul—for this must not be said only once—it belongs to be invisible, to possess knowledge, to be intelligible, and to participate in memory and reason in the transformations of both evens and odds. <note>This refers to the mathematical and rational nature of the soul's movements, often associated with the "circles" of the Same and the Different in Platonic cosmology.</note> But since there are five bodies—fire, water, thirdly air, fourthly earth, and fifthly <term>ether</term> <note>Ether was considered the "highest" element, making up the substance of the heavens.</note>—by the leadership of these, they produce many and various individual living beings. This we can learn in one instance: let us first posit that the earthly genus of living beings includes humans, many-footed animals, and those lacking feet, both those that move and those that are stationary and connected by roots. One must think of this everywhere: that although all things are made of all types of bodies, nevertheless the nature of earth and solidity is most abundant in this genus. 

Another genus of living beings must be posited, which is also born and can be seen, and it possesses the most fire; it also has small particles of earth, air, and all the others, and therefore we must say that various visible living beings are born from this. These we think are the celestial living beings—the divine genus of the stars—constituted with the most beautiful body and the most blessed and best soul. To these living beings, we think one of two lots must be assigned. For either they are entirely immortal and divine by necessity, individually without destruction; or they live a long-lived life, sufficient for each to the point that they need nothing longer. 

Let us consider these, I say, as two genera of living beings. And again, let us say that both are visible, of which one seems to be entirely of fire, the other of earth. But the earthly genus moves without order, while the fiery genus moves with every ordination. That which is borne without order must be thought of as mindless—which is what the living beings among us mostly do. But that which proceeds in order in the heaven is demonstrated to have a Mind sufficiently by this track: that it always proceeds through the same paths and in a similar way, and acts and experiences the same things. 

Indeed, the necessity for a soul to possess intellect is the greatest of all necessities; for it leads, but is not led, and it governs. When the soul, which is the best thing, conducts itself by counsel according to the best intellect, then that which it truly performs according to intellect will necessarily happen without any persuasion, and <term>adamant</term> <note>original: "adamas," referring to the hardest, most unbreakable mythical substance.</note> itself could not be more solid or immovable. Indeed, the three Fates preserve as perfected what each of the gods has deliberated with the best counsel. It was therefore necessary for it to be an argument for men that the stars and that entire circuit possess Mind, because they always perform the same actions. For they deliberated what they must do already long ago in a greatest and wonderful span of time. They do not approve now this and now that by counsel, moving up and down. Therefore they neither err, nor do they revolve outside of the ancient order. To many of us, however, it has seemed the opposite: that because these stars always perform the same and similar things, they do not have a soul. The common people follow this insane opinion, thinking that the human race possesses life and mind because it is moved [erratically]...

# **Epinomis, or, The Philosopher. 621**

...provides: Now, regarding why we say these things <note>referring to the heavenly bodies/planets</note> are not without reason **endowed with souls**, first their very size bears witness to it. For they are not only as large as they appear to the eye, but each one is of incredible magnitude. This is to be believed because it is shown by sufficient proofs <note>original: *demonstrationibus*; likely referring to the geometric calculations used in ancient astronomy to estimate the size of the sun and moon</note>, by which we understand that the whole sun is larger than the whole earth, and that all the stars that are carried along possess a marvelous magnitude. 

Let us consider, then, how it could be possible for such a great magnitude to be carried around in such a cycle <note>original: *circūferri*; to be carried in a circular orbit</note> for so long a time by any mere nature <note>meaning a purely physical or material force</note>. I therefore assert that **God is the cause**, and it could not happen in any other way. For a thing cannot become **ensouled** <note>original: *animatum*; having a "psyche" or soul that provides life and movement</note> except through God, as we have already declared. Since, therefore, God is able to do this, it was an easy matter for Him, first, to grant life to every body and every mass; and then, to lead them according to the plan He thought best. Finally, concerning all these matters, this true opinion...

Again, we say there are **eight** <note>In the Platonic system, this includes the five visible planets, the Sun, the Moon, and the outer sphere of the "fixed" stars</note>. Three of these have already been mentioned, and five remain. The fourth and fifth <note>the planets Mercury and Venus</note> are carried in their course and circuit at nearly an equal speed with the sun, so they are neither slower nor faster. Intellect is always a sufficient leader for these three—I speak of the Sun, of **Lucifer** <term>Lucifer|The Morning Star</term> <note>original: *Luciferi*; the Latin name for the planet Venus when it appears in the morning</note>, and of that third one, which cannot be named because it is unknown. 

The reason for this ignorance is that the first observer of these things was a **Barbarian** <note>original: *Barbarus*; to a Greek writer, this meant anyone non-Greek, specifically referring here to the advanced astronomers of Egypt and Mesopotamia</note>. For an ancient region nourished those who, because of the clarity of the summer season, first observed these things. Such were **Egypt** and **Syria**, where all the stars are always, so to speak, clearly seen; because clouds and rains do not obstruct the view of the sky. From there, these proven observations spread here and everywhere else over infinite time. Therefore, let these things be sanctioned by laws with great confidence. For to think that divine things should not be worshipped, or that these celestial bodies are not divine at all, would be the height of madness. 

As for why they lacked names, the cause has been stated; nevertheless, they hold the titles of gods. For Lucifer, which is also the Evening Star, is said to be the star of **Aphrodite** <note>original: *Appoditus*; a variant for Aphrodite</note>, that is, of **Venus**. 

<margin>He followed another copy, different from our own.</margin>

This name is very fitting for the Syrian author of names. The star that runs at nearly the same speed as the sun is the star of **Mercury**. There remain three more motions of those who move to the right with the sun and moon. Furthermore, one must speak of the eighth around the one: which someone will rightly call the **Upper World** <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, which moves contrary to the others and pulls the rest with it—as it appears to men who know little about these things. 

But it is necessary to say those things which we know sufficiently. For true wisdom appears in a certain way to him who has attained even a little bit of right and divine intelligence. The remaining are three stars: one of which is slower than the rest, which is surnamed by some with the name of **Saturn**; the one placed after this in position and slowness is said to be **Jupiter**; then **Mars**, which is the reddest of all. These things are not difficult to explain by intellect, if one tries, but once you have understood, you must think of the gods as we have said. 

Every Greek should also know this: that we inhabit a region almost the best of all for virtue. In this the praise of this region chiefly consists: that it is midway between the nature of winter and summer. But because we are further from the summer serenity than the Barbarians, as we said, we understood the order of these gods more slowly. 

But whatever the Greeks received from the Barbarians, they returned it better. And we should think this also in these matters we are now treating: that although these things are difficult to find, there is great hope for us that the Greeks will honor all these gods with a more excellent cult than they received from the Barbarians, and then, warned both by discipline and by the **Delphic oracles**, will pursue them diligently with every lawful observation. Nor should any of the Greeks think it improper for mortals to treat divine things; but on the contrary, he should think that God is not without mind, nor ignorant of the nature of the human race. For He knows that men will follow Him as He teaches, so that they may thoroughly learn what they are taught. Moreover, He is not ignorant that He teaches us number and how to count, and that we ourselves learn it; for if He were ignorant of that, He would be the most foolish of all—and certainly that which is commonly 

[Column 2]

said would happen. For He would be ignorant of Himself if He envied those capable of learning rather than rejoicing that they become good because of God. 

Indeed, it is likely that when men first began to think about the gods—that they existed, what they were like, and what they did—they did not judge as wise men, nor as second-best, when they thought that fire and water and other bodies were the most ancient things; but the wonderful **soul** was later...

# Epinomis, or, The Philosopher. 623

...and let him consider, but rather that one which involves the **eight** circuits, and how the **seven** are moved in relation to the first <note>In the Platonic cosmos, the "first" is the outer sphere of the fixed stars, which carries the seven inner spheres of the planets, Sun, and Moon in the opposite direction</note>, and in what order each completes its own circles. No nature except one that is wonderful <note>original: *mirabilis*; implying a divinely gifted or exceptional intellect</note> will ever easily perceive this, as we have just said, and shall say again, declaring what ought to be learned and how it ought to be learned. 

First, then, let it be said that the **Moon** unfolds its circle most swiftly, and thus completes the first full moon and the month. The **Sun** must be looked at next, which by its circuit brings about the solstices and the changes of the seasons; furthermore, those that run together with the Sun <note>Referring to the planets Mercury and Venus, whose orbital periods appear closely linked to the Sun from a geocentric perspective</note> must be considered. 

Finally, lest we discourse too often about the same things, we must contemplate all the courses which we touched upon a little while ago, and which are not easily understood; so that our natures may be prepared beforehand by the teachings pertaining to these things, discovered through long practice and labor—indeed, even from childhood. Therefore, there is a need for the teachings which are called **mathematical** <term>mathematical|mathematicae</term> <note>From the Greek *mathematikos*, meaning "related to learning"; in this period, it specifically refers to arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music</note>.

### Book Thirty-Six

Indeed, he considers the **power** <note>original: *potentia*; referring to the active capacity or potentiality of a being</note> of the divine intelligence to be both its source and its mirror. For since it has the capacity to understand, it therefore understands, and in the act of understanding, it contemplates that very same power.

Traces of these principles also appear in nature. For in all things that are naturally composed—whether they be stones and metals, or plants and animals, and most especially in the heavens themselves—nature is so arranged that from its innermost power and natural vigor, a certain order proceeds. This order is found both in the very forms of these things and in their actions and effects. 

Such an order, which is evident from the outside and accompanies the inner vigor of that power, seems to manifest a certain **wisdom**. For nature does not proceed in one way in its ordered progressions while wisdom proceeds in another; rather, the progression of both is entirely similar. In human art as well, whether practiced in private or in public, a similar relationship between power and wisdom is seen...

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical relationship between divine power and intelligence, arguing that the visible order in nature—from minerals to the celestial spheres—is a reflection of internal divine wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>divine intelligence, power vs. wisdom, natural order, metaphysics, celestial harmony, philosophy of nature</keywords>
