<meta>Continuity from page 624: The text continues exploring the metaphysical relationship between human intelligence and the divine, moving from the order of nature to the direct contemplation of God as the "Immense Good."</meta>

On the Epistles of Plato. 625

The mind is deceived regarding God, just as the common people are misled by their senses and imagination, and many learned men are driven back by their own emotional disturbances. For the intellect, judging according to its own nature, compels us to assert that God is either a certain intellect or something that can be understood. However, the **Immense Good** is not an intellect—which, as if in need, turns toward what is understandable so that it may be perfected by its light—nor should it be called "understandable" <note>original: *intelligibile*; referring to an object of thought that the mind can grasp</note>, for that shares a common nature with the intellect, through which it maintains a proportionate relationship with intelligence. But the Immense Good has no common nature with finite goods, and no proportion. Hence, in the *Parmenides*, Plato proves that we have neither a name, nor a definition, nor scientific knowledge of God, insofar as He exists beyond the limits of intelligence. Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: *Mercurius*; the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings</note> asserted the same before him. After him, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th century who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity</note> said the same, proving that God should not be called "being" or "understandable," but rather something above both. 

Because God surpasses both the intellect and the understandable by an infinite interval, no one can reach the divine substance through any active effort of intelligence; however, one can sometimes attain it through **passion** <note>original: *passione*; here meaning a "receptive undergoing" or being acted upon by God, rather than emotional passion</note>. By passion, I mean a gracious state, brought into us through the beneficial action of the infinite Good itself. It is brought, I say, into the very unity that is the head of our mind, specifically when the mind gathers itself entirely from every side into its own unity—which is the expressed image of divine simplicity. But that which shines beneath the divine Sun upon a mind clothed in this unity vanishes when the soul puts off that unity and once again puts on the "multitude" of worldly things. 

From these points, it is clear from the opinion of our Plato that divine things are not found by us, but are rather revealed from above. Neither can the substance and property of divine things be grasped by the mind, much less explained in words and letters. Therefore, one must discuss and write about these things with the intent that, through words and letters, we might hope to exhort and prepare souls for the divine, rather than to demonstrate them. Thus, Plato writes nothing concerning the definition of the divine substance and its properties. He does, however, write many things which—whether through negations, relationships, exhortation, or instruction—might eventually lead the mind to that state to which the home of almighty Olympus is finally opened from on high. 

There, after the soul has withdrawn from lower things into itself, and turned from itself toward higher things, it immediately attains that unity, stability, and simplicity (if I may speak thus) in a single, simple state. But what it attains "is not lawful for a man to speak" (as Paul says) <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:4</note>, and in Plato's view, it is much less lawful to write, "lest that which is holy be given to dogs." <note>original: *ne detur sanctum canibus*; a quote from Matthew 7:6</note> While he trusts neither words nor letters for the explanation of divine matters, he nevertheless judges that they are more safely committed to spoken words than to writing, for letters make things common to anyone. Yet he allows these things to be spoken only to the most select people. He entirely judges that the dignity of divine things requires them to be transferred from mind to mind through speech rather than being translated into external materials through writing. For this reason, the Jews say the mystical sense of their Law was handed down from God Himself through Moses, not so much in letters as commended to their souls. But let them see to that. Certainly, the Pythagoreans observed this, and Plato preserved it. For even here, he promises that he will send certain things through Archedemus rather than through letters. 

He asserts, moreover, that the things written by him belong to Socrates, whose specific duty was in **purification** <note>The Socratic method of "clearing" the mind of false opinions to prepare it for truth</note>. But why is it added that Socrates was "beautiful even in his youth," that is, divinely illuminated? So that we may understand that Socrates, both through the perfection of his early education and a fortunate nature, received from God (through his familiar "daimon" or spirit) those things which others barely attain after great labor. Furthermore, these same mysteries, received through divine revelation, were poured into Plato, and through Plato’s exhortations, they can be poured into men who are similarly disposed. 

Lest anyone think I am dreaming in this exposition, one must listen to Proclus confirming these things as follows: "For those who desire to reach the highest Good, there is no need for science or the exercise of wit, but for firmness, quiet, and tranquility." This is indeed divine faith, which draws and joins us to the highest Good and all divine things in an ineffable way. Truly, we ought not to seek the highest Good or aspire to it through science or any action of the wit, but rather offer and commend ourselves to the divine light, and with our senses closed, rest in that unknown and hidden unity of beings. For this kind of faith is older than all doctrine. It is certain that Proclus received this from Plotinus. 

If anyone considers these things diligently, let him not demand from Plato that usual "doctrinal order" found among human debaters in his dialogues, but let him be content with that style alone which leads to God by a straighter path. Such a style or order consists in **purging** and **converting**. For it is necessary both to purge the eye of the mind from the dark filth of matter and, once purged, to direct it rightly toward the light of the divine Sun itself. One ought not to search further or struggle beyond this. For the immense light, present everywhere by its very nature, pours itself in as soon as the eye of the mind—created for it—looks upon it purely and rightly. If the intellect uses its own activity to receive God—an activity which is both accidental and manifold, and in its own way changeable—it will surely be separated by that very activity from the most simple substance of God, which is most remote from every image of motion. Therefore, it is enough to have purified and directed the mind after a suitable inquiry. Hermes <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> attributes the rest to a "sacred silence of the mind." For he judges that God is pronounced by the mind through its own silence rather than through speech. All of Plato's dialogues, therefore, are occupied with this: some consist only in purging, others only in converting, and others in both. These mysteries are confirmed again in the *Letter to the Syracusans*. And these confirmed things support the Gospel precepts in a wonderful way.

->### ARGUMENT FOR THE<-
->### Third Letter.<-

This letter of Plato is written to Dionysius the Younger after Plato's second departure from him. First, he responds to things Dionysius asked; then, he dissolves a slander fabricated against him by Dionysius. In his response to the question, he teaches that there is no **pleasure** in God—specifically, the kind of pleasure that has an opposite in pain, and which consists in a certain motion or the filling of a deficiency. However, he does not deny that in God is all that "Good" for the sake of which pleasure *seems* good. He adds that pleasure (the changeable kind) is a cause of harm, specifically regarding money and honor; likewise, it causes pain in the body. Furthermore, it takes away sharpness of mind, memory, judgment, and dignity. After this, against Dionysius's accusation, he proves that he set out for Sicily for the most just reasons: to give counsel regarding the restoration of once-ruined cities and a fair form of government.

->### ARGUMENT FOR THE<-
->### Fourth Letter.<-

After Dionysius was expelled from his tyranny, Plato writes to Dion, who had now returned to his homeland, admonishing him and also Heraclides, Theodore, and other friends who held power, to live far from tyranny and to maintain a form of government tempered mostly by the rule of the best men <note>aristocracy</note> and, in a certain way, by the people <note>democracy</note>. Here are certain precepts to be committed to memory: 
1. First, that it properly belongs to princes to excel all in truth, justice, magnificence, and temperance. In short, they should surpass others in prudence as much as men surpass boys in prudence. 
2. Second, they must show themselves to be exactly as they wish to be seen. 
3. Third, they must look around and see that the eyes of all are turned toward them, remembering that neither can their vices be hidden, nor will they satisfy the highest expectations with only mediocre virtue. 
4. Fourth, they should imitate the most proven lawmakers and avoid discord among colleagues like a plague. 
5. Fifth, they must remember that common benevolence is exceedingly necessary for getting things done, and this can only be acquired and preserved through humanity <note>original: *humanitate*; kindness, civility, or philanthropic spirit</note>.

->### ARGUMENT FOR THE<-
->### Fifth Letter.<-

Even if custom ascribes this fifth letter to Plato, it seems rather to be by Dion, who is fashioning himself entirely after Plato’s strengths. He instructs Perdiccas, who has been established as a prince in a monarchy, to remember that he is young and therefore in need of the counsel and service of elders—not just any elders, but the most proven ones, and not in every matter, but in the form of government, who understand what is most...

### Arguments

[He] hands it over by pact and law alone: by a legitimate pact, I say, with sacred rites duly performed, established by mutual agreement, and with an oath interposed, by attesting and beseeching God himself as the author and preserver of union. By attesting, I say, and beseeching under the odd number, in which God is said to rejoice. For he brings forward here the three highest principles of things, which he also touched upon in the first epistle. For where he says, the leader of all things present and future, he wishes the world-soul to be understood, which, as the principle of motion, leads all things by temporal reason from the future into the present, and from the present into the past. But where he speaks of the father and lord, he signifies the supreme God and the Good itself. Yet he seems to insert a certain divine mind in the middle between these two, when, while repeating "of the leader," he also adds "and of the cause." For in Plato, "king" often signifies the Good itself, "cause" signifies the mind, and "leader" finally the soul. And since he refers the cause to the mind, for that reason the Platonists in the *Timaeus* argue that the Intellect emerged as the son of the Good itself, and the immediate architect of the world. Concerning which it is written in the *Epinomis*: The most divine Reason, or the most divine Word, adorned the visible world. Moreover, he calls the Good itself here both "father" and "lord": so that by the first he might designate the father of the mind, but by the second the lord of the soul. Thus perhaps the Platonic number explains it. Thus also the Christian Platonist, but an Arian one. Someone might also understand the Holy Spirit by the leader, and the Son by the mind. For where Plato says "father," he likewise implies "son." But if anyone should posit even a single essence, he will seem to oppose many Platonists, yet he will not manifestly conflict with Plato. Furthermore, he exhorts to more graceful studies of doctrines at the same time, and to certain more pleasant disciplines related to these, namely eloquence, poetry, and music. He commands one to apply oneself to all these with the purpose that, investigating the divine scent through these as if they were footprints, they may love him alone, and by loving, may moreover attain the savor. He says, therefore,: if you truly wish [it], let us philosophize our life, that is, either let us investigate by loving, or love by investigating. Finally, we shall all undoubtedly know him himself. Certainly, the name of philosophy seems to carry with it a certain inquiry, yet it properly carries love and an amatory inquiry. Pythagoras, therefore, knew, and Plato also knew, that we relate to finite goods in one way, and to the infinite good in another: and indeed, that finite goods are known by us before they are loved, and must be loved so that they may be known; but the infinite is loved before it is known, nor is it to be investigated so much that it may be known, as it is to be loved. But why must it be loved before it is understood? Because, clearly, love transfers the lover into the beloved; that which was lacking in proportion, it supplies by a transforming affection. Is not God often named "fire" in the sacred [texts]? By the same metaphorical indulgence, therefore, an angel may be named a transparent body, but the soul an opaque body, as long as it is enclosed in this blind prison. Therefore, just as a transparent body under fire—that is, a clear one, like air and water—suddenly admits light both outside and inside, but earthly bodies must first be heated intensely, and first thinned by heat into a transparent likeness before they receive the fiery light: so spirits separated from the body suddenly receive the divine light; but spirits joined to earthly bodies need the fire of transformed love, by which indeed, being purified and translated into a divine likeness, they may finally be illuminated by the splendor of knowledge from above. Hence Porphyry says: the inquiry of divine things indeed purifies the soul, but love deifies it. For he expresses the matter here with its own word, and indeed not unjustly, for from no material does fire come from that which [merely] receives light, but from that which receives fiery heat. It is therefore a Platonic sentiment that divine things must be investigated—namely, that they exist, and what sort they are by a certain common perception—but meanwhile they must be loved not with a common, but with a singular and incomparable charity: for only thus can we somewhere clearly understand what will be, and become blessed. How much these things harmonize with sacred letters, no one but the profane is ignorant.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE SEVENTH EPISTLE.

Plato’s seventh epistle was written to the kinsmen and friends of Dion, the fatherland having now been liberated by Dion, and Dion having been unjustly slain. But so that many things pertaining to the history, both in this epistle and in others, may be clearly understood, one must look back a little further. Plato set out for Syracuse three times. Once indeed in the time of the elder Dionysius, being forty years of age. Twice thereafter, while the younger Dionysius held the tyranny. What he did in each journey, or for what cause he set out, appears partly in the life of him written by us, and partly in these epistles. Dion indeed seems to have been from the same family as Dionysius: moreover, he was variously entangled in affinity with him. For the elder Dionysius had Dion's sister, Aristomache, in marriage. But Dion himself had Dionysius's daughter, named Arete, as his wife. Dionysius the younger, however, was born not from Dion's sister, but from another wife named Doris. On the first journey, Dion having been made a listener of Plato, directed his life toward virtue, and began to desire the public good of the fatherland. Therefore, when Dionysius the elder died, and Dionysius the younger succeeded to the tyranny, and while still a boy was governed almost entirely by Dion's counsel, Dion, wishing to lead him into a desire for the philosophical life, called Plato to Syracuse with many prayers, and induced Dionysius to summon him. Plato therefore obeyed, led primarily by the hope that by his counsels he would bring it about that the state there would become either a republic or a kingdom. But almost a month after Plato's arrival, [Dionysius], led by false slanders, expelled Dion as if he had invaded the tyranny. He nevertheless welcomed Plato freely. But Plato, indignant, returned to his fatherland with the matter unfinished. He arrived a third time, intending to reconcile Dion to Dionysius, having been beseeched again and again by both, and also asked by Archytas and Archidemus the Pythagoreans, and by very many nobles. At that time, Dionysius promised both the recall of Dion and that he would moreover preserve the best form of governing. But he performed none of those things which he had promised. When indeed Plato openly rebuked Dionysius because he had failed his word, both concerning the recall of Dion and concerning his own [promise] to Theodotus about preserving Heraclides, he thereafter held Dionysius as an enemy. Thus he lived in the greatest danger of being killed by the soldiers. But Archytas of Tarentum sent the orator Salmictus to Dionysius along with a ship, asking that he release Plato. He released him and provided provisions. Plato returned safely to his fatherland. Shortly after, Dion, having secretly gathered forces and set out for Syracuse, expelled Dionysius, and liberty was restored to the Syracusans. But shortly after, he himself was killed by the deceit and envy of his own people. After these things, Hipparinus the son of Dion, and Hipparinus the brother of Dionysius [and] nephew of Dion by his sister, holding Syracuse, deliberated by the counsel of the nobles concerning the better form of governing. Meanwhile, Dionysius was attempting to return to the principate with the support of his enemies. Plato therefore writes to these, exhorting them and instructing them toward the best form of governing, that is, a kingdom obedient to laws and supported by the authority of the nobles. Specifically, precepts of this kind are gathered from this epistle: It is not foreign to a good nature to desire the rudders of the state, especially when necessity demands it; but it is foreign to a good citizen to desire to obtain these with all license. It is not the part of a prudent man to involve himself rashly in public affairs, especially where he is subjected to danger without hope of public safety. Philosophy alone can discern what is good and just in both public and private affairs, and what is not of that kind. The human race will not cease to be involved in evils until either philosophers rule, or those who rule, by God's illumination, philosophize. A delicate and luxurious education depraves even divine natures. No intemperate person can be prudent. A city in which the citizens are incontinent can be contained by no power of laws, because it suffers frequent changes, and always for the worse. Violence must be brought neither upon the fatherland nor upon parents, but one must consult the interests of both far from violence. The authority of the ancients is to be preferred to the speeches of the [modern] makers. Nothing evil can happen to a good man. The soul, separated from this body, pays the penalties of its crimes under the sentence of divine judgment. It is better to suffer the most grievous injuries than to inflict them. The greedy and intemperate are blind and deaf to divine things, so that they neither see them themselves, nor can they endure to hear them from others, or perceive them when heard. Impiety is mixed with all sins, and vice versa. Impiety itself, mixed with sins, is the stimulus by which sinners are especially troubled both in this life and tortured in the other. After these things, where he writes about his familiarity with Dionysius and about the study of philosophy, he proves that no one will make progress in philosophy unless, kindled by the love of wisdom, he both sustains all its labors for its sake and despises its pleasures. Then indeed, since it is the part of a wise man to contemplate divine things, he opportunely shows that divine things can never be expressed to the common people in writing or in words—nay, they even ought not to be. They cannot be, because what is greater is also understood entirely by the mind. They ought not to be, because those who are the lowest among the common people would laugh at them as old wives' tales; and those who are slightly higher among the common people, having heard these things, would either fall into false heresy, or would turn out vain beyond measure and contentious on account of a slight opinion of higher things. Plato does not say anywhere that nothing true or certain can be understood about divine things; but rather that what is understood about them cannot be expressed, nor can their proper truth be understood by the same reasoning as other things. Some forms are entirely joined to bodies, others are entirely separate. The former are called natural, the latter divine. There are also intermediate ones, joined indeed in a certain way, and in a certain way separable, that is, rational souls, intermediate between divine and natural things. Insofar as these are joined to bodies, they are necessarily disjoined from divine things. For they cannot be joined to forms separated from matter except by separation. But they are separated from matter in two principal ways: both by moral purgation and by contemplative resolution.

[[page number: 627]]

The study of philosophy does both: and just as one who dries out moist wood first by the sun, then moves it to the fire, provides the occasion for the wood to be kindled, yet he himself does not kindle the wood, but the fire does; so the study of philosophy both prepares the soul for divine things through moral discipline and purification, and through contemplative resolution moves and joins the mind to divine things: yet it does not itself form the mind with divine truth, but God himself, like a fire, suddenly illuminates the mind with his own light, which has been prepared and brought near by the benefit of philosophy as if it were material. Therefore, when Plato said that our inquiry into divine things does not both prepare and form the intellect for perceiving: although in perceiving divine things, the most purified and eminent inquiry indeed prepares, but does not form. For that reason, he says there is need for long-standing familiarity with divine things, signifying the constancy of speculation; likewise by the conjunction of life, or communion, signifying the purification perfected by moral discipline. He adds that finally, in a mind so affected, the light of truth is kindled not gradually by some human love, but suddenly. But from where? From the fire—that is, God—leaping forth or sparkling. By "sparks" he designates the ideas, the exemplars of things in the divine mind. He also designates the formulas of ideas innate in us. These, once put to sleep through sloth, are awakened by the fanning of doctrine, and like rays of the eyes flashing out, are illuminated by ideas as if by the rays of stars. He adds that light of this kind is not only kindled but becomes *in* the soul, to show that souls were both formed and innate, and that such splendor becomes familiar. And lest the mind in that state be ambiguous and anxious, he added: "It now nourishes itself," that is, this light first kindled divinely in the mind, thereafter by its own power draws an abundance of divine rays, and fills the mind with nourishing joy. Here the mind feeds itself, that is, seeking nothing from without, it lives content with itself, and however blessedly it is affected within, even if it wished, it cannot, and knows not how to express it. Plato contemplates five degrees in this contemplation, which you may read more diligently explained by us in the *Theology*. For he commands the one desirous of truth to proceed first through what is heard from the name of the thing itself, then through sight and other senses from the accidents of the thing itself to the definition of the thing itself, through this to the formula of the thing innate in the mind, and finally through the formula to the Idea, the procreator of both formulas and things. And he teaches meanwhile that the Idea differs far from the rest in four principal ways. Because, clearly, the Idea is a substance, simple, immobile, and unmixed with its contrary. But the remaining four—that is, the name, the accidental image, the definition, and the formula/notion—degenerate from the substance, simplicity, stability, and purity of the Idea. For that reason, they do not sufficiently imprint the Idea upon us, but they accommodate us, as best they can, to the divine impression. Finally, the mind impressed divinely, if it should ever strive to express the characters of the ideas in words and letters, will produce deformed images of the most beautiful things. But if one believes the Pythagoreans, one will not strive so much to depict the ideas as to cultivate the souls of the listeners, and to polish them like tablets on which divine forms may finally be painted by the divine finger. Indeed, she herself, looking up at the celestial rays, will not attempt to describe the forms of the rays in vain to the blind; once they are incurable, she will let them go. If they are curable, she will only undertake to purge the vision and raise it upward, as one who understands that she would otherwise labor in vain.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE EIGHTH EPISTLE.

In the previous epistle, instructing the Syracusan princes, he was then occupied with matrimonial precepts and with the deeds performed by himself and Dion. In this one, however, he comprehends his own institutions in briefer terms, always maintaining a middle path between vanities and the government of the people, but most of all studying that the citizens be reconciled rather than expelled, and that as much as can be done without injury to others, the state of the republic be stabilized. Soon in the beginning, he asserts that men polluted by impious crime are incurable, and that no counsel will profit them. Likewise, in all things, both in speaking and in thinking, a beginning must be made from God. In the whole epistle, you will observe how cautious and at the same time merciful a governor Plato is, and how diligent a reconciler of minds. He approves, as is his custom, a government similar to the Lacedaemonian. In which there is a great deal of the nobles, there is also a certain royal form, and there is also something of the people. He condemns extreme servitude, through which all things are subjected to human lust. He also disapproves of extreme liberty or license, in which anyone almost without selection is allotted the rudders of the republic. But he approves the middle. Note the golden saying: "Moderate servitude is that which serves God, immoderate that which serves men." To temperate men, law is God; to the intemperate, however, it is lust.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE NINTH EPISTLE.

In the epistle to Archytas the philosopher, who was very busy with public affairs, he gives counsel for contemplating, lest he desert an honest and at the same time necessary action. For to profit men both publicly and privately, he calls an honest and necessary action. Honest indeed, because just as any member of the body is not for itself alone, but also for others, and especially for the whole, so men are for one another, and most of all for the species. Necessary, however, because unless you live for others, you cannot live for yourself, and unless you succor your household and fatherland, your family and public affairs, destitute of governors, will either waver or, governed by worse men, will be endangered and finally suffer shipwreck.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE TENTH EPISTLE.

He confirms Aristodemus, a familiar of Dion, who philosophizes primarily through the elegance of his manners, in his opinion and life. Asserting that the substance of philosophy is indeed moral virtue, which the name itself declares by a certain love and cultivation; [this is] the definition. Human speculations, however, are either certain extrinsic ornaments of philosophy, or ways toward attaining that firm purity of mind which pertains to morals. When this is attained, contemplation follows, divine rather than human, and infused from above rather than acquired; to which, if that prior speculation is compared, it is called a "game" by Plato. That, moreover, is the greatest precept of Pythagoras and Socrates. But where we translate "ornaments," the Greek word "ornament" signifies something mixed with a certain subtle vanity and pride. As if he should say: Knowledge puffs up, charity builds up. Likewise: Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul. He places sincerity or health in a simple and tranquil mind; faith indeed in words, and finally firmness in gestures and actions.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE ELEVENTH EPISTLE.

To the prince Laodamas, consulting him about the best government, he gives that accustomed counsel of his: that all laws will be vain unless, moreover, the most proven men through whom the laws live have great power in the republic, and unless some magistrate is constituted in the city, and indeed one with the greatest authority, who as a censor of morals may diligently observe the actions of individuals through scouts, always intent on this, that the daily life of the citizens may lead their minds toward fortitude and temperance.

### ARGUMENT FOR THE TWELFTH EPISTLE.

The twelfth epistle is proof to us of how liberal and simple Plato was; as one who entrusted his certain more secret commentaries, not yet finished, to Archytas. It is also an argument that Archytas, philosophizing no less in manners than in words, was worthy to have the dearest things entrusted to him. Perhaps indeed these commentaries pertained to filling out the unfinished *Critias*, and to composing the *Hermocrates* not yet written. But the epistle to Dionysius which is added by those ignorant of these things, we have not translated for that reason, because both the words of the epistle themselves and all the learned deny that it is by Plato. It is, moreover, worthwhile to notice in these epistles with how great and constant a mind our Plato was, especially in the affairs of his friends, and how many grave dangers he often underwent for the safety of a friend. Furthermore, how freely and kindly he quite often corrected the tyrant, being most of all alien to adulation, but yielding to no one in charity and duty, so that he can profit us for living well and blessedly no less by his life and manners than by his disputations.

# Book Thirty-Six.

## THE THIRTY-SIXTH BOOK OF PLATO: THIRTEEN EPISTLES.

### DION TO DIONYSIUS, TO ACT WELL [GREETINGS]. EPISTLE I.

While I was among you for a long and great time, and so faithfully administered your empire that you perceived utility therefrom above the rest, I sustained heavy slanders. For I knew that, with me supporting you, a cruel deed would nonetheless seem to have been done. All, however, who were involved in the same government can be witnesses for me. Many of whom I liberated from no mediocre losses with the greatest effort. Even exercising power among you, I quite often guarded your city. Finally, however, I was expelled by you more ignominiously than it is fitting for some beggar to be expelled, commanded to depart by you, I who bestowed such long-lasting labor upon your interests. Therefore, hereafter I intend to lead a solitary life. You, however, such a tyrant, shall govern alone. But that distinguished money sent by you for travel expenses [viaticum], I send back to you through this Bacchis together with these letters. For it is neither sufficient for travel expenses, nor is it useful enough for the rest of life; and it would bring the greatest disgrace to you giving it, and not much less to me receiving it. Therefore I was unwilling to receive it. But it matters nothing to you, both to give and to receive the same amount; but that being received, you shall honor some other of your people, as you have honored me. For I have already been honored enough by you. And it is opportune for me now to say that [verse] of Euripides: that you, when the affairs require it, will wish such a man were present to assist you. I want you to remember, however, and many other tragedians, when they introduce some tyrant perishing, they attribute voices of this kind to him: "Alas, wretch, I perish supported by no friends." But no poet has yet depicted anyone perishing from a lack of gold. That poetic [saying] is also highly approved by those who have a mind: "The glitter of gold is not the rarest thing in the wretched life of mortals; not adamant, not silver tables which are prized among men, so flash to the eyes; nor do broad estates or cultivated fat lands avail so much for life, as the mind of good men agreeing among themselves." Farewell; and consider that so much has been erred toward us, that you may conduct yourself more rightly toward others.

### PLATO TO DIONYSIUS, TO ACT WELL [GREETINGS]. EPISTLE II.

I heard from Archedemus that you judge that not only I, but even my familiars, except for Dion alone, ought to speak or do nothing evil against you. This, however, which you except concerning Dion, shows that I do not have power over my familiars. For if I had power over both others and over Dion and you, very many good things, as I think, would come to both you and the rest of the Greeks. But now I am great in this alone, that I present myself obedient to my reason. Which things I say because Cratištolus and Polyxenus brought nothing sincere to you. One of whom they say said that he heard at the Olympics many of those who were with me disparaging you. Perhaps he hears more acutely than I. For I heard no such thing. It seems to me, however, that hereafter as often as he brings something of this kind to you, you ought to act so that you write to me and investigate the matter itself. For I shall neither fear nor blush to confess the truth. Moreover, between me and you it is such that neither are we (to speak freely) unknown to any of the Greeks, nor do the men of this age keep silent about our familiarity; hold that also as certain, that posterity will not be silent. Such are those who know it, being neither small nor obscure. To what purpose is this? I shall reveal it immediately, having begun the matter somewhat deeper. By the law of nature indeed, those excelling in wisdom and power tend toward the same thing. And those two things always affect each other, pursue each other, and come together. Then also men are greatly delighted by these, as often as they either in the poems of poets or in private conversations relate or hear such things: as when men speak of Hiero and Pausanias the Lacedaemonian, they rejoice to commemorate the familiarity of Simonides which he had with them, and to relate what he said and did among them. Similarly, they were accustomed to celebrate together Periander the Corinthian and Thales the Milesian; Pericles and Anaxagoras; Croesus and Solon as wise; and Cyrus as powerful. And indeed, the poets having imitated these things introduce Creon and Tiresias together; and Polyidus and Minos; Agamemnon and Nestor; Ulysses and Palamedes; and as it seems to me, for the same reason the ancient men joined Prometheus to Jove. Some of these they introduce agreeing, others disagreeing; some indeed sometimes in concord, sometimes in discord. And they sing of their disagreements as well as their agreements. I have said all these things, however, for this reason: to show that even when we are dead, men will not be silent about us. Wherefore, care for the subsequent time must not be neglected by ourselves. For it happens by a certain nature that the most idle men care nothing for what the future opinion about them will be; but the most proven men do everything so that they may be well heard of among men in future ages. From which I make a conjecture that there is some sense for those who are dead of the things which are done in life. Since the best perhaps so divine; the worst indeed in no way. But the presages of divine men are stronger than those of others. I think, however, clearly that those superior deceased ones of whom I speak, would amend their familiarity; they would apply the greatest effort so that they might spread a better opinion of themselves than now. This indeed is permitted to us even now, God favoring; and if anything was sinned in our previous familiarity, to amend and correct that both in deeds and words. Indeed, I say this: that the opinion will be true (especially as pertains to philosophy) concerning us; so that if we are good, we shall have a good reputation; if evil, an evil one. And we, caring for those things, could do nothing more pious; and neglecting them, nothing equally impious and profane. How, moreover, this should happen, and can happen justly, I shall say thus. When I came to Sicily, the fame was that I excelled greatly among those who then philosophized. I desired also, when I had come to Syracuse, to have you as a witness of that opinion: so that philosophy might be in honor for me even among the multitude. But that matter did not succeed prosperously enough for me. I say, however, that the cause of this was not that which most people thought, but I assert that futile cause: that you seemed not to trust me enough, but in a certain way to wish to dismiss me: but to call others: and to inquire what business I had, disagreeing clearly as it seemed to me. And because many were affirming concerning what they spoke, that you indeed despised me and had intended your mind toward other things. This fame therefore then increased. What, however, ought to happen after these things, hear thus: so that I may respond to that which you ask, in what way we [should behave] toward each other.

---
[[page 629]]

In what way we ought to conduct ourselves mutually. If you indeed altogether despise philosophy, let us bid it farewell. But if you have either heard from another, or found better things for yourself than those which are handed down by me, embrace those. But if our things please you, you ought also to honor us most. Now, however, as if from the beginning, you go first, I shall follow. For honored by you, I shall honor you; not honored, however, I shall rest. Furthermore, if you first begin to honor me, you will seem to honor philosophy; and that among the multitude, which you especially desired, will produce glory for you as a lover of wisdom. But if I shall honor you, who do not honor me in the least, I shall seem to admire and follow riches; and how shameful this is judged by all, we are not ignorant. But to speak summarily: with you honoring, there will be honor to both; but with me honoring, there will be infamy to both. And concerning these things indeed, enough. But the little circle [orbiculus] itself does not hold itself rightly. Archedemus himself will tell you, however, when he returns to you. But that more precious and divine thing, about which you ask me through him, must be accurately shown to him. For you say, as he relates, that it was not sufficiently demonstrated to you by me concerning the first nature. It must be told to you now, therefore, through certain enigmas: so that if anything should happen to this tablet by sea or land, he who reads it may not be able to understand. It is thus: Around the King of all are all things; all things are for his sake; he himself is the cause of all beautiful things; around the second are second things; third things around the third. The human soul affects to understand what sort of things those are, looking into those things which are kindred to you. None of which things holds itself sufficiently. But in the King himself, and in these things which I have said, there is no such thing. But that which is after this, the soul says. But what sort of questioning is this of yours, O son of Dionysius and Doris? And how much is it the cause of all evils? Nay rather, is not a certain stimulus of this innate in our soul? Which unless one uproots, he will certainly never attain the truth. You said in the gardens when we were under the laurels, that you had thought this out: and it was your discovery. And I, I say, if this seemed to you to be thus, you would have liberated me from many disputations. Nor have I ever found another discoverer of this; and my very great investigation is occupied around it. But you perhaps, having heard from someone, by some divine chance arrived there. But you have never held firm demonstrations of that matter, but at one time you brought them forth one way, at another time another: insofar as you were conjecturing by phantasy. This, however, is no such thing, and this does not happen to you alone. But know for certain that no one, when he first hears me, is affected otherwise. And one indeed more, another indeed less exhausted, only with difficulty finally cease from labor. Almost all, however, labor not a little. Since these things are and have been so, we have almost found, as I think, what you asked through the epistle: how it is necessary for us to conduct ourselves toward each other. After indeed you have discussed these things both by yourself and compared them with the opinions of others: if only you have performed a right examination, you will show yourself agreeing with us and our things. In what way, therefore, will these and other things which we have said, hold themselves? You indeed rightly for that reason sent Archedemus to us. And after he has returned to you and reported my sentiment to you, other doubts will perhaps seize you; you, however, if you consult rightly for yourself, will send Archedemus to me again; he in turn, like a merchant, will return not without profit; which if you do twice or thrice, and diligently examine those things which we send, I shall wonder indeed if you do not have yourself much better than now toward those things which you doubt. Boldly therefore do these things. For neither you nor Archedemus can undertake any negotiation which is either more honest or more acceptable to God. Beware, however, lest these ever fall into the ears of men unskilled in discipline and erudition. For there are none, as my opinion holds, which said to the people seem more ridiculous; nor which brought forth among the ingenious, seem more wonderful and divine. But often said and always heard and for many years, only with difficulty finally, like gold, are they purified with great labor. For listen to what is accustomed to happen in this matter that is wonderful. There are many men who have already heard these things: powerful in teachability, powerful in memory, skillful in examining and judging, now advanced in age and having heard these things for no less than thirty years; these nevertheless affirm that things which once seemed most incredible to the hearing, now for the first time seem to them very credible and clear; and things which then seemed most probable, now on the contrary seem so to them. Looking at these things, therefore, beware lest you ever repent of those things which have now escaped you unworthily and rashly. The greatest custody of this matter, however, is to write nothing, but to learn. For things which are written cannot be contained; for this reason I have never written anything about them, nor is there any prescribed work of Plato, nor will there be. Those things which are now said, are of Socrates: who even while he was a young man, was clear in virtue. Farewell: and believe us. And this epistle, when you have read it quite often, burn it immediately. And concerning these things indeed, enough. But you wonder that I did not send Polyxenus to you. I, however, concerning Lycophron also and the rest who are with you, affirm that which I have for a long time and now: namely, that you excel those as much as possible both in genius and in art: nor does any of them willingly yield to you in disputation, as some suspect, but unwillingly. And yet you seem to have used them very humanely, and to have honored them with honest gifts. But concerning them indeed, many such things may be said. Use Philistion as much as possible, if it happens to use him. And if it can be done, use the work of Speusippus; and send him back. Speusippus indeed also has need of you. Philistion promised me, however, if he were dismissed by you, that he would seek Athens immediately. It would be laudable to have dismissed him from the stone quarries [latomiae]. But there is a light petition concerning his relatives, as well as concerning Hegesippus the son of Aristo. For you also wrote to me: if anyone should wish to bring injury to him or to those, and you should perceive it, you would not permit it. Concerning Lylychides, furthermore, it is becoming to confess the truth. For he alone of those who set out from Sicily to Athens, has changed nothing in your and my familiarity. But those things which were done, he daily honors more with words as much as he can.

### TO THE SAME.
### EPISTLE III.

You ask whether it is more rightly placed in salutations, "Plato to Dionysius, to rejoice [Gaude]": or in the way I am accustomed to write to friends, "to act well [Bene agere]." You indeed, as those say who were present with you in Delphi, so blandly addressed the God himself, and similarly wrote: "Rejoice, and preserve the pleasant life of a tyrant." I, however, would salute neither a God nor a man in this way. Not a God: because I would speak against his nature. For divinity is far from trouble and pleasure. Not a man: because pleasure quite often brings detriment and pain to him, producing sluggishness in the soul and oblivion, ignorance and petulance. And let these things be said by me concerning salutation. Which, after you have read them, you will take as you wish. Many indeed report that you are accustomed to say to certain legates, while they come to you, that you had in mind to restore the Greek cities in Sicily and [Syracuse]...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato’s Epistles, specifically discussing the Seventh Epistle's famous "Seventh Letter" passage regarding the limits of language and the necessity of divine illumination in philosophy. # On the Epistles of Plato. 627

[Left Column]

The study of philosophy does both: just as one who dries wet wood <note>original: "humidum lignum"</note> first by the sun, then moves it to the fire, provides the opportunity for the wood to be ignited—yet he himself does not ignite the wood, but the fire does—so philosophical study, through both moral discipline and purification, prepares the soul for divine things. By resolving the soul through contemplation <note>The term used here is "contemplatio," referring to the Greek "theoria," the act of looking upon divine truths.</note>, it moves the mind toward divine things and joins them. Yet, philosophy itself does not form the mind with divine truth; rather, God himself, like a fire, illuminates the mind with the light of his own truth. In this process, the mind acts as the "matter" <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic thought, "matter" is the potentiality that receives "form."</note> prepared by the benefit of philosophy and drawing near to the light. 

Therefore, since Plato had said that divine matters can be expressed neither by letters nor by words, he signified further that they can neither be taught nor found by the same method as other things. For in perceiving other things, our inquiry both prepares and forms the intellect; whereas in perceiving divine things, inquiry or the most purified <note>original: "purgatiss," likely "purgatissima" or "purgatissimum."</note> [state of soul...]

<summary>This page uses the metaphor of seasoning and igniting wood to explain that while philosophy prepares the human mind, only God can provide the final "fire" of divine truth. It reflects on Plato's assertion that the highest truths cannot be captured in writing but require internal illumination.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Epistles, illumination, purification, contemplation, divine truth, allegory of fire, philosophical study</keywords>

**W**hile I was staying among you for a long and considerable time, and was so faithfully administering your empire <note>original: "imperium vestrum." ...we ought to take turns. If you indeed utterly despise **philosophy**, let us let it be. But if you have either heard from another or found better things yourself than those which are handed down by me, embrace those. But if our teachings please you, you ought to honor us most of all. Now, however, as if from the beginning, you lead the way and I shall follow. For if I am honored by you, I will honor you; if I am not honored, I will remain quiet. Furthermore, if you begin to honor me first, you will appear to honor philosophy; and that, among the multitude—which you especially desired—will produce glory for you as a lover of wisdom. But if I honor you while you do not honor me at all, I will appear to admire and chase after wealth; and we are not ignorant of how shameful this is judged to be by everyone. To speak briefly: if you honor me, there is honor for both; but if I honor you, there is infamy for both. And enough on these matters. As for the <term>small sphere</term> <note>original: "Orbiculus." This likely refers to an astronomical model or a geometric device Archedemus was bringing to Dionysius.</note>, it is not in good condition. Archedemus himself will tell you about it when he returns to you.

But that matter which is more precious and divine, about which you ask me through him, must be shown to him accurately. For you say, as he reports, that the <term>first nature</term> <note>original: "prima natura." This refers to the ultimate principle of reality, often identified with the "One" or the "Good" in Platonic thought.</note> has not been sufficiently demonstrated to you by me. I must, therefore, speak to you now through certain riddles, so that if anything happens to this tablet either by sea or by land, anyone who reads it may not be able to understand it. 

It is thus: All things are around the King of all; all things are for his sake; he is the cause of all beautiful things. Second things are around the second; third things are around the third. The human soul strives to understand what quality these things have, looking at those things which are kindred to itself. None of these are sufficient. But in the King himself, and in those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of that sort. But what follows this, the soul asks. Yet what sort of question is this of yours, O son of Dionysius and Doris? <note>Dionysius II was the son of Dionysius I and Doris of Locri.</note> And how much is it the cause of all evils? Rather, it is a certain stimulus born within our soul. Unless one roots this out, he will certainly never attain the truth. 

You said to me in the gardens, when we were under the laurels, that you had thought this out and that it was your own discovery. And I said that if it seemed to you to be so, you would have freed me from many arguments. I said I had never found any other discoverer of this, and that most of my own investigation was occupied with it. But you, perhaps having heard it from someone else, reached that point by some divine fate. Yet you never held firm demonstrations of that matter, but brought them forth differently at different times, insofar as you were guessing by your imagination. But this matter is nothing of the sort, and this happens not to you alone. But know for certain that no one, when they first hear me, is affected otherwise. One is more exhausted, another less, and they only just cease from their labor at last. Almost all of them labor not a little. 

Since these things are and have been so, we have found, I think, what you sought through your letter: how we ought to behave toward each other. After you have discussed these things by yourself and compared them with the opinions of others—provided you have performed a correct examination—you will show yourself in agreement with us and our teachings. In what way, then, will these and the other things we have said stand? You did indeed act rightly in sending Archedemus to us for that reason. And after he has returned to you and reported my opinion to you, other doubts will perhaps seize you; but if you consult your own best interest, you will send Archedemus to me again, and he, like a merchant, will return not without profit. If you do this two or three times, and diligently examine those things we send, I will indeed be amazed if you do not have a much better grasp on the things you doubt than you do now. Do this boldly, therefore. For neither you nor Archedemus can undertake any business that is either more honorable or more acceptable to God.

Take care, however, that these things never fall into the ears of men unskilled in discipline and learning. For there are no things, in my opinion, which when spoken to the common people seem more ridiculous; nor any which, when brought forth among the gifted, are more wonderful and divine. Often spoken and always heard over many years, they are only just purified like gold with great labor. For hear what usually happens in this matter that is wonderful. There are many men who have already heard these things—men powerful in teachability, powerful in memory, skillful in examining and judging—who are now advanced in age and have heard these things for no less than thirty years; yet these men affirm that the things which once seemed most incredible to hear, now for the first time appear very credible and clear to them; and those which then seemed most probable now seem to them to be the opposite. Looking at these things, therefore, take care lest you ever regret those things which have now escaped you unworthily and rashly. 

The greatest safeguard for this matter is not to write, but to learn by heart. For things which are written cannot be kept secret. For this reason, I have never written anything about these matters, nor is there any prescribed work of Plato, nor will there be. Those things which are now said belong to Socrates, a man who, even while he was young, was famous for virtue. Farewell, and believe us. And as for this letter, when you have read it several times, burn it immediately. 

And enough on these matters. You wonder why I do not send Polyxenus to you. But concerning Lycophron and the others who are with you, I affirm now exactly what I have for a long time: namely, that you far excel them both in natural talent and in the art of discourse; and that none of them yields to you in dispute voluntarily, as some suspect, but against their will. Yet you seem to have treated them very kindly, and to have honored them with respectable gifts. But concerning them, many such things may be said. If it happens that you can employ Philistion, use him as much as possible. And if it can be done, use the work of Speusippus, and then send him back. Speusippus also has need of you. Philistion promised me that if he were dismissed by you, he would seek Athens immediately. It would be praiseworthy to have dismissed him from the stone-quarries. My petition is light concerning his relatives, as well as concerning Hegesippus, the son of Aristo. For you wrote to me: if anyone wished to bring injury to him or to those others, and you perceived it, you would by no means permit it. Furthermore, it is right to admit the truth about Lysiclides. For he alone of those who set out from Sicily to Athens has changed nothing in his friendship toward you and me. Rather, he daily honors what was done with words as much as he can.

**Y**ou ask whether it is more correctly placed in greetings for Plato to bid Dionysius "to rejoice," or, as I have been accustomed to write to friends, "to act well." <note>original: "gaudere" (to rejoice/joy) vs "bene agere" (to do well/act well). Not a man, because pleasure very often brings loss and pain to him, producing dullness in the soul and forgetfulness, foolishness and insolence. And let these things be said by me concerning the greeting. When you have read them, you will take them as you wish. **Letters.** **633**

<margin>Cicero. Words from *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 5.</margin> <note>original: "Cicero. verba ex Tuscul. 5." The printer notes that Cicero quotes or references this specific passage of Plato in his own philosophical works.</note>

[Column 1]
...should obtain the **government**: or those who govern, by some divine chance, should truly **philosophize**. <note>This is a restatement of Plato's famous "Philosopher King" argument from *The Republic*: that societies will only find peace when rulers become philosophers or philosophers become rulers.</note> With this mind, I went to Italy and Sicily; this was my first journey to those places. When I had come there, that "blessed life" which was spoken of, full of **Italian** and **Syracusan tables**, <note>A common ancient expression for extreme luxury and gluttony. Syracusan feasts were legendary for their excess.</note> pleased me in no way: to be stuffed twice a day, and never to spend the night alone, and the other things which accompany this life. For no one of all who are under heaven, if he were nurtured in such habits from youth—even if endowed with an excellent nature and intellect—would ever emerge as **prudent**. He certainly will never care to be **temperate**. And the same reasoning will apply to the other virtues. Moreover, no city will be able to rest easy under laws if its citizens think everything should be spent on superfluous expenses; and having set aside all other things, they think they should strive only for banquets and sexual pleasures. It is necessary for such cities to change now into **tyrannies**, now into <term>the power of a few</term> <note>original: "paucorum potentiam." This is the definition of an Oligarchy.</note>, now into a <term>popular state</term> <note>original: "popularem statum." This refers to a Democracy, which Plato often viewed as unstable.</note>: and never to rest. Indeed, those who are powerful in these cities do not even wish to hear the very name of a just and equal government. 

Considering these things along with those previous ones, I set out for **Syracuse**; perhaps by some chance of fortune. It seems, however, by the work of <term>those who are above us</term> <note>original: "eorum opera qui supra nos sunt." A reference to divine providence or the gods.</note>, a beginning was then given to all things which recently happened to **Dion** of Syracuse: and I fear lest, though I am now consulting the living again, you should by no means agree with me. But as to how I say my journey then to Syracuse was the beginning of everything, listen. I was then frequently conversing with **Dion**, who was then a young man, and what things I judged would be best for men, I persuaded him by what reasons I could, and advised him to do. 

But in saying these things, I seem, secretly and beyond my intention, to have then prepared that ruin of the **tyranny** which followed. <note>Plato is reflecting on how his philosophical teachings to Dion eventually led to the political upheaval and the overthrow of the ruling family.</note> For Dion, since he was of the sharpest intellect—both for all other things and for those things which were then said by me—seized them so quickly and vehemently, more so than any of all the young men whom I have ever met. And he decided to lead the rest of his life much more excellently than many other Italians and Sicilians, pursuing **virtue** rather than pleasure and delights. Therefore, he lived hostile to those who spent their lives in tyrannical institutions; and this continued until the death of **Dionysius**. <note>Dionysius I, the "Elder," who ruled Syracuse with an iron fist.</note> 

But afterward, he noticed that the opinion which he himself had conceived through right reason existed not in himself alone, but also in certain others (though not many), in whose number he hoped **Dionysius the younger** <note>The son and successor of the previous tyrant. Dion hoped Plato could mentor the young ruler.</note> would be, the gods helping; if that happened, both he himself and the rest of the Syracusans would obtain wonderful happiness. Wherefore he judged that I ought to come to Syracuse as quickly as possible, so that I might join myself as an ally and helper to these men: holding in memory how easily my companionship had just recently drawn him into a desire for the most beautiful and best life. Which desire, if he should fulfill it in Dionysius as he had begun, he had great hope that without slaughter and blood, and without those evils which have now happened, he could establish a true way of living and a **blessed life** in that whole region. Dion, rightly considering these things, persuaded **Dionysius** to call me: and he himself also asked that, setting aside all things, I should hasten to come: before any others clinging to Dionysius, having neglected the best life...

634 **Book Thirty-six.**

We were afraid that Dionysius might perhaps punish one of us as if we were accomplices in that crime. <note>The "crime" refers to the alleged conspiracy of Dion, Plato’s friend and Dionysius's brother-in-law, to overthrow the tyrant.</note> A rumor, however, arose in Syracuse that I had been killed by Dionysius, as if I were the instigator <note>original: "autorem"</note> of all the things that had then happened. But he, sensing that we were all so affected, and fearing lest something more serious might perhaps happen from our fear, received us all very kindly. He certainly comforted me personally and told me to have good hope, and he asked me most earnestly to stay. For for him, there was nothing honorable in my flight; but there was honor in my staying. And therefore he made a great pretense of pleading with me. **But we are not ignorant that the prayers of tyrants are mixed with necessity.** <note>A famous observation on power: when a tyrant "asks" or "prays" for something, it is effectively a command backed by force.</note>

Indeed, to prevent me from devising a way to depart, he settled me in the citadel: and he willed me to inhabit those places from which thereafter no sailor would take me away—not only if he prohibited it, but unless he himself commanded and sent them. Nor would any merchant or any prefect of the maritime coast have seen me going out alone without suddenly returning me as a captive to Dionysius; especially since it was now rumored, contrary to what had been spread before, that Dionysius was once again "embracing" Plato <note>original: "complecti." Here meaning to show great favor or to hold someone in high esteem.</note> with great intensity.

And in a certain way, it was so. Nor should the truth be kept silent. He indeed "embraced" me more and more every day, and he delighted in our manners and our company. He desired to be praised by me more than by Dion, and to be considered far more of a friend. And to this end indeed he strove most mightily. But he neglected the method by which this would have best been done, if only it could have been done. For the method was this: that he should more freely apply himself to me in hearing and learning the principles of philosophy, and should come to an agreement with me. But in truth, he was too distrustful of this: fearing, as his slanderers <note>original: "calumniatores"</note> asserted, that if he became entangled in those philosophical principles, Dion would have already attained all the things he desired.

I, however, endured all things, persevering in the same opinion with which I had set out from the beginning: trying if by any means it could happen that he might come into a desire for the philosophical life. But he, striving against it, defeated me. And thus the first period of my journey to Sicily, and of my actions there, was spent in all these things. But in later times, I returned again to Sicily; to which Dionysius recalled me with all zeal. For...

...he might compare himself to his equals, and be in harmony with virtue. But above all, [our goal was] that he might show himself to be consistent and steady within himself. We were pointing out that he lacked this quality more than anything else—though we did not use open words at the time, for that would not have been safe. <note>Plato is treading carefully; directly telling a tyrant he is unstable or lacks character could be a death sentence.</note> Instead, we used a more hidden way of reasoning that carried the same meaning, teaching that only in this way can any man save both himself and those over whom he rules: by observing these principles. ### Commentary.

[[notes: This section continues the speech of Diotima from Plato's *Symposium*, as interpreted by Marsilio Ficino (the 15th-century Florentine priest and philosopher who led the Platonic Academy).]]

Love is a vehement, clever, and sagacious hunter. He is always weaving new traps, a seeker of prudence, eloquent, a philosopher throughout his whole life, a powerful enchanter and charmer (*fascinator*), a sorcerer, and a sophist. He is neither entirely immortal by nature, nor mortal. Instead, sometimes on the same day he flourishes and lives, as long as he is abundant; at other times he withers away and then comes back to life because of his father’s nature. But whatever he acquires slips away from him; therefore, Love is never a beggar, nor is he ever wealthy. Furthermore, he is placed in the middle between wisdom and ignorance. 

These are the words of Diotima. We shall explain them as briefly as we can. Although these qualities are present in all kinds of love, they appear more clearly in the three "middle" kinds, as they are more manifest to us. Being born on the birthday of Venus, Love follows Venus—that is, being born among those higher spirits we have called "Venuses," he leads the souls of men back to the heights. He is captured by the desire for the beautiful since Venus herself is most beautiful; that is, he inflames souls with the desire for the highest and divine beauty. Since he had his origin in those spirits who are closest to God, they are illuminated by the highest divine splendor and raise us toward those same rays. 

Furthermore, since the life of all living creatures and trees, as well as the fertility of the earth, consists of moisture and heat, Diotima hints that Love lacks both moisture and heat to demonstrate his "want." This is why she called him dry, lean, and squalid. For who does not know that things deserted by moisture are dry? Who would say that pallor and squalor come from anywhere other than a defect of the blood's heat? Indeed, mortals become pale and lean through long-lasting love. 

The force of nature is almost never sufficient for two tasks at once. The "intention" (*intentio*) of the lover’s mind is entirely occupied with the constant thought of the beloved; all the force of his natural constitution is focused there. Therefore, food is not perfectly digested in the stomach. Thus, the greater part is expelled as waste, and the smaller part—which is raw—is drawn to the liver. There, for the same reason, it is poorly cooked. Consequently, only a small amount of raw blood is spread through the veins; hence, all the limbs become thin and pale due to the lack and rawness of nourishment.

Furthermore, wherever the constant intention of the mind is carried, the *spiritus* (spirits)—which are the chariots or instruments of the *anima* (soul)—fly there too. The spirit is created in the heart from the most subtle part of the blood. The lover's mind is snatched away toward the image of the beloved fixed in the *phantasia* (imagination), and toward the beloved himself. The spirits are drawn to the same place. Flying there, they are continually dissolved. Therefore, a very frequent supply of blood is needed to recreate the consumed spirits. Where the most subtle and clear parts of the blood are daily exhaled in refreshing the spirits, the pure and clear blood is dissolved, leaving behind what is spotted, thick, dry, and black. 

From this, the body becomes dried out and squalid; from this, lovers turn into "melancholics." For from dry, thick, and black blood, *melancholia* (black bile) is produced. It fills the head with its vapors, dries the brain, and never ceases to disturb the soul with foul and horrific images day and night. We read that this happened to the Epicurean philosopher Lucretius because of love. Harassed first by love and then by insanity, he finally laid hands upon himself. 

These things usually happen to those who abuse love, transferring what belongs to contemplation to the lust for embraces. For we tolerate the desires of seeing more easily than the desire of both seeing and touching. When the ancient physicians observed this, they said that love was a passion close to the disease of melancholy. The physician Rasis (the 9th-century Persian doctor al-Razi) prescribed that it be cured by sexual intercourse, fasting, drunkenness, and walking. 

Not only does love make men this way, but those who are such by nature are more prone to love. These are the people in whom bile (which they call *cholera*) or black bile (*melancholia*) prevails over the other humors. Bile is hot and dry; black bile is dry and cold. The former holds the place of fire in the animal body, the latter the place of earth. Therefore, dry and parched melancholics are understood to be like the earth; squalid and pale cholerics are understood to be like fire. Cholerics, because of the impetus of their fiery humor, are carried headlong into love; melancholics love more slowly because of the sluggishness of their earthy humor. But because of the stability of their humor, once they are ensnared, they persevere for a very long time. 

It is with good reason, therefore, that Love is depicted as dry and squalid, since men who are like this usually indulge in love more than others. We believe this happens primarily because cholerics are scorched by the fire of bile, and melancholics are corroded by the harshness of black bile, as Aristoteles (Aristotle) affirmed in the seventh book of the *Ethics*. A troublesome humor always angers both, forcing them to seek some great and continuous solace against the constant annoyance of the humors. 

Delights of music and love are of this kind. For we can apply ourselves to no other pleasures as constantly as to the charms of music and voices, and the allurements of beauty. Other senses are quickly satiated. But the sight and the hearing are fed longer by "empty" sound and painting. Not only are the pleasures of these senses firmer, but they are also more akin to the human constitution. For what is more suitable to the spirits of the human body than human voices and figures? Especially those that please not only by a likeness of nature but also by the grace of beauty. 

Therefore, choleric and melancholic men seek the delights of song and form as a unique remedy and solace for their very troublesome temperament. Thus, they are more prone to the allurements of Venus. And Socrates, whom Aristoteles judged to be melancholic, was—as he himself confessed—most inclined of all toward the art of loving. I can judge the same of Sappho, who was melancholic as she herself testifies. And even our Maro (the poet Virgil), whose image indicates he was choleric, was nevertheless quite prone to loving, although he was modest.

**Barefoot.** Diotima depicted Love this way because a lover is so occupied in amorous matters that in other duties of life, both private and public, he does not walk cautiously as is proper, but is reckless, carried wherever he goes without any discerning foresight. Therefore, in his progress, he incurs frequent dangers, just as one who does not support his feet with leather [[abbrev: sassulciat: provides soles for]]; hence they are struck by frequent thorns and pebbles. 

**Humble.** The Greek word in Plato (Eros) means "on the ground" and "flying through the lowest things." For he saw that lovers oftentimes, because of the abuse of love, live without sense, and great goods perish for the sake of light cares. These people surely give themselves up so much to the beloved that they strive to pass entirely into them, and they fashion themselves into the beloved by both words and gestures. Indeed, through the very frequent imitation of boys and girls, who would not become effeminate? Who would not turn into a boy or a woman? 

**Without a home.** The home of human thought is the soul itself. The home of the soul is the spirit. The home of this spirit is the body. There are three inhabitants; there are three homes. Each of these wanders as an exile when its natural home is lost. For all thought turns not to the discipline and tranquility of its own mind, but to the service of the beloved person; and the soul deserts the ministry of its own body and strives to leap into the body of the beloved. The spirit, the chariot of the soul, flies out by exhaling in another direction while the mind hastens elsewhere. Therefore, thought leaves its home, the soul leaves, and the spirit leaves. The first exit brings madness and restlessness; the second, the weakness of death and dread; the third, trembling, fear, and sighing. Therefore, love is deprived of its own hearth, its natural seat, and its desired rest. 

**Without bedding or any cover.** For he has nowhere to rest and nothing to cover himself with. Since every thing seeks its own origin, the little spark of love—ignited in the lover’s appetite by the object of a beautiful body—strives to fly back into that same body. By this impetus, it carries both the appetite and the wanter along with it as it flies out. O cruel lot of lovers! O life more miserable than any death! Unless perhaps your soul, snatched from its own body by this violence of love, neglects the figure of the beloved and receives itself into the temple of divine splendor, where it will finally rest and be fulfilled. 

Who would deny that love wanders naked and without cover? For who hides a love that the whole gaze, fixed in songs, betrays? That interrupted speech declares? The redness and paleness of the face, frequent sighs, the tossing of limbs, perpetual complaint, untimely praises, sudden indignation, boasting, procacity, petulance, vain suspicion, and the lowliest services indicate it? Just as light accompanies the heat in the sun and fire, so external signs follow the internal fire of love. 

**He sleeps at the doors.** The doors of the soul seem to be the eyes and ears; for from here, many things are carried into the soul, and the affections and habits of the soul shine out most clearly through the eyes. Lovers linger mostly in looking at figures and hearing voices. Rarely does their mind collect itself into itself. More often it wanders through the eyes and ears. Therefore, they are said to lie at the doors. 

They are also said to **lie in the road**. For the beauty of the body ought to be a certain road through which we begin to ascend to a higher beauty. But those who prostrate themselves to foul lusts, or even dwell on the sight more than is proper, seem to remain in the road itself; they do not travel to its end. 

**Under the open sky.** Quite rightly. For being entirely occupied in one thing, they consider nothing in the conduct of their affairs. Thus, they live their lives by chance, exposed to all the dangers of fortune and all storms, just like those who live naked under the open sky. 

**Always needy because of his mother’s nature.** Surely, since the first origin of love was from want, and what is natural cannot be entirely uprooted, love is always needy, always thirsty. For as long as something is lacking to be obtained, the heat of love blazes. When it is possessed entirely on all sides, the heat ceases because the indigence has ended, rather than enduring without want.
