[[page number: 274]]

### 274 On the Banquet.

### WHAT GIFTS LOVERS HAVE
### because of love's
### father.
### CHAPTER X.

These things follow from "Want," the mother of love; but the opposite things come from "Plenty," his father. Anyone who understands the above will recognize what the opposites are. Above, Love was described as simple, careless, lowly, and unarmed; here, the opposites are introduced. For he is called clever, a sagacious hunter, a schemer, a plotter, a seeker of prudence, a philosopher, manly and bold, vehement, eloquent, a magician, and a sophist. 

The same love that makes a lover uncaring and inert in other affairs makes him astute and clever in amorous matters, so that he hunts for the favor of the beloved in marvelous ways—either entangling them with guile, or capturing them with services, or soothing them with eloquence, or charming them with song. The same fury that made him mild in service also supplies weapons: ferocity toward those indignant at the beloved, and for those fighting for him, security and unconquered strength. 

Love, as we said, takes its origin from sight. Sight is in the middle between vision and touch; hence the lover's mind is always distracted and tossed up and down in turn. Sometimes it falls into the desire for an embrace; sometimes it is won over by the modest desire for celestial beauty, and now this, now that prevails and leads. In those who are most honorably educated and strong in mental sharpness, the latter usually overcomes the former. 

Whoever prostrates themselves to the filth of the body is rightly considered dry, naked, humble, unarmed, and inert. **Dry**, because they are always hungry and never filled. **Naked**, because like reckless people subjected to all dangers, they are considered infamous as impudent and unrefined. **Humble**, because they think nothing high, nothing magnificent. **Unarmed**, because they succumb to shameful desire. **Inert**, because they are so dull that they do not know where love draws them, and they stay on the road without reaching the goal. 

Those of the opposite kind appear affected in the opposite way: for feeding on the solid goods of the mind, they are more filled and love more tranquilly; they preserve modesty, neglect the shadowy appearance of the body, and are raised higher. As if protected by armor, they flee empty lusts and subject the senses to reason. These are described by Diotima as **philosophers**, the most skillful and prudent of all, who walk most providently through the figures of bodies as if through certain footprints or scents. From these, they sagaciously investigate the sacred beauty of the mind and the divinities; and thus, by hunting prudently, they happily attain what they desire. 

Surely so great a gift of love proceeds from his father, "Plenty"; for the ray of beauty, which is both plenty and the father of love, has this power: it is reflected back to where it came from and draws the lover with it. It descends from God first; then, passing into the angel and the soul as neighboring materials, and flowing easily from the soul into a body prepared for its reception, it shines out from that body of the younger person, especially through the eyes—the brightest windows of the soul. It flies straight through the air, penetrates the eyes of the elder person, transfixes the soul, ignites the appetite, and leads the wounded soul and the ignited appetite toward its medicine and refreshment. Meanwhile, it snatches them along with it to the same place from which it had descended: step by step, first to the body of the beloved, second to the soul, third to the angel, and finally to God, the first origin of this splendor. 

This is a useful hunt, this is the happy fowling of lovers. Indeed, a certain friend of Socrates in Plato's *Protagoras* attributes this hunt to him: "Do you see, O Socrates? I think you are returning from that hunt to which the honorable nature of Alcibiades is accustomed to call you." 

Furthermore, she calls love a **Sophist** and a **Magician**. Plato in the dialogue *The Sophist* defines a sophist as an ambitious and subtle disputant who, by the craftiness of fallacies, shows us the false as true and forces those who dispute with him to contradict themselves in their speeches. Both lovers and beloveds sometimes suffer this. For lovers, blinded by the clouds of love, often accept the false for the true, while they judge their beloveds to be more beautiful, sharper, and better than they are. They contradict themselves because of the violence of love. For reason advises one thing, but lust follows another. They change their plans at the command of the beloved; they oppose others to follow their whims. Often also, the beautiful are ensnared by the cunning of lovers and become easy when they were previously stubborn. 

But why do we think love is great? Because the whole power of **magic** consists in love. The work of magic is the attraction of one thing by another out of a certain kinship of nature. All the parts of this world, like members of one animal, all hanging from one author, are joined together by the communion of one nature. Therefore, just as in us the brain, lungs, heart, liver, and other members draw something from each other and mutually help each other, and when one suffers they sympathize—so the members of this huge animal, that is, all the connected bodies of the world, mutually borrow natures and are borrowed from. From their common kinship, common love is born; from love, common attraction. This is true magic. 

Thus, from the concavity of the moon’s orb, fire is drawn upward because of the kinship of nature; from the concavity of fire, air is drawn; from the center of the world, the earth is drawn to the lowest parts; and water is snatched from its place. Hence the magnet turns iron, amber turns straw, fire turns sulfur; the sun turns many flowers and leaves toward itself; the moon turns the waters. Mars is accustomed to stir the winds, and various herbs invite various kinds of living creatures to themselves. Even in human affairs, his own pleasure draws each person. 

The works of magic, therefore, are works of nature. Art is but the servant. For where natural kinship lacks something, art supplies it through vapors, numbers, figures, and qualities at opportune times; just as in agriculture, nature produces the crops, but art prepares them. The ancients attributed this art to "daemons" because they understand the nature of the society of natural things, what fits each thing, and how the concord of things, if it is missing anywhere, may be restored. 

Some are said to have become friends with daemons either by a certain likeness of nature, like Zoroaster and Socrates, or by the worship of a beloved, like Apollonius of Tyana and Porphyry. Therefore, signs, voices, and portents are told to have happened to them while awake, or oracles and images while sleeping. Those who have become friends of daemons seem to have turned out to be magicians; just as daemons are magicians knowing the friendship of the things themselves, and all nature is called a "magician" out of mutual love. 

Moreover, every beautiful person fascinates us with tender eyes. They soothe men with the powers of eloquence and the measures of songs, as if with certain incantations, and win them over; furthermore, they appease and capture them with devotion and gifts no differently than with sorceries. Therefore, let no one doubt that love is a magician, since the whole power of magic consists in love, and the work of love is fulfilled by fascinations, incantations, and sorceries. 

He is neither entirely mortal, nor entirely immortal. Not mortal, because the two loves in us—those two daemons we spoke of—are perpetual. Not immortal, because the three "middle" ones of these change daily; they grow and decrease. Furthermore, an unquenchable inborn fervor is planted in the human appetite from the beginnings of life, which does not permit the mind to rest and always impels it to apply itself with zeal to a certain thing. 

The characters of men are diverse, and they do not live by one wish. Hence that continuous fervor of desire, which is natural love, impels some to the study of letters; others to music or figures; others to the honesty of morals or a religious life; others to honors; some to accumulating money; many to the luxury of the belly; others to other things. Indeed, it impels the same man to different things in different ages. 

Therefore, the same fervor is called both immortal and mortal. **Immortal**, because it is never extinguished and changes its matter rather than vanishing. **Mortal**, because it does not always dwell on the same thing; instead, either from a change of nature or from satiety arising from long-lasting frequenting of the same thing, it seeks new delights; and what almost failed in one thing revives in some way in another. 

It is also called immortal for this reason: that a figure once beloved is always loved. For as long as it remains the same in the same man, it is loved in him; but when it flows away from him, the same figure you loved before is no longer in him. You do not burn for this new one, because you did not burn before; but you do not stop loving that prior one. However, there is this difference: you used to see that one in another person; now you see it in yourself alone, and you always love it fixed in the same memory, and as often as it meets the eyes of the mind, so often it burns you, the lover. 

Therefore, as often as we meet that person once dear to us, so often we are moved, or the heart skips and trembles, or the liver melts, or the eyes shake, and the face takes on various colors in his presence. For his presence suggests the hidden figure in the mind to the eyes of the soul and, by blowing on it, rouses the fires sleeping under the ashes. For this reason, love is called immortal. 

But it is also held to be immortal because, although the faces remain always fixed in the breast, they do not offer themselves equally to the eyes of the mind; therefore, benevolence seems to boil and cool down in turn. Added to this is the fact that both bestial and human love can never be without indignation. Who would not be indignant at one who has stolen his very soul? For just as liberty is pleasing above all else, so slavery is burdensome. Therefore, they hate and love the beautiful at the same time: they hate them as thieves and homicides; as mirrors shining with celestial splendor, they are forced to admire and love them. 

What can you do, miserable one? Where can you turn, alas, lost one? You would not want this homicide of yours to exist, yet you would also not want to live without the blessed spectacle. You cannot be with this person who destroys you, who kills you; yet you cannot live without this person who steals you from yourself with such marvelous allurements, who claims all of you for himself. You desire to flee him who burns you with his flames; yet you also desire to cling to him, so that you who are possessed by him may also be close [[page number: 275]] to yourself. 

Miserable one, you seek yourself outside of yourself, and you cling to your captor so that you might one day redeem yourself. Surely you would not want to love, insane one, because you would not want to die; yet you would also not want *not* to love, since you judge that you must serve the image of celestial things. Therefore, by this alteration, it happens that in every moment (so to speak) love withers and revives. 

Love is also placed by Diotima as the middle between wisdom and ignorance. Furthermore, love follows beautiful things. Wisdom is the most beautiful of all things. Therefore, he appetites wisdom. He who appetites wisdom does not possess it entirely. For who would seek what is present? Yet he does not lack it entirely either. In this one thing at least he is wise: that he recognizes his own ignorance. But he who does not know he is ignorant knows neither the things themselves nor his own ignorance, and does not seek knowledge, of which he does not know he is deprived. Therefore, the love of wisdom, because it is partly deprived of wisdom and partly wise, is located between wisdom and ignorance. 

This, says Diotima, is the condition of Love. But the nature of the Beautiful itself—that is, of the supreme Beauty—is that it is delicate, perfect, and blessed. **Delicate**, insofar as it allures the appetite of all things to itself by its own sweetness; **Perfect**, insofar as it illustrates those who approach with its rays and perfects them; **Blessed**, insofar as it fills those illustrated with eternal goods.

### WHAT THE UTILITY OF LOVE IS
### from its definition.
### CHAPTER XI.

After Diotima explained the origin of love and what kind of thing it is, she now reveals where it tends and what it contributes to men. 

We all certainly desire to have good things; and not only to have them, but to have them always. But the individual goods of mortals change and fail, and all would quickly vanish unless new ones were made daily in the place of those departing. Therefore, so that good things may always endure for us in some way, we desire to recreate perishing things. Recreation happens through **generation**. Hence the instinct of generation is inborn in all. 

Since generation makes mortal things similar to divine things through continuation, it is surely a divine gift. To divine things, beautiful things are related, while ugly things are contrary; the beautiful are similar and friendly. Therefore, generation—a divine work—is perfectly and easily consummated in that which is beautiful, and the opposite happens in the opposite case. Therefore, that endeavor of generation seeks beautiful things and flees their contraries. 

What do you ask human love is? What does it contribute? It is the desire for generation in the beautiful to preserve perpetual life in mortal things; this is the love of men living on earth, this is the goal of our love. 

Indeed, in the very time when each of the animals is said to live and to be the same (as from childhood to old age), although it is called the same, it never contains the same things in itself; but it is always being made new, as Plato says, and old things depart—according to hair, flesh, bones, and blood, and the body entirely as a whole. And this happens not only in the body, but also in the soul. Morals, customs, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears are changed constantly; nothing from these remains the same and similar; prior things are abolished, new ones succeed and grow. 

And what is more marvelous, even sciences: not only do some vanish and others rise, and we are not always the same according to our sciences, but even any one of the sciences suffers almost the same. For meditation and reminiscence are, as it were, the resumption of a passing science. For forgetfulness seems to be the exit of science. But meditation, always restoring new memory in the place of the departing one, preserves science, so that it appears to be the same. 

In this way, whatever things are mutable in the soul or body are preserved: not because they are always entirely the same (for this is characteristic of divine things), but because that which decays and departs leaves something new and similar to itself. By this remedy, mortal things are made similar to immortal things. 

Therefore, in both parts of the soul—the part that looks to cognition and the part that governs the body—the love of generation is inborn to preserve life perpetually. The love that is in this part accommodated to governing the body does not immediately from the beginning impel us to take food and drink so that humors may be generated from these nutrients, by which what flows away from the body may be resumed. Through this generation, the body is nourished and grows. When the body is adult, the seed itself becomes restless and provokes the lust of procreating offspring, so that what cannot remain always in itself may remain everlasting, preserved in an offspring very similar to it. 

The love of generation attributed to the cognizing part of the soul makes the soul desire truth—its own nourishment—through which it may be nourished and grow in its own way; and if anything falls away from the soul through forgetfulness, or becomes numb because of sloth and neglect, it "regenerates" it through the study of record and meditation, and calls back to the mind what had perished through forgetfulness or had become sluggish through idleness. 

When the mind is adult, it stimulates it with the most burning desire to teach and write, so that science generated either in writings or in the minds of disciples—the teacher’s intelligence and truth—may remain eternal among men. And thus, by the benefit of love, both the body and soul of every man may seem able to survive always after death in human affairs. 

Each love follows beautiful things. Surely the one who rules and governs the body desires to nourish his own body from feasts as delicate, pleasant, and beautiful as possible, and to generate beautiful offspring with a fair woman; and the one who pertains to the soul strives to imbue it with the most adorned sciences and disciplines, and to produce a writing most similar to his own science in an ornate and beautiful style, and to generate through teaching in a most beautiful soul—I mean a soul that is sharp and best. 

We do not see the soul itself, and therefore we do not look at its beauty. But we see the body, the shadow and image of the soul; thus, suspecting from its image, we conjecture that there is a fair soul in a beautiful body. For this reason, we more willingly educate beautiful people.

### ON THE TWO LOVES,
### and that the soul is born with the aforementioned truth.
### CHAPTER XII.

We have now said enough about the definition of love; now let us declare the distinction made in Plato between the fecundity of the soul and the body concerning love. 

All men, he says, are pregnant and heavy in body, and pregnant in soul. To the body, all its parts are inserted from the beginning. Hence, in fixed cycles of time, teeth erupt, hair comes forth, the beard grows, and the seeds of procreation flow down. 

If the body is fecund and heavy with seeds, much more is the soul—more excellent than the body—most fertile, and it possesses the seeds of all its things from the beginning. Therefore, the soul was allotted the "reasons" (*rationes*) of morals, arts, and disciplines long ago, and from there it brings its offspring into the light at fixed times if it is correctly cultivated. 

That it has the innate reasons of all its things, we recognize from its appetite, investigation, invention, judgment, and comparison. Who would deny that the soul, immediately from a tender age, desires true goods, honorable things, and useful things? But no one desires unknown things. Therefore, some notions of these things are in the soul even before it desires them; through these as their forms and reasons, it judges them desirable. 

The same is proved from investigation and invention: if Socrates seeks Alcibiades in a crowd of men, surely, to find him one day, it is necessary that some figure of Alcibiades be in Socrates' mind, so that he may know which man he seeks above others, and be able to discern Alcibiades from others when found in a gathering of many. So the soul would neither track down those things it seeks, nor ever find them, unless it had some notion of them—that is, of Truth, Goodness, Honesty, Utility—through which it might seek them to find them, so that as often as it finds what it had investigated, it may recognize it and discern it from its contraries. 

Not only from appetite, investigation, and invention, but also from judgment is this proved. For whatever it judges to be its friend or enemy, it is not ignorant of what friendship or malevolence is. In what way then would we daily judge many things true or false, good or bad, as we are accustomed to, and judge rightly, unless truth and goodness were in some way pre-known to us? 

Again, how are the works of architecture, music, painting, and external arts, as well as the inventions of philosophers—even by many not versed in these arts—very often proved to be rightly judged or reproved, unless some form and reason of those things were granted to them by nature? 

Comparison also shows us the same. For whoever, comparing honey to wine, pronounces one sweeter than the other, recognizes what sweet flavor is; and he who, comparing Speusippus and Xenocrates to Plato, thinks Xenocrates more similar to Plato than Speusippus, undoubtedly knows the figure of Plato. 

In the same way, when we rightly judge one good better than another among many, and one appears better or worse than another by a greater or lesser participation in goodness, it is necessary not to be ignorant of goodness. Furthermore, since among many diverse opinions of philosophers or others, we often judge best which is more similar to the truth and more probable, it must be that we do not lack some intuition of truth, so that we are not ignorant of what things are more similar to it. 

Therefore, some in youth, some even without a teacher, and most from the very few rudiments of doctrine demonstrated by teachers, are told to have turned out most learned: which could never have happened unless, as we said, nature were helping. Socrates demonstrated this abundantly to the boys Phaedo, Theaetetus, and Meno; and he taught that boys could respond rightly in individual arts if someone questions them prudently: surely because they are endowed by nature with the reasons of all arts and disciplines.

[[page number: 276]]

### THE LIGHT OF TRUTH IN THE SOUL.
### CHAPTER XIII.

But in what way such reasons are in the soul appears ambiguous in Plato. If anyone follows those books which Plato wrote as a younger man—the *Phaedrus*, *Meno*, and *Phaedo*—he will perhaps think they are painted in the substance of the soul almost like figures on a wall. This has been touched upon often by me and by you in the previous sections, for he seems to hint at it there. 

But in the sixth book of the *Republic*, that divine man reveals the whole matter and says that the light of the mind for understanding all things is God himself, by whom all things were made. For he compares the Sun and God to each other in such a way that as the sun is to the eyes, so God is to minds. 

The sun generates eyes and provides them the power of seeing. This power would be in vain and overwhelmed by everlasting darkness unless the sun’s light were present, painted with the colors and figures of bodies: in which light the eye sees the colors and figures of bodies. Nor does the eye behold anything else but light. It seems, however, to behold various things because the light infused into it is adorned with various formulas of external bodies. Indeed, the eye perceives this light reflected in bodies, but it by no means sustains the light itself in its source. 

In the same way, God procreates the soul and grants it a mind, the power to understand. This would be empty and dark unless God’s light were present to you, in which you might look up at the reasons of all things. Whence through God’s light it understands, and it recognizes only the divine light itself. Yet it seems to recognize diverse things because it understands that light under the diverse ideas and reasons of things. 

When someone, seeing a man with his eyes, fashions an image of the man in his imagination (*phantasia*) and revolves for a long time in judging it, he raises the sharp edge of his mind to look up at the reason of man existing in the divine light. Then a spark immediately flashes in the mind, and in truth, the nature of man itself is understood; and so for all other things in the same way. 

Therefore, we understand all things through the light of God, but we cannot see that pure light and its source in this life. In this clearly consists the whole fecundity of the soul: that in its inner chambers shines that eternal light of God, most full of the reasons and ideas of all things, to which the soul turns as often as it wishes by purity of life and the greatest intention of study; having turned, it flashes with the sparks of the ideas.

### WHENCE LOVE TOWARD MALES, 
### WHENCE TOWARD FEMALES.
### CHAPTER XIV.

Thus the body of men is pregnant, as Plato wishes, and the soul is pregnant, and both are stimulated by the incitements of love toward birth. But some are more fit for the offspring of the soul than the body, either because of nature or because of education; others, and indeed most, are the opposite. The former follow celestial love, the latter vulgar love. 

The former love males by nature, and those almost adult rather than females or boys, because in them the sharpness of the mind flourishes more, which is most fit for the discipline they are going to generate, because of its more excellent beauty. The others, on the contrary, for the sake of the pleasure of venereal intercourse and the effect of corporal generation. 

Since that genital force of the soul, being void of cognition, has no discrimination of sex, it is nevertheless incited by its nature to generate as often as we judge some beautiful body to be present. It happens for the most part that those who associate with males, to settle the stimuli of the genital part, mingle with them. These are especially those in whose horoscope Venus was in a masculine sign and with Saturn, or in the bounds of Saturn, or opposite Saturn. 

But it was necessary to observe the incitements of that genital part, not to affect this vain work of loss, but the duty of bearing and procreating, and to transfer it from males to females. We believe that through a certain error of this kind, that nefarious crime arose which Plato, in his laws, detests most sharply as a kind of homicide. Surely he who snatches away a man about to be born is to be considered no less a homicide than he who takes a born man from the midst. He is bolder who cuts off a present life, but more cruel who envies the light of one about to be born and kills his sons not yet born.

### THE SOUL IS ABOVE THE BODY,
### THE ANGEL ABOVE THE SOUL, GOD ABOVE THE ANGEL.
### CHAPTER XV.

But so much for the double fertility of the soul and the double loves. Next, let us discuss by what steps Diotima raises Socrates from the lowest things to the highest: from the body to the soul, from the soul into the angel, and from the angel she leads him back to God. 

One can argue that these four levels of things must be in nature as follows:
Every body is moved by another thing; but it cannot move itself by its nature, since it can do nothing through itself. But it seems to be moved by itself because of the presence of the soul, and to live because of the soul. And indeed, when the soul is present, it moves itself in a certain way; but when absent, it is moved only by another, since it does not have this nature from itself, but the soul properly possesses the power of moving itself. 

For whatever it is present to, it imparts the power to move itself; but what it itself imparts to others by its presence, it must have much earlier and more so itself. Therefore, the soul is above bodies, as it can move itself according to its essence, and therefore it ought to be above those things that do not move themselves from themselves but by the presence of others. 

When we say the soul is moved by itself, we do not speak transitively (as Aristoteles wanted to be taken from Plato), but we utter that word absolutely, as when we assert that God stands through himself, the sun shines through itself, and fire is hot through itself. For one part of the soul does not move while another part is agitated; but it is moved entirely from itself, that is, by its nature. This means it runs by reason from one thing to another and carries out the works of nutrition, growth, and generation through intervals of time. 

That temporal discourse begins from the soul itself, because what is above it understands all things at once in one point of eternity, not at different moments. Therefore, the first motion and the first interval of time are rightly placed in the soul by Plato; from there, both motion and time pass into bodies. 

Since it is necessary that rest exist before motion (since rest is more perfect by reason), above the mobile motion of the soul, some stable intelligence ought to be found, which is intelligence according to its whole self and always intelligence in act. For the soul does not understand by its whole self, nor always, but from a certain part of itself and sometimes; nor does it have a certain power of understanding, but an ambiguous one. 

Therefore, so that what is more perfect may precede what is less perfect, above the mind of the soul which is mobile, partial, intermittent, and doubtful, there must be placed the **Angel**: a mind entirely stable, continuous, and most certain. Just as the soul, moved by itself, precedes the body agitated by another, so the stable mind, stable by itself, precedes the soul agitated by itself. 

And just as the body has from the soul that it moves itself (and thus not all bodies, but animate ones seem to move of their own accord), so the soul has from the mind that it always understands. For if the intellect were in the soul by its own nature, it would also belong to the souls of beasts, just as the power of being agitated. Therefore, the intellect does not belong to the soul through itself and primarily; wherefore it is necessary that what is through itself and primarily composed of mind should precede it. Such is the Angel, a more excellent mind. 

But surely the One itself, that principle of things and supreme good which Plato calls the "One itself" in the *Parmenides*, necessarily towers over the mind of the angel. Indeed, above all the multitude of a composite thing, the One itself must be simple by nature; for all things are from one, and all composition is forged from simple things. 

That mind, although it is immobile, is not the pure simple One itself. For it understands itself; where these three seem different among themselves: that which understands, that which is understood, and the understanding itself. It has besides the power of knowing, which is entirely formless before the act of cognition; it is formed by knowing, and by understanding it desires and takes the light of truth, which it seems to have lacked before it understood. It also has in itself the multitude of all ideas. See how great and how varied is the multitude and composition in the angel! 

Therefore, we are forced to place the pure and simple One before it. But we can place nothing before God—the One itself—because the true One is void of all multitude and all composition. If it had anything above it, it would surely be made by that; wherefore, depending on it, it would degenerate in this very thing from it, as every effect is accustomed to from its cause. And therefore it would no longer be the One and simple, but at least composed of two: namely, from the cause and its own gift or its own effect. 

Therefore the One itself, as Plato wishes and Dionysius the Areopagite (the Christian mystic) confirms, towers over all things; and the most excellent name of God—the One itself—is judged by both. 

Reason also shows us its sublimity by this: that the most eminent cause ought to be the most ample gift, and by the excellence of its power extend itself to all things. The gift of the One propagates itself through the universe. For not only is the mind one, and every soul one, and every body one, but even formless matter itself and the privation of things is called one in some way. For we say one silence. One darkness. One death. 

Yet the gifts of the mind and the soul do not extend that far. For the mind grants an artificial species and order; the soul provides life and motion; but the formless and first matter of the world and the privation of things is void of species and life. Therefore, the One itself precedes the mind and soul, since its gift is more widely diffused. 

By the same reason, the mind seems to exceed the soul because life—the gift of the soul—is not given to all bodies. Yet the mind grants species and order to all these.

[[page number: 277]]

### WHAT THE COMPARISON IS BETWEEN
### God, the angel, the soul, the body.
### CHAPTER XVI.

Therefore, we ascend from the body into the soul, from this into the angel, and from this into God. God is above eternity. The Angel is entirely in eternity; surely both his operation and essence remain stable. For rest is proper to eternity. The soul is partly in eternity, partly in time. For its substance always endures the same without any change of increase or decrease; but its operation, as we showed a little before, runs through intervals of time. The body is entirely subject to time. For both its substance is changed, and its whole operation requires a space of time. 

Therefore, the One itself exists above rest. The Angel is in rest. The soul is in rest and motion equally. The body is placed in motion alone. 

Again, the One remains above number, motion, and place. The Angel is placed in number above motion and place. The soul is in the number of motions, but above place. The body is subject to number, motion, and place. Indeed, the One itself has neither any number nor composition of parts; nor is it changed in any way from what it is; nor is it enclosed in any place. The Angel has a number of parts or forms, but is free from motion and place. The soul has a multitude of parts and affections and is changed by the progress of reasoning and the variety of perturbations, but is exempt from the limits of place. The body, however, is obnoxious to all these.

### WHAT THE COMPARISON IS
### between the beauties of God, the
### angel, the soul, and the body.
### CHAPTER XVII.

The comparison between these four and their forms is the same. Surely the form of the body consists in the composition of many parts, is constrained by place, and slips away in time. The species of the soul suffers the vicissitudes of time and contains a multitude of parts, but is absolute from the boundaries of place. The species of the Angel has number only and exists immune from the other two. But that of God suffers none of these. 

You see the form of the body. Do you wish to behold the species of the soul also? Take away from the corporal form the weight of nature itself and the limits of places, leave the rest; now you have the species of the soul. Do you want that of the angel too? Take away, I pray, not only the spaces of place but also the progress of time; retain the manifold composition, you will immediately obtain it. 

Do you also desire to see the beauty of God? Take away furthermore that manifold composition of forms; leave the entirely simple form, you will have immediately attained the species of God. 

But what will finally remain for me after these are subtracted? Will you see anything other than light, the leader of beauty? Furthermore, the beauty of all bodies is that light of the sun which you see, infected by those three: by the multitude of forms (for you behold it depicted with many figures and colors), by the space of place, and by temporal change. 

Take away its seat in matter so that it retains the other two besides place: the beauty of the soul is exactly of this kind. Take away from here, if you like, the change of time, leave the rest: a most clear light remains without place and without motion, but engraved with the reasons of all things. That is the angel, that is the beauty of the angel. 

Finally, take away that number of diverse ideas; leave one simple and pure light: like that light which remains in the globe of the sun itself and is not dispersed through the air; now you comprehend in some way the beauty of God—which at least precedes the other forms by as much as that light of the sun, pure in itself, one, and inviolate, surpasses the splendor of the sun divided, partitioned, infected, and obscured through the cloudy air. 

Therefore, the source of all beauty is God. Therefore, the source of all love is God. 

Furthermore, the light of the sun in water is a certain shadow compared to the clearer light of the same in the air. The splendor in the air is similarly a shadow compared to its glow in fire. The glow in fire is a shadow compared to the light of the sun shining in the sun itself. The comparison between those four beauties of the body, soul, angel, and God is the same. 

God is never so deceived that he loves the shadow of his species in the angel, but neglects his own true beauty. Nor is the angel so captured by the species of the soul, which is its own shadow, that, detained by its shadow, it deserts its own figure. 

Our soul, however—which is most greatly to be lamented, for this is the origin of our whole unhappiness—our soul alone is so soothed by the allurements of the corporal form that it postpones its own species and, forgetting itself, follows the form of the body, which is but a light-shadow. From here comes that most cruel fate of Narcissus in Orpheus. From here comes the miserable calamity of men. 

Narcissus indeed, a youth—that is, the soul of a reckless and inexperienced man—does not behold his own face. He by no means notices his own substance and virtue. But he pursues its shadow in the water and tries to embrace it: that is, he admires beauty in a fragile body and like flowing water, which is the shadow of the soul itself. He deserts his own figure and never attains the shadow, since the soul neglects itself by following the body and is not filled by the use of the body. For it does not truly desire the body itself, but it affects the higher species, allured by the corporal form which is the image of its own species, just as Narcissus affects it. Since it does not notice this, while it desires one thing and follows another, it cannot fulfill its desire. 

Therefore, dissolved into tears, it is consumed; that is, the soul, placed outside of itself and fallen into the body, is tortured by pernicious perturbations and, infected by the filth of the body, it as it were dies—since it now seems to be a body rather than a soul. 

So that Socrates might avoid this death, Diotima led him back from the body to the soul, from this into the angel, and from that to God.

### HOW THE SOUL IS RAISED FROM
### the beauty of the body to the beauty of God.
### CHAPTER XVIII.

Come, dearest guests, imagine Diotima addressing Socrates thus: "No body, O Socrates, is beautiful on all sides. For either it is beautiful in this part and deformed in that; or beautiful today and not at all other times; or judged beautiful by one and ugly by another. Therefore, the beauty of the body, defiled by the contagion of ugliness, cannot be pure, true, and primary beauty. 

Furthermore, no one ever suspects beauty itself to be ugly, just as no one suspects wisdom to be foolish. But we think the disposition of bodies is sometimes beautiful and sometimes ugly; and at the same time, different people feel differently about it. Therefore, primary and true beauty is not in bodies. 

Add that many bodies are called by one name of beauty. Therefore, there is one common nature of beauty in many bodies, through which they are similarly denominated as beautiful. But consider that one nature of this kind—just as it is in another, that is, in matter—so it depends on another. For what cannot be sustained in itself can much less hang from itself. 

Will it depend on matter? Not at all. For nothing deformed and imperfect can adorn and perfect itself. But what is one ought to arise from one. Therefore, the one beauty of many bodies depends on some one incorporeal artificer. The one artificer of all is God, who through angels and souls makes all the matter of the world beautiful daily. Therefore, one must believe that the true reason of beauty is found in God and his ministers rather than in the body of the world. 

To that, you will ascend again by these steps, as I think, O Socrates. If nature had given you eyes like a lynx, my Socrates, so that you might penetrate anything occurring to your sight, that most beautiful body of your Alcibiades on the outside would appear most foul to you. How much is it that you love, friend? Only the surface, indeed, color snatches you—indeed, a certain reflection of lights and a very light shadow. Either a vain imagination deceives you, so that you love what you dream rather than what you see. 

But lest I seem entirely to oppose you, let it be that this Alcibiades is beautiful. But in what part is he beautiful? Surely in all members except for his snub nose and eyebrows higher than is proper. These, however, are beautiful in Phaedrus. But the thickness of the legs in him does not please. These are becoming in Charmides, unless he showed a slender neck. So if you observe individual men, you will praise none in every part. 

Whatever is right everywhere, you will collect; you will fashion a complete figure in yourself from the observation of all, so that the absolute beauty of the human race, which is found scattered in many bodies, may be collected in your soul by the thought of one image. You will value the figure of any man little, O Socrates, if you compare it to that one. But you possess that one not so much by the benefit of bodies as by the benefit of your soul. Therefore, love that one which your soul has fashioned and the soul itself, its artificer, rather than that exterior maimed and dispersed beauty. 

But what do I command you to love in the soul? The beauty of the soul. Light is the beauty of bodies; light is also the beauty of the soul; the light of the soul is truth—which alone your friend Plato seems to ask from God in his prayers: 'Grant me, O God, that my soul may be made beautiful, and that those things which pertain to the body may not impede the beauty of the soul; let me think only the wise man rich.' 

In these, Plato declares that the beauty of the soul consists in truth and wisdom, and that it is granted to men by God. Truth is one, and the same is granted to us by God: in its various affections, it receives the names of various virtues. Insofar as it demonstrates divine things, it is called **Wisdom**, which Plato asked from God above others. Insofar as it demonstrates natural things, it is **Science**; as human things, **Prudence**. Insofar as it makes men equal, **Justice**; as it makes them unconquered, **Fortitude**; as it makes them tranquil, it is called **Temperance**. 

From these, two kinds of virtues are numbered: the **Moral virtues**, I mean, and the **Intellectual virtues** which are more excellent than those. The intellectual virtues are Wisdom, Science, and Prudence. The moral virtues are Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance. The moral virtues are more known because of their operations and civil duties; the intellectual virtues are more hidden because of their secret truth. Furthermore, he who is educated in honest morals, being purer than others, is easily raised to the intellectual virtues. 

Therefore, I command you first to consider the beauty of the soul which consists in morals, so that you may understand that there is one reason of all morals, through which similarity and honesty are established."

### Commentary.

[[margin: Eulogy of Socrates]]

[[notes: The text here resumes a new section regarding the character of Socrates and his "true" way of loving.]]

...his frequent correction of others' crimes had rendered many and great men—as truth is accustomed to—hostile to him: especially Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon, citizens most powerful in the republic; and the orators Thrasymachus, Polus, and Callias. Furthermore, he had the most sharp persecutor in the comic poet Aristophanes. 

But neither those citizens in the accusation by which they dragged Socrates to judgment inscribed dishonest loves; nor did his enemies the orators object any such thing to Socrates; nor did Aristophanes the comic poet, although he collected many other absurd slanders against Socrates in the *Dionysia*. Do you think that if he had defiled himself with such a foul stain—nay, unless he had been most remote from the suspicion of this crime—he would have escaped the poisonous tongues of such detractors? 

Did you not notice that, best of men, in the previous sections? That while Plato fashions Love itself, he paints the whole image of Socrates and describes the figure of that deity from the person of Socrates? As if true love and Socrates are most similar, and therefore he, above others, is the true and legitimate lover. 

Come now, recall the picture of Love in your mind. You will see Socrates figured in it. Place the person of Socrates before your eyes. You will see him thin, dry, and squalid: a man who was, as they say, naturally melancholic and hairy. Lean from hunger. Filthy from neglect. Naked besides, that is, covered with a simple and old little cloak. Walking without shoes. Phaedrus in Plato shows that Socrates was always accustomed to walk this way. 

Humble and flying through the lowest things. The gaze of Socrates was always fixed on the ground, as Phaedo says. Furthermore, he frequented lowly places: for he was found either in the shop of Simon the cobbler or in the workshops of sculptors. He used rustic and unpolished words, which Callicles objected to him in the *Gorgias*. He was so mild besides that, provoked by many injuries, often even struck, he is told not to have been moved in his soul. 

Without a home. When Socrates was asked where he was from, he said: "A citizen of the world." For there is the fatherland where there is good. But he had neither his own hearth, nor a soft bed, nor delicate food, nor beautiful furniture. Sleeping at the doors in the road under the open sky. These signify the open breast and heart lying open to all in our Socrates. Furthermore, he was delighted by sight and hearing, which are the doors of the soul; and also that he walked secure and intrepid, and lay anywhere if necessary, wrapped in his cloak. 

Always needy. Who does not know that Socrates was the son of a sculptor and a midwife? And up to old age, he sought his living by his own hand in carving stones, and never had enough to nourish himself and his sons. He confessed the indigence of his mind everywhere, questioning everyone, preaching that he knew nothing. 

Manly: for he was of a constant mind and unconquered opinion, who even spurned King Archelaus of Macedon, and Scopas of Crannon, and Eurilochus of Larissa with a high soul: when he did not accept the money sent by them, nor did he himself want to go to them. 

Bold and fierce. How great his fortitude was in bellicose matters, Alcibiades explains most copiously in the *Banquet*: to whom Socrates, when he had won at Potidaea, is said to have spontaneously conceded the victory. 

Vehement: he was indeed, as Zopyrus the physiognomist had rightly judged, most excitable; and often during speaking, because of the vehemence of his speech, he was accustomed to toss his fingers and pull his hair. 

Eloquent. For him, reasons in almost every part seemed equal while he discussed. Although he used unpolished words, as Alcibiades says in the *Banquet*, he moved the souls of the audience more than Themistocles and Pericles and all other orators. 

A plotter against the beautiful and the good. Alcibiades says that Socrates was always plotting against him; surely, captured by the love of those who appeared endowed with an honest nature, Socrates captured them with his reasons for the study of philosophy. 

A clever and sagacious Hunter. It was said enough in the previous sections that Socrates was accustomed to hunt for the divine species from the form of the body, and Plato testifies to this in the *Protagoras*. 

A Schemer in many ways: as the dialogues of Plato indicate, he refuted the sophists, exhorted the youths, and educated modest men. 

A seeker of Prudence. For he was of such great prudence and so sharp in foreseeing that whoever dared anything against his counsel was ruined, as is told in the *Theages* by Plato. 

Philosophizing throughout his whole life. In that defense of his before the judges, he declared to the judges that if they acquitted him of death on the condition that he never philosophize afterward, he would prefer to die rather than stop philosophizing. 

An enchanter, charmer, sorcerer, and sophist. For Alcibiades says he was more soothed by Socratic words than by the melody of Marsyas and Olympus, the excellent musicians. That a "daemon" was familiar to him, both his accusers and his friends testify. The comic Aristophanes also called Socrates a sophist, and so did his accusers. Surely because he had an equal faculty for exhorting and dehorting. 

Middle between wisdom and ignorance. "While all men are ignorant," says Socrates, "I differ from others only in this: that I do not ignore my ignorance, while others are entirely ignorant." Thus he was in the middle between wisdom and ignorance: because although he did not know the things themselves, he recognized his own ignorance. 

For these reasons, Alcibiades judged Socrates to be most similar to Love and therefore the truest lover after Love itself was to be praised, so that in his praise we might understand that all who love similarly are praised. What the praises of Socrates are, you have heard here, and they are most clearly open in the words of Plato from the mouth of Alcibiades: also in what way Socrates loved, he who remembers the doctrine of Diotima can know. Socrates loved her exactly as Diotima taught above.

### ON BESTIAL LOVE,
### which is a kind of insanity.
### CHAPTER III.

But someone perhaps asks: What does that love of Socrates contribute to the human race? Why is it to be celebrated with such great praises? What is its contrary? 

I shall say, starting from a bit deeper. Our Plato in the *Phaedrus* defines fury as an alienation of the mind. He gives two kinds of alienation. He thinks one arises from human diseases, the other from God. He calls the former **insanity**, the latter **divine fury**. By the disease of insanity, a man is cast down below the human species, and from a man is turned into a brute in some way. 

There are two kinds of insanity. One is born from a vice of the brain, the other of the heart. The brain is often occupied by burnt bile, often by burnt blood, sometimes by too much black bile; hence men are sometimes rendered demented. Those who are vexed by burnt bile are most vehemently angry even when provoked by no one; they shout loudly, rush upon those in their way, and strike themselves and others. Those who labor with burnt blood break out into excessive laughter, boast beyond all custom, promise marvelous things about themselves, delight in song, and exult in dancing. Those who are pressed by black bile mourn perpetually; they fashion dreams for themselves which they either dread as present or fear as future. 

And these three kinds of insanity indeed happen by a defect of the brain. For when those humors are retained in the heart, they produce anguish and anxiety, not dementia; but then they produce amentia when they have overwhelmed the head; therefore they are said to happen by a vice of the brain. 

But we think that insanity is properly made by a disease of the heart, by which those who love "desperately" (*perdite*) are afflicted. To these, the most sacred name of love is falsely attributed. But lest perhaps we seem to know too much against many, for the sake of arrangement let us also use the name for them.

### VULGAR LOVE
### is a certain fascination.
### CHAPTER IV.

[[notes: This section explains the Renaissance medical/physiological theory of how "love at first sight" actually works through the eyes.]]

But you, apply the attention of your ears and mind to what is to be said. Blood in youth is subtle, clear, hot, and sweet. For as age proceeds, with the more subtle parts dissolved, it becomes thicker; therefore it also becomes darker. Surely what is thin and rare is pure and translucent; the opposite is the opposite. 

Why hot and sweet? Because life and the beginning of living—namely, generation itself—consists in heat and moisture, and the seed, the first generation of living things, is hot and humid. Nature flourishes in such things in childhood and youth. In the following ages, it is necessarily changed little by little into the contrary qualities of dryness and coldness. Therefore, blood in a youth is subtle, clear, hot, and humid: because it is subtle, it is clear; because it is recent, it is hot and humid; because it is hot and humid, it therefore seems to be sweet. For sweetness is made in the mixture of the hot and the humid. 

To what end is this? Namely, that you may understand that the **spirits** in this age are subtle and clear, hot and sweet. For since they are generated by the heat of the heart from the purer blood, they are always such in us as the humor of the blood is. 

Just as the vapor of the spirits of this kind is created from the blood, so it also emits rays similar to itself through the eyes as if through glass windows. And just as the sun, the heart of the world, sends its light and its virtues through light to the lower things by its circuit; so the heart of our body, by its perpetual motion, agitating the blood closest to it, diffuses from it spirits into the whole body, and through them sparks of lights through individual members, but most through the eyes. 

For the spirit, since it is the lightest, flies out especially to the highest parts of the body; and its light flashes more abundantly through the eyes since they are themselves transparent and the most bright of all parts. That there is some light, however small, in the eyes and brain, many animals that see at night can be testimony, whose eyes sparkle in the darkness. And also if anyone, in a certain way, presses and twists the corner of the eye with a finger, he seems to behold a certain lucid circle within himself. 

It is told that even the divine Augustus had eyes so clear and bright that when he looked at anyone more sharply, he forced him to lower his face as if before the glow of the sun. Tiberius is also told to have had very large eyes, and which (what is marvelous) saw even at night and in the darkness: but only for a short time and when they first opened from sleep; then they grew dim again. 

But that the ray emitted from the eyes draws a spiritual vapor with it, and from the vapor, blood, we perceive from this: that bleary and red eyes force the eyes of a person looking at them nearby to labor with a similar disease by the emission of their own ray. Here it appears both that the ray is extended as far as the object, and that along with the ray, the vapor of the corrupted blood emanates, by whose contagion the eye of the beholder is infected. 

Aristoteles writes that women, when the menstrual blood flows, often foul a mirror with blood-colored drops by their gaze. This, I think, happens because the spirit, which is the vapor of the blood, seems to be a certain most thin blood, so much so that it escapes the sight of the eyes; but being made thicker on the surface of a mirror, it is clearly perceived. This, if it falls upon some matter like cloth or wood, is not seen because it does not remain on the surface of that thing, but penetrates it. If it falls on dense but rough matter, like stones and the like, it is dissipated and broken by the inequality of that body. 

But a mirror, because of its hardness, stops the spirit on its surface; because of its equality and smoothness, it preserves it unbroken; because of its brightness, it helps and increases the ray of the spirit itself; because of its coldness, it forces the very rare mist of it into little drops. For almost the same reason, as often as with open mouths we breathe onto glass, we sprinkle its face with a certain most thin dew of saliva; for the breath flying from the saliva, compressed in that matter, falls back into saliva. 

Therefore, what wonder if the eye, opened and intent upon someone, hurls the stings of its rays into the eyes of the one standing by? And also along with those stings, which are the vehicles of the spirits, it directs that bloody vapor which we call the spirit? Hence a virulent sting pierces the eyes; and since it is sent from the heart of the striker, it seeks the heart of the person struck as its own proper region. It wounds the heart; and on its harder back, it grows blunt and returns into blood. 

This foreign blood, in some way alien to the viscera of the wounded man, infects his own blood; the infected blood becomes sick. From here follows a double fascination. The gaze of a foul old man, and of a woman suffering menstruation, fascinates a boy. The gaze of a youth fascinates an elder. 

But since the humor of the elder is cold and very slow, it hardly touches the back of the heart in the boy; and being unfit for passage, unless the heart is most soft because of infancy, it moves it very little. This is therefore a light fascination; but that one is most grave, through which the junior transfixes the heart of the senior. This is that "best love" about which the Platonic Apuleius complains: "The whole cause and origin of this present pain, and even the only medicine and health, is you yourself to me. For those eyes of yours, having slipped through my eyes to my innermost heart, stir up a most sharp fire in my marrows. Therefore, have mercy on one perishing because of you." 

Place before your eyes, I pray, Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian and that orator Lysias captured by his love. Lysias gapes at the face of Phaedrus; Phaedrus fixes the sparks of his eyes in the eyes of Lysias; and along with the sparks, he also transmits the spirit. The ray of Phaedrus is easily coupled to the ray of Lysias; spirit is also easily joined to spirit. A vapor of this kind, generated from the heart of Phaedrus, seeks the heart of Lysias: by the bluntness of which it becomes more compact and falls back into the prior blood of Phaedrus; so that the blood of Phaedrus, which is marvelous, is now in the heart of Lysias. 

Hence both break out into a shout immediately: Lysias to Phaedrus: "My heart, Phaedrus, most dear viscera!" Phaedrus to Lysias: "O my spirit, O my blood, Lysias!" Phaedrus follows Lysias because his heart asks for its humor. Lysias tracks Phaedrus because the bloody humor demands its own vessel, it requires its own seat. But Lysias tracks Phaedrus more ardently. For the heart lives more easily without a small part of its humor than the humor itself lives without its own heart. The stream needs the source more than the source needs the stream. Therefore, just as iron, having accepted the quality of the magnet, is drawn to this stone indeed, but does not attract the stone; so Lysias follows Phaedrus more than Phaedrus follows Lysias.

# Letters. 637

to argue: as if he had heard everything I had ever thought of. For he is not slow to learn, and he is vehemently inflamed by a desire for honor. Perhaps he was pleased by what was being said, and he was clearly embarrassed that he had heard nothing from me when I had first come to him. Therefore, partly a desire to hear more clearly had seized him, and partly a desire for glory spurred him on. Why he did not listen during that first journey of mine, I have explained in the preceding pages. When I had returned home as a guest, and I had refused his second invitation—as I mentioned—Dionysius then seemed to me to be truly burning with care for his own reputation. He feared that men would interpret my refusal as a total contempt for him, as if I had found his nature, character, and way of life lacking through my own experience. It is only right that I confess the truth: I must endure it with a calm mind if anyone, hearing what happened, despises my philosophy but thinks the tyrant <note>referring to Dionysius II of Syracuse</note> possesses a great mind.

For Dionysius sent a trireme <note>a swift ancient warship with three banks of oars</note> to me a third time, so that I might sail easily. He also sent Archedemus, whom he believed I valued most among all the associates of Archytas in Sicily, along with other noblemen from Sicily. All of them affirmed to me with the same words that Dionysius was marvelously devoted to philosophy. He himself also sent a very large letter, as he knew how I felt toward Dion, and that it was Dion’s great desire that I should travel to Syracuse. The letter was composed with all these things in mind, beginning in this way: **Dionysius to Plato.** Having offered the lawful and customary greetings <note>original: "Legitima & consueta ratione," likely referring to the standard Greek greeting "Chairein" (Rejoice/Greetings)</note>, he says: "Nothing should be more important to you than coming to Sicily at our request. First, regarding Dion, things will be handled exactly as you wish. I believe you will wish for moderate terms, and I will grant them. But if you do not come, you will obtain nothing of what you desire for Dion, neither in other matters nor in those things concerning his person which are now most desired." Thus he wrote. The rest was lengthy and not particularly relevant to recount.

Letters also arrived from Archytas and other Italians and Tarentines <note>Greek colonists in southern Italy</note>, praising Dionysius’s zeal for wisdom. Furthermore, they added this: that if I did not go, the friendship I had forged between them and Dionysius—which was of no small importance for political affairs—would be entirely subjected to slander. Since I was being summoned in this way at that time—with some from Sicily and Italy pulling me, and others at Athens almost pushing me with their prayers—reason dictated to me that it was not right to betray Dion and my Tarentine hosts and friends. It also occurred to me that it would not be surprising if a talented young man, who previously refused to hear discourses on great matters, might change his mind and be set on fire with a passion for the best life. It was necessary to test his disposition to see which way it inclined, rather than betraying him or making myself the cause of such a great reproach against him, if his affairs truly were as reported. 

Protected by the defense of these reasons, I began the journey, fearing many things and divining that many things would not be very happy—as indeed they turned out to be. Finally, I set out for the third time, "under the Savior" <note>a Greek expression for a lucky or third attempt, often dedicated to Zeus the Savior</note>. For I truly achieved safety: I was once again fortunately saved. For this, after God, I owe thanks to Dionysius; because while many desired to kill me, he resisted them and showed some degree of respect for my situation.

When I had arrived, I judged it to be of primary importance to examine this very thing: whether Dionysius was truly inflamed by a love of philosophy as if by fire, or whether the rumor that had reached Athens was empty. There is a certain way of conducting this test; it is not inelegant, but truly suitable for tyrants, especially those who have already heard many lectures. This is exactly what I perceived had happened to Dionysius as soon as I arrived. One must show such people how great a thing philosophy is, how much zeal it requires, and through what great labors it is acquired. 

Whoever hears this, if they truly love wisdom and are naturally related to it and worthy of possessing it—being, as it were, divine—thinks that a wonderful path has been shown to them, and that they must march along it with every effort, and that they cannot live while doing otherwise. Therefore, such a person encourages themselves and their guide on this journey, and does not stop until they have either reached the end of all things or at least acquired the faculty by which they can lead themselves to the goal without a guide. Considering things by these and similar reasons, throughout their entire life, in whatever they do, they are always intent on philosophy above all else. They use a daily diet that best allows them to preserve their intellect, memory, and judgment, remaining sober and always hating the opposite way of life.

But those who are not truly lovers of wisdom, but are merely colored by opinions from the outside—like those who are tanned and colored by the sun—when they hear how many things must be learned, how much labor is required, and what temperance of daily life is necessary for the study of philosophy, they judge it to be a hard and impossible thing for them, and they cannot be induced to apply themselves to the work. Most of them persuade themselves that they have already heard everything sufficiently and need no further study. 

This method of testing is clear and not at all deceptive against those who cannot follow through because of their own softness; thus they can never cast the blame on the teacher, but they themselves are refuted as being incapable of doing what befits philosophy. This was the method of examination I used with Dionysius then. I did not run through everything, nor did Dionysius require it. For there were many and very great things in which he strove to be thought sufficiently learned because of what he had heard from others. 

I hear, however, that he later wrote about the things he heard then, as if composing his own textbook; yet I hear he understood none of these things truly. I know nothing for certain about this. I know some others have written about these same things, but whoever they are, they do not even know themselves. I will say this much about all who have written or will write, claiming to know the things I seriously study—whether they heard them from me or others, or discovered them themselves—in my judgment, they can perceive nothing of the matter. For there is no writing of mine on these subjects, nor will there ever be. For it can in no way be expressed in words like other disciplines; but from long association with the subject itself, and a life joined to it, a light suddenly shines out in the soul—as if from a flickering fire—and thereafter nourishes itself. 

And yet I know this much: that things written or said by me are said in the best way; but if they were badly written, it would cause me no small distress. If I thought these things should be written down or spoken to the common crowd, what finer thing could happen in our lives than to bring such a useful thing to humanity and bring nature into the light for all? But I do not believe the effort of publishing these things is useful for men, except for a very few who are able to find it for themselves through small hints.

<meta>This page continues Plato's Seventh Letter. After explaining his third journey to Syracuse to meet the tyrant Dionysius II, Plato now pivots to a profound philosophical digression. He explains why Dionysius’s attempt to write a book on the "highest truths" of philosophy was a mistake, by outlining his famous theory on the limits of language and the nature of knowledge.</meta>

[[original page: 638]]

# Book Thirty-Six.

...having been demonstrated, they might be shrewd in finding them for themselves. Others, however, he had filled partly with wicked contempt, and partly with high and vain hope, as if they had already learned something magnificent. Therefore, I thought to speak at greater length about them. For perhaps if these things are said, what I am saying will appear somewhat more clearly. For there is a certain true reasoning that stands against those who dare to write anything at all <note>original: "nihil omnino audet scribere" — here Plato critiques the act of writing down the most sacred philosophical truths, which he believes cannot be captured in text.</note> about such matters; it is a reasoning often spoken by me elsewhere, and now, it seems, needing to be said again. For every existing thing, there are three means through which knowledge must necessarily be gained. The fourth is knowledge itself. The fifth, however, must be placed as that which is knowable—that is, what can be truly known and truly exists. The first of these is the **name**; the second is the **definition**; the third is the **image**; and the fourth is **knowledge**. Take any single thing you wish to learn about, as was just mentioned, and think of all things in the same way.

Something is called a **"Circle,"** which is the name we were just pronouncing. Next follows its **definition**, composed of names and verbs. For "that which is everywhere equidistant from its extremities to its center" <note>This is the classic Euclidean definition of a circle.</note> is the definition of that which we designate by the names "round," "circumference," and "circle." The third is the **image**: for a circle may be painted or erased, turned on a lathe or destroyed. None of these things happen to the "Circle itself" <note>The "Circle itself" refers to the Platonic Form or Ideal—the perfect, abstract concept of a circle that exists independently of any physical drawing.</note> which all these other things relate to, for it exists as something else entirely. The fourth is **knowledge**, **intellect**, and **true opinion** regarding these things. This whole category must be placed as one: it exists neither in sounds nor in the shapes of bodies, but in the mind and intelligence. Therefore, it is clear that this is something other than the nature of the Circle itself, and different again from the three things mentioned before. Among these, **intellect** <note>original: "intellectus"</note> stands closest to the "Fifth" in kinship and likeness, while the others are more remote.

The same can be said of straight and curved figures, and of color; of the good, the beautiful, and the just. It applies to every body, whether handmade or natural, whether fire or water, and all such things; similarly of every animal, and the character of souls, and of all actions and passions. For unless someone somehow grasps those four, he will never perfectly participate in the knowledge of the "Fifth." Furthermore, those four attempt to show "what sort" <note>quality</note> a thing is no less than "what" <note>essence</note> it is, because of the **weakness of language** <note>term: <term>weakness of language</term> (original: "rationum debilitatem") — Plato's belief that words are inherently unstable and cannot fully capture the true essence of reality.</note>.

Therefore, no one of sound mind will ever dare to commit the things he has understood to the same medium, especially an unchangeable one <note>i.e., written text</note>, as those four things represent. This is something clearly suffered by things designated by shapes. But this point we are making must be considered again. Certainly, any circle among those painted or made on a lathe by human hands is plainly contrary to that "Fifth" thing. For it participates in "straightness" everywhere <note>Plato means that any physical circle, if magnified or examined closely, is made of imperfections or straight segments, unlike the perfect Ideal.</note>. But the Circle itself, we affirm, has neither more nor less of anything; that is, it has nothing at all of a contrary nature. Furthermore, we say that none of these names have any stability. For nothing prevents the things we now call "round" from being called "straight," and the "straight" being called "round"; the names would have no less stability if they were swapped for their opposites. The same reasoning applies to the definition: since it is composed of names and verbs, it possesses no firm stability at all.

It can be proved in many ways that none of these four are certain or firm. The greatest point of all is what I said a little while ago: that since there are two things—**essence** and **quality**—whenever the soul seeks to know "what" a thing is rather than "what sort" it is, the soul is filled with ambiguity and obscurity. This happens unless each of the four has been thoroughly discussed by the soul through reason, affection, and finally the senses, passing through all that is said and shown. In matters where we are not accustomed to seeking the truth due to poor education, we think ourselves satisfied if we touch upon the presented "images." Are we not then a laughingstock to each other when we are questioned by those who are able to tear apart and refute those four things?

Whenever necessity compels someone to show the "Fifth," anyone capable of overturning and retracting the argument wins the day. He makes the person who is explaining—whether in speech, writing, or debate—appear to many listeners as if he understands nothing of what he attempts to say or write. In such cases, it is often ignored that it is not the mind of the writer or speaker being refuted, but rather the nature of those four elements, which are inherently flawed. Only through a process of "rubbing" these things together—moving up and down through the names, definitions, and visions—does knowledge finally shine forth from within. I mean knowledge of that which is naturally well-disposed in the soul toward that which is also naturally well-disposed.

But if someone is poorly disposed by nature—as is the natural state of the soul in many people toward learning and morals—not even Lynceus <note>A mythological hero famous for his keen sight, said to be able to see through trees and stones.</note> could make such a soul see. To put it briefly: neither quickness of mind nor memory will ever make someone see if they are not kin to the matter at hand. For the principle does not take root in alien habits. Therefore, those who are not naturally inclined toward justice and other beautiful things—even if they are clever and have good memories for other subjects—and those who are indeed kin but are dull and have weak memories, will never reach the highest truth of virtue or vice. For it is necessary to learn these together: the false and the true of the whole essence, through total practice and a long period of time, as I said from the beginning.

After the names, definitions, sights, and senses of these things have been rubbed against one another and worn down through "friendly refutations," and discussed through questioning and answering without envy, finally **prudence** and **intelligence** flash out regarding each thing, striving for the very summit of human capacity. For this reason, a serious and studious man writing for people about things truly worthy of study would be far from subjecting himself and his works to envy and ambiguity. One can understand this from a single point: whenever you see someone's writings—whether it be a lawmaker's laws or any other works—believe that these were not his most serious or most studious efforts, if the writer is himself truly serious. Those truest thoughts lie in the most beautiful region of his own being. If, however, he truly committed these "serious" matters to writing, then it was not the gods, but men who "robbed him of his wits." <note>A quote from Homer's Iliad, suggesting the person has gone mad or lost their reason.</note>

Whoever follows this discourse and digression will clearly understand that if Dionysius wrote anything about the highest and first principles of nature—or if anyone else, whether lesser or greater, did so—in my opinion, he had heard or learned nothing sound regarding what he wrote. Otherwise, he would have venerated these things just as I do, and would never have dared to subject them to absurdity and indecency by publishing them recklessly. Nor did he write them as a "memory aid." For there is no fear of forgetting these things once they have been grasped by the mind, as the whole matter is captured in the briefest of terms. Perhaps, however, he did it out of a base ambition: either claiming these ideas as his own, or seeking glory by pretending to participate in a discipline of which he was unworthy. Truly, from one...

He describes the breakdown of his relationship with the tyrant Dionysius II and the subsequent betrayal regarding the property of his friend Dion.</meta>
