# Letters. 639

...at least in that assembly it happened to Dionysius, it might perhaps be conceded. But "Jupiter knows," as the Theban says. <note>original: "sed id nouerit Iupiter, (vt inquit Thebanus)" — an ancient Greek idiom used to express that only God knows the truth of a matter, or to suggest a sense of resignation.</note> I certainly ran through these matters with him once, in the manner I described, and only once; but never again after that. After this, however, one must consider—just as we must take care to find the cause of what happened to us regarding those events—why it was that we did not discuss them a second or third time, or even more often. Did Dionysius, having heard them only once, think he knew them sufficiently and understood them well enough (whether he discovered them himself or learned them from others before)? Or did he think the things being said were frivolous? Or perhaps a third thing happened: namely, that he judged the material to be beyond his own strength or too great for him, and in truth saw that he was not at all fit to live under the diligence of wisdom and virtue. For if he is said to have thought them frivolous, many witnesses will certainly fight against our cause on the other side—witnesses who have far greater authority in judging such matters than Dionysius. But if he found or learned them, and they seemed worthy to be applied with a liberal mind to his education, who would not find it strange that Dionysius, being so affected, would so easily despise the leader and author of these things?

How he despised them, I will now say. Certainly, not long after this time, he now completely forbade the agents of Dion's estate to touch it, though he had previously permitted Dion to possess it freely and receive the fruits from it. He also stopped the money from being sent to him in the Peloponnese <note>The southern peninsula of Greece, where Dion was living in exile.</note> as had been the custom—acting as if he had entirely forgotten that letter he had written to me. For he asserted that those things did not belong to Dion, but to Dion's son; since the boy was his nephew by his sister, he claimed the boy was under his own legal guardianship. These things, then, were done up to that time. When I considered these events, I clearly perceived how Dionysius was disposed toward philosophy, and I was deeply troubled, whether I wished to be or not. It was already summer by then, and ships were frequently sailing. It seemed to me that I should complain not so much about Dionysius as about myself, and about those who had impelled me to come a third time into the strait of Scylla and to re-measure the perilous Charybdis. <note>Plato uses these two famous sea monsters from the *Odyssey* as a metaphor for the dangerous political situation in Syracuse.</note>

I was therefore compelled to tell Dionysius that I could not possibly remain with him while Dion was being so ignominiously despised. But he tried to console me and begged me to stay, thinking it would not be honorable for him if I myself should go as the messenger of these actions so soon. When he could not persuade me that I must stay, he said he himself would prepare those who would carry me away and determine how they would do it. I, however, had decided to cross in the transport ships, thinking that all things must be endured if he forbade me to leave—especially since I, clearly doing no injury to Dionysius, was being injured by him. But when he realized that I was in no way willing to stay, he devised the following schemes to hinder my sailing. The next day, he held a gracious speech with me, suited for persuasion.

"Let the matters of Dion and his property," he said, "insofar as they provide a cause for our discord, be removed from between us. For your sake, I will do these things for Dion. I decree that Dion, receiving his own property, shall live in the Peloponnese, not as an exile, but as one who is permitted to travel here whenever it seems right to him, to me, and to you, our common friends—provided he does me no injury. Of this matter, you and your associates, as well as Dion’s friends living here, shall be my guarantors. Dion himself must also sufficiently confirm to you that he will observe this. All the money he receives shall be deposited in the Peloponnese and in Athens with whomever you see fit. Dion may receive the income from this money, but he may not take the principal itself without your consent. For I do not trust that if he receives the money, he will keep faith with me, as it will be no small amount. I have greater faith in you and yours. Consider, therefore, if these things please you; stay here for a year for the sake of these terms, and once it has passed, you shall depart with this money. I know Dion will be very grateful to you when you have accomplished these things for him."

Although I replied that I would consult on this matter, I took time until the next day to respond. And agreeing on this, we then departed. Afterward, I consulted with myself, being indeed very uncertain. However, the first reason occurred to me as a guide for my counsel: "Come now, even if Dionysius intends to keep none of these promises, if I leave, he could plausibly write to Dion through himself and his friends the things he now tells me—that he offered them voluntarily, but I refused and utterly neglected Dion's affairs." Furthermore, I added this: "If Dionysius, being unwilling to let me go, does not give me a ship or provisions, and indeed easily signals to everyone that I wish to depart against his will, who would dare to carry me away in a ship from the very house of Dionysius?" I was living, to add to the inconvenience, in the very gardens that were around the house. From there, not even a doorkeeper would have permitted me to go out unless Dionysius ordered it. But if I stay for a year, I will have something to signal to Dion, and I can make known the situation I am in and what I am doing. And if Dionysius keeps even some of what he promises, this work and endurance of mine will not seem entirely ridiculous. For the estate of Dion would be valued at no fewer than one hundred talents, <term>Talent: A massive unit of currency. 100 talents would be a staggering sum, equivalent to millions of dollars today.</term> if one wished to estimate it correctly. But if things turn out as they are likely to turn out, I do not know where I shall turn. Nevertheless, perhaps it is necessary for me to endure Dionysius's machinations for another year and refute them with the facts themselves as much as I can.

When I had so consulted with myself, I reported to Dionysius the very next day that it seemed I must stay. But I added: he should not think I could do everything with Dion as if I were his master, and therefore it would be worthwhile for he himself to write to Dion alongside me, explaining these plans of ours and asking whether these terms satisfied him or not, and whether he required anything else besides them. "And that," I said, "must be written as soon as possible." In the meantime, no new action should be attempted regarding Dion's affairs. These things were said between us. We agreed on these points, nearly as I am now telling them.

After this, however, when the ships had already left and I therefore had no further opportunity for sailing, Dionysius—as if remembering something overlooked—said: "Half of Dion’s goods ought by right to remain with his son, and the other half should be sent to Dion. I will therefore see to it that this half is sold. When it is sold, I will hand over half of the money to you to be carried to Dion; the other part will be reserved by us for the son, for so the law itself requires."

Struck by these words of his, I thought it ridiculous to speak further on the matter. I said, however, that we were waiting for a response from Dion and would report these very things to him again. But later, Dionysius quite boldly sold the entire estate of Dion at whatever price he wanted, and in whatever way and to whomever he pleased. He made absolutely no mention of the matter to me. And I, likewise, spoke nothing further of Dion's business thereafter, since I judged that I would accomplish nothing more. To this extent, and in this manner, I provided help to both philosophy and my friends. After these things, Dionysius and I lived in such a way that I was always looking outward, like some bird—

# Book Thirty-Six.

...desiring to fly away from there somehow. He, however, was constantly devising ways to restrain me, conceding nothing regarding Dion's affairs. In all other matters, however, we claimed to be friends throughout all of Sicily. At that time, Dionysius attempted to reduce the pay of the veteran soldiers, contrary to his father's custom. Enraged, the soldiers gathered together and threatened that they would not tolerate it. Consequently, he closed the gates of the citadel itself and tried to coerce them. But they suddenly advanced to the walls, raising a certain barbarian and warlike cry. Terrified by this fear, Dionysius conceded everything they were used to—and even more—as they flocked together. However, there was a rumor that Heraclides was the cause of the entire tumult. Heraclides, sensing this, secretly took flight. When Dionysius sought to capture him and could not find him, he summoned Theodotes to him in the gardens. I happened to be walking in the gardens myself at the time. As for the rest of what was discussed between them, I neither know nor did I hear it while they were talking; but I both know and remember what Theodotes said to Dionysius while I was present.

"O Plato," he said, "I am persuading Dionysius here that if I can bring Heraclides here to answer the charges brought against him, and if he then does not wish to remain in Sicily, Dionysius should at least allow him to take his wife and son and depart for the Peloponnesus. He would live there, plotting nothing against Dionysius, and receiving the income from the honors <note>original: "honorum... fructus," likely referring to the revenues from his estates or properties.</note> he possesses here. Therefore, trusting in this, I have already called for Heraclides, and I will call him again. Whether he comes here from the first summons or the second, I was establishing and asking of Dionysius that no harm befall Heraclides either outside the city or within it; but if it seems best, he should only be sent beyond the borders until Dionysius sees fit otherwise. Do you," he asked, "concede these things, Dionysius?" 

"I concede them," he replied, "nor shall he suffer any other harm even if he should appear in your own house." 

On the following day, at twilight, Eurybius and Theodotes flew to me in a state of wonderful terror. Immediately Theodotes said, "O Plato, you were present yesterday when Dionysius agreed with me and you on the conditions regarding Heraclides." 

"I was present," I said. 

"But now," he said, "the guards are running about to seize Heraclides, and there is a danger that he is somewhere nearby. Follow us, therefore, with all haste to Dionysius." 

So we went; and having entered his presence, they stood in silence, weeping. But I said, "These men, Dionysius, are afraid that you might act against what was agreed yesterday regarding Heraclides. For it seems to me that he has turned aside somewhere nearby and is clearly present." 

Dionysius, hearing this, flared up in anger, and his face changed into various colors, such as anger is accustomed to bring. Theodotes, falling at his feet and taking his hand, begged him with many tears not to do such a thing. Then I took up the conversation to console him, saying, "Be of good cheer, Theodotes. For Dionysius does not dare to do otherwise than he promised yesterday." 

But Dionysius, looking at me with an excessively tyrannical expression, said, "I promised you nothing, whether great or small." 

"By the gods," I said, "you certainly did promise not to do these very things which this man is now begging you not to do." Having said these things, I went out. 

After this, Dionysius continued trying to capture Heraclides. Theodotes, however, sent messengers to signify this to him, warning him to take flight. Dionysius had indeed sent a certain Tisias with guards, ordering them to pursue Heraclides everywhere. But he, as it is said, anticipated them and, by avoiding the guards by a small space of a day, retreated within the borders of the Carthaginians. <note>The Carthaginians controlled the western part of Sicily; fleeing there meant escaping Dionysius's immediate jurisdiction.</note>

Now indeed, from the enmities arisen against me, it seems probable that Dionysius had finally secured the opportunity he had long sought through treachery—namely, that no money should be sent to Dion. First, he dismissed me from the citadel, using the excuse that the women were to perform ten days of sacred rites in the gardens where I was living. Therefore, he ordered me to stay outside the citadel with Archedemus during those days. Meanwhile, Theodotes called me to him and complained much about Dionysius regarding what had been done then. When Dionysius heard that I had gone to Theodotes, finding again this opportunity for hatred against me similar to the previous one, he sent someone to me to inquire whether I had indeed been summoned and stayed with Theodotes. I freely confessed that I had been there. 

Then he said, "Dionysius has ordered me to tell you that you are not doing right: for you always value the friends of Dion and Dionysius <note>original: "Dionem Dionisiūque amicos," possibly a scribal error or referring to the political faction of Dion and those like him.</note> more than himself." 

These things were said. Nor did he ever call me into his house again after that, treating me as a manifest friend of Theodotes and Heraclides, and as his own enemy. He was incensed because Dion's affairs had now completely perished. I lived then outside the citadel among the mercenary soldiers. Certain others, and some servants who were Athenians by birth, came to me and indicated that slanders against me had been spread among the soldiers. Furthermore, they said some had threatened to kill me if they found me anywhere. 

I therefore devised an escape of this kind: I sent word to Tarentum, to Archytas <note>Archytas was a famous Pythagorean philosopher, mathematician, and statesman of Tarentum, a friend to Plato.</note> and other friends, indicating the danger in which I was placed. They, devising a pretext for an embassy in the name of their country, sent Lamiscus, one of their number, together with a ship of thirty oars. When he came to Dionysius, he asked that he permit me to depart safely, entirely according to my own will. He assented and sent me away, providing provisions. I did not ask for Dion's money, nor did anyone give it. 

After this, when I had arrived in the Peloponnesus and found Dion there watching the Olympic Games, I narrated what had been done. He, calling Jupiter to witness, immediately declared to me and my relatives and friends that he would exact punishment from Dionysius—both because he had deceived me, his guest (for so he both said and felt), and because he had expelled him quite unjustly. Hearing this, I urged him to call together other friends for this purpose, if it seemed right. But as for me, I said that since he and others had by their efforts—and almost by violence—pushed me into an intimacy with Dionysius, I was bound by the communion of living, food, and sacred rites, and I felt I ought to be a sort of mediator, fair to both sides. I added that although many had long slandered me to Dionysius as if I were plotting with you against him and his tyranny, he did not actually kill me, but held me in some respect. To this I added that my age was unfit for warlike matters, and that I could be a middle-man between them if ever there was a need for a conciliator who could repair their friendship if they wished. "But as long as you strive with hatreds," I said, "you will call upon other helpers." I said this because I loathed the error and the fortune that had been adverse to me in Sicily. Since they did not obey my reasoning, they themselves provided the cause for all the evils that followed. Truly, if Dionysius had restored Dion's property, or rather if he had been entirely reconciled, nothing adverse would have happened, as far as human conditions go. For I could easily have restrained Dion by my will, counsel, and authority. On the contrary—

# Letters. 641

...on the contrary, now making an assault upon one another, they have filled everything with calamities. Dion <note>Dion was Plato's student and the brother-in-law of the tyrant Dionysius II; he successfully overthrew the tyrant but was himself murdered by former allies.</note> certainly held the same will that I would say I, and others who are moderate, ought to hold: namely, that power—whether one's own, or that of friends, or of the city—should be used to perform just deeds. This does not happen if someone, especially in matters of great importance, seeks to fill himself, his family, and his country with benefits through treachery and cruel conspiracies. Such a man, being poor and unable to restrain himself, but rather succumbing to pleasures due to a narrowness of spirit, would then judge wealthy men as enemies, slaughter them, and seize their money. Meanwhile, he might tell his associates and family that he, being needy in these matters, should not be blamed. In the same way, if someone similarly benefits his city and is honored by it, but then distributes the property of the few to the many through his own decrees; or if someone presiding over a great city that rules many smaller ones unjustly assigns the money of those smaller cities to his own. For in this way, neither Dion nor anyone else ever proceeds of his own will toward a destructive power that would be perpetual for himself and his descendants. A prudent man, however, approaches the establishment of a Republic <term>Republic: original Latin "Rempublicam," referring to the state or organized political community</term> and the framing of the most just and best laws, and does so without civil slaughter and expulsions.

While Dion was doing exactly this—choosing to suffer impious injuries rather than inflict them, though taking care not to suffer them himself—he nevertheless fell, just as he had reached the height of overcoming his enemies. It should not seem strange to anyone what happened to Dion. For a pious, temperate, and prudent man is never entirely deceived by the impious in such matters. But it is also not surprising if the same thing happens that might happen to a good pilot, from whom a coming storm is not entirely hidden, but the unusual and therefore unforeseen magnitude of the storms can remain hidden, and by being hidden, sink the ship. In this way, fate seems to have deceived Dion somewhat. For it was not hidden from him that his enemies were evil, but how deep the ignorance, iniquity, and voracity within them was, did remain hidden. Being deceived in this matter, he fell, subjecting Sicily to incredible grief. 

Therefore, my advice to you following these narrated events has been stated thus far. As for the reasons why I myself returned to Sicily as if compelled, I thought it necessary to show them, lest my return seem absurd or undertaken without reason to anyone. Therefore, if what I have now said seems probable to anyone, and if the reasons for why it happened seem sufficient, we shall consider that enough has been said.

# PLATO TO THE KINSMEN AND FRIENDS OF DION. LETTER VIII.

BY WHAT way of living matters might most successfully prosper, I will truly attempt to narrate to you to the best of my ability. I hope, however, to consult not only for your interests—though for yours most of all—but also for everyone who is in Syracuse; thirdly, even for your enemies and foes; and beyond that, for anyone among them who has polluted himself with impious crime. For these crimes are incurable, and no one could ever expiate them. Consider, then, what I say at present. Your entire plan and study concerning all of Sicily, now that the tyranny has been dissolved, turns on these things: Some certainly strive to revive the tyranny again; others to utterly extinguish every memory of tyranny. In such matters, a "right" plan usually seems to many to be one where things are arranged so that enemies are afflicted with the greatest possible evils, while friends are brought the most benefits. Yet it is by no means easy for those who inflict much damage on others not to suffer much in turn from others. There is no need to search far for examples of this, since what recently happened in Sicily can be a sufficient example for us. For everything seems to have happened in this way while some sought to inflict evil, and others sought to repel it and take revenge. In narrating these things, you can be suitable teachers of others everywhere, so that there is almost no difficulty in perceiving them. But what things are useful for everyone—both enemies and friends—or at least what would hinder these people the least, these very things are neither easy to see, nor easy to achieve according to one's wish once they are seen. This consultation and inquiry, therefore, seems very much like a prayer. And so, let this be for us entirely like a prayer and a certain entreaty. For in all things, both in speaking and thinking, the beginning must always be taken from the gods. A prayer of this kind, once completed, will signify to us a reasoning that is profitable to you and your enemies alike.

From the time when war was first waged in Sicily, one family has continuously dominated, which your ancestors placed in charge of public affairs when they were in the greatest danger, being pressed by the Carthaginians. <note>The Carthaginians were a North African power and the primary rivals of the Greeks in Sicily.</note> The situation had reached an extreme crisis, lest Sicily, which was cultivated by the Greeks, be overturned and devastated by the Barbarians. At that time, they elected Dionysius <note>Dionysius I (the Elder), who rose to power during the Carthaginian invasion of 406 BCE.</note> as a young man vigorous in war to preside over the necessary military matters; but they wanted Hipparinus, <note>Dion's father and a prominent Syracusan statesman.</note> as the elder, to moderate affairs with counsel. Granting these men absolute authority for the safety of all Sicily, they called them "tyrants," as it is said. Furthermore, whether one considers a certain divine fortune, or a god, or the virtue of those to whom the matter was committed, or both together with the citizens of that time, to have been the cause of that safety—let it be as each person thinks. Certainly, safety was obtained for them in this way at that time. Therefore, since they had conducted themselves thus, it was just that thanks be returned by those who had been saved. If, however, the tyranny itself later committed any evil by abusing the gift of the state, it has the judges of its crime, from whom it may pay the penalty. 

But what penalties can necessarily and rightly be applied to them for what was done? If you could easily repel their force without great danger and labor, or if they thought they could easily recover their domination, we certainly could not advise you on the things we are about to say. But now, both sides ought to consider and remember how many times each has already come near to a almost certain hope of obtaining what you desired, thinking only a little was lacking to achieve everything according to your will. Yet that very "little" has everywhere been the cause of huge and numerous evils, and it has not yet reached an end; rather, in a certain continued succession, an old evil appears and a new beginning arises at the finish line. This kind of cycle and vicissitude of things seems likely to destroy both the tyrannical and the popular factions; and as far as can be feared by likely reasoning, all of Sicily seems destined to fall into the oblivion of the Greek tongue, <note>Plato fears the Greek language and culture will be wiped out by non-Greek invaders.</note> transferred to the power and domination of the Phoenicians and the Opicians. <note>The "Opicians" or Oscans were ancient peoples of Italy, often seen as "barbarians" by the Greeks.</note> Therefore, all Greeks ought to apply a remedy against these things with all foresight. If anyone, therefore, brings forward a better and truer plan than what will be said by me, he will deservedly be named a "Lover of the Greeks." What my opinion is, in a certain way, I will now attempt to state quite freely for the common

# Book Thirty-Six.

...relying on reason and law to explain. I, therefore, assuming the persona of an arbiter for myself—as I have long been accustomed to do—will counsel both the one exercising and the one enduring tyranny in common. And first of all to every tyrant: I advise that he flee this title and the thing itself, and transfer it into a kingship, if it can be done. That it can indeed be done, Lycurgus, a good and wise man, demonstrated in practice. For he, when he saw that his own kin in Argos and among the Messenians had already transitioned from kingship into tyranny, and that consequently both these peoples were destroying themselves as well as their respective cities, feared for both his country and his kin. He applied a remedy by creating the senate and the office of the Ephors <term>Ephors: powerful Spartan magistrates intended to balance the king's power and ensure the law was followed</term> for the safety of the kingdom. On account of this, it has been preserved for so many centuries with glory; for indeed, law—full of authority—was made queen of men, and not men the tyrants of the laws.

To this very end, my reasoning now exhorts all men, persuading those who affect a tyranny to decline and flee, with a certain untiring zeal, that kind of "happiness" belonging to famished and foolish men. Instead, they should transfer themselves as much as they are able to a royal form of government and obey royal laws, for they will eventually receive the greatest honors from men and from willing laws. 

However, for those who prefer liberty above all ways of living, but flee the yoke of slavery as an evil, I warn them to beware lest, through an insatiable greed for untimely liberty, they fall into the greater disease of their ancestors. This is exactly what those ancestors suffered because, being unwilling to obey anyone, they abused their love of liberty immoderately. For those who governed in Sicily before Dionysius and Hipparinus <note>Hipparinus was the father of Dionysius I; his name was also given to Dion's son and a son of Dionysius I.</note> seemed to themselves to live happily, dissolved in lusts and commanding their own leaders. Furthermore, they drove out and deposed the ten leaders who preceded Dionysius, judging no one according to the law, so that they might be subject to no man who judged justly, nor be dominated by the law, but might be entirely free in every individual matter. It was for this very cause that tyrannies arose for them. 

For both slavery and liberty, if they exceed measure, are bad; if they observe measure, both are good. Moderate slavery is that which is shown to God; immoderate is that shown to men. For temperate men, God is the law; for the intemperate, pleasure is the law. 

Since these things are so by nature, what I counsel and command to the friends of Dion, let it be promulgated to all Syracusans, according to the common opinion of Dion and myself. Indeed, I shall set before you what he, while still breathing, spoke. What reasoning, someone might ask, does Dion bring to us concerning our present affairs? Receive this now as the first of all points. In the beginning, let the laws be such that they do not turn minds toward the acquisition of wealth and money, nor toward lusts; but since there are three things—the soul, the body, and money—let them place the virtue of the soul first. In the second place, let the virtue of the body serve the virtue of the soul. And in the third and final step, place the value of money, as a servant to the soul and the body. Whatever law accomplishes this is right, truly bringing blessedness to those who use it. To call the wealthy "blessed" is the speech of a mad and unhappy person, suited to women and children, and making those who believe it into such people. But that I now exhort you toward true goods, you will understand by the work itself, if you will only taste what I have said concerning the laws; for such examination seems to be the truest in all things.

Since these types of laws have been received, and while Sicily is placed in a moment of crisis—where you neither sufficiently overcome nor, on the other hand, are greatly overcome—it will perhaps be just and useful for all of you to strike a middle path, both for you who are fleeing the bitterness of domination and for others who desire to obtain domination. Their ancestors once—and this must be emphasized most of all—saved the Greeks from the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbaris," referring here to the Carthaginians who frequently threatened Greek Sicily.</note>, so that today it is possible to consult about a Republic <term>Republic: original Latin "Rempublicā," referring to the structured political community or state</term>. Otherwise, if things had been lost then, it would not be permitted to speak of these things now, nor would any hope remain. 

Now, therefore, let some have liberty along with royal power; for others, let there be power subject to a kingdom, with laws dominating not only the other citizens but even the kings themselves, if they should act against the laws. In all these things, with a mind free from deceit and healthy, create kings with the help of the gods. First, create my son <note>This refers to Dion’s son, whom the persona of Dion is here "speaking" of.</note> for a double grace: for my sake and for his grandfather’s. For the latter liberated the fatherland from the Barbarians in a time of storm, and I have now twice liberated it from tyrants. You yourselves are my witnesses of these things. Secondly, create as king the one who has the same name as my father, I mean the son of Dionysius <note>This refers to Hipparinus, the son of Dionysius I and brother of Dionysius II.</note>. And do this being mindful of his present service in the fatherland and his pious character, who, though born of a tyrant father, voluntarily attempts to liberate the fatherland, choosing eternal glory for himself and his kin over a very brief and unjust tyranny. Finally, it is necessary to invite the son of Dionysius, Dionysius himself <note>Dionysius II, the exiled tyrant.</note>, to the Syracusan kingship, if the city is willing and if he is willing, though he is now the leader of an army of enemies. If, I say, he wishes to live content with the form of royal dignity, fearing as is natural the turns of fortune, and pitying the fatherland and the sacred things and tombs of his ancestors, let him not destroy everything utterly in strife, gratifying the Barbarians through the fatherland's misfortune. 

These three kings you shall have; whether you add or take away anything, you shall establish it by common consent in such a pact as was spoken before, and hear it now again. If the family of Dionysius and Hipparinus wish to put an end to these calamities which now press upon Sicily for her safety, obtaining honors for themselves and the whole family not only for the present but for the future—on this condition, as was said before, call them to the kingdom. Choose ambassadors whom they themselves wish for the sake of harmony with public authority, whether from your own citizens, or from foreigners, or from both, as many as they shall allow. Let these, by common opinion, establish laws and constitute the Republic in such a way that it is fitting for kings to be masters of sacred rites and of such other things as are proper to be granted to those whose benefits to the fatherland are evident. 

Furthermore, let the guardians of the laws themselves <note>original: "custodes ipsi legun," likely referring to the *nomophylakes*</note>, thirty-five in number, together with the people and the senate, have the judgment of war and peace. Let there be distinct courts for different matters. Let the authority over death and exile rest with the thirty-five men; and besides them, with certain other judges elected from those who have most recently performed their magistracies, so that one is chosen from each magistracy who appears best and most just. These, in the following year, shall pass sentence concerning death, imprisonment, and exile. But it shall not be permitted for a king to be present at these trials, seeing as he is a priest, and it would be a sin for him to be contaminated in the passing of a sentence of death, prison, or exile. 

These things I was thinking of doing while I lived, and even now I think they should be done. And then, when I had overcome my enemies together with you, I would have established them as I had decreed, had not foreign forces and furies stood in the way. Therefore, if things had proceeded according to my wish, I would have filled the rest of Sicily with colonists. I would have expelled the Barbarians from those places they now occupy, except for those who fought for common liberty against the tyranny. I would have restored the former colonists of the Greek places to their ancient and ancestral seats. Therefore, I counsel everyone in the present to deliberate and act upon these same things by common counsel, and to exhort everyone to do these things; because if any dissent, they should be considered enemies by common opinion. Nor are these things such that they cannot be done. For those things which exist in the souls of two...

I speak, however, of two souls: specifically Hipparinus <note>The son of Dionysius I and brother of the younger Dionysius</note>, the son of Dionysius, and moreover my own son. For I believe if these two agree, the other Syracusans and all who care for their fatherland will also agree. But offering honors with prayers to all the gods, and to others besides to whom it is proper to vow alongside the gods: furthermore, urging and inviting friends and enemies alike and kindly, do not cease until you most perfectly fulfill those things spoken by us, which are like divine dreams appearing to those who are awake, clearly visible and fortunate.

# PLATO TO ARCHYTAS OF TARENTUM, TO DO WELL, LETTER IX.
<note>The greeting "to do well" or "to fare well" was a standard Platonic opening, contrasting with the more common "greetings."</note>

Archippus and Philomedes have come to us, bringing the letter you gave them, and reporting what was necessary concerning your affairs. They completed the public business of the city without difficulty, for it was not particularly laborious. But they reported that you find it very troublesome that you are unable to be freed from the public occupations of the city. Indeed, it is manifest to almost everyone that the most pleasant kind of life is to spend time in one's own pursuits, especially if one chooses to do the kind of things you do. But you ought also to consider this: that none of us is born for himself alone, but our country claims a part of our birth, our parents a part, and our friends a part. <margin>Cicero cites this in *On Duties*, Book 1, and *On Ends*, Book 1.</margin> Many things, moreover, happen to us according to the diversity of the times, by which our life is occupied. Therefore, when the fatherland itself calls you to govern the republic, it would perhaps be absurd not to obey—especially since it would simultaneously happen that an entrance is left for wicked men, who approach public affairs with no regard for what is best. Enough regarding these things. We have a care for Echecrates at present, and will have in the future: both for your sake, and for his father Phryniomis, and for the sake of the young man himself.

# PLATO TO ARISTODORUS, TO DO WELL. LETTER X.

I hear that you are, and have been for some time, a close friend of Dion, and that through all this time you have especially practiced the wisdom of character regarding philosophy. For I judge that steadfastness, faith, and sincerity are true philosophy. As for other sciences and skills which incline toward other things, if someone calls them "ornaments," he will, I believe, name them correctly. But fare well now, and persevere in these present habits.

# PLATO TO LAODAMAS, TO DO WELL. LETTER XI.

I wrote to you previously as well, that it matters much for all the things you mention that you yourself come to Athens. But since you say you cannot come, the second best thing would be if either I or Socrates <note>Not the famous Socrates, who was long dead by this time, but a younger associate of the Academy known as "Socrates the Younger"</note> could go there, as you signaled in your letter. However, Socrates is at this time hindered by the disease of strangury <note>A painful condition involving restricted urination</note>. For me, traveling there would be a disgrace if the things for which you call me were not at all accomplished. Indeed, I have very little hope that they can be accomplished. If someone were to attempt to report all the reasons why I am so distrustful, a lengthy letter would be needed. Furthermore, because of my age, I am not physically well enough to complete the journey and undergo the dangers of sea and land that such a trip usually presents, especially at this time when all things are full of danger for travelers. Nevertheless, I can give counsel to you and the founders of cities, which—as Hesiod says <note>Referring to the poet Hesiod's *Works and Days*</note>—is a deceptive thing to think of as easy, but difficult to understand. For if they think a city can ever be well-constituted without the placement of some laws, unless there is someone presiding over the city with authority, a daily moderator of everyone's life so that it is temperate and strong among both slaves and free men, they do not think correctly. Accordingly, if there are already men among you worthy of this power, it could be done. But if there is need of someone for instruction, there is, I think, neither one who can teach nor one who can be taught among you; the only thing left is to pray to the gods. For almost all cities that existed before this time were constituted in this way from the beginning, and later well-cultivated by the opportunity of great events, both in war and peace, when in such times a famous and upright man attained great power. First, however, it is necessary to care for these things with the utmost readiness; yet consider them as I say: do not attack them rashly as if they could be done lightly, but think of what can be conveniently accomplished. Fare well and be happy.

# PLATO TO ARCHYTAS OF TARENTUM, TO DO WELL. LETTER XII.

It is marvelous with what great pleasure we received the commentaries sent by you, and we were delighted by the genius of their author. Indeed, the man himself seemed to us worthy of those ancient ancestors of his. They say there were ten thousand men who were the most excellent of all the Trojans who withdrew under Laomedon <note>A mythological king of Troy</note>, as the story goes. As for the commentaries which you requested from me by letter, they are not yet finished. Nevertheless, such as they are, I have sent them to you. Regarding their custody, we both feel the same way. Therefore, no exhortation seems necessary.

# LETTER XIII.

Let this be the beginning of the letter to you and simultaneously the sign that this letter is mine. When you once received the young men of Locri at a banquet, and you were reclining far from me, you rose and came to me, and kindly and humanely said something witty, as it seemed both to me and to him who sat next to me. He was one of those polished men then present; "Truly, Dionysius," he said, "you are greatly aided by Plato in the pursuit of wisdom." To which you replied, "In many other things as well. For since I ordered him to be summoned, suddenly for that very reason that I had summoned him, I perceived a benefit." Therefore, this must be preserved, so that this mutual utility may perpetually increase more and more between us. Now, therefore, study this very thing; I send to you from Pythagoras, concerning divisions <note>likely referring to mathematical or musical divisions</note>, and furthermore a man whose services you and Archytas (if he comes to you) might use, just as it then seemed to us. His name is Helicon: his homeland is Cyzicus, a disciple of Eudoxus <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus, a famous mathematician and astronomer</note>, in all whose doctrine he was elegantly instructed; and he has had dealings with one of Socrates' disciples and with Polyxenus, the companion of Bryson: and what is furthermore rare, he is kind and affable, nor does he seem malicious; rather, he would be judged light and candid. I speak, however, cautiously and timidly, for I am expressing an opinion about a man, not an animal that cannot be lost, but something that can easily be changed and corrected, except in certain cases, and those very few. # Book Thirty-Six.

I was hesitant and suspicious when speaking with him, and I asked about his fellow citizens, but no one reported anything bad about him. You should also consider this carefully and exercise caution. Whenever you have leisure, learn from him with the greatest care, and from others who have studied philosophy. If you are not teaching someone yourself, continue to learn during your spare time so that you may become better and more illustrious; do not cease to be helped by me. But enough on these matters for now.

As for what you requested in your letter—that I send you an image of **Apollo**—I have done so. Leptines <note>A trusted associate of both Plato and Dionysius</note> has undertaken to bring it to you. It was made by a learned and excellent craftsman whose name is Leocharis <note>A famous Athenian sculptor of the 4th century BCE, often associated with the Apollo Belvedere</note>. There was another work at his studio, truly remarkable as it seemed to me. Therefore, I bought it to give as a gift to your wife, because she took care of me in both health and sickness in a manner worthy of both of us. You shall give it to her, unless you decide otherwise.

I am also sending twelve amphorae <note>Large ceramic storage jars</note> of sweet wine for the boys, and two of honey. The dried figs had already been stored away before we arrived. The gathered myrtle berries had rotted, but in the future, we will take more diligent care. Regarding the plants, Leptines will tell you the details.

As for the money for these purchases and a certain tax to be paid to the city, I received it from Leptines. I told him what seemed most honorable and true for both of us. The money we spent on the Leucadian ship is approximately sixteen <term>minas</term> <note>An ancient unit of currency; 1 mina was roughly 100 days' wages for a laborer</note>. I accepted that sum and used it for these things.

Now, hear how matters stand concerning your money and my own here in Athens. I will use your money, as I told you before, just as I use the resources of my other friends—using as little as possible, and only for those things that seem necessary, just, and honorable for both me and the one from whom I receive it. Such a situation has happened to me at this time. I have four grand-nieces, the daughters of my nieces who died while I—at your command—was not crowned. The first is of marriageable age, the second is eight years old, the third a little over three, and the fourth is not yet a year old. For those who marry while I am still alive, I and my friends must provide dowries; for those I do not survive, they must fare as best they can. If their fathers were wealthier than I, I would not need to provide the dowry. As it is, I am richer than they are; I previously arranged the marriages of their mothers with help from others and from Dion <note>Dion of Syracuse, Plato's close friend and Dionysius's brother-in-law</note>. One is now being given to Speusippus <note>Plato’s nephew and eventual successor at the Academy</note>, who is her mother's nephew. He needs no more than thirty minas, for such dowries are respectable and suitable for us. Furthermore, if my mother should die, no more than ten minas will be needed for the construction of a monument. These are my current necessities.

If any other expense arises, either private or public, on account of my relationship with you—as I once mentioned—it will be my task to struggle and fight so that the expense is kept very small; whatever I cannot avoid will be charged to you. 

But next, let us speak of the expenditure of your money in Athens. First, if I must spend anything on a <term>Choragus</term> <note>A wealthy citizen who financed the costumes and training for theatrical choruses</note> or something similar, there is no guest-friend of ours who will repay you. It is very important to you that money spent is for your benefit. If it is not spent, but merely delayed until someone comes from you, it brings you loss; besides being difficult, it would also be shameful for you. I attempted this with Andromedes, and I urged Erastus of Aegina—from whom you had ordered me to take what was needed as your guest-friend—but he was more interested in sending the larger sums you had written about. He replied (as was fair, since I am a stranger to him) that he had difficulty recovering what he had previously spent on your father's behalf; he would not refuse a small amount now, but would certainly refuse a large one. Therefore, I took the money from Leptines, who is worthy of praise—not just because he gave it, but because he gave it gladly and promptly. In other matters, too, he appears to be your friend and well-wisher in both word and deed.

It is necessary for me to report to you these things, and their opposites, so you know how everyone is disposed toward you. Therefore, I will openly tell you the truth about the money, for it is only fair; and having tested your domestic staff, I will speak of them as well. Those who constantly promise they will advise you on necessary expenses only want to advise you when they are sure they won't offend you. Therefore, you must accustom them and force them to explain these and other matters to you. For you ought to know everything as far as you are able, and be a judge of these things, fleeing from the knowledge of nothing. This is the most advantageous way to maintain and preserve your rule. If you handle expenses correctly and settle your accounts, you will rightly say that you have the greatest opportunity for high achievements and the preservation of wealth. You should also ensure that those who boast of being your supporters do not slander you among men. This does not seem to help your reputation at all.

Come, let us speak of Dion. I cannot report the rest until the letter you mentioned is brought to me. Regarding the things you did not want me to mention to him, I have made no mention or memory of them. I did, however, test whether he would bear it heavily or easily if those things were done; it seemed to me he would be no small amount of angry if they came to pass. Otherwise, Dion seemed to me to be well-disposed toward you in both word and deed.

We shall give to Cratinus, the brother of Timotheus and my companion, a very ornate military breastplate of the type used by infantry. For the daughters of Cebes, we will give three tunics, not expensive ones like those of Hermogine, but of Sicilian linen. The name of Cebes is very well known to you. He appears in the *Socratic Dialogues* and in the *Dialogue on the Soul* <note>The "Phaedo," which depicts Socrates' final hours</note>, where he disputes with Simmias against Socrates; he is a man who is both familiar and well-disposed to all of us.

Regarding the **mark** on my letters, which indicates whether I write seriously or not, I think you remember it, yet pay close attention. Many people ask me to write to you, and I cannot easily refuse them openly. Therefore:
The beginning of a **serious** letter is: **"GOD"** <note>original: "DEUS" (Singular)</note>.
The beginning of a **not serious** letter is: **"GODS"** <note>original: "DII" (Plural)</note>.

The ambassadors also asked me to write to you, and not without reason. They very gladly praise both you and me everywhere. Among them, Philager is not the least, though he was suffering from pain in his hand at the time. Likewise Philedes, coming from King Darius, spoke great things of you; if it did not require a very long and wordy letter, I would write out all he said. Now, ask Leptines whether you should send the breastplate or any of the other things I wrote about; if you wish to entrust it to him, do so—otherwise, entrust it to Terillus. Among those who sail constantly, he is our friend and is not at all unskilled in philosophy. He is the son-in-law of Tiso, who was helping us when we were sailing. 

Farewell, and study philosophy, and rouse and exhort other young men, and greet your playmates in the ball-game for me. Command Aristocritus and others that if any message comes from me in words or letters, they should see to it that it is delivered to you as soon as possible; let him remind you of what has been written so that you take care of it. Now, see to it that Leptines is repaid his money as soon as possible, so that others, looking at his example, may serve us more promptly and eagerly.

# PLATO'S AXIOCHUS ON THE CONTEMPT FOR DEATH, TRANSLATED BY RODOLPHUS AGRICOLA.

<note>The "Axiochus" is a Socratic dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato, though modern scholars believe it was written by a later member of the Academy. Rodolphus Agricola (1444–1485) was a preeminent Dutch humanist who translated this from Greek into Latin.</note>

### SOCRATES, CLINIAS, AXIOCHUS.

**SOCRATES.** As I was heading out toward the Cynosarges <note>A public gymnasium outside the walls of Athens</note> and had reached the Ilissus river, I heard the voice of someone calling out, "Socrates! Socrates!" When I turned and looked around to see where it came from, I saw Clinias, the son of Axiochus, running toward the Callirhoe spring with Damon the musician and Charmides, the son of Glaucon. One of these was teaching him music; the other loved him out of friendship and was loved in return. It seemed right for me to turn aside and meet them, so that we might gather as soon as possible.

**CLINIAS,** however, was bathed in tears. "Socrates," he said, "now is the time for you to show that wisdom which is so widely praised. For my father has suddenly been deprived of his strength and lies near the end of his life. He is distressed that his end is at hand, even though previously he used to despise those who depicted death in horrific images, and he would mock them kindly. Therefore, go and encourage him according to your custom, so that he may follow necessity wherever it leads with a willing heart, and so that he might be honored by me for this very act of devotion more than for anything else."

**SOCRATES.** Clinias, you have never asked me for anything moderate and honorable in vain, and all the more so now when you call me to these duties of piety. Let us hurry then. If things are as you say, there is need for haste.

**CLINIAS.** As soon as he sees you, Socrates, he will feel better. It has often happened to him before that he was revived after being questioned.

**SOCRATES.** To arrive more quickly, we went by the path near the wall toward the Itonian gates. For he lived near the gate that is by the Amazonian column. We found him with his senses returned and his body robust, but failing in mind and utterly in need of consolation; he was frequently sighing and crying out with tears and the wringing of his hands.

Looking at him, I said: "Axiochus, what is the meaning of this? Where are those magnificent words of yours from before, your constant praises of virtue, and that strength of mind in you that was greater than words could describe? Like a cowardly athlete, you showed yourself distinguished in the gymnasium, but you have failed at the actual contest. Will you not, as a man of such great age and a follower of reason—and if nothing else, an Athenian—circumspectly consider nature? For it is a common saying, tossed about by everyone, that life is a kind of pilgrimage; it is necessary that those who complete it do so cheerfully and, almost singing a *paean* <note>original: "pęana" — a song of praise or triumph</note>, approach the final necessity. To behave so softly and with such difficulty, being torn away like a child, in no way shows the wisdom of a man of your years."

**AXIOCHUS.** You seem to speak truly, Socrates. But I do not know how it is that when danger draws closer, those brave and grand words secretly fly away and are neglected. A certain fear arises, tearing my mind apart in many ways, thinking that I shall be deprived of this light and these goods, and that I shall lie senseless and without feeling wherever I may rot, turned into dust and worms.

**SOCRATES.** Axiochus, because of your lack of experience, you are incorrectly joining together the loss of senses with the act of sensing, and you are doing and saying things that contradict yourself. You do not consider that while you loathe the fact that you will lack senses, you simultaneously grieve over the putrefaction and the loss of life's pleasures, as if you were going to pass into another life after death rather than into a total abolition of the senses—returning to the same state you were in before you were born. For just as when Draco and Cleisthenes <note>Athenian lawgivers from the 7th and 6th centuries BCE</note> governed the republic, no evil touched you (for you had not yet begun to exist so that anything bad could happen to you), so it will be after death. You will not exist, so nothing can be bad for you. Therefore, discard all this foolishness by realizing this: once this frame is dissolved and the soul is restored to its proper place, this remaining earthly body, being void of reason, is no longer the "man." For we *are* the soul, an immortal living being enclosed in a mortal fortress.

Nature has surrounded us with this "tent" <note>A common metaphor for the human body</note> not without evil; its joys are hidden and fleeting, mixed with many pains, while its sorrows are sudden, long-lasting, and utterly empty of joy. I mean the illnesses, the sores of the sensing limbs, the internal diseases. Because the soul is distributed through the passages of the body, it necessarily suffers with it, and thus it longs for the celestial and kindred ether, and thirsts eagerly for the company and joys of that life above. Therefore, departure from life is a change from a certain evil into a good.

**AXIOCHUS.** Since you think life is an evil, Socrates, why do you persist in living, especially since you are a seeker of truth and excel the rest of us—the multitude—in intelligence?

**SOCRATES.** Axiochus, you do not give a true testimony of me. You think, as the Athenian commoners do, that because I investigate things, I also possess knowledge. I am so far from knowing the more hidden things that I would pray to even know the common ones. What I am saying are the teachings of Prodicus the Wise <note>A famous 5th-century BCE Sophist known for his lectures on language and ethics</note>, some bought for two obols, others for two or four drachmas. For this man teaches no one for free, and he always has that saying of Epicharmus <note>A Greek comic playwright and philosopher</note> in his mouth: "One hand rubs the other; give something and take something."

Recently, when he was declaiming at the house of Callias, son of Hipponicus, he spoke so much against life that I have added it to my own thoughts. From that moment, Axiochus, my mind has leaned toward death.

**AXIOCHUS.** And what did he say?

<margin>The misery of life.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** I will tell you those things that come to my mind. "What part of life," he asked, "is free from calamities? Does not an infant cry immediately from the start, as soon as it is born? It begins life with tears. What trouble does not press upon it? It is always urged on by either poverty, or cold, or heat, or beatings. Even before it can speak, how much does it suffer? It cries, of course, and this is the only complaint it has for its anxiety. When it has completed its seventh year and exhausted many labors, then come the guardians, the gymnastics masters, and the schoolteachers. Then, as an adolescent, there are critics, geometers, and masters of military affairs—plainly a huge multitude of masters. After these, when he is enrolled among the *Ephebi* <note>Young men of military age (18–20)</note>, there is first the fear of the Lyceum, the Academy, the gymnasiarchy, the rods, and absolutely no measure of evils. The entire time of youth is under moderators chosen from the council of the Areopagus to preside over the youth. Then, when he is freed from these, cares openly emerge, and he must deliberate on which path of life he should especially take. Compared to the troubles that follow, those earlier childish ones seem like mere nursery terrors. For then come military expeditions, wounds, and constant..."
