...chastens. In this way, he redeemed the young Phaedo, who had been prostituted in a public brothel, from that calamity and made him a philosopher. He compelled Plato, who was devoted to poetry, to commit his tragedies to the fire and to embrace more precious studies. He led Xenophon from common luxury to wisdom and sobriety. He made Aeschines and Aristippus rich men instead of poor ones, Phaedrus a philosopher instead of an orator, and rendered Alcibiades the most learned of men instead of an ignorant one. He made Charmides grave and modest; Theages he made just and brave—a citizen for the Republic. Euthydemus and Menon he transferred from the quibbles of the Sophists to true wisdom. Thus it happened that the companionship of Socrates was not so much pleasant as it was useful; and, as Alcibiades says, Socrates was loved much more ardently by the youths than he himself loved them.

->centered: #### HOW THANKS OUGHT TO BE GIVEN ####<-
->centered: to the Holy Spirit, who has illuminated and kindled us toward this discussion.<-
->centered: ##### CHAPTER XVII. #####<-

**I**t seems now, best guests of the banquet, that we have happily discovered—first from your discussion and then from mine—what Love is, who the true lover is, and what utility the lover gains. You should undoubtedly believe that the cause of this most happy discovery and its teacher was Love himself, who has now been revealed. For by being kindled with the love of finding Love, so to speak, we sought Love and found him, so that thanks must be given to him equally for the inquiry and the discovery. O wondrous magnificence of this divinity! O incomparable kindness of Love! For while other divinities hardly reveal themselves for a moment after you have sought them for a long time, Love even meets those who are about to seek him. Wherefore men confess they owe themselves much more to him than to the others. 

There are some who dare to frequently curse the divine power as the thunderer against our crimes. Some even hate the wisdom that explores all our disgraces. But we cannot help but love Love, the bestower of all divine goods. We shall worship this Love, who is so favorable to us, with our minds so that we may venerate him; we shall admire his wisdom and power, so that with Love as our guide we may have, so to speak, the whole of God as our favor. Loving him entirely with the fire of Love, we may also enjoy the whole of God in perpetual love.

->centered: # PLATO’S BANQUET #<-
->centered: # OR, ON #<-
->centered: # LOVE #<-

**APOLLODORUS, FRIENDS OF APOLLODORUS, GLAUCON, ARISTODEMUS, SOCRATES, AGATHO, PHAEDRUS, PAUSANIAS, ERYXIMACHUS, ARISTOPHANES, DIOTIMA, ALCIBIADES.**

[[notes: This begins the actual translation of Plato's *Symposium* by Marsilio Ficino (the 15th-century Florentine priest and philosopher).]]

**I** BELIEVE I am sufficiently prepared regarding the things you ask. For yesterday, when I was returning home to the city from Phalerum, a certain acquaintance of mine saw me from behind and called from a distance. Joking as he called, he said, "O Phalerian Apollodorus, won't you wait?" I stopped and waited. He said, "I was just looking for you, desiring to hear what discourses were held concerning Love at that dinner where Agatho, Socrates, Alcibiades, and several others gathered. For another person told me, who had heard it from Phoenix the son of Philip, and he added that you knew of it. But he could report nothing certain about the matter. Therefore, you should tell me. For it concerns you to narrate the speeches of your friend. But first, tell me this: were you yourself present at the discussion, or not?" 

"In truth," I said, "that man seems to have reported nothing certain to you, if indeed you think they gathered so recently that I could have been present." "I did think so," he said. "How so?" I asked. "Do you not know, O Glaucon, that for many years now Agatho has not visited here? Indeed, from the time I began to associate with Socrates and to observe his words and deeds more diligently every day, not yet three years have passed. Before that, wandering wherever chance took me and thinking I was doing something important, I was the most miserable of all men, just as you are now, who think anything else should be done rather than philosophizing." "Do not bite," he said, "but tell me at what time the banquet was celebrated." 

To this I said, "While we were still boys, when Agatho won the victory in his first tragic contest. On the day following the victory, after the sacrifices for the victory had been celebrated, the discussion was instituted at a prepared banquet." "That is certainly a long time ago," he said. "But who told you? Was it Socrates himself?" "No, by Jove," I said, "but the same person who told Phoenix: a certain Aristodemus of Cydathenaeum, who was of small stature and always went with bare feet. He was present at the discussion, for he was one who loved Socrates most of all those then living, it seems to me. Moreover, I questioned Socrates himself about some things Aristodemus had reported, and he agreed with him." "Why then," he asked, "do you not tell me? The road that leads to the city is well-suited for both hearing and speaking." 

Thus as we went, we talked of these things. Therefore, as I said at the beginning, I am sufficiently prepared in these matters. If you want these things recounted to you again, I will recount them. For as often as I either have a discourse about philosophy myself or hear others speaking, besides thinking it profits me, I am wonderfully delighted. But as often as I hear other discourses, especially yours, who always study the piling up of money, I am both vexed and pity you, because you think you are achieving something when you achieve nothing. Perhaps you think me unhappy, and I suspect you think truly. I, however, do not merely think it of you, I know it for certain. 

**FRIEND:** You are always the same, O Apollodorus; you are perpetually disparaging yourself and others, and you seem undoubtedly to think yourself most unhappy first, and then all others except for Socrates alone. I do not know where you got that nickname 'The Madman.' For in speaking you always treat yourself and others bitterly and harshly, approving of Socrates alone. 

**APOLLODORUS:** O dearest man, it is clear from this that I am insane and raving, because I think this way about myself and about you. 

**FRIEND:** It is not fitting to contend over these things at present, Apollodorus; rather, comply with our prayers and explain to us what those discourses were. 

**APOL:** They were indeed as follows. Or rather, I will now try to recount them to you from the beginning in the same order as Aristodemus reported them. For he said he met Socrates washed and with his feet adorned with shoes—things he rarely did. He asked where he was going so adorned, and Socrates replied that he was going to Agatho's house for dinner, having avoided yesterday's dinner because he feared the crowd gathered for Agatho's victory, but he had promised to be present the following day. For that reason he had adorned himself, so that he might go as "a beautiful man to a beautiful man." 

He asked further, "Aristodemus, how is it that you are going to dinner uninvited?" "As you command," I said. "Follow me then," he said, "that we may destroy the proverb, changing it in this way: 'to the banquets of the good, the good also go uninvited.'" [[margin: Iliad 10]] Homer, however, seems not only to ignore but to violate the proverb. For when he had portrayed Agamemnon as a man strenuous in military matters and Menelaus as soft, while Agamemnon was celebrating a banquet after a sacrifice, he brings Menelaus to Agamemnon's table coming of his own accord. Thus he made the inferior man come uninvited to the table of the more excellent man. 

Hearing this, I said, "Perhaps, O Socrates, I shall not be as you say, but as Homer portrayed: a common little man coming to the banquet of a wise man uninvited. Since you are leading me, see what reason you will assign for my arrival. For I will not confess to coming uninvited, but will say I was invited by you." "On the way," he said, "since there are two of us, we will perhaps consult on what we shall say; but let us go now." 

After they had disputed such things between them, he said they went; and Socrates, being meditative and walking with too slow a step, was left behind. When Aristodemus waited for him, Socrates finally ordered him to go ahead. When he approached Agatho’s house, he found the door open and a ridiculous thing happened: right on the threshold a certain servant met him and led him where the others were reclining, whom he found already about to dine. As soon as Agatho saw him, he said, "O Aristodemus, you have come at an opportune time to dine with us. If you want anything else, defer it to another time. I was looking for you yesterday to invite you and saw you nowhere. But why do you not lead Socrates to us?" 

"And I," he said, "turning around, saw Socrates nowhere, and replied to Agatho: 'I came with him, having been called here by him to dinner.'" "You did well," he said, "but where is Socrates?" "He was just walking behind me. Therefore I too wonder, and I do not know where he is." "Boy, look for Socrates," said Agatho, "and bring him in to us. You, Aristodemus, recline next to Eryximachus. Hey you, give him water for his feet so he may sit now." 

Then Aristodemus said another boy entered and announced that Socrates himself had withdrawn into the nearest vestibule and refused to enter when summoned. "You tell of an absurd thing," he said. "Call again, and do not let go until he comes." "Not so, O Agatho," Aristodemus replied, "but let him be; for this is Socrates' custom. Sometimes he is accustomed to stop and stand wherever he happens to be. He will come quickly, I think. Do not disturb him, but permit him to come at his own will." "If it seems so to you," Agatho said, "so it must be done. But you, boys, bring the feast to the others and set out whatever you please. For no one presides over us. I have never done that. Therefore, thinking that I now, along with the others, have been received by you at the banquet, take care of everything diligently, so that we may approve of your work." 

After this, he added that they began to dine, and Socrates, though often called by Agatho’s command, did not enter until he had exercised himself somewhat in his usual way, and he came in the middle of the dinner. Agatho, who was sitting last and alone, said to him, "Here, O Socrates, recline next to me, so that touching you I may enjoy that wise thought which you devised in the vestibule. For it is clear that you have found it and possess it; otherwise you would not have ceased." 

Socrates sat down and said, "It would be well for our affairs, Agatho, if wisdom were such that it flowed from the fuller man into the empty one by touch alone, just as water flows from a full cup into an empty one through a wool thread [[notes: an ancient method of siphoning]]. For if wisdom is so, I value greatly that I sit by you. For I think I shall be filled by you with a most abundant and beautiful wisdom. My own is indeed thin and ambiguous, like a kind of dream; yours, however, is quite brilliant and powerful, seeing that in your youth it shone and flashed so clearly yesterday in the sight of more than thirty thousand Greeks." 

"You are insulting, O Socrates," said Agatho. "Yet later you and I shall judge this matter of wisdom with Dionysus as judge; but now, let us dine." 

After this, Aristodemus said, when Socrates had reclined and dined, and the others also had finished dinner, they made libations and tasted the wines in the ritual of sacrificers, and began to sing to the god. Having done other things as is custom, they turned to drinking. Whereupon Pausanias began to speak thus: "We must see, O men, by what means we may drink more lightly and pleasantly. For to confess the truth about myself first, I feel myself still weighed down by yesterday's unmixed wine, and I need a certain intermission. I think most of you are similarly affected, for you were there yesterday. Consider therefore how we may drink more lightly and healthfully." 

To him Aristophanes soon replied, "You speak wisely, Pausanias; a certain moderation in drinking must be applied. For I too am among those who gorged yesterday." When Eryximachus the son of Acumenus heard this, he said, "You speak rightly. And I desire to hear this from you besides, Agatho: how much strength do you have for drinking?" "Very little indeed," Agatho said. "It certainly benefits us—I mean myself and Aristodemus and Phaedrus and these others—that you who are very strong at drinking are now weary of it. For we are always weak, except for Socrates, who is fit for either. Therefore, whatever we do, it will be the same." 

Here Eryximachus said, "Since no one of those present seems to want to gorge, perhaps if I speak the truth about drunkenness, I shall be less troublesome. For from the skill of medicine, it is clear to me that drunkenness is a grave thing for men. For neither would I ever wish to drink excessively myself, nor would I advise another, especially if someone is suffering from yesterday's carousal." 

To him Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian said, "Indeed, I have always had faith in you, especially in medicine. Now similarly, provided the others also agree." When all heard this, they consented that they should drink not to drunkenness in the present banquet, but for pleasure. Then Eryximachus: "Since it has been decided that it will be in each person’s judgment how much he drinks, and no one should be forced beyond what he wants, I will explain what remains. I think the flute-girl who just entered should be sent away, to play the flute for herself or, if she wishes, for the women who are inside. I judge that we ought to converse with one another today. If you wish, I will reveal what our discourses should be." 

To this all said it pleased them, and ordered him to explain. Eryximachus then said, "The beginning of my speech will be according to Euripides’ *Melanippe*. For the story I am about to begin is not mine, but Phaedrus’. Phaedrus here often complains to me, asserting an absurd thing: that while poets have fashioned songs and hymns to the other gods, no one of so many poets has ever written any praise for Love, such a great and significant god. Yet if you wish to look, Eryximachus, you will surely find that eloquent Sophists have praised Hercules and others in prose, just as the most skilled Prodicus did—though this should seem less wondrous to anyone. But I have also read a book by a wise man in which salt was extolled with wondrous praises for its utility to life; and one can find many other things of this kind celebrated with praises. That men should be studiously occupied in these things, yet no man has dared until this day to praise Love according to his dignity, but he is so much neglected, even though he is so great a God—is this not unworthy? 

To me this speech of Phaedrus seems true. Therefore, I desire both to confer this gift upon him and to gratify him, and I judge it decent that this god be honored by us. If it also seems so to you, a congruent discussion will arise among us. I think Love should be praised by each one of us as skillfully and as excellently as we can. Let Phaedrus begin, since he both sits first and is the inventor of this discourse." 

Then Socrates said, "No one would oppose you, O Eryximachus. How could I refuse, who profess to know nothing except matters of love? Nor will Agatho and Pausanias oppose, and Aristophanes much less, whose whole study revolves around Dionysus and Venus; nor any other of those I now see. Although an equal lot does not cover us who sit last. For if the first ones depict him skillfully and abundantly, it will be enough for us. But let Phaedrus now begin with happy auspices and honor Love." All assented to what Socrates had said and ordered similarly. 

But Aristodemus did not remember every single thing said by each, nor do I remember every single thing he related. Therefore I will now report to you the speech of those who said things worthy of remembrance. First, they said Phaedrus began in this manner.

->centered: #### PHAEDRUS’ PRAISE ####<-
->centered: #### OF LOVE ####<-

**L**ove is a great god, and to be wondered at among gods and men, both for many other reasons and especially because of his origin. For since he is among the most ancient of the gods, he appears worthy of honor. We argue this from the fact that parents of Love neither exist nor are reported by any poet or anyone else. But Hesiod asserts that in the beginning Chaos existed; these are his words: "Earth, the wide and stable seat of all forever, and Love"; namely asserting that after Chaos these two existed, Earth and Love. Parmenides says of his generation: "Before all the gods she first brought forth Love." Acusilaus also seems to agree with Hesiod. And so it is conceded everywhere that Love is among the most ancient. 

Since he is such, he is the cause of the greatest goods for us. For I do not find what better thing could happen to a youth than an excellent lover, or to a lover than an excellent beloved (*amasius*). There are two things which ought to lead a man from boyhood through his whole life if he is to live excellently: shame in shameful things and the study of glory and praise in honorable ones. These things neither lineage, nor riches, nor honors can provide more quickly or better than love. Without these two, neither a city nor a private person will ever be able to achieve anything noble and magnificent. 

I assert indeed that a lover, if he is caught doing something shameful or suffering it from someone through cowardice, and does not resist and take revenge—whether from his father, or from friends, or from any other man—is not so vehemently pained as if he were caught by his beloved. Similarly, we see a youth blush most of all then, when a lover finds him committing something base. If a city or an army could be made in some way partly from those who love and partly from those who are loved, they would act and administer each thing bravely beyond what can be said; while through shame they would abstain from shameful things and contend for honorable ones as if by a certain emulation. Such men would overcome in battle. A lover would surely blush more vehemently to desert his post or throw away his arms before his beloved than before all other men. Indeed, he would often prefer to die than to desert the beloved and not help in dangers. [[margin: Iliad 23]] 

Nor is anyone so cowardly that Love does not inflame him and render him divine toward virtue, so as to persuade even the bravest man. For what Homer says—that a god inspires force and fury in certain heroes—this Love has given to lovers. Furthermore, only lovers choose to die for another, not only men but also women. Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, exhibited a manifest testimony of this discourse to the Greeks; she alone chose to die for her husband, though he had both a father and a mother. Because of love, she so surpassed them in charity that she showed them to be strangers and connected to their son in name only. This deed was judged so noble not only by men but also by the gods, that while the gods had attributed the gift of returning to life to very few and the most excellent among many who had done many great things, they immediately raised her from the underworld, being delighted by such an egregious deed. Such is the study and virtue concerning love that the gods value. 

But they sent away Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus [[margin: Orpheus is harshly criticized]], failing in his prayer, from the underworld. For they did not restore the woman for whose sake he had descended, but showed him her phantom, since he did not dare to die for the sake of love, as Alcestis did, but, as a cithara-player, was deterred by a certain softness and devised certain machinations by which he might descend to the underworld while living. They decreed that he should pay the penalty for this crime and ordered that he be torn apart by women. 

Achilles, however, the son of Thetis, they honored [[margin: Iliad 23]] and sent to the Islands of the Blessed, because when he had heard from his mother that if he killed Hector, he must die immediately, but if not, he would return to his fatherland and finally die as an old man, he boldly chose to fight for Patroclus his lover and to avenge his death, and not only to die for him, but to be killed over his corpse. Greatly approving of this, the gods decorated him with signal glory because he had valued his lover so highly. 

Aeschylus, however, plainly raves when he says Patroclus was loved by Achilles, who surpassed not only Patroclus but indeed all heroes in beauty, and was still beardless and much younger in age, as Homer says. In truth, the gods value this virtue in love most highly. But they admire and delight more vehemently, and confer greater benefits, when the beloved protects and loves the lover than when the lover loves the beloved. For the lover is more divine than the beloved, since he is rapt by a divine fury (*furore*). On which account they honored Achilles more than Alcestis: indeed, they transferred him to the Islands of the Blessed. 

From all these things I assert Love to be the most ancient of all gods, and the most honored, and the one most conducive for men, both living and dead, toward attaining virtue and beatitude. Aristodemus related that such was the speech of Phaedrus. After Phaedrus, some others spoke, but they fell from memory. Passing over them, he related the speech of Pausanias, which I shall now report.

->centered: #### PAUSANIAS’ PRAISE ####<-

**I**t seems to me, O Phaedrus, that the discourse proposed to us was not quite right, in which we are simply ordered to praise Love. For if Love were one, it would have been well said. But since he is not just one, it is better to first express which one is to be praised. Therefore I will try to amend this. First I will explain which love it is fitting to praise, then I will strive to extol him according to the dignity of that god. 

Surely it escapes no one that without Love, Venus never exists. Wherefore if there were one Venus, there would be one Love. But since there are two Venuses [[margin: Twin Love]], there must also be a twin Love. Who denies that this goddess is twin? Is not one indeed the older Venus, born of Heaven and without a mother, whom we call the Celestial Venus (*Caelestem*)? The other, however, is the younger, born of Jupiter and Dione, whom we call the Common (*Pandemum*) and Vulgar Venus. It is necessary, therefore, that the Love who is the companion and helper of the former Venus be called Celestial, and the other Vulgar. 

Indeed it is fitting to praise all gods, but the works of each love must be distinguished. This is the condition of any action: that by its own nature it is neither honorable nor base—such as the things we are doing now: drinking, singing, disputing. None of these is base or honorable in itself. But the manner of doing gives a certain name to the action. For that which is done well and rightly is honorable; that which is not right exists as base. By the same reason, not every love and every manner of loving is honorable and to be praised. Rather, only that one which exhorts us to love honorably. 

For the love of the Vulgar and Common Venus is indeed vulgar itself and performs whatever happens to it. And this is the one by which base and abject men love. Furthermore, they love women no less than males, and bodies more than souls, and men without minds rather than prudent ones. They gape only to fulfill their desire; they do not care at all whether they fulfill it honorably. Thus it happens that they perform whatever chance offers them, good and evil alike. For an affect of this kind flows from that Venus who is much younger than the high one, and who participates in both sexes in generation. 

But the Love who follows the Celestial Venus, who participates not in the female but only in the male sex, is of boys only. Then, since he is the companion of the older Venus, he himself is free from all petulance. Therefore, whoever is inspired by this love loves the male kind, which is by nature more robust and generous, and more a participant in mind. And those who are rapt by this love sincerely and perfectly are clearly distinguished by this: that they do not love young boys, but adolescents, when they have already begun to prevail in mind—which happens when they are close to puberty. For I think those who begin to love from this point are prepared to live together and in common for their whole life, not to deceive the beloved, nor to go from one to another to be loved, nor to love boys still lacking in mind, whom they might later mock as they grow old and abandon. 

It ought to be instituted by laws that no one loves boys, so that such great study would not be placed in vain upon an ambiguous matter. For it is uncertain where either the body or the soul of boys will finally end up, whether toward virtue or vice. Good men propose this law for themselves voluntarily. It is also necessary to subject those vulgar lovers to the same law by necessity, just as we prohibit them from loving free women according to their powers. For these are the ones who have provided the occasion for reproaches and for the opinion of some who say it is base to comply with a lover. They say these things about vulgar lovers because they recognize and disapprove of their importunity and injustice. But nothing that is done modestly and legitimately should be censured. 

The law about love instituted in other cities is easy to understand, because it is handed down simply. But among us and the Lacedaemonians [[notes: Spartans]], it exists variously. For in Elis and among the Boeotians, where men lack the art of speaking, it is simply established by law that compliance should be shown to lovers; nor does anyone there, young or old, call it base. I think this was done by them so that they would not have to labor in persuading adolescents, seeing that they are inept at oratory. In Ionia, however, and among many others subject to the Barbarians, this is judged altogether base by law. For among the Barbarians it is held base because of tyrannies, and also because of the study of wisdom and gymnastics. For those studies do not benefit tyrants, which make the minds of subjects sharp and generous, and which produce indissoluble friendships among them and frequent societies—which are accustomed to be born from other things, but most of all from love. 

Our tyrants learned this from the matter itself. For the love of Aristogiton and the confirmed friendship of Harmodius dissipated their tyranny. And so wherever indulgence of Love has been fundamentally removed, it has been forbidden by the depravity of those who made the laws—the beginning of avarice and the study of increasing empire through the cowardice of subjects. But where it is allowed without limit, it is allowed because of the sluggishness and laziness of those who so established it. 

Here [[notes: in Athens]], however, it is instituted much more rightly, but as I was saying, it is not easy to know. It seems clearly conceded, if one notices what is said, that it is more honorable to love openly than secretly, and especially those who are generous and best, even if they seem less beautiful than others. The common exhortation of everyone favors the lover as much as possible, as if he attempts nothing base. For commonly, if someone catches the beloved, it seems a beautiful thing; if he does not, it is base. And the law concedes certain wondrous machinations to the lover to reconcile the beloved to himself, and permits him to be praised: things which if anyone dared to attempt for the sake of anything else, he would incur the greatest censures among philosophers. 

If someone, for the sake of receiving money from someone, or obtaining a magistracy or other power, should attempt those things which occur everywhere among lovers toward beloveds—beg suppliantly, entreat, lie at doors by night, serve with a certain sedulous observation, and comply in all things which any slave would neither wish nor be forced to do—he will be scolded equally by enemies and friends. The former will censure his servile flatteries and assents. The latter will rebuke him, and his friends will be ashamed of his servitude. But the lover when he does these things gains favor, and as if he were doing something noble, he is permitted by law to do those things without any mark of infamy. 

And what is greatest of all, it is commonly said [[margin: Only to amatory perjuries do gods give pardon]] that only to amatory perjuries do the gods give pardon. For they say a Venereal oath is worth nothing [[margin: Venereal oath]]. Thus both gods and men have granted every license to a lover, as our law testifies. If we look at these things that have been said, love will seem to be esteemed as something most noble in this city, and it is honorable for the beloved to indulge the lover. If, on the other hand, we notice what I shall say, we will think this is held most base among us. 

For parents entrust their sons to tutors (*paedagogis*), who prohibit the beloveds from speaking with lovers. Companions and peers also censure whenever they see such a thing, and while they pluck at such things, the old do not reprimand them, nor do they rebuke those who err. Therefore, I think it holds thus: that the thing itself in itself, as was said at the beginning, is neither honorable nor base. It is not simple; rather, what is done rightly is honorable, and on the contrary, what is done wrongly is base. 

It is indeed base to comply with the wicked and to do so basely. But it is honorable to comply with the good, and honorably. The vulgar lover is wicked, he who loves the body more than the soul. For he is not stable, since he loves a thing that is least stable; as soon as what he desired has deflowered, he goes away and flies off, keeping none of the things he promised. But the lover of good character perseveres in friendship through his whole life, seeing that he was pursuing a stable thing. 

Our law commands us to examine these men diligently, to comply with the latter and flee the former. It orders us to follow these and flee those, judging and examining what each person loves and what is loved in each. And for this reason, it is judged base to be caught easily and quickly, so that time may intervene, which is required for examining character; then, it is base to be caught either by the abundance of money or the power of magistracies—whether he is ensnared by a certain fear rather than will, or if, having received money or acquired civil gifts, he does not despise them. For nothing from these seems solid and firm, besides the fact that a generous friendship cannot arise from them. 

One way according to our law remains, by which beloveds can rightly gratify lovers. For just as that law was related among us concerning lovers, in which it is said that no voluntary obedience of the lover to the beloved is to be thought flattering and infamous; so also another certain voluntary servitude remains according to the law, which undergoes no infamy. This is the one which concerns virtue. For it is instituted in our laws that if someone wishes to serve someone, thinking that through him he may profit either in a certain wisdom or in any other part of virtue, this voluntary servitude again will not be a disgrace to the servant, nor should it be called flattery. 

It is necessary that these laws lead to the same end: namely, the one about lovers and this one about philosophy and other virtue, if it is to happen by any reason that it is fitting for beloveds to comply with lovers. For as often as the lover and the beloved meet in the same place, each having a law—the one prepared to minister and serve the beloved justly in all things, the other in turn prepared to obey his teacher of knowledge and character justly in each thing—and the former is able to contribute to wisdom and other virtues, while the latter is in need of erudition and wisdom; then indeed, with these laws meeting in one, it alone happens that it is honorable for beloveds to show compliance to lovers, and otherwise in no way. 

In this, at least, it is not base to be deceived. In all other things, such compliance is judged base, whether the opinion deceives the one complying or not. For if someone gratifies a lover as if he were rich for the sake of riches, and is deceived, and does not receive money because the lover is found to be poor, he is nonetheless censured. For he seems to have shown a servile habit of his mind, because for the sake of money he would serve anyone in each thing—which is not at all honorable. By the same reason, if someone gratifies a man as if he were good, hoping himself to emerge better from this association, and is deceived when that man is found to be wicked, it is a kind of honorable deception. For he seems to have demonstrated his affect, being prepared for all ministries for the sake of attaining virtue. This is surely judged most noble. Therefore, it is always honorable to gratify and serve for the sake of virtue. This is the love of the Celestial goddess herself, celestial itself; which is precious both privately and publicly, and compels both the lover and the beloved to take up the care and study of virtue. 

The other loves are companions of the Vulgar Venus. These things I bring to you about Love at the present time, O Phaedrus, as if spontaneously." 

When Pausanias had made a "pause" (*pausam*)—that is, an end of speaking—(for thus the wise men teach me to play on the word) Aristodemus said it was necessary for Aristophanes to speak, but he was hindered by a hiccup occurring either because of fullness or some other cause. Wherefore he immediately spoke to Eryximachus the physician sitting after him: "O Eryximachus, it concerns you now either to repress my hiccup or to speak for me until it ceases." To this Eryximachus replied, "I will do both. I will speak in your place, and you in mine, after the hiccup has gone. Meanwhile, while I speak, if you hold your breath for a while, the hiccup will cease. If that does not please you, at least wash your throat inside with much water. And if it is very vehement, tickle your nostrils so that sneezing is provoked. For if you do that once or twice, even if it is most vehement, it will be removed." "Before you finish speaking," said Aristophanes, "I will do what you command." 

Eryximachus spoke thus.

->centered: #### ERYXIMACHUS’ PRAISE ####<-

"**I**t seems necessary to me," he said, "that after Pausanias began rightly but finished insufficiently, what is lacking be now fulfilled by me. I approve indeed of that distinction in which Love is distributed into two. But I seem to have found through our art of medicine that Love is present not only in the souls of men toward beautiful things, but also toward many other things and in other things: both in the bodies of all animals and in those things which grow from the earth—and finally, in all things that consist in the nature of things, so to speak. This great and wonderful god extends himself most widely through all things, both human and divine. 

I will first take an example from the skill of medicine, so that I may honor my art. Surely the nature of bodies contains this twin Love. For that which is well in our bodies and that which is ill are different and dissimilar. What is dissimilar desires and loves what is dissimilar. Therefore, the Love which is in a healthy body is one thing, and that which is in a sick one is another. And as Pausanias was just asserting that one must gratify tempered men but not at all intemperate ones, so also in the bodies themselves, one must indeed comply with the good and healthy parts—in which the rationale of medicine mostly consists—but not at all with the bad and sick ones, if one wants to be a skillful physician. 

Medicine is, to put it briefly, the science of how the amatory affects of the body are known regarding repletion and evacuation [[margin: Medicine]]. And whoever discerns the beautiful and deformed love in these is a most skilled physician. He who can so change these things that one love is born in place of another, or who can send in Love where it is absent and needed, and remove it where it is ingrained, is an educated craftsman. For it is necessary to be able to reconcile those things in the body which are most hostile and to insert mutual love into them. The things which are most hostile are those which are most contrary: cold to hot, bitter to sweet, moist to dry, and others of this kind. 

When our progenitor Aesculapius knew how to insert mutual love and concord into these things, as these poets testify and I myself believe, he composed our art. Therefore all medicine speaks in that manner and is governed by this god. Similarly also agriculture and gymnastics. It can be clear to anyone who notices even for a little while that the same rationale applies to music. Which Heraclitus perhaps felt, but explained poorly in words. 'One thing,' he says, 'discordant with itself agrees, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre.' But it is an absurd thing to say that harmony discords, or is made of discording things while they are in dissonance. 

But perhaps he meant to signify this: that from things which previously discorded—namely, the low and the high notes—harmony is produced when they are subsequently made to consonant by the musical art. For harmony is never blown from low and high while they discord. For harmony is a concord (*concentus*). Concord is a certain agreement. Agreement cannot occur from discording things while they discord. What discords and is not in agreement cannot sound together, just as rhythm is constituted from the fast and the slow, previously discording, but later sounding together. And just as medicine gives concord to the humors, so music gives consonance to voices, producing Love and mutual consent. Music is the science concerning harmony and rhythm, judging amatory affects and forces. 

Surely in the composition of harmony and rhythm, the amatory force can be easily perceived; but the twin Love is not yet distinguished here, but only then when one must use rhythm and harmony for others—either by fashioning them (which they call melody-making) or by using those things already made, the melodies and meters (which they call education). Here that superior discourse returns: namely, that one must gratify modest men and those who are not yet sufficiently modest so that they may become so, and the love of the good must be preserved. And this is the decorous and celestial love of the Muse Urania. But that of the Muse Polyhymnia is vulgar. This must be indulged with the greatest caution so that men may draw pleasure but avoid incontinence. Just as in our art it is arduous to use rightly the desires which allure us to the sweet feasts of cooks, so that we may eat sweetly without detriment to good health. 

Wherefore both in music and in medicine and in all other things, both human and divine, we must observe both loves which are in all things according to our strength. Furthermore, the constitution of the seasons of the year is full of both of these. For as often as those things I just mentioned—the hot and the cold, the dry and the moist—obtain a congruent love for one another and receive harmony and opportune tempering, they bring a healthy and fertile year to men, to all animals, and to plants, and they harm nothing. 

On the contrary, when petulant and contemptuous love prevails in the seasons of the year, it corrupts with much injury. For plagues are accustomed to arise from these, and many other diseases in various brutes and plants. For frost, ice, hail, the blights of crops, and rots come from the immoderate and exceeding love of qualities; the science of these things—of the movements of heaven and the seasons of the year—is called astronomy. 

Moreover, all sacrifices and those things over which divination presides—namely, the communions of gods and men with one another—revolve around nothing else than the curation and custody of love. For all impiety is accustomed to approach then, when one does not indulge modest love nor honor and venerate it in all things, but wanders around the other love, not using congruent duty toward parents, living and dead, and toward the gods. To discern and cure these loves is the purpose of divination [[margin: Divination]]. And furthermore, divination is the craftsman of friendship between gods and men, because it understands what most pertains to right or wrong among human loves. 

And so love contains in brief much and wide, or rather all, power. But the love that revolves around good things with temperance and justice has the highest power and exhibits all beatitude to us. For it reconciles us to one another in common life and makes us friends to the gods who are more excellent than human nature. Perhaps I too pass over many things which pertain to praising Love, though not willingly. What is lacking, Aristophanes, is yours to fulfill. Or if you wish to honor this god in another way, honor him, since the hiccup has ceased." 

"It is already settled," said Aristophanes, "yet not before it was repressed by a sneezing. Wherefore I wonder if the congruent affection of the body requires such noises and ridiculous sounds as a sneezing. For as soon as the sneezing arose, the hiccup immediately stopped." "See what you are doing, good Aristophanes," replied Eryximachus. "You move laughter against yourself before you have even spoken, and you force me to become an observer of your speech to see if you happen to bring forth something laughable, when you could have spoken securely." 

"You speak well, Eryximachus," Aristophanes said. "Let those things be as if unsaid; but do not observe me, for I do not fear that I might bring forth something that moves laughter—for that would be the gain and proper property of our Muse—but I fear I might bring forth things to be laughed at." 

"Having thrown your javelin, Aristophanes, do you hope to flee?" Eryximachus replied. "But apply your mind to speaking as if you were to render an account of all your words; but perhaps, if it seems so, I will let you go."

->centered: #### ARISTOPHANES’ PRAISE ####<-

"**I** intend to speak of Love differently than you and Pausanias. For it seems plain to me that men have altogether ignored the power of Love until now. For if they knew it, they would dedicate signal shrines, altars, and victims to him; none of which are done in these times, though it is most fitting of all to observe these things toward him. For he is, beyond the other gods, exceedingly beneficial to the human race, the curator and tutor of men, and the physician whose healing would lead our race to the highest felicity. 

Therefore I will try to explain his power to you. You, in turn, will teach others what you perceive from me today. It is necessary first to learn what the nature of men once was, and what were its passions. For it was not once as it is now, but far different. 

In the beginning there were three kinds of men, not only the two we have now, male and female, but a certain third kind was present, composed of both. Only its name remains to us; the thing itself has perished. For it was then 'Androgynous' (*Androgynum*) both in species and in name, mixed from the male and female sex. The thing itself failed, leaving only an infamous name. 

Furthermore, the whole species of each man was round, having a back and sides in a circle, four hands, as many legs, two faces on a round neck, and altogether similar. One head for both faces turned in opposite directions. Four ears, two genitalia, and other single parts as one can conveniently imagine from these. It walked then both upright as now, in whichever direction it wished; and whenever it contended to go more quickly, like those who, with their heads down and legs up, perform a circular dance, it was then borne in a swift circle supported by eight members. 

The three kinds were such because the male was generated from the Sun, the female from the Earth, and the mixed from the Moon. For the Moon participates in both. They were spherical in figure and motion because they were like their parents. Hence they were of robust body and elated mind. Wherefore they attempted to fight with the gods and to ascend into heaven, as Homer writes of Ephialtes and Otus [[margin: Iliad 1]]. 

Jupiter and the other gods consulted on what should be done. There was no small ambiguity in the matter. For they did not find how they might kill them and destroy the race with lightning as they did the Giants—for if the human race were extinct, the human cult and veneration of the gods would perish—nor did they think they should be permitted to persevere in such insolence. Finally Jupiter explained his opinion. 

'I have found,' he said, 'a way by which it can happen that men exist and yet are more modest. And that will be if they are made weaker. I will now divide each one into two parts. From this they will be both weaker and it also benefits us more. For those who worship us will be more numerous. They will walk rightly on two legs. But if they seem again to rise up impiously, I will cut them into two again, so that they are forced to hop on a single leg, being lame.' 

Having said this, he divided each into two, like those who divide eggs to pickle them in salt, or those who cut eggs with hairs. He commanded Apollo that, as soon as the partition was made, he should turn the face and neck of each toward that part where it was cut, so that seeing his section he might become more modest; and he ordered him to heal the rest. 

Apollo immediately turned the face and, drawing the skin from everywhere into what is now called the belly—like contracted pouches—and making one mouth, he tied it in the middle of the belly. This knot they call the navel (*umbilicum*). And he smoothed most of the other wrinkles and distinguished the breasts part by part, using an instrument such as tanners use when they polish the wrinkles of hides; but he left some around the middle of the belly and the navel, so that they might represent our ancient passion as a kind of scar. 

After the nature of men was thus divided, since each desired his own half, they ran to one another and, throwing their arms around each other, they embraced, desiring to be fused into one. Whence they failed from hunger and torpor, because they never wanted to be separated. And when one half died and the other remained, the survivor sought another half and joined with it, whether it was the half of a whole female—which we now call a woman—or of a man. And so the race of men was perishing. 

Wherefore Jupiter, taking pity, devised another remedy: he changed the genitalia and transferred them from the back to the front. For before, since they had these at the buttocks, they did not generate in one another but, scattering seed on the earth like cicadas, they conceived and generated. But when he transposed them to the front, through these he made generation be fulfilled in one another: by the male in the female, for this reason—so that if a man were mixed with a woman in embrace, they might propagate the species of men. But if a male with a male, they might be moved away from the embrace by satiety and, turned to the management of affairs, they might take care of life. 

From that time, mutual love has been innate in men, the reconciler of the ancient nature, striving to make one out of two and to heal the nature of men. Each of us is therefore a half of a man, like the little fish called *Plecttae* [[notes: flatfish like sole]], who being cut become two from one. Each perpetually seeks his own half. 

Wherefore those men who are a portion of the promiscuous kind, which was once called Androgynous, are fond of women and adulterers are mostly found from these. From this kind also adulteresses take their origin. Whatever women are fond of men and adulteresses are born from this stock. But those women who are a part of a woman do not desire men much, but affect women more, and hence women who desire women are born. 

But those who are a part of the male follow males. While they are boys, seeing that they are a particle of the male, they love men and rejoice in constant familiarity and congress with men. These are the most generous of all boys and adolescents, seeing that they are by nature more virile than all others. Some falsely call these impudent. For they do this not from any impudence, but from a certain generousness, fortitude, and masculine nature—for they congratulate their like. 

The evident argument of this is that when they have grown up, they alone turn to civil administration and emerge as excellent men; and established in the age of manhood, they love adolescents, but by nature they despise marriage and the generation of children, though they are forced by law. A celibate life pleases them. Altogether, then, such a man loves virtue in males and is studious of friends, always congratulating his kinsman. 

Therefore, as often as someone's half meets him, whatever sex he may be eager for, they are most vehemently stirred and stupefied, and they burn with friendship, familiarity, and love, and they do not allow themselves to be separated even for a moment, so to speak. These are the ones who proceed to love through their whole life, yet they cannot express what they especially expect from one another. For it does not seem to be Venereal coitus for the sake of which one delights so much in the company of the other. It is certainly something else that the soul of each desires, which it cannot express, but rather divines and conjectures, and marks its innate affect with obscure traces. 

But if Vulcan [[notes: Hephaestus]] were to stand over them as they lay together with his tools and ask, 'What is it, O men, that you require from one another?' and as they hesitated he asked again, 'Is this what you long for—to meet as much as possible in one and the same, so that you are separated from one another neither by day nor by night? If you affect this, I will melt you and confound you into the same, so that from two you become one, and both in this life and among the dead you may always remain one. See if this is what you burn for, and if it will be enough for you if you become masters of this.' 

If Vulcan were to ask so, it is clear that no one would refuse, or would seem to desire anything else than this. For it is clear that each would think he had found what he had once desired—namely, to be made one from two by congress and mixture with the beloved. The cause of this is that the ancient nature of men was this, and we were whole. The desire and effort for restoring the whole took the name of love. 

Once indeed, as I narrated above, we were one. Then because of injustice we were split by God, just as the Arcadians were by the Lacedaemonians. It is to be feared, moreover, that if we are less modest toward the gods than is fitting, we may be divided again and become such as those who are figured on columns, having our noses cut like those of the thinnest animals called *Lispae*. 

But for the sake of these things, it is fitting for each to worship the gods with the highest piety, and to exhort others to this, so that we may avoid these things and attain those, as our leader Love and commander admonishes us; whom no one would dare to oppose. He opposes him who is an adversary to the gods. For if, being reconciled to God, we have him propitious, each will find and attain his own longed-for half. Which few indeed do in these times. 

And let not that Eryximachus of yours scold this speech of mine, as if I were speaking of Pausanias and Agatho—for perhaps they are of these, and both are males by nature. I assert indeed of all men and women, that our race will finally be happy if we fulfill the impetus of love, and each enjoys his own delights, being restored entirely to the ancient nature. If this is something most happy, it follows that from those things now granted to us, that which is closest to it is best: that is, that each should find those who are by nature dear to his heart. Praising the God who is the cause of this, we ought rightly to praise Love, who in the present time helps us exceedingly while he leads us to that which is proper to each, and for the future offers us the highest hope—if we piously worship the gods—of restoring us to our old figure and healing us to make us most blessed. 

This is my speech about love, Eryximachus, different from yours. I pray that you do not scold it, so that we may hear what each of the rest brings forth—or rather, what both of them bring forth. For only Agatho and Socrates remain." 

"I will comply with you," said Eryximachus, "for your speech pleases me. And unless I knew Socrates and Agatho to be eloquent in amatory matters, I would vehemently doubt lest words fail them, because so many and various things have been said. But I still have confidence in them." 

"You yourself have also struggled strenuously, O Eryximachus," Socrates said. "But if you were established in that degree in which I am now—or rather in which I shall be when Agatho has also spoken skillfully—you would then especially dread and be pressed on all sides by difficulties." 

"You wish to circumvent me with incantations, O Socrates," Agatho replied, "so that I may tremble in your sight, because you have a great expectation of me as if in a theater, as if I were about to speak most elegantly." 

"I would be too forgetful, O Agatho," Socrates said, "if I thought you would be terrified now by us, who are so few men, when I saw you so bravely and generously ascend the tragic pulpit along with the actors, and bring forth your poems without any movement of terror before such a great multitude of spectators." [[margin: A prudent man should fear the judgment of a few wise men more than many fools.]] 

"Do not think me so studious of the theater and devoted to its favor," said Agatho, "as to ignore that for a prudent man, the judgment of a few wise men is more to be feared than that of many fools." 

"I would judge unfairly, Agatho," Socrates said, "if I thought anything rustic of you. I know indeed that if you met some who were wise in your judgment, you would care more for them than for the crowd. But see that we ourselves are not such. We were there too, counted in the number of the common people. But if you met other wise men, would you not fear lest you did something inept in their sight? Or do you say otherwise?" "No." "For you report the truth," said Agatho. "But you would not fear the crowd if you thought you committed something inept," said Socrates. 

Here Phaedrus said, "O friend Agatho, if you proceed to answer Socrates, he will care nothing for how other things are done here, provided he has someone with whom to dispute, especially a beautiful one. Indeed, I gladly hear Socrates disputing. Nevertheless, I must take care that love is praised by each in a certain order. Therefore, praise the God both of you first; afterward you shall dispute with one another at your own pleasure."

->centered: #### AGATHO’S SPEECH ####<-

[[margin: Right reason for praising.]] "**Y**ou speak excellently, Phaedrus," Agatho said, "nor does anything prohibit me from speaking. With Socrates, indeed, it will be possible to dispute often at other times. But I will now first show how one should speak, then I will speak. 

It seems to me that everyone who has spoken until now has not praised the God himself, but has narrated to men the benefits which are happily conferred by him. But what he himself is like, who is the cause of these goods, no one has yet expressed. The only right reason for praising in all things is that by which the nature of the one being discussed is shown first, then the things of which he is the cause are declared. Thus also in the present, it is fitting to show first what love himself is, then to explain his gifts. 

I assert that since all gods are happy, Love—if it is permitted and tolerable to say—is the happiest of all, seeing that he exists as the most beautiful and best of all. That he is the most beautiful is clear first because, O Phaedrus, he is the youngest of all the gods. He himself provides an evident argument for this, as he flees old age—swiftly indeed, as it arrives faster than it ought; love by nature hates it and flees it, but mixes with youths. [[margin: Like rejoices in like.]] The old proverb is rightly carried about: that like always clings to like. 

And though I concede many things to Phaedrus, in this one thing I do not at all assent: that love is older than Saturn and Iapetus. Rather, I say he is young beyond the other gods, and always young. Those ancient deeds of the gods which Hesiod and Parmenides describe are to be attributed to Necessity rather than to love, if indeed they told the truth. For they would not have castrated and bound one another, and many other violent things would not have happened to the gods then, if love had been with them; but benevolence and the highest peace would have reigned, as they do now, from the time when love began to rule the gods. 

Therefore he is young, and moreover tender and soft. There is need of some such poet as Homer was to demonstrate the tender softness of love. Homer says that Ate—that is, Calamity—is a goddess and soft. Namely, to show that her feet are tender, he says she never treads the floors but walks upon the heads of men. He seems to have used a clear conjecture that he is tender because he does not walk through hard things, but touches soft ones. 

We must use the same argument for those wishing to show that Love is tender. For he does not go through the earth and skulls, which are not at all soft, but fixes himself in the softest of all things and remains. Namely, he places his seat in the souls and minds of gods and men. Nor yet in just any souls; for if he finds a soul of hard habit, he flees; but if he finds a mild and soft one, he inhabits it. Since therefore he always touches the softest parts of the softest things with his feet and his whole self, it is necessary that Love be most tender. Wherefore Love is both young and tender beyond all others. 

Furthermore, he is liquid and slippery like water. For he could not flow around every soul from every side, and flow in and out secretly, if he were hard and rigid. His beauty of form, which Love is decorated with beyond all others, can be an argument for his aptly composed and flexible shape. Furthermore, between deformity and love there is a perpetual battle. The decorum of his color also signifies the constant habitation of this God among flowers. For in that which lacks flowers or has deflowered, whether body or soul or whatever else it may be, Love himself does not sit. But wherever there is a flowery and fragrant place, he rests most gratefully. 

Many more things could be brought forth concerning the beauty of this god, but these suffice. Next, one must speak of the virtue of love. What is to be valued most of all is that Love neither inflicts injury on God or man, nor suffers injury from God or man. For he himself does not suffer by force, if he suffers anything. For violence does not touch love. Nor does he do anything by force, if he does anything. For everyone obeys love voluntarily in each thing. Whatever someone contracts willingly with another who is willing is held just, as the laws of the royal city establish. 

Nor is he a participant in justice alone, but also in the highest temperance. [[margin: All pleasures are overcome by love.]] Since it is agreed among all that temperance is to rule over lusts and pleasures, and no pleasure is more powerful than love. But if all pleasures are weaker than love, they are surely overcome by him, and he rules. Therefore Love, because he rules over lusts and pleasures, is wondrously temperate. 

Regarding fortitude, moreover, not even Mars resists Love. For Mars does not hold love, but the love of Venus, as it is said, holds Mars; and that which holds is more powerful than that which is held. But he who rules over the bravest of others is undoubtedly to be judged the bravest of all. Concerning the justice, temperance, and fortitude of this god, enough has been said. 

It remains to speak of his wisdom, which must be carried out according to our strength. First, so that I may honor my own art just as Eryximachus honored his, this god is a poet so wise that he can make others poets too. For anyone, though he was previously rude, emerges as a poet as soon as love has breathed upon him. From which one can clearly conjecture that love is a skilled poet, and in short, that he contains all musical numbers of poetry. [[margin: What one does not know, he cannot give or show to another.]] For what someone neither has nor knows, he cannot give or show to another. 

Who would doubt that through the wisdom of love all animals are begotten and born? Moreover, do we not seem to be given the faculty of the arts by this God? And that the man of whom he is the teacher excels in any art and emerges as famous? On the contrary, he who is not touched by love lies in obscurity? For Apollo, who is the disciple of Love, found the skill of archery, medicine, and divination with appetite and love as his guide. Similarly the Muses found music. Vulcan found the art of working in bronze. Minerva found the craft of weaving. Jupiter found the governance of gods and men. 

Wherefore the affairs of the gods were disposed with love intervening—love, I say, of beauty; for love does not follow deformity. But before, as I said at the beginning, many and atrocious things happened among the gods because of the reign of Necessity, as it is said. But after this god was born from the desire for beautiful things, all goods came forth both to gods and to men. Thus it seems to me, O Phaedrus, that love himself is first most beautiful and best, and then he bestows such things on others too. 

Something metric occurs to me at present: 
'This is the god who bestows peace on the human race, 
Peace on the sea and a serene face to the deep, 
Rest to the winds, a bed for man, 
And permits sleep for cares.' 

He removes rusticity from us, he reconciles us with familiarity, congregating all such assemblies. In solemn and festive days, in dances, in sacrifices, he is our leader and president. Bringing forth mildness, exterminating ferocity, the bestower of benevolence, the expeller of all malevolence; propitious, beneficial, to be looked upon by the wise, pleasing to the gods, longed for by those who lack him, to be possessed and held by those who participate in him. The father of delights, of soft allurements, of the sweet perfusion of graces and of desire. Studious of the good, the despiser of the evil; in labor, in fear, in desire, in speech, he is the governor, the perfect helper, and the primary savior. The glory of all gods and men, and the most beautiful and best leader. Whom every man ought to follow, and every man who is a participant in that song which love himself sings should venerate with noble hymns, sooting the minds of gods and men. 

Therefore, Phaedrus, let this speech of mine be vowed to the god, filled partly with jests and partly with serious matters according to the faculty of my genius." 

When Agatho had said these things, as Aristodemus related, all the guests approved of the speech with a certain greatest applause; seeing that it was seen to have been held as was worthy both of Agatho and the God. Wherefore Socrates, turning to Eryximachus, said, "Do I not seem now to have rightly feared before, O son of Acumenus, when I prophesied what truly happened—that Agatho would speak most elegantly, wherefore I thought words would fail me?" 

"In one thing," Eryximachus replied, "I think you prophesied correctly: that Agatho would speak skillfully. But that facundity would fail you, not at all." 

"Who," said Socrates, "neither I nor anyone else would be deterred in speaking, who must speak after such a brilliant and copious oration? And other things indeed which are aptly composed in any way do not seem so wondrous; but the elegance of names and words which he used at the end of the oration—if anyone notices it, he will be immediately stupefied. Since I myself understood that I could not come near to his eloquence, I was nearly moved by shame to go elsewhere from here, if it had been permitted. Indeed the speech of Gorgias [[notes: a famous Sophist]] reminded me of what Homer said. I feared that Agatho, imposing an end to his words, would transmit the head of the eloquent Gorgias from his speech into mine, making me mute and rendering me a stone instead of a man. 

Then at last I recognized that I had rashly promised that I would praise love among you to the best of my power, and that I had ineptly professed amatory matters, when I altogether did not know by what reason each thing should be praised. I thought indeed, on account of my rudeness, that true things ought to be reported about whatever is praised by us, and that this should be present and allowed; and that from these, selecting the most beautiful, we ought to ascribe them as decently as possible. Wherefore I was elated with a certain great hope, as if I were about to speak rightly, since I had, as it seemed, the true rationale for praising. 

But finally, this method of praise appeared not congruent. For it seems necessary to ascribe all the greatest and most noble things of the thing we praise, whether they are truly present in it or not. [[margin: Praise is censured in which true things are reported but false ones are preferred.]] For it matters nothing whether they are false or true, since it is proposed not how love himself is praised, but rather that each one should seem to praise love as much as possible. Wherefore you have attributed everything to love, and have affirmed that he is such and the cause of such and so many things, so that he may appear most beautiful and best—namely, to the ignorant. For to those who understand, such a broad and pure thing would never be judged right. 

Indeed I was altogether ignorant of this method of praise. Unknowing, therefore, I agreed with you that I too would praise him among the others. My tongue therefore promised, but my mind not at all. Let such a praise be absent from me. For I could not extol him in that way. Nevertheless, if you wish, I desire to speak true things in my own ritual, and to look at myself rather than to contend with your orations, lest I move laughter. See therefore, Phaedrus, whether it pleases you to hear such an oration now which narrates only true things about love, proceeding with whatever composition of words and names happens to occur." 

Phaedrus said, "It certainly pleases me and the others that you speak in your own judgment." "Concede to me, O Phaedrus," Socrates said, "that I may ask Agatho a few things, so that having been confirmed by him I may speak." "I concede indeed," Phaedrus replied. "Just ask." Then he narrated that Socrates made this beginning of speaking.

->centered: #### SOCRATIS’ DISCOURSE ####<-

"**B**est friend Agatho, you seem to have laid the foundations of your oration when you said that first what love is should be shown, and afterward his works enumerated. This beginning I indeed greatly approve. Come, therefore, since you have spoken so ornately and magnificently of love in other respects, declare this to me besides concerning his nature: whether love is such that he is the love of something, or of nothing. I do not ask whether he is the love of some mother or father. For that would be a ridiculous interrogation—namely, whether the love of a father or mother is love. But if I were to ask whether a father was the father of someone or not, you would surely reply, if you wished to speak congruently, that a father is the father of a son or a daughter. Is it not so?" 

"Entirely," Agatho said. 

"And is not a mother the mother of someone?" And he consented to that. "Answer furthermore," Socrates said, "a few things, so that you may better understand what I mean. Is a brother, in what he is, the brother of someone?" He said yes. "Is he not of a brother or a sister?" "Of these surely." 

"Try similarly to show us about love, whether love is the love of something or of nothing." "Of something, certainly." "Keep this in memory, of what he is the love. And answer to this: whether love appetites that very thing of which he is the love, or not." "And most of all, indeed." "Does he have this very thing with him, and yet appetite and love what he has? Or rather, does he not have what he both loves and appetites?" 

"It is likely that he does not have it." 

"Consider furthermore whether it is necessary, instead of just likely, that whatever appetites, appetites that which it lacks; and if it does not lack, it does not desire. To me indeed this pleases in a wondrous way, as being necessary. But how does it seem to you, Agatho?" "The same as to you," replied Agatho. 

"You speak well. Would a great man wish to be great, and a robust man wish to be robust? From those things which we conceded above, it seems to me that it cannot happen. For he would not be in need of those things which he already contained in himself." 

"He says true things. For if he who is robust should wish to be robust, and he who is swift to be swift, and finally he who is healthy to be healthy—perhaps someone would believe that these, and others, appetite those things they have. Lest we be deceived here, I say these things for this reason. If you notice these things diligently, Agatho, you will see it is necessary that whatever they have in the present time, they have the same in the same time, whether they wish or not; but who would desire this very thing? 

When someone adds: 'but while I am healthy, I indeed wish to be healthy; and while I am rich, to be rich; and therefore, I desire what I have'; to him we immediately reply: 'O good man, you having attained riches, health, and strength, wish to possess these also in the future time: since in the present you have them whether you wish or not.' Do you see, therefore, when you say 'I desire what is present to me,' whether you infer anything else than this: 'what is present to me now, I also long to have present in the future.' Do you think, Agatho, this man would answer this or something else?" 

"Nothing else," said Agatho. "Love of this kind surely looks to that which is not yet at hand nor possessed: namely, that those things be present and preserved in the time that follows." "It is so altogether." 

"And he therefore, and anyone else who appetites, appetites what is not yet exposed and prepared, and what is not present, nor what he has, and what he himself is not, or what he lacks. Such things are those of which there is appetite and love." "Such things undoubtedly." 

"Come," Socrates said, "let us repeat what was said above. First, indeed, love was said to be of some things, then especially of those which he lacks." "Certainly," he replied. "Remember furthermore of what things you asserted love to be. I will reduce it to your memory if you wish. Indeed I think you said thus: 'all things among the gods were disposed on account of the love of beautiful things, for of shameful things there is altogether no love.' Did you not say so?" 

"So indeed." 

"You speak probably indeed, O friend. And if it is so, love certainly is the love of beauty, and not at all of ugliness." "I consent." "Is it not conceded that he loves that which he lacks and does not have?" "Conceded plainly." "Therefore love lacks beauty and does not have it." "Necessary." "What then? Do you call that beautiful which lacks beauty and does not have it?" "In no way." "Furthermore, if these things hold so, do you assert love to be beautiful?" 

"I seem to have understood nothing of those things I said above." 

"You spoke rightly. But answer a little further: do not good things seem beautiful to you?" "To me indeed." "If therefore love lacks beautiful things, and good things are beautiful, he also lacks good things." 

"I can in no way resist you, O Socrates. Let it be, therefore, as you say." 

"You could never, O beloved Agatho, oppose the truth, though you could easily oppose Socrates."

**B**UT I will now dismiss Agatho, and I will relate to you, O guests, a discourse about Love which I once received from a fatidical [[notes: prophetic]] woman, Diotima, who was skilled in these matters and understood many other things wisely; she once gave the Athenians a delay of the plague for ten years by performing sacrifices. She instructed me in the amatory faculty. Those things which she said, I will try to express to you by myself according to those things which were agreed between me and Agatho. 

It is necessary first, O Agatho, as you also explained, to show what and of what kind love is, then to enumerate his works. It is better, it seems to me, to relate it to you now in the same order as that guest-woman handled me when she examined me. For I predicted nearly the same things to her as Agatho just did to me: that love was a great god and looked to beautiful things. And she redargued me with the same reasons with which I redargued Agatho: that love was neither beautiful, as I said, nor good. 

To her I then said: 'What do you say, O Diotima? Is love therefore base and evil?' And she: 'Speak better things, I pray. Do you think it is necessary that whatever is not beautiful be base?' 'Most certainly.' 'And what is not wise, you think is ignorant? Have you not noticed that there is a certain middle between wisdom and ignorance?' 

'What is that?' 

'To opine rightly—that is, to participate in the truth without a certain rationale. [[margin: Between wisdom and ignorance the middle is right opinion.]] For this is indeed not science, for science is never without a rationale. Nor is it ignorance either. For that which is master of the truth is not called ignorance. Something of this kind is right opinion, a middle between wisdom and ignorance.' 

'You tell true things,' I said. 

'Therefore do not force what is not beautiful to be base, or what is not good to be evil. By the same reason, although you concede love to be neither beautiful nor good, you should not therefore think he is necessarily base or evil, but a middle between these. [[margin: Love is middle between base and beautiful.]] But in this all consent: that love is a great god.' 

'Do you say all the ignorant,' she asked, 'or the knowing?' 'All,' I said. 

'In what way,' she asked laughing, 'would they confess him to be a great god, who do not even want him to be a god at all?' 'Who are these?' I asked. 'You are one,' she said, 'and I am another.' 'In what way do you assert I said this?' 

'I will show you easily. Tell me, do you not affirm all the gods to be beautiful and happy? Would you dare to say any of the gods was not beautiful or not happy?' 'Not by Jove.' 'And do you not call those happy who possess good and beautiful things?' 'Only those.' 

'But you admitted in the prior parts that love, on account of his lack of beautiful and good things, appetites these very things which he lacks.' 'I admitted it indeed.' 'In what way then is he a God,' she asked, 'who is devoid of beautiful and good things?' 'In no way. So you do not think love is a God?' 

'What then?' I asked. 'Is love mortal?' 'Not at all.' 'What then?' 'Like the ones above, a middle between mortal and immortal.' 'What is he, O Diotima?' 

'A great *daemon* [[notes: spirit or intermediary]], O Socrates. For the whole nature of *daemones* is middle between mortals and gods.' [[margin: Nature of daemones.]] 'What power does he have?' 

'He interprets and carries human things to the Gods, and divine things to men: of the former their prayers and sacrifices, of the latter their commands and solemn sacred rites, institutions, and order. Being established in both as a middle, he completes the whole, so that the universe is connected with itself by such a link.'

[[summary: This text presents the opening of Plato's Symposium as translated and commented upon by the Renaissance philosopher Marsilio Ficino. It covers the various speeches given in praise of Love (Eros), moving from historical myths and social ethics to the philosophical definition of Love as an intermediary spirit (daemon) between humanity and the divine.]]

# On Justice.                                                                 649

[Left Column]

**SOC.** You might also say this: what do those skilled in the art of measuring do when they distinguish between the Large and the Small? Do they not measure? 
**HO.** Certainly. 
**SOC.** What? Do those who judge concerning the Heavy and the Light not weigh <note>original: *appendunt*. This refers to the act of hanging items on a balance scale.</note> them? 
**HO.** They weigh them. 
**SOC.** Now, what will you say of those who pronounce judgment on matters of the Just and the Unjust? Answer. 
**HO.** I truly cannot. 
**SOC.** Would you not say they are reasoning <term>reasoning: the Latin *ratiocinari* implies a process of calculation or logical deduction, suggesting that justice is a "math of the soul"</term> correctly? 
**HO.** I think so. 
**SOC.** Therefore, judges, who pass sentence among us, surely reason when they judge concerning the Just and the Unjust. 
**HO.** I agree. 
**SOC.** But those who practice the art of measuring measure the Small and the Large. For we said that **Measure** <note>original: *Mensura*. Here used as the specific tool or standard of the art of geometry.</note> is that by which such things are judged. 
**HO.** We did say that. 
**SOC.** But again, those who have devoted their study to the art of weighing weigh the Heavy and the Light. For the **Scale** <note>original: *statera*. A balance or steelyard.</note> was for us that very thing by which those things are usually discerned. 
**HO.** It certainly was.

<summary>Socrates uses the analogies of measuring size and weighing objects to argue that judging Justice and Injustice is an art of "reasoning" or "calculation." He establishes that just as scales are the tool for weight, reasoning is the specific tool used by judges to determine what is right.</summary>

...are men born good? And by examining this very thing in this way, perhaps we will find out. This refers to a "techne"—a specialized craft, art, or branch of knowledge that can be taught.</note> by which they may recognize the natures of good horses, and thus understand which horses are both physically fit for racing and brave in spirit, and which, on the other hand, are sluggish? **FRIEND.** There are. **SOCR.** What then is that skill?
