652 [tab] On Deliberation.

[Left Column]
...of those very ones who give counsel, as is fitting, to be able to provide just that. Wherefore I can devise no reason why the eagerness of those who think they are able to give you counsel should not appear ridiculous. But regarding the vote <note>original: *suffragium*. In a Greek city-state context, this refers to the formal casting of a ballot or show of hands in the assembly.</note> which you intend to cast, I am in great doubt as to what its power might be. For will you decree that those who know <note>The "experts" or those with specific knowledge of the matter at hand.</note> should give counsel? Yet will they not give the same advice, no more than one person would, and not in different ways about the same thing? For which reason it will not be necessary for you to cast a vote regarding them. Or will you appoint the unskilled, and those who do not give counsel as they ought, to give counsel? But these are no more to be consulted than madmen. But if you will pass judgment neither on the skilled nor the unskilled, whom will you judge from the beginning to be fit for giving counsel? How indeed is it at all fitting for others to give you counsel, if you yourselves are able to judge these things? But if you cannot judge, what benefit can votes be to you? Or in what way is it not ridiculous that you—as if you were in need of counsel and not fit to find it for yourselves—have assembled; yet, once you have assembled, you think that a sentence <note>original: *sententiam*. Here, a formal opinion or decision reached by the group.</note> must be passed by you, as if you were able to judge? For it must not be said that you were each individually unrefined <note>original: *rudeis*. Lacking training or education in the subject.</note>, but after you came together in one place, you became wise; nor, moreover, that you doubted in private, but as soon as you came here, you no longer doubt, but have become fit to perceive those things which must be done by you—even though you have learned these things from no one, nor have you found them out yourselves, which is by far the most difficult thing of all. For unless you are able to know what must be done by you, you will never be able to judge whether he who gives you counsel does so rightly. Nor, moreover, will any single person who gives you counsel say that he [will show] you what you [must do]...

<summary>This page presents a Socratic argument regarding the paradox of deliberation: if a group of people is ignorant of a subject, they are incapable of judging which advisor is actually an expert, making the act of voting on counsel logically absurd.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue "On Deliberation" (the pseudo-Platonic *Sisyphus*). Socrates is continuing his inquiry into how one can judge the truth of a speaker's words and whether a single perspective is sufficient for understanding.</meta>

On Deliberation. [space] 653

...how will it be possible that he does not understand the matter? Therefore, as I listened to these men, I began to doubt, nor did I have a basis for what I should judge. Some others, indeed, who were present, were affirming that the first speaker spoke the truth. I ask you, therefore, if you have anything to bring forward <note>original: *in medium proferas*, meaning to offer for public consideration or debate.</note> regarding these matters: whether it is possible, when only one person speaks, to understand what he says; or is there a need for a second person to respond, if it is to be possible at all for someone to know whether the speaker speaks correctly? Or rather, is it not necessary to hear both? Or what do you think?

A little while ago, a certain man was accusing another, because he was willing neither to lend him money <note>original: *argentum*, literally "silver." In antiquity, silver was the standard for currency.</note> nor to trust him with it. And indeed, the one who was accused defended himself. But another person from among those who were present asked the accuser this: "Did this man indeed err, who did not trust you nor lend to you? Or did you not also err, you who did not persuade him to lend?" "How then," he said, "did I err? Which of the two..."

<summary>Socrates explores whether a listener can judge the truth of a statement by hearing only one speaker or if a dialogue between two parties is necessary. He illustrates the complexity of persuasion through an anecdote about a man failing to secure a loan.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue "Sisyphus," where Socrates challenges the definition of political deliberation, and then begins a new dialogue, "Eryxias," which explores the nature of wealth.</meta>

On Deliberation. 655

**Socrates.** Which, then, Sisyphus, do you think a person should do if they do not know something—seek it out, or learn it? **Sisyphus.** By Hercules! <note>original: *mehercule*, an oath to the god Hercules.</note> They should learn it. **Socrates.** You are quite right. But do you think learning is better than seeking because someone can find what they need more quickly and easily if they learn from those who know, rather than seeking it while they themselves are unskilled? Or is there some other reason? **Sisyphus.** No, it is for that reason. **Socrates.** Why then did you all yesterday—both you and the leaders of the city—not cast aside the plan of deliberating and seeking out what you did not know was best for the Republic, and instead learn from someone who knows how you might achieve the best results? Instead, as it seemed to me, you sat there the entire day mixing things together and guessing blindly <note>original: *ariolantes*, referring to the practice of soothsayers or diviners guessing at the future.</note> about what you did not know, utterly neglecting the pursuit of learning. Perhaps you will say that I say these things to you only for the sake of a joke in our discussion, rather than demonstrating them seriously; but I ask you, Sisyphus, to attend carefully to this now. If it were granted that "Deliberation" is a specific thing, and that what we are saying now is not true—namely, that it seems to be nothing other than knowledge, conjecture, and invention (even if a more serious name is used for it)—do you think that in the matter of deliberating well and showing themselves to be good counselors, men differ from one another just as they do in all other disciplines? For instance, do blacksmiths differ from other blacksmiths, doctors from doctors, and flute-players from flute-players? And as all other craftsmen are themselves different from one another in the same arts, do you think that in deliberating, too, some people differ from others? **Sisyphus.** I certainly think so. **Socrates.** Tell me then: do not all who deliberate—whether they do so well or poorly—deliberate about the future? **Sisyphus.** Very much so. **Socrates.** And what else can we say here, except that future things do not yet exist? **Sisyphus.** Nothing else. **Socrates.** For if they already existed, they would no longer be "future," but would already be here; would they not? **Sisyphus.** Indeed. **Socrates.** If, therefore, they do not exist in any way, then by the same logic they have not happened, since they do not exist. **Sisyphus.** Not at all, by Hercules. **Socrates.** If, then, they have not yet happened, they have no nature as yet that is properly theirs. **Sisyphus.** None at all. **Socrates.** Therefore, do not all who deliberate—whether well or poorly—deliberate about things that neither are, nor were, nor have any nature, since they are deliberating about the future? **Sisyphus.** It seems so. **Socrates.** Does it seem possible, then, for someone to achieve—either well or poorly—that which exists nowhere? **Sisyphus.** What is your reasoning for saying this? **Socrates.** I will explain to you what I mean; please pay attention. Among many archers, how would you recognize who is skilled and who is unskilled? This does not seem difficult to know. For perhaps you would order them to aim their arrows at a target; <note>original: *σκοπὸν* (skopon), a mark or goal to aim at.</note> would you not? **Sisyphus.** Certainly. **Socrates.** You would then judge him to be the winner who most often sends his arrows so that he hits the mark accurately. **Sisyphus.** I certainly would. **Socrates.** But if no target were set up at which they were to direct their arrows, but each person shot wherever he wished, how could you know who shot well or poorly? **Sisyphus.** In no way. **Socrates.** In the same way, you would not know how to distinguish those who deliberate well or poorly if they do not know what they are deliberating about. **Sisyphus.** True. **Socrates.** Certainly it is true; for if those who deliberate are deliberating about future things, are they not deliberating about things that do not exist? **Sisyphus.** Exactly. **Socrates.** But it is not possible for someone to reach that which exists nowhere. For by what logic does it seem possible to you that someone could achieve what is nowhere? **Sisyphus.** None. **Socrates.** Since, then, it is not possible for anyone to reach what does not exist, there will no longer be anyone who deliberates about things that are not. For "Fortune" is numbered among those things that do not exist; is that not how it stands? **Sisyphus.** It seems so to me. **Socrates.** Therefore, no one who fails to reach future things can be either a good or a bad counselor. **Sisyphus.** It does not seem so. **Socrates.** Indeed, no one will be able to be a better or worse counselor than another, unless they either reach what does not exist more happily, or miss it more unhappily. **Sisyphus.** They will not. **Socrates.** Toward what, then, are people looking when they call certain men good and bad counselors? Is this not something, Sisyphus, that seems worthy of our thinking about again and again?

## ->OR OTHERWISE,<-
## ->ERASISTRATUS,<-
## ->SOCRATES.<-

While I and Eryxias of Stiria <note>note: A "deme" or district in ancient Athens.</note> happened to be walking in the Portico of Zeus the Deliverer, <note>original: *porticu Iouis Liberatoris*. Known in Greek as the Stoa of Zeus Eleutherios, a famous meeting place in the Athenian Agora.</note> Critias and Erasistratus (the son of Phæax and nephew of Erasistratus) came toward us. Of these, Erasistratus, who had then recently returned from Sicily and those regions, approached more closely and said, "Greetings, Socrates." "And greetings to you," I said; "do you bring us any news from Sicily? Do you have anything fine to report to us?" "Very much so; but," he said, "do you wish for us to sit down? For I am still tired from the journey, having set out from Megara yesterday." "Let it be so, if it seems right." "What then," he said, "do you first wish to hear of the things there? Whether it is what the Sicilians are doing, or how they are disposed toward our Republic? For it seems to me they are disposed toward us no differently than wasps; which, if they are slightly irritated or provoked, become invincible until someone attacks them and extinguishes them utterly. Such is the disposition of the Syracusans. For unless someone intending to wage a great war sets out there with a massive fleet, that city will never come under our jurisdiction and power; instead, it will be so irritated by these small fleets that it will be most troublesome to us in the future. Now, however, they have sent ambassadors to us, with the intent (as it seems to me) of deceiving our city." Meanwhile, while we were talking in this way, the ambassadors of the Syracusans arrived by chance. Therefore, Erasistratus, pointing out one of them to us, said: "That man, Socrates, is the wealthiest of all the Sicilians and Italians." "And why," I said, "should he not be the wealthiest, who has land so broad that it can provide opportunity for anyone who wishes to practice agriculture far and wide—and such land as could not easily be found elsewhere in all of Greece? And who has other things that pertain to wealth separately: slaves, horses, gold, and silver?" Seeing that he was now being led to say even more about the man's resources, I asked him: "What then, Erasistratus? What sort of man does he seem to be in Sicily?" "He seems to be," he replied, "the most wicked of all the Sicilians and Italians—and he is as wicked as he is wealthy. So much so, that if you were to ask any Sicilian who they thought was the most wicked and the wealthiest...

[[margin: Divination and magic are granted through spirits (*daemones*).]]

Through this, every prophecy (*vaticinium*) proceeds, as does the diligence of priests concerning sacrifices, expiations, incantations, all divination, and magic. Indeed, God does not mix with man, but through this medium, all commerce and colloquy between the Gods and men is conducted, both while we are awake and while we sleep. Whoever is skilled in these matters is called *daimonios* (divine), that is, a happy and wise man. But those who are clever in other arts and faculties that are performed by the hands are called *banausos* (menial), that is, mercenaries. For indeed, these

[[margin: Love is one of the spirits (*daemones*).]]

spirits (*daemones*) are many and varied. One of these is Love (*Amor*). I asked, "Who then are the parents of Love?" "Though it is a lengthy tale to tell," she said, "I will nevertheless explain it. When Venus was born, the other gods sat down for a prepared banquet, including *Metis* (Counsel), who is the son of the god of abundance. When they had dined, *Penia* (Poverty), acting as a beggar for food—since the feast there was abundant—came and waited about the doors. *Porus* (Resource), indeed, being drunk on nectar (for wine did not yet exist), entered the garden of Jove (Jupiter) and, heavy with sleep, began to slumber. Penia, compelled by her own lack, devised a plan for how she might conceive a son from Porus by a kind of ambush. Therefore, she lay down next to him and conceived Love. Hence Love was born as a follower and servant of Venus, because he was begotten on the birthday of Venus. By his fifth nature, he is seized by a desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is beautiful. Because Love is the son of Porus and Penia, he happened to turn out like this: First, he is always poor, and far from being soft and beautiful as most people think; instead, he is dry and squalid, barefoot, always flying on the ground, without a home, without bedding or any covering, sleeping at the doors or in the street under the open sky, and preserving the nature of his mother, he is always in need. Second, according to the lineage of his father, he lies in wait for the beautiful and the good; he is manly, bold, vehement, a sharp hunter, always weaving new stratagems, a seeker of prudence, eloquent, philosophizing through his whole life, an incantator, a powerful fascinator, a sorcerer, and a sophist. He is not entirely immortal by nature, nor is he mortal; but sometimes in the same day he flourishes and lives, as often as he overflows; at other times he fails and then lives again because of his father's nature. But what he acquires continually flows away beneath him. Therefore, Love is never a pauper, nor is he ever wealthy. Furthermore, he is established between wisdom (*sapientia*) and ignorance (*inscitia*). For this is how the matter stands: None of the gods philosophizes or desires to become wise, for they are already so. Nor does anyone else who is already wise philosophize. On the other hand, those who are entirely ignorant do not philosophize, nor do they desire to become wise. For ignorance has this worst quality: that he who is neither beautiful, good, nor wise nevertheless thinks himself to have these things sufficiently. Therefore, he never seeks those things of which he does not realize he is unworthy." "Who then, Diotima," I asked, "are those who philosophize, if neither the wise nor the ignorant do so?" "Surely even a child would understand this," she said: "namely, those who are in between these two, among whom is Love. Wisdom is indeed something most beautiful, and Love is concerned with the beautiful. From which it necessarily follows that Love is a philosopher; and since he is a philosopher, he holds the middle ground between the ignorant and the wise. The cause of these things lies in his birth. For he was begotten of a wise and wealthy father, but of a mother who was least wise and certainly poor. Such is the nature of this spirit (*daemon*), my friend Socrates. It is no wonder you imagined Love to be such as you did from the opinion you held of his nature. For, as I gather from your words, you thought Love was the one being loved (*amatus*), not the one loving (*amans*); and for that reason, I think Love seemed to you to be all-beautiful. For that which is lovable is indeed beautiful, delicate, perfect, and most blessed. But the lover has another such nature (*idea*), such as I have described above." "Let it be as you say, stranger," I said, "for you speak excellently. But since Love is such as this, what use is he to men?" "This, Socrates," she replied, "I shall next endeavor to teach. Love is indeed of this sort and thus begotten. Moreover, he is of beautiful things, as you yourself say. But if someone should ask: 'For the sake of what is Love of beautiful things, O Socrates and Diotima?' Or more clearly: 'He who loves beautiful things, what does he especially seek from them?' What shall we answer?" "That they should be present to him," I said. "But this response requires a further question of this sort: 'What will he have to whom beautiful things are present?'" "I have no answer ready," I replied. "But if someone," she said, "changing the words and using 'the good' instead of 'the beautiful,' should ask: 'He who loves good things, what does he seek?'" "That they be present to him," I said. "What will he have to whom good things are present?" "The answer to that is easier," I said, "for he will be happy (*felix*). By the possession of good things, those who are blessed are made blessed; nor is there any need to ask further why he who desires happiness wants to be happy, for the answer seems to have reached its end." "You speak the truth," I said. "But do you think this will and this love are common to all men? And that all wish for good things always to be present to them?" "It is clearly common," I replied. "Why then, Socrates, do we not say that everyone loves, since everyone always loves the same things? But instead, we say some love and others do not?" "I wonder at that myself," I said. "But do not wonder. For selecting a certain species of lovers, we name them 'Love,' attributing the name of the whole to them. But in other cases, we use other names." "Give me an example," I asked. "Behold: you know that 'to make' (*facere*) is something broad. For 'making' is generally called the cause by which anything proceeds from not-being into being. Wherefore all actions of every art are 'makings' (*effectiones*), and all artisans are *poetae* (poets), that is, makers (*factores*)." "You tell the truth," I said. "Yet you see that they are not called poets, but are allotted other names. From all making, one selected part—specifically that which concerns music and verses—is called by the name of the whole. For this alone is called 'poesy' (*poësis*), that is, 'making'; and those who possess this part of making are called poets." "These things are true," I said. "The same thing also happens regarding Love. For in sum, every appetite for good things and for happiness is a most great and insidious love for everyone. But those who proceed toward the good through the study of money, or gymnastics, or wisdom, are neither said to 'love' nor are they called 'lovers.' However, those who strive toward it according to a certain species take the name of the whole—namely, Love, and loving, and lovers." "You seem to speak rightly," I said. "Some say that those who seek the half of themselves are 'loving.' But I say that Love is neither of the half nor of the whole, unless it is in some way the good. For men are even willing to cut off their own hands and feet if they seem to be an evil and a ruin to them. For each person does not love what is his own, unless perhaps someone calls that which is good 'his own' and his proper property, and calls that which is evil 'alien.' For men love nothing else besides the good. Does it not seem so to you?" "It certainly does." "Then should it be said simply that men love the good?" "Without a doubt." "And should it not be added that they desire the good to be present to them?" "It should be added." "And not only present, but always present?" "And always." "Love is therefore, in sum, the appetite by which someone desires the good to be always his." "You speak very truly." "Since universal Love is always of this sort, can you say what the primary condition of seeking is, or the mode of pursuing it, and in what

[[page number: 294]]

[[heading: Book Twenty-Five]]

[[margin: Love is the desire for immortality.]]

action or study Love is properly named?" "If I could show that," I said, "I would never have marveled at your wisdom, Diotima, nor would I have come to you for the sake of learning." "Then I shall tell you," she said. "This is a birth in the beautiful (*partus in pulchro*), both according to the soul and according to the body." "One needs a prophecy to understand what you say," I replied, "for I do not perceive it in any way." "I shall speak more plainly. The body of all men is pregnant and heavy, Socrates, and so is the soul. And as soon as we reach a certain age, our nature desires to give birth. But it cannot give birth in the ugly; it can only do so in the beautiful. Surely from the union of man and woman, offspring and birth proceed. This work is divine; and in the mortal animal itself, this is the immortal part: namely, conception and generation. These cannot be completed in that which is out of proportion and dissonant. But the ugly is dissonant from everything that is divine, while the beautiful is consonant with the divine. Therefore, beauty itself is the Fate and the *Lucina* (goddess of childbirth) for generation. Because of this, as often as that which is pregnant draws near to the beautiful, it exults with joy, and is diffused with hilarity and pleasure, and it gives birth. Contrarily, when it approaches the ugly, it is contracted by a certain sadness and pain; it is frightened and restrained and does not beget, but is tormented while retaining the fetus. For this reason, that which has conceived and is now overflowing, gasping toward generation, hovers mostly around the beautiful, since it is relieved from sharp anxiety thereby. For Love, Socrates, is not of the beautiful as you think." "But of what then?" I asked. "Of generation and birth in the beautiful." "Really?" "Really," she said. "Why of generation? Because generation is something everlasting and immortal, as much as can be in a mortal thing. But it is necessary to desire immortality together with the good, from those things which we conceded above, since Love is the appetite by which everyone desires the good to be always present to him. From these things, it is concluded that Love is also the desire for immortality." All these things Diotima handed down to me when she spoke about matters of love. Moreover, she asked this: "What do you think is the cause of this love and desire, Socrates? Do you not see how gravely all living things are affected—both those that walk and those that fly—when they are driven toward generation with their whole force, and are driven mad by the heat of love? First, for the sake of generation, they desire to couple vehemently. Then, how they labor concerning the nourishment of their offspring! For the sake of these, even weak animals demand battle against the most robust, and are prepared to die for them and to perish of hunger, provided they nourish their children, and they boldly undertake anything else. One might think men do these things by a discourse of reason, but what is the cause of such burning love in beasts? Can you assign this cause?" "Not at all," I said. "Do you believe," she asked, "that you will be skilled in amatory matters while you are ignorant of these things?" "For this reason, Diotima," I said, "as I mentioned before, I flee to you, because I recognize that I need a teacher. I pray you, therefore, to bring forward the cause of these and other things pertaining to love." "If you believe the nature of love to be that which we have often said, do not wonder. For from this,

[[margin: Constant change in body and soul.]]

similarly as from what went before, mortal nature strives as much as it can to be always and immortal. But it attains this only by generation, because it always substitutes another young thing in place of the old. For indeed, in the very time when each animal is said to live and be the same—as from childhood to old age—although it is called 'the same,' it never contains the same things in itself, but is always made new and sheds the old, according to hair, flesh, bones, blood, and the whole body. And this happens not in the body alone, but also in the soul. Habits, customs, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears change continually. None of these stays the same or similar, but the prior ones are abolished and new ones succeed them. Furthermore, what is more wonderful, not only do some sciences vanish and others arise—and we are not always the same in our knowledge—but even each individual science suffers the same. For what is called 'meditating' is said to happen as if the science had exited. For forgetfulness is the exit of science. Meditation, however, always restores a new memory in place of the departing one, and thus preserves science so that it seems to be the same. In this way every mortal thing is preserved—not because it is always entirely the same as the divine is, but because that which wastes away and departs leaves behind something new and similar to itself. By this remedy, Socrates, that which is mortal—whether body or anything else—becomes a participant in immortality; but the divine and immortal does so in another way. For this reason, you ought not to wonder if every nature holds its own sprout most dear. For for the sake of immortality, this kind of effort and love is inherent in everyone." When I had heard these things, moved by admiration, I said, "Is it truly thus to be judged, O most wise Diotima?" Then she, as the most perfect sophists are wont to do, said, "Know for certain, Socrates. Indeed, if you wish to consider the pursuit of glory that is in men, you will wonder at your own rudeness [[notes: i.e., lack of refinement]] because you did not sufficiently comprehend what I said. You will see how vehemently they desire to show themselves known to all, and to attain immortal glory in the future. For the sake of this more than for their children, they undergo dangers, spend money, refuse no labors, and finally expose themselves to death. Or do you think Alcestis would have wished to die for Admetus, or Achilles to perish in the vengeance of Patroclus, or your Codrus to die for the kingdom of his sons, unless they had presaged that they would attain an immortal memory of virtue, such as exists among us?"

[[margin: Iliad s.]]

"Far from it," she said. "On the contrary, I believe everyone does all these things for immortal virtue and an honorable reputation; and the better men are, the more they strive toward these things. For they love immortality. Therefore, those who are fertile in body turn themselves more toward women, and love in this way, and hope to attain immortality, memory, and happiness through all time by the generation of children. There are also those who have a soul more pregnant and fertile than the body. These surely conceive those things which it is fitting for the soul to have conceived and to conceive. But what is fitting? Prudence, namely, and the other virtues, of which things all poets are the begetters, as are those artisans who are called inventors. But the greatest and most outstanding prudence of all is that by which civil and domestic matters are governed, the name of which is temperance and justice. Whoever, therefore, is full and pregnant by nature with virtues of this sort—and is thus divine—when the proper age is imminent, he now affects to give birth and generate, and therefore he wanders everywhere and seeks the beautiful in which he may generate. For in the ugly he would not generate at all. Therefore, he rejoices in beautiful bodies more than in deformed ones, being as he is pregnant. But if he should also find a soul that is beautiful, generous, and teachable, with both beauties concurring, he is wonderfully delighted, and in the presence of that man, he is immediately eloquent in speaking about virtue—what a

[[page number: 295]]

[[heading: The Banquet, or, on Love.]]

good man ought to be like, and what his duty is—and he strives to imbue him with this doctrine. Adhering to the beautiful and using it familiarly, he brings forth and gives birth to those things which he had once conceived, being mindful of them both in his absence and in his presence; and what is born from this, he nourishes and educates together with him. Hence they contract a more august communion and a firmer friendship than the parents of mortal children, insofar as they communicate together in children who are more immortal and more beautiful. Indeed, anyone would choose such children rather than human ones, especially if he considers Homer and Hesiod and emulates other poets, seeing what kinds of children they left behind: which being immortal, provided immortal glory and memory for their parents. Such children, if it pleases you, as Lycurgus left to the Lacedaemonians—the saviors of Lacedaemon and almost all of Greece. And among you, Solon is honored for the generation of laws, as are many others elsewhere among the Greeks and Barbarians, who demonstrated many and noble works, progenerating all virtue. For whom many sacred sites and temples have been dedicated because of such offspring, but never yet for human children. In these amatory matters, Socrates, you yourself might perhaps be initiated by your own industry. But whether you can proceed further and reach the perfect amatory state, or those things which look toward the sublime—for whose sake these things exist, if anyone seeks correctly—I do not know if you are able to perceive. I shall tell you, however, and I will help you with all my study. You, however, strive to follow me to the best of your strength. It behooves him who is to progress by the right path toward this, to contemplate beautiful bodies immediately from adolescence: and first, if indeed he is led correctly, to love one body and there produce beautiful reasons; then to think that the beauty which is in any body is related to that of another body. And if it is fitting to follow what is beautiful in species, it is absurd to believe that the beauty which is in all bodies is not one and the same. And he who observes this ought to become a lover of all simply beautiful bodies, and for this reason relax the vehemence of love toward one, and think little of the species of one. After this, he should estimate the beauty which is in souls to be more excellent than that which is in the body, so that if someone is of an ingenious mind, even if the form of his body yields to certain others, he should nevertheless think it sufficient, and love him, and care for him, and bear such reasons, and seek all speeches which can make adolescents better; so that from here he may be led to inspect the beauty which is found in duties and laws, and understand that it is all uniform and related to itself, so that he may think little of the beauty concerning the body. After duties and laws, let him pass to the sciences, so that he may contemplate the beauty of sciences; and while he beholds that which overflows with ample beauty, let him no longer admire the species of one boy as a slave; nor should he be content with the beauty of one man or one duty. For whoever fails in this is a meager and abject slave. But let him plunge into the deep sea of beauty, where by that very intuition he may abundantly give birth to many noble and magnificent reasons and intelligences in philosophy, until there, confirmed and strengthened, he may now behold one such science, which exists of such beauty. Apply the edge of your mind to me now with all your strength. Whoever is led step by step through amatory matters this far, having beheld beautiful things in the right order, will now arrive at the end of the amatory affection, and will suddenly behold a certain beauty wonderful in nature: This is that for whose sake we underwent all preceding labors. In the beginning indeed it always is; it neither is born, nor perishes, nor grows ever, nor decreases. Moreover, it is not beautiful in one part and ugly in another, nor beautiful at one time and not at another. Nor is it beautiful in comparison to this and ugly in comparison to that. Nor beautiful here and ugly there, as if it were beautiful to some but not at all to others. Nor again will beauty itself be tinged by any imagination, as if it were a beautiful face, or beautiful hands, or anything else of which the body is a participant. Nor like a certain speech, or science. Nor will it be thought to lie in another, as in an animal, or the earth, or the sky, or any other thing, but it is itself through itself with itself, always existing as uniform. But all other beautiful things are beautiful by participation in it, under that condition that while others are born and perish, nothing is subtracted from it, or added, nor does it incur any passion. When indeed someone ascending from these by rightly loving boys begins to behold beauty itself, he almost touches the end. This is surely to proceed correctly toward amatory matters, or to be led by another, when namely someone begins to ascend from these beautiful things for the sake of that beauty, using them as if they were certain steps, and passing from one first into two, and from two into all bodies that are beautiful, and from beautiful bodies to beautiful duties, and from beautiful duties turned toward beautiful doctrines, and finally from many doctrines arriving at that doctrine which is of nothing else than that beauty itself; and thus at last he contemplates what beauty itself is. In this state of life, O friend Socrates," said that prophet-stranger, "if anywhere else, is it for a man to live, namely while beholding beauty itself. Which if ever you see, you will judge it precious beyond what can be said of gold, and ornate garments, and beautiful boys and adolescents. Whom now both you and many others, while you behold them, are too much stupefied by, and if it could be done, you would choose to be always among them, neglecting food and drink. How happy do we think that spectacle will be,

[[margin: Cicero, book 2 of Duties.]]

if it should happen that he beholds beauty itself, sincere, integral, pure, simple, not contaminated with human flesh, colors, or other mortal trifles, but beholds beauty itself divine according to itself. Would you think little of a life of this sort? namely, of the man himself who looks up there, who beholds so noble a spectacle, who adheres to it. Do you not think that he, seeing beauty only for himself with that eye by which it can be perceived, will bring forth not images of virtue anymore, but virtues themselves? since he touches not a simulacrum, but the thing itself. And when he brings forth and nourishes true virtue, he will be made a friend of God, and if any other of men is so, he especially will exist as immortal." These things, O Phaedrus and other guests, Diotima told me. In whom I place my faith, and I study to persuade others that human nature cannot easily find anything more conducive to the possession of blessed immortality than legitimate love. Therefore I judge that love is to be honored by all men. And indeed I cultivate amatory matters, and I exercise myself in them exceedingly, and I exhort others. And now indeed and always I praise the power and strength of love according to the faculty of my genius. This speech, O Phaedrus, if you wish, consider as a certain laudation of love; but if it pleases you to call it otherwise, call it so. When Socrates had said these things, all the rest approved; Aristophanes, however, was trying to say something; who, since Socrates said it, had made mention of him in a certain place. But suddenly the door of the

[[page number: 296]]

[[heading: Book Twenty-Five.]]

vestibule was struck and gave a sound, and the clamor of revelling youths and a flute-player was heard. Then Agathon said, "Ministers, see who the men are that have arrived, and if any friend of ours is among them, summon him to us. If no one, announce that we are no longer drinking, but are already resting." But a little later they heard the voice of Alcibiades, insulting in his drunkenness, and crying out loudly in the vestibule. He was asking where Agathon was, and ordered that he be led to Agathon. Therefore the flute-player and others led him in, and they stood at the doors of the vestibule, Alcibiades crowned with a certain wreath of ivy and violets and his head surrounded with many ribbons, and crying out, "I bid you hail, men! Receive a very drunk man as a companion. Or let us depart, having crowned Agathon alone, for the sake of which we came. I could not be present yesterday. Today I have come bearing ribbons, so that from my own head I might bind the head of the wisest and most beautiful, if I may say so. Will you mock me as a drunkard? Even if you laugh, I know that I speak the truth. Answer clearly whether you permit me to enter on these terms: will you drink with me or not?" Here everyone shouted and ordered him to enter and lie down. Agathon also summoned him. The companions therefore led him in, and he, taking off the ribbons to surround Agathon's head, did not see Socrates, although he was in sight. He sat down near Agathon, in the middle between him and Socrates. For Socrates had moved aside. When he had sat down, he congratulated Agathon and crowned him. Agathon said, "Boys, take off Alcibiades' shoes, so that he may lie down as a third." Alcibiades said, "Quite so," and asked who the third guest was. Turning around, he saw Socrates, and when he saw him, he exclaimed, "By Hercules! What is this? Have you sat down here too, O Socrates, lying in wait for me? Thus you are always wont to meet me suddenly where I least expected you. And now why have you come here? Why do you sit here rather than near Aristophanes, or someone else who is ridiculous and wishes to be seen? But you have cleverly devised it, to sit here next to the most beautiful of the guests." Socrates, turning to Agathon, said, "See, Agathon, if in any way you can help me. For the love of this man has become no light matter for me. For from that time when I began to love him, I am never permitted either to look at any beautiful person or to speak to one, without this jealous man—that is, one captured by amatory suspicion—becoming envious and doing strange things and reviling me; indeed, he can hardly restrain himself from laying hands on me. See therefore that he does no such thing in the present, but reconcile us; or if he tries to use force, help me. For the fury and amatory impetus of this man terrifies me greatly." To this Alcibiades replied, "Between me and you no reconciliation is possible, but for the sake of these things I will avenge myself on you elsewhere. Now, however, Agathon, give me some of these ribbons so that I may also adorn this wonderful head, lest he be angry with me that I crowned you and not him, who surpasses all men in speech, not just recently like you, but always." Taking the ribbons, he crowned Socrates and sat down. Sitting down, he said, "Come now, men. You seem to me too sober; I do not think this should be permitted to you. For we must drink. For that was agreed among us. Therefore, I propose myself to you as the leader of the drinking until you have drunk enough. Agathon, order some large cup to be brought if one is at hand. But there is no need; rather, boy, bring that vessel here, which seems to hold more than eight *paterae* (drinking bowls)." When he had filled the vessel, he himself drank first, then ordered it to be poured for Socrates, and said, "Against Socrates, O guests, I accomplish nothing by this trick. No matter how much anyone orders, he will drink it off, and you will never see him drunk." Socrates, when the boy had poured, drank. Then Eryximachus said, "What are we doing, Alcibiades? Do we neither say anything over the cup, nor sing, but just gorge ourselves like thirsty people?" To him Alcibiades said, "Hail, best Eryximachus, son of the best and most prudent father." "And you hail," Eryximachus added. "But what should we do?" "Whatever you prescribe," said Alcibiades. "You indeed must be obeyed. 'One medical man is worth many others.' Command therefore whatever you please." "Listen then," said Eryximachus. "Before you entered, it seemed good to everyone present, starting in order to the right, each in turn should praise Love according to the faculty of his genius. We indeed have each spoken; you also, since you have not spoken but have drunk, ought rightly to speak: and when you have spoken, then at last you shall command Socrates whatever you wish. Socrates also similarly to the one who follows on the right, and the others in turn." "You speak noble words, Eryximachus," said Alcibiades. "But it ought not to seem a fair ratio for a drunk man to compare his words with the speech of sober men. But, O blessed man, did Socrates persuade you of anything by what he just told? Or do you know that it is entirely the opposite? For if I praise anyone in his presence—whether God or another man besides himself—he will not keep his hands off me." "Good words, please," Socrates said. "Say nothing to these things," Alcibiades replied; "for by Neptune I would praise no one else while you are present." "It seems it should be done this way," said Eryximachus, "and if you wish, praise Socrates." "What do you say?" asked Alcibiades. "It seems necessary, Eryximachus, that I should approach this man and avenge myself before you." "What are you thinking," said Socrates, "will you praise me by some ridiculous things? Or what will you do?" "I will speak true things," said Alcibiades, "do you permit it?" "Indeed, I permit you to speak the truth," said Socrates, "and I even command it." "I will obey most willingly," said Alcibiades, "provided I can achieve it. But you observe, and if I relate anything less than true, interrupt as you please, and refute the lie. For I will never lie willingly. Nor should you wonder if one thing or another comes back to my memory from here or there. For it is not easy for a man so affected to enumerate your strange habits eloquently and in a certain order. O men and guests, I shall endeavor to praise Socrates through images. He himself will perhaps suspect that I turn my speech to ridiculous things. But the image will be taken for the sake of truth, not for the sake of a joke."

[[margin: See the proverbs in Erasmus, 'The Sileni of Alcibiades'.]]

[[page number: 297]]

[[heading: The Banquet, or, on Love.]]

...attracts, and because it is divine, it shows who needs the gods and mysteries. You, however, differ from him only in this: that without any instrument, with naked words, you accomplish this same thing. We certainly, as often as we hear another relating the words of another—even if he is a very good orator—we make nothing of them, so to speak. But when someone hears you, or your words being related by any other—even if he who relates them is inept, and whether a man, a woman, or a youth hears them—we are indeed stupefied and seized in mind. For my part, unless I suspected I might seem too drunk, I would affirm under oath what things have happened to me from his words at other times, and happen even now. For as often as I hear him, my heart is moved much more than those who are carried away in the manner of the Corybantes [[notes: ecstatic priests]] at his words, and I shed tears, and I see this same thing happening to many others. And when I heard Pericles and other good orators, they indeed seemed to me to speak nobly, but nothing such happened to me; neither was my mind stirred, nor did it condemn itself as living a slavish life. But by this Marsyas of ours, I am often so moved that I think it is in no way for me to live in this state of life. Do not deny these things, Socrates. For I know for certain that if I were willing to lend my ears to him now, I would least endure it, but those same things would happen to me. For he compels me to confess that while I myself fail in many things, yet I neglect myself and care for the business of the Athenian people. Therefore, by force, as if plugging my ears against the Sirens, I flee from him and avoid him, lest I grow old sitting near him. I suffer toward him alone what no one would believe, being restrained by shame or modesty. But I fear him alone. For I am conscious in myself that I cannot defend myself against doing what he commands; but when I depart from him, I am overcome by popular ambition. I therefore flee him and avoid him, and as often as I look at him, shame takes me because I have not kept my promises, so that I often wish he would depart from life. But again, if that should happen, I know I would endure it much more bitterly. Therefore, I do not know where to turn or how to use this. And from the melodies of this Satyr, such things have happened to me and to many others. But hear the rest, how he is like those to whom I said he was similar, and see how wonderful a power he has. Know that none of you knows Socrates. But I will show you, since I have already begun to speak. Do you see how vehemently Socrates is affected toward the beautiful? And how he always dwells among them and is stupefied? And how he is ignorant of all things and knows nothing? Surely this figure is very like a *Silenus* (a statue of a satyr). Know therefore that he is clothed externally in this form of habit, like a carved Silenus. But inside, if he were opened—O men and guests—there is a wonderful chastity and integrity. Nor does he value the beauty of anyone's body at all, nor riches, nor honors, nor other things which the common people admire; but he utterly despises all those things beyond what can be imagined, and leads them as nothing. Therefore I tell you that we are as nothing to him; yet he ironically feigns otherwise, and never ceases to joke openly about these matters. But when he is acting seriously and is opened inside, I do not know whether any of you has ever inspected the divine images that lie hidden within. I certainly once saw them, and they seemed to me so divine, and golden, and beautiful, and wonderful, that I thought it in no way lawful to act otherwise than as Socrates prescribes. Once upon a time, O men and guests, I thought Socrates was truly delighted by my appearance, and I thought I had found this wonderful and happy occasion for what I affected. I decided to gratify Socrates so that he might communicate to me whatever he knew. For I thought my beauty was something great and wonderful, and I trusted it most. And since before I had never been accustomed to speak with him without a companion, once, having dismissed the companion, I remained alone with him. All the truth must be opened to you. Attend, I pray. If I lie, Socrates himself refute me. I remained, O men and guests, alone with him alone, hoping he would say the same things to me that lovers are wont to say to their beloveds when they are alone. Wherefore I was very glad; but nothing of these things was done, but as he was accustomed, when he had discussed until evening, he departed. After this I challenged him to the palaestra and exercised with him, as if I were going to accomplish something in this. We were thus often alone together in gymnastics. What need is there for many words? Nothing succeeded for me. After this had in no way succeeded, I decided to approach this man with harder engines of war, and not to desist from my undertakings. Hear how vehemently I laid wait for him here. I invited him to dinner just as a lover lies in wait for his beloved. He did not easily nor at first obey, but at length he complied. He came therefore; but having taken food, he immediately rose to depart. Then I, restrained by shame, permitted him to depart. But laying other more vehement ambushes, I protracted the conversation after dinner until late at night; and when he wished to depart, I compelled him to stay, objecting to the unseasonable night. He rested therefore in the next bed, on which he had sat and dined, and no one else besides us slept there that night. What has been said so far can be brought forward everywhere without a blush. But what follows, you shall not hear until I have recited that proverb:

[[margin: Proverb.]]

"Wine, both with youth and without youth, is truthful." Moreover, it seems wrong that he who praises Socrates should pass over in silence his proud and unconquered deed. Furthermore, I am affected no differently than he whom a viper bites. For they say he does not wish to open what his passion is like, except to those who are similarly sick, as if these alone—being not ignorant of the evil—might forgive him if anyone, compelled by torture, does not hesitate both to speak and to do everything. I therefore, being bound more than others by the vehement bite of philosophy—which is the sharpest of all—and whether heart, or soul, or whatever it should be called, being wounded by the desire for speeches in philosophy, which bite more sharply than a viper and occupy a youthful mind when they touch it (if it is not entirely lazy), and compel it to do and say whatever at length it may—and beholding Phaedruses, Agathons, Eryximachuses, Pausanias, Aristodemuses, Aristophanes, and finally Socrates himself and the others. (For you all are seized with me in the fury and revelry of philosophy.) Therefore, hear all of you. For you will give me pardon for those things which were then done by me, and are now said. But servants, and anyone else who is profane and rustic, let them plug their ears. When the lamp was extinguished and the servants had departed, it seemed to me, O men and guests, no longer to be dissembled and deferred, but what I felt must be opened ingenuously. I touched him therefore, saying: "Socrates, are you sleeping?" "Not yet," he said. "Do you know what has seemed to me so far?" I said. "About what, and what do you ask?" he said. "You alone have seemed to me a lover worthy of me," I said, "yet you have been too modest in love. Since the matter stands thus, and I am such as I am, I would lead it to be foolish unless I gratified you in this too,

[[page number: 298]]

[[heading: Book Twenty-Five.]]

and in all other things, whether it be my possessions or my friends you might need. To me indeed nothing is more important than that I should become the best man possible. Toward this, no one can help me more than you. I, however, would fear the rebukes of the wise much more for not obeying such a great man than I would fear the words of the foolish for obeying." When he had heard these things, dissembling with his usual irony, he responded thus: "O friend Alcibiades, you seem indeed not to be lazy or base, if what you relate about me is true, and there is in me a certain power through which you yourself can be made better, and you see a wonderful beauty in me, far more excellent than your own form. If, knowing these things, you desire to communicate with me and to exchange beauty for beauty, you strive to carry back much more than I, like a money-lender. For you endeavor to gain the truth of beautiful things in exchange for opinion, and to receive gold for brass. But, O blessed man, observe more diligently, lest my condition escape you, since I am of no price. Surely the eye of the mind begins to see sharply only when the eye of the body first begins to fade. You, however, are far from this age." When we had heard these things, I said, "My things are such as I have said; for I do not have one thing in my mouth and another in my heart. You, however, deliberate as you think will be better for you and for me." "You speak well," he said, "therefore hereafter, consulting together, we will do what we think will be most conducive to both of us, both in these and in all other things." When I had heard these things and had 'thrown my spear,' as it were, I thought he was hit; rising up, I permitted him to say not a word further. And surrounding him with this cloak which you see—for it was winter—I lay down under his old pallium (*cloak*) and, embracing this happy and wise and entirely wonderful man with these arms, I thus rested the whole night. I know you will not deny these things, O Socrates. He, however, despised the form in which I most trusted, as if it were ridiculous, and proudly contemned it. I call all the Gods and Goddesses to witness, O judges—for you are the judges of Socratic pride—that I rose up no differently than if I had slept with my father or my elder brother. What kind of mind do you think I had after this, when I considered myself indeed contemned, yet I admired his genius, temperance, and fortitude, having found such a man as I had believed no one to be for prudence and tolerance? Therefore I found no reason why I should be angry with him, nor how I might depart from him, nor again by what allurements I might reconcile him to me. I knew indeed that he could be conquered by money more difficultly than Ajax by steel, and that in which I had hoped he would be more easily ensnared had failed me. Ambiguous, therefore, and more enslaved to this man than any other to another, I wandered about. All these things were done by me then. After this, as time proceeded, military service happened to him and to me together against Potidaea; and Socrates and I were tent-mates and mess-mates in that army. First, in the endurance of labors, he far surpassed not only me but all others; and if in any place, as is wont to happen in war, provisions failed, none were found equal to him in enduring hunger and thirst. But again, in the abundance of things, and in revelry, and at the military table, he alone seemed able to enjoy himself. And although he did not want to drink, yet if he was compelled, he immediately surpassed everyone in drinking; and what is most wonderful of all, no one ever saw him drunk. But this, I think, can still be refuted by me hereafter. Against winters and cold, which are most harsh in those places, he did wonderful things. For once when a very great and intolerable frost occurred, so that no one dared to go out of their tents—and if any did go out, it was only if they were very much wrapped up, and their feet and legs carefully wound about with skins and woolen cloths—Socrates at that very time went out with the other soldiers such that he added nothing to that garment which he had been accustomed to wear before. Barefoot indeed he walked through the ice more easily than others with shoes. The soldiers, beholding these things, suspected they were being despised by him. And in these matters Socrates was such. But what that most tolerant man did in the same army is worth hearing. For when a certain thought once fell upon him, he stood thinking in the same spot from the morning time; and since it was not given to him to explain what he was thinking, he persisted thinking, and did not leave off. And it was now noon, and the soldiers had noticed it and were wondering, and one was telling another that Socrates had been standing since dawn thinking. Finally, some soldiers from Ionia, when night was now imminent, having dined first (for it was then summer), placed their bedding around him, then lay in the cold, observing him to see if he would persist through the night also. Socrates, however, stood until the following dawn and the rising of the sun. But then he departed, when he had now greeted the rising sun. In battles also, what he was like should not be passed over in silence. For when that battle occurred from which the leaders of the army gave me rewards as the best fighter, no one else saved me but Socrates. For seeing me gravely wounded, he in no way deserted me, but leaping before me, he protected me and my arms and saved me from the enemies. And I then tried to persuade them that the gifts should be handed over not to me, but to this Socrates, by whom I had been saved. Nor will you refute this, nor deny it as false, Socrates. Then surely the leaders, looking at my rank, preferred to give to me, while you, O Socrates, were beseeching them in the first place that the honor should be exhibited to me, not to you. But it was noble, O men, to see Socrates when our army fled from Delium. For I was present also at this battle, and indeed fighting from a horse, while Socrates himself was on foot. Our men being routed and everyone's flight having already happened, Socrates and Laches together were retreating. And when I happened to fall upon them, I told them to be of good courage, and said I would never desert them. Here indeed I could behold Socrates better than at Potidaea, because I was safer on a horse and less fearful. First, therefore, one could see with what great caution and presence of mind he surpassed Laches. Then it seemed to me, O Aristophanes, that he was doing what you say he does here: walking proudly, and with his eyes quietly surveying all around, and cautiously examining each thing. For he was looking back at enemies and friends alike, showing by his eyes and look, and demonstrating even to those further off, that if anyone should attack him, it would not be done with impunity. Therefore he and the other departed safely. For almost no one attacks those who walk 이렇게 (thus), but they attack those who are carried away in headlong flight. In many other things Socrates can be wonderfully praised, but such are they that perhaps some others also might deserve the same praise; but those things are special in this man, through which he is found to be similar to none of other men, neither of the ancients nor of the new. For what kind of man Achilles was, someone might guess Brasidas to have been, and certain others; and as Pericles was, so were Antenor and Nestor. There are others also who can be compared to each other in this way. But what kind of man Socrates is, and what

[[page number: 299]]

[[heading: The Banquet, or, on Love.]]

and of what kind is his wonderful way of speaking, no one comes close to his likeness, neither of the ancients, nor of those who are now, except as I have now said and assimilated him. For he is similar to none of men, but to Sileni and Satyrs himself, and his speeches are too. For this also had been omitted by me before, that his speeches are very like opened Sileni. For if someone should hear his speeches, they seem at first, as it is said, to be too absurd in appearance. For names and words in their external aspect present the habit of a certain contemptuous Satyr. For he always has in his mouth asses, and blacksmiths, and shoemakers, and tanners, and he seems to say the same things always about the same people, so that almost all who are less experienced or skilled might mock his words. But if anyone looks within his speeches, first indeed he will find that they alone of all others have a depth of sense, and furthermore are most divine, and contain very many most beautiful images of virtues, and extend themselves to very many things; indeed, they comprehend all precepts by which he ought to be instructed who is to live honorably and well. These are the things, O men and guests, in which I praise Socrates, and also about which I complain. For you have heard meanwhile what injuries he has brought upon me. Nor has he behaved thus against me alone, but also against Charmides the son of Glaucon, and against Euthydemus the son of Diocles, and many others he has done the same, whom he deceived under the species of a lover: for instead of a lover, he turned out to be the one loved. Therefore I also warn you, Agathon, that you beware of his simulations and dissimulations, and knowing him from these things which I have suffered, take care of your business, nor according to the proverb, like fools, become wise only after receiving an inconvenience. When Alcibiades had said these things, Aristodemus related that laughter was excited in all by his audacity and freedom of speaking, since he seemed to be captured by the love of Socrates. "You seem to me to be sober, O Alcibiades," Socrates said. "Otherwise you would never have so artificially made such a long circuit of words to hide that for whose sake you said all the rest: which at the heel of your speech, so that you might seem to bring it forth besides your purpose, you finally added, as if you did not say all those things for the sake of separating me from Agathon. You think I ought to love no one besides you alone, and that Agathon should be loved by no one else but you. But your Satyric and Silenic figment did not escape us. But, O friend Agathon, effort must be given so that neither his machinations profit him, nor cause a division by any calumny thrown between me and you." "Truly, O Socrates," Agathon responded, "you seem to speak the truth. Which I gather from this, because to separate us, he interposed himself in the middle between you and me. But this will profit him nothing: for rising from here, I will sit near you." "It must surely be done thus," said Socrates. "Sit here below me." "Pro Jupiter!" Alcibiades exclaimed, "What things does this man compel me to endure? He wishes to surpass me in all things. But if nothing else, O wonderful man, at least permit Agathon to sit here in the middle." "It is in no way fitting," Socrates responded. "For you have praised me. It behooves me now to praise this man sitting to my right. Therefore, if Agathon remains after you, he will not praise me again before he is praised by me. But let it go, happy man, and do not envy this man my praises. Indeed, I desire vehemently to praise him." "Hui, hui, Alcibiades," Agathon said there. "Why do I delay here? I am departing from here now so that Socrates may praise me." "That is the custom of Socrates," Alcibiades responded, "that while he is present, it is permitted to no one else to reconcile the beautiful to themselves. See now, I pray, how easily and by what probable reason he has drawn him to himself." Agathon therefore rose to rest near Socrates. Then suddenly many revellers, having found the doors open—for someone had gone out just before—entered and sat around them. By whose noise all things were disturbed, nor was any measure in drinking served after this. Aristodemus recounted that Eryximachus, and Phaedrus, and some others departed, and that he himself slept for a long time, for the nights were long then, and rose about dawn when the cocks were already crowing. Woken from sleep, he found that the others were partly sleeping and partly had departed. But Agathon, and Aristophanes, and Socrates alone were still awake, and were drinking from a certain large phial, passing it in a circuit to the right. Socrates, however, was disputing among them. Aristodemus said he did not remember the other things—for he was not present from the beginning and had been heavy with sleep—but the sum of that disputation was that Socrates was compelling them to confess that it is the duty of the same man to compose tragedy and comedy, and that he who is tragic by art is also comic. When they had conceded these things, compelled rather than persuaded, Aristophanes first gave himself to sleep, and then Agathon as light was already arising. But Socrates, while they were sleeping, set out for the Lyceum, with Aristodemus himself following as he was accustomed, and having washed in his usual manner, he exercised the whole day, and at last toward evening rested at home.

# PHAEDRUS,
## OR, ON THE
### BEAUTIFUL.
*
### THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.
[[notes: Ficino (the Florentine Platonist) provides a preface or "Argumentum" to the Phaedrus here.]]

Our Plato, pregnant with fury from the poetic Muse—whom he followed from a tender age, indeed from his Apolline birth—first brought forth a book that is almost entirely poetic. And most white (*candidissimus*), he published the most white work, beautiful concerning beauty and Love simultaneously, and most worthy of the love of all, so that deservedly he published other books thereafter full of charm and grace. Having inaugurated a happy beginning from the Venerean Muse, he alone of all joined charm everywhere with dignity. Since indeed we have explained many mysteries of this book in our *Theology* and in the book *On Love*, we will touch upon its argument very briefly. The *Symposium* indeed treats primarily of Love, and consequently of beauty. But the *Phaedrus*, for the sake of Beauty, disputes concerning Love. Nor is the speech of Lysias and the oratory dispute inserted entirely without reason. For beauty pertains both to the mind and to sight and hearing. Whence it happens that where beauty of souls and names is discussed, and likewise the beauty of the body, the beauty of speech is deservedly disputed. Immediately in the very beginning, Socrates, while walking, hands down very serious precepts: that all things must be utterly contemned for the sake of the study of wisdom, and that the most powerful study of wisdom is to consider oneself. Among these things, the most artificial description of the place allegorically signifies the Academy: the plane tree signifies Plato; the chaste shrubs signify the chastity of Platonic and Socratic love; the fountain signifies largesse in communicating wisdom; the other ornaments signify the oratorical and poetic flowers with which the Academy of Plato abounds. Lysias is rightly rebuked because he inquires into what the affection of love is like, but did not first define love itself nor distinguish it. Considering meanwhile the modesty of Socratic love—for he is about to pronounce some things less honorable—

[[page number: 300]]

[[heading: Book Twenty-Six.]]

he begins with a covered head. Soon he invokes the Muses, so that they might at least honor a less honorable matter with their own splendor of elocution. But before he vituperates the base lover, lest he be in the same crime as Lysias, he defines base love as being a certain desire or lust rebellious against reason, which overcomes the opinion tending toward right things and ravishes toward the pleasure of form. While he proceeds to define that, he gives us two leaders: one indeed is the innate appetite for pleasure, the other truly a certain legitimate opinion acquired gradually through discipline and leading toward honorable things. But these leaders internal to us are moved by two external ones: a certain airy spirit (*daemon*) moves opinion, and a watery one moves lust. After he has defined it, he separates adolescents from base lovers by many reasons. Then meanwhile, note a wonderful mystery, similar to the Mosaic mystery. In the very beginning of many evils, some spirit (*daemon*) mixed in pleasure. Because, however, he acts the poetic rather than the philosophical persona, he submits himself as if seized by a spirit, because he vituperated Love with the name of a God. And he does this so that, about to distinguish Love, he may be distinguished in a poetic rather than a dialectical manner. In these things, observe that it is a most grave sin to offend against the name of God. Again, there is a presage in the soul. Then he separates the art of poetic ambiguities from the base. He divides fury into divine and human. The divine into four: namely prophecy (*vaticinium*), mystery, poetry, and love. He confirms providence and religion. He prefers wisdom inspired by divine fury far above human wisdom. Before he proceeds to the treatment of particular souls, he brings souls in common into the middle: namely the soul of the world (*anima mundi*), which he names Jove, and under it the twelve souls of the twelve mundane spheres, under which he subordinates as many orders of spirits (*daemones*) and as many particular souls. To each indeed he accommodates a chariot (*currus*), that is, celestial and everlasting bodies. He disputes concerning rational souls, both divine and human, concerning the circuit of both; and by what reason the souls of men follow the contemplation of celestial souls in heaven, as they follow the wonderful things above the angelic heaven. What indeed is in the soul—the chariot, the vehicle, the wings, the charioteer (*auriga*), the horses, Fate, and the fall into the body, what again Great Jove is in heaven and the other Gods following—we explain in our *Theology*. It will be enough for you at present to understand the twin wings as twin innate instincts of the mind, elevating the soul to the supernal: in the intellect indeed an instinct toward the divine true; in the will an instinct toward the divine good, converting it according to its strength. When indeed these are relaxed, the inclination of the vegetative nature is intensified toward governing bodies; the Pythagoreans think that souls, with their wings now broken, descend into the elements. After these things, they distribute the soul falling from heaven into nine degrees. In all these things he uses both poetic license and follows the Pythagoreans rather than his own narrative. Among these things, observe that a similar fall of souls is described by the Pythagoreans, and of spirits (*daemones*) by the prophets. Also the number nine, fitting both the angelic choirs and the spirits fallen from there. I pass over now that Pherecydes the Syrian narrates a certain similar fall happening to spirits. And he adds that *Ophion* (the serpent-daemon) was the head of the rebellious army from the divine mind. Similar to this is what is contained in the divine mysteries: namely that Jove thrust down the inferior spirits to the lower regions. But let us return to the dialogue. Finally, a man with a purged mind dedicated to god is filled from there with all goods, and is sober and wise, although because he is placed outside himself, he is mocked by the common people as if insane. After this he descends to the divine legitimate fury of love, which he thinks is kindled in the soul when, beholding the beautiful form of the body, it easily remembers the divine beauty which it once had contemplated, and is inflamed with the desire for recovering it, and goes mad. But contrariwise he describes as a feral fury that which does not ascend from the form of the body to the divine intuition, but basely descends to Venerean coupling. He describes again a certain human fury between the divine and the feral, kindled in the mind of him who, occupied by the admiration of bodily form, neither hands it over entirely to the oblivion of the divine, nor remembers it perfectly. From which it happens that he is neither entirely intemperate nor yet always temperate, but appears sometimes as if incontinent, sometimes continent. Seeking afterward the causes for which one loves more or less, he flies to the stars, of which from the beginning souls are companions. For he disposes as many orders of human souls in the *Timaeus* as there are stars in heaven. From here he returns again to dividing the powers of the soul: and he calls the reason the charioteer, the genuine appetites the genuine horses; the rational appetite the good horse, the irrational appetite the evil horse. But in this genus of appetites, that which verges toward anger is less evil; but that which dominates toward concupiscence is more evil. Then he depicts the passions of lovers, both the continent and the incontinent, and mutual love, like a poet. Whence it happens that these must be indulged allegorically no differently than the *Songs of Solomon*. These things being done, when he had treated of the beauty which pertains to the mind and that which pertains to sight, he now proceeds to examine the speech of Lysias and to demonstrate the office of the orator, so that it might appear what the beauty of speech is, which pertains to hearing. He places the beauty of speech in order, so that it should have a head differing from the end, and have a middle, necessarily coupled to the head and the end and to each other. He commanded such an order to be observed by the orator in the first place. But he proves that no one can be a true orator unless he has a science of things, especially of human matters and of minds. In order that the orator might attain this, he commands that he learn the dialectical faculty of dividing and composing, which he wishes to be the principal instrument for tracking and finding the truth, and in the *Phibus* [[notes: Philebus]] he calls it a gift of the god, because just as in the world it is the perpetual office of god to divide and compose, so it is for the dialectician in his art. And therefore he judges the consummate dialectician—that is, the metaphysician—as if he were to be a god. After this he compares orators among themselves; and he vituperates those who, putting the probable before the true, speak to the people and deceive themselves, and stupidly trust they can know what is most likely true even without the knowledge of the truth itself. Soon some best and famous precepts are given. Three things are first necessary for an orator: Genius, Doctrine, Exercise. Philosophy is necessary for the maximum perfection of each art. From dialectical exercise and the contemplation of sublime things, a sublimity of mind and an efficacy for acting is finally acquired. Which two indeed are greatly necessary for the perfection of the greatest arts. Then he compares the orator who is not legitimate to cooks and flatterers, as in the *Gorgias*; but the legitimate one to a doctor. Furthermore, he gives a rule by which the nature of the soul as much as the body—indeed of everything—must be known, and immediately returns to the office of the orator. He adds concerning the office of writing that letters were found in Egypt by a certain spirit (*daemon*) called *Theuth*, together with the other disciplines. He derides moreover the study of writing, in those who think they can make truth perfect for posterity by trusting in letters. And in the manner of the Pythagoreans, he proves that the contemplation and tradition of truth in souls is better than in books. Which he confirms also in his epistles. Finally, he praises only that orator who is a philosopher by genius and study. He concludes the dialogue with a prayer, and with beauty of the soul for those seeking it from god. In which consider that Socrates, having contemned all other things entirely, is content only with the beauty of the mind—that is, wisdom—yet nevertheless he indicates that this very thing is acquired not so much by human study as by divine gift.

#### SOCRATES, AND
##### PHAEDRUS.

**SOCRATES.** My friend Phaedrus, where to and from where? **PHAEDRUS.** From Lysias, O Socrates, the son of Cephalus. But I am going for a walk outside the city. For I sat with him a long time, spending from the morning until this very hour there. But by the persuasion of your and my comrade, Acumenus, I exercise by walking; which kind of exercise he thinks is easier and more healthful than running in a gymnasium. **SOC.** He advises well indeed, O friend. But Lysias, as it seems, was in the city. **PHAED.** He was. For he stayed with Epicrates in this house near the Olympium, formerly the house of Morychus. **SOC.** What business was going on there? Or did Lysias receive you with a banquet of speeches? **PHAED.** You shall know, if only you have leisure to walk along with me and listen. **SOC.** What then? Do you not think that, according to Pindar, I prefer even beyond business to hear your and Lysias's conversation? **PHAED.** Proceed then. **SOC.** Just speak. **PHAED.** And that discussion was, O Socrates, congruent to your ears. For the speech that was held was, I know not how, amatory. For Lysias wrote of a certain one of the beautiful being solicited, but not by a lover; and in that very thing...

[[page number: 301]]

[[heading: Phaedrus, or, On the Beautiful.]]

...he showed himself off in that he proved that gratification should be given not to the lover (*amans*) more than to the non-lover. **SOC.** O generous man!
