<meta>Continuing from the previous page, this text continues Diotima’s famous "Ladder of Love" speech from Plato’s Symposium. Having described Love's parents—Resource and Poverty—she now explains Love's character as a philosopher and the biological and spiritual drive for immortality.</meta>

...[always poor, and far from being soft and beautiful as most people think; instead, he is dry and squalid, barefoot, always flying on the ground,] without a home, sleeping always on the bare earth **at the door** <note>original: *ianuam*</note> and in the streets under the open sky. Following his mother's nature, he always lives with want. But according to his father, he is a schemer after the beautiful and the good, brave, impetuous, and intense, a clever hunter, always weaving some stratagem, desiring wisdom and resourceful in **finding** <note>original: *inuenientem*</note> it, a philosopher <note>Literally, a 'lover of wisdom' in Greek.</note> throughout his whole life, a formidable sorcerer, charlatan, and sophist.

# Love as the Philosophical Mean

<margin>Love occupies a middle ground between wisdom and ignorance.</margin>
When I, Socrates, was thus **refuted** <note>original: *refutatus*</note> by her, I asked: "Who then are those who seek wisdom, if they are neither the wise nor the ignorant?" She **responded** <note>original: *reſpõdit*</note> that it is obvious even to a child that they are those in the middle, among whom is Love. For wisdom is among the most beautiful of things, and Love is the love of the beautiful; therefore, Love is necessarily a philosopher. 

"I want you to be **taught** <note>original: *docearis*</note> further," she said. "If someone loves the good, what do they desire?" I replied, "To possess it." "And what will he have who possesses it?" I could not answer **hastily** <note>original: *feſtinanter*</note>, so she said: "He will be happy. For by the acquisition of good things, the happy are happy." 

# The Universal Desire for Good

<margin>The definition of Love as the desire for eternal possession of the Good.</margin>
This **teaching** <note>original: *doctrinâ*</note> regarding the good is not **innate** <note>original: *innata*</note> in all men as a conscious thought, yet all men desire the good always. One who is **supplicating** <note>original: *ſupplicãs*</note> for the truth must see that Love is the desire for the perpetual possession of the good. "In what way," she asked, "must they pursue it? What is this **deed** <note>original: *facinus*</note>?" I told her that if I knew that, I would not be admiring her wisdom and coming to her to **attain** <note>original: *adipiſci*</note> these very things. 

# Procreation and Immortality

She said: "The **deed** <note>original: *facinus*</note> is birth in beauty, whether according to the body or the soul." All men are pregnant in soul and body, and our nature desires to give birth. But it cannot give birth in the ugly, only in the beautiful. When the pregnant one **encounters** <note>original: *offenderet*</note> the ugly, it becomes sour, and because it **suffers** <note>original: *pateretur*</note> and is pained, it shrinks and does not give birth. But the beautiful delivers the possessor from great pains. 

<margin>Why animals and humans labor for their offspring.</margin>
"Why do you **labor** <note>original: *elaboraris*</note> so much," she asked, "and even die to **provide** <note>original: *præſtare*</note> for your offspring? It is because mortal nature seeks, as far as it can, to be eternal and immortal. This is only possible through procreation, which leaves behind a new and different being in place of the old."

<summary>Diotima defines Love as a philosophical intermediary seeking the "Good" and explains that the human impulse toward procreation is actually a quest for immortality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the "Eryxias," a pseudo-Platonic work on the nature of wealth. Following the anecdote about Prodicus, Socrates leads his companion through a series of logical steps to define what actually constitutes "wealth" by linking it to "utility."</meta>

**On Wealth.** [Page number:] **659**

[Column 1]

...matter? If we cannot say [otherwise], let us consider it this way again: Come now, if a man could live without food and drink so that he was never hungry or thirsty, would he ever need these things, or silver, or anything else to acquire them? It certainly does not seem so to me. The same thing, then, I say, would happen in other matters if we did not require these things for the care of the body—things we currently lack, such as heat, cold, and other necessities that the body, being born in a state of need, must have. 

For what are called **riches** <note>original: *pecuniæ*. While this often means money, in this philosophical context it refers to all material wealth or property that has exchange value.</note> would be of no use to us if a human being lacked absolutely none of those things for which we desire to have money—so that we might supply the desires and necessities of the body with those things we frequently lack. But if a man is in need, then the possession of riches is certainly of use for the care of the body for those who are needy. Truly, if this [need] were driven from our midst, as we say, we would not need riches, and perhaps riches would not exist at all. 

*That appears to be the case.* 

It also appears, it seems, that those things which are useful for this same purpose are "wealth" to us. But this little bit of reasoning greatly disturbed him. Therefore I said: "What? Can we say it is possible for the same thing to be useful at one moment and useless at another for the same action?" 

"I would not say so," he said, "but if we have need of something for a certain action, it seems useful to me; if we do not need it, it is useless." 

"If indeed, then," I said, "we could make a bronze statue without fire, we would have no need of fire to make it; and if we had no need, it would not be useful. The same reasoning can be applied to other things as well." 

*That is clear.* 

"Therefore, nothing without which something can be accomplished seems to be useful to us." 

*Nothing.* 

"If we, therefore, without silver and gold and other such things—which we do not use for the care of the body in the same way as food, drink, clothes, bedding, and houses—could satisfy the desires and necessities of the body so that it needed nothing further, then neither silver, nor gold, nor other things of this sort would be seen as wealth <note>original: *pecuniæ*</note> in this regard, provided this could be done without them." 

*They would not.* 

"These things, certainly," I said, "if they are of no use, cannot be seen by us as wealth; but it must be that those things by which we can acquire what is useful are wealth." 

"I could never be led, Socrates," he said, "to believe that gold and silver and other things of that kind are not wealth to us. I am certainly firmly persuaded that whatever is useless to us is not wealth, and conversely, whatever is useful ought to be counted among those riches which are most beneficial. But I will never allow myself to be persuaded of this: that these things we just mentioned are not useful to us for the uses of life, provided that by them we acquire the things necessary for living." 

"Come now, what shall we say about these matters? Are there not men who teach Music or letters, or hand down some other science <note>original: *scientiam*; in this context, it refers to any specialized branch of knowledge or skill, often translated as 'art' or 'craft'.</note>, and who, by demanding a fee for these things, provide themselves with the necessities of life?" 

*There are.* 

"Do not these men themselves acquire necessary things through their knowledge, exchanging it just as we exchange gold and silver?" 

"I believe so." 

"If indeed, then, they acquire for themselves by this very means the things they use for life, it must be that this [knowledge] itself is useful for life. For we said silver was useful for this reason: that by it we can acquire the things necessary for life." 

*We did.* 

"Since, therefore, the sciences themselves seem useful to us for this purpose—because for the same 

[Column 2]

cause for which gold and silver are wealth—it is manifest that those who possess them are also wealthier; even if a little while ago we did not so easily allow that they were the wealthiest. Indeed, from what has now been conceded, it must follow that those who are more endowed with knowledge are also, at times, wealthier. For if someone were to ask us whether we think a horse is useful to any man, would you say 'yes,' or would you rather say it is useful to those who know how...

<summary>Socrates argues that wealth is defined solely by its utility in satisfying bodily needs; consequently, if knowledge can be traded for life's necessities, knowledge itself must be considered a form of wealth.</summary>

**Definitions. 661**

[Column 1]
**Virtue** <note>The OCR "lis" is likely the suffix of *Virtutis* or a misreading of *Virtus*. # On the Universe 663

->### A FRAGMENT OF PLATO’S TIMAEUS TRANSLATED BY MARCUS TULLIUS, CORRESPONDING TO THE PLACES WE HAVE MARKED IN THE MARGIN.<-
*

**W**hat is that which always is, and has no beginning? And what is that which is born, but never truly is? The first of these is grasped by the intellect and reason, being that which is always one and the same; the other is that which prompts sense-perception and opinion, lacking reason—which is entirely a matter of opinion; it is born and it perishes, and can never truly exist. Now, everything that is born must necessarily be born from some cause. For if the cause is removed, the origin of nothing can be found. Therefore, if he who strives to complete some task gazes upon that form <term>Species: in this context, the Platonic "Form" or eternal Idea</term> which is always the same, and sets it before himself as a model, he must necessarily produce a noble work. But if he looks to that which is born <note>That is, the physical, changing world.</note>, he will never achieve the beauty he desires. Let all the heavens, then—or the world, or whatever other name it delights in—be so called by us. Regarding this, let us first consider what must be considered at the start of every inquiry: whether it has always existed with no beginning of its birth, or whether it arose from some starting point in time. For it is seen and touched, and is everywhere corporeal. Now all such things move the senses; and those things that move the senses are the same that rely on opinion, which we said have a beginning and are born. But nothing can be born without causes. And indeed, to find the one who is, as it were, the parent <margin>difficult <note>original Greek: *chalepon* (χαλεπόν)</note></margin> of this universe is difficult; and once you have found him, it is forbidden <note>original: *nefas*. A term meaning something that violates divine law or is religiously prohibited to speak of.</note> to declare him to the common people. So we must look again at whether the maker of so great a work imitated an eternal model—that which is always one, the same, and like itself—or that which we say is generated and born. Now, if this world is beautiful, and if its craftsman is good, surely he preferred to imitate the form of eternity. If otherwise—which is a thing forbidden even to say—he followed a born model instead of an eternal one. There is no doubt, then, that he preferred to pursue <margin>To pursue means to imitate.</margin> eternity, since nothing is more beautiful than the world, and nothing more excellent than its builder. If, therefore, it was born, toward that...

<summary>This page contains Cicero's Latin translation of Plato's Timaeus, focusing on the metaphysical distinction between the eternal world of "Being" and the physical world of "Becoming." It argues that the world's creator must have used an eternal, perfect model to craft the universe because of its inherent beauty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marcus Tullius Cicero’s Latin translation of Plato’s *Timaeus*. The previous page concluded with the necessity of a "cause" for all things that are born. Here, the text moves into the mathematical and physical structure of the universe, explaining how the Creator used geometric proportion to bind the elements together into a unified whole.</meta>

664 On the Universe.

[Left Column]

...union or proportion can be said. For when, among three items—whether numbers, figures, or any kind of things—it happens that the middle term is related to the first in the same proportion as the last is compared to it; and conversely, as the extreme is compared with the middle, so the middle is compared with the first: then that which is the middle becomes both the first and the last, while the last and the first become the middle. 

<margin>Or "bound together"</margin>
<note>The margin note *An deiuncta* suggests a variant reading in the manuscript: *deiuncta* (separated) versus *devincta* (bound). Cicero is discussing how distinct elements are unified.</note>
Thus necessity compels that those things which were *separated* should become the same. And since they have been made the same, it follows that all things are one. Now, if the body of the universe were being explained as a flat and even surface, and required nothing else, a single intervening middle <term>Middle: in mathematics, a 'mean' or bridge that connects two values</term> would bind both itself and those things between which it was placed. But since solidity was sought for the world—and all solid things are never joined by a single middle, but always by two—it thus happened that between fire and earth, God placed water and air, and compared them to each other and joined them in proportion, so that just as... 

<note>Plato’s logic here is that while a 2D plane needs only one middle term to connect two points (e.g., A : B : C), a 3D solid requires two middle terms to bridge the gap between two extremes (e.g., Fire : Air : Water : Earth).</note>

<summary>This page describes the mathematical harmony of the cosmos, explaining how the Creator used geometric proportions to unify the four elements into a single, solid body. It argues that while a flat surface needs one "middle" to connect its parts, a three-dimensional world requires two (air and water) to bridge the gap between fire and earth.</summary>

On the Universe. 665

[Left Column]
...and by that motion which was always in the same [state] and driven in the same manner, he [the Creator] surrounded them from all sides. And so, when he had embraced the outer circle as one and the inner as another, he designated the former as being of the "Same" nature and the latter of the "Other" nature. He turned the circle of the "Same" sideways toward the right; but this closer one he directed from the middle line toward the left. Yet he gave supremacy to the upper one, which alone he left undivided. As for the inner one, after he had divided it into six parts of the heaven, he commanded seven unequal orbits to be moved by double and triple intervals, with courses contrary to one another; of these, he made three move with equal speeds, but the other four with speeds different from one another and from the remaining three. 

Therefore, when that God, the progenitor of the world, had generated the Soul from his own mind and divinity, he then finally placed all that was solid and corporeal beneath that Soul, making it internal, and thus joined them by fitting center to center. So the Soul, proceeding from the middle, enveloped the extremity of heaven from the highest region in a circular path, and turning within itself, began the starting point of a divine, eternal, and wise life. And while the body of the heaven was made visible, the Soul escapes the sight of the eyes. Now, the Soul is a partaker and participant in all the ratios of composition <note>original: "ἁρμονίαν" (*harmonían*), meaning harmony or musical proportion</note> of eternal things and those falling under the understanding; nothing better than this was ever produced by the best and most excellent parent. Indeed, since it is bound from the nature of the "Same" and the "Other," and with matter added through a tempering of three parts and a compact proportion, the Soul, turning within itself, when it has grasped mutable matter, and then again the undivided and simple nature through which everything is moved, it discerns what is of the same kind and what is different, and judges all other things: what is most fitting for each thing, and in what place or manner or time it happens, and what distinction exists between those things that are born and those that are always the same. 

Now, true reason, which is occupied with those things that are always the same, and moves of itself without voice or any sound within the "Same" and the "Other," when it touches that part where sensation can occur—and the orbit of that "Other" kind, unchanged and upright, announces everything to the soul and mind—then firm and true opinions and beliefs are born. But when it turns toward those things which, remaining always the same, are contained not by sense but by intelligence, so that the course of the Moon should most closely encircle the Earth, and the revolution of the Sun should be closest to it above the Earth. Then Lucifer <note>The Roman name for the planet Venus</note> and the holy star of Mercury have a course equal to the speed of the Sun, but a certain contrary power; by the running together that Lucifer, Mercury, and the Sun have among themselves, some overtake others and are overtaken in turn. As for the reason for the placement of the remaining stars, and what their placement is, that must be deferred to another discussion, lest a greater speech be spent on what was merely to be touched upon than on the subject for whose sake we touched upon it. 

Therefore, when each of these stars attained its proper course, by which the movement of time was to be marked, and their bodies were bound with vital links, and when living beings were born and learned to obey authority, then, from the transverse motion of the "Other" nature running into the motion of the "Same" nature, and being held and hindered in them: as some traversed a larger orbit and others a smaller, the larger more slowly and the smaller more quickly, by the motion of the one and the same nature: those which moved most swiftly seemed to be overtaken in speed by the slower ones, and though they were surpassing them, they seemed to be surpassed. For he turned all their orbits...

[Right Column]
...as if in the twist of a spiral <note>Latin: *Helicis inflexione*</note>, because they were proceeding in two opposite directions at once, so that what was slowest became closest to the swiftest. And so that there might be some evident measure which would declare the speeds and slownesses in those eight courses, God himself kindled the Sun like a light at the second circuit above the earth, so that the heaven might shine as much as possible for all, and so that living beings who were entitled to be taught might learn the nature and power of numbers from the motion of the "Same" and from that which was similar to it. 

Day and night, therefore, were generated in this manner and for these causes, making one most wise and excellent circuit of the orbit. A month occurs when the moon, having traversed its course, catches up with the sun. A year occurs when the sun has finished its whole circle and traveled through its orbit. But as for the orbits of the other stars, men—except for a very few—are ignorant of them, and neither call them by name nor measure them against one another by number. Thus they do not know that these wanderings of the stars are what is rightly called "Time," endowed as they are with infinite multitude and admirable variety. Nevertheless, it can be seen and understood that the absolute and perfect number of time is finally fulfilled in the "Perfect Year," when the eight circuits, having finished their courses, have returned to the same starting point, and when the same orbit, always similar to itself, has measured them out. For these reasons the stars were born, which, penetrating through the heaven, would turn back at the summer and winter solstices, so that this whole visible living being might be most similar to that eternal living being which we perceive, in imitation of eternity. 

And indeed, he had fashioned other things up to the birth of time, impressed by those things he was imitating; but because he had not yet included every living being within the world, the likeness of the image fell short of the proposed model in that respect. Therefore, as many and of what kind of forms of living beings as the mind could perceive in the appearance of things, so many and of such kinds did he think to fashion within this world. Now there were four kinds of living beings: one divine and heavenly, another winged and of the air, a third terrestrial, and a fourth of divine animation <note>Cicero's translation of the "aquatic" or "water-dwelling" category. The text refers to fire-based beings (stars) as the "divine" type.</note>. He made the [heavenly] form mostly out of fire, so that it might be the most splendid and beautiful to behold. And since he wished to make it similar to the nature of the universe, he rounded it for mobility, and with wisdom as its companion, he made it of the best possible mind, and distributed it equally throughout the heaven, so that this heaven, distinguished by variety, might be called by the Greeks "Cosmos" <note>original: "κόσμον"</note> and by us the "Shining World." He gave to the divine [stars] two kinds of motion: one which would always be in the same state and equal, and the same in all things, and would move with speed in one way; the other, which he moved earlier, toward whatever part it might be driven by the revolution of the "Same" and the "Similar." But for the five remaining motions, he willed that orbit to be immobile and standing; of which kind are those stars which, fixed in the heaven, do not move from their place, which are living beings...

Cicero details how the Sun, Moon, and planets define time and lead toward the "Great Year," concluding with the four categories of living beings created to populate the cosmos.</summary>

### On the Universe (*De Universitate*)
**[Page 666]**

...at times they [the celestial bodies] are hidden from our sight, and emerging again, they strike terror into those devoid of reason. If we should attempt to explain these things in words without any image of these matters being placed before the eyes, the labor would be undertaken in vain. But enough has been said of these things by us: let what we have prefaced concerning the nature of the Gods who are discerned, and those who have arisen, have this limit.

As for the rest, whom the Greeks call *daimones* [δαιμονας], our people (as I think) call *Lareis*—if only this can be seen as correctly translated—both to know and to announce their origin is a task greater than what we would dare to profess or write. Doubtless, belief must be given to the ancients and to the men of old, as they say, who claimed to be the progeny of the Gods; and thus they have handed down their names to us. Moreover, they were best able to know their own progenitors. And it is a very difficult thing not to have faith in those born from the Gods, although their speech is confirmed neither by arguments nor by certain reasons. Because they seem to speak of things known to them, the ancient law and custom must be obeyed. Thus, therefore, as it has been handed down by them, let the origin of these Gods be held and described: so that we may record that *Oceanum* and *Salaciam* were generated and brought forth by the breath of heaven and the conception of the earth. From these were born *Saturnum* and *Opem*; thereafter *Iouem* and *Iunonem*, and the rest whom we are accustomed to use and call brothers among themselves and kinsmen, and their—to use an ancient word—progeny [*prosapia*].

When, therefore, all those who both move and show themselves openly, and those who reveal themselves to us only insofar as they themselves wish, were created, then that God who generated all things spoke these things to them: "Attend, you who have been born by the breath of the Gods. Of which works I am the parent and maker; these are indissoluble by my will, although everything that is bound together can be dissolved. But it is by no means the part of a good being to wish to dissolve that which is bound by reason. But since you have been born, you cannot indeed be immortal and indissoluble. Yet you shall never be dissolved; nor shall any fates of death destroy you: nor is any deception more powerful than my counsel, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those by which you were bound when you were being begotten.

"Learn, therefore, what I intend. Three genera [of life] remain for us, and these are mortal; if these are passed over, the absolute perfection of heaven will not be complete. For it will not hold all genera of animals within its embrace. But it will be necessary that it holds them, so that those which are made by me may be able to equal the life of the Gods. Therefore, so that they may be generated in a mortal condition, you yourselves undertake it; imitate, in begetting them, that power of mine which you remember me using in your own birth. Among these, those who are created such that they ought to be, as it were, of the same kin as the immortal Gods, let them be called of a divine race; let them hold the sovereignty over all living things, and let them obey you willingly by right and law. The beginning and status of these is handed over to you by me. You, however, weave a mortal part onto that which shall be immortal. Thus shall arise living beings whom you may both nourish while alive and receive into your bosom when consumed.

"He spoke these things; then he returned to the previous tempering [mixing]. In which, tempering the whole soul of the universal nature, he mixed it, and pouring out the remainder, he made it equal to the previous mixtures, in nearly the same way, except that it was not so incorrupt as those which were always the same, but he took second and even third degrees. Therefore, the whole being constituted, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars, and joined each one to each star, and so placed them, as it were, in the chariot of the universe, and pointed out the fatal and necessary laws: and he showed that the first birth of each would be the same for all, and that it would be moderated and constant, and diminished by no one. Moreover, he said that when the souls were, as it were, scattered, in certain intervals of time, a living being would arise which would be most fit for the worship of the Gods. But since the nature of the human race was twofold, things were so held that the more excellent genus was of those who were to be men.

"But when he had sown the souls into bodies by necessity, and when by necessity an accession to the bodies occurred, and then a departure [death], it was necessary that one sense should exist, common to all, excited by a more vehement motion and joined to nature; then love mixed with pleasure and distress, after that anger and fear, and the remaining motions of the mind, companions of the former, and even those contrary and dissenting: he who rules these by reason shall have lived justly; but he who gives himself over to them, unjustly. And he who has correctly and honestly finished the circuit of living given by nature shall return to that star to which he was fitted; but he who has lived immoderately and intemperately, a second birth shall transfer him into a feminine figure. And if not even then shall he make an end of vices, he shall be tossed even more gravely, and shall be transferred into the figures of beasts and wild animals most similar to his own habits: nor shall he see a limit to his evils before he begins to follow that rotation which he had within himself, innate and implanted, of the same and the one. Which shall finally happen when he has driven out by reason those things which, consisting of fire, air, water, and earth, are turbulent and devoid of reason, and reaches the first and best effect of the mind."

When he had so designated these things—and had placed himself outside of all fault or cause if any deception or vice should happen afterward—he sowed them as if scattering them, some into the earth, some into the moon, and others into the remaining parts of the world, which are established as marks for the signification of the spaces of time. After that sowing, he permitted the younger Gods, so to speak, to fashion mortal bodies, and whatever was left of the human soul that ought to be added, all that and what followed they should polish and perfect: then that they should provide themselves as a prince and leader to this living being, and rule and govern its life most beautifully, except insofar as it might seek some misery for itself by its own fault.

And indeed he who composed all things remained constant in his own state; but those who were created by him, when they had recognized the order of the parent, followed it. And so, when they had received the immortal principle of a mortal living being, imitating the generator and maker of themselves, they borrowed particles of fire and earth, and water and air from the world (which they were to return again), and coupled them together, not with the same bonds by which they themselves were bound, but with such as could not be seen on account of their smallness [*paruitatem*]; by many "wedges" [cuneoli], as it were, driven in, they made one body out of all: likewise, they bound the circuits of the divine mind within that inflowing and outflowing body. Thus they, immersed in a river, neither held nor were held, but by great force were now carried and now were being carried. Thus that whole animal was moved indeed, but immoderately and by chance, so that it was carried by six motions: for [it moved] forward and backward, to the left and to the right, and upward and downward, now here, now there. But if it settled in splendor, then either the same appearance or sometimes a changed one returns, when the fire of the eyes has confounded and betaken itself with that fire which is poured out before the face. Things which are on the left appear on the right, because with contrary parts of the eyes, they touch contrary parts.

**[Page 667]**

### On the Universe (*De Universitate*)

...they touch. Moreover, right things respond to right, and left to left, by the conversion of the lights, when these do not cohere among themselves. This happens when the smoothness of mirrors has assumed depth on this side and that; and thus it has thrust the right into the left part of the eyes, and the left into the right. Faces are also seen upside down by the repulsion of the lights, which, by turning, makes the lower parts what are the superior.

And yet all these things are of that genus which assist the causes of things, which God uses as ministers, when he effects the appearance of the best insofar as it can be done. But most people estimate that these are not assisting causes, but are themselves the causes of all things, which have the power of cold and heat, of solidifying and liquefying: but they [these elements] lack all intelligence and reason, which are found in no other nature except in the soul. Moreover, the soul escapes every sense of the eyes. But fire, and water, and earth, and air are bodies, and these are seen. He, however, who professes himself a lover of intelligence and wisdom, must seek out the primary causes of an intelligent and wise nature: then the secondary causes of those things which necessarily move others, being themselves moved by others. Wherefore, it seems to me that we must do it thus: that we speak of each genus of causes separately—as much of those which, with intelligence, are the effectors of the most beautiful and best things, as of those which, being void of prudence, produce inconstant and perturbed things.

And concerning the causes of the eyes indeed, that they might have that power which they now have, I think enough has been said. Moreover, let their greatest utility, given to the human race by the gift of the gods, next be explained. For the eyes have brought to us the knowledge of the best things. For this discourse which has been held by us concerning the Universe would never have been discovered if neither the stars, nor the sun, nor the heaven could have fallen under the view of the eyes. But now, days and nights having been known by the eyes, then the revolutions of months and years have devised number and measured the space of time, and we have attained philosophy for [all] things: than which boon none more desirable, none more excellent, has either been given to the race of mortals by the grant and gift of the gods, nor shall ever be given.

**THE END.**

### Translator’s Notes on Abbreviations and Readings:
*   **Lareis**: Cicero's idiosyncratic translation for the Greek *daimones* (spirits/divinities). The text notes "(vt opinor)"—as I think—reflecting Cicero's uncertainty about the term.
*   **q; / q:**: Standard abbreviation for *-que* (and).
*   **eorū, Deorū, operū, etc.**: The tilde or macron indicates a missing "m" or "n" (*eorum, Deorum, operum*).
*   **colligatū**: *colligatum* (bound together).
*   **cōditione**: *conditione* (condition).
*   **animātium**: *animantium* (of living beings).
*   **ē / ā / ō**: Used throughout the index for *em/am/om* (e.g., *scientiā* for *scientiam*).
*   **m / p / f**: In the index, these refer to *medium* (middle), *principium* (beginning), and *finis* (end) of the page column.
*   **prosapia**: An archaic Latin term for lineage or family, which Cicero explicitly notes as a "veteri verbo" (old word).
*   **Abaridis**: Reference to Abaris the Hyperborean, a legendary priest/sage.
*   **Agathos / Achos / Aither / Alphos**: These entries include Greek terms transliterated into Latin/Roman characters.

<meta>This page concludes the fragmentary Latin translation by Marcus Tullius Cicero of Plato's Timaeus. It follows the discussion of the physical properties of the world and the creation of the human body, moving here into the physics of optics and the philosophical purpose of human sight.</meta>

**On the Universe. 667**

[Left Column]
The right side corresponds to the right, and the left to the left, through the turning of the light, when the reflections do not cross over one another. This occurs when the smoothness of the mirrors <note>Cicero is describing the behavior of light in different types of mirrors—likely curved or concave mirrors which can flip or preserve the orientation of an image.</note> has assumed a certain height on this side or that, and thus it has pushed the right toward the left part of the eyes, and the left toward the right. Faces are even seen upside down by the downward thrust of the light, which, by turning, makes the lower parts into the upper.

Yet all these things belong to that class of things which serve as auxiliary causes, which God uses as ministers while he brings about the appearance of the best world, as far as it is possible. But most people estimate that these are not merely aiding causes, but are the actual causes of all things—possessing the powers of cold and heat, of solidifying and liquefying. However, these elements lack all intelligence and reason, which can be found in no other part of nature except in the soul. But the soul entirely escapes the perception of the eyes. On the other hand, fire, water, earth, and air are bodies, and these are seen. 

But he who professes himself a lover of intelligence and wisdom <note>original: "sapientiae... amatorem," a literal translation of the Greek "philosophos."</note> must first seek out the primary causes of an intelligent and wise nature; then, he must seek the secondary causes of those things which of necessity move others while being moved by others themselves. 

<column-break/>

[Right Column]
Wherefore, I see that we must do likewise: we shall speak of each kind of cause separately—both of those which, acting with intelligence, are the producers of the most beautiful and best things, as well as those which, being void of wisdom, produce effects that are inconsistent and disordered. 

Regarding the causes of the eyes—that they might have that power which they now possess—I think enough has been said. Next, let the greatest utility of the eyes, granted to the human race as a gift of the gods, be explained. For our eyes have brought us the knowledge of the most excellent things. Indeed, this very discourse we have held concerning the Universe would never have been discovered if neither the stars, nor the sun, nor the heavens could have fallen under the gaze of our eyes. 

But now, days and nights have been made known to the eyes; then the cycles of months and years have created the concept of number, have measured the passage of time, and have driven us to the investigation of the nature of the whole. From these things we have attained philosophy: no greater good than this, nor any more desirable or more excellent, has been given to the race of mortals by the grant and gift of the gods, nor will it ever be given.

**T H E   E N D.**

<summary>This final page of Cicero's translation of Plato's Timaeus explains the physics of mirror reflections before arguing that physical elements are merely tools (secondary causes) for a divine, intelligent primary cause. It concludes by praising the gift of sight, which allowed humans to observe the heavens and thereby invent mathematics, timekeeping, and philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>optics, reflection, primary causes, secondary causes, providence, vision, astronomy, origin of philosophy, Cicero, Plato</keywords>

[[page number: 314]]

## Book Twenty-Six.

...you would have spoken the truth. But in what way and from where can we claim for ourselves the art of true and persuasive oratory?

**SOCRATES.** Is it not enough, O Phædrus—or rather, is it not necessary—that a person be perfected in this struggle just as in others? Certainly, if nature has granted you the potential to be an orator, you will be an excellent one if you add doctrine and practice. If you lack any of these, you will be incomplete. As for how great such an art is, it seems to consist not in the path followed by Gorgias (the famous Sophist) and Thrasymachus, but rather in another. 

**PHÆDRUS.** Which path is that, especially?

**SOCRATES.** It seems, my good man, and not without reason, that Pericles (the Athenian statesman) stood out as the most perfect of all orators. 

**PHÆDRUS.** Why so? 

**SOCRATES.** All great arts require dialectical practice and the contemplation of the sublime in the nature of things. For the very sublimity of the mind and the effective power in perfecting any task seem to proceed from this. This is what Pericles added to his natural sharpness of wit. 

[[margin: When an orator is excellent.]] 
[[margin: Great arts require practice.]]

Relying on his familiarity with Anaxagoras (the pre-Socratic nature-philosopher), a searcher into these kinds of things, Pericles gave himself over to contemplation. He grasped that nature of the mind and of mindlessness about which Anaxagoras discoursed so diffusely. From there, he translated into the art of speaking whatever seemed useful to him. 

[[margin: Pericles was a student of Anaxagoras.]]

**PHÆDRUS.** How do you mean? 

**SOCRATES.** The method for the art of healing and the art of speaking is almost the same. 

**PHÆDRUS.** In what way? 

**SOCRATES.** In both, it is necessary to divide nature: in one, the nature of the body; in the other, the nature of the *anima* (soul). This must be done if you intend to provide medicines and nourishment to the body—not merely by practice and use, but by art—so as to make it healthy and robust. Likewise, you must apply persuasion and virtue to the soul through rational and legitimate institutions. 

**PHÆDRUS.** That seems likely, Socrates. 

**SOCRATES.** But do you think the nature of the soul can be sufficiently known without knowing the nature of the whole? 

**PHÆDRUS.** If we are to believe Hippocrates (the father of medicine), the successor of Aesculapius, we should not think the nature of the body or its doctrine can be understood without this method. 

**SOCRATES.** He speaks wisely, my friend. But besides Hippocrates, we must consider whether the reasoning of our discussion harmonizes with it. 

**PHÆDRUS.** I agree. 

**SOCRATES.** Observe, then, what Hippocrates and true reason say about the investigation of nature. 

[[margin: On the reasoning of nature.]]

Should we not consider the nature of each thing in this way? First, whether that thing—about which we wish to possess an art and give it to others—is simple or manifold. Then, if it is simple, we must investigate its power: what it does and to what it acts, or what it suffers and from what it is acted upon. But if it has many species, once these are numbered, one must inquire into the natural power of acting and suffering in each one, just as in the single case. 

**PHÆDRUS.** So it appears, Socrates. 

**SOCRATES.** Proceeding without these is like the journey of a blind man. However, someone who treats something by art should not be compared to the blind or the deaf. It is clear that whoever applies speeches to someone by art will exquisitely demonstrate the substance of that nature to which he applies the speeches—and that is the soul. 

**PHÆDRUS.** Without a doubt. 

**SOCRATES.** Does not his entire effort strive toward this: to persuade the soul thoroughly from within? 

**PHÆDRUS.** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES.** It is established, then, that Thrasymachus or anyone else who applies himself to teaching rhetoric must first, with the greatest diligence, describe and declare whether the soul is naturally one and uniform, or manifold according to the form of the body. For we say this is what it means to "show nature." 

**PHÆDRUS.** Absolutely. 

**SOCRATES.** Second, he must show what it can do to each thing, or what it can suffer from each. 

**PHÆDRUS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** Third, having distinguished the types of speeches and souls and their affections, he must run through all the causes, matching each speech to each type, teaching what kind of soul is necessarily moved to belief by what kinds of speeches and for what cause, and why another is not moved at all. 

**PHÆDRUS.** That would be most excellent, as it seems. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, my friend, neither this nor anything else will ever be treated artistically if it is treated otherwise. But our current writers of this art, whom you have heard, are clever; they know the nature of the soul most beautifully but hide it from us. Until they speak and write in this manner, we will never admit they write according to art. 

**PHÆDRUS.** What manner do you mean? 

**SOCRATES.** I cannot easily say the words themselves. But I will explain, as far as possible, the manner in which one ought to write if one is to write by art. 

[[margin: How one must speak by art.]]

**PHÆDRUS.** Tell me, I beg you. 

**SOCRATES.** Since the power of speech is a certain drawing and delighting of the soul, the future orator must know how many species the soul has. These are so many and of such a kind that from them, some people are made this way, and others that way. Once these are distinguished, there are also so many and such species of speeches. Thus, souls of a certain kind are easily persuaded to certain things by certain speeches for a specific reason; while those affected differently are not persuaded at all for another reason. 

Therefore, he who has sufficiently perceived these things must later be able to mark them in actual affairs and catch them in the moment they are perceived by the senses. Otherwise, he still has nothing more than the words once handed down to him by teachers. 

But when he can sufficiently say who is persuaded by what speeches, and acutely perceives the person before him to be endowed with that character about which he previously discoursed—that *this* is the very person to be compelled to such things by such speeches—if he is so instructed, then finally he will have perfectly attained this art. This happens when he adds to these previous things the knowledge of the opportunity for speaking and keeping silent, and recognizes the proper use or misuse of brevity, of pity, of sharp vehemence, of amplification, and of the other parts of oratory handed down by teachers. Not before. 

He who lacks any of these in speaking, teaching, or writing, yet claims to speak by art, will fail to persuade. Perhaps, then, a writer will compel us thus: "O Phædrus and Socrates, do you think the art of speaking is to be grasped in this way, or otherwise?" 

**PHÆDRUS.** It is impossible, Socrates, to do it otherwise, although it appears to be no small task. 

**SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. Because of this, one must revolve all speeches up and down to search whether any easier or shorter way to that art occurs, so we do not wander aimlessly through a long and rough path when we might walk through a short and level one. Therefore, if you can bring any help from what you have received from Lysias or anyone else, recall it to memory and explain it. 

**PHÆDRUS.** For the sake of trying, I could perhaps do so, but not at present. 

**SOCRATES.** Do you want me to recount a speech I once heard about these matters? 

**PHÆDRUS.** Why not? 

**SOCRATES.** They say, then, Phædrus, that it is just to give even the wolf's side of the story. 

[[margin: A proverb.]]

**PHÆDRUS.** You should do so. 

**SOCRATES.** They say there is no need to extol and magnify these things so much, nor to seek the discussion from so high and far away. For, as we said at the beginning of the discussion, a future orator does not need to know the truth about what is just and good, whether regarding things or men who are such by nature or education. For in the courts, no one cares about the truth of these things at all, but

[[page number: 315]]

## Phædrus, or, On Beauty.

rather about persuasion. That is what is "likely," and it is what he who intends to speak by art must aim his mind toward. Sometimes, deeds should not even be told unless it is probable they were done; rather, in both accusation and defense, one should always introduce "verisimilitudes" (things like the truth). The speaker should pursue the likely and neglect the true. If this is observed in every speech, they say the perfect oratorical art is exhibited.

**PHÆDRUS.** You have recounted the things said by those who profess the rhetorical art, Socrates. I remember we touched on this briefly in earlier parts. This seems to be a great matter for those who dwell in this art. But you have also persuaded Tisias (an early Sicilian rhetorician) himself quite seriously.

**SOCRATES.** Let Tisias tell us this then: does he call anything "probable" and "likely" other than what seems so to the common crowd?

**PHÆDRUS.** What else could it be?

**SOCRATES.** He seems to have found and written this clever and artificial example: that if a weak but bold man, having beaten and robbed a certain robust but timid man, is brought into court, neither of them ought to confess the truth. Rather, the timid man should say he was not beaten by the bold man alone, while the bold man should repel this, showing they were alone, and take refuge in this: "In what way could I, being weak, have attacked this robust man?" The other will not mention his own timidity but, devising some other falsehood, will perhaps argue against his adversary. And in other cases, there are such things said by art. Is it not so, Phædrus?

**PHÆDRUS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Oh, how cleverly Tisias—or whoever it was, or by whatever other name he delights in—seems to have found this hidden art! But shall we say this to him, my friend, or not?

**PHÆDRUS.** What is that?

**SOCRATES.** "O Tisias, long before you arrived, we were affirming that this 'probable' and 'likely' thing arises for the crowd only through a likeness to the truth. We were asserting that likenesses of the truth are most aptly found everywhere by him who *knows* the truth." Therefore, if you say anything else about this art, we will listen; if not, we will trust what we said a little while ago: namely, that unless one knows and distinguishes the characters of the listeners, and divides things themselves into their species, and again comprehends each under one idea, he will never attain the art of speaking as far as is permitted to man. 

This, however, will never be attained without long study. A prudent man will not sweat over this so that he can speak and act before men, but rather so that he might be able to speak and do things that are pleasing to the gods, according to his ability. For men wiser than us, O Tisias, say that a man of sound mind ought not to meditate on how to please his fellow-servants (except as it happens), but how to obey good masters born of the good. Therefore, if the circuit is rather long, do not wonder. For it must be circled not for the sake of the things you think, but for the sake of great things. But these results, as reason dictates, will be most beautifully effected from those efforts if someone is willing.

**PHÆDRUS.** This seems to be spoken very beautifully, Socrates, if only someone could attain it.

**SOCRATES.** But it is noble to always strive for noble things, and to endure whatever happens.

**PHÆDRUS.** Truly.

**SOCRATES.** Let this be said regarding the art and the ignorance of speech.

**PHÆDRUS.** Sufficiently indeed.

**SOCRATES.** It remains for us to speak of what is becoming and unbecoming in writing.

**PHÆDRUS.** Plainly.

[[margin: On the decorum of writing.]]

**SOCRATES.** Do you know how you can best please God in speaking or doing things regarding speeches?

**PHÆDRUS.** Not at all. Do you?

**SOCRATES.** I have heard some things handed down by the ancients; but whether they are true, they alone know. If we could find the truth ourselves, would we have any further care for human opinions?

**PHÆDRUS.** A ridiculous question indeed; but recount what you say you have heard.

**SOCRATES.** I heard that around Naucratis in Egypt, there was one of the ancient gods, to whom the bird called the Ibis was dedicated; the name of the *daemon* (divinity) himself was Theuth. He was the first to invent number and calculation, geometry and astronomy, and also games of dice and lots, and letters. 

At that time, Thamus was king of all Egypt, living in the great city which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and they call the god himself Ammon. Theuth went to him, demonstrated his arts, and said they ought to be distributed to the rest of the Egyptians. Thamus interrogated him on the utility of each; as Theuth explained, Thamus praised what seemed well said and blamed what was the contrary. 

Thamus is said to have shown many things to Theuth regarding each art in both directions, which would take too long to narrate. But when they came to letters, Theuth said: "This discipline, O King, will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memory. For it is an invention that is a remedy for memory and wisdom." 

But Thamus replied: "O most ingenious Theuth, one man is suited to creating the works of an art, another is prompter at judging what portion of advantage or harm they will bring to those who use them. And now you, the father of letters, out of benevolence, have affirmed the opposite of what they can actually do. For their use will produce forgetfulness in the souls of learners because of the neglect of memory; since, relying on external written monuments, they will not revolve the things themselves within their own minds. Therefore, you have found a remedy not for memory, but for reminding. 

You also hand down to your disciples the *opinion* of wisdom rather than the truth. For when they have read many things without the doctrine of a teacher, they will seem to be experts in many things while they are usually ignorant. They will also be more troublesome to deal with, since they are not endowed with wisdom itself but are adorned with the opinion of wisdom."

**PHÆDRUS.** Socrates, you easily make up speeches about Egyptians or any other nation you please.

**SOCRATES.** But, my friend, those who dwell in the temple of Zeus at Dodona assert that the first prophetic speeches erupted from an oak. To those ancients, since they were not wise like you youngsters, it was enough in their simplicity to listen to rocks and oaks, provided they told the truth. You perhaps think it matters who the speaker is and from where. For you do not consider only whether the things said are true or false.

**PHÆDRUS.** You have rebuked me rightly, and it seems to me that it happens with letters just as the Theban king said.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, whoever thinks he can either hand down an art through letters or receive it as if something certain and firm will come from letters, is quite foolish. He truly ignores the prophecy of Ammon, believing that there is something more in writings than a way to remind someone who already knows the things signified in the letters.

**PHÆDRUS.** Most rightly.

**SOCRATES.** Writing has this grave quality, Phædrus, truly similar to painting. For the works of painting stand as if they were alive; but if you ask them anything, they keep a very modest silence. You will think speeches likewise speak as if they understood something. But if, being greedy for knowledge, you inquire about something said, the same thing is always signified in them, and only one. 

And every speech, once it is written, is rolled about everywhere equally among those who understand and others for whom it is not at all suitable; it does not know to whom it

[[page number: 316]]

## Book Twenty-Six.

ought to speak and to whom it ought not. When it is unjustly affected by undeserved contumely, it always needs the protection of its father. For it can neither repel an adversary nor bring help to itself.

**PHÆDRUS.** These things also seem to be rightly said by you.

**SOCRATES.** What further? Do we see another speech, the brother of this one—how it is legitimate, and how much better and more powerful it is than the other?

**PHÆDRUS.** Which one is that? And how do you say it is made?

**SOCRATES.** I mean the one that is written with knowledge in the soul of the learner, because it can help itself and understands among whom it should speak and among whom it should be silent.

**PHÆDRUS.** You speak of the speech of the one who knows as being living and animated, of which the written speech might not unjustly be called a certain image or shadow.

**SOCRATES.** Entirely. But tell me this also: Would a farmer of sound mind, with seeds very dear to him from which he expects fruit, sow them with great zeal and diligence in the gardens of Adonis in the heat of summer, and rejoice to see them becoming beautiful within eight days? Or if he ever did so, would he do it for the sake of a certain festive day and game? But when acting seriously, applying the study of agriculture, would he not sow where it is suitable and think he has achieved enough if his sowing reaches fruit in the interval of eight months?

**PHÆDRUS.** Exactly so, Socrates; he would do the former in jest, as you say, and the latter seriously.

**SOCRATES.** And shall we think the man possessing the science of just, honest, and good things is less skilled than the farmer in sowing his own seeds?

**PHÆDRUS.** Least of all.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, he will not studiously sow them in black water with a pen along with speeches, since he cannot help them when they are in danger, nor can he sufficiently show the truth from them.

**PHÆDRUS.** Certainly, that is not consistent.

**SOCRATES.** Not at all. But he will sow and describe the "gardens of letters," as it seems, for the sake of play; and when he has written them as monuments and treasures against the forgetfulness of a future old age—both for himself and for others following the same tracks—he will surely rejoice seeing his tender fruits already born. While other men follow other games, celebrating banquets and similar things, he, meanwhile, setting those aside, will lead his life in the delights of speeches.

**PHÆDRUS.** You describe a most excellent play, Socrates, compared to the base play of others—the play of one who can play in speeches and converse about justice and the other things you mention.

**SOCRATES.** It is so indeed, friend Phædrus. But in my opinion, a much more excellent study occurs in these things when someone, using the dialectical art and finding a suitable soul, plants and sows speeches with knowledge. These can help both themselves and their sower, and produce fruit and yield seeds. From these, others born in other characters can always preserve that immortal gift, and they make the one who has them as blessed as is possible for a man.

**SOCRATES.** That too is much more excellent. 

**SOCRATES.** Now, Phædrus, these things being granted, we can distinguish the following.

**PHÆDRUS.** What things?

**SOCRATES.** Namely, those for the sake of which we descended to this point: to discuss the reproach against Lysias in the art of writing itself, and the speeches themselves, whether they are written with or without art. What is artistic and what is devoid of art seems to have been sufficiently declared.

**PHÆDRUS.** So it appears.

**SOCRATES.** It is necessary to remember again that no one can be highly skilled in the art of speaking for persuasion and teaching, as our superior reasoning showed us, until he has known the truth of those things he says or writes, and knows how to define the whole matter, and having polished the definition, knows how to divide it again according to species down to individuals. 

By this reasoning, having contemplated the soul and caught what is congruent to each character, he should thus especially dispose and adorn his speech, accommodating varied speeches to varied souls and multiple harmonies, and simple speeches to a simple soul.

**PHÆDRUS.** So it appeared entirely.

**SOCRATES.** But what shall we say of that question we touched upon above? Whether it is honorable or shameful to pronounce and write orations, and how this study can be justly blamed or not? Have not the superior points declared this sufficiently?

**PHÆDRUS.** Which ones?

**SOCRATES.** Truly, if Lysias or anyone else ever wrote or writes anything, and writes anything privately or publicly (such as civil constitutions), such that he thinks there is some great stability and certainty in his writings, that is to be thought shameful for the writer, whether it is said by anyone or not. For to be ignorant of what is true and what is false concerning the just and unjust, the good and bad—even if the entire crowd praises it—can never happen without being truly most shameful.

**PHÆDRUS.** Most shameful.

**SOCRATES.** On the contrary, consider the man who thinks that play and jest are necessary in any speech written on any subject, and thinks no speech, whether in prose or bound in meter, is worthy of great zeal in composition (like those who recite poems just for persuasion without judgment or doctrine). 

Instead, he believes the best of those speeches were composed for the sake of reminding those who already know. In those speeches spoken for the sake of teaching and learning—which are truly written in the soul concerning just, honest, and good things—he thinks there alone is perspicuity and perfection, and he considers these alone worthy of study. 

He says such speeches are to be called his "legitimate sons": first the one found within himself, then whatever sons and brothers of this offspring are born in his own mind or the minds of others as is fitting. All other speeches he postpones. This man, I say, Phædrus, seems to be the kind we should wish to be.

**PHÆDRUS.** I certainly desire and pray for it exactly as you say.

**SOCRATES.** But enough from us about the art of speaking, as if these things were said in play. Therefore, tell Lysias that we, having gone to the stream of the nymphs and the Muses, heard certain speeches that ordered us to say to Lysias and the other writers of orations—and further to Homer, and whoever else composed naked poetry or poetry adorned with song, and finally to Solon and all who committed civil institutions to letters: that if, being conscious of the truth, they composed such things and can defend them in discussion, and by speaking make their writings appear cheap compared to their words, they should not be named after these things they played with using a pen, but rather from those they seriously thought out.

**PHÆDRUS.** What names do you provide, and in what way?

**SOCRATES.** The name of "Wise," Phædrus, seems great and suitable to God alone. But we might more conveniently and modestly call such men as we just described "Philosophers" (lovers of wisdom) or some similar name.

**PHÆDRUS.** It certainly is not unbecoming.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, will you justly call the one who has nothing more excellent in himself than what he wrote—and who composed it by turning it up and down, adding or subtracting in long emendation—a poet or a writer of orations or laws?

**PHÆDRUS.** Why not?

**SOCRATES.** 

[[page number: 317]]

## Apology.

**SOCRATES.** You should report these things to your friend. 

**PHÆDRUS.** But what will you do? For your friend must not be overlooked. 

**SOCRATES.** Who is that? 

**PHÆDRUS.** The noble Isocrates. What will you announce to him, Socrates? What shall we say he is? 

**SOCRATES.** Isocrates is still a youth, Phædrus. But I am inclined to say what I augur for him. 

**PHÆDRUS.** What is it then? 

**SOCRATES.** He seems to me to be of a greater genius than to be compared with the orations of Lysias. 

[[margin: Cicero says this in *The Orator* in these words.]]

Furthermore, he has a greater natural disposition toward virtue, so that it would be no wonder if, as he advances in age, he either stands out in this genre of orations which he now studies as much as he surpasses all other boys who ever touched orations, or if, not content with these, he should desire greater things by some divine movement of the soul. For a certain natural philosophy dwells in the mind of this man. This message, received from these gods, I bring to Isocrates, who is most dear to me. You bring those things to Lysias, who is most dear to you. 

**PHÆDRUS.** So it shall be. But let us depart from here, as the heat has now somewhat subsided. 

**SOCRATES.** Prayers must be made to these gods before we go. 

**PHÆDRUS.** Why not? 

**SOCRATES.** O friend Pan, and all you other gods who inhabit this place, grant that I may become beautiful within; and whatever I have externally, let it be friendly to my internal things. Let me consider the wise man alone to be wealthy. And let me have only as much gold as no one else can bear or carry, except a temperate man. Do you think anything else should be prayed for, Phædrus? For me, the prayer is enough. 

**PHÆDRUS.** Pray the same for me. For among friends, all things are common. 

**SOCRATES.** Let us depart.
