# [SOCRATES' SPEECH]

I do not know, men of Athens, how you have been affected by my accusers. I certainly was so affected that I almost forgot myself, so persuasively did they speak—though they brought almost nothing true to you. But of the many things they falsely asserted, I admired this most: that they warned you to be on your guard lest you be deceived by me as if I were eloquent. 

For they were not at all ashamed to assert that which I was mox about to refute by deed, since in your presence I appear far removed from eloquence. This, I say, seemed to me the most impudent of all, unless they perhaps call "eloquent" one who speaks the truth. For if they say that, I would confess myself to be a rhetorician, though not in their manner. 

For while these men, as I say, spoke nothing true, you will hear from me all true things. And by Jove, men of Athens, you will not hear from me a painted oration like theirs, with elegance of words and names, nor otherwise adorned, but you will hear one woven with whatever words happen to occur by chance. For I trust that I speak just things, and let none of you expect me to speak otherwise; for it would not befit this age, men, to enter here before you in the manner of young boys with studiously formed words. 

Therefore, men of Athens, I earnestly pray and beseech you: if you hear me using the same words in my defense that I use in the marketplace at the money-changers' tables—where many of you have heard me—and elsewhere, do not wonder, nor be angry. For thus it is: I come now for the first time into court, being more than seventy years old, so that I am truly a stranger to the manner of speaking used here. 

And surely, just as if I had come to Athens as a stranger, you would forgive me for speaking in a foreign voice and style, according to the custom of my upbringing; so also now I pray you—and not unjustly—that you pay no attention to the form of my speaking (which may be better or worse as it happens), but consider only this and apply your mind to it: whether I say just or unjust things. For this is the duty of a judge; but the duty of a rhetorician is to speak the truth.

It is just, men of Athens, that I first respond to the first false accusation and the first accusers, and then to the newest. For many have falsely accused me to you for many years now, and I fear them more than the supporters of Anytus, though they too are powerful in persuasion. 

But those are more powerful, men, who occupied most of you from childhood, accusing me far from the truth and persuading you: namely, that there is a certain wise Socrates, a searcher of the things above the air and below the earth, who usually makes the worse cause appear better through discourse. Those who spread this rumor about me, men of Athens, are my most powerful accusers. For those who hear these things think that searchers of such matters do not believe the gods exist. 

Indeed, such accusers are many, and they have accused me for a long time, and they persuaded you at an age in which most of you were boys or certainly youths—easily believing it in an empty cause, with no one defending me. And what is most alien to the nature of defense, it is not even possible to know or speak their names, unless perhaps one of them is a comic poet (referring to Aristophanes). 

But whoever persuaded you through envy and calumny, and whoever being persuaded then persuaded others—all these are entirely infinite; I cannot bring any of them into court or refute them, but it is necessary to fight against them as if in the dark, defending and refuting with no one responding. 

Consider, then, as I was saying, that my accusers are twofold: those who accused me recently, and those of long ago, whom I just described. Judge then that I ought to respond first to those whom you yourselves heard first and much more often. 

Come, then, I must respond, men of Athens, to those crimes, and try in this so brief a time to remove that opinion which you, deceived by calumnies, have conceived against me over so long a time. I wish to refute my adversaries and succeed, if it is better for you and for me. Although I think it will be difficult. Nor does it escape me what kind of task it is. But as it pleases God, so let it happen. We must obey the law and bring our defense. 

Let us repeat from the beginning what the accusation is, from which that calumny was born against me, which Melitus relied on when he brought this suit. What then do my accusers say? As if they were present in court, let their accusation be recited, in which they swore regarding the calumny: 

"Socrates acts unjustly and searches too curiously into the things under the earth and in heaven, and makes the inferior cause superior. Furthermore, he teaches the same things to others." 

Such is the accusation. Indeed, you have seen such things in the comedy of Aristophanes: for the character of Socrates is carried about there, affirming that he wanders through the air, and many such trifles. Of these things, I know nothing, neither much nor little. 

Nor do I say this as if I make little of the science of these things, if anyone is wise in such matters (lest I be accused of so great a crime by Melitus), but because truly, men of Athens, I know nothing of them. I bring most of you as witnesses. I ask that you teach and explain to each other, however many of you have ever heard me talking—and most of you have. Recount to each other, then, if any of you ever heard me disputing about these things at all, whether much or little. And from this, finally, you will know that the other things many people say about me are of the same kind. 

But none of these things is true. Moreover, if you have heard from anyone that I teach men and make money from it, that is not true either. Although it seems noble to me if someone can teach men, like Gorgias of Leontini, and Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis. Each of these, men, has that faculty by which, going to individual cities, they persuade youths—who could have committed themselves to the discipline of their own citizens for free—to leave their own discipline and follow them, giving them money and being grateful besides. 

There is also another wise man here from Paros, who I heard had arrived. For it happened that I once met a man who has spent more money on the Sophists than all the others: Callias, son of Hipponici. I interrogated him (for he has two sons): "O Callias," I said, "if your sons were colts or calves, we would have someone to hire and set over them who would make them beautiful and excellent in their kind, and he would be either a horse-trainer or a farmer. But now, since your sons are men, whom do you think to set over them? And who has the science of this human and civil virtue? I think you have thought about this, since you have sons. Is there such a person," I asked, "or not?" 

"There is indeed," he said. "Who is it?" I asked, "and from where? and for how much does he teach?" "Evenus of Paros," he said, "and the fee is five minae." And I judged Evenus happy if he truly has this art and teaches so diligently. For I myself would also boast and make much of myself if I knew such things. But certainly, men of Athens, I do not know them. 

Someone might perhaps ask: "But Socrates, what is your work? And from where did these calumnies arise against you? Unless you were doing something outside the custom of others, so great a rumor would never have been raised about you. For from where does such frequent talk come, unless you had done something different from the rest? Tell us then what it is, lest we judge anything rashly about you." 

This seems a just interrogation; and I will try to show you what it is that has produced this name and calumny for me. Listen now, though I fear I may seem to some of you to be joking. But know that I will tell you the entire truth. 

Truly, men of Athens, I have attained this name for no other reason than for a certain wisdom. But for what kind of wisdom? Perhaps for that which is human wisdom. For in this, I truly seem to be wise. 

Those others whom I mentioned a little while ago perhaps have a wisdom greater than human, or I do not know what to call it; for I am not endowed with it. If anyone says I possess it, he lies and speaks this to calumniate me. But let it not be troublesome to you, men of Athens, nor be moved if I seem to say something great to you; for I will not speak from myself alone, but I will bring a witness worthy of trust. 

If there is any wisdom in me, I will provide the Delphic god as a witness to you of what kind it is. You certainly knew Chærephon. He was familiar to me from youth, and a friend to the Athenian people, and he fled into exile with you and returned with you. You know what kind of man Chærephon was, how vehement he was in whatever he turned himself toward. 

Once, having traveled to Delphi, he dared to ask this of the oracle. Do not take it badly, men, what I am about to say. He asked if there was anyone wiser than me. The Pythia (the priestess) responded that no one was wiser. Regarding these things, his brother here will testify to you; for Chærephon himself has passed away. 

Consider why I say these things. For I must open to you from where this calumny against me arose. When I heard these things, I thought to myself: "What does the God say? Or what does he signify? For I am conscious to myself that I am wise neither in great things nor in small. What then does he mean when he asserts I am the wisest? It is not to be believed that the God lies, for that is not permitted to God." 

And so for a long time, I was ambiguous, searching for what the oracle meant. At last, after long wanderings, I found a way of this kind. I approached one of those who seem wise, hoping that if anywhere, the prophecy could be refuted there, and shown to the oracle that not I, whom he had preferred, but this man was to be preferred in wisdom. 

While I was examining him—his name it is not necessary to mention, but he was one of those active in the republic—while I was examining and discussing with him, men of Athens, I was affected in this way: that man seemed to me to appear wise both to others and especially to himself, but not to be so at all. Then I tried to show him that he thought himself wise, but was not. 

Because of this, he became hostile to me, and many who were present took it badly. So, returning to myself, I thought: "I am surely wiser than this man. For it appears that neither of us knows anything beautiful or good. But the difference is this: that he, while he knows nothing, thinks he knows something; I, on the other hand, as I do not know, so I do not think I know. I seem, then, in this little thing to be wiser than this man, because I do not even think I know what I am ignorant of." 

After this, I went to another of those who are held to be even wiser than he, and in considering him, I judged entirely the same, and I made him and many others hostile to me. 

Hence, I proceeded likewise to others, not ignoring how much hatred I was exciting against myself, and so I proceeded not without a certain pain and fear. Nevertheless, it seemed necessary to me to prefer the divine oracle to all things, and to go everywhere searching for what the oracle meant, and for the sake of this, to visit everyone who seems to know anything. 

And by the Dog, men of Athens—for I must tell you the truth—such a thing happened to me in this search from the divine oracle: those who were most approved in the opinion of men, I found to be almost the most imprudent of all; while those who were held to be inferior seemed to be more probable regarding prudence. 

It is worthwhile to recount my errors and labors to you, which I sustained while the oracle was so proven by me that it could not be refuted. After the men in the republic, I went to the poets, the authors of tragedies and dithyrambs and other poems, as if I would clearly catch myself being more ignorant than them. 

Taking their books, in which they seemed to have labored most, I inquired after their meanings, so that I might learn something from them. I am ashamed, men, to open the truth to you here, but it must be said. Almost all others present could speak better about the things they themselves had written in their poems. 

I caught this quickly in the poets: that they do not do what they do by wisdom, but by a certain nature from a divine agitation of the soul, just as those who prophesy are inspired by divine fury. For these also say many and excellent things, but they understand nothing of what they say. I saw the poets were affected in the same way, and at the same time I perceived that because of their poetry, they judged themselves to be the wisest of all men in other things in which they were not wise. 

I departed, then, with the same opinion I had of the politicians. Finally, I went to the craftsmen, being well conscious of how little I knew there, and I knew they knew many and beautiful things, and I was not deceived in this. For they knew things I did not, and in this part, they were wiser than me. 

But, men of Athens, I caught the skilled craftsmen in the same error as the poets. Because they performed their own craft rightly, each of them thought himself most wise in other things, even the greatest. And this error obscured even that wisdom they did possess. Therefore, I asked myself in place of the oracle which I would choose: to be as I am, knowing neither what they know nor being ignorant of my own ignorance, or having both as they have them. I answered myself and the oracle that it is better for me to be as I am. 

Because of this inquiry of mine, men of Athens, many most difficult and grave enmities have arisen against me, from which many calumnies followed. The name of "Wise" arose for me because those present think I know those things in which I refute others. 

But it seems, men of Athens, that in truth only God is wise, and in this oracle he means this: that human wisdom is to be weighed as little or nothing. He names Socrates as wise to use my name as an example, as if to say: "He, men, is the wisest who, like Socrates, knows that his wisdom is truly worth nothing." 

Therefore, I was thus affected then, and now I do not cease searching and inquiring everywhere in obedience to God, meeting anyone, whether citizen or stranger, whom I think to be wise. And if ever he does not seem so to me, then I, supporting and obeying the God, demonstrate that he is not wise. And because of such occupations, almost no leisure is left to me either to do anything worthy of mention for the public or for my private affairs, but I am placed in extreme poverty because of my service to God. 

Furthermore, the wealthiest youths, who have time from their business, follow me voluntarily and delight when they see men refuted by us. Moreover, they themselves sometimes imitating me, strive to confute others. In which thing they find a great crowd of men who think they know something, when they either know nothing or very little. 

Those who are convinced by them are angry not so much at them as at me, and they cry out that there is a certain most wicked Socrates, a corruptor of youth. But if anyone asks them what I do or teach that corrupts them, they can assign nothing; indeed, they are entirely ignorant. 

But lest they seem to lack material, they fly to those things which are commonly objected to those who philosophize: namely, that he cares for things in the air and under the earth, and does not believe in gods, and persuades that the bad cause is good. 

For the truth, I think, they do not want to confess: that they are indignant because they have been convicted of pretending to know what they do not know. Since they are ambitious and vehement and many, and as if by agreement and with the diligent study of persuasion, they have filled your ears, both long ago and recently, with calumnies diligently fashioned against me. 

From among these, Melitus, Anytus, and Lycon rose against me: Melitus hostile because of the poets, Anytus because of the craftsmen and governors of the republic, and Lycon for the sake of the rhetoricians. 

Because of this, as I said from the beginning, I would wonder if I could remove from you in so short a time this opinion conceived from so many calumnies and so long established. These things, men of Athens, I speak truly to you, and I hide nothing, nor do I subtract anything great or small, although I almost know that in saying these things, I will be troublesome to them. 

Which is an argument to you that I speak the truth, and that this calumny has arisen against me, and its causes are as I have said. And whether you inquire into these now or later, you will find it to be so. Toward those things which the first accusers brought, let this be a sufficient defense before you. 

[[notes: Socrates now turns to address Melitus directly. He uses a dialectical method to show that Melitus has never cared about the education of youth, despite his claims. Socrates argues that if he corrupts the youth, he must do so either willingly or unwillingly. If willingly, he would be harming himself by making his neighbors worse; if unwillingly, he should be instructed rather than punished. He then addresses the charge of atheism, showing that it is contradictory to believe in "daemonic things" (as the indictment admits) without believing in daemons or gods.]]

[[notes: Socrates concludes by asserting that he will not stop philosophizing, even under threat of death, because he must obey God rather than men. He compares himself to a "gadfly" sent by God to rouse the "noble but sluggish horse" of Athens.]]

### Book Twenty-Seven.

It seems to me to be quite the opposite. For it is well known, O men of Athens, that if I had long ago entered into public affairs, I would have perished long ago; and thus I would have brought no benefit either to you or to myself. I pray you, do not be angry with me for speaking the truth. For no one can remain safe for long if they honestly and bravely oppose either you or any other [[abbrev: quā → quam: than/any other]] people, in order to prevent the many unjust and lawless things that are accustomed to happen in a city. But it is necessary for him who truly fights for justice—if he is to remain safe even for a short time—to live as a private citizen and not to touch the republic. Of these things I shall bring you great proofs—not words, indeed, but what you value more highly: deeds. 

Hear now what has happened to me, so that you may perceive more clearly that I would never have yielded to anyone against justice for fear of death, and that by not yielding, I would have perished at once. I will relate to you some troublesome and legal matters, yet true ones. For I, O men of Athens, have held no public office until now, except that I was elected to the Council [[notes: the *Boule*]]. It happened that my tribe, Antiochis, was presiding at the time when you all hastened to condemn the ten generals together—unjustly indeed, as was later known to all of you—because they had not picked up those who perished in the naval battle [[notes: the Battle of Arginusae, 406 BCE]]. 

At that time, I alone of all the *prytanes* (that is, the senators) opposed you, so that you would do nothing contrary to the laws, and I resisted with my vote. At that time, though many orators were prepared to report my name and drag me into judgment, and you yourselves ordered the same with a great shout, I thought it was more fitting for me to undergo the danger for the sake of law and justice than to side with you in sensing what was not just, out of fear of prison or death. And these things were done while the city was still established under the liberty of the people. 

But after we came to the power of the few [[notes: the oligarchy of the Thirty Tyrants]], those thirty who occupied the republic summoned me and four others into the *Tholus* (the Dome) [[notes: the *Tholos*, the seat of government]]. They ordered us to bring Leon the Salaminian from Salamis so that he might be put to death—such things as they used to command many others at that time, so that they might involve many people in their own crimes. Then I showed again, not by words but by the deed itself, that I care nothing at all for death—even if it seems a bit crude to say so—but that I care entirely for this: that I should do nothing unjust or impious. That terrible power did not frighten me in the least into doing anything unjust. But when we left the Tholus, the other four set out for Salamis and brought back Leon under arrest; I, however, went home. And perhaps they would have killed me for that, had their power not been dissolved shortly thereafter. And of these things you will have very many witnesses. 

Do you think then that I could have lived so many years if I had handled public affairs, and acting as a good man, had supported justice and, as is proper, preferred it above all else? Far from it, O men of Athens; for neither could any other human being have remained safe for long while conducting himself in this way. But throughout my whole life, whenever I handled public business, I proved myself to be such a man, and privately I was the same, never yielding to anyone in anything that was not just—neither to others, nor to any of those whom my accusers claim are my disciples. 

I, however, have never been anyone’s teacher. But if anyone desired to hear me speaking and going about my business, whether young or old, I never denied it to anyone. Nor am I one of those who disputes for money and remains silent when not paid; rather, I offer myself to be questioned by the rich and poor alike, and even if someone wants to hear what I say by responding. And if any of these people becomes good or not, I could not justly be blamed for it, since I never promised or handed down any *doctrina* (teaching) to anyone. If someone says they have learned or heard anything from me privately that I did not make common to everyone else, they do not speak the truth. 

But hear, O men of Athens, why some are delighted by my company. It is entirely true what I told you above: men are delighted when they are present while those who think they are wise—when they are not—are cross-examined. For it is not an unpleasant thing. But to me, as I said, this task has been enjoined by God through oracles, dreams, and every way through which any other divine fate has commanded a human to do anything. These things, O men of Athens, are both true and easily proven. For if I am now corrupting some of the youth, and have long ago corrupted others, it would be natural that some of them, now having become older and realizing that I gave them bad advice when they were adolescents, would rise up against me and demand punishment. Or if they themselves were unwilling, at least some of their kin—fathers, brothers, and other relatives—if their kin had suffered any evil from me, would now commemorate it and demand punishment. 

But many of them are present here, whom I see. First, there is Crito [[notes: Socrates' wealthy friend]], my contemporary and fellow tribesman, the father of this Critobulus. Then Lysanias of Sphettus, the father of this Aeschines. Furthermore, there is Antiphon of Cephisus, the father of Epigenes. There are others too whose brothers have been my familiars: Nicostratus, son of Theodotides and brother of Theodotus. (And Theodotus has died, so he cannot entreat his brother). And here is Paralus, son of Demodocus, whose brother was Theages. Also Adeimantus, son of Ariston, whose brother is this Plato. Finally, Aeantodorus, whose brother is this Apollodorus. I can mention many others, any one of whom Meletus [[notes: one of the accusers]] ought to have produced as a witness in his speech. But if he forgot then, let him produce one now; I will allow it. Let him bring forth such a person, I say, if he has one. 

But you will find, O men of Athens, that the reality is entirely the opposite. For all, as you see, have come forward willingly to bring aid to me—the man who corrupted their kin and brought them detriment, as I am accused by Meletus and Anytus. If those who were depraved themselves were to help me, it would not be surprising; but their older relatives, who were never depraved by me—for what reason would they support me, except for a right and just one? For they know that Meletus is lying and that I am telling the truth. 

These, then, O men of Athens, are roughly the things I have for my defense, and perhaps others like them. But perhaps one of you, returning to himself and his usual customs, might be annoyed that while defendants even in smaller cases are accustomed to beg with many tears and supplications, and to produce their children in court to move the jury to pity, along with many other household members and friends, I will do none of these things, even though I am established in the extreme of danger, as it seems. Someone offended by this might be more stubbornly irritated against me and, in that very anger, might cast their vote against me. 

If anyone among you is of that mind—though I do not think so—I will address him in this way: "I too, my good man, have some relatives." For as Homer says, I was not born from an oak or a rock, but from humans [[notes: cf. Odyssey 19.163]]. And so I have relatives, O men of Athens, and three sons, one of whom is already an adolescent, while two are small children. Yet I will bring none of them here [[margin: Odyssey 19.]] 

[[page number: 325]]

### Apology.

to beg for my acquittal from you. Why then will I do none of these things? Not from any stubbornness, nor from contempt for you, men of Athens. Whether I am bold in the face of death or not is another matter. However, for my reputation and yours and that of the whole city, I do not think it is fitting that I should do these things at my age and with the name I have acquired, whether that reputation be true or false. Nevertheless, it is already a common opinion among men that Socrates excels many in some particular way. If those among you who are thought to stand out in wisdom, or courage, or any other virtue, act as I have often seen some act when they were being judged, it will be a great disgrace. 

When they were thought to be of some value, yet in court they strove for pity in a marvelous way, as if they were going to suffer something grave if they departed from this life—as though they were going to be immortal if you did not kill them. Yet these men seem to me to bring shame upon the city, because some foreigner might think that those among the Athenians who excel in virtue and are held superior in magistracies and other honors are no different from women. 

These things, O men of Athens, are not fitting for those of you who seem to be of some authority to do, nor even if we wished to do them should you permit it. Rather, you should show that you would much more readily condemn the man who, by introducing such piteous displays, makes the city look ridiculous, than the man who quietly awaits judgment. 

Furthermore, O men of Athens, in addition to what has been said about the reputation of the city, it does not seem just to me to beg a judge, nor to be acquitted by begging, but rather to teach and persuade. For a judge does not sit for this purpose—to grant favors—but to judge according to the laws. And he has promised this by an oath: that he will not grant favors to whomever he pleases, but will judge according to the laws. Therefore, it is not right either for us to accustom you to swearing falsely, nor for you to become so accustomed. For neither of us would be preserving *religio* (religious duty). 

Do not, therefore, O men of Athens, require me to do such things before you which I consider neither honorable, nor just, nor holy—especially, by Jove, when I am accused by Meletus of impiety toward God. Certainly, if I were to persist in persuading you and bending you by begging when you have sworn an oath, I would be teaching you not to think that gods exist, and truly, while I prepare a defense for myself, I would be accusing myself of not believing in the gods at all. But it is far from being so. For I believe there are gods, O men of Athens, more than any of my accusers do; and I permit you and God to judge concerning me, so that it may be beneficial both to me and to you. 

That I am not distressed, O men of Athens, that I have been condemned by you, is due to many factors, and especially this: that it did not happen contrary to my expectation. Indeed, I wonder much more at the number of votes on each side. For I did not think I would miss acquittal by so small a number of votes. But now, it seems, if only three votes had fallen differently, I would have escaped. I seem to have escaped Meletus certainly, and not only escaped, but it is clear to everyone that unless Anytus and Lycon had risen to accuse me, he would have had to pay a thousand drachmas, since he would not have received a fifth part of the votes. 

So, this man proposes the death penalty for me. So be it. But I, O men of Athens, what penalty should I propose for myself? Is it not clearly what I am worthy of? What then? What is it fitting for me to suffer or pay, because I did not remain silent about what I learned, but neglected what the crowd values most—profit, family affairs, military commands, powers, and other magistracies—and besides, I avoided the conspiracies and factions that occurred in the republic, judging that I was truly born for more equitable duties than to think my safety depended on these things? 

To these things, I say, I did not turn, for being occupied with them I would have been of no use to you or to myself. But I devoted myself to this one duty alone: applying myself privately to each of you to bring the greatest benefit (as I indeed believe), persuading each one of you not to care for his possessions before caring for himself—that he might become as good and as prudent as possible—nor to care for the affairs of the city before caring for the city itself, and to have a care for other things in the same manner. 

What then, being such a man, do I deserve to receive from you? Something good, surely, O men of Athens, if you would truly estimate it according to my dignity; and indeed such a good as would befit me. What then befits a man who is poor and a benefactor, for whom it is advantageous to be free from other occupations so that he may exhort you toward virtue? There is surely no other reward, O men of Athens, that more befits such a man than to be fed in the Prytaneum [[notes: the town hall of Athens]] at public expense—and much more so than if any of you had won at Olympia with a horse, or a two-horse chariot, or a four-horse chariot. For that man indeed makes you *seem* happy, but I make you *be* happy. Furthermore, he does not need sustenance, but I do. Therefore, if I must be estimated according to dignity and justice, I judge myself worthy of this: that food be provided for me publicly in the Prytaneum. 

Perhaps, in saying these things to you, I seem as arrogant as I did in the earlier matters when I rejected pity and supplications. But it is not so, O men of Athens; it is rather of this sort. For I am persuaded that I voluntarily do injury to no one. Yet I do not persuade you of this, because we have had only a short time for speaking. But if there were a law among you, as there is among others, that where death is the penalty, the trial should last not just one day but several, I believe I would have persuaded you. But now it was not easy to dissolve great slanders in so short a time. 

Since, therefore, I am persuaded that I must do injury to no one, I am far from doing injury to myself and saying that I am worthy of evil, or that I deserve some such penalty. What then? Should I, fearing that I might suffer what Meletus thinks I deserve (which I say I do not know whether it is good or evil), choose instead one of those things which I clearly know to be evil, and judge myself worthy of it? Should it be chains? And why should I spend my life in prison, always serving the Eleven [[notes: the officials in charge of prisoners and executions]]? Should it be a fine, and to remain in chains until it is paid? But that is the same thing I said above, since I lack the means to pay. 

Or perhaps exile? For perhaps I might be judged worthy of this. But a too great desire for life would possess me, O men of Athens, if I were so foolish as to think that if you, my fellow citizens, could not bear my company and my words—but my company and speech became so heavy and hateful to you that you now decree to free yourselves from them—others would tolerate me so easily. Far from it, O men of Athens. A fine life indeed it would be for me at this age, wandering in exile, moving from one city to another, living in continual rejection. 

For I clearly understand that wherever I go, the young men will listen to me just as they do here; and if I repel them, they in turn will persuade their elders to drive me out. And if I do not repel them, their fathers and kin will expel me for their sake. 

Perhaps someone will say: "Cannot you, Socrates, live in silence and quiet in exile?" But this is the most difficult thing of all to persuade some of you. For if I respond that this would be to disobey God, and therefore I cannot keep quiet, you will not believe me, as if I were speaking with irony. And if I say that it is the greatest good for a man to speak every day about virtue and other things about which you hear me talking daily, and thus to examine myself and others—and that an unexamined life [[notes: *vitam inconsideratam*]] is not worth living—you will believe me even less. 

But these things, O men of Athens, are as I say, though they are not easily persuaded. And at the same time, I have never been accustomed to think myself worthy of evil. If I had money, I would propose a fine as large as I could pay, and it would not hurt me to lose it. But now I have none, unless you wish to estimate it at as much as I am able to pay. I can pay perhaps one mina of silver. I therefore estimate the penalty at that much. But Plato here, O men of Athens, and Crito, and Critobulus, and Apollodorus, order me to propose thirty minae. They themselves will be the guarantors for so much money. I therefore estimate it at that much; and these men will be sufficient guarantors to you for this silver. 

For the sake of not much time, O men of Athens, you will gain a reputation and provide a pretext for those who wish to revile the city to say that you killed Socrates, a wise man. For they will say I am wise, even if I am not, when they wish to revile you. If then you had waited but a short time, my death would have happened of its own accord. See my age, how far it is already from life and near to death. I do not say this to all of you, but only to those who condemned me to death. I say this also to them: Perhaps you think, O men of Athens, that I was defeated in judgment by a lack of such words by which I might have persuaded you, if I had thought I should do and say everything to be acquitted by you. 

But it is far otherwise: Certainly, I was condemned for a lack, not of words indeed, but of audacity and impudence, and because I was unwilling to say such things to you as would have been most pleasant for you to hear—namely, hearing me weeping and lamenting, and doing many other things which I said were unworthy of me, and such as you are frequently accustomed to hear from others. But neither from the beginning did I think it fitting to do anything unfree to avoid danger, nor do I now repent of having used this manner of defense. I prefer indeed to die having relied on such a defense than to survive by the opposite. 

For neither in judgment nor in war ought I or any other do everything possible to avoid death. For in battles it is often clear that death can be avoided if one throws down his arms and turns as a suppliant to his pursuers. There are other devices in individual dangers by which one might escape death, if one is not ashamed to do and say anything. But consider, O men of Athens, that it is not difficult to escape death, but it is much more difficult to escape wickedness. For she runs faster than death. 

And now I, being slow because of old age, have been caught by the slower runner; but my accusers, being vehement and fast, have been caught by that which is faster: wickedness. And now I go away, condemned by you to undergo death; but they go away condemned by truth itself to wickedness and injustice. And I am content with my penalty, as are they. Perhaps these things had to be so, and I think they are well enough. 

After this, O you who condemned me, I desire to prophesy to you. For I have already reached that point where men are accustomed to prophesy—namely, when they are near death. I predict to you indeed, O men of Athens, that if you kill me, a punishment will come upon you immediately after my death [[notes: *supplicium vobis statim post mortem meam*]] and, by Jove, one much harder than that which you have inflicted on me. For now you have done this thinking to free yourselves from being compelled to give an account of your life to anyone. 

But the opposite will happen to you. For I think there will be more people to cross-examine you, whom I was holding back, though you did not notice it; and they will be all the more troublesome as they are younger, and thus you will take it more heavily. Truly, if you think that by killing men you can free yourselves from being reviled, you are very much mistaken. For this is not a liberation that is either effective enough or honorable. But that which is both easiest and best is not to suppress others, but to prepare oneself to be as good as possible. Having prophesied these things to you who condemned me, I make an end. 

But with you who acquitted me, I would gladly speak about this thing that has happened, as long as the magistrates are occupied and I have not yet gone to that place where I must die. But, O men, stay with me for this time. For nothing prevents us from conversing with each other while it is permitted. I wish to show you, as to friends, what has just happened to me and what it signifies to my mind. 

To me indeed, O judges—for I can rightly call you judges—something marvelous has happened. For that prophetic voice of the *daemon* [[notes: the *daimonion*, Socrates' internal divine sign]] used to offer itself to me very frequently in the past, and even in the most trivial matters it would oppose me if I were about to do anything not quite right. But now, these things which you see have happened to me—things which someone would surely think and judge to be the extreme of evils. But the sign of God did not oppose me as I left home this morning, nor as I ascended this platform on which I plead my cause, nor in any part of my speech while I was talking, although at other times it frequently used to stop me in the middle of a sentence while I was speaking. 

But now in this whole affair it has nowhere opposed me either in deed or in word. What then do I think is the cause of this? I will tell you. It appears to me that what has happened is a good thing. Nor do we judge correctly when we think death is an evil. This is a great conjecture for me, because my sign would have opposed me as it was accustomed to do, unless I were about to do something good. 

We can think of it in this way: there is much hope that it is a good thing. For death must be one of two things: either death entirely removes all sensation, or as it is said, it is a migration by death from these places to some other place. Therefore, if sensation is extinguished and death is like a sleep which sometimes, even without visions of dreams, brings the most peaceful rest—good gods, what a gain death is! 

I believe indeed that if someone had to compare that night in which he passed so quietly that he did not even see a dream with the other nights and days of his whole life, and had to say how many nights and days in his life he had traveled better and more sweetly—I think that not only a private person but not even the Great King [[notes: the King of Persia]] himself could count many. If then death is something like that, I say it is a gain. For thus all time seems to be nothing more than a single night. 

But if the things that are told are true—that death is a migration to those shores which those who have departed from life inhabit—that is much more blessed. When you have escaped from those who want to be counted in the number of judges, you come to those who are truly called judges: Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus [[notes: the judges of the underworld]], and any others of the demigods who lived justly. Can this pilgrimage seem mediocre to you? And to be able to talk with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod, and Homer—at what price would you estimate that? 

Indeed, I would often wish to die, if it were possible, so that I might find those things of which I speak. [[margin: Cicero *On Divination* 2.]] [[margin: Almost all these things are described from Cicero's *Tusculan Disputations* 1.]] 

[[page number: 327]]

### Crito, Or, on what must be done.

Especially since that habitation and company will be wonderfully pleasing to me, when I am together with Palamedes and Ajax the son of Telamon, and any others of the ancients who died by being circumvented by a judgment [[notes: i.e., heroes who were unjustly condemned]]. It would not be unpleasant, I think, to compare my misfortunes with theirs. And besides, the greatest thing would be to spend time there searching out and examining each person, as I have done here, to see who among them is wise, and who thinks he is wise when he is not. 

Furthermore, O judges, at what price should one value the chance to test the prudence of the great king who led the vast forces to Troy, or of Odysseus, or Sisyphus, and many other men and women one could mention? To talk with them and live in examination of them would be an inestimable happiness. For surely those who live there no longer die, and they are both more blessed than we are in other things and, moreover, they remain immortal for the rest of time, if indeed the things that are said are true. 

You too, O judges—those of you who acquitted me—should not fear death. Think of this one thing as true: that no evil can happen to a good man, either living or dead, and that his affairs are never neglected by the immortal gods. Nor has this happened to me by chance; rather, it is clear to me that it was better for me to die now and be freed from my labors. And for this reason, that divine sign did not hinder me. 

Truly, I have no reason to be angry with those by whom I was accused or those by whom I was condemned, although they did not accuse and condemn me with this intention, but because they believed they were harming me. For this, they are indeed to be blamed. (But now, having returned to those same men, I address them thus): 

I only ask this of you, O men: that when my sons have grown up, if they are troublesome to you just as I was, you should punish them in the same way—especially if they seem to you to care more for money or any other thing than for virtue. And if they want to seem to be something when they are nothing, rebuke them as I rebuked you, because they do not attend to those things to which they ought to attend, and they think they are something when they are of no value. If you do this, I and my sons will have suffered justice from you. 

But it is time to depart hence—I to die, and you to live. Which of the two is better, the immortal gods know; I think no human being knows.

---

### CRITO, OR, ON WHAT MUST BE DONE.
### THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO.

[[image: initial 'Q']] JUST as with the *Apology*, so the disposition of the *Crito* is so orderly and plain that it does not need a lengthy argument. Note, however, first that just as Socrates prophesied while awake in the *Apology*, so in the *Crito* he prophesies while sleeping. Thus you may know that God is always present to a wise and pious man, both while he is awake and while he is sleeping. 

From all this, gather a confirmation of the Gospel teaching [[notes: Ficino often links Plato to Christian doctrine]]. The approval of martyrs. An exemplar of justice. Incomparable fortitude. Contempt for mortal things. Desire for eternal things. Finally, the foundation of religion. 

Why should I mention that the opinion of the crowd is to be held in contempt? That only the judgment of the wise man—or rather truth itself—is to be cherished? Why again, that one should not wish merely to live, but to live *well*? Likewise, that one must never do harm in return for injuries, nor should injuries be avenged? Again, that the danger of death and destruction should be undergone rather than sinning? 

Why should I recount his singular observance of the laws and his inestimable love for his fatherland? Which he undoubtedly puts before parents and life itself, for this reason (as he says): so that when he has set out for the other life, he may be able to give a fair account of his past life to the eternal judge. Nor should he be compelled to tremble before the laws that rule there—the sisters of human laws. 

Finally, he concludes that the reasons for justice ring in the ears of his mind so loudly that he cannot hear anything else, and that anyone who persists in trying to dissuade him will labor in vain. He adds that one must proceed only by that path along which God—that is, the reason divinely infused—leads.

---

### SOCRATES, CRITO.

[[image: decorative initial 'C']] **SOCRATES:** Why have you come at this hour, O Crito? Is it not still very early? 
**CRITO:** Very early indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** Exactly how early? 
**CRITO:** Just the first light of dawn. 
**SOCRATES:** I wonder how the keeper of the prison was willing to listen to you. 
**CRITO:** He is already familiar with me, O Socrates, because I come here frequently. Moreover, he has received some benefit from me. 
**SOCRATES:** Have you just arrived, or some time ago? 
**CRITO:** Some time ago. 
**SOCRATES:** Then why did you not wake me at once, but sat there in silence? 
**CRITO:** By Jove, Socrates, I would never have woken you. For I myself would not wish to remain so long in wakefulness and grief. But I have been admiring you for some time, seeing how sweetly you sleep. And I deliberately did not wake you, so that you might spend your time as peacefully as possible. Truly, I have judged you happy for your character both many times before and throughout your whole past life, but especially in this present calamity, because you bear it so easily and calmly. 
**SOCRATES:** Indeed, Crito, it would be quite absurd if someone of my age should take imminent death heavily. 
**CRITO:** Nevertheless, O Socrates, others just as old are overwhelmed by similar calamities; yet their age does not help them from bearing their present fortune heavily and with distress. 
**SOCRATES:** That is true. But why have you come so early? 
**CRITO:** I bring bitter news, Socrates—not to you, it seems to me, but to me and all your familiars, both bitter and heavy. Which I indeed, if anything else, would bear (I think) heavily and with distress. 
**SOCRATES:** What is this? Has the ship from Delos [[notes: whose arrival signaled the end of the religious stay on executions]] already returned? Upon its return, I must die. 
**CRITO:** It has not yet returned, but it seems to me it will return today, from what some people coming from Sunium [[notes: a cape in Attica]] report, who left it there. It is clear then from these reports that it will arrive today, and therefore it will be necessary for you, O Socrates, to depart from life tomorrow. 
**SOCRATES:** Good fortune, O Crito. If it so pleases the gods, so be it. However, I do not think it will return today. 
**CRITO:** From where do you conjecture that? 
**SOCRATES:** I will tell you. For on the day after, or that very day on which the ship returns, I must die. 
**CRITO:** So say those who have power over this matter. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore I do not think it will arrive on *this* day, but the other [[margin: *in the home]]. I receive this conjecture from a certain dream which appeared to me just a little while ago tonight; and you seem opportunely not to have disturbed my sleep. 
**CRITO:** But what sort of dream was it? 
**SOCRATES:** It seemed to me that a certain woman was approaching, beautiful and pleasing to look upon, wearing white garments, calling me and saying: "O Socrates, on the third day from now you shall reach fertile Phthia" [[margin: Iliad 9.]] [[notes: a quote from the *Iliad*, where Achilles speaks of going home to Phthia]]. 
**CRITO:** What an absurd dream, Socrates! 
**SOCRATES:** Manifest, however, as it seems to me, O Crito. 
**CRITO:** Manifest indeed. But, O blessed Socrates, even now listen to me and save yourself. For if you die, not only one [[margin: *In Greek: no other calamity will happen.]] calamity threatens me; but besides being robbed of such a familiar as I shall never find another, I shall certainly seem to many who do not know either of us well enough that, although I could have saved you if I had been willing to spend money, I neglected to do so. And what reputation could be more shameful than to seem to value money more than friends? 

[[page number: 329]]

### Crito, Or, on what must be done.

[Socrates continues to argue that the opinion of the crowd does not matter compared to the opinion of the expert/truth...]

...is that an evil, and where does it tend, and into what part of the one who does not obey? 
**CRITO:** Into the body, obviously; for this it corrupts. 
**SOCRATES:** You say rightly. Is it not the same with other things, O Crito? Should we not run through almost all of them by the same reasoning? Concerning things just and unjust, shameful and honorable, good and evil—about which we are now consulting—should we follow and fear the opinion of the many, or rather that of the one who understands, whom it is fitting to respect and fear more than all others? Unless we obey him, we shall be harmed and corrupted in that which is accustomed to become better through justice and to be corrupted by injustice. Or is that nothing? 
**CRITO:** I think it is so, O Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** Come then, if that which is made better by what is healthy but corrupted by what is unhealthy—not having followed the judgments of the experts—will we have to live with it destroyed? That is the body, is it not? 
**CRITO:** That very thing. 
**SOCRATES:** Should we then live with a vicious and corrupted body? 
**CRITO:** By no means. 
**SOCRATES:** Or perhaps should we live with that part of us corrupted which is harmed by injustice but helped by justice? Or do we think it is more vile than the body, whatever it is of ours, concerning which justice and injustice revolve? 
**CRITO:** By no means. 
**SOCRATES:** But it is more precious? 
**CRITO:** Greatly. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, O best of men, we should not care much about what the many say of us, but what that one says who understands just and unjust things, and truth itself. Therefore, first you did not rightly suggest that the common opinion concerning things just, honorable, and good (and their opposites) should be of any value. But truly someone will say: "But the crowd can kill us; is this not manifest?" 
**CRITO:** That certainly can be said, Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** You speak the truth. But, O admirable one, this reasoning which we have run through seems similar to the previous one. And consider this again: whether it remains for us or not—namely, that we must not value *living* most highly, but *living well*. 
**CRITO:** It remains indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** And does this also remain? That to live well, honorably, and justly are the same thing? 
**CRITO:** It remains. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, from what we have confessed, this must be considered: whether it is just for me to try to go out from here without the Athenians dismissing me, or unjust. And if it appears to be just, let us try; if not, let us omit it. 
As for the considerations you bring about the expense of money, about (common) opinion, about the education of children—beware, O Crito, lest these be considerations truly for these "many," who easily kill, and if they could, would bring one back to life, and that indeed without any reason. 

But for us, since reason so requires, nothing else is to be attended to except what we were just saying: whether we shall act justly in paying out money and giving thanks to those who lead me out from here—whether, I say, in this we act justly, both we who are led out and they who lead—or whether instead, if it appears we act iniquitously, we should not even think of it, but it befits us to undergo both death and any other punishment rather than acting iniquitously. 
**CRITO:** You seem to speak rightly, Socrates. Consider, however, what we should do. 
**SOCRATES:** Let us consider together, my good man. And if you can refute me in any part of what I say, refute me; I will assent. Otherwise, I beg you, O blessed man, stop repeating the same words to me so many times: that I ought to go away from here against the will of the Athenians. I value it highly to act having been persuaded by you, but not against my will. 

Attend, therefore, whether the beginning of the consideration seems to have been spoken conveniently enough to you, and try to answer what is asked in the way you most think you should answer. 
**CRITO:** I will try indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** Do we say that in no way should injury be done voluntarily? Or is injury to be done in some way, and in another way by no means? Or is it in no way either good or honorable to do injury, as we often confessed in the past? Which indeed has just recently been confirmed. 
Or have all those previous agreements of ours evaporated in these few days, and have we, such old men, O Crito, who have been discussing so studiously together, failed to notice that we differ in no way from children? Or rather is the matter exactly as we used to say: whether the multitude affirms it or denies it, and whether we must undergo more grave or lighter things than the present ones? Yet to do injury is altogether an evil and a shameful thing for the one who does it. Do we admit this, or not? 
**CRITO:** We admit it certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** In no way, then, must injury be done? 
**CRITO:** In no way indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** Nor, if you have suffered an injury, should you retaliate, as the crowd thinks? Since in no way must injury be done. 
**CRITO:** So it seems. 
**SOCRATES:** What then? Is it fitting to do evil to anyone, O Crito, or not? 
**CRITO:** Certainly not, O Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** What then? If he who suffers evil refers evil in turn to the one who inflicted it, would that be just as the crowd says, or unjust? 
**CRITO:** Unjust. 
**SOCRATES:** Truly, to inflict evil on men does not differ from injury. 
**CRITO:** You speak truly. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is neither fitting to retaliate nor to do evil to any human being, whatever you yourself have suffered from others. And see, O Crito, lest in conceding this, you assent to us contrary to your own opinion. For I know that very few think or will think this. 
But those who think thus and those who think otherwise have no common deliberation; it is necessary that they despise each other when they look upon each other's counsels. Observe therefore diligently whether this opinion is common to you and me, and whether you think with me. 
And should we deliberate starting from this principle: that it is never right either to do injury, or to retaliate with injury, or, having been affected by evil, to return evil to him who inflicted it? Or do you depart from us here, not consenting to this principle? To me indeed it has long seemed so, and it seems so now. If it appears otherwise to you, speak and teach me. But if you remain in the previous view, hear now what follows. 
**CRITO:** I consent indeed and remain; speak then. 
**SOCRATES:** I say therefore next—or rather I ask: whether the things someone confesses to another to be just, he ought to do, or to deceive? 
**CRITO:** He ought to do them. 
**SOCRATES:** From these things, consider this: if we go away from here without the consent of the city, shall we be doing evil to some people, and indeed to those whom it is least fitting, or not? And do we remain in those things which we agreed were unjust, or the opposite? 
**CRITO:** I cannot answer these things, Socrates. For I do not understand. 
**SOCRATES:** But consider it thus: as if, while we were wishing to flee from here (or however this should be called), the Laws and the Republic of this city should come and, standing over us, ask: 

"Tell us, O Socrates, what do you intend to do? Do you not understand that by this deed you are attempting, you are planning destruction for us Laws and for the whole city, as far as it lies in you? Do you think any city can stand longer and not be subverted in which public judgments have no force, but are made void and rescinded by private men?" 

What shall we say to these things, O Crito, and other things of this sort? For anyone, especially an orator declaiming for a law thus violated, could bring many arguments in this direction—specifically a law which commands that sentences passed in a public judgment be valid. Shall we answer them that the city did us an injury by not judging rightly? Thus, or otherwise? 
**CRITO:** Thus, by Jove, O Socrates. 
**SOCRATES:** But then the Laws themselves would answer: "O Socrates, was it not agreed between us and you that you must stand by the judgments which the city passed?" And if we were to marvel at the Laws speaking thus, perhaps they would say: "Do not marvel, Socrates, at what we have just said; rather respond, since you are accustomed both to question and to answer. Come, tell us, what do you accuse in us and the city that you strive to dissolve us? First, did we not beget you? And through us your father took your mother and brought you forth? Tell us then, do you find fault with those of us who are the laws concerning marriages, as if they were in some part not right?" 
"I find no fault," I would say. 
"But what about those laws concerning the education and erudition of children, in which you yourself were educated? Or did those laws established for this duty not dispose correctly when they ordered your father to educate you in music and gymnastics?" 
I would concede they disposed correctly. 
"Come then, after you were born through us, and educated and erudite, can you first deny that you are our offspring and servant—both you yourself and your progenitors? Then, since that is so, do you think justice is equal between you and us, and that whatever we attempt to do to you, it is just for those same things to be referred back to us by you? 
"Or, while you have no equal right against your father, or your master if you had one, so that you could return what you suffered from them—neither if they provoked you with a quarrel could you quarrel back, nor if they struck you could you strike back, nor do other such things to them—will it be permitted to you against your country and the laws? 

"Are you so wise that it escaped you that the country [[margin: In Greek, *Sorte* (Fate)]] is to be preferred before father and mother and all progenitors? And that the country is something more venerable, more holy, and in a higher place both among the gods and among humans of sound mind, and that one ought to cherish it more and obey it, and to be more submissive to it even when it behaves harshly and roughly than to a father? And if it commands anything, one must either persuade it or do it, and suffer most patiently whatever it orders to be suffered—whether it commands you to be beaten, or thrown into chains, or sends you into battle to receive wounds and undergo death, one must obey entirely. 

"For justice so dictates; and one must not turn back, nor flee, nor desert the rank. But both in war and in judgment, and everywhere, those things must be done which the republic and country command—or certainly one must persuade it and show it where its command is just. But to use force is a nefas (wickedness), whether against a mother or against a father, and most of all against the country." 

What shall we say to these things, Crito? Do the laws speak truly, or not? 
**CRITO:** It seems so to me. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore the laws might perhaps say: "Observe, O Socrates, whether we speak truly: that you are attempting unjust things against us. For we, who begat you, educated you, instituted you, and made both you and all other citizens participants in all the goods we were able to provide; nevertheless, we permit any of the Athenians, once he has recognized and approved the customs and laws of this city and the form of governing the Republic, if we do not please him, to take his things and go wherever he pleases. 

"Nor does any of us laws hinder or prohibit it, whether any of you whom we and the city do not please wishes to depart into some colony or transfer his habitation elsewhere; he may do so by his own judgment and take his things with him. But whoever of you, after he has known how we exercise judgments and rule the city in all other things, remains—him we assert to have agreed with us in deed that he will do whatever we command. 

"And we affirm that he who does not obey does injury in a threefold way: because he does not obey us who are his parents, and because he does not follow us who are his nurturers, and because having pacted to obey us, he neither obeys nor strives to persuade us if we seem to do anything not quite right. And although..."
