### Phædo, Or, On the Soul.

[[page number: 335]]

-> Phædo, Or, On the Soul. <-

I know he will do so; on the fourth day, tell him what he must answer. "Tell him the truth, O Cebes," he said, "that I did this not to compete with him or his poems—for I knew that would not be easy—but to test certain dreams and to ensure I was not failing in my duty, if perhaps this was the 'music' they have so often commanded me to practice." For it was like this: often in my past life, the same dream occurred to me, though appearing in different forms at different times, always charging me with the same thing: "O Socrates, make music and practice it."

In former times, I assumed this was an exhortation to what I was already doing. Just as we are accustomed to cheer on runners, I thought the dream was urging me on in what I was already practicing—thinking that philosophy was the *maxima musica* (the highest music) and that I was laboring in it. But after the sentence was passed against me, and the festival of the God [[notes: referring to the mission to Delos for Apollo]] prevented me from dying, I felt it necessary—should the dream so often command me—to practice this "popular music" and not resist it, but to obey. For I thought it safer to free myself from this duty and obey the dream by making poems before I departed from life. 

Therefore, I first made verses in praise of the God whose festival was then being celebrated. After the God, judging that he who is to be a poet must create not mere speeches but fables—and as I was not a myth-maker myself—I took some of the fables of Aesop (the Greek fabulist) which I knew and had at hand, and put into verse whichever ones I first encountered.

"Report these things, then, to Evenus (the poet and sophist), O Cebes, and bid him farewell; and if he is wise, let him follow me. For I depart from here today, it seems. So the Athenians command."

Then Simmias said, "What a thing to command Evenus, O Socrates! For I have often met the man, and from what I perceive of him, he will by no means be willing to obey you."

"What?" said Socrates. "Is Evenus not a philosopher?" 

"He seems so to me," Simmias replied. 

"Then Evenus will be willing, as will anyone who is a worthy participant in this pursuit. However, perhaps he will not lay violent hands upon himself. For they say it is not *fas* (divinely lawful)." And as he said this, he lowered his legs from the bed to the ground. Sitting thus, he disputed the rest.

Cebes then asked him, "In what way do you say this, O Socrates? That it is not lawful to violate oneself, yet the philosopher should desire to follow the dying?"

"What, O Cebes? Have you and Simmias not heard such things from Philolaus (the Pythagorean philosopher), with whom you were familiar?"

"Nothing clearly, O Socrates," said Cebes.

"And yet I too speak of these things from hearsay," Socrates said. "Whatever I have heard, there is no envy in reporting it to you. For perhaps it is most fitting for one about to migrate there to consider and imagine in the mind what kind of thing we think this migration is to be. For what else should one do until the setting of the sun?"

"For what reason, then, O Socrates, do they say it is *nefas* (an impious act) to lay hands on oneself? For I have already heard from Philolaus, when he stayed with us, and from some others, that it is not fitting to do this; but I have never heard anything clear about this matter from anyone." [[notes: Socrates is referring to the Pythagorean doctrine of the body as a prison.]]

"But attention is needed," he said. "For even if you have heard it, it may perhaps seem marvelous if this alone out of all other things is simple—that it never happens to a man, as in other cases, that it is better for him to die than to live. And perhaps it will seem marvelous to you if those for whom it is better to die are not allowed to benefit themselves, but must wait for another benefactor."

Then Cebes, smiling, said in his own dialect: "God knows!" 

"And yet," said Socrates, "it might seem absurd in this way. But perhaps it has a certain reason. Indeed, that discourse which is held in secret about these matters—that we humans are in a kind of *custodia* (guard-post or prison), and it is not fitting for anyone to release himself from it or run away—seems to me a great saying, though not easy to understand. Nevertheless, O Cebes, this seems to me rightly said: that the Gods have care for us, and that we humans are one of the *possessions* of the Gods. Does it not seem so to you?"

"It does to me," said Cebes.

"Therefore," he said, "if one of your own slaves were to kill himself without you signifying that you wanted him to depart from life, would you not be angry with him? And if you had the power, would you not inflict some punishment?"

"Certainly," he said.

"Perhaps, then, in this way it is not beyond reason that one should not kill oneself before God imposes some necessity, such as he has imposed on us at present."

"That appears consistent," said Cebes. "But what you said just now—that philosophers should easily be willing to die—seems absurd, O Socrates, if indeed what we just said has reason: namely, that God takes care of us and we are His possession. For it makes no sense that the most prudent men should not be grieved to be removed from that care provided by the Gods, who are the best governors of all things. For a prudent man would never think he will take better care of himself once he has escaped to freedom. Perhaps some foolish person might think he must flee from his master, not reflecting that one should not flee from what is good, but rather remain in it as much as possible. Thus he would flee without reason. But he who has a mind always desires to be with him who is better. And thus, O Socrates, the opposite of what was said a little while ago is more probable. For it is fitting for the wise to bear death heavily, but for the foolish to bear it gladly."

Socrates, having heard this, seemed to me to be delighted by the shrewdness of Cebes. Turning to us, he said, "This Cebes is always searching out certain reasons, and is not at all willing to admit easily whatever anyone says."

Then Simmias said, "To me also, Cebes seems to have a point. For with what intent would wise men flee those who are truly better than themselves, and easily suffer to be without them? And it seems to me that Cebes directs his speech at you, because you so easily leave both us and the Gods, who are, as you yourself admit, good rulers."

"You speak justly," said Socrates. "For I think you are saying that I must clear myself as if in a court of judgment."

"Most certainly," said Simmias.

"Come then," he said. "I will now try to defend myself before you more accurately than I did before the judges. Indeed, O Simmias and Cebes, if I did not think I was migrating, first to other Gods who are wise and good, and then to deceased men who are better than those here, I would be acting unjustly in not bearing death with annoyance. But now, be certain that I hope to go to good men—though I would not affirm this absolutely. But that I shall go to Gods who are very good masters, be certain that I would affirm this if I would affirm anything of the kind. Therefore, I am not at all annoyed by death, as I would be if the matter were otherwise, but I am of good courage and hope that something remains for those who have died, and as has been said for a long time, it will be much better for the good than for the evil."

"What then, O Socrates?" said Simmias. "Do you intend to depart with this opinion for yourself alone? Or will you leave us to share in it? For I think this good is common to us as well. Moreover, you will only have cleared yourself before us if you persuade us of what you say."

"I shall try to do so," he said. "But let us first listen to Crito. For he has seemed for some time to want to say something."

"What else, O Socrates," said Crito, "except that the one who is to give you the poison has been telling me for a long time that you should be warned to speak as little as possible? For he says that those who dispute grow too warm, and nothing of that sort is suitable for those who are to drink the poison. Otherwise, those who do so are sometimes forced to drink the poison twice, or even three times."

Then Socrates said, "Let him be. Let him only prepare his duty, as if he were to provide it twice, or even three times if necessary."

"I knew that would be your answer," said Crito. "But he has been bothering me for a long time."

"Let him be," Socrates said. "But I, O judges, want to render to you the reason why it seems to me that a man who has applied himself to philosophy throughout his entire life rightly expects imminent death with great confidence, and is in good hope that he will obtain the greatest goods there after he has migrated from here. How this is so, O Simmias and Cebes, I will try to open to you. For whoever handles philosophy rightly seems to be hidden from other men in this: that they themselves study nothing else but *mori* (to die) and *esse mortuos* (to be dead). If this is true, it would be utterly absurd if, when they have studied nothing but this through their whole life, they should be grieved when this very thing they have long pondered and practiced arrives."

Here Simmias, smiling, said, "By Jove, O Socrates, you have drawn a laugh from me, even though I was not much inclined to laughing. For I think there will be many who, if they heard this, would think it a most fitting thing said about philosophers; and our people [[notes: the Thebans or Greeks in general]] would agree, and quite strongly too, that philosophers truly are dying, and that they are not unaware that philosophers deserve to suffer this very thing."

"Perhaps they would speak rightly, O Simmias, except in adding that they are 'not unaware.' For it is hidden from them in what way true philosophers both study to die and are worthy of death. But let us leave them now and speak to ourselves. Do we think that death is something?"

"Certainly something," said Simmias.

"Is it anything else," he asked, "than the *solutio* (release) of the soul from the body? And that this is 'being dead': namely, the body released from the soul existing by itself apart, and the soul released from the body existing by itself? Is death anything other than this?"

"Nothing else," said Simmias.

"Consider, then, my good man, if the same thing seems to you as to me. For from these things I think we shall more clearly understand what we are seeking. Does it seem to you the duty of a philosopher to pursue those which are called pleasures, such as those of feasts and drinks?"

"Not at all, O Socrates," he said.

"But what of those of Venus (sexual pleasures)?"

"In no way."

"What of the rest of the care of the body? Do you think the philosopher makes much of it? For instance, having fine clothes, shoes, and other ornaments of the body—does he seem to you to value them highly, or to think nothing of them, except insofar as great necessity forces their use?"

"It seems to me a true philosopher holds these all as of no account," said Simmias.

"Does it not seem to you," he said, "that the study of such a man does not incline toward the body, but as much as possible departs from it and turns toward the soul?"

"It seems so to me."

"Therefore, in such things, is it not first manifest that the philosopher, more than other men, separates the soul as much as possible from communion with the body?"

"It is manifest."

"But most people think, O Simmias, that for a man to whom nothing of such things is sweet, and who does not enjoy them, it is not worth thinking he is truly living; he is almost dead, since he does not study the pleasures of the body."

"You speak the very truth," he said.

"But what about the acquisition of wisdom itself?" asked Socrates. "Is the body an impediment if one takes it along as a companion in the investigation, or not? What I mean is this: Do sight and hearing have any truth for men? Or is it as the poets are always singing, that we hear nothing and see nothing *sincerum* (pure or certain)? And if these bodily senses are not pure and certain, neither are the others; for all the rest are somewhat inferior to these. Do they not seem so to you?"

"Entirely," he said.

"When, then, does the soul touch the truth?" he asked. "For whenever it tries to investigate something with the body, it is clearly deceived by the body."

"You speak truly."

"Is it not in reasoning, if anywhere at all, that some of those things which truly are become manifest to it?"

"It is so."

"And it reasons best then, when none of these things disturb it—neither hearing, nor sight, nor pain, nor pleasure—but when it most gathers itself into itself, abandoning the body and communicating with it as little as possible, not touching it, but reaching out toward that which truly is."

"It is so."

"Is it not here, O Simmias, that the soul of the philosopher most despises the body, flees from it, and seeks to live by itself?"

"It appears so."

"What of these things, O Simmias? Do we say that *Justum* (Justice itself) is something, or nothing?"

"Something, by Jove!"

"And again, *Pulchrum* (the Beautiful itself) and *Bonum* (the Good itself) are something?"

"Of course."

"Did you ever perceive any of these with your eyes?"

"Never," he said.

"Or did you touch them with any other sense of the body? I speak of all things, such as Magnitude itself, Health, Strength, and in short, the *essentia* (essence) of all other things—that is, what each thing is. Is the truest part of these perceived through the body? Or is it that whoever among us prepares himself to think most accurately and deeply with the mind upon the thing he sets out to consider, he will come closest to the knowledge of it?"

"Certainly."

"Would not he do this most purely who approaches each thing with thought alone as much as possible, neither employing sight in his thinking nor joining any other sense to his reasoning? But using pure thought by itself, he would strive to hunt down each pure thing as it is in itself, as free as possible from eyes, ears, and, in short, the whole body—on the grounds that it disturbs the soul and does not permit it to attain truth and wisdom whenever it is taken into communion? Will not this man, O Simmias, if anyone, attain to that which truly is?"

"You speak marvelously well, O Socrates," said Simmias.

"Therefore," he said, "from all these things, it must necessarily follow that such an opinion remains with true philosophers, so that they say such things among themselves: 'A kind of path of reason seems to lead us to this consideration: that as long as we have the body, and our soul is mixed with such an evil, we shall never abundantly attain what we desire.' For the body provides almost innumerable impediments because of its necessary nourishment. Moreover, diseases falling upon us from it impede the investigation of truth; it fills us with loves, desires, fears, and various images, and in short, much nonsense, so that it is most truly said that we are never permitted by it to be wise about anything. For nothing else but the body and its desires incite wars, seditions, and battles."

[[page number: 337]]

-> Phædo, Or, On the Soul. <-

"For all wars occur for the sake of money. And we are compelled to seek money for the sake of the body, serving its cultivation. Thus it happens that because of all these things, we are abstracted from the studies of philosophy. The final blow of all is that if any leisure happens to us from it, and we apply ourselves to considering something, it everywhere opposes our investigations, disturbs the soul with tumult, and strikes it with such astonishment that we cannot perceive the truth because of this obstacle. But it has truly been demonstrated to us that if we are ever to know anything purely, we must withdraw from the body and consider the things themselves with the soul itself. And then, it appears, we shall obtain that which we affect, and of which we profess ourselves lovers—namely, wisdom—at the time when we are dead, as our speech indicates, but by no means while we live. For if nothing can be purely discerned with the body, one of two things must be: either we can never attain knowledge, or only after death. For then the soul will be by itself apart from the body, but before that, in no way. And while we live, it seems we shall come closest to knowledge if we have as little commerce with the body as possible and do not communicate with it, except as far as extreme necessity compels; and we shall not be filled with its nature, but keep ourselves pure from its contagion until God himself releases us. And thus being pure and liberated from the foolishness of the body, as is consistent, we shall be with those who are like us, and we shall know through ourselves everything that is sincere—that is, perhaps, the truth itself. For it is not *fas* (lawful) for the impure to touch the pure. Such things, I judge, O Simmias, all true lovers of learning must say to one another and think. Does it not seem so to you?"

"Most certainly of all, O Socrates."

"If these things are true, then, O friend," he said, "there is great hope that he who arrives there where I am now setting out will, if anywhere, abundantly obtain that for the sake of which we have undertaken so much business in this present life. Therefore, this migration now imposed upon me, I undertake with good hope; and similarly any other man will undertake it who thinks his mind is prepared, as if purified."

"Entirely so," said Simmias.

"And does not purification," he said, "consist in this which we have been saying for a long time: namely, that we separate the soul from the body as much as we can? And that we accustom it to withdraw and collect itself from the contagion of the body from everywhere, and thus—as far as possible—to dwell, both in the present time and in the future, alone by itself, as if released from the chains of the body?"

"Most certainly," he said.

"Is not this called death: the release and separation of the soul from the body?"

"Exactly," he said.

"To release it, as we confess, is the constant and sole study of those who rightly philosophize. And this is the very meditation of philosophers: to release and separate the soul from the body. Is it not so?"

"It seems so."

"Would it not then be ridiculous, as I said at the beginning, if a man who so prepared himself in life that he lived as close as possible to death, should then be indignant when death arrives? Would it not be ridiculous?"

"Of course."

"Truly, then, O Simmias," he said, "those who rightly philosophize meditate on death, and they are the least of all men terrified by it. Consider it thus: since they everywhere despise the body, but desire to have the soul itself by itself, would it not be the height of absurdity if they were terrified and grieved when this happens, and did not gladly go there where there is hope of obtaining what they loved in life (for they loved wisdom) and of being liberated from that whose commerce they bore with annoyance? Or have many people voluntarily wanted to go to the underworld for the sake of deceased boys, wives, or children, hoping to see them there and be with those they loved? Will a true lover of wisdom, who is vehemently drawn into this same hope—that he will not obtain it worthily anywhere else but in the underworld—bear death with grief and not go there gladly? One must think, O friend, if he is truly a philosopher, that this opinion will be very strong in him: that he can find pure wisdom nowhere but there. And if this is so, would it not be altogether beyond reason, as I said just now, if such a man feared death?"

"By Jove," said Simmias, "it would be against reason."

"This will be a sufficient conjecture, then," he said, "that if you see someone grieving at the approach of death, he is not a philosopher but a *philosōmaton* (body-lover), that is, a lover of the body, and probably also a *philochrēmaton* (lover of money) and a *philotimon* (lover of honor), desiring one or both of these things."

"It is altogether as you say," he said.

"Therefore, O Simmias, what is named Fortitude—does it not especially belong to such men?"

"Most especially," he said.

"And Temperance (which even the many say consists in not being a slave to desires, but despising them and keeping modesty)—does it not belong only to those who most despise the body and live in philosophy?"

"It must be so," he said.

"For if you wish to consider the fortitude and temperance of others, it will seem quite absurd to you."

"In what way, O Socrates?"

"You know that everyone else considers death one of the greatest evils."

"Most certainly," he said.

"Therefore, is it not out of fear of greater evils that those among them who are 'brave' sustain death, when they do sustain it?"

"Indeed."

"So everyone except philosophers is brave through fearing and through fear; although it is absurd that someone should be brave through fear or cowardice."

"Certainly."

"And what of those among them called 'temperate'? Is it not in a similar way that they are affected: temperate through a kind of intemperance? Although we say that is impossible. Nevertheless, an affection similar to this happens to them in that fatuous temperance of theirs. For fearing that they will be deprived of other pleasures, and desiring them, they abstain from some because they are overcome by others—even though they call it 'intemperance' to be overcome by pleasures. Yet it happens to them that by being overcome by pleasures, they overcome other pleasures. And this is similar to what was just said: that in a certain way, they become temperate through intemperance."

"It seems so."

"But look, O blessed Simmias, whether this is at all the right path to virtue: to exchange pleasures for pleasures, pains for pains, and fear for fear, and the greater for the lesser as if they were coins. Perhaps there is only one right coin for which all these things should be exchanged—namely, *Prudentia* (Prudence or Wisdom). In this, and with this, all things are truly bought and sold: fortitude, temperance, justice, and in short, true virtue exists with prudence, whether pleasures and fears and other things of the same kind are present or absent. But if they are exchanged for one another apart from prudence, such virtue is a kind of shadowy thing, truly slavish, possessing nothing healthy or true. The truth of virtue consists in the purification of all these things; and temperance, justice, fortitude, and prudence itself are a kind of purification. Wherefore, those who established the mysteries for us seem not to be despised, but in truth long ago they secretly admonished us that whoever migrates to the underworld unexpiated and uninitiated will lie in the mud; but whoever arrives there purged and initiated will dwell with the Gods."

[[page number: 338]]

-> Book Twenty-Nine. <-

"For there are, as the common saying goes, many who carry the thyrsus (the staff of Bacchus), but few who are truly Bacchants. These, in my opinion, are none other than those who have rightly philosophized. To be numbered among them, I have left nothing undone in my life, as far as I was able, but have contended in every way. Whether I have contended rightly or achieved anything, we shall know for certain when we arrive there, if God wills, a little later, as it seems to me. This defense I offer to you, O Simmias and Cebes: why I do not bear it heavily or feel indignant to leave you and those who are my masters here. For I hope that there I shall find good masters and friends no less than here. Many people, however, do not believe this. If, then, my defense has persuaded you more than it did the Athenian judges, it is well."

When Socrates had said these things, Cebes took up the discourse and said: "The rest, O Socrates, seems rightly said. But as far as the soul itself is concerned, men are very doubtful whether, once separated from the body, it is anywhere at all, or whether it perishes on the day a man dies, and is immediately dissolved and dissipated like wind or smoke as it exits the body, and exists no more. Truly, if it were collected into itself somewhere, and liberated from those evils you just described, there would be much good hope, O Socrates, that what you said would be true. But perhaps not a little persuasion and faith is needed to believe that the soul survives after the death of the man, and that it has some power and intelligence."

"You speak the truth, O Cebes," said Socrates. "But what do you think should be done? Shall we perhaps converse about these very things—whether it is probable that it is so, or otherwise?"

"I would gladly hear," said Cebes, "what you think about these matters."

"I do not think anyone hearing this," said Socrates, "not even a comic poet [[notes: an allusion to Aristophanes, who mocked Socrates]], would say that I am now talking nonsense and speaking about things that ought not to be discussed. If it pleases you, let us consider it this way: whether the souls of the dead are in the underworld or not. There is an ancient saying, which we remember, that souls which have gone from here are there, and return here again, and are born from the dead. And if this is true—that the living are made again from the dead—then our souls must be there. For they would not be born again if they were not. And this is a sufficient conjecture that it is so, if it truly appears that the living are made from nowhere else but from the dead. But if this is not the case, another reason will be needed."

"Altogether," said Cebes.

"Do not consider this in humans alone," he said, "if you wish to understand it more clearly, but in all animals and plants, and in short, in everything that is born. Let us see if everything is produced in this way: that contraries come from nowhere else but from their contraries, in whatever things such a condition occurs. Just as the Beautiful is in some way contrary to the Ugly, and the Just to the Unjust, and countless other such things we see. Let us consider whether it is necessary that for whatever has a contrary, it is made from nothing else but its contrary. For example, when something is made greater, it must necessarily have been smaller before it became greater."

"It is so."

"And if it becomes smaller, will it not become smaller from what was previously greater?"

"Exactly so."

"Furthermore, from the stronger comes the weaker, and from the slower the swifter?"

"Certainly."

"And what of this? If something becomes worse, does it not come from the better? And if more just, from the more unjust?"

"Of course."

"In all things, then, we have explored this sufficiently: that all things are thus made—contraries from contraries."

"Certainly."

"What again? Is there also something like this between the two contraries: two generations or progressions from one to the other, and back again from the other to the first? For between greater and smaller, there are 'increase' and 'decrease'; and we say one increases and the other decreases."

"Yes," he said.

"And similarly with being separated and being joined, growing cold and growing warm, and all things in the same way? And even if names are lacking in some places, yet in the thing itself it must necessarily be so: namely, that all things come from one another, and there is a generation of each into the other."

"Altogether," he said.

"What then? Is there something contrary to 'living,' just as 'sleeping' is contrary to 'waking'?"

"Certainly," he said.

"What is it?"

"Dying," he answered.

"Do these not come from one another, since they are contraries? And since there are two, are there not also two mutual generations between them?"

"Nothing prevents it."

"I will tell you one pair," said Socrates, "both the things themselves and their generations. You tell me the other. I say 'sleeping' and 'waking'; from sleep comes waking, and from waking comes sleep. And their generations are 'falling asleep' and 'waking up.' Is that sufficient for you?"

"It is certainly sufficient."

"Now you tell me similarly about life and death. Do you not say that living and dying are contraries?"

"I do."

"And that they come from one another?"

"Yes."

"So from the living, what is produced?"

"The dead."

"And from the dead?"

"One must confess: the living."

"Then from the dead, O Cebes, living things and living people are produced."

"It appears so."

"Therefore, are our souls in the underworld?"

"It seems so."

"And of the generations concerning these, is not one of them manifest? For dying is manifest, is it not?"

"Entirely so."

"What shall we do then? Shall we not render the contrary generation in turn, or shall we say that nature is crippled in this one part? Or is it necessary to render to 'dying' a certain contrary generation?"

"Altogether."

"And what is that?"

"Coming back to life."

"Therefore, if there is a coming back to life, is this not a progression from the dead to the living?"

"It is indeed."

"It is agreed between us, then, for this additional reason, that the living are made from the dead no less than the dead from the living. Since this is so, it is a sufficient conjecture that the souls of the dead must necessarily be somewhere from which they may return again."

"It seems to me, O Socrates, that this necessarily follows from what has been granted."

"Observe then, O Cebes, that we did not grant these things without reason, as I think. For if things were not continually rendered to one another, revolving as if in a circle, but instead there were a kind of direct progression only from one thing to its opposite, and they did not reflect back to the other or make a return, then all things, believe me, would finally have the same form and condition, and they would cease to be produced."

"In what way do you say that?" he asked.

"It is not at all difficult to understand," he said. "Just as if everyone were to fall asleep, but no one ever rose again to waking, you would clearly see that all things would finally come to such a state that the ridiculous fable of Endymion [[notes: a youth granted eternal sleep by Zeus]] would seem like nothing, nor would he appear anywhere, since all other things would similarly be oppressed by sleep. Furthermore, if all things were mixed together but never separated, the saying of Anaxagoras (the Pre-Socratic philosopher) would suddenly come true: that all things were together. In the same way, O friend Cebes, if all things that received life were to die, and having died, remained dead and never came back to life, would it not be necessary that all things would finally be consumed and nothing would live? For if living things were made from other things, but then perished, what would prevent everything from being consumed by death?"

"Nothing at all, O Socrates," said Cebes, "but you seem to me to speak the absolute truth."

"It is certainly so, O Cebes," he said, "most especially so in my view. We have not confessed these things as if deceived, but in truth there is a coming back to life, and the living are made from the dead, and the souls of the dead survive. And it is better for the good, but worse for the evil."

"And according to that principle, O Socrates," said Cebes, "which you are accustomed to use frequently—if indeed it is true—that our learning is nothing else but *reminiscentia* (recollection): according to this, I say, it is necessary that we learned in some former time those things which we now remember. But that could not happen unless our soul had been somewhere before it came into this human form. Wherefore, for this reason too, the soul seems to be something immortal."

"But what demonstrations of this matter do you have, O Cebes?" asked Simmias. "Bring it back to my memory. For I do not remember well at present."

"One most beautiful reason," said Cebes, "is that when men are questioned, if someone questions them rightly, they themselves answer everything as it is. Yet they could never do this unless knowledge and right reason were within them. Then, if one turns them to geometric figures and diagrams, or something similar, one will clearly find that it is so."

"If this reason does not satisfy you, Simmias," said Socrates, "consider whether it seems the same to you as to us if you consider it this way. For you doubt that what they call 'learning' can be 'recollection.'"

"I do not exactly doubt it," said Simmias. "But I need to learn the very thing we are talking about: namely, to remember. And almost from what Cebes began to say, I already record it and believe it. Nonetheless, I would very gladly hear from you the reason by which you were just beginning to prove it."

"By this reason," said Socrates: "we confess surely that if anyone remembers something, he must have known it at some time before."

"Certainly," he said.

"Do we not also confess this," he said, "that whenever knowledge arises in this way, it is recollection? I mean in this manner: if someone has seen or heard something, or perceived it by another sense, and not only knows that thing but also recognizes something else, of which there is not the same but a different knowledge—should we not rightly say he remembers that thing which came into his notion?"

"How do you mean that?" asked Simmias.

"This," said Socrates. "The knowledge of a man is one thing, and the knowledge of a lyre is another. Is it not?"

"Of course," said Simmias.

"Are you unaware that this happens to lovers when they see a lyre, or a garment, or anything else which the boys they love were accustomed to use? For they both recognize the lyre and at the same time form in their mind the image of the boy whose lyre it was. This is 'remembering.' Just as if someone sees Simmias often, he might be reminded of Cebes, and infinite other things of the same kind."

"Infinite, by Jove!" said Simmias.

"Is not such a thing, then, a kind of record?" he asked. "Most especially when it happens to us in those things which we have already surrendered to oblivion through length of time and neglect?"

"Certainly," said Simmias.

"What then?" said Socrates. "Can it happen that someone who has seen a painted horse or a painted lyre remembers a man? And when he looks at a painted Simmias, does Cebes come into his mind?"

"Yes, indeed," he said.

"And does it not also happen that one who looks at a painted Simmias remembers Simmias himself?"

"It certainly happens."

"In all these cases, does it not occur that one remembers someone from similar things? And is it not necessary to realize whether this similarity falls short or not of that thing whose memory is recalled?"

"It is necessary."

"Consider then, whether this is so. We say something is 'Equal'? I do not mean one piece of wood to another piece of wood, nor one stone to another stone, nor anything else of that sort, but beyond all these, do we say 'Equal itself' is something, or nothing?"

"We say so, by Jove! And marvelously so."

"And do we know what 'Equal itself' is?"

"Entirely."

"From where did we receive the knowledge of it? Was it not from those things we just mentioned—namely, having seen woods, or stones, or other equal things, from these we thought of that which is something else besides these? Does it not seem something else to you? Consider it this way: Do not equal stones or woods, while they are the same, sometimes appear equal and sometimes unequal to us?"

"Indeed."

"But can the 'Equals themselves' ever appear unequal to you? Or can 'Equality' appear to be 'Inequality'?"

"Never, O Socrates."

"Therefore, these equal things and 'Equal itself' are not the same."

"In no way do they appear the same to me, O Socrates."

"Nevertheless, from these equal things, which are different from that 'Equal itself,' you simultaneously thought of and perceived its knowledge. Is it not so?"

"You speak most truly."

"Whether it is similar to them or dissimilar?"

"Exactly."

"It makes no difference. For as long as you have seen one thing and from that perception understood another, whether similar or dissimilar, it is necessary that recollection comes from this."

"Most certainly."

"What of this? Does it happen to us in the same way regarding those things we were just mentioning—the woods and other things? Do they seem to be equal in the same way as 'Equal itself' is? Or do they fall short in some way of being such as 'Equal itself' is, or not at all?"

"They fall far short," he said.

"Do we not confess that when someone, looking at something, realizes that this thing he sees desires to be like some other thing that exists, but falls short and cannot be such as that thing is, but is inferior—is it not necessary that he who realizes this must have previously known that thing which he says this resembles in some way, but does not fully reach?"

"It is necessary."

"What then? Does something like this happen to us or not, regarding equal things and 'Equal itself'?"

"Very much so."

"It is necessary, therefore, that we had knowledge of 'Equal itself' before that time when, first seeing equal things, we recognized that all these desire to be such as it is, yet fall short of its perfection."

"It is so."

"And we also confess this: that we did not recognize it from anywhere else, nor could we, except from sight, or touch, or some other sense. For I judge similarly of all these things."

"They are similar, O Socrates, for what we are trying to show."

"But from the senses, one must understand that all things subject to the senses desire that which is 'Equal,' although they do not attain it. Or do we say otherwise?"

"Not otherwise."

"Therefore, before we began to see, or hear, or use other senses, we must have had the knowledge of 'Equal itself'—namely, what it is—if indeed we are to refer these equal things which lie under the senses to it, judging that they all strive to be like it, yet are left inferior."

"It follows necessarily from what was said before, O Socrates."

"And were we not born with sight and hearing and the other senses?"

"Altogether."

"But we must, as we said, have had the knowledge of 'Equal itself' before these."

"Yes."

"Wherefore, as it seems, it is necessary that we grasped it before we were born."

"So it appears."

"And if we obtained it before birth and were born possessing it, we knew both before birth and immediately upon being born not only 'Equal itself' and the Greater and the Lesser, but all things of the same kind? For our discourse now is no more about 'Equal' than about 'Beautiful itself,' 'Good itself,' 'Just itself,' and 'Holy itself,' and as I say, about everything to which we assign this very term 'what it is,' both in questioning and in answering. Thus it is necessary that we had the knowledge of all these before we were born."

"It is so."

"And if, having received these knowledges, we did not always forget them, we would be born with them and always know them through our whole life. For 'to know' is to retain the knowledge of something once received and not to have lost it. Do we not call the loss of knowledge 'oblivion'?"

"Exactly, O Socrates."

"But if, having received this knowledge before birth, we lost it upon being born, and then later, by using the senses regarding those same things, we recovered those knowledges we previously had—would not what we call 'learning' be the recovery of our own knowledge? And in calling this 'Recollection,' would we not be naming it rightly?"

"Rightly."

"For it appeared possible that when someone has sensed something, either by seeing or hearing or some other sensation, he recognizes from this something else which he had forgotten, to which this thing was in some way related, whether it be similar or dissimilar. So as I have been saying for a long time, one of two things must be: either we were born knowing and we all know through our whole life, or those whom we later say are 'learning' are merely remembering, and learning is recollection."

"It is altogether so, O Socrates."

"Which then do you choose, O Simmias? That we are born with knowledge, or that we remember later what we previously knew?"

"I cannot choose at present, Socrates."

"What of this? Can you choose what you think about this: Can a man who knows give a reason for the things he knows, or not?"

"He must be able to, O Socrates."

"And do you think everyone can give a reason for these things we were just discussing?"

"I would wish so," said Simmias, "but I much more fear that by tomorrow there will be no man here who can do so worthily."

"Then you do not think, O Simmias, that everyone understands these things?"

"In no way."

"Then they remember what they once learned."

"It must be so."

"When did our souls receive this knowledge? Certainly not after we were born as humans."

"Certainly not."

"Therefore, before."

"Yes."

"Then, Simmias, souls existed before they came into human form, apart from the body, and they possessed intelligence."

"Unless perhaps, O Socrates, we receive these knowledges at the moment we are born. For that time still remains."

"Be it so, O friend. But at what other time do we lose them? For we are not born possessing them, as we just confessed. Or do we lose them in the very moment we receive them? Or can you suggest another time?"

"In no way, O Socrates; I did not realize I was saying nothing."

"Is it then like this for us, O Simmias? If those things exist which we are always talking about—the Beautiful, the Good, and every such essence to which we refer all things perceived by the senses, which was ours before and which we find again as our own, and to which we refer these things as to their exemplar—it is necessary that just as those things exist, so also our soul existed before we were born. But if these do not exist, this whole argument would be in vain. Is it not so? Is there an equal necessity that both these things exist and our souls existed before we were born, and if the one does not exist, neither does the other?"

"Marvelously so, O Socrates," said Simmias. "The same necessity seems to apply to me. And the argument leads us to a most beautiful conclusion: that our soul existed before we were born, just like that essence you mentioned. For I hold nothing so certain as that all such things exist most truly—namely, the Beautiful itself, the Good itself, and all the others you just spoke of. And as far as I am concerned, it is sufficiently demonstrated."

"But what does it seem to Cebes?" asked Socrates. "For he too must be persuaded."

"I think he too is sufficiently persuaded," said Simmias, "although he is the most resistant of all men and the slowest to believe. Yet I think it has been sufficiently proved to him that the soul existed before our birth. But whether it will still exist after our death does not seem to me, O Socrates, to have been shown yet. There still remains that doubt of the many which Cebes brought forward: that perhaps when a man dies, the soul is simultaneously dissipated and ceases to be. For what prevents it from being produced and constituted from elsewhere, and existing even before it fell into a human body, but then, after it departs from it, perishing as well?"

"You speak rightly, Simmias," said Cebes. "For only half of what is necessary seems to have been proved: namely, that our soul existed before we were born. It is necessary also to show that after we are dead, it will exist no less than it did before we were born, if the demonstration is to reach its end."

"That has already been demonstrated even now, O Simmias and Cebes," said Socrates, "if you are willing to connect what has just been proved with what we granted before: namely, that every living thing is made from the dead. For if the soul exists before, and when it comes into this life and becomes a man, it must necessarily proceed from nowhere else but from the dead, why is it not necessary that it also remains after the death of the body, since it must return to this life? Thus what you ask has been demonstrated even now. Nevertheless, you and Simmias seem to want to discuss this again more diligently; and perhaps, like children, you fear that the wind might truly dissolve and disperse the soul as it exits the body, especially if someone dies not under a clear sky but when the winds are blowing violently."

At this Cebes, smiling as if they were indeed afraid, said: "O Socrates, try to persuade us otherwise—or rather, not as if we were afraid, but perhaps there is a child within us who fears such things. Let us then strive to persuade him not to fear death like a *larva* (a ghost or bogeyman)."

"Certainly," said Socrates, "he must be healed by daily 'incantations' until he is made sound."

"But where, O Socrates, shall we find such a 'healer' of this sort, since you are leaving us?"

"Greece is large, O Cebes," he said, "in which there are many good men, and there are many barbarian nations. Through all of these you must search for such a healer, sparing neither money nor labor. For there is nothing on which you could more profitably spend money. You must also search among yourselves; for perhaps you will not easily find anyone who can do this better than you."

"It shall be done," said Cebes.

[[page number: 341]]

-> Phædo, Or, On the Soul. <-

"But let us return, if it pleases you, to where we left off."

"It pleases me," he said. "For why should it not?"

"You answer rightly," said Cebes.

"Should we not ask ourselves something like this?" he said. "To what kind of thing does it belong to suffer this—to be dissolved? And for what kind of thing should we fear it might suffer this? And to what part of it? Then we must consider whether the soul is such a thing, and from these things, either have confidence or fear for our soul."

"You speak the truth," he said.

"Therefore, is it not for that which is composed and already a composite that it is natural to suffer being dissolved, insofar as it is composed? But if something is not composed, to this alone it belongs not to suffer the same things as any other."

"It seems so to me," said Cebes.

"And is it not those things which always remain in the same state and manner," he asked, "that are most likely to be simple? But those which are different at different times and never in the same state, are they not composite?"

"So I think."

"Let us return to those things we proceeded to in the earlier dispute. That essence itself, to which we assigned 'what it is' in our questions and answers—does it always remain in the same way and state? Or is it different at different times? Namely, Equal itself, Beautiful itself, each thing that is being itself—do they ever receive any mutation? Or does each of them, being uniform and existing by itself, always remain in the same way and state, and never, nowhere, and in no way undergo any mutation?"

"It is necessary, O Socrates," said Cebes, "that these always remain in the same way and state."

"And what shall we say of the many things," he asked, "which are called by the same names—such as beautiful men, horses, garments, or any other such things which are called beautiful or equal? Do these always remain in the same way? Or rather, are they altogether the opposite of those others, so that neither in themselves nor with one another, to speak simply, are they ever in the same state and manner?"

"These, O Socrates," said Cebes, "are never in the same state."

"And these can be touched, seen, and reached by the other senses. But those which always remain the same can be perceived in no other way than by the intelligence of the reason alone, and are invisible; for such things are not seen."

"You speak the absolute truth," he said.

"Do you wish, then, that we posited two species of things: one visible, and the other invisible?"

"Let us posit them," he said.

"And that the invisible always remains the same, but the visible never remains the same?"

"Let us posit this also," he said.

"Come now, is there anything else in us but the body on one hand, and the soul on the other?"

"Nothing else," he said.

"To which species do we say the body is more similar and related?"

"To no one is it doubtful that it is to the visible."

"And what of the soul? Is it something visible, or not?"

"Not to men, O Socrates," he said.

"But we were speaking only of those things which can be seen or not seen by the nature of men. Or were we discussing those which relate to another nature?"

"Only those which relate to the human," he said.

"What then did we say of the soul? Is it visible or invisible?"

"Not visible."

"Invisible, then?"

"Yes."

"Therefore, the soul is more similar to the invisible species than the body is. And the body is more similar to the visible."

"That is altogether necessary."

"And did we not say this also in what went before? That when the soul takes the body as a companion to consider something, either through sight, or hearing, or some other sense (for to consider through the senses is to consider through the body), then it is dragged by the body to those things which never remain the same, and it wanders, and is disturbed, and staggers like a drunkard, because it has touched such things."

"Certainly."

"But whenever the soul itself considers by itself, it goes there to that which is pure, eternal, immortal, and always remains the same. And as if related to it, it always dwells with it, whenever it returns to itself and it is permitted, and it ceases from error. And regarding those things, it always remains in the same way and state, because it has touched such things. And this affection of the soul is called *Prudentia* (Prudence or Wisdom)."

"You speak most beautifully and truly, O Socrates," he said.

"To which species again does the soul seem to be more similar and related, from what was said both before and now?"

"I think, O Socrates," he said, "that anyone, even the most unlearned and stubborn, would confess from this discourse that the soul is in every way more similar to that which always remains the same than to the opposite."

"And what of the body?"

"To the other species."

"Consider it again in this way. As long as the soul and body are together, nature commands the one to serve and be subject, and the other to rule and dominate. According to these things, again, which of them seems to be similar to the divine, and which to the mortal? Do you not think the divine is such by nature that it rules and leads, and the mortal such that it is subject and serves?"

"I do think so."

"To which of these is the soul similar?"

"It is clear, O Socrates, that the soul is similar to the divine, and the body to the mortal."

"Observe now, O Cebes, whether these things follow from all that has been said by us. Namely, that the soul is most similar to the divine, immortal, intelligible, uniform, indissoluble, always in the same way and state as itself; and the body is most similar to the human, mortal, unintelligible, multiform, dissoluble, and never in the same state as itself. Can we, O friend Cebes, bring forward anything else against this?"

"We cannot."

"What then? Since these things are so, is it not fitting for the body to be quickly dissolved, and for the soul to be altogether indissoluble, or something very close to the indissoluble?"

"Of course."

"You see, then, that after a man has died, what is visible in him—the body—placed in a visible place, which we call a corpse, whose nature it is to be dissolved, fall apart, and flow away, suffers none of these things suddenly, but remains for a long time, especially if someone died with the body in a fine condition, and even in that very bloom of youth. For the body, dried and preserved as they do in Egypt [[margin: cf. Herodotus, Book 2]], remains almost whole for an incredible time. Moreover, even if it rots, some parts of the body—the bones, nerves, and such—remain, so to speak, immortal. Do they not?"

"Yes."

"But the soul, which is an invisible thing, migrating to another similar and excellent place—pure, invisible, and hidden from us—truly to the good and wise God (where, if God wills, my own soul is also shortly to migrate): shall such a soul, endowed with such a nature, as soon as it is liberated from the body, be dissipated and perish, as many people think?"

"Far from it, O dear Cebes and Simmias! Rather, the matter stands much more like this: if it departs pure, trailing nothing of the body with it, as one that had no willing communion with it in life, but fled from it and gathered itself into itself, as if always meditating on this—which is nothing else but to philosophize rightly and truly to meditate on dying easily. Is this not the meditation on death?"

"Altogether."

"Does not the soul so affected, then, go to that which is like itself: divine, immortal, and wise? Where, when it arrives, it becomes happy, liberated from error, ignorance, fears, fierce loves, and other human evils; and as is said of the initiated, it truly spends the rest of time living with the Gods. Shall we say this, O Cebes, or otherwise?"

"This, by Jove!" said Cebes.

"But if it departs polluted and impure from the body, as one that always embraced the body and cultivated and loved it, and was soothed by its pleasures and desires as if by certain spells, and was so captivated that it thought nothing was true except what is corporeal—what can be touched, seen, drunk, eaten, or used for sexual pleasure—but was accustomed to hate, fear, and flee what is obscure and invisible to the eyes, yet intelligible and to be grasped by philosophy: do you think such a soul will escape purely by itself?"

"In no way," he said.

"But infected and entangled, I think, by the corporeal contagion, which the custom and constant familiarity of the body has made almost innate through continual attendance upon it?"

"So we think."

"And we must think, O friend, that this which the soul trails with it is heavy, ponderous, earthly, and visible. Therefore, it is weighed down by it and dragged back to the visible place by fear of the invisible and the hidden. And as it is said, it wanders around monuments and tombs, around which certain shadowy phantasms of souls have appeared—such as those souls provide which did not depart purely from the body but trail something visible, by which they can be seen."

"That is consistent, O Socrates."

"Consistent indeed, O Cebes—yet these are not the souls of the good, but of the evil, which are compelled to wander about these places, paying the penalty for an improperly lived life. And they wander about for so long until, with the desire for the corporeal nature accompanying them, they again put on a body. And they put on, as is fitting, such characters as they practiced in life."

"What kind of characters do you mean, O Socrates?"

"Those who lived a life devoted to the belly, petulance, and gluttony, and had no regard for shame, it is fitting they should enter the forms of asses and such brutes. Do you not think so?"

"You speak consistently."

"But those who pursued injuries, tyrannies, and robberies above all others, it is equal that they should pass into the genera of wolves, hawks, and kites. Or where else should we say they migrate?"

"Most likely there," said Cebes.

"And similarly in the rest," he said, "for they go into whatever genera they contracted similar habits with in life."

"That is manifest, of course."

"Are not the happiest of these, and those who go to the best place, those who practiced that popular and social virtue which they call temperance and justice, acquired from habit and exercise without philosophy or mind?"

"In what way are these the happiest?"

"Because it is fitting that these should demigrate into some such civil and mild genus as bees, wasps, or ants, or even back into the same human genus, and modest men be made from them."

"That is fitting."

"But into the genus of the Gods, it is not *fas* (lawful) for anyone to arrive, except for those who, burning with the desire for learning, have both philosophized and departed altogether pure. For the sake of these things, O friends Simmias and Cebes, those who rightly philosophize abstain from all the desires of the body and thus persevere, never surrendering to them; they do not fear the loss of their estate or poverty, like many who are lovers of money; nor again do they fear contempt and ignominy, like those who seek magistracies and honors, and then abstain from them."

"For that would not be fitting, O Socrates," said Cebes.

"Not by Jove! Wherefore, those who care for their soul and do not serve the cultivation of the body, having despised all these things, do not walk in that way where those others we described go, because they do not know where they are going. But they, thinking they must not resist philosophy and its release and purgation, follow her in the way she leads them."

"In what way, O Socrates?"

"I will tell you," he said. "The lovers of learning know that philosophy truly receives their soul bound in the body and entangled, and compelled to consider things through it as if through a certain prison. And since it does not do this through itself, it is involved in all ignorance. They know, moreover, how philosophy, perceiving how severely the corporeal bond tightens the soul—since it happens through desire, by which the bound soul is an assistant to its own binding—the lovers of science know, I say, that philosophy, receiving their soul thus constituted, gradually instructs it and begins to release it, showing how deceitful the judgment of the eyes is, how deceitful the ears, and the other senses. She persuades it to depart from these, except as far as absolute necessity does not compel it to cling to them, and to recall and collect itself into itself, and to believe nothing except itself, insofar as it understands through itself whatever exists by itself. But whatever it considers through other things, existing in others, it should think nothing of it as true; for such a thing is sensible and visible, but what the soul considers by itself is intelligible and invisible. The soul of the true philosopher, judging that it must not resist this release, thus abstains from pleasures, desires, pains, and fears to the best of its power—judging that when someone is vehemently delighted, or fears, or is pained, or desires, he does not suffer as much evil from these as one might think (namely, if someone were to grow sick or spend money because of his desires); but that he suffers what is the greatest and extreme of all evils, yet does not perceive it."

"What is this, O Socrates?" asked Cebes.

"That the soul of every man is compelled to be delighted or pained at the same time about something vehemently, and to think that that about which it suffers this most is the most manifest and truest thing, when it is far otherwise. And these are most especially those things which are visible, are they not?"

"Altogether."

"Is it not in this passion that the soul is most especially bound by the body?"

"In what way?"

"Because every pleasure and pain, as if holding a nail, fastens and connects the soul to the body, and makes it so corporeal that it already thinks those things are true which the body says. Indeed, because it thinks the same things as the body and is delighted by the same things, it is compelled, I think, to become of the same character and the same nourishment—so that it can never depart pure into the other life, but always exits full of the stain of the body. Therefore, it quickly falls back into another body and is born again as if sown, and thus becomes altogether alienated from the commerce of the divine, pure, and uniform essence."

"You speak the very truth, O Socrates," said Cebes.

"For these reasons, O Cebes, those who are justly lovers of learning follow temperance and fortitude, but not for the reasons the vulgar think. Or do you think so?"

"Not at all."

"Certainly not. But the soul of the true philosopher would think thus, and would in no way think that, when philosophy has released it, it ought to surrender itself again to pleasures and pains, and be bound again, making its work in vain, like reweaving the web of Penelope [[notes: the wife of Odysseus who unwove her shroud every night]]. Rather, seeking the tranquility of these things, following reason and always remaining in it, it contemplates the True, the Divine, and that which is beyond opinion. Nourished by this, it judges it must live thus as long as it lives, and hopes that when it departs, it will migrate to that which is related and like itself, and be removed from human evils. From such an education and exercise, there is no reason for it to fear, O Simmias and Cebes, lest when it recedes from the body, it be distracted and dissipated, and its whole life recede into the winds and nothing remain."

WHEN Socrates had said these things, a long silence ensued. Socrates himself, as it seemed, was repeating to himself what had been said; and most of us were doing the same. But Cebes and Simmias spoke a little further with each other. Socrates, looking at them, said: "What do you think of what has been said? Does it perhaps seem to you that something is lacking? For many doubts and objections still remain, if one is to handle it sufficiently. If you are discussing something else among yourselves, I say nothing. But if you are in doubt about these things, do not be afraid to speak and go over it, if you think it could be said better in any part. Moreover, take me as a companion, if you think it can be done more conveniently with me."

"I will confess the truth to you, O Socrates," said Simmias. "For a long time each of us, doubting, has been impelling the other and bidding him to question you because of our desire to hear. But we fear lest this be ungrateful to you because of your present calamity."

Socrates, hearing this, smiled gently and said: "Papae! O Simmias, how difficult it would be to persuade others that I do not consider this fortune at all adverse, when I cannot even persuade you! For you fear lest I be more difficult and mournful now than I have been in my previous life. And, as it appears, I seem to you inferior to the swans in divination. For they, when they perceive they are shortly to die, then sing much more sweetly and loudly than they were accustomed to before, being glad that they are about to migrate to the God whom they serve [[notes: Apollo]]. But men, because they themselves dread death, falsely accuse the swans, saying they lament death and emit a song out of pain. They do not realize that no bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or afflicted by any other pain. Not the nightingale itself, nor the swallow, nor the hoopoe, which they say sing lamenting out of sorrow. But to me, neither these birds seem to sing out of pain, nor the swans. But because they are sacred to Phoebus (Apollo), as I think, being endowed with divination, they presage the goods of the other life; and therefore they sing more alacritously and rejoice more on that day than in former times. And I too think I am the fellow-servant of the swans and sacred to the same God, and that I have no worse vaticination (prophecy) from the same master than they do, nor do I depart from life with a more remiss mind. Wherefore, you may speak and question whatever you please, as long as the Eleven of the Athenians [[notes: the officials in charge of prisoners and executions]] permit."

"You speak beautifully," said Simmias. "Therefore, I will open to you in what thing I doubt, and Cebes here will say what he does not admit from the earlier dispute. For it seems to me, O Socrates—as perhaps to you also—that the manifest truth about these matters is either impossible to understand in this present life, or only with the greatest difficulty. Furthermore, not to explore what is said about them in every way, and not to stop until you are exhausted by examining everything, I judge to be the mark of a man who is too soft. For one must achieve one of these: either learn and find how they are; or if this cannot be done, choose the best and safest of human reasons, upon which one may sail through the storms of this life as if on a raft, unless one can sail through more safely and with less danger on some firmer vehicle or some divine word. And now I shall not be afraid to question you, especially since you yourself exhort us to do so—lest I should blame myself hereafter for not having said what I think. Indeed, O Socrates, when I reflect on your words with Cebes, they do not seem to me sufficiently confirmed."

"Perhaps, O friend," said Socrates, "you think truly. But say in what part you think they have been spoken less than sufficiently."

"In this part," said Simmias. "Namely, one could say the same thing about harmony, the lyre, and the strings: that harmony is something invisible, incorporeal, very beautiful, and divine in a rightly tuned lyre; but the lyre itself and the strings are bodies—corporeal, composite, earthly, and related to the mortal. When, therefore, someone has broken the lyre or cut the strings, he could affirm by the same reason as yours that it is necessary that that harmony remains and is not destroyed. For in no way could it be that the lyre still exists after the strings are broken—the strings being of a mortal genus—but the harmony, which was related to the divine and immortal, has perished before the mortal. He would say that the harmony is still somewhere, and that the wood and strings will rot before it suffers anything. Indeed, O Socrates, I think you have observed that we think the soul is something of this sort: that there is in our body a certain tension and complexion from the hot, cold, dry, moist, and other such things, and the temperance and consonance of these is our soul—resulting in our body once these things have been well and moderately tempered with one another. If, then, the soul is a kind of harmony, whenever our body, through diseases or other evils, is immoderately loosened or tightened, it is necessary that the soul, although most divine, immediately perishes, as other consonances are accustomed to do, whether those in voices or in other works of craftsmen; but the remains of each body stay for a longer time, until they are either burned or rot. Consider, then, what must be answered to this reason, if someone should think the soul is a certain temperament of those things in the body, and perishes first in death."

Then Socrates, as he often did, looking sharply and smiling, said: "You speak justly, Simmias. If any of you has a more abundant faculty for answering than I do, why does he not answer him? For he seems to have touched upon the reason not badly. I judge, however, that before an answer is given, we must hear what Cebes also condemns, so that we may have time for deliberation. Then, after hearing these things, we must either concede to them if they seem to bring forward things consistent with the truth, or if not, the earlier reason must be defended and retained. Wherefore, come, O Cebes, say what most disturbs you and prevents you from assenting."

"I will say," said Cebes. "It seems to me to revolve back to the same thing and to be liable to the same charge as we mentioned in the earlier parts. For that our soul existed before it descended into a human form, I do not retract; it was most beautifully said, and unless it were a grave thing to say, I would assert it was sufficiently demonstrated. But that it survives after we are dead does not seem to me proven in that way. Yet I do not concede to Simmias' objection that the soul is not stronger and more durable than the body. For it seems to me to excel all these things by far. This earlier reason, then, would say to me: 'Why do you still doubt? Since you see that after a man has died, that which was weaker in him survives, does it not seem to you that that which is more durable must also be preserved during this time?' Observe, then, what I answer to that. I too need a similitude, just as Simmias did. Indeed, it seems to me these things are said just as if someone were to say about an old deceased weaver that he had not yet perished but perhaps survived somewhere; and to bring forward as a conjecture the garment which he himself had woven and wore, asserting that it was still sound and had not perished. And if someone did not believe it, he would ask which is more durable: the genus of man, or the garment which one uses daily. And if the answer were that the human genus is more durable, he would think it demonstrated that the man is much more safe, since that which was more fragile in him has not yet perished. But I do not think this is so, O Simmias. Consider also what I say. Anyone would understand that such an argument is foolish. For this weaver, who had worn out many garments and woven many, died after many garments—when there were many—but he died before the last one. Nor does it follow that a man is viler or weaker than a garment. I think the same similitude of the soul to the body can be made; and if someone should bring forward those same things, he would seem to speak congruously: namely, that the soul is more durable, and the body weaker and less durable. But he would say that each soul consumes many bodies, especially if they live many years. For if the body flows away and is dissolved even while the man is living, and the soul continually reweaves what is consumed, it will nevertheless be necessary that when the soul perishes, it then has its last garment, and perishes before that one alone. But when the soul has perished, then at last the body shows the weakness of its nature, quickly rotting and vanishing. So by this reason we cannot yet be confident, even when we have departed, that our soul survives. For if someone granted even more than what you say, and confessed not only that the soul existed before our birth, but even that nothing prevents the soul of some from remaining after death and frequently returning and departing—for the nature of the soul is so strong that it is often put into a body and preserves itself and the body—even if these things were granted, he would not yet grant you that the soul is not exhausted in many generations, but would say that finally, at some death among many, it is altogether destroyed. Moreover, he would add that no one can know that death and dissolution of the body which also brings destruction to the soul; for it is impossible for any of us to perceive it. If this is so, no one is not foolishly confident in death unless he can demonstrate that the soul is altogether immortal and indissoluble. Otherwise, it is consistent that whoever is about to die must fear for his soul, and always be solicitous lest in that dissolution of the body which is most imminent, it altogether perishes."

When we all heard them say these things, we were troubled, as we later confessed to one another. For although we had been greatly persuaded by the earlier dispute, we seemed to be disturbed again and to have lost faith not only in the reasons already brought forward but even in those yet to be said—fearing that either we were by no means good judges, or the matters themselves were unworthy of faith.

ECHECRATES: I give you pardon for that, by the Gods, O Phaedo. For as I was listening to you just now, such a thing came into my mind: To what reason shall I trust hereafter? Since the reason of Socrates, which was so probable a little while ago, has now lost its faith. It is marvelous how much that reason which proves our soul to be a kind of harmony has always been able to influence me; and now, having heard it, it suddenly recalled to my memory that the same thing had previously seemed so to me. Thus it happens that I need another reason again, as if from the very beginning, which might persuade me that the soul does not perish with the body. Tell me, then, I pray by Jove, in what way Socrates finished the dispute, and whether he himself also, as you confess of yourselves, seemed to bear it heavily, or on the contrary, benignly defended his reason; and moreover, whether he sufficiently protected it or not. Report all these things to us as diligently as you can.

PHAEDO: Indeed, O Echecrates, although I have often admired Socrates, I never admired him with greater pleasure than then when I was present. That he should have something to answer to the objections is perhaps not to be wondered at. But this I especially admired in him: first, how pleasantly, benignly, and kindly he received the words of the young men; then, how sagaciously he perceived that we had been moved by their reasons; and finally, how opportunely he applied the medicine to us, and recalled us as if we were fleeing and defeated, and turned us back to following and considering the discourse together.

ECHECRATES: In what way?

PHAEDO: I will tell you. I happened to be sitting to his right on a certain low stool, next to the bed. He himself sat much higher. Stroking my head and smoothing my hair on my neck (for he was accustomed sometimes, when the occasion permitted, to play with my hair), he said: "Tomorrow, perhaps, O Phaedo, you will cut these beautiful locks." [[notes: a sign of mourning]] "So I think, O Socrates," I said. "Not certainly if you listen to me," he said. "What is this?" I asked. "Indeed, today I shall cut mine, and you yours, if our reason dies and we cannot raise it up again. And if I were you, and the reason fled me, I would swear as the Argives did not to let my hair grow until I had defeated and overcome Simmias and Cebes." "But against two," I said, "not even Hercules is said to have been sufficient." "Then call me as your Iolaus (Hercules' nephew and companion) while there is still light," he said. "I call you indeed," I said, "but not as Hercules called Iolaus, but rather as Iolaus called Hercules." "It makes no difference," he said. "In the first place, however, we must take care lest something happen to us." "What?" I asked. "Lest we become *misologoi* (haters of reason)," he said, "just as some become haters of men. For no greater evil could happen to us than this: if we hate reasons. Hatred against reasons arises in the same way as hatred against men. Hatred against men usually enters when we trust someone too much without art, and we think him to be altogether a true, sincere, and faithful man, but then shortly after we find him to be wicked and unfaithful, and again another in the same way. So when this has often happened to someone, especially from those whom he considered most familiar and friendly..."

[[vocabulary: Socrates, Cebes, Simmias, Philolaus, Evenus, Phaedo, Echecrates, Hercules, Iolaus, anima mundi (world-soul), harmonia (harmony), immortalitas animae (immortality of the soul).]]

[[summary: This excerpt from Ficino's translation of Plato's Phaedo covers Socrates' arguments for the soul's immortality—including the Argument from Opposites and Recollection—and addresses objections regarding the soul as a harmony or a wearing-out garment. It emphasizes the philosopher's duty to separate the soul from the body to attain pure wisdom.]]
